# The Complete Works of Philip of Harveng

[Col. IV]

## Dedicatory Letter

To Albert, Archduke of Austria, Duke of Brabant, most serene and most merciful Prince of the Belgians.

When I first brought forth this Philip of ours from the darkness—as I had long ago promised him—so that he might behold a light he had never previously seen, he did, it seemed to me, precisely what a man condemned to a long, almost eternal night would naturally do if he were once permitted to gaze upon heaven. Certainly he would not cast his eyes upon one of the lesser stars, but upon the sun itself, shining pre-eminently, while the lesser fires merely gleam by a light bestowed upon them from that native light. Thus this author of ours, although nearly consumed by neglect, as soon as he was received into my hands, began at once to shine out, as though night and dust had been wiped away; and he fixed his gaze not upon anyone among your subjects inferior to you, but upon you yourself, seeming to seek your protection so that he might be kept forever in the light he had attained.

Whenever I read him, I always judged him most worthy to see the light of day; yet I earnestly wished that, though so modest a work, he might appear under the protection of so august a name. What I promised, therefore, is now before you. It is a great thing to receive; it is something to be able to give to the great. Nor do they confer less of a benefit when they deign to receive than when they give. Thus this highest favor shall be reckoned by me and my brethren among the countless benefits which Your Most Serene Highness has bestowed upon us: namely, that, though you are the prince than whom no age has seen one more illustrious at home or abroad in martial valor, justice, piety, and gentleness, you do not disdain our small offering, which we humbly and solemnly present with devoted hearts.

Indeed, our means of support, our shrines, and the ornaments of our altars acknowledge themselves to be owed to you. Thus whatever comes from us to you comes, assuredly, to be received as your own, because unless our Bonne-Espérance had been supported by your hands and shoulders, it would have wholly lost every hope of recovering its former beauty and splendor. For after the monstrous fury of traitors had brought most grievous devastation far and wide upon our lands and those of our neighbors, and had set fire to this house and to its sacred church itself, every hope of assistance, wherever we turned for it, had perished.

But when Your Highness, with the eyes of your mercy, beheld what remained of the ruins—mere fragments—you then stirred us to restore it; and finally, in order that we might do what you encouraged us to do, you bestowed the aid of your generosity, which is accustomed to be most lavish toward religious persons and holy places. Yet what a small part is this of your benefits toward us! Whenever I reflect upon them in my mind, or speak of them with my brethren, I feel within myself a strong desire to find some means by which the gratitude of my own heart and of all those with me toward you may be publicly attested.

Our prayers, indeed, most invincible Prince, and our almost continual vows for you and yours—for the peace of your rule, the prosperity of your fortune, your life, your safety, and that of the whole country—strike heaven and call upon those above; and I firmly hope this from your most admirable humanity. The light of your generosity shines upon me. You will grant that this is enough—

But let it be so: although our devotion toward you will always grow warmer and greater, it is nevertheless not enough for us unless we can establish that we are not ungrateful to so great a prince. This book is therefore dedicated to Your Most Serene Highness for that end: that all may understand that you yourself are the foundation of our hope, never to collapse at any time.

Its author is that Philip, contemporary with Blessed Bernard and second superior of this our monastery. I shall not speak of the greatness of his modesty, piety, religious devotion, and other virtues—virtues, as it were, of not a man but some blessed spirit dwelling among assemblies of mortals. No one saw them without being filled with the utmost admiration. His writing flows in a gentle style, yet one that sweetly expresses what is pious, lofty, learned, and profound. In it is found this rare quality: that its speech is as pleasing and sweet as finely refined gold, and that, developed in almost equal periods, it falls with a corresponding cadence. No one who knows that in his life and character nothing ever existed that was discordant will wonder that he delighted in this manner of speaking and writing.

Nor, consequently, is it surprising that, while he lived, he had as his most familiar friends men equally distinguished by titles of nobility and learning. For every one of his characters, as it were, savors of something from which the reader’s mind, once it has perceived it, can readily recognize that he was a man who could rightly win the affection of both classes. To say everything in a word: everywhere he breathes forth that Norbert who was founder of our order and our house. Philip stands next to him not only in rank and in the office of prelate, but also by the outstanding merit of his holiness—indeed, more nearly on this latter account than on the former. [Col. VI] Therefore whoever has a heart inclined toward that first man with any great devotion will without doubt extend the same kindly inclination of mind to this one also.

Immortal God! How splendid is nobility when holiness renders it splendid! Both were supreme in Norbert, if the former is considered to arise not merely from lineage but also in an exceptional degree from the dignity of his person. No one will doubt that Philip ought to be considered his heir in both respects. Therefore I come to dedicate to your august name this little work, an enduring memorial of teaching distinguished by religious devotion, because you, who pray to and venerate Norbert as an exceptional patron, cannot but love Philip too.

From this I have conceived the following firm hope: that he who has not merely looked with serene eyes upon our shattered, ruined, and prostrate condition, but has also raised with his own resources those things which, lying in ruin, had survived unharmed despite the violence of a hostile fate, will look upon this work in no other manner. A particular consideration of the work itself also supports this hope: for its greater part consists of an exposition of the Song of Songs. May he to whom these pages are dedicated live as long as his country can never sufficiently wish, yet only as long as nature permits—never departing later than his country wishes. I should therefore like Philip to seem to have sung beforehand what his own soul will someday sing most happily among the choirs of spirits. Let him be small, if you will, and less worthy of so great a patronage, provided only that he may foretell to his protector the happy events of another life which the condition common to nature makes necessary. You will be that man, most serene Prince; when summoned into heaven, your soul will sing these things—late indeed, if God hears us, but nevertheless recalled there someday.

But even now, through your goodness and mercy, incomparable with those of any other, I shall obtain that, together with these few labors of Philip, I and all my brethren may be, and may seem to be, devoted to you.

Meanwhile, may God, the Best and Greatest, preserve Your Most Serene Highness safely for us for many years; protect you from every evil of both soul and body; and at last bring you, through Norbert’s intercession, to the glory of heaven, the sole reward for labors undertaken in defense of the Christian commonwealth. This shall remain the prayer of

Your Most Serene Highness’s most devoted client,  
**Brother Nicholas Chamart**,  
humble abbot of the monastery of Bonne-Espérance.

[Col. VI]

## Life of Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance

(LEPAIGE, *Bibliotheca Praemonstratensis Ordinis*, Paris, 1633, folio, p. 508.)

The venerable Philip of Harveng, surnamed the Almoner, second abbot of the monastery of Bonne-Espérance of the Premonstratensian Order in the diocese of Cambrai, was a most eloquent and wonderfully learned man, pious and holy, and intimate with St Bernard of Clairvaux. He sprang from parents of modest means. For in his thirteenth letter he says of himself: “Lest, as a commoner, I seem to flatter one nobler than myself, and to seek your favor more by words than by deeds,” etc.

From childhood he was exceedingly devoted to learning. He was afflicted by an illness, though intermittently; and, in order to feel its discomforts less keenly—or rather to ward them off more easily—he applied himself more eagerly to reading. When he was a growing boy, he voluntarily presented himself to his bishop. Clothed by him in clerical dress and marked on the crown of his head with the sign of the tonsure, he was transferred from lay status into the clerical profession.

After passing beyond adolescence, while his tender youth, as it were, occupied an inner chamber, divine grace, which is stronger than nature, suddenly struck him with the blow of fear and shook from his hands both the amusements of his former vanity and the deceptive hope of the world which he eagerly embraced. It moved him—indeed, compelled him—so that he who rejoiced to profess himself a cleric would no longer delay being restrained by the laws of clerical religious life. Drawn by this welcome compulsion, he did not refuse to obey the admonitions. Thus, bidding farewell to the world, he cast away whatever he had mistakenly sought within it, holding in contempt many things which he had formerly loved exceedingly.

He soon went to Odo, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance, renowned for the holiness and austerity of his life, that he might use him as master and guide on the narrow and sublime way of perfection. Having received from him the habit of the Premonstratensian Order in the church of Bonne-Espérance, he enclosed himself there in the shelter of the cloister. There, while seeking pardon for the past and, so far as he could, avoiding present evils, he felt that the place and its example were a very great help to him in these aims, and he rejoiced not a little at having found a harbor.

He remained there for nearly a full year before he was promoted to holy orders and before he was in any way admitted to minister at the altar. Afterward, when he had been initiated into these orders, he was elected and appointed prior of his church of Bonne-Espérance. In this office, although he spoke and wrote eloquently many things concerning the instruction and consolation of his brethren, and governed them most holily for nearly eighteen years, he nevertheless suffered grave persecution and the most severe conflict through the envy and spite of certain persons, as is clear from his two letters appended below.

“Certainly,” he said, “the wrongfulness of our times is lamentable, and especially the habitual and obstinate wickedness of religious persons, or those dedicated to God. Forgetting their condition and calling, blinded by the spirit of spite and envy, they commonly do not fear to persecute with bitter hatred men more learned and capable, and more pious and religious; to overwhelm them with storms of injuries; and by every means in their power, with blind and audacious mind and purpose, either to remove or to obliterate their deeds and good works.”

Especially when he was harassed by these conflicts of adversity, the venerable Philip remained unshaken; and his piety and unwavering, tested patience became manifest and shone forth to the whole world. For he knew that “tribulation produces patience; and patience, proved character; and proved character, hope; and hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:3–4). Therefore, the more he was attacked, the more humbly he devoted himself to fasting and prayer and delighted in meditating upon heavenly things, pouring forth floods of tears. By the gentleness of a patient heart, bearing everything happily and cheerfully, he never neglected, by any means available to him, to show offices of charity to his rivals. He complains of them, as also of certain leaders of the order, in Letter Nine, addressed to Bartholomew, Bishop of Laon, and in Letter Twelve, addressed to Pope Eugenius III.

This blessed man, illustrious in sanctity and learning, adorned not only the Premonstratensian Order but shone upon the whole Church of God. For he left to posterity monuments of his divine genius, of great benefit to God’s Church, by which the truth of the Catholic faith and monastic and clerical discipline are elucidated, vices are put to flight, and the devout minds of believers are wonderfully kindled toward the love of God and desire for the heavenly homeland.

Having succeeded Odo, the first abbot of Bonne-Espérance, he wonderfully restored there the monastic discipline which had in some measure declined through discord among the brethren, and he governed those committed to him in a spirit of gentleness, with the utmost holiness and mercy. He rose to such a height of liberality and charity toward the poor and needy that he deserved to be distinguished by the name of Almoner. Finally, conspicuous in the renown of holiness and glorious in many titles of virtue, after faithfully and religiously administering the duty of his office for about twenty-seven years, he resigned it in the Advent of the Lord in the year 1182; and in the following Lent, having directed his life according to the example of Christ the Savior, he laid aside the body and passed straightway to Christ himself.

[Col. VIII]

## Historical-Literary Notice

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, IV, 292.)

Philip of Harveng, second abbot of Bonne-Espérance of the Premonstratensian Order in Hainaut, in the diocese of Cambrai, called from almsgiving, or “the Almoner,” whose life, compiled from his letters and other writings, is found in Jean Lepaige’s *Bibliotheca Praemonstratensis*, pp. 508–513, flourished from the year 1159; among other things, he composed an epitaph for Urban III, who died in 1187. His writings were published together by Nicholas Chamart, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance, at Douai in 1621, folio.

[Note: To these must be added the letter in which, in A.D. 1159, he congratulates Alexander III upon his elevation to the papal dignity; published by D’Achery, vol. II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 453 (vol. III of the new edition, p. 527).]

They are as follows: twenty-one Letters, the tenth of which is a rebuking letter addressed to St Bernard of Clairvaux; a mystical Commentary on the Song of Songs; Moral Reflections on the same Song; *On Nebuchadnezzar’s Dream*; *On the Salvation of the First Man*; *On the Condemnation of Solomon*; and six treatises *On the Instruction of Clerics*: 1, on the dignity of clerics; 2, knowledge; 3, justice; 4, continence; 5, obedience; and 6, silence.

*Life of St Augustine, Bishop of Hippo.*

*Life of St Amand, Abbot and Bishop of Maastricht*, also in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. I, 6 February, pp. 857–872.

*Passion of Saints Cyricus and Julitta.*

*Passion of St Salvius, martyr.*

*Life of St Foillan.*

*Life of St Gislenus, confessor and abbot.* Compare Charles Le Cointe, at A.D. 651, vol. III, p. 303 ff.

*Life of St Landelinus, Abbot of Crespin in Hainaut.*

*Life of St Oda, virgin*, also in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. II, 20 April, pp. 773–780.

*Life of St Waldetrudis, virgin.*

*Passion of St Agnes, virgin and martyr*, in elegiac verse.

Various poems, epitaphs, and logogriphs. Among the epitaphs, that on Ivo is also found in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. V, 20 May, p. 248. The others concern Anselm of Canterbury, Peter Abelard, William of Conches, Bernard of Clairvaux, Urban III, etc.

[Col. 0001]

# Letters of Philip of Harveng, Abbot of the Renowned Monastery of Bonne-Espérance (G)*

## 1. First Letter. Philip to Wederic

He inquires concerning the works of the six days: whether God accomplished them simultaneously or successively; and concerning the time of the creation of the angels and of the fall of the first parents.

[Col. 0001A]

You ask—and ask insistently—that, since you see two persons disagreeing with one another before you, while each believes that he understands one opinion better than the other, I should write to you which of them you ought chiefly to follow. I wonder why you seek such a judgment from me so insistently; why, to pass over others, you do not ask your uncle’s learning on this subject. He would both rejoice more religiously in your religious zeal and answer you, when you inquire, more pleasantly and wisely. For he is as distinguished by religious conduct as he is especially [Col. 0001B] learned in letters, so that he can both provide you with a model of fitting holiness and impart to you instruction in truth.

But because it pleased you not only to ask this of me, but to ask it insistently and humbly, I shall at last endeavor to answer you as best I can, lest you think me contemptuous of you if I choose to keep entirely silent.

You ask whether God created all things simultaneously, or made his works one after another, so that a corresponding duration and order of works should be understood according to the duration and order of the six days. You ask, further, that what is read—that God first made one thing and afterward another—may receive the grace of spiritual understanding, yet without excluding the literal sense.

This question is certainly obscure and difficult; [Col. 0001C] accordingly, some earlier writers debated it long ago, and the dispute is still unresolved. For in the divine Scriptures some things are found so different that they seem contrary to one another: in one place God is shown to have made his works, as it were, one after another; elsewhere it is more plainly found that he created all things simultaneously. But since it is not permissible to assert that divine Scripture says anything contrary to itself, lest, by contradicting itself, it be convicted of falsehood, it remains to recognize it as altogether truthful and harmonious with itself, if the prudent reader, aided by grace, attains understanding.

For such a reader, however, as it is difficult to penetrate the hidden meaning of that Scripture with a fitting understanding, so, once it has been penetrated, it is much more difficult to explain it in adequate words. For although his own words seem sufficiently plain and clear to one expounding them, they nevertheless [Col. 0002A] often seem obscure and difficult to the hearer. Hence the view about which you inquire does not seem sufficiently clear to us, and we possess no certain and fixed conclusion about what we can especially affirm concerning it. This is because it is so obscure that even our predecessors did not see it completely clearly; or rather, because they explained it in words that were less than adequate; or, what may more truly be said, because we readers are weighed down by laziness and dullness, and our intellects, darkened for grasping what we read, are too slow.

Thus, even if those who preceded us in time and learning discerned this same question as they ought, and by expounding it made it, as they thought, sufficiently clear, their exposition nevertheless seems to us to need another exposition—to us, I say, [Col. 0002B] who, lazy in reading and dull in understanding, can scarcely retain even easy matters. For in many places they seem either to say contrary things, or rather things so different that we cannot easily discern which of their assertions should more rightly be chosen. Each seems, being fully persuaded in his own view, to think correctly for himself; nor is either more plainly convicted of falsehood by the other.

For those who interpret the divine utterance strive to establish their own understanding without presuming to disprove another’s, unless perhaps they know that person to be departing from sound faith or that the context of the passage more manifestly opposes him. They know that divine Scripture produces many meanings in many passages, [Col. 0002C] none of which deserves to be rejected, although one may be approved more than another. Therefore, many choose and commend one interpretation in such a way that they do not maintain that those who have understood otherwise are in error.

They therefore understand in different ways what is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), and the words that follow. It would be both lengthy to bring forward here their diversity of views and superfluous to burden this little letter with such material, especially since you did not ask me to recount in order what each person thinks about it, but to answer which of the two alternatives you proposed seemed preferable to me. If, therefore, I knew what Moses, the writer of the divine history, intended to be understood in these words, I too would judge that interpretation to be preferable; [Col. 0003A] indeed, setting ambiguity aside, I would affirm that it should be preferred to all others. Yet if another understood differently, I should not have to reject his view, provided it were established that it did not deviate at all from the rule of truth.

For the same Spirit who dictated his words to Moses, his servant, for writing, and who inspired in him the fitting meaning of those same words, can, I say, show another meaning to another person in the same words, while depriving neither of the knowledge of truth. Moreover, it is more likely that, in the things Moses wrote, whatever his successors could truly discern—though they understood them differently and in different ways—Moses himself also understood completely clearly, and that God deigned to grant him the grace of seeing [Col. 0003B] not contradictory but diverse meanings harmonize in his words.

But because it would be lengthy to gather this diversity point by point, I shall endeavor, as you ask, to select the interpretations which seem weightier, those which I find ecclesiastical doctors have more highly commended and whom I judge to have penetrated the secrets of the Scriptures more diligently and subtly.

“In the beginning,” he says, “God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). The Beginning is the Word of God, the Wisdom of God, in whom, as David testifies (Ps. 103 [104]), God is believed to have made all things. This Wisdom is creator, not created; through it both spiritual and bodily things were created. By the name “heaven,” Scripture intended to signify spiritual nature; by “earth,” bodily creation. God created these “in the beginning,” that is, the Father [Col. 0003C] in the Son, or in the very beginning of his work.

For the words “in the beginning” can suitably be understood to signify the commencement of action, when God began to carry out in actual operation those things which he had eternally predestined within himself. At this beginning of his work he created spiritual, rational, intellectual nature, which he wished to designate by the name of heaven because he willed it to aspire to heavenly desires: free from earthly affections, it should adhere to its Creator by bonds of love; subject to him alone, it should rule over all irrational creatures, surpassing them all.

[Col. 0003D] The angels and human souls belong to this spiritual or rational nature. The angels were created together and all at once from the beginning; but human souls were created and are created in the course of time, and will continue to be created until the end of the age. Yet although new souls are created daily, a new nature is not said to come into being, because the nature of souls is spiritual and rational, and the creation of this nature had already preceded in the angels from the beginning.

At this same beginning—that is, in the same commencement of action—earth was created: namely, a certain formless and confused matter, out of which earth was made, that is, everything bodily. This means not only what we now call earth in ordinary language, but also water, air, and heaven, which we designate by distinct names as bodily things. [Col. 0004A] When that formless and confused matter was created, from which all things were afterward made, all things were in a certain sense made, because they are not improperly said already to exist in that from which it is clear that they proceed materially.

Since, therefore, God in the beginning created heaven and earth—that is, incorporeal and corporeal creation—it is not incongruous to affirm that he created all things simultaneously, since everything created is either incorporeal or corporeal. Observing this, a certain wise man, wishing to praise the Creator himself excellently and briefly, seems to have commended this creation in quite clear words: “He who lives forever,” he says, “created all things together” (Ecclus. 19 [Sir. 18:1]).

For all things were created together, since at the [Col. 0004B] beginning both the nature of spiritual beings and the matter of bodily beings were created. Nor afterward is anything said either to be created or to arise whose likeness cannot be found in the angels or whose origin cannot be found in formless matter. Yet, although all things were created simultaneously in the manner stated, nevertheless, as is written elsewhere, “wisdom was created before all things.”

[Note: [Col. 0003] On this passage from Ecclesiasticus, see St Thomas, I, part, question 41, article 3, reply to objection 4, where he explains that the passage may be understood both of created and uncreated wisdom.]

This does not mean Wisdom coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father, but wisdom which is a creature, not a creator: namely, rational nature. It is called wisdom because it is made capable of divine wisdom; and it is not inappropriately named by the term of that Wisdom to which it was created similar through understanding.

It was created before all things, not by priority in time but rather in causality and dignity. For time did not exist when it was created, and therefore [Col. 0004C] that which was not created under time is not prior to all things in time. But it is prior to all things in cause, because all things were made for its sake, and all things are referred to it; and all things which were created with it in pre-existing matter were created in accordance with it. Since it was made rational while the rest of creation was made irrational—this one in order that it might wisely obey God, to whom it was made similar through reason; the other in order that it might humbly serve this rational nature, for whose sake it was made—it is undoubtedly prior to all things in the dignity of its creation, since it was set above all by the merit of reason.

There is another reason why it may not inappropriately seem to be called prior to all things. While [Col. 0004D] this invisible nature and that matter of visible things were created together, the former was created formed, not formless; the latter was created not formed but formless. For that pre-existing matter was made from nothing in such a manner that, once created, it was almost comparable to nothing; and unless it afterward came to form and appearance, no one would know what that formless confusion was for.

But rational nature was so created that it had no pre-existing matter; from the very beginning of creation it was personally distinct, so that no mingled confusion or confused mingling held it; it received a form suitable to its condition, so that it did not thereafter need to be formed; and it attained everything pertaining to distinction and number, [Col. 0005A] so that in these respects it possessed nothing less than what was due.

For it is naturally implanted and inborn in that nature that it should possess an immaterial substance, personal distinctness, rational understanding, and a power of free choice so free that it could incline its own will either to good or to evil: toward good, indeed, not compelled but aided by preceding grace; toward evil, not impelled but slipping away when that same grace abandons it. Innate in that nature are uniform immortality, keen subtlety, manifold perfection, and a power of discernment conformed to its Creator; and for this reason it rightly ought to be called not formless.

Since, therefore, angelic nature was created formed, and for it to be is in some sense to be formed—for from that from which it has being, it has also being in this manner—whereas all visible things are plainly created as though imperfectly, so that they have being in matter before they are formed, Wisdom is rightly remembered as having been created before all things, its creation being perfected by an inborn formation, not one subsequently added. Nevertheless, in one respect it is judged to have been created unformed, because its creation did not bestow upon it everything necessary. For although it had experienced the manifold bounty of creative power, it still remained for it to receive the benefit of assisting grace. It was necessary, indeed, that it should turn, through love, the freedom given to it toward Him whom it knew as its Creator; and, with grace cooperating, should choose—indeed, should love—to cleave to Him in whom and with whom it might happily possess for ever the gifts it had received. [Col. 0005B]

For by this conversion and love it would be sufficiently formed, and by this formation firmly established; nor could it thereafter dissent from Him even in the slightest degree, once it had chosen, through love, to obey. This conversion—[Note: [Col. 0005] He means the stability mentioned shortly before, that is, the grace of confirmation or, as he calls it below, firmness.]—that is, this form, was not conferred upon angelic nature in its creation, but offered to it: so that, if it chose it, it might be counted as merit; but if it turned itself away, it might justly be punished with eternal punishment. Thus it was created: though receiving many things, it was nevertheless not self-sufficient, but unformed. But when turned to love the true light, it becomes wholly conformed to it as was fitting. The part, however, which chose to turn away not only remained, or continued, unformed, but, rejecting the light offered to it, became dark and deformed.

It was fitting that a rational creature should be made in such a way that it should not possess by nature everything that it ought to possess; but through intelligence and free choice it should both perceive what its creation bestowed upon it and be able to attain what its Maker offered it; that it should come to this not without its own merit, and should fall away from it only by spontaneous will. [Col. 0005C] Therefore, immediately upon being created, without any intervening interval, it turns and embraces in love Him from whom it was; and, though by free choice it could be borne either toward better or toward worse, it beheld and loved that which was worthy to be preferred.

For the freedom of will naturally present in it could not remain idle, even briefly, without at once turning to will something; otherwise, I do not know how it could rightly be called will. [Col. 0005D] For if it willed nothing, it would not be will, since will is so called only from willing, although what ought to be willed is not distinguished by that name.

Moreover, since it is the property of will to will, what can it will except good or evil, in opposition to one another? Willing, indeed, belongs to will; willing good or evil belonged to freedom. And what else was it to will good than to turn toward God? What else was it to will evil than to turn away from Him?

Therefore angelic nature, because it possessed free will, immediately both willed by will and chose by freedom what it would will. One part of them willed God, whom it both knew and loved as its Creator; the other part, though no less free in will, declined to will something else. [Col. 0006A] The former is confirmed in its purpose by grace and by the merit of free will, and receives from Him whom it willed the grace of firmness, so that, though mutable by nature—namely, because made from nothing—it can now no longer be changed by grace, because it has joined itself by spontaneous will to the immutable Good.

Yet freedom of choice must not therefore be said to suffer an injury if it can no longer, as at first, cleave to evil. Rather, it is now more properly and fittingly called free, when by the gift of grace it is delivered from every misery and from fear of misery. But that other part, which likewise had free will, as was said, immediately turning toward itself lost the dignity in which it had been made; and because it perversely chose to cleave to itself rather than to God, it could not remain in that which it was. [Col. 0006B]

Having fallen, therefore, and been plunged into the depth of darkness, it is tortured by eternal punishment and reserved for torment on the day of judgment. Together with all who stubbornly imitate it, it is assigned alike to the living worm and the unquenchable fire. But because we do not linger very pleasantly over the things belonging to the devil, let us leave these matters and return to the good angels. [Col. 0006C]

The angels were created mutable by nature, since, being made from nothing, they could change; but they were not changed by grace, because they clung to Him by whom they were made. Cleaving to Him, they remained and continued eternal, though by no means coeternal with the eternal Creator. For His eternity knew neither beginning nor end; theirs had a beginning but no end, because, while it impressed itself upon Him in burning desire, it did not depart from His firmness through the gift of grace. [Col. 0006D]

Hence, delightfully cleaving to sweetest contemplation and holding their own mutability in check by His stable firmness, they know no succession or varying motions of times; but, surpassing everything transitory, they rest eternally in His eternity. In that eternity, there is not “now this, now something else,” which belongs to time; rather, blessed sameness—or the same blessedness—is possessed all at once and simultaneously. No change or shadow of succession enters into it, for it does not range through diverse and varying things in a diverse and changeable manner.

Because of this eternity, by which angels are known to cleave to God and God likewise to remain eternally in angels, the Apostle called those angels an eternal house when he invited the minds of the faithful to hope for a heavenly dwelling: “We have,” he says, “a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5). [Col. 0007A] That house is both ours and God’s: ours, because we hope to come to dwell in it, if we are willing or able to serve God according to the law due to Him; and God’s, because God deigns to dwell in it and, dwelling there, adorns it with beauty.

David, while still placed upon earth, already saw this beauty; and, fervent in spirit, loved what he saw. Because he envied no one the joy of that same dwelling, he did not suppress in silence the grace he had received: “Lord,” he says, “I have loved the beauty of thy house, and the place where thy glory dwells” (Ps. 25). [Col. 0007B] This is heaven, or the heavens, in which God is said both to be and to sit, and in which He delights to accomplish His will, as is taught in the Lord’s Prayer and frequently proclaimed in the Psalms: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6); “The Lord—his seat is in heaven” (Ps. 10); and: “Our God is in heaven; he has done whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113).

And because no succession of time is found not only before this heaven but even in heaven itself—for in its blessedness it loses nothing, nor is anything future there temporally concealed—Scripture, when it records its creation, is silent about times and days, because this creature surpasses every creature of time. Rightly, therefore, no mention of time or day is made in its creation, in which no variation of temporal appearance is found. For where “now this, now something else” is not observed to vary, time or day ought not to be named. [Col. 0007C]

Likewise, when the earth itself is remembered as having been made in the beginning, no time or day is named in its creation, because that underlying matter of bodily things, denoted by the name “earth,” is declared to have been without form or appearance, without fitting distinction. But where there was no form or appearance, order, change, or succession, there was doubtless as yet no time or day, because the various forms of mutable things bring forth the alternations of times or days.

Yet this formlessness is not said to have remained in that matter; indeed, the Creator willed to remove it even so swiftly that, although formation followed creation itself, no interval of time occurred between the two. Matter was created first and formed afterwards; but the former did not precede the latter in time, because, as has been said, no delay of time intervened between them. Thus both were made simultaneously, although they are said to have been made one after another: for in one and the same moment of time matter and its appearance came into being, though they had by no means one and the same order or origin. [Col. 0007D]

For matter was prior to appearance, not in time but in origin, just as sound precedes song, flame light, and body shadow—not by any interval of time, but truly by the order of origin. This seems to be what our Augustine says in Book XIII of the *Confessions* (ch. 32):

> “Of created matter, whose formlessness you formed without the interposition of time: for since the matter of heaven and earth is one thing, and the appearance of heaven and earth another, you made the matter indeed from absolute nothing, but the appearance of the world from formless matter; yet you made both simultaneously, so that the form followed matter with no intervening interval.”

You see that, as is understood here, the Creator made simultaneously the matter of the world and its appearance or form, because He inserted no span of time between them. Yet the former is not doubted to be prior and the latter subsequent, as Augustine himself declares in Book XII of the *Confessions* (ch. 19): “It is true that everything formed from the formless is first formless, then formed.” [Col. 0008A]

Since, then, as you see, every formlessness is earlier and its formation later, and thus the matter of the world is primordial while its form or appearance is coeval with it, it remains to ask what sort of appearance this was that is said to have clung inseparably to its matter, so that no interval of time is known to have occurred between them.

Some hold that this formless matter was at once so formed that the four elements were separated from one another and assigned to their fitting places, as we now see them, and adorned with all things in them, animate as well as inanimate—things described in Genesis as completed within the number of six days. For they think it insufficiently fitting for the Creator to have made anything imperfect at the beginning of His work and to have brought it to perfection by the passage of time, when, just as He could create the underlying matter from nothing, so He could form from it the world that followed without delay of time. [Col. 0008B]

Therefore, they say, the enumeration of the six days is not to be taken literally; rather, a mystical interpretation is to be sought in it, since, as we understand from their teaching, God completed in a moment everything described there. According to this meaning, not only was humanity created from the beginning together with the angels, but also all the other things over which, once created, humanity was set. This sudden and perfect production is called the form of things, which Scripture says was completed through the interval and number of six days.

No wise person presumes to set his face against such an opinion, lest, by obstinately maintaining that this could not happen, he seem to weaken the divine power; for he cannot confirm what he asserts by open testimony of the Scriptures. Yet Scripture does not seem to deny that it could have happened otherwise; indeed, it seems almost to murmur if nothing in it is maintained according to the letter, especially since it is truly believed to have been written for human beings and is not judged unworthy to serve their understanding by fitting condescension. [Col. 0008C]

Therefore it cannot be denied that the distinction of the six days may be understood literally, and that God completed His works through intervals of time. Nor is anything thereby detracted from His almighty power, because this is attributed not to His weakness but rather to His will. He could have done otherwise if He had willed; but perhaps He willed to do it in the way which He foresaw to be more fitting for the rational creature, for whose sake He was making the world and the things in the world.

Accordingly, God made that formless matter which Scripture called by various names, because of certain likenesses which it judged not unfitting to be present in it; so that, when a person heard it called by such diverse names, he might know that it was properly none of those things but was so called by likeness. It is called earth, and earth invisible and unformed; it is called the abyss, whose face was oppressed by darkness; and it is called water, over which the Spirit was borne. [Col. 0009A]

It is called invisible earth because of darkness, and unformed because of deformity: invisible because it had not yet been illumined by light; unformed because it had not yet been adorned with fitting forms. It is called abyss because of its hidden depth, but water because of its readiness: abyss, because its depth does not offer itself to be traversed by human inspection; water, because it offers itself readily to the Creator for formation. For just as all things that are generated have their generation from watery moisture, so, when God speaks, all things are brought forth formed from that formlessness.

When He said, “Let there be light,” “there was light” (Gen. 1). By the shining of that light the formlessness of the matter was immediately formed, but the form or appearance of all things was not immediately completed. [Col. 0009B] Nor should Augustine’s statement trouble you—[Note: [Col. 0009D] *Confessions*, Book XIII, ch. 32.]—that God made simultaneously the matter of heaven and earth and the appearance of heaven and earth, and that no interposition of time separated form from matter, but the swift hand of the craftsman joined both without intervening delay.

For elsewhere, while disputing about the same formless matter and comparing it to the grain or seed from which a tree grows, he said that all things could be found invisibly in that formlessness, but arise from it into light through delays of time:

> “Just as,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0010D] Book V, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, ch. 23.] “in the grain itself all things were invisibly present together which would arise over time into a tree, so the world itself must be conceived, when God created all things simultaneously, to have possessed simultaneously all things that were made in it and with it, potentially and causally, before they arose through delays of time in the way in which they are now known to us.”

[Col. 0009C]

You see that the works of that first creation are not brought to completion immediately in every detail, but arise through delays of time; and although that formlessness is the mother of all things, its form or appearance is completed through the interval of six days. Augustine spoke in this way according to the differing opinions of different people, lest he seem to reject one if he pursued only the other, knowing that no injury is done to the Creator of all if, in doubtful matters, now one view and now another is preferred according to the capacity of those disputing.

Yet he himself seems to me to incline rather to the opinion that God completed His works through the interval of six days. What he says—that God made simultaneously the matter and appearance of heaven and earth—does not conflict with what he says about completing them through delays of time. For something is often said to be made which nevertheless has not yet been wholly completed: it has what belongs to a thing begun, but does not yet have everything that belongs to it when completed. [Col. 0009D]

Thus, when a shoot springs from a seed and a tree is produced from the shoot, as soon as it is drawn out of darkness and summoned into the air of light, the appearance of a tree is displayed to all who look at it. The observer says, “This is not earth; it is not stone; it is a tree”; perhaps he also says what kind of tree it is. Yet there is not yet there the shady spreading of branches, nor the countless multitude of leaves; not yet the beautiful variety of flowers, nor finally the fruitful sweetness of fruits. But although all these things are not yet seen to spring from or with that new tree, they can nevertheless be found in it, not actually but causally and potentially. Though the curious hand of the cultivator does not draw them out from it, the natural power implanted in it does, through the power of the Creator. [Col. 0010A]

So indeed, when that dark matter of the world became luminous at God’s word, “Let there be light,” the appearances of heaven and earth—indeed, of the four elements—began to shine out in it, but the individual things did not yet fully stand forth in their individual places and properties. Before God said, “Let there be light,” that matter was so formless that it was neither visible nor tangible, even if someone had existed who attempted to examine it. But God immediately formed this formlessness to some extent when, by creating light and illuminating it, He made manifest the principal parts of the world in a certain degree of appearance. [Col. 0010B]

For that light was made in order to illuminate that unformed chaos and, by its preceding radiance, to disclose the world hidden within it, so that when the full distinction of the individual parts followed, it might take place in light and not in darkness. And this is what God “saw to be good” (Gen. 1): namely, that light should be made, infusing a certain appearance into the four elements, by whose gift it could be seen what property was assigned to each—without which no one would know what the invisible matter contained.

“And there was evening and there was morning, one day” (Gen. 1): that is, that light, declining from its rising to its setting and returning from its setting to its rising by a moving circuit, completed the space of a day. By its brightness it so removed the formlessness of that matter that it was no longer unformed, although its formation was not yet complete. [Col. 0010C]

On the second day—that is, in the second circuit of this light—God made the firmament, which He called heaven: He separated it fully by distinction from the other elements; assigning it its proper place, He established it in revolving motion, and so arranged everything suited to its nature, and willed what He had arranged to be firmly established, that it should not be found to depart from the law then imposed upon it until the end of the age.

On the third day—that is, in the third circuit of the light already mentioned—the waters beneath heaven were gathered and assigned to their proper channels or beds; and the dry land, which is also called earth, appeared. Being heavier and immovable than the other elements, it occupied the lower place. Between the upper heaven and the lower earth, air occupied the middle place; on that same day the industrious hand of the Maker made it clear, when the spacious receptacles of the earth received the waters which had been spread from heaven itself down to earth in cloudy thickness. [Col. 0010D]

These things just described were made on the first three days. In them the fabric of the world was so sufficiently constituted that each of its elements received its own place, order, form, or appearance. In these three days the world was ordered by a perpetual law; in the three following it was adorned with diverse creatures, lest it be regarded as useless and superfluous if it seemed to have been made solely for itself.

Thus the heaven, which is found to have been created before the other elements, was on the fourth day adorned with the sun, moon, and varied stars. The sun was commanded by its native brilliance to illumine the day, while the moon and stars were to shine during the night. For although days had undoubtedly existed earlier through the operation of the light of which we spoke, they had not possessed so great a light; and the greater brilliance of the new sun was instituted so that the day might thereafter be completed by its service. [Col. 0011A]

On the fifth day air was adorned with flying creatures and water with swimming creatures. On the sixth day animals, beasts, and creeping things were produced on earth; and lastly, on that same sixth day, God fashioned humankind from the mud of the earth and breathed a soul into the formed body. Because He made humanity in His own image—not in bodily form but in excellence of reason—He willed humanity to hold a rank more worthy than and above all the things He had made in the world. This is the being for whose sake God made the world and the things in the world; and therefore He set humanity over all the things He had made before and for humanity, just as, in the cultivator’s judgment, fruit is preferred to the tree, since the cultivator’s labor is devoted to its cultivation only for the sake of its fruit. [Col. 0011B]

Thus humanity, for whose sake the world was made, is in a sense the fruit of the world itself: prior in cause and usefulness, though later in time, just as an apple, though it comes from a tree later, is far more useful.

Perhaps it is not unfitting that humanity, made after all things, be compared not to the tree but rather to the apple itself: for just as a tree, in its sixth stage of growth, is pleasantly laden with fruit, so the world, on the sixth day—as it were in the sixth stage of its growth—is finally adorned by the making of humanity. After the grain or seed, mentioned above, which invisibly contains the tree, the root seems to occupy the first stage of growth, the trunk the second, branches the third, foliage the fourth, flowers the fifth, and fruit the sixth and last. [Col. 0011C]

So, after that formless matter of the world which is found to have been made first in the creation of temporal things, the sixth day reaches humanity, so that God might be found to complete His works in the one whom He wished to exalt above the rest as the fruit of all things. Up to humanity, then, the formation of the world appears to have received growth; in humanity it was brought to perfection. Thereafter no new thing is formed in the world, because whatever happens later is judged to have been made earlier. [Col. 0011D]

Thus the world was perfected by the progress of time when it had fully received every kind of thing; and on the sixth day it was made, as it were, higher or more excellent because of the worthier human being, just as the sixth hour holds a higher rank in the day. For when, at morning twilight, the darkness of night is dispersed and, as night departs, day rises without an interval of time, the new sun poured upon the earth undoubtedly brings daylight; yet the day does not immediately shine with meridian light. The night which existed has already departed and some light has already arrived; but it does not yet have all the light or warmth that it will have when the sun reaches the middle of the higher heaven. [Col. 0012A]

In the first hour dark gloom is scattered and a somewhat dim appearance of things is revealed; as the sun advances, brightness increases, and at length, in the sixth hour, the fullness of that brightness is completed. For as the sun rises through the intervals of six hours to the meridian center, it naturally illumines and warms the day in such a way that it is sufficiently regarded as full and perfect in both respects and seems thereafter not to advance but to decline.

Likewise, that formless matter of the world was as night when it was made invisible and unformed. But when God said, “Let there be light,” a kind of morning sun shone, by which a certain brightness immediately shone upon that matter. Its presence, beyond doubt, removed the darkness, but did not bring the same matter to its due perfection. This advancement occurred gradually through the interval of six days, but on the sixth day the form of all things was completed. Once all things earlier in time, though not in dignity, had been perfected, humanity was made last, in the sixth hour, as it is said, of that same day. [Col. 0012B]

Thus the world and the day seem in some manner to correspond and alike to reach perfection in the number six: the world, as has been said, receives on the sixth day humanity, worthier than the rest; and the day attains its higher rank in the sixth hour.

Whoever understands the works of the six days in this way is not condemned for error, nor does anyone soundly wise oppose this understanding. For although a manifold mystery is contained in these matters, it is not contrary to the literal sense. For in many places of Scripture there is such depth that it is evident many profound mysteries are contained in it; yet the literal understanding is not removed from it. And one reaches the inward fruit more pleasingly because the surface of the letter is found not only leafy in words but fruitful in truth. [Col. 0012C]

Accordingly, it may fittingly be believed that humanity was not created from the beginning with the angels, but was afterwards fashioned from the mud of the earth on the sixth day, as is written. Receiving a soul immortal and incorporeal by nature, humanity surpassed every irrational creature by the dignity of inborn reason.

Finally, a certain man of our age, distinguished in religious habit and conduct and not moderately learned in both sacred and secular letters, who left us no small memorials of his intelligence, in which are found not contemptible teachings of sound faith—when in one place he discussed that first human being and affirmed that the body was created from mud but the soul from nothing—said as follows: [Col. 0012D]

> “The Catholic faith chooses this view rather, and judges it more consonant with truth: that we should believe that the soul of the first human being, when it was made, was not made from any pre-existing matter but created from nothing; nor was it made in the beginning when the angels were made, but afterwards, when the very body into which it was to be infused had been formed by the Creator himself, and that it was at once made and joined to the body.” [Note: [Col. 0013D] Hugh of Saint Victor, Book I, *On the Sacraments*, Part VI, ch. 3.]

You see that, according to this author, the Catholic faith chose and judged more consonant with truth the belief that the human soul was not made at the beginning with the angels, but afterwards, once the body had been formed, and was both made and joined at the same time to that body. Thus it is coeval with the human body, yet neither it nor the body is coeval with the angels created in the beginning. [Col. 0013A]

Nor should it trouble us if it is said that God made nothing imperfect (Deut. 2), though He made His works one after another; for He made each thing in its own kind so that whatever He made was perfect. For example, when God said, “Let there be light,” light was immediately made so perfect that it seemed not morning but as though noon, so that it suffered no delay in advancing. This is not said to have been granted to the second, third, or any subsequent day.

For after that first day, every day receives a dim beginning in the morning twilight; through the moments of the hours it increases until the sixth, and then gradually declines and at last closes at evening. But that one day, though it had evening darkness, did not have morning darkness: at its very rising its light was found to possess such perfection that noon added no increase of shining to it. [Col. 0013B]

Likewise, when it is said that God made the firmament (Gen. 1), it must be understood that He made it perfect. He did not begin at the top and work toward the bottom over the passage of time, as a woman weaves cloth when she begins it by setting up the warp. I judge the same to be understood concerning the other elements: they are completed on the day or at the time at which they are recorded as made.

Similarly, when God is said to have created swimming or flying creatures, we should not believe that He began their creation from an egg, so that, when the egg had been quickened by suitable warming, He produced the smallness of young offspring and then, by the passage of time, reared them to their due size. [Col. 0013C] They were not made in this way and knew no such birth or growth at all; rather, they immediately received at their beginning whatever perfection befitted each of them.

Again, when animals, beasts, and creeping things were created on earth, they did not begin from conception or birth, as happens now. Rather, setting aside the slow nourishment we know, they were created such as we now see them, perfect in strength or age. Shrubs and trees likewise did not begin from the formlessness of seed or the tenderness of sprouting, so as to spread into branches and leaves over the passage of time. Instead, in their very creation, sterile trees were made beautiful with due strength, branches, and foliage, while fruitful trees were laden also with fitting fruits. [Col. 0013D]

Finally, that paradise which is remembered as planted from the beginning—from that beginning, I mean, in which the earth was adorned with herbs and trees—was filled with an abundance of different fruits. Although this abundance seemed to proceed from the trees, it was not later than them by an interval of time. Therefore, when the first human being was made, he is said to have been placed in that same orchard, so that sufficient nourishment might be supplied to him by that abundance of fruits—except that he was forbidden, with the utmost care, to touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, not because it was evil, but so that his obedience might be tested. [Col. 0014A]

For God did not begin to form that human being as a child, as from then onward one is formed in the womb: at that stage a person neither needs nor is able to be sustained by fruits, nor is yet fit to be burdened with new loads of commandments. Rather, God made him such that he immediately possessed the maturity of puberty and could, being capable of reason, obey the laws of holiness. Therefore he was endowed with the blessing to increase and multiply, and was restrained from the aforesaid fruit in order that his merit might be increased. [Col. 0014B]

But that angel who had been created in the beginning, and who, having turned away from the Creator, had become the devil—when he observed that human being standing in the righteousness bestowed upon him, and envied his happiness, having himself been irreparably lost—was unable to crush him by force and therefore sought by snares to deceive him, lest the human being might reach by the merit of obedience the place from which he himself had fallen.

Nor is it surprising that humanity was forestalled by the devil’s deceits: the devil is found to have been made in the beginning, but humanity on the sixth day. The one, burning with malice, had already become accustomed to envying his betters; the other, simple and inexperienced, [Note: [Col. 0013D] “Inexperienced” (*rudis*) means untried. It is read in much the same sense in the homily on Adam and Eve in Chrysostom, vol. I, though it is not by Chrysostom but by a later Latin author: “So great a grace shone in the inexperience—that is, the simplicity and lack of experience—of the first human being that he might give it a name and foretell the future.”] had not yet learned to guard against hostile snares. [Col. 0014C]

But if, as some maintain, the works of the six days are separated from one another by no interval of time and humanity and the devil are asserted to have been created simultaneously, it is not necessary to ask how the former could have been overthrown by the latter, although both were created at the same time; and if it is asked, the answer can easily be given.

For the question which, you say, you found in a certain little book—though you state that you do not know who its author was—is not worth much consideration, nor should it trouble anyone, since a prompt solution can remove its little snares. [Col. 0014D]

“How,” it asks, “did humanity fall by diabolical persuasion, when both were created in the same moment?” And it adds: “The devil was created and fell simultaneously; but humanity remained in obedience from the sixth hour to the ninth.”

If, as this writer maintains, it accords more with truth that humanity and the angel were created together, and that the angel immediately fell by wickedly following his own truth, while humanity preserved the holiness of the obedience enjoined upon him from the sixth to the ninth hour, could the devil not, within this interval—from the sixth to the ninth hour—have contrived snares against humanity, and humanity eventually have been tripped by those snares? [Col. 0015A]

A greater and far more perplexing question, as I see it, would arise if, just as the angel is said to have been created and fallen at the same time, so humanity also, created together with the angel, were said likewise to have fallen with him. For it is not clear how someone persuaded can truly be said to have fallen together with the persuader, when the wicked persuader seems not unfittingly to have fallen beforehand.

But when humanity remained in obedience from the sixth to the ninth hour and the angel fell immediately upon being created, who can doubt how the former could have been overthrown by the latter’s evil persuasion, since the latter had so much time for persuasion? [Col. 0015B]

Yet from the assertion that humanity remained in obedience from the sixth hour to the ninth, another question seems to me to arise, one which may prompt even little children to ask and perhaps exercise some grown people in solving it. For if the angel was made in the beginning, as no one who thinks rightly doubts, and if humanity is asserted to have been created with that same angel, as this writer pleases, why is humanity said to have been obedient from the sixth hour to the ninth rather than from the first hour to the ninth, since the sixth hour cannot truly be called the sixth unless five have preceded it?

But no five hours preceded that beginning. The hour which precedes all the rest is figuratively called not the sixth but the first; and therefore humanity’s obedience is rightly commended as extending from the first, not the sixth, hour. [Col. 0015C] But because I recall reading nothing certain about this hour in the canonical Scriptures, and I do not dare define at what hour humanity was made, we must leave judgment in this matter to the person who strives to affirm both that humanity was made with the angels and that it was made in the sixth hour—the person who wonders how humanity can be said to have fallen through the devil’s persuasion, when the devil fell immediately upon being created, whereas humanity seems to have remained in obedience from the sixth to the ninth hour.

This may be truly affirmed without reproach, because canonical Scripture attests it: namely, that humanity, for whose sake the world was created, was fashioned on the sixth day, later than the other living creatures. Although a spiritual understanding accords with this assertion, the literal sense is not discordant with it: so that, although something mystical is subtly traced in it, it is not denied that it can nevertheless be received according to the letter. [Col. 0015D]

To the question you asked—whether God made his works simultaneously or successively—I have thought this should be the answer, committing to your prudent judgment whether it should be retained or perhaps rejected.

But concerning your question whether anyone who has committed a grave offense ought to confess it to someone other than the person to whom he was once entrusted, prepared both to weep worthily over what has been done at that person’s judgment and thereafter to restrain himself by fitting observance: with your leave, brother, I forbear to answer at present, [Col. 0016A] considering that such an answer requires an abundance of words. For to anyone arguing about it, so many objections may be raised, and to those raising objections so many counterarguments may in turn be offered, that it seems to me lengthy and difficult to define everything exhaustively. And, to confess the truth, my strength is insufficient to unravel a difficulty of this kind. Here, then, let this answer of mine end, lest useless prolixity produce weariness in the reader. Farewell.

## LETTER II. PHILIP TO HERVARDUS

He teaches that three things are necessary for one reading Holy Scripture; he asks and resolves how Christ contracted original sin from Adam, and yet was contained in him according to the flesh.

[Col. 0016B]

You used to send me simple little letters, and I would reply to you in like fashion, in which nothing was indicated except our mutual affection, or something of no or little importance was discussed. But not long ago you sent me another letter, by which you burdened my smallness no little: for in it you set forth a rather difficult question, whose solution you carefully demanded from me.

This question, as you say, you have very frequently dropped into the ears of your teachers, whose learning you judged able to dispel your ignorance. Yet while you were, as it were, awaiting their answer, their earnest discourse, as you say, verbally debating the matter, was found as unworthy as it was ineffective for untangling this question. In saying this, moreover, you seem somehow to exaggerate the weight of the same question and to burden me further indirectly: as though you asserted that I ought to be accused of rashness if I should presumptuously attempt what your teachers cannot manage to unravel.

But perhaps I ought not even to suspect that you thought this; and what was said simply should not be charged to craftiness, lest I be found readier to accuse the simplicity of your expression than to untangle the perplexity of the question proposed. Setting this aside, therefore, I shall try to answer you, who inquire carefully, yet without prejudging one who thinks better; for although I may not be able to satisfy you in your doubt, I do not begrudge one who argues more subtly and effectively.

You doubt and ask: since Christ’s flesh was in Adam’s loins, as ours also was, how did it not contract sin from there, as ours did? And lest perhaps your own words have slipped from your mind, I shall briefly repeat them and afterward answer them as Christ himself has supplied the answer.

“When we say,” you say, “that we all were in Adam, this universality gathers within the embrace of its expression human beings descended from the seed of human propagation in such a way that it includes Christ with us. But when we say, ‘We all sinned in Adam,’ this universality, now with its embrace shortened, its circle narrower, and its scope more restricted, is so confined within the bounds of the human race that it hesitates to include Christ, whose nature was incorrupt. Yet it is certain and indisputably true that one and the same sinful and corrupted material of Adam’s flesh preceded both our flesh and Christ’s flesh. Therefore, since Adam’s flesh, through the sin of disobedience, stripped itself of the splendor of immortality, it was either partly corrupted or wholly and entirely corrupted. But how Adam’s flesh, like mine, could be partly corrupted by the sin of concupiscence, I have not read, I have not understood, and, I think, could not be taught. But if it was wholly and entirely corrupted, how will Christ’s flesh, which flowed down from the loins of sinful Adam, be preserved unharmed? I have read it, but have not understood it; I do not say that I could not be taught it, but that I am not able to be taught it.”

This is the substance of your question; this is what you doubt, and concerning which you consult me. I rejoice, then, that you are striving to be instructed in the divine writings; but in them I want you to be found teachable, lest either dull grossness make your study foolish or the sickness of pride hinder your intellectual agility.

For, as I judge, three things are especially necessary for a reader of the divine Scriptures, without which perfect knowledge of those Scriptures is not acquired: study, intellect, and humility. Study, as you know, is diligent constancy in reading. Intellect is the natural quickness of understanding. Humility is the lowliness of mind, whether the grace of understanding is given or not given.

Study is so necessary for the person who wishes to know the divine writings that without it he can scarcely know them. For only the laborious constancy of the reader can grasp so vast and profound an ocean—of the reader who does not devote to idleness a mind sluggish and negligent, nor spend his study upon fruitless and worldly business. For all that must be known cannot be found in one place; and therefore many things must repeatedly be reviewed by frequent reading, so that the darkness of ignorance may be dispersed through repeated reading.

Indeed, among secular writers someone says that no one can be wise unless he has read much. Therefore, when the Apostle instructed Timothy, he said: “Attend to reading” (1 Tim. 4). And lest brief attention to reading should be thought sufficient, he adds: “Meditate on these things; be occupied with them” (ibid.). If, therefore, you desire to know the Scriptures, you must occupy yourself with them, remain in them, and meditate upon them with suitable constancy; for what is closed to the fastidious and negligent is opened to the studious and more persistent knocker.

Intellect likewise is very necessary to the reader, without which one labors in vain at literary toil; for no one gains any knowledge, or only slight knowledge, by constancy in reading unless the grace of understanding is present. Hence Paul says of certain persons: “Always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim. 3). This intellect, however, is not situated within the choice of human will, but is the gift of God’s generosity alone; for, as he gives human beings to be born or to live according to his will, so he distributes to them the gifts of understanding according to his will.

Therefore God must be entreated to grant fitting understanding, lest the desire to learn suffer rejection at a barred entrance. For although intellect, when possessed, must be sharpened by the file of study, yet unless one possesses, through his gift, that which can be sharpened, one does not possess it.

[Col. 0018A]

For this reason, when the Apostle had said to Timothy, “Understand what I say,” he immediately added, “For the Lord will give you understanding” (2 Tim. 2), making sufficiently clear that the measure of understanding is not situated in human will, but in the Lord’s freely bestowed generosity. Isaiah also proclaims that generosity, saying: “The Lord God opened my ear” (Isa. 50). And Luke the Evangelist says: “He opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

You see that the Lord gives understanding to Timothy, opens Isaiah’s ear, and opens the minds of the apostles so that they may understand the Scriptures. Conversely, he closes the minds of those of whom the Apostle says: “They understand neither what they say nor the things about which they make assertions” (1 Tim. 1).

But when someone sees that both study and intellect abound in him, and begins to penetrate the hidden mysteries of Scripture, he must hasten also to add humility, without which he will gather the rest to no purpose. This humility is necessary not only when the secrets of Scripture are disclosed, but also when they are hidden: lest the person who understands glory in himself rather than in the Lord, or the person who does not understand judge not his own slowness but rather the Scripture itself to be blameworthy.

For many, when they understand what they read, glory proudly; but when they do not understand, they complain even more proudly, judging entirely worthy of censure whatever they see cannot be comprehended by human reason.

[Col. 0018C]

But the prudent reader, when he understands something, ought to glory not in himself but in the Lord; and what he does not understand he ought humbly to revere, knowing that whatever canonical Scripture declares is true, even though it is not equally grasped by all.

Some things are hidden so that they may be sought more diligently, and, when found, held more firmly; and, if perhaps they are not found, the reader may revere them with due humility. Sometimes, indeed, a reader may advance more by being humbled through a rebuff than if he suffered no rebuff at all. Therefore, since I do not doubt that both study and intellect are present in you, it remains that both be fortified by the grace of humility. Thus may you rejoice in what you understand, while what you do not understand does not seem discordant to you. Humbly attribute the difficulty of understanding not to the disputation of learned men but to your own slowness; and do not stone a closed door with blasphemies, but greet it with due reverence.

You wonder: since Christ was in Adam, as we were, why did he not also contract sin from him as we did? When it is said, “We all were in Adam,” Christ too is contained in this universality; but when it is said, “We all sinned in Adam,” Christ is excepted from this universality. For he did not sin in Adam who never sinned anywhere or at any time, “of whom Scripture says: ‘He committed no sin.’”

Therefore, when the Apostle, speaking of Adam, says, “in whom all sinned” (Rom. 3), although he does not there expressly except Christ, he nevertheless shows elsewhere that Christ must be excepted, where he says of him: “Him who knew no sin” (2 Cor. 5). Hence it is clear that not all who were in Adam sinned in Adam.

[Note: [Col. 0019D] See cols. 22 and 23 passim.]

But this is truly said: all who sinned, sinned in Adam. For as all of us who were going to be born from Adam were in Adam, so all of us who were going to be born sinners from Adam sinned in Adam.

First, one must see how we were in Adam, though at that time we did not yet exist. For just as those who will be born many years hence do not yet exist, so we who now exist did not yet exist in Adam’s time. But we are said to have been in him because we took from him the origin of our existence. In him there were, by God’s creation, seminal nature, and, by reason of sin, carnal concupiscence; from these the propagation of the human race took its beginning, and each of us assumed them at the time of his conception.

When that first man—or the first human beings—had been made, God said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1). From this it is understood that God willed those whom he had made to multiply and other human beings to be propagated from them; and, once these were brought to completion in the course of time, he would transfer them to heaven through the power of their merits, to make good the diminished number of angels.

Thus already in Adam there was the seed-bed of posterity, by which he could have begotten children at the prompting of free will. As husband, he would have entered his wife’s womb without the impulse of lust, and she, conceiving without loss of integrity, would have given birth at the due time without groaning. Since those who generated would have transmitted nothing but flesh to those begotten, and those begotten would have received nothing but flesh from those generating them, children would truly be said to have been in their parents only according to that flesh, from which they derived the origin of that flesh alone.

But before this happened, the first human beings transgressed God’s command, and, guilty of transgression, were struck by this sentence: because they had not wished obediently to adhere to God, their superior, they were miserably compelled to endure the rebellious insubordination of their inferior, that is, their body.

For concupiscence was inflicted upon the members called the genitals, and they perceived in them a movement of which they were deservedly ashamed. Before sin, like their other members, they were subject to the choice of the will; after sin, whether they wish it or not, they are moved by the prompting of lust.

These same members were indeed generative organs before sin, but not shameful parts, because in them there was no concupiscence, no unseemly desire, no opposition, and absolutely no disturbance; rather, there was honorableness, purity, tranquility, obedience, and holiness. After sin they are deservedly called shameful parts, since they struggle so greatly against the spirit that they are moved to procreate only by lust.

[Col. 0020A]

This is how Adam infected his children and, as it were, blighted the succession of his posterity in its root: since in procreation not only flesh but also carnal concupiscence is at work, whoever is begotten in that manner is held under the guilt of the same concupiscence.

For though a man and woman are joined not by adulterous but by marital union; though the marital embrace is undertaken not for indulgence but for procreation; though Abraham, a hundred years old, and Sarah, ninety, are joined to beget the promised Isaac (Gen. 18; Luke 1); though Zechariah and Elizabeth, in begetting the Lord’s forerunner, in some way serve the angel who announces him—yet righteous parents cannot beget a righteous son, because they cannot beget without concupiscence.

Therefore John as well as Isaac needs the remedy of circumcision to abolish the contagion of generation.

[Note: [Col. 0019D] These statements appear contrary to what is said in Luke 1:15 by the angel himself to Zechariah, where a son is promised who will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from the womb. Yet, after considering these words, Augustine, *Letter 57 to Dardanus*; St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 27, article 6; and Blessed Bernard, *Letter 174*, still leave doubts concerning the sanctification—that is, the justification—of St. John in the womb. For he could have been filled with the Holy Spirit in order to do what is read in Luke 1:41; just as St. Elizabeth herself is there said to have been filled with the Holy Spirit, and Zechariah likewise in verse 67. Yet no one would say that this filling should be understood as justification itself. Therefore St. John was filled with the Holy Spirit just as Jeremiah was sanctified—that is, chosen for the prophetic office, which is holy. Indeed, he showed himself already to be a prophet endowed with the spirit of prophecy when “the infant leaped in the womb” (Luke 1:41).]

For from those from whom they receive that they are human beings, they receive that they are unrighteous human beings, since from them they draw not only the substance of flesh but also the concupiscence of the flesh.
