In this respect they are said to have been in their parents, namely, according to what it is certain they received from their parents; and therefore they are judged in some manner to have sinned in those through whose concupiscence they are generated.

Thus the Apostle, speaking to the Hebrews of the Levitical priesthood and attempting to show how greatly it differed from Christ’s priesthood, said that when Melchizedek the priest met Abraham, Levi, who was in Abraham’s loins, in some manner paid tithes in Abraham (Heb. 7).

Levi was in Abraham’s loins according to what he would receive from him in the course of time: according to the seminal principle by which, through concupiscential intercourse, he would be born of his mother much later. In the same way Abraham himself had been propagated from the loins of his parents. Hence both he and Levi fittingly paid tithes to Melchizedek.

That tithing, by which Melchizedek was not tithed but rather received tithes, signifies that remedy by which Christ was not healed but healed. He took from us that by which he might mercifully heal us, since in assuming our flesh he was born not for himself but rather for us.

For Levi and Abraham—indeed, all of us—need healing medicine, since we contracted a deadly disease in the workshop of our generation. There, because the appetite of carnal concupiscence boiled up, no one emerged who was not entangled in the stains of that same concupiscence.

All of us, therefore, who are born in this so disadvantageous manner are bound by the chains of original guilt. Indeed, before we come into this light, in conception itself we are miserably destined for death and are condemned, though not by actual sin, yet by original sin.

This sin is deservedly called “original,” because the first human beings were first inflamed, as their disobedience required, by the heat of concupiscence through which the acts of procreation are accomplished; and from them other human beings are propagated by a concupiscential origin.

Or perhaps it is not undeservedly called “original” because that unseemly movement or itching is, as it were, a defect and origin of our flesh: since through the union of male and female no one at all is generated unless first the flesh of the begetter is aroused by the impulse of lust. Therefore, because the flesh first desires and then generates, not so much the flesh as its concupiscence should rightly be judged our origin; and thus the sin said to be imposed upon us through it rightly deserves to be called original.

From Adam to Christ all, without doubt, are bound by this sin, because all are generated through concupiscence. Therefore they need to be tithed by Christ—that is, purified by his saving sacraments. But Christ required no purification, because he received flesh from the Virgin in such a way that she experienced no male embraces and sensed no concupiscence in conceiving.

Since none of us is generated without the union of male and female, and that union is completed only through concupiscence, Christ willed to take flesh in his mother’s womb without the approach or seed of a father, so that he might entirely exclude all concupiscence and the origin of his flesh might not be stained by original defilement.

Therefore he drew from his mother not the heat of lust—which she experienced in conceiving neither as her own nor as another’s—but the material of flesh, found pure, tranquil, and stirred by no tempest: the Holy Spirit descending upon her in more abundant grace and driving from her every uncleanness of tumultuous lust.

“The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1). He will come upon you so that, like the bush, you may burn without being harmed (Exod. 3); he will overshadow you so that you may not suffer the heat of carnal concupiscence. He will come upon you, I say, to make you fruitful in a new and wonderful manner; he will overshadow you so that no appetite of lust may render that fruitfulness unclean.

He who did whatever he willed both willed and was able to become incarnate in the Virgin’s womb in such a way that the same flesh would derive its origin not from carnal concupiscence as ours does, but from the Word. Thus his flesh is rightly judged to differ from ours in that it is said to have a very different origin.

For, as was said shortly before, carnal concupiscence provided the origin of our flesh, inflaming our parents when they came together to generate. Hence that same concupiscence is often called our mother in the Scriptures, from whose womb our carnality is propagated: “My father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up” (Ps. 16).

Our father was the devil, and our mother concupiscence: for, at his suggestion and by her enticement, we are conceived and born in sins, and remain subject to death until the grace of divine mercy regenerates those born in this way. Once regenerated, we are no longer held by the original bond; yet the tinder of concupiscence remains in the flesh, by which we are exercised for the increase of merit—not so that it may thereafter harm us, provided that it is restrained by the prescribed laws, but so that it may infect posterity if anyone is generated through that same concupiscence.

Melchizedek, whom you know to have borne the figure of Christ, is aptly introduced by the Apostle (Heb. 7) as having been “without father, without mother, without genealogy,” because it is clear that Christ was neither begotten in that manner nor begot anyone in that manner. For in his own generation he did not preserve our order, nor did he derive the origin of his flesh from carnal concupiscence; because lust did not precede his mother in conceiving, but a spiritual infusion came upon her so that she might conceive.

For this reason he says: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me”—nothing, certainly, that belongs to him. For the Virgin conceived by the Spirit, and the origin of what was conceived is from the Word, as the angel’s testimony declares and our confession of faith professes: “For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1).

My Augustine says:

> “The principle of his conception came not from male seed, but in a far different manner from above.”

[Note: [Col. 0021D] *On Genesis according to the Letter*, book 10, chapter 20.]

Hilary, orthodox preacher of the Catholic faith, says:

> “Mary did not give origin to the body, although she contributed all that was natural to her sex for the body’s growth and birth.”

And below:

> “The flesh derived its origin from no other source than the Word.”

And much further on:

> “Although he was born according to the law of human beings, he was not conceived according to the law of human beings: possessing in his birth the constitution of the human condition, while himself existing outside the constitution of that condition in his origin.”

And again:

> “His origin is not from a human being, since he was born from the conception of the Holy Spirit.”

You see that when the Son of God is incarnate, it is not carnal allure but God’s Spirit that works; the mother’s integrity is in no way violated by male intercourse; no concupiscence is supplied, but the substance of flesh alone.

Therefore he who drew the origin of his flesh not from carnal desires in our manner, but from above, plainly did not contract an original defect in conception. For sin is ascribed to any person born only because it is conveyed to him by the concupiscence of his parents through the seminal principle.

If I too could have been conceived without the concupiscence of my parents, perhaps I would not have been bound by original chains, because I would have received nothing from them except the substance of flesh, by which I would have been a human being only, not a fallen human being.

[Note: [Col. 0021D] He says “perhaps.” For if it occurred miraculously that actual concupiscence or lust were entirely removed while intercourse remained, nevertheless the offspring would still contract original sin, says Blessed Thomas, *On Evil*, question 4, article 6, reply to objection 16. It would be otherwise if someone were conceived without the concupiscence of parents in such a way as to be born from them only materially, and not seminally: St. Thomas, article 7 and *Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 81, article 4.]

Likewise, because the Virgin, filled with the Holy Spirit, did not conceive from carnal concupiscence, and because the Son of God received from her nothing except flesh, Christ himself is rightly free from sin, since he was neither born nor conceived in sin.

Whether, therefore, Levi is said to have paid tithes in Abraham (Heb. 7), or Adam’s posterity is said to be bound by the guilt of transgression, it is truly asserted that none of this pertains to Christ, although it is not denied that he was in their loins. For he was in them only according to that which he drew from them; and he drew from them nothing other than what he drew from his mother. He drew nothing from his mother except flesh; he drew nothing from his mother except flesh.

He was, therefore, in them according to flesh alone, which is God’s good creature, not according to concupiscence, by which the generation of us all is infected. But he who was in them according to flesh alone, which is good, and not according to concupiscence, which is evil, plainly did not transgress in Adam and therefore did not pay tithes in Abraham.

For just as he was not in Adam who drew nothing from Adam, so no one was in him except according to what he drew from him; and no one drew anything else from him except what he drew at conception from his own parents. Thus we, who drew flesh and concupiscence from our parents, were in them according to both; and because of this we are said not only to have been in Adam but also to have sinned, when that one man sinned from whom the concupiscential origin of us all flowed by succession.

Accordingly, it is fittingly said both, “We all were in Adam”—that is, both we and Christ—and “We all sinned in Adam,” but only we and not Christ. For as all who were in him were in him, so all who sinned in him sinned in him.

This is like the statement: “Who enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1), namely every person who is enlightened; and, “who wills all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. 2), namely all who are saved. We were in Adam, and Christ was too; but we in a twofold manner, Christ in a single manner: we according to flesh and concupiscence, Christ according to the substance of flesh alone.

[Col. 0023D]

We were therefore born richer than Christ, only in respect of what we drew from our parents: for we drew two things, while Christ drew from his mother only one thing. And ours is the voice: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50), a voice surely far removed from Christ.

Would that I did not possess such riches! Would that I were not hindered by such an encumbrance! Would that, by the benefit of poverty and nakedness, I might run unencumbered along the narrow path of virtues!

Christ’s poverty and nakedness are fittingly commended; and inviting us also to them, he says: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John 12). Since we cannot either go before him or in any way equal him, let us strive at least, though from afar, somehow to imitate him by following him.

Blessed indeed is Christ’s poverty, which refused to experience the thorns of our riches, and which deserved to be heard when crying to the Lord in its own voice: “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” (Ps. 33)—poor in crime, poor in vices, poor not by laying down but by never assuming the hump of camels; poor while pronouncing blessed his imitators, because “yours,” he says, “is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

Blessed also is his nakedness, which was not wrapped in our little rags, indeed which was free from the stains of all sins. It does not put upon itself Adam’s tunic of skins, but by its own simple purity consumes that tunic in us.

The tunic of skins, which is made from a dead animal, signifies the death of sin with which our nature is, as it were, clothed over when concupiscence is poured upon our flesh; when, according to Paul’s saying (Rom. 8), the body is judged dead because of sin, although the spirit seems alive because of righteousness.

The Apostle himself lamented that he was clothed with this garment of sin, this body of death; and he mournfully asked who would free him from it: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). “Of this death,” he says. Of which death? Of that, namely, of which he had previously said: “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive in the law of sin” (ibid.).

And seeing that no one can be freed from it unless divine grace chooses to assist him, he answers: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (ibid.).

Therefore anyone, whether the Apostle himself or any one of us, is freed through Jesus Christ from this body of death by whose covering the Apostle was burdened, because through him divine grace is supplied to us so that the Apostle’s command may be fulfilled: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, concupiscence” (Col. 3).

These are the members of this body; these are the forms of this death; this is the death itself which we must put to death with much and continual labor—not so that it may no longer exist at all in the present life, but so that it may not prevail. That is, when the inborn inclination to sin is stirred in us, no effect may be yielded to it.

For while we live here, the incentive to sin cannot be uprooted from us completely; but through divine grace it can be restrained, so that the spirit, strengthened with manly vigor, may check its tumult, and it may lie hidden, ineffective, as though extinguished beneath ashes.

John the Baptist symbolically displayed this death of sin and the mortification of this death when he girded his loins with a leather belt (Mark 1). Because he had been conceived through the concupiscence of his parents’ loins, and had contracted from them not merely a body but a body dead because of sin, it was necessary for him to mortify that same death by the rigor of discipline, lest the carnal allure that his parents had transmitted into him might weaken him by its enticements.

He therefore fittingly girded his loins with a leather belt, because he so bound the wantonness of the flesh with the thong of continence that he granted it no freedom to wander, but shattered the serpent’s head at its very source with the hammer of mortification.

And when he was thought by the crowds to be Christ because of his excellence of life, lest this false opinion spread any longer, he replied: “I am not the Christ” (John 1). “I am not,” he says, “the Christ, for I was conceived not only by the transmission of flesh but also by the transmission of sin, and thus I am infected by original impurities. Although I have obtained cleansing from them through the benefit of circumcision, nevertheless, while I live here, I am truly judged imperfect because of the remnants of inborn concupiscence.

“But Christ, who contrary to our custom was conceived without male seed and born from a virgin without concupiscence, is not girded with a leather belt because he is not clothed in a tunic of skins. For he who, at the entrance into this life, is hindered by no covering of concupiscence, and therefore does not feel in his loins a law opposing the spirit, is surely protected by no constriction of a girdle, because there is found in him nothing at all needing to be restrained.

“Therefore, do not suppose that the one whom you see girded with a leather belt is Christ. For even though I seem to excel you in the merit of holiness, I cannot be compared with him who was neither born nor conceived in sins.”

Thus John declared, in speech and dress, that he differed greatly from Christ: he proclaimed himself bound by original chains, but Christ as taking away the sins of the world: “Behold,” he said, “the one who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

Christ is therefore rightly said both to have been in Adam and nevertheless to have contracted no stain from him, because he was able, contrary to the laws of flesh, to take flesh without concupiscence in his mother’s womb, just as he was able to be born of a virgin by a wonderful and new birth.

But lest I seem to be more wordy than is proper, I shall set an end to my answer and perhaps not impose the weight of divine reading upon you, who may rejoice in its brevity—even though what has already been said deserves to be accused of prolixity, if it is judged insufficient for your question.

But if it has not departed from the rule of truth and has satisfied your concern, a somewhat longer digression will more easily and justly obtain pardon when the delay of reading is relieved by the benefit gained. And if, despite many words, the perplexity of the question has not yet been sufficiently resolved, even so pardon should not be denied where the writer’s will is found more ready. For it is clear that he does not at all begrudge the studious reader, nor deliberately keep silent about anything he has been able to understand.

But, to confess the truth to your affection, I judge that I grasp the truth of this matter more readily than I can explain it in words. Therefore, in my final recourse to excuse, my inability will cry out that prophetic saying: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53).

For it is impossible—or difficult—not only to recount his divine generation but also his human generation. Therefore humility is necessary: humility which, if something is closed to it, does not know how to become indignant, but either merits a fuller grace for attaining what it desires, or, if it does not attain it, is nevertheless not held guilty of presumption and obstinacy.

May, therefore, both your inquiry and my answer be completed in this humility, so that whatever they lack—indeed, because they will lack something—may be supplied by its fullness. Farewell.

## LETTER III. PHILIP TO HEROALDUS

He rebukes the name “Fortune.” He teaches that Christians ought not to linger in pagan books, but hasten to the sacred Scriptures. Praise of the Parisian academy.

The letter which your affection, mindful of me, sent me, [Col. 0026B] as though to rouse my lethargy and heavy drowsiness by the striking of a watchman, know that I have both read attentively and received gratefully when read; for in it I seem to have discerned your progress as a learner. For although the vessel in some respects still retains the scent with which it was formerly impregnated, yet in other respects it is clear with what nectar it has subsequently been sprinkled: since you do not yet keep silence about those matters with which the seductive workshop of the pagans fumes, while at the same time you speak of those things which the more serene discipline of divine reading has bestowed upon you.

Nor, I think, will you take it ill if I confidently administer a blow to you, so that, when the blow has been given, I may shake you like someone holding nuts: that, once the childish things full of emptiness have been shaken off, only the riper book of honourable truth may be retained. When you say that some people “smile upon smiling Fortune,” [Col. 0026C] and that, when she has mocked anyone, they too mock the mocked man in like manner, the surface of such words somewhat strikes and offends sound ears, because ecclesiastical faith condemns their sense—or rather their senseless meaning. For God, who was both able and willing to create all things, according to his will grants and arranges for us prosperity or adversity; and he governs all things by a discriminating order and an ordered rule in such a way that no place or efficacy is left in them for fate or Fortune.

That pagan says: “Fortune rules in every matter.” And another says [Note: [Col. 0025D] Juvenal, *Satires*, 7.]:

> “If Fortune wishes, you will become consul from being a rhetorician.”

And whatever similar expression you find is judged so erroneous and incongruous that the majesty of truth enjoins silence upon us concerning its assertion. Hence, although [Col. 0026D] we lawfully use certain words by which we say that something hidden or doubtful is denoted—namely “perhaps,” “by chance,” and other such terms which seem to derive from *fortuna*, or which seem to be derived from Fortune—nevertheless the word *fortune* itself [Note: [Col. 0026D] Compare St Augustine, *Retractations*, book I, chapter 1.] is not permitted to us by the same rule of speech, because truth does not admit its divergent and perverse meaning. For the error of the Gentiles supposes that Fortune is a goddess, who turns a revolving wheel and by a powerful will brings one man down into misery and restores another; and when Marius rejoices in new power, then she smiles, but when Sejanus is dragged by the hook, then she mocks.

Since it is not Catholic to think this with them, surely it is not truthful [Col. 0027A] to speak with them either. And since I know with certainty that you hold the truth of the faith, I wish that speech may be found to agree more earnestly with one who thinks truly. You have in the Psalm to whom this ought more certainly to be ascribed: “He humbles this one,” it says, “and exalts that one” (Ps. 74). Who? “A cup,” it says, “is in the hand of the Lord, and he has inclined it from this to that.” And Hannah says: “The Lord brings down to hell and brings back; the Lord makes poor and makes rich” (1 Sam. 1). Therefore, since both welcome prosperity and troublesome adversity are in God’s hand, be certain that neither fate nor Fortune accomplishes anything in them. Rather, paganism, deceived by its manifold error while seeking gods for itself, invented this fiction, because in its misery it did not find the true God.

Finally, you have read in the title of a Psalm, “The understanding of Asaph,” and you have found “Asaph” more frequently in the Psalm titles, [Col. 0027B] concerning whom you also wished to speak to me in your letter. You hold, through knowledge, that although he was held in the pressure of the winepress, he was found not to be a grape—or rather wine—nor dregs, but oil. This is what I said pleased me in your letter: namely, that you seem to have devoted effort to divine reading. In it Asaph and Jeduthun, and others of this sort, are commended not moderately: men who, by their own labour and study and that of others, are commended as attaining a rightly ordered life.

If you acquire their commendable understanding; if you choose to pass—indeed, to leap—from progress to progress; if through art, heart, and hand you compose a harmonious concord of conduct, then you too will surely sing psalmody before the ark of the covenant, pleasing to divine ears. [Col. 0027C] In this, as in a gymnasium—as your letter intimates—you are already wrestling and voluntarily bearing the pressure of the winepress upon your shoulder: perhaps intending to leave behind, like a grape, that old flavour of worldly life and learning, and by vigorous agility to pass over into a new sweetness both of knowing and of living.

For what else do the divine readings to which you devote yourself resound? To what other end do the blows of this literal exercise labour, except that they may render the one whom they have undertaken seriously learned and, by the hammer of learning, equipped to enter upon the path of a better life? You know that some languish in manners so sluggish and lethargic that they are unwilling to apply any, or only slight, diligence to learning. Others, however, possess an intellect so crude—indeed, so dull—that although they are always learning, [Col. 0027D] they never arrive at perfection.

Thus many among the people are so inert through a certain rustic dullness that they have no experience whatever of the price at which wine is sold. They regard it as superfluous to direct their minds toward investigating this, being content with a cistern, a pool, or flowing waters. Others, however, of what they suppose a better disposition, unwilling to remain shut up in their own cottage, delight in frequenting streets, marketplaces, crossroads, and gatherings of their betters. Passing along, they recognize from the sign of a circle on an inn that there is wine there; perhaps from a herald’s testimony they know that it is good as well. Yet they have not immediately experienced by inward taste the sweetness of that whose knowledge they acquired only through use or outside report. Knowledge that comes first offers them no healthful benefit [Col. 0028A] unless the experience of taste comes to the aid of that prior knowledge.

Even if someone advances so far that, assuming a herald’s office, he wishes and is able to cry aloud through streets and lanes, and to boast with smacking lips of how great is the pleasantness of clarified must and how sweet is ancestral wine, nevertheless, whatever he thus mixes for others and serves to them, if he has not himself perceived it by taste, he does not nourish inwardly his own self who serves it. Do not follow their example through equal dullness or negligence. Rather, wisely instructed by a better counsel, put aside the watery flavour of that fabulous Helicon, and strive to be brought into Solomon’s true wine-cellar; not so that you may speak more copiously and noisily about wine or the vine of Soreth, but that you may be intoxicated by eager draught and full taste.

[Col. 0028B] I do not want you to remain inexperienced in this abundant intoxication, because the fruitful cups of Helicon will never make you eloquent. Rather, through that wine you will not be ignorant of true knowledge; indeed, you will know because you will feel that “the Lord’s intoxicating cup—how splendid it is!” (Ps. 22). For here a man is said truly to know when he is also granted to experience: when what is found life-giving and most healthful in the Scriptures is not enclosed merely in the reader’s memory, but is experienced by the eagerness of one who tastes.

Hence the Prophet says: “Taste” (Ps. 33); and another says: “Friends, drink and be intoxicated” (Song 5). But one who is badly sober and does not taste the cup of this intoxication, whose abstinent throat is constricted by weakness and dry thirst, [Col. 0028C] plainly does not possess the true knowledge of Scripture. Though he remembers its words, he has not deserved to obtain its meaning. He does not obtain the meaning who, though seeking flesh or skin, may have found them, has nevertheless not yet reached its life-giving spirit; who does not yet feel the spiritual sweetness of Scripture; who does not consent with an attached affection of mind to the reading he has heard; who, although by zeal for reading he receives the words into memory, has not yet tasted with his dull palate their inward sweetness. Therefore, although he is already thought great among men in the place of Apollo, he is accounted nothing by the testimony of Scripture itself.

“If anyone,” it says, “is perfect among the children of men, if your wisdom is absent from him, he shall be accounted nothing” (Wis. 9). And below: “All men are vain,” it says, “in whom there is not knowledge of God” (Wis. 13). You see that Scripture calls wisdom and knowledge the same thing, or at any rate so harmonious and altogether so alike that whoever is not endowed with such knowledge and wisdom deserves to be accused of vanity and accounted nothing.

For it calls that the knowledge of God by which God is known, by which he is experienced, by which the affectionate mind of readers experiences his sweetness in the Scriptures. Devout readers draw this knowledge from the inexhaustible cellar of wine-filled abundance; and the giver of it himself loves it more than the sacrifices of those who offer them. “I desired,” he says, “the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings” (Hos. 6). But that he means by the knowledge of God not a knowledge content with the leaves of his reputation or words, but one which, experiencing and tasting God, is intent upon fulfilling [Col. 0029A] his will, he subsequently indicates by the opposite statement. He says that those have fallen into the precipice of transgression whom he wishes us to understand have not attained the knowledge of God: “I desired the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings; but they, like Adam, transgressed the covenant.”

Where he ought to have said, “But they did not at all possess the knowledge of God which I desired,” he says what those who lack God’s knowledge consequently chose to do; so that, through what is openly declared to have been done, he may plausibly signify what efficient cause preceded it. And beautifully: “Like Adam,” he says, “they transgressed the covenant.” When Adam stretched himself forth in Paradise to touch what was forbidden, he showed this not by compulsion of nature nor by ignorance of mind, but, deciding with enervated softness to conform himself to feminine passion, he proved deliberately and knowingly disobedient to reason.

Had he held God by the aforesaid knowledge—that is, by present experience in taste, feeling, and judgment—he would not by will or contempt have passed over the covenant he had received. For whoever rejoices to know one whom he experiences in this manner, consequently loves to obey him also.

Therefore those who, like Adam, are not ashamed deliberately to sin and transgress the covenant are rightly said not to possess knowledge but to labour in ignorance. For the increase of knowledge lies not in speaking fluently many true things from the Scriptures, but in obeying more affectionately in conduct once their meaning has been received. Nor should you therefore believe that divine reading is rightly judged superfluous because not every [Col. 0029C] reader of it advances by reading to this understanding and agreement. It does not contain such living power or effect as necessarily to render every reader thus disposed.

Grace alone invisibly grants the increase of this progress, but outward reading supplies no slight assistance. Welcoming the reader in its kindly bosom in order to teach, it teaches in many ways how one ought to live and by what antecedent merits of life one ought to arrive. While it unfolds mystical and moral meanings enclosed beneath the covering of the letter; while it says that the literal shell contains spiritual wine; while it displays, as it were, that wine’s colour, commends its flavour, and proclaims its usefulness, it exhorts and incites the hearer to drink it. Through this exhortation [Col. 0029D] he investigates more carefully what has been commended.

And while, gladly provoked by the insistent commendation, he drinks, the drinker’s inward appetite is sharpened. What appeared of little or no use to the one who did not drink becomes pleasant and healthful to one who drinks more fully. For taste receives a pleasing increase through appetite, and appetite through taste; and, advancing, it supplies the inward person with more solid nourishment, so that he may either grow stronger as with bread or, as if elegantly intoxicated with choice wine, become cheerful.

[Col. 0030A] That spiritual knowledge—or, to speak more precisely, that life-giving meaning—which is experienced in the divine writings when their Author grants more abundant grace to a devout reader, is called both bread, by which the inward person is strengthened, and wine, by which, advancing into an ecstasy of mind, he is intoxicated. It is bread when he is granted to attain unconquered fortitude; it is wine for a man when, longing for heavenly things, he forgets earthly and visible things. It is bread when he manfully bears and overcomes every opposing thing; but wine when, seeking not the things that are his own, he hides himself wholly in that sanctuary of God.

Observing this, Zechariah says: “What is his goodness, and what is his beauty, except the grain of the elect and wine that makes virgins flourish?” (Zech. 9). What good, he says, is in [Col. 0030B] Scripture except bread or grain? Removing shameless dogs from its food, it admits only those whom Christ deigns to choose as friends—those who abhor the husks of swine and the empty chaff of beasts, and with refined desire seek to feed upon the wheaten fine flour of sons. To them Solomon says: “Eat, friends” (Song 5).

And what is beautiful in Scripture except wine? Those who have drunk it are carried away into a kind of ecstasy; having driven off the tumult of wakefulness, they are soothed by the tranquil rest of the mind. Whatever disturbs this sleep they hold so hateful that, bidding it farewell, they follow Christ with undivided wholeness of spirit. On account of this wholeness they are also called virgins, because they are not held by a varied affection for vices; but, despising the enticements by which all carnal persons [Col. 0030C] do not fear to be corrupted, whatever their regard for holiness, they rest in the chaste embrace or reclining companionship of Christ alone.

This was beautifully foreshadowed by that young man in the Gospel who, when the Jews raged and wished to seize him, let go his linen cloth, choosing to flee naked (Mark 14), and to experience the peaceful purity of spirit rather than be entangled in the ragged malice of the tumultuous crowd. Christ recalled him from his purpose, he wishing, as they say [Note: [Col. 0029D] He rightly says “as they say.” Certain persons indeed inferred this from the preface to John circulated under Augustine’s name; but it is certainly not Augustine’s, both from its difference of style and from the final tractate on John. Baronius rightly proves, from Ignatius, Jerome, and Epiphanius, that Saint John never attempted marriage: vol. I of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 31. Nicephorus, book VIII, chapter 3, judges that the wedding related in John chapter 2 was that of Simon the Canaanite.], to take a wife, and reclined him upon his breast during supper (John 18), because he adorns with the entire purity of virginal spirit those whom he admits more intimately to the depths of spiritual knowledge.

[Col. 0030D] And rightly, he to whom it is granted to recline above Christ’s breast at supper, to whom Christ wished more abundantly to pour spiritual knowledge, is rightly, I say, proclaimed to have been a young man and a virgin, so that this twofold grace may be held more commendable through its pleasing union. For, while some at this age, as though released from the laws of chastity, delight in unrestrained excess, every prudent person strives to restrain himself by virginal modesty, considering that the useful strength of a young man is that upon which the beauty of virginal modesty is laid.

Finally, a certain comic poet says [Note: [Col. 0030D] Plautus.], “It is fitting that a young man be modest.” [Col. 0031A] And John says: “I write to you, young men, because you are strong and have conquered the evil one” (1 John 2). Since a young man, by a certain impulse proper to him, burns intensely to obtain his desires, by the tender love of which he has been strongly entangled, he rightly signifies vehement strength, or strong vehemence, which is customarily ascribed to that age—indeed, to that will.

To this strength a certain wholeness of a modest spirit must be joined, so that it may not permit strength to be immersed in empty and harmful desires, but, calling it back from public business and the noise of the streets, may make it dwell with itself in the flowering chamber of the Scriptures. When these two dispositions are joined in an indivisible covenant and, like John, sleep leaning upon Christ’s breast (John [Col. 0031B] 13), nothing more fruitful can be found anywhere for readers in such leisure, and scarcely anything more serene or pleasant can be experienced in such an occupation.

Isaiah speaks of this: “The young man shall dwell with the virgin” (Isa. 62). For when Christ deigns to visit the reader with his grace and to inflame his chaste and vehement desire, so that in reading he may understand and love what he understands, there comes to be a gracious cohabitation of young man and virgin, fruitful not through the agreement of carnal things but through the advancement of spiritual things. According to the aforesaid Zechariah, the spiritual knowledge of Scripture bears or makes flourish such strong men and virgins—that is, the strong wholeness of virginal spirit—when either the diligent reader eats as bread in sweat, or, more advanced, receives it as wine in a gentler draught.

[Col. 0031C] This is surely what that understanding of Asaph already rejoices both to know and experience: through the gift of grace it has advanced to obtain this benefit, so as to drink clarified wine, pressed by the strong winepress of divine reading and freed from sediment, in Solomon’s quiet cellar. Just as the queen of the Sabaeans is recorded to have come there with a great company, so that she might make more certain to herself through the sight of her eyes what she had heard of from afar by report (1 Kings 10), so you too, led by love of knowledge, came to Paris and found Jerusalem, sought by many, through a desired short route.

Here David touches the ten-stringed psaltery with his hand; here with mystical touch he plays the psalms. Here Isaiah’s prophecy is read and, through reading, disclosed; here the other prophets produce diverse modes in harmonious melody. Here wise Solomon is opened to [Col. 0031D] gathered learners; here his storehouse is opened to diligent knockers. Here there is so great a concourse at the knocking, such a multitude of clerics, that it strives to exceed the numerous throng of laypeople.

Happy city, in which the holy books are turned over with such zeal, and their intricate mysteries are resolved through the bestowed gift of the Spirit; in which there is such diligence of readers, and finally such knowledge of the Scriptures, that it may deservedly be called, after Kiriath-sepher, “the city of letters.” In it I wish you, after the pattern of Othniel, to be educated not so much literally as spiritually: to receive the Scriptures in such a way as to delight in experiencing their inward sweetness; and to make the musical psaltery sound in such a way that the accompanying harp may be found to sound in harmony: “For the psaltery,” as you have read, “is pleasant with the harp” (Ps. 80). Farewell.

## LETTER IV. PHILIP TO ENGELBERT

**The study of letters is to be directed toward the spiritual perfection of the inward person.**

[Col. 0032A]

As you know grammarians say, *vir* (“man”) is derived from *virtus* (“strength” or “virtue”), because he ought to have a spirit not soft, not feeble, not, so to speak, feminine, but strong, steadfast, and masculine in unconquered vigour. Such a man must not grow vainly inflated when prosperity smiles upon him in abundance, nor grow effeminate when adversity presses upon him with trouble. Therefore, if you wish to advance into the perfect man—or rather, if you remember that you are a man—act manfully and strengthen yourself more stoutly. Do not refuse, for the sake of mere words, to endure whatever hardship may meet you.

For just as a soldier does not receive the palm [Col. 0032B] who is lulled by soft indolence, who, unable to bear labour, is constantly pampered by shade, feathers, and a wife’s embrace, so one reaches the heights of knowledge only by labour and study. Hence you see very many everywhere distinguished by the clerical name, but very few trained with corresponding progress; instead, repelled by some difficulty, they either remain completely unlearned or rinse their lips at the horse’s fountain, so as suddenly to come forth as poets.

Both errors were more carefully avoided by all who wished truly both to be called and to be learned. As followers or servants of philosophy over no small length of time, they advanced so far as to become masters of others. Plato, a citizen of Athens, though he had already learned Greek letters to perfection and had surpassed his fellow pupils in Socrates’ school, nevertheless still burning with love of learning, went down into Egypt and acquired no small knowledge among foreign and barbarous nations. Perhaps he had heard that Moses, born and raised in Egypt, had been instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, as the divine page relates; and Plato, not moderately curious about this wisdom, became eager to investigate it.

Not content with this investigation, he then sought Italy and acquired much knowledge among the Pythagoreans as well. Devoted to such study, he reached his eighty-first year, in which he found no end of study save with the end of life.

[Col. 0032D]

Socrates, Plato’s master, is said to have lived ninety-nine years and to have spent them in constant literary labour. Themistocles, when he had completed one hundred and seven years and sensed the end of life was near, complained, as they say, that he was compelled to leave life at the very time when he seemed first to be beginning to become wise. Cato the Censor, though advanced in mature age and appearing already perfect in learning among the Latins, nevertheless burned with youthful eagerness to learn Greek letters, and, though a teacher of the Latins, was not at all ashamed to become a pupil of the Greeks.

Therefore, since the harshness of labour did not break these men and others like them, nor the long span of advanced age turn them back from giving such diligence to literary study [Col. 0033A] that their love of learning made them feel no obstacle whatsoever, it is not prudent for your energy to wither because of an approaching little fever, and for your manly spirit to languish together with your weakened body. For it is not honourable merely to have been in Paris; rather, it is honourable to have acquired honourable learning in Paris.

Therefore let it not suffice you if you have seen the Muses and the Heliconian spring, if you have drawn a small drop from its stream, or if you see yourself sprinkled with its exceedingly slight dew while its abundance has not yet been more fully poured into you. Indeed, philosophy itself, which sets before students Helicon’s clear fountain, judges that the mere benefit of seeing it is not enough. To the person to whom it gives Plato’s keen and sharp intellect, Cicero’s flowers and adorned eloquence, the teachings of your Socrates, [Col. 0033B] and a clearer disclosure of Aristotle’s arguments, it surely does not wish merely to give a small sprinkling of drop or dew; it wishes him to bend over or immerse himself longer in its living fountain.

What temporal riches or bodily pleasures can be compared with this knowledge, when any fool may sometimes abound in them, but cannot at all deserve to acquire this? Hence divine Scripture says: “What does it profit a fool to possess riches, when he cannot buy wisdom?” (Prov. 17). Therefore neither Croesus’s riches, Alexander’s power, Polyphemus’s dreadful size, Hercules’ unconquered strength, Nereus’s admirable beauty, nor other things of this kind are to be compared equally with literary knowledge. Rather, refined letters are unquestionably deservedly [Col. 0033C] preferred to them.

Therefore, when by God’s will you return to us in health and bring back with you not so much money as literary knowledge, I shall, to speak truthfully, regard you, even if shipwrecked, not as poor but as laden with honourable wares and adorned with precious riches. Yet those riches appear not primary but secondary; indeed, to one who examines more carefully, they are not truly to be considered riches at all unless they humbly and religiously serve those riches which are spiritually possessed by the truly rich alone. Divine Scripture speaks of these: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Prov. 13).

[Col. 0033D] A man’s own riches are faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues by which one reaches heavenly glory. Whoever lacks them is found foolish and without glory before God, rejected by God himself, the knower of the truly wise, even if you approve him as Socrates, Plato, or Aristotle. “Has not God,” says the Apostle, “made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1 Cor. 1). And again: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (ibid.). And the Lord says: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent” (ibid.).

Therefore no prudence, knowledge, or abundance of learning is sufficiently worthy of commendation unless it strives to be augmented by the superadded fortress of virtues. Indeed, those who are not redeemed by the merits of virtues as by their own riches are grievously weighed down by the riches of learning as by foreign shackles.

[Col. 0034A]

For this reason virtues are called one’s own riches: because they make truly rich those upon whom they are freely bestowed, granting them in the present a grace of advancing merits and in the future an unfailing glory of rewards. Therefore, whenever a prudent man strips himself, as though to wrestle in the school’s gymnasium, whenever he keeps watch or abstains, grows cold or sweats, he must consider diligently what he is aiming at, and what he sets before his intention and literary labour.

For it is not fitting that in present labour he should be encouraged by windy and empty hope, like the animal said to live on wind and air, lest he should someday glory vainly within himself in being trained in literary studies. This motive for glory, when it calls and induces miserable students to learn, completely trips and deceives them with its agreeable enticement. It gives them an insatiable desire for knowledge yet never leads them to the perfection of knowledge. Of them the Apostle says: “Always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of truth” (2 Tim. 3).

The knowledge of truth is to know God, and, through the benefit of knowing, to experience him more fully—not as demons do, who, knowing him, were tormented by their knowledge, but as the good angels do, who are called Cherubim because of the merit of their knowledge. “We know,” say the demons, “who you are, Son of God. Why have you come to torment us before the time?” (Matt. 8). But *Cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge.” Therefore both those and these know God: the former, so that they may experience him as an angry punisher; the latter, as a gracious and freely-giving protector. The former know him in order to desire and beg to flee from him; the latter, in order more intimately to follow and know him as merciful.

Imitating these latter, Hosea says: “We shall know, and we shall follow in order to know the Lord” (Hos. 6). I want you also to know with this purpose, to devote much diligence to letters so that, aided by learning, you may know God more fully and follow him; and, through persistence in following, may finally deserve to know him face to face. Would that all who are given over to literary labour studied in this way, enduring the many hardships of the schools to this end: namely, that the inward eye, cleansed by the applied eye-salve of knowledge, might be rendered readier and clearer for seeing God. Farewell. In my name greet most warmly your companions who are with you, my friends.

## LETTER V. PHILIP TO JOHN

**He defends the books of Blessed Hilary on the Trinity and explains two difficult statements therein: (1) that Mary did not give origin to Christ’s body; (2) that Christ’s body was impassible. He shows the Catholic understanding of these statements.**

[Col. 0034D]

I have understood your affection toward me not only now from your letters, but long since from your deeds. And I, to speak truthfully, love those who love me; and “those who keep watch to love me find me loving them.” But in this your affection is greater, because you loved me first, and by loving deserved to be loved; thus yours freely does what belongs to it, whereas mine in some measure responds as a duty.

I know, moreover, that your prudence is not unaware [Col. 0035A] that love nurtures the confidence by which the beloved is encouraged to speak, even though he is dust and ashes, because he judges that patience will not be lacking in one who loves him. Therefore I shall speak confidently to my lord, and I ask you to hear patiently. May my love embrace both confidence and patience, on one side and the other, so that it may not turn aside even a little from love’s side. For neither confidence nor patience is found commendable unless bound by the indissoluble bond of love. Indeed, without love confidence rises into pride, patience is overthrown by anger, and thus at last that peace is uprooted which is first and chiefly commended among the servants of God.

Having read your letter, by which, as you say, you wished to make my fraternity more cautious, you have made it unsettled and more doubtful, compelling it to depart somewhat from what I previously thought I understood prudently. For I did not think that Athanasius’s book—which, as you asked and directed, I had sent you to read—ought to be rejected altogether. Rather, I read it in such a way that I gladly embraced what I could understand in it, and humbly revered as secret and hidden what I could not understand.

I also judged your knowledge of the divine Scriptures to be so prudent, and your prudence so knowledgeable, that just as you held nothing in them contrary to the rule of truth, so you perceived the hidden things of truth itself with lynx-like understanding. But because you affirm that the aforesaid book says many false things about Christ and therefore, laying doubt aside, reject it, my dullness is more astonished than can be expressed and, with your leave, does not yet know to which it ought to give assent.

[Col. 0035C] Until now I did not think that he spoke falsely in any, or in so many, matters, and I commended your learning to no small extent. Now, since one is held so openly contrary to the other, I am secure in neither. Since I cannot commend both together, I must choose one. If, God revealing it, I learn that your opinion is in every respect truer, I shall rejoice to have acquired fuller knowledge and shall render no small thanks to your perspicacity, through which I shall obtain such a benefit. But if I become certain that he does not make such false assertions about Christ, my smallness will not follow your opinion in every respect. I ask that your excellence not be offended by this: wherever truth is found, it ought to be held.

[Col. 0035D] Certainly, when I consider that from childhood you have learned the sacred writings in the cloister and have made no small progress in their knowledge, I judge approved in them what you approve, and hold suspect what you reject to the contrary. But when I consider that Athanasius is remembered as the author of that book, and that Athanasius’s sound faith and profound learning are solemnly commended, I seem to incur blame for fickleness if I quickly believe that heretical falsehood is present in that book.

[Col. 0036A] Finally, my Augustine is found to commend highly the book which Athanasius wrote against heretics [Note: [Col. 0035D] Letter 48, to Vincentius.]; and both its prefixed title and the course of the work itself seem to show that this book too was written against heretics. If, however, your prudence does not at all think that this one was written by that commendable Athanasius, and both its title and our opinion are rejected, I neither wish nor ought to oppose you contentiously on this point, since at present I find no certain evidence supporting me.

Whoever wrote it, its words must be examined more carefully, and the truth of an appropriate interpretation sought in them, so that neither the writer’s authority may commend or excuse falsehood when found, nor the reader’s presumed quickness may distort hidden truth. [Col. 0036B] In that book, when I read it, I know I found very many things that appeared so obscure to my small understanding that I could scarcely reach their meaning or discover the author’s sense, whether because of difficulty of expression or corruption of the manuscript.

There are other things too which, to speak truthfully, disturbed me; because of some novelty in them they did not sufficiently please me. Yet I did not dare immediately to impute the offence they caused me to falsehood; I preferred to attribute it to my own slowness. Since I have not deserved to be perfect in the Scriptures, I do not presume rashly to pronounce judgment on obscure writings, lest, by carelessly condemning matters in which my blindness stumbles, I should deservedly lose the rest which my understanding has somehow grasped.

Rereading these very matters more carefully, I eventually seemed to discover what meaning the obscurity of those passages appeared to conceal. Although the author strives to explain it in many words, it did not choose to open itself to me except when I knocked. Therefore, as I now judge, the author of this book is not to be accused of error, nor is the book itself to be rejected by prudent judgment, provided that what I think ought to be judged commendable and that it can be truly demonstrated that he thought this.

To pass over other matters which you did not wish to specify by name: the points which you say are obstinately and falsely proclaimed in the tenth book of this work, and which seem contrary both to Bede and to many other orthodox writers, your prudence, had it wished to attend a little more carefully, could either have accommodated or at least tolerated without harm to the faith. He proclaims indeed, as you assert, that Christ did not take the beginning of his body from Mary, but, as it were, from the Holy Spirit; and that in his Passion he was neither sorrowful nor suffered pain. Such teaching, as you say, is not to be heard; rather, thanks should be rendered to him who did these things willingly and without sin.

In the aforesaid book, its author aims to show that Christ’s flesh had a wondrous and unprecedented generation for us, and was therefore by nature endowed with a wondrous strength unknown to us; so that, just as in the conception, contrary to the human manner, no sin was present, but pure holiness, so also that man, conceived and born, possessed a certain natural strength surpassing the human manner. [Col. 0037A] That book endeavors to show this; it is wholly occupied with this, refuting certain heretics who presumed to blaspheme the Son of God because, having become man, he could not avoid human distresses.

Accordingly, in commending that body which the Word of God is said to have assumed, it says that it did not receive its beginning or origin from the contagion of sin, since his Mother is found to have been physically pregnant, yet no concupiscence of the flesh preceded her conception. For although Mary is not denied to be Eve’s daughter, nevertheless, just as no one of sound judgment asserts that Eve conceived from anyone, because Eve is shown to have supplied bodily matter for her own conception in such a way that the result of this supplying follows upon preceding [Col. 0037B] concupiscence. From the time when Eve contradicted God by disobedience, divine vengeance so inflicted upon her flesh the heat of lust that afterwards she could by no means attain the effect of conception unless she experienced the concupiscence of flesh, both her own and another’s.

And since, when one comes to physical procreation, the flesh of the begetter is first enticed by fleshly concupiscence, that same concupiscence may not inappropriately be called the origin or beginning of our flesh, without whose prior allurement our generation cannot be completed. Those, indeed, who supplied the material of their flesh for our begetting also transmitted to us the concupiscence of that flesh; and this transmission naturally infects the generation of us all, because vice is said to have become, as it were, nature. For this reason the Apostle calls both us and others “by nature children of wrath” (Eph. 2), since we are generated through that concupiscence and bound through it by original bonds.

Thus also the same sin by which each of us is naturally bound before doing anything good or evil is not inappropriately called original, because our flesh seems in some way to have received its origin from it, and because bodily generation has brought this beginning upon it. Yet Mary did not give this origin, or beginning, to Christ, although she physically bore him; for in begetting him she supplied the seed-bearing material of her flesh, and, while supplying it, was not inflamed by any onset of lust. This is what Athanasius [Col. 0037D] says: “For Mary did not give an origin to the body, although she contributed everything natural to her sex for the body’s growth and birth.”

He says that Mary did not give Christ’s body its origin, yet contributed everything natural to her sex. In this he shows that she both supplied what is proper to a mother—that is, the material of flesh—and yet brought in no stain of original vice. This is what this book proclaims, repeats, and multiplies by inculcating it in various ways: namely, that Christ’s body, although naturally held to be like ours, was by no means begun in the contagion of our vices. Of it he says that “although she bore by the office of her sex, yet he did not receive the elements of an earthly conception”; and below: “A body not begun from earthly elements.”

What he means by “earthly elements” or “the elements of earthly conception” seems to be shown a little later, when he is found briefly describing the beginnings of our bodies: “But if earthly bodies,” he says, “that is, bodies begun according to the elements of common causes.” He therefore calls the common causes, whose concurrence begins our bodies, earthly—that is, defective—elements; and because of them he calls our bodies earthly, indicating not their material but the vices which are certain beginnings of those bodies. For after Adam’s sin, unless our parents were inflamed by the vices of concupiscence, they surely would produce no offspring physically.

Concerning these vices he says elsewhere: “Even if Christ had been conceived from the origin of our vices.” If Christ was not conceived from the origin of our vices, from what was he conceived? From the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin and effected the origin of this conception: filling the Virgin so that, in conceiving, she might impart the material of her flesh; overshadowing her so that she might not feel the heat of lust. Therefore, when either the Virgin is said to have conceived by the Spirit, or Christ to have received from the Spirit the origin of his flesh, this is not understood to mean that the divine substance passed into flesh or became the material cause of this conception. Rather, it denotes his coming upon the Virgin and the wondrous operation by which the Virgin bears and Christ is wondrously born.

The union of man and woman effects our conception; but that conception was effected by the Word of God, or by the Spirit abiding in the Virgin. Thus the principle of the one is shown to come from below, whereas that of the other is commended as coming, in a far different manner, from above. My Augustine says of this in *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 20: “The principle of his conception came not from male seed, but in a far different manner from above.” I take the statement that the principle of this conception came “in a far different manner from above” to mean that it received its origin from the Word of God or the Spirit, because the Word of God, coming from the bosom of the Father, remained in the Virgin, and because, as he says, “the Holy Spirit shall come upon thee” (Luke 1).

Therefore Athanasius says: “The flesh had received its origin from no other source than the Word.” And below, concerning Christ: “He himself is the origin [Col. 0038D] of his own body.” And again: “He testified that its origin was from the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the Virgin.” And below: “What the Virgin brought forth from the conception of the Holy Spirit.” And much else of this kind.

Whether, therefore, the Word of God or the Spirit is said to effect this origin, this ought not to be considered discordant or contradictory; for “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. 9)—that is, the Son of God built his own body—and: “That which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1). Yet when this operation is ascribed either to the Word or to the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0037D] He explains the words of St. Hilary from Book X of *On the Trinity*.], Mary is not denied to have done what was hers. Indeed, it is certain that she supplied the material of her flesh and was the material cause of this [Col. 0039A] conception.

But the Holy Spirit, as your prudence has very well written, was not the material cause in Christ’s conception, but the efficient cause. And, I ask, what use would a material cause have been had the efficient cause not been present—the cause which in a wondrous and unprecedented manner made the barren Virgin fruitful, transforming the seed-bearing flesh of the Virgin, without a man’s agency, into the body of the Son? Thus that Son can rightly be said to have received his origin from the Spirit, because he was conceived by him; and nonetheless to have received his origin from Mary, because he was made from a woman. The former is the efficient cause, the latter the material cause; and she is the true mother of a true man.

For just as he was a true man, so she was a true mother, bringing him forth from her own flesh. Eutyches and those with him presumed to deny this and maintained [Col. 0039B] that he received nothing from the Virgin’s flesh. They said that, although he had been incarnate in the Virgin’s womb, he had nevertheless not been begotten of her seed—perhaps lest they should seem to inflict injury upon him if they admitted that he had been born from such material. The Venerable Bede, to whom you referred me, strives to overthrow their erroneous opinion and to convert them—or rather, those like them—to the faith, asserting that he took flesh not from nothing, not from elsewhere, but from the Virgin’s own seed [Note: [Col. 0039D] In Bede, Book IV on Luke, chapter 49, it reads thus: “but he derived it from maternal flesh.”], “otherwise,” he says, “he would not truly be called the Son of Man, if he did not have his origin from a human being.”

In this I do not think that Bede says or thinks anything contrary to Augustine or Athanasius, nor, conversely, that they dissent from such an opinion; [Col. 0039C] for Bede speaks of the seed-bearing material of the body, whereas Athanasius speaks of the divine operation. Since the principle of this conception came from above, the conception can not inappropriately be said to have received its origin from there; but since he drew flesh from the Virgin, he is rightly said also to have had his origin from a human being. Bede undertook to establish this against Eutyches; Athanasius repeatedly commended the other point. Neither appears to me to conflict with the other in this, but each courageously attacks his own adversaries.

Nor, I think, does Bede fail to know that the principle of this conception came from above, nor does Athanasius deny that Mary supplied a seed-bearing portion of her body. But Bede takes up for proof that which serves as a secondary element, while Athanasius takes up that which works as the first and principal element. Yet Athanasius, speaking of the principle of conception—which is rightly judged first and principal—does not pass over Mary, who, concupiscence being removed, performs what remains of a mother’s office. Rather, he acknowledges both that she bore the Son from herself and that she received him only from God: “The Virgin,” he says, “begot what she begot only from the Holy Spirit; and although she gave from herself for the birth of the flesh as much as women, whose generative origins have been received, supply from themselves for the production of bodies”; and so forth.

And elsewhere: “When we proclaim that the true Son of God was born as the true son of man.” And below: “Using her maternal office, she carried out the nature of her sex in [Col. 0040A] the conception and birth of the man.” And again: “She bore from herself a body, but one conceived from the Spirit.”

In these words he confesses quite plainly both that she was truly a mother and that he was truly the son of man—something which could by no means be said if he were not truly born from her flesh. But because he did not receive his beginning from the vices of our origin, or from our original vices, since bodily concupiscence did not infect the material prepared beforehand for him, Athanasius rightly both commends his origin as wonderful and marvels at it as worthy of commendation. The Word of God, or the Spirit, coming down into the Virgin in a new manner, effected it.

Consequently, he who was thus received by the Word of God was conceived by the Spirit; and though Athanasius knows him to be like other human beings in the truth of human [Col. 0040B] substance, he nevertheless says that he was very unlike them in a certain natural power. Thus, just as in conception he suffered nothing contrary to holiness, so afterward he suffered nothing in soul or body contrary to his own will.

We, undoubtedly, because we are generated through our parents’ concupiscence and are bound by the chains of sins in that very origin, are, once born, subjected to a condition so wretched that, even against our will, we suffer the constraints of punishments. Thus our nature is corrupted in conception itself; thus, through the prevailing power of guilt, it is unavoidably weakened, so that, willing or unwilling, it is afflicted by pressing troubles and compelled to lose the strength it had received in Adam before sin. Since this weakness, already inborn, cannot be avoided by any of us, it has deserved to be called “nature” by customary usage.

We are now naturally weak; now we are naturally afflicted by fear and sorrow, hunger and thirst, heat and cold, scourges and wounds. We can neither wholly remove these hardships nor, when they occur, avoid pain. This is that sweat in which, after sin, we miserably eat our bread; this is that weakness in which we naturally toil; this is the nature from whose bonds we most earnestly desire to be stripped, so that at last we may suffer nothing contrary to our will. Athanasius says that this nature was not in Christ; he does not believe Christ possessed this weakness, namely, so that he should suffer unwillingly any trouble in either soul or body, however much seemed to be inflicted upon him [Note: [Col. 0040D] Various passages of St. Hilary explain this excellently.].

[Col. 0040D] For because his Mother knew no union with a man, because fleshly concupiscence did not defile her in conceiving, but the Spirit coming upon her and the overshadowing power of the Most High made her fruitful, he says that the one thus born had a nature so powerful that he could avoid the troubles of impending punishment. As our defective origin formed us and subjected us to suffering and pain against our will, so his origin, free from defect, strengthened him and removed every kind of trouble altogether from his will.

Therefore sufferings could not exercise their own nature upon him, since they could introduce nothing contrary to his will. Although he seemed to endure all that came upon him, nothing of it could prevail against him. For his strength was so great that he could not be deprived of the rightful possession of his will; nor could our natural weakness or feeble necessity obtain mastery in him, but his own will remained sovereign in all things. Thus, as he was born when he willed, so he suffered what he willed, afflicted as he willed; not having a nature by which he was compelled to feel pain as we are, but having a will by which, through sharing our pains, he might heal them [Note: [Col. 0041D] Note this concerning St. Hilary’s meaning and mind.].

This book of which we are speaking seems to proclaim—and repeatedly to commend by proclaiming—that Christ, whose generation was free from every vice, did not feel pain by nature in response to sufferings inflicted upon him [Note: [Col. 0041D] Compare Blessed Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 14, articles 2 and 3; *Sentences*, distinction 15, article 2.]. It does not deny [Col. 0041B] that he endured the sufferings of our body and soul, or that he suffered pain in enduring them. Rather, it says that this pain was brought upon him not by natural necessity [Note: [Col. 0041D] Not such necessity as exists in us; for Christ voluntarily assumed, in his humanity, the necessity of feeling inflicted sufferings, and through his will—both divine and human, insofar as the latter is an instrument of the Word—could turn away sufferings, prevent pain, and avert death. Philip must be understood accordingly when he explains St. Hilary. See the asterisk near the end of this page.], but that he himself received it by his will.

“The Lord Jesus Christ,” he says, “suffered when he was struck, when he was hung up, when he was crucified, when he died; but the suffering that rushed upon the Lord’s body was indeed suffering, yet it did not exercise the nature of suffering, because it raged in its penal ministry in such a way that the power of the body received, without a sense of punishment, the force of punishment raging against it.”

Suffering appears to exercise the nature of suffering when it can compel the sufferer, willing or unwilling, to feel pain—when, according to the measure or force with which this affliction comes upon him and grows heavy, he is forced to waste away in soul or body. [Col. 0041C] But Christ’s suffering by no means exercised the nature of suffering, because its bitterness could not prevail against him. For although a grave and manifold tumult of sufferings was inflicted upon him, he was afflicted only when, as much as, and in the manner that he willed.

For this reason he says that Christ in a sense did not feel what he did feel, and that he received the force of raging punishment without a penal sensation, because one who is not burdened by punishment seems not to feel it, and one who moderates its weight by the command of his will seems not to be burdened by it. “The power,” he says, “of the body receives, without a sense of punishment, the force of punishment raging against it.” And because it perhaps seemed highly troubling to say that he received the force of punishment without a sense of punishment, he subsequently shows more plainly how this should be understood, [Col. 0041D] when this quasi-insensibility is ascribed to his nature—unless perhaps someone more discerning thinks it ought to be understood otherwise—provided it is agreed that truth is contained in these words.

“Indeed,” he says, “the body of our Lord had the nature of our pain, if our body has it in its nature to tread the waves and walk over the billows.” He does not wish Christ’s body to be of the same nature as ours, nor conversely ours to be of the same nature as his—not because he is not a true man as we are, but because he was not naturally defective as we are. He shows this more plainly in what follows: “That man is from God, having indeed a body capable of suffering, and he suffered; but not having a nature capable of pain, for his body belongs to a nature proper and his own.” And a little later: “For he had a body, but one proper to its own origin and not arising from the vices of human conception.” And below: “The appearance and truth of the body testify that he is a man; but let him be ignorant of the natures of vices.”

He was therefore ignorant of the natures of vices because he endured the defects of our weakness not naturally but voluntarily. Hence elsewhere he says: “From the things shown, it is beyond doubt that in the nature of his body there was no weakness of bodily nature, and that, although that suffering was inflicted upon the body, it did not bring upon the body a nature of feeling pain. For although the form of our body was in the Lord, he was not in a body of our defective weakness, because he was not in the origin which the Virgin brought forth from the conception of the Holy Spirit—an origin which, although she brought it forth by the office of her sex, nevertheless did not receive the elements of an earthly conception. For she bore from herself a body, but one conceived from the Spirit, having in itself the truth of its body, but not having the weakness of nature; for that body is truly a body which is born from the Virgin, and it is outside the weakness of our body because it received its beginning from a spiritual conception.”

These words show that Christ surpasses other [Col. 0042C] human beings by a power of nature, that he was not of such a nature as to feel pain, and they add the reason: namely, because he knew none of the defective elements of our origin—an origin which naturally entangled us wretches both in sin and in the punishment of sin. Natural weakness inflicted neither upon him; nor did any trouble, whether in soul or body, oppose him. Rather, as he was able both to be born without sin and to remain born without sin, so he was able * either not to suffer the troubles of punishment or, having suffered them, not to feel pain.

Bishop Maximus says: “Christ’s hunger as a man was not bodily frailty but a sacrament of heavenly grace.” And below: “I see him hungry, and I do not see in him a necessity to eat.”

Therefore, his hunger, or anything else that he endured, [Col. 0042D] was not contradiction, not necessity, not an involuntary injury to soul or body, but a sacrament of heavenly grace. Since his purpose was to impart to human beings the remedy of healing, he appeared visibly to them, in the truth of a substance or form like their own, as he knew their ailments required: possessing from his origin a wondrous strength of nature, yet mercifully inclining his will to suffer weak things; possessing by nature the ability not to be weighed down by sufferings, and possessing by will the ability to assist the weak by suffering with them.

For his body or soul differed from ours in this: his own weakness did not compel him to feel pain; but because his pain was necessary for us, he bore voluntary pain for us, not for himself. For just as he could avoid pain if he willed, so he could feel pain when he willed. He willed it when, and as much as, he saw it necessary for us, since he had come not so much to suffer pain as to benefit us. Thus he felt pain only willingly, whereas I feel pain even unwillingly; and therefore, although he was like me by reason of the assumed truth of human substance, he was nevertheless far unlike me through the wondrous strength of the nature of which I speak.

My Augustine also seems to commend this strength [Col. 0043B] when, in his sixtieth tractate on John [Note: [Col. 0043D] Tractate 60.], he spoke of Christ’s troubled soul: “There is no doubt whatever that he was troubled not by weakness of mind but by power, lest despair of salvation arise in us when we are troubled not by power but by weakness.” Thus he was troubled by power; we, not by power but by weakness. A wondrous difference, concerning which Augustine immediately adds [Note: [Col. 0043D] In the same place.]: “By an ineffable difference, he surpassed the whole human race in strength of mind; did he perhaps labor under precisely the same bodily weakness as we do? Rather, I think that, as he differed from us in strength of mind, so also in bodily strength—a difference which his pure conception bestowed on him. As that conception was new, knowing no course natural to other human beings, so it bestowed upon him, in a new manner, a singular strength.”

[Col. 0043C] His body was weak in that it could suffer and feel pain—a weakness which by the grace of the resurrection he willed to abolish—but it was strong because it lacked a defective nature, or a natural defect; and it had derived this strength from a spiritual conception. Because of that weakness, assumed both by power and by will and brought to an end through the benefit of the glorious resurrection, he is truly proclaimed to have been passible and mortal; and Isaiah the prophet declares that he bore our sicknesses, infirmities, and wounds (chapter 53).

But because of that strength which belonged to him by nature, bestowed upon him by a generation not of concupiscence but of the Spirit, he is said to have surpassed the entire human race [Col. 0043D] by an ineffable distance, so that the devil, astonished by it, was filled with wonder. For, as Pope Leo says [Note: [Col. 0043D] Homily for the First Sunday of Lent.], the devil wished to test this difference when, after the fast, he dared to tempt Christ: “Astonished by his fast of forty days and nights, he craftily wished to discover whether he had this abstinence as a gift or as his own possession, so that he might not fear that the workings of his deceptions would be undone if Christ were of the same condition as his body.”

For Christ had not newly received as a gift the abstinence by which he had eaten nothing for forty days, as Moses and Elijah did, but possessed it as his own from [Col. 0044A] the beginning—that is, naturally. Though he had our body, he was not of our condition, because just as there was nothing defective in his origin, so in action he experienced nothing resisting or contrary to himself. But when, for the certain purpose of a mystery, he had taken our hunger upon himself, the devil rejoiced that he had found in him a sign of a passible nature. Thinking Christ to be of the same condition as his body, he at last boldly set before him the snares of his deceptions, hoping to deceive one whose hunger showed him to be a true man.

Yet his hope and deception attained nothing of what it hoped for. Indeed, it was deceived by the one whom it believed could be deceived: for where the disposition to hunger was found, no necessity of eating was found; because, just as he could endure hunger when he willed, so no food was found necessary to remove it. Therefore, recognizing both that he who hungered was a true man and that he who did not need food was not a man of our weakness, the devil withdrew in wonder and confusion, while the joyful host of angels came to minister to him.

For this reason Athanasius, speaking of Christ’s sufferings, ascribes them not to a weak nature or natural weakness but rather to will, knowing and firmly holding that Christ both felt pain and felt it not naturally but voluntarily. “He suffers pain for us,” he says, “but he does not suffer pain with the sensation of our pain, having in himself a body subject to pain but not a nature capable of pain.” And below: “It is not for one who is to give life to weep, nor for one who is to glorify to feel pain; and yet he who wept and felt pain gives life.”

Here [Col. 0044C] he openly acknowledges that Christ both wept and felt pain, although this was not his own—that is, although it did not happen to him by necessity or nature. “Ascribe weakness,” he says, “if there is necessity and nature for him, and if there is force there” [Note: [Col. 0044D] Not from the principles of human nature in such a way that, had he wished, he could not have prevented it.].
