He does not wish necessity, nature, or compulsion to exist in Christ’s sufferings; rather, whatever Christ endured or suffered, he says was will, sacrament, power, and triumph. “What madness, I ask,” he says, “is it to turn all this into an insult against a weak nature, when it is both will and sacrament, both power and triumph?”

No doubt now seems to remain that Athanasius acknowledges Christ to have felt pain, and to have felt pain voluntarily, whereas pain is naturally implanted in us so that we suffer it not by will but by punitive necessity. In this matter, as I seem to see, he agrees with all who think rightly, and the faith of right believers does not dissent from him. That faith says, in accordance with Isaiah (Isa. 53), that Christ was a “man of sorrows,” as you also write very well, and that with our flesh he voluntarily assumed our affections without sin.

Accordingly, I greatly wonder why you have thought the reading of this work useless, indeed have declared it to be rejected as contrary to faith. In my judgment, you would by no means have done so so freely if you had given it somewhat more careful attention. For even if something is found there which, considered by itself, perhaps ought to be criticized, it can, unless I am mistaken, be excused when what precedes and follows is considered. In condemning any book, one must not seize upon the difficulty of one or two expressions, but consider the whole sequence of its reading. For all things cannot be said at once; some individual statements may rightly be contradicted. But when all are considered together, things which appeared to be rejected are often protected by the support of what surrounds them.

But if one can find there a statement which cannot in any way accord with the rule of truth, is the book therefore to be despised, or rather, as you write, entirely rejected by those who have a cloven hoof? Is it because of one falsehood [Col. 0045B] that the remaining truths should be excluded from prudent people’s reading, when the Apostle commands that all things be read and what is good retained? (1 Thess. 5.) Yet neither, I think, does one have a cloven hoof who knows how to reject truth together with falsehood; rather, it is the one who, reading both, knows how prudently to distinguish them from one another.

I have not said or written this because I presumed to teach you and sit, worthier of a footstool, in a semicircular seat. Rather, I wish humbly to remind your prudence to deign to give careful attention to what has been said. If you see that it can accord with truth, deign to assent with benevolent affection; but if you discover that I hold anything contrary to the rule of truth, then grant to one sick and ignorant—or ignorantly sick—both healing knowledge and suitable correction. For I do not so love the flattering caresses of compliant agreement that I reject the instruments of a cutting physician, knowing that the wounds, even bloody wounds, of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates (Prov. 27).

Therefore, concerning what has been said, I wish you not to remain silent but to answer as seems fitting to you; for whatever you say will not injure my littleness, provided truth accompanies it, and love of truth. Farewell.

Finally, after I had composed this letter and added the final “Farewell” by which a letter is customarily closed, I learned from Master Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, that this book of which we are speaking was written not by Athanasius, as the title of our copy states, but by Hilary of Poitiers, whose faith and teaching are likewise found worthy of commendation. For three days ago, when I was in Paris and that same Master and Bishop Gilbert deigned to converse with me, in the course of speaking he cited a certain verse from that book: “Thus,” he said, “says Hilary in *On the Trinity*.”

Recognizing the verse very well, I immediately asked whether Hilary was truly the author of the work from which that verse had been taken, since the title in our codex named Athanasius. To prevent the mistaken title from making me uncertain, he recited from memory the whole beginning of the work as far as the middle, adding by what number of books it was concluded and in which of them the verse he had cited occurred. Since I recognized that all these things truly belonged to this work, I further asked whether [Col. 0046A] the whole work should be judged worthy of faith. He replied: “Everything contained in it is worthy of commendation.”

Thus through him my error concerning the author of this work was removed, and my understanding concerning the truth of its doctrine was confirmed. Farewell again.

## LETTER VI. PHILIP TO JOHN

*On the same subject.*

I am glad that, although my littleness maintains something contrary to your prudence, nevertheless, as you say, our love remains unshaken with you. I want you to know that I have no doubt that our book which you read was written by Hilary, as I afterward heard some teachers affirm and saw stated in the titles of other codices.

Concerning the question which is debated between us, you sent me one written reply; and because it did not seem sufficient to you, you added another. Receiving both on one and the same day, after reading what you had written first and finding at the end of its discourse that apostolic saying, “If anyone wishes to be contentious, we have no such custom” (1 Cor. 11), I confess that I resolved to make no reply at all, lest I might displease you as contentious. But when, reading the second, I found also at its end: “Consider these matters, dearest friends, and write back what seems right to you concerning them,” [Col. 0046C] I changed my intention and wished to write something in reply, lest I should seem to scorn your command by silence.

You express surprise, as you say, that in my letter I wrote the Apostle as saying: “Read everything; hold fast to what is good” (1 Thess. 5), whereas the text there is, “Test everything” (ibid.). Yet you would not regard this as remarkable at all if you recalled Jerome’s letter to Pammachius and Oceanus. For in it, he says: “The Apostle commands us to read everything, retaining what is good.” But although the Apostle commands that everything be read and what is good retained, you nevertheless judge that Hilary’s book—in which, you do not deny, many things are said with the greatest perfection—should be wholly rejected without hesitation because you consider him blameworthy in certain respects.

You also disapprove of the book which the same Hilary wrote on Matthew, because of certain statements in it which, as you say, are either false or perplexing. From this you make clear that, just as you reject what is false, so too you reject what is perplexing. To demonstrate this more openly you add: “There is an abundance of simple Catholic books, so that perplexing books ought rightly to be avoided because of the stumbling-block they cause, since the Apostle says: ‘Let no one deceive you by subtlety of speech’” (Col. 2).

It is clear that you wish only simple books—that is, books plain and easy to understand—to be read, while perplexing books—that is, subtle and difficult ones—are to be avoided, lest one incur that offense of deception against which the Apostle either commands or exhorts the Colossians to guard themselves. Yet Jerome does not forbid the reading even of works containing something open to the charge of falsehood, provided that usefulness of truth is likewise found in them. Indeed, he frequently read Origen’s books, which he knew to be blameworthy in many respects, and did not at all censure those who read them.

“Origen,” he says [Note: [Col. 0047D] Letter to Tranquillinus], “ought, in my judgment, to be read for his learning as Apollinaris and certain ecclesiastical writers are read: that we may select what is good in them and avoid what is contrary.”

But let it be so: let Origen’s books, or any works of this kind, be rejected, lest simple persons be led into error by maintaining falsehoods as truths; and let the deception of falsehood, when it is not understood, harm as much—or rather more—than learning gained from discovered truth benefits. Must things that are perplexing and subtle also be avoided, however? Or, once read but not understood, must they be condemned by rash judgment, with their very perplexity and subtlety counted as a fault rather than honored on that account far more, and with far greater reverence? What Apostle, what apostolic man, ever said or wrote this: namely, that simple books should be read, but perplexing and subtle ones should rightly not be read because of the offense they occasion, as you write?

When the Apostle warned the Colossians not to be deceived by subtlety of speech, did he wish to induce them to refuse to read writings that are perplexing and subtle, and to read only simple ones? Certainly the course of that passage does not seem to contain such an intention—to remove them from reading subtle works. Rather, in it the Apostle shows his concern that the Colossians be more fully instructed, lest, being untrained and simple, they be deceived by pseudo-apostles speaking subtly.

“For,” he says, “I want you to know what concern I have [Col. 0047C] for you and for those who are at Laodicea, that their hearts may be comforted, being instructed in love and into all the riches of the fullness of understanding, into the knowledge of the mystery of the Father of Christ Jesus” (Col. 2).

He who endeavors to instruct them into all the riches of the fullness of understanding, so that they may know the mystery of God the Father—which is, “The Word was made flesh” (John 1)—does not wish them to be content with reading simple books. Rather, he wishes them to devote themselves to those which contain the hidden mysteries of God the Father, so that they may resist the arguments of heretics and destroy their subtle snares by the stronger propositions of subtle books. Therefore he adds: “But this I say, lest anyone deceive you by subtlety of speech” (Col. 2); and shortly afterward: “See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit” (ibid.). And above: “We do not cease,” he says, “praying and asking for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding” (Col. 1).

The Apostle wishes the Colossians to make progress in all wisdom and spiritual understanding: by reading and understanding subtle things, they are to resist subtle arguments wisely. Otherwise he would write in vain either this letter to them or other letters to others, if he did not greatly desire perplexing and difficult matters both to be read and understood. For he often writes things so subtle that they are not easily grasped except by the wise and spiritual; often things so perplexing that many, not grasping them, are rashly led into error—as he himself seems to indicate to the Corinthians, and as Peter more clearly demonstrates in his own Epistle.

To the Corinthians: “If anyone,” he says, “seems to be a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge what I write to you” (1 Cor. 14). And Peter: “Just as,” he says, “our most beloved brother Paul also, according to the grace given him, wrote to you, as also in all his letters, speaking in them of these matters, among which are some things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort to their own destruction” (2 Pet. 3). If perplexing and subtle things are rightly avoided because of offense, as you write, why does Paul write things known only by the wise and spiritual, and things in which the unlearned and unstable suffer the perplexity of error?

[Col. 0048B] The Lord Jesus Christ himself also speaks so subtly in the Gospels that not even the Apostles grasp the subtlety of his discourse; hence at times he sharply rebukes their slowness: “Are you also still without understanding?” (Matt. 15). He speaks so perplexingly that some are horrified, charging his saying with intolerable harshness, and withdraw from following him because they cannot explain the difficulty placed before them. “Many of his disciples,” he says, “when they heard it, said: ‘This saying is hard’; and they went back and no longer walked with him” (John 6). And in Matthew (ch. 15): “Do you know,” they say, “that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this word?”

Although such subtlety and such perplexity are known to be present in apostolic and evangelical writings, it is nevertheless not the counsel that their reading should be rejected because of the offense they occasion. Rather, one must apply oneself to it much more diligently, so that the prudent reader, by seeking and knocking, may attain an appropriate understanding of it.

Likewise, Hilary’s writings, although perplexing and subtle, should not, in my judgment, be deemed contemptible; nor should their reading be wholly banished either from the wise or from the simple. They will furnish no small benefit to both: the wise person will wisely penetrate their obscurities, while the simple person, remaining outside, will humbly salute those same writings. I therefore wonder that your prudence does not fear to condemn those writings and does not defer to the judgment of learned men, both earlier and present, who succeeded Hilary and accused him of no heresy, but, as was fitting, extolled him with worthy praises.

When Jerome, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, introduced Hilary and individually listed the books he had written, he seems to have mentioned among and above the others this very book about which we are speaking; and he stamped neither this nor the others with a charge of heresy.

“Hilary,” he says [Note: [Col. 0048D] See the letter of the same Jerome to Florentius], “bishop of the city of Poitiers, having been exiled to Phrygia, composed twelve books against the Arians; another book on synods, which he wrote to the bishops of Gaul; commentaries on the Psalms; a little book addressed to Constantius, and another against Constantius; a book against Valens and Ursacius, containing the history of Rimini and the Synod of Seleucia; a book of hymns and another of mysteries; commentaries on Matthew; a treatise on Job; another elegant little book against Auxentius; and several letters to various persons. Some say that he wrote on the Song of Songs, but this work is unknown to us.”

While Jerome was composing a catalogue of Hilary’s books, he presumed to condemn none of them—though in the same book he does not fear to show the little works of many others to be blameworthy. Perhaps he would not have been silent about the fault of these works if, sharing your opinion, he had perceived in them something so detestable.

You affirm that this book of his, which you judge should be rejected without prejudice, is in certain places contrary to itself: namely, because it says both that Mary did not give an origin to Christ’s body and yet discharged a mother’s office in conceiving him; and because it says both that Christ himself at last endured wounds, the cross, and death, and yet received, without a natural sensation of pain, the force of pain raging against him. You say that the two middle propositions agree with right faith, but that the first and last wholly contradict truth.

Since I judged that these things were not mutually contradictory, and in another letter showed, as best I could, how they agree with truth, you say that I did not make such a demonstration appropriately, but violently twisted writings of falsehood to the rule of truth. For, as you write, Mary gave Christ’s body a material origin, not a defect; and you add, as if in astonishment: “How different Mary and defect are!” You say that I put one in place of the other, when I maintain that Mary did not give the origin which defect did not give.

To this I reply:

I know indeed that defect and Mary differ greatly, and I have put neither Mary in place of defect nor defect in place of Mary. But if, by our law, defect worked everything in Mary, then what it worked could not improperly be said to have been worked by Mary. For what flesh works through fleshly desire is not undeservedly attributed to the flesh as its agent. And what the flesh does while a person, willing or unwilling, is inflamed by fleshly desires, that person truthfully declares himself to do: “For,” says the Apostle, “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I hate, that I do” (Rom. 7).

The Apostle, consisting of spirit and flesh, saw these different elements working in such a way that he felt one resisting the other. He said that he performed fleshly deeds because of the allurements of inborn pleasure, yet that he hated them because of the resistance of spiritual will. If he calls his own that in which the flesh delights carnally, though the spirit—which is his better part—resists that delight, how much more rightly and properly would he call this inclination his own if, with the spirit lulled asleep, he brought it to effect?

For then works of the flesh can properly be called ours, when we do not feel them opposed by a resisting spirit; when the conceived desire is indulged with looser reins so that it is consummated through bodily intercourse, even though lawful. But we can neither call spiritual works ours in the same way, nor ought to do so, because we do not have them from ourselves. Rather, through the Spirit of God giving them, we obtain both the inclination and the accomplishment of spiritual works. Therefore they are not so much ours as his, by whose gift and grace we remember that we obtain them.

Since, therefore, every fleshly desire is utterly excluded from Christ’s conception, it is not incongruous to deny that Mary gave an origin to his flesh. For she would properly be said to have given it if she had been drawn to conceive by her own desire. And because the Spirit who comes upon the Virgin performs that conception, the origin of this flesh is rightly assigned to that Spirit; and he is not undeservedly called the author of this origin, by whose gift and work the Virgin, remaining and continuing a virgin, is wonderfully made fruitful.

Thus not Mary, but the Spirit gave origin to that holy body: she felt no natural and personal desire in conceiving, while he, working, came upon the Virgin who was to bear; she, knowing no man, endured none of the impulses of flesh which, under the wretched law of our conceptions, are primary; he, in his marvelous generosity, bestowed upon her gifts completing this marvelous conception, with the natural defect ceasing. Yet this does not deny that she supplied the seminal material from which the Wisdom of God built for himself the workshop of a body, so that he should not be believed to have constructed it for himself elsewhere or from nothing, but truly to have assumed a body in the Virgin’s womb and from the Virgin’s womb.

[Col. 0050C] In this assumption certain persons, as I have heard recently, experience a difficulty. Though instructed by the divine writings, they strive to maintain firmly that, although Christ took flesh in the Virgin’s womb and from her womb, he did not take that particle from which we others are conceived. They shrink even from believing or saying that Christ assumed in the Virgin that liquid flesh which physicians call either seed or semen, and did not instead choose within her some other flesh holier, or at least worthier; as though it were unfitting for a body of such surpassing holiness to have been conceived from that common material of our universal vileness.

In short, faith, as they think, does not require the assertion that Christ was conceived from the Virgin’s seed; but every Catholic must confess that he was conceived from the Virgin’s flesh. They judge it far more credible and much more fitting that he should appear to have assumed not that particle, but another particle of flesh. In this judgment, to the extent that they pay honor to Christ, they seem to detract from the Virgin. It is certain that an injury to the mother rebounds upon the son, and no one can honor either of them with worthy praises who does not fear to arrogate unacceptable honors to the other.

From the time when the angel Gabriel greeted that Virgin, from the time when, after the greeting, “the power of the Most High overshadowed her” (Luke 1), ineffable grace so wholly cleansed her, and the marvelous cleansing so wonderfully adorned her entire being. And just as our flesh, both solid and liquid, is accused of sin and disgrace because the law of the members is punishably opposed to the law of the spirit, so, after it was said to the Virgin, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (ibid.), that saying of Solomon was fulfilled: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song 4).

I therefore judge that the Virgin’s seminal flesh possessed nothing shameful, nor did any other flesh adjacent to it possess any greater dignity; rather, it was from that flesh, ordained from the beginning by God for the forming of conceptions, that the Wisdom incarnate as man fittingly built his house. On account of the material he received from Mary, Christ can be said to have had the origin of his flesh from her; on account of the Spirit working in her, he is rightly said to have received his origin not from Mary but from the Spirit. Hence it is said: “For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1).

[Col. 0051B] As to Hilary’s statement that Christ did not suffer pain in the Passion, he determines in many places in the same book how it should be understood; and I made this more than sufficiently known in another letter, even if I have not yet satisfied your prudence. Because his conception was peaceful and serene, free of every disturbance of desire, his flesh was far removed from the defects of our nature. Therefore what we, conceived in sins, suffer through natural necessity, he—whose flesh is touched by no defect because it lacks a defective beginning—suffers by free will.

In the first of your replies to which I now respond, you think soundly and prudently concerning this will to suffer; but, as it seems, you dissent from the same view in the other. In the first you agree with Hilary’s teaching, as is just; in the other, unless I am mistaken, you proclaim views far opposed to it. For in the first you say that I labor for nothing by striving through many words to demonstrate what every simplest person in the Church knows well, and the affirmation of which has moved no learned person. You even seem somewhat offended that I expend more parchment than necessity requires by showing in lengthy discourse what could be conveyed without saying very much.

For you say: “I lament as your loss the parchment which you expend in teaching that he suffered not by necessity but by will, since every simplest person in the Church knows this.” In this place your prudence rightly understands and confesses that Christ was not driven to suffer by coercive necessity, but was moved by free will, so that no one, however simple, doubts it. If anyone should presume to think the contrary, he is to be charged with error, as your same prudence subsequently confesses: “Moreover, whoever has thought contrary to this faith—whether Augustine, Hilary, or anyone else—must be believed either to have corrected the error itself before death or to have remained unbelieving.”

Since, then, Christ’s Passion involves will and not necessity, and anyone who has thought contrary to this faith is, as you rightly write, held guilty of error, I wonder why in another reply you do not fear to oppose this assertion [Col. 0052A] by assigning necessity to the suffering Christ—the necessity which you previously remove from him. For you say: “We therefore wish there to be in Christ’s sufferings both will, sacrament, power, and triumph, and also the things which your book, along with you, denies: necessity, nature, and violence; but we also wish these to be voluntary.”

There you say Christ suffered not by necessity but by will; here you wish necessity to be in his sufferings. I confess that I do not know how this can be consistent with itself—unless perhaps you understand there to be two necessities, one of which belongs to Christ in suffering while the other is not present in his sufferings. Yet even so I do not see how what you wish irrevocably to affirm in this little clause can stand, since you name not some other necessity which you might perhaps have understood, but the very necessity which our book, along with us, denies.

For I judge that the necessity or violence of which Hilary speaks was not present in Christ’s sufferings, in which both Hilary and you say that will and power were present. What Christ endured by free will, surely he did not endure by necessity; and violence certainly did not compel him to do willingly, under the command of his power, what he did. For necessity prejudices will, and violence prejudices power.

Thus, when he endured spittings, blows, wounds, and the cross, he indeed suffered pain by will; he laid down his life by power. Though his enemies inflicted such insults on him, they did not compel him by necessity either to suffer pain or to die. The force of those inflicting injuries did not prevail to bring these things about; rather, it was the voluntary power of the one enduring them. In the same way, he accepted disturbance of soul and bodily hunger by a will possessing power, or by voluntary power. By the gift of his spiritual conception he possessed the innate capacity not to be burdened by such things, contrary to the manner known and customary in us, unless our weakness seemed to require that he be shown to be a true man through human affections, and that, suffering with sufferers, he might be regarded as the physician bringing us salvation.

Therefore, that he could fast for forty days must be assigned not to a miracle, as you write, but to his own power, lest our dullness judge him equal to Moses or Elijah, whose conception was far different and whose strength was far different from human nature.

[Note: [Col. 0051D] Performed through a power foreign to Christ. See the following column. Otherwise, there is no reason to deny that it was a miracle, but one accomplished through divine power proper to Christ.]

[Col. 0052D] You indeed say that after the fast he necessarily became hungry; and that after becoming hungry, unless he ate, he necessarily would have failed, unless perhaps he wished to remove these burdens by the benefit of a miracle—a kind of miracle that we can observe also in Moses, Elijah, and certain others. For you say: “Truly a man, he truly suffered pain, having a nature such that unless he ate he would fail; he would sink if he walked upon the waves; he would die if he were crucified—unless by a miracle he willed this not to happen. Some such things he himself also performed in certain others, as in Elijah and Moses, Peter and Maurus.” And below: “We say that Christ had the strength to fast longer not by nature but by miracle; for when the miracle ceased, nature at once became hungry.”

Marvelous is this miracle: by whose gift Christ could abstain from food for forty days, but when it ceased nature could not endure hunger longer; indeed, he would suffer hunger by necessary weakness, and, being hungry, would be compelled to fail unless he ate. If then, when the miracle ceased, nature at once became hungry, as you say, why, I ask, did he not eat when hungry, or why did he not fail when he did not eat? For it is written that after the fast he was hungry (Matt. 4); yet it is not written that he ate while hungry, nor is it found that he failed while not eating.

But after the fast, being hungry, he ought either to have eaten or, if not eating, to have failed. Yet, as I have said, though hungry he did not refresh himself, and though not refreshing himself he did not fail. You must therefore say either that the miracle did not cease or that Christ did not fast at all through the aid of a miracle. For if he fasted with the miracle’s help and, once he became hungry, that same miracle had already ceased, you will admit that after hunger he necessarily failed, since nowhere do you read that he ate while hungry. But it is impious to admit this. If, however, the miracle did not cease, how will you say that he endured hunger, when you say that his nature became hungry only once the miracle had ceased? In order, then, to avoid the objections that can thus be advanced as inconsistencies, I should like this miracle to be explained to me better, because it seems wrapped in such great obscurities that I cannot see through it unless you resolve them.

Christ, as I thought, walked upon liquid waves in one way, Peter or Maurus in another. Christ also fasted in one way, Elijah or Moses in another. For they, infirm and heavy by nature, could do nothing of the kind by themselves, and therefore did it through the power not of themselves but of another. To take one example of them: Peter truly perceived this in himself and of himself when, seeing Christ upon the sea, he wisely and humbly said: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters” (Matt. 14). It was as if he said: My nature will walk upon the liquid sea not by my power but by yours; and that unfamiliar burden will not weigh me down if I command it, but if you command it.

Therefore, when Christ commanded, Peter walked fearlessly upon it; but, considering who did what, he became afraid when he saw the strong wind. His faith weakened, and he would already have descended to the depths through natural heaviness had Christ not mercifully stretched out his powerful hand to him. Thus, as I have said, Peter walked upon the liquid element in one way and Christ in another: Peter was sustained by a power not proper to himself, Christ by his own proper power.

Christ had, of course, acquired that power from the fact that God the Word had assumed human nature to himself by a spiritual conception in a virginal womb—an assumption such as no other human being experienced either before or afterward; and therefore no such human being was found either before or afterward.

Because the leaden talent of iniquity did not weigh down his nature, but he came wonderfully here in a light cloud from the Spirit by whom he was conceived, the wave of the sea did not withdraw from its unbroken course beneath his foot, nor did it engulf him as he walked through its flowing opening. Because neither his origin nor his conception departed from the rule of holiness, no element of the Creator found him contrary to itself while he lived here. Rather, he had such a body that it was of free will and in every respect of voluntary power.

He could therefore, if he wished, not suffer pain; and when he wished, he could suffer pain. He suffered pain when he wished medicinally to suffer with us in our pain; he did not suffer pain when he wished to retain the privilege of his innate power.

To be able to suffer pain is a certain weakness; not to be able not to suffer pain is a greater weakness. The first weakness is common to us and Christ, from which both we and he are free after the resurrection, when our strength—or his—can no longer become weak, and this inability is not feebleness but perfected strength. Through this weakness, namely the ability to suffer pain, Christ both could and wished to endure human pains. On its account he is prophesied by true prophecy to be “a man of sorrows and knowing weakness” (Isa. 53), and is solemnly proclaimed by the Apostle to have been “crucified from weakness” (2 Cor. 13).

But the weakness which consists in not being able not to suffer pain must be believed naturally to adhere to us alone. Pressed and oppressed by it, no one of us who is permitted to remain on earth even for one day can avoid being burdened. Christ, however, in my judgment, should not be thought to have been unable, while living this life, not to be troubled. For he whose holiness both of body and mind was incomparable surely possessed an incomparable strength of both.

Hence my Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0053D] *Tractates on John*, 60]: “By an ineffable distance he surpassed the whole human race in strength of mind.” This is that strength by which he differed from all of us beyond expression: while the unavoidable necessity of being troubled, according to our manner, did not hold him, and while he could, with unimpaired vigor of nature, avoid all human sufferings, nevertheless by voluntary power he was troubled for the salvation of us all. Therefore Augustine prefaces this statement [Note: [Col. 0054D] In the same place]: “There is no manner of doubt that he was troubled not by weakness of mind but by power.”

Augustine does not wish any believer to doubt that Christ was not compelled to be troubled by weakness of mind. He so excludes weakness from that disturbance of mind as to attribute voluntary power to Christ. But you, in order that the little clause may be explained according to your view, wish the word “only” to be supplied there incongruously. Where Augustine says, “Christ was troubled not by weakness of mind but by power,” you say, “not by weakness only, but also by power.”

I wonder how Augustine either failed to see that “only” ought to be added, or perhaps saw it but begrudged it. Elsewhere, in expounding the Gospel, he has greatly expanded himself in a multitude of words; I wonder why here, by omitting one particle, he so confused the sense of the text. But if you are willing to consider the sequence of that reading more carefully, it seems to me to show neither before nor afterward what you claim. Rather, as he removes from us the power over being troubled and attributes only weakness to us, so conversely he removes weakness from Christ and attributes voluntary power to him.

For after saying, “There is no manner of doubt that he was troubled not by weakness of mind but by power,” he added: “Lest despair of salvation arise in us when we are troubled not by power but by weakness.” Clearly, when he says here that we are troubled by weakness, not by power, he does not add “only”; nor, when he says there that Christ was troubled by power, not by weakness, did he add “only.” Therefore, if I am not mistaken, he judged that it should be added neither here nor there; and I judge that it should consequently be removed from both. If you wish it to be added there, it appears that it must be added here as well; and then no small absurdity will arise: just as you say that Christ was troubled both by weakness and by power, so we too will be asserted to be troubled both by power and by weakness. Augustine denies both propositions.

If you were disposed to reread more carefully those two discussions on John in which Augustine speaks of Christ’s disturbances—namely, where he discusses Christ’s troubled soul, or Christ troubling himself when he was preparing to raise Lazarus (John 11)—you would see, I think, that no one who thinks rightly can doubt that Christ was troubled not by necessary weakness but by voluntary power.

Likewise, in Maximus’s sentence, “That Christ hungered as a man was not a bodily frailty but a sacrament of heavenly grace,” you say that “only” is to be understood after the words “was not a bodily frailty,” so that that hunger may be not bodily frailty only, but also a sacrament of heavenly grace.

Accordingly, as with Augustine, so with Maximus it is not enough to wonder why, by omitting that particle, he wished the sense of the text to be obscured; and how did it happen besides that both agreed in this, that they wished the same single particle to be understood in these little clauses? But neither this author nor the other added that “only,” nor, if I am not mistaken, judged it should be added. Therefore it must not be inserted by us into these same clauses. For as Augustine says that Christ was not troubled by weakness of mind, so Maximus says that he did not hunger through bodily frailty; and because he hungered by voluntary power for the help of the salvation of us all, he says that this hunger is a sacrament of heavenly grace.

I hold, have held, and wish henceforward to hold in mindful remembrance what your kindness nevertheless deigns to teach me as though I did not know it: namely, that Christ’s death and all the other things which, Scripture testifying, his humanity either did or willed to suffer, are both literally true and contain the sacrament of our salvation. Thus neither may the letter prejudice the spiritual sacrament nor the spiritual sacrament the literal sense.

I know, therefore, that his soul was troubled; that he troubled himself; that he wept before the Jews (John 11); that, seeing the city Jerusalem, he wept over it (Luke 9); that, after fasting forty days and forty nights, he afterward hungered (Matt. 4); that he was wearied by the journey (John 4); that he rejoiced in spirit (Luke 10); that his soul was sorrowful (Matt. 26); and that he was seized, crucified, and died (John 18). But he did all these things by voluntary power, not, as you write, by necessity and violence. It was not that he could not pass through the course of this present life without them, but that he saw them to be beneficial for us who travel it. It was not that a strength naturally inborn in us, grievous and harmful, oppressed him, in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col. 2), but that we might strive to be bound to him by a closer bond of love when we perceived that he had voluntarily taken up our troubles. It was not that he did not differ from us by an ineffable distance in strength both of body and mind, but that he might not be thought not to pity us if he did not endure our miseries.

God therefore assumed man when he wished; the man assumed endured what he wished. Thus he often avoided the wrath of his persecutors when he did not yet wish to suffer, and offered himself to those seeking him when it pleased his own will. Origen plainly appears to demonstrate this in his homily on Genesis [Note: [Col. 0055D] Homily 8], unless perhaps you wish to reject his testimony, or rather to understand in his words the aforesaid “only,” and by supplying it to obstruct the plain truth both here and elsewhere.

“Wisdom,” he says, “has built herself a house” (Prov. 9); and: “He humbled himself unto death” (Phil. 2). “And whatever you read concerning Christ, you will find done not by necessity but willingly.”

You see that necessity is wholly removed both from Christ’s incarnation and from his Passion, as well as from the other things read of him, and that spontaneous will is attributed to them. Thus it is certain that Origen agrees with Hilary, Augustine, and Maximus, while you differ very greatly both from him and from them.

But now I put an end to this letter, lest its wordiness deserve to displease you and I again compel you to grieve over the loss of expended parchment. Yet it is not so lamentable for much parchment to be spent in writing as for writers to lack the skill worthy of writing.

For this reason I earnestly exhort you in conclusion to pray more earnestly: that, if either I or you think otherwise in any matter, divine grace may deign to reveal it, granting us both to sit thirstily beside the streams of the divine Scriptures, and, for those who thirst, to have the cheeks of the turtledove and the eyes of doves. For, I confess, what is needed for the depths of divine reading is a necessary, not disdainful, fullness; not the corrupted ease of adulterous cruelty; not the swollen importunity of raven-like chatter; but, conversely, the inexhaustibility of deer-like longing, the undefiled chastity of turtledove-like faith, and the modest humility of dove-like simplicity.

In these, indeed, I think that both the knowledge of the righteous and the justice of knowing are brought to completion without *debitum* (what is due; the wording is uncertain). But lest, by detaining you long, I displease you by detaining you, this letter should fittingly end here. Farewell.

## LETTER VII. FROM PHILIP TO JOHN. On the same subject.

Meas mihi epistolas, quas vobis miseram, remisistis, sed eas primitus tam crebro glossis marginalibus repersistis, ut quasi transire in colorem alterum compellantur, et jam non esse quod fuerant videantur. Cum enim glossa textui ad hoc soleat superponi, ut possit idem textus non tenebrescere, sed exponi, vestra glossa econverso illas epistolas obscuravit, et tam pergamenum exterius, quam sensum interius deturbavit. Vultis quidem, ut video, non solum quod [Col. 0057B] contra vos, sed etiam quod ad vos dicitur, infirmare, et meum infirmando, vestrum sensum tenaciter confirmare, et ideo pene cuncta corrumpitis mordaci pipere superfuso, sed sufferre diligentis et dilecti vulnera non recuso. Scio enim hoc vos intendere, ut qui recte et salubriter sapere vos putatis, me pauperem et insulsum sapore fructifero condiatis; sed 32 piper vestrum errore aliquantulum amarescit, et, pace vestra dixerim, falsitatis nubilo tenebrescit. Cui si voluero seriatim per omnia respondere, et a meis litterulis qnae objecta vel injecta sunt omnia removere, non potero sufficienter per epistolam hoc implere, sed necesse erit librum, vel libros potius adhibere.

You returned to me my letters which I had sent you, but first you so repeatedly over-wrote them with marginal glosses that they seem compelled, as it were, to change into another colour and no longer to be what they were. For whereas a gloss is ordinarily placed over a text so that the text may not be obscured but expounded, your gloss, on the contrary, has obscured those letters and has disturbed both the parchment outwardly and their sense inwardly. You wish, as I see, to weaken not only what is said against you [Col. 0057B], but also what is said to you; and, by weakening my meaning, stubbornly to establish your own. Therefore you corrupt almost everything by sprinkling it with biting pepper. Yet I do not refuse to endure the wounds of one who loves and is loved. For I know that this is your purpose: that you, who think yourselves to savour rightly and wholesomely, may season me, poor and insipid as I am, with a fruitful flavour. But your pepper is somewhat embittered by error and, if I may say so without offence to you, darkened by a cloud of falsehood. If I wished to answer it point by point in every respect, and remove from my little letters everything objected or added to them, I could not accomplish this adequately in a letter; books—or rather, several books—would be required.

[Col. 0057C] Caeterum quia scio ad faciendum libros idoneum me non esse, mihique nec otium, nec peritiam praesto esse, non omnibus quae in me dicitis, sed aliquibus respondere tentabo, et vel refellam ea, vel me saltem aliquatenus excusabo. Cum enim me videam a vobis graviter accusari, necesse est accusatum, vel ad modicum excusari, non ut per hoc majoris acquiram meritum sanctitatis, sed ne vos mei causa inconsideratum judicium incurratis. «Qui judicat, inquit, fratrem suum, judicat legem (Jac. IV).» Superbiae et stultitiae meam arguitis parvitatem, qui tamen cordis mei occultam non satis perspicitis veritatem, et scitis quia quod loro judicii, tam in melius quam in deterius, potest flecti, utile est et sanctum ad melius potissimum id reflecti. Dixi in epistola mea [Col. 0057D] (epist. V). «Si Deo revelante vestram esse cognovero sententiam per omnia veriorem, gaudebo consecutus scientiam ampliorem: vestraeque perspicaciae grates non modicas exhibebo per quas hujusmodi beneficium obtinebo.» Huic versiculo superposita glossa vestra obloquitur, dicens: «Superba humilitas,» etc. Dico vobis, non est in me tanta superbia ut recusem quae recta sunt, vel a vobis audire, vel auditis humiliter consentire; si tamen Deus dignetur mihi intelligendi gratiam impertire, sine quo quidquam boni, nec ego, nec quispiam potest scire. Si autem vel modicam scintillam scientiae vestrum mihi conferret documentum, vestroque labore et merito Deus mihi praebere: incrementum, [Col. 0058A] ut verum fatear, pro posse meo vestro beneficio responderem, etsi par pari referre non praevalens, saltem gratias humiliter exhiberem. Neque enim refert, ut extimo, a quo quis accipiat et percipiat utilem veritatem, cum illa recte intelligenti suam per se commendet puritatem, nec tam propter doctorem veritas teneatur, quam propter veritatem doctor commendabilis habeatur. Itaque tam libenter a vobis perciperem doctrinam veritatis, ac si mihi loqueretur majoris quispiam dignitatis, quia nec cathedra sublimior doctrinam reddit commendabilem quae mentitur, nec inferior eam contemptibilem quae verax et utilis invenitur.

[Col. 0057C] Yet because I know that I am not fit to make books, and have neither leisure nor skill available for it, I shall attempt to answer not everything that you say against me, but some things; I shall either refute them or at least make some defence of myself. Since I see that I am gravely accused by you, it is necessary that the accused person make at least a small defence, not in order thereby to acquire a greater merit of holiness, but lest, on my account, you incur a rash judgment. “He who judges his brother,” he says, “judges the law” (James 4). You accuse my smallness of pride and folly, though you do not sufficiently discern the hidden truth of my heart. And you know that what can be bent by the strap of judgment, either for better or for worse, is useful and holy especially when it is bent back toward the better. I said in my letter [Col. 0057D] (Letter V): “If, by God’s revelation, I discover that your opinion is in every respect truer, I shall rejoice to have attained fuller knowledge; and I shall render no slight thanks to your discernment, through which I shall obtain such a benefit.” Your gloss placed over this sentence objects: “Proud humility,” etc. I tell you: there is not in me such pride that I should refuse either to hear from you what is right, or humbly to agree with what I have heard—provided that God deign to grant me the grace of understanding, without whom neither I nor anyone else can know anything good. But if your instruction imparted to me even a small spark of knowledge, and God, through your labour and merit, granted me increase, then [Col. 0058A], to speak the truth, I should respond to your kindness according to my ability; although unable to return like for like, I should at least humbly give thanks. For, in my judgment, it makes no difference from whom one receives and learns useful truth, since truth itself commends its purity to one who understands rightly; truth is not to be held because of the teacher so much as the teacher is to be deemed commendable because of the truth. Accordingly, I would receive instruction in truth from you as willingly as if some person of greater rank were speaking to me; for neither does a loftier chair make commendable teaching that lies, nor does an inferior one make contemptible teaching found truthful and useful.

Quantum recolo, cum scholas junior discendi gratia frequentarem, et vel conferri vel praeferri [Col. 0058B] quibusque melioribus praesumptivo more scholarium praeoptarem, ab his tamen, qui vel aetate vel gradu quolibet inferiores se credebant, non contempsi et audire et discere quae sciebant, nec adeo tumui superbia, ut attenderem quis cui loqueretur, dum tantum quod audirem commendabile videretur. Quanto magis nunc, cum religionis habitum gerens jam vel tenuiter incanesco. contra vestram reverentiam non procaciter intumesco, quam aetate, scientia, sanctitate et scio et fateor praeeminere, longe infra cujus pedes his tribus gradibus video me jacere. Quod ergo vobis respondeo, scitote non fieri superbia, et studio contendendi, sed sciendi amore et gratia colloquendi, ut cum, ejus quem diligo [Col. 0058C] non fruar vel auditu vel visu corporali, eum saltem et audiam et audito respondeam internuntio litterali. Paulo infra in eadem epistola mea: «Cum attendo, inquam, quia in claustro sacras litteras ab infantia didicistis, et in eadem scientia non mediocriter profecistis, approbandum in eis extimo quod probatis, et suspectum habeo quod econtrario reprobatis.» Super hunc versiculum vestra glossa: «In claustro, inquit, et alibi, in scholis scilicet, didici; nec juxta quorumdam praesumptionem ipse me docui, sed a magistro Ansello didici, quod non dico ut me commendem, sed ut vos tangam.» Pro hoc dicto, ut extimo, displicere vobis non debui, pro hoc tangi moleste non merui, cum per hoc vestrae scientiae nil dedecoris inferatur, sed commendationis [Col. 0058D] plurimum conferatur.

As far as I recall, when as a younger man I attended schools for the sake of learning, and in the presumptuous manner of schoolboys wished to be compared with or preferred to [Col. 0058B] any who were better, nevertheless I did not disdain either to hear or to learn what was known by those whom I considered beneath me in age or in any rank. Nor was I so swollen with pride as to consider who was speaking to whom, provided only that what I heard seemed commendable. How much more now, when I wear the religious habit and am already becoming, if only slightly, grey-haired, do I not insolently swell up against your reverence. I know and acknowledge that you excel me in age, learning, and holiness; in these three degrees I see myself lying far beneath your feet. Therefore know that what I answer you is not done from pride or love of contention, but from love of knowledge and for the grace of converse: so that, since I cannot enjoy the bodily hearing or sight of him whom I love [Col. 0058C], I may at least hear him through the messenger of a letter and answer what I have heard.

A little further on in that same letter of mine: “When I consider that from childhood you have learned the sacred writings in the cloister, and have made no slight progress in that same knowledge, I judge what you approve in them to be approved, and I hold suspect what you conversely reject.” Over this sentence your gloss says: “I learned in the cloister, and elsewhere—that is, in the schools; nor, in accordance with the presumption of certain persons, did I teach myself, but I learned from Master Anselm. I say this not to commend myself, but to touch you.” On account of this statement, I think, I ought not to have displeased you, nor deserved to be hurt by your being offended; since by it no dishonour is brought upon your learning, but very great [Col. 0058D] commendation is bestowed upon it.

In claustro enim ubi locus non facile conceditur vanitati, sed praecipue datur opera sanctitati, ubi die et nocte justus divinae subditus jussioni, vacat hymnis, precibus, silentio, fletibus, lectioni; ibi, inquam, defaecata vitae sinceritas permundat intellectum, quo mundato, scientia facilins et efficacius adducitur ad perfectum. Vobis autem scientia commendabilis non videtur, nisi scholarum saecularium tumultu fabricetur, tanquam inter eos quos in scholis forensibus, longo tempore certum est erudiri nullus error, nulla possit haeresis inveniri. Vos indignamini, quia dixi vos in claustro sacras litteras didicisse, tanquam per hoc videar vobis contumeliam intulisse: [Col. 0059A] et commendabilius extimatis quod Laudunum discendi gratia requisistis, et in magistri Anselli celebri auditorio resedistis. Sed beatus homo, non qui magistrum Ansellum audivit, non qui Laudunum vel Parisius requisivit, sed «Beatus, inquit, homo quem tu erudieris, Domine, et de lege tua docueris eum (Psal. XCIII).» Et: «Audiam, ait, quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus (Psal. LXXXIV).»

For in the cloister, where room is not readily granted to vanity but attention is given chiefly to holiness; where the righteous person, subject day and night to the divine command, devotes himself to hymns, prayers, silence, tears, and reading—there, I say, the clarified sincerity of life thoroughly cleanses the understanding; and once it has been cleansed, knowledge is brought more easily and effectively to perfection. But knowledge does not seem commendable to you unless it is fashioned amid the tumult of secular schools, as though no error or heresy could be found among those known to be trained for a long time in the public schools. You are indignant because I said that you learned the sacred writings in a cloister, as though I had thereby offered you an insult; [Col. 0059A] and you consider it more commendable that you went to Laon for the sake of learning and sat in the celebrated lecture-room of Master Anselm. Yet blessed is not the person who heard Master Anselm, nor the one who went to Laon or Paris, but: “Blessed,” he says, “is the man whom thou instructest, O Lord, and teachest him out of thy law” (Psalm 93). And: “I will hear,” he says, “what the Lord God will speak in me” (Psalm 84).

Utinam in claustro sacras ab infantia litteras doctus essem, ut toto tempore vitae meae sacris studiis interessem, in domo Dei nutritus a puero ad similitudinem Samuelis, 33 sciendi aestuans desiderio ad similitudinem Danielis. Quod quia mihi commendabile videbatur, ut scilicet in schola religionis quis a puero nutriatur, ideo non putavi aliquam [Col. 0059B] a vobis mereri laesionem, cum vestram commendans scientiam, claustri potius quam scholarum feci forensium mentionem.

Would that I had been taught sacred letters in a cloister from childhood, so that throughout my life I might have devoted myself to sacred studies—nurtured from boyhood in the house of God in imitation of Samuel, 33 burning with desire for knowledge in imitation of Daniel. Since it seemed commendable to me that someone should be nurtured from childhood in the school of religion, I did not think that I deserved any injury [Col. 0059B] from you when, in praising your learning, I made mention of the cloister rather than of the public schools.

In eadem epistola mea: «Vestram, inquam, aestimabam divinis in Scripturis scientiam tam prudentem, et prudentiam tam scientem, ut sicut in eis nil praeter veritatis regulam sentiretis, ita et ipsius veritatis occulta intellectu lynceo videretis.» Ad hoc glossa vestra respondens: «Stulta, inquit, aestimatio de aliquo hujus temporis homine, nedum de me, qui multa adhuc habemus a Deo audire, quae non possumus portare modo.» Non aestimavi quod omnia nota vobis vel cuipiam praesentium habeantur, quaecunque in Scripturis sub tegumento litterae multipliciter [Col. 0059C] occultantur, sciens quia multa multi adhuc habent audire, quae nondum in praesenti conceditur eis scire. Non hoc, inquam aestimavi, neque hoc me aestimasse uspiam affirmavi, neque hoc me affirmasse quispiam poterit veraciter affirmare, si verba mea velit attentius retractare. Non enim dixi quod omnis veritatis occulta, vel omnia veritatis occulta, videretis, sed ipsius, inquam, veritatis occulta videretis. Ipsius inquam, non totius, neque omnia occulta, sed occulta. Quod si alicujus vel aliqua videtis veritatis occulta, profecto constat quia videtis occulta; et cum videatis veritatis occulta, non solum alicujus vel aliqua, sed ut plus dicam, multae vel multa, dici non debuit aestimatio mea stulta. Hoc enim pie de vobis debuit aestimari, quod videtur rei veritas demonstrare. [Col. 0059D] Si autem paulo amplius de vobis aestimavi quam rei veritas habeatur, indignum est ut propter hoc, aestimatio mea tam graviter arguatur; nec stulta, sed forte ignara debuit appellari, quae, quod satis non noverat, pie voluit arbitrari. Sicut enim de quolibet malum incognitum affirmare est praeceps temeritas, sic de justo quidquam perfectius aestimare, pia credulitas: quae, quem veraciter novit vel justum vel doctum, extollit amplius et honorat, non more invidentium, detractionis caligine decolorat.

In that same letter of mine: “I regarded your knowledge of the divine Scriptures as so discerning, and your discernment as so knowing, that, just as you perceived in them nothing beyond the rule of truth, so you saw, with lynx-like understanding, the hidden things of truth itself.” To this your gloss replies: “A foolish estimate of any man of this age, much less of me, since we still have many things to hear from God which we cannot bear now.” I did not suppose that all things whatsoever hidden in the Scriptures under the covering of the letter in many ways [Col. 0059C] were known to you or to any present person, knowing that many people still have much to hear which they are not yet granted to know in this present life. This, I say, I did not suppose; nowhere did I affirm that I supposed it; and no one can truthfully affirm that I did so, if he is willing to reconsider my words more carefully. For I did not say that you saw “the hidden things of all truth” or “all the hidden things of truth,” but that you saw “the hidden things of truth itself.” Of truth itself, I say—not of all truth; nor all hidden things, but hidden things. If you see the hidden things of some truth, or some hidden things of truth, it plainly follows that you see hidden things; and since you see hidden things of truth—not merely of one truth or a few things, but, to say more, of many truths or many things—my estimation ought not to have been called foolish. For this ought piously to have been thought of you, as the truth of the matter appears to show. [Col. 0059D] But if I thought somewhat more highly of you than the truth of the matter warrants, it is unworthy that my opinion should for that reason be so severely censured. It should not be called foolish, but perhaps uninformed, because it piously wished to suppose what it did not sufficiently know. For just as it is rash recklessness to assert an unknown evil concerning anyone, so it is pious belief to think something more perfect of a righteous person; such belief raises and honours more highly one whom it truly knows to be righteous or learned, rather than, in the manner of the envious, disfiguring him with the darkness of detraction.

Sciebam quidem in Scripturarum scientia plurimum vos valere, et hujus, de qua nobis sermo est, [Col. 0060A] aestimavi notitiam vos habere, et ab aestimando, nec volui nec debui sententiam removere, donec audirem vestram mihi prudentiam respondere. «Lex nostra, inquit Nicodemus, non judicat quemquam: nisi prius audierit ab ipso, et cognoverit quid faciat (Joan. VII). Audito igitur quid de hujus Scripturae involucro sentiatis, cognovi, ut arbitror, non hanc esse regulam veritatis, ad quod tamen confirmandum tam glossas, quam epistolas fabricatis, et odorem semel imbibitum, ut testa lutea, diutius reservatis. Quibus glossis vel epistolis et respondi, et adhuc forte plurima responderem, nisi vestram quam diligo reverentiam pertimerem: quae, quia me intelligit sententiae suae nullatenus assertorem, verborum suorum me clamitat venatorem. Cum enim de regula [Col. 0060B] fidei disputatio inter nos habeatur, et ad reprehendendum verba vestra, mea ut dicitis, locutio deflectatur, non videtur vobis haec mea deflexio proposito convenire, et ideo non parcitis, objecto illo poetae versiculo [Note: [Col. 0059D] Horatii Flacci *Ars poet.*, vv. 21–22.], me ferire:

> Amphora coepit  
> Institui; currente rota cur urceus exit?

I knew indeed that you possessed great strength in knowledge of the Scriptures, and I supposed that you had knowledge of the matter of which we are speaking [Col. 0060A]. Nor did I wish, or ought, to remove my judgment from that supposition until I heard your discernment answer me. “Our law,” says Nicodemus, “does not judge anyone unless it first hears from him and knows what he does” (John 7). Having therefore heard what you think about the obscurity of this Scripture, I learned, as I judge, that this is not the rule of truth; yet in order to establish it, you compose both glosses and letters, and retain for a long time, like an earthen vessel, an odour once absorbed. To these glosses or letters I have answered, and perhaps would still answer many more things, unless I greatly feared your reverence, which I love. Because it sees that I am in no way an advocate of its opinion, it cries out that I am a hunter of its words. Since our dispute concerns the rule of faith [Col. 0060B], and my speech, as you say, strays aside in order to reprove your words, this digression of mine does not seem to you to fit the purpose. Therefore you do not spare to strike me by throwing at me that verse of the poet:

> “A jar began  
> To be fashioned; why, as the wheel turns, does a pitcher emerge?”

[Note: [Col. 0059D] Horace, *Ars Poetica*, verses 21–22.]

Sed quoniam verbis meis, et vos dignamini respondere, ostendendo quae quantum veritatis amatoribus debeant displicere, non debetis, si et ego vestris respondeo, succensere, nec mihi venatoris vel figuli vitium intorquere, ne hoc ipsum in vos videamini retorquere. «Beatus, ait, qui non judicat semetipsum in eo quod probat (Rom. XIV).» Verumtamen [Col. 0060C] apud me non amphora, sed urceus institui coepit, et urceus exit, quia non alta sapiens, sed humilibus consentiens, beatum Hilarium non desisto honore debito venerari, cujus doctrinam audio a sanctis doctoribus commendari. Vestra vero amphora, tantae confidentiae, tantae est granditatis, ut eumdem Hilarium arguere non timeat haereticae pravitatis, et quia me super hoc suum non invenit assensorem, ejusdem erroris arguit defensorem. Mihi quippe frequenter objicitis, quia haereticum facit, non errare, sed errorem defendere, ut scilicet non perseverem diutius Hilarium excusare, sed vobiscum sentiens, doctrinam ejus accelerem accusare.

But since you deign to answer my words too, showing how greatly they ought to displease lovers of truth, you ought not to be angry if I also answer yours, nor charge me with the fault of a hunter or a potter, lest you seem to turn this very charge back upon yourselves. “Blessed,” he says, “is he who does not judge himself in what he approves” (Romans 14). Nevertheless, [Col. 0060C] in my case it was not a jar but a pitcher that began to be made, and a pitcher comes out; for, not aspiring to lofty things but agreeing with the humble, I do not cease to venerate blessed Hilary with due honour, whose teaching I hear commended by holy doctors. Your jar, however, is of such confidence and such magnitude that it does not fear to accuse that same Hilary of heretical perversity; and because it does not find me agreeing with it in this, it accuses me of defending the same error. For you frequently object to me that what makes a person a heretic is not error, but defence of error; your purpose being that I should no longer persist in excusing Hilary, but, thinking with you, hasten to accuse his teaching.

Sed si erroris defensio facit haereticum, quae rogo est haeresis damnare Catholicum? «Disperdat, inquit, [Col. 0060D] Dominus linguam magniloquam (Psal. XI)» et apud Zachariam invenitur super amphoram impietas residere, quae magna falso loquentibus dicitur praesidere, et in medio amphorae paulo post eadem impietas est projecta, et ori amphorae massa plumbi protinus est injecta (Zach. V). Et recte, ne libera diutius feratur impietas, in amphorae profunda projicitur, unde ne possit egredi, os amphorae massa plumbi obstruitur, quia sic intra magniloquos plerumque sensus erroneus debacchatur, ut os iniqua loquentium obstruatur. Eadem vero amphora sublata de medio recte confitentium Judaeorum, defertur in terram Sennaar inter medium Chaldaeorum, quia [Col. 0061A] cum fides mundaverit fines ecclesiasticae regionis, lingua magniloqua gratanter requiescit in errore confusae Babylonis. Vellem ergo ut vestra anphora in urceum verteretur, vestrum grande principium fine humili 34 clauderetur, ne tanta granditas quae damnare Hilarium non veretur, submota a Catholicis, deputari cum haereticis mereretur.

But if defence of error makes a heretic, what, I ask, is the heresy of condemning a Catholic? “May the Lord destroy,” he says, [Col. 0060D] “the boastful tongue” (Psalm 11). In Zechariah, moreover, impiety is found sitting upon a jar: impiety is said to preside over those who speak great things falsely. Soon afterwards that same impiety is cast into the middle of the jar, and immediately a mass of lead is placed over its mouth (Zechariah 5). And rightly so: lest impiety continue to be borne about freely, it is cast into the depths of the jar; and, lest it be able to come out, the jar’s mouth is sealed with a mass of lead. For thus erroneous opinion commonly rages among boastful people, so that the mouth of those speaking wickedly may be stopped. That same jar, removed from the midst of the Jews who rightly confess, is carried into the land of Shinar, into the midst of the Chaldeans; because [Col. 0061A] when faith has cleansed the borders of the ecclesiastical land, the boastful tongue gladly rests in the error of confused Babylon. I would therefore that your jar were turned into a pitcher, and that your great beginning were 34 concluded with a humble end, lest such greatness, which does not fear to condemn Hilary, be removed from the Catholics and deserve to be counted with the heretics.

Hieronymus, de quo dicitis quia si dignum laude librum Hilarii judicasset, qui laudare nonnullos invenitur, eum procul dubio collaudasset, non solum vestrae sententiae non consentit, sed de Hilario longe aliud praedicat, aliud longe sentit. Scribens enim ad Paulinum (sub finem): «Sanctus, inquit, Hilarius Gallicano cothurno attollitur, et cum Graeciae floribus adornatur, longis interdum periodis involvitur, et a [Col. 0061B] lectione simplicium fratrum procul est.» Cum dicit enim Hieronymus et Graeciae floribus adornari et longis periodis involutum Gallicano cothurno sublimari, manifeste judicat scriptis ejus inesse et verborum floridam venustatem, et dignam reverentia occultorum sensuum gravitatem: propter quam et a lectione simplicium procul eadem dicit esse, non quia tanquam reproba indigna sint legi, sed quia tam difficilia, ut a simplicibus non facile possint intelligi. Neque in hoc arguitur scriptoris celsitudo, si scripta cothurnata simplicium non capit hebetudo, sed potius et profunda illius scientia commendatur, et istorum vel probatur humilitas, vel studium excitatur.

Jerome, of whom you say that, if he had judged Hilary’s book worthy of praise—as he is found to praise certain persons—he would undoubtedly have praised it as well, not only does not agree with your opinion, but proclaims and thinks something very different about Hilary. For in writing to Paulinus, near the end, he says: “Holy Hilary rises in the Gallic buskin; though adorned with the flowers of Greece, he is sometimes involved in long periods, and is remote from the reading of simple brethren.” When Jerome says that Hilary is adorned with the flowers of Greece and, involved in long periods, raised aloft in the Gallic buskin, he plainly judges that his writings contain both the richly flowering beauty of language and the reverence-worthy weight of hidden meanings. On account of this, he says that they are remote from the reading of simple people—not because they are, as blameworthy works, unworthy of reading, but because they are so difficult that they cannot readily be understood by the simple. The writer’s loftiness is not blamed if the dullness of simple people cannot grasp writings in the buskin style; rather, his profound learning is commended, and their humility is either approved or their zeal stimulated.

Idem Hieronymus ad Amandum presbyterum scribens, [Col. 0061C] hujus libri de quo nunc agimus, non solum non probat lectionem, sed etiam illius facit cum veneratione debita mentionem, admirans quiddam a se exponendum inquiri, quod in illo potest expositum inveniri. «Miror, inquit, te hoc a me quaerere voluisse, cum sanctus Hilarius Pictaviensis episcopus undecimum librum contra Arianos in hac quaestione et solutione compleverit.» Inquisitus hujus operis liber undecimus hanc quaestionem, de qua illic agebatur, invenitur diligentius explicare, ad quam iterum explicandum Hieronymus extimat superfluum laborare, ex quo luce clarius innuit, et hoc opus ab Hilario scriptum esse, et idem Hilario dignum laudis meritum non deesse. Meus etiam Augustinus, ne laudes Hilarii tanquam invidus premere sub silentio [Col. 0061D] videatur, in sexto de Trinitate libro (cap. 10), et ipsius Hilarii et hujus operis laudabiliter memoratur. «Quidam, ait, cum vellet brevissime singularum in Trinitate personarum insinuare propria, aeternitas, inquit, in Patre, species in imagine, usus in munere. Et quia non mediocris auctoritatis in tractatione Scripturarum, et assertione fidei vir exstitit; Hilarius enim hoc in libris suis posuit,» et caetera in secundo hujus operis libro haec Hilarius verba ponit, quae satis elegantia satisque difficilia ducens, Augustinus ad medium sic exponit, ut plane pateat ea, et commendatione intelligentium digna esse, et juxta Hieronymum a lectione simplicium procul esse. Haec autem sibi assumens Augustinus ipsum Hilarium [Col. 0062A] non mediocris auctoritatis, et Scripturarum fuisse tractatorem, et fidei asserit assertorem: quod quantum aestimo non fecisset, si hoc opus esse contrarium fidei cognovisset.

Writing to the presbyter Amandus, [Col. 0061C] that same Jerome not only does not disapprove the reading of the book with which we are now concerned, but even mentions it with due veneration, expressing astonishment that he is asked to expound something that can be found expounded in it. “I wonder,” he says, “that you wished to ask this of me, when holy Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, completed the eleventh book against the Arians with this question and its solution.” The eleventh book of this work, when consulted, is found to explain more carefully the question then under discussion; Jerome judges it superfluous to labour to explain it again. From this he indicates more clearly than light both that this work was written by Hilary and that Hilary does not lack merit worthy of praise. My Augustine also, lest he seem enviously to suppress Hilary’s praises in silence, [Col. 0061D] makes commendable mention in the sixth book of *On the Trinity* (chapter 10) both of Hilary himself and of this work. “A certain man,” he says, “when he wished to indicate most briefly what is proper to each person in the Trinity, said: eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift. And because he was a man of no slight authority in the treatment of Scripture and the defence of faith—for Hilary set this down in his books”—and so forth. In the second book of this work Hilary sets down these words, which Augustine, regarding as sufficiently elegant and sufficiently difficult, explains in such a way as to make it wholly clear that they are worthy of the commendation of those who understand them and, in Jerome’s words, remote from the reading of the simple. By adopting these words, Augustine affirms that Hilary himself [Col. 0062A] was a man of no slight authority, an interpreter of the Scriptures, and a defender of the faith. In my judgment, he would not have done this had he known this work to be contrary to the faith.

Sed ad quaestionem de qua nobis sermo est redeamus, et quid inde doctores sancti sentiant, et quomodo eidem Hilario consentiant, videamus. Dicit Hilarius necessitatem in Christo passionibus non fuisse, id est eum non sicut nos necessario doluisse, sed dolores nostros ita, cum voluit, suscepisse, ut posset eas non solum divina, sed etiam humana tam animi quam corporis fortitudine poenaliter non sensisse. Quod contra vos dicitis Christum ejusdem infirmitatis, cujus et nos per omnia excepto peccato naturaliter exstitisse, sed passiones, vel dolores passionum, [Col. 0062B] operante divino miraculo, differre potuisse, cessante autem miraculo post jejunium sicut et nos necessario esurisse, vulneratum necessario doluisse, crucifixum diutius vivere nequivisse. Sicut enim operante divino miraculo quadraginta diebus Moyses jejunavit, operante miraculo super undas Petrus liquidas ambulavit; cessante autem miraculo, nec ille inediam diu ferre, nec iste grave corpus elemento liquido potuit superferre: ita Christus, ut dicitis, passionum molestiis naturali et propria infirmitate credendus est necessario praegravari, cum in eo divinum miraculum destitit operari.

But let us return to the question under discussion, and see what holy doctors think of it and how they agree with this same Hilary. Hilary says that sufferings were not necessary in Christ; that is, he did not necessarily feel pain as we do, but took up our pains, when he willed, in such a way that he could have failed to feel them painfully not only by divine power, but also by the human strength of both soul and body. Against this you say that Christ was naturally, in every respect except sin, subject to the same weakness as we are, but could postpone sufferings, or the pains of suffering, [Col. 0062B] through a divine miracle at work. When the miracle ceased, however, you say that after fasting he necessarily became hungry as we do, that when wounded he necessarily felt pain, and that when crucified he could not remain alive longer. For just as Moses fasted forty days by a divine miracle at work, and Peter walked upon the liquid waves by a miracle at work, but when the miracle ceased the former could not long endure lack of food and the latter could not carry his heavy body upon the liquid element, so Christ, as you say, must be believed necessarily to have been weighed down by the troubles of suffering through a natural and proper weakness when the divine miracle ceased to operate in him.

Ubi non satis diligenter perpenditis, natura humana quem locum in rebus habuisset, si, ut creata [Col. 0062C] fuerat, sine peccati macula permansisset, quomodo humanus animus ad imaginem Dei factus, nec angelis minor vel inferior videretur, sed eo solus Deus major et superior haberetur. Qualem animum suscepit Dei Filius cum voluit humanari, qui animus nullo vitio potuit depravari, propter quem solo Deo minor fuisse praedicatur, propter corpus vero solum paulo minus ab angelis minoratur. Unde Augustinus contra Maximum (lib. III, c. 25): «Natura, inquit, humana, qualem naturam Christus humanae mentis assumpsit, quae nullo peccato potuit depravari, solus Deus major est.» Iste ergo animus, qui nullo potuit vitio depravari, non est credendus humanis affectionibus necessario praegravari; qui, etsi corpus habuit paulo minus ab angelis minoratum, illud tamen nullo [Col. 0062D] etiam fuit vitio depravatum. Et quia corpus quod peccato corrumpitur, non ejus animam aggravavit, sed totum illum hominem spiritalis conceptio levigavit: idem homo nostras ut nos molestias non creditur coactus pertulisse, sed imperio potestatis, et beneficio voluntatis 35 pro nobis misericorditer suscepisse. Quod in quarto decimo *De civitate Dei* invenire potestis evidenter, ubi de quatuor animi affectionibus Augustinus satis disputat diligenter: quas inesse nobis insignis ille poeta Virgilius ostendit [Note: [Col. 0061D] *Aeneid*, book VI, verses 733–734.], brevique eas versiculo comprehendit:

> Hi metuunt, cupiuntque, dolent, gaudentque, neque auras  
> Suspiciunt.

Here you do not consider carefully enough what place human nature would have held among created things had it remained, as it was created [Col. 0062C], without the stain of sin; how the human soul, made in God’s image, would appear neither lesser nor inferior to the angels, but God alone would be held greater and superior to it. Such was the soul assumed by the Son of God when he willed to become human: a soul that could be corrupted by no vice, on whose account he is proclaimed lesser than God alone, whereas on account of the body alone he is made a little lower than the angels. Hence Augustine, *Against Maximus* (book III, chapter 25): “God alone is greater than human nature—the nature of the human mind which Christ assumed, and which could be corrupted by no sin.” Therefore this soul, which could be corrupted by no vice, must not be believed necessarily to have been weighed down by human affections. Although it had a body made a little lower than the angels, that body too was corrupted by no [Col. 0062D] vice. Since the body corrupted by sin did not weigh down his soul, but spiritual conception made that whole man light, the same man is not believed to have endured our troubles under compulsion as we do, but mercifully to have taken them up for us by the command of power and the benefit of will. This you may plainly find in Book XIV of *The City of God*, where Augustine discusses carefully enough the four affections of the soul, which the notable poet Virgil shows to exist in us [Note: [Col. 0061D] *Aeneid*, book VI, verses 733–734.] and sums up in a brief verse:

> “They fear and desire, grieve and rejoice, and do not look up  
> To the air.”

[Col. 0063A] Cum de his Augustinus affectionibus- disputaret, et eas etiam in Christo fuisse patenter affirmaret; quomodo et in nobis sint, et in illo fuerint distincte declaravit, et a sensu clare intuentium dubietatis surculum amputavit. «Verum, inquit (cap. 9), ille hos motus certae dispensationis gratia, ita cum voluit suscepit animo humano, ut, cum voluit, factus est homo.» Et infra: «Habemus, inquit, has affectiones ex humanae conditionis infirmitate: non autem ita Dominus Jesus Christus, cujus infirmitas fuit ex potestate.» Quid evidentius, quid distinctius potest dici? quis contendat huic dicto posse merito contradici?

[Col. 0063A] When Augustine discussed these affections and plainly affirmed that they also existed in Christ, he distinctly explained how they exist in us and how they existed in him, and cut away the shoot of doubt from the minds of clear-sighted observers. “But,” he says (chapter 9), “he took up these movements in his human soul, when he willed, for the sake of a definite dispensation, just as he became man when he willed.” And below: “We have these affections from the weakness of the human condition; but the Lord Jesus Christ did not have them in this way, for his weakness was from power.” What could be said more plainly or more distinctly? Who could maintain that this statement can rightly be contradicted?

Suscepit ille, cum voluit, nostras affectiones certae gratia dispensationis, habemus eas nos ex infirmitate [Col. 0063B] humanae conditionis: habemus, inquam, nos ex ea quae nobis naturaliter ingenita est infirmitate, non autem ita Dominus Jesus Christus cujus infirmitas fuit ex potestate. Habemus itaque nos, habuit et ille, sed aliter nos, aliter ille. Habemus nos, quia sic geniti non possumus non habere; habuit ille, quia sic genitus, cum voluit, se habentem potuit exhibere. Nec solum has animi affectiones, sed etiam corporis passiones non ex humanae sicut nos conditionis infirmitate, sed ex misericordiae pertulit voluntate; sicut idem Augustinus in quarto *De Trinitate* (cap. 2) insinuat dicens: «Mors peccatoris veniens ex damnationis necessitate, soluta est per mortem justi venientem ex misericordiae voluntate.» Et infra in eodem (cap. 13): «Qui posset, inquit, [Col. 0063C] non mori si nollet, procul dubio quia voluit mortuus est.» Mortuus est, inquit, non quia cessante miraculo, sicut dicitis, vivere non potuit, sed quia mori voluit: voluit, inquam, non solum Deus ut moreretur homo, sed etiam mori voluit ipse homo: Ut facerem inquiens, voluntatem tuam, Deus meus, volui (Psal. XXXIX);» et: «Voluntarie sacrificabo tibi (Psal. L);» et: «Qui dilexit me, tradidit semetipsum pro me (Galat. II).» Tunc autem ex humanae conditionis infirmitate, mors ejus sicut nostra rectissime venire diceretur, si cessante miraculo lege nostra omnium mori necessario cogeretur; si genitus ingenitum hoc haberet, ut morti resistere non valeret.

He took up our affections, when he willed, for the sake of a definite dispensation; we have them from the weakness of [Col. 0063B] the human condition.
