We have them, I say, from the weakness naturally inborn in us, but the Lord Jesus Christ did not have them in that manner, since his weakness was from power. Thus we have them, and he also had them, but we in one way and he in another. We have them because, being born as we are, we cannot fail to have them; he had them because, being born as he was, he could, when he willed, show himself as possessing them. Nor did he endure merely these affections of the soul but also bodily sufferings, not from the weakness of the human condition as we do, but from a will of mercy. So the same Augustine indicates in Book IV of *On the Trinity* (chapter 2): “The death of the sinner, arising from the necessity of condemnation, was undone by the death of the righteous one, arising from the will of mercy.” And later in the same work (chapter 13): “He who could [Col. 0063C] fail to die if he did not will to die, undoubtedly died because he willed.” He died, he says, not because, once the miracle had ceased, he could not live, as you say, but because he willed to die. God willed, I say, not only that the man should die, but that man himself willed to die: “To do thy will, O my God, I have willed” (Psalm 39); “I will sacrifice to thee willingly” (Psalm 50); and “He who loved me gave himself for me” (Galatians 2). His death could rightly be said to come, like ours, from the weakness of the human condition only if, when the miracle had ceased, he were necessarily compelled to die under the law common to all of us; only if, having been born, he possessed this as an inborn property, that he could not resist death.

Quia vero ex hoc quod homo factus est, habuit ut [Col. 0063D] posset mori, ex eo autem quod sine peccato factus est, habuit ut posset et non mori, recte dicit Augustinus, quia ejus infirmitas fuit ex potestate, et mors ejus venit ex misericordiae voluntate. Ejus quippe infirmitas, non moriendi necessitas, sed moriendi fuit possibilitas; qui cum posset, quia homo erat, mori, quia homo sine peccato erat, nihilominus et non mori; eligit ut pro nostra omnium salute moreretur, non ex necessitate sua, utpote qui nullo vitio teneretur. Quod etiam in vicesimo quarto *Moralium* ostendit (cap. 1) papa Gregorius, dicens: «Ille autem quia nulli admistus est culpae, nulli ex necesitate succubuit poenae.» Videtis necessitatem ab omni poena ejus penitus removeri, et remotionis causam pariter admoveri: «Nulli, ait, ex necessitate succubuit [Col. 0064A] poenae, et hoc, quia nulli admistus est culpae.»

But because by becoming man he had the capacity [Col. 0063D] to die, while by being made without sin he had the capacity also not to die, Augustine rightly says that his weakness was from power and his death came from a will of mercy. His weakness, indeed, was not a necessity of dying but a possibility of dying. Although, because he was man, he could die, yet because he was man without sin, he could also not die; he chose to die for the salvation of us all, not from any necessity of his own, since he was held by no vice. Pope Gregory also shows this in Book XXIV of the *Moralia* (chapter 1), saying: “But because he was mingled with no fault, he succumbed to no punishment from necessity.” You see necessity wholly removed from every punishment of his, and at the same time the reason for that removal given: “He succumbed to no [Col. 0064A] punishment from necessity, because he was mingled with no fault.”

Non ergo, sicut dicitis, ideo tantum potuit non mori, si mori non vellet, quia Deus qui in illo erat, poterat quidquid vellet. Cum autem sicut in Moyse et Petro cessaret in illo divinum miraculum operari, cogeretur ipse homo morte necessario praegravari sed ideo ex necessitate nulli poenae succubuit, quia nulli culpae admistus fuit, quamvis hoc ipsum quod sine culpa ille homo creatur, non hominis, sed Dei esse beneficium non negatur. Sicut enim quod ambulare fortiter; quod currere possum velociter, rectissime attribuitur corporis sanitati, corporis agilitati, et tamen hoc totum est veraciter Dei donum, a quo est omne bonum, ita Christus quod nulli ex necessitate succubuit poenae, ex eo fuit, [Col. 0064B] quod nulli admistus est culpae, quamvis illa munditia negetur opus esse gratiae creatricis, et eidem homini tam inseparabiliter assistricis, ut sicut potuit non pati cum nondum pateretur, sic posset et non mori cum non moreretur, si vellet non solum divinitas quae in illo suaviter omnia disponebat, sed etiam ipse homo qui disponenti personaliter cohaerebat.

Therefore, contrary to what you say, he was able not to die if he did not will to die not merely because the God who was in him could do whatever he willed—while, if the divine miracle had ceased operating in him as it did in Moses and Peter, the man himself would necessarily have been weighed down by death—but because he was mingled with no fault and therefore succumbed to no punishment from necessity—although it is not denied that the very fact that that man was created without fault was a benefit not of man but of God. Just as my ability to walk vigorously and run swiftly is rightly attributed to bodily health and agility, yet all this is truly God’s gift, from whom comes every good, so Christ’s not succumbing to any punishment from necessity arose from [Col. 0064B] his being mingled with no fault—although that purity is not denied to be the work of creative grace, which so inseparably attended that same man that, as he could avoid suffering when he was not yet suffering, so he could avoid dying when he was not dying, if not only the divinity that gently ordered all things in him but also the man himself, personally united to the one ordering them, so willed.

Quod ergo mihi objicitis illud de Evangelio: «Non sicut ego volo, sed sicut tu (Matth. XXVI),» vox est membrorum, vel capitis in persona membrorum, quibus proprie dicitur: «Alius te cinget et ducet quo tu non vis (Joan. XXI).» Quod autem objicitis illud de propheta: «Praevaluerunt insidiantes mihi (Job XXX):» insidiantes visi sunt praevalere, [Col. 0064C] cum suam ad effectum malitiam perduxere, cum juxta quod optaverant, Christum occidere potuerunt, et tamen potentiores eo quem occiderant non fuerunt. Non legistis Jacob ad angelum invalere, et abire volentem tanquam invitum aliquandiu retinere? (Gen. XXXII.) Et tamen quis nesciat eidem Jacob angelum praeeminere, et imbecilli fortiorem affectu spontaneo subjacere? Ita Christus, infirmus quidem voluntaria potestate et affectus potenti voluntate, passioni succubuit non naturaliter, id est non infirmitate coactus naturali, quia non conceptus lege nostra omnium generali. Quod etiam cujusdam nostri temporis, 36 et vidit et scripto commendatur prudens subtilitas; si tamen vestrae prudentiae [Col. 0064D] cujusquam modernorum placet auctoritas, qui cum de Christo homine loqueretur, ex quo ait conceptus et animatus exstitit, per unitionem deitatis ab omni peccato et poena peccati naturaliter mundus fuit, quamvis quasdam peccati poenas habuerit sua voluntate. Videtis illum hominem non solum ab omni peccato, sed etiam a poena peccati mundum naturaliter exstitisse: quem tamen sua voluntate quasdam poenas peccati certum est habuisse. Unde infra subjungit: «Postquam in utero conceptus est, ita divinitas eum omni parte confirmavit, ut omne peccatum et poenam peccati ab eo naturaliter removerit.» Ecce ab illo homine, et peccatum et poena peccati naturaliter sunt remota; cui tamen non peccatum, sed poena peccati, cum [Col. 0065A] voluit, est admota, quia conceptus sine culpa unito sibi Deo ita est confirmatus ut non nisi voluntate, non nisi potestate fuerit infirmatus.

What you object to me from the Gospel—“Not as I will, but as thou wilt” (Matthew 26)—is the voice of the members, or of the head in the person of the members, to whom the words properly apply: “Another shall gird thee and lead thee where thou dost not will” (John 21). What you object from the prophet—“Those lying in wait for me prevailed” (Job 30)—means that those lying in wait seemed to prevail [Col. 0064C] when they brought their malice to effect, when they were able to kill Christ as they desired; yet they were not more powerful than the one whom they killed. Have you not read that Jacob prevailed over the angel and held him for some time, as though unwilling, when he wished to depart? (Genesis 32.) Yet who does not know that the angel was superior to Jacob, and that the stronger submitted voluntarily to the weaker? So Christ, weak indeed by voluntary power and submitting by a powerful will, yielded to suffering not naturally—that is, not compelled by natural weakness—because he was not conceived under the general law common to us all. The prudent subtlety of a certain man of our own time also perceived this and commended it in writing, 36 if the authority of any modern writer is acceptable to your discernment. Speaking of Christ as man, he says that from the time when he was conceived and ensouled, through the union of divinity he was naturally clean from every sin and punishment of sin, although by his own will he had certain punishments of sin. You see that this man was naturally clean not only from every sin but also from the punishment of sin; yet it is certain that by his own will he bore certain punishments of sin. Hence he adds below: “After he was conceived in the womb, divinity so strengthened him in every respect that it naturally removed from him every sin and punishment of sin.” Behold: from that man both sin and the punishment of sin were naturally removed; yet not sin, but the punishment of sin, was added to him when [Col. 0065A] he willed, because, conceived without fault, he was so strengthened by the God united to him that he was weakened only by will, only by power.

His et horum similibus acquiescat vestra prudentia documentis, non contendat grossis et inefficacibus argumentis, quia veritas ad hoc plerumque latet sub cujusdam nebulae tegumentis, ut eam non capiat intellectus grossior imprudentis. Quod propter nonnulli «semper discentes, et nunquam ad scientiam veritatis pervenientes (II Tim. III),» nihil in Scripturis aestimant contineri, nisi quod vident passim ab omnibus obtineri; et quae latentia vel volunt vel nequeunt intueri, digna putant a fide recte scientium removeri. Vident quidem Adam factum fuisse mortalem, alioquin nequaquam moreretur, [Col. 0065B] et hoc facile potest sciri quod tanta experientia retinetur; sed non vident eumdem factum et immortalem, cum immortalis non mori praedicetur, et mortalem immortalemque simul esse consentaneum non videtur. Sed utrumque simul erat, non necessitas, sed potestatis, non quod ille ad istud sive illud necessario cogeretur, sed quod ejus optioni neutrum negaretur. Qui quoniam per peccatum ad mortalitatem electione libera declinavit, tanta necessitate per peccatum genitos omnes posteros obligavit, ut praesentis vitae molestiis quae primo illius meritis irrogantur, isti tam justi quam injusti necessario patiantur. Ideo Propheta, imo omnis justus: «De necessitatibus meis, inquit, erue me (Psal. XXIV)» id est non solum a peccato, sed etiam [Col. 0065C] a poena pro peccato, quam incurri, non sicut Adam electione libera, sed necessitate misera.

Let your discernment rest upon these and similar proofs, and not contend with coarse and ineffectual arguments. For truth often lies hidden beneath the coverings of a kind of mist, so that the coarser understanding of the undiscerning cannot grasp it. For this reason some, “ever learning and never attaining to the knowledge of truth” (2 Timothy 3), judge that the Scriptures contain nothing except what they see commonly attained by everyone; and whatever hidden things they either will not or cannot perceive, they think should be removed from the faith of those who rightly understand. They do see that Adam was made mortal, otherwise he could not have died [Col. 0065B]; and this may easily be known because so great an experience preserves it. But they do not see that he was also made immortal, since an immortal being is said not to die, and it does not seem consistent for one to be mortal and immortal at once. Yet he was both at once—not by necessity, but by power: not because he was necessarily compelled toward the one condition or the other, but because neither was denied to his choice. Since through sin he freely turned toward mortality, he bound all descendants begotten through sin under such necessity that both righteous and unrighteous must necessarily suffer the troubles of this present life, which were first inflicted upon him as his due. Therefore the Prophet—or rather, every righteous person—says: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Psalm 24), that is, not only from sin but also [Col. 0065C] from the punishment for sin, which I incurred not, as Adam did, by free choice, but by miserable necessity.

Quam precem miserator et misericors Dominus a tempore Abel primi justorum audiens, et fine saeculorum efficacius tandem exaudiens, filium suum voluit incarnari, incarnatum cum hominibus conversari, ita tamen ut sine culpa, sancti Spiritus opere gigneretur, et ideo nullius necessitatis vinculo stringeretur. Peccato enim necessitas debebatur; ipse autem nullo debito tenebatur. Liber autem a debito, id est tam poena quam peccato, cum posset non mori, non solum si Deo, sed etiam si ipsi homini complaceret, eligit tamen mori, ut aeternae nostrae mortis debitum aboleret. Reddens quippe [Col. 0065D] quod non debuerat, solvens quod non rapuerat, quia elegerat Adam mori, elegit etiam ipse mori, ut par pari referret, sed causa utilitasque differret, dum ille a vita per inobedientiam declinavit, iste se ad mortem per inobedientiam inclinavit; ille moriens aeternae mortis caligine nos involvit, iste moriens ab eodem debito nos absolvit.

The compassionate and merciful Lord, hearing this prayer from the time of Abel, the first of the righteous, and finally answering it more effectually at the end of the ages, willed that his Son should be incarnate and, having been incarnate, live among human beings. Yet he willed him to be begotten without fault by the operation of the Holy Spirit and therefore bound by no chain of necessity. Necessity was owed to sin; but he was held by no debt. Free from debt—that is, from both punishment and sin—although he could have avoided death, not only if it pleased God but also if it pleased the man himself, he nevertheless chose to die, in order to abolish the debt of our eternal death. For, rendering [Col. 0065D] what he did not owe and paying what he had not taken, because Adam had chosen to die, he too chose to die, so that he might return like for like; but the cause and benefit differed. The former turned away from life through disobedience; the latter inclined himself toward death through obedience. The former, by dying, wrapped us in the darkness of eternal death; the latter, by dying, released us from that same debt.

Unde grates non modicae, non solum Deo qui unitus est homini sed etiam ipsi referendae sunt homini, qui, ex quo Deo personaliter est unitus, ita eidem est voluntate per omnia counitus, ut sicut eum hominem pro nobis voluit Deus pati, ita idem ipse homo pro nobis voluit pati: et assumptus assumenti nec ad modicum obmutiret, sed disponenti suaviter ipse assensu spontaneo fortiter obediret. [Col. 0066A] Etsi enim sicut duas naturas, divinam scilicet et humanam, ita duas, ut dicitis, voluntates asseritur habuisse, non tamen Deo quidquam contrarium ille homo credendus est voluisse, sed sicut in unitatem personae conjuncta est humanitas deitati, ita hujus illius unita per omnia voluntas voluntati, et assumens assumpto in assumendo contulit tale munus, ut cum eo sicut persona, ita et voluntate maneat semper unus. Si vero aut illa caro spiritui suo, aut ille spiritus Deo suo, vel ad modicum obviavit, quid nisi a rectitudine aliquantulum deviavit, et ita fatebimur Christum fuisse divisum, quem teneri vult Apostolus indivisum? (I Cor. I.) Quam divisionem etsi omnis per peccatum genitus in se cogitur experiri, non tamen putet eam posse etiam in Christo [Col. 0066B] inveniri: ne naturam illius secundum nostram nimis carnaliter metiatur, et eum infirmari naturaliter et necessario mentiatur. Quem si infirmatum, passum, mortuum confitetur, (quod quidem non solum nullus fidelium, sed nec infidelis quilibet diffitetur) non est satis si etiam non attendat illum esse conceptum opere spiritali, et ideo naturae suae fretum privilegio speciali, ut necessario non gravetur conditionis nostrae privilegio generali. In quo et illius charitas amplior comprobatur, et nostra credulitas amplius commendatur, dum ille cognoscitur et suae merito puritatis non pati potuisse, et affectu charitatis pro nobis aegrotantibus voluisse. Quod quidem et videre et tenere non mediocris est profectus, si tamen dignum fide perfectorum 37 indicatur [Col. 0066C] intellectus: et ideo tam mihi quam vobis id desidero plenius revelari, ut fidei praesentis merito mereamur Deum revelata facie contemplari. Volo autem ut meo huic desiderio dignemini subvenire; et vos vestro Philippo, quod Paulus suis Philippensibus impertire: «Deus, inquit, meus repleat omne desiderium vestrum, secundum divitias suas in gloria, in Chisto Jesu (Philipp. IV).» Vale.

Therefore no slight thanks are due not only to the God united to the man, but also to the man himself. From the time he was personally united to God, he was in every respect so united to him in will that, just as God willed that this man should suffer for us, so that same man willed to suffer for us. The assumed one did not become silent even briefly before the one assuming him, but himself strongly obeyed, with spontaneous assent, the one who gently ordered all things. [Col. 0066A] For although, just as he is said to have had two natures, divine and human, so too, as you say, two wills, that man must not be believed to have willed anything contrary to God. Rather, as humanity is joined to divinity in unity of person, so the will of the one is wholly united to the will of the other; and in assuming him, the one who assumed conferred such a gift on the one assumed that he remains forever one with him in will as in person. But if either that flesh opposed its spirit, or that spirit its God, even to a small degree, what else would this mean but that it had departed somewhat from rectitude? Then we shall confess Christ divided, whom the Apostle wills to be held undivided (1 Corinthians 1). Although everyone begotten through sin is compelled to experience this division in himself, no one should suppose that it can be found also in Christ [Col. 0066B], lest he measure Christ’s nature too carnally by ours and falsely say that he was weakened naturally and necessarily. If he confesses Christ to have been weakened, to have suffered, and to have died—which indeed no believer, nor any unbeliever whatever, denies—it is not enough unless he also attends to the fact that Christ was conceived by a spiritual operation and therefore enjoyed a special privilege of his nature, so as not necessarily to be weighed down by the general condition of our nature. In this both his love is shown to be greater and our faith is more highly commended: he is known to have been unable to suffer by reason of his purity and yet to have willed, through love, to suffer for us who are sick. To see and maintain this is no small progress, provided it is judged an understanding worthy of the faith of the perfect. 37 [Col. 0066C] Therefore I desire that it be more fully revealed both to me and to you, so that through the merit of present faith we may deserve to contemplate God with unveiled face. I wish you to deign to assist this desire of mine, and to grant your Philip what Paul granted to his Philippians: “May my God fill every desire of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4). Farewell.

## LETTER VIII. FROM PHILIP TO GREGORY. A religious person ought not to disparage other religious orders.

Si quia, unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma, omnium fidelium jure esset cor unum et anima [Col. 0066D] una, quanto magis eorum qui concessam vivendi latitudinem arctiori proposito supergressi, religionem, vel clericalem, vel monachicam voce et habitu sunt professi? Eos quippe etsi ab invicem locorum secernit longinquitas, sive reddit foris dissimiles habitus vel professionis diversitas: debet tamen unus eos spiritus, una dilectio sic ignire, ut inveniatur spiritalis conflatio diversorum animos counire. Talis illa legitur Ecclesia fuisse primitiva, quae accipere meruit tanta vehementis spiritus incentiva: ut ab ea procul fieret livor et contentio praesumptiva, et in unum eam manipulum devinciret dilectio collectiva. Felices qui illis in diebus converti meruerunt, imo qui sic et conflari et conflatione mirifica uniri studuerunt, qui abjecta multiplicitate [Col. 0067A] pristinae mansionis, erant, sicut scriptum est: «Omnes unanimiter in porticu Salomonis (Act. V).» Processu vero temporis cum ad fidem convolant nonnulli salvandorum numerum supergressi, rite piscatorium Ananias et Saphira sunt ingressi (ibid.), ipsamque religionem, voce magis quam opere multi Simones sunt professi (Act. VIII), quorum illi non parum sibi retinent de pannosa pristinae consuetudinis facultate, isti vero appetunt gloriari de optata exteriorum munerum sanctitate. Utrique arguendi, utrique falce judiciaria feriendi: nisi forte divina visitante gratia resipiscant, ut juxta Jeremiam (cap. XVII) non diem hominis concupiscant. Cum enim sermo evangelicus perfectionis intuitu venundari et dari praecipiat omnia quae habentur, [Col. 0067B] satis est incongruum si fraudulenter eadem retinentur, si, qui perfectionem vultu et habitu profitentur, eamdem retento, non tam nummorum quam morum sacculo diffitentur. Nec sufficit cuiquam perfectionis gratia pecuniarum contemnere facultatem, si non etiam relinquat morum pelliceam pravitatem, si non, juxta Apostolum, sic se terreni hominis exuat vetustatem ut, deponens mendacium, loquatur veritatem (Ephes. IV). Mendacium deponit et veritatem loquitur, qui assumptam professionem probabili conversione morum exsequitur, qui sic, juxta promissum, studet mandatis perfectioribus inhaerere, ut non sicut Ananias et Saphira quidquam sibi velit proprium retinere.

If, because there is one Lord, one faith, and one baptism, it would rightly be the case that all the faithful had one heart and one soul [Col. 0066D], how much more should this be so for those who, having surpassed the latitude permitted in ordinary life by a stricter purpose, have professed the religious life—clerical or monastic—in word and habit? Although distance of place separates them from one another, and diversity of habit or profession makes them outwardly dissimilar, yet one Spirit and one love ought so to kindle them that a spiritual fusion may be found to unite the souls of diverse persons. Such is the primitive Church which we read of: it deserved to receive such promptings of the mighty Spirit that envy and presumptuous contention were far removed from it, while gathering love bound it into one sheaf. Happy are those who deserved to be converted in those days—indeed, those who endeavoured thus to be fused together and united in a wondrous fusion. Casting aside the multiplicity of their former habitation, [Col. 0067A] they were, as it is written, “all of one accord in Solomon’s porch” (Acts 5).

But in the course of time, when certain people flocked to the faith in excess of the number of those to be saved, Ananias and Sapphira properly entered the fishing-net (ibid.), and many Simons professed religion more in speech than in deed (Acts 8). The former retain for themselves no small portion of the ragged wealth of their former manner of life; the latter desire to glory in a hoped-for holiness of outward gifts. Both are to be rebuked, both struck with the judicial sickle—unless perhaps, visited by divine grace, they repent, so that, according to Jeremiah (chapter 17), they do not desire the day of man. For when the Gospel word commands, with a view to perfection, that all one possesses be sold and given away, [Col. 0067B] it is quite incongruous if those same things are fraudulently retained; if people who profess perfection in face and habit deny it by retaining a purse not so much of money as of corrupt morals. Nor is it sufficient for anyone, for the sake of perfection, to despise the possession of money unless he also leaves behind the skin-clad perversity of his conduct; unless, according to the Apostle, he so strips off the oldness of the earthly man that, putting away falsehood, he speaks truth (Ephesians 4). He puts away falsehood and speaks truth who fulfils the profession he has undertaken by an approved conversion of morals, who thus strives, according to his promise, to adhere to the more perfect commandments, so as not, like Ananias and Sapphira, to wish to retain anything as his own.

Ille etiam promeretur non mediocriter reprehensibilis [Col. 0067C] judicari, qui assumpto humilitatis habitu praesumit inaniter gloriari: qui dona spiritualia, vel quae optat, vel forte jam meruit obtinere, ad privatae laudis aucupium tanquam Simon Magus satagit retorquere. Plerique enim cum religionis ingressi fuerint officinam, ut in ea regularem vivendi fabricent disciplinam, proponitur quidem eis velut matoria malleus et incudo, et a quolibet doctiore describitur exsequendi operis pulchritudo, sed vel pressi ignavia, strenuitate debita non laborant, vel hebetes nihil aut parum opus propositum meliorant. Vidisti plerosque et insignitos exterius titulo militari, et animo tamen degeneres nunquam graviter praeliari, et innumerabiles clericos in scholarum [Col. 0067D] gymnasio convenire, et eorum tamen raros ad perfectum scientiae pervenire. De qualibus Paulus: «Semper, inquit, discentes, nunquam ad scientiam veritatis pervenientes (II Tim. III).» Ita et hoc tempore perplures quasi mandatis evangelicis obedimus, dum relinquentes saeculum, claustrale conflatorium introimus; sed quia illic corda nostra non satis digno charitatis incendio counimus, nimirum, opus assumptum ad unguem nullatenus expolimus. Hinc accidit, ut arbitror, quod ii qui in diversis vel Ecclesiis vel ordinibus conversantur, rupto pacis internae vinculo, sibi invicem adversantur, et cum deberent in osculo sancto, amplexu mutuo, confoveri, mordentes et consumentes invicem, vix possint ab invicem sustineri.

He too deserves to be judged not slightly blameworthy [Col. 0067C] who, having taken up the habit of humility, presumptuously glories in vain; who strives, like Simon Magus, to turn spiritual gifts—whether those which he desires or perhaps has already deserved to obtain—to the pursuit of private praise. For when many enter the workshop of religion in order to fashion there a regular discipline of life, a hammer and an anvil are certainly set before them as tools, and the beauty of the work to be performed is described by anyone more learned. Yet either, crushed by sloth, they do not labour with due vigour, or, being dull, they improve the proposed work little or not at all. You have seen many people outwardly distinguished by the title of soldier and yet so degenerate in spirit that they never fight seriously; and countless clerics gather in the training-ground of schools [Col. 0067D], yet few of them attain perfection in learning. Of such people Paul says: “Ever learning, and never attaining to the knowledge of truth” (2 Timothy 3). So too, in this age, very many of us appear to obey the Gospel commandments when, leaving the world, we enter the cloister’s furnace of fusion. But because there we do not sufficiently unite our hearts in the worthy fire of love, we certainly do not polish the work undertaken to the nail. Hence, I think, it comes about that those living in different churches or orders, having broken the bond of inward peace, oppose one another; and though they ought to cherish one another with a holy kiss and mutual embrace, they bite and consume one another and can scarcely endure one another.

[Col. 0068A] Those who are thought to embrace a milder rule do not fear to disparage the holier, and bitterly mock their strict observances as superfluous inventions. But those who seem to themselves to practise something more mature and stricter are not ashamed to boast of it, both among themselves and before others, and to judge those who act differently as of lesser merit. I have wished to mention this so that you may not be led by the multitude of such persons, nor, under their guidance, be drawn away from the path of truth and, once led astray, be brought into error and ruin; from which, with your heart blinded—or perhaps hardened—you may afterwards not easily be brought out.

For I want you to be distinguished not so much outwardly by a religious countenance and habit as to be found adorned with religious conduct: fervent in spirit, flourishing in dove-like simplicity, and no less skilful in serpent-like prudence. For neither is one religious who does not burn with the spirit; nor is fervour perfectly commended if it is not softened by lovable simplicity; nor is simplicity freed from the snares of opponents unless it is fortified by shrewd prudence—simplicity which is “like a deceived dove, without understanding” (Hos. 7). Therefore do not suppose it enough that you have transferred yourself to the fellowship of the righteous or, for religion’s sake, have taken on their appearance and habit; for it profits little or nothing to associate with righteous people unless one diligently strives also to imitate their righteousness. Thus Lot, though a citizen of Sodom, earned the title of praise; and Judas Iscariot is not held excusable, since the perversity of his fellow-citizens did not bend the former, while the holiness of the latter’s fellow apostles did not advance him to a like manner of life.

[Col. 0068C] Therefore have the likeness of the dove: disparage no one, bite no one, be found harmful to no one; but, with an enlarged heart, embrace all in benevolent affection—not only those in whose flock or order you are included by your own choice, but all whom you see either to be religious or to bear the title of religion. For just as one who holds the more honourable rank in the Church is often of lower merit, so one lower in rank sometimes has a life superior in merits; and I do not think that the merit of inward holiness should be measured by the degree of one’s order or by any outward dignity.

Accordingly, lest dove-like simplicity lapse into foolishness and, deceived and without understanding, be wrapped in the darkness of ignorance, have also the prudence of the serpent, which discerns, which with keen understanding both chooses what is beneficial and rejects everything harmful. If you possess this, then, while reverencing all religious persons with the fitting service of humility, you will not nevertheless be induced through misplaced credulity to admire, in foolish simplicity, whatever all of them do, and through erroneous admiration to think it ought to be imitated as though it were just. “There is no man,” says Solomon, “who does not sin” (3 Kings 8). And James says: “In many things we all offend” (Jas. 3). For just as something worthy of praise is often found in any unjust person, so a righteous person sometimes does what cannot accord with his merit; and as benevolent simplicity does not pervert that good because of the person, so discerning prudence does not turn that evil into good by foolish commendation.

[Col. 0069A] It belongs to an undiscerning person both to condemn whatever he sees in an irreligious person and to commend whatever a religious person does. For Simon Magus believed what Philip, his preacher, asserted ought to be done (Acts 8); and Simon Peter dissembled in a matter for which Paul, his fellow apostle, reproved him when he understood it (Gal. 2). “Woe to those,” says Isaiah, “who call good evil and evil good, who make sweet bitter and bitter sweet” (Isa. 5). Therefore, if virtue, wherever it may be found, ought to be approved, and vice rejected by discerning judgment, reverence all religious persons, of whatever order they may be, and embrace in benevolent affection the virtues of them all.

If among them you perhaps detect, with lynx-like discernment, something imperfect; if you reprove someone’s fault with a judgment not so biting as truthful—nevertheless, do not let that person’s religion become worthless in your eyes as though it were nothing, nor let your spirit swell against him as though you were more religious. Although you neither can nor ought to imitate him in that wherein he is imperfect or perhaps blameworthy, you ought nonetheless humbly to reverence his other good qualities, whether open or hidden; to value him more highly, reckon yourself inferior in merits, judge yourself unworthy, and think better of the other. Thus the religious man whom the householder wished to invite to his wedding is found occupying the lowest place at the banquet (Luke 14), and is honourably raised from the footstool to the chair—not by his own advancement, but by that of the householder. But the one who had chosen a high place in a presumptuous spirit is degraded.

[Col. 0069C] Finally, “man does not know,” as it is written, “whether he is worthy of hatred or love” (Eccl. 9); and therefore no one ought to presume upon his own merit or rank, nor ought anyone to disparage another person or order. For as, of two grinding at the mill amid the tumult of the populace, and of two in the field amid pastoral labour, so also of two in bed amid monastic repose, one will be taken and one left (Luke 17). He will be taken who, in his place and order, has chosen the better things, forgetting what lies behind and earnestly stretching himself toward what lies before; who, according to the prophet, “will not contend nor cry out” (Isa. 42), yet according to the Gospel will call himself an unprofitable servant (Luke 17). But he will be left who, glorying in an outward habit, claims religion for himself more by words than by conduct; who, falsely flattering himself, disparages others; who, avoiding labour, reclines in soft ease; who bends his malevolent heart to excuse himself and accuse his neighbour.

But to desist completely from these things and apply oneself more fully to those; to draw the mind away from vices and shape virtues into a settled disposition—this is not within the power of all who are like us; indeed, it is no small difficulty even for any who are more perfect. Yet no labour seems difficult to one who desires, if the desired reward is set before the labourer; for, while what is loved is believed delightful, the weight of present heaviness is lightened by love for the sweetness hoped for.

[Col. 0070A] That the labourer in the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is followed by a most sweet fruit, if he vigorously and earnestly carries through the task he has undertaken, that mighty Samson declares in an elegant riddle—a riddle to be spiritually solved not by the Philistines but by you and those like you: “Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness” (Judg. 14).

For the converted sinner eats ashes as bread, is fed with the bread of tears, and eats the bread of sorrow when he humbly laments his past transgressions and strives to blot them out with a flood of tears. Yet food proceeds from this eater, because he who eats the bread of humble sinners merits to be refreshed with the bread of the exalted angels: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77). And: “I am the living bread; if anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever” (John 6). Since the sorrowful eating of the sinner is grievous and laborious, while the refreshment of the Creator is sweet and joyful, when Samson had said, “Out of the eater came forth food,” he added, “And out of the strong, sweetness”: namely, because he who bravely eats the bread of mourning in the present life will receive in the life to come the sweet fruits of angelic bread.

[Col. 0070B] Nor do I say this so that you may be taught by me as though you were ignorant, you who are better and more perfectly instructed by those far better than I; you who have at hand living books, not written over in perishable ink, but inscribed and furnished with the more splendid teaching of the Holy Spirit. You observe their conduct more diligently than a prudent reader observes constant reading, and by their example you are fully taught likewise to live [the printed *ad uniendum* is probably corrupt]. Therefore I do not teach you, but remind one already taught that you should carefully recall what you have done, what you began, and why you began it when you assumed the religious habit. Know that if you labour to persevere—or rather, if while labouring you persevere in what you have begun—he who willed to establish labour as a command will refresh you in your labour.

Know that I rejoice in your present and future good not a little; that I smile upon your laborious grief in hope of future sweetness; and that, although the Apostle Paul admonishes us to weep with those who weep (Rom. 12), I was more constrained to lament you when you were laughing. Yet I want you not to consider it burdensome to repay me in some small measure, and, solicitous for me, to beseech God also with concern: that, mercifully forgetting my sins, he may deign to receive me into the number of the elect. Farewell.

## LETTER IX. PHILIP TO BARTHOLOMEW. On the unjust persecution inflicted upon him.

[Col. 0070D] When the vast expanse of the sky is darkened by the deep horror of night, if suddenly a ray of the appearing morning star shines forth, the mind of one who sees it is greatly cheered, even though day has not yet come in its full office. For the sun alone, when present, can drive away all the darkness of night; alone restore sorrowful minds to their former state. Yet, though delaying its own coming, it does not fail to comfort those sitting in darkness when it sends the light-bearer before it.

Your consolation, therefore, seems to me to fulfil the office of that morning star. Although it cannot remove all that is dark within me, it nevertheless instils in me a most welcome hope of full light—a hope which, through the benefit of your charity, does not put me to shame. But when the sun’s radiance shall graciously pour itself in full measure upon the horn of the earth, when Christ present shall pour upon me the fullness of his light, then my adversary will no longer cast over me the dark shadows of grievous wrongs, nor, through prevailing malice, blunt my endurance.

[Col. 0071A] Since my lowliness lies far from that fullness because of my merits, your visitation meanwhile is very pleasing to me: it both refreshes me with a good and consoling word and advances me, by a mystical gift, to whatever small measure of strength I possess. For you did not think it sufficient merely to write to me, a little one, unless with more abundant grace you also sent a mystical gift, by which I am much more subtly and frequently urged, amid whatever troubles I endure patiently, to strive not to be moved from patience.

For one oppressed by a superior height requires a remarkable strength of patience; though that height may exert little effort to press down, the lower person is nevertheless intolerably burdened. Thus a certain woman, when she cast a fragment of millstone from the summit of a tower, killed King Abimelech as he fought below (Judg. 9); and what she above could cast down with easy effort, he below could not endure with the constancy of life. If, however, the woman had encountered the king on horseback while he was fighting, she would perhaps have harmed him little or not at all, because an equal would easily have resisted an equal with equal strength; indeed, the man would have scorned the woman with royal disdain.

[Col. 0071B] But if that same king sat in the lofty stronghold of a tower, how many little women placed below, I ask, could he alone crush? Or rather, if he gathered many kings and princes there with him, how, with their help, would he overwhelm a single man with the weakness of a woman? If, sparing stones, they wished merely to smear him with spittle, many strong persons of female sex could overwhelm one man, nor could the poor man resist such showers of spittle unless God’s mighty hand graciously hastened to assist him.

It is therefore no wonder that the martyr Stephen died when the heavy multitude of his own people pressed upon him. For when it stoned him, though innocent, with one unanimous spirit, Saul at least—though not himself stoning—kept the garments of those who stoned him (Acts 7). When that same Saul afterwards became Paul, he stirred up even his own people against himself and became an enemy by speaking the truth. As he was about to go up to Jerusalem to visit his brethren, he heard that there he would suffer many grave things. For the prophet Agabus took Paul’s belt and, binding his own hands and feet with it, said: “The Jews in Jerusalem will bind in this manner the man whose belt this is” (Acts 21).

[Col. 0071D] And he, girding his loins with strength and hearing the saying addressed to Job, “Gird up your loins like a man” (Job 38), said: “I am prepared not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem” (Acts 21). Blessed Paul, whom such courage girded that the hostile multitude of the Jews did not terrify him, who was ready bravely to suffer all the things which he knew beforehand would threaten him from men of his own nation.

You have urged me, similarly afflicted and already suffering many things less than justly at the hands of the rulers of the people, to possess the same courage as Paul; and, lest a letter should not suffice, you offered a reminding gift. Even if this contained no value or mystery in itself, it would still please me because of the sender’s goodwill; for when the author is held in gracious esteem, the gifts he makes are consequently precious. But now both the lofty authority of the giver and the moral usefulness of the offered gift have, by God’s ordering wisdom, come together and reached me at a fitting time of tribulation to console me.

[Col. 0072A] For the belt which your dignity has chosen to send me to be girded with suits me and admonishes me to endure all things bravely, so that, with the folds of my garment drawn tight, I may be rendered manfully ready; when those folds are left loose, everyone is found hindered in running the course of strength. Thus, “The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself” (Ps. 92). And: “Gird yourself upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. 44), so that, when he has been strikingly marked by a powerful girding, all may know how greatly he is fortified with strength.

Yet he whose strength has no comparison, whose willing is power, and whose patience is not confined by our straits, declares that he endures much more grievously from those whose goodwill he ought to have received—ought, I say, both because he himself is God and that people was his people, or at least because he was a man and born from their people. “I have laboured in enduring,” he says (Isa. 1). And: “If my enemy had cursed me, I would have endured it, and perhaps hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my familiar friend” (Ps. 54). And elsewhere: “The man of my peace, in whom I hoped, has magnified his heel against me” (Ps. 40).

[Col. 0072C] Therefore, when men of my own nation, men of my peace, in whom I hoped, likewise magnify their heel against me, perversely inflicting injury in return for favour and repaying undeserved evil for good—whether because they have not fully known the truth of the matter or perhaps because they have not loved it sufficiently even when known—what wonder if my lowliness is stunned by so grave an offence and, unequal in strength to so great a burden, languishes? “For the strength of stones is not my strength, nor is my flesh bronze” (Job 6).

Paul commands that fathers should not provoke their children to anger, but should show them beforehand the path of life in God’s patience and teaching (Col. 3). Yet they themselves—if it is lawful to say so—have transgressed the apostolic command and with a united spirit have undertaken to provoke me, a little one. And although the Law says through Moses, “You shall not respect the person of a man in judgment” (Deut. 16): you shall hear the great and the small alike, wishing them to have neither one weight nor another but to render the same judgment to the greater as to the lesser—these men have rejected, in my case or on my behalf, the written rule of justice and, showing partiality, have refused to hear me, a little one.

[Col. 0073A] “Our law,” Nicodemus says, “does not judge anyone unless it first hears him and knows what he does” (John 6). But when the assembled leaders judged me unheard and, by the authority of their power, pronounced sentence against me, I wonder that no Gamaliel was found to utter a word, to give sound counsel to those in error with freedom of spirit—advising them, namely, to leave alone the man whom they were disgracefully accusing of no crime, whom they were bringing forth, after the manner of Susanna, to the shame of grievous infamy (Dan. 13).

Even if perhaps there was someone to whom the outcome of this affair was displeasing because he had hitherto known nothing similar about it, as in the case of Susanna, still there was no one to refute whatever those accusing judges asserted in their testimony—judges whom not truth but received authority caused to be heard. Yet because God knew Susanna to be of far greater merit than I, he was moved by mercy and was immediately found not wanting to her: he sent Daniel, who convicted the dishonest witnesses of falsehood and brought the error of the others back to the path of truth.

[Col. 0073B] But I, like Joseph, have been left in disgrace; like one guilty of adultery, I have been consigned to prison (Gen. 39). I was compelled to endure dishonour not by decree of law but rather by the king’s anger—dishonour which the equity of judgment might more truly have turned against another. But the queen, unwilling to be held guilty by human judgment or to have a punishment fully deserved turned upon herself, craftily hastened to break out first in a cry and, retaining the man’s cloak, summoned her servant-witnesses. The king, then, judging from evidence not so much true as plausible and from these testimonies unfairly favouring the queen, thought falsehood to be truth; and he consigned the man to penal disgrace not so much justly as by sheer power. Thus through the craft of the accuser and the ignorance of the judge, Joseph, though innocent, paid the penalty.

And she who deserved it was not swept up in the immediate ruin, by that judgment which none of us fully knows, since God has not yet advanced us to knowledge of his secrets.

[Col. 0073C] But I do not wonder that an unbelieving king or an Egyptian woman acted thus: neither served divine religion or justice; the dark land and race of Egypt held them, and the welfare of an Israelite man concerned them little or not at all. For it is written: “The Egyptians hated the children of Israel” (Exod. 1).

But if children of Israel delighted in oppressing one another, if the elder patriarchs disparaged Joseph their younger brother (Gen. 37), the prophet Amos—or rather the Holy Spirit speaking through him—plainly shows why such things are inflicted on such persons: “Woe,” he says, “to you who are wealthy in Zion, the chief men, heads of the people; who are set apart for the evil day and draw near to the seat of iniquity; who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd; who sing to the sound of the psaltery like David; who think they possess instruments of song; who drink wine in bowls and suffer nothing over the affliction of Joseph” (Amos 6).

[Col. 0074A] When this prophet had enumerated several things by which the rulers of the people are darkened and for which they deserved, by just judgment, the “Woe” he pronounces, he added at the end: “and they suffered nothing over the affliction of Joseph” (ibid.), plainly showing that the summit of all wickedness is completed in this: that the younger brother is crushed by the power of the elder; that, while the former suffers, the latter is stirred by no mercy; that, while the former wastes away, the latter seems cheerful.

Thus, when the elder patriarchs suffered grievous hardships in Egypt; when they were said to have come to spy out the weaker parts of the land; when, having been brought from prison, they were nevertheless compelled to leave one behind in chains (Gen. 42): they considered no cause more responsible for their deserving these misfortunes than that they had formerly refused mercy to their youngest brother. “We suffer these things deservedly,” they say, “because we sinned against our brother, seeing the distress of his soul when he entreated us, and we did not listen; therefore this tribulation has come upon us” (ibid.).

[Col. 0074B] If a brother is rebuked for crushing his brother (Mal. 2), should not also a city be rebuked for crushing its citizen, when the greater the multitude of wise persons within it, the greater ought to be its rectitude of justice? And if it is not Babylonian city, whose name means confusion, but the city Jerusalem, titled with the name of peace—a city formerly, as it is written, full of judgment (Isa. 1); the holy city; the city chosen by the Lord, that knowledge of his name might be poured into it, that the law might go out from Zion and the word of the Lord spread from Jerusalem (Mic. 4)—if this city, I say, does something indiscreetly rather than wisely, not justly or piously but rather violently by mere power, who would not be amazed, who would not mourn, who could endure it patiently?

“Seeing such a city, Jesus wept over it” (Luke 19). And elsewhere he says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you” (Luke 13). We have indeed been sent to this Jerusalem that we may be saved; that, under its teaching and guidance, we may be freed from Babylon; that, according to the prophet, it may meet everyone who has been led forth with bread, and bring forth the waters of heavenly mysteries for one fleeing in thirst (Isa. 21). But if it offers stones in place of bread and poison in place of health-giving waters, who would not recoil, who would not shrink from such nourishment—or rather, from such intolerable and detestable injury?

[Col. 0074D] Paul, having rightly experienced the confusion of this city, which inflicts anger upon its citizens in place of a spirit of gentleness, preferred to be handed over to the Gentiles rather than sent back again to that confused and detestable city. It was indeed confused when it mercilessly scourged that same Paul after he had been brought out of the Temple (Acts 21), when it insatiably thirsted for his death and would have carried out its intention unless Lysias, the military tribune, had hurried to come and with great force rescued him from the hands of those striking him. “It was reported,” he says, “to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion” (Acts 21).

[Col. 0075A] Two days later, when that same Paul was being held at Caesarea and was speaking in his own defence before the governor Festus while the Jews stood by, showing that he had sinned in nothing against either the Temple or the law of the Jews and that he had unjustly endured their lashes and insults, Festus, wishing to please the Jews who accused him, is recorded to have replied to Paul as he spoke: “Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there to be judged concerning these matters before me?” (Acts 25).

“Do you wish,” he says, “to go to the royal city, that there you may more fully attain what you believe just; where your law is in force; where the rulers of your nation live; who abhor one weight and another; who reject a deceitful balance; where the fountain of mercy and the seat of justice are found; where, according to Moses, the superior and the inferior alike are heard?” But Paul, knowing that no such thing was found in Jerusalem, and that it was held neither by the bond of law joined with mercy nor by the balance of justice, recoiled and refused to be presented for its judgment, wisely choosing rather to be judged among foreigners. “I stand,” he says, “before Caesar’s tribunal; there I ought to be judged. I have done the Jews no wrong; no one can give me over to them. I appeal to Caesar” (ibid.).

[Col. 0075B] Paul does not wish to go up to Jerusalem to be judged there, lest, when he ought to be judged, he should instead be stoned; for the scribes, Pharisees, chief priests, and elders of the people were readier to stone than to judge rightly. That same Paul wished, but was unable, to calm their confusion, restrain the tumult, and dissolve the ruinous combination. He repeatedly gave both them and others an account that he had inflicted no injury upon Temple, Law, or people, and fortified his position with so many and such weighty testimonies that Festus the governor, because of Paul’s great learning and eloquence, said that he was mad: “Paul, you are mad; much learning is turning you to madness” (Acts 26).

But if so great a man did not calm the leaders of his own nation or bring them back by his words, although true, to the line of truth, who am I that I should be able to bring my elders to knowledge of the truth and make them readier to spare me? When or how shall I be able to reach their houses, distant from one another, or find them sitting there, so that I may give each one an account and cause them to think differently, and to repair, with a changed purpose, what they wished to destroy? Or when or how shall I be able to gather them again, or perhaps incline them, once gathered, to hear me, a little one, in whose assembly, as many assert, scarcely anyone is heard unless he is distinguished by an equal or perhaps greater eminence of name?

[Col. 0075D] “For the rich man,” as you have read, “speaks, and all are silent. But the poor man speaks, and they say: Who is this?” (Ecclus. 13). Therefore the wealthy readily joined the speaker who was rich, and by the privilege of their power oppressed the absent poor man. With such eagerness did they carry out what was pleasing in their own eyes, and, persecuting me without the restraint of a defender, that they did not even spare a feast day: “lest perhaps there should be a tumult among the people” (Matt. 26).

For when their feast day was being celebrated and, with the council assembled, deliberation was held concerning me, certain persons not forgetful of their old anger, having gained the desired opportunity, informed against me—though I was hidden and had until then been unknown to many present there—and compelled me to be named before all and displayed, hanging in the sun, as known to everyone, indeed as notorious. A strange thing! My insignificance lies concealed in a corner among them, yet in their council my disgrace becomes known to all. When, the session dissolved, they each went away to their homes, they paid back at great interest, far and wide, what they had received about me.

[Col. 0076A] Thus, as they carried reports and filled everything with malicious rumour, while the sentence pronounced against me was being circulated by them, knowledge of my name was spread everywhere; and what had hitherto been enclosed within narrow boundaries was now disseminated among all peoples, not through a proclamation of holiness but through the contrivance of falsehood. Therefore a great dispute arose in the talk of different persons, who were mutually opposed because of the novelty of this report—or slander: some saying that he is good, others saying, “No, but he deceives the crowds” (John 7).

Some think that this disgrace was justly inflicted on me, supposing true whatever they hear confirmed by such eminent leaders. Others say that an enemy has sown tares upon the wheat (Matt. 13), and that the accuser of the brethren has subjected truth to falsehood. Which of them judges more truly, speaks more justly, and embraces the same justice with more upright zeal—the Judge of all, from whom nothing is hidden, knows; he has not wholly withdrawn the knowledge of sincere truth from everyone. For it has become known to some, and perhaps will yet become known to more; and at some time it will shine more fully upon your prudence: namely, that I am compelled to suffer their anger for the very reason for which I ought to have obtained greater favour.

[Col. 0076C] For if I did not make known Noah’s shameful nakedness, but, after the manner of Shem and Japheth, threw a cloak over him, why, I ask, is the curse of Canaan inflicted on me, when Noah rightly bestows the gifts of blessing upon Shem and Japheth? (Gen. 9). If, while Saul relieved himself, I did not draw the sword upon him but recalled and restrained the soldiers rushing upon him, why does that same Saul oppress and persecute me, a little man, gathering the camps of the strong against a feeble flea? (1 Kings 24).

To confess to you, it is not plainly clear why I have become hateful, unless it is because, to the best of my power, I became useful to those to whom I owed service, according to what—as though recalling it in a dream—a certain pagan says beautifully, introducing a fruit-bearing tree as speaking:

> I have committed no wrong, unless it is called wrongdoing  
> to render each year its fruits to its cultivator.

[Note: [Col. 0075D] Ovid, *Elegy on the Nut-tree*, vv. 5–6.]

[Col. 0076D] Since, therefore, evil is inflicted upon me for good, as I suppose, and since I endure it not without strong patience—and since I have not deserved to be Paul, who is not merely unweakened by any tribulations but even rejoices in them, glorying in hope of reward and crown—I beg your dignity to come mercifully to my aid and support, with the shoulders of your prayers, me labouring beneath this burden, so that, since my littleness is now failing under an unequal weight, it may be strengthened by your merits to endure it.

I beg you to pray to the good Lord for the boy grievously tormented and, by your intercession, in the place of the centurion, restore him to his former health: so that the desired remedy may be bestowed also upon the paralytic and worthy praise rendered to your faith. I beg you to lay the one lying in bed at Jesus’ feet through the tiles, and by welcome importunity bend the delaying physician, so that he whom sickness bends toward death, unable even to support his own body, may be raised by him who is powerful and commanded, once walking, to take up his bed (Matt. 8; Luke 5).

[Col. 0077A] But because, according to a certain pagan, it is sweet to speak to the wretched, I have spoken rather long, and have pursued my misery with words—not sufficient, perhaps, but at least numerous—thinking that some remedy might be afforded me if I should deserve even to be heard by your dignity. But if you will not consider it burdensome to reply to me with a more abundant benefit, a greater and more effective consolation will be given me; for the wound of the mind, made raw by the grievous iron of those who trouble it, is greatly eased by the soothing balm of consoling words.

At the close of this discourse, then, I say that I desire you to fare well, and with you all the others who do not refuse to grieve with me in my tribulations.

## LETTER X. PHILIP TO BERNARD. He complains about a member of Prémontré received by the Cistercians against the will of the Premonstratensians.

[Col. 0077C] I wonder whether your holiness will deign to hear me and, hearing, follow my discourse to its end, and whether you will not rather be indignant that I dare even utter a word and address your reverence—I, a man of no merit. Yet pressing necessity gives me both matter and boldness for speaking, and your humility gives confidence that you will hear; for a righteous man, knowing himself debtor to wise and foolish alike, does not consider it burdensome to make himself a patient hearer of little ones.

When I see what trouble threatens the little Church of which I am a son, and how it removes its peace and quiet far away, I confess that I cannot help grieving; and in this I neither think nor deserve to displease your holiness. For he is sick with a foolish insensibility, or more than ordinarily inhuman through beastly savagery, who, seeing his mother’s inward parts shaken by disturbances, forgets ten months and does not pity her with the compassion due to her.

[Col. 0077D] What the cause of this disturbance is, you do not fail to know; and would that you had known nothing at all of it, for, as I see it, that widow would bear her grief more lightly if your reverence had not inflicted it upon her.

I beg you not to take it ill if I report to you what she complains of within herself—indeed, how grievously she is afflicted in complaining. For although you have already heard from another why she grieves, perhaps you have not yet clearly learned how deeply she grieves. When she considers that it is not an enemy—a man who takes what is ours is indeed an enemy, she says—but [Col. 0078A] a man of such peace, such holiness, such renown, one who seems to strengthen other Churches by word and deed, who nevertheless does not shrink from burdening her intolerably: she is saddened beyond all expression, and wonders beyond comprehension when or where she deserved this from you. For even if by sinning she deserved that the just judgment of the divine will should permit her to be afflicted, she did not deserve at your hands that you should rejoice to be her tormenting threshing-sledge (*tribula*). Rather, she hoped that, if adversity pressing upon her from elsewhere threatened her with any trouble, your holiness, which she loved greatly, would mercifully confront the threat.

She had a little ewe-lamb, which had grown up with her, eating of her bread and drinking from her cup, and was to her as a daughter (2 Kings [Samuel] 12). Leaving its flock and bearing the mark of disobedience, it came [Col. 0078B] to your sheepfolds; there it knocked but did not find an open door, because after it our Church sent its shepherd, and your affection, as was fitting, then sent it back to its own place. But shortly afterward, when the same little ewe was again seized by the disease of wandering fickleness, having once more broken the little cord of obedience, it ran back there also. For an unstable mind does not know how to stand still, and a childish eye delights in gazing after novelties rather than things long known. Yet because a certain newly arrived guest found no small favour with you, you at last received our sheep, our brother, against his own Church, while wishing, as they say, sufficiently to comply with that guest’s will.

From this, reverend Father, our province is scandalized, our [Col. 0078C] Church disturbed; that little flock which Christ himself consoles in the Gospel is inconsolably saddened by this action of yours. It cannot see how it accords either with justice or with charity that your holiness should have been pleased to act thus against it. For it knows that Pope Innocent, of blessed memory, commanded—and committed this same command to a written record—that without permission of our abbot and chapter none of our brethren should depart from us, and that no one should presume to retain a brother who has departed. It knows also that it has been agreed between the abbots of our and your Order, and more carefully forbidden for the preservation of peace, that neither should presume to retain the other’s brother unless he can obtain his own abbot’s permission. There are also some other matters [Col. 0078D] which ought to have been observed between your Church and ours, if your holiness had thought them, as our lowliness does, worthy of observance.

How you answered all these points to our brethren sent to you to reclaim their brother, you wished to make known through those same brethren, both orally and in writing. They said that you grieved over the scandal to our province and Church, yet nevertheless refused to send back our brother in order to quiet that same scandal. You say, as they report, that when you received our brother without the leave of his chapter, you did not know Pope Innocent’s command; but now that you know it, you will receive no one further, lest through disobedience you oppose a command which it is not lawful to oppose.

[Col. 0079A] But if, once the command is known, it is a fault for you to receive any one of ours without the permission of our abbot and chapter, is it not likewise a fault to retain one already received, when the same command prohibits not only receiving but also retaining? For the written text reads thus: “Of your brethren who have promised stability and obedience, no one shall depart without the permission of his own abbot and chapter; and no one shall presume to retain one who departs.” Therefore both the departing brother and the one who retains the departing brother without permission fall under the same sentence. Nor is failing to observe a command already known in receiving a brother a greater fault than retaining him after becoming aware of the command. For what purpose, indeed, shall we say that apostolic writings or privileges have force, except that by their protection each person may lawfully possess in due peace what is his? And if another has perhaps seized these things either by violence or through ignorance, should he not restore them more promptly when he learns of the apostolic writings?

You say that someone came to you and said: “The abbot of Prémontré, and our abbot, and others—I do not know who—have granted permission to the aforesaid brother; and the man whom until then you had refused to receive you then first committed to your probation.” But, as you know, the abbots of Prémontré, Laon, Breine, and Stenveld denied this in your presence by word of mouth, steadfastly asserting both that they had not granted him permission and that they had not sent this man as a messenger to you. Their truth, it seems, ought to have borne sufficient witness, [Col. 0079C] rather than the assertion of someone ignorant—or, not to say, lying.

Finally, when, at the instigation of certain of yours, the lord Apostolic caused our abbot to be summoned into his presence at Paris, and when, after he was presented, he deigned in sufficiently humble words to urge him to give the brother permission, our abbot, as you know, replied that, if this permission were granted by him, no small scandal would be brought upon our province, our Church, and indeed the whole Order. Therefore, under no terms and on no advice would he himself grant this permission, unless perhaps he were compelled by an unavoidable command.

But the lord Pope acted mercifully, lest he should seem to burden either our Church or our Order. Though he urged, he did not command; [Col. 0079D] and though, as an apostle of Christ, he could have imposed a burden, he declined to exercise the power he had received, knowing that he possessed it not for the destruction but for the edification of our Order. God provided well for the Church when he granted her such a pontiff, who became all things to all people in order to gain all. Yet, as you say, he would undoubtedly have commanded had your reverence wished to advise him to do so; and what was not done freely through the disposition of a consenting will would have become, as it were, necessary by the command of authority. I think you declined to advise this because you truly knew that it ought not to be advised, lest you turn against us little ones the greater favour than others which you enjoy with him.

For what difference does it make whether someone seeks to oppress his neighbour by his own power or another’s, so long as that neighbour suffers scandal thereby? Though scandals must indeed arise, nevertheless for one who contrives scandal for even one of these little ones who believe, it is better that a millstone be hung about his neck (Matthew 18; Mark 9). “Do they not oppress you by their power,” says James, “and themselves drag you before the courts?” (James 2). James does not judge that oppressing an undeserving neighbour and dragging him before the tribunal of authority is either justice or charity, since neither the more powerful should oppress the powerless nor the greater molest the innocent.

Believing that you remained committed to this purpose of not molesting one’s neighbour, that little flock humbly sent certain brethren to admonish you [Col. 0080B] to order its brother, who had presumptuously come here against prohibition, to return to his own Church, as seemed just. You answered them, as they say, that it is not your Order’s practice that you should return anyone once received and compel him unwillingly to return to his own Church; rather, they should endeavour to bear this injury with equanimity, and you would endeavour, if life attended you, to compensate them by an equivalent benefit. This seems to our people like the answer which someone gave his brother when the latter diligently demanded back what belonged to him by hereditary right: “I hold it,” he said, “and I shall hold it long.”

Is it not your Order’s practice, then, that you should be willing, to brothers of yours—if indeed you deign to judge those of our Order to be your brothers—to restore in the debt of charity what is theirs? But it is your Order’s practice that, even against their will and protest, you should receive what you then retain in order to increase their scandal. It is not your Order’s practice to preserve mutual peace and not to be a stone of stumbling even to those who in some fashion desire to serve God; but it is your Order’s practice to inflict upon them by power what you do not wish inflicted upon yourselves, wishing them to bear what, if inflicted by another, you would not willingly endure? A strange Order! Some who hear this, they say, wonder who ordained this Order, what prophet or apostle proclaimed it praiseworthy, when fraternal peace and love are so highly commended in Holy Scripture that without them no other virtue is judged sufficient.

What profit is there to you in their blood while they descend into distress, [Col. 0080D] because they think that you count their injury as nothing and seek the prosperity of your Church in such a way that your prosperity impedes their advancement? What profit, I ask, if, when they are intolerably afflicted, they are forced to utter that prophetic imprecation: “Give them, O Lord” (Hosea 9). What will you give them? “Give them a barren womb and dry breasts” (ibid.), because their fruitfulness turns to the ruin of your little ones, and their importunate abundance does not fear to disturb the peace of the weak. And the Apostle, who was accustomed to grieve at others’ disturbances, seems, in compassion with the troubled, to invoke something similar with them: “Would that those who trouble you would cut themselves off!” (Galatians 5).

But if you say that they are unjustly stirred against you, [Col. 0081A] and that what you wished to do ought neither to be nor can be forbidden by them, because in receiving our brother you had the assent of the lord Apostolic, to whom they themselves ought not to have contradicted and whom you ought to have satisfied: they know assuredly, as they say, that the lord Apostolic did not impel you to receive him, nor did he compel them, with that discretion which is his, to give him permission. But because you deserved to find favour with him, he appears to consent to your or your associates’ will, not by commanding but by permitting. For he would not permit this injury to be inflicted upon our people unless, at the urging of yours, he were pressed to allow it; and your people think and maintain that what they were thus able violently to extort is lawful for them. But let it be so. All things are lawful for them—but are all things expedient? (1 Corinthians 10).

“Am I not free,” says the Apostle, “am I not an apostle? Do I not have power to do this and that, as the other apostles do? Yet I have not used this power, lest I scandalize my brother; lest we burden any of you, lest we give any occasion of stumbling” (1 Corinthians 9). The Apostle does not wish to do what he sees that discretionary permission authorizes him to do, because he recognizes that it conflicts with the laws of charity when in doing it another’s benefit is impeded—another to whom, by the right of brotherhood, he ought to prove useful. Finally, he does not wish to give an occasion to those who love occasions for sinning, who draw from the deeds of the greater as though material for taking offence, and who do not fear to trouble their neighbours with the poison of malice, while imitating saints of greater renown only externally by action, not inwardly in intention. “What I do,” he says, “I shall do, that I may cut off the occasion of those who desire an occasion, so that in what they boast they may be found just as we are” (2 Corinthians 11 [printed: II Cor. II]).

What malicious person, hearing that, whether our Church wishes it or not, you receive its fugitive, would not conceive from you—or increase once conceived—a motive for doing the same harm, rejoicing if he can accomplish the malice he has conceived and glorying in this act as though he appeared like you? For there are many who display the habit of religion but devote their zeal not so much to fraternal peace as to disturbance. They rejoice more if they have drawn someone away from another monastery by the seductive flattery of falsehood than if they lead him [Col. 0081D] out of the world by the example of righteousness or the word of truth. They think that they attain the highest honour if someone chooses to transfer to their colony; if, spurning the monastery in which he imbibed the milk-like rudiments of religion, he migrates to them, as though to receive a worthier increase belonging to a greater Order.

Such people should not be granted the opportunity they seek; their presumption should be checked by prudent counsel. A well-disposed person rightly loves to withdraw his hand even from things lawful, lest the malicious person, having received an occasion, presume to occupy by unlawful means what belongs to another. Even those whom it is clear are not elevated by deep knowledge, not understanding what they see their elders doing, suppose themselves invited by a kind of example [Col. 0082A] not to fear doing similar things. When they falsely imagine that what they have conceived is similar, they confidently do unlawful things; and when the knowledge of their elders thus goes before little ones along a dark path, these people’s weak conscience perishes. Thus the Apostle says: “By sinning against the brethren and striking their weak conscience, you sin against Christ” (1 Corinthians 8). But if they judge that what is set before them is not to be imitated at all, they undoubtedly maintain that it ought not even to be set before them by their elders, and immediately judge their liberty without understanding the truth of heart or action. “Why,” says the Apostle, “is my liberty judged by another’s conscience?” (1 Corinthians 10). And again: “Commending ourselves,” he says, “to every conscience of men” (2 Corinthians 4).

The person who chooses to abstain both from things not lawful and from things not expedient will be able to remove inconveniences both for himself and for another: from the former, that he may keep himself undefiled from this world; from the latter, that he may remedy the weaknesses of his neighbours.

Both duties ought to be observed with such care that one without the other should not be judged sufficient, since no one shows himself sufficiently acceptable to God unless, so far as lies in him, he also gives no offence to his neighbour. But he is pleasing to God and approved by men [Col. 0082B] who has embraced not only righteousness but peace also: he strives to serve God through righteousness and to live in harmony with his neighbours through peace. “The kingdom of God,” says the Apostle, “is righteousness and peace” (Romans 14); and, “Pursue peace, without which no one shall see God” (Hebrews 12). Again: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4). And Zechariah: “Love only truth and peace” (Zechariah 8). This peace must be maintained firmly not only in the same house or cloister, but also among those at a distance. It ought to be extended to all who desire to serve God in such a way that neither side causes the other any offence. “Be without offence,” says the Apostle, “to Jews and Greeks and the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 10). And again: “That you may be sincere and without offence” (Philippians 1). And this: “Giving no offence to anyone” (1 Corinthians 6 [printed citation]).

[Col. 0082D] But if no offence at all is to be given to any of the faithful, how much more ought monks to show deference to clerics, so that spiritual love may make one heart and one soul of those whose religious life is, as it were, kindred? Is God the God of monks only? Is he not also the God of clerics? Yes, of clerics also: one God justifies both clerics and monks from faith and through faith, not so that zeal and contention may again destroy those found justified, but so that by mutual affection they may strive continually to polish their progress to the utmost. Yet when such peace, such concord, such love ought to exist among those who, whether clerics or monks, desire to be disciples of one Christ—to whom he says, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14), and, “By this all will know [Col. 0083A] that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13)—it is astonishing, reverend Father, that we see this turned into its opposite and the just bounds of peace so overthrown that many seem to embrace the summit of religion, yet are found to turn aside from peace and concord with their neighbours.

Therefore, when I observe religion advancing, I rejoice; but when I observe love failing, I waste away. Considering both together, I am bewildered, because I cannot at all grasp how these things can be reconciled. I once thought that in modern times would be fulfilled what the Lord promises through Isaiah (chapter 28): “I will set judgment by weight and righteousness by measure”—that is, that among religious persons one would judge another as he would prefer to be judged by another, and would not do to another what he would not wish done to himself. But now many who have entered the gate of religion by a more relaxed way dare to disparage those who have undertaken a stricter purpose; and those who seem to themselves to live a little more religiously are found to despise somewhat men of a less rigorous purpose, not knowing—or rather not holding fast to—that saying of the Apostle: “Considering one another superior to yourselves” (Philippians 2).

This plague, this contagion, spreads widely; it plucks away the pleasing little blossoms of religion in such a way that one scarcely reaches the fruit of the Spirit, in whose catalogue peace and love are named. What Order now lives without complaint? What Order does not complain of another Order, while one does not bear another with tender affection but carries off what belongs to another?
