One strives to seize another’s lands or minds [perhaps *animum*, “soul/mind”], narrowing another’s boundaries in order more greedily to enlarge his own; commending his own institutions, disparaging another’s reputation or name; diminishing what belongs to another and arrogating somewhat more to himself.

You know how greatly the old monks who wear the black habit, who walk the well-trodden path of religion according to the institutions of the earlier Fathers, complain of the austere novelty of the Cistercians. By the growth of the latter, they think, they themselves are diminished both in fame and in number. You know how greatly the Cistercians themselves criticize the softness and gentle luxuries of these monks, and contend that such things do not belong at all to monks [Col. 0083D] who, because they have attained the height of a more sparing diet and clothing, do not sufficiently, as is said, accommodate themselves to others’ weaknesses. From both sides the regular clerics suffer certain injuries, as they say—though they too endeavour in some fashion to serve God. Although they would wish, and ought, to be aided by monks labouring alongside them, they complain greatly that those resisting them burden them.

It is therefore no longer surprising if we see Egyptians clash against Egyptians, as the Lord threatens through Isaiah (chapter 19); or if the wicked devours one more righteous than himself, as the prophet Habakkuk (chapter 1) marvels; or if, among the people of Israel, each devours the flesh of his own arm, according to the prediction of Isaiah (chapter 9): Manasseh Ephraim, Ephraim Manasseh, and together both [Col. 0084A] against Judah. And what else is this than monk against monk, and both together against the cleric? But the Apostle says: “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians 5).

I would that no such biting be found at all in our Order and yours; that, on the path of religion which they have undertaken, neither be hindered by the other, but each be humbly instructed by mutual examples; and that they be united not by habit but by affection, not by place but by spirit. Thus those who seem to devote to religion a somewhat greater care than others would also strive to outdo one another in honour and love. So mutual peace would flourish and love abound; surely the wickedness of many would grow cold. Not only would he who is on the opposing side, having nothing evil to say, fear to speak, but concerning both, thus united, this prophetic saying could rightly be spoken: “He walked with me in peace and equity, and turned many from iniquity” (Malachi 2).

Indeed, it would help many, religious and secular alike, no little if these two Orders walked together in peace and equity; if, when one observed that through zeal for penitence he endured somewhat more than the other, he did not on that account presume to exalt himself over the other. For not a greater bodily suffering but a humble spirit and greater love are held acceptable—provided God graciously turns to accept what we do. “Who knows,” says Jonah (chapter 2 [printed]), “whether he may turn and forgive, and turn back from the fury of his anger, and we shall not perish?” Therefore, if you judge anything lawful for yourselves, take care that this liberty does not become a stumbling-block to the weak—weak persons, I say, both yours [Col. 0084C] and ours. For just as there are many imperfect persons among us, so among you—not all, with your peace, shall I say, are perfect. Indeed, some of them, when they take from you what either is lawful or seems to be lawful, presumptuously add many things of their own.

Those of them whom you have sent and who dwell in our regions boast in the people’s hearing that our brother, once he has become a monk, will be sent back to them; they will gain glory from his presence, and our Church will be put to shame and confusion. This boasting, this provocation, is not taken from the Apostle Paul but presumptuously invented by themselves. The same Apostle warns them not to hunt for popular glory and not to contrive any injury against their neighbours: “Let us not become desirous of vain glory,” he says, “provoking one another, envying one another” (Galatians 5). But when I see or hear these and very many like matters discussed among those who both appear religious and are religious, I am compelled to grieve beyond expression. And since I do not yet see what can console me in this matter, I may fittingly declare that prophetic saying: “Consolation,” he says, “is hidden from my eyes, because he divides among brothers” (Hosea 13).

One cannot sufficiently marvel whence or where this hell proceeds, which divides brothers whom he said were bound together by a bond of friendship—especially since they make no small effort alike to serve God; those serving God are commanded to love one another; and those who love one another ought to give not the bites of bitterness but the kiss of peace. Would that Christ, eager for our salvation, might bite [Col. 0085A] this hell—indeed, would that he might mercifully swallow up this death! It seems to bury in the tombs of dissension those whom life-giving love ought to unite. I would know whence this division among brothers arises, but it is a great labour for me to discover it, because I cannot yet enter into that sanctuary of God whose height seems to conceal such a secret.

Would, then, that I could obtain your favour, so as to deserve to be instructed by your answers! Since you have entered Christ’s wine-cellar, there, I suppose, you have found this knowledge also. Would that you would deign to answer me, a little one, and by this matter instruct not only me but many together with me! Would that you would deign to grant even a short delay to this reply, since it is your office mercifully to teach the ignorant! If I saw that I possessed any merit in your sight, I would certainly press you more urgently to answer, and, an eager claimant, would not keep silence until I had extracted this from your holiness, whether more opportunely or importunately. For, to confess the truth, you would confer no small favour if you said something on this question to me—or rather to us—in our ignorance: namely, how some of us are found to agree in serving God and yet to disagree so greatly with one another.

But if our dryness does not deserve to be watered from the fullness of your knowledge, we both wish and ask to be helped at least by your prayers, that God may grant us both to taste nothing except what we ought, and to taste more fully [Col. 0085C] what we ought. Farewell.

## LETTER XI. PHILIP TO BERNARD

He marvels that, while new religious reforms increase, their mutual love does not increase.

Just as the eminence of their merits makes very many people illustrious when the good reputation of such persons reaches the knowledge of many, so the ugliness of blameworthy renown nevertheless makes known certain people who lack the desirable brightness of virtues. I recall reading something similar in a certain pagan author, who records that different things of this kind befell different young men:

> So evil a fame prevented Thersites from remaining hidden  
> as Nereus’ beauty made him fit to be seen.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, book IV, epistle 13, verses 15–16.]

[Col. 0085D] Now, although Nereus’ blooming beauty does not commend me to you, the hideous ugliness of Thersites does indeed make me known; and though you do not know my bodily face, by the working of sinister whispering you have learned a disgraceful report—or infamy—about me. My lowliness does not greatly rejoice in being known in this way; indeed, to confess to you, it blushes no little. I did not seek to have you know me in order that I might seem vile in your eyes. Nor had I resolved to imitate that shameless man who, insatiably desiring to spread his fame far and wide, and being unable to accomplish anything worthy or outstanding, devised a plan and set fire to the city’s temple. When the citizens asked who had dared to be the author of this fire, and why, he sprang forward into the midst and said, “I am he who wished to be known.”

Since, therefore, I did not at all desire this title of perversity, it was nevertheless imposed upon me against my intention, when a wicked friend—or rather, an enemy—who named me before you while absent and unknown, sowed tares upon the wheat with a hostile hand (Matthew 13). How he did this, what wise person would not, with still greater astonishment, be utterly amazed—if only the truth of the matter becomes plainly known and he considers carefully how true and sincere a love brother ought to show brother, and father son, especially those who profess holiness by speech and habit? Yet often no one is found more grievously poised to harm any wretch than the one who ought to have appeared near at hand to help him—particularly if the person wishing to harm is considered richer or more powerful, so that he believes himself entitled to command popular support.

At this very time—or rather, in this storm—one can find very rarely anyone who, according to Moses’ command, will listen equally to the small and the great, anyone who either chooses, by keeping silence, to abstain from judgment or takes due care in giving it. “You shall hear,” says Moses, “the small as the great, because judgment belongs to the Lord” (Deuteronomy 1). But when, at Clairvaux, one of your brethren told you our truth and a more powerful person, on the other hand, his own will, the outcome of the affair made sufficiently clear to which you inclined the ready ear of your fatherhood. For while he was silent—the one who will in due time “save the children of the poor and humble the slanderer” (Psalm 71)—your reverence likewise did not choose to remain silent, nor did it drive the slanderer from his purpose with a peaceful word. Instead of turning his heard slanders into truth and mercy, you compelled me, by your counsel and judgment, to be pressed down and oppressed.

By your own, I say; for, as you know far better, it is shown to be a human and not the Lord’s judgment when the powerful person’s will is preferred and the poor person’s truth is not heard, whereas that highest Judge accepts no person’s greatness but looks only upon the justice of his countenance. Nor do I doubt that your judgment was produced by a hasty assumption rather than by presumptuous malice, for I ascribe no envy and no malice to your holiness. Your simple assessment, not a prudent obstinacy, harmed my lowliness. Nevertheless, lest that righteous man be considered rash and harmful to someone through an incautious assessment, and be held guilty both of the sentence so pronounced and of his own ignorance: “The cause which I did not know,” he says, “I diligently investigated” (Job 29).

But my misery, my injustice, deserved to endure this. When grace failed, it refused to abstain from forbidden things and could move that highest Judge to such anger that he would not remove from miserable me such grievous troubles. For although I do not recall having done wrong against you or against those who were grievous to me, yet I know that before the sight of the inward Judge I have offended so repeatedly that he justly permitted both my lowliness to be grievously oppressed and your holiness to be deceived to my misery. But just as you were willing to say that I should fall under an oppressing hand, so I wish that, with your purpose changed, you would say: “May God deliver the poor from the powerful”—the poor man, I say, “who has no helper” (Psalm 71)—the poor man whom the multitude of the powerful attacks so fiercely in order to wound him that the exhausted remnant, half-dead, can scarcely breathe or draw breath.

But if you do not wish also to give help to one whom you wished to harm, deign at least, I beg, to instruct his ignorance. For I waste away not only under the burden of wounds inflicted upon me, but I likewise languish grievously from lack of knowledge. Your greatness, unless I am mistaken, can heal this double illness; and your rich fullness can wipe away my parched want. Indeed, it would seem an interest not injurious but fitting for you if, for a single injury, you rendered a double benefit. Yet if both are beyond your ability—or rather, your will—then at least grant me mercifully one of them, as I have said: that, if you do not supply a costly medicine for the wounds inflicted, you turn at least the gentle reed of instruction toward me.

Three years ago I sent you a certain letter, in which, as I recall, I earnestly asked you that your holiness would deign to open what was closed to me; but, as I was afterward told, that letter did not deserve to reach your hands. The depth of that same well still seems so great to me that the dullness of my little drawing-vessel cannot reach it. A wonderful mist of difficulty spreads itself before one wishing to draw, and the secret sought hides itself by a deeper evasion. I do not doubt that you have touched this depth more fully and more clearly, since it has been granted you to enter the wine-cellar and the Lord’s sanctuary; to you the Lion of the tribe of Judah has chosen both to unseal the seven seals and to open the book (Revelation 5), and through your ministry to provide nourishment to the crowds reclining at table.

It moves me that in our times I see religion expanding and fraternal love greatly contracting; that more people glow commendably with zeal for living well [Col. 0087D] and yet grow cold toward loving one another. In no earlier days was religion clothed in so many varieties, distinguished by so many modes of life, by so many, so to speak, Orders. Once the ash has been driven away, that fiery condition kindles the desolate coals more abundantly and the vehement flame more eagerly stretches itself into diverse furnaces. Hence new monasteries of both clerics and monks grow together with fruitful increase, and old ones, recovering their former vigour, blossom again. Though we see them restrained neither by one habit nor by the same rules, it is nevertheless certain that they advance toward the heights of religion.

But although, in the same as well as in different monasteries, they are bound and joined by divine love and strive, despising present things, toward things to come, [Col. 0088A] they nevertheless kick against one another so violently in their conjunction that, while commendably making progress in keeping the command by which they are commanded to love God, they are found blameworthily to forget the second command, which is like it. So great a plague, so great a disturbance, now prevails among them that Order complains no little of Order, and man of man; and since one is considered exceedingly burdensome to another, due love or reverence is seldom given to anyone. Many, moreover, who appear to devote no small labour to holiness defer rather to the will of the great than to the truth of the poor, holding what Antipater is said to have answered Caesar: that he was a friend not of the man but of the Roman name.

By what means cleric is troublesome to monk, monk to cleric, or even cleric to cleric and monk to monk, I recall having discussed more fully in that letter; in the present letter I refrain from recounting it, especially lest I be found to detain your reverence too long with prolix words.

Therefore I beseech you by him who has bestowed upon you his knowledge and his holiness: deign to instruct my lowliness on this matter. How can such great agreement be present among religious persons in their desire for heavenly things, and yet such great disagreement among themselves? How do they hurry so eagerly to hold the summit of religion, and yet turn aside so far from mutual love? How can they walk with straight steps toward divine love and limp so blameworthily in brotherly love? “Would that I were a man without the Spirit and spoke lies instead” (Micah 2). I do not say this to disparage the holiness of the greater, but to disclose my thoughts to your majesty, so that, once known, your knowledge and goodwill may deign to remove them—unless perhaps, because you know that I am foul among the worms of poverty and the dunghill, you disdain to answer one becoming worm-eaten and foul. Farewell.

## LETTER XII. PHILIP TO POPE EUGENIUS III

He asks the pontiff for aid against his persecutors.

If your condescension allowed me to speak with you a little, if your patience deigned to hear me as I speak, I would recount to you the history of my tribulation, that I might gain some consolation either from my narration alone or equally from your reply. For when someone is weighed down by a burden unequal to his strength, he thinks that he bears it more lightly if he speaks—if he tells a willing listener either how great is the weight of the burden threatening him, or how inadequate is the strength of the one burdened. Thus Jeremiah, when he saw the city of Jerusalem given over to destruction and could not bear in patient silence this heavy load, undertook to narrate the miserable course of events in tearful words and to commit the weeping narrative to enduring writing. Unable either to help the city which he loved dearly or not to feel the most grievous pain at its destruction, he broke silence and turned to lamentation, finding no remedy more fitting for his sorrow.

Indeed, a wound which becomes more dangerously inflamed while it is kept closed sometimes beneficially subsides when uncovered; for, just as an architect does not repair a ruin he has not known, so a physician does not know how to apply medicine to a covered wound. Therefore every sick person, as I observe, bears silence with difficulty, but seeks some remedy by speaking; and if perhaps he does not deserve another listener, he nevertheless often offers himself both as narrator and listener to himself alone. But if he happens to find a benevolent listener who both wishes and knows how to impart consolation to the sorrowful, he is refreshed by the medicine of that listener’s words, so sweet and so well prepared, that he is no longer aggravated even by the slight pain of the wound inflicted.

Therefore Holy Scripture says: “If you see a man of understanding, rise early to him, and let your foot wear away the threshold of his door” (Ecclus. 6). And below: “Grace will be found in the words of a man of understanding” (Ecclus. 21). Since, therefore, I read that the words of the wise are not found without grace, and hear that the person to whom I speak is proclaimed wise, my foot desires and strives to approach and enter his threshold, and by frequent coming to wear it away—unless, God forbid, it suffers repulse. But I hope that the good Spirit of God will both pour truth into my mouth and spread charity in your heart, so that I may set forth without fear of falsehood the things known to me concerning myself, and that you may gladly hear the true things I shall say.

Having assumed in the cloister the countenance and habit of a religious rule, warned by the divine Spirit, I chose to live there, so that, putting aside the tumult of the world and the pompous pride or exaltation of secular life, wholesome quiet and lowliness might contain and cherish me. I had lived in this purpose for several years, holding no pre-eminent office of authority in the Church, except that, called by the election of those whom I had resolved to obey, I had remained for almost nineteen years in the office called the priorate. Now although, as prior, I had not attained a sufficiently fitting pinnacle of holiness, nor extended my reputation far and wide by the merits of virtues, nevertheless I strove so to live among my brethren that, to the best of my ability, I might avoid giving them an example or occasion of sinning. For I wished so to please God, to whom I had offered myself, that I would not displease the people among whom I had placed myself; I wished so to direct my life before God that I would not have my reputation stained among men. For I judged it honourable and useful that, though few knew me in my lowliness, even they should be unable to say anything unfavourable of me; that, by grace granted, I should conduct myself toward all in such a way as to obtain good testimony both from those within and from those without [Col. 0089D]. Of this Solomon says: “A good name is better than great riches” (Prov. 12).

When my lowliness seemed, according to its measure, to have attained this in my church and neighbourhood, and when, as I thought, almost no one complained of me, I confess that I was so content with the honour—or burden—of the priorate undertaken among the brethren that I did not stretch myself toward seeking the heights of a greater prelacy.

May your holiness believe this, and may knowledge of the truth cleanse you of every doubt; for no one at present presses me to lie. Believe, I say, that I preferred to be kept in a quiet and humble condition rather than advanced to ecclesiastical honours for which I knew, and had known, myself unequal [Col. 0090A]. May your holiness believe that, if my superiors had received my lowliness with tender affection, if, according to my desire, they had hidden me under the shelter of their wings from the disturbance of men, I would have preferred to be nourished by their care in a peaceful bosom rather than exposed to the tumultuous occupations of public affairs.

This our wholly wicked enemy saw and envied. Being a craftsman of harm, as you know far better, he loves nothing more than either to inflict real injuries on the morals of the faithful, or at least to damage their reputation by fabricated lies. Considering carefully where he could harm me more, and threaten many others more secretly and more hurtfully, since truth did not serve the purpose of his perverse will, he skilfully devised a deceptive likeness of truth. For the serpent was more cunning than all the other animals in paradise (Gen. 3). This serpent, this twisting snake, did not pour out its gathered poison all at once in one vomit or with one hissing sound; rather, choosing a vessel, it poured itself in by a slippery course, so that, when that vessel had become fully infected with malice, falsehood, and deceit, the plague might from it be poured out more effectively, far and wide, to the destruction of many.

He understood, I suppose, that a reputation which had long prevailed could not easily be damaged, and that an attacking lie would not be sufficiently believed unless, just as it was aided by an ingeniously plausible resemblance to truth, it also employed a suitable bearer of the lie to increase the deception. Having therefore found a man whom he thought useful to himself, whom an externally assumed appearance of religion concealed, he made him conform to his own character and purpose and appointed him as the first and chief agent for carrying out what he had planned [Col. 0090C]. That man then began, as he had been instructed, to murmur and to fabricate evil reports about me in biting whispers. He approached some whom he saw to be eminent in our order and endeavoured to persuade their ears of evil in place of good, falsehood in place of truth.

But they knew that a man can be shaken by many and diverse temptations, and that there is no one who, if grace be lacking, cannot be corrupted. They heard what had been said once, twice, and often; and, as human suspicion behaves, they believed true what seemed plausible. Those among them who investigated the matter more carefully and wished to lend a kindly ear to truth learned with what intention it had been said, and, since I had been attacked gratuitously by false calumnies, forgave me, as seemed just to them. But those to whom the truth of the matter was not quickly clear—or, if it may be said, to whom it did not sufficiently please even when revealed—clung somewhat more obstinately to the evil reports and spread them in many ways through the ears of very many.

Thus in a short time the report—or rather, ill repute—extended its power, and made its adulterous shoot fruitful through wandering talkativeness; and things which had put down no deep roots of truth nevertheless presumptuously grew into wild, spurious offshoots [Col. 0090D].

But perhaps it will seem harsh to a religious listener—as indeed it seems harsh to me who recount it—that any man who had undertaken a religious profession and had loved to maintain it in countenance and habit, indeed in morals also, should have been or be thought the first sower of this falsehood, since true religion does not know how to serve shameful lying. For it is written: “Do not wish to tell any lie; for persistence in it is not good” (Ecclus. 7). And below: “A thief is better than the persistence of a lying man; yet both shall inherit destruction” (Ecclus. 10). Therefore, since lying is compared with theft—indeed, since Scripture declares persistent lying worse than theft—I do not presume to assert that a religious man is guilty of lying, lest I offend religious persons, who love to judge of others what they think of themselves.

Yet I shall say with certainty what perhaps will not offend your reverence, and for which, I think, no one will maintain that I deserve blame: if he was not that man, he was at least as it were a man [Col. 0091B]. For that wicked one, “Satan, transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 2), in such a way that those upon whom he has shone are not illuminated but scorched. It is therefore not discordant with faith to say that he transforms himself also into a man when he strives to sow tares over the wheat. Of him it is said: “An enemy, a man, has done this” (Matt. 13).

This enemy, not knowing Christ to be God but regarding him as a mere man, and desiring to weaken him with diverse temptations, wished, I suppose, to appear to him in the form of a man, hoping that a man would more easily adhere to the counsel of a man. It is therefore no wonder if this man presented himself also to our superiors, if he accused me before them with feigned calumnies—he who has existed from ancient days as the accuser of the brethren (Apoc. 12), and through whose envy death is said to have entered the world (Wis. 2). This being, wholly devoid of true holiness and holy truth, and, like a certain pagan, schooled in a thousand arts of doing harm, having obtained a time suitable to his malice, has often spoken many wicked things concerning me to many people. For he stubbornly asserted that I had done things which I had never done, and turned into their opposite things which I had done well. He laboured to compose malicious inventions so that he might fasten a stain upon me and others. Hence it is written: “The plotter turns good things into evil, and fastens a stain upon the chosen” (Ecclus. 11).

This plotter won credit from very many and so infected them by insolent insistence that bare truth had no place with them, but falsehood hidden under the appearance of truth prevailed [Col. 0091D]. Like an infant and tender thing, it came forth from the mouth of that most wicked person, but in its course it acquired exceedingly great strength; a fierce enemy to all who resisted it, it passed with shameless brow toward its appointed end. For though the serpent had first crawled and coiled among men of our order, and though there it was afforded not merely a path but an open road, it nevertheless did not suspend its ill-sounding instrument among them, but extended itself among others to sing its song. For this rumour was known not only to monks and those called secular clerics, but also to popular crowds, because what had been reported to the leaders of our priests was more widely repeated by them to religious and secular persons alike [Col. 0092A].

What so many and such eminent narrators publicly proclaimed, most hearers judged worthy of belief; and many who still did not know my face spread my name abroad with grave reproach. Clerics spoke of me, laypeople spoke of me, abbots spoke of me, bishops spoke of me; and, knowing nothing clearly about the matter, they followed rumour as their guide. And because they knew more certainly from report that I was prior in my church, everywhere among peoples and places there was much talk about the prior.

“The prior,” they said, “of Bona-Spe conducts himself wickedly; the prior stubbornly acts against his religion and order. The prior has purchased the goodwill of his brethren by trafficking; the prior bestowed his favour upon them for the sake of ambition. The prior,” they said, “is a violator of peace, a sower of lawsuits, guilty of treachery, author of dissension; he has violated rights, thrown the order into confusion, broken faith, usurped what was not due, and, not content with what was lawful, has boldly extended himself to things not granted.”

These and similar things were said concerning the wretched prior and were believed by many to be entirely true, since there was not always someone present to confront those repeating them and bring the hearers back to certain knowledge of the truth. They knew indeed that it was written: “Do not believe every word” (Ecclus. 19); and again: “Before you inquire, do not reproach anyone; and when you have inquired, rebuke justly” (Ecclus. 2). And concerning uncertain things, the command is: “Do not judge” (Luke 6; John 7); but concerning manifest things: “Judge righteous judgment” (Zech. 7) [Col. 0092C]. They knew, I say, that these and many similar sayings were contained in the Scriptures, by which they might be restrained from rash judgment and inconsiderate reproach. But because the authority of those reporting was judged not to be disregarded, the ready credulity of the hearers seemed proper.

All these things converged toward my ruin, while both groups ran as one, as though to stones; and those who, relying upon sounder counsel, confronted the stoners, nevertheless gave little or no help to wretched me. For so great was the multitude of persecutors—indeed, so great the strength of that same multitude—that scarcely anyone dared to speak the truth on my behalf, and one who dared undertake it found no favour among them. “You also are one of them,” they said; “for your speech makes you known” (Matt. 26).

Finally, such wave upon wave of flooding waters came over us, and the growing whirlwind of words brought matters to such a point that those who harassed me said no peace could possibly be given to affairs unless I were expelled from my church and compelled to live elsewhere [Col. 0092D]. Our bishop did not assent to a plan of this kind; indeed, by the authority he possessed he strongly forbade it, especially since our church then lacked the provision of its own abbot and the care of us belonged directly to him. He knew and said that I was being unjustly defamed and that our church was being afflicted in a manner far from right order. He set himself in authority against those raging over us, but he did not restrain their overwhelmingly powerful fury.

For, wishing us to be freed from their calumnies, he humbly offered to cast himself at their feet if, for the sake of peace, they would desist from what they had begun and no longer resist the truth which he knew. Several abbots of our order likewise proclaimed this truth and, having investigated it more carefully, judged me innocent, maintaining that no abbot who had been entrusted with a church possessed such power as to lead brethren out of it against the will of themselves and their chapter [Col. 0093A]. Nevertheless, they did not listen either to our bishop, to the aforesaid abbots, or to many other leaders among us; but with unwearied zeal they persisted in what they had begun. They neither relaxed the thunder of anger nor of threats, promising neither me nor our church any peace unless I, with certain brethren, hastened to leave the church, since this kind of tribulation seemed to rage because of us.

Yet some who had perhaps pledged themselves well disposed toward me, when I consulted them on this matter, replied kindly: “Brother, your oppressors have spoken concerning you and your absent companions to the other abbots, to that abbot of Clairvaux who is most renowned among them, to bishops, and moreover to an archbishop. They have prosecuted their case in those men’s ears as they wished, obtained the counsel they wanted in accordance with their own account, and now stand in this obstinacy upon their authority. For your bishop will not resist the archbishop; no one like us can stand against the abbot of Clairvaux. Whatever your oppressors assert concerning you, those men think entirely true; whatever these men seek, the others do not refuse to grant. If they all decide to persist in oppressing you, who are you that you can resist the effort of so many? It is good, therefore, that for the present you comply with their wishes, lest by resisting you appear hard and stubborn, and so that your church, to which they are wrongly bringing trouble while you are present, may—if God so disposes—receive peace when you are absent.”

Our bishop at last yielded to similar advice. He now allowed our departure, which he had previously forbidden; and because the violence pressing upon him did not permit him to exercise his own legal authority, he left us, as though casting away the helm amid the waves [Col. 0093D]. Although he did not cease to will what his goodness prompted, broken by adversities he ceased to contend for us; seeing that his efforts achieved nothing, and despairing of himself, he henceforth commended us to divine providence.

Thus seven of us, who had been named in writing and were not sufficiently acceptable to the majesty of the leaders, went out; and, like persons charged with crimes, we lived for some time in their cloisters under their power. But after we had gone out, the disturbance begun long before did not cease; rather, great tumult grew in the church and great tumult in our province. It became clear that our departure had not brought peace to affairs, as had been said, but had introduced the cause or material of a greater scandal [Col. 0094A]. The brethren within the monastery were intolerably burdened; outside, secular persons wondered greatly that our leaders should press us or our church so harshly, when they had no reason for pressing us except the violent impulse of their own will.

The brethren with whom I had lived for more than twenty years brought no accusation against me. Outsiders, moreover, bore sufficiently good testimony, and were more vehemently—and, as they thought, more justly—angry with those who everywhere recounted evil things about me more fabricated than known. But those who still did not dislike what they had done approached the powerful persons and leaders of our province and, having made them hostile to patience, brought still greater violence upon our church. Nor did they keep silent about me: they added worse charges to the earlier ones [Col. 0094B].

For when both greater and lesser persons wondered and asked what I had done that I ought to be violently expelled from my church—since they had never heard such a thing from our brethren before, nor had themselves learned it in any way—these men, in order to excuse more credibly what they had done, laboured to accuse me much more gravely and much more wickedly in my absence. One publicly proclaimed that I had committed something which ought not even to be spoken. Another judged me most worthy to be burned, in the hearing of secular people. They intended to turn toward hatred of me those whom they saw bearing better testimony concerning me.

Someone else, desiring to please our superiors through eagerness to flatter, denied what they denied and likewise affirmed what they affirmed. Impatient of peace, he rode about our province as a wanderer and, lavish with words, he heaped things heard upon things unheard with great increase. Since, according to Solomon, this evildoer “rejoiced in most evil things” (Prov. 2) and insulted those grieving over our ruin, when reproved by some people he could find no more suitable excuse than: “I wish, and I ought, to assist my lord” [Col. 0094C]. By “his lord” he meant the leader of the priests, by whose permission he himself, a lesser lord, exercised command. To that greater lord this lesser one wished to render service in obedience both just and unjust, since he saw him consenting with sufficiently ready spirit to his own desires.

This man strove, either personally or through his messengers, to meet more diligently the men of our order whom he saw unwilling in this affair to depart from the truth and willing to oppose our superiors with words, though with little effect. He flattered with entreaties and frightened with threats, lest they presume to dissent from his lord. He and men like him proclaimed so many and such mutually consistent allegations against me, and shamelessly defamed me with so many calumnies, that even secular people recoiled from so great a crime, wondering how religious persons could endure to say such things concerning any brother of their own [Col. 0094D].

Even though they did not know the Scripture which says, “Do not proclaim it in Gath, nor publish it in the streets of Ascalon, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised rejoice, lest the daughters of the Philistines exult” (2 Kings 1)—even though, I say, they had not read these words—they nevertheless seemed to hold their meaning. Though ignorant of the fall of Saul and Jonathan, they spoke similar things concerning me: “Even if,” they said, “the men of his religious order knew that he had sinned grievously and fallen into the abyss of some execrable crime, they should not have revealed it among us secular people, nor stirred up the bold minds of those outside to insult one who had fallen. For when so great a reproach is inflicted upon him by them, their whole order is certainly disparaged. Therefore, even if they had not wished to spare him because their hatred had grown, they ought at least to have spared themselves.”

These and similar things the Ascalonites, Gathites, and Philistines said among themselves about our Israelites; in amazed astonishment they lamented the destruction of this religious order. Most of them added on oath that, even if they felt themselves close to death, they would nevertheless not go over into the colony of these men for the sake of remedy [Col. 0095B].

Meanwhile, in the foreign cloister to which I had been sent to live, the leaders ordered that I be watched closely, fearing that I might do something new that would weaken their purpose, or that someone coming might bring me some useful news. But divine benevolence chose to soften these cloistered men, among whom I lived as among the guards of a prison and whom I had at first suspected would be harsher toward me because of the leaders’ commands. They knew and acknowledged that I was bearing my present troubles unjustly.

When they, together with most others, spoke with me out of humanity, they earnestly sought to console me in my distress, declaring that they grieved greatly over my scandal and piously exhorting me to bear it with an even mind. “Humble your heart and endure, and have patience in your humiliation” (Ecclus. 2), they said; “truth will set you free.” Yet when the exhortation of many seemed insufficient to me, especially because the promised and desired outcome did not follow quickly, I confess that the saying which a certain pagan is recorded as giving in a nearly similar matter occurred to me more often: “All forgive; no one helps” [Col. 0095C].

Those who loved truth and knew that I was oppressed unjustly forgave me very mercifully; but they did not bring their gentle feeling to the effective result of assistance, since they drew no sword of defence for me against the leaders. I saw that those seeking to injure me had more power than those who, together with me, were burdened by undeserved injury. The former pressed my disgrace both threateningly and effectively; the latter resisted the oppressors only with truthful goodwill, not with courageous freedom [Col. 0095D].

Therefore I was afflicted more and more day by day because, among those ignorant of the truth, I was accused as deserving a thousand deaths; and although I was not considered a person of great power, great learning, or indeed great merit, yet, as the report worsened, I became known everywhere among nations. This, to confess the truth, was what I most abhorred and what I had taken the greatest pains to avoid: I who formerly wished to lie hidden without the scandal of wickedness in a corner of poverty now heard myself named reproachfully through streets and crossroads, cities and palaces [Col. 0096A].

Thus falsehood thundered far and wide with unrestrained cries, while truth, still with downcast face, whispered in a hoarse murmur. At last abbots of our order arrived from different parts of the world and, as was customary, gathered at the Church of Prémontré for consultation. Many of them passed through our church and many through the province; they heard both the order and origin of the widespread scandal. Although they did not sufficiently approve what our leaders had inflicted upon us, they referred the matter for more discerning treatment to the common judgment of the Convenae.

There, after earlier as well as later events had been unfolded from the bottom up, and after what seemed obscure and doubtful had been more clearly resolved, they learned that our church was being disturbed less than justly and that I was vexed not through my own but through another’s fault [Col. 0096B]. Once the truth was known, very many of them grieved over so great a scandal; but they did not wish to pronounce judgment against their superiors or equals. They determined to give us some remedy in such a way as to leave unpunished the things that had been done.

Accordingly, they ordered that we who had been violently expelled from our church be brought before their assembly. Once brought, they graciously and humbly deigned to exhort us that, being somehow forgetful of the past, we should return to our church and strive to restore the disturbed minds of the brethren to peace. For they knew that peace could not be given to the brethren, nor those outside who had been grievously stirred up be calmed by a fitting silence, unless the return of those whose departure had turned into scandal brought back some measure of tranquillity [Col. 0096C].

And because two years earlier I, a poor man, had been accused in my absence before their assembly, and they had judged me unworthy of the honour of the priorate, now in this assembly, with me present, they deigned to acknowledge that they had been compelled to move against me by a false report. “We were told,” they said, “that he had been unwilling to render obedience worthy of his superiors, and that for this reason he deserved to bear our sentence. But since it has now become known to us that he committed nothing wrongly, we readily remit whatever offence he was believed to have committed.”

Having heard everything they decreed concerning the present affair, everything that they wished to say against us or on our behalf, as it was fitting to rejoice in those things which seemed suitable, so we had to endure what seemed more burdensome. For they decreed that we should patiently bear, by authority, the things violently inflicted upon us or our church, perceiving that our oppressors were unwilling to turn away from what they had begun—except only that they permitted us to return to our church [Col. 0096D].

Even this some of them did not desire with sufficient openness; but they did not wish to oppose or resist the common decree of all, understanding that they had gained no honour among those men by presuming, more through anger than justice, to inflict violence upon us. Although the multitude decreed that what had been done by a few should stand, their rectitude did not plainly judge that it ought to have been done. Indeed, many of them individually were greatly troubled by this injury; but, as I have said, they feared to offend their equals or superiors.

Therefore it is beautifully written: “A rich man who is shaken is supported by friends; a humble man is deceived, and besides is reproved” (Ecclus. 13). If I wished to recount in order what things, and how great, some of them inflicted upon me during the aforesaid two years while reproaching me, and what things they said about me everywhere while I was absent—and I do not know where—your hearing, I think, could not endure it [Col. 0097A]. For although, contrary to my intention, I have already said much in this little work, I have nevertheless not pursued a hundredth part of it, knowing both that they would not like it if I committed to enduring writing what I have omitted, and that no small volume would result if I rehearsed everything from memory.

Let it suffice to have said this: I judge that no plague, no persecution can be called more grievous than when those believed to be brethren or members of one’s household appear as enemies; when the man persecutes me in whose bosom I ought, fleeing to him, to have been refreshed, if perhaps I found myself assailed by the stones of outsiders. Nothing is more absurd than for a sick person to perish beneath the heavy hand of the physician, or to find shipwreck where a harbour was expected; when, according to the prophet, those who fled a lion encountered a bear more dangerously. That prudent Tully complains befell him: “The place,” he says, “which seemed likely to be one of rest and tranquillity became the scene of the greatest troubles and most turbulent storms” (Amos 5).

Concerning this, may your fatherhood, holiness, discernment, and compassion not be unwilling to stretch out a hand to me, nor disdain to lead into the inn one left half-dead, so that you may pour oil upon him as the good Samaritan did upon the man whom priest and Levite passed by—indeed, bruised (Luke 10) [Col. 0097C]. For although my present lowliness does not deserve to see your face—would that divine power favourably grant this to me!—yet when your excellent fatherhood gives a good and consoling word in reply, it will in some manner make present to me its gracious presence.

For if you had been here with me, “Lazarus would not have died” (John 11); but even now I know that whatever you shall ask of God, God will give him (ibid.). Therefore say to this Lazarus—say, I pray, with power; say mercifully—that he may rise again, and that wicked death may not rise up anew against him. For the power joined to your majesty will bring both your word and your affection of justice, mercy, and goodness to effect [Col. 0097D]. But if your dignity wishes more fully to know the things I have omitted, provided it does not close its ear in weariness even to these things which have been said, a faithful narrator will recount them much better in living speech; and here, setting an end to my purpose, my lowliness will be silent. Farewell.

## LETTER XIII. PHILIP TO ***

He discourses elegantly on the virtues of prelates.

“To the most beloved of those who love him, the least of his own.” Does the heading prefixed to this letter not show who writes to whom, since it does not set forth either name according to the usual custom? If the novelty of this kind strikes and reproves the wonder of some reader, he has not yet, I think, sufficiently grasped the reason for the silence. Let him first read—or, if he wishes, read through—what the letter contains, and, if he is prudent, he will be able to conjecture why neither my name nor yours appears in the title.

Wonderful and marvellous is God’s dispensation: when he brings forth into this laborious light those born in one manner, in the course of time he so pours the diverse gifts of his generosity into them that some are counted poor, others rich; some fear, others are feared; some love and yet are not loved, or, even if they were perhaps loved once, are rejected because of their poverty.

When you and I, as boys, were occupied in the schools for the sake of learning, and were kept under the master’s rod lest untimely liberty harm us as wanderers, a certain tender affection bound us together in welcome love and tied our different minds into one bundle [Col. 0098B]. And although boys are easily moved by native fickleness, now loving one another, now rejecting one another, this instability did not press upon us as boys: once begun, our affection remained fixed and steadfast.

Then, as time advanced, when childhood gave way to years and succeeding adolescence made us older and perhaps more discerning, such change did not bend the course of our mutual affection but strengthened us more ardently in love, as though in a stronger furnace. For the more I grew day by day in understanding, the more carefully I examined your affection toward me; and the more certainly I saw it to be steadfast, the more gratefully and intensely I loved you who loved me.

Moreover, there seemed to be in you a certain composure of character which deserved to be loved by the truly wise—a quality scarcely found in other young men who see themselves distinguished by nobility of blood [Col. 0098C]. For a young man commonly takes pride in noble lineage, disdains the company of those whom he judges inferior, and thinks it unworthy to render familiar service to lesser persons, since, as he supposes, they ought to serve one more worthy, namely himself.

But you, though pre-eminent in the greatness of your birth and yet displaying nothing of the overbearing Maecenas, gathered together not merely equals but even inferiors with benevolent affection. A young man of good disposition, you made yourself lovable to all. Above all, at that time you joined yourself to me in one spirit: you loved me as an equal, even respected me as a superior; and though you were regarded as somewhat inferior merely in number of years, you did not hesitate to prefer me, as though I surpassed you in other respects also [Col. 0098D]. Your condescension reclined in gentle intimacy upon me; you greatly desired to speak with me and to hear me; and neither my lack of usefulness nor my inequality of station turned back your affection, but your freely bestowed goodness urged you to love me.

Reflecting that you abounded in these and many similar merits, I could not but love one so deserving and so loving; and him whom I saw so well-disposed toward me I embraced also with the inward arms of sincere affection [Col. 0099A]—and rightly, sincere affection. For, to confess the truth, I did not desire to grow rich in temporal things through this affection, nor did I seek from you any gift by right of friendship. Although my desire stood in need of many things, it did not love you in order that this want might be supplied. It was not the hunt for financial gain that attached me to you, but the manifest proof of a character worthy of love: namely, that moral integrity shone forth in you, and by a certain worth of its own drew me to love you.

Thus Tullius Cicero also says that true friendship arises and, having arisen, is nourished by suitable encouragements; and that he is found to be a true friend who rejoices in his friend’s virtue, not one who is enticed by his own advantage. [Note: [Col. 0099D] In *Laelius*.] And since, just as he described the outlines of friendship, my conscience perceived that we loved one another, I thought that we were rightly [Col. 0099B] to be counted among those pairs of friends of whom we were then reading together in pagan literature. Indeed, it then seemed to me a great and commendable thing that our affection, as I supposed, deserved to be placed among rare and illustrious lovers: that, as Theseus and Pirithous, Pylades and Orestes, Tydeus and Polynices, Patroclus and Achilles, Laelius and Scipio, so you and I were bound together by mutual affection and were not turned aside from the same purpose by any causes that might rush upon us.

And because, carefully considering matters as they stood, I perceived you to be the more capable, I sought the highest honours for you rather than for myself; as though I were certain that your advancement would in no way weaken our shared purpose if, [Col. 0099C] while I remained in humility, any pre-eminent dignity should raise you on high. These things and very many like them I felt moving secretly within me; yet at that time I did not care to speak of them in your hearing, lest I should seem, as a commoner, to flatter one nobler than myself, and to seek your favour more by words than by deeds. For both the moral writings of the pagans taught me this, and, what is more, reason itself had already persuaded me that our affection should not display itself outwardly in word and tongue, but should rather occupy the inner mind with steadfastness, truth, and deed.

In this truth of loving, the youth of us both passed; nor did any disturbance during that time compel us to quarrel, because love itself so drove away everything adverse to it that the harmony which had reduced us, as it were, to one soul was strengthened. [Col. 0099D] While this was taking place, I first passed beyond the boundaries of adolescence and, in the customary order, entered the adjoining limits of youth; within these, leaving what was behind, I proceeded toward what lay ahead, and I went before you, who followed upon the path I had passed. And now, as though my tender youth were dwelling in an inner house, while yours, still more tender, was held as it were in the vestibule, divine grace struck me—who had lived longer and perhaps through a more prolonged life had contracted much offence—with a sudden blow, and knocked from my hands the deceitful hope of the world which I greedily embraced.

Therefore, bidding farewell to the world, I cast away all that, deceived, I had pursued within it. I held in contempt many things that previously I had loved greatly; fleeing to a monastery, I left my former dwelling, [Col. 0100A] and, having assumed the religious habit, shut myself up in a cloistered lodging. There, while I sought pardon for past sins and, as far as I could, avoided present evils, I felt that the place and its example greatly aided me in these things, and I rejoiced greatly at having found a harbour.

But because you, who seemed to me as half my own soul, were still in the world and entangled in the things I had left, that harbour of which I have spoken did not yet seem sufficient to me, and the repose I had found was troubled by the tender remembrance of you. The prow of my ship indeed rested somewhat in the desired anchorage; but its stern, exposed to the waves, lay subject to grave danger. And as much as I rejoiced in the benefit of safety on this side, so nearly as much was I weighed down on the other by sorrowful anxiety.

[Col. 0100B] For since two friends are said to depend upon one and the same soul when they are firmly bound together by mutual loving affection, my soul did not believe itself to live fully where the deadly sweetness of the Sirens held you in the shipwrecking sea of this world. 56 Therefore my whole soul could not contain itself within me, nor wholly remove from itself everything that was in the world, when it was often compelled to remember you, who were no negligible part of it—or rather, if it can be believed, was compelled never to forget you. For just as no one can easily commit himself to oblivion, so no less can he forget one whom he loves as himself, especially when he attends over him with watchful concern in such a way that, through the union of love, he perceives himself to depend upon him.

And this union of lovers, which I had first learned from pagan writings [Col. 0100C]—to which I had devoted my attention with you in the schools for several years—the authority of the divine Scriptures likewise seemed commendably to proclaim; these Scriptures, the former books having been set aside, were now frequently read by me in my leisure.

When the patriarch Judah sought to indicate more explicitly how closely his father Jacob was united to his son Benjamin by the bond of love, he said to Joseph: “If I go in to my father and the boy is absent, since his soul depends upon this one’s soul, he will die” (Gen. XLIV). You see that the father’s soul depends upon the soul of his son, because he is held toward him by so great an affection of love that the son’s prosperity gives the father vital consolation, and conversely adversity brings intolerable loss.

[Col. 0100D] And lest this affection be thought to arise from the bond of kinship alone, and not from the aforesaid evidence of worthiness in the one loving and the one loved, hear elsewhere how great a love is found among strangers, by what tender and sincere love each is bound to the other. When young David, taken from the pastures, stood before King Saul at the king’s command, and Jonathan his son, of noble character, regarded the shepherd, “the soul of Jonathan,” it says, “was bound to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul” (I Sam. XVIII). Behold: Jonathan’s soul is bound to David’s soul, and each is declared to love the other as his own soul; yet among them there is found neither kinship nor equality of birth, but one was reared in the palace and the other in the pastures [Col. 0101A].

Reading or hearing this, I did not judge it in any way alien to religion that I should esteem you to be loved as my own soul, since that holy David loved the loving Jonathan so greatly and, above all the young men, the lyre-player or shepherd chose the king’s son. Nor should it be deemed unfitting to your nobility that you deigned to be joined in affection to one of humbler birth, since royal dignity distinguished Jonathan and yet he did not disdain the lyre-player coming from the pastures.

Therefore, while I lived in a cloistered lodging and at times prayed for the advancement of myself and of those dear to me, concern for you above all pressed me so strongly that it seemed to me it would never find a remedy until, after delay, it attained the object of its desire. [Col. 0101B] Anxious for you, I frequently implored divine mercy on your behalf; day and night I commended you to it with suppliant prayer. And while commending you, to confess the truth, I sighed deeply, and, unable to restrain my grief, drenched my face with a flood of tears.

Although we were separated far from one another by distance of place, now devoted to different purposes and occupied with different affairs, nevertheless I pursued you everywhere, not with my feet but with anxious affection; I embraced you, though absent, as present. And wonderfully, although you neither saw me nor believed me to be with you, nevertheless, by the power of love, I could not but be with you. Indeed, as it seems rather to me, you dwelt with me in my lodging; you were united not with my [Col. 0101C] body, but—what is more—with my spirit. You spoke with me without any human witness; you seemed to hear me speaking, though you no longer seemed to obey as before.

I had assigned you a hidden seat in the secrecy of my heart; there I had placed you, unremoved, as my companion in solitude. There you held an equal share by the privilege of companionship, second only to God, whom I had resolved to follow with my chief desire. In desiring the blessing of salvation, I joined you to myself, since I wished for you, without distinction, the same things and in the same measure as for myself. Yet in prayer I frequently preferred you to myself; almost neglecting myself, I offered the sacrifices of my prayers for you.

In everything which I believed myself to be doing well, I beheld you with me; I would not suffer you to be absent from me even for a little while. I wanted whatever I did, [Col. 0101D] if it pleased God, to be yours; nor did I fear that I incurred any loss through this. For spiritual benefits are certainly of such a nature that, when one bestows them on another, one does not thereby find oneself deprived; rather, the more generously one enriches one’s neighbour with them, the more gratefully and abundantly one possesses them. Therefore whatever I attempted in any way to do for the sake of my salvation, I ardently desired to be transformed also into your advancement, so that I might obtain more joyfully and happily in heaven eternal life with him to whom, as has been said, I had given a friendly seat in my heart.

Meanwhile, in this seat of my heart you dwelt with me; in it you in no way declined my companionship or my conversation. Although you seemed present [Col. 0102A] to me as if to no one else, you were nevertheless held closer to me than all others, because more inward than all. My spirit conferred this benefit on me: while my love preferred you above everyone else, it presented you to me frequently, though distant and unaware; indeed, it removed your absence from me altogether. For the spirit has power to present to itself the one it has loved, and by a kind of memorial power to keep that person present, willing or unwilling; to mingle conversations, render familiar service, urge with prayers, and admonish by inward speech concerning whatever matters may arise.

While I laboured in this without interruption for several years and wished unceasingly for your salvation, behold, the divine counsel which no wise person reproves, whose depth “neither [Col. 0102B] wise man nor scribe nor investigator of this world has discovered” (I Cor. I), willed to raise you—whom I wished to withdraw from the prosperity of the present world—to far greater ecclesiastical honours. I confess that I grieved, groaned, and wept, not accusing God’s subtle counsel or envying your prosperity, but fearing that such exalted dignity, as often happens, might entice your mind so that you would despise the humble things of religion and the hardships of holiness.

For although “all authority is from God” (Rom. XIII), some, enticed by the charm of power, refuse to bend down to bear the burden of holiness; and the more worthy the rank they hold in the Church, the farther they stray from holiness. Hence anxious, hence troubled, I could not rejoice in your honours, which a perfect lover of holiness is found to abhor greatly, [Col. 0102C] because through them he is occupied with outward business and is often, willingly or unwillingly, entangled in attendant vices.

But when, by God’s ordering counsel, you attained honours, you gathered many new friends about you; for dignity, which often disturbs the inward mind, enriches the person who receives it with outward friends. Hence it is written in Solomon: “The friends of the rich are many” (Prov. XIV); and again: “Riches add very many friends” (Prov. XIX). Enriched by their services and attendance, and regarded as usefully occupied in fulfilling their wishes, you relaxed somewhat—or rather, as I think, if you will permit me to say so, you set me aside altogether.

Nor is this surprising. For the human mind, when scattered and divided among many things, becomes less capable for each; and when it chooses to give its attention to outward matters, it is compelled to recoil from inward ones. It is therefore no wonder if, when new things came upon you, you cast aside the old; if you wished to put aside something useless for the sake of many useful things, since, even if you stood above many others at the summit of dignity, you nevertheless required many people in order to attain that same summit.

[Col. 0102D] But I, sitting silently in my corner of poverty, displaying not so much a well-ordered character as the outward habit of holiness, though I seem to have assumed some newness, nevertheless see much oldness remaining in myself. For I confess that I am still held by love of you, and my tenderness cannot be altogether removed from it. But the older it is, the sweeter my inward taste finds it; as a certain Wise Man is found to say in the divine writings: “New wine, a new friend: let it grow old, and you will drink it with sweetness” (Ecclus. IX).

New wine, indeed, ought not to be wholly rejected, but old wine deserves much approval: the former may be drunk, but it bites with the sharpness of novelty and roughens the palate, whereas the latter, clarified through the benefit of age, soothes and sweetens it. Concerning this, a certain pagan speaks well [Note: [Col. 0103D] Horace.]:

> Let those in haste drink new must;
> 
> for me, let an earthen jar pour ancestral unmixed wine.

Just as ancestral unmixed wine is tasted more sweetly and delightfully, so an older friend is retained more gladly and faithfully [Col. 0103B]. Conversely, one sins against the ancient command of Scripture who abandons with an unstable mind one whom age commends. “Do not forsake an old friend,” Scripture says, “for a new one will not be like him” (Ecclus. IX). For what new person can I find like you, who may strive to anticipate me with tender affection and service, and in whom, even if some indication of strong character should shine forth, still—passing over other matters—the recommendation of long standing is absent?

Indeed, for anyone sitting in a corner whom outward prosperity has not preceded, an abundance of friends certainly does not easily occur. For just as most people reject enemies burdensome to themselves, so some do not receive as friends those whom they see to be poor. But when wealthy eminence received you in its free embrace, and abundant advantage shone within it to carnal eyes, immediately a new abundance of friends poured into your mind; their welcome influx drove old me outward. Yet, though driven out, I did not in turn drive out you who had driven me out. [Col. 0103C] And I poured nothing over that which had long been poured in, lest blameworthy fickleness should be attributed to me, “since a jar long preserves the scent with which it was newly impregnated.” [Note: [Col. 0104D] Horace.]

Therefore, since, as I have said, I was not freed from love of you, but was urgently concerned for you with my former affection, I often desired to address you more familiarly and to disclose to you in outward words what I turned over in my mind. But how could one obtain access to the presence of so great a majesty—especially one pressed by the barrier of poverty, one, I say, confined in the prison-house of lowliness—to one who is enclosed in a palace amid many attendants? [Col. 0103D] How could he pass through so many doors and so many doorkeepers, arrive at the master’s chair or the inner chamber, or rather find you there free for this purpose, willing to grant even a little time to one speaking with you? How could you endure for long the conversation of one in whom you thought there was no weight and from whom you expected no advantage, when nothing seems more intolerable to many people than a poor person talking idly and at length with a rich one?

Even if, perhaps, such humility were in you that you would deign gladly to hear one speaking, and such usefulness were in the speech that it deserved fittingly to be heard, still the arrival of greater persons, not easily to be turned away, or the hearing of cases, not to be deferred without loss, would not permit your majesty to be free for me for long; and your attention, willingly or unwillingly, would be compelled to turn back to them.

[Col. 0104A] For this reason, returning to myself, I resolved to speak with you in the secrecy of my heart, where no intermediary was present and limitation of time caused no hindrance; where no interruption disturbed either speaker or hearer; where the intrusion of a greater business did not strive to break in; where, finally, not even you yourself, whether unwilling, would refuse to hear, or, whether kindly disposed, would complain of whatever trouble the encounter might cause.

And because inward speech commonly does not satisfy a desiring mind unless outward speech is joined to set forth what it has conceived, I have spoken, as I could, of some things among many, not only in my heart but also with my pen; and I have addressed you familiarly in speech as though present, and in writing though absent. For this is precisely what writing accomplishes: it does not shrink away in any manner, nor does it evade either lack of time or inconvenience of place; for just as I can think many things secretly without any human witness, so, with none of them aware, I can write some things alone.

[Col. 0104B] I have therefore written this address of mine, not knowing at all whether it will ever come into your hands, or, if it should arrive, whether it will please you; for works beneficial to great persons are sometimes not presented to them, or are rejected as though harmful because of an obstacle of distaste. But even if it is not granted either to come into your presence or, having arrived, perhaps to find your favour, nevertheless, because it may suit not you alone but many others also, it will not be unfitting if someone besides you wishes to hear it.

And if no one does, it will nevertheless benefit me that my will works as it can, while it exhorts in writing as well as in desire the person whom it loves to strive, according to the office undertaken and the measure of dignity attained, to possess a corresponding merit of holiness. To attain this, it is of great value if each person measures himself prudently, if he discerns what rank or order he holds; if he keeps firmly in memory what the Holy Spirit declares in the divine writings through Solomon, threatening terribly the soul betrothed to himself: [Col. 0104D] “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go after the tracks of the flocks and feed your kids” (Song I).

You hear truth resounding in the divine writings; you hear it thunder terribly even while sparing, so that it is certain that one who is found hardened in obstinacy is dead rather than asleep upon hearing this thunder. For he dies who does not hear—not by that visible death which alone the impious fear, since they do not see invisible things and cling only to visible ones, but by that terrible death which God foretold to the first parents lest they sin and inflicted upon them when they sinned, that they might prove his sentence true. “On the day,” he says, “when you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. II). And through the prophet Ezekiel (ch. XVIII): “The soul that sins, it shall die.”

[Col. 0105A] Just as the soul gives life to the body while it is joined to it, and when it departs the body is necessarily compelled to die, so certainly the soul dies when it sins, because God, who is its life, abandons it. Abandoned by God, when it is no longer nourished by his life-giving pastures, it is not restrained from going after the tracks of the flocks—that is, after its own desires—and it feeds its kids: that is, it cherishes, loves, and embraces worldly thoughts, and rejoices to lead them, by most wicked progress, into the effect of action. “Go,” he says, “after the tracks of the flocks and feed your kids” (Song I). By what judgment? By what desert? “If you do not know [Col. 0105B] yourself,” he says (ibid.).

Therefore, lest, going after the tracks of the flocks, he feed his kids, let everyone who is rightly wise know himself. Let him know himself, and let this understanding not slip away from him, so that he may not “be made like the horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. XXXI). He knows himself who prudently understands what he is and for what purpose he was made; finally, in what rank or order he has been placed, and what manner of life has been assigned to that order by the law of obedience.

For we have all been made human beings, and to serve him by whom we were made, so that what is lower in us may obey the reason implanted in us, and that reason itself may submit with diligent concern to the divine dominion. Hence the prophet Micah (ch. VI): “I will declare to you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requires of you: namely, to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk attentively with your God.”

[Col. 0105C] Besides this law, which is imposed generally upon all human beings and to those who do not keep it attaches fitting condemnation, a special law, as it were, is imposed upon certain persons to whom a higher spiritual order and rank is assigned. For while the whole multitude of believers is divided into clergy and people, less is assigned to the people, but something more to the clergy. Neither is commanded anything other than to serve God; but the clergy are directed to render a greater diligence in service.

Among the clergy, priests are set above the lower orders; their hands are anointed with the sacred liquid of chrism, so that by priestly right they may consecrate that most holy body and blood of Christ [Col. 0105D] and administer the other sacraments of salvation. Among the priests themselves, those take precedence in the order of dignity who, having received the pastoral staff, are called either abbots or bishops. The former owe their cloistered subjects the discipline of the Rule; the latter owe both those in cloisters and all others an example and teaching for life.

Great is the honour, but a grave burden is imposed upon this honour; and its splendour will injure its bearer severely if the person whom divine ordering wills to preside over others in an honourable rank does not love, with the utmost zeal, also to benefit those same people. For this reason some are set over others in the Church by God, and others, in the same purpose, are placed beneath them by divine order: that those of greater rank may give faithful care to those below, and those below may strive to obey those of greater rank with due humility. [Col. 0106A] Let the former minister spiritual teaching to inferiors with paternal concern; let the latter show filial obedience to superiors. And let binding love—not physical descent, but what is stronger—make them mutually fathers and sons, names which are relative to one another.

Indeed, the name *abbot* is derived from fatherhood. For *abba* is “father” in Hebrew and *pater* in Latin; and *bishop* (*episcopus*) means “overseer,” because he is commanded not to extend himself above others through the allure of domination, but to direct his attention over their care through the desire to benefit them. Thus the bishop is to be regarded as one not extended over his subjects but attentive to them, and as bound toward them not by a tyrannical desire to rule but by a paternal concern to help.

Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “But we shall not glory beyond measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God has apportioned to us, a measure reaching even to you; for we do not overextend ourselves as though not reaching to you” (II Cor. X). The one who does not presume to overextend himself, lest he seem to exceed the measure God has apportioned, oversees with paternal concern according to the name of bishop, as he clearly shows a little later: [Col. 0106B] “My daily pressure: concern for all the Churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (II Cor. II).

Therefore he does not know how to be a bishop who does not know how to oversee but rather loves to rule; who shines with assumed dignity but does not fortify that dignity with the holiness imposed upon him. Holiness is assigned to this dignity as an inseparable companion, that it may be fortified by its fellowship like an impregnable wall. If dignity is found not to possess this protection, it will necessarily be subject to loss and just contempt.

For just as holiness becomes brighter and more renowned when raised to the throne of dignity, so dignity becomes firmer and worthier when fortified by the protection of holiness. Holiness indeed has grace even without outward dignity; but dignity, if it lacks holiness, not only does no good but does very great harm. For when anyone unworthy is placed on the lofty [Col. 0106C] throne of dignity, that dignity is proved harmful both to him and to others; and what ought to offer salutary discipline to all is, on the contrary, turned into a detestable ruin.

First, the dignity which makes a person higher in rank and order also consequently makes him more widely known than others. The life of such a person is debased and defiled by unworthy conduct; but his dignity, as though by a light set before it, reveals his defilement. Sallust rightly observes this [Note: [Col. 0105D] In Caesar’s speech.]: “Those who spend their lives in an eminent position have all their deeds known by all mortals.”

Therefore outward dignity ought not greatly to be sought by one unworthy of it. Its restless talkativeness does not remain silent if it knows anything deserving rebuke, but forces widespread notice upon one who wishes to lie hidden beneath the shadow of vices, indignantly refusing, by silence, to collude with the sinner. The higher someone is outwardly exalted in dignity, the more plainly he is shown to be unworthy in merit; dignity does not make him worthier according to the word’s name, but makes his reputation more shameful according to the merit of his life.

On this point prudent Boethius says [Note: [Col. 0107D] Book II of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, prose 6.]: “Dignity conferred on the wicked not only does not make them worthy, but rather betrays and reveals them to be unworthy.”

[Col. 0106D] Dignity inflicts harm not only upon reputation but also upon character. It gives someone willing to sin no small increase in his capacity to fulfil that desire, since it offers him both the seductive flattery of present licence and the welcome protection of future impunity. For when, supported by dignity, he sees others subject to him and rejoicing to comply with his wishes in order to please him—or, if something displeases them, nevertheless enduring it without due rebuke—he thinks that whatever pleases him is permitted, and with presumptuous spirit does not fear to do what is thus considered permitted.

Far happier would that person be without the summit of dignity, under whose protection he fulfils the wickedness of his wretched will. The happier he appears to himself because permission or opportunity yields to his will, the more miserable he becomes by freely accomplishing what he wickedly burns to do. Therefore Seneca says to Nero [Note: [Col. 0107D] *On Clemency*, book I, chapter 3.]: “It is a destructive power to be able to do harm.” And Tullius, the most eloquent of the Romans, says of someone: “O wretched man, to whom it was permitted to sin!”

[Col. 0107B] But this is a licence arrogated by unjust powers, not one confirmed by the laws of justice; and what the perversity of a wretched will considers liberty, the most just law of truth denies to be liberty. The aforesaid Sallust, affirming this, says [Note: [Col. 0108D] In Caesar’s speech.]: “Thus, in the greatest fortune there is the least licence.” Since, as he says, all mortals know the deeds of those who spend their lives in an eminent position, he says that they have the least licence, lest those who are commanded by the rank of prelacy to benefit others be found by perversity of deeds to harm them; and lest their perversity cause greater harm because eminence of honour makes it more widely known.

Indeed, such is the rigorous judgment of religious truth: whoever is raised to the higher throne of ecclesiastical dignity has imposed upon him at the same time the burden of more perfect holiness; and the more exalted he is, the more perfect he is commanded to be, and the tighter the bond of law by which he is bound to live justly.
