[Col. 0107D] Divine justice wishes ecclesiastical dignity to shine with due honour without being cheapened by the unworthiness of its holder; and wishes its reputation to spread very widely without also spreading the smell—or rather the stench—of a bad reputation. But it does spread this if the person who loves to be exalted above others in honour does not fear to be disgraced by the merit of his life; if he who presides over others by rank and order of dignity does not strive both to preside over them and to benefit them by the fitting splendour of holiness.

When someone has stained his life with the blackness of vices and through love of sin despised his reputation, he not only fails to invite his subjects to a better life but opens before them a broader path to sin. For because his conscience is not sound but sick, his tongue is surely dulled when it comes to correcting his subjects; and the evil which he loves and foolishly multiplies in his own conduct, he patiently tolerates in the conduct of others. [Col. 0108A] If perhaps, forgetful of himself, he presumes to thunder against the conduct of his subjects, or, compelled by his office of government, to preach something just, almost everyone refuses to hear his preaching or, hearing it, despises obedience.

Thus it happens that, when the merit of the holiness imposed upon him does not commend the prelate, the excellence of his very dignity is held in contempt; and when he sometimes speaks a word of necessary truth, he repels his hearers by the merit of his own wickedness. Thus subjects everywhere fall into the ruin of bad conduct when their prelate does not maintain a discipline of life; and, because of him, they incline with ready minds toward the worst things and embrace more eagerly the example set before them.

The person who is condemned by the guilt of his own fault alone is damnably judged also for the transgressions of his subjects. Being insufficient, he is compelled to bear the burden of others, and the blood of the lost will be required from his hand. Whatever subjects do without shame in imitation of their prelate, whatever condemnation they merit because such an offence prevails, the just Judge surely demands more strictly from the prelate, who has either impelled them to sin or at least not driven them back from sin.

[Col. 0108B] Therefore, the more one who presides is raised above other inferiors, the more abundantly he is bound both by his own chains and by those of others; and when he has been wrapped in more ropes of sins, he will be punished more severely, cast down into deeper darkness.

But lest he seem to thunder with threats beyond what is just and falsely affirm so grave a judgment upon a prelate, hear how terribly divine Scripture threatens. As it threatens, so it bears true witness: “A most severe judgment,” it says, “will be made upon those who preside” (Wis. VI); and, “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (ibid.); and, “A stronger punishment awaits the stronger” (ibid.).

The meaning of these words may appear more clearly if it pleases us to rehearse in order the chapter itself in which divine Scripture is found to warn prelates terribly, so that they may hear and beware what awaits them if they live badly:

> “Give ear, you who rule multitudes and take pleasure in crowds of nations; for power has been given you by the Lord, and might by the Most High, who will examine your works and search out your thoughts. For, though you were ministers of his kingdom, you have not judged rightly, nor kept the law of justice, nor walked according to the will of God. Terribly and swiftly he will appear to you, because a most severe judgment will be made upon those who preside. For mercy is granted to the lowly, but the powerful shall suffer powerful torments. For the Lord will exempt no person, nor will he fear anyone’s greatness, because he himself made both small and great, and he has equal care for all. But a stronger punishment awaits the stronger” (Wis. VI).

[Col. 0109A] You hear that God’s severe justice does not flatter prelates, spare the great, or comply with their perversities; but because he made all and has care for all, he will punish the powerful powerfully, and the stronger more severely. I wish this chapter were so familiar to all prelates that it could not easily slip from their memory; indeed, that it might be turned over upon their lips so frequently that not only the sense but also the sequence of the words would be retained.

I wonder whether any person could be found so obstinate or hard that he would not be compelled by this furnace to soften somewhat; who would not fear threats at once so true and so terrible, and, stirred by fear, abolish the vices long rooted in him. But because not all take care, or perhaps have leisure, to read divine writings, and if they have read some, do not wish or are unable to commit everything to memory, ecclesiastical discipline prudently chose to ordain that certain prelates should carry a rod or staff, in which they might carry before themselves, as in a book, their own reminder.

For when Joash became king, he received into his hand the book of the law to be held, which the priest Jehoiada commanded to be offered him mystically, so that Joash and all others might know that the king ought to obey the divine law (III Kings XXIII) and mark his hands—that is, whatever he does—with its testimony. [Col. 0109B] Likewise, when those among us called abbots or bishops are appointed by God’s ordering counsel to a position of rule, they receive in their hands a pastoral rod or staff, so that they may have continually before them, as it were, a mystical herald.

Its form appears to contain no small mystery, by which, like a book set before him, it never ceases to remind the prelate himself how great the virtues are which he ought to possess within himself and with what grace of virtues he ought outwardly to shine before the eyes of his subjects. For that rod is straight and smooth, so that it has neither crookedness nor roughness, but remains without every impediment of unevenness. Its lower part ends in an attached goad; the part which looks toward heaven is adorned with a hook placed above it.

[Col. 0109D] A remarkable form. Whoever looked upon it would not be struck with wonder, unless familiarity through frequent use had already made him acquainted with it. But since many rods of this kind are now seen quite often, the constancy of seeing them prevents observers from wondering; and although most people do see the remarkable form that has shown itself to many again and again, they do not attend to it with due amazement. Nevertheless, the bearer of it is commanded to look attentively upon it, and much more attentively upon the mystery known to be contained in it, lest, as Uriah (2 Sam. 11) carried letters in which the death of one unaware of it was contained, so this man too, through lack of foresight, carry that by which he deserves to be struck.

For if he understands wisely, he will possess a stable preeminence, according to Solomon’s saying: “He who understands shall possess the helm” (Prov. 1); but if he does not understand, he will by no means escape the scourge, as is written in Hosea (ch. 4): “He who does not understand shall be beaten.” Therefore the rod is placed in his hand for this purpose: that what ought not to be hidden from him may be known; but what is hidden is precisely that which he is shown not to see with due understanding. And he who is convicted of lacking understanding—or an understanding heart—is compelled to bear on his back the rod taken from his hands. Of this Solomon says: “A rod is upon the back of him who lacks a heart” (Prov. 10).

Thus the rod in the hand is the honor and glory of its holder; the rod on the back is the grievous misery of the one who bears it. For he who wisely understands what he holds is crowned with honor and glory, whereas he who does not understand is bent down to endure the lash. Hence David too says: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bow down their back continually” (Ps. 68). For when the eye is darkened so that it may not see—that is, when the heart is darkened so that it may not understand—the back is undoubtedly bent to suffer what it has deserved; and voluntary contempt for necessary sight is followed—indeed, pursued—by the fitting endurance of suffering.

The pastoral rod is therefore placed in the prelate’s hand, so that he may wisely understand what spiritual mystery lies hidden in it; and that what he has grasped by understanding he may not cease to fulfill in works, so that the hand may not oppose the understanding of the mystery. Now the mystery of this rod is as follows. That hook by which the rod is distinguished at its upper end, and which is usually found both more beautiful and more elaborately worked, seems to express the prelate’s gentleness, by which he ought to draw his subjects to himself, so that they may love him with filial affection; and, once loved, he may be heard more willingly and effectively.

For a subject is not readily willing to listen to, nor to obey either the commands or wishes of, one who—ignorant of the honorable and highly beneficial nourishment of affectionate gentleness—displays himself toward his subjects as an excessively savage lion. Divine Scripture, if indeed it is heard, offers such a man salutary instruction and recalls his ferocity to the soothing influence of gentleness, lest he who ought to gather his subjects in a dove-like embrace repel and scatter them with a beastly roar. “Complete your works,” it says, “in gentleness, and you shall be loved above human glory” (Ecclus. 3). And: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (ibid.). And a little below: “Do not,” it says, “be like a lion in your house, overthrowing those of your household and oppressing those subject to you” (Ecclus. [Col. 0110D] 4). And much later: “Have they appointed you ruler? Do not exalt yourself; be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32).

When divine authority imposes this gentleness upon a prelate, it places upon him the mystical hook of the rod of which we speak, teaching that authority is deprived of its principal honor if the one set above others lacks social kindness. Pagan teachers too seem to confirm this when they endeavor to invite rulers to clemency, even setting merciful gods before them as examples—gods who do not send thunderbolts upon people whenever they offend. “If gods,” says Seneca, “are placable and just, and do not immediately pursue the faults of the powerful with thunderbolts, how much more just is it for a man set over men to exercise authority with a gentle spirit?”

Perhaps Paul, Seneca’s friend, having read this, showed himself to possess such gentleness and, by its hook, drew to himself the hearts of the Thessalonians, wisely recognizing that subjects cannot effectively be invited to obedience if one seeks only to be feared by them and not to be loved. “We became,” he says, “little ones in your midst, as if a nurse were cherishing her own children” (1 Thess. 2).

[Note: [Col. 0111D] This is maintained by D. Philippus, who does not approve the letters commonly read as Seneca’s to Paul and Paul’s to Seneca; but because in the Acts of Paul’s Passion, recorded by the hand of Linus, it is said that the emperor’s instructor was bound to Paul by an intimate friendship. Baronius reports this under the year of Christ 66.]

A nurse who earnestly undertakes to cherish her children pays no attention either to the age of her body or to the greatness of her lineage, but lovingly accommodates herself to their infancy; and, lest the life-giving nourishment she strives to pour into them should perhaps be rejected, she adds the seasoning of gentleness. So too one appointed to nourish the souls of his subjects ought to attract to himself their unformed and various dispositions; and if he sees some, oppressed by disgust, withdrawing from following him, he ought to recall them with the hook of gentleness and bind those recalled to himself in gentle embraces.

But lest gentleness be found excessive and defective—for it is certain that whatever is excessive turns aside into vice—uprightness must necessarily be joined to this gentleness; by its addition gentleness obtains mature holiness. As a figure of this, a straight shaft is set beneath the aforesaid hook; by its aid the hook becomes higher and more conspicuous. Without it, the hook falls to the ground and grows dark through ignoble abasement; with it present, it shines like a lamp set upon its supporting candlestick.

Although a prelate’s gentleness bends down to gather his subjects, it must nevertheless not bend down toward earthly vices, but must rest firmly upon uprightness as upon a vessel, lest, by condescending more than is right to those who have fallen, it too collapse through unstable weakness. The prelate should indeed make himself lovable to others, yet he must not wish to cleave to their vices; he must be a lover of his subjects, but not also a lover of their vices. He is shown not to love those vices when he takes care to grant them no consent, when he does not flatter the excesses of his subjects through harmful fear or affection, and when he is not softened by their fawning services.

He therefore has a straight shaft when he is delighted neither by their deceitful favor nor, under the rule of avarice, hunts after their money; when he loves them in such a way that he does not refuse to say what is true and holy, and does not excuse the vices of those he loves for love’s sake. He has a shaft when he strives to bring back to straightness and smoothness whatever he sees discordant, perverse, and harsh in their conduct, not only by introducing saving teaching with resounding words, but by setting before them the pattern of holiness through his hand—that is, through his deeds.

But since, as it is written, “The perverse are corrected with difficulty” (Ecclus. 1), and are not withdrawn from their purpose of sinning by either entreaties or blandishments, when they have been warned once and again they must necessarily be struck, and their very broad ways enclosed with thorns and a wall. For when any perverse person who refuses correction is not struck, a broader road to sin is opened for him; and an indulgence too readily granted to perverse conduct supplies an incentive to wrongdoing.

Rightly, therefore, a point is attached below the shaft in the pastoral rod—a point that touches the ground, or rather is driven into it. The mystical rod also ends in this point, just as it begins from the upper hook already described. This point signifies the severity of punishment, by which the earthly carnality of offending subjects is struck, so that where the soothing of oil or ointment is of no avail, a medicinal instrument may cut away their corruption. Proper uprightness is not sufficiently preserved among them unless their fault is struck by the point of discipline, unless the festering wound undergoes cutting and disobedience endures fitting punishment. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “We have readiness to punish every disobedience” (2 Cor. 10).

But because anger or ignorance often abandons the proper measure of punishment and, with the rein loosened, proceeds to excessive striking, the aforesaid point is beautifully joined to the straight shaft, while it is not the point but the shaft that is held in the striking hand. This significantly indicates that the bitterness of punishment ought so to punish sinners that uprightness never falls from the hand of the one who strikes. Thus, whether the prelate extends the point from the necessity of striking or raises the hook from a gentle desire to soothe—whether, that is, he seeks to restrain subjects by deserved blows or to make himself lovable to them in a spirit of gentleness—the middle shaft does not leave his hand, so that uprightness may be maintained in both cases. And the hand that holds it is nearer to the hook than to the point.

For although, on account of the office he bears, he ought both to be loved and feared by his subjects, he must nevertheless seek more to be loved than feared; and, more remotely placed from the point of punishment, he ought to keep nearer to himself the gentleness that draws others. Yet a prelate cannot present himself in this fashion outwardly toward his subjects unless he has first applied inward diligence to cultivating his own conduct, and, carefully advancing from progress to further progress, has, with grace assisting him, brought those advances themselves to perfection.

I judge that a subtler and more spiritual mystery of this is signified when his hand is marked by the pastoral staff, in whose mystical form he is taught—or, once taught, compelled to remember—with what diligence and in what order he ought to advance toward perfection. For he is not found able to benefit others worthily enough unless he has first endeavored to be good to himself, unless he begins first with himself the fabric of goodness in which he is to clothe others, being himself clothed first and foremost. Hence divine Scripture says: “He who is wicked to himself, to whom will he be good?” (Ecclus. 4).

Therefore the pastor is mystically admonished by the pastoral rod what manner of person he ought to be when he is promoted to the excellence of the pastoral office, so that, if human speech has no opportunity to address him, or perhaps fears to do so, the elegant silence of his mystical rod’s form may speak to him. As has been said, the lowest part of the rod has a point, the middle part a shaft, while a hook rises at the top; and thus its threefold form seems to signify the threefold progress toward which the spiritual pastor is commanded by the decree of divine law to aspire.

For, according to Ecclesiastes (ch. 4), a threefold cord is not easily broken, because this threefold progress is joined together with such a tenacious bond that it is either scarcely, or not at all, broken by violent assault. By the point is signified the chastisement of this rod: the mass of earthly pleasures is subjected to the sovereignty of reason when the prelate mortifies his members which are said to be upon the earth, so long as they are wrongly given over to freedom and are not restrained by the law of the spirit. Of these the Apostle says to the Colossians (ch. 3): “Mortify your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil concupiscence, and avarice.”

From these members is formed the old man of sin, who is fittingly said to be not in heaven but upon earth, because heavenly life, granted only to the virtuous, does not admit one who abandons himself through a slippery affection to such vices. Therefore the prelate ought to put off the old man with his deeds and with such members as these; and, in order to put him off, he should undertake fitting bodily chastisement, so that when the body has been chastised and reduced to due servitude, the spirit may prosperously advance from virtue to virtue. “I chastise my body,” says the Apostle, “and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9).

For if the body is not chastised with the point of discipline, the very one who preaches is surely rejected; and although he may perhaps proclaim truth to others on some occasion, God does not regard the man whose life does not look toward righteousness. Of him the Prophet says: “His countenance has seen righteousness” (Ps. 10). God sees—that is, approves—righteousness, but rejects verbose falsehood; and when He perceives that fitting bodily chastisement is absent from someone, He does not wish His righteous ordinances to be recounted by him. “Why,” He says, “do you recount my righteousnesses and take my covenant into your mouth? But you hate discipline” (Ps. 49).

Therefore, lest the divine word rebuke and accuse him so severely, he must not refuse once more to pierce his own earth with the point of discipline; that is, by undertaking chastisement, he must press down within himself the earthly affections, for unless these are subdued he is not raised to spiritual progress. He presses down his earth when he loves to abstain from its pleasures, to endure vigils, abstinence, and fasts; when he frequently weeps at the remembrance either of past transgression or of the future judgment; and when he is fittingly and continually occupied with the things of God.

By these and similar pursuits the insolent spirit is weakened—the spirit which, devoted to carnal pleasure, rises up stubbornly in pride. The very desire of the flesh also fails, or desires ineffectually against the spirit. But when the flesh has been fittingly chastised and, as the spirit is subject to God, so the flesh is made subject to the spirit, chastity will consequently arise from that chastisement; or rather, having arisen, it will be carried onward, enduring and unfailing.

For just as the rod rises from the aforementioned material point and is adorned with slender length, so from the restraining of carnal pleasures there is produced beautiful chastity. It may be called slender because it is sought amid burning desires, acquired by abstinence, fasting, vigils, and labors, and finally made smoother through the frequent practice of many prayers. Indeed, a material rod is in no way perfectly polished while it is crowned with spring flowers or native leaves, or covered by the juicy tenderness of its natural bark; but when it has been stripped of leaf, flower, and bark, and its shoots cut off, it is polished, its brightness displaying the figure of chastity.

Such a rod is placed in the pastor’s hand when the care of governing souls is entrusted to him. Its bark having been scraped away, it gives no impediment to its holder; and its polished whiteness suggests its mystery to the observer. For flesh that is softened with linen, purple, and silk; flesh that, impatient of labor, is nourished with luxurious comforts; flesh immersed in earthly things, which neither restrains its natural desires nor withdraws itself from carnal and harmful allurements—such flesh surely can scarcely, or never, attain the whiteness of fitting chastity that the excellence of pastoral dignity urgently requires.

And this same pastoral excellence is commanded to embrace chastity in such a way that it may not only fail to fall away from it, but may not even bend away from it; so that the beauty of purity may honor strength, and, in turn, inflexible strength may protect that purity. Hence the mystical rod is not merely white and polished by the scraping away of its bark, signifying chastity acquired through much labor and effort after carnal enticements have been driven away; it is also long and inflexible, because one comes to the perfection of chastity only through inflexible endurance.

Its inflexibility signifies the strength of chastity; its length signifies the untiring duration of perseverance, so that, according to Ecclesiastes, “Let your garments be white at all times” (Eccl. 9), and do not heed the deceitful counsels of enemies rushing upon you: “Bow down,” they say through Isaiah (ch. 51), “that we may pass over.” As long as the strength of chastity and purity stands upright, however great the multitude of enemies, they cannot pass over it. But if it is weakened and bent down by carnal enticements, they pass over it and glory in their victory.

Therefore let the pastor’s garments be white at all times, so that he may never admit the blandishments of plotting enemies; and if they should attempt to bring the seduction of impure perversity, let him resist them with the persevering strength of chastity. The angelic powers in the Song of Songs admire this chastity, by which ecclesiastical pastors are adorned and strengthened by steadfast perseverance against the temptations of enemies; and in their admiration they rightly inquire what it is, or how great it is: “Who is this,” they say, “who comes up through the wilderness like a rod of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and frankincense, and from every powder of the perfumer?” (Song 3).

By the name “rod,” chastity is appropriately signified: it is polished by the razor of heavenly discipline and made slender by fasts and abstinence, so that, with the heavy flux of lust removed, it may ascend to heavenly things with no burden retarding its step. “Who is this,” they say, “who ascends like a rod of smoke?” (Song 3). And aptly, “of smoke,” because smoke has its origin below and rises above, spreading far and wide either its fragrance, if it is good, or its stench, if it is bad.

For there is an evil smoke whose fire burns rather than enlightens, whose stench corrupts and defiles; proceeding from the deep furnace of vices, it chokes the throat, blocks the nostrils, and blinds the eyes of the wicked. Such smoke is recorded as proceeding from the burning of Sodom, when God exacted vengeance for the wicked ways of those ruined people, who, overturned by the slippery pleasure of the body, had transgressed far beyond the bounds of lawful chastity. “Abraham looked,” it says, “upon Sodom and Gomorrah and the whole land of that region; and he saw ashes rising from the earth like the smoke of a furnace” (Gen. 19).

Such smoke is also said in the Apocalypse to have risen from the pit of the abyss and, by its darkness, to have corrupted the sun and the air—although it would have been much more fitting for such smoke either not to have been in the pit at all, or at least to have remained confined within its narrow bounds. “He opened,” it says, “the pit of the abyss, and smoke rose from the pit like the smoke of a great furnace; and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit” (Rev. 9).

The pit of the abyss, or great furnace, is the burned-out depth of the sinful conscience, stirred and set aflame by “that dripping honeycomb,” as Scripture says, “from the lips of the harlot” (Prov. 5), when the wretch burns in mind through suggestions of bodily pleasure and, breaking forth into deeds, fears neither God nor man. The smoke of the pit or furnace is its dark reputation—indeed, infamy—by which the bright appearance of sun and air is darkened. For the open manifestation of the ruler’s crime not only dishonors himself, but also stains his subjects by the contagion spread abroad either from his example or from their shared guilt.

If the sun shines with the purified beam of its light, the air receives light from it so that it becomes day; but if its face is covered with a cloudy veil, the air is undoubtedly darkened with nocturnal gloom. So too, if the life and teaching of the prelate shine with the worthy light of holiness, the people subject to him are suffused with the timely gift of brightness. But if he grows black with the smoke of disgrace, they too are consequently darkened by a corruption that is either unwelcome or perhaps welcome.

Therefore, lest that rod in the Song of Songs, said to ascend from the wilderness with wonderful progress, should be thought to belong to this smoke, after the admirers had said, “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness like a rod of smoke?” (Song 3), they added what sort of smoke it was: “Smoke,” they say, “from the spices of myrrh and frankincense, and from every powder of the perfumer” (ibid.). Good smoke proceeds from spices—from the spices, I say, of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer.

With myrrh the bodies of the dead are embalmed, and through the benefit of this spice they are preserved from all corrupting decay. Therefore it fittingly signifies the chastisement of the flesh, by whose merit the flesh itself is preserved from the eternal decay of damnation. Flesh which does not consent in the present life to suffer with the humbled spirit is compelled to endure eternal pain; but flesh which, sorrowing, wastes away under afflicting repentance does not afterwards decay in punishment, once the harmful humors of its vices have dried up.

Frankincense, however, was offered in divine sacrifices when, after various offenses, God had to be appeased and the devout priest presented himself at the altar, humbly offering prayers to God both for himself and for the people (Lev. 2). Accordingly, frankincense is properly understood as the devotion of prayer, directed from the secret chamber of the heart like incense before the divine presence, praying God to grant the grace of necessary chastity and, by the benefit of His generosity, to preserve what He has granted. “When I learned,” says a certain wise man, “that I could not otherwise be continent unless God gave it, I went to the Lord and made supplication” (Wis. 8).

Every powder of the perfumer is the collection of diverse virtues, gathered in the little mortar of discipline through the diligent practice of a good life, and reduced to fineness by the attrition of flesh and spirit. The more strictly flesh and spirit are worn down, the more they are sprinkled with the finer powder of virtues. From such myrrh, frankincense, and perfumer’s powder is made a precious ointment, with which the feet of Jesus—or perhaps His head itself—is anointed; and the saying of the Gospel is fulfilled: “The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 12).

The fragrance said to fill the house is the reputation and esteem of chastity, which fills the house—that is, the Church—with the ray of its brightness, when chastity not only grows strong within itself with worthy fortitude, but its strength also becomes known far and wide to all. Paul says of this: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (2 Cor. 2). And the patriarch Isaac says: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 2). What Paul or Isaac calls a fragrance, Scripture in the Song of Songs calls smoke: “Who is this,” it says, “who ascends like a rod of smoke?” (Song 3).

The rod of smoke is chastity of good fragrance, good repute, and good fame. This chastity—or the fragrance and smoke of this chastity—ascends and advances before the divine majesty. It is certain that chastity does not displease God, since even its smoke, that is, its reputation, is found to please Him not a little. John speaks of such smoke in the Apocalypse: “The smoke of the incense rose,” he says, “from the hand of the angel before God” (Rev. 8).

In Scripture an angel is sometimes understood as a priest, because the priest becomes God’s messenger on earth when, sent to men, he announces to them the divine will and preaches to them, both in word and example, the truth they must hold. Hence the prophet Malachi says (ch. 2): “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the Angel of the Lord of hosts.” But if, as the prophet testifies, a priest ought to be called an angel—a testimony that cannot be contradicted by any worthy objection—how much more so the man distinguished above other priests by the honor of prelation, whose teaching and command other priests obey by the ordering of divine ordinance, and through whose ministry other priests are consecrated and chrism is blessed, by which those born under sin are reborn unto righteousness?

Such an angel should certainly have an angelic life, distinguished by the privilege of purity and worthy merits of virtue, lest by living perversely he turn away from Him who made him an angel and, after the manner of that first apostate, be changed from an angel into Satan. According to the Apocalypse, smoke of incense rises before God from the angel’s hand when the priest’s devout way of life and commendable reputation please God, when the good report of his devotion is spread abroad on every side, and when not so much his preaching as his praiseworthy conduct exhorts others to live well.

As has been said, the angelic powers admire in the Song of Songs the rod of this smoke, and they rejoice in wonder at its ascent—that is, its progress—when the priest adorned with the pastoral mitre of dignity holds within his heart and outwardly in his hand the inflexible rigor of chastity.

But because no virtue obtains the merit of perfect holiness unless it is more strongly protected by the added preeminence of charity, the hook signifying charity is rightly placed above the pastoral rod, which, as has been said, signifies chastity. “I show you,” says the Apostle, “a still more excellent way: ‘If I should deliver my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing’” (1 Cor. 12). Much chastisement of the flesh is found even among pagans, and their conduct is sometimes distinguished by an inflexible rigor of chastity; but because through the virtue of chastity they do not advance into the virtue of charity, chastity itself does not suffice for their salvation.

The hook is therefore beautifully placed upon the pastoral rod. Joined to the rod, it extends somewhat upward, then bends its arched head back into itself in such a manner that, by its own curve, its summit is drawn downward and, having made a circuit, is again turned upward. This is that charity which, loving, is assuredly loved; which draws God to itself and is drawn upward by God. Through it chastity draws down and brings toward itself the God who is above it, and God raises and draws back to Himself the chastity that draws Him. Thus He Himself says: “I love those who love me” (Prov. 8); that is, “I draw those who draw me.” And through Jeremiah (ch. 31): “I have loved you,” He says, “with everlasting charity; therefore I have drawn you in mercy.” And she who loved in the Song of Songs said in supplication to her beloved: “Draw me after you” (Song 1).

This love makes chastity useful and honors it; it improves to the utmost whatever good is done. The catalogue of all other virtues does not attain the beauty of fitting holiness unless it is distinguished by the diadem of this brightness. Hence divine Scripture says: “O how beautiful is a chaste generation with brightness” (Wis. 4). A chaste generation is rightly called the integrity of the flesh, generated from the point of bodily chastisement as a rod from its root. It is then beautiful, and truly declared beautiful, when it is crowned, as with a diadem, by its own brightness—that is, by fitting charity.

This charity, of which that hook is the type and figure, is the brightness of virtues that will never fail; for charity never fails, as apostolic Scripture declares. It has its beginning here and will have its consummation in heaven (Rom. 8). Therefore whoever wishes to hold the pastoral rod or staff in his hand, whoever wishes to hold such dignity without shame, ought to look more diligently upon the form of that rod and advance toward its mystery not only in understanding but also in the effect of deeds. Let him chastise with the point of abstinence his members that are upon earth; let him make body and mind chaste by the rigor of continence; let him draw God to himself by the hooked affection of love.

But if he does not keep this rule of holiness, he will surely be deprived of the merit of that dignity; and, according to the Boethius mentioned above, dignity itself will display him as unworthy, while he will, according to Tully, disfigure dignity. For just as Boethius says: “Dignity conferred upon the wicked not only does not make them worthy, but rather betrays and displays them as unworthy,” so Tully, speaking of Caesar, says: “While he wished to adorn some men more highly, he did not honor them, but disgraced the ornaments themselves.”

[Note: [Col. 0117D] Book II of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, prose 6.]

I would have you avoid both outcomes with the utmost effort and care, lest dignity be harmful both to you and you to it, and the loss of both of you be irreparable; and lest the Church lament, ready to fall under such a ruler. Solomon says: “When the wicked rule, there is the ruin of men” (Prov. 28). And below: “When the wicked assume authority, the people groan” (Prov. 29). But who am I, that I should either rebuke or teach, or even offer a reminder by way of counsel, to an ecclesiastical pastor and teacher, when I hold the lowest place at the banquet and he a more worthy chair? I, hidden in a corner, ought to do nothing but be silent and, beneath the shadow of silence, show myself teachable by my betters.

Yet one who loves greatly truly discovers that great love does not measure what or how much it ought to do; and since love knows no judgment and cannot endure it, it surely does not easily rest within due limits. Breaking forth, it hopes for what it cannot accomplish at all; and though met by many obstacles, it nevertheless perseveres obstinately, and its affection is not relaxed from its purpose, although the achievement of the work does not follow it.

Therefore, if anyone reading this letter should perhaps be indignant because such a very little man addresses so great an excellence in this manner, I think he will moderate the rein of his indignation more gently, because he will have no one against whom he can plainly be angry. Since the title of this writing does not identify the writer’s name, the reader will be uncertain to whom he ought particularly to assign it. And truly, one cannot reasonably deny to an unknown person that what I say to you might be said by another, and said to another.

But if, through someone else’s disclosure or perhaps through my own refusal to deny it, you understand that this has truly been said to you, and receive it with understanding, I ask that, although after the fashion of the wealthy you are occupied with many things, still, when you are at leisure, you will not find it burdensome not merely to read it but to reread it. For reading, immediately wearied of at first sight, profits little or nothing; but it profits very much if, having pleased the reader, it is repeated ten times.

But perhaps by now I seem to have been too wordy and to have changed the purpose of a letter into the size of a little book, whereas a letter requires pleasing brevity and this little work has now attained extensive length. On this account too, I think, pardon ought to be granted me, because my mind overflowed with the desire to converse with you somewhat longer; and since I was not granted the opportunity of your presence, I chose that my smallness might speak more freely even to one absent. I shall put an end to this discourse with this final line, and will not impose upon you, busy as you are, a longer burden of reading: I am ready to give God thanks to the best of my ability if this address should merit the approval of your majesty. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0119D] That the same Philip who wrote the preceding letters is the author of this most learned letter is plainly shown by its style and learning. This I attest, having read them attentively: Franciscus Silvius, Doctor and Professor of Sacred Theology at Douai, 27 September 1617.]

## LETTER XIV. PHILIP TO RALPH.

He philosophizes excellently concerning manifold death and martyrdom.

Some people are such that, though they do not know how to speak, they cannot be silent. Others, recoiling from such folly, often fall into the stubborn hardness of that singer Tigellius, who never made up his mind to sing when asked, but sang when unbidden.

[Note: [Col. 0120D] Horace, *Satires*, book I, satire 3, verse 1.]

Thus, according to the poet, the avoidance of one fault leads into another vice; and only a prudent and strong mind avoids both falls. Happy is the man who inclines toward neither. When I was at your house on one occasion and afterwards you at mine, you asked—and by the right of hospitality demanded—that I should write something for you about any martyr or about martyrs, as though you yourself had not read of their contest, full of labor and sweat, and of the triumphal crown endowed with glory and honor.

When at first I refused and excused myself as neither learned nor free for this task, you stubbornly persisted with multiplied requests and, in order that I might at last show myself foolish by speaking, compelled me by the urgency of your entreaties. Therefore, if I say anything that should be judged worthy or useful, I think it ought to be credited not to my labor but to your merits. But if I am found unequal to your desire, do not be surprised, and do not take it ill if, perhaps hoping for great things, you find little things. Rather, learn to grant pardon to one who is willing though unable, by recalling that poetic saying as though it were prophetic:

> No one can teach what he knows only a little.

[Note: [Col. 0120D] Ovid, *Tristia*, book II.]

As I am about to speak of martyrs, I find nothing in the present context more fitting to serve as the beginning of this small work than what the divine voice announced from heaven to John and, lest it perhaps be forgotten, carefully commanded to be committed to writing: “Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14). Although this saying does not concern martyrs alone, it undoubtedly includes them; and we should therefore speak principally of them, though not remain wholly silent about the rest.

“Blessed,” it says, “are the dead who die in the Lord.” Of the dead, some are blessed and others are not blessed; and among the blessed, some are martyrs and others, as some say, are not martyrs. *Martyr* is a Greek word, translated into Latin speech as “witness.” Although ordinary usage could call one who is a martyr a *testis*, “witness,” Latin preferred to employ the Greek word, so that *martyr* might properly designate that witness who, bearing testimony to God, does not fear to suffer death in that testimony and for the sake of that testimony.

A witness is one who testifies to something, by whose testimony that which is true is affirmed to be true and that which is false to be false. Yet not everyone who does this is called a martyr among churchmen, but only the one shown to do it for God’s sake and, while doing it, to suffer the death inflicted upon him.

For no one is known to bear witness to the truth more perfectly or more plainly than one who is compelled, in bearing it, to endure death; for when death is present, the false judgment of a deluded conscience no longer flatters him, but the truth of the matter itself is found in the secret place of the heart, and the martyr truly discovers how much he is willing and how much he is able to endure.

For sometimes a man, inspired by heavenly grace, serves God with sufficient devotion, and judges himself strong and steadfast in His service; he performs great things, promises still greater things, and is a most ready executor of his resolve—but only while peace smiles upon him and the persecutor has not yet drawn near. But if, when serenity has been disturbed, a raging wind should thunder forth as though from a desert region; if flashing fire should rage—not illuminating, but burning; if the malice of the persecutor should cut, burn, and press on toward death—the weak mind of the sufferer does not resist or stand firm. Rather, weighed down and overwhelmed by a certain love of the flesh, and conquered by natural softness, it yields and retreats when spiritual grace does not assist.

Therefore, those whom God, the searcher of hearts, understands to be thus weakened, yet whom He wills to save by His abundant grace, He does not allow to be more grievously pressed by the torturer until He makes them stronger through a more generous gift of grace. You have read (John XIII) that Peter judged and promised that he would be strong and steadfast, that he would lay down his life for his Master, and that he would in no way deny Him, even if it were necessary to die. Yet, when the persecutor threatened, he did not perform what he had promised, as the Master, who knew him better, had foretold.

And when Peter made this affirmation, “Likewise,” says the Evangelist, “all the disciples also said” (Matt. XXVI); and concerning both him and them: “Having left Him,” he says, “they all fled” (ibid.). The gracious Master saw that they were still too weak to endure death for Him, yet purposed to save them by His grace. Therefore the persecutor struck them with the blow of fear, but not with the hammer of death, because He repelled that man’s assault with a most powerful word. “Whom do you seek?” He said. And they: “Jesus of Nazareth.” And He: “If you seek Me, let these go their way, that the word which He had spoken might be fulfilled: ‘Of those whom Thou hast given Me, I have lost none’” (John XVIII).

The Master, aware of hidden things, wills that the disciples not be held with Him or forced, as malice bears down, to undergo death, lest, if they are crushed by the imminence of death at an untimely moment, they may not yet die for the Lord and consequently not die in the Lord.

If they were not dead in the Lord, they would not be blessed dead. Divine grace had not yet strengthened them by a fuller benefit to such a point that, steadfast in spirit, they would be willing to die for Christ’s testimony. Thus, if they had perished denying Him and fleeing at the hands of their persecutors, they would undoubtedly not have deserved salvation but would have perished. Therefore, in order that the saying which He had uttered concerning their not being lost might be fulfilled, the persecutor was restrained and none of them was taken. Rather, for their salvation, He Himself chose first to die, so that afterward, made strong, they might render the same service to their Savior.

For after His death such grace of the Spirit was bestowed upon them that they bore witness to the truth before kings and governors; and in defending it they now endured not only every danger but also offered themselves, with unshaken minds, to those inflicting death. They were therefore afflicted by many and various sufferings, and, to answer their Master more fully, were at last slain for Him. Because they were killed not by their own death but by the violence of the wicked, they were, beyond all doubt, found to be true witnesses—that is, martyrs.

In that martyrdom they resisted the will of their persecutors, not by bodily strength but by the power of the Spirit; and with unbending minds they persevered even to the shedding of blood. Once it had been shed, they were judged not conquered but conquerors, by a new manner of victory; and, by right of their victory, they were crowned with honor and glory.

Certainly, from ancient times, if war is undertaken between adversaries in this temporal world, whoever survives and kills his enemy is undoubtedly proclaimed victor; the killer’s hand is adorned with a green palm, and his head with a golden crown studded with jewels. By contrast, in martyrdom, the one who does not prefer flesh to spirit or present things to future things; who does not answer threats with threats or blows with blows; who, when the sword comes upon him, sets devoted patience before it; who, when the adversary presses him, finally lays down his life—such a man is rightly found victorious in the judgment of the wise, and is distinguished not with palm, laurel, jewels, or gold, but with the rewards of eternal glory.

Therefore, when you read that a crown is placed upon the head of a martyr—whether Christ or another—and that it is golden or made of a precious stone, this is not said of earthly material, which Paul compares to hateful dung, but of recompense. That recompense, perfect, whole, and more desirable than gold or the stone deemed precious by the judgment of the covetous, renders the ruling part of his mind glorious by the merit of his passion.

You have concerning Christ: “We see Jesus, because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor” (Heb. II). And concerning the martyrs: “Blessed,” He says, “are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. V). Although this may be understood of all who are known to live in Christ, according to that saying of the Apostle: “All who wish to live godly lives in Christ Jesus suffer persecution” (II Tim. III), yet He spoke especially to the apostles, whom He exhorted to suffer for righteousness’ sake. And in order that He might present Himself to them more effectively as an example, He willed to endure death inflicted upon Him, both for them and before them.

But they, more clearly instructed by His word and example, and afterward strengthened more abundantly by the inward grace of the Spirit, all suffered martyrdom, as heavenly providence prepared it for them in different places and at different times—except only the one whom wicked betrayal separated from them. Although he too, driven by repentance, brought upon himself a grievous death, an impious death; yet because he did not attend to Christ’s love and testimony, when, hating the present life, he hanged himself with a noose, he is believed not to have suffered martyrdom but to have committed a wicked homicide. Being guilty of Christ’s death, he also incurred, what is worse, guilt for his own death.

Thus what they say is plainly true: it is not punishment but the cause that makes a martyr. For not everyone whom a grievous occasion has overtaken is a martyr, but the one whose suffering a sound intention commends.

> **Note: [Col. 0121]** Augustine, in the sermon on Saints Gervasius and Protasius.

Such a person does not presume in any way to inflict final death upon himself, but receives death inflicted by another as though with hands raised to heaven, so that his whole intention is only to please Him whom he knows presides over martyrs by saving grace. Of such persons John says: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those slain for the word of God and for the testimony which they held” (Apoc. VI).

Therefore, not all who are killed, but those killed for God’s word and testimony, are crowned with martyrdom or with the reward of martyrdom, and are proclaimed blessed because they thus died in the Lord. To this blessedness Christ, as has been said, invited His disciples when He declared blessed those who suffer for righteousness’ sake, knowing that, having received greater grace, they too would endure persecutions with equanimity and would attain, through the merit of patience, to the glory of the promised blessedness.

For from among those whom the Father had given Him to save, He lost none, because He did not permit them to be killed at an untimely time. And that wicked traitor had undoubtedly not been given to Him—a fact which, though at first hidden, the outcome of events declares more plainly.

But those whom He knew had been given to Him, He preserved by His grace; yet afterward He offered them the bitter cup which He Himself had first drunk. That is, when in the course of time He saw them strong enough to drink it, He did not begrudge them either martyrdom or the reward of martyrdom.

John alone, whom Christ is believed to have loved above the rest, is said to have yielded up his soul in the bosom of peace. While all the others endured the hand of a killer, he descended into the tomb and died like one asleep. I think this happened not because God, sparing and pitying him as weaker, made such provision, nor because, regarding him as less worthy, He begrudged him the glory of a greater reward; but because in John’s peaceful end He wished to prefigure the rest of contemplatives—a rest not injured by death, but delighting to be consummated more sweetly in a blessed sleep.

Indeed, Christ is rightly said to have loved him above the others because he loves less whatever is prevented from remaining longer. Now the labor and temporal affliction of the righteous are prevented from remaining; but the mind’s repose and spiritual contemplation remain and endure. Otherwise, it must not be believed that John either did not wish or was unable to suffer death for Christ, or that he was inadequate to bear witness to the truth—not so much in word as in deed. For although, when Christ was seized, he fled naked, leaving behind his linen cloth (Mark XIV),

> **Note: [Col. 0123D]** He has similar statements elsewhere. Some deny that John was the young man mentioned by Mark, ch. XIV, v. 51. Nevertheless, St. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XIV, ch. 23; book VI of the *Exposition of the First Book of Kings*, ch. 2; Chrysologus, sermon 78; and Bede, in his commentary on Mark, hold that he was John the Evangelist.

yet after receiving the Spirit in tongues of fire (Acts II), he never fled from the threats of persecutors. Rather, willingly offering himself, he endured torments, hastening to martyrdom as though invited to a feast. Hence you have: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts V).

For John rejoiced when he spoke the word of God with boldness before the rulers (Acts IV), when he suffered both harsh words and harsher blows for it, when he could no longer pass over in silence what he had heard and seen concerning Christ, choosing to obey God rather than men (I John I). He rejoiced when he was cast into a vessel of boiling oil, when he was held on the island of Patmos for the sake of exile, and finally when no suffering seemed worthy to be compared with future glory and death was considered by him far more precious than life.

It follows that John too was by no means excused from martyrdom or defrauded of the reward of martyrdom when afflicted and distressed. Though he did not end his final day by fire or sword, many and varied tribulations so wore him down that all who attend devoutly possess certain assurance: neither strong patience nor patient fortitude was lacking to him for the completion of martyrdom.

The one whom divine equity rendered thus afflicted, advancing him from virtue to virtue and bringing him to perfection—though we do not know him to have been killed by a persecutor’s hand—nevertheless converted his ready will into accomplishment. In the secret of His knowledge, inaccessible to human understanding unless perhaps the mind, aided by grace, is caught up in ecstasy, He knew him to be His martyr by the merit of his virtue, and granted him, as to the apostles, fellowship with the martyrs.

Christ Himself seems to indicate this in the Gospel (Matt. XX), when He wished to instruct James and John, who had zeal but not yet according to knowledge, so that the brothers, more wisely taught by His instruction, might be made more capable of gaining what they desired. For when they asked that one might sit at His right hand and the other at His left in His kingdom—perhaps so that they might seem to preside over the others as preeminent—He did not immediately promise what was requested. Rather, checking the unlearned pride of the young men, He answered: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” And they: “We can” (Matt. XX).

No one doubts that by the name “cup” He signifies the draught of suffering, which He endured to drink for the wiping away of the stains of our uncleanness. Although our weakness was seen to recoil from it in Him, His spirit was nevertheless found ready to rejoice in it. Concerning this, in the Gospel He says: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me” (Matt. XXVI). And again: “Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, Thy will be done.” “The spirit,” He says, “is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mark XIV).

John and James answered that they could drink this cup of suffering, and afterward, with Peter, promised it in ready speech. Christ clearly did not then rebuke them as liars; rather, recalling them from presumption, the good teacher instructed the uninstructed. “You do not know,” He says, “what you ask. To sit at My right hand or at My left in My kingdom is not Mine to give to you, but to those for whom it has been prepared by My Father” (Matt. XX).

He did not judge them yet fit to obtain what they sought; therefore He reproved the premature impulses of the young men. Before striving to prepare themselves for it by fitting discipline and labor, they wished certainty to be given them concerning the reception of the reward. But that session in the kingdom admits not those who presume rashly, but those who deserve it by afflicted bodies and humbled spirits.

When they answered concerning this deserving, “We can,” Christ, knower of the future, did not deny it, but declared that they would drink the cup under discussion. And just as He did not exclude from drinking James, whom we read was killed by Herod’s sword (Acts XII), so neither did He exclude John, whom we have said fell asleep in the bosom of peace. “You shall drink,” He says, “My cup” (Matt. XX).

He did not say, “You shall drink My cup,” addressing one of them, so as to instruct us to understand only one of the two and, once James had been received, to remove John from drinking the cup. Rather, He said, “You shall drink,” in order to show that John and James alike would drink and would endure the bitterness of suffering for Christ’s name.

Although Christ plainly agrees with them when they make this assertion, if you consider it carefully, He seems in some respect to disagree. For they could not yet do so while pressed under the burden of weakness, whereas He knew more perfectly how much they could do. Therefore, although the brothers answered their superior in ready speech and upright heart, “We can,” concerning the present, Christ added, “You shall indeed drink My cup,” declaring this to be future: neither brother was then able to drink, but each would drink it later.

For He did not say, “You are indeed able to drink My cup,” which was the judgment that their own ability was present, but, “You shall drink,” which His knowledge more truly foresaw. For fitting strength to drink was not yet at hand for them; rather, He, the author of this gift, declared that it would come.

It is therefore clear that they drank the cup of suffering, and that in the course of time they became able to do what they were not yet able to do. Although we do not know when or how John drank it, since we do not hear that final death was inflicted upon him by a persecutor, nevertheless He whose word and knowledge do not err truly discerned it. Whoever is found to think rightly does not contend against His testimony.

So too, whoever does not contentiousy oppose the authority of the Gospel says that the Virgin Mary was a martyr, since that saying of Simeon was foretold and written: that the sword of suffering would pass through her soul. “And a sword,” he says, “shall pierce thine own soul also” (Luke II).

If one whose flesh is pierced by a bodily sword is a martyr, who would deny that one is a martyr whose mind is tormented and, as it were, deprived of life by temporal tribulation? The suffering that torments the naturally immortal soul is much more bitter than that endured by flesh, which quickly fails and is mortal. For many grieve so inconsolably, and are tortured by such pain and misery, that when they cannot apply a remedy to their torment, they prefer the death of the flesh to enduring their present distress.

When Mary saw Him who was both her God and her son unjustly judged, scourged with reproaches, mockery, spittle, and blows; His hands and feet pierced with nails and His side with a spear; stretched upon the cross and condemned to a most shameful death—who can reckon how great an injury that loving mother bore in her soul, or with what feeling she received her son’s suffering into her heart?

She was found to have grieved so deeply for her son that what the son endured in the flesh, the mother must be believed to have endured in her soul. Not the points of nails but of sorrows were driven into her, and while living with her son she was crucified with him in death. I think that when her son was dying on the cross before his mother’s eyes, had the same mother been offered a choice, she would have preferred swiftly to die by crucifixion in the body rather than to live longer and suffer thus in her soul.

Who then can doubt that she was a martyr, when such inward sorrow is found to have afflicted her, when tribulation sharper than every saw or two-edged sword cut and pierced her as her son died and was pitifully deprived, as it seemed, of every aid? Simeon, considering this, said: “A sword shall pierce thine own soul also.”

He also who, through the Holy Spirit, arranged the canon of the Mass, secretly affirmed that both Mary and John are martyrs: for in the catalogue of saints, where he commemorated none but martyrs, he named Mary above the others and John with the others. Finally, your Gregory, when he spoke devoutly and memorably about the mother of the seven brothers, who is reported to have urged her sons to constancy of faith amid the hands of persecutors—because she alone endured in her soul the deaths of them all—called her, as you know, more than a martyr.

It follows that not only those are rightly regarded as martyrs who are proved to close their final day by the hand of a killer, but also those who are temporally afflicted for love of righteousness, ready rather to die than to be turned aside from a right purpose. Since God alone, the searcher of hearts, knows all who are thus ready, and our dim eye does not recognize many of them, we chiefly, and as it were properly, call martyrs those whom we do not doubt to be not merely dead in the Lord but slain for the Lord.

Yet no rightly thinking person separates Mary or John either from their number or their merit, for it is not so much common assertion as the Gospel reading that proclaims them to have suffered martyrdom. All the rest whom we know to shine by excellence of merits and to end their present life in the bosom of peace—the Church’s custom calls them confessors, distinguished from martyrs, because they are more illustrious by the title of worthy confession than by that of final suffering.

For the one who with steadfast mind professes the things that are of God, and confesses God, who is worthy of praise, by a certain excellence of life, is rightly distinguished both by the name and merits of a confessor when he is found finally to end his day in the peace of the Church. Nevertheless, just as confession adorns the contest of a martyr, so too the confessor is not without a certain martyrdom of his own. For no one is granted to shine with brighter merits in this life who either will not or cannot endure present troubles.

To say nothing of others: are not those committed to a certain martyrdom who profess either Augustine’s canonical rule or Benedict’s monastic rule? Under the shepherd’s rod and staff, they are enclosed together, as it were, in one workshop, and are restrained at the command of a superior by cloistered discipline.

You know by experience how harsh are the trials suffered by cloistered persons in the chamber of obedience; by renouncing their own will, with how many troubles they are shaken. Though they are not immediately killed by the violent hand of an executioner, they nevertheless die daily for Christ’s name. In their person the Prophet says: “For Thy sake we are killed all the day long” (Ps. XLIII). And Paul says: “I die daily, brothers” (I Cor. XV).

Considering this, the heavenly herald, as was said, proclaimed blessed not those slain but those dead in the Lord. In this he gave our cloistered brethren hope of attaining blessedness: although they are allowed, as it were, to live because the executioner has been removed, they die daily by a death quite wretched, yet plainly saving. Since this death is medicinally inflicted by the Lord and endured by them with an even mind, grace assisting, those who endure it are led by a laborious path to another death, which, ending labor, introduces them to blessedness.

For the righteous do not have one and the same death, any more than the unrighteous do. To speak now about their difference is not foreign to our purpose—provided it does not seem long and superfluous to you, who know equally well. Besides, many people, just as they gladly hear things unheard before, also sometimes rejoice to have things already heard recalled to memory; nor does it burden them to hear more often what, because it is necessary, they desire to know by heart.

Death may also be called “passing” (*transitus*). For death is a certain passing from one thing to another. Not that every death which passes from one thing to another is judged to be such a transition, but because everyone who dies is not unfittingly said to pass over. For sometimes we cross either a doorway’s threshold or a riverbed, and yet are not said to die—lest, since a human being never remains in the same state but, coming forth like a flower, passes away like a fleeting shadow, he be said in this life not to live but rather to die, and life be falsely called life but in truth named death.

Although some think even this can be said quite fittingly: namely, that a human being does not live here but rather dies, since whatever he does temporally is undoubtedly known to pass away, and, in passing away, to perish by the destruction of a certain death. For when, for example, we pass from sitting to standing, from standing to walking, and thus from leisure to action, from action to leisure, or from one action to another, when the latter comes, the former is no longer. And what has ceased to be is in a certain sense said to be dead, since to die is nothing other than no longer to be what one was.

And because nearly everything done here is found to pass from being to not-being, according to their opinion the present life is found full of a thousand deaths; and only that knows no death which is not ended when another thing comes upon it.

Therefore, although there are so many deaths that their number is infinite, the number of those which make men blessed is finite. And, as I see it, you will find in Scripture certain deaths as though preeminent, of which one kind belongs to those being saved and another to those perishing. There are four which Scripture properly calls deaths, and, if you attend carefully, it assigns all men to them in such a way that none can be found, from the beginning through the whole succession of those who follow, who is not known to experience either all of them or at least some of them.

The first death is passage into injustice. God first threatens this death terribly to man, warning him not to fall into it through a wandering mind, lest, should he expose his soul to death in that first death, evil advancing from worse to worse, he finally fall into the second. “Of the tree,” He says, “of the knowledge of good and evil, do not eat; for on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. II).

On whatever day, He says, you pass from righteousness to injustice, from obedience to disobedience, from what is commanded to what is forbidden, you shall die by death—by the death, I say, of sin, of which the prophet says: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Lev. IV). And in the Gospel: “Allow the dead,” He says, “to bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII).

> **Note: [Col. 0127D]** These words are not to be understood as though, in those words of Genesis II, God had threatened only the soul’s death. For from Romans V, death came through sin; and from Romans VIII, the body is indeed dead—that is, subject to the necessity of dying—because of sin. Indeed, from the Lord’s own words in Genesis III, “because thou hast eaten,” etc., “thou shalt return to dust,” it is certain that the words “thou shalt die by death” in Genesis II must also be understood of bodily life. Hence Symmachus correctly translates, as St. Jerome testifies in his *Hebrew Questions*: “Thou shalt be mortal.” But Philip wishes to show that spiritual death of the soul followed from sin; that bodily death likewise followed from the same sin as a punishment, he teaches in what follows.

Those dead who are permitted to bury their dead die not in flesh but in spirit, since they do not fear to make passage to what is forbidden, to injustice. By a forbidden passage they deserve to be made far from Him who is life.

Because the first Adam thus fell from righteousness into injustice, he infected his nature with the defect of carnal concupiscence in such a way that none could be begotten from his union, or that of his descendants, except through concupiscence; and one thus begotten could be born through sin only as dead to sin. The Prophet affirms this when he says: “In sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. L).

For the abolishing of this, God finally willed to become man, to have His flesh circumcised, to be baptized in the washing of water, to die with blood shed, to be raised when buried—so that by a mighty sacrament He might grant a remedy to the world and the law, just but harmful, might be dissolved by a more just mercy. Yet this did not mean that inborn death would not remain in those being born, but that it would thereafter not harm those born and now reborn by the saving remedy.

For the death which had reigned from Adam to Moses with a looser rein, and from Moses to Christ with a somewhat tighter one, Christ’s birth, martyrdom, and resurrection so destroyed—and more powerfully abolished what that first man had brought in—that this death no longer held the reborn in the bond of original sin, and the second death possessed no legal claim upon them.

For whoever has once been washed from the stains of sin by saving sacraments and released from the harsh and long-enduring bonds of paternal transgression, if, with grace assisting, he is not thereafter enslaved by actual vices but resists them with conquering hand and effective strength, rejoices because, with the snare of the first death of the lost now broken, he is no longer held. He must also rejoice because he will not be harmed by the second death. Of this John says: “He who conquers shall not be harmed by the second death” (Apoc. II). And below: “Over these,” he says, “the second death has no power” (Apoc. XX).

But whoever has not been released from ancestral stains by any sacramental remedy, or has, after release, precipitously fallen into actual sins, passes in a wholly just order, ruined, from the first death—which either his own iniquity or that of his parents compelled him to undergo—to the second.

The second death is passage into the punishment of injustice. Just as passage into sin is sin, and sin is death, by which the soul is separated from God who is life—and certainly separation from life is not undeservedly judged death—so passage into the punishment of sin is punishment, and punishment is death. For once it has been made far from the repose in which every life naturally delights, it is miserably tortured by toil and misery.

For that life is rightly called non-vital to which pleasing repose is not made a companion, which, worn down by troubles, has so miserable an existence that for one existing badly it would be better not to exist. Eternal Truth indicated this in that lost man whom He assigned, guilty of wickedness, to harsher punishments: “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Mark XIV).

And indeed a pagan says: “How can a life be vital which does not rest?” You see that even the pagan knows that a life which does not hide within the bosom of rest is not vital—a life which does not incline itself toward the friendly favor of repose and lay its head down in it as on a soft couch. Therefore, on the testimony of Scripture, those who, sin demanding it, are transferred to the sufferings of punishments are rightly said to die. Although their substance in some manner does not cease to remain, they do not remain in the pleasing repose by which life becomes vital.

Of the punishments to which one comes by the merit of sin, one is found temporal and transient, another eternal and unending. The temporal punishment is assigned alike to all living in this life by an equal law, though not without distinctions; the eternal is reserved for the lost alone.

For because the first man, as has been said, corrupted his nature by being guilty of disobedience, he bound all his descendants so inexorably that they were struck by a general sentence owing to their father’s guilt: that in the sweat of their faces they should miserably eat their bread (Gen. III). This sentence, by which they sweat and labor, is so common to all that not even the Son of the Virgin is exempt from it. Though He was neither born nor conceived under the law common to all, in sins, He nevertheless endured under the law common to all the punishments for sins (Ps. LXVIII).

For He paid what He did not owe, so that by mighty mercy He might render free those wrapped in the stains of debts, and so that temporal purification might prevent those whom penal death holds by the merit of sin from being seized by eternal death. Of this you have read: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them” (Wis. III).

Therefore He paid what He had not taken, so that the second death might not utterly swallow those wounded by the first; rather, God might mercifully abolish both deaths in those whom He had chosen, bringing them out from the most evil death of sins and causing them to die by the happier death of the blessed.

For the blessed also have their deaths. Their first death is passage into righteousness: when, leaving behind what they had contracted either originally or committed actually, they turn to righteousness and return by fitting satisfaction to Him whom they had abandoned through the merit of sin.

For those live—and live badly—whose passions press and keep watch, whose actions advance from bad to worse, whose members are freely ruled by the law of sin, and whose carnal mind resists when the commandment has been received. Hence Paul says to the Romans (ch. VII): “When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins which were through the law worked in our members, so that they might bear fruit unto death.” And when he described these same passions to the Colossians—namely, fornication, impurity, lust, evil concupiscence, and avarice, which is the service of idols—he added: “In these you too once walked, when you lived in them” (Col. III).

In these passions, therefore, the Colossians once walked; and, walking, they rejoiced in living—that is, in making wicked progress—when, forgetful of heavenly things, they hungered only after things transitory and hurried at headlong speed to fulfill their evil desire. But when, following Paul’s admonitions, they put away wrath, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and [Col. 0130A] the other things of this kind, and stripped off the old man, setting their heel upon vices, they no longer lived, as before, with a perverse purpose, but passed by a happy death from that state to another. To them the same Paul says: “If you have died to the elements of this world” (Col. II). And below: “For you have died, and your life is hidden” (Col. III). Happy is he who has now crushed the venomous head of the serpent with a strong hammer; whose inward passion and evil action no longer live; who, execrating that which either knowingly he had sought as injustice, or, deceived, had asserted to be justice, no longer puts forth desires to obey them, his hands and feet shut up as though in a tomb and bound in fetters.

Of him the Lord says: “Lazarus, our friend, sleeps; [Col. 0130B] but I am going to awaken him from sleep” (John II). That man, he says, who flees worldly things and is grievously hostile to them, is rightly, according to his merits, a friend of those things which are God’s. When grace visits him, he has now ceased from his evil purpose of sinning; and, withdrawn from the tumult and love of temporal things, he has fallen asleep. But I wish by mighty mercy to raise him from his present sleep—that is, to preach more diligently to my hearers—that one enduring this sleep will undoubtedly rise again: that is, renouncing sin, he will receive the reward of life and salvation.

The disciples answer: “Lord, if he sleeps, he will be safe” (ibid.). If by this new mode of speech you teach or affirm that he who has ceased to devote wakeful attention to perverse works is asleep, then, since this sleep is not one of fault [Col. 0130C] but of virtue, he undoubtedly has hope of salvation. The Lord also wished this sleep to be called death, though his hearers could not yet understand this, supposing that one asleep would more easily rise to wakefulness than one who was dead would return to life. “Jesus,” it says, “spoke of his death, but they thought that he spoke of the sleep of slumber” (ibid.). That Jesus said that one who does not sin had fallen asleep amounts to saying that he had died, because sleep is sometimes called death in the Scriptures, and whoever is struck down from vices may be said to sleep as well as to die. But those who had not yet fully grasped his words affirmed what was easier and more probable, thinking that, if the outcry of sins gives way to rest, sleep suited better than death.

“Then Jesus said to them plainly: Lazarus is dead” (ibid.). He whom I first said in mystical speech had fallen asleep, he says, is also said to have died, to speak more expressly and plainly; for he rightly dies whose passion, once alive, has now come to an end, when either his inclination is no longer stirred or is not carried into effect. But the man whom divine grace visits with a fuller gift, so as to grant him a happy death, passing from sin to righteousness, is rightly called Lazarus by the Lord’s own testimony, since the interpretation of the name declares a benefit received. For Lazarus means “helped”; and indeed God helps the one whom he thus puts to death with most mighty hand, [Col. 0131A] cutting off and pruning away his harmful acts and inclinations. Withdrawn from worldly clamour, love, and business, shut up as though in a tomb, he binds him like one dead with a saving bond: “Lazarus is dead; but let us go to him” (ibid.).

Let us go, that I may both grant grace of resurrection to one thus dead, and, before your eyes, grant hope of life after such a death, so that, observing in this man, both living and dead, the benefit of my bounty, you may desire a like death and a life not unlike it. Thomas understood this wisely: “Let us also go, that we may die with him.” Let us go, that our soul too may die with the death of the righteous, so that by the merit of this death we may be granted life; for he who so generously grants his own people to die [Col. 0131B] will also grant them life with a full horn—or rather, with one fuller still. Promising this through Moses, he says: “I will kill, and I will make alive” (Deut. XXXII). And Hannah says of him: “The Lord kills and makes alive” (1 Kings II).

The perverse do not know how to rejoice at this deed; inflamed by malice, they choose to envy. And the more people they hear preached as like Lazarus, the more severely they are known to be tortured by unrest of mind. They come, through the passage of time as well as their progress in wickedness, even to plot cruelty against Lazarus; and the person whom they plainly see surpassing the rest both in word and example, they persecute more fiercely and desire that he should perish before the others. “The chief priests,” it says, “plotted to kill Lazarus, because many, on account of [Col. 0131C] him, were departing and believing in Jesus” (John XII).

Is not Paul like Lazarus? He declares himself, as though shut in a tomb, crucified to the cross; dead to the law, he lives to God; with oldness dead in him, Christ’s newness lives. Speaking to the Galatians: “I have been crucified with Christ” (Gal. II). And below: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI).
