And above: “I have died to the law, that I may live to God; yet now it is not I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II). Through Paul, or because of Paul, many are led to the haven of faith; many, having received faith, love and follow Christ, while they are bathed, as it were, in the ray of a star by his preaching or letters, and are spiritually kindled by his life and example as by a destructive coal.

When the malicious leaders of the elders see this and envy it, when those most wicked Jews disparage so great a progress, they judge no remedy more suitable to their envy than to allow Paul no longer to live in any way. Paul says: “I proclaimed to all the region of Judea and to the Gentiles that they should turn to the living God; for this cause the Jews, when I was in the temple, seized me, wishing to kill me” (Acts XXVI).

You see that, when Paul wishes to convert Jews and Gentiles, some Jews, wasting away with the poison of envy, seize him in the temple, where he ought to have been safer, wishing to kill the man whose life they reproach as opposed to themselves. Yet he is not abandoned by the One who presides over the [Col. 0132A] temple; according to the meaning of the name Lazarus, he is helped against the malice of his persecutors, since among their hands—though grievously burdensome to their will—he remains steadfast and fearless in his purpose. “Helped,” he says, “by God’s assistance, I stand to this day” (ibid.).

Every envious person attempts to kill Paul or Lazarus standing firm when he strives by threats or deceits to draw him back from divine worship, or when, by that shamefulness of character through which he, being most wicked, disfigures his own life, he labours to make the other like himself. But, helped by divine assistance, he frustrates the enemies’ wiles and terrors and does not put forth readier hands for works of darkness. Thus he flees both the first and second death of the lost, so that after the first death, in which he rejoices, he may desire the second death of the blessed with still greater joy. [Col. 0132B] Finally, Lazarus is believed not only to have undergone one bodily death, but, after the first, to have encountered another; plainly signifying that every righteous person is enriched with grace so fruitful that, having first died holy, he dies more holily a second time.

His second death occurs when, after the mortification of the old life and the destruction of vices, he finishes, as it were, his course and passes to the joy of rewards; when, with present trouble or labour lulled to sleep, he passes on to obtain the glory he has desired with honour. Of this Paul says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). So long as the soul is bound to the body by visible *gomphi* (Γόμφος, “a wooden nail”) and, subjected to vanity, dwells amid struggle and contest; so long as it groans in present distress as though in childbirth, and, still living by faith, longs for those courts of the Lord, [Col. 0132C] it rejoices that it is dead by only one death, grieving that it is not yet allowed to come to the other. “Alas for me, for my sojourn has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the dwellers in Kedar; my soul has been a sojourner for long” (Ps. CXIX).

Although I rejoice that by a happy death I have passed to righteousness and have found there, according to Job’s words (ch. III), a secret place of contemplation like a tomb, nevertheless, because I am still compelled to dwell with the inhabitants of Kedar, who presume to trouble the sweetness already tasted with the poison of bitterness, I grieve that this sojourn, which by the law of guests I had hoped to pass through, seems to me in my misery to be prolonged while I remain as though a citizen. Thus Paul, seeing himself placed in such great misery, so that he cannot complete his course while wrapped in the folds of tenacious life, wishes to be cut off like cloth in the middle of the weaving, for fresh vine-shoots to be pruned more swiftly by the cutting-hook, for the summer suns of Cancer to be shortened more pleasantly by the approaching Capricorn, and for the stretched limits of life to be confined within a shorter term. [Col. 0132D] He desires that the woven sequence of days should not be unrolled along the journey begun; and, not content with one death, he wishes to be dissolved into the other death (Phil. I), so that he may be with Christ, upon whom angels look with longing, and with whom, according to Peter’s testimony, it is good to be.

With this prospect he was willing, with an altogether tranquil mind, and was enabled by help, to endure whatever the world’s adversity—or rather perversity—wished to inflict upon him. Nor could anything which, amid the world’s raging malice, he saw threatening him painfully, turn him back toward the wicked love of living. For he endured many and varied dangers from robbers, rivers, the sea, his own people, and the Gentiles; hardships of hunger, thirst, nakedness, and cold; and in enduring them, though his flesh was worn, his spirit was not exhausted (2 Cor. II), so that when tribulation raged against him with all its strength, he might by death’s benefit pass to the crown laid up for him.

So too Stephen, whom that same Paul—or rather Saul—made a martyr when, seeking to free all, he killed him by the hands of those who were to be freed. Stephen, I say, fortified by patience, did not throw stones back at those stoning him; nor, because of love for present things, did he cast away care for things to come. [Col. 0133A] Rather, when his course was completed, he wished to pass to the crown signified by his name; bidding farewell to his stoners, he desired to fall asleep in the Lord whom he loved. That it is written of him (Acts VII) that “he fell asleep” means nothing other than that he passed over: he who was tortured by wakeful labour in the exercise of righteousness rejoiced to pass, freed from the body, into rest.

David too, sweating in this contest, hopes gladly for this passage, and confidently affirms that by it he will rest, knowing that this benefit is awaited by all the faithful and that they too are not deprived of the same gift from sin. “In peace,” he says, “I shall sleep and rest together” (Ps. IV). In that peace in which he understands and desires that he will rest, he sees and foresees that the wicked man will not be, because the wicked man does not find the same passage with the righteous, nor, when the passage has been made, arrive at the same rest. “I saw,” he says, “the wicked exalted and raised up; and I passed by, and behold, he was not” (Ps. [Col. 0133C] XXXVI). I saw, he says, the wicked man exalted in this present hovel, and lifted like chaff, carried away by the wind of pride; but when I passed—that is, when I foresaw in the Spirit that I should come from labour to the grace of sleep and enjoy that saving and delightful salvation—I knew beyond doubt that the same wicked man was not there, and that no place exists for the wretchedly evil among the blessed faithful.

To this passage, which the wicked man neither knows nor desires, but avoids like a plague when ruined in mind, God’s Wisdom invites us in gracious speech, so that those whom desire for it has made contemptuous of the world may by passage to it become possessors of the promised inheritance. “Pass over to me, all who desire me” (Ecclus. [Col. 0133D] XXIV). You, he says, whose devotion desires not the world but God’s Wisdom, whose longing for salvation or for the courts of the Lord causes you to faint with desire: love that death by whose benefit you pass to me; undertake the passage by which, once completed, you find the inheritance you have deserved. For you do not come to me except by death or passage intervening; nor do you attain the inheritance unless you sleep worthily and savingly. For although it is prepared in sweat and labour for every busy and watchful person, nevertheless hereditary rest is not granted except to one who passes over, except to one who falls asleep. Hence you have: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. CXXVI).

For this reason the humble hearer is invited to pass over: that, once he has passed, he may enjoy the sweetness he desires, putting far away whatever bitterness he experiences in death or passage [Col. 0134A] and, having found the inheritance, being soothed by its incomparable sweetness. Indicating this, Wisdom, after saying, “Pass over to me, all who desire me” (Ecclus. XXIV), adds shortly afterward: “My inheritance is above honey and the honeycomb” (ibid.).

Since among all things which our taste loves to experience carnally, nothing sweeter than honey and honeycomb can be found, the promised inheritance is commended as above them both, so that nothing desirable and earthly may be known comparable to it. Christ, the Power of God and the Wisdom of God, wished not only to forewarn us prophetically by word that we should make this passage, but afterward also to instruct us historically by deed and example. Made man for us, he wished to die, or to pass over, [Col. 0134B] thereby granting us a pleasing and clear instruction concerning whence and whither we pass. Of him the Evangelist says: “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John XIII).

Let none of us hope or love to remain in this world, however much he seems in it either to abound in successes or to excel in good works. The Son of God himself, who had come to endure labours in the world, did not wish to obtain a permanent dwelling in it. Dying, therefore, he departed from the world into which he had come, and by a fruitful passage returned to the Father from whom he had proceeded. He gives us hope and grace that we too may pass there—that is, that by death intervening we may come from the labour of this world to eternal rest.

Who would dare deny that those dead by this death are blessed? And what soundly wise person would not rejoice in the hope of this death, when one who so dies is proclaimed to die with Christ, and by the merit of this death is shown to live with him? “If we have died with Christ,” he says, “we believe that we shall also live together with Christ” (Rom. VI). And below: “If we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him” (Rom. VIII). Those who thus die—that is, die with Christ—are therefore rightly called blessed, since, according to the testimony of the divine utterance, they die in the Lord. They are not truly said to die in him—that is, in his good pleasure, by the grace of whose dying—who are not found like Christ in death or passage.

I want you therefore to know that some of the dead die from the Lord and in the Lord; others from the Lord but not [Col. 0134D] in the Lord; others neither from the Lord nor in the Lord. And whoever die in the Lord also die from the Lord; but the converse does not hold, since not all who die from the Lord consequently die in the Lord. Those, however, who die neither from the Lord nor in the Lord surely die by that death of which it is written: “A man indeed kills his own soul by malice” (Wis. XVI); and: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII). For it is certain that God did not make sin and was not the author of this evil. Those who, deserted by grace, die in sin, plainly die neither from the Lord nor in the Lord.

For God, as Scripture says, did not make death (Wis. I): he did not first kill the angel through sin, nor afterward man. Rather, the devil is plainly the inventor of his own sin and death, [Col. 0135A] and, after man’s creation, the instigator of his sin. Created good by the good God, he became proud in miserable perversity; dissatisfied with what he had received, he sought the likeness of God which he had not received. A liar and father of lies, as the truth of the Gospel declares (John VIII), he fell through his own will alone, whence he is called the devil. Fallen and lost, when he saw himself irrecoverable and envied the blessedness set before newly made man, he deceived man, in the form of a serpent, into eating what was forbidden.

> **Note: [Col. 0135D]** This does not conflict with what the Apostle says in 1 Tim. II.14: “Adam was not deceived,” because Adam was not tempted by the devil in the serpent’s form to eat what was forbidden; rather, the woman herself—who is truly human and, together with Adam, the seed-bed of the human race—was so tempted. Yet Blessed Ignatius the martyr, in the Epistle to the Trallians; Hilary, Canon 3 on Matthew; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 38; Augustine, on Psalm LXVIII, [Col. 0136D] at the words “what I did not seize”; and certain others concede that Adam was in some sense deceived. Saint Philip himself likewise explains the manner of the deception, cols. 595 ff. and 606 ff.

And thus he introduced into the world the death which he had brought down from heaven. Of this it is written: “By the envy of the devil death entered into the world; but those who belong to his [Col. 0135B] side imitate him” (Wis. I). When simple and unwary man heard the envious counsellor, he did not immediately reject, at its first appearance, the false promiser; neglecting God, he turned aside into the errant party of the counsellor and did not refuse to imitate him, dying by death.

As stated before, God is believed neither to have made this death nor to have inflicted any sin upon those who sin; otherwise, if sin were inflicted upon anyone by the good Author, the sinner would be considered not blameworthy but rightly excusable. Of this Scripture says: “God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living” (ibid.).

This death, then, since it is not in the Lord, is likewise not inflicted by the Lord; and by a just judgment another death is consequently imposed upon it, because it is fitting and just [Col. 0135C] that sin, shown to be contrary to God, should be followed by the deserved punishment exacted by him. Punishment, moreover, is death, of which it is written: “Injustice is an acquisition of death.”

> **Note: [Col. 0136D]** Wisdom I, according to some books; for the older and more correct manuscripts of Wisdom I do not contain that sentence.

Those who are on his side are worthy of death. For whoever loves to commit injustice and, with stumbling step, turns aside into his party is found worthy of death—that is, of penal afflictions—acquiring it for himself when he summons it by his words and deeds. Since this death is justly inflicted upon the sinner according to his deserts, God is not inappropriately proclaimed its author: as perfect goodness accords with him in not sinning, so it is not incompatible with his justice to punish the sinner. “For the Lord is righteous and loves righteous deeds; his face beholds equity” (Ps. X).

Therefore he punishes whatever is committed against righteousness, and the punishment of sinners is assigned to him as just judge. Although it is sometimes called evil because it does not accord with the will of those who suffer it, it is good for God because it does not depart from justice. Hence Scripture testifies that God thinks or makes evil, yet he is not accused by the judgment of soundly wise persons, since, justice dictating, he does not permit human characters and acts to go unpunished. Through Micah: “Behold, I devise evil against this family, from which you shall not remove your necks” (Mic. II). And Isaiah: “Making peace and creating evil” (Isa. XLV). And Amos: “Is there evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” (Amos III).

God, therefore, who is nothing but good, is not denied to make evil when, by his striking, the sinner is burdened with afflictions—not because the evil, that is, fault, belongs to God who inflicts it, but because it is evil, that is, grievous and harsh, to the sufferer. This evil, this harshness, ranges so broadly throughout humankind that it embraces all Adam’s children; no one sees himself released from this heavy yoke, so as to boast like the son of a white hen.

Indeed, pagans who observed the present life more prudently considered carefully that it was not vital but penal; and, grieving that they were oppressed in it by punishments and hardships, they preferred more clearly to call it death rather than life. Hence that writer says:

> “I live—if it is life to possess a kind of death.”

> **Note: [Col. 0136D]** Ovid.

Because he was deprived of home, country, wife, and household, and was held in harsh exile among the Getae and Sauromatae; and, what was graver than these, was sustained by no remedy of hope, such a life seemed to the wretched man a grievous kind of death. But for this pagan, or any false Catholic, this death or affliction by which he is punished, by which in the present life he experiences the most weighty hand of the avenger, is, just as it is by just judgment the repayment of preceding fault, so surely the beginning or foretaste of punishment to follow. Thus in the present life his death and destruction begin as a punishment [Col. 0136C] and, after this life, are consummated with an immense and unending increase.

For then the deep abyss of hell receives him, an irretrievable flood according to the saying of the pagans; a tomb pressed by a stone which the hand of mercy does not roll away; a binding with fetters which no divine mission unlooses; and the passage of a heavy rod, founded, according to the testimony of Scripture, in such a way that the wretched man is consigned to it without end and without remedy. And because the worm that does not die (Isa. XXX), the burning of fire, the everlasting confusion of darkness, intolerable and eternal adversity, and all such things inflicted there upon buried sinners are a repayment of deserts and the vengeance of the just Judge, this death is rightly proclaimed to be from the Lord, [Col. 0136D] who is shown to render just evil to the evil and unjust. “Vengeance is mine,” he says, “I will repay” (Deut. XXXII; Heb. X).

This condemnation rightly deserved to be called by the name of death, in which every lost person is known to be burdened with such great afflictions that, being far removed from God, who is life, he is compelled, as though failing, to expire and can no longer either desire or be able to breathe for praising him. Hence you have: “The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all who descend into hell” (Ps. CXIII). Just as those who die wickedly by sinning do not praise God, neither do those who suffer in hell the punishments deserved for sin; and while in sinners the will is reprobate, upon those descending to hell an incurable incapacity is added. This incapacity, though it is from the Lord, who is not denied to inflict punishments upon the lost, is nevertheless not proclaimed to be in the Lord—that is, in his grace—because his benevolence in no way delights or rejoices in the infernal punishments which his severity wills to inflict.

Showing this, Scripture, after saying, “God did not make death” (Wis. I), adds: “Nor does he delight in the destruction of the living” (ibid.). It calls sin death, which, as has often been said, [Col. 0137B] God did not make; but it calls the eternal punishments of the lost the destruction of the living. God is indeed believed to bring them about, yet his benevolence does not rejoice in them, since he would rather that man be saved than perish, though he is compelled to bring evil upon the lost according to their deserts.

But leaving the death of the lost, which we know insufficiently because we have not experienced it—and whose experience we do not wish to come upon us, but rather to be turned away—let the course of our speech return to the death of martyrs, which divine goodness works by a kindly design. When it sees those whom it wishes to come to the grace of salvation and to the number of the elect serving either original or actual vices, it deigns, when and as much as it wills, to bestow its benefit upon them, causing their badly living inclinations and actions to perish.

In the figure of this death we know baptism to be consecrated: the pursuing Egyptians drowned in mighty waters (Exod. XIV); in a venerable mystery the depths of the sea crossed; the people of God brought out and renewed with oldness dead. That is: by the saving washing our vices are driven far away, and, with Egyptian habits buried, we are conformed to Christ who died. “We were buried with him,” Paul says, “through baptism into death” (Rom. VI).

When, at grace’s visitation, a person renounces Egyptian slavery; when, execrating sin, he devotes himself to virtue; when, with enemies overcome, he is granted to cross the Red Sea on dry foot; when he is granted by a happy passage to arrive from Egypt in the wilderness; when, with a view to peace, he banishes the old cries and tumults of vices, [Col. 0137D] washed in new grace, he appears buried with Christ, who died for us. The breadth of the wilderness receives him buried or washed; having received him, necessary strength cherishes him, and in cherishing advances him. For though the multitude of Egyptians has been submerged in mighty waters, fullness of rest is not granted to those who inhabit the desert.

For enemies arise, who are known to envy the progress of the good and who presume to hurl terrible threats at those who pass through. Since they cannot turn them from their purpose, they strive at least to extract from them some delays in advancing. In this the children of Israel are not found worthy of blame; rather, all upright and vigorous persons are praiseworthily exercised, while they confidently meet and resist their adversaries, overcome those who resist, and do not abandon their journey begun. Thus, indeed, when divine grace brings us out from the darkness of sins and, washed in baptism or penitence, leads us into righteousness, we have died, because the old malice no longer lives in us; yet our devotion has not yet entered the sanctuary of complete rest. For certain things creep in from the side, as though the old life had revived, or perhaps incentives to new vices arise; if they were given free rein, they would become altogether oppressive, unless God, going before, mercifully brought purifying evils.

In this sojourn, therefore, both righteous and unrighteous people are afflicted as punishment and suffer the troubles of penalties for either their own sins or those of their people; nor is anyone, though he has departed from Egypt, so blessed that he passes through the present [Col. 0138B] wilderness untempted. But the unrighteous, abandoned by grace, are brought into the temptation set before them; while the righteous are brought out purified like gold from the furnace (Ps. XCIII). Divine justice does not call the former back as they rush headlong from their course begun, but mercy mercifully shapes labour for the latter into a commandment. For when the righteous choose to render obedience to God’s command and, according to his command, bear present troubles with equanimity, then the labour without which this present life or way is never traversed is wonderfully found to be shaped into a commandment, because patience and humility are maintained in labour according to the precept or rule established by Scripture. “My son,” it says, “when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear; prepare your soul for temptation; [Col. 0138C] humble your heart and endure” (Ecclus. II). And below: “Endure in sorrow, and in your humility have patience; for gold and silver are tried in the fire, but acceptable people in the furnace of humiliation” (ibid.).

Therefore, the labour which, as I said before, is for the reprobate the beginning or foretaste of punishment to follow, performs for the elect the function of a poultice, oil, and bandage. What justly draws the former, according to their deserts, to greater ruin, the latter experience, through grace at work, as medicine. By this surgical instrument the spurious excrescences of vices are cut away; by this fire light and useless chaff is burned; by this poultice health wounded by a blow is restored; by this oil the inconvenience of swelling and pain is eased; by the strength of this bandage things twisted and broken return to soundness; by this medicine at last all infirm things are turned to healing.

Moreover, by this furnace or kiln gold and silver are made brighter, and the righteous person’s righteousness receives an increase of desired purity; and where the leaden or tin-like iniquity of the lost becomes ashes, there the golden or silver perfection of the elect shines forth. For this purpose divine goodness wills those who have died to sin and passed to righteousness, who are crucified to the world and have left works of darkness—for this purpose, I say—to be scourged and, while they are in the body, disciplined by stripes and troubles: either that their stains may be erased as by a sharp razor, or that, once their stains are erased, their merits may be increased by greater merits. [Col. 0138D]

But just as the sinner’s most wretched death receives an increase from evil to worse evil (Ps. XXXIII), while he either multiplies his faults or finds first grievous and then more grievous loss for them, so the martyr’s death, precious in the sight of the Lord, is found fruitful in commendable progress: in the present life it repeatedly makes him pass from virtue to virtue, and, when virtue is perfected, it more happily passes to salvation. This death, by which he now dies—or repeatedly advances in dying—when, that is, through love of righteousness he patiently bears such frequent evils; when oppressed by severe affliction, he does not refuse for Christ’s sake to suffer something more severe, and thus passes from righteousness to greater righteousness—this death, I say, for which the grace of heavenly gift is granted to be present, makes him, as it appears, a martyr.

For when either the inner [Col. 0139B] soul of anyone is struck by injury or the outer flesh is oppressed by an inflicted suffering, if, after Christ’s example, he remains a strong fighter in the contest, making a good passage with reward or crown in view, he is rightly believed even now to be a martyr, since he is known both to suffer grievous things and not to lack grace while suffering. Since this grace is granted to a martyr only from the Lord, the martyr is not inappropriately said to die from the Lord, from whom, being propitious to him, he merited to obtain that he might be willing and able to endure his present martyrdom with equanimity.

Because this same martyrdom is believed to be wrought not by anger but by God’s mercy—mercy which through it washes away stains and causes merits to increase by merits; which, while cleansing grain on the threshing-floor, rejoices that the chaff is burned; which, while testing gold, wishes it to be brought forward to a greater purity [Col. 0139C]—whoever is not found rebellious and unbelieving toward that grace rightly acknowledges this death also to be in the Lord. For if there is joy among the angels when a sinner, led by repentance, turns himself away from sins (Luke 15), and, aided by grace, is converted by a new purpose to righteousness, how much more must He be believed to rejoice in that person thus justified, who by His gift and grace has merited to attain righteousness? When the Lord sees him pass from sin to righteousness, knowing that the reality of this passage has proceeded from Himself, and knowing what is beneficially fitting for the one who passes—fitting for healing disordered impulses and building up character—He, the wise physician, neither grudges nor refuses to bestow it upon him.

He therefore gives them many and varied bodily labours and torments of mind, by which that person, grievously but beneficially [Col. 0139D] trained, having now tasted a useful death, passes from progress to progress with greater diligence, until by diligent care and effort he comes to perfection. The Apostle Paul affirms that he is engaged in this death, and that in it he prospers by fitting progress through grace’s gift; showing that, not merely without sadness under the pressure of painful punishments, but also with a certain expansiveness of mind, eager for progress, he glories. Speaking to the Corinthians, he says: “Always carrying about in your body the mortification of Jesus” (2 Cor. 4). And again: “We are always delivered unto death for Jesus’ sake” (ibid.). And in another Epistle: “Why also,” he says, “are we in danger every hour? I die daily, brothers” (1 Cor. 15). But by what death he dies always, every hour, or daily, and by what stage or order he is advanced to fuller [Col. 0140A] righteousness, he indicates to the Romans: “Not only so, but we glory also in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience; and patience, tested character; and tested character, hope; and hope does not put to shame” (Rom. 5). He indicates that tribulation and prolonged endurance are a kind of death; and because he considers it the cause of manifold progress, he declares that he is not burdened by experiencing it but, eager to advance, glories in it.

When he recounted to the Corinthians the history of his misery and arranged, as it were, a series or catalogue of the evils inflicted upon him, he clearly showed that he received from them not failure but progress, enduring all these things not under compulsion but willingly: “In labours more abundant, in prisons more abundant, [Col. 0140B] in stripes beyond measure, in deaths often” (2 Cor. 11). Having enumerated in a rather long succession many further things that follow—which I refrain from adding here for brevity’s sake—he added: “Most gladly will I glory in my infirmities” (2 Cor. 12). And again: “I take pleasure,” he says, “in infirmities, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ” (ibid.). In all that he seems to suffer grievously for Christ, he declares that he glories with the bosom of his heart expanded and is pleased with himself, knowing that whatever he suffers for Him—provided also that it is in Him, that is, in His grace—will be turned into the progress of a good death and an increase of righteousness.

Therefore he also takes care to admonish the Corinthians more diligently that they should strive to remain steadfast in what they suffer, affirming [Col. 0140C] that labour is by no means unfruitful when, by the merit of constancy, it is acceptable to the Lord. “Be steadfast,” he says, “and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Cor. 15). If, standing firm and pressing on in good works, you labour; if, labouring in the Lord, you abound in good works: know that the labour which your constancy suffers in His good pleasure is not considered empty or useless. Hence he says also to the Thessalonians: “Now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord” (1 Thess. 3).

And when he took care to exhort the Ephesians to obedience, he wished to show what sort of obedience is commendable, lest either one who commands or one who obeys should be deceived by error, go astray, and make the command of obedience conflict with the laws of righteousness. [Col. 0140D] “Children,” he says, “obey your parents in the Lord, for this is just” (Eph. 6). Since it is certain that many servants obey masters or children obey parents, whose obedience does not deserve to find commendable fruit, Paul wished, by a quite brief indication, to define what obedience ought to profit those who obey well. For it is not always just to obey parents; but it is always just to obey parents in the Lord, when, that is, in obeying the counsels of elders, the obedient person is found truly to please God.

But if a father should presume to command his son something found contrary to the divine good pleasure, nothing is more fitting for a good son to do than confidently to reply with apostolic teaching: “We must obey [Col. 0141A] God rather than men” (Acts 5). Therefore, although much labour and distress are often endured in carrying out the counsels of elders, it is plain that no fruit of righteousness follows from this unless, as has been said, that same labour is endured in the Lord. And whatever a strong person who obeys suffers in the Lord will not lack saving fruit, as Paul affirms to the Corinthians: “Knowing,” he says, “that your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Cor. 15; 2 Cor. 11). Thus Paul, knowing that he himself labours harshly even in the Lord and endures, in His good pleasure, the grievous evils which he carefully enumerates, glories not only in the Lord but also in the labour which he suffers in the Lord, observing that labour and tribulation gradually produce fitting progress.

[Col. 0141B] But one who is so engaged in this death, or in this progress of righteousness—who rejoices with untiring spirit in suffering so many and such great things so often—will you say that he is not yet rightly to be judged a martyr, and that, while he is tormented with martyrdom, he still ought not to be called a martyr? If dying quickly by fire, sword, or any kind of gibbet makes a martyr, is one not a martyr who is oppressed not by a momentary but by a more prolonged punishment? If one who dies once, never again to suffer anything of that sort, is a martyr, is one who dies daily, and will die again and again, not a martyr?

But perhaps one who dies the first death, although he suffers many grave things and, through suffering, advances from righteousness to fuller righteousness, is nevertheless not yet declared a martyr by human judgment because the end, to which worthily commendable praise is given, is unknown. For just as you see many whose misery does not correspond to martyrdom but conflicts with it, so you have very many whose end does not accord with their beginning: though they propose to assume, or do assume, much patience amid adversities from love of righteousness, they do not bring it to completion, their weakness overcoming the firmness of their purpose. [Col. 0141C]

But this man experiences the matter much more surely in himself and is found to demonstrate it much more clearly to others: the man who for Christ endures not only the threats and blows of a persecutor, but, his course completed, also bears the most grievous hand of one who kills him. Even if formerly he had either not known Christ or suffered nothing grave for Him, if at the last he is killed on account of His testimony, he is undoubtedly proclaimed a martyr in everyone’s judgment. But if, conversely, someone is first found to have shown much reverence to Christ and to have endured a sufficiently grave and prolonged first death, by which one passes to righteousness, yet at last passes to the reward due him and the eternal benefit of a more welcome recompense in a peaceful end, without a killer’s hand—such a one will not receive among human beings the name or glory of martyr. But who will rashly presume to affirm that this is also so before God?

Who will contend that the death of the righteous person—whether the first death by which he passes to righteousness, or the second death by which he passes to the reward—is wholly unfruitful of martyrdom both before God and before human beings, if in the former he is sometimes compelled to endure grave and prolonged human sufferings, while in the latter the hands against him are found restrained by God’s hidden counsel? [Col. 0142A] For although the rage of the enemy and the murderous sword are far away, the axe and the hatchet that cut down are nearer at hand: that is, when God, through severe illness and the most grievous force of pain, causes the righteous person to pass to the remedy of fuller glory.

But because it is not mine to penetrate all the counsels of the heavenly height, I neither ought nor dare to affirm anything to you concerning such matters. I refer you to those who, having attained the grace of greater understanding, have spoken more plainly about the uncertain and hidden things of divine wisdom. This one thing has been granted me to know, and my smallness confidently declares it: whoever is proved first to pass to righteousness and afterward to the reward of righteousness, works both passages not except by the Lord and in the Lord, in whose good pleasure [Col. 0142B] the perfection of both is completed. And because I have said that deaths of this sort are called passages, you should rightly know that those dead in the Lord are proclaimed blessed, in whom God’s grace lovingly works so kindly that they are found to glory more fully not only in the first death but also in the second.

And if we and those like us are not granted the grace of martyrdom, namely to be killed for the Lord by the hands of persecutors, it is at least fitting that we strive with our utmost power to die in the Lord, so that, being dead, we may enjoy the blessedness proclaimed: “Blessed indeed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14). Your profession, moreover, and the humble habit which it displays, already show you dead through the first death of the righteous. If you do not prove yourself delicate and idle in its exercise, [Col. 0142C] I shall not easily say that you are without experience of martyrdom.

The second death will complete its labour, perhaps grievous indeed, but far more happily, when that spirit of yours departs from this present wicked age; when, the bond of flesh by which it is held being broken, it is brought into that long-desired sanctuary of God. When it has come there, it will no longer seek instruction from me, a little man, but, seeing the Creator, will know more fully who in that fellowship of saints glories in the title of confessor, and who is crowned, by a greater grace, with the glory of martyrdom. May He bring us alike to either of these and introduce us into His Lordly joy—He who, in the goodness that is His own, called us though undeserving, and, having made us dead by the first death, mercifully invited us to the second. Farewell.

## LETTER XV. PHILIP TO ADAM. A Letter of Remonstrance.

[Col. 0142D]

“Among you the first shall be last” (John 5)—indeed, as I seem to see, not even last. For I have no man, when the water has been stirred, to put me into the pool. For while I wish to come, another stronger than I goes down before me; and so hope, once lively, now grows sickly, and, while the matter is prolonged beyond what is right, loses its greenness and turns ashen. Once your graciousness promised a fire that knows no ashes, and, to confess it to you, hope smiled upon me in my credulity. But because a certain change, as it were, in the atmosphere did not permit the truth to follow at its due time, my credulity has now ceased to trust in promises.

No one ought to doubt how much truth pleases Christ, since He wished quite plainly to call Himself Truth: “I am,” He says, “the truth” (John 14), so that we may know that whatever is done contrary to truth does not please Christ Himself, and that what does not please Him has no glory before God. Nor are you unaware that in many places of divine Scripture mercy and truth are coupled, that all the ways of the Lord are called mercy and truth, that “God loves mercy and truth” (Ps. 83), and that “mercy and truth have met one another” (Ps. 48). To what end is this, unless it is to show that a social grace flourishes between these virtues, a certain welcome kinship held by an indissoluble bond, so that in all things which we are commanded to do justly and beneficially they may wish to stand together and not be separated [Col. 0143B] from one another?

Mercy leads us to will a good thing; truth brings us to carry that same thing out. And so that harmonious love between them may be worthily celebrated, serene peace forbids an alien perversity to interrupt such fellowship. For it is not lawful that any unseemly intermediary should break in between mercy and truth, interrupting them as they meet one another, presuming to find a place of its own between them and, once it has found it, compelling them to recoil from one another.

Mercy is present when we desire to do any good thing, when with devout affection we especially wish to benefit someone. In this we show mercy not only to our neighbours but also to ourselves, for it is first necessary that we ourselves be stirred with devout spirit toward the good. Hence you have read: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Sirach 30). And: “A merciful man does good to his own soul” (Prov. 11). But when mercy has arisen in us for willing, truth must immediately meet it for holding firm: truth which preserves unbending the affection of mercy and the purpose of a devout will, and fortifies them against the assault of harmful perversity. [Col. 0143C]

For there is a certain perversity more certainly and plainly called falsehood, which always lays snares for a devout purpose, acting and striving so that the necessary presence of truth may not bring the benefit of sought holiness to effect. Since truth is always hateful to that falsehood, while it is by no means unwelcome to the aforesaid mercy, that wicked and crafty thing, envying the good which mercy has already proposed, places itself in the middle so that it may not be brought to completion by truth’s meeting it. Raging in many ways, it wishes utterly to remove the seed that has sprung up; and if it does not uproot it entirely, it at least strives to delay it, so that falsehood joined with delay may assail mercy and wage war against truth.

For they contrive that either a richer person, or a more tender affection of the flesh, or perhaps some other plague, may presume to leap into the middle, repelling mercy and striving to forestall truth. When truth has been forestalled, the enemy rejoices and envy exults; saddened truth laments because it does not meet its friendly virtue. For, considering a good thing mercifully begun but not truly completed because the aforesaid plague intervenes, it complains that those who should be undivided are divided, an inseparable companionship separated, right unjustly depressed, and justice utterly violated against justice. [Col. 0144A]

Mercy seems to forget its promise; truth, driven far away, can scarcely remember mercy. With hard obstacles cast between them, they no longer seek their friendly intercourse and cry to one another: “An unseemly chasm has been fixed between us.” Truth is indignant because, when it ought to meet mercy, a richer person intervenes; it is indignant again because a more tender affection of the flesh finds a place before it. And since there is no one who fittingly restores the separated pair to union, truth, striking deaf ears, thunders terribly through Scripture: “God does not accept the person of man” (Deut. 10). And again: “He who loves him or her more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10).

You know that these and similar things are contained in truthful Scripture, by which it is clear that truth does not wish to be prevented from a righteous purpose, but to be set before private concerns and our own wills, to meet mercy more surely, with nothing contrary interposed. After, therefore, at mercy’s prompting, you spoke a good and consoling word [Col. 0144B] and, moved by its impulse alone, promised a benefit: who bewitched you? Who hindered you from yielding to truth, from giving place instead to injustice, from opening the door to earthly power? If rank or kinship ought to have moved you, who more worthy, who by right nearer to God, ought to have appeared to you than He from whom, your Creator and the Creator of all—as no one doubts—you both existed and could do this very thing of which we speak? For you have read: “He made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. 99). And: “All power is from the Lord God” (Rom. 13).

Therefore you received from Him, who also granted you existence, the ability to give freely the freely promised benefit. But in choosing to turn aside to another party, you presumed, with insufficiently cautious confidence, not from Him but against Him who truly is Truth. In this not only is truth injured, because it does not meet the preceding mercy, but peace also complains because justice does not go before it; and since peace is not likewise allowed to find justice coming to meet it, it has no one to whom it wishes or is able to grant a welcome kiss.

For as mercy and truth rejoice to meet one another, so justice and peace kiss one another by a certain bond of covenant; and this kiss of theirs follows in due order when the meeting of the former pair duly precedes it. [Col. 0144D] For as soon as truth meets or encounters mercy, and the good purpose is fulfilled with no contrary thing intervening, justice is present, watching and carefully considering; and what it understands to have been rightly done it commends, approves, and confidently exalts.

But whatever is done with truth removed, justice does not recognize at all, nor does it wish to be present at an action in which carnal affection prevails. Rather, it works hard to strike more severely with an opposing point and to condemn more sternly whatever injustice disfigures. Thus, raging against the perpetrator of fault, it gives a threatening sentence; with stern countenance and harsh hand it brings troubles, drives away peace; and when our impatience judges that it is treated too unjustly, justice cries that we are rightly burdened according to our deserts. For it belongs to justice to leave absolutely nothing unpunished, but to pursue by chastisement whatever is found irreverent or undisciplined; and sometimes it wishes to be considered all the more swift toward vengeance because, once guilt has been punished, it intends at times to show mercy.

But if the fault has not been committed through grace’s gift and our own effort, or, truth having been recovered, has already been dismissed through the merit of repentance, justice—which knows how to be gentle only toward good works—loves to stand by us when we hold to truth. [Col. 0145A] Favouring our purpose, it now threatens terrible punishments to our enemies, presents to the just Judge what we do justly, and asks that God, who is Truth, may advance our truth: “His eyes,” as you have read, “behold equity” (Ps. 16). The just Lord does not turn His ears from its prayers; rather, hearing and answering, He turns its petitioning hope into reality. And lest perhaps a delay in the thing He promises burden the petitioner, He immediately sends peace to meet justice, to confirm the covenant.

I mean the peace by which we now hold with firmer confidence that we are reconciled to God; by which, our faults now deleted, we do not fear to suffer future punishments; by which the refreshment of a sounder conscience feeds and satisfies us, counting light whatever threats or more grievous troubles the world brings. Hence it is written: “A secure mind is a continual feast” (Prov. 15). This peace—than which nothing is more praiseworthy or desirable in this life, and which many desire as more wholesome and sweeter than any deceit—seems to wish to console us more firmly, and so loves not merely to meet justice but also to kiss it.

In this is sufficiently made clear what justice deserves and what, by its own merit, it gains not only in the future but also in the present, lest anyone falsely suppose that he receives the benefit of peace without having merited either just truth or true justice. For peace does not think that truthful justice ought to be deferred from its reward, but meets it more swiftly, smiles upon it more joyfully, and greets it; rushing into an embrace, it offers a kiss with uniting affection, marking enduring love with a confirming covenant. [Col. 0145C]

You see that when truth, as is fitting, meets or encounters mercy, justice is immediately present, and peace meets justice; they strike a firm covenant and form themselves into a four-horse chariot, appointing Christ as leader or charioteer of its foursquare form.

The first wheel is mercy, which always runs ahead in good works; the second is truth, which must immediately meet it. Joined upon one and the same axle, they rejoice to be borne together, proceed at equal pace, and not be removed from one another. But if truth is withdrawn from mercy, its purpose having been injured, the two-horse chariot falls, lies powerless, and is reckoned as nothing; lacking one foot and leaning too much upon the other, which is owed its counterpart, it cannot move, but is fixed, as it were, more deeply in mud.

The rear part of the four-horse chariot places first the wheel of justice, the inseparable follower or companion of the preceding virtues. For what they delight to accomplish by their mutual meeting, justice commends, judging it worthy of reward. For this reward it immediately wishes peace to be present, which makes the conscience of the worker secure from distrust; which removes from it the biting stings [Col. 0146A] of fear, cherishes love, advances faith, and makes hope serene. Hence Paul says: “The Lord, the just Judge, will render to me” (2 Tim. 4). Justice and peace, therefore, are likewise joined on one axle and follow the union of their predecessors in equal fellowship. When these are rightly arranged, the vehicle becomes foursquare, right order is enacted, and the work is made complete.

Upon a vehicle of this sort, made foursquare by the aforesaid number of wheels, all our action must rely and our whole conduct must be established, so that, supported and undergirded by such protection, it may proceed securely and, through saving progress, be happily carried from the depths to the heights. For without this vehicle no person’s work can be carried to perfection; without it Elijah, Elisha’s master, was not caught up on high. But the disciple recognizes this foursquare form in his master when he asks that his spirit may be present with him twofold: “Let the spirit that is in you,” he says, “be double in me” (4 Kings 2).

When I consider those men borne and lifted up by the foursquare order of the virtues mentioned above, but see you, on the contrary, carelessly recoil from that same union, I am astonished and grieved that the divine law places the same yoke upon you, yet your negligence does not put its neck beneath that yoke. You too, surely, like them, are the chariot of Israel; you are the charioteer; you ought to be carried in the four-horse chariot, at whose first front, as has likewise just been said, truth is the second wheel. Once its integrity is injured, the remaining series is unfruitful and vain. [Col. 0146B]

Feeling that the rims, spokes, hub, and axle of this wheel are shattered in an unexpected crash, and that the noise harshly strikes his ears, he cries out—whoever loves the worthy foursquareness of a work, whoever hates with the hatred proper to such foursquareness its defect or breaking: “My soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab” (Song 6). Aminadab is interpreted “the willing one of my people,” signifying Christ, who willingly offered Himself for His people, so that each person might in return offer to Him both what is his own and himself.

This Aminadab wishes whatever is offered to Him to be made foursquare by the aforesaid virtues: at the front of the work, truth joined to mercy; in the final—or rather the highest—part, justice and peace kissing one another; and whatever we do consecrated in this fashion or order by the fourfold arrangement. We shatter such a fourfold structure or chariot with a heavy hammer and wickedly violate the sacred mystery when we separate truth’s presence [Col. 0146D] from mercy and, justice being banished, do not taste the grace of peace.

For this reason every saint who is a fervent champion of truth, a lover of equity, a censor of conduct, and our corrector when we err, grieves deeply and wastes away, gnashes his teeth and is angry; his soul, zealous with its zeal, is troubled over the chariots of Aminadab. For seeing these chariots not carried at their due course but broken by our fault, and harmful affections set before them, he cannot, in zeal for truth, fail to be troubled, grieving over the wrongs which he sees inflicted upon Aminadab Himself.

Much more does Aminadab Himself, Christ, who, as stated above, wished to be called Truth, grow indignant when He feels truth injured and perceives that justice is not truly loved. Angry with one who does not love what He commanded or firmly keep His law, He rightly denies him His peace. Once it is denied, He reproaches through Isaiah, saying: “If you had attended to the commandments, your peace would have become like a river” (Isa. 48). David agrees with Him, saying: “Great peace have they who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Ps. 118). [Col. 0147A]

It is plain, therefore, that through contempt for truth and neglect of the commandments peace is denied, stumbling is introduced, and the force of evils prevails. Yet I do not wish it to prevail over you—even though I have said these things; for I do not judge it fitting to rejoice in the sad evils of one’s neighbours. Indeed, to speak truthfully, I long and deeply desire that you be freed from your present burden, that your sorrows be stilled and your joys prosper more sweetly; that you be brought back to the love of truth by a stronger anchor, and more sweetly led into the desired harbour of repose and peace.

## LETTER XVI. PHILIP TO PHILIP. He commends virtues worthy of noblemen.

[Col. 0147B]

Philip, to his Philip.

The heading above whispers that you are mine and I am yours; and would that no destructive thing might arise against such a whisper! Would that mighty grace, remaining in you as it has begun, might work until it completes its course and be perfected without end! This is indeed the grace which by its will made you a human being when you did not exist; which, by greater goodness, washed you in the living font when you already existed; which brought you to the years of puberty and the bloom of adolescence, and, as you entered the threshold of youth, now shone upon you more abundantly and clearly.

Your father lives and has not yet failed in strength; and with his consent, not a human being but grace made you a count. What is far greater, it did not reject your lordship as Saul’s was rejected: while it removed far from a powerful youth the pride of a courtier and youthful desires. These and such things made you mine—that is, welcome and worthy of my embrace—and commendable; though I have not yet seen your face, they made you not unknown to me. For I do not yet know even my own face, and nevertheless know myself far better than anyone else.

Since, therefore, I know and feel divine grace working wonderfully in you, and you effectively and willingly submitting yourself to grace at work, I love more and rejoice more to see your inner mind thus than I should to see your outward face, which you will display even to those who do not love you. Thus seeing you, and not begrudging your excellence though I am not yet known to you, I too am yours, since I am devoted to your progress. I am yours in favouring you, rejoicing affectionately with you, and lightly urging you with the spur that you may bring the journey well begun to perfection. [Col. 0147D]

For though you have many learned and devout persons to stand by you—for such as a prince is, such are those he finds to serve him—and though their exhorting voice does not cease rightly to urge you on, I think that a spur secretly applied to a horse already admitted to the course will not hinder it. Know, then, that it is not deemed specially praiseworthy to be of great family, since often in a nobleman a spirit basely degenerate grows weak; nor is it a great thing to stand pre-eminent by the eminence of any rank if the excellence of fitting virtue does not adorn that rank.

But whoever attentively sees that, in the principality, lineage, and youth by which you excel, you are endowed not so much with these as with knowledge and virtue, cannot, unless held by hatred or envy, fail to rejoice or fail to marvel at this rarity as at the unique phoenix bird. For if a noble young prince does not incline his body to the enticements of passive male prostitutes, but reclines only in lawful marriage-bed and embraces that are lawful alone; if, when gifts are offered, he does not bend his hooked hand toward avarice, nor fatten its hungry ardour by stripping the poor—this is a wonderful and remarkable thing, not easily found in marketplace or crossroads; and the rarer and more splendid it is, the more it is sought by a distinguished prince. [Col. 0148A]

A good prince not only withdraws foot and inclination from what is unlawful, but by fuller grace hastens more eagerly toward perfection. Thinking little of being sluggish toward vices as though he were powerfully ill, he stretches forward toward the things before him and burns more vehemently with love of righteousness. If, therefore, he perceives anyone even murmuring against the laws; if any rich person rages against a poor person; if a robber dares to rage against the Church—lest harmful poison spread while discipline languishes feebly—he swiftly draws the sword from its sheath. Though the dullness of some carnal people murmurs against him (for strength always finds opponents and is a sign that is contradicted), nevertheless, aflame with zeal, he goes forth like Phinehas (Num. 25) and does not withdraw the dagger until he has exacted worthy punishment from the presumptuous.

There are some who, when they hear a zealous prince praised, and hear it proclaimed how severely he has punished this or that offence, bite and pervert what is justly done with satirical tooth; and, as if horrified, wash their hands with Pilate the judge (Matt. 27). He burns, but with love; not suddenly, but in accordance with settled custom. Yet these wicked interpreters attribute it to anger and indiscriminate impulse. He drives out one nail with another, judging a wound rightly to require a wound; the envious murmuring of detractors falsely says that the physician is mad. Their detraction is false, though it wants to be thought truthful criticism; it wishes to draw the prince back lest he strive to advance to the summit of justice, lest under his protection orphan and widow rejoice to be cherished and Christ’s monasteries be protected from the teeth of robbers. [Col. 0148C]

But should this somehow come to the prince’s ears or attention, far be it from him to consent to recoil from a just purpose. Rather, he should love to outrun wicked tongues and unjust lips, so that he may seem to throw at those labouring in vain the saying of a certain pagan: “Your horse is panting at the beginning of the slope.” Nevertheless, lest Satan, the tempter, seize anything in the prince, and lest that wicked and crafty one stain the purity of justice with any blemish, the prince should return into himself, humbly remember God, and pray to Him in David’s words or something similar: “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God” (Ps. 142); and, “Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it. Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice” (Ps. 118).

If he has perhaps learned letters—knowledge of them is not confined to clerics, for many in lay rank or order know letters—then, sometimes free from military tumult or business, he ought to take up a book and, as in a mirror, contemplate himself. [Col. 0149A]

There are polished treatises, letters, and writings, both of pagans and of orthodox authors, that offer to noblemen lessons of no small usefulness: they adorn rank, order military service, strengthen youth, build character, sharpen minds, and advance men to virtue; they rebuke sluggishness, rouse zeal, describe equity, moderate anger, commend clemency, and recommend gentleness. A prince of noble mind does not disdain to read or hear these and similar works, nor does he utterly crush the remembrance of them beneath temporal concerns. He judges it unworthy to lend his ear to tales or his hand to dice, rather than to take up a little book, at least furtively, at a suitable hour.

I saw, as I recall, Count Charles, while he stood at the divine altars, reverently and fittingly occupied with the psalms that were to be read; and as a polished sword was fitting when the time came to exact vengeance, so a little book was fitting to the devout prince at the time for reading. I also saw Count Ayulf, noble by birth, distinguished in appearance, formed in character, who rendered great thanks to his parents because they had made him learned from childhood. In speaking with me he showed himself so Latin that he seemed nothing but a cleric; yet he showed himself so much a soldier that shortly afterward he died fighting pagans for his homeland. [Col. 0149B]

For strong military service does not detract from learning, nor does honourable literary learning detract from military service. Indeed, in a prince such a union of the two is so useful and fitting that, as the aforesaid Ayulf maintained, a prince whom literary learning does not ennoble is, through no small degeneracy, rustic and in a sense bestial.

For, since both your parents’ care enabled you from childhood to know letters, and since heavenly grace has enabled you to do what letters proclaim and commend, continue as you do—or rather, make progress, and in progressing bring to completion what you have begun—loving purely Him from whom you received both the will and the power to do this. For it is not by your own merit, but by His benefit, that you are granted both to live and to live rightly; nor is it through yourself, but through Him, that your power rules over others. He often grants kingship, at least for this present time, even to evil men; yet, though making them kings, He does not crown them with His own honor or glory. “By me,” He says, “kings reign” (Prov. VIII).

When He raises certain persons up, He permits them to flourish in whatever power, while nevertheless, by a judgment known to Himself, He determines not to grant them heavenly things. Thus the better sort may take heed and reflect, and may not love ruling here beyond measure, since they see that it is not peculiar to the good but shared by them with the reprobate. But those to whom, by the goodness that is His own, He grants knowledge of the rule of truth, and upon whom He bestows grace to hold fast to it—these He raises on high and gives a seat upon the throne, so that the benefit received may not remain hidden from others.

Therefore, since you understand what is just and gladly pursue with devotion what you understand, grace favors you and indeed provides for your advancement. If, however, you were a private person, dwelling humbly as an equal among inferiors, you would not possess the reward promised to the just except by the merit of justice. Yet because that same grace has set you over not merely one person, one rank, or one province, but rather has made one man ruler over many, I see this as advantageous not only for you but for all your subjects: for the peace and tranquillity which their multitude requires for itself are nourished and guarded for them by you—by your strong diligence and your equally diligent strength.

Happy are those who have deserved to have as their defender one who is still passing through the years of tender youth, yet possesses the character and prudence of mature old age: a man of counsel, prudent in speech, abundant in charity toward Christ’s poor, steadfast in justice, effective in purpose, and fruitful in his concern for his subjects. The more securely flourishing discipline makes them live, and the more it keeps them free beneath your wings from tumult and plunder, the more they should recognize themselves as bound and indebted to you; they should be worthily anxious to repay you and, because of their obligation, readier to do so.

For all and each must pray to the divine majesty on your behalf, and with untiring devotion renew their prayers and offerings, that His goodness may confirm you in goodness; that, according to the Apostle (I Tim. II), peace and tranquillity may be preserved; and that He may increase what you have not yet strength to accomplish, though it may perhaps not be owing to your merits. Nor are only those who enjoy your protection and are sheltered by your defense, who through your patronage obtain the desired benefit of peace, your debtors. All foreigners or distant persons also, if they are lovers of God, are rightfully beholden to you and without doubt your debtors. For whoever are bound together everywhere by unity of faith and love must rejoice, like the mutually joined members of a body, in one another’s health; and, seeing in another what he has not yet deserved to obtain in himself, a person cannot fail to rejoice.

Since, therefore, within your borders one part of the Church now flourishes and rests, while another still labors abroad, the latter is nevertheless made joyful by the health which it sees or hears of in the former. It smiles not only upon those to whom it sees so great a benefit happily given, but also upon you, whose vigilance is devoted to this end. Accordingly, whenever all who are children of the Church faithfully worship and adore God hear that you are such a man, they favor you, love you, and pray for you. Whatever their devout intercession can do—if it can do anything, or rather, because it can—this you make your own and acquire, not being content with your own merit alone.

Thus all those are yours through whose abundance you are found richer; and you are theirs, through whose prayer and goodwill you are guarded. For your sake they stand in their own place and labor in the spiritual battle; they sustain you as you labor in temporal rule and business. Relying on that defense, you will safely penetrate the camps of malignant enemies. A guest in the world, not a citizen devoted to it, you will not love the world’s contagions. With your side girded with a sword, you will serve not the world but the Church; you will reject the blind tyranny of Nero, Alexander, and any men like them.

Nor will the non-deceptive prompting of many persons now present mislead you; nor will the example of other rulers induce you to tear your subjects apart. Such rulers, possessing an appearance of faith but lacking merits and virtue, oppress and crush with Egyptian servitude those whom they ought to protect and soothe. Divine Providence has already in some measure foreshadowed that you will remain free from their disposition and conduct, when at your recent birth it assigned you a proper name; when, from among so many diverse names, it chose one to be set apart, and by a sufficiently provident counsel decreed that you should be called Philip.

Now Philip is interpreted “mouth of a lamp,” or “mouth of hands.” Such an interpretation, as I seem to see, suits your rule. You do not follow the multitude of other rulers with a blinded or greedy eye, concealing the grace of inner light entrusted to you beneath dug earth or a bushel; rather, like a lamp with a broad and open mouth, you pour it forth and diffuse it more brightly. Nor is it inconsistent with this that Philip is also called “mouth of hands,” since the fact that God has made you a ruler is declared by the speech of your deeds; what either your devotion or the divine ordering conceives and intends in your rule, your hand—that is, your action—plainly speaks and shows.

Therefore both “mouth of a lamp” and “mouth of hands” seem rightly applicable to you; and regenerating grace chose to find for you a very suitable name, because a luminous generosity of spirit commends your rule, and none of your actions is compressed into silence, but is outspoken. Yet the more precious this height is—not so much of name as of merit—the more rarely it is possessed by the multitude of other rulers. Many who are exalted upon a throne are cast down into the abyss of vices, and, not knowing the Lord, are nevertheless unknown by Him. Of such persons He says: “They have reigned, but not by me; they have been princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. VIII).

May the merciful power and powerful mercy of God turn you away from following them; and, having turned you away from the reprobate, may He convert you ever more fully to the love of justice. Thus, when the course of this present life is ended, when not rulers simply but righteous rulers shall dare to present themselves to the supreme ruler—who does not reject the mighty, since He Himself is mighty—may He deign to place you, mighty as you are, with Himself upon His throne.

## LETTER XVII. FROM PHILIP TO HENRY. On the same subject.

[Col. 0151D]

Many great men send great gifts to you, a great man, whether they already possess your favor or hope for it; and the gifts sent are welcome to you either because of their own value, or because their donors perhaps make them precious through their own favor. But I can neither present myself to you as welcome—indeed, I have not yet deserved even to be known by you—nor do I seem to add anything great to your abundance. Therefore I fear that I may seem presumptuously to stretch out a short hand toward lofty matters, since I, a little man, send you, a great man, nothing but small prayers and worthless pages.

Yet the report of certain people has repeatedly encouraged me to do this. It has commended you as a noble man endowed with a still nobler grace, because so distinguished are the gifts of grace present in so great a ruler that they may be found quite rare in other rulers of this kind. For, they say, you graciously hear and regard one who is poor and wretched indeed, possessing a patient heart and a hand open to give. You know that merciful devotion and the almsgiving of one who has compassion act against the incentives of sins like water that extinguishes fire.

Be present, then, with favor to the cries of orphans, the groans of widows, the sick lying helpless, and lepers; ward off or relieve their want with abundant gifts. Thus no one can now doubt that this charity, so widely poured out, has passed into you, his son, from your father, both by example and by merit. For just as the sins of fathers are punished to the third and fourth generation in children resembling them, so it is not unreasonable to believe that the good merits of parents are displayed in the same order; and their justice is found to benefit their children considerably, since the character of the latter frequently conforms to the model of those who went before.

Moreover, that father of yours, distinguished by marvelous generosity toward the poor, whose mind greed did not ensnare and whose hand avarice did not bind—he fortified you, whom he intended as his heir, with honorable learning, by prudently educating you from boyhood in the liberal studies. And rightly so. Since noble blood and lineage make a man noble; possessions make him rich; and servitude or the service of dependents makes him a lord, it was fitting that literary knowledge should lead you forth from the ignorance of common people and the stupid blindness of brutish men, and make you endowed with splendid freedom.

For this reason the pagans rightly call literary learning “liberal”: because literary grace, obtained through labor and study, frees the person who receives it from confused association with the crowd and from the common multitude, lest he be kept weighed down and oppressed by the fetter and dullness of rusticity. Therefore you owe much to your father, whose care and diligence thus provided for you. He did not begrudge his son not only what was his own, but also what he himself had not deserved to obtain; and when he arranged that the excellence of your countship should make you ruler over many peoples, he wished you also to be raised above other counts by knowledge of letters.

You likewise owe much—indeed, very much—to God’s grace and such great goodness. By its help and working, you and your father jointly accomplished something honorable and useful: your father through care, command, exhortation, persuasion; you through affection, study, character, and obedience. Through the concurrence of these things, after pursuing school discipline for several years beneath the master’s rod, you attained liberal learning. According to the measure of your time and rank, you have been so thoroughly imbued, as they say, with letters that you surpass very many clerics, though you are by no means counted among their number.

Although, in applying yourself to letters, you did not foresee that you would become a cleric, but expected to be girded with the sword-belt and entangled in military affairs, you did not grow sluggish toward letters through hatred or contempt. Rather, by labor together with grace, you acquired for yourself a commendable learning. Moreover, though you have attained through letters the grace and progress of understanding, you devote to them a certain diligence and affection of mind. A noble soldier and commander of soldiers, you love and honor armored warriors in such a way that, in the manner of a cleric, you love letters and generously welcome learned men.

At times you lay aside military business, the causes of disputants, and the noise of courts; claiming yourself for yourself, you return to clerical leisure. Taking up a book, you rejoice in the course of reading as it unfolds, in which, as in a mirror, your perfected countenance shines for you. For whether you reread the writings of pagans or of Catholics and search books, provided you do not find it burdensome, as a prudent reader, to separate the precious from the worthless according to the counsel of the prophet (Jer. XV), you discover what befits the people, the soldier, the ruler, or the prelate; and for what purpose either fortune, according to the pagans, or God’s grace, according to Catholics, has given you rule above others.

You discover also what your high rank owes to superiors, equals, and inferiors—beyond or short of which due measure uprightness cannot stand. Uprightness abhors crooked deviation and loves, and declares worthy of love, whatever accords with nature, character, and worthy honor; whatever is due to God, to one’s neighbor, and to religious holiness.

When you read and frequently reread these and similar matters in Scripture, understanding them prudently and taking care to distinguish the profitable from every harmful thing, you do not cease to be a ruler or a noble governor of peoples, nor do you degenerate into idleness. Rather, you in some way regenerate yourself in the liberal waters of the ancients. The turbid waters of Rezin are offered by the dullness of the popular law-courts; but the depth of the literary well contains the waters of Siloam. Those waters are poured out through streets and squares in streams like rainwater; these are enclosed, as though under a seal, within a flowering garden and beside a clear spring.

The condition of a servile mind and the brutish men of the forum are overwhelmed by the flood of the former waters; the rarity of the latter is more pleasingly attained by those noble in understanding, eager in affection, and free in spirit. And while many approach and attain the lofty presence of the spring, so far as I can see, just as those who do not understand do not drink, so only those who love are refreshed.

There are indeed innumerable persons who pass over letters with a deaf understanding; there are more who understand them but neglect to embrace them in affection. They know, yet do not inwardly perceive: languishing through disgust rather than love, like an ass eating thistles, they are moved neither by juice nor flavor. Others, quite rare amid the many ranks just described, are agile in understanding, patient in study, and not ignorant of learning. When they have found letters, they are so greedy in love of them that, however distinguished they may be by wealth, birth, or the eminence of rank, they nevertheless do not allow letters to slip away through lavish contempt. Rather, they hold and preserve them with a hooked hand; indeed, to say more, they anxiously gather them ever more often with open eye or ear.

Although occupied by outward cares, such persons do not lay aside their love and concern for letters. They never say, “It is enough”; they set no limit to learning. When time and care permit, they revisit and frequent letters; withdrawing from business, they give themselves to literary leisure. Nor is it idle leisure to serve letters, but useful business: in them one more frequently discovers what rightly gives pleasure or advantage. God, I think, wished them to be cultivated in the Church for this purpose: that through frequent use of the letters, He whom they proclaim might be known and more deeply loved.

For although God has chosen to employ several dissimilar languages among the various nations of humankind, and to distinguish many regions from one another by differing speech or unite them by the same tongue, He wishes, unless I am mistaken, that language to be preferred by a certain privilege of reverence and love which He wishes to be used among sacred ecclesiastical matters and transmitted to posterity in writing. Hebrew and Greek were indeed given in that order to the fathers of old; yet because they come to us, as it were, from afar not by use but only by report, our understanding, having taken leave of them, applies itself as best it can to the Latin before us. And unless we are hard and reprobate, affection follows understanding.

Each person should therefore revere with affectionate veneration the language through which he hears the true God more expressly proclaimed to him; through which our redemption, the resurrection of all, and the glorification of the saints are more truly made known; and through which, to state the matter briefly, knowledge itself of God and of the things that are God’s dawns upon those who read and do not neglect to read. Therefore the noble workshop of letters rightly pleases a noble man, since through its exercise is forged the saving discipline of character, knowledge, and faith. Even if every other common language is ready at hand to anyone, if Latin is not, then—with his permission, I would say—an asinine dullness holds him captive.

Recognizing this rightly, you do not neglect the Latin language and literary learning, and you love and honor those whom you perceive to be especially learned: showing reverence to all who are your superiors, rewarding many inferiors with gifts, and rescuing needy men from oppressive necessities. Because of this, devouring Envy—who, according to a certain pagan author, delights in assailing the highest things, and, though perhaps she does not dare to bite the face of the greater, always dares to bite the heel—

> [Note: [Col. 0153D] Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, Book I.]

—seeing that you love learned men and gather them with a liberal hand, and being unable to endure this, adds and spreads poisonous speeches.

Envy also sees that, as a wise architect, you lay new foundations for churches, build walls, and hasten to add roofs.

> [Note: [Col. 0153] Note the foundation of the priory of Saint Martin of the Fields.]

Loving the beauty of God’s house, you give fitting ornaments to its interior: gold, silver, stones, books, chalices, vestments. Finally, whatever you judge fitting for ecclesiastical use or adornment, you prepare with such diligence that you seem not to feel the loss involved in the expense. Seeing, I say, that you are so concerned in such matters, Envy cannot but waste away and cannot remain silent.

It is also a sign spoken against that in these same churches you delight to gather clerics, whom secular custom has chosen to call “secular” because of a certain freedom in their manner of life.
