You gladly provide them with the necessary and regular revenues, so that they may gladly and continually offer themselves there willingly for service. When they gather and solemn psalmody is sung, when harmonious melody resounds with hymns, canticles, and sweet organs, you delight, as they say, in something like the harmony of the firmament and stars—or, more correctly, in a foreshadowing of angelic symphony and heavenly songs.

In these matters, as I judge, you ought not rashly to be condemned, nor should what is done well be wickedly reckoned evil. For no one doubts that Christ wills churches to be dedicated to Himself, and we know that from ancient times, by apostolic authority, clerics have been ordained in them. Far be it from any wise person so to presume to accuse these clerics as also to judge those who wished to gather such men in churches, since the purpose of those who gather them is set upon this end and directed to this intention: that God may be served in churches through clerical ministry and literary labor.

From one end of the world to the other, antiquity has exalted the clerical order and assigned it the chief rank among all other orders. Divine ordering, although it sometimes bestows a greater gift of holiness upon a soldier or a peasant, nevertheless chose to prefer the cleric by the excellence of ecclesiastical dignity. Thus the Roman Church, and the very many churches which have flowed from it in different places and times, have shone with clerics in an unbroken succession reaching down to us. Although many of them, as human beings, incline toward the weak and needy elements of the world, authority and power do not depart from their order and title on that account.

They hold both the Apostolic See and all other bishoprics everywhere. By the merit of their authority, they judge soldier and populace alike. By hand and mouth they consecrate the sacraments of baptism and of the altar; they establish laws for all and teach the path of saving life. Even those who, because they are thought to bind more tightly the relaxed rule of life, are called by the special name “religious” or “regular”—over them too, I say, apostles, archbishops, bishops, and their clerics preside and rule by the privilege of their rank. Let those religious persons themselves see whether they also possess the fitting holiness owed to that rank.

Holiness befitting the dignity of clerics who preside is commanded to all, but it is not immediately attached to each of them as an inseparable companion. For in cleric and layperson alike holiness exists only through God’s grace or love; dignity, however, is sometimes a cause of wrath and of heavier judgment. It is written: “A most severe judgment shall be for those who rule” (Wis. VI).

Therefore, when you carefully raise the cleric above the layperson by discriminating honor and reverence, and when you give him more abundant gifts of money or revenues, you embrace, as I judge, more the order than the individual by divine understanding; and you extend your hand in affection not to the man, but to the name. Paul says: “To whom honor, honor; to whom tribute, tribute” (Rom. XIII). You pay honor to an order established by the ancient fathers; you give the tribute of sustenance necessary to the Church militant, knowing that a branch lies low and does not attempt to rise upward unless the prophetic elm—or some other support—sustains it.

Let no one judge you in this; let no one dare to twist your purpose toward the sinister side, lest a rash judge deserve, with far greater justice, to displease God. For this action of yours can be pleasing to God and profitable to you, and divine propitiation need not fail those whom you gather. Finally, just as Judas Iscariot, ruined by wickedness, was found among the holy and chosen apostles (Matt. XXVI), so among secular pagans a centurion was found more pleasing to God (Acts X). Thus no one should place excessive confidence in a religious habit assumed, nor should anyone rashly despair beforehand of those who seem to have left behind the linen garment.

I hope, however, that divine justice will not render void your work, both in building churches and gathering clerics. If perhaps you understand something differently, God’s own goodness will reveal this to you; and what has been begun by a ruler’s hand so liberal and solicitous, once what is partial has been done away with, will be brought more fully to perfection. For He who willingly ordained that churches should be founded for Himself, that the primacy of the whole Church should from ancient times be assigned to clerics, and that so solemn an institution should be transmitted down to us through a long succession of days—He, I say, will not permit in these days the wrath of the envious or the words of detractors to prosper. Rather, He will advance with saving honor the clerics and all who rightly love clerics; He will foster their good deeds and more mercifully spare their faults.

Whoever, among whatever peoples or places, desires to be a cleric ought, as a debtor and beneficiary, to repay you for your love of clerics. He ought to pray to God more devoutly and unceasingly offer the sacrifices of prayer, that God may at last will you to be with Him among those clerics whom merit together with grace will make perfect in glory. Nor should one doubt that the benevolent majesty of God hears—indeed, answers—the prayers of such persons. In the present Church He bestowed upon them an eminent dignity for this purpose: that, about to pray for their own ignorance and that of others, they might approach with greater confidence because more familiarly; and that, presuming upon the benefit by virtue of their office as prelates, they might intercede for the errors of all.

Their intercession is found especially living and more powerfully effective for the person whom it renders God propitious and to whom it grants the desired benefit: namely, the one who in reciprocal affection loves the order through which such diligent help is given to others, and repays like with like in a willing spirit. Thus a devout layperson makes his own, as though by a price paid, what belongs properly to the cleric: the cleric readily satisfies by prayer; the layperson by ready affection. The former, somewhat more confident, performs and perseveres in the role of envoy going beforehand; the latter, loving the envoy, joins himself steadily to him and stands beside him. And truly, those to whom God now gives such a great gift of mutual love in return, He Himself also loves, receives, and crowns in the kingdom of heaven. Those whom, during the time of their earthly sojourn, He makes rejoice in one another, when the world’s end is closed He grants eternally to glory in Himself, the Lord. Farewell. May those also fare well who desire that you fare well.

## LETTER XVIII. FROM PHILIP TO RICHER. Literary studies are necessary for ecclesiastical men.

[Col. 0157A]

Concerning you, dearest brother, many people have spoken to me one after another. Perhaps their feelings differed, but they were unanimous in offering very favorable praise. With kindly speech they have reported to me things known to themselves and pleasing to me; but they have not yet afforded me an opportunity of seeing your face. Yet the more I hear so many and such things recounted about you alone, the more I desire, as is customary, to behold your face: not to send a message to one absent, but to give a word of grace or greeting to one present, and to venerate your gray hairs, which have acquired the reverence of old age.

My mind, whatever its quality, is not wholly deprived of the benefit of seeing, since it more gladly beholds your inward rather than your outward face: that face, I mean, which neither grows pale, burns with fever, nor falls ill; which is not wrinkled by the old age of years, but ripens through the pursuit of virtues. Seeing it, I understand; and understanding it, I delight to see it. It is presented to me; I sense that it smiles upon me. Though the face of dying flesh is far removed and unknown, the form of the mind, destined to end under no limit, shines forth for me.

Such ought to be those who inhabit the schoolroom, who forge the discipline of learning by the hammer of study or the anvil of knowledge—such as faithful report commends you to kindly ears; and there is no one who would criticize the one who commends you, unless perhaps malicious Envy. So far as I understand, you have studied, indeed still study, to devote yourself to scholastic pursuits. You love to be a disciple, desiring not so much to be heard as to hear, so that, taught by hearing, you may more cautiously reject harmful things, and, freed from them, may more affectionately love and more diligently choose profitable things.

For to know what must be done and not to perceive it with diligent affection is not merely useless but harmful, since any petty learned person, if ill-disposed, thereby gathers an incentive to sin. Wisdom refuses to enter an ill-disposed soul (Wis. I); and when it is set outside, a person is convicted of not inwardly perceiving what he knows.

When knowledge does not taste good to the person who knows, when its flavor is not felt in the inward taste, when one holds merely the words and does not experience sweetness, when one does not apply love or affection to the good things understood, what does such a person produce except an understanding empty, needy, and utterly useless? Indeed, just as knowledge forms and instructs, ennobles and illumines the diligent person, so the same knowledge puffs up and destroys, accuses and rebukes the negligent conscience (I Cor. VIII). Devoid of weight and withdrawn from solid truth, like chaff exposed to the wind, it delivers that conscience into the precipice of sin.

Thus you see very many who learn very much, even constantly, but arrive late or never at the knowledge of truth (II Tim. III). The more curiously they apply labor and study to learning, the farther they wander from wisdom. Ecclesiastes, representing their type, says (ch. VII): “I said, ‘I shall become wise,’ and wisdom itself departed farther from me.” For when they have collected Aristotle’s opinions or Plato’s, Quintilian’s rhetorical colors, and Cicero’s gathered flowers; when they have drunk and been saturated with a flood of turbid waters; when they have acquired, through many labors, the ragged learning of pagans—they do not by this study free themselves from error or truly excuse themselves from negligence, since they either wholly fail to know or refuse the waters of Siloam, which flow silently.

Of such people a certain pagan says: “You drink another water.” If perhaps, using sounder counsel and applying their minds to reason, they sometime undertake to devote themselves to divine reading, they generally merely rinse their lips, as it were, at the Hippocrene spring. They do not thirst for what they read or draw it in by inner love. Because there is so great a multitude of such persons, whom the hammer and anvil of study exercise in the scholastic furnace, I would call happy and excellent the one whom the rectitude of divine grace so cherishes and advances that love of learning does not abandon him and holiness of life holds him fast.

For holiness without knowledge often wanders into error or does not shine forth fully; and knowledge without holiness teems with the worms of vices and is defiled. But when these are united in what is plainly an indivisible bond, nothing more useful and nothing more honorable can be found in human life.

Happy, therefore, is the person who has received this benefit of grace, who is polished by the file and study alike for knowing and for living. Such a person moves among scholarly companions and fellow students in such a way that he is held to be their model or mirror in both respects. For amid young people, not to follow youthful ways; amid broad license, not to range about with looser reins; amid restless and slippery persons, to restrain oneself by strict moderation—who would not judge this worthy of praise? What wise person would not strive to imitate it?

But if—God forbid—the disorder of the assembled students is so great, if Babylon’s confusion is such that neither reading nor the example of a life proposed moves them to live better, still the citizen of Jerusalem possesses grace and holiness possesses its merit; the multitude of those around him, or perhaps of detractors, does not bend his purpose. Just as moral or spiritual reading strikes those who live childishly, so the honorable conduct of any persons offends the perverse and reprobate. From that from which the good person is corrected and receives an increase in virtue, the wicked person incurs a more grievous loss and becomes worse.

But, as you know, a school is like a field indiscriminately planted with trees of every kind, or like a marketplace into which everyone flows and where they do not all remain in one quiet condition. In the former, a good cultivator raises some trees and uproots others; in the latter, a buyer rejoices and gathers goods, while a seller laments and begs. So, as you know better, is scholastic discipline: in it, one person is advanced by a more agile intellect and eagle-like subtlety; another is held back by crude sense and asinine dullness. One makes progress toward a better life through reading and instruction; another, lying according to his own ways, remains lying in a wallow or sewer.

But the one who excels in study and understanding among the idle and obscure, and what is more excellent, burns with spirit and advances in life and character amid the hard-hearted—what is he but a fruitful olive among barren and thorny brambles, or a shining carbuncle among dark stones? Therefore, as I seem to see, a school ought to be called a second cloister: it supplies many examples worthy of imitation to those gathered there; it calls those more diligently devoted to reading away from public affairs and turns them aside; it either weakens or converts their reprobate affections.

Although a superior person cannot always succeed in rousing an inferior to act, nevertheless one devoted to reading provokes others to read by example. Reading once undertaken has a certain grace and profit of occupation, although occupation alone suffices for no one’s perfection. Yet, apart from those things which unquestionably produce true wisdom and virtue of mind, by whose benefit each person gathers merit for himself and reaches certain salvation, I judge nothing more fitting for a cleric than to cling to literary studies, hold a book in hand, and sit frequently at reading: to practice this not only in childhood, adolescence, and youth, but, far more pleasantly and sweetly, in old age flourishing with gray hair.

Finally, whoever, whether younger or older, loves to profess himself a cleric—I wonder with what hardness he refuses to look upon letters, with what pride or contempt he resists frequent reading, and why he lives more eagerly among riches than among the delights of letters. I wonder why those who possess ability, leisure, and resources do not also possess an insatiable desire and delight in knowing. Why do they prefer to frequent markets rather than schools, crossroads rather than places of retirement; why do they prefer to display gilded chalices rather than written books, money rather than learning? I wonder, I say, why they do not set literary exercise before all else—unless perhaps they expend something more necessary, saving, and spiritual upon themselves or their neighbors. For no age or rank among clerics ought rightly to be blamed if, rejecting public affairs, it loves to be occupied with reading.

Therefore the regular cloister rightly holds the first and chief place among clerics. In its reclining-place is celebrated leisure—or rather, saving work—where private possessions having been cut off, grafted activity prevails and bears fruit, divine reading is cultivated, and contemplative perfection is forged. But scholastic life ought to claim the second place for itself. For love of it, the prudent cleric chooses to leave secular things behind, so that, if lacking the fare and fitness to board the ship of the cloister, he does not suffer ruinous shipwreck but takes hold of a nearby skiff or plank.

If, abandoning even that, he flows down to the weak and needy things of the world, which erase letters and are recognized as foreign to a cleric, he has become far removed from the right hand. As shipwreck gains strength, he veers toward the opposite side, from which scarcely, or never, either salvation or honor swims out or emerges. Since you have prudently considered this, I wish to urge you more diligently to persevere. If you do not enter upon the first course, beware of turning your purpose toward the last. Flying between the two, continue what you do: hold fast to the plank you hold and cling to it, a prudent inhabitant of the schools, rejecting wandering rather than sitting still.

Read—indeed reread—the holy books, which compose and set before you the vehicle or four-horse chariot of virtues. They establish as its guide and charioteer not the typical Elijah but Christ. Carried upward by it, if you close the evening and final day of old age, you will come to the desired prize, to the goal of life and salvation.

## LETTER XIX. FROM PHILIP TO RAYNALD. He congratulates a noble, learned, and pious man on having been raised to ecclesiastical prelacy.

Among the many and great affairs to which you are compelled to devote your care, I think this present page will scarcely find you unoccupied; and for this reason it is not surprising if, at first encounter with it, you hasten immediately to pass on, and, busied with the greatest matters, disdain whatever is smallest and most trifling. Yet sometimes a prudent man condescends, amid serious matters, to lighter ones; amid lofty business he seizes even a brief leisure. Amid the roar of arms, he withdraws and steals himself away for himself—or rather, restores himself to himself; [Col. 0160B] he reads, listens, reflects, and meditates upon something useful.

Happy are human affairs when their governance and management are entrusted to such men: men who are strong and discerning, confidently dispatched to every task; who are not broken when the sea rages with hardship and adversity, nor, when the sky has cleared, rely upon prosperity beyond what is fitting. By grace bestowed, they are commendably equipped not only with courage and the sword, but with prudence and counsel; they keep watch for the Church, fight for their country, promptly resist and press their enemies, knowing that, just as strength of hand and courage made Judas Maccabaeus illustrious (1 Macc. III), so the surpassing depth of profound counsel made his brother Simon illustrious (1 Macc. XIII). Finally, in Solomon’s words: “As deep water, so is counsel in the heart of a man” (Prov. XX).

If, by God’s ordering, the care of affairs is entrusted to such a [Col. 0160C] man; if command is added more powerfully to his counsel, or counsel to his considered strength: government flourishes, the Church prospers, the crowd settles into a people, enemies are subdued, pride lies low, and unbelief gnashes its teeth and wastes away.

From the beginning divine goodness wisely ordained, and in its providence did not deny its benefit to its realm or to its Church, when it gave to you, a noble man, both the clerical profession and, with a more generous hand than is customary among nobles, literary learning. For certain nobles devoted to literary study are so idle that they delight in the open streets, or in fleshly things and carnal pleasures in their chamber; and they think nothing harder than [Col. 0160D] prolonged study and instruction, thus making themselves unworthy of advancement to ecclesiastical eminence. Observing this, that Prince by whose hand and authority dignities are bestowed—and likewise clergy and people, whose office it is to choose clergy as their leaders—were truly neither deceived nor led astray by ignorance or error when they advanced you, illustrious in letters, character, and rank, to a worthier station.

There you have deserved an exceptional favour of birth, while, as a prelate, you seem to embrace a good work more than an honour. Desiring to obtain a name from the thing itself, you watch and labour more than others; fighting for the peace of those entrusted to you, you show yourself an enemy to their enemies. Although in this warfare you do not yourself draw the sword from its sheath, nevertheless you lead forward against the enemies of the realm those who do draw it. You sustain them by expenditure, advance them by encouragement, govern them by counsel, strengthen them by integrity; [Col. 0161A] and, lest anyone rightly find fault with you, you go before them in the honourableness of your life.

For as your magnanimity makes you burdensome to enemies in war, so your manner of life makes you hateful to rivals, because most malignant envy finds in you no blemish of disgrace; and therefore, sharpening its tooth, it reproves only what is worthy of praise. Rightly, then, as I see it, has ecclesiastical dignity been conferred upon you; rightly has the highest direction of affairs after, and from, the prince been entrusted to your counsel. In it, as a prudent craftsman, you have found suitable material for administering affairs—a material that makes you conspicuous; or rather, you anticipated it by your conspicuous integrity.

For dignity did not confer integrity upon you, but raised up the integrity it found; and integrity once found makes dignity worthy. In a remarkable way, integrity makes you good, but dignity does not thereby make you [Col. 0161B] worthy; for dignity, sometimes bestowed upon an unworthy man, does not adorn him, but reveals him as unworthy. Integrity, however, always adorns and makes dignity conspicuous. Thus dignity requires integrity as inseparable from itself; if it is lacking to one who seeks dignity, he who was previously base becomes baser, and the light of dignity makes his disgrace more plainly visible to many.

Integrity, then, possesses grace even when it lacks the summit of dignity; while dignity, when deprived of the benefit of integrity, possesses only punishment. Yet the blind ambition of many thirsts for and insatiably seeks dignity, whereas the sound love of a few strives for, and by striving attains, integrity. Therefore let your graciousness consider and attend more carefully to what the Giver of this grace intends and purposes, [Col. 0161C] when with a more generous hand he extends gifts to you—great gifts indeed, since they make men great, though they do not yet bring them to completion.

If you rightly defer to the prince, and reverence his majesty with faithful service, because he has given you, not alone, that dignity which you share with the unworthy: consider what you owe—what love, reverence, and affection—to him who alone has bestowed on you upright character, honourable learning, and prudent understanding. Certainly he must be believed to have conferred on you not only these things, which no human being has been found able to bestow upon another, but also ecclesiastical dignity itself. For his excellence and majesty above all kings are so great that through him kings reign, and from him comes all power whatsoever for all persons (Prov. VIII).

[Col. 0161D] Therefore know that whatever good you have received, you have from him; whatever you are and whatever strength you possess, you owe first and chiefly to him. Rejoicing in present glory and honour through his gift and grace, bind yourself to him—not with a rope of tow, but more strongly by affection and love. For who, unless he is mean in spirit, does not become a giver back, whether immediately or later, to one who first gives? Who does not become the follower of the giver of a reward? Though unequal in resources and unable to repay measure for measure, who at least does not strive to be found devoted and well-disposed toward him?

If a lover of empty glory wishes to be thought generous and lavish toward a seller, will you refuse to show yourself grateful and indebted to the Giver of heavenly grace? He who first loved you wishes to be loved in return. Giving you his gifts, he asks that yours be given to him—or rather, seeking you yourself, he wishes you, not your possessions, to be offered for his good pleasure. Yet he does not reject your possessions; rather, he wishes you to be preferred before all that belongs to you. He does not regard and accept you for the sake of your possessions, but rather your possessions for your sake. He to whom belong the world and its fullness [Col. 0162A] (Ps. XXIII) does not contend for the offering of bulls and rams. Desiring only you, he is not troubled by covetousness for your things; he judges that gift base which is not adorned by the love or affection of those who offer it.

But that he should will and seek you, and delight more in you yourself than in your gift, is not merited by your nobility, your magnanimity, or, finally, your dignity. It comes from his goodness and grace, which is his own and mercifully goes before you; it has made, or will make, you worthy to be chosen and loved—it did not find you so. Hence, when necessity demands it, you lead forth the battle-line, and in grave danger find victory standing by your side; and when you triumph, you give spoils and the victor’s laurel to the soldier, while you bow your neck beneath the yoke of humility with remarkable strength of mind. As you deigned to indicate in your letter to me, you did not wish to ascribe to yourself any of the things victoriously accomplished; rather, since the flight undertaken showed many overthrown by few, you plainly affirmed that this was the work not of yourself, nor of man, but of the divine Name.

[Col. 0162B] You perceived the truth of the matter well with keen understanding, and did not suppress it, like the envious, in miserly silence. You remembered that mighty David, when he rejoiced in the trophies of victory, asked that glory be given not to himself but to the Lord. “Not unto us,” he says, “O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory” (Ps. CXIII). David saw that peace through victory had been won for him not by his own bow, sword, or arrow, but by the mighty arm of God. When, triumphing over enemies, he gloried not in himself but in the Lord, he looked upon his humble conscience far more victoriously and fruitfully.

For, seeing prosperity smile more sweetly upon him with a serene countenance, he deemed it fitting to applaud it with the same steadfastness of mind as though from above; [Note: [Col. 0161D] That is, to applaud.] and, praising amid a great people (Ps. XXXIV), he was not carried away like chaff by every wind, but, attributing all things to God, humbly rested upon the foundation of an instructed conscience.

Therefore you are wise, and it neither disgraces your learning nor your dignity that, amid vain and worldly things, you confess the truth with your [Col. 0162D] own lips. Seeing, once clouds have been dispersed, the favourable sun shining forth, you do not ascribe it to human beings, lest you seem wickedly to begrudge divine works. You are wise, I say, when, seeing soldier and people glory in victory after the human fashion, you do not join them in like manner, but congratulate them with due moderation. With the prophet you rejoice so as to fear, and fear so as also to rejoice, remembering adversity in the day of prosperity (Ecclus. XI).

Therefore, when the multitude perhaps is swept into rejoicing with hearts not so much devout as unrestrained, you wisely summon humble and devout persons to prayer. Not relying upon the pleasing smile of circumstances as upon a reed-staff, you ask to be aided by the urgency of prayers, without becoming lax concerning their efficacy. This indeed I desire you to do; rather, I desire you to advance more earnestly in what you have begun, and to watch over the Church in such a way that you may fulfil the burden laid upon you more fruitfully. Since Imperial Highness has wished to impose upon you military responsibility, render in it saving obedience to the highest King.

For an earthly king, as you know much better, does not prejudice the supreme King—unless, heaven forbid, he perversely opposes the highest law. But when he is understood to command for the Church and for the country, [Col. 0163A] the subject ought without doubt to obey a saving command. Thus we often see some set out on campaign who desire not to shed blood but to obtain peace through victory; whom not the frenzy of malice, but the law of obedience, girds with the sword-belt; who rejoice not in the slaughter of enemies but rather in a triumphant conclusion.

It is fitting that you likewise be such in the actions of war which you have undertaken: that you take part in secular affairs in such a manner and with such an intention that, while in the sight of the proud both authority and necessity show you as a singularly stern man, within the enclosure of a composed mind the presence of fear and love may preserve you in the rule. Thus, serving as a soldier of God according to Paul (2 Tim. II), you will not entangle yourself in secular affairs; and according to the laws of princes, you will draw arrow from quiver and sword from sheath. As a priest and a victim, you will show yourself approved in the frying-pan of fear; as a leader or standard-bearer, you will restrain the enemies of the empire from carrying their presumptuous malice into effect.

Modesty of character, meditation upon the Scriptures, the maturity of watchful honourableness, care for the altar, reverence for the Church, and worthy consideration of your dignity [Col. 0163C] will preserve you as a cleric, as a priest, and as a bishop to us in reality as well as in name—although royal authority, necessity of affairs, and integrity of faith may sometimes bring you into military service. In this service, however, as a soldier of Christ, you will rightly take courage if you do not presume upon hatred of darkness, rage, or malice; but, as a provident steward, lead forth armed men into battle in such a way that you would prefer to make enemies sons of peace rather than cast them out, slaughtered like beasts, through pathless fields.

Thus Church and peace will perceive you as their defender and lover; the soldier as a vigorous leader, and the field of Mars as a warrior. Thus you will appear father to sons, soldier to soldiers, enemy to enemies; thus, finally, in a manner sufficiently difficult but still possible, you will make yourself all things to all people. [Col. 0163D] Strongly equipped with prudence, you will be able to do all things—not by your own arm alone, but aided by another. You will be able, I say, if you cling bravely to the stronger God, if you ascribe your power not to man but more truly and humbly to the Creator.

That you may more effectually desire and be able to do what I say, do not be ashamed to take your model more carefully from a beggar. As he diligently seeks his necessary alms from door to door, so do you, with unwearied course, recall in order the fathers who have gone before.

Moses, leader of the people, described by Scripture as the meekest of all in converse with God (Num. XII), and accustomed to the hard exercises of war (Exod. XIX), now advances, orders, and arranges the battle-line; now prays, and opposes himself to God’s anger for the sinful people (Exod. XVII). When, because of the destroyed sons of Korah, an unbearable scourge of fire that had gone out from the Lord raged among the people [Col. 0164A] (Num. XVI), Aaron, the first high priest—whose place you hold in the office of bishop—stood between the dead and the living, offered incense, pleaded with the Lord, appeased wrath, and stopped the burning. Though a great part of the sinners was slain, the greater part was delivered.

Joshua, not by weapons of war but by sounding trumpets signifying the word and doctrine, and by a sevenfold circuit prefiguring in spirit the commendable discipline of character and deeds, shook the city of Jericho. When its walls fell of themselves, he entered, sparing no one except Rahab and whoever obeyed her warnings (Josh. VI).

Gideon, about to engage the Midianites in grievous battle (Judg. VII), placing no hope in bow or sword, instructed three hundred men, after his own example, to sound trumpets and to reveal lamps placed inside broken jars. By a marvellous means he triumphed over the innumerable host of enemies, and showed you, who are to succeed him, a model of victory not to be despised. As I see it, the strength of those fighting lies in trumpets, jars, and lamps; if you attend to them, there is much beauty of sacred mystery. In the trumpets is figured the exhorting voice and resounding preaching of prelates; in the broken jars, mortification of the flesh and the subduing of lighter impulses; [Col. 0164B] in the displayed lamps, good repute and a form shining worthily and illuminating the eyes of subjects.

Concerning the trumpets, the Lord says through Isaiah: “Cry aloud, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. LVIII). Concerning the jars, Paul says: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected” (1 Cor. IX). Concerning the lamps, Christ himself says: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works” (Matt. V).

David, the noble king and most powerful conqueror of his rebels, compassionate toward those he had conquered and their humble merciful protector, forbade the sons of Zeruiah to lay hands upon Saul, the Lord’s anointed (1 Sam. XXIV). Later, when Saul had died in battle, grief-stricken, he cursed the mountains of Gilboa (2 Sam. I). Thus he rejoiced that the palm of victory or honour should be given to Joab, commander of the army, yet he could not deny Saul the mourning and honour due to mercy.

Later, when internal sedition raged throughout the whole land, and a son had armed the cruel minds of a perverse [Col. 0164D] legion against his father, David so favoured the victory of his own men that, conversely, he mourned Absalom’s death (2 Sam. XVIII). Thus he honoured divine grace that he could scarcely endure the anger of its just vengeance.

Do not cease prudently to recall these and similar persons, whom divine reading indicates as exercising military service, not malice. In the grave peril of war, they neither thought that they should lie idle under the shadow of shelter in degenerate cowardice, nor wished men who had been killed to be cast aside; rather, they mercifully and manfully desired the conquered to be subjected.

Whatever a soldier, a member of the populace, or any unlearned person of this order may do—one to whom discernment of the divine law and the sequence of Scripture are unknown—a prudent man, learned in letters and occupying a position of oversight, disdains to be held in enervating softness either at home or in warfare. Rather, pressing on with a robust mind, he attacks more severely and persistently the malice of those who resist, while not ceasing, according to the written law, to love human beings because they are human beings. [Col. 0165A] “Do this, and you shall live” (Luke X). Indeed, you do and will do this, and you will undoubtedly not lack victory, because, now victor over yourself, you will rejoice more over yourself than over another. For everyone is said, justice so judging, to be worth more as ruler of himself than as conqueror of many cities. Farewell.

## LETTER XX. PHILIP TO RICHER. He commends the study of letters.

You do what is yours to do. It is characteristic of lovers to seek what they love; and neither the eye by sight nor the ear by hearing is satisfied with it, especially when sound conscience is joined to love. For some love [Col. 0165B] and seek what they love, but do not seek it rightly because they do not love rightly. But those who love rightly also seek rightly what they love; and right love follows, and worthily attains a right end—yet not failing, but rather advancing toward perfection.

As I have perceived, you love letters—indeed, sacred letters. Their reading, according to Paul (1 Tim. IV), instructs toward salvation; their love advances one from virtue to virtue. Their reader and lover does not lack the fruit or reward of loving, but one who seeks finds, provided that he comes by the right way of seeking.

Yet when you ask that these same writings be poured out to you from a dry spring, from a poor vein, you do not sufficiently consider that you err, nor do you moderately confuse me. For when you demand from [Col. 0165C] me what I am altogether unable to provide, you do not sufficiently consider that you are mistaken, while I, being unequal to it, am greatly embarrassed. In this, however, you are not deceived: you do not ask for the fables and inventions of poets, the snares of sophists, or the arguments of deceivers; nor, finally, for anything else by which vanity may exult, truth be disturbed and shaken. You ask for that which may nourish and, as you say, refresh your soul.

You testify that this gift is dearer to you than any gift, indeed more precious; and, as your letter declares, you suppose that it can be sent by me. You do not consider that carrying wood into a forest is judged useless, not to say foolish; and in my field there grows not even sturdy timber, but fragile reed. You possess and inhabit Kiriath-sepher, the city, as it is read, of letters; you possess the divine books, the abundant storehouses of Scripture. You possess the wine-cellar, that house of spices, Solomon’s portico; you possess what the sequence of divine reading declares useful for refreshing the soul.

You read and understand what is useful for doctrine, character, and holiness; you add love, and join understanding to charity. What reading proclaims and the understanding of the reader grasps, the love and inward affection of the lover embrace. Since, therefore, apprehension of present things will certainly lead you to the attainment of supercelestial things, why you should demand my words or counsels, which are of no importance, is not apparent—unless perhaps because intemperate love judges nothing sufficient for itself as long as it sees anything delayed or lacking.

Thus the people, who think themselves empty [Col. 0166A] and void, rightly groan with Jeremiah and, suffering hunger, seek bread; and every carnal person gives what the world considers great and precious in order that spiritual food and refreshment may be supplied to him. Yet whatever he receives, his soul is not yet satisfied here, and love of heavenly things does not yet rejoice in the fullness it desires. Since his hunger or beggary can be satisfied by no present things, he nevertheless prays for and rejoices to receive them for the refreshment of his soul. “All the people groaning and seeking bread; they gave all their precious things for food, to refresh the soul” (Lam. I).

But when some carnal people see spiritual persons thus worn down, begging for spiritual things, hindered from transitory gains, despising visible things and ensnared by love of invisible things, [Col. 0166B] they scorn, mock, and reject them as refuse, often inflicting loss upon them either by words or by blows. Hence it is added in Lamentations: “See, O Lord, and consider, for I have become vile” (ibid.). God, who inspires and turns the soul to love him, does not turn his merciful eyes away from that same soul; but he looks within the lover and carefully considers one who is outwardly vile, weighing love worthily and compensating lowliness with the benefit of a better hope.

Those whom contempt for present things has made vile in the eyes of fools, hope bestowed will surely make safe—or rather, has made safe. For though present life was able to have them as strangers and pilgrims, it could not hold them; hope, fortified by certainty of the thing hoped for, has already made them citizens of the saints.

[Col. 0166C] Therefore, as I have observed, you rightly call yourself a pilgrim from time to time in your letters. Whoever thinks rightly knows that while living here he is a sojourner. And not only in Paris, where you sometimes reside for the sake of letters, but wherever on earth or in whatever place you may be, you lodge as a traveller in transit. A guest for a single night, since he does not intend to remain long there, does not lay a stable foundation for a house but pitches a tent for himself. When morning comes, he takes it down and goes elsewhere; his foot does not rest until he is at last granted arrival in the country he desires.

This is your understanding, this is what you remember, this indeed is what I perceive you to think. I rejoice to find it not once but repeatedly in your letters; nor do you show it only by word or tongue, but by life and character, [Col. 0166D] stretching yourself by the gift of grace not backward toward the last things but forward toward the best. To this end every trumpet or literary horn sounds and resounds; to this end tend the books of the Gentiles and the spiritual page of divine books. Finally, to this end all reading or Scripture is given to us, in which, if you read devoutly, either the Maker or his work is understood.

It is decreed by the highest law, and more firmly implanted in every creature, that nothing begotten is constant, but is of mutable nature; and whatever among bodily and spiritual things, whether together or one after another, began to exist, did not receive natural immutability. If, however, any human or angelic spirit is now found to stand immutably, it receives this not by merit of its condition, but through the grace of him who [Col. 0167A] created it.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] The author does not deny that angels and human souls are ungenerated and incorruptible by nature, since they can altogether be reduced to nothing by God. For he alone is essence; and the rest, a little below. Yet, as is elsewhere said, that portion of angels who love God is confirmed in its purpose by grace and by the merit of free will, . . . so that what was mutable by nature . . . cannot be changed by grace; and: grace confirmed better the angels who had been created good. Likewise: he has already established certain angels by the benefit of his will, not of their nature. For confirmation in grace comes from grace.]

What the law of nature denies to all creatures made from nothing, the all-powerful grace of the Creator bestows, who, whenever he wills, has power over creation. The wise ought to know this natural mutability of things for this purpose: that with utmost effort they may beware of being ensnared by error or love of such things, and that no one may presume in any way to cling to things which cannot themselves remain in a stable state by their own power.

You must therefore pass onward, and in pilgrim fashion continue to journey and make progress. You must judge that every creature, like a tent, is insufficient for you; nor must you cease advancing until you arrive and find something great surpassing every creature—namely, him who created all mutable things and alone is immutable by nature. He alone is essence, and naturally shines forth in essential excellence; he knows no motion of change, no shadow of alteration: from eternity he is truly the great, almighty, immortal God, special not through the grace of anyone greater, but by the peculiar privilege of his nature.

[Col. 0167B] Not only the preaching and Scripture of teachers, but the creation, mutability, and nature of all things proclaim and exalt him. Since all things show themselves to have been created with the manifest evidence of inherent mutability, they establish and commend an uncreated and immutable Creator.

Therefore, since the prudent reader can understand him in every Scripture, and the discerning interpreter admire him in every creature, considering every created thing worthily, he will always seek the face of the Creator. Nothing below him and nothing above him will satisfy the soul of the lover. Below him there is indeed nothing that ought to suffice [Col. 0167C] or be preferred; above him there is nothing, since he is known to surpass all things in the excellence of eternity. The understanding of the truly wise perceives him as first and last; the love and affection of those who understand rightly perceive him as the highest good, truly and supremely worthy of love.

Concerning him, when, as you say, with loving zeal you seek new things as an emulator of those who study well, you deserve to find in him, not in me, what you ask. For as the wicked will seek and not find (John VII), so he offers himself to the good and is found; whoever asks receives, and to one who knocks his sanctuary is opened (Matt. VII). You rightly profess yourself an emulator of those who study well; in this you neither hide beneath a bushel nor are held by the vice of presumption. You remember that pagan who called himself not a *sophos*, as his predecessors had done, but a philosopher; [Col. 0167D] he proclaimed himself publicly not wise, but a lover of wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 0168D] Pythagoras.]

Those who inhabit the schools ought to know that none of them yet studies well enough if he does not labour with fitting diligence to knock at the sanctuary just mentioned; if he does not read, understand, and love this labour to the end that, by suitable progress, he may desire and be able to follow and attain the Creator (1 Cor. [Col. 0168A] XIV). Finally, just as one who turns away from the sanctuary, being ignorant, is unknown, so animal wisdom is judged foolishness—or folly (1 Cor. III). Although any lost person may seem to know many things, he is not wise but unwise while he does not care to enter the Lord’s sanctuary.

Ask, seek, knock, enter the bridegroom’s chamber, where peace kisses righteousness and the soul is united to the Word of God by a nuptial covenant. When you arrive there and say within yourself, “It is good for us to be here” (Matt. XVII), bidding farewell not only to vices but also to worldly affairs, you will rejoice to dwell among angels.

I ask, moreover, that, when things go well with you, you remember me at least a little, that, standing before the divine countenance, you may pray more affectionately for me. And when divine goodness has poured into you a fuller gift of grace, attend to your joy in such a way that you make me a participant [Col. 0168B] in your richer abundance. For that charity which, according to Paul (Rom. V), is poured out in our hearts through the Spirit, abounds more in one who pours more of it back upon his neighbour. Whereas most other things cannot both be given and retained whole by those who give them, this, though bestowed upon many, is found in a marvellous way to be possessed more fully by those who have bestowed it more fully.

I pray that this charity may build up your learning and raise it to saving progress, so that, when what is partial has been done away with, you may at last pass more happily to perfection. Farewell.

## LETTER XXI. PHILIP TO WILLIAM. A letter of recommendation.

I have heard good news. Divine goodness has poured and infused joy and gladness into my hearing, and “my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; moreover, my flesh also rested in hope” (Ps. XV). A good word, a good report, has reached the ears of my old age; ears long deafened by the harsh noise of wicked living, frequently battered by it, now breathe again with the new melody of a better reputation.

“The smell of my son is as the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. XXVII), spreading far and wide. The more fully it refreshes and nourishes those who are present and love him, the more sweetly it does so. By divine grace it has not defrauded me in my absence, and I have heard what I long desired to hear and have rejoiced.

Fame has presented to me that Samuel—yes, that Samuel—who, succeeding the aged [Col. 0168D] Eli in place and office, was chosen as a prophet (1 Sam. VII): to anoint others, both prophets and kings; boldly to rebuke and reject Saul, guilty of disobedience; and to anoint, admonish, and advance the better David to an everlasting kingdom (1 Sam. XV). It has also raised up for me the spirit of the boy Daniel (Dan. XIII), who restores judgment to the rule of truth, condemns the shameless elders, and [Col. 0169A] through zeal for justice frees and acquits Susanna, oppressed and crushed by the wrongs of the wicked.

“Blessed be God, who has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid” (Luke I): who has not despised the devout prayers of the Church or the voice of a widow pouring forth groans; who has given her such a father and such a son, one who watches over and devotes himself to her with paternal affection and filial love, receives her reverently as a mother, and diligently protects her as a daughter. Blessed, I say, be God, who has bestowed upon a young man, unusually fleeing youthful desires, grey-headed and discerning judgment, and, as the reward of a spotless life, the venerable throne of old age.

A rare bird indeed is a man young in years, noble by birth, distinguished in learning, eminent in dignity, solicitous for the churches, a hearer of the poor, and steadfast for what is just. “Who is this, that we may praise him?” (Ecclus. XXXI). Not to praise such a man belongs to the envious; yet we ought to praise not so much him as him who made him such. For the life of such a man is not the work of man but of God—or rather, of God and man: of God through grace that works, [Col. 0169B] and of man through obedience that cooperates. Thus both God and man should receive fitting praise.

Do, therefore, what you do; rather, advance and complete what you have begun, so that, with the help of him who bestowed upon you such grace and affection, you may lead and bring your intended holiness to perfection. Let not your majesty be offended, nor let it be imputed to insolence, if I, so small a little man, offer counsel and admonition to one so great. For, according to a certain pagan:

[Col. 0169C]

> There is no harm in applying the spur to a horse already set in motion.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] Ovid, *Epistles from Pontus*, book II, elegy 6.]

Nor is it considered absurd if an old man humbly urges a younger. Although you are far superior in dignity, you are much younger in age. As Paul says, it is fitting for a young man to flee (2 Tim. II); and an old man is commanded to meet the fugitive with loaves.

All look toward you as one placed on the watchtower (Isa. XXI), as one set in an eminent position; all observe you with greater curiosity. As all well-disposed persons will rejoice in your progress, so the wicked—whose number is beyond reckoning—will bite, slander, and devour you as bread for food (Ps. XIII). Since the eyes of all are fixed upon you, be watchful: like the two-faced Janus or many-eyed Argus of the fables, or rather, according to our writings, imitate more earnestly the four living creatures full of eyes before and behind [Col. 0169D] (Rev. IV). Through vigilant care see yourself thoroughly, examine yourself, know yourself, according to the saying of the Wise Man:

[Note: [Col. 0169D] Solon.]

> “Know yourself, O man.”

You will know yourself if, the greater you are, the more you humble yourself; if you recognize yourself not as one ruling over the clergy but as the servant of the servants of God; if you restrain, by fitting authority, not persons but the excesses of persons. You will know yourself if you swiftly cut off and more severely punish anything shameful or harmful that may perhaps break out from you, lest it grow strong, become wild, and the authority granted you seem to be permission to sin. For that pagan says:

[Note: [Col. 0169D] Sallust.]

> “In the highest fortune there is the least licence.”

Meditate upon these things; be occupied with them, so that your progress may be manifest to all, and, following the Apostle’s instruction to the young Timothy, “you may save both yourself and those who hear you” (1 Tim. IV). Farewell, and farewell for ever.

## LETTER XXII. JOHN TO PHILIP. On statements of Blessed Hilary in the book *On the Trinity*.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] Philip replies to this letter in the fifth of his letters.]

Brother John to his dearest kinsman Philip, greeting in the Saviour. Let every doubt be removed from your heart that my affection for you is great and everlasting; and let us speak of other matters.

I thank you for having sent the book I requested; I returned it quickly, however, because it seems to me to have had some erroneous author rather than blessed Athanasius, though it is falsely entitled with his name. Although in many matters it thinks rightly concerning the consubstantiality and distinction of persons in the Godhead—for no false doctrine fails to mingle some truths with itself—nevertheless in more matters it argues in a most questionable manner, and in some even stubbornly teaches error. For this reason it ought deservedly to be wholly rejected by those who chew the cud and have the cloven hoof.

For, among other things, in the tenth book, near the beginning, it says that our Lord did not receive the beginning of his body from Mary, but as it were from the Holy Spirit. The Catholic Church, however, maintains that in the conception of the Lord Jesus the Holy Spirit was not the material cause but the efficient cause, while the flesh of the holy Virgin was the material cause, so that she may be his true mother.

[Col. 0170C] Note what Bede, a man of Catholic authority, says on the Gospel saying, “Blessed is the womb that bore thee” (Luke XI), and on the words, “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I).

Likewise, contrary to the teaching of the orthodox, it declares that our Lord was neither sorrowful nor suffered pain in his passion. It ought not at all to be believed in this; rather, thanks should be given to him who, together with our flesh, voluntarily assumed even our affections without sin, and who, according to Isaiah (chapter LIII), is called a man of sorrows and is said to have borne our sorrows.

I have written these things in order to make your fraternity more cautious. Farewell, and pray for us.

## LETTER XXIII. JOHN TO PHILIP. On the same subject.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] Philip replies to the following letter in the sixth of his letters.]

To Brother Philip, John sends greetings in the Lord. There must be absolutely no doubt that love is most steadfast; we must proceed to the matter. Burdened with many affairs, I reply briefly. As I rejoice that you keep your eye upon the Scriptures, so I desire that it be a single eye. For, given the subtlety of minds and the multiplicity of Scriptures, it is easy for anyone to find supports for a dissenting opinion: just as, by his nimbleness, the hare finds many winding paths, and, by reason of the forest’s darkness, the wolf finds many hiding places. Thus perhaps that “fool who said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13), if patiently heard—even if he could in no way prove it, since falsehood is not proved—would nevertheless attempt to urge this point, saying at least to us: “Where is your God?” (Ps. 41). But we must not “overstep the boundaries set by the fathers” (Prov. 22).

I rejoice, moreover, that it is now agreed among you also that that book is not by the most trustworthy Athanasius, so that even its title must now be erased. Yet as to the body of the book, there is no doubt among us that many things in it are stated most excellently. For, as is written, there is no false doctrine which does not mingle in some truths. Nor are we ignorant why lepers, who are rejected by the Law even if leprosy is spread over only part of them, signify heretics. When you say that the Apostle says, “Read everything; hold fast to what is good,” we are surprised, since the text there is: “Test everything” (1 Thess. 5). We are not surprised that you have read that book, but that you approve it; for Ambrose says of such writings: “We read them so that they may not be read.” I therefore thought that this book should be read cautiously by the wise, but not at all by the simple; and I communicated my opinion to you as to one most dear.

But you—to whom I speak confidently, in accordance with what is written of certain persons in the descriptions of falsehood: “The labor of their lips shall cover them” (Ps. 139)—labor by saying many things in order to cover falsehood. “But even if an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel other than that which you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1). These are not my words, but the Apostle’s. We have received that the Lord Jesus Christ is one person from two natures: according to the divine nature, existing eternally from the Father; according to the human nature, beginning in time from his mother; and truly suffering with the perception of pain, truly dying, rising again, and possessing the remaining articles of faith. That you expend parchment in teaching that the conception of our Lord Jesus Christ was of the Holy Spirit, and therefore most exalted, pure, and holy; and that he suffered not by necessity but by will—I grieve for your loss of effort, since every simplest person in the Church knows this. I say this in jest.

But whoever thought contrary to this faith—whether Augustine, Hilary, or anyone else—must be believed either to have corrected the error itself before death, as your Augustine and ours corrected many things even in himself; or to have purged that very sin by virtues, as the blessed martyr Cyprian, according to Augustine’s testimony, expiated in himself the error of the Donatists by the virtue of his suffering; or to have remained unbelievers, as Origen did. We too possess an exposition on Matthew bearing the name of blessed Hilary. Although we venerate Hilary as most holy, we do not approve certain opinions set forth there, either because they are false or because they are troubling. Catholic books suited to simple people abound; therefore books that are troubling on account of the danger of offense ought rightly to be avoided, since the Apostle says: “Let no one deceive you by subtlety of speech” (Eph. 5). What you brought forward concerning blessed Maximus as testimony is irrelevant.

You know Origen, of whom Jerome says: “Where he is good, no one is better; yet because of certain things he is rejected.” When I found one of Origen’s books, without a title, in the library of a church in our region, I read it with great diligence and pleasure at the request of that church’s prior, because it was excellent in some respects. When I happened to find errors in it, I pointed them out and warned him not to read it thereafter. He willingly accepted this, and put the book out of his hands. Most dear friend, while burdened with many affairs and having scarcely leisure even to think, much less to write, I have written this reply, adding the Apostle’s statement: “If anyone wishes to be contentious, we have no such custom” (1 Cor. 11). I earnestly and affectionately request a special remembrance of me in your prayers. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIV. JOHN TO PHILIP

[Note: Philip replies to this following letter in the sixth and seventh of his letters.] On the same subject.

To Brother Philip, John sends greetings in the Lord. Since I did not reply sufficiently to the words of your letter, because its bearer was hurrying to return almost in the very hour in which he had arrived, I later added something: namely, that the book seems to contradict itself, and that you interpret it by force.

It contradicts itself, indeed, when it says: “Nor did it say that Mary gave origin to the body”; but below: “She used, it says, the office of a mother,” and the remaining words of that chapter. Likewise, from another chapter: “The Lord Jesus Christ suffered,” it says, “while he was struck, while he was suspended, while he was crucified, while he died; but the suffering which assailed the Lord’s body was not suffering, nor did it exercise the nature of suffering, although it raged in its penal operation, and the strength of the body received, without perception of pain, the force of the pain raging fiercely against it.” What is proclaimed here except contradictions, when he is said both to suffer and not to suffer?

You labor with much violence to explain this: whereas he says that Christ suffered without perception of punishment—the very point at issue—you say that he suffered willingly, a matter not doubtful even to children. And where the book says, “Nor did Mary give origin to the body”—which truly is an error, since the Psalm says, “Truth sprang up from the earth” (Ps. 84)—you explain it as meaning that he did not receive from her the vices of our origin. That is open doctrine. For Mary gave material origin to that body, not vice; and how different Mary and vice are, though you put one in place of the other.

In that conception, in which God was made from a human being, the righteous one from a sinful mass, unleavened bread from what was leavened, sanctification began not only in the one being born but also in the conception, or in her who was to conceive. Thus a righteous mother, by a righteous conception, might provide a righteous material origin for her righteous Son. The angel says: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). And the prophet: “Let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45). And: “As rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but water the earth” (Isa. 55)—that is, Mary—and soak it and cause it to bring forth fruit. For the mother herself to have no sin, “the Holy Spirit shall come upon you,” that is, in a more excellent manner; but in order that there might be neither the tinder of sin then nor thereafter, “the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). The prophet signifies both by snow, which is white and cold.

Therefore Christ’s body took its origin, not from vices, but from Mary wholly cleansed; just as the orthodox Church proclaims, as faithful and great Athanasius says: “God is begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages, and man is born from the substance of his mother in time.” On this chapter, all the divine books should suffice you, in which among other things it is written that what makes a man a heretic is not erring, but defending error.

On the second matter, in which Christ is proclaimed not to have suffered pain and to have possessed, even according to the flesh, a certain extraordinary strength—proved, as it were, by his walking upon the waves—we say that this is contrary to authorities and is supported by inadequate argument. We refute the argument thus: if the Lord’s body did not have the nature of our pain because it trod upon the waves, then Peter’s body also did not have the nature of our pain because it trod upon the waves. The same cause would yield the same conclusion—which is false.

But authorities proclaim Jesus weak. The Apostle says: “We preach Christ crucified” (1 Cor. 1); and again: “Though he was crucified from weakness” (2 Cor. 13); and again: “What is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1). And that great Adam received not bone for bone, but flesh for bone. Again: “In the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. 8), but not in sinful flesh. For there were, as you know, two things in the human race: sin and the punishment of sin. One of these—guilt—was not in Christ; the other—punishment—he assumed. Hence he says: “Then I paid for what I did not seize” (Ps. 68). Hence he is called “a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness” (Isa. 53): acquainted, that is, by experience, though he who is Wisdom itself is ignorant of nothing.

Jerome, on “By his bruise we are healed”: “It is clear that, as the body was scourged and torn, so the soul truly suffered for us, lest truth in part and falsehood in part be believed of Christ.” For the true man truly suffered. He had a nature such that, unless he ate, he would grow weak; if he walked upon the waves, he would sink; if crucified, he would die—unless by miracle he willed that this not occur. He himself also performed some of these things in certain others, as in Elijah, Moses, Peter, and Maurus. The punishments of certain martyrs also became refreshment: for Vincent, the roughness of potsherds was the sweetness of flowers. He too, when he wished, “passed through the midst of them and went his way” (Luke 4). But these things are to be ascribed not to his human nature, as you and your book say, but to divine miracle. Human nature, however, was weak before the resurrection, though he sometimes showed himself strong by divinity in miracles. The Church says of him in the Song of Songs: “His belly is ivory, adorned with sapphires.”

I also criticize what you said in your letter: that if one finds in it some opinion which can in no way agree with the rule of truth, that book is nevertheless not to be rejected. Truth is otherwise where faith is concerned. Therefore, in Christ’s sufferings we affirm both will and sacrament, power and triumph; and we also affirm as voluntary those things which the book, together with you, denies: necessity, nature, and compulsion. We must now come to the authorities of the saints which you opposed.

Pope Leo: “The devil wished to discover whether he had this self-restraint as a gift or as his own,” etc. We have determined this above, where we said that Christ possessed this strength of prolonged fasting not by nature but by miracle. For when the miracle ceased, nature immediately hungered; and by this the devil was deceived, so as to crucify the Lord of glory.

Augustine: “It must in no way be doubted,” he says, “that he was troubled not by weakness of mind, but by power”—one must supply “only.” For he was troubled not only by weakness but also by power, as we said above. He was troubled by weakness, as the Apostle teaches: “Though he was crucified from weakness,” etc. (2 Cor. 13). And he himself says: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Mark 14).

Bishop Maximus: “That Christ hungered as man,” he says, “was not bodily frailty, but a sacrament of heavenly grace”—one must supply: not bodily frailty only. This may indeed be said of all Christ’s sufferings and deeds. For example, Christ’s death was a sacrament, because it signified in us the death of sins or punishments, and the manner itself signified a manner; nevertheless, historically, he died.

Consider these things, dearest friend, and write back what seems to you concerning them; and pray for us. Farewell.

## LETTER XXV. HUNALD TO THE PROVOST

On the same subject.

Brother Hunald to Lord John, provost. The whole of your controversy, as it seems to me, consists in two chapters. I do not presume to settle it by my own judgment, but humbly seek with you the truth of the question proposed.

The first part of the dispute contains this: while each attacks the other, one defends Hilary’s denial that Christ had the beginning of his body from Mary. Yet in this, I judge that you do not think so differently, but merely contradict one another in words. You both agree that the Holy Spirit was the beginning of the virginal conception, and each of you likewise confesses that the blessed Virgin supplied seminal flesh for the conception. You both also call each a cause of Christ’s body, and hence a beginning—but, I think, equivocally.

For example, as Boethius testifies, “beginning” is predicated equivocally of point and unity, when one is affirmed to be the beginning of a line and the other the beginning of number. But equivocation, or any multiplicity of meaning, does not admit contradiction. Thus, although either one may affirm that Christ had a beginning from Mary, while Hilary says that he did not, the words indeed differ, but the senses do not contradict one another. For Hilary faithfully believes both beginnings. In writing, “The Virgin generated the body from herself,” he in some manner proclaims Mary to be a beginning. But when he confesses that Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit, he declares the Spirit too to be, in another manner, a beginning. “The body,” he says, “was not received from the elements of earthly conception, nor begun from earthly elements.” This, I think, is to be understood as follows.

He calls the elements of things their beginnings—that is, those causes which, under the governance of divine providence, produce the conception of bodies. These causes, or natures, unfold in the procreation of bodies those numerical principles which God created when he created all things together, assigned to them, and scattered in them seminally in the very act of creation; yet he did not bind his own power to them. By “earthly conception of bodies”—whence he likewise calls the bodies themselves earthly—he means that they are frail and weak, subject to corruption. He also judges the elements themselves by the same term, using the figure of speech in which the name of an effect is transferred back to the cause. Your adversary, however—but not your enemy—preferred to interpret “earthly” as “vicious,” unusually, though I do not say wrongly.

Those common causes, then, as I began to say, operate in generating bodies, as when grain or a tree arises from its seed. But in the virginal conception, it was not the customary course of nature, but an altogether different cause which first acted, though other causes followed. Another, uncreated cause came upon it: it set apart from the Virgin’s flesh the flesh to be personally united to the Word of God, and cleansed that flesh from original sin. Hilary, I think, spoke of this cause, or beginning, of Christ’s body when he said: “Christ did not have his beginning from Mary.” For that beginning he truly did not have from his mother, though he had another. For the Virgin generated from herself. This, as it seems to me, Hilary understood faithfully; and whoever thinks rightly does not depart from that faith. It is therefore unworthy of learned men to contend about words when the things are agreed, and to dispute over a name.

Let us now proceed to the second question. It is this: Was Christ’s flesh so weak that, just as we necessarily feel pain when suffering is inflicted, he likewise could not fail to feel pain unless the divinity worked by a miracle beyond nature? Lord Philip, so far as I can infer from his letters, proclaims the Lord’s body to have had so robust a constitution that he attributes to the nature of Christ’s body the fact that he fasted beyond ordinary human health and trod the currents of the sea; but he says that Christ’s suffering pain and dying in pain occurred beyond nature and by miracle. Thus he proclaims an extraordinary strength in the assumed man, by which he did whatever he willed and did not suffer pain except when, or to the extent that, he willed. He indeed proclaims this strength, and no believer denies it. But he differs from us in thinking that Christ acquired it from the nature of his humanity, whereas we believe that he had it by grace. For the personal union with divinity granted him this: that he should rule over every nature of things, and that nothing should resist his will—that rational will, by which the same one willed as man what God willed.

For there is another will, properly called appetite, according to which one is said to wish to eat, even while, in keeping a fast, he wishes to abstain from food. Thus the same person both wills and does not will to eat. Many things contrary to this latter will befell Christ, but nothing contrary to the former. Therefore that man was most strong, according to Augustine’s words: “By an ineffable distance he surpassed the human race in strength of mind.” He was as strong and as wise as the omnipotent Word—but not by nature; rather, by grace. Therefore, when Philip removes from Christ’s humanity the necessity of death, I fully agree with him on this point. For he who was omnipotent was subject to no necessity of that kind.

But the question remains whether he was freed from necessity by the nature of the Word or by that of humanity. Since “necessity,” as you also know, is not said in only one sense, let us not dispute over a word. In my view, a thing is necessary when its not being is equivalent to impossibility. If such necessity seems to you to have existed in Christ because that manner of our redemption was ordained and foreseen by God, then everything else foreseen would, by the same reasoning, be subject to necessity. Since this is not true of other things, it must also be false of this. Therefore the teachers of the Church remove this necessity from Christ, whom Origen summons as witnesses to his opinion: “Whatever you read concerning Christ, you will find was not done by necessity.” And Maximus: “I see Christ hungry, but I do not find that he had a necessity of eating.” Augustine likewise says: “We have these affections from the weakness of the human condition.” By these words he signifies necessity, and therefore adds: “But not so the Lord Jesus Christ, whose weakness was from power.” Therefore Augustine does not remove weakness of actions from Christ, but denies that it came from necessity. And elsewhere: “It must not be doubted that Christ was not troubled by weakness of mind,” that is, he was not troubled because strength was lacking to him.

Maximus must be understood in the same way: “That Christ hungered was not bodily frailty”—not that he did not possess it when he hungered, for otherwise he could not have hungered, but because the frailty he assumed did not compel him; that is, it did not force him against his will to undergo hunger. And he rightly adds that this was a sacrament of heavenly grace. For whatever God did or suffered in man was, as regards its own nature, a miracle unheard of from the beginning of the world. Hilary likewise: what else does he deny in Christ under the name of nature except the necessity of suffering pain? “He did not have,” he says, “the force, nature, necessity of suffering pain.” And elsewhere: “Without perception of punishment, he received the force of raging punishment.” Here “perception” is not the name of an act, just as “sight” sometimes is not; for we say that someone has sight though he does not exercise the act of seeing. Hilary therefore calls perception the capacity for feeling. In his usage, I think, to do something “from nature” is the same as Augustine’s “from the condition of birth,” that is, from necessity. Yet, as Cicero says, nature itself is difficult to define.

As to the words of the modern authority which are also introduced into the discussion, let its author see what he means. I understand them thus: “Christ was naturally free from sin and punishment”; that is, he was naturally free from those things without which he could have been born. But we are naturally bound by them because we cannot be born without them. Yet this may also be referred to the nature of divinity.

Therefore, since both we and Lord Philip agree, on these testimonies of the doctors, that Christ lacked the necessity of death, observe nevertheless where I differ from him. May I not rightly say that Christ had to die—not absolutely, however, but with this qualification: unless God willed to work beyond the nature of flesh? Boethius and Cicero teach that there are two kinds of necessity: absolute and conditional. But someone will ask: does this twofold necessity seem likewise to apply to, or be removed from, certain other human beings? Were not the three children in the fiery furnace necessarily to be burned? And would not Moses and Elijah, while fasting, necessarily have failed unless they had divinely received power—those to endure flames, these to endure hunger? Yet there is a great difference here. Christ, even by that nature whereby he was God, did what he willed; whereas other human beings had what they did not from themselves, but from elsewhere and by grace. But what then? Did not the assumed man also have his power by that same grace? In what, therefore, was his perfection greater than that of others?

It was far greater indeed. For that man received grace fuller than all human beings, “from whose fullness we all received” (John 1). Whatever the Son of God had by nature, the Son of Man also had by grace. But concerning Christ, who alone was both God by nature and man, the question was what he had by grace. Does Lord Philip disagree in this? Or perhaps he will say that Christ’s pure conception was by grace, and that this, as he thinks, gave him extraordinary bodily strength; and therefore that strength is said to have existed in that man by creative grace, but no less by nature. Must this be conceded to him: that the pure conception of Christ gave him strength of assumed human nature above that of man? If so, we seem to proclaim this with him; and what appeared to be a great controversy between us has been reduced to great agreement, and we dispute only about words. For I think that what a thing acquires from conception is natural. Conversely, it cannot be denied that that most sacred conception gave him a great defense against every suffering. For if John, who had not felt the heat of lust, deserved not to feel the heat of oil, how much more did his purity free from the necessity of suffering him who was not only a virgin, but also the son of a virgin?

Or must it be believed that Jesus acquired the same power from a pure conception as from union with the Word? If so, I fear that we again fall into the opposing position. I confess that this matter is perplexing and therefore requires more careful attention from your prudence. Yet, as it appears to my small understanding, the pure conception of the man whom God assumed contributed nothing to him except what the one assuming willed. It pleased his goodness to assume, without sin, the condition of our weakness, as will shortly be shown.

Therefore the bodily strength which Philip proclaims was not possessed by Christ from the nature of humanity. For Christ did not put on that condition in which Adam was before sin, as Lord Philip thinks. Rather, since there are three conditions of human nature, he assumed something from each of them, according to Boethius. For the fact that he had a mortal body was from the condition in which God punished man after sin; but the fact that he could not sin was according to that condition to which man would have been transferred if he had not yielded to the tempter. The third condition remains, which Boethius calls intermediate: in it man before sin could hunger, digest what he had taken, and fall asleep. No one denies that these and similar things were in Christ. Even if Christ had assumed this condition without qualification, nevertheless by the nature of man he would not always have been able to fast. Adam was not so resistant to hunger that he could have lived without food. Boethius clearly shows this in these words: “Nor should it be believed that such want was absent in Adam that, unless he ate, he could not live.” I am not unaware, however, that different readings of this author are found in different manuscripts on this point. Yet whoever carefully considers what follows will easily grasp the meaning.

Therefore God united flesh naturally weak, but displayed it as strong to a maiden [the printed reading is *puellae*].
