By contrast, Lord Philip says: “He assumed it naturally strong, but for a time bore our infirmities.” The testimonies of Scripture which he produces against us on this point favor us no less than him. And those which he violently wrests in support of his opinion can readily be turned back in defense of our faith.

For they proclaim Christ’s strength and free him from necessity; and in this, according to the tenor of the explanation already given, there is no disagreement between us. The issue is this: which condition of humanity did Christ assume? The whole force of this question rests here. For, as it seems to me, Philip has contributed nothing effective toward its solution. Against the argument which he repeatedly urges—that Christ was free from natural frailty because he was conceived without sin—Boethius sets forth an indubitable judgment, to which Gregory does not stand opposed when he says: “Because he was mingled with no guilt, he succumbed to no punishment by necessity.” For since Christ was born without sin, he did not assume by necessity the condition imposed on man as punishment after sin. Gregory does not mean that Christ therefore had no natural frailty because he had no sin; rather, that he did not possess it necessarily. But what then? Does he not remove necessity from Christ because of his purity? If that is true, did not the pure conception itself give him supreme strength, since it removed the coercion of necessity? Once this is granted, we almost fall back into the opposing position. The difficulty must not be concealed.

Let your subtlety consider this. Does Christ’s pure conception remove every kind of necessity from him? For I conceded shortly before that conditional necessity existed in him. Unless he willed otherwise, would he not have had to die, as Peter did? Therefore Christ’s flesh had as much natural frailty as Peter’s. Did he have as much necessity of death as man? Let these verbal entanglements not weary you as childish; I cease to pursue them.

But I wish to pursue the opinion which denies that Christ, from his conception, assumed the frailty of our flesh—namely, mortality and every affection—which man deserved by sinning, with this sole exception: that sin could not occur in him. Against this opinion, with a certain concession granted to it, I proceed as follows. It confesses that Christ assumed from his conception this weakness: that he could feel pain when suffering was inflicted upon him, and that this is common to him and us. If this is true, did he not assume the natural capacity for suffering pain? For I call natural what a thing receives from its Creator. How did he suffer pain beyond nature and by miracle, when he did not lack the bodily capacity for pain? If a stone had received at creation the capacity for pain, then, when struck, it would beyond doubt not suffer pain beyond nature or by miracle. But because the sun had no natural capacity to stand still, we say that its standing still occurred beyond its nature and by miracle.

Further: what cause, I ask, was there for Christ to fear death, which was so far removed from him that it could not befall him unless he assumed it in himself by a great exercise of power? But, he will say, Christ assumed fear for a time, just as he assumed pain, so that his greater love toward us might be proved: he who was naturally strong deigned to be made weak for us, and thus our love, owed to him, might be rendered greater. I answer: because the mediator of God and men wished, through the mediation intervening between his own natures, to reconcile two extremes opposed to one another, the nearer he became to our frailty, the more abundantly he displayed his goodness toward us; and therefore greater love should be shown to him.

Further, since the two natures in Christ are joined without confusion, whatever Christ did or suffered, he must have done or undergone according to one or the other of them. What he neither did nor suffered according to either nature, he did not do or suffer at all. But he suffered pain according to neither nature: if not according to the human, then much less according to the divine. It follows that he did not suffer pain at all. But it is impious to think this of Christ. Therefore it is utterly false that he did not possess a nature capable of pain. If, however, Philip means by “nature” necessity, as blessed Hilary repeatedly associates force, nature, and necessity, then this whole dispute concerned only a word, and he must either disagree with himself or yield wholly to our position. Thus there will no longer be more reason to be angry with him than with blessed Hilary.

But perhaps this manner of speaking, and its seeming novelty of words, offends you. This fault of novelty in modern writers must indeed be criticized considerably. But I do not think that holy Hilary, if he thinks rightly, should be judged by moderns because of his words. For that philosopher is of the highest subtlety, and wished to retain this freedom of expression. On this proposed question, most of what has been said has been offered not rashly as assertion, but as inquiry. Now, if Lord Philip—should he happen to read it—replies anything to these points, I would wish to be informed.

[Note: While attentively reading these twenty-one letters of Philip, surnamed “of the Alms,” formerly abbot of the monastery of Bonne-Espérance, I found them not only consonant with the Catholic faith, but also solidly learned and full of the abundant erudition usually found in the most careful ancient readers of the divine Scriptures. They have therefore, not undeservedly, until now been desired by learned men. They will thus be profitably printed. Attached to them are three other letters written to Philip himself, and one from Hunald to John the provost, on the same subject as the fifth, sixth, and seventh letters; these too will be usefully published.]

Drawn up at Douai, 2 November 1617.

Francis Sylvius, Doctor of Sacred Theology and professor at the University of Douai.

## LETTER XXVI. PHILIP TO POPE ALEXANDER III

He congratulates Alexander upon his elevation to the highest dignity, and reports that the kings of England and France had met in order to win him to their side.

(From D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, new edition, vol. III, p. 527.)

“Having received the letters of your graciousness, etc.” It survives among various letters to Alexander III, under the year 1159.

## COMMENTARIES OF PHILIP OF HARVENG, ABBOT OF BONNE-ESPÉRANCE, ON THE SONG OF SONGS

### THE PROLOGUE OF THE SAME AUTHOR BEGINS

You ask of me a work weighty and arduous, beyond my powers, without sufficiently considering what you request so urgently and anxiously, or from whom. To tell the truth, I neither know nor perceive in myself an understanding so subtle that I can bring to completion what you desire. A poet is indeed found to have carefully warned his hearers—among whom I remember sitting as a boy—that writers should not be hasty in rashly undertaking every great subject, but should rather be cautious and take up material proportioned to their powers:

> You who write, he says, choose material equal  
> To your powers; ponder long what your shoulders refuse  
> And what they can bear.

[Note: Horace, *Art of Poetry*.]

If consideration of one’s powers is required for narratives in pagan poems, much more is it required in the nuptial and spiritual Song of Songs, which surpasses not only the ditties of the Muses and the empty fables of poets, but even our own hymns and the songs of prophets. Indeed, so many interpreters of this work, both modern and ancient, are found that I do not know what later writers could add; and, since there are so many commentaries on this Song, any later writer appears not so much to forge new things as to steal things already discovered.

Yet whatever objections I make seem not to satisfy you. You wish me to undertake what lies neither in my learning nor in my eloquence. Spiritual subject matter burdens and heavily weighs down shoulders already burdened, since, according to Paul, “the natural man does not perceive” (1 Cor. 2). Thus, knowingly and prudently, I put my hand into the fire, or entrust myself in a frail little boat to the deep perils of the sea, trusting only in him who wills that his own should not be worn down by labor in vain, who, being good and merciful, says to those speaking of him and laboring for him: “I am present.” Before him, I ask you, commend me by your prayers; and obtain for me the grace by which I may accomplish what I desire—a grace which, though just and true, he will not grant for my merits, yet, being compassionate and merciful, will not deny to your prayers.

> You ancients know only one moon;  
> In our times another and greater is present.  
> The sun, once alone, marvels at a greater novelty:  
> For a new moon gives birth to a new sun.  
> If you wish better to know who or what these are, I shall unfold it:  
> Christ the sun arises; Mary the moon gives birth.

## PREFACE TO THE SONG OF SONGS
[Col. 0181C] A certain King of kings and Lord of all things (and whatever name more worthy or excellent may be given, by which his power and mighty excellence can be commended) possessed a realm of marvellous and unheard-of extent, in which he had decreed that no share should be apportioned to any other. It seemed fitting to his good pleasure that his kingdom should remain undivided for himself, and that there no one greater than he, or even his equal, should be found, who, with equal power, might be driven by rebellious and insolent presumption into contempt.

One part of this realm was held to be higher, brighter, more honourable, and more worthy of his frequent presence; another part was far lower, rougher, and darker, perhaps less pleasing to its Lord Himself in proportion to its merits. In that part over which he presided above, a great order of many princes stood beside him. They had received the command to serve their Lord with bowed neck and to sing fitting praises to him with unwearied devotion. Therefore he made them marvellous and admirable, pre-eminent and conspicuous in dignity, and endowed them, as it were, with a secondary authority upon the throne of the kingdom: so that they should preside in excellence over all dwelling throughout the kingdom, while themselves remaining subject to their own Lord in due reverence.

One of them, who did not seem inferior to the rest, rejoicing in the gift he had received of beauty and honour, conceived something lofty and rash against his Lord; and, seeking greater things, supposed that he would be like him. Very many of that great multitude of exalted beings agreed with him, presuming to think themselves equal to the Most High. Immediately the King stripped them all of the glory bestowed upon them and, when stripped, assigned them to the lowest part of his realm. For in the highest region he endured nothing resistant, unsuitable, troublesome, or, indeed, dishonourable to remain; but by a severe judgment he at once cast down the evil once it had arisen, and removed the wicked far from the serene glory of his countenance.

But though removed far away, they nevertheless did not abandon wickedness (Wis. 12); rather, they infected the inhabitants of that lowest region with the poison of their crime, compelled them to rebel against the Lord of all, and incited them to a like injury through threats and force, deceit and flatteries. There, indeed, that supreme King, for reasons known to himself, endured evil to grow wild and increase in strength; nor did he immediately restrain every wicked person with the hasty sickle of punishment. Though by a mere nod he could either prevent their coming into being or swiftly avenge every harmful act once committed, he appeared wonderfully patient, as though forgetful of those advancing toward worse things.

Thus, in a short time, through the instigation of the greater and the consent of the lesser, that entire lower part of the kingdom was corrupted; and all flesh, once corrupt, worshipped neither from fear nor love its King and Lord. Him whom it did not see present with the eye, and no longer perceived in its ill-disposed heart, it did not obey in his commands, even if it chanced at some time to hear them. Yet sometimes, looking down upon them from on high, he sent them his messengers; and, speaking in many portions and in many ways, he recalled those wandering in error to better things and to what was near salvation. But very many of them, entangled in harsh and long-lasting bonds of vices, [Col. 0183C] were softened neither by his warnings nor by his promises.

Very few, to whom spiritual teaching had become brighter and more pleasing, or whom natural reason and understanding perhaps admonished, looked back in humble regard to their King with sounder judgment, and, good among the wicked, worshipped the Lord according to place and time. Yet throughout so many expanses both of places and times, persons of this kind were found so rarely that, since all flesh had been corrupted, as was said above, that King could easily know his own by name among every people, whereas the multitude of the wicked could no longer be comprehended by any human count.

This endured not merely for many years, but through many ages of years, during which the people hardened their neck against their King and against his law. All were at last deservedly brought, together with their guilt, into the eternal darkness of the prison, except the few who had previously been restored to his favour.

Throughout the whole succession of times during which the people were found held in the aforesaid error, that King had purposed to have mercy on them at the end of times: in the last age to bestow his grace more abundantly upon the wretched, whom he saw perishing alike through ignorance and wickedness. He chose a marvellous and altogether astonishing method of showing mercy; but why he chose this method in preference to another cannot clearly be comprehended, except that he saw it to be more pleasing to his good pleasure, and therefore no one of sound judgment doubts it to be better.

This mercy which he was to show to the erring people in the last days, and the means by which he was to accomplish it, he willed to be revealed in different nations, places, and times to a very few, whom, because they saw through a more abundant grace, he willed to be called prophets. With the eye of their minds enlightened, they wished to disclose the mystery to others who did not know it; yet they took pains to disclose it through figures and riddles. Proclaiming to peoples the future benefits of the King mentioned above, they indeed uttered much by tongue or pen, but obscurely: so that they might neither wholly conceal the King’s grace after the manner of the envious, nor yet make the holy mystery common to unworthy unbelievers.

Some of them committed these things, understood and foreseen, to enduring writing, and thus transmitted them to those who would come long afterwards, so that not only those then present but, still more, their successors might read in the Scriptures truths which the understanding of their predecessors foresaw and did not begrudge to those to come. While these wrote one after another, a certain man places himself between them, whose knowledge and teaching ecclesiastical authority does not rank below that of the others. Receiving the secrets of the future by the prophetic Spirit, he brought them to the knowledge of others by a marvellous kind of writing.

The supreme King of whom the discourse speaks—having neither an end nor a beginning of existence, possessing not the grace but the immutable nature of persisting; against whose mighty power no one is granted the ability to resist, but to whom he wills he gives the welcome ability to assist in whatever manner he wills—had a Son, of the same nature, substance, and majesty, coeternal, coequal, and in every respect of one power with him. Him he had determined to send to that perverse and pestilential race of human beings, so that he might make a lasting dwelling among and with them, [Col. 0184C] and might take from them a virgin for himself in a nuptial covenant, whom nevertheless, beyond the law of marriage, he would preserve whole in virginal mind and body.

For he saw that, through the benefit of marriage, anger, quarrelling, hatred, and hostility are driven far away, while joy, equity, welcome fellowship, peace, and love are restored; and that for this purpose not merely two, but many thousands together are brought together, who, though different and—what is worse—hostile, are effectively induced to will and not will the same things. He saw that nations differing in language and customs, regions separated from one another by land, sea, and vast intervening distance, are joined together through the reconciled marriage of one bridegroom and one bride; and thereafter they obey, honour, love, and revere one another.

Finally, through the benefit of marriage the desired offspring of children is acquired, and a welcome brotherhood of hearts flourishes among them. As both brothers and cousins multiply, natural love and affection grows without measure; and thus the original benefit of the marriage bond is extended to many. In this manner—indeed, in a manner far more excellent—that King determined to recall his enemies; and, taking a bride from among them, he wished to turn them into friends, so that human beings might render a brother’s due to the bridegroom of their sister and, finding a suitable degree of relationship, might advance in love unto eternity.

For the Father who determined to send the Son for this purpose, and the Son who loved in every respect to obey the One sending him, is God: immortal, impassible, and by nature invisible, whom no visible creature could visibly see or contain. Therefore the Son of God himself willed to be received among human beings in the virginal bridal chamber of the Bride, so that, coming forth from it as Bridegroom, he might be seen and touched in nuptial form and habit.

Before this came to pass in reality, certain persons, as has already been said, foresaw it in the Spirit and left it set down in their writings, some more obscurely and others still more obscurely. One of these is found to have described the mutual affections of Bridegroom and Bride more plainly, weaving, as it were, a subtle and noble, spiritual and modest drama. That man knew that male and female singers are employed at temporal weddings, offering melodies of songs and various praises; that, skilful with their hands, they touch lyre, cithara, and symphony, and weave harmonious melody with sambuca, pipe, and psaltery, so that in all these ways they are found to rejoice fittingly in the nuptial chamber and to invite the other assembled guests to rejoice with them.

In this form or after this example, our writer, wonderfully instructed, pursued this distinguished bridal chamber with epithalamic praise. He composed a new and unheard-of drama after the fashion of comic writers, who introduce various persons of the stage speaking. Antiquity, certainly, knew no such kind of writing before him; but from him, it seems, later generations adopted it at a great distance below his achievement. For the later schools of the Greeks, not sufficiently able to grasp what things he wrote mystically about which persons, nevertheless transferred this mode of writing itself to their vanities and follies.

## EXPLANATION OF THE TITLE OF THE SONG OF SONGS

The title of this work is: *The Song of Songs of Solomon.*

[Col. 0185B] Since in this little work he wrote nothing but harmonious praises of Bridegroom and Bride, he inscribed “Song” or “Songs” in its very title, so that the prudent reader might be prepared at once, by this reminder on its very front, for praises of the bridal chamber, and might render them in loving fashion, not with melody of voice but with harmony of character.

But since many are found, before and afterwards, to have produced songs in their writings, though they did not describe the praises of this bridal chamber so excellently, for the commendation of these Songs and to distinguish them from the unequal productions of others, he set down here not merely “Songs,” but “Song of Songs.” For just as the Holy of Holies and Sabbaths of Sabbaths are raised in eminence above holy things and sabbaths, and ages of ages are preferred to ages in dignity and glory, so, although there is much commendation of songs in the writings of the ancients, the *Song of Songs* promises and contains something greater and far holier.

And lest the writer of this work should be unknown to readers and the authority of the writing be diminished through ignorance of its writer, he deliberately added mention of himself as author, plainly naming Solomon in the same title: “The Song of Songs of Solomon.” This Solomon was a king and a king’s son; and therefore he fittingly reveres the supreme King, the Son of a King, describing how great a grace of peace shines forth in his marriage, and with what rest and glory the noble Bride lies hidden in his bosom.

Finally, as the interpreters say, peace is signified by the name Solomon, and the peaceable character of his kingdom is indicated by the testimony of Scripture: the Egyptian hand did not come to its aid in war as though it were powerless, but rather Satan, or an adversary, was not encountered from Dan to Beersheba. “He had peace,” it says, “on every side round about, from Dan to Beersheba” (3 Kings 4). And below: “My God has given me rest round about, and there is no Satan nor evil encounter” (3 Kings 5).

By him is signified the One who by his own power made the two one; who presented himself as the cornerstone to Jews and Gentiles coming from opposite directions (Eph. 5); who, coming from the Father’s bosom, did not abandon heavenly things; who, coming to the unjust, brought salvation and righteousness near to them. He gathered into one, as though by a bond of concord, earthly and heavenly beings whom not so much difference of place as inequality of merits had long separated from one another, when in the bridal chamber of the Bride he celebrated spiritual nuptials, by which he marvellously united divine and human nature in personal unity.

Therefore the writer of this work is rightly called Solomon—that is, “peaceful”—indicating that no troubled person can worthily sing such a song, lest anyone suppose that he has attained the contemplative or theoretical summit of knowledge who has not first been diligently formed in moral and natural learning. To teach this more effectively, he who was about to write this book is found to have prefaced it with two others, carefully describing distinct matters in each: in the first, that discipline which they call ethical or moral; in the second, that which they call physical or natural.

In the first he teaches the untrained and forms us toward elegance of conduct; and while thus forming us, he occasionally introduces the Father and frequently the Son. Moreover, even in the title he calls himself king and son of a king, so that both his father’s dignity and royal fear may constrain us: “The Proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel.” In this book he instils fatherly discipline into the untrained and little ones, declaring that one who does not hear falls more grievously into ruin, while one who understands possesses the helm of his own life, because an obedient man ought rather to speak of victories than remain silent (Prov. 21).

In the second book, however, he teaches the well-ordered man, now endowed with mature age, that every creature under the sun is subject to vanity; no generation remains in the same state, but everything generated tends by nature toward destruction. [Col. 0187A] And since the things of this world will not endure in a fixed condition, but their appearance and form pass away by an unavoidable law, he plausibly indicates that we should not cling to such things, but seek something else, greater and nearer to salvation.

But because it is rare and difficult in a sense not to see visible things—that is, not to adhere to visible things with any affection of mind—in the title of this book too he calls himself king and son of a king, and, as though by royal authority, addresses the assembly, that is, the Church: “The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Jerusalem.” He wished royal authority, pressing as it is, to shake and impel those whom the suitable sweetness of teaching does not sufficiently attract, and to advance them to the more developed stage of natural knowledge, so that they may judge contemptible whatever they know to be unstable by the privilege of temporal course.

In the third volume he makes no mention of royal power, but, that having now been laid aside, simply calls himself Solomon. He shows that those who come worthily to this reading, lulled by the peace due to them, desire only the vision of the Bridegroom. Such a reader, utterly despising everything he understands to be transitory and having learned by every diligent care that it is oppressive, now holds with freer spirit the contemplative place, from which the Bridegroom’s presence excludes everything unsuitable and harmful that may present itself.

Thus in these volumes he embraces moral, natural, and contemplative knowledge. In the first, the son gains a father’s discipline, not money; in the second, he discovers that all transitory things beneath the sun are vain; in the third, forgetting the things below, he stretches himself wholly toward divine and heavenly things. In the first, every untrained person is formed in good morals by the father’s watchfulness; in the second, the visible world is shown to him as deformed because of its changeability; in the third, that lower human being is re-formed with cleansed face and, brought into the sanctuary, is conformed by a pleasing likeness to him whom he sees.

In the first, he hears Abraham giving command, hastens to depart, and is prepared for moral obedience (Gen. 12). In the second, Isaac digs wells, seeks waters, and investigates natural things (Gen. 26). In the third, Jacob sleeps upon a stone, attends upon angels, and contemplates divine things (Gen. 28); indeed, as it says, he sees God himself face to face and is saved.

In the first, he nourishes, restrains more strictly, and wraps about with moral precepts, rules of discipline, and a saving bond the future Bride, still untrained and little. In the second, he frees and releases her now grown up from the deceits of suitors and the bonds of deceivers. In the third, the Bridegroom claims and joins to himself alone the Bride now fit for marriage, to whose chaste union no one joins himself incestuously.

Therefore that first book, as the pursuer of precepts, is rightly called ethical or moral; the second, as the pursuer of visible things, physical or natural; the third, as the pursuer of invisible things, contemplative, theological, spiritual—the later it stands in order, the more eminent and principal in excellence.

In this book Solomon saw and foresaw a certain virgin to be born of royal stock, who would be more pleasing than all others to the supreme King and his Son; in her the Son of God would consecrate for himself a temple, tabernacle, and bridal chamber, so that there he might celebrate nuptials known beforehand to a few but wholly unexperienced by all. Lest anything honourable or fitting should seem absent from these nuptials, he says that the friends of the Bridegroom are present with the Bridegroom, and young women with the Bride; and thus he arranges a spiritual epithalamium, as though four persons were speaking to one another, whose frequent entrances and departures weave the nuptial drama.

The virgin whom Solomon sees as thus to be loved by the Son of God and specially chosen for this ministry—or, if one prefers it, mystery—is she noble in lineage, distinguished in conduct, beautiful beyond the daughters of men, wise in letters, humble in spirit, glorious in merits: she, I say, to name her at last, is Mary, descended after Solomon from his offspring, who joyfully occupies the first part of this drama. For although many before the Virgin had spoken here and there at length concerning nuptials of this kind and had set forth their praises and preliminary approaches, Solomon in this book brings none of them into the midst; rather, he suddenly introduces the aforesaid Virgin speaking.

# BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER ONE

[CANT. 1.] “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

Here the first question which arises is this: since in this drama four persons, as it were, are introduced speaking to one another—the Bridegroom and the Bridegroom’s companions, the Bride and the young women accompanying her—why does the Bride, more hasty, come forward first to speak, when it seems that this office ought to be granted to the more worthy Bridegroom?

But this indicates that the Virgin is not darkened by ignorance, but investigates with instructed spirit the words of the preceding prophets; and, just as Solomon and the others are known to have foreknown future things, so she too knew what had been foretold concerning herself. She knows, therefore, that God had formerly spoken in many portions and in many ways in the prophets (Heb. 1), and had set forth everything necessary for bringing about the nuptials. From the days of Moses and long before, through many figures of things and riddles of words, he had signified beforehand that this would occur: namely, that by the grace of marriage he would come into a virgin’s bosom.

But the Virgin wishes all these foreshadowing things now to be silent, and figures and riddles to have no further place as before; she wishes him who is promised finally to show his presence and no longer to restrain by delay the longing of one waiting to behold him. “For,” she says, “promises are not enough for tender love; the sickness grows more grievous if fulfilment is delayed beyond due measure. Since I ought not and cannot bring compulsion to obtain what I love, I judge it fitting simply to offer supplicatory words: ‘Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.’”

“I know,” she says, “that Scripture relates how it was once said to Abraham that the nations would rejoice to be blessed in his seed (Gen. 12); and that this is not considered worthy of faith in Isaac his son (Gen. 21, 22), but will be fulfilled more effectively at the fitting time in me. Isaac too, begotten by a father already old, ready, obedient, and prepared for sacrifice while still a boy—what else did he signify but this joy of mine, which my God assigned to me before I came into being?

“As the world grows old, I grieve that he whom I desire does not draw nearer; that the One to be sent does not more swiftly obey the One sending; that my joy is not bestowed upon me, though I love and desire it; and that I seek it all the more because it is not taken away from him who possesses it. I know that Jacob, when about to sleep, did not place a cushion beneath his head, but, with a stone placed beneath it, slept most sweetly (Gen. 28). In this I do not doubt that he is figuratively signified who, when he has given me a kiss, will be cut from the mountain without hands.

“In Judah, Leah’s son, whom the aged father wills to be praised by his brothers (Gen. 49), from whom the Jews are most certainly derived both in race and in name, no one seems to me more fittingly signified than he who confesses God the Father to be Lord of heaven and earth (Luke 10).

“I know Joseph, to whose brothers his death is found more welcome than his life (Gen. 37); after he became a dreamer, he was clothed in a richly variegated tunic (Gen. 39). His chastity is read to have been assailed by the threats and blandishments of a shameless mistress, but his young mind, unencumbered, leaps over the snares laid before it. He is, as I see, the One who, having given me a kiss, will be clothed in a new garment, varied with virtues, and, proceeding as Bridegroom from the bridal chamber, will endure many envious persons. He will flee the malice of this present life as an unchaste harlot, having as his companion the purity of highest chastity and chaste goodness.

“He is the One before whom all others will bow their knees to the Lord of things; whom stars, sun, and moon, kings and princes will worship; who will sustain Egypt, suffering more from death than famine, with marvellous prudence (Gen. 41), and will minister life-giving food to all who fittingly ask for it.

“What need is there for me to recount Moses, Aaron, Joshua, the order of the judges, David, the other kings, or to name each of the prophets? In their catalogue no one at all is noted who does not, by word or deed, speak beforehand of him whom I desire. But because he sent all these before him as certain heralds and drummers, in whose preludes he had not yet given his presence but had promised it, impatient of delay, I count their proclamations as worthless, since he himself is not received in presence.

“My understanding has already grasped, from their promises, that he will come; but such love for the One to come has seized my longing as I wait that whatever promise enters my understanding or memory, I now almost disdain as trumpets and pipes, sistrums and psalteries, and whatever makes noise outside at the door. I desire that he alone be led into the midst and introduced more sweetly and laboriously into my bridal chamber.

“Therefore let him who is to come not prolong delay any longer; let him not suspend my longing as I wait by intolerable postponement. Let him, promised from ancient times, finally descend as dew upon the fleece; let him not greet me from afar, but show himself nearer to one who desires him (Judg. 6). For I wish that he should no longer hide himself in the Father’s bosom; that from there he should no longer deafen my ears with the wordy multitude of messengers; but that he should pour over me, who have long endured and can endure no longer, a fuller grace, and, by a complete entering-in, wholly pour himself into my bosom.

“For what benefit is it to soothe a suspended mind with so many promises and yet experience absolutely no fulfilment of what is promised? Rather, sickness leads to death if health is always absent and the Beloved is not at last presented to the one who loves him in welcome union. Let him therefore kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

Moved by the heat and desire of her request, though he does not immediately fulfil the impatient mind of the waiting Virgin, he still adds by sending her a more welcome messenger, one who may tell her in private conversation that the Lord is nearer. Though there was much holiness in many of those who went before, in this one there was found much strength, both in reality and in name; and because he announced that the most mighty Defender of Israel was at hand, he deserved fittingly to be specially called Gabriel.

Sent to the Virgin, and not forgetting the excellence of the One who sent him, he does not remain outside at the door as though hindered by servile chains. Rather, with greater confidence he enters a kind of vestibule of the inner bridal chamber, already declaring by word and expression who he is and why he has come. “Hail,” he says, “full of grace” (Luke 1).

The angel marvels that the Virgin’s secret is inaccessible even to himself, perceiving carefully that it is granted to her Lord alone; and he rejoices to find the place of the bridal chamber so serene that, open to God alone, it rejects every stranger. “Hail,” he says, “Virgin, fittingly joyful above all virgins, already filled with the worthy gifts of all grace. To you my Lord and the Lord of all has sent me before him; indeed, I now see that he who sent me is with you. ‘Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.’

“I thought that I came as a herald by command of the One sending me, but the Commander seems to have preceded the messenger; perhaps because he wished first to find the Virgin alone, lest I should appear to approach her, inexperienced and timid, without him.”

The angel, whom the Lord he was sent by had already preceded, I suppose, did not find the aforesaid Virgin in market or street, in tumult or dancing. He did not find her occupied with spindle, needle, comb, wool, or flax; in short, detained by no servile work of weaving, but free for leisure—or rather, spiritual business—wholly devoted to the Scriptures with understanding and affection that was holy, not carnal. Therefore the angel himself reveres her when so found, intent upon divine study with all observers removed, and, marvelling at a youth robust not in years but in spiritual progress, gives the Virgin the entrusted greeting with great reverence: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke 1).

“You,” he says, “so devoted to leisure or work so honourable and modest, ought worthily to be declared blessed among, indeed above, all women. Such a blessing will attend you, full as you are of grace, that neither the first woman has an equal nor any later woman will equal you.”

“And when she had heard, she was troubled at his saying, and considered what manner of greeting this might be” (ibid.). Seeing the unfamiliar appearance of a man, the Virgin is alarmed; and hearing something new, she likewise shudders in disturbance, because a man was not accustomed to be present at her spiritual leisure and because she had not yet understood herself worthy of such great excellence. She turns and returns in her mind what this greeting portends, what the angel standing by intends, or what the Lord sending him intends, since she does not yet openly comprehend the secret of the mystery. It seemed fitting in every respect that the Virgin should fear lest she offend.

And the angel says: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with God” (ibid.). “Let sudden fear not disturb your maidenly mind, since you have found saving grace with God. Do not reject in fearful heart the holy purpose and good pleasure which he has toward you, since that Lord, whose messenger I am in bringing these greetings, grants you salvation.”

And he adds: “Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (ibid.). “In your womb the Son of God will celebrate marvellous nuptials, and your very womb will bear as man that same Bridegroom whom you will call Jesus, because of his goodness; for he will save his people from their sins.”

And Mary says: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” (ibid.). “Since I,” she says, “have resolved not to enter a carnal marriage, and you truly assert that I shall shortly bear a son, allow me to say, I certainly wish to know the means by which this apparently unsuitable thing can fittingly come about. I had read Isaiah writing that this marvellous thing would occur, but neither he nor anyone else had said that it would occur in Mary. And because this sandal seems bound about with a perplexing strap, I want you, to whom it may perhaps have been granted, to loosen it for me.”

And the angel answered and said to her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (ibid.). “Know that you will experience no union with a man; but by the operation of the Holy Spirit you will conceive—possible indeed, but ineffable—for he will wholly remove from you whatever is called or conceived as indecent, and by interposing himself as a kind of shade he will prevent every heat of shame.

“And since the Spirit of God will bring about this birth in holiness and wonder, what is born will without doubt be holy; and from God no one other than the Son of God will arise, when God and man are personally united in you.”

And Mary says: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.). Having heard the manner in which the marvellous birth could take place, by which God is born from a Virgin to know no union with a man, the humble Virgin is ready to obey the Lord, and what she understands to be holy she now hopes and loves to happen swiftly.

“Since he whom you proclaim is Lord,” she says, “and I know myself to be the Lord’s handmaid, I now ask that your word be fulfilled and that it be done to me according to it; rejoicing that the good and merciful One did not despise me, though unworthy, but that the gracious and most high One regarded me, lowly and humble as I am.

“Therefore, once you have faithfully completed the ministry entrusted to you, and once I have understood with sufficiently certain faith the mystery you have spoken, your announcement has left me even more suspended and, as it were, restless. Nothing is enough for me unless I feel present him who sent you. Therefore let him himself no longer send another in his own stead, and let him not promise by a messenger things to come to my eager mind; rather, let him himself now present himself to me at the fitting time, and, present in person, kiss me personally as one present.

“Let him kiss me, I say, with the kiss of his mouth. Let this union occur in me, I say, not with lips but through the meeting of two natures, so that both may marvellously be the nature of one person; and so that those which guilt and diversity of nature had hitherto made far apart may now be joined by an undivided personal unity in firm peace.

“For I understand that the fullness of deity will come into my womb, preserving uninjured the seal of my virginal chastity; and in this bridal chamber the Son of God himself, by the sweet kiss of marriage, will join two unlike natures in the unity of his person. God will indeed become man, neither defiling nor consuming the excellence of his own nature, but powerfully purifying and assuming human nature. And, assuming it, he will give the assumed nature a marvellous and incomparable gift: namely, that the assumed and the Assumer may become one through their wondrous union.

“One, I say—not God only, nor man only, but one God-man, one Christ. This is not so that the substance of God is confused, but so that humanity is assumed into God. This assumption, this union by which God willed personally to unite a human being to himself and to make or unite a covenant of peace between nature and nature in the Virgin’s womb, is here called by the honourable name of a kiss, because peace restored between those at variance is confirmed by a kiss.

“The Virgin, then, desires that concord between God and man should be restored in her womb, and that concord, once restored, should be strengthened by an unshaken covenant, so that he who was God and Son only of God the Father may become, in a new and marvellous manner, Bridegroom and Son of a mother.

“Let him become Bridegroom by joining the Virgin to himself in a kind of marital covenant, resting in her bridal chamber after peace has been made by the nuptial kiss; by her, or in her, generating spiritual children through spiritual efficacy, so that both he and she may rejoice in the fruit and offspring of children. Let him become Son by taking true flesh in her womb, while keeping the Virgin wholly entire and undefiled; consecrating in her every holy person as God, making them sons and heirs of God, and, born from her as man, making them his co-heirs.

“The Virgin rejoices and exults in this benefit, ancient indeed in promises but new in reality, and asks that it may abide forever. Considering that by this good an evil both subsequent and inveterate can be destroyed, she desires that, once the kiss has been given to her, he should make with her an everlasting covenant. For she sees that he judges it wholly unsuitable and unworthy that peace should not be unshaken after someone has given a sign of peace; and therefore she desires him to be enfolded by that bond which, once confirmed, neither ought nor can ever afterward be dissolved.”

## CHAPTER TWO
“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Every holy person or prophet through whom the Lord discloses his thoughts and secrets to human beings is called the Lord’s mouth: through such a one he reveals the past to us, foretells the future, commands good things more sweetly, and forbids evil things more sternly.

Moses is evidently known to have been formerly the Lord’s mouth. God seems to have granted him such grace that he was made aware of this secret long beforehand and, as a faithful messenger, spoke of what was to come: “God,” he says, “will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren like me; him you shall hear” (Deut. 18).

No believer doubts that David was the Lord’s mouth. In the prophetic Spirit he reverences this mystery, already known beforehand; and, lest he seem to envy others what he foresees, he takes up the psaltery and sings praises and canticles to him: “He,” he says, “as a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber, rejoiced as a giant” (Ps. 18).

That Isaiah’s word may be commended with due reverence, and that the utterance may not be judged contemptible because of its speaker, he speaks to a stiff-necked people, not easily moved to faith; and, so as either to attract or perhaps to frighten them, he sometimes declares himself to be the Lord’s mouth: “The mouth of the Lord,” he says, “has spoken these things” (Isa. 1). And, just as Isaiah declares himself to be the Lord’s mouth, so Jeremiah also ought to be believed and may likewise be called so; instructed by the Spirit, they spoke beforehand of the Virgin’s childbearing and proclaimed coming mysteries in prophetic speech.

Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isa. 7).

Jeremiah says: “The Lord shall make a new thing upon the earth, and a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31).

Finally, the angel Gabriel himself is found to be the Lord’s mouth. He personally addresses the Virgin, now grown and of marriageable age, concerning so great a mystery; and, lest even a small cloud of ignorance leave her uncertain, he explains both that she will give birth and how she will give birth. Therefore the Virgin, now sufficiently assured, wishes no longer merely to hear the Lord’s mouth, but, burning with love, desires to feel the kiss of his mouth: that by the welcome coming of the Bridegroom she may be cherished in firm peace and unshaken presence, according to what is announced by prophet or angel as the Lord’s mouth. “Let it be done to me,” she says, “according to your word” (Luke 1).

Let it be done: let the fullness of grace make me blessed among women; let the royal beauty of the coming Bridegroom adorn my bridal chamber; let the holiness of the Holy Spirit alone make my womb fruitful; let him be my Son—the Son of God, salvation, righteousness, wisdom, and strength. By this kiss may that Bridegroom lovingly incline himself to me; by it may he lay me down, his bride, mother, and Virgin, in a peaceful bosom and welcome embrace. By it may he soothe me, refresh me, make me serene, and claim me for himself, setting me apart from all who would oppose me.

But let this be done according to your word: a word which you uttered not from your own mouth but from the Lord’s mouth, since you became not your own mouth but rather the Lord’s mouth. For you are reckoned not as your own angel, herald, or messenger, but as his who speaks to me through you and wholly makes you his own, so that you may speak. Therefore I do not say to you, “Kiss me with the kiss of your mouth,” but rather say of him: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” that he may at last deign to make me blessed by his own kiss—the kiss which it was granted to you, his mouth, to proclaim in a message.

## Chapter III

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Hearing that she had been betrothed to the Son of God, that she would bear God and man, and that in conceiving she would altogether not experience a man, while preserving her purpose, but that the overshadowing Holy Spirit would come upon her with effective power [Col. 0194B], the Virgin rejoices in what she hears with certain faith, strong hope, and fervor of Spirit and love; yet she wishes to rejoice more fully in the more welcome fulfillment.

Therefore she desires that Spirit of such great grace, such great peace—so sweet, so kindly, so wondrously effective in power—may be given to her more fully: the Spirit who wards off the injuries of the flesh, strengthens her resolve of chastity, gives fruitfulness, and preserves the seal of virginal purity. She desires, I say, that the gifts promised her may be confirmed by that kiss.

“Let,” she says, “the voice of the angel that promises me such benefits cease, and let the Son of God himself, who betroths me as a virgin to himself alone, draw nearer. Let him touch me with his mouth, whose touch will flood me with abundant grace. Let him deign to kiss me with his own kiss and make me fruitful by his own Spirit.”

In the kiss of a mouth, there is not merely an outward joining of lips; a certain breath from within is also received and felt. If the inner parts are pure and filled with sweet savor, the mouth that kisses infuses, as it were, a sweet spirit into the one kissed. Therefore, since the Spirit is breathed forth, as it were, from the heart and mouth of the Son—for the Spirit is proclaimed to proceed from the Son as from the Father—and since nothing is truly thought to be purer and sweeter than that secret reality, the Virgin rightly asks to be kissed by the Bridegroom, that is, the Son of God, so that she may taste the inward good by drawing in and receiving the saving Spirit.

“I desire,” she says, “that he in whom I have believed and whom I have loved may come and stand nearer; that this Bridegroom, admitted familiarly into my chamber, may purify, magnify, and gladden me with a sweet kiss—not so that there may be the merely external joining of lips which ordinarily occurs, but a welcome and sweet infusion into me of the Spirit of his mouth.”

Finally, after God first formed man from the clay of the earth, he breathed, as we read, “the breath of life into his face” (Gen. 2); and just as man is understood to have been made or fashioned by God as though by hands, so by the breath of his mouth he was animated for temporal life.

Far beneath this, when Elisha wished to raise the dead man, he bent over the body and wished to place not only hand upon hand but mouth upon mouth, so that, touched by the breath of the living man, he might receive a living soul; and, as Elisha bent over him, the deceased received not loss but advancement (4 Kings 4).

But much more exaltedly and far more sacredly, the Virgin desires the Son of God to be present with her, much more sweetly and much more effectually present in the kiss: namely, that he may impart the kiss—that is, make the Spirit of his mouth perceptible—and touch her with a fuller Spirit of grace and efficacy.

“You, my Bridegroom, my God,” she says, “kindly grant me your presence. Give the kiss to her who asks: that is, grant me to feel your Spirit. May your breathing upon me be so useful, fruitful, and delightful that I may remain a virgin according to my vow and yet, in conceiving, be fruitful. Breathe upon me, I say, not merely so that I may be able, like others, to labor in accordance with a command; but kiss the Virgin, so that through a kiss you may grant the Virgin a conception surpassing that of all others. Let your kiss work in me wondrously and in a wondrous manner, so that by a singular privilege both fruitfulness may be preserved to the Bride and virginity to the Mother.”

Therefore, all and each of you standing here in this assembly: if you think worthily and reverently on anything from the word you have heard, consider and love both the kiss which the Son of God the Father offers and the singular merit and solemn miracle of so great a Mother. Knowing and feeling the mysteries of the bridal kiss, seeking nothing else and being satisfied with no alternative, she directs herself as though principally to obtaining it. Thus at the beginning of her discourse she especially asks for it to be granted her, wishing to experience its sweetness and efficacy.

## Chapter IV

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” “May he whom I love, whom I choose above all, be wondrously united to me. May inward sweetness be poured into me through his kiss, through his Spirit; through whose aid and work the integrity of my flesh may be safeguarded [Col. 0195C], and the Word be personally united with flesh, God with man, in me.”

See the miracle of the Lord’s Mother. The Virgin receives the Bridegroom’s kiss and receives the Spirit of him who kisses; and in the kiss she, now a mother, conceives, while through the Spirit’s working she receives conception.

The angel Gabriel had previously proclaimed this when he announced that the overshadowing Spirit would come upon her (Luke 1); afterward the Evangelist Matthew confirmed it, when, recalling the event, he commended the Virgin Mother: “She was found,” he says, “with child of the Holy Spirit.” And below: “For what is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1).

The Virgin desires this grace and efficacy to be granted her when she asks the Bridegroom so pointedly to kiss her: desiring not to feel, in the kiss, the Bridegroom’s outward kisses, but that his inward Spirit might pour forth effective grace upon her.

In this figure, as you know, when we are presented at the altar and consecrate the sacred mysteries, we too are consecrated to the Lord himself. Since through the merit of so great an office we are then filled with the Holy Spirit, religion judges it fitting that those standing by should likewise exchange kisses. Let us kiss, I say, not so that we mingle lip with lip, but so that we pour forth to others the grace of the Spirit received; and that those who attend the same sacred mystery humbly and attentively may, through the Spirit’s working and the kiss as its sign, become participants in the sacrament.

Therefore the Virgin wishes the Bridegroom to give her the pledge of a bridal kiss; she wishes, through the Spirit of his mouth, to receive a certain communication of spiritual efficacy, so that both the integrity of her chastity and special purpose may remain inviolate, and that she may conceive in a new manner and a virginal womb may give birth to the conceived child.

This gift, this benefit, this grace, this Virgin alone deserved to find: that she might be found with child, preceded not by knowledge of a man but by the infusion of the Spirit; that she alone, by a kiss alone, as a virgin alone, might give birth to both God and man; and that in her childbearing things so diverse and discordant might meet in a harmonious miracle.

But the Bridegroom, sensing the devout impatience of her ardent longing, does not turn his ear away from the desire and prayers of her who calls upon him; nor does he retain any longer within himself the mercy that is his own, or his ancient counsel. Rather, drawing nearer, he presents himself more sweetly to the one who loves him. [Note: [Col. 0195] An allusion to Matt. 13:52 and Song of Songs 7:13.]

He presents himself, I say, and gives the eagerly desired kiss to the one who asks. By giving the kiss, he gives greater confidence to her who speaks, so that she may not immediately withdraw as though the matter were completed, but may proceed confidently, having once begun to speak.

For you too, brothers, know that this sometimes happens when two persons from different places seem to meet together: if the lesser succeeds in finding favor with the greater, the greater deigns at the outset to bestow a kiss upon the lesser. Having received it, the lesser is strengthened with greater confidence, so as afterward boldly to say whatever he judges fitting. Having felt the other’s goodwill in offering the kiss, he becomes more confident and readier to speak.

Thus the Virgin, having received the Bridegroom’s presence and been strengthened by the bridal kiss, knowing that through the infusion of the Spirit she will become a mother with a virginal womb, turns somewhat more confidently away from prayer and toward the Bridegroom present before her, addressing him in worthy praises.

## Chapter V

“Because your breasts are better than wine.” Rightly, she says, I greatly preferred your coming to the time of promise, and asked that the kiss of your coming be given to me, because I knew and experienced—not led by the sensation of the flesh, not taught by my own spirit, but by the divine Spirit—that your breasts are far better than wine.

Since in the Bridegroom’s kiss she had felt not breasts but, apparently, lips, and therefore should consequently have praised lips rather than breasts, what does it mean that, without remembering lips or speech, she mentions breasts, as though through a simplicity that errs?

Moreover, it is the breasts not of bridegrooms but of brides that are customarily praised, because boys are plainly not suckled at men’s breasts. And just as we judge worthy of praise those things we know to be fruitful, so we rightly leave without praise those which remain idle and without fruit.

Besides, it is implanted somehow naturally in everyone that, setting aside what is wholly unfamiliar to him, he turns to what he knows more intimately and uses as an example what is certain to his own art or occupation. Thus, a sailor, speaking of every prosperity, calls it calm breezes, a smooth sea, a strong sail, oarsmen, and a ship’s keel; but adversities he calls swift winds, a swelling sea, and waters running down into the bilge. Likewise, in nearly all the things he likes to talk about, a soldier draws examples from matters belonging to military service; scarcely anything sounds in his mouth except spear, sword, shield, helmet, or breastplate. Even if cowardly fear sometimes makes these hostile to him for battle, familiar habit makes them friendly to him in speech.

What, too, do scholarly clerics speak of except books or authors of secular literature? What do more religious people speak of except testimonies from the divine writings? What, finally, do we poor people speak of except things impressed upon us by poor people, authors, or guardians—we, I say, for whom both noble rank and the abundance of the rich are inaccessible?

Therefore, because what belongs to women is familiarly known to the Virgin, women by whose breasts little infants grow into larger children, she simply assigns womanly things to the Bridegroom; indeed, she compares the fruitfulness of his grace to breasts. In this she also draws us away from the literal sense of the words, indicating that they are pregnant with spiritual meaning. For she attributes to the Bridegroom what is more easily found in the bride, because she knows perfectly well that this applies to him only for the sake of comparison.

“Because your breasts are better than wine.” The Virgin indeed knew and had read in the books of the ancients that righteous Job, deprived of possessions, bereaved of his children (Job 1), wounded from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head by harsh blows (Job 2), and then wearied by his wife’s most painful reproaches, at last complains and laments bitterly and miserably that death, coming at a suitable time, had not freed him from such great evils:

“Why,” Job says, “did I not die miserably in the womb and expire as I came from the uterus? Why did I not immediately end my life in a danger worthy of it? Why, to increase my misery, was I strengthened by being laid upon knees? Why, finally, to complete it, was I suckled at breasts?” (Job 3).

I think that the breasts at which Job laments and complains that he was suckled—judging it far better that he had first been weaned from his mother—poured into him not saving milk or life-giving nourishment, but the venom of an asp, or wine in which there is debauchery. Of it you have read: “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 32).

This wine or poison is the persuasion and doctrine disseminated and spread by the serpent-like perversity of wicked people. It makes its hearers drunk and deceives them; it turns and leads them from faith into error and from righteousness into unrighteousness.

Therefore in Egypt, as the Psalmist testifies, the Lord struck the vineyards of the wicked (Ps. 77); and Moses, in his song, accuses the vineyard of the Sodomites (Deut. 32). For Egypt and Sodom mix poisonous wine for those who recline at their table: a pattern of perversity, the teaching of malice, and the twisting path of unrighteousness.

By contrast, in Jeremiah the sons of Jonadab deserved praise (Jer. 35), because, having heard their father’s command, they did not drink wine of this kind. Their minds were not made mad by the thought of deceivers or by ruinous consent; according both to their father’s command and to his example, they maintained the rule of truth.

Heretics indeed have evil wine; false Catholics have it too. Through it, their minds ruined and their feet broken, they fall into various errors of faith or morals; and in a similar manner they corrupt and lead astray their little hearers. The Jewish people too have wine, and so do the Gentiles; each, wickedly made drunk by it, is held fast and darkened in miserable error, and one sometimes draws and urges the other into headlong ruin.

Of such people a certain poet aptly says [Note: [Col. 0197D] See Prov. 7:7 and ch. 14:18.]:

> …a procession worthy of report met me:  
> a drunken old woman was dragging an old man who had been drinking.  
> [Note: [Col. 0198D] Ovid, *Fasti*, book 1.]

Judaism and Gentilism are not without reason said to have grown old, since both peoples are known to have existed from ancient times. Neither was content with its own ceremonies; each frequently strayed into the other’s error.

Did not Gentilism, drunk to evil purpose, seem to you to drag along the Jewish people when it urged that people, by every means it could, to worship the gods? And that people, miserably held by a like drunkenness, followed the leader before it as an ox led to slaughter.

When Elijah saw such a procession advancing against him, he could not endure it without angrily mocking it, or without hastening in anger to deride it openly: so that he might strike the erroneous leaders with rebuking ridicule, lest they lead, and correct the wandering hearers with a chastising word, lest they follow. “Elijah,” Scripture says, “came near to all the people and said: ‘How long do you limp between two sides? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal, follow him’” (3 Kings 18). And below: “Elijah mocked the prophets of Baal, saying: ‘Cry with a louder voice; for he is a god, and perhaps he is talking, or is in an inn, or is on a journey, or perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened’” (ibid.).

Nor are Jews alone deceived by the deadly persuasion and error of Gentiles; Gentiles too are sometimes led into Jewish superstitions and absurdities. And Judaism, grown old in evils, does not permit the wretched Gentile to be released from the bond; but, having drunk evil wine, it leads the drinker, the blind leads the blind, even to the final pit.

In the Gospel the Lord condemns their procession not so much mockingly as censoriously, and threatens them with a coming woe all the more terrible because it is true; so that, when they have heard his stern and truthful warnings, both the leading guides and their followers may be either corrected or rendered inexcusable. “Woe to you,” he says, “scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who travel over sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves” (Matt. 23).

Paul too, seeing such a procession, seemed not to laugh but, burning with zeal, steadfast for righteousness and intolerant of wrong, to recoil from it. With free speech he did not spare Peter, who seemed first and more worthy among the apostles, because Peter was regarded as leading in that procession through a fearful error. Paul did not want Peter to drink muddy wine, nor a crowd equally muddied to follow him once he had drunk it badly, lest from this procession there arise not merely laughter or mockery, but the truth of the Gospel—which must not be—suffer shameful danger.

“When Cephas came to Antioch,” he says, “I withstood him to his face, because he was blameworthy” (Gal. 2). And below: “When I saw,” he says, “that they were not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Cephas before them all: ‘If you, though a Jew, live as a Gentile and not as a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?’” (ibid.).

Observing both the leader and his followers made drunk by the cloud of error, and seeing that evangelical truth was not kept among them with sufficient purity, Paul judged this a grave sin, would not allow it to pass unpunished, immediately came forward, and, extending the rod of correction, interrupted the blameworthy procession.

The same Apostle judged this worthy of recounting and, speaking to the Galatians, repeated it among other things pleasingly and memorably—perhaps so that not only the Galatians, but also we, might learn by his teaching what those greater than ourselves owe to us, and what we owe to those greater than ourselves.

For the lesser person owes no consent to the faults and errors of the greater; if some grave and intolerable matter is found in the greater, the lesser must rebuke it from hatred of fault and zeal for a more pleasing righteousness, taking all the more care not to introduce anything of swollen insolence or resentment. But the greater person must not scorn the lesser’s warning with haughty disdain, nor repulse a worthy reprover by the privilege of authority; rather, with a kindly ear, he must obey the admonisher—or rather the admonitions—provided that they are shown truly and humbly to serve charity.

The Virgin says and affirms that the Bridegroom’s breasts are better than this wine, by which Cephas or any wandering person is led astray and staggers with limping step, whether leading or following in such a procession. She knows by experience that they are more delightful not only to outward hearing but also to inward taste.

The Bridegroom’s breasts are his pattern and teaching, example and word, life and speech. By them he cherished and nourished little hearers as with milk; he fed and strengthened those more advanced as with bread and solid food. For this reason he was born a child, to offer himself suitably to little ones, and advanced in age, to show himself a man to those more advanced. In all that he did and said, he led and taught little ones or greater ones according as they had made themselves more ready to receive smaller or greater things.

“Coming forth from the bridal chamber, fair in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44), he was abundant in the incomparable fullness of saving teaching. He first wished, by the merit of his form, to please not only the Virgin but also us; afterward, by word and teaching, to instruct all who would be teachable. Because we are unwilling to offer obedience sufficiently worthy to his word, we are compelled deservedly to shrink from the first appearance of him whose face we ought to love.

Jesus, as you have read, “began to do and to teach” (Acts 1), so that through the attractive beauty, as it were, of his deeds he might call and draw us, attentive and favorably disposed, and gently lead those whom he has attracted firmly into his school.

With his right breast, doing great things, he shows himself commendable and ensnares those who gaze more carefully in the net of his beauty. With his left breast, saying great things, he makes those whom he already holds learned and blessed hearers; but he teaches that despisers will by no means go unpunished.

Who would not call these breasts of the Bridegroom better than corrupting wine? Who, except one drunk with wine, would contradict the Virgin who declares it? For those drunk on the wine of the condemned, both drinkers and those who have drunk, run—or rather fall—blindly; while those who have drunk from the Bridegroom’s breasts are blessed. “Blessed,” he says, “is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law” (Ps. 93).

## Chapter VI

“Because your breasts are better than wine.” Finally, in the Bridegroom’s breast are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, wholly concealed from the prudent and wise of this world. The Bridegroom who had concealed their secrets for so long a time from so many who were comparatively grown now comes forth from the bridal chamber and, in his own goodness, reveals them to little ones.

For in ages past incomparable treasures lay hidden in him; but when he took the Virgin’s flesh, they burst forth wondrously like swelling nipples from a breast. They poured out not dry drops but streams and rivers, and poured themselves forth from a full horn into all who approached worthily.

For this reason, after receiving the kiss, the Virgin does not immediately turn away from the Bridegroom as though saying farewell, but reclines on his breast for the sake of progress. Applying the vessel of her pure mind all the more capaciously because more eagerly, she drinks and is satisfied with the welcome abundance of his breasts and their flowing streams.

There she thirsts with lofty desire for knowledge and wisdom, concealed by deep counsel from many, and perceives them revealed to her more openly. And now, without consulting the angel or the earlier prophets, she alone, leaning upon the only one, draws and attracts wisdom from hidden places, in accordance with Job (ch. 28).

I am mistaken if that disciple whom the Bridegroom loved did not also understand wisdom and knowledge to flow from the Bridegroom’s breast. At the Supper, he rested not so much in wine and material feasting as in a welcome reclining upon Jesus’ breast, between the very breasts. There he saw the Word abiding in the most secret bosom of God the Father (John 1); he saw the Word made flesh in the virginal bridal chamber of the Bride-Mother; he saw the treasures of wisdom and knowledge shining in a clarity visible to him, yet dark to the prudent and wise of the world beneath a certain veil spread over them.

He saw, I say, and did not begrudge their revelation—not to all, but to believers. With the swift pen of a scribe he committed them to lasting writing, so that the intelligent hearer might desire to breathe toward the mysteries of that same breast, and from his own poverty of merits find relief in the presence of those treasures.

Porphyry did not approach this breast, nor Aristotle, Socrates, or Plato; not the first Cato, not the second, nor that third Cato said to have fallen from heaven; nor, finally, did anyone approach who, blinded by malice, rejected the newness of grace while holding and retaining the antiquity of his own knowledge or wisdom.

Their knowledge, by a true judgment, is said not to heal but to puff up (1 Cor. 2); and their wisdom is judged by God to be grievous folly. Yet they remain fixed in it through ignorance of the truth, deceiving themselves by a certain privilege of antiquity. One of them says:

> “Let those who hasten drink new must;  
> let an earthen jar pour ancestral unmixed wine for me.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0201D] Ovid, *The Art of Love*, book 2.]

He wishes not to drink the new must of grace from the Bridegroom’s splendid breast, but to have poured out for him the old wine of error from a muddy vessel. Its sweetness seems to him the more welcome and complete because use has confirmed it and ancestral antiquity has sanctioned it.

But let those drink the new must, which old vessels cannot contain, who hasten—who love to behold the Bridegroom coming forth from the bridal chamber; who, warned by angels, come quickly like the shepherds, and do not silence what they see and love, but proclaim it in eager announcement (Luke 2).

No one was found to hasten to him before, or more perfectly than, she who deserved to prepare for the coming one the bridal chamber of her womb. Reclining on his breast, she drank and perceived his knowledge and wisdom to be more welcome in perception and meaning, and better than philosophical error.

## Chapter VII

“Because your breasts are better than wine.” The Bridegroom’s breasts may also be called his mercy and truth, which are known to work in a special way in the Virgin Bride and Mother. The Law given through Moses neither ought nor can be made equal to them, although it may be judged good and necessary in its own time. “The law is good,” indeed, “if anyone uses it lawfully” (1 Tim. 1).

But in the Law there is found a certain harshness of wine: it works wrath and does not bestow grace; it demands tooth for tooth and eye for eye (Exod. 21), that one who strikes be struck in return, and that the other cheek not be offered (Matt. 5; Luke 6). The Law commands many and great things, but does not bring its obscurities into the light. If it produces anything life-giving, it covers it with clinging chaff; it burdens blind minds, weighs down and dulls stiff necks, and does not pour in the gentleness of grace or the sweetness of the Spirit.

The Law rightly gives or promises temporal things according to merit; it afflicts the offender and does not remit deserved punishments. It works severe judgment and stern justice; it does not know mercy and is not appeased freely and without price.

Who sucks such a grape without having his teeth more harshly set on edge? Whose taste and palate are not made more bitter by such a draught? There wrath reigns without mercy and judgment is exercised, whereas mercy ought worthily to exalt itself above wrath and judgment (James 2).

Therefore the Virgin, considering the commandments of the Law—which in a sense deceived the people by enjoining hard and unbearable things without the Spirit of grace—praises the Bridegroom’s breasts, which received her more graciously and sweetly: “Lord,” she says, “according to the Psalm, your mercy and truth have upheld me” (Ps. 39).

Mercy is that by which the Lord of heaven wished to enter the bridal chamber: having an unbegotten Father, he wished to have a virginal mother. Truth is that by which he consummated this will in a happy work: “The Word was made flesh” (John 1), and God wondrously dwelt as man in the Virgin.

Mercy is that by which he did not compel the world to undergo its deserved punishments, but chose this time, these nuptials, and this Virgin in order to wipe them out. Truth is that by which he happily illumined the chosen time through his coming and made the chosen Virgin fruitful through the Spirit’s working. “Mercy and truth,” he says, “have met one another” (Ps. 84).

Mercy ran ahead so that the Virgin might become worthy; truth immediately came to meet her so that she might truly become a mother. It was not, as with us, a departure or flight of virtues because of deserved guilt; rather, in her there was their welcome meeting and encounter.

Mercy ran ahead to prepare a place for the coming Bridegroom, driving harmful things far away and adorning the bridal chamber with the flowers of virtues. When it had been adorned, truth likewise presented itself, which, in accordance with the purpose, ineffably made God human in the Virgin.

God’s mercy toward the Virgin, then, is a more ready will and affection; and truth is the fulfillment or effect of that will. Mercy, not merits, made the Virgin gracious; and truth made her, now full of grace, glorious.

You have read and heard it foretold: “For God loves mercy and truth; the Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 83). In the Virgin God loves to work mercy and truth: he wishes her, freely chosen, truly to glory in grace; he purifies her by the incomparable gift of spiritual grace, and gladdens her by the singular privilege of special glory.

“He has regarded,” she says, “the lowliness of his handmaid; and from this all generations shall call me blessed” (Luke 1). In his regard for her lowliness, she wishes merciful grace to be commended; in the proclamation of blessedness, truthful glory to be marked. For the humble handmaid is made rich in gifts of grace; and of you, city of the great King, we worthily say: “Glorious things are spoken.”

The Virgin therefore rightly says that the Bridegroom’s breasts are better than wine, because no former age bestowed anything like this, nor did the censorious severity of the Law bring this with it: that mercy should come to the Virgin, truth should be born so that she might be made full of grace, and that she should be gladdened with incomparable glory.

## Chapter VIII
Because your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments [Col. 0202D]. The Virgin, reclining in the Bridegroom’s bosom, resting against his breast, reposing between his breasts, withdrawn from external matters and resting in inward and more secret things, feels wonders and tastes sweetnesses—not with her palate, but through the joyful experience of her heart; she delights to be suffused with the sweet fragrance of sweet things.

For the Bridegroom’s breasts contain not the simple drink of milk, but ointments: marvellous compounds, preparations of healing substances, which, gathered and prepared from exceedingly precious ingredients, had been known beforehand to few and fully bestowed upon none in all preceding ages or days. Their inward abundance is not drawn forth by every little child and suckling; rather, the Virgin Bride, fuller in grace and more advanced in growth, experiences it presently. In her bridal chamber this very composition or mixture of ointments was made, destined first and far more abundantly to benefit her, but ourselves, little ones, less and later.

For when mercy and truth, as was said above, met one another, they wisely and carefully gathered certain things as though they were ingredients; bringing them from different quarters, they collected them into one bundle and, by the art of the perfumer, reduced them to most fragrant ointments. For an ancient discord existed between God and humankind, because human injustice had no agreement with God’s justice. But the Bridegroom, on his coming, brought justice and gave peace; he caused the one going before and the one following to be joined by a welcome kiss: “Justice and peace have kissed” (Ps. [Col. 0203B] 84).

For when, by conferring justice, he made righteous the one who had been unrighteous, the discord which had long persisted between the righteous and the unrighteous gave way; and peace immediately followed. Since she perceived nothing in the justified person except what was righteous, she gave and received the long-desired kiss of justice now found. Therefore the righteous human being had peace with the righteous God; and by a wondrous assumption God became man—God, I say, assuming humanity and giving his own justice to the assumed one, while the power of the assuming one’s justice was not exhausted.

Moreover, just as mercy and truth meeting one another make a compound or ointment, so justice and peace, kissing one another, likewise make a certain preparation by which health, or surely a wholesome soothing remedy, is given to the person whom the Samaritan has mercifully lifted onto his own beast [Col. 0203C] (Luke 10). Finally, they met in the Virgin’s bridal chamber as in a little mortar, and in their most welcome meeting prepared an ointment—or rather, ointments—of great benefit: the Father’s command, the presence of the Word, the overshadowing of the Spirit; the obedient ear, more steadfast faith, and the Virgin’s flesh.

In this earthen vessel there is no rustic mixing of these ingredients, but a certain pounding by learned hands and medical skill.
