When they have been distributed in fitting number, measure, and weight, precious ointments result: remedies which mitigate pains and restore health. Their preparation is indeed of such fragrance and scent that the Bride, to whom the greater benefit of grace is granted, delights in and marvels at the fragrant sweetness of the ointments, which are not merely good, but undoubtedly the best among better things.

For although before the Law and under the Law very many things were found which are medicinally transformed, through the merits of devout faith, into ointments—things which God, ever loving good things, is said to have smelled and is believed often to have delighted in with the most pleasing scent of sweetness—yet she in whose proximity to the bridal chamber, or rather in whom the bridal chamber itself is found, experiences these ointments of which we speak to be the best of all those before them.

Into her earth God sent spittle from his own mouth [Col. 0203D] (John 9), and in a manner wonderfully unlike anything above or below made clay; its touch and application restores light long denied from the ancient time of birth, and its sweet fragrance ineffably delights the sense of smell. Isaac is believed to have perceived this sweet fragrance from afar [Col. 0204A] and, taught by the Spirit, to have foretold it mystically when Jacob his son presented himself to him in very fine garments and the most sweet scent of the garments reached his father’s nostrils: “Behold,” he said, “the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 17).

To this field was given the incomparable holiness of a new blessing and, consequently, an unfailing fullness of flowers, fruits, and scents. Isaac, perceiving it from afar, rejoices and marvels; the Virgin, sensing it close at hand and experiencing it in reality, rejoices ineffably. From her, indeed, and through her, a perception—even a faint one—of that same fragrance comes to us, at last scarcely reaching us because it found us far away; yet, having found us, it made us as happy as joyful at its arrival—though not through our merit, but through the Virgin’s intercession.

Although such ointments were composed in the Virgin, they were not held confined within narrow bounds with her. Rather, through abundant grace they reached those more remote and, by their fragrant touch and health-giving scent, anointed us. That ointments are spoken of in the plural, rather than ointment in the singular, indicates that not one kind of evil alone is found in us. Our misery has brought upon itself many ailments and many infirmities, which the physician, when he came, removed with medicinal ointments. “Truly,” says Isaiah, “he himself bore our ailments and carried our infirmities” (Isa. 53).

Truly he bore and took away, carried and removed, our ailments and infirmities, which were many and diverse and required not the touch or fragrance of one ointment [Col. 0204C], but different ailments required different medicinal treatments from different ointments. Yet we, burdened with much sickness, have no leisure to learn what is healthful; dullness of intellect or the lethargy of weariness weighs us down, so that we apply little diligence to such matters. We do not know, I say, what infirmity requires what ointment; and though we have experienced many diseases, we are blind in the art of healing.

But our physician, presiding alone within his own workshop, prepares a medicine suited to each illness. By his own skill, he does not wish the sick indiscriminately to participate in it, nor for his art or knowledge to pass over to them, but rather for it to benefit them. Nevertheless, insofar as anyone can experience it in himself, to whom the physician loves to grant healing care: this physician appears to have brought forth for us three ointments successively and, through them, to have supplied us sick persons with a suitable remedy [Col. 0204D].

The first, indeed, biting and harsh, violently shook us; and, as though applying an outward liniment, immediately struck an inward heaviness. Disturbing and removing a disease long inbred, it increased it and presented it, as it were, all at once to feeling and knowledge. Once it had been brought to light, the wicked mind raged and groaned, scarcely able to bear itself, as it reviewed recent things and old. Pricked and compuncted, it wrapped itself in harsh memories of its iniquities and cast itself among the thorns and briars of thoughts that accused—or even defended—it.

Thus the troubled mind at once began to abhor its own foulness and, deservedly, to displease itself more vehemently on account of its own ugliness. Through hatred of itself, it began to bear witness to new things contrary to its former state, and, judgment having changed, to detest what had previously pleased it. This fragrance of ointment introduced a dreadful fear, like a cup; having cleansed the channels of the veins, it brought us to a health-giving vomiting, so that, freely rejecting with disgust the former blandishments of vices, which had previously been falsely thought gains, we might truly count them losses.

The penitent man indicated that he had been touched by this scent: laboring in groaning, he washed his bed with tears; his eye was troubled by dread of the Judge because of his sins; and, in this health-giving vomiting, he confessed that he had grown old among his enemies (Ps. 6). For fragrance and stench neither agree well nor remain in one abode. When, through grace, the nostrils are opened and the scent of precious ointment is admitted [Col. 0205B], the stench of vices, unable to endure its companionship, is expelled. And the more vigorously this health-giving draught is administered, the more abundantly and freely the foul sediment comes out.

For that scent is “living and effective and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Heb. 4). Therefore, when it is impressed upon someone, seasonably or unseasonably, with the physician’s devout care—when it has entered the damaged boundaries of the sick person as powerfully as mercifully—no channels of veins, no hiding places or recesses of marrow, indeed no place from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, is inaccessible to it. It runs to and fro, wanders about in the manner of a swallow circling, investigates every deep and hidden thing with the office and penetration of a judge, and whatever it finds contrary to life, liable to guilt, and given over to vanity, it gathers with a strong broom and carries away once gathered, preparing a place for health [Col. 0205C].

The second ointment breathes more healthfully and gives forth the scent of a gentler benefit. It restores hope of life and also brings in love, so that the sick person, feeling himself relieved of a heavy burden, may now hope for better things and, in hope, love to act. At this scent the spirit formerly languishing revives; with appetite returning, it desires life-giving food. Refreshed by the food of grace, it rejoices that the necessary strength is restored and that weakened hands and feeble knees are strengthened (Isa. 35).

Accordingly, warmly embracing the gift of strengthening grace, it goes out to its work, finding the exertion of labor welcome [Col. 0205D]. Its hands, released from torpor, it diligently employs in labour; it hears and obeys, that it may go and bear more pleasing fruit. Forgetting what lies behind, it applies itself more attentively to virtue; it chastises its body and duly reduces it to servitude (1 Cor. 9). What had previously seemed bitter or perhaps impossible is, conversely, judged as easy in proportion as it is healthful.

Hence it embraces fasts, vigils, continence, and patience; it considers it fitting to be governed and subjected to the counsel of its elders. Out of love of what is right, it renounces the pleasures of the flesh—indeed, even its own wills—so that it may subject its body and itself to God. For God wills this order to be maintained in us: that all things should be restrained within their proper law and established bounds [Col. 0206A], so that the spirit, ruling the flesh, may act upon it and reduce it beneath itself, while the spirit itself, obeying the greater, may be one spirit with God.

Who, miserably situated in the foul hovel of this body, or entangled in so many stains and snares of malignant spirits, could thus advance, freed from the threats or ambushes of attacking enemies, unless he were anointed with this ointment of strengthening grace? Who would not recoil from the entrance because the bolt of excessive difficulty had been set against it, or fail in progress through the manifold encounter of hindrances, unless he were touched so sweetly and effectively by the scent of this ointment that, both beginning and advancing, he should not be broken?

Finally, whoever rightly traces the course of those who advance knows that the Father corrects and chastises the son whom he loves (Heb. 12) [Col. 0206B]. He does not wish one to glory in having gained the benefit of the promised inheritance if he has not first permitted him to be scourged by many tribulations of sufferings. But if the righteous person gives way a little and wavers under the assault of vices or scourges, the scent of this ointment, coming to meet him, quickly revives him. Such sweetness does not allow him to be struck down and fall into utter failure, but, putting a hand beneath him, gently supports and carefully advances him to greater progress.

Therefore impending evils do not wholly draw him back from what he has begun; rather, grace mercifully shapes his labours and contests according to the command. The one whom, by its merciful design, it permits to shiver and sweat, it strengthens after sweating by the promised restoration of health and makes stronger.

The third ointment calms the sea, moderates wrath [Col. 0206C], quiets the winds by its majesty, and with its hand makes the turbulent motions of the mind serene. It levels the road, holds the right hand, steadies the steps, and, as though a harbour had now been found, makes one secure and confirms him. For the strong traveller is now in some measure serene within himself, happily removed from the attacks of vices or from debased consent. United in patience, he already confidently and humbly presumes upon what is certain.

Although every sort of adversity still murmurs and presses upon him from behind, it does not effectively resist him face to face by its insolence, while, forgetting what lies behind, he longs for and faints in the courts of God alone (Ps. 83). Turned wholly toward him in affection, he desires, as it were, to join face with face. “My face has sought you,” he says; “your face, O Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. 26) [Col. 0206D].

Touched by the fragrance of this ointment, he either does not feel adverse things at all, or counts them empty and reckons them as nothing; he does not consent to them. He burns with so great a desire for the things ahead, which he already senses, that he passes by with a deaf ear whatever sounds discordantly and dissents. Let every temporarily harmful thing then rage and make noise with threats or blows; let things seemingly profitable entice by fraud, falsehood, entreaty, or price. What will this person do but joyfully and bravely hold to his sure path and, like one on a mountain ridge above those barking below, answer with that apostolic saying: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? I am certain that neither death nor life …” (Rom. 8).

Since such certainty of perseverance confirms him that he does not care what hostile force makes a clamour against him [Col. 0207A], he already seems to himself to possess the reward laid up for him, which is known to remain unfailingly promised to those who persevere. “I have finished the course,” he says; “there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness” (2 Tim. 4). And again: “We were saved in hope” (Rom. 8).

Whoever has experienced the fragrant sweetness of this ointment becomes as certain of future things as though they were present, and advances so greatly, strongly, and sweetly from virtue to virtue that he hopes for salvation and holds the salvation hoped for as though it were already given. Thus the first ointment purged away the wickedness of the old leaven; the second, by the new gift of the mixture, prepared unleavened deeds of merit; the third confirmed those who feast upon the certain privilege of restored health.

The first, with a heavy scraper and a discerning ladle, turned over the house, overthrew it, and emptied the bilge; the second poured strengthening medicine into the sick mind [Col. 0207B]; the third made hope more certain, so that it might no longer fear a fall or ruin. Therefore the first may be called purgative, the second strengthening, and the third confirming: because by the first every sick person is cleansed from the dregs of vices; by the second, through the welcome file and desired labour, health is restored; by the third, the mind is strengthened in its purpose both by a certain humble joy in present gifts and by assured confidence in future ones.

The holy Virgin had perceived the Bridegroom’s breasts to abound in these ointments. She did not, like the envious, keep their grace for herself with the outlet closed; rather, she offered their most sweet fragrance outwardly to the devout and humble, and by their benefit nourished minds previously barren with an abundance of merits. But because one does not arrive at so great a benefit of this fragrance by human powers, unless, when one comes, one is first anticipated by divine hand and help, the Virgin shows by what gift one undoubtedly comes to it, so that, once this has been shown, one who hears but does not love may be held without excuse.

## CHAPTER IX

“Your name is oil poured out.” The Bridegroom’s name is Jesus, which was called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb (Luke 1). And who understood this name more truly, loved it more sincerely, or preached it more fittingly than the Virgin Mother herself, to whom the angel first announced: “Behold,” he said, “you will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus” [Col. 0207D] (ibid.).

Jesus is called in Latin *Salutaris*, “the Saving One,” or *Salvator*, “Saviour.” His name accords with his work; he has his name from the thing itself, “for he shall save his people” (Matt. 1). Thus he is rightly called Jesus, since he will be the salvation of the people, and “whoever calls upon his name shall be saved” (Joel 2). For the Lord’s right hand gives strength to the person who calls upon it devoutly, and he has become an answerer unto salvation for the person who confesses worthily (Ps. 117).

The Bride calls this name oil. For *eleos* is Greek, and in Latin it means mercy, because it was not our justice but his mercy that enabled Jesus, or the Saviour, to will to be our Saviour. Our merit had cast us far away from his face, but he called us back and by the mercy which is his own saved us. Hence the Apostle says: “Not from works of righteousness [Col. 0208A] which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus 3).

When God purposes to save the undeserving, after wrath he remembers this mercy; through, or because of, this name—that is, this oil—he has compassion on the unworthy and wretched. By the power of this name he drives our enemies far away and, freeing us from vices, brings us back to himself as friends. The person who had long stood wandering in the way of sins now hopes, grace visiting him, and joyfully promises himself this; for he knows that God’s gifts and calling are not conferred from his repentance, but that the name and oil of mercy are poured above every liquid of merits.

“For he gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, and every tongue confess that Jesus is Lord” (Phil. 2) [Col. 0208B]. Therefore that penitent says: “For your name’s sake you will give me life” (Ps. 142), and adds: “In your mercy you will destroy my enemies” (ibid.). And in another psalm: “For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be propitious to my sin” (Ps. 24).

The Lord himself does not contradict this hope or assurance. Rather, through Isaiah, taught by the Spirit, he mercifully foretells this, so that the penitent who hears it may presume with strengthened and fuller confidence, and may know in what he ought to glory, as healthfully as truly: “All who love your name, O Lord, shall glory in you” (Ps. 5). Of this name he says through Isaiah: “For my name’s sake I shall put my wrath far away” (Isa. 48).

For the sake of the name, or oil, which sheds the dew of mercy, he puts his judgment and wrath far from those who had deserved them [Col. 0208C]. If he were not regarded as Saviour, merciful and compassionate, what would remain for each wretched person except to be justly crushed beneath his intolerable justice?

But what does it mean that the oil is said to be poured out? As long as oil is kept in a little vessel, it is either unknown, or its grace and usefulness are not felt. Although the physician himself, who knows all things, knows it, the sick do not, since he has not yet applied it to their wounds requiring healing. At one time this oil was held, as it were, in a sealed vessel, when the Son of God was held in himself to be good indeed and merciful, truly possessing in affection the purpose of showing mercy, but not yet fully making the wretched rejoice in the result.

This oil seems to have been kept in its vessel when, in a hidden judgment, he did not will to have mercy on the angels who grew proud: he neither turned them away from their fall by preventing grace, nor converted them after their fall by aiding mercy [Col. 0208D]. But he granted the angels who stood to feel this oil, mercifully deigning to preserve them lest they too should fall, and increasing and adding to them so effective a soothing virtue of this oil that they received from it a sure and unwavering support for standing.

But perhaps we should say that this is above us and does not concern us, unless we too experienced the benefit of the same oil—or rather, unless he inclined toward us more liberally and abundantly the open vessel, and, the oil being poured out entirely, caused his whole mercy, as it were, to bend down toward us. For both our need and his goodness seemed to require that greater mercy should be granted to greater misery; and because there is no distinction, since manifold sin gathers and confounds both Jews and Gentiles (Rom. 10), the whole abundance of this oil must be poured out upon both, so that the yoke might decay.

Foreseeing and praying for this in the Spirit, the Prophet says: “May God have mercy on us, may he make his face shine upon us, and may he have mercy on us” (Ps. 66) [Col. 0209A]. Why does he say, “may he have mercy,” and again, “may he have mercy”? He adds: “That we may know your way on earth, your salvation among all nations” (ibid.). “Because,” he says, “both Gentiles and Jews have sinned, and there is no distinction, this outpouring of oil must reach both, that you may graciously recall us Jews to him who is the Way, and that together we may know your salvation among all nations.”

Oil shut up in a vessel preserves the holy angels; oil poured out gathers together the scattered bands of chosen human beings. And mercy, which hides itself within the sanctuary of heaven in order to protect the healthy, pours itself out, when the vessel is inclined, in order to heal sick human beings. “O Lord,” he says, “incline your heavens and come down; touch the mountains and they shall smoke” (Ps. 143).

He who offers to the standing angels a vessel full of mercy inclines that vessel to heal sick persons on earth. What seemed to be held within it he now pours out with lavish and bountiful hand, and he pours abundant mercy over those who have great need of mercy. At its medicinal touch harmful swellings subside, stings are restrained, and the pains of wounds are softened. Like smoke, the vanity of proud minds vanishes; the disease being driven away, renewed health gains strength [Col. 0209C].

## CHAPTER X

“Your name is oil poured out.” The Bridegroom’s name is Christ; and *Christus* means “anointed,” because God “anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions” (Ps. 44). He may be called not only anointed but also oil, because by his own power he wipes away harmful phlegm from us and anoints us, languishing and dry as we are, with sweet grace.

For the name Christ, rightly defined in its meaning, teaches that God and man are personally united, and that by the marvellous and incomprehensible force of this union one Christ is made, although the natures of God and man are very dissimilar. For just as a rational soul and corruptible flesh make one human being [Col. 0209D], so God assuming humanity and the assumed human being likewise make one Christ.

> [Note: [Col. 0209D] Athanasius, in the Creed.]

And although the unconfused diversity of both natures is maintained, nevertheless the unity of person is proclaimed in Christ himself. If faith in this name is poured upon us by the sprinkling of his mercy, if we love the union of the natures and the unconfused unity of person, then, because he overflows and abounds in abundant chrism and wondrous charism, he makes us altogether joyful while he makes us fruitful in the merits of virtues.

But this oil, or name, is no longer enclosed within the narrow boundaries of Judaea; it has been poured out among the nations to the very ends of the world. No one rightly judges that he comes to salvation [Col. 0210A] unless he first advances in virtue through faith in this name. “There is no other name under heaven in which we must be saved” (Acts 4). Therefore no one can hide from the true light of this oil, since its ray pours itself powerfully to the ends of the earth and enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1), provided that person has not rendered himself unclean through obstinate wickedness.

For everyone who has happily received, by grace, the gift of ears to hear, everyone wisely instructed in faith in this name, knows that Christ is the cornerstone joining Jews and Gentiles; that he is the head of the Church, the one mediator of God and humankind, our bone and our flesh by nuptial exchange and natural fellowship, himself anointed and anointing those near to him through spiritual power and grace [Col. 0210B].

He poured out this oil or name far and wide among both Jews and Gentiles when his love was poured into their hearts: first, so that the apostles might truly confess Christ among the Jews; then, so that many among the Gentiles might be anointed with the same chrism. When the apostles were asked whom people said the Son of Man to be, they replied that not all spoke or thought alike. Then, after their own understanding had been examined more closely, Peter, speaking both for himself and for the rest, gave this learned answer: “You are the Christ.” And he said: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16).

After this oil or name had flowed mercifully in Judaea, Idumaea too received its outpouring [Col. 0210C]. There, when Christ came, he extended his sandal so that he made friends of those whom he found alien through the fault of error. Since they received this name with firm faith and with a hope undoubtedly not empty, they were generally called Christians by Christ himself; and whoever proved worthy to be retained in the register of the faithful desired, as he was a Christian, so also to be designated by the name.

This name is therefore rightly called poured out rather than poured in, because it is not assigned particularly to Jew alone or Greek alone. Although the Jews first glory in faith in this name, those more distant are not excluded from the same glory. For the sound of this name has gone into all the earth (Ps. 18), and its outpouring has passed to the ends of the world, granting the saving benefit alike to distant and nearby persons—provided they have loved to adorn faith with works.

For all believers dispersed from east to west, from north to south, are sprinkled with the Christian name or Christ’s oil; it is not shut out from any by land, sea, or any interval whatsoever, but has been poured out to all upon whom God has willed to have mercy [Col. 0210D].

## CHAPTER XI

“Your name is oil poured out.” The Bridegroom’s name is God. This is the name which the Father is believed to have imparted to the Son when he is said to have begotten him coequal and coeternal with himself; when the unbegotten one gave the begotten one naturally to be God, and willed that none but God should participate in this giving.

For, just as whatever God is, so whatever has been substantially derived from him has been imparted to this Son in fullest measure: no one is excluded by beginning, end, place, or time [Col. 0211A]. From him from whom he has being, there has been granted to him essentially that which is naturally inaccessible to every creature.

He who is God in some sense poured out his own name as oil when he did not confound the newly created angels with a cloud of ignorance, but, by the generosity of him who made them, they understood by whom they had been made and received that Father and Son are inseparably one God. Nor did this outpouring instruct angels in heaven alone; the same instruction also passed down to human beings on earth. Judaea was marked by the certainty of divine knowledge, and in Israel the majesty of this most illustrious name was received (Ps. 75).

“Worship him,” he says, “all his angels; Zion heard and rejoiced” (Ps. 96) [Col. 0211B]. The angels in heaven venerate as God and Lord the one at whose name the citizens of Zion on earth rejoice when they hear it. In that people the name of God is celebrated and the poured-out oil is active, though grace has not yet been poured out more abundantly among the nations.

But when the long-desired fullness of time came, by which the depth of the divine purpose was made known to us, the Son, sent by the Father, willed to become human in the Virgin and from the Virgin. Thus the name God was more fully proclaimed among Gentiles as well as Jews. “Let the nations know,” he says, “that your name is God” (Ps. 82). “And all kings,” he says, “shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71). Whom does “him” mean? He adds: “His name remains before the sun” (ibid.). What benefit is in this name? “All tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him” (ibid.).

What is this name? “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel [Col. 0211C]” (Luke 1); “and blessed be the name of his majesty.” The name of his humility is “Man”; the name of his majesty is “God” (ibid.). Of him the Apostle says: “Who is over all, God blessed for ever” (Rom. 9).

This God, remaining in the Father’s bosom and inhabiting inaccessible light, possessing from him, or with him, equality denied to angels and human beings alike, willed before the Virgin’s childbirth that his name should be poured out among a few. But after her childbirth, he willed that it should be poured out everywhere upon all with greater force. The nations of the Gentiles did not know him hidden; a few Jews, taught by the Spirit, had some perception of him. But after he was poured into the Virgin’s womb at the end of time, he was poured out through streets and squares like water.

“I am poured out like water,” he says, “and all my bones are scattered” (Ps. 21) [Col. 0211D]. Like water he poured himself out into the common knowledge of all when his love was poured out into our hearts, when he scattered the gifts of his charisms, gave to the poor, and gave to human beings the bread of angels, which strengthens them.

Therefore, he whom Isaiah says long before was hidden, we now see, poured out as oil, exposed to all: exposed so that he may pour healing oil over the sick, hidden so that he may hide us, once healed, in the hiding place of his face. “Truly,” he says, “you are a hidden God, God of Israel, Saviour” (Isa. 45). He is hidden when, in God, God conceals himself far from human sight in the Father’s bosom; he is exposed when, from his mother’s womb, he pours himself out for Israel’s salvation. He is hidden when, as God in God, he veils his face from us; he is exposed when he reveals that he has come to save his people.

The angels ever burn with desire to look into the hidden one; human beings now love to love him poured out and exposed. Though the desired hiding place does not yet possess those burdened by the corruptible weight of the body, this outpouring of oil makes them now fervent in spirit [Col. 0212A]. Therefore, after the Virgin had said, “Your name is oil poured out,” she added, “Therefore,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XII
[Col. 0212B] Therefore the young women loved you. “Because,” she says, “you poured out your name like oil, when, coming forth from the bridal chamber, you truly taught that you are not only man but also God.” Those taught by God did not at all neglect this teaching; rather, they loved you with a renewed spirit, whom before they had not known. He did not call them young women in error but deliberately, thereby indicating the tender affection of those who love; for this age both loves more tenderly, adorns itself more carefully, and busies itself more continually—restless in its glances, unsettled in its movements, unable to keep still—while its desire remains unfulfilled. Therefore those whom the condition of harmful old age does not disfigure, whose inward face no wrinkle of former perversity furrows, whose eye does not grow dim, whose tooth does not fall out, whose complaining voice does not grow hoarse, whose trembling step does not falter, whose spine does not bend with age, but in whom such heat flourishes and the vigor of the mind is renewed—these indeed burn more vehemently to love, endure delay more heavily, faint more sweetly, and languish more pleasingly.

[Col. 0212C] Finally, while young women desire to attain the end of their longing, they strive more carefully to please those whom they love; and, so that they may render themselves more pleasing to their sight, they exert the utmost care and effort to appear more beautiful. Thus, giving attention either to preserving or acquiring beauty, they set a mirror before themselves, consider the condition of their face, rejoice in the good qualities which they perceive nature has granted them, and supply by watchful care what nature has given less fully. The more beautiful they offer themselves for pleasing, the more pleasing they become for begetting; for those whose greater beauty delights the eyes of their bridegrooms are more gladly rewarded by them with a kiss and made fruitful by their embrace.

[Col. 0212D] One such woman, anxiously holding a mirror in her hand and carefully discerning in it what she is like, bore children; for “the body that decays discolors the soul’s beauty, and the earthly dwelling weighs down a mind devoted to much toil” (Wisdom 9). To restore this soul, pressed down but perhaps not crushed, both to righteousness and salvation, she chastises her body and duly subjects it to servitude (1 Cor. 9). Looking toward love, she does not shrink from enduring danger or death; she wipes away whatever stain she judges displeasing to the bridegroom. She wishes her forehead to be bright, her cheeks softly flushed, her lips to breathe modesty, and

[Col. 0213A] her words restraint; in short, she wishes her whole face to shine with new grace, so that she may worthily please him to whom she wishes to commend herself. But when she had shown herself approved and lovable, with forehead cleansed and face so pleasing, she did not remain barren through the merit of this labor and love. Rather, by the Spirit making her fruitful, conceiving in the womb of generation, she bore children to the bridegroom by spiritual word and deed. To them she also says: “My little children, whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4). And again: “In Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4).

Another young woman, when she was fervent and promised to remain fixed and steadfast in that very fervor, paid insufficient attention, with a judgment worthy of her weakness; still untrained and inadequate, she was found somewhat too confident. “Lord,” says Peter,

[Col. 0213B] “I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death” (Luke 22). But he whose it was to know Peter himself, as he knew all else, more fully—knowing that Peter indeed wished what he had said, but could not accomplish it—said: “I tell you, Peter, the cock will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know me” (ibid.). And because the denial of one lacking confidence would have brought him wholly to ruin, unless the powerful grace of the merciful one had lent him its hand, desiring that Peter should not merely recoil from a rash fall but afterward, strengthened, bring forth spiritual children, he said: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have at last turned, strengthen your brethren” (ibid.).

Later, visited by the regard of divine mercy and strengthened by the more abundant gift of the Spirit breathed into him, this same Peter burned more strongly in love and stood more firmly in perseverance; and, by the merit of his stronger love, he deserved to hear from the bridegroom himself: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these? Feed my sheep” (John 21).

[Col. 0213C] Therefore the apostles and apostolic men are not improperly called young women, who in this drama are said to accompany the Virgin Bride. It is not fewness of days or of age that makes them young women, but more fervent faith, impatient love, and the grace of bestowed renewal. For the error widely disseminated in Judaea was driven out—the error preached by the Pharisees, that Galilee could not produce the Christ, and that, in their judgment, it was in no way credible that the carpenter’s son, the brother of James, should be Christ (Matt. 13; Mark 6); he who, in their estimation, deserved stones not for a good work but for blasphemy

[Col. 0213D] (John 10), because, though he was a man, he claimed to be God. When this error, I say, was driven out, newness of faith was bestowed upon the young women, and what the Bride had first secretly received was communicated to the apostles.

“O God,” says the Bride, “your name, your oil, poured itself into me when your dew moistened my fleece, when your divinity flooded me, when I perceived within myself the whole God—the Word of the Father, the Son of God—and I myself, wholly full of complete affection, loved you. But after I had been filled, this oil was poured back upon those nearby; and, so that it might be received, it was poured out upon the young women. What, when poured into me, they neglected because they could not receive it, they loved when poured out upon themselves in fervor of spirit.”

For no one followed that same Virgin more familiarly,

[Col. 0214A] or more fully attained, through her mediation, knowledge of the Bridegroom, than the apostles, who lived with her for a long time before and after Christ’s passion and heard from her more frequently the mystery of the Word incarnate. “All these,” it says, “were persevering with one accord in prayer with Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1). One of them, above the rest, took care of that Virgin, and, at Christ’s command, diligently devoted himself to serving her; he gave her the obedient care of a son as to a mother, and served her, received into his own home, with the ministry of a provider.

But who could reckon with what affection she embraced John and the others with whom she had lived so long; with what care she strove to teach them what she had known first and more perfectly; and how often and insistently she recounted the wondrous order both of her conception and of her birth?

[Col. 0214B] For what she saw fulfilled in herself by a deep and ineffable counsel, she did not begrudge to those standing with her, to young women such as these. Rather, she rejoiced to recall it often in their hearing, wishing them likewise to attain a share in the grace granted to her. Accordingly, when she had said, “Therefore the young women loved you,” she added: “Draw me,” etc.

## CHAPTER XIII

“Draw me; we will run after you in the fragrance of your ointments.” Although the Virgin is raised to such excellence that by the gift of grace she is brought to the Bridegroom’s kiss, she indeed draws joy and spiritual confidence from this, yet presumes nothing concerning her own strength. For as she did not conceive the willing of good by her own merit, so neither did she receive the power to accomplish it except from another.

[Col. 0214C] And from him from whom she has everything which she knows to be useful and desirable, she asks to be drawn after him, to whose service she has devoted herself. For she neither is, nor aims to be, so swift as to run ahead. She strives only for this and judges it sufficient: to run after him. Yet even for this, in her own judgment, she has no strength unless she is drawn; unless she is not dragged back by the burden of her own weakness; unless, by the sweet Spirit of grace, she is impelled toward the things before her and not driven back toward the things behind by the breath of the evil spirit.

Therefore she asks to be drawn after him by him—not unwillingly, but hindered still by the fetter of corruptible flesh. Though its strength may now be sufficiently firm in a ready spirit, the flesh nevertheless remains somewhat weak through a certain natural heaviness.

[Col. 0214D] The ready spirit burns to follow him whom it loves, earnestly desiring that the flesh may no longer delay it beyond what is right; so that, as the Virgin’s spirit loves to cling to God, so the flesh may be unable to wrest anything injurious away from that same spirit. For a readier will urges and raises some persons toward higher things, but bodily weakness calls those same persons back and softens them. By its grievous softness it either casts them headlong into failure or at least does not permit them to advance to perfection.

What, then, is necessary for such wretches, whom misery draws back with a soft bond, except that they be drawn and attracted by a stronger spirit, so that, when the softness which wickedly pulls them back has been pressed down and overcome, the merciful hand of the one drawing may at last prevail? “Therefore,” he says, “I have drawn you in mercy” (Jer. 31).

There is also that drawing by which the flesh is not now compelled

[Col. 0215A] to obey, but rather the spirit itself is soothed: a drawing, I say, of a far sweeter inward delight, when the spirit takes pleasure in the taste and love of truth once tasted. In the place of this drawing the Bride-Mother wishes to be held by grateful desire, and thereby to be sweetly advanced toward those things which delight the spirit; not to be frightened away from their sweetness by any disturbances of temporal things, but to be wholly absorbed by the serene face of him whom she loves.

If such a face is shown, even briefly, to one who loves, and if a clearer eye directs itself with right judgment upon what has been shown, the one showing and the one gazing are joined by such a bond of love that the lover is drawn to the beloved by an indissoluble bond. Drawn, I say, not by violence, trouble, fear, or hatred of either the drawn or the drawer, but by love: by that drawing through which a child is drawn after its nurse, or a son follows his father, or a daughter her mother; indeed, by that drawing through which the lover is drawn into the beloved—more gladly as he languishes more sweetly, while he desires to attain and desires insatiably to desire.

[Col. 0215B] Of this Hosea says: “I will draw them in the bonds of charity” (Hosea 2). And the drawn one answers: “My soul has clung after you” (Ps. 62).

Thus our Virgin desires and asks to be drawn after her beloved: namely, that by his grace he may give effect to her loving and following; that with affectionate love the Bride may burn after the Bridegroom, the Mother after the Son; and that not flesh to flesh, but soul to God may cling more strongly. For just as she recalls that she was weighed down by the loss of a certain death, when her unhappy soul had once clung to the pavement, so this Virgin, because after the Bridegroom’s kiss she loves nothing but life, desires to be drawn after him through whom she may live—not unwillingly, but eager in affection, fervent in spirit, free through merits.

And because, when thus drawn and thus aided, it is not fitting that she should linger, this woman will surely not follow the one who draws her with a limping step. Rather, with ready stride, agile pace, and swift foot, she will run and hasten by an unhindered path to him for whom she longs. “We will run,” she says, “in the fragrance of your ointments.”

[Col. 0215C] She says, “We will run,” in the plural, though she had begun in the singular: “Draw me.” “If you draw me to yourself by special affection and grace, making me pleasing and blessed by the nuptial kiss; if you cleanse and make fruitful the Bride by the sovereign Spirit, so that I may rejoice in a new and unprecedented kind of virginal childbirth—if,” she says, “you draw me thus, then not I alone will rejoice in the spiritual gift, but with me the young women will rejoice in a certain common benefit. They will, according to their measure, imitate me who run ahead more devoutly, and they will be declared to run together with me after you whom they love.”

Therefore, “Grant me first, grant me especially, the kiss; draw me by the bond of charity; grant me to know and feel the greater grace of your goodness. And this will not benefit me alone, nor shall I be found running alone; rather, we will run, and all who love, though not with equal speed, will come to you together.”

Through the example and merit of the Virgin, who is found to have run first and more perfectly, the apostles and their successors believe they have found grace. Casting off, as though a wrinkled tunic, old age, they are renewed like an eagle—not in feathers but in renewed habits.

[Col. 0215D] The Virgin was drawn and attracted by a certain cord granted to none besides, by which she clung to the Bridegroom and Author with a heart wholly untiring. She was drawn up and lifted up while the Holy Spirit overshadowed her so strongly and so sweetly that, nature’s customary law being set aside, she conceived God. He who is conceived is the one whose word runs swiftly, who, leaping on the mountains and bounding over the hills, runs ahead of the others as a giant (Song 2). The Virgin sees that she must necessarily be drawn in order to follow him; she can grasp him only when her native slowness has been cast aside.

Who, then, is found readier to be drawn or made swifter to run than the Virgin, whose flesh has been altogether lightened of the burden of sin and, through the lightening draw of God, wonderfully united to the God who draws? Thus drawn, the Virgin—having received what she knows was granted to no other—

[Col. 0216A] now runs, now advances, now hastens more eagerly toward the object of her desire, teaching and leading the fervent young women toward perfection, although none, however swift, arrives at equal progress.

Perhaps, therefore, the Virgin asked singly to be drawn, but declared that she would run not alone but together with the others, because the Son, choosing her especially as Mother of God, drew her to himself, yet she did not draw the fruit of this work to herself alone. For from the fact that she was singularly exalted to the prerogative of motherhood, no small benefit was granted to the young women who followed; while they strove worthily to imitate that Virgin, each ran according to her measure in loving the Bridegroom. “Two ran together,” it says, “but John ran ahead faster than Peter” (John 20). And another says: “Thus I run, not as toward an uncertainty” (1 Cor. 9).

[Col. 0216B] “We will run,” they say, “in the fragrance of your ointments.” The fragrance of the ointments is the sweetness of spiritual gifts. When each of the elect has perceived it with a keen sense of smell, not envying it to others but rather rejoicing in their companionship, they hasten with eager running to reach it—or rather, to enter into it. They cannot bear delay and scarcely tolerate waiting to find what they have sensed beforehand.

You know that it naturally belongs to dogs to perceive with their noses what they do not see with their eyes; and if they have been properly trained in hunting practice, they run about, hasten, bark, cry out, until they have caught up with it. To such persons Paul says: “Run thus, that you may attain” (1 Cor. 9). But if anyone with a keener nostril smells something anointed or an ointment, he follows the allurement of the absorbed fragrance with such desire

[Col. 0216C] that neither promises, threats, death itself, nor life recalls him from it. He counts all things as loss, so that he may gain only what he desires.

How great, consider, are the ointments in their own fullness, when they are kept under the perfumer’s hand behind lock and chamber-door—if, before they are actually and fully found from afar, their sweetness of scent makes hearts so attentive? How great is the fullness of those things that refresh persons now present, whose fragrance, streaming outside, makes those who inhale it so ardent that, their feet being strengthened at the soles, it makes them not only come, but, in hatred of grievous delay, run?

Who will grant us, far off as we are, to perceive this fragrance even a little? Who will give stronger movement to our weakened feet and feeble knees, so that by merciful grace we too may sometime be found running, or at least may follow at a slow pace from afar the young women who run ahead? Blessed are those women to whom the Bride-Mother indicates that she will grant her companionship, with whom she declares that she will run in the fragrance of the ointments. For she truly runs with those young women in such a way as to run ahead; and while they still remain outside, she herself runs more swiftly and more familiarly within. Indicating this, she adds:

## CHAPTER XIV

“The king brought me into his storerooms.” She who shortly before had asked to be drawn by him whom she loves now confesses that she has been drawn and brought into his storerooms. She does not conceal through envy the grace she has found,

[Col. 0217B] nor dishonor it by obscure silence; rather, she makes it known to the young women for the praise and glory of the Bridegroom. Since she burned with greater desire and shone with greater merits, the Bridegroom brought her, as if suddenly, into his secret chamber. To one thus admitted he showed the wondrous abundance of spiritual things, the presence of ointments, and the truth of promised gifts.

Entering and beholding Solomon’s incomparable storehouses, she was astonished and, as it were, stupefied by the grace of this new vision. Having no further strength and unable to contain herself for joy, she runs back outside, announcing the benefit which she had deserved to obtain. “You,” she says, “to whom divine grace has now granted that you may run, take care not to incur a blameworthy failure through delay or exertion. Rather, run steadfastly and bravely toward riches which are not uncertain—perhaps unknown to you, but not wholly untried by me. He who brought me into his fullness has not yet led you to what you desire, according to the counsel which he himself knows.

[Col. 0217C] Yet he wishes you to rejoice in my present good things and, by my example, to have more certain confidence concerning your own.”

The Bride wished here to name him not “Bridegroom” or “Beloved,” but “King,” wishing, I think, to indicate the royal power of the Bridegroom and to commend his resources, riches, and every fullness of possessions—since the storerooms of kings are found to overflow beyond those of others. Now no rightly minded person can doubt that he is powerful, since truthful Scripture affirms by many testimonies both that he does not cast off the mighty, because he himself is mighty (Job 36), and that “he has done all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113), and that he has power to act whenever he wills (Wisdom 12). That he is rich, the Apostle says: “He who is rich,” etc. (Rom. 10); and the Gospel: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward” (Luke 16)—undoubtedly signifying God.

[Col. 0217D] Finally, who is richer than the Lord, whose “are the earth and its fullness, the world and those who dwell in it” (Ps. 23)? Therefore the Virgin’s Bridegroom is not inappropriately called King, a name which commends both his power and abundance. He is said, moreover, to have not one storeroom but storerooms, in order that his abundance may be shown to be far greater; for it is certain that more is contained in storerooms than in a single storeroom, and that many things in many places are filled with diverse supplies. The Virgin says that she was brought into many rather than one, indicating that she attained the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

[Col. 0218A] In these she deserves to receive not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God (1 Cor. 2), in order that she may know what things have been given her by God; and, knowing them, may revere them. Thus, although she sees and loves in herself the Word of God made flesh, having the mind of Christ she no longer knows him according to the flesh (2 Cor. 5).

The hidden things of divine wisdom, uncertain and concealed from others, are made known to the Virgin by an incomparable gift and in an ineffable manner. She rejoices to be brought into that sanctuary of secrets, to which the other virgins rejoice to be led not abreast of her but after her. She received first and more perfectly both the announcing angel and, according to his word, experienced the overshadowing Spirit. She knew that in conception she had undergone neither fault nor intercourse, and that in childbirth she had uttered no groan according to Eve’s law.

[Col. 0218B] She knew that he whom she cherished and embraced according to the natural need of little children was life and the life-giving nourishment of angels; that he whom she held in her lap and nursed at her mother’s breast was God, eternally hidden in the bosom of God the Father. By a marvelous newness she knew herself to be the mother of God and man, and the nurse of her own Nourisher and Author—and of all things.

These perhaps are the storerooms into which the Bridegroom brought the Virgin Mother, which none but the wise Architect constructed with his own hand, and which, when he constructed them, he filled with such an abundance of spices that the very sweetest fragrance of the ointments stirs every sluggish person to run. One storeroom, as it were, is that into which divinity descended into humanity without being consumed; another is that in which humanity was assumed into God.

[Col. 0218C] These two—namely, the Word and the flesh—are joined to one another by such a marvelous work that in Christ they are naturally distinct and yet not personally divided. If anyone seems to understand and receive one without the other—if he confesses either Christ as man without God or God without man—he appears to have entered one of the King’s storerooms but, through either ignorance or obstinacy, to have recoiled from the other.

But the Virgin Mary entered not one only but both together. She confessed that he whom she bore was at once God and man; she relied upon him all the more devoutly because she did so more certainly, retaining in memory and sweetly recounting what, whom, and how she had borne.

[Col. 0218D] For she bore not merely man but also God. His wondrous humanity and his divinity made human were disclosed to the Virgin who had been admitted, but for some time remained hidden from the young women themselves. Running in the fragrance after the Mother and Virgin, they will be led into these same storerooms when time and merits coincide. The Virgin declares that she will rejoice when they are led in, indicating that through them she will receive an increase of joy; for, already secure in herself concerning the gift she has received, when they also receive it she will enjoy greater joy on their behalf. This is what she adds: “We will exult,” etc.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0219A]

“We will exult and rejoice in you, mindful of your breasts more than wine.” Turning—or rather returning—to the young women, she announced to them her joy; and by this announcement invited them to run more steadfastly. When she had briefly finished this, she immediately turned both word and face back to the Bridegroom, since she judged speaking to him sweeter than speaking about him.

Everyone who loves tenderly, although he willingly speaks to others about the one he loves, finds it much more pleasing to speak to that person himself, if the choice is granted. Speaking about him, he desires to commend him to his hearers; speaking to him, he rejoices to taste his own grace. Thus the Bride, when speaking of the Bridegroom, appears to do so for the young women’s sake: namely, to exhort them to love him whom she loves.

[Col. 0219B] For so great is her love that she does not fear a rival or concubine, nor count it a loss if another woman is prompted to love him. Indeed, she judges that the joy which, as a lover, she desires to have in the beloved will be made greater if others also attain a share in him. Therefore, returning quickly to the Bridegroom, with whom she gladly converses more often, she declares that she rejoices not in her progress alone, but in theirs together with her. “We will exult,” she says, “and rejoice in you.”

One word does not suffice for the lover to declare her joy; she doubles it, so that by doubling it she may express its abundance more clearly. Yet even if she uses the same or similar words, as though explaining at greater length, she cannot worthily express all that she feels. Or perhaps, when she says “We will exult,” she denotes a joy that she does not hide within, but pours outward in voice or some action in such a way that the appearance of love is displayed before the eyes of beholders and that whoever attends rightly may likewise be inflamed to love. “I have not hidden your righteousness,” he says, “in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation” (Ps. 39).

[Col. 0219C] But because every hypocrite sometimes does or says many things which have a good appearance while inwardly conscience contradicts them, the Virgin adds: “And we will rejoice in you,” denoting that joy which, God bearing witness, lies hidden in the secret place of the heart, when the heart inwardly rejoices in accord with what is shown outwardly.

The Prophet seems to indicate this in one verse, distinguishing them more clearly and assigning each to its own sphere: he calls joy that which is held inwardly, but exultation that which is expressed through outward signs. “Therefore,” he says, “my heart has rejoiced, and I exulted under my tongue” (Ps. 15). And elsewhere: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice” (Ps. 104). And again: “Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, God of my salvation; and my tongue shall exult in your righteousness” (Ps. 50).

From these passages it is inferred that this is the difference between rejoicing and exulting: rejoicing belongs to the heart; exulting belongs to action. For every righteous person ought to rejoice in him both in affection and in effect, from whom he hopes to obtain both present grace and future glory.

[Col. 0219D] Yet exultation is sometimes also assigned to the heart, and a person is said not only to rejoice but to exult inwardly, so that exultation seems to differ little or nothing from joy, since it too is said to be inward. “With my mouth,” he says, “I cried to him, and I exulted under my tongue” (Ps. 65). “Under my tongue,” he says, means in the heart, as later in this Song: “Honey and milk are under your tongue.” And Anna, in her Song: “My heart exulted in the Lord” (1 Sam. 2). And this Virgin Mary herself, in hers: “My spirit exulted in God my Savior” (Luke 1).

Therefore, when she says, “We will exult and rejoice,” she signifies by the doubled term an overflowing joy which she understands that both she and the young women will receive, rejoicing through the gift of more abundant grace in both future and present things. For to the devout person who deserves to be brought into the aforesaid storerooms, their Author promises the joy of the life which now is and of that which is to come (1 Tim. 4). And, having given what was promised,

[Col. 0220A] he already bestows present blessings in reality and future blessings in hope, by which the cloud of sadness being wiped away, the heart of those who seek the Lord is soothed.

Moreover, in the present he advances knowledge and refreshes and calms conscience; in the future he wholly removes both from every darkness and disturbance. This reality and this hope exhort one to love, enable one to run to him, and enable the runner not to fail but rather to advance until he comes to that same end. Therefore, when the Bride says, “We will exult and rejoice,” she adds, “in you,” so that, whether exultation or joy is granted us from present things or from blessings to come, none of us may glory in himself but in the Lord. Forgetting himself—for from himself he has nothing but death and sorrow—let him remember with tender affection him from whom life comes, or rather, who is life. “Mindful,”

[Col. 0220B] she says, “of your breasts more than wine.”

“You nurse, nourish, and refresh the thirsty with your breasts, while you grant and sustain those who love by free gifts; while you make those who love your grace, once they have attained it, perfect by a desirable progress.” Those who have cast aside the substance and thrown away the purse of their own perversity rejoice in the hundredfold recompense of voluntary poverty. Made stronger by the present benefit and the milk of the left breast, they become more certain, through the gift of the right breast, of receiving the reward of eternal life.

Breasts such as these are above wine—that is, better than wine—because present perfection and the promise of the future are offered to the righteous more profitably and more pleasingly than the tribulation and anguish inflicted upon all evildoers, who are tormented in the present by wounded conscience and await an irremediable punishment in the future. “Tribulation,” says Paul, “and anguish [will come] upon every soul of a human being who does evil” (Rom. 2). And Jeremiah: “Crush them, Lord, with a double destruction” (Jer. 17).

[Col. 0220C] This wine, harsher than gall, most bitter in taste and flavor—this deadly cup of the Lord’s wrath or fury—is drunk by all the lost, through the merit of their worse life. They do not touch the Bridegroom’s breasts, full of grace and more pleasing nourishment. “You have drunk,” Isaiah says, “from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath; you have drunk to the bottom of the cup and drained it to the dregs” (Isa. 51). Explaining what this cup is, he says below: “Two things have befallen you: devastation and destruction, famine and sword” (ibid.).

The Bridegroom’s breasts are far better than this wine or cup: they promise or give more pleasing things both to the Bride and the young women; they keep them far from wrath and fury, from severe judgment, by the hand of mercy; their desire is satisfied by both present perfection and the reward to come. Or: “We shall be mindful more than wine,” that is, we shall be more mindful of the breasts than of wine.

[Col. 0220D] By “wine,” it seems, he means the passing suffering of this life, which brings no slight harm of trouble to those who long for eternity: the corruptible body and the necessary dwelling amid earthly things weigh down the soul and depress the mind by the burden of very many thoughts. Although such a burden destroys or purges vices in every righteous person, when God burns and chastises the one whom he loves with the severe but useful cautery of scourges, nevertheless, because it stings and such a draught becomes bitter upon the palate of one who tastes it, whoever burns to drink heavenly things more sweetly wishes it far removed from him. Of this the royal Prophet says: “You have made us drink the wine of compunction” (Ps. 59).

The harshness of punishments, from which neither poor person nor rich person is found exempt or immune—when even an infant one day old experiences it under a severe law—is a troublesome sting and a draught suited to medicine, bringing the hateful yet plainly fruitful bitterness of discipline. Every wise person carefully rejects it considered by itself, yet judges it must be endured patiently in view of the fruit that follows.

[Col. 0221A] Though present experience has compelled him to remember it, a more perfect fruit and sweeter hope nevertheless urge him to forget it. He remembers spiritual goods and salvation that will remain longer more gladly than a bitter draught and compunction that will pass more quickly. The grace of this seems to be bestowed not upon all but upon very few, whose foot is found worthily set upon the rock, so that unbending uprightness may carry one, firmly established, upward, and that through the merit of uprightness he may receive a far fuller and more perfect certainty. Therefore follows: “The upright,” etc.

## CHAPTER XVI
The upright love you. For whoever does not descend to the lowest things with bent knee and flexed hamstring, but hangs poised toward the highest and most arduous things in fervent desire; whoever is not bent in accordance with the counsels of malignant spirits, so as to offer them the desired ease of passing through him—such a one is surely upright. He is judged to hate what he rejects; and, abhorring forbidden things, he is proved to love the one who forbids them. [Col. 0221D] Thus you have: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Ps. XCVI).

He hates evil who does not incline the vessel of his heart toward it, who does not cast down his eyes into its depths or to the earth (Dan. XIII); who does not calmly endure one who evaporates a foul smoke from the dung-heap of this life—a smoke that afflicts the nostrils with incense, blinds the eyes, and discolours the inner countenance. But, in hatred of evil—which he finds tending downward—he loves what is better and suited to salvation, and raises heart, hands, and eyes upward. Not only, when pressed and oppressed by an evil burden, does he bend downward; rather, erect toward things above, he clings to them inseparably with his whole desire.

Since these things stand and are directed for standing by an unbending uprightness, those who are raised toward them through advancing merits are plainly made upright. [Col. 0222A] And just as those who make idols or images of the Gentiles become like them (Ps. CXIII), so they are conformed to heavenly things by cleaving to their uprightness. These heavenly things—which are not inappropriately called heaven or heavens, and are prepared as house or dwelling, place, seat, and throne for the Lord—truly embrace the Lord himself and him who sits there with ardent desires; nor can they fail to love him whom they behold ruling powerfully and reigning sweetly within themselves.

“Our Father,” he says, “who art in heaven” (Matt. VI). And: “I have loved,” he says, “the beauty of thy house, and the place where thy glory dwells” (Ps. XXV). And: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII). And: “The Lord: his seat is in heaven” (Ps. X). And: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. LXVI). You will find many such sayings [Col. 0222B] which declare that God dwells in heaven or in the heavens, presiding with gracious good will over seat, place, and house. But there can be no mutual delight between the seat and him who sits there except where, by grace’s gift, uprightness corresponds with uprightness.

For God is upright and wishes to have those like himself; nor is he loved except by those who love to cleave to his uprightness. No one cleaves to that uprightness except through love, and no one is truly made loving except through uprightness. The Virgin Mother, perceiving this, says: “The upright love thee,” because those who do not turn their intention aside toward the desire of the flesh, but turn themselves with willing heart toward him who is supremely good, are plainly travelling the straight way, the royal way, and by right progress attain the Good that they desire.

Thus: “God is good to Israel, to those who are upright in heart” (Ps. [Col. 0222C] LXIX). For those who follow serpentine windings and the meanders of crooked perversity do not taste how sweet and pleasant is the rule of divine goodness, because the crookedness of malice or injustice neither accords nor cleaves to the uprightness which is good, just, and supremely praiseworthy. But whoever, with a free aversion to earth or earthly things, suspends himself above them and, seeking what is above, grasps them more with an uplifted heart than with his hands, perceives indeed the great and greatly praiseworthy abundance of divine sweetness. Yet though he learns of its sweetness by report, he does not experience it in inward perception unless he is found like the good God through uprightness of heart.

[Col. 0222D] The Lord seems to order such uprightness by fitting progress, and in the Gospel to invite the apostles toward it: wishing not only to make them readier to seek it, but also more certain concerning the order of that which they ought to seek: “Let your loins,” he says, “be girded about, and lamps burning in your hands; and be yourselves like men awaiting their lord” (Luke XII). This prudent craftsman, arranging the fortress of a well-proportioned uprightness, first lays, as it were, a base and casts the foundation of the work. When the base is laid, he establishes the support of the column and sets above it the capital, the ornament of the same uprightness.

By the loins are understood the will or affection of this life, the lust of the flesh, and the will’s acquisition of what it desires. For this reason the divine judgment of justice wills the loins [Col. 0223A] to be girded, since it wishes us to be restrained not merely from things unlawful, but even from things not expedient. To set aside what is harmful; to abstain from desirable things; to prevent fleshly appetites from reaching their completing effect; to restrain unstable impulses with the strong girdle of chastity—this is a kind of solid base and the beginning of holiness.

Whoever desires to attain uprightness of life must first take care to abstain from unlawful and useless things, so that, when he has laid the necessarily preceding base of self-restraint, he may confidently place upon it the burden of the structure which follows. Perhaps this is why, when the man suffering grievously in his feet sat at the gate of the Temple asking alms of those entering, Peter, moved by compassion, gave him not money’s help. For grace had given the Apostle power, not gold or silver; rather, by a powerful word he restored health to the lame feet, and, with his foundations strengthened, the man walked, rejoicing and leaping (Acts III). [Col. 0223B]

Peter rightly first granted health to the feet, and then the man, walking upon his strengthened bases, leapt up; for weakness must first be brought to an end, and then, once this base has been laid, the structure rises more strongly toward progress. Accordingly, after saying in the Gospel, “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII), he added: “And lamps burning in your hands” (ibid.). When someone has cast away works of darkness with due abhorrence, the lighting of lamps follows in fitting order: that his holiness may shine before people, and that the uprightness of morals and justice may stand out like a pillar of fire.

A lamp in the hands signifies brightness in works: when, upon the base of self-restraint by which you abstain from things not expedient, you add eminence of works and uprightness of morals; when you strive, in the manner of an unbending column, to remain stable and immovable, and to excel all things beneath you in life and conduct. [Col. 0223C] Yet it does not suffice for anyone to shine in great works unless through them he aims to please, not people, but the Lord. Therefore he adds: “And be yourselves like men awaiting their lord” (ibid.). The intention or expectation by which you do not desire a passing reward, but with watchful care await your Lord from above, is a bulwark of the uprightness already described, and like the capital is the commendable ornament of the column.

A column is bare and unsuitable if it is not adorned with a capital set upon it; and insufficient is the uprightness that is not held fast by expectation of the Lord. By this expectation, as by a summit, it surmounts and transcends all things of the world and, in the manner of Jacob’s ladder, lays hold of the heavens above. Hence Paul says: “Our commonwealth is in heaven, from whence also we await the Saviour” (Phil. III). [Col. 0223D] The Apostle declares that he lives there, whence he lovingly awaits his own and all people’s Saviour. Whatever is proclaimed upright and stable by worthy judgment is completed, as it were by a covering, through this waiting.

The Bride-Mother, more fully instructed in this matter and having attained the same uprightness by greater progress, loves the Bridegroom [Col. 0224A] and is joined to him in chaste union, learning by experience that his union is not denied to one who loves rightly. For, according to the prophet, “The Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him” (Deut. XXXII); therefore he looks with gracious countenance upon the Virgin’s equity, and the strength of his peaceful kingdom possesses her—she whose uprightness corresponds to so great an equity. For the same prophet says to him: “A sceptre of uprightness is the sceptre of thy kingdom” (Ps. XLIV).

The Virgin herself, I think, is for this reason called a rod in the Scriptures, where she is mystically prefigured: by the name “rod” is understood not only the Virgin’s flourishing beauty, but also her pure and likewise fruitful uprightness. You know that Aaron’s dry rod put forth leaves on the next day (Num. XVII) and, without aid from natural fertilising agencies, [Col. 0224B] bore nuts in wondrous newness. In it, without doubt, is prefigured the Virgin’s uprightness: nature standing amazed, she who knew no man is advanced to bear a son.

Isaiah likewise, seeing a rod to come forth from the root of Jesse (Isa. XXI), knew that the Virgin would be born from Jesse’s stock. What else could the flower which rose from her in incomparable emergence signify but her Son? In this very pageant the angelic spirits marvel, when they behold the same Virgin ascending through the desert like a rod of smoke (Song III): namely, because, abandoning what lies below, the Virgin stretches herself more freely toward higher things and, treading the earth beneath her former purpose, grasps heaven with her desires.

But since this uprightness is attained only by the file and by labour, and since, as Scripture declares, one enters the kingdom of God only through many tribulations (Acts XIV), the Virgin wishes the young women not to be scorched by present troubles, but to be refreshed amid temporal distress by contemplation of spiritual things. [Col. 0224C] The young women might indeed have been troubled that she who appears already brought to the Bridegroom’s kiss and, by her own testimony, introduced into the king’s wine-cellars, still labours under afflictions, is wearied by a wretched burden, and—though she claims, as it were, to be beautiful—has her face charged with ugliness. Concerning this, the Virgin seems anxiously to anticipate them and to instruct them more diligently that they may weigh each point rightly: the apparent ugliness will pass swiftly away, while a beauty fixed in an unbending state will remain to follow.

## Chapter XVII

[Col. 0224D]

“I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like Solomon’s skin.”

The blackness which disfigures and stains this Virgin’s beauty is the adversity of the present life, which weighs and afflicts her against her will; it does not permit the joy of the Spirit and the grace of peace begun to be brought to the harbour of consummated beauty. To the Bride, fervent in spirit, sighing for continual peace, and aspiring through sight of the Bridegroom to perfect beauty, there come fear, danger, the trouble of harmful injury, tribulation and distress, inward pain, and the sword of suffering. These cast a cloud of sadness and dark blackness over her countenance, which spiritual gladness and the light of grace sometimes suffuse.

For not even to the Virgin herself did this present life give unbroken peace or unfailing joy. She suffered and groaned, assailed by many troubles; and in the numbering of her days she brought forth white pebbles in such a way that many black ones were nevertheless not lacking among them. The pagans, indeed, distinguish and reckon their sad and prosperous days, in order to determine by certain knowledge which outweigh the others; just as they mark the succession of prosperous days with white pebbles, so they mark sad and adverse days by the blackness of pebbles. [Col. 0225A]

Therefore the Virgin is black when she feels herself afflicted by temporal troubles; when she sees him whom she bore crucified by mockers; and when she sees him whom she knows to be author and Lord among angelic spirits, God in the bosom of God the Father with equal glory, made flesh in her and from her, now subjected to the power of persecutors—with many attackers and no defender of him at hand. [Col. 0225B] The Mother is black when she sees her own flesh, loved not by vice but by nature, cruelly crushed in her Son by untimely death; when every evil that he suffers by the Father’s command rebounds miserably, in the circuit of a natural sling, upon the Mother’s heart.

The Bride is black when, even after he has risen from the dead, she hears the Bridegroom blasphemed by those sharing her tribulation; when she sees his preachers, the apostles, scourged; when she considers that everything which she herself knows concerning him, or which the holy sayings declare, is a sign contradicted by the rebellious and unbelieving. In all these circumstances, who can reckon with what grief, what sorrow, her spirit wastes away; by what wrinkles it is contracted; with what pallor her face withers? For the sadness which inwardly weighs down and afflicts the mind often appears in the countenance, and the outward ugliness of the flesh displays it. [Col. 0225C]

As Solomon asserts when he says: “A sorrowful spirit dries up the bones” (Prov. XVII). Thus sorrow, by drying the bones, blackens and disfigures the Virgin; driving joy far away, it seizes and usurps the first place for itself. It does not allow the present form to rejoice in greater beauty, since the corruptible body darkens it with a blacker dye. Nor is it surprising that the more sorrowful Bride calls herself black and misshapen, since in this she is not unprofitably likened to the Bridegroom whom she loves. Because he is burdened by troubles while held in corruptible flesh, Scripture testifies that he has neither beauty nor comeliness: “There is no form or comeliness in him” (Isa. LIII), and, “We saw him, and there was no appearance” (ibid.). [Col. 0226A]

But one who has neither comeliness nor beauty is understood to be black and misshapen. Therefore the Virgin is not to be blamed for being conformed to him in blackness, since blackness is not to be charged to either as shame or disgrace; rather, the present condition of life, given over to misery and toil, makes them misshapen. Christ did not will to be free from enduring these things; rather, he offered himself as an example both to others and to his Bride-Mother, so that the Virgin too might not shrink from appearing black and misshapen, but might patiently show herself conformed to the Bridegroom in this also.

Thus later in this epithalamium the Bride says of the Bridegroom himself: “His locks are black as a raven” (Song V). Since he is darkened and blackened like a raven, the Virgin is in no way ashamed to confess herself black as well. [Col. 0226B] But lest anyone suppose that this blackness is the more burdensome because it is enduring, the Virgin, immediately upon mentioning it, declares herself beautiful: “I am black,” she says, “but beautiful.” Although, she says, I suffer punishments deserved by human perversity,

> [Note: [Col. 0225D] The same Virgin, with anxious hand, wipes away the stains of her inward beauty (col. 227). And those stains are wiped away through the benefit of cleansing grace (col. 245). There are other similar passages in which the Blessed Virgin is described as sprinkled with slight actual sins. But first the reader should observe that the author says the following concerning the most Blessed Virgin at col. 246: “With dry foot, pure step, and clean life, you pass along such a way, assailed by no contact whatever with vices.” And at col. 291: “Encircling darkness does not obscure her blooming light; threatening threshing-sledges do not crush her unimpaired beauty.” And elsewhere: “Inferior to Christ alone, she rules over the other saints”; and: “She is held in the bodily covering not of vice but of nature.”
>
> Further, this author loved the Blessed Virgin in a remarkable degree (col. 280), and by her help overcame great tribulations (col. 27). Accordingly, he did not speak of her thus with evil intent. Rather, he did so because of what he had seen in Chrysostom, Homily 45 on Matthew chapter XII, and Homily 20 on John chapters I and II, where, in accordance with his own opinion, he attributes certain faults to the Virgin, though using the manner of a homilist. Or, more probably, our author had in view the remnants of original sin, among which is liability to undergo the penalties and miseries of human mutability. This sequence and chain of disadvantages is certainly like a certain stain, or net woven from stains and wounds, enveloping the Virgin herself, from which she could not wholly free herself before blessedness came upon her. For even if, by the overshadowing of the Most High, the tinder of sin which had remained bound in her until then was removed (St Thomas, III part, question 27, article 3), nevertheless a sword afterward pierced her soul (Luke II, v. 35). Moreover, the word *macula* (“stain”) in this author very often signifies something quite other than ugliness or filth.]

though I am vexed in the present furnace and purified by the cautery of passing heaviness, yet beneath this burden beauty lies hidden and loveliness is nourished: justice gladdens it, and unfailing duration establishes it. “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of righteousness” (Rom. VIII).
