And though, he says, a manifold death of punishments afflicts bodily life by reason of the first sin, fastening me daily, as one dying, to a heavy gallows, yet that inner person, rich before God, is renewed from day to day; he lives because of righteousness and is adorned by the merits of virtues. And the more present misery discolours the outward person, [Col. 0226C] the more love of future things advances and adorns the inward one. To him grace even now gives strength to love things above, and, when virtue is completed, promises glory and salvation.

The Prophet says: “Lord, in thy favour thou hast bestowed strength upon my beauty” (Ps. XXIX). He who is more beautiful in form than the children of men, by the privilege of his own will, the brightness of eternal light and the mirror of divine majesty, likewise by his own will imparted to his Mother and Bride a strength whose beauty he himself, the King and Lord who had bestowed it, desired. Speaking to her below, he says: “Show me thy face; thy face is beautiful” (Song II).

Just as she is called black and misshapen because she suffers temporal evils, so she is beautiful or fair because she lovingly desires spiritual things. Their inestimable beauty so affects its lover that it makes the blackness of the sufferer pass into whiteness. Hence the Prophet: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house” (Ps. XXV). And the Lord says in the Gospel to those who love him: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John XVI). As affliction makes her black, so love makes her beautiful. The former belongs to the present time and will soon end; the latter, though it began in time, shall never end.

Therefore the Virgin did not rightly say that she was beautiful and black, but black and beautiful: because blackness first took possession of her, when tribulation was allowed freer rein to rage against her and, both by its arrival [Col. 0227A] and by its departure, to come before the beauty that was to arrive. [Col. 0227B] John says of this: “Death shall be no more; neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more, for the former things have passed away” (Rev. XXI).

This mass of evils therefore came first to the Virgin’s heart, but did not find there a settled dwelling or stable place. Rather, as an unwelcome intruder it anticipated her coming beauty, and so was compelled to depart when that beauty afterward came upon her more fully. The Virgin’s beauty consists in this: with spirit aflame, desiring the countenance of God, she anxiously wipes the inward stains from her face with her hand; she clears the eye, cleanses the conscience, makes the heart serene, and by severe judgment removes the attacks of clamouring thoughts. Finally, with pure and active mind, she is carried away in ecstasy and reaches the throne of majesty, inaccessible to the slow and negligent. [Col. 0227C]

Of this, he who sat on the throne adds: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. XXI). The Lord makes things new when, by the hand of mercy, he wipes away the oldness of our inner person; when he strikes ignorance, heals the conscience, and directs the will; when, the error of falsehood wiped away, he enables us to speak truth with our neighbour; when he gently instils delight in that same truth; and finally, when, to establish the beauty of inward grace, he hides us from the tumult of people in the hidden place of his countenance.

Thus she who, exposed to threshings and sufferings, considers herself black and misshapen rejoices, hidden in the secret place of the divine countenance, to be made like it. Whom the furnace of tribulation renders dark, as it were, by its own soot, the beam of contemplation makes bright and beautiful by its outpouring. [Col. 0227D]

## Chapter XVIII

“Like the tents of Kedar, like Solomon’s skin.”

Having said herself to be black and beautiful, she shows how she is black and beautiful. “Black,” she says, “like the tents of Kedar; beautiful like Solomon’s skin.” *Kedar* is interpreted “darkness.” Tents are called not permanent houses but movable huts, which are set up either by shepherds in pasture or by soldiers on campaign. Placed for a time, they are not secured upon a stable foundation; rather, when expedient, they are moved elsewhere without loss.

Therefore the Virgin appropriately confesses herself black like the tents of Kedar, indicating that the condition of this life, by whose bonds she is still held, is indeed darkened by much cloudy colouring or gloom of troubles and embittered by many stings and punctures of sufferings. Yet its hateful and dark bitterness is not established in a lasting condition, but passes like a tent and does not remain, like a guest. [Col. 0228A] Job affirms this: “After darkness I hope for light” (Job XVII). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John XVI).

The Virgin’s grief, groaning, and suffering of temporal life’s troubles pass away and are transformed into the light of spiritual joy. She complains not so much of the presence of night, which will pass, as she rejoices in the certain hope of light, which will remain longer. Strengthened by the gift of this hope, she makes little of momentary distress while her pure and secure mind is conformed to glory yet to come. When the frost or old age by which she is drawn tight and made sick for an hour has been wiped away, she blossoms anew in joyful spirit and, like an eagle, grows young again.

Solomon says beautifully: “A joyful mind makes a flourishing age” (Prov. XVII). For whose inner person’s age would not blossom, whose broken old age would not be made young again by the benefit of the rock? This is true where pure faith, secure hope, and enduring love meet in the conscience, all of them steadfastly obeying God alone in all things. Therefore the Virgin is rightly said to be beautiful like Solomon’s skin: having cast aside awareness of the flesh, she is as though ignorant of the troubles of passing suffering. Her continual obedience, and her cheerful conscience in obedience, make her commendable and serene; they adorn her countenance and make her face clear of the grime of dust. [Col. 0228B]

Skin is stripped from a dead animal and separated from flesh by an iron rather than a fleshly razor. Once separated, it no longer knows bodily injuries or sufferings: struck, it feels no pain; troubled, it does not grieve. It proves flexible, manageable, and suited to varied uses, provided that the labour and skill of a prudent craftsman work upon it. If the craftsman diligently chooses to bestow care upon it, it is found readier to obey in innumerable ways.

So too the Virgin is separated from the things of the flesh by that strong razor which is proclaimed sharper than every two-edged sword and able to reach even to the division of spirit and soul (Heb. IV). Drawn and stripped by this blade, as though ignorant of bodily affections and afflictions, she loves to forget them and, stretched toward things above, especially to remember those things. [Col. 0228C]

That supreme craftsman, designated by the name of Solomon yet of far greater benevolence, wisdom, and power, adapted her—withdrawn from bodily affection—to his spiritual good pleasure. Having anointed her with the oil of grace, he fashioned her for every fitting purpose, so that there was in her no rebellion and no opposition whatsoever, but like a skin she was made agile in every way for obedience. “Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word” (Luke I).

You see that, having heard the message, she devotes herself as handmaid to the Lord according to his word. In nothing does the thing formed oppose its maker, nor the vessel the potter; but Solomon’s throne is subjected to the command of him who sits upon it—indeed, the heaven of heavens, his seat, is stretched out according to the will of him who sits there. God stretched out heaven like a skin so that the prophetic saying may stand: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. LXVI), and: “The Lord: his seat is in heaven” (Ps. X). [Col. 0229A]

But who can more worthily, who can more fittingly, be called heaven than the Virgin, who deserved to be adorned with the stars of so many virtues? Their varied brilliance mitigates the burdensome darkness of this life as it recalls the errors of the ignorant multitude to knowledge. She brought forth the moon, which would shine for those darkened by night, when she raised up the Church so that it might show itself radiant to all. By example and teaching she instructed the holy apostles, whose manner of life bestowed necessary light upon the earth’s inhabitants.

Finally, the Virgin herself, or heaven, brought forth that greater luminary which provided fuller saving remedy to a languishing world. Because he alone is God and none can be made equal to him, he is worthily called the Sun by a singular privilege. Thus this Virgin alone, and no other, bore so great an offspring; this wondrous heaven brought forth in wondrous manner the Sun alone. He makes day for those who are awake when by his presence he illumines and suffuses our atmosphere; he brings night upon sleepers when, concealed by the interposed mass of earthly sins, he hides himself. [Col. 0229B]

But if this Sun alone, bright among and above all things, beautiful in the light of his countenance and in form beyond the children of men, loves by his grace to make the earth—heavy under so great a weight—fruitful, how much more does he make heaven abound in more ample gifts? Scripture reads that he stretched it out like a skin, wherein he seems to have displayed its ready obedience; for the Virgin, who is deemed comparable to heaven, indeed commendable above heaven, resists the pleasure of her commander in nothing, not even slightly.

But I, as I see, am not a skin in the Lord’s hand: I am hard and rebellious when he calls and commands; I do not open my ears to his voice and instructions but stop them up; and if perhaps it happens that I hear, I harden my heart lest I obey what I have heard. If, however, sometimes visited and softened in penitent heart, I promise obedience to the commandments and perseverance in them, and begin to concern myself with amending either my own conduct or that of my own people, then behold: a wind rushes in, thunders, tests, destroys, and I abandon what I had begun. [Col. 0229C]

For the most evil tempter gathers many darts for himself; when he inflicts them, he either terrifies the mind more harshly or softly caresses and weakens it. The flesh draws the conquered spirit into its own domain, and love of fleshly things seduces me so that I become wholly flesh. “Who, then, shall deliver me, wretched as I am, from this body of death?” (Rom. VII.24). Who shall separate me from this flesh by the strong sword of the spirit, so that, after the flesh has been killed and surrendered to the beasts and birds of Babylon, I may be found to be skin alone and stretched out at Solomon’s command?

But if this gift has not yet been granted to me or to anyone like me—one to whom the Bridegroom’s chamber and God’s sanctuary still seem inaccessible—nevertheless the true Solomon did not deny this grace to our Virgin. He fashioned her like a skin according to all his will. For having withdrawn her from the flesh’s concupiscence and the harmful affection of perversity, he raised her by the hand of mercy to the height of purity. [Col. 0230A] Having scraped away desires like varied colours, he laid upon her a starry beauty; indeed, he brought in the merits of virtues and heavenly grace.

The Virgin wished that this should not be unknown to the daughters of Jerusalem, because she did not know how to envy those close to her the grace she had found. Thus, those who might be troubled by the Virgin’s blackness if they regarded it carelessly might be shown both a worthier cause of that blackness and its shorter duration.

## Chapter XIX

“I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.”

She calls daughters those whom a little earlier she called young women, thereby indicating both their tender affection and their fervent desire. Because daughters, more gently inclined to listen and more eagerly to see, attend more closely and love more tenderly the praises of beauty set before them, she says: “You whom dull stupidity does not hold back from understanding, attend and see how commendable my beauty is. You are certainly not darkened by Babylon’s confused blindness; rather, the grace of inward vision enlightens and reveals your eyes.”

Therefore I pointedly call you daughters of Jerusalem, by which name I compel you to see more diligently. When you hear and observe that you are called by such a name, know that the name ought not to be empty but rather derived from the reality. You are truly daughters of Jerusalem if you see; if you grasp intellectually what is said obscurely; if you judge what sounds harsh externally to be a shell or chaff, and desire what is sweet and life-giving within as kernel, grain, and fine flour. [Col. 0230B]

Finally, know that I myself, who invite you to understanding [Col. 0230C] and do not permit you to grow dark in ignorance or to wander in darkness, am rightly called Jerusalem by merit of seeing; for to me these divine mysteries and heavenly sacraments are known to be revealed. Since I bring you forth, as in childbirth, from the darkness of ignorance; since through zeal and labour I lead you to the light of truth and knowledge; since with affectionate concern I form you by more perfect rules of life—what do I do but conform you to my womb, or rather to my character, in the place of a mother?

Indeed, the Bridegroom says to one of you: “Behold thy mother” (John XIX). You are her daughters, doing good and not gazing upon my blackness with an attention as though clear-sighted. Its cause is beneficial, and its end is already near at the door. Do not, perhaps, encounter a present stumbling-block through excessive curiosity, if you attend more than is right merely to the fact that I am black. Therefore she says: “Do not,” etc.

## Chapter XX
“Do not look upon me because I am black, because the sun has darkened me.” “See to it,” she says, “that you do not fasten carnal eyes upon my burdens; lest the adversity that has shaken my resolve breed a stumbling-block for you; lest your consideration childishishly be amazed at my troubles, as though it were unfitting that my manner of life should be embittered by tribulations. Have, I beg you, an understanding worthy of daughters of Jerusalem, and weigh rather the cause of this matter than its effect. What is seen by all, I want you to regard as though it were not seen at all; and what is hidden from the foolish, I want you more wisely to behold.

“That I am black, that I am sorrowful, [Col. 0231A] that a cloud of momentary injury circles about me, that waters enter even to my soul, that the sword of suffering passes through me—this the true Sun has done; He has brought me to this by His counsel; He has spread such cosmetic colouring, or blackness, over my face. That Sun, in whose absence a night more dreadful and ugly falls, and all the variety of things is found colourless and without form, but at whose presence heaven shines, earth rejoices, its surface is restored to manifold beauty, and the very countenance of things is in some way made conformable to beauty—that Sun, I say, who by the regard of His countenance renews and adorns all things, by a certain absence of Himself darkens me for a little while.

“For He withdraws Himself in strict judgment from those who afflict me, while He does not yet present Himself to me who suffer, for the kiss; perhaps so that they may advance yet further into evil by wickedly inflicting evils, and, conversely, that I may advance into good by patiently bearing troubles. Thus a prudent virgin, eagerly desiring to preserve or increase her beauty in the literal sense, sometimes applies a covering to her face in many ways, so that the desired beauty may grow beneath its veil and appear of greater grace when it has been nourished by the medicinal covering. And certainly her lover—provided his uprightness is not unacquainted with such things—does not despise the virgin whose face is covered, knowing that the beauty which for a time is darkened by the veil laid over it will afterwards shine forth more pleasingly when that veil is removed.

“So too I am black, wrapped in a certain cosmetic covering; and while I live in the flesh, I am not yet altogether freed from troubles, because that Sun of mine, who [Col. 0231C] wills me still to be in the poor dwelling of this night, does not will me to be wholly free from its injuries. For the place and time in the midst of which you still see me are, by a law inherent in them, not a state of complete peace or rest—a state which not even my Bridegroom Himself chose to obtain here by prerogative of power; rather, as you know, He chose to be afraid and distressed (Mark 14). And He who, oppressed by many hardships, finally willed to undergo death, also wills that I, placed here, should not lack the same sufferings. I endure them patiently in memory and love of Him, assured that He not only wills this, but will also bring it about accordingly.

“For He who does not yet honour my face with its full colour, by His delay—as I seem to see—darkens it; and He who wills that I be blackened by a burden [Col. 0231D] soon to pass, I do not refuse to acknowledge as doing the very thing which He ordains to be done. Therefore, since in this arena my patience struggles more fully, I ask that you, daughters, may not be scandalized by considering these things. Do not attend to what I suffer, lest your weakness be thereby offended; but attend to who wills me to suffer, knowledge of which commends you.

“Nothing that I suffer for Him is worthy of scandal. Rather, it is a greater suffering to lack sufferings apart from Him, because he who is unhappily fortunate enough to be spared the scourge here grieves miserably hereafter at not being included among the number of the elect. My Bridegroom Himself, who also endured being black in the present life, wills the same blackness to be in me and in all His own. When the fitting time comes, He will remove this colour, turn sorrow into joy, and transform the cosmetic colouring into whiteness.

“Accordingly, what was said—‘The sun has darkened me’—may be understood instead as ‘the sun will darken me’: the past tense for the future. For He who made the things that are to come was indeed going to do this in the Virgin; and the Virgin confidently asserts that He has already done what He was going to do. What the Virgin already knows beforehand concerning her future glory, taught as she is and full of the Spirit, she does not predict nor request; but, secure of its fulfillment, she rejoices and affirms as already fulfilled what faith and hope possess, while reality alone murmurs that it remains unfulfilled.

“Do not,” she says, “judge my blackness worthy of your attention, as though it either harms now or can remain for long; for ‘I passed by, and behold, it was not’ (Psalm 36), nor is there a trace of it to be found. Nor will it remain for you, if you too wish to pass through in a like manner. For that true Sun who [Col. 0232B] has bestowed His light upon this world, who rose for us in order to draw His own from the deep, will soon wipe away my cosmetic colouring or blackness with a gracious hand; He will utterly remove wrinkle and stain, pain and every tear.

“Indeed, to speak better and with far greater certainty, He has already removed it: He has already refreshed my sick soul with the desired remedy, because by His grace He has advanced me to such certainty that I possess as though already accomplished what my understanding foreknew would shortly be done. Therefore, as your worthy consideration is not burdened by the sight of my blackness, because of Him who consoles me by His benefit, so it is expedient that those who harass me by their malice should know that both their way will perish and they themselves will not rise in the council of the righteous (Psalm 1). What sound-minded person would carefully weigh or consider with grave concern anything inflicted by those whose power will soon pass away? Would he not rather hold cheap both them and the troubles inflicted by them, when he finds in them nothing firm, nothing stable?”

## CHAPTER XXI

“The sons of my mother fought against me; they made me keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.”

Those who ought to have spared the Virgin and defended her from the injuries of others, who ought to have met attackers as they came and resisted those assailing her, to have given their lives for her and preserved their sister by their own death—these, on the contrary, attack her and delight in harassing her with persecutions. With affection crushed, law violated, and right altogether broken—though even among beasts the law of nature establishes that such ties ought to be maintained—the mother and her sons do not shrink from persecuting, troubling, tearing, torturing, disembowelling, and in nothing pitying daughter and sister. [Col. 0232D]

I judge that Judaea, or the Synagogue, was the Virgin’s mother: according to the law of the flesh, she is believed to have borne her, cherished her in a tender bosom with maternal care until the years of mature youth, and instructed her in the ordinances of the Law. The mother’s sons, both by flesh and by character, are the Jews: blind guides of the blind, Pharisees more by malice than knowledge. Forgetting the covenant of brotherhood, they afflicted their sister all the more grievously when they fastened her Son to the cross with tongues more venomous than iron nails. Of them the prophet Amos says: “They have not remembered the covenant of brothers” (Amos 1).

Sick with poisonous perfidy, they refused to remember more healthily that covenant by which brothers ought to be bound to their sister with deeper affection. But as though alien from her race and far removed from nature, they do not render the rights due to a sister—indeed, not even those due to a human being. And what sound-minded person can think soundly of Judaea, which is a mother but does not love, as the tales report of Medea? That mother had no love or care for her children, but, inflamed by hatred, removed them from her midst by untimely death. Like Medea, Judaea tries to make false the argument which nature has woven as a defence of the love due from a mother—an argument advanced and affirmed not only by the modern loquacity of disputing clerics, but also by the experienced sagacity of pagans from ancient times: “If she is a mother,” they say, “she loves.”

But because Medea was a mother and did not love, they say that she put off, rather than neglected, a mother’s nature. Since even a beast is bound to its offspring by natural affection, a woman who is not softened even by animal feeling is proved not to be a mother. Moreover, Solomon, to whom God gave wisdom as the companion seated beside His throne, proved by this argument that the woman was the mother—the harlot who preferred that her own infant be given alive to the lying woman rather than cut apart by the sword brought forth at the king’s command:

> “She whose son was alive said to the king—for her bowels were moved over her son—‘I beseech you, my lord, give her the living child, and do not kill him.’ But the other said, ‘Let him be neither mine nor yours, but divide him.’ The king answered and said, ‘Give her the living child, and do not kill him; for she is his mother’” (3 Kings 3).

And elsewhere it is written: “No one has hated his own flesh” (Ephesians 3).

Yet Judaea is unwilling to obey either the testimonies of Scripture or the commands of nature. Instead, she rages against her daughter with incredible cruelty; exceeding the bounds of laws, she gives scope to and exercises the most wicked fury of mind—nor does more considered regard restrain her sons from malice. For they are like their mother: they neither fear God nor reverence man. With obstinate malice they deny that God is man, and do not think it fitting for His majesty and profound counsel that He should be willing and able to descend to endure our miseries.

They further maintain that Christ’s mother conceived by Joseph; that she was neither a virgin in conception nor remained a virgin after giving birth; and that everything reverently proclaimed concerning her integrity [Col. 0233D] or her Son’s majesty is rejected by their testimony as fictitious and frivolous. “If,” they say, “a virgin gave birth, she first had intercourse.” Therefore they persecute her Son, as they say, not for a good work but for blasphemy (John 10), and they strive to erase His memory from the earth. Their ground is that, among themselves—who are merely human beings—He claims something more for Himself and, though a man, presumes to make Himself God.

At length, when malice presses on, they condemn the innocent man to death, accusing Him as one who does not render due reverence to law and king. They bind Him, smear Him with spittle, strike Him, hand Him over to the judge, and the judge to the soldier. A harsh clamour resounds; they crucify Him—these with their clamorous tongues, those with nails. What else is all this than raging against the Virgin, sounding a furious trumpet against her, struggling against the walls of patience, attacking and assailing the tower of constancy with a heavy battering ram? They shake it, immovable though it is, but cannot conquer it because grace stands in their way.

And it should be noted that, although both Gentiles and Jews rage against the Virgin—Pilate and the soldiers doing by deeds what the Pharisees demand in words—yet here, where the battle is recounted in prophetic spirit and nuptial song, the Virgin remembers only her own people; no mention is made of outsiders. “The sons,” she says, “of my mother.” Why this, unless because, as you know, it rightly hurts more when the person who ought to have shown honour brings dishonour; when someone in whose bosom one might hope for rest as in that of a friend hands over to the enemy the person whom he ought to have cherished?

For when an enemy curses, the curse is borne more patiently; when an enemy rages against an enemy, he does not deserve to be accused—or severely accused—for it. When a stranger does not generously assist a stranger, just as he gains no praise, so neither does he incur much blame. But “the man of my peace, my close companion, my acquaintance” (Psalm 54) sins more unjustly when friend or neighbour approaches more harshly against me; when, instead of loving me, he venomously slanders and attacks me; when for good things he displays evils, and for love hatred. How then can I endure, act patiently, and not rather complain that the faithless man rages with deceit?

Therefore, passing over the Gentiles in silence, the Virgin complains of the Jews. Their malice is presently brought forward: they, the sons of her mother, so grievously wounded the Virgin, to whom they rendered assault instead of defence, hindrance instead of help. But so that we may know that the evils which they more zealously carried out became profitable to us who are far removed, by God’s ordering wisdom; and that their malignity and the injury inflicted upon the Virgin became our benefit and a desirable increase of grace, the Virgin adds:

## CHAPTER XXII

“They made me keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.”

Every soul may rightly be called a vineyard. One soul seems comparable to another by a certain likeness, because, as a vineyard or vine consists of many things—namely leaf, cluster, and shoot—so too the soul is distinguished by many powers or virtues. “Let not the sons of my mother,” says the Virgin, “glory that they fulfilled their wickedness against me; that, raging against me, they filled my soul with bitter sorrow; that my watchfulness did not keep it safe from their violence, but their sword passed through it.

“For in taking away my own soul more violently, they unknowingly transferred me to the keeping of many souls; and, while they inflicted a grievous loss upon my vineyard, they bestowed a useful benefit upon you, daughters of Jerusalem. The desolation or failure of my own vineyard is beyond doubt your spiritual advancement. In injuring me, as they suppose, for a time, they made me a keeper necessary for you, to whom I pass.

“Not only individual souls, but also communities of souls gathered in groups, may fittingly be signified by the name ‘vineyards.’ For just as many shoots possess the name and produce of the vine, so many souls together make a flock or congregation, to which the Lord says: ‘Do not fear, little flock’ (Luke 12). And the Prophet says: ‘You transplanted a vine from Egypt’ (Psalm 79). Elsewhere: ‘The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel’ (Isaiah 5).

“Therefore the mother’s sons who inflicted the aforesaid sufferings on the Virgin transferred her, driven from her own vineyard, to many others. For she who was wickedly despised by brothers and fellow-tribesmen was received by many vineyards, or congregations, of the Church. But the Virgin did not fortify her own vineyard with her guardianship, because that wicked people obeyed neither her admonitions nor her examples. Rejoicing in its own will, abandoned to itself by a hidden judgment, with hardened neck it incurred Isaiah’s curse: ‘Woe to the sinful nation, a people weighed down with iniquity, an evil seed, criminal children!’ (Isaiah 1).

“Perhaps also the Prophet and the Virgin called them sons rather than daughters because, by the masculine term, they designated their perverse strength: powerful and strong against the Virgin’s soul, drunk with the wine of the condemned whose merits they rejoice in, they will suffer their punishments. Thus: ‘Woe to you who are powerful at drinking wine and strong at mixing drunkenness’ (Isaiah 5); and, ‘The mighty sought my soul’ (Psalm 53).

“These mighty and powerful men, when they drove the Virgin away from their own guardianship, compelled her to pass to the keeping of our vineyards. What was rightly taken away from those nearer to her because of their merits has been bestowed, by the grace of God’s gift, upon us who are more distant. How many communities throughout the world today rejoice that they are fortified by this Virgin’s protection and that their churches are kept by her welcome care! Though they rightly detest the malice of her lost sons, they nevertheless rejoice that she has been useful and necessary to themselves.

“But, not to speak of others, brothers, is not this your own community gathered in honour of this Virgin? Is not this place and church dedicated in her name? Do you not rejoice in her special care and protection, embracing your guardian with a kind of spiritual affection and tenderness? Who among you, when he recalls her memory or even hears her name, does not rejoice in devotion, does not applaud with devout service, hoping to find her Son merciful and gracious if he can first honourably show reverence to His mother?

“Happy fault, useful conflict, fruitful perversity: by which an odious brotherhood raged against our Virgin; by which, leaving those who rage, gracious blessing passes to us; by which the Virgin rejects her brothers, disowns her household, and hates her own people; by which she puts our vines in order, surrounds them with a hedge, prunes and digs them, and—in brief—keeps us with every diligence.

“Yet, because even in these vineyards there can sometimes be found those who presume to destroy the same vineyards by their evil habits, the Virgin turns to the Bridegroom and wishes to be instructed by Him more fully as to who they are, so that she may beware of those whom she knows not to be numbered among His own. Therefore she says: ‘Tell me,’ and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 0236A]

“Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

“You,” she says, “whom I love not in word, not with the tongue, not by the mere sound of lips, but with heart and mind and with all the powers of my inner being: show where You pasture, where a pleasing refreshment is prepared for You, where You find food by which Your hunger is satisfied. For ‘I was hungry,’ He says (Matthew 25).

“I know that a prudent shepherd does not remain in all places or in every pasture, but wisely seeks out those in which benefit is found. Abhorring and passing by what he knows lacks life-giving nourishment, he feeds and refreshes himself in what he knows does not recoil from life. And she beautifully asks so carefully not about the food, but about the place, [Col. 0236B] because perhaps she knows well enough the fodder in which He delights. She is certain that His food is purity, justice, truth, and other things of this kind which effectively produce true holiness.

“But who knows where this holiness is truly and firmly found, except one taught by Him who teaches humanity knowledge? For a human being does not know what is in a human being, nor can one worthily judge another (1 Corinthians 2), whose face indeed appears but whose conscience is not seen. The Virgin therefore wishes not to be deceived by the outward appearance of people, but to be led as it were into truth’s inner chamber; and to reach, not with a material foot but with a spiritual eye, the place in which the Bridegroom delights to find pasture and rest.

“Thus Joseph also is sent by his father’s care to look again upon his brothers in the pasturelands. Arriving at Shechem and finding a man, he carefully asks where they are feeding; the boy does not understand that he will be a burden to his elders and that he will not rejoice in the desired discovery as he hoped:

> ‘I seek my brothers,’ he said; ‘tell me where they are feeding.’ And the man said to him, ‘They have departed from this place; for I heard them say: Let us go to Dothaim.’ Therefore Joseph went after his brothers and found them in Dothaim” (Genesis 37).

It is rightly said that Joseph found his envious brothers in Dothaim. They are reported to have gone to that place not by chance but deliberately, perhaps knowing that there they would find not so much life-giving pasture as an opportunity to fulfill their wicked will and criminal design. Dothaim is interpreted “their green fodder,” or “sufficient failure.” Their green fodder—that is, the fodder of the envious—is envy itself: they taste it and chew it over; it grows strong in their minds; with its pestilential savour it becomes sweet within their throats. It is not trodden under a censuring foot, it does not wither through swift repentance, but remains green with tireless rancour until the height of wickedness.

Nothing is more pleasing to the faithless than to envy their betters, slander those who are absent, sometimes rejoice at the presence of others, smile with a feigned expression when they lack the power to harm, and, when the time to harm has shone forth, hurl a poisoned dart. Therefore, as in Hosea Ephraim feeds on the wind when it vainly desires what it hopes to come to pass (Hosea 12), so every envious person is not unfittingly said to have come to Dothaim when he delights in the poison of envy as in green fodder.

But Dothaim is also interpreted “sufficient failure.” From the very source by which that wicked person more vehemently advances toward the accomplishment of malice, the guilty man falls into a greater failure of conscience; and the very thing he loves—to inflict harm on another—plainly suffices as torment for one labouring under envy. A certain pagan aptly suggests this:

> “The Sicilian tyrants,” he says, “did not devise a greater torment than envy.”

[Note: [Col. 0237D] Horace, *Epistle to Lollius*.]

Anyone known to endure poisonous envy in his soul—a torment greater than any the Sicilians devised—is certainly proved to lack a tranquil state of mind, and such failure sufficiently brings about the death of the one who fails. For the envious person is found to harm himself more than his neighbour, and to suffer first what he attempts to inflict on another. His envy, which the other person often does not even feel, destroys the one from whom it proceeds as a moth destroys a garment.

Thus Joseph’s brothers, who, as you have read, were found in Dothaim—that is, already overtaken by a certain inward failure and by envy—see Joseph and speak among themselves as they meet him coming. They offer the unaware man not greeting or a kiss, but hatred: “Behold,” they say, “the dreamer comes. Come, let us kill him” (Genesis 37).

A wicked place, an accursed and abominable place, a place detested in the judgment of all who think soundly; a place to be called not refreshment but rightly failure, where charity perishes, brotherhood fails, and detestable envy prevails. [Col. 0237C] Since many are known to feed in Dothaim and other places like it, and whoever follows them is struck by some punishment, the careful Virgin asks not about the broad generality of the many, but about the particular place and solitude in which the Bridegroom feeds. For she knows that His place is not possessed by many, that His pasture has not many masters; she knows likewise that not every pasture belongs to the Bridegroom, and therefore she eagerly wishes to know which is His.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“Tell me where You pasture, where You lie down.”

“I know,” she says, “that You do not pasture in the covert of reeds; Your purity does not rest in marshy places, in which Behemoth hides in repose pleasing to himself (Job 40), where he cherishes and advances his wicked perversities and brings evil desires into effect through pestilential food. In these Your soul takes no pleasure; You have no will in them, as You truly declare concerning the Jews by Isaiah’s prophecy. Since they are not subject to Your will or good pleasure, they have been cast far from Your refreshment and Your countenance.

“For how do You pasture where You have not yet chosen to dwell, where under pressure of distress You do not desire to walk freely, where the appetite for feeding is turned back by a certain bitterness of what is set before it, when an evil seed and an exasperating house are found? I am certain that Mount Gilboa is not regarded as pasture pleasing to You: there Saul, David’s enemy (1 Kings 31), did not shrink from entering battle; there the mighty fall; there death gives Saul and Jonathan over to its laws; and upon it neither dew nor rain comes, as David in lamentation curses.

“I know likewise that the plain of Shinar is not offered as Your pasture (Genesis 11), where, since pride reigns, reverence is not shown to You; where the presumption of an unwise multitude is struck by diversity of tongues; and where, with people divided from one another, the tower of infinite greatness is not completed. Nor do I think that the plain of Megiddo is pleasing to You for pasture (2 Chronicles 3), where archers struck the righteous Josiah to death, and justice, which was already rejoicing in the hope of victory, is brought back utterly dead through the reversal of battle.

“But did You choose the valley of Topheth as pasture suited to You (4 Kings 23)? Though lovely in situation, You knew it to be foul with sacrilege. There the children of Israel, in wretched superstition, paid homage not to You, God, but to Moloch, and in blind ritual passed sons and daughters through fire for him. The attractiveness of this valley was not pleasing to You, nor to Josiah; that king’s sagacity abolished its pestilential rite. The very aspect and most lovely beauty of the place invited people to sacrilege, but the foulness of scattered bones of the dead and heaped-up corpses repelled them.

“Since, therefore, You do not pasture in mountains, plains, and valleys of this kind, I ask You to teach and show more carefully where You do pasture, if perhaps You are said to have other mountains, plains, and valleys in whose bosom You delight to pasture or lie down.”

The Virgin knows indeed that other mountains are commended in the Scriptures, mountains in which no one is said to perish but to be saved. The Bridegroom Himself loves them, visits them with friendly affection, makes them worthy of Himself, and fit for His special pasture. The prophet Joel says: “On Mount Zion there shall be salvation” (Joel 2). David says: “He chose Mount Zion, which He loved” (Psalm 77); likewise, “Mount Zion, the city of the great King” (Psalm 47); and, “The Lord loves the gates of Zion” (Psalm 86).

What wonder, then, if that mountain which the Lord embraces with benevolent affection is said to offer pleasing fodder to the One who embraces it? In the one whom He loves, the Lover cannot be denied pasture, since He has no refreshment at all except where His love is. Therefore perhaps John says: “I saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion” (Revelation 14). But why was He standing, except to feed? The Lamb stands while He feeds; when He rests, He lies down.

The Virgin, concerned not only with one but with both, asks where the Bridegroom pastures and where He lies down, as though the place of feeding were one and that of resting another. For the Bridegroom is the Lamb. Of Him of whom John elsewhere says, “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3), he also said: “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1).

The Bridegroom, therefore—or Lamb—feeds on a mountain: not the mountain which Isaiah calls dark (chapter 13), nor that great mountain which Zechariah says will be made into a plain before Zerubbabel (chapter 4), but Mount Zion, commended for vision, whose name comes from the thing itself and which, with near objects set before it, looks farther into the distance. Of this mountain Isaiah prophesies: “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isaiah 16).

Finally, through Ezekiel the Lord promises: “Behold, I myself will feed my sheep” (Ezekiel 34); and, specifying where He will feed them: “I will feed them on the mountains of Israel” (ibid.). Israel is interpreted “seeing God.” Therefore I would call those mountains good and fertile to whom it is granted to behold God, and upon whose pasture the good Shepherd promises to feed His sheep. For the saints who excel in virtues are lifted high by their merits; living in heaven, they are flooded with the light of contemplation. They indeed refresh God’s good pleasure, God’s desire, God’s will; they offer to His command the fertility of manifold spiritual obedience.

“Concerning the saints who are in His land,” he says, “He has made all my desires wonderful in them” (Psalm 15). “He has made wonderful,” that is, He has fed, cherished, and brought wonderfully to fulfillment, so that whatever I willed might be done in them, and their great and wonderful works might be sought out in accordance with all my desires (Psalm 110).

Finally, in the Gospel the disciples say: “Where do You wish us to go and prepare for You to eat the Passover?” (Mark 14). And He says: “The master of the house will show you a large upper room, furnished; prepare it there” (ibid.). The upper room is high and elevated; it is large, broad and sufficient; it is furnished, beautiful and inviting. The upper room in which the Bridegroom’s refreshment lies is commended by its loftiness of dignity, because “the heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but the earth He has assigned to the children of men” (Psalm 113). It is expanded by great spaciousness so as to be more sufficient, because He does not delight in a narrow bench and a stingy three-legged stool. And so that it may always attract Him, it is spread and adorned with elaborate coverings and fragrant flowers, because He who is beautiful beyond the children of men rejects what is impure, dishonourable, and ugly.

The Bridegroom also feeds in a field: that field, namely, which is levelled when the heaps of rubble are removed; which, uprooting thorns and briars, is beautified with a pleasant surface; which, cleansed of barren frost, is made fruitful by springtime mildness; which smiles with green grasses and is varied with flowers of many colours. The first and chief of these says: “I am the flower of the field” (Song 2).

That field is rich and must not be passed over in negligent silence. Upon its surface Ezekiel sees many bones, exceedingly dry (Ezekiel 37). By hearing they received the ineffable word of the Lord; through marvellous joining they received sinews, flesh, and skin; and at last they lived again when the spirit came from the four winds. Finally, in the Gospel (Luke 6), the Bridegroom descends from the mountain and stands in a level place. Because in that place the power of healing and fullness of grace shone forth, a great multitude of people came together to Him from every side. The good Shepherd, seeing them eager to hear and be healed, generously refreshes them with the word of life, with saving pasture.

The Bridegroom also feeds in valleys, which David says abound with grain (Psalm 64), and in the valley of Jehoshaphat, which seems to shine with the grace of humility. The greater anyone is, the more he lowers himself in all things; and the person whom his neighbour worthily commends and exalts darkens himself in his own judgment. “When you have done all good things,” He says, “say: ‘We are useless servants’” (Luke 17). And again: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 2).

In mountains, fields, and valleys of this kind the Bridegroom feeds, because loftiness of life, equality of conduct, and humility of judgment are the Bridegroom’s pleasing refreshment. As a wise craftsman, He Himself works these things in His faithful, rejoicing to bring His purposes in them to fulfillment. “My food,” He says, “is to do the will of Him who sent me” (John 4).

## CHAPTER XXV
“Tell me where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.” Having asked where the Bridegroom pastures, the Bride adds that she seeks where he also lies down at noon [Col. 0240B], touching upon the custom of shepherds who, after attending to pasture during the first part of the day, turn aside and recline at noon for rest. Since foxes are known to have dens and birds of heaven nests (Luke 9), into which many wretches, with blind countenance and wandering foot, tumble: the Virgin wishes to know more certainly where the Son of Man chooses to turn aside, and where he wishes to lay his head down for rest.

For the time warns us, when the world is hot and burning, when the noonday quarter glows under a fiercer sun, that the provident Shepherd should turn aside somewhere and rest, while the little flock, fleeing to him, hides itself quietly. The sun is hot; heat falls upon the minds of the wicked when a mass of evil vices pours into them: when avarice, lust, and ambition rule them [Col. 0240C], when the inward face of their souls is blackened by the burning of such things. Therefore, in this noon, whose heat that world cannot endure—the Holy One, to whom nothing unclean pertains—where he turns aside, where he pauses, where he finds a welcome resting-place, I myself would, if it were possible, wish to know not so much by knowledge as by experience.

For when pride raises us up because of goods of either nature or grace; when persistent anger inflames us, envy torments us, lust softens us; when prayer is burdensome, divine reading is loathed, when the preaching voice is not heard because the ear is shut like that of an asp: we must fear lest that Shepherd, burdened by this heat and untimely disorder, leave us and flee beneath a fitting shade. The world, placed in evil, burned under a heavy and parching sun [Col. 0240D], and Egypt or Ethiopia suffered under the noonday heat, when the Holy Spirit overshadowed the incorrupt Virgin and prepared in her a pleasing shelter for God, the Son of God (Luke 1).

The same heat or disorder had lain heavily enough upon the Pharisees and had spread with looser rein among the Jews, when Christ, leaving them, turned aside to the few apostles and gathered them, as a hen, beneath the shade and covering of his wings. But when Jews and Gentiles raged against him even to the cross at noon, some with tongue, others with hand, pouring out the poison of burning wrath, he—leaving, not so much with his feet as in affection, more with his mind than with his eyes, those whom he rejected—saw standing beside the cross his Mother and the disciple whom he loved (John 19). And when he had received the vinegar [Col. 0241A], tasting it rather than drinking it, he thus fulfilled the mystery; upon these, over whom the Spirit cast his shadow, he rested all the more gladly because more sweetly. While outside the sun burned fiercely, whose rage had filled him, he bowed his head toward these, gave up his spirit, and fell asleep.

Thus, no longer bearing the noon and the raging heats of Cancer or Leo, completing at the sixth hour the contest or mystery of the Passion, he turned aside and loved the Spirit’s shade, the serene resting-place of the tomb. The stone set upon it did not hinder him when he rose. “For he lay down as a lion” (Gen. 49). The tomb indeed could have held him as long as he willed; but, his will fulfilled, he was not detained by the obstacle of the stone. Rather, divine power made him strong as a lion for rising in the morning and likewise for repaying, at noon, the retaliation due to those who raged.

[Col. 0241B] Nor do I consider it unworthy if we believe that the same Bridegroom also lies down in you, if we proclaim that he finds some little rest in us. For it is, by the gift of his grace, our will both to serve him and to soothe him, although the power is not yet wholly free even for those who will it. But if we ourselves, or perhaps anyone else, judge it insufficiently fitting that we should attribute to ourselves what even the greatest scarcely manage to attain, we must fear, on the contrary, that we distrust the righteous one more than is right and equally incur danger through base distrust.

Therefore, between these two extremes, may not Daedalus but the Father of spirits teach us to fly; may he guide our unknown path and be willing to grant the grace of journeying, lest we be plunged into mud and filth while we cling, like carnal persons, to things nearer the earth [Col. 0241C], or lest we be cast down from glory while we foolishly assault higher things after the manner of Icarus.

For the Bridegroom lies down in us if we are proved to love him, if we prepare ourselves for his service with diligent zeal; if we hasten to wipe away with broom or razor whatever makes a clamor or gives offense; if, for love’s sake, we adorn the secret place of our heart with the flowers of affection. For nothing is more pleasing to him, nothing does he desire more eagerly, than to be loved: namely, when we truly embrace him with singular love; when, because of him, we cast far away as refuse whatever the world offers; when in the world or in ourselves we love nothing besides him.

Thus John (chapter 13) is said to have reclined upon the breast of this same Bridegroom, because that Bridegroom loved him, as he reclined, above the others. Nor, as you know, is anyone else said there to have reclined [Col. 0241D], except him whom Jesus is repeatedly and openly declared to love. And rightly we read not that Jesus reclined in John’s bosom, but that John reclined in Jesus’ bosom: for we are believed not to have loved him first, but he to have loved us first. And where anyone truly understands that he is loved, there he rejoices to recline and delights in sweet repose.

Before his Passion Christ understood John, like the others, to be weak, and understood himself to be loved less than sufficiently by the disciple whom he loved. For at that time neither John nor Peter either wished or was able to endure death for him—something which, after they received the Spirit following his resurrection, none of these failed to achieve. Yet Christ was found so to love those whom he chose, and his love for them so compelled him who loved them, that he willingly gave his life into death for them [Col. 0242A], and, dying, defended from death those whom he held in his bosom.

After his resurrection, appearing to these same disciples, he breathed upon them (John 20) and by a most serene breath conferred the priestly power of binding and loosing. Shortly afterward the mighty Spirit inflamed them with tongues of fire (Acts 2) and strengthened them unbendingly against the world’s threats, entreaties, and rewards. The death which he first was willing to endure for them they repaid—not entangled in the cords of avarice, but by prodigal generosity.

The Bridegroom should deservedly be believed to lie down in such persons and in those like them, among whom he finds nothing by which his rest can be injured: in whom devotion flourishes, discipline burns yet more fervently; no furnace merely smokes, but the entire workshop of love burns. For, as has been said, the Bridegroom desires to be loved; and love is fire. Those whom he sees kindled and burning with love, in them he wishes to lie for rest, as in a bed.

[Col. 0242B] And for this reason he is said to lie down only at noon: when the sun, nearer heaven, is farther removed from earth; when it emits purer rays, more fervent than usual; when with a greater blaze it terrifies the wider fields of the sky. Perhaps he pastures in the morning, when the troublesome darkness of night has already withdrawn, when the sun, necessary for those rising to work, goes before; when its turning wheel, with laboring horses, climbs upward and, unable to stand in one place, does not aim at remaining still but at moving forward and advancing.

During its delay the sun gives useful nourishment to the day; warmed and advanced by it, the day gradually receives increase [Col. 0242C], until the sun hastens to and reaches the middle of heaven and stands fixed, where, having risen higher, it is compelled either to remain or to descend. So indeed, brethren, when you sat in darkness, the Sun of grace brought you morning light. Casting aside the error of night, you hastened to take hold of discipline; and the more fully he spread out for you clearer rays, the more gladly you labor and make greater progress.

Therefore, while you discipline the opposing body by vigils, fasting, sweat, and cold; while, devout and humble, you bind your patience with the cords of obedience; while, with regard to the commandments, you banish your own will; while you labor for food which does not perish but endures, and with tireless zeal eat the labor of your hands: surely the Bridegroom pastures among you, with you [Col. 0242D], and labors, just as the devout lover and seeker of wisdom prays: “Give me wisdom,” he says, “that she may be with me and labor with me” (Wis. 9).

For in pasturing there is indeed the fruit of life, but undoubtedly joined with labor; labor is a slight burden, bearable because of the more pleasing fruit. Therefore, when the righteous person invites patience to labor with him, he loves not so much labor itself as its better fruit. Accordingly, the Virgin anxiously desires to know not only where the Bridegroom pastures but also where he lies down, that she may attain his more pleasing condition. For although, while he pastures, he grants us no slight advancement, still, while he lies down and rests, he advances us more pleasantly and securely to perfection.

Therefore, when, with the body disciplined, the murmur of the passions lulled—not wholly laid aside, but for a time set aside together with the labor of temporal activities—prayer, devotion, and meditation upon the reading heard make you inwardly serene, and divine grace lifts you, suspended from earth, as though into the height of vision; when, though swiftly and briefly, you seem to be among angelic spirits; and when, in some manner beholding the Lord’s glory, you say with Peter, “It is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17); when you burn sweetly as with fire through love of such things, and the Sun brighter than the sun bathes you in the ray of his splendor: then indeed the Bridegroom pastures in you and delights in loving rest. He rejoices in such a noon: day rejoices with day, light with light.

[Col. 0243A] For as the wicked enemy, author of evil and prince of ruined Babylon, loves the deep darkness of night and the cold of the north, so the Bridegroom, who is God, unfailing light and burning fire, making his gracious presence far from those unlike and unworthy of him, lies down and rests in those whom he feels to be burning with the fiery torch of divine love; whom, caught up in ecstasy, he sees shining—not being burned—in noonday light.

They have forgotten present things and are intent upon heavenly ones; not content with dawn or the morning sun and the works of beginners, but raised up to the perfect day and burning noon. They are one spirit with God, though not yet perfect solely because they still share the dwelling of the flesh. Blessed is one who, forgetting what lies behind, has merited thus to stretch forward; who, despising morning’s temperate state, is so kindled by noonday advancement and excessive heat; who holds the Bridegroom in the bosom, embraces him in affection as with an arm, fixes the eyes upon the Sun alone, and does not turn aside toward the corpses of this flesh.

Blessed, I say—provided [Col. 0243C] that person does not fear the fall from this benefit, provided the noon of such heat and splendor does not decline toward sunset; provided the flesh does not draw one back, together with nature’s still weaker law, which cannot yet bear the glory of lasting blessedness. Blessed therefore is that day whose noon does not set, in whose ever-fiery light the Bridegroom remains and reclines; whoever reaches it perseveres there in stable degree and, having found its good, declares that nothing is better, nothing more delightful.

In it the holy angels always behold the face of both Father and Son; nor are the souls of the saints kept apart from that vision. Rescued now from the wicked world and the prison-house of flesh, they have been received, together with the angels, into the Bridegroom’s peaceful chamber. There is found a fuller and more perfect noon, where day does not decline and is not ended by approaching evening; where there dawns only one day, neither advancing nor failing, whose brightness is not darkened and whose splendid heat does not grow tepid.

[Col. 0243D] Therefore no one fully receives such a noon in this life, but only tastes it beforehand; there one is fully satisfied, where a delay, though shorter, does not constrict, where love for God in all things burns continually and unceasingly, and he who is loved gladly lies down and rests in all.

On earth, then, he pastures only in one to whom he grants righteousness, pouring in the abundance of grace; one whose good works, like grasses and flowers, refresh his will; whose conduct he accepts, whose justice he delights to behold; one in whose merits he rejoices, whose virtues he embraces, whose holiness he receives; one for whom the morning day and the sun shine with imperfect light while that person labors and advances, “because toil is fashioned in the commandment” (Ps. 93).

But in heaven the Bridegroom lies down, where day does not dawn with dimmed light, but the sun, as at noon, gleams with maturity now complete. Its warmth of splendor and splendor of warmth have nothing imperfect, but stand perfect, as though at a solstice, upon an immovable axis. Therefore day lies down sweetly in day, light in light, sun in sun, and rests: because the righteous shines brightly as the sun in the kingdom of his Father (Matt. 13), and the Bridegroom, the Sun of righteousness, receives in that righteous person a chamber and rest so pleasing because it is not confined by space or disturbed by an assault of trouble.

Accordingly, the anxious Virgin deservedly asks to be shown where he whom she loves with singular love pastures and where he lies down, so that, once it has been shown, she may gladly follow him there in security, lest—if it remain shut—she wander after the flocks of his companions [Col. 0244B].

## CHAPTER XXVI

“Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.” A companion of Christ is one who wishes to be identified by his name, who says that he belongs to him, who chooses to profess his faith; one who proclaims his word, preaches the way of truth, and associates himself with Christ either in reality or in the appearance of holiness.

But since there are many who possess no true reality but are colored with an appearance; who detest in feeling and deed what they maintain in word or countenance—the Virgin chose to call them not “a flock” but rather “flocks,” knowing that the singular name is more suitably attributed to the righteous. Thus later in the Song: “Your hair is like goats; your teeth like a flock of sheep” (Song 6). And in the Gospel: “Do not fear, little flock” (Luke [Col. 0244C] 12).

The flocks of his companions, then, are the false multitude of believers: among them is an appearance of piety, but no strength, no power of works; among them appears the display of Christian religion, and the preaching or teaching of Scripture is sometimes heard, but their life has no right savor and does not sufficiently breathe forth the discipline of morals. These persons commonly injure and seduce the consciences of the weak, turning aside from the path of righteousness into the broad way of error. By open conversations, hidden counsels, or worse examples, they corrupt good morals; they either entirely remove, or at least temporarily interrupt, the narrow way of religion.

The most prudent Virgin does not wish to be led after such seducers, but to discern wisely who ought to be preferred to whom, lest, if she takes Nicholas for Stephen or Judas for John, she be considered like them or become a daughter of Gehenna twofold. The Virgin knows that this evil is done by the prompting of evil spirits, whom iniquity cast far from and removed from the heavenly seat. For they did not see divine excellence with an eye sufficiently humble, but, desiring inaccessible likeness, fell from heaven like lightning.

Knowing that they would never return to the place from which they fell, but that human beings made from clay would ascend through grace and merits, they are corrupted by malice, suffer and are tortured by wondrous envy, and strive with utmost effort to harm those whom they see receiving this grace. Since, therefore, their disposition for envy is tireless, and, according to a certain pagan writer, they have a thousand arts of harming, they spread their nets both at midnight and at noon; and with either an arrow in darkness or a noonday attack they seize the unwary and wretched (Ps. 90).

[Col. 0245A] The arrow flying in darkness, which strikes grievously while unknown, is a hidden suggestion by which our mind is enticed: beneath a sort of covering veil it promises itself to be either no sin or a venial one, and with a small wound, as it were, introduces deadly poison into the wretched heart. The noonday attack, on the other hand, is the open malignity of the assailant, when the impudence of the evil one violently pours out all its strength, when it grievously casts us down from the throne of patience, obedience, and continence; or perhaps, if we resist, more plainly threatens and inflicts losses, dangers, and martyrdoms.

But if the evil spirit should find anyone stronger, so that he does not fear its terrible threats or its fiercer attack, it lays aside threats, is silent about dangers, introduces nothing violently, but fraudulently turns toward a certain appearance of religion. For, observing that some take pleasure in vigils, prayers, abstinence, fasting, and manual labor, it does not resist but presses on and first encourages them to persist in these more rigorously; then, lest they should be surpassed in them by one another, it urges them to guard more anxiously against each other; and afterward, at the fitting time, it induces them, dissatisfied, not to keep the regularly prescribed measure.

Thus, while a person fervent in spirit tries not to be inferior to the others and does not restrain the admitted horse of desire with the bridle of moderation; while one anticipates the appointed vigils in order to pray more devoutly or meditate more pleasantly upon something from Scripture; while one fasts and abstains lest the stomach seem burdened by quickly passing foods [Col. 0245C]; while one still strong in body applies oneself beyond due measure to manual labor; while one extends oneself to these or similar practices with looser reins: there arise on every side gusts of vainglory, love of praise, presumptuous self-estimation, contempt for others, rash judgment, and harsher, harmful rebuke.

For condemning others, whom one sees, as lukewarm, keeping a more relaxed measure, that person already judges oneself, more fervent in effort, better than all. And the more thoughtlessly one burns toward greater things, the more, wounded by the wind of pride, one withers wickedly and becomes emptier in a more shameful fashion. For vanity, secretly introduced, receives the person whom fervor drives headlong; and a certain appearance, once introduced, deceives that person’s conscience. Pretending to be good with false light, it dulls and darkens the eyes, through the subtler work of him who transforms himself into an angel of light [Col. 0246A].

By his work, this wretched person does not at all suppose oneself deceived, but imagines oneself bathed, as it were, in a ray of the noonday sun. Looking only at the surface, like a visible flower, one hopes for a surer fruit and does not detect the defect in the root. Thus deceived, one already wanders after the flocks of the companions, while, apparently doing good, one is defrauded by the craft of evil spirits. Such spirits are discovered to be, in a sense, Christ’s companions and associates, since the person supposes oneself to please Christ and is nevertheless found to please them.

The more prudent Virgin does not wish to wander after companions of this sort, nor to be defrauded by their noonday appearance of good. Rather, she wishes to perceive their wiles with clear-sighted eye and to find Christ in his own light and in a noon that does not deceive. “I wish,” she says, “to find your light true, useful, and serene, lest, deceived by error, I run after an alien light; lest fallen Lucifer falsely assume for himself Michael’s likeness; lest Satan present himself to me in Gabriel’s form and appearance. I wish,” she says, “not to be deceived by the noonday attack and demon, nor carried away by the beguilements and deceptive pretense of those who falsely claim to be your companions, who rejoice in the name of angels but do not enjoy angelic blessedness.”

Therefore, lest their aforesaid light and day flatter me craftily, show me in what human being or angel a pleasing rest is found for you—a rest which in yourself shines and burns not merely in daylight but at noon, being perfect: neither begun in the morning nor declining toward evening in its course.

[Col. 0246C] Thus far the Virgin Bride has spoken about and to him whom she loves more tenderly, pursuing her love and desire in uninterrupted speech. Now she takes up silence, yet does not wholly cease speaking, but pauses briefly in order to listen. Let us likewise, at this point, take up silence and rest awhile; and let us at last impose an end upon this first book, since it asks that an end be put to its own length, and our weakness asks that the labor undertaken be at least briefly set aside.

If day dawns, I shall endeavor to bend back the resting pen to discuss what the Bridegroom deigned to answer the Virgin; if that Holy Spirit graciously comes to teach me in silence what may please him for me to speak rather than to keep silent.

# BOOK II

[Col. 0245]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0245D]

“If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out, and go after the tracks of the flocks.”

After the Virgin’s many words, by which she showed the heat of her soul and asked that the desired kiss be given her and the Bridegroom’s chamber shown to her, not hardness, contempt, or, finally, a prolonged silence holds the Bridegroom any longer. Rather, having carefully heard her vows and prayers, he gives an answer.

[Col. 0246D] And indeed, the Virgin, who so anxiously wishes to be taught where the Bridegroom lies down, he first warns diligently not to neglect looking upon herself, that, turning toward her own condition, she may not fail to know her own beauty, lest neglect or disuse discolor what is unknown. For one does not prudently kindle oneself to acquire other things who does not first examine with the eye of worthy consideration what has already been acquired, and who rashly heaps up desired riches by labor while failing to preserve with diligent care what was long ago stored up.

As the poet describes, a hunter greatly errs and fails who catches at things fleeing while despising and leaving behind what has been caught. Likewise the prophet Haggai showed him worthy of rebuke who placed gathered wages in a bag with holes (Hag. 1). Therefore the Bridegroom first sends the Virgin to consider her own beauty and does not allow her to consign past things to forgetfulness. He reminds her of the very thing which he warns her to remember, so that she may more readily incline her ear to the admonitions: “O beautiful one,” he says, “among women.”

That Virgin whom the Son of God chose for himself from eternity as Mother of God; in whom, at the fitting time, taking flesh, he confined himself within contracted limbs; from whom he willed to be born, without the flesh being broken, by a new kind of birth; whose son he became before childbirth and after childbirth, her chastity remaining wholly incorrupt—that this Virgin, I say, was beautiful among others, that is, more beautiful than other women, I think worthy of belief, nor is faith of this sort blameworthy.

[Col. 0247B] For it is not believable that God, the Son of God, chose as his mother one dark-complexioned, one-eyed, conspicuously goitrous, or hunchbacked, rather than one beautiful with snowy face, rosy color, lovely eyes, and a full figure: so that she who was selected for an office more worthy than that of other women might be not only free from every stain of ugliness, but also fairer and more perfect in bodily appearance than all others.

Yet the statement that she is called beautiful among women applies not so much to grace of countenance and bodily beauty as to her perfect morals and her marvelous holiness. The angel testifies that she alone was “full of grace”—something nowhere said of any other woman—and therefore merited to become the mother of Christ alone. Beholding such beauty, the angel said: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1).

For she is blessed in women, that is, among women, upon whom the harsher curse has been imposed through Eve’s guilt; women who are conformed to the first sinner under that unhappy law and, liable to sins, are deformed by likeness to their mother. Among these wretched and deformed women a greater beauty was granted to this Virgin. Passing beyond the old curse and hereditary law, through the Spirit’s overshadowing she drove far from herself every heat of evil and every stain of sin; and by the merits of innocence and the beauty of her mind she set herself above all women.

[Col. 0247D] Moreover, rejoicing in the integrity of her body as an increase of her beauty, she became fruitful by a new manner unknown to all; and in an ineffable childbirth, while a virgin, she brought forth one such that no other woman, either before or afterward, bore one greater or equal. What then is this so great and incomparable eminence except the marvelous and outstanding beauty of this Virgin, by which she was found not merely unsurpassed by other women but herself far more beautiful and excellent than all?

The Bridegroom calls her back and leads her to consider this, yet does not fully introduce her to the desired chamber, so that she may first know with what great grace she is adorned and remember with mindful humility whence and how far she has come. “You,” he says, “who have already obtained a grace greater than that of all women, who, remaining a virgin, have wonderfully become the Mother of God: while you do not find what remains and have not yet reached what you desire, consider more diligently what has already been granted you by my gift.

[Col. 0248A] For although eagerly desiring future things, you are not yet able to obtain them, if you take care humbly to remember the grace already received, your perception of present things will establish your faith more firmly; and faith so established will await future things more sweetly and securely. But if you set aside and do not know what you already experience as present, and, while seeking what you have not experienced, are found negligent of what you have experienced: ‘Go out’—this I say to you not as counsel or command, but, foreknowing the future, as a threat.

“‘Go out,’ that is, you will go out and deserve to recoil from the secret place; you will be far from the sanctuary into which you seek to enter; you will be driven away from the very pleasant chamber which you wish shown to you; and you will seem to go out because you are not allowed to go in. Thus those who do not deserve to be inscribed with the righteous in the eternal book are said to be blotted out of the book of the living; and in customary speech we say that those things are taken away which we know are at last not granted to us although hoped for or desired.

[Col. 0248B] Thus the Virgin too will complain that she goes outside when, through her ignorance, she suffers rejection from entrance; when, forgetful of her beauty, she appears ugly and discolored; when from remembrance of present things she does not have certain confidence concerning future things.

“But if, Virgin, you rememberingly consider that you possess the pledge and earnest of the Spirit, which none of the elect has deserved to obtain in precisely that manner, you will surely know that whatever you worthily ask is neither taken away nor is the righteous desire of one who burns defrauded, but is delayed. For you who received so many and such great things beyond all women, who conceived the Son without a father through the working of the Holy Spirit, who, according to Gabriel, found marvelous and ineffable grace with God, who gave birth without intercourse and without pain to him whom you conceived—what can you rightly suppose will hereafter be denied you, provided the time comes when it is worthy to be given?

[Col. 0248C] “Therefore await from him who granted such great things what remains; and if, as often seems to be the case, he causes delay for your desiring soul, wait again. And lest the delay perhaps burden you, remember what you have already received; strengthen yourself by the memory of those gifts toward faith and patience. For in what you already possess you have surpassed all women’s beauty and preceded all Eve’s daughters by your beautiful countenance of mind. If you know this and give worthy thanks to the giver, then, sighing for what remains, you will not utter an undeserved complaint against the one who delays.

“For this reason he delays: that the desire delayed may groan more fervently and steadfastly, not fail through impatience with faith shaken; that during the time of delay you may cultivate and adorn your beautiful countenance more fully, rather than more carelessly discolor it with the dust of forgetfulness and base ignorance. Therefore, if you do not know yourself, go out from my assembly, from my bosom, from me, and finally from the face of him whom you loved; and go after the tracks of the flocks whom you feared a little earlier.”

“Go out,” he says, “and go.” For one who has gone out from the sanctuary into which one ought to have entered, advancing toward worse things, is no longer allowed to stand but must go; and because one did not fear to forget oneself or the counsel of the one who warned, one is compelled to go far from oneself and farther still from the one who warned.

[Col. 0249A] One goes after the tracks of the flocks who follows their preceding perversity: those who love errors and sects and do not know the unity of faith; or those who live in a beastly manner, entice and deceive their followers, and grievously pursue those whom they precede by their perverse morals.

## CHAPTER II

“And feed your kids beside the tents of the shepherds.” When anyone has gone out and gone away, already possessing a darkened understanding, that person is said to feed kids while bringing perverse affections to effect, fostering and advancing instability of mind, wantonness of conduct, bodily impurity, and loving to lead an animal life.

Perhaps one feeds lambs who, strengthened by the spirit of merciful grace, possesses innocent acts and pure, simple thoughts. The supreme Shepherd approves their fruit and loves their whiteness, and exhorts his beloved to feed them: “If you love me,” he says, “feed my lambs” (John 21). But one feeds kids who, with corrupted mind, deceived spirit, and ruined will, does evil, delights in wickedness, is burdened by justice, and pursues those things which the righteous Judge judges to be placed at the left hand (Matt. 25), so that the avenging angel may rage harshly against them together with his ministers.

Such kids are not said to be fed in the tents of the shepherds, from whose fellowship one is kept by one’s own pressing malice. The shepherds’ life does not attract such a person; their works do not delight but offend, nor does one desire to imitate what they set forth beforehand in teaching and conduct.

[Col. 0249C] And because such a person is not found dwelling in the shepherds’ tents, where the voice of exultation and salvation is heard together, one at least remains nearby; nor are one’s pastures found farther away, while one retains Christ’s name, the same baptism, and common sacraments. Thus, abhorring virtue, one glories in an appearance of piety; and, not possessing the reality, is visibly overshadowed by the sacrament of faith. For this reason one is said to feed not within but beside the shepherds’ tents: although one is, in some manner, outside, the appearance of one’s own condition is nevertheless near.

The shepherds are any perfected persons who pursue right faith not so much in name as in works; who, washed once in the laver of regeneration, are often cleansed by devout tears; who devoutly celebrate the Church’s sacraments for their salvation, possessing not so much their outward form as their power. In these tents they set their perversities straight, subject their own wills to the divine good pleasure, govern with discerning moderation both their works and their affections, and daily advance to greater progress.

[Col. 0249D] But those do not dwell in them, though they come somewhat near, who destroy faith by works while not abandoning the sacraments of faith; who, lacking virtue, are adorned with its outward title; who imitate those whom they see as good shepherds not in reality but in name.

But perhaps it may seem harsh and austere to some that the Bridegroom addresses the Virgin Mother in this way, that, at the beginning of his reply, he threatens her who had spoken sweetly with such tender words.
