For it is certain that after the aforesaid kiss she will not in this manner go out or go away from him; and therefore things so grave and superfluous do not seem fitting for one who kisses or loves.

Although these words may be assigned more suitably to any soul, or even to the Church, to which, when it sins, Christ frequently judges it useful now to promise and now to threaten, yet her beauty is believed to be more steadfast in a special manner—the one in whom God is made human and the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. I therefore think it worthwhile to examine a little more attentively how the Bridegroom may answer fittingly in like manner to the Virgin speaking amorously, and how, having already perceived her prayers, vows, and tireless desire, he returns praises for praises and does not dissent from her desire.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0250B]

If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out and follow the tracks of the flocks. The Bridegroom, wishing to advance the Virgin step by step toward greater perfection, teaches her how she may deserve to obtain the grace of progress: namely, if she so stores away within herself, as though in hiding, the gifts she has received, that the crafty enemy may not set his pitch-covered hand upon them, even for a little. For he often applies a harmful touch to the higher gifts of greater grace and holiness, when he pours over them the dark cloud of wicked vanity as a calamity: either by a heavy blast of pride he overwhelms and hardens a mind endowed with gifts, or at least by a light breeze he somewhat darkens the beauty of a tender countenance. For it is difficult for any Virgin to look upon herself as endowed with higher gifts and either not be struck by the battering-ram of proud [Col. 0250C] vanity, or not be moved by even the slightest breath of it: to perceive herself distinguished in form and praiseworthy in appearance, yet never to consent with a yielding mind to one who praises her frequently.

Therefore she who does not wish pride to touch her must not hold a mirror before herself, lest, seeing herself beautiful, she perhaps place herself before others. Rather, lest she consent even a little to the flattering deceiver, she should offer her countenance, unknown to herself, to be known only by her chaste lover. Thus the chaste lover, desiring that the Virgin please none but himself, wishes her not to know the appearance of her own face; he wishes the Virgin not to know herself or marvel at her own beauty, lest, admiring or praising herself, she glory more in herself than in the Lord.

That angel would have been happy if [Col. 0250D] in some manner he had not known himself, when in the delights of paradise he surpassed Lucifer in splendor; happy, I say, if he had not been proud of what he had received, and, though created by God, had not imagined himself God’s equal. Far better and happier did Abraham not know himself when, as though ignorant of himself, he sought divine converse; when, forgetting that he was regarded as great in merits and more illustrious in life, he confessed in prudent counsel that he was nothing but dust and ashes. “I will speak to my Lord,” he says, “though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII).

Happy also was King David, who, because he refuses to know the learning of the letter which he had acquired, and sets his own aside, deserves to enter into the powers of the Lord. Not establishing his own righteousness, he serves with bowed neck under God’s righteousness; forgetting what is his own, he remembers only what belongs to the Lord. [Col. 0251A] “Because I have not known learning,” he says, “I will enter into the powers of the Lord; Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone” (Ps. LXX).

On the other hand, wretched Nebuchadnezzar did not remove from himself knowledge of himself. He knew himself to be rich, exceedingly powerful, and endowed with varied successes; he attended more to himself as ruler than to him through whom kings rule, and, beholding himself as great, he slighted the author of his greatness. “Is not this great Babylon,” he says, “which I have built by the strength of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Dan. IV).

But if someone objects that some people are found to have reviewed their own distinguished works, although Scripture does not judge them thereby blameworthy, let him distinguish the time and the cause 142 in which this is found to be done; and let him know [Col. 0251B] when and why it is found both permissible and necessary. For when a person feels himself being more severely compelled to suffer or commit evils, if by prudent counsel he wishes to be drawn from them as feet from a snare, he can—and indeed ought—to recall lovingly the good things he has already attained, so that the memory of better things may remove the evils threatening him.

Thus Job, when he was shaken by a great weight and number of evils, and his wife urged him at last to curse God, recalled and reviewed the good things he had already received. Mindful of his good deeds, he did not allow the mass of evils to envelop him in the stains of impatience. “I comforted,” he says, “the heart of the widow, and I clothed myself with righteousness; I put it on as a garment. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the poor. And when I sat [Col. 0251C] like a king surrounded by an army, I was nevertheless a comforter of the mournful” (Job XXIX). “But now those younger in time mock me” (Job XXX). And above: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” (Job II).

The good man did not think his good deeds unworthy of being pressed into silence when such a multitude of evils hemmed him in on every side, so that the sweet remembrance of good things might make light the burden of the pressure weighing upon him—as Scripture later advised through a certain Wise Man: “In the day of evils, do not be forgetful of good things” (Ecclus. XI).

To this, I think, belongs that saying which the writings of the Gentiles so favorably extolled and handed down to posterity as a memorable dictum. [Col. 0251D] Some maintain that one of the seven sages of Greece uttered it; others assert rather that Apollo gave it in an elegant oracle: “Know yourself, O man.” Since the sages of the world knew that man consists of a rational soul and a body, of which they said one part was shared with the gods and the other was common with beasts, those whose teaching was sounder preferred reason to the body; by this judgment they disparaged beasts and, more fittingly, deferred to the gods. They wished man therefore to be governed under the guidance of reason, and bestial flesh to be subjected to the rational spirit; so that, when the spirit was raised up, man might be removed from among the beasts and, if not in place, at least [Note: [Col. 0251D] “At least” in place of *saltem*.] in merit be transferred into the fellowship of the gods.

[Col. 0252A] Indeed, they thought that man was made for this and for this reason, and that this is the natural difference between man and beast: the beast freely hungers after earthly things, whereas man is commanded to aspire to heavenly things—a point which the lofty position of the human face itself seems to indicate [Note: [Col. 0252D] Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, I.]. Apollo wishes man prudently to remember this matter: to know whence he comes and whither he ought to advance by the worth of reason; to forget his lower, posterior part, as though given over to sleep; and to awaken to that which is before him with the quickness of his powers.

But since many decline from and wander outside the path of reason—who, in beastlike fashion, plunge into the filth of earthly activity; who entangle and involve their hands in grave offences, put their feet into voluntary sins, and do not free themselves from the crimes laid before them; among whom scarcely anyone is found who lives according to man, [Col. 0252B] but rather, according to the philosopher, is found to live like a pig or an ass—therefore the seer cries aloud, does not permit the tripod to be silent, the oracle resounds, and the censorial voice issues teaching. Great Apollo thunders and, having hurled his lightning, wishes to be feared; he wishes horse and mule, pig and ass, to be deterred from error and ignorance; he wishes all better persons to be admonished toward honorable knowledge and his hearers to be advanced to understand the excellence of reason. “Know yourself, O man,” he says.

Paul was not ignorant of this saying when he was compelled to endure severe things and, tenderly sharing in the weakness and scandal of the Corinthians, burned with concern, lest he be too heavily burdened by another’s load—or perhaps so that he might be deemed more worthy of a hearing by those burdened. He has recourse to knowledge and professes that he knows himself to be a man: one who does not serve the flesh, but who glories in being joined to heaven. “I know,” he says, “a man in Christ caught up as far as the third heaven; and I know such a man—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know, God knows—that he was caught up into paradise and heard secret words, which it is not permitted for a man to speak” (II Cor. XII). [Col. 0252C] And he added: “On behalf of such a one I will glory” (*ibid.*).

Do you see that Paul knows himself to be a man exalted to the third heaven, visiting paradise, and glories in so great a grace? This was so that the Corinthians might not defer more to false apostles and prefer deceitful teachers to his doctrine and merits. Otherwise, if this or a similar cause or necessity had not existed to compel the wise man to this seeming folly, [Col. 0252D] he would surely have remembered what was said in the Gospel to his fellow apostles and would have held it worthy of remembrance both in speech and in conscience: “When you have done all good things, say: We are unprofitable servants” (Luke XVII).

In this saying it is made clear that not everyone is proved to do every good thing, unless this statement is added to his other good works. Nor does he adequately give a worthy appearance to a mass of good deeds who, for the sake of avoiding vanity, does not remain ignorant of it. Therefore, so that you may know the Bride to be perfectly holy and humble, the Bridegroom teaches that this ignorance belongs to her: while she hastens toward the remaining things which the Son does not yet give but promises, she does not commit to self-glorifying memory the things she already possesses. [Col. 0253A] “If you do not know yourself,” he says, “O beautiful one.” For his “if” is not a doubtful but an affirmative conjunction, as that poet says: “Gods, if there is any piety in heaven.”

The Bridegroom therefore says: If you do not know yourself, O beautiful one—which indeed is difficult, but nevertheless 143 is the part of a man—go out. But go out: from where and to where, if not from contemplation of yourself to your work? Go out from considering your own beauty to fashioning the beauty of others. Neglectful, as it were, of yourself, be solicitous for very many: form disciples; teach the apostles what you have learned more perfectly concerning me; condescend to John, whom you have received as a son in the capacity of mother. Go out, I say, and follow the tracks of the flocks.

Those who preside over flocks walk after their tracks and are known to keep their care before their eyes. [Col. 0253B] Lest anyone stray or anyone, exhausted, sit down, they cast their watchful eyes about; they rejoice at the healthier one, and carry every weak one on their shoulders or lead it back. Thus it is the mark of authority to preside over flocks; and the apostles are instructed to attend upon the Virgin who presides, so that the Virgin may command them, act as mother in caring for all, and they may heed their mother, as the Gospel declares: “Woman, behold your son” (John XIX); and to the disciple: “Behold your mother” (*ibid.*).

For when the care of John is entrusted to the Virgin Mother, the care of the others is not, I think, excluded from her; but what is assigned more specially to one because of a certain mystery is shown to be generally necessary for all. For John alone does not receive and venerate Mary when received, nor does the Virgin embrace John alone with the affection of devoted care. Loving all, she endeavors to make herself useful to all and, preeminent in teaching, presents herself as an example to be imitated by all. [Col. 0253C] “All,” it says, “were persevering unanimously in prayer with Mary, the mother of Jesus” (Acts I).

Therefore the Virgin is admonished to follow their tracks, that with a careful eye she may examine their progress—what they do, whither they tend, and by what paths they go; that she may promote what is worthy of praise, and not pass over the wandering but correct them. The flocks are the apostles and those joined to them in faith and works, who, instructed in the evangelical mysteries, are separated from the error of the ignorant; who, reverencing the Virgin and believing her teaching, long for eternal pastures and hold in contempt the things of this world. [Col. 0253D] Of these it is said through Ezekiel: “But you are my flocks, says the Lord” (Ezek. XXXIV).

Perhaps he wished to call them “flocks” in the plural because the apostles, commanded to preach the word of the Gospel to the nations who would believe, separated from one another under the Spirit’s guidance and chose different regions of the world. There, through zeal in preaching, they gathered many flocks and assemblies of people, many churches. Although they differ in place, time, and the worth of their virtues, nevertheless, when all come to the Catholic faith and evangelical teaching, many flocks are gathered into one, and the many are brought together into one Church; all are united by the undivided mystery of faith and baptism.

## CHAPTER IV

And feed your kids beside the tents of the shepherds. He calls the apostles “kids,” because, though they are not denied to have advanced to great holiness through the Virgin’s word and [Col. 0254A] example, nevertheless, while they live a mortal life and are held in the prison-house of the flesh, they confess themselves, according to the Bridegroom’s counsel, to be unprofitable servants. Ignorant of their own righteousness, they confess their sins with humble voice (Luke XVII). One of them says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us” (I John I). And another: “In many things,” he says, “we all offend” (James III).

Those whom purity of conscience, the beauty of innocence, simplicity of conduct, and the eminent holiness of merits render lambs, confession of sin with fear also renders kids, while a person does not yet know whether he is worthy of hatred or of love. Therefore, when any righteous persons are called lambs and innocence earns praise for them—a quality that is not regarded as worthy of commendation except by Christ’s gift—he says, “my,” as he indicated much later to Peter when he entrusted to the loving man the care of those who love: [Col. 0254B] “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my lambs” (John XXI).

But when he wishes those persons whom James and John declare not to be without sin to be reckoned as kids because of sin’s desert, he says “your,” so as to impose upon the Virgin a fuller care for them, that she may watch over their treatment and advance them to a better condition. So it was said to Moses: “Go down; your people have sinned” (Exod. XXXII). Or else, because, just as lambs are allotted the right hand according to Gospel testimony, so kids are known to be set at the Bridegroom’s left hand (Matt. XXV), by “kids” he not inappropriately wishes to signify all the Virgin’s actions—that is, whatever the Virgin is commanded to perform temporarily [Col. 0254C] in this life.

For self-correction, care for others, preaching or teaching, toil and cold, vigils, fasting, discipline—these are indeed gifts of Christ, but they seem to belong to his left hand because, not established at a stable rank, they quickly deserve to reach their end. Yet, if they are fed, they also bring increase: not as in Hosea, “Foolish Ephraim feeds the wind” (Hos. XII), but the Bride should take care to feed beside the tents of the shepherds—that is, to conform herself to the precepts of the Scriptures and to their authorities.

The shepherds are Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Moses and David, the patriarchs and prophets. Some of these are found, in the literal sense, to have labored in feeding flocks; all, in governing and correcting morals, watched with much greater care. [Col. 0254D] Perhaps 144 for this reason such shepherds choose to dwell in tents: because they teach and love to hasten from virtue to virtue, and nothing present is enough for those striving toward greater progress until that which is partial is done away and they finally come to perfection.

Beside their tents—that is, according to their teaching and example—the Virgin is commanded to govern and direct her actions, so that she may follow the rule of Scripture, which the long preceding succession of prophets set forth as something to be known and kept. Although the Virgin Mother already surpasses those same authors by a certain special grace, their authority nevertheless precedes her in time; nor is it unfitting that she be invited to their commendable pattern and teaching, so that she may follow in example those whom she now seems [Col. 0255A] to surpass in merits.

The Bridegroom then shows the Virgin how she may be able to do what she is commanded—how, not knowing herself, she may go out and rejoice to feed the kids—namely, by glorying in the Lord alone and, ignorant of her own face, admiring his face alone. Therefore he adds: “To my cavalry,” etc.

## CHAPTER V

I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots. He calls her beloved whose mind wholly agrees with what she hears, whose conduct no longer departs even a little from the commandments, and who strives so to do and accomplish all that is commanded that, loving him who commanded, she deserves to be loved by him. As it is written in the Gospel: “You are my friends if you do [Col. 0255B] what I command you” (John XV).

Moreover, in order that she might become beloved, he compared her to his own cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots. He alludes to a historical event and touches upon the history which describes the children of Israel crossing the depths of the sea on dry tracks, while Pharaoh’s chariots and indeed his whole army perished. It is fitting to consider in what respect the Virgin Mother is held similar to this people. For such a comparison seems to lack a sufficiently fitting correspondence, especially since in that crossing the people of Israel are not found to have had horses, nor was there any cavalry, since they plainly lacked horses and horsemen.

For it is written of Pharaoh: “Horse and rider he cast into the sea” (Exod. XV), and below: “Pharaoh’s chariots and [Col. 0255C] his army he cast into the sea” (*ibid.*). But when the children of Israel crossed, no mention is made of horses or chariots; nor did they escape Pharaoh’s threats by such protection, lest anyone think that what God’s hand alone wondrously chose to accomplish should be attributed to horses or chariots. Finally, although perhaps one may cross the sea by ship, one does not cross it on horseback or in a wheeled vehicle. In that crossing the people used neither ship nor vehicle; rather, with the waves divided and standing like a wall on both sides, they crossed on dry foot, never again to feel the assaults of the Egyptians.

Thus it is rightly called cavalry for no other reason than that God sat upon it spiritually and mercifully presided as ruler over the people subjected to him. That people became his chariot or four-horse chariot, and [Col. 0255D] he chose to be the leader and driver of the chariot upon which he sat. To him Moses says: “You were a leader in your mercy to the people whom you redeemed” (Exod. XV). And Habakkuk: “You who ascend upon your horses, and your chariot is salvation” (Hab. III).

“I made this cavalry mine,” he says, “as in Pharaoh’s chariots—that is, above all Pharaoh’s chariots I consigned it to my service when I brought it out of Egypt and freed it from the hands of its pursuers. So, by a profound mystery, I bound you to a wonderful ministry, when I blessed you, chosen Mother and Bride among women—that is, above all women. All the impulses, all the assaults suggested by the flesh or accumulated by the enfeebled mind, all the crowds of vices which Egypt, ruinously corrupted, sends forth and brings in, I drowned and extinguished beneath the flood of crushing water; I washed away your stains by the benefit of cleansing grace.

[Col. 0256A] But when the enemies had been extinguished, and you had been more freely assigned to my service, subjected with willing neck to my light and pleasant yoke, I—a mighty horseman, a skilled charioteer—lead you through the midst of the sea. With the waves removed to either side, I bring you through to the solid land of the living. On the right and left stands the threatening height of waters, held fixed like a wall by an invisible power. They stand astonished and marvel that, in a new and unheard-of manner, they are held in place, that a way is given to the chariot, and that the unstable waves are not feared.

So, moving and turning amid the midst of sinners—on this side the foolishness of the Gentiles, on that observing the scandals of the Jews (I Cor. I)—you contract from their wickedness neither fault nor sin. You are not broken by reproaches; you do not abandon the path shown beforehand. Not only does the mass of threatening waves fail to press down or overwhelm your head, but not even a passing stream stains the feet as you walk. Rather, with dry foot, pure step, and clean life, you pass along the way of this world, assailed by no touch of vices.

How, then, after receiving so great a gift, could you not be beloved? Your conduct in a world so unclean is so modest; you have become the guardian of my mind, the confidante of my spiritual secret, a true mother, unknowing of the marriage-bed. That in conceiving she knew no marital bed—and indeed that from then onward no erotic contact 145 injured her virginal mind—the Bridegroom seems to intimate in the following words, by which he wished to commend her modesty more plainly.

## CHAPTER VI

Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove. The Virgin’s beauty is especially evident in her cheeks, [Col. 0256C] where a snowy color is found to redden slightly. Indeed, whiteness and redness seem to vie with one another, as each competes to occupy alone the surface of the cheeks. Or, if it pleases more—rather, because it does please—while whiteness pours itself by lavish gift over the whole face, redness is lightly spread over the cheeks. They smile upon one another, and a kind of friendly fellowship of colors arises: from snow-white comes rosy, and from rosy the snowy becomes more pleasing.

Thus the Virgin’s cheeks are made beautiful by a commendable color; grace adorns them, not confusedly but diffusedly. In them red color, or sanguine blush, is joined to whiteness; neither disdains the other, but each is ever sated by an eager mouth. The Virgin’s whiteness [Col. 0256D] is the purity of her flesh and virginal integrity, which no stain and no bodily corruption harms; strengthened more securely, it is not defiled by the violent assault of a ravager; guarded more diligently, it does not grow pale under the harder blowing blast. The blush, fittingly joined to the snowy color, is the fervor or warmth in which the inward mind rejoices to burn. Since, as though in a furnace, it can scarcely contain itself within, it appears outwardly in works as though in the cheeks.

For however greatly the Virgin burns inwardly with spiritual love, she cannot fully express it outwardly in bodily action; but from the abundance grasped by inward conscience, a kind of red spark shows itself outwardly in the face. I think that the Virgin’s cheeks are declared beautiful by this blush and whiteness. Her lover [Col. 0257A] delights to behold their beauty; and though, as said above, he wishes the Virgin not to know it for humility’s sake, he himself is not envious but loves to bestow fitting praises upon her.

Nor should it be thought that he inflicts any injury on her beauty when, in praising her, he mentions the turtledove. For although the turtledove is believed to possess no merit or holiness, it nevertheless presents a type of chastity and a pattern of modest continence. Having obtained one mate, it knows no other thereafter; preserving faith to that one alone, it is ashamed to know another. If that mate is perhaps lost, it does not even then wish another; it grieves like a widow and refuses to sit upon a green branch.

How great its love, faith, and longing for chastity; how holy and worthy of imitation the form of modest honor which it presents! It loves uniquely, whether present or absent, the one it chose, with whom it once joined itself in fellowship under the pledge of faith. [Col. 0257B] To what turtledove could that Virgin of virgins in whom God willed to be incarnate be compared more fittingly or worthily? She was drawn with all her desire to love him alone, so that she shunned every man and was troubled even at an angel’s coming.

After the Son’s birth, likewise, no desire for a man injured the mother; but after giving birth, the Mother, the Bride, clung to the Bridegroom with indissoluble love, so that thereafter no fleshly impulse brought harm to her chaste spirit and she felt no more enticement of another love. Clinging to heaven alone, she did not know the frail pavement of earth; she loved in her Son, as in her Bridegroom, the sacrament of the flesh.

[Col. 0257C] With firm faith she loves to cling to the Bridegroom and to present herself as a chaste virgin to him, her one husband. She rejoices for a time in his bodily presence and is proclaimed blessed through spiritual love and communion. “Blessed are you who believed,” says Elizabeth (Luke I). But when he seemed to be lost—namely, when, having died and risen, he put aside human fellowship and was now returning whence he had come, that is, to the Father’s right hand—she, shunning public life, persevered like a mourning turtledove, with chaste heart and modest face, as a widow.

And because she no longer possessed the Bridegroom whose presence had been flourishing and delightful, she kept faith with the absent one and now sat only upon dry wood. No other Bridegroom possessed equal privilege over her, although perhaps another, like a son, stood by her through the grace of service. Therefore, I think, when Christ upon the cross commended his Virgin Mother to John who stood by and carefully entrusted the disciple to her service, he significantly did not say, “Woman, behold your Bridegroom,” nor to the disciple, “Behold your Bride”; but he said, [Col. 0257D] “Woman, behold your son”; and to the disciple, “Behold your mother” (John XIX).

For in many sons a mother’s fruitfulness is commended without injury to conjugal faith, whereas among many bridegrooms chastity is accused of incontinence. Therefore, so that the Virgin might be preserved for one husband even in his absence, another bridegroom did not stand beside her in the present, but another son did. Finally, another John—the greatest of those born of women, as he plainly indicates to all—understood this mystery. Although he could be believed to be Christ, who was the Virgin’s own Bridegroom, John nevertheless explicitly declares that he is not Christ and that he is not the Bridegroom.

“You yourselves,” he says, “bear me witness that I said, I am not the Christ. He who has the Bride is the Bridegroom; but the friend of the Bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the Bridegroom’s voice” (John III). [Col. 0258A] You see that John, carefully 146 measuring himself with a worthy eye of consideration, while others lie about him, wisely chooses not to lie about himself. Knowing his own limits, he declares himself not the Bridegroom but the friend, lest, by usurping falsehood, he make himself an enemy instead.

Therefore the Virgin has no Bridegroom but Christ, who celebrated wonderful and incomparable nuptials in her womb and made her fruitful not by male intercourse but by the divine Spirit. By his presence that ever-Virgin continually flourishes, and the loving virgin rejoices in his greenness. [Col. 0258B] For as long as the Bridegroom is with her, she cannot fail to rejoice in him, in whom she sees that her flesh has no stain of flesh. In the chamber of her womb he became one flesh with her—an union indeed containing no fault, but suited to the salvation of all.

Because such a spiritual communion felt nothing contrary in its union, the birth plainly introduced no fault in the conception; and Christ, once born, unlike others and not by nature a child of wrath, lived in pure flesh, destined to die not by necessary impulse but voluntarily. Finally, when about to die, he said: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke XXIII).

The Bridegroom calls himself the green wood: his root is not bitten by the little worm in hidden conception; his trunk—that is, his life—is not held by even the slightest decay; the spreading of his words [Col. 0258C], like branches, does not wither under a harmful blast. In short, the whole timber flourishes with innate vigor. To whom does what Paul says better apply: “If the root is holy, so also are the branches” (Rom. XIII)?

Any other human being, however, is rightly called dry wood: his conception is not sufficiently cleansed, and his life is assailed by vices. He does not sprout of himself or through himself, nor is he fruitful with righteous growth, unless the Bridegroom, bestowing the dew of divine grace, pours it down upon him from above. Therefore, while the Bridegroom is with her, the Virgin delights in green wood; when he is absent, she judges every wood dry. She finds no other on which the turtledove’s foot may rest even briefly that is not dried out by the touch of either original or actual sins.

[Col. 0258D] Therefore, showing that she grieves at the Bridegroom’s absence, since she neither has the one whom she loves nor wishes to have another in a similar place, she sits upon dry wood and, mourning, displays herself as a widow; by both her posture and her lament she represents the figure of the turtledove. Nor should it be thought that her beauty is thereby deprived of its grace because the sorrow of widowhood compels her to sit and mourn. For as the Bride’s face fittingly brightens in the Bridegroom’s presence, so it is not foreign to grace if it wastes away in his absence.

Thus he rightly commended the Virgin’s beautiful cheeks as like those of a turtledove: the Virgin who kept due faith toward him both when present and when absent; who, knowing him to be the sole man endowed with united divinity, gave herself wholly and devotedly to him in modest chastity. To her the Bridegroom adds:

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0259A]

“Your neck is like necklaces.” In praising the Virgin, the Bridegroom employs unheard-of comparisons, which at first appearance do not seem sufficiently apt to express the likeness: for neither cheeks with a turtledove nor a neck with a necklace seems to agree, unless the diligent reader strives to discover the hidden correspondence. A chain is fastened around the neck, so that whoever is bound may be held, drawn now this way, now that way, elsewhere according to the will of the one holding him; and if the one who draws him away is malevolent, the person dragged off is miserably enslaved and, having lost freedom, becomes subject to the rule of the stronger.

By this the merciful Lord once meant a certain Virgin, pressed down and oppressed, who, deceived and enticed, did not at first reject fraudulent flatteries; but afterwards, [Col. 0259B] offering her neck to chains, she carelessly allowed herself to be led into disgrace, and, forgetting her inborn freedom, turned herself toward harmful slavery. Seeing and pitying her, the Lord recalls her to what she had lost, warns her not to permit herself any longer to be held by another chain, and bids her—who, by the loosened enclosure of modesty, allowed the corrupter to enter—to hear a chaste and saving counsellor, that she may be loosed from his bond. “Loose,” he says, “the chains from your neck, captive daughter of Zion” (Isa. 52).

“You,” he says, “who were once worthily called the daughter of Zion, when, seeing God with the mind, you seemed in return to be seen by him with favour: from your neck, where neither precious stone nor gleaming gold nor necklace now shines—but which a corrupted mind, the heat of the flesh, youthful desire, have disfigured—loose, I beseech you, the chains, so that what has been prostituted to forbidden shamefulness and lies defiled [Col. 0259C] may be wiped clean by a strong hand and, being set free, restored to honour.”

The neck of this Virgin whom we have before us was not defiled by that stain; it was not hardened by a stiff neck or an untamed heart. Rather, the Bridegroom rubbed it clean with gentle speech and a soft hand; and, once cleansed and smoothed, he laid upon it a light burden and a sweet yoke. Of this you have also received the command: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11).

The Virgin’s neck, then, is her gentle humility, the meekness accustomed to the laws of humble obedience. The Bridegroom himself willed to offer himself as its pattern or example when, obedient to the Father, God willed to appear as man in a virgin’s womb. The Virgin understood his obedience to be most worthy and imitable; loving this form, [Col. 0259D] she did not raise her neck proudly, but, hearing by obedient hearing, bore a yoke—not that which Adam made heavy upon his children, but that which is light and sweet, and more graciously adorned the neck that bore it.

For just as, according to the pagan poet, that which injures its bearer is not an honour but a burden, so conversely that which adorns is not a burden but an honour. And indeed Christ’s yoke does not burden one who loves it, but honours him; it does not dishonour the neck of the obedient, but adorns it. How great an ornament of mind do you think shines forth in the Virgin’s words; how many necklaces, not chaff-bundles, hang from her neck! At the angel’s word, by which she was forewarned that she would bear God, she does not declare herself noble by royal descent, but confesses herself a humble handmaid. Nor was obedience to divine commands a new and sudden thing for her, [Col. 0260A] since for very many preceding days she had been accustomed to serve God; so much so that she vowed that she would remain a virgin, though she had neither a command for this in the Scriptures nor a precedent among those who had gone before.

Taught only by the Spirit, who graciously presided within her, she resolved to preserve her chastity inviolate. She deserved not to be disappointed in her hope and desire; indeed—and what is more extraordinary and wonderful—to be made fruitful while that purpose remained. By a new mode she remained both virgin and fruitful, whereas before and after, no woman who was fruitful remained a virgin, nor did she who remained a virgin become fruitful. Yet regarding so great a prerogative she was unwilling to say or think anything lofty or disordered, nor to differ from him whom she knew as a Master meek and humble of heart.

Thus no human being bore the light burden and sweet yoke in such a manner, nor did anyone else conform himself so fully to the obedient Bridegroom, as she who supplied him with the garment of her flesh. Her obedient neck seems an ornament to those who consider it worthily. Finally, she is found to be so subject to Christ the head that there is no doubt that she stands above the rest of the body. She seems to hold a middle place between head and body; nor can the sons of the Bridegroom reach the Bridegroom except through the mediation of the Mother. With the Bride present for us, it is good to cling to her; in her absence the members cannot adhere to the head. For us, placed far below, the Son of God descends through her; and our weakness cannot ascend to him except through her.

She first, she more blessedly receives the great gift by which many and diverse persons are made as one; by which the two [Col. 0260C] walls are united in one faith and one baptism and, converging upon Christ, are personally joined to him. Finally, by her intervening mediation she commends us to Bridegroom and Son; she invites us to pray and reminds him to attend. Mother and handmaid of the Bridegroom, sovereign lady of us all, she joins those whom Eve, the harmful divider, had separated; and, powerful and effective mediatrix, she keeps them joined.

For, seeing that we were dry and had no wine at the wedding, and knowing that without wine the wedding could not be sufficiently pleasing, she compassionately pities those about to perish from thirst, hastens anxiously to forestall the need, and confidently approaches her Son concerning the lack of wine. “The mother of Jesus says to him,” it is written, “They have no wine” (John 2). And, observing that the humble intervention of her devout prayer was not made void but brought benefit to us—indeed, to all reclining at table—she says to the servants: [Col. 0260D] “Whatever he tells you, do” (ibid.).

When they incline their ears to the command according to the Virgin’s word, the jars are filled with water and purified wine is returned. By a miracle worthy of the deed, our foolishness is changed into savour, torpid cold into fire, and neglectful contempt into love. A good neck, a good intervention, finally a good mediatrix: she joins those whom Eve, the harmful separator, had divided; she invites her Son to generosity and us to obedience, and brings it about that neither we fail to render service nor he to bestow favour.

Nor is it without reason that the Bridegroom praises this same neck as “necklaces,” which bear the insignia of matronly wealth and honourable chastity. Fashioned from gold and precious stones by skilled artistry, with surpassing beauty, they adorn the neck, cover the breast, and fasten the double edge of the garment. You know that gold commonly signifies understanding and wisdom, while stones signify virtues and works; and the craftsman sets stones in gold and arranges them carefully when he acts strongly and orders his deeds wisely.

The Bridegroom therefore fittingly distinguished the Virgin’s neck by the comparison with necklaces, because her humble meekness—by which the Virgin bore the yoke the more sweetly the longer she obeyed—and her prerogative of merit—by which, nearer to the head, she surpassed the other members of the body and effectively interceded with the Bridegroom as mediatrix for his sons—shine with the gold of wisdom, are made firm by the stones of works, and are adorned by the hand of the craftsman in a worthy union of virtues. For who bore the sweet yoke more strongly and wisely in love, who loved [Col. 0261B] more ardently, who obeyed more graciously him who sweetly orders all things, than the Virgin in whom the Word coeternal with the Father, the Wisdom of God, willed to be clothed in flesh so that he who remained what he was deigned to be found in outward form as a man? (Phil. 2).

Strengthened by the gift of this sacrament, the Virgin’s prerogative, like a golden necklace, fastened the upper edge of the garment. It not only bestows beauty on the Virgin but also protection, so that within the bosom of the flesh she may not feel a deceitful robber. For as she repelled every harmful thing from her mind, so also from her flesh; indeed, the shameless robber did not even knock at the chamber of her repose, seeing with envy that she was wonderfully fortified by grace from above, so that no malevolent person could find entrance anywhere.

Perhaps for this reason the Bridegroom called them not a necklace but “necklaces,” indicating a multiple, or at least double, prerogative of grace: namely, that the Virgin’s spirit grows faint in tender love for her salvation, and that her flesh, now subdued, desires nothing against the spirit. In Paul, as he says (Rom. 7), two laws struggle against one another, so that neither his spirit nor his flesh fully accomplishes what they will. Since his mind serves the law of God, he is believed already to possess one necklace; but since his flesh serves the law of sin, he has not yet prevailed in gaining the other.

Therefore, as Paul is more unhappy, still drawn in opposite directions—his spirit desiring the things above, his unruly flesh the contrary—so the Virgin is more blessed, to whom the double necklace has already been given: her spirit clings to God and her flesh does not struggle against the spirit. Blessed, I say, is she who, guarded by necklaces, does not admit the shameless robber; who keeps the enemy far from the doors of virginal chastity; who does not even allow the unruly dogs, the vices of the flesh, to bark at the door, from which her loving Bridegroom willed to keep her chamber serene.

Nevertheless, he did not so entirely banish every other assault from that same chamber, nor deny any entrance at all when they attacked fiercely. In this, although the cruel malice of the assailant deserves blame, the humility of the one enduring it does not equally incur fault. Therefore the Bridegroom says:

## CHAPTER VIII

“We will make for you golden little fishes, patterned with silver.”

A *muraenula* is a fish which, nourished in the waters, endures being struck and driven repeatedly by their surging flood, yet rejoices that the water’s force does not drive it to death. Shaken by a storm, it does not fear being swallowed in the deep; putting, as they say, its tail in its mouth, it folds itself into a circle. Caught by a fisherman’s skill, it enriches the tables of diners and invites us to desire it by its pleasing flavour.

Perhaps the Bridegroom seems to promise the Virgin such a fish, were it not made clearer by the very promise that this literal interpretation is altogether excluded: for he calls the same fish golden or silver. Finally, he does not say, “We shall give you,” which could be understood of food, but “We shall make for you,” which is understood of possession. A fisherman indeed gives little fishes but does not make them; the Bridegroom, however, not only gives his gifts but makes them. For the gifts are his, who as their author makes them precious.

In this unstable but surging condition of life, in this exceedingly dreadful sea, made shipwrecking by loss of faith, the Virgin feels herself assailed by many troubles and tribulations, but she is not weighed down unto collapse and impatience. For the Bridegroom works in her a certain strength like that of fishes, by which, standing amid the waters, she is not weakened by the manifold flood. Invoking him for whose love she burns and by whose unquenchable heat she is held, she does not fear the deluge nor is swallowed by the deeper waters. “Save me, O God,” she says, “for the waters have come in unto my soul” (Ps. 68). And fittingly thereafter: “Let not the deep swallow me” (ibid.).

The restless depth of the waves and the shifting multitude of tribulations are not enough to make one wonder that they hasten to gather against the Virgin as though in battle array; yet by no assault or onset can they break her resistance as she remains uninjured among the waves like a fish. They drive her, but do not expel her; shake her, but do not uproot her; disturb her, but do not cast her from her state of solid firmness. They stand astonished, beholding a Virgin of such steadfastness. Just as new grace, incomparable beauty, and unheard-of prosperity do not exalt her, so harsh tribulation, the persecution of the wicked, and the fluid mass of waters do not soften her.

Remaining in the flesh, she was not fleshly in spirit but golden—that is, rich with the gold and treasure of spiritual wisdom. She retained in herself nothing soft, nothing fluid, nothing of ignorant dullness; but was solid and bright, weighty in understanding, endowed with a treasury of outstanding strength. For in the furnace of tribulations she was found not like chaff, hay, or stubble, forestalled by the smell of fire, but like gold of the first rank (1 Cor. 3). And as the flood of waters in the depth of the sea did not sink the prudent Virgin, so the furnace of fire did not stain her with soot but cleansed her.

The greatness of tribulations found in her no small flaw, no obstacle to which any harmful or dishonourable shame might cling. Though waves and fires passed over and through her in rivalry, the waves found her indeed a *muraenula*, and the fire found her golden.

But when the Bridegroom affirmed that he would make not one *muraenula* but “little fishes,” he signified, I think, not one virtue but many, which the good craftsman formed by the skilled hand of his power, joined together by wondrous workmanship, and prepared for the Virgin’s adornment and protection. Further, a *muraenula*, bringing its tail to its mouth, appears to make from itself a circle or ring when the end is turned back to the beginning from which the good work of virtue began: when the Virgin’s patience, for the sake of him whom she loves, chooses to bear every burden, and no adversity can remove her from her purpose.

Another *muraenula* may be called her obedience, by which, from the time she was greeted by the angel, she is found so devoted to heavenly commands that, in accordance with Gabriel’s word and through the Spirit’s working, faithfully united to the one Bridegroom and rejecting every other, she sought to please him alone who sees in secret. And who can say or conceive anything concerning that *muraenula* which may seem adequately suited to its praises? [Col. 0263B] With no human speech intervening, an angel speaks to her; he declares her blessed among women, and she calls herself a handmaid; he promises that she, though knowing no man, shall become the mother of the Lord now present (Luke 1); she gives faith, yet responds humbly; she bears the new man who in the beginning was God with God (John 1), and remains lowly and humble, returning nothing lofty or proud.

There is also a greater and more excellent *muraenula*: that called love or charity, which, seated upon a throne, rules the others with a kind of royal sceptre; which, surpassing faith and hope in dignity and invested with noble power, advances more effectively and rejoices more securely when introduced into the very chamber of the Bridegroom.

From little fishes of this kind a cord or chain is woven, as though from certain spots: firmer indeed than gold and free from the defilement of dust; fashioned by the learned hand of the goldsmith in the furnace of tribulation, not reduced by waters to softness or by smoky fire to ash. Does it not seem to you that Paul joined together diverse *muraenulae*, and wove them, joined together, into one cord or little chain? For him the pressure of tribulation became furnace and anvil, from which by wonderful workmanship there issued the golden beauty of little fishes: “Knowing,” he says, “that tribulation works patience; and patience, tested character; and tested character, hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the charity of God has been poured forth in our hearts” (Rom. 5).

You see, therefore, that from the furnace and anvil of tribulation the metalwork of patience is produced, forming the root and immovable foundation of the cord or chain. Upon it rests the height of the virtues which follow, and the beauty of charity, surpassing all in gold, brings them to completion. This is unfeigned charity and a union of virtues worthily commended, which the pleasing mixture of silver patterns and distinguishes. Thus the more laboriously interwoven cord of little fishes is found to have silver patterning inserted into it.

Vermilion, which is a red colour, or the little worm (*vermiculus*) which is of the same colour as vermilion, signifies Christ’s Passion, which must be remembered in everything we do, so that, when we think that we serve, obey, and love him, we may diligently recall what he undeservedly suffered for us. For his garment, Isaiah testifies, was reddened for us (Isa. 63), and his clothing was soiled like that of one treading the winepress. In its type, you know, an ancient command was promulgated that a red heifer should be sacrificed for sins (Num. 19).

The red heifer is he who says in the Psalm: “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21). Whoever desires more perfectly to obtain the little fishes promised to the Virgin ought more diligently to remember this worm and outcast, this reproach. For a golden union of virtues does not furnish sufficient adornment unless the red little worm and silver are interwoven.

Finally, the little worm is twisted into a manifold sphere and circle, to signify in it the worthy perfection of the memory already mentioned. Though cut and divided into two separated parts, it still lives, signifying him who, struck upon the wood of the cross, slept briefly, but immediately awoke: “He dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6).

In faith, love, and loving memory of him the Virgin lived rightly, even when the persecutor harshly fixed the sword not so much in his body as in her soul. And when the Son’s death reached the tender heart of his Mother, death nevertheless did not find her faith and love. Was not he dead who escaped death by timid denial (Mark 14)? And he who, shaken by fear, fled naked after leaving his linen cloth? And those who, leaving him, all hastened into flight and did not hold fast either the significance of the little worm or that of the silver?

For bright and resonant silver is said to represent speech, whose purity, tested in furnace and fire, does not fear to give voice; which has nothing leaden or tin-like, is not darkened by the fire, but passes through unharmed and emerges brighter and more resonant. You have that “the word of the Lord is a pure word, silver tested by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11). And through Isaiah: “If you pass through the fire,” he says, “you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not harm you” (Isa. 43).

Peter’s speech is found not resonant in the fire but foul like lead (Mark 14); John’s speech likewise is not found sufficiently bright, since, when reproaches were directed against him, the former did not answer a good and truthful word, while the latter, taking flight, hid himself in silence. They had read but neglected what is written: “Do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth” (Ps. 118); and again: “I shall answer those who reproach me with a word” (ibid.).

But the Virgin, diligently embracing Christ’s Passion in the arms of faith, does not negligently suppress love for him in silence. Rather, what she believes and loves she openly proclaims when the time requires, as one who truly loves confidently utters the word of faith. She is therefore worthily granted the special adornment of the little fishes, patterned and distinguished with approved silver, because the Bridegroom places amid her perfect virtues the loving remembrance of his Passion—a remembrance which the Virgin does not neglect either to bear out in her conduct or to set forth in speech.

The Bridegroom says that he will make, rather than has made, this adornment for the Virgin, showing that in this life the gift is not yet present to her but future. While the Virgin labours, toils, and strives bravely in the contest, she is given not the completed attainment of the way, not the joy of reception, but the promise of the crown. For here, as on an anvil, the spot is beaten out; the promised perfection is produced, and, as grace prospers, bent back so as to become complete, so that [Col. 0265A] the tail may adhere to the head, the end be conformed to the beginning, and this completing conformity be secured with a firm nail.

In its type Moses commands that the head and tail of the animal be offered, indicating that spiritual conduct must turn the end back to the beginning, so that the spot may be completed, a ring made, the *muraenula* rounded, and a work well begun brought to completion by a like end. Since the Virgin does not yet fully attain this while she lives here, but awaits it, the Bridegroom does not cast fear or distrust upon one who waits. Rather, he strengthens her expectant spirit by hope, cherishes her by his promise, and gives assurance, declaring that he will do whatever pertains to her perfection.

Nor should it disturb us that he says not, “I will make golden little fishes for you,” but “We will make.” Although the Son alone appears here to speak or promise, he does not alone bring about the effect of the promised gift. Rather, it is certain that the Father works with the Son, and equally the Holy Spirit, who are certainly separated from one another neither in nature nor in operation. “My Father works,” he says, “and I work” (John 5). And again: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (ibid.); and without doubt the Holy Spirit also. Of these, the Son says in the Gospel: “We will come and make our dwelling with him” (John 14). Speaking to the virgin Bride, he likewise says: “We will make for you golden little fishes, patterned with silver.” And she:

## CHAPTER IX

“When the King was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.”

After uttering the praises by which the Bridegroom commended the Virgin’s cheeks and neck, and after making the promise of little fishes by which he strengthened her maidenly heart, he now seems, as it were, to yield and withdraw from the Virgin’s sight; yet, not withdrawing from her speech or love, he is held in grateful remembrance. For the Virgin, turning to the maidens who dwell with her and attentively await their mutual words, delights to speak of the Bridegroom, to commend his excellence, and to proclaim what his surpassing goodwill has bestowed upon her.

“When the King,” she says, “was at his table.” My Bridegroom, she says, is neither base-born nor common nor of inferior and feeble power, but the Son of the supreme King, and himself a King of no lesser excellence. From the paternal assembly, the royal seat, the hidden place of inaccessible majesty—where angels see and unweariedly desire his face—he willed to come down to earth for the salvation of perishing souls and rested in my bridal chamber in the delightful love of marriage.

I say, this King gladly reclined in my womb, a reclining most pleasing to him who reclined; and though he found no repose pleasing to himself in foxes’ dens or birds’ nests, he complained of finding nothing in me that displeased his resting. Reclining there, he wonderfully filled me with his grace: preserving the Virgin, he abolished the Virgin’s barrenness; he kindled me wholly as a burnt offering by his effective fire; and the whole house was filled not by the smell of flesh but by the most sweet fragrance of ointments.

For as in this his reclining that Majesty more sweetly laid down his head, and as God the Son of God bowed himself in my womb in order to assume flesh, my strength received no small increase, a more abundant advance of grace; and I became like nard, fragrant within through its strength and giving forth a fitting fragrance without.

Nard, literally, is a low-growing herb, hot in nature, rich in oily juice, dense with leaves, strong in fragrance, and suitable for preparing perfumes. By it the virtue of the Virgin Mother is not unfittingly figured: before the Bridegroom’s coming she seemed small and known to God alone, but in his presence she spread far and wide the sweetness of fragrance, pouring out to others the benefit of fuller knowledge.

While the Bridegroom reclined in the Virgin’s womb, righteous Joseph marvelled at the unknown mystery; but when the angel revealed it, he perceived the fragrance of the sacrament’s magnificence (Matt. 1), understanding that the Virgin had not been corrupted, nor conceived by another womb, but had received a marvellous conception through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Elizabeth likewise appears to have perceived this fragrance with prophetic sense when the already pregnant Virgin is read to have gone up into the hill country; at the greeting of her voice, the infant John leapt in the womb (Luke 1), and the entire mountain dwelling resounded in great joy as though with a ringing echo. Elizabeth perceived it, and so did the child in her womb: they perceived the reclining of the incarnate Word and smelled the sweet fragrance of this precious nard. Priestess with voice and infant with movement applaud the Virgin as she comes, exalt the one who greets them, and render fitting service to her who surpasses them: “Whence is this to me,” says the priestess, “that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (ibid.). And she adds concerning the Son: “For behold, when the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leapt for joy in my womb” (ibid.).

Rejoicing with those who rejoice, the pregnant Virgin nevertheless remains humble like nard; fuller in grace and richer in more abundant merit, the young woman serves the older woman with dutiful attentiveness. For she chose to stay with the priest for three months, deeming it fitting during that time to live with the elderly matron, care for her, bring assistance, sit more anxiously beside her in childbirth, sympathize with her pains, soothe her groans, and offer welcome consolation.

Nor did the Virgin merely offer the consolation of an attendant to the woman in childbirth; rather, as some think, she performed the office of midwife. This was not because the inexperienced Virgin had been accustomed to such service, but in order meekly to show her ready affection toward the mother; and so that, first holding and beholding the newborn infant, she might make better the one whom she knew to be the prophet of the Most High and the forerunner of the Christ who was to be born (ibid.).

Elizabeth sees the Virgin’s humility and, considering it, marvels. By the Spirit of prophecy she perceives the humble excellence of this nard: she sees that wonderful bush, to be proclaimed in every age, burning unharmed (Exod. 3); she sees nard, naturally hot—indeed fervent in spirit—not consumed. She perceives that the humble nard has richer juice; that in the Virgin’s womb a purer fountain of mercy springs forth. She sees the humble nard dense with leaves; the Virgin abounding in words of modesty and saving teaching.

Although the Virgin’s nard does not yet show the fuller effect of all these things, nevertheless it gradually gives fragrance to some whose nostrils are sound, so that even with limited understanding they may perceive how great is the virtue in the Virgin, how great the grace of that virtue, and how great in aromatic nard is the hope of health for the sick. Whoever feels sickness or weakness in himself, if with eager perception and due love he receives this fragrance, will not grieve that he is burdened or falling into weakness, but will rather rejoice that he is soothed and passing onward to advancement.

Indeed, the fragrance of the nard itself is found to receive increase, as in the course of time the Virgin imparts a fuller knowledge of herself. After the birth of the Son, who advanced in wisdom [Col. 0267B] and age, she is known to be his mother while the Virgin’s chastity remains uncorrupted (Luke 2). For while the Word in flesh, God in man, lived among men, and was called by many merely a man, either through ignorance or malice, yet many recognized him by true judgment as God and man, and believed that his Mother was a Virgin after birth as before birth.

Therefore, “when the King was at his table”—that is, when God, great in man, presented himself as humble and was hidden from unbelievers, concealed from outsiders, appearing only to his own chamberlains—“my nard gave forth its fragrance”: that is, my light beneath the bushel, my virtue in obscurity, did not remain hidden, but became known to Peter and the others who possessed the true faith. Thus, when he asked, “Whom do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16), and again, “But whom do you say that I am?” (ibid.), Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid.).

Questioning concerning himself, he called himself my Son of Man. Peter, having drawn in the fragrance of the nard, affirmed that he was the Son of the living God, understanding that Christ, my Virgin’s Son, is such that he is rightly proclaimed Son not of a man, but of God. The gentiles do not perceive this fragrance with sound perception, nor do the Jews, who, not knowing me to be a Virgin, deny that he is the Son of God. Deriding the Mother—whose Father was altogether absent from the union—they do not weigh the inexpressible generation of both the begetting and the begotten.

Accordingly, with hardened nostrils, blind sight, deaf hearing, and impious hands, they afflict me; failing to perceive the fragrance, they crucify Christ as a mere man. The centurion rightly contradicts their unsound judgment, when, seeing the earthquake, he says that Christ is God’s Son: “Truly,” he says, “this was the Son of God” (Matt. 27).

But my nard gave a far greater fragrance, and its virtue shone forth, when the King reclined upon the royal throne and seat of rest. There, removed from earthly things, he found a more pleasing place and, far from the envious, endured neither injury nor labour. For while he lived in this world and was placed in a life subject to death, in which he seemed as though abandoned by divine protection, he endured so many and such great things, walking through the straits of a harder path, that this dwelling is rightly judged to be one not of rest but of labour. In it he says: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27). And of it: “I have laboured in bearing” (Isa. 1). And Jeremiah: “Lord,” he says, “you have given them a shield of the heart—your labour” (Lam. 3).

But when, dying, he had completed the laborious journey by conquering death, and, risen immortal, ascended into heaven whence he had come, he sat down at the right hand of Majesty on high, having become so much better than the angels as he inherited a name more excellent than theirs (Heb. 1). When this King possessed his due peace upon that royal seat or throne, reclining in the paternal assembly and rejoicing in coeternal glory, the Virgin’s nard was found to give a more abundant and fruitful fragrance, and virginal fruitfulness to shine more pleasingly in proportion as it shone more richly.

For when the Spirit was sent and descended in tongues of fire, and suddenly a mighty sound came from heaven upon the disciples (Acts 2), the blindness of ignorance and the distress of fear were driven far from them; and they spoke as prudently as confidently the things they knew about Christ. The Virgin had long before, in many successive accounts, explained to them the Bridegroom’s kiss or the nuptial covenant, and, by no bodily act, his bodily conception and birth. She had explained that the one assuming and the one assumed had been personally united: the former not diminished in the assumed nature, the latter not consumed by the glory of the one assuming; that God was true man; that Christ advanced in wisdom and age; and that he finally both laid down and resumed his own soul by free power.

These and very many more things—which are not easy to recount in the present place, especially because they are so many that they could scarcely be contained in a book—the Virgin had repeatedly studied to explain over many years to many whom the same Bridegroom had willed to attach to himself more intimately. Because, when the Spirit was sent from heaven, all these things were more fully understood, they were more gladly accepted with fuller understanding; and things which, while the Bridegroom laboured and was mortal, had pleased less when veiled, pleased more when uncovered while he, immortal, reclined in rest.

The Virgin’s nard, therefore, gives its own—that is, a fragrance suited to them—to the faithful when her virtue and holiness exhibit a fuller knowledge of themselves; when, as the Bridegroom reclines at the right hand of the divine Majesty, the knowledge of the truth already spoken of becomes more fully known and more sweetly delightful.

I wonder whether the woman who wished to offer Christ, as he reclined, a pound of precious spikenard ointment appears to have signified this very thing (John 12). With due reverence she poured it over his feet, and with more abundant grace over his head; and that blessed house of Simon was wholly filled with the fragrance. Jesus himself bears witness concerning this: “She has performed a good work upon me” (Matt. 21). Truly it was a good work, and one can scarcely find a better: while Jesus reclined among his guests, he rejoiced that his feet and head were anointed with spikenard—his humanity not oppressed by the silence of ignorance, and the height of his divinity raised by the proclamation of fuller knowledge.

Our Virgin strove to commend this not so much by words as by conduct, to proclaim it commendable as much by living as by speaking, lest she seem like a talkative soldier discoursing about battle and victory though, being delicate, he had been unwilling to endure the burdens of camp or the engagements of such warfare. Therefore she adds:

## CHAPTER X
A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; he shall dwell between my breasts. Myrrh is a bitter spice which, according to physicians, if one carefully anoints dead bodies with it, gives corpses so effective a remedy by its bitterness that for a long course of days they suffer neither the corruption of worms nor decay. Thus the Virgin’s Spouse is rightly figured by the name of myrrh, whose bitter bundle does not burden her conscience; rather, what another who does not love judges heavy and most bitter is judged by her, eager for salvation, to be as sweet as it is salutary.

The bitterness of myrrh is the word or command of the Spouse. Some are found to abhor even its first taste; its initial appearance and its hearing so displease them that, hardened in heart, they not only refuse to consent, but hasten to recoil far from it as from something harmful and opposed to them. You know that when Christ in the Gospel spoke to a certain young man concerning perfection and urged him to despise riches and embrace voluntary poverty, he rejected the offered taste as sorrowful and bitter. He did not retain what he heard, proclaiming himself avaricious more by deed than word: “When the young man heard the word,” it says, “he went away sorrowful, for he had many possessions” (Matt. XIX). Elsewhere Jesus said: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.” “Many of his disciples,” it says, hearing this, said: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” “From that time many of his disciples,” it says, “[Col. 0269C] went back and no longer walked with him” (John VI).

You see that these people give no faith to what they hear and cannot endure the hard word as the bitterness of myrrh. They find no useful consent with such an adversary, but in a ruined frame of mind abhor that saving command: “Be reconciled,” he says, “with your adversary while you are on the way with him” (Matt. V). But the Virgin now before us does not reject such a command. She willingly endures the bitterness of myrrh; and what those whose palate is ill pampered reckon too sharp, she, with sounder judgment and a concordant spirit, loves to find more pleasing. Therefore she called it not a *fascis*, a burden, but a *fasciculus*, a little bundle of this same myrrh, thereby signifying, so to speak, the sweet bitterness [Col. 0269D] of the divine command. It does not press upon the neck or shoulders, nor weigh down the one who bears it; rather, love is increased in it, and love makes light the yoke imposed by the beloved.

For whatever she judges necessary to herself in this life, she rejoices to accomplish or carry out, not like Simon under compulsory service, but for love of the Spouse. By this little bundle she preserves her flesh and strives to establish herself in an abiding state, while she seeks to commend wholly to her Beloved that which she bears in the flesh. Certainly our miserable toil, or miserable action, decays whenever Christ’s love grows cold within us. And even if the spirit, eager through love of him, burns warmly, myrrh is a bitter bundle for us when the flesh either becomes weak or rises insolently against the Spirit. For we cannot wholly break our own wills, nor utterly banish [Col. 0270A] the pleasures of the world or the body; unhappy as we are, we bear such a burden with much labor, while fear by turns is overcome by hope, and hope again by fear.

But the Virgin embraces her Beloved so tenderly and sweetly; her consciousness takes such delight in the sweetness of his love that whatever bitterness she is compelled to endure at present she counts light and small, through love of him whom she already tastes and will taste more fully hereafter. Therefore she says, “My beloved is to me.” Although others, she says, seem to bear a hard burden because they have not yet deserved to obtain harmony of flesh and Spirit, nevertheless my Beloved has already chosen to show himself to me as a little bundle. The struggle of the flesh having been lulled to sleep, I have been granted to cling to his continual embraces.

For the Virgin, considering him whom she loves, sees that he is King, and therefore powerful, rich, and noble. She does not care if any harsh things make an uproar without, since within she already rejoices securely in his embrace. The one whom she shortly before calls King—“while the King was at his table” (Song I)—she now loves to call Beloved, in order to show that she loves no weak, needy, or ignoble one. Suspended in his embrace with burning affection, she counts as nothing, with fitting disdain, whatever lies beneath or behind. Therefore, having said, “A little bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me,” she adds: “Between my breasts,” etc.

## CHAPTER XI

“He shall dwell between my breasts.” This little bundle is good and exceedingly desirable to one who loves; [Col. 0270C] it neither bends the back or shoulder nor produces disgust in the bearer, but dwells with welcome sweetness between her breasts. There we see what is loved not so much borne as held and clasped. It is not like him of whom it is written: “He turned his back away from burdens” (Ps. LXXX). And you have read that the shepherd carries the lost sheep, when found, back to the flock upon his shoulders (Luke XV). Concerning it he complains: “I have labored, bearing it” (Isa. I).

Yet the Virgin who bears the aforesaid bundle of myrrh does not think herself to labor, nor does she say that she bears this little bundle upon back or shoulder. Instead, by a new manner of speech, she gladly says that it dwells between her breasts, where the seat of the heart is and where love is said to rule. The Virgin’s breasts appear [Col. 0270D] to signify her twofold love, by which the Virgin loves the Spouse as God and as man: God, as Creator and Lord of the whole creation; man, as Son by the grace of a wondrous and ineffable birth. To him rightly applies what is said through the Prophet: “God of my heart, and God my portion” (Ps. LXXII).

Indeed, no one fails to know that a mother embraces her son between her breasts, a son whom, because she is a mother, she is proved by a certain law of nature to love. And the Virgin compared her own Son, by reason of love, to a little bundle; the prophetic word calls him, because of his humility, a child or little one: “A little one,” it says, “has been born to us” (Isa. IX). This little one dwells sweetly between his mother’s breasts. She embraces him strongly not by nature but by prevailing grace; and with unrelenting love she holds and does not let go, loving him here as God and there as man—indeed, as her whole Son at once—and she never ceases to love because of any impulse of bitterness. Of him she says below: “I held him, and I will not let him go” (Song III).

Nor does the mother alone embrace the Son tenderly: the Bride also embraces the Spouse; and as she rejoices, so does he in their mutual embrace. When, as was said at the beginning of the drama, he kisses her, he surely dwells more sweetly between her breasts. For in a kiss—if it is consummated with sufficient eagerness and sincerity—not only mouth is joined to mouth, but breast also, it is said, to breast. Nor is the love of kissers proved to advance to the full if the kiss given by the mouth is not confirmed by a grateful embrace. Rightly, therefore, the Virgin declares that the Spouse dwells between her breasts: [Col. 0271B] that is, the tender love of their embrace is made firm with the glue of union. And lest it be thought brief and perfunctory, after the manner of others, she is said never to grow weary of it, but the Spouse to make his dwelling in it. “He shall dwell between my breasts,” she says. Of him she adds: “A cluster,” etc.

## CHAPTER XII

“A cluster of Cyprus is my beloved to me, in the vineyards of Engaddi.” This Beloved is wonderful and greatly lovable; no understanding of mine or like mine can comprehend his excellence. Yet that it may in some manner apprehend him, I hear him called now myrrh and now a cluster—knowing, nevertheless, that he is none of these things, but is figured under these names.

A cluster is fruit which, through the progress of time, once it has attained ripeness, becomes fit to eat; afterwards, when pressed in the winepress, it strains out the liquid of wine for drinking. By this name the Virgin’s Spouse is not undeservedly called: his knowledge matures in the hearts of right believers through fitting growth; and once matured, he is eaten by the eager affection of those who love him, while by spiritual food the life of those who eat is spiritually sustained. Affirming this in the Gospel, he says: “He who eats me shall live because of me” (John VI).

Blessed is the one who desires and is able, after selling his substance, to obtain this food and prepare the eager throat of the heart for such a meal; who by its sweetness restores inward powers that had languished, and, casting away care for the flesh, diligently strengthens the Spirit. Blessed, I say, is the one in whose conscience knowledge of this cluster ripens, whose desire burns, in whose throat it is sweet, whose loving palate delights to be anointed with its welcome flavor, [Col. 0271D] and who feels its life-giving juice pass inward to the vital organs. When it has passed, the flesh withers and the spirit is made rich; the outward person grows faint, the inward is renewed; the sense of the flesh subsides, the spirit receives increase; the one becomes as though dead, while the other hastens more eagerly toward its growth.

For one is no longer content merely to eat the cluster with a hungry mouth. After vital food one desires to drink a fruitful cup; the desired eating does not seem sufficient unless it is seasoned with a sweeter, more welcome cup of wine. Therefore one presses the now-ripe cluster vigorously in the winepress of devotion and the press of love, casts out the grapes, and strains a wine more pleasantly pleasing. One who until then had eaten with some labor now drinks more sweetly and is more completely gladdened, since in love one feels nothing contrary. Thus food appears in a manner to be transformed into drink, and the cluster into wine, when someone is so sweetly intoxicated with divine love that, forgetting present things, he is held solely by longing for things to come and, knowing no sadness, seems already to enjoy the joy of his Lord.

The most blessed Virgin tasted this sweetness more fully than all others and burned much more vehemently with its wine or love, especially when, after the death of her Son—which, when she saw it, the Mother could not but grieve—his flesh was found to bloom again through the benefit of the resurrection. She who, as he died, tasted the sad bitterness of a kind of myrrh, exulted more sweetly, as though having drunk wine, when he arose. And that her joy may plainly be known to surpass that of others, the cluster of which the discourse speaks is suitably commended from its place: “My beloved is to me a cluster [Col. 0272B] of Cyprus.”

Cyprus is an island, first rather than second among the surrounding islands, as those who have seen it say. It is so fertile in excellent wine that its abundance is not merely welcome and sufficient for itself: its wine is deservedly transported thence into other regions as well. Its cluster is found fairer to behold, more pleasing to eat, and sweeter to drink when, in its ripe season, it undergoes the winepress of those who tread it. It seems to smile upon sight and taste alike, and the heart of the lover rejoices to answer its invitation. Thus the Virgin rightly chose to call her Beloved a cluster of Cyprus, since he deigned to provide her, his loving one, with such joy that, once the grief brought by his dying passion had been wiped away, she was rendered as it were drunk by the most sweet taste of his resurrection.

Although he became a cluster for many others too, so that through the grace of his resurrection they might have hope of rising in flesh and spirit, yet the Virgin declares that to her he became none but a cluster of Cyprus: for the Spouse is believed to have given her fuller and more perfect joy. The Virgin knew that her Son’s death would avail for the blotting out of vices and that his resurrection would bestow the merit of justification. While others variously doubted both, she did not doubt; the more firmly she believed, the more strongly she loved, and the more greatly she rejoiced. Worthily, then, she understood him in whom she believed and whom she loved to be in some manner comparable to a cluster of Cyprus: in her his love ripens with incomparable growth, and having tasted it more fully and sweetly, she rejoices more strongly and gladly.

That this cluster may be commended with still greater grace, mention of the vineyards of Engaddi [Col. 0272D] is not passed over. Though Cyprus seemed named sufficiently, Engaddi is added lest anything be wanting to the commendation: “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi.” He appears to say that a cluster of Cyprus is in the vineyards of Engaddi; yet the literal truth of the matter contradicts this statement, since Engaddi is known to be far distant from Cyprus, and neither custom nor necessity requires clusters to be carried from vineyards into vineyards.

If anyone undertook to carry clusters from vineyards into vineyards, prudent judges would accuse him of a certain absurdity—as though, deprived of sense, he carried wood into a forest or poured water into a sea completely full, when a thing should rather be brought where it certainly does not abound. Finally, Engaddi is said not to have vineyards, but certain little trees, known to surpass vines. If these are pierced by skilled hands at a fitting time, they are known to sweat oil, indeed balsam liquid.
