Because their owners cultivate such trees with great care, making them more ready, as it were, to produce liquid like vineyards, perhaps divine speech called them vineyards, thereby indicating that they are both subject to cultivation and rich in precious fluid.

Since, therefore, a cluster of Cyprus is not to be found in these vineyards or trees, nor can what has been said accord with the letter, spiritual understanding must be sought in this expression; as you have already received, it has the greater authority in this drama. In a tree or little tree the Virgin’s Spouse is not unsuitably figured. If he is pierced by the touch and love of worthy believers, [Col. 0273B] he sweats oil, yields the liquid of precious balsam, brings much grace to the lover, and pours out a more pleasing spirit. “Therefore,” he says, “I love those who love me” (Prov. VIII). And in the Gospel: “Someone touched me,” he says, “for I perceived power going out from me” (Luke VIII).

When this Spouse is touched by the acceptable affection of one who loves him, he pours forth sacred balsam, the power of the abundant Spirit: that which soothes diseases and by its presence drives away every injury; that which, once error and ignorance have been driven out, teaches concerning all things by an anointing. This benefit, moreover, seems indicated by the name of the place itself, if anyone unfolds or is able to investigate it more explicitly; for *Engaddi* is interpreted “fountain of the goat,” or “eye of temptation,” and this interpretation serves the mystery of so great a matter.

The goat is rejected in the Law, being sent into the wilderness by the ministers (Lev. XVI), and in the Gospel it is likewise placed at the left because of sin (Matt. XXV). For this reason sin or the sinner is not unfittingly figured by it: one who, by his own deserts, is rejected by him who loves righteousness alone. The fountain of the goat, however, is the Spirit himself, whose outpouring washes away sin, cleanses the sinner, makes the flesh of leprous Naaman cleaner than that of a child (IV Kings V), changes a goat into a lamb, giving the merit of innocent life (John IV), and becomes in the one who drinks an abundant fountain, a fountain of springing water.

The eye of temptation is also not undeservedly said to be this same Spirit. By his light and grace temptation is foreseen far in advance; teaching human beings knowledge, forming wisdom, and directing understanding, he clears away the darkness of night and leads them to the perfect day. [Col. 0273D] Therefore the cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi is the Beloved of our Virgin, because the love and joy by which her soul is moved are established in Christ himself and in his worthy Spirit: loving him in himself, she rejoices in him and not in another. To her he is a fruitful tree, healing balsam, a living fountain, a washing away of unrighteousness, the light of knowledge, and a spiritual eye. Whatever is judged necessary either for driving away evils or obtaining goods is truly proclaimed to be possessed in him and from him.

That we may not be judged wholly strangers to this benefit—although we are by no means equal to the great merit of this Virgin—we have received certain visible things in the sacrament of holy baptism as memorials of invisible realities. For we are anointed with oil as a figure of heavenly medicine: with sloth driven far away, we are prepared for active discipline, so that our spirit, anointed by the divine Spirit, may be stronger in the struggle and may escape more readily from the hand or snare of the adversary. Afterwards we are washed with the pure fountain of visible water, that we may be cleansed spiritually from the filth not so much of flesh as of soul; that we may change the harsh impulses of the goat into all gentleness; and that we may reserve within ourselves nothing leftward, nothing worthy of judgment. Thirdly, a light is kindled for us, so that our eye may not grow dark, and that when it foresees anything harmful, it may forbid or punish it; that, not ignorant of Satan’s wiles—what they feign and what they intend—it may walk honorably as in daylight [Col. 0274B] and not be overtaken by darkness.

Thus the baptizer instructs a vigorous athlete when he is newly equipped for the contest, more by signs than by speech, so that, once he has received a living understanding of these things that have been said, he may strive with all effort, through grace, to attain their effect. In all these respects the Virgin is believed equal to none: not second, but far before all others, she rejoices in the love of the Spouse. And by a special privilege that saying rightly belongs to her which, as we know, is still forbidden us through our deserving: “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus, in the vineyards of Engaddi.”

After the Virgin had spoken these things to the young women concerning her Beloved, and had set forth mystically what patience and what joy she possesses in him, he, turning as it were toward her, does not delay to answer graciously, praising and commending what he perceives and loves to be preeminent in her.

## CHAPTER XIII

“Behold, you are fair, my friend; behold, you are fair; your eyes are those of doves.” You, he says, who above all women are my friend, the enemy of every malice and every ugliness. “Behold”—that is, not merely with all the righteous in the life to come, but much more praiseworthily than all others in the present: behold, I say, you are fair, endowed with a singular beauty to which no woman before or after can be compared. For it is fitting that he who is fair in form beyond the children of men should possess one who displays a special beauty through singular grace: one whose face is not darkened by degrading and unworthy ugliness, but whom love makes like the Beloved in the sight of him by whom she is loved.

But when he has said, “Behold, you are fair, my friend,” why does he repeat: “Behold, you are fair”? What does “fair and fair” mean? Perhaps he repeated it in order that no one might doubt the aforesaid beauty, but that the subsequent assertion might confirm the prior testimony; for every word is proclaimed to stand in the mouth of two witnesses (II Cor. XIII), and the authority of the Law and the Prophets is said to hang upon two commandments (Matt. XX). Some say that he called the Virgin fair twice in order to indicate that she possessed a twofold beauty: she remained miraculously Virgin in conceiving and bearing, and in so great a prerogative truly declared herself humble. For one often finds someone either humble but corrupted, or a little proud if she happens to be uncorrupted. Rightly, therefore, she is fair whom no injury to integrity disfigured; and fair again, whom incomparable humility adorned. Thus the flower of virginity renders one who is humble in spirit more splendid; glorious in virginal flower, more beautiful in humility of spirit.

But I, without prejudging those who are known to have held this view irreproachably, think that by repetition the Spouse expressed something proper to a lover. One who loves tenderly rejoices to be loved by the one whom he loves, speaks pleasing words, and is not satisfied to say only once what he loves. Love’s force has this as its familiar and proper trait: when affection has drawn someone in with a dearer bond, it stirs that person to speak graciously of what he loves, and unless the same things are repeated, they do not seem sufficiently fruitful to him. Love urges the lover to speak more willingly and, in order to express affection, to repeat the word more frequently. Nor does such reading seem excessively repeated to a lover, even if, according to the poet, it were repeated ten times.

Thus David, when he wished emphatically to express the love he had borne toward his son and could not suppress in silence the grief of his death, walked mourning and with covered head, forgetful of royal dignity, and as he spoke of his son repeatedly said the same words: “Absalom, my son, my son Absalom” (II Kings XVIII). Likewise in the Psalm: “God, my God” (Ps. XCII). And elsewhere: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us” (Ps. LXVI). You see that for a lover it is not judged enough to say once what pleases him; rather, tenderer affection rejoices to repeat what it has said, because whatever can be spoken is still thought little by love in comparison with what the soul comprehends beyond explanation in words.

Therefore when the Spouse begins to address the Virgin with tender words and, as you have heard, chooses to call her fair for the second time, he aims not so much, by repetition, to commend her beauty—great though it is—as to disclose to his hearers the affection that binds him to her. Since a great deal of beauty shines forth in the eyes of maidens, he declares in praise of her that she has the eyes of doves. These, I think, he intends to be understood not as the carnal eyes of this head, but as the spiritual eyes of that inward person.

Doves have certain properties implanted in them by nature, which by an ineffable law of generation they pass on from predecessors to successors. In these they are reported to differ greatly from other birds, to whom not all these gifts of nature are granted. They are said to possess seven natures, or natural virtues, by which they seek useful things and are kept from harmful ones. I defer, for brevity’s sake, to another occasion perhaps, the task of naming them individually and comparing them with the virtues of holiness. Finally, the Holy Spirit was seen to appear in the form of a dove (Luke III), indicating to us that he has no small likeness to it: he himself is found distinguished by seven chief gifts, and it, as said before, by the pleasing sevenfold number of its nature.

When, then, the Spouse declares the Virgin’s eyes to be those of doves, he commends in her the seven gifts of grace: not the perishable light of the head, but the discerning virtues of the soul, which distinguish the just and unjust rather than days and nights. He rightly praises her whom he sees so conformed to his Spirit as to possess the sevenfold grace of virtues. Driving far from her the sleepiness of the flesh and feminine lethargies, he gave her spiritual wakefulness and dovelike eyes. Indeed, the Spirit himself rested more abundantly in no woman than in this Virgin, in whom he rested sevenfold; all that material doves possess figuratively by nature, he gave her in spirit, in truth rather than figure. Therefore, rejoicing and not ungrateful for the praises received from the Spouse, she too calls him fair, likewise doubling the praise; she rejoices to render a return to her praiser, and so mutual love is strengthened by reciprocal praise.

## CHAPTER XIV

“Behold, you are fair, my beloved, and beautiful.” Because your holiness has bestowed beauty upon me by cleansing my heart, I have learned from this that there is much beauty also in you. For if ugliness still held my eye uncleansed, your bright form could in no way have appeared to me. But now, adorned with spiritual eyes like those of doves, I perceive more keenly how polished your countenance is. I see you possess a form fairer than the children of men, though many see you as having neither form nor beauty.

For raven-like sight, oppressed by foul blackness, beholds you only as ugly, only as human; and, detained by error, condemns you with unworthy judgment when it says that you are John, Elijah, or one of the former ones (Matt. XVI). But to me, whose faith is unshaken, whose sight is not raven-like but endowed with sevenfold grace, and whose vision is dovelike and ready, your mortality is far removed from infirmity, your appearance far from ugliness; and the incomparable beauty of both natures shines sweetly forth.

You are indeed fair in your wonderful and preeminent Godhead, endowed with substantial unity with the Father and the Spirit; with them you have the same natural excellence, coeternal greatness, and equal kingdom and power. Among the gods none is found like you, nor is any other God distinguished by so great a prerogative of beauty. For although personal distinction makes the Father another and the Holy Spirit another, natural substance nevertheless makes them one God and not another God. Therefore whatever beauty the Father and Spirit are known to possess, my Beloved, I see shining in you by certain faith. This draws me to love you and choose you as Beloved, to follow you and not cease until I attain, come, and reach perfection.

And because the height of your divine beauty is not hidden from me in the present, the wondrous beauty of your humanity also greatly pleases me. As man among human beings and mortal among those dead through sin, you are such that, though you endure punishment, you are not burdened by the guilt of mortals. No child of Adam merited to obtain this beauty by nature, because no one’s conception and no one’s birth was without fault. But singular purity and special excellence adorned you alone, whom a virginal womb alone brought forth, conceived by the divine Spirit.

And this you reveal before and beyond all other human beings to none but me, my Beloved. By singular merit you honor me in such a way that I bear you in sure truth as God and man: mother of the Spouse, bride of the Son, in wondrous and incomparable chastity. Therefore you are fair to me, and especially beautiful you shine forth to me: you are known as God in man and as holy man above human beings; equality of nature conforms you to God the Father as Son, while the law of sin and the common conception of humankind do not darken you.

You are fair, I say, because you are the radiance of eternal light, the spotless mirror of the divine majesty, the splendor of the Father’s glory, the figure of his substance, the image of truth (Heb. I); light from light, the rising sun bringing morning day to the world, day from day, reclining at noon, knowing no evening setting. Carried away in ecstasy and raised in the Spirit from visible things, I behold you, so fair, with the purified sight of the mind. As though forgetful of myself, I cannot help loving you whom I behold thus; I burn to commend you, my Beloved, and your beauty.

## CHAPTER XV

“Behold, you are fair, my beloved.” Not only does the wondrous beauty of your Godhead please me—that excellence which, equal with the Father and Spirit, your majesty possesses—but you have also kindled me greatly by that beauty whereby, abounding in grace, you descended from the heights to lowly things. Not small is that beauty with which you girded yourself and were mightily clothed, when you were established by the Father upon his holy mountain Zion (Ps. II); when, taking flesh in me and being personally united to it, you went forth as the Bridegroom from his chamber (Ps. XVIII), splendid in power through humility.

In that flesh, above the law of flesh, you did not experience the vices of flesh; conceived by the Spirit, you flourished with inborn strength. Though enduring the punishment of flesh, you failed in the sight of your persecutors; but in the sight of believers you accomplished the mystery that brings salvation to the world. For it was necessary that, living in flesh under punishment, you should teach us and show yourself a master of life by conduct as well as speech; that you should forge the rule by the anvil and hammer of the Gospel; and that, suffering death in the flesh, you should triumph over Zabulus, the author of death.

Having been given over to death, on the third day you rose; made immortal, you strengthened faith and gave hope. To the heavens whence you had come you raised the substance of our flesh; and, having given your Spirit, you lifted there the minds of those who are yours. Who that worthily considers that you could thus be born and live, die and rise, and that in high counsel you chose to do these things as man for human beings, would not be astonished, marvel, love this beauty, and eagerly embrace so mighty and so benevolent a giver?

Although this is hidden from others, from whom, because of sin, such grace is either withdrawn or, by a hidden judgment, its bestowal is now deferred to the future, the course of this matter is nevertheless declared to me in the present. To me it is evident; to me it is pleasing what your Godhead works in man. “Behold,” I say, “you are fair, my beloved, and beautiful.” “Behold”—that is, the beauty of your majesty is manifest to me; the excellence of your Godhead presents itself to the opened eye of faith. By its generous gift it pours understanding into my mind, and, once understanding has been made clear, it produces the effect of unbreakable love.

Behold again, the saving dispensation of your humanity is not hidden from me: its conception, birth, life of singular merit, power, purity, patience, praiseworthy teaching, shining miracles, integrity of conduct, and perfection of discipline. In all these you are adorned as man above human beings; and in your distinctive beauty you are comparable neither with prophet nor apostle. Therefore I love you above all, choose you alone, my Beloved—though still, while life is lived here, imperfectly, as I seem to see.

Yet, that my imperfection may not trouble me beyond measure, I desire your presence to reveal itself more closely to me. And lest I seem to invite the fair and beautiful one to unseemly things, I have endeavored to prepare a place fitting for the lover.

## CHAPTER XVI
The little bed is ours, flowering; the beams of our houses are of cedar, our ceilings of cypress.

Because the noble Virgin has found her lover beautiful and fair, she does not, in rustic fashion, invite him to work. Refined love does not know how to be worn down by base labour or torture; rather, it loves rest and leisure and rejoices in a kiss or an embrace. That lover, still inexperienced in this matter, seems to have been untrained, nor did his love provide sufficiently worthy rest for the one he loved: he asks that she whom he loves be given to him so that they may labour together, [Col. 0278C] but may not yet rejoice in repose. “I loved her,” he says, “and sought her out, and sought to take her as my bride; and I became a lover of her beauty” (Wis. VIII). And below: “Send her from the throne of your majesty, that she may be with me and labour with me, and that I may know what is acceptable to you; for she knows and understands all things” (Wis. IX).

This man still saw labour as fitting for himself, and wished that Wisdom, whom he loved, might work with him, so that the lover, still less wise, might be taught by their shared labour; and, once taught, might be brought onward to the rest of the bed. Thus the woman whose praiseworthy strength is commended is said to lay her hand to the distaff and grasp the spindle with her fingers; and she seems to become pleasing to her husband because she did not eat her bread [Col. 0278D] in idleness (Prov. XXXI). But our Virgin, surpassing far both this woman and that lover, seeks rest rather than tumult; she now possesses leisure, not labour. She offers her lover not the training-ground of an athlete but a little bed, which she has taken pains to adorn and furnish with more elegant ornament.

The Virgin’s little bed is the secret place of her heart. She cultivates and cleanses it by diligent labour and care, lest anything dishonourable or unseemly appear to the Bridegroom when he comes; and, that it may provide a sweet resting-place worthy of such great dignity, she supports and fills it with the welcome softness of carefully wrought work. And because a noble lover rejoices not only in softness spread beneath him but also in beauty, the Virgin, understanding this, adorns the little bed with pleasing flowers. By scattering the flowers of wondrous chastity with much care, she makes that same little bed like a garden of delight. [Col. 0279A]

For lest anyone, hearing of the Virgin’s bed, should take offence, doubt her progress, and stray from the path of holiness through a gross and carnal understanding, the Virgin herself declares that it is adorned with gathered flowers; and the flowers are chastity and the reputation of that chastity. Virgin chastity adorns her hidden knowledge like a flower; it makes the little bed pleasing, pouring out the grace of beauty and fragrance. For it is that which excels in outstanding virtue and merit, and which shines forth conspicuously both in reputation and in name, so as to present a pattern. In this there is nothing bodily, nothing bestial, nothing given over to sin, but everything wholly spiritual; for this drama, or song, or nuptial epithalamium blossoms with mystical words and contains nothing of hay or flesh.

Yet, although the bed which love has prepared so carefully thus blooms and prospers, [Col. 0279B] the Virgin calls it not a bed but rather a little bed. By this word she fulfils the rule well known to her, by which she is accustomed to embrace humility both in word and deed. Therefore, she says, I call this little bed not properly mine but ours in common; and—what is worthy of praise—I do not presumptuously claim it for myself. For although I was found obedient in consenting to him who called and helped me, his prevenient grace and subsequent mercy nevertheless chose to bestow efficacy. Therefore the little bed should rightly be called not mine but ours, since it is plainly prepared by the work and diligence of us both: you have made it bright by the hand of grace, I by labour and effort; you have adorned it by your gift, I by practice; you with flowers of virtues, I with flowers of moral conduct.

I have wished to mention this so particularly in order that, drawn by its beauty, you may graciously come to its dwelling; and that, far from tumult—which I know you do not often frequent—I may rejoice in that than which nothing is better: being with you in a flowering secret place. [Col. 0279C] For although it is necessary to go out and speak for the brothers and neighbours, it is far more delightful to enter into silence in order to behold you; and, in the leisure of rest, to be soothed by your presence, to enjoy mutual embrace, and to experience the fruit of love, the joy of the Spirit.

My houses also seem to emulate my effort to merit this; and though with slow step, they follow me as I rest upon the little bed. Although they are not yet able to advance so far as to become a little bed, they are nevertheless already found worthy to obtain no small grace. In this I rejoice, and shall rejoice, because you please not only when your presence is now held upon the little bed, but also when, according to the Prophet, you will be known to be in the houses (Ps. XLVII): those, that is, to whose cedar beams you give an incorruptible support, and to whose cypress ceilings you likewise give enduring ornament.

## CHAPTER XVII

The beams of our houses are of cedar; our ceilings of cypress.

By houses he means the churches of the faithful, congregations of the righteous, and monastic communities. In these, the simpler members may be considered stones, while the greater and wiser are more suitably called beams and ceilings. Beams are set in sequence over a building in the form of a vault and arranged opposite one another on its two sides. Below, [Col. 0280A] extending like arms, they embrace the building’s breadth; above, joined like heads, they are connected by a firm nail. The ceilings, however, are laid beneath the height of the beams and spread in length from one wall to the other; they hold and bind those same walls as it were by a fastening, lest under a harmful impact they lean away from uprightness or stature.

By the name of beams is fittingly represented the order of prelates: raised above earthly things, they are commended by the loftiness of their merits. Bearing the annoyances of rains and winds—that is, the harsh assaults of the wicked—they shelter and protect from them the tender conduct of their subjects. Erect toward heavenly things, they concentrate themselves upon contemplating that one thing necessary, more strongly bound by the nail of love. [Col. 0280B] The more they see, the more closely they cling; and the more sweetly they taste. They judge it better to be with Christ (Phil. I), while contemplating his excellence; yet they regard remaining in the flesh as necessary for the brethren.

Those, therefore, who suspend themselves through subtle desire upon knowing the things above stoop down through benevolent care to revisit their neighbours. Gathering them beneath their wings, they cherish and protect them as a hen does; they strengthen them for virtues by examples and teaching. And since these are commended by a worthier merit of virtues, the beams whose role they fulfil are said to be cedar. For cedars, as they say, are naturally incorruptible and tall, and possess such a strong scent that serpents are said to abhor them. Therefore those are worthily found fit to be advanced to the height of prelacy [Col. 0280C] who, lofty in merits, love to behold heaven in desire; whose works always flourish in steadfast virtue, lest they rot; whose reputation is so great that all ill-disposed persons recoil from it.

Nor is it unfitting in prelates that cedar is said not to burn in fire. It bears the image of those who will not perish in the blaze of passions, whose strength is wondrous: the desire of the flesh does not know how to break them, nor does their most sweet fragrance turn to ashes amid the smell of fires. The ceilings, said to be of cypress, signify those whose discipline flourishes and excels among the rest. By their strong work and obedience of perfect will, a pattern of perseverance is given to the lesser members assembled in the Church. Cypress too is said to be incorruptible and fragrant; [Col. 0280D] moreover, it is knotless and has no roughness in it. It fittingly signifies one who, made readier and smoother by divine gift rather than by nature, obeys without delay and never kicks back in the joint.

For in some persons the virtue of obedience is so knotty, so full of murmuring, so beset by complaints, that when a command arrives it does not find a smoother path prepared beforehand, but more often meets with graver contempt or anger. But those who have been granted to flourish with cypress smoothness delight in a discipline of obedience that is knotless and polished. They love whatever the discernment or teaching of their prelates commands, and the sudden stain of impatience does not set itself against the command.

By such beams and ceilings spiritual houses advance, are roofed and fortified, and avoid ruinous [Col. 0281A] and carnal falls. Their holy and wondrous beauty flourishes, since, as has been said, “holiness befits the house of the Lord” (Ps. XCII). The Virgin wished these houses to be called ours in order to show that she has communion with the Bridegroom beyond others, since by nuptial right the Bride counts as ours even that which belongs to the Bridegroom. And, as Christ is concerned, so too the Virgin is concerned for the spiritual advancement of us all.

Therefore, seeing not only herself but also her own people advancing spiritually, and seeing prelates and subjects attain the likeness of cedar and cypress, she exults and invites the Bridegroom to rejoice in these too, and, leaving the restless, to delight in the welcome repose of the houses. And he says:

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0281B] [CHAP. II.] I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.

“If,” he says, “the Bride’s little bed is springing with flowers, shining with virginal beauty; if it gleams and is fragrant with spiritual adornment and beauty; if, rich in royal cultivation, it seems to smile upon those who consider it worthily—what does it have that it can truthfully claim not to have received from another? For it does not possess of itself the fact that it shines with flowering beauty; nor does that which the Bride calls flowering bloom except by a flower. Therefore let not the flowering thing glory in itself, but in the flower; since it certainly does not have from itself that it blooms, but from the flower.

“But if anyone who blooms wishes to know more carefully whence he blooms, lest shameful ignorance strip beauty and bloom from him: I, God the Son in the Father, light dwelling in inaccessible light, became the flower of the field, possessing unfailing beauty. The root of Jesse put forth a shoot [Col. 0281C] and the flower came forth from the root; nor did it wish to lie hidden in a chamber beneath a bushel, or in a bed beneath a coverlet. Rather, it became the flower of the field, so that it might be more plainly known to all and none might deserve excuse who fails to know one so conspicuous.

“For I, who from eternity was God, hidden lest I be seen, descending from this mountain was received by the field so that I might be grasped. I did not enter the gates and walls of cities, nor did I again climb a steep mountain, lest I either be unknown or be not more easily grasped by one who knew me. For if a strong man climbed the mountain, the weak man left behind would be excused; in a city, the citizen would exclude the stranger; [Col. 0281D] and so, as injustice prevailed, one would accuse another of being readier, and Habakkuk would charge me with silence (ch. I), while the wicked devoured one more righteous than himself.

“Therefore I wished to be a flower in a field and not in cultivated land, which the farmer claims for himself by hereditary right; which he breaks with the plough, furrows with the ploughshare, and diligently digs with the hoe, because it answers fruitfully only to the labour of human hands. A field, however, is assigned to no person as private property; it does not know the hand of a cultivator and is not sown by broken ground. But warmed by the sun and drenched with heavenly rain or dew, it grows warm and germinates, and in the fitting course of time smiles with flower.

“Nor is it unsuitable if this field is said to signify the Virgin of virgins, in whom no human being and no carnal intercourse operates. With her flesh intact, she is made fruitful and germinates as spiritual rain descends upon a fleece; she rejoices in flowering, snow-white beauty. The hand of a greedy worker has not injured this field, nor has a rustic hand ploughed it. [Col. 0282A] No harmful swelling raised it up, but overflowing humility made it level. I am the flower, proceeding certainly not from human effort or cultivation, but brought forth by a heavenly gift, endowed with an incomparable birth.

“I am the flower by which this field’s pleasing levelness is adorned. It does not bloom by itself, but is thus blessed by my gift; therefore, although the Virgin may rightly rejoice in so great a benefit, she should nevertheless glory in me and not in herself—in the flower, not in the flowering thing. For although a flower does not produce fruit as soon as it is born, still, since it will give fruit in its proper season, it already promises it. And just as no flower other than mine, or superior to mine, is found, so no one finds better fruit in another.

“But lest I seem to have provided mercifully for the Virgin alone and to have begrudged my mercy to lesser persons, I who became the flower of the field, granting the Bride a special privilege, have also bloomed in the valleys—abundantly indeed, but not with an equal benefit.”

## CHAPTER XIX

And the lily of the valleys.

Valleys—or rather, low valleys—which are shaded on either side by neighbouring mountains and watered from both sides by flowing streams lest they dry out through thirst, seem to me to signify the humble and lowly, whom love of discipline keeps tirelessly under the laws of their superiors. They entertain nothing lofty or swollen from their overbearing patron; they judge themselves useless servants in humble holiness, incline their ear to the admonitions of Scripture and to each Testament with greater diligence, desiring to abound more in a wealth of merits than in grain.

Christ acknowledges himself as the lily of such valleys [Col. 0282C] because, though he is most high, he is said nevertheless to look upon lowly things (Ps. CXII); and his Spirit rests only upon the humble and gentle person whose conscience shines with humility made clean and cleanness made humble (Isa. LXVI). He fittingly chose to be called a lily, thereby signifying what he came to do among the valleys, for the valleys’ sake, so that those who attend rightly may not fail to perceive the cause of his coming; and so that, after making them learned, he may conform them more effectually to himself.

The lily, whiter in its petals, is encircled round about like a valley, and has within it something red in its depth: in the petals it displays what is fair and bright, while in the red it represents the appearance of blood. The whiteness of the lily signifies the purity of assumed flesh, which neither conception before nor conduct afterward stained black. Rather, flesh born of flesh knew nothing of the poison proper to flesh, and shone by merit of virtues as with snowy brightness. [Col. 0282D] That red thing, however, brings the welcome remembrance of the Passion, by which, when he shed his blood, he erased the written bond of the long-made covenant—an unhappy covenant which the first parents made with the author of sin when, at his will, they touched the forbidden tree.

Thus Christ is a lily when he glows with the merit of an innocent life, when in the flesh he is not held by the stain or adhesive taint of clinging vice; when, as man, human malice attacks and accuses him; and when, for human beings, he as man does not refuse to suffer harsh and bitter things. He is the lily of the valleys when he gives the rejected and humble an example and grace for living, commends innocence, implants love of self-restraint, and, having first suffered grievous things, calls them to the virtue of suffering: teaching great things, doing greater things, and proclaiming the time for doing them. [Col. 0283A]

But if it is said that the redness within the lily has the appearance of fire—“God is fire,” as Scripture certainly declares (Deut. IV)—then that redness, as I see it, surrounded by snowy brightness, is God clothed in the robe of a man’s pure flesh. He hid himself in this covering from the wise and prudent, but revealed himself to believing little ones and the humble (Luke X), who so look upon the covering or whiteness of assumed flesh outside as to see within the fiery redness of hidden deity. Of these Peter says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI); Nathanael: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel” (John I); and the centurion: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark XV).

Christ made himself the lily of these valleys when, within the man, he revealed himself to his humble followers as not merely man but God; to them his innocent humanity was displayed in such spotless whiteness that they also saw, without stumbling, the hidden Deity by faith. [Col. 0283B] Having taught them what they ought faithfully to think concerning him, he resumes the Virgin’s praises and invites them to consider more carefully how she imitates the Bridegroom amid this life’s troubles, while full rest and unfailing peace are not yet possessed.

## CHAPTER XX

As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.

Although, as you have heard, I called myself the lily of the valleys, know also that I still dwell among more grievous thorns. I allow myself frequently to be touched by them and more painfully pricked; but though touched and pierced, I do not lose my proper state or whiteness. In this manner my beloved lives among the evils of this age, and by wondrous virtue light is proved to shine in darkness. The darkness surrounding her does not obscure her flowering light, nor do threatening thistles crush her unbroken beauty.

She rises and grows like a lily among thorns; among the dark she shines, among harsh things she grows gentle. Blown and driven by the wind, she seems to feel certain effects, but suffers no injury to her whiteness or fragrance. I think the grievous thorns are the cares and anxieties of this life, by which the minds of the righteous, while they live here, are assailed; they groan [Col. 0283C] and long to be more fully freed from them, that at last, having attained the fruit of peace, they may rejoice with Christ.

The thorns are likewise Jews and Gentiles: grown old in malice, childish in ruined understanding, execrating faith and wrapped in thicker darkness, they persecuted Christ and his Mother with bitter hatred. Among them Son and Mother flourished like a lily, and alike preserved their unharmed whiteness and proper fragrance, contracting no guilt from their persecutors’ malice and repelling slanderous tongues with unconquered patience. Indeed, the more the life of malicious people is darkened by blacker soot, the more brightly shines the holiness of these two when worthily considered; the unstained beauty of the lily loses none of its loveliness and grace if the harsh ugliness of thorns is seen beside it. [Col. 0283D]

Thus the lily among thorns has a fuller title to praise, retaining a more pleasing form while they grow dark. For while both Gentiles and Jews rage with serpent tongues against the Lord and against his Christ (Ps. II), Christ, the flower and lily, is gentle in conduct and shines in miracles and teaching. The Virgin strives most diligently to resemble this flower and lily, loving and desiring to glory in so great a likeness. And as the lily among thorns is made lovely by radiant beauty, so the Bride is adorned among the daughters by the merit of virtues.

By “daughters” he means those who, lacking manly firmness and a masculine spirit, are dull through womanly softness and asleep in feminine drowsiness; weak for honourable work, effective in soft and harmful pursuits, crafty in flattery, and faithless or insolent in detraction. [Col. 0284A] Seeing or hearing that the Mother rejoices in her Son, they are clothed in perverted understanding and deny that she is either virgin or fruitful. Although endowed with a unique gift, they measure her carnally by the common rule of all persons, lying that she bore only in the manner experienced by other women.

They suppose the one whom she bore to be Joseph’s son and testify that he has many brothers, though he is the only one. They do not know him to be a man born from man without a father; they recoil from hearing that he is God, the Son of God, without a mother. Among these people and their blasphemies the Virgin is neither broken nor withered. Rather, her mind is strengthened by faith; flowering in the joy of the Spirit, she grows young again. She embraces that tender and unfading flower of the root, and imitates his beauty by striving not so much to follow his footsteps as to make progress after his pattern. [Col. 0284B] Finally, according to Solomon: “A joyful spirit makes flourishing youth” (Prov. XVII).

Therefore, just as the Son, a flower and lily rising among thorns, does not feel the thorns, because he does not consent with like affection to their malice, so the Mother and beloved, living among the daughters, does not know the daughters’ darkness. As a daughter of light, she shines and has no works of darkness. Indeed, to say more: not only do thorns do the lily no harm, but the lily also bestows much ornament upon the thorns; and the surpassing whiteness which, by a natural gift, spreads itself in the lily pours no small grace upon neighbouring thorns.

Did not the lily spread incomparable benefit on every side when Christ poured out devout prayers for his persecutors? When by the hand of mercy he scraped away the ugliness of thorns [Col. 0284C] and changed bramble into flower, and prickles into fruit? “Father,” he says, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII). As though sprinkled by the dew of this prayer, the harshness of the thorns becomes gentle, their inward dryness gives way, goodwill turns green; in a new manner the little branch buds, puts forth leaves, and blossoms, and the little flower rejoices to imitate the lily in even a small measure of whiteness.

Who does not know that sometimes thorns, formerly dry, bloom by the gift of the summer season, and that not so much their old prickles as fresh little flowers stand out upon them? Standing beside the lily, although far unequal to it in size or beauty, they yet enjoy some likeness of whiteness and a closer neighbourhood. Thus, as we draw near to Christ, the lily’s beauty contracts no ugliness for itself from us; rather, our ugliness gains for itself no small grace from it. And while the lily’s loveliness thus admits us, like the abundance of a planted garden, our solitude, once dry, now at last rejoices exceedingly in bloom. [Col. 0284D]

Foreseeing this, Isaiah says: “The wilderness and trackless places shall rejoice, and the solitude shall exult; and it shall germinate like a lily” (Isa. XXXV). Our mind is rightly called a wilderness and trackless place when, abandoned by God, it is inhabited neither by the citizens of virtues nor of works; when its benevolent creator does not walk in it or love to look upon it, seeing it besieged in solitude by the prickles of vices, like thorns. When divine grace visits it like spring mildness and calls the white lily into the garden plantings, it will indeed rejoice and exult in the gift of a new benefaction, because, joined to the lily, it will germinate like a lily.

Rejecting the bramble which the harshness of thorns would have produced—because harsh punishment awaits thorny ways—it will bring forth sweet little flowers rivaling the lily in whiteness, and, with first shoots budding, will exult in hope of fruit. [Col. 0285A] Among thorns of this kind that white lily—or rather the brightness of eternal light—works wondrously, rejoicing to turn harshness into smoothness and the prickle into flower. By the goodness that is its own, it will at some time bring the matter to such a point that the flower bears fruit and enjoys the fruit it is to enjoy.

So too the beloved is rightly believed to live among the daughters, to care for them, and to work more diligently for their salvation. Those once wandering in mind, haughty in eye, insolent in tongue, and barren in works, she at length deigns to make, by her companionship, active and fruitful. [Col. 0285B] Those whom she admits into the noble inner chamber of her hearing, she does not allow to remain barren as they stand before her. Rather, instructing by word, fortifying by example, and helping by intercession, she invites them to love, urges them to work, and gladdens them by their progress.

Thus those who had once been daughters of Babylon by the merit of their life, once they have entered, she makes daughters of Jerusalem, daughters of vision. Among them, rejoicing, she sees the Bridegroom, loves to embrace him, and reveres him with worthy praises, just as he reveres the Bride. Therefore she says: “As,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXI
“Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.” The Bride, hearing herself praised with worthy praises of the Bridegroom—by whom she has what makes her worthy to be honoured with laudatory proclamation [Col. 0285D]—hastens, lest she seem ungrateful, to repay her praiser in turn; knowing that reciprocal praises are pleasing to a lover. Rightly enough she chose to compare him with an apple tree, since among woodland trees it is acknowledged to stand out, not so much more highly as more excellently: for whereas the trees of the forest bear no fruit fit for human food, in the apple tree one finds good fruit and the finest refreshment.

For Christ is a tree whose strength sustains no injury, whose leaf does not yield to the wind when it rages fiercely (Ps. 1); all things belonging to it prosper, and in its season it will give fruit, by which it now invites the hungry and will afterwards satisfy them. Christ is the tree of life for all who grasp him firmly, who stretch themselves out with strong desire to seize his fruit; who do not strive, by wandering understanding, to grasp whatever else they encounter, since they do not observe that life-giving fruits hang from them.

I believe that all human beings may be called trees of the forest: although they have the leaves of words, they undoubtedly lack saving fruit, because in them there is no salvation, no life, no unfailing vigour of nature, but a certain barrenness of virtues, the fault of the flesh bringing forth through the defect of generation. For matters are not so in them that anything living, commendable, or gracious comes from them; there is nothing in one person that is saving for himself or fruitful for others. For whatever worthy and necessary thing is found in anyone—if indeed anything is found in anyone—is known by whoever truly experiences it to come not from that person’s own resources but from Christ’s.

But Christ, as man among men, is not inappropriately compared to an apple tree. Conceived [Col. 0286B] by the Spirit, he is not accused of barren nature. His root is harmless; his denser shade shelters us from harmful heat; his wholesome fruit and utterly sweet fragrance spread abroad. In short, these three things may equally be found in an apple tree; nor is there another tree in the woods that can pride itself on being distinguished alike by all three. But in the apple tree especially shade, fruit, and fragrance are joined by a natural bond; and from him who is God and man they proceed in spiritual abundance.

By these he refreshes, feeds, and delights those who have received him, who by receiving mercy have deserved to be called and to be sons: those who, because they have passed by faith from darkness into light, have through a blessed change been transformed from woodland trees into sons of God. Christ, beholding them as sons and heirs of God, is not ashamed to call them brothers and to love them as co-heirs [Col. 0286C] (Matt. 25), so that he himself may stand forth as the firstborn in chief honour among many brothers, and he who was once the only Son may rejoice in sons now plural in number.

For he, God from God, was the Father’s only-begotten Son; and, born as man from a virgin, he was likewise his Mother’s only son. But, providing for the elect, he opened the bosom of grace more generously, and by the benefit of adoption made brothers those whom nature had denied him. The Son of God and man surpasses such brothers or sons as far as a fruit-bearing apple tree surpasses the trees of the forest: for its fruitfulness is preferred to their barrenness, and no human being—however just—can be compared with Christ.

Peter understood this when the centurion showed him more honour than was right and gave to a mere man the reverent devotion owed to Christ [Col. 0286D]. Peter did not rashly appropriate for himself what he knew was not his own, but showed who he was, how barren, and how unlike the apple tree. “Cornelius,” he says, “fell at his feet and worshipped him. But Peter raised him up, saying: ‘Rise; I too am a man, as you are’” (Acts 10). And below: “Proclaiming peace,” he says, “through Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all” (ibid.).

You see that Peter neither wishes nor permits Cornelius to worship him, showing that a mere man ought not to be honoured in this way; and making it understood that this privilege is due to Jesus Christ, that he alone, man among men, is to be venerated with divine worship. I think that not even an angel wishes such worship to be rendered to himself; and although greater than a human being, he is nevertheless found to revere a human being. In that human being he now perceives [Col. 0287A] something new, unexperienced by all preceding generations, hidden from the ages and disclosed in the fullness of our time.

Thus, when John rejoiced that many things were shown him by an angel, and, wishing to venerate his instructor with what he supposed to be a fitting service of humility, fell at his feet in order to offer him the honour due to one greater than himself, the angel, measuring himself rightly, appeared to recoil. “After I had heard and seen,” he says, “I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed me these things; and he said to me: ‘See that you do not do it’” (Rev. 22). And above: “I fell,” he says, “before his feet to worship him; and he said to me: ‘See that you do not do it; for I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus. Worship God’” (Rev. 19).

The angel does not wish to be made equal to Christ, the servant to the Lord, nor the barrenness of forest trees to be compared to the fruitful tree. But just as the apple tree is plainly pre-eminent among woodland trees, so the angel knows Christ to be pre-eminent among the sons.

Indeed, angels too are sometimes called sons in the Scriptures, and are proclaimed always to behold the face of God the Father. According to Job, moreover, the sons of God are read to have come to stand before the Lord, among whom that wicked angel Satan is also read to have been present (Job 1). Moses likewise says: “He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel” (Deut. 32), calling angels “sons of Israel.” Another translation makes this clearer: “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.”

For some believe that God has chosen from the nations as many to be saved [Col. 0287C] as there remain angels after others fell, so that there may be prepared for him from among human beings as many sons to behold him as are already counted among the angels who behold him and are likewise sons. Yet among these sons the Bride’s Beloved is pre-eminent like an apple tree. For just as there is no salvation in a mere human being, so too there is none in an angel; but salvation is in Christ, who, although lower than the angels because of his suffering of death, is nevertheless far more exalted because of the union of God and man.

Therefore, when the angel said to John, “See that you do not do it,” he adds the reason: “I am your fellow servant, and the fellow servant of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus. Worship God.” “I,” he says, “am worthily the servant not merely of God, but of God made man; I am the fellow servant of you and of those who bear witness to Jesus by faith and works. It is not fitting for a servant to take away the Lord’s rights, when every creature ought rather to render all things to its Creator.

“Therefore worship not an angel but God: God who, in order to save the angel, did not lay hold of an angel, but took hold of the seed of Abraham in order to save it; God who emptied himself and took the form of a servant” (Phil. 2), “so that he was found in fashion as a man.” According to this humanity, although he was found lower than the angels, he is not found much lower, but is reckoned only a little lower, if what Scripture declares is understood without wandering interpretation. David says: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8). And Paul: “Him who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death” (Heb. 2).

Christ, certainly, consists of God and man; and man consists of soul and [Col. 0288A] body. The soul is the greater part of the human being—greater, I say, not in bulk, but in dignity and excellence—because in the soul the human being was made in God’s image and likeness. The body, however, is the lesser, that is, the inferior, part of the human being. According to that part Christ is found lower than angels, because angels are not clothed in the covering of mortal flesh; rather, that immortal spirit, strong in understanding and endowed with reason, remains, in that in which it was made, without the injury of death.

The human spirit too is said to be of the same or a similar nature, likewise endowed with reason; it has a beginning, but is not confined by the limitation of an end. Yet, poured into a body generated corrupt through original fault, it is, by a wondrous and very pitiful law, burdened with that body’s deserts. Hence you have read: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9).

Thus the soul, which is of the same or a similar nature as an angel—for such creatures are, as it were, of one kind by reason of their rationality—first disfigures its original beauty through association with flesh, and then by the assent of the will slips into the ruin of vices. But because Christ’s flesh, conceived by the Spirit, did not contract original fault, it did not draw into guilt the soul infused into it, a soul which knew no guilt. Rather, as both conception and manner of life preserved this flesh undefiled, so creation and the condescension of its Creator rendered that soul free from every stain.

But what kind of soul should Christ be believed to have assumed into personal unity? A soul whose nature is ennobled by immortality, understanding, and reason; which neither a prevailing [Col. 0288C] embodiment nor any defilement can dishonour. Nor is he believed, in assuming it, to have consumed the dignity of the soul assumed. No angel, no creature whatsoever, is greater than such a soul; he alone is greater, to whom, as Creator, no creature can be made equal.

According to this soul, Christ ought not to be thought lower than angels. Endowed with native dignity, it could be corrupted by no vice. Although the maker does not confer this incapacity upon his creature merely by making it, he conferred it upon this soul by assuming it. What neither angel nor soul possesses by the privilege of condition or force of nature, the Creator bestowed upon the creature whom he willed and when he willed. And he who had formerly granted to angels that none could thereafter fall or fear falling, afterwards gave to the soul he assumed that holy steadfastness might likewise remain unshaken.

It remains, therefore, that Christ be declared lower than angels only according to the flesh, which, as stated above, is judged the other, lesser, or inferior part of the human being. Thus he is rightly read to have been made lower not by much, lest he seem so according to the whole human being, but by a little, that it may be recognized that reference is made to the flesh alone.

But sin has made us wretches much lower than angels, since both conception has infected our flesh and embodiment our soul, so that we deservedly accuse our generation as culpable in both respects. We are held under a harsh law because vice has been turned into nature. Hence Paul says: “We were by nature children of wrath” (Eph. 2).

Although the burden of fault did not weigh down the good angels, but grace confirmed them, well created as they were, yet more excellently: nevertheless Christ must be believed to be pre-eminent among them just as among human beings, and, like an apple tree among the trees of the forest, to hold primacy among such sons. Angels venerate Christ not merely as God but as God and man; in him they contemplate the fruit of salvation and a protecting shade. Through him they see, without envy, human beings crushed and oppressed by the heavy burden of condemnable sins converted and restored to the saving excellence of merits.

Neither crops, nor ram, nor calf, nor indeed human being or angel could accomplish this; nor was any other name given in which we might be saved. Thus life is won from sickness, salvation from loss, so that every creature is powerless to provide fruit or healing [Col. 0289B]. Since, therefore, neither the barren forest nor the workshop of any craftsman supplied life, fruit, or the efficacy of a powerful remedy, and the world, sick as it was, had come to hate those who promised relief because of their delay, the tree of life arose in the midst of paradise: the fruitful apple tree.

Its most pleasing shade banishes burning impulses; its fruit freely refreshes those whom oppressive hunger had injured. It not only restored humanity to the fellowship with angels once lost, but also raised human nature above angelic dignity. For the angel beholds our nature now united to God in Christ; considering its fruit, he rightly confesses himself barren, because one who was unable to restore either a fallen fellow angel or a lost human being ought not to compare himself with Christ, who was able to do all that he willed.

Observing this, the Virgin rightly says: “Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.” Of him she adds:

## CHAPTER XXII

“Under his shadow, whom I had desired, I sat; and his fruit was sweet to my throat.”

“If,” she says, “as you have heard, I have wished to commend my beloved, if I have compared him to a fruitful apple tree among barren trees, do not suppose that I am uncertain of what I set before you, or abundant in words but unacquainted with the things praised. By experience I have learned how useful and good this apple tree is; I have felt how great a refuge, how great a refreshment, how great a salvation there is in it. For under its shadow it has been granted me not only to be, but to sit—to flee harmful heats and obtain the grace of rest.

Good is that rest which was fashioned not by the anger of a pursuer but by the hand of loving grace; over which not gloomy death but the apple tree, broad with branches and leaves, cast its shade; in which the sinner is not buried in the tomb of despair or ignorance, but the just mind is soothed by the sweet refreshment bestowed through progress.

Wretched is that people which long wished to remain in darkness and in the shadow of death, forgetting heavenly things and clinging carnally to earthly things. Not knowing life that gives life, it grew dark beneath the obscuring death of sins, whose body is the death without end that will follow. For sin, by which the soul is pierced as by a sword and is found to be made distant from him who is life, is the soul’s first death—pleasant now, more sorrowful in the future; but the eternal condemnation which rightly follows is the second death [Col. 0290A].

The former is both death and the preceding shadow of the death that follows; the latter is both death and the reality of the preceding shadow. Although it may happen that we are in the first, it is not prudent for us to sit there—that is, to obtain a lost repose without concern for repentance. For one who sits in the shadow does not fear to forestall the death to come, while that death, coming on, hastens to find him sluggish; and whomever it finds in darkness, as it were under its own right, it binds and holds in prison with the insoluble force of its bond.

Yet the merciful Spirit frightens some people violently, shakes them with a sudden sound, and, visiting from on high as the Dayspring, floods them with morning light. Having been brought forth from sleep, from the shadow of harsh danger and of night, they are received by a joyful day [Col. 0290B] and by a sweeter, daylight shadow.

The day is illuminating faith; the virtue of hope is a sweeter shadow of the foreknown appearance, in which it is good to be, better to live, and best to sit, until at last it is granted us to obtain the full light more fully. One is in the daylight shadow who knows that not only present things but also things to come exist; who sees through a mirror what is certainly not yet visibly at hand; who by undoubting faith understands that God is invisible and believes him to be the rewarder of those who hope in him.

Paul says: “Whoever approaches God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him” (Heb. 11). Without this faith no one pleases God, nor is that conscience worthy which is not held by the knowledge of God. For, as you have read, the ignorant person is said to be unknown; and truly one who is not known cannot be accepted by one who does not know him (1 Cor. 14). Therefore the Prophet says: “He believed; therefore he spoke” (Ps. 115): “You yourself are my God.”

Without faith, then, no one can be just. Indeed, to say more: one who has not believed ought not even to be said to exist; and one who does not exist is consequently not even in the shadow. Of such persons it is written: “Do not deliver your kingdom to those who are not” (Esther 14). He is rightly said not to be who does not know that God is, to whom the one by whom he was made has not yet made himself known; who, blinded in mind, is far removed from the merit of existence, not yet having attained faith, which is the shadow or beginning of subsistence. Of this Paul says: “If only we hold firm to the end the beginning of his substance” [Col. 0290D] (Heb. 3).

Whoever, then, has faith, firmly holding that God is, exists and is in the shadow; but it is not enough to be there. Rather, one who already exists by the merit of faith must labour so that, living in it, he may deserve also to be just. For to be in faith is not yet to be just; but to live by faith, or to live in faith, is reckoned righteousness, because dead faith works, even though it does not love. Love, indeed, is the life of faith; and therefore it is not one who merely believes, but one who believes lovingly, who is proved to live. And one who lives in faith, worthy of praise, is proclaimed commendable in righteousness.

Thus Habakkuk says: “My just one lives by his faith” (Hab. 2). One may indeed be in faith without being just, but no one lives in faith except the just person. For one is in faith to whom, when saying, “Lord, Lord” (Matt. 7), the door is nevertheless not opened; and one lives in faith who, doing the will of the Lord, is heard.

And because faith is not the presence of the desired reality, but, as stated above, the substance and shadow of the hoped-for appearance (Heb. 11), the just, whose merits do not yet admit them into that same appearance, promise themselves meanwhile not so much to be as to live in its shadow. “In his shadow,” they say, “we shall live among the nations” (Lam. 4).

The just will live in the shadow when they lovingly labour in faith, when they strive to conduct themselves justly, piously, and holy; when it is granted them to rejoice in living faith among the nations—that is, among human beings—though they are not yet granted to glory in the appearance found among angels. They will indeed live in the shadow when they firmly hold by faith that he who was incarnate in the Virgin’s womb was God born before the ages; [Col. 0291B] when they love as God, coeternal with and like in majesty to the Father, him who was found as a human being to suffer harsh things for human beings.

In short, they will live when, putting behind them, as it were, those unworthy things which that man chose to endure among men, they understand and love God, blessed for ever, to be pre-eminent above all; when, leaving behind what any merely animal-minded persons can see and hold, they keep especially before their eyes that which only spiritual persons deserve to possess (ibid.). Therefore they first declare: “Christ the Lord, the Spirit before our face.”

Christ the Lord is held as Spirit before our face when our faith now beholds him not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit; when, recognizing that his flesh alone profits nothing, it knows him who gives life to be God, Spirit (John 6). For those who are still flesh-minded embrace very childishly the many things proclaimed of him according to the flesh; they do not place the things of Christ that come later after the earlier things, but, through impaired faith and ignorance of the order, put them first.

When Peter heard the prediction of Christ’s imminent passion, he was found to embrace the flesh rather more tenderly than the Spirit. He had Christ before his face, indeed, but as a human being who would die, not as the Spirit who raises up, not as God who will restore life to the dead. “May it be far from you,” he says (Matt. 16); “this will not happen; you will not die.” But Christ says: “Go behind me; you do not savour the things that are of God” (ibid.).

Therefore Paul, removing his hearers from human things, wishes them to become more ready for those things that are [Col. 0291D] God’s, judging rightly that the things of the flesh are to be put behind and that God and what belongs to him are to be placed before the face. “That you may walk,” he says, “worthily of God” (1 Thess. 2). And elsewhere: “Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus” (2 Cor. 5).

In this shadow or faith, in which, as was said above, unjust people may be permitted to be, though only the just may live, there is much labour while one lives in it; for wretched man does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or of love (Eccl. 9). But the Virgin Mother, who found grace with God beyond all others, keeps Sabbath in it and obtains a blessed jubilee. She not only lives—which is the common lot of all who labour—but, secure, sits, which is the special possession of one at rest.

For she is the one upon whom that Holy Spirit came, in whom the power of the Most High found a rest pleasing to itself. By the covering of its shadow, making her far removed from both fault and fear, it granted her a tranquil seat in love alone. “Under his shadow,” she says, “whom I had desired, I sat.”

With desire she had desired that God, the Son of God, should come into her; that grace wholly unknown to all should precede both his conception and his birth; that, after kissing her, he should fortify her with the seal of chastity, and preserve both mind and flesh in the uninjured flower of virginity. Having received this, the Virgin—now ignorant of fault or fear—sits as though upon a throne beneath the shade of most grateful refreshment. While the rest below still labour, hemmed in by poverty of merits, she already tastes in the great, prepared upper room an ineffable sweetness.

“And his fruit,” she says, “was sweet to my throat” [Col. 0292B]. The fruit of the shadow, or of the overshadowing Spirit, is eternal sweetness. The Virgin’s palate now senses it, and her inner mind tastes it more sweetly; but that flavour is still held, as it were, in the throat, while the belly hungers, its appetite not yet filled.

Certainly, in this life whatever heavenly sweetness is perceived beforehand, whatever divine and incorporeal reality the mind clothed in flesh experiences, is still, as it were, only in tasting: by it the desire of the taster is soothed, but it has not yet reached the belly, where perfect satiety is found. Thus the Virgin rightly says, to show both that she has obtained no small sweetness and that all sweetness is imperfect as long as life is lived here: “His fruit is sweet to my throat,” not yet “to my belly.” For she rejoices now to be delighted by a most sweet taste, and she awaits being fully satisfied when his glory shall appear.

Anyone who has observed the act of eating with slightly closer attention knows that food in the throat has not yet indeed been swallowed, but is being swallowed; and swallowing comes so near that it cannot, or scarcely can, be drawn back from outside to the mouth. The eater may therefore reckon as eaten what he feels already moving in his throat. So too, while the Virgin still lives under the law of mortals in this life, she is kindled by a love sweeter than that of other mortals, so that the fruit of love, or of the Beloved, is already sweet in her throat; and, through prevailing confidence, no threatening fear makes it bitter there.

For she has experienced that supreme and desirable good of the world to come in such a way that, while advancing toward perfection, [Col. 0292D] she is not uncertain of what remains. She already holds in her throat what we, far unequal to her, still hunger for, what we, still poor, scarcely perceive on the very tip of the tongue or with the lips. For neither we nor those like us have yet been brought to the point of rejoicing more fully, being introduced into that sanctuary of God. Although still living in the flesh, the Virgin draws no small confidence from it, and confidently already presumes as accomplished what will be more fully fulfilled.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“The King brought me into his wine-cellar; he set love in order within me.”

Whom and why she calls “King,” I recall having said above, when the Virgin mentioned that she had been brought into the King’s cellars. Though those cellars are considered to be richly furnished with many treasures, they are not, however, called wine-cellars [Col. 0293A]. Now the Virgin declares that she is brought into the wine-cellar, indicating that, through the passage of time, she is led onward toward progress of conscience. There she now rejoices not merely in the grace already received, but is intoxicated with incomparable joy as with an abundance of wine.

For if that most splendid cup of which you have read (Ps. 22) intoxicates any just persons, so that, when the Spirit descends from heaven, it makes them eloquent as though drenched with new wine (Acts 2), what should we judge to be the merit of the Virgin in whose womb God hid himself, and to whom the whole wine-cellar pours itself out more graciously than to one who has merely been brought inside? How could her mind, once brought in, fail to be intoxicated, when not a narrower cup, nor wisdom mixing wine in a bowl, but an overflowing cellar—the house of wine—produced abundance poured forth, and drenched her more richly like the rushing of a river through a city?

For the Most High, desiring his own particular tabernacle to be made beautiful and this holy one, holier than the rest, to be adorned with fitting virtues, did not bring forth small gifts from his inner sanctuary with a miserly hand; rather, he graciously brought her into the inner mysteries of his sanctuary itself. There the beloved alone is joined to her sole lover, and from the source itself, or in the source itself, she draws waters with fuller joy (Isa. 12). Washed in them, she is made radiant; drinking them, she is sweetly gladdened, intoxicated with joy, and strongly inflamed as with wine.

But this intoxication does not disturb the soul, confuse the virgin mind, darken the memory, or take away knowledge; rather, it pours knowledge in. It does not think evil, does not act perversely, loves righteousness, does not take up anger, does not inflict hatred, nourishes love, [Col. 0293C] and sets charity in order (1 Cor. 13): “He set love in order within me.”

It is no small merit and, indeed, no small holiness in her that not only charity but also the order of charity is pre-eminent. While love is poured out in many others, in her its outpouring remains especially unconfused. For many, although they love, do not maintain order in their love: either darkened by ignorance or oppressed by graver negligence, they love more what ought to be loved less, or less what ought to have been loved more; or they place last what ought worthily to have been set first.

But the Virgin, wisely taught in all these matters and hindered by no stains of negligence from fulfilling what she knew, loves herself in the Lord as is fitting; she loves, as it is written, every neighbour as herself (Matt. 22). Yet among those whom faith or nature makes neighbours, and whom the authority of written law commands to be loved in due measure, the prudent Virgin knows how to distinguish whom to embrace with lesser and whom with greater love, to whom to give less deference and whom to honour with greater diligence.

Finally, in Christ, whom she conceived by the Holy Spirit and bore, and in whom personal unity joined God and man, the true Mother loved each nature with such discriminating judgment that the charity which the same Son set in order within her did not go astray. First, she loved with all her heart and all her strength, without measure, God—whom she knew to be the Creator of heavenly and earthly things and the most orderly lover of the things he created—united to true flesh and wondrously made man [Col. 0294A].

In this love no limit or measure is commanded; no writer or Scripture has taught how greatly God is to be loved. Whoever is found to have expressed more subtly the measure of loving seems to have taught not how much God ought to be loved, but from how much of oneself he ought to be loved. “From your whole heart,” it says, “and from your whole soul, and from all your strength” (Luke 10).

This is the measure—if indeed it is a measure—by which the Virgin Mother rejoices to love God in Christ; its depth human speech cannot express fully. Even if a more fervent soul can somehow experience so great a sweetness, one who can easily explain it in words can scarcely be found. Therefore, from all that she had and all that she could do, she loved in her Son; she directed a stronger devotion toward the mightier power, toward incarnate deity. She preferred the Creator to every creature with fitting reverence, and held God united to man as more precious than all things.

But she loved as herself the man whom she knew to be her own virginal flesh, conceived without a man and born without her, his Mother’s, groaning; whom she knew to be her neighbour by nature and by the natural bond, as she had read it was fitting to do. For since no one hates his own flesh (Eph. 5), as you recall having read, even though one knows that any fault may have belonged to that flesh, how greatly must the Virgin Mother be believed to have loved the Son in whom there was no fault and in whom nature stood astonished at having lost its accustomed right?

For the Virgin, conceiving, underwent no embrace or sexual union; in giving birth she felt no bodily pain, no injury. Original sin, which long before had, as it were, been turned into nature, grieved at being driven far away and could not at all lay hold on such a birth [Col. 0294C]. From ancient times the law of sin used to anticipate every childbirth and drive both mother and son, as though tributaries, toward payment of usury. It stamped upon all who were born alike the impress of its own coinage, and none was so fortunate as to escape this pressure.

The Virgin alone, bringing forth in a wondrous manner the unique firstborn, experienced neither in conception nor in childbirth the universal sentence. She rejoiced to have such a neighbour—indeed, such a son—in whom the injury of original sin could assert no claim of its own. Therefore the Virgin rightly loves this neighbour as herself; and, if it is lawful to believe it, she must be said to love him more than herself, because she judges so great a man to be loved above every human being and embraced more tenderly and eagerly than either herself or all others.

What, taught by the Spirit, she understands, she lovingly understands must be done; and, through the working of that same Spirit, she is neither powerless nor ineffective in fulfilling it. Therefore she can—and does—love more than herself the human Son whom she has brought forth from herself in a manner beyond telling, just as she understands him ought to be loved.

We wretches, certainly, either cannot grasp in understanding those things which are perfect and supreme, or lack perfect and effective grace to fulfil them. Thus perhaps God, pitying our weaknesses, commands us for the present to love any human being as ourselves. But the Virgin, filled with God and rich in the fuller gift of grace, is borne up to the heights and to a loftier degree of merit. The man whom she knew to be born from herself materially, unencumbered by any original stains, pure in flesh and in Spirit united to God, inaccessible to all creatures—him she loves above all those whom she understands to have been endowed with lesser merits and grace. She judges it fitting not merely not to prefer herself to him, but not even to compare herself with him in love.

The one who is loved himself inspired this order of love, and set this special charity in order in his loving Mother, so that he who at his birth had wondrously granted that the Virgin should be both virgin and fruitful might in a similarly wondrous manner render her, if not equal in merits, yet second to himself. For, inferior to Christ alone, she surpasses all others in the brightness of holiness; and holiness is made radiant only by the excellence [Col. 0295B] of charity, which, the more subtly and clearly it apprehends the necessary order, the more perfectly and effectively shows itself to be nearest to Christ.

This benefit Christ works in the wine-cellar, into which the Virgin has been introduced and rejoices to burn with the fire of charity, judging nothing more welcome or delightful than to burn, nothing more healthful in this present life than to be affected or to languish with the heat of charity. Of this she adds: “Strengthen,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXIV
“Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love.” Those who love unlawfully and have not yet attained the object of their desire are said to grow sick and waste away as their longing is delayed; and their ruined mind incurs the pains of languor if fulfilment of its wretched wish does not come to its aid. Thus Amnon, who loved Tamar, Absalom’s sister, when he could not yet accomplish what he had wickedly desired, fell ill; and, despairing of being able to bring his intended wickedness to completion, he grew thin and declined day by day. “It came to pass,” he says, “that Amnon, son of David, loved Tamar, Absalom’s sister, and wasted away exceedingly for her, so that he fell ill because of his love for her. And Jonadab said to him: ‘Why are you, the king’s son, growing so thin day after day?’ And Amnon said: ‘I love Tamar, Absalom’s sister’” (2 Kings [Samuel] 13).

If one burdened by unlawful love falls ill and wastes away, if, oppressed by lustful desire, he is worn down day after day, how is the Virgin Mother, loving the Bridegroom, to be thought sick—she who wastes away not through Venus’s incestuous passion, but through the ardour of a chaste wound into her own salvation (salutare)? For she loves; and in loving, as though wounded, she slips into a kind of faintness, since she has not yet grasped what she seeks. Yet she so fixes the eye of her mind upon perfection that, not content with what she has, she pours out all her desire upon what is yet to be had; and, as though she possessed nothing, she burns to cling to what she is to obtain.

Thus, reaching toward what she desires and not yet sensing it accomplished, she languishes and fails. She cannot obtain what she desires; she yearns and waits, and complains that she still does not have the fulfilment. What could the Virgin experience in this life that was healthier than this languor, or more languid than this health? She was unwilling that anything tasting of earth should be found within her soul; she wished to cling to God alone in unbending embraces, [Col. 0296A] and perhaps was still compelled to remain here for the sake of others.

She wished, but was unable, to enjoy God without hindrance; to be released from the heavy body; not to be worn down by labour; to rejoice in jubilation. She judged it good to enjoy invisible goods, while she still seemed necessarily held by visible things. Therefore, for one who wills but cannot, her bodily life is somewhat burdensome, but certainly no little fruitful for the young women who must be nurtured. For the example and teaching of the Virgin benefited the holy apostles, while through her the order of life and the discipline of morals flourished among them.
