Seeing herself delayed from Him whom she loves more greatly, she wishes some consolations to be afforded her expectation; and she invites the young women living with her to make progress, so that, upon seeing Him, she may endure her own incompleteness more patiently, as it were.

“If,” she says, “the presence of perfect rest does not yet receive me; if faith cannot yet pass into the rule of sight; if impossibility causes languor because possibility has not yet been fulfilled; if I am afflicted with groaning so long as imperfection is not healed by perfection—then at least I desire that you meanwhile be advanced toward fitting progress, and that by my word and example alike you may merit with me the same blessedness.

“If that supreme and discerning disposer of all things wishes me to remain here longer; if by profound counsel He wishes my presence to benefit you; if He delays me from glory, I do not accuse the good pleasure of Him who delays me, and, for as long as it pleases Him, I do not refuse the labour imposed upon me. Meanwhile, while there is time, gather about the bed of my seeming sickness; support me, labouring under delayed desire, with spring flowers—[Col. 0296C] that is, with your good affections. Remove far from yourselves the former dryness and the harshness of winter, and with flowery diversion and springtime consolation revive me, languishing in love’s heat.

“For it will be no small consolation, no slight refreshment to one burning; it will be reckoned a poultice, oil, or bandage to one who is ill: namely, if, having driven winter frost far away, you bloom in springtime beauty; if after the flowers of affections you produce the riper fruits of works. A good tree, indeed, is adorned with lovely flowers in the welcome season of spring; not content with beauty, it is afterwards laden with the fruit of its works. When the country husbandman who laboured upon it sees himself surrounded by these fruits, he rejoices that his labour has been recompensed with a fruitful gift.

“So too the Virgin wishes the young women who are with her to take the place of a good tree; placed in the Bridegroom’s garden, she wishes them to bloom in faith and desire, and in the passage of time to abound in good works. Supported or surrounded by these, she may await the Bridegroom all the more richly for having awaited Him longer. For the more persons shall deserve to profit by her word and example and, when the Bridegroom comes, be found in her company, the richer and more joyful she herself will appear to Him at His coming; and she will obtain greater glory not only for her own merits but also for theirs.

She therefore rightly desires and asks to be supported with flowers and surrounded with apples: since she does not yet know God face to face, she may meanwhile rejoice in the progress of those whom she teaches, and, when the time comes, may glory more abundantly because of them and together with them. Nor does she ask merely to be supported with flowers, but also to be surrounded with apples; for a hungry person cannot be satisfied with flowers without fruit. Although the latter must necessarily be preceded by the former, the flower delights the eye indeed, but is certainly not found sufficient for food.

And truly, just as without virtue the appearance of piety is not fruitful, so faith without works is read and understood to be idle (James 2); affection is not enough if, when it has time and opportunity, it is not brought to effect; and “understanding is good for all who have it”—or rather, who put it into practice (Psalm 110 [111]). “Support me,” therefore, she says, “with flowers; surround me with apples,” that I may rejoice when I hear you say: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5). And this: “We cannot but speak of what we have heard and seen” (Acts 4). Let me rejoice also when I perceive [Col. 0297B] that you go away rejoicing from the presence of the council (Acts 5), because you have been judged worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus.

“Support me,” I say, “because I languish with love”—not from an injury to the head, not from paralysis of the limbs, but from love; not from the oppression of fever, not from any bodily discomfort, but from love. Nothing more ardent, nothing more vehement can anyone experience when what is loved is tasted, seen yet not possessed, believed to be offered and ardently sought, yet unable to be found.

But she immediately adds how both His presence is felt and His absence grieved; and in one verse she thus sets forth the favour of His presence and the delay of His absence.

## CHAPTER XXV

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” [Col. 0297C].

The Bridegroom’s left hand beneath the Bride’s head indicates that He is present, whereas His right hand as one that *will* embrace rather than *is* embracing suggests that He is absent. Thus, while a sorrowful complaint is made concerning His absence, there is nevertheless good reason to rejoice in whatever measure He is present. For after saying, “His left hand is under my head,” she adds, “and his right hand will embrace me,” not “embraces me”; thereby indicating that the benefit of the left hand is already possessed in the present, whereas the present embrace of the right hand is not yet possessed.

Since the Virgin had said that she languished with love’s fire, she indicates, in order to accord with the languor, that she lies down. For she appears to say that the left hand is not placed upon but placed beneath her head; and it is certain that a consoling hand lies beneath one who is lying down, not one who is standing. Thus in the Gospel the centurion’s servant is said to lie down; and if you ask the reason, it is because he was paralysed and grievously tormented. For him the centurion hastens, having sent a messenger, to anticipate the Lord, praying that He may deign to help the one lying down by His most powerful word. “Lord,” he says, “my servant lies at home” (Matthew 8). Why does he lie down? “He is paralysed,” he says, “and grievously tormented.” What do you wish to be done for you? “I am not worthy,” he says, “that you should enter beneath my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant will be healed” (*ibid.*).

Again, a great multitude is said to lie in the five porticoes, and the cause given is nothing other than various bodily illnesses. They await the angel’s customary descent into the pool to stir the water, so that whoever first descends after the water’s movement may feel healing when his body has been washed. “In these porticoes,” he says, “a great multitude lay.” Why did they lie there? He explains: “Of sick persons.” Why in the porticoes? He adds: “Waiting for the moving of the water” (John 5).

If then the multitude and the centurion’s servant are said to lie down because they are held by sickness or paralysis, it is not incongruous that the Virgin, who says she languishes by love’s violence, should also be understood to lie down, as is proper to one languishing. To her, languishing and lying down, the Bridegroom does not long remain absent; rather, in gracious favour, the Beloved presents Himself to His beloved. And lest love languish more harshly and sickness endure a harsher delay, He places His left hand beneath her head, softer than a pillow or any soft support.

The Bridegroom’s left hand, as some maintain, is temporal prosperity: strength, riches, beauty, lineage, literal learning, and whatever in this world appears to smile upon one for a time—things which no one can obtain unless God gives them. They are quite fittingly called the left hand because such things are not denied in this present life equally to evil and good persons, and because they are especially sought with all their efforts by those who are set at the left hand of the strict Judge in that true and severe judgment.

The Bridegroom, being present, places all these beneath the Bride’s head when He sets her holy mind above all transient things. What a perverse person, in corrupt judgment, considers supreme enticements, the Virgin presses down and despises, judging them losses for Christ. For as the seeker of such things exults and dances when he obtains them, so—indeed, far differently—the wise Virgin rejoices in despising them. And whereas she pleases the Bridegroom by despising all else as though her head were set above it through regard for Him, that man displeases Him by putting himself beneath those same transient things.

But the Bridegroom’s right hand is that sweeter, fruitful, and life-giving grace which the merely natural person, blinded in heart, does not perceive. Only that person knows it—or rather, His immortal Spirit knows it—to whom the spiritual anointing gives understanding and teaches knowledge. The Virgin, while still placed in this body, already tastes this grace; but the body’s presence confines it, so that she cannot receive it in an expanded bosom. She perceives it, and takes the greatest delight in what she has perceived; she delights and hungers, yet, hungering, is not yet able to be satisfied.

This delight indeed has a beginning here but no end. It pours itself into those who love it; to those who desire it, it promises an end; but it gives to those who worthily persevere that end [Col. 0298D] whose beginning knows trouble, but whose consummation knows no end. Seeing this, the Prophet says: “Delights are at your right hand for ever” (Psalm 15 [16]). Since this right hand is not yet granted fully to one who loves and waits, while the present life, like the left hand, is preferred before it—and is the more burdensome the longer it lasts—she feels this left hand yet does not assent to it, but surpasses it by the excellence of her mind. She hopes for the other and declares it future, which, though not in time, is already preferred by its own merit. “His right hand,” she says, “will embrace me.” He who has not wholly denied me His presence or visitation, while bringing these temporal gifts from Himself into contempt, will be seen to present Himself to me far more fully and sweetly when His right hand, and life unfailing, deigns to embrace me.

[Col. 0299A] Some wish a different meaning to be found in the left hand placed beneath her: namely, that it signifies spiritual gifts which the Bridegroom, by divine grace, wishes to bestow upon the Bride, adorning her with them while she lives here and sweetly refreshing her as she labours beneath the sun. For she had confessed that she languished in love’s heat; and, held by languor, as has been said, appeared to lie down. Therefore, lest the languor of one lying down decline into weariness under the pressure of delay, the Bridegroom puts His left hand beneath her head, so that she may rest her weakness upon it.

The Virgin indeed grieves that the fuller vision of the Creator has not yet been granted to her; she wishes to be released, because that vision is inaccessible to all mortals. The inner mind languishes and lies down, as though weary, under grievous delay; beneath it are placed steadfast faith, more certain hope, and tireless charity. The welcome companionship of these virtues, or their shared grace, is present concern, faithful guardianship, and spiritual consolation. Since flowers and apples are not enough to surround the Virgin, they serve for her languishing mind, her seemingly weary head, as a pillow.

“While time weighs upon me,” she says, “while the days are evil, here I shall rest a little. While I languish with love, while I lie down in sickness, I shall hide in your bosom. Here is rest; here is a dwelling-place, until at last I grow old—not by a century of years, but by a century of merits. When this is completed, may my long-lasting languor depart, and may I be renewed like an eagle. For then and thereafter, according to the poet, I shall count the years in Nestor’s stead by the right hand; indeed, passing from the left hand to the right, according to the Prophet, I shall keep watch in the morning. In the morning I shall stand watching, and contemplate the One desired—or rather, my Desire—and beneath His right hand, [Col. 0299C] when His glory appears, I shall be satisfied” (Psalm 16 [17]).

No longer will the left hand—that is, the consolation of present virtues—be placed beneath my languishing head; instead, the right hand and the full, eternal vision of God will be granted. It will embrace me, standing and seeing, in dearer arms; it will surround me wholly, and leave nothing languishing anywhere. Meanwhile, while I await the future glory of His right hand, I shall not despise grace already present or the consolation of the left hand. Hidden in it, I shall rejoice as place and time permit; when faith has passed into sight and hope into possession, I shall glory.

But the Bridegroom, seeing the Virgin stirred by so great a love and lulled in the soft bosom of the left hand beneath hope of the right, speaks thus: “I adjure you,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 0299D]

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not awaken or make the beloved wake until she herself wishes.”

As the Bridegroom speaks to the young women, He conforms Himself to our customs and solemnly entreats—indeed, sternly adjures—them in human fashion. He knows that negligence or forgetfulness sometimes closes and blocks the ears of the weak, and that transgression of commandments does not long remain unpunished. Therefore, lest He seem to command carelessly and they fail to take pains in observing the commandment as though it were most trivial, He binds them more sternly and introduces an oath, so that the sacrament may inspire fear in those whom weakness renders sluggish.

“I do not wish,” He says, “that you should call my beloved back [Col. 0300A] to temporal business or care: she to whom I have given my spiritual left hand beneath her, and to whom, resting in grace, I have granted the expectation of eternal glory—until she herself judges that the same care will be salutary for you. For she knows better when she ought to devote herself to spiritual leisure or spiritual work; when she ought to care for you by word and temporal provision; when to read more devoutly, pray more urgently, meditate more intensely, and when to turn herself to you, of whom she is not forgetful.

“When she sees that her return and presence are necessary to you—she who certainly loves not so much to be put forward before you as to benefit you—she will inflict upon spiritual leisure something like an injury, and convert necessary acts into voluntary ones. I wish you, then, to bear her return to you patiently until she wishes it; for she will wish it when she sees the fitting time approaching for you. She knows that your affairs must not be wholly abandoned, whereas her spiritual leisure is above all to be preserved, though nevertheless sometimes interrupted.

Those who are placed above others in the Church by care and office are instructed by this teaching, if they are willing to consider it more carefully: they should devote their highest effort to spiritual leisure, and not recoil from it because of temporal attractions and enticements. Very often we are bound by such great cords of negligence in regard to spiritual matters, and are found so lukewarm—or rather cold—toward them, that we hasten rather to run about, hear, see, and chatter, judging nothing more burdensome or more troublesome than to sit, read, write, and meditate.

To crown the evil, if we see some persons unwilling to cling to secular business, despising roving about, speaking sparingly, abhorring gossip, devoting themselves to reading, more gladly labouring in meditation, and committing to lasting writing whatever they understand, [Col. 0300C] we mock them with pursed lips, hooked nose, and raised eyebrow; and when stones are lacking, we stone them with a slanderous tongue. Why is this? Unless it is because we do not hear the Bridegroom’s warnings, by which He adjures the daughters of Jerusalem; or rather, though hearing, we do not obey at all when malice intervenes. Thus we surely incur the anger of Him who, as the stricter Judge, hates and persecutes slanderers: “He who slanders his neighbour,” He says, “him I persecuted” (Psalm 100 [101]).

Nevertheless, it is proper to those who seem to preside over others in the Church not to lord it over the clergy but to offer themselves as an example to their subjects; not to entangle their minds in external cares and secular business, but with an eager mind to devote themselves to spiritual pursuits; not gladly to take part in legal cases or worldly disputes, but to be ready, with fitting attention, for literary study and spiritual leisure. Let their whole will be devoted to these higher matters; let necessity, not pleasure, call them back to lower things. Let them hide themselves in those higher matters, diligently drawing forth the hidden things of wisdom; let them return to these lower matters patiently, for the sake of brothers and neighbours.

But those who desire to disparage them and draw them away from their spiritual purpose should fear the Bridegroom’s warnings, by which the Bride is aided and the daughters of Jerusalem adjured. For the studies of such persons will not be harmed by our envious murmuring, while unjust detractors will be pursued by the indignation and punishment of the strict Judge.

But why are the daughters of Jerusalem adjured by the gazelles and stags of the fields, as though they were known to fear or love animals of this kind, so that by mention of them they might be more attentively moved to keep the command they have heard? Who could believe that the command of one adjuring them in this way would be observed more carefully rather than judged useless and wholly frivolous, when scarcely anyone would be held by the reverence of any oath if that by which one is adjured were considered of no weight or importance?

Yet in this sacred drama, though things carnal and contemptible seem to be named, a sounder understanding loves to seek spiritual things in them. Rejecting what the literal surface sounds and clamours, it values highly only what spiritual meaning shows itself to those who seek it.

The gazelle, then, they say, has this implanted by nature: it is not content to feed in plains and valleys, but with the greatest care seeks the lofty peaks of mountains, as though it could nowhere else find a pleasant sufficiency. It passes by, with a certain disdain, the broad expanse of fields and the low, sunken valleys granted from the beginning, by nature’s laws, to all grazing animals alike; it approaches rocks inaccessible to the rest, delights to feed there, to leap confidently, and to remain there without weariness.

By it may fittingly be figured that virtue which, not content with transient goods, strives to contemplate things highest and heavenly; which surpasses the matters in which the common weakness of many seems to linger, and gladly wills and is able to embrace certain heights inaccessible to lesser persons. Forgetting the troubles of this present life as things left behind, joined to the companies of angels—indeed, advancing beyond angels in desire—it has passed beyond the plain of lower things, is carried away in love of things above, and, hanging upon the highest summits, feeds upon the sweetness of eternal things.

But the stag, which through fitting hunger and eagerness devours serpents and venom—things which other animals abhor and judge foreign to food—signifies that virtue of mind which delights to swallow deadly sins and applies a hungry diligence to destroy them. For there are some who do not attain the excellence of contemplation, but gird themselves with a strong sword to destroy vices. They devour the multitude of the lost as bread for food, and by a wholesome repast annul the power of sins. When the deceit of attackers clings to them like an arrow, they compel it to rebound by a skill quickly sought; nor do they permit the harmful iron to rule long in the wound, but, once it has been drawn out, they recover through healing medicine.

Since it is clear that this virtue belongs to humble persons of every kind—those who are known to be not harsh through perversity but level through benevolence of character, and who, even if they have done great things, nevertheless say that they are unprofitable servants—He therefore calls them stags of the fields: those, namely, who bravely embrace the broad commandment of twofold love, and run the way of the commandments when their heart and soul are enlarged.

Finally, when stags prepare to cross deep waters, they arrange themselves in the crossing so that the head of each follower rests upon the haunches of the one before, and in the same manner each supports the one who follows it. But the one that has placed itself before all the others and is sustained by none preceding it, when weariness hinders it from bearing the labour of swimming and carrying, leaves the one supported by it and hastens to take its place at the end, knowing that this one is still free and is not bearing another follower. Thus, bearing one another’s burdens, they strive to fulfil the law of Christ (Galatians 6); they imitate a building in which one stone loves to sustain another. Their mutual support is wrought by the affection of charity; in its strong ship they are drawn away from shipwreck and led to the harbour of the will.

“I adjure you,” He says, “daughters of Jerusalem, [Col. 0302B] by the gazelles and stags of the fields. You whom it befits to be Jerusalem—that is, daughters of peace, without which the present vision of God can in no way be yours—I wish to adjure you by those virtues through which vices are trampled underfoot and rewards loved, lest, by a misguided counsel, you presume to oppose the Virgin’s sounder desire.

“By those virtues, I say, which are lifted higher in seeking and contemplating God, and likewise by those which are extended more broadly in love for one’s neighbour, I adjure you not to assail your neighbour at rest with troubles and be found resisting God, in whose left hand she reclines. For this rest of hers is useful and pleasing to her who rests, and not displeasing to Me, who more fully know what benefits each person. Therefore, when the time comes, I wish her to apply herself diligently to rest, and I forbid you who are weaker from murmuring or judging.

Who will grant me that I may not only neither awaken nor make awake any persons who sleep, nor be found guilty of the commandment by rashly judging those at rest, but may also rest in the left hand of the Bridegroom, who gives His own grace, and hide in the secret place of the tabernacle from heat, storm, and rain? Happy am I if I may deserve to die thus, to sleep thus; if the Bridegroom deigns to refresh me with the benefit of this death, with the grace of sleep; if the daughters of Jerusalem are forbidden to hinder this, lest I be compelled, that is, to return either to life’s troubles or to the wakefulnesses of sin (Numbers 23).

Happy, I say, if my soul, dying the death of the righteous and failing in longing for the courts of the Lord, may desire this (Psalm 83 [84]); if it may fall asleep either in the Bridegroom’s left hand or at least in the Bride’s lap; if it may learn by experience how sweet and pleasant was that sleep for the Virgin—the sleep from whose kiss the first book took its beginning, and in whose sleep this second book receives its end. For I judge it fitting that, for the present, my pen should not hasten to pursue what remains, but, while the Bride sleeps, should itself recline a little. When she wishes to awaken, and charity constrains this watchful woman to speak, the pen will, according to its strength, gird itself again for the labour interrupted rather than abandoned.

## THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0303]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0303A]

“The voice of my beloved.”

The Bridegroom rightly wished to warn the daughters of Jerusalem under oath, lest they presume to remove the Beloved from sleep or repose before she wished it. He knew that, when the suitable time came, she would awaken more fittingly and return to those whom charity compelled her to remember. Having tasted the sleep in which she deserved to fall asleep in the left hand, she does not wish to pass over in silence the savour she drank there. But, for the sake of her neighbours, interrupting for a little while what she had begun, she rises, awakens, and reports to us what she has perceived.

First, however, she indicates that she has heard the Bridegroom speaking and recognized the speaker’s voice as well known. Concerned for her sleep, He not only places His left hand beneath the sleeper’s head, but also opposes Himself to the troubles that come upon her with a terrible oath.

## CHAPTER II

“The voice of my beloved.”

This voice, I say, which makes me serene amid repose and sweet silence; which excludes worldly troubles from the calm chamber of one at rest; which thunders and adjures, driving troublesome assaults far away; which satisfies, not wholly but in part, the desire of one asleep—this voice, I say, is undoubtedly the voice of Him whom I loved, whom I have often found already favourable to me in cherishing and defending me.

I recognize Him whom I love; I sense His voice now present; by hearing I perceive that He loves and does not neglect one who loves Him. His voice sounds on my behalf, speaks concerning me, bestows a protection favouring me, and gives you who are set below an instruction neither useless nor contemptible. His voice declares me beloved, plainly indicates that my will pleases Him, teaches you discipline, teaches knowledge, and teaches goodness also (Psalm 111 [112]). It admits me into a chamber—or rather, a kind of vestibule—of welcome peace, and permits me to sleep a little; while you wait, it does not keep silent about what it judges inwardly expedient.

Therefore I, the Bridegroom’s friend, stand and rejoice because of the Bridegroom’s voice (John 3). When He who is heard appears, I shall rejoice more abundantly; and would that, until I see Him, I may not see death. But when will He come? Why does He weave delays? Do you think I shall see Him? Would that He might rend the heavens and come (Isaiah 64)! I desire now that no herald speak beforehand and no forerunner go before; rather, I desire Him who speaks to draw nearer, so that my heart may see and rejoice when the word of that prophecy is fulfilled which He uttered through Isaiah’s mouth in truthful proclamation: “I am He who spoke; behold, I am here” (Isaiah 52).

Yet, as far as I seem able to foretell—or rather, as far as I already seem to sense—behold, He comes: He has found the way of wisdom, the manner of journeying, and the fitting time. And He whom I desire, for whom I sigh, whom I embrace with continual prayers—behold, He comes with force, and is now nearer, at the doors.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0304A]

“Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.” The Virgin burns to look more closely upon him whom she loves, seeing—and not grudging—that his presence is not possessed uselessly; and she who first perceives him coming announces it to every hearer, so that, hearing the announcer’s word, each may run to meet the one who comes. For she is not stirred by envy if an abundance of him is given to others also, if the beloved, on arriving, offers himself to be seen by the rest as well, so that he may be loved: his love reconciles those who love him and instils in them spiritual harmony, so that one who first burns with love does not fear to have a companion, not a rival.

Thus here too the virgin beloved does not conceal the beloved’s presence or arrival, but announces it to the daughters, desiring him to come to the benefit of all. For this reason, a little above, she proclaimed him gracious in beauty [Col. 0304B], in order subsequently to show that he is fruitful not for herself alone, but for others also. Above she says: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely” (Song 1). And a little later: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved” (Song 2). But why does she here proclaim as coming one whom, by declaring him beautiful there, she plainly implies was not absent? For there she did not say that, after his presence had been granted, he withdrew, such that she must necessarily say that he came again.

But, as those with experience know, it is characteristic of lovers, or of love, that he who loves and desires to be held in the bond of a closer affection sometimes withdraws himself, so that he may draw his beloved after him and be anxiously sought; and sometimes returns, that he may soothe her and be held more eagerly. Thus he goes and returns, and he who, as sounder faith believes, is never and nowhere absent, is now said to be absent and now present to us [Col. 0304C]. For he who is always and everywhere present by the privilege of his unbounded majesty is nevertheless called absent when he withholds, and present when he bestows upon us the grace of his goodness.

Now, therefore, the Virgin rejoices and announces that he is coming, signifying that in his coming there is no delay and that he finds no obstacle; rather, he leaps upon mountains and passes over the hills that confront him, so that he seems by swift progress to arrive at his intended destination. But speaking mystically, the Virgin intended “mountains” to mean the good angels, whom it is certain shine with the excellence of primordial holiness. Created lofty, they did not fall through the breath of pride or the impulse of greed; rather, through the merit of perseverance—or by grace alone—they advanced [Col. 0304D] to an unwavering firmament.

God leaps upon them when he does not keep hidden within himself alone the secrets of his counsel, but shows himself to them as wonderful in his counsels above the children of men; when he deigns to reveal all at once to the angels in the heavenly court what he purposes in the course of time to accomplish among human beings. For the salvation of humankind, which God chose to work in the midst of the earth, distributing it through different places and times by a saving dispensation and providence, he first chose to make known all at once to the angels in heaven, through whose ministry he would afterwards bestow his benefits upon the earth.

“Are they not all,” he says, “ministering spirits sent forth for service on behalf of those who shall inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1). Therefore, when God comes to the Virgin, in whom he works a wonderful mystery, he first leaps among the angels, to whom swift and complete knowledge is presented. He makes known to Gabriel what Gabriel, once instructed, will afterwards bring to Mary. God unfolds the prophecy to the angel all at once; the angel unfolds it successively to the Virgin: “Hail,” he says, “full of grace; behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” (Luke 1), and so forth.

God also leaps among the angels when, not through himself directly but through them, he approaches us to instruct us, give counsels of salvation, or bestow whatever benefit; and when they are found suddenly to advance or leap toward us, whether to teach or to govern us [Col. 0305B], he may be said to do this, since it is evident that those who do it obey him. “I heard,” says Daniel, “the voice of a man between the banks of the Ulai; and he cried and said: Gabriel, make this man understand the vision” (Dan. 8). And when Mary asks, “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1), the angel says: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you” (ibid.).

Whether, then, God is said to leap among angels—that is, toward angels—or perhaps toward human beings through angels, so that he may lavishly grant them the presence both of himself and of his own; nevertheless, he passes over the hills when he deprives them of the grace of this gift and does not enlighten them by the like benefit of his knowledge. The hills are the demons, whom it is certain surpass earthly human beings by the privilege of nature [Col. 0305C], but cannot be compared with heavenly spirits because of the desert of their sin. Having fallen from among those spirits, they no longer rise to equal eminence; having fallen down to human beings, they swell more wickedly above them.

From them God conceals the mystery hidden from the ages; he does not reveal the grace of his coming, the mystery of great godliness. But, passing over those whose good nature the perversity of pride disgraces, he reveals himself and his wisdom to better angels or human beings: “We speak wisdom,” says Paul, “among the perfect; wisdom which none of the rulers of this age knew” (1 Cor. 2). And when Micaiah prophesied more truly, Zedekiah son of Chenaanah said: “Has the Spirit of the Lord then left me and spoken to you?” (3 Kings 22).

Indeed it is so. The Spirit of truth leaves and passes over the proud and false [Col. 0305D], but saves those humble in spirit and teaches them by the gift and presence of his goodness. Toward these he hastens like a giant exulting, and permits himself to be more sensibly felt as present; those abandoned to forgetfulness he flies over with a light leap and does not admit to knowledge of himself.

Nor is it foreign to an appropriate meaning if the Virgin herself is said to possess mountains and hills, so that her eminence in spiritual and temporal goods may be commended. Her spiritual goods are rightly compared to mountains; her temporal goods to hills, which, although great, are not equal to spiritual goods. The mountains in the Virgin are especially the gifts of those virtues through which, or because of which, we know that it was granted to that Virgin to deserve pre-eminence over others in the Church by a lofty distinction, and worthily to please him who is truly called the Mountain of mountains [Col. 0306A]. Her love is a mountain; humility is a mountain; chaste integrity of purity is a mountain. Upon these the Bridegroom leaps—that is, he shows himself present in the magnificence of divine majesty. Into these he pours himself wholly, according to the angel’s word, “fullness of grace” (Luke 1), so that in them the incomparable height of the Bride may excel and rejoice.

That her love was great—not because more forgiveness was remitted to her as one who had sinned, but because the grace of the Beloved entrusted more to her as one who loved—she herself indicates a little above in this drama, saying: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2). And she first stated the merit: “For I languish with love” (ibid.). What excellence and merit her humility must be believed to possess she too indicates; nor is any doubt to be entertained, since that regard of God chose her to behold her, and the Virgin, once chosen, believed that she might answer more confidently concerning herself: “For he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 2).

Finally, Isaiah did not fail to discern the integrity of her purity in body and heart; and the angel, much later, confirmed the ancient prophecy. Since nothing like it was heard before or afterwards, it is clear that this was fortified by the excellence of singular holiness: “Behold,” they say, “a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7; Luke 10). Such mountains the one who came and leaped wished to take from and confer upon the Virgin; the Virgin strove to return and offer those same mountains to their giver. In these he rendered himself present to her with a lavish hand, full of grace; in these she rendered herself pleasing to him above all women (Ps. 44).

Finally, the daughters of Tyre are read to entreat the face of the King with gifts; and here he is presented upon the mountains—that is, in the most exalted gifts [Col. 0306C; reading uncertain]. Seeing her own gifts and his gifts, by which he raised the Virgin to such exceptional eminence, returned to him, he gave himself to her in them, as it were wholly, by a grace-bestowing leap.

The hills, however, over which he is said to leap are those gifts of the Bridegroom which, though he wished to bestow them greatly upon the Virgin, do not contain the summit of religion or perfection of life. They display rather an honourableness suited to the person, not an inseparable companion of religion. For beauty, family, and learning, which flourished in the Virgin with a certain excellence, were fitting for honourableness, but not so necessary for salvation that, without them, a place at the banquet cannot sometimes be found for some persons, or that, in their absence, anyone’s holiness may despair of being brought into the joy of his Lord [Col. 0306D].

Yet the Bridegroom, wishing that nothing honourable or necessary should be lacking to the Virgin, made her holy in inward goods and graceful in outward ones. He gave himself wholly to the former, nor did he forsake what was to remain with enduring rank; he attended to the latter in passing, as things that would pass away by the privilege of nature. In passing over, or leaping over, these, he did not despise them in arrogance or hatred; but he did not behold with a fixed gaze things shining with transient bloom. Comparing with better things those things which present grace had elevated, but which their end would impair, he transferred himself rather to the former and did not cling to the latter, which have an end.

Beauty of face has an end; bodily appearance is not held by a permanent tether; parental glory passes away; the succession of lineage is not long esteemed as a great thing. Prophecy shall cease, as you have read (1 Cor. 8), and knowledge shall be destroyed [Col. 0307A]. These and things like them he who gives them does not reject, but beholds them as one passing by. For the Virgin is proclaimed commendable not chiefly because of these things, but rather because of those which incomparable holiness produces. Upon these, as upon mountains, he who comes wishes to leap; those of unequal merit, like hills, he wishes to pass over.

He himself is the supreme giver of good things and the lover of all that he gives; in him all justice is found, and no injustice. While distributing many things to his own, he does not measure all things by one mode or weight, but distinguishes each and bestows on each fitting care. Therefore the Virgin adds concerning him: “My beloved is like,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER IV

“My beloved is like a gazelle and a young stag.” [Col. 0307B] Many people are not led by fitting discernment toward what must be done, but are either held back by negligence or led astray by ignorance. And when the slower foot sticks fast or the understanding that should go before is darkened, they do not seek worthy things or bring good undertakings to their intended result. I think no one among human beings has been unacquainted with this kind of plague; it was inevitably implanted in all the descendants of the first parent by that first parent. Thus they commonly either do not see, or cannot go, where they might rejoice to find life and light both for themselves and for their own.

For what happened to the first parent when he first sinned through fault alone, not nature, exists in us later and far more miserable people through both fault and nature. By a sufficiently wretched law we now either do not wish, or cannot, free ourselves from such stains. And Paul is altogether truthful when he says: “By nature we are children of wrath” (Eph. 2). Would that you, Paul, were a man without the spirit and spoke falsehood instead (Mic. 2)! Would that you were not led against the law of the spirit by another law of the flesh! Yet, though you now rightly will but still cannot wholly accomplish, you judge that there is no condemnation for you, because God reckons as done whatever you thus will but cannot yet fully do.

But I, wretched and far inferior to Paul—my eye grows dark, my spirit languishes, and bends toward destruction under its languor. Corrupt nature is at work; natural vice prevails; bound by the law of the flesh, I do not obey the spiritual law. Therefore, when someone reads me the new Gospel or presents the old prophecy; when David more frequently sounds psalmody upon the ten-stringed psaltery; when Paul spurs me on, urging me with stern counsels to advance, worthily following those set over me and likewise going before those subject to me [Col. 0307D]—I, stiff-necked, am nothing but an ass before a lyre, and, with the goad accomplishing nothing, a heavy ox standing in anger beneath its natural weight.

For when I take up a psalm and the harmony of both New and Old Scripture, and am commanded to sound the timbrel and render a concordant symphony, I know only how to bray, how to make a badly sweet melody resound. I do not wish to follow Deborah (Judg. 5) or imitate Moses and Miriam (Exod. 15). Unhappy man that I am, whose soul has been branded with this cautery by the corruptible body, whose intent mind earthly habitation has thus weighed down with many concerns (Wis. 9), whom ass-like dullness makes obtuse and foolish, and an indolence like that of sluggish cattle makes slow and backward in goodness.

On the other hand, happy is that man whose mind, conceived of the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0307] An allusion to the article of the Creed: “Conceived of the Holy Spirit.”], is not dulled by the burden of flesh; whose willing of what is always good is not blunted by inability; who contemplates with keen understanding things uncertain and hidden from others, and by effective power accomplishes whatever he wills. Happy, I say, is the man who knows neither the dullness of an ass nor the sloth of an ox; who, by innate power alone, effectively prevails both in subtle matters and in remote ones; who prevails in both, having sight like a gazelle and being also like a young stag, which in swift course passes more quickly to what it seeks, as those who know the diverse natures of beasts report.

For among different creatures there is much diversity of nature. Although the gazelle is slower than the stag, it sees more sharply and more subtly perceives and distinguishes what is suitable, or perhaps unsuitable, for it as it grazes. Indeed, it is said to possess within itself a certain liquid by which, if someone prudently anoints the eye, it is sharpened for better sight. Thus the gazelle itself not only possesses a sight more ready in sharpness, but the anointing of this inward liquid grants us too the grace of seeing [Col. 0308B].

Who is worthily like this except he to whom every will speaks and the hidden thing of every heart lies open: the Bridegroom and beloved of the Virgin, from whom nothing is hidden; who judges and distinguishes the causes of all things by strict and penetrating examination, and widely separates and sets apart the evil from the best, and the good from the worst? Alone among human beings truly human, he beholds at once the eastern and western regions; he is prevented from viewing neither by distance nor by obstacle. In examining things he is not deceived by a false appearance, and error or forgetfulness does not lead him away from true judgment.

Indeed, in him is found that liquid suited to healing, as he knows far better who experiences it not merely by knowing but by feeling. If anyone eagerly pours it more carefully over the eye in order to see, blindness is removed and dimness does not cast its mist over the sight. This liquid is the Spirit of Christ, the water of wisdom, the fountain of living water, the power that went forth from him to heal the woman who sought healing (Luke 8); it is the water of Siloam in which the man who did not sin so as to be born blind washed his eyes, first smeared with spittle, not without effect (John 9).

But the young stag is borne over the flatness of fields in rapid course, and outruns not only gazelles but stags more mature in age. While he has strength suited to the task, an agile body, and still youthful age [Col. 0308D], he scorns obstacles, overcomes thickets, leaps fences, and recognizes no boundaries. Thus he does not heed or fear the bite of dogs, traps laid in ambush, or snares encountered; rather, he flies past all pursuers. When he is thought to be present, he makes himself absent quicker than speech; when he is judged absent, he makes himself present by a sudden arrival.

The beloved of the Virgin is fittingly likened to this young stag. Though God has assumed flesh, he is not burdened by the weight of flesh, but wills and is able to leap over everything displeasing; and he can reach whatever he wills as soon as he wills it. He runs past the cords stretched into a snare (Ps. 139); he passes by the stumbling-block set beside him; he does not fall with a slipping or unsteady foot into the snare hidden in the way in which he walked (Ps. 141) [Col. 0309A]. He outruns in far greater merits the fathers from whom, according to the flesh, he was born. From us, being slower, he withdraws at one time and meets us at another according to his will.

He withdraws when, with a gazelle-like gaze, he observes us not so much in our outward appearance as in the secret of conscience, and discovers hearts grievously wounded and dispositions of the inner being harshly formed. When he sees us empty of merits, burdened with vices, unkind in character, he judges us unworthy of his presence—that is, of his grace. When we do not feel grace present within us, and while he watches, sleep heavily under the shadow of vices; when we suppose that he more negligently forgets our transgressions, that he is occupied elsewhere and has gone far away—then, without our foreseeing it, like a young stag he suddenly meets us, punishes vices, and condemns the vicious, unless mercy first outruns judgment.

Often too, when, as we think, vices have been cast off, we labour at better pursuits and rightly await, on their account, the blessed hope and gracious coming of the Lord. Yet with our understanding darkened, we place bitterness for sweetness and darkness for light. Clinging more than is just to recognized goods, we do not adequately correct evils that are unrecognized. Therefore, while we offend in many ways and do not perceive our ignorance, uncertain beyond doubt whether we are worthy of love or hatred (Eccl. 9), this young stag suddenly rushes swiftly and flies down from above, and the subtle eye of the gazelle searches our Jerusalem with lamps [Col. 0309C] (Zeph. 1).

It searches, I say, the hidden things of a mind darkened by certain ignorances, bringing in light and dispersing the heavy darkness that had seemed whitened. Seeing clearly whatever is unseemly and hidden by our blindness, it regards our supposed righteousnesses as a menstrual cloth (Isa. 64). Therefore it strikes; and in striking what had been thought worthy of reward, what else occurs but that this young stag suddenly presents himself to us? He seemed absent and far away while he spared us and deferred the falsely hoped-for reward.

Sometimes, pitying our error, he draws the avenging sword back into its sheath and piously warns us to embrace saving discipline (Ps. 2), lest, foolish and deceived, we await a reward in place of punishment. Rather, according to Jeremiah, let us search out our ways with anxious inquiry (Lam. 3). But since searching is sluggish in darkness and more effective amid lamps, he comes as a gazelle, wonderfully enlightening from the everlasting mountains; and he pours that liquid of his Spirit over the inward eyes, so that they may see disclosed whatever harmful thing hides itself in our conscience.

Once this has been overthrown and wiped away, we rejoice in our cleansing and desire to love him whose gift and grace enable us to work so great a work in ourselves. Thereafter we desire him to be more graciously present, to mingle conversations with us, to deserve his favor, and to feel him nearer. Perceiving that we love him and assenting to the prayers of those who love him, he grants us a certain abundance of himself, soothes us with gifts, and does not assail us with blows. He puts far away whatever painful thing from the past troubles us, so that we may taste how sweet he is [Col. 0310A], revealing his sweetness to those who desire him.

And while he is thought to stand as though before our eyes and already to be felt in our hands, he withdraws like a young stag, wishing to be sought more ardently. He makes himself absent without abandoning us, not as inflicting punishment, but watching to see whether unrestrained love is suspended in desire for the absent one. If he sees that we are held by tender love, burning for him when absent and refreshed by no present things; if he sees us aflame with longing and counting nothing dearer than him, he does not allow his absence to torment us longer.

The one whom, not seeing, we believe to have gone far away suddenly comes and again shows himself near. Looking down from on high, like a gazelle, upon our now sound desire, he protects us in humility by his sudden arrival, like a young stag. Perhaps for this reason he deserved here to be called not a stag but “a young stag of the stags”: he who also wished to be proclaimed through Isaiah as a child and a little man (Isa. 9) [Col. 0310B]. For he who is exalted above all gods, containing all things within himself and hiding himself, pours himself out by humble condescension to those humble in spirit (Ps. 95).

Because this is known to no one better than to the Virgin—for everyone unworthy grieves that he has not sufficiently experienced so great a gift—the Virgin rightly and confidently testifies to this, declaring him to be the one like a gazelle or a young stag. But if any hearer wishes more curiously to know where he tends with such haste—the one who is said to come leaping and bounding, like the gazelle and young stag—and where at last he fixed his step, let him hear that he is where the Virgin said he halted his course.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0310C] “Behold, he himself stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattice.” Though he has come, this one desired more sweetly and awaited more longingly has not yet, as I seem to see, arrived completely. But approaching the Bride, whose love he knew could not be nourished by another remedy, he stands behind the wall, wishing to be known rather than seen.

The wall in this place is not unfittingly called the present life, built, as it were, of hours and days, months and years, like stones laid beside or upon one another. While we are temporally confined within its narrownesses, we either do not know God or do not yet contemplate his face. Hence God says to Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). That is: no one within this prison of time, enclosed within the boundaries of this life—however great his merit or however diligently polished his mind—shall see me in my nature, in the glory of my nature. That glory shall appear beyond this wall to those who go forth, to satisfy them.

Therefore the darkness of the present life does not admit the vision of so great a glory; amid its shadows that face does not permit itself to be seen. No one bearing flesh, wrapped in the prison-house of time, sees the brightness of God freed from temporal mists. Seeing this, John says: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4). “Ever,” that is, in time: while the creature is subject to vanity—that is, to transitory time—it does not see God himself in his form or nature, though sometimes it knows, indeed feels, that he is near, stirring it to prayer and ready to hear prayers [Col. 0311A].

And significantly the Virgin does not say, “Behold, he stands within the wall,” but “behind our wall.” This wall of ours is temporal, always tending toward sunset and oppressing those who likewise tend toward it. It is dark with an inward darkness, as befits evening; neither rising dawn nor morning sun receives it. Set within its limits, we do not see the face of the Bridegroom, the glory of Christ; but beyond it—that is, after we have passed its boundaries. When, having crossed its limit, we shall know nothing transitory any longer, then after evening we shall come to morning, and after darkness to light. Hence David says: “In the morning I shall stand before you and see” (Ps. 5). And Job: “After darkness,” he says, “I hope for light” (Job 17).

The Virgin also beautifully said, “behind our wall,” not “my wall.” Although the Virgin, fuller of grace in a greater measure, is already free from the guilt of our sins, this wall of the present life is common to us all. In it, it is no longer guilt, nor flesh burdened by guilt, that—as it seems—withdraws the Virgin from seeing truth; rather, it is that she too, as a creature, remains subject to the vanity already mentioned. We, far below the Virgin, are weighed down by the burden of sins and darkened by fleshly enticements and denser shadows. As many movements and affections of the inner spirit as oppress us, so many dividing walls do we set between ourselves and God [Col. 0311B].

But the Virgin, whom the pressure of such things no longer assails because she is full of grace, is nevertheless still detained under time by present life alone, unwillingly and against her will. She therefore says that not many walls but rather one intervenes, and that it is not peculiar to herself but common to all. She whom the excellence of grace had long removed from many walls did not immediately cast aside, at will and desire, the one wall that was hers and everyone’s alike. Living with us, she did not consent to retain our sins any longer; yet she felt life itself, like a wall, to be burdensome and opposed to her.

She willingly desired to see face to face him whom she loved, but that law, written with an iron stylus, delayed her desire: the law proclaimed from God to Moses, and from Moses to human beings many ages before, confirmed then, now, and henceforth by indelible writing: “No human being,” he says, “shall see me and live” (Exod. 33).

“Behold,” says the Virgin, “I understand that the Bridegroom stands behind our wall. However near he may come, he does not wish to reveal himself clearly to those living here. And though he may perhaps be far from certain others, since it is certain that many walls intervene for them—behold, he stands near me, who sense that only one wall is opposed to me [Col. 0311D]. He stands in order to attend to me with diligent concern, to show himself ready as a helper to one desiring to depart; to strengthen one delayed, stretch out his hand to one striving, console one amid present things, and promise better things to one who follows.”

Thus Stephen, while enduring the stones and insults of the Jews, grieving not so much for himself as for the wickedness of the lost (Acts 7), was intent upon prayer and was caught up in a sweet ecstasy; he saw Jesus standing, inaccessible to the miserable men who stoned him. Jesus stood in order to give strength to the one struggling, hope of victory to the dying man, and, extending a hand to the trusting, to break down the wall for the one about to depart; to receive him as he departed and, having received him, rescue him from the tumultuous course of this world, thereafter to sit in the beauty of peace and rest in abundant repose.

Thus, while the Virgin is held back only by the wall of present life, the Bridegroom is said to stand, as it were outside, behind that wall, so that he may meanwhile encourage her, who is about to depart, to remain steadfast in keeping watch over herself, and so that she may await him as the guardian of her departure, standing and remaining steadfast with manly courage [Col. 0312A]. Meanwhile, while the Virgin endures delay, enclosed within this wall, desiring indeed to be dissolved but not yet wholly released, the Bridegroom is said to look through the windows and gaze through the lattices: caring for the Virgin, he consoles her by the gaze of his grace.

Lest the house be badly blind and its interior dark, gracious light is poured in through windows and lattices. Windows and lattices appear to me to differ from one another in this: windows are extended lengthwise, while lattices present a round form like an eye. Therefore the Bridegroom seems to look in through the oblong windows when he makes luminous, by the hope of one who endures long and by constant patience, the Bride’s sojourn in which she is held for a long time within the wall. Without the grace of this light, nothing is more deserving of hatred, nothing more wearisome.

David, oppressed by weariness, says: “Alas, for my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. 119). But when filled with joyful light: “You are,” he says, “my patience, O Lord, my hope from my youth” (Ps. 70) [Col. 0312C]. The Bridegroom gazes through the lattices when, by the undisturbed grace of his presence, the Virgin more subtly surveys her own actions; and, finding nowhere among transitory things where she may allow her foot to rest (Gen. 8), fixes the eyes of her mind on him for whom she waits with sounder desire.

He gazes through the lattices when, removing animal affections and motions far from the Bride, he pours into her—or, in pouring, enlightens—the spiritual eyes. With these eyes the circumspect Virgin not only does not cling to present things or eagerly attend to what will pass away; but, when her pupils have been made clear, she sees and loves more eagerly those things which remain without end. Into these eyes God’s vision pours itself, not only to cleanse but also to preserve cleansing; and through them it is subsequently diffused throughout the whole structure, as it were. Their smooth and rounded perfection, opened externally by a narrower opening and internally by a wider one, renders all things covered with the infused light (Ezek. 40 and 41).

I wonder whether the prudent builder of the Church did not see this very thing. Understanding one part of it as worthier in merits, he built it round and wished to call it a lattice, in which he wished more significantly to place the Holy of Holies and the altar [Col. 0312D]. This part deserves first to receive the grace of the divine regard; first sanctified, it is not held by the sickness of avarice. But with its opening expanded and filled with the eminent light of mysteries, it pours back upon the whole Church everywhere, like an eye, the benefit of the sacrament.

For this reason lamps or candles are especially lit there, and these are clearly shown to signify the grace of the light already mentioned. From them it is understood that God’s vision is first presented there and then extended to the remaining parts, as though light were scattered abroad [Col. 0313A]. Thus he who, standing behind the wall, does not yet allow himself to be seen loves to behold his beloved through the windows and lattices. Seeing and not seen, yet able not to remain unknown, he wishes his speaking voice to be heard as though from an oracle.

## CHAPTER VI

“And my beloved speaks to me.” To me, I say: to me who am still held within the wall, even against my will, and, if no longer hindered by other stains, still impeded by those of present life. He who stands behind the wall, awaiting my desire to depart although I am not yet able to do so, and meanwhile looks within through the eyes of windows and lattices of mercy, adds even this to the fullness of his benefit: he speaks, and in gracious speech pursues the sweet lines of love.

And rightly is speech said to follow sight, because when we happen to see someone beloved, we immediately wish also to address her. As a trumpet urges those who fight, or a spur or heel urges a horse sent forward, so we urge her by a pleasant word to greater watchfulness in love [Col. 0313B]. Therefore the Bridegroom speaks, delighting to soothe her by his speech. He makes his will known to her and teaches the humble one to obey; he teaches her to confess herself his handmaid, especially after she has heard Gabriel’s message of salvation, and to hold in memory the saying which she knew had long before been written of Samuel: “Speak, O Lord, for your servant hears” (1 Kings 3).

Therefore the Lord speaks to this handmaid—indeed, the beloved to the Bride who listens. The loving and ever-watchful Bride lends an open ear to the speaker; he gives joy and gladness to her hearing by speaking (Ps. 50), while she humbles herself by more gladly hearing the Bridegroom’s voice. And she does so worthily the more gladly, because he does not, like an adversary, speak harmful or sorrowful things; rather, his benevolence speaks sweet and useful things. For he who loves and is loved does not rage against or grow angry with his beloved, but offers her peace, although it is not yet perfect, as though a wall still intervened.

What peace he offers her, and what peaceful thing he speaks to her, is made clear in the following verse, lest you remain long in ignorance.

## CHAPTER VII
“Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my fair one, and come.” Here one may first object: why does he who a little earlier warned the young women not to disturb her, nor to rouse her as she rested between the left hand and the right until she herself wished it, now, as though forgetting his warning, urge her to rise? He even presses her [Col. 0313D] to hasten, as though it were no longer to be deferred. Yet he who restrained the daughters of Jerusalem—whose eyes have not been opened for this purpose—but left the Virgin’s rising to her own will, as you know, knows far better what, when, is fitting or advantageous to holiness; for from him the Virgin has the grace wisely to devote either leisure or activity to truth.

When, after her repose of leisure, the Bridegroom inspires in her a desire for activity, he stirs and raises up her love toward concern for her neighbours. He sweetly spurs her delay toward a work now necessary, so that “he who hears may say, ‘Come’” (Rev. VI): that she who has been taught may teach the truth. What does he say or command to her except, “Arise and hasten”? That is: as in [p. 179] leisure, so in activity, promptly obey me. [Col. 0314A] “You,” he says, “who sweetly lie concealed above my left hand and beneath my right; who within the wall rejoice, not vainly, at my regard—arise. For a little while leave the unfruitful embraces of pleasant leisure; go swiftly into the streets and lanes, and bring in here the lame and the weak” (Luke XIV).

“Because you will what I will, and do not will when I do not will, I rightly call you my friend, since you are hostile to every desire displeasing to me.” Not only the present truth of the Song, but also the true saying of the pagans, aptly accords with this statement.

> [Note: [Col. 0313D] Cicero, *On Friendship*.]

“The same willing and the same unwilling,” he says, “is in the end firm friendship.” You are my friend because in everything you wish to think with me, are conscious of my secrets, and keep the will of my mind. You are likewise a dove because you do not aspire to the things present in the world, [Col. 0314B] but, because eternal things are absent, you grieve and sigh without consolation. For although you sometimes willingly offer yourself to instruct your neighbours, you do not put aside the longing in which you burn toward me (Luke XI). Though you undertake very many things, you do not abandon that one necessary thing; you only for a while interrupt your leisure for stillness and contemplation.

And because you excel in fitting discernment, in both pursuits you acquire praise and merit from each, and in neither do you show yourself unattractive, but fair—mine by the merit of this beauty, that is, not moderately pleasing to me. Therefore, my friend, my dove, my fair one: arise, hasten, and come. Arise from leisure; gird yourself courageously for labour. Hasten: obey without delay, lest the need of your neighbours [Col. 0314C] find you too slow. And come—not going far from me after the tracks of the flocks, after the flocks of your companions, but labouring while I stand beside you, without any loss or harm.

For when you have risen and hastened, do not, as though impatient, desist from what you have begun: I shall be present, strengthening you and shaping labour into a commandment (Ps. XCIII). Nor, when your strength has failed, shall I abandon you as though far away. When you come to me in labour, you will find yourself near me (Rom. XIII). Arise, because it is now the hour for you to arise from sleep; hasten, because God loves a cheerful giver (II Cor. IX); and come, because “I am with you,” says the Lord. That it is the hour he declares next, saying: “For winter is now past,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0314D]

“For now winter is past; the rain has gone and departed; flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come.”

While it is winter and the earth is harshly constricted by cold frost; while its surface is weighed down by a covering of snow and its face is not truly coloured; while the north wind delights in raging through these fields of air with looser reins, and the south wind does not appear, and the coming of the west wind is delayed—then, of course, the farmer does not hasten to go out to his work or bring forth his plough. He remains at home, is free for himself, delights in the fire, and fills himself with more lavish feasts.

Likewise, while rain endures, with showers pouring down long and unseasonably, and pools and ponds now occupy fields long dry; while torrents plunge with violence from high mountains, rivers overflow their banks and stray far and wide; while crops are overwhelmed, houses float, trees are uprooted, and the waters of the flood are neither restrained by command nor repelled by obstacle—what ploughman goes out to yoke his oxen? What husbandman applies the pruning-hook to the vine to cut away what is harmful or superfluous?

But when a stronger hand sternly rebukes and checks these things, and, the air having cleared, spring’s sweetness pours itself upon the earth; when the troublesome violence of rain and winter has been wiped away, and, the cloud having been cleared, the world’s own countenance has returned—then at last the ploughman rejoices, the spirit of work returns, and a man goes out to the vineyard, because the time for pruning is suitable.

Our winter is that time when we are held fast in the harsh cold of the mind, when ignorance or negligence prevents us [Col. 0315B] from loving God; when the wicked spirit, like the north wind, continually hardens us, and the world, set in wickedness, conforms us to its own malice. Our rain, however, is when the outpouring of carnal affections pours itself into our minds, and their enervating softness spreads everywhere in a wave-like rush; and a great flood is found to exceed its bounds and overstep its measure, since it is neither restrained within the channel of discipline nor met in advance by the hand of justice.

For then passion rages like a torrent; the filth of vices roars; it submerges and suffocates the mind, rendering it ignorant of the commandments. And if anything good had been sown and conceived in hope, whether seedling or blade, the water of the flood carries it off, the Egyptian river takes it away, bitter death overwhelms it. Finally, the mind, now lost, stretches outward [Col. 0315C] [p. 180] to desire unlawful things; it draws into its own use whatever it finds softer and sweeter. It is caressed by the pleasure of foods and the soft touch of women; it tastes only flesh and whatever thus flatters miserable flesh.

But if divine grace should deign at some time to have mercy amid such great calamities, to look upon the aforesaid hardness of the mind with eyes of mercy—so that it may at last wish it, long pressed by harmful frost, to be loosened by the Spirit’s warmth, and us to be absolved from the guilt of death through the benefit of pardon—then winter, tenacious and harsh, hitherto crushing the wretched, shaken from its ruinous state, becomes transitory. It passes, I say; and in its passing greenness and revived mildness return. The south wind comes, the west wind breathes, and the sweetness of spring and summer follows; [Col. 0315D] the beauty of flowers smiles, promising the fruits to follow; the vine rejoices in the pruning-hook that cuts away its useless branches.

As the same grace blows, the air is cleared and the great inundation of rains diminishes. The flood dries up, and the river is recalled within its banks. Discipline does not vainly prescribe moderation to the self-indulgent and continence to the luxuriant; when the stream of vices has dried up, the inner workshop of the mind is adorned with virtues. Once cleansed and made fruitful by an inward gift, it is not only that the flowing rain goes away and departs; a new adornment and a certain new appearance of the earth also now arrives. And where winter has passed and rain has gone and is no longer seen, there the flower of good works appears—namely, the hope of the reward to come.

Because the Bridegroom wished to impart such grace to the daughters of Jerusalem, so that, when the rubble of perverse will had been uprooted, [Col. 0316A] they might now desire to attain greater progress, he exhorts the Virgin, rejoicing in leisure, to go to meet and assist them. He shows at what time, and after what preceding fitness, this may worthily and profitably be done. “Arise,” he says, “for winter is now past”: that hardness, namely, which for some time could hinder the minds of hearers from either hearing the word of God or loving to obey it once heard; which pressed itself upon them with a heavy hand and harsh dominion, made waters hardened with cold stand still instead of flowing, cast cold snows upon the earth like a heavy cloak, and by long pressure killed tender sheep.

Such hardness was plainly found to hold Peter under its heavy hoof when he answered, concerning him whom he knew, that he did not know the man (Mark XIV). And so that he might be unable even to speak the truth, a servant or maid struck him with the blow of fear; lest the disciple help his Master, his sluggish hand remained under his armpit (Prov. XIX). You remember, I think, what Gospel truth affirms: when Peter denied him and warmed himself, it was cold (John XVII). Therefore at that time the Virgin is not commanded to arise in order to speak; rather, by grace’s mercy, he who denied is first looked upon so that he may weep. [Col. 0316B]

For he wept bitterly, feeling himself held by harsh cold (Luke XXIII), and that the fire beside which he stood was not sufficiently suitable to drive it away. But, once that same winter had passed through the merciful regard of grace, Mary is sent to Peter to announce the power of the risen one (Mark XVI).

Again, did not the heavy rain—the many waters of the evil time or day—seem to hold John of Zebedee? [Col. 0316C] With his spirit, as it were, suffocated and the rigour of chastity bent, he hastened to embrace the soft union of the flesh—the nuptials of a pleasure destined to perish. But a very great rain, much uncleanness, suffocated him when Peter, more confident, three times denied the Master near his Passion (Mark XIV), while John himself, terrified by the aforesaid Passion through love of this life, was driven headlong into flight and fled naked, leaving behind the linen cloth.

And truly he is guilty of no small fault, nor does he stray or offend only a little, who in the flood of passions leaves behind the pure linen cloth of love for heavenly things. No one can be more honourably or more usefully clothed than in it—provided Christ grants that we be buried in it according to his own likeness. “He wrapped him,” it says, “in a clean linen cloth [Col. 0316D] and placed him in the tomb” (Matt. XXVII).

But John’s self-love stripped him naked as he fled, having despised the linen cloth; Judas was enfeebled by hatred of his Master, the sickness of avarice, and the guilt of crime. In short, the water carried all away, the flood harmed them, guilt drowned them; but while the others escaped by grace, Judas, lost, did not emerge. For he, suffocated by despair, hanged himself with a noose around his throat. John attained the citadel of grace, the height of vision, because Christ, suffering on the cross, banished care for Judas far from his own goodwill, but lovingly entrusted care for John to the Virgin Mother: “Woman,” he says, “behold your son” (John XIX).

Therefore, after he wished by faith in the risen Christ to remove far away the troubles of winter and rain, and for liberating grace to appear more eminently in those whom he had chosen, [Col. 0317A] he earnestly invited the Virgin not to be slow in arising, hastening, and coming. For it is now time to speak, since the earth is not held by the rain or winter described above. Nor has such great harshness merely gone and departed: spring sweetness, flowering beauty, and hope of fruit have also come. In our land flowers of obedience, patience, and continence now shine forth; in only a little while they will produce their desired fruit.

Therefore there must be no delay in bringing forth meanwhile the pruning-hook and the purifying admonition, which diligently cuts away the shoots of revived negligence (Wis. IV), scrapes off ignorance, instructs faith, and prunes conduct, so as by careful effort to make them more ready and worthy to bear fruit. For when vintage-time, the day of fruits, dawns, there will no longer be pruning; both basket and hoe will rest. These instruments, after winter has passed, are more fittingly brought forth when fresh greenness springs and varied flowers display themselves in the land.

[p. 181] “Flowers,” he says, “have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come.” And he adds: “The voice,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER IX

“The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land; the fig tree has put forth its early figs; the flowering vines have given their fragrance.”

The voice of the turtledove is not raised, according to musicians, in high notes, nor is it pleasing to their ears. It does not sing very sweetly, as, according to a certain pagan writer, the nightingale does; rather, it dwells in low tones, sorrowful with a subdued kind of groaning—not welcome to those who rejoice, but pleasing to those [Col. 0317C] who wish to mourn. He appears to imitate such a voice in lament who bitterly complains that his sojourn on earth is prolonged; who, not clinging to present things and refusing consolation in them, does not cease to lament with groaning because future things are absent.

“Alas for me,” he says, “for my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX). And again: “She has wept, weeping in the night, and her tears are upon her cheeks; she has none to comfort her” (Lam. I).

If you remember, this voice was heard among the disciples when their tender love, their hope provoked by deferred desire, made them debate and sigh among themselves; they complain like a turtledove, and amid their complaints many doubts and varied discussions arise. “What are these words,” he says, “that you exchange with one another as you walk, and are sad?” (Luke [Col. 0317D] XXIV). And they reply: “We hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (ibid.).

When, therefore, the voice of this turtledove is now heard in the land, the Virgin is rightly summoned to the task of advancing faith, so that she may know that her preaching is neither vain nor ineffective when it is preceded by such devout groaning, by such a grieving spirit. For the turtledove loves to dwell in mountains and more secluded places. It does not delight in gatherings of birds, in public places, or in popular crowds. It bears the form of that spiritual wisdom which neither the wandering multitude of public places nor the natural man receives.

Of this Job says: “Wisdom is drawn forth from hidden places” (Job XXVIII). David says: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. L). And Paul says: “We speak the wisdom of God [Col. 0318A] in a mystery, which is hidden” (I Cor. II). Paul, who knew himself debtor both to the wise and to the foolish, while speaking among the perfect draws wisdom from hidden places; and he reveals the uncertain and hidden things of wisdom to those whom the dullness or blunt ignorance of people of the public square does not trouble, and whose ears are equally receptive.

Thus the voice of the turtledove is that which, concealing from darkened crowds the hidden or uncertain things of wisdom, uncovers them for the eyes or ears of very few. While covering the mystery from the multitude, it sweetly whispers the secret of Isaiah, the prophecy of Elizabeth, the oracle of Zechariah, only to those who, having received the Spirit, hasten to the mountains—those whose ears the crafty asp does not stop against hearing.

Finally, that woman appeared to merit the voice of the turtledove who rejoiced that she had seen the Lord [Col. 0318B] as he rose from the dead, and, her desire now fulfilled, announced him whom she alone had seen, not to crowds in the street but privately to the apostles: “Mary Magdalene came,” it says, “announcing to the disciples, ‘I have seen the Lord, and he said these things to me’” (John XX). Mark, however, says: “Jesus, rising early on the first day of the Sabbath, appeared first to Mary Magdalene; but she went and announced it to those who had been with him” (Mark XVI).

Those disciples too remain privately, in the manner of the turtledove’s excellence, who, in Thomas Didymus’s absence, rejoice at seeing the Lord. When Thomas returns they tell him, thinking he too will rejoice at such news; but he, disbelieving, declares that he will not believe unless he sees. Nor is it unfitting, if you wish, to call the same Lord a turtledove as well: [Col. 0318C] after rising from the dead he wished to appear both to women and to disciples, while he showed himself wholly hidden from crowds rejoicing in the marketplace or street, to be seen only by his own people in private in Galilee.

I judge without doubt that his voice as turtledove is that by which he made himself known to his own as present, in order that they might believe: a voice kept far from the hardened hearing of the wicked, and brought only to those whom he found held by an incipient affection of love. “Peace be to you,” he says; “it is I” (Luke XXIV). This is the good voice of the turtledove, a voice from lofty mountains, a secret voice which the clamouring crowd cannot grasp, accustomed as it is to the disputes and tumults of the public square. Only a few know it—those whose ear hears worthily, whose eye is not darkened by obstinacy, and whose vigorous understanding more diligently investigates the secrets [Col. 0318D] of wisdom.

Of this voice it is written: “His voice shall not be heard in the streets” (Isa. XLII). Once this voice sounded upon the earth and was heard by the disciples, the earth opened its joyful bosom, previously hindered by harsh cold. In a newly springing mildness it became worthy to be called ours—the earth which, cursed in the first man, deserved to be blessed when the second rose again. For the Lord once sternly forbade it to sin; when it transgressed the prohibition, he cursed it more severely in anger and wrath. But when he rose from the dead, he blessed that same earth with his regard and his grace; renewed by his gifts, he called it ours by right of its newness.

[p. 182] ## CHAPTER X

“The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” Once, [Col. 0319A] when it sinned, that land enslaved itself to another’s lordship and usurped a new god and another possessor for itself. But once it has been breathed upon by a new Spirit and made free from the errors mentioned above, it is rightly called ours, since its possession is now common to both.
