For those who are one spirit and one flesh are to be said henceforth to possess nothing not held in common. What belongs to the bride, the bridegroom fittingly claims as his own, since he wishes to keep even what is his not as his own property, but to share it with her, so that together they may rejoice in possessing all things in common.

“Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. VI). If, I say, I call the Father who is in heaven not mine exclusively but ours in common, I rightly call the bride’s land not yours but rather ours. For just as by gift I have [Col. 0319B] made you a sharer in what is mine, so, by the gift of me who give—more mine than yours—I am a sharer in what is yours.

Otherwise, if the land were regarded as yours alone and not rather ours, perhaps the voice of the turtledove mentioned above would not be heard in it, nor would the fig tree put forth the early figs which it produced on hearing the turtledove; and if these were not produced, it would not bring forth later fruits in their season.

Nearly all trees whose kind or appearance differs have this as something proper and implanted by nature: a tree which will produce its fruits at their mature time first rejoices in a certain offspring of flowers that is destined to pass away. Of this it is written: “In the morning let it flower and pass away” (Ps. LXXXIX). But when the tree has been deprived of its transient flower, nature working, [Col. 0319C] it becomes fruitful with the arrival of the fruit that follows. Whatever grief it felt before, whatever loss it endured in being bare of its fading flower, it makes good with new joy and changes for a better abundance.

The fig tree, however, is found unlike the others in this respect. Its abundance of fruit is not preceded by the grace of flowering; rather, while the others flower, it is said to produce its first fruits, and later, as time advances, other fruits that pass away. Thus the fig tree becomes fruitful in a manner unusual among all trees: without any preceding flower, rich in a first and second abundance of fruits. The early figs (*grossi*) which come first do not possess the grace or flavour of those which come later; the later they are in time, the better their juice, beyond doubt.

Yet among the early figs, which are said to precede others, it is sometimes possible to find a few—though very few—that both come first and [Col. 0319D] do not yield place in location or time to those following. When others fall, they stand longer and remain with those to come. For an early fig is sometimes found growing between two little branches, guarded, as it were, by the diligent surrounding protection of its neighbours; resting in the corner, drawing sap and nourishment from both sides, it not only does not fall but grows to a larger size than the others. Those of its own age which fall are not equal to it in excellence; nor do those which come later deserve, beyond doubt, to be compared with it. Rather, it merits preference over both, in fragrance and flavour, fit food for nobles and worthy to be placed on a royal table.

The fig tree can not unfittingly be called the Jewish people. When they heard Christ commending [Col. 0320A] heavenly things and teaching that earthly things were not to be loved, being imbued with the sacred Scriptures, they immediately produced people who would believe—but who would not remain firm in the word of faith through firmness of works. Having quickly come forth, taking on the appearance of piety but denying its power and lacking the weight of truth, they fell at the first gust of wind while still unripe; or, before the wind even blew, they dropped through their own weight.

Perhaps people of this sort are not undeservedly called *grossi*, “early figs,” because with a gross or dull mind more than with the body they wickedly reject hidden and subtle things. In Paul’s phrase (Eph. IV), they have an understanding darkened by grossness; they believe for a time, but in time of temptation collapse into falling away.

I consider those to have been sufficiently—indeed more than sufficiently—gross who are read in the Gospel as having stood by [Col. 0320B] Christ while he spoke. When he discoursed mystically concerning eating his flesh and drinking his blood, and asserted that only those who ate would possess eternal life in him, those from whose sides very gross fat seemed to hang, unable to grasp the mystery, were found to recoil from the mystical saying. “This saying is hard,” they said; “who can hear it?” (John VI). Miserably shaken by the hardness of this saying, and unable, as unstable people, to endure the north wind’s blast of truth, they took badly the pure stumbling-block concealed in the saying. Plainly, like early figs, they fall before their time. “From this,” it says, “many went back, and no longer walked with him” (John VI).

But when they withdrew, [Col. 0320C] do not suppose that thereafter none from the same people wished to hear Christ or to be among those who heard him. Later he sent before him seventy-two others to every place where he knew he would come; taking them from that people, he did not permit the fig tree to remain utterly barren. Finally, Judas the traitor, who had followed the Master among the apostles for some time and pursued him to the end in betrayal and incurable hatred, when he found himself, like an early fig, fallen into the depths through his own weight, brought himself back upward much more grievously by hanging himself with a noose.

But lest the apostle’s place long [p. 183] remain vacant and the worthy perfection of the sacred number be diminished by one man’s fall, Matthias, as you have read, was chosen by lot as an apostle. Thus neither was the fig tree empty [Col. 0320D] nor the number twelve imperfect. If this seems too little and insufficient to any hearers, if the diligent reader thinks that something here contains a matter worthy of inquiry, let him turn to those who afterwards believed from that people at Peter’s word and filled up the number of those who had fallen—now three thousand, now five thousand. There is no doubt that, the later they were in time, the better they should be called than Judas and the aforesaid apostates. Christ was far more pleased with their evening succession and conversion than with the morning withdrawal and fall of the others.

But those early figs which, when others fell, stood firm—very few indeed—and, without falling with the fallen, remained even with those who followed, may rightly be understood as the apostles. They were [Col. 0321A] among the first, perhaps the very first, chosen by Christ; and they were not driven away from him by entreaty, price, or the force of threats. When the good Master carefully approached them to ask whether, while the others went back, they too wished to go, Peter, more ready to speak, did not conceal what he intended; but before the others, as their first and chief, he answered: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have words of eternal life; and we have believed and known that you are Christ, the Son of God” (John VI).

Peter, therefore, lies hidden as it were between two little branches—between Law and Gospel. Drawing nourishment from both sides, he grows strong to persist courageously. Resting at the border of both, he gently inclines himself upon each, carefully relying on the one while in no way turning away from the other. For he [Col. 0321B] understands that the old Law prefigures the new by signs and enigmas; the new makes the old understood, not obscure. The old does not prejudice the new, but precedes it; the new does not oppose the old, but meets it.

To Peter the lawgiver and the giver of the Gospel do not seem to differ from one another, since the Law foretells Christ and Christ does not wish to abolish the Law but to fulfil it. In him, as in a corner, the old Law is joined to the new by a certain harmony. Peter, leaning firmly upon it, is guarded by a double defence. Of this he himself says: “We have the firmer prophetic word, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark [variant: gloomy] place” (II Pet. I). This concerns the old. What of the new? “Repent,” he says, “and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts II).

To Peter, therefore, and his fellow apostles, who first believed in Christ and [Col. 0321C], when some withdrew, remained with him in their temptations, Christ wished to impart such maturity of conduct and sweetness of grace that it is certain they surpass both contemporaries and successors by their merit in life. No rank could compare itself with this rank, no other man with an apostle, as some think; none could be preferred before them in life and merits, whether earlier or later. They become so sweet in fragrance and so mature in works that both those present and those to come rightly yield to them.

When the fig tree had brought them forth—not merely as preferable to the bad, but as certainly better than the good, great as mountains, “gross,” or abundant, in the richness of merits—the [Col. 0321D] Bride is rightly invited not to postpone too long visiting such persons, but sometimes to set the business of her neighbours before her special leisure. The Bridegroom wishes that the Virgin, not long absent, should not be burdensome to the apostles, who are still young; but that she should speak graciously to them, disclose manifest things concerning hidden matters, strengthen their faith, instruct their untutored understanding, advance their beginning affections, and lead them to perfection.

He wishes, I say, the Virgin to labour in watchful care, so that the untrained apostles may be able to rest their heads beneath their own vine and fig tree. While present iniquity passes away and fuller day shines upon them, may each rest beneath the [Col. 0322A] mighty hand of Christ and meanwhile beneath the shadow of the Holy Spirit.

And in order that the Virgin may labour patiently in caring for these same young men and hope for near fruit if she perseveres diligently, he says: “The flowering vines have now given their fragrance; they will give autumn grapes, having flowered already at the first season.” I take the vines to mean individual souls already converted to faith, in which God’s merciful calling works the grace of merits. Warmed by the mildness poured into them, they now visibly produce their flower. The flower, not yet rich in fruit, meanwhile gives its fragrance.

Just as the presence of the flower makes the place of the vine pleasant, so its fragrance makes that same place cleaner and calmer, because it does not allow a serpent or crawling thing, nor poison, to remain there; by a certain undivided force it makes the place alien [Col. 0322B] to all such things. I would call that a good flower and good fragrance by which recent conversion so adorns the soul that it first drives far away whatever inwardly dishonours it; so that the eye of the beholder may rightly rejoice at its first fruits, and poisonous envy, unable to bear its good fragrance, may recoil in alarm.

The wicked either do not wish or cannot bear to see the good with equanimity, and a more righteous place cannot be possessed by two masters. But when a fresh flower and comely fragrance diffuse themselves through abundant grace, guilt flees, poison is shut out, and iniquity hides itself far away. For fragrance and stench are sternly opposed to one another: they do not agree and do not remain in the same dwelling. But when virtue rightly flowers and its reputation sweetly grows strong, vice is annulled and everything foul-smelling in evil vanishes.

When Simon Peter, flowering in the summer [p. 184] grace, spread his fragrance far and wide and promulgated with generous liberality the new rule of possessing nothing as one’s own, some people who wished with clean conscience to feed upon this good fragrance sold their possessions and laid their prices at the apostle’s feet (Acts V). But Ananias and Sapphira, who laboured in poisonous deceit and a ruined mind, burning with the disease of avarice as with inward fevers, unwilling generously to aspire to the height of apostolic poverty, were compelled miserably to expire at the fragrance of this word.

Thus Peter, and thus the brothers who assembled, shine with a new flower before human beings and fill the whole house with their fragrance. Such rigour is found to prevail in the Church that [Col. 0322D] Simon Magus cannot endure Peter, nor Nicolaus Stephen.

> [Note: [Col. 0321D] Thus cols. 244, 330, and 361 present Nicolaus as condemnable, one of the first seven deacons, from whom came certain most foul heretics called Nicolaitans. Whether he was in fact such a person or not is commonly examined by those who write on the Acts of the Apostles, ch. VII, v. 5; Rev. II, 15. See especially the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, under the year of the Lord 68.]

Good indeed were the vines which flowered thus in that time; very happy were the souls which produced so powerful a fragrance. In their company the serpent of envy and poisonous fraud do not persist; the stinking malice of the lost cannot resist the life-giving fragrance. “They could not resist,” it says, “the wisdom and Spirit that spoke” (Acts VI).

But our vines now, since the days are evil, grow dull to no small degree. Virtue is more obscure, love weak, merits languish more negligently. A disease making baleful progress creeps within the enclosures of [Col. 0323A] our conscience and discolours the flowers above, while at the root it tears us down while we are tender. Therefore, as I see it, the most holy Virgin lingers too long away from us; for us she sleeps, is free for herself, and delights in her repose. Lying upon the Bridegroom’s left hand, she contemplates his right; perhaps forgetful of us, she rejoices to attend only to her own concern.

Who will awaken her? Who will say to her, “Arise; why do you sleep?” (Ps. XLIII). Because weariness and sloth have turned us away from labour and watchfulness, and the enemy, observing us, has already mocked our torpor and our Sabbaths, the Virgin does not visit those who are full of leaves but poor in flower and fragrance; and, as our sins demand, she has long ceased to visit them.

But if she sees our flower bloom again and perceives its fragrance, she will not refuse to arise and bestow more welcome diligence. [Col. 0323B] She who was found mercifully to assist her own young men will deign to impart greater mercy to us, who are far more wretched. For she does not fail those in whom she sees that her Bridegroom also does not fail; those in whom she knows his present grace to be so present that they do not lack fragrance and do not wish to withhold it from their neighbours, but freely give to others what has freely been given to them.

For those who, lacking virtue, assume for themselves the appearance of virtue; who do not strive to obtain the grace of living well but presume upon it—these dispense not their own fragrance but another’s, while they endeavour to give others the form of a virtue presumed rather than possessed. But those who truly rejoice to possess the gift of some virtue, and who wish it not to be hidden under a bushel but to appear before the eyes of their neighbours—[Col. 0323C] if from it they seek more their own glory as exhibitors than the glory of those who behold it—they are more truly said not to give their fragrance but to sell it.

Passing over, therefore, those who are convicted either of giving an alien fragrance or of selling their own, and mentioning those who are known, like flowering vines, to give their own fragrance, he urges the Virgin to arise for them, to hasten with watchful care, and, lest she delay once admonished, he loves to repeat the very command.

## CHAPTER XI
“Rise,” he says, “my friend, my bride, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the wall.” It does not suffice for one who loves to admonish once the woman whom he loves; rather, he repeats and presses the matter, unwilling that she should be sluggish in fulfilling his injunctions. And, that he may more readily induce her, forgetful of the body, to comply voluntarily, he seeks to soothe her with caresses and affectionate names. Therefore, she whom, when he first said “Rise,” he called friend, dove, and beautiful, when he says again, “Rise,” he nevertheless calls friend and dove again; inserting the name “bride,” which I do not recall his having used anywhere above, although he is found elsewhere to have addressed her more frequently by other names.

Because a bride loves leisure with her beloved and clinging to the embraces of the bridegroom, and because nothing is harder for her than to turn the attention of her mind away from him toward public actions, when the Bridegroom admonishes her and repeatedly urges her to withdraw a little from that which she loves more, he puts before her the name by which he knows she is held more strongly to obedience. For Bridegroom and bride seem to be bound by some sacred, or consecrated, mystery in such a way that he sets her a boundary which she may not pass: namely, that the Bridegroom should exercise care, command as one who has power, and write the law; while the bride should lend her ear, obey what is spoken, love the command, and subscribe to it.

Therefore, when the Virgin hears herself more carefully called “bride,” recalling not so much the burden as the honor by which she loves to be bound to the caller, she understands that she ought not to oppose the Bridegroom even in the least, but should always judge his good pleasure to be the merit of her salvation. For he does not abandon her when he invites her to provide an example for others abroad, when he suggests that she suspend for a time the pleasing leisure of contemplation. Nor does he begrudge her progress when he wishes her service to be seen by those around her; rather, he wishes those to progress who love to contemplate her good works.

185 For he wishes her holiness to be set before those who look upon it in such a manner that she may rejoice to be set before them, yet not exposed to winds and storms; he wishes her to go forth into public and to be shown to others, even unwillingly, in such a way that she nevertheless perceives herself guarded by the vigilant care of the one commanding. This is perhaps what he says: “My dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the wall.” “I wish,” he says, “that the bride should sometimes be shown to the young women, so that they may be able and rejoice to be strengthened by a necessary example; but that she should nevertheless be held within the clefts of the rock, and that the assault of the hawk and hostile snares should be kept far away.”

The rock, as is well known, is called Christ figuratively: when struck by Moses’ mystical rod, it yielded a spring, poured out water, and bestowed streams in abundant gift; the people and their beasts drank when badly parched with thirst. The clefts of this rock are called Christ’s wounds, passion, and death; faith in and love of these bestow a saving defense. Whoever lies hidden in watchful remembrance of them, or in a remembering watchfulness, in hope and silence, will neither be crushed by present troubles nor fear future afflictions.

Nor do I consider it absurd if Christ’s clefts are called law and grace, mercy and truth, justice and peace, and anything similar: things which, disclosed and experienced, protect us from the onrush of the malignant. If anyone lies hidden in these—that is, in a worthy understanding of them—they raise him toward progress and free him from harmful failure.

A wall is called a simple heap of stones, stretched out like a hedge and not held together by mortar in between; but, joined by a light kind of workmanship for the protection of vineyards, it encloses them and frees them from the harmful attacks of beasts. This wall may be that society of angels which, long ago ordered by the Creator’s command for the protection of the elect, has no need, in order to stand more firmly, of the binding force of Law or Gospel; its original condition, confirmed by grace, has sufficient solidity.

The caves and inner little dwellings, or recesses, of this wall are found open by whoever has worthily entered the vineyards: they are the care and love which angels seem to show to human beings, whom, like doves, they desire to keep from malignant attacks. Therefore, to the Virgin who is invited to revisit the flowering vineyards, in order that, postponing leisure for a time, she may give those who behold her a model of conduct, he who invites her promises the clefts of life and the hollows of the wall, so that the dove, relying upon such protection, may confidently fulfill what is commanded.

“You,” he says, “whose devotion of mind burns to be at leisure and to behold, rise and hasten, and let no fear delay you. For although your mind, longing for secrecy, as it were hates public exposure, nevertheless you have no cause for fear, since the rock already guards you in its clefts.”

A good rock, which the anxious hand of those who dig opens, and which, once opened, grants a saving defense to the digger; and which the Bride not by digging but by longing merited to open, and in which she found not deceptive confidence but faithful protection. She, indeed, unable to bear base labor, disdained to dig the earth; flourishing in praiseworthy pride, she did not desire to sink herself in muddy desires. Unlike that wicked servant who, having received his Lord’s talent, being excessively anxious about loss, covered it in a pit in the ground and would not return it with interest: “Going away,” he says, “he dug in the earth and hid his master’s money” (Matt. 25); and below: “Being afraid,” he says, “I went away and hid your talent in the earth; behold, you have what is yours” (ibid.).

That man would have been far happier had he not devoted himself to this labor, had he not dug muddy earth in soft negligence; had he answered the avaricious master more pleasingly with doubled interest, and had merited to be hidden in the rock rather than cast into outer darkness: “Cast,” he says, “the useless servant into outer darkness” (Matt. 25). Finally, those who dug Christ’s hands and feet and pierced his side with a lance, being devoted only to earth, did not come to the solid rock; clinging to softer things, negligently sunk into the deep, ignorant of the first commandment, they did not keep either the like or the second.

Therefore the Virgin, although she knows the Word made flesh from the womb most fully, nevertheless she no longer knows his excellence according to the flesh. Rather, she is raised upon the rock, sets her foot above the solid rock, and, as a dove nesting in the clefts of the rock, arranges and orders her young. Established above the rock—or rather, in the clefts of the rock—she avoids predatory assaults and remains safe from snares. Standing at the mouth of the cleft, she rejoices to behold the flowering vineyards and, that they may progress more, permits herself to be seen by them.

Rightly, then, the hollows of the wall are not shut to this same Virgin, but are spread wide in an open recess to receive her more fully. They do not permit her, while caring for the vineyards, to labor in the heat and rain beneath the open sky; rather, the angels surrounding her do not omit to care for her. Indeed, from ancient times caves have stood open in this wall, ever since angels fell from it in ruinous descent. The prudent architect did not wish to repair them with stones of the same kind, but that human beings should enter through grace and merits in place of those who fell.

And because the interrupted wall awaits repair through human beings, it delights to be opened more to none than to the Bride; and it displays for her all its entrances, all its openings, that the Virgin may freely enter whichever she sees will benefit her. To her, who thus has refuge in the clefts of the rock and in the hollows of the wall, and who, fortified by this protection, no longer fears any assaults of the malignant ones, the Bridegroom, adding speech, wishes her face to be shown to him—perhaps being curious to know whether anything blameworthy can be found in it.

## CHAPTER XII

“Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears; for your voice is sweet and your face beautiful.”

After the Virgin is said to be a dove in the hollows of the wall and in the clefts of the rock, I judge her to be not so much mourning as rejoicing in secure protection. She is admonished to offer for the Bridegroom’s sight the face nourished by such great benefits, desired on account of the merit of its beauty. For the Bridegroom now judges that nothing remains in her which, when offered to the beholder, ought to displease; since, with a secure mind as though at an unceasing banquet, her face grows cheerful, and her inward purity shines more clearly upon its surface.

Solomon intimates this when he says: “A joyful mind makes a flourishing age; a sad spirit dries up the bones” (Prov. 17). Therefore, when the mind languishes in sadness, the soul sickens; consequently the bones dry up, the face wastes away, and, conscious of its ugliness, it blushes to go out in public. Even if it desires to be seen by the one who loves it, it fears to do so.

But the Virgin—if any ugliness had formerly existed in her—now has a joyful mind; the beauty of her conscience flourishes. Having heard the Bridegroom’s voice, she will not cover herself with the cloak of base shame, but will show her form, which certainly shines forth more fully in the face.  
[Note: Col. 0325. This refers to what is said near the end of Genesis 34.]

Adam, conscious of sin, immediately withdrew into gloomy darkness; ugly with a sad face, he did not go out to meet God who called him. He knew that the stains of filth which sad guilt had brought upon his face would not please God, who is described as a lover of beauty.

But the Virgin’s face, which the Bridegroom so carefully wishes to be shown to him, is known by him to be neither filthy nor reproachable through sordid ugliness. Hers is a conscience endowed with a certain singular grace, before which no other can be preferred and with which, finally, no other woman can be equaled. For she seeks leisure more ardently, knows how to rejoice more sweetly than others when she finds it, and bears the task imposed upon her all the more soundly the more patiently she endures it. Knowing no halting now along this path and now along that, she proceeds in such a way as to run toward the commandment without exceeding the boundaries set for her.

Such a conscience shows itself confidently to none but the Bridegroom. At the voice of the one commanding, it considers nothing its own; when a difficulty is proposed, it does not hold out the cloak of excuse, but whatever he commands, it grasps with outstretched hands. The Bridegroom expressly asks that this face be shown to him because he recognizes neither the Virgin nor any other human being except through the face; and the more free from the soot of sin he sees her, the more he rejoices that his knowledge of her is fuller.

“Because it has been given to you to excel in many goods, I wish you, from your reception of present gifts, to have such confidence that you need not fear to appear before me face to face, displaying your conscience openly before my sight. And when it shows itself to me, the more purely, the more securely, then your voice will also sound in my ears. For when your face has been presented, you no longer rightly shut your mouth; rather, thanksgiving and the voice of praise confidently burst forth.”

For once the face has been seen so serene through the privilege of grace, the lovely voice no longer contains itself within the bounds of silence. As the face is worthy to be seen and beautiful to the sight, so the voice becomes sweet and resonant to the hearing. But she who still either fears or offends the Bridegroom on account of imperfection, and therefore does not show a secure face to him who asks—or perhaps refuses—the voice of such a one has not yet broken forth in a sufficiently harmonious sound in his ears; her turned-away face interrupts its sound, lest it become sweet.

Therefore the Bridegroom wishes the Virgin’s voice to sound in his ears—a voice which exceptional sweetness is found to commend, whose sweet and delightful harmony of sound rings among women’s voices more sweetly than the voice of a swan among the cries of geese. No woman so readily stretches out her hands to commandments; consequently no one’s exultation or confession is so welcome. No one’s face shines with so much grace or beauty, and therefore no one’s voice resounds with sweeter melody.

“Your voice,” he says, “is sweet, and your face beautiful.” “Therefore,” he says, “my ear, with its open bosom, desires to hear your voice, because it is found to charm that ear with harmonious sound; and the voice of one whose visible face rightly pleases by such beauty adds grace by its harmony with the face already seen.”

It is a good order that first the face of the inner conscience should be adorned, and then the voice, sounding worthily, should be declared praiseworthy. For the praise or teaching of one whose face still does not deserve to be shown because of ugliness does not appear sufficiently sweet in sound.

Perhaps anyone’s face has a certain grace in silence and is praised when that person lives justly, and there is neither opportunity nor necessity to speak; when, more secretly before God, that person presents a clean face of heart and does not publicly display even this fact by a proclamation of the voice. But a clamorous voice never profits, and sometimes harms, unless a beautiful face has preceded the voice; for, as is written, praise is not precious in the mouth of a sinner, and a recital of justice is likewise hateful where there is hatred of discipline (Ecclus. 15).

But the Virgin, who is understood to be led onward more than others, whom Bridegroom and Son wished to lead to perfection, blossomed in a beautiful face as she advanced into marvelous virtue, and sounded forth in teaching and example worthily for the salvation of her hearers. 187 Her inner face still desires to be shown to us today, while she loves us, warns us by example, speaks to us, and cries aloud to us. In both she diligently provides for us and favors us: no longer anxious for herself, she trembles and fears for us.

But if our eye is dim and our ear—like that of asps—deaf, and if her face is hidden from us and her voice grows hoarse, nevertheless the Virgin’s beauty is believed to have flourished both now and then in the Bridegroom’s eyes, and her praising and exulting voice to have sounded sweetly in those same ears. Therefore perhaps he says pointedly: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears.” “Although you do not show your face to those who desire to see it, and do not grant the benefit of your voice to those who stop their ears, yet your face is shown to me, who cannot fail to see my own gifts, and your voice sounds in my ears, to which I judge it worthy to give attention.”

And so that the Virgin’s presence might not be idle for those around her, but might become fruitful for the young women who worthily behold her, the Bridegroom wished every harmful thing to be removed from them, so that they might merit to behold her revisit them more fruitfully. Therefore he adds: “Catch for us,” etc.

## CHAPTER XIII

“Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards; for our vineyard has blossomed.”

Whom does the Bridegroom seem to invite to catch the little foxes, unless his dogs, lest these seducing little beasts dare to hide among the vineyards? In the absence of the dogs they are found to gnaw, injure, and destroy them; hence it is necessary that the dogs be found zealous to catch them.

Accordingly, the Bridegroom admonishes those whom he has already placed over the care of the vines, whom he has made prelates of churches, skilled in hunting down every harmful thing, to keep watch, pursue the deceitful little beasts with shrewd tracking, press on, and not cease until they catch what they hunt. Of such people Jeremiah says: “I will send many hunters, and they will hunt them” (Jer. 16). And in the Psalm: “The tongue of your dogs” (Ps. 67).

These dogs, with whom the Bridegroom wished our care to be joined, stand by us when we begin, preventing loss or damage. They diligently urge that evils threatening us may already fade at their very beginning, before they grow more grievously through our negligence or ignorance. For sometimes our present manner of life burdens us with hidden faults; their gentle seduction secretly insinuates itself like a fox, and, running deceitfully through blind winding paths, wishes to remain unknown and to destroy us, ill-provided as we are, all the more freely because more secretly.

When our elders visit us with their teaching, instruct the ignorant, and correct the erring by discipline, they show from where temptation comes, whither it proceeds, and what destruction—or finally what death—follows each suggestion. When with their censorial tongue they rebuke fresh maladies, like watchful dogs they catch the little foxes within us.

Hence those commanded to do this diligently but who do not care, those who are lazy in hunting and make sleep the image of their negligence, are called through Isaiah, as by another dog, “dumb dogs” (Isa. 51), sleeping and loving dreams, although appointed in the place of watchmen. And surely this care lies much more upon us as well: namely, that we should endeavor to be found equally watchful in the capture, and should pursue the foxes within ourselves with diligent tracking until we wisely reach their hiding places by the hunting scent.

When we reach them, we must crush the evil seeds of disease while they are new, according to the poet;  
[Note: Col. 0327D. Ovid.]

and dash our little ones against the rock, according to the Prophet (Ps. 136), lest either ignorance obscuring us or negligence drawing us away should seduce us down the path of error and lead us into deadly falls and the snares of temptations.

For sometimes subtle temptation pretends to be either nonexistent or very small, and flatters a negligent mind with deceptive charm, so that, when it denies or minimizes what is secretly perceived as desirable, it subsequently makes us despise what we actually consent to. And when the seduced mind does not look carefully enough at how the cancer creeps or what the conceived wickedness intends, the destruction of the vineyard itself clearly shows that the fox, formerly little, which secretly entered, has done no small harm.

We are therefore commanded to attend to, hunt, and diligently catch foxes of this sort which deceitfully insinuate themselves into our minds, so that what first lay hidden, as if in a chamber and reverently beneath a cloak, may burst forth, come out, and at last rejoice to show itself shamelessly. “Some rejoice,” as it is written, “when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2).

But some say—if your attentive memory has retained what it heard—that this present little book, which Solomon, as stated above, arranged in the manner of a drama, contains the words only of four, as it were, persons, who speak of nuptial love and of the spiritual chastity of marriage.  
[Note: Col. 0329D. See above at the beginning, before the exposition of chapter 1 of the Song of Songs.]

For the Bride and the young women, the Bridegroom and the Bridegroom’s companions, are introduced as four, as it were, characters. They are brought, as it were, from the stage into the middle in order to weave the drama, so that speech may pass from these to those and back again, and a reciprocal dialogue may fulfill the nuptial drama.

Therefore, the Bridegroom, who above has spoken now to the Bride and now to the young women, and has pursued with pleasing care what suits the Bride, now seems to turn his speech to his companions, exhorting those present at the wedding to catch the foxes. The Bridegroom’s companions, however, are said to be the holy angels, who are certainly known to attend this wedding; as you know, Gabriel was sent to the Virgin in the beginning, and both he and the others are not absent from service to humankind.

At this wedding the Bridegroom is driven by no slight care to provide what will benefit the Virgin and those attending her: first, that the Virgin may rejoice more excellently in the bridal chamber; second, that the young women may not lack spiritual progress. It has been said far above that by the name “young women” are figured the apostles and apostolic men, who seem more especially to attend the Virgin, the Bridegroom’s Mother, with devoted affection: while they lovingly venerate her childbearing with earnest wonder and firm faith, and imitate her fruitfulness by themselves bearing children—not through sexual union, but through the Spirit.

The Bridegroom wishes these pastors and teachers not to be burdened by the attack of malignant spirits, but to be freed through the favorable love and protection of angels, so that the vineyards may not wither in the flower of their first season through the foxes’ deceit, but may grow strong toward late fruit through the care of good spirits. Therefore the Bridegroom admonishes the good spirits, who in this wedding song are the companions, to be zealous, to aim at the advancement of the marriage, to stand nearer to them, and worthily to care for those whose ruin or injury the solicitous Virgin does not wish.

For the Virgin has great concern for the young women, or apostles, whose way of life will benefit her greatly and others greatly as well. The angels’ care is commanded diligently to keep harmful things away from them—a service or ministry greatly pleasing to both Bridegroom and Bride. Speaking to them, the Bridegroom says: “Catch,” etc.

## CHAPTER XIV

“Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.”

“You angels,” he says, “whom flesh has not made equal to human beings, nor sin equal to evil spirits; whom pride or disobedience has not cast out from the Creator’s presence; who remain and abide with me from the beginning forever as companions, sharing in glory but not equal in eternal greatness: while I and the Bride celebrate the wedding, I wish you to stand by us attentively, so that whatever strives to oppose may through you be ineffective and powerless.

“For some, when they no longer advance by open violence along a plain path, creep in by dark winding ways and whisper poisonous deceits. They speak ill of the Virgin and labor to resist her purposes, by deceitfully disfiguring what she affirms concerning Christ. They seek to dissuade people from allowing the hidden divinity of Christ to be seen by faith’s eye; or, if faith has seen it, from loving it firmly in the mind. They strike those who will deny with the hard blow of ignorance or fear, or implant love for visible things in those who will neglect faith in invisible things.

“Who are these, if not wicked demons, learned in malice and full of deceit? They love nothing holy, seek nothing worthy of praise; when violence is lacking, love and skill in seducing are present, and, according to a certain pagan writer, they possess a thousand arts—and more—of doing harm.”  
[Note: Col. 0330D. Ovid.]

By marvelous cunning of craft, not by right of power or strength, these seduce Judas Iscariot, who loved money more than salvation. By manifold deceit they dissuade him from loving his Master, and persuade him, guilty of hatred, to become a traitor: “When,” he says, “the devil had put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him” (John 13).

These same spirits shortly afterward shake Simon Peter, who a little earlier had promised his lot for steadfastness, with the thunderbolt of fear so as to deny him. He would suddenly have perished as a denier within the subtle jaws of beasts had the powerful prayer of his merciful Master not helped him: “Simon,” he says, “behold, Satan has sought you, that he might sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22).

Nor did the cunning of the malignant ones merely diminish the number of apostles before Christ’s resurrection; after the resurrection it also prepared a snare for the chosen deacons. Though it did not draw into it Stephen, full of faith and the Spirit, or the other five, it nevertheless led the seventh, the foreigner Nicolaus, into a new heresy.

The Bridegroom rightly designated their deceitful cunning by the name of foxes. Nature has not armed animals of this kind with many powers, but has protected them by such cleverness and so great a refuge of varied deceits that they are said in the Gospel to possess many recesses of dens within us: “Foxes,” he says, “have dens” (Luke 9). Demons have hidden recesses and dark lurking places; they have tracks impossible to follow and winding footprints, so that a simple person cannot easily set foot in tracing them out, since one either cannot see them, or, if one happens to see them, immediately loses them.

At times, when hunger seems to press a fox hard, it runs to the refuge of deceit and pretends to lie dead. When birds come near, hoping to find food in the dead carcass, it seizes them unawares and rejoices in gaining victory over the living. So too that wicked spirit, always found to hunger for our ruin: when it cannot ensnare any winged creatures with open nets—for, as Scripture recalls (Prov. 1) and the truth of experience affirms, a net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures—it pretends to be dead and to have absolutely no power against the righteous. It yields and seems already to grant that they may prevail in whatever good things they choose.

When they think themselves standing, as though they will henceforth not fall, rejoicing in long progress and already secure through much experience, they sometimes approach this carrion of the world, desiring transient things a little too immoderately, believing that nothing harmful lies in them but rather that they benefit necessary uses. But that wicked one, remembering that the former Law forbids touching carrion (Lev. 2), sees the righteous now held guilty, even slightly, under the written Law; judging the unsuspecting desireers of temporal things to be under his power, he suddenly comes wickedly to life and lays a strong hand upon the birds destined to perish.

Thus those who thought they were catching it and turning it to their own uses are found to be caught, and the living are subjected to the dead. For while the living desire a little too incautiously the carrion of sins, that which seemed dead comes vigorously and truly to life for the destruction of the living.

That prudent Samson, abhorring deceitful foxes, caught them alive—no fewer than three hundred. Binding them two by two, with their heads free and their tails tied, and placing fire beneath their tails, he fashioned a mystery worthy of praise (Judg. 15). This prudent Samson, who is said also to be strong in arm, and who by prudent strength is believed to have removed the gates of death, is the beloved of this Virgin of whom we speak—he whom a true understanding of faith proclaims God and man.

He caught not one or merely two but three hundred foxes together, because he has perceived all the malice of all malignant spirits. As man, so also as God, he observes all things circumspectly, and nothing appears imperfectly to his sight. As you know, every perfection is figured by the number one hundred; and it is not unfitting to speak of perfection, a hundredfold, as tripled, since for whatever malignant spirits have suggested to us, whether only slightly, in affection, whether by word, or whether by deed they have brought to any effect, this stricter Judge gathers all of them completely in his hooked hand and, preparing fire for all, draws them all into miserable ruin.

For now wicked spirits rage, as though with their heads unbound and mouths free; but their tails will be bound unbreakably. When, at the end of all things, they are forbidden the power to rage, the fire rendered according to their deserts will press them into unceasing suffering. Of this the Gospel says: “The eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). And Paul: “Whose end,” he says, “is in burning” (Heb. 6).

Meanwhile, while that consummation is still deferred, while the final burning has not yet been inflicted upon the gathered foxes, the Bridegroom wishes more carefully to admonish his companions—that is, the good angels—to apply diligence in catching the evil ones. For human beings attacked by demons and filled with many miseries cannot stand unless ministering spirits resist the snares of the harmful spirits. The good ones therefore come, discover the deceits of the evil ones, and, having discovered them, show them beforehand to human beings, so that they may guard themselves carefully.

For this purpose ministering spirits have been set over human beings; for this purpose they have been assigned to their care and guardianship: that what people, slower through nature and negligence, cannot prevail to do, these spirits—whom both nature and merit have made far keener—may foresee, guard against, warn human beings of, and help them guard against. Thus enemies may not exult and insult, saying, “We have prevailed in doing harm.”

The weaker human being, wishing to prepare or rebuild the inner walls of holiness, to restore Jerusalem, and to repair the old breaches of the ruined city, has many who attack and impede the harsh labor of one so diligently engaged. When they see it, they envy it, and, to say the least, mock the watchful diligence of the laborer. When they perceive him not sufficiently strong by himself to escape, even with his steps unharmed, the enemies’ mockery or pressure, they despise the work begun and declare that it cannot be brought to perfection; rather, they say that foxes will lightly leap over what remains incomplete, with a mocking leap.

Thus Tobias the Ammonite says in Ezra: “If a fox goes up, it will leap over their stone wall” (2 Ezra 4). And it is added: “Hear, our God, because we have become an object of contempt; do not cover their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before your face, because they mocked the builders” (ibid.).

You see the wicked rivals mocking the labor of the builders and, as they progress, already rejoicing at the future leap of foxes. Their weakness cannot fully resist this mockery, or the leap already presumptuously anticipated, unless the skilful guardianship of angels stands by them as they labor. Therefore, because the diligence of the righteous works hard in restoring the mind’s building, and the work begun is sometimes disfigured by the mockery or oppression of malignant beings, the Bridegroom more urgently admonishes and incites his companions, whose stronger care more fully investigates the deceits of the assailants.

“You,” he says, “who can forestall with swift sight the cunning of envious spirits, catch for us the foxes which think they will leap over the wall of the builders, lest their disgraceful leap dishonor what those builders construct, or any deceit of enemies disfigure the city that is being restored.” Isaiah says: “Those who say to my soul, ‘Bow down, that we may pass over’” (Isa. 51). Against this Nahum the prophet says: “Belial shall no longer continue to pass through you” (Nah. 1).

Who will grant that Belial may no longer proceed through us, nor foxes leap contemptuously over the work of building, unless the Bridegroom’s companions, who are commanded to assist human beings in this matter, wisely and watchfully forestall mocking leaps or assaults? Let them therefore catch the foxes for us while they appear little and still weak, lest they grow large and cross the wall—which, while small, they can easily leap over. If they are allowed to test its smallness by a free leap, progressing toward worse things, they will hasten to destroy our vineyards.

When the vineyards are flowering and hope to advance toward fruit in summer’s mild weather, the little foxes must be removed far away from them, or their frauds must be discovered by worthy foresight so that, even if they wish it, they may not have power to harm those who are advancing.

## CHAPTER XV

“For our vineyard has blossomed.”

He who shortly before named “vineyards” now consequently names the singular “vineyard,” whereas one usually passes in counting from the singular number to the plural. By this he indicates that the souls to whom the Bridegroom has willed to give saving life are gathered by unity of faith and agreement into a united people. “We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. 99). They call themselves “people,” that the singularity of faith may be commended, and call themselves “sheep,” that the diversity of many may be shown; for fitting unity gathers many into one bundle or sheaf, and one Lord and one faith make one people.

That this kind of unity may appear to be commended more expressly, among those whom Christ wished to gather together as apostles (Acts 4), love in common possession of all things long ago removed every inconvenient obstacle, so that there was one soul in all and one heart for all (Acts 2). Perhaps this vineyard is said especially to have blossomed, into which the Bridegroom is read to have poured his Spirit on the fiftieth day. Rich in a new gift, burning with a new love of holiness, it brought forth new and unheard-of little flowers of voluntary poverty.

Of it it was foretold: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5). Rightly is the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, producing marvelous flowers and about to bear equally marvelous fruits, called the house of Israel: not a house obscured by blindness, certainly, but a house seeing God in hope at present, later to behold him, rejoicing greatly in faith now and destined to rejoice still more in sight.

Within the enclosure of this vineyard little foxes ought not to be admitted; or, if perhaps admitted, they ought not to be allowed to remain long. When hidden avarice has already destroyed Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5), still wickedly tender, they should quickly be caught, lest they go on and fulfill the desired malice of their deceit. For the Bridegroom’s companions, faithfully attending Peter and revealing the hidden bite of the little fox in false brothers, do not permit its poisonous little snares to be spread everywhere among the rest. The seducers grieve that their design is broken and their deceits discovered.

For those whom angels perceive themselves to govern for salvation, and concerning whom they know that the Bridegroom truly has care, they neither wish nor allow to be devoted to the earth and become the foxes’ portion (Ps. 62); rather, they warn and help them not to be subject to the foxes’ deceits. Therefore, at this time the foxes are not undeservedly called little, since they are easily restrained from plunder by angelic ministry. But when the end of time comes, they will become more maliciously great: with their powers unrestrained, they will blaze forth into violence all the more freely because only briefly remains (Rev. 20).

Then angelic care, as though insufficient, will summon them to a greater hearing, and our Samson himself, placing fire beneath, will bind the tails of all. The sending forth of foxes will hasten to rage against the harvests of the Philistines, so that the works both of these and of those may deserve to perish in one fire. For then wicked spirits will perish in a destroying but not consuming fire, and evil human beings will likewise perish miserably in a death that is nevertheless immortal. The former, their ends bound unbreakably, will not return to the freedom of wickedness; the harvests of the latter, as of Philistines—that is, both their works and the hope of their works—will perish.

Because the Bridegroom, in his benevolence, wishes this to be kept far from his vineyards, and wishes angels to be employed in restraining it while the time is favorable, the Bride rejoices. And she loves to answer the loving Bridegroom in a corresponding manner all the more because she sees him to be more kindly disposed toward her young women. Of this he adds: “The Beloved,” etc.

## CHAPTER XVI
My beloved is mine, and I am his—he who feeds among the lilies—[Col. 0334C] until the day breathes forth and the shadows decline. What is meant by this: that, when the beloved woman speaks here about her beloved, her utterance seems somewhat incomplete? Nor is a fuller sense found in it unless something external is understood to be supplied. But what, more truly or more certainly, she who speaks herself intends to be understood is, I think, not easily discovered with precision—especially by those plainly hindered by the darkness of their minds and not deserving to have the hidden things of Scripture opened to them. Therefore, since I am slight in understanding and do not abound in merits, I shall supply this expression for myself and for no one else, in such a way that I neither criticize the speaker nor weaken her words by a wandering interpretation; for whatever I may say here will be conjecture rather than assertion.

A little above, when the Virgin said [Col. 0334D] “My beloved to me,” she added “speaks”: “My beloved,” she said, “speaks to me.” Nor does that construction seem clouded by an implied addition; furnished with the necessary elements, it is plainly found sufficient. But now, saying, “My beloved to me,” she has not added what he does or says; thus it remains uncertain which of these she wishes understood. And the more uncertain it is, the more freely anyone is permitted to discover whatever seems suitably applicable in the present place.

For unrestrained love, scarcely able to endure its own impulses, often cannot find words fully expressive of its feelings; and so its speech is sometimes suspended, or—to say more—defective through scant verbal resources. For when it stretches itself with its whole desire toward that for which it burns, longing to hold that alone, it counts all else as of little worth. And if it happens to speak a word about it, it pays no attention to time, manner, or order; and while it desires all of it, it does not strive to express all of it in words.

Thus that woman in the Gospel, when what she loved had been taken away, knowing only how to weep and holding in her mind alone him whose tomb she grieved to see empty, suddenly saw someone and, her eye wandering, supposed him to be the gardener. Not remembering grammar sufficiently and fearing no Priscian, she said: “Sir, if you have taken him away, tell me; and I will take him away” (John 20). She introduces “him,” although she had said nothing about him before, and does not explain by a suitable preceding word to whom she refers him; thinking it enough for the hearer that she herself fully thinks and fully feels it, even if her outward, half-complete speech does not correspond more fully [Col. 0335B] to the full sense within her.

Nor is it surprising if hidden love, when it needs another’s help to display itself, judges half-complete speech sufficient for itself—love which often speaks through a sigh, often even through desire alone, and does not despair of being heard even though it does not speak with a full clamor of words. Therefore our Virgin, carefully weighing the grace of this love and not repaying its abundance with abundant eloquence, encloses within the hidden place of her heart wondrous movements in an inexplicable way. Breathing out only faintly in few words, she thus responds to him: by speaking she makes this love known to the hearer, yet with a curtailed store of words leaves the hearer in suspense.

“My beloved,” she says, “is mine, and I am his.” That is: he gives me what is his, and I give him what is mine [Col. 0335C], so that his things may be mine and mine his; and thus we may possess ours together and rejoice that all things are common to us, as the laws of betrothal require.

If such a meaning can be believed to emerge most suitably from these words, the Bride seems to answer the Bridegroom in response to what he had said. When he commanded the foxes to be caught because the vineyard had blossomed, he called it “our” vineyard, but did not show in the following words whence this commendable communion had arisen. For he did not say, “My vineyard” or “your vineyard,” but “Our vineyard has blossomed.” The prudent Virgin, attentively receiving that word with a diligent ear, as though the Bridegroom had departed, turns again to the aforesaid young women. She rejoices to speak of him and, in few words, makes known whence comes this communion [Col. 0335D] which the Bridegroom wished to signify.

So that it could be called not his, not mine, but rather “our vineyard,” there has been a reciprocal exchange through which the two are equally friends. For he, in his condescension, looked upon me, his lowly handmaid; and my humility did not despise the grace of him who looked upon me. Perhaps not by my merit but by his good pleasure, he loved me; and the faith of his beloved understood that he was to be loved worthily according to his merits. The Word, intending to become flesh, poured himself into the womb of me, his handmaid; taking flesh in me and from me, by his grace he flooded me. I offered myself, gave him my flesh, devoted myself to obedience, and set no measure, limit, or order upon the good pleasure of him who commanded. By my flesh—which, in assuming it, he so exempted from every fault—he purchased or redeemed for himself the vineyard said to have blossomed. And that vineyard, when it is purchased or redeemed by our flesh while still withering, is, once it blossoms and is loved, significantly called ours.

If the patriarchs of old, who, as is clear, were born one after another of one father, though—as you remember—not all of one mother (Gen. 29–30), say of the next-to-last, Joseph, “For he is our brother and our flesh” (Gen. 37), how much more may the Mother of the Bridegroom, the Bride of the Son, say, “our flesh”? And of the vineyard redeemed by this flesh, may the Son likewise say, “ours”?

“My beloved,” she says, “gave to me what was his; his benefit, his mercy in all things, goes before me. And I offered to him what was mine in a worthy return, so that henceforth there may graciously be communion between us both in things and in words. He also gives me admonitions and a command to rise; and I offer him [Col. 0336B] a ready ear for hearing. He urges and diligently advises me to rise and hasten; renouncing idleness, I patiently bear labor.

“My beloved is to me”—what is he, except loving or beloved? And what do I return to him, except gifts of like diligence or affection? Thus his love, who is first and far pre-eminent, is the originating love; mine is only a subsequent return through his gift. My beloved gives me a command; together with the command he gives a blessing. I run for him in the way of his commandments, with heart enlarged. He gives me help; I give him service. He gives me goodwill; I give him obedience. He gives me what belongs to grace and to love; I give him what belongs to reverence and honor. He is beloved to me; he confers on me, needy as I am, the saving gift. I return to him [Col. 0336C] voluntary affection, though he requires it; and he, the great and almighty God, who willed to be born a human being from me, rejoices to feed not so much between my breasts as among the lilies.

He who once fed the patriarch Jacob from his youth, and who much more recently satisfied five thousand men from five loaves (Matt. 14)—how is he thus needy, or so neglectful of his power as to be fed, when being fed seems a matter not of power but of need? Indeed, after he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he afterward hungered (Matt. 4). When that wicked devil set stones before him to tempt him, he did not suggest that he change them by a word into lilies; for he thought that Christ hungered through necessary lack, as other human beings do, and that therefore bread, rather than lilies, suited one who was hungry.

“You,” he says, “whose jaws, as I perceive, are empty through the exhaustion of fasting, command that these stones by effective power become bread. For while hunger is unfed through the lack of bread, the appearance of lilies—even if perhaps suitable for the eyes—is not suitable for the jaws.” Yet sometimes the eyes too seem to suffer their own hunger: when they itch to see and cannot restrain themselves; and when the covered appearance of a desired thing is granted to them, their curiosity is not inappropriately said to be fed.

Perhaps this is what the Virgin declares when she says that the Bridegroom feeds among the lilies: because the thing desired gives his eyes an answer not so much in word as in appearance; and the gracious eagerness and more ardent heat of lovers are fed not by taste or flavor but by the sight or fragrance of lilies. Therefore [Col. 0337A] he is significantly said not to feed *on* lilies but *among* lilies: dwelling and conversing among them, he rejoices in their fragrant beauty. And just as the Virgin, sick with love, desires to be supported by apples or flowers, so he desires to be delighted among the lilies by their pleasing gift.

For what shines more brightly or breathes a sweeter fragrance than virginal integrity, faith purifying the heart, the fruitfulness of matronly chastity, purity, innocence, spiritual love, sweetness of character, the form of righteousness, and the excellence of special merit in the Bride who is Mother? Among these the Bridegroom walks as though along a broad path; seeing them and smiling upon them, he is fed by their pleasing sight. He delights in the beauty and fragrance of outstanding merits; he himself, flower and lily, rejoices in the resemblance he has found.

For he confesses himself to be “the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys,” and in the Virgin Bride [Col. 0337B] he also beholds the flourishing grace of the lily. Thus he shows that he feeds with a certain joy between the two, while in a subtle movement he now presents himself more fully to the Virgin, now refers himself back to his own proper place, renders himself incomprehensible, and withdraws. For neither does he constantly hide himself in the Father’s bosom, begrudging himself to us, nor does he continuously pour himself out in the Mother’s lap as though through perpetual favor. Rather, coming forth from the Father, he now hastens to her in humble condescension; and withdrawing from her, he now returns to the Father’s inaccessible throne.

“His going forth is from the Father,” says Ambrose, “his return is to the Father.” [Note: [Col. 0337D] In the hymn *On the Nativity of the Lord*.] The Virgin, loving and beloved, experiences as her own this will of the Bridegroom: by it he is now absent from her, now found more present; now he is discovered to be present above human measure, now beyond humanity—while the shadows still remain [Col. 0337C] and the grace of the coming day has not yet arrived.

## Chapter XVII

“He who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathes forth and the shadows decline.”

For when night has declined, nothing obscure and nothing harmful in us will any longer come upon us; and when the gentler breeze breathes at dawn, unfailing light will arrive. Perhaps then the Bridegroom will no longer roam among the lilies in order to feed, since, once seen by us, he will not again return in order to hide himself in his proper place. From that point and thereafter, he will not feed between the two lilies; he will not show himself by forsaking one or referring himself to the other. Rather, he will be so in one that he is constantly present to the other—indeed, so in both that [Col. 0337D] he is absent from neither even for a moment.

“I am in the Father,” he says, “and the Father is in me” (John 14); and below, concerning the Spirit: “He will remain with you,” he says, “and will be in you” (ibid.). Therefore God in God, God remaining in himself, will always contain all things; and nonetheless God will be all things in all. He who now breathes when, how, and where he wills, flooding all with daylight—or rather, with enduring light—will then breathe upon them.

For the person upon whom, while living here, that Holy Spirit worthily breathes, and upon whom he breathes himself by gracious gift not merely unto life but unto life that gives life—for that person a brighter day will then breathe with an ineffable increase. Against that day the ancient night and the future importunity of shadows will not conspire. For God is day: day [Col. 0338A] knowing no setting, one day, whose breathing now and whose still greater breathing then are no small blessing.

It is the day at whose fuller breathing the shadows decline, the nocturnal darkness yields, and wicked spirits or spiritual wickednesses are driven from among those above and cast down even to hell. Wretched indeed are those shadows that, as the day breathes forth, are forced to decline, their necks broken and weighed down by infernal punishments. Their power to rage is lost, though not their capacity to suffer; they curse their grievous existence and their eternally miserable state of being. They would be far happier if they deserved to be reduced to nothing—if, as they are deprived of wicked power, so they were wholly deprived of existence. For it would be better for an evil human being or angel no longer to exist than always to exist in so great a misery of not harming but suffering.

But such shadows—the confusion of darkness, the obscure voice, the power of malicious spirits—will at last receive more fully what they have wickedly done. Unable to endure the breathing day, they are heavily bowed down beneath a hard burden and irrevocably consigned to avenging fire and the living worm.

Meanwhile, while the consummation of the world and the final end of things is delayed, or while the end of her days is not yet at hand for the Virgin mentioned above, the Bridegroom is found to go and return, rather than to remain steadily; and he does not grant to his loving one a fuller abundance of himself. Now, as though made far nearer to heaven than to the Virgin, he wishes to be sought; now, approaching the earth, he allows himself to be felt quickly and only briefly [Col. 0338C]. There he seems more present, though farther absent from here; from there he seems to return when he wishes to be near the Virgin.

Therefore he is not inappropriately said to move among the lilies, delighting in a going forth and return like those of things that are unstable: feeding between two shores, not turning with fixed step toward either of them; now absent, now present; departing quickly and soon returning. To him the Virgin adds: “Return,” etc.

## Chapter XVIII

“Return, my beloved; be like a roe or a young stag upon the mountains of Bethel.”

She who in the preceding chapter spoke of the Bridegroom to the young women—or perhaps, standing alone within the secret chamber of her mind, spoke to herself—does not continue long in that course of speech. Instead, she turns directly to him by whom she believes herself deserted [Col. 0338D]. Love, being insufficient, is consequently found impatient: it does not wish to be without him whom it has once experienced as delightful, once as most sweet. Whatever is offered or conferred upon the yearning soul apart from him, it eagerly rejects with fitting disdain; nothing suffices it until it returns to him.

Since she cannot yet enjoy him by more fully beholding his face, she wishes frequently to address him in speech. And when she speaks about him to him, she is immediately compelled to turn her words into prayer, so that she may be worthy to be seen by him whom she desires to see, with a desire fitting for him. But because in her mortality she feels that he more often withdraws or turns away, nothing does she ask more anxiously [Col. 0339A] than that he return: so that, returning and observing with what love the tender Virgin is held, he may grant the lover grace and a more abundant share of himself.

And lest he prolong his departure or his delay, the Virgin judges it fitting to add merit to her petition, so that even if he perhaps does not intend quickly to hear her prayers, compelled by his own justice he may not set aside the merit of her who asks. “Return,” she says, “my beloved. For if I were begging some great thing from one whom I do not love, I should not wonder at being repulsed and disappointed of my desire. But when I pour out prayers and stretch forth suppliant hands to my beloved, whence comes your hardness, that you do not bring about what I ask?

“For who is so harsh, so austere, that, if he perceives himself tenderly loved, he does not repay it with ready goodwill in equal measure, and does not grant to his loving one the benefit she requests, lest he violate the rights or laws of love by being too hard? True and sincere love does not long turn away its ear; it does not deny like things to one who gives what is welcome and desired, nor confer contrary things. It is held and stirred by much care for her who loves purely; it embraces the lover and responds to tender affection with increase.

“Indeed, by the testimony of Scripture you have said that you love those who love you (Prov. 8); indeed, some—as those who have experienced it proclaim—you loved before they loved you (1 John 4). Since you are laudably proclaimed the first to love, with no preceding merits, who would not judge it harsh if you despise the prayers of those who have well merited? It is certain that one who loves deserves to be loved, and she who is worthy to be loved does not deserve, in consequence, to be disappointed of her desire by the Just One [Col. 0339C]—especially since she does not, after the manner of certain fleshly persons, hunt after what is her own, but asks only for you, and asks that you be present only for your own sake.

“Return, my beloved. You whose love holds me, in comparison with whom all other things are foul to me; you whose absence weighs me down while present things sting or bite me; you who, when believed to be at hand, suddenly turn away, inflicting a burden scarcely bearable upon the untrained and inexperienced: turn, I pray, so that you may show yourself kindly toward one who calls you back—or rather, to say more, return, so that you may make yourself present to the loving one in the sweetness she desires.

“More willingly restore what you have already willingly and often given. Give back to the lover what she has merited, though you loved her before she merited it. Now repeat as a debt what you formerly bestowed freely [Col. 0339D]; or rather, at last return by granting what you promised to those who love you. For at the end of life’s course you promised that we should see you face to face (1 Cor. 13); that those who see you should be satisfied with fullness, and that the satisfied should not be possessed by weariness; that your presence should make us glad and your absence should no longer burden us; that, oppressed by no distress, we should always rejoice with you in your glory.

“Therefore, my beloved, I wish and ask you to return for this: that what I have tasted a little and seen imperfectly through a mirror, I may now hold and see more perfectly with unveiled face, the obstruction of flesh removed and mortality entirely banished.”

But because fervent desire is not filled by the abundance of things present, and unfilled love is not sufficiently patient in awaiting absence, the Virgin asks not merely that he whom she loves return, but that when returning he be like a roe and a young stag [Col. 0340A]. “Be like a roe,” she says, “and a young stag” (above, ch. 4).

As you know it has been said above, the roe has a natural power in its eyes to see and quickly discern food suitable to itself, and even while running to judge what is useful to it, what is fit to eat, and what is unsuitable and therefore rightly to be rejected. But the young stag, aided by both younger age and stronger nature, speeds in swift course and is suddenly present wherever it wishes. It rejoices in such a privilege of speed that among other wild animals it seems to have not merely feet but winged feet.

Therefore, when the Virgin asks the Bridegroom to be like such animals, she shows that she does not lack a conscience confident and secure in itself—a conscience which she does not accuse, at present, either of ignorance or negligence. Since she desires swift recompense, she does not refuse first to be seen. “You,” she says, “whose presence my loving soul longs for, at whose return my conscience in no way trembles: search and observe with what longing, with what earnestness, I love you; with what affection, with what love, setting present things aside, I wait for you alone who are to come.

“Be like a roe, that you may search my inward parts more diligently and not disdain to examine or distinguish what I set aside or place first, whether well or better. And when you know certainly what each virtue deserves in me, let your justice, like a young stag, be swift in giving what it has earned. For I am so eager to receive the benefit of the reward [Col. 0340C] that I am not frightened by the preceding scrutiny and sudden examination. With such ardor do I desire the swift goodwill of the young stag to arrive that I do not refuse to experience the subtle watchfulness of the roe.

“For I know that the grace of the young stag will not come to me for fuller joy unless the truth of the roe first comes to examine my inward conscience; nor will the expectation of his joyful coming fulfill my desire unless his true examination first judges me worthy of fulfillment. ‘Judge therefore and distinguish my cause,’ not only ‘from the unholy nation’ (Ps. 42), which is in no way comparable to me, but also from the holy nation, whose holiness, compared with mine, is not equaled. Perhaps it is this nation which, fearing examination, wishes to be clothed with the coming glory in such a way that it is not first compelled to undergo the winnowing fan of examination.

“For, not knowing whether it is worthy of hatred or love (Eccl. 9), it serves in fear and rejoices in the Lord with trembling. Now, raising itself toward him in hope of the desired gift, it becomes glad; now, turning back upon itself, it fears the scrutiny—severe precisely because true. ‘Who knows,’ it says, ‘whether he will turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him?’” (Joel 2).

But the Virgin knows without doubt that her beloved will turn; having turned, she confidently asks him to return. She wishes her inward parts to be observed by the subtle gaze of him who returns, firmly assured that the steadfast building of her mind will not be overthrown by any battering ram. Therefore, in her whom the sharp eye of the roe finds nothing that is not its own, the goodwill of the young stag will consequently make its leap; and her conscience, approved by judgment that runs before, will have its purity rewarded by the swift grace of the recompensing one [Col. 0341A].

For the roe loves to look more subtly and discerningly, while the young stag wishes to appear glad and benevolent in the swiftness of its course. Both rejoice to be borne over mountain ridges, the summits of virtues: the latter, in rewarding what is just, follows; the former, in considering everything subtly, goes before.

“Upon the mountains,” she says, “of Bethel.” As those who think themselves to possess knowledge of Hebrew names say—a knowledge of which we have deserved either none at all or very little—*Beth* means “house,” and *el* means “God”; and *Bethel* is called “house of God” in Latin speech. [Note: [Col. 0341] The author had some knowledge of the Hebrew language.] The house of God is not inappropriately understood as the inward conscience of the Virgin: that is, the spiritual bridal chamber prepared for God the Son of God, chosen by the majesty of the divine presence as a dwelling place, and adorned and honored by the wondrous excellence of holiness.

This house or dwelling is rightly called mountainous, not because of rough and uneven ridges but because it is rich in the varied merits of virtues. The plain country of us lower beings lies far removed from their height; and among human beings the Bridegroom alone is declared worthily to rise above her. He is indeed borne above, like a roe or a young stag, and the height of any mountains cannot compare with his excellence. Above the mountains of the Virgin and the heights of her conspicuous merits, he is both the subtle knower and swift giver of rewards.

And while the desired glory of rewards has not yet come to the Virgin—a glory which she knows will not come unless the worthy examination of the giver first precedes it—she desires and asks that him whom she loves should not delay longer [Col. 0341C], but swiftly return in the likeness of a roe and a young stag: so that over the mountains of merits and the virtues of virginal conscience, examination may go before and friendly recompense follow.

For that recompensing one is the stag of friendship and the offspring of graces. Although he graciously hears the Virgin’s affectionate prayers, he does not immediately fulfill her desire. Seeing the Virgin, he does not yet wish to be seen face to face; but, like lovers, he hides himself by withdrawing and wishes to be sought. Of this the text continues: “On my bed,” etc.

## Chapter XIX

[Chapter 3.] “On my bed, through the nights, I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him, and did not find him.”

This bed, I think, can be called a certain narrowness of mind, in which the will or intention of one who loves gathers and constrains itself: namely, when she desires with supreme longing to please him whom she loves, to speak with him alone, and to cling to his close embraces. Burning with this purpose, she wishes to recoil from sensible things, turn away from earthly things, and feel the invisible one alone. As though unaware of the flesh, drunk with the love of the Bridegroom whom she tastes beforehand, she constrains herself as one spirit with him into a narrow space, as it were a short bed.

In contrast, the truthful speech of Isaiah—or rather, the truthful spirit of prophecy through Isaiah—accuses and rebukes a woman who does not commit herself to a like narrowness, who, with mind unrestrained, lets in ruined affections: [Col. 0342A] “You have received an adulterer; you have enlarged your bed” (Isa. 57). When the prophetic word says that the shameless woman received an adulterer, it adds, to show that she is not a friend of sufficiently narrow solitude: she has not reduced the breadth of her couch to a short bed, nor compelled herself within narrow bounds by shortening the bed.

For she enlarged her bed when she poured her ruined mind outward; and she received another—or rather, an adulterer—when she introduced the seduction of sin. Enervated by effeminate softness, with legs spread apart and body loosened, she has been defiled in the widened bed with illicit lovers. But the Virgin, ignorant of the aforesaid breadth, encloses herself in a certain narrowness of mind. She admits no one beside him with whom she is one spirit; and she sought upon this bed within herself him [Col. 0342B] whom she loved, hoping that he would be present, she who had admitted absolutely no other.
