For she had read in the Psalm: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him” (Ps. 144). Therefore the Virgin seeks the Bridegroom, but night dulls the seeker’s sight. Night covers itself with a dark face over one wishing to find what she seeks; and, once it has covered her, the sought light does not pour forth full rays, but, withdrawing its brightness, hides itself as though beneath a veil. Not one night but many oppose themselves to the seeking Virgin, placing an oppressive wall between her and the sought one so that he cannot be found. Therefore the Virgin rightly speaks not so much of night as of nights, by whose obstruction she perceives that her desire is still denied.

Night is the difficulty of seeking; night is delay in finding. Night is the distress of postponement; night is the misery of endurance. Night is the unfulfillment of spiritual desire; night is flesh destined to die, even though one’s manner of life is now no longer fleshly. Finally, night is the burdensome presence of this life, however polished by labors and the virtues of one who labors [Col. 0342C].

Through these nights the Virgin declares that she sought the Bridegroom; and because he did not appear to remain in the first, she did not abandon her purpose. Though she sought again and again, she had not yet found him as she wished, proving by experience that light has no complete correspondence with these darknesses. “Through the nights,” she says, “I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, and did not find him.”

The Virgin could not find the Bridegroom when she sought him because the dim night seemed to anticipate the seeker; indeed, as though by agreement, a crowd of nights gathered together, striving and exerting itself to hinder the seeker’s hands and eyes. For although the Virgin strongly restrains herself from other occupations and, confined upon the bed, applies herself more anxiously to seeking, she nevertheless does not reach that inaccessible light of the Bridegroom as long as the crowd of aforesaid nights presses itself against her endeavor.

Hence the same Bridegroom says: “You will seek me and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come” (John 7). The Son is indeed in the bosom, in the council, at the right hand of God the Father—equal in glory, of one substance, of the same majesty; coeternal with the eternal one, equal to the invisible one, dwelling also in inaccessible light, granted not only to any one of us but even to his Mother [Col. 0343A] while she lived here.

For neither John, nor James, nor finally the Virgin Mother attained to the throne of glory in which the Son is in the Father and the Father remains in the Son. As the right or left hand is not given to them for sitting, so neither is it given to the Mother, who by the law of the Son’s humanity is a servant among mortals. Therefore, although the Bridegroom is sought here, whether by their longing or by that of the Mother, he is not found at the right hand or in the glory of God the Father. This being not removed but delayed, she seems to have formed this resolution and either spoken it only to herself or perhaps addressed it to the young women: “I will rise,” etc.

## Chapter XX
Surgam, et circuibo civitatem: per vicos et plateas quaeram quem diligit anima mea. — “I will rise and go about the city; through the lanes and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves.” Since, confined to my bed, I cannot find him whom I love, I will rise; [Col. 0343B] I will undertake to traverse the city’s expanse. I will rise from the leisure and attentiveness of contemplation, and gird myself for the zeal and business of action. Nor will I imitate Dinah (Gen. XXXIV): I will not go out merely to see the women abroad; I will not purchase an estate or go into the country for secular business. Rather, I will go round the fortified city within its circuit; for the sake of calling and strengthening others, I will enter Jerusalem’s heart.

I will not ascribe my nights to fault, to the body, or to idleness; rather, to bless him I will lift up my hands in the nights (Ps. CXXXIII), and seek more diligently through the lanes and squares him whom I love—him whom I cannot find upon my bed—if perhaps I may be able to find him among them. For sometimes we find more abundantly, amid the business of speaking, a progress which we do not perceive in leisure; and when we bestow due care upon brothers and neighbours, he to whom we render obedience through this service is more immediately present.

I think that “lanes” are those whom the rectitude of faith and the steadfast certainty of hope directs; while “squares” are those whom the sweeter breadth of mature charity receives. Through these the Virgin declares that she will seek the Bridegroom, because, by imparting care to them, she judges that she will please him. Since above the Bridegroom had invited her to rise—“Rise,” he said, “make haste, my beloved”—in order, that is, to visit her neighbours for their instruction, the Virgin obeys these counsels, interrupts for a little while the leisure she had taken up, and promises to rise and seek the Bridegroom through lanes and squares.

For she lovingly considers it worthy of her care to visit and go about among those contained within the religious circuit of the fortified city, those who acknowledge themselves to be fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household within the Church’s enclosure [Col. 0343D]; by her intercession she removes every harmful thing and by her example supplies what is profitable. She walks through lanes and squares in the same city when she assists and instructs those upright in faith, steadfast in hope, and expansive in charity, striving to advance them to better things, so that she may deserve increasingly to please him to whom she has proved herself faithful.

For thus he is sought by the diligent, and wills to be sought: and those who seek deserve the grace of him himself whom they seek. Thus, through those narrow and subtle in understanding, and those widened in knowledge, the concern of seekers is exercised; and, though they do not yet sufficiently advance to finding, they are at least advanced toward greater merit. Thus, I say, he wills his countenance to be sought through the people of the Church, as through the city’s lanes and squares; yet he wills that countenance, though invisible, not yet to be found through visible things [Col. 0344A]. For although, by giving the grace of seeking, he wills greater merit to be acquired, he does not yet will that those seeking should experience the desired fullness of that which they seek.

Therefore, when Isaiah cries, “Seek the Lord while he may be found” (Isa. LV), he does not seem, in my judgment, to mean that seekers here can perfectly find the one sought. Rather, those who strive to apply watchful diligence in seeking can at present obtain not the reward of merit, but merit for the reward. Those, therefore, who must still live by faith and by hope in what is to come seek the Lord God: they will find him not immediately, but afterwards. Through nights they seek the day; they will not immediately enjoy his presence, nor attain full joy until the day has dawned.

For through the nights, although worthy zeal is bestowed in seeking [Col. 0344B], not light itself but the merit of finding light is found. While the nights are present, this is the fitting time for seeking; and, once merit has been found, the obtaining of the reward remains. For who would suppose that day can be found through the nights, when, unless the nights give way, the more welcome day refuses to come? The presence of night can be called nothing other than the sun’s absence; and when the sun rises, it is clear that flight is at once commanded to the nights.

While night is present, the sun does not send forth its brightness over the world; and while darkness remains, it does not permit its own face to be seen. But hastening toward its rising, it sends ahead the morning star as its herald, by whose indication it promises itself not to be present, but soon to come. Yet that morning star—by whose announcement the coming sun is anticipated—is found by seekers while the nights still remain [Col. 0344C]. Once it is found, the shadows of night begin to thin, though they wholly vanish only when the sun has risen.

Therefore, while the absent sun is sought through the nights, the morning star sometimes shows itself. It does not intend to show the sun while the nights are still present, but teaches seekers where they should tend, where they should direct the eye by which they will find, from what quarter, that is, they should hope for the sun’s coming presence. For as long as deep night holds and oppresses the world, and the unclean dregs of our wretchedness weigh upon our consciences, who knows—before the morning star is seen—from where the sun is to rise, when, without a guide going before, even the way to it cannot be found?

But when one who seeks the sun beholds the preceding morning star, instructed by that herald he is already held in a kind of certainty [Col. 0344D]: he knows that the sun’s presence is far from the one who announces it, but that, because night intervenes, its face is not yet seen. Thus, seeking light through the nights, he finds light, but nocturnal light; by this light he will afterwards find light, but daylight. This approaching day—the sun that is to come—wills its presence to be delayed, so that it may be reached more certainly; it wills the morning star to be set forth first.

This is what one receives who asks; this is what one finds who seeks; this is the door opened to one who knocks. To one seeking the sun as reward, the way is first shown, as it were, by the morning star. First, I say, merit is given by grace to the labourer; and then, as though from merit—or rather, it will be given—the sun is bestowed as reward upon one who waits. For the Bridegroom does not immediately give reward along with merit, even though perhaps every man sets good wine before that which is inferior [Col. 0345A] (John II); but he is the true sun, who alone deserves to be loved above all things. He wills indeed to be seen, yet is not seen unless the morning star has first been sent.

Perhaps for this reason, after the Gospel had said, “Everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds” (Matt. VII), thereby indicating that the benefit of merit is given in the present, it showed that something else remained to be given hereafter: “And,” it says, “to him who knocks it shall be opened” (ibid.). He who rejoices, it says, that the prior merit is granted him through asking and seeking, will afterwards rejoice, through knocking—that is, through persistence—that the door is opened to him. For one who through the nights is advanced by grace together with merit, as by a morning star, will, when the sun’s palace is opened, enjoy the glory of full light.

A little earlier, when he said, “Ask, seek, knock,” and appended to each word its corresponding response, he gave nothing in the present but set forth promises in the future tense [Col. 0345B], leaving us in suspense whether they were to be fulfilled amid the nights—that is, in this time—or whether they would bring us at once to the desired presence of the eternal sun: “Ask,” he says, “and you shall receive; seek and you shall find; knock and it shall be opened to you” (ibid.). But, lest there remain long doubt whether nothing is granted to the desire of us who ask in the nights, and whether nothing is deferred until the day dawns and the sun—not rather the morning star—rises, he immediately added: “For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds” (ibid.). This concerns the present time. For he does not say, “will receive and will find,” but “receives and finds.” “And,” he says, “to him who knocks it shall be opened.” This concerns the coming sun. For he does not say, “it is opened to him who knocks,” but “it shall be opened,” in order to distinguish between that which we are granted to obtain in the present and that which is promised to be granted much more fully hereafter.

Thus Jacob, asking and seeking not Leah but Rachel in marriage (Gen. XXIX), received first Leah, according to the custom of the country, from her father rather than Rachel. At the wedding he set the elder before him: not of equal beauty, indeed, but fruitful, promising that afterwards the young man would gain entrance to the second. Likewise the Virgin, through the nights, seeking through lanes and squares him whom she knew to be beautiful above all others, first receives and finds the fruitful gift of merit. But because she now longs not so much for merit as for reward, for labour as for rest, she is believed to have found nothing as long as he does not reveal his face. Therefore she repeats: “I sought,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 0345D]

Quaesivi illum, et non inveni. — “I sought him, and did not find him.” Behold, now for the third time the Virgin declares that she has sought him whom she loves, and complains that, though sought, he has not yet been found according to her desire. Yet, not finding him, she is not broken by labour nor does she despair of her purpose; rather, in hope of finding, she perseveres in the zeal of seeking.

It belongs to one who loves to seek once, again, and many times what is loved; if delay intervenes, not to desist from what is hoped for. And if one suffers harshly because what is sought does not quickly appear, still hope comes to aid, lest one fail under desire too long deferred. The Virgin therefore seeks to behold the face of him whom she loves; and nothing suffices for the seeker as long as she perceives herself prevented from attaining her desire. Not content with the bed—where maidenly modesty might suitably seem to be preserved [Col. 0346A]—she goes around the city, walks through the lanes, and now does not shrink from being found amid the squares.

So great a love presses her; such ungoverned ardour inflames her—a love that despises persons, pays no heed to what suits whom, and, once it has burned, no longer cares for reason’s judgment, but conforms those whom it has made burn to its own excess. This Virgin, burning more strongly and therefore more delightfully in such excess, is not recalled by fear of the night, nor frightened by public hostility toward virgins. She seeks him whom she loves; and, not content to seek once, as she repeats her search and hastens here and there, she is found by those whom she encounters.

## CHAPTER XXII

Invenerunt me vigiles qui custodiunt civitatem. — “The watchmen who guard the city found me.” While she wanders about and moves anxiously to and fro [Col. 0346B], running and seeking, while the presence of the one sought is not offered, those to whom the city’s care or guard has been entrusted—who keep watch upon its walls with the vigilant concern of charity—come and find her not languishing in base sleep, but loving vigils and rejoicing in the Virgin’s watchful love.

For this purpose the Bridegroom’s companions, angels lofty in dignity, upheld by wonderful grace and steadfast in their holiness, are sent for ministry and keep watch over our city: that they may see the progress of those who love and foster their ready will. These, then, find her; and having found the Virgin, they rejoice. They regard her as one who loves and marvel at love’s greatness. Having known many lovers commended in a long succession from former times, they see that the Bridegroom is now loved more by the Virgin, and do not envy her [Col. 0346C].

Reviewing in order, from above downward, the citizens and household members of that city to whom grace had been given to love the Giver of grace and Author of truth, they perceive that in all of them the grace of loving had been less; and they rejoice that the Virgin has found no equal among mortals in loving. Significantly, it is not the watchmen who are found by the Virgin, but the Virgin by the watchmen. For the watchmen’s concern over the city is directed to this end: that they may diligently inquire who receives a diminution and who an increase of holiness, and may grieve with one and rejoice with another in the affectionate goodwill of charity.

But the Virgin sought neither men nor angels. Rather, with supreme desire she strove to find the Lord of angels. Therefore, if she perhaps perceives any approaching her [Col. 0346D], she says that she is found by them rather than that she finds them. When those who found her perhaps wished to address her, to ask whence and where she was going and what she intended to find, she, forgetting her female sex, hastens to forestall those about to speak and, impatient with love, disclose her desire to them.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Num quem diligit anima mea vidistis? — “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” The Virgin ought more modestly to have waited in silence while those who had attained a higher rank of dignity spoke first, until the angels who met her should offer counsel to the woman, and, after they had spoken first, she should then answer as instructed. But love without measure knows neither moderation nor restraint: it fears neither sex nor rank nor overstepping bounds [Col. 0347A]. In a certain exaltation of mind it seems to forget every claim of law, judging it right to remember incessantly him alone whom it loves: “Lord,” she says, “I will remember your righteousness alone” (Ps. LXX).

Holding him alone, therefore, in unfaltering memory—the one by whose grace righteousness loves the unworthy and the worthy—when she perceives angels present to guard the city, to admonish the imperfect and not fail the more perfect, she does not judge their presence sufficient for her until she finds him whom she believes to be far above angels. Therefore, not enduring to be approached by those who vigilantly attend to the care of the citizens, she herself approaches them eagerly. Love, stronger than fire and unable to be contained beneath ashes, flames out more visibly and desires to be seen by those standing around.

Since she is slower to be silent and quicker to speak [Col. 0347B], she keeps only him upon her lips and does not speak at length of another: him, I say, whom she loves; him whom, as beloved, she seeks more ardently to find; and, since she has not yet found him, concerning whom she wishes at least to hear new things more eagerly. “You,” she says, “to whom it has been granted always to behold the Father’s face, whom neither fault, flesh, nor any affliction prevents from beholding it: have you not seen him whom I love, whom I desire to find—God the Son equally in God the Father?

“Has that happiness been bestowed upon you, his companions, which is so far denied to me, his betrothed, under a grievous law: namely, that you may behold my Bridegroom in his glory with a discerning eye, while he does not yet allow himself to be seen by me, his mother and Bride? Him, I beg you, in whose presence you have found so blessed a grace, if it pleases you and seems fitting [Col. 0347C], tell me whether you have seen him; and to me as I burn with longing either show him upon whom you desire to look, or at least announce with a consoling word your own vision.

“For it will be no small comfort to me if you announce that you have seen him whose vision I do not yet deserve to find. I am not one to grieve that any happy persons have gone before me to that place which I, far slower, do not yet rejoice to have reached. Tell me, I say, whether you have seen him—or rather, since you have seen him, worthily announce it; commend in saving teaching what you have perceived more fully concerning him. For I judge it fitting to lend an ear to you who have deserved, while we still remain in darkness, to contemplate his face.

“You indeed, not suffering hunger in your mouths but blessed, desiring without weariness yet, all distaste being far removed, satisfied [Col. 0347D], eat in his kingdom the living bread, incorruptible nourishment; refreshed by its richness, you know no affliction at all” (Matt. XVIII). “Although you are now present to console us who labour on earth, you nonetheless always attend his table and banquet; and, while hunger presses us fasting amid troublesome nights, in the courts of that Lord one full day provides you refreshment.”

The angels are not represented as answering the Virgin’s question, perhaps because the Virgin did not wish to endure the delay of an answer: every delay now troubled her burning mind. Therefore the author makes known what she did in her impatience of delay.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0348A]

Paululum cum pertransissem eos, inveni quem diligit anima mea. — “When I had passed them by a little, I found him whom my soul loves.” She knows that he whom she loves is not one of the angels, and that one who remains far above angelic excellence cannot be shown by an angel. She is certain that the Bridegroom and Son, the face of her God, so veils himself that none sees him unless that same Son chooses to reveal him. Therefore, unwilling to remain longer among them or wait anxiously to hear their answers, the Virgin hastens to pass them by in order to seek the Bridegroom, whom she could find only by passing them by.

Or perhaps, as was said above, the watchmen, questioned about the Bridegroom and not dulled by ignorance, were ready and swift to answer. They do not keep silent that they have seen him in his glory, lest they seem to envy the seeker’s affections or progress [Col. 0348B]. They teach the Virgin that he whom she loves is not to be seen among them, but must be sought far beyond them with diligent watchfulness, and that the seeker must make a passage beyond them if she is to see him; and, once this has been done, the Beloved will show himself to the diligent seeker according to the will of him who reveals himself.

“We,” they say, “O Virgin, rejoice with those who see him whom you love, and we testify to what we have seen and heard. And, if you truly desire that his vision may likewise strengthen you, you must not stand still or cling here, but rather pass beyond. Perceive the mutable nature of the whole creation, which indeed has a beginning, though it will not have an end in the same manner; pass beyond, and you will find him to be of another and dissimilar nature, one to which no change or shadow of alteration can ever come.”

Perhaps the watchmen replied these or similar words to the Virgin and promised her the finding of him whom she so loves. But the Virgin, more hasty, did not recount their words in order; she explained more briefly what she herself did: “When I had passed them by,” she says, “I found him whom my soul loves.” “By the consoling words of those by whom I was found while seeking the Beloved, I was detained for a while; but, burning insatiably and not content with such consolation, I stretched myself with looser reins toward what lies beyond.

“For, seeing that angels did not supply my desire, and that the city’s guardians lacked the effective grace to supply it, I passed beyond them, considering whether cherubim and seraphim and spirits of more excellent rank might confer upon my burning heart a fuller gift of sufficiency [Col. 0348D]. For just as there are angels sent in the ministry of salvation to serve the heirs, so perhaps there are others more worthy, who are not sent by the Lord but stand before him. As far as these higher spirits are set above the lower, ministering angels, so are they subject to him whom they rejoice unceasingly to attend.

“I passed beyond angels when I ascended to those worthier spirits. I passed beyond them when I perceived that neither group could fulfil my desire; when I understood that angels possess not merely an insufficient rank but a created nature, and that absolutely no creature can suffice for my desire. I passed beyond when I reflected that the watchmen, or angels, were made. I passed beyond when I considered that they were made not by themselves but by another, and that he who made them is the author of them and of all things in such a manner that he himself has absolutely no creator—not himself, nor any other” [Col. 0349A].

“I passed beyond when it was truly granted me to know this: that angels, being made, can do absolutely nothing without him who made them. I passed beyond when I considered that he who is Maker can do all things through himself, and that he alone suffices for me in all things by giving himself. But what is passing beyond the watchmen—or rather passing the watchmen by—except finding him whom my soul loves? He cannot be more fully found unless creation is passed beyond; and this cannot be fittingly experienced except by one who passes beyond.

“Thus, passing beyond the watchmen, I found him whom I love; thus I came to the excellence of him who is not made but Maker. I found the Creator to surpass every creature beyond measure, and therefore that nothing apart from him ought to be loved.”

But when the Virgin says that she found him whom she loves, why does she preface this by saying that she passed the watchmen only “a little,” when she seems to have passed beyond all things by a very great distance, rejoicing to have found him who is far above all things? Because, while she is held under the law of mortals and the more burdensome bond of flesh, however much she advances in purer longing, she does not find the Bridegroom except with the eye of faith or love. She rightly says “a little,” in comparison with fuller grace [Col. 0349B].

For although through zeal and grace she purifies and advances her understanding, and in marvellous progress passes beyond angels and comes to the Beloved, still, because this arrival is imperfect while one lives here, the eye of faith considers itself to have crossed by only a small passage. This passage could rightly be called great if she already perceived that no burden of flesh opposed her; if she rejoiced greatly not by faith but by reality, not by hope but by sight; if she enjoyed the Bridegroom’s face and no disturbance recalled her from enjoying it.

The passage would be great if she saw herself stripped of inborn mortality and clothed over with glory, worthily exalted above angels; if she sat, by royal right and not wrongful presumption, upon the Bridegroom’s throne; if, as Bride and mother, she cleaved to her Son by a singular privilege. Meanwhile, since such reality or vision is not granted [Col. 0349C], she embraces by faith and hope him whom she loves; and the one whom she says she found by passing the watchmen a little, she declares that she has held with a most firm bond.

## CHAPTER XXV

Tenui eum, nec dimittam donec introducam eum [Col. 0349D] in domum matris meae, et in cubiculum genitricis meae. — “I held him, and I will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her who bore me.”

The Virgin, as said before, sought the Bridegroom with repeated purpose and did not find him whom she sought until she passed beyond the intervening watchmen. For as long as anyone else seems to stand between seeker and sought, the one sought does not sufficiently allow himself to be exposed to the seeker’s desire. When, therefore, she seemed to pass the watchmen with the lynx-eyed gaze, she rejoiced to find more clearly the one she sought—as far, at least, as a living human being can prevail; indeed, she obtained above other human beings the grace of prevailing.

The Virgin found him because he, invisible, could not be perfectly found or seen by a living human being, nor could he, being beyond sense, be sensed. And the more subtly she discovered by contemplation that he is incomprehensible [Col. 0350A], the more strongly she loves him and intends to love nothing apart from him. Thus she judges that he must be pursued not by the foot but by affection; and, pursued, she finds him not with the eye but with keen understanding. She holds him not with clasps, glue, or a binding cord, but with love; she binds him not with an iron chain but with a stronger embrace.

She holds and binds him, I say, and does not relax hands eager to hold. She does not interrupt love, affection, or the intense zeal of advancing. The one long desired she brings into the chamber of her secret heart; she rejoices in the presence of him whom she has brought in, and does not allow him, once present, to go away again. Some are indeed found to have held him at times and to have drawn him by certain bonds toward their own will; yet he seems to be admitted within their snares in such a way as at last, impatient of delay, to ask to be released.

“I see,” he says to Moses, “that this people are stiff-necked. Let me go, that my wrath may be angry against them and that I may destroy them” (Exod. XXXII) [Col. 0350B]. The righteous Lord, whose eye sees and approves equity, abhors the people’s hardness and the perverse wickedness of idolatry. Against that people he purposes to be grievously angered, to be indignant with sinners, and to exact swift vengeance upon them. He wills to unleash his wrath more harshly against the idolaters; but Moses stands in the way and strives to restrain the enraged one (Judg. X). He holds him whom he loves and understands that he sometimes obeys the prayers of those who love. He restrains him when angry and does not permit him to rage according to his purpose against the guilty.

“Either forgive them this sin,” he says, “or, if you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written” (Exod. XXXII) [Col. 0350C]. God does not often alter his writing after our fashion, nor, as though moved by repentance, erase marks once inscribed. The one whom he has already decreed by his grace to save as enrolled among the eternal citizens, he does not later erase or remove from the book of the living.

Thus Moses, asking either that he himself be removed from the book which God had already written, or that God, once the people’s sin was forgiven, have mercy upon them, provokes divine justice, through that which he knows can in no way accord with it, to do what he judges more fitting. He holds it more firmly and, as it were, binds it even against its will, lest the unrestrained hand of conceived wrath extend itself in vengeance.

But justice, so held back from vengeance, seems to wish release because it wills no offence to be left unpunished; and Moses considers that so great a crime would justly be avenged by the death of all, unless the avenging hand were forestalled by mercy’s placid countenance [Col. 0350D]. Therefore, lest he rage so against them that all are utterly destroyed, they are aided not by their own merits but by Moses’ merits. The Lord does not will to heed Moses’ plea that he be released, but, bound more firmly by Moses’ prayers, mercifully compels himself to obey.

Long before, Jacob is read to have wrestled with a man who is called now a man, now an angel, and now even the Lord. Perceiving that his opponent could not easily be overcome, he says: “Let me go, for now the dawn has risen” (Gen. XXXII). But Jacob says: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (ibid.). Jacob does not wish to release God, with whom he wrestles mightily, unless he is redeemed by a price—unless the defeated one grants the victor the grace of blessing, without which the victor himself rejoices in no victory.

“And,” it says, “he blessed him in that same place” (Gen. XXXII) [Col. 0351A]. In order to deserve release, he gives the requested gift; and the Lord renders his releaser enriched by grace. Thus at last, having received the freedom he requested, he is released; and the one who releases rejoices in the newness of the desired gift.

But the Virgin rejoices not in gifts already given, but in the Giver. She seeks no benefit other than more abundant enjoyment of his presence: to hold him whom she loves, not to be drawn away from his embrace, and not to be induced by any price to let him go. “I do not wish,” she says, “that he whom I hold should come to me by grace in such a way that, once the gift is received, the giver of the gift departs; that the blessing of the Beloved be presented to the beloved woman in such a way that he whom I love is absent once he has blessed.

“For I love his gifts only for his sake, and whatever he may give me does not suffice without himself [Col. 0351B]. Indeed, if he denies himself to me as one who loves, let him give himself to others; content with him alone, I shall sleep in peace altogether. Nor do I hold, or shall I hold, him of whom I speak for myself alone; I shall see to it that others hold him with me. For I shall not, through the disease of avarice, envy what benefits others; rather, the more I advance, the more I shall rejoice in the advancement of others.

“Therefore I shall hold him whom I hold and shall not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house—indeed, into her chamber also—so that the mother may subsequently rejoice to find herself experiencing the good which the daughter first and more abundantly deserved to perceive.”

The mother, or she who bore this Virgin, is Judaea. Judaea first bore her in the flesh, in the pain of one giving birth; later, by legal sacraments, she gave her birth unto the worship of the one God [Col. 0351C]. Perhaps she is called both “mother” and “she who bore” so that, by the repeated name, a double begetting may be signified. The Virgin promises to return a benefit to her who bore her. She returns it when she brings the Beloved into that woman’s house or chamber.

Judaea’s house is faith: the faith by which it knows the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of both to be God; the faith by which it has withdrawn itself from the deeds and fellowship of unbelievers. Hidden and resting securely beneath the sheltering shade of this covering, it will not feel the oppressive heat of the sun, nor storm or rain. The unbelief of the Gentiles is not fortified with such a roof: it is not covered by shade, by a roof-peak, or by the tiles of faith. Rather, like a wild ass, it is found free in the open fields or under the open sky; it knows no house, endures no restraint, and is not enclosed by wall or fence.

Therefore, when foul weather comes—snow, hail, ice, storm-winds, or finally some power of darkness—it rejoices immediately to seize one whom it finds wandering and uncovered [Col. 0351D]; and that one is tossed like chaff, fixed by no weight. Judaea, however, its house shut and fortified as with the strength of a castle, rejoicing in its lofty roof and distinguished by certain ramparts, drives far away the grave threats of the air with a strong defence, and, in faith’s hidden place, rests its head and now makes its conscience serene.

For when winds rush, the sky thunders, and the air rages—as it is accustomed to rage threateningly and with excessive persistence in our region—nothing seems calmer than to be covered steadfastly by faith’s defence, provided that defence rests upon a stable foundation [Col. 0352A]. For an architect gathering masses of timber and stones in a structure, if he is properly concerned or afraid of its collapse, digs deep and strives to find the rock upon which he can establish the building with firm footing. Otherwise, though the house itself is raised on taller columns and completed by remarkable labour and workmanship before the eyes of beholders, the greater and more laborious it is, the more grievous a ruin it is liable to suffer under the impact of floods and the force of winds, because it does not rest upon a stronger rock.

Therefore, that Judaea’s house—that is, its faith—may receive a worthy support, the Virgin, providing for her mother, promises to introduce the foundation: that rock which is Christ. By its own firmness it does not permit the building set upon it to fall. God, as you have read, was known from ancient times in Judaea (Ps. LXXV); but Idumaea did not yet know the extension of his sandal. For in those days he imparted some manner of knowledge of himself to believing hearts, but did not personally clothe himself in visible flesh before their eyes.

But when new grace came, when the fullness of time arrived, when God’s strength, condescending to the weak, willed to become weak: the Virgin, fruitful in spirit, bore God incarnate and brought forth to humanity one invisible in divinity, yet shod in flesh [Col. 0352B]. Knowing surely that thereafter none would come to salvation except those who believed in Christ, the wisdom and power of God—Christ, I say, begotten before the morning star from the womb of God the Father, but at the end of the ages made man from the womb of his own mother—the Virgin took the greatest care that this knowledge of the matter should be imparted to Judaea and that the edifice of faith should be made firm upon this as its foundation.

Holding him, therefore, the Virgin promises that she will not loosen her eager hands until she makes him known to her people as one to be held more firmly: until she presents him newly born to believing shepherds, and afterwards commends him, grown greater, to the slower apostles. Indeed, in these words and merits of Mary, the faith of the Jews is instructed, lest the abandoned house fall; through her assistance and work it is upheld. As she gives birth and more truly reveals the one born, Judaea receives and honours Christ: it believes him to be God and man, loves and worships the one believed [Col. 0352C].

Perhaps this is what the Virgin’s promise signifies when pleasant mention is made not only of the house but also of the chamber: namely, that Judaea in the apostles will rejoice both to believe in Christ and to love him, and will obtain this twofold benefit through the Virgin’s intercession. A house, as more spacious, receives indiscriminately many who gather together; but a remote chamber privately admits only those who love. Therefore the house indicates faith, which we see to be common to many, while the chamber indicates love, which you know belongs particularly to the elect.

It does not suffice for the Virgin that she preach Christ to Judaea in such a way that he is believed. She takes the greatest care that he may also be loved by Judaea, while she declares that he is both God born of God before the ages without a mother, and truly made man anew from herself without a father. By counsels and merits alike she leads Judaea to believe and love this; she brings Christ into its house and chamber [Col. 0353A]. Nor does she cease from her zeal until she sees her poor desire answered and rejoices that the Beloved is found in the secret place of those who love.

Once he is found, she does not envy; she does not waste away as a rival. Rather, she breathes again after labour and recovers from weariness, because, burning with charity, she is made glad by the goods of those who advance. In that resting place, as it were, she rests with a joyful conscience. Favouring this rest, the Bridegroom says: “I adjure you,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXVI
“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the stags of the fields: do not awaken or rouse the beloved until she herself wishes.” The Bridegroom warns the apostles, and those who seem likewise to have believed from Judaea and, through the Virgin’s word and care, to have received Christ in the secret place of faith [Col. 0353B]. He warns them, I say, not to make light of the grace once received, and through contempt for present things to stretch themselves out toward former things, or perhaps toward things worse than the former. For if their faith or love should be more grievously shaken, they will make a noise against her sleep, striking the Virgin’s ear more harshly; and she will be compelled unwillingly to awaken to troubles from the joy of repose which the Virgin wished to attain through their conduct.

Therefore the Bridegroom warns them lest Judas’s betrayal thunder harshly among the apostles; lest the teaching of Nicolaus, discordant with the others, sound evilly; lest, on hearing the mystical discourse, many of the disciples be struck by scandal and, going back, no longer walk with him, their purpose harshly broken. Nor did only those apostates, or anyone else who did not truly cleave to Christ in like manner, but also the fear of the elect [Col. 0353C], injure the Virgin’s ears not a little. Peter’s denial, John’s stripping, and the flight of them all resounded grievously and compelled the Virgin, while at rest, to be awakened for watchfulness.

The Bridegroom, therefore, tenderly concerned for the Virgin whom he loved, warns those whom he understood to be disturbed by fear of persecutors, that they may not fail away from the pattern and teaching which the Virgin had given them, or, if they do fail, may perhaps more swiftly recover their senses. “Daughters of Jerusalem,” he says, “it is not fitting for you to will what you find that she who warns you does not yet will; nor are you free to will anything harmful or unbecoming until she too wills it—she whom it is certain [Col. 0354A] never to will it at all.” The apostles indeed, when grace deserted them contrary to the prohibition, willed such things, since they could not resist the fault that confronted them to the utmost. But she willed nothing of the sort, being able worthily to withstand faults as they came upon her; and for this reason she was found to be roused from her pleasing rest, not by her own disturbance but by that of her followers.

Afterward, however, rightly mindful of this adjuration, and more fully visited by the presence of the strengthening Spirit, they are adorned, as it were, in the chamber of their conduct and merits; and they rejoice that through the Virgin’s help and action the Bridegroom is brought in. Once he has been brought in, the Virgin herself likewise rejoices greatly and rests in the sleep she most desired within their conduct. The Bridegroom’s love forbids her to be awakened from it, lest she suffer punishment, though she is not found conscious of fault.

Above, therefore, when with the same words [Col. 0354B] the Bridegroom wished to adjure the daughters of Jerusalem not to presume to awaken the Bride while she rested in the Bridegroom’s embraces, the Virgin was shown to rejoice in their progress, or in progress arising from them—those whom she was said to have gained for herself by grace and merits. Here, however, when the same adjuration is found repeated, the Virgin is understood to rejoice in the merits of others, whose concern is enjoined by the Bridegroom’s love not to reject the grace found so welcome to the Virgin’s desire. There she delights in welcome rest amid the Bridegroom’s embraces; here she rejoices that the Bridegroom rests in her neighbours’ chamber. There she falls asleep amid the progress of her own; here amid that of her neighbours; and in either sleep, holding the Bridegroom, she desires him in his courts.

But since there the same verse has in some fashion been explained, I did not think it necessary [Col. 0354C] to repeat the same explanation here, lest, if what has already been said is said again in the present place, needless repetition produce weariness in the hearer. Therefore, as the second book of this work there took its end where, for the sake of rest, the Virgin made herself recline upon the Bridegroom’s left hand, so here I judge it fitting that the present book be brought to its close or conclusion where the Bride rejoices that the Bridegroom is brought into his mother’s house or chamber: so that where the Bride is granted to fall asleep amid delightsome progress, there our pen may rejoice to be refreshed by silence, as by sleep.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0353]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0353D]

“Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a slender column of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powdered perfume?”

Thus far in this drama the Beloved and the Virgin have spoken to one another or concerning one another, and have pursued in reciprocal speech what belongs to love and grace. No others appear to have been introduced to speak, although the young women or companions have likewise been brought in to hear. But now the Bridegroom grants those to whom he had given place and grace to hear a more ample benefit: he gives the companions opportunity [Col. 0354D] to speak, so that the nuptial epithalamium may become more pleasing to them, since in it they too have together contributed, as it were, a social token.

The companions, that is, the angels, who are said to attend the Bridegroom at such nuptials—who, although they minister to human beings, are nevertheless not barred from his presence—consider with what affection the Bridegroom is bound to the Virgin, and by what grace and merit the Virgin is advanced above all women. They are amazed, stand astounded, and cannot sufficiently admire her as she deserves; nor can they discover with what praises they may suitably honour her. Loving devotion indeed urges them to say something, [Col. 0355A] but consideration of her wondrous greatness holds them back from saying anything. For whatever they say seems to them too little and inadequate; yet they think themselves worthy of blame if they say absolutely nothing.

The very abundance of what may be said makes them poor indeed in speech [Note: [Col. 0355D] That is, of what is to be said.], and certainly their great poverty does not satisfy their desire. Yet they speak in order to awaken in us a desire to listen, and to give us, their hearers, some confidence to speak. For none of us would venture to utter praises of so great a Virgin if the excellence of the angels, as though conscious that it was insufficient for the task, rejected it altogether. But the example and concern of those who are ministering spirits admonish us also, according to whatever ability we possess, to honour the Virgin with praises.

For they themselves show that they act as their ability permits, not as the Virgin’s dignity demands [Col. 0355B]. They have not yet sufficiently apprehended how great the Virgin’s merits are, and therefore do not undertake to express them exactly in words or praises; rather, they marvel, and in marvelling inquire who she is whom they behold to be so wonderful.

“Who is this?” they say. “We review the succession of women present and preceding from ancient time, from the point at which Eve, who was made first, gave assent to the Enemy. Many of them received gifts of diverse charisms. Yet, though the beauty of the inner mind has been cultivated by the hands both of grace and of effort, we can find none of them like this one; rather, she is found to surpass all by ineffable grace. Who, then, is this, to whom alone a singular excellence is granted, so that no woman before her and none after her is her equal; so that she now appears not even to need our aid; indeed, so that she surpasses not merely human beings but angels—not by nature, but by grace?

“Who is this who does not walk with bent knee like a delicate woman, but walks and advances manfully with a strong and tireless step? She undertakes a difficult path untried by women’s feet, and, having grasped the ladder which Jacob scarcely deserved even to see, she ascends boldly through the wilderness [Col. 0355C]. The wilderness, as I see it, is a singular path and manner of life, unknown to the crowd and not worn by the hoof of the populace; it is not touched with mud, nor sprinkled with the dust of the streets; no fault stains it, nor does any superfluity of chaff cover it.

“When Jacob, with a stone apparently supporting his head, was sunk in mystic sleep, he scarcely deserved to see such a ladder [Col. 0355D] (Gen. 28). As it appeared to him, it was forbidden to those living in the human manner and reserved for angels alone as they ascended and descended. For the angels descend, joyfully and favourably meeting the Virgin’s progress. They ascend, preceding her progress with festal praises. Hastening to meet the Lord who leans upon the ladder, they ask: ‘Who is this, who hastens by merits to surpass angels superior by nature?’

“Who is this,” they say, “to whom virginal fruitfulness, or fruitful virginity, has been granted—something inaccessible in all preceding ages both to angels and to human beings? Who, living in a body wrapped in the necessities of death, runs the course of a life liable to vices with unstained step?”

[Col. 0356A]

“For she ascends like a slender column of smoke,” which, when thin and narrow, rises from below and, lifting itself into the fine air, itself becomes finer. Thus it advances upward, entrusting itself to the hidden place of the clouds and, as though emptying itself, eludes the eyes of those looking on. The Virgin, certainly, though begotten of earthly parents, was nevertheless refined by the pursuit of discipline after earthly dregs had been scraped away. She advanced to such a height of merits above human beings that she is rightly said to have surpassed the capacity of those who marvel at her.

As she thus advances, she gives forth far and wide a most sweet fragrance: the teaching of righteousness, a more pleasing pattern of discipline. She grants assistance and rejoices to show goodwill; to those who consider rightly, these seem to breathe fragrance like spices. Perhaps for this reason the smoke, with the slender column of which the advancing Virgin is compared, is said to come forth [Col. 0356B] not from the pit of the abyss but from spices. For the making of these perfumes requires a collection of many kinds of ingredients; they are made from myrrh and frankincense and every powdered perfume.

Myrrh gives marvellous healing to dead bodies, and by a certain natural power drives corruption away from flesh that is slack and soft. Frankincense, burned in fire, is offered to God in sacrifices, and the devotion of those making sacrifice is commended by its fragrant smoke. Myrrh, therefore, seems to resemble the virtue by which the Virgin worthily subjects her body to service, so that through fasts, vigils, and purity corrupt vice may be far removed, and, nature’s claims being restrained, nothing soft or fluid may rot within it.

But by frankincense is figured the Virgin’s humble devotion, or devout humility. When it is burned in the censer of her mind [Col. 0356C] by the fire of the Holy Spirit, melted into love, it is directed upward like smoke; indeed, like a slender column, contracting itself into narrowness, it hastens more intently toward eternal things. By the perfumer’s powder, the whole heap of which is, as it were, added above, is expressed the totality of the remaining virtues. The perfumer—from whom the healing salvation of all has been discovered—carefully gathers and wisely grinds this totality into perfumes.

When all these things, suited to saving medicine, have been gathered and crushed in the Virgin’s heart as in the mortar of discipline, smoke rises before the perfumer and fragrance breathes forth—something at whose worthy wonder the companions’ contemplation scarcely arrives. Who, then, is this in whom, as though a multiplicity of ears of grain had been reduced into a sheaf [Col. 0356D], indeed, the totality of ingredients has been gathered into her mortar; whose merits are ground down, like powder, by the most searching examination; and who is borne upward before the perfumer like smoke, indeed like a slender column of smoke, in marvellous ascent?

When these have been brought and offered, the same perfumer does not turn away, but reclines with welcome goodwill in the offerer herself as upon a little bed. He encloses that same little bed with a rampart of strength, by which he keeps far from it whatever is unseemly and whatever is harmful. Of this the companions add: “Behold the little bed,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER II

“Behold, Solomon’s little bed: sixty mighty men surround it [Col. 0357A], of the mightiest of Israel.”

He whom I had called the perfumer they seem to name Solomon: he who is the author and lover of peace wished to prepare for himself a little bed on which, hidden from the disturbance of human beings, he might lay down his head for repose and show himself truly peaceable not only in name but also in reality.

I think that his little bed can be called the Virgin herself. Through the grace of love she is found so devoted to Solomon’s service that she permits no alien person to take rest within her and does not admit, even for a little while, the crafty enemy within the narrow confines of her mind. For this reason she deserved to be called not a bed but a little bed, so that this diminutive may seem to indicate a certain narrowness in her: not enlarged so as to receive another along with him, she strives to please the Bridegroom alone and is content with him alone, whom she lawfully loves.

To her suitably applies that prophecy of Isaiah; prophecies uttered at different times agree with one another, showing every attentive person that a certain narrowness of mind befits one who loves: such a person does not embrace many and does not serve two masters. “The bed,” he says, “is narrowed, so that one falls out; and the blanket is too short to cover both” (Isa. 28). The bed of the mind is commendably narrowed when it intends to be open and pleasing only to the lawful spouse, when it grants no dwelling, place, or space within itself to another, when the other is forced to fall away or, perhaps frightened from afar, does not approach.

Finally, the garment of virginal modesty, which dissipation does not weave and excess does not make, draws itself close about the lawful spouse; another is in no way covered by it. Nor does the Bridegroom receive a common portion with the adulterer, nor does he permit him to lodge with himself beneath the same garment [Col. 0357C]. Therefore the Bridegroom is found, through the same Isaiah, more severely to accuse her who did not narrow her little bed or shorten her garment but wickedly enlarged everything by admitting the adulterer; and he refuses the unworthy partnership both of adulteress and adulterer. “You have enlarged your bed,” he says, “you have received an adulterer” (Isa. 57).

But the Virgin, with her little bed narrowed, admitted no stain of any adulterer; with her garment shortened, she permitted no crafty person to be covered beneath it. Rather, she removed from the narrow rest of her mind everything contrary to it and, keeping faith with the Bridegroom, devoted herself wholly and singly to him. Therefore Solomon, the lover of peace, who nevertheless has care for battles, furnishes with armed soldiers and makes secure by a strong defence her who, through striving together with grace [Col. 0357D], wished and was able to offer herself as a little bed, so that enemies and rivals must necessarily shrink away.

She is not surrounded by walls, towers, or material fortifications. Rather, under the provident hand of the aforementioned Solomon, she remains unafraid amid sixty mighty men by a mystical number: they provide guards, and enemies inflict no harmful injury. The guards, who deserve to be called mighty only if they are so, are the spiritual virtues by which the Virgin is strengthened. They do not stand by her from one side alone, without the other; prudently arrayed, they surround her in an ordered circuit.

[Col. 0358A]

Their perfection is figured in the number sixty, which is completed by multiplying six and ten by one another. Six indicates perfection of works or labours; ten, the perfect consequent attainment of rewards. Since God, the Creator of all things, completed his works in six days, and, as you know it is written, rested on the seventh day from the works he had performed (Gen. 2), perfection in working is rightly signified by six, a perfection whose fuller attainment is laboured for throughout the whole span of days.

There are some who hold that six should not be judged perfect because God chose to complete his works in it. Rather, they say that the primordial works were once made in six days because God knew this first number to be perfect, so that by the perfection of the number God might commend his works and, having completed them in a perfect number, show them likewise to be perfect [Col. 0358B]. By ten, moreover, the perfection of reward is rightly said to be signified, because the master of the household orders it to be given to the labourers in the vineyard; and whoever has faithfully persisted in the labour assigned to him out of regard for obedience is content with this additional number at the end of time.

Therefore six multiplied by ten, or ten by six, makes sixty, when the Virgin is strongly girded both with the labour of the day’s burden and with the sure hope of future reward; when in the present she rejoices to devote herself to perfect works, and fears and doubts nothing whatever concerning what follows. [Col. 0358C]

Why either six or ten ought, according to mathematicians, to be judged perfect, and by what perfection the number sixty is found to be commended, I undertook to explain more fully in the *Response concerning Obedience* [Note: [Col. 0357D] See below.]; here, for brevity’s sake, I chose to pass it over in silence.

For those do not yet seem fully to possess the six who perform great things but cannot fulfil greater ones; who, although perhaps sufficiently watchful and cautious in avoiding wicked acts, are nevertheless still less perfect than they should be in speech. “Whoever does not sin in speech,” he says, “is a perfect man” (James 3). Some likewise, although they guard their ways so as not to offend with a slipping tongue, and thus already hold the six, nevertheless do not yet approach the ten sufficiently. For although they hope that they will receive a reward for their labour, they do not yet fully know whether they are worthy of hatred or of love [Col. 0358D].

The Holy Virgin is found to pass beyond—indeed, far to surpass—both in grace and merits the defective merits and advances, so to speak, of all these persons (for no one like them has deserved to attain complete perfection in this life). While she is still dwelling among us, she is thus encircled by the mystical sixty, so that the observance of works and labours renders her perfect, and the entirely certain expectation of future things makes her secure. And those who surround her fittingly deserve to be called “mighty men of the mightiest of Israel,” because among all the virtues whose merits seek to behold God, those by which the Virgin is encircled, and by which she loves to be kept secure once encircled, are known to be mighty and distinguished by exceptional strength.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0359A]

“All holding swords, most skilful for wars.”

How great is the strength with which these surround the Virgin, and how great their care, is shown both by the mystical number and by their armour; otherwise, if they came or assembled to fortify her unarmed, the more numerous they were, the more justly they would be condemned as worthless. Each, therefore, holds and draws a two-edged sword, so that if some robber should perhaps attempt to pass through the enclosure, his presumption may immediately be driven back and altogether vanish—or rather, may recoil in terror far away at the sight of the sword.

This sword is not of iron, by which wicked material things are sensibly struck. It is the sword of the Spirit, which the Apostle declares to be the word of God, because the word of God is proclaimed living, effective, and more piercing than every sword [Col. 0359B], penetrating the recesses of the soul and the inward conscience (Heb. 4). The sword is the faithful testimony, the bright commandment, the book of the law, which the priest Jehoiada wished to place in the hand of King Joash (2 Chron. 23), so as to show all that knowledge of the divine law befits a king; indeed, that a king ought not so much to know the law as to hold it in his hand—that is, in his actions. “They gave,” he says, “the law into the king’s hand to hold, and made him king.”

Thus the sixty are said not merely to have but to hold swords, because not everyone who has one immediately holds it, whereas those who hold one cannot be denied to have it. And it is of little, indeed no, use to possess a sword in its sheath if the hand—that is, the discipline of works—does not draw it. All the mighty men, therefore, who are said to surround the Virgin hold swords: they obey the word and are exercised in worthy works. By so great a defence they render the Virgin strong and secure, so that, enemies being driven back from afar, she suffers neither injury nor loss.

Those who thus fortify her are surely most skilful for wars. Their training is no novelty, being marked more by progress than by time; for to know what is right but not yet to do it is an elementary, crude, and, as it were, immature kind of instruction. Understanding grants progress not only in knowledge but also in conscience to those who act, rather than to those who merely possess understanding. As conscience without knowledge is not sufficiently trained, so knowledge without conscience is found crude and more imperfect [Col. 0359D]. Therefore they should be called not only instructed but most skilful who, in carrying out battles, obey the word and put their hand to the sword; whose concern for repelling hostile assaults so proceeds that it is terrible to all, since their hand does not depart from the sword. Concerning a sword of this kind it is added: “Each one’s,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER IV

“Each one’s sword upon his thigh, because of the terrors of the night.”

The companions carefully consider and more attentively marvel at the manner and order in which those sixty work for the Virgin’s protection: how provident and sagacious they are in guarding her, and how effective they prove to be not only in strength but also in prudent resolve. Each one, not laying aside the sword he has once received, but placing upon his thigh the one which he is said to hold in his hand, is so watchful to fight whatever may harm from without that [Col. 0360A] he is not negligent of himself but keeps watchful care of himself.

The thigh signifies flesh, which is propagated from the thigh; and flesh is weak and is shown to fail by nature. Therefore by the thigh, or flesh, is signified weakness or failure, which our steadfastness or progress incurs as if by nature. However greatly human virtue may be raised in magnitude, it does not have from itself the power to remain firm in its purpose. If grace deserts it and it relaxes a little from diligence, then, as though its wings had been lost, it does not stand with steady step.

Thus a virtue seems to place the sword upon its thigh when, by the bright word of the Lord, proclaimed more piercing than every sword, it worthily restrains and chastises its own weakness and strengthens by the severity of the word what it finds naturally feeble. It holds the sword upon its thigh when it worthily watches over and attends to its own guardianship, recognizing itself not merely as weak but as naturally weak. Accordingly, it guards itself more carefully against failure and ruin, so that it crushes even the causes of failure—the thigh, as it were—by the discipline of the word [Col. 0360B].

Thus, surely, the Virgin’s virtue, watchful and intent upon removing every harmful thing, rejoices not to fear the terrors of the night. Everything which the crafty enemy or dark temptation strives to devise is rendered wholly futile by this instructed and formidable vigilance. Observing this, the angels—who, as was said above, are called the Bridegroom’s friends and companions—marvel ineffably at this little bed of Solomon and its protection. They continue to commend it in other words, judging whatever they say in praise of the Virgin far from sufficient.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0360C]

“King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon; he made its columns silver, its reclining-place gold, its ascent purple; he paved its midst with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem.”

What they had called a little bed, they also call a litter, upon which many dishes are carried to Solomon, and to him as he feasts is set food that does not perish but endures. The Virgin, then, is the litter through whom the souls of the saints are commended to God and, through her prayers and merits, raised to the Bridegroom’s banquet. For this same purpose the Bridegroom wished to prepare her for himself: that those who could not be presented through themselves might deserve to be presented through her.

For although the souls of the saints are distinguished by various virtues and, like dishes, seasoned in manifold fashion with the flavour of graces [Col. 0360D], nevertheless they lie far from Solomon’s banquet, as though altogether forsaken, unless they are aided by the Virgin’s intercession as by an offering-table. Therefore the Bride herself is rightly called the mediatrix of us all and, not incongruously, the mother-empress. Entreating the Bridegroom and commanding her Son, she turns his wrath into favour, his anger into sweetest love; by the little meal of her prayer she changes us from bitter persons into sweetness.

Those, therefore, who had first been hateful with wild bitterness, when received upon the litter become acceptable through the merit of the one receiving them. No one deserves to please at Solomon’s banquet unless he rejoices to be offered to him by the Virgin, as from a propitiatory table. For the aforesaid litter, or table, is of such merit that all those upon whom its propitiation has been diligently bestowed may confidently present themselves at Solomon’s banquet; while those alien to the table consequently absent themselves from the banquet as well.

For it is made from the woods of Lebanon [Col. 0361A]. Lebanon is a mountain raised by conspicuous height, adorned by its aspect, and clothed with the beauty of groves; its trees are uplifted by lofty size, beautified by wondrous appearance, and strengthened by incorruptible firmness. “Lebanon” is interpreted as “whitening,” signifying Christ, who is the brightness of eternal light and is prepared as the mountain of the house of the Lord: the good tree whose fruit is shown to be only good; whose wood, planted beside the waters of Siloam, does not dry out, is not stripped of foliage in autumn, does not wither in winter, but renews its youth with untiring durability and incorruptible strength.

[Col. 0361B]

From these woods, the companions say, the litter is constructed, so that the work may rightly seem commended, as it were, by its material; for the Virgin’s holiness is built from Christ’s virtues and reduced into a table and litter for the advancement of us all. Since mighty Solomon constructed it so from strong and incorruptible material, it did not experience the worm nor admit decay, but drove it away. Her integrity of strength was not injured by the hammer, broken by the age of time, or disrupted; it remained and endured incorrupt.

Moreover, lest this table ever depart from Solomon’s presence, or ever incline in any direction, Solomon wished it to rest upon a noble support, placing beneath it not unstable tripods but immovable columns of silver [Col. 0361C]. The Virgin’s table was presented to Solomon by eminent loftiness, and the silver, unbending uprightness of the columns held it immovable. Solomon’s goodwill received and confirmed her bright conduct, her ringing reputation, the moderation of her speech, and the force of her utterance.

Silver, shining in brilliance and giving a ring when suitably struck, is made into columns, and what is placed upon it stands fortified, when the Virgin, abiding by the power of the Most High, has brought forth the Word of the Father and firmly relies not on her own strength but on his. In her is also said to be found a golden reclining-place, because nowhere did our Solomon appear to experience a more pleasing rest, where he might wish or be able to lay down his head—to bow the excellence of deity in order to assume flesh.

It is fittingly said to be not leaden but golden [Col. 0361D], because among all metals nothing is considered better than gold: it is more precious in price, heavier in weight, and stronger beneath the hammer; hence a reclining-place is deservedly said to have been made from it. I judge that gold figures the Virgin’s love, which is certainly pre-eminent among her other virtues. Although faith, hope, and very many others are worthy of praise, none of them can deservedly be compared with love.

Balanced by its own weight, that love is so weighty that it does not slip, bent by fickleness, toward the right or the left; it does not run about or fluctuate, nor burst forth to love anyone else. It embraces the Bridegroom alone, and a third person does not break apart the embrace of the two. Finally, it desires to cleave to the Bridegroom with such strong longing and solid strength that it is not broken by adversities or worn out beneath the hammer of tribulation. When Peter broke, John recoiled, and all fled, unable to bear the raging hammer, the Virgin alone stood firm and did not cease to love the Bridegroom dying for the Bride’s sake.

Therefore Solomon made for himself in the Virgin such a reclining-place [Col. 0362A], commended by love that was weighty, steadfast, and comparable to none. Upon it the maker himself laid down his head, away from the disturbance of human beings; and, as though about to refresh us, he invited us also to the same feast. But such a reclining-place is not easily found among persons like us; it is not reached except with labour and great effort. To attain it, as experience has shown, no one fully arrives unless, intending to ascend, he girds himself with worthy strength.

[Col. 0362B]

For there are steps, or ladders, by which ascent is made to the reclining-place. The Virgin expended no small labour upon them; and because, considering rightly, she knew that they were not dark with soot but purple, she advanced by them to the summit in an honourable likeness. In ancient times purple belonged to kings alone. Its form or colour showed royal dignity, so that when common people observed that no one except a prince was clothed in purple, they might be reminded to reverence one marked by the royal signs.

Since, therefore, one reaches the reclining-place, where welcome repose is imparted to Solomon, not by a presumptuous leap but by a purple ascent, the most prudent Virgin, desiring to arrive at so great a merit that she might be shown to be a queen, clothed herself in royal purple. She showed herself to be a queen by fitting signs when she eagerly assumed a discipline of a new kind; when she was the first to dare to enter the path of virginal continence, consecrated by the chaste purpose of her mind and unattempted throughout all preceding ages [Col. 0362C].

She showed herself to be a queen when she put upon herself purple, that is, the virtue by which she imposed harsh servitude upon her most tender body; when she gave her blood not to the executioner’s hand to be shed, but consecrated to God alone the unpierced vessel of her virginal body. She strove to mark herself out as a queen not in womanly but in purple garments when, by loftiness of mind, she chose not to experience bodily allurements, and chose to rule her flesh—something, I think, not sufficiently known to anyone who, fleeing the training-ground of this exercise, has shown himself untried in it.

Therefore the Virgin, not corrupted by womanly softness but made red and suffused with the martyrdom of royal suffering, came and arrived at the point of becoming Solomon’s reclining-place. By an ascent only of purple she advanced to so excellent a merit that Solomon, reclining in her, took food with unwearying hunger. But Solomon paved the middle of this litter not with tapestries from Egypt or with the fleeting novelty of flowers, but with love, by a far better design, so that absolutely nothing might appear in it from which the eye of the reclining guest, eager for what is honourable, would recoil [Col. 0362D].

For love’s ornament must necessarily be added to all the virtues by which the Virgin is made pre-eminent and distinguished—virtues fitting to the aforesaid litter in their outstanding and worthy merits. Without love all the rest become as useless refuse. [Col. 0363A]

Nothing sufficient can be placed upon the aforesaid litter unless diffused love is necessarily laid over it; indeed, all things set around it are not worthily gathered unless the middle of them is filled in with the cement of love. Therefore love is necessarily placed in the midst of all, so that from there a kind of nourishment may be spread to all things surrounding it; so that this binding may hold together all things rightly done lest they fly apart from one another; and, if anything perhaps lies wrongly placed, it may have sufficient covering.

“For love is the bond of perfection” (Col. 4), and “covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4). I judge that this is said not so much for the Virgin’s sake as for the daughters of Jerusalem, to whom it had been granted to be present while Bridegroom and Bride spoke together. It was said lest, on hearing silver columns, a golden reclining-place, and a purple ascent proclaimed [Col. 0363B], they should presume to think that they could attain such things, and should see themselves as driven far from that litter, of which they possessed no likeness, even a slight one.

When they hear that love is found in the midst of these things, with its welcome covering by which a multitude of sins is covered, they do not despair that they too may belong to that litter if they love and choose to cleave still more diligently to the diligent one. Although many things are said to be placed upon that litter which are not sufficiently comparable to persons like us but belong more specially to the Virgin, nevertheless the love said to be placed in their midst is undoubtedly not foreign to the daughters of Jerusalem. Rather, it greatly benefits and heals their moderate condition, to whom both an ease of approach and an effective hope of progress are thereby given.

[Col. 0363C]

Such a litter Solomon—the Bridegroom, Christ—wished the Bride, the Virgin, to offer to himself: one which deserved to surpass all in excellence of virtues, yet did not seem to prohibit the daughters of Jerusalem from following her, if, though not in every respect entirely, they wished at least through love to cleave to her footsteps. But that they may cleave to her and see Solomon, in whom they ought to rejoice, the companions or angels who are speaking seem to admonish them. They turn toward them perhaps not so much their faces as their speech, so that, instructed by it, they may hasten carefully to behold Solomon.

## CHAPTER VI
[Col. 0363D] “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him, on the day of his betrothal and on the day of his heart’s joy.” Since the companions had foretold that the Virgin was now Solomon’s bed, now his litter, and had described the former as adorned with great strength and the latter with great beauty, lest they should seem in this to have attributed more to the bride than to the bridegroom, and, in commending the Virgin, to have rendered Solomon less than his due, they invite the daughters of Zion to a more ample effort of understanding, that they may consider attentively what glory or honor the things previously mentioned have brought to Solomon.

For this reason they are careful expressly to warn them to go forth: that is, not to remain in the hovels either of their vices or of ignorance’s darkness, since those whose life is entangled in vices are unfit to see, as are those whose understanding is hindered by an overcast gloom. “Therefore,” they say, “you whom we especially invite to see, know that you must no longer remain in the things behind; and for this reason we desire you to come out from darkness, from the evil covering, and, as you go forth, to free your feet from the stains that impede them. Come out, therefore, from the hovel of life that darkens understanding; come out from the midst of benighted ignorance; come out from the gross and rustic understanding of benighted peoples. Advance into daughterhood; take concern for your progress. Go forth, and by going forth worthily become daughters who behold; with diligent hand cleanse eyes afflicted with bleared vision. Wipe the stains from your face as though before a mirror, and, like maidens, devote care to acquiring beauty.

[Col. 0364A] “By this departure and advance from the inward negligence of a blameworthy workshop, by this zeal of contemplation and this mirror of discipline, you will obtain the vision necessary for you: you will be granted to see Solomon in his diadem. Solomon, I say—the king whom none can see in his beauty except the holy, whose face has indeed been washed and whose eye is clearer; those who burn with maidenly care to acquire beauty, who can behold what is inaccessible to clouded eyes with a purified eye.

“Solomon’s diadem is the passibility of his flesh, with which the undefiled virginity of his mother crowned him, when the Lord did a new thing and a woman encompassed a man, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy (Jer. 31); yet she was a Virgin conceiving and giving birth, according also to Isaiah’s testimony (Isa. 7). Such flesh, or such passibility of flesh, is not undeservedly honored with the name of diadem. For although to clouded eyes it is reckoned disgrace or ignominy, yet whoever rightly understands that whatever is shameful is unworthy of Solomon, and, understanding, loves the end intended in such suffering—how great a struggle there is in the flesh, and how great the usefulness in that struggle—surely attributes to it a name not of ignominy but of honor, not of disgrace but of crown. ‘We see,’ says Paul, ‘Jesus, because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor’ (Heb. 2).

[Col. 0364B] “For this crown the Virgin Mother supplied the material in her womb; the craftsman Spirit fashioned the supplied material with skilled hand and wove it into a circle with work so perfect that it incomparably surpasses gold, precious stone, or electrum. The Jew, looking upon it, esteems it nothing but thorns and toil; the unbeliever, considering it, thinks that it has neither appearance nor beauty. A more purified eye beholds him as beautiful in form beyond the children of men, not only because he is God, but because, though man, he is not bound by human debts.

[Col. 0364D] “Indeed, the material of his flesh is naturally shared with human beings; but that very community is exempt from fleshly vices. By the power of this mystery he personally admits us into unity with himself, and, once joined to him, does not allow us to be divided from him. The circular perfection of the diadem beautifully signifies this: no division at all breaks its wholeness. Thus the diadem is said to signify the removal of division, because whoever is enclosed by the circumference of this crown does not know how to be divided.

“In this crown, therefore—that is, in his flesh—he couples and joins us to himself; and he does not separate those who share his struggle from honor and glory. In some sense the Mother is said to have bestowed this glory upon Solomon when the Virgin is believed to have conceived God made man in her womb. Who would not offer praise to the Virgin? Who would not make worthy mention of her, who crowned Solomon not with gold or stone but with her own flesh; who gave the King that in which he might and could glory, by which he might conquer and worthily be crowned for victory?
