[Col. 0365A] “They declare that this took place on the day of his betrothal; by the deed itself they indicate that night or darkness was far away, since the betrothal present in the bridal chamber did not bring in darkness, but a sanctified and sanctifying day, a light, shone upon it. For when the Bridegroom entered, incomparable light arose. No other is admitted, and the door is open to no outsiders; rather, with equal consent they shut every entrance against all comers, while the companions, or angels, dance and applaud festively before the doors.

“Therefore, on a bright day the mystical betrothal is celebrated: the chaste Virgin is joined to one man by spiritual union; a woman encompasses the man; Solomon is crowned with a diadem; mortal human nature is personally united to God, who is immortal by nature. But on this day, when the Creator of the Virgin became her Bridegroom, who can relate what or how great was the joy of her heart? In her womb our humanity was assumed into God, yet not consumed, because the Spirit overshadowed it with the fellowship of him who assumed it.

[Col. 0365B] “How great was the joy of her heart is not ours either to speak or to conceive, since we have not deserved to enter so holy and secret a sanctuary. She herself, to whom God willed more fully and perfectly to disclose it, could scarcely pour out even a little of the joy commanded in her heart. ‘My spirit rejoiced,’ she says, ‘in God my Savior’ (Luke 1).

“Whatever, therefore, takes place in the Virgin knows no night. For day is poured upon her as she crowns the King; light shines forth; her motherly spirit is gladdened by a daylight—or rather, an enduring light—whose worthy apprehension does not brighten our weak eyes. For she is not that Bathsheba whom David, without Uriah’s knowledge, defiled by adultery, but Mary, the flower of virgins, whom the Holy Spirit uniquely claimed to make fruitful. Nor is this that Solomon who is said to have reigned from Dan to Beersheba for forty years, but Christ, whose kingdom has no end, whose dominion has no boundary.

[Col. 0365C] “Neither Jew nor Gentile, nor any accursed person—though, under the name Christian, he is whitewashed with the appearance of piety, yet, denying its power, is darkened by poverty of merits—can worthily weigh the glory of this flesh, this diadem. Therefore the companions, or angels, to whom it had already been granted through the merit of blessedness to see, lest they should seem to begrudge others the benefit they had received, do not think it should be hidden under a bushel or covered by silence. Rather, they invite the daughters of Zion to prepare themselves with fervor and zeal for seeing.

“For in this not only is praise offered to Solomon, but also to the Virgin; nor is the glory bestowed upon the crowned one taken away from the one who crowns him. Indeed, whatever the assumption of flesh in the Son appears to accomplish worthy of glory is reflected back upon Mary, from whom that same Son willed to take flesh. Therefore the Bridegroom did not long turn his presence away from her; after the companions’ words he turns again to her praises, in order to show that he who is crowned with a diadem is so beautiful in glory that it is clear that the beauty of the crowning crown is not lacking either.”

## CHAPTER VII

[CH. 4.] “How beautiful you are, my beloved; how beautiful you are! Your eyes are those of doves, apart from that which lies hidden within.” Since these words, as you may remember, were set down earlier and in some fashion expounded in the second book of this work, they are not to be expounded again in this place or at this time; the care of readers must be referred back to the book already mentioned.

Yet, as I see, something is changed in these words, and this praise of the Virgin is here introduced by a different phrase. There it was said, “Behold, you are beautiful; behold, you are beautiful”; here, however: “How beautiful you are, how beautiful.” There “behold” is said—clearly the pointing-out of one making an affirmation; here “how” is placed—the intensification, that is, of one expressing admiration. There is understood a merely demonstrative testimony to beauty; here, an expression of admiration at great beauty. “How beautiful you are,” he says, “my beloved, how beautiful! How greatly beautiful you are, with what great beauty you are adorned—you who are my beloved and are proved to be privy to my secret! Who can utter it with a swift tongue and passing sound, or what hearer can comprehend it even if it is spoken?

[Col. 0366C] “The addition found here, which had not yet been said and therefore was not expounded above, serves to confirm this more firmly: it indicates both that the Virgin’s beauty is great and that no deceitful ugliness exists within that beauty: ‘apart from that which lies hidden within.’ There are some whose outward beauty and lovely surface are ready at hand, while inwardly there is the rapacity of wolves and serpentine deceit; what appears outwardly is made beautiful by an overlay of hypocrisy, while what lies hidden within is darkened by malicious ugliness.

“There are others who, although they are not whitened outwardly by deceitful hypocrisy and are not inwardly infected by a persistent poison, nevertheless, while they are held in the body, are so grievously burdened, as punishment, by a certain law of sin that at times, willing or unwilling, they slip even into slight fault.

> [Note: Col. 0365. He alludes to Romans 7:15: ‘What I do not will, this I do,’ etc.]

“Since not everything evil our thought conceives can immediately appear to others, and since we ourselves are often unaware of what in us deserves, by right, to displease us, when the Bridegroom says that the Virgin is ‘apart from that which lies hidden within,’ he proves her free not only from evident faults but from hidden faults as well. Which of the saints is there who can glory that he is without that which is hidden, rather than pray, as one who does not understand his sins, to be cleansed from secret faults? Who, I say, is not anxious about hidden things and serves the Lord in fear, fearing because he does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or of love? (Eccles. 9.)

[Col. 0367A] “The Virgin, therefore, who was by no means conscious of sins, and yet was not ignorant of her hidden things, the Bridegroom rightly declares beautiful once and again; with her, as outwardly so inwardly, there was nothing unbecoming. He proceeds to describe her beauty part by part, adding: ‘Your hair,’ and so forth.”

## CHAPTER VIII

“Your hair is like a flock of goats, which have ascended from Mount Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep, which have come up from the washing.” By the hair, I think, the bodily senses may be represented: coming forth from within, they seek to spread outward and, when liberty is granted them, are found to wander more widely than is right unless they are recalled by regular correction and restraint. Hence Job also says: “I made a covenant with my eyes” (Job 31); and David: “Turn away my eyes, that they may not see vanity” (Ps. 118). And so with the rest.

[Col. 0367B] In order that hair may remain worthily as an ornament of the head, it is rooted in and adheres to that same head. Otherwise, once it has been plucked up by the root, the pleasing tresses no longer remain; and once the tresses have been cut away, baldness disfigures the head. So also the bodily senses, all of which are situated in the head, receive their powers there and act there principally. If, as though driven from their proper seat, they are displaced when the head is disturbed, not only the head itself but also the remaining members are deprived of very great honor.

But if, with the head sound, they stand firm and tenacious as though in a root, and are sufficiently effective for fulfilling their natural office, then, like hairs, they are sometimes loosened into wandering license and stray too far unless restrained by an applied hand and an imposed law. Thus a certain force of nature makes the Virgin’s hair well rooted, while the fittingness of regular restraint binds it in outward chastity: she makes her senses firm in affection by subtle foresight and, by powerful correction, restrains them from unbridled activity. The Virgin also brings her hair worthily under correction when she keeps the senses of her inward mind carefully within measure; when she does not permit those senses by which she ought to perceive spiritual and life-giving things to consent, through wandering license, to transitory and destructive things.

[Col. 0367C] Such senses, bodily or likewise spiritual, that we little ones—still carnal in our senses—may more easily understand what is said, the Bridegroom compares to goats: rustic animals feeding among rocks and upon the very summits of lofty mountains. The Bridegroom rightly wished to compare the Virgin’s senses to goats, because, despising lower things, the Virgin loves to aspire only to higher things. Though in the swift leap of contemplating and loving she grasps what is inaccessible to us, she nevertheless regards herself, in rustic fashion, as humble and lowly. “He has regarded,” she says, “the lowliness of his handmaid” (Luke 1).

“And he significantly compared the Virgin’s hair not to goats but to a flock of goats. In this he invites the diligent hearer to understand the gathered unity of the senses, because wandering movement or stealthy dissipation has not driven them apart from one another; rather, chaste fellowship has brought them back into a flock beneath the shepherd’s care and staff, so that no wild beast would dare to rush upon any one of them, but, wearied by hunger, would stand amazed with jaws opened but untried.

[Col. 0368A] “To commend such goats still further, they are said not to descend but to ascend from Mount Gilead. Yet, just as ascent is made from the plain to the heights of a mountain, so, in the proper sense of the words, there is descent from the mountain to the plains. ‘Jesus, coming down from the mountain, stood in a level place’ (Luke 6). And of Moses: ‘Moses went up the mountain and was there forty days’ (Exod. 24). And later the Lord says to Moses: ‘Go down; your people have sinned’ (Exod. 32).

“Since, then, one may more correctly speak of descent rather than ascent from a mountain, what is meant by the statement that the aforesaid goats are remembered as ascending, not descending, from Mount Gilead? Unless it is that the great progress of the hairs—that is, of the senses—is indicated; and the literal connection, referred to them, finds a worthy appropriateness which does not seem literally suitable to material goats. For the Holy Spirit was not concerned to discuss goats’ ascent, but to show us weaker persons, by such comparisons, the progress of the Virgin, who strives to advance from mountain to mountain—that is, from virtue to virtue—by the grace of spiritual pasture, and seeks to attain not mountain ridges but the heights of progress.

[Col. 0368B] “Hence also this mountain of which the discourse speaks is called Gilead. The Hebrews declare that its name is interpreted ‘heap of witness,’ because, when Laban had calmed the fury of his threats and stubborn anger and was preparing to enter into a covenant of peace with his nephew Jacob, they raised a heap of stones with stones gathered by both hands and left it to succeeding generations as a testimony of the peace they had made.

“But no excellence seems to bear witness to Christ more than the Virgin’s love, which by its merit is found to surpass all others. It is piled up from living and chosen stones, raised for increase, and gives an indelible memorial to those present and those to come. Thus the Virgin advances and ascends from Mount Gilead when she attains the summit of holiness through accumulated virtues. And she does not, as though descending, hunt after her own glory from this; but, with fitting progress, testifies only to Christ’s mighty mercy. ‘He who is mighty has done great things to me,’ she says (Luke 1).

[Col. 0368D] “Therefore the Bridegroom next praises the Virgin’s teeth, in order that not only her beauty may appear plainly in her hair, but great usefulness may also be shown in her teeth—if, however, what has been said is understood not literally but spiritually. ‘Your teeth,’ he says, ‘are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing.’ The Virgin’s teeth, with a strong bite, root out the pestilence of heresies, lest shoots of falsehood strongly oppose truth; and they chew over, with fitting arguments, the hardest teaching concerning the incarnate Word, so that little ones may now more readily devote themselves to this faith.

“These teeth are fittingly compared to a flock of sheep—not sheep weighed down by the harsh burden of wool and sweat, but those which, once their fleeces have been shorn, show that they now possess nothing superfluous and, if they seem perhaps to have possessed anything, condemn it by washing confession. Thus the Virgin, who burns with the lawful love of one who loves, is rightly said, as a bride, to come up from the washing like one shorn, because she has sought to be more cleanly freed from the superfluous burdens of sins in proportion as she wished to be found more credible in commending the Bridegroom. Of these it is added: ‘All with twin offspring,’ and so forth.”

## CHAPTER IX

“All with twin offspring, and none among them is barren.” All, namely, both the goats that ascended from Mount Gilead and hung with fearless step upon its highest summit, and the sheep that washed themselves once their fleeces had been shorn and, coming forth from the washing, lacked the harsh burden of wool and sweat.

[Col. 0369B] All, I say, are equally fruitful by grace, so pleasing through the abundant gift of fertility that no one among them is condemned for barrenness, and each rejoices in the more abundant gift of twin offspring. A thing worthy of wonder: that in the flock no goat and no sheep is found barren; that none of the fruitful creatures is content with a single birth; that the virtues of the Virgin, which we have understood to be represented by the hair or teeth, are made fruitful by love and are not content with a single love.

“For they love God and they love human beings; they neither despise God for humanity’s sake nor humanity for God’s sake. Rather, according to the new and old law, they reverence the first and second commandments as alike, while in the same Christ they embrace with two arms the twofold substance of the giant. For in the one Christ, whom the Virgin loves as her bridegroom and her son, she sees two substances personally joined to one another. Their natures are indeed distinct and unlike—for they are the natures of God and of man—yet in their union they constitute one Christ, one person.

[Col. 0369C] “To love him tenderly and delight in tender love is to be not barren and to be fruitful with twin offspring. For the Holy Spirit is not greatly concerned with goats or sheep, but rather with virtues and the praiseworthy offspring of virtues. Continuing their praise, he adds: ‘Like a scarlet ribbon,’ and so forth.”

## CHAPTER X

“Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet.” The Virgin’s closed lips preserve knowledge of the law and gather up, in the secret chamber of the heart, what they know should be kept. Their closure is not to be blamed as unfruitful silence, since the wise person keeps silence until the proper time, and the silent heart meditates prudence. Thus: “Mary,” it says, “kept all these things, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2).

[Col. 0369D] But when the things gathered and stored are shaken for utterance by the hand of one knocking, and the bolt or bar is at last struck loose from her closed lips, obedience knocks and, having received the time for speech, she brings forth nothing but instruction for those who have ears to hear. To obtain this the prophet wishes to have a door, so that he may restrain his lips by a fitting law: lest either excessive silence make him see himself cast down and repent, or, by no smaller fault, light verbosity carry him into excess. “Set, O Lord,” he says, “a door of restraint about my lips” (Ps. 140).

“Lord,” he says, “give my lips a fitting closure and, when the time comes, an opening as well, so that they may turn on the hinge of discernment like a door: neither closed when it is time to be silent nor opened for speech except at the fitting time. ‘Woe is me,’ says Isaiah, ‘because I have kept silence’ (Isa. 6). And another says in contrast: ‘A wordy man shall not be justified’ (Job 2). To avoid danger on either side, the Virgin’s lips found the right effectiveness and, by worthy guardianship, forestalled the faults both of silence and of excessive speech. To avoid speaking what was superfluous, they restrained themselves by praiseworthy closure; and at the fitting time they expressed what seemed honorable and useful.

[Col. 0370A] “Therefore they are not undeservedly compared to a scarlet ribbon, by which the hairs of the head are drawn back lest they flow out without restraint. A maiden’s hair, lest it wander through innate lightness, is bound and restrained and pressed under the power of command. For this purpose the Virgin prepares for herself a clean and slender ribbon: when, as time passes, she feels her youthful hair grow, she places it over the hair with suitable restraint, lest the latter display itself at an untimely moment or in an unseemly manner.

“But when the prudent Virgin sees the time approaching when it is fitting for her hair to appear more freely and openly, with diligent hand she loosens the slender ribbon and for a time frees and releases the hair, as it were, from its authority. The hair then seems more pleasing to beholders’ eyes in proportion as it was previously held longer beneath the ribbon’s guardianship. Hidden under its binding, it is arranged and cherished, and merits to attain a pleasing beauty; it shines forth more honorably when, with the ribbon set aside, it is allowed to come before human sight—provided it never ceases to remember the ribbon that has been set aside.

[Col. 0370B] “So, indeed, when the discernment of one speaking has been trained under silence and polished over a long course of time with lips kept closed, then when they are at last opened, speech leaves its native workshop and, proceeding into human ears, resounds with fitting instruction. Hence it is well added: ‘And your speech is sweet.’ For when the lips, like a ribbon, have worthily restrained inward affections and have prudently shaped on the hammer and anvil of silence what must be uttered, their opening, like the laying aside of the ribbon, is neither blamed nor cheapened. Timely speech pleases, and the utterance becomes sweet to its hearers.

[Col. 0370C] “Otherwise speech grows obscure in emptiness, and an utterance becomes bitter when it is not formed beneath the lips or matured in silence; when, before anything is uttered, the lips do not serve as a ribbon, but ineptly bring forth with open mouth whatever comes into it. But why are the Virgin’s lips compared only to a scarlet ribbon, unless because in this too they are set far above our very dissimilar lips? Although ours show themselves to be closed and opened at different times, to worthy observers they represent not scarlet but perhaps rather mud.

“Scarlet, bearing the appearance of fire, rightly signifies love—love inflamed, or fire itself, which purifies gold as in a furnace; which makes the righteous, more precious than gold, fervent and burning; which burns but does not consume, but refines and makes lovers clean. The Virgin’s lips are likened to this scarlet, or fire: in both silence and speech they serve tender love; ignorant of mud, they do not grow pale like ashes, but modestly glow and kindle with scarlet redness.

[Col. 0370D] “Closed and devoted to silence, they give themselves to God; they meditate upon the ineffable, cling to the invisible, rejoice in him, and with burning desire suspend themselves upon inward and eternal things. They hold in eager embrace him whom they apprehend as incomprehensible. ‘How great,’ they say, ‘is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you’ (Ps. 30).

“But opened, though not unrestrained, they stretch themselves toward outward things; they begin to speak and, in speaking, accommodate themselves to their neighbors. What they had tasted beforehand within, they now bestow outwardly upon those in need; and even in this they show themselves to burn or glow red with scarlet. ‘For the sake of my brothers,’ says he, ‘and my neighbors, I spoke peace concerning you’ (Ps. 121). Therefore, because the Virgin’s lips are made lovely by the likeness of a ribbon and are blamelessly commended by red scarlet or fiery love, as her silence and meditation know no shadow of bitterness, so her speech shines with the grace of sweetness. Of her praise he further adds: ‘Like,’ and so forth.”

## CHAPTER XI

“Like a fragment of pomegranate are your cheeks, apart from that which lies hidden within.” The beauty of this Virgin whom we have in hand is so great that our dullness cannot easily comprehend it fully. Her praiser, choosing to have mercy on our weakness, proposes various comparisons, that through them we may somehow behold her. Although none of these can be thought sufficient, some nevertheless appear fitting in part—so far as material things can be adapted to spiritual things, and base, transitory dwellings likened to beautiful realities.

[Col. 0371C] Thus the Virgin’s cheeks, flourishing with a blush of modesty, are likened to a pomegranate, which shines with ruddy rind and, when broken, reveals within a gathered multitude of seeds, in which no slight beauty of whiteness also gleams. In a young woman’s cheeks, as in the prominence of her face, the excellence of beauty places its throne; sitting there, it holds royal sovereignty, resting upon grace and not strengthened by privilege.

“Desiring, then, to commend the Virgin’s beauty, the Bridegroom loves to compare her cheeks to a pomegranate—indeed, to a fragment of one—so that the double color of one fragment, red outside and snowy white within, may proclaim the Virgin’s praises, sound with equal proclamation, and neither contradict the other. The red color, bearing the likeness of blood, is a type of suffering which the holy Virgin endures from desire for her Solomon. Whatever the world proclaims by promises or thunders by terrors, she despises with a strong mind, repels with steady foot, and does not distinguish the greatest things from lesser things.

[Col. 0371D] “Against shearings and pressures she sets the rind as a shield, firmly embracing that praiseworthy ordinance of Solomon which promises blessedness to the one who now dashes little ones against the rock, and which teaches that everyone who does not reject living devoutly must suffer. Thus the patient Virgin does not grow troubled at pressure and breaking; indeed, if she is not pressed and broken, she blushes. But when broken and crushed, she does not grow pale with sickly exhaustion; rather, she shines with inward beauty and is made white by a joyful conscience.

“A pomegranate unbroken offers its pleasing redness to sight; broken, it offers fitting flavor to taste. Unbroken, it gives a fragrance of marvelous sweetness to open nostrils; broken, it does not diminish but diffuses a far greater fragrance. So too the Virgin, not crushed or struck by hammer or persecutor, shines with pomegranate color and glows with desire or love. Her manner of life is ruddy to beholders’ eyes, flourishing in mature conduct, modest gaze, and bashful countenance.

[Col. 0372A] “But if a heavy hand presses her, breaks her, and reduces her as it were to a fragment; if an unwelcome sword or tribulation passes through not so much her body as her soul: inwardly no foul blackness appears, but another beauty of no lesser grace becomes manifest—namely, inward purity and the cheerful security of a cleaner conscience. Whoever wisely considers such a fragment apprehends its sweetness not with the tooth but rather with the mind. He understands that it is delightful to the eyes not merely by whiteness or redness, but fruitful in sweetness and flavor to the inward palate and sound taste.

“Moreover, its fragrance—or reputation—especially gives forth its scent when not only its works but also its examined conscience comes to light; when its patience is struck by pressures and fractures, its mind shaken, and nothing is shown in it but an assemblage of virtues and their brightness or purity. The Bridegroom praises this beauty of the Virgin, which may somehow be known both by herself and by another, if any human knower of her can be found, under the name of cheeks, which show themselves in the face and represent the double beauty of redness and whiteness like the aforesaid fragment.

[Col. 0372B] “But what he does not presently give to the Virgin, but sets before her, he does not expound through praises or comparisons of this sort. He wishes that chief thing to remain hidden from us who are too weak to grasp it, in order to show that it far excels everything received here. ‘Apart from that,’ he says, ‘which lies hidden within.’ ‘On the basis of that,’ he says, ‘which is manifest, you, Virgin, ought to be proclaimed praiseworthy for the gifts of grace which can in some fashion be compared to temporal things; apart from that—that is, leaving unspoken what is still hidden and not seen, wholly incomparable, and kept far from sight under seal.’

[Col. 0372C] “From this you would deservedly receive a preeminent praise if it could be spoken, or if, once spoken, it could be comprehended by human beings. But what eye does not see, ear cannot endure, and has not ascended into the human heart, the present discourse does not undertake to expound. Sparing, therefore, those whom I introduce into the audience of this drama, I return to set forth what can be grasped. Leaving unspoken what mortal understanding has not yet the power to comprehend, I shall speak in human fashion of your praises and advances.”

## CHAPTER XII

“Your neck is like the tower of David, which was built with battlements.” Since the Virgin’s beauty was commended in cheeks compared to a pomegranate or its fragment, her strength is next commended in her neck: it does not bend itself down toward the feeble and needy transitory things of the world, nor does it turn its uprightness aside from its purpose through enervating softness.

[Col. 0373A] She herself bears the present life, the burden of flesh, the heavy load, as something sweet through strong patience and the constancy of patience. Whatever the world inflicts, it does not shake her from her position or cause her, in the manner of the weak, to stumble—though that world strikes the necks of all who are present. For she is filled with such love and such fervor of spirit that she weighs burdens as trifles, as though accustomed to them; and like a heifer taught to love the yoke or the threshing-floor, she judges the practice of bearing heavy things a benefit, not an injury.

“Therefore her neck is said to be like a tower, which, fixed by its own weight, is not moved by the force of winds or the battering of floods; which is of such strength that it does not surrender its place to the power of evil spirits and affords impregnable defense to the whole city. It is said to be David’s tower. David, whose name is interpreted ‘strong of hand,’ signifies Christ: the good experience his unconquerable and invincible hand as ready to help; the evil experience it for vengeance.

[Col. 0373B] “Such a tower is raised in Jerusalem so that, through vigilant watchfulness, it may foresee enemies from afar; and, should they dare to draw near, may defend itself against their attacks or assaults and, by its strength, make light of whatever they bring. Its defense benefits not itself alone but the whole city: it gives that city necessary strength and no unseemly ornament. When the weaker city is attacked by the enemy, it immediately flees to the tower; and the stronger tower gives confidence and aid to the city that flees to it.

“So too the Virgin, like the Davidic tower, sees the enemy from afar—indeed, despises him—and does not care about him. At the sight of her he shudders and flees, and does not persist in his intended boldness. Whatever threats or frauds he ventures to devise are dashed to pieces, and the malice of the presumptuous one recoils upon himself: so great a terror does the face of the one beholding inspire, so powerfully does it strike back the enemy.

[Col. 0373C] “For it is a tower built with its battlements. Battlements joined to a tower seem to project outward, to fortify the tower strongly, and to menace enemies heavily. From them are cast spears, javelins, stones, and other such things, by which, while the tower is defended, enemies are vigorously beaten back. These, I think, are the commands or admonitions of Scripture, the sayings of the prophets, and spiritual knowledge of sacred writings. They are shown to adhere, through steadfast memory, to the Virgin’s strong mind and, through the varied progress of her works, to keep harmful things farther away.

“For the subtlety of Scripture and spiritual understanding, a tenacious memory of commandments, and clear literal knowledge make the Virgin’s conscience unshakable in its projection outward and repel the enemy’s assaults with the ready missile-shots of works. With battlements of this kind the Davidic tower defends itself and, to drive back the wicked, stretches itself out with certain arms, as it were. For the unbending strength of the Virgin, which is said to be represented by the neck, rejoices to be strengthened by the added protection of Holy Scripture.

[Col. 0374A] “There she receives what makes her stronger and safer, what enables her to restrain enemies and faithfully protect friends. This seems to adhere to her more firmly for her own defense, while from it there also hangs down to us a benefit that, although not equal, is not contemptible. Hence it is added: ‘A thousand,’ and so forth.”

## CHAPTER XIII
A thousand shields hang from it, all the armor of the mighty. In the battlements, and likewise in the shields, he seems to signify Scripture, commending it by varied names because of its varied effects. For since its efficacy in giving aid is found to be manifold, it is not surprising if it is distinguished by many titles. Therefore the Bridegroom says that shields hang from the tower; and, lest we think them few, he adds a number rather than leaving it unspoken, so that when enemies do not attack, we may resort not only to the hanging shields, but may also place undeceiving confidence in the number of the shields. A thousand—the highest number in the order of numbers—is said to be the most perfect of perfect numbers, because it is formed from perfect numbers: as ten is completed from ten units, a hundred from ten tens, so a thousand is completed from as many hundreds; and among numbers there is no greater single number.

By this number are commended the strong defense of the shields, their perfect usefulness, and the beneficial suspension of those that are perfect. They are arranged not merely for the ornament or protection of David’s tower, but are also offered in abundant defense to us who flee to the tower. The Virgin, whose neck, as has already been said, is compared with the tower 215, is prepared with manifold strength for the defense of us all; she elucidates and expounds for us the sequence of the Old Scripture, showing fulfilled in herself in reality what that Scripture sets forth as to come in mystery. For what Jeremiah long before foretold concerning a woman who would encompass a man (Jer. 31), what Isaiah prophesied concerning a Virgin who would conceive and bear a son (Isa. 7), what Ezekiel foretold in a sufficiently obscure riddle concerning the unopened gate (Ezek. 44), what Moses wonderfully prefigured in Aaron’s rod (Num. 17), what prophecy formerly testified in many places and in many ways without displaying it—those who attend perceive to hang forth for us more evidently from Mary.

It hangs forth, I say, from her; it is not shut up within her by bolts and bars, but has been poured out by manifest grace even to our knowledge, so that, returning to the Virgin, we may rejoice to find more plainly what greedy antiquity wished to cover over for us in the cloud of mystery. These mysteries, which we say hang forth to us from Mary—that is, shine out for us from her and through her as we look upward—the Bridegroom rightly designates by the name of shields in this nuptial song. In setting them before us below the tower, he assigns them to us more closely and especially. For the Virgin herself first and more perfectly knew the mysteries of the Scriptures which had both been spoken and foretold concerning her in the dark utterance of the prophets. Instructed more subtly and excellently by their riddles, she brought them forth to us and offered them to those who love her as shields.

The hollow, flat surface of a shield protects and conceals a citizen, checks or blunts head-on the malice of an assailant. So too the depths of Scripture and its breadth, inaccessible to the enemy, become through the Virgin’s abundant aid the strength of us citizens. Indeed, through her the day, once dark to us, has now dawned; through her, in the shield of the Scriptures, the sun of our understanding has shone. Through her we now see, now hold Christ, once promised under figures and wrapped in riddles, now that the promises of Scripture have been fulfilled. Through her the luminous perfection of Scripture has condescended to us far beneath it and, with opened bosom, shows itself to all who advance in zeal and understanding. There one may see the ordered series of perfect commandments, profitable to those who love them: a way of life, an order—in short, all the armor of the mighty.

For whoever wishes to be armed with worthy strength finds in Scripture a ground for rightful boasting. In it life-giving edification lies hidden under the shadow of the letter, and, for those who worthily seek the Virgin, shines forth through her favor. But those who do not care to seek diligently or advance strongly cannot find useful armor in Scripture, because to those who do not know the Virgin the face of Scripture is obscure. It is not armor for the ignorant, but for the strong in faith. Hence the Gentiles, harshly buffeted by foolish unbelief, and the Jews, scandalized no less disastrously by the Virgin’s childbirth, do not find in Scripture Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God—though for us knowledge of him hangs forth from the Virgin without obscurity. Since they do not approach the Virgin with worthy reverence, they do not worthily believe in the wondrous conception or in so ineffable a birth. Thus they remain unable to see—or, seeing, they recoil from—the hanging shields; unarmed, they languish and perish in their languor, making no use of the armor of the mighty.

Those whose left hand is not armed with the hanging sword, whose present conduct is not healthfully instructed by the understanding of the Scriptures—their right hand does not glory in salvation or in future blessedness; indeed, their judgment does not reach the right hand but is deceived. Therefore the Virgin’s neck is not unfittingly likened to a tower, through which so manifold a benefit of Scripture is proclaimed to us; through which the mystery of the incarnate Word is disclosed to us; through which the Word of the Father passes before our ears—indeed, before our eyes. For that good Word, which the very heart of God the Father uttered ineffably, when he ordained to come to human beings and be seen by them, took up the neck of this Virgin as though it were a vehicle of speech and made for itself a path through it. Having passage, it presented itself to those who were neither seeking nor questioning it.

By the passage of this Word, the path itself is so magnificently adorned and the Virgin’s neck strengthened with such might that it is not considered unequal to bearing the burdens of us infirm people, but, like a mighty tower, protects us who are weak. Finally, a tower, as some maintain, is named from protecting (*tuendo*), because it protects both itself and whatever lies beside it; and the hope of those who flee to it is secure in its protection—especially if a thousandfold array of shields and all the armor of the mighty hang there. Since the Virgin appears to surpass abundantly in these things, the Bridegroom continues to add praise to praise; and, loving his beloved, he does what is proper to a friend, who judges that whatever praiseworthy thing may be said of his beloved should be said alike. Therefore he says: “Your two breasts,” etc.

## CHAPTER XIV

“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle, which feed among lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline.”

Earlier, the Virgin commended the Bridegroom’s breasts and declared that they were better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments [216]. Perhaps recalling this, the Bridegroom, even though what seems an interval of time has intervened, would not allow her breasts likewise to pass without praise. After the neck, therefore, which he compared to a most strongly fortified tower, he passes to the breasts and fits to them too a wonderful likeness. He brings forward, not something of the same kind according to the letter, but fawns which feed rather in the time of shadows than of daylight.

The breasts signify, as I think I see, that abundance of the Virgin by which she cherishes and advances our littleness in infirmity; by which she gives us milk and does not wean us until she brings us to growth, until the day arrives and the night at last comes to its end as the shadows grow thin. It moves me that, in bringing forward the Virgin’s breasts, he says “two,” although every woman literally has no breasts except two. Thus, if he had said only “breasts,” leaving “two” unspoken, no right-thinking person would understand anything except two. But perhaps by this he wished to signify the twofold abundance of which I have spoken: for a single abundance would not pour forth enough fullness upon us, but the double one sufficiently nourishes us with its united benefit; nor does any sound-minded person seek to discover a third, much less anything beyond that.

For the Virgin has a certain overflowing affection of benevolence toward those whom she sees to need stronger protection: those whom she sees to will and strive to be redeemed by her Son, yet not to be permitted, pressed beneath their own weight, to attain perfection. The Virgin therefore loves to pour out tender milk for such persons and, with kindly affection, to advance the weak toward every kind of strength. For the holy Mother knows certainly that it does not please her redeeming Son that those should perish whom he wished not to remain guilty of the original debt. But since this breast and this affection of benevolence would be considered insufficient unless a stronger effect were joined to the kindly affection, the Virgin has and obtains from her Son the efficacy or power to bring those who are weak effectively to the advancement she wills. To whom she has mercy with affectionate concern, she brings aid and healing with effective power. With one breast, as it were, she inclines herself to compassion for the miserable; with the other she now supplies the necessary assistance to those in need.

From these two breasts—that is, affection and effect—the Virgin pours into us nourishing milk. With watchful hand she hides us from whirlwind and rain; whatever the lion thunders, she drives back with stronger threats and blunts; whatever the venomous asp has poured over us, she heals with medicinal milk. Therefore the breasts are not unfittingly compared with fawns, which reject harmful things and freely pass over to useful ones; which see suitable things from afar and distinguish them with keen sight; and which leap over every harmful thing by effective power or agility. This, plainly, they are known to have received from the mother gazelle, to whom powerful nature is believed to have given this gift: to see more sharply and distinguish more discerningly whatever may be beneficial, to reject more carefully, and to pass more swiftly over harmful things.

So the Virgin’s affection and effect receive from Mother Grace this power: that they may discerningly see whom they should carefully advance toward salvation; that they may pass over those whom they perceive not to belong to grace; and that they may abhor the filthy and allow the reprobate to become still more filthy. The fawns are called not unlike but rather twins because, born from one mother, they are fed together on one milk. This seems fitting for the aforesaid affection and effect, which one mother, Grace, has willed to bring forth by gracious favor. They are joined by a kind of brotherhood, by a binding covenant: what the first undertakes, the second pursues in completing action; the former does not desire what the latter cannot accomplish, nor does the second bring to completion what the first does not more diligently perceive and desire.

“They feed among lilies” when they delight in the virtues of those who advance, when they flourish in the brightness of their conduct and the fragrance of good testimony; when inwardly they burn more healthfully, not with redness but with love, and outwardly grow white through whitening works as though with leaves. They indeed do not cease to flourish through the Virgin’s abundant favor, and the Virgin likewise does not cease to rejoice in their progress, until, their spirits polished to the utmost, a sweeter day breathes upon them and the shadowy obscurity impatient of that day expires. For when morning light arrives, knowing no evening, the night of present ignorance and every night of distress departs; and the lilies, gathered, are offered in festal joy to the supreme King, in whose sanctuary they enjoy sevenfold and unfading beauty.

There is no hunger there; there the fawns no longer feed; there the Virgin’s breasts are poured out for none who are advancing; there the Virgin no longer rears anyone, teaches anyone, or has mercy on anyone, because there is no infancy, ignorance, or misery. Here, then, the Virgin feeds, where she is said still to feed us; where, while shadows still remain, the face of day is not seen; where, when the day is already bright, one person is not taught by another; where, according to the prophecy (Jer. 31), God shall be known from the least to the greatest.

Having praised the bride’s breasts, the Bridegroom, as though withdrawing himself from her and returning himself to his companions, speaks to them about her. For his loving concern is so vehemently fixed upon her that in this song he knows how to speak only to her or about her.

## CHAPTER XV

“I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense.”

For one who loves, it is not enough to go to the mountain which he loves; he also chooses to precede his journey with speech. While he delays revisiting it rather than omitting to do so, he promises that, though his word runs before, he will afterward go there himself. “If,” he says, “I have withdrawn myself a little from the mountain’s presence, I have not withdrawn from it tender memory or love. I have not contracted contempt, anger, or hatred for it; rather, I have thereby drawn still more strongly to myself its love and longing for me.”

Now the mountain is the loftiness of this Virgin of ours, made commendable by fixed and immovable steadfastness. Though blasts of winds, gathering as though in an army, threaten it on every side, they do not cast the mountain down from grace or from its abiding station. For enemies frequently hurl arrows and javelins at this Virgin, and as their malice advances they add the assaults of battering-rams and heavy engines of war. Yet the mountainous height and immovable firmness of the Virgin cast all these far away; their efforts defeated, the enemies are more harshly repelled and thrown down to the depths.

For whether the pledged hand of the Mighty One is considered present or absent, so great is the Bridegroom’s love for the Virgin, so great his care concerning her, that she is secure, like a mountain, under his protection, and whatever the raging fury of the winds might bring is rendered void. When the Bridegroom seems to depart from her, he does not allow her to yield; sometimes withdrawing himself, he promises to return more quickly. Since he himself knows when he ought to go and return, he declares that he does so according to what he knows to be greatly expedient for the Virgin. Though departing, as it were, from the Virgin, he does not escape the marks of love; after being absent a little, he goes again to her. Neither coming nor going serves sluggishness, but love, so that they may be bound more closely and cleave to one another with a stronger bond.

For this purpose the Bridegroom withdraws himself: lest his presence, being too freely granted, become cheap. For this purpose he goes to the Virgin: that love may revive more tenderly, and that he who loves and wishes to be loved more by the Virgin may make her burn more vehemently in that furnace. Therefore he goes to the Virgin, that her love may blaze more ardently and he himself may rejoice more fully as she loves more. When he perceives that she is more greatly scorched with heat—or with love—he loves her as she advances and cherishes her in a more welcome embrace.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0378C]

Hence another translation has: “I will go for myself to the mountain of myrrh.” I will go to the Virgin; and lest I seem to go in vain, I will go for myself: seeking indeed to care for her and to satisfy her, but also for myself. Certainly I shall not go there empty-handed or superfluously; I shall confer something upon her and bring much back to myself when I return.

I will go to the Virgin, whose height myrrh now wonderfully claims; whose intact flesh no native corruption disfigures; whose integrity a marvelous chastity renders more excellent than that of all women, and whose excellence is made solid, not swollen, by that chastity. This is a great mountain, known to be so devoted to chaste actions that it may be called not soft and yielding, but specifically a mountain of myrrh: for seductive softness did not enervate the Virgin, but unblemished rigor and the myrrh of continence preserved her.

The Bridegroom also not unfittingly calls her a hill of incense, because she spreads a good fame among both those present and those to come; and, kindled by coals and by the violent heat of love, she rises in a mass and offers God a sacrifice of fragrance. Her devotion and ardent affection, sweeter than all incense, offer her to the Creator and exalt her above creation. She is a mountain that knows not how to bring forth what is ridiculous, yet a hill choosing to entertain no lofty thoughts of herself. When she restrains and extinguishes, and does not allow the enticements of flesh even to mutter; when she strives by the most approved myrrh to prevent affections breeding worms; when she puts a yoke upon her own wills and sets them a law; when she checks and disciplines with salt whatever the flesh savors—then indeed she is a mountain, possessing such incomparable height, great virtue, great constancy, and great strength of wisdom.

But when she frees herself from transitory pursuits and works, considers in her mind how sweet heavenly things are to the inward palate, melts herself into liquid incense with fiery love, and, forgetful of earthly things, wholly enwraps herself in contemplation of things above—then she truly becomes a hill, because the more lofty she is in merits and devotion, the humbler she is in heart and, as it were, no more removed than others.

When the angel found her alone in her chamber, devoted to meditation, and the Lord who sent him himself anticipated the angel’s announcement of the coming birth, she, hanging with most devout love upon the angel’s word—indeed, upon the Father’s Word—and condescending to us below, who were not yet able sufficiently to comprehend great things, said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1). When the Virgin’s mind, by new grace, surpassed our lowliness, and he who had come as messenger saw himself anticipated, with what humility did the most devout Virgin abase herself, who, already called Mother of God, granted herself no title except that of little handmaid? When strong fire is applied, incense melts into a cloud of smoke; the smoke rises on high and the sweetness of its fragrance spreads. The world far and wide seems occupied by the excellence of this mountain, and yet the humble Virgin still compels herself to be called a hill. To this mountain in merits, this hill in humility, the Bridegroom promises to go; and, more swiftly than his word, is already present to answer the speaking Virgin—or rather, he anticipates and commends her before she speaks, that she may be more closely inflamed in love for the One who commends her.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0379C]

“You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.”

From the time when the angel announces to the Virgin the word and greeting entrusted to him, and when the Holy Spirit comes upon her and overshadows her with power, the law of iniquity does not retain its privilege in her; no recent or ancient stain of sin remains. Now one woman is ugly, another wholly ugly; one is beautiful, another wholly beautiful. Ugly is she whom the former wrath, the law of nature, darkens and bends down—she who contracts guilt for herself from the beginning and from the defect of generation. That defect has such overwhelming and inextricable force that there is neither power nor capacity utterly to be without it.

But the wholly ugly woman subjects her corrupted will to the perverse law and, by deadly consent, fashions an accursed unity: what the oppressive law suggests—or rather, imposes—she pursues by will and serves by completing action. By contrast, beautiful is she who understands that the written law, the sequence of commandments, is good; who, now that the Spirit has given the gift, loves it as given; who is moved by voluntary impulse to fulfill it more diligently, yet has not deserved to obtain power to prevail. The willing is indeed present, but she experiences contradictory conflict, because the door of possibility has not yet been opened to her will. While the one forcefully knocks, strives obstinately, and persists, the other repels more strongly, opposes more stubbornly, and resists. The former seeks, with the hand of diligence cultivating her face, to strive so that, cleansed of every blemish, she may be able to enter where she desires; the latter endeavors to resist and oppose this purpose and sometimes, being stronger, rejoices to gain the victory first.

But she is wholly beautiful whom the defective law, nature’s disgrace, and the disease of wrath no longer press down, overpower, or suffice to hinder, so that her will is stirred by desire to repel sins and a worthy possibility assists it as it goes before. She is wholly beautiful whose mind’s keenness flourishes and whose spirit does not languish; whose flesh is at rest and does not rise insolently against the spirit; whose spirit, suffering no rebellion from that which is subject to it, obeys God alone and no longer limps in obedience to the commandment. She is wholly beautiful who has now attained, by a kind of example rarely found, this summit: upon whom has come so great a grace of the overshadowing Spirit, and from whom the mighty hand of mercy has wiped away every blemish so completely that not only guilt but even anxious fear of guilt remains no more.

Whether anyone like us can attain this while the present age rolls on, as one groans and laments remaining under it—to tell you the truth, I do not claim certain knowledge; and therefore I do not rashly presume to affirm what I do not know. For although the light of new grace has been poured into our eyes, and at its rising the darkness poured over us by our parents’ fault has disappeared, there is nevertheless a certain blemish, as it were, impressed upon our face. So long as we live here, pressed by it, we are liable to fault even in small matters. Of this it is written: “No one is clean from filth” (Job 15). “There is no human being who does not sin” (2 Chr. 6). This severe law seems to have impressed such a blemish upon us wretches and infected our beauty with it as though with a cautery, so that, although we strive to polish it with the hand of carefulness, we still cannot wholly free it from this wrongful right.

A blemish, moreover, is a more tenacious mole, a shameful mark, a discordant ugliness by which the neighboring and adjoining beauty grieves to be infected—or, rather, affected. Although much care is employed to wipe it away, it does not eliminate what has already become ingrained and turned into nature. But if anything of natural defect was in this Virgin, the spiritual grace that came upon her cleansed and removed the stain; and what endures more harshly in us by a miserable or tenacious law, the medicinal hand of grace in her washes away effectively. Because the general iniquity of us all does not darken her, but the special excellence of her merits now makes her shine in the Bridegroom’s sight, the Bridegroom rightly loves and invites her more tenderly, that in coming to him she may commit herself to him more devoutly and attentively.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come.”

The Bridegroom admonishes her who is wholly beautiful, so that not even a slight blemish holds her, lest she perhaps seem to have labored for beauty without fruit: she is to come, namely, from great beauty to greater beauty; from what has been given, she is to pass with instructed foot to the Giver [219]. For no one is permitted to remain in the things received, clinging to them with whole desire and grasping hands. Rather, not in contempt or hatred of them but through advancement and discernment, one must turn the eyes of the mind toward him who bestowed them, and possess not those things themselves but now him—while possessing those things for his sake—more dearly.

Lebanon, it seems to me, signifies that whiteness which the Bridegroom wished to designate for the Virgin—or rather to designate the Virgin by: namely, the whiteness of continence and virginal purity, which the Son, the Bridegroom, bestowed as a gift of his goodness upon his mother, the bride. For the Bridegroom wished his mother to dwell in whiteness, so that her excellence might be commended as though by the place; so that Mount Lebanon itself—that is, the whiteness of virginal excellence—might consecrate her fruitfulness in such a way that her fruitfulness became spiritual.

Nevertheless, if it may be said—indeed perhaps because it can be said—the Virgin seems not so much to be sanctified by the place as to sanctify the place. The Virgin is not made commendable by the mountain, but the mountain by the Virgin; and this whiteness has not so much exalted the Virgin as the Virgin has exalted this whiteness and made it altogether more pleasing in the eyes of worthy beholders. For before the Virgin, just as Mount Lebanon could be found, so virginity too could be found, but it was said to be marked with little or no honor. Nor was anyone found commended by virginal beauty, or by whose merit virginity itself might rejoice to be made illustrious.

We know that this was reserved for our time and for this Virgin: lifted up by this mountain, she rather rendered the mountain lifted up; and, in a wondrous way, she herself, whiter than Lebanon, made Lebanon whiter, and by her own merit adorned virginal beauty. Therefore the Virgin is great and incomparably worthy of praise, comparable with no women before her or after her. To virginal whiteness, which had previously possessed no merit or honor from anyone, she brought merit and a more abundant gift of grace. Thus what for many earlier ages had been dishonorable and burdensome among women became from that time onward pleasing and beautiful. What Jephthah’s daughter, grieving, as it were devotes and laments, the rod of Jesse, wisely choosing, raises more sacredly and honors.

But because the Virgin possesses no grace and no merit that she has not received, she hears and receives from him who gave it this command: that from so great a whiteness, in which she herself first rejoices by his gift, she should refer herself to him through whose agency virginity itself becomes fruitful. “Come from Lebanon, my bride,” he says. “You who have made Mount Lebanon white by a new gift, who have exalted virginal whiteness by excellence of merits, come—but without laying aside virginal beauty itself. Not content with it, prefer the Bridegroom’s grace. Come, not to cease now from your resolve of virginity, but to be joined and stand nearer to me, your Giver; so that you who rejoice securely in virginal purity may rejoice more eagerly in the bride’s privilege, in the nuptial covenant.”

Thus it is said, “Come from Lebanon, bride.” But when “Come from Lebanon” is repeated and “bride” is not added, he intended, as I judge, to admonish her twice about that to which he knows the Virgin clings more firmly the longer she has possessed it, so that, thus admonished, she may turn herself away from it—not from hatred, but as counsel directs—and turn with easier passage toward the things offered. When he repeats “Come” a third time and adds neither “from Lebanon” nor “bride,” he urges her not only to withdraw from the things she now possesses through advancing merits, or to advance in present reality to the bridal things set before her, but also to do whatever progress she makes—as though she had labored in a double contest—wholly for love of the reward and wholly in hope of the crown.

“Come, then,” he says, “turn away from the things you now possess for the sake of advancing; come a second time, turn more intimately toward bridal embraces. Come a third time, so that you may rejoice not only in virginal honor and in the bridal chamber, but that you, the mother, may be crowned in glory with the Son upon the royal throne.” Hence follows: “You shall be crowned,” etc.

## CHAPTER XIX

“You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.”

The Bridegroom’s Virgin Mother is so earnestly urged to come in order that she may be worthily honored for her merits with royal insignia, and that a crown may be given to her—not one fashioned from gold, silver, electrum, or gemstones, but, by a new kind of workmanship, one made from lofty mountains. Its supreme craftsman first places Mount Amana, then sets Mount Sanir and Hermon above and upon it; the prudent artist inserts the dens of lions and the ridges of leopards, and thus with marvelous wisdom fashions and composes a marvelous work.

But why, from so many mountains throughout the world, did he choose three which he specifies by name and bring them into this wonderful work in such a manner as to arrange Amana first, Sanir second, and Hermon third, joining in this work those separated from one another by location? What mystery is figured by this deed does not readily appear, unless perhaps the interpretation of the names themselves gives assistance. Carefully examined, this interpretation makes clear the darkened understanding and mystically brings the Virgin’s crown to perfection.

Amana means “watchful tooth,” signifying the wicked spirit known to envy all who are sound in mind, who in his constant envy loves and desires always to bite us, press us through deadly biting toward death or vices, and sometimes rejoices to prevail in such business. For this great crime he is found not to be dulled by sluggish sleep, but to remain constant and watchful in evil. Although, wicked as he is, he does not reveal himself to those who are vigilant and keep watch over themselves, yet he watchfully bites and attacks those given to sleep and insufficiently wary of themselves.

Sanir, mentioned next, is not dissimilar. Its interpretation clearly expresses the same watchfulness, and this name too seems to signify the same wicked spirit, whose malice is known to be assigned only an ever-watchful character. For Sanir means “night bird” or “stench.” A bird uses the rowing motion of its feathers and holds itself aloft by its wings; when it is believed to be far away, it suddenly appears by swift flight. If daylight is perhaps thought not to favor its purpose, the bird of spiritual malice becomes nocturnal in order to deceive the wretched. It becomes nocturnal when temptation fraudulently seeks a person who is unwary and secure; when, perhaps having been detected, it stealthily introduces itself under another appearance; when it mocks and derides one overcome by languor and sleepiness; when the sluggard is led—indeed, seduced—like an ox to slaughter and does not see it.

Nor without reason is Sanir also said to mean “stench,” because temptation, although it avoids being foreseen, nevertheless wishes to be sensibly present. While it strives, like a crawling serpent, not to be heard in silence, it nevertheless wishes to be felt by inflicting a venomous stench through its bite. Temptation not foreseen is not felt, as though by an open nostril, when the tempted person, oppressed in mind, experiences the heavy burden of guilt. Wherever he turns himself on the bed of darkness beneath the coverlet, he perceives the product of the stench, perhaps uncertain of its root. The root full of vice is stealthily oppressive suggestion; the foul fruit is the consent or consequent completion. When its stench infects the nostrils and affects the inner sense of smell, it renders the whole person weakened by poisoned inward parts.

Hermon is fittingly added, meaning “execration” or “his anathema.” From that point onward, this lost being not only does no good, but with greater malice execrates the good which he hears, because such a collection or cesspool of vices flows in through the crevices of the nostrils that no instruction of the word can find a way into the heart itself. Once the word is excluded, that wicked one hardens the miserable heart further; and when it is hardened, he likewise closes and stops up the ear after the manner of an asp, so that it no longer believes or loves to obey right hearing, but afterward chooses not even to hear what is rightly put before it.

Thus he execrates whatever uprightness of conduct suggests, so that wickedly introduced dullness closes every entrance to it, delighting only to offer open nostrils to the stenches of vices and to fill the lakes of the inward recesses with unclean floods. Since admonition and Scripture are not admitted to the hardened mind, it treats as anathema whatever true religion or worship contains; loving to be held by the softness of mud and unclean dregs alone, it judges nothing more execrable than to be removed from such things. Hence it is written: “Wisdom is an abomination to the sinner” (Ecclus. 1). Advancing toward worse things, he is not only wicked toward himself but wishes to harm others also; strong in malice, he delights to be a terror to those beneath him. His ensuing savagery, like a lion lying in wait from its den, wishes all the rest to sink before him in servile fear.

For some people’s cruelty is not easily restrained within the narrow confines of the mind, but roars and boils, seeking to extend itself so as to harm others. When the furnace or kiln has been kindled with the heat of malice, leonine fury desires outwardly to rage against all those subject to it. If such a person perhaps sees that the force of his power is insufficient, he seeks a new form of hunting: namely, the deceit of falsehood. Now, raging like a roaring lion, he seeks someone to devour; now he shows himself a leopard, spotted with manifold deceit. For that wicked spirit is manifoldly belligerent: now using power to overcome the wretched, now deceitful; now agreeable to the willing and unwilling alike, now rebellious; harmful through a thousand arts and, like a leopard, change-skinned.

Significantly, the Bridegroom assigns lions to dens and leopards to mountains, thereby signifying both the deceitful strength and the strong deceitfulness of malignant spirits. Sometimes savage strength proceeds from a den or ambush; sometimes, from the height of power, a no less deadly multitude of deceits. Whether deceitful and crafty spirits openly exert themselves in strength, or whether the strong and exalted descend to weave nets of deception, they wage destructive war against both the unwary and the weak. Unless the Virgin comes and mercifully brings aid, they carry off the banner of triumph.

But the holy Virgin hastens to meet such wicked enemies, grieving that any of the elect should deviate from her Son’s purpose. She pities those whom hostile and wild malice has already destroyed; she intercedes with her Son and reconciles to him those whom he redeemed. When the Son has been appeased, she turns confidently to attack the enemies: she breaks their powers, lays bare and overturns their deceits; and whatever Mount Amana swells with, whatever Sanir or Hermon raises on its lofty summit, the Virgin strongly tramples and softens like the mud of the streets. Therefore, when complete victory has been won over them, her hand is rightly adorned with laurel and the Virgin’s head crowned with gold; and she is said to be crowned from these same mountains, since she is now granted full glory in victory over them.

## CHAPTER XX
From the head of Amana, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, etc. Yet I do not think it unsuitable if the aforesaid mountains are beautifully interpreted in a sound sense, so that they figure not evil demons but people converted to the faith. The Virgin rejoices in their faith, is solicitous for their progress, cherishes them with her goodwill, and advances them through her intercession. As has been said, Amana means “watchful tooth.” A “watchful tooth” is fittingly the preacher to whom, as one who watches, the keeping of us who are weak is entrusted; to whom, when a sheet full of animals—or rather, of creatures living in an animal fashion—is offered, the command is given, not literally but in a spiritual mystery, to kill and eat: “Kill and eat,” he says (Acts 10).

For a shepherd does not worthily undertake watchfulness over his flock if he does not consume its hardness by the admonition of teaching; nor, when something worthy of rebuke presents itself to his watchful eye, does he fail promptly to apply the biting tooth for cutting it away. Conversely, it is written of others: “They shall eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4). After the mountain Amana, the Bridegroom wished to name Mount Sanir, whose interpretation seems to signify a nocturnal bird. For, while we are benumbed by the long-standing habit of vices, the ever-watchful shepherd undoubtedly becomes a bird of the night.

When blind softness invites us to sin—or rather, to persist in sin—the good shepherd, [Col. 0384D] who neither sleeps nor slumbers over our guarding, seems, like a nocturnal bird, to arrive importunately and suddenly, and to confront more sharply with the sword of the word habits made wickedly secure. Thus Judas Maccabaeus, when he perceived that the nights were already being pressed by silence and that the opportunity of time suited his bold enterprises, fell upon his unsuspecting enemies, courageously inflicted great slaughter, and triumphed in vigilant warfare over those resting in secure torpor. For the warrior judged it of little consequence whether he dared attack his enemies by night or by day, provided only that the sluggish and cowardly heedlessness of his enemies yielded to greater caution, and victory was granted to the fighter either by cunning strength or by military stratagem.

Moreover, among the ancients this maxim was famously proclaimed and, lest forgetfulness erase it, was committed to writing among the pagans: in war one should seek not only excellence in courage, but also fitting stratagem, so that the enemy’s malice may be cleverly crushed. “What man would inquire whether it is deceit or valour in an enemy?” says Virgil, *Aeneid* II. [Col. 0385A] Therefore the prudent leader, when he wishes to subject hostile malice to servitude, applies his hand as need requires now to stratagem, now to valour: so that, if the enemy resists by deceit, he may fall crushed by the hammer of valour; and, if the sun has not scorched him by day, he may not escape the deception of night.

In this manner the good teacher, coming upon us in our torpor like a bird, provides for our salvation, importunate to our will and unwelcome to our habits. He confronts those weighed down with sleep and shakes from us our accursed sluggishness; once awake, he provokes us to fly as an eagle does its young. But with what confidence or effectiveness can he undertake or accomplish this, [Col. 0385B] unless he first loves and keeps what he preaches ought to be kept? He does not embrace the darkness of this present night with any desire, but, soaring beyond like Sanir and Hermon, abhors what he sees below.

For he invites us effectively to teaching precisely because he confidently commends by his conduct the discipline which he preaches in words. He does not neglect himself while offering medicine to others, but abhors and flees whatever the world smells of as a bilge. “The things that were gain to me,” he says, “I reckon as dung” (Phil. 3). Hermon, moreover, is said to mean not only “abhorrence,” but also “anathema”; and the addition made to it—namely, “anathema of anathema”—means “separation of separation.” Thus a teacher may deservedly be called its anathema when he himself separates with all diligence from that from which he teaches others to separate.

“I did not yield to flesh and blood,” says Paul (Gal. 1). Thus Paul is “its anathema,” that is, “anathema of anathema,” “separation of separation”: separating from himself what he strives to separate from others, or separating from others what he had first taken pains to separate from himself. And the diadem of this Virgin is marvellously woven: in it are set the watchful tooth, the nocturnal bird, and the anathema of anathema. Yet, if anyone wishes to examine the sequence of words more carefully, it is not expressly said that the Virgin is crowned from these mountains. For it was not said, “You shall be crowned from Amana, Sanir, and Hermon,” but, “You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon.”

The head, as everyone knows, rules the remaining members and the whole body; [Col. 0385D] the crown of the head is called its summit. The head is not contained in the summit, but the summit in the head; for the head is not a part of the summit, but the summit is the upper part of the head. By the head, therefore, the order of prelates is fittingly figured, whom the prophet calls the nobles, the heads of the peoples. By the summit, however, the apostolic choir seems to be designated, which is evidently pre-eminent in the order of prelates by a certain excellence.

Or perhaps the apostolic order itself may be called the head; 222 and the summit is Peter, who is clearly proclaimed first and chief. As he was among the apostles, so he was set before the apostles as keeper of the keys of heaven; while John remained as he was, Peter followed Christ in a special manner. These apostles are also figuratively the dens of lions, in which kings and lofty princes of lands lay themselves down when, having put aside the fierceness by which they commonly terrify their inferiors, they bow to them and do not refuse to submit to their merits.

For when an emperor, laying aside the diadem by which he shines forth, forgets his sceptre and does not indulge his royal dignity; when he humbles himself, obeys Peter, and accepts Paul’s admonitions—what is this except a lion lying at rest in an apostolic den? These likewise are mountains, lofty in merits and firm in holiness: they are eminent not in earthly height but in spiritual dignity. Whoever desires to be adorned with a radiant countenance lifts his eyes to them, recognizing himself as a leopard variegated with a spotted skin. He who, under the burden of many vices, is not secure in his own strength and has no confidence of victory, and must fight against spiritual wickedness in valley or plain, passes to [Col. 0386B] their heights to seek help and instruction; lest he perish, he embraces the discipline of their learned teaching. “I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains,” he says, “whence help shall come to me” (Ps. 120).

Thus the apostles are rightly called both lions’ dens and mountains of leopards. Kings and rulers alike, and those held fast by the manifold multitude of vices, listen to them; having listened, they obey through the grace of the divine gift, lay aside beastly ferocity, and follow an ordered rule of life. When the Bridegroom arranges and disposes these very guides as living stones, then, after disposing them fittingly, he surrounds and crowns the Virgin Queen. For her honour he makes them worthier in merits, so that within the choir of righteous people they may become closer to the Bride by a special excellence.

Since he does not immediately find that he can bestow this more fully upon her whom he loves, he grants her the hope of promise. Having received the promise, the Virgin now rejoices in the presence of hope and, more truly, awaits the future with sure confidence. “You shall be crowned,” he says. By what merit, however, the Virgin is worthy to attain the presence of hope, the Bridegroom seems to recall by his grace, so that all may know that a perfect reward is bestowed on no one whose worthy merit has not first been found.

## CHAPTER XXI

“You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes, and with one lock of your neck.”

Enemies are accustomed to be deterred by enemies through fear of wounds; and one who has inflicted a wound may perhaps earn greater hatred. As much as the person able to injure and inflict wounds rejoices at his strength, so much—indeed, more—does one compelled to suffer them grieve. But here the Virgin wounds, and the wounded one does not return hatred. She seems to prevail, yet he does not stretch out his hands in retaliation. She, assured of victory, brightens in countenance and claps her hands; he seems pierced, and, though pierced to the heart, does not complain but applauds.

For a hand trained for battle and an arrow inflicting a powerful wound are not anger, loss, or injury to the one who receives them; rather, wounds from one who loves in this way are judged more welcome and better than the deceitful kisses and treacherous frauds of one who kisses wickedly (Prov. 27). The Bridegroom loves to be strongly wounded—but by love; to be pierced, not by a sword, but by the stronger affection of those who love. From the depth of that wound grace flows, love breathes more sweetly, and, pouring out not blood but sweetness, loves more vividly and does not die. [Col. 0387A]

Rightly, therefore, he declares that his own heart—not his head, foot, or anything similar—is wounded. We sometimes see a person survive when such things have been wounded; but the heart itself, even slightly wounded, admits no healing hand and, having neither time nor remedy, immediately gives up the vital spirit. Therefore, when he declares that his heart is weakened, as it were, by the Bride’s wound, and by repeating the word wishes to confirm the certainty of the same wound, he indicates that the wound must be understood as neither destructive nor mortal: for the heart is not bodily or subject to death, but living.

But because the heart of the body is the seat of the soul, the place of life, and the dwelling of hatred or love, by naming the heart he means the secret place [Col. 0387B] of a more welcome love. There he receives and accepts her who has deserved to come there in a special way and to enter the sanctuary of grace by singular merit. He expressed this entrance by the name of a wound: not bloody, not violent in rage but in love, not in anger but in benevolent affection. For no sleepy weakling penetrates there, but one clean of heart, keen in spirit, and forceful in unrelenting constancy.

Moreover, no one exerts effective force upon this sanctuary who, walking on a path that is less than straight, turns himself toward the love of temporal things. Rather, it is the person who strives with prevailing effort to forget all things that pass away and, cleaving to God alone, desires to attain eternal things alone. Thus in this passage he calls her at once bride and sister, in order to signify by these names the stronger affection of shared goodwill: for what belongs to the Bridegroom is not denied to the bride by right of marriage, and the divine law requires that a sister be regarded as participant and co-heir with her brother in the paternal inheritance.

The Virgin is Christ’s sister, and Christ is likewise the Virgin’s brother. They have one kinship on earth and are said to have one Father in heaven. Though he grants not one identical portion to all on account of sex, but according to merits, still, distributing justly, he disinherits neither daughter nor son. Accordingly, the Virgin, as this Father’s daughter and heir, is rightly called Christ’s sister and co-heir. Her more gracious affection—sisterly and bridal love—wounds her brother and bridegroom, not with the point of a javelin but with the spiritual point of the eye.

## CHAPTER XXII

[Col. 0387D] “With one of your eyes.” By this saying he indicates that the Virgin is radiant with two eyes, but more gracious and sweet through one of them. In approving one, he plainly does not rebuke the other; without accusing the other, he esteems the one more highly. Perhaps the other eye is that which has been given to behold visible things: the world and all that is contained within the compass of the world; which attends to and understands those things which the order of events or nature unfolds together or successively, as things destined to pass away through shifting change or changeable movement.

Indeed, it sees that whatever has been created naturally hastens toward some kind of passing away; and that, in spirits no less than bodies, nothing is stable in itself, except those angels whom the mighty Author of things and Lord of creation has already established by the benefit of his will, not by nature. But the first and chief eye is that spiritual eye which withdraws itself far from contemplation of temporal creation and, transcending angels and every creature altogether, raises itself to behold the face or nature of the Creator. Because, ignorant of the world, it laudably pines for God’s salvation, is not disturbed by many things, but desires that one necessary thing, it is rightly called one: that is, not many-formed through love of many things, but single in loving the one God alone and beholding him alone.

This eye does not pour itself outward to live among many things, but, gathering its gaze, pours itself into Christ’s inner chamber.
