It wounds his heart, because it hides itself there more keenly than a sword, where Christ conceals no eye except one and simple. [Col. 0388B] Nor does the Bridegroom say that he is wounded only by the eye, but also by a lock, and by repeating the word he plainly indicates that the wound itself is repeated. For it was not enough for the Virgin, as it were, to have inflicted one dart, nor was it enough for the Bridegroom, with the second left unmentioned, to have reported only one.

The Bridegroom, therefore, is wounded by the Virgin’s eye and, as he declares, also by her lock, because the multiplicity of hairs, loving propriety and enduring discipline, is not carried away by the wind or scattered through the emptiness of harmful freedom, but is maturely gathered and, as it were, brought under the rule of unity itself. I think no woman has been found in all former ages who, after her hair was cut off, was uniquely content with one single hair, or who could so deserve praise on account of one hair, unless the crowned multiplicity is restrained into one by a rule of discipline.

So too the Virgin, rejoicing to be adorned with many hairs—that is, virtues—lest this very multiplicity be compelled to be blown about by the breeze of vanity, gathers them all together and binds them in a certain unity; by wondrous discipline she brings them under one love. For whatever is acquired through a multitude or abundance of merits, if it is not bound by the bond of love, lacks the glory of rewards. No worthy praise approves whatever is manifold in merits if it is not united, like hairs, by the binding fillet of charity.

Paul rightly judged this of her (1 Cor. 13), calling love the bond of perfection when he wished to commend it. Although the accumulation of the other virtues is countless, unless it is bound by this bond it remains wholly imperfect. But when bound, it strengthens and adorns the Virgin’s faith [Col. 0388D] and, like a lock, adorns rather than burdens the neck. Faith glories in such an ornament and such a work, worthily indeed, since through love it performs what the divine law commands.

For those whom a heavy and, as it were, bodily mass removes and separates from the head, faith, like a neck, binds and joins us to Christ. Without it, not even the Virgin herself can please God; by its intervention Elizabeth wished to call her blessed: “Blessed,” she says, “are you who believed, because the things spoken to you by the Lord shall be fulfilled” (Luke 1). And the Apostle says: “That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith” (Eph. 3). In the lock of this neck, united by the aforesaid bond of love—and by whose honour, not burden, the Virgin’s faith is distinguished—the Bridegroom declares with joyful exultation that his heart has been wounded. He indicates that her tender affection powerfully moves, but does not trouble, him through the Virgin’s strong love. In her praise he adds: “How beautiful,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! Your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments above all spices.”

He calls the Virgin’s breasts those by which she instructs little ones so that they may grow, and cherishes those somewhat grown so that, with the passing of time, they may reach youth. He declares them beautiful, so that they may not seem contemptible to Jews who glory in the letter of the law, but may shine forth more pleasingly both for them and for other hearers. Whether they are first called *mammae* (“breasts”) or later *ubera* (“teats, breasts”), they are declared more beautiful in comparison with the wine of the law: for the law’s harshness makes the Jews like drunken and senseless people, whereas their sweetness makes us pleasing and harmonious to God.

Because you know that the Virgin’s breasts were set forth not far above and, insofar as God granted, expounded there, I refrain from delaying longer to expound them anew, referring the attentive hearer to what has already been said. But because beauty here is said to reside not only in the *ubera* but also in the *mammae*, of which no mention was made there or anywhere above, he seems perhaps to intimate something new with greater subtlety—something to which I have not applied hand or effort in a more careful exposition.

The *mammae*, as it is said, do not give milk to little children, but, when the time comes, promise that they will give it forth. Meanwhile they lie concealed beneath the shadow of immature time, not yet rich in fitting fruit but swelling in hope of the future. For as long as the Virgin observes us undisciplined, hardened, and not yet born to vital life because our sins demand it, she keeps the benefit of teaching within her breasts and does not bring it forth, not presuming to nourish those whom a fitting birth has not brought forth to life.

For she knows that it belongs to Christ to give life to us long dead, to renew us from uterine darkness into the grace of light; but once we are born, she is permitted to bestow that benefit upon us and pour out her breasts more abundantly for those now capable of receiving it. “If,” she says, “you would cause your chosen ones to be born into that grace of light which I especially desire, so that, when you gave life, they might be fed by whatever benefit you chose, then my *mammae* would become the abundance of *ubera*, and, living in the Spirit, would more effectively nourish them with worthy milk. [Col. 0389D] Then I would gradually unfold for them your conception and birth, and reveal to the listener’s ear the secret mystery; and what neither Gentiles nor Jews comprehend with unbelieving mind, John, son of Zebedee, sucking my breasts, would drink in.”

The Bridegroom praises such breasts and teats in the Virgin Mother. To conclude their praises with a fitting and equally mystical end, he adds a commendation not of the nourishment of milk, nor of its streams or flows, but of the surpassing fragrance and ointments preferred above all spices: “And the fragrance of your ointments above all spices.” From the aforesaid breasts, by which the Virgin is distinguished through her wondrous childbirth, there is found to issue not womanly milk but an abundance of ointments. Even if the entire succession of perfumers from all former times were assembled to prepare ointment, every one of their compounds would be surpassed, not in time but in marvellous fragrance.

Whatever the ingenuity of the ancients produced from the beginning; whatever pagan curiosity grasped from the wondrously created world; whatever sophists or, following Pythagoras, philosophers devised with deceptive subtlety, by which they infected their disciples as teachers with a corrupting spice—all this is far surpassed by the Virgin’s preaching and teaching, in which truth rules and the discipline of life prevails. Whatever patriarchs and prophets, relying on the gift of foresight, veiled in obscurities of words or in mystical sacraments; whatever the fathers of old perceived with prophetic scent, who agreed to proclaim with wakeful announcement the advent of the true light—the Virgin, queen of virgins, surpassed all this by special advancement, she who bore in her virginal womb the man who is humanity’s salvation. [Col. 0390B]

The completed novelty of her conception and birth, the new preparation, the effective remedy first given in the virginal chamber, and the sound reading afterward conveyed to us by the Virgin’s certain teaching proceed in such a way that what she herself bestows transcends all that precedes as promise. For none of those before her so expressed the truth that was to come as did the holy Virgin, to whom divine goodness granted that she should know the mystery of the incarnate Word more expressly and perceptibly than it could be told by a human being or an angel.

Her knowledge and the sweet recollection of that knowledge are so wondrous a preparation and such an abolition of the ancient wound that the Virgin, anointed with them as with spices or ointments, no longer knows the wound inflicted by the malice of Eve or of the serpent. These ointments of the Virgin, by which she deserved to be medicinally anointed, are closed under a certain seal and cannot be fully explained in our speech. For the light that prepares ointments deigned to arise in the Virgin in such a way that no other human being can perceive it as it is.

But the fragrance, or report, of these ointments breathes sweetly and healthfully upon us. Its sweetness now restores breath to our languishing mind; having drawn into our nostrils, as it were, the fragrance of that little which the Virgin spoke from her certain fullness, our spirit has revived. Rightly, then, he does not set above all spices the Virgin’s ointments, [Col. 0390D] which she does not present to us who are far inferior, but what is less—their fragrance. No earlier knowledge and no spices can be compared with the grace granted to the apostles through the Virgin to smell it.

Not without reason, when Christ returned to the Father from whom he had come, and the apostles had been left behind before the Spirit was granted in tongues of fire, the apostles thought it fitting to persevere unanimously in prayer with Mary the mother of Jesus, so that they might affirm more constantly—and therefore more certainly—what they had received from her. Upon those on whom the sun of understanding shone with more abundant splendour, a honey-sweet fragrance flowed from the Virgin herself in such a way that, if it were compared with the understanding or hearing of any predecessor, it would undoubtedly deserve to surpass it in sweet delight. Of this he adds: “A honeycomb,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“A dripping honeycomb are your lips, O Bride; honey and milk are under [Col. 0391A] your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.”

The Virgin’s lips should rightly be called a honeycomb, because the Virgin herself is figured by the name of a bee. By a natural privilege the bee feeds on flowers, lives on dew, knows no intercourse, and marvellously gathers its offspring with its mouth; it is made fruitful with progeny without groaning or pain. Thus the Virgin becomes a chaste mother in her womb, not by lust but by love. Active in skill, shrewd in ingenuity, it does not grow idle in its diligence; with remarkable industry it makes its prudence known, building a honeycomb for itself, arranging distinct cells in order, and diligently storing honey in their narrow spaces with its mouth.

The Virgin is fittingly judged like this bee. She delights to feed spiritually on the flowery beauty of virtues; living in the Spirit, she receives divine grace from above as dew; knowing no man, she conceives and bears a son without labour. By diligent effort she heaps up spiritual riches, gathering and preserving in her heart words heavy with meaning. She fills the secret place of her conscience with a sweetness so delightful that inwardly, like a honeycomb, she may be called honeyed.

Yet she does not confine this sweetness, which she herself tastes more perfectly and fully, through the sickness of envy or the key of avarice. Rather, opening her lips, she permits to drip for us who stand by what the divine Spirit wished to instil in her from above as dew and sweetness. For the Virgin considers what is suitable for us to hear first and what afterward. She does not disclose all at once what she judges worthy of concealment; nor, like an overturned vessel, does she immediately pour out all that it contains. Instead, because we are less fit for everything, she sprinkles us with a thin dripping.

The Old Testament, the figurative speech of the prophets, the riddles of the ancients, and the obscure surface of the Scriptures did not, I say, deserve in the same way to be or to be called a dripping honeycomb. Although they were a honeycomb, they were held closed under a seal. For we may call the obscurity of the earlier writings a honeycomb: it held honey within but did not know how to drip it, because it did not convey mystical senses, inner sweetness, and spiritual advancement to our darkened understandings. [Col. 0391C]

That honeycomb, then, weighed down by its own weight, lay for a long time, not pressed out by the hand of builders. No one came who, pitying it for our sake, might lift it up and, having lifted it, with a pleasing hand squeeze it into the mouths of the hungry. But the Virgin, full not so much of honey as of sweetness of mind, rich not in money but in spiritual teachings, did not pour out with sudden force, as from an open vessel, what she had stored in the honeycomb—sweeter than honey, more delightful than all wine. Instead, regulating the opening of her lips by the occasion at hand, she chose to bring forth only what the capacity of her hearers was able to bear.

Thus her lips dripped less while Christ still lived among humankind as a human being, but more after he had conquered death and now lived again in greater glory. For then the Jews’ obstinacy was oppressed by blindness poured over them, whereas now greater knowledge has been poured into the apostles by the gift of the Spirit. Therefore the Virgin’s lips are dripping like a honeycomb: they are not shut by a bolt or fastened with a nail; rather, while one part of the mouth is closed, the other is open, revealing to hearers what suits the time.

For she does not, like a talkative woman, suddenly chatter whatever comes into her mouth. She regulates hidden things by the discerning silence of secrets, judging that certain matters should be held back more carefully under the covering of the tongue, and, when the time is at hand, entrusting them to the lips to be dripped forth. Perhaps for this reason she is said to have honey and milk under her tongue, in whose hidden chamber a twofold knowledge is contained: one that appears suited to little children and sucklings, the other fitting those more advanced and grown.

For little children must be nourished with milk, while those somewhat older are brought on to eat honey: the former confessing Christ truly born as man from the Virgin; the latter venerating the same one as God born from God before the ages. Milk, coming from flesh, may signify Christ’s humanity; honey, coming from flower or dew, his true divinity. The Virgin keeps knowledge of these beneath her tongue in secret and does not indiscriminately or immediately scatter it abroad in speech. [Col. 0392B]

Yet when Christ, God and man, first shows himself as man so that, through knowing what is visible, the heart of the knower may rise to what is invisible, what does it mean that he says not “milk and honey” but “honey and milk” are beneath the Virgin’s tongue, though she first teaches that he is man and afterward that he is God? There is no doubt that in Christ divinity comes first in dignity. Therefore he judges it fitting that, in speech also, his humanity should not proceed first; but if speech openly or mysteriously concerns both alike, that which excels in dignity should also be placed first in the order of speaking.

Or rather, wishing to show the Virgin’s twofold knowledge, which she had wished to keep concealed for a long time beneath her tongue, he significantly expresses in speech which of the two was not only worthier but also prior, making mystical mention of honey first and milk afterward. For the angel first announced to the Virgin that God was present with her; afterward, once he was present, he indicated that she would conceive a son. Thus, knowing him to be present, the Virgin might trust more firmly, and, having already received the greater gift, might not doubt the lesser.

“Hail,” says the angel, “full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke 1). And concerning the other he adds: “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” (ibid.). Through the angel the Lord teaches the Virgin that he is present; he pours in knowledge made sweeter than honey. Having first given the taste of this honeyed knowledge, he promises through the same messenger the conception, as it were, of milk. For she could not be adequately prepared to believe the conception unless she rejoiced to be more certainly instructed about the divine presence; unless she knew and felt that the Holy Spirit was coming upon her from above, by whose shadow whatever she is said to bear is made holy.

This knowledge of God’s presence and of the Son’s conception lay hidden for a long time beneath the tongue, within the Virgin’s own understanding. Yet virginal discernment does not entirely deprive us of this benefit: it does not suddenly make the stored-up spring manifest, but draws it out and channels it drop by drop. Such great discernment and discerning action clothe and commend her, if there are any able worthily to weigh her merits: [Col. 0393A] those who know beforehand how, among the obscure and negligent, she chooses not even to utter a word, but loves to pour out in drops, not with prodigal hands, for the diligent.

As is well known, our nakedness is covered with garments, and virginal nobility is distinguished by the glory of garments. Perhaps none pleases the Bridegroom except she who is clothed in fine linen and purple in such a manner that she not only fears no cold but also appears comely in her attire, being found adorned with double garments. Though in the present passage he has not described the quality of the garments or stated their number, he reserves this for the woman who, as was said elsewhere, is found by someone and whose price is far off, coming here from the furthest bounds.

That woman, indeed, may be said to be any soul who, solicitous for those belonging to her, is found so devoted to its work that, guarding against heat, cold, and sudden attack, it puts its hand to strong things and labours as though seated at a loom. Here, however, he considers not just any soul generally fearful of want, but a particular soul of special merit or excellence. Her garments do not cover shame or ward off cold, but her ornaments present her festively before the Bridegroom.

Because the oppressive blindness of the mind does not allow us to see how solemn and festive she appeared in the Bridegroom’s eyes, he has not here expressed to us the number or beauty of those garments. Yet, lest he say nothing at all, he turns to their fragrance. For in what the Virgin either inwardly knows of Christ or has now consented to drip forth, how industrious she has been, as a bee rejoicing in honey, and how intent, as a dripping honeycomb, upon the study of discerning moderation—all this fully pleases him alone, to whose eyes all is open. To us it comes like the fragrance of frankincense placed upon coals. [Col. 0393C]

For when virginal incense immerses itself in divine fire, it is in an ineffable manner wholly transformed into a saving exhaustion. Yet it is not consumed to destruction by the power of the stronger, but is delightfully taken up by reason of its love and beauty. We do not perceive how intensely it burns or how it pleases through this burning; we scarcely draw in even its faint fragrance as those standing far away. For when the incense is melted, its smoke rises toward the Bridegroom’s vastness, while its fragrance or report extends itself in breadth toward us.

Therefore the virtues by which the Virgin is nobly adorned, and through noble beauty presented to the divine gaze, are certain garments: not necessary for covering nakedness, but suited for displaying her beauty with greater confidence. She is presented and offered to the divine gaze like frankincense—not conspicuous in gold or clothing, but in conduct pleasing to God. Its welcome sweetness seems so to please the Lord that it touches us also by its fragrance, because he pities us in his goodwill.

For she does not love to wander abroad for anything else, but rather to be enclosed within these two things by the rampart of strength: namely, that she may present herself to her Bridegroom more fully commendable in beauty, and, dripping more delicately, may fill us with her fragrance. Therefore he adds: “A garden,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXV
A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain. [Col. 0394A] Because in the first garden the serpent overthrew the first woman, God, the Son of God, then planted another garden for himself when he filled the blessed Virgin, beyond the measure bestowed upon other women, with his grace: a garden rich not in many kinds of herbs, but in virtues. For in that garden woman’s simplicity was deceived; the man tasted what was forbidden; after the tasting, nakedness was discovered; death forestalled those who were to live forever because of their transgression; and the curse of mortality came upon both them and their descendants.

This garden, however, contains no shrubs, herbs, flowers, dense-leaved trees, perishable fruits, or scents; it possesses other things worthy to be compared with such things—or, more truly, to be set above all perishable things. For it has that which a sound and wise taste judges fruitful; that which smell judges, with right discernment, precious; that which inner sight, when its darkness is cleared away, finds gracious; that which, in wondrous abundance, wipes away every lack. [Col. 0394B] For the tree of life is planted in it with roots fixed fast; whoever eats from it—as experience has shown those who have done so—is not harmed by grievous death, but lives, by a happier decree, with that life which, once obtained, does not cease.

It also has marvellous frankincense, praiseworthy spice, and ointment, found not in Arabia but in the land denied to the dying. Whoever has inhaled its fragrance will know no serpent-like stenches, nor, when drowsiness prevails, will he feel sudden bites. It has, moreover, the pleasing flower of the rose, violet, or lily—or whatever flower is acknowledged to be more delightful to the eye. Whoever attends to it worthily and fixes upon it a penetrating gaze will pass beyond whatever sorrow the night mutters into joy—not transitory joy, but enduring joy. [Col. 0394C]

For in this garden the tree of life, the poured-out oil, and the beautiful flower is the Bridegroom of the Virgin himself, fairer in form than the children of men. With him present, neither shameful want nor impoverished ugliness besieges it; rather, in him “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2). For it is certain that God is in Christ, and Christ in the Virgin, not shadowily but truly; and for this very reason the garden is full of sufficient goods. He who planted it willed, by wise counsel, that it should be enclosed in such a way that whoever sees and envies it may grieve at being shut out.

And indeed, as it is by no means closed to the faithful and the friendly, [Col. 0394D] so, fortified with strength, it is shut against the enemy. It admits neither Jew nor Gentile nor anyone empty of faith; and whoever it judges worthy of hatred, it sends far away by a powerful repulse. Therefore, in it, unlike in the ancient garden, the serpent does not creep deceitfully; it does not poison its fruit, contaminate its fragrance, or pluck its little flowers. Perverse softness does not hunger there; hunger does not proceed to its effect; woman does not obey the serpent, nor man the woman.

Yet no weariness injures it as deserted or solitary; grief does not sting it, because its very maker walks joyfully within it. At his cheerful countenance things in the garden bear fruit; the forms of things flourish; the abundance of kinds smiles beneath the beauty of him who is fairer than men. For as he walks there, in whose countenance is beauty and upon whose lips grace has been poured out, the Virgin’s garden answers with joyful spirit and unconfounded face. [Col. 0395A] It pleases him as he walks, every ugliness having been so wholly excluded that within there remains nothing but beauty, surrounded by a strong defence.

But what is meant by this: that it was not enough to call the garden “enclosed” once to the Bridegroom, but that he repeats the very expression in the same words, unless it is because—as I recall having already said—the power of love has this excess: by repeated speech it expresses the greatness of a more welcome affection? Or perhaps he wished to call the garden enclosed twice in order to show that a twofold evil was excluded from that Virgin: both that a feeble spirit may not be attended by the softness of tender flesh, and that flesh may not stubbornly resist the stronger spirit.

For although in mind we serve, through grace, the law of God, yet through the law implanted in us we are in some degree enslaved by the flesh; and when, with the spirit awake, we seem watchful, we are found greatly imperfect because the flesh has been loosened in sleep. [Col. 0395B] Or this garden deserved to be called enclosed twice because the Virgin is found to embrace a twofold pursuit, yet in neither shows herself at all blameworthy, but with watchful mind defends herself against the attack of every enemy.

Thus, when necessity demanded it, she gave herself to practical work, yet did not, by giving her hands to it, detract from the spiritual life. Conversely, she fixed her spiritual eye upon contemplation in such a way that she did not shrink from active work—the work to which God, because of sin, assigned a curse as punishment. In the honeyed sweetness of contemplation she was raised out of herself; in milky affection she stooped down to gather in her neighbour. Fortified on both sides, or rather on every side, she gave no opening to any of the many assailants seeking entry. [Col. 0395C]

But because a garden needs watering lest it dry up, and rather needs suitable plantings to abound and grow luxuriant, this garden is said not so much to be watered by a fountain as, more expressly, to be called a fountain. A fountain, some assert, is named from pouring forth, because it seems to pour living water from hidden places and, bubbling with an unfailing vein, to live by an abundance not external but inward—not, like a pool, by torrents, nor, like a cistern, by rainwater (Prov. 5).

Accordingly, this Virgin ought quite fittingly to be called a fountain: her understanding does not dry up, nor is her perception parched by dry heat; instead, by the grace of an inner gift she is taught and enriched ineffably, and with a marvellous constancy beyond expression is made glad. [Col. 0395D] Yet she long conceals, as though beneath a seal, the mystery revealed to her; she does not disclose her living abundance to those less able to contain it. She keeps enclosed within knowledge, as though in a sealed fountain, the manner of her fruitfulness, the form of her marriage, and the excellence of her celibacy.

For he who bestowed upon her such knowledge and such singular inward awareness did not leave her like a vessel without a lid, but sealed her, lest unworthy hearers, hearing but not understanding, be disturbed into scandal and hasten to stones rather than reverence the mystery. Therefore the author of the gift himself closes with a bar the virgin’s bridal chamber, the inner rooms of her secrets, the fountain of leaping water, and her wondrous knowledge of divine things; with David’s key he seals them for himself, and does not unseal them for the darkened blasphemer who lacks the due worthiness.

The popular crowd stands outside; the undiscerning mob makes a clamour. [Col. 0396A] The seal not having been opened, it does not grasp so secret a fountain. The ingenuity of philosophers and the rulers of the world remain hungry; barking, they do not understand, and in their importunity they achieve nothing. There is indeed great abundance and great subtlety in the fountain; the water leaps, and the spring’s leap is perpetuated by the vein flowing forth from within. But the key placed upon it appears so to conceal it from all outsiders that it deigns to open nothing at all to unbelievers, but only a little to believers.

Yet that little, in relation to the abundance which remains, so overflows for us and so exceeds our smallness that only a gathered mind and an undivided love can receive it, because this kind of paradise admits no envious serpent. Hence follows: “Your shoots,” and so forth.

## Chapter XXVI

[Col. 0396B] Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruits of orchard-trees. What this enclosed garden, or fountain fortified with a seal, sends forth—though it admits none, or very few, into the secrets of its fullness—is like a paradise, or delight, of pomegranates, white within and red without. For if a garden has been planted by prudent hand or counsel and, at fitting times, moistened with the irrigation of living water, what more fittingly can be said to issue from it than that which hunger seeks for eating or sickness judges wholesome and effective for healing?

Thus the Virgin’s shoots—she who is figured under the name of garden or fountain—are attested by him who praises her to resemble paradise. Indeed, speaking more expressly, he says that they are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of orchard-trees, [Col. 0396C] and the other things which follow, which are known to be medicinal.

Long ago there was a paradise of the serpent’s persuasive wickedness, the birthplace of a new deceit and the destroyer of holiness. In it the strong man yielded to the woman’s soft counsel, and the tasting of the forbidden fruit brought to those who experienced it the fruit of death. But this paradise, which issues from the Virgin’s garden or fountain, restores more powerfully what was more inquisitively lost in that one. It consists of pomegranates, white within and red without, and of other fruits whose taste is most healthful to those who eat them.

The red colour displayed outwardly by pomegranates represents the love and endurance of suffering, which one may behold in the Virgin’s life and conduct if one wishes to be taught by her example to suffer likewise. [Col. 0396D] The whiteness within is the flower of conscience: a secure mind which, while the world rages outside or impending suffering threatens, embraces purity and does not abandon virginal cleanness; it is not disturbed by injuries and, when assailed by troubles, does not sin.

The fruit of the other orchard-trees sent forth with the pomegranates consists in her good works. These are not only pleasing to the sight when first displayed, but also richly fruitful to those who taste them—that is, imitate them—and precious not because of a deceptive colour but because of a most useful flavour. But since one or two kinds of things do not sufficiently please an eye that looks more inquisitively, he adds many varieties to augment her praises, so that her manifold shoots may cause us greatly to admire and, in fitting ways and with many praises, reverence her as worthy.

## Chapter XXVII

[Col. 0397A]

Cyprus with nard; nard and crocus; cassia and cinnamon, with every tree of Lebanon; myrrh and aloe, with all the finest ointments.

The cyprus plants are slender shrubs that rise to great height. Their grains are boiled in oil through the skilful care of physicians; such a preparation makes a praiseworthy ointment, by which those who are anointed find desirable relief from pain. So also the Virgin’s virtues, exceedingly refined and upright, have been raised to the height of dignity, not by branches but by merits. Their fruitful acts are cooked in spiritual oil when, in holy love, they are stripped of harmful or carnal moisture.

Nard, a small tree, is joined to these cyprus plants when the excellence of virtues is lowered by regard for humility. The more the Virgin is raised among women by singular titles, [Col. 0397B] the more humble and lowly she appears in her own eyes. Cyprus with nard, therefore, are fittingly placed first in this catalogue of medicines—these things which, like paradise, issue from the Virgin’s garden—because humility joined to excellence of virtue so commends it that this great preparation may safely extend to our knowledge.

Again: nard and crocus. From nard alone, it is said, without another species or mixture, comes a praiseworthy ointment and beneficial preparation. Mary Magdalene wished to anoint the Lord’s feet with this ointment, as the testimony of the Gospel reading has made sufficiently known: “She took,” it says, “a pound of costly pure nard ointment and anointed the feet of Jesus” (John 12).

Nard is contrition of heart, offered by the humble and devout. By a contrite spirit they are raised to such grace that they anoint the feet of Jesus, advance further even to his head, and fill the nostrils of those around them—or rather the whole house—with fragrance. [Col. 0397C] “The house,” it says, “was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (ibid.). And earlier in this bridal song: “My nard,” it says, “gave forth its fragrance” (Song 1).

Crocus sits and stands beside this nard, both as tree and ointment. It drives away fevers already present, meets and resists those that approach; on its surface it bears a golden beauty or colour, signifying charity, and it occupies a loftier throne. This charity delights to stand ready beside devout humility and to remain the inseparable companion of a contrite spirit, so that whomever it knows to be pierced and anointed with more devout affection, it makes love more deeply and does not permit separation from the one loved.

For if some feverish bitterness of sadness or sloth intervenes, threatening harm, charity immediately comes near. Weakening the harmful force, it urges the devout spirit to stand firm in what it has begun, lest the malevolent enemy win a triumph from the deceived. [Col. 0397D]

“Cassia,” he says, “and cinnamon.” Cassia, reddish in colour and possessing a hard bark, signifies the strength of constancy which does not yield to encroaching troubles. It loves to provide such unceasing companionship to the virtues already named that for their sake it refuses neither the loss of blood nor the torment of martyrdom. This constancy rightly seems necessarily associated with the preceding species, lest fatigue prevent devotion from bringing to completion what it loves, and lest a good resolve, if sudden violence does not break it, be gradually weakened by a hand prolonged and stretched out over time.

And because, according to the command, a wise person is always mindful of his last things (Eccles. 7), cinnamon is immediately present, resembling ash in colour. It warns that in all things toward which the wise person deserves to advance by suitable progress, he should never cease to remember who he is, whence he comes, and where he is going. “You are earth,” it says, “and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). And Job says: “I repent in ashes and dust” (Job 42). [Col. 0398A]

Finally, when Abraham raised himself to speak to God with prosperous affection and effect, even at that lofty summit he regarded himself as ashes. He showed that he so rejoiced in the benefit bestowed that, remembering himself worthily, he seemed to venture nothing as from his own resources. “I will speak,” he says, “to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18).

These are aromatic shrubs, effective for healthful medicine, especially suited to the cultivation of character and fitting for true instruction, along with very many others, diverse in appearance and effect, which Lebanon together brings forth for healing. For Christ, whom many say is figured by the name Lebanon, wills the series of his virtues to be conveyed to us through the Virgin; and what prophetic promise proclaimed many ages before, the Virgin’s outpouring has brought into effect in our hands.

“Myrrh,” he says, “and aloe, with all the finest ointments.” Having described above, under enigma or figure, those virtues by which the love of the inward mind is spiritually instructed for what lies ahead, [Col. 0398B] he seems to pass to kinds of other gifts which are known, through a medicinal mystery, to suit bodies.

For flesh, to which from conception a natural law has been imposed—that, whether it lives more or less fully, it must necessarily be mortal—may have its morning flower struck down by evening decline, yet not dissolve into corruption or serpent-like worms. Mighty myrrh commands this and seems to prevail by its command; in its presence flesh does not fear to undergo what is natural. For myrrh is an ointment with which dead flesh rejoices to be anointed. When it has been anointed, its integrity is marvelled at for not being dissolved under its innate law; although deprived of living strength and knowing itself now feeble and defenceless, nevertheless, by the wondrous protection of myrrh, it does not know the worm of long-established corruption.

Aloe accomplishes this same thing by the power of its strength, and therefore it is fittingly joined to myrrh in this bridal song, so that a certain shared friendship or affinity may be recognized between things whose operation or result is one though they are different. [Col. 0398C] Yet aloe possesses, by a special right and privilege, something which myrrh could not attain through their common partnership: besides preserving the anointing of dead bodies, it also becomes a draught that purges the entrails of the living.

Myrrh, therefore, is persistence in fasting, the harshness of abstinence, restraint in continence, the exercise of labour, frequency in meditation, and zeal in learning. At the first taste these produce extraordinary bitterness, but through a more vigorous operation of practice they expel carnal corruption. Yet because this effect is fully powerful only in dead flesh, the sweetness and affection of living must be removed; and in order that the affliction sought outwardly may benefit us more sufficiently, this present life must be taken away from us who are flesh.

For though we are sometimes afflicted outwardly by some grievous activity, we nevertheless live badly while the virulent root, the living passion, remains. It is expedient that the prudent physician, having touched the vein of our inward motions and obtained knowledge of them, should make the wrongly living humours depart by a purgative draught. [Col. 0398D] This draught is aloe—or rather, it is an inward love of virtue, which produces a wholesome hatred of fault and destructive slavery. Casting out from the depths of the heart the shameful dregs of Pharaoh, it makes that portico of Solomon thoroughly cleansed for Christ.

A certain pagan, neither inexperienced in nor ignorant of a similar medicine, aptly set forth such oppressively clinging dregs and filth, and the draught of love and efficacy of virtue that expels them—not to wandering and negligent people, but to those seated in the school of discipline.

[Note: Col. 0399D. Horace, Book of Epistles.]

“The good hate to sin,” he says, “through love of virtue.”

Good love is likewise a good virtue of love: it condemns with perfect hatred the sewer of baser impurity; with the strict broom of judgment it sweeps away whatever it finds filthy, and spreads a pleasing marble pavement for the coming Bridegroom. After the inward parts have been cleansed by love of virtue, as by the efficacy of a draught, from then on myrrh and aloe work together: will and action become for us an ointment that provides fleshly beings, not through vice but through nature, a sufficient defence against everlasting corruption (Rom. 8; Eph. 2). [Col. 0399A]

For will without action, languishing in idleness, would not attain merit; nor would action without will find glory before God. Rather, affection rejoices to shine outwardly through action in a praiseworthy way, and action bears evident testimony to affection. Since, then, will—or love of virtue—seems to hold the first place, and no one doubts that action follows a preceding will, what does it mean that in this bridal song the speaker does not first name aloe, which, though not as an ointment, precedes as a draught?

For he does not say “aloe and myrrh,” but “myrrh and aloe with all the finest ointments,” because the labour of action, figured by myrrh, as we have said, leads out and presents publicly the love of virtue—which was said to act in place of a draught. For labour does not show itself through love, but love shows itself through labour, as though visibly; therefore myrrh is named first, since it wishes first to appear as guide and forerunner, through whose office love deserves to be made known. “By their fruits,” he says, “you will know them” (Matt. 7). [Col. 0399D]

Nicodemus rightly, in the Gospel, brought a mixture of myrrh and aloe weighing one hundred pounds, preparing this ointment in precisely that order. He wished to anoint Christ’s dead flesh with this mixture, showing that it would not pass, under the law of mortals, into corruption. Here likewise myrrh is named first and aloe afterward, namely because the will is now demonstrated in visible action; and they came together into one mixture before the eyes of right believers, and by that union prepared an ointment beneficial for our pains. “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53); and “Christ,” it says, “died for us” (Rom. 5).

That Nicodemus is recorded to have brought one hundred pounds of this mixture indicates that Christ bestowed his benefit upon us in weight and number; and that what had formerly been prophesied in passing words and signs was at last brought to fulfillment in certain weight and perfect number. “It is finished,” he says (John 19). [Col. 0400A]

I would be mistaken if the Virgin did not prepare such a mixture, if by this preparation she did not keep worms and corruption far away, if in making it she neglected either weight, number, or the very order, rather than sending forth here a paradise of fragrant fullness. And lest this one thing perhaps appear insufficient to anyone, since manifold need is often not supplied by one benefit, he adds, “with all the finest ointments,” to indicate the Virgin’s abundant outpouring, which with myrrh and aloe gives us ointments of her other gifts.

The first and chief ointments are those of twofold charity, which this enclosed garden brings forth from the storehouse of holiness. The Virgin distils them upon worthy hearers through saving admonitions and teaching, strengthening teaching by example, conduct, and discipline. Since she deserved above to be called not only an enclosed garden but also a sealed fountain, the Bridegroom, having now explained what may be more particularly assigned to the garden, does not delay to pass in his speech to those things which seem more fittingly to belong to the sealed fountain as well. [Col. 0400B]

## Chapter XXVIII

A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters flowing with force from Lebanon. As your shoots are pomegranates and the other things which follow, suitably produced from the garden of delight for food or healing, so your outpouring is not the fountain of one garden, but rather a fountain of gardens, by which the fruit-bearing hearts of many desire to be watered.

For whoever wishes to become a garden and to excel a barren field, whoever wishes to bring forth blooming beauty and useful fruit, ought zealously to resort to this clear and unmuddied fountain, and perhaps not to take as an insult the rebuff of freely offered refusal. For the Virgin’s goodwill—which much wisdom is known to direct—wished to offer herself to us weaker people as a fountain, lest the difficulty of drawing should inflict a harsher rebuff upon those whom eagerness seems to urge toward the hope of drinking. [Col. 0400C]

We take pleasure in sweetness when discovered by perception, but excessive labour in searching seems to close the entrance. Her fountain-like fullness does not exasperate us, but rather moderates itself; and it receives in its spaciousness those already eager but not yet strong. But because to greater persons, burning more fully to be heard, the shallow plainness of a fountain seems too quickly exhausted, the Virgin’s wisdom withdraws itself into the deep of mystery and admits them to its fullness through labour.

The more they consider that what they desire is removed from them and hope that the well contains a more abundant supply of water, the more, inflamed by desire, they gird themselves for strenuous effort, knowing that depths are not reached without a drawing-vessel. Therefore, not content with what appears open and common to many, they lower a vessel into the depth of the well on a long rope. They persist in uninterrupted work until they draw back the full vessel on an unbroken rope. [Col. 0400D]

When they taste its draught, they are astonished at such sweetness and are not strong enough by their own powers to contain it. Filled with its abundance, they finally do not wipe away their dry thirst, but, in hydropic manner—or by hydropic love—immerse themselves in the well itself.

But since, according to a certain pagan:

[Note: Col. 0401D. Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*.]

“They acquire a defect if the waters are not stirred,”

they find at the bottom of the well waters that are not stagnant, not degenerated by foul standing, and not corrupted by the defect of remaining still. Having found them, they draw living waters, displaying both great fullness and marvellous sweetness. Nothing dead or harmful approaches these waters; no serpent hisses, nor injures with poisonous breath; no branch fallen from above disturbs them; no flowing mud enters them. Their guardian, the Bridegroom, allows nothing turbid to be present. [Col. 0401A]

He himself is Lebanon, ever white with unmelted snows—or rather the brightness of supreme light and the mirror of divine virtue. From himself he pours out waters and fills, through a hidden channel, the virginal fountain or well with a spiritual abundance of waters. Although we do not draw from its deep pools in fuller supply, for we come with a narrow vessel and an inadequate desire, whoever can weigh the abundance with which Lebanon pours out waters knows with what force their plenty flows into this well.

Come, you who are far away, to this fountain of living waters; and you whom worldly wisdom holds, free yourselves from its shackles. Vomit out philosophical swelling in repeated vomitings; drunk on the wine of dragons, repair the ruin of your study by drinking living water. A good garden is this, which has received the name of fountain or well: distinguished by many kinds of fruits and medicinal species; rich in irrigating water, not stagnant and putrid, breeding worms, but flowing with force from Lebanon and springing, in living vigour, into life. [Col. 0401B] Its Bridegroom tends it with such solicitude and care, increasing its growth and so perfectly removing harmful things, that he has not only sealed it as enclosed, lest it lie open to a violent thief or plunderer, but protected it from above as well, lest even a wicked wind touch it in the slightest degree.

## Chapter XXIX

Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; breathe through my garden, and its spices will flow. A beautiful order. He first addresses and sends far away the north wind, lest it rush in before the other and occupy the region, spread freely across the plains of the wide air, and pour down grievous blasts or hail upon the garden rich in fruits.

“You,” he says, “who have established for yourself a throne as though royal at Arcturus, intending to rule and bring the world under your servitude: rise. Let this presumption no longer keep you secure; I want you to depart far away and not rage over the garden’s beauty. You thought that you would be like the Most High—you who were once called Lucifer—although he who alone is, is not made so by another light; and the very name you put forward is known to contradict your wickedness. For when there is one like him, he can no longer be called Most High. [Col. 0401C]

Rise, therefore, and now restrain the swelling bellows of this seat. Driven from your puffed-up throne, vanish into thin air; scatter yourself among those like you, as finer dust, or immerse yourself, as emptier smoke, in the eyes of the proud. Among our serious concerns neither your mockeries nor the sport of mockers is welcome. In the garden of holiness, lost to you because you corrupted Eve in paradise, laughing and prevailing over her, the Virgin—or the Virgin’s garden—shuts its door against you, now scorned.

Rise, therefore, you whom self-estimation harms and swelling pride empties further; since, according to your false hope, you do not rage within the bounds of this garden. Do not vainly trouble yourself any longer to circle the strongly enclosed garden. Make room for the more powerful one, whom it is fitting should enter as he comes.” [Col. 0401D]

“And come,” he says, “south wind.” Once he has been removed far away, whose presence and neighbourhood are rightly grievous, come, south wind—most wholesome and sweet for the garden—sent here by the southern pole and gentler sun, whose arrival does not admit the cold north wind. You, therefore, who do not delight in his harmful companionship and do not allow him to enjoy dominion in the garden of holiness: because, once he is sent far away, the Virgin is not yet content with such a benefit, present yourself to her with gracious countenance, to supply what she needs.

Come, south wind, breathing more sweetly from that hidden abode in which there is no darkness or impurity, rich in pure light. Breathe and blow—or rather, blow through: that is, act by a gentle breath, so that this garden may be adorned and rejoice in its enduring adornment. [Col. 0402A]

The south wind seems to me to bear the figure of the Holy Spirit, whose sweet breath the north wind cannot endure. When the latter detects him coming, even by a faint scent, he shudders and hastens to abandon the primacy he had presumed to claim. For the powerful kindness of the one so opposes the malice of the other that by its presence it destroys whatever the other wickedly does. Those whom the north wind holds pressed down by frost, fixed in hard error, the south wind loosens; and, once loosened, it makes them run like torrents into love.

This south wind visits the enclosed garden with a fuller coming, cherishing and advancing its diverse fruits with gentler air, so that spices may be produced from them, suited to medicinal disciplines, and may flow—indeed, flow into—not the bodies but the inward loves of those needing healing. And rightly the Bridegroom either commands or urges the south wind to come, because, as the Father sends the Spirit, so the Son testifies that he sends him: though the Spirit is believed to be present and beneficial wherever and whenever he wills, nevertheless he is sent by him with whom he has one being by nature. [Col. 0402B] “When the Paraclete comes,” he says, “whom I shall send to you” (John 15).

Therefore the Son sends the Spirit to the virginal garden or bridal chamber, so that, coming, he may breathe upon it, soothe it with spiritual breath, and, having infused into it through sweet breathing a marvellous urging toward virtues, cause the garden, fragrant with spices, to flow out and overflow for our healing.

## Chapter XXX

Rise, north wind, and come, south wind. Or, if it seems preferable to someone, by the words just mentioned the Bridegroom does not wholly remove the north wind, but allows it the free choice to rise if it wishes. For although it is full of malice, it cannot come against us unless sent, nor rise to evil action unless permission is granted it.

Seeing, therefore, that the garden is sufficiently strong through incomparable enclosure; that it does not fear horrible threats, the brandished sword, or cruel death; that it cannot fail under the troubles of assaults or attacks, but can be proved and, by the merit of its testing, be crowned more worthily and gloriously: he turns to the one who always delights to become a persecutor and, ignorant of the outcome, dares to lay hands upon any righteous persons. [Col. 0402C]

“Rise,” he says, “north wind; break out from the hiding-place of wickedness, display all your strength and the malice of your perverse will. Thunder, flash lightning, make a tumult, bring in whirlwinds, heap up whatever hailstorms and tempests you can; add new ones to the old. But do not suppose that unrestrained malice can prevail against the Virgin: the south wind comes, giving the Virgin strength to endure with equanimity whatever you bring. It blows through the garden within and intoxicates it with marvellous sweetness, so that it either feels nothing at all or at least does not fail under torture.

“You, north wind, rise and attack, and rage violently outside. You, south wind, breathe within and grant that what the other thunders may be patiently borne. You, malicious one, exasperate the house so that the neighbouring wall seems to burn; you, benevolent one, strengthen the bridal chamber so that, being well protected, it need not fear even fire.” [Col. 0402D]

Did not the north wind seem to rage more harshly when it drove the Jews, Mary’s kinsmen by race, into madness against her, so that they denied the Virgin’s integrity on account of her childbirth and maintained, by the law common to us all, that he—her son and the begotten Son of God—had been begotten? Does it not thunder harshly when the Jews persecute that same Son, when human beings of another nation are joined as companions in their wickedness, when the persistent fury and discordant cry of his kinsmen urge on outsiders, and when both crucify him who deserved it not—the former with their voices, the latter with nails?

It is not easy to say what a blow to the mother—indeed, what a heavy hammer—so great a force of persecutors struck. Yet it did not strike the beauty of her faith and patience from her garden, because the south wind reigning within enclosed it with a rampart of strength and excluded every oppressive force from faith and patience. [Col. 0403A]

Thus south wind and north wind are engaged with varying inclination and contrary effect; thus they clash with different and hostile face like combatants; thus the heavy assaults of a river strike against a strong foundation, and are rebuffed by victorious constancy and an unharmed building. Through this conflict and pressure the Virgin does not dry up like cremium [uncertain word], but, like a fruitful olive, is medicinally enriched. From her flows an oil more precious than every ointment; worthy spices flow forth, comparable neither to gold nor to silver.

The contention of the north and south winds, whose purposes remain so different, therefore benefits not them alone; the resulting usefulness reaches even to us, an outstretched hand rejoicing to give, not to close everything in silence. But because, after recounting so many praises of the Virgin, the Bridegroom has now wished to be silent at this point, I have judged it fitting that our pen too should for a little while lay a finger upon its mouth, and that the fourth book of this work should now set upon itself an appropriate end.

# Book V

[Col. 0403]

233 **Chapter I**

[Col. 0403D]

[CAP. V.] Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his apple-trees.

The Virgin, seeing and approving that the likeness of a garden belongs to her—planted with virtues, flourishing with corresponding merits, and, by a marvellous advance, burning for nothing but the Bridegroom’s face—can no longer keep her desire under silence. For the more diligently he fortifies her in order to defend her, and the more carefully he raises, commends, and protects her when fortified and defended, the more she loves, the more she desires to see the face of her beloved, judging what she possesses to be little while grieving that she does not yet possess what remains.

“Let him come,” she says, “who, mighty in hand and not weak in word, planted his garden by rooting it, and, when it was rooted, willed to water it with living waters; who willed to enclose it and shut it against every harmful thing, so that these might not prevail against it—indeed, might have no claim whatsoever upon it. Let him, I say, come and deign to look more closely upon what is his, and by his kindly gaze increase and guard its grace. For whether the north wind is commanded to rise or permitted to rage fiercely, and whether the south wind is, on the contrary, commanded to come gently: it will take place, and the garden will feel the effect; and it will be beneficial to it that feels it, if the beloved comes to grant his presence to the one who loves him. With him present, the malevolent north wind will gnash, yet, though harmful, will not harm; the south wind will appear sweeter and more effectual. The former, by afflicting, will work patience; patience, testing; testing, hope that does not put to shame. The latter will work love, which is poured out in our hearts.

“And who would deny his presence or coming for long to the garden which he planted, watered, and even gave increase; from whose enclosure the judicial broom cast far away everything harmful, and which, enclosed by a strong defence, he made especially his own? Who, moreover, would not be moved because he is beloved—the one whom the loving woman begs to come—and because that to which he is invited as Lord is none other than his own? For it befits an owner to come to his possessions even uninvited; and love itself is a cry, so that one so loved cannot fail to be called.

“Therefore let the beloved come into the garden—not another’s, not into another’s right, but into his own—and there show himself loving and serene. And, finding pleasing what he sees there to be useful and honourable, let him pluck it by hand—indeed, let him eat it—unless perhaps he finds it unseasonable. My fruits, I think, show themselves fit to be gathered; indeed, they are his fruits, for they do not claim ripeness except by his gift. They are not like the fruits of certain persons, which please when seen but vanish immediately when touched; rather, they ripen with savoury fragrance and substantial taste. Let him come and eat not merely the outward surface of these fruits, beautiful to the eyes, but rather their ripeness, fruitful to eager taste; that is, let him delight to take them to himself, remove them from the midst, and rejoice to lay them up in his own treasury. For although it is necessary to remain here in order to gain merit, I judge it far better there to rejoice in the reward. Therefore I would rather be in the storehouse of rest than in the field of labour, and have my cultivator feed and refresh himself upon his own harvest.”

The Bridegroom hears the words—or rather, the desire—of the bride, and answers. He does not promise that he will come, or even eat, according to the Virgin’s prayers; rather, what is far more, he shows that he has come sooner than she spoke, and that he did not, with deaf ear, delay even briefly the coming she requested.

## CHAPTER II

“I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.”

Just as the Lord was said above to have sent an angel beforehand to the Virgin, and the Virgin was said before him to have found grace, so here, when asked to come, he does not promise his coming to her who asks; he declares that he has already come and done what seemed fitting to him.

“You anxiously ask that I come,” he says, “but I have already come. I have anticipated the time you seemed to appoint and the hope of the gift requested. More willingly than you could ask or seek, I hastened to come; and I visited my garden not by a forerunner, but by my own presence. For it would not be fitting that I should leave bare in the hands of deceivers that which I planted with my own hand, and which, when planted and watered, I urged toward suitable growth; or that I should weaken the earlier gifts of its progress by later and worse things. Therefore, the garden which I made by grafting into it varied virtues, I made my own by granting it profitable protection. What I enclosed and sealed, excluding all things harmful, I cherished and advanced by giving it my continual presence.

“For how could I deprive of my care and presence a sister whom my only Father gave me to love with kindred affection? How could I deprive a bride, whom mystical unity has taught me to embrace in a severe and sincere union? How, I say, could I fail rather to commend good beginnings with a better ending?”

Since the meaning of the titles “Sister” and “Bride” has in some measure been explained above, I refrain from repeating it, lest what is so often repeated produce weariness. The prudent reader will surely not cling only to what is present, but will more carefully turn mind and eye to what precedes.

But he shows what he has accomplished in the garden by his gracious condescension—he whose coming was sought with such desire—lest one suppose that he did nothing there through sluggishness and negligence, although he had not yet done everything according to the Virgin’s wish.

“I have gathered my myrrh with my spices,” he says. Strict discipline, the stern austerity of abstinence, virgin continence, integrity both of body and mind—by a marvellous unction these preserve virgin flesh from eternal corruption, and, above the law of nature, above the nature of wrath, heap up a store of merits. The Bridegroom, coming into his garden, has now gathered such myrrh, because the Mother’s continence so perfectly pleased the Son that, when he was incarnate and nature marvelled at the inexpressible birth, the novelty of the event introduced neither the decay of pride, nor worm, nor injury.

For the Bridegroom carried off fertile integrity, granted to no virgin before or after, as though harvested from the threshing-floor into the granary. By his good pleasure and protection he willed to fortify it so that no beast of the field and no lofty-wise bird could enter it. Carnal pleasure, which is accustomed brutishly to anticipate fertility, marvels to find nothing belonging to itself in the Virgin’s conception; it marvels that in an earthly field a harvest grows so ripe and is carried away as if by stealth, to suffer no ravaging.

The birds of heaven, which sow nothing honourable or useful for salvation but often greedily destroy the crops of others—indiscriminate presumption and empty self-exaltation, which are accustomed to arise from good achievements and, by innate perversity, delight to feed upon their defects—grieve that the aforesaid harvest of myrrh has been removed from their midst in such a way that neither violence nor fraud can gain even the slightest access to it. The little birds complain that they slept longer than they should, and that the love and watchful diligence of the reaper forestalled them. Now they have hands awake and outstretched for plunder, but are held back by the enclosure of the granary and its unopenable bar.

The Bridegroom likewise shuts his spices in such a granary; and, sealing them with the Davidic key, he does not heed the barking voices of slanderers. He gathers, as it were, the Virgin’s modesty in a harvest, lest, exposed in the field to beasts, it be injured by an envious whisperer. The hostile man who commonly sows tares among wheat, and who, unable to injure a life, at least stains the reputation of the good, he drives out from contact with the Virgin by his opposing hand; he banishes far from modesty’s enclosure the enemy of chastity. For he does not wish that her reputation, more fragrant than spices or ointments, should be disfigured by the powerful arguments of any sophist; rather, firm faith maintains and truthfully proclaims that she is both Virgin and fruitful, although this is unknown in the experience of others. Thus he removes myrrh and spices from the hostile reaper’s plucking sickle, gathers them, and entrusts them to a granary that preserves them more faithfully, while by the strong protection of truth he accumulates and preserves her chaste purpose and the most sweet fragrance of chastity.

## CHAPTER III

“I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.”

Rich in the year’s yield of myrrh and spices, he does not say, following the literal sequence, that he has anointed himself; rather, he says that he has eaten, although myrrh does not appear suitable for food, and drunk, although no one says that spices are thirsted for. But because the Virgin’s manner of life is exposed to pressures and cuttings, because perfection of merits is acquired not through soft sleep but through wakeful endeavours, and because whatever the Virgin gathers for herself in the present through labour gives the Bridegroom who gives and loves not bitterness but sweetness, he therefore declares that, the harvest now complete, he has eaten: thus showing that he has hungered for the Virgin’s progress.

Finally, in the Gospel, the rich man says: “Soul, you have many good things laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, make merry” (Luke 12). This rich man, then, is not one whose soul is demanded on account of its misdeeds during the night; rather, with his granary shut and harvests brought in, he is rich. He does not extend a false hope toward many days or years; nor does he apply threshing or winnowing to these same harvests. For by a marvellous manner of speech, what he called myrrh or spices while harvesting he now finds to be honeycomb, now declares to be honey when eating, because the eater’s taste experiences nothing sweeter than honey, and no integrity is found more pleasing to Christ than his Mother’s.

You know that a honeycomb is called a kind of storehouse, which the skilful bee is found to make, divided into waxen cells. Ingenious in its work, it hides itself under a sort of covering, within which it carefully stores the comb and, in the comb, honey. This honeycomb—the one whose protection delights to cover it and whose sleepless care protects it all around—he, I say, does not allow to be injured or to dry up; but, with the honey implanted in it, brings it to his own table, according to his good pleasure.

A tender honeycomb is severely injured and dries out; deprived of its honey, it is ruined by dryness and becomes empty. So too, when bodily integrity is not sweetened by the savoury love of Christ, and virtue does not shine by its own worth through hatred of sin. For fragile flesh is rightly called wax; a more zealous and austere way of life turns it into a honeycomb. Honey is placed within it and incomparable sweetness lies concealed when the love of Christ is the sweeter motive for embraced chastity. Therefore Christ does not take as his food, nor the Bridegroom as his favour, the honeycomb which inward emptiness dries and consumes. The chastening or integrity of a girl's flesh is rightly rejected when it presumes to be presented and offered dry, without honey. But that integrity confidently presents itself to his sight and as his food which is richly fattened with abundant honey and gracious love. The eater rejoices in its rich sweetness—or sweet richness; and the more he feasts, the richer the food grows.

Because drinking appropriately accompanies eating, the Bridegroom indicates next not only that he drank but what he drank, in order to show both the Virgin’s learning and richness as hostess, and the commendable drink which refreshes and nourishes its drinker.

“I have drunk my wine with my milk,” he says. The prudent Virgin, diligently intent on pleasing by her ministry, mingled wine in the mixing-bowl for her beloved when he had fittingly eaten, so that, refreshed by food and cheered also by wine, he might be more generous in granting whatever was asked of him. Rightly, therefore, being devoted to an incorruptible, divine service, she gives the Bridegroom not turbid water but wine, more fittingly and wisely; showing that in her nuptial embrace and service she is not cold through want, but burns with spiritual affection.

This is not the incurable wine, comparable to the poison of asps and dragons (Deut. 32), through which the destructive error of the nations rages and wanders astray. Wine, I say, signifies a love denied to rustic and ragged poor people, by which the rich in grace and noble in mind are carried into ecstasy. Thus Wisdom, inviting us to divine love, does not mix tasteless waters but wine with prudent mystery, so that our childish or infantile manner of life may grow young and, having drunk wine, may mature in worthy advances. “Drink the wine which I have mixed for you; leave infancy and live” (Prov. 9).

“You,” she says, “whom not infancy of years but weakness of character holds captive; not age, but who suffer not through lack of strength but through languid attachment after the manner of carnal people: drink the wine I have mixed for you—not Falernian wine, but spiritual love, by which those made drunk deserve to live eternally. Leave infancy, which cannot aspire to greater things, which does not love—or rather, knows how to love only carnally—which hinders and darkens those who love with unconsidered love, and makes the darkened resemble it in its harmful dullness.”

Such lovers their love does not advance toward light but removes from light; their pleasure does not make them serene, but harsh clamour alienates them further from sweet rest. The deceptive appearance of love shakes their hearts and inflicts blindness; by most evil progress, at last and in its final stage, it brings oppressive death. Of such people a certain pagan says:

> “I will tell you what has destroyed you: you do not know how to love.”

These are not perhaps drunk with wine, or with the wine of dragons and asps, but are far removed from the saving cup of Wisdom. She offers it to her hearers with an ungrudging hand; having given them drink, she refreshes them, and, having refreshed them, makes them wonderfully drunk with sweetness. This wine of Wisdom, the cup of grace and virtue, by drinking which one receives the power of life and salvation, the Virgin who bears God drank more fully; drinking, she rejoices more sweetly, she who in an inestimable manner remains Virgin while becoming fruitful.

The Son born from God and from herself—the one whom she conceived in her virginal womb, of whom she is sponsus and sponsa [bridegroom and bride]—she holds in her chaste bosom by high counsel and nuptial mystery, gathers to herself in spiritual affection, and loves with filial love: as Son in the bridal relation, so also Bridegroom. In such nuptials the water-jar is not exhausted; the royal cup knows no water; no ruler, ignorant of the mystery, is astonished at the banquet. No one complains through fear or the presence of poverty; the Bridegroom is not accused of ignorant or ill-ordered generosity.

For he who comes forth from the highest heaven, from the secret bosom of the Father, enters the bridal chamber whose seal of inviolate firmness remains intact; and from it he comes forth as Bridegroom in the celebrated mystery of the nuptials. He brought with him, and willed to be present at the nuptials, such fullness that it is certain that nothing honourable or necessary is lacking to them.

Since nuptials ought not to be celebrated without wine—especially those held not for the sake of flesh alone but for God—in these nuptials wine does not fail but abounds; it both refreshes and makes fruitful the very celebrants of the marriage. Spiritual love, known to glow more strongly than wine, is found to intoxicate the Virgin with such fervour of spirit that, forgetting waters, by whose flood the purity of chastity is in danger of being crushed, she passes wholly, with unwearied desire, into the love of truth. Truth, moreover, is Christ; and Christ is God and man.

Therefore the Virgin loves Christ God with a love undoubtedly not carnal but spiritual, because God is Spirit. She loves God, who is Spirit, with vehement spirit, powerfully and effectively crushing everything that tastes wrongly to the flesh. For God, who is Spirit and does not will to be seen visibly, delights to be held by likeness and an invisible bond; and he especially takes pleasure, as in ancestral wine, in that love by which a lover embraces him spiritually.

He bestowed such love upon angelic spirits from the beginning. Had the one who chose to become an enemy from a friend remained in it, man would not have been deceived, nor would he have grieved at having incurred the due of death, which through that one’s envy is read to have entered the world (Rom. 5). But because this love was found to have diminished among the angels, God wills that it be restored not in them but in human beings. Before the Law and under the Law he asks patriarchs and prophets to love him spiritually; when the days of grace dawn, he recognizes this love more expressly in the Virgin Mother.

Feeling it to abound more fully in her by the grace he himself gives, he willed to receive it as wine, all the more joyfully because more sweetly; and with eager taste he drank the draught offered by the Virgin, enclosing it in the hidden place of his good pleasure as firmly as irrevocably. Rightly, therefore, the Bridegroom declares that he has drunk his own wine: that is, he has received with grateful draught the divine love which he gave to the Virgin—the love by which she desired to embrace Christ God with all her heart, all her soul, and all her strength, and which Christ himself receives and is believed to delight in when received.

But because the Word made flesh, God made man, chose to be born from the Virgin, the Virgin who loved God gave herself also, as Mother, to love him as man. She knew that the commandment of the Law is neither sufficiently useful nor fruitful unless the similar or second commandment is added to the first and greatest. Therefore, fulfilling Law and Scripture, she loves her neighbour; mindful of the inexpressible birth, she loves Christ the man. She does not hate her own flesh in her Son with a stepmother’s hatred, but embraces it with maternal affection and loves it by natural right.

For her hardness is not the hardness of stones, nor can her mind be called bronze (Job 6). Rather, the Mother is found so devoted to tender love that, considering Christ made man from herself, she loves him as herself—or, if it may be said, more than herself. This love, this affection or care of the mother, is represented by the name of milk, which a mother naturally gives to her child. For the mother holds or lays up her son in her bosom or lap and, with tender love and anxious affection, pours milk into him.

This vigorous, milk-like love, sweet with natural sweetness, does not derogate from divine love, does not prejudice the wine, and is not always opposed to the spiritual; rather, it deserves to find no small grace with God, if it loves to serve in union rather than to rule alone. Thus the giver of the evangelical Law, saying, “He who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10), did not condemn nature’s privilege, but wisely ordered the union of the two affections: love of God, as the higher love, is without measure, while natural love holds the second place within the union.

Although some persons first grasp natural love, because they more readily comprehend it and are not yet fit either to understand or to love spiritual love, yet the love which is God's is certainly first and greatest; and, as if in a union, it desires the second to be present beside it. The second, indeed, is sometimes found without the first in those forestalled by ignorance or debased negligence. But the first, flourishing in perfection and knowing no envy, introduces the second and always desires to see it joined with itself.

Accordingly, when Paul presents what is first as though it were second, by persistently preaching to the Corinthians only Christ—and him crucified—he spares weakness, provides for progress, and advances faith, so that those who could not yet grasp Christ’s divinity might at least understand and love his charity toward them; and, knowing that he suffered freely for them—indeed, for all—they might return something, by loving him, for so great a goodness. “I judged,” he says, “that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2). And a little later: “As to little children, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3).

But he who thus nourishes and advances the imperfect with milk, knowing what to give to each, speaks wisdom to the perfect; he preaches Christ, the Son of God, as eternal God, born before the ages and coequal with the Father who begot him. Thus he gives milk to little children and wine to those more grown, marking differing advances, or stages of progress: he can teach both those weaker persons by whom natural love is more easily grasped and those more mature persons for whom spiritual love is now fittingly suitable.

But from the time when, in a new manner, the Virgin became a mother, she was raised by the grace of the divine gift to so great a summit of perfection that she loves Christ, truly God, with supreme desire and just right, and likewise grants to the same one as man the due right of nature. In the Son she loves the excellence of divinity with a pure mind, and naturally loves her own flesh tenderly and sweetly. Toward the former she is carried and raised to love by a stronger ardour; toward the latter she is, as it were, drawn back and lowered by a gentler step. Drunk, she raises herself more vehemently toward the former; sober, she inclines herself more gently toward the latter. To the former she offers the wine of strength, to the latter the milk of tenderness. A twofold love flourishes in the Virgin, and neither detracts from the other; Christ receives and accepts the harmonious union of both.

Isaiah says: “Come, buy without silver, and without any exchange, wine and milk” (Isa. 55). The prophet knew that Christ is not pleased by solitary love, but delights in a twofold gift corresponding to his twofold, giant-like substance. He therefore wished wisely to instruct us to buy wine and milk, indicating that wine suits God, milk man—or rather, that wine and milk suit Christ as God and man.

But since, according to the prophet’s teaching, this wine and milk must be bought, what does it mean that no exchange, no silver, is admitted to this purchase, unless that the twofold love by which Christ, God and man, wishes to be loved cannot be compared with gold, silver, or any earthly price? For that kingdom, in which everyone who rightly loves Christ remains with him eternally, is bought and gained not by a heap of money but by poverty of spirit. In the present, too, love for him knows no cheap price and does not wish to be possessed by one swollen with temporal abundance.

Rightly, then, Isaiah calls to this purchase those who make no mention of silver in buying, but instead offer a lowly spirit, purity of the inmost mind, continence of the flesh, and nakedness after laying aside soft linen. Armed, I believe, with this price, the Virgin entered the nuptial market; having found and bought wine and milk, she mingled both together for the Bridegroom, serving Christ God and man with a twofold cup, knowing that he would not thirst for one without the other.

Having drunk and been refreshed, he turns again to his companions and diligently invites them to the nuptial feast, so that those who serve like attendants in the chamber, knowing its secrets, may also be counted guests and fellow-partakers at the rich table.

## CHAPTER IV

“Eat, friends; drink and be drunken, dearly beloved.”

He calls the angels friends: those who remained in his friendship when Lucifer and many who agreed with him ceased to love.
