They stood by the celebration of the wedding after those who did not love had been driven far away, and they devoted themselves more intimately, in worthy ministry, to knowing the hidden mysteries. The Bridegroom does not allow those who stand and attend to gain fitting advances in knowledge to remain poor or hungry. Instead, opening the cellar and displaying the abundance of gifts, he invites them as it were to a table of rich marrow and clarified vintage wine (Isa. 25).

“Eat, friends,” he says. “You whom I willed to take part in the present nuptials as companions and friends, and, after those who did not love had been removed, to be present at the kisses of those who love: eat at my table with me what is set before you; that is, understand what, once understood, will deserve to please you. Understand what grace or savour the solemnity of the nuptials and the depth of the mysteries contain; what glory and honour belong to the Virgin’s fruitfulness and the Mother’s integrity. Understand what sacrament is contained in ‘the Word was made flesh’ (John 1), and what aid divine things bring to human beings, heavenly things to earthly.”

This understanding is rightly called eating. When an angel or anyone of this kind is invited to eat, the divine word does not mean to dispel bodily need, but indicates that spiritual understanding must be sought. Thus, when in a vision the hand of the Lord was sent to Ezekiel and brought him a book enclosed under a seal: “Son of man,” it says, “eat this roll, and go, speak to the children of Israel” (Ezek. 3). Since little or nothing is gained by the sent hand’s bringing a sealed book if the prophet does not know what is written in it, he is necessarily urged to eat the roll: namely, that he may grasp with mind, not tooth, what the roll contains.

For the eater is not satisfied merely with the appearance or beauty of food, but burns rather to be refreshed by its taste and flavour. Everyone who rightly understands is nourished not by the tinkling sound of Scripture, nor by mere feeling, but by understanding suited to spiritual advancement. Because one cannot be nourished by this through the powers of one’s own will alone, but receives it by grace and the benefit of divine generosity, the prophet, after hearing the Lord’s voice and command, is not yet sufficient for himself but states that he was fed by God: “And I opened my mouth, and he fed me with that roll” (ibid.).

“I strove to open my mouth at his invitation to eat; at his admonition to understand, I applied myself to obedience. And he, finding me already prepared by the admonitions offered, fed me as I gave attention to the opened roll; that is, he gave me abundant knowledge and literary understanding. ‘He spread it before me,’” he says, “‘and said: Eat this roll’” (ibid.). “The book which the hand sent to me brought rolled up I did not, by any effort or power of mine, unroll. Rather, the very hand which brought it removed the surpassing or covering veil and made evident and spread open what was shut in the roll. For though it is mine to obey the one who admonishes, to offer, as it were, hands ready for progress, it belongs to his grace to grant me—or anyone else—quick understanding. It is mine to open my mouth, lest I deserve to be wholly driven away from the food; it is his to fill it, that is, to grant right understanding. ‘Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it’ (Ps. 80). And elsewhere: ‘Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments’ (Ps. 118). And he says: ‘I will give you understanding and instruct you’” (ibid.).

Thus, speaking to the companions whom the Bridegroom willed to be present at the hidden mysteries, he did not wish them to be rustic and hungry at the nuptials; rather, having set before them a table of profound greatness and exquisite fullness, he kept his friends far from the hunger of the ignorant multitude. “Eat, friends,” he says: “that is, understand the wonderful mystery, the inexpressible sacrament, whose veil ignorance opens to others who are not friends. But to you who serve and stand beside me, I have granted the power, resting solely on my grace, to know what nature does not attain.”

For, contrary to what some say, angels did not naturally possess from the beginning the knowledge of mysteries which remained more fully hidden in God. When the fullness of time came and God the Son of God chose to celebrate the nuptials, he willed first and more familiarly to reveal them to the angels. Hence the Apostle says: “What is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God, that the manifold wisdom of God may become known through the Church to the principalities and powers in heavenly places” (Eph. 3). God’s wisdom, remaining uniform in itself while acting outwardly in many and varied ways, deserved to be called manifold; it becomes known, as it were, in more ways to angelic principalities and powers when the mystery of the incarnation of the Word shines more clearly upon them.

But because understanding does not sufficiently avail angel or human being for merit unless the sweeter affection of love is joined to understanding, the friends are rightly and freely admonished after eating as well, so that learned nourishment and perfect refreshment may produce life-giving sufficiency. “Drink,” he says, “and be drunken, dearly beloved. If, by my gift, you grasp hidden mysteries with the understanding, do not yet be content with that; be zealous for progress. And that you may sufficiently advance and appear, as it were, to perfect what you have begun, drink while eating: that is, love what you have understood.”

For it profits little or nothing to understand things that are great and perfect unless we love what we understand with a more powerful grace. As the people without understanding will be beaten, according to Hosea’s testimony (Hos. 4), so the wicked servant who does not love what he understands will condemn himself as guilty of negligence. Therefore the companions or friends are rightly urged not merely to understand, but also to love, so that, having gladly perceived deep things, they may admire their most sweet savour; and those who once grieved, as it were, over the sinner’s miserable fall may now, from joy, be astonished at the Redeemer’s marvellous counsel.

When they seize the height of this matter with hands of understanding and love, drunk with astonishment and joy they are suspended in a kind of ecstasy. Forgetting the wounds which the serpent’s deceit formerly inflicted upon humankind, they think now only of the physician and the present remedy. They eat when they understand that the life-giving mystery and saving nuptials are being celebrated; they drink when they love that humankind is restored to its former—indeed, greater—grace; they are drunk when they marvel and cling in astonishment, and through joy cannot sufficiently admire that humanity, assumed into God, deserves to be exalted above angels.

The Bridegroom calls those who know this secret “friends”; calling them “dearly beloved,” he magnifies them as drunk with love and joy. He indicates both that those are pleasing to him who apply spiritual understanding to subtle knowledge, and that the same persons become most pleasing when they come to, and advance in, the progress of love. When the friends have been refreshed with food and made drunk with more pleasing drink, the bride reclines her head in sweet consciousness or love, forgets visible things, is suspended in invisible things, and does not envy us what she tastes and feels, but shows it to us.

## CHAPTER V

“I sleep, and my heart watches.”

While the companions and friends attending so divine a work gaze in wonder, drunk with astonishment at the profundity of its greatness and not with wine, the bride reclines within the chamber in gentler repose; the Bridegroom has just offered her the desired cup of marvellous savour. While the friends keep watch, as it were striving to comprehend and astonished at the measure of so profound a matter, the Virgin judges whatever does not give delight in lofty silence to be the public forum. She rests in the bridal chamber and closes her eyes, if only briefly, in sleep.

For with business and the clamorous anxiety of business driven away, the noise outside excluded, and the door, as it were, of the pure mind closed, she falls asleep among the Bridegroom’s embraces all the more eagerly because more sweetly. Failing into him and advancing by that failing, she desires only things beyond sensation. Remaining in the body, her serene mind is carried in ecstasy away from the things of the body, forgetful of cares. Raised by peaceful rapture, she rejoices to forget all that is lower, sleeping and resting in those things which above all she desires to attain.

But lest this sleep appear to bring negligence or sluggishness, to inspire confidence in the ambushes of enemies, or to open a freer entrance, the Virgin sets a watchman who keeps indefatigable guard and foresees from afar whatever clamours improperly. While she sleeps, dissolved in the Bridegroom’s tender embraces, forgetful of what lies behind and released from temporal cares, her heart watches. It drives far from sleep the clouds of fantasies, empty phantasms, the heavy clamours of the world, and the seductive melodies of sirens.

Her heart watches with vigilant care lest the burden of public affairs, cast upon her, disturb the sweetness of sleep she has found; lest any annoyance enter secretly into the chamber’s hidden place, rage once admitted, and violently shake off sleep. Finally, her heart watches so that, after anxiously repelling every adversary, it may listen and hear the Bridegroom whispering in a gentle murmur; and, closing the door, as it were, against every harsher disturbance, may lend its ear to the Bridegroom who speaks more sweetly and subtly.

For the more eagerly she loves to be joined to him more closely and cling to him more desirously, the more gladly she hears him and wishes to rejoice for joy at the Bridegroom’s voice. Lending her ear to hearing, she thinks herself severely injured if, for the sake of his voice, she does not reject whatever else sounds out. For he, cherishing sleep and favouring the sleeper’s desire, when he has thus allured her, speaks to the heart of the woman who loves; and he sets for her, as he wills, the limit both of repose and of activity, as he is recorded long ago to have promised through the prophet: “I will allure her, and I will speak to her heart” (Hos. 2).

“I will allure her,” he says, “when, with head inclined, she lays herself in my bosom and, in mutual embraces, permits nothing to come between us; when, greedy for silence, she delights to fall asleep beneath my shadow and, thirsting to drink in the sweetness she has found, drinks and thirsts. But I will speak to her heart when I admonish her to wake, when I restrain her from her own enjoyments for the sake of her neighbours, so that, setting aside for a little while the draught of sweetness already tasted, she may go out to work, watchful in brotherly love.”

Thus the Bridegroom allures the Virgin when he brings her into the hidden things of his breast; he speaks to her heart when he calls and brings her back to us awake, when, after tasting the sweetness of sleep in which she delights to forget temporal things, he commands her to wake for love and care of her neighbours. While she sleeps and tastes how sweet it is to rest, and her heart watches in more diligent concern to serve, behold: a sudden interruption of the sweetness already perceived strikes, as it were, a hand knocks at the door, and the beloved’s voice shakes her ear. Understanding herself to be stirred by such a shock—for she recognizes the voice because she has heard it often already—the Virgin seems to answer either herself alone or the young women attending her, and recounts in mindful speech what voice, and whose, she has heard.

## CHAPTER VI
“The voice of my beloved knocking.” When, she says, I am held in my desired repose by the welcome gift of sleep, and yet with a heart sufficiently wakeful I remain intent upon the Bridegroom’s good pleasure, from concealment, as I perceive, a voice suddenly breaks forth, as it were into public, which anxiously interrupts my progress in sleep, lest it come, as I wish, to perfection. Its importunity strikes my ears somewhat harshly and repels me from that which I was burning more firmly to grasp. And I should bear this repulse with difficulty, to confess the truth, were I not rightly to prefer his good pleasure to my own will.

Yet I know that it is by no means displeasing to his will that the door of a holy mind should be found closed to outsiders: so that whoever passes along the wandering paths of worldly seduction may find it shut, not open like a brothel. Even the Bridegroom himself, when he wishes to come to that same door, prefers to find it closed rather than open; and to discover its seal so firm, so inviolable, that he may never at all know it opened unless he himself has knocked.

For a holy mind, keeping itself within its spiritual workshop, ought so to cultivate contemplation, so to embrace the discipline of leisure or silence, that it does not open its enclosure for itself, nor break forth into the office of preaching unless it has been knocked upon and received the voice of one commanding. Therefore the Virgin, asleep and soothed by delightful slumber, rejoicing to be confined within her enclosure as though entangled by gentler chains, hastens to open not merely for anyone whatever, but not even for the Bridegroom, until at last she is knocked upon, commanded, and compelled to obey. [Col. 0415C]

She certainly does not summon her teacher in order that he may command; rather, she recognizes more quickly even the faint voice of one knocking. And just as she does not listen or give heed, in order to open, to every warning of a deceiver, so she does not stop her ear when the teacher’s voice sounds. He sounds and knocks at the door—or at the repose of one at rest—when he wishes, through the benefit of teaching, to provide for those who are outside; when, pitying the blindness and poverty of the unlearned orphan, he wishes it to be wiped away by virginal labour and the merit of the labourer to be increased.

But what that voice proclaims besides, or what it says—what it tenderly commands or announces to the sleeping bride—the Bridegroom wished the bride to know not only more secretly and more sacredly, but also wished it to reach outsiders, however faintly.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0415D]

“Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled one; for my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.”

You, he says, who have firmly barred the chamber of your mind against the malevolent robber; who have strengthened the virginal enclosure and watchful guard against everything hostile: open the doors to me—not one who envies, but one who desires your advancement, your crown, and the advancement of those who are yours—and set aside for a little while your leisure or silence.

Rise, awaken, hear more healthfully my voice as I knock; remove the bolt from the door. For nothing whatever that you rightly shut against the enemy, the world, or any outsider ought to be shut against me. Make sure that you open to me alone, as one worthy of merit and praise. When I allow you to be at leisure and to indulge in peaceful sleep, to attend to yourself, to devote your hands to leisure or to silence, then, I admit, the bridal chamber ought to be closed, the door bolted, the virginal secret not opened to vice or worldly business. [Col. 0416A]

For with the door shut, that Father of spirits wishes to be prayed to, his face to be sought, and the kiss of the seeker to be made serene; he wishes leisure so fruitful not to be disturbed by crowds of business, but to flourish under a gentler breeze and with the most effective course. But when I stand and knock earnestly at the enclosure, when my voice resounds and asks that an opening be given to it, it is not prudent for you to remain hidden longer beneath the shadow of silence; rather, stand ready for the command and show yourself subject to him.

Open to me, then, after interrupting for a little—not casting aside—the sweetness of sleep, so that what you have received in the chamber you may preach upon the housetops; and, as though forgetful of yourself, may remember for my sake those who stand with me, and may not be reluctant to speak for brothers and neighbours of the peace already tasted. For you ought not to indulge only your own desires, nor draw out the sweetness of heavenly milk only for your own lips; rather, when the time requires it, you must also provide for the benefit of others, lest you seem to begrudge to those unable to obtain it what you have been able to draw first or more abundantly.

Finally, a sister ought not to shut the door against a brother when they serve together as heirs—indeed, as fellow-heirs—under the highest Father; when kinship of flesh, the mighty force of nature, one love, and one concord rightly make them of one mind. Therefore, just as you shut the door—and rightly shut it—with the bar of watchfulness against the enemy, so, as a friend, draw back the bar and remove the bolt for your brother and friend alike: you who have become a friend by diligence of mind and the bond of charity, the faithful keeper of secrets, aware of my truth. [Col. 0416C]

And because you do not, like a peacock, take delight in or swell with pride at the blind beauty of your eyes, but, with my grace shining upon you, grow gentle in the spirit of innocence: you who are sister and friend are rightly called also my dove, cheerful in hope of things to come, yet groaning because those same things are not yet fully present. In these and other such gifts abundantly endowed by me, you are worthily called the undefiled and perfect Virgin: perfect, I say, not because nothing whatever is lacking to the present life, but because you are wholly beautiful, so that there is now no blemish in you.

You therefore, who are distinguished by names of this kind—indeed, by the realities signified by those names—and who experience me as so gracious in the abundance of these gifts, hear the voice of him knocking; open the closed doors; and, lest you think the insistence of the knocker idle, see the reasons.

“For my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.” Christ’s head, according to the testimony of Paul, is God. Dew, which the cold night pours over the earth, the sun dissolves as, with its morning beam, it disperses the mist together with the things upon the earth: it is the coldness of unbelievers and the subtle malice of the faithless by which the nations are held; it is the iniquity of the Jews that grows cold (1 Cor. 2). [Col. 0416D] While they do not understand or confess that Christ the man is God, the Son of God, what do they do except dare to weigh down and offend his head, and fill it with such burdens and troubles that it can scarcely bear so complete a load?

Hence God says through Isaiah: “I am full,” he says (Isa. 1); and again: “I have laboured in bearing” (ibid.). You burden me, he says, with such dew, with such nocturnal cold, that I seem to myself to be worn out and filled with disgust at your perversity; and I, who cannot be disturbed, who in tranquillity judge the world, am wearied in bearing the loads of your iniquities.

The Jewish dew, and the cold malice of one who does not believe, speaks in the Gospel words that oppress more harshly. Seeing Christ as a man, he understands nothing else, nor loves anything else; and he especially takes offense because Christ truly declares himself to be God. “For a good work,” they say, “we do not stone you, but for blasphemy; because you, being a man, make yourself God” (John 10). And above: “Therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he called God his Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5).

You see Christ’s head oppressed by very cold dew, and Christ rightly complaining of a more grievous malice, by which not only his head but also his locks are weighed down with similar cold, while unbelievers persecute them with hatred and insults. [Col. 0417B]

Locks are called clusters or masses of hair. Rooted in and adhering to the head, they are joined outwardly to it by a certain bond of nearness; and, while each keeps its proper place and arrangement, together they provide the head both covering and honour. By them, as I see it, the saints are fittingly signified: called to the faith from different places and nations, made to adhere more firmly to the Head by the steadfastness of the same faith, and outwardly made to cling together like bees by brotherly closeness.

Such, I think, were those in the primitive Church who are read to have gathered to Christ in a devoted spirit: those who, before his Passion, followed him who was about to suffer, few in number; or who, after he had risen, received more abundantly faith in the Resurrection. Of them Mark says: “He called to himself those whom he himself wished, and he made twelve to be with him” (Mark 3). And Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of people together was about one hundred and twenty” (Acts 1); “and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in various tongues as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2). And below: “They were baptized, and on that day about three thousand souls were added” (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “The number of men became five thousand” (Acts 4). And much later: “When Paul preached, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus; and there were altogether about twelve men” (Acts 19).

These are the Bridegroom’s locks, for whose advancement he has no small care and whose oppression he bears with distress. [Col. 0417D] Often the nights become oppressive through drops of rain—or rather, through downpours—when, the sun having long departed, they grow dull in colder darkness. As every righteous person is called a day by the merit of life, so the impious and sinner living wickedly is called night; for, since the light has not risen for him and the sun of righteousness has not shone, he has drawn upon himself the dreadful cold and darkness of ignorance.

Such a night, the dark conduct of sinners, hates justice and condemns the innocence of better people; and it prevents that innocence from walking openly, as it were, beneath the naked air of the world, while it harasses it with frequent troubles, like drops of rain. Does not that night seem to you to have been especially troublesome, which rejoiced to oppress the apostolic choir more harshly? Though it did not wholly tear away from the Head the entire lock once joined to it, it shook one hair loose and brought it into the pit of perdition.

For when the leaders of the Jews wished to seize and kill Christ, they employed many deceits and schemes to seduce and induce Judas Iscariot—whom they perceived to be grievously troubled by avarice—to sell his own Saviour cheaply. All the others indeed were severely shaken by the wind of fear, but they were not shaken loose from the foundation laid beneath them or the root planted within them. The Bridegroom’s hand recalled them and wished them to be restrained under a rule, so that thereafter they might bear more patiently both the threats of rulers and the drops of the nights. [Col. 0418A]

Thus, after the Resurrection, when the chief priests thundered with threats and imprisonments, words and beatings, in order to turn the disciples back from their purpose of preaching by fear, they said: “Judge whether it is just to listen to you rather than to God; for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4). And below: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5).

Nights attack from outside such locks as charity binds, social love joins, and inward faith and spiritual devotion cause to adhere to God; the dark hands of unbelievers burden them with colder drops and more frequent malice. For as the prophet declares, “a cistern makes its water cold” (Jer. 6), so it has made its malice cold. Therefore, so that the locks of believers may be protected against enemies and their burdens, and may not be wickedly oppressed either through ignorance or voluntary consent, the Bridegroom urges the Virgin to open to him the door of her secrets and, explaining what she knows, to instruct the minds of her neighbours. [Col. 0418C]

For although the anointing of the Spirit is said to teach the righteous concerning all things (1 John 2), the Virgin is nevertheless not commanded in vain to apply diligence. It does not hinder, but indeed promotes, the effective growth of spiritual grace if a fitting foundation is first laid by planting and watering. But because it is sweeter to be at leisure and behold the sweetness of rest and the delight of contemplation than to labour in speech and the anxiety of preaching, the Virgin, choosing to remain enclosed and unwilling to be torn from her purpose, answers as though grieved that she is being driven out to business.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0418D]

“I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?”

Adam was made naked, placed beneath the open sky, not enclosed in a chamber or wrapped in garments, so that he might look up to heaven with a face unimpeded by any covering, and might walk with unencumbered step to behold God. But because, devoted to his wife, he yielded to the will of the deceived woman and, offending the Creator, reached out for what was forbidden, he entangled himself and his descendants in the guilt of death, miseries, and labours; and, having lost nakedness, clothed himself in wretched mortality.

Thus after disobedience he was clothed in skins, so that, deprived of the simple life and naked justice, he might know that the loss of miserable punishment threatened him—an image represented by a garment made from dead animals. To such punishment, as I see it, belongs the anxious labour by which we desire either to learn or to teach; and until we see that which is perfect with the eye of a sound mind more fully unveiled, we eat our bread in the sweat of our face. [Col. 0419A]

We breathe a little from this heat or sweat when, laying aside the burden of cares, we breathe toward invisible things; and we are stripped of the ragged tunic of labour by sweet leisure when, with the door of the mind shut, we contemplate the sweetness of inward rest. Since the bride already senses this sweetness with eager taste, she does not quickly consent to open for the disturbing Bridegroom; rather, fleeing away after leaving behind her garment, she delights to behold naked truth, fearing to be turned from so happy a leisure to business.

“After laying aside,” she says, “the anxiety in which I toiled more laboriously, and stripping myself, with a view to peace, of the tangled tunic of outward things, how shall I interrupt the sweetness I have found and send myself back to worldly cares, which I do not love? I do not refuse the command; I do not reject obedience; but I fear being subjected once more to a burden that will weigh me down. Having tasted inward things, I no longer care to revisit outward things; and yet I do not, like an asp, stop my ear against one commanding.

“I had laid aside the spoils of old heaviness and found for myself the joys of pure nakedness. I rejoiced that I was no longer where I had been, indeed that I was no longer what I had been; through a progress sufficiently pleasing, I seemed naked to be among naked angels. Forgetting visible things, I more gladly beheld invisible things. I knew no troubles; I was not confined by narrow barriers. In this breadth of mind nothing opposed me; what I love, what I desire, was more abundantly present to me. [Col. 0419B]

“Therefore, if my own will draws me back, I deserve accusation; if necessity presses upon my will, I seem oppressed. Thus a kind of danger threatens from either side, since it is hard to do anything unwillingly or unjustly. Free, therefore, from ragged anxiety, how shall I again become entangled? Stripped of temporal things, with what patience shall I again put on the tunic? How shall I bring washed feet back to the mud of the streets, so as to defile them with the troubles either of sins or of cares?

“For though in speaking to my neighbours and carefully setting forth what I already know, I have not departed from the path of righteousness, as most people are accustomed to do, still I seem to have incurred certain defilements, since I have felt the troubles of cares come upon my heart. For whatever, even slightly, meets and resists one contemplating divine purity, or fails to assist that contemplation by favourable service—if it is compared by fitting consideration with that purity—although holy in its own kind, will nevertheless rightly be judged defiled.” [Note: [Col. 0419D] “Defiled” means “imperfect.”]

“How, then, after tasting that sweetness, shall I again endure this bitterness and turn back the steps of such great advances to the defilements of decline? For what advantage shall I place myself under another’s burden, when I now desire not to undertake conflict further, but to receive the crown?” But while I hesitate, while I doubt, as though not knowing how to find a way by which I might or could return to that which I had interrupted; while, rejoicing in silence, I delay returning to the accustomed burden—behold, I feel the hand of my beloved inserted through the opening.

## CHAPTER IX

“The beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch.”

He does not permit me, though warned by his voice, to remain longer in hesitation. The beloved pierces the enclosure and puts his hand through a narrow opening: he opens in the shut mind a subtle understanding, like an aperture; and, once it is opened, he inserts what he knew would be useful for my advancement.

That grace of the Bridegroom which opens the understanding, works effectively once it has been opened, and more subtly pours and breathes into the opened understanding the means and order by which one may more perfectly strive and aspire to please the Bridegroom, is not incongruously called his hand. By its help and operation, therefore, the subtler understanding perceives that neither rest nor labour brings advancement without the Bridegroom’s good pleasure. One must devote oneself to leisure when his goodwill invites us to it; and one who wishes to cease from it when commanded will not escape his anger and judgment. [Col. 0420B]

For someone may displease God by stubbornness in leisure and obtain merit by humility in activity; and neither condition is found sufficiently useful if it is not preceded, as it were, by obedience to Christ’s good pleasure. When this is subtly understood, she no longer strives to resist violently. Instead, what in her had become, as it were, hard, is made soft like a belly; and her heart, softened by the gracious hand, is strongly shaken and trembles. Fearing to offend, she now desires nothing but the Bridegroom’s good pleasure.

Good is the hand of grace, which mightily pierces dim places, giving light to the understanding so that it may see more clearly what will be beneficial. At its subtle touch, whatever was hard softens; and when it has become soft, trembling grows strong toward obedience. Who will grant that he may put this hand through the narrowness of the opening into us and, having opened our understanding, not allow anything to grow hard, but, when he has given subtle understanding to see, may subsequently infuse active diligence to accomplish?

Happy, then, is the Virgin touched by the hand of him who works, whose soft heart trembles at the touch or efficacy of him who commands; who, having heard the command, does not withdraw into the lodging-place of negligence, does not grow dim in understanding, does not limp in affection, but obeys. Hence she adds: “I rose,” etc.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0420D]

“I rose to open to my beloved.”

She who shortly before shuddered at resuming the tunic she had laid aside, and seemed not to know how she might again defile her washed feet, now, perceiving more fully in what matter and to whom she ought to obey, rises and hastens to open to him whom she loves. She had been held in a pleasing place or chamber of her own, and, as in a private room, rejoiced in sweet leisure. Delighting in soft repose, she rested with head reclined; she knew nothing of wakeful tumults or whatever made noise outside.

Rising from repose of this kind, or peaceful sitting, the Virgin shakes herself free and girds herself for the contest. What the Bridegroom’s spoken voice did not obtain from her, his inserted hand prevails to accomplish more fully. For a heard voice teaches one to act, but does not itself bestow action; and an ear responsive to hearing is not immediately made ready also for accomplishment. Rather, what the voice of one commanding declares beforehand for us to know, the touch of operative grace brings about for us to perform.

Hence Isaiah says: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. 63). The words of prophecy sound in the ears of all everywhere, but, when the Bridegroom’s hand is absent, they do not give faith to Isaiah; for the word that strikes the outward ears of unbelievers becomes like a sounding cymbal (1 Cor. 13) if grace does not touch their minds. [Col. 0421A]

Therefore, after the voice by which the Bridegroom advised the Virgin to open, because she delayed obeying the warning given, he applied his operative grace to soften her heart and, by the touch of his hand, to render her ready to accomplish what he had commanded. Elsewhere Solomon is also found praising the same Lord, showing that what he declares beforehand with his mouth, he completes with his hands; thus making clear that it is not sufficient for him to be ready to speak unless he also applies the more gracious favour of his hand to perform: “With your mouth,” he says, “you have spoken, and with your hands you have completed” (3 Kings 8).

Thus the Bridegroom advised the Bride with his mouth to undertake labour, but made her readier by the touch of his outstretched hand. With his mouth he made her, resting in sleep or leisure, wakeful to hear; with his hand, active, so that she might rise and open more watchfully. “I rose,” she says, “to open to my beloved.” She who, lying down, could not—or perhaps would not—open, shaken by the touch of the hand rises and hastens to obey. She rises, I say, lest by delaying she seem to keep the knocker waiting, judging it beneficial to herself whatever she finally perceives to please him. [Col. 0421B]

Having therefore interrupted her silence, she rises and prepares herself for teaching, so as to implant moral discipline in the hearts of her hearers. She makes her hands active in order to furnish others with a pattern of life; and by word as well as deed she opens to the Bridegroom a path by which to come. For Christ’s way is effectively opened when truth is found in the teacher’s word and seriousness in the teacher’s action; when preaching or teaching so instructs the minds of hearers that the discipline of the virtue displayed beforehand builds them up more fully. Showing this, the Virgin adds: “My hands,” etc.

## CHAPTER XI

“My hands dripped myrrh, and my fingers were full of the finest myrrh.”

When the Virgin rose and, as it were, went to open, hoping that with the door opened Christ might enter more fully, as she went she perceived that the door itself would not readily open unless she strove to employ strong hands to lift the bolt. The door was not opened immediately when she reports herself to have risen; nor does she assert that it opened as soon as she rose. For although she undoubtedly confesses that she rose in order to open, immediate success in opening is not granted her. She does not say, “I rose and opened,” but, “I rose in order to open.”

Because, perhaps, some difficulty opposed her as she rose, the Virgin prudently applied her hands to remove it: hands, I say, not sluggish with leisure, not dry, not deceitful, but strong in active virtue and effective in worthily accomplishing their purpose. “My hands,” she says, “dripped myrrh.” [Col. 0422A]

By hands she appears to mean actions; by myrrh, judicial strictness, because the Virgin wished to judge everything she did with greater rigour. She knew that one rightly need not fear the judgment to come who has humbly chosen to endure judgment in the present. Therefore the Virgin’s hands dripped the bitterness of myrrh when all her acts observed the rule of discipline, when she diligently restrained everything she endeavoured to perform in this laborious flesh, lest it presume to wander negligently.

For myrrh is said to strengthen soft and yielding flesh and to preserve it from decay to which it is subject by nature. Likewise, regular strictness strengthens the works of our hands lest they perhaps fall into a natural failure, and leads them to perfection. And since it is not sufficient for the Virgin, by living strictly, to make great progress in virtue unless she also instructs others and draws them with her toward salvation, she says not that her hands hold or possess myrrh, but rather that they drip it, thus showing that she pours the advancement of her works out to outsiders.

For this purpose she rises: so that her teaching may not remain fixed in one place or falter anywhere, and so that she may not keep enclosed what she knows to be useful to others, but may let it drip, benefiting those with her not merely by the desire of her will but by a displayed model of righteousness and an example of strict holiness. [Col. 0422B] Therefore, eager to open, the Virgin stretches out her hands; eager to instruct her neighbours, she first displays the dripping of myrrh. She holds it certain that she teaches more effectively when strictness of conduct hastens to precede instruction in words.

But because the severe strictness of life is not considered fully sufficient if it does not maintain prudent moderation, or moderated prudence, within itself, after commending the fragrant anointing of hands dripping myrrh she next makes mention of the fingers. “My fingers,” she says, “were full of the finest myrrh.”

Although the fingers cohere below by one root, as it were, or one joint, they emerge outwardly distinct and in unequal size or measure. Their distinction is fashioned by so prudent an artifice of nature that, serving the hand, it is considered both useful and fitting. The discerning virtue is therefore rightly understood through the fingers; if it is joined as an inseparable companion to our actions, whatever strictness does not afflict, oppress, or confine in them severely, it renders more perfect and adorns by its companionship. [Col. 0422C]

Although it sometimes extends itself more sparingly, sometimes more abundantly, according as it sees and judges that the business at hand requires, it nevertheless neither strives to pass beyond due limits nor deems it indiscreet and harmful to stop short of them. Hence this one and same virtue, which is called discernment, is applied so variously to many and diverse affairs that it is not unfittingly represented by the name not of a finger but of fingers, since it works in many ways, distributing to each as it wills.

The most prudent Virgin, wishing to commend fingers of this kind, declares them to abound in the finest myrrh, because, just as strictness achieves little or nothing when indiscreet, so discernment does not shine unless accustomed to hard burdens. Discernment shines and is adorned with rosy beauty when the accompanying strictness is not confined by a miserly limit; when myrrh has been poured into the fingers not from an empty horn but a full one, and when this fullness is worthily approved, not confused. [Col. 0423A]

That strictness may fittingly be called approved or tested to which our life of labour strives to be so committed that any stain contracted from interruption in the present workshop is carefully boiled away by the severity of superadded discipline. But the Virgin calls the myrrh with which she declared her fingers full not merely “approved,” but “most approved,” perhaps indicating that the approved kind may be given to others labouring with grace, while the most approved is truly and specially assigned to her.

Approved myrrh is that which chastises the restless body and subjects the chastised body to servitude, lest the law implanted in its members wholly resist life and salvation; which restrains the unruly motions and burgeoning passions that incite the body, and does not allow them to become oppressive. But most approved myrrh is that which utterly denies every vice an entrance; which so banishes the cunning devices of enemies by the barred door of the mind that it not only does not permit conceived wickedness to be brought into effect, but, through stronger progress, no longer even opens the door to its conception.

It is most approved when the hand not only commits no unlawful deed, but the mind, far purer, admits nothing blameworthy; when the stronger spirit not only does not consent to the law of the flesh, but both flesh and spirit no longer feel anything requiring pardon. [Col. 0423B]

Although myrrh of this kind seems far removed from our limits, it is nevertheless certain that it is not lacking to this great Virgin. Rather, by an excellent gift it is so available to her fingers that she declares them not poor but full. For she is the one whose discernment embraces more fully the bitterness of strictness, and whose strictness is governed by discerning moderation. Mighty in both, she delights, with the doors closed, to find the welcome sweetness of silence; yet when touched by the Bridegroom’s hand, she does not wholly refuse to open.

Hence she adds: “The bolt of the door,” etc.

## CHAPTER XII
Pessulum ostii mei aperui dilecto meo: at ille declinaverat, atque transierat.  
“I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved; but he had turned aside and passed on.”

After the Virgin had displayed her hands and fingers, worthy through myrrh, and had prepared herself for opening by a discerning discipline, she unfastened the previously closed door by removing the bolt, and, at the command of him who knocked, disclosed what she had kept hidden within [Col. 0423D]. For she who had formerly rejoiced in sweet silence now judges it fitting, when the Bridegroom knocks at the door, to speak; feeling that she pleases him no less by speaking, whose favor she had rejoiced to obtain in silence.

Therefore she consents to open the door to him whom she loves—that is, she breaks silence and begins to instruct her neighbors: laying a foundation of faith in the young and unformed, and building up in the advanced and mature the structure of loftier righteousness. She opens the door not for herself but for her Beloved; she unfastens the enclosure not for herself but loosens the doors for him who knocks and sets an opening before him, because, when she puts out the Lord’s talent for the benefit of others, she is concerned not for her own glory or name, but for his.

For the love by which the Mother embraces the Bridegroom, the Virgin her Son, does not seek its own interests [Col. 0424A], nor hunt after anything private to itself. Whether she seems to devote herself to the leisure of contemplation or to the labor of preaching, she serves him alone whom she loves, with a devoted and whole spirit. And although she prefers leisure to labor, nevertheless, cleaving to him, she does not wholly reject the latter. Rather, when she applies herself to labor for his sake, it becomes more plainly known what motive holds her when she clings more diligently to leisure.

Leisure is not considered worthy of the highest praise unless its sweetness is sustained by a commendable cause; nor does that supreme Judge wish leisure to be presented to him as merit, but wishes a commendable cause to be displayed in its face. Understanding this, the holy Virgin says not that she opened the door, but the bolt of the door, so that the bolt may not be commended by the door, but the door by the bolt. For that invisible and most penetrating examiner of invisible things [Col. 0424B] is an eager lover not so much of the effort that follows as of the cause that precedes. “I opened,” she says, “the bolt of my door to my beloved.”

In the literal sense, whenever someone is found knocking at a door, as you know, it is not the bolt but rather the door that is opened. The person wishing to grant entry to the knocker pushes back the bolt which he had pushed inward when he wished the door to remain shut. Here, however, it is said not that the door but that the bolt of the door is opened. This means that a spiritual, not a literal, understanding is required; for just as the bridal chamber is not to be understood as constructed of wood or stone, so the door and bolt do not admit the crudeness of literal interpretation.

Thus, by the name “door,” silence is not inappropriately figured, beneath whose covering the Virgin lies concealed and rejoices in her hiding-place [Col. 0424C]. The bolt placed upon the door so that it may not turn is the love of the Bridegroom, for whose sake the Virgin embraces silence. When the outer doors have been closed and the Virgin lies shut away in silence, love for the Bridegroom is the cause stronger than every bar; and as cause and effect concur, the Virgin, a handmaid of repose, rejoices ineffably in her progress.

But if the Beloved knocks and asks the Bride to open, he surely wishes to find her love in that very silence. He proves that he is the cause of her adopted silence if, for the sake of him in whom she rejoices in silence, the Virgin also endures being occupied with outward matters. Otherwise, if the Virgin should resist with a stubborn mind while the Beloved knocks, there is no doubt that she clings to silence from a desire that is not true. For one who truly loves, knowing that she cannot fail to hear him whom she loves, rejoices, in order that she may be loved more, to disclose her love to him whom she loves [Col. 0424D].

Therefore, when the Bridegroom knocks, the Bride plainly does not remove but brings forward the bolt: that is, she carefully reveals the reason in which she rejoices in leisure, while she sets aside and dismisses leisure for the Bridegroom’s love; and, for the sake of him for whom she had devoted herself to leisure, she now does not refuse to devote herself to labor. For his sake she had wished to remain enclosed within, accustomed to the trophies of victory; for his sake, now going outside, she again becomes an athlete, showing in labor what cause had sustained her in leisure, and singing that prophetic saying contained briefly in the verse of the Psalm: “If I remembered you upon my bed, in the mornings I will meditate on you” (Ps. 62).

By “bed” he means repose, in which she delights in her chamber when, as though the door were closed, she is set apart from the turmoil of outward affairs. But the things that return in the morning after the quiet silence of night may quite properly be called temporal activity and teaching [Col. 0425A]. Therefore one who truly lies hidden in welcome silence for Christ’s sake also consents, for his sake, to devote himself to outward matters; and he shows whose remembrance or love he keeps upon his bed when he is called in the morning to work.

So too, when the Virgin receives, as though in the morning, the command to speak, she opens to the Bridegroom the bolt by which her door was secured. She shows by what love and what spirit she was held in silence, since she does not refuse obedience when she is asked to go forth in public. She opens, I say, in order to satisfy by her response him who had knocked and first moved her to open, and to rejoice in finding him outside; so that him whom in silence she could not yet sufficiently bind to herself, called into public she may be able to ensnare by the merits of obedience.

“But he had turned aside and passed on.” The Beloved knocks upon the Bride’s door and asks her to open to him; yet, when the bolt has been opened, he cannot be found. In a wondrous manner he inclines himself toward her by his presence, and, when he is thought already to be held, he at once turns aside, fleeing back to his own things. For the excellence of his nature is so incomprehensible that, when by generous favor he pours himself into a mortal creature, he seems to offer his whole self and grant the lover hope of holding him; yet, when her desire is stretched out, his immensity cannot be grasped.

He kindles and expands the sweet desire of one burning with love; he provokes the burning one and promises the presence of the one who provokes her. Yet, when he is thought present among the inmost veins of her tender embrace, he escapes eager hands and withdraws from the mouth that longs for him [Col. 0425B].

He flees the Virgin, I say, not because of blameworthy offense, but because she is pressed down by corruptible flesh. He turns away from her eyes his face, which cannot be granted to her—not by taking the reality away, but rather by postponing it. He gives tireless hope and strengthens her faith, he who dwells in inaccessible light. Turning from his mother’s gaze the desired face, he passes to the bosom of the Father; and, though he wills that his immortality should be loved by mortals, he reveals to none of them a light which has not been revealed to mortals, nor does he wish to be presented sufficiently to any of them.

For although he wills to be abundantly present, ever more and more, to help others, he nevertheless wills that something should always be lacking to all, so long as sin seeks remedy, weakness seeks healing, or this corruptible thing labors to lay aside its natural corruption [Col. 0425C]. For not only sin but also corruption darkens us and conforms us to the world in which we live. It binds us, lest we fly away more freely from it, by a bond that cannot be fully untangled; by this tether our eye is not utterly overwhelmed, but it grows dim.

Seeing, therefore, that the Virgin is still subject to this bond and wrapped in the fragile covering of flesh—not of vice but of nature—he frequently presents himself to her in the manner and order he wills; yet his immortal excellence quickly withdraws itself from the mortal. For though the Immortal promises in some manner to be known and felt, he does not admit a mortal eye to see him more fully. When he comes and asks the Virgin to open, he immediately turns aside and hastens to pass into invisibility.

He comes when he pours himself more pleasantly and sweetly into a pure mind; he passes on when he hides himself from that mind so that he may not be seen face to face [Col. 0426A]. He comes when he leads it to a true and sincere hope of the supreme vision; he passes on when he withdraws himself from one who still hopes and hastens in desire. He comes, I say, when he gives the Virgin thirst for the bright fountain of good; he passes on when he does not allow the thirsty one more fully to find what she seeks. He comes when he grants the Virgin’s faith to attain the highest merit; he passes on when he does not yet allow faith to pass into reality and hope into sight. Finally, he comes when, by commanding or knocking, he bears the Virgin forward to progress in obedience; he passes on when she, not yet arriving, seems to dissolve into a kind of failure. He comes when the Virgin stretches herself forward in a prosperous course; he passes on when, though running, she has not yet grasped the prize.

Withdrawing his hand rather than his affection from her, he adds: “My soul,” etc. [Col. 0426B].

## CHAPTER XIII

“**My soul melted when my beloved spoke. I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me.**”

The Virgin marvels and is astonished beyond what can be said; inwardly she wastes away in overwhelming amazement, because she obediently consents, at his commands or admonitions, to hold him whom she loves, yet still gains no strength, through any powers or merits, to obtain him. He speaks and urges the Virgin to open; she rises and hastens to obey the speaker more carefully. Indeed, upon hearing the word she is so reduced to tender affection that she seems to herself melted as by a mighty fire.

With that Spirit present who greatly delights to abide, the Bridegroom’s word, like fire burning in a furnace [Col. 0426C], powerfully scorches the whole Virgin, removes every dross far away, and melts her into love of himself as though she were fusible material. Melted, she seems to retain nothing that is her own or peculiar to herself, but offers herself pliable and workable, as if for every form: whether she is permitted to remain hidden within and to attend to spiritual things, or commanded to go out, speak to her neighbors, and benefit them. Let her heart not be troubled; let it bring no complaint against the command, but let it rejoice to stand by the one commanding and persevere in what has been begun.

Therefore, although she rejoices to be occupied only with spiritual leisure or spiritual labor, having put behind her what lies behind and stretching herself only toward what lies ahead, she seems almost to complain that he whom she seeks with such great zeal and with vision so purified is not yet found, and that she has not yet come to him with unveiled face [Col. 0426D]. “Him,” she says, “I love with all my heart, all my soul, all my strength. I do not cease to call; I join prayers to prayers and vows to vows. Yet when sought, he immediately slips away and does not yet fully give what he promises. And though he hears when called, he does not adequately answer my desire.

“What, then, is this: when he speaks—that is, when my soul tastes and recognizes his sweetness—I melt altogether in fiery love; but when I seek more eagerly, he withdraws himself as though begrudging me and does not answer my call, that is, he does not present the face I seek? Yet, seeing that I am placed in so great a desire, he does not allow me to be wholly deprived of consolation. Rather, lest I seem too greatly deceived by the postponement of what I sought, while I seek, I am sought; while I do not find, I am found” [Col. 0427A].

## CHAPTER XIV

“**The watchmen who go about the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my cloak.**”

Long before, the watchmen were said to have found this same Virgin (above, book III, ch. 22), and the Virgin carefully to have approached those who found her: they who diligently strive to go about the city of the faithful and, neglecting the reprobate, to bestow due care upon the elect. I recall having said there what then occurred to me; whether it deserved to please or suffice the reader, I do not know. And lest a repeated exposition of the same matters become burdensome, I pass on to explain only what has now recently been heard.

“They struck me,” she says, “and wounded me” [Col. 0427B]. The companions of the Bridegroom, to whom the care of the faithful is entrusted, keep unremitting watch over their flock. They go about Jerusalem, praising the name of the Lord upon the walls, and cherish and advance those whom they see will come to him. Nor is it enough for them to visit once; they do not find it burdensome to visit again. They examine the dispositions of those who are progressing and rejoice to bring them to completion; and those whom they know to be passing more firmly and freely from virtue to virtue, they love more often to find, after seeking them out, steadfast in their purpose.

Thus they are said to find again the Virgin whom they had found before; and they support her burning love with due favor. Since it is their care to awaken and kindle lovers, they exalt and commend the one who is loved, so that he may be loved more. In commending the ineffable magnificence of the Creator [Col. 0427C], they instill a greater force of love into the Virgin’s mind; while they desire to describe, yet cannot adequately describe, how great is the excellence of him who is loved. The Virgin, struck powerfully, is wounded by a keener dart.

For the praise of the Beloved is a certain dart or arrow. When the mind of this Virgin has fittingly been struck by it, she rejoices not so much to be painfully pierced as sweetly pierced; and she considers herself not so much transfixed by a dart as soothed by a healing draught. More sweetly dissolved into love by this dart or draught, she seems more gladly to be stripped of bodily things; and as the sense of bodily things is weakened, in which she had been more harshly entangled, she loves more tenderly because her mind is more freely established in heavenly things.

Thus the Virgin indeed rejoices that her cloak is taken away, when she feels herself, as though mentally naked, lifted up into heaven [Col. 0427D]; when she hears the watchmen proclaim the Bridegroom’s surpassing praises and, through the incentive of those praises, feels herself stripped of concern for bodily things. For one who is joined to bodily things, whether by the law of mortality or by love of the flesh, is covered, as it were, with a cloak that is difficult to bear. Hence, if she is stripped bare either in deed or in disposition by the devoted spirit, she rejoices to open herself to the Bridegroom and, with her face uncovered, to cleave to him more openly.

Since the watchmen exhort the Virgin to this by admonitions or praises, they are said to strike and wound her and to take away her cloak. While her mind attends to their presence or conversation, forgetting her flesh, she stretches herself wholly into the love of the spirit. For this purpose ministering spirits are sent to human beings; for this purpose, once sent, they exert themselves with much care: to instruct lesser people in lawful things lest they sin, but to urge greater people to abandon even lawful things with stronger desire [Col. 0428A].

When they find the Virgin burning with the torches of love, they lay wound upon wound and endeavor to inflame her still more. They take away from her the cloak in which she is naturally wrapped: that is, the concern by which every mortal is found to care for himself. For they proclaim him whom she loves so admirable and preach him so inaccessible that they draw the whole virginal mind into ecstasy, so that, forgetting the body whose oppressive presence she commonly grieves to be enclosed in, she may reckon herself freed, even if only a little, from that burden.

Yet the watchmen do not show themselves long to the Virgin either; they quickly withdraw from her to whom they sometimes condescend. They yield not entirely to her will, but rather, with subtle prudence, to holiness; and they return to care for others and to guarding the walls [Col. 0428B]. By the name “walls,” however, I think the apostles are figured, by whose care the Church rejoices to be defended. Raised high and elevated, they surround the city, strongly equipped for its protection—not, as is usual, with stone or cement, but with a mass of virtues and the indissoluble foundation of charity—provided that they are worthily guarded by the watchmen.

The most devout Virgin, seeing them raised to progress and being not yet able fully to attain her Beloved, turns to them, wishing to use fraternal consolation—not envying them, but rejoicing in their grace and salvation.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0428C] “**I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him that I am sick with love.**”

After the Virgin, as stated above, had been anticipated by the Beloved’s admonitions and, when he turned aside, had been found by the watchmen, and after they too withdrew themselves, she wishes to return to the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, the apostles—and to address them concerning him whom she loves with such great longing.

“You,” she says, “who, like daughters, burn more vehemently with love’s tenderness; you who prepare the inner chamber of the mind for the invisible Bridegroom: I admonish you—or rather, lest admonition be judged insufficient, I adjure you. For I desire that no one should pass lightly over what is so firmly adjured. Therefore, if by any means or order it should be granted you to find the Invisible, to attain the Inaccessible [Col. 0428D], announce and proclaim that I am burdened with tender love, so that through your intercession I may deserve to be commended to him whom I love.

“If delay has held you back while purified, if it has brought you to the Bridegroom with eager desire and a thoroughly cleansed vision, announce my ardors, my tireless love, my powerful languor; ask him to remember the wound of charity and give heed. And if a longed-for day removes any one of you from the body, if you arrive first after casting off the garment of flesh and with face wholly unveiled—for often the last rejoice to become first, while those who seemed first complain of becoming later—if divine grace gives you an unhindered path and you find first the one whom together we seek, I wish you to tell him, once found, by what ardor I am held, by what love, by what exhaustion I languish, and by what desire or languor I fail.

“If, I say, the king’s table receives you, if found light first pours itself over you, while I remain in darkness and am still held in prison with Joseph [Col. 0429A], remember me who am held there. Let not recent prosperity lead you into forgetfulness, but ask the mighty Lord to bring me too outside more quickly. And so that he may be moved more powerfully by swift mercy, say that I languish and that my languor presses upon me intolerably. And lest he should laugh at my pains and at my grievous incapacity to endure them, announce that this languor is born not from hatred of him but from love.

“It is an excessive languor, which heats my very soul with a vehement fever—indeed, which melts it like wax in a stronger fire. Melted by this heat, it grows wholly numb toward the transitory things of the world [Col. 0429B]; and, knowing now how to speak only of the Bridegroom, it falls silent more feebly concerning everything else.”

Perceiving this, the daughters of Jerusalem reply: “What is,” etc.

## CHAPTER XVI

“**What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have so adjured us?**”

Hearing themselves carefully adjured by the Virgin, so that, if they find the Beloved, they should report that she is weakened even unto languor, the daughters of Jerusalem seem to be more inflamed to find him, and set themselves more earnestly to ask what sort of one he is whom they seek.

“You,” they say, “who already know your Beloved by a marvelous privilege of love, since by a new manner you have made yourself known to him as Bride, Mother, and Virgin; therefore you now seem to us worthily the most beautiful among all women [Col. 0429C], since you are not held by the blindness common to us all and by equal merit with us. Since divine generosity granted this to no woman in earlier ages, and no woman has thus approached the pleasing of him of whom we speak, we know that no one can better instruct our ignorance or impart to us any knowledge whatever of him whom we seek.

“Perhaps for this reason he has not yet wholly released you from the present age or admitted your desire into full repose; but by his providence he has left you among us, even against your will, that you may teach us who he is that visits you so often. For the more frequently and lovingly you behold him, although through a mirror, the more you deserve to obtain greater knowledge of him. And when he visits and knocks, you are undoubtedly urged to open for this purpose: that you may not be reluctant to pour out to lesser persons the knowledge received from him [Col. 0429D].

“Tell us, then, what sort of one he is whom you wish to be sought by us together, and to whom you send us as messengers if he allows himself to be found. Tell us what he is like, lest we be led astray rashly in seeking him and, darkened by error, be induced to substitute one for another. Since you have adjured us so firmly and so lovingly, we wish not to despise but rather to heed what you asked; and indeed we regard the word of your oath as a command. Only tell us what your Beloved is like above another beloved.

“We know indeed that you love the Father, whose Son you thus cherish, and that in loving the Begotten you do not fail to unite the Begetter with him. But since no one has seen the Father except the Son, and except through the Son, while that same Son has not wholly withheld himself from you [Col. 0430A], tell us, if you possess anything concerning the quality of that Son, of whose greatness we hear and understand little or nothing.

“And because we rejoice that we too love, in no small measure, him whom you love, we ask this question of love not merely once but again; so that, when you hear the inquiry of attentive people repeated, you may wisely understand with what affection he is sought by those who love him. Let, then, the pointed repetition of the inquiry move you not to delay in answering the lovers’ questions. Tell what your Beloved ought to be considered like, and how God-and-man may be firmly believed and loved.

“He is God from God, light from light, and flesh from flesh, man from a virgin. We wish to be taught by you what we owe him, so that to each substance may be rendered what properly belongs to it [Col. 0430B]. For this reason the foregoing question is fittingly repeated, because a twofold love of a twofold substance is expounded therein. Since the knowledge of this is folded up, as it were, in a book, earnest inquiry is urgently applied to break its seal.

“Thus they ask once, and ask again, that it may be more plainly explained to them how that giant of double substance wishes to be loved; what he wishes to be thought to be, according as he is called *dilectus ex dilecto* (“beloved from beloved”); and what according as he is called ‘beloved’ without *ex dilecto*. For the first question, having said ‘beloved,’ immediately adds *ex dilecto*; the second, repeating ‘beloved,’ according to some manuscripts does not add *ex dilecto*. By this it gives us to understand that God, worthy of love, is from the Father, who is likewise to be loved; while the man, though to be loved, is not equally worthy of being embraced as from a human being [Col. 0430C].

“For the Son’s divinity is loved equally in the Father; but his humanity, which does not know the Father, is not thus loved in the mother. The double question appears subtly to indicate this: the first included *ex dilecto*, while the second chose to omit it. But if someone says that the first included it and the second did not omit it either, I do not wish to contend too strongly or oppose him stubbornly, for I have found many manuscripts supporting this reading. Although not all the manuscripts I could find do so, most of them have *dilectus ex dilecto*—‘beloved from beloved’—in the second inquiry as well as in the first. Nor have I sufficiently ascertained whether the phrase was repeated by the author, or instead written through a scribal defect or error [Col. 0430D].

But *dilectus ex dilecto* (“beloved from beloved”) can be said of man from man, because the Virgin loves her Son both because he is man and because of that from which he is. For she loves her own flesh, since “no one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5). We love him because, having become man, he shares our nature, and because our Creator assumed the lowliness of the creature. But the Virgin loves not merely him who became man, but him who became man from herself; and she loves herself, from whom he became man, more for his sake.

Although his becoming human rightly deserves to be loved by angel or human being, it belongs more fittingly to her to love him in whose virginal womb he became human. And whereas the obedience of the whole creation necessarily renders what is due to him made human, the Virgin, richer in grace, acts by a certain voluntary force of nature. This the daughters of Jerusalem seem to suggest in their question when they say not, “What is our beloved like?” but, “What is your beloved like?” They thereby indicate that that Beloved is rightly assigned to the Virgin as though in a special manner, because both nature and grace powerfully produce her love for him [Col. 0431A].

Questioned about this Beloved, the Virgin does not delay to answer, nor does she appear to begrudge his knowledge to those who seek it. She understands that she desires to be dissolved, but that it is nevertheless necessary for her to remain, so that what she drank in the chamber she may endeavor to teach upon the rooftops.

## CHAPTER XVII

“**My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands.**”

“My Beloved,” she says, “whose knowledge you have not yet, as it seems, acquired, though you have now earnestly sought it with desire to acquire it, shines with not one but a double splendor: a whiteness beyond estimation, to which a lovely redness is joined. Whiteness is unfailing light, inaccessible to those in darkness; day knowing no evening, not diminished by succeeding darkness; light eternally bright, and likewise the brightness of eternal light, illuminating angels and human beings alike, present both to those who endure and to those who pass away [Col. 0431B].

“It is, I say, the brightness of light: light present to all yet not displayed, truly shining in darkness, yet not comprehended by the darkness (John 1); brightness more luminous than the sun, light exceeding the brightness of snow, assuming a red garment yet enduring no stain upon that garment. For God—the Word of God, the Father’s Only-begotten, the image of the Begetter—clothing himself in a servant’s body, a tunic of misery and toil, living among human beings as a man, lived a life so humble that, to those who look worthily upon him, he presents, as it were, a ruddy face.

“For, taking true flesh from others, he was made so like human beings that, in the eyes of those whose sight is dim, neither beauty nor comeliness remains to him. Poor and weak, and, according to Zechariah (ch. 3), wearing filthy garments, he is sickly with ugliness and pale of muddy countenance [Col. 0431C]. But I, his mother, whose mind is not darkened and whose understanding is not dull, to whom my offspring was made known and his conception shone forth above all others, know that my Son’s flesh was wholly free from every vice: that he assumed nature but took from guilt nothing except punishment.

“Therefore he, who, as one fleeing every vice, blushes at every vice while bearing its punishment alone, is undoubtedly not defiled but ruddy. It is not injury from guilt, but rather flight from injury, when his cheeks are suffused with the blood-red blush of passion. Nor are only his cheeks red: the whole garment of his body is red; passion makes the whole beautiful, and penal suffering gives it a purple adornment. What is shame and intolerable loss to every sinner is for him nothing but grace and a commendable increase of glory.”  
[Note: [Col. 0431D] An allusion to Luke 2:52 and Philippians 2:9.]

“Finally, fire is red and is found to be the color of blood. If mercy does not intervene, guilt cannot endure its heat; and wood, hay, and stubble experience in it not light but burning, whereas it saves gold, silver, and stone, rendering like recompense to each (1 Cor. 3). Therefore my Beloved is a fire consuming chaff [Col. 0432A], drying up mud, bringing the reprobate to nothing, and mercifully chastising the dissolute: fire enclosed in an earthen vessel, red with judicial power, shaking all around by judging in red power.

“For God willed him whom he had desired from before the ages to be substantially united to himself to be found, at the end of time, in the form of a man. His becoming human cannot readily be known by anyone except one to whom he wills to impart grace for that purpose. He wishes it to be sought by the desire of the studious and the study of those who desire; and, as I understand, he wishes to grant it to you who seek worthily. I do not begrudge you this, though I seem to have been anticipated by the same grace; rather, I teach you who seek and rejoice that you are effectively instructed.

“Therefore he is the radiance of glory, the figure of substance, the image of the Father’s Godhead, the brightness of eternal light [Col. 0432B], the mirror of divine majesty” (Heb. 1). “He is white in the white Father, untouched by any stain and always pure; yet, though he submitted to have a mother, he willed to become ruddy. Bright, I say, as light from light, he likewise desired to be red; but though red for our aid, he never ceases to be eternally bright in himself.

“Among the choirs of angels, the crowds of human beings, or their assemblies, no giant more powerful than he, nor anyone like him, has been found. For this reason the Father carefully chose him from among thousands: he was sent by will, not compelled by a harsh law or necessity. Made priest and victim, he offered himself in sacrifice by his own will, laying down the life he had assumed and taking it up again by a like authority.

“This number is excellently defined as stated before, when a finite number is put for the whole infinite: so that from among all angels and human beings, who cannot be comprehended by any number, he alone was chosen for the ministry of offering [Col. 0432C]. No other human being or angel could offer in this way; no one else’s offering could effectively confer this. Therefore, ‘from among thousands’—that is, from the infinite number of all—this one was uniquely chosen, who accomplishes more perfectly what the imperfect cannot accomplish. And that he is worthy to be chosen, through whom this benefit is bestowed, is set forth by the worthy sequence of praise that follows.

## CHAPTER XVIII
His head is finest gold; his locks are like the tall shoots of palm trees, black as a raven. This Beloved of the Virgin, since he is not held to be of one generation, is likewise believed not to be of one substance or nature: for from the Father alone he is believed to have that by which he is God, and from his mother alone that by which he is man. Thus Christ remains at once God and man, of a twofold substance or nature. In this union, in which two natures are held to meet in one person, one thing is found to be primary and another secondary. The former may indeed be called the head by privilege of dignity; the latter may be fitted, if it seems appropriate, to some other likeness.

The head of Christ, therefore, is that primary nature in him which, begotten from the Father, is believed coequal with the begetter; according to which, just as he is not greater than the Father, [Col. 0433A] so neither is he less than him [Note: [Col. 0433D] This must be read cautiously.], while he is greater both than every human being and truly than himself. This head is not inappropriately compared to gold—indeed, to the finest gold, approved above all others—which rules over all metals by the worthiness of its price and, even if lying in mud, is not made ugly by a muddy nature.

For Christ’s divinity, which he is known to possess coeternally and in common with the Father, assumed our flesh while preserving itself immune from fleshly sins. And, mercifully bending down by lofty counsel toward our mud, it lay hidden beneath the shadow of flesh, unpolluted by any of its defilements. Therefore, by this mystery in which God bent himself down while remaining in his own nature, he was wonderfully made a creature by the rightful freedom of his power. As these natures came together, neither suffering loss [Col. 0433B] of which to complain, Christ, God and man, was given to us from such a union.

In this union God or divinity is set above, as the head; man or humanity is placed beneath, as the feet or body. The head, like gold, is more precious than every base metal, because the Creator is believed to surpass all creatures. But the feet, or body, are an earthen or clay vessel, taken from wounded material yet rendered free from every vice. Above it, as a head, rises he who assumes it, advances what he has assumed, illumines what he has advanced, and does not consume it.

Such a head in Christ does not improperly claim primacy for itself: no ugliness of baldness strips it, nor does unseemly baldness disfigure it. Rather, safeguarded from every ugliness and endowed with inborn beauty, it is adorned, for its manifestation, with fitting locks [Col. 0433C] of hair. These locks are undoubtedly the virtues of heaven: the more worthy creatures, the pre-eminent choir of angels. While others slipped away and fell irrevocably into hell, these, adhering more firmly to the head, remain fixed for ever.

By the privilege of their excellence and the merit of their acquired dignity, they are likened not to any ordinary trees but to lofty palm trees, which warriors carry in their hands after defeating their enemies, when on a festival day they wish to display themselves in radiance as victors. Those are said to be the tall shoots of palms which rise above the others in straight height and which, once lifted up, stand more firmly at the summit on high, remaining alike at every season unbent in both harshness and beauty.

So the virtues of heaven are raised high above the rest, since they rejoice to enjoy him by whom they were saved when the others fell; they hasten always to lift themselves up to behold his face, and, abiding in desire, do not turn aside through languishing weariness. Thus, as though triumphant, they rejoice to bear the lofty palm, since now secure concerning themselves they glory in the marks of victory; fear having been put far away, they celebrate the festival day, carrying in their hands the visible branch of the gift they have obtained.

They indeed set themselves before those seeking to see God, and do not display Christ’s naked head indiscriminately to everyone. The brilliance of the gold does not admit the eyes that gaze upon it; but, so that it may in some measure be endured, the intervening hair puts itself forward. [Col. 0434A] This hair does not remove the presence of that head but promises it, and by a fitting progress afterwards ushers us into it. Though it first and more closely clings to that head by a kind of glue of love, it nevertheless condescends to us who follow far behind, through a certain likeness.

Clinging to the head, the beauty of the locks shines; condescending to us, their blackness appears. The locks are white as a lily when they present themselves to the golden head; but when they stand before us, they display the blackness of a raven. Those who contemplate Christ’s head—his naturally being one with God the Father—rejoice that the lofty, shining shoots of palms are like it. But those who consider that everything they understand has been made see it, when compared with the radiant Maker, as black.

Therefore angels, uplifted in their efforts to contemplate the Maker, see the Creator as far surpassing every creature. They see him as shining white—or, if anything clearer can be conceived—and themselves as though dull and like blackening ravens. For the more eagerly they cling to him in love, the more they discover that not only human beings are black, but angels too. And to those for whom the excellence of the head shines more brightly than gold, their humble consideration of themselves becomes darker.
