Thus Christ’s locks are, as has been said, like lofty palms when they attentively consider the height of his divinity; yet they are not inappropriately said to grow black like a raven when they confess with their own cry that they are far unlike him. For, while strongly and uniquely loving his eternal beauty, [Col. 0434C] they cry in humble voice that they are black and lowly, recognizing that what receives its beginning from another and cannot lack an end except through another is not comparable to that which remains through itself, without beginning and without end. This consideration, by which they exalt Christ’s head while angels humble themselves in the contest, neither diminishes nor detracts from their merits or their crown. Rather, they seek and confidently obtain the branch of victory precisely insofar as they openly proclaim themselves black and humble, like a raven.

## CHAPTER XIX

His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed and resting beside full-flowing waters. The Bridegroom has eyes with which he surveys and searches out all things; by their mighty circuit he advances and illuminates what is seen [Col. 0434D]. He delights to open them in order to bestow his gifts upon us, and, lest he condemn us on account of our merits, hastens to cover them. Therefore these eyes are said not to possess the eagle’s severity, but through a more gracious affection to possess the dove’s simplicity. For the eagle sees more severely and sharply for plunder; the dove more innocently signifies a gentle and simple discipline.

Since such eyes are likened rather to doves than eagles, I think it not unfitting to call them grace and truth. For by grace and truth God made all things; he saw the things made to be very good, and deigns to honour good angels and human beings with reward or crown. For he gave existence to angels who had not existed; when some of them fell, he willed not to fail those who remained. Those whom he saw by grace, so that they would not fall through proud perversity, he made fixed and stable in truth, so that they might no longer be able to fall.

But that angel whom God did not regard with the eye of grace turned himself away from the rectitude in which he had been made. Not being forestalled by grace, he did not receive a stable step in truth; turned away from both eyes, he wretchedly deceived himself beyond repair. Blessed, therefore, is that man upon whom divine goodness looks with the eye of grace. Although, under the tree, he was already held guilty because he had preferred his wife’s false counsel to the rule of truth and feared the voice he heard because of the recent shame of his nakedness, [Col. 0435B] God mercifully illumined him, dark beneath the fig tree, by the sight of grace and then recalled him, in an order sufficiently gracious, to the light of truth. Crushed by labours, so that he might pay for presumptuous perversity, grace instructed him in order to render him steadfast in truth.

But in order to confer this benefit upon the whole human race, and to set mercy above judgment over its wounded origin, when the world was already pressing toward evening, a light of sudden newness arose: the Word was made flesh, full of grace and full of truth. When his brighter rising poured itself upon us who were in darkness, it poured these two lights upon us. Having deigned to become man, he saw us with a double eye: that is, he joined indivisible truth as companion to grace that foresees.

For those whom grace saw, so as to endow us, though undeserving, with merits, truth also saw, so as now to heap rewards upon us as deserving persons. Certainly, he grants first merits only to those undeserving of them; and again, he crowns only those who are deserving with the rewards of merits. Thus he saw us with grace when he called us undeserving; having called us, he urged us toward righteousness and the merits of righteousness. He saw us also with truth when, as we gave assent, he offered himself as helper—he who had first offered himself freely as promiser.

The calling and the promise of one who strengthens were grace; the fulfilment, or benefit, of one who helps was truth. It is of no sufficient use if grace lavishly promises us some good thing unless truth, its companion, answers the promise. Rightly, therefore, the Bridegroom is said to have eyes by which he looks innocently and simply upon all the elect: the one, going before, does not begrudge but freely sees the undeserving; [Col. 0435D] the other follows them as though deserving and performs the office of truth.

Since these eyes do not view us harshly but observe us with harmless simplicity, they do not devise plunder, but extend themselves wholly toward our salvation. Rightly, then, the holy Virgin says that they are like doves, which their own nature makes simple and innocent. Doves dwell beside streams of water and full-flowing waters, so that they may foresee birds of prey which wickedly attack the more simple creatures—as those who investigate the natures of birds more curiously say, supporting the matter by certain conjectures.

That the doves are said to be washed, not with water but rather with milk, indicates that they are far removed from material doves. Since neither custom nor reason admits that doves are washed in this way, [Col. 0436A] this language plainly directs us to a spiritual interpretation. Therefore the Bridegroom’s eyes, as already said, are like doves not merely over waters but over rivulets of waters, when his grace and truth teach us the contents of the Scriptures, showing from where, through what, and toward what end the passing doctrine of the prophets tends.

For, drawing joyfully from the springs of the Saviour, they carry to us the Creator’s manifold promises. These do not cease to approach and pass us by with their murmuring promise until the thirst of those who wait is refreshed by the gift of fulfilment. Finally, the Bridegroom’s eyes are said to stand over this overflowing abundance of waters, and grace and truth behold us as placed there, in order to teach us that nothing begotten, like a stream, remains fixed, but hastens toward destruction by a natural flow and its own motion.

Since the form of this world passes away, things roll on in their course, and the instability of times and days permits nothing to remain, a purer and simpler understanding is necessary, so that our progress amid these transitory things may be firmer and more solid. Perhaps this is why the doves to which the aforesaid eyes are compared are said to be washed not with water but with milk: for snowy whiteness is naturally attributed to milk, and in it is signified the clean simplicity of dove-like grace.

This grace sees us in such a way, and also gives us sight in such a way, that it neither harms us nor wishes us to harm another. It wishes the mirror of the Scriptures to shine before our eyes, so that we may foresee the harmful attacks of others. Commending this purity of sight in the Lord himself, the prophet Habakkuk says: “Your eyes are too pure to see evil, and you cannot look upon iniquity” (Hab. 1). These are good eyes, shining with so great a purity that they mercifully choose not to see our wickedness. They cannot turn their gaze toward our iniquity, but rejoice to direct their vision toward our advancement.

Accordingly, they are said to rest beside full-flowing waters, because they illumine us and make us sit beside those streams when they teach us to approach and embrace with a more gracious affection the evangelical Scriptures, which flow with fuller teaching. Prophetic Scripture, like waters, makes us fruitful; evangelical Scripture, however, flows far more fully and abundantly. In the former, spiritual meanings are wrapped in figures and enigmas; in the latter, they shine fully and are unfolded in plainer words. The bright fountain of good formerly poured itself upon us in a remaining rivulet; afterwards it drenched us more abundantly in the mighty torrent of a river. Thus it offered us the useful irrigation of the old Scriptures and afterwards more fully satisfied our thirst through the Gospels.

Who would not commend these eyes of the Bridegroom, like doves, which mingle for us the rivulets and the fullest streams of Scripture? Their sight, ignorant of our evils, promotes and makes good fruitful; and, by a second advancement, cleanses us as with milky whiteness. That eyes, or the doves to which the eyes are compared, are said to sit beside waters or to use a milky washing [Col. 0437A] should be judged not frivolous but useful, not superfluous but rather mystical: in this the Bridegroom delights to work our salvation through grace and truth. Of him it follows: “His cheeks,” etc.

## CHAPTER XX

His cheeks are like beds of spices, planted by perfumers. After praising the eyes, the Virgin passes also to the cheeks, which she judges by no means unworthy of praise. In them, as was said long before (above, book I, ch. 2), the beauty of the face shines forth; and by reason of its comeliness the face deserves praise. Therefore the Virgin praises the Bridegroom’s face—that is, the beauty of his divinity—which blossoms with a kind of smile and glows with the bloom of nobility. It appears cheerful and pleasant to those who behold it devoutly, and is found useful and fruitful by those who reverently worship it [Col. 0437B].

Indeed, he is “fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44), whose beauty is beyond estimation and more fruitful than can be expressed. Although the Virgin judged nothing properly comparable to him at all, she nevertheless compared him, by a certain licence of speech, to beds of spices. Such beds are little gardens, rich not in gold, silver, or things of that sort, but in aromatic trees and many kinds of plants. From these a perfumer, with skilled hand, makes a medicinal ointment by which wounds are healed and pain is relieved.

So too the Bridegroom’s face—that is, his divine beauty—in which there is nothing polluted and no unseemly ugliness, is distinguished by inborn splendour and by a form adorned with worthy virtues, not by a transitory bloom of colour or a colour more deceitfully produced by art. In that beauty eternity is the beginning; immortality knows no end; tireless light shines; immutability stands firm; peace rests; power is able; wisdom is wise; the presence of charity burns. There flourishes a kind of commonwealth, confederated not by citizens but by virtues.

Their confederation is found neither feeble nor useless; rather, whoever loves it experiences it as powerful and beneficial, since its aromatic ointment, its compound or salve, proves a powerful and sufficient medicine for us who are sick. No garden-bed is planted by a hand so prudent as to become rich in such spices and such potent medicine; no perfumer has adorned a little garden with plantations so effective, nor crushed such herbs or spices in a mortar [Col. 0437D].

Or, certainly, the Bridegroom’s cheeks are his two substances or natures. The Creator willed to be united personally with the creature, and a twofold substance was found to meet in the one and same Bridegroom, marking, by its wondrous union, one face as it were. The meeting of these natures united God and man, who had formerly been far separated; it dissolved the wall set between them and joined heavenly things to earthly. In condescending to human beings, it brought them example and teaching, poured in the gift of grace, and supplied healing medicine.

Therefore these cheeks are compared to beds—that is, gardens—from which herbs and spices suited for aromatics are produced. Perfumers cultivate them with beneficial care; concern for healing the sick occupies those taught in the medical art. For when God had endured the world’s perishing through sin for many thousands of years, and neither human nor angel was able to uproot it, at last the perfumers wisely chose for themselves certain beds from which they gathered medicinal aromatics and remedies of salvation.

They joined together divine and human nature, assigning to them by lofty counsel a kind of exchange for healing. Having joined them in one person, as cheeks are joined in one face, they prepared an aromatic compound and restored the sick world with the grace of health. The perfumers seem to me to be none other than the Father, the Son, and their Spirit. They are said to take part, with a common counsel, in this aforesaid exchange. Although the Son alone must rightly be believed to be incarnate, the Father and Spirit are nevertheless said to work the incarnation with him [Col. 0438B].

Therefore the Bridegroom’s cheeks—that is, the two natures which wonderfully met in one person—like beds planted by perfumers, brought forth aromatic remedies. Their compound and the display of their remarkable art bestowed upon us the desired benefit of saving medicine. Worthily, then, the Bridegroom deserves to be loved also because of his cheeks. Their union contains the fruitful height of the mystery, which this same perfumer turns into ointment for us who are sick, and into a compound for those advancing, with the Father and Spirit working together. It follows: “His lips,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXI

His lips are lilies, distilling the finest myrrh. Anyone who is a teacher and not lacking understanding knows, I think, that in the Scriptures the efficient cause is sometimes put for the effect. Since we do not attain the effect of speaking except through mouth and lips, mouth and lips are often found used for speech. By the Bridegroom’s lips, therefore, the Virgin intended to signify his words. In a new figure of speech she compared them to lilies, because lilies, when seen, signify innocence more simply through their whiteness, and when crushed, more wisely supply a richer medicine.

The Bridegroom’s words know neither deceit, fraud, nor falsehood; when carefully examined, they put forth firm truth. When more graciously understood, they teach goodwill, innocence, and chastity; when more perfectly loved, they bestow true holiness upon those who love. These words, or lips, are said to distil the foremost or choicest myrrh—that is, to proclaim teaching effective and necessary for all—because although the wise of this world have wished, both in writings and speech, to condemn vices and commend virtues, they lacked spiritual efficacy, like “a sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal” (1 Cor. 13).

But the Bridegroom’s lips, uttering both the Old and the New Testament, provide saving instruction to their hearers in each. Although perhaps that which came first is called imperfect in some respect, because the time of grace and fitting hearers had not yet been found, that which came later provided the completion when the acceptable time arrived: the sun looked upon darkness, and light came to those sitting in shadow.

The two Testaments aptly correspond to the lips, one of which must necessarily be placed upon the other for speech. Their sound teachings form us; the Old, by itself, seems weak and insufficient, while the New, coming afterward, fulfils its insufficiency. When these Testaments are uttered by the Bridegroom’s two lips and fashioned by wise art for the instruction and salvation of us all, the Bridegroom likewise urges his hearers toward a twofold advancement—those, however, who have received through his gift spiritual understanding.

He invites them to love God and to care for their neighbours; while administering temporal matters, not to forget eternal things; and to let every righteous person put his hands to temporal employment or business in such a way that, at appropriate times, he may devote himself more eagerly to spiritual leisure. Since the Bridegroom’s teachings instruct us in these two pursuits, his lips are rightly two, and the Testaments likewise two, so that where no discord is caused by the diversity of things or acts, the same number may not be discordant in a like form [Col. 0439B].

For this reason lilies intervene by a fittingly graceful likeness. In form or colour they do not exceed the aforesaid number two; in their middle is found a little red, surrounded by spreading petals gleaming in whiteness. This central redness indicates laborious action which, while life is lived in this world, brings much suffering. No one is so blessed as entirely to avoid the presence of burning; some attain even to the shedding of their own blood [Col. 0439C].

The whiteness of the petals prefigures that blessedness in which the Bridegroom conforms our bodies to his own body. When whiteness is laid over us—the whiteness which reaches us through merits with grace—he hides, indeed absorbs, what was mortal, and girds us with immortal glory. Thus lilies corresponding to the lips in their twofold form or colour signify present things in their brief redness and future glory in whiteness. Their appearance then distils the finest myrrh—that is, most useful teaching—when its meaning does not waver in us who are capable of it.

## CHAPTER XXII

His hands are rounded, golden, full of hyacinths. By the Bridegroom’s hands, I think, the Virgin named his works, which he performed both before his birth and after being born from the Virgin. In them the praise of the one performing them is so incomparable that it proves that whatever he wills, he can also accomplish with easy effectiveness.

For this reason she calls these hands rounded, indicating that nothing obstructs the will of the worker. A carpenter is found to do nothing more easily than to work with a lathe, and what is done upon a lathe is found wholly round. Thus in the lathe is understood the ease of the worker, while roundness bears the praise of the finisher: whatever he wills, he brings to effect as soon as he wills; what he brings about willingly he also completes powerfully, knowing no relapse into failure.

This easy and smooth perfection of the lathe belongs neither to angel, nor human being, nor any simple creature, but only to him who alone willed to be born from a Virgin as God and man. He could do whatever he willed, not simply as man but also as God. It fittingly accords with this that the Virgin called the same hands golden, signifying, as it seems, divine power in gold. For as gold is said to prevail over other metals, so divine power prevails in the Bridegroom’s works.

To say nothing of other matters: that the Creator became, through his own work, a creature; that God willed to use his power, not his nature [Note: [Col. 0439D] See Letters 5 and 7.]; and that, while performing wonderful things in a human being, he also endured grievous things—all this was not, as it appeared, a defect of strength in submitting himself, but power. “I have power,” he says, “to lay down my life” (John 10). And the prophet says: “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53).

Therefore in all that God, made man, willed to do, neither lead nor tin—as some have thought—is believed to rule. Rather, to those who see rightly, gold appears and shines; though not comprehended by darkness, the light shines in darkness [Col. 0440B]. Divine power, brighter and more precious than all gold, though invisible to blind human beings, flourishes as if hidden more secretly in a treasury. Concealed from the eyes of unbelievers by the cloud of flesh set before it, it spreads outward, though unknown, into the branches of works.

Those worthy to understand this power rightly are not held merely by love for visible works; rather, they are kindled by hope of invisible goods and hang upon them in love and longing. Therefore the Virgin called the rounded hands not merely golden but, with equal testimony, declared them full of hyacinths. By hyacinths—stones like the air in colour—she signifies the heavenly goods which we are commanded to seek in love.

The works which God made man was seen to perform are plainly full of heavenly goods to those who behold them worthily: through manifold teaching they lead us into their true understanding, and through certain promises they bring us to hope for them. The dispensation of the incarnate Word contains nothing other than hyacinths. He invites all who are active and girded up to purchase them, because Christ’s temporal activity, which tends only toward heavenly goods, intends to make us ready and watchful to obtain those same goods through the merit of faith. Of his praise it follows: “His belly,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXIII

His belly is of ivory, distinguished with sapphires. Since the belly is regarded as the softer and more tender part of the body, it is rightly said to signify the Bridegroom’s flesh or humanity. Though he had long been God, he finally willed for our sake to become weak and to be like other human beings in nature, not through a defect of nature.

But because the Word made flesh (John 1) was wholly ignorant of fleshly sins, the Virgin significantly calls his belly not fleshly. The manner and order of his generation, though he knew it, had not been harmed by the softness of our customary condition or nature. For the vice which immediately attached itself to the first human beings when they sinned so wounded the generation of us all through their fault that no one who begets can wholly free himself from it; rather, he makes guilt pass, as if naturally, into what is begotten [Col. 0441A].

This vice, this transmission—now as it were a second nature—compelling both begetters and the begotten to lament their wound, weakens and enfeebles the belly of all, that is, flesh so begotten. No labour or skill removes its vicious softness. The Virgin alone, in conceiving, is believed not to have experienced this law harshly implanted, because she is known to have conceived of the Holy Spirit while knowing no man. The guilt which did not precede the mother who bore him in the ordinary manner did not reach the Son born of a mother without a father.

His conception not only inflicted no injury upon his flesh, but, through the working of the Spirit, supplied it with considerable strength. Just as our generation instils in us a nature deserving wrath, so his flesh, conceived of the Spirit, became stronger and firmer by nature. Because both man and guilt were absent from that conception, contrary to ordinary custom, and because the Holy Spirit further imparted to it a purer efficacy, he who was conceived, though flesh in substance, was not fleshly in vice [Note: [Col. 0441D] See the letters mentioned.]. He received a new strength of a certain eminent natural character.

Endowed with this nature, he was wholly ignorant of the inciting passions of the body that generally oppress other human beings living in this flesh. But those sufferings which are not punishments for his own fault but penalties on account of sins, he rendered subject to himself by a strength like ivory. For hunger, thirst, sleep, weariness, and other things of this kind, which Scripture records that he endured, did not come upon him necessarily by the law common to us all because of weakness of strength. Rather, by an innate power he surpassed the law implanted in us; he suffered none of these things except because, when, and as much as he willed.

Whereas we are generally compelled by necessity’s restraint, he exercised a will effectively endowed with power. Although as a man conceived of the Spirit he could have borne no human sufferings and suffered no injury, he nevertheless willed to bear injuries so that he might be believed by human beings to be human—the very purpose for which he had come. He came so that, having assumed the substance of flesh, he might truly be believed human, and that by suffering voluntarily he might heal the necessary sufferings of believers. Thus the ivory belly—that is, the hidden, inborn strength of the humanity displayed beforehand—might be turned into a remedy by which the sickness of us who are truly weak might be healed [Col. 0441D].

Such a belly was not only clothed and girded with ivory strength but also distinguished with precious sapphire stones. The true flesh, which a singular conception strengthened with wondrous power, was beautified by the added divinity with the excellence of miracles. Sapphire is like the sky when it is serene, appearing, as with a clear face, free from dark clouds. By this stone are rightly signified those works of the Bridegroom which are far above humanity and especially assigned to divinity.

To man belongs that he is flesh and does not know the unruly motions of flesh; that he is found harder against soft heats and becomes cold; that he performs the function of ivory, since, if linen cloth is placed beneath it, the cloth is not burned by a coal placed above it. To man also belongs that he could, by a natural privilege, forbid from affecting either his body or soul all the sufferings which we are compelled to endure as penalties; and that he could nonetheless admit them when he wished and as he wished, and, once admitted, restrain them so that they might have no more or less force than his dispensation required.

But to God belongs that amid these things he changed water into wine by a wondrous mystery; that with a small quantity of bread he satisfied many thousands of people; that he strengthened all the sick with the desired remedy; and finally that he raised the dead by the command of his voice alone. Therefore the ivory belly—that is, the robust sequence of human works—is distinguished with sapphires, that is, with the beauty of divine works. Amid those things which, as man, he could stoutly suffer as he willed, heavenly excellence rejoices at times to shine forth in miracles [Col. 0442B].

For he does not choose always to work merely human things, nor always divine things, but to adorn the sequence of his works with distinction. Thus, by ivory strength, he commends himself as more than Jonah or Solomon in his humanity, so that he may also show himself as God in humanity through the beauty of sapphires to those who believe rightly.

## CHAPTER XXIV

His legs are marble columns, founded upon golden bases. The Bridegroom’s legs signify the paths or journeys by which he visibly came to us when he found us weak, sluggish, and unable to travel. Though invisible in himself and by nature far unlike humanity, he condescended to human beings and appeared and became known as a creature.

One leg consisted in all that pertained to his incarnation and his temporally passing life; the other leg consisted in what pertained to his death and burial. Thus all his action and all his passion were as two legs by which salvation came to us, while those legs passed away and salvation remained [Col. 0442C]. These are not inappropriately compared to marble columns, because his paths are proved upright and strong: in willing what he could, there was righteous rectitude; in accomplishing what he willed, there was equal and sufficient strength.

And since no one doubts that a whole accumulation of works collapses if what seems well built is not founded upon a solid base, the marble columns are said to be founded upon golden bases. With these placed beneath them, the columns are not denied to be stable and praiseworthy. Whatever God, made man, willed to do or suffer, he is believed to have done or endured not under compulsion. Rather, he seemed to rest upon that twofold charity, more precious than gold, which gives firmness to all that is laid upon it.

For he loved God, whose command he willed to obey; and he loved human beings, for whom he knew his obedience to be beneficial. In the former he understood the first and greatest commandment to be contained; in the latter he did not neglect the second, which is like it. The Son loved the Father, because the Father loved the Son; he loved human beings, whom he and the Father together planned to save. He possessed this twofold love as certain underlying causes, for which he endured to become human and, as human, to do and suffer so many things [Col. 0443A].

## CHAPTER XXV
His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen as the cedars. Since above the Virgin commended the Bridegroom, as it were, part by part, proclaiming his praises individually from head to legs, she now, abbreviating her discourse, embraces him almost wholly at once and esteems his appearance highly by comparison with Lebanon. Among the other mountains said to occupy the land of the Jews—whose level expanse, according to those who know it, is constrained by the frequency of mountains—Lebanon rises higher, is more fertile in trees, and is whitened with perpetual snow. It is rightly said to bear the type of the Bridegroom, because no one among the saints can be compared with him in this excellence: made fruitful with plantings of virtues and a dense abundance of works, he does not know the burning of native vices, being whitened by the frost of the flesh. God the Father, indeed, chose him for the salvation of us all, so that through him every righteous person may advance from virtue to virtue, and so that the Church’s fabric may be constructed from his examples, character, and teaching, as though from incorruptible beams. The cedar, incorruptible by nature and knowing no sudden decay, by the abundance of its diffused scent repels the assaults of serpents; Solomon prudently wished to employ it when he strove to furnish either a house for himself or the temple promised to the Lord. [Col. 0443B–C]

Thus too the Virgin’s Bridegroom is of an incorruptible nature, knowing no injury from fault from the beginning of his generation. The fragrance of his works, the renown of his virtues, and the praise of his teaching drive every harmful thing far from the thresholds of discipline. Therefore he was chosen to be placed in the building, so that through him the house of God might be strengthened with worthy firmness; so that no one may perform anything at all worthy of praise unless it is commended by his good will, as by the strong presence of cedars. Whatever is raised by builders’ efforts cannot stand if it is not fortified by this cedar-like strength; and the heedless worker who does not measure himself by worthy judgment finds whatever he does without cedars liable to ruin. But one who chooses the Bridegroom as the safeguard of his whole work finds no ruin and suffers no loss, because his good will both gives builders a grateful endurance of their labours and bestows the far more pleasing strength of cedars upon the building. Of him it is further said: “His throat,” etc. [Col. 0443C–D]

## CHAPTER XXVI

His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable. Since taste resides in the throat and holds the nearer place in which it judges things savoury or flavourless, I consider taste to be figured by the name “throat,” according to that manner of speaking in which the container is commonly named for what it contains. The Bridegroom’s taste is therefore said to be not merely sweeter but sweetest, lest, if anything less were said, one should suppose that something is lacking to him; for whatever proceeds from him, if tasted with a sound throat, has no sweetness sweeter, no pleasantness more delightful.

Whether one considers distinctly that he is God or that he is man, and devotes oneself eagerly to discerning what belongs properly to each, one sees nothing more subtle than this distinction, nothing more wonderful than this union, and tastes nothing sweeter than so subtle and manifest a vision. For one sees that the divinity which assumes humanity is in no way consumed; nor did humanity fail, but rather advanced, when it was wonderfully assumed into God. There occurs no confusion, no conversion of one nature into the other, but a personal union in the mystery of a virginal generation. If heavy phlegm does not constrict the eye that contemplates this, and if the mind tastes the sweetness of this mystery with an open throat, what can be found sweeter than this taste, or more blessed than this throat, to which it is now granted to experience what angels desire? [Col. 0444A]

And if angels desire God, whom they contemplate without ceasing, and venerate him made man with inexhaustible wonder, then human beings too rightly both desire and marvel at the same one in his entirety; with their whole desire they embrace him who is altogether desirable. For he is God, and there is no other besides him; he is a man clothed in human form for his own sake. He is worthy to be loved, not only because he is God, not only because he is man, but because, by the saving mystery, he is at once the same God and man. He is a man, I say, not such as any other man, but one through whom every human being may be saved; so that, just as a man was the downfall or ruin of humanity, so—indeed, far more—this man may be humanity’s remedy. [Col. 0444B]

Who, then, would not wholly desire such a one, wholly love him, wholly admire him? Who would not rejoice to embrace with whole desire one who is God and neighbour alike? Who would not seek such a one more earnestly, hold him more eagerly if he should find him, and strive to instruct others by fitting admonitions to seek him? Therefore the prudent Virgin, who knows no rival in love and fears no concubine, everywhere proclaims the one she loves so that he may be loved; and having deserved to see him thus, she does not wish to envy him to others, but gladly provides for those standing with her with anxious affection. Therefore she concludes thus: “Such is,” etc. [Col. 0444C]

## CHAPTER XXVII

Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem. Such, I say, is he by whose tender love I am held; and, as it seems to me, I have not been deceptively ensnared, nor has unrestrained love, as sometimes happens, deceived me, because fleeting speech has still not worthily praised him. Although much has been said by which he is shown to be commendable, this praise must nevertheless still be judged insufficient, because I cannot yet fully express in transient words the one whom I joyfully feel him to be.

I have undertaken to continue his praises so extensively, although what ought to be said has not yet been adequately expressed, so that he whom I love may become known to you to some degree, and that your mind also may grow warm with love for him. For he cannot be loved unless he has been understood; nor does he seem to be understood unless he has also been loved. Therefore I desire that the one whom I have loved, and whom I have understood to become a friend to those who truly love him, may himself be understood and loved by all. [Col. 0444D–0445A]

You therefore, daughters of Jerusalem, strive with all your strength both to love him and to be loved by him; for nothing is holier than loving one so benevolent and so powerful, and nothing is happier than being loved by one who does not know how not to love one who loves him. “I love those who love me” (Prov. 8). When the praises of the Bridegroom, expressed in such diverse kinds of figures, have been concluded, the Virgin is silent for a little while and awaits the daughters’ reply, considering whether perhaps through this hearing they have received a fuller grace by which they may be carried more vehemently into love for him whom she proclaims. But before their response is set forth, I have thought it fitting that my pen should withdraw somewhat from its labour; and where the Virgin has fallen silent, let the pen also choose silence, so that here at last the fifth book may gladly attain its end. [Col. 0445A–0446A]

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0445]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0445A–B]

Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned aside, that we may seek him with you? Having heard the praise of the Bridegroom, the daughters of Jerusalem are stirred and provoked to love him with a greater longing. They rejoice that the Virgin has spoken beforehand so much concerning him and has pursued the character about which they had earlier inquired. For above they had said, “What is your beloved more than another beloved?” Now they rejoice that he is understood by mystical likenesses; but because he does not yet permit those who understand and in some measure love him to see him clearly, they ask where he has gone, so that he may be sought by them more certainly.

Earlier, when the Virgin hastened to open the bolt of her door (Book IV, chapters 10–12), hoping to find closer at hand the one whose voice she had heard knocking at the doors, “he,” she says, “had turned aside and passed on.” He did not offer himself to the Virgin’s sight, perhaps in order that, by withdrawing the vision, he might make her more intent on seeking. Since, therefore, the Virgin is found to have commended the Bridegroom in many ways, and since he is known—as has already been said—to have turned aside, the daughters of Jerusalem ask and wish to be instructed more carefully: to whom and to what place did he go and turn aside, as though he wished to make himself present there?

“This one,” they say, “whose praises you have woven in so many forms, concerning whom you so earnestly commanded that your love—indeed, your love-sickness—be announced: how shall we seek him, or be able to find him when sought, when we do not know the place to which, after escaping us, he chooses to go? Tell us, then, whether he hastened to the left or rather to the right. Tell us, if you know, to what or to whose merit he turned aside, so that in seeking we may not be led astray by a wandering error, but may follow in imitation of the merit of the one to whom he came. [Col. 0445C–D]

For when, under your instruction, the place or the merit of the place becomes known, our minds will burn more ardently to hasten there; and in seeking the Bridegroom we shall be carried away with a desire not equal to yours, perhaps, but at least like it. Without your accompanying favour we shall not enjoy finding him. We know indeed that whoever seeks him while neglecting you will prove altogether imperfect in that search; nor does the Bridegroom wish to be found by us or by other seekers unless he sees that they are first accompanied by your favourable fellowship. With you, therefore—that is, with your favourable patronage—we shall seek him whom we cannot find without you and your good will. By your benefit our devotion shall follow him, having been taught beforehand in what place, or through what merit of a place, he dwells. [Col. 0446A]

And indeed no one else can better teach us where the Bridegroom has gone or where he has chosen to make himself present than you, who have entered the sanctuary by the gift of his grace and have more fully known the secrets of spiritual understanding.” To this the Virgin replies: “My beloved,” etc. [Col. 0446B]

## CHAPTER II

[Chapter 6.] My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices, to feed in the gardens and to gather lilies. You wish to know where he whom I love goes or turns aside, when he does not yet wholly incline himself to your desire, when he does not set before you, as though you were hungry, full refreshment, and in what places he displays himself more fully and abundantly. He has delayed your hope, indeed, but has not rejected your desire, choosing to go down into the garden which he has made his own by the gift of grace, so that he may honour it with a favourable vision as a bed of spices, and, having found lilies, may rejoice in their ripe harvest.

When he does not answer the apostles fully according to their wish, and does not favour their prayers with a consummating result, perhaps he descends to deacons as to a pleasing garden, in which he finds Stephen more worthy than the rest to reap. For Stephen, diligently cultivated as a bed, humble in conflict, and crushed by manifold suffering like spice, both displays lilies in the whiteness of an innocent mind and, when the sickle comes, shows himself fit for harvest. Considering what the compassionate Saviour undertook for the salvation of the saved, what wounds he endured, and finally what death, Stephen burns—indeed, is on fire—to imitate what Christ displayed beforehand, judging it far too grievous if he is not the first to render the due return. [Col. 0446B–D]

Therefore, in suffering martyrdom, fearing that he may be preceded by another and impatient of delay, he strives to be found readier, believing that he will have somewhat greater glory in martyrdom itself if, by shortening the time, he can attain it first. To him and to those like him the Beloved loves to turn aside when he wishes to carry them from the threshing-floor into the granary; for, as though withdrawing himself from those whom he wishes to remain longer in this life, he hastens to present himself to those who depart from here prematurely and more swiftly. Of this she adds: “I am my beloved’s,” etc.

## CHAPTER III

I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine, who feeds among the lilies. “I know,” she says, “that my beloved displays himself more closely and openly to those whom he now intends to gather white as lilies for harvest, those whom, threshed on the floor and stripped of the ragged covering of chaff, he wishes to convey to the granaries and to the full repose of souls. Therefore I strive with all my strength to please him: to make myself a garden, a bed, a shining lily, so that, when he comes and finds me flourishing with due cultivation, he may take me from the midst and make me cleave to himself for ever.

“I, I say, prepare a pleasing repast for my beloved, that he may feed and suffer no wound of bitterness. For him, fed and refreshed in me, I prepare a dwelling, so that, detained by the dwelling, he may thereafter make no mention of flight. And the beloved, as I perceive, prepares himself for me, that he may love and gather me and draw me to himself; when I have been gathered and drawn, he will give me nothing better than himself, so that, with anxieties driven far away, I may sleep and rest together in peace. [Col. 0447A–B]

“He, I say, while I am still placed upon earth, raises me to the love of heavenly things; and lest I cling long to earth, he seems to sharpen the harvesting sickle. He delights to feed on my lilies, not only while they are still rooted in the earth, but also if, when the time is ripe, they are set before the table already reaped. Therefore I strive to prepare myself for him for this purpose and desire to obtain the hoped-for joy by merits; he rejoices to render me a return—indeed, to add more than a return—for his good will delights in bestowing benefits.”

## CHAPTER IV

You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army arrayed in battle order. Seeing that the Virgin is ready in his praises and desires to be dissolved sooner and to be always with him instead, the Bridegroom, though he does not yet hasten wholly to fulfil her desire, nevertheless inclines himself in benevolent affection to console her. “You,” he says, “who burn with so great a desire to see me, and feed upon my praise while you are not yet able to obtain what you hope for, form for yourself a wonderful beauty by this affection and effort, and conform yourself by a beautiful likeness to him whom you love.

“Like the beautiful one, therefore, you may fittingly be called beautiful, since you rejoice and strive to devote yourself to imitating him in such a way that, diligently rejecting every defilement of the enemy, you may rejoice as a friend in those things which are salutary and pleasing to the friend. In this affection and advancement you do not know how to envy others, but seek to advance everyone to better things by example and teaching: rival of none, detracting from none, burdensome to none, but solicitous for all, drawing all, and sweet to all. For nothing is sweeter than, by loving God, to embrace one’s neighbour in such a way that one who rightly loves chooses not to turn away from either; to love God and embrace him with tender arms in such a way that one does not at all envy, but even rejoices that he is loved by any neighbours whatever.” [Col. 0447C–D]

But the Virgin, rightly loving the Bridegroom, knows no envy—greater than which, according to a certain pagan writer, even the Sicilians have devised no torment [Note: Col. 0447D, Horace, *Epistles*, Book I, to Lollius]. She does not fear a rival and is not tormented by suspicion of a concubine; indeed, she gathers together all whom she sees loving the one whom she herself loves. She flourishes, indeed, with so sweet and peaceful a spirit that she rejoices for the Bridegroom to be loved by all; she grieves that he is not loved, and judges that her spirit is burdened in no other way than when the one whom she so greatly desires to be loved is not loved.

Seeing, therefore, that the daughters of Jerusalem love him without envy, she chooses rather to rejoice, and with a joyful spirit strives to do whatever she can, so that those who behold the beauty of her works may rejoice to imitate them. She is sweet when she desires that the daughters of Jerusalem should please the Bridegroom; she is comely when she strives by words and deeds to show herself as a pattern of pleasing him. She is sweet, indeed, because she desires them to possess the same glory as herself—except perhaps that she wishes to be the unique mother of the only Son. [Col. 0448A]

Yet she does not envy them even the dignity of mothers, knowing that whoever worthily does the will of the Bridegroom, or Son, shall deserve to be called his brother, sister, and mother, as he himself is found to declare in the Gospel (Matt. 12). But because among mothers she deserved to hold an outstanding primacy, she who by singular grace bore God incarnate from herself: although no small height of merits is granted to others, her comeliness, sweetness, and beauty are especially commended beyond the rest. She is beautiful as she burns with love for him who is “fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44), whose sweetness shines in his character and whose beauty shines in his deeds; incomparable with any human being, she resembles that Jerusalem which, established in heaven, contemplates God without ceasing.

For that holy and mutually harmonious multitude of angels, fortified like a city by indissoluble strength, shines with such beauty that nothing worthy of blame seems visible in it; and it burns with wonderful desire that humanity too may deserve to attain this same end. Because the Virgin is believed to have attained it through the Bridegroom’s grace and, while remaining in the flesh, to have found merit above flesh, she is rightly proclaimed beautiful like Jerusalem; and when the enemy beholds her beauty, he marvels in terror. [Col. 0448B–C]

For, seeing her fortified with so many and such great virtues, and finding no access anywhere, as though before an army arrayed in battle order, he is amazed that the firmness of angels flourishes in a human being and that the order of battle and power of an army exist in a single Virgin. In angels there is such order and such steadfastness of battle-line that the enemy recoils at the first sight, and, shaken by great terror, attempts nothing against them, dares nothing against those whom he sees, supported by extraordinary order, prevailing in strong prudence. When Jacob once saw them, he said: “These are the camps of God” (Gen. 32). And Elisha said to his servant: “Do not fear, for there are more with us than with them” (4 Kings 6).

Elisha does not fear, nor does an enemy assault shake him, because the ordered battle-line of angels repels it far away. Their stronger order admits no oncoming assaults of enemies and does not permit the threatening sword to enter the circuit of the camp. With equal terror the enemy flees the Virgin after attempting her, marvelling at her order of virtues and ordered strength. Considering that a human being possesses the likeness of the heavenly armies, he fails at the first encounter and, recoiling farther away, cannot sufficiently abhor her. [Col. 0448D]

The holy Virgin is rightly compared both to armies and to angels, because in both the excellence of chastity is commended: neither flesh nor intercourse of flesh ever harms angels, and “camp” (*castra*) received its name from chastity (*castitas*) because camps are removed from domestic embrace. Thus the Virgin is found terrible as an army in battle array: although she bears God in the flesh, she experiences no union of flesh. Hearing her proclaimed chaste in conception, the enemy is terrified and flees; nor does he comprehend so great a mystery by understanding. [Col. 0449A]

## CHAPTER V

Turn your eyes away from me, because they have made me fly away. Although in my judgment you are proclaimed beautiful, sweet, and comely, I nevertheless wish you not to search into things higher and inscrutable, nor suppose, while you live here, that you can obtain fully those things which I will show to no mortals except after this life. Recall, then, as it were, and restrain the eyes with which you stretch yourself toward invisible things, when you recognize that you cannot yet reach them. And while you stretch yourself toward the things before you in hope and desire, know that you do not yet apprehend them fully or effectively.

Thus you will seem to turn your eyes away from me when you compel them humbly to turn back toward yourself; and when, still living mortally, you turn to your own inadequacy, enduring not a rejection from my excellence, as it were, but a postponement, you turn away. Long ago through Moses, the most truthful prophet, I declared that no living human being had attained my vision; whoever is mortally wrapped in the girdle of flesh is obscured and darkened until released. “No man,” I say, “shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). [Col. 0449A–C]

So long as a human being is bound by the stains of this present life, he is darkened by a kind of cloud—not damnably, indeed, but punitively—and cannot behold my divinity as it is unless he ceases to live and to be confined in the fellowship of flesh. Therefore, the more intently you fix your eyes upon the inaccessible light, the more you perceive it to be withheld from you. When you strive to see and yet are compelled to recall your eyes, I seem to fly away before those very eyes, repelled as they are. For because they strain with every effort to see and yet do not fully apprehend what they desire, I fly away from them when they find themselves darkened and weak, or even when, though clear-sighted, they discover me to be incomprehensible.

What I carefully tell you about turning these eyes away is not a rejection or a command; rather, I declare it so that you may know that the full vision of me cannot be given to any human being unless that person first rejoices to be stripped of the burden of flesh. [Col. 0449C–D]

## CHAPTER VI

Your hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of sheep that have come up from the washing; all are bearing twins, and none among them is barren. Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from what is hidden within you. Lest the Virgin be disturbed because she cannot yet behold the Bridegroom’s face, and because he swiftly flies away when he is truly believed already to be held, the Bridegroom hastens to soothe her by repeated praises, so that, her ears being delighted, she may bear the delay more patiently.

Since these praises were set forth above (Book IV, chapter 8) in almost the same words, and were expounded there, so far as God gave, I refrain from repeating the exposition here, lest I seem to impose delay upon the reading and weariness upon the reader. Yet when the Bridegroom repeats these praises and brings them forward so often, he does not act idly or speak carelessly; rather, it belongs to one who loves—if he burns intensely—to recall what he loves, indeed to repeat it diligently. [Col. 0449D–0450A]

## CHAPTER VII

There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number. The Bridegroom considers those who attain the Catholic faith by the gift of grace and pursue the firmness of that faith either in reality or in appearance. Wishing figuratively to indicate their differing merits, he seems mystically to assign them different names. By the name “queens” are fittingly figured those who, protected by a royal enclosure, are overcome neither by the enemy’s deceit nor by violence. As they guard their ways so as not to offend in word or deed, they approach the bed of the eternal King through progress in spiritual things. There they are filled with lofty knowledge, rejoice in humble conscience, rest pleasantly in the Bridegroom’s embrace, and are made fruitful by his benefit; and by the fruitful seedbed of teaching they bear him spiritual children, through whose fertile birth the nuptial chambers are enriched and gladdened.

They are rightly said to be comprehended in the number sixty, because the perfection of the law and of works is known to be commended in ten and six, and multiplying one by the other produces sixty. For just as six times ten, so ten times six, makes sixty. Whoever rejoices to fulfil the ten commandments of the law in deeds, therefore, or who orders whatever he does in temporal life according to the form of the law, is fittingly included in the number sixty; that person’s fruitful dignity is said to please the highest King. [Col. 0450B–C]

In this number one may also find five and twelve, whose multiplication appears to arrive at sixty; for twelve multiplied five times, or five twelve times, unquestionably reaches the sum of sixty. Five is rightly said to be multiplied by twelve in the person who moderates the five bodily senses in the manner and order wisely prescribed by the pattern or institution of the apostles, whose perfection is commended by the number twelve.

“And eighty concubines,” he says. As those who love the Bridegroom chastely and bear him children are queens, so those who do not love sincerely yet nevertheless preach are concubines. Their knowledge and preaching do indeed bear spiritual children, but because their conscience is wounded, those who bear them remain animal, or carnal. They are not unfittingly said to be eighty, because they are known to hold the law’s number ten in word and knowledge, but, lacking the twofold love, fall back into the number eight by embracing in life and morals the things of the world. [Col. 0450D]

For there are four seasons of the year, four elements of the world, four regions of the earth, and finally four passions by which each person is carnally affected and troubled, and by which one stains with a ruined will whatever one rightly knows. The wise philosopher commands and urges that such passions be repelled, knowing that one ruled by carnal passion errs. Even if one does not uproot it completely, though it is naturally implanted, one nevertheless errs if one does not repel it by fitting discipline.

> “Drive away joys,” he says,  
> “Drive away fear,  
> And banish hope;  
> Let no pain be present.”  
> —[Note: Col. 0451D, Boethius, *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, Book II, metre 7.]

Whoever, bereft of understanding, is found to double the aforementioned four—that is, to strengthen carnal passions, contrary to the philosopher’s prohibition, by adding another passion—such a person, completing the number eight, is not yet permitted to reach the number ten, because in the evils that he performs no pattern of twofold love is found. [Col. 0451A–B]

“And maidens without number.” When queens and concubines preach and sow the spiritual word, although the desire of the former is righteous and that of the latter carnal, a new offspring is surely produced by their effort or labour, which receives the Bridegroom by faith and follows him with readier affection. Whether the preachers of the word are righteous or unrighteous, many are begotten through their word in faith and knowledge; and, just as from the good, so also from the evil, abundant offspring is born—numerous not to any human being but rather to God alone. Of them he says: “I shall count them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. 138).

Those who assent to teachers preaching the faith are fully known to him who numbers the multitude of the stars. But to us, observing the fish of every kind gathered into the net, their multitude is altogether innumerable as the sand. Since they have received the rudiments of the faith they have heard but have not yet advanced to proclaim to others the teachings of that same faith, they are called maidens by reason of their newness or imperfection. They are unknown to a human being whose knowledge is still dull and whose eye is darkened. Whether they are good and later chosen into vessels, or evil and cast out and rejected, so long as they are held in the net in a confused order, they are not countable by any human being. [Col. 0451B–C]

## CHAPTER VIII

My dove is one, my perfect one; she is one to her mother, chosen for her who bore her. It is certain that many cleave to me in lawful love, and that many, having renounced [something unspecified in the supplied text], attain the sole appearance of truth. So many everywhere are begotten in faith through the word and teaching of preachers that they seem altogether innumerable to anyone who carefully considers them. But the Virgin, pleasing, useful, and fitting to me above the rest (2 Tim. 2), knows no plural number, but is one: burning with desire for me alone, she is held in religious unity; one is joined to one, in singular, or unique, dignity.

She is one, I say, because she is not carried away into diverse and perverse desires; she is never taken, even for a little, from him whom, as the one, she uniquely loves; she is not bound away from the Bridegroom’s full contemplation by enticements of earthly things or by ties of many affections, but only delayed by the burden of flesh. Rejoicing in hope of future things, grieving amid present transitory things, she despises what is present and groans for eternal things still absent, like a dove. While she is held in the flesh, she seems to herself harshly wandering; nothing satisfies her until she beholds the Bridegroom more fully with joy. [Col. 0451D–0452A]

She is one because, cleaving to him, she loves nothing except him; and if she seems perhaps to love anything, she loves it only for his sake. Thus whatever she does, she refers it to no one but him, watching over herself as one for the one, until at last she sleeps together in peace. And because, awake in purpose, she is so gathered into love for the one, she has deserved by the merit of this unity to be called my perfect one: one to whom, as far as present life permits, no holiness is lacking, and in whom, while I dwell, the fullness of the whole divinity dwells.

Nor is there another to whom I would promise so great a gift of grace, while she still complains that she is held in the prison-house of flesh. Yet if she takes care to look at herself while living mortally, let her dare to confess herself imperfect. “Not that I have already received,” says one, “or that I am already perfect” (Phil. 3). And another: “Your eyes saw my imperfection” (Ps. 138). If Paul and David truly know themselves imperfect, although not despised in your eyes, O God, on account of their merits, to whom may such great or such pre-eminent praise be given among either the new or the old, unless perhaps to the Virgin, who is rightly preferred before all others? [Col. 0452A–B]

She, therefore, is one to her mother and singular in this excellence. At her singularity the remaining multitude and common society are astonished; every person marvels at the Virgin so exalted and so perfect; her mother rejoices in such a unique and singular daughter. But what is the mother who wished to rear such a daughter for herself, cherished and advanced her, and enabled her to reach so great an excellence, if not grace itself, so worthily and rightly proclaimed? The angel Gabriel testifies that the Virgin is full of its gift: “Hail, full of grace” (Luke 1).

Grace itself, by its own goodness, wiped away the stains of our sins and filled the aforesaid Virgin with such an outstanding benefit that, though she bore the one One, she nevertheless remained an intact Virgin; and, remaining a Virgin, she answered the fruit-bearing grace with a new and singular offspring. She is therefore one to her mother, because grace, her mother, seems to have had neither a first nor a second like her, one who displayed herself equally Virgin and fruitful. Grace honoured no other with so many titles of virtue, but adorned this one—or unique one—with a singular privilege. [Col. 0452C–D]

But lest anyone should think that she earned this privilege and was not chosen beforehand, but rather herself chose, she is said to be, just as one to her mother, also chosen for her begetter, so that not only her perfection but also her prior election may be commended. Grace, indeed, chose her and, as it were, begot her when she did not exist; when she existed, the same grace received, nourished, advanced, and assisted her. In choosing or begetting, grace holds the place of a begetter; in nourishing and advancing, it performs the office of mother or nurse. The grace which foresaw and chose the Virgin by provident knowledge also mercifully received and gathered her by maternal affection: there it was like a begetter, when it foresaw in secret that she would come; here, mother or nurse, when it more visibly advanced her to incomparable progress.

For grace advanced her and formed her in its own workshop: it formed her in desire, character, and discipline; it also formed her in letters, mature judgment, and serpent-like prudence. Dove-like simplicity and perfection completed what had been formed. Perhaps for this reason she is called at once “my dove” and “my perfect one”: so that the dove-like perfection present in her may be recognized, and so that those seven virtues naturally bestowed, as it were, upon doves may be understood as spiritually perfected in her in the same number. As those who have examined the natures of birds more carefully say—not attending to wandering report but rather to known truth—the dove is naturally marked by a certain sevenfold set of virtues, in which the perfection of our Virgin is found to be spiritually figured. Since I am found to have delayed speaking about these long above (Book II, chapter 13), when this epithalamium first seemed to introduce doves in the second book, I shall now pursue, as I can, what I promised there, since no mention of doves occurs in what follows. [Col. 0453A–B]

A dove lacks gall. Our Virgin also, from the time when the angel Gabriel greeted her and when the Holy Spirit came upon and overshadowed her, offered God no bitterness either of actions or affections, but distilled the honeyed sweetness of her character, sweeter than a honeycomb.

A dove does not tear with its beak. The Virgin likewise did not repay due retaliation to any who injured her; rather, in every affliction she displayed unbending patience, so that even when she saw her only Son handed over and crucified, she preferred that the ungodly be converted rather than afflicted according to their deserts.

A dove nourishes the young of others. In the sea of this life the Virgin keeps her mind so serene that she does not judge it alien to give merciful help even to strangers and the unworthy. Rather, to all who are in need—to Jews as much as to Gentiles—she gives useful teaching in words and shows instruction in conduct with equal benevolence. [Col. 0453B–C]

A dove willingly lives beside streams. So too the Virgin diligently attends to the streams of the Scriptures: she embraces books, lives by the prophets’ admonitions, is continually intent upon divine readings, devotes herself to spiritual study, and is not detained by outward concerns.

A dove chooses the better grains. Likewise, when the Virgin gives care or study to the Scriptures, she not only prefers whatever is useful to all harmful things, but, with discerning eye, chooses better things among the good, embracing more eagerly whatever she knows to be more pleasing to the Bridegroom.

A dove willingly nests in the rock. The Virgin likewise performs whatever she can in firm faith; her activity is established by the rocky safeguard of faith. Her surpassing faith is not disturbed by a flood of waters, does not grow weary in stormy fury, and is not shaken by the hammer of fear.

[Col. 0454A] **The dove groans instead of singing.** The Virgin, although she modestly rejoices in the aforesaid sixfold array of virtues, nevertheless, because she does not yet behold with unveiled face Him whom she loves, and although in these things, as in six days, she strives to accomplish everything exceedingly well, yet because she is not yet granted fuller rest on the seventh day, still, like one in need and displaying the nature of a dove, she groans: while she cannot attain what she desires, while she is held back and longs the sooner to be released. By this groaning the Virgin detracts nothing from her merits, nothing from her holiness; nor does the dove’s lament take anything away from that unity for which, to the best of our ability, we have commended her above. Rather, she is perfect in accordance with place and time; indeed, if she did not now groan, she would more rightly be called—and would be—imperfect. Of her it is added: “They saw her,” etc.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0454B]

**The daughters of Zion saw her and called her most blessed; queens and concubines also praised her.** Above, the daughters of Jerusalem are called daughters of Zion: they are those who, as was said before, accompany the Virgin in this nuptial song; who truly behold the present marriage by faith, and, while others are darkened, are not held in wandering error or ignorance. Observing the Virgin distinguished by such great virtues, perfected through labour together with grace so completely and incomparably, they are astonished, marvel, and proclaim her not merely blessed—which they see to be common to very many—but rather most blessed, that is, more excellent than all the rest.

For although many others may deservedly be called blessed, both the Angel and Elizabeth declare that this woman is blessed among all—that is, above [Col. 0454C] all women—she who, contrary to the ordinary course of the flesh and against nature’s powerful prohibition, while remaining a virgin alone brought forth the blessed fruit of her fruitful womb. Since they see this and cannot adequately unfold so great a mystery, nor find anything comparable among women, the daughters of Zion exalt her and confidently call her most blessed, plainly proclaiming her excellence in speech untainted by envy.

For the Apostles, perceiving with lynx-like understanding that Christ was born of the Virgin and begrudging this benefit neither to Jews nor to Gentiles, affirmed not only the Son but also the Mother to be most blessed; through such a vision they themselves deserved blessedness according to their measure. “Blessed,” he says, “are the eyes which see what you see” (Luke 10). Not only the Apostles, but other teachers succeeding them in place and time, became in the Church praisers of this great Virgin. Some of these, through the fruitful merit of chaste desire, are queens; others, who do not love but feign love, are more rightly called concubines.

For in these days, when faith fruitful throughout the whole world increases, charity grows cold among certain people as wickedness abounds. Many praise the Virgin, stirred by most devout love; many, denying virtue, are coloured with an appearance of piety. For the Virgin’s honour has grown to such a degree, and her fame or renown has filled the whole world so thoroughly, that not only true but also false believers seem to rejoice in her praises; and those whom devotion does not move are made to praise her by opportunity. Therefore this Virgin may be called marvellous and greatly to be marvelled at: the Angel and the prophet declare her blessed above all.

[Note: [Col. 0455D] Blessed Elizabeth is meant.]

Those who love her rightly rejoice to exalt the blessed one in praise; and those who neglect to love her nevertheless now dare not cease from praising her. In her praise it follows: “Who is this?” etc.

## CHAPTER X

**Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed for battle?** The Bridegroom invites devout hearers to marvel, so that they may become more readily disposed, as is fitting, to praise the Virgin. When they hear the question, “Who is this who comes forth like the dawn?” they are admonished by her progress to marvel all the more at what precedes.

At the rising of dawn darkness is alarmed, night thins out, obscurity is scattered, the denser shadow vanishes; new light arises, a certain aspect of the world shines forth, things receive their colour, and the earth’s surface grows cheerful. Our Virgin, therefore, resembles this dawn: she visits us oppressed by deeper darkness and denser shadow; when, as it were, she strikes them with sudden terror by the majesty of her hand, they disappear, and she brings us the morning brightness.

The moon, as they say, does not shine by its own light, but rather by another’s; what it receives from the sun it reflects to others with its full orb. It is assigned especially to give light to the night, inferior only to the sun, yet preferred to all the other stars. So too the Virgin: whatever light, grace, or honour she possesses, she knows to be from Christ, who is of higher excellence and to whom alone she is inferior; she presides over the other saints, drives away our darkness, and rejoices to restore light to us. She is therefore fair to us—indeed fairer than the moon—she who at last refreshes with timely light those oppressed by a long night; who leads us back by a guiding torch when we wander and grope for the way; and who, through watchful care, introduces us into the desired presence of the sun.

She is also chosen as the sun. The sun was made to appear a greater light than both stars and planets; wherever it turns, it is seen to shine pre-eminent. It knows no shadow of night, does not grow dim at the onset of the mighty, travels around the world in a steady course, and is not chastised by repentance for a fall. But from the time when the Virgin entered the sanctuary of fuller grace, she surpassed not only every saint but also the earlier Apostles. Burning with excessive love, tirelessly radiant in holiness, she cares for us all, suffering nothing deadly within herself. She rejoices to traverse the world oppressed by darkness with sleepless care; to restore its growing-cold ruins with most fervent affection; to drive away the clouds of our sins by her radiant intercession; and to make fruitful the soil of our minds by her most gracious regard.

In this she remains and perseveres; to this she has been divinely chosen: that in affection and effect she may be perfect among the other saints, distinguished like the sun by the steady brightness of virtue’s rays, never neglectful of herself and not forgetful of us, though far beneath her. Since she is found, acting as the dawn, to shine upon us in our darkness; since she knows that she has the moon’s beauty only from another; and since she seems to continue in her begun course as the sun with steady step—she is as useful and welcome to those who rightly contemplate her as she is terrible to enemies, like an army arrayed for battle. Since you may recall the character of this battle-line or terror, as it has been set forth and explained above, it is unnecessary to repeat the earlier exposition.

## CHAPTER XI

**I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys, and to observe whether the vine had flowered and the pomegranates had budded.** Why the Virgin is likened, as stated before, to the moon and sun, and why she is adorned with such an excellence of virtues as to be preferred to others, is not hidden: the Bridegroom confesses that he descends to her, showing that this is mercifully bestowed upon her through his presence.

Thus in Egypt he showed that he would grant a benefit to the children of Israel when, after they had been oppressed with mud and brick, he at last descended from heaven’s lofty throne; when he visited the afflicted in their misery with a merciful regard, and, having visited them, freed them from slavery by a most mighty hand. “Seeing, I have seen,” he says, “the affliction of my people, and I have come down to free them” (Exodus 3). Likewise, in the Gospel he is said not to have descended without purpose (Luke 6), but in order to console the crowds assembled in a level place. Though he understood that they were weak and poor in spiritual goods, he did not raise them to the heights by the counsel that he knew; yet he did not disdain personally to visit them where they stood on the plain, and he did not neglect to bring forth gifts of blessing from the fullness [Col. 0456C] of his treasure.

If this descent into Egypt or into the plain is found to have been fruitful, far more rightly will his descent to the Bride not be judged idle. For she is like neither dark Egypt nor the turbulent plain, but a garden of delight, rich in fruits and nuts. The Virgin is a garden of nuts, into which the Bridegroom says that he descends, because no difficulty or inconvenience whatsoever opposes his descent. Although the heaven of heavens and the dwelling of angels delight him, nevertheless the nuts of the garden, the flowers of the vine, and the shoots of pomegranates do not displease him.

In a nut, the outer husk is rather bitter; beneath the husk lies a hard but brittle shell; enclosed beneath the shell, however, the kernel provides sweeter pleasure to the eater. The Virgin, therefore, is a garden of nuts when she is troubled by the bitterness of sufferings and temptations; when the malice of persecutors wickedly opposes her repose; when whatever this world either flatters or thunders at her becomes utterly bitter to her; when everything that shines to those of corrupt taste is foul to her. She is a garden when, like a harder shell, she is strengthened by wonderful fortitude; when she is found unfailing in vigils, fasts, and prayers; when she is in no way softened by the reproaches of the Jews or the swords of the Gentiles; when in every distress she is found to stand bravely with untiring firmness.

Although she is found fixed and stable in all things, she nevertheless longs to be broken and dissolved, and to appear more openly before Christ. For she knows that he delights not in shell, husk, [Col. 0457A] or any bitterness, but in the kernel offered to him—the sweeter it is, the more joyfully he feasts. The hidden kernel is the inward sweetness of the loving soul, concealed from the eyes of the persecutor deceived by malice. When the shell is broken, it is not taken away but presented, as though by the hands of one offering it; it is set before the Bridegroom, who presides over the same table or banquet.

The loving Bridegroom then descends into this garden of nuts when he shows himself near and gracious to his beloved in her labour; when, diligently wishing to advance her “from strength to strength” (Psalm 83), he desires to see there, with a favouring gaze, the fruits of the valleys. For what the humble virtues strive to accomplish in the Virgin, and what they lovingly expect from their labour or merit in assured faith, the Bridegroom sees and approves; he makes all things prosper and ripen under favourable grace as though beneath a blowing west wind.

The fruits of the valleys are the labours of humble virtues, diligent endeavours, hands readier for works: fruitful actions more pleasing in a well-planted garden. Although they are not yet entirely ripe for harvesting or storing, they delight the eye and will soon pass to eating. When he has seen the fruits of the valleys, the Bridegroom nevertheless desires to see whether the vine, blooming worthily, hastens to answer its cultivator: whether the ordered succession of virtues is found to shine with fragrant beauty; whether, by its flowery scent, it keeps every harmful poison from its boundaries.

For fear that poisonous envy might wound the tender Virgin, fitting renown fortified her and flower-like beauty raised her up. Though by a new manner she brought forth among us the swelling of the womb, she nevertheless put far away the stain of unlawful suspicion and the serpent’s poison. Not only did the presence of sins in her conscience not confound her, but neither did adverse rumour flush her face with shame. So abundant was the vine’s flower, so great the vigour of its fragrance, that her integrity was free both from guilt and from shame.

In such a garden the Bridegroom sees that pomegranates too are not lacking: hidden in the will is a spirit ready for suffering, willing to endure not only death but also the threatening sword; and, if not yet in effect, already in affection growing red with the shedding of blood. The pomegranates do not yet openly show themselves, but to the attentive observer they display themselves as though in bud. Passion does not yet grow red, because the executioner has not drawn his sword; but the will, more firmly rooted, already puts forth a bud on its shoot. To inspect this, the Bridegroom did not send a messenger beforehand; rather, with humble goodwill he himself strengthens and revisits the Virgin. By his gracious descent he cherishes the garden, rejoices to ripen the fruits of the valleys, causes the vine to flower, and the pomegranates to bud.

## CHAPTER XII

**I did not know: my soul was troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab.** Seeing that the Bridegroom had wondrously descended into her garden, and that by his wondrous descent he had brought equally wondrous grace, the Virgin cannot adequately express what she beholds spiritually within herself. Rejoicing in present knowledge, she confesses her former ignorance.

“I did not know,” she says, “before the Angel announced that I was full [Col. 0458A] of grace, and the Holy Spirit overshadowed me with a sufficiently radiant cloud; before the Son of God made me fruitful by his kiss, and new fruitfulness honoured my virginal conscience—I did not know that so much grace and so great a gift could be imparted to me, that I, a lowly handmaid, so inexperienced compared with others, could receive such experience.

“Before he enclosed his garden—not, however, with hedge, wall, or rampart; before he sealed the fountain—not, however, with an iron lock, bar, or metal; before he descended into that same garden and inspected it with his abundant gift of goodness—I did not know him to be so powerful, so gracious, and so rich in such great generosity. Therefore, when he descended to me and in some measure showed himself to me, I was troubled, alarmed, and astonished, marvelling at so great a benefit. My soul laboured in a fortunate failing toward its salvation: failing in a saving labour—or rather, being advanced, I was troubled.”

“For I see that the Bridegroom came down not poor or needy, not as just any person from the people, but arrived, as the powerful do, on horses or in chariots. I had no strength remaining, as I considered that he both powerfully works salvation and fitting religious worship is preserved in that very power: ‘You ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation’” (Habakkuk 3).

You know that the ark of the Lord, captured and held for several days by the people of Ashdod, was finally returned free when they were compelled by injuries to their buttocks.
