Placed upon a new cart, it was brought back into the house of Aminadab, where more reverent worship and more fitting religious observance were rendered to it. Aminadab means “willing.”

[Note: [Col. 0457] The author reads 1 Samuel 5, “Aminadab,” that is, “a willing people,” instead of “Abinadab,” that is, “a willing father.”]

It signifies him who willingly chose to come from the Father’s bosom and unite human nature to himself in the Virgin’s womb; who presides like a king or charioteer over angelic powers, while all serve him in swift harmony as a chariot-team. When the Virgin more attentively observes such rule and service, she confesses that, having formerly been ignorant of them, she is somehow troubled by this knowledge. She recalls that festive gatherings of people were customarily arranged for former weddings, whereas angelic chariots and invisible drummers were not seen. Perhaps they bear in this nuptial song the name or image of chariots because this wedding solemnity reaches and aids the fourfold world; and because the four living creatures described in the prophecy of John or Ezekiel are enlisted as heralds or yokefellows in the same undertaking.

Therefore the Virgin, formerly ignorant, is troubled because of Aminadab’s chariots when, brought into his sanctuary, she marvels at the thousands upon thousands who minister to him; when, as though delivered from the enemies’ territory, or from Ashdod, she is received both by the king’s mighty excellence and by the priest’s worship.

Aminadab, speaking to her, adds: “Return,” etc.

## CHAPTER XIII

**Return, return, Sunamite; return, return, that we may look upon you.** Lest the Virgin seem to return to Aminadab’s house through her own merits—for she is the ark of God, held captive for a time under the law common to us all—Aminadab shows that the effectiveness belongs not to the one returning, but rather to the mercy and mighty goodwill of the one who calls her back.

The Bridegroom therefore calls back her who is called Sunamite, that, released from bonds, she may return with unencumbered steps; that she may not remain among the people of Ashdod and the enticements of carnal senses, but may be voluntarily borne back, in the vehicle of a four-sided newness, to the house of the loving one.

[Note: [Col. 0459D] An allusion to Hosea 14:5.]

Sunamite means “captive,” “despised,” or “scarlet.”

[Note: [Col. 0459D] Here, as elsewhere (cf. cols. 284, 447, 449), the author excepts Christ alone from original sin. He had evidently read Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, I.ii, ch. 24; Ambrose, *On Psalm 118*, sermon 6; and Athanasius, sermon *On the Mystery of the Incarnation*. He wrote at the same time as St Bernard and maintained the same view as Bernard in Epistle 174 and Book I on the Song of Songs. He had also seen what St Fulgentius says in *On the Faith to Peter*, chapters 2 and 26. St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 14, answer to objection 1; Bonaventure on III, distinction 3, question 2; and others all held this view and spoke as they thought. But today we must observe the constitutions *Cum praeexcelsa* and *Gravissimis*, Book III, *Extravagantes communes*, title “On Relics and the Veneration of Saints.”]

But the Virgin, like others, was naturally a daughter of wrath. Her manner of life could not wholly free her from the stains attaching to that condition; although she possessed virtue capable of driving out damnable sins, she was still burdened by a bond and captive under nature’s laws. Since she was naturally conceived in sins, her manner of life was infected by faults, even if slight; by reason of that infection she was despised in the purer eyes of God, but finally her humility was regarded through grace. For he “looked upon the humility of his handmaid”; and he called her back once and again, freeing her by a twofold calling from captivity and contempt, so that the divine law might afterwards keep her wholly free from guilt whom the law of wrath, the law of birth, had held guilty.

For this reason the Bridegroom adds that he calls her back once and again, and with repeated speech more earnestly invites her to return. The calling first draws her from the harsher sentence; the second makes her firm through a condition—or a grace—more abundant. For after first saying, “Return, return, Shulammite,” he adds: “Return, return, that we may look upon you.” “I desire her return,” he says, “so that she may no longer be held captive and despised; I desire her return so that she may be more pleasing to me, may love the one calling her back, and may burn—not with fire, but with love—and may worthily be called scarlet because of merit, not colour.”

Scarlet dye bears the appearance of fire, signifying love; for one who loves burns. But because this fire, or the Virgin’s love, is necessarily twofold, since, as I recall having already said, she embraces in the Bridegroom both God and man, the Bridegroom twice invites to this twofold love her whom he enriches before others with so great a gift that she is like scarlet twice dyed. Thus the first repetition calls back one captive and despised; the second makes her, far more firmly, loving and beloved. Both he and the companions whom he wishes to be present at and aware of this mystery delight to see and behold her as she is—so scarlet. When the angels observe her freed from guilt, contrary to the usual law of nature, and scarlet with love beyond the capacity of visible creation, they cannot sufficiently marvel at such excellence; rejoicing with the Bridegroom, they desire to inquire concerning the Bride.

## CHAPTER XIV

**[Chapter 7.] “What will you see in the Sunamite,” they say, “except choirs of camps?”** “You invite the Virgin,” they say, “and again and again desire her to return; through a wondrous advancement you desire to turn all of her toward your good pleasure, so that neither the guilt proper to her may retain any power in her nor she fail to delight us who behold her as one worthy by the privilege of love.

“What, then, will you see in this Sunamite, who returns so often? What will you judge concerning her when she is presented before your sight? For we see in her such perfection of character that not human beings but rather camps of angels correspond to her.” Scripture calls angels camps because the violence of enemies cannot penetrate their ranks, and because the Emperor presiding over them gives them such confidence that every attacker, repulsed far away, flees. Of them Jacob says: “These are the camps of God” (Genesis 32).

They may also fittingly be called choirs because they are harmonious in affection and musical in unwearied praise. Such melody sounds in the ears of their presiding Lord that neither the harmony of heaven, of stars, nor even of planets compares itself with it. Whatever virtues the angels see themselves to possess, they also see the Virgin surpass in them without envy; and because they recognize in her, by a wondrous novelty, an angelic life, they marvel and now ask the Bridegroom whether he knows something further.

“What will you see,” they say, “in this Sunamite whom you call back, except a wonderful harmony of praise and exquisite strength; except praiseworthy choirs and the ancient armies of angels; except virtues in harmony and unwearied strength, like that of camps? We already see these things in the Virgin whom you love so greatly; and if anything remains hidden, we should gladly desire to see it. We wish you yourself, whom we know more certainly to understand these matters, to recount to us both these things and the rest in which we rejoice to behold her.”

To this the Bridegroom replies: “How beautiful,” etc.

## CHAPTER XV

**How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince.** The Bridegroom does not delay graciously to answer what has been asked. Yet in answering he chooses to turn his speech toward the Virgin, thinking that he will not displease the aforesaid companions if, while they ask questions, he chooses to show himself affable to her. He therefore does not cut off their hope by silence when they ask; rather, he turns to her, to whom he does not tire of speaking more often. As he begins to address her with new praises, he wishes the attendant bridal companions to hear everything he says.

Now he begins to recount her praises from her steps, whereas above (Book IV, chapters 7 and 22), when he praised her, he chose to begin with her eyes. Perhaps, if repetition of praises makes drowsy hearers weary, a different order and varied colouring may render them wakeful and attentive. Thus above (Book IV, chapter 23), when he frequently wished, as it were, to praise the Virgin part by part, he did not pass over her breasts; but, beginning with the upper parts, his praise proceeded so that he spoke from the breasts downward, not of the remaining limbs. The Virgin herself, in the preceding book (Book V, chapters 18–27), praising him in detail or limb by limb, descended in sequence from head to legs and their bases. The Bridegroom, returning the favour, arranged the series of his praises in this order, but altered that very order for the sake of variety.

I judge the Virgin’s steps to mean her deeds. She wished them to be hidden from us, though we are far more distant; yet through them she wished to come into our knowledge, for her holiness would remain hidden from us if she had chosen sluggish or uninterrupted sitting still. These steps were not marred by a halting limp; girlish frivolity did not accuse them of wandering and instability; a withering disease did not turn them back toward the weak and beggarly elements of this world; nor did an unjust tax-collector extort from them any tribute. They possessed such lovely health and such vigorous beauty, and persevered with such constancy in that beauty, that admiration rather than description befits their praiser; for not only full expression but even a foretaste is sufficient for the hearer.

To show that nothing necessary is excluded from these steps, as they proceed over the uneven ground of this life they are not bare. Rather, lest the drought of the sun or the harshness of winter inflict any burden, a certain mortification of pleasure clothes them, as it were, with shoes. Whatever pleasant or painful thing threatens to overthrow in them anything useful or honourable, a patient insensibility advances to repel it, permitting nothing destructive to reach the tender foot. In such sandals lies hidden the beauty of the steps, which is not fully apparent to us but is better known to the Bridegroom, who loves to be present to the Virgin in all things and makes her like himself as a daughter.

Perhaps for this reason he now calls her “daughter,” a term he has nowhere used above: because he has especially shod her after his own pattern and caused her, in sandals, to correspond to him more expressly and closely, by granting that, while placed in the flesh, she should not feel the claims of the flesh. He is rightly called the prince of the prerogative of this gift: having become flesh, he refused to be bound by fleshly things; he willed to preserve unharmed by vices the humanity he assumed, and to conform the chosen Virgin to himself as a daughter. Removing from the midst the privilege of obstinate wrath, he is rightly called, by Isaiah’s testimony, the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9). Whoever is granted truly to experience this peace within himself—for many say “peace, peace,” among whom peace cannot be found—whoever, I say, is found by the gift of grace to share in this peace is rightly marked with the filial name because of likeness.

## CHAPTER XVI

**The joining of your thighs is like necklaces fashioned by the hand of a craftsman.** By a beautiful manner of speaking he commends the Virgin’s integrity when he compares the joining of her thighs with skilfully made necklaces. For in the thighs carnal generation is commonly figured, and the denial of generation and barrenness of the thighs in their joining. Thus the sinful soul which embitters God by fleshly enticements, as the prophet recalls (Isaiah 51), spreads apart her feet to every passer-by; not content with a lawful husband, she receives other men—indeed adulterers—under a dissolved law; she does not endure the narrow limits of the marriage-bed but prostitutes herself to seductions in an enlarged bed.

But the Virgin, who in conceiving knows no man whatsoever, who by the ancient privilege of nature does not consent in body any more than in mind to such things, holds through thighs joined with an unbreakable union a firm covenant of perfect chastity from that time onward. For as she is recorded to have been at conception, when the Angel proclaimed it (Luke 1), so she is believed, by pious faith not departing from truth, to have continued. Her body was not afterwards separated from her mind, nor her mind from her body, but both remained undivided in continuous agreement and uninjured affections.

This joining was rightly compared to necklaces, which are known to be fashioned by a skilled hand from gold and stones. They not only bring the beauty of ornament through their own worthy value, but also join the upper edges of the garment to protect the virginal breast. Thus the joining of the thighs, more precious than gold or stone, preserves flesh and makes the spirit industrious in gaining merit. It protects the Virgin from admitting a corrupting seducer and also admonishes her to love him through whose benefit she is so adorned.

For necklaces, as some say, are named either from protecting (*muniendo*) or from admonishing (*monendo*), because those protected by such a gift are admonished by it to drive far away the envious corrupter with such a defence, and in return to love their benefactor graciously. A skilled craftsman made these necklaces with his own hand; though denied to many, he did not deny them to the Virgin Mother. Paul earnestly desired that they might be granted to him; I do not know whether, while living here, he perhaps deserved to be blessed in this way.

## CHAPTER XVII

**Your navel is a rounded bowl, never lacking cups.** The navel joins and binds together the surrounding parts of the belly; lest they sag through natural softness or perhaps flow away, it draws them back and constricts them. In it a woman is said to have the seed-bed of generation, although in men this is chiefly held in the loins.

[Note: [Col. 0461D] An allusion to Job 40:11.]

The Virgin’s navel, therefore, is her steadfast teaching. While the Apostles were giving way through fleshly fear and feminine softness, she stood firm in manly faith; she did not give way with similar levity, but by a certain steadfastness recalled those who were light and more wandering than was right. For when the men saw that they had too lightly abandoned their purpose of faith, while she, though shaken by overwhelming grief, remained firmer still—after the accomplished resurrection had been shown in several visions, while the Virgin was intent upon contemplation and devout prayers—they humbly returned to her, ashamed of what had gone before. Henceforth they cleaved more credibly and steadfastly to her teaching.

For her rounded bowl is a fuller and more perfect shaping, because the birth of the risen Christ had become more fully known to her. Everything that is read in Scripture concerning him over the long succession of ages she drank in more abundantly and poured out to her hearers in due measure. Her rounded bowl—or her easy perfection in exposition—does not dry up through want and is not confined by narrow capacity. Filled with cups and intoxicated with the wine of wisdom, it is offered to peoples far and wide; it suffices for all and, when offered, never fails.

## CHAPTER XVIII

**Your belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies.** The belly is humanity, weakness, or temporal life, which needs the fostering of clothing and bodily nourishment. Its very softness requires such care of natural support that spiritual progress and eminence are thereby accumulated within it. For although the Virgin does not hate her flesh but preserves it, she does not weaken the powers of the spirit in caring for it. While necessarily cherishing it, she reserves herself for hard labours, in which she heaps up an abundance of merits like wheat.

As this abundance rises upward like a point, without exalting itself through the windy multitude of chaff, it is both pleasing to the cultivator for making bread and fruitful for sowing seed. The Virgin’s manner of life is shown to please not only the Bridegroom; it also works like a seminal power in those who attend upon her, as she instructs them, calls them toward all that is better, and admonishes them to grow and advance to higher things not by word but by example.

Lest robbers violently presume to take away such great merits, thieves plunder them, or mice stealthily carry them off, they are surrounded not by stakes, stones, or mortar, but by lilies—that is, by the gracious charm of inviolate purity.

## CHAPTER XIX

**Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle; your neck is like an ivory tower.** The force of love causes these same words, spoken above, to be repeated; they need not be explained again, for brevity’s sake. Yet it may be asked what the change means and what ought to be figured in it, since it may be regarded as different. Above it was said (Book IV, chapter 12), “Your neck is like the tower of David”; here, however, it is “like an ivory tower.”

The tower figures a certain strength of the Virgin; ivory, the chaste and pure beauty of that same strength. For the tower shows her fortified by virtues against enemies; the cold natural to ivory shows her cleansed from burning passions. Thus the Virgin is a tower when she bravely defends herself from enemies; she is an ivory tower when she shows herself free from fleshly heat. She is a tower, I say, when the encounters of malicious persons dread the mass of her virtues; ivory, when she shines white in cold sternness like winter frost.

## CHAPTER XX

**Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude.** I think enough has been said about the eyes in the second book (above, Book IV, chapter 7, and elsewhere); nor do I think it necessary to repeat what has been said. But since a new comparison seems to be introduced here, that novelty itself requires explanation.

Heshbon is a city inhabited by a multitude of peoples. Pools are springs, or lakes and a fitting abundance of waters, which, being situated at the city gate, refresh the inhabitants of the city itself with manifold generosity. Therefore the Bride’s eyes, not infected with serpent-like dregs but, as the second book explains, conformed to dove-like ways, are perhaps here likened to pools because they impart saving teachings to those who have been washed, or wash those who have been instructed. For those upon whom the Virgin deigns freely to look with her eyes, those upon whom she graciously chooses to have mercy with a benevolent regard, she calls back from the open-field error and brings us to the useful gate through which we are introduced to the citizens, household members, and assembly of those who worthily deserve admission.

Heshbon means “girdle of sorrow.” By her regard the Virgin restrains us from public licence; having entered the narrowness of the gate, necessary sorrow girds us. She does not allow us to remain happy any longer amid all the clamour outside, but wishes us, afflicted in misery, to be worthy of mercy. When the Virgin looks mercifully upon people in this condition, she protects us as citizens and members of the household of the daughter of the multitude. This daughter—that is, this city—admits many strangers who come to her, but by a wondrous law she admits none except the sorrowful and miserable.

This is their present refuge; this is the protection they presently use: the Virgin cherishes them with the fitting benefit of her eyes and visits the sorrowing with diligent care, graciously refreshing them now in such a way as to promise them something much better hereafter. I have experienced what I say. When, under the pressing judgment of God, the sons of my mother fought against me; when, though strangers spared me, those whom I believed to be my own flesh injured me; the ashes of this Heshbon—my own sorrow—would have forced me to perish, had not the Virgin deigned quickly to help with outstretched hand. She stood by me and did not cast away care for me far from herself; rather, she placed herself in the midst against the tongues of the malicious. Seeing that they raged not with zeal for justice but through hostile faction, she shut the mouths that spoke such wicked things with the strong hand of mercy. To her rightly belongs what follows: “Your nose,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXI
Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks out toward Damascus. Pestilent men, who are the devil’s champions and athletes, resembling him by whom they are sent, indiscriminately stir up quarrels; blinded by malice, they do not know the rule of judgment, and if perhaps they do know it, rancour and envy corrupt their knowledge. But the Virgin, seeing that some need a greater protection, does not know how to fail those whom she knows are suffering injury. She shows herself, to those who consider rightly, to have a strong nose: not flattened like a monkey’s, not weakened by softness, not shaved away.

For although, as though silent, she sometimes permits her own to be afflicted—perhaps insofar as it is expedient that they be amended by afflictions—nevertheless, when the malice of the envious grows more violent and attacks, the discernment of this strong one rises and resists like the tower of Lebanon. Moreover, she prevails and opposes the malicious more effectively because she is firmly established in Christ, who is the mountain of Lebanon; set and built upon him, she looks out and keeps watch toward Damascus, so that by her vigilant gaze she may call it back and turn it from its purpose. Damascus is interpreted “thirsting for blood.”

[Col. 0465A] The city of the lost ever thirsts for our blood; but lest it drink it all, the Virgin prevents it by the regard of her eyes. These both bestow a saving defense upon us when we devoutly ask, and powerfully inflict harm upon that evil thirst. For her discernment knows when and how to console those who suffer unjustly; but those who inflict injustice, whether to strike with punishment or to await in patience. She knows whom to look upon with a pitying countenance as humble and cast down, and conversely whom to despise as Damascenes, their malice thus deserving it.

In all these things she does not attend to her own pleasure alone, but greatly esteems the will of the Bridegroom, whom she desires to please. Loving his friends, she rejoices at their advancement; over his enemies she wastes away, as it were, with a perfect hatred. To her the following is fittingly added: “Your head,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXII

[Col. 0465B]

Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head like a king’s purple bound in channels. The Virgin’s head may not inappropriately be called her mind or intention. Her remaining works, like dependent members, appear so subject to it that they deserve neither to be directed toward progress nor raised toward pleasing God unless they are governed by a preceding intention as by a head.

Since wickedness does not weigh this intention down, nor weakness soften it, but it raises itself toward higher things with the sound desire of pleasing, it has deserved to attain both the height and name of a mountain, whose interpretation is found not to lack the fruit of mystery. Carmel is interpreted “knowledge of circumcision,” or “knowing circumcision.” Circumcision, as the Jews know, is an incision of the flesh, cutting away the foreskin—that is, figuratively, carnal desire. The Jews held this figure given through Moses literally; but those held it spiritually who endeavoured to put aside what the flesh suggests.

Therefore the Virgin, whose intention is plainly pre-eminent in desire, is rightly called Carmel, knowing nothing of subjection to carnal things. Circumcised spiritually in heart, ears, and all her senses, she pleased not a man but God alone, undivided, in giving birth to her Son. That new mother indeed beheld in herself the wondrous excellence of a mountain when, uniting herself to the Bridegroom, she circumcised carnal desires; when the Spirit so overshadowed her, and spiritual circumcision so cleansed her, that in bearing a child she did not transmit to the one born the inherited guilt of flesh.

The hair of her head—that is, her holy and most subtle thoughts—

[Col. 0465D] by which no slight beauty or adornment comes to the head, is compared to kingly purple bound in channels, while it is dyed purple, as it were, by a certain blood: faith in and love for Christ’s Passion. Among those said to be skilled in this craft, purple is customarily bound in bundles within narrow channels; water is then poured over the bound material in a due manner and measure, so that through this pouring the dye may be useful in dyeing wool purple.

Or, according to some, at Tyre and Sidon, where this craft especially flourishes, fine white wool is confined in channels; when the blood of the shellfish is poured over it, it is changed into a purple colour, and thereafter, being purple, indeed is called “purple.” It is said to be royal purple because it was formerly, as it were, the special prerogative of kings to be clothed in purple garments, and by this sign kings were undoubtedly distinguished from others.

Thus in the Gospel (Matthew 27; John 19), because Christ had, as it were, presumed to assert himself king, the Jews who persecuted him seemed intolerably enraged; and before killing the one whom they did not wish to reign over them, they mockingly clothed him in a purple cloak.

The hair of the head is arranged in narrow channels when the Virgin’s thoughts are subjected to spiritual exercises; when faith in Christ’s Passion prepares for itself a purer place; when rain descending upon the fleece turns all of it into love. The blood of the sea-fish is the love itself of the Redeemer, who was made man in the world at the command of the eternal Father. Upon the Virgin, whom he sees enclosed in the dye-vat of discipline, he pours and infuses love for his blood by the grace of healing.

[Col. 0466B] From this she is said to become purple—indeed, purple dye—and thereafter she is offered to the highest King so properly and specially that she is fitted no longer for human but only for divine use; and she is shown to know and love not a human man, but God and man. This God-man may also fittingly be called the Virgin’s head: he who, in chief excellence, is proclaimed the mountain of the house of the Lord above the tops of the mountains. His name is assigned, perhaps, to no other mountain than Carmel, because he both knowingly and powerfully removes the true foreskin from Israel.

The hairs, however, which are known to cling to the head at the root yet to wander farther unless discipline strives to restrain them, are all the Virgin’s acts. In Christ she has established them more firmly from their root, and by judicial strictness has called them back

[Col. 0466C] from excessive progress. She willed them to be brought into channels—that is, into lowly and humble narrow places—and that the joy of the Passion, like purple dye, be laid upon them. Her whole manner of life knows not how to think lofty thoughts, but to fear, and to shine in red martyrdom as a living sacrifice.

## CHAPTER XXIII

How beautiful you are, and how fair, dearest one, in delights! Your stature is compared to a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters. Since the praises begun from the feet have come in a straight sequence to the head and hair, and have found nothing in all the foregoing that is not praiseworthy, he gathers the Virgin’s beauty into a kind of brief summary, calling her “dearest,” in whom he finds nothing blameworthy.

“How beautiful you are,” he says, with a will knowing no sluggishness but vigorous; “how fair,” pursuing a just will by an effective hand. And, that the praises may be strengthened by a worthier cumulative conclusion: “dearest to me in so many delights.” In one so praiseworthy I complain of no loss, because your stature is like the commendable palm tree: narrower below, spacious above; you rejoice in a good beginning and are fruitful with a better end.

For just as a palm is set before a girded warrior, so surely it is given to the ungirded warrior as victor; and what had led and stirred up the spirit of the combatant to labour is raised in praise when borne in the hand of the triumphant. Your stature, therefore, is found like this palm when persevering labour is adorned with so many titles of praise; when, beginning from below, you are enlarged by fruitful progress; when, with the world conquered, you rejoice as a champion in the now-certain prize.

[Col. 0467A] Your stature is rightly said to resemble a palm because it is known to stand in an upright purpose rather than bend; and because its standing is granted to advance unwaveringly to perfection, it deserves to obtain the palm—that is, the worthy title of victory. And your breasts, by which you nurse or abundantly feed those around you—that is, your pattern of life, by which you instruct the ignorant both morally and spiritually—are like not useless plants or fruitless trees, but fruitful clusters rejoicing in stored wine.

Those who attentively perceive you to be perfect both morally and spiritually, and thus raised from the bosom of earth to the lofty likeness of a palm, marvel and are astounded; they cannot remain within their own limits when, among all women, they see none like you. Therefore, squeezing your breasts with hands, as it were, of reflection, and foreseeing more fully that the perfection of both kinds of life flows from them, they seem to have pressed out for themselves certain clusters and brought forth the intoxicating wine of astonishment and admiration.

## CHAPTER XXIV

I said: “I will climb the palm tree and seize its fruits; and your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine, and the fragrance of your mouth like the fragrance of apples.” In the following verse the Bridegroom clearly indicates whence such grace above others is bestowed upon the Virgin, so that her breasts are considered like clusters and her stature like a palm; he shows that what he foretold, he afterwards fulfilled.

“I said,” he says,

[Col. 0467C] “I will climb, and your breasts shall be clusters.” His saying is his purpose: what he willed to be ordered from eternity, what he willed, remaining fixed within himself, to conceal for a very long time. At last, when the happy fullness of times shone forth, the evident certainty of this saying was given to this Virgin.

For he who had long been hidden within himself or in the Father, being presented to the Virgin—an angel indeed having been sent, but he preceding the angel—willed that wonderful saying to be displayed as though visible, when he granted himself, invisible by nature, to be seen by grace. “I said,” he says, “and what I said I shall not keep silent longer, but I shall climb the palm tree”—that is, I shall appear visibly. I shall ascend into the Virgin; through her I shall show myself to others; through the flesh assumed from her I shall triumph over the prince of the world.

For the depth of my divinity was inaccessible to human beings. Led by love for them, I shall ascend on high, so that, when I have been visibly exalted from the deep, hidden, and invisible, I may draw all things to myself, not deprived of the power of drawing.

[Col. 0467D] The Virgin, therefore, is a palm tree, lofty through the privilege of merits. The Bridegroom willed to climb into her as into a sycamore tree. His ascent—that is, his assumption of flesh—is regarded by every believer as a wild fig (*ficus fatua*); but for one who looks worthily and receives humbly, it produces saving fruit.

The Bridegroom gladly seizes this fruit when he finds absolutely nothing displeasing to himself in it; when he accepts it, approves it, and rejoices that what the palm’s fruitfulness is given to bring forth—the salvation of the faithful—accords with his good pleasure. He seizes it, I say, when its most faithful guardian draws near, when he fortifies it beforehand and takes care that it leave nothing exposed to birds; when he cherishes the palm itself and advances it into such strength that everything fitting for the salvation of the world depends upon it.

[Col. 0468A] From it depend Christ’s flesh, the Passion of his flesh, the wood of the cross, the blotting out of sins, the flight of night, the return of true light, the reconciliation of the world, steadfastness in virtues, and confidence of rewards. He gladly seizes all these things, being their author and disposer. When these have been seized, the Bride’s breasts are compared to clusters of the vine because, through her benefits, the minds of worthy contemplators are made drunk; and her scents—or the fragrance of her mouth—become like apples, because her reputation and teaching taste sweetly in the nostrils of hearers. The following is added: “Your throat,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0468B]

Your throat is like the best wine. If what is conveyed to outsiders as a proclamation of faith is like clusters and apples, what and how great are the things that may be believed, which are felt by the Virgin herself, who with lavish hand offers what is suitable to the throats of the hungry? Who but one blind would think that she is unfed amid things so great and so many?

She herself rejoices beyond others to perceive so many and such eminent things. Above all she drinks in how great a sweetness is found in the Bridegroom; what others scarcely taste, since they are not adorned by so great an excellence of merits, she feels and savours more fully with eager draught. The Bridegroom figuratively called this taste her throat; desiring to commend it, he compared it with the best wine. For anyone to whom the Virgin’s taste or throat becomes known seems to himself to have drunk, because he is made unspeakably joyful.

[Col. 0468C] For the Virgin, not begrudgingly, makes her taste known to whoever she chooses; she gladdens that person’s heart as though with wine. So much is she granted to know and feel in the secret of her heart that one to whom it has been granted to share it cannot fail to rejoice. The Bridegroom rightly calls this wine the best: whoever has drunk it judges none better. Neither Naboth’s vineyard nor perhaps the vineyard of Sorek offered a like draught; Noah did not drink better wine from the first vineyard that he planted.

But because this taste or throat of the Virgin is more fully disclosed to no one, nor does any other rejoice more in its perception, than the Bridegroom—who has no need to be taught by passing speech, for he sees and approves whatever is usefully thought—the Virgin, knowing that this wine is more worthily pleasing to its praiser, as if snatching the word from his mouth, hastens to reply.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Worthy for my Beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew over. “He commends,” she says, “my throat—or rather, what has now become sweet in my throat—which no one thoroughly approves whose dull palate is numbed. But he, by whose gift so great a grace shines forth to me, drinks it with a full draught; his cup does not run dry through want.

“I have experienced the wondrous sweetness of this wine; and, since the Bridegroom declares it best, I am not uncertain concerning it. Lest I be accused of silence, I have spoken confidently and followed up with worthy praise what he rightly began. That discerning knower calls the wine best; relying on his statement, I accordingly declare it worthy—worthy, I say, to be offered in a welcome cup to him for drinking, to whom surely whatever is unworthy ought not be given.

[Col. 0469A] Whatever is best ought to be given most worthily to him who must be judged best of all. Just as he by no means wishes to drink from a dreg-filled cup, so he demands that I offer him unmixed wine. Therefore I judge my throat, which he called the best wine—that is, the affection of my heart, which has tasted from him such great and ineffable things—worthy to be carefully presented to his sight and to satisfy his thirst by offering a fitting drink.

“For he thirsts—he thirsts for the good of us all—yet he does not accept the gall of dragons and the wine of asps (Deuteronomy 32). He does not drink, but refuses, the vinegar of the Jews and the bitterness offered him; and he puts the wicked far away, whom he accuses thus in the Gospel: ‘Depart, you cursed; for I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink’ (Matthew 25).

“Therefore I judge it worthy to offer the best wine to one who thirsts: wine that is pleasing not only in its first taste but also when repeatedly tasted, so that, drinking it eagerly and finding what he has drunk pleasing, he suffers no weariness but loves it all the more when chewed over. The lips and teeth, by which clean animals are known to chew the cud, I judge to signify reconsideration and, in reconsideration, strict examination. By these the benevolent and most sharp-sighted Judge revisits and examines strictly whatever he loves in the Bride so as to approve it.

[Col. 0469C] He drinks when he gladly embraces either her understanding or her affection; he chews it over when he revisits and strictly examines what is loved. And the more fully he sees that nothing unsuitable appears either before or after, the more he loves to rejoice in what is searched out and pleasing. But just as the Law willed an animal that does not chew the cud to be called unclean, so an understanding or affection that does not endure being reconsidered is not sufficiently clean. Yet whatever lies hidden in the Virgin does not fear repeated judgment, and the subtle chewer-over finds in her nothing to cut away.” Therefore she adds: “I,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXVII

I belong to my Beloved, and his turning is toward me. “I,” she says, “rejoice to be found serving and obeying my Beloved, clinging to him more pleasingly, and experiencing his welcome sweetness. Whatever I feel within myself does not fear to be more plainly laid open to him; my conscience does not shrink from being brought before his scrutiny.

“I, indeed, am not scattered through the empty and varied windings of the world by feminine fickleness, but with mature steadiness am intent upon him alone whom I love. I have not turned from him, in act or affection, even for a little while, but am turned toward his face with devoted desire. And my Beloved does not sleep while guarding me,

[Col. 0469D] nor does he snore; he is present when I call, and shows himself kindly to one calling. He turns not his face away from my prayers alone, but even from my affections; rather, he turns toward my desire with a cheerful face.

“And because not a turning-away but a mutual turning is proclaimed between us, it pleases me that my speech also should turn again toward him, so that my face, gazing while diligently seeking his desired face, may address that very face familiarly, as though mouth to mouth.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Come, my Beloved; let us go out into the field; let us remain in the villages. “You,” she says, “whom I love, who above did not refuse to come when called, whom I know to impart a more abundant grace to me when you come—come still, if you desire to find me ready and prepared, so that I may now be willing and able to consent to your command.

“Above, I had somewhat feared that my washed feet would be defiled and that, rejoicing in my welcome bed, I would again be summoned to outward affairs. But because I now understand this to be expedient for the needs of many, I do not refuse anything that I see accords with your good pleasure. Come then, my Beloved, and let us hasten to go out together into the field, that we may proclaim your name and your grace to the world; that what you formerly ordained in concealment may no longer remain hidden, but become known to all who are worthy to obtain this benefit.

[Col. 0470B] “Let our knowledge be spread not only in Judaea, which is called, as it were, our city, where our fellow citizens are and the generation of our flesh is propagated, but also in the villages—that is, outside, among the Gentiles. And, that it may be spread more effectively, let us not be reluctant to remain there longer.

“The Beloved and the beloved are seen to go out into the field, and are no longer shut in with the door of the bridal chamber closed, when the world lovingly embraces in faith the Word made flesh and venerates the mother from whom the Word willed to be incarnate. But mother and son have not yet gone out to those who, in rustic dullness, have not professed the catholic faith: scandalized, they do not worship God and man together, and, abhorring the fruitful Virgin, do not honour her with due reverence.

[Col. 0470C] “Therefore, seeing that this should no longer be delayed, the Virgin wills that knowledge of hidden things should finally be brought forth publicly; that the firm faith transmitted in the apostles should be carried to the Jews, and that the Idumaeans should not become strangers to the grace of the same gift. For Christ did not refuse to extend his shoe over Idumaea, and transformed enemies into friends and foreigners into members of his household, when he disclosed teaching and grace to distant nations: namely, that his immortality had shod itself with our mortality.

“The Virgin urges him to remain among these nations, and he does not refuse her urging. In this she secretly rebukes and accuses the hardness of the Jews, who, quickly abandoning Christ’s faith after the apostles, so remain that they postpone conversion until the end of the age. But mother and son come to the villages—that is, nations foolish and distant from the citizens, still unlearned and uncultivated, knowing not the prophetic teaching—and make a long stay among them, while they cleave to the Son in such a way that they also keep grateful remembrance of the mother.

[Col. 0470D] The Virgin lovingly rejoices in their advancement, understanding that this itself likewise pleases the Son; she continues to urge him and confidently entreats him to persist in advancing for the better what has been well begun.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Let us rise early for the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the flowers bear fruit, whether the pomegranates have blossomed. There I will give you my breasts. Since every one of the faithful has experienced our goodwill as beneficial, and is not uncertain, if grace remains, about his own advancement, let us rise early. As the night is now compelled to turn into light, let us make them watchful by labour and diligent effort.

The careful cultivator wishes to go out early to the vineyards: to provide what is useful for them, remove what is useless, prune away what is superfluous, bestow care upon necessities, and rejoice if he finds that they answer his efforts with fitting progress. Let us therefore rise early—that is, let us hasten to remove evening terror, give dawn to the vineyards, and pour in the morning sun. Let our visitation drive ignorance’s darkness far away and beat it back, and pour the new light of grace upon the churches of the Gentiles.

[Col. 0471B] Let the Gentiles know your name, Lord; let them know it, go forth, and begin their work. Let those who had formerly been barren and dry, weighed down by nocturnal dullness, advance and flower in the morning, so that they may be accounted fruitful vineyards. Let our visitation, our sight of them, grant them increase; let it not permit them to be afflicted beyond what is just, but make an outcome also with the affliction. Let us persist in the work: you going before powerfully and mercifully, and I diligently and confidently interceding for the churches.

“Let us see whether it has flowered”—that is, let us gladly approve that the vine appears to have flowered: it already shows that it has received our grace; it is already green, already flowering, already rejoices to have given the careful cultivator hope and to have supplied, in its flowery appearance, sure signs of progress. Since a flower is not enough unless it is allowed to attain fruit, let us see and approve that the flowers appear to bear fruit, because the Gentiles who are taught to come into the hearing of faith do not delay in adorning that faith itself with worthy works.

[Col. 0471C] Let us also see whether the pomegranates have flowered; let us consider that many among them have grown strong with such great courage that, burning with love, they expose themselves to endure martyrdom, even though executioners do not apply the material sword outwardly. The repeated syllabic conjunction *si* (“if”) is not an expression of doubt but an affirmative manner of speaking: for what the Virgin foretells is by no means uncertain but certain, nor does the subsequent course of events contradict her utterance.

For many among the Gentiles, upon whom mother and son bestowed their goodwill, like a vine have produced a flourishing appearance by labour and diligence; and by the progress of grace have brought flourishing dispositions into fruitful effects, and by both example and teaching have led others to fruit. But some, burning with the torches of a greater desire, flower like pomegranates: they redden under afflictions and endure so many and such great hardships in their contest that only the suffering of death separates them from the fruit of martyrdom.

[Col. 0471D] For the spirit which does not cease from envy and falsehood often inflames itself with unbridled malice against some people, striving with utmost zeal either to weaken their life or at least to defile their good name with malicious rumours. It goes forth, therefore, and infects those whom it finds more prone to malice; it arms with shamelessness elders by rank of presbyter rather than by teaching, who, when they cannot fulfil their own lust as they please, determine to cast the entire weight of accusation upon Susanna.

An evil report flies abroad and shakes the whole city; people are astonished and marvel at the disorderly novelty. The innocent woman would have perished under a wholly false judgment unless divine mercy at last came to her aid by sending Daniel. Who would dare not praise this woman, Marina, Eugenia, and others of this kind—or dare deprive them of the reward of martyrdom—when the deceit of accusers and shameless falsehood attacked them, and not a sword of iron but a sword of suffering pierced their souls?

[Col. 0472B] Finally, when God sometimes permits certain people to be deceived and perish, he allows a spirit of falsehood to rage in their ears; and prophets who deserve not to see what is true and useful prophesy by their own spirit whatever they know will please the king. Thus, deceived themselves, they deceive Ahab, whose ears itch, and declare by false prophecies that victory is at hand. But Micaiah, alone openly testifying to the truth, is first struck with a slap and immediately consigned to prison.

There are some who love to speak vain things and to divine lies, and who in no way wish anyone truthful to oppose them. Both the prophet and the one to whom flattering wicked prophecy is given, failing sufficiently to foresee his own fate, rejoice in a brother’s suffering. A disease or pestilence of this sort still spreads widely today, ranging farther abroad; this stain occupies many and extends over a broad space. Very many are found who, displaying an appearance of love in face and dress, maliciously slander and curiously listen to slanderers.

[Col. 0472C] Darkened by malice, they think more is added to their own praise if they perceive that due honour is not rendered to their brothers. If they can weaken another’s reputation by any reproach whatever, they suppose their own will either stand more firmly or be increased more abundantly. Thus, hating Micaiah, they do not follow his truthful prophecy; but lying to the king, they comply with his desires. And though both king and ministers are deceived by flattering falsehood, those whom they unjustly and wickedly persecute are not abandoned.

For the Virgin is present and deigns to look upon those whom she prudently understands to be crushed by unjust injury. Lest the injured fail, but rather, being tried, rejoice more over the outcome, she frees them from present evils and by her intercession advances them to better things. Therefore she says to the Bridegroom: “There I will give,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXX

[Col. 0472D]

There I will give you my breasts. “When,” she says, “I see the vine adorned with new flowers, when subsequent fruits are brought forth with the beauty of preceding flowers, when anyone oppressed is afflicted beyond what is just, and is coloured like a pomegranate in our sight—there, that is, then, at the fitting hour and suitable time, I shall pour out my breasts: I shall give my help to one in need.”

The Virgin fittingly promises to give not a breast but breasts, because many are willing whose action does not answer their will. Many indeed seem to feel compassion when they see us miserable, but, hindered by poverty or avarice, they do not extend a helping hand. Of such persons a certain pagan says: “All forgive; no one comes to help.” But the Virgin both pities our miseries with an affection of goodwill

[Col. 0473A] and, with a most powerful hand, accomplishes whatever she sees to be necessary for us. And lest faith grow faint beneath a hard burden and hope waver, she quickly comes, so that she may refresh us with both breasts.

But because her kindness pities none of us except for the sake of the Son, whom she sees to be most merciful toward us, and lest she seem to refer the cause of her kindness to us rather than to him—for she does not love him because of us, but loves us because of him—she therefore did not say, “I will give them my breasts,” but “I will give you.” “Whatever,” she says, “I spend upon those who so need help, I shall attribute wholly to you, whose good pleasure I see at work in them. I do not wish this favour to be credited either to them or to myself; rather, I desire both them and myself to glory more rightly in you alone.

[Col. 0473B] “Whatever, therefore, I may be found mercifully to impart to those who flourish like vines, whom I see producing good works, or finally whom I perceive, while suffering injustice, to resemble pomegranates—to those who sigh only for us and await our protection—whatever help, I say, I bestow upon such persons, I give to you, because I shall help through you, for you, and referring everything to you.”

## CHAPTER XXXI

The mandrakes have given forth fragrance at our gates. Since the Virgin previously named villages, vineyards, and pomegranates, in which she symbolized the churches of the Gentiles and their various advances, she turns toward the Jews and likewise predicts, under enigma and figure, that their conversion will someday take place.

Her prophetic nose, most keen in sensing, smells their conversion and rejoices in the most certain hope of their conversion, knowing and foreseeing the conversion of the Jewish people—delayed indeed, but to come at the end of the ages. Foretelling this, she says: “The mandrakes have now given forth fragrance at our gates; our nostrils, not dulled by ignorance, have foreknown that, after the fullness of the Gentiles has been permitted to enter, then the remnant of the Jews, then all Israel, will be converted.”

[Col. 0473C] Mandrakes, they say, are herbs suited to medicinal uses, bearing a human likeness except for the head. By them the prudent and the erring Jews are quite fittingly represented: like human beings, they are instructed for divine worship by the written Law. But because they neither know nor worship Christ, the head of the faithful, mutilated and disfigured, they discolour all the rest of the body. Though conformed to believers through knowledge of the Scriptures and legal commandments, they are deformed through the absence of the head and unbelieving ignorance.

They also provide no small remedy to the sick when they read the Law to us, set forth a discipline of life, preserve for us the books—as a furnace of moral teaching and workshop of spiritual teaching—and bring to us, for instruction, the severe judges whom they possess. Yet they do not as yet produce fuller fruit in the dwelling or bridal chamber, but at the gates—that is, in spiritual senses—they give the Virgin a welcome fragrance. For what divine goodness purposes to bestow upon them in the last days is already granted to the Virgin, smelling it from afar, to foresee.

[Col. 0474A] She perceives that, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, Judaea—which now, erring, has gone out from the boundaries of the Church, and which, suffering hunger, does not receive even crumbs from the table of the masters—will then be converted to the faith and eat the bread of children.

## CHAPTER XXXII

All new and old fruits, my Beloved, I have kept for you. That the Gentiles, newly called to faith by the gift of grace, bring forth worthy fruits and works appropriate to holiness is my desire, indeed my earnest endeavour and concern: I diligently care for whatever I know will please you. Likewise, that the Jews, who now roam about as though their bonds had been broken, should be recalled in the last days to the ancient bond of faith, is also the object of my solicitude, desire, and entreaty; I compassionately grieve and forgive them as they stray.

Therefore, my Beloved,

[Col. 0474B] I keep new and old fruits for you when I diligently gather together the merits of both peoples; when I do not allow the good beginnings of Gentile and Jew to perish, but strengthen the purpose of the former and endeavour to repair the injured zeal of the latter. Perhaps the Virgin chose to call these merits, fruits, or works “fruits” (*poma*) because she rejoices to present gifts of this kind to the Bridegroom for eating, so that he may be captivated by their pleasing appearance and, lest he recoil as though cheated, be held by their useful and commendable reality.

She keeps the fruits of the Gentiles when she cherishes and embraces their newness; when she rejoices that they are grafted in and that those grafted into the olive tree receive more abundant fruitfulness; when she shows herself powerful and benevolent toward them in their labours and devoutly presents their fruitful labours to her Son. She seems likewise to preserve the fruits of the Jews when, finally pitying them, she wills that they should wander no longer; when she strives to restore members of her own race to their ancient state and, extending her hand, turns a people long hostile to faith into a friend.

[Col. 0474C] She keeps new and old fruits when she so helps the Gentiles, now converted to the newness of faith, that she does not at all wish them to turn away from the older Jews; when she lovingly seeks the Jews’ return to faith now lost—or rather interrupted—without begrudging that the Gentiles were grafted in beforehand. “I have kept these,” she says, not seeking for myself nearer glory, but entirely for you, that is, for your honour. For when the Virgin, solicitous about them or on their behalf, rejoices, she glories not in herself but in the Bridegroom, as was said a little earlier.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Col. 0474D]

## Chapter VIII

“Who will grant me that you may be my brother, nursing at my mother’s breasts, so that I may find you outside and kiss you, and no one will now despise me?”

The Virgin desires that those things which she already foreknows, though still absent, concerning the Gentiles and the Jews, may become known openly to a world which recognizes nothing unless it is evident; and that knowledge of the Bridegroom—which is already disclosed to her as though in the bridal chamber—may go out into the field, where the sun shines more broadly. “Who,” she says, “will grant me this? That is, who will bless me with so great a gift, who will so enlarge my desire, cramped by narrowness, that I may find you outside as my brother and disclose to others, still ignorant, those things known to me?

“Your birth in the flesh makes you indeed my brother—indeed, the brother of all; your mother feeds you for a time, not from necessity but by nature. [Col. 0475A] You suck her breasts; you do not refuse to receive from her the nourishment of little children, when you make use of food, drink, clothing, and sleep—things by which you do not deny that you are human. Who will grant that I may find in the street, outside, him whom my mother proclaims to be such and so small? Find, I say, not merely a man—which the eyes of unbelievers do not deny—but God made man, which is disclosed only to believers.

“I wish,” she says, “that Gentiles and Jews, accustomed to know only visible things, may see, understand, and love you as God; and that you who are proclaimed in prophetic utterance as the hidden God may be seen by these people with certain faith, when the eye of the heart has been unveiled. If this is granted, so that I find you there, I shall rejoice and gladly kiss you, once found among human beings: that is, I shall delight in love and honor for your name [Col. 0475B] when I contemplate that you are loved and praised by humankind.”

Yet the Virgin wishes not simply to kiss the one found, but rather to kiss him all over (*deosculari*); the compound form of the word suggests not diminution but increase. And we are told, as some have thought, that this *deosculari* is used when, in many places, we kiss in order to express a greater longing. Therefore the Virgin wishes, if she finds him among human beings, to kiss him wholly and to be compelled to pass over nothing without joy: she wishes to see him honored by them as God and man, and, kissing him distinguished with a twofold honor, to delight in rejoicing.

When such honor is worthily rendered to the Son, the reverence due also to the Virgin herself will not be taken away. In the eyes of those who seek rightly, she will not be despised, she who was chosen above all women to bear such a one. For whoever rejoices to understand and love him as both God and man [Col. 0475C] will not regard as contemptible her from whom he was born. Nor will such a person be wounded by the stumbling-block of the Jews or by the folly of the Gentiles, when, by the just proclamation of truth, the wondrous integrity of the mother is established. Whoever, I say, wishes to render honor to the Son according to his good pleasure also resolves not to withhold due honor from the mother; for no good son accepts the service of anyone who does not likewise desire to render honor to his Virgin Mother.

## Chapter XXXIV

“I shall take hold of you and lead you into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her who bore me; there you will teach me.”

When I perceive that you are wisely understood and newly loved, I shall favor those who love you and seize the Beloved, as it were, with my hands. [Col. 0475D] Holding him once seized, I shall not permit you to be drawn back from your purpose, but shall cause you to be brought more fully into my mother’s house. Far be it from me to fail those who love, to despise one who is not despised; rather, I shall cherish more diligently what is imperfect until it becomes perfect. I shall love those who love; and, that they may love more, I shall advance them. I shall remind you, Beloved, by unwearied prayers that you may help them.

Thus I shall endeavor to lead—or bring—you into my mother’s house, when I prepare it with devout care for your entrance; when you attentively obey me as a son obeys his mother, and pursue not their former merits but my desire. The Virgin’s mother, as stated above, is mortal nature itself, which brings us all forth into this light by a similar birth and which, that it may have for itself a house in which it is to remain until the end of the age, begets human beings in a succession that never ceases. [Col. 0476A]

Into this house—that is, into human beings—the Virgin promises to lead the Bridegroom, so that he may mercifully accomplish their own salvation within them, walk among them, and joyfully arrive at the chamber where he may lie down, rest, and find the repose of rest. The solicitous Virgin leads the Bridegroom into the house and chamber of her mother when, compassionately pitying us, she leads him by devout prayers to dwell in us, walk in us by the grace of his goodness, and remain in us—not to be recalled from there because of the merit of our wickedness.

“There,” she says, “you will teach me.” When it has come about that I rejoice to bring you into each of the elect and that you are not withdrawn from accomplishing their salvation because of their sins, then you will teach me [Col. 0476B] and make me certain of hidden things. Then I shall know both that they are elect and that I am concerned for the elect. You will teach me, I say, when, by more abundant grace, you turn into fulfilled reality the hope of promise which you formerly gave me; when, at the better end of the promise having ceased, you grant the effect of that glory for which you give longing to those who await it.

## Chapter XXXV

“And I shall give you a cup of spiced wine, and new wine of my pomegranates.”

When you make me learned through the experienced knowledge of fuller grace, I too shall give you gifts of greater abundance. I shall offer you a cup most sweet in taste and flavor: wine indeed that has been spiced, love compounded with labor. [Col. 0476C] I shall gather, as it were, into a mixing-bowl the merits of those whom I know to please you—their loves and labors—and offer them to your sight, or rather to your drinking. That you may receive them more gladly, I shall commend them by devoted goodwill.

When aromatic spices are added to wine, they are made into a spiced drink through the application of a skilled hand. Likewise, if tribulation and the distress of suffering are added to love, that love, offered to the Bridegroom, obtains the place of a welcome drink. Emphasizing this, she says: “And new wine of my pomegranates.”

New wine seethes and bubbles with raging tumult and disturbance, forcefully casting off all impurities from itself. It signifies that love which does not care to be soothed by the tranquility of this life, but, hastening to martyrdom, burns to be refined by pressures and beatings. By pomegranates, however, she wished those to be figured in whom many virtues are gathered like seeds; [Col. 0476D] the inward collection of virtues makes them precious, and the ruddy appearance of their sufferings makes them beautiful in the eyes of those who see rightly.

Perhaps the Virgin says “my pomegranates” because whoever loves Christ devotes himself to the Passion and martyrdom: she rejoices to bestow help and care upon him, and reckons as wholly her own whatever progress he makes. Thus the new wine of pomegranates is the unrestrained fervor, or ardent love, of those who show themselves ready patiently to endure everything which the world either threatens horribly or delights in inflicting violently.

The Virgin loves to offer the cup of this wine or new wine when she rejoices that those fervent in spirit shine with virtues, and that, removed from the midst, they finally pass without failing to the Bridegroom’s table or banquet, [Col. 0477A] soothing the taste of the one feasting with the sweet excellence of their merits. Lest she be thought to ascribe this to herself beyond what is right—or rather, that she may testify that whatever she rejoices in concerning them is a divine gift—she turns to the young women standing by and says: “His left hand,” etc.

## Chapter XXXVI

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.”

That I lead the Bridegroom into my mother’s house and into any of the elect, that I serve the cup and heap gifts upon gifts—this is his benefit, his left hand, his temporal consolation, which receives me as I recline, more gently than the feathery softness of a pillow. For by this consolation he cherishes and sustains my insufficiency in the present; he who will embrace me with a fuller right hand in the future, and who now [Col. 0477B] so governs me that he never wholly forsakes me, will at some time govern me so that he provides every sufficiency on every side.

Already I hide sweetly in the fruit of that reality and in the shadow of this hope; I rejoice greatly over present things and still more over future things. For this reason I make it known to you who stand by, so that you too may love him by whose gifts I am already so enriched.

This verse, however, is found and explained earlier. There it is preceded by another verse denoting the Virgin’s weakness, because, when the Virgin asks to be sustained with apples and strengthened with flowers as one languishing, mention is immediately made of the left hand, which is understood to support her as she lies down. Here, however, where salvation is at the door and no mention is made of languor, where her age is more advanced and the progress of merit stronger, she is already secure about her own affairs and concerned for the progress of others. Forgetful, as it were, of herself, she rejoices in the perfected merits of the elect. [Col. 0477C]

She sees that they are to be endowed with the sweetness of love, with wine, with new wine, with the fervor of the Spirit, and are to be offered more worthily to the royal table and divine taste. She desires the fulfillment of their offering so ardently that, with that end in view, she patiently suffers her own fulfillment to be delayed. For, considering with what fruit her conception and the integrity of her childbirth become known to believers’ hearts, and to what end more people grow ardent over time in loving the Bridegroom, she cannot fail to rejoice in such things, both future and present. Foreseeing their glory, she seems to await her own more gladly and calmly. Seeing this, the Bridegroom says: “I adjure you,” etc.

## Chapter XXXVII

[Col. 0477D]

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not awaken or rouse the Beloved until she herself wishes.”

“You apostles, you teachers of the Church,” he says, “go, teach all nations; and take care that those whom the Virgin foresees by prophetic understanding as destined for salvation are not, through your negligence, held back from the progress foreseen for them. Take care that, if perhaps you watch too little over their keeping, you do not awaken her desire from the repose already found.”

This adjuration, by which the watchfulness of teachers is so earnestly urged, is likewise found in the second and third books of this work. There it has been sufficiently worn down by exposition, if that pleases the reader, and need not now be explained again in this final repetition. [Col. 0478A] Yet this may be said. At first, caring for herself, she rejoices in spiritual leisure, from which she is forbidden to be recalled to temporal business or disturbance, lest, while she loves to be at leisure and contemplates spiritual things, she be compelled, before she wishes, to return to concern for her neighbors.

In the second instance, she takes care that Judaea may not be led astray through hardness of heart, but that knowledge of the Bridegroom may be brought into her house or chamber. Nor does it suffice for her to become gladly an assistant to the Bridegroom or Son if she knows that her mother is altogether abandoned by grace. The Bridegroom also prevents her from being recalled from that concern, both in affection and in effect, lest apostolic teachers be found, through their negligence, to thwart her. Rather, they must take care and strive to apply vigilant diligence, so that the Virgin may not cease to rejoice in the progress of her own people.

[Col. 0478B] Thirdly, she is concerned either only for the Gentiles or equally for Jews and Gentiles, calling her mother the weakness or nature of humankind. Into her house—that is, into all flesh—she wishes knowledge of the Bridegroom to be brought; and the Bridegroom wills that she not be drawn away from this desire by any trouble. Thus may be fulfilled what is written: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3).

## Chapter XXXVIII

“Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her Beloved?”

The angelic spirits, standing by while Bridegroom and bride converse, aware of the bridal secrets and contemplating the profound mysteries, are held fast and cannot sufficiently marvel or be astonished [Col. 0478C] at who or how great is the Virgin whose marriage they see being celebrated.

They observe indeed that she is endowed with wonderful understanding, rejoices at the present good of others, and is concerned for their future progress; that here she burns with desire for the Bridegroom, there with concern for her neighbors; that she is distinguished by virtues and beautiful in the eminence of her merits. They observe too that the Bridegroom so rejoices in her leisure and rest that he utterly excludes every approach of any indiscreet person, admits no importunate person within the enclosure of her repose, and does not permit the resting one to be roused until she herself wishes.

When they perceive that the Virgin excels in these and other such qualities, and when they scarcely comprehend so great her grace and merits, they speak to one another and inquire in mutual speech who or how great she is [Col. 0478D] whose eminence they contemplate.

## Chapter XXXIX

“Who is this who comes up from the wilderness,” etc.

Earthly habitation, deserted now through a long succession of ages, had, because sins required it, been deprived of experience of heavenly goods. Astraea had abandoned it, fuller of nettles, thorns, and briars, and, returning to the stars, took there a more pleasing place.

> [Note: Col. 0477D. *Metamorphoses*, Book I.]

In this solitude, mortal nature lay prostrate under weakness, while, with the vigor of the spirit corrupted, it gave itself over to carnal allurements. Submerged beneath a heavy flood, it did not know a way of emerging; it was heavily burdened by mud, and there was no possibility of cleansing itself.

From there, in a new manner—by a novelty incomparably wondrous, a miracle almost monstrous, an event matched by none in all the preceding ages—the Virgin rises and stands forth. No longer infected by the filth of vices, she is raised by a marvelous ascent to the eminence of merits. [Col. 0479A] Who, then, or how great is she? Who can worthily consider her eminence, she who rises thus from former horror and vast solitude: though remaining there in body, she maintains a higher step in mind; she no longer overflows with the vices of her conduct, but, contrary to custom, abounds in the delights of merits?

And indeed we see her abounding in excessive delights and leaning upon the one she loves, like a delicate woman. Though walking upon earth, she scarcely dares touch it; her Beloved lifts and sustains her delights above. Who can worthily consider her? Who does not marvel at her height, since neither before nor afterward is she compared with any woman? Leaning in a special way and with confidence upon him whom she loves, she has no need of our assistance for progress, because she does not distrust the perseverance of her advance.

That the angels so earnestly ask who she is has, if you wish to recall it, been repeated a third time. Whenever anyone is introduced asking such a question, the question itself makes mention of the Virgin’s progress.

First it is asked: “Who is this?” She is made slender like a little rod by many disciplines and compared with the smoke of spices and every powder of the perfumer; yet, while still dwelling in the flesh, she stretches herself upward in desire so that whoever attends more carefully is delighted by her fragrance or example.

Second it is asked: “Who is this, who comes forth like the dawn?” Leaving behind the things that are past, like the darker shadow of nights, she attains the beauty of the moon, indeed even the likeness of the sun or daylight; and, striking terror into her enemies, she is comparable to an army drawn up for battle. [Col. 0479C]

Third it is asked: “Who is this?” Like a delicate noble matron, forgetful of all things and delighted only in him whom she loves, she so fails from her own things that she does not wish to remain in them even for a little while; she so advances in him that she loves to recline all of herself upon him.

So that she may know and recall whence and where she has come, she hears the Bridegroom saying: “Under the apple tree,” etc.

## Chapter XL

“Under the apple tree I roused you; there your mother was corrupted; there she who bore you was violated.”

“You,” he says, “who lean upon your Beloved with such delicate tenderness, who, hunger driven far away, now recline upon my breast at the banquet—to whom do you owe whatever you have? Who raised you to this height of merit, except he who roused you as you lay weak beneath the tree?

“That first woman, who wickedly desired the forbidden fruit and by unlawful eating wickedly ensnared her husband, was immediately given over beneath the apple tree to weakness—or rather to death; and that same death was left to her descendants as though by hereditary right. Under that tree, then, made lovely by its mystical fruit, all posterity lies weighed down under the laws of death, since every creature born by a similar generation from those parents languishes and groans in the fault brought in by the tree. [Col. 0480A]

“Under the same tree the Virgin was held by a like bond, until divine goodness—which had been hidden within itself through many preceding ages—looked upon her more kindly and chose her above all women, in order through her to redeem those whom hereditary death had compelled to be condemned. Thus it transferred the chosen Virgin from tree to tree: drawing her out from sin, it raised her to the summit of greater grace; freeing her from the stain of paternal and inherited injury, it transferred her to faith in and love for his future Passion.

“For when the Virgin understood that God, taking flesh from her, was to be born a human being, she consequently recognized that he was, according to the flesh, to die. In that death, because she understood our life and the salvation of us all, she loved—if not death itself—certainly the gift of grace which it brought. Therefore, when she had been snatched away from beneath the apple tree which brought death, she was nevertheless brought beneath the apple tree which bore the fruit of life. Under its shadow she was raised to such a height that, in grace and merit, she is perfect above all women. [Col. 0480B]

“But if the words, ‘There your mother was corrupted,’ are referred to the first tree, which brought death, then human nature is not unfittingly called the Virgin’s mother: under that tree it suffered so great an injury and loss that, having itself been corrupted, it corrupted others and turned vice into nature for us. If, however, beneath the tree of the cross the bride’s mother is believed to have been violated, Judaea is rightly understood to be called her mother. For where the Bridegroom raised the Virgin, by the merit of faith, to singular grace, there the mother, demanding that the Bridegroom be killed, violated her heart through obstinacy.

“Thus beneath the wood of the cross both the bride’s faith flourishes and Judaea’s chastity is violated. Denying the true Bridegroom, she clings obstinately to the corrupter; and him to whom she ought lovingly to cling and be fastened, she, with a corrupted mind, repeatedly demands be crucified.”

Where the Virgin has been roused, she hears the Bridegroom next saying: “Set me,” etc.

## Chapter XLI

“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death, and emulation is hard as hell.”

“Because your mother, having lost herself in error, cast me out from her heart, she also removed from that heart’s chamber the salvation which was close at hand. But you, my Beloved, who are roused there by incomparable grace, love him who rouses you, so that, loving, you may be loved more fully.

“Yet because in loving you appear sufficiently vehement, not weak, I see that this must be added: do more perseveringly and confirm what you do. Close your heart, in which my love seems to be contained in abundant fullness, [Col. 0480D] by placing upon it a seal which no cunning can erase.

“This seal, which I urge you to set over your heart as a covering, is subject to no cunning and no injury. What more subtle art cannot newly devise, what more learned hand cannot fasten together, cunning cannot unseal and violence cannot break. Therefore place me—me, whom no device can in any way injure or corrupt—upon your heart as a seal. When I seal it, no entrance or exit that causes harm will lie open; and when none lies open, constant and unfailing love will remain.

[Col. 0481A] “I also wish you to place the same seal upon your arm: that is, do not undertake to do anything except from me and through me. When you have rightly sealed whatever you do with such a protection, know that your arm is subject to no harm at all. I advise that what you do and what you love be sealed by my being placed upon them because, protected by such a seal, your heart or arm will not be injured, but will prevail with incomparable strength against all things and will fear nothing encountered, being comparable even to death.

“For just as death comes with equal strength and fearlessness to all, and no power or skill can resist it when it comes, so love, if it is truly protected by the seal described above, is found to prevail strongly against every harmful thing. Likewise, when hell delights in raging harshly against any miserable persons, neither labor nor the groans of the miserable can soften the hardness of its rage. So too, the emulation by which the loving Virgin burns to imitate God refuses to be recalled from its purpose by prayer, price, or softness. [Col. 0481B]

“It is fitting, then, that this strong and inflexible love and this emulation be found in you, so that remembrance of me may not be taken from your heart and arm, from love and deed. Whoever lacks that seal is easily violated; and, by the testimony of the Law, a vessel without a covering is judged unclean (Numbers 19). But the vessel which burns with the fire of love and is covered by the hand of my care—the strong heart of one who loves, guarded by me placed upon it as a seal—is a commendable vessel, unable to be emptied, abundant; it is a bright heart [perhaps *lucibile*, “luminous”], a heart like a lamp, [Col. 0481C] not shadowy.”

Therefore he adds: “Its lamps,” etc.

## Chapter XLII

“Its lamps are lamps of fire and of flames; many waters cannot quench love, nor will rivers overwhelm it.”

“It is not you alone, Virgin,” he says, “who are commended by a worthy title of praise because you are preeminent both in the grace of merits and the excellence of love. Whoever loves is also called a lamp of fire and flames: resisting adversity, yet not fleeing afflictions.
