“The lamp which stretches itself with open mouth toward the attainment of love, while outwardly presenting itself as contemptible among wrongly disposed rich people, is shown and understood by those who consider worthily to be a lamp of fire, hiding its fire from the unworthily darkened. For it burns and is delightfully kindled with inward heat; yet it does not appear to burn for external things, but grows cold toward them, since it no longer cares for whatever belongs to this life as for barren frost, and conforms itself by inner desire to the burning seraphim. [Col. 0481D]

“Nevertheless, lest it be evident that this lamp is kindled uselessly and the neighbor complain that no benefit is bestowed upon him from it, the lamp which was first called a lamp of fire is afterward called also a lamp of flames. Thus it appears, to careful observers, to lack neither for itself nor for its neighbor. For one who loves and is strongly consumed by the fire of love is not numbed by weakness or idleness, but works more vigilantly. To eyes that are not bleary, such a one pours forth welcome light with generous gift and presents himself as an example to those at work and a guide to those walking.

“Many waters do not extinguish one who burns and gives light. The lover, or the lover’s strength, yields neither to threats nor blandishments; nor, finally, will rivers, nor an inundation of greater afflictions, nor famine, nor sword overwhelm the abundance of his fire or flames. For love flourishes with such force and vigor that it cannot be overwhelmed by either a small or a greater assault of tribulations; for the sake of spiritual reward it endures in love the multitude of waters, drops of rainy dew, and the greater onrushes of rivers. [Col. 0482A]

[Col. 0482B] “To this love, therefore, nothing half-hearted is rightly compared. Rather, love is worthily set before whatever can be possessed here. Whoever has a sound head and is not deprived of truth of judgment chooses and loves it above every transient thing offered here.”

Therefore he adds: “If a man gives,” etc.

## Chapter XLIII

“If a man gives all the substance of his house for love, he will despise it as though it were nothing.”

Whoever does not rejoice merely in the lot of senseless or irrational beings, but, possessing human form, exercises eminent reason—if such a person gives all that he has in order to obtain love, he will seem to himself to have given nothing, if he has gained possession of this desire.

“Substance” means whatever our need or desire gathers together in the present and whatever management either expends for temporal uses or preserves. Substance, I say, is not that by which we essentially subsist in living, but that which is said to stand beneath or support us, who are alive, for our use. [Col. 0482C] It is not unfittingly called the substance of a person’s house because human need is supported by such resources. The person who is solicitous enriches and honors his house with them, whether prudently laboring to ward off poverty or greedily laboring to increase wealth.

One lavishly squanders and disperses such substance when he immerses himself in a profound desire to acquire love. When he has given that substance and perceives that he has received this love, comparing what was given with what was received, he will seem, on more careful consideration, to have given nothing. With such eagerness does he love and embrace what has been received that, considering as nothing and despising all that he had given, he sees no comparison between what passes away and what does not perish. The former is nothing and perishable; the latter remains and is regarded as something great and outstanding. [Col. 0482D]

Nor is it out of place if the human body is called “substance” here, since it is shown that a human being subsists in it or through it. Scripture therefore adds mention of the person’s house, because there the soul’s treasure has its dwelling, as it were, in a fertile vessel. If, then, a sensible person gives this body, to which the soul is plainly so closely joined that it cannot easily be restrained from attachment to it—for no one is found who wishes to be stripped of this house or body, since Paul too wishes rather to be clothed over than unclothed, and love did not draw Peter, though he loved three times, wholly away from this law of the flesh; rather, as Christ foretold, another led him where he did not wish to go—if, I say, a person gives this body, to which the soul is bound by such tenacious bonds, he rightly judges that he has given nothing (Romans 8). [Col. 0483A] “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared.”

The Bridegroom exalts and commends this love so often for this reason: that the loving Virgin may value so highly what has been so greatly commended, and, when she recognizes that she has attained no small summit of this commended love through the Bridegroom’s gift, may understand that she is not despised in his eyes. Concerning her the companions add: “Our sister,” etc.

## Chapter XLIV

“Our sister is little, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken with?”

[Col. 0483B] “We see,” they say, “that the Virgin has advanced not a little in the grace of love, yet has not fully attained what she desires. Although, for love’s sake, she has now come to despise the substance mentioned above, she still does not find him whom she so loves in his own beauty.

“And because she is our sister—not by her exalted merits but by nature, destined afterward to receive with us the inheritance of one God the Father—let us speak together a little about her, and, if perhaps she needs anything from us, let us all bring it together, not individually. As far as it seems to us, the reason why this our sister, who, as was said above, has deserved already to be brought into the chamber, does not yet rejoice that she has been led from chamber into chamber, is that she is not yet sufficiently capable or mature, but suffers from smallness and has not been brought, as it were, to marriageable years. [Col. 0483C]

“Dishonorable love, preceded by excess or lust and seized and defiled by Venus, the wicked counselor, or by desire, is accustomed, I say, to snatch away a Virgin before she is mature in age, yielding more to pleasure than preparing what will benefit the Virgin. But this love which we have before us, although more vehement, nevertheless wishes to be more prudent; and the lover wishes this love to benefit not so much himself as the Virgin. The Bridegroom waits and waits again, and has patience in love while the Virgin advances in fuller merit and grace.

“She is therefore still little, and we see that she has no breasts. Although above she was shown not to lack breasts, she is said not to have those things which, though they wish to appear to the Bridegroom, are not yet sufficiently able to do so, because they do not yet seem to possess complete sufficiency. Virgins are not fit for marriage while they remain childish, while their age is little, while their breasts do not yet swell. Even if they project a little and give a sign of future maturity, they still retain the former tenderness of immaturity. [Col. 0483D]

“Since, then, she is so little and is plainly without breasts, what shall we do for her? What more can we now provide? What further thing belonging to us can be bestowed, that she may finally rejoice that the day of her marriage is no longer delayed? She is indeed to be spoken with and led into the more secret bridal chamber; but first she must be led out from present things, which are not yet sufficient. And that she may be able to be led out from them, what further must we do, so that she may advance to gain that longed-for day?

“On that day—that is, with regard to and in the progress toward that day—what can we give to this sister? By what greater zeal or love of ours shall we prepare her, that she may reach the day for which she is now regarded as impatient and so concerned, when her noble lover, the law of betrothal having been fulfilled, will speak with her? Though above he has spoken with or concerning her in many ways and modes, he has not yet pursued a completing gift, but an endeavor conducive to merit. Now it remains for her to follow him into the inner chamber of the chamber, and for him, in the manner he knows, to speak ineffably with her whom he has thus followed. [Col. 0484A]

[Col. 0484B] “A spiritual mystery is concealed in the word ‘speaking with,’ because this bridal epithalamium makes familiar use of figures. This speaking with, by which we desire and foretell that Bridegroom and bride will meet, is the very union in which the face of the seeker is granted to find the face of the one sought. There is ‘speaking with’ when the one present does not conceal from the one presented something fitting to be said, but reveals his face to her who is free from corruption; without intermediaries, one is joined to the other in secret, and the Virgin, seeing the Word, will be satisfied in love now brought to completion.”

## Chapter XLV

“If she is a wall, let us build upon it silver battlements. If she is a door, let us fasten it with cedar boards.”

When the companions ask what they should do suitable for the day on which the Virgin will see the long-desired glory of the divine countenance, they do not delay in answering, as though by delegated speech; and they resolve to provide for the Virgin with solicitous goodwill. [Col. 0484C]

“If she is a wall,” they say, “compacted of stones and mortar—indeed, of virtues joined together by the binding of charity in their midst—it remains for us to build silver battlements upon it and strengthen the wall’s firmness by adding defense. Jerusalem is the city of the Holy One, the numerous gathering of believers, devoted in the present to fruitful labors and glorious in unfailing hope. One Lord and one faith join and bind it together into one sheaf, as it were; and the holy Virgin encircles it by example and teaching, merits and intercessions.

“If, therefore, she is a wall—or rather, because she is one—rejoicing to have citizens placed about her, it is fitting that some defense be set upon the surrounding wall. Thus our care and exhortation may keep watch and give attention from above, lest the enemy extend himself even a little toward penetrating it. Though we cannot yet transfer the laboring Virgin hence, as she desires, we ought and wish at least to bestow this upon her while she labors: that our protection may make her fortified against all things that arise and that frequent exhortation may teach her to endure patiently. [Col. 0484D]

“Thus we prepare not stone but silver battlements for the wall, when we strengthen the Virgin by careful defenses and exhortations; when we strongly prevent the malice of attacking enemies from approaching and cry out to her that she should be secure concerning the outcome.

“Lest, however, this city seem to be so enclosed by the surrounding wall that it is excluded through it from benefits which it has not from itself but, as it were, from outside, she who is the wall is likewise called a door, through which whatever is necessary for the city is supplied. For through the Virgin the Bridegroom loves to enter the gathering of believers; through her also he loves to aid all who trust in her. Though closed to every man, she is opened to God alone by the little key of faith, so that through her the Word made flesh may visibly be brought to human beings.

“If, then, she is a door, let us fasten her with cedar boards: that is, let us add invincible strength to this grace already mentioned, so that fragrant breadth may confront any detractor and unfailing strength resist anyone who presses too harshly. [Col. 0485A] Meanwhile, while the noble Virgin labors and sweats in the contest, let us prepare and strengthen her patience by hope of the crown. And truly, what she hopes and asks to be given is not far away: as we perceive, she will soon see and rejoice in the Bridegroom revealed with unveiled face.”

## Chapter XLVI
“I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower; from the time when I became, in his sight, as one finding peace.” Hearing that the angels were not indifferent or idle toward her, but were concerned for her and promised their protection or service, the Virgin briefly shows what she rejoices has already been granted to her, hoping that, after a longer delay, what remains will not be deferred. “I,” she says, “by grace bestowed and by the work of industrious hands, am now a wall, binding together in the middle by charity a mass of living stones that will not fall; my breasts rise above it like a tower, conferring honor upon the wall and striking terror into approaching enemies.” As the wall signifies the gathering of virtues and the inward bond of charity, so the breasts signify the pattern of life and the teaching of truth, which come forth and hasten to appear openly to all, that they may instruct those who love and compel adversaries to shrink back.

In these respects, although she is not yet perfected for the completion of the present marriage, she nevertheless attained them many years before, namely from the time when she deserved, before him, to find as it were peace: she longs for another peace and expects shortly to find it. For when the Holy Spirit overshadowed her for conception, the Son who was to be born brought her not peace, but as it were peace: peace from vices, peace in grace, peace from the tumult of carnal generation—but not the peace of vision, nor the peace of abiding permanently in eternal glory. Nor does she show herself rejoicing only in her own progress; she also shows that others have attained no slight progress, who through her, grace being bestowed, advanced so far that the vineyard deserved to become rich, not in tendrils, but in peoples. Concerning it she adds: “There was a vineyard,” etc.

## CHAPTER XLVII

“There was a vineyard belonging to the peaceful one, in that which has peoples. He entrusted it to keepers; a man brings a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit.”

From the time when the Spirit worked, I found before him as it were peace: the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts achieved effective growth. What had formerly been confined within the narrow boundaries of Judaea is now found more broadly and fruitfully in that which has peoples. “That which has peoples” may be called faith, or unity, or love, to which diverse peoples are known to be devoted in one-minded spirit, so that, while the apostles preached, not only did many thousands of Jews believe, [Col. 0486A] but their sound went out into all the earth and their preaching was heard.

He entrusted such a vineyard to the apostles and apostolic men for keeping: their preaching spread it not only in Judaea but also among the nations. And when Paul sees Judaea hardening and being perverted, from that point onward he declares that he is turning to the Gentiles. With grace prospering, it grew in so short a time, put away the newness and tender weakness of infancy so thoroughly, that a man—that is, one powerful not so much in strength as in virtue—gives all that he possesses for its fruit: a thousand pieces of silver. The flower of the vineyard is conversion of life; its fruit is the perfection to follow. Whoever desires to be a man for the sake of its hundredfold return casts away passing things. Finally, the fruit is itself the recompense of the spiritual reward [Col. 0486B] which a man obtains for himself by contempt of temporal value.

For one who is found to act not womanishly but manfully does not measure out how much he can give for the fruit of that vineyard. Greedy for spiritual reward, that he may receive it with increase, prodigal of temporal value, he brings it without weight, number, or measure. For the thousand pieces of silver—that is, whatever he possessed, either infinite in number or great in price, whatever smiled deceptively upon his eyes or rang pleasantly in his ears—he brings to the apostles’ feet, casts away, and holds in contempt as dung, that through the loss of temporal things he may receive eternal fruit.

When the Virgin has thus recounted both her own advances and those of others, and commended the vineyard which flourishes more in peoples than in the multitude of its vines, she now hears, not the angels answering, but the Bridegroom with attentive ears: he favors and applauds the praises of both Virgin and vineyard.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

“My vineyard is before me: a thousand are yours, O peaceful one, and two hundred for those who guard its fruit.”

The Bridegroom shows that the vineyard which follows him and gives temporal things for his sake does not walk in darkness, but is in light before him. Favoring and approving it because, after giving away its own goods, it now remains in him, he repays it not merely like for like, but doubly—or a hundredfold—with himself.

“He,” he says, “who for my sake holds temporal possessions in contempt, should know, for greater strengthening, that he is before my eyes. Let every inexperienced reader or hearer know that I, loving one who loves me, do not turn away my gracious face from him. Those thousand pieces of silver, which according to your word a man loves to bring—he who, according to your pattern, loves to prefer invisible things to visible—will belong to the peaceful one: that is, they will deserve rewards of peace. He will confer peace on those who freely give their own things for eternal goods.

“Nor will they be called only peaceful, but also two hundred: that is, they will bestow a double peace on the giver. For the peace or perfection which the distribution of possessions merits is great in the present and will be greatest in the future. As perfection is understood in the thousand, so it is also understood in the hundred. These are certainly doubled when the vineyard is brought to such effective fruitfulness that, after superfluities are cast aside, whoever loves with wakeful care to guard its fruit deserves to find a double peace.” 284

For whoever wishes to preside by example and to be of benefit through praiseworthy teaching, and loves to be a diligent guardian of the aforesaid fruit, introduces through the thousand pieces of silver the first, but not the chief, peace; and, changing a hundred into two hundred, afterward brings in the second and better peace. Having briefly shown that the grace common to all the perfect applies, he immediately returns to the Virgin with special love and concern. He desires her, for whom he cares above all the branches of the aforesaid vineyard, to pass more quickly from transitory peace to abiding peace.

## CHAPTER XLIX

“You who dwell in the gardens, friends listen: make me hear your voice.”

“Although,” he says, “I still delay both those who bring and those who postpone bringing a thousand pieces of silver for two hundred, and I do not yet permit them to be led to the desired attainment of the ensuing reward, I do not wish to restrain you, whom I love above all, any longer from your desire. Rather, granting you a choice, I desire you to have immediately whatever you choose.”

“You therefore, whom I have led out from the dwelling-place of darkness, from the shadow of hard death, and who by outstanding grace dwell not in a dry place but in gardens—choose a pleasing word; utter your voice; speak yourself. Your companions stand by; your friends listen and desire to hear from you yourself. I myself, who know better whatever you are now preparing to say, desire to hear your voice and the good pleasure of your inward choice, so that the manner of speaking may become known not to me but to the others, to whom your choice is hidden unless it shines forth in speech.

“With you, love for vainly passing things and fear of things coming upon you do not wither; rather, faith, hope, and love shine like gardens bright with dewy bloom. The grace of these is so wondrous that it delights your desire in such a way that no disturbance bends you down to things below. You indeed wish to depart or at once pass to things above. Loathing whatever belongs to time, you wish more swiftly to grasp eternal things; whatever I have bestowed for the present, you wish to exchange for the desire of future things; casting off the cloak of flesh, you desire to greet in presence the face of me, your beloved.”

And she says: “Flee,” etc.

## CHAPTER L

“Flee, my beloved; be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.”

In many passages and on many occasions above, the loving Virgin invited her beloved and asked him in many ways to come. At the beginning of the Song itself she more earnestly desired his kiss, and throughout this epithalamium she showed that this is what she willed and sought. What then does it mean that she now repels him, whose desire for him she earlier cries makes her languish? What reason, we may ask, is there that she bids flee the one whom she so loves, unless perhaps because lovers have quarrels in hope of sweeter reconciliation, as a certain writer [Note: [Col. 0487D] Terence, *Andria*.] declares:

> “The quarrels of lovers are the renewal of love.”

But, as I seem to see, the Virgin’s love knows no quarrels; rather, she burns to see sooner the one whom she so loves. Since she knows that he cannot be seen in this place or body, she desires to go with him to that place where she may behold him.

“Flee,” she says, “my beloved, to the secret sanctuary of the Father; return quickly; call me there with you, where I may no longer be harmed by any troubles. Strip me quickly of the corruption of this body, and, where it is permitted and insofar as it is permitted, reveal yourself visibly to me. Since you were formerly accustomed to be likened to a gazelle and a young stag, be now also in this matter swift, agile, and discerning. Let your consideration see worthily what befits a bride who is a mother, and distinguish me from all merely human beings by a higher privilege.

“The mountains of spices are the heavenly and angelic powers, which bring us, while we labor, various necessary healings. By their ministry useful spices are prepared for us, yet under the direction of him by whose art of compounding they are blended. I no longer desire that you speak with me beneath those angelic mountains; flee above them, that you may be held far more excellent. Keep your seat at the Father’s right hand, inaccessible alike to angels and human beings, and now, as I see, granted to me with you—to the mother with the Son.

“Take, therefore, my right hand and lead me according to your will. I shall follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. XIV), with no halting delay. Flee quickly, that I too may flee; for I am ready to flee. Fleeing, I shall see you going before me, exalted above the angels.”

But after the virgin Bride, the Mother, was received more gloriously by the Son and obtained a glorious seat with the Bridegroom above the angels, I judge it better to be silent about the honor in which she rejoices and the joy with which she sees herself honored than to dare speak at length of such things. For what my understanding, or one like mine, does not grasp, what manner or effect of utterance can there be? Even what the understanding in some measure judges that it contemplates cannot easily be explained in fitting words.

Yet this may be said: where the Son is, who placed the flesh he assumed at the Father’s right hand—whatever that is which Scripture truly calls the right hand—there is his Mother, who furnished him with her own flesh, who from her womb, with her integrity preserved, bore God made man. 285 There, I say, she is: crowned with glorious honor or honorable glory; she rejoices in, from, and with him whom she bore, having attained her desire. As bride she clings to her Bridegroom in true and sincere embraces, so that, though love is satisfied, the unrelaxed desire of love endures.

Therefore the Mother is with the Son not only in spirit, concerning which there is not even the slightest doubt, [Col. 0488D] but also in body. This indeed does not appear incredible, because although canonical Scripture does not proclaim it with evident proofs, devout faith is nevertheless led to it by probable arguments. Though one who is quick in word and knowledge may not prove it sufficiently, our Augustine nevertheless declares it worthy of belief. Nor is it troublesome to angels if they see the Bride with the Bridegroom, the Mother with the Son, occupying a royal throne; if they see her who formerly held him in her lap now holding him upon the heavenly throne; if they see human flesh gloriously honored above themselves in Mother and Son, and the marriage begun happily among us consummated there more happily.

Since concerning these matters I have spoken as I could, although not as I wished, and have reached the end of my discourse with a sufficiently slow foot, I beg you, holy Virgin, now that you stand with your Son in heaven, not to cease from care and concern on behalf of him who is yours. I am yours indeed, if not by merit sufficiently worthy, at least by an affection somewhat more ready: yours, serving you, though I do not yet know whether I am worthy of hatred or of love (Eccl. IX); yours, desiring to please you with services and gifts, if only you grant that I may effectively prevail in my purpose.

You therefore, holy Virgin, receive from my hand this small gift. It is not gold, not silver, not a stone suitable for the gifts of kings; but an unadorned offering of words, produced with a rather coarse understanding: a very small offering, yet full of vigils and labor. When I devoted myself to its exercise as to a rough gymnasium, [Col. 0489B] I was struck by many troubles and severely driven back, as it were from the front, by the attacks of malicious persons. I often interrupted the work I had begun because of harder pressures; [Col. 0490A] but, recalled and helped by the sweeter memory of your grace, I did not abandon it.

You, therefore, by whose aid I did not fail in the furnace of pressures beneath the heavy hammer, but somehow, taking breath, have now completed the work begun in your name: receive it now when offered. Correct the offerer mercifully; amend him; love him when amended; and commend me, when loved, to your Son. For I know that if I am commended to him by your goodwill, the venomous serpent either will not bite me at all, or, if it bites, its bite will not harm me. Either your Son will call back the tongues of detractors to modest silence, or he will transform their poisonous reports into a health-giving antidote.

Thus I hope, through your intercession, to be delivered from all who harm me by your grace; and, when delivered, to be enriched through grace with greater gifts. When enriched, you will grant that through you I may rejoice in the Son; and, to bring this book to an end, that at last, freed from evils, I may glory with you in heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0489]

This commentary on the Song of Songs, which Master Philip of Alms most learnedly and with sublime understanding composed, is a good word, a refined and chaste utterance. Therefore, whoever desires to be intoxicated by the breasts of the Bride and to be introduced by ordered love into the Bridegroom’s wine-cellar, look upon and receive this work dedicated to the Queen, in which she, the most beautiful of women, is described as standing amid the variety of her merits beside her beloved, fairer in form than the sons of men.]

John Gallemart, Doctor of Sacred Theology and professor of catechesis at the University of Douai, 7 February 1618.

[Col. 0489]

# MORAL INTERPRETATIONS OF THE SONG OF SONGS BY PHILIP OF HARVENG, ABBOT OF BONE-ESPERANCE 286 (G)*

[THE FIRST VOLUME BEGINS.]

## PROEM

[Col. 0489C]

To his lords and fathers worthy in every respect of reverence for holiness, MILO, bishop of the Morini, and HUGH, abbot of Prémontré: the worse and least of the servants of God, whose name is contained in the first five letters of the first five parts of the first volume, wishes them to have the discriminating hoof of Ezekiel’s calf.

By grace of God going before me, I began the following little work on the Song of Songs, at the urging and encouragement of a certain faithful man who had once heard me disputing concerning certain doctrines of divinity. Moreover, a certain illness, which from my childhood, though intermittently, has nevertheless often assailed and still assails me, moved me in large part to this work. [Col. 0489D] For I thought that, if I applied myself more ardently to this work, I should sometimes feel less the annoyances of the illness that assails me. I thought, I say, that the urgency of this work would drive from me the harassment of the aforesaid sickness. Yet I confess the truth of the matter to all: the work was indeed begun by me with God inspiring, but the aforesaid sickness has still been little alleviated for me.

But perhaps there will be some, of my own order or another, who, pretending to have zeal for God, though not according to knowledge, will say: “Who is this man? What is his person, his life, or his wisdom, that he has presumed to do this?” To them I say: I indeed, as I said above, am the worse and least of the servants of God; my bodily person is weak, my speech contemptible, my life sufficiently despicable before God, and my wisdom is none.

[Note: [Col. 0489] Some material is missing here which could not be read in the autograph, everywhere filled with erasures.] “Great,” he says, “is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. XXX). Truly great and wonderful is the abundance of God’s sweetness, which God has hidden for those who fear and love him—here, in the divine Scriptures, and in the age to come, in contemplation of his majesty. But lovers of the world cannot receive this sweetness, because, filled with vain pleasures and deadly desires, they do not at all long for the ineffable joys of the heavenly homeland. [Note: [Col. 0489D] A few words are missing here.]

Therefore we place this brief preface before the book, so that we may make our hearer diligent and attentive to understand the mysteries of divine reading, [Col. 0491A] lest in this little book he seek anything bodily or carnal. For the letter of this little book is quite remote from what it seems to sound like; and unless we believed it had certainly been produced by the Holy Spirit, we should judge it wholly unworthy of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

For who, hearing kisses, eyes, cheeks, and the Bride’s lips named, would not immediately and rightly be offended merely by hearing that such things were found in divine utterances, unless, with the Holy Spirit dictating, he believed that these things had been written concerning the coming of the Son of God to humankind and the salvation of faithful souls? Yet the more harshly the letter repels us from carnal and outward understanding, the more sweetly it introduces us to its inward understanding, beloved by God.

Certainly, it is believed that this book is composed by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit because all and each of the sentences found in it seem to contain at least seven things: namely, [Col. 0491B] the divinity and humanity of Christ; the union of Bridegroom and Bride, that is, of Christ and the Church; according to rhetorical ornaments, a one-membered, two-membered, three-membered, or four-membered sentence; and, according to secular disciplines, the seven liberal arts and the three parts of philosophy—logic, ethics, and physics, that is, the rational, moral, and natural disciplines—without which parts of philosophy this book cannot be expounded.

Moreover, the title prefixed to this little book appears to contain within itself the meaning of the entire book. For just as the sun, placed in heaven, diffuses its rays everywhere and, spreading its marvelous brightness, illumines the whole world by its presence, so this title placed before this little book already reveals to us in large part what the book seeks to say: “The voice of one desiring Christ’s coming.”

It is asked concerning this first title: since two persons seem to be introduced, namely Christ and someone who desires him, why is the proper name of this desiring person not expressed, while Christ’s name is manifestly named? The answer is that if any person were expressed by name or set down specifically, the other persons who speak in various ways in this book might perhaps appear excluded. Christ’s name, however, is set down openly and without veil because the prophecy of this book treats of the coming and incarnation of no one other than the Son of God alone.

Further, some may wonder why Christ, who is the worthier and more excellent person, does not begin speaking first in this book. But sound reason, supported by authority, required that the inferior person should speak first and humbly beg him—without whom it could not be saved—to come for its deliverance, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I).

The blessed Apostle Paul teaches us, saying: “All things that happened to our fathers happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. X). If, therefore, it was a figure among them, it ought to be truth among us. Turning over much Scripture of the Old Testament in my mind, I sought a figure of this truth: whether perhaps one of the patriarchs or prophets had anywhere kissed his wife, so that the preceding figure might reveal the subsequent reality more clearly. Yet I found this written of no one except Jacob the patriarch alone. For it is written of him alone that he once kissed his wife, that most famous Rachel, concerning whom no one doubts that she bears the figure of holy Church. Jacob, moreover, is recognized as having borne the figure of Christ both in the interpretation of his name and in the operation of his virtue.

For it is written in the book of Genesis (chap. XXIX) that the patriarch Jacob once journeyed to the eastern land. Coming to a certain [Col. 0492B] well, he spoke with the shepherds of that region; and behold, Scripture says, Rachel was coming with her flock, for she herself pastured her father’s flock. When Jacob learned that she was his cousin, he watered her flock and kissed her.

Afterward Jacob wept and told her that he was her kinsman. Who then is he who journeys to the eastern land, except Christ, of whom the prophet says: “Behold the man: East is his name” (Zech. VI)? And what is the eastern land except the blessed and everlasting Virgin Mary, Mother of God, from whom Christ deigned to arise, whom Ezekiel (chap. XI) calls the eastern gate? What did that well prefigure except the mystical and hidden Scripture which foretold that Christ would be born? What did Rachel’s flock, which Jacob watered, signify except the flock of prophets, whom Christ gave to drink from water springing up into eternal life? What did Jacob’s weeping suggest except the compassion which Christ had for us when he purposed to die for us? And what is it that holy Jacob tells Rachel—that he is her kinsman—except what the Lord said through the prophet: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI), and in the Gospel: “Go, tell my brothers,” etc. (Matt. XXVIII)?

What, moreover, does the kiss which Jacob gave Rachel signify except that Christ joined the nature of humankind to himself through the mystery of the Incarnation? [Col. 0492D] Hence humankind itself says in this place concerning Christ: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Let that same one who was formerly prefigured by the patriarchs and foretold by the prophets—that one, I say—come, assume from my nature immaculate flesh, and wonderfully restore me to the joys of paradise which I lost through Adam.

Let holy Church also say concerning Christ: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” that is, let the Word become flesh; and, just as Eve was fashioned from sleeping Adam of old (Gen. II), so let the same Word made flesh (John I)—that is, God made man—dying on the cross, betroth me to himself as his bride, pledged with his blood.

Let blessed Mary, Mother of Christ, also say—let her herself say concerning Christ: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”; that is, just as he formerly promised through Isaiah the prophet, saying, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive” (Isa. VII), let the Son of God come into me and receive from my virgin flesh a most holy body, so that, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber (Ps. XVIII), he himself, adorned with the purple cloak of my flesh, may proceed from my womb.

Let every faithful soul likewise say concerning Christ: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”; that is, let him unite me to himself through faith and works in this age, so that in eternal blessedness I may deserve to become one spirit with him. Of this kiss of Christ and holy Church—that is, of the mystery of the Incarnation—the prophet David says: “Righteousness and peace have kissed” (Ps. LXXXIV). Join, therefore, if you please, a lily to a violet or a rose: such is the kiss of Bridegroom and Bride, of Christ and Church—that is, the union of divine and human nature.

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” In this sentence you will find seven mysteries: Jacob and Rachel; God and humankind; Christ and holy Church; the Son of God and blessed Mary; Christ and the faithful soul; peace and righteousness; lily and violet.

## RECAPITULATION OF WHAT PRECEDES

With the utmost purpose and a pure heart, we must entreat God, whose unfolding of words gives light and reveals spiritual understanding to those childish in malice (1 Cor. XIV), that he may deign to open the eyes of our heart, so that we may be able to consider the wonders which are in his law. No truly wise person doubts that the Holy Spirit is the author of this book. Nor does anyone instructed in ecclesiastical letters fail to know that Solomon was the instrument of the Holy Spirit when he composed this book. For without the grace of the Holy Spirit he could not utter such great and such profound mysteries of Christ and the Church.

Since, therefore, we firmly hold that the Holy Spirit made this book, we must ask why that same Holy Spirit began the same book with the letter O, and what pleased him in this letter more than in the others. Yet he himself deigned to show how great is the authority and dignity of the mystery of this letter O, who gave himself the name of that same letter, saying: “I am α, alpha, and ω” (Rev. I), that is, the beginning and the end. “I am the beginning,” he says, “giving beginnings of existence to all creatures. I am the end,” that is, completion; because, when all human beings fail, I alone remain, since I am God and am in no way subject to changeability. Hence the Apostle James says: “With whom there is no change nor shadow of turning” (Jas. I).

Paul shows that Christ is the end, that is, completion, when he says: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X). Finally, if we wish to investigate more subtly the mystery of the letter O, in no other letter shall we find so great a figure not only of the whole world but even of God himself. For it is found rounded and complete on every side of itself, just as the philosophers describe the world of this age as rounded in the form of a sphere.

Moreover, if we examine more closely according to the Greek letters, we undoubtedly find that this letter ω is three-membered, that is, has three parts. What then do the three parts, rising upward in the one letter ω, signify except the three persons in the substance of the one supreme Trinity? Therefore the Holy Spirit begins the opening of this book with the letter ω not by chance but by a sure mystery of divinity, because throughout its whole text this book proclaims him who created the whole world from nothing and who declares himself in the Gospel to be one in the Trinity, saying: “I and the Father are one” (John X).

The three upward-looking parts of the letter ω thus declare, as we have said, three persons in the one substance of the Trinity. And fittingly the parts of the same letter look upward and, as if coming down from heaven, make one letter below: for knowledge of the holy Trinity descended to us through the Lord Jesus, and through unity of faith established its seat in the one holy catholic Church. Therefore in the Gospel the Lord Jesus himself says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII)—with the Holy Spirit understood—to be the one true God.

Certainly, I think that the prudent reader should not pass over carelessly the fact that this book takes its beginning from a kiss, which is a sign of love and peace. For in mystical and open expressions it points us to him at whose birth the angelic multitude cried: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

There is, moreover, another mystery which may still be said concerning the kiss: a kiss cannot be made except by two. Two sets of teeth, one opposite the other, come together in a single kiss of peace, and thus, with lips joined, accomplish a kiss in love. These two coming from opposite directions and meeting in one should not inappropriately be understood as the divinity and humanity of Christ. They came from very different places when one from heaven and the other from earth came together in one womb of blessed Mary ever-Virgin, and these two natures gave one another, as it were, a perfect kiss. For by the working grace of the Holy Spirit they are so inseparably united that, without danger to faith, God must no longer be spoken of apart from man, nor man apart from God.

This, then, is what our same nature seems to say in our book: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” as if to say: “I desire that God the Son of God should so assume me into the Virgin’s womb—that is, that the Word become flesh—that he may remain what he was, always true God, and may, with me changed from mortality to immortality, eternally constit—” [The supplied source breaks off at this point.]

We have learned by the authority of sacred Scripture (Job V) that nothing happens on earth without cause, because we and our words are in God’s hand. Since, therefore, it is beyond doubt that both we and our words are in his hand, it is plainly evident that we cannot say anything well unless either he cooperates or permits it. Further, although nothing is said to occur on earth without cause, neither do we judge that this happened without reason: that at the beginning of the exposition of this little book we made use of lilies, violets, and other flowers.

It was altogether fitting that our exposition should take its beginning from flowers, because, with his help, we intend to speak of him who says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II). He is indeed that wondrous flower which, according to the prophet Isaiah (chap. XI), rose from the root of Jesse—that is, Christ, who assumed flesh from the Virgin Mary. And as a sweetly fragrant flower sends out its most pleasing scent everywhere, so he spread throughout the world knowledge of his divinity and humanity.

Moreover, just as flowers without human cultivation produce honeycombs and honey of themselves, so the Virgin Mary bore from herself God and man without contact with a man. Let us therefore call this book, which speaks of that wondrous flower, “the flower of flowers”: that is, the flower of other books, apart from that supreme flower himself, Christ.

For all the saints are called flowers in holy discourse; hence the saying: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree,” etc. (Ps. XCI); “The righteous shall flourish like the lily before the Lord.” Certainly, all books of sacred Scripture may be called flowers because they make us flourish with flowers, that is, with spiritual virtues. Therefore, as Christ is the flower of other flowers—that is, the honor, glory, and beauty of his saints—so this book called the Song of Songs is, as we said above, apart from Christ’s Gospel, the flower of flowers, that is, the flower of other books.

Behold, as we have heard, the Bridegroom, that is Christ, calls himself a lily in this book, because in nearly every passage of sacred discourse the lily signifies virginity, chastity, and purity. Since he himself was a virgin and the son of a Virgin, he especially commended chastity to us in his Gospel among the other virtues, saying: “Let our loins be girded” (Luke XXII). As though he said: “Since you do not doubt that I am a lover of virginity, chastity, and purity, take care to preserve in thought, speech, and deed the chastity which is more pleasing to me than all other virtues.”

Moreover, I was reared in Nazareth, which is interpreted “flower,” because that soul feeds and nourishes me delightfully through devout works which breathes virginity, burns with chastity, and loves purity.

Therefore, as the Bridegroom, Christ himself, may be understood by the lily in this book, so his Bride, that is, holy Church, ought likewise to be interpreted by the flower of the violet. And rightly is the devout Mother Church designated by this flower, the violet, which is purple or sky-blue in color: she continually exhorts her children to the glorious contests of the martyrs and to the heavenly joys of everlasting blessedness. By the purple color, therefore, is understood the glory of martyrdom; by the sky-blue color, the blessed and glorious expectation of God’s kingdom.

Nor should this pass over in silence: the same flower, the violet, is described as temperate in nature, so that it can heal those whom an immoderate burning of the flesh beyond their strength afflicts. [Col. 0496A] This should fittingly be assigned to holy Church, which applies to her children, wounded by every kind of assault of temptations, the soothing poultices of devout confession and repentance. Hence every faithful person ought to say to his mother, the Church: “According to the multitude of my anxieties in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul.”

## THE SECOND ALLEGORY CONCERNING JACOB
In the abundance of memory, and in the delight of the Holy Spirit, we must recall that in the preceding part of this book we spoke of the departure of the patriarch Jacob for the eastern land, and that (so far as the Holy Spirit at that time supplied us with strength) the poverty of our understanding examined Jacob himself and the eastern land by interpreting them in an allegorical sense. It remains, therefore, [Col. 0496B] that we likewise return to the matter and, not as it deserves, but as the scantiness of our understanding can in some measure grasp it, seek out the sweetly fragrant flowers of a second allegory. For the divine page is a certain field overflowing with flowers, in which the faithful soul ought to delight itself by gathering the various flowers of allegory—that is, by meditating on spiritual meanings. Hence the prophet David says: “Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart” (Ps. 36).

The eastern land, therefore, is rightly called the heavenly Jerusalem, namely the dwelling-place of the citizens above, of which the Psalmist says: “My portion is in the land of the living” (Ps. 141). Whoever can indeed reach it by good works will taste death no more; for then every holy person is reborn in God through eternal birth, when his temporal life is ended by conditional death. [Col. 0496C] Therefore the elegant custom has become established in the holy Church that we proclaim the birthdays of the saints precisely when we know that they have departed from this light.

Who, then, is that Jacob, whose name means “wrestler,” except our spirit 290, to which an unceasing struggle against spiritual wickedness is appointed? Let our Jacob therefore set out for the land of the East; that is, let our spirit hasten by the steps of good action toward the land of promise. Paul yearned for that promised land when he said: “Let us hasten to enter into that rest” (Heb. 4). But as we hasten toward the heavenly Jerusalem, we encounter a well shut by a great stone, because, as the prophet David says, “The judgments of God are a great abyss” [Col. 0496D] (Ps. 35). Solomon agrees with him, saying: “All things are reserved for a human being as uncertain after death” (Eccl. 9).

What, then, do we say this well, shut by a great stone, is, except the hidden and terrible counsel of God, which is in no way disclosed until the day of judgment? In dread of this the prophet says: “Come and see the works of God: terrible in his counsels toward the children of men” (Ps. 65). And what do the shepherds there with their flocks, lying about the well, signify except the faithful souls both of prelates and of subjects, who await God’s judgment? Hence it is rightly said that, when the shepherds had gathered together with their flocks, the stone was removed from the mouth of the well and the sheep were watered: for, when all people come to God’s judgment, his terrible counsel, [Col. 0497A] now hidden, will be revealed.

Then at last the sheep will be watered from the water of the opened well, when each person is condemned or saved according to the just judgment of God’s hidden counsel: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared” (Matt. 25); but to those on the right: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (ibid.). And thus, in a wondrous and ineffable manner, Jacob will recognize the face of his kinswoman Rachel, when our spirit beholds in heaven the contemplative life for which, while still placed on earth, it long yearned. Hence Rachel is interpreted “the beginning seen,” because then our spirit will contemplate God himself not in a riddle or through a mirror, but face to face (1 Cor. 13).

The kiss which Jacob gave Rachel [Col. 0497B] may be interpreted by that saying of the Lord: “Father, I will that, as I and you are one, so they also may be one in us” (John 18). Thus it is clearer than light that, when one gives another the kiss of peace, the mouth is joined to mouth in loving affection, with no thing interposed. Hence blessed John says: “We are the children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; but we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). Therefore there will be no opposition between Creator and creature; otherwise there would not be true and perfect blessedness.

## Recapitulation of What Has Gone Before According to Ethics, That Is, Moral Interpretation

[Col. 0497C] As we approach morality and desire to discourse upon morality, we must ourselves be well behaved. For we cannot speak elegantly of human morals unless we have in some degree been instructed or adorned by morals. Above we said—unless perhaps it has slipped from our memory—that this book begins from perfection, that is, from the letter O, which signifies perfection. According to the Latins, as philosophers say, this letter suggests within itself the form of the whole world; and, as formed according to the Greeks, it represents to us in its pattern the holy Trinity.

Therefore you who read or hear this book, strive for perfection; labor to be perfect. Hear not me but the Lord saying in the Gospel: “Be [Col. 0497D] perfect, as your Father who is in heaven is perfect” (Matt. 5). Yet you will by no means be able to be perfect unless, having put away iniquity, you adhere perfectly to the highest perfection, which is God. David desired this perfection when he said: “But for me it is good to adhere to God” (Ps. 72).

You can therefore be perfectly perfect if you believe and retain in your heart the faith of the holy Trinity, and fulfill that same faith by good works. I say that you will present yourself perfectly perfect to God on the day of judgment if, in this age, so far as you can, you keep yourself free from every sin. But because, as blessed Gregory says, a good work is of no value without chastity, just as chastity is of no value without a good work, lilies rightly follow in our recapitulation and signify virginity, [Col. 0498A] chastity, and purity.

There are, moreover, certain people who are virgins and chaste, but are not pure, because they pride themselves insolently upon preserving virginity or chastity. For Eve, our first parent, was indeed a virgin and chaste in body, but unclean in mind, because she obeyed the devil who falsely promised rather than God who truly threatened. Hence divine Scripture says: “He who exalts his heart is unclean before God”; nor does it profit one at all to be bodily virgin and chaste, if one is incestuous in mind.

Therefore let spiritual lilies bloom anew in us—the emblems of virginity, chastity, and purity of heart—so that, made chaste in body and soul, we may deserve to be marked by that evangelical blessing by which those are ennobled to whom the Lord says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they [Col. 0498B] shall see God 291” (Matt. 5). Thus violets rightly follow in the order of recapitulation, gleaming with heavenly brightness, because those preserve chastity well who seek, through its observance, to attain the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

The other flowers, not expressed by special name in this exposition, fittingly suggest the remaining virtues by which the virtues mentioned above are adorned. For without humility, obedience, charity, patience, long-suffering, perseverance, prudence, and discretion—the mother of all virtues—no one can retain perfection or perfectly possess peace or concord, which are designated by the kiss of the Bridegroom and Bride.

## First Moral Interpretation of Jacob

[Col. 0498C] In the old Law divine Scripture teaches us (Lev. 1) that one who offers God from the flock a ram, or any animal suitable for sacrifices, must first remove its skin; second, put its flesh to the sacred fires; third, offer to the Lord as a whole burnt offering the fat and the things covered by fat. A ram or heifer is any statement taken from the Old Testament. We remove, as it were, the skin from this statement when, treating its historical meaning, we affirm it to be true. The flesh, however, is delivered to sacred fires when its allegory is explained as understood through spiritual meanings. We consider that we offer the fat and the parts beneath it to God when we investigate its moral meaning, and those things that depend upon morals, for the profit of faithful souls [Col. 0498D] and the praise of God himself.

Since, therefore, in the foregoing treatment we interpreted the historical Jacob in an allegorical and spiritual sense, we have, as it were, removed the skin and burned the flesh in the sacred fire. It remains for us to apply the fat to the divine fire—that is, to bring moral meaning to light through a moral and higher understanding. Our flesh indeed becomes the eastern land when vices are put to death in it and spiritual virtues arise. The spiritual Jacob—that is, Christ—will deign to visit it if it is such as to be judged worthy of his visitation.

The well to which the historical Jacob came signifies our heart. If it loves God perfectly and keeps his word, Christ will come to it and remain in it. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: [Col. 0499A] “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14). The stone by which the well is shut is rightly understood as the hardness of our heart. The Lord mercifully promises to remove this hardness from us when he says through the prophet Ezekiel (chs. 11 and 36): “I will take away from you the heart of stone, and give you a heart of flesh, and make you walk in my commandments.”

The three flocks of sheep with their shepherds, which Jacob finds beside the well, are the three kinds of thoughts that move about our heart. For in our thoughts we often remember the evils we have done; by God’s help we guard against present evils; and we entreat God concerning future evils, lest they overwhelm us submerged. [Col. 0499B] The history rightly reports that those flocks were watered when the stone was removed, because, when the hardness of our heart has been removed, the aforesaid thoughts are made drunk with spiritual compunction and the health-giving sprinkling of tears.

The shepherds who guard the aforesaid sheep are faith, hope, and charity, which nourish our simple thoughts. It is therefore clear that one who mourns over past sins, guards against present ones, and fears future ones in prayer, makes himself free in every way from every sin. Thus at last he returns to that virtue called sinlessness, in which God created the first human being in his own image.

Finally, the history describes in elegant language that Jacob there recognized his kinswoman Rachel, because without doubt the creature is then more perfectly recognized by its Creator [Col. 0499C] when a human being, according to his ability, keeps himself from sin. Hence Rachel is rightly interpreted “sheep” or “the beginning seen,” because the creature clearly returns to the beginning of its creation when, through simplicity and sinlessness, without the blemish of sin, it is presented to its Creator.

The weeping with which Jacob wept at the sight of Rachel signifies the ineffable joy and incomprehensible jubilation which God, appearing to his faithful, will grant them. For we often weep from excessive joy, just as this Jacob is known to have wept in exultation when he recognized his kinswoman Rachel. The kiss which Jacob gives Rachel signifies that unity by which we shall be united to God himself. Of this unity the Apostle Paul seems to me to speak when he says: “He who adheres to God becomes one spirit [Col. 0499D] with him” (1 Cor. 6).

Moreover, the fact which the history does not pass over—that Jacob told Rachel that he was her blood-relative—may fittingly be interpreted thus: when judgment is ended, we shall recognize our substance in our Creator, which he long ago assumed in pity for us when he willed to be born from the blessed Virgin Mary.

## 292. Here Begins the Second Moral Interpretation, Intermingled with the Flowers of Allegory

The text of the history has related to our ears concerning the patriarch Isaac how he once commanded his servants to dig a well. Digging more deeply, they found water in abundance, and therefore called that well “Abundance.” What, indeed, did that well [Col. 0500A] which Isaac’s servants dug foreshadow except the Old Testament, which, before it was expounded by teachers, remained buried beneath an obstacle of earth? Let us therefore dig this well with a spiritual hoe, and without doubt we shall find abundant waters—that is, spiritual meanings.

In the preceding treatment above we spoke of Jacob allegorically and morally. Now let us return to this same Jacob by a spiritual journey and seek in him a second moral meaning through a higher understanding. This moral interpretation is sometimes intermingled with certain allegorical flowers, lest it be judged unadorned by prudent and vigorous men.

Look upon yourself, O human being; and, when you have considered yourself, you will find figuratively within yourself the whole world—and, to speak more boldly, if you live well, your very Creator. If, then, the human being is of such dignity as somehow to contain within himself not only the likeness of the entire world but even of God himself—for the human being was made in the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1)—no one should find it absurd if we choose, by turns, to interpret our spirit or soul now as Jacob, now as the eastern land.

Let us say that our spirit itself is the eastern land, and meanwhile the spiritual Jacob. For just as the historical Jacob wrestled with the angel and prevailed against him, and just as the allegorical Jacob—that is, Christ—triumphing over death and the devil, overcame them on the wood of his cross, so the moral Jacob—that is, our spirit—must crucify this world to itself and fight against itself, so that, ruling its own mind, [Col. 0500C] it may be stronger than conquerors of cities.

The spiritual person, I say, must crucify the world to himself, so that he may say with the Apostle Paul: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6). The inner human being must, I say, labor beyond strength to conquer himself and the world, encouraged by the example of the Lord Jesus, who says: “Take courage, for I have conquered the world” (John 16). Nor should he strive any less earnestly to become the eastern land, from which vices are continually uprooted and in which spiritual virtues arise.

The spiritual way of Jacob—that is, of our spirit—must rightly be understood as Christ, who says: “I am the way” (John 14). The straight way which leads to God is simple obedience. Hence, according to the history, Jacob obeyed his mother Rebecca [Col. 0500D] when he traveled along this way of which we speak. Therefore no way is straighter than obedience; and obedience is not true and straight except in him who said: “I am the truth and the life” (ibid.).

The place to which Jacob is reported to have come at his first stopping-place—namely, the house of God, or Luz—is interpreted “Beth-el nut,” that is, “almond.” Therefore let our spirit, intent upon continual prayers, become the house of God, because the Lord says: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. 21). Yet whoever desires to become the house of God should not refuse to become a nut or an almond. For our spirit cannot be God’s dwelling without fortitude, patience, long-suffering, and prudence; these fruits’ very hard and almost unconquerable shell signifies this.

That Jacob wished to rest after sunset signifies that our spirit then rests perfectly in God when it puts to death and slays within itself everything that belongs to sin. The stones that he gathered and placed under his head signify the examples of the saints, which, storing in our head—that is, in our mind—and living according to them, we perfectly despise the world. That saints are called stones is attested by the Apostle Peter, who says: [Col. 0501A] “And you, like living stones, are built up into a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit” (1 Pet. 2). Nor is this surprising, since the Lord Jesus himself is called in David “the cornerstone” (Ps. 117), and in Daniel, “a stone cut from the mountain without hands” (Dan. 2).

Jacob’s falling asleep signifies that we must renounce the world perfectly and adhere to Christ; or it signifies contemplation of the supreme Divinity and forgetfulness of all secular vanity. The ladder consisting of two timbers, which Jacob saw on high and whose summit pierced heaven’s secrets, is the two Testaments, which teach and instruct us and lead us to knowledge of the divine majesty. Hence the history rightly says that Jacob saw the Lord leaning upon the summit of the ladder. For by no means can we come to the Lord himself unless, according to our measure, we spiritually fulfill the commandments of the two Testaments.

O how great is the mercy of our Redeemer! For what did God’s leaning upon the summit of the ladder prefigure, except his descent for the redemption of humankind, which from that time he was already in some manner preparing? [Col. 0501C] The stone which Jacob anointed after he had completed his sleep, in preference to the other stones, signified Christ, filled above all saints with the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

## 293

Of this spiritual anointing and incomprehensible outpouring of the Holy Spirit, the prophet David speaks to the Son of God: “Because you loved righteousness and hated iniquity, therefore God your Father anointed you with the oil of rejoicing above all your saints” (Ps. 44). The stone which Jacob anointed and set up as a pillar signifies that Christ, through the mystery of the Incarnation, was to obtain in the holy Church a place of pontifical dignity and possess throughout the whole world the sceptres of royal authority. Hence Jacob rightly says: “For truly the Lord is in this place” (Gen. 28), because outside the catholic Church no one can be saved or please God.

Moreover, if we wish to interpret this ladder morally, we may fittingly understand its two timbers as faith and hope, which receive us, as it were, on earth and bring us, lifted up, into heaven’s secrets. Faith and hope are necessary to us in this age, but in heaven they will have no function (Rom. 8), because, as Scripture says, in the age to come we shall see as he is the God in whom we believe and hope, and whom we await through patience (1 John 3); and therefore we shall have no further need of faith and hope.

The rungs inserted into the two timbers of this ladder may be understood as the remaining virtues, without which faith and [Col. 0502A] hope are altogether useless. For as our body dies without the soul, so faith without works, as James testifies, is called dead (Jas. 2). Thus charity rightly follows faith and hope in order; it is divided into two, namely love of God and love of neighbour. For one who merely believes or hopes in God, but neither loves God himself nor loves his neighbour for God’s sake, and who moreover refuses to perform what is good, is plainly like the demons. Of them the Apostle James says: “The demons believe and tremble” (ibid.).

Let us therefore place upon this ladder which leads to heaven its first rung: humility; love of God and neighbour; good thoughts; better words; best actions; chastity of body and soul; purity of heart; fraternal peace; concord; confession; penitence; bodily discipline; fasts; vigils; prayers; bodily exertions for God; spiritual meditations upon God’s law; contempt for the world; disdain for our body; and spiritual desires. Upon the summit of this ladder let us place obedience, because it is this that leads us to the contemplation of the supreme majesty. Thus divine Scripture says concerning obedience: “Through obedience they arrive at knowledge of God’s hidden things” (2 Cor. 2).

Let our spirit therefore ascend this ladder: “From virtue to virtue,” until it sees God reigning below in Zion (Ps. 83). Finally, for this reason the Lord seems to stand upon obedience, which is placed on the summit of this ladder: because through obedience [Col. 0502C] he planned to reconcile humankind to himself and, according to the Apostle Paul (Col. 1), to make peace through spiritual concord between things in heaven and things on earth. Hence the same Paul says: “Christ became obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. 2). And elsewhere: “From the things which he suffered, though he was the Son of God, he learned obedience” (Heb. 5).

Jacob’s words when he awoke—“Truly the Lord is in this place” (Gen. 28)—plainly declare that God truly dwells in our heart when our spirit has perfectly possessed within itself the aforesaid ladder, and our mind, despising the vanities of the world, has fallen asleep in sweet repose in the love of God. We too can morally be an anointed stone if we have received an anointing from the Holy Spirit, as did those to whom the Apostle John said: “And you have received an anointing from the Holy Spirit, and have no need for anyone to teach you, because his anointing teaches you about all things” (2 John 2).

The field in which Jacob finds the well may fittingly be understood as our spirit or soul, provided that it is filled with the fragrant sweetness of spiritual flowers, as was the one who said: “We are the sweet fragrance of Christ” (2 Cor. 2). In this place, however, the well must be understood as the Holy Spirit, of whom the Lord Jesus said in the Gospel: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and living waters shall flow from his belly.” [Col. 0502D] “This,” however, “he said concerning the Holy Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive” (John 7).

The Holy Spirit himself, I say, is “the fountain of gardens, [Col. 0503A] the well of living waters flowing with force from Lebanon” (Song 4): that is, the holiness, refreshment, purification, cleansing, joy, and jubilation of faithful souls who desire to be with Christ. Therefore let our soul labor to possess this well within itself; that is, let it strive through good works to become a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit.

Yet the waters of this well, said to flow from Lebanon, signify that the Holy Spirit is possessed only in a chaste body and a purified heart. Thus Mount Lebanon itself is interpreted “whitening.” The statement that this well was shut by a great stone elegantly declares that the Holy Spirit in no way dwells in a body subject to sins (Wis. 1). For the huge stone is the mass of our crimes, which without doubt hides the Holy Spirit from us lest he be seen. Hence the prophet says: “The hand of the Lord is not powerless to save, but our sins have made a wall between you and God” (Isa. 59).

But neither should we carelessly pass over what Wisdom says: “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful” (Wis. 1). Let the wall of our crimes, or the millstone, therefore be removed; and let spiritual discipline be embraced and maintained by us—that is, let us confess our sins 294 [Col. 0503B] and submit ourselves to spiritual correction, so that we may be able to become the most holy dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit.

Let our spirit, I say, be a field blossoming with every kind of flower of virtues; let the well be found in it by Jacob, pouring forth health-giving streams—that is, let the Holy Spirit be found to dwell therein through Christ. His presence will plainly be manifested in this way: if in all things we are meek, humble, and peaceable, [Col. 0504B] and abound in the fruits of good action with chastity and sobriety.

[Col. 0503] Here ends the first tome, that is, the first volume on the Song of Songs.

## Here Begins the Second Tome, on the Words: “Your Breasts Are Better Than Wine, Fragrant with the Best Ointments”

[Col. 0503B] In order that the things which follow in this book may shine more clearly for us, it is necessary that the preceding matters of this book not depart from our memory. For blessed Jerome says: [Col. 0503C] “The divine discourse coheres with itself, and what follows depends upon what precedes.”

For just as the manna which once descended from heaven to earth was one thing and signified another, so divine utterances certainly display one thing outwardly and conceal another inwardly. The manna which God rained upon the children of Israel was bodily food, but spiritually it signified the flesh of Christ, who says in the Gospel: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6). The dew, which descended from heaven together with the manna, bore a figure of that blood.

Accordingly, just as the Israelites, gathering manna (Num. 11), ground it in a mill and, making bread from it, prepared for themselves every delight and every sweetness, [Col. 0503D] so the children of spiritual grace and enemies of the killing letter ought to examine and ruminate upon the divine Scriptures in spiritual meanings, and thence serve spiritual food to their hearers.

Let us not therefore be among Abraham’s servants who remain at the foot of the mountain, guarding the ass; rather, let us ascend the high mountain with Abraham and Isaac, so that we may be able to see the angel and the ram caught by its horns among the brambles (Gen. 22). Who, then, are those who remain at the foot of the mountain and guard the ass, except those who do not seek a spiritual and higher sense in sacred speech? For it is like guarding a brute animal beside a mountain not to seek allegorical and moral meaning in the divine writings.

The angel who appeared to Abraham on the mountain after he had dismissed the ass signifies allegory, which discloses itself more fully to those whom historical [Col. 0504B] interpretation does not delay from ascending to spiritual understanding. The same angel, set forth in the figure of allegory, is rightly said to have cried from heaven, because spiritual allegory always proclaims ecclesiastical mysteries and heavenly sacraments.

[Col. 0504C] The ram caught by its horns among the brambles signified, not unfittingly, moral meaning, which depends upon the harshness of the letter. Hence the same ram is rightly said to have been neither impaled nor bound among the brambles, because moral meaning is found fully among the sequence of the letter either rarely or never; rather, as a ram hangs caught by its horns among brambles, so moral meaning itself is prudently drawn out by prudent and learned men from the history to which it subtly clings.

Let us therefore consider how reasonably the Bride addresses the Bridegroom—that is, how the holy Church turns to Christ and says: “Therefore I desired your coming,” that is, “your kiss,” “because your breasts are better than wine.” In this place we may, with sound understanding, understand Christ’s two breasts as his mercy and clemency, provided that mercy is attributed to his humanity and clemency to his divinity. Hence the prophet Jonah says to the Lord (ch. 4): “I know, Lord, that you are clement and merciful”; as if to say: “I know certainly that you, who are now known to all only as God, will in the future, having assumed our humanity, become a human being for us.”

Moreover, wine, known to have a harsher taste, fittingly signifies the severe justice of the Mosaic Law. Let the Bride therefore say to the Bridegroom—that is, the Church to Christ: “For this reason I desired your coming, because your breasts are better than wine”; that is: “Your clemency and mercy are better than the severe and merciless justice of the ancient Law.”

Finally, if we understand spiritually Christ’s two breasts in the divine page as allegory [Col. 0504D] and moral interpretation, and wine as history, we do not depart from the true sense. Let us too say with the Bride to the Bridegroom: “Your breasts are better than wine”; that is, moral interpretation and allegory are sweeter than the often harsh and irrational understanding of history.

Otherwise: “Your breasts are better than wine.” God’s two breasts were indeed the Law and the Prophets, which killed those whom they nursed. Hence Paul says: “The Law works wrath”—that is, death—“and the Law brought nothing to perfection” (Rom. 4). Of these breasts Isaiah says: “Whom will he teach 295 knowledge, and whom will he make to understand what is heard? Those weaned from milk, torn away from the breasts” (Isa. 29); as if to say: “Christ will teach that person the spiritual knowledge and hearing of his Gospel who utterly removes from himself the carnal and tasteless meanings of the Law and the Prophets.”

[Col. 0505A] Of these breasts David says: “From my mother’s breasts I was cast upon you” (Ps. 21); that is: “I abandoned the killing letter and the Jewish understanding of the Law, and immediately came to you, who are the supreme truth of the Law.” Thus the Law and the Prophets are in this place God’s breasts, but the wine is the Gospel, of which Christ says: “New wine must be put into new wineskins” (Matt. 9), that is, the apostles. Christ himself is the cluster; the Gospel is the wine. As wine comes from a cluster, so Christ composed the Gospel.

This was fittingly prefigured in the history which relates that two men once brought on their shoulders, upon a piece of wood, a cluster with its branch from the promised land (Num. 13). These two men carrying upon the wood the cluster with its branch are the two peoples who killed Christ on the cross: the Jews, crying, “Crucify him” (Luke 23; John 19), and the Gentiles, who placed him upon the cross. Let the Bride therefore say to the Bridegroom, the Church to Christ: “Your breasts are better than wine”; that is, the utterances of the Law and the Prophets, tempered and bedewed by the grace of evangelical preaching, have been greatly improved—that is, made sweeter and better.

For the Law said: “If anyone commits this or that sin, let him die” (Exod. 21). But the Gospel cries: “If anyone sins, let him confess, do penance, and he shall not die.” Your breasts, therefore, have been greatly improved—that is, made sweeter.

“Fragrant with the best ointments.” Ointments are made from various sweetly fragrant spices. Let us therefore seek these ointments. The Apostle John says: “You have an anointing from the Holy Spirit, and his anointing teaches you about all things” (1 John 2). Let us now consider the ointment which was placed on Aaron’s head and descended into his beard. Aaron signified Christ, and his beard the apostles, who, like a beard, clung more closely than the other saints to Christ their head. The ointment placed upon Aaron’s head and descending into his beard is the diverse gifts of the Holy Spirit descending from Christ upon his apostles.

Filled with these ointments, Paul said: “We are the sweet fragrance of Christ in every place” (2 Cor. 2). And elsewhere: “We give thanks to God, who has made manifest through us in every place the fragrance of the knowledge of himself” (ibid.). Therefore, anointed and perfumed with these ointments—that is, with the gifts of the Holy Spirit and apostolic teachings—the Bridegroom’s [Col. 0506A] breasts, that is, the Prophets and the Law tempered with the new wine of the Gospel, have become far more fragrant—that is, more redolent—than they were before.

Strive, therefore, O hearer who hears and reads what the Bridegroom’s breasts are; strive, I say, that you too may have breasts of your own, as Peter and Paul had. One of them said: “I gave you milk to drink” (1 Cor. 3); the other said: “Like newborn infants, desire milk” (1 Pet. 2). If, therefore, you ask what these breasts are, I answer: they are the two commandments of charity, love of God and of neighbour—that you may love God above all things and your neighbour as yourself.

But those who love the world do not possess these breasts, because the more closely they are joined to it, the farther they withdraw from God. Let such people therefore hear the Apostle James crying terribly: [Col. 0506B] “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4).

## Recapitulation of What Has Gone Before
By the inspiration of the grace of the Holy Spirit, we said above and instilled through the ears of the body into the minds of our hearers that the manna which God once rained from heaven upon the children of Israel truly bore the figure and image of Christ’s body. But perhaps some will now say—whether because this interpretation displeases them, or because they are filled with a more spiritual and elevated understanding—“This interpretation will produce distaste, because we have strayed greatly from divine understanding in equating a corruptible thing, namely manna, with an incorruptible thing, namely Christ’s body.” Yet if they disdain to give credence to our words, let them see and consider [Col. 0506C] what the historical text in Exodus declares to us even when we are silent:

> “There appeared in the wilderness something small, and as though pounded with a pestle, resembling frost upon the ground. When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another, ‘Manhu,’ which means, ‘What is this?’ For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them: ‘This is the bread which the Lord has given you to eat’” (Exod. XVI).

Let us see, then, whether perhaps we can find Christ called bread anywhere. The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever; and the bread which I shall give is my flesh, for the life of the world” (John VI). See how fittingly the Old and New Testaments agree with one another.
