[Col. 0506D] Therefore, what Moses calls manna and heavenly bread, the Lord in the Gospel calls bread descending from heaven and his own flesh.

Yet let us consider, having for a little while put aside the tumult of worldly thoughts, why the Holy Spirit says through the prophet Moses that it appeared “small.” Then, why is that same manna described as pounded with a pestle, and why is it reported to have lain upon the ground “in the likeness of frost”? For if, according to the character of the grammatical art, we examine carefully this word, *minutum* (“small”), we undoubtedly find that it is derived from the verb *minuo, minuis*—“I lessen, you lessen.” Thus manna is described as small not by chance, but by the certain mystery of reason, because it bore the figure of Christ’s body. Of him the prophet David speaks to God [Col. 0507A] the Father, saying: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands” (Ps. VIII).

Thus it is not without reason that manna, appearing from above, is said to have been found small upon the earth, because that supreme Majesty of the only-begotten Son greatly diminished himself when he came down to bear the injuries of our mortality; and, taking the form of a servant, according to the Apostle Paul’s expression, “emptied himself” (Phil. II). This manna was greatly diminished when the Creator of heaven, earth, and all things lay hidden among human beings without any estimation of rank. This manna appeared greatly diminished when the Creator of humankind endured so many reproaches from his creatures.

Accordingly, the book of Exodus continues that this heavenly manna appeared as though pounded with a pestle. This clearly corresponds to Christ’s humanity, which, as we have already said, endured so many dishonours and insults from wicked people. This spiritual manna was indeed greatly pounded when Christ’s body was smeared with spittle, harshly handled with scourges, dishonoured by a crown of mock honour, and moreover made the object of everyone’s derision. This spiritual manna was battered by the pestle of cruel suffering when a soldier’s spear pierced Christ’s side, and the hardness of nails bored through his hands and feet. [Col. 0507C]

Therefore, all ambiguity being put aside, it must be confessed that Christ was true God and true man, and that ancient manna bore his image or figure. He was undoubtedly man: enduring the pain of suffering, he died and commended his spirit into the hand of God the Father, saying, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII). But he was true God, and the Son of God—not adoptive, but consubstantial and coeternal—who said in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John X).

That the same manna had the likeness of frost does not at all turn us away from divine and mystical understanding; rather, it subtly introduces us to the truth of so great a depth. It is plain to almost all who exercise human reason that frost is nothing other than water congealed by cold. It appears especially when the sun’s burning heat [Col. 0507D] is somewhat moderated and the wintry air freezes, by the severity of its cold, the water which it finds upon the earth. Therefore, as we suppose, manna appeared upon the earth in the likeness of frost in order to indicate to us the hardness or unbelief of the Jewish people.

Thus it is written in the Gospel: “The Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter” (ibid.). Therefore the Jews surrounded Christ and said: “How long do you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (ibid.). It is therefore clearer than light that the coldness and numbness of unbelief possessed the hearts of those who strove to entrap Christ by their plots and refused to believe in him who had come for their salvation, as though they did not know who he was. To indicate the hardness of the Jews’ hearts, the Evangelist says that it was winter [Col. 0508A] when the Jews said to the Lord Jesus: “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”

Thus Exodus fittingly continues that when the children of Israel saw the manna, they said, “Manhu,” meaning, “What is this?” For they did not know what it was. Behold: the fathers in the wilderness, when they saw manna, said, “What is this?” But their children, seeing him whose figure that manna bore, said, “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” Who, then, filled with so great amazement, would not rightly stand astonished when the ancient Law and the new preaching of the Gospel proclaim one and the same thing? The historical text of the old Law says concerning the Jews that they were wholly ignorant what manna was. But concerning their children Paul the Apostle, the eminent preacher of the new Law, says: “For if they had known the Lord Jesus, they would never have crucified the King of glory” (I Cor. II).

Therefore, even to this day the ignorance of *Manhu* remains among unbelieving Jews; but among faithful Christians there remains uncorrupted faith and knowledge of the Lord Jesus. Let the Jews, then, ask Moses what *Manhu* is; let Moses answer them: “This is the bread which the Lord gave you from heaven to eat.”

But let us, silencing our own question, receive with the attentive ear of the heart what the Lord said to the Jews in the Gospel: “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and died” (John VI). But why did they die? Because they believed nothing else concerning that manna than what they saw with bodily eyes. Likewise their children, struck by their fathers’ unbelief and blindness, [Col. 0508C] thought Christ to be merely human, and disdained to believe that he was true God and the true Son of God.

It is therefore established beyond doubt that both fathers and children were condemned by a like death of unbelief. To them the Lord fittingly says in the Gospel: “I told you that you will die in your sin” (John VIII). This Ezekiel the prophet had fittingly prophesied long before, when he said: “And why will you die, O children of Israel? For I do not will the death of the sinner, says the Lord, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII). Thus he who prophesies not concerning the present but the future, saying, “You will die,” plainly announces the Jews’ unbelief and that they would not believe in him who was to be born for them. [Col. 0508D]

## RECAPITULATION OF WHAT PRECEDES: ON THE BRIDEGROOM’S BREASTS

In the earlier treatment of this book, when we discussed, according to our measure, the Bridegroom’s breasts, we interpreted those breasts in the spiritual sense as clemency and mercy: clemency being referred to his divinity, and mercy attributed to his humanity. Figures of these spiritual breasts of the Bridegroom, namely clemency and mercy, are found in many places in the sacred utterances.

Thus, in the Third Book of Kings it is said (ch. VI): “Solomon made at the entrance of the oracle two doors of olive wood, and carved upon them figures of cherubim and palms, and sculptures projecting very prominently; and he overlaid both the cherubim and the palms and the rest with gold.” The figure of these spiritual breasts of the Bridegroom—that is, clemency and mercy—is also found in the same Book of Kings (ch. X) under the designation of hands, as it is written: [Col. 0509A] “King Solomon made a great throne of ivory, and covered it with exceedingly bright gold. It had six steps; the top of the throne was rounded at the back; and two hands, one on either side, held the seat; and two lions stood beside each hand, and twelve lion cubs stood upon the six steps, on either side.” Afterwards the history of Kings adds that “no such work was made in any of the kingdoms” (ibid.).

These, I say, are the Bridegroom’s two spiritual breasts, which the prophet Zechariah calls the two olive trees in his book (ch. IV). As it is written there: “I saw, and behold, a lampstand wholly of gold, with its lamp upon its top, and its seven lamps upon it, and seven funnels for the lamps which were upon its top; and two olive trees over it, one at the right of the lamp and one at its left.” And afterwards, when the same prophet asked the angel who spoke with him what were the two olive trees, or the two olive branches beside the two golden beaks in which are channels of gold, the holy angel answered him: “These are the two sons of the oil of brightness, who stand before the ruler of the whole earth” (ibid.).

If now we return to the order of our argument and show how the two doors of olive wood set at the entrance of [Col. 0509C] the oracle signify the Bridegroom’s two breasts, clemency and mercy, we must first, having set aside the veil of the killing letter, tell the friends of spiritual grace that he who is called the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs is also called the temple’s oracle and the ivory throne in the Book of Kings. Zechariah the prophet likewise, in the Holy Spirit, called him the golden lampstand.

As breasts are set in the human body bodily, so these two virtues—clemency and mercy—are naturally inherent in Christ. Therefore they are rightly called his breasts, because by the sweet abundance of these virtues the whole world is filled, nourished, and sustained. Of this abundance David the prophet says: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. XXXII). For how could this world, weighed down by so many iniquities, endure? Or how could the mortal race gain salvation, if it were judged with God’s clemency and mercy removed? It is evident that neither the world nor humanity could endure for even one hour of the day if God chose to look to the evils done by people in this world rather than to his own clemency. Therefore David the prophet also says: [Col. 0509D] “O Lord, do not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities” (Ps. CII).

Thus the Bridegroom’s breasts are fittingly understood through the two doors of the oracle. As those entering the oracle entered by those doors, so those who are to enter the kingdom of heaven will enter not by their own merits [Col. 0510A] or works, but by God’s clemency and mercy.

But what, we may ask, does it mean that cherubim, palms, and also raised carvings are said to have been sculpted upon the doors of the oracle? It is plain that *cherubim* is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge or wisdom”; and many know that in ancient times the hands of victors were adorned with palms as an emblem of praise and victory. An *anaglyptum*, so far as may be understood, is said to be a kind of carving whose rear part lies hidden within, while its front, formed by the sculptor’s art of human skill, projects extraordinarily far outward.

Thus cherubim, which signify a multitude of knowledge or wisdom, are not without reason found carved upon the doors of the oracle. It is just, I think, that those who hope in God’s clemency and mercy should in no way depart from true knowledge or wisdom. For there is no greater wisdom than for a person wholly to withdraw from evil and constantly do the good by which God is pleased. The Psalmist took care to summarize this wisdom in few words: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI). The figures of palms rightly follow after the cherubim, because the hands of those are justly adorned with the victor’s palm [Col. 0510B] who labour with devoted purpose in good works and, so far as is permitted to mortals, diligently guard themselves against evils.

Accordingly, ecclesiastical authority has long established, by eminent custom, that the right hands of Christ’s martyrs and virgins should be marked with palms worthy of praise: they conquered by despising this present world, and by preserving their virginity and chastity did not hesitate, for love of the heavenly kingdom, to give their bodies to martyrdom. It is indeed a great victory to preserve integrity of mind and body in this world, and by overcoming oneself, together with the present world, even unto death, to despise it. Therefore the Creator of the world himself, who had trampled down this wicked age by despising it, said in exhortation to his soldiers: “Take courage, for I have conquered the world” (John XVI). We can by no means conquer the world better than by wholly renouncing both it and the things that belong to it.

But whoever now abstains from evil and does good, preserves virginity or chastity, and seems to have perfectly renounced the world, must take care not to rein in the course of his progress from desiring the other virtues. The raised carvings which are found sculpted upon the doors of the oracle are recognized as spiritually bearing the figure of these virtues. For, as we have said above, raised carvings are sculptures whose rear portion is hidden within, but whose front portion is plainly manifest to all who see. [Col. 0510D]

Thus whoever inwardly abounds in the affections of charity and outwardly bestows the works of that same charity abundantly upon neighbours; whoever preserves obedience in the mind and at times displays the works of that obedience in action; whoever is humble and gentle in heart and has indications of that same humility and gentleness in outward conduct; whoever expresses in himself the marks of the remaining virtues—from that person’s mind and body, without doubt, spiritually proceed raised carvings projecting very prominently. The same judgment is to be made concerning the remaining virtues.

If anyone inwardly loves chastity, outwardly mortifies the flesh, fasts, keeps vigil, labours, and prays, that person, all doubt removed, makes manifest that raised carvings have been sculpted in his flesh. Since it is impossible to be saved without faith, the history therefore fittingly adds that Solomon overlaid the cherubim, palms, and raised carvings with gold. Whoever abounds in the aforesaid virtues signified by the cherubim, palms, and raised carvings, but lacks the Catholic faith, can in no way be saved. Blessed Peter teaches that gold signifies the Catholic faith in the sacred Scriptures, saying: “That your faith may be found much more precious [Col. 0511B] than gold which is tested by fire” (I Pet. I).

Behold, we have shown that the Bridegroom’s two spiritual breasts, namely God’s clemency and mercy, are to be understood through the two doors of the oracle.

For Christ himself is the true and spiritual oracle, because through him our prayers are heard by God the Father. Hence blessed John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (I John II).

## RECAPITULATION OF WHAT PRECEDES: ON THE IVORY THRONE MADE BY SOLOMON, AND HOW IT SHOULD BE REFERRED TO THE PERSON OF CHRIST

We said above that the Lord Jesus, who is called the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs, is also called the temple’s oracle and the ivory throne in the Book of Kings. We further added that God’s clemency and mercy, namely the Bridegroom’s breasts, are to be understood through the two doors of the oracle. Finally, we supplied the sufficient reason: just as those entering the oracle went in through those doors, so those who are to be saved will indeed be saved through God’s clemency and mercy.

It remains, therefore, for us to approach the throne made of ivory and, according to our measure, discuss how this throne was made by Solomon as a figure of Christ. Then it will be necessary to investigate allegorically in a spiritual sense how the two hands of which we spoke in the preceding passage—[Col. 0511D] the hands which hold the seat upon the ivory throne—spiritually bear the figure of clemency and mercy, namely the Bridegroom’s breasts.

Yet we should devoutly consider whether anything is said anywhere in the divine utterances about a throne, so that what we wish to say may be strengthened by the authority of the sacred utterances. In the Apocalypse John says: “From the throne proceed lightnings, voices, and thunders” (Apoc. IV). That is, from Christ, who is the golden throne in whom the fullness of divinity rested, proceed lightnings—that is, the signs of miracles—along with the voices of Gospel preaching and thunders, namely the terrors of the future judgment and final condemnation.

Moreover, no one should fail to know that the throne of which we strive to speak, and which we intend to refer spiritually to Christ’s person, is described as made not only of ivory, but also of most brilliant gold. It is therefore clear, without any remaining ambiguity, that by gold we should understand divinity, [Col. 0512A] and by ivory, his humanity. That gold possesses the signification of Christ’s divinity needs no difficult interpretation. As gold surpasses all metals by its preciousness, so Christ’s divinity surpasses not only his humanity but all creatures by the excellence of its dignity.

Therefore, after the Holy Spirit had said through the mouth of the historian that Solomon made a great throne of ivory, he immediately added: “And he covered it with exceedingly bright gold,” in order to show how greatly the prerogative of divinity surpassed the assumed material of humanity. For it is certain, and no one doubts, that a thing which clothes another thing is placed over that which it seems to cover. Thus, as most splendid gold adorned, embellished, and glorified with its brightness and radiance the throne which it covered, so undoubtedly divinity raised that human being whom it assumed to such a glorification that the man himself, through participation in divinity, was made God.

Our humanity therefore advanced greatly: in the assumption of the assuming divinity, it was glorified and raised to participation in the heavenly Godhead. Indeed, as its descent into hell in the first Adam was more grievous, so its ascent into heaven in the second Adam was more glorious and excellent. As there was no more unhappy way in which, deceived by the devil, it could be cast down from paradise, so there was no more blessed or glorious way in which it could be exalted by Christ. [Col. 0512C]

Our flesh was therefore exalted in Christ above every creature and above itself. I say “above itself” because it had not at all merited the dignity to which it came. This is what the prophet prophesied long before it happened: “Let your ancient counsel, O Lord, come true” (Isa. XXV). This counsel, indeed, was from eternity—and before eternity, if it is lawful to say so!—in the purpose of the highest divinity: that our flesh, to be assumed and glorified by Christ, should be raised to the contemplation of divine majesty.

Filled with spiritual contemplation, Ezekiel the prophet (ch. XVII) seems to me to speak of this glorification or assumption of our humanity: “A great eagle, supported by the great strength of its wings and adorned with great variety of feathers, came to a cedar that was in Lebanon; it took from the pith of the cedar, carried it away, and set it upon a holy and high mountain.” What, then, is this eagle except the one of whom the prophet says: “As an eagle provokes its young to fly and, hovering over them, spreads its wings, takes them up, and carries them upon its shoulders?” (Deut. XXXII). And, as though someone asked of him which eagle he meant, he at once plainly added that he had said this of God: “The Lord alone was his guide” (ibid.).

This eagle came to the cedar in Lebanon and took from its pith for itself when the Word uttered from the Father’s heart came to blessed Mary and received for himself from her virgin flesh a most holy and undefiled body. And as the prophet says of that eagle that it set upon a holy and high mountain the pith which it had taken from the cedar, so the Son of God—the Father’s Word—raised up with himself, at the right hand of his Father in the seat of his majesty, our flesh which he assumed from the blessed Virgin Mary. [Col. 0513A]

That blessed Mary is called the cedar of Lebanon is plainly recognized more from ecclesiastical usage than through any difficult interpretation. For holy Church says in her daily office: “I was exalted like a cedar in Lebanon” (Ecclus. XXIV). Since *Lebanon* is interpreted as “whiteness,” it is not without reason compared to the virginity of blessed Mary. For as a material cedar was exalted in Lebanon, so blessed Mary, on account of the singular privilege of her virginity, is glorified and chosen before others with God.

But now let us return to the golden and ivory throne mentioned above and behold with spiritual eyes how it bore the figure of the Lord’s body. “Solomon made a great throne of ivory” (III Kings X). This throne was truly great in wondrous loftiness, because, as the Psalmist says, “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no end to his greatness” (Ps. CXLIV). We have also explained a little earlier why this throne was clothed with most precious gold. It remains for our minds to bring into the light why this throne, which bore the figure of the Lord’s body, was of ivory.

As those before us who have discussed the natures of things with prudent skill have said, ivory is of such wonderful power and coldness that, if a linen cloth is thrown over it and a live coal is placed upon that linen cloth, the ivory by its power keeps unharmed the cloth adhering to it, so that it cannot be wholly consumed or burned by the live coal laid above it. Who, then, cannot clearly—or at least in some degree—perceive how this comparison should be applied to Christ’s body? [Col. 0513C] As ivory by its natural power keeps the cloth laid over it uninjured by the heat of fire, so the divinity that was hidden in Christ’s body kept that body free from every stain of sin. Therefore blessed Peter the Apostle, speaking of the Lord Jesus, said: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Pet. II).

The sacred history teaches us by evident reasoning that the six steps on the throne, by which one ascended gradually to its seat, signify the six ages of the passing world, through which God the Son promised in mystical and hidden ways that he would come in his incarnation. In the first age, from Adam to Noah, he promised that he would come when he announced to the woman: “Your seed shall crush the serpent’s head” (Gen. III). In the second age, from Noah to Abraham, he indicated that he would come when he said to Noah’s sons: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. VIII). In the third age, extending from Abraham to Moses, he foreshadowed that he would be present when he blessed the offspring of that prophet, saying: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). In the fourth age, from Moses to David, he indicated that he would be present in the manifold observance of sacrifices. In the fifth age, from David to the birth of blessed Mary, he announced figuratively through kings and priests that he would come, because he is “King of kings and priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). The sixth age is that which now continues from the birth of the blessed Virgin Mary to the day of judgment. In it the Son of God graciously deigned to come in his incarnation, just as by the sixth step one came to that glorious seat in the midst of the golden and ivory throne (III Kings X). [Col. 0514B]

The statement that the top of the throne was rounded at the back must not be passed over negligently by the discerning reader. For scarcely anyone endowed with some measure of understanding is ignorant that whatever is round is perfect in every part. Concerning Christ, whose figure that throne bore, holy Church proclaims to her children: “Perfect God, perfect man, subsisting with a rational soul and human flesh.”  
[Note: [Col. 0513D] Athanasius, in the Creed.]

The two hands which on the aforementioned throne hold the seat, one on each side, should not inappropriately be understood as our Saviour’s clemency and mercy. These accomplished this: that for the redemption of humankind Christ should take flesh and should for a time taste the death of which he had been wholly ignorant. Hence David the prophet says: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. CIX). These, I say, are the Bridegroom’s spiritual breasts in the Song of Songs: the two hands holding the seat of the golden and ivory throne in the Book of Kings, namely clemency and mercy, which brought it about that God became man and wonderfully restored us to the joys of paradise which we lost through Adam. [Col. 0514C]

Finally, let us see what the historical text related to us above: “Two lions stood beside each hand” (III Kings X). From the preceding discussion we clearly understand that there were no more than two hands there; and if two lions were assigned to each hand, we hold with certainty that no more than four lions stood there. What, then, do the four lions set beside each hand signify except the four Gospels, which everywhere proclaim God’s clemency and mercy? For thus you have it written in the Gospel: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark XVI). And elsewhere: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. IV).

The twelve lion cubs which sacred history reports to have stood upon the six steps signify the fullness and perfection of spiritual gifts, which no one doubts rested and remained upon Christ. “In Christ,” as the Apostle says, “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II). And John says: “From his fullness we have all received” (John I). Meanwhile, if we wish to understand these twelve lion cubs as the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which Isaiah relates rested upon Christ, together with the virtues which holy Church especially commends, our interpretation will be judged worthy of due praise even by the enemies of truth. For Isaiah says: [Col. 0515A] “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and upon him shall rest the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI).

If, then, you add to these seven gifts of the Holy Spirit five virtues—namely faith, hope, charity, good work, and chastity—you will without doubt complete the number twelve. Seven and five, when united, undoubtedly make twelve. These spiritual lion cubs, I think, are of greater and worthier value than those which Solomon caused to stand upon the six steps in the midst of the golden and ivory throne.

After this, history relates with a kind of amazement that “no such work was made in any of the kingdoms” (III Kings X). And history has fittingly and quite rightly said this. For in all the kingdoms no work such as this has been made: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). No such work, I say, has been made in all the kingdoms as that God should become human and redeem by his blood the human race which had perished. Truly, no work so glorious has been made in all the kingdoms as that our nature, now wholly despairing of salvation, should be drawn out from hell and placed in heaven at the right hand of God the Father. [Col. 0515C]

## RECAPITULATION OF WHAT PRECEDES: ON THE GOLDEN AND IVORY THRONE MADE BY SOLOMON, AND HOW IT SHOULD BE REFERRED TO THE PERSON OF HOLY CHURCH

Nearly all sacramental expressions which are found set forth figuratively in the divinely inspired Scriptures are sometimes referred to our Head, who is Christ; sometimes they should be assigned universally to holy Church, which is the body of that same Head of ours; and sometimes they can fittingly be applied to each individual faithful person, who is a member of the aforesaid Head and body. [Col. 0515D]

For let us know with certainty that, just as the ivory throne of which we have often already spoken is fittingly applied to the Lord Jesus Christ, so consequently it is appropriate to the holy Church, which is his body. But since, as far as the capacity of our understanding allowed, we have above allegorically assigned the said throne to Christ our head, it remains now for us to ascribe it in an allegorical sense to our body, the holy Church.

[Col. 0516A] “Solomon,” he says, “made a great throne of ivory” (III Kings X). Since Solomon’s name is interpreted “peaceful,” it is not without reason that the Lord Jesus Christ is understood through Solomon. Of him the Apostle Paul indeed says: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II). Therefore this our peaceful king made an ivory throne, because, as the divine page testifies, “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. IX); and because the holy Church, in all her teachings, proclaims chastity above all to be observed, it is fittingly established that the throne which prefigured the holy Church was made of ivory.

For ivory is the bone of an elephant; and that animal is said to be so cold in nature that it either rarely, or scarcely more than once a year, as we suppose, approaches to render the dues of natural intercourse. [Col. 0516B] This suitably alludes to the sacraments of the holy Church, which utterly forbids marital acts to some of her children, while to others she indulgently permits marital relations for the restoration of human offspring.

Moreover, there is another mystery commonly told concerning the elephant and the dragon, which without doubt must be assigned especially to the holy Church. For the *draco*, as blessed Augustine says, is a serpent or animal twelve cubits in length, which pursues the elephant because its blood is a drink most delightful to it. Therefore, when it wishes to kill the elephant so that it may pleasantly drink the blood it desires, it entangles the elephant’s feet with the length of its body and tail, so that the elephant can neither turn aside anywhere [Col. 0516C] nor proceed. And thus, in a wondrous manner, while the elephant, its feet entangled, is crushed down upon the constricting dragon, it presses down and kills by the mass of its own body that very dragon which had been plotting to bring it death.

What, then, does this elephant signify except the holy Church? And what does that dragon signify except the devil, who persecutes the same holy Church with unceasing stratagems? Thus also John the Apostle says in his Apocalypse: “And the dragon persecuted the woman, and the woman fled into the wilderness. And the dragon sent a river after the woman, that he might cause her to be carried away by the river” (Apoc. XII). This woman is the holy Church of whom Solomon says: “Who shall find a strong woman?” (Prov. XXXI).

Furthermore, it should be known that the holy Church, which in the Song of Songs is called bride, dove, and [Col. 0516D] beloved (ch. II), is herself called the ivory throne in the book of Kings. And she whom Solomon calls a strong woman, John in the Apocalypse names the woman fleeing into the wilderness. She is, finally, the house built by Wisdom, standing upon seven pillars.

But the statement that the throne made by Solomon of ivory was great is in no way contrary to the holy Church. For she is the one who, in her head—that is, Christ—has pierced the height of heaven, and who, borne by her feet, namely the Apostles, has reached to the utmost bounds of the whole world. This too is fittingly prefigured in the prophet Daniel, when, in a vision shown to the most impious king Nebuchadnezzar under the image of a great [Col. 0517A] tree, the holy Church is displayed. As it is written there: “I saw, and behold, a certain great tree stood in the midst of the earth, whose height reached unto heaven, and whose branches spread to the ends of the earth” (Dan. IV). “The beasts of the field dwelt beneath it, and the birds of heaven lived in its branches; food for all was in that tree, and all flesh fed from it.”

The tree in the midst of the earth is the holy Church, of which it is said: “God has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. LXXIII). Its height, reaching to heaven, is Christ, the head of the holy Church, of whom Paul says: “We have a great high priest, Christ Jesus, who has passed through the heavens” (Heb. IV). Its branches are the Apostles, to whom the Lord said: “I am the vine; you [Col. 0517B] are the branches” (John XV). Thus it is well said that its branches spread to the ends of the earth, because “their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

The Prophet further states that the beasts of the field dwelt beneath the tree, while the birds of heaven lived in its branches. By the beasts, brutish human beings may be understood; by the birds, spiritual persons ought to be understood. For the former, being animal or fleshly, occupy the lowest place in the holy Church; but the latter, as spiritual persons, raise themselves to lofty things upon the wings of virtues. The food of all, said to have been in that tree, is evangelical preaching: namely, the nourishment of faithful souls, preached in the Church. And since at the end of this vision it is added that [Col. 0517C] all flesh fed from that tree, it is plainly made known that all flesh which is to be saved on the day of judgment must live according to Christ’s Gospel and by no means depart from the holy Church.

The statement added by the history of Kings—that Solomon clothed the throne he had made with gleaming gold—does not estrange us from ecclesiastical mysteries. For the holy Church is clothed in most brilliant gold, because she is adorned with every ornament of wisdom. Wisdom is indeed signified by gold, as a certain wise man says: “Hidden wisdom and concealed treasure: what profit is there in either?” (Ecclus. XL).

Moreover, if we wish to understand through gold the adornments of spiritual virtues, let us hear with devout mind how the Psalmist meets our understanding: “All the glory,” he says, “of the king’s daughter is within, clothed about in golden fringes with varieties” (Ps. XLIV).

The six steps upon the said throne signify the six ecclesiastical ranks which exist in the holy Church: readers, doorkeepers, acolytes, subdeacons, levites, and priests. [Col. 0517D] For just as one ascended by those six steps to the throne’s seat, so by these six ecclesiastical ranks one reaches the most holy altar. The statement in the book of Kings that the throne was round signifies that the holy Church, ascending from virtue to virtue, always tends toward perfection. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your belly is like a turned bowl” (ch. VII). For whatever is fashioned on a lathe is plainly shown more perfect to human sight.

The two hands holding the seat are Christ’s divinity and humanity, which construct for us the most holy altar in the holy Church. For unless God had become man, his flesh would by no means be daily offered upon the holy altar. And unless the God who became man were true God, he would by no means be worshipped with equal honour together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

The four lions standing there beside the hands signify the four virtues: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance, which hold a triumphal standard in the holy Church. The twelve lion cubs standing on the six steps on either side are the twelve Apostles, namely the preachers of the holy Church. For since lions are strong animals and bear the type of royal dignity and authority, the Apostles are fittingly understood through lions, whose royal dignity and royal authority are preached throughout the four quarters of the world.

At the conclusion of this exposition, the history of Kings adds: “No such work has been made in all kingdoms.” The history of Kings speaks truly: no work so wonderful as the holy Church has been made anywhere in the world, she who daily opens the kingdoms of heaven to her children through faith and works.

## RECAPITULATION OF WHAT HAS GONE BEFORE: CONCERNING THE IVORY THRONE, AND HOW IT SHOULD BE APPLIED MORALLY

Whoever wishes to instruct people in morals ought [Col. 0518C] himself to be instructed in moral conduct. But because it is difficult to find someone adorned in every respect with good morals, we nevertheless ought not altogether to cease from building up moral character. For by the authority of the divine utterances we maintain that our mind ought always to be intent upon good conduct and works, and that our tongue should proclaim to all the praises of its Creator with tireless devotion.

Whoever reads or hears that passage of Scripture which tells how Solomon made a great throne of ivory, should not attend merely to that material throne; rather, look to your own body and your own soul, since what was materially done in that throne you can find spiritually [Col. 0518D] and morally in yourself. You may indeed be a golden and ivory throne spiritually and morally, if you devote yourself to true wisdom, signified by gold, and perfectly strive after chastity, signified by ivory, in mind and body.

You likewise have within yourself those six steps by which one ascended to the perfect seat: namely, the six works of mercy. Since we consider that we have already expounded these above, we pass them over here, to avoid wearying the reader. And because the throne is said to have been round, it plainly indicates that whoever desires to be the throne of God should strive after every perfection and guard mind, tongue, and body from every sin.

The two hands holding the seat are two things: namely, the will of God and the present life, which retain the soul in this body. [Col. 0519A] That the soul of each faithful person may be called a seat is proclaimed by the divine page even while we are silent: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wis. VII).

The four lions beside the aforementioned hands may rightly be understood as four virtues, namely fear and love, contempt and affection. For we ought both to love and fear the will of God; but this present life we ought, as is expedient, both to cherish and to despise.

The twelve lion cubs standing on the six steps on either side are the twelve sacraments of the holy Church: the threefold renunciation of the devil; the threefold profession of the Catholic faith; reception of holy baptism; communion in the body and blood of Christ; confession; penance; forgiveness of sins in the Holy Spirit; [Col. 0519B] and perseverance in good works until death. These, therefore, are the spiritual lions which keep far from the souls of the faithful that lion who prowls about seeking whom he may devour, and by their power and sanctification drive him away, lest he dare thereafter to dwell in them.

Afterwards the historian concluded this exposition with these words: “No such work has been made in all kingdoms” (III Kings X). Whoever is well ordered in conduct, whose morals breathe forth a most sweet fragrance far and wide, who constantly pursues and cleaves to good conduct, who daily offers himself as a sacrifice to God, whose morals God approves and praises, and who, through the correction of his conduct, is made spiritual from animal: such a person can without doubt say of himself that no such work has been made in all kingdoms.

## RECAPITULATION OF WHAT HAS GONE BEFORE: CONCERNING THE IVORY AND GOLDEN THRONE, AND HOW, UNDER AN ALLEGORICAL INTERPRETATION, IT SHOULD BE APPLIED TO THE PERSON OF THE BLESSED, GLORIOUS, AND EVER-PERPETUAL VIRGIN MARY

[Col. 0519C]

“Solomon,” he says, “made a great throne of ivory, and clothed it with exceedingly brilliant gold” (ibid.). I beseech you, my most renowned Lady: if I say anything less worthy than your dignity deserves, may this not bring harm to my soul, but rather increase my merit and heavenly glory. For I know, I know, that if all my limbs were turned into tongues, I would not be able worthily to utter your praises, which the sublime glory of your singular virginity deserves.

I know, I say, my Lady, that even if all things that are mine could speak, they would still find no one in heaven or on earth like you. In heaven no one is like you, because, if we speak of God, God is greater than you, and therefore is not your equal. But if our tongue wishes to speak of saints, angels, or any creatures created by God, it is manifest that your dignity surpasses and excels all creatures; for, as it is written, “You have been exalted above the choirs of angels unto the heavenly kingdoms.”

Again I beseech you, my Lady, dearer a thousand times over than all who are dear: help by your prayers and merits all your servants who gladly honour you, serve you devoutly, and speak fittingly of you as is worthy; sustain them, strengthen them against every sin, preserve them, and bring them to the immortal joys of your Son.

[Col. 0520A] You, then, are that throne—not the one made by Solomon, the mortal king, namely the son of King David, but rather that throne which God, namely the Son of God, the immortal King, chose and chose beforehand from eternity as his dwelling. You are that throne of which the Psalmist says: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. XLIV).

You are, I say, my Lady, dearer than all who are most dear, a throne formed from heavenly gold and spiritual ivory. Through gold is understood the divinity of Christ your Son; through ivory, which is of a cold nature, your most holy virginity. You are therefore formed from the gold of divine majesty and the ivory of perpetual virginity, because the divinity of your Son, through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, was ineffably overshadowed in you, and your virginity remains and has remained inviolate.

Moreover, I do not think that what investigators of natural things commonly say about the nature of ivory should pass over in silence. It accords with the dignity of blessed Mary and with the sublime power of her aid. For they say that if ivory is very often applied to an aching head, it naturally assuages and removes every headache. Therefore those who suffer wounds in the head—that is, in the mind—from the darts of vices must without doubt implore the help and assistance of holy Mary, Mother of God, and say from the inmost affection of their hearts: “We flee to your protection, where the weak have received strength; and therefore, O Virgin Mother of God, we render thanksgiving to your dignity.”

You, I say, Lady, are the house which Wisdom—that is, the Son—built for himself (Prov. IX), and [Col. 0520C] in which he established, in everlasting firmness for splendour and glory, seven spiritual pillars: virginity, chastity, continence, humility, faith, hope, and love.

Truly, in blessed Mary shone forth the singular privilege of incomparable virginity and the fragrant sweetness of perfumed chastity; for unless she had been a virgin and chaste, the Son of God would by no means have chosen her as his dwelling. For it was fitting that she who redeemed the world should be a virgin, because that first parent who had lost the whole world was a virgin. Since, therefore, blessed Mary, Mother of God, was a virgin, she was consequently chaste and continent.

But what worthy thing can we offer in praise of her inexpressible humility? Indeed, when this most holy and [Col. 0520D] thousand-times blessed Virgin, mother of the Son of God, was chosen by the angel, she confesses herself with humble devotion to be the handmaid of that same Son, saying: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke I).

The Mother of God had unblemished faith, because she believed the angel’s announcement that she could become the Mother of God. In that most blessed Virgin hope had fixed its lofty citadel: although what she heard was strange and unheard of in past ages and generations, she most certainly hoped in faith that it ought to come about as the angel proclaimed.

No one who has received even a little instruction in the knowledge of divine law can fail to know how the Mother of God overflowed with the bowels of love. For just as her Son incurred the curse of the law for the redemption of the human race—Moses says, “Cursed is he who hangs upon a tree” (Deut. XXI)—so she too preferred, while preserving virginity, to lie under the curse of the law rather than, having lost her virginity, leave carnal children in Israel. Thus the Mosaic law said: “Cursed is the man or woman who has not left seed in Israel.”

You are therefore brighter and more splendid than every brightness and splendour of the sun; incomparably more precious than every precious stone; you are found more radiant than all the shining of the stars, as the star of the sea. For you are the brightness of eternal light and the spotless mirror of divine majesty. You are the inheritance of the Lord; in you the Son of God dwelt. You can say: “The Creator of all things, who created me, rested in my tabernacle” (Ecclus. XXIV).

You are the tabernacle set in the sun, [Col. 0521B] from which tabernacle the Son of God came forth “as a bridegroom from his chamber” (Ps. XVIII). Your womb is the silver bed in which is that golden apple of which Solomon says: “Golden apples in silver beds: a word spoken in its proper time” (Prov. XXV). For the special birth of your only-begotten Son could not have been expressed by a worthier and more splendid comparison. The apple set forth in silver beds is the Word made flesh in the Virgin’s womb.

The six steps described as being upon the ivory throne especially signify the six degrees of humility which blessed Mary had in her heart. Thus the Holy Spirit fittingly speaks in the Song of Songs: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song I). Nard is said to be an aromatic tree of low growth, through which the humility of blessed Mary is suitably understood. This virginal humility pleased the king while he rested at his table, when that king, namely the Son of the eternal King, descended from heaven and assumed most holy flesh in the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary.

But now let us see what the six degrees of humility are. The first degree of humility is that a person confess that he was created from the earth and, because of the desert of his perversity, confess that he shall return to ashes. The second degree is that a person never become proud because of any grace received. The third is that he unceasingly give thanks to his Creator for benefits bestowed upon him by the Lord. The fourth is that a person consider himself inferior to all in merits. The fifth is that he judge himself equal to no one. The sixth is that he by no means reckon himself better or superior to anyone.

These are the six spiritual degrees of humility by which God descends to the heart of one humbling himself, and through which a human being ascends to knowledge of the God descending to him.

After this, the history informs us that the throne was round in its outer part. I remember having said in the preceding exposition that whatever is round appears perfect. What, then, does the roundness and perfection of the golden throne indicate to us except that the Virgin Mary was a virgin before giving birth and remained an inviolate virgin after giving birth? The hands which held the seat of the ivory throne signify the two Testaments, which everywhere proclaim Christ’s humanity, which he assumed in blessed Mary.

[Col. 0522A] Therefore the four lions standing beside the said hands are the four Gospels, which proclaim the same thing as the two Testaments. The twelve lion cubs said to have stood upon the six steps on either side are the twelve virtues which blessed Mary certainly possessed: spiritual life, joy in the Holy Spirit, long-suffering, patience, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, incomparable modesty, virginity, compassion, and perseverance in a holy purpose.

Blessed Mary led a spiritual life, for unless her life had shone full of virtues, she would by no means have pleased God. She indeed possessed joy in the Holy Spirit, because she herself, filled with spiritual jubilation, said in her hymn: “My spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour” (Luke I). Long-suffering did not fail her, because although what she heard from the angel was unheard of and unfamiliar, she nevertheless waited in long-suffering for its fulfilment in herself. She was strongly fortified by the virtue of patience, because she endured with a patient spirit the insults which she saw inflicted by faithless Jews upon her Son—indeed, upon herself as well.

Who could deny that she possessed goodness and kindness, she whom we confess beyond doubt to have flourished in every abundance? Gentleness held a chief place in her, because unless she were gentle, the Holy Spirit would by no means have chosen her as his dwelling. As we have already recalled above, incomparable faith illumined the inmost parts of her heart; for although it was contrary to the laws of human nature that a Virgin should be chosen as Mother of God, she believed that this could come about by God’s will, as the angel [Col. 0522C] proclaimed to her.

With what praises can we worthily exalt her modesty—that is, her religious devotion—when we know with certainty that the angel found her occupied in prayer and silence? And with what praises, as is fitting, shall we proclaim the gates of her virginity and the marks of her most unimpaired chastity, when she had so ceased to delight in converse with human beings that she was alarmed even at an angelic entrance and address? Thus the angel said: “Do not fear, Mary; you have found grace with the Lord” (ibid.). For when the angel Gabriel proclaimed to her that glorious and ineffable “Hail,” sent from God, he saw that she was afraid and immediately urged her not to fear anything.

No one can fully convey to human hearing the compassion and grief which blessed Mary endured at the death of her Son. For she saw God and the Son of God, whom she, a Virgin Mother, had conceived by the Holy Spirit, crucified by the most impious Jews and condemned with thieves as though guilty of some crime. How could the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary remain without experiencing grief, when she saw her own flesh, which the Son of God had taken in her womb for the salvation of the human race, hanging upon the cross?

We can readily demonstrate the perseverance in holy purpose and good works which blessed Mary possessed, because it is established beyond every uncertainty that from her birth to the end of this mortal life she pleased God in all things.

[Col. 0523A] After this, the book of Kings concluded the foregoing exposition with these words: “No such work has been made in all kingdoms” (III Kings X). O how admirable is this conclusion! Truly, no such work was made in all kingdoms as this: a Virgin conceived by the Holy Spirit; a Virgin bore the Son of God; a Virgin remained inviolate after giving birth.

[Col. 0524A] No such work, I say, has been done since the beginning of the world as that a Virgin Mother should nurse the Son of God at virgin breasts. Therefore, since the breasts of the Bridegroom gave the beginning to this second throne—that is, volume—it is fitting that the breasts of the Virgin Bride and Mother should give the same throne a suitable ending.

[Col. 0523] Here ends the second volume on the Song of Songs.

## HERE BEGINS THE THIRD VOLUME: ON THE WORDS, “YOUR NAME IS OIL POURED OUT; THEREFORE THE YOUNG WOMEN LOVED YOU EXCEEDINGLY”

[Col. 0523B] Whoever is pleased to enter a garden planted with trees of diverse kinds and adorned with blooming flowers is pleasantly refreshed by the taste of its fruits and wonderfully delighted by the sweet fragrance of its flowering blooms. What, then, do we say that this garden is, except the most delightful text of the divine Scriptures? And what are the trees and flowers? Surely, the spiritual sayings of the Scriptures.

Let us therefore enter this garden in mind and spirit, and see what the Bride says to the Bridegroom: “Your name is oil poured out.” As those who discuss the natures of things say, oil is reported to possess seven powers or properties in itself, which appear most fittingly applicable to the name of Christ, because, according to the prophet Isaiah (ch. XI), the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are said to have rested upon him: namely, “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord.”

[Col. 0523C] But let us now proceed to discuss the seven properties of oil and apply them to the Lord Jesus. Oil is said to float above every liquid in which it is placed. This fittingly applies to the Lord Jesus, because, as Paul says: “God gave him a name which is above every name” (Phil. II); and he himself “is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. IX).

Oil receives no foreign liquid, because no stain or contagion of sin defiled Christ, as Peter says: “Who did no sin” (I Pet. II). Oil refreshes people, and Christ gives us drink and satisfies us with his blood and flesh. It heals wounds, because, as Isaiah says, Christ “healed our wounds” (Isa. LIII). Its inward nature is like its outward appearance, because our nature, assumed by Christ’s divinity, was entirely without fault through participation in that same divinity. Applied to fire, it gives light to those sitting in darkness; and Christ enlightens every human being coming into this world (John I). If it is poured out in one place, it seems to spread over the ground around it: Christ, indeed, was born in Bethlehem, but was announced to the Eastern peoples by a star shining from heaven.

Compare, then, if you please, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit with the seven properties of oil, and you will consider wonders in the law of God. [Col. 0524B] There is no greater wisdom than that a human being should know his Creator, “who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.” No one can have a worthier understanding than to know the good that he understands and to admit no work of the devil into the secret place of his heart. Our body and soul then use wise and perfect counsel when, after confession and penance have preceded, they are refreshed by Christ’s body and Christ’s blood. Our mind attains stronger health when it imitates Christ according to its ability.

Certainly, we cannot attain fellowship with Christ unless we strive to possess true knowledge, bodily chastity, and purity of heart. We shine with a great radiance of love when we bear the bowels of piety toward all people with a sincere heart. We truly confess that we have the holy fear of the Lord when, by doing good in one place, we allow a sweet-smelling example to flow forth from us far and wide.

[Col. 0524C] Let the Bride therefore say to the Bridegroom, “Your name is oil poured out,” as though she said: Just as oil poured out in one place seems to spread over the ground around it, so you were crucified for me in Jerusalem, but were preached by me throughout the whole world; and therefore the young women—that is, faithful souls—loved you. Since you died on the cross for them, those young women loved you so greatly that they themselves, as martyrs, died for you.

Let us therefore strive, as Paul says, to suffer with Christ and die with Christ (Rom. VIII), so that we may be able to rise with him to the blessed life; for if we are companions in his sufferings, we shall likewise share in his resurrection and joy (II Cor. I).

## RECAPITULATION OF WHAT HAS GONE BEFORE
Goldsmiths who are accustomed to work in gold and silver or precious stones, when they fashion some costly vessel with their hands, may have people who praise and admire the vessel they see, delighting in the remarkable variety of the craftsmanship. Yet the artisans still place the vessel they hold beneath their hammers, refine it with files, and adorn it with gems; and although to the bystanders the vessel may already seem perfect in every respect, to the artisans it still appears insufficiently polished and perfected. In the same way, when we previously treated that saying, “Your name is oil poured out,” [Col. 0525A] although what we said may perhaps please some, yet with the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit we can still add something to the earlier discussion that will not displease the hearing of readers and listeners alike.

“Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens loved you” (Song of Songs 1). This is the voice of the holy Church, praising in this two-part utterance the mercy of her Bridegroom and his ineffable love. Nor is it surprising that the Bride praises the mercy of her Bridegroom, since the Bridegroom himself does not keep silent about the affection and compassion he has shown toward his Bride. For through the prophet Jeremiah he says: “With everlasting love I have loved you; therefore, in mercy, I have drawn you” (Jer. 31). Concerning this very ineffable love [Col. 0525B] with which Christ loved the holy Church, the apostle John says: “In this the love of God is made perfect in us: not because we loved him, but because he first loved us” (1 John 4).

Moreover, it is worth considering whether anything may be found said concerning oil in the Old Testament or in the prophets which suits the name of the Bridegroom and may fittingly be applied in mysteries to the Bride, namely the holy Church. Thus in Exodus the Lord says to Moses: “Command the children of Israel to bring you the purest oil from olive trees, crushed with a pestle, so that the lamp may always burn before me in the tabernacle of testimony” (Exod. 27). Isaiah the prophet also, mentioning oil, says: “A vineyard was made for my beloved [Col. 0525C] on a horn, the son of oil; and he fenced it round, chose stones out of it, planted it choice, built a tower in its midst, constructed a winepress in it, and expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes” (Isa. 5). In the prophet Zechariah it is written concerning oil: “These are the two sons of the oil of splendour, who stand beside the ruler of the whole earth” (Zech. 4).

For in the preceding treatment, aided by the help of Christ’s divinity and somewhat made fruitful by the dew of spiritual understanding, we discussed—though not as worthily as we should, but according to the measure of our ability—the seven natures of oil, and assigned those seven natures to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are present in Christ in their fulness. It remains now for us to say something further concerning oil in an allegorical sense which may suit both Christ and the holy Church, [Col. 0525D] and may also apply morally to each believer.

Let us therefore see what the distinguished prophet Isaiah says: “A vineyard,” he says, “was made for my beloved on a horn, the son of oil.” O Lord Jesus Christ, who are the Son of the highest oil, open the spiritual eyes of my heart, that I may be able to consider the wondrous mysteries that have been hidden from eternity in your holy and most blessed law. *Eleos* in Greek is called *misericordia*, “mercy,” in Latin. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful” (Luke 6). David the prophet likewise, refreshed by the overflowing grace of the Holy Spirit, speaks thus of God: “My God, my mercy” (Ps. 58). Therefore almighty God, ineffably kind and especially merciful, who in Isaiah is called oil, [Col. 0526A] is indeed called merciful in the Gospel, and so is his Only-begotten Son; and he is proclaimed by David the prophet as mercy.

For the most beloved Son of this ineffable and incomparable oil, a most dear vineyard was made upon the most excellent horn—that is, in the humanity which he assumed from our sinful mass. That humanity surpasses the remaining mass from which it was assumed by the power of the assuming divinity, just as a horn is accustomed to surpass the flesh from which, in growing, it seems to proceed. Concerning this horn, that is, the incarnation of the Lord Jesus, Zechariah, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, said: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people” (Luke 1). And as though someone were asking him what mercy the God of Israel [Col. 0526B] had shown to his people, he immediately added: “He has raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant” (ibid.).

If we wished to interpret this horn otherwise than the truth of the matter requires, truth itself, supported by authority, and authority, strengthened by faithful truth, would contradict us. For it is plain that the royal Virgin of David’s line was chosen, from whom and in whom this horn—that is, our humanity—was assumed by the Word of the Father. Unless this had happened, the human race, which had perished, could in no way have been saved. And this is the horn of salvation raised up for us: namely, the Word made flesh for our salvation, who dwelt among us (John 1). Therefore in this horn a most dear vineyard was made for the beloved Son of oil: that is, through the humanity which [Col. 0526C] he assumed, the Son of almighty God acquired the holy Church for himself.

That the Son himself is called “beloved” is declared by his Bride in the Song of Songs: “My beloved,” she says, “is white and ruddy” (Song 5): ruddy because of the shedding of blood on the cross, white because of the prerogative of virginity and chastity. Again, in the same little book his most dear Bride speaks thus of this same Bridegroom: “My beloved,” she says, “will dwell between my breasts” (Song 1). Therefore the holy Church, which in Isaiah is called a vineyard, is in the Song of Songs called the Bride. This vineyard was made a delight to the most dear beloved Son of oil, because he took flesh from it; for, as Paul says, “No one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5).

[Col. 0526D] Elsewhere the same Paul states more plainly how great the Bridegroom’s love for his Bride is: “Husbands,” he says, “love your wives as Christ loved the holy Church and gave himself up for her” (Col. 3). Hence the same Bridegroom says of his Bride in the Song of Songs: “How beautiful you are, my friend, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are those of doves!” (Song 1). The Bridegroom repeats and doubles the declaration of his Bride’s beauty because he foreknew that she would be virgin and chaste both in soul and in body. He compared her eyes to doves because he foresaw that she would possess the simplicity of faith which heretics lack.

But what are we to think is meant by the prophet’s saying that God fenced round his vineyard, that is, the holy Church? The holy Church is called a vineyard [Col. 0527A] not only in Isaiah, but also in the Gospel book and in the Song of Songs: in the Gospel, where the householder hired labourers for his vineyard (Matt. 20); and in the Song of Songs, where it is written, “A vineyard belonged to the peaceful one,” and, “Our vineyard has blossomed” (Song 2). The Lord therefore surrounded this vineyard with a hedge when he fortified it with the utterances of the prophets, and instructed it with apostolic teachings as with a strong defence, so that it might not be trampled down and torn apart by heretics.

Hence it fittingly follows in the same prophet that “he chose stones out of it” (Isa. 5). Stones are selected out of a vineyard by people in order that, being harmful, they may be thrown out of that vineyard. Thus the heretics, who are called tares in the Gospel (Matt. 13), are called stones in Isaiah the prophet and [Col. 0527B] are described in elegant language under the name of foxes in the Song of Songs, as it is written: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy our vineyards” (Song 2). What the prophet says, “[And he planted it choice],” is precisely what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Therefore I chose you out of the world, that you may go and bear fruit and that your fruit may remain” (John 15). And the apostle Paul says in his epistles: “I planted,” and, “You are God’s field” (1 Cor. 13). Of the apostles it is said: “While living in the flesh, these men planted the Church with their blood.”

The tower which the prophet Isaiah testifies was built in the midst of the vineyard is the name of the Lord, of which Solomon says: [Col. 0527C] “The name of the Lord is a very strong tower; the righteous man will run to it and be saved” (Prov. 18). For people flee to a tower so that they may be delivered from the attack of enemies. The Lord’s name is therefore rightly compared to a tower in which people are saved, because, as the apostle Peter says, “There is no other name given under heaven in which we must be saved, except in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 4).

The winepress constructed in the aforesaid vineyard represents to us the figure and image of the most holy altar. For just as a grape is squeezed in a winepress or press, and, when squeezed, is strained into the sweetest wine, so Christ’s body and blood are daily consecrated and offered gloriously and wonderfully on the altar. What follows in Isaiah—that the Lord expected his vineyard to produce grapes and, behold, it produced wild grapes—we should understand as spoken of heretics and false Christians. For heretics, who do not agree with the Church’s sacraments [Col. 0527D] but rather oppose and resist them with perverse doctrines, and false Christians, who profess to know God but deny him by their deeds: these without doubt produce and bring forth for the Lord thorns and wild grapes instead of grapes, that is, useless and harmful fruits.

Yet the prophet in what follows makes known what ought to be done to such persons on the day of judgment, saying: “Now then, men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem, judge between me and my vineyard,” that is, concerning my vineyard (Isa. 5). [Col. 0528A] By the men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem we must understand especially the apostles and the other saints, whom we undoubtedly know to be citizens and inhabitants of that heavenly Jerusalem above which is our mother. The Lord, removing every ambiguity, promises them in his Gospel: “You who have followed me shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19). And the apostle Paul says: “Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (1 Cor. 6). Elsewhere it is written concerning all the saints: “The saints shall judge nations and rule peoples” (Wis. 3).

Concerning these apostles and other saints, already exalted before God’s majesty in eternal predestination, Zechariah the prophet, contemplating their glory [Col. 0528B] prophesied: “These are the two sons of the oil of splendour who stand beside the ruler of the whole earth” (Zech. 4). The prophet indicated the apostles and the other saints by the number two because there are two commandments of love, whose observance and fulfilment make people saints and friends of God. Who is signified by oil, however, we have already briefly stated while expounding that saying from Isaiah. It should further be known that the prophet Zechariah says something more than Isaiah. Almighty God, because he is both truly merciful and true mercy, is simply called oil in Isaiah; but in Zechariah, with an addition, he is called oil of splendour. Nor without reason [Col. 0528C] is God the almighty Father called oil of splendour, since his Only-begotten Son is called by the Apostle “the splendour and figure of his substance” (Heb. 1). The Father, therefore, is splendour; the Son is splendour; and likewise the Holy Spirit is splendour; yet there are not three splendours, but one splendour. In the same manner, in the Catholic faith, we believe and confess: God is Father, God is Son, God is Holy Spirit; yet there are not three gods, but one God. [Note: [Col. 0527D] Athanasius, in the Creed.]

Therefore, since, as we said above, Greek *eleos* means “merciful” or “mercy” in Latin, oil consequently signifies him who is merciful, God the Father of mercies. If, then, we understand God the Father by oil, we are given to understand his Son as the splendour of oil. Thus, the oil of splendour [Col. 0528D] and the splendour of oil are the unbegotten begetter and the only-begotten Son of God the Begetter.

## Recapitulation of What Precedes: How This Saying about the Vineyard Must Be Referred to the Synagogue

“A vineyard,” he says, “was made for my beloved on a horn, the son of oil” (Isa. 5). The same prophet states more plainly what the vineyard is when he says: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his delightful shoot” (ibid.). David the prophet also speaks of this vineyard: “You transplanted a vineyard from Egypt; you cast out the nations and planted it” (Ps. 79), and the other things which follow [Col. 0529A] in that psalm concerning the same vineyard, which can easily be understood without any interpretation.

This, I say, is that vineyard, namely the Jewish people, concerning which the Saviour says in the Gospel: “A certain man, a householder, planted a vineyard and leased it to husbandmen. When the time of vintage drew near, he sent his servants to the husbandmen, that they might receive the vineyard’s fruit from the husbandmen. But the husbandmen, seeing the servants of the householder, seized them, subjected them to many insults, and killed them. When the householder heard what had happened, he said: ‘I will send my only-begotten, most dear son to them; perhaps they will respect him.’ But when they saw the son of their Lord, they said to one another: ‘Behold, this is the heir. Let him therefore be killed, and so the inheritance will pass to us’” (Luke 20).

Who, then, can more rightly be understood by this householder than God the almighty Father of our Lord Jesus Christ? For he is the true householder, who governs and rules the whole world in merciful compassion and orders Christians, Jews, pagans, and heretics according to his blameless wisdom. These are the households of which this householder is said to be father, and whose care he does not disdain to undertake. [Col. 0529B] For this most merciful householder provides for Christians, namely his sons, on this condition: that if they wish to obey his commands, they may avoid the punishments of hell and find the unfailing joys of paradise. The same householder shows that he has care for the Jews because, in his merciful goodness, he waits for them to return [Col. 0529C] to him. He by no means excludes pagans and heretics from his providence, because although, like wicked servants, they are ungrateful for his benefits, the Lord nevertheless still waits with patient forbearance for them to abandon heresies and idols and return to him.

This householder planted the vineyard when he led the Israelite people out of Egypt with mighty hand and uplifted arm, and made them dwell in the land of promise after expelling foreign nations. And he leased it to husbandmen when he commanded the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees to instruct that people according to the law of Moses, and, as far as is permitted to mortals, restrain them from the desire for every evil. The same householder sent his servants to the aforesaid [Col. 0529D] vineyard when he dispatched the prophets to instruct that Israelite nation. But the husbandmen, recognizing the servants of their Lord, subjected some of them to insults and inflicted undeserved death on others.

For if we are willing to attend more diligently to the pages of Holy Scripture, we can find very few of the elect who were not either subjected to insults by the impious or unjustly handed over to a most cruel death. It is plain indeed that the most impious Jews condemned Isaiah and Jeremiah to a cruel death and disgraced almost all the remaining prophets with many insults and reproaches. The son of the householder whom the husbandmen kill is the Lord Jesus Christ, who was crucified by the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees.

But now let us return to the preceding [Col. 0530A] saying, which we had resolved to discuss under the type of the Synagogue. “A vineyard,” Isaiah says, “was made for my beloved, on a horn, the son of oil.” Since we have said something, though not sufficiently, about the vineyard, it remains for us now to indicate where the Son of God is called beloved. For it is written in the Gospel that the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord Jesus in the appearance of a dove, and the voice of the Father was heard saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Luke 9).

The Bride speaks of this beloved, this most dear one, in the same book of which we are speaking: “My beloved,” she says, “is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline” (Song 2). That is to say: My beloved will be united to me in faith, and therefore I shall be united [Col. 0530B] to him in faith and works; he feeds among lilies—that is, he delights in chaste, devout, and just works—until the day breathes and the shadows decline, that is, until the day of judgment appears and the images of sins are reduced to nothing.

Therefore the vineyard was set against this beloved upon the horn: that is, the Synagogue greatly opposed the humanity Christ assumed, so much so that it would never believe in him whom it saw subject to human sight as a mere man and not as God. This vineyard, I say, became exceedingly bitter to this beloved when the Synagogue gave the Lord Jesus, in the humanity with which he was clothed, gall and vinegar to drink. Remember, you who hear these things, that above I said that the humanity of the Son of God should be understood by the horn, and I sufficiently demonstrated the reason by the authority of sacred Scripture. [Col. 0530C] Why the Son of God is called by Isaiah the son of oil must be briefly repeated, since we have already taught this adequately above. For *oleos* in Greek is called “mercy” in Latin. Therefore, because the Father is merciful and is mercy, it is certain that Christ is the Son of God who is oil, because he is the Son of the merciful God.

Thus this beloved son of oil, that is, Christ the Son of God, fenced round his vineyard, namely the Synagogue, when he instructed it by the examples and institutions of the patriarchs and fortified it with the books of the prophets, so that it might not admit another Lord besides him and so that the solitary wild beast of which the Psalmist complains (Ps. 79), namely the devil, might not lay it waste. [Col. 0530D] For a vineyard is fenced so that its fruit may be preserved unharmed for the lord of the vineyard, and so that its barriers may not easily be opened to enemies and animals.

As to the statement, “The Lord chose stones out of it” (Isa. 5), it is clear that after the election of the apostles the Synagogue itself was expelled and rejected by God. Concerning this rejection it is aptly written in Isaiah, where the Lord speaks of Shebna, the scribe and prefect of the Temple: “Behold,” Isaiah says, “O Shebna; behold, the Lord will cast you out from your station and cause you to be carried away as a capon is carried away” (Isa. 22). Similarly, concerning the rejection of the Synagogue it is written under the person of King Jeconiah: “Though Jeconiah king of Judah were like a golden ring upon my hand, says the Lord, I would pluck him from there and cast him away” (Jer. 22).

For the Bride was cast out from her station when the Synagogue, on account of its iniquity, was thrown down from the glory of its former state; and the same Synagogue was carried away like a capon when, because of its barrenness and imperfection, it was removed from the outward understanding and Jewish observance. We know a capon to be a castrated and unfruitful animal, to which the old law is aptly compared—a law which, as blessed Paul says, brought nothing to perfection. Hence it fittingly follows in Isaiah the prophet concerning this same Shebna: “What are you doing here, or as though you were someone here?” (Isa. 22). [Col. 0531A] Without doubt, we are accustomed to say, “What are you doing here?” to a person whose work we do not approve at all. And “as though you were someone”: he occupies a position, not truly as a person of any perfection, but nevertheless does not perform work worthy of the merits of his office or place. [Col. 0531B]

We may indeed refer that choosing of stones, of which we spoke above, to the kings and prophets whom we do not doubt were chosen by God in the Synagogue. As for Isaiah’s saying that the Lord planted that choice vineyard, it is plainly understood that kings, prophets, and the entire Israelite nation derived their origin from the stock of Abraham, who was chosen by God. Yet this planting greatly degenerated from that glorious, ancestral life, from whose root it seemed to draw its offshoot. The Lord reproved this degeneration to the Jews in the Gospel with most kindly rebuke, saying: “If you are Abraham’s seed, [Col. 0531C] do the works of Abraham; and why do you seek to kill me? Abraham did not do this” (John 8). we are accustomed to say, “What are you doing here?” to a person whose work we do not approve at all. And “as though you were someone”: he occupies a position, not truly as a person of any perfection, but nevertheless does not perform work worthy of the merits of his office or place.

We may indeed refer that choosing of stones, of which we spoke above, to the kings and prophets whom we do not doubt were chosen by God in the Synagogue. As for Isaiah’s saying that the Lord planted that choice vineyard, it is plainly understood that kings, prophets, and the entire Israelite nation derived their origin from the stock of Abraham, who was chosen by God. Yet this planting greatly degenerated from that glorious, ancestral life, from whose root it seemed to draw its offshoot. The Lord reproved this degeneration to the Jews in the Gospel with most kindly rebuke, saying: “If you are Abraham’s seed, [Col. 0531C] do the works of Abraham; and why do you seek to kill me? Abraham did not do this” (John 8). The Jews had indeed greatly degenerated from the glory of the blood of Abraham, their patriarch and father. For Abraham loved, honoured, and worshipped God; but the Israelite people hated, dishonoured, and condemned God upon the most cruel cross.

The tower which the prophet says was built by the Lord in the middle of the vineyard signifies the Temple in former times, most renowned because of its dignity, which everyone knows was built in the midst of the Jewish people by God’s command. The winepress that stood in the above-mentioned vineyard signifies the altar which the Israelite people held in great veneration in their midst. That altar is rightly compared to a winepress, [Col. 0531D] because, just as many grapes are pressed in a winepress into liquid wine, so the diverse and numerous victims laid upon the altar and burnt were, by signification, referred to one sacrifice, namely Christ.

The prophet’s statement that the Lord expected his vineyard to produce grapes and it produced wild grapes plainly indicates that this saying pertains especially to the Jews. Did not those Jews bring wild grapes instead of grapes when they denied their Creator before Pilate’s face? (John 19.) Blessed Peter reproaches them for this, saying: “But you asked that a murderer be granted to you, while you handed over the author of life to death, whom God raised from the dead” (Acts 3). Did not the most wicked Jews make wild grapes for the Lord instead of grapes when they said to Pilate [Col. 0532A]: “Crucify him,” and, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19)?

Therefore Isaiah’s subsequent words, “Now, men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem, judge between me and my vineyard” (Isa. 5), clearly pertain to the general resurrection, in which the holy apostles will judge and condemn this vineyard. The Lord himself testifies to this in the Gospel when the Jews disparage him: “If I, as you say, cast out demons by the prince of demons, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Matt. 12.)
