Therefore they will be your judges. The prophet Isaiah also declares this when he prophesies of the Lord’s and the holy apostles’ coming on the day of judgment: [Col. 0532B] “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3).

Solomon likewise undertook to comprehend Christ, the holy Church, the holy apostles, and the day of judgment in a brief saying: “The man of the holy Church is noble in the gates when he sits with the elders of his people” (Prov. 31). Thus the apostles, who in the Gospel are called the twelve judges and sons of the Jews according to the flesh, are the very persons called in Isaiah men of Judah, inhabitants of Jerusalem, and elders of the people; and Solomon calls them senators of the people. These are indeed the two sons of the oil of splendour whom the prophet Zechariah (chap. 4), in the spirit [Col. 0532C] of prophecy, says stand beside the ruler of the whole earth. He described them by the number two because he foresaw in the prophetic Spirit that they would proclaim Christ’s divinity and humanity.

Moreover, we should understand the same prophet’s statement, “These are they who stand beside the ruler of the whole earth,” as said not only of the apostles but also of all the saints. Hence the Lord himself says in his Gospel: “Father, I will that where I am, there also may be my servant” (John 12). This is also affirmed by blessed Augustine, the distinguished teacher [Note: [Col. 0531D] *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chap. 79] and most faithful defender of the Catholic faith, when he says: “Let us know for certain that, after the Lord’s ascension to heaven, all the souls of the saints are with Christ, and that, leaving the body, they go to Christ, as it is written: ‘The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God’ [Col. 0532D] (Wis. 3), awaiting the resurrection of their bodies, so that in whole and everlasting blessedness they may alike enjoy Christ. Likewise, the souls of sinners are placed in hell, awaiting in fear the resurrection of their bodies, so that they may be turned over with the devil to eternal punishment.”

## Recapitulation of What Precedes According to the Moral Sense
Although it is exceedingly grave and dangerous for an inexperienced and ill-disciplined person to discourse on the good conduct of others, nevertheless we must not, with our senses asleep, neglect the fact that we are commanded always and without interruption to bless and praise God, as [Col. 0533A] the Psalmist says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. XXXIII [34]).

For if we wish to wait to speak of goodness until we are good, or to be silent about perfection until we are perfect; and if, again, we keep silence from the praises of God until we have become worthy to praise God, it is plainly evident that we shall never praise God anywhere, because, as necessity requires, in this life we shall never at all be good and perfect and worthy of God’s praises. Therefore let good will not fail us, even though effective power is lacking; and so, with God increasing our strength, we may at last attain the point at which we are good and perfect, and fit for the praises of God.

But now let us examine this sentence according to a moral interpretation: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women [Col. 0533B] loved you” (Song of Songs I.3). Blessed is that man, though mortal, whose name has already obtained, through the merit of a good life, such a prerogative that it can truly be said to him: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women loved you.” Certainly such a man must be earnestly sought; and, once found, must be loved not moderately.

For to him who lives well and religiously in the world; who gives abundant alms from his substance for God’s sake; who does not do to another what he does not wish done to himself; who seeks in all his works that God may be praised; and who presents himself in such a way that he is venerated by all people because of his holiness—to him indeed it may be said: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women loved you,” that is, faithful souls.

Likewise, he who proceeds to conversion [i.e. enters the religious life], [Col. 0533C] lives well, holy, and religiously in the cloister, and by the good report of an irreproachable life encourages and draws others to turn to the Lord; moreover, he who by dovelike peace and brotherly love makes himself beloved in the souls of his brethren, so that he is loved by all with the pure intention of the mind—to him without doubt it must be said: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women,” that is, the souls of the brethren, “loved you.”

Furthermore, concerning what we set forth above in the first recapitulation—namely, that the Lord commanded Moses to tell the children of Israel to bring oil from olive trees—if we are true Israelites, in whom there is no deceit, our spiritual Moses likewise commands us (Exod. [Col. 0533D] XXVII), namely the Lord Jesus Christ, to bring him oil from olive trees: that is, to follow and imitate the examples and deeds of the holy Fathers, whom we know pleased God in ancient times through works of mercy.

Yet because obscurity in the divine page is not good, but indeed is very harmful to those of lesser capacity, I judge it fitting to speak somewhat more fully about olive trees and oil, so that what we wish to say may be answered with clearer understanding. Therefore the olive trees are our holy Fathers, of whom blessed Paul says: “These are men of mercy, whose acts of righteousness have not been forgotten before God.” These indeed are the olive trees of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “A good tree cannot bear evil fruits” [Col. 0534A] (Luke VI.43).

The oil of these trees is every good, devout, modest, chaste, religious, and holy work. That a good work ought to be understood by oil is made most plainly clear by the Gospel according to Matthew: “The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like ten virgins,” and the rest that follows there (Matt. XXV). Solomon seems sufficiently to agree with this saying when, among his other words, he says: “At all times let your garments be white, and let oil not fail from your head” (Eccles. IX.8).

Our garments, then, are the members of our body, with which our soul is clothed while, according to God’s ordering, it dwells in this little body. These members must always be white, because they ought not to be subject to any sin. Thus Isaiah the prophet says: “A garment [Col. 0534B] mixed with blood shall be for the burning of fire” (Isa. IX.5). And the Apostle says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires” (Rom. VI.12). And again: “Just as,” he says, “you presented your members to serve impurity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (ibid., VI.19).

Oil never fails from our head when our mind always abounds in devout work and good desire, and indeed wishes constantly, if it were possible, to do more than it can ever bring to completion. Hence the Psalmist says: “My soul has longed to desire your justifications at all times” (Ps. CXVIII [119].20). [Col. 0534C] We therefore offer oil from olive trees to God when we strive to please him through works of piety and righteousness, through which we do not doubt that our fathers once pleased him.

Further, the fact that the oil offered to God was most pure was not expressed thus by Moses without reason, for he foresaw that this would come to our knowledge. The same prophet could have said “pure” or “purer” oil, but he preferred to use “most pure,” in order silently to indicate to us how we ought to examine the work by which we intend to please God himself, who is supreme purity. Oil is pure when our work is free from sin in its outward performance. It becomes purer when no sin is found even in our speech. [Col. 0534D] But if, when our mind sets itself to carry out a good work, it is able to avoid vainglory within, then assuredly the oil is most pure which it offers to God in the sacrifice of its heart.

Certainly, the statement that this oil was to be beaten with a pestle (*pilo tusum*) ought by no means, I think, to be passed over negligently. Pounding with the pestle signifies the tribulations and pressures of this world. What, then, does oil beaten from the pulp suggest to us, except that we ought to imitate the deeds and examples of those Fathers whom we know, according to the Apostle (Heb. XI), entered the kingdom of God through many tribulations?

The command that a lamp should always burn before God in the tabernacle of testimony (Exod. XXVII) plainly signifies that the intention [Col. 0535A] of our heart ought never to be removed from consideration and contemplation of God’s majesty, just as the heart of him who said, “The meditation of my heart is always before you” (Ps. XVIII [19].14), never withdrew from God. For, as the Lord says in the Gospel (Mark VI), “the lamp of your body is your eye.” Our holy Fathers interpreted this eye as the intention of the soul, or the sincere disposition of the mind.

The tabernacle of testimony may rightly be understood as our body; hence blessed Peter says: “I know, brethren, that the putting off of my tabernacle is swift, according as the Lord Jesus Christ deigned to reveal to me” (II Pet. I.14). Therefore in this tabernacle—that is, in our body—the lamp must always burn before the Lord, because the simple and pure [Col. 0535B] intention of the mind must continually rule our body; and we must never allow anything to rule our mind which we know displeases our Judge.

Or the lamp continually shines in our tabernacle when the ardor of charity never grows cold in our heart. Thus the lamp of charity shone in Paul’s heart with the splendor of wondrous brightness, so that Paul himself said: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the indwelling Spirit who was given to us” (Rom. V.5). Or the lamp shines with unfailing brightness in the tabernacle of testimony when, through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, our heart continually considers the things that are God’s.

As we have examined the chapter in Exodus according to its moral meaning, [Col. 0535C] so it is fitting that we should discuss morally that saying taken from Isaiah: “A vineyard was made for my beloved upon a horn, the son of oil.” Oh, how blessed is that soul which, by truly and devoutly working, becomes God’s vineyard! But let us now consider what a vineyard is, what a vineyard consists of, and transfer its earthly cultivation into moral and spiritual edification.

A vineyard appears to consist of vines; and the vine (*vitis*) is so called because it holds itself in the place where it is planted by force (*vi*). Whoever, therefore, desires to be a vine or vineyard must not abandon the purpose of holiness and religion which he has undertaken for God’s sake: he must not be loosened by prosperity or broken by adversity, knowing that “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” [Col. 0535D] (Matt. XI.12).

But this also—that the vine, unlike the custom of other trees, conveys the moisture which it draws from the earth through its pith to the tops of its branches—must be considered with admiration for its great mystery. Other trees receive moisture from the earth between the bark and the solid wood, and pour that moisture into the little branches growing from them, so that they may bear fruit. What, then, does it signify that the vine receives moisture in its pith—that is, in its inner part—and afterward abundantly diffuses it through its outer branches? Surely it signifies the perfect soul of every faithful man: though its body appears openly before people, it remains hidden in God’s presence, because it strives more to please God inwardly than people [Col. 0536A] or the world outwardly. Hence the Psalmist says: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. XLIV [45].13). Paul likewise says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I.12).

This same mystery may also be considered in the vine, which, unlike other trees, conveys sap through its inner pith, with which it gradually afterward waters the outer branches naturally growing from it. For holy men pour into religious people the charisms of the Holy Spirit which they receive by God’s hidden gift in the secret place of their heart, through the performance of good works and the preaching of the heavenly word; and, in the manner of a good vine, what is invisibly wrought in them is visibly manifested outwardly.

There is, furthermore, another thing which can authoritatively be said of the rational vine, [Col. 0536B] and which may be found by the prudent diligence of distinguished clerics in the divine utterances. This tree, namely the vine, is low in stature; and while it lives it is adorned with leaves, fragrant with flowers, pleasing to every eye with jewel-like fruits. But if it is cut down, the more dear, precious, acceptable, and lovable it was before, so much the more worthless, degenerate, and useless it afterward becomes.

The Lord himself makes this clear through the prophet Ezekiel when he says: “Son of man, what will become of the wood of the vine, which is more precious than the other woods of the forest?” (Ezek. XV.2). “If it is cut down, can anything useful be made from it? Is a peg made from it upon which any vessel may hang?” But it is useful for nothing except [Col. 0536C] to be cast into the fire.

What these things signified is made clearer when the following discourse is found to concern the children of Israel. So long as the children of Israel obeyed God’s commandments and did not depart from his cultivation, they remained, like a good vine, in the beauty of their flower and fruit. But after they began to oppose his commands, and moreover inflicted the punishment of the cross upon him who is the author of life, they were assigned to eternal fire like a useless, severed vine.

Likewise Christians who have been imbued with the Church’s sacraments and instructed in faith and works by the Church’s teachers, so long as they exercise their faith by good works within the bosom of the same Church, flourish in the vineyard of God with the verdure of faith like a fruitful vine. But if—God forbid!—[Col. 0536D] they fall into some heresy, abandon the grace to which they had long ago been entrusted, and voluntarily infect themselves with perverse doctrines, do they not, by the merit of their own iniquity, hand themselves over to avenging flames, like a severed and useless vine?

To them, without doubt, most aptly applies what Moses the prophet says in his song: “Their vine is of the vine of Sodom,” as far as the place where, speaking in God’s person, he says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay them”—understood to mean, on the day of judgment, what they deserve (Deut. XXXII).

But what shall I say of converts and religious men who, as the Lord declares in the Gospel (Luke VIII), “believe for a time, and in the time of temptation fall away”? I have known certain men of great religious observance and very demanding purpose—would that I had not known them—[Col. 0537A] who, so long as they are permitted in cloisters to exercise their own will, or to wander and run about through the monastic workshops, throughout the whole world, and among relatives, are retained within the precincts of the monastery only in name, under the appearance of some sort of religious life; although, as I said above, with ruined mind and wandering spirit they rove throughout the whole world.

To them aptly applies what the Lord says through the prophet: “Ephraim has become like a deceived dove without a heart; strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it” (Hosea VII.11, 9). The strangers are demons, opposing vices, evil thoughts, and carnal desires, which estrange us from God if, through our own sloth, they obtain dominion in us. David complains of these strangers, saying: “For strangers have risen up against me, and the strong have sought my soul” (Ps. LIII [54].3).

Solomon likewise says: “Do not give your honor to strangers” (Prov. V.9). And as though we asked Solomon who these strangers were, he immediately adds: “and your years to the cruel one” (ibid.), namely the devil, of whom the Lord testifies: “He was a murderer from the beginning” (John VIII.44). Whoever has wickedly given himself to the aforesaid strangers—that is, demons, vices, and desires—while he lives in the course of this present life will without doubt, after this life, be delivered into the power of Satan, that is, of this cruel one. This is the cruel one who, in Isaiah [Col. 0537B] XIX, is written to persecute human beings cruelly.

[Col. 0537C] Therefore these religious men—if indeed those who conduct themselves as we have just portrayed, or even, shameful to say, worse still, ought to be called religious—if they are ever corrected by their masters for their salvation, or constrained to remain in their cloister and keep their order, immediately cast aside the fear of God and abandon the purpose of their religious life and order. Under the pretext of stricter religion, they disorderly leap out of their cloister and roam as wandering monks through various regions of the world; or, alas, what is still more disgraceful, return to the world.

To them aptly applies what the blessed apostle Peter says in his epistle: “A dog has returned to its own vomit, and a washed sow to wallowing in the mire” (II Pet. II.22); and: [Col. 0537D] “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to go back” (ibid., II.21). These converts, therefore, while they remained in their holy purpose, were like the vine of Sorek, that is, the chosen vine, rooted and founded in charity in God’s vineyard. But now they have been estranged backward, turned to a reprobate mind, and, according to the prophet Ezekiel, made utterly useless and degenerate; they are henceforth fit for nothing except to be cast into the fire and burn.

We have wandered far from the order of our discussion while disputing about the nature of the vine and vineyard. Yet it is now fitting to return to what we began. “A vineyard,” says Isaiah (ch. V), “was made most dear to my beloved upon a horn, the son of oil.”

[Col. 0538A] The beloved, then, is he to whom the bride in the Song of Songs sends her messengers, saying: “Tell my beloved that I languish with love for him” (Song V.8). Oh, how fortunate and blessed is the soul that languishes with love of God! In it, without doubt, love for this deceiving world has already utterly perished, and the false glory of the passing age has been reduced to nothing.

To this beloved bridegroom the same most dear bride speaks again in delight in the same little book: “Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field; let us see whether the vineyard has flowered, whether the flowers bring forth the fruits of brightness and good work” (Song VII.11–12). But certainly, he says, this vineyard—that is, our soul—has been made most dear to this beloved son of oil, namely of almighty God, “upon a horn.”

It is plain to everyone, even to those only rarely illumined by understanding and intelligence, that every horn rises above the flesh from which it grows; and therefore every spiritual virtue is rightly understood through a horn. Hence Moses the prophet, because of the excellence of his merits and the singular prerogative of spiritual virtues in which he wholly flourished, alone among mortals appeared horned through sharing in converse with God; as it is written: “When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, he did not know that his face was horned” (Exod. XXXIV.29)—that is, glorious and wonderful through the intimacy of God’s conversation.

But the Lord Jesus, who before Moses—indeed before the world was made—was God, and after Moses appeared in the last times as a mortal man in this world through the mystery of the Incarnation, is said by the prophet Habakkuk [Col. 0538C] (Hab. III.4) to have horns in his hands, in which his greatest strength is recognized to have resided. Thus it is written in the song of that prophet: “Horns are in his hands” (ibid.), namely Christ’s; and afterward: “There,” he says, “his strength is hidden; there death shall fall before him” (ibid.).

Moreover, if we now wished to bring forward everything that the divine utterances customarily say about these spiritual horns, daylight would fail us more readily than material for speaking. Yet we shall not be wholly silent. “The horns of the just man,” says the Psalmist, “shall be exalted” (Ps. LXXIV [75].11). Who is so dull and foolish as to dare say that the righteous person has horns? Rather, the virtues of the righteous are his horns, by which [Col. 0538D] he fights against the devil and by which he is raised and exalted before God.

Let Isaiah therefore say that the vineyard was made most dear to the beloved son of oil: that is, because of the virtues it possesses, our soul is loved and held in great honor by the only-begotten Son of God. This is what is said through the prophet: “If you separate what is precious from what is vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. XV.19). To separate what is precious from what is vile is to distinguish virtues from vices.

But who is the son of oil? Since this has already been said so often, it is very tedious to repeat the same thing repeatedly. As for the Prophet’s statement that the Lord fenced in the vineyard, we ought to understand this enclosure as referring to our soul, which is God’s spiritual vineyard. Oh, how glorious and outstanding in virtues is the soul for which God has such care that he fences it about with devout diligence! For the Lord himself says through the prophet: [Col. 0539A] “I will hedge in your ways, and you will go after your lovers and will not overtake them; and then you will say, ‘I will return to my former husband, for it was better for me then than it is now’” (Hosea II.6–7).

Furthermore, pausing briefly over this point, it is pleasing to consider how those who enclose gardens make hedges. A closed garden, morally interpreted, is called by God a most blessed soul. It is known to all that hedges are made from stakes and rods: the stakes are driven into the earth below and adhere to it, while their raised tops look upward toward heaven; then rods are woven crosswise between them, and in this manner a hedge protecting God’s garden is completed.

But what more rightly can we call the stakes of this spiritual hedge than the saints of God? Though they still remain on earth because of the weakness of the flesh, they are nevertheless continually with Christ in heaven and cleave to him through spiritual desires. Hence one of these spiritual stakes, living on earth, said: “But our citizenship is in heaven” [Col. 0539B] (Phil. III.20). And what are the rods but their examples and good works and catholic doctrines? By these stakes and such rods God hedges in his vineyard, because through the examples and teachings of his saints he daily cultivates, teaches, instructs, and admonishes the souls of his faithful.

Hence David said: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will guard them” (Ps. XXXIII [34].8). Another prophet likewise testifies in God’s person, saying: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. II.8). It is plainly evident that, among all the members a human being possesses, the pupil of the eye appears more tender and delicate. Therefore, if we are of such worth that we are compared to the pupil of God’s eye, we ought not to be ungrateful for his benefit; rather, we must live in such a way that we deserve to be guarded and fenced in by him like a good vineyard.

Also, Isaiah the prophet insists strongly that God selected stones out of his vineyard. Let us not doubt that this refers to our soul, if indeed, as we have already shown above, we are God’s vineyard by living spiritually. The stones in God’s vineyard may be understood as vices, desires, and impure longings, which, just as stones make a vineyard barren, [Col. 0539D] make our soul barren. But now God must be entreated that he may deign to select and cast out stones from this vineyard—that is, to uproot from our soul every vice displeasing to him—so that our soul, remaining as a good branch in him who is the true vine, may hear with the apostles: “Without me you can do nothing; and as a branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me” (John XV.5, 4).

What Isaiah subsequently says in his discourse, that “God planted his vineyard as a chosen vine,” we should know to refer morally to our body and our soul. “For man was made in the image of God and after [Col. 0540A] his likeness” (Gen. I.26). That planting was surely chosen indeed, having been created in God’s likeness and image. Moreover, it is found written in the book of Wisdom: “God made man simple and upright, but he involved himself in infinite questions” (Eccles. VII.29).

“After this,” Isaiah says, “God built a tower in the midst of his vineyard.” If, then, our soul desires to be God’s vineyard, it must without doubt have within itself that tower built by God. When a tower is constructed, it rises from bottom to top in a square form. Build, therefore, Lord God, in my vineyard a four-sided tower: that is, establish and root in our soul these four virtues—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—and likewise in our body abstinence, sobriety, chastity, and true repentance. Let the remaining virtues be the stones of this spiritual building.

Let the cement which binds and embraces the stones be charity itself, without which no work is called good, and in which every good work is made firm and founded. Thus Paul says: “Be rooted and founded in charity” (Eph. III.17).

“The Lord,” Isaiah says, “constructed a winepress in his vineyard.” Everyone knows the work carried on in a winepress. In the winepress grapes are pressed; and, once pressed, they melt into liquid in order to be changed into sweetest wine. Although the Lord says of his Passion through the prophet: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and there was no man with me from among the nations” (Isa. [Col. 0540C] LXIII.3), there is nevertheless another spiritual winepress which, would that the Lord Jesus might deign to construct in the vineyard of our body.

Holy compunction and the pouring forth of blessed tears for love of Christ may fittingly be called the winepress of the soul. That most dear bride, in delight, of whom the Song of Songs speaks, had this spiritual winepress built within her, when she sighed concerning her bridegroom: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke to me” (Song V.6). This saying therefore displays the inestimable and incomparable affection of the bride for her bridegroom: she loved him with so sincere a love that she wholly melted even at his word.

Yet the same bridegroom loves his bride with a much fuller affection and loftier charity: for love of her he not only descended from heaven, made a little lower than the angels, but even came to the punishment of an ignominious death. Jeremiah the prophet indeed declares this in his Lamentations, saying: [Col. 0540D] “The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah” (Lam. I.15).

That most blessed soul which is called the Bride in the Song of Songs is called the virgin daughter of Judah in Jeremiah. The soul wedded to God is called a virgin because of the integrity of faith and the chastity of the body with which it is clothed. It is called a daughter of Judah because of its humble confession of sins and glorious perseverance in the praises of God. For Judah is interpreted “confession,” which applies to confession of sins and praise of God.

Although much still remains that could be said about the winepress, I think these things may suffice for modern hearers, who, though they gladly listen, cultivate brevity, lest a volume stretched too far burden the minds of weary hearers. But must we fear offending the lazy and weary so greatly that we omit what can help, instruct, and edify energetic men trained in meditation on God’s law? By no means.

Let us see, then, what follows in the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah says: “The Lord expected his vineyard to produce grapes, and behold—alas!—it produced wild grapes.” This saying should plainly be feared rather than expounded. “For behold,” says the apostle James, “the farmer waits for the precious fruit [Col. 0541B] of the earth, patiently enduring until he receives the early and the latter rain. You also be patient, and strengthen your hearts in the service of God until the Lord himself comes” (James V.7–8).

Furthermore, lest we leave wholly unexamined what was said above, that the Lord expected his vineyard to produce grapes and it produced wild grapes, it must be said briefly: woe indeed to those whom their Creator awaits throughout their entire life to bear fruit, but who, once the course of this present life is ended, are found fruitless. For all Christians generally who have received the faith and have been imbued with works of faith, if they live badly, if they close their final day without the working of faith, undoubtedly bring forth wild grapes instead of grapes.

[Col. 0541C] But you also, whoever are called a convert: even if for a time you seem to be within the enclosure of a monastery or cloister, if before your final day comes you withdraw from holy conversion [the religious life] and from God’s service, without doubt—if it can be said—you produce for your Lord God, instead of grapes, something more grievous than, alas, wild grapes.

[Col. 0542A] Yet blessed and happy are those who, conversely, bring precious grapes to God, who awaits them for salvation, instead of wild grapes. These are those who once clung to this deceitful world with excessive love, but afterward, realizing that they had erred, turned with all the affection of their heart to holy religion and, despising the vanity of the world, devoted themselves with all their strength to God’s service. Zechariah the prophet seems to me to speak of them: “These are the sons of shining oil, who stand before the Lord of the whole earth” (Zech. IV.14).

Since we have often already said above that oil signifies mercy, and mercy denotes him of whom the Psalmist says, “My God, my mercy” (Ps. LVIII [59].17), we avoid repeating this again, lest we produce weariness in our hearers. But this is certain: if God is called oil, those who are sons of oil may equally be called sons of God. Blessed John the apostle agrees with this saying in harmonious voice: “Brethren, we are children of God, and it does not yet appear what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (John III [I John 3].2).

Let us therefore consider who is speaking. He was a convert, an apostle, and an evangelist; he had renounced the world; therefore he boldly said: “We are children of God.” It is therefore evident that whoever renounces the world more perfectly [Col. 0542C] and cleaves more intimately to God in the manner of the apostles is a son of God and may truly be called so.

[Col. 0541] Here ends the Third Volume.

THE FOURTH VOLUME BEGINS: On the saying, “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.”

[Col. 0541C] As we approach the exposition of the fourth book of this work, it is fitting that with pure mind and utmost intent we invoke him who, in making the lights of heaven on the fourth day, illuminated the world, so that he may deign to remove for us the veil of the letter of the Old Testament, and that, according to his will, we may be able to discover the spiritual sense in writings covered by a rather dark veil. For indeed a great veil is laid over this saying: “Draw me after you”; as likewise over the eightfold work of God in the book of Genesis, and over the eight sayings of the prophet Amos, where it is said: “For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn back” (Amos 1); and over the eightfold vision of the prophet Zechariah. Nevertheless, having briefly tasted of these sayings, let us direct our pen to the matters of which we have spoken above, and investigate by spiritual inquiry whose voice this is that says, “Draw me after you,” and to whom she speaks. No wise person doubts that this is the voice of holy Church, which says, “Draw me after you”; and all the authority of both the New and the Old Testament proclaims in harmonious voice that her Bridegroom, to whom she speaks, is Christ, the Son of God.

But it is very remarkable on what grounds holy Church asks to be drawn after the Son of God—that is, after her Bridegroom—since this spiritual drawing to the Father belongs especially, on the authority of his Son, to the Father himself. For the same Son of God says in the Gospel concerning that same most beloved Father of his: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John 6). Finally, that same most merciful Father says through the prophet Jeremiah concerning that same illustrious and chosen Bride of his Son, namely holy Church: “I have loved you with everlasting love; therefore, in compassion for you, I have drawn you” (Jer. 31). It must therefore be confessed that God the Father, by the abundance of his sweetness, in the invisible love of inward charity, drew the mind of his Son’s Bride to this end: that this same most beloved Bride might ask to be drawn by her same Bridegroom, namely the Son of God.

But surely, O hearer, do not believe that this drawing, which the Bride desires her Bridegroom to perform upon her, is violent. [Col. 0543A] It is not violent, but in every way loving and voluntary. Hence the Psalmist, inflamed by spiritual desire so that he might worthily utter the praises of God, draws to himself the grace of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “I opened my mouth, and drew in the Spirit” (Ps. 118 [119]); “Holy” is understood. He plainly added what purpose he had drawn him in for, saying: “Because I desired your commandments” (ibid.). We are therefore given to understand that the grace of the Holy Spirit is drawn in through desire for God’s commandments.

There is, moreover, another very praiseworthy and commendable drawing: when someone is known to be placed in some distress, and a friend, sympathizing and grieving with him, bears that same distress with him in compassionate sorrow, so that he may be able to free him from it. In this way it also happens that the person freed from that distress through the aid and compassion of his friend is compelled to love that same friend more than usual, and is drawn toward love of him by a wonderful and inestimable affection of charity. Thus, in this most merciful manner, holy Church, kindled by divine love of charity and considering the compassion of ineffable mercy which Christ had for her when he underwent death for her, says: “Draw me after you”; as though she said: “As you died for me, so grant that I too may be able to die for you.” Or rather, “Draw me after you,” that is, make me attain knowledge of your majesty, so that I may see—not now through a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face (1 Cor. 13)—how you are in the Father and the Father in you, and how [Col. 0543C] the Holy Spirit proceeds from you and from the Father.

“We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments”: this appears to be the voice of the young women, that is, of faithful souls speaking to the Bridegroom. Our mother, holy Church, trusting in the excellence of her merits in her stronger members—that is, the apostles and martyrs—prays to you that she may deserve to attain knowledge of your majesty. But we young women—that is, weaker and more feeble, though still faithful, souls—have not yet laboured so much for you that we dare to aspire to the inaccessible light in which you dwell. Yet we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments: that is, by living well in this world, we shall follow the examples of your saints, in order that after death we may be able to attain their fellowship. Or again, “we shall run in the fragrance [Col. 0543D] of your ointments,” that is, we shall walk in the way of your commandments, so that, enlarged by your love, we may be able to receive within the little casket of our heart the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Let us therefore run, dearest brethren, in the fragrance of God’s ointments, so that it may be said of us: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118 [119]). Let us run, I say, with the apostle Paul (Phil. 3), so that with him we may lay hold of eternal life. For he runs well who, living piously and justly, brings the last day of his life to a religious conclusion. Finally, one who runs leaves the place in which he was and hastens toward the place in which he was not. So let us leave behind the glory of this world; let us flee the desires and pleasures [Col. 0544A] of this age; let us zealously seek, with Paul (1 Cor. 12), the better gifts, which are fragrant ointments—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—so that, drawn out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth, we may be able to reach the everlasting joys of paradise.

## Recapitulation of the foregoing according to the allegorical and mystical sense

317 With the help of him who said, “If I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12), we have spoken above concerning the saying in the Song of Songs, namely, “Draw me after you.” It remains now, with his aid, to speak for his praise concerning the sevenfold or eightfold work of God, and to bring to light how each work corresponds to the eight ages of this world. Yet [Col. 0544B] first it is necessary that we distinguish the world into eight ages; then we shall more properly assign each work separately to the distinction of each age.

The first age of this world extended from Adam to Noah. The second, from Noah to Abraham. The third, from Abraham to Moses. The fourth extended from Moses to David. The fifth, from David to the coming of Christ. In the sixth age the Lord Jesus Christ came; this age lasted until the time when persecution ceased in holy Church. The seventh age is that which is now taking place, until the day of judgment. The eighth age will be after the day of judgment has passed; it will be without end.

Certainly, it is especially remarkable that the things which God is read to have made in those seven days correspond, in an elegant order and by a most wise arrangement, to these aforesaid seven or eight ages. Let us therefore hasten to discuss the work of the first day. Relying on the most holy inspiration of him who made the first day, let our mind not fear to bring to light what mystery this work contains, while preserving in every respect the exposition of the holy Fathers.

“Moses says: ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth’” (Gen. 1). O Moses, dweller with God! O hidden revealer of divine secrets! Who disclosed to you that God made heaven and earth in the beginning, except he himself, who created all these things for the praise, honour, and glory of his name? But in what beginning? Surely in him who says in the Gospel: “I am the beginning, who speak to you” (John 8). In him, I say, concerning whom [Col. 0544D] John the Evangelist testifies: “In the beginning was the Word, and all things were made through him” (John 1). In him, I say, concerning whom the Psalmist says to the Father: “And you, Lord God the Father, in the beginning founded the earth in your Son, and the heavens are the works of your hands” (Ps. 101 [102]).

Consider, most kindly hearer and most gentle lover of spiritual utterances, that only two things shine forth in the work of the first day: namely, the Creator who made the creature, and the creature which was made by its God and now serves him. You will find absolutely nothing else in that work, even if you were to scrutinize the work of the first day for a thousand years. There the creature made by God the Father through the Son is declared; likewise, the Holy Spirit is proclaimed as borne over the waters, in order that he might sanctify them for us to convey the grace of baptism. And just as the holy Trinity is shown in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit through the effect of the work, so the work itself which was made in some way represents within itself the likeness of the most holy and undivided Trinity.

For everything created by God, from the moment it was created, had being; it was subject to quantity; and it necessarily had to be subject to quality. Let us clarify what we have said, lest perhaps we leave the understanding of a simple hearer beset by obscurity. It is evident that whatever exists has being either through itself, or with another, or through another, or in no way. God alone exists solely through himself. But that which was created by him, in order to subsist through him who created it, is necessarily known to exist through itself and without another: this is one thing which properly belongs to God. To exist through another and not to be able to exist without another is shown to be proper to the creature, which cannot exist without its Creator, even though it may in some manner appear to exist. What is created is subject to quantity, because it is either small, great, or middling. The creature is necessarily subject to the laws of quality, because it is either white, black, or coloured with an intermediate colour.

Behold, in a few words, with God’s inspiration, our pen makes clear how reasonably every creature represents within itself the image of the holy, undivided Trinity. Moreover, if with the eyes of the inner person we scrutinize still more closely the very surface of this sacred page, [Col. 0545C] we shall find all the rules of those seven arts called liberal according to philosophy. To begin with the art of rhetoric: according to the modes of expression called figures, the first sentence—“In the beginning God created heaven and earth”—is known to have one member. But those who glory in skill or eminence in that art will clearly acknowledge that the second sentence—“The earth was empty and void, and darkness was upon the face of the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters”—has three members.

Certainly we must by no means pass over in silence that the first sentence, which has one member, proclaims one God to us; but the second, which has three members, likewise confirms and declares to us that the true God consists of one substance and three persons. Let these remarks suffice to strengthen the foundation of our faith concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—a faith repeated not only in this book, 318 but also in all the divine volumes.

Blessed Augustine offers this interpretation of heaven and earth: “God made heaven and earth in the beginning,” that is, the angelic or heavenly creature and the earthly creature. We also may, without departing from the sense of the ecclesiastical rule, refer heaven and earth allegorically to the person of our first father Adam. For before he sinned he was like heaven; but after sinning he heard from God: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). Adam may rightly be called heaven before the commission [Col. 0546A] of sin, because undoubtedly, as Saint Augustine says, if he had not incurred that miserable guilt, he would have attained heavenly glory without tasting death.

Adam can still be called heaven and earth in another way, because he had a soul of heavenly nature, while his body took its origin from the earth. For Scripture says: “God made man from the clay of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. 2). There is also another reasonable interpretation by which our first parent ought to be called heaven and earth. For Eve was made from him, as it is written: “God cast a sleep upon Adam, took one of his ribs, and built that rib into a woman” (ibid.). If, therefore, we understand Adam by heaven and Eve by earth, our interpretation proceeds by the straight path of ecclesiastical teaching.

Let us say it differently. We may not unreasonably interpret heaven and earth in Adam, because holy Church was to spring from his offspring; in the elect she may be called heaven, and in the reprobate whom she contains, earth. Or again, Adam can fittingly be called heaven and earth because it was to come about that one descended from his stock through the lines of generations would reconcile heavenly and earthly things together through his blood, and would restore, from the children of that same Adam—though regenerated by the saving font—the loss which the heavenly court had sustained in the fall of Satan and his companions.

The statement that the earth was empty and void must be understood thus: after Adam and Eve consented in sin to the devil rather than to God, they immediately remained empty and bereft of the grace of the Holy Spirit and of the other virtues with which they had previously shone. The following must be understood in the same sense: “Darkness was upon the abyss” (Gen. 1). The abyss, as Saint Augustine says, is a certain depth without a bottom; and indeed, the deeper it is, the darker it is beyond doubt. Do not those seem sufficiently dark who thought that they could hide from the face of God? For after the transgression Adam said for himself and his wife: “I heard your voice, Lord, and hid myself” (Gen. 3). Therefore darkness was upon the face of the abyss, because the obscurity of sin, the boldness of self-defence, and the covering of falsehood besieged [Col. 0546D] the hearts of those who strove to deceive by words him of whom Solomon says: “You alone know the hearts of the children of men” (2 Chron. 2).

But we ought to interpret the statement that the Spirit of God was borne over the waters so as to understand that, even from that time onward, the grace of baptism was consecrated through the power of the Holy Spirit—a baptism by which Adam’s offspring was to be cleansed from this transgression. And the words God said, “Let there be light, and light was made” (Gen. 1), can fittingly be applied to Adam himself. For he shone out like light before the other creatures over which he was set; and so, through participation in the most wise light hidden within him, he gave names to all things. “And God saw the light, that it was good” (ibid.). [Col. 0547A] It would certainly have pleased God if Adam had remained in the same state in which he had been created by him. But because Adam sinned, there was a great division between the state he possessed before his fall and the state in which he remained after tasting sin; and this is the division of “light from darkness. And he called the light day, and the darkness night” (ibid.). That is to say: before transgression Adam was righteous—that is, light and day; after the guilt of transgression, he remained night and darkness—that is, a sinner.

“And evening and morning were made one day” (ibid.). If we wish to understand Adam’s soul, which was of heavenly nature, by morning, and his body by evening, this interpretation of the sentence may be given: “Evening and morning were made one day,” that is, from soul and body one human being was made. Or, if by morning, which belongs to light, we wish to understand that glorious condition in which God created Adam, and if by evening, which looks toward darkness, we understand the unhappy guilt which Adam incurred, we may say that Adam, whom God created righteous, although he made himself a sinner, nevertheless remained the same person, except that he did not lack the stain of sin. Our purpose, therefore, is this: that, with the aid of him who made the first day, we may refer allegorically to the events of the first age of the world what was done on that first day.

[Col. 0547] Here ends the fourth book on the Song of Songs.

## Here begins the fifth book, on the words: “The king has brought me into his wine-cellars; we shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts; the upright love you more than wine” (Song 1).

[Col. 0547B] 319 As the sacred history of the Old Testament, when it was read, intimated to the minds of its hearers in spiritual melody: Isaac, the holy patriarch, son of that most noble and eminent patriarch Abraham, once, as evening was already drawing on, went out to meditate in the field (Gen. 24). And while he walked about in meditation, he lifted up his eyes and saw Rebecca, his bride, coming; he met her and brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah. He loved her so greatly that he largely assuaged the grief which had befallen him through the death of that same mother.

Because Isaac means “laughter” or “joy,” we rightly understand by him in a spiritual sense our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the joy and gladness, jubilation and exultation, and unfailing delight [Col. 0547C] of his saints. That the Lord Jesus himself is Abraham’s son according to the flesh is attested by Matthew the Evangelist when he says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1). The fact that holy Isaac went out into the field for meditation as evening was already drawing on signifies that the Lord Jesus Christ came into this world as the end of this age approached, in order to fulfil the mystery of his most holy incarnation. Isaac’s walk into the field thus signifies to us the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ into this world. Hence his most beloved Bride says to the same Lord Jesus in the Song of Songs: “Come, my beloved, let us remain in the woods; let us go out into the field” (Song 7), although blessed Ambrose interprets the field itself as a fortress.

Moreover, Isaac’s bringing Rebecca into his mother’s tent and moderating the grief of his mother’s death for love of her signifies that the Lord Jesus Christ joined holy Church to himself in spiritual nuptials and nuptial songs. He loved her with such spiritual love that he even [Col. 0548B] consigned the Synagogue—namely, his carnal mother—to oblivion. Finally, Rebecca herself means “patience,” which Isaac brought into his tent; this, indeed, elegantly alludes to the mysteries of holy Church. At the end of the conflict of this age our Lord Jesus Christ will bring her into the everlasting dwelling places of heavenly glory. To the founders of this Church, namely the holy apostles, he himself says: “By your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21).

Therefore, contemplating in this little work that most blessed and happy bringing-in of Christ’s Bride, and rejoicing with unutterable joy and incomprehensible jubilation as though what is still to come after the day of judgment had already taken place, she addresses the young women thus: “The king has brought me into his wine-cellars” [Col. 0548C] (Song 1). Now who is this king by whom the Bride says that she has been brought into the wine-cellars? Surely he of whom the prophet David says: “O God, give your judgment to the king and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71 [72]). The same king, son of the highest King, makes this clearer in the Gospel when he says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

What are these wine-cellars, except those tabernacles or courts of which the prophet David sang: “How beloved are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts; my soul longs for and desires the courts of the Lord?” (Ps. 83 [84]). The Lord Jesus himself calls these tabernacles or courts “dwelling places” in the Gospel when he says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14). Therefore holy Church, Christ’s Bride, contemplating spiritually these dwelling places, tabernacles, or courts, and panting for them with the whole desire of her soul after setting aside love of the world, says as though she already possessed in present reality what she does not doubt that she will possess after the day of judgment: “The king has brought me into his wine-cellars.”

Truly, says holy Church, the King has brought me into his wine-cellars, because what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2), he has faithfully granted me as he promised. Hence the prophet Isaiah says: “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you” (Isa. 64). Therefore the young women—that is, faithful souls—kindled by love of this ineffable joy, by the affection of incomprehensible jubilation, and by contemplation of the supreme and unutterable Trinity, say: “We shall exult and rejoice in you.”

For then, when the mystery of the resurrection and the general judgment has been completed, when the Son of God says to his faithful: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25); and when the corruptible body will no longer weigh down the soul, nor the earthly dwelling depress the mind that thinks many things, but the soul, seeing God as he is face to face (1 Cor. 13), will through participation in the vision of the supreme and incomprehensible Trinity make its flesh wholly spiritual—then, I say, [Col. 0549B] these young women, that is, faithful souls, will more truly say: “We shall exult and rejoice in you.” For while we lived on earth and faithfully obeyed your commandments, you promised great things indeed; but in heaven you gave greater things. Therefore we shall exult and rejoice in you.

“Remembering your breasts,” that is, your commandments, through observance of which and through the grace of the Holy Spirit we have attained contemplation of the brightness of your majesty. Or again: “We shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts more than wine,” that is, your words. Those words became sweet and honeyed to us beyond wine—that is, more than the teaching of the Mosaic law, which is rightly compared to wine because of the severity of its commandments. This wine is said to kill little children, because, as Paul says, “The law works wrath”—that is, death (Rom. 4 [Rom. 4:15]).

Therefore, King Christ, because you have bestowed so many benefits upon your Bride, the children of that same Bride—that is, the upright—love you. They love you upright in thought, upright in speech, upright in action. Those who do not return to sin after confession and repentance are rightly called upright.

We may indeed refer this saying to the person of Christ, so that Christ says: “The king has brought me into his wine-cellars”; that is to say: my Father, who is King of kings, commanded me to take flesh within the womb of the blessed Mary, ever Virgin. The womb of the most holy Virgin is rightly called the wine-cellar of God the Father, because it was predestined by him from eternity and, at the end of the ages, prepared and consecrated by him for the birth of his Son. Recognizing this birth, the young women—that is, the angelic and heavenly powers—sing glory to God in the highest and announce peace on earth to people of good will (Luke 2), as though they said to the Father: “Rightly shall we exult and rejoice in you, because by the incarnation of your Son you intend to restore our number, which had been diminished by the devil’s fall.”

“Remembering your breasts more than wine,” as though it said: “We remember your mercy and your wondrous compassion, by which you now temper the severe sentence of just condemnation [Col. 0550A] that you formerly imposed upon the first man, when, his iniquity requiring it, you excluded him from the joys of paradise and expelled him into this vale of tears and miseries.” Therefore, considering these benefits graciously bestowed upon them by you, the upright love you, because neither in heaven nor on earth do they find anything dearer or more worthy than you. For you created the whole world from nothing when it did not exist; with wondrous power you fashioned man from the clay of the earth; and the same man whom the devil deceived and ruined by his fraud, your most kindly mercy restored and saved for the joys of paradise. Therefore the upright love you, because they find nothing better or more just to love than you.

Let us, then, brethren, also bring Christ into our wine-cellars. Our wine-cellars are our body [Col. 0550B] and soul, into which the Lord promises that he will enter if, after all evils have been excluded, he finds them prepared and clean for himself, as he says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens the door to me, I shall enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3). But what joy, jubilation, gladness, or exultation, do we suppose, will the young women—that is, all the powers of our soul—then possess, when they see Christ present in their wine-cellars? Then, moreover, the Bridegroom will say to these young women: “No one shall take your joy from you” (John 16).

## Recapitulation of the foregoing according to the mystical and allegorical sense, on the saying: “The king has brought me into his wine-cellars.”

[Col. 0550C] Perfumers, who prepare fragrant spices from diverse ingredients, and who frequently handle balsams or other such aromatic substances, first themselves enjoy, as it were the reward of their labour, the wondrous scent of those spices or balsam; then those who come afterward and draw nearer are suffused with and enjoy the most pleasing fragrance. Moreover, this is most certainly evident: the more those aforesaid perfumers crush their spices, grind them finely, or pour out their balsams and transfer them from vessel to vessel, the more surely they bring a fresher odour to their own nostrils and offer a sweeter scent to those standing at a distance. What, then, are these precious spices or balsams, if not the most sacred utterances of the divine books? [Col. 0550D] Hence the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved has gone down to the bed of spices, to gather lilies” (Song 6).

What, then, is the bed of spices, if not the Catholic Church, in which is contained an immense abundance of divine books? By “perfumers,” moreover, I think none can more fittingly be understood than the rulers and preachers of God’s Church. Following the manner of aromatic substances, they crush by exposition the divinely inspired Scriptures and divide them into small parts; and just as balsams, when poured from vessel to vessel, breathe forth a most sweet odour, so they produce rational and pleasing meanings as they pass from history to allegory and from allegory to moral interpretation.

321 If, therefore, as we have said, the sacred utterances are spices, and if they give forth more fragrance the more they are crushed, [Col. 0551A] let us see what fragrance this statement emits or contains within itself: “The king brought me into his storerooms.” The storerooms of this king, according to allegory, are in general all the books of the divine law. We are spiritually and mystically brought into them by the Lord when he himself instructs and teaches us to understand their hidden and mystical meanings. Thus those blessed disciples were brought by the Lord Jesus into these storerooms, of whom the Gospel says: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

The Gospel is, indeed, a certain secret storeroom, overflowing with every divine grace and spiritual wealth. Hence the Bride cries out exultantly in the Song of Songs: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar, [Col. 0551B] and ordered charity within me” (Song 2). For the Gospel teaches and declares how charity ought to be possessed and practised among Christians: namely, that God should be loved first, before all creatures, above all creatures, and before all things; and then, in the second place, one’s neighbour should be loved with the sincere affection of charity. This is the most blessed and sacred ordering of pure charity which every faithful person can find in the storeroom of Christ’s Gospel.

There are besides other storerooms of this great and exceedingly rich king: namely, the book of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, the book of Numbers and the book of Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the twelve prophets, together with very many other books of the divine law; these are Christ’s storerooms. But what shall I say concerning David, chief and most excellent among [Col. 0551C] the prophets? In the first part of his book he manifests more clearly than light whose storeroom he is, when he says: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence” (Psalm 1).

We do not, therefore, judge that this is the time to run through all the books individually and explain how each book is a storeroom of this supreme king, for we have by no means sufficient understanding for carrying this out, and we know that our holy Fathers of old have accomplished it more fully. Yet, lest anyone think that we wish to conceal ourselves in silence through bodily sluggishness, let us enter the storeroom of which we spoke above, and, through the generosity of him whose storeroom it is, bring to light what it contains hidden within itself [Col. 0551D] and what fragrance it gives forth.

“Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly,” etc. In the divine page, O searcher of the spiritual law, three things lie open to your inquiry: history, allegory, and moral interpretation, which always accompanies and clings inseparably to our condition. Indeed, these three things exist in the nature of things, and they are not easily found unless they are sought out with care by an attentive reader. The historical understanding of this verse, namely, “Blessed is the man,” should therefore be referred to the person of the earthly king David; the allegory should be assigned to the Lord Jesus Christ; and the moral interpretation should be applied to the correction of our actions.

But how can we refer this verse historically to David—“Blessed is the man,” etc.—when we know that he sinned in thought, speech, and [Col. 0552A] action? For it is certain that David sinned in thought when, looking incautiously from his bed, he saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, bathing and desired her. But because he did not restrain the unlawful thought within himself, he descended to the guilt of speech when he inquired through messengers who that woman was. And who does not know that he fell by a miserable lapse in deed, when he committed adultery with that same Bathsheba (2 Kings 11), and afterwards delivered her [Col. 0552B] husband to be slain by the swords of the sons of Ammon, lest the adultery become known to all?

What blessedness, then, will be granted to David, who is proved guilty in thought, speech, and deed? And who would dare call David a blessed man, when he committed adultery so lightly and, what is worse, joined homicide to that adultery? But according to the word of the Apostle Paul (1 Corinthians 6), he was washed, justified, and sanctified in the name of our Lord and in the Spirit of our God. He was justified, I say, through confession, when he said to the prophet Nathan: “I have sinned against the Lord; pray for me.” And Nathan the prophet said to him: “Do not fear; you shall by no means die, because the Lord has taken your sin away from you” (2 Kings 12). Behold how swiftly this man, through confession, was washed, justified, and sanctified.

Moreover, let us hear what the Lord says concerning him: “I have found David my servant, the son of Jesse, who does all my wills” (Acts 13). And elsewhere: “I have found David my servant; I have anointed him with my holy oil” (Psalm 88 [89]). [Col. 0552C] “My hand,” he says, “will assist him” (ibid.), and the rest that follows in the same psalm, which the plain wording proves to have been spoken in praise of David himself. Who, then, would dare condemn one whom God washes, justifies, and sanctifies with words of this kind?

But let us surely inquire whether perhaps we may discover somewhere that David did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, did not stand in the way of sinners, and did not sit in the seat of iniquity. For it does not befit the majesty of God to justify the ungodly, any more than it befits him to condemn the just. God would by no means justify or praise righteous David unless some good work pleasing to God himself were found in him.

The history of the book of Kings is well known. It relates that Saul, a most impious king, once unjustly persecuted David; and it happened one day that this same Saul entered a cave for the necessities of nature. And behold, David, fleeing from Saul’s presence, was hiding with his companions in that same cave. His companions therefore said to him: “Behold the day of which the Lord spoke to you, saying, ‘I will deliver your enemy into your hand, that you may do to him whatever you wish.’ Rise, therefore, and kill him.” But David rebuked the words of the men who were with him and did not permit them to kill him, but said: “As the Lord lives, unless the Lord himself strikes him, or his day comes for him to die, or he goes down and perishes in battle, I will not lay my hand upon the Lord’s anointed” (1 Kings 24). Behold how David did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly.

[Col. 0553A] Although the Law said, “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Leviticus 19), he, despising the ordinances of the old Law, was already making a passage to the mysteries of the new Law. For in the new Law it is said: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5). Having therefore, with God’s help, shown how David did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, it remains for us, with his aid, to demonstrate how he did not stand in the way of sinners.

For likewise in the same book of Kings it is found that, on another occasion, that same utterly wicked King Saul, spurred on by envy, persecuted holy David. And it came to pass, as the sun was declining to its setting and approaching evening was now about to place an end to the day, that Saul prepared to rest where he was, his tents and [Col. 0553B] pavilions spread out. And when tranquil sleep held the limbs of all, David, having noted the place where Saul slept, said to his companions: “Who will go down with me to Saul in the camp?” (1 Kings 26). Some of his companions went down with him.

When he came to the place where Saul slept, one of those who was with him said: “Behold, God has delivered your enemy into your hand. Now therefore allow me, and I will pin him to the ground with the spear at one stroke; there will be no need for a second.” But David said: “Do him no harm, nor stretch out your hand against him. For who, having laid his hand upon the Lord’s anointed, will be innocent?” (ibid.) “Let the Lord know this: unless the Lord himself strikes him, or his day comes [Col. 0553C] for him to die, or he goes down and perishes in battle, I will not lay my hand upon the Lord’s anointed” (ibid.). Behold how David did not stand in the way of sinners, because he refused to heed the counsel of those who urged him to murder.

Having thus shown, by certain proofs drawn from the deeds of holy David, and by clear authority, that he at some time neither walked in the counsel of the ungodly nor stood in the way of sinners, we must still show with watchful mind that he did not sit in the seat of pestilence. After Saul ended this temporal life with the sons of Israel by the lot of battle on Mount Gilboa (1 Kings 31), it is written that the house of Judah anointed David king over themselves in Hebron and placed him in a royal seat according to royal custom.

[Col. 0553D] “Behold,” says the history, “certain men came and reported to David that the men of Jabesh-gilead had honourably buried Saul, his enemy.” And he sent them word, saying: “Blessed are you by the Lord, who have shown this mercy to Saul your lord. And I also will repay you with favour for the deed which you have done for him” (2 Kings 2). Moreover, later in the book of Kings it is said that David took the bones of Saul and Jonathan and buried them with great honour in the land of Benjamin (2 Kings 21).

Indeed, by what words can we adequately explain how David wept when he heard of the death of that same enemy Saul, at whose destruction you, surely, ought to have rejoiced with exultant minds? For it is written: “David bewailed this [Col. 0554A] lament over Saul and over Jonathan his son: ‘Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who provided golden ornaments for your adornment and clothed you in luxury. O Saul and Jonathan, how lovely and graceful you were in your life! You were swifter than eagles, stronger than lions. Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you, nor fields of firstfruits be found on you, because there the shield of the mighty was cast away—the shield of Saul—as though he had not been anointed with oil. Jonathan’s arrow never turned back, and Saul’s sword did not return empty. O how the strong, noble, and distinguished men have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!’” (2 Kings 1).

[Col. 0554B] The fact, too, that David ordered the man who reported to him, saying, “I killed Saul on Mount Gilboa,” to be killed accords greatly with works of piety and mercy. Behold, as we have said, David did not sit in the seat of pestilence and iniquity: at the death of his enemy he not only poured forth lamentations of grief, but by most devout words urged others to mourn with him.

Above, therefore, we stated that the historical sense of this verse, “Blessed is the man,” should be referred to David, the allegory to Christ, and the moral interpretation to each one of us. Yet the allegory of this verse may readily be applied to the Lord Jesus, since he who committed no sin did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, did not stand in the way of sinners, and in no way sat in the seat of pestilence and iniquity.

Let us therefore investigate with close scrutiny how the moral interpretation of this verse concerns each of us, and how it surrounds us on every side in our inward [Col. 0554C] action. For, O lover or hearer of the divine word, you ought to consider in this verse—“Blessed is the man”—three kinds of falls belonging to human frailty, and carefully ponder the ways in which our nature is subject to sin. For just as in this verse three things are denoted—walking, standing, sitting—so every sin to which we are liable is committed by us in three ways. But who these three ways are, we know more from daily experience, which we cannot mention without deep sorrow, than from the indication of any exposition. It is difficult for the human condition not to fall in thought, speech, or action.

[Col. 0554D] For the mind seems, as it were, to walk in the counsel of the ungodly when, given over to the vain thoughts of evil spirits, it wanders here and there. It stands in the way of sinners when it speaks things contrary to God. But it sits in the seat of pestilence when, casting away the fear of God behind it, it acts wickedly.

RECAPITULATION ACCORDING TO THE ANAGOGICAL AND MORAL SENSE IN THE STATEMENT: “THE KING BROUGHT ME INTO HIS STOREROOMS.”

All the arts of human learning, while they are being taught—that is, when they are taught or practised—provide their students with certain pleasant diversions outside themselves. Such are, for example, polishers, wood-cutters, those occupied in quarries, goldsmiths, builders, and practitioners of any other art known to belong to human skill. For all these have, amid their work, certain idle consolations. While polishers polish marble, they talk, tell stories, laugh, and amuse themselves—sometimes even with matters shown to have no bearing whatever upon that craft. But our art, namely that of spiritual writings, requires the whole person to attend to it in learning or teaching. Either a person gives his entire self to our art, or he will never attain a clear mastery of it. For who has ever been able to become a good cleric with a divided heart, distracted senses, or a wandering and unstable mind? [Col. 0555A–B]

Therefore, one who wishes perfectly to attain what is offered to human understanding in the divine books must necessarily consign not only the things of this world, but even himself for the most part, if one may say so, to forgetfulness. Thus, with earthly pleasures lulled to sleep and wicked deeds despised—deeds which often plunge unwary people into the depth of an abyss—let us approach the Bridegroom not with a divided heart but with an undivided mind and sincere affection. Let us beseech him, together with his most beloved Bride, in humble words, that he may deign to bring us, his devoted servants, into his storehouses.

Above I confessed that I had said that the storehouses of this Bridegroom and King were, allegorically, all the books of divine law. Now I likewise say that, morally, the storehouses of this same Bridegroom and King are all the virtues that may be found scattered everywhere through the sacred utterances. But since we wish to begin a discourse on virtues, it follows that we should direct our pen to the head or source of all virtues. The head or source from which all virtues proceed is undoubtedly charity. Hence blessed Gregory says:

> “As many branches proceed from one trunk of a tree, so many virtues are generated from one charity; and the branch of a good work possesses no greenness unless it remains in the root of charity.”

Let charity itself, therefore, be the beginning of our discourse, because it is believed to be a storehouse of this great Bridegroom and King. Yet with what presumption shall we dare to speak of charity, when we neither love nor possess that same charity perfectly as we ought, and when we appear in no way charitable toward your brothers? Still, this presumption springs from love of charity, which incites us gladly to discuss the works of charity. “God,” John says, “is charity” (1 John 4). This virtue could not be compared with anything greater than being equated with the almighty Creator. Although one may say, “God is obedience, humility, chastity, peace, patience,” and likewise of the other virtues, yet of none is it said so particularly as of charity, “God is this or that virtue.” God, therefore, is charity. [Col. 0555C–D]

God is rightly said to be charity, and rightly declared to possess charity, because, though he alone existed in his glory, divinity, and majesty, he did not wish to possess alone the kingdom of heavenly blessedness. Rather, he sought companions—angels and human beings, whom he created for the praise and glory of his name—to share with him the blessed and immortal joys of everlasting delight.

Of his inestimable charity, incomparable loving-kindness, and ineffable mercy, blessed Augustine speaks thus:

> “O inestimable love of charity that you had: in order to redeem a slave, you gave up your Son.”

For Augustine considered with what compassionate charity and charitable compassion almighty God pitied humankind after its miserable fall. To raise it up, he caused his Son, consubstantial and coeternal with himself and the Holy Spirit, to put on the slave’s girding of flesh and to endure the suspension of death.

The prophet also, in Isaiah 63, saw in the spirit of prophecy the Lord Jesus [324] clothed with the mantle of zeal, treading the winepress alone, with no man from among the nations beside him. Let no one fail to understand that to be clothed with the slave’s girding of flesh is the same as to be clothed with the mantle of zeal; and that what denotes suffering the loss of an undeserved death plainly signifies treading the winepress alone. For the Lord Jesus Christ greatly loved us, since for our sake he perished in the winepress—that is, on the cross—pouring out his blood. Thus Isaiah says: “He was wounded for our iniquities, he was crushed for our crimes, and by his death we were saved” (Isa. 53). Hence John says: “He loved us and washed us in his blood” (Rev. 1). [Col. 0556A–B]

Moreover, this incomparable charity, inestimable love, and inexplicable compassion of the Lord Jesus Christ was long ago aptly prefigured in holy David. The history in the Book of Kings relates that David’s son Absalom, coveting his father’s kingdom, once cruelly persecuted him and, had difficulty not stood in his way, intended to inflict an undeserved death upon him (2 Sam. 18). But as David was returning according to God’s ordering, death itself fell upon its own agent, and a very thick oak held Absalom suspended between heaven and earth. For he was worthy—not merely, I do not say, to look upon heaven as he died, but neither was he such as earth could worthily receive—he who, contrary to every law of nature, strove to bring the peril of death upon his father’s beloved person.

Yet David, as a most loving father, when he heard of the death of his son and persecutor—if indeed one may call him a son who had proved so abominable a persecutor—David himself, I say, poured out inconsolable tears. For thus it is written of him:

> “King David, walking with covered head, mourned his son, saying: ‘Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Who will grant that I might die for you, my son Absalom?’” (ibid.)

See how David had been brought into the storehouses of charity: he wept with irreparable tears for the death of his persecutor. But someone may say: “You are doing violence to divine Scripture. How, then, do you know that David’s grief over the destruction of his son was a figure of the passion and death which the Lord Jesus Christ endured for the salvation of humankind?”

Listen not to me but to the apostle Paul, who says that all these things happened to our fathers as figures and were written for our correction (1 Cor. 10). If David, therefore, was a figure, then in the Lord Jesus Christ the undefiled reality undoubtedly remained. Yet let us examine carefully whether David’s lamentation corresponds to Christ’s passion and death; once this has been examined, our objector will have nothing left that he can justly object to us. [Col. 0556C–0557A]

For in the Gospel we read that the Lord Jesus Christ wept in two places and afterwards endured death for us. “When he saw the city Jerusalem, he wept over it, saying: ‘For if you too had known’” (Luke 19)—understand: the things that were to come upon you—you would weep; but because you now do not know them, for a little while you dissolve into foolish joy and rejoice.

Likewise, at Lazarus’s tomb, the Lord Jesus Christ, as true man, deigned to weep (John 11). Of this weeping holy Augustine says that he did not weep for the dead man, whom he himself raised, but for death, which humankind acquired for itself by sinning. For he considered in what glory humankind had been created by its Creator, and into what misery it had come through disobedience.

After this twofold weeping, the Lord Jesus came to pay the debt of death that he did not owe, because he had been sent by the Father into the world in order that, by dying, he might redeem humankind. Let us see, then, how David’s lamentation fittingly corresponds to the twofold weeping and single death of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“King David,” it says, “walked with covered head” (2 Sam. 19). What, then, should we think is signified by David’s walking with covered head, except that the divinity which assumed was hidden in the humanity assumed? For, according to the apostle Paul, “the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11). David, as it were, walked with covered head when God was hidden in the assumed human being.

Does it not seem to you that the Lord Jesus walked with covered head when human opinion considered him to be Elijah, Jeremiah, or one of the ancient prophets?
