But the apostle Peter uncovered the Lord Jesus’s head when he said to him in a truthful voice: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16). Therefore, when the Lord Jesus performed miracles through the power of his divinity, David walked with covered head, because God hidden in a human being appeared by manifest signs. [Col. 0557B–D]

But when, passing through the field of this world, he suffered and did solely human things for our sake, then David, as though walking with covered head, mourned his son, saying: “Absalom, my son, my son Absalom” (2 Sam. 18). Accordingly, the Lord Jesus endured the injuries of our nature in order to save humankind, which is signified by Absalom, whom he himself created for the praise and glory of his name.

Thus Absalom is aptly interpreted as “the father’s peace,” or as “the devil,” because the ancient enemy gloried that he had subjected our race to himself through disobedience; and because the Lord Jesus Christ, through the flesh that he assumed from the human race, reconciled and restored that same human race to peace with his Father.

That David, while walking and weeping, repeats his son’s name tearfully—“Absalom, my son, my son Absalom”—plainly signifies [325] that the Lord Jesus shed tears twice in the Gospel and truly underwent death for humankind’s salvation. The Savior’s compassion and death, which he endured for the salvation alike of our soul and body, may be understood through this double and tearful repetition of the name. For whatever perished in our first parent, the second Parent wholly assumed and saved. By his death, indeed, he redeemed humankind. [Col. 0558A]

Let us be convicted of falsehood and branded as false interpreters of divine law if the following history does not itself indicate what we say, when it cries out in clear words: “Who will grant that I might die for you, my son Absalom?” (ibid.). If, then, as we have said above, we understand our Lord Jesus Christ through David and humankind through Absalom, it is certainly plain that the death David desired for his son’s destruction points to the death which the Lord Jesus endured for the redemption of humankind.

I beg you, reader of this lesson, spare me and do not be angry with me because I said metaphorically that humankind should be understood through Absalom, and our Lord Jesus Christ through David, the most compassionate and charitable king. For this custom is very frequently found in the divine writings: under an allegorical sense, one person is taken for various meanings. Thus blessed Gregory understands our Lord Jesus Christ metaphorically through Saul, a most impious king; while through Mount Gilboa, on which Saul was slain, he understands the Jewish people.

But while we have discussed figuratively, according to the capacity of our understanding, the charity of David and Christ, we have lingered rather long in the storehouses of charity. Let us consider still more closely whether any of the ancient fathers, besides David alone—who mercifully prayed for his persecutors Absalom and Saul—dwelt in these storehouses of charity. [Col. 0558B–C]

O Moses, inhabitant of these chambers, tell us what you did and how, placed amid persecution, you entered the storehouse of charity. The children of Israel once made a golden calf to worship, and by that sin provoked to anger the God of majesty, who had bestowed so many benefits on them. When Moses learned of the deed—Moses, who was gentler than all human beings dwelling on earth—he said to the Lord:

> “I beseech you, Lord: this people has committed a great sin and made for themselves gods of gold. Either forgive them this offense, or, if you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written.”

The Lord answered him:

> “Whoever sins against me, I will blot him out of my book. But you, go and lead this people” (Exod. 32).

And it is written in what follows that the people wished to stone Moses. The same Moses said to the Lord: “I beseech you, Lord God, forgive this people’s sin according to the multitude of your mercy.” And the Lord said to Moses: “I have forgiven according to your word” (Num. 14).

See how he had been brought into the storehouses of charity; see how holy Moses abounded in the inward affections of charity. With such feeling did he beseech God’s majesty for idolaters and for his persecutors that he even asked to be blotted from the book of eternal life, in which he was already recorded, if God did not remit this offense to them. [Col. 0558D–0559A]

But while I speak of holy Moses’s charity, I cannot consign David’s charity to forgetfulness. The Second Book of Kings relates that God was once greatly angered against the Israelite people over whom David ruled. He sent his angel, who killed as many as seventy thousand men of the Jewish people. But when David saw the angel of the Lord striking the people, moved by compassion he said to the Lord:

> “I am the one who sinned; I acted wickedly. But these sheep—what have they done? Let your hand, I pray, turn against me and against my father’s house” (2 Sam. 24).

When God saw David’s charity, since he wished to die for the people entrusted to him, he said to the striking angel: “It is enough now” (ibid.). The raging plague was restrained from Israel, and the Lord was reconciled to his land.

Furthermore, the prophet Samuel had formerly been rejected by that same people and driven from his leadership; yet the same people who drove the prophet from his position begged him to entreat the Lord for them. Let those who scarcely, or perhaps never, pray for their friends with a sincere heart hear what he said, answered, and spoke to his enemies:

> “Far be this sin from me against the Lord, that I should cease praying for you; and I shall show you the good way by which you ought to walk” (1 Sam. 12).

Again, the same prophet is found in the same book to have mourned for Saul, a most impious king, on whose account Samuel himself had also been driven from his leadership. Therefore the Lord said to him: “How long will you mourn for Saul, when I have rejected him?” (1 Sam. 16). [Col. 0559B–C]

See how these three men already at that time observed what the Lord would later say: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5). No one, indeed, has greater charity than to pray for persecutors and give up his life to death for them (John 15).

We shall scarcely be able at last to leave the storehouses of charity, for so many and such great works and examples of that charity present themselves to us. There are still other storehouses of this great and illustrious Bridegroom and glorious King: namely, all the virtues, as we have already said, which are found in the books of divine law. We shall [326] here take care to name some of them, lest we seem through negligence to have passed them by untouched.

Charity will always be the principal and first; it is followed by humility, faith, hope, frugality, sobriety, virginity, continence, chastity, mercy, obedience, peace, patience, long-suffering, perseverance, repentance for sins, and pure confession; the observance of God’s commandments out of true love; goodness, concord, kindness, gentleness, brotherly love, spiritual fellowship in God, the giving of alms, rational ordering of conduct, contempt of self, disdain for the world, rejection of worldly glory, renunciation of one’s own will, spiritual love, poverty, fasts, vigils, prayers, tears, mortification of the flesh, constant meditation on God’s law, the ever-unwearied contemplation of heavenly things by our soul, joy, exultation, jubilation—not in earthly matters, but in the Holy Spirit—moderation in prosperity, and courage in adversity. [Col. 0559D–0560A]

With God’s inspiration, I have assembled forty-two virtues in this catalogue, in which I have prepared an unobstructed way to heaven for those who desire to ascend. For if anyone wishes to climb step by step through these virtues, he will without doubt be able to penetrate to heaven’s heights.

Finally, this should be observed: in this catalogue charity itself is the chief virtue, and unfailing courage is itself the last, because, as Solomon says in the Song of Songs, “Charity, or love, is strong as death” (Song 8). Charity cannot in any way be preserved without spiritual courage, nor courage without true charity. If, then, we truly believe that both we and our words are in God’s hand, it is surely not thought accidental that forty-two virtues are found set out in the sequence of this catalogue. For there were forty-two encampments through which the children of Israel, departing Egypt, came to the promised land.

Moreover, when the Lord Jesus Christ descended from heaven to earth at the command of God the Father for the salvation of humankind, he came through forty-two generations to the womb of the blessed, perpetual, and ever-Virgin Mary. [Col. 0560B–C]

O if there were some scribe learned in the kingdom of God! O if someone could bring forth new and old things from the treasury of his heart! O, I say, if someone were so learned in the divine law that he knew how worthily and elegantly to fit and assign each thing to each: namely, how each of the virtues which we have just touched upon corresponds in rational order to each generation and encampment; again, how each generation corresponds to each virtue and encampment; and again, in what sequence each encampment can be fitted to each virtue and generation.

For who is so great and such a person as to dare to say, “I opened my mouth and drew in the Holy Spirit” (Ps. 118), or to whom God speaks in the secret place of his heart and says, “Open your mouth, and I shall fill it” (Ps. 80)? Such a person could explain and unravel the depth of so many mysteries hidden within the compass of these virtues, generations, and encampments together.

But although this work exceeds the poverty of our little talent, nevertheless, trusting in him who said to his disciples, “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10), we shall attempt only to touch upon the beginnings of these virtues, generations, and encampments. Under the interpretation we set forth, we shall leave what remains for our hearers themselves to understand. [Col. 0560D–0561A]

The first encampment of the children of Israel is called Ramesse; at the beginning of the genealogy of Jesus Christ the patriarch Abraham is placed; and in the catalogue of virtues which we composed, charity is put first. Abraham is interpreted “father of many nations”; Ramesse, “the stirring of a moth”; and, according to the apostle John, God is charity (1 John 4).

What, then, do we understand by the many nations of whom Abraham is called father, except a great multitude of diverse virtues? And what should we understand by the stirring of a moth, except the insolent assault of sins and vices? Thus God, who is charity, gives by his grace to whom he wills the ability to be father of many virtues; and he himself removes, uproots, and takes away from the person upon whom he has mercy all stirrings, assaults, and insolences of every vice and sin.

Under this interpretation—and under a better one, if God should reveal it to someone—we should understand the second encampment of the children of Israel, the second generation of Jesus Christ, and the second virtue of our catalogue. For it is written: “The children of Israel departed from Ramesse to Sochoth, a place interpreted ‘tabernacles’” (Exod. 12). In the sequence of the genealogy of our Lord Jesus Christ, Isaac is recognized as Abraham’s son; and in the catalogue mentioned above, humility follows charity in order. [Col. 0561B–0562A]

A truly marvelous thing, worthy through the ages of admirable and manifold praise! Now it is most pleasing to consider how the tabernacles correspond to the generation, and the generation to the virtue. For Isaac, as Saint Paul says (Heb. 11), dwelt in tabernacles with the fellow-heirs of the heavenly kingdom; and in him shone the marks of incomparable humility. Who, indeed, can adequately explain the wonderful humility Isaac displayed (Gen. 22), when he did not at all oppose his father as he wished to offer him to God?

Furthermore, Isaac is interpreted “laughter” or “joy,” because “the voice [327] of exultation and salvation is in the tabernacles of the righteous” (Ps. 107). But true salvation is acquired only in sacred humility, since, as divine Scripture says, “Only the humble in spirit shall be saved” (Ps. 33).

If anyone knew how to proceed interpretively through the remaining encampments, generations, and virtues, I confess the truth of the matter: the greater part of time would fail him rather than his abundance of speech. We shall therefore provide our hearers with material for thought, because if we explained everything, they themselves would remain dull, idle, and overcome by weariness. [Col. 0562B]

[Col. 0561] Here ends the fifth volume on the Song of Songs.

THE SIXTH VOLUME BEGINS: From the words, “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem,” as far as “My own vineyard I have not kept” (Song 1).

[Col. 0561C] Those who seek gold and linger in gold-bearing mountains remove the upper earth and search the lower and deeper parts of the ground, in order that with labour and sweat they may deserve to reach the long-desired weight of gold. When after long digging they perhaps find gold, even though they see it covered with an overlay of rust and blackened by the filth of earth, they do not despise it at all. For they know that if it is put into fire and comes into the hands of hammerers, it will immediately shed its accidental blackness along with its rust and dirt, and without delay recover the natural brightness of gold with flaming brilliance.

Who, then, are those who seek gold, except those who love the wisdom and spiritual understanding of the divine Scriptures? And who are the gold-bearing mountains, except the holy teachers—namely, the prophets and apostles? Of them it is written: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help will come to me” (Ps. 120). What, then, does the mass of gold covered with rust and dirt signify, except the Scripture of the prophets, which is very obscure and wrapped in diverse riddles and figures? We must refine it for so long by the fire of the Holy Spirit, until, having cast off the dross of the killing letter, we arrive at wisdom and spiritual understanding.

Therefore, just as gold, though outwardly discoloured by rust and dirt, is not despised because its inward gleam and brightness are considered, so the Scripture of the prophets, though surrounded by the hard shell of the outward letter, must not be despised, because precious spiritual understanding lies hidden within. [Col. 0561C–D; 0562C]

To make what we say clearer, let us consider what it means that the Bride—that is, the holy Church—speaks to the young women: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” Black outwardly, but beautiful inwardly; as though she said: “I am gold darkened by the blackness of accidental rust; but if I am consumed when fire is applied, I shall appear as most shining gold—that is, as refined gold.” For Scripture says: “As gold is tested by fire, so tribulation of temptations tests the righteous” (Prov. 17).

Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace”; and by “daughters of Jerusalem” she means faithful souls, whom above she called young women. Their zeal and highest purpose is to be able to please God alone, who, according to the apostle Paul (Eph. 2), “is our peace and made both one.”

Let the holy Church therefore say: “O daughters of Jerusalem, that is, O faithful souls who constantly desire to see God, who is our peace, do not be disturbed; do not wonder that I am black in the suffering of my martyrs. Rather, rejoice and be glad, because I am beautiful in receiving eternal rewards. I am black indeed and mourn because of the present persecutions inflicted upon me by heretics and evil Christians; but I am beautiful and rejoice, knowing that through many tribulations I must enter the kingdom of God.” [Col. 0562C–0563A]

She now adds a comparison of her blackness and beauty, saying: “I am black as the tents of Kedar, and beautiful as the skin of Solomon.” Kedar was the son of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, and Kedar is interpreted “darkness.” It is reported of him that he endured the greatest persecution from his neighbours and, constantly moving his tents from place to place, fled. This fittingly corresponds to the holy Church, which, set amid the darkness of afflictions and the persecutions of adversaries, says: “We do not have here an abiding city, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13).

The same Church complains concerning these adversaries, saying in the Psalms that “they hated me without cause” (Ps. 24; John 15). But concerning the skin of Solomon, I do not recall finding anything written except in this passage alone, neither in the New nor in the Old Testament. Therefore a great question arises for us. Yet we should know that what is found in the divine writings only with such difficulty and obscurity that it is scarcely understood is not without a great mystery. Unless we understand the whole from a part, we shall certainly derive no spiritual understanding in this passage.

For it is the custom of sacred Scripture sometimes to take the whole from a part, sometimes a part from the whole. This is what we must do here. We read in the Book of Kings [328] that in his time Solomon, a most powerful king, assembled all Israel and proceeded with great display to Gibeon, because there was the greater high place (1 Kings 3), and the tabernacle which the Lord had commanded to be made through Moses his servant when the children of Israel left Egypt. [Col. 0563A–C]

That tabernacle was made in the image and likeness of a certain spiritual and heavenly tabernacle shown on the mountain to Moses, the servant of God. Thus the Lord further says to Moses: “See that you make the tabernacle according to the pattern of that tabernacle which you saw on the mountain” (Exod. 25). The earthly tabernacle, therefore, was made after the pattern of the heavenly tabernacle.

David testifies that the tabernacle established by Moses was made of skins, when he said to Nathan the prophet: “Do you see that I dwell in a cedar house, while the ark of God is in the midst of skins?” (1 Chron. 17), that is, in a tabernacle made of skins.

Whom, then, did Solomon—whose name is interpreted “peaceful”—signify except Christ, of whom Paul says that by his blood he made peace with the things in heaven and the things on earth? And what does it mean that Solomon went to Gibeon with all Israel, except that Christ ascended into heaven with those whom he drew out from the underworld? Hence David says: “Christ ascending on high led captivity captive” (Ps. 67).

What is that greater high place except the knowledge of the supreme and incomprehensible Trinity? For we cannot ascend to a higher height than to know that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are from eternity, as they are, one true God. [Col. 0563C–0564A]

Of what was that tabernacle, constructed from the skins of dead animals, a figure, except the present Church, founded and established by our holy fathers—the prophets and apostles? Therefore, by “the skin of Solomon” we must spiritually understand the entire tabernacle made of skins, that is, the whole from a part. Otherwise we shall find no spiritual understanding whatever in this expression.

Let the Bride, that is, the holy Church, therefore say: “I am black as the tents of Kedar: that is, just as Kedar once suffered persecution from his neighbours, so I suffer daily attack from heretics and false Christians. But I am beautiful as Solomon’s skin: that is, as Solomon’s tabernacle, constructed from skins, which shone with inestimable and incomparable brightness because of the many gold and silver ornaments it contained within.

“Do not look upon me because I am dark,” that is, do not despise me because of the countless oppressions I endure from adversaries, because for them I await heavenly glory from the eternal Judge on the day of judgment. “Because the sun has discoloured me”: therefore, she says, you should not regard me with contempt if I appear dark—that is, black—amid tribulations, because the sun has discoloured me; that is, because for Christ’s sake, who is the Sun of righteousness, I gladly embrace and suffer these things. I know with certainty that the more humble and abased I am in this world for his love, the more glorious and acceptable I shall be before his majesty in eternal blessedness. [Col. 0564A–C]

“The sons of my mother fought against me.” Where a sick person suffers greater pain, there he is more often compelled to apply his hand. The holy Church seems to do this in repeatedly complaining of heretics and false Christians, saying: “The sons of my mother fought against me.” The mother of the holy Church is the grace of the Holy Spirit, from which heretics and false Christians were regenerated in holy baptism; yet they fight against that same Church in words, deeds, and wicked teachings. Of them John says in his Epistles: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2). Hence Paul says: “I know that after my departure grievous wolves will enter among you, not sparing you” (Acts 20).

“They placed me as a keeper in the vineyards.” Here the holy Church speaks in the person of the holy apostles, who were clearly made planters and keepers of vineyards—that is, churches gathered from the nations. “My own vineyard I have not kept”: that is, we abandoned the synagogue from which we were born, because of its unbelief and blindness of heart, and passed over to the nations, who received the word of God with joy. Thus Paul says to the Jews: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts 13). Therefore the apostles were set as keepers in the vineyards of the nations when they were told: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. 28). But then they did not keep their own vineyard, when the faithless Jews expelled them from the synagogue, threatening them not to speak to anyone in the name of Jesus (Acts 4). [Col. 0564C–0565A]

RECAPITULATION FROM THE PRECEDING MATERIAL: HOW THE STATEMENT, “I AM BLACK, BUT BEAUTIFUL,” IS TO BE REFERRED TO THE PERSON OF CHRIST.

This sentence—namely, “I am black, but beautiful”—may reasonably, in a sound interpretation, be referred to the flesh of Christ hanging upon the cross, as though saying: “O daughters of Jerusalem,” that is, “O faithful souls, I am indeed black because of the pain of the Passion now at hand and of the most grievous death [Col. 0565B]; but shortly I shall be beautiful and comely because of the glorious Resurrection and the wonderful Ascension.” Hence Paul says: “We see Jesus, for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour” (Heb. II).

“Like the tents of Kedar”: that is, just as Kedar was formerly persecuted by his neighbours, so also the Jews—my friends and my neighbours—stood against me and raised their voice against me, crying: “Crucify him” (Luke XXIII; John XIX). Jeremiah the prophet had also prophesied this long beforehand in the person of Christ, saying: “My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; it has raised its voice against me” (Jer. XII). It is reported of the lion that it goes about the forest [Col. 0565C] in which it dwells, roaring; and it does this so that the animals remaining within the forest may have no opportunity to come out, in order that afterwards it may more easily inflict death upon whichever animal it wishes.

This may quite fittingly and appropriately be applied to the Jewish people, who, like a lion going about the whole forest of this world, say: “You see that we are gaining nothing; behold, the whole world is going after him. If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him” (John XII). This Jewish people also raised their voice against Christ when they cried to Pilate: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John XIX); and immediately added why they said this: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die” (ibid.).

Therefore, by Kedar, which is interpreted “darkness,” we should understand the darkness of death; but by Solomon’s skin [Col. 0565D] we should understand the glory of the Resurrection. Let Christ’s flesh hanging upon the cross therefore say: “I am black like the tents of Kedar, but beautiful like Solomon’s skin”; that is, they may seem able to bring upon me the darkness of death, but they cannot take away the glory of the Resurrection.

“Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me.” That is: Do not look at me in the calamity and misery in which I now hang upon the cross for you; rather, look upon me already made glorious by the Resurrection and coming in my majesty for judgment. “Because the sun has discoloured me”: that is, because the Sun of righteousness, who dwells in me, willed that I should thus be darkened through death, and after the Resurrection will make me glorious with incomparable glory. Hence the same Son says in the Gospel: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had [Col. 0566A] before the world was made” (John XVII).

“The sons of my mother fought against me.” The mother of Christ according to the flesh was the Synagogue, since it too derived its origin through the patriarchs and kings, and through blessed Mary. How the Jews, who are the sons of his mother—that is, of the Synagogue—fought against him in the Passion, the Psalmist attests, saying: “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI).

“They made me a keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.” It is plain that the faithless Jews persecuted Christ both living and dead, so far as even to guard his tomb with vain anxiety; and the more they drove him away from themselves by cruelty, the more they sent him on to the Gentiles, who were to believe [Col. 0566B] in him. “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts,” as Isaiah says, “is the house of Israel” (Isa. V). Therefore the Jews made Christ keeper in the vineyards of the Gentiles when, refusing to believe in him, they expelled him from their hearts. And Christ then did not keep his own vineyard when, compelled by their faithlessness, he abandoned them. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke XIII).

## Recapitulation of What Precedes: How This Sentence, Namely “I Am Black, but Beautiful,” Should Be Referred Allegorically to Our Nature

I think, therefore, that we do no wrong if we refer this saying, “I am black, but beautiful,” allegorically to our nature [Col. 0566C]. For the spiritual person understands all things spiritually. Let our nature therefore say—not existing in the state in which it was created by the supreme Creator, but rather in that state in which it remained after being deceived by the devil:

“I am black because of the disobedience and sin of my first father Adam; but I shall become beautiful because of the obedience and justification of the second Adam, namely Christ my Redeemer.” Hence Paul says: “As through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one righteous man many shall be made righteous” (Rom. V).

“Like the tents of Kedar”: that is, just as Kedar was formerly made unstable because of the persecution which he suffered from his neighbours, so from now on I shall be unstable and shall never remain in the same condition, because of the proud hope of empty glory which the devil falsely promised me when he persuaded me to believe him, saying: “If you eat of the forbidden fruit, your eyes shall be opened and you shall be like gods” (Gen. III).

“Like Solomon’s skin.” The Catholic Church firmly holds and believes that blessed Mary, who remained ever an inviolate virgin, drew her origin from our corrupted nature and sinful mass. This blessed Virgin became not only the skin, but also the tabernacle of Solomon—that is, of Christ the true peacemaker—when Christ himself deigned to be born from her for the [p. 330] salvation of the human race. Let our nature therefore say: “Through the first Adam, a sinner, I was made black; but through the second Adam, my Redeemer, I shall become beautiful [Col. 0567A]. I am black because I believed the devil more than God; but I shall become beautiful because the Son of God will take flesh from me and will restore me to the contemplation of the glory of the divine majesty. From the state in which I was created, I would have passed to that glory without the pain of death, had I not been miserably fallen through being deceived by the devil’s empty hope.”

“Do not look upon me because I am dark”: that is, do not contemplate me as I became when the ancient enemy persuaded me; rather contemplate me as I was created by the supreme Creator.

“Because the sun discoloured me.” If by “sun” we understand temptation, we have a true and well-established sense. For the Lord says in the Gospel concerning seeds sown upon rock—that is, concerning unbelieving Christians and perverse heretics—that “when the sun had risen, they withered” (Luke VIII); that is, when temptation arose, they failed in faith and conduct. Finally, it is written in the book of Psalms: “By day the sun shall not burn you” (Ps. CXX); that is, in prosperity no temptation will deceive you.

Let our nature therefore say: “Because the sun discoloured me”: that is, the temptation brought by the devil took away from me the colour of immortality and innocence and discoloured me with the colour of death and the blackness of sin.

“The sons of my mother fought against me.” The mother of our nature and of the angelic nature is the most merciful grace of God the Creator, from whom human beings and angels were wonderfully created, as is said in Genesis: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I); that is, in himself, who is the beginning of all creatures, God created the angelic and earthly [Col. 0567C] natures. Those angels withdrew from that angelic nature through pride and became apostates; afterwards, having become demons, they fought against our nature in Paradise through the serpent. Our nature rightly complains of them in this passage, saying: “The sons of my mother fought against me”; as though it said: “Those who were mercifully created with me by the supreme Creator cruelly drove me out of the Paradise in which I had been placed, through the serpent’s suggestion.”

“They made me a keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.” We may interpret this saying according to the passage written in Genesis: “The Lord had planted a Paradise of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed, to work it and keep it” (Gen. II). Our nature was placed, as it were, as a keeper in vineyards when God sent the first man into Paradise, planted with trees of diverse kinds, so that by thinking and speaking what pleased God he might work there and keep himself, lest he be deceived by the devil [Col. 0567D]. Our nature was made ruler, as it were, over the vineyards of Paradise when it heard from the Lord: “Eat from every tree of Paradise, but do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (ibid.). Yet because our nature did not keep this obedience, but subjected itself to the devil through disobedience, it consequently lost the vineyards of Paradise over which it had been set, and kept itself badly—that is, its own vineyard.

## Recapitulation of What Precedes, According to the Moral Sense

Since, with God’s help, we have expounded a threefold allegory of this sentence, it remains now, with his help, to bring to light the moral meaning hidden in it and reasonably apply it to ourselves—that is, to our soul.

Let our soul also, worn out by diverse and innumerable temptations, surrounded by thorns and stings, by the calamities and miseries of its flesh, weighed down by the putrefaction and corruption of its flesh or body, say: “I am black because ‘the flesh lusts against the spirit’ (Gal. V), and my body unceasingly draws me into sin” (Rom. VI). “I am black,” it says, “because I see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind and [Col. 0568B] leading me captive into the law of sin.”

It has now indicated how it is black, namely, “like the tents of Kedar.” That is: I am sluggish and unstable in what is good, but inclined and fickle toward evil. The Psalmist laments over this Kedar when he says: “Woe is me, because I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (Ps. CXL), that is, with those who love darkness and are unstable in mind and body.

Hence the Lord speaks to Ezekiel, saying: “Son of man, you dwell among scorpions” (Ezek. II). The Lord called his prophet “son of man” so that the prophet might not become proud on that account and fall into empty glory because his God spoke to him. A scorpion has a gentle and mild appearance, but usually strikes from behind with the curved wound of its tail. Who then are these scorpions but deceptive human beings, demons, vices of the flesh, our lusts, and pleasures? For all these things, like scorpions, show us a pleasant and most sweet appearance when they attract us to sin by giving delight; but afterwards they strike from behind like a tail and kill us, because, since we gave them consent for sinning, on the last day of judgment we shall incur the torments of hell with all these things, without remedy. This, surely, is what it means for scorpions to strike and kill with the tail.

Those whom Ezekiel calls scorpions, David in the Psalms and Solomon in the Song of Songs call Kedar. But you also, whoever you are, standing in the Church of God and praying or chanting psalms: whenever you wander in mind and soul throughout the whole [Col. 0568D] world and are inwardly devastated by unclean, foul, and shameful thoughts, know that you dwell with the inhabitants of Kedar.

And what follows in the same verse is very much to be feared: “My soul has been a sojourner for a long time” (Ps. CXL); that is, my soul has for a very long time taken delight with the inhabitants of Kedar—that is, with vices and lusts, with pleasures and unclean desires. All these are Kedar, that is, darkness, because they make a person dark. Hence Paul says: “You were once darkness,” that is, sinners; “but now light,” that is, righteous persons, “in the Lord” (Eph. V).

“But I am beautiful like Solomon’s skin.” A little above it gave the comparison, namely the tents of Kedar, to which it likened itself in saying: “I am black like the tents of Kedar [Col. 0569A].” Now, however, it supplies the corresponding comparison, namely Solomon’s skin, to which it likened itself in beauty, saying: “But I am beautiful like Solomon’s skin.” By this skin of Solomon, we said above, the entire tabernacle is signified, which was constructed of skins. But we must say something concerning it according to the moral sense.

“The tabernacle was constructed of red-dyed skins, hyacinth-coloured skins, and goat-hair cloths” (Exod. XXVI). By the red-dyed skins we understand martyrs, who shed their blood for God; by the hyacinth-coloured skins we understand confessors, who laboured throughout the course of their lives for love of the heavenly homeland; and by the goat-hair cloths we understand sinners. Therefore, if our soul wishes to be God’s tabernacle, let it possess within itself the charity of martyrs, the faith of confessors, and the hope of sinners. For amid adversities and prosperities it must have the courage and patience of martyrs; in good works, the perseverance and long-suffering of confessors; and the penitence and humble confession of sinners.

Moreover, it is good for our soul that it should itself be spiritually the ark of the Covenant which was in God’s tabernacle. The ark was made square from incorruptible wood, overlaid with the finest and most precious gold, and set upon two poles by which it was carried (Exod. XXV). Therefore, if our soul imitates the examples of the saints, who are the incorruptible woods; retains in memory the four Gospels, signified by the square form of the ark; applies itself to spiritual wisdom, signified by gold; and spiritually understands the Old and New Testaments, figuratively denoted by the two poles [Col. 0569C], then our soul will be a spiritual ark in the tabernacle of God.

Finally, in the tabernacle there was an urn containing heavenly manna, the two tablets of the Covenant, and Aaron’s rod which blossomed (III Kings VIII; Heb. IX). We must possess all these things spiritually: that is, we must have the urn containing heavenly manna, so that we may believe Christ to be both true God and true man. For by the urn his humanity is understood, but by the heavenly manna his divinity. Likewise, the two tablets of the Covenant are necessary to us, so that after we have perfectly believed concerning Christ that he is true God and true man, we may hold a sound and Catholic understanding concerning the Father [Col. 0569D] and the Holy Spirit, who are signified by the two tablets: believing that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.

When, therefore, we have confessed the Holy Trinity—that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—to be one God, I think it necessary that we should hold the Catholic faith concerning the humanity of Christ, which he took in blessed Mary and which is shown by Aaron’s rod. Namely, we must believe without doubt that, just as that rod blossomed and bore fruit without cultivation by human aid, so blessed Virgin Mary conceived and bore the Son of God from the Holy Spirit without human contact.

Therefore, if our soul is God’s spiritual tabernacle, and spiritually contains within itself the ark, urn, tablets, and Aaron’s rod, then it will be able truly to say: “I am beautiful like Solomon’s skin [Col. 0570A].”

“Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me.” When, for love of God and with the heavenly homeland in view, we preach the Gospel to our hearers, if perhaps through our own speech we incur empty glory—whether because we speak well or because we are gladly heard by the people—then our soul, darkened by the infection of empty glory, ought to say: “Do not look upon me because I am dark”; that is, do not despise me because I have sinned, since I incurred the fall of empty glory through love of Christ. This does not mean that he is pleased if I have done wrong in his work; rather, unless I had undertaken the office of preaching for love of him, I would never have reached this stain of sin.

Or indeed: “Do not look upon me because I am dark”; that is, do not judge me to be sinful by my nature, for I was created by the supreme God without the stain of sin. If I now appear sinful in the present, I do not possess this naturally from myself, but because it pleased the Sun of righteousness—that is, God—who, according to his just will, sent me into this sinful flesh. Through dwelling in it, my nature contracted sin, though it had previously been created without sin’s stain by the good Creator.

For just as good wine, when poured into a corrupted vessel, is immediately spoiled—not because it has by nature the property of becoming spoiled, but because it is spoiled through participation in the corrupt vessel into which it has been poured—so our soul is not sinful and corrupt by nature; rather, through participation in the corrupt body in which it is placed, though incorruptible by nature, it becomes accidentally corrupt [Col. 0570C]. Certainly, no one knows how this happens; but because it so pleases God, it has pleased him from the beginning—he who from eternity has ordered all things blamelessly in his holy dispensation. And this is what follows: “Because the sun has discoloured me.”

“The sons of my mother fought against me.” Allegorically, the sons of our soul’s mother may be called the five senses of the flesh: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. By these the human body is ruled and governed, just as a mother is supported and aided by her children. How these sons of the flesh fight against the soul in daily conflict may be shown by sufficiently convincing experience.

Does not sight fight against the soul when the eye sees a woman in order to desire her [Col. 0570D]? Hence Jeremiah says: “My eyes have plundered my soul” (Lam. III). Truly unhappy eyes plunder and assail the wretched soul when they report inwardly to it the unlawful things which they see outwardly and strive to take from it that simple chastity by which our soul is intimately united to God.

Anyone can readily show the conflict which our hearing continually wages against the soul. For whatever we hear that is sinful and discordant with the good of true religion undoubtedly wounds our soul. What then shall I say of smell, which sends to the soul all that it draws inwardly from the outward breath? While it infects the soul with outward delights, it weakens and kills it as though by wounds inflicted.

Let Solomon, when questioned, answer how our mouth kills the soul by lying; for he says: “A lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. I). David indeed testifies to this, saying in the book of Psalms: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. V). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “By your mouth you will be justified, and by your mouth you will be condemned” (Matt. XII). Therefore, according to the Lord’s saying, our mouth condemns us by speaking and eating unlawful things. But if we eat what is necessary to us and say what pleases God, then our mouth justifies us.

By what weapons touch assails the soul, Christ’s soldiers know, who daily wage the Lord’s spiritual battles. Hence Holy Scripture testifies: “As one who touches pitch is defiled by it, so one who touches his neighbour’s wife is made altogether unclean” (Ecclus. XIII). Let our soul therefore say: “The sons of my mother fought against me”; that is, the five senses which rule in the flesh assault me in unceasing warfare, and because, while I am in the flesh, I must make use of their assistance, I am wholly unable to pass even one hour of the day without their conflict [Col. 0571B].

“They made me a keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.” It is plain, and no one living religiously doubts, that the more diligently any person keeps watch over the actions of others which need guarding, the less carefully he sometimes observes his own actions. Blessed Gregory testifies in his writings that our actions are called vineyards [Col. 0571C].

Let our soul therefore say: “They made me a keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.” That is to say: While I desire to watch over and correct the actions of my neighbours, I give less diligent care to my own actions. For even those who guard the temporal vineyards of this world often encounter the dangers of blowing winds and rushing rains; nor do they fear, for the sake of guarding those vineyards, to suffer loss to their own bodies, because they love the temporal rewards which they think they may receive from the lords of the vineyards.

Thus, indeed, thus do the prelates of the holy Church. When they serve in gathering souls through preaching, they sometimes take less care of themselves than is necessary; and not infrequently they willingly accept bodily death from persecutors for the sake of their preaching itself, because they set before their eyes the eternal rewards which they await from God. This, certainly, is what the apostles and martyrs did [Col. 0571D].

## How This Sentence, “I Am Black, but Beautiful,” Is Ascribed to Blessed Mary

Therefore, after bringing to light, with God’s help, the threefold allegory and the simple moral sense of this sentence, it is fitting that we direct our pen to the person of blessed Virgin Mary. For we do not doubt that this whole book, composed by the Holy Spirit through Solomon’s mouth, was written in her praise and for the honour of the holy Church.

Let blessed Mary herself therefore say: “I am black, but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem”; that is: “I, daughter of the heavenly Jerusalem which is above, our mother [Col. 0572A] (Gal. IV), am black in the present world—that is, contemptible, despised, and consumed with sorrow—while I see my son crucified through the envy of the Jews and drenched in his blood. I am black, I say, because of present grief, since the anguish of my son reaches even to the pain of my own heart.”

Hence Simeon said to blessed Mary: “A sword shall pierce your own soul also” (Luke II); as though he said: “The pain of Christ your Son’s Passion and death will reach and wound the innermost chambers of your heart; and thus you will prove yourself to be his true mother, when you compassionately suffer with him as he dies on the cross with the inmost affection of your heart.”

Let blessed Mary therefore say: “I am black through pain and grief because I see my son dying upon the cross; but I am beautiful”—that is, “I rejoice and exult because I consider him now about to rise from death [Col. 0572B]. I am black like the tents of Kedar, but beautiful like Solomon’s skin.”

By the tents, which change from place to place as they are carried, is understood the transitory and changing sorrow of this present life; but by the skin—that is, Solomon’s tabernacle—is signified the heavenly glory in which God dwells. Let blessed Mary therefore say: “I am now afflicted with transitory and temporal grief for my son’s death; but shortly I shall rejoice with him as he rises, ascends to heaven, and reigns in heavenly glory.”

“Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me”: that is, do not hold me in contempt or despise me because you see me afflicted in the present tribulation, since I, O Jews, am troubled and afflicted on account of my son, who is the Sun of righteousness and whom you killed. Or indeed, do not look upon me as blackened by calamity and misery because of my son’s death; rather consider me already placed at his right hand and reigning with him in eternal brightness [Col. 0572C].

“The sons of my mother fought against me.” Spiritually, the sons of the mother of blessed and perpetual Virgin Mary were the wicked Jews, who were sons of the Synagogue; and they fought mercilessly against her when they killed her son upon the cross. For she was by no means free from the pain and Passion which her Son endured upon the cross. Moreover, it must be believed that the anguish of Christ’s death as he died upon the cross reached even to the inward parts of his most loving Mother; nor could she look upon him hanging upon the cross except with great sorrow, since she knew that he was both true God and had truly assumed flesh from her flesh.

“They made me a keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.” “Exult and praise, O dwelling-place of Zion” (Isa. XII): that is, O Church gathered from the Gentiles, which is guarded and governed by so great a guardian. Rejoice, I say, because the Queen of heaven and Lady of the angels has been appointed your keeper. For you are the spiritual vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth—that is, of hosts. Over you has been set the guardian who is empress of the world and exalted above the choirs of angels.

Of her it is rightly said that she did not keep her own vineyard, and that she abandoned the Synagogue because of the faithlessness and pride of the Jews. She might indeed seem to have been bound to guard it with carnal affection and foster it with the aid of her prayers, because she is known to have derived her carnal origin from it [Col. 0573A]. Yet because that Synagogue—that is, the faithless Jews—despised her as though she were their sister and were unwilling to honour her, by God’s just judgment they shall lack her intercession and aid in this world and on the day of judgment.

“You therefore, Jerusalem, praise the Lord; and praise your God, O Zion” (Ps. CXLVII): that is, O Church of the Gentiles, which are spiritually called Jerusalem and Zion because you are shown to cleave, by faith and works, to God, who is supreme peace; and, standing upon the watchtower—that is, in the height of spiritual life—you behold your enemies from afar. Praise God, I say, O Church [Col. 0574A], who has given you so great an advocate, namely his own glorious mother. The Jews despise her because they say that according to the flesh she was their sister.

Therefore, having driven Jewish faithlessness and impiety from our hearts, let us honour and magnify with due praise the Mother of our Redeemer. Let us know this for certain: the honour, praise, glory, and magnificence which we render to his mother on earth will make him well-disposed toward us in heaven, and gracious in his majesty when he comes for judgment with angels and archangels.

[Col. 0573] Here ends the sixth volume.

## The Seventh Volume Begins, on the Saying: “Tell Me, You Whom My Soul Loves, Where You Pasture, Where You Rest at Midday, Lest I Begin to Wander after the Flocks of Your Companions” (Cant. I)

[Col. 0573B] Among the twelve precious stones, whoever wishes to discover the topaz, more precious than the other stones, must naturally know the sizes and colours of all the stones, lest, led astray by error, he indiscriminately take one for another. For among the twelve there are two stones somewhat similar to topaz, namely chrysolite and chrysoprase, which seem golden in colour, as topaz is. Yet topaz differs from the other stones in this: it is rarer to find and, as is said, shines with every colour.

This stone is found in Ethiopia and in the region of the Thebaid; and it is reported that in the same province there is an island called Topazion, where this topaz stone is found. That topaz comes from Ethiopia the Lord makes known when speaking to blessed Job. For when the Lord spoke to Job concerning wisdom, he said: “The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equal to it” (Job XXVI).

Who, then, are the twelve precious stones, if not the twelve apostles founded upon the foundation which is Christ? And whom else does the topaz, rarer and more precious than the other stones, signify except our Lord Jesus Christ, who is “more beautiful in form than the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV) and is humbler than all human beings? Thus he himself is reported to have said to his disciples in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. XI).

Hence it is rightly said that topaz shines with every colour, because “in him dwells all the fullness of divinity” (Col. II), and he is adorned with the ornament of every spiritual virtue; for according to John, “We saw him as the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I) [Col. 0573D].

Moreover, that this same topaz stone gave its name to the island where it is found, so that the island is called Topazion after topaz, is believed not to have happened without a great mystery. For just as Christ is understood by topaz, so the holy Church is understood by this island. And just as this island received its name from the topaz stone and is called Topazion after it, so the holy Church has been named Christian after Christ, the cornerstone, and all faithful Christians delight in being marked by Christ’s name.

Certainly, in comparing the holy Church to an island, we speak in accordance with the prophet Isaiah, who by the spirit of prophecy calls all Churches islands, saying: “Listen, islands, and give heed, peoples from afar” (Isa. XLIX). The Churches of the Gentiles are rightly compared to islands because, just as islands are beaten by gusts of wind and often shaken by the tumult of rushing waves, so Churches dispersed through diverse regions of the world are oppressed by great persecutions and agitated by innumerable temptations.

Moreover, that, according to the saying of the Lord speaking to Job, topaz is said to be found in Ethiopia, and that this same topaz is in no way equal to wisdom, is very suitably applied to the Lord Jesus. By wisdom Christ’s divinity is understood; by topaz, fittingly, his humanity. This topaz is taken from Ethiopian soil because his humanity is assumed from our sinful and dark nature; and we cannot compare his humanity to his divinity, because according to his divinity he is equal to the Father, but according to his humanity he is less than the Father [Note: [Col. 0573D] Athanasius, in the Creed.].

The Son himself makes this known in the Gospel, saying: “I and the Father are one” (John X), which pertains to his divinity; and elsewhere: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV) [Col. 0574D], which pertains to his humanity. Hence David the prophet also testifies in the Psalms: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. VIII). The Son of God was made a little lower than the angels because, though he was immortal and invisible God, for us he became mortal and visible man. And because, by the command of his Father, he humbled himself so greatly for the salvation of humankind, he therefore received from that same Father the name which is above every name, so that at his name every knee should bend, and that by every creature in heaven and on earth (Phil. II) he should be worshipped as one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

And this is what follows in this verse: “You crowned him with glory and honour, O Lord, and set him over the works of your hands” (Ps. VIII).

Accordingly, after this brief distinction which we have made, let us now return to that from which we had wandered rather far, and with the attentive ear of the heart hear what the Bride says to the Bridegroom, the Church to Christ: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you rest at noon,” etc. As though she said: You are a topaz; you are a precious stone. It is you whom I seek, you whom I desire, you whom I love above all things. Show me yourself, because among so many precious stones I cannot find you; and this is what follows: [Col. 0575B] “Lest perhaps I begin to wander among the flocks of your companions,” seeking you in the way that those once wandered and went astray, of whom the Lord said in the Gospel: “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” The disciples replied: “Some, Elijah; others, Jeremiah; or one of the prophets” (Matt. XVI).

All these, therefore, began to wander after the flock of the companions—that is, they wandered among precious stones while seeking topaz. They wished to take chrysolite or chrysoprase for topaz, because in some respect they resemble it, being, like it, golden in colour. For they had heard that the prophets had worked miracles as Christ did; this was to be golden in colour like topaz. But Peter, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, leaving the other stones behind, [Col. 0575C] recognized the true topaz when he said: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid.). It was as though he said: Certainly the prophets were men of great authority in their own time—that is, they shone like precious stones in the glory of miracles—yet they were in no way what you are, the Son of God.

Let us therefore, setting aside the tumult of worldly concerns, hear the prayer in which the holy Church beseeches Christ to deign to make himself known to her by sure signs, lest she should perhaps—God forbid!—adore and worship one of the saints in his place and, led astray by an error of her simplicity, fall into idolatry. Let us next consider what Christ answers the holy Church, and how [he] removes from all saints the worship belonging to divinity alone, and assigns it to God alone, to whom it is rightly due. For we ought [Col. 0575D] to honour the saints, not adore them. God alone, however, is to be adored and honoured; the saints, for love of him, are only to be honoured, not adored.

Let Christ therefore say to the holy Church: You ask me to assure you, with every ambiguity removed, where—that is, in what place—I pasture or recline; and I shall answer you that I pasture and recline at noon—that is, I rest and remain in my Father, in whom from eternity I have remained equal to him in all things. That the Son remains ineffably and eternally in the Father, and the Father in the Son, is proclaimed with one harmonious voice by the whole authority of both the New and the Old Testament. Hence the Lord says to the Father concerning his disciples: “Father, I desire that, as you are in me and I in you, so they too may be one in [Col. 0576A] us” (John XVII). And elsewhere the Lord says to Philip: “Philip, whoever sees me sees my Father. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John XIV). “Otherwise, believe because of the works themselves.”

Since, then, by the authority of the divine Scriptures we have sufficiently shown how the Son remains in the Father—that is, how Christ reclines and pastures at noon—it remains for us to show where in the divine utterances God the Father is called noon. This is found rarely—indeed, most rarely—and the rarer it is, the more precious. Almighty God, “the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation” (II Cor. I), to whom the evils we do displease and the good things we do please, himself speaks in the prophet Isaiah, [Col. 0576B] saying: “I shall rest in my place and shall consider, as the noonday light” (Isa. XVIII).

What, then, does he mean when he says, “I shall rest in my place”? When did he labour, that he should now seek rest? And why does he compare himself with the noonday light rather than with a breeze or another hour of the day? Further, what does he mean when he says, “I shall consider,” since considering belongs to one who either does not know or does not understand a matter? For he knows and understands all things before they come to pass.

What then is God’s rest, unless it is peace in the heart of the faithful and devout Christian? Thus it is written: “In peace, in that same place, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. IV). And in Isaiah we find the Lord saying: “This is my rest: refresh the fallen one” (Isa. XXVIII). We therefore give great rest to our God when we exhort a fallen sinner to turn from [Col. 0576C] his sin. Elsewhere Scripture says: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet man who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI).

But what is God’s place except peace and justice, devotion and mercy, and obedience, the mother of all virtues? Hence the prophet David says: “His place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. LXXV). Zion, indeed, is interpreted as “watchtower.” A watchtower is a high place, from which a man, if stationed there, can see very far beyond himself. Therefore by Zion, which is interpreted “watchtower,” is understood obedience, the begetter of all virtues. If anyone deserves to persevere in it until the final day of his life, without doubt he will be able to attain to the contemplation [Col. 0576D] of the brightness of the divine majesty. For divine Scripture says thus concerning obedience: “Through obedience one arrives at knowledge of God’s hidden things.”

But what does God the Father behold, except what, according to the prophet Job (ch. XXXI), he himself does—namely, he counts all our steps, that is, our deeds—in order that after death he may render to each of us according to what he has done? Thus the apostle Paul says: “We must all be manifested before the judgment-seat of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V). Blessed Augustine likewise says: As we now stand in the Church and see one another present, so on the day of judgment we shall stand before God’s judgment-seat. For we shall then have this same soul [Col. 0577A] which we now have, and we shall be raised in this very body in which we are now clothed. We were not made like horses and oxen, to perish in eternal death; rather, after we have lived here, we shall be judged elsewhere, so that we may receive either eternal rewards for good works or everlasting punishments for our sins.

Hence the Prophet also says: “God has spoken once” (Ps. LXI), that is, from eternity he has established and predestined immovably. What? “These two things I have heard” (ibid.). What are they? All “power belongs to God” (ibid.), the almighty Father. Here you have one. “And to you, Lord Jesus Christ, belongs mercy.” Here you have the other. For you will render to each person on the day of judgment according to his works (Rev. XXII). But that judgment belongs to the Son and not to the Father, hear him himself saying in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V).

Almighty God the Father therefore beholds in his place, as the noonday light, everything that we do in this world, in order through his Son to render to us on the day of judgment according to what we have deserved. Hence it is written: “The Most High God is a patient requiter” (Eccles. V). And God is rightly called Most High, because no thing is comparable to his sublimity. Divine Scripture calls God a patient requiter because, while he patiently awaits sinners so that they may turn, he finally condemns more harshly those who do not turn.

But let us now consider why Almighty God compared himself with noonday brightness, and why [Col. 0577C] he who is the Creator of all creatures likened himself to his creature—that is, to the brightness of the sun. For among all creatures he could find, in relation to us, no creature brighter than the sun. Therefore, just as the sun surpasses and shines above all the elements and lights of this world in dignity and brightness, so Almighty God appears worthier and more eminent than all things which he created for the praise and glory of his name. And just as the sun, at the burning hour of noon, spreads its rays everywhere and illuminates the whole world with the wonder of its brightness, so every creature, considering God Almighty’s omnipotence and mercy, trembles and adores him.

Of this mercy the Psalmist says: “The earth is full of the Lord’s mercy” (Ps. XXXII); and again: [Col. 0577D] “I shall sing the mercies of the Lord for ever” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Truly the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy, because every creature living in it has received its continued existence not from its own merit but from God’s mercy. And the same Psalmist rightly says that he will sing the mercies of the Lord for ever, because both our good work here and our introduction after death into the joys of paradise proceed wholly from the mercy of God: he created us when we did not exist, and in his mercy saved us when, at the devil’s persuasion, we had been deceived and ruined. According to the apostle Paul (I Cor. II), he also wills no one to perish, but wills all to come to knowledge of himself.

But if it is certain that God wills no one to perish, but [Col. 0578A] all to attain knowledge of his divinity, why do those who perish perish? They perish, surely, because they disdain to obey God’s commandments. Behold, by God’s gift we have shown, as far as we could, from the Gospel words that the Son remains eternally in the Father. And from the utterances of the prophet Isaiah we have set forth the statement in which God the Father calls himself, by comparison, the noonday light.

## CONCLUSION OF THE ARGUMENT

Accordingly, it is certainly established and no one doubts it: if the Father is noon, and if the Son remains in the Father, then without doubt he remains at noon. It is right, therefore, that Christ answer the holy Church and say: You ask me to tell you where I pasture and recline; and I answer you that I pasture [Col. 0578B] and recline at noon—that is, I remain in my Father, who is the true noon, as I have remained from eternity.

## RECAPITULATION OF THE FOREGOING: HOW THIS STATEMENT, NAMELY, “TELL ME,” ETC., SHOULD BE REFERRED TO THE PERSON OF THE FATHER

He who waters the everlasting mountains from his upper chambers, who satisfies and makes drunk the earth lying below with the fruit of his works (Ps. X), is able to give us the spirit of spiritual wisdom, so that, filled with it, we may be able to understand the hidden mysteries in the Scriptures of the divine law which we desire. For just as the eminent prophet Moses (Exod. XIX) once first ascended the mountain and afterwards held familiar discourse with the Lord concerning hidden things, so it is necessary that the holy Church now do the same.

For she climbs, as it were, a great and lofty mountain [Col. 0578C] when, despising all transitory things and transcending herself, she approaches the discourse of her Bridegroom—that is, the Son of God—and asks him, saying: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you rest,” etc. Having therefore ascended the highest mountain—that is, after enjoying the most sweet discourse of the Son of God the Father—it is necessary that she humbly approach God the Father himself and seek from him, with suppliant devotion, where he pastures and where he reclines.

Let us therefore return to the beginning of our discourse and examine carefully what the everlasting mountains are, what the heavenly waterings are, what the earth lying below is, and what the satisfaction and inebriation produced by the fruits of God are. I think that the everlasting mountains should be understood as those of which the Psalmist says to the Lord: [Col. 0578D] “You give light wonderfully from the everlasting mountains” (Ps. LXXV). The everlasting mountains, then, are the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, by whom we have been wonderfully enlightened, because through the examples of the patriarchs, the words of the prophets, and the teaching of the apostles, we came to know the faith of the Christian religion. Formerly we sat far removed from the knowledge of God, in darkness and in the shadow of death. Hence the prophet Isaiah says: “The people of the nations who walked in darkness saw a great light; upon those dwelling in the land of the shadow of death, light arose” (Isa. IX).

Truly a great and wonderful light arose for the peoples of the nations when the faith of Christ was planted and rooted in their hearts through the preaching of the apostles. Thus they began to have Christ dwelling within them, whereas before they received into the lodging-place of their hearts the devil, the most wicked deceiver and most cruel murderer of their souls. Hence Paul also says: “That Christ may dwell in our hearts through faith” (Eph. III). Finally blessed Augustine [Note: [Col. 0579D] *Tractates on John*, vol. 9.] says: “Faith in your heart is Christ in your heart.”

It is therefore clearer than light that unless the light of faith shines in our hearts, we shall sit in the darkness of unbelief and shall in no way have Christ dwelling within us. Of these mountains the Psalmist says: “The high mountains are for the stags; the rock is a refuge for hedgehogs” (Ps. CIII). The apostle Paul teaches that the rock signifies Christ, saying: “And the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X). The high mountains are those who above [Col. 0579B] were called holy mountains—namely, the prophets and apostles.

The habit of stags is said to be that they flee to the mountains when they are pursued by hunters. Everyone knows that hedgehogs are full of prickles and spines. By these two animals two kinds of sinful people, contained within the bosom of the holy Church, are signified. One kind is that which repents and weeps for its sins and, distrusting its own deeds, hopes to attain God’s mercy through the intercessions and prayers of the saints. This kind of people is rightly compared to stags, which flee to the mountains in order to be delivered from death.

The other kind of people is subject to hidden and public sins; and the more it despairingly gives itself over to various crimes, the farther it withdraws from God. Casting aside the fear of God and not fearing to sin before [Col. 0579C] men, it shows itself to be like a hedgehog, full of spines and prickles. Yet at times this kind of people is pierced with compunction at the point of death; considering the weight of its sins, it is grievously tormented in its inner person. Since it does not doubt that it is going to the punishments of eternal torment, touched by divine inspiration it hastens to return to Christ, who is the true rock. Opening to mortals the bosom of clemency and the fountain of devotion and mercy, he cries through his prophet: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII).

The high mountains, therefore, are a refuge for the stags, and the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs, because just as repentant sinners who do good works are saved through intercessions [Col. 0579D] and prayers, so miserable and despairing persons, surrounded by the spines of their sins, are received by Christ, provided that they turn to him at the last hour of their lives. For divine Scripture says: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (ibid.).

Behold, with God’s help we have shown, as far as we could, what the everlasting mountains are. It remains to show what the heavenly waterings are. Moses says: “May my teaching thicken like rain, and my speech flow like dew” (Deut. XXXII). Isaiah likewise says to the Lord: “For your dew is the dew of light” (Isa. XXVI). It is therefore clear that the divine Scriptures are called heavenly waterings, [Col. 0580A] by which the prophets and apostles were watered and made fruitful, as it were, by a heavenly mouth.

The apostle Paul speaks of this watering when he says: “The earth, drinking the rain that comes down upon it and producing a crop useful to those by whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing” (Heb. VI). David again speaks of this heavenly dew, saying: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV). The city of God is the body or soul of the righteous person, which is then made glad more fully when it is pleasantly sprinkled with the flowing streams of divine utterances. Thus David says again: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV).

The house of God is the holy Church; the abundance of that house is divine Scripture, by which the faithful soul is soberly and devoutly made drunk [Col. 0580B] when, lulled into a spiritual ecstasy, it forgets all things of this world and is joined to God alone in purity of mind. The torrent of God’s delight, however, is renunciation of this world. For just as a torrent overwhelms and sweeps away everything placed before it, so the person who perfectly renounces the world despises prosperity and adversity alike, gladly crucifies his flesh with its vices and desires, and has nothing able to delay the purpose of his mind until he can attain him whom he loves above all things and above himself.

Since, therefore, renunciation of this world is a great delight and pleasure to God, it is clear that those who renounce neither themselves nor the desires and lusts of the world prepare in their hearts no pleasure at all acceptable to God. Let the wicked, then, go and abound in this world’s riches; and let them know beyond doubt that the more they serve this world and their own flesh by living wickedly, the farther they withdraw from God and join themselves to the devil, their cruel master. For the apostle John says: [Col. 0580C] “Little children, do not love the world or the things that are in the world; for if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (I John II). These words make it plainly apparent that love of this world removes the love of God from human hearts; and since God is called love, when love is removed from our heart, God too is undoubtedly removed.

Accordingly, now that the everlasting mountains have been shown and the heavenly waterings disclosed, our mind, breathed upon by the dew of the Holy Spirit, will attempt to make clear what that happy and blessed earth is which is satisfied by the fruit of God’s works. But while we are about to speak of earth, let us not go far away from ourselves, because we ourselves are earth. For the Lord says to Adam: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III).

Let us take care, then, lest perhaps—God forbid!—we are that earth which the Lord granted to the serpent as food. For the book of Genesis (ibid.) says that God struck the devil in the serpent with this curse: namely, that he should eat earth all the days of his life because he had by his fraud deceived the man who had been created by God with a [Col. 0581A] straightforward and simple nature. Scripture also attests this, saying: “God made man simple and upright” (Eccles. VII): simple, that he might never do evil; upright, that he might never depart from God himself.

But because our first parent, led on by vain hope, thought that he could obey both God and the devil, he incurred duplicity instead of simplicity. For the uprightness of mind which he had received from God—and by which he ought thereafter to have pleased God alone—he bent toward the knowledge of evil, being coaxed by the blandishments of the woman. By God’s dispensation it came to pass that he lost the state of eternal uprightness; and because, when he could stand, he refused to stand, now, even when he would wish to stand, he cannot stand.

But now let us return to the earth of which we began to speak a little earlier. The earth given to the devil for food was the Jews, who desired to kill the Lord Jesus. To them the Lord himself says: [Col. 0581B] “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to fulfil your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth” (John VIII). It is as though he said: You are the devil’s earth; therefore you desire to be satisfied by the fruit of his works. And because he is proved to be a murderer and never to have stood in the truth, you, following your father, wish to kill me, and in me, who am truth, you neither wish to stand nor to believe.

Let us, then, be that earth which, bearing fruit, received blessing from the Lord, as David says: “The Lord will give goodness, and our earth will give its fruit” (Ps. LXXXIV). The Lord gives goodness to our earth when he inspires in our heart the sweetness of his love, so that for his sake we may gladly endure harsh and bitter things and utterly cast away from ourselves the vices of human flesh which bring the soul to death. The Lord, I say, gives us his goodness when he imparts to our minds knowledge of himself. Drunk, as it were, with a spiritual draught by that knowledge, our minds account the joys of this world as nothing, because, despising the deceptive glory of the age, they strive to attain him whose knowledge is eternal life. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: [Col. 0581C] “This is eternal life: that they may know you, and that your Son whom you sent is the one true God” (John XVII).

But our earth gives its fruit when our mind, caught up in heavenly contemplation, sighs toward God and, forgetting its frailty, desires to become one spirit with him, whom with the sincere love of charity it loves, as is fitting, above all creatures. Our earth, I say, will then give its fruit when our body, through the good works which it now performs, after the end of this frail life and after having been tested by many temptations, gives back its spirit to God, saying with the Psalmist: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Ps. XXX).

The fruit of this flesh will then be doubled in blessed joy, when that same flesh, glorified through the glory of resurrection, is granted eternal blessedness together with its spirit; so that, just as both endured punishments and tribulations for God in this world, so after the day of judgment they may receive with equal joy [Col. 0582A] the dwellings of that highest and incomparable glory promised by God. Of these dwellings the Lord himself says to his disciples: “In my Father’s house there are many dwellings” (John XIV).

Since the intention of our mind, so far as its powers support it, has laboured to show what the earth is which is satisfied by the fruit of God’s works, it remains to speak, for the praise and glory of his name, of God’s works themselves and of the fruit of his works. The works of God, generally or universally, are all creatures, which were created by God himself in most wise order. Concerning this wonderful creation the authority of divine Scripture declares: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Eccles. XVIII). Hence the prophet David says to the Lord: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. [Col. 0582B] CIII).

God indeed made all things in his wisdom, because he created all things ineffably in his Son, who is his wisdom, word, and power. The same prophet, understanding this in the Holy Spirit, declares elsewhere: “And you, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands” (Ps. CI). Here the Prophet calls the Son of God “the beginning,” whom in the preceding psalm he had called God’s wisdom. By heaven and earth, moreover, we ought to understand the things contained in these two elements, since we believe that all creatures made by God exist within the compass of these elements.

They judge that Moses, the most eminent of prophets, understood this in the Holy Spirit when, expounding the creation of the world, he says: “In the beginning [Col. 0582C] God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I). It is as though he said: In his Son, who is the beginning of every creature which he himself made, he created heaven and earth and the things contained in them.

Yet among the other works which Almighty God is believed to have created through his Son, the Son himself is read to have performed a certain wonderful and special work. Concerning this work, the prophet Isaiah, touched by the divine Spirit, declares thus: “His work was foreign to him, so that he might do his own work; first he did the foreign work” (Isa. XXVIII). Since these words of the holy prophet are very obscure, and cannot easily be found in the other prophets, they ought to be weighed by us with careful attention, because so great a prophet did not utter them without the weight of a great mystery.

For these words contain within themselves a vast mystery, covered, as it were, by a veil under the outward bark of the letter. Unless the words are more fully examined, the hidden mystery within cannot be brought to light. What, then, does the prophet mean when he says that the work of the Son of God was foreign to God himself? What does he mean when he says, “In order to do his own work, he first did a foreign work”? Let us seek some example which, once introduced and considered, will more clearly show the hidden mystery which we wish to disclose in this statement.

A certain master says to one of his servants (Matt. XXI): Go first and work in my vineyard; afterwards you shall work in your own vineyard. Know for certain that you shall in no way work in [Col. 0583A] your own vineyard unless you have first worked in mine. Hearing this, the man works in his master’s vineyard and afterwards does work in his own vineyard; thus he first performs a foreign work in order later to perform his own work.

So indeed, so did the Lord Jesus Christ. He first performed a foreign work in order afterwards to perform his own work. To be born, suffer, be crucified, die, and rise again was a work foreign to his divinity. For he is invisible, impassible, and immortal, being coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father and the Holy Spirit. The proper work of the Son of God was the redemption of the human race.
