But unless he had first been born, suffered, died, and risen again, he could in no way redeem from death the human race which had destroyed itself through its free choice.

The Son of God therefore performed a foreign work in order afterwards to perform [Col. 0583B] his own work, because he first endured death, which did not befit his divinity, in order afterwards to redeem the human race, which did befit his divinity. Behold, we have shown, though not as worthily as we should, what the general works of the Father and Son are, and what are those special works of the Son alone, such as suffering death—which does not befit the divinity either of the Son himself or of the Father. Human death pertains only to Christ’s humanity; but the divinity of the Father, of Christ himself, and of the Holy Spirit remains and has remained entirely without experience of death or any suffering.

Let us therefore show what the fruit of God’s works is, with which fruit we, who are earth, ought to be satisfied. We judge this to be the fruit of God’s works: that, considering the works of the Lord himself, who made all things, we praise and glorify them. We should know, I say, that this is the fruit of God’s works: that from contemplating creatures we return thanks and praise as is fitting to their Creator. For from no pre-existing matter he wonderfully created all things that were made; and he first created man from the mud of the earth by ineffable power, and breathed into him the insensible breath of life. Moreover, what is of greater glory and more excellent dignity, he deigned to bestow upon that same man, above other creatures, his image and likeness. For divine Scripture testifies of no creature except man alone (Gen. I) that it was formed or created in the image and likeness of God.

Come then, O man—come, I say—give thanks to the clemency and goodness of your Creator. I beg you, do not be ungrateful for the benefits conferred upon you by him; respond as far as you can to the depths of his charity. If you wish, you can answer him according to your ability, on this condition: if you are willing to obey his commandments which he gave you for your salvation, preserve yourself free from every sin, [Col. 0584A] and persevere in his service to the final end of your life.

You are therefore of great authority and dignity, O man. Almighty God created you in his image; his Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, redeemed you by his blood; you have been graciously enlightened by the Holy Spirit; by the sevenfold grace of that same Holy Spirit you have been instructed in the knowledge of the holy Trinity.

You represent God’s image in yourself so long as you do not sin. But if you ever consent to sin, God’s image departs from you and you become like the devil himself, who by sinning and pride departed from God and irretrievably condemned and destroyed himself—he who had been the seal of the likeness of God’s glory, as the prophet Ezekiel says (ch. XXVIII).

Above we said [Col. 0584B] that, just as Moses once first ascended Mount Sinai and only then held solitary discourse with the Lord about hidden and mystical matters, so the holy Church had done. For she ascended, as it were, a great and lofty mountain when she approached the solitary discourse of her Bridegroom, who is “beautiful in form above the children of men” (Ps. XLIV), and asked him, saying: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you rest,” etc.

Let her therefore approach the solitary discourse of the almighty Father and, putting away from herself the stains of all iniquity, seek from him in a like affection of charity where he reclines and where he pastures. Accordingly, before God the almighty Father speaks with the Bride of his Son, or before the Bride herself deserves to hear from the Father of her Bridegroom: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline [Col. 0584C] your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and then I shall tell you where I pasture or recline”—before this happens, it is necessary for our mind to inquire with watchful attention where in the divine utterances the Son of God is called a mountain. Otherwise our discourse might be charged with falsehood by someone less learned, especially because we have called Christ a mountain and likened him by comparison to Mount Sinai.

Leaving aside many authorities which attest what we say, let one sufficient and suitable authority be brought forward as is fitting. May the spiritual children of grace and friends of the divine law gladly lend it their spiritual ears, and may enemies of truth or persons less wise have nothing to contradict. Daniel the prophet, privy to God’s secrets, is reported, from the abundance of the sweetness of the Holy Spirit, to have recounted the wonderful dream of that great and terrible vision which the king of Babylon had seen. Expounding it, among other things which he declares to him, he interprets Christ as a mountain, saying: “You saw,” etc.

[Col. 0585]

## CONCERNING THE DREAM OF KING NEBUCHADNEZZAR. (G)*
[Col. 0585A] 340 You were looking, O king, and behold, a single statue stood before you, whose appearance was exceedingly terrible. The head of this statue, I say, was of gold; its breast and arms of silver; its belly and thighs of bronze; its legs of iron; and part of its feet was iron and part clay. You continued looking until a stone was cut from a mountain without hands, and struck that statue upon its feet of iron and clay, and shattered it. But this stone which struck the statue, as Daniel says (ch. II), became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.

The stone, then, cut from the mountain without hands, is Christ, who took his origin from the sinful mass of humankind without carnal intercourse. Of this stone it is rightly said that it became a great mountain and filled the whole earth, [Col. 0585B] because the Gospel which the Lord Jesus established and handed over to his disciples to preach filled the whole world, as he himself says to his disciples: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16). Yet this mountain was a little stone when God was known only in Judaea; but this stone becomes a great mountain when “from the rising of the sun to its setting the name of the Lord is praiseworthy” (Ps. 112), and “there is none who can hide himself from its heat” (Ps. 18): that is, from the preaching of the Gospel which was preached through the apostles to the whole world.

The stone, therefore, became a great mountain and filled the whole earth when, according to the prophet Isaiah (ch. IX), he who was born to us as a child and given to us as a son, a star showing the way [Col. 0585C] from heaven, appeared as the exalted God throughout the world. This stone, I say—that is, Christ—grew into a great mountain because all nations which he himself made now come, worship him, and glorify and praise his name forever.

But let us now see what that statue which this stone struck and shattered signifies. For so wonderful a dream and so unusual a vision could by no means have been shown to the king of Babylon without the weight of a great mystery. “Its head,” he says, “was of gold; its breast and arms of silver; its belly and thighs of bronze; its legs of iron; and part of its feet was iron and part clay.” This statue, then, is divided into seven parts and appears to be composed of five materials. If, [Col. 0585D] therefore, we understand this statue figuratively as this age, and understand by its seven parts or by the five materials of which it consists five or seven ages of the world, we shall have a probable and reasonable interpretation.

For those people who lived in the first age of the world, from Adam to Noah, were like the golden head [Col. 0586A] of this statue. As the head is the beginning of the body, so they were the beginning of the succeeding age and of the human race. Or, as gold surpasses all metals because of its worth, so that first age of the world was more glorious and excellent than the ages to come.

By silver, which is the second material after gold, is understood the second age of the world, from Noah to Abraham. For as silver is known to be far inferior and worse than gold, so the second age is shown to have been much worse and inferior to the first age of the world. Indeed, on account of that age’s wickedness, the Lord is said to have brought the flood upon the earth.

By bronze, which we sometimes employ as a figure of endurance and strength, we fittingly understand the third age of the world, from Abraham [Col. 0586B] to Moses, because in that age men were strong and patient amid adversity and prosperity—namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and many others who faithfully kept God’s commandments through endurance and strength of spirit.

By the material of iron we ought to understand the fourth age of the world, known to have lasted from Moses, the outstanding prophet, to David.

The fifth age, however, which extended from David to Christ’s coming, is fittingly understood through the clay and earthen material, which, although joined to iron, nevertheless could not adhere to it. In the age before Christ’s coming, the Gentile and Jewish peoples existed mixed together in Judaea; [Col. 0586C] but as clay in that statue could not be made firm with iron, so the Gentile people had no true concord with the Jewish people.

In the sixth age, therefore, the stone was cut from the mountain without hands: that is, Christ was born of the Virgin Mary without a man’s touch. He struck and shattered the statue—that is, he showed how vile and contemptible the glory of this world was. For when he said to his disciples, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Matt. 5), he preferred spiritual poverty to gold and silver, bronze and iron, and all the riches of this age. Thus it is rightly said that the stone struck the statue upon its feet of iron and clay, because Christ, who is the cornerstone, through the preaching of spiritual poverty reduced to nothing and destroyed the clayey [Col. 0586D] and muddy glory of this world. Afterwards this stone grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth, when Christ, through the preaching of the Gospel, became known as God throughout the world.

341 We may also, by allegorical interpretation, understand the seven [Col. 0587A] members of this statue as the seven ages of the world in a spiritual sense. Certainly, by the statue’s golden head we fittingly understand the people of the first age of the world. For as gold has no colour except its natural one, so the people of that first age had no law by which they might know God except the natural law: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself” (Deut. 6). Through the creation, indeed, they knew the Creator: “For the invisible things of God were made known to them through the visible things that were made” (Rom. 1); and every creature directed the minds of those who beheld it toward its Creator.

The eternal and wonderful splendour of that Creator likewise appeared in the distinctive working of the sun, moon, and stars, [Col. 0587B] rendering inexcusable those who did not believe in him. For he who had bestowed such brilliance and beauty upon his creatures was undoubtedly much more radiant, splendid, and beautiful in his own majesty.

But because thoughts dwell in the breasts of mortals, not without reason do we understand through the breast of the statue the people of the second age. Their perverse thought and malicious action are said to have moved the God of majesty to such a point that, if it may be said, the Creator himself became angry with his creature and, their wickedness demanding it, destroyed the whole race of mortals by the waters of the flood, leaving only a few survivors, from whom he afterwards restored the entire world.

By the arms, by which the labour and strength of human exertion are customarily expressed, may be designated the people of the third age, [Col. 0587C] from Abraham to Moses. They remained strong in faith amid this world’s adversity and prosperity, and endured great struggles to keep God’s commandments. Such was the outstanding patriarch Abraham, who, as the Apostle says (Heb. 2), faithfully believed in hope against hope and, obedient to the prompting of God’s will, left the land of his birth. He was ready to fulfil an obedience unheard of and unprecedented in former ages and generations, when he wished to sacrifice to God his son, in whom he had received the hope of the promise, thereby showing us a perfect example of obedience.

In that same age was Isaac, son of this great patriarch (Gen. 22), who willingly endured the scourge of bodily blindness given to him by God. As formerly he had yielded assent to his father in the offering of himself, so in the bodily blindness which he suffered he strove to give thanks to God. Therefore he deserved to receive from God the gift of prophecy, and, in ecstasy, with the eyes of his heart opened, he blessed his son Jacob in these words: [Col. 0587D] “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field” (Gen. 27).

Whom, then, does Isaac call his son in the spirit of prophecy, except Christ, who was to be born from his seed through the lines of generations? And the fragrance of what full field did Isaac spiritually perceive, except the fullness of divinity which, as Paul says, rested bodily in Christ? (Col. 2.) Hence John, in whom was the grace of the Holy Spirit, says: “From his fullness we have all received, grace for grace” (John 1). The fragrance of the full field, therefore, is the fullness of Christ’s divinity.

Moreover, Jacob, living in the same age, when he joined two wives to himself in carnal marriage, indicated how greatly two peoples were to be embraced, as Christ joined them to himself in the unity of faith; or how greatly the two blessed modes of life—namely, the active and contemplative—were to be embraced.

By the statue’s bronze belly, in which the human inward parts are contained, are designated the people of the age from Moses [Col. 0588A] to the time of the apostles. For as many things beneath the belly are not exposed to human sight, so what was done under the period of the given Law was by no means clearly evident to our understanding.

Since human offspring proceeds from the thighs, the age that is known to have existed in the time of the apostles and the primitive Church is fittingly understood by the thighs of this statue. For the holy apostles, together with their mother the Church, then begot many children for God through faith, the regeneration of sacred baptism, and the glorious preaching of the Gospel which they learned from God himself. Thus Paul said to some: “In Christ I begot you through his Gospel” (1 Cor. 4). And elsewhere the same man says: “My little children, whom I am again bringing to birth until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4).

We rightly understand the age of the apostles and doctors of the Church through bronze thighs, because bronze is a very resonant metal. Accordingly it is said of the apostles: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends [Col. 0588B] of the world” (Ps. 18).

By the statue’s iron legs is understood the age in which we live. For as iron subdues and breaks hard things, so the fervour of holy religion, which through God’s grace has grown more abundantly than usual in the holy Church, has shattered and crushed, by the strength of the Holy Spirit, the pleasures and delights of this passing age and the desires of the flesh.

By the iron and clay feet, which are customarily the furthest part of our body, is rightly understood the final age, which will come in the time of Antichrist. In that age, as the Lord says in the Gospel, “There will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the world, so that, if possible, even the elect might be led into error; but for the sake of those elect the days themselves will be shortened by God” (Matt. 24; Mark 13).

Moreover, as iron and clay 342 cannot be made firm in one structure, so the people of that age will be unable to be contained in the one bosom of the holy Church. The followers of Antichrist will strive to uphold his perverse teaching and heresy; but the children of the holy Church will defend their mother and the doctrine of the Catholic faith and the Gospel. Thus, as different persons think different things and are drawn to opposed sides, iron cannot adhere to clay, and they will be unable to agree with one another.

After this, that stone which was once ineffably cut from the mountain will come for judgment: namely, Christ, who long ago came forth from that shadowy and dense [Col. 0589A] mountain of divinity and from his hidden dwelling. But what will that stone do? It will strike and destroy this statue—that is, this world—and by the wondrous power of his divinity restore it to a better condition.

That this world must lay aside its present state and receive another, better state, the Lord declares in the Gospel when he says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24). Thus Paul says: “For the form of this world passes away; and that which grows old and ages is near to destruction” (1 Cor. 7). Hence the apostle Peter says: “But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, on which the heavens shall pass away with a great rush, and the elements shall be dissolved by the heat of fire. But we await new heavens and a new earth, and his promises” (2 Pet. 3). John the apostle likewise says in the Apocalypse: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. 21). For the first heaven and the first earth passed away, and the sea is no more.

Whoever desires to be refreshed by a loftier mystery and instructed in allegorical senses may, if he wishes, apply this statue allegorically to the person of the holy Church. Since the head of this statue is said to be golden, and since the Lord Jesus Christ is called the head of the holy Church, we should not improperly understand the golden head of this statue as the Lord Jesus himself. For as we know that the head is the beginning of the body, so we do not doubt that the Lord Jesus Christ is the head and beginning of the holy Church.

Moreover, as the limbs [Col. 0589C] of our human body are governed by the head, so faithful Christians, who are the members of the holy Church, are directed toward salvation by their head, Christ, if they obey him.

By the breast of this statue we rightly understand the holy apostles, because secret counsels are customarily hidden in the breast, and the holy apostles were privy to God’s secrets. Thus the Lord says to these apostles: “All things whatsoever I heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15). And elsewhere: “To you,” he says, “it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Matt. 13). Hence the apostle John, truly the intimate revealer of God’s hidden things, reclined upon the breast of the Lord Jesus; and afterwards he poured forth for us the fountain of divine wisdom which he had drawn from that [Col. 0589D] breast.

By the arms, through which the strength of human labour is expressed, are rightly understood the holy martyrs, who fought courageously for love of their heavenly homeland and, for the sake of God’s glory, spared not themselves even to the shedding of blood.

By the bronze belly we understand the holy confessors and modern doctors of the Church, whom we know to have been filled with every spiritual knowledge and wisdom and with holy preaching. For as solidified humours in the belly, derived from food, flow into and nourish the upper and lower parts of the body, so holy teachers wrote down the lives of saints who went before them and handed on to us the spiritual rules by which we ought to live.

Certainly, as those who define the structure and nature of the human [Col. 0590A] body say, the propagation of our flesh proceeds from the thighs. Therefore the order of married faithful persons contained in the holy Church is understood through the thighs of this statue. Those to whom the ability to beget children has been granted use the marital acts in the sacrament of marriage in such a way that they nevertheless do not exclude God from the dwelling-place of their minds.

By the iron and strong legs are understood religious men living a celibate life. For as the legs support and carry the whole body, so they assist the holy Church by prayers poured out to God and commend it to God by continual supplications.

In the iron and clay feet we should understand the final and weaker part within the holy Church: namely, that part which is neither bound by the bond of marriage nor, renouncing the world, willing to give itself to God’s service. Such people, having received freedom to sin, confess that they believe in God; yet they refrain from sins neither through fear nor through love of him. They are therefore as iron and clay because, though they have faith, they by no means perform the works of faith. Paul rightly says of them: “They profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1).

## Another Allegory

If we were worthy to hear the voice of that heavenly trumpet which John, as he says in the book of the Apocalypse, heard speaking to him: “Come up here, and I will show you what must happen after these things” (Rev. 4); and if we could be in the spirit with him—that is, become wholly spiritual, so that nothing carnal, nothing earthly, [Col. 0590C] 343 should remain in us at all—then we would be able to apply the figure of this statue in an allegorical sense to the text of the whole divine Scripture.

Since we know that the book of Genesis is the beginning of the divine Scriptures, we not improperly understand the head of this statue through that book. And because the Gospel which the Lord Jesus Christ established was always hidden in the Old Testament, as the prophet Ezekiel testifies (ch. 1), declaring that he saw “wheel within wheel”—that is, the Gospel within the old Law—we rightly associate the Gospel with that same book of Genesis in the portion corresponding to the head. For we do not doubt that the Law and the Gospel say the same thing in every respect and contain precisely the same things, although in dissimilar words.

As the head of this statue is understood through Genesis and the Gospel, so it is fitting that its breast be understood through the books of the prophets. For secret counsels are hidden in the breast, and the holy prophets are known to have foreknown God’s secret counsels before they came to pass. Hence one of those prophets said: “Let your ancient counsel, O Lord, come to pass in truth” (Isa. 25).

Since, as we have already said, human labour is customarily represented in the arms, the arms of this statue may rightly be prefigured through the book of Psalms, because those psalms very often mention human labour, as in: “See my humiliation and my labour” (Ps. 24), and: “They are not in the labour of men” (Ps. 72), [Col. 0591A] and many other similar passages.

By the books of Kings we ought to understand the statue’s bronze belly, because as many things are hidden in the belly that do not appear outside, so in the books of Kings many mystical and figurative matters remain hidden from us. And because, as we have already said, human offspring proceeds from the thighs, the thighs of this statue are not inappropriately understood through the Epistles of blessed Paul and the other apostles.

Although Paul was caught up to the third heaven, and although in ecstasy he heard certain secrets which human beings cannot comprehend, he nevertheless humbly descended to regulate carnal marriages, saying: “Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband; and let each have his own wife because of fornication” (1 Cor. 8).

By the legs, which seem to support the weight of the whole body, we ought to understand the writings of modern doctors. These are rightly described as iron, because as iron subdues everything, so the writings of the saints—namely Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory—destroy and eliminate all the doctrines of heretics.

By the iron and clay feet we ought to interpret the teachings of Catholics together with those of heretics who will exist in the last days. For as iron cannot be made firm with clay, so orthodox teaching cannot agree with the perverse doctrines of heretics. As Paul says: “What fellowship has light with darkness, [Col. 0591B] or what share has the believer with the unbeliever?” (2 Cor. 6).

## Another Allegory

If we wish to examine this statue morally, we shall undoubtedly find in it a moral interpretation. By the gold of which this statue’s head was made is signified true wisdom, which consists in two principles: that we utterly turn away from evil, and that we do not omit any good which we are able to do.

By the breast and arms are signified sincere thoughts and holy works, because it is fitting that whatever good a person thinks, he should strive to accomplish without delay in deed.

By the belly, which can never suffer emptiness without danger to health, our mind is signified; it must by no means be emptied, to its harm, of holy thoughts and [Col. 0591C] spiritual meditations.

By the bronze thighs, from which mortal offspring customarily proceeds, our chastity ought to be figured: through it we ought inwardly to please God alone, and outwardly to set before people a good example without desire for vain glory.

By the iron legs, let us understand our strength and patience, so that we may be strong in prosperity and patient in adversity, and strengthen the weak knees of wavering brothers by the spirit of courage.

By the iron and clay feet our steps may be signified, because we ought diligently to avoid evil paths and carefully walk upright ways, so that it may truly be said of us: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118).

We have strayed rather far from the order of exposition while discussing more subtly that wonderful statue which King Nebuchadnezzar saw. But now I think it is a fitting time to return to that from which we digressed and hear [Col. 0592A] how almighty God shows the Bride of his Son where he himself feeds and where he reclines: in the south, that is, in love of God and neighbour.

Above we showed how the Bride addressed her Bridegroom, saying: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you lie down at midday” (Song 1); and how the same Bridegroom answered his Bride: “For I feed and recline at midday—that is, I remain in my Father, who is the true midday—as I have remained from eternity.”

It remains, therefore, that almighty God answer the Bride of his Son how he likewise reclines and feeds—that is, rests and remains 344 at midday, namely in his Son, whom he begot eternally and in every respect like himself. That the Son remains eternally in the Father and the Father in the Son is proclaimed in a harmonious voice by all the authority of both New and Old Testament.

Thus the Son himself says of the disciples in the Gospel: “Father, I will that, as you are in me and I in you, they too may be one in us” (John 18). And he says to Philip: “Philip, do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14).

Therefore, as above the Bride asked not only her Bridegroom but also the Father of her Bridegroom where he fed and reclined, and was answered by both that this was at midday—that is, the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father—so now, if the same Bride wishes to ask the Holy Spirit where he feeds and where he reclines, the Holy Spirit himself will answer her: “Because I proceed ineffably from the Father and the Son, so indeed I feed and recline in both—that is, I rest and remain—because I am one God with them, as I have been from eternity.”

[Col. 0593]

# Response Concerning the Salvation of the First Man

## Prologue

[Col. 0593A]

When I would often converse with my brothers about the divine Scriptures, and, knowing nothing, was nevertheless thought to know something, they asked me on several occasions about certain matters which troubled them, either because they seemed difficult to understand or not sufficiently credible. When I answered that I did not know them, or that at present I lacked leisure to recount to them the testimonies of Scripture, this answer did not satisfy them. Rather, their affection accused me either of feigned ignorance or of the obstinacy of someone occupied with other concerns. For this is the character of supreme desire, if it is ardently kindled: it almost knows no patience if it is delayed even a little. Hence the saying of a certain pagan is fittingly repeated: “Nothing is hurried enough for a desiring mind.” [Note: [Col. 0593C] Sallust.]

Therefore, lest, by not answering, I seem grudging toward those who desire knowledge and inquire, and lest I deserve to displease those to whom I owe whatever I possess if I contribute nothing, I judged it fitting to answer some of their inquiries by dictation rather than conversation. This is not because I presume to resolve their questions to the last detail—for perhaps that would be rash to promise—but because I may offer whatever answers I can; and this, if God helps, may more easily be accomplished.

If, however, what I have written should come into the hands or ears of some wise person, I ask that he not hasten to judge it presumptuous that I wished to commit my answers to writing. For though this may seem unnecessary to the learned, it will not be useless [Col. 0593C] to me and to those unlearned persons like me. Since memory is not a sufficiently trustworthy guardian of those things which I may sometimes think usefully, but many of them slip away by the slippery paths of forgetfulness into the region of destruction, I wished to bind some of them by the bond of writing, so that by it I might recall to memory things that had fled.

To a wise man who retains the divine Scriptures by heart, a written work flowing from a poor vein is, I confess, not greatly to be embraced. Yet it is not to be rejected by the simple and less educated. Finally, it ought not to be attributed to presumption when it is humbly rendered to brotherly love. Let this, if it seems good, suffice for the preface, so that the first answer may now begin.

345 Chapter One

[Col. 0594A]

You ask, brothers, whether the first Adam is saved, since Genesis plainly acknowledges that he sinned damnably, while it does not there openly record that he repented. We all know, not only by reading but also by experience, that he sinned; for both by living miserably in this life and by departing most miserably from it, we feel the punishment of his sin.

It is not superfluous to say what sort of man he was when formed before sin and how he was disfigured after sin, although this is known, since it seems necessary to my purpose. For man was made in a state in which no man after him was made. He was made mortal and immortal: mortal, indeed, so that he could die; immortal, however, so that he could [Col. 0594B] avoid dying. He was given free ability to sin and not to sin, and the reward of each condition was set before him: death and non-death. Thus, if he sinned, death would follow; if he did not sin, he would never die.

But because, as it is written later, “Every animal loves its like” (Ecclus. 13), a helper like himself was given to him (Ecclus. 17); and woman was fashioned from no other source than the rib of the sleeping man, so that she might be joined to him lovingly through a certain natural affection and he might enjoy such consolation.

He was placed in paradise, planted with trees of various kinds, so that he might both eat their fruit and delight in their beauty. There also stood, among the others, two trees whose names seem to disclose what they were. One was called the tree of life, the other the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, from their effect—that is, because they produced such effects.

Adam was therefore permitted, by eating from the tree of paradise, to escape the troubles of hunger; and, by eating from the tree of life, to avoid death and old age. Lest, established in such great glory, he should rashly become proud like the Angel before him, a command was imposed upon him, which he might obey for his own good. Thus he who surpassed the other living things upon earth in dignity would nevertheless be humbled beneath the yoke of obedience and subject to God alone.

He was therefore told that, while eating from every tree of paradise, he was not to eat only the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil; if he did so, he would die the death. That tree, certainly, was not evil, having been created by the good God. Rather, it was good for the created human being to obey the Creator, so that he might, as it were, be exercised in the training-ground of obedience and thus attain heavenly glory by his merit.

For if he had humbly remained in what was commanded him, then, after completing the life he had earned, he would undoubtedly have been transferred without the intervention of death into the company of angels, if it seemed fitting to God. Ceasing to be mortal as he was, he would become immortal in a way different from that in which he had been immortal. For he was immortal in that he could merely avoid death; but he would become immortal in that he could by no means die. This inability would not be a weakness or a defect of infirmity, but the strength and summit of perfection.

A human being thus created rightly owed obedience to such a great Creator and giver of so many and such great goods, loving the good of patience and aspiring to the greater things promised.

Who, however, could worthily either express in words or conceive in mind how greatly he sinned when he turned away from all these things and, abandoning the Creator’s command, listened to the voice of his deceived wife? The devil envied him this great glory, in which he then rejoiced in the present and rejoiced still more in hope of the future. As it is written (John 8), the devil was a murderer from the beginning—that is, from the time humankind was created. And because he had lost the true life, which is God, he wished to take that same life away from man, lest man should ascend by the merit of obedience to the place from which he had fallen through the vice of pride.

Seeking suitable steps by which to cast him down, he clothed himself in the crafty serpent and, hiding in it, first approached the woman. Since he knew her to be weaker in sex, he hoped that she would be easier to lead into sin. Coming to her, he very shrewdly renewed her memory of the divine command, lest, when she was subsequently accused of transgression, she might defend herself by pleading forgetfulness.

## Chapter II

“Why,” he said, “did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” But she said: “We have been told to eat from every tree that is in paradise; but the tree of the knowledge of good and evil has been forbidden us, lest perhaps we die.” To her he said: “You shall not die at all. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3).

God, who will be like you? Who among the clouds will be made equal to the Lord, or who is like God among the sons of God? The woman believed the deceiver, thinking false what God had said and true what the wicked enemy asserted. But lest she sin alone, she approached the man and, with feminine importunity, persuaded him to eat the forbidden fruit and, in accordance with the serpent’s word, become as God.

He, however, knew such an assertion to be false, while knowing God beyond doubt to be truthful in all that he had said; yet he preferred to comply with his wife rather than, by offending her, obey the Creator. For he could not bear, with a husband’s affection, to grieve her whom he had received as his companion by the law of marriage, hoping that through repentance he could be reconciled to God. This is what the Apostle later wrote: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression” (1 Tim. [Col. 0596A] 2).

For she was deceived when, as I said before, she believed that what God had said was untrue; but he was not deceived in that he knew false what the serpent had urged. Wretched were both. For what is more detestable than to judge God a liar? Again, what is more wicked than, having despised him whom a man knew to be the truthful God, to yield to a woman’s enticements? Both sin, eat the forbidden fruit without hesitation, and, as the serpent had said, their eyes are opened. What does this mean? Did they not see before? Is it not written: “The woman saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance; and she took of its fruit and ate, and gave it to her husband” (Gen. 3)? And immediately it adds: “He ate, and the eyes of both were opened” [Col. 0596B] (ibid.).

They were opened, then, not to see what they had previously seen, but to discern what they had previously not known: namely, the difference between the good which they had lost by sinning and the evil which they had found by experiencing it. Many people understand better then how pleasant health is when severe illness presses upon them. Therefore that tree is called the tree of knowledge of good and evil, because through tasting it such knowledge is acquired.

For divine vengeance, which leaves no fault unpunished, immediately struck both with its blow; and in the members called shameful they were afflicted with the itch of lust, so that those who had refused humbly to submit to the divine law might be compelled to feel the law of the flesh resisting the law of the mind. Having learned this, and being deprived of the garment of immortality, they blushed to be naked; and, having taken flight and wishing to hide, they covered their shameful parts with fig leaves.

And fittingly this disobedience—the recompense of disobedience—rules especially in the moist parts, so that, because all their offspring is bound by the stain of transgression, this may appear most especially in those members through which that offspring itself is propagated. For a human being bound not only himself, but also those who would come after him, in such guilt; and he who through disobedience deserved to die compelled all others to die. For he who before sin, although mortal, would nevertheless not have died if he had not sinned, made all those whom he begot through sin so mortal that, however justly they might thereafter live, they would nevertheless necessarily die.

For none of them, whether [Col. 0596D] he sins in the likeness of Adam’s transgression or does not sin, now escapes the straits of death, since even of Christ himself, who did not commit sin, it is written: “The issues of death belong to the Lord God” (Ps. LVII). If Adam had obeyed the divine commands, neither he himself nor any of his descendants would have fallen into such miseries; indeed, no ruin would ever have been felt, since that first disobedience alone is the cause of this ruin.

Yet God, who is rich in mercy, did not wish the man whom he had made to perish, but to return; he seeks him that he may be corrected, rebukes him that he may come to his senses, showing what he would later say: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live” (Ezek. 18).

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0597A]

“Adam,” he says, “where are you?” And he: “I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.” And the Lord: “Who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the forbidden tree?” And he: “The woman,” he says, “whom you gave me as my companion, gave it to me, and I ate” (Gen. 3).

Wretched man: when he ought humbly to have acknowledged his own fault alone and, by confession, to have obtained pardon, he attempted to turn it back upon the woman, and she upon the serpent—although another person’s inducement to sin is sufficient excuse for no one. The man said that he had been persuaded by the woman, while the woman said that she had been deceived by the serpent. This indeed was true, but it did not excuse them, lest the sin which could be washed away by a pure and simple confession should be doubled by a needless [Col. 0597B] excuse.

Accordingly, they received the penal sentence together: the man, namely, to eat his bread in sweat; the woman, to give birth in pain. Then they were expelled from paradise and excluded from the tree of life; and, lest easy return thither be granted them, an angel bearing a flaming sword was stationed before the gates of paradise. Yet, lest hope of return be removed altogether, the same sword is called turning or ever-moving.

After this, in the same book of Genesis (ch. 4), nothing is read concerning Adam except that he knew Eve his wife and begot Cain, Abel, and Seth, sons and daughters; that he lived nine hundred and thirty years; and that he died. We must therefore now inquire and investigate more carefully—provided that the Spirit of God, who searches all things, even the deep things of God (1 Cor. 2), helps us—whether perhaps something may be intimated to us from the words of that very book from which the salvation of that man ought to be assessed.

I would never have presumed to assert that this can be done, unless I had been instructed by other passages of Scripture, in which matters are more openly stated that are here covered by the veil of the letter. Thus, indeed, one Scripture makes another [Col. 0597C] clearer; and when more is read, it makes not merely an unlearned person but even a wise person wiser. Since not everything is said in one place, or what is said is said obscurely, it is necessary to read more; and thus Solomon’s saying will prove true: “The wise hearer will become wiser” (Prov. 1).

Indeed, those things are often received more sweetly which are drawn out with some labor from more obscure passages. Thus the Prophet, according to another translation only, joyfully sings to God: “How sweet are your utterances to my throat, more than honey and honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. 119). Honey is called that which is bare and open, whereas honeycomb is that which lies hidden in skillfully constructed waxen cells and is strained out from them with some labor. Therefore it was not enough to say that God’s utterances are sweeter than honey; he adds “and honeycomb,” wishing honey to signify the things in Holy Scripture that are more evident, and honeycomb those which in it are more hidden.

Let us therefore briefly repeat the words of Genesis itself relevant to the present matter, so that from the very cells of the letter we may draw out something, if God grants it.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0598A]

“God,” he says, “called Adam and said: ‘Adam, where are you?’ And he said: ‘I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself’” (Gen. 3).

I wonder whether perhaps, in Scripture’s statement that God called Adam, some grace, some mercy of the Creator, some benefit, some advantage for the sinner may be understood. In many passages of Scripture God is found to call; there one must carefully consider what he is said to call, or to what end.

There is one kind of calling by which each thing is called by its own or its common name: for example, when we say, “This man is called Moses, that other one Aaron”; or, “This animal is called a horse, that one a lion”—that is, it is named. By this calling God, in the establishment of the world, called the firmament heaven [Col. 0598B] and the dry land earth (Gen. 1), which means nothing other than that he named them by their names.

There is another calling indicated to us by the prophet Haggai—or rather, by God through him: “I called dryness,” he says, “upon the earth, upon the grain, upon the wine, upon the oil, and upon whatever the ground produces” (Hag. 1). And David says: “He called famine upon the earth and broke every support of bread” (Ps. 104). I suppose no one is so childishly minded, however little instructed in the knowledge of Scripture, as to think that famine or drought was some person able to hear a speaker’s words. Hearing is indeed proper to a rational, or at least an animal, creature; but famine and drought are no creatures at all, but rather a plague and affliction of creatures.

The ancient people of the Gentiles, however, were held in such an error, believing such sufferings to be gods or persons, as a certain pagan says:

> “And she saw the famine she had sought in a stony field.”

[Note: [Col. 0597D] Ovid.]

This was said of one of the mountain goddesses, seeking Famine in obedience to Ceres’ command. Therefore, when God is reported to call famine and drought upon the earth, it seems to me to mean nothing other than that, when God determined to punish the inhabitants of the earth for sins demanding punishment, he commanded famine or drought to occupy the land.

There is also a calling by which God is read to call human beings through a human messenger; and there is another by which he calls them himself, without any human ministry. Thus this fourfold calling of God can be found in Holy Scripture [Col. 0598D]. The first may be called by another name naming or designation; the second, command; the third, admonition; the fourth, transformation. The first assigns names to things so that they may be distinguished; the second commands that people be punished; the third admonishes so that they may be corrected; the fourth pours in grace so that they may be transformed.

The next-to-last of these, by which people are called through people, is in a sense general, because it is bestowed alike upon good and evil persons. Since a human being does not perfectly know God’s secret counsel, he calls all alike to the kingdom, although God has prepared glory for some of them and eternal fire for others. I judge this to be the kind of calling of which we read in Solomon: “I called and you refused. I also will laugh at your destruction” (Prov. 1); and in the Gospel: “Many are called, but few chosen” (Matt. 22).

That this calling, which is sometimes found to be profitable, should be understood to have been made through human beings seems to be shown by the preceding words in both books, if one is willing to attend carefully. “Wisdom,” Solomon says, “preaches outside; in the streets she gives her voice” (Prov. 1). A few words later he adds: “I called and you refused” (ibid.), and so forth. The Wisdom of God is the Son; the Wisdom of God is Christ, who is surely said to preach outside and give his voice in the streets when preachers sent by him bring God’s word not into human hearts—which belongs to God alone—but into human ears, and cry out without ceasing in the broad public spaces denoted by the name “streets” [Col. 0599B], lifting up their voice like trumpets. They labor, with the Apostle, to plant and water, yet accomplish nothing unless God, speaking inwardly, is willing to give the increase (1 Cor. 3).

Likewise, in Matthew, where it is said, “Many are called, few are chosen” (Matt. 22), a little earlier in the same chapter this is prefaced: “Go therefore to the exits of the roads, and call to the wedding as many as you find. And his servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, evil and good. And the wedding was filled with those reclining at table. And immediately that man who was found without a wedding garment was cast out” (ibid.). The chapter thus ends: “For many are called, but few are chosen.” What is understood in the Gospel by roads and road-exits seems to be denoted by Solomon under the name “streets.”

Such too is that passage in Isaiah: “All of you shall fall by the sword, because I called and you did not answer; I spoke and you did not hear” (Isa. 65).

## CHAPTER V

The final calling of God is special: by it he is found to call people himself, in the manner he himself knows, where no human intermediary is found. Sometimes this occurs openly, as when he called Moses from the bush; often secretly, as with countless thousands from the beginning of the age. This calling is assigned the special prerogative that it is rarely found fruitless—indeed, it seems that the prophet Joel spoke of it by antonomasia: “On Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be salvation, and among the remnant whom the Lord shall call” (Joel 2).

[Col. 0599D] For he intended the excellence of this calling to be understood as so great that the benefit of salvation follows it, and that to be called by God in this way is nothing other than to be effectually summoned to salvation. Therefore, as it seems to me, the divine historian did not wish the statement, “God called Adam” (Gen. 3), to be noticed casually, but instructed us to understand in it the gracious disposition of the caller and the great advancement of the one called.

If I wished, or were able, to turn over the divine Scriptures and bring forward all the passages in which God is said to call by himself, whether openly or secretly, and expound how great the benefit of this calling is, this collection, in my judgment, would be of such magnitude as to exceed the suitable scope of a volume. Yet, lest I seem to affirm wordily what I cannot demonstrate [Col. 0600A] at least a little, I shall bring forward certain examples that occur to my memory, so that your charity may know that no slight benefit is contained in this calling of God.

## CHAPTER VI

In Exodus we read that, “when Moses was feeding the sheep of Jethro his father-in-law and had driven the flock into the interior of the desert, the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush. Seeing the bush burn without being consumed, he said: ‘I will go and see this great vision, why the bush is not burned.’ But when the Lord saw that he was approaching to see, he called him,” it says, “from the midst of the bush and said: ‘Moses, Moses!’ He answered: ‘Here I am.’ But he said: ‘Do not come near here; remove the sandal from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground.’ And he said: ‘I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’” (Exod. 3).

You see that great grace is signified in this calling by which God calls Moses, when he who had come from Egypt is commanded to remove his sandals. Since sandals are made from the skins of dead animals, they fittingly signify dead works—that is, sins—which are undoubtedly committed in Egypt, that is, in darkness: “For whoever does evil hates the light” (John 3).

Therefore Moses, wishing to go and see the vision, is rightly forbidden, and is divinely taught in what order this must be done: namely, that he should hasten to lay aside the old coverings which he had acquired while living in Egypt; and so he will merit the divine vision—or rather, come to know God himself. Hence a certain knowledge of God is given to him as though he had already removed his sandals, or rather was now prepared to remove them, when it immediately adds: “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” [Col. 0600C] (Exod. 3).

## CHAPTER VII

In the same book of Exodus, when God was speaking to Moses about making the tabernacle of the covenant and the ark of testimony, and no craftsman capable of so great a work could be found: “Behold,” he says, “I have called Bezalel by name, the son of Uri, of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in every work; and I have given him Oholiab as a companion,” etc. (Exod. 31). And he concludes: “They shall make all that I have commanded you” (ibid.).

What all these things are which Bezalel is said to make is beyond my powers and beyond the scope of this place to expound. Yet let your charity know this: the Prophet especially commends those who remember God’s commands in order to do them (Ps. 103). From this it can be inferred that Bezalel is not called by the Lord without fruit, since grace is also given him to do what is commanded, especially since he is said to be filled with God’s Spirit and called by name—an expression rarely found unless spoken of the righteous.

For the Lord knows not only the way of the righteous, but also their names. Thus Moses is told: “I know you by name” (Exod. 33). And the prophet says of God: “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by names” (Ps. 147). And in the Gospel parable, while the unjust rich man’s name is left unspoken as though unknown, the beggar is called Lazarus by name [Col. 0601A] (Luke 16).

## CHAPTER VIII

In the First Book of Kings, when the replacement of the old priesthood was under discussion and the new was figuratively brought forward, Eli the aged priest having been rejected, the boy Samuel is chosen; and in this election the divine calling is not passed over in silence. “Samuel,” it says, “was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was; and the Lord called Samuel: ‘Samuel, Samuel!’ And Samuel said: ‘Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening’” (1 Sam. 3).

You see that this calling is full of heavenly grace, since such prompt obedience follows it. For as nothing is more perverse than to refuse to hear, so nothing is more perfect than to obey quickly.

In Isaiah, when the Father is introduced speaking to the Son and foretelling what would be as though it had already occurred: “I, the Lord,” he says, “have called you in righteousness, have taken hold of your hand, preserved you, and given you as a covenant to the people” (Isa. 42). A little later, when the Son himself speaks prophetically to the people who would believe from all nations and mercifully exhorts them to better things by calling them: “Do not fear,” he says, “for I have redeemed you and called you by your name: you are mine. When you walk through fire, you shall not be burned, and flame shall not burn in you, because I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior” [Col. 0601C] (Isa. 43). And a little below: “Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call” (Isa. 48). And in the following chapter Christ himself says: “Listen, islands, and give heed, peoples from afar: the Lord called me from the womb” (Isa. 49). And in Joel, as was said above: “On Mount Zion there will be salvation, as the Lord has said, and among the remnant whom the Lord shall call” (Joel 2). And Zechariah: “He called me and spoke to me” (Zech. 6).

## CHAPTER IX

If we turn to the New Testament, we shall find there also that Christ’s calling is not idle, but incomparably fruitful, since his calling appears to be nothing other than a certain infusion of spiritual grace. Thus the evangelist Matthew, speaking of James and John, says: “Jesus, going on, saw two other brothers, James of Zebedee and John his brother, mending their nets, and he called them” (Matt. 4).

What he intended to be understood by the words “he called them”—that is, what grace this calling was—he makes clear when he adds: “But they, leaving their nets and father, followed him” (ibid.). For just as a little earlier Peter and Andrew, on hearing, “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men,” immediately left their nets and followed him (ibid.), so indeed James and John left their nets and father and followed him, although they are not read to have been invited with such words, but only called. Mark (ch. 3) and Luke (ch. 5) also attest this, having spoken of their calling.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0602A]

When Mark the evangelist was setting out the catalogue of the apostles, he says: “Jesus went up the mountain, called to himself those whom he himself wished, and made twelve to be with him; and he gave them power to heal infirmities and cast out demons” (ibid.). Enumerating individually those whom Christ called, he concludes the number with Judas Iscariot.

But if anyone asks what grace Judas himself gained through this calling, since it is certain that, while the others were chosen, he was rejected, let him know that no slight grace was also given to him, since with the others he received power to heal infirmities and cast out demons. But the saving grace which, in my judgment, is bestowed on those specially called by God ought, as it seems to me, to be referred not to Judas as the twelfth but to the number twelve: that is, he was called and pleased the caller.

And this, unless I am mistaken, the evangelist himself seems secretly to suggest, if one attends to his words not casually. For when he had said, “He called to himself those whom he wished,” he himself added, “And he made twelve to be with him.” Since the number twelve of the apostles was full of great mystery, that one was undoubtedly called, that one chosen; nor was it diminished when Judas fell, since another was substituted in his place.

“He made [them],” he says, “to be twelve with him.” For Matthias was already then more truly with him, having already been chosen by him in the secrecy of his counsel, than Judas Iscariot, who walked with him for a time only outwardly. Indeed, Christ so willed twelve to be with him that Judas could not bring it about that there should be only eleven; when Judas fell into the precipice, Christ’s own perfection nevertheless preserved the number twelve.

For eleven signifies transgression, whereas twelve is established by the power of perfection. Thus, lest the number should be deprived of its saving mystery, not merely eleven but twelve remained in the ministry. But if someone says that the word “called” in Mark is to be understood improperly, namely in the sense of “called together,” so that by the figure called apheresis the word loses a syllable at its beginning, then no question about Judas remains; rather, the gathering together—that is, the uniting—will apply to him as to the others.

For “to call together” and “to call” do not seem to have the same meaning; but whether this simple word is compounded in this manner or in any other, its signification is, unless I am mistaken, altered somewhat. Christ is said to go up the mountain to call together—that is, unite—the twelve disciples; this is clearly expressed by the other evangelists, Matthew and Luke. “Having called together,” Matthew says (ch. 15), “his twelve disciples, he gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out.” And Luke (ch. 9): “Having called together the twelve, he gave them power over all demons and [uncertain reading: stolis], that they might cure diseases.”

Christ is found to call together not only Judas but also blasphemous Jews, where nonetheless no benefit to them is found. Mark, in the same chapter of which I have just spoken, says that when the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem declared, “He has Beelzebub, and by the prince of demons he casts out demons,” “having called them together, he spoke to them in parables: ‘How can Satan cast out Satan?’” (Mark 3), and the rest. In this calling together no benefit to the blasphemers is stated, unless perhaps one understands what is at one point read in John: “And many of the crowd believed in him” [Col. 0603A] (John 2).

Certainly different is that calling, and different its result, of which Martha says to Mary in John’s Gospel: “The Master is here and calls you” (John 11). And later John himself says: “He called Lazarus and raised him from the dead” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0603B]

Paul too, at the beginning of his Epistle to the Romans, which all his other Epistles follow, declared himself called; and by that declaration he in a sense commended everything he was about to say. “Paul,” he says, “servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle” (Rom. 1). Writing to the Galatians, he plainly disclosed by whom he had been called: “Paul,” he says, “an apostle not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead” (Gal. 1).

How great was the grace, or with what result was he called? A little later in the same letter he explains: “But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles” [Col. 0603C] (ibid.). And lest this grace be thought casual and useless—because, as the Apostle himself testifies, many proclaim Christ from rivalry and not sincerely—he writes to Timothy: “Share in suffering for the Gospel according to the power of God, who delivered us and called us with his holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and the grace given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal ages” (2 Tim. 1).

Intending to say “and called,” he first says “delivered,” so that it might be plainly known how holy and saving that calling is which deliverance precedes. For the first Adam involved the entire mass of the human race in the stain of transgression; from this, God’s predestination, in its own goodness, frees certain persons. Having freed them from that entanglement and already delivered them in the secrecy of his counsel, he later called them with his holy calling: that is, he inspired them and enlightened them with his knowledge, so that from the same mass from which, according to desert, vessels unto dishonor were made, vessels unto honor might be made—not with nature removed, but purified by grace.

Speaking to the Romans, he thus declares the riches of this gratuitous deliverance and fruitful calling: “That he might show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory, whom he also called: us, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles” (Rom. 9). And to commend what he had said with prophetic language, he adds, as he says in Hosea (ch. 2): “I will call ‘not my people,’ ‘my people’; and ‘not my beloved,’ ‘beloved’; and ‘not having received mercy,’ ‘having received mercy’; and it shall be, in the place where it was said: ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called children of God” [Col. 0604A] (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XII

Throughout the whole body of his Epistles the Apostle very frequently speaks of this calling, but nowhere more plainly and concisely than a little earlier in Romans, where he thus comprises four stages of divine benefits:

> “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. 8).

You see that God’s first benefit toward us is predestination, by which we are ordained beforehand to eternal life; the second is calling, by which we are invited and inspired to seek eternal life; the third is justification, by which, our sins having been forgiven, we merit eternal life through good works; the fourth is glorification, when justice having been turned into judgment, we possess eternal peace and life.

The first occurs in him, not in us; the second, from him in us; the third, from him with our cooperation; the fourth, from him after we have already merited it. By the first he chooses us before we exist; by the second he admonishes us that we may be good; by the third he makes us just; by the fourth, glorious and immortal. The first is nothing other than the truth of divine foreknowledge; the second, the infusion of grace; the third, the working of justice; the fourth, the reward [Col. 0604C] of glory. By the first he foreknows those who are to exist much later; by the second he calls the undeserving; by the third, forgiving sins, he grants merits; by the fourth he crowns without end those who have already merited well.

Therefore, just as none are glorified except the justified, nor justified except the called, so undoubtedly none are called except the predestined. This is that special calling of God which is attributed to no one except him, by which none are called except those who will be holy—those who, according to the Apostle (Rom. 8), “are called saints according to [God’s] purpose.” This is not according to their own merit, but according to God’s purpose, because “the gifts and calling of God are without repentance” (Rom. 11).

If the book of Genesis does not openly say that Adam was called by this calling, it does not forbid such an understanding; nor does it maintain that he is excluded from salvation, since its words rather seem to allude to his salvation.

## CHAPTER XIII

“God,” he says, “called Adam and said: ‘Adam, where are you?’” (Gen. 3). Great is the Creator’s condescension: he seeks his own creature and does not allow it to remain in the hiding-place of iniquity, but wills it to come forth and return to the light of truth. On this anvil, under this hammer of inquiry, the sacrament of our reconciliation was already then being forged, while he who had sinned through the fault of wrongful consent was invited to the remedy of worthy confession, so that by the same mouth through which an unjust eating had been committed against salvation, a true confession might now be made unto salvation.

“Adam,” he says, “where are you?” As if he said: It is not good for you to remain hidden any longer. Come out; step forward; confess; declare your iniquities, that you may be justified. And he says: “I heard your voice and was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself” [Col. 0605A] (ibid.).

Before sin, man could more than sufficiently glory and be judged more than sufficiently happy: God had freely bestowed upon him innumerable benefits and bound himself to him by so great a bond of love. For, to omit the other things, which have been stated above and need not be repeated here, it was great happiness for him to dwell among angels and, finally, great glory visibly to behold God, who, although invisible by nature, was visible to him through an assumed visible creature.

The man placed in paradise saw God in the same manner in which the patriarchs and righteous persons of old later could see him while still living in the flesh: appearing to them in an assumed visible form, as an angel or a man, they recognized beyond doubt that he was God. Thus it is written of Jacob: “Behold, a man wrestled with him until morning” (Gen. 32). And a little later Jacob himself says: “I have seen God face to face, and my life has been preserved” (ibid.). And when Joshua was in the field near Jericho: “He saw a man standing opposite him, holding a drawn sword; and he went to him and said: ‘Are you ours or our enemies’?’” (Josh. 5). A little later it adds: “And the Lord said to Joshua”—undoubtedly the one to whom Joshua himself had been speaking.

Likewise, “when Gideon was threshing and cleaning grain in the winepress so as to flee Midian, the angel of the Lord appeared to him and said: ‘The Lord is with you, most valiant of men’” [Col. 0605C] (Judg. 6). A few words later it adds: “When Gideon saw that he was the angel of the Lord, he said: ‘Alas, my Lord God, because I have seen the angel of the Lord face to face.’ And the Lord said to him: ‘Peace be with you; do not fear; you shall not die’” (ibid.).

An angel likewise appeared to Manoah, concerning whom Scripture says: “Manoah understood that he was the angel of the Lord and said to his wife: ‘We shall surely die, because we have seen the Lord.’ The woman answered him: ‘If the Lord wished to kill us, he would not have received burnt offerings and libations from our hands’” (Judg. 13).

You see that him whom Scripture calls a man or an angel, it also calls God, in order to show that in a man or angel appearing to them in some fashion, people understood God—who, as has been said, is invisible by nature, but appeared visibly to those whom he willed and in whatever manner he willed. Finally, three men are read to have appeared to Abraham, but two angels to Lot, in whom nothing other than God is understood to have been present (Gen. 18–19).

This is why those first humans, once after sin they knew themselves naked—not because clothes they had not previously possessed had been removed, but because they had lost the holiness in which they had been created—blushed and feared to be seen by God, whom they had been accustomed to see in the manner described above. For this reason they fled among the trees of paradise to hide themselves, covering with fig leaves the parts which had now become shameful, leaves which perhaps first came to hand as they fled in their distress [Col. 0606A].

For although by sinning and fleeing they could bring it about that they did not see God, they could not bring it about that they were hidden from him. “For the eyes of the Lord behold good and evil” (Prov. 15), and “the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. 34). He sees even those who do not see; he overtakes them however much they flee.

For if, as a certain pagan says, kings have long hands—

[Note: [Col. 0605D] Ovid.]

—how much more should the King of kings and Lord of lords be believed to have long hands, from which no one can escape unless he chooses to flee to those very hands?

## CHAPTER XIV
Adam understood this; when he heard himself being sought, he did not wish to remain hidden any longer by silence, but to appear by confession. And he said: “I heard your voice, Lord, and I was afraid, [Col. 0606B] because I was naked, and I hid myself” (Gen. III); as though he were saying: I know that, while obedience remained within my bounds, I was clothed in the robe of immortality, innocence, and holiness; nor did I fear your face when, appearing holy before you, I came to see your power and glory. But when, having burst the barriers of self-restraint, I fell into the precipice of disobedience, I was stripped and put to shame; and, in order to find some remedy, however inadequate, for my shame, ill taught, I sought a hiding-place. In this I sinned, and in this I confess that I have sinned. I confess, I say, that I sinned not only by eating, but also by hiding. “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” (Ps. CXXXVIII). After sin I ought indeed to have fled, [Col. 0606C] but to you, not to myself. “For my soul was troubled within me; therefore from henceforth I shall remember you” (Ps. XLI).

And the Lord, both to complete the fitting shame and to provide an instrument of amendment, repeats the misery and the cause of the misery, so that, hearing what he had done and what he had deserved, the man might be more deeply afflicted and, being afflicted, might deserve to be cleansed. “Who,” he says, “told you that you were naked, unless because you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?” (Gen. III). That is to say: Who gave you awareness of this nakedness, unless because you did not preserve obedience? Because you did not remain in that which you had received, you experience evil and know what you did not know before.

And he said: “The woman whom you gave me as companion gave it to me, and I ate” (ibid.). Such, he says, was the perversity of my [Col. 0606D] will that a very easy persuasion inclined it to sin, and feminine softness enervated a manly mind. You gave me a woman as a companion for living with me, not as a guide into sin: she who was later in order of creation was also to be lower in rank, subject to me in obedience to my command, and to follow me as I followed you. But I, in an inverted and perverse order, followed one who went before me, listened to one who persuaded me, did not repel one who offered, did not instruct one who had been deceived, but destroyed myself; deceived not by error but led on by love. For what she, through wrongful credulity, urged upon me, I, through wrongful wifely attachment, brought to completion; and lest I grieve her, I grieved my God. Nor did I sin any [Col. 0607A] less because I sinned knowingly and deliberately. “She gave it to me, and I ate.” I, I say—I who ought even to have forbidden her while she ate, and by right of authority recalled her from guilt—not only did not forbid her, but ate as well; so bound, indeed conquered, by conjugal affection that, deprived of marital firmness, I weakly submitted myself to her.

But if to some persons the words, “The woman whom you gave me gave it to me, and I ate,” appear not to have been a humble confession but a kind of excuse—so that, in having despised obedience to the divine command, he sought to attribute the whole fault not to himself but jointly to the woman—I do not dare to disagree, especially since many saints have thought thus and have left it written in their little works. He may indeed have erred in this, because he did not think it would displease God so greatly that in his answer he accused the woman; he did not suppose that so grave a charge would be laid against him because, although he spoke the truth, he attempted to excuse himself. Therefore, he who was not deceived in eating was deceived in excusing himself: in the former he offended God knowingly, in the latter unknowingly. For to God, who is supreme justice, not even truth itself is pleasing in the excuse of sin; nor does he will that incautious defence should increase guilt, but that pure and simple confession should wipe it away. It remains, therefore, that every excuse being dismissed, the sinner should say to him: I have sinned, Lord; have mercy on me.

But this inexperienced athlete had received no instruction concerning this matter; he had been taught by no preceding example. Though he knew that it was evil not to obey the divine command, he did not know that what is true displeases eternal Truth. He knew, indeed, that the apostate angel had fallen because [Col. 0607C] he did not obey; but he had not understood that the angel had incurred offence by speaking truth. Yet whether the saying, “The woman whom you gave me gave it to me, and I ate,” is taken in this manner or in that, the woman is rightly reproved because she offered the man the taste of death and, by persuasion and flattery, though unwittingly, compelled him to sin.

## Chapter XV

“And the Lord said to the woman: Why have you done this? She answered: The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (Gen. III). This was spoken truthfully, though not wisely. For she was deceived by the serpent. Nevertheless, she ought neither to have transgressed through deception nor to have added an excuse to her transgression.

Nor should anyone be troubled because, after the calling by which, as I said, Adam was called by the Lord, he is found to have committed sin. I did not say that this calling conferred upon him the power never again to sin at all, but rather the power not to remain obstinately in sins. For who is so deficient in understanding as to say that, after he was called by God, Adam committed no sin, when he lived for so long afterward—he who had already lost through disobedience that state in which, had he remained, he would have experienced no sin whatever? But because he lost it, he fell into this misery and pitiable life, in which life is no longer lived without sin. Yet a person is delivered from it when he is commendably called by God through this calling. You certainly know that Moses (Num. XX), after the grace of the divine calling, provoked God at [Col. 0608A] the waters of contradiction and therefore did not enter the land of promise; nevertheless, he was not excluded from the bounds of eternal blessedness.

## Chapter XVI

And the Lord said to the serpent: “Because you have done this, you are cursed above every living creature and beast of the earth” (Gen. III). You see that God neither asks the serpent—or rather, the devil concealed in the serpent—where he is, nor asks why he did this; but because he did it, God pronounces upon him the deserved curse. He does not foretell it as a future curse, as though threatening, but declares it as present: “You are cursed,” he says. For since he was not being recalled to hope of pardon, nor granted time for repentance, he is rightly said not to be going to be cursed, but already to be cursed: he who had previously sinned irreparably [Col. 0608B] and incurred the punishments of eternal cursing.

He is beyond doubt cursed, both because he exalted himself against God in pride, saying, “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV), and because through envy he cast down the man whom he saw subject to the Most High. Therefore this iniquity is not the beginning but an addition to his curse: by it he is now punished more severely, though he was already being punished, perhaps more mildly. “You are cursed,” he says, “above every living creature and beast of the earth.” By the living creatures and beasts of the earth I consider that we should understand those who are animal and bestial, who think nothing heavenly but only earthly things, and who therefore incur the eternal curse; concerning them the Apostle says: “Their end is destruction, and their glory is in their shame—those who think earthly things” (Phil. III). [Col. 0608C] Among these this one is declared cursed—that is, cursed more than all the cursed. For just as the Virgin Mary is proclaimed in the Gospel “blessed among women” (Luke II), that is, more blessed than all women, so this one, through whose envy death entered into the world (Wis. II), is cursed among all—that is, more cursed than all who from that time until the end are found cursed throughout the whole world.

## Chapter XVII

“Upon your breast,” he says, “you shall go” (Gen. III). Since he had begun to speak as though to a serpent, he preserves the metaphor, and shows literally in the serpent what applies spiritually to the devil. The breast is the dwelling-place of the heart and thoughts. Therefore, by the name “breast,” every perverse person is not inappropriately designated, one upon whom the devil freely rolls about. And he goes, as it were, over such a person when, pressing and oppressing him, he compels him always to bend toward earthly things and does not permit him to rise to heavenly things.

This perverse person, because he always clings to earth, is no longer called merely earthly, but emphatically “earth”; and this earth is granted as food to the aforesaid serpent, so that he may wholly swallow it within the belly of his malice, hide it from the light of justice, and wrap it in the covering of eternal condemnation. This is what follows: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (ibid.). The days of his life are rightly understood as all this time during which he received licence to rage, until, at the end, all those belonging to his party having been gathered, they fall together into Tartarus to be punished by eternal death.

But lest in the meantime he should boast of this licence, or rejoice too long that he had deceived the woman, there is added the punishment by which he should also be punished in the present: while he always burned with the desire to do harm, he would nevertheless sometimes lack the power to accomplish it. “I shall set enmities,” he says, [Col. 0609A] “between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed” (Gen. III). The seed of the devil is evil suggestion, whose fruit is eternal condemnation; the seed of the woman is fear of God, whose final benefit is the vision of God. “She,” he says, “shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (ibid.). She shall crush the contrivances of your suggestion with the battering-ram of divine fear, disabling your deceits by the counsel of her prudence, and repaying your malice in kind: so that you, who deceived, may be deceived by one deceived; you, who cast down, may be cast down by one cast down; and, struck back from the front, you may be able only to lie in wait for her heel, without being able to prevail and boast.
