After the devil is consigned to eternal cursing, what is inflicted upon each human being is, as it seems, not the same curse but temporal affliction. And because the woman first incurred guilt, she first receives the penal sentence, so that the same order should be preserved in receiving sentence as is known to have existed in committing the fault.

## Chapter XVIII

“And God said to the woman: I shall multiply your sorrows and your conceptions. In pain you shall bear children, and you shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. III). If these words, with the historical sense set aside, are understood spiritually alone, they are rightly assigned to any holy soul or to the universal Church, whose sorrows and conceptions are multiplied, which bears children in pain—that is, the fruits of good works with labour—and serves under the power of the husband, that is, Christ; and he rightly rules over her. But if they are understood historically, it is not unfitting for them to be said to apply especially to Eve. For if this sentence is thought universal, so that what was said to Eve is asserted to apply to every woman, then, to say nothing of other objections, the childbirth of the Virgin Mary will stand against that opinion; for although she gave birth, she nevertheless gave birth without pain.

Therefore, whether the things said to Eve are understood literally or spiritually, not all of them apply to every woman, but different things to different women. Yet whatever the Lord said either to the woman herself or concerning the woman to the serpent [Col. 0609D] ought to be believed capable of applying to that same Eve. Thus, just as we read that it was said to her, “In pain you shall bear children,” and do not doubt that this is true, so we should without doubt believe that what was said to the serpent, “I shall set enmities between you and the woman, and she shall crush your head,” was said concerning that same woman. She who, under the punishment of divine justice, bore children in pain—this being a penal sentence—also, through grace visiting her, crushed the serpent’s head—this being a spiritual victory.

And it should be noted that the words said to the woman, “I shall multiply your sorrows and your conceptions; in pain you shall bear children; and you shall be under the power of your husband,” admit [Col. 0610A] both a spiritual and a literal sense, so that the woman is believed both actually to have endured all these things and spiritually to have fulfilled them. But what was said concerning her to the serpent—“I shall set enmities between you and the woman; she shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel”—excludes the historical sense and admits only the mystical sense, since it would appear quite useless if understood according to the letter. For what benefit would there be if the head of a material serpent were crushed, when no profit to the soul would result from it? Therefore I judge that the crushing spoken of is that of which Paul says to the Romans: “May God crush Satan swiftly beneath your feet” (Rom. XVI).

Hence, in what follows, the same woman is called the mother of the living, that is, of good works, to which sins are contrary and which are very often designated in the divine Scriptures as “the dead.” Thus the Apostle, speaking to the Corinthians, says: “What shall those do who are baptized for the dead, that is, for sins?” (II Cor. XV). And to the Hebrews: “The foundation of repentance from dead works” (Heb. VI). Finally, when the same Apostle spoke to Timothy concerning this same woman, he said: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression; yet she shall be saved through the bearing of children, if they continue in faith and love” (I Tim. II). The one whom he calls deceived in transgression, he seems to call saved through the bearing of children—that is, through the exercise of good works, which are understood under the name of children. Hence the Psalmist says: “Look upon your servants, and direct [Col. 0610C] their children” (Ps. LXXXIX).

But what the Apostle adds concerning the children, “if they continue in faith and love” (I Tim. II), should not be believed to have been said with doubt. For the causal conjunction *si* (“if”), just as in some places it is used doubtfully, is also frequently used affirmatively in both divine and secular writings—more often, indeed, when joined to the indicative, but sometimes when joined to the subjunctive. Through the prophet Malachi God says: “If I am a father, where is my honour? If I am a lord, where is my fear?” (Mal. I). And that eminent poet says: “If there is any compassion of the Lord in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0609D] Virgil.]; certainly not doubting but affirming that pity exists in heaven. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII), knowing certainly that they would have love for one another. Therefore, in order to make known what he intended to take place spiritually, the Apostle brings Eve forward and says concerning her what he knew to be true.

## Chapter XIX

You have heard what was said to the woman; now hear, if you please, what sentence was afterward imposed upon the man. Genesis continues: “But to Adam he said: Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your work. It shall bring forth thorns [Col. 0611A] and thistles for you, and you shall eat the herbs of the earth. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. III).

“Curse,” as it seems to me, designates every sin by a general name, while the particular meaning is understood, so that each sin is reckoned by its special name. The prophet Hosea seems to have done this (ch. IV), when, after setting down the genus, he proceeded to add several of its species: “Cursing, lying, theft, murder, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood.” Therefore, when man sinned, he committed a curse, to which curse a penalty is due, lest he boast of impunity. Accordingly, it is inflicted upon him that his earth—that is, his mortal flesh—should be cursed: that is, liable to the penalties of the curse and given over to labours and sorrows.

By this mode of speech Christ himself is called cursed, indeed a curse, because he bore the troubles of our mortality, which the curse imposed upon the first man had brought in. Writing to the Galatians, the Apostle says: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us” (Gal. III). And, to prove the truth of what he had said, he adds prophetic testimony: “For it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. XXI). You see that Christ, hanging on the tree, is called a curse, or cursed—which is nothing other than to say that he was afflicted by the punishments that arise from the curse. By a similar figure of speech the same Apostle calls him sin in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us” (II Cor. V).

Hence, when God said to man, “Cursed is the earth,” he added, “in your work,” so that this curse should be understood as the affliction of earthly labour, not eternal condemnation. It was written above that “the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and guard it” (Gen. III). There too, then, it was said that he should work; but in that work there is contained not affliction but delight, not misery but guardianship. For he was placed in the paradise of delight so that he might cling perfectly to the divine commands, serve God with delight, and, persevering in his service, continually preserve for himself the delight granted to him. [Col. 0611D] For if he had maintained perseverance in divine service, he would never have felt any burden in any of his work. This is what was said: “He placed him in the paradise of delight to work and guard it.” “It,” that is, the paradise of delight: that he might not lose through negligence the delightful state which he could retain through diligence.

Nor should anyone be disturbed if paradise is found here or elsewhere in the divine Scriptures to be masculine in gender, although modern grammarians maintain it to be feminine. But if grammarians please, so that *illum* (“it”) is referred not to paradise but to man, there is no need to contend, since the sense does not thereby depart far from the same meaning. “God,” it says, “placed man in the paradise [Col. 0612A] of delight that he might work.” The man was to work—without doubt, to obey the command he had received—and God, without doubt, would guard him while so working in that delight in which he had placed him.

In certain manuscripts there occurs not *illum* but *illud*: “that he might work,” it says, “and guard it.” Man was placed in the paradise of delight in order to do what God commanded and to guard—that is, to preserve—his own work by persevering in it. Therefore, the man’s earth could rightly be called blessed in its work when he felt in his work no discomfort, affliction, or opposition, because neither sin nor the punishment of sin was found in his work. But now, conversely, it is deservedly called cursed in its work, since either sin reigns in it if he lives badly, or the penalty of sin burdens it even if he lives well. For life is now no longer lived without misery; yet, through God’s mercy, this misery already becomes useful for some.

For evil persons it is only harmful and penal; for good persons it is fruitful and medicinal, because God changes evil into good, as the Apostle says: “For those who love God, all things work together for good” (Rom. VIII). For if one lives well in this misery, so that it is loved not as a bedroom but endured as an inn; if one does not murmur against God’s sentence; if one longs for the eternal homeland: then without doubt our very misery is changed into merit, and the human being, made good, is restored into something better. Hence the Prophet says: “You who fashion labour into a commandment” (Ps. XCIII). [Col. 0612C] For God fashions our labour for us into a commandment when he wills us to endure patiently the evils which he wills us to endure in this life; and he reckons the good of this patience as merit for obedience.

Therefore, when it had been said, “Cursed is the earth in your work,” there was added: “In labours you shall eat it”—that is, in labours you shall obtain fruit from it. “My tears,” he says, “were my bread” (Ps. XLI); and: “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, you are blessed” (Ps. CXXVII). Your earth, he says, will henceforth not be fruitful if, despising labour, it wishes to be luxurious. This is what the Apostle says figuratively: “The widow who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (I Tim. V).

Our flesh is not unfittingly called a widow when it is not lawfully ruled by the spirit as by a husband, but, wickedly free from the spiritual law, prostitutes itself in the brothel of its pleasures. Thus, living for itself, it is dead to God; just as, conversely, it is said: “You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III).

## Chapter XX

“It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III). The thorns and thistles that our earth brings forth are the anxieties and cares which our flesh lays upon us, while, in order either to protect it lest it fail or to cherish it so that it may thrive, we seek usefully to arrange the spiritual goods that are at hand and prudently to acquire those that are absent. Because these things are necessary and this life cannot be lived without them, our mind is distressed by heavy anxiety concerning them: while, under God’s inspiration, it already strives to aspire to heavenly things, it is nevertheless often compelled by present necessity to think of transitory things.

Yet if this anxiety and care do not pass beyond a definite measure and their proper limits; if heavenly things are not neglected on their account; if they are not extended to the pursuit of unlawful things; if, even in lawful things, they are restrained with discernment—then they are in some manner manageable and tolerable. They are, as it were, herbs: though they prick somewhat, they do not overwhelm; indeed, they serve our benefit. Hence it is said: “And you shall eat the herbs of the earth” (Gen. III), as though it were said: You shall cut down the temporal cares by which you labour in pursuing or arranging transitory things, lest they grow luxuriant; [Col. 0613B] you shall feed upon them and turn them to your own use, so that they may appear imposed not for destruction but for improvement. For thorns and thistles are then found to be not timber logs but manageable, indeed useful, herbs, if temporal cares are endured not out of love for present things but in hope of heavenly things.

Therefore the Apostle says to the Romans: “Creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope, because creation itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VIII). For creation is subjected unwillingly to vanity when a person is afflicted by temporal sorrows not through loving them but through obeying; and, lest he fail in them—indeed, that he may improve—he is strengthened by hope of deliverance, because, passing into the freedom of the glory of the children, he shall be delivered from the bondage [Col. 0613C] of corruption.

And temporal miseries are appropriately designated by the name of herbs, the food of animals, because the life of the faithful labours and makes progress in them: insofar as we are earthly and, as it were, animal, we need earthly food; but once made spiritual—if indeed we become spiritual—we are refreshed by the sweetness of heavenly bread. For as animal beings feed on herbs, so spiritual persons feed on bread, concerning which it is added concerning Adam: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread” (Gen. III).

## Chapter XXI

The saying, “It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the herbs of the earth,” may also be understood differently. Thorns and thistles are tribulations and suggestions [Col. 0613D] of sin; they spring from the earth—that is, from our flesh—and assail the very thing from which they arise. For just as a little worm is born from a garment or piece of wood, by which that very garment or wood is consumed, so suggestions of sin are born from the flesh, by which the flesh of sin itself is pricked and often consumed.

When these stir within us the desire to sin, if, through the spirit’s manly resistance, they do not reach the point of action, they can indeed prick us but cannot overwhelm us, because our prudence, aided by grace, devours and crushes them as herbs. Yet we find them to be oppressive and crushing beams through consent and negligence. Therefore it was said: “And you shall eat the herbs of the earth.” For our earth produces the bitter and harsh herbs of sin, namely its enticements; and we are admonished to eat them, that is, to consume them with the mouth, lest they grow and from thistles become timber logs.

What is meant by “with the mouth”? Fasting and prayer. For one who does not endeavour to oppose prayer and fasting to the demands of belly and throat and to the incitements of lust is shown to submit himself weakly to them. That our enemies are weakened by arms of this kind was elegantly signified by Balak, son of Sephor, king of the Moabites, in the book of Numbers. When he saw the Israelite people entering the borders of Moab, he remembered how they had defeated Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, together with all the rest through whose lands they had passed. Terrified, he said to the elders of Midian: “This people will thus destroy all who dwell within our borders, just as an ox is accustomed to crop herbs down to the roots” (Num. XXII).

Because an ox was customarily slain in sacrifice, that ox is not inappropriately the one who says: “I chastise my body and subject it to slavery” (I Cor. IX), which appears to refer to fasting. He crops the herbs down to the roots when the holy man consumes by prayer the movements of his flesh and the impulses of youth, lest they grow luxuriant; so that, even if sin cannot fail to exist, it may nevertheless not reign in his mortal body. Therefore he is an ox, and he crops the herbs, who by fasting and prayer represses rising vices, lest from the muddy root of carnality a sapling of wickedness should sprout and run wild.

Balak rightly feared that his people—namely, the Midianites and Moabites—could be defeated in the same way as he knew the Amalekites had been defeated. For it had not escaped him that, when the people of Israel came forth from the desert of Sin, encamped at Raphidim, and Amalek met them, Moses, having the rod of God in his hand, ascended to the summit of the hill and, lifting his hands, with Aaron and Hur supporting them, did not cease praying until sunset, until, as it is written (Exod. XVII), Joshua put Amalek and his people to flight by the edge of the sword. [Col. 0614C] Balak, wisely understanding the effect of this victory, ascribed it to merits rather than forces: to prayer and fasting rather than hands, to prayer and fasting rather than spear and sword. He remembered well what he had heard proclaimed: that when Moses raised his hands in prayer Israel prevailed, but when he relaxed them a little, Amalek prevailed.

Finally, he knew that innumerable other peoples, although equipped with a multitude of weapons and surrounded by much fortification, had yielded to Israel, though Israel appeared greatly inferior in number, if not in merit. The Gospel seems to commend something similar: “This kind,” it says, “is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. XVII). Thus also Christ, about to go to his passion, said: “Pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Luke XXII). But to those labouring and sweating in the contest of fasting and prayer, the welcome refreshment of bread is due, lest the distaste caused by continuous labour overwhelm them. For strengthened by inward refreshment, while they are more sweetly encouraged to hope for heavenly things, they are more strongly fortified to endure temporal troubles.

## Chapter XXII

Therefore it follows: “In the sweat of your face [Col. 0615A] you shall eat bread” (Gen. III). It is not added, “What bread?” but only, “In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread.” Therefore, by antonomasia, that bread is understood of which it is elsewhere mystically written: “He gave them bread from heaven to eat” (John VI). This bread, indeed, is a spiritual infusion or refreshment, by which our inward person is renewed, advances, and is strengthened, while the outward person decays and is continually afflicted with temporal miseries.

This is the bread of which we say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. VI). It is necessary every day, and without it one does not live on any day or at any time—provided one lives well and spiritually. But one who does not live spiritually does not live, even if he seems to live. This bread is the taste of divine sweetness, of which the Prophet says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII). How great the sweetness of that savour is can indeed be felt, but cannot be spoken. And wondrously, when the mind is commonly enlarged to receive it, it seems shut up against recounting it even to itself; the power of discourse is not given, though the grace of feeling is present.

Yet one does not come to this ineffable sweetness except through labour, nor does one receive the fruit of such sweetness who does not sweat and labour in the contest of holiness. This labour consists of fasting, vigils, reading, prayer, meditation, compunction, and weeping. We ought to labour in these things in this land of the dead if we wish to eat and be refreshed by the bread of angels. But when we have come into the land of the living, we shall indeed eat that bread, but now without labour and [Col. 0615C] sweat; for this refreshment has a laborious beginning in this life, but a glorious consummation in the other.

Therefore it was said: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken.” That is to say: You must labour to eat this bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken—that is, until, at death’s approach, you become inanimate earth, just as you were at first inanimate earth before the spirit came to you. After the dissolution of the body, however, you will cease to labour, having found more fully that which you here deserved to taste beforehand; you will enjoy bread now without suffering, since with the end of this life misery too will end.

It follows: “And he made,” etc.

## Chapter XXIII
[Col. 0615D] “And God made garments of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them; and he said: ‘Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil’ (Gen. III).” Because skins are stripped from dead animals, bodily mortality is not inappropriately signified by garments of skin: the mortality inflicted on them when, deservedly through disobedience, they were stripped of the robe of immortality. Thus, by the very attire of the body, the body’s punishment was marked: those who were now mortal—or rather, destined to die—were clothed in the skins of the dead, though until then they had been naked and yet had needed no clothing. Such a garment, plainly, became for them not only a necessary covering for their new shame, but also a medicinal reminder of their weakness; for, looking upon it, they were reminded whence and whither they had come, [Col. 0616A] and by this reminder were restrained from becoming proud again.

For this reason, I think, John the Baptist is also read to have worn a leather belt around his loins (Matt. III): namely, so that he might remember that, through the stock of sin, he had come forth mortal, and might not grow proud because Christ was thought to be he. But so that the heavenly physician might apply a more biting poultice to the harmful swelling, when he had clothed them in garments of skin, he adds: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil.” In the words “of us,” the Trinity is understood, in which there is plurality of number: Father is God, Son is God, and Holy Spirit is God; yet they are not three gods but one God.

“Therefore he has become as one of us”: that is to say, he has become God, which each one of us is [Col. 0616B] God. In this saying he seems in some manner to mock the sinner’s pride, and moreover to strike fear into those who would sin, showing that man has not only failed to obtain what he wrongly desired, but has not even preserved that which he had rightly received. “He has become as one of us, knowing good and evil”; as though he said: While he perversely desires to be as God, behold, he has rightly been reduced to becoming like horse and mule; and while he unjustly covets the Creator’s divinity, he has justly fallen into the mortality of beasts.

Now man knows good and evil—both of which I also know—but he knows them by losing the one and experiencing the other, in a manner in which I do not know them. I know good, indeed, by always possessing it; I know evil also, but by never experiencing it. Adam, however, while wishing by knowing [Col. 0616C] good and evil to become like God, was made far from him precisely through knowing both: he knows one by losing it, and the other by suffering it according to his deserts.

The saying, “Behold, Adam has become as one of us,” may also be understood otherwise, so that it is not judged irony or mockery but rather taken as a serious statement. “Behold,” he says, “Adam has become as one of us,” that is, truly one outside us. “As” sometimes expresses resemblance, sometimes the reality of a thing. It expresses resemblance when Peter says: “Like newborn infants, desire milk” (I Pet. II). It expresses reality when John says: “And we saw his glory, as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John I).

“One of us,” that is, one made outside us; as one says: [Col. 0616D] “one of the consuls,” of a man who was once consul but is so no longer, and who is more plainly and commonly called an ex-consul. For as one who holds the consulship is called consul, so likewise one deprived of it is called ex-consul. Thus we also say ex-bishops, ex-abbots, and ex-advocates, of those who once held this dignity but have laid it down.

Adam, however, was made in the image of God in order that he too might be God by always cleaving to him. “He who cleaves to God,” he says, “is one spirit” (I Cor. VI). Therefore, so long as he remained obedient to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in them, he too was undoubtedly God with them—though not substantially but by designation; not by nature but by grace; not by the merit of his own labor but by the Creator’s gift. But after he ate what was forbidden and obeyed the voice of his wife, [Col. 0617A] wretchedly he departed from their fellowship; and he who through righteousness was one in them, that is, among them, through unrighteousness became one of them, that is, outside them. 358 For by cleaving to God he was God; but by withdrawing from him he became not-God—more explicitly expressed, if ordinary usage allowed it, as an “ex-god.” For just as a man who was once consul and is consul no longer is called an ex-consul, so, if usage allowed it, he might aptly be called an ex-god, because he once was and now is not a god.

“Behold,” he says, “Adam has become as one of us”; as if he said: Truly, while we remain what we are, Adam, who was also God, has gone out from us “and has become knowing good and evil,” not as he formerly knew it, and as we too know it, but as he had never known it, and as we certainly do not know it.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“Therefore, lest perhaps he stretch out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat and live forever, the Lord God sent him forth from the paradise of delight, to till the ground from which he had been taken; and he placed before paradise cherubim and a flaming, turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life” (Gen. III).

Because, through the tree of life, as I recall having said above, Adam formerly avoided death and old age, but had now, by sinning, incurred the desert of death, he is expelled from the paradise of delight lest he touch the same tree as before; thus he might be removed from his former state of immortality both in place and in desert. In my view, this may be ascribed to divine mercy: God willed that man’s sin be annulled by this punishment, so that, cleansed through bodily death, man might return to life, lest, living forever and sinning forever after sin, he should lead an ever-miserable life.

For if, after sin, man had remained bodily immortal, and no intervening death had abolished his sin, he would have been like the devil, who lived immortally after sin and never rose again from the death of sin. Therefore man is beneficially excluded for a time from the tree of life, and cherubim—which means “fullness of knowledge”—and a flaming sword, that is, the straits of tribulations, are interposed, so that through fullness of knowledge, by which charity is signified, and through the straits of death, there may be a return to the tree of life, which is Christ. Therefore the sword itself is said [Col. 0617D] not to be fixed and motionless but, though flaming, to be turning: so that return to life is indeed difficult, yet possible.

You have heard, brothers, what is first read in Genesis: what punishment is justly inflicted for sin and what return to life is granted. I have wished to recall this so that your charity may observe that the words of Scripture do not seem to declare Adam’s eternal destruction. Rather, as they show his sin and death without any doubt, so they intimate repentance and life by testimony that, though hidden, is not absent.

I know, indeed, and I judge that no one doubts, that the things said of him after sin truly apply to his posterity: through his sin it too was cast out from the immortality of paradise and thrown into this region of death; it too suffers the thorns and thistles of anxieties [Col. 0618A] and sins; it too eats bread, whether temporal or spiritual, in the sweat of its face; it too returns by dying to the earth from which it was taken; and finally, returning to paradise through love and tribulation, as through the cherubim and the sword, it enjoys without end the tree of life—that is, Christ, the living bread.

But if, as I have said, this is not inappropriately assigned to Adam’s posterity, who would dare object if it is also said to apply to him: that he incurred death by sinning and returned to life after sin through repentance? Let the affection of piety agree—indeed, rejoice—in this view, since the rule of truth does not disagree with it but agrees with it.

Thus David, after receiving the promise of divine generosity concerning the long continuance of his posterity, when he entered before the Lord, humbled himself, and humbly praised God for the benefits granted him, said: “Who am I, O Lord God, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far? Yet this has seemed too little in your sight, O Lord God, unless you should also speak concerning the house of your servant for a long time to come” (II Sam. VII). And he added: “For this is the law of Adam, O Lord God” (ibid.); as though he said: You did not begin to act mercifully toward human beings only in modern times, but showed yourself merciful even to the first man. He lived under this law: though he deserved punishment, he found a benefit; you did not, according to his deserts, cast him away from your grace, but recalled him by benefits to serve you. So too today, O Lord God, you confer undeserved benefits upon me, whose merits did not precede them.

“This is the law of Adam, [Col. 0618C] O Lord God”: namely, that you have mercy on man without merit, and man serves you by obligation.

In Hosea, when the Lord showed with how great a love he had loved the children of Israel and brought them back when they had gone astray, he said: “I will draw them with the cords of Adam, with the bonds of charity” (Hosea XI). That is to say: With the cord and bond of charity by which I did not neglect Adam when he sinned, but corrected him—not allowing him, a wretched fugitive, to wander to his ruin, but binding and drawing him that he might return—with that bond of charity, I bound the sinful children of Israel and, once bound, recalled them, so that through the rough and steep paths of repentance they might return to the way of salvation, lest they incur the loss of servitude through the downward slopes of perverse freedom.

But if anyone should think and say [Col. 0618D] that these testimonies which I have brought forward concerning Adam cannot be understood of the first man, but only of “man,” so that Adam there is taken as meaning “man,” he should not be charged with a false opinion if he has perhaps inferred this from learning and reading. For perhaps he has read that what David says in the Book of Kings, “This is the law of Adam, O Lord God,” Hebrew tradition explains thus: “This is the law of man, O Lord God.” Likewise, where we have in Hosea, “I will draw them with the cords of Adam,” the Septuagint and other translators, as Jerome testifies, rendered: “I will draw them with the cords of men.” Thus “man” or “men” may here be understood generally; yet this does not contradict the possibility that the first man, or the first human beings, are understood particularly.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0619A]

I have found another testimony in which that first man is shown quite clearly, although his proper name is not there given. If the book entitled *Wisdom* is brought into the discussion, it is evident that it bears witness to the salvation of the man who was formed first. While commending wisdom and affirming that through it all who pleased God from the beginning were healed, it adds: “She preserved him who was first formed by God, the father of the world, when he alone had been created; and she brought him out of his transgression and gave him power to govern all things” (Wis. X).

Blessed Augustine seems to maintain that these words suit no one better than Adam himself, when, writing to Evodius, he wished to insert these same words in his letter. “Concerning that first man,” [Col. 0619B] he says, “the father of the human race, that Christ delivered him from hell, nearly the whole Church agrees; and it must be believed that she has not believed this vainly, from whatever source it has been handed down, even if express authority for it cannot be produced from the canonical Scriptures. Although what is written in the Book of Wisdom—‘She preserved him who was first formed by God, the father of the world, when he alone had been created; and she brought him out of his transgression and gave him power to govern all things’—seems to support this opinion more than any other interpretation.”

Nor should anyone be troubled if, in Book XIII of *The City of God*, or perhaps elsewhere, he reads Augustine saying that Adam was made disobedient unto death, as though he had thereby meant that Adam never came to his senses but remained stubborn and obstinate in his disobedience until death. If that were so, he would undoubtedly never escape eternal death. For whoever does not repent before death finds nothing after death except eternal punishment. But to think this of him—what else is it than to dissent from Augustine, who, as he says, knew that the whole Church agreed concerning him?

Therefore, when Augustine says that Adam’s disobedience was all the more detestable because he was made disobedient unto death, he appears to me not to have marked its temporal duration, or the extent of Adam’s great age, but the magnitude of the disobedience itself: namely, that the disobedience was so great that he deserved death. For although every disobedience is evil, it is nevertheless certain that one may be much worse and another worst of all. When an easy thing is commanded, and the one commanding threatens death to the transgressor, yet the servant despises the command, he undoubtedly incurs a mortal sin and ought to undergo punishment all the more severe because he could more easily have obeyed.

Adam therefore is rightly said to have been made disobedient unto death because he despised a light command and a grave punishment—not because he remained unrepentant until he died, but because he sinned so greatly as to deserve death. To sin unto death is to deserve death by sinning. If anyone now commits murder, adultery, or any other grave sin, he is rightly said to sin unto death, [Col. 0620A] yet repentance is not thereby excluded from the sinner; rather, the magnitude of the sin itself is expressed.

Conversely, Christ is likewise read to have been “made obedient unto death” (Phil. II), that is, to have rendered such obedience to the Father that the Jews judged him to have deserved death. Thus, when he remained fixed and steadfast in doing the Father’s command, they cried: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. XXVI). And when Pilate wished to spare him, they answered: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die” (John XIX). Nor did they keep silent about what death he deserved, crying: “Crucify, crucify” (Luke XXIII). This is what the Apostle says: “He was made obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. II).

Although Christ remained in his obedience until the end of this life and may therefore be called “made obedient unto death,” it nevertheless seems better, as stated above, to understand the Apostle to mean by this the quality of his obedience: not a long obedience, such as many weak persons also possess, but one so perfect and strong that he despised—or deserved—death. In this mortal life, where many obstacles exist, strength is especially commended; and if obedience maintains that strength even to contempt of, or desert of, death, it is deservedly judged praiseworthy.

After this life, however, unfailing length of days will accompany obedience, and such strength will not be needed. For without end the Lord will command the good servant, and without struggle the good servant will obey. That long, tranquil, and glorious obedience is commended there where it is said: “When he has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father, then he himself also will be subject to him who subjected all things to him” (I Cor. XV).

## CHAPTER XXVI

The strength which, I said, is necessary for this life seems to be commended elsewhere by a certain Wise Man, who confidently promises: “My soul will praise the Lord unto death” (Ecclus. LI). What is “will praise unto death”? Will it not praise also after death? Indeed, much more after death. Hence, when the prophet exhorted and said, “Praise the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. CXLV), the soul elegantly replied: “I will praise [Col. 0620D] the Lord in my life” (ibid.). That is to say: So long as I am in this mortal life—which ought rather to be called death than life, where whatever praise is offered to God is counted as nothing in comparison with future praise—I cannot praise him who, as it is written, “is God of the living and not of the dead” (Matt. XXII); but I shall praise him in the region of the living, where I shall live, and truly live, because I shall live without misery.

Therefore, when that Wise Man says, “My soul will praise the Lord unto death,” he intends not to designate long praise but strong praise, for the sake of which he is ready, even if he does not actually suffer them, to endure the very dangers of death. In the corresponding way Adam is said to have been made disobedient unto death, although by God’s mercy he repented before death.

Blessed Augustine also says in some places [Col. 0621A] that Adam received the sentence of condemnation—not because he understands Adam to have been condemned eternally, but to have been afflicted temporally. For condemnation is not always that eternal condemnation of which it is said, “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV), but often means either bodily death itself or any temporal affliction. Hence, in the Second Book of Maccabees: “He acquitted Menelaus, guilty of every wickedness, of the charges; but he condemned to death the wretched men who would have been judged innocent even if they had pleaded their case among the Scythians” (II Macc. IV). And Origen, in the fifth homily on Luke, says that Zacharias, John’s father, “was condemned to silence because he did not believe the angel.”

The condemnation by which Adam was condemned, therefore, seems to be that of which it was said above: “Cursed is the earth in your work; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you. In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread” (Gen. III).

## CHAPTER XXVII

Finally, the man who, according to the Gospel parable, went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers (Luke X) is understood to have been Adam, and what is said of him is asserted to apply particularly to Adam. When a certain wise man interpreted this parable concerning Adam himself, he said that Jerusalem was paradise, Jericho the world, the robbers the hostile powers, the wounds disobedience, the priest the law, the Levite the prophets, the Samaritan Christ, the beast Christ’s body, the inn the Church, the innkeeper the head of the Church, the two denarii the Father and [Col. 0621C] the Son, and the Samaritan’s return Christ’s second coming.

Origen says, in the thirty-third homily on Luke, that all these things were beautifully and reasonably said and apply not to every person but particularly to Adam. It should be noted that the robbers left him not dead but half-dead: though they cruelly inflicted the wounds of sins, they did not take from him the hope of healing.

Likewise Origen, in the sixteenth homily on Genesis, says: “‘I will bring you back from there at the end,’ I think, means that at the end of the ages his only-begotten Son descended even to hell for the salvation of the world and brought back the first-created man. Therefore, what was said, ‘I will bring you back from there at the end,’ will be fulfilled more truly in Adam than in Jacob.”

Augustine, in *On the Baptism of Infants*: “As those first human beings are rightly believed to have been delivered from eternal punishment by the Lord’s blood through subsequently living justly.” Pope Gregory, speaking of Adam in the *Register*, says: “His soul was not so dead as not to exist, but so dead as not to be blessed; yet Adam afterward returned through repentance.” Who would dare doubt Adam’s repentance, when Augustine and Gregory so openly dare to affirm it?

John the bishop also, in a sermon entitled *On the Fall of the First Man*, bears witness to this man’s salvation. For he says: “The Lord God both abhorred the enemy’s cruelty and pitied man’s fall; in fatherly compassion he grieved for the deceived man. Finally, the Lord God said: ‘Adam, where are you?’ He calls him to confession; he wishes him to confess his sin; he seeks to show mercy; he intends pardon; he reproves the fault so that he may grant forgiveness, so that those whom he did not wish to form by instruction he might cleanse through confession.”

And he adds: “They receive garments of skin, so that those who had already confessed their transgression might receive forgiveness through the humility of their clothing. The Lord showed that sins can indeed be purged by benefits; he showed that pardon can most easily be obtained through confession and the unseemliness of humble attire.” These are the words of John Chrysostom concerning Adam.

Therefore, what the teachers of the Church—indeed, as Augustine says, the whole Church—think of him, we too ought to think, and no authority of Scripture is found to dissent from it. [Col. 0622C] Finally, the Encratites, also called Tatianists, are charged with heretical perversity, Augustine testifying, because among the other things which they perversely think and say, they deny the salvation of the first man.

But because, to confess the truth, 361 I have spoken longer than I intended, while pursuing, not as I ought but as I could, the matters to be said concerning Adam, it is now time to set an end to this response of mine, since what has been said can suffice for the brothers’ inquiry. Let this response therefore come to an end thus: I shall pass to another after restoring myself for a little while by silence.

[Col. 0621]

# RESPONSE CONCERNING SOLOMON’S CONDEMNATION

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0621D] It is easy to argue in whatever fashion concerning obscure matters, when no one presumes to oppose the disputant. But when someone attempts to bring something doubtful into the light, and anyone openly resists his efforts, greater uncertainty arises among the hearers, since they do not know whom they ought rather to believe—unless perhaps one of the two is refuted by more numerous and stronger testimonies.

In this second response, therefore, God must be entreated to direct my steps in the path of truth and to fortify the true things I shall say with the protection of unconquerable firmness.

# RESPONSE CONCERNING SOLOMON’S CONDEMNATION

[Col. 0623]

[Col. 0623A] You ask, brothers, whether Solomon, king of Israel, ought to be considered saved or rather—as some maintain—judged lost. For so many good and evil things are read concerning him in canonical Scripture that many people, when it happens to them to review them by reading or hearing, are left uncertain which ought to prevail. Some, setting doubt aside, say that he ended good beginnings with a ruined end; others, conversely, that he changed evils he had committed into better things through repentance.

At your request, brothers, I have resolved to answer this opinion, which thinks so differently and contrarily; and, insofar as ability is granted, to admonish them to think the same and, if they agree, to join in agreement. Let the love of you all know first, therefore, that the things read in canonical Scripture concerning Solomon are distinguished in three ways, so that a prudent person may, with careful consideration, see when he reads or hears them what and how he ought to understand.

That Solomon in many of his acts prefigured Christ, I think no one doubts; that he prefigured him in every act, no one should presume to affirm. Of the things said concerning Solomon, therefore, some apply to Solomon himself literally and also to Christ mystically; some apply to Solomon in such a way that they neither can nor ought to be fitted to Christ; and some are said—or rather seem to be said—of Solomon in such a way that they do not apply to him at all. Yet according to spiritual understanding they apply to Christ.

I judge it fitting that several examples be brought forward from among the many, in which what I have said may be more certainly recognized as true. Scripture says that Solomon built the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem; in that work he prefigured our Lord Jesus Christ more clearly than light. Christ builds a temple for God the Father—that is, the holy Church—when he cuts and squares living stones, that is, holy men, and binds them together with the cement of charity, so that, brought into one soul and one heart, they may rise into a spiritual building and ascend to behold the Creator’s face.

But Scripture says that when Solomon was old, his heart was corrupted; he loved foreign women, concerning whom God had said, “You shall not go in to them”; and, abandoning the living and true God—the God, I say, of his fathers—he worshipped Ashtart, goddess of the Sidonians, and Chamos, god of the Moabites. No allegory commends or excuses this deed; it is maintained as plain history, so that it is believed that he truly did this and understood that in it he displeased God not slightly.

We do indeed read that the prophet Hosea took a prostitute as wife. Whether this happened literally or rather, as some wish, is to be understood only spiritually, matters little, provided it is established that he acted not through the sickness of incontinence but under the bond of obedience. [Col. 0624A] For in that marriage he obeyed a divine command and undoubtedly prefigured Christ. But it neither should nor can in any way be applied to Christ that Solomon is read to have committed fornication against God; having despised him from whom he had received such great gifts, he inclined his side to foreign women and moreover worshipped their gods.

Again, something is said to David as though concerning Solomon, which yet is most clearly proved not to apply to Solomon: “When your days are completed and you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you, which shall come forth from your womb, and I shall establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I shall establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (II Sam. VII). If anyone carefully considers this promise made to David, by which his seed is promised to be raised up—raised up, I say, not before his death but after it—he will find that Solomon is not announced in it, for Solomon was undoubtedly raised up before David’s death.

Divine Wisdom wisely arranged that Solomon was both born and reigned before his father’s death, something not read of any other king, so that this prophecy might not be fulfilled in him, since it says: “When you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed.” For it is not openly read of any of those other kings that he was appointed king before his father’s death, or named king by anyone.

Although, while King Uzziah was still living as a leper and dwelling apart because of his leprosy, his son Jotham, as it is written, governed the palace [Col. 0624C] and judged the people of the land, Jotham was nevertheless not called king, nor does divine Scripture declare that he reigned until his father Uzziah is declared to have been deprived of the gift of this life. Jotham could indeed preside by governing the palace and judging the people and nevertheless not be king, because not everyone to whom the ministry of judging is assigned immediately enjoys royal anointing and title.

Solomon, however, while David was still alive, was anointed king at Gihon; and when the people cried out, “Long live King Solomon” (III Kings I), he was from that time constantly called king and freely elevated to the royal throne. Thus the divine promise which declares that David’s seed would be raised up after his death is necessarily understood to be fulfilled not in Solomon but in Christ. Setting aside the literal sense, it is fulfilled in Christ by spiritual understanding: Christ, who was to be born temporally from David’s seed long after David and to reign eternally in his saints.

“I shall establish his kingdom,” he says; “he shall build a house for my name.” Lest this appear to have been said of Solomon, because Solomon built God a material house, he added: “And I shall establish the throne of his kingdom forever.” [Col. 0625A] As it is known to all that the throne of Solomon’s kingdom was not everlasting, so it is certain that Christ reigns forever; thus this prophecy is manifestly recognized to have foretold him, although it seems to allude to Solomon.

What follows—“If he does anything wickedly, I shall rebuke him with the rod of men; but I shall not take my mercy away from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I removed from my presence”—is nevertheless truly referred to Christ, but according to the property of his members alone, in whose voice he says in the Psalm: “The words of my offenses are far from my salvation” (Ps. XXI).

A threefold manner of understanding may indeed be found in the books of the prophets—indeed, in all Scripture called the Old Testament—so that some things are suitably understood only literally, others only spiritually, and others in both ways at once; and not everything is to be interpreted in any single way according to each person’s preference. This is, in my view, why some people often stumble in the divine Scriptures: they insist that Scripture must be understood according to their own sense, and, because they do not weigh sufficiently carefully the things they say or affirm, defend their error with a verbosity less truthful than insolent.

Because they seem to themselves rather keen in understanding and perhaps are somewhat ready in speaking, they disdain to submit to their elders in speaking; impatient to leave the nest, before they have grown feathers they rush forth to argue. This, I think, is why different people think differently about Solomon, and why many dissent from canonical Scripture, whose authority is fixed: they do not plainly agree with those who have understood it and expounded what they understood.

Therefore I judged it fitting, in this response which I have undertaken to give the brothers concerning Solomon, to compile what the elders have thought and said about him, and to confirm by their testimony the things I shall say about him. But first I wish to recount what canonical Scripture says concerning him—only such things as seem relevant to the present response.

After the death of the little son whom Bathsheba bore King David through adultery, “David,” it says, “comforted Bathsheba his wife. He went in to her and slept with her. And she bore a son and called his name Solomon, and the Lord loved him. And he sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet and called his name Beloved of the Lord, because the Lord loved him.” In Hebrew, as they say, it reads: “He called his name Jedidiah,” that is, “beloved because of the Lord.”

Concerning this, Hebrew tradition holds that God loved him because of his own mercy, although Solomon was not worthy of divine love, being born from that woman whom David had taken as wife contrary to the Lord’s advantage. But in being called beloved because of God, he whom I think is signified: he of whom the Gospel says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XII). For even that man whom the Word of God assumed to himself in unity of person had merited nothing either to be assumed or to be loved. Thus whatever the one assuming bestowed on the one assumed, the assumed person ascribed not to merits but to grace. Of him the prophet foretold: “Blessed is he whom you chose and assumed” (Ps. LXIV). Blessed indeed was he who was chosen without choosing, so that to him also may be said what was said to us: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV).

As time went on and David became old, at his command Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anointed Solomon king over Israel, leading him to Gihon. And while David was still alive in Jerusalem, Solomon reigned. Thus, when the king’s servants entered and said to him, “May God make Solomon’s name greater than your name,” the king, it says, worshipped upon his bed and moreover spoke these words: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who has today given one sitting upon my throne, while my eyes see it” (III Kings I).

After David had entered upon the way of all the earth: “The kingdom,” it says, “was established in Solomon’s hand, and he joined himself in affinity to Pharaoh, king of Egypt. For he took Pharaoh’s daughter and brought her into the City of David, until he should finish building his own house, the house of the Lord, and the wall around Jerusalem. Yet the people sacrificed in the high places, for no temple had been built for the name of the Lord up to that day. Therefore Solomon loved the Lord, walking in the precepts of David his father, except that he sacrificed in the high places” (III Kings III).

They seem to me, in these words, to set forth together both Solomon’s evils and his good qualities. For in that, once the kingdom had been established [Col. 0626C] in his hand, he entered into an alliance with Pharaoh, taking Pharaoh’s daughter and bringing her into the City of David, he sinned seriously. For he had read that the Lord, through Moses, had forbidden the sons of Israel to unite in marriage with the daughters of foreigners, lest, enticed by feminine blandishments and led astray into their idolatry, they fall away. If anyone objects that Moses too is said to have had Zipporah, daughter of Reuel, and likewise the Ethiopian woman—that is, Tharbis, daughter of the king of the Ethiopians—for whose sake Miriam and Aaron were later charged with murmuring; and that Joseph also, in Egypt, took as wife the daughter of Potiphar, a priest, the answer will be that no such law had yet been given by the Lord; and where there is no law, neither is there transgression.

But after the law had been given [Col. 0626D], Samson is rebuked by his parents because he loved a woman of the daughters of the Philistines whom he had seen at Timnah, and sought her as his wife. “Is there no woman,” they say, “among the daughters of your brethren and among all your people, that you wish to take a wife from the Philistines, who are uncircumcised?” Since he could find no just excuse for this, he gave only the reason that is almost always evil: his own will. For he said to his father: “Take her for me, because she has pleased my eyes.” Let law and reason cease, he says: so I will; let will stand in place of reason.

But in what is added concerning Solomon—“until he had finished building his own house, and the house of the Lord, and the wall around Jerusalem” [Col. 0627A]—he indeed acted well, for he built the mystical temple for the Lord as commanded, and enclosed the city of Jerusalem with a wall. “Nevertheless,” it says, “the people were sacrificing in the high places.” Again, this is the fault not only of the people, who sacrificed in the high places, but also of Solomon, who did not recall the erring people. Leaving the city of Jerusalem, where the Ark of the Lord had been placed in the midst of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it, the people sought high places for sacrifice, prompted not by the holiness of the places but delighted by their pleasantness.

The following statement seems in some measure to excuse this deed, and, as though it were not a sin—or rather, as though it were a slight sin—to cloak it: “For the temple had not yet been built to the name of the Lord until that day.” [Col. 0627B] Yet this was not said as though such conduct were commendable before the Temple’s construction, but because after the Temple had been built the sin was greater and altogether inexcusable. For this noble Temple was commanded to be built with such varied workmanship, adorned with such great plates of gold, and dedicated with such festive solemnity, so that the people might gather there to worship and sacrifice; and both the Temple’s holiness might invite them and its wonderful structure delight them. Therefore, one who afterward sought high places for sacrifice, now having no excuse, deserved greater condemnation.

It follows: “Therefore Solomon loved the Lord, walking in the commandments of David his father.”

Here again is Solomon’s righteousness: namely, that he is said [Col. 0627C] to have loved the Lord and walked in David’s commandments. But that he did not yet love the Lord perfectly, nor walk perfectly in David’s commandments, the divine discourse seems to indicate when it adds: “Except that he sacrificed in the high places.” For this is found neither to have pleased the Lord nor to have been commanded by David. There is no doubt that this sacrifice is reproved, since it is judged an exception to love of God and to David’s commandments.

Moreover, Solomon did many other things which undoubtedly pleased God, and which David had commanded before he died. Then it is said that the Lord appeared to Solomon by night in a dream, saying: “Ask what you wish me to give you.” And Solomon said: [Col. 0627D] “You will give your servant a teachable heart, that he may be able to judge your people and distinguish between good and evil.” Therefore the saying pleased the Lord, because Solomon had asked for such a thing. And God said to Solomon: “Because you asked for this word, and 364 did not ask for yourself many days, nor riches, nor the lives of your enemies, but asked for wisdom to discern judgment: behold, I have done for you according to your words, and have given you a wise and understanding heart, so that none before you has been like you, nor shall any arise after you. Moreover, I have given you even those things which you did not ask: riches and glory, so that among all kings in former days none has been like you. But if you walk in my ways, as David your father walked, I will make your days long.” Therefore [Col. 0628A] Solomon awoke and understood that it was a dream (3 Kings 3).

Here again are Solomon’s righteousness and honorable desire: namely, in that he asked for wisdom to discern judgment. God, in the goodness that is his own, not only granted what had been sought, but also added by free generosity what he had not sought—riches, namely, and glory. Yet I confess, your love, I am troubled; I say, I am troubled by what is added: “Therefore Solomon awoke and understood that it was a dream.” After this follow the great and splendid works Solomon performed in judging, in writing, in building the Temple of the Lord and its vessels, and the many other things enumerated in the Third Book of Kings and highly commended by the testimony of that Scripture.

How perceptive he was in rendering judgment after receiving wisdom in a dream is shown by the dispute of those harlots [Col. 0628B], one of whom said, “Your son is dead, but mine is alive,” while the other replied in turn: “You lie; my son is alive, and your son is dead” (ibid.). To end this contention, the king ordered a sword brought to him and the living infant divided into two parts, so that one half might be given to one woman and the other half to the other. At hearing this, a mother’s entrails were moved, and she who truly was the mother preferred that the whole infant should remain alive with her rival rather than possess half of him herself. Therefore she said: “I beseech you, my lord, give her the living infant, and do not kill him” (ibid.). Conversely, the other woman, whose heart was not softened by maternal affection, said: [Col. 0628C] “Let him be neither mine nor yours, but let him be divided” (ibid.). At this the king, the mist of doubt now dispelled and truth’s face recognized by such a test, said: “Give her the living infant and do not kill him, for she is his mother” (ibid.).

His subtlety in writing is shown by those three books which canonical authority receives into the catalogue of the divine Scriptures: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. In the first he is ethical, as he forms us in good morals; in the second, physical, as he declares that the things under the sun are naturally perishable; in the third, theological, as he joins us in an indissoluble embrace to God and our Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 0628D] In the first he teaches us to love our neighbor; in the second, to despise temporal things; in the third, to cling to heavenly things. In the first he instructs the untrained and the little ones; in the second he advances those somewhat more mature; in the third he raises those already advanced to the things that are heavenly. In the first he teaches us to behave well among human beings; in the second to scorn what lies below the human being; in the third to embrace what lies above the human being.

Finally, he himself is found to be called by three names, to which these three books seem suited. For he was called Idida, that is, “beloved by men”; Ecclesiastes, that is, “preacher”; and Solomon, that is, “peaceful.” Because in the first book he taught how a person should conduct himself blamelessly among other persons—what compassion he should show to inferiors, what humility [Col. 0629A] to equals, what reverence to superiors, and what love to all—this being very useful and sufficiently easy for human beings, he pleased human beings greatly; and he was called by the name whose reality he attained in writing.

In the second book he delivered a sermon—that is, he invited all people collectively to despise temporal things, by showing that those temporal things are perishable and short-lived, and asserting that everything begotten under the sun hastens toward destruction. And because he preached—that is, he did not speak as though in some corner of a house, but publicly addressed all—he was rightly called Ecclesiastes, that is, “Preacher.”

In the third book, whose title is the Song of Songs, he surpasses the dignity of the others, in that he leads us, cleansed from vices and strengthened in contempt for temporal things, into the bridal chamber; and, placing Christ’s left hand beneath us and drawing his right hand over us, he delightfully conceals us in his embrace. Thus righteousness, enduring sweat and cold, runs swiftly ahead; peace, rejoicing triumphantly, festively comes to meet it; and lest it ever grow faint through lack of reward, it happily comes to its aid by counting. These two virtues rejoice together in their mutual meeting, rush into kisses, and what is written comes to pass: “Righteousness and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84).

When, however, Solomon wrote of that peace which is counted as righteousness, rejoicing in the divine vision after being brought into the bridal chamber, he is not inappropriately called Solomon—that is, “peaceful”—prefiguring him who became our peace and, making both one, reconciled [Col. 0629C] us to God through his death, so that we who by our own nature were children of wrath might through grace become children of mercy.

Furthermore, as it is written, he discoursed concerning trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that comes forth from the wall; and he treated of beasts, creeping things, and fish. This Scripture is found neither among us nor among the Hebrews nor anywhere else, though there is no doubt that it once existed. There are, however, two books whose reading is frequent in our Church, one called the Wisdom of Solomon, the other Ecclesiasticus. Because of some similarity of style, some suppose that Solomon wrote them; but those who are older and wiser judge this opinion false.

Indeed, the first of them, namely the Wisdom of Solomon, has, as Jerome says, a Greek eloquence [Col. 0629D]; and, since it is nowhere found among the Hebrews, is affirmed to have belonged not to Solomon but to a certain Philo. Ecclesiasticus, however, is said to have been written by Jesus son of Sirach, who is found to have lived in the time of Simon the high priest. This Simon succeeded the high priest Onias and preceded another Onias—namely, the Onias whom Andronicus, at Menelaus’s instigation and without fear of justice, murdered, as the Second Book of Maccabees shows.

As for his prudence in building the Temple of the Lord and its vessels, the construction itself, if carefully considered, indicates how great it was: according to the letter, no mean beauty appears in it; and according to the spiritual understanding, a wonderful loftiness stands forth. [Col. 0630A] He is said to have received knowledge of this matter through God’s inward infusion and through the outward instruction of his father David. He is also found to have completed the work with the cooperation of many, both foreigners and natives.

That God taught him is made plain by the Third Book of Kings, which says: “God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding, and breadth of heart like the sand that is on the shore of the sea” (3 Kings 4); and shortly afterward: “God gave Solomon wisdom, as he had spoken to him” (3 Kings 5). That David carefully instructed him for accomplishing the aforesaid work is plainly shown by the First Book of Paralipomenon: “David,” it says, “gave Solomon his son the plan of the porch and the Temple, [Col. 0630B] and of the storerooms, upper chambers, inner rooms, and chambers of the inner sanctuary, and of all the courts and surrounding halls which he had devised, of the treasuries of the house of the Lord and the treasuries of the holy things, and of the divisions of priests and Levites for all the work of the house of the Lord, and for every vessel of service in the Temple of the Lord” (1 Paral. 2). David also gave Solomon, as follows in the same place, pure gold by weight and silver for making the vessels of the house of the Lord.

So that this plan might be regarded as commendable and might appear to have been given not from David himself but rather from God, David adds: “All these things came to me written by the hand of the Lord, that I might understand every work of the pattern” (ibid.).

Finally Scripture concludes, saying: “King [Col. 0630C] Solomon loved many foreign women, including Pharaoh’s daughter, and Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women, from the nations concerning whom the Lord had said to the children of Israel: ‘You shall not go in to them, nor shall they go in to yours, for they will certainly turn your hearts so that you follow their gods.’ Solomon, then, was joined to these women with most ardent love; and the women turned away his heart. When he was already old, his heart was corrupted by women so that he followed foreign gods. His heart was not perfect with the Lord his God as was the heart of David his father; but Solomon worshiped Astarte, goddess of the Sidonians, and Chemosh, god of the Moabites, and Moloch, idol of the Ammonites. [Col. 0630D] And Solomon did what did not please the Lord and did not fulfill the charge to follow the Lord, as David his father had done. Then Solomon built a shrine for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, on the mountain opposite Jerusalem, and for Moloch, the idol of the sons of Ammon. Therefore the Lord was angry with Solomon because his mind was turned away from the Lord God of Israel, who had commanded him not to follow foreign gods; and he did not keep what the Lord had commanded him. The Lord raised up an adversary against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite, of royal seed. Jeroboam also, son of Nebat, Solomon’s servant, raised his hand against the king. Solomon therefore wished to kill Jeroboam, but he fled into Egypt and remained there until Solomon’s death. The rest of Solomon’s words, and all that [Col. 0631A] he did, and his wisdom—behold, all are written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon’s Days. And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father” (3 Kings 11).

These are the final things found in canonical Scripture concerning Solomon. Though they seem open and plain, some nevertheless deserve consideration that is not superficial. In them we are warned and taught how the misery of humanity must be lamented, and the righteousness of God alone remembered and feared. For our righteousness is either nonexistent or almost worthy of being reckoned as nothing, because it can neither begin from itself nor attain completion through itself and in itself. Hence the prophet, as one having no righteousness, or perhaps as one forgetful or contemptuous of it: “Lord,” he says, “I will remember your righteousness [Col. 0631B] alone” (Ps. 70).

Who, then, reading or hearing that Solomon was supported by so many and such great goods—wisdom, power, riches, and glory, bestowed upon him by divine generosity—would not extol him with praises? Who would not judge him to have been happy, if only he had enjoyed that happiness without failure? But when one subsequently reads that this same man, now advanced in age, was plunged into the whirlpool of lust and, endowed with such great wisdom, fell into the error of idolatry—366 who would not lament the so unstable condition of human life? Who would not fear the so severe judgment of divine righteousness?

It remains, therefore, that whoever glories should glory not in himself but in the Lord, remembering what is written: no one can “be continent unless God grants it”; and therefore, “I went,” he says, “and implored the Lord” [Col. 0631C] (Wisdom 8).

As I see it, not even the strength of a diamond remains firm unless God preserves it by his merciful protection. Hence, according to the Septuagint interpreters, the prophet Amos saw the Lord standing upon a diamond wall, and holding a diamond in his hand. The diamond is a precious stone of such strength, they say, that it is not harmed by hammer and anvil, not worn away by a file, not destroyed by fire, nor consumed by any passage of time. Yet the one that remains unconquerable against all these things cannot withstand the warmth of goat’s blood; if it is defiled by contact with it, all that strength is dissolved.

Accordingly, the Lord is fittingly said to hold a diamond in his hand and to be seen standing upon [Col. 0631D] a diamond wall, because unless that stone’s strength is fortified by his power, not one stone will remain upon another that will not be destroyed. The stone which did not fear the sound of hostile trumpets, which mocked the assaults of warriors, which did not yield to the attacks of ballistae—if it is sprinkled even slightly with goat’s blood, it trembles, falls, and is utterly shattered.

The diamond stone signifies any saint of wondrous strength; goat’s blood signifies the uncleanness of lust. Therefore, however strong anyone may be through gathered virtues, if he is stained by the blemish of lust alone, he falls, perishes, and is wholly enfeebled. It is not surprising, then, that Solomon, formerly supported by such a great abundance of virtues, afterward defiled by such unrestrained lust, fell grievously from evil into worse evil; so that he who did not take care to gird his loins with the belt of strength did not even fear [Col. 0632A] to depart from divine worship.

But perhaps we wonder why God permitted so grievous a sin in one whom he had first wished to adorn with so many virtues. Let us recall that the angel who, through excellence of holiness, was called Lucifer fell from heaven by divine permission. Yet the balance of divine equity is not to be accused on this account, but rather the unchangeable malice of the one who fell is useful. Therefore we should not investigate why God permitted it to happen thus, but should know with fear that God permitted it to happen thus. For by a hidden but just judgment he permits the diamond not to be snatched from his hand, but to slip away; and although the hand that holds it is sufficiently strong to preserve it, the very will of the slipping one nonetheless suffices for its fall. Once slipped away, although it thinks itself able somehow to repel other assaults, [Col. 0632B] it cannot remain unharmed in resisting goat’s blood.

This is very suitably applied to Solomon, who, though he seemed for a long time to be held by the divine hand, at last slipped away and descended into so many crimes that he neither remembered having been there nor, rather, feared being far from it. Therefore let what I said—that Scripture introduces this at the end—be considered a little more carefully, so that, with the Lord’s help, the way it should be understood may appear. For a past course of life, however splendid, is in some manner weighed by its end; and it is not those who at one time lived well, but those who have persevered, who are commended.

“The king,” it says, “Solomon loved many women, including Pharaoh’s daughter, Moabite and Ammonite women, Hittite, Edomite, and Sidonian women, concerning whom the Lord had said: ‘You shall not go in [Col. 0632C] to them.’” I am troubled why, when divine Scripture has made known to us generally the foreign women whom Solomon is reproved for loving—Moabite women, Ammonite women, and the rest—it has singled out Pharaoh’s daughter. It seems to me to have done this either because Solomon is not read to have taken any Egyptian woman except her; or because he must be believed to have loved her more than the others; or because he is found to have had her earlier and much longer than the others.

For it was said above that, once his kingdom was established in his hand, before he dreamed that he would become wise, he entered into an alliance with Pharaoh, took his daughter, and brought her into the City of David. Although Scripture there does not openly rebuke him for this alliance, nor does he then appear to have forsaken his God because of her or worshiped foreign gods, yet at the end it is made sufficiently plain that he is judged worthy of rebuke on account both of her and of the others. For Pharaoh’s daughter would not be placed among those whom he is reproved for loving unless it were proved that he sinned in loving her too.

For when Scripture says that “Solomon loved foreign women, including Pharaoh’s daughter,” [Col. 0632D] and the others whom it lists, it clearly indicates how and to what end he loved her and the rest by adding: “Solomon was joined to these with most ardent love of heart, and the women turned away his heart.” It follows: “When he was already old, his heart was corrupted by women.”

[Col. 0633A] A remarkable perversity is made known by experience: although the heat of sexual desire burns in adolescence and youth, it nevertheless cools in old age; and one who rages in the workshops of the loins while strengthened by the vigor of age is compelled by a certain law of nature to be silent when, in the passage of time, age bends toward old age. Thus, when a son was promised to Abraham already old, he replied: “Do you suppose that a son will be born to a centenarian, and that Sarah, ninety years old, will give birth?” (Gen. 17). And shortly afterward Sarah herself said: “After I have grown old,” 367 she said, “and my lord is aged, shall I devote myself to pleasure?” (Gen. 18).

That is to say: when the incitements of the flesh have already cooled with advancing age, how shall we again perform the offices of pleasure? In this it is evident that Abraham and Sarah came together not so much from a desire for intercourse as from hope and desire for procreation. Finally, when David grew old and had, as Scripture says, many years of age, a young virgin was sought for him, that she might warm him and, sleeping with him, keep him warm. Abishag the Shunammite was found, a girl exceedingly beautiful, who slept with the king and ministered to him; “but the king,” it says, “did not know her.” [Col. 0633B] You see a virgin at the beginning of puberty sleeping with the king without loss of virginity, because the king, being far removed from the boundaries of youth, was free from lust through the protection of old age. But Solomon, when old and by natural law already bound to grow cold, burned with lust in a perverse order; and he was so corrupted by love of women that he even followed their gods.

“And his heart,” it says, [Col. 0633C] “was not perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father.” This perfection, which divine Scripture says Solomon lacked, is also read to have been lacking in certain other kings, who, although they performed great and splendid works, did not remain in the same purpose. Of Abijah, son of Rehoboam, it is said that his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God. That Abijah also, whose heart was not perfect, was reprobate is plainly shown by the very text of the history, which says: “He walked in all the sins of his father which he had committed before him.”

His father was Rehoboam, of whom it is said in Paralipomenon that, when Rehoboam’s kingdom had been strengthened and fortified, he forsook [Col. 0633D] the law of the Lord, and all Israel with him. And finally it is added that he did evil and did not prepare his heart to seek the Lord. If, therefore, Abijah walked in all his father’s sins, it is clearly established that, like his father, he did not end his life well.

Of Amaziah likewise it is read that he did what was good in the sight of the Lord, yet not with a perfect heart. That he did not act with a perfect heart is plainly indicated when it adds: “But after Amaziah had slain the Edomites and brought in the gods of the sons of Seir, he set them up as gods for himself, worshiped them, and burned incense to them” (2 Paral. 25). You see that these two kings, by Scripture’s testimony, had reprobate lives, whose heart is said not to have been perfect with God.

Finally, when Scripture wished to commend King Asa [Col. 0634A], son of the same Abijah whom I have just mentioned, it says: “Nevertheless Asa’s heart was perfect with God all his days” (2 Paral. 15). In this perfection I see nothing other than perseverance, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10). For although Asa is found to have sinned at some time, he must nevertheless be believed to have ended his life well; otherwise it would not be said: “His heart was perfect with God all his days,” but perhaps, “perfect during some of his days.”

That Asa was perfect—that is, persevering—with God throughout all his days is indicated a little earlier in other words, where it is said of him: “Asa did what was right before the Lord, as David his father did” (2 Paral. 14). David, indeed, although he committed sin, did not utterly fall away from the way of righteousness; but, recalled to righteousness by divine regard, he was found to have finished in it. Hence David himself is frequently commended in the same Scripture of Kings, and his perfection is often brought forward either for the commendation of good kings or for the shame of evil ones.
