Of Jehoshaphat, the righteous son of Asa, it is read in Paralipomenon: “And the Lord was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the ways of David his father” (2 Paral. 17). Of Hezekiah, in both the Book of Kings and Paralipomenon, it is said: “He did what was pleasing before the Lord, according to all that David his father had done” (4 Kings 20). Of Josiah in the Book of Kings: “He did what was pleasing before the Lord [Col. 0634C] and walked in all the ways of David his father” (4 Kings 22); and in Paralipomenon: “He did what was right in the sight of the Lord and walked in the ways of David his father” (2 Paral. 34). But concerning Abijah, whom we said above to have been reprobate, the Book of Kings says: “His heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father” (3 Kings 15). Of Amaziah: “He did what was right, yet not as David his father did” (4 Kings 14). Of Ahaz: “He did not do what was pleasing in the sight of the Lord his God, as David his father did” (4 Kings 16).

You see that none of these kings is said to have had a perfect heart like David’s, or to have walked as [Col. 0634D] David walked, unless Scripture’s testimony identifies him as righteous; and this is denied to no one unless his life is judged reprobate. David’s likeness or perfection is ascribed to Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah, whom the divine discourse attests to have remained righteous. The same perfection is denied to Abijah, Amaziah, and Ahaz, whom the same Scripture declares to have been reprobate.

This perfection is frequently found in the books of Kings and Paralipomenon, and seems to be nothing other than persevering righteousness. Concerning it Jehoshaphat speaks in Paralipomenon: “When Jehoshaphat had appointed Levites, priests, and heads of families in Jerusalem, that they might judge the Lord’s cause and judgment for its inhabitants, 368 he commanded them, saying: ‘Thus you shall act in the fear of the Lord, faithfully and with a perfect heart’” [Col. 0635A] (2 Paral. 19). What does “Thus you shall act faithfully and with a perfect heart” mean except: You shall do well and bring it to completion? In saying “faithfully,” it signifies faith working through love; in “with a perfect heart,” perseverance is signified.

Hezekiah likewise, when the prophet Isaiah said to him, “Give orders to your house, for you shall die and not live,” turned his face to the wall and prayed to the Lord, saying: “I beseech you, Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart” (4 Kings 20). Recalling his past life and considering his present conscience, he saw that he had persevered in the Lord’s commandments up to that time; and therefore, although he wept, he rejoiced in such perfection.

To this same perfection, as it seems to me, David himself invites Solomon: “But you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a perfect heart” [Col. 0635B] (1 Paral. 28). But because this is not fulfilled by human effort unless divine grace gives aid, David himself prays to God, saying: “Lord God of Abraham, give a perfect heart to Solomon my son” (1 Paral. 29). He also prays for himself in the Psalms: “Make my steps perfect in your paths” (Ps. 16).

If this perfection is perseverance, as it seems to be, then perseverance appears to have been lacking in Solomon—unless perhaps he alone is exempted from what is found to be ascribed only to reprobate kings. For if the list of the kings of Judah from David to Zedekiah, who was the last king, is reviewed, none of them, as I have carefully considered, is denied to have had a perfect heart with his God like David’s unless, as I said shortly before, his life is judged reprobate. Nor is anyone read to have had a perfect heart with God like David, or to have walked in David’s ways, unless he is known to have brought a good life to an excellent conclusion.

I wonder, then, whether it is perhaps vainly said of Solomon alone what is ascribed to other kings as evidence of condemnation: namely, that in his case alone the statement that his heart was not perfect with his God like David’s has no effect. If this is so, I am troubled by what is still added. For when Scripture had said of Solomon, “His heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as was David’s heart,” it shortly afterward added: “And he did not fulfill the charge to follow the Lord, as David his father did.” It did not say, “He did not begin to follow the Lord,” but “He did not fulfill the charge to follow the Lord.” [Col. 0635D] What does “fulfilled” mean? It seems to mean nothing other than: he did not complete it, did not bring it to an end, did not carry it through to the finish.

If he were affirmed to have done penance, certainly he would have fulfilled the charge to follow the Lord. For who fulfills the charge to follow the Lord except one who finds a good end? Or who finds a good end except one who fulfills the charge to follow the Lord? But if Solomon is said not at all to have fulfilled the charge to follow the Lord because he sinned while following him, David too could be said not to have fulfilled it, because he too sinned. Yet it seems impious to say this of David, since that same Scripture especially commends his fulfillment. For precisely in that Solomon is reproved [Col. 0636A] because he did not fulfill the charge to follow the Lord as David did, it is elegantly shown that David himself did fulfill the charge to follow the Lord. Otherwise it would not be said of Solomon, “He did not fulfill the charge to follow the Lord as David did,” but: “He did not fulfill the charge to follow the Lord, nor did David.”

It is established, then, that David fulfilled the charge to follow the Lord; but Solomon, as Scripture says, did not fulfill the charge to follow him. If, however, some other sense seems present in these words, which both maintains the rule of truth and yet does not conflict with Solomon’s salvation, I do not prejudge one who understands better, provided that what he says he can establish either from divine Scripture or by the testimony of the elders. It follows:

“Then Solomon built a sanctuary for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, on the mountain opposite Jerusalem, and for Moloch, the idol of the children of Ammon.” Since Scripture had said that his heart had been corrupted by women so as to follow foreign gods, it now says how he followed them, plainly in order to show that he was not merely corrupted but also a corrupter of others. “He built,” it says, “a sanctuary for Chemosh on the mountain opposite Jerusalem.” It was not enough for him to incline himself to foreign women unless he also worshipped their gods and invited others to worship them. For this purpose he built Chemosh’s sanctuary: so that the people might gather there and, prompted by the royal example, openly devote themselves to the worship of demons.

For who among the people, seeing the wisest of kings build a sanctuary and bend his knees to demons, would not be stirred up to the same sacrilege [Col. 0636C]—especially since that people is always recorded as having been prone to it? For if you wish to review the ancient Scriptures, you will find that people exceedingly stiff-necked, forgetful of divine worship, and repeatedly fallen into idolatry; and although recalled from it by divine scourges, nevertheless frequently relapsing into the same thing. Thus, taking occasion from the king, the people of God became idolaters; abandoning the temple established by the Lord’s command on Mount Moriah, those same people worshipped the idol Chemosh in the sanctuary which the king had built on the mountain opposite Jerusalem.

And appropriately that sanctuary is said to have been situated on the mountain opposite Jerusalem: so that, just as one worship was opposed to the other, so one mountain might be called opposed to the other mountain. For the temple of the Lord stood on Mount Moriah. Such is the astonishing envy of the ancient enemy: since he cannot possess the same things as God, he at least wishes to possess a daughter. Therefore, because he saw divine worship being celebrated on a mountain, he wished a sanctuary to be dedicated to himself on a mountain, so that the Lord’s temple might in some measure be overshadowed by his sanctuary, and Mount Moriah pressed down by an opposing mountain. This is surely what he boasts in his heart: “I will sit,” he says, “on the mountain of the covenant, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV).

And it should be observed that the mountain on which the Lord’s temple was built was called Moriah—that is, “the mountain of vision”—whereas the mountain on which Chemosh’s sanctuary stood was called the mountain of offence. For since God deigns to behold those who make offerings to him in his temple, that place is rightly [Col. 0637A] adorned with such a name, so that the truth of the matter may be shown in the very word and the devotion of those making offerings strengthened by the hope of being seen by God. This is indeed the mountain on which God, by reason of Abraham’s obedience, beheld him offering his son Isaac; whence, as it is written, “To this present day it is said: On the mountain the Lord will see” (Gen. XXII). But the mountain on which Solomon built Chemosh’s sanctuary was rightly called the mountain of offence, because there God is offended, as are the worshippers of the divine religion.

These are the high places which Solomon is found to have left to posterity as a memorial of his error, and which, long afterward, Josiah, that most righteous king, is recorded to have destroyed. “And in this manner,” it says, “he did for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.” This shows [Col. 0637B] that he made sanctuaries or idols not for one gentile god only but for many; that he worshipped not one but many. For when it is said that he acted in this manner for all his foreign wives, it is evident that, in order to satisfy the wishes of all those for whose love he was wasting away, he worshipped their gods, voluntarily conquered by error. From this too it follows that he did not love Pharaoh’s daughter without fault, and that on her account he worshipped Egyptian gods, as he did the rest.

It follows: “Therefore the Lord was angry with Solomon, because his mind had turned away from the Lord God of Israel, and because he had not kept the things which the Lord commanded him.” After these words, nothing is read in canonical Scripture about Solomon by which his repentance can be plainly demonstrated, or even to some extent inferred.

[Col. 0637C] Since, then, I have said as much as I could concerning the preceding chapter—what seemed to me right—I now think it necessary to show by what testimonies my statement is supported, lest perhaps I seem to begrudge Solomon salvation and for that reason twist the Scriptures presumptuously according to my own desire rather than truthfully. For I know that some are deeply troubled if Solomon’s repentance is denied; they are more ready to believe the talkative report which they hear Jews chattering and spreading than what ecclesiastical teachers are found to affirm in their writings.

Isidore, bishop of Seville, after briefly treating allegorically matters recorded before this chapter concerning Solomon—namely, the building of the temple, Solomon’s wisdom in which he flourished as a writer, the judgment of the harlots, and the queen of the South—concluded at the end:

“But what shall I say now concerning the rest of his works, when holy Scripture vehemently rebukes and condemns him, and makes no mention whatsoever either of his repentance or of God’s forgiveness toward him? Nor does it occur at all what good this lamentable submersion of his might signify even allegorically, unless perhaps someone should say that the foreign women for whose love he burned signify churches chosen from among the Gentiles. This might perhaps be understood without absurdity, if they had abandoned their gods because of Solomon and worshipped his God. But since he himself offended his God because of them and worshipped their gods, there is no good that can be conjectured from this. Yet I do not think that nothing is signified, but rather evil, as we said concerning Lot’s wife and daughters. There appears [Col. 0638A] in the person of this Solomon a marvellous excellence and a marvellous submersion. Therefore what existed in him at different times—good earlier and evil later—is shown in the Church, still in this present age, simultaneously at one time. For by his good, I think, the good people of the Church are signified; by his evil, the evil people of the Church: as in the unity of one ark, or as in that one man, good people in the grain and evil people in the chaff; or in the unity of one harvest, good people in the wheat and evil people in the tares.”

When Isidore says that holy Scripture makes no mention whatever either of Solomon’s repentance or of God’s forgiveness toward him, he sufficiently shows that in Scripture itself Solomon’s repentance can neither be plainly understood nor in any degree secretly inferred. When he says below that in Solomon good existed first and evil [Col. 0638B] later, he plainly intends us to understand that Solomon began well and ended badly. For he did not say: “In him good existed first, evil later, and good again”—which he certainly would have said had he wished to establish Solomon’s repentance. Rather, he says, good existed in him first and evil later, and he says nothing again of his good.

Moreover, in order that this same Isidore might commend both these matters and the others scattered throughout the whole body of his little book by the authority of the elders, he says thus in the preface to the entire work:

“These things, therefore, have been taken from the authors Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Cassian, Fulgentius, and Gregory, outstandingly eloquent in our own times.”

Whether, however, all these 370 men spoke about Solomon, or what they said of him, I have not yet discovered with certainty, for I have not read all their books. Indeed, I do not remember having yet read any book of Victorinus; of the others I have read not all, but a number. Whatever, therefore, I have found about Solomon in their books, or even in those of some others, I shall bring forward—provided that importunate forgetfulness has not erased what reading at one time supplied to me.

Origen, in the twentieth homily on the book of Numbers, speaking of Solomon, says:

“If you reread what has been written about Solomon, you will find that, although he was very wise, he inclined himself to many women. Therefore, although he was very wise and possessed great merits before God, yet because he gave himself over to many women, he was deceived. I think [Col. 0638D] that the many women are called many doctrines and the diverse philosophies of many nations. Since, as a man most learned and most wise, he wished to know and investigate each one, he could not keep himself within the rule of divine law; rather, Moabite philosophy deceived him and persuaded him to sacrifice to the Moabite idol—likewise the philosophies of the Ammonites and of the remaining nations. It is therefore a great thing, and truly the work of God, to associate with so many doctrines as though with women and yet not depart from the rule of truth, but steadfastly to say: ‘There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number; yet my dove is one’” (Cant. VI).

In these words of Origen, no repentance of Solomon is heard of; rather, he is declared to have been deceived because he gave himself to many women and could not keep himself within the rule of divine law. “And therefore,” he says, “it is a great thing, and truly the work of God, to associate with so many doctrines as though with women, yet not depart from the rule of truth, but steadfastly to say: ‘There are sixty queens and eighty concubines; yet my dove is one.’” By this he seems to imply that Solomon indeed said this, but did not say it steadfastly. To speak steadfastly is nothing other than to persevere to the end.

Hence Bede, commenting on Luke, says: “It is not the beginning of endurance but perseverance which bestows the glory of the heavenly kingdom; for perseverance, which is also called constancy, is a certain strength and fortitude of mind and the pillar of all virtues.”

The same Origen, in his twenty-seventh homily on Luke, in which he shows that Matthew and Luke could have had different authors for Christ’s genealogy, says:

“In Matthew there is named the wife of Uriah, who violated her husband’s bed. Since our Lord and Savior had come for this purpose, to take upon himself the sins of human beings, he therefore descended into the world, took on the persons of sinful and vicious human beings, and wished to be born from the stock of Solomon, whose sins are written down, and of Rehoboam, whose offences are related. But when he rises from the washing-bath and is described as born a second time, he is born not through Solomon but through Nathan, who rebuked his father concerning Uriah’s death and Solomon’s birth.”

In these words too Origen quite plainly accuses Solomon, just as he accuses Rehoboam, and excuses him by no assertion of repentance. Matthew, whose purpose was to trace Christ’s line of birth by descending from those above to those below, wished to insert into that genealogy the persons of vicious human beings, in order to show him born from sinners who came in the flesh to condemn sin. Thus he named Solomon and Rehoboam, “whose sins,” as Origen says, “are written down.”

But Luke, ascending from those below to those above, describes Christ not as descending into the world but as ascending from the washing-bath of baptism; beginning the genealogy with Joseph, he carries it all the way to God himself. For after saying of the baptized Christ, “Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, who was of Heli, who was of Matthat, who was of Levi,” he runs upward [Col. 0639D] in sequence and completes the list of names by saying, “who was of Shem, who was of Adam, who was of God.” Therefore, in this catalogue, to which he wished to assign God as end or boundary, Luke was unwilling to insert Solomon and Rehoboam, lest the rope which is brought to completion by so holy an end should be defiled by the insertion of Solomon, whose sins are written down. In his place he inserted Nathan the prophet, who is not merely free from rebuke but rebuked David, Solomon’s royal father, for presumptuous conduct.

Some, however, maintain that Nathan the prophet, who rebuked David over Uriah’s death, was not David’s son but the son of Shammah, David’s brother. They say that he is also called Jonathan by another name; but when he is called a prophet, he is not called Jonathan, but Nathan only. Nevertheless David fathered a son Nathan; whether this Nathan was a prophet or not, Luke inserted him in his genealogy in place of Solomon.

Augustine, in the second exposition of Psalm 89, says:

“God promised something eternal from his seed, and Solomon was born. He became a man of such wisdom and prudence that God’s promise concerning David’s seed was thought fulfilled. But Solomon fell, and gave occasion to hope for Christ. Here God was about to say to you: ‘I swore indeed and promised, but this man was unwilling to persevere.’ What then? Lord God, did you not foreknow that he would not persevere? Certainly you knew it. Why, then, did you promise me in one who would not persevere something which was to be eternal?” [Col. 0640B]

The same Augustine, in his exposition of Psalm 126, says:

“Solomon was a lover of women and was rejected by God. But if, when he fell, the things spoken through him are erased, it would be judged that they were spoken by him, not through him.”

You see that Augustine, in the psalm previously cited, says that Solomon did not persevere, and in the following one that he was rejected by God, although what he wrote was not rejected.

The same Augustine, in Book XVII of *The City of God*, speaks thus of David and Solomon:

“David reigned in the earthly Jerusalem, a son of the heavenly Jerusalem, greatly commended by divine testimony, because even his great offences were overcome by such piety through the most health-giving humility of repentance that he is altogether among those of whom he himself says: ‘Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered’ (Ps. XXXI). After him Solomon, his son, reigned over the same whole people, beginning to reign while his father was still alive. He had good beginnings and bad endings; for the favorable circumstances which wear out the minds of the wise harmed him more than wisdom itself benefited him—a wisdom memorable even now and thereafter, and then praised far and wide.”

Augustine could not have pronounced a clearer judgment concerning Solomon than by saying: “He had good beginnings and bad endings.” He certainly would not have said this had he known Solomon repented. For if he truly repented at the end, he had not bad but good endings. Finally, before his death, after having been trained in the divine Scriptures for forty years, Augustine carefully reviewed the books he had written from the beginning of his conversion until that time. Finding two hundred and thirty-two, besides his letters and popular discourses, he gathered into one volume everything in them which seemed worthy of criticism, partly by criticizing it and partly by defending and explaining how it ought to be understood. He therefore reviewed *The City of God* among the rest, yet did not judge worthy of correction what he had said concerning Solomon. Had he, over so great a span of time, perceived Solomon’s repentance either from canonical Scripture or from the truthful writings of the preceding Fathers, he either would not have said that Solomon had bad endings or would without doubt have censured that statement.

[Col. 0641A] Pope Gregory, who is known to have been far removed from Augustine in rank and time, is found to have assented to the same opinion. For he says in the second book of *Moralia*:

“The end of an action is expressed by the quality of its time. Thus Judas is said to have gone out by night to the faithlessness of betrayal, from which he would not return; for when he went out, the Evangelist says: ‘And it was night’ (John XIII). Hence it is also said to the wicked rich man: ‘This night they demand your soul of you’ (Luke XII). A soul which is led into darkness is recalled not in the day, but is spoken of as recalled in the night. Hence Solomon, who received wisdom and was not going to persevere in it, is described as receiving it in sleep and at night.”

These are Gregory’s words. See, then, what he says: “He received wisdom, not going to persevere”; and therefore he received it in sleep and at night. That he intended this perseverance to mean the end, he makes sufficiently clear when he says: “The end of an action is expressed by the quality of its time.” That Judas and the wicked rich man ended badly is beyond doubt; this, Gregory says, is signified by the quality of the time. But if Solomon, whom he associates with them, returned through repentance to the light of true wisdom—to which, without doubt, every person who truly repents returns—then in Solomon’s case the quality of the time expresses not the end of the action but its middle.

When Gregory had said, therefore, “The end of an action is expressed by the quality of its time,” he ought not to have proved this by Solomon’s example, if Solomon’s action had a bright end through repentance. What therefore moves me is what I said above moved me: namely, what is meant by sacred Scripture’s saying: “Solomon awoke and understood that it was a dream” (III Kings III). While he was held in a happy sleep, perhaps he thought what he saw fixed and firm; but when he ceased sleeping, he understood that what he had seen was fleeting and transitory. What does this signify? What, I ask, except that he was not to remain in the wisdom he received while dreaming, just as he did not remain in the very sleep in which he was made wise?

For we do not remain in what we see in dreams; and we first know with certainty that we have slept when we cease to sleep. Happy, then, would Solomon have been had he never awakened: what he merited to obtain while dreaming he could not—indeed, would not—preserve while awake. The cessation of dreaming therefore suggests the cessation of wisdom; the night in which he found himself after awakening signifies the darkness of sins into which he came after becoming foolish.

Finally, you will scarcely find any saint who became wise by dreaming; indeed, whoever is found to have attained wisdom attained it only while awake. Although God spoke to some ancient fathers through visions or dreams, as he says to Aaron and Miriam: “If there be among you a prophet of the Lord, I will appear to him in a vision and speak to him in a dream” (Num. XII), nevertheless, unless I am mistaken, he is not recorded as having bestowed the gift of wisdom upon anyone while dreaming, lest he appear to encourage those seeking it not to study and diligence but to leisure and sleepiness.

Luke says concerning the apostles while awake: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV). John the Evangelist too, who drank streams of God’s word from the fountain of the Lord’s breast—for waters are drunk more pleasantly from that fountain—is not recorded as having slept upon Christ’s breast at the supper, but as having reclined there (John XXI).

In secular literature, I seem to remember, as though in a dream, reading that Ennius dreamed on Mount Parnassus and thus suddenly emerged as a poet. Hence that poet is not greatly commended by later generations; rather, in his writings and deeds alike, he is judged not merely to nod, as even good Homer sometimes did, but to sleep and snore feebly. Solomon’s wisdom, however commendable because it was granted by God, was of no benefit to him because he did not remain in it; for, to use Augustine’s words: “The favorable circumstances which wear out the minds of the wise harmed him more than wisdom itself benefited him, a wisdom memorable now and thereafter and then praised far and wide.” Pope Gregory affirms the same thing when, using Solomon’s example, he says that the end of an action is expressed by the quality of its time.

Fulgentius, in *Without the Letter* [Note: [Col. 0641D] That is, in the work *Without the Letter*. Concerning this Fulgentius, Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. II, p. 213, has the following:

“Fabius Claudius Gordianus Fulgentius, a man of consular rank, author of a prose work divided into twenty-three little books, entitled *A Marvellous Work on the Ages of the World and of Man, Without Letters*. For throughout the first book, on Adam, there is no letter A; in the second, on Abel, no B; in the third, on Cain, no C; and so in the rest. Jacobus Hommey published it from a Sorbonne manuscript—in which, as with Sigebert, ch. 28, it was incorrectly attributed to Fulgentius of Ruspe—and illustrated it with notes (*Journal des Savants*, 1694, p. 757), Poitiers, 1694, octavo. He also added a specimen of Peter of Riga’s recapitulations of the two Testaments in elegiac verse, which Polycarp Leyser published entire in his *History of Medieval Poetry*, pp. 705–727. Likewise, the first section or division contains no A, the second no B, and so on up to Z.

“[Col. 0642D] Nestor of Laranda had formerly written such a lipogrammatic *Iliad* (λειπογράμματον), with one letter omitted in each successive book, in Greek verse; and Tryphiodorus did so with an *Odyssey*. They are discussed in Book II, chapter 5 of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*. Sanderus, in Part II of the manuscript *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 23, cites another handwritten manuscript of Fulgentius’s work, but lacking the later books. In it he is called not Fabius, as by Hommey, but Flavius Claudius Gordianus Fulgentius. Yet Bollandus, using the same mutilated manuscript, also calls him Fabius, in vol. I for January, p. 972. The author acknowledges himself Libyan or African in more than one passage, and says that he undertook this work in imitation of the Greek poet Xenophon. Someone might conjecture that he was Claudius, son of Gordianus and father of Fulgentius of Ruspe, who returned to Africa from Italy, whence the fury of Genseric had driven out his father, and, despoiled of ancestral estates and home, might with good reason in Book I have inveighed against public plunder, etc.” These are Bollandus’s words.], Book VIII, without the letter H:

“My God, what does this so secret dispensation of your judgment mean? Why does the offspring of a stained crime enjoy the success of his father’s kingdom? Was it fitting that Solomon, defiled by the contagion of an adulterous womb, should either gain the merit of building the temple, [Col. 0643A] discover treasures of wisdom, or become successor to his father’s kingdom and greater in power? But see: the son of crime incurred crime, and the adulterous offspring did not come to a good end. Although he discourse from hyssop to the cedars of Lebanon, although he await the queen of the South admiring his wisdom, although he construct an ineffable temple, command spirits, abound in prudence, possess skill in judgments, shine with riches, gleam with gold, and blaze with jewels—yet in life he branded whatever he had drawn into himself from nature; and, worst of all, in old age he was no longer a most wise man, but an indecent worshipper of Gentile gods.”

When Fulgentius says that Solomon, the son of crime and adulterous offspring, did not come to a good end, he quite openly denies his repentance, adding how hostile Solomon’s old age was to religion: it was preserved not by prudence but, as he says, “defiled by indecent worship.”

Paschasius, deacon of the Roman Church, a man most thoroughly learned in divine writings, whose sanctity and learning Gregory commends in the fourth book of the *Dialogues*, speaks thus of Solomon:

“‘His seed shall remain for ever, and his throne as the sun before me; and as the moon it shall be perfect for ever, and a faithful witness in heaven.’ Therefore those who wish to understand this as said of Solomon should consider how his throne was like the sun before the sight of God the Father, when holy Scripture says that his heart was turned away because of desire for women, and that he worshipped Astaroth, Chemosh the god of the Sidonians, and the other monstrosities of the nations. Scripture finally concludes that God was not with Solomon. If, therefore, God was not with him, how did his throne shine as the sun before the sight of God the Father—especially since he was stained with every uncleanness of lust and condemned for idolatry? Or how was he a faithful witness in heaven, when he was found a false witness on earth by worshipping idols? But since this cannot possibly be understood of him, the enemy must, willing or unwilling, interpret it concerning Christ.”

These are Paschasius’s words concerning Solomon, in which he says both that Solomon was found a false witness on earth through worshipping idols, and that he was condemned for idolatry.

[Col. 0643D] Bede, a priest, who is found to have read the books of the preceding Fathers with such study and assiduity that he is found to have placed in his own writings many things exactly as they stand in theirs, when he was commending Josiah in the little book which he wrote to Nothelm, “the least,” on certain questions from the book of Kings, spoke thus:

“And the high places which were in Jerusalem, at the right side of the Mount of Offence, which Solomon king of Israel had built for Astaroth, the idol of the Sidonians, and Chemosh, the offence of Moab, the king—namely Josiah, of whom he was speaking—defiled and broke the statues.” And he added concerning Solomon: “Here, unless I am mistaken, it is shown—would that it were not shown—that Solomon never perfectly repented of the crime of idolatry which he had committed. For if he had produced fruits worthy of repentance, he would above all have laboured to have the idols which he had built removed from the holy city, rather than leave them as a scandal to fools, as things made by himself, when he was most wise, in error as though wisely and rightly made.”

Anglosmus and Rabanus, who came after Bede, also placed these same words, as they stand in Bede’s book, in their own books.

Since I have stated certain things which are found, clearer than light, to oppose Solomon’s repentance, I shall now set forth the opposing evidence—those things in which, as some wish, that repentance appears to be affirmed—lest I seem deliberately silent concerning what they refuse to leave unmentioned. For I found certain little leaves in which some statements had been written as testimony for his repentance, excerpted from works of the holy Fathers. I shall therefore bring forward what I found collected there, lest by silence I offend those who pity Solomon more than is right.

“What Saint Augustine, the eminent doctor, thought concerning King Solomon’s transgression; what Jerome, interpreter and expositor of the divine law, wrote about his repentance; and where Ambrose, defender of the Catholic faith, called him holy—I shall briefly make known.” Then it adds:

“In his literal exposition of Genesis, Book XI, Augustine says of him: ‘Solomon, a man of such great wisdom—must one believe that in the worship of images he thought there was any divinity? No. But he could not resist the ways of women drawing him to this evil, doing what he knew ought not to be done, lest he grieve his own deadly delights, for which he was wasting away and dissolving.’”

Augustine indeed says this in Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*. But whoever attends more carefully to the context of the passage will find in these words not Solomon’s excuse but his accusation. Augustine does not say this to prove that Solomon repented, but to show that he sinned prudently—that is, knowingly—since he undoubtedly knew that it ought not to be done, yet despised God and obeyed the will of women.

So too the first Adam sinned knowingly: though knowing that what the woman urged ought not to be done, he nevertheless did what he saw that she persistently wished, lest he grieve the companion he had received, whom he believed would waste away in sorrow if he did not grant her consent even in evil. Hence the Apostle says: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression” (I Tim. II): that is, she believed true what the serpent hissed, while he knew it false and nevertheless yielded.

For Augustine speaks in the aforementioned book about the very Adam whom the Apostle says was not deceived; and for Adam’s sake he brings Solomon forward, likewise asserting that Solomon was not deceived—that is, that he sinned not ignorantly but knowingly. He also makes this plain in Book XIV of *The City of God*, when he similarly speaks of Adam:

“Just as Aaron did not consent through persuasion to the people’s error in making an idol, but yielded under compulsion; nor is it credible that Solomon believed in error that idols should be served, but was compelled into those sacrileges by feminine blandishments: so we should believe that that man was induced to transgress God’s law in joining himself to the woman not because he was deceived into believing her words, but because he yielded to the bond of companionship.”

Lest Augustine seem to have excused Adam or them, he adds concerning Adam: “Yet no less guilty, if knowingly and deliberately …” Therefore, in these words no repentance is commended; rather, harmful knowledge is condemned, in accordance with the saying of the Apostle James: “To one who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin” (James IV).

Again, the little leaves say: Ambrose, in the book *Hexaemeron*, mentioning Solomon, says: “Know yourself, O human being: it is not, as they say, from Pythian Apollo, but from holy Solomon, who says, ‘Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women.’”

Again Ambrose, in the *Apology of David*: “What shall I say of David? What of holy Solomon? Since the Jewish crowd thought that he had come as Christ, he fell by divine ordinance, lest he seem to be above human nature.”

These are Ambrose’s words. Lest we should seem uncertain why Ambrose called Solomon most holy, the man who wrote these words in the little leaves added, as though on his own authority:

“David is not called holy, because everyone knows that he is holy; but Solomon is named holy for us, in order to remove from us uncertainty concerning his repentance.”

Gregory the pope says this concerning Aaron, whom David calls holy, in the seventh homily on the final part of Ezekiel the prophet, when he brings forward the verse from the Psalm: “They provoked Moses in the camp, Aaron the holy one of the Lord” (Ps. CV). “Moses,” he says, “is not called holy, because everyone knows that he is holy; but he calls Aaron holy in order to remove uncertainty concerning his life.”

Thus this man presumptuously attributes to Solomon what Gregory says concerning Aaron, although the same Gregory who gives Aaron the testimony of holiness denies Solomon’s repentance, as stated above.

Finally, Ambrose himself, in the same *Apology of David*, where he calls Solomon holy, nevertheless does not affirm his repentance. Indeed, if anyone wishes to examine more carefully, he will find Ambrose denying Solomon’s repentance. For Ambrose says:

“What shall I say of holy Solomon, whose later years were not without grave error, though the Jewish crowd thinks that he himself came as Christ? And how many people did the scandal of his grave error recall? Thus the greater fault was more beneficial, so that he might not be believed to be above humanity, since he was not free from human vice.”

When Ambrose says that Solomon’s later years were not without grave error, he plainly asserts that they lacked repentance; had they, as some contend, embraced it, they would without doubt have been free from grave error. The same Ambrose seems also to indicate why God permitted Solomon to sin thus at the end: namely, lest the people should think him Christ if he brought the holiness he had begun to its due conclusion.

Therefore, as Ambrose says, the scandal of this grave error recalled many people from error: by showing Solomon to be merely human, lest he be thought Christ. The fault serving the salvation of the elect was more beneficial than persevering righteousness, useful to one man but destructive to many. Therefore let it not trouble anyone that Ambrose calls Solomon holy in the places mentioned above, and even in certain others which it is unnecessary to seek out and produce, since it is enough to have found this once or twice.

Philip also, in his first book on Job, calls him holy: “For, as holy Solomon says, ‘The fruits of the ungodly are sins.’” Elsewhere in subsequent writings, and perhaps in other works of the Fathers, something similar may be found, if anyone wishes or is able to apply himself more carefully to reading. But, in my judgment, Solomon’s repentance is not proved by this; nor does his being called holy compel us to understand that he returned at the end [Col. 0646B] to the rule of holiness, but only that he had once been holy.

For just as Peter is called Satan—because he had in mind not the things of God but those of men—yet did not remain in that intention, so Solomon may rightly be called holy although he did not remain in the holiness he possessed. If anyone says that Peter is found called Satan only when he wished to oppose Christ, and, once the fault marked by that name had been rejected, is never afterwards called Satan, let him recall the Scriptures and heed reading, as the Apostle commands; he will find many called what they no longer were, but once had been.

When Judas Iscariot came to Jesus and kissed him, Matthew says: “Jesus said to him: [Col. 0646C] Friend, for what have you come?” (Matt. 26.) It is clear that he calls him friend whom he knew was no longer, but had once been, a friend. For it should not be believed that Judas had never loved Christ, although he did not remain at all in that love. For just as an unjust person is often converted through God’s mercy and becomes just, so conversely a just person is sometimes perverted through God’s abandonment and becomes unjust. This is declared in Ezekiel (ch. 28), where it is said: “If the wicked man does penance and performs judgment and righteousness, he shall live and shall not die. But if the just man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity in the transgression by which he has transgressed, and in the sin which he has committed, in those things he shall die.” Nor [Col. 0646D] should it be said what is added there: “The way of the Lord is not just” (ibid.).

But since it is not necessary, in order to prove this, to bring forward many testimonies from the Scriptures—when, in the unstable course of this life, we ourselves see it not so much read as happen—let it suffice to have said one thing, and let us return to the subject. When Matthew composed the catalogue of the apostles, he calls himself among the others “the tax collector”: “Philip,” he says, “and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew the tax collector.” Now tax collectors at that time were called those who did not fear to entangle themselves in public business—which can scarcely, or not at all, be conducted without sin—or in crimes and shameful acts; and who, scorning the discipline of good living, were permitted to carry out whatever disorderly thing pleased them, not by decree of law, but by decree of a perverse will. Yet far be it from us to suppose that Matthew was such when he wrote the Gospel and named himself a tax collector in it; but he was without doubt such when he sat at the customs-post. Afterwards, admonished by Christ’s call and inspiration, he abandoned both the customs-post and everything else that he either did or possessed wickedly; and, though the reality denoted by the word had been put aside, he did not lose the designation of that reality.

In the same Matthew the Lord says: “Pharisees, tax collectors, and sinners go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21). How, I ask, do tax collectors go before Pharisees in the kingdom of God, when, unless they have ceased to be tax collectors, they never enter it? Therefore he calls those men tax collectors who were tax collectors; and when they go before others into the kingdom of God—whether those others do not enter it or enter more slowly—they have undoubtedly ceased [Col. 0647B] to be tax collectors.

When Mark the Evangelist (ch. 2) spoke of this same Matthew’s calling, he said: “He saw Levi sitting at the customs-post and said to him: Follow me. And rising, he followed him. And it came to pass, when he reclined in that man’s house, that many tax collectors and sinners reclined together with Jesus and his disciples.” I do not think that these tax collectors and sinners reclining with Jesus in Matthew’s house were what they had formerly been. Rather, I think that they had received no small grace, since Christ called those whom he had judged worthy of his own table to repentance. Hence he answered the scribes and Pharisees when they murmured over this: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (ibid.). That is to say: I did not come to call you, who think yourselves righteous—though you are not—but [Col. 0647C] those who, by accusing themselves, have merited no longer to be what they were.

Luke the Evangelist says: “One of the thieves who were hanging blasphemed him, saying: If you are the Christ, save yourself and us. But the other answered and rebuked him, saying: Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation?” (Luke 23.) And he said to Jesus: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.” When Luke says that one of the thieves who were hanging blasphemed him and that the other rebuked him, he calls both the blasphemer and the one rebuking the blasphemer “thieves,” although the blasphemer was indeed held fast by the vice of theft, while the other was now no thief, [Col. 0647D] but was regarded as a most devoted confessor.

These things have been said because Ambrose calls Solomon holy; in this matter, so far as appears, he in no way contradicts the other teachers, among whom Augustine says: “This man had bad endings after good beginnings.” By saying this, Augustine clearly enough indicates that Solomon began well and ended badly; because of those beginnings Ambrose assigns him the name of holiness. Thus the divine word says that certain other kings, both of Judah and of Israel, had holy beginnings of reign, though it likewise declares that their endings were evil. For as the first works of Joash, Amaziah, and Uzziah, kings of Judah, are commended, so their last acts are certainly condemned. All the kings of Israel, whose first king after the division of the kingdom was Jeroboam son of Nebat and whose last was Hoshea son of Elah, are known to have been reprobate, though some of their deeds are commended.

To omit the rest: how greatly the divine word praises Jehu son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi, and how greatly subsequent reproach darkens him, may readily be heard if you will grant silence to the reader: “The Lord said to Jehu: Because you have zealously done what was right and pleasing in my eyes, and have done against the house of Ahab all that was in my heart, your sons to the fourth generation shall sit upon the throne of Israel” (4 Kings 10). And Scripture immediately adds: “After these things Jehu did not take care to walk in the law of the Lord God of Israel with all his heart; for he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam [Col. 0648B] who made Israel sin” (ibid.). Just as this King Jehu is first read to have performed works pleasing to God and then to have set upon those same works a detestable ending, so Scripture says likewise that Solomon at first pleased God, but at the end, when he had become old, incurred the divine wrath through women.

There follows in the *Foliola*: “Testimony concerning Solomon’s repentance.” This has been taken from a little book by a certain Bacchiarius, but his name is not given there. Bacchiarius indeed, in the little book which he writes to Januarius, while maintaining that one must not despair of a certain brother who had fallen into the pit of fornication, brings forward Solomon’s fall and repentance.

“Solomon,” he says, “that wonderful man who deserved [Col. 0648C] to be joined to God’s attendant—that is, Wisdom—fell into the embraces of foreign women; ensnared in the bond of lust, he also defiled himself by the error of sacrilege, because he made an image of Chemosh, the Moabite idol. But because through a prophet he acknowledged the fault of his error, is he therefore deprived of heavenly healing? But perhaps you will say: I never read in the canon that he repented or received forgiveness. Hear then, brother: some perhaps say that his repentance, which is not written in the books of the Law, was acceptable for this reason, that he repented not before the face of the people but in the secrecy of conscience, with God as witness. And we know that he received forgiveness from this: when he was released from the body, Scripture records that he was buried among the bodies of the Israelite kings. [Col. 0648D] Yet we know that this was denied elsewhere to sinful kings who remained in their chosen perversity to the end of life. Therefore, because he deserved to be buried among just kings, he was not excluded from forgiveness; and he could not have earned forgiveness itself without repentance.”

These are Bacchiarius’s words. “Because,” he says, “through a prophet he acknowledged the fault of his error, is he therefore deprived of heavenly healing?” I wonder in what manuscript Bacchiarius read that Solomon acknowledged his sin through a prophet and, through this acknowledgment, did penance, since he could not have found this at all in canonical Scripture. For if he reviews the books of Kings, Chronicles, or the other books which the Catholic Church reads as established by canonical authority, he will not find—unless I am mistaken—that any prophet either rebuked Solomon in sin or exhorted him to repent. Yet this he will be able to find concerning David, Asa, and certain other kings, both just and unjust.

Indeed, God is read to have spoken to Solomon four times, but no prophet appears as intermediary in any of these instances. Once the kingdom had been established in his hand, when he was at Gibeon: “The Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, saying: Ask what you wish me to give you” (3 Kings 3); and below: “When he had roofed the house which he was building with cedar ceilings, and had built a story over the whole house, the word of the Lord came to Solomon, saying: This house which you are building—if you walk in my commandments—I shall establish for you my word [Col. 0649B] which I spoke to David your father” (3 Kings 6), etc. Long afterward: “When Solomon had completed the building of the house of the Lord, the Lord appeared to him a second time, as he had appeared at Gibeon. And the Lord said to him: I have heard your prayer” (3 Kings 9), etc. Finally, when he had incurred divine displeasure through both lust and idolatry: “The Lord was angry with Solomon because his mind had turned away from the Lord his God and he had not kept the things which the Lord had commanded him. Therefore the Lord said to Solomon: Because you have held this in yourself and have not kept my covenant and my commandments which I commanded you” (3 Kings 11), etc.

Neither here nor anywhere else afterwards is Solomon read in canonical Scripture to have acknowledged his sin through a prophet, [Col. 0649C] so that by this means he should be thought to have found heavenly healing. Finally, when Ahijah the Shilonite prophet foretold to Jeroboam son of Nebat that he would reign over the ten tribes of Israel: “Ahijah took hold of his new cloak, tore it into twelve parts, and said to Jeroboam: Take ten torn pieces for yourself. For thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand and give you ten tribes, because he has forsaken me and has not 376 walked in my ways as David his father did; but I shall take you, and you shall reign” (ibid.). When Ahijah the Shilonite had finished speaking, Scripture adds: “Therefore Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam” (ibid.). From this it may be inferred that Solomon indeed knew what the prophet had said—namely, that Jeroboam would reign—but did not apply heavenly healing to his wound by that knowledge, since, guilty of envy and homicide, he wished to kill the man whom the divine will had appointed to reign. But Jeroboam “arose,” it says, “and fled into Egypt, and was in Egypt until Solomon’s death” (ibid.).

But if Bacchiarius wishes to appeal to Josephus, the writer of *Jewish Antiquities*, in order to defend with his authority what he asserts concerning Solomon, he will not find that Josephus says Solomon repented, even though Josephus says that a prophet came to him. Lest I seem unfairly to withhold Josephus from Bacchiarius, I shall bring forward Josephus’s words:

“Solomon,” he says, “bound by irrational [Col. 0650A] love, taking seventy wives and three hundred concubines, besides these also the daughter of the king of Egypt, was suddenly captured by them, so that he followed their worship as well. For, as age advanced and reason likewise weakened with time, when he could no longer maintain his father’s practices, he continually honoured the god of two of his wives. Therefore a prophet came, sent by God, saying that his iniquity was not hidden from him and that he would not long rejoice in these things. On hearing this, Solomon trembled, was deeply disturbed, and was suddenly changed from nearly all the good things in which he had been.”

These are Josephus’s words concerning Solomon. How he was suddenly changed from nearly all the good things in which he had been, Josephus explains by adding: “Not much time,” he says, “[Col. 0650B] having passed after the prophet had foretold that these very things would happen to him, God immediately raised up against him an enemy named Hadad. And a little later, at the time when Solomon was in evils because of the aforesaid transgressions and had been abandoned by God [the intervening reading is corrupt], Hadad came from Pharaoh into Idumaea; and, since Solomon could not capture him because he was protected by many guards, his hated countenance withdrew, and rising from there he came into Syria. There he joined himself in friendship with a certain man named Raazon; having a very great multitude of robbers about him, he advanced, seized Syria, and became its king. Then he too, ranging about, afflicted the province of the Israelites and continued to ravage Solomon. Meanwhile Jeroboam, son of Nebat, [Col. 0650C] rose up against Solomon; and Solomon, learning his purpose and plot, sought to seize and kill him.”

In these words of Josephus no repentance of Solomon is sounded, but rather his sin and, as that same sin required, the affliction both of himself and of the whole country. Josephus concludes: “Thus Solomon died at a very great age and was buried in Jerusalem, surpassing all kings in prosperity, prudence, and riches, apart from those matters in which, deceived in old age by passion for women, he transgressed.” That he transgressed but did not repent, Josephus himself makes clear much earlier when he says: “While Solomon was the most glorious and religious of all kings and surpassed all who had held dominion over the Hebrews before him in wisdom and riches, he did not remain so until the end of his life; for, abandoning the observance of his ancestral solemnities, he shamefully burned with passion for women and sexual intemperance, and his course had not the same end as David’s.” You see that Josephus too says that Solomon’s course did not have the same end as David’s, just as canonical Scripture says—something sufficiently discussed above—that his heart was not with the Lord as David’s was, and that he did not fulfil the command to follow the Lord as David did. But if he had truly repented, as David unquestionably did, it could truly be said that his life had had the same end as David’s. Therefore nothing else is expressed in these words of Josephus than [Col. 0651A] Solomon’s sin, and no repentance of his after that sin.

Let us return to canonical Scripture and to Bacchiarius. “Solomon,” Scripture says, “slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David” (3 Kings 2). Bacchiarius also tries to argue from this that Solomon should be judged saved because he is not found excluded from the tombs of the kings, from which certain kings are read to have been excluded.

“He was buried,” he says, “in the city of David. The city of David is called Zion, which is also Jerusalem. For when David had been anointed king over Israel, ‘he went,’ it says, ‘to Jerusalem; this is Jebus; and he took the stronghold of Zion, which is the city of David.’ David dwelt in the stronghold, and therefore it was called the city of David. David was buried there, as it is written: ‘David slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David’ (ibid.). There all twelve kings of Judah after David, both just and unjust, down to Hezekiah, are read to have been buried; but, as the same Scripture testifies, some are excluded from the tombs of the kings.

“For concerning Jehoram it is written in Chronicles: ‘They buried him in the city of David’ (2 Chron. 22), but not in the tombs of the kings. Of the leprous Uzziah, who is also called Azariah, we read in the book of Kings: ‘They buried him with his ancestors in the city of David’ (4 Kings 15). In the second book of [Col. 0651C] Chronicles (ch. 26), concerning the same man: ‘They buried him in the field of the royal tombs, because he was a leper.’ Here one must ask whether to be buried in the field of the royal tombs is one thing, and to be buried in the tombs of the kings another. That they are different would not appear at all unless the appended phrase somehow taught us to understand it so. For Scripture, wishing as it were to show the reason why he was buried in the field of the royal tombs, added: ‘because he was a leper.’ This seems to be added not for his honour or glory, but for disgrace and ignominy.

“It may therefore be understood that the field of the royal tombs was more extensive than the space or enclosure of the tombs, and that Uzziah should be believed to have been buried in some remote part of it, apart from the tombs of the others, since he plainly remained a leper until the day of his death. For just as, while alive, he was expelled from the temple and lived, as it is written, [Col. 0651D] in a separate house because of leprosy, so perhaps in death he too was buried in a separate grave because of leprosy. Therefore what is said in the book of Kings, that they buried him with his ancestors in the city of David, must not be understood to mean that he was so buried with his ancestors as to be within their tombs with them, but only in the same city with them.

“So too it is written in the book of Kings concerning Jehoram: ‘Jehoram slept with his fathers and was buried with them in the city of David’ (4 Kings 8). Likewise, in the same book, concerning Joash: ‘They buried him with his fathers in the city of David’ (4 Kings 12). Yet Chronicles declares that they were excluded from the tombs of the kings, as was said a little earlier. Likewise concerning Ahaz it is written in Chronicles: ‘They buried him in the city [Col. 0652A] of Jerusalem, for they did not receive him into the tombs of the kings’ (2 Chron. 28).”

Only these four kings, from David to Hezekiah, are read to have been excluded from the tombs of the kings—if indeed Uzziah is counted among them; but divine Scripture declares that none of the others was excluded. Yet among the others are found Rehoboam, Abijah, Zechariah, and Amaziah, who are undoubtedly reprobate. Therefore Bacchiarius’s argument is neither sufficiently fitting nor sufficient: namely, that Solomon should rightly be judged saved because he is not reported to have been excluded from the tombs of the kings. For burial among kings is not an argument for eternal holiness, but a merely formal addition to a certain dignity; while exclusion from them is not a judgment of eternal damnation, but demonstrates the enduring hatred of a subjected people toward its king.

Finally, divine Scripture neither openly says nor secretly suggests anywhere that one should be judged just because one is found buried with the just. Saul and Jonathan are read to have been buried under an oak at Jabesh-gilead: Saul was unjust, whereas Jonathan is declared just. Likewise Manasseh king of Judah and his son Amon were both buried in the garden of his house, in the garden of Uzza; of these, Scripture says that Manasseh, after many crimes, performed great repentance before God, whereas Amon persevered obstinately in his perversity.

There is also in the *Foliola* another testimony concerning Solomon’s repentance: “Jerome, in the thirteenth book on the prophet Ezekiel himself: ‘Solomon sinned and offended God, although afterwards he did penance, writing the Proverbs, in which he says: At the end I did penance and looked back, that I might choose discipline.’”

This little verse, which Solomon is here said to have spoken in Proverbs, is not found in Proverbs, even if they are read through a thousand times from beginning to end. Jerome himself translated Solomon’s Proverbs from Hebrew into Latin, and in that translation he did not include this verse; had he discovered it in the Hebrew truth, he would undoubtedly have put it in his translation. For Jerome was so faithful an interpreter that, as he himself often confesses, he added, subtracted, or altered nothing in the divine Scriptures, but carefully conveyed Hebrew truth to Latin ears, rendering either word for word or sense for sense.

But since, before Jerome interpreted the divine Scriptures, the translations of others were read in the churches—namely those of the Seventy translators, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and also the Fifth Edition—someone may say that he perhaps took the aforesaid verse from one of them. For Jerome brings forward many scriptural testimonies in his works not only according to Hebrew truth but according to the edition of any interpreter whatsoever, “lest, as he says, he should seem to mint new things and be accused of destroying old ones.”

To this one must reply that Origen, who was much earlier than Jerome, does not appear to say this, although he knew all those editions thoroughly. From all of them, except that of the Seventy translators, he made one library, arranging six columns on a single page and assigning one edition to each, so that the diligent reader, finding all of them successively together, might easily see wherein one differed from another or agreed with another. This is what Jerome means when he says that the Greeks carefully read Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, interpreters of the Old Law, and through Origen’s labour dedicated the *Hexapla* in the churches; and elsewhere: “Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion are received as Judaizing heretics, who concealed many mysteries of the Saviour by a crafty interpretation; [Col. 0653A] yet they are included in the *Hexapla* in the churches.” *Hexapla*, that is, copies or libraries having six columns. Origen himself, in the second homily on Leviticus, says: “Perhaps to some it will seem that an error of expression was made by the translator; but, after more carefully investigating, I have found that all the translators rendered it alike.” From this it is clear that Origen possessed the translations of all the interpreters.

It may be asked: since Origen, as has been said, arranged six editions in six columns in one library, who was the translator of each? We have plainly identified translators for four of them: the Seventy, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion. But Jerome says that Origen discovered the fifth, sixth, and seventh editions through wonderful labour; and, apart from the one translated by the Seventy wise men and then most commonly used in the churches, he joined the three following editions—the fifth, sixth, and seventh—to the three remaining editions, those of Aquila, Symmachus, [Col. 0653C] and Theodotion, and arranged them in one library as stated above.

Who the translators of these last three—the fifth, sixth, and seventh—were, we do not know well, unless perhaps we suppose that Aquila was the author of one of them, so that he issued two translations, though we do not know what compelled him to translate a second time. For Jerome plainly shows in his Commentary on Ezekiel that Aquila issued two translations: there he sometimes speaks of Aquila’s first edition and sometimes of his second. But because Jerome himself and other teachers, whenever they bring forward something from any one of these editions, rarely mention their order—that is, whether they took it from the first or the second—they do not often make this clear. Hence some suppose that Aquila had only one edition, because this distinction has either not yet been discovered by them or perhaps has not been retained in memory.

This distinction is more clearly noted in the passage on Ezekiel in which Jerome names both the first and the second edition together: “The first edition,” he says, “of Aquila rendered it ‘staff’; the second, as did Symmachus and Theodotion, rendered it ‘firmament.’” Here both the first and the second are plainly named, as stated; and it is shown that Aquila said one thing in one edition and another in the other. I judge that Origen placed both in his library, since it was made known above that he possessed all the interpreters’ translations.

Origen himself, however, is not easily found to maintain Solomon’s repentance; rather, in the passages mentioned above, he says that Solomon too was deceived by women, and that he did not firmly utter what is there stated concerning the Song of Songs. He also says that Solomon and his son Rehoboam were excluded from the genealogy of Christ which Luke composed, beginning from below and carrying it up to God, lest, in the line whose prerogative is consummated in God, there be mention of those whose sins are recorded—although, to omit others, David is expressly named there, and both his adultery and his homicide are contained in the sacred writings. Yet David’s sins, as the prophet Nathan testifies, were removed from him; but the sins of Solomon [Col. 0654B] and Rehoboam are not read to have been erased by repentance. If canonical Scripture testified that they had been erased, there would be no reason for Solomon, a man of such wisdom, merit, and renown, to be excluded from the catalogue of the just when his father David is entered there by the merit of repentance.

The remaining ecclesiastical teachers who had some reputation or name before Jerome, or in Jerome’s time, and who knew the divine Scriptures according to other translations, since Jerome’s edition had not yet been made or circulated, likewise did not report finding the aforesaid verse in Proverbs. I do not say this because I have read all their writings, but because I do not think it could have escaped Augustine, Gregory, Paschasius, Bede, Fulgentius, and Isidore, who flourished in the Church in different places and times and read the writings of earlier Fathers with great zeal; nevertheless, concerning Solomon they delivered one and the same judgment.

I also think that Jerome’s Commentary on Ezekiel did not escape them; but when they read it, either they did not approve the testimony concerning Solomon’s repentance found there, or rather they did not find it. For it is credible that Jerome either did not say this at all in his Commentary, or did not say it so absolutely; but perhaps through a reader’s ingenuity, or rather through a copyist’s carelessness, the manuscript has been corrupted and its sense altered by the corruption. This is indeed what Jerome himself often complains of: Greek and Latin copies of the Scriptures had been corrupted through the fault of scribes; and his friends therefore often compelled him either to correct old versions or to produce new ones.

For I do not dare to affirm—indeed, I do not dare even to suppose—that Jerome, a man of such learning and authority, held anything in the canon of Scripture against all others, or all others against him; especially since it is one thing to differ in matters of Scripture while still agreeing in truth, and another to hold contrary opinions while truth itself resists. Therefore, just as Jerome, when expounding another book of Solomon, namely Ecclesiastes, did not affirm it himself but assigned the assertion to the Hebrews, so perhaps in his work on Ezekiel, when speaking of Solomon, he should be believed to have expressed a judgment that was tentative rather than fixed, although the manuscripts now contain it otherwise.

For in his work on Ecclesiastes he says: “The Hebrews say that this book belongs to Solomon while doing penance.” Jerome did not say: “This book belongs to Solomon while doing penance.” He could certainly have said this as confidently as truthfully if he had discovered that Solomon repented in Proverbs. For who would doubt that Ecclesiastes is a book of Solomon while doing penance if Proverbs testify that he repented, since the universal Church holds that Solomon wrote Proverbs first and Ecclesiastes afterwards? But if he wrote Proverbs after repentance, then much more Ecclesiastes, which he wrote after Proverbs. Jerome could therefore have said affirmatively, “This book belongs to Solomon while doing penance,” and need not have attributed the statement to the Jews, to whom he is accustomed to attribute not only in this place but often elsewhere what he either knows to be false or, not knowing it to be true, does not presume to affirm.

For they say many things in which they contradict the truth, as Jerome himself states in many places; and, what is more, the angel testifies this in Revelation, where they are called not Jews, as they falsely claim to be, but the synagogue of Satan. Ecclesiastical teachers believed that Solomon wrote the books which the Catholic Church reads as his not after repentance but before that detestable sin; and, lest what they thought should be unknown to us, they left it written in their works. Hence Augustine, on the eighth Song of Ascents mentioned above, says: “Solomon was a lover of women and was rejected by God; but if the things spoken through him were erased when he fell, it would be judged that he had spoken them himself and that they had not been spoken through him.” These words show that Solomon wrote first and fell afterwards; but by God’s providence for us rather than for him, what he had written did not fall when he fell.

Finally, sacred history first narrates that he received wisdom while sleeping, then that he devoted himself to writing, and finally that, when he had already become old, he abandoned God by cleaving to foreign women. So much for these matters; let us return to Jerome.

[Col. 0655D] Therefore he who, in his commentary on Ecclesiastes, did not presume to render a hasty judgment in establishing Solomon’s repentance but cautiously attributed it to the Jews, should be believed to have maintained the same or a similar manner of speaking in his commentary on Ezekiel. Thus he is rightly to be believed neither to have reproached the remaining holy men—so many and so learned—with folly and ignorance, nor himself to have incurred a blameworthy error. We can suitably avoid both inconveniences if we choose to attribute what is displeasing there to the fault of copyists. While copying Jerome’s Commentary, carefully dictated and perhaps corrected still more carefully, whether compelled by command or hired for payment, they were turning one thing over in their mouths and pondering another in their hearts, or perhaps sleeping; and they carelessly omitted what was in the exemplar, or still more carelessly added from themselves what was not in it.

Jerome himself recalls copyists from this negligence in a certain passage, saying: “For it will be of no benefit to have corrected a book unless the correction is preserved by the diligence of scribes.” Finally, in his exposition on Hosea, when Jerome spoke of just kings, he composed their catalogue as follows: “When we read that David, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah were just kings.” Here I wonder no little why he omitted Solomon, though Solomon was more famous than the others for wisdom, power, wealth, and glory, and should deservedly have been placed among the just kings if he returned in repentance to the righteousness which he abandoned by sinning.

And if Jerome did not place among the just Manasseh, whom he knew on Scripture’s testimony to have repented, it is not especially surprising, since in his entire life no just work at all is found of him until it is declared that at the end he repented. But Solomon, who before that most grave sin of both luxury and idolatry shone with such wisdom, flourished with such power, was eminent in such illustrious works, abounded in such riches, and glittered with such fame and glory—even if for a time he turned aside from the path of righteousness—should nevertheless not have been excluded from the number of just kings, when we read that David and Asa at times sinned gravely, though not only Jerome but canonical Scripture calls them just.

Elsewhere, however, the same Jerome vehemently [Col. 0656C] accuses Solomon; and, having accused him, excuses him by no testimony of subsequent repentance. Rather, he declares both him and King Ahaz, a reprobate, entangled in impious deeds, without then adding that they were absolved through repentance. For, speaking to Vitalis the priest about Solomon and Ahaz, king of Judah, son of Jotham and father of Hezekiah, he says that both were defiled with the filth of idolatry, yet does not say that they were cleansed in the course of time:

“Let us consider,” he says, “that Scripture accuses Solomon and Ahaz of self-indulgence and impiety. For each, though he was of the stock of David, departed from the Lord; and one of them followed lust to such an extent—without doubt Solomon—that he had seven hundred wives, and three hundred [Col. 0656D] concubines, and young women, and passive prostitutes beyond number; and, neglecting the God of his fathers, he built idols for very many nations and became not, as formerly, Jedidiah—that is, beloved of the Lord—but a lover of women.”

Here Jerome adds nothing concerning Solomon’s repentance; rather, he joins him to the reprobate King Ahaz in impiety, so that, just as he openly shows them agreeing in idolatry, he seems also to imply that neither differed from the other through repentance. But if you wish to hear a clearer testimony of Jerome, one plainly at considerable variance with Solomon’s repentance, consider what he says elsewhere to the monk Rusticus, where he quite openly contradicts Solomon’s repentance:

“What was wiser than Solomon?” he says. “Yet he is made foolish [Col. 0657A] by the loves of women.”

And lest anyone should presumptuously interpret “made foolish” in an improper sense, the same Jerome explained its meaning in the words that follow, when he introduced the saying from the Gospel:

“Salt,” he says, “is good; but if it becomes foolish, it is cast outside, and loses the dignity of its name so completely that it is not even useful for the dung-heap.”

Thus, by saying that Solomon was made foolish, and adding that foolish salt is cast outside and is no longer useful, Jerome quite plainly declared Solomon reprobate—that is, never recalled to the savour of repentance. For it is certain that salt which has become foolish is irreparably drained away; having lost its proper savour, it is not salted again, but is found everywhere and always wholly useless, since neither it itself is seasoned by another thing, nor does it season anything else [Col. 0657B] by itself.

Therefore, when the Gospels discuss salt that has become foolish, they signify nothing other than any reprobate person who, having lost the savour of righteousness, is corrupted by tasteless and insipid perversity and is recalled to his former state by no repentance. David observed this when, speaking of a certain reprobate and knowing assuredly that his counsel would in no way be pleasing to God, he humbly asked that this very counsel be made foolish—that is, rejected from the good pleasure of the divine will:

“Make foolish, I beseech you, O Lord,” he says, “the counsel of Ahithophel.”

This petition itself was not made foolish; rather, Ahithophel’s malice was rejected, because by his perverse and unjust counsel he offended the Creator’s righteousness; and, failing to achieve his counsel, he set his house in order [Col. 0657C] and hanged himself with a noose.

Rightly, then, salt which has become foolish is cast outside. In that casting-out nothing other than this very rejection is shown, by which every perverse person is irreparably condemned. The outward casting-out is eternal reprobation, by which miserable persons, bound hand and foot, are cast outside and are not allowed to enter into the Lord’s joy.

David seems to have recoiled from this casting-out when, considering the multitude of his sins, he saw it as though impending over him; and what at that time he said tremblingly, when his fear had been somewhat eased, he sang joyfully from memory:

“I said in my alarm: I am cast out from before your eyes” (Ps. 30).

“When I feared,” he says, “the burden of my offences, [Col. 0657D] I said, ‘I am cast out from before your eyes,’ judging myself unworthy of aid from your grace, as though my great iniquity obstructed your great mercy. But because I feared, I was humbled by fearing; having become humble, I called upon you. Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer when I cried to you.”

What he cried, however, he says in another psalm: “Do not cast me out from before your face.” “Do not cast me out from before your face,” he says, “but hide me in the hidden place of your face; for one cast out from before your face is driven down into outer darkness, while one hidden in the hidden place of your face rejoices to be delivered from every disturbance caused by men.”

Let us also say: Good Jesus, do not make us foolish; do not cast us out from before your face, lest we perish with Ahithophel or with the wicked servant cast outside, [Col. 0658A] but may we rejoice in everlasting security in the hidden place of your countenance. Therefore, when Jerome declares Solomon foolish and cast out, it is plain that he does not affirm his repentance. He is shown to be contrary not only to other teachers but also to himself, if he declares one thing concerning Solomon in his commentary on Ezekiel and another in his letter to Rusticus.

John Chrysostom likewise, when in his little work *On the Restoration of the Fallen* he highly commended David’s repentance and there brought Solomon into the discussion, made no mention of Solomon’s repentance. Yet it would have been entirely fitting that, just as he held up David as an example of repentance to the fallen man whom he was striving to recall to repentance, he should also have held up Solomon—especially since, as I said before, he there [Col. 0658B] introduced Solomon’s memory. For he says:

“Blessed David fell by the same fall as you now have; and not only this, but he added another, graver thing. For he joined murder to adultery. And after this, did he remain fallen? Did he not rise, and stand again against the enemy? And so he subdued him that even after his death his merits benefited his descendants. For when Solomon had committed that monstrous crime and deserved a thousand deaths, the Lord nevertheless says that, because of David, He would grant him the kingdom intact. For He says: ‘I will surely tear your kingdom and give it to your servant. Nevertheless, I will not do it in your days, for the sake of David your father; but I will take it from the hand of your son’” (3 Kings 11).

Likewise, when Hezekiah came into [Col. 0658C] extreme dangers, though he himself was righteous, the Lord says that He will bring him help because of the good David.

See: John commends David’s repentance and calls Hezekiah righteous; and, placing Solomon between them, he calls him neither repentant nor righteous, but says only that David’s merits benefited him so far that his kingdom was not divided in his own days, though he deserved a thousand deaths.

In his homily on the fiftieth psalm, the same John also exalts David’s repentance with great praises and there introduces many repentant persons: namely Peter, Paul, Matthew, the publican, Mary the sinner, and the thief. Among them he nowhere commends Solomon as repentant, though he ought more solemnly to have proclaimed the repentance of no one than of a king so rich, so powerful, and so wise, if he had read that Solomon repented either in Proverbs or anywhere in the canonical Scriptures, or at least in writings of the Fathers which he judged worthy of faith and authority.
