Finally, the Venerable Bede, when he expounded the very Proverbs of Solomon according to Jerome’s translation and showed in many places what was contained in the old translation, did not say that he had found anything in them concerning Solomon’s repentance, nor that he knew anything to have been found by others. Rather, in the little work which he writes to Nothelm, as was said above, he affirmed that Solomon never repented perfectly.

The loose leaves continue:

“The Hebrew books say that Solomon was dragged five times through the streets of the city [Col. 0659A] as an act of repentance. They likewise say that he came into the temple which he had built carrying five rods, and gave them to the legal experts so that he might be beaten by them. Having taken counsel together, they said that they would not lay hands upon the Lord’s anointed. Frustrated by them, he then deposed himself from the kingdom.”

So much in the loose leaves. Jerome translated from Hebrew into Latin all the Scriptures contained in the Hebrew canon; and in these one cannot find that Solomon was dragged through the streets of the city as an act of repentance or offered rods to legal experts to beat him. The remaining Scriptures which they possess are apocryphal, and their authority is not suitable for establishing matters that have come into dispute. Thus the books of Jesus son of Sirach, Judith, Tobit, and First Maccabees, though they are found among them, are reckoned by them among the apocrypha because they are not included in their canon.

But if they say that they have any other books which assert that Solomon’s repentance is contained in them, those books are not to be believed, since such testimony is drawn from the Jews’ own assertion: whatever is not in the canon is in no way to be considered worthy of belief. Finally, Josephus, writer of Jewish antiquities, asserts that he has read such material, yet he learned from no Scripture, canonical or apocryphal, that Solomon repented. From this it is plainly gathered that lying is not alien to the Jews; rather, it is quite peculiar and familiar to them either to deny what is true or affirm what is false. For this reason Sophronius compelled Jerome [Col. 0659C] to translate the Davidic psalms according to the Hebrew truth: when Sophronius was disputing with a certain Hebrew and produced against him certain testimonies from the psalms according to the Septuagint translators, the Hebrew man, chattering and mocking him because he did not know Hebrew letters, said at almost every word that the Hebrew either did not contain what it did contain, or contained what it did not contain.

The loose leaves continue:

“The words of Solomon, writing Ecclesiasticus after he had voluntarily lost the kingdom: ‘Solomon reigned in days of peace, to whom God subjected all enemies, so that he might build a house in His name,’ and the rest which follows in the same chapter” (ch. 47).

Solomon did not write *Ecclesiasticus*, as Augustine says in the seventeenth book of *The City of God*, and as Jerome had said in many places before Augustine. Jerome says that he found this book in Hebrew, entitled not *Ecclesiasticus*, as among the Latins, but *Parables*. Two others, he says, were joined to it: *Ecclesiastes* and the *Song of Songs*, so that by the similarity of their writers—that is, Solomon—it might equal them not only in number of books but also in kind of subject matter.

Therefore, because of this similarity of style, the custom prevailed among the unlearned that *Ecclesiasticus* should be called Solomon’s; but the older and wiser say that it belongs to Jesus son of Sirach, who, as was said much above, lived in the time of Simon the high priest. When, in the final part of the same volume, he praised the mighty deeds of the preceding fathers, he highly commended that same Simon in the conclusion, exalting him more fully and loftily because he knew him more closely and perfectly. This Jesus is said to have written *Ecclesiasticus*, as he himself seems to show at the end of Simon’s praise:

“Jesus son of Sirach of Jerusalem wrote in this book instruction in wisdom and discipline, and renewed wisdom from his heart.”

When, therefore, after recounting David’s praises, he came to narrate Solomon’s deeds, he first extolled Solomon’s wisdom, renown, and riches with high praises; then he brought forward that grave sin and disgrace of his, thus keeping in his description of Solomon’s life the order which Solomon had kept in living it:

“He was instructed,” he says, [Col. 0660B] “in his youth, and was filled with wisdom as with a river.”

Then, turning to him directly, he adds:

“Your name was proclaimed to distant islands, and you were loved in your peace. The nations marvelled at you in songs and proverbs. You amassed gold as though it were bronze, and accumulated silver as lead.”

Thus far the praises. Then he adds:

“You bent your thighs to women; you exercised power over your body.”

It may be asked what he means by saying, “You exercised power over your body,” since the Apostle says: “You are not your own, for you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6). Whoever knows that he belongs to God does not use his body freely and at random for his own pleasure; rather, he chastises it and subjects it to servitude according to the will of Him to whom he remembers that he belongs.

For as a tame and broken horse uses its body not according to its own will but according to that of its rider, so indeed the righteous person, having God as ruler, does not himself but God has power over his body. But concerning those who, in a perverse order, have power over themselves and live rather by their own will than that of their Lord, a certain wise man says elsewhere: “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6).

Accordingly Solomon, when he no longer feared God—wrongly free from the bridle of holiness—nor respected man, swollen with the sceptre of royal power, exercised power over his body, indulging its pleasures all the more freely and extravagantly because God deigned patiently to endure him and man did not presume to restrain a king from his purpose. Hence he incurred what follows:

“You gave a stain to your glory, and profaned your seed, to bring wrath upon your children and to stir up your folly among the rest, so that you made the empire twofold and caused a harsh kingdom to rule from Ephraim” (Ecclus. 47).

This plainly shows that, just as David’s righteousness, Scripture bearing witness, benefited his descendants beyond expression, so Solomon’s iniquity did no slight harm to his seed and children: divine wrath is said to have been brought upon them, and because of their father’s folly they did not deserve to retain the kingdom undivided.

But what is added there—“God, however, will not abandon His mercy, nor destroy the descendants of His chosen one from the stock, nor corrupt the seed of him who loves the Lord” (ibid.)—calls David His chosen one and the one who loves the Lord. God did not utterly extirpate David’s seed and stock, lest that promise by which He swore His truth to David should prove empty: “Of the fruit,” He says, “of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131).

He therefore gave, as follows there, a remnant to Jacob, and to David from that very stock. That is to say: because of David, God gave from that same stock a remnant—that is, Rehoboam—so that David’s illustrious merit might avail more with God for preserving the descendants of his race than Solomon’s iniquity could avail for utterly extirpating them. Thus Rehoboam’s being given from that stock is said to be due to David’s merit; but Rehoboam’s perversity is earned by Solomon’s iniquity. This is perhaps what was said shortly before to Solomon: “You profaned your seed, to bring wrath upon your children” (Ecclus. 47).

How profane Rehoboam was may be read both in this *Ecclesiasticus* which we have in hand and more fully in the books of Kings and Chronicles. His son Abijah too was no less wicked, so that the dreadful saying was truly fulfilled: “I am a jealous God, repaying the iniquity of fathers upon children to the third generation of those who hate me” (Exod. 20).

For here it is said of Rehoboam that Solomon left after him, from his seed, the folly of the nation and Rehoboam, deficient in prudence, who turned away the nation by his counsel. In his time the empire was divided in two, [Col. 0661C] and from Ephraim a harsh kingdom proceeded. Rehoboam himself ruled only the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, which are called by the one name Judah; but Jeroboam son of Nebat grievously oppressed with a most harsh rule the remaining ten, which were called Israel.

This is what was said to Solomon: “So that you made the empire twofold and caused a harsh kingdom to rule from Ephraim.” For Jeroboam, who exercised harsh rule over the ten tribes, was of the tribe of Ephraim. When Israel had been separated from Judah, Jeroboam made two golden calves, placing one in Bethel and the other in Dan. He commanded the people to assemble there for worship, fearing that if, in accordance with custom, they went to Jerusalem to worship, they might on that occasion turn to Rehoboam king of Judah, and the divided kingdom would thus be reunited.

Therefore it is written of him: “He caused Israel to sin” (3 Kings 16). And when the perverse life of his successors—the reprobate kings—is later described, it is said of almost every one of them that “they walked in the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.”

Rehoboam himself also oppressed the children of Judah with a harsh rule, as he arrogantly replied to the people when they requested relief from this severity:

“My father made your yoke heavy; but I will add to your yoke. My father struck you with whips, but I will strike you with scorpions” (3 Kings 12).

These indeed were the heirs whom Solomon left to his kingdom and impiety: Rehoboam, who, as Jesus says, [Col. 0662A] overthrew the nation by his counsel; and Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin and gave Ephraim a way of sinning.

It is plain from this that in this narrative Jesus includes not only righteous men but also some unrighteous ones, perhaps so that the holiness of the righteous might shine out more clearly when the dark perversity of the reprobate appeared alongside it. For no one, to say nothing of Solomon, is ignorant that Rehoboam and Jeroboam were reprobate unless he possesses no knowledge, or only a slight knowledge, of the divine Scriptures. Therefore it is not surprising, when Jesus describes the succession of kings, that Solomon is named after David, since Rehoboam and Jeroboam, whose reprobation is beyond doubt, are named there as well.

But this troubles me: if Jesus intended, in praising Solomon, to establish him as righteous, why did he take pains to bring forward Solomon’s sin after his praises, when he is found to have done this concerning none of the righteous whom he had enumerated in great number before and after Solomon? For if you wish to examine the catalogue which he composed, from Enoch, with whom he began his praises, to Simon son of Onias, whom he praised in the conclusion, you will find that he brings forward the sin of none whom he praises except Solomon, though some of them are found to have sinned gravely if other Scriptures are examined more closely.

Finally, in that whole catalogue, in which he set forth many ancient fathers who succeeded one another in the people of God and presided by holiness or dignity, he accuses no one at all of unrighteousness except Solomon, Rehoboam, and Jeroboam. That Rehoboam and Jeroboam were reprobate is not in the least doubtful; but no repentance of Solomon, nor any righteousness after his sin, is mentioned there at all. If he judged Solomon to be excepted from the lot of Rehoboam and Jeroboam, I wonder why he either mentioned Solomon’s sin at all, when in that passage he had not sullied any righteous man’s praises by mention of sin, or at least why, after the sin, he did not add Solomon’s repentance, so that his praise might be commended by a worthy conclusion and he might be judged fit to be numbered among the righteous without hesitation.

But after this same Jesus had extolled Josiah among the other righteous with fitting praises, he adds: “Except David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, all committed sin.” Here it must be asked whom he means by “all,” or what sin he intends. For if we take “all” to mean all those whom he had named earlier, we must beware of accusing them of sin beyond what is just, since among them are some whose sins are not read of in the sacred writings, and others who, though they sinned, are nevertheless reported to have sinned less than David. How then shall we say that all those sinned except David, when David himself is found to have sinned more than some of them?

Let us, if you please, consider the following verse, to see whether we may perhaps draw from it in some way whom he means to have committed sin. Having said, “All committed sin,” he adds: “For the kings of Judah forsook the mighty law.” By this he seems to imply that, when he said “all,” he meant kings: that is, all the kings of Judah, or of the people of Israel, committed sin, except David, Hezekiah, [Col. 0663A] and Josiah, who were certainly kings.

But when we have established that all kings must be understood, I think we must still ask whether he means all those named in the books of Kings and Chronicles, or whether some of them are excluded by this general statement. For if we say all of them, Asa and Jehoshaphat confront us, whom canonical Scripture declares to have been righteous. Of Asa it says: “Asa did what was right before the Lord, as David his father”; and of Jehoshaphat: “Because he walked in the ways of David his father.” Those who are read to have walked in David’s ways are not to be accused of unrighteousness; nor should we suppose that Jesus charges with dissimilarity those whom canonical Scripture makes equal by so great a likeness in holiness.

We must therefore return only to those kings whom Jesus named in his book. For when there he included patriarchs, prophets, judges, and priests who, as I said above, belonged to the people of God, he also inserted not all, but certain kings of that people: David, Solomon, Rehoboam, Jeroboam, Hezekiah, and Josiah. After Josiah, since he did not wish to name another king thereafter, he said what has often been quoted: “Except David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, all committed sin”—that is, all the kings he had named: Solomon, Rehoboam, and Jeroboam.

We must now see what kind of sin these committed, from which David, Hezekiah, and Josiah were free. For he does not mean every sin, but a particular sin, just as the Lord says in the Gospel when speaking of the Jews: “If I had not come, they would not have sin” (John 15). He does not mean every sin, but a particular sin—namely, one which they did not have before His coming but had when He was present.

This sin which Solomon, Rehoboam, and Jeroboam committed, as I judge, is idolatry: abandoning their ancestral laws for the rite of the nations, they built high places, fashioned idols, and worshipped demons. This seems to be implied there when it is added: “For the kings of Judah forsook the mighty law.” The mighty law is to worship God, to adore God, according to that command: “You shall worship the Lord your God.”

If anyone is unfailingly devoted to this law, although he wanders astray through certain byways, he can nevertheless easily be recalled to the One whom he worships as long as he is found bound by this bond of faith. For it is no slight benefit of divine grace, nor a merit of human effort to be despised, for each person to retain the seal of faith and, though he sins—for there is no human being who does not sin—to turn his mind nonetheless toward worshipping God: to bend the knee to Him alone, bow the neck, offer God the service owed to Him, and not faithlessly worship another god alongside Him or in His stead.

Accordingly, when the souls of believers are commended to God, this merit is elegantly set before Him: “Although they sinned, they did not deny you; but, marked with the sign of faith, they faithfully worshipped you, who made all things, including them among all things.”

But if a person breaks bonds of this sort, so as shamelessly to attribute to a creature the worship owed to God the Creator, he is proved utterly to have forsaken the mighty law, being so far from pardon because he no longer even outwardly venerates the giver of pardon.

Thus, in the Second Book of Maccabees, when, through the wicked and unheard-of crime of the impious priest Jason, the priests and their fellow tribesmen adopted the customs of the nations and, despising the temple, as it is written there, and neglecting sacrifices, hastened in every respect to become like the nations, the divine word adds: “To act impiously against the divine laws does not go unpunished” (2 Macc. 4).

How it did not go unpunished for them, it shows a little below when it says that “King Antiochus, returning from Egypt, with savage minds took the city by arms” (2 Macc. 5). “In the whole three days eighty thousand were killed, and forty thousand taken captive.”

By departing from this law through idolatry, both in heart and deed, the aforesaid kings fell away utterly from all holiness. Recalled by no fear, they worshipped demons in place of God. Hence it adds: “They fell away and despised the fear of God. For,” it says, “they gave their kingdom to others, and their glory to a foreign nation” (Ecclus. 49). They could truly have reigned had they remained humbly subject to the divine command, according to what is written: “By me kings reign” (Prov. 8). But they gave their kingdom and glory to others—that is, to demons—when they weakly submitted themselves to them, while those demons ruled and gloried in this.

After these words, *Ecclesiasticus* is found to offer nothing from which the repentance of these kings might be inferred in any degree.

Nor should it move anyone that the Book of Kings says concerning Solomon: “The rest of Solomon’s words, and all that he did, and his wisdom—behold, all are written in the book of the days of Solomon’s words”; and that Chronicles says: “The rest of the deeds of Solomon, first and last, are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, in the words of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the vision of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam son of Nebat.” These books are found nowhere, either among us or among the Hebrews; and therefore neither we nor they can in any way know what those remaining matters are which they contain. Nor does our Scripture say that Solomon’s repentance is found in them. Hence I do not see how one can establish, or even conjecture, what is wholly unknown.

Let it therefore suffice for us to know, on the teaching of canonical Scripture, that those books once existed, though they do not now exist. But to contend that something was written in them which we can demonstrate by no evidence is merely words. For just as Chronicles says concerning Solomon that the rest of his deeds were written in the words of Nathan the prophet, in the words of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the vision of Iddo the seer, so, a little later, it says also of his son Rehoboam: “The deeds of Rehoboam, first and last, are written in the books of Shemaiah the prophet and Iddo the seer.”

Therefore, if someone contentious should say concerning Solomon that his repentance perhaps was written in those books which we do not possess, it can likewise be said contentiously concerning Rehoboam that his repentance perhaps was written in those books which we do not possess. Yet no one knowledgeable in divine Scripture doubts that Rehoboam was rejected by God; and Augustine says concerning Solomon, in his exposition of the eighth Song of Ascents—which I recall having cited above—that Solomon was rejected by God.

Whatever Scriptures we cannot know, whether because we do not possess them or because, possessing them, we do not understand them, ought to be committed to the divine fire, according to the command in the law concerning the flesh of the lamb. Those Scriptures which, as I said, are not found either among us or among the Hebrews were indeed long ago irreparably burned by fire.

In the time of Zedekiah, the last of the kings of the children of Judah, in the eleventh year of his reign, the hostile Chaldean army invaded Judaea and destroyed Jerusalem after besieging and capturing it. Among other things, it entirely consumed by fire the library which had been gathered there with great care. Afterwards Ezra the scribe, by permission of Artaxerxes king of Persia, came up from Babylonian captivity; and when he returned to Jerusalem, supported by marvellous knowledge—or rather, filled with ineffable grace—he restored to their former state, from the vast multitude of books which the fire had utterly consumed, the few which we now use.

If it seems incredible how this man, though gifted with a brilliant mind and trained in divine letters from childhood, could hold in memory so vast an ocean of Scriptures and recall to human knowledge from a remembering heart books consumed by fire, let us remember that nothing is impossible for God, who first willed that they be written and willed that they be rewritten through Ezra. Indeed, it is true what is written of Him: “It is in His power to do when He wills, and He has done whatsoever He willed.”

Since it is not incredible that He alone should work wonders—for His name alone, as He says to Manoah, is “Wonderful”—Ezra himself is therefore called “a ready scribe in the law of Moses,” and King Artaxerxes writes to him: “To Ezra, priest and most learned scribe of the law of God, greetings” (1 Esdr. 4). And a little later: “You are sent,” he says, “to inspect Judah and Jerusalem according to the law of your God which is in your hand” (1 Esdr. 7).

[Col. 0666A] Moreover, Ezra at that time devised new letter-forms, while retaining only the sounds and number of the old ones. Because these characters were readier and more legible than the earlier ones, the Hebrews gladly received them and use them to this day. Previously they had used, in both sounds and characters, the same letters as the Samaritans. Thus, even today, Jews and Samaritans retain identity in the sounds of their letters, but great diversity in their shapes.

Since I have brought forward what I found written concerning Solomon, it is fitting that I should now impose silence upon this response, leaving to the judgment of the prudent reader which of the things said he should prefer by a true judgment, and to whom. For I do not think that any reader, provided he is prudent, will dissent from those with whom he sees Augustine, Paschasius, Gregory, Bede, Fulgentius, Isidore, Anglosinus, and Rabanus agree, since these are not found to oppose the divine Scriptures but rather to agree with them in every respect.

Who would be so petty-minded—or rather so perverse-minded—as to dare say that these men either envied Solomon’s salvation and for that reason denied his repentance, or did not understand the divine Scriptures and therefore all alike erred in denying his repentance? It is therefore safe to revere such teachers and guides by following them, since to know the truth in the Scriptures through them is commendable, or perhaps to be ignorant with them is excusable.

If a choice were given me, I would rather know in the Scriptures what they knew and not know what they did not know, than, failing to know what they knew and presumptuously claiming what is unknown, either deny in them what they affirmed or affirm what they denied. Therefore, my brothers, whenever any matter comes into doubt, the loose leaves of unlearned persons are not to be brought forward, but the writings of venerable Fathers are to be examined more carefully, so that our ignorance may be wiped away by the assertions of those whose teachings make the Church shine like the sun and moon.

May your charity receive what I have been able to understand and collect concerning Solomon; for the response that follows demands an end to be set to these matters.

[Col. 0665]

# SIX TREATISES ON THE INSTITUTION OF CLERICS

## I. ON THE DIGNITY OF CLERICS

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0665D]

If in the preceding responses I found God’s help, though unworthy of it, I see that I shall need Him far more in this which follows. I am not slightly shaken at undertaking it, and seem, as it were, checked from the outset by the weight set before me. For while I still stand at the entrance, looking from afar toward its end, I judge the difficulty of reaching it to be so great that I think it better to greet it from a distance and return to my own affairs than commit sails to the winds and proceed further.

For one must travel between Scylla and Charybdis; to sail between them is full of danger, but to escape from them is worthy of a miracle. Yet if that pilot is willing to steer my little vessel—the one who, giving Peter His hand when he began to sink, made him rise again; who commanded wind and sea when the apostles were in peril and caused their turmoil to cease—I shall be led and brought by a swift course to the desired goal, though carried in a frail craft.

For what seems impossible to me when I measure my own strength is entirely easy to Him whose ways are in the sea and whose paths are in many waters. It will not be my own merits but those of my brothers that commend me to this pilot; and they will assist me, as I serve Him in this work, by their vows and prayers. With Him, then, holding the helm, I shall venture to attempt the danger.

## CHAPTER ONE

You ask, brothers: since every order of those living in the Church is of great holiness, provided each keeps the rule of the truth prescribed to it, which of them is nevertheless more worthy, and which truly holds the foremost rank in dignity—monastic or clerical?

I think this has come into doubt because for some time the virtue of humility has failed in both groups; and, with eyes clouded by the smoke of pride, the purity of truth is either not apparent or not pleasing. For one of them proudly despised what it was, while the other, with no less pride, sought to seem what it was not. Thus the scales of equity tipped on both sides, and consequently many now do not know the measure of dignity belonging to either.

To examine the boundaries of this matter is full of envy and labour, since those who investigate such questions are commonly accused of hatred or affection. For if I disparage clerics beyond measure, among whose number I rejoice to be, I shall seem to hate what I am and love what I am not. This fault ranges far and wide throughout the human race; thus a most satirical writer in secular literature greatly wonders:

> “How does it happen,” he says, “that no one loves the lot which either reason has given him or chance has cast in his way—”

[Col. 0667D] “May he live content with his lot, and praise those who follow different paths?” HORACE, *Satires*, I.1. The wise man saw that most people, dissatisfied with their condition, did not love what they were, but rather, afflicted by the disease of inconstancy, praised more highly what they were not. But if I do not commend monks as is just, that evangelical blow will strike me (Matt. VII): “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do likewise to them”; and that apostolic saying (Phil. II): “Considering one another superior,” although this statement of the Apostle seems to be understood not of the evident order of rank, but of the hidden merit of holiness. Great moderation, therefore, must be employed, and one must turn aside neither to the right nor to the left, so that, although I may not be able in [Col. 0668A] all respects to satisfy the wishes of those who think differently, I may nevertheless do no injury to the truth. Since, however, the order of clerics seems to me the more ancient, let it take the first place in this reply, so that we may first discuss that which is beyond doubt the first to have existed. What, then, was from the beginning the dignity of this order, and what its office, must be carefully investigated; and this, as I judge, can be found in the books of Moses.

## CHAPTER II

For we read in Exodus that, while the people of Israel were dwelling in the wilderness, God commanded that an ark be made for them from shittim wood, and that it be placed within a tabernacle constructed of curtains, skins, and boards, so that prayers and offerings might there be made to Him dwelling therein, [Col. 0668B] and that there He might be gracious toward those who made supplication and brought gifts. In order that this divine dwelling might be served with fitting religious observance, He chose Aaron and his sons to exercise the priesthood, so that, receiving the gifts of those who offered them, they might present them before the divine presence and pray that God Himself would be made propitious to the people.

But since, as the Apostle says, “all these things happened to them in figure” (I Cor. X), and were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, clerics ought to understand what the things just mentioned prefigured, and how even then they commended their dignity and office. Now, to recount here all that was said through Moses concerning the ark and the tabernacle would be lengthy, and to explain their many meanings and interpretations far more difficult. Yet I should like briefly and summarily to touch upon a few points, in order to show in them how the dignity of clerics is prefigured in image.

The ark made in the wilderness from shittim wood—which, of course, is incorruptible—signifies Christ’s body, which was made in this world from an incorrupt virgin and remained incorrupt: not only because it did not see the corruption of decay in the tomb, but because it was neither gnawed by the worm of lust nor corrupted by the destructive decay of age. A certain sinner laments these two afflictions of the flesh, that is, of the carnal life—perhaps one not fashioned from incorruptible wood. “I have grown old,” he says, “among all my enemies” (Ps. VI). And again: “For my loins have been filled with mockeries” (Ps. [Col. 0668D] XXXVII). To show more plainly of what corruptible material he consisted, he added: “And there is no health in my flesh” (ibid.). Moses therefore suitably made the ark from incorruptible wood, because no contagion of sin caused Christ’s body to decay.

The tabernacle, composed of curtains, skins, and boards, signifies the Church of the present time, which consists of diverse kinds of believers. Although they differ in merit, office, and dignity, they nevertheless establish one structure of the Church through the bond of charity. While this Church hastens from this pilgrimage to the joys of the divine vision, it passes, as it were, from the wilderness to the land of promise. Lest it grow weary through the labor of this journey, it possesses no slight protection, since in its inner sanctuary it contains the saving sacrament of Christ’s body. While it appears to preserve this sacrament within itself, it is rather preserved by it: so that the ark is not so much protected by the tabernacle as the tabernacle by the ark.

Aaron and his sons, who both preside over and serve the tabernacle, are the clerics. Since they receive the dignity and office of clerical rank in the Church, they not only minister to that Church but also govern it. Aaron indeed represents those whom we now call bishops; his sons represent the presbyters of lower rank, who consecrate Christ’s body with their sacred mouths and distribute it to the other faithful for reception. Since Aaron and his sons could not themselves perform all that had to be done in the tabernacle, the sons of Levi, from whom they too sprang, were joined to them, so that they might minister to the Lord under them and carefully attend to the tabernacle itself [Col. 0669B] and everything pertaining to its worship. For thus the Lord spoke to Moses:

> “Bring near the tribe of Levi, and make them stand before Aaron the priest, that they may minister to him, keep watch, and observe everything pertaining to the service of the multitude before the tabernacle. And you shall give the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons” (Num. XIV).

These Levites too were held in such great dignity that, when Moses counted the other tribes of the children of Israel by households and families, they alone were not numbered among the rest, but were selected from the others by the Lord’s command and devoted to divine ministry. As it is written:

> “Do not number the tribe of Levi, nor include their sum with the children of Israel; but you shall appoint them over the tabernacle, and they shall be in ministry” (Num. I).

These Levites, who keep watch in the tabernacle under Aaron and his sons, represent those clerics who minister in the Church under bishops and presbyters. Set apart from the people and placed over the people, they reconcile God and the people through their intercession. For interceding for the people belongs not only to presbyters, but to all clerics. Just as Aaron and his sons, who were from the tribe of Levi (Num. III), and the other Levites, taken by the Lord in place of the firstborn sons of Israel, are devoted to the service of the tabernacle so that by their office both their own sins and those of the people may be removed, so likewise clerics, whether of higher or lower order, are separated from among the people to serve God, so that, devoted to the divine offices, they may protect not only themselves but also the people subject to them.

But because the prerogative of clerical dignity is not sufficient for this protection unless a fullness of holiness is joined to dignity, God willed that these same clerics be formed in such holy conduct that through the merit of their lives they might conform themselves to God, not to the world. And indeed it is unfitting that those who hold the summit of ecclesiastical dignity should not also shine with the light of holiness, since dignity is to be regarded as a burden rather than an honor if it is not supported by the aid of holiness. The deeds of any private person, if wicked, either remain hidden or become known to few; but one eminent in dignity finds no hiding place for blameworthy deeds, because dignity itself brings what is shameful into the light.

The prudent man Boethius bears witness to this:

> “Dignity conferred upon the wicked not only does not make them worthy, but rather betrays and reveals them to be unworthy.”

And a certain historian says:

> “The deeds of those who spend their lives on high are known to all mortals; thus, in the greatest fortune there is the least liberty.”

When a prelate is disfigured in life and reputation, he is found to harm those whom he ought to benefit. For when the poison of the head is conveyed to the limbs, the health of the whole body is weakened. Since the life of clerics ought to be the model for laypeople—so that clerics may go before as leaders along the heights of justice, while laypeople follow as flocks—the fickleness of the populace is nevertheless far more prone to pursue what is worse than to imitate what is arduous. Therefore, lest clerical dignity should burden clerics by making their lack of holiness more conspicuous, and lest it produce a stumbling-block to life for those to whom it ought to offer an example, God rightly ordained that those to whom He freely granted dignity should receive holiness appropriate to that dignity: that the more worthy they were than the people, the holier they might be for those same people.

For it was not fitting that those far unequal in dignity should be equal in the quality of their lives. Subjects should live in such a manner as to deserve to please God; prelates, however, in such a way that they may be considered above those who live well, not so much by position as by merit. This holiness of clerics, like their dignity, is prefigured in the Law by many enigmas and figures and commended by many testimonies, so that none who is willing to incline his ear to the Scriptures may doubt it. So many things are read, written through Moses about Aaron and his sons and the other Levites, in which matters pertaining to clerics are undoubtedly prefigured, that it is now easier not to love them than to be wholly ignorant of them. It seems fitting, then, to bring forward some of these matters and, as ability permits, show how they apply to clerics, so that the less learned may learn what they do not know, while those who contemptuously love to forget what they know may, willing or unwilling, be compelled to remember.

## CHAPTER III

Aaron, then, was the first priest chosen by God—not because there had been no priests before him, but because those earlier priests had been made such, as it were, by their own spontaneous will rather than by divine authority. It is therefore useful to go back a little and say something about the earlier priests, so that the necessity of this priest’s election may be apparent, since many preceded among the nations, whose usefulness is judged either not so great or wholly nonexistent.

In Genesis, Melchizedek is found to have been priest of God Most High (Gen. XIV), and is read to have brought out bread and wine to Abraham returning from the slaughter of his enemies. The Apostle Paul greatly reveres the mystery of this action, recalling that the prophet David declares Christ to have been made priest according to this order:

> “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

Yet divine Scripture does not recount when, how, or why this Melchizedek was made a priest; rather, it introduces him while remaining entirely silent about these matters. His way of life, indeed, was among foreigners; and although he is known to have ruled them by royal right, he is not believed to have ministered to them in the office of priest. Scripture seems, as I judge, deliberately to make this distinction: it does not assert that Melchizedek was both king and priest of a city, but calls him only king of Salem, while separately naming him priest of God Most High. Scripture thus appears to intend us to understand that he possessed royal authority in the city, but served God alone—and not the people as well—through the ministry of a priest. For thus it is written in Genesis:

> “But Melchizedek king of Salem, bringing forth bread and wine—for he was priest of God Most High” (Gen. XIV);

and the Apostle says:

> “This Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings” (Heb. VII).

Nor is it incredible that a faithful and just king should rule unbelievers, since we often read of this very thing and of its opposite, and see it happen in the present day. Unbelieving kings frequently ruled over the children of Israel who worshipped the true God; conversely, Israelite kings or rulers, having subdued their enemies by the law of war, made them tributaries, even if they were not Jews. In our own times Christian kings impose upon Jews scattered everywhere in unbelief, and upon many Gentiles, not indeed the worship of Christian religion, but the yoke of dominion. Conversely, among barbarian nations many Christians, although they do not depart from the Catholic faith, nevertheless bow their necks beneath the dominion of kings.

It is therefore not surprising if Melchizedek too, who served the true God, ruled unbelieving Gentiles, so that his priesthood appears not so much necessary as voluntary: for by it he seems not to minister to the people but to please God. Perhaps that people had priests of its own through whom idolatrous worship was maintained among them. Possibly in order to distinguish him from these, Melchizedek is called priest of God Most High. Before priests are found among God’s people, priests are recorded as existing among foreign nations, so that the Jews may seem to have received priesthood from the Gentiles rather than the Gentiles from the Jews.

For when Pharaoh king of Egypt had brought Joseph out of prison and made him ruler over the whole land of Egypt, changing his name and calling him, in the Egyptian language, “savior of the world,” Scripture says that he gave him as wife Aseneth, daughter of Putiphar, priest of Heliopolis. Later in the same book:

> “Joseph bought all the land of Egypt, each man selling his possessions because of the severity of the famine, except the land of the priests, which had been given them by the king; for they were supplied with fixed rations from the public granaries, and therefore were not compelled to sell their possessions” (Gen. XLVII).

And in Exodus: “Moses was feeding the sheep of Jethro his father-in-law, priest of Midian” (Exod. III). You see that priests were maintained among the Egyptians and Midianites, through whom their sacred rites—or rather sacrileges—were certainly celebrated, while no priest was yet found among God’s people. At the time when Moses, after killing the Egyptian, fled to Midian, the people of God were dwelling among the Egyptians. The Gentile nations had already been dispersed far and wide; they worshipped various gods in diverse superstition, established temples, images, and sacrifices for them with perverse devotion, and almost all were utterly ignorant of God, their true Creator.

## CHAPTER IV

The Egyptians, among whom the children of Israel were then living, especially worshipped Serapis. He had been king of the Argives, crossed by ship into Egypt, and there died, receiving divine honor. While still alive he was called Apis; but when, after death, he was worshipped, he was called Serapis—as though “buried Apis.” For it seemed fitting to them that, when they rendered him the service of divine honor, they should also honor him by enlarging his name. Miserable men did not understand that this distinction was dishonor both to themselves and to him, since such an addition indicates the tomb of a dead man.

In honor of this Serapis they carefully and delicately reared a snow-white bull marked with certain spots; deceived by astonishing error, they rendered divine honors to this bull. When it died—or, as some say, was sacrificed to the aforementioned Serapis—they sought another of the same color to rear. Since they found the sought animal without difficulty, they believed this occurred through divine providence. This bull was called Apis after the one said to be Serapis, its name shortened by aphaeresis. Perhaps this was because, even though it was to be venerated with divine honor, it was not to be made equal to the god Serapis; or perhaps it was called Apis lest, if it were named Serapis, the reckless error should seem obvious, since this animal was worshipped while alive, whereas the other had been worshipped after death.

Miserable Egypt was held in this miserable error while the Israelite people there were oppressed with the labor of clay and brick. This error proved ruin and a stumbling-block to those same children of Israel, because many of them, abandoning the worship of the one true God, turned to worship Egyptian inventions. Seeing temples carefully built, images devoutly adored, priests ordained, sacrifices celebrated, and the Egyptians prospering while doing these things—seeing these things, I say—they were moved by popular fickleness and urged to do the like. Since they did not visibly see the true God, they served the Egyptian gods whom they could see. They were driven to this worship either by fear of Pharaoh, drawn to it by the allurements of Egyptian prosperity, or perhaps deceived by the darkness of error and ignorance.

They therefore worshipped Apis, that bull to which the Egyptians also bent their necks and to which they perversely rendered the worship owed to the Creator. Hence, I think, when in the wilderness they asked for gods to be made for them, saying to Aaron, “Make us gods to go before us; for we do not know what has happened to this Moses who brought us out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. XXXII), Aaron remembered that they had worshipped Apis in Egypt and, casting their earrings into the fire, fashioned a calf. He thought that they either would not accept another idol, or at least would not hold it so dear. Thus, seeing the new molten image and recognizing in it, as it were, their former god, they cried out with joy:

> “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (ibid.).

That they served foreign gods in Egypt is clearly attested by divine Scripture, which afterward seeks to recall them from that worship:

> “Put away the gods whom your fathers served in Mesopotamia and in Egypt, and serve the Lord” (Josh. XXIV).

## CHAPTER V

Since, then, the children of Israel were led astray by idolatrous error among the Egyptians and, as was said, were grievously oppressed with labor in clay and brick (Exod. II), when King Pharaoh died, and divine grace visited them in his death, some of them cried to the Lord from their labors—although perhaps not all; or perhaps all cried with contrite hearts. Moved by their cry, God had pity on their error and remembered the covenant which He had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He did not suffer their children to perish utterly, but kindly admonished them to return, sending Moses to them from the land of Midian.

Since Egypt is darkness, while Israel is “one who sees God,” and there is no fellowship of light with darkness—for although the light shines in darkness, the darkness does not comprehend it (John I)—the Lord willed to bring them out of Egypt, that is, out of the darkness of idolatry, and place them in the wilderness of repentance. There they might acquire the merit of holiness and, by holy living, regain—or rather increase—the height of Israelite dignity.

But because no religion seemed commendable to them unless it was occupied in offering sacrifices, and because they regarded only that devotion as fruitful which was commended by the offering of carnal gifts, God, nursing them as little children, did not abolish their custom of sacrifice. Rather, He ordered it, so that what they were unwilling to refrain from doing they might gladly offer not to gods but to the true God. This is why Pharaoh grew violently angry and implacably indignant. When Moses and Aaron came in to him and said, “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me in the wilderness” (Exod. V), he was greatly offended at the saying:

> “Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go.”

And they said:

> “The God of the Hebrews has called us, that we may go three days’ journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the Lord our God.”

And he said:

> “Why, Moses and Aaron, do you distract the people from their work? Go to your burdens” (ibid.).

And below: “They are idle, and therefore they cry out, saying: ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God’” (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “You are idle, and therefore you say: ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord.’ Go, therefore, and work” (ibid.).

Nothing seemed so grievous or troublesome to Pharaoh as that the people of Israel should leave Egypt in order to sacrifice to the true God. The spiritual Pharaoh—that is, the devil—foresaw or suspected that a great loss would be inflicted upon him if the priesthood were divinely bestowed upon the children of Israel, through whose ministry sacrifice would be offered to God Himself by that people. Accordingly, material Pharaoh strove with all the strength he could command either to nullify this plan entirely or at least to alter it somewhat.

When he saw that it could not be wholly annulled, and that, having been struck by three plagues, he was oppressed more heavily than usual by the addition of a fourth, he was compelled to soften his hardness somewhat—or rather, to pretend that it was softened. He said: “Go; sacrifice to the Lord in this land” (Exod. VIII). It was as if he said: I know that you want to sacrifice to your God in the wilderness, but go and sacrifice to Him in Egypt, so that some middle ground may be arranged between you and me, by which concord may somehow be maintained: I partly consent to your request, and you obey my command in some measure.

Moses replied: “It cannot be done so; we shall go three days’ journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to our God as He commanded us” (ibid.). The holy man, or the Spirit speaking in him, clearly saw that the people of God must have no concord with Pharaoh, and that a sacrifice cannot please God if the one who sacrifices intends not to go forth into the light of holiness but to remain in the darkness of sins. Finally, at Israel’s departure from Egypt (Exod. XIV), the same people were commanded to sacrifice the mystical lamb; but this sacrifice was designed to avail not for remaining behind, but for going out.

## CHAPTER VI

They went forth from Egypt, whether Pharaoh wished it or not, and under Moses’ leadership were settled in the wilderness, where they were instructed as novices and reared as though on tender milk. God saw that they were inclined to sin and could not, or could scarcely, be torn away from Egyptian custom—for, as you have heard, they had grown accustomed to venerating idols, occupying themselves with sacrifices, and imitating Gentile rites. He therefore did not immediately forbid them every old practice, lest, clinging more tightly to it, they should utterly reject every novelty.

For a weak mind then allows itself to be led, however imperfectly, toward better things when its guide allows it to remain in some small measure of its former delight. It more patiently endures the scalpel of the physician who cuts when it at the same time feels the gentle poultice of that same physician soothing it. Accordingly, God revealed to them a new form of religion without wholly taking away the old; He left them their old practices, yet in a sense renewed them. He granted them carnal sacrifices—that was old—and instituted that those sacrifices should be offered to Himself—that was new.

Thus, accommodating Himself to their weakness, He also provided for the benefit of us who would come long afterward. What He granted them to perform literally, He gave us to understand spiritually, so that the carnal figure might attract them as earthly-minded people, while its spiritual meaning might benefit us. For through what He commanded them He wove for us a hidden sacrament, so that we might love more deeply the things fulfilled among us when we knew them to have been prefigured long before. In commanding them to do carnal things, He foretold those things which were to be fulfilled spiritually in us; and the literal history of that time became prophecy for us.

I seem to have woven a rather long digression while showing that priesthood was received not by the Gentiles from the Jews, but by the Jews from the Gentiles—or, more truly, from God. At last we must return to the matter with which I began and show, as I promised, how the old things correspond to the new. For I promised, if I remember rightly, to mention some among the many matters written through Moses concerning Aaron and his sons and the other Levites, and to show how they can and ought to be applied to clerics, and how both the dignity and holiness of these latter are found prefigured in them.

## CHAPTER VII

Therefore, when God had given the children of Israel, settled in the wilderness, commandments for living and had earnestly forbidden them henceforth to worship the gods of the Gentiles, saying, “You shall have no strange gods before me” (Exod. XX), and again, “You shall not make gods of silver with me, nor shall you make gods of gold for me” (ibid.), He commanded that the ark and tabernacle, as was said above, be constructed, and that sacrifices be offered to Him there.

In order that the offering of sacrifices might be held commendable, and that the untamed neck of the people might be restrained by reverence for their superiors, God willed that priests should exist among that people through whose ministry He wished such worship to be rendered to Him. For He did not wish every person who offered sacrifice to be a priest to Himself and to trust, in presumptuous pride, that he was sufficient to appease God; lest the prerogative of so great an office should become more despised because every unworthy person everywhere freely assumed it for himself.

Therefore, among the other tribes of the children of Israel, He chose the tribe of Levi for a certain mystical reason; and in it He chose Aaron and his sons as priests before the rest, so that Aaron might hold the supreme primacy of the priesthood and his sons a certain secondary precedence. That they might be distinguished from the others in clothing as well as dignity and office, He willed those who ministered in the tabernacle to wear a new kind of garment, so that its reminder might render them more devoted in ministry and cause them to be held in greater reverence by the others.

Thus Moses, by the Lord’s command, made for his brother Aaron certain garments which he alone possessed as his own, and others which he shared with his sons, so that their very dress might indicate the respects in which the high priest surpassed all the others and those in which he was joined with the other priests. Thus chosen and thus clothed, Aaron and his sons perform the priesthood; they minister to the ark and tabernacle, to God and to the people: to God, that they may deserve to please Him; to the people, that they may instruct and exhort them to live well and please Him. In this is plainly shown that clerics promoted to exercise the priesthood ought not to force themselves in, but to be chosen; not to be stripped, but clothed—lest, if they exercise the priesthood without being chosen and clothed, they deserve not aid but burden from such an office.

## Prologue on the Election of Clerics

I would therefore like to linger a little longer upon this election of clerics and to examine more carefully how election is commended in the Scriptures, both New and Old, so that if, with God’s help, knowledge of it is revealed to us, then, with His grace poured in, it may be loved more deeply when known. For a person more easily loves what he knows at least somewhat; but I do not know whether one can love what one does not know. Finally, as the Apostle testifies, the hardness of certain people did not attain to love of the Lord because knowledge of Him had not first come to be in them: “For if they had known,” he says, “they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II). It is as though he said: They did not love Him because they did not know Him.

## CHAPTER VIII

Not only Aaron, of whom you have heard enough, but also his son Eleazar, is chosen by God, so that after Aaron he may serve the tabernacle with supreme care and become high priest not so much by carnal succession as by divine election. Thus God speaks to Moses:

> “Take Aaron and his son with him, and lead them up Mount Hor. When you have stripped the father of his garment, you shall put it upon Eleazar his son; and Aaron shall be gathered and shall die there” (Num. XX).

That none but the high priest wears such a garment is clearly declared in Exodus:

> “The holy garment which Aaron shall use, his sons shall have after him, that they may be anointed in it and their hands consecrated. For seven days he who is appointed high priest in Aaron’s place from among his sons, and who enters the tabernacle of testimony to minister in the sanctuary, shall wear it” (Exod. XXIX).

Who that son is who must be clothed in this garment and appointed high priest in place of his father seems to be specified in Leviticus, where the divine discourse speaks of the offering of the high priest:

> “This is the offering of Aaron and of his sons, which they must offer to the Lord on the day of their anointing: the tenth part of an ephah of fine flour, to be offered in a perpetual sacrifice” (Lev. VI).

But the priest who succeeds his father by right shall offer it warm as a most sweet odor to the Lord. Here it must be noted that it does not simply say, “the priest who succeeds his father,” but carefully says, “who succeeds his father by right,” so that the succession is understood to be just which is ratified not by descent of flesh alone but by divine election.

For Aaron himself is read to have had two other sons older in age, Nadab and Abihu, who were found worthy neither of paternal succession nor of divine election. Moses therefore did not know who ought to be advanced to the high priesthood after his brother Aaron, and he consequently had to be taught by God—especially since Aaron had another son, Ithamar, who, though found praiseworthy in life, was nevertheless not called to the rank of the supreme priesthood.

Moses himself, when he knew by divine revelation that he was to die, though he left sons to succeed him carnally, did not leave to any of them responsibility for governing the people or the honor of office. Instead, he entrusted leadership to Joshua son of Nun, chosen by God. Thus Moses says:

> “May the Lord, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over this multitude, lest the people of the Lord be like sheep without a shepherd.”

And the Lord said to him:

> “Take Joshua son of Nun, and lay your hand upon him, that the whole assembly of the children of Israel may hear him” (Num. XXVII).

Moses, I think, did not begrudge leadership to his sons. Rather, the holy man, inspired thus by God, foresaw that advancement to ecclesiastical honors was not to be sought ambitiously, but that election according to the divine will was to be awaited and commended.

Jethro also, priest of Midian, commended this election when he gave salutary advice to his son-in-law Moses. When Moses was laboring intolerably in governing the people and alone bore their cases and disputes from morning until evening, his father-in-law Jethro saw this, judged it quite unfitting, and wisely advised him to choose assistants:

> “Provide from among all the people capable men who fear God, in whom is truth, and who hate avarice; appoint from among them tribunes, centurions, commanders of fifty, and commanders of ten, to judge the people at all times. Whatever is more important, let them refer to you; let them judge only the lesser matters, and the burden will be lighter for you when it is divided among others. If you do this, you will fulfill the command of the Lord.”

When he had heard these words, Moses did everything Jethro had suggested, and, choosing able men from all Israel, appointed them rulers of the people, tribunes, centurions, commanders of fifty, and commanders of ten (Exod. XVIII).

You see that these rulers were not advanced to a more worthy rank through the impulse of their own will, but were elected by the order of divine disposition; and that dignity itself did not flatter their ambition, but served the welfare of the faithful. Since those chosen are declared to fear God, love truth, and hate avarice, it is clear that they did not seek the summit of dignity.

## CHAPTER IX

Election appears to be of great efficacy not only in governing the people, but also in danger to the people, as the reading of the divine Scriptures plainly indicates. For when Amalek was fighting against the people of Israel at Rephidim, and Moses was arranging how war should be undertaken against those who opposed them, he said to Joshua: “Choose men, go out, and fight against Amalek.” Joshua, it says, did as Moses had said, and put Amalek and his people to flight by the edge of the sword (Exod. XVII).

See: none of the children of Israel were equipped to fight against Amalek except those chosen by Joshua—that is, by Jesus—lest, if the unchosen presumed to undertake war, they should be compelled to find ruin rather than victory.

Later, when the people of Israel were dwelling at Shittim in the plains of Moab and were oppressed in disgrace, conquered not by war but by the deceit of the Midianites through the idol Peor, God willed that this injury should be avenged, so that the enemy might not rejoice longer in its deception and that Israel’s disgrace might be cleansed by a new victory:

> “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Avenge the children of Israel upon the Midianites, and afterward you shall be gathered to your people.’ Immediately Moses said: ‘Arm from among yourselves men for battle, who may exact the Lord’s vengeance on the Midianites. Let a thousand men be chosen from each tribe of Israel to be sent to war.’ And they gave a thousand from every tribe. When they had fought against the Midianites and conquered, they killed all the males” (Num. XXXI).

Something similar is found in the book of Judges. When all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, came together with one purpose and one counsel against Benjamin of Gibeah, because the men of that city had gone far beyond the bounds of lawful chastity and, tormenting the wife of a certain Levite with an unbelievable frenzy of lust, had inflicted on her a shameful death, all the children of Israel assembled before the Lord at Mizpah and decreed that war should be made against Benjamin of Gibeah, lest so great a crime go unpunished. They said:

> “Let ten men be chosen out of every hundred from all the tribes of Israel, and a hundred out of a thousand, and a thousand out of ten thousand, to bring provisions for the army, so that, fighting against Benjamin of Gibeah, we may repay it for the crime it deserves” (Judg. XX).

You see election greatly commended when war is waged against enemies, lest anyone presume to avenge others without the support of election. For whoever presumes, without being chosen, either to avenge others or to rule over others is found to bring ruin upon both himself and the rest, because presumptuous strength does not attain a desirable end unless perhaps worthy repentance has corrected it.

## CHAPTER X
Unaware of such presumption, David is chosen both to wage war [Col. 0678C] and to rule; and in both capacities he is found to have followed not his own will but the Lord’s. Thus the wise woman Abigail says to him: “The Lord will surely make for you, my lord, a faithful house, because you, my lord, fight the battles of the Lord” (1 Sam. 25). Who, I ask you, fights the battles of the Lord except one who, in battle, seeks not his own glory but the Lord’s, and grieves when he sees enemies slain, although he rejoices that victory has been granted him? Hence the same David is not moderately grieved at Saul’s death and is indignant against the mountains of Gilboa, upon which he fell (2 Sam. 1). Concerning his kingdom he says to Michal: “As the Lord lives, I will dance before the Lord, who chose me and commanded [Col. 0678D] me to be leader over the people of the Lord, Israel” (2 Sam. 6). And in Chronicles this same election is repeatedly mentioned, so that by repeating it the text seems especially to commend it. “The Lord God of Israel chose me,” he says, “that I should be king over Israel; and again, it pleased him to choose me as king over all Israel” (1 Chron. 28).

It seems superfluous at present to recount when or how God chose David himself, since I judge that the sequence of this matter is not unknown to your prudence. For you know that Jesse the Bethlehemite, having brought forward his sons in order, from the eldest downward, heard Samuel say of each one: “The Lord has not chosen this one either.” But when the young David came from the pastures, the Lord said to Samuel: “Rise and anoint him, for he is the one” (1 Sam. [Col. 0679A] 16).

Many more such examples from the Old Testament might be added to those already stated; but, lest an extended multitude produce weariness, we must at last turn aside to the writings of our own time. In them too election is found commended, and it is fitting to dwell upon this consideration.

## CHAPTER XI

When our Lord Jesus Christ dwelt with us on earth, he formed his Church by words and deeds, and carefully appointed those who were both to preside over it and to benefit it. Therefore, as you know, he chose twelve disciples, whom he also called apostles. He sent them throughout the whole world to preach and baptize in his stead, to loose and bind, to heal diseases, to command demons; and [Col. 0679B] to provide for the Church itself with paternal care, while presenting themselves to others as a pattern of life.

Finally, he bestowed such grace upon them that they performed not only the works which he himself performed, but even greater ones, as he himself declares in the Gospel (John 14) and as Holy Scripture confirms. For none in all preceding days—whether patriarchs, prophets, or any saints who served the Lord in different places and times—shone with so great a grace either of holy living or of working miracles as did the apostles themselves, who were counted worthy both to see and to love God in the flesh.

No one approached this apostolic rank unless chosen; no one thrust himself into it by swollen presumption. For Christ wished, in that first and foremost [Col. 0679C] order of the apostles, to show that the eminence of ecclesiastical dignity is not the pursuit of one’s own will, but an honour and ministry of holiness. Therefore he chose those upon whom he laid such a ministry, as he himself says to them: “I chose you” (John 15).

Moreover, when the number of those apostles had been reduced by the fall of Judas Iscariot, so that nothing might be lacking to the number, 393 which had been established by Christ himself, the apostles wished another to be substituted, to take Judas Iscariot’s place and carefully complete both so sacred a mystery and the number belonging to the sacred mystery. Therefore, as it is written, they put forward two: Joseph, called Barsabbas, and Matthias. And praying, they said: “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen [Col. 0679D] to receive the place of this ministry.” And they gave them lots, and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles” (Acts 1).

You see that only one who is chosen succeeds to Judas’s place, and that no one approaches apostolic dignity except one who is called. Matthias, indeed, is chosen by lot when he is ordained an apostle through the apostles. And those who in that time were ordained pastors of the Church were, as some maintain, chosen by lot; whence they are also called clerics. For *clericus* means “one chosen by lot.” *Cleros* is Greek and *sors* Latin; hence *clericus*, “one chosen by lot.” Thus the name “clerics” arose from the apostles, who are assuredly both clerics and princes of clerics. Being themselves chosen, they both chose others and, by choosing, taught that others ought to be chosen.

[Col. 0680A] Nor did they choose only presbyters or bishops, who hold a more worthy rank in the clerical order because of their priesthood; they also chose deacons, whom they wished to be inferior to presbyters. For when, in the early Church, the apostles saw the number of believers increasing and could not suffice for the ministry of all, it pleased them to appoint seven men of good repute to serve the faithful, so that they themselves might be freer to devote themselves to the word of God and prayer. “And they chose,” it says, “Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timotheus, and Parmenas, and Nicolas, a proselyte of Antioch; and, praying, they laid hands on them” (Acts 6).

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0680B] Saul of Tarsus also was chosen to become an apostle, as the Lord says concerning him to Ananias in a vision: “Go, for this man is a vessel of election for me” (Acts 9). Then, when the same Saul was at Antioch with the prophets and teachers, among whom were Barnabas, Simon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen: “While they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.’ Then,” it says, “fasting and praying, and laying their hands upon them, they sent them away” (Acts 13). And indeed, sent by the Holy Spirit, they departed.

Behold Saul and Barnabas, chosen from among the rest, are sent to preach the word of God, leaving a fitting pattern to which later generations ought to conform themselves. For no one ought to undertake the office of preaching unless divine election commends him; lest, if the Holy Spirit has not sent him but he has been rashly impelled by his own spirit, harmful presumption weigh him down.

Accordingly, the same Paul seems aptly to commend the bishops—that is, presbyters—of Ephesus [Col. 0680C] when he earnestly exhorts them to govern the Church: “Take heed,” he says, “to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God” (Acts 20). It is as though he said: Take heed to your own salvation and that of all the faithful, over whom you did not set yourselves by arrogant ambition, but obeyed the Holy Spirit, who set you there.

He also declares elsewhere that this is how matters ought to be done. Writing to the Hebrews and speaking of high priests, he says: “Every high priest, taken from among men, is appointed by men” (Heb. 5). He says, “taken” and “appointed,” as though to say: he does not take the high priesthood upon himself, but is taken up to it; he does not appoint himself, but is appointed. He states this openly when he adds: “Nor does anyone take the honour for himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (ibid.)—that is to say: a high priest ought to be appointed in such a way that he does not take or presume the honour, but is taken; that he does not love or choose it, but is chosen.

He confirms this by the authority of the Law, adding a little later: “The Law appoints men priests” (Heb. 7). And when instructing Titus concerning the appointment of presbyters, he says: “For this purpose I left you in Crete, that you might correct what is lacking and appoint [Col. 0681A] presbyters in the cities.” “You,” he says, “are to appoint presbyters, not they themselves” (Titus 1).

Finally, in the Gospel the Lord is found rebuking those who hasten to choose the foremost places at banquets, whereas one invited to a wedding ought to sit in the lowest place until he hears himself told: “Go up higher” (Luke 14). By these and many other testimonies of Scripture, both old and new, it is sufficiently shown that only one who is chosen ought to rise to ecclesiastical honours, lest, when the master of the house comes to inspect those reclining at table, he compel the person whom he himself did not advance to go down.

Therefore clerics must take the greatest care not to be charged with this presumption: lest they choose before they are chosen; lest, if they wish to choose while unchosen, they possess the name but not the reality. For a cleric is called “one chosen.” [Col. 0681B] The interpretation of “Levites” also accords with this interpretation, because, as a cleric is called chosen, so a Levite is called taken up. For the Lord took the Levites in place of the firstborn sons of Israel, that they might minister to him in his sanctuary (Num. 3). Thus those who are promoted to the dignity of this office ought to be chosen and taken up; otherwise they will not enjoy that blessedness of which the prophet says: “Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken up” (Ps. 64). That is to say: blessed is the cleric and Levite.

And he fittingly put the cleric first and added the Levite, because the cleric, though not earlier in time, is prior in dignity; for the Levite is the type and figure of the cleric, while the cleric is the reality which will endure until the end of the age. For the dignity and office of clerics will not fail until the coming end [Col. 0681C] of the age carries us over into the eternal ages of ages.

## CHAPTER XIII

But although, as has been said, only one who is chosen ought to be promoted to ecclesiastical honours, in our times we see things done very differently. For the number of those has grown and multiplied who glory less in the reality than in the name of clerics. Since many burn with the torches of greed and desire beyond measure either to be enriched or to be honoured, when they cannot prosper as they wish, they shamelessly thrust themselves forward and seek ordination, so that what is not bestowed upon them from their own inheritance may be bestowed through the commerce of orders.

Accordingly, when the eagerly desired day for the celebration of ordinations is announced as approaching, we see so many hurrying toward orders that they might be thought to have heard that poetic proclamation: “Let the itch seize the lowest place.” For, seeing those who have been ordained flourish, and attain to honours and riches not so much through integrity, learning, or birth as through the advantage of orders, they regard it as disgraceful if they are left in a lowly position and are not themselves somehow reckoned rich.

Thus, possessing no holiness, they assume the office of holiness—not in order thereby to serve God, but to attain their own desires more effectively. And because God was not their reason for seeking ordination, since they care not to minister to God but to the world, the very office which is refreshment and spiritual nourishment to the righteous becomes for them a snare and ruin. [Col. 0682A]

For although presbyters of this sort are commanded to feed the people spiritually, they are proved instead to feed themselves temporally; and although they appear to stand at the altar praying for the people, they await not so much divine benefits from heaven as they pursue the earthly offerings of that very people. The Lord rebukes their greed through the prophet Malachi, saying: “Who is there among you who will shut the doors and kindle my altar without payment?” (Mal. 1). God wishes the ministry of his Church and altar to be performed freely—that is, not from the impulse of greed but from zeal of charity—because what is offered is not acceptable to him if it is not brought forth from the treasury of good intention. Therefore he adds: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not receive an offering from your hand” (ibid.).

[Col. 0682B] Because God finds in them nothing pleasing to himself, he does not approve the gift externally offered either; and he who is the inward examiner of all hearts receives the gift rather without them than they without the gift. Therefore, when they set God’s glory not upon their heart but upon their offering, when they do not place purity of heart before glorifying him, they not only fail to obtain what they think to earn by offerings, but are justly rejected for the malice of their hearts. And when their outward offering alone blesses God, God, the just recompense-giver, curses their blessings.

He clearly indicates this when he says a little later: “O priests, if you will not lay it to heart to give glory to my name, says the Lord of hosts, I will send upon you [Col. 0682C] want, and I will curse your blessings; and I will curse them, because you have not laid it to heart.” Because, he says, you have not laid it to heart, because you were unwilling to understand that in which I am glorified, I will send upon you a want of good works; on account of inward perversity I will reject the outward holiness of your ministry. “For you,” he says, “have departed from the way and caused many to stumble in the Law” (Mal. 2).

Greedy priests teach perversely among the people, and by that perverse teaching cause many to stumble, while they wish both to exercise the ministry of holiness and yet not to lay aside the habits and deeds of former perversity. Of such persons Micah says: “The rulers of Jerusalem judged for gifts, its priests taught for a wage, and its prophets divined for money” (Mic. 3). Priests of this kind hold the body of Christ in no small contempt: they sell it for earthly gifts, and what was sufficient by its own price to redeem the whole world, presbyters of this sort do not refuse to dispense for the meanest alms. [Col. 0682D]

## CHAPTER XIV

All indeed utterly detest Judas Iscariot; all execrate his greed. Yet, if we wish to consider somewhat more carefully, he valued Christ’s body much more highly, since he demanded no less than thirty pieces of silver for delivering him up. But our presbyters very often offer Christ at the altar for a coin, very often for an obol, [Col. 0683A] not considering that Christ did not will himself to be valued at such a price, nor that the mystery of his passion should be celebrated with this in view.

This may be proved from his words by anyone willing to examine them more carefully. For when Christ, at the point of his passion, was in agony, and, leaving his beloved disciples the surest pledge of himself, entrusted to them the mystery of his body and blood to be celebrated, he expressly stated with what intention he wished it to be done. He said: “As often as you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me.” I ask you, presbyters, to attend more carefully to Christ’s words and understand with what regard the mystery of his body and blood ought to be celebrated. “As often as you do these things,” he says, “you shall do them in remembrance of me.” [Col. 0683B]

What does “in remembrance of me” mean? It means: not in remembrance of money, not in remembrance of the world, not in remembrance of any earthly advantage, but in remembrance of me—that is, that you may please me, love me, render a fitting return for my passion; that, as I, under the compulsion of charity, offered myself to the Father for you, so each person, through reciprocal charity, may offer himself for me. Whoever therefore does these things and does not do them in this remembrance acts against Christ’s command.

But it is certain that sacrifices do not profit when set against obedience, since, as the Lord says through Samuel: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (1 Sam. 15).—“As often as you do these things,” he says, “you shall do them in remembrance of me.” And fittingly, when Mass is celebrated, this same little verse is repeated in the canon, so that the priest may set Christ’s command before him through his own mouth, lest he be able to excuse himself—lest, that is, the fault may in any way be obscured by the covering of ignorance or forgetfulness. [Col. 0683C]

For this verse gives the righteous an incentive to love and gives the unrighteous an increase of punishments and sorrow: the former, repeating it, are more ardently stirred to imitation; the latter, despising it, are judged more severely. Yet the multitude of those who despise it is so great that marketplaces rather than churches are now filled by them; and mingling indiscriminately with the people, they are treated as though they were the people. Hence the prophet lamented: “As the people, so the priest” (Hos. 4).

For although those ordained to the ministry of the Church ought to remain within the church or its precincts [Col. 0683D] and to be separated from popular tumult and crowds in both life and rank, because they cannot endure to be restrained from such company by any barrier of discipline, we now see marketplaces, streets, and crossroads filled with them. This is also what Jeremiah laments in his Lamentations (ch. 4): namely, that the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street—that is, the ministers of the Church run unbridled through the expanses of worldly affairs.
