And what wonder if we see our ordained men wandering through the byways of conduct, when they hurried to be ordained for no other reason than that through orders they might conform themselves more openly to the world? How can anyone’s conduct be purified when that person’s intention, like a spring and source, is defiled with the mud of greed?

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0684A] As these people go astray by unjustly seeking orders, so, conversely, we see many depart from the same path by proudly fleeing them. Because perhaps their own estates support them and the necessities of the present life are readily at hand, they utterly disdain to be ordained—not because they do not wish to be honoured or enriched, but because they do not wish, through orders, to be recalled from freedom to sin.

They fear, certainly, that if they were burdened with the weight of orders, they would thereafter be compelled to live better; and, since they do not wish to abandon the will to sin, neither do they wish to lose their freedom. Therefore, when a bishop, dean, or any superior of theirs wishes to promote them to orders, because perhaps the Church seems to need their ministry, they stubbornly refuse and do not deign [Col. 0684B] to obey the commands of their superiors. They say that they fear to be adorned with sacred orders while they do not possess a life of holiness.

They wish indeed to be sustained by the Church’s temporal benefices, but they do not wish to assist that same Church in spiritual matters; they wish to live from the altar, but do not wish to serve the altar. Hence we see some churches full of canons, yet so lacking in deacons and presbyters that scarcely can anyone be found to perform such an office, unless vicars are hired like mercenaries.

But if these despisers of orders see ecclesiastical honours smiling upon them—honours which they cannot obtain without orders—they set aside the fear which they previously pretended and run toward the orders which they previously fled. Their younger age no longer holds them back; nor does unlearned foolishness, nor a life entangled in vices. But, all consideration of these things set aside, lest they fail to attain the imminent prelate’s office, they submit their necks to sacred orders, under which they will undoubtedly collapse. [Col. 0684C]

Thus in our times many churches are seriously weakened because prelates of this sort rule them by a hidden judgment. When their own presumption, rather than love of Christ, has raised them to a more worthy rank, in that very dignity they “seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2). They apply their whole minds to perishable things and, like children, clinging to present things, think nothing of things to come. “Woe to you, O land,” Scripture says, “whose king is a child” (Eccl. 10).

That is to say: Woe to you, O Church, whose prelate retains a childish life, assuming neither the gravity of old age nor the strength of youth. He does not do everything with counsel, as befits mature old age; nor is he strong, as befits youthful age. He does not sit except to eat and drink, like the children of Israel, nor rise except to play. That is, in what he does, he is captivated only by passing bodily and mental pleasure; he does not, with Paul, stretch himself toward the things that will remain without end. “I considered,” he says, “the days of old, and held the eternal years in my mind” (Ps. 76).

He does not cast away nuts and knucklebones—that is, the idle and playful things which his age seemed to have permitted to boys; nor has he taken in hand the book of the Law, which we read that Joash took when he became king (2 Chron. 23). Therefore, when such a child has been ordained by his own choice and, under the protection of orders, attained the height of some ecclesiastical principate, the people groan, as Solomon says, and lament miserably; for, while the child performs childish things, the people too do not mature. Of such people the Lord says through Isaiah: “I will give children as their princes, and effeminate men shall rule over them, and the people shall fall” (Isa. 3). [Col. 0685A]

## CHAPTER XVI

Nor does this ambition for ordination occupy only those whom we call secular clerics; it also creeps among those who seem regular in manner of life and habit. For the malignant spirit is not content, as though easily, to claim for himself those who live in public, unless he also tries in some degree to weaken those whom he sees to embrace a stricter purpose.

Thus, when they have been gathered in [Col. 0685B] a cloister under a rule, in order, having cast aside worldly things, to strive with utmost care for holiness, nevertheless within the very purpose of religious life they do not wish to appear inferior to the rest; indeed, perhaps they wish to stand out a little more highly. If, therefore, they see—or rather think—that they surpass the others in life or learning, they wish also to obtain a more worthy place among them, so that they may be held in greater reverence among those whom they consider themselves to exceed in the merit of whatever grace.

For this reason they desire to be raised to sacred orders; they either openly offer themselves or secretly seek to be invited, so that, once ordained a little more highly than the rest, they may obtain a position fitting, as they suppose, to their holiness. But if they see the day pass on which they thought their superiors would remind them, and, their hope disappointed, they are not promoted to the desired [Col. 0685C] orders, they murmur and assert that they are treated more unworthily than they deserve, since their persons ought, as they think, to have been more highly honoured.

But if they see persons whom they regard as their inferiors promoted to orders alongside them, and persons whom they do not dare deny are their equals secretly preferred to them by an ordering beyond their sight, then, judging from both considerations that their own promotion is delayed beyond measure, they complain that no small injuries are being inflicted upon them. For they refuse wisely to weigh the weakness of their own merits or to ascribe their delay altogether to God’s counsel—who either does not wish to burden them with orders beyond their strength or perhaps, by delaying, wishes to test their patience.

Paying attention to none of this, they dispute the discernment of their teachers or accuse their love toward the brethren, as though they did not know how more discerningly to see the degree in which each brother ought to be loved or in whatever manner he ought to be treated with deference. [Col. 0685D]

But those who, under regular discipline and habit, truly devote themselves to holiness wage war against vanity with utmost care and earnestness. They seek not to be honoured among the brethren, but to honour them, remembering that Christ came not to be served but to serve (Matt. 20). If, therefore, their ordination is delayed, they do not murmur that this is done through the negligence or error of their teachers; rather, they regard themselves as unworthy of so holy an office or honour. Attending solely to pleasing the divine majesty according to their purpose, they humbly entrust their care to that same will.

But if they are called to orders, they do not love to be raised up so much as they fear to be weighed down by orders, lest they who could scarcely walk in the way of God while unburdened be compelled either to fall under the load or in some degree to retard the journey they had begun. Therefore, in accepting orders they follow not a hidden desire but a compelling obedience, lest, if they desire too greatly to remain hidden, they hear that refusal to comply is a kind of divination (1 Sam. 15). [Col. 0686A]

Yet many, though they do not rashly seek ordination, nevertheless wish to be invited to it through obedience—not because they wish, as they suppose, to be more highly honoured, but because they judge that they will serve God more devotedly and assist those whom they love more effectively by prayer. Thus they rejoice if both lesser and greater brethren are ordained, so that they too may be invited, if not before the others, at least together with them.

[Col. 0686B] When invited, however, they rejoice beyond measure to obey commands they desired; when not invited, they grieve that the purpose of their conceived desire is frustrated. And because they grieve for themselves and rejoice for themselves, it must be feared that they are shown to consent not so much to God as to themselves. For the truly obedient person ought, by following and loving the divine counsel, to commend it—not to apply divine counsel to his own will.

That ancient enemy, who has a thousand arts of harming, diligently strives to overthrow those whom he sees ascending to higher things by a stricter purpose. Either he confronts them from the front and turns them back through open assaults toward the things they have left behind; or, coming at their side, he hurls at them the dart of proud vanity; or, following from behind, he extorts from them, as though a tribute, some admixture of their own will.

[Col. 0686C] Therefore whoever takes care to escape all his snares must set before himself nothing except what obedience dictates; undertake nothing that it forbids; and despise nothing that it commands. For it belongs to a religious man—that is, one who does not feign religion but loves it—to love obedience, not because it accords with his own will, but because it pleases divine goodness.

Finally, human will is judged commendable when it serves as the humble handmaid of obedience, not when, in a perverse order, it seeks to go before it and loves obedience itself only because obedience obeys it. Therefore that person is safely—indeed, beneficially—promoted to ecclesiastical dignity who, in that very promotion, follows not his own will but God’s; and who, if it were possible, would prefer to remain more safely in a lowly place than to stand more dangerously in an exalted one. [Col. 0686D]

## CHAPTER XVII

There is, however, a certain election which every religious person ought truly to desire: that by which, insofar as he is permitted, he ought to choose himself, and which he is commanded by the testimony of the divine Scriptures to love. It is that which our master, the teacher of all, marked out in the Gospel reading when he earnestly instructed us to embrace it, teaching what we ought and ought not to choose if we sincerely desire to become his imitators. “When you are invited to a wedding,” he says, “recline in the lowest place” (Luke 14).

He spoke this parable to guests whom he observed choosing the foremost places at banquets. Therefore it is ours to choose the lowest [Col. 0687A] place and not presumptuously to raise ourselves to higher things. But if the outward lowering of a person is not possible in a given case, its disposition must nevertheless be preserved in the heart, so that true inward humility may be maintained, although outward deference is rendered to each person according to his proper rank.

The same Master also clearly expressed this elsewhere, saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). It is as though he said: Even if, because of the dignity of some office, you hold a higher place, nevertheless, following my example, embrace a lower one in humility of heart, so that what belongs to dignity may be rendered to it, without injury to humility.

For there are many who, when they attain dignity, lay aside [Col. 0687B] the humility which they previously seemed to maintain, as though dignity and humility did not agree well or dwell in one seat. But neither does humility prejudice dignity nor dignity humility; indeed, dignity especially requires humility, and only humility is worthy of dignity.

David is known to have possessed both. He is recorded as having been a king, yet he remained humble. “The Lord chose me,” he says, “and commanded that I should be leader over the people of Israel” (1 Chron. 28). Behold dignity. “I chose to be cast down in the house of my God” (Ps. 83). Behold humility. Observe how pointedly he took care to distinguish these two elections, wishing to ascribe one to God and the other to himself: for it belongs not to us but to God to raise us to a rank of dignity, whereas it belongs to us, by the inspiration of his grace, always to choose humility.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0687C]

When, therefore, a cleric has been chosen for ecclesiastical dignity—not taking the honor to himself, but called by God as Aaron was (Heb. 5)—it remains for him to be clothed as Aaron was, lest, while his election is held commendable, his unsuitable nakedness be reproved. For election alone is not enough to commend a cleric: just as none but one chosen should minister at the altar, so none but one clothed should do so. The garment by which he ought to be covered and adorned, so that his ugliness may not appear, is a certain interweaving of virtues and an admirable beauty. If he is found not to possess these, he cannot please Him by whom he was chosen.

That election alone does not suffice to commend a cleric may be established by the testimony of many who, though chosen, are found to have been rejected because they lacked the garment of virtues. Thus God is said to have chosen Saul to be king over the people of Israel; yet, because he did not remain worthy of his election, he is known to have become reprobate. “Saul,” it says, “stood in the midst of the people, and he was taller than all the people from the shoulder upward. And Samuel said to all the people: Surely you see him whom the Lord has chosen, for there is none like him among all the people” (1 Sam. 10). But afterward, when through disobedience he had been stripped of the covering of virtues: “The word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying: I repent that I have made Saul king, because he has forsaken me and has not fulfilled my words in deed” (1 Sam. 15).

Since, therefore, he did not fulfill God’s words in deed, God cast him away, as it is written [Col. 0688A], so that he should no longer be king over His people Israel; and he fell on Mount Gilboa (2 Sam. 1). For Saul’s death signifies the fall and ruin of those who, after attaining ecclesiastical dignity, neither acquire new holiness nor even retain their old holiness. The more highly they are set above others, the more grievously they are cast down. For the ancient enemy strives to assail more intensely those whom he sees preferred above others, and often succeeds in overcoming them through the allurements of dignity.

Thus the mountain on which Saul died is called Mount Gilboa; and Gilboa is interpreted as “slippery,” because, plainly, no one plants firm steps upon the lofty summit of ecclesiastical dignity unless he possesses the gravity of mature holiness. Often one who seemed to stand safely on level and humble ground, and to walk steadily [Col. 0688B], when he comes to steep and slippery ground, does not withstand his more fiercely attacking adversary and does not persevere in the holiness he had begun. Beholding this, the mystical David mourns bitterly and laments with tears that those who had formerly been strong have fallen. “How,” he says, “have the mighty fallen?” (ibid.).

Saul had indeed been strong while he fought on the plain and forcefully overcame the enemies of Israel with an unconquered hand. But when he ascended Mount Gilboa to fight, not only was he unable to obtain the victory that fled from him; in a new fashion, unable to stand, the unhappy man fell into a snare and into ruin. For the prophet Samuel attests that, while he lived as a private man, he was humble in his own eyes; but when he had become king, he was condemned for stubborn disobedience (1 Sam. [Col. 0688C] 15). His humility, therefore, gave him an impregnable defense; dignity, producing pride, brought him the harm of death.

For this reason David, as though indignant, curses Mount Gilboa upon which Saul had fallen—or rather, by the spirit of prophecy foretells the curses inflicted upon many prelates: “Mount Gilboa,” he says, “let neither dew nor rain come upon you” (2 Sam. 1). Dew signifies the inward sweetness of heavenly inspiration, while rain signifies the outpouring of divine preaching. Certainly that dignity is not enriched by these, in which a prelate is proved not to conquer but to fall. Hence he adds: “For there the shield of the mighty was cast away—the shield of Saul” (ibid.). As if he said: that splendidness of honor does not receive the gift of saving grace, in which even strength falls; in which, the shield and defense of the one resisting having been knocked away, the malice of the attacking adversary triumphs and rejoices.

But because the carnal malice of the envious sometimes insults the spiritual downfall of the righteous—more ready, should it see them slip, to laugh mockingly than to sympathize mercifully with them as they fall—David interweaves into his lament and says: “Do not announce it in Gath, nor proclaim it in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult” (ibid.). Gath and Ashkelon are cities of the Gentiles; the Philistines, or “the uncircumcised,” are the Gentiles themselves. By them are appropriately denoted people of secular life who, according to the Apostle, walk in their desires like the Gentiles who do not know God, undertaking nothing narrow, nothing holy, but proceeding by the broad and spacious way that leads to death.

When such people see or hear that persons of a higher order, abandoning their profession, are carried down into the depths of vices—persons whom they knew ought to be preferred to themselves, both by the prerogative of dignity and by the merit of holiness—they mock, laugh, and rejoice because they have found an occasion for detraction and, as it were, freedom to sin more securely. “Look,” they say, “those whom the excellence of their rank set above us and proposed as examples of better living are found to sin far worse than others and to depart from the way of truth far more shamelessly. Is it not therefore enough that we should never begin so great a profession, rather than bring to such an end one rashly begun?”

Since they have the will to live badly, they seize upon such an occasion as greater license; and they rejoice to become worse by the example of those whom a worse life makes more contemptible even in their own eyes. Nor do they any longer receive words of correction reverently from persons whose conduct and life they despise; rather, taking up the brazen boldness of resistance, they further add the insults of biting chatter. Therefore David says: “Do not announce it in Gath or Ashkelon, lest they rejoice.” As if he said: Do not report to secular and envious people the fall of those who stand preeminent in ecclesiastical dignity, because they are readier to fall together, rejoicing at the victory of the wrangling deceiver, than to wash their hands in the blood of the sinner.

Nor was Saul alone chosen for rejection: Solomon also is found to have been chosen. For David says in Chronicles (1 Chron. 28): “From among my sons the Lord chose Solomon my son, that he should sit upon the throne of the kingdom of the Lord over Israel”; and to Solomon himself: “Now, because the Lord has chosen you to build the house of the sanctuary.” And below: “The Lord chose Solomon my son alone, still a boy and tender.” Yet I pass over for the present how Solomon was rejected, because this has been said more than sufficiently in the preceding answer. We have produced two examples from the Old Testament; let us seek two more in the New.

## Chapter XIX

When Christ chose the twelve disciples, whom, as was said above, He named apostles, He also chose among them [Col. 0689D] Judas Iscariot, whom He unquestionably rejected after choosing him. Christ Himself briefly indicated both his election and his rejection, saying: “Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6).

Likewise, when, after Christ’s ascension, the apostles chose seven deacons, they chose among them Nicholas, a proselyte of Antioch. When he fell away into heresy, the other six remained in the faith. It should be noted that, whereas the others are simply named, to him alone his national designation is expressly added: he is called “a proselyte of Antioch.” It is as though Scripture wished thereby covertly to convey that the others were natives and therefore perhaps members of God’s household and fellow citizens with the saints, whereas this man, remaining and continuing a stranger and foreigner, did not share the grace of the others.

The interpretation of his name also seems to agree with this, for it is known to mean “foolish people.” For *Nicolaus* is interpreted “foolish people”; *layas* means “people,” whence also *laicus*, “layman,” that is, “of the people.” Rightly, therefore, was he called Nicholas, for, abandoning the wisdom that is God’s and is God Himself, he fell away into the ignorance—indeed, the folly—of the people.

Let these four examples suffice for your charity, so that you may know that no one should place confidence in his own election unless, seeing himself commended by an election fitting to him, he strives, by putting on the garment of virtues, to adorn himself. This garment, in my judgment, ought to be twofold, so that it may sufficiently avail for all necessities. Otherwise, if a cleric thinks a single garment sufficient for him, constrained by a poverty proper to the common people, he may suffer loss of salvation [Col. 0690B].

For although a layman may perhaps be regarded as content with one garment, and may be so poor that he cannot even obtain that unless it is bestowed upon him through clerical generosity, it is nevertheless unfitting for a cleric to conform himself to that likeness. He ought to be exalted by a far richer prerogative of virtues. For one who ought to instruct the layperson both by words and by conduct must unquestionably shine more brightly in both, so that, having labored to distinguish himself by the garments of fitting virtues, he may freely undertake diligently to clothe others.

## Chapter XX

Therefore, as has been said, let the cleric have a twofold garment, which grants him a twofold grace [Col. 0690C]: an ornament suitable to his dignity and an unfailing protection against the discomforts of sun and cold. For clothing is judged necessary on these two grounds: that a person may be suitably adorned and may be fortified, as by a means of repelling, against encroaching discomforts.

The garment that adorns and protects the cleric is knowledge and righteousness. Each is so necessarily joined to the other that either without the other is held insufficient to clothe the cleric. For it is not enough that he be clothed either in uninstructed righteousness or in unrighteous knowledge. Rather, he must be clothed with two tunics—that is, distinguished alike by knowledge and righteousness.

Thus Aaron, the first high priest under the Law, who is a type and figure of our clerical order, is said to have been clothed in tunics by the Lord’s command. Moses, at the Lord’s bidding, clothed him with two tunics: one inner tunic of fine linen, that is, linen; the other, an outer tunic of hyacinth-blue (Exod. 28). In the linen is signified the subtle and inward knowledge of the Scriptures, in which the cleric ought, through reading and meditation, to be wholly occupied, delighting in it as in a soft and delicate garment. In the blue outer garment, the color of the air, is shown the righteous practice both of living and preaching, through which the cleric is proved to seek heavenly things. Thus, while inwardly he burns with desire for the Scriptures, outwardly he must not grow sluggish in righteous works; rather, both in living and teaching, his holiness should become known everywhere.

Although the sons of the same Aaron are found clothed not in two tunics but only in one linen garment [Col. 0691A], they are not believed exempt from what those two signify. For they too are commanded to possess knowledge and righteousness; yet it is fitting that the greater one, the high priest, should excel more in them. In the pontifical attire of Aaron the priest, eight particular insignia are described; of these only four are assigned to his sons. This does not mean that these priests also should not be distinguished by every kind of virtue, but that the one set over them ought to be more honorably and richly clothed.

Those garments signify different ornaments of virtues, with which every cleric ought to shine; but to discuss them individually belongs neither to this place nor to this time. Omitting them, then, we must return to what I proposed and discuss the twofold garment which, by God’s gift, now comes to mind.

## Chapter XXI

When the Holy Spirit spoke through Solomon concerning the valiant woman—by whom, as no one doubts, the Church is figured—He declared her clothed in a double garment, saying: “Fine linen and purple are her clothing” (Prov. 31). In the fine linen is figured subtle, pure understanding acquired with much labor, to which the incomparable treasure of divine wisdom is revealed. While it delights to hide itself entirely, as it were, from the disturbance of men, it rejoices, having put off the tunic of its former ignorance, to be wrapped in a new linen cloth.

In the purple, added over the linen, righteousness is fittingly understood. For its sake the unruly flesh is worn down by worthy chastisement, often even to the shedding of blood [Col. 0691C]. Thus, by the benefit of knowledge, strength grows in the hidden bosom of conscience through the cooperation of grace; from this proceeds the manifold beauty of righteous works. Hence the passage adds: “Strength and beauty are her clothing” (ibid.).

And so that what is assigned generally to the universal Church may be known to be ascribed individually also to her members, it says shortly beforehand: “All her household are clothed in double garments” (ibid.). Who are the household of the Church but clerics? They enter the tabernacle while the people remain, as it were, outside in the open court; completing the offices of sacrifice, they enter also the Holy of Holies, where the ark of acacia wood was commanded to be placed, where, that is, they make Christ’s body with their own hands upon the altar.

For there is the ark, there the manna, there the mercy-seat, there the two cherubim—that is to say, there is Christ’s body, there Christ’s divinity, there Christ Himself, there the ministry of angels. Among all these things clerics’ dignity and office deserve to move and, as it were, to contemplate them. These are the household who, because of the prerogative of this contemplation, are said to sit beside Solomon’s bed and to serve Solomon Himself more intimately and closely, while, holding swords and thoroughly trained for war, they labor to guard that same bed—that is, the Church. “Behold,” it says, “Solomon’s bed; sixty of the mighty men of Israel surround it, all holding swords and thoroughly trained for war” (Song 3). Certainly these members of the household are clothed in double garments when they are said to be both learned for battle and strong for battle.

But if one recalls what was said to the apostles, “Do not have two tunics” (Mark 6), one must understand that something different is meant there—something which preachers of God’s word should by no means possess. They ought not to possess double clothing out of fear of future nakedness, since hearers ought to provide the necessities for preachers of truth. Or perhaps those who preach evangelical truth ought not to embrace fleeting vanity, lest, though they seem fittingly to commend heavenly things in speech, they be convicted of loving and seeking earthly things, and, for the sake of things that will pass away more swiftly, of imparting to their hearers those things which remain forever.

For this is, in a sense, to possess two tunics: outwardly to display holy speech while inwardly concealing an evil intention. Hence the Prophet says: “They spoke with heart and heart” (Ps. 11). And another Wise Man says: “Woe to the double heart, to wicked lips, to hands that do evil, and to the sinner who walks upon the earth by two ways” (Sir. 2).

## Chapter XXII

Nevertheless, John the Baptist says this concerning two tunics: “He who has two tunics, let him give to him who has none” (Luke 3). That is to say: he who possesses knowledge and righteousness should share them with one in need. And he fittingly did not say, “He who has two tunics, let him give one to him who has none,” so as to command him to keep one and give the other, which indeed seems appropriate according to the letter.

For in no other way can someone with two tunics clothe both himself bodily and another person, except by giving one away and keeping the other. If he keeps both, he gives none to another; if he gives both, he suffers the discomforts of nakedness. He therefore did not say, “He who has two tunics, let him give one to him who has none,” but simply, “Let him give to him who has none.” By this, I judge, he wished to convey that one may mercifully assist another from one’s spiritual tunics and yet suffer no harm or loss. Spiritual gifts are indeed such that, although given to others with a generous hand, they are not in any way diminished in the giver; rather, the more abundantly you strive to distribute them, the more abundantly you find them increasing within you.

A pagan poet expressed this elegantly in one verse, though perhaps he did not know what he was saying:

> “Who would wish light, once set beside another light, to be taken from it?” —Ovid

For light is a spiritual benefit, bestowed upon one who lacks it without failing in the person who bestows it. Thus the Lord says to the apostles: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see” (Matt. 5), wishing people to be enlightened through the apostles, yet not wishing those apostles themselves to be blinded.

Finally, when John the Evangelist spoke of that true light which enlightens every person coming into this world, he said: “We all received from his fullness” (John 1). When the fullness of that true light enlightened John, was the greatness of that fullness diminished in itself? Certainly not. Perhaps for that reason he did not presume to say, “We all received his fullness,” lest, if he testified that it could be received by a human being, he might seem to detract from so great a fullness. Instead he said, “We all received from his fullness,” indicating that much from that fullness had been bestowed upon himself while nothing whatsoever had been diminished in that fullness.

John the Baptist signified this when he said: “He who has two tunics, let him give to him who has none.” As though he said: I do not say, “Let him give one,” nor do I say, “Let him give both,” lest, while providing for the one who lacks, I seem to inflict loss upon the giver. Or perhaps it was not proper to say, “He who has two tunics, let him give one or both to him who has none,” lest a fixed limit and measure seem imposed upon the one commanded to give, while the recipient’s capacity was disregarded in favor of the giver’s discretion.

For although anyone burning with charity is a lavish distributor of spiritual gifts, the hearer is nevertheless often not capable of receiving them. Therefore they must be brought forth not so much according to the giver’s ability as according to the hearer’s capacity. A cleric, then, ought to possess two tunics and give to one who has none: he ought to be formed by knowledge and righteousness, and to form others by the same.

## II. On the Knowledge of Clerics

## Chapter XXIII

To speak separately of each matter: if anyone wishes to know more carefully than he already knows with certainty that knowledge of the Scriptures properly belongs to clerics, he may easily discover this by turning through the Scriptures themselves.

In Exodus, when the divine discourse speaks of building the tabernacle, and Bezalel is summoned with Oholiab to construct it, it says: “The Lord filled them with the spirit of wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and every kind of learning, to devise and accomplish the work” (Exod. 31). By the tabernacle built in the wilderness the present Church is signified; by Bezalel and Oholiab, the clerics to whom the care and concern of building that Church are entrusted.

And lest the unlearned should unjustly boast in the name of clerics, when clerics hold the place of teachers [Col. 0693C], they must be filled with the spirit of wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and every kind of learning. Otherwise they must fear lest the clerical state be for them not so much a summit as a ruin. For, being appointed to establish the Church, what will they accomplish unless they have acquired the adze of teaching?

It is right that Bezalel and Oholiab are said to figure clerics, since the interpretation of their names appears consonant with this statement. Bezalel is interpreted “in the shadow of God”; Oholiab, “my father’s protection.” Those dwell especially in the shadow and protection of God the Father who are divinely ordained to the dignity and office of the clerical state for the building up of the Church. And lest they be cut off at the root through the dryness of barren ignorance, they are made fruitful by the shade and refreshment of saving knowledge.

In Deuteronomy, where Moses carefully instructs the people whom, at God’s command, he had undertaken to teach concerning what they ought to do, it is made abundantly clear to all how much knowledge is necessarily assigned to clerics. “If,” he says, “you perceive that a judgment is difficult and ambiguous among you, between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and leprosy—and not leprosy—and if you see the words of the judges vary within your gates, arise and go up to the place which the Lord your God shall choose. And you shall come to the priests of the Levitical race and to the judge who shall be in those days, and you shall inquire of them. They shall declare to you the truth of judgment; and you shall do whatever they say and teach you according to his law” (Deut. 17).

We perceive a difficult and ambiguous judgment among us, between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and not leprosy, whenever our dull understanding cannot distinguish between sin and sin, righteousness and righteousness, sin and unrighteousness. By “blood and blood” he signifies sin and sin; hence Hosea also says: “Blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4). By “cause and cause,” I judge that righteousness and righteousness are figured; hence David says: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42)—that is, my righteousness from an unrighteous nation. By “leprosy and not leprosy” are understood sin and non-sin; hence Leviticus says: “If there is a plague of leprosy in a man, he shall be brought to the priest” (Lev. 12).

Often we regard a greater sin as lesser, and conversely; we regard a greater righteousness as lesser, and conversely; we regard what is leprosy as not leprosy, and conversely. Therefore, when we feel that now one thing, now another is more rightly judged within us, it is as though we see the words of judges varying within our gates. For that is what the text says: “And if you see the words of judges vary within your gates” (Deut. 17).

I judge that these gates figure our five senses, through which either death or life is accustomed to enter our soul. Hence Jeremiah says: “Death entered and climbed through our windows” (Jer. 9). And David says to the righteous soul: “For he has strengthened the bars of your gates” (Ps. 147). The judges, however, are our thoughts, which by judging either accuse or excuse us. Hence the Apostle says: “Their thoughts accusing or even defending them” (Rom. 12). The words of judges thus vary within our gates when uncertain thoughts move within our heart, and we do not know to which of them we ought especially to yield, since one appears justly to resist another.

And lest this doubt persist too long, he says: “Arise and go up to the place which the Lord your God shall choose; and you shall come to the priests of the Levitical race and inquire of them” (Deut. 17). The place chosen by the Lord is the Church. Of it Jacob says: “Truly this place is holy” (Gen. 28). And Moses: “Take care not to offer your burnt offerings in every place you see, but in that which the Lord shall choose” (Deut. 12). And the Lord says to Solomon: “I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice” (2 Chron. 7). And a little later: “I have chosen and sanctified this place, that my name may be there forever” (ibid.).

The place chosen by the Lord, dearest brothers, is the congregation of holy clerics, the assembly of holy religious observance. To it Moses—that is, the divine law—admonishes those humbly to come whom he sees perishing from the disease of ignorance. There are found Levites and priests, that is, clerics of the tribe of Levi—not by descent of the flesh, but by the dignity of their office; not by a passing succession, but by enduring religious observance. Of them the Lord says in Exodus: “They shall be my priests by an everlasting religious observance” (Exod. 29).

“And you shall inquire of them,” he says, “and they shall declare to you the truth of judgment” (Deut. 17). Those declare the truth of judgment to inquirers who sit continually over divine readings, adhere wholeheartedly to their commands, strive diligently to fulfill what they have learned, and instruct others, both by word and example, to fulfill the same. “And you shall do,” he says, “whatever they say and teach you according to his law.” We should obediently hear those whom we see obeying the pages of the divine Scriptures; since they are sufficiently taught by reading, they are also prepared to live well.

Those can teach others according to the law who have learned the law. For, as a certain pagan says:

> “No one can speak what he does not know.” —Ovid

And how, I ask you, can a cleric know the law except by reading, except by applying himself diligently to divine reading? Hence it is added a little later: “He shall write for himself a copy of this Deuteronomy of the law in a book, and he shall read it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the Lord his God and keep his words and ceremonies commanded in the law” (Deut. 17).

Clerics, therefore, must give constant attention to reading if they are to satisfy the command of the divine will: by reading they are to learn how they ought to serve God and to keep His words and ceremonies commanded in the law. That such persons are pleasing to God may be doubted by no one, since through Jeremiah He promises to give them as a great gift to His people: “I will give you shepherds after my own heart, and they shall feed you with knowledge and doctrine” (Jer. 3). No one doubts that God declares those who feed with knowledge and doctrine to be pleasing to His heart; hence it may be understood that those who do not feed with knowledge and doctrine perhaps displease Him. Therefore the Lord says through Hosea: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I too will reject you, that you may not exercise priesthood for me” (Hos. 4). And below: “And it shall be, as the people, so the priest” (ibid.).

## Chapter XXIV

Likewise, when the prophet Ezekiel (chap. 3) was sent to teach the children of Israel, he says: “I looked, and behold, a hand was sent to me, in which was a rolled-up book. He spread it out before me and said to me: Son of man, eat this scroll, and, going, speak to the children of Israel. And I opened my mouth, and he fed me with that scroll.”

Metonymy is a figure in which the container is taken for the contained thing, or the contained thing for the container. This manner of speaking is frequently found in both divine and secular writings. Therefore no one doubts that by “book” or “scroll” Scripture is figured metonymically, Scripture being literally contained in a scroll.

The prophet and priest sent to the children of Israel is fittingly first fed with the scroll, because a cleric whose office it is to enrich others by the page of knowledge ought not himself to suffer hunger. One who is commanded to bring forth the abundance of saving doctrine ought certainly not to fast from that same knowledge. For how can one oppressed by weariness, who has refused to uproot the deadly languor of ignorance with the file of study, supply the life-giving nourishment of doctrine to those in need? Ignorance is indeed inexcusable when negligent will itself is at fault.

But when Jeremiah the prophet was called to the office of preaching and, upon carefully considering himself, believed that knowledge was lacking to him, he humbly declined the imposed work because of ignorance and elegantly excused that ignorance: “Behold, Lord, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child” (Jer. 1). As if he said: Do not impose the office of teacher upon me, since I am untaught—not because I was unwilling to learn, but because I have not yet been able; not entangled in the stains of negligence, but hindered by childhood.

The Lord, knowing that he had answered modestly, did not condemn him for falsehood, but mercifully removed his anxious fear through a free promise: “Do not say, ‘I am a child,’ for you shall go to all to whom I send you, and you shall speak whatever I command you” (ibid.). That is: Do not stubbornly refuse what you are commanded because of childhood, since no age may oppose divine commands; and the humility that is commended is that which truthful obedience accompanies.

And as though Jeremiah asked, “How can I fulfill what you command, when one who has not learned to speak ought to remain silent?” the Lord added: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth” (ibid.). As if He said: What does not come to you through the benefit either of age or of time, my powerful grace grants in generous measure. I give you my words, so that you may be regarded as learned and may no longer complain that you, an unlearned man, are compelled to teach others.

## Chapter XXV

Finally, in the Gospel the Lord rebukes the Sadducees because they did not know the Scriptures and therefore did not believe that souls would return to bodies through the benefit of resurrection. When they asked concerning the wife of seven brothers, whose she would be in the resurrection, He answered: “You err, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God” (Matt. 22).

When the Lord had said, “Not knowing the Scriptures,” He pointedly added, “nor the power of God.” You see what great impropriety follows ignorance of the Scriptures: whoever does not know them is convicted of not knowing even the power of God. If the Sadducees knew the Scriptures, they would by no means be ignorant of God’s power; for, understanding the Scriptures, they would not doubt the power of the resurrection which those Scriptures proclaim.

In John’s Gospel, when there is wretched dispute about Christ among the people and Christ is truly unknown by the disturbed crowd, certain lost persons produce testimonies from the Scriptures and, not knowing what they say or concerning what they make their affirmations, introduce error to those who are perishing. Some said, “This is truly the Prophet”; others, “This is the Christ”; but certain persons replied: “Does the Christ come from Galilee? Does not Scripture say that Christ comes from the seed of David and from the town of Bethlehem?” Therefore dissension arose in the crowd (John 7).

You see how great the crowd’s dissension is because they lack understanding of the Scriptures. Without this, they cannot become knowers of Christ, even though they may behold Him bodily. A little later, the chief priests and Pharisees said to the officers whom they had sent to seize Jesus: “Why have you not brought him? Have you also been deceived? Has any of the rulers or Pharisees believed in him? But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed” (ibid.).

Perhaps they speak truly: the crowd that does not know the law is accursed; therefore they too, who think they know the law and do not know it, are accursed. Nicodemus, one of them, says to them: “Does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him and knows what he does?” They answered and said to him: “Are you also a Galilean? Search the Scriptures, and see that no prophet arises from Galilee” (ibid.).

You see that in every matter they return to the Scriptures and endeavor to convict one another by their testimony; but the wretches, while judging themselves victorious, are convicted by their own judgment. They rightly urge Nicodemus to search the Scriptures. Had he and they searched them more carefully, they would certainly not have withheld but would have borne witness to the truth. Thus elsewhere in the same Gospel of John, the Lord Himself exhorts them: “Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and they indeed bear witness to me” (John 5).

Who can doubt that a person has deservedly incurred divine wrath if he has not been diligent in searching the Scriptures, when he hears the Lord commanding this in the Gospel? And He fittingly did not say, “You have eternal life in them,” but “You think that you have eternal life in them,” because, though they believed themselves to understand the Scriptures, they did not understand them; and though they supposed it falsely, they did not have eternal life in them.

He therefore says: “Search the Scriptures.” Why? “They,” He says, “are those which bear witness to me.” As if He said: If you truly wish to have eternal life—which is nothing other than myself—search the Scriptures that bear witness to me, so that by searching them you may find me in them, and, having found me, may have eternal life. Therefore He says to them: “And you are unwilling to come to me, that you may have eternal life” (ibid.). Those who are unwilling to search the Scriptures thus seem unwilling to come to Christ; nor can they be seen to possess that life, though they may falsely suppose that they do.

## Chapter XXVI
Finally, the Lord himself, when he chose apostles who were unlearned and without letters in order to confound the wise, nevertheless did not wish them to remain unlearned; rather, as time went on, he took care to advance them into the profound mysteries of knowledge. Therefore, going up the mountain and opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V), etc. And below, when he had finished many parables with the same apostles, he concluded with these words: “Have you understood all these things? They say to him, Yes. He said to them: Therefore every learned scribe is like a householder, who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matt. XIII).

He gives worthy testimony to those who understand, calling them like householders because they worthily understand the things spoken, the new and old things brought forth from this [Col. 0698C] treasure. For the householder is Christ himself. His treasure is Holy Scripture; the new and old things are the rewards of the righteous and the punishments of the wicked. Since, by the revealed grace of the Gospel, the rewards of eternal life are conferred upon the righteous as a new gift, while punishments are imposed upon the unrighteous, as from ancient times, by hereditary right, the householder is fittingly said to bring new and old things from his treasure, when through his Scriptures Christ promises both punishments to the unrighteous and the joys of life to the righteous.

The learned scribe is like Christ himself when he prudently understands what is said in the Scriptures; when he does not neglect to inscribe it with the stylus of memory upon the tablets of his heart; and when he does not doubt that these same things are salutary [Col. 0698D] for all who understand worthily. Thus the Lord invites the apostles and their successors to study by encouragement; yet shortly afterward, when Peter said to him, “Explain this parable to us,” he answered by rebuke: “Are you also still without understanding?” (Matt. XV). He wished to arouse them to study not only by encouragements but also by rebukes, lest, serving sluggishness and idleness, they presume to provoke him to anger.

Accordingly, he fittingly rebuked the two disciples going to the village of Emmaus, as Luke relates: “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken” (Luke XXIV). And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. Thus, shortly afterward, when they had recognized [Col. 0699A] him and he vanished from their sight, they said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV).

John the Evangelist likewise states that the disciple who ran with Peter to the tomb believed that the Lord had been taken away, as the woman had said; and he seems to add, as it were, the reason why he believed so rashly: “He saw,” he says, “and believed; for he did not yet know the Scripture” (John XX). As if to say: if he had known Scripture, he would not so rashly have believed what was false. The unbelief of those going to Emmaus in Luke, and the credulity of this man in John, are condemned; and ignorance of the Scriptures is proved to be the cause of each error.

Therefore, after [Col. 0699B] his resurrection, when the Lord was about to ascend into heaven and to leave his disciples on earth for a time, he did not wish them to remain longer ignorant of the Scriptures, lest through ignorance they stray from the straight path of life or teaching. For although until then he had taught them many things as time allowed, he had nevertheless left many things yet to be taught—perhaps so that they might desire their acquisition more ardently and preserve what they had acquired more firmly. But when he was about to leave them, saying, “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI), lest preachers of truth should be lame in knowledge and unsteady in faith, he said to them: “It is necessary that all things written concerning me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke XIV). And the Evangelist adds: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” [Col. 0699C] (ibid.).

What Scriptures? Surely the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms—these three terms signifying the whole content of the Old Scripture, which, Luke testifies, was made fully clear to the apostles.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Lest anyone suppose that understanding of the Scriptures belongs only to them and not also to the clerics who occupy their place in the Church, and therefore, impatient of study and labor, choose in disgust to serve idleness, let him hear how Paul endeavors to instruct his disciples, whom he had ordained clerics, and worthily and commendably praises them once instructed.

To Timothy he says: “Give attention to reading, exhortation, and teaching” (I Tim. IV). As if to say: Do not suppose that you are a cleric in order that you should [Col. 0699D] wander about idly or perhaps become entangled in secular business; but, if you are truly to make progress, embrace reading, and, so that your progress may be manifest to all, teaching and exhortation. And lest anyone believe that a little time suffices for carrying out such things, rather than that one must persevere in studies of this kind with suitable constancy, the Apostle adds: “Meditate on these things; be occupied with them, that your progress may be manifest to all” (ibid.).

How much such constancy first benefits the reader himself and afterward benefits the hearer, he declares when he adds: “For in doing this, you will save both yourself and those who hear you.” You see how useful it is for a cleric to remain occupied with reading and exhortation: by doing these things, not only may he himself deserve salvation, but he may also glory more abundantly in the salvation of his hearers.

In another Epistle, [Col. 0700A] the same Apostle praises Timothy thus: “But you,” he says, “have followed my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, long-suffering, love, patience” (II Tim. III). Being about to mention the other virtues, he set teaching first, in order to show it as a school and a kind of forge from which, by the file and discipline of the virtues, the catalogue of virtues might spring forth.

A little later, when he admonished the same man, saying, “But remain in those things which you have learned and which have been entrusted to you” (II Tim. IV), as though Timothy were saying, “Whence do you think such power will come to me, that I may attain the holiness of perseverance which you command?” he added: “Because from childhood you have known the sacred writings, which can instruct you unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus” [Col. 0700B] (ibid.). For all Scripture inspired by God is useful.

In instructing Titus likewise, he says: “In all things show yourself an example of good works, in teaching, in integrity” (Titus II). Here too, being about to say “in integrity, in gravity,” he first said, “in teaching,” lest a cleric falsely hope to offer himself to others as an example of good works if he refuses to embrace teaching, the mother of virtues.

Hence he also greatly praises certain Corinthians, saying: “You have been made rich in him, in every word and in all knowledge” (I Cor. VII). And in another Epistle to the same people: “You abound,” he says, “in speech and knowledge” (II Cor. VIII). Finally, lest the Apostle himself be held [Col. 0700C] by the Corinthians in greater contempt than is right because of ignorance, he too humbly glories in his knowledge in the same Epistle: “I consider,” he says, “that I have done nothing less than the great apostles; for though I am unskilled in speech, I am not in knowledge” (II Cor. II).

By “speech” here he means a certain fluency and elegant arrangement of expression, which some pursue with the greatest care: they prefer speaking well to living well, appearing wise to being wise, being set above others to being useful to them. One may safely lack such charm of words and rhetorical ornament; but a cleric cannot lack knowledge of the Scriptures without fault.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

For when from childhood he is assigned to literary studies [Col. 0700D] and, other occupations being set aside, is devoted to these alone, who is so dull that, if life is his companion, he cannot attain knowledge, provided he is willing to apply more diligent care? He must therefore be reproved for negligence and sloth if, in a perverse order, he chooses to know nothing, because he has been chosen for this purpose: to surpass others in knowledge.

Yet most, once they have passed beyond the limits of childhood and reached the years of puberty, wish to exercise the privilege of a perverse freedom. Impatient of study and labor, they cast aside discipline; deserting their former nest, they find not so much flight as ruin. Freed from the servile fear of a schoolboy, they run about through the vices of reckless youth; and because they now see that no rod of an elder restrains them, they rejoice to wander more freely through the broad plains of [Col. 0701A] pleasures.

If perhaps they see riches coming to them, or any honors smiling upon them as they wish, they become all the more hostile to literary studies as they delight more in deceptive excesses. For they think themselves sufficiently learned if they see themselves exalted by riches and honors. They judge it happier to glory in monetary prosperity than to be afflicted with troubles and labors for the sake of learning. Since knowledge seems useful to them for no other purpose than attaining temporal honors and riches, if they see themselves abounding in these without effort, they consider laboring to acquire knowledge superfluous. They do not sufficiently consider that command of Wisdom: “Take hold of discipline, and not money; choose instruction rather than gold” [Col. 0701B] (Prov. VIII).

Thus what they may have acquired in childhood, while by reason of their age they remained subject to parents and teachers, they are compelled in time to forget through the predominance of idleness, when they ought already to have attained greater progress. Hence we see many heaped with riches and revenues, many adorned with ecclesiastical dignities, yet so simple, unlearned, and illiterate that, when they come among clerics assembled together for any cause, they scarcely dare to utter a word of Latin among them; and if they presume to do so, their speech does not smell of school discipline. Of such people divine Scripture says: “What profit is it for a fool to possess riches, when he cannot buy wisdom?” (Prov. XVII).

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Col. 0701C]

Just as these men are drawn back from the labor of learning by harmful prosperity, so many others, as they say, are hindered by poverty. Seeing that the financial resources at their disposal do not suffice according to their desire, and unprepared to endure even the small discomforts of poverty, they prefer to remain uneducated among their own people rather than be needy among strangers for the sake of learning.

Flattering themselves with this excuse, and miserably deceiving themselves with flattering enticements, while they refuse to devote effort to study and labor, they indulge pleasantly in idleness and [Col. 0701D] sloth. And the less they are occupied with literary studies, the more they succumb to deadly pleasure, because idleness, by withdrawing their desire from honorable labors, undoubtedly supplies abundant material for sinning.

Thus, while through the discomforts of poverty they refuse to attain knowledge, they are compelled to find moral ruin; and while with blameworthy languor they are sluggish toward honorable and useful things, they burn even more blameworthily for things wicked and harmful. For when they observe that they cannot attain the joys of passing prosperity through the benefit of clerical integrity, they do not hesitate to fall into every sort of disgrace, in order somehow to obtain their desires.

Accordingly, they become entangled in secular business and revere the marketplace more than the church: imprudently—indeed, shamelessly—eager in acquiring temporal things, but wholly without zeal for preserving clerical honor. And now, setting before themselves no barrier to sin, they retain nothing of the cleric except the name, in whose outward appearance they falsely glory, since they are shown to possess the name without the reality.

Many, moreover, to complete their own ruin, presume to approach sacred orders; and although they know nothing—indeed, because they know nothing—they hasten to seize the place of knowledge, which they ought especially to have avoided because ignorance cannot accord with that order. Since knowledge is beyond doubt fitting for every cleric, it is particularly fitting for him who is exalted to the summit of priesthood, lest an ignorant priest seem to contradict that saying of Malachi: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge” [Col. 0702A] (Mal. II).

Yet in order that they may compensate for the disadvantages of their ignorance by a new trade, they do not shrink from arrogating to themselves the priestly rank by rash presumption. They are ensnared all the more dangerously [Col. 0702B] unto ruin because the more rashly ignorant men seize the position of the learned. For because, laboring in sloth, they desire to know nothing from the Scriptures, they do not know how to preserve their life and order by fitting religious observance; and what they do not first endeavor to attain by knowledge, they cannot afterward exhibit in works.

Against this divine speech declares: “A disciplined and instructed man keeps himself” (Ecclus. XL). Yet though they have neither knowledge nor fitting self-guarding, they presume to teach an ignorant people and do not fear to usurp the position of teacher which many a wise man avoids occupying. Divine Scripture elegantly condemned their presumption when, to confound them, it commendably praised Ecclesiastes: “Because Ecclesiastes was most wise,” it says, “he taught the people” [Col. 0702C] (Eccl. XII).

As though it said: Be ashamed, you who, knowing nothing, do not fear to invade the place of knowledge; you who, without having experienced the footstool of discipleship, sit down by a precipitate leap in the teacher’s chair—when Ecclesiastes did not presume to instruct the people until he had first deserved to obtain wisdom. Therefore, because they despise wisdom, they cannot find spiritual progress or minister saving teaching to others; instead, by their example they destroy those whom they ought to have given life, since they chose not to live through wisdom but rather to die through ignorance.

In contrast, divine Scripture says: “Instruction and wisdom have this: they give life to their possessor” (Eccles. VII). Thus indeed, though there is a great multitude of clerics in the world, the number of ignorant men is infinite; and none or scarcely any among them can excuse his ignorance, whether poverty or riches abound to him. For they refuse to hear the counsel of a certain wise man—indeed, of Wisdom itself—who thus gives us wholesome admonition: “Draw near to me, you unlearned, and gather yourselves into the house of discipline” (Ecclus. LI). And another Wise Man says: “He who rejects wisdom and discipline is unhappy” [Col. 0702D] (Wis. III).

## CHAPTER XXX

Not only those who offer such excuses are drawn back from the study of learning by harmful sloth; many also who renounce the world and devote themselves to a cloistered rule are so drawn back. Although they seem commendably zealous in serving God, they are sluggish with blameworthy languor in diligent reading.

For since God has brought them out of secular life so that thereafter in the cloister they may devote the greatest care and diligence to spiritual work, they ought not, in my judgment, to be considered blameless if they disdain to meditate on the divine law with fitting constancy. The divine law is Holy Scripture; a cloistered cleric ought to be wholly occupied with its reading, if he takes care, in accordance with his profession, to oppose the world more perfectly and, cleansed of earthly things, to have his conversation in heaven with the Apostle.

Of this law David the prophet says: “The law of the Lord is spotless, converting souls” [Col. 0703B] (Ps. XVIII). Holy Scripture is appropriately called “spotless law” from its effect, because with the help of grace it cleanses its readers from earthly affection; and it converts the souls that the enticement of temporal things has perverted through the error of ignorance, by recalling, forming, and enlightening them.

For while it bears witness that these visible things will pass away swiftly, whereas those things which are not seen will remain without end, what else does it do but endeavor to draw those childish in understanding away from love of visible things and train them toward desire for invisible things? Hence the same prophet adds: “The testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones” (ibid.).

The testimony of the Lord is Scripture, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Search the Scriptures: these are they which bear testimony concerning me” (John V). Therefore a cleric ought to remain in this law day and night, if he seeks more fully to glory in the blessedness of the perfect; and, having learned it by reading and meditation, he ought to give it back in preaching to those who seek it.

Thus Malachi, speaking mystically concerning the cleric, says: “They shall seek the law from his mouth” [Col. 0703C] (Mal. II). And another Wise Man says: “Let not the account of the elders pass you by” (Ecclus. VIII), “for from them you shall learn understanding, and in time of need you shall give an answer.”

But many cloistered persons, as I had begun to say, refuse to apply themselves more diligently to reading; and, what is worse, they frequently accuse, openly or secretly, those who do apply themselves, judging them to be idly inactive because they do not see them busy with temporal tasks. Therefore, because they find sitting, reading, and meditating burdensome, they desire to be occupied with outward matters; and if no duties happen to be entrusted to them, they complain with hostile murmuring about their superiors’ distrust.

For they say that those who impose upon them no outward obedience do not place sufficient trust in them, although, as they say, they are ready to obey commands and serve the needs of the brothers. But if they undertake any outward task, they rejoice because they are no longer compelled to sit and read; and, flattering themselves because of the duty imposed upon them, they give themselves up more than is right to running about and talking. And since they extend themselves with looser reins toward the outward affairs they covet, they return very seldom to the inward and spiritual matters of reading and meditation.

Even if they sometimes attempt this, weariness intervenes and drives them back to a welcome habit. Many, moreover, neglect to give reading prolonged attention because they do not understand everything they read; and, because Scripture is found difficult, they think that such reading will not profit them. Therefore, closing the book, they turn back to temporal affairs; and if opportunity or permission for action is lacking, they at least turn these matters over in their thoughts—more ready to wander freely abroad, or in mind, than to search out the obscurities of Scripture with diligent persistence [Col. 0704A].

## CHAPTER XXXI

But Scripture itself requires a reader who is diligent, not wandering or fastidious, because it is often obscure in order that it may be sought more laboriously and, once understood, retained more gratefully. Therefore, when it presents itself as obscure, one must not immediately recoil from reading; rather, one must persist all the more, so that fitting persistence may deserve to find what Christ refuses to grant to a negligent reader.

Christ himself must also be knocked upon by devout questioning; he delights to open the enigmas of Scripture to questioners, provided that those who question can find him alone. Mark the Evangelist, as it seems to me, elegantly indicated this after recounting that Christ had spoken the parable of the sower to the surrounding crowds: “And when he was alone,” he says, “those who were with him, the Twelve, questioned him concerning the parables. And he said: To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” [Col. 0704B] (Mark IV).

When, I ask you, my brothers [Col. 0704C], do we find Christ alone, unless it is when we drive from our hearts every worldly tumult, so that nothing unsuitable may disturb our reading and nothing hinder our meditation, but we apply ourselves to the sacred pages with this intention: that through the benefit of reading we may know Christ more fully, love him once known, and hold fast to him once loved?

Therefore, when we remove everything that disturbs reading, and in reading think of nothing except pleasing Christ, we undoubtedly find him in a certain manner alone; and to such finders he gives spiritual understanding of the Scriptures. Hence he says to them: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God.” To you, namely, who steadfastly desire to know; to you who question me when I am alone. To you, I say, it has been given to know the mysteries contained in the Scriptures, which are hidden from those who sleep and are fastidious.

Thus also in Matthew, after saying, “To you it has been given to know the mysteries [Col. 0704D] of the kingdom of heaven,” he added: “But to the rest it has not been given” (Matt. XIII). And why it had been given to the apostles but not given to the rest, he stated as follows: “For to him who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound; but from him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away” (ibid.).

This is to say: he who has diligence shall receive understanding; he who has persistence in seeking and reading shall find the grace of comprehension. But he who does not have it—even if he has natural ability or a little knowledge—what he has, I say, shall be taken from him, because he will derive no future benefit from it.

Therefore Christ, found alone, must be prayed to, that from above he may remove the veil of obscurity from the letter and remove from our heart the cloud of blindness; for the book offered to us who know letters does not delight us while it remains sealed with unbreakable seals [Col. 0705A].

## CHAPTER XXXII

But if simple prayer is perhaps insufficient to obtain the opening of the book and the unsealing of its seals, one must nevertheless not cease, lest the reader or petitioner seem to have failed through negligent weariness. Rather, one must do what John the Apostle says that he did: “For when he saw in the right hand of the one seated upon the throne a book sealed with seven seals, and no one in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth could be found through whom the sealed book could be opened, I, John,” he says, “wept much, because no one was found worthy to open the book or look upon it” [Col. 0705B] (Apoc. V).

And he indicates the fruit of his weeping when he adds: “And one of the elders said to me: Do not weep; behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, to open the book and its seven seals” (ibid.). And after this was said: “I saw,” he says, “in the midst of the throne and in the midst of the elders a lamb standing as though slain; and he came and received from the right hand of the one seated upon the throne the book, and opened it” (Apoc. V).

Therefore, when those things which are hidden in the Scriptures under the envelope of the letter, sealed over, are not disclosed to us who read and desire to know, that supreme Teacher must be knocked upon with prayers. And if a wordy prayer does not move him to give generously, an outpouring [Col. 0705C] of tears must be added. This is often found more effective with God; by it his severity is softened, and what he does not wish to grant to one who entreats, he cannot endure to deny to one who weeps.

If, then, while we are occupied in reading, we feel that our understanding is clouded and that the veil of the letter, set before us, obstructs our effort, a stream of tears must be drawn forth, that it may wash away and abolish the obscure surface of the Scriptures. For when a diligent reader weeps from desire to understand, the outward eye is thereby darkened for a time, but the inward eye is thereby made clear in a new manner; and what had previously appeared obscure becomes plain to him.

Although it is not Scripture but the face that is watered with tears, yet by such irrigation it is not the face but Scripture that is purified in an ineffable way. And although the former is materially washed, there can be no doubt that the effect of the washing passes to the latter [Col. 0705D]. But this transfer is not seen by carnal eyes; spiritual understanding sees it more clearly, when it sees that what before tears lay hidden, wrapped in sealing clouds, is after tears freed from every darkness.

A marvelous matter, and one which we, though speaking of it, know not so much by the experience of feeling as by the unquestionable testimony of divine reading: for not to all to whom the benefit of this knowledge is granted is also given the grace of experiencing it. The Apostle John knew it by experience. When no one was present who could open the sealed book, “I,” he says, “wept much”; and after tears, what had previously remained hidden was made clear to him [Col. 0706A].

From this it is plainly shown how much persistence in reading and ardor in understanding one ought to have. Even if, because the eye is clouded, we cannot bring our affection for so great a good to its result, we ought nevertheless both to invoke God by prayers and to obtain his grace by tears.

It has now been made more than sufficiently clear, through many and various testimonies, that knowledge of the Scriptures properly belongs to clerics and that they ought with the greatest care to devote themselves to studies of this kind. This does not mean that, whenever they do something else, it must immediately be counted a fault, provided that work befit the clerical order. For they may lawfully undertake ecclesiastical concerns and sometimes give themselves to manual labor, provided they are moved to these not by the vice of frivolity but, as it were, forcibly by either charity or necessity.

For the Apostle bore the care of the churches [Col. 0706B] because charity pressed him, and he labored with his hands when necessity weighed upon him. Indeed, when he instructed Timothy, he did not wholly remove labor from him, but rather set it in order, in order to show that it is not foreign to a cleric sometimes to labor, if only he knows how to place it in its proper place.

For he ought to place the study of the Scriptures first and cling to it more diligently; but he ought to endure manual labor not pleasurably but tolerably, so that spiritual delight may chiefly draw him to the former, while temporal necessity, as it were against his will, compels him to the latter. “Exercise yourself,” he says, “unto piety; for bodily exercise is profitable for a little, but piety is profitable for all things” [Col. 0706C] (I Tim. IV).

By “piety” he means attentive study in the Scriptures, through which, with grace assisting, a cleric ought both to know God more fully, love him more tenderly once known, and worship him more perfectly once loved; so that, advancing in these matters, he may become spiritually God’s temple, giving others a holy example by knowing and living. Hence shortly afterward he adds: “Give attention to reading, exhortation, and teaching.” And again: “Give attention to yourself and to teaching; for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.”

For this reason he chiefly admonished Timothy toward these things: “For bodily exercise,” he says, “is profitable for a little.” Timothy knew that Paul had often devoted himself to manual labor [Col. 0706D], especially since among the Corinthians he says that he had done so very much. Timothy wished to imitate him in this too, as a good disciple, so that he might resemble his master in all things. But because neither did the same necessity press upon him as upon the Apostle, nor did he have bodily strength sufficient for much labor, the Apostle takes care, as it were moderating him, to restrain him: not wholly removing the impulse of zeal, but recalling it to a fitting measure.

“Bodily exercise,” he says, “is profitable for a little.” He does not say, “It is useless,” for otherwise he would seem wholly to condemn labor; rather, he says, “for a little,” wishing to indicate the limits of its usefulness more precisely. For labor is useful to many, because through it bodily health is sometimes preserved [Col. 0707A] and one returns more eagerly to the use of reading. It is useful, I say, when it serves reading and the other spiritual offices as an inferior, not when in a reversed and perverse order it stubbornly rules over them.

It is useful when, for the cleric, it does not presume to claim the foremost place at table, but, not forgetting its own rank, chooses to remain concealed in the last place. It is useful when the cleric imposes a rule upon it, lest it run beyond the bridle and, through the vice of frivolity, take precedence over the study of reading. Therefore it is profitable for a little in comparison with piety, which, according to the testimony of apostolic truth, is profitable for all things: “Piety,” he says, “is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come.”

For through this piety spiritual riches and glory are more abundantly acquired in the present life, and in the life to come the eternal joys of righteousness are conferred by merit. Hence David says: “Glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness remains for ever and ever” [Col. 0708A] (Ps. III). And Solomon: “In her right hand are years of life; in her left, riches and glory” (Prov. III).

Therefore a cleric ought to have as the first and chief intention of his will the desire to devote himself to seeking and studying the knowledge of truth; but he ought not to serve manual labor or ecclesiastical concerns through the curious impulse of frivolity, but through the obedience of pure and sincere charity.

# III. ON THE JUSTICE OF CLERICS

[Col. 0707]

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Col. 0707B]

Enough, it seems, has been said about the knowledge of clerics. At last we must also speak of their justice; for although, as you have heard, knowledge is commended in no slight degree, it is nevertheless insufficient unless justice is joined to it. To show this, there is no need to compile many testimonies of Scripture, for I think that no one, however unlearned, can doubt it.

For who doubts that knowledge alone grants salvation to no one, when, to say nothing of others, Solomon is known on the testimony of Scripture to have been the wisest of all, and yet, as has been sufficiently shown in another response, to have been rejected because of injustice? Justice must therefore necessarily be joined to knowledge, so that the cleric may be considered perfect in every respect as is fitting; for, as I recall having said above, neither unlearned justice nor unjust knowledge is proved sufficient for him.

Indeed, it is that second tunic with which, we said, the cleric ought to be clothed. Certainly it is not expedient that he be content with a single tunic, because Moses gives two tunics to Aaron the high priest, who is a type of clerics, and because that strong woman and her household are said to be clothed in double garments.

Just as knowledge produces justice, so justice in turn nourishes knowledge, because by its merit it obtains for knowledge spiritual progress, without which knowledge is never brought to perfection. Hence a Wise Man says: “My son, desiring wisdom, preserve justice, and God will give it to you” [Col. 0707D] (Ecclus. I). Wisdom is fittingly said to be given through the merit of justice, because without justice wisdom cannot be deemed praiseworthy; rather, however great it may appear, it is empty swelling, not solid fullness.

Thus the Apostle says: “Knowledge puffs up” (I Cor. VIII). Whom, I ask, does it puff up, except the one whom charity does not build up? Charity is love of God; and to love God is justice. For nothing is more just than that the Creator should be loved; hence love of him must be understood as true justice. Therefore, whoever does not love and preserve this justice vainly either desires or possesses knowledge; indeed, knowledge itself is reckoned harmful to him, since because of it he is accused of greater folly.

Hence the Apostle says: “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” [Col. 0708B] (Rom. I). Since all knowledge has its beginning from Christ and receives its end in him—that is, it is not brought to completion unless it makes or finds him its end, as David wisely perceived: “I have seen the end of every perfection” (Ps. CXVIII)—anyone who does not strive to be perfected by such an end, though he seem wise, nevertheless deserves to be condemned as foolish.
