For there is no truer or greater folly than that our knowledge should not know Christ. Therefore, although some attempt falsely to cloak it under the name of wisdom, the Apostle preferred to call it folly, as it truly is: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (I Cor. III). The world—that is, worldly-wise people—often consider foolish people wise; but God, who is pure truth and admits no falsehood, reproves those who do not know him for rash vanity. Hence the Prophet says: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain” [Col. 0708C] (Ps. XCIII).

## CHAPTER XXXIV
Brothers, you see that there is no true knowledge without justice as its companion. Justice drives from it the swelling of deadly vanity and fortifies it on every side with the solid bulwark of charity. It is clear, then, that many whom we see laboring greatly to acquire knowledge nevertheless stray far from the straight path of knowing; and the more earnestly they toil from a desire to know, the more—strange indeed, or rather pitiable—they go astray. For while they think themselves satisfied, as it were, with turbid waters, and take no care to be made drunk with the abundance of the limpid fountain, they abandon Him who is the beginning and end of saving knowledge, and wander off to the left, down the slopes and byways of secular wisdom. Hence Solomon says: “The Lord knows the ways that are on the right; but those that are on the left are perverse” (Prov. 4). The more vigorously and swiftly clerics run along these paths in heedless impulse, the farther they run from Christ, who is the way of truth; and because, oppressed by the darkness of vanity, they do not return to Him whom they ought to hold, they finally fall irrevocably into the pit of perdition.

[Col. 0709A] That harmful swelling which seems to spring from knowledge leads them to this end, when that same knowledge is neither acquired nor retained with justice in view, but so that they may either amass temporal riches, or boast, with others—or perhaps above others—of pompous reputation and honor. For this reason parents entrust their children to literary study and redeem their teachers at no small price, so that the little ones, still tender in age, may be imbued with letters and rendered fit to obtain the things of the world. Even the children themselves, for the most part, when with advancing age they grow up and the honorable or useful things of the world become more fully known to them, begin to burn with zeal and diligence for school discipline because they now fear being seen as inferior to others. And those who, when little, learned through fear of being whipped, when somewhat older study through love of glory: hastening to surpass those whom they see compared with themselves in equality of learning, and envying those whom they understand to be preferred because of more outstanding progress.

They therefore study and labor to compose verse well, to be judged commendable in making prose and rhythm, and to be found ready and agile in the various kinds of metre, lest anyone be able to equal them in such study. Through love of this pursuit they often endure many hardships: fasting, vigils, and self-contempt. Although these oppose the tenderness of their age, they nevertheless please them because they serve study and advancement. For one too devoted to bodily care cannot fittingly serve in the ranks of letters, since a fat belly, frequent sleep, and delicate softness are found to weaken the powers of the mind. Neglecting these things, they also make a practice of reading secular authors and carefully noting the manner of speech used by tragedians, comedians, and satirists; and they commit both these and those to memory because, as doctors and masters affirm, a morality not to be despised is contained in them.

[Col. 0709C] As time goes on, when they grow stronger both in age and in learning, they burn insatiably for the reading of the greater authors. Having read Priscian—within whom, as they say, the whole fullness of grammar is contained—they turn to the flowers and colors of rhetoric, so that they may know how to speak elegantly. But because the subtlety of dialectic is of no small benefit to the other arts, since by it falsehood is separated from truth, or truth from falsehood, they think that they know either nothing or very little unless they also strive to follow—or rather to outstrip—the rest in this art. They therefore take pains, by the aid of dialectic, to entangle others in the nets of verbal blemishes and skillfully free themselves from the cast nets of those others. And because nothing is sweeter to the talkative than chatter, they rejoice that they have at last found a talkative and wordy kind of knowledge.

Many are found to value this so highly that they do not shrink from devoting many years to it, spending countless coins upon it, and enduring many long labors—fasting, vigils, sweat, and cold. Others, for whom knowledge of the arts mentioned above does not suffice, proceed to the study and pursuit of the remaining arts; and after spending much labor and time in attaining the trivium, they finally judge that they must apply themselves to the quadrivium. Such is the ardor of excessive desire: despising what it has acquired, it presses more eagerly toward what remains to be acquired; and so long as it sees that anything is lacking, it cannot say, “It is enough.”

[Col. 0710A] Having learned grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic—which the wise men of the world chose to call the trivium—they desire to be taught arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy, which they judged should be called the quadrivium. These, indeed, are sought more inquisitively by some because they are unknown to many who know many things; and they more eagerly desire to acquire that knowledge which they understand most people, though highly learned in letters, do not possess. Some, moreover, are stirred even to read the books of divine law and are instructed by the pages of both Testaments, being more curious to know them by memory than to obey their commands unto salvation. For it is clear that not all devote themselves to knowledge with one purpose, but that different persons seek different ends of learning; and according to the merit of each individual intention, a varied fruit is given from knowledge of the Scriptures.

## Chapter XXXV

Some learn, seeking nothing else than knowledge: this is the vice of restless curiosity. Others, that they may know how to know: this is the vice of windy vanity. Others, that after learning they may sell it: this is simoniacal wickedness. Others, that they may be spiritually built up: this is pious and holy humility. Others, that, having been built up, they may also build up others: this is pure and true charity. For these five reasons care is bestowed upon every kind of knowledge. For the first three, which precede, a perishable reward awaits; but no loss destroys or corrupts the final two. Sound hope advances them, and the hoped-for reality brings them to completion, free from decay or end.

## Chapter XXXVI

But to speak of each in turn: what is more useless than to expend labor or study in acquiring knowledge, seeking from this nothing else except merely to know—being curious to gather many and various things, and, once they are gathered, to brood upon them listlessly? Thus the miser, for the most part, gathers and hides much money, feeding more on the delight of possessing than enjoying the benefit of its use; he prefers that it decay in a pit or pouch in his own possession rather than be brought forth for his own use or another’s. Hence a certain Wise Man fittingly says: “A hidden treasure and an unjust wisdom: what profit is there in either?” (Ecclus. 41).

[Col. 0710D] What, again, is more foolish than for a man to endure long labors in the schoolroom merely in order that, through the favor of fleeting fame, he may be known to know many things—judging nothing sweeter than to hunt after empty rumors and to give his sweat for the popular ear to drink? He who thinks it fine to be pointed at and called, “This is he,” delights only in human praise; he boasts not so much in being wise as in being known to be wise. He grasps no other fruit of knowledge than the cloud of a passing breeze. Hence the satirist Persius sharply rebukes him:

> “Your knowledge is nothing, unless another knows that you know this.”

And what is more wicked than for anyone to labor in acquiring knowledge so that by it he may procure temporal wealth for himself; so that, in his eyes, a spiritual office may occupy a low and last place, while he arrogates to himself the first and chief place for a temporal office? Was not Simon Magus, as Peter testifies (Acts 8), deservedly rejected from the lot of the saints because he thought the gift of the Spirit could be bought with money? The knowledge acquired is owed to Him from whom the grace of learning is received, so that what is given by the benefit of divine generosity may be rendered with charity alone in view. Hence Christ says: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. 10).

[Col. 0711B] Therefore, when these three motives have been driven far from every student, let the remaining two be pursued: let the study of knowledge be undertaken with the intention of spiritual advancement, either one’s own or another’s, so that each person may humbly strive with all his might to be instructed for the sake of knowing and loving God, and, when necessary, may charitably share acquired knowledge with others.

I pity you, scholarly clerics, who apply such diligence in learning and endure so many and such great labors in acquiring what seems to be wisdom; for the more learned you are considered—whether by yourselves or by others—the farther you wander from true wisdom through pride. In their person Ecclesiastes aptly says: “I tried all things in wisdom; I said, ‘I shall become wise’; and wisdom itself withdrew farther from me.” And, as though in wonder, he adds: “And deep profundity—who shall find it?” (Eccles. 7). Truly it is high and profound, and few can discover why many always learn and yet cannot attain true knowledge. Of them the Apostle says: “Always learning, and never attaining to the knowledge of truth” (2 Tim. 3).

[Col. 0711C] Who, then, will find the breadth of this depth—why those who are always learning never attain the knowledge of truth—except one who at last understands, by grace inspiring him, that it is firmly established that no one is truly wise who does not desire to be? But he rightly understands this to be a true statement who does not neglect, but loves, to maintain justice.

## Chapter XXXVII

[Col. 0711D] He understands that knowledge is profitably ordered who does not intend to remain among the Egyptians with it. Rather, if he has endeavored to acquire it in Egypt, the riches acquired among the Egyptians by pleasing labor, just as they greatly harm while they are carnally cherished in their native bosom, so they benefit in many ways when they are spiritually transferred elsewhere from there. This seems to be signified through the children of Israel in Exodus, when they are read to have been delivered from among the Egyptians by the hand of Moses. “The children of Israel,” it says, “asked the Egyptians for vessels of silver and gold, and very much clothing” (Exod. 12). I think this signifies refinement of morals, in which we see the Egyptians—that is, the wise men of the world—abound.

Therefore, when the children of Israel plan to pass from Egypt into the wilderness, they do not wish to set out empty-handed. But, instructed beforehand by the Lord, they first endeavor to acquire Egyptian riches. Thus, when clerics, inspired by grace, are converted from secular life to the desert of penitence, if they have been fortified with prudent counsel, they do not transfer there empty or vacant; rather, they first strive to acquire by polishing and study the riches of knowledge, by which they are afterward usefully fortified against the sickness of ignorance.

[Col. 0712A] For in those things called the liberal arts there is a certain golden and precious subtlety, a certain graceful and well-ordered eloquence, and also a morality not to be despised. But they are known to be useful for salvation only when they are transferred from Egypt into the wilderness for the purpose of pleasing God. A person must not persist obstinately in Egypt with these riches and boast with pompous swelling of acquired knowledge. For that same knowledge is not bestowed on anyone except by divine gift, so that everyone who boasts may boast not in himself but in the Lord.

The divine discourse indicates this in the same place when it adds: “The Lord gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they would lend to them; and they despoiled the Egyptians” (ibid.). Who, I ask, can acquire even secular knowledge unless God’s generosity is willing to pour grace into him? For this reason He wills that the Egyptians be despoiled by an artful stratagem, lest clerics departing from Egypt deserve to be reproved for ignorance. “When you depart,” He says, “you shall not go out empty; but you shall despoil Egypt” (Exod. 3).

[Col. 0712B] God indeed wills that they should someday leave Egypt, yet not empty, lest they deserve to be charged with a double fault: because they have at times lived in Egypt, amid mud and brick, and because in it they have been enriched by no learning. It is blameworthy, indeed, whenever a cleric loves to dwell in Egypt; but he greatly aggravates the same fault if he chooses to be idle there. If, burdened by sloth, he acquires no literary knowledge for himself, since the ignorance of a layman does not become this name. But if, with wakeful care, he strives to gather much knowledge for himself, yet loves Egypt too much and does not care to hasten toward the wilderness mentioned above, he falsely seeks to have the name of wise man bestowed on him, since this knowledge is not yet worthy to be called wisdom.

Who would judge the deception of the children of Israel commendable in itself, unless justice overshadowed that seeming injustice; unless their subsequent departure from Egypt excused it and, with grace favoring them, transformed it in the course of time into something better? So, certainly, that seeming folly is changed into wisdom when every kind of knowledge humbly serves justice—when the person who strives, or has striven, to serve literary advancement seeks nothing further than to obey God more wisely and more perfectly.

[Col. 0712D] But whoever does not love to have such a desire in learning, although he understands many things, as he thinks—or as he is thought—to do, is not wise but foolish, as the Apostle is remembered above to have said. Another Scripture also confirms him in this. For when Solomon seemed repeatedly to commend wisdom, lest it be believed that wisdom alone was sufficient, or even truly wisdom, he subsequently asserted that he who loves to do unjust things is called foolish:

> “By wisdom a house shall be built, and by prudence it shall be strengthened; by instruction the storehouses shall be filled. A wise man is strong, and a learned man robust and powerful; for salvation lies where there are many counsels” (Prov. 24).

And he added:

> “Wisdom is too high for a fool. He who devises evil shall be called foolish; the thought of a fool is sin” (ibid.).

You see that one who acts wrongly is truly called foolish, although he may appear wise to himself or to those like him.

## Chapter XXXVIII

At times Scripture calls sense, understanding, wisdom, or knowledge improperly—that is, according to the estimation of the unlearned—and at other times properly, according to the truth of the matter itself. When it uses these names properly, they are found to cooperate with justice; but when improperly, they certainly oppose it. “Sense” is understood as an adversary of justice when Ecclesiasticus says: “Better is a man who lacks wisdom than one who abounds in sense and transgresses the law of the Most High” (Ecclus. 19). For it is clear that the sense which transgresses the law of the Most High is evil. Therefore the Apostle says: “For this reason God gave them up to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1).

[Col. 0713B] It is taken in a good sense when it is said in the same Ecclesiasticus: “I desired, and understanding was given to me” (Wis. 7). And again: “Honor and glory are in the speech of a sensible man” (Ecclus. 5). And much further on: “A sensible man believes the law of God” (Ecclus. 33).

Useless understanding is that of which the Apostle says: “For God revealed it to them. For His invisible things are perceived through the things that have been made, so that they are without excuse; because, though they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God” (Rom. 1). This is the understanding which, because it would not do what is just, deserved to be rejected by Him who is the just Lord and loves just deeds. In contrast, concerning good understanding it is said: “Good understanding belongs to all who do it” (Ps. 110). The Apostle comprehends both kinds of understanding—useless and useful—in one verse when he reproves those whom he had learned possessed the useless without the useful:

> “Though they knew the justice of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death” (Rom. 1).

[Col. 0713D] “Though they knew the justice of God”: behold, they seem to have had understanding. “They did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death”: behold, they are said to have lacked useful understanding. For they would not understand what they ought to have understood. Hence David says: “He was unwilling to understand, that he might do good” (Ps. 35). Elsewhere he summons them to that understanding, saying: “Understand, you foolish among the people” (Ps. 93). Of this good understanding Solomon also says: “The understanding man shall possess the helm” (Prov. 1); and Ecclesiasticus: “An understanding servant is acceptable to a king” (Prov. 14).

## Chapter XXXIX

Foolish wisdom is that of which Solomon says: “There is no wisdom against the Lord” (Prov. 21); and the Apostle: “God has made foolish the wisdom of this world” (1 Cor. 1); and again: “I will catch the wise in their craftiness” (1 Cor. 3). Hence Jabin, whose name is interpreted “wise,” is read to have been caught and subdued in the torrent Kishon—that is, in his own hardness—and to have perished at Endor, reduced to nothing like the dung of the earth. “They became,” it says, “like the dung of the earth” (Judg. 4).

[Col. 0714A] Let the wise blush, whose wisdom is compared to dung, since it is proved not to be raised toward things highest and divine but rolled back toward things lowest and base. They do not deserve to be chosen and assumed as clerics and Levites, but to be cast from the midst of this life like refuse. For their glory, as it is written, “is dung and a worm” (1 Macc. 2). Jeremiah most fittingly contemplates their glory and laments it with a compassionate spirit in his Lamentations (ch. 4): “Those who were nourished in saffron have embraced dung.” Those are nourished in saffron who are delicately instructed, as it were, in the Scriptures; but wretchedly they embrace dung when they long for perishable things.

Therefore that wisdom is rightly called wisdom which is truly wisdom: returning to Him from whom it receives its being, it seeks nothing other than to be with Him forever, knowing that it is of no benefit to begin, as it were, happily unless one is granted a happier completion. Of this Solomon says: “I will show you the way of wisdom; I will lead you by the paths of equity” (Prov. 4). And another wise man says: “To you, kings, are these my words, that you may learn wisdom and not fall away” (Wis. 6). And Ecclesiasticus: “A wise and understanding heart will refrain from sins” (Ecclus. 3).

[Col. 0714C] And below: “A wise man does not hate commandments and just deeds” (Ecclus. 33). From these testimonies it is plainly clear that wisdom in the proper sense is that which works justice, which glories not merely in knowing, but in knowing and loving God. Finally, even evil angels are shown to know very many things; hence demons are interpreted as “knowing ones.” Yet their knowledge is ignorant of God, the Creator of all, since it neither believes in, loves, nor worships Him. For when they say in the Gospel, “We know who you are, Son of God” (Luke 4; Mark 1), this is the knowledge by which all reprobate beings are compelled to know God’s power: unable to resist His wrath, they are worthily punished according to their deserts; and Him whom they would not love so as to enjoy His sweetness, they experience, whether they will or no, as harsh, and are tormented.

[Col. 0714D] They appear not to be silent about the nature of this knowledge when they add: “Why have you come before the time to torment us?” (ibid.). It is therefore miserable to know God not with joy but by undergoing what has been prepared for the devil and his angels; but it is glorious to know Him as it is written: “To know You is perfected justice” (Wis. 15). For this reason *cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge”: while evil angels, becoming foolish and therefore falling into the abyss of eternal damnation, these wisely adhered to divine love, which is the bond of perfection.

It is a fine distinction: evil angels are assigned merely the name of knowledge, but good angels the term “full knowledge”; thereby misuse is indicated in the former, but perfection of the thing in the latter. For the former are called “knowing” improperly, concerning whom Jeremiah says: “They did not know how to do good” (Jer. 9); but the latter glory in fullness of knowledge, according to what the Lord says through the same prophet: “Let him who glories glory in this: to understand and know Me” (ibid.).

## Chapter XL

Since it is clear, therefore, that the knowledge or wisdom of clerics is nothing, and that what seems to be something is of no benefit unless it is supported by the aid of justice, we must consider what kind of justice this is, which is judged so necessary. A little above I said that nothing is more just than to love the Creator; and therefore His love must be understood as justice. But since many say that they love God while refusing to obey His commandments—and this profession certainly contradicts the truth according to John’s testimony, for love does not know how to serve lethargy or idleness, or, worse still, to entangle its hands in evil works—we must consider what kind of life is imposed upon clerics, by which their love or justice is proved.

[Col. 0715B] “By their fruits,” He says, “you shall know them” (Matt. 6). Faith must be given not to their words but to their works; and one must hold not common opinion but the truth of the matter. The one God has mercifully bestowed many precepts for living upon humankind, whether under the Law or after the Law, and by them He fittingly instructed all who proved teachable in their respective times. Although these precepts are many and diverse, they are not opposed to one another; rather, they are assigned to different classes of persons and conditions of times in such a way that different precepts are known to be profitably imposed on different people.

For some were given under the Law and others under grace; under the Law some were imposed upon priests and Levites, others upon the people; under grace, some upon clerics and others upon laypeople. Under the Law, indeed, the Lord commands that eye be rendered for eye, tooth for tooth, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, bruise for bruise (Exod. 21; Deut. 19). Under grace, however: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5). And again: “I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven” (ibid.).

[Col. 0715D] Under the Law many things are also specially imposed upon priests and Levites, by which the other children of Israel are in no way bound. They are commanded to minister in the tabernacle, to present at the altars the sacrifices of those who make offerings, to shine in a distinctive kind of clothing, and to do many other things which anyone who reads the books of Moses can verify, though it would now be long and superfluous to enumerate them. But other things are read as being imposed on the remaining children of Israel, in which priests and Levites are not joined—for example, they are commanded to share many gifts from their labors with those who minister at the altar, so that those known to serve the altar may live from the altar.

Finally, at the dedication of the altar performed by Moses, when the princes of each of the remaining tribes offered gifts on the day it was anointed, no prince of the Levites is recorded to have offered anything of the kind. For those specially assigned to the ministry of the altar, though still under mystery and figure, perhaps in its dedication did not offer gold or silver or any perishable thing. Therefore Levi, as stated above, is interpreted “assumed,” because in the ministry not his possession but he himself is rather assumed.

[Col. 0716A] Under grace, however, we read that certain things were commanded to the apostles, who are clearly the first and chief of clerics, which were not assigned to the lower crowds. For preaching and baptizing, absolving or binding, and other matters of this kind are imposed upon them and their vicars, from whom the condition of laypeople is far removed. Conversely, laypeople themselves must do certain things which are not to be imposed on clerics—not because the privilege of lesser holiness is sufficient for clerics, but because they have transcended these humble matters by the height of ecclesiastical dignity.

For men whom the lay condition compels, as it were, to occupy themselves with secular business—business in which a cleric serving God ought not to become entangled—are told, I say, to pay tribute to Caesar (Matt. 22), whose image is impressed upon the denarius. The cleric is free from this obligation, since his order is more perfectly conformed to God. Since, therefore, as was said, different things are imposed upon clerics and upon the people under both Law and grace, it is certain that lesser things are assigned to the people and more perfect things to clerics. Thus those who are set above others by the dignity of their order should likewise surpass them in holiness, and should strive to conform themselves more expressly to God alone, so that the people may confidently imitate them as a regular pattern.

[Col. 0716C] Hence it seems to me that the justice of clerics is in some manner different from that of the people. For although the people are divinely commanded to live justly, it is nevertheless unjust if a cleric equals them in his manner of life. The justice of clerics must surpass that of the people by as much as ecclesiastical order precedes secular order; and clerical holiness ought to be of such singular merit that, by comparison with it, the life of the people, though just, is called secular. Therefore clerics are also called canons—that is, regulars—because while the people range, as it were, more freely through wider expanses of life, the cleric, whose latitude is restrained, is confined by the rule of a more rigorous life.

## Chapter XLI

[Col. 0716D] It is not permitted for the life of clerics to pass from rule into free measure after the fashion of musicians. Clerical life harmonizes with the heavenly melody only when no enticement of the flesh grates within it, but spiritual maturity resounds continually. Musical art is known to grant singers this rule or license: they may now leap from free measure into rule, now from rule into free measure. For those still captivated by transitory pleasures are known, just as they gladly hear varied sounds, to be considerably wearied by those held in sameness.

The condition of the people, as I see it, receives a similar liberty. To it a path of life is opened now narrower, now more spacious, so that, while it is permitted some scope for its own will in certain matters, it may more readily be drawn to a rule of however small a holiness. For if it always kept to free measure, it would undoubtedly incur death, since the broad and spacious way leads to death; and if it were continually compelled to keep a stricter rule, the brutish multitude would be burdened by an intolerable weight.

[Col. 0717A] Does not the Apostle Paul seem to you like a kind of notary, healing the weakness of carnal persons by a learned composition? At one time he seems to grant them a welcome freedom; at another, he strives to bend them back toward a fitting rule. “Because of fornication,” he says, “let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (1 Cor. 7).

The rendering of the carnal debt is a certain pleasurable latitude, which the multitude of the people, unable to maintain the height of continence, willingly embraces. Such rendering is permitted in the marital union so that they may not, what is worse, commit fornication with the bond of modesty wholly broken. “But this,” he says, “I speak by way of concession, not command” (ibid.). Since the naming of concession indicates that fault has preceded, he recalls them, as it were, from freedom to rule and advises them to devote themselves to prayer, that by devotion and tears they may in some degree restrain the freedom granted them.

[Col. 0717B] To devote oneself to prayer is, as it were, a regular musical chant which, at the Apostle’s counsel, married people ought to sing. They are not commanded but permitted to return from it to carnal union, as from a regular note to a free-measure note, so that enticed by this concession they may not presume wholly to leap away from the rule. “Return,” he says, “to the same, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control.”

Much later in the same Epistle, when the discussion concerned alms to be given and the same Apostle urged the same Corinthians toward them, he set before them a rule of generosity to be observed, yet allowed them, as it were, scope for their own will. This was not because he begrudged them a more perfect good, but because he saw them as too weak to attain it. “Concerning the collections made for the saints,” he says, “as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also must do. On the first day of the week, let each of you lay aside with himself, storing up what pleases him” (1 Cor. 16).

[Col. 0717D] It is as though he said: “I indeed wish you to give alms, but I do not command you to leave everything, because although perfection of holiness requires this, the weakness of your will does not bear it.” On this subject he says to the same Corinthians in another Epistle: “Not that others should have relief and you distress” (2 Cor. 8). That is to say: I do not demand that you spend what is yours upon the poor with so lavish a hand that the hardship of poverty befalls you yourselves. Rather, let your generosity supply their want without bringing upon you the loss of neediness. “Let your abundance,” he says, “supply their want, that their abundance may also supply your want, so that there may be equality” (ibid.).

[Col. 0718A] Equality comes about, indeed, when you moderate the poverty of the saints with your gifts without impoverishing yourselves in any way; and they share with you the merits of their virtues without suffering poverty in those same virtues. Thus the Apostle Paul, as a learned scribe, brought forth new things and old from his treasure, arranging the life of the people both in free measure and in rule: advising them to pursue the things of justice, yet not commanding them to abandon lower things.

But because the clerical condition is far more exalted, this general justice does not suffice for it. Rather, another, special justice is enjoined upon it, because only a spiritual life befits a spiritual order. “To you,” He says, “it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Luke 8); “but the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2).

The justice of clerics—or rather the working of their justice and love—is therefore, to select two among many, voluntary poverty and continence. These two are so specially enjoined upon clerics by the testimony of the divine Scriptures that I do not know whether those called clerics can truly be what they are called without them. It is a hard saying, but full of truth: one is not sufficiently truly a cleric whom the treasure of poverty does not enrich, whose loins the girdle of chastity does not bind. Both are prefigured symbolically in the Law and shown in reality in the Gospel, so that no cleric who refuses to obey such virtues can find an escape.

## Chapter XLII
The Lord indeed commanded through Moses that the tribe of Levi should by no means receive an inheritance by lot among its brethren, but that the people and the rest should provide it with first-fruits and tithes of produce and cattle, and the firstborn of the flocks, so that those assigned to the service of the tabernacle or altar might not be occupied in increasing or preserving possessions. This institution, however, is only a type and figure of what was long afterwards to be fulfilled in clerics: that what was foreshadowed in them in shadow might be fulfilled in these in reality. For clerics ought principally to serve the altar, and, longing for God alone, ought not to seek a transitory inheritance; rather, they should be so content with moderate food and clothing that, seeking nothing further, they are not even for these necessities more occupied with external things than is right.

Therefore, as I have said, seeking nothing transitory, they ought by hereditary right to possess God alone, and in return to offer themselves to God as an inheritance pleasing to him, so that God may be their unique inheritance and they themselves God’s distinguished, chief, special inheritance. Hence the Lord says to Aaron: “In their land you shall possess nothing, nor shall you have a portion among them: I am your portion and your inheritance” (Num. 18). And to Moses: “You shall consecrate and separate the Levites from among the children of Israel, that they may be mine” (Num. 8).

This seems also to be indicated by the very name *cleric*, because *cleros* in Greek corresponds in Latin to *sors*, that is, “lot” or “inheritance” [Col. 0719A], so that he who glories in such a name may be regarded both as God’s inheritance and as having God for his inheritance. I do not therefore think that a money-bag befits a cleric; nor is it his place to spring out toward enlarging the bounds or boundaries of possessions, lest one who ought to pass nimbly through the eye of a needle be forced, burdened by the hump of riches, to recoil like a camel.

Therefore the Lord also, who wished in the Gospel to set forth the realities signified in the Law—for he did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfil it—when he assigned to his apostles the dignity and office of preaching, commended to them the incomparable treasure of poverty, saying: “Do not carry a money-bag” (Matt. 10; Mark 3). It is as though he said: You who are sent to preach words of life to others and with utmost zeal to invite them to the love of heavenly things, I do not wish you to turn the ministry of so great a dignity into a means of hunting after earthly profit [Col. 0719B]. For it is not fitting that you who invite others to the riches of the heavenly kingdom should carry a bag for storing temporal money, lest you be found to commend one thing by word and—to God forbid!—to demonstrate another by example.

For a hearer does not know how to accept the preaching of preachers unless he sees their life agree with their speech. Therefore, so that their speech might be held commendable and might effectively exhort others to contempt for temporal things, Christ wished those same preachers to possess nothing, but to present to others a model of poverty.

## Chapter XLIII

Elsewhere in the same Gospel, when the same Lord commended the chief virtues and assigned them especially to the apostles and apostolic men, he wished to place poverty first, as the necessary and immovable foundation without which the structure of perfection receives no sufficient growth. “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor, because yours is the kingdom of God” (Matt. 5).

That this blessedness is assigned especially to the apostolic—that is, clerical—order was elegantly marked by the Evangelist Luke, who expressly recalled that the Lord lifted up his eyes toward the disciples when about to say this: “And he, lifting up his eyes upon his disciples, said: Blessed are you poor, because yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke 6). It is as though he said: Although this popular multitude, which deserves to be called worldly because worldly things have been granted to it in the wilderness, either does not wish or cannot attain the summit of this blessedness [Col. 0719D], yet I see that you both wish and can do so—your order, like your holiness, being singular. You have abandoned the broad way and hold to the strictness of the regular way and life. Thus, to look upon those who are known to remain below, I lower my eyes; but to behold you, I raise my eyes, rejoicing that you dwell in heaven.

Matthew likewise indicates this when he says: “When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him, and there they heard from him the series of the eight beatitudes” (Matt. 5). In this catalogue Matthew also placed poverty first, indicating that apostolic holiness is not perfect without it, because voluntary poverty is a certain height of the mountain which clerical dignity is commanded to attain, not the popular multitude [Col. 0720A].

For this reason Christ admitted no one into the number of the apostles unless he had cast away his own resources, showing that clerics, upon whom ecclesiastical care was to be imposed, were suited to the treasure of poverty, not to perishable possessions. The Apostle Peter glories that he has found this treasure and carefully asks how great its reward is, so that, when he has heard it, he may not only rejoice deservedly but may more effectively exhort the clerics who follow him to seek it: “Behold,” he says, “we have left all things and followed you: what, then, shall we have? We have done what you commanded: what have you promised to those who do this?” (Luke 10.) You see us forsake all earthly things: what may we expect in return? And he says: “You who have left all things and followed me, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).

You, he says, who have placed your neck beneath the bond of voluntary poverty, will receive the riches of eternal freedom. You who have so liberally practised righteousness—not the righteousness of the populace, but that suited to your dignity—when the Son of Man sits in his majesty, will likewise sit, having received power to judge; and your holiness will enjoy its due honour, because, as it is written, “righteousness shall be turned into judgment” (Ps. 94).

This, my brethren, is the righteousness by which the apostles and their vicars are known to excel: because for Christ’s sake in this world they love to possess nothing—not gold, not silver, nor any other perishable things—but, having despised these [Col. 0720C], freely cleave to heavenly things. This righteousness, I say, will be turned into judgment when Christ the Judge appears to all upon the throne of his majesty; and voluntary poverty will sit with him, judging not only human beings but also angels.

Christ himself confirmed in the Gospel that it would judge human beings; the Apostle Paul declared that it would judge angels. Christ says: “You who have left all things and followed me shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” This concerns human beings. And the Apostle Paul says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6). This concerns angels. This power of judging is promised and rendered to voluntary poverty. Christ therefore wished to impose this poverty upon apostolic dignity, so that those whom he established as temporal judges of the Church might also be eternal judges in heaven [Col. 0720D].

## Chapter XLIV

If, therefore, clerics know that they possess apostolic dignity in the Church, since in the apostles’ place they hold the power of binding and loosing, let them know that voluntary poverty too is imposed on them, as it was on the apostles; unless they keep it, they cannot be joined to the number of judges. For power to judge is granted only to the poor, although the grace of salvation is granted to many wealthy persons among the people.

Indeed, perfection and poverty are so closely connected that no one can possess that evangelical perfection which Christ wished the apostolic—that is, clerical—order to possess without poverty [Col. 0721A]. Since it was a great thing for them to hold the summit of ecclesiastical dignity, he wished their life to be one of perfect holiness, so that perfection of life might correspond to a perfect order, lest the dignity, ashamed by discordant life, become mute.

However generous, chaste, righteous, and holy anyone may be considered, he is nevertheless not judged perfect so long as he is known to possess his own riches. This is sufficiently declared in the Gospel, where Christ testifies to the same thing both by deed and by word. For when he allowed the apostles, whom he wished to present as perfect, to retain nothing as their own, what else did he intend to teach by such a deed except that he who wishes to possess his own riches is not accounted perfect?

To a certain young man asking what he should do to possess eternal life, Christ likewise recounted the general commandments and admonished him that fulfilling these was sufficient for attaining life (Matt. 19). But he, as though what he had heard did not satisfy his desire, replied that he had kept all these things from youth. To him Christ said: “One thing is lacking to you: if you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and come, follow me” (ibid.).

If you desire to crown the accumulation of general virtues with the grace of perfection, you must distribute all that you have to the poor, so that, laying down the burden of property—which, though it may not oppose holiness, opposes perfection to no small degree—your holiness may deserve the judicial seat of the perfect. On hearing this, the young man, as it is written, went away sorrowful [Col. 0721C], for he possessed many estates. Though he had kept the righteousness generally commanded to both the new and the old peoples, he could not—or would not—aspire to that righteousness which is specially assigned to the apostles and apostolic men.

When Christ said to him, “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor,” this saying sufficiently made known that no one attains such perfection while retaining anything as his own. This, assuredly, is the rule of perfection; this is the pattern of generosity first proclaimed by Christ in the Gospel and afterwards kept by the apostles and some of their successors. Christ proposed it generally to all with the generosity that is his own; but out of a certain special love he expressly imposed it upon the apostles and their vicars, so that these might be compelled to keep it as though by command, lest they be found to possess a perfect order but not a perfect life—which would be incongruous [Col. 0721D]. Others, however, are left in this matter to the breadth of their own will, since their lower order permits them to possess a lesser holiness. Indeed, we find nothing of this kind either proposed or imposed upon anyone in the ancient writings; rather, we find that they were permitted to have possessions of their own.

## Chapter XLV

No one among the ancients is either commanded or exhorted to lay aside the bag of property and embrace the rule of voluntary poverty, although in many places the benefit of generosity, produced by the unfailing spring of divine charity, is commended.

That most holy Abraham, whose faith and obedience are praised, who at the Lord’s command went out from his land, kindred, and father’s house, is nevertheless recorded, during that very pilgrimage, to have been exceedingly rich in silver and gold; nor did he receive a command to leave these things behind [Col. 0722A]. Joseph, whose chastity is commended, was incomparably enriched in Egypt and, in accordance with his name, increased in riches and honours. For *Joseph* is interpreted “increased.”

Even the tribe of Levi, which, as stated above, did not receive an inheritance among its brethren, is nevertheless found to have possessed cities and their surrounding pasturelands in the midst of their territory, so that it might dwell there by its own right and there sustain its own beasts of burden and livestock. For it is written: “The heads of the Levitical families came to the priest and Joshua son of Nun and said: The Lord commanded through Moses that cities be given us to dwell in, and their surrounding pasturelands for feeding our animals. And the children of Israel gave from their possessions, according to the Lord’s command, cities and their surrounding pasturelands” (Josh. 21). And below: “Thus all the cities of the Levites in the midst of the possessions of the children of Israel were forty-eight, with their surrounding pasturelands” (ibid.).

You see that even the Levites did not lack the bag of property, and that they did not hold the apostolic life, but only in certain respects its figure. Finally, when the prophet Isaiah, taught by the divine Spirit, spoke of the grace of generosity and humbly exhorted his hearers to it, he neither commanded nor advised anyone to give away everything utterly, but to share something of what he possessed with the needy: “Break your bread for the hungry,” he says (Isa. 58). One who breaks his own bread for another plainly gives some to the other and keeps some for himself.

Such breaking is certainly judged not blameworthy but praiseworthy, so much so that Jeremiah, seeing it not done, laments: “The little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. 4). After Isaiah had said, “Break your bread for the hungry,” he added: “And bring the needy and wandering into your house” (Isa. 58). He did not say: “You who have a house, abandon it in order to attain evangelical perfection”; but: “You who have one, receive those who do not,” in order that you may deserve the rewards of salvation [Col. 0722D].

Evangelical perfection was due to you, clerics, who follow apostolic footsteps; for you was reserved the privilege of such holiness, namely that the poorer you are than others, the richer you may be in the merit of perfection. For the eternal goodness of God did not begrudge the holy ancients, or those who lived in former times; but for you, established under grace, it provided what is more perfect. Nor should Christ be thought to have hated them, but rather to have loved you as more tenderly.

Therefore, opening to you the treasury of lavish generosity, with liberal hand he bestowed the gifts of blessed poverty, so that, bearing its burden, you might not also carry a bag of money, but entrust what is to be borne to him who knows both how to keep it safe and, at the fitting time, to restore it.

## Chapter XLVI

[Col. 0723A]

Perhaps this is what that wisest Solomon said when he foresaw Christ’s lavish kindness toward you. For, seeing how great were the benefits Christ would bestow upon you especially, he said: “He took with him a bag of money, intending to return on the day of the full moon” (Prov. 7).

Christ took the bag of money with him when, having conquered death, he carried his flesh—indeed, our flesh as well—clothed in immortality, into heaven in his glorious Ascension, and placed it at the Father’s right hand. There, clerics, you ought to gather your money as in a bag and entrust your sweats and chills under a faithful seal, because there “neither rust nor moth destroys, nor do thieves break in or steal” [Col. 0723B].

And Christ is beautifully raised into heaven not before the people but before the apostles, so that it may principally be indicated to them and their vicars that all their desire ought to be carried there, since they see their own bag specially borne before them. In this bag, as in a nest, that Davidic turtledove places its young: the one who loves to be separated from the people, not so much in place as in merit, and, leaving behind the market square, embraces the narrow solitude of clerical life.

There, I say, the turtledove places her young on high, warms, encourages, and nourishes them until they grow feathers, so that, mature, they may fly through the free air and not grow sluggish under worldly heaviness. But just as that turtledove’s nest does not decay, so neither does that clerics’ bag grow old; no tear harms it in the passage of time, because no perishable money is put into it [Col. 0723C].

For incorruptible soundness does not preserve the bag into which the insatiable miser heaps transitory gains. “He who gathered wages,” says Haggai, “put them into a bag with holes” (Hag. 1). If therefore you clerics gather any gains in these marketplaces, see that you do not put them into a perforated bag, lest, when the integrity of perfection has been broken, what you labour to pour in from above should be lost, as it were, through a hole below.

Accordingly Christ, after saying to the same persons, “Do not carry a money-bag,” later said: “Make for yourselves bags that do not grow old” (Luke 12): bags into which neither rust nor moth nor thieves have permission to enter, and in which every depositor has certain confidence of recovering what belongs to him [Col. 0723D]. For he to whom the deposit is entrusted—the one who, as Solomon declares, took the bag of money with him—will undoubtedly return to you on the day of the full moon, restoring your deposit to you with a hundredfold increase.

By the day of the full moon the last judgment seems to be signified, in which the universal Church is to be brought to completion in its members, when all who are to be saved have been gathered and it receives its perfect increase, never thereafter to suffer diminution. Of this full moon John says in the Apocalypse (ch. 6): “It was said to them that they should rest yet a little while, until their fellow-servants and their brethren should be completed.” In this full moon Christ will appear visible to all [Col. 0724A], and the choir of the faithful will rejoice unspeakably at his sight—especially those who, obedient to the Gospel, did not carry an earthly bag of money, but entrusted it to Christ himself, the faithful repayer, at fruitful interest.

On that day he will grant judicial dignity to those who on earth embraced voluntary poverty for his sake: those whom the imperfect righteousness of the laity did not weigh down and oppress, but whom the perfection of clerical excellence raised and advanced.

## Chapter XLVII

The Apostle Peter rejoiced in this perfection when he confessed that he had neither gold nor silver; and, though he gave the lame man no assistance from monetary generosity, he bestowed the more pleasing little gift of unexpected health. “Silver and gold,” he says, “I do not have; but what I have, this I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk” (Acts 3).

You see how great riches he brought forth from the treasury of poverty who had no bag of gold or silver: he confidently commanded the laws of nature, and at the word of the one commanding, the lame man leapt up and walked [Col. 0724B]. Neither that rich Croesus, whose wealth secular literature exalts, nor powerful Alexander, to whom the greater part of the world seemed to submit, could have conferred this; for nature does not know how to render obedience to those who love possessing honours and riches.

Whence, then, did Peter possess such efficacy in generosity, unless through the merit of his poverty, as he himself seems covertly to indicate, if one looks a little more carefully at his answer? For, about to say, “What I have, this I give you,” he expressly prefaced it with, “Silver and gold I do not have,” so that it might be understood that, because he did not possess silver and gold for the sake of perfection, he deservedly received the grace of healing. Religious want is accompanied by an abundance of virtues, so that the poorer one is in relation to the world, the richer one is accounted before God.

Peter was rich and yet possessed nothing; and though he had no bag, nothing was lacking to him. For Christ knows how to bless his poor in such a way that the less they possess, the more abundantly he makes them abound. Therefore, when he spoke in the Gospel to Peter and the other apostles, he said: “When I sent you without bag and wallet, did anything lack to you?” And they said: “Nothing” (Luke 22). A wonderful thing: nothing is lacking to those who possess nothing [Col. 0724D].

How can these opposites be reconciled, these incongruities agree: that they should be found to lack nothing and yet possess nothing? How, I say, except because both the lack of earthly resources and the grace of poverty to be loved are present to them: so that they possess nothing and desire to possess nothing, and the perfection of life which they have found delights them more than the perishable possession of gold and silver?

This is needy abundance and abundant need; for one to whom poverty accords well is rich, and the poor person is not one who has little but one who desires more. Thus Christ wished to make the apostles and their vicars poor, and, having made them poor, to exalt them above others in the Church, so that they might be judges on earth by merit of clerical dignity and judges in heaven by merit of voluntary poverty [Col. 0725A].

This poverty, surely, is the patrimony of clerics; this is their possession; this is their treasure. Enriched with it as a great gift of the New Testament, they are heirs and have become principal co-heirs of Christ, who commends poverty.

## Chapter XLVIII

Nevertheless, because no one is commanded to serve as a soldier at his own expense, but necessary maintenance from public resources is granted to one who serves, it has been permitted to clerics to live from the Church, over which they are said both to preside and to be of service, lest they be burdened by lack of bodily sustenance. Accordingly, many things have been bestowed upon churches through the generosity of kings, the gifts of princes, or the offerings of any faithful persons; many things have been assigned to them by proprietary right, so that necessities might be supplied from them to clerics, lest on their account they be occupied with external matters more than is right.

Hence, I think, the practice which we see in certain places through a depraved custom ought sufficiently to be judged improper: namely, that some persons, ignorant of—or rather contemptuous of—the institutions of both the New and the Old Law, demand tithes and taxes from these very clerics [Col. 0725B]. Those who, leaving worldly things behind, have chosen to be maintained under the clerical title, serving the Church in the apostolic manner, supported by the offerings of the faithful, or—what is more perfect—imitating the Apostle Paul by seeking their livelihood through manual labour, are unjustly compelled to pay taxes or tithes, since they are known to have all things in common and nothing as their own.

Accordingly Ambrose of Milan, speaking mystically of Levi under the figure of a cleric—or rather seeming to introduce God himself as speaking—says: “He is not tributary to another, nor subject to tithe; he is not generous from his possession. From him I seek neither tithes of produce, nor gifts, nor offerings; he himself is a gift to me, he himself is a tribute to me. He is not generous to me from his possession, but he himself is my possession: he himself is my produce, he himself is my revenue.”

When Pope Gregory answered the questions of Augustine, bishop of the English, and instructed him how he should conduct himself toward his clerics who lived a common life, he showed that portions ought not to be made from the goods of those clerics, since they expended not a part but everything in pious causes and religious acts: “With regard to clerics living a common life, of whom he was speaking, there is no doubt what we should say concerning the making of portions, since everything left over must be expended upon pious causes and religious purposes” [Note: [Col. 0725D] From the decrees of the blessed Pope Gregory, Response 2.].

It is therefore clear that the common little possessions of clerics who choose to imitate the apostolic life ought not to be tithed; indeed, others are commanded to offer them oblations and tithes, so that those appointed in the apostolic role to the ministry of the altar may live from the altar. But since ecclesiastical benefices are commanded to relieve clerics’ necessities, not to serve their pleasures, it is not fitting that they should crave them bestially. That is, they love not the things of Jesus Christ but their own things.

For who would judge it worthy of pardon if a cleric receives temporal nourishment from the Church [Col. 0726A] and does not seek in it spiritual progress, when the Lord commands spiritual things to be sought first, declaring that temporal things, even when not sought, are then added? “Seek first,” he says, “the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6).

Therefore clerics ought not to thirst for the milk and wool of the sheep—that is, they ought not to seek honours and riches—lest the Lord complain through Ezekiel that from them earthly rather than spiritual profit is sought: “You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool, but you did not pasture my flock” (Ezek. 34). Those who delight in consuming the sheep’s milk and clothing themselves in their wool nevertheless do not impart due pasture to the same sheep: they glory beyond measure in the reverence paid them by the sheep; they are heaped with the sheep’s offerings, yet do not help them by word or example, but only hunt private advantages among them.

For when certain clerics delight to shine in ecclesiastical dignities, acquire for themselves many revenues from the Church, join house to house and field to field, heap new coins upon those long stored, fatten their extended belly with exquisite dishes, surround themselves with a large household, gleam in costly clothing, decorate horses of great value at great expense, sweat over the useless labours of bird-hunting and hunting, and occupy their uncertain hands with the sport of dice—when they love to entangle themselves in these and similar things, who can doubt that they pursue neither their own salvation nor that of others through such pursuits?

Such men, deprived of the truth of clerical office [Col. 0726C], are adorned only by the falsehood of the name. Of them Jeremiah says (ch. 7): “Their clergy shall not profit them.” Their clerical status does not profit such clerics, because the humility of religious service does not please them, but the eminence of pompous lordship exalts them. The poverty familiar to religious life does not conform them to Christ, but secular vanity and property deform them.

What ought to be common to poor clerics they perversely make their own by a distorted claim of right; and no equality is preserved among them, while each embraces greater riches according to his ability. Such a clergy also confers no benefit upon the people, since it does not aim to teach its subjects by word and example; captivated by love of money, it does not care for the salvation of souls; occupied with earthly things, it does not strive to attain heavenly things [Col. 0726D].

When the popular multitude observes such a clergy, it does not so much pity it compassionately as reproach it mockingly; and, defending itself insolently by objecting to that clergy, it more freely extends itself into further sin. Therefore poverty is especially assigned to clerics, because it is the mother of virtues, as the Gospel indicates, so that, once they are found to possess nothing as their own, they may attain the remaining virtues more easily and more perfectly.

For just as riches provide no slight fuel for vices, so poverty surely promotes the growth of virtues. Without it the catalogue of virtues cannot be fulfilled, since their perfection is said to be cherished in its bosom. Finally, Christ does not wish his clerics—teachers and leaders of holy religion—to have anything in common with the clerics and priests of Pharaoh [Col. 0727A].

## Chapter XLIX

You know that, while the distress of famine pressed the Egyptians, they sold their possessions to Pharaoh through Joseph’s agency, and all Egypt was subjected to his dominion. Only the land of the priests endured nothing of the sort, but, as Scripture says, remained free from this condition: “Joseph bought all the land of Egypt, each person selling his possession because of the greatness of the famine, except the land of the priests, which had been given them by the king; and to them fixed rations from the public granaries were supplied” (Gen. 47). Therefore they were not compelled to sell their possessions.

You see how great is the devil’s skill in deceiving. According to a certain pagan writer, he has a thousand arts for doing harm. To those whom he wishes to set over others in order to seduce them, he is found to grant land of their own; and while others distribute what is theirs, he does not take away these men’s private possessions [Col. 0727B]. The Egyptian famine did not burden Pharaoh’s priests, but their necessary sustenance came to them from the public granaries, nor were they compelled to sell their possessions, because Pharaoh dealt more mercifully with them.

Why was this so, except that the more they appeared to be indulged by him, the more tightly they might be bound to him in stronger chains? Pharaoh saw that avaricious priests delight in earthly gifts—for, as it is written, “the eyes of the wise are blinded by gifts” (Exod. 23)—and, knowing that they desired nothing but transitory things, he craftily strove to reward them lavishly with the objects of their desire, so that he might entangle them in chains all the tighter as they were softer, and bind them to his service by love rather than fear.

Since he wished through them to teach the Egyptian people the sect of dark religion, he judged it fitting to show these teachers of falsehood more friendly to himself than others, so that by pleasing familiarity that wicked one might make them more wicked than the rest, and more ready through favourable inclination to teach the commandments of darkness [Col. 0728A]. Wondrous—indeed dreadful—is this craftiness of Pharaoh, who sets such snares of intrigue for his priests: they, their judgment ruined, rejoice at being delightfully ensnared, and do not care to free themselves from that which brings greater ruin.

By contrast, true and sincere is the wisdom of our Solomon, who conforms his own to himself by the model of the evangelical command. When he wished to appoint masons and stonecutters to build the spiritual temple, he instructed them to place their treasures in heaven, so that they might have no share upon earth, but might themselves receive God uniquely and God might receive them specially [Col. 0728B].

Pharaoh, who knows nothing of heavenly things and delights in making his dwelling only among earthly things, while cutting off vital breath from his priests, grants them an earthly portion. Thus, while the righteous man says, “My portion is in the land of the living” (Ps. 141), Pharaoh, with his own, says: “My portion is in the land of the dying.”

But Christ, who was poor on earth and commended poverty by his example, and who, in order to obtain eternal riches, returned by wondrous ascension to the heavens from which he had come—having freed the apostles and their vicars, whom he appointed to preach to others his poverty and riches, from the birdlime of earthly property—assigned to them the heavenly patrimony alone.

Therefore the cleric who wishes to possess earthly things by proprietary right wishes to have fellowship with Pharaoh’s priests; and you know that Christ and Belial cannot agree, and that no one can serve these two masters at the same time (Matt. 6) [Col. 0728C].

## IV. On the Continence of Clerics

[Col. 0727]

## Chapter L

[Col. 0727C]

These points, however briefly made concerning the poverty of clerics, we judge sufficient. Let us now pass to their continence. For we have said that their righteousness consists in this as in the former; and that without it they may indeed be called clerics, but cannot truly be held to be such. Since, therefore, it is beyond doubt—as has been said more than sufficiently above—that Aaron and his sons bore the type of clerics, though they did not fully express the reality, we must return to them briefly here also and consider carefully what is said concerning them. When God spoke to Moses about making their vesture, and Moses himself was taught how he ought to clothe them as ministers of the tabernacle, after the other general garments, which are there described with subtlety and mystical meaning, mention is also made of linen breeches:

> “You shall make also linen breeches, that they may cover the flesh of their nakedness, from the loins to the thighs; and Aaron and his sons shall use them when they enter the tabernacle of testimony, or when they approach the altar to minister in the sanctuary, lest, guilty of iniquity, they die” (Exod. 28).

Here the first question that arises is whether the children of Israel customarily used breeches and concealed their private parts by them, or whether, content with other garments, they are to be thought ignorant of the use of breeches. Since we have no certain proof from Scripture, and ought not abruptly to affirm uncertain things as certain, it remains to conjecture and, by conjecture, to investigate the hidden truth, so that in the end we may either discover it beyond doubt, if possible, or at least form a fitting opinion. For sometimes what is not disclosed by manifest authority is somewhat illuminated by diligent inquiry; and either the truth of the matter sought is found, or the conjecture itself is supported irresistibly by analogy.

Moses, indeed, who by the Lord’s command wrote the Law for the children of Israel, said little about their clothing; and although he spoke at length in many ways concerning how they ought to live, he did not greatly pursue the question of how they ought to dress. In some places, to be sure, he forbids them certain kinds of garments; elsewhere he commands fringes to be woven into their cloaks, so that it is evident that both by abstaining from forbidden garments they obeyed the precepts of the Law, and by having fringed cloaks they likewise served obedience.

In Leviticus: “You shall not put on a garment woven from two materials” (Lev. 19). And in Deuteronomy: “A woman shall not wear a man’s garment, nor shall a man use a woman’s garment” (Deut. 22). In Numbers: “Let them make for themselves fringes on the corners of their cloaks, putting blue cords on them” (Num. 15). Likewise in Deuteronomy: “You shall not wear a garment woven from wool and linen. You shall make cords in the fringes at the four corners of your cloak” (Deut. 22).

These words plainly show both that they possessed cloaks by prior custom and that afterwards, by the Lord’s command, they added fringes to those same cloaks. Finally, divine Scripture testifies that Joseph—whose sale into Egypt is sufficiently known to all—used a cloak. When his mistress, having seized the hem of his garment, said to him, “Sleep with me,” “he left his cloak,” it says, “in her hands, fled, and went outside” (Gen. 39). The same Joseph, while still a boy, is found to have received from his father a patterned tunic, which his brothers are said to have taken from him: “Israel loved Joseph and made him a patterned tunic” (Gen. 37); and a little later: “His brothers stripped him of the long, patterned tunic” (ibid.). From this it may be understood [Col. 0729C] that the children of Israel were clothed not only in cloaks but also in tunics, both of which they had in use before and after Moses, not by command but by the discretion of their own will. Of these, long afterwards, the prophet Micah says: “You have taken the cloak from over the tunic” (Mic. 2). But concerning breeches I do not recall finding anything in the books of Moses—namely, anything showing that he either commanded them to have them or stated that they had them.

## Chapter LI

Many, however, say and wish to establish as true that among many of the ancients there was a custom of possessing no breeches. Using closed and circular garments, they supplied a covering which they considered sufficiently adequate for the private parts. But as time went on, when more careful concern for decency arose and other clothing seemed incapable of adequately concealing the shame of nakedness—because many were sometimes compelled to blush fittingly when the shamefulness of their flesh was exposed—the use of breeches began to spread far and wide.

I think this explains why that blessed Benedict, who wrote the Rule for monks, when he wished to teach them not only useful holiness but also religious propriety, commanded that monks sent outside on Church business should take breeches from the wardrobe and wear them, lest those who ought to provide others with a model of decent holiness provoke laughter through the occasion of shameful nakedness. Since the use of breeches was not common throughout that region, but perhaps only the more respectable or busier persons used them, not the ordinary or lowly multitude, the holy man fittingly instructed monks going out in public to conceal their private parts by them; but upon their return to restore all such garments to the wardrobe. For outside there was greater need to be covered in this way, while in the cloister there was greater ease in adequately safeguarding modesty without them. If all men had customarily worn breeches, he would not, it seems, have commanded returning monks to restore them to the wardrobe.

In our own times as well, in western Scotland not everyone wears breeches; only soldiers or townsmen of any kind put them on. The rest of the populace is content with a garment common to all, closed before and behind and whole, but open below at the side hem. Clerics who had left those regions and come here for the sake of study once told me this; and several persons of that people, travelling through our country on foreign journeys, are most plainly known not to have breeches. Nor should it seem surprising if we believe the use of breeches not to be general in that province, when we know that in places nearer to us there is among some an even worse custom.

In a recent year, when our brethren, sent for the benefit of the Church, came during the summer to certain parts of Flanders, they saw most men walking everywhere through lanes and streets, stripped not only of breeches but of every kind of clothing for the sake of cooling themselves; they worked at their own tasks naked, neither respecting the gaze of passers-by nor restrained by the laws of their elders. When our brethren rebuked them, asking why they walked about so beastially naked, they replied: “It is not for you to impose your laws upon our will.” Therefore I wonder not so much at the beastly shamelessness of the peasants as at the blameworthy forbearance of others, who do not hasten to overwhelm them, if not with stones, at least with spittle, lest rustic rashness presume to exceed the bounds of human modesty.

## Chapter LII

What then? Must we suppose that the children of Israel also were unaccustomed to using breeches, and that either shamelessness or custom prevailed against so great a concern for decency? Who but an impudent person would say that they were so immodest that, forgetting human propriety, they were not ashamed, like beasts, of the bodily shame of nakedness? Even though Isaiah is read, much later, to have walked naked through the streets of the city (Isa. 20), it is certain that not shamelessness but obedience compelled him to this; for, when the Lord requires it, the cheerful giver judges nothing burdensome, and the truly obedient person nothing dishonourable.

But the children of Israel had received neither any such command from the Lord nor instruction from Moses. Rather, that natural law—which is the natural humanity of all living human beings—so instructed them that they knew clothing ought to surround the indecent parts of the body, lest dreadful nakedness injure human modesty. What garment could be found more suitable for adequately covering their nakedness, especially for people who could rarely, if ever, be free for leisure or rest, but were almost always disturbed by the concern of work, the hardship of travel, or the tumults of war?

And, to omit other matters, how could they confidently act in the hazards of war: drive away their enemies, yield, as often happened, to those who were putting them to flight; engage those who attacked; press boldly upon those who resisted; and, with sword drawn, join battle hand-to-hand? How, I ask, could they move freely and confidently in these and similar circumstances if they feared that the native shamefulness of their bodies might be exposed by some chance of battle? Such exposure would fill them with intolerable shame—not so much a protest of their modesty caused by leaving behind horse or chariot as, in that very protest, the possible uncovering of their private parts.

For such are the vicissitudes of war: now these men, now those, press upon fugitives and yield to pursuers; now they cast down those whom they strike, now, when struck, fall themselves. And when they fall, sometimes a certain integrity of modesty is preserved, so that they appear almost to have descended voluntarily; at other times disgrace twists them so that their head is below and their feet above. Whose bold attack would not such a fall somewhat delay? Whose manly spirit would not be enfeebled by fear of exposed nakedness—unless the Israelite, standing most bravely in the battle line, knew that his private parts were protected no less by breeches than his hand by a sword?

From the time when the children of Israel left Egypt under Moses’ leadership until after Moses’ death, they were rarely free either from war or from fear of war. Even before they left Egypt, Moses himself went to Ethiopia for war, overcame it by both military strength and wisdom, and subjugated it to himself. There, with wise consent to his suit, he took Tharbis, daughter of the king of the Ethiopians, in marriage. Although this is not found in our writings, which are marked by the privilege of canonical authority, Josephus, the writer of Jewish antiquities, took care to impart knowledge of the matter to us; and in this point the divine page appears to agree somewhat. For in Numbers, chapter 12, it says that Aaron and Miriam murmured against Moses because of Moses’ Ethiopian wife, since some believed her to be this same Tharbis.

## Chapter LIII

[Col. 0731D] But if it is asked when Moses could have gone into Ethiopia for war and there attained the crown of victory through both courage and wisdom, then, as it seems to me, it was before, as avenger of his brother’s injury, he concealed the slain Egyptian in the sand and, after the matter became known, fled to Midian in fear of Pharaoh.

For although the book of Exodus joins Moses’ birth in Egypt and his flight from Egypt with such brevity that there appears to have been little interval, even in age, between the two, and it cannot clearly be inferred from that account that he was yet fit for so great courage or wisdom, elsewhere divine Scripture plainly indicates how old he was when he fled Egypt, and that at that time he was a man of no small merit.

In Exodus: “The woman received and nursed the child; and when he was grown, she handed him over to Pharaoh’s daughter” (Exod. 2). It immediately adds: “In those days, after Moses had grown up, he went out to his brethren and saw their affliction; and he saw an Egyptian striking one of his Hebrew brethren, and he struck the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. Pharaoh heard this report and sought to kill Moses; but he fled from Pharaoh’s presence and remained in the land of Midian.” Nothing is here expressly distinguished concerning Moses’ wisdom, military deeds, or age, except that the woman handed over the grown boy to Pharaoh’s daughter; and that, in those days, after Moses had grown up, he hid the slain Egyptian in the sand (ibid.). Nor do I recall finding anything thereafter in his books concerning his age until, returning by the Lord’s command from Midian into Egypt, he is said to have stood before Pharaoh: “Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three, when they spoke to Pharaoh.”

When he had led the children of Israel through the wilderness for forty years and, through the Lord’s revelation to him, perceived that the day of his death was approaching, he said to them: “I am one hundred and twenty years old today, and can no longer go out and come in, especially since the Lord has said to me: ‘You shall not cross this Jordan’” (Deut. 31). That he died about this time is indicated by the words that follow, when the book of Deuteronomy, bringing both itself and Moses to an end, concludes with this closing statement: “Moses was one hundred and twenty years old when he died,” and so forth (Deut. 34).

But Stephen, the protomartyr, in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 7), defined more certainly how much of his life Moses spent in Egypt and at the same time indicated that he had made no slight progress there:

> “Pharaoh’s daughter took him and brought him up as her own son; and Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in his words and deeds. When he reached the age of forty years, it came into his heart to visit his brethren, the children of Israel. And seeing one of his race suffering wrong, he avenged him by striking the Egyptian” (Exod. 2).

And shortly afterwards: “Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian.” How long he remained in Midian before returning to Egypt by the Lord’s command, Stephen then plainly declares: “When forty years had been completed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in the flame of a burning bush; and God said to him: ‘I have surely seen the affliction of my people, and I have come down to deliver them; and now come, and I will send you into Egypt.’”
