Nor does Stephen omit the third period of forty years, when he adds: “God sent this Moses as ruler and redeemer; he led them out, performing wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years.” Thus Stephen is found to have divided Moses’ life into three periods of forty years, the first of which, he declares, Moses spent before fleeing Egypt. During this period, according to the same Stephen, he became mighty in his words and deeds and was taught all the wisdom of the Egyptians; and, according to Josephus, he was distinguished by triumphant campaigns after conquering Ethiopia.

Divine Scripture does not sufficiently clearly state how Moses lived in Midian, where he spent the second forty-year period of his life, except that he took as wife Zipporah, the daughter of Jethro the priest, by whom he begot two sons, and that he tended the sheep of his father-in-law Jethro (Exod. 3). But in the third period of forty years, how greatly he brought the children of Israel out of Egypt through fear and toil, led them across the Red Sea, endured the adversities of wars that met them in the wilderness, and obtained victory through courage and prudence, the narrative text carefully makes known. It frequently joins wars to wars and fears to fears. It is established that Moses, whether younger or older, rarely ceased from military unrest, unless perhaps when he is said to have tended the sheep of his father-in-law Jethro in Midian.

Therefore this Moses, worn down by such extensive experience of war and instructed in remarkable wisdom, is not to be thought to have permitted anything indecent to remain hidden in the dress of himself or his people which could weaken their manly courage—lest those whom native vigor impelled toward the love of victory should be disgracefully held back by that secret fear. This fear, known to arise from the absence of breeches, I judge more suited perhaps to women than to men, since the weaker sex is known to be hindered in conducting external affairs, while in domestic and private work the remaining clothing can more easily be kept in place.

## Chapter LIV

Nevertheless, to speak more boldly, I do not think even the Amazons lacked breeches. Leaving behind the quiet which feminine nature seemed to have bestowed on them, they rushed to bows and quivers, light shields and swords, and with manly spirit attacked their enemies courageously. In order that they might mount horses and chariots more easily and descend from them again more readily, more nimbly protect themselves by carrying their *peltae*—that is, round shields—and hurl a javelin more powerfully at their enemies, they bound their breasts with a chest-band, lest they hang freely in their natural softness.

Thus the Lord, reproving his people through Jeremiah for forgetfulness, says: “Does a virgin forget her adornment, or a bride her breast-band? Yet my people have forgotten me” (Jer. 2). And through Isaiah, when threatening punishment upon the daughters of Zion: “Instead of a breast-band there shall be sackcloth” (Isa. 3).

Some say that in battle these Amazons bound one of their breasts so tightly with a chest-band that they left the other free and exposed it naked, in order that they might not only crush their enemies manfully by arms, but also emasculate them in womanly fashion by the enticements of their nakedness. Hence that distinguished poet, speaking of Penthesilea, their queen, says:

> Penthesilea in fury leads the ranks of the Amazons  
> with crescent shields, and burns amid the thousands,  
> fastening golden belts beneath her exposed breast.  
> —Virgil

[Col. 0734A] Penthesilea compressed one breast with a golden belt and exposed the other, so that by the benefit of the belt she might free herself, as stated, with regard to the one, and by the other entangle her adversary. These Amazons, whose queen was Penthesilea and who waged a grievous and prolonged war with the Danaans, laboured in continual martial exercise and prepared themselves by suitable means to conduct it manfully and decently. I judge that they did not lack breeches, lest, when fleeing in battle, they offer their enemies not so much hope of triumph as material for mockery when they fell.

In our own times, too, women in certain parts of the world are said to wear breeches—not all of them, but the nobler women, who, being set apart from the condition of the common people, more frequently ride horses and endure military disturbance. Though I have not seen them, I have learned with certainty from people who have. If women take such care for decency as to use breeches to conceal nakedness, who could believe that the children of Israel in Moses’ time suffered from such shamelessness or ignorance that, though occupied with such great affairs, they did not cover their private parts with breeches?

But if they are to be believed to have possessed breeches, as the suitability of the matter suggests, what then does it mean that Aaron and his sons are expressly commanded to have breeches in the ministry of the tabernacle and altar, “that they may cover the flesh of their nakedness,” when, even without command, they covered it with breeches according to the custom of their people? Are all the other tribes to be believed to have had breeches while the tribe of Levi alone lacked them? Or rather, when they minister at the altar, are they clothed in a new kind of garments, with new breeches added to the rest, so that they put aside not only their old remaining clothes but also their old breeches, and take up together new breeches as well as everything else?

For it was not fitting that, when a pleasing and mystical newness appeared in outward things, the minister presented at the sacred altars should be like a whitewashed wall. Therefore the priest is commanded, when he ministers at the tabernacle or altar, to be adorned with new linen breeches, as also with a linen tunic, so that by this dress he may not only provide a covering for his nakedness but also indicate a sacrament to those who put it on. But since it is not for our leisure or purpose to show what each garment signifies, let us at least attempt, however briefly, to explain what we have proposed: namely, what the linen breeches signify, which the divine word so expressly willed to be assigned to those who minister at the altar.

## Chapter LV

You know that breeches clothe and bind those parts of the body through which human generation is propagated, through which a man is joined to his wife in carnal intercourse, and through which—to speak a little more immodestly—the itch of lust is consummated: a bodily pleasure than which none is proved greater. In breeches, therefore, continence is signified, through which the fulfilment of this pleasure is wholly banished; through which not only adulterous or fornicated intercourse is restrained, but even marital intercourse, which is allowed to spouses for the sake of remedy or offspring.

For he seems, as it were, not to have breeches who is found indulging in such acts, who does not endeavour to restrain himself from such union, nor wholly remove feminine contact from himself: “It is good,” says the Apostle, “for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Cor. 7). The divine word therefore fittingly declares these to be especially suitable for those who minister at the altar, so that they may strive to cover the shamefulness of their flesh, lest their conduct be found at variance with their office if anyone should presume to serve at the altar without them.

For no one ought to undertake the ministry of the altar who does not strive to join continence to the other virtues; because, just as only a holy person ought to serve the altar, so only one who is continent can be made holy for such service. It may therefore seem surprising why Aaron and his sons are read to have been sanctified to serve the altar, though they are known not at all to have possessed this kind of continence. For since they had wives and children in unbroken succession until Christ’s coming, it is clear that they did not practise such continence.

But it must be understood that, as said above, they did not express the life of clerics in reality but prefigured it in figures and riddles, so that in them there might be a shadow destined to pass away in its time, whereas in the latter there might remain the truth. “All these things,” says the Apostle, “happened to them in a figure; but they were written for our sake” (1 Cor. 10). Their garments, then, signify the virtues of clerics, without which those who serve at the altar or tabernacle are not sanctified.

Thus it is written: “Make garments for Aaron, in which, being sanctified, he may minister to me. And these,” it says, “shall be the garments which you shall make” (Exod. 28). After listing certain garments with which both Aaron and his sons were to be clothed, it adds: “You shall clothe with all these things Aaron your brother, and his sons with him; and you shall sanctify them, that they may perform the priesthood for me” (ibid.). And immediately it adds concerning the breeches what was quoted above: “You shall make also linen breeches, that they may cover the flesh of their nakedness, lest, guilty of iniquity, they die” (ibid.).

The fact that it is not added here, “And you shall clothe Aaron and his sons with them,” as was said previously concerning the other garments, seems to some worthy of more careful attention, as though it had not been omitted without reason. In certain other places also where Moses is commanded, or obeys, to clothe Aaron and his sons, the sacred garments are brought forward but breeches are not named among them, as though they were either separated from the number of sacred garments or Moses himself was in no way commanded to clothe Aaron and his sons in breeches.

It is said in Exodus to Moses:

> “When you have washed the father with his sons in water, you shall clothe Aaron in his garments: that is, the linen tunic, the ephod, and the breastplate, which you shall bind with the belt; and you shall place the tiara on his head and the holy plate upon the tiara. You shall also bring forward his sons and clothe them in linen tunics; you shall gird them with a belt—Aaron, that is, and his sons—and place mitres upon them; and they shall be my priests by a perpetual ordinance” (Exod. 29).

Nothing is commanded concerning breeches. Likewise in Leviticus:

> “Moses immediately presented Aaron and his sons. And when he had washed them, he clothed the high priest in a linen under-tunic, girding him with a belt and clothing him in a hyacinth-blue tunic; over it he placed the ephod and, fastening it with the belt, fitted on the breastplate. He also covered his head with the turban and placed upon it, before the forehead, the golden plate. Having presented his sons also, he clothed them in linen tunics, girded them with a belt, and placed mitres upon them, as the Lord had commanded” (Lev. 8).

Here again nothing is added concerning breeches. From this, as some wish, it may be understood that the divine Law is represented by Moses. For the Law given through Moses does not impose continence upon ministers of the altar, but merely proposes that it should be undertaken: that is, the Law teaches how praiseworthy, how it must be maintained, and how fitting for priests continence is. This is what is said to Moses: “You shall make breeches”; but they are to take them upon themselves, not from command but from spontaneous desire. This, they say, is what is meant by: “Let them cover the flesh of their nakedness” (Exod. 28). It belongs to Moses, they say, to make breeches—that is, to teach continence; but it belongs to them, and not to Moses, to cover the shamefulness of their flesh.

But, as it seems to me, from many passages of the same Scripture it can easily be proved that those who serve the altar ought to be constrained by breeches; and the other garments do not confer sufficient adornment upon them unless they also provide the special covering of breeches.

## Chapter LVI

It is certainly established that Moses is commanded to consecrate Aaron and his sons and their garments, lest any of them presume to minister either unconsecrated or without consecrated garments. It is said in Exodus: “When you have taken some of the blood which is upon the altar and of the anointing oil, you shall sprinkle Aaron and his garments, his sons and their garments; and when they and their garments have been consecrated, you shall take the fat from the ram,” and so forth (Exod. 29).

Moses is commanded to clothe Aaron himself and his sons in these holy garments, as is read later in the same book of Exodus: “You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, and, having washed them with water, you shall clothe them in the sacred garments, that they may minister to me” (Exod. 40). But if anyone should think that breeches ought not to be counted among those garments which Moses is commanded to consecrate and with which he is commanded to clothe Aaron and his sons, that person will find, if he investigates, that divine Scripture openly contradicts him:

> “Behold,” says the Lord, “I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, and have given him as companion Oholiab, son of Ahisamach; and I have put wisdom in the heart of every skilled person, that they may make the holy garments for the ministry of Aaron and his sons” (Exod. 31).

The following words declare what these garments are: “Bezalel and Oholiab made woven linen tunics for Aaron and his sons, and mitres with their crowns of linen; also fine linen breeches, and a belt of twisted linen,” and so forth (Exod. 19).

Behold: breeches are plainly counted among the holy garments; and in Leviticus they are called holy still more plainly:

> “Speak to Aaron your brother, that he may not enter at all times into the sanctuary which is within the veil, lest he die, unless he has first done these things: he shall put on a linen tunic, conceal his private parts with linen breeches, gird himself with a linen belt, and place a linen turban on his head. For these are holy garments, in all of which he shall be clothed after he has washed” (Lev. 16).

You see that breeches are called holy, and that ministers of the altar are clothed in them after they have been washed. But by whom are they washed or clothed after washing? Surely by him to whom it is said: “When you have washed the father with his sons in water, you shall clothe Aaron in his garments.” And again: “You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tabernacle; and, having washed them with water, you shall clothe them in the holy garments.”

Therefore it is clearer than light, and no authority resists it, that continence, signified by breeches, is not merely commended by Moses—that is, by the divine Law—but the Law willed also to command it for those ministering at the altar. Without doubt, then, those who minister without devoting themselves to chastity are to be regarded as transgressors of the command.

This sort of continence, perhaps, is imposed not on a human being as such but on an order: that is, not every person whatsoever is necessarily commanded to be continent, but the person raised in sacred orders to the ministry of the altar. The marital remedy is permitted to every person; but the clerical rank rises above that permission. For continence is assigned as an inseparable companion to the ministry of the altar to such an extent that the minister guilty of iniquity dies without it, as you heard shortly before:

> “Speak to Aaron your brother, that he may not enter the sanctuary at all times, lest he die, unless he has first done these things: he shall put on a linen tunic and conceal his private parts with linen breeches.”

And again: “You shall make linen breeches, that they may cover the flesh of their nakedness, lest, guilty of iniquity, they die.” It is clear, therefore, that what is punished by death if neglected is imposed upon them by the command of the Law.

What was said—“Let them cover the flesh of their nakedness”—seems to me to signify their ready will, which ought to cooperate with the divine command: namely, that it should hasten to embrace the yoke of continence and not resist with stiffened neck when it is laid upon it. Thus Moses clothes us, and we ourselves cover our nakedness: he teaches and commands, while we obey his commands by cooperating with them.

For we ought not to take up or bear his yoke under compulsion, as Simon of Cyrene bore the cross, but should gladly run to meet him who offers it, so that what is his benefit in imposing it may become our merit in accepting it. Finally, the ploughman lays the yoke upon the gentle ox, and the eager, well-trained ox voluntarily places its neck under the same yoke. As though to the ox, the ploughman says: “Take my yoke upon yourselves, for my yoke is sweet” (Matt. 11). And the ox replies: “Set your law before me, Lord, in your way, and direct me into the straight path” (Ps. 118).

## Chapter LVII
If, however, we refuse to embrace continence together with the ministry of the altar, we must necessarily lay aside that ministry; indeed, we must by no means presume to undertake it, because it cannot be laid aside once it has been undertaken, and it cannot be useful if it is presumed upon without continence. “Command Aaron and his sons,” he says: “This is the law of the burnt offering: it shall burn upon the altar all night until morning; the fire shall be from the altar itself. The priest shall be clothed in a tunic and linen breeches” (Lev. 6). You see that Aaron and his sons are commanded by Moses—or rather, by the Lord—to be clothed in breeches; otherwise they are shown to act contrary to the law of the burnt offering.

The law, as the Apostle writes to the Hebrews, “has a shadow of good things to come” (Heb. 10); that is, the matters literally contained under the title of the law signify those which are spiritually bestowed in the time of grace. Therefore what is said concerning the sacrifice of the burnt offering must be understood figuratively. A burnt offering occurs when nothing from the victim sacrificed is left for eating, but the whole is consumed upon the altar by fire sent from heaven. A priest invites the people to offer a burnt offering when he commends to them the summit of a more perfect life, so that by fitting discourse he may strive to stir up those capable of receiving it, and strengthen those who have already begun, that they may remain in their resolve.

For even among the people one can sometimes find persons who do not refuse to hear stricter counsels for living; who, inflamed by the exhortations of their superiors, cease to serve carnal concerns and, aspiring after the better gifts, rejoice to obey spiritual commands. These seem to offer a burnt offering to God through Aaron’s hand when, through his teaching and ministry, they gladly set aside worldly matters for the sake of perfection. But how can any teacher instruct others in this rule of perfection unless he strives to present himself as its model, unless among other things he is known to practise continence, without which perfection of life can by no means be completed?

Accordingly, when the law of the burnt offering is described, the priest is fittingly commanded to put on breeches, lest one divinely commanded to offer and commend to God the perfect works of others should deserve to be rejected through the obstacle of his own imperfection. For the perfection which a layman offers freely, a priest is commanded to offer as a duty, because, when he is ordained to the sacred ministry of the altar, perfection of life is assigned to him as an inseparable companion.

This is well suggested by the following passage in the same Leviticus (ch. 6), which establishes that every sacrifice of priests must be a burnt offering, commanding that absolutely nothing be left from it for eating, but that it all be consumed by fire, as was said a little earlier [Col. 0738D]. Divine speech never seems to command the people that they must offer only a burnt offering, since many kinds of sacrifice are permitted to them, by which, if they have sinned, they may deserve to make God favourable to them. But a burnt offering alone is imposed upon Aaron and his sons, so that they may savour nothing carnal, nothing imperfect; presume to retain for themselves nothing pleasurable; but strive to offer themselves wholly to the divine fire.

“This,” he says, “is the offering of Aaron and his sons, which they must offer to the Lord on the day of their anointing” (ibid.). This anointing is the ordination of clerics, by which, through the laying on of hands, they are consecrated to the Lord and anointed with spiritual grace both to perform the ministry of the altar and to handle the sacred mystery. Concerning this Paul, speaking to Timothy, whom he had ordained, says: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1 Tim. 4) [Col. 0739A]. And in another Epistle to the same man: “I remind you,” he says, “to rekindle the grace which is in you through the laying on of my hands” (2 Tim. 1).

What, then, is the offering which Aaron and his sons are commanded to offer to the Lord in this anointing, in this their consecration? “A tenth part,” he says, “of an ephah of fine flour in a perpetual sacrifice” (Num. 28). Fine flour, or flour of the finest kind, is bread that is tender, pure, and delicate; through it is figured the law given through Moses, concerning which Paul says: “The law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good” (Rom. 7); and again: “We know,” he says, “that the law is good” (ibid.).

The minister of the altar is commanded to offer this law, for the sake of which he was anointed; and lest he think himself free from offering it on the following day, he is taught more carefully how long he must offer it: “In a perpetual sacrifice,” he says. It is remarkable how this specification could apply to that symbolic Aaron—that he must offer a perpetual sacrifice on the day of his anointing—when neither that anointing nor the legal offering had a perpetual permanence. Rather, when the Holy of Holies came, the anointing of the Jews ceased; and it is certain that no temple, altar, priesthood, or sacrifice remains to those same Jews, but that all these things have reached their end.

A perpetual sacrifice is therefore assigned more truly to our clerics, for it does not cease until the end of the age. Then, indeed, it finds no end other than that of which it is written: “I have seen an end of all completion” (Ps. 108 [CVIII]); and for which many psalms are entitled, “Unto the end.”

## Chapter LVIII

But in what order should such a sacrifice be offered by clerics? “Half of it,” he says, “in the morning, and half of it in the evening” (Lev. 6). The law has two halves—that is, a double sense: namely, the literal and the spiritual. Its literal sense we must offer in the morning, its spiritual sense in the evening.

Morning is that period from the giving of the law until Christ’s coming, when the law itself is said, through carnal observances and ceremonies, to have infused among the Jews a certain rudimentary and new knowledge of God, and to have removed from them somewhat the darkness of ignorance. Hence David also says: “God is known in Judah” (Ps. 75). Evening extends from Christ’s coming until the end, when the mystical sense of the law is more fully unveiled to us, when knowledge of Christ is proclaimed not as begun but, as it were, completed: for he is preached not as still to come, but as having already come. He is no longer dimly disclosed in shadows to those still sleeping through calf, ram, sheep, goat, turtledove, and dove, but is truly made known through his own body to those long awake.

Of that morning the Apostle says: “All these things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10); and of the evening he adds: “But they were written for us, upon whom the end of the ages has come” (ibid.). In that morning Moses’ face was veiled for the children of Israel, and the Holy of Holies was sealed off by the curtain drawn across it. In this evening, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, we are transformed from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.

Therefore, in the morning let us offer half of the law—that is, let us concede its literal understanding to the people of that time. Let us recognize that carnal sacrifices suited them, and that they might lawfully attend to carnal concerns. Thus we seem to offer, as it were, half the law when we examine carefully when and upon whom it was imposed, knowing that those must be accused of disobedience not because at that time they did not keep the law spiritually, but because they refused—or perhaps, owing to their scrupulousness, were altogether unable—to keep it literally.

But in the evening we must offer the other half of the law, that is, assign its spiritual understanding to the clerics of the new grace, so that they may hold in actuality the perfection which the offering of Aaron and his sons intimates figuratively, from the time that they are anointed into sacred orders [Col. 0740B]. For if a cleric, cleaving carnally to the law, wishes to compare himself with Aaron and his sons, he wishes to offer both halves of the law in the evening, contrary to the command: whereas one is rather to be offered in the morning and the other in the evening, and each must be distinguished in a definite order. For neither is the spiritual sense prescribed to those persons or times, nor, conversely, is the literal surface prescribed to us; rather, its proper half is assigned to each time, so that then the letter might lawfully be observed, but now the Spirit must necessarily be kept.

Accordingly, let Aaron and his sons sacrifice a material calf, ram, sheep, and goat, as the letter of the law commanded them to sacrifice; but let our clerics offer the body and blood of Christ, as Christ himself willed to command: “Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke 22). Let those men be clothed figuratively in linen breeches in a temporal sacrifice; let these men be girded with holy and honourable continence in a perpetual sacrifice.

For this is especially imposed on them by the divine word when, concerning the aforesaid offering of Aaron the priest, it adds: “It shall be fried in a pan, sprinkled with oil” (Lev. 6). The offering of clerics is truly fried in a pan when, by the ardour of chastity, they restrain the wandering impulses of the loins, so that when the innate urge to wander is aroused, no effect at all is permitted to it. A cleric is fried in a pan when he wholly removes from himself soft and wanton touches; when he restrains the incitements of lust within the bounds of continence; when he burns his flesh with the cautery of chastity; when he sufficiently consumes its vicious impulses.

For nothing is more unseemly than that one who stands at the altar both for himself and for others should wallow in moist places and in the mud of luxury. For just as divine fire is commanded always to burn on the altar, so the minister of that altar ought, by sacred fire, to restrain the wantonness of the flesh. This offering, this frying, is greatly commended—provided that, as the law commands, it is mixed with oil. “It shall be fried in a pan,” he says, “sprinkled with oil.”

Oil signifies mercy, because *eleon* is Greek for “mercy”; and when someone wishes to cure another’s infirmity, he first mercifully applies the gentleness of compassion. Of this the Apostle says: “If a man has been overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6) [Col. 0741A]. But the first and chief mercy is that by which each person has mercy on himself and deserves to please the true God, according to the saying of a certain wise man: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30). And another wise man says: “The merciful man does good to his own soul” (Prov. 11). For one who is wicked to himself—toward whom can he be found good, when everyone ought to begin the fabric of goodness from himself?

Therefore it is necessary that the frying be sprinkled with oil—that is, that the cleric embrace continence with the intention of pleasing God, and, because he manfully weakens carnal impulses, seek not temporal but spiritual advancement. Otherwise the frying is found altogether too dry, too tasteless, and wholly useless, if it is not seasoned with this oil of mercy. Many pagans, indeed, are found to have practised continence; but because they did not strive through it to please the true God, they lacked the worthy fruit of continence.

Therefore the offering of clerics is perfect when they strive to fulfil the spiritual sense of the law; when they love to practise restraint for God’s sake; when they love to consume the wanton desires of the flesh with divine fire and assign none of them to themselves as their own. For this reason the divine word thus concludes concerning Aaron’s offering: “Every sacrifice of the priests shall be a burnt offering” (Lev. 6). If in these words, with the surface of the letter removed, the spiritual sense is attended to, no marital union is left to those who exercise sacred orders; nor is so great a bodily pleasure permitted where every sacrifice is commanded to become a burnt offering—that is, to be consumed wholly by fire [Col. 0741C].

## Chapter LIX

Nor should it disturb anyone that much later in the same Leviticus it is said concerning the high priest: “He shall take a virgin as his wife” (Lev. 21); and in Ezekiel concerning priests: “They shall not take a widow or a divorced woman as wife, but a virgin from the seed of Israel” (Ezek. 44). If our priest wishes to take these words literally, let him know that he is also bound to perform the whole law: namely, that he must materially sacrifice a calf and a ram or other such things, and literally observe all that the law commands.

But because, as the Apostle says, “the law is spiritual” (Rom. 7), this must necessarily be understood spiritually, so that the virgin whom the priest is commanded to take as wife is understood to be she of whom the Apostle says: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11). For the Church is a virgin because she does not subject the integrity of her faith to the corrupting devil; and she is a mother because she begets spiritual children for Christ. Our priest ought to take this woman as his wife, spiritually make her fruitful by the seed of God’s word, and beget children from her in the name of the deceased brother—that is, Christ.

For this same purpose Christ ordained, instructed, and left the apostles as his successors: that they should become zealous helpers in increasing the faithful peoples of the Church. Hence Paul says: “We are God’s fellow workers” (1 Cor. 3). But Christ chose to demonstrate by his life, rather than merely command in speech, what kind of life he wished those same apostles to have, so that his teaching might be deemed altogether beyond reproach, appearing to proceed not so much from facility in words as from gravity of conduct.

Accordingly, Christ chose for the continence of which we speak to be sealed in himself with such integrity that he allowed it to be violated by no stain, nor even the suspicion of a stain. He preserved the ornament of this chastity so intact that he allowed no harm to be done to it from any quarter. Finally, in the Virgin from whom he was born the same continence shone forth: as she was continent before giving birth, so she remained afterward. Chastity bestowed upon her did not impair fruitfulness, nor did fruitfulness prejudice chastity.

When Christ took human flesh in a virginal womb, he joined the Church as his bride in the bridal chamber; and he neither took integrity from his mother when he was born from her nor diminished the chastity of his Bride when he was joined to her [Col. 0742B]. From this it is sufficiently indicated that those whom he wished to raise up in his stead to govern and instruct the same Church, and to be ordained to beget spiritual children, he also wished to conform to himself in life. Thus, from the time they aspired to so holy an office, they were to set aside all carnal embraces and devote themselves solely to promoting the fruitfulness of the Church.

For he did not consider it fitting that they should choose two wives—a carnal wife, that is—and divide their time in order to please both; rather, he wished their whole attention to be devoted to serving and pleasing the Church, not entangled in the carnal allurements of a carnal bride. Therefore, when he chose his disciples, he wished none who was married to remain in the apostolic rank, none occupied by the bonds of a carnal union. Just as he did not permit those who had not yet taken wives subsequently to be bound in marriage, so he wished those who had taken them to be released from those same bonds.

This is well shown in the Gospel, where Peter asserts that both he and his fellow apostles had left everything, among which everything Christ himself is found expressly to have included a wife. Peter says: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall we have?” (Matt. 19). But Jesus said to them: “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold” (Matt. 10) [Col. 0742D]. You see that one who left everything did not retain a wife for himself. Rather, if anyone happened to be entangled in bonds of this kind, when he came to the apostolate he was wholly released from them; otherwise Peter, or any of the others, would not have left everything if he had wished to retain the wife who delights more than other carnal things and is counted among the things to be left.

## Chapter LX

This is also elegantly indicated in Luke, where the rule of perfection is commanded to the same apostles: “Sell what you possess,” he says, “and give alms; make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven” (Luke 12). And lest renunciation of outward possessions should seem to fulfil the whole measure of perfection, he immediately adds the matter of continence [Col. 0743A], showing that if it does not become a teacher of the Church to possess a purse of money, much less does it become him to cling to marital embraces. “Let your loins be girded,” he says, “and your lamps burning” (Luke 12).

In these words continence is sufficiently plainly commended; carnal union is sufficiently plainly rejected. For where girding of the loins is commanded, no scope at all is allowed to the effect of lust. Otherwise the loins will be regarded not as girded but ungirded if they obtain the freedom they desire for the flow of lust. This is, indeed, mystically figured in Leviticus, where the priest is commanded to be girded with a linen belt: “With linen breeches,” he says, “he shall cover his shameful parts; he shall be girded with a linen belt” (Lev. 6). Lest the breeches of those men hang loose, they are commanded to gird them with a belt; lest the continence of these men be relaxed, they are commanded to gird their loins.

From this it is clear that Christ wished them to be wholly free from marriage and to await their Lord watchfully when he should return from the wedding, “so that, when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him” (Luke 12). And fittingly, “immediately.” For he who delights to fall asleep amid marital embraces cannot immediately open to the Lord when he knocks. Burdened by the sleep of carnal allurements, he must necessarily be awakened by repeated knockings; and when awakened, he does not even then hasten to meet the Lord who knocks, because the delight of recently disturbed sleep often returns and still labours, with many oppressions, to hinder one whom it had until then been able to entangle in its stains.

But one who zealously strives to serve the Lord in the camp of continence and the battle-line of chastity—not to repose with loosened loins amid the blandishments of the flesh, but, because of terrors in the night, keeping a sword upon his thigh and standing watch in sleepless vigilance—such a person lawfully awaits the coming of the Lord who knocks; indeed, he scarcely endures patiently even the intervention of any delay. Such was Paul when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1). “I desire,” he says, “that he may knock, because I am ready to meet him when he knocks, since I keep watch and am not lulled asleep by the blandishments of the loins.”

Of such persons Christ adds: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, shall find watching” (Luke 12). By what kind of watchfulness the Lord wishes such servants to watch, he chose to show in the preceding words, commanding them to await with girded loins the Lord returning from the wedding; and in the following statement he greatly commended that same vigilance, repeating it in many ways through an added comparison: “And if he comes in the second watch,” he says, “or if in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants. But know this: if the householder knew at what hour the thief would come, he would surely watch and would not allow his house to be broken into. Therefore, you also be ready” (ibid.) [Col. 0743D].

But Peter, wishing to know whether this parable concerning watching and awaiting the Lord with girded loins should be assigned generally to all or specially to some, said to him: “Lord, do you speak this parable to us, or also to all?” (ibid.). That is to say: “Do you bind us, to whom you now speak, under this rule of continence, or do you impose the same rule indiscriminately upon those far off as well as those present?” And the Lord, to show that the people are released from this law and that it is specially assigned to teachers of the people, answered: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord appoints over his household, to give them their measure of wheat in due season?” (ibid.).

As if he said: “It is the person whom I appoint as steward over my household, to distribute to them the measure of wheat—that is, the word of life according to the capacity of each hearer—and to do this in season, that is, when he has reformed his own conduct, while correcting others, whom I specially instruct in these rules of continence.” Otherwise he will not be a faithful steward, nor a commendable teacher, if he presumes to teach that things ought to be done which he himself does not do, or if, being incontinent, he urges continence. But if he does and so teaches, he will not be found premature or ill-ordered. Therefore he will enjoy a particular blessedness, contained there in the following verse: “Blessed,” he says, “is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he shall find so doing” (ibid.) [Col. 0744B].

What does “so doing” mean? Clearly, keeping watch with girded loins, faithfully dispensing in due season the measure of wheat, and commending the summits of virtues not so much through words as through conduct. Whomsoever Christ finds thus ready with girded loins, not hindered by the rheums of lust like soft and flowing garments, he will reward with swift blessedness; and, girded himself, he will duly minister to one who is girded. This is what he says: “He will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, will minister to them” (ibid.).

For then Christ girds himself in order to reward the good servant—that is, he is hindered by no obstacles—when, at his knocking, that servant is found awake in the battle-line of continence. He does not put forward works of the flesh which in the course of time must be punished by judicial fire, but an angelic life, which ought immediately to be rewarded with angelic blessedness. For it is angelic to live in the flesh without being held by the laws of the flesh; and it is certain that one who does so will be admitted more swiftly to angelic fellowship.

But whomsoever Christ finds asleep amid marital embraces, with his belt loosened and impeded by flowing garments, Christ too is found, as it were, impeded and slow in rewarding him, while he grants him heavenly glory either never or late, according to his merits. This does not accuse Christ of inability, but charges that man’s troublesome weakness. Therefore he did not wish the apostles, whom he intended to distinguish by the summit of perfection, to be entangled in such stains; but from those from whom he took away the purse of monetary resources, he also took away the seductive pleasures of a wife, lest, thinking of worldly things and how they might please their wives, they should lack minds free to devote themselves and to please God alone [Col. 0744D].

## Chapter LXI

Therefore none of them, after becoming an apostle, is read either to have taken a wife, retained one already taken, or begotten children; rather, it is established that thereafter they lived a celibate life, so that they are found to have done absolutely nothing marital. Finally, John, son of Zebedee, who, as they say, wished to take a wife, Christ recalled from this intention; and later, while hanging on the cross, he entrusted the Virgin Mother to that Apostle, a virgin [Col. 0745A].

We know, indeed, from the Gospel account that Christ did not refuse to attend the wedding of someone among the people, lest he seem to have condemned marriage. Rather, at the beginning of his signs, he consecrated marriages, so that no one might doubt that they were commendable. Yet none of the apostles is read to have invited him to his own wedding; none is read to have commended his own marriage by Christ’s presence. Rather, as was said, Christ took care to call John back from his intended marriage, since he wished soon to raise him through the grace of the apostolate.

Why was this so, unless to show both that he permits marriage to those who are among the people and that he prohibits apostolic men from marriage, lest those whose profession was so different should have an equal rule of life? What benefit would Christ, born of a virgin, have brought to clerics if he had left them in the condition in which they had been under the law, when he bestowed upon the people no small measure of holiness, chastity, and honourableness? Is it credible that, at his coming, the condition of the laity should advance, while the clerical condition, which is much more worthy, should receive no advancement? Or that his benefits, more lavish than usual, should reach the people so as to pass over clerics, who are first and foremost?

Rather, the first and chief gifts ought to have been bestowed on clerics, whom divine grace willed to set before the rest, so that God might grant them, as mountains, a special peace, and through them righteousness might come down to the lowliness of the hills. Therefore the Davidic speaker lifts his eyes to the mountains, from which he thinks help will come to him, knowing that the mountains first receive what is afterward poured into the hills (Ps. 120).

You know that the old law and the tradition of the fathers before the law, although they condemned fornication and adultery, nevertheless did not greatly tighten the reins of chastity, but allowed the cord of continence to be loosened to such a degree that one man might lawfully be joined in marriage to many wives at once. Hence Jacob, Elkanah, David, and many others, both righteous and unrighteous, are read to have had several wives at the same time, yet not thereby to have incurred the stain of adultery.

For the mystery of this practice, which fittingly suited that time, offered an appropriate excuse for such marriages. For at that time, although especially the Hebrew people appeared to worship God—being separated from the rest and regarded as a peculiar people—yet among many other and diverse nations some loved God and served him in ways pleasing to him, whether by faith alone, by offerings of victims, or by whatever means. Melchizedek is read to have been priest of God Most High; Job is read to have greatly pleased God; the sons, friends, and comforters of the same Job are believed to have worshipped the true God, though they certainly were not Hebrews.

Likewise, in Egypt those midwives who received the command to kill the male children of Hebrew parents feared God rather than the king: “The midwives,” it says, “feared God and did not do according to the king’s command, but preserved the males” (Exod. 1). And below: “God did good to the midwives; and because the midwives feared God, he built houses for them” (ibid.) [Col. 0746A]. And who would suppose that only those whom I have mentioned here were devoted to divine worship, rather than that others too, inspired by the same Spirit in different places and times, put far from them the error of the nations, worshipped their Creator and the Creator of all, and cleaved to him in true faith and righteous works?

But because, in comparison with those who, deceived by various falsehood, served demons everywhere among the nations, those who worshipped the true God were very few, no or only rare mention of them is commended in the divine Scriptures. Yet from the few whom we have mentioned it may be inferred that they were more numerous. Finally, the magi who, from the East, guided by the radiance of faith, sought Christ born of the Virgin at Bethlehem neither before nor afterward asked to become Jews; but by true faith and offered gifts they made Christ favourable to themselves—the Christ whom the Hebrews, enveloped in the mist of blindness, despised.

Therefore, because in ancient times some persons in many and different nations served the true God and, abandoning the worship of idols, cleaved to him in the bond of faith, what was far more holy in the spiritual realm was fittingly signified typologically in carnal marriage: just as one man was permitted to have many wives at once, so the one God was rightly believed to join to himself the souls of many nations. And many wives were fittingly and lawfully joined to one husband, not one wife to many husbands, because many nations fittingly served one God, not many gods; nor did one nation or soul serve many gods. “You shall worship the Lord your God,” he says, “and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 10); and David says: “You shall not worship a foreign god” (Ps. 80).

## Chapter LXII

[Col. 0746C]

But when Christ, born of a Virgin, brought an increase of holiness to the whole world, he commended in himself and in his mother the holy purity of virginity. Although he did not compel the faithful peoples to the precipitous summit of that same virginity, he nevertheless reduced their marriage chambers to union with one wife, so that thereafter no one might be joined in marriage to several wives at the same time, but one man might be content with one woman in a holier mystery.

Thus by his preaching Christ called the many diverse nations of the Gentiles to the catholic faith; thus he joined to those nations the diverse tribes and families of the Jews, in order to construct from these walls the building of the Church and unite both—indeed, many—by the cornerstone. And truly, many. For among the Gentiles themselves there were not one but many peoples, who, worshipping different demons, were held in diverse error. Though the general seduction of error made them, as it were, one, the particular superstition of each nevertheless made them many and diverse.

Even those few who perhaps among them rendered due worship to the true God did not have the same rite of worship or the same ceremonies among themselves; rather, each offered gifts to God according to his own judgment, according as the divine Spirit bestowed grace upon each. We read that Melchizedek the priest, of whom we spoke above, offered one thing, and blessed Job another; yet we believe their different little offerings pleased God. These persons had been instructed in no sacraments of faith and in no legal doctrines, yet they pleased God by true faith and righteous works. Having no such law, they were a law unto themselves: they did not have the law written on parchments or stone tablets (Rom. 2), but showed the work of the law itself written in their hearts [Col. 0747A].

Therefore, when Christ, both personally and through his apostles, preached the kingdom of heaven to all, he called all—whether Jews or Gentiles—to unity of faith in such a way as to allow none to remain in his former condition, but compelled all, in season and out of season, to pass over to Gospel teaching. Thus he would no longer permit many and diverse peoples to serve him, but only one: namely, the catholic, Christian people obedient to Gospel commands. He chose that this also should be beautifully figured in carnal marriage, and therefore he permitted one man thereafter to be joined in marriage to only one wife.

For circumcision, uncircumcision, Judaea, and Gentile status were no longer to serve him according to their former manner, but the Church alone, not having spot or wrinkle, was worthily to please him according to her merits. Though formed by the influx of many newcomers, she is nevertheless one and admits no other into the marriage chamber of her nuptials. Therefore, in order to demonstrate the inviolate sacrament of this union, he also willed every man to be content with one wife.

This is commended so clearly in evangelical and apostolic writings that no doubt remains to attentive readers; and it is now so established in the Church by visible practice that not so much reading as the thing itself demonstrated makes anyone learned. For in our times no one is joined by the marital bond to many wives simultaneously; should anyone presume to do so, he is judged an adulterer without question [Col. 0747C].

The Lord fittingly indicated this in the Gospel when he recalled that first marriage, in which both an evident example of lawful union is given and the sacrament of Christ and the Church is expressed. “Have you not read,” he says, “that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’?” (Matt. 19).

Christ wished those who are married among us to strive to conform themselves to that first marriage which God willed to establish in the beginning: just as God joined only one wife to the first man, so in the time of grace no one should presume to have a greater number. Therefore he repeats in the Gospel what is said in Genesis, so that, having come to commend chastity by word and example, he might restore it to its former rank by setting forth the first marriage: “He shall cleave,” he says, “to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). He did not say, “He shall cleave to his wives, and three or four or more shall be one flesh.”

Paul, speaking to the Ephesians, carefully explains what mystery this contains. Introducing these same words, he then adds: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5). As if to say: The marriage of Christ and the Church is figured by carnal marriage rightly celebrated only between two, where no trinity or larger multiplicity is found, but a simple duality is united. “The two,” he says, “shall be one flesh.”

And so that what is spiritually commended in Christ and the Church might be truly maintained in carnal marriage also, the same Paul adds: “Let each man love his own wife as Christ loves the Church” (ibid.) [Col. 0748A]. Here he did not say, “Let each man love his wives,” but “his own wife, as Christ [loves] the Church,” in order to show that no one ought henceforth to be joined to many wives if he wishes to be fitted to Christ and the Church by the requisite likeness.

In many other places the same Apostle is found to commend this same principle and to remove all doubt from the hearts of his hearers. Christ, appearing as a man, brought this rule of chastity and this advance in holiness when, by saving teaching, he raised the whole world to better things, lest his coming should appear contemptibly worthless in everyone’s sight if, in the course of time, it appeared superfluous and useless.

## Chapter LXIII
What further distinction, then, do we find conferred upon clerics—whom we know to be worthier than the people—in this fullness of time, if this rule of marriage, to which the people are advanced by the evangelical law, is likewise granted to the same clerics? As I see it, their holiness has made no further progress in this respect if the divine law has made them equal to the people, whereas those who must furnish others with an example of life, both by word and by example, ought rather to have received an increase of holiness. But far be it that Christ should have raised inferiors to better things [Col. 0748C] while disregarding their superiors! Rather, those whom he raised to the heights of ecclesiastical dignity he also advanced to the summit of greater holiness. This the patriarch Jacob fittingly signified when he foretold things to come concerning Judah his son, in whom Judah undoubtedly prefigured Christ. “His eyes,” he says, “are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk” (Gen. XLIX).

You clerics are the eyes of Judah, that is, of Christ: set in a higher rank as though in the head, and illuminated by the light of greater knowledge, you penetrate the remote and hidden things of the Scriptures with lynx-like understanding, and show others the fitting path of life. Wine, therefore, aptly denotes the knowledge of the people, which the saving Passion of Christ instructs unto faith. Of this Paul undertakes to preach nothing save Jesus Christ, and him crucified, wishing somehow to intoxicate their minds with such a flavor [Col. 0748D] or love. Perhaps for this reason Christ, invited to the wedding, turned water into wine: lest the people’s knowledge should thereafter remain tasteless if, through aberrant faith, it did not behold Christ crucified for the salvation of all.

But in this one respect Judah’s eyes are far more beautiful: they not only reverence Christ crucified with believing minds, but contemplate Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God. One of them says, “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI); and another, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God” (John I).—“And his teeth,” he says, “are whiter than milk” (Gen. XLIX).

The teeth of Christ are likewise the clerics: gathered in the Church in the twofold rank of sacred orders, namely the presbyterate and the diaconate, and rooted as it were in the mouth, in the secrets of profound knowledge, [Col. 0749A] they are neither gnawed by the little worm of heretical perversity nor corrupted by the mold of bad habits or negligence. Rather, the strength of sound faith confirms them, and the blooming beauty of perfect chastity commends them. For chastity is signified by whiteness; thus the Bride is praised by the Bridegroom’s voice in the Song of Songs: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Cant. II).

By milk, however, which is the food of little children, we rightly understand the life of laypeople. Since they are unable to feed on solid bread, they are nourished by milk’s sustenance; that is, shrinking from the higher precepts of life, they are left within lower lawful things. For since they cannot attain the lofty condition of virginal integrity, nor reach the second rank—the height, that is, of widowed continence—they are permitted to live amid the low and humble things of [Col. 0749B] marital union. Thus, while they are colored by this whiteness, though weak and tender, they may deserve to be counted among Christ’s little ones, rather than, blackened by the foulness of fornication, being rejected from the assembly of the faithful as their deserts require.

Christ’s teeth, therefore, are rightly said to be whiter than milk: that is, clerics are chaster than the chaste married persons among the people, since clerical continence far surpasses the permitted and lawful union of laypeople. For just as Christ, when he came, recalled the ordinary man to union with one wife, so he deprived the cleric distinguished by sacred orders entirely of every wife, so that the former is content with one and the latter with none. For an ordinary man is found in the Law to have lawfully joined many wives to himself, while the priest is found to have had only one.

Neither Aaron nor any priest after Aaron do I find to have had many wives at the same time; and the divine utterance in Leviticus seems expressly to have observed this: “He shall take a virgin as wife” (Lev. XXI). It does not say, “He shall take virgins as wives.” This virgin, whom the priest of that time joined to himself in a typological marriage, prefigured the Church, as I recall having said above—the Church whom in our times the priest was to receive as his own and from whom, by the seed of the Word, he was to have spiritual children.

Therefore, when Christ came and by his presence removed the shadows of things and presented to himself a perfect priestly order, he wholly separated it from carnal marriage and assigned it to the chaste embraces of the Church alone, so that the type and figure of the former marriage might finally [Col. 0749D] come to an end in him, now that the truth of the figure was present and would never pass away.

Thus it is evident that, at Christ’s coming, both clergy and people received fitting advances; each attained a holiness greater than usual. The former, who had previously lawfully used many wives, was recalled to the allowance of one; while the latter, who by decree of the Law had been carnally joined to one virgin only, is now joined carnally to none, but spiritually to the Church alone. A cleric cannot conform himself more expressly to Christ, the master, nor a disciple to his teacher, unless he strives to imitate him not so much by following with his feet as by following in character, so that this Gospel saying may properly be recognized as spoken of him: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John II). And this servant, who for Christ’s sake has left both wife [Col. 0750A] and all else, will be a judge together with that Judge. Hence it is added: “And where I am, there also shall my servant be” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER LXIV

Therefore Paul, who imitates Christ through continence, glories that he will be a judge: “Do you not know,” he says, “that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. VI). Carefully inviting his disciples Timothy and Titus to this continence, he instructs them also in governing the Church, so that they may know that the office of presiding is not salutary for them unless they strive to attain the surpassing height of continence.

He says to Timothy: “Let no one despise your youth; but be an example to believers in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, in chastity” (1 Tim. IV). The Apostle, weaving a certain catalogue of virtues, placed chastity at its conclusion, making it understood that this catalogue is shapeless and quite unpolished unless it is adorned with the crown of chastity. And a young man is aptly warned with special care to preserve chastity, lest, even in the dignity of the presbyterate, his youth be held contemptible if he weakly yields to the desires of the loins.

For young persons are customarily assailed more violently by such desires and, when the barrier is removed, wander more unrestrainedly down the slopes of pleasures. They are restrained less by the due rule of holiness because they think that the protection afforded by their age permits them greater indulgence. Therefore the Apostle does not wish the presbyter whom advanced age does not commend to be held by the birdlime of youthful desire; rather, he wishes the young man to oppose youthful things in such a way that he deserves to be called presbyter not so much by years [Col. 0750C] as by character. Accordingly he says to Timothy: “Flee youthful desires” (2 Tim. II).

By modest language he wished to call the desires of the loins “youthful,” desires by which, as was said above, young men are found especially to burn. For he who had become debtor by right of priestly office both to the wise and the foolish, both to men and women, so as to impart the benefit of teaching to all not only by living but also by speaking and admonishing—how, to say nothing of others, could he instruct young women by his conversation if he had not manfully freed himself from their allurements by a commitment to continence? Therefore he adds: “Entreat older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all chastity” (1 Tim. V).

Here the Apostle seems entirely to separate both older and younger women from a presbyter’s embrace, when he instructs Timothy to treat the former as mothers and the latter as sisters, so that in neither case may the presbyter be held by a husbandly affection, but in all chastity may be regarded by all women as a brother or son. Hence also below: “Keep yourself chaste,” he says (ibid.). Speaking to Titus, he called this chastity “continence,” thereby showing that the presbyter must not be married but free from every marriage: “A presbyter,” he says, “must be sober, just, holy, continent” (Tit. I).

This is the continence which the same Apostle had proposed to preserve in himself and carefully commended to Timothy and Titus, so that good disciples might follow a good master in it [Col. 0751A] and urge others to pursue the same purpose. Of this purpose he says to Timothy: “But you have followed my teaching, conduct, purpose” (2 Tim. III). He intended “teaching” to be understood in knowledge, “conduct” in morals, and “purpose” in continence. Timothy had effectively followed all these things by imitation, just as Paul himself had previously set them forth by preaching and showing them.

And because Paul knew that Timothy was already abiding in these things, he accordingly exhorts him to remain firmly in the same course: “But you,” he says, “remain in those things which you have learned and which have been entrusted to you” (ibid.), knowing from whom you learned them—“knowing,” he says, “from whom you learned them.” Namely, from me, who demonstrated by deeds what I communicated in words. And lest he should seem either to have taught what was improper or that Timothy had learned from him inappropriately, he commends his teaching by the testimony of the Scriptures. Timothy had been educated from infancy in their pages and therefore could not easily be ensnared by the traps of false teaching: “Knowing from whom you learned them, and because from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which can instruct you unto salvation.”

It is as though he said: You have found in the sacred writings those things which you learned from me, so that, when my exhortations move you to hold what I have proposed, you may be confirmed more firmly by the authority of the divine Scriptures, which you know particularly well.

## CHAPTER LXV

That Paul’s purpose was continence, no one doubts who is willing to review his Epistles. Speaking to the Corinthians, he says: “I wish all to be as [Col. 0751C] I myself am. I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain thus, as I also am. But if they do not contain themselves, let them marry” (1 Cor. VII). It is clear from these words that Paul was bound by no wife; and he glories that Timothy and Titus remain in this same purpose, while earnestly exhorting them to remain in it.

What then is meant by his saying to Timothy: “A bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife” (1 Tim. III); and to Titus: “Appoint presbyters in every city, if anyone is without reproach, the husband of one wife” (II Tim. I)? There are some who read these words with a rather gross understanding, wishing it to be understood that the Apostle commanded or permitted a presbyter to be married and that he should not be recalled from marital union on account of sacred orders—provided only that he is distinguished from the people in this respect: if his first wife perhaps dies, he does not enter upon a second marriage. For although, as stated above, an ordinary man is not allowed to possess two wives at once, he may take another after one has died.

But if we wish carefully to consider Paul’s teaching, conduct, and purpose—which no one can doubt Timothy and Titus had followed—we must understand these words much more subtly and truly, and fulfil them in a much more sacred and spiritual manner. Paul knew how Christ had instructed his disciples, by what examples and admonitions he had invited them to continence. For this reason he had conferred concerning the Gospel with James, John, and Cephas, who seemed to be pillars, lest perhaps he should differ in any respect from Christ or from them, should he himself teach other presbyters otherwise than they had been taught. But the aforesaid apostles added nothing to him, since they found nothing in his teaching contrary to Christ’s teaching or their own.

Therefore, just as Christ wished to instruct the apostles, so Paul proposed to conform himself to them; and he carefully commended the same purpose to Timothy and Titus and the other presbyters. Consequently, when he says that a presbyter must be the husband of one wife, this must not be understood as though he ought to associate a wife with himself upon receiving sacred orders. Paul himself is not found to have done this, and it is certain that Timothy and Titus were not married. Rather, it must be understood to mean that before sacred orders he had had no more than one wife, if indeed he had had a wife.

Paul then saw many persons of different conditions and ages coming to the Catholic faith and to Christ’s baptism, and foresaw that many more would come later. Some of these, whether before baptism or even after baptism, had devoted themselves to secular life and would necessarily later have to be ordained to govern the Church. He therefore wished to provide a sure indication of what sort of persons they ought to be—not only after ordination, but also before it—so that carnal life might in some manner be a type of spiritual life and, although they differ greatly in the merit of holiness, they might nevertheless agree, not in reality but in the image of chastity.

“A bishop or presbyter,” he says, “must be the husband of one wife; [Col. 0752C] and deacons are husbands of one wife” (1 Tim. III). This is to say: I wish that such a man be promoted to sacred orders as, before orders, was content with only one wife, so that hope of continence may be inferred from the fact that he is shown not to have entered into more marriages even in a lawful state.

For as one content with one wife did not seek a second marriage, so a consecrated presbyter or deacon, consecrated to the Church and as it were betrothed to her, ought thereafter to seek no one’s embraces but rest in her bosom or lap alone, so that neither bodily allurement of the loins nor the spiritual fornication of heretics may tear him away from her. Thus, I say, he who is ordained as either minister or overseer to the Church alone must cleave to her in lawful affection and be bound by an indissoluble bond, so that he does not turn his mind back to union with a carnal wife, nor introduce any heretical perversity into the chamber of his heart, lest he be found no longer monogamous as before, but bigamous or trigamous, contrary to the apostolic life.

The apostles indeed, and apostolic men, say of the Church to whom they are joined by a spiritual covenant: “My dove, my perfect one, is one” (Cant. VI). In order figuratively to designate this unity, monogamy is commended in the presbyter or deacon; if he has perhaps been content with it, he is judged suitable for election. This is not because bigamy causes some injury to future holiness, but because it does not preserve the sacrament of this aforesaid unity.

The Lord says something similar through Moses in Leviticus (ch. II), when he forbids a person who is blind, ruptured, or similarly afflicted to offer him the legal sacrifices. This is not because such bodily infirmities are found entirely incompatible with perfect righteousness—indeed, they often even assist it—but because they do not sufficiently prefigure the image of the holiness required, since the figure ought to agree in outward appearance with the truth.

## CHAPTER LXVI

The Apostle also commands that a widow of sixty years be chosen who has been the wife of one husband (1 Tim. V), so that in her may shine forth both the maturity of completed age and the mystery of unity mentioned above. It should be noted that he does not command the selection of a woman who either has a husband or intends to have one, but of one who is both widowed from her husband and chaste in purpose, lest either ecclesiastical religion or reputation [Col. 0753B] be disgraced if a woman living in luxury is supported from the temple treasury. Hence he says: “Avoid younger widows, for when they have become wanton, they wish to marry” (ibid.).

When, therefore, he teaches that a widow of sixty years should be selected—one in whom youthful desires have cooled, whose wantonness has subsided, whose womanly capacities have failed—what is meant by his so pointedly specifying this very requirement, unless it is that he commended a mystery? For what could it have harmed in so aged a woman’s living well if the widow chosen had been the wife of two husbands, or three, or even more? Often she devotes herself more fervently to holiness who remembers having given freer rein to pleasure.

Did Christ in the Gospel condemn the woman who had successively had seven brothers as husbands, or declare that she had erred because she had married so many times? When the Sadducees asked which of the seven would have her as wife in the resurrection, or which would lack her whom they had all had, “You err,” the Lord said, “not knowing the Scriptures” (Luke XX). It is as though he said: It is not she but you unbelievers—you—who err, imagining that marriages are celebrated in the resurrection. You see that Christ rebukes not the woman with seven husbands but the unbelieving Sadducees, because repetition of marriages does not prejudice holiness, nor are widows with many husbands condemned, but widows’ luxuries are. “The widow,” he says, “who is in luxuries is dead while living” (1 Tim. V).

When, therefore, the Apostle commanded the selection of a widow who had been the wife of one husband, no one can doubt that he wished to show the sacrament mentioned above, which he also wished to commend in the presbyter or deacon. For just as he says of the widow, “who has been the wife of one husband,” so I judge it must be understood of the presbyter: “who has been the husband of one wife,” not one who wishes either to take a wife with orders or after orders, or to retain with orders a wife taken before orders.

For it would seem quite incongruous for a greater liberty of carnal pleasure to be granted to a presbyter than to a widow: that, while widowed continence were imposed upon a poor woman, the pleasure of marital union were allowed a presbyter. Women are not set before presbyters for imitation; rather, presbyters are set before both them and all others in the Church as examples to be imitated. Hence it is evident that, just as continence is imposed upon widows who are supported from the temple treasury, so it is imposed upon clerics also—indeed, much more upon clerics—through whom ecclesiastical religion ought to flourish. When they have passed from the low ground of secular life to the heights of sacred orders, they ought to surpass everyone in the Church both in station and in the ordered character of their life.

This was the view of the ecclesiastical teachers who preceded us in faith and knowledge. Thus they understood the Apostle’s aforementioned statement concerning the cleric who is the husband of one wife, and thus in their treatises they left it for us to understand.

## CHAPTER LXVII

Our Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory, and Jerome—men elevated by the merit of sound teaching, and placed by the Catholic Church upon the height of authority—though they lived in different places and times, nevertheless agreed in this, under the teaching of the Holy Spirit: ministers of the altar must never indulge in the mire of carnal union; even if married before sacred orders, they must nevertheless practice continence after orders by apostolic authority.

I wonder, therefore, whence such a custom has grown among the Greeks: that presbyters freely have intercourse with their wives, and, as I have heard from some, that none are ordained without wives. Indeed, when men who previously had no wives are raised to the rank of priesthood, they are at the same time, as it were, necessarily compelled to take wives, lest, fortified by such a remedy, they fall into the precipice of fornication. They say, “Let each man have a wife because of fornication” (1 Cor. VII)—a remarkable thing, and quite worthy of ridicule, and unworthy of so great a ministry or so sacred a mystery.

Others, however, say that the custom mentioned above does not exist among the Greeks, but another, more fitting one: namely, that the man ordained presbyter is given the choice whether to practice continence or not. If he chooses continence, he may not afterwards take a wife, but remains in the chastity he has undertaken. But if he chooses marriage, he may either retain the wife he has or take one if he does not have one—provided only that, should she first die, the presbyter does not thereafter obtain another. “A presbyter,” they say, “must be the husband of one wife.”

The Fathers mentioned above did not understand or expound the Apostle’s words in this way; nor was this observed in this manner by them or by any other saints, whether earlier or later. Origen, who was Greek by nation, did not preach thus to the Greeks themselves. Rather, both in life and speech he most diligently commended clerical continence. And, to confirm his opinion more surely, having zeal for God but not according to knowledge, he physically castrated himself out of love for purity, lest he ever depart from the aforesaid purpose of due chastity.

Our Augustine also, though born and raised among Latins, was exceedingly learned in Greek letters. He declares that he has read nothing of this sort in Greek codices and found nothing of it among the Greek teachers whom he knew to be saints. Rather, relying on the testimonies of Greeks as well as Latins, he imposes continence on the sacred orders of clerics. Hence he writes a little book *On the Singleness of Clerics*, in which he endeavors to withdraw them from all association with women, so that they may not presume to live with them in the same house; “because,” he says, “unless the manner of life of these men is separated from living with those women, their life or their reputation is stained by an unavoidable contagion.”

Jerome, who was skilled in three languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—and searched Hebrew, Greek, and Latin codices with such diligence that the outer eye grew dim through constant reading while divine grace brightened the acuity of his inner eye—Jerome, I say, declares that the Apostle’s aforementioned words must be understood in no other way than that continence is assigned as the inseparable companion of sacred orders.

Thus, speaking to Pammachius, he says: “Let them be angry not with me but with the holy Scriptures—indeed, with bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the whole priestly and Levitical choir—who know that they cannot offer sacrifices if they serve the work of marriage.” And elsewhere, when he thundered against the blasphemies of Vigilantius and labored to call the minds of the faithful back from his opinion, he says: “For this—an outrage!—he says that bishops have accomplices in his crime, if indeed those should be called bishops who do not ordain deacons unless they have first taken wives.” And shortly afterward: “What will the churches of the East do, what Egypt, what the Apostolic See, which accepts as clerics either virgins or continent men, or, if they have had wives, men who cease to be husbands?”

You see that continence is commended quite openly in these words, and that men distinguished by sacred orders are not at all released from it. Who, then, expounded the Apostle in this way to the Greeks, saying that he gave presbyters a command or permission to be joined to wives not only before orders but after orders as well? Origen, Augustine, and Jerome, who are known to have been trained in Greek letters, are found in their writings to have left us the contrary teaching. Should we believe that what Greek teachers were able to teach in writings or exhibit in deeds could have escaped men of such great learning? Or, what is more likely, no saint among the Greeks, any more than among the Latins, expounded the Apostle as requiring this interpretation; rather, a depraved custom prevailed because it pleased many who minded carnal things and perhaps could not be uprooted by the few who opposed it.

Thus a certain pagan said: “What is sinned by many is just.” For just as among the Latins, in very many places—to say nothing of other evils—the custom of lending at interest has so prevailed through the attachment of many to usury that no power is now given to the prelates of the Church to uproot it. Not only common and low-born persons, but very many nobles, delight that they flourish in such wealth; and the outcry of those rebuking them may fail to prevail amid the protests of many. So perhaps among the Greeks something blameworthy is found which has as its patron not the authority of Scripture but the perversity of a multitude or custom.

But leaving the Greeks to their custom—if what rumor has spread among us concerning them is true—let us return to the path of our own teachers. Let us hold firmly to their meaning in the evangelical as well as apostolic Scriptures, so that what, by God’s generous grace, they deserved to understand in them, we too may take care both to hear more attentively and to obey more diligently what we have heard.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

The Apostle’s words must not always be understood as they seem to sound. Rather, we must believe that a subtler meaning lies hidden in them, one not easily disclosed to the unlearned and negligent, as he himself is found on several occasions to declare. He says to Timothy: “Understand [Col. 0756B] what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in all things” (2 Tim. II). And to the Corinthians: “If anyone seems to be a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge the things that I write to you” (1 Cor. XIV).

By these words he indicates that his hearers need spiritual understanding and wisdom, lest they pervert his words by a reprobate or carnal meaning, as did those of whom Peter says: “As also our most beloved brother Paul, according to the grace given to him, wrote to you; as also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these matters, in which are certain things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable pervert to their own destruction” (2 Pet. III).

Therefore, lest we fall into the pit of destruction, let us hold the Apostle’s words as the aforementioned saints understood and expounded them: namely, that continence is unquestionably imposed upon clerics, and that good repute must be joined to this same continence.
