For those chosen so as to please God through continence, and to admonish others to please him by their own example, must ensure that neither their life nor their reputation is corrupted by any stain, so that their life may be useful to themselves and their reputation useful to their neighbors.

The reputation of chastity is precarious, and anyone is quickly believed to have fallen into bodily lapse, even though it is clear that he has maintained continence for many preceding days. Christ, attentive to this, imposed upon his apostles not only continence but also carefully instructed them to preserve the reputation of that continence, lest their light lie hidden under a bushel but, displayed and raised aloft, shine far and wide for the advancement of all.

Therefore, placing a belt upon their loins—by which continence is undoubtedly signified—he commanded them to be “girded in front” (*praecincti*), in which a certain display of continence seems to be marked. This was not so that their empty, boastful pride might glory vainly, but so that God, the giver of this gift, might be praised by those who behold them: “Let your loins,” he says, “be girded in front” (Luke XII).

Since the loins are not in front but behind, what does it mean that he did not command them simply to be girded, or girded about, or, so to speak, girded behind—which could have been said more expressly—but carefully commanded them to be *praecincti*? Taken literally, this is not fitting language, unless by adding the prefix *prae-* (“in front”) he wished to signify the manifestation of continence mentioned above. He thereby taught clerics not merely to preserve continence in secret, with conscience as witness, but commendably to display it for imitation, not for boasting.

Among the ancient saints, indeed, we find Elijah and Jeremiah girding their loins, but not “girding them in front,” because although they refused to have wives in disregard of the Law’s curse—“cursed is he who has not left seed upon the earth”—they nevertheless did not presume to invite the people of their time to the same continence. This preaching was properly reserved for the apostles and apostolic men, when grace had been revealed and the excellence of chastity was commended; when the true lamp-wick, trimmed not by a material but by a spiritual snuffer, was made clear—that is, when the somewhat obscure mystery of the Law was unveiled by Gospel preaching.

Once the Lord had said, “Let him who can receive it, receive it” (Matt. XIX), it was fitting that clerics should not only maintain this continence, but that no one should doubt that they maintained it. Thus, as incomparable holiness made them pleasing to God, the beauty of good reputation would make them venerable to the people. For the Church’s teachers are not sufficiently served by the truth of their own chastity unless, so far as lies in them, its reported truth invites others also to the same thing.

Foreseeing them in the Spirit, a certain Wise Man exclaimed: “O how beautiful is the chaste generation with glory!” (Wis. IV). The chastity of clerics, upheld by the protection of its own truth, may perhaps be good; but it is not beautiful without the benefit of due renown, because goodness itself is no slight degree disfigured if the stain of suspicion is credibly cast upon it.

Hence some think that *clerus* (“clergy”) is so called, as though *clarus* (“bright” or “renowned”), from *claritas* (“brightness” or “renown”): because, just as one who is illustrious shines with the radiant beam of preeminent dignity, so the clergy ought also to shine in reality and in name with holiness, lest either a discolored life darken dignity or sinister rumor obscure noble holiness. Thus the aforesaid Wise Man fittingly marvels when, in the spirit of prophecy, he contemplates the saints of our time, whom he sees raised to so great a height both by conspicuous chastity and by renown that in both respects they deservedly surpass the saints of old.

## CHAPTER LXIX
The lengthy discussion of clerical continence, and its affirmation by the testimonies of the divine Scriptures [Col. 0757D] as true, may suffice, so that no doubt about these matters is left to anyone—unless perhaps one perversely resists the truth. Yet, although I had proposed to speak of the dignity of clerics, so much has been said about their holiness that I may seem, as though forgetful of my purpose, to have gone off upon something else in place of what I undertook, and to have woven an excessive discourse concerning their virtues. But if what was said at the beginning of this reply is recalled, it will not seem irrelevant that an account of clerical virtues has been introduced. For their dignity itself shines forth more brightly precisely because such distinguished holiness necessarily cleaves to it. For God willed, as was said at the outset, that those whom he set above others by ecclesiastical dignity should likewise excel in a certain special and eminent holiness, lest so great a [Col. 0758A] prerogative of dignity should deserve to be cheapened if ordinary righteousness appeared sufficient for it.

It was therefore fitting that clerical holiness itself should be brought forward, and that the special virtues by which it ought to be distinguished should be shown with the supporting testimonies of Scripture, so that, once the holiness known to be inseparably joined to the aforementioned dignity has been recognized, it may more easily be judged how highly that dignity itself ought to be valued. For faith, hope, charity, and the acquisition of other virtues of this kind are known generally to suffice for bringing lay righteousness to completion. But besides these, those four virtues of which I have spoken hitherto—namely, election, learning, poverty, and continence—are assigned especially to clerics, so that without them they are deservedly accused [Col. 0758B] of being unworthy to glory in the name of clerics, since they have not more zealously embraced the reality denoted by that name. But those who have attained these four virtues together with the others are plainly persons of great and, as it were, perfect holiness; and therefore they are rightly marked out by the lofty rank of clerical dignity. For only such holiness deserves to be raised to so high a summit, and no dignity is more fittingly honored by such holiness than this one.

Great, therefore, and pre-eminent is the dignity of clerics. It is so placed in the middle between God and the people that, while subject to God, it is set above the people; nor is anyone released from the bonds of sins except through it, since the power of binding and loosing has been granted to it by the Lord. Thus, in Leviticus, when someone is commanded to offer sacrifice for sin, the divine word frequently [Col. 0758C] concludes: “The priest shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him” (Lev. IV).

Finally, when Moses is sent into Egypt to lead the children of Israel out of Pharaoh’s hand, he shrinks from so great a task; and, as though too weak to fulfill what is commanded, he begs that another be sent: “I beseech thee, Lord,” he says, “I am not eloquent; send whom thou wilt send.” And the Lord says: “Aaron thy brother, a Levite—I know that he is eloquent—shall speak for thee to the people and shall be thy mouth; but thou shalt be to him in those things which pertain to God” (Exod. IV). And below: “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Moses said: Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips; how shall Pharaoh hear me?” (Exod. VI).—“And the Lord said to [Col. 0758D] Moses: Behold, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet. Thou shalt speak all that I command thee; he shall speak to Pharaoh” (Exod. VII).

You see that, for leading the children of Israel out of Egypt and for reproving Pharaoh, Moses confesses himself inadequate. Therefore God promises him the assistance of Aaron his brother, so that what Moses cannot accomplish may be supplied through Aaron’s help, and so that not Moses alone but Aaron too may be commended before God and the people. Moses bears the figure of the Law, because through him the Law was given; Aaron, however, bears the figure of the priesthood, upon which dignity was first conferred. Therefore, because the divine Law, to which all the people ought to be obedient, cannot reach human knowledge except through the ministry of preachers, Aaron, Moses’ brother, is fittingly appointed [Col. 0759A] for this purpose: through his office the precepts of the Law may become known to all, lest, lacking a preacher, they be silenced under the weight of silence.

This is what Moses says: “I beseech thee, Lord, I am not eloquent”; and the Lord says of Aaron: “Aaron thy brother, a Levite—I know that he is eloquent” (Exod. IV). For the Law, which by itself is silent as though tongueless, requires that Pharaoh, as one foolish, be chastised and that the wise Israelite people be delivered from his hand. Aaron is rightly called the brother of Moses, because clerical dignity is joined to the divine Law by so close a kinship that they ought not be separated from one another. The Law needs a clerical preacher; and the preacher ought not act except according to what the Law has prescribed. The divine Law ought carefully to make known to the cleric those things which pertain to God; and [Col. 0759B] the cleric ought to preach that same Law to the peoples in fitting speech. Thus Moses, as it is written, shall be to his brother Aaron in those things which pertain to God, and Aaron shall speak to the people for his brother Moses.

## CHAPTER LXX

It is clear, therefore, that clerical dignity is figured in Aaron, to whom the office of preaching is specially entrusted, lest Moses alone should seem to glory in the salvation of the faithful, but Aaron also should be granted a share in the same glory for the assistance bestowed. The Apostle Paul too glories in this assistance when he considers that through it his merit is increased: “We are God’s fellow-workers” (I Cor. III). God could certainly have taught sufficiently, [Col. 0759C] without Paul or Aaron, whomever he wished; but he chose to employ them as his helpers, so that their merit might be increased by their collaboration, and their dignity might stand out because the lower people were commanded to hear them. “He who hears you,” he says, “hears me” (Luke X).

Aaron, Moses’ brother, is commanded to hear Moses alone and to speak to the people what he has heard from him, because the chief pontiff of clerics obeys the divine Law alone, while he is found, by the privilege of doctrine, to be set above all others. Perhaps for this reason, when divine Scripture names Moses and Aaron together, it almost always puts Moses first: “Moses and Aaron said”; “the Lord said to Moses and Aaron”; and much else of this kind. It does not so yield precedence to Moses as to wish in any respect to detract from Aaron, who is named after him; rather, by this too [Col. 0759D] it wished to show that the priest ought not to go before the divine Law, but to follow it.

But when Joshua son of Nun and Eleazar the priest are brought forward together, as those known to succeed Moses and Aaron respectively in governing and teaching the people, that same Scripture significantly puts Eleazar first. By this, as it seems, it intends us to understand that no one—not only among the people, but even among the rulers of the people—is to be preferred to the chief pontiff; indeed, he himself is to be regarded as prior by right of priesthood to the greater no less than to the lesser. Thus it is written in Numbers: “These are the names of the men who shall divide the land by lot: Eleazar the priest, and Joshua son of Nun, and one prince from each tribe” (Num. XXXIV). And in the book of Joshua itself: “The chiefs of the families [Col. 0760A] of Levi came to Eleazar the priest, and Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders of the kindreds” (Josh. XXI). And elsewhere in the same book (Josh. XXII), whenever Eleazar and Joshua are mentioned together, they are arranged, unless I am mistaken, in the order I have stated.

Phinehas also, the priest and son of Eleazar the priest, is named before the other rulers when he is sent with them to the children of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in the land of Gilead. For when those two and a half tribes had built beside the Jordan an altar of immense size, “the children of Israel,” it says, “sent to them Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest, and ten princes with him, one from each tribe”; and a little later: “When they heard these things, Phinehas the priest and the princes of the embassy who were with him were appeased.” You clearly see [Col. 0760B] priests named before the leaders and princes of the people. By this, I think, their dignity is shown forth: for while a material sword, reaching to the division of soul and body, is granted to the latter, to the former is granted the living and efficacious word of God, sharper than every two-edged sword, which the Apostle Paul declares reaches to the division of soul and spirit (Heb. IV).

Lest the fact that Eleazar the priest is named before Joshua the ruler should appear accidental and weightless, divine Scripture itself makes sufficiently clear elsewhere that it did not arrange their list in this way without mystery. When Moses, forewarned by the Lord, knew that the day of his death was near, he was concerned about appointing a ruler; and he is read as replying thus to the Lord who spoke with him [Col. 0760C]: “May the Lord, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over this multitude.” And the Lord said to him: “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit of God” (Num. XXVII); for, if anything must be done, Eleazar the priest shall consult the Lord. At his word Joshua himself shall go out and come in, and all the children of Israel with him.

Behold, Joshua, appointed in Moses’ place at the Lord’s command, is commanded to go out and come in at the word of Eleazar the priest, so that, just as all the children of Israel, he too may hear the priest: the priest is to command and the ruler to obey. Thus, although he knows himself to be set above all the people, he may recognize the far more worthy precedence of the chief pontiff.

## CHAPTER LXXI

[Col. 0760D]

It is honorable and very useful that the more persons anyone sees deferring to him, the more carefully he should consider whom, and in what respect, he ought to prefer before himself; lest, if he scorns to render due honor to his superiors, he deserve to suffer the same scorn from his inferiors. King Uzziah of Judah was unwilling wisely to observe this, or to render priests the honor he owed them. He rashly attempted what was not lawful for him, supposing that whatever pleased him was lawful. For he entered the temple of the Lord and wished to burn incense upon the altar of incense. Azariah the chief priest and the other priests wished to prevent him, followed the king swiftly into the sanctuary, and, burning with zeal for righteousness, addressed him boldly:

“It is not thy [Col. 0761A] office, Uzziah, to burn incense to the Lord, but that of the priests, that is, of the sons of Aaron. Leave the sanctuary, lest thou hast despised [the command], for it shall not be accounted to thee for glory” (II Chron. XXVI).

But he, swollen with the sceptre of royal power and reckoning the lofty dignity of the pontificate of no consequence, not only refused humbly to be recalled from his purpose, but, adding rashness to what he had wickedly begun, held the censer in his hand and angrily began to threaten the priests. Therefore God immediately struck him with leprosy upon the forehead, so that, smitten at last, he might recognize that priests are to be honored not only by the people but by kings and rulers, and that they must not be resisted with arrogant obstinacy.

When Azariah and the other priests saw that he was covered with leprosy, they rendered him what was due [Col. 0761B]: scorning the scorner, they drove him from the house of the Lord as an outcast and most contemptible person. He himself, realizing that he was leprous, hastened out; and, as it is written there, he lived in a separate house because of his leprosy. Thus he who, swollen with royal pride, had refused humbly to bend his ear to the admonitions of priests deserved to endure the divine vengeance intolerably. Nor could he, nor dared he, brazenly oppose their expulsion of him, having at last learned what priests ought to command kings.

Just as Azariah the pontiff expelled leprous Uzziah from the temple, lest he should remain king (II Chron. XXIII [an apparent erroneous reference]), so, conversely, Jehoiada the pontiff brought Joash into the temple that he might become king, placed him upon the royal throne amid the people’s acclamation, and, after Joash’s grandmother Athaliah had been slain, established his kingdom [Col. 0761C] with due security. What, then, is commended in all this except pontifical dignity? Without it royal power itself is not established; and whatever is not fortified by its mighty blessing, however lofty and eminent it may be, is found neither enduring nor worthy of commendation.

That this is repeatedly signified in the ancient Scriptures is certain; but Christ wished to demonstrate it in reality in the Gospel when, choosing his disciples, he bestowed on them apostolic dignity and granted this dignity great and wonderful power. “Having summoned the apostles,” [Col. 0761D] Luke says, “he gave them power and authority over all demons, and to heal diseases” (Luke IX). And in Matthew: “Amen, I say to you, whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. XVIII). And in John: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain are retained” (John XX).

Wonderful dignity! Wonderful power! By its command demonic powers and the diseases of the soul are subjected; at its decision whatever is loosed or bound on earth is also loosed or bound in heaven. Having received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, it discerns by prudent examination what ought to be shut or opened; and, with God himself confirming the act by mighty power, it sees itself separating some persons from others for God.

## CHAPTER LXXII

[Col. 0762A]

Lest this dignity or power be believed to have been given only to the apostles and not also to their vicars, seventy-two others are designated, to whom the Gospel declares similar things to have been granted. They are sent to preach before Christ’s face, like lambs among wolves, and they receive Christ’s office just as the apostles do. For it is said to them: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke X). And again: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (ibid.).

Therefore Christ entrusted the office of preaching to the apostles and apostolic men—that is, clerics—and especially assigned to them the pontifical power of binding and loosing, so that by preaching they may teach how the dead may return to fellowship with the blessed living, and may allow those raised by Christ [Col. 0762B] to depart when released from the bonds of sins. Thus he said to them concerning Lazarus: “Loose him, and let him go” (John XI). It was certainly easy for Christ, by the same word by which he raised Lazarus, to loose him also; but by commanding him to be loosed, he commended the ministry of those who loose, lest perhaps anyone later, when divine grace raised him to repentance, should think ecclesiastical authority unnecessary for himself.

For just as Christ reserved to himself the raising of the dead, so he gave to clerics the loosening of the bonds of those raised, so that through their ministry the raised may be given free power thereafter to run unhindered along the path of holiness. Therefore no repentance is shown to please God [Col. 0762C] which is not committed to the judgment of clerics; for just as it belongs to sinners to do penance for their sins, so it belongs to clerics to give those penitents, and prescribe for them, the rule of truth. Nor is this alone assigned to them—the solemn office of preaching, or the pontifical power of binding and loosing. The prerogative of baptizing is also entrusted to them, lest anyone falsely claim that he can enter the kingdom of heaven without being reborn of water and Spirit through their ministry: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). And to Nicodemus: “Unless a man is born again of water and Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God” (John III).

This excellence of regeneration, by which both original and personal sins are forgiven [Col. 0762D]; of which the pursuing Egyptians are drowned in the Red Sea as a type; through which the ragged garment of the old life is destroyed and the new person is adorned with the brightness of a new linen robe—this excellence, I say, has been so assigned as peculiarly proper to the apostles and their clerical successors that no other order or condition is permitted regularly to exercise that ministry, even if it possesses the same holiness or perhaps greater.

## CHAPTER LXXIII

Finally, John, son of Zechariah—than whom no greater arose among those born of women—who baptized many in the river Jordan, was indeed great by the merit of his illustrious holiness; yet in baptizing he did not enjoy the privilege of apostolic dignity. Although he merited to baptize Christ among others, he could not nevertheless [Col. 0763A] remit the sins of those whom he baptized, because his washing, of little or no benefit to those washed, was not the reality but the figure of divine baptism.

That baptism is divine by which Christ, who is God, baptizes through the apostles and their vicars; for although he is truly believed to baptize, he nevertheless chose to entrust to them the ministry of baptizing. Thus the Evangelist says: “Jesus makes and baptizes more disciples than John, although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples” (John IV). But that baptism is rightly called human by which John, who was a man, baptized both Christ and others. Thus Christ himself called that baptism not God’s baptism but a human baptism: “John’s baptism,” he says, “is it from heaven, or from men?”

Who, then, can doubt that divine baptism is worthier than human baptism; Christ’s baptism [Col. 0763B] worthier than John’s baptism; the baptism in which there is reality worthier than that which is a figure of reality? For by the washing of the former every stain of guilt is cleansed away, whereas the latter is ineffective for this work. But since the baptism by which Christ baptizes is far worthier than that by which he himself was baptized, why did Christ not grant John the ministry of the worthier baptism, when he raised him to such an excellence of holiness that he himself bore witness that none born of women rose above him? Why, when he gave him holiness greater than that of others, did he not also grant him greater dignity, so that he might exercise the ministry of saving baptism and, at his decision, every obligation on earth and in heaven [Col. 0763C] might be loosed?

Why, I ask, did Christ refuse to assign this gift to John, a prophet and more than a prophet, unless because he wished to commend apostolic dignity by a certain special grace, lest the prophetic order be thought either superior to it or even equal to it, if John, like the apostles, received Christ’s office in the Church? John is fittingly proclaimed holier and worthier than the apostles, so that apostolic dignity may appear to be conferred not from merit but from grace, and that each may defer to the other in reciprocal humility: the Apostle sees greater holiness in John, and John reveres greater dignity in the Apostle.

Although apostolic [Col. 0763D] holiness is undoubtedly understood to surpass all the saints of old, prophets as well as others, John is nevertheless judged holier than certain apostles, because it is said that no one greater than he rose among those born of women—if, however, that testimony has no other meaning. Some indeed say that Christ’s words ought not to be understood as asserting John to be greater than others, but only not less than them. For it was not said that among those born of women he himself rose as the greatest, but that no one greater than he rose. Thus, they say, it remains possible to understand that another might be found not greater but equal to him; and they contend that no necessary force of the wording prevents this sense.

But if this is so—if John is not greater than the others, but none of the others is greater than he—who is more fittingly judged equal to him [Col. 0764A] than any of the apostles? Their holiness is so great that it is set before all the faithful for imitation, and the universal Church is entrusted to their protection. But if, on the contrary, someone says that John is without doubt proclaimed holier than the others because none is affirmed to have risen greater than he among those born of women, he should not be contentious in opposition, as though this were entirely unsuitable, provided this meaning is drawn from sound arguments.

For there is a figure of speech which secular learning calls *lyptote* [litotes], which says less and signifies more. For example, when it is said that a man is neither stronger than Samson nor wiser than Solomon, this means nothing other than that he is weaker than Samson and less wise than Solomon. So, when it is said that no one greater than John [Col. 0764B] the Baptist arose among those born of women, perhaps not someone’s equality but John’s greater holiness is indicated by the *lyptote* we mentioned. Yet by this no detraction is made from the holy apostles; rather, Christ’s lavish generosity toward his Baptist is declared.

## CHAPTER LXXIV

Yet someone who carefully considers the Evangelists’ words may perhaps still oppose this opinion, and endeavor plausibly to show that John is not greater than the apostles. Matthew says: “No one greater than John the Baptist arose among those born of women” (Matt. XI). But Luke seems to specify more precisely whom we should understand as the one whom Matthew says was not greater: “Among those born of women,” [Col. 0764C] he says, “no prophet is greater than John the Baptist” (Luke VII). Therefore no prophet, not no apostle, is greater than John; hence he was called by the Lord more than a prophet: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Indeed, I say to you, and more than a prophet” (ibid.).

Moreover, the apostles are by no means called prophets; indeed, with the prophets’ pardon, the apostles are raised above prophets. But the Lord rightly called John a prophet and more than a prophet, because he whom others prophesied from afar, John pointed out with his finger by being born, preaching, baptizing, and prefiguring him. Furthermore, it should be noted that Matthew says: “No one greater than John the Baptist arose among those born of women.” Luke, however, says: “Among those born of women [Col. 0764D] no one is greater.” The former speaks of the past, the latter of the present; neither speaks of the future. From this it may be understood that no one who then was or had been is indicated as greater than John, or as having been greater than him; but perhaps it is not denied that someone might be greater than he.

For it was not said, “No one greater shall arise,” or, “No one shall be greater”; rather, Matthew says, “No one greater arose,” while Luke says, “No one is greater.” It is certain, moreover, that when these things were said, the apostles were still weak and little, and far inferior to John in holiness. He was already ready to die for love of preaching the truth, whereas they only acquired such steadfastness after Christ’s death. For when Christ spoke these things of John, although he had already called the apostles to the rank of apostolic dignity, he had not yet [Col. 0765A] bestowed upon them the perfection of promised holiness. Rather, he wished first that, in his school, they should gradually be formed by examples and admonitions, and after his ascension be perfected by the Paraclete sent from heaven.

Thus none of them is rightly said then to be greater than John, since their simplicity is so often charged with imperfection: when, frightened in the boat, they are rebuked for little faith; when, not understanding the parable, they are reproved for still lacking understanding; when the sons of Zebedee prematurely and ambitiously seek to be placed at Christ’s right and left; when they dispute among themselves which of them ought to be judged the greater; when Philip, supposing that he sees the Son, asks that the Father be shown to him; when Peter, lying from fear of the Passion [Col. 0765B], denies his Master; when John, leaving his linen cloth behind, flees naked to save himself; when all scatter, abandoning their dying Master; and when Thomas does not believe him risen unless he sees the nail-marks. Since they were beset by these and many other weaknesses, what wonder if they are judged inferior to John?

But after Christ’s ascension, when the Spirit descended upon them in tongues of fire and they were made drunk with the new wine of grace; when, putting off the garments of childhood, they were renewed with more perfect clothing; when they proclaimed Christ everywhere, no longer held back by fear as before; when the sick of every kind were restored to health even by their shadow or their handkerchiefs; when they adorned the beginnings of the Church being born with wonderful [Col. 0765C] works; when, shut up in the glowing workshop of all holiness, they were found to fashion its whole rule; and, to conclude, when they shone forth in a new religion unheard of in all previous ages—what wonder if someone judged them not only no less holy than John, but perhaps now holier? Although Christ nowhere openly declares this through any Evangelist, nevertheless, in bearing testimony to John, he does not seem to deny it.

But because it is not ours, where we have no warrant from the Scriptures, to weigh in an unconsulted balance the hidden merits of the saints, lest, while we seem to defer to some, we be found to disparage others, we must leave their judgment to Christ, the supreme and true Judge. He who bestowed their gifts may distinguish between their holiness, if he sees anything requiring distinction, and may give more or less honor to whomever he wills, if he judges it fitting to do so. Yet I think that, without offense [Col. 0765D] to John, this may be said: whether he is considered holier than the apostles or inferior to them in holiness, he seems to yield to them somewhat in a certain ecclesiastical dignity, since in baptizing, binding, loosing, and administering the other sacraments of the Church, the Apostle is found to exercise Christ’s office—a power or ministry which John did not receive.

## CHAPTER LXXV

[Col. 0766A]

To the apostles and their vicars this gift is specially assigned: that through the laying on of their hands the Holy Spirit may be poured into believers. No one is in any way fully worthy either to be or to be called a faithful person unless he has been instructed in the sacraments of faith through their ministry. This was indeed performed in the primitive Church with manifest signs, when every believer who received the Spirit spoke in various tongues. Now, although signs so evident do not follow, priests are nevertheless known by certain faith to do the same thing spiritually. For they give the Spirit by the laying on of hands in ordaining; and though far inferior to the apostles in holiness, they exercise a vicarious power for conferring divine gifts upon believers.

For the holiness of the apostles was so great that, although any cleric can imitate them in some manner, he cannot in any degree be made their equal. Although their dignity is in some fashion transmitted even to us, their holiness remains, as it were, singular and proper to themselves. When, after the Paraclete had been sent from heaven, they spoke in every tongue and, as the miracle became widely known, were held in reverence by all, such a new flowering of holiness [Col. 0766B] appeared in them that it inspired fear in the eight thousand who had assembled; and these promised that henceforth they would live according to the apostles’ judgment and willingly submit their necks to Christ’s sweet yoke.

Accordingly the apostles established for them a new rule of life, setting themselves forth as the pattern of that rule, and advanced them to a perfection such as no earlier age had known. For, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “All who believed were together; and the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. Nor did any one of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common. And as many as possessed houses or lands sold them, brought the prices of them [Col. 0766C], laid them at the apostles’ feet, and distribution was made to each according as anyone had need” (Acts II).

O new thing! Who, whether before the Law or under the Law, heard of so many thousands of people reaching such unity of spirit, embracing voluntary poverty with such ready mind, attaining such agreement in living together, and unanimously obeying the laws of such new and perfect holiness? “They were all,” it says, “with one accord in Solomon’s portico.” That portico was rich, not so much with the gold, silver, or other metals of Solomon of old, as with the treasure of virtues and the splendor of the new religion. With the south wind blowing and driving away from the furnace the ashes of cold antiquity, the fire sent from heaven [Col. 0766D] fashioned, by marvelous workmanship, the pattern of regular holiness.

Rich, I say, was that portico, in whose furnace the divine fire grew—not burning, but illuminating; in whose forge the unheard-of beauty of the Church came into being, binding the hearts of so many thousands with the bond of such unity that, through the gift of a united will, they were not many but one.

## CHAPTER LXXVI

I recall that the ancient saints Abraham and Lot are highly commended in the Scriptures (Gen. XIII), and yet were at one time so separated from one another that they were unwilling to remain together not only in the same dwelling but even in the same region, lest either their great [Col. 0767A] possessions be diminished by harmful proximity or a quarrel arise between their shepherds. Thus, when one chose the right hand, the other turned to the left; and each, as far as he could, accumulated wealth for himself.

But the saints of the new Law, coming from right and left, are gathered into one shared dwelling; and, with fear of quarrels laid to rest, they rejoice to unite their houses, lands, estates, and whatever else they possess, so that each retains nothing as his own and, in a new manner, all possess everything. When the eleven patriarchs were tortured by miserable envy, they did not hesitate secretly to sell Joseph, the twelfth; brothers could not bear to have their brother dwell with them in one house, lest, if the prophecy of his dream came to fulfillment, they might someday be compelled to revere him.

But the saints of whom we have spoken, coming from many and different tribes, leave behind the many houses they possessed and grow together [Col. 0767B] into one portico. They are so melted by the fire of brotherly love that they satisfy the unity laid upon them not only by living together but also by being of one mind in all things. The children of Israel opposed their leader Moses with manners so perverse that, although they frequently promised obedience, they rarely fulfilled it; and because they refused to be held even by the more relaxed reins of the commandments, they could not be endured by their teacher Moses.

He was therefore burdened, I think, not so much by the innumerable multitude of peoples as by the harsh and untamed diversity of their minds. He could not bring them back to one will by entreaty, payment, or any threats; or perhaps, having brought them back, could not preserve them in the same purpose. But the saints of whom we have spoken [Col. 0767C] are so formed by the apostles’ admonitions and so conformed to their way of life that, renouncing at the apostles’ teaching all that they had loved to possess, and living in the same portico, they rejoice, together with others who possess nothing, in possessing nothing themselves. “They were,” it says, “persevering in the teaching of the apostles” (Acts II).

Blessed is this teaching, which merited to obtain such grace that it could teach others both by words and by conduct; which raised the structure of the primitive Church to the summit of perfect religion, so that those present were astonished at the rigor of so great a novelty, while those to come adopted for themselves the rule of an admirable holiness.

## CHAPTER LXXVII
But the ancient enemy, whose characteristic is to begrudge human salvation, could not endure such advances of the Church; and regarding the growth of this new religious life as his own loss, he stirred up certain perverse persons to attack it. When wickedness prevailed, it bent somewhat the strictness of their purpose. For, once persecution had been unleashed, he caused Stephen the Levite to be stoned, and those whom love of religion had gathered together to be separated from one another through fear, so that, seeking the protection of flight, they chose to scatter in every direction; nor did any of them, apart from the apostles, dare remain in Jerusalem. Thus it is written: “Having driven Stephen out of the city, they stoned him; and on that day a great persecution arose against the Church which was in Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles” (Acts VII). [Col. 0768A] And below: “Those,” he says, “who had been scattered by the tribulation which occurred under Stephen travelled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch” (Acts VIII).

Therefore, when the rest of the multitude was geographically separated from the society of the apostles by the pressure of persecution, and wandered dispersed among the nations in uncertain dwellings, the same pattern of life could not be preserved in every respect among them; rather, the strictness of discipline was compelled to relax. For although in some there remained a desire for the holiness they had undertaken, the bond of that unity was nevertheless loosened: when they lived together, having left everything, they possessed nothing of their own, but, preferring what was held in common to private property, distributed it according to each person’s need. But when that distribution from a common stock began to fail, and regular strictness no longer restrained those separated from one another as formerly, they turned to keeping a purse of private money, in order to avoid—or at least lessen—the temporal poverty of life.

The apostles, however, who, as has been said, remained in Jerusalem, together with some who afterward joined them, maintained the purpose of voluntary poverty and, living together, the strictness of their intended holiness. Hence the brethren who had been scattered through diverse regions and maintained whatever holiness they could among barbarian nations often made a collection according to the measure of their own means and sent it to Judea for those adhering to the purpose of the aforesaid poverty. For when Agabus came to Antioch (Acts XI) and foretold by the Spirit the coming famine, [Col. 0768C] “the disciples,” he says, “each according to what he had,” resolved to send aid to the brethren dwelling in Judea; and they did so. “The disciples,” he says, “each according to what he had.” Therefore these persons no longer possessed all things together, but each possessed what was his own.

The apostle Paul also, speaking to the Romans, says: “Now, therefore, I shall go to Jerusalem to minister to the saints; for the Macedonians and Achaeans have approved making some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem” (Rom. XV). And to the Corinthians: “Concerning the collections,” he says, “which are made for the saints, as I instructed the churches of Galatia, so do you also: on the first day of the week; those whom you approve, I shall send with letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem” (I Cor. XVI). And in another Epistle to the same persons: “The sharing,” he says, [Col. 0768D] “in the ministry performed for the saints” (II Cor. VIII).

Paul calls “saints” by antonomasia those who had surpassed the broad level of ordinary holiness by the summit of voluntary poverty: those who had left their possessions so as to possess all things together, and possessed all things so that no individual possessed anything privately. Although the other virtues yield no small profit for life, without this poverty they do not lead to perfection; for the more earnestly anyone strives to acquire or preserve things that perish, the less he thinks upon things that will endure without end. Rightly, therefore, those are called saints in an eminent sense who, in view of a more excellent holiness, devote themselves to poverty: just as one labours to enrich his own house by gathering countless riches, so they enrich the Church by possessing nothing. [Col. 0769A]

Paul further urges that disciples who, on receiving the faith, had retained temporal property should receive spiritual goods from those who had left everything, by ministering to them; so that the abundance of the former might supply the need of the latter, lest excessive want injure their intended holiness, and lest the former, by mercifully helping, should make their own the holiness of those poor persons which they themselves had not been strong enough to attain by similar action.

But as time went on, when the apostles departed from one another for the sake of preaching, and, together with the elect, many who were not to be saved also flocked to the faith; when almost everywhere among the nations persecution was inflicted upon believers by unbelievers, so that Christ’s name might be wholly removed from the earth—then, whether the adversary wished it or not, the multitude of believers began to increase, but that primitive religion gradually grew so weak that at last few could anywhere be found who either sought or persevered in being united with its former strictness. [Col. 0769B]

The authority of the Church was indeed extended in many ways, and its dignity was commended far and wide by favouring grace; and although singular holiness enlightened many in various places, the regular community of which we have spoken contained few. For as individual bishops were appointed to individual cities, presbyters were stationed through villages and towns, and clerics were distributed to govern churches, the multitude of believers increased through their teaching; but their own beauty was somewhat darkened, because, while they strove to raise every weak person to whatever degree of holiness they could, they themselves, whether compelled or perhaps voluntarily, fell away from due strictness. [Col. 0769C]

Thus the religion of the clerics gradually weakened. As the multitude of believing peoples increased, they burned more eagerly to obtain among those subject to them the dignity of clerical rank than to display holiness befitting so great a dignity. For, seeing that this order was preferred to all others in the Church, and that all truly wise persons, kings as well as peoples, properly deferred to it, many who desired not so much service as honour turned the reverence bestowed upon them into pride. And from that for which they ought rather to have feared and loved God—who raises the needy from the dust (Ps. CXII; Job V), and, as Scripture says, lifts up the sorrowing by restoration to safety—they offended more grievously, being unworthy of so great and pre-eminent a dignity. [Col. 0769D]

Therefore, although they preached the Gospel everywhere, invited unbelievers to the Catholic faith, and confirmed those invited in the same purpose, they did not do this chastely or sincerely, as the Apostle says, since in it they sought not what belonged to Jesus Christ but what belonged to themselves (Phil. II). This weakness, this failure, this dissolution among the clerics was, in my opinion, a kind of fountain and origin of the monks.

## Chapter LXXVIII

Since the clerics, whose order is older, have been discussed first, the monks must now be discussed afterward, as I proposed; so that, just as it has now in some manner become known whence and how the order or dignity of the clergy proceeded, so it may likewise become known what origin and development the religious life of monks has had. When, therefore, a multitude of nations had flocked far and wide to the Catholic faith, and the institution of the apostles asked no more of them than that they should abstain from idolatry, fornication, things strangled, and blood (Acts XV), and that, having cast these aside, they might lawfully possess the remaining things of the world—this liberty, which had been granted discreetly and beneficially to the weak and untrained, so weakened the greater persons, who ought to have been stronger, that Jew and Gentile alike thought this rule of holiness sufficient for himself, and clergy and people alike declined into this broad plain of freedom. [Col. 0770A]

At last some of the faithful, more carefully considering this and recalling the strict purpose of that primitive Church, burned with zeal of spirit for living well. They reckoned worldly things as nothing for love of heavenly things, despised the worn-out breadth of popular life, and manfully transferred themselves to the narrowness of solitary life. Leaving houses, fields, parents, the tumult of the city, and, along with worldly possessions, the seductive allurements of their own wills, they built monasteries for themselves in suburban and remote places. There, under the discipline of a strict rule, they corrected their former habits.

Because, having left parents, spouses, and the multitude of the people in order more perfectly to leave secular occupations, they lived in private places, few in number and in a manner solitary, they were called *monozantes* or monks from that same singularity, so that their very name might mark them as separated from the crowd of the people. For *monos* means “one” or “single”; hence one who withdraws from the multitude of the people for the sake of quiet is rightly called a monk. [Col. 0770C]

Or, as some wish, *monachus* is said as though from *monoculus*, that is, “having only one eye.” For one who formerly seemed to use, as it were, a double eye—while appearing both to seek the world and yet specially to love God—now, rejecting all the things in which he was accustomed to delight temporally, loves to contemplate heavenly things alone with undivided desire. And because he has closed—indeed, plucked out and cast away—the eye by which worldly things are too eagerly sought, while retaining and cleansing that eye by which heavenly things are known, he rightly deserves to be called a monk, as though one-eyed: one who did not shrink from glorying in the reproach of a blessed blindness.

Indeed, in secular literature a certain man is called Monichus, who was said to have a single eye in his forehead: “Monichus,” it says, “hurls ash-trees.” Our monk, however, is said to have a single eye not in his forehead but in his heart, by which he sees invisibly; and he plucks out for himself the eye that seemed to be outwardly in the face, by which he carnally admired carnal things. [Col. 0770D]

Blessed is this blindness, by which the eye that loves external things is blinded; John the apostle exhorts us to embrace it: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world; for friendship with this world is enmity toward God” (I John II). Christ brought this blindness upon—indeed, bestowed it upon—those who wished to love him: those who despised visible things for love of invisible things. As he indicated in the Gospel, with the Jews listening, when he proclaimed the benefits of his generosity to those who did not understand: “For judgment,” he says, “I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX). [Col. 0771A]

That is to say: I came for this purpose, that the eye desiring invisible things may be restored, and that the eye loving external things may be blinded; so that one who wishes more rightly to see the direct rule of perfect life may not be troubled to endure the blindness of the harmful eye. For the greater loss this eye suffers, the greater increase the other receives; and while the desirable injuries of blindness are inflicted upon the one, gifts of fuller light are bestowed upon the other.

But the unhappy Jews, interpreting spiritual words carnally and considering the blindness they heard of a punishment or disgrace, answered: “Are we also blind?” [Col. 0771B] As though to say: If you came here to restore sight to the blind, what have you bestowed upon us in this respect, when we are not disfigured by the disgrace of any blindness, nor lack the benefit of the generosity which you proclaim? And the Lord, wishing to recall them to spiritual understanding and commend the blindness which he had come to confer, said: “If you were blind, you would not have sin; but now you say, ‘We see’; your sin remains” (ibid.).

That is to say: If you wished to turn the eye of your mind away from the things that are outward, and to regard me not as a mere man like other mortals, but to love God in man with a pure heart and a good conscience, you would not have sin—namely, the sin of unbelief, the sin of iniquity—because true faith would train you for good, and perseverance in righteous work would confirm you in it. But now you say, “We see”; your sin remains. “But now,” he says, “you maintain that you see, since you consider only those things which you see appearing outwardly; and because you love to cling to them more than is right, it is evident that your sin remains in you without failing” (ibid.). [Col. 0771C]

Therefore, because our monk, as has been said, gladly plucks out and casts away this eye, which knows how to attend only to visible things, while with utmost care and diligence he strives to cultivate that eye alone which, like an eagle, he can fix upon the rays of the sun, he rightly deserves to be called a monk on account of this unity (*monas*): refusing to have several eyes, he is content more happily with one single eye.

## Chapter LXXIX

[Col. 0771D] Lest the monk should turn his mind back to having two or more eyes—that is, lest outward occupation should divert him from the desire for heavenly things—the first institution ordered this profession in such a way and formed it by certain laws that it would neither wish to be exalted by ecclesiastical dignity nor become entangled in secular concerns. It wished it to be of such humility, indeed, of such lowliness, if one may say so, that at Christ’s banquet it should occupy a place as though rejected and last, and that every dignity should shrink from its lowliness.

Therefore, just as this profession banished secular business far from itself, in order that it might deserve more perfectly to attend upon God, so it also fled ecclesiastical dignities, lest it be caught more than was right by their allurements. For although it is fitting that only spiritual men should hold them, nevertheless their occasion has commonly removed many from the summit of perfection. Its purpose, however, was, for the sake of perfection, to avoid utterly all hindrances and to occupy itself so completely with private pursuits that it might both devote itself to manual labour, as the necessities of this life required, and strive to please God alone, as perfection of life demanded. [Col. 0772A]

Finally, it took no special care to select persons of any age or condition, but gathered all indiscriminately and everywhere. Whereas clerical dignity admitted none but the educated, monastic humility received persons untrained in letters. For the monastic profession did not judge it alien to itself if one coming to it for the sake of conversion was ignorant of letters, since its purpose was not so much to devote itself to the study of literary learning as to exercise fasting, vigils, and manual work.

It undertook manual work with such diligence and zeal that it laboured at it not only by day but also by night, so that each person might by his own labour supply what was necessary for himself and, by continual mortification of the flesh, subdue the insolence of the spirit. Thus, indeed, as some say, Mark the Evangelist ordained; thus he established a rule of life for monks. [Col. 0772B]

For Mark, burning with zeal of spirit, wished to avoid the ecclesiastical dignities offered to him and, reclining in the lowest place, to lie hidden like a lamp kindled in concealment. Having zeal for God but not according to knowledge, he presumed to cut off his thumb, so that the Church might rightly reject him. But because it is written, “There is no counsel against God” (Prov. XXI), the divine choice prevailed so greatly that his desire was frustrated and he was forcibly carried, against his will, to ecclesiastical honours. Whether he wished it or not, he attained the grade of priesthood and was made first bishop of Alexandria, at the summit of dignity.

Yet although he could not, through remaining hidden, obtain what he had desired, he did not cease to love it; and the lowliness which, divine counsel opposing, he could not maintain in his own life, he established for others to maintain. A few men, indeed, of outstanding worth, who at that time were counted under the name of monks at Alexandria in Egypt, received from him a rule of life. Taking up from the Acts of the Apostles what is written, “No one called anything his own, but all things were common among them” (Acts IV), [Col. 0772D] and similar passages, they also wished to add for themselves that saying of the Prophet (Ps. CXXVIII): “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, you are blessed,” and that of the Apostle: “Whoever does not work shall not eat” (II Thess. III).

Instructed by Mark through these and similar admonitions of Scripture, they proposed to devote such diligence to holiness that their example would invite not only unlearned and simple persons, whom the breeze of fickleness often carries away, but also learned and discerning men, whom the maturity of due gravity commends. Therefore, as both educated and uneducated persons flocked together in the suburb of Alexandria, Mark established a monastery of monks. He imposed upon them both a rule of life and strict discipline, wishing them to devote themselves so diligently to manual work that, by vigorous activity, they might resist both lethargy and idleness, and that, without depending upon the small gifts of others, they might obtain for themselves from their own labour the necessities of life. [Col. 0773A]

For since the office of preaching was not imposed upon them, nor the governance of a Church, nor care for the faithful entrusted to them, but rather subject lowliness, continual work, and quiet silence, it was fitting that they should not presume to seek the people’s offerings, lest by usurping what was not due they deserve to be burdened by another’s load. For it was granted to those to live by the Gospel and be supported by the offerings of the people to whom the ministry of preaching had been granted and who deservedly presided over the Church of the faithful by doctrine. But upon these men was imposed such humility that they should consider themselves lower than others and desire not so much to excel at the summit of dignity as to remain hidden in silence. Hence they also wished to wear rough and uncultivated clothing, so that they might show by their outward appearance the contempt in their minds and invite others, by dress as by conduct, to despise the world. [Col. 0773B]

## Chapter LXXX

Thus many persons, as this religious life was spread far and wide and desired with the same fervour of spirit, took leave of parents, possessions, and their own wills, fled to it, and voluntarily subjected themselves both to so strict an order and to so orderly a strictness. And the same religious life was spread not only about Alexandria but throughout all Egypt and the Thebaid; once spread, it multiplied, and monasteries were built in many places through abounding grace, in which the humble in spirit were gathered to live with one mind. [Col. 0773C]

Then monastic strictness spread into Palestine, Mesopotamia, Cappadocia, and the whole East. Through it the dissolution of clergy and laity alike was put to shame, and many, execrating their own pride, humbly embraced the grief of repentance; leaving their former manner of life, they professed the monastic life. These, according to the character either of places or times, or according to differences of disposition, wished to add some things for themselves, remove some things, and alter others. They did not preserve in every respect what had been instituted by the earlier Egyptians, but adopted the strictness and purpose of monks in such a way as nevertheless to accommodate themselves in some respects to the weakness of the many. [Col. 0773D]

For uniformity produces weariness in weak minds, while agreeable variety brings refreshment. They therefore resolved to suspend for a short time at certain fixed hours the manual labour which they had proposed to do almost without interruption, so that, leaving it aside, they might devote themselves more attentively to spiritual offices and celebrate devoutly the solemnity of the psalms, which among them was called the *synaxis*.

Accordingly, besides the evening and night hours, in which they agreed with the Egyptian monks, they gathered together at the third, sixth, and ninth hours to celebrate the aforesaid *synaxis*. They limited it to only three psalms, so that they might freely yield to devotion for the appropriate time and return as quickly as possible to manual work. For they performed the latter as though under obligation, but the former freely; since their purpose was both to exercise manual labour more diligently and, at times, to give themselves, as it were swiftly and briefly, to spiritual offices. [Col. 0774A]

Thus refreshed by a pleasing alternation, they believed that they could more easily devote care to holiness, because a weak mind is weighed down by intolerable weariness if compelled always to attend to the same thing. But those monks who lived within Egypt, especially the Tabennesiotes dwelling in the Thebaid, maintained the monastic purpose so inflexibly that from morning until evening they did not cease from manual labour, nor did they gather together to celebrate solemnly the aforesaid hours of the day.

While praying, meditating upon psalms, and repeatedly pondering short prayers, they continued at the work they had undertaken; and they performed both, not alternately like those whom we mentioned above, but together with tireless strictness, so that anyone arriving would be in doubt which seemed dependent on the other. For they did not omit psalms on account of labour, nor labour on account of psalms; rather, they fortified each by the other, so that labour removed the weariness of prayer and prayer lightened the continual exercise of work. [Col. 0774B]

Only at evening and night times did they chant psalms solemnly together; and after the nocturnal *synaxis*, each returned to his cell in complete silence, where he spent what remained of the night in vigils and manual labour. Thus, as was said above, they toiled at work not only by day but also by night, lest at any time they should deviate from their purpose. Indeed, they considered themselves by no means free from blame if, when the rising light of day arrived, they were found sluggish in sleep or idleness. Therefore they awaited the coming of day while awake, and commended their vigils by continual manual work. [Col. 0774C]

For they believed that they attained so much greater a perfection as they strove more fully to forget the things behind; and the constancy of labour made no small contribution to this forgetting, restraining harmful thoughts by suitable strictness. On Saturday and Sunday they assembled together at the third hour for communion; and, having partaken of the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, they required no Mass solemnities during the remaining days of the week.

## Chapter LXXXI

[Col. 0774D] For at that time it was not their custom either to celebrate Masses frequently or to promote monks everywhere to holy orders. In a monastery scarcely one or two exercised the priestly office, and these nevertheless appeared more worthy than the rest of such an office. Thus bishops and the other rulers of the Church allowed this to be done and mercifully met their needs: because they could not keep clerical priests among themselves to celebrate the ministry of the altar, they promoted some monk to orders, lest they lack the ministry of the saving sacrifice, and lest those who had chosen, for Christ’s sake and removed from the crowd, to dwell in solitudes should there be compelled either to pass their present life without Christ’s sacrament or to end it more perilously. [Col. 0775A]

Much later, when the renown of the same order had spread through almost the whole world and monasteries of monks had been built through many cities, towns, fortified places, and villages, the former custom nevertheless remained: namely, that very few among them celebrated Masses, and that they celebrated them not publicly but privately—that is, for themselves, not for the people. For their office was not to stand at the altar to celebrate the divine mystery; they were permitted to do this for the sake of receiving communion, lest they lack the saving ministry. Therefore only a few among them were permitted to be raised to holy orders, and it was not customary to summon the people to their Masses. This was properly assigned to the order of clerics, upon whom the care not only of the people but also of monks had been imposed. [Col. 0775B]

If anyone finds it incredible to hear this asserted concerning monks because he sees it somewhat changed in our times, let him read—or read again—more carefully the writings of the ancient Fathers, and without doubt he will prove it true and, his murmuring silenced, will agree with our assertions. So few among them were formerly accustomed to be promoted to holy orders that, although a monastery was often known to contain many monks, scarcely one, as was said above, was found among the others to exercise the office of priesthood in celebrating the divine mystery.

## Chapter LXXXII

It is found in the Register that the community of monks established in the monastery of Praecoritanum required the service of a priest for carrying out the sacred solemnities of Mass. [Col. 0775C] It therefore humbly asked Pope Gregory to allow one of its monks to be ordained, so that the sacred solemnities of Mass might be celebrated there by him. Pope Gregory kindly agreeing to this petition, deigned to admonish Victor, bishop of Panormus, in whose bishopric the same monastery was situated, that he should set aside delay and hasten to fulfil the monks’ desire, which plainly concerned their religious purpose and the salvation of souls. That is, he should promote to ordination the man whom the monks, unanimously, should offer from their own community for consecration, “so that,” to use Gregory’s own words, “the community which asks that he be ordained for them may, as often as necessary, be refreshed by celebrating the solemnity of the sacrifice with due reverence.”  
[Note: [Col. 0775D] St Gregory, *Register*, book IX, indiction II, epistle 92; *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVII, col. 1018.]

Urbicus also, abbot of the monastery of Saint Herma, situated at Panormus, since the community of monks with him had no priest among them, petitioned the same blessed Gregory; and Gregory ordered the aforesaid Victor, bishop of Panormus, by written instruction to ordain one of them priest. For he says: “We have judged it necessary by these present letters to exhort your Fraternity that he who shall be selected from that community for this ministry, whose life, conduct, and manner of action can be fitting for so great a ministry, ought, with the Lord’s help, to be consecrated without delay, so that he need neither leave his monastery for this reason nor be compelled to bring in a stranger for performing the sacred work.”  
[Note: [Col. 0775D] From the same *Register*, book VI, indiction XIV, epistle [Col. 0776D] 42, col. 830.]

You see that in the monastery of Praecoritanum or of Panormus Pope Gregory permits one monk to be promoted to holy orders, so that, as often as necessary, the community may be refreshed by celebrating the solemnity of the sacrifice and may not need to employ an outside priest for performing the sacred work.

## Chapter LXXXIII

That it was not their custom to celebrate public Masses, but in a sense private ones—that is, not solemnly to summon the people to them—was clearly made known by Gregory himself, who sharply rebuked Felix, bishop of Pisaurum, for transgressing this ancient custom. Speaking of a monastery of monks built by a certain John and dedicated by the aforesaid bishop Felix, he says: “As has come to our attention, a chair having been set up, the sacred solemnities of Mass are publicly celebrated there. If this is true, we exhort you in these words that, setting aside every excuse, you have your chair removed from there by every means and do not again celebrate public Masses there.”

Lest blessed Gregory should appear unwilling for monks to live there, where he so strictly forbids the celebration of public Masses, he adds: “But in the same monastery we wish, by God’s grace, that the community of servants of God should remain as it now is.” And lest he should seem altogether to deny them, while remaining there, the consolation of Mass, he took care to remove this inconvenience from them more diligently: “If,” he says, “they wish Masses to be celebrated there for themselves, let a priest be sent by you.”  
[Note: [Col. 0776D] St Gregory, *Register*, book VI, indiction XIV, epistle 46, col. 832.]

“For themselves,” therefore—that is, for the monks, not for the people—he permits Masses to be celebrated there: private, not public Masses. And because perhaps they did not have a priest, he allows one to be delegated there by the bishop: “If they wish Masses to be celebrated there for themselves, let a priest be sent by you.” Thus Gregory wished monks to be removed from the concourse of the people, so that they might not be joined to them in any way even on the occasion of Masses; lest, perhaps, by usurping an office foreign to themselves, they should decline with secular persons toward secular matters. [Col. 0776D]

For he knew that it did not at all belong to their order to endeavour to govern peoples; and therefore he wished them so to exercise what had been granted them that they should in no way presume to aspire to what was not due. Accordingly, when the same Gregory knew that a certain church of Saint Pancras, entrusted to clerics to celebrate Mass there and minister by performing divine rites to the people who duly gathered there, was declining for the worse through clerical negligence—and that, at the appointed hour, the clerics were not found there and the people returned home complaining—[Col. 0777A] he wished to entrust it to a neighbouring monastery of monks and to assign its revenues henceforth for the monks’ use, in such a way that the abbot of the monastery should thereafter be considered the overseer of the same church, while he should appoint there for the performance of the sacred work not a monk but a clerical priest.

The former clerics, who gladly received from it their temporal maintenance, did not adequately repay the gathering people with spiritual provision. He therefore wished to transfer the temporal benefit to religious men, so that, with them providing more diligent care, the Church might no longer suffer loss. Yet because public Masses had to be celebrated in that church, since the people regularly gathered there to hear the sacred office, the same pope wished the abbot to take care to employ there not a monk but a clerical priest, whose duty it was to instruct the people both by word and example. Thus he says to Abbot Maurus:  
[Note: [Col. 0777D] Epistle 18 from the Register of Lord Gregory, book III, indiction XII, chapter 18.]

“We decree that the lands of the aforesaid church, whatever may enter into it, and whatever may accrue from its revenues, shall be assigned to your monastery and belong to it there without any diminution; provided, however, that whatever must be done or repaired in that church shall undoubtedly be done and repaired by you. But lest, with the priests removed, to whom that church had formerly been entrusted, it should appear to be without the mysteries, we therefore command you by the tenor of this authority that you do not cease to employ there a visiting priest who can celebrate the sacred solemnities of Mass, so that henceforth no neglect may be found in the aforesaid church.” [Col. 0777C]

It is clear that Gregory, who wishes ecclesiastical benefices to be transferred to monks because of the clerics’ neglect, nevertheless does not wish to confer upon them the additional office of presuming to celebrate public Masses before the people, but rather wishes to reserve that as proper to clerics.

## Chapter LXXXIV

Therefore, because monks celebrated Masses only for themselves and not for the people, few at that time aspired to holy orders; and at an earlier time far fewer still, although they were then stronger in monastic strictness. When the virgin Marina, still a little child, was brought by her monk-father to a monastery of monks and, her being a girl concealed, was made a monk with them; when, having been brought up there from childhood and instructed in sacred letters, she was regarded as of marvellous holiness and marvellous patience, and until, in mature age, she ended her life in death, it remained wholly unknown that she was a woman—then, I think, it was not customary for monks in monasteries to be ordained so generally as we see done in our time. For it is not credible that one who both lived among monks for so long a time and was proved to possess such holiness and patience would either, when called to orders, presume stubbornly to recoil from the command, or, forgetting her female sex, presume by unlawful daring to obey such a command.

[Col. 0778A] Eugenia likewise, a virgin, burning with the ardour of the divine Spirit and shrinking from the broad way of secular life, desired the narrow path of living. She laid aside female dress and, being thought a man, entered a monastery of men, where she became not only a monk but, in time, abbot of the monks. Who, then, could believe that such a monk—indeed, such an abbot—was raised to holy orders, performed the divine mysteries, and ministered at the sacred altars? For not just any ordained priest was sought to govern monks, but one formed in good conduct, who would strive to benefit the other brothers by religion, learning, and the example of his whole monastic life, rather than to preside over them by the eminence of the priesthood.

Finally, that blessed [Col. 0778B] Benedict, who built many monasteries of monks, who formed monks to the last detail by his life and writings, and who left to posterity a praiseworthy memorial of his holiness by providing no slight instruction for regular living, is not recorded to have been a priest; nor is he thought to have lacked anything of monastic dignity. For, seeing that the aforesaid promotion to holy orders does not make a monk, but rather self-abasement, labour, silence, discipline, stillness, and religion, Benedict did not think that he inflicted any injury upon the monastic profession if he strove to surpass the monks not in holy orders but in holy conduct.

But because the rulers of the Church, although they did not confer this as a matter of obligation, nevertheless granted it freely—namely, that [Col. 0778C] monks should exercise holy orders, lest, being removed from the people, they should appear also to be removed from the saving sacrifice—this permission is found to have grown so greatly in our times that now in monasteries one can scarcely find not only an abbot but even any monk who does not see himself promoted to orders. Moreover, many who receive holy orders in the clerical profession, leaving clerical service, pass over to monastic life for the sake of quiet; and although they cease to be clerics, their orders are nevertheless not taken from them. Thus, just as those who had not possessed orders are permitted to receive them, so those who previously possessed them are permitted to retain them.

Thus, although distinction by holy orders is in a certain sense proper to clerics, for the reasons [Col. 0778D] we have stated it was transferred also to the monastic order, so that, as Gregory says, when necessary, the community may be refreshed by celebrating the solemnity of the saving sacrifice, and it may not be necessary to employ an outside priest for performing this work. Nor should clerics take it ill that this office has been conferred upon monks, since they see that it has not been taken from themselves; and though it has been mercifully granted to the latter, nothing of the former dignity has been diminished for the clerics. Even if some either will not or cannot perceive the dignity of clerics, their blindness does not obscure the truth; rather, when it is closed to those who have failed through pride or negligence, it is opened to others who have advanced in humility and learning. [Col. 0779A]

## CHAPTER LXXXV

But as to ecclesiastical revenues being transferred to the use of monks, and monks being maintained contrary to the original institution not by the labour of their hands: with your leave, clerics, I shall say that it seems to me that your worldliness brought this about, and your laxity bestowed this benefit upon them. For because, despising the churches to which you especially ought to have rendered service, and neglecting the people by whose offerings you lived in temporal matters, you declined through corrupt conduct into the pursuit of transitory things, and in harmful blindness preferred not so much what is lacking as what belongs to the world: it seemed good to blessed Gregory and the other shepherds of the Church that the temporal revenues of churches should be transferred to [Col. 0779B] religious men, so that churches might be governed more diligently and holily through their watchful care.

There is also another reason why ecclesiastical revenues are transferred to monks and what had been proper to clerics is granted for their use. When the monastic order was no longer content with suburbs and solitudes, but, as its numbers increased, occupied cities and towns, forts and villages, many delicate persons flocked to it for the sake of conversion. Hindered by frailty of body and mind, they could by no means maintain the former rigour. With reins loosened, both because of the surrounding populace among whom they lived and because of the aforesaid weakness from which they chiefly suffered, they abandoned the manual labour which their predecessors had maintained; dwelling in cloisters, they preferred to lie concealed more loosely under the shade of rest and leisure. [Col. 0779C]

Observing this, the doctors of the Church did not fail even such persons, but mercifully met their infirmities, so that those who could not or would not satisfy the former purpose might at least accomplish, in a more indulgent manner, the good that they desired. Therefore, lest, freed from manual labour, they should either wholly withdraw from the monastic profession because of poverty or entangle themselves in secular business for the sake of passing sustenance, the pastors of the Church allowed them to be supported from church revenues, so that, relieved of anxiety concerning provisions, they might occupy themselves more freely with divine reading.

Thus Pope Gregory rebukes Abbot John and the monks with him because they presumed to receive church revenues for their own use, yet devoted their attention to idle leisure rather than to the work of reading. For he says:

> [Note: [Col. 0779D] Extract from the Register of Lord Gregory, Book II, indiction X, chapter 42.] “Among the very brothers of your monastery whom I see, I find none occupied with reading. Hence it is necessary to consider how great a sin it is that God has sent you sustenance from another’s offering, while you neglect to learn God’s commandments.”

Therefore, although monks deserved to obtain ecclesiastical revenues for the reasons stated, some of them in the course of time undertook to possess so much that, having amassed riches—which true religion is always known to have abhorred—they [Col. 0780A] seem to have forgotten poverty, which it is certain was formerly familiar to this order. This poverty, indeed, is found to have given birth to this order; in her bosom or lap she nourished it with spiritual food, and, having brought it up from the rags of infancy, led it to its due age and strength, so that it seemed to lack nothing for the summit of perfection.

Yet when it had acquired strength, the same order seemed to curse poverty, judging nothing more intolerable than to be constrained longer by her laws. And her whom it had possessed as mother and nurse through the benefit of spiritual love, it persecutes as an enemy, as though she were to be accused of stepmotherly hatred. Not judging it enough to be sustained in moderate measure by granted benefices, it hastens in rivalry to accumulate riches and honours, not considering [Col. 0780B] how great an injury it does to holiness while with such effort it renounces poverty.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI

But some monks, seeing themselves richer than clerics, think themselves no less more worthy; and, darkened by the cloud of presumption, they imagine that those whom they surpass by a certain appearance of holiness they also surpass in the eminence of dignity. Therefore, when they compass sea and land to make one proselyte, when they exhort someone living a secular life to become a monk, they entice him with such flatteries as these: they say that their order is worthier than other orders and that monastic life is second to none, but higher than all in rank and merits.

“If you desire conversion,” they say, “you will do better to join us and to incline your ear more suitably to our counsels. It is not our advice [Col. 0780C] that you should enter another order, since you cannot attain one more exalted than ours. Our order is plainly found worthier than the others; this path of life is surpassed by no shortcut. Therefore, if you wish to find worthy advancement, know that you cannot elsewhere ascend to so perfect a rank. No one can be raised higher,” they say, “than by becoming a monk, since this order is considered worthier and more exalted than the rest, and clerical dignity, which presides over the lower orders, is in no way equal to our sublimity.”
