By these and similar assertions some monks exalt themselves when they wish to draw the minds of their hearers to themselves. They lead not only the ignorance of ordinary laypeople into such an opinion, [Col. 0780D] but compel some clerics also to think it. For to many clerics whom fullness of learning does not enlighten, this claim of the monks now seems true; and because they see little holiness both in themselves and in other clerics, they accordingly think the clerics’ dignity slight. Both parties, it seems, deserve no slight rebuke; both must be more carefully instructed in knowledge of the truth, lest, if through their negligence the truth be unknown to them, they incur what God threatens such persons through Solomon:

> “Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women, go forth after the tracks of the flocks and feed your kids” (Song of Songs 1).

For one who lacks due knowledge of truth—what does he do except feed and foster the impurity of falsehood, turning over and over within himself, in wandering error, either that what is false is true or, conversely, that what is true is false? In such persons you will find neither simplicity of thought nor purity of deeds; rather, you will see the disorderly impulses of wanton presumption running riot, while, wrapped in darkness, a man either does not consider what order he belongs to or does not carefully weigh what dignity that order possesses. [Col. 0781A]

It is good for a person to know both the order in which he is established and the appointed goal or limit of that order, so that he may neither presumptuously leap beyond fixed bounds nor, retreating short of them, feebly fall away from them. For if anyone happens to remain either beyond or short of definite limits, he cannot perform rightly what is right; since, when knowledge—which is the foundation of every perfect work—is darkened, the work itself suffers no slight loss.

Hence, in a certain historian the noble Metellus is praised, commendable not so much for birth as for prudence, because he ordered his army properly and in no way allowed that order to be confused. “He would make the rounds of the watches with the legates; likewise, in a march, he would be present now among the foremost, now among the rearmost, often in the middle, lest anyone depart from his rank.” [Col. 0781B] This man, skilled in war, saw that he would not easily gain victory if his army did not hold its due order: if confusion arose between noble and common soldiers; if infantry were improperly mixed with cavalry or cavalry with infantry; if superiors declined downward through degrading abasement or inferiors presumptuously occupied the place of superiors.

The prudent Boethius also seems to bear witness to this, saying that what abandons a fixed order has no happy outcome:

> “That which abandons a fixed order has no happy outcomes.”

Therefore a certain poet also gives this careful warning:

> “Let every particular thing hold fittingly the place allotted to it.” —Horace

Finally, to come to our own writings: when Isaiah commended the simplicity of certain persons, he did not leave unmentioned the dignity of order joined to that simplicity, knowing that the simplicity of the innocent is not sufficiently adorned unless it is suitably ordered:

> “And the lambs shall feed according to their order” (Isaiah 5). [Col. 0781D]

He beautifully says that lambs feed according to their order, because simplicity finds the pasture of saving nourishment when, turning aside to neither hand, it holds to the straightness of the regular path. Then it does not abandon its shepherd and guide upon the way, when through insolence it does not forsake the appointed boundary. Hence Scripture chose to call those who feed according to order not kids but lambs, because a kid, a wanton animal, does not know how to restrain its unruly impulses. Ignorant of order, in the heat of wandering desire it loves to roam through slopes and heights, so that, separated from the fellowship of the lambs, it may at last deserve to be placed at the left hand. [Col. 0782A]

Therefore the Lord commands through Moses in Numbers, chapter 2, that the children of Israel should march in order: “Each one,” he says, “shall set out according to his place and his order.” Let no one, then, doubt that each person ought to act according to his order and be formed in deeds and conduct according to his order. For every action regularly conformed to its own order is terrible as an army drawn up in battle array. Therefore the Apostle says: “Let all things among you be done honourably and according to order” (1 Corinthians 14). The Apostle fittingly wished that what was honourably done should also be done according to order, because in our works there is no due appearance of honourableness unless both the truth of order and the order of truth are maintained in them.

But how do we do all things according to order if we do not even know order itself? If, through mistaken judgement, we deem what ought to be preferred to be postponed, and conversely falsely assert that what ought to be postponed should be preferred? Does not she in the Song of Songs who loves ask for love to be ordered within her, lest, if she embraces later what ought to be loved first, [Col. 0782B] or considers what ought to be judged more worthy as more unworthy and vile, she deserve to be accused of error because the order of love is confused?

> “Order love in me” (Song of Songs 2).

It is therefore good for both cleric and monk to know what dignity his order possesses and what holiness each ought to possess in his own order, lest he recklessly presume to arrogate to his own order or another’s more or less than is just, but may know and willingly assign humbly to each what belongs to it. [Col. 0782C]

If monks think themselves worthier than clerics because, as stated above, they see themselves much richer—their churches more lavishly adorned with gold, gems, and silk, their tables heaped with many and varied dishes, and themselves prospering temporally in the other matters which it would be lengthy and superfluous to recount—there is no doubt that this judgement deserves rejection, since no dignity ought to be estimated according to the measure of riches. For who would grant that the richer a man is, the worthier he is, when we see many subjects overflowing with abundance of riches, while prelates are worn down by poverty, whether unwilling or voluntary?

But if they wish to establish themselves as worthier on the ground that perhaps they are somewhat holier—since clerics, abusing looser reins, appear to mingle in secular affairs, whereas monks, restrained by tighter cords, are confined beneath cloistered rule—I do not think that for this reason it should be granted them that, setting the former aside, greater deference should be paid to their order. For although the holiness of clerics is weakened, their dignity is not thereby annulled; and the dignity of an order is not to be judged according to its members’ morals, since the degree of dignity does not depend upon the quality of life. Great and splendid holiness is indeed enjoined upon this dignity, but it is not so inseparably joined to it that, if holiness should decline through someone’s corrupt impulse, the excellence of the dignity itself must necessarily collapse. [Col. 0783A]

Monks therefore ought not to be deemed worthier than clerics because they see the holiness of clerics somewhat weakened; for greater holiness cannot obtain the privilege of taking precedence over a greater order in the Church. Otherwise, if it were fixed and immovable in the present Church that the holier person must be considered worthier than the less holy, not only would a monk now be preferred to a cleric, but a peasant to a priest; less reverence would be paid to the teacher and much more to the disciple. For we often find greater holiness in a peasant than in a priest, yet we do not attribute to him greater dignity. Indeed, although the peasant is more to be imitated by us because of his merit of life, nevertheless the priest is more to be revered by us because of the dignity of his order.

To go higher: when we see one bishop ordained over many thousands of people so that the present Church may be governed through his teaching, who would despair that somewhere in a corner of a city there may be found a commoner better than the bishop in the merit of holiness? Yet who would presume to say that this commoner—whom perhaps even the bishop himself does not doubt to be holier—is worthier than his bishop? Because the priestly or episcopal dignity with which the bishop is distinguished is greater than the popular order in which that commoner is found, the bishop is rightly judged worthier and more exalted, even though that commoner’s holiness is greater. Thus a king is said to possess greater dignity than a soldier and a soldier than a peasant, though one of lesser rank sometimes surpasses one of greater rank in the merit of holiness. [Col. 0783B]

## CHAPTER LXXXVII

That greater deference ought to be paid to the higher order has been judged both by pagan and ecclesiastical writers, who transmitted it in writings to posterity lest forgetfulness erase it. When Gnaeus Pompey presided over the Roman empire and held the city and fatherland by royal power, what subject did not show him reverence? What soldier did not render him fuller deference according to his place and rank? But when, defeated by Julius Caesar, he had abandoned the Roman forces and, stripped of assistance and with hope lost, fled as an exile to foreign nations, and finally lost his life by poison, Julius obtained that empire, and the supreme government and royal power were transferred to him. [Col. 0783C]

When Prince Antigonus approached him in Syria, he began vehemently to complain about Antipater, alleging that Antipater violently took certain things from him. In order to stir Caesar’s anger against Antipater and more easily incline Caesar himself toward his own side, he began indirectly to cast against Antipater the charge of friendship with Gnaeus Pompey, to whom Antipater had familiarly rendered military service. But Antipater did not fear to answer before Caesar what was true, and by a prudent answer to remove the slander cast against him:

> “He charges me with Pompey’s favour. I confess, Caesar, that I was a friend not to the man, but to the Roman name.”

The pagan understood well that greater deference must be given to the greater name. Therefore, as long as he knew Pompey to be exalted by the royal name, he did not neglect humbly to render him the service due. But when he knew the royal power and name had passed to Julius Caesar, he did not refuse to submit to him with the same reverence. Thus the prudent pagan rendered deference not to the man but to the name, since he knew that the office-name, not its individual bearer, was to be preferred above others. [Col. 0784A]

Likewise, in Holy Scripture Hushai the Archite declares that this ought to be done when David was driven out and his son Absalom was exalted, though only briefly, both in royal position and in royal name. When Absalom anxiously asked Hushai why he had not gone with David his lord, Hushai answered Absalom:

> “By no means; for I shall belong to him whom the Lord has chosen” (2 Kings 16).

That is, as though he said: If the Lord has chosen you to reign, I know and acknowledge that greater deference must be given to you.

When the Apostle Peter urged the faithful to render reverence to superiors, he commended in those superiors not so much holiness as excellence of dignity:

> “Be subject for God’s sake to every human creature, whether to the king as pre-eminent, or to governors as sent by him” (1 Peter 2). [Col. 0784B]

He did not say, “to the king as holier,” or “to governors as holier,” but, “to the king as pre-eminent, or to governors as sent by him.” By this he plainly teaches that those whom God sends to rule others ought indeed to receive deference because of the excellence of their dignity, even if a fully worthy pattern of holiness does not shine in them. For if inferiors disdain to be subject to superiors, they are undoubtedly proved to resist God himself, as the Apostle Paul says:

> “Every authority is from God; and those that are, have been ordained by God. Therefore he who resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Romans 13).

Paul does not say here, “He who resists holiness,” but, “He who resists authority resists God’s ordinance,” lest anyone, sheltered under a show of whatever holiness, presume to despise the lofty rank of a superior. [Col. 0784C]

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII

Finally, if an order itself is judged inferior because of lesser holiness, who does not see that the same judgement is turned back upon monks, and that their order then suffers the loss of honour from which they draw an argument against the clerical order? For just as in the clerical order it is easy to find many whose conduct and actions seem not to accord with their order, so too in the monastic order there are perhaps some who, though monks in dress, are not monks in conduct. If anyone calls me rash because I dare even whisper about the morals of monks—for it seems presumptuous to censure the lives of better men—I shall bring forward holy men who burned not with the poison of envy but with zeal for justice, and who, burning in spirit, did not fear to rebuke monks.

Gregory and Jerome, who are known to have flourished in life and learning, who we know to have been monks both in fact and in name, and who loved the monastic order as was fitting, did not keep silent about the faults of monks, either through excessive fear or harmful affection. [Col. 0784D]

Pope Gregory, rebuking Abbot Urbicus and the monks with him, says:

> “I see how the rule of the monastery has been relaxed, since the monks of the same monastery were not prepared to obey you, nor were you then able steadfastly to arrange anything; and I groan deeply because I find your monastery otherwise than I had thought.”

Speaking to Abbot John, he says:

> “The reputation of the monastery has been defiled through your negligence.”

He writes also to Abbot Valentinus:

> “It has reached us that women commonly enter your monastery; and, what is more serious, that your monks make women their spiritual co-mothers and thereby have with them an incautious intimacy.”

Likewise, to the subdeacon Anthemius:

> “We have learned that some monks have gone so far into such wickedness as publicly to take wives.”

And to all the monks dwelling on the Mount of Christ he says:

> “It has reached us that you observe none of the precepts of the monastic rule.” [Col. 0785A]

Secunderinus, a monk who, after the carnal lapse into which he had fallen, ought to have restrained himself more strictly than usual under regular discipline and blotted out the stain of dreadful incest by mourning and tears, nevertheless did not fear to promote himself to the office and rank of abbot and to sit with rash daring in the teacher’s chair. Gregory, indignant, ordered this Secunderinus, forgetful of his grave offence, to be deposed and Theodosius substituted in his place.

In these and many other passages, too numerous to collect, Pope Gregory—himself a monk—vehemently accuses monks. Burning with zeal for justice, he does not excuse their laxity because of likeness of order; indeed, the more tenderly he embraces the monastic order to which he himself belongs, the more fiercely he hurls the sharp darts of deserved rebuke against monastic offences. [Col. 0785B]

## CHAPTER LXXXIX

So too Jerome—indeed, far more so—abhors the insolence of monks and is implacably indignant against them, seeing that the monastic order lamentably complains because it endures many destroyers within its own walls. Thus, above all others, he rebukes Jovinian, whose name he says is derived from the idol Jupiter. He did not allow him long to boast in noble phrases, but crushed him with worthy invectives, plainly demonstrated to all that his teaching was false, and by holy and evangelical discourse recalled the minds of the faithful from the erroneous following of his sect.

Jovinian, having assumed the monastic habit and displayed to the eyes of simple people an appearance of religion, became such an enemy of all holiness and such a plunderer of chastity that he was proved the foulest imitator of Jupiter, from whom he had drawn his name. For just as, in secular literature, Jupiter is found to overflow with the streams of lust and, as an impure lover, to overcome many virgins with deceitful persuasions, so our monk, burning with a new heresy and overflowing with poisonous doctrine, shakes the citadel of virginity and the precious walls of continence. [Col. 0785C] He teaches that virginity ought not to be praised—indeed, that its barrenness ought deservedly to be condemned according to its merits—and that carnal union is to be approved much more justly and much more highly, without which the human race cannot be propagated.

O monastic monster! O monstrous monk! His unheard-of doctrine is so perverse that this novel assertion seems deserving of rejection not only by Catholics but even by pagans. For I do not think that anyone is so educated in the erroneous doctrines of pagans, or that anyone among them is so perverse, as to dare either to think or to agree with a monk who thinks that marriage is to be preferred to virginal integrity and carnal intercourse to continence. Indeed, even if someone either does not care or lacks the strength to abstain from such embraces, he nonetheless thinks, and does not deny, that continence is of greater merit. [Col. 0786A]

Finally, in the temple of Vesta—whom their writings affirm to have been a virgin—and in which a perpetual fire was kept, no women except consecrated virgins were permitted to serve, so that all things alike might accord with the merit of holiness. For what is more fitting than that in the temple of a virgin a perpetual fire should shine, and that the luminous virginity of nuns should correspond to that perpetual brightness? As fire shines more than the other elements, yet nothing is generated from it, so virginity, though sterile, should be preferred to fruitful embraces.

Therefore, if any virgin consecrated to Vesta’s service was convicted, after the light of virginity had been extinguished, of being violated, she was lowered into an excavated pit up to her breasts and, before all who watched, was compelled there to die as her deeds deserved. What else did they intend to signify by this punishment except that one who presumed to judge sexual union preferable to virginity did not fly upward to heaven on the wings of virtues with the sterile fire, but, cast down into fertile earth, added himself to the number of earthly things and made himself fruitful? The pagans thought better than our monk about continence: they wished Vestal nuns to be virgins only; and, though through erroneous superstition they paid divine honours to Jupiter, they did not judge his incontinence to be imitated. [Col. 0786B]

## CHAPTER XC

In this matter Jovinian seems to agree with Jupiter himself: what Jupiter delights to do, Jovinian does not neglect to praise. The emissions of the loins by which Jupiter does not shrink from defiling the titles of his divinity, this man, uncircumcised in heart and lips, is not ashamed to proclaim preferable to angelic celibacy.

> “And what wonder if such a thing is asserted in his preaching, since it is written, ‘Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks’?” (Luke 6).

From a muddy spring no clear stream can flow, nor can a sweet fragrance exhale from a foul bilge. Such as is the monk’s life, such is his preaching made known; and he who ought to have been the good fragrance of Christ is corrupted, to corrupt others by the error of a depraved doctrine. But Jerome comes forward and shows that the doctrine of a monk whose luxurious way of life is condemned is not sufficiently approved. [Col. 0786C]

For his conduct was so perverse and so opposed to the monastic profession that no fitting devotion lay concealed in it, nor did any holy or imitable practice appear outwardly. For, as Jerome says:

> [Note: [Col. 0787D] Book I against Jovinian.] “Though he boasts that he is a monk, after a filthy tunic, bare feet, bread for food, and water for drink, he has betaken himself to white garments and a polished skin, to sweet wine and carefully prepared meats, to Apicius’ sauces and *paxamates*, to baths and rubdowns, and to taverns. It is most plain that he prefers earth to heaven, vices to virtues, and gold to Christ; and yet this handsome monk is fat, sleek, whitened, and always walks as though a bridegroom,” and so forth.

In these words Jerome shows plainly enough what becomes and what does not become a monk, while at the same time severely rebuking Jovinian on both grounds: because he disgracefully cast aside what properly befitted him as his own, and no less reprehensibly adopted what was unfitting to the monastic profession. When he says that, after a filthy tunic, bread for food, water for drink, and the rest of that sort, Jovinian betook himself to white garments, a polished skin, prepared meats, Apicius’ sauces and *paxamates*, baths, rubdowns, and taverns—and became a handsome, fat, sleek, whitened monk—Jerome clearly indicates what way of life he judges holy, honourable, [Col. 0787A] and regular for a monk, and what way of life he judges devoid of religion, forgetful of its profession, secular in reality rather than merely in name.

He wishes, I think, that the monk’s tunic should display the dirtiness of poverty, and that food and drink should display the sober frugality of abstinence, so that contempt for the world may be shown through the meanness of dress, and flight from carnal enticements proved through moderation in food. On the contrary, Jovinian, and perhaps those who love to imitate Jovinian, judge it intolerable to be disfigured by poor clothing; and in the monastic habit, however much it bears an appearance of holiness, they nevertheless seek the luxuries of vanity. They wish indeed that their clothing may display an appearance of religion, but that the same garment may nonetheless be soft, delicate, and rather becoming, lest either its roughness afflict tender flesh or its cheapness shame a mind swollen with glory. [Col. 0787B]

But true religion does not know how to pursue such luxuries or glory. It delights to glory not in a carefully arranged garment but in the cross set before it, striving truly to imitate the Apostle Paul in this matter. Paul does not rejoice in being soothed by delicate clothing, but in being crucified with Christ’s sufferings:

> “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6).

And to the Romans:

> “We glory in tribulations” (Romans 5).

And to the Philippians:

> “Even if I am poured out as an offering, I rejoice and congratulate you” (Philippians 2).

And to the Colossians:

> “I rejoice in sufferings” (Colossians 1).

You see Paul glorying in the cross and in sufferings, not rejoicing in soft and delicate clothing, in accordance with the saying of a certain wise man:

> “Never glory in clothing” (Ecclesiasticus 11). [Col. 0787C]

If, Scripture forbidding it, no one at all ought to glory in clothing, how much more detestable does it appear in a monk, if in the habit which he assumes to show humbly his voluntary poverty, he seeks luxury or the vanity of secular glory? Hence Jerome writes to Rusticus:

> “If you wish to be a monk, let the dirtiness of your clothes be an indication of a pure mind; let a cheap tunic prove contempt for the world.”

And Pope Gregory says:

> “What is a monk’s habit except contempt for the world?”

Accordingly, Jerome rebuked the monk Jovinian, who, having cast aside the religious dirtiness of the monastic tunic, shone in luxurious clothes, and desired to be called a monk while abhorring everything regularly appropriate to a monk. [Col. 0787D]

Nor does Jerome show him only in dress as a despiser of the poverty he professed; in diet also he shows him forgetful of due frugality. Having fallen headlong through greedy desire to prepared meats, exotic sauces, rubdowns, taverns, and baths, Jovinian, he says, attained a sleek complexion, comeliness of face, and immoderate fatness:

> “This handsome monk, fat, sleek, whitened.”

Jerome does not think it belongs to a religious monk to strive to shine in bodily beauty, to swell with fatness through serving elaborate kinds of dishes, or to immerse himself in the excessive vapours of baths in order to nourish that same fatness. [Col. 0788A]

## CHAPTER XCI

Finally, in secular literature certain persons are said to refuse baths when they wished to claim for themselves the name of poets, knowing that those who crave the effeminate softness of bath treatments are unworthy of the honour or the name of poets.

> “A good part of mankind,” he says, “does not care to trim its nails,”

“Does not trim his beard, seeks secluded places, shuns the baths.” (Horace, *The Art of Poetry*, 297.) If, then, a man seeks solitude because he wishes to be freer for writing poems, if he refuses the baths because he wishes to seem a poet or philosopher, who could patiently endure a monk’s indulging in the luxuries of baths, so that, unable to bear solitude, he may appear more polished in the eyes of onlookers? Can false superstition exert greater power among pagan philosophers than the religion of truth among monks, so that what the former do not consider burdensome to endure for human favour, the latter endure for the sake of holiness—or perhaps do not endure at all? For although, in food or baths, whatever necessity requires is mercifully allowed to a religious man, excess is nevertheless most emphatically forbidden, because suitable moderation sustains nature’s need, while unsuitable excess produces unbecoming corpulence. Therefore the Apostle says: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” [Rom. 13]. And our Augustine, when establishing a rule of life for religious clerics, says: “The bathing of the body, when required by the necessity of illness, is by no means to be denied.” And the aforementioned Jerome, writing to the monk Rusticus: “Do not seek the comforts of baths, you who desire to extinguish bodily heat by the rigor of fasts.”

What, therefore, is granted to necessity is undoubtedly denied to pleasure; and holy men do not wish one who professes to become religious to be fattened with meats and fried dishes, taverns and baths. Indeed, Jerome says against Vigilantius that the monk has the office of one who mourns. But a monk who is plainly so diligent in nourishing his body does not seem to perform this office, since religious sorrow does not know how to nourish corpulence, but to put it to sleep through fasts and labours. For there is no one who has not learned, either from his own experience or from the unquestionable testimony of those who have experienced it, that spiritual meditation, religious devotion, and frequent weeping do not allow bodily bulk to expand beyond due measure, but, when these are present, constrain it within proper bounds.

For these aforesaid practices take to themselves abstinence, fasts, vigils, and labour, by which they press down and suppress the pleasures and swelling of the flesh; and whatever overflowing fat they find in it, they fry in the pan of heavenly discipline. Indeed, that workshop of spiritual pursuits, in which what we call heavenly discipline flourishes, does not allow even a stout man to remain long within its bounds—provided, however, that he proves tractable enough to be formed by rule. Whoever, then, you see to be fat, either has not yet entered the aforesaid workshop, or perhaps refuses there to undergo fitting discipline; for immoderate bodily corpulence cannot agree with the fires and hammerings applied by the spiritual furnace, hammer, and anvil.

For who would believe that a man is kindled to the marrow by divine fire, suffused with continual mourning and tears, afflicted by abstinence and fasts, worn down by vigils and labours, if his face swells with fat like a bee stung by its barbs, and his belly grows large like a sack packed with goods? Such fatness surely does not smell of that spiritual occupation—labour, vigils, abstinence, fasting—but, to speak truthfully, of satiety, abundance, and idleness. Thus also, in Ezekiel, the city of Sodom is rebuked: having cast off the rigours of virtues, it fell into the enticements of vices; refusing to be emaciated by fasts and abstinence, it chose to grow fat through satiety and idleness. “This,” he says, “was the iniquity of Sodom: satiety, abundance, and idleness” [Ezek. 16]. And rightly is that shameless city rebuked on these grounds, because these things are bitter enemies alike to spiritual and bodily chastity; nor is the perfection of mature holiness found where satiety reigns in bodies made fat. Indicating this through Jeremiah, the Lord says: “They have grown fat and sleek, and have most wickedly transgressed my words” [Jer. 5].

## CHAPTER XCII

[Col. 0790A]

It is therefore not credible that, if undue corpulence is found in a monk, due holiness can also be found in him. Rather, the covenant of religion which he pledged with God is annulled, as God declares through Moses in Deuteronomy: “When they have eaten, and are full and grown fat, they shall make my covenant void” [Deut. 31]. And a little later: “The beloved grew fat and kicked” [Deut. 32]. Because the monk has made himself fat by unsuitable satiety, driven by the heat of corpulence he has kicked against the goad of religion; and he who ought to have emaciated his flesh by fasts and abstinence has presumed to annul such a covenant. For, having cast off the yoke or burden of due holiness, he wanders as a vagrant over the plains and byways of pleasure; and setting aside those serious matters that compel a contrite heart frequently to water its face with tears, he prefers, when full, to relax in childish amusements. Hence also in Exodus: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” [Exod. 32].

You see that after the pleasure of food and drink follows the frivolity of play: when fasting and abstinence are banished, abundance of food is accompanied by vanity and dissipation. Thus, in the Book of Judges, Eglon, who is described as exceedingly fat, is also declared king of the Moabites: “Eglon king of Moab was exceedingly fat” [Judg. 3]. *Eglon* is interpreted “round” or “orbital course.” He is aptly called “round” or “orbital course” who, not content with what moderately sustains nature, is swept by unrestrained appetite toward richer foods; and because sameness generally produces disgust, he rolls in a circular course through novel and varied dishes.

Moreover, Scripture significantly affirms that this man, who is shown to make provision for the flesh in its desires with such zeal, is king of the Moabites. *Moabite* is interpreted “flow” and “outpouring.” Such a household is aptly assigned to a fat king, because flabby thoughts and dissolute deeds attend corpulence; and when excess of elaborate eating goes before, Moabites follow in familiar company. But Ehud, the judge of the children of Israel, who used either hand as his right hand—or, according to other interpreters, was ambidextrous—is said to have attacked this same king of Moab with resolute spirit. Drawing a two-edged dagger from his right thigh, he struck the king’s fat belly so powerfully that the hilt followed the iron into the wound and was enclosed by the richest fat.

This Ehud is interpreted “praise.” Such a judge is deservedly called not merely praiseworthy but, emphatically, “praise,” because he is by no means subjected to the fat king whose people are dissolute; rather, such strength of spirit flourishes in him that he pierces the king’s belly, wherein the greater corpulence overflows. As I see it, Jovinian is deservedly compared with King Eglon: he grows fat on meats and taverns, fried dishes and baths; his morals are perverse and his works dissolute, so that such a people seems worthily to have followed his fatness. But the ambidextrous Ehud is rightly understood as Jerome, who attacks the fat monk with the sword of the word of God and so effectually condemns both his life and teaching that none of the faithful is thereafter led into his opinion.

He teaches especially those who profess the monastic life both whom they ought to flee and whom they should profitably imitate: he rebukes Jovinian and his imitators for vanity, and rightly commends himself and those like him for poverty. “The fat, polished, whitened men,” he says, “favour you. All whom I see handsome, all with curled hair, with dressed locks, with ruddy cheeks, are from your herd—indeed, they grunt among your swine. From our flock come men sad, pale, soiled, and as though strangers to this world; though silent in speech, they speak by dress and bearing.”

In these words Jerome shows that a monk who is fat, polished, whitened, handsome, curled, with arranged hair and ruddy cheeks, is not particularly to be commended, but is to be counted among Jovinian’s herd and among the grunting swine. But he who is sad, pale, soiled, and a stranger to this world in bearing and dress—speaking more by these than by speech—is undoubtedly worthy of fellowship with religious persons. In that fellowship it is unfitting that even the slightest trace of vanity should remain; rather, sadness, pallor, and silence should exist only through desire for holiness. Jerome indeed wishes the monk to accustom himself continually to ruminate upon this holiness, not to belch forth the drunken excess of yesterday’s drink.

## CHAPTER XCIII

There was a monk whose name I neither wish nor ought to disclose, especially lest, deceived by error, I name one man in place of another. When he had been buried in wine during the evening and came with the others to celebrate the night synaxis—perhaps more from habit than devotion—he was found to be meditating not so much with fitting devotion on what was being said as repeatedly recalling from memory the drink that had been offered. When the course of psalms had ended and, as usual, they came to read the lesson, and the reader at the lectern requested a blessing, the monk, thinking that drink was being offered him in the customary manner, blessed the reading with the “ninth blessing.”

For when the reader said, “Lord, command the blessing,” he replied: “May the Son of God bless the drink of his servants.” Whom among those standing round did such a blessing fail to shake? Whose laughter did it perhaps fail to draw out, whether secretly or openly—unless indeed one among them was found of such gravity as to attend rather to tears than laughter? Had Jerome happened to be present at this jest, I would not suppose that he would laugh with the others so much as angrily rebuke the thirsty monk, who was bodily present amid sacred psalms and readings while his whole mind was occupied with drinking cups.

We do not say this because we wish to disparage monks or to write something like a satire upon their collected faults, but to restrain somewhat the arrogance of those who, because of the disordered morals of clerics, presume to judge their order inferior. One should not measure the order of either clerics or monks by their morals, since many unsuitable things may be found among both. For just as very great religious devotion plainly shines in many monks, so fitting holiness appears in not a few clerics, who, having left the world—indeed, the harmful vanity that belongs to the world—rejoice to be guided in that truth which is Christ.

Some, abandoning the seductions of secular life, set aside houses, fields, estates, honours, riches, parents, and, greater than all these, the latitude of their own will; they embrace the narrowness of silence, continence, and poverty. Retaining nothing as their own and following Christ, who is perfection, they are found to live under the clerical rule in such a way that in them the apostolic life seems truly restored. They love to devote themselves to spiritual studies, to tame the insolence of the flesh by fasts, vigils, and labours, to be instructed by divine readings, and to be soothed by psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. In short, they are found in every respect such that their holiness deserves to be marked by clerical rank.

If, then, the measure of dignity depends upon the merit of one’s life, let the excellence of these men’s holiness be weighed; and if we happen to find among them persons holier than monks, let us at least not hesitate to call them likewise more worthy. Yet a particular dignity assigned to each order is not so changeable that it is judged now greater, now lesser, according to the merit of those belonging to that order. Rather, he who is presently of lesser holiness before both God and men is often of greater dignity in the present Church. For divine generosity is not so constrained that it must give greater gifts of virtues to those of higher order: we read that Saul, exalted to royal height, was more dignified, while David, dwelling in the pastures, was holier. Holiness is bestowed solely by the grace of a merciful God; dignity, however, is often bestowed by the wrath and judgment of an angered God.

Let monks, therefore, keep for themselves the greater holiness, humbly leaving the greater dignity to clerics; lest by unjustly desiring what they neither ought nor are able to obtain, they may deservedly lose what they seem to possess. Although holiness does not prejudice dignity, nor dignity holiness, their respective pursuits are nevertheless often found to conflict so greatly that those who strive to attain one do not wish to seek the other. For those who truly seek holiness refuse transient dignity; and conversely, those who devote themselves to acquiring dignity inflict no slight injuries upon holiness. Therefore the more worthy are not to be envied, nor are they to be disparaged by their inferiors; rather, they must mercifully be aided by vows and prayers, lest the higher rank by which perhaps an unworthy life is adorned should be regarded not so much as honour that raises up as a burden that weighs down.

I read in a poet a certain little verse saying:

> It is not an honour but a burden; its appearance will harm the bearer.

And our prophet says: “For by raising me up, you dashed me down” [Ps. 101].

## CHAPTER XCIV

[Col. 0793A]

Jerome, therefore, rather plainly maintains that the rank of clerics is more worthy, although he sees the holiness of monks as greater. When he was restraining the first impulses of wanton youth by the harshness of the desert, and earnestly inviting to that same desert Heliodorus, whom he loved, he strove to extol the monastic rank with deserved praises, yet did not hesitate to give clerics precedence in dignity. Writing to Heliodorus, he says: “The case of the monk is one thing, that of clerics another: clerics feed the sheep; I am fed. I may not sit before a presbyter; they, if I sin, may deliver me to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. But if the pious entreaties of the brethren also invite you to that same order, I shall rejoice at your ascent, but fear for your fall.”

More than sufficiently, Jerome’s words declare which dignity is greater: he attests that clerics feed while monks are fed; that the monk ought not sit before the cleric; and that, should he sin, he is subject by the cleric’s authority to destruction of the flesh. Thus, if Heliodorus wishes to be raised to that order, Jerome, as he says, will “rejoice at his ascent” but “fear for his fall,” because he does not envy his friend the greater dignity and regards monastic lowliness as safer.

A little later he accordingly adds, by way of counsel: “Brother, recline lower down; from him to whom more is entrusted, more is required. It is not easy to stand in Paul’s place or hold Peter’s rank. If you are to build a tower, reckon the cost of the future work. If a monk falls, a priest will pray for him; but for the fall of a priest, who will pray?” Likewise, writing to Paulinus: “Let bishops and priests have before them as examples the apostles and apostolic men, and, possessing their honour, strive also to possess their merit. But let us,” he says, “have as leaders of our own profession Paul, Hilarion, Antony, Macarius; and, to return to the authority of Scripture, our leader is Elijah, our Elisha, our guides the sons of the prophets, who dwelt in fields and solitudes.”

You see, on Jerome’s testimony, that the order of monks is lower; if they fall into sin, they rise through the intervention of clerics. Monks have as leaders of their order solitaries and prophets, whereas clerics possess the office and honour of the apostles. The prophets are said to be the leaders of monks because, removed from the crowd of people, they chose to live in solitudes so that there, turning the eye of the mind away from outward things, they might contemplate God more familiarly and freely. Jerome says of them to Rusticus: “The sons of the prophets, whom we read were monks in the Old Testament, built themselves little huts near the streams of the Jordan; abandoning crowds and cities, they lived upon gruel and wild herbs.”

For this reason John the Baptist too is said to be the leader of this order, as is found in the writings of certain Fathers. John Chrysostom says: “As the apostles are leaders of priests, so John the Baptist is leader of monks.” Jerome, writing to Eustochium, says: “I come to the third class, whom they call anchorites; having left the coenobia, they carry nothing further into the desert except bread and salt. Paul was the founder of this life; Antony its illuminator; and, to ascend to higher things, John the Baptist was its leader.” Therefore, as you have heard, John the Baptist is leader of monks, not because he was worthy to baptize Christ, but because he chose to dwell in the desert.

## CHAPTER XCV

For the ministry of baptism is not granted to the monastic order; it is specially assigned to the clerical order, unless perhaps so urgent a necessity for baptizing arises that postponement would involve danger. Even then it is not denied to a layperson. In the absence of a cleric, if a layperson, under the pressure of necessity, immerses a child in the sacred font after invoking the name of the Trinity, this ministry ought neither to be condemned in the layperson nor the baptism repeated in the child. Yet what necessity compels to be done temporarily ought not to be practised presumptuously; nor should this office be assigned as though due to a lay person, when the cleric’s absence and the urgency of such danger render it in some measure excusable.

Taking account of this necessity, Pope Gregory permits Bishop Candidus to take monks from monasteries and ordain them to govern people through churches.

> [Note: Col. 0793D. Book V, indiction XIV, chapter 127.]

“For your Fraternity,” he says, “has informed us that it has no presbyters and suffers no small hardship on this account; and because it reports that in certain monasteries situated in its parish there are monks who may be suitable for this office, and that it wishes, with our authority, to promote them to this order: therefore, by this present letter, we grant you permission, with the consent of their abbot, to take monks from monasteries situated in your parish and ordain them presbyters.”

This permission given to Bishop Candidus, that monks be taken out of monasteries and set over the people in place of clerics, is not granted everywhere and generally to all; indeed, elsewhere the same Gregory most emphatically forbids it. For when, as stated above, he removed clerics from the church of Saint Pancras because of their negligence, and assigned the revenues of that church to a neighbouring monastery for the monks’ use, Gregory nevertheless did not wish a monk from that monastery to be sent to the church to minister to the people. Rather, by the abbot’s provision, a visiting presbyter—that is, a cleric—was to be placed there, who, receiving temporal sustenance from the monastery, might fittingly minister spiritual sustenance to the people gathering at the church.

Again, when Gregory learned that a baptistery was being used in the monastery situated above Mascalas, he was greatly angered and ordered it removed, lest the community of monks grow insolent through usurping what was not theirs and, finding an occasion, grow lukewarm in the strictness of their order’s profession. Writing to Bishop Secundinus, he says:

> [Note: Col. 0795. Letter from the Register of Saint Gregory, Book II, indiction II, chapter 95.]

> We previously ordered that the baptistery be removed from the monastery of Saint Andrew, which is above Mascalas, on account of the monks’ insolence, and that an altar be established in the place where the fonts are, so that the aforesaid monks may more safely celebrate the Divine Office.

It is not, then, the office of this order to baptize; it is not its office to consecrate believers’ marriages by mystical blessing; it is not its office to ordain ministers for celebrating the mysteries of the altar; and there are many other functions which the clerical order seems to reserve so exclusively for itself that the monastic order neither can nor ought to obtain them.

Finally, writing to Furia concerning widowhood, Jerome declares that the monastic order is subject to the clerical order and explicitly calls clerics the fathers of monks. He says: “As though whatever is said against monks did not redound upon clerics, who are the fathers of monks! The loss of the flock is the shepherd’s disgrace. Conversely, the life of that monk is praised who holds Christ’s priests in reverence and does not disparage the order through which he became a Christian.” No ambiguity is now allowed to remain: the flock of monks ought to be subject to clerics as shepherds, and to render them the service of reverence, since through them it has obtained the sacraments of Christian faith.

## CHAPTER XCVI

One may therefore ask: if the dignity of clerics is so great and so pre-eminent, why does Jerome chiefly invite those whom he loves to the monastic life? Either he ought to have judged higher that to which he invited them, or he ought to have invited them to what he knew to be higher. True love, surely, does not know how to envy another’s advance in religious dignity; true religion does not know how to disparage the loftier height of holiness. But I neither dare nor ought to accuse Jerome of envy or detraction, since neither I nor anyone else presumes to doubt his merits.

If it please you, let a second, similar question be joined to this one, so that both may be resolved together by one similar brief answer. Jerome himself, and John Cassian also, say that there are three kinds of monks in Egypt. The first kind are called Sarabaites, the second coenobites, the third anchorites.

[Col. 0795D]

They call Sarabaites those who live two or three together in cells, so according to their own will that among them no order, rule, or discipline is observed. If they have performed any work and sold what they have made, it is valued at a higher price. They fast when they please; when a feast-day comes, they stuff themselves to vomiting. They remain rarely in their cells and frequently in hamlets; they go about little houses, visit little women, hunt for small gifts, flatter with ingratiating words, disparage clerics, envy monks, and oppose their betters. In short, repudiating the reality signified by their name, they glory only in the name of monks.

But they call coenobites those who, gathered in a monastery, renounce their own will; having all things in common, having cast away secular property, they are kept under the authority of one father by regular discipline. Through love of the brotherhood they set aside private advantages; by the laws of obedience they subject their own wills. They strive to be found lowly and humble, so that they are ashamed not to outdo one another in humility. Bound together by the glue of love, like bees they cling to one another; they are inflamed by mutual examples; they hide themselves in the haven of silence; they rest in holy work and holy desire.

They call anchorites those who, after a long practice in the coenobium and formation of character through diligence, hasten to the desert with a view to the perfection of holiness. There, separated from human companionship and sight, they strive more strictly to withdraw themselves from the things of this life and to cling to God alone in loving embraces. By fasts of two, three, four, or more days they restrain the appetite of the flesh; they banish the delights of food far from their islands. With bread and water, and at most with added salt or wild herbs, they restrain nature’s need; and by such food they grow fat not outwardly in flesh but inwardly in mind. They are worn down by continual labours and enjoy sleep so furtive and scanty that they seem rather to doze than sleep, lest even fullness of sleep should in any degree impede their purpose.

Thus they meet bodily necessity, both in these matters and in all others, so as to give no place to deceptive pleasure; choosing to live, as far as it is permitted for a human being to be separated from human things, with angels in the continual suspension of a fervent spirit. I find these three kinds of monks named in the writings of the Fathers. Of the first I hear nothing good said; but I know the other two to be highly commended. Yet, though the kinds of coenobites and anchorites are extolled with fitting praises, the latter is judged more worthy and more perfect, because although a religious multitude lives holily and justly, solitude demands something holier and more perfect.

Thus Jerome, writing to Demetrias, says: “There is commonly among many a debate whether the solitary life or life with many is better; the former is preferred to the latter.” Why, then, although Jerome knows and affirms the anchoritic kind to be more perfect, does he invite those whom he loves to the fellowship of coenobites? Why does he not wish those withdrawing from the world for the sake of conversion to become anchorites, but urges, advises, and incites them to become coenobites? It is not the part of a just man to envy those whom he loves the degree of perfection; but it is the part of a just man to provide what he knows to be safer.

Jerome himself resolves this question, lest we suffer any doubt about it: he shows that he does not envy but provides, does not disparage but draws upward, does not lower one whom he loves so that he becomes contemptible, but acts lest, raised up, he perhaps vanish more quickly like smoke. He judges it better for someone to live more safely in lowliness than, placed on high, to fall down to what is low and base; better to gain victory in the field with the assistance of many than, rushing alone to lofty things, perhaps shamefully to forget the contest he has undertaken. For he knows that the enemy attacks the solitary person more fiercely, that fault is near at hand, and that one who is solitary does not easily rise again after a fall. Scripture testifies that “if two are together, one is warmed by the other; if one falls alone, he has no one by whose aid he may be raised” [Eccles. 4].

When the enemy sees an ordered battle-line of camps, he retreats in fear; when a hawk finds a dove wandering alone, he rejoices. Under the shepherd’s staff and in the presence of dogs, the wolf does not presume to break into the flock; but a sheep separated from the flock can scarcely escape the bold snares of the lion that prowls about. Thus, as Jerome himself says, solitary life is dangerous even for men, lest, withdrawn from human company, they be exposed to foul and impious thoughts; become full of arrogance; despise all others with lifted brows; and arm their tongues to disparage clerics or other monks.

Therefore, when instructing the monk Rusticus and inviting him to what he knew to be safer, he says: “It pleases me that you should have the companionship of holy persons, neither teach yourself nor enter without a guide upon a way you have never entered, lest you immediately turn aside in another direction and be exposed to error.” Jerome then shows how one who refuses the companionship of holy persons and lives alone in the desert is exposed to error and compelled more readily to turn aside in another direction: “In solitude,” he says, “pride quickly steals in. If a man has fasted a little and seen no other person, he thinks himself someone of importance; forgetting himself—whence and whither he has come—he wanders inwardly in heart and outwardly in tongue. He stretches out his hands to whatever gluttony demands; he sleeps as much as he wishes; he does whatever he wishes; he fears no one; he thinks everyone inferior to himself.”

And lest he seem, in saying this, to be accusing the solitary life, he took care to excuse what he had said before by adding: “What then? Do we condemn the solitary life? By no means; indeed, we have often praised it.” If, therefore, Jerome by no means condemns the solitary life, why does he not kindle the monk Rusticus by exhortation toward it, except because solitude demands persons so perfect and strong that strength suitable for solitude is found in few? Thus, after saying that he did not condemn the solitary life, which he had often praised, he adds: “But from the training-ground of monasteries we wish to send forth into the desert soldiers whom the hard first lessons of the wilderness will not terrify: men who have long displayed the character of their life; who have been least of all in order to become first of all; whom neither hunger nor satiety has ever overcome; who rejoice in poverty; whose dress, speech, face, gait, and teaching are a doctrine of virtues.”

Since it is the privilege of few to glory in such perfection, and since it is not expedient for the imperfect to live alone in the desert, Jerome exhorts the man whom he loves to seek the companionship of holy persons, so that his weakness may be supported by the assistance of many. For in the community of holy persons, perfection of holiness suffers no loss, while imperfection receives an increase toward progress: the fervent workshop of obedience preserves the strong in virtues already acquired, and regular discipline forms and advances the weak toward acquiring them.

This is the good workshop of religion, in which the perfect regularly form the imperfect and the imperfect strive to conform themselves to the more perfect; and if the adversary presumes to attack anyone there, he is repelled by the encounter with the multitude and is not permitted to triumph. For when the elders burn with brotherly love and the younger members retain nothing of their own will, such a multitude is rendered so secure and unconquerable that the adversary’s deceitful strength cannot prevail against it. Therefore, a little later Jerome says to the same Rusticus:

> [Note: Col. 0797D. Jerome, *To Rusticus*, Letter 13, Book II.]
>
> My discourse aims at teaching you that you ought not to be left to your own judgment, but to live in a monastery under the discipline of one father and in the fellowship of many: that from one you may learn humility, from another patience; that this man may teach you silence, that one gentleness; that you may not do what you wish; that you may be subject to one whom you do not wish; that you may come weary to bed and, walking, as it were, sleep; that you may be compelled to rise before your sleep is finished; that you may serve the brethren; that, having suffered an injury, you may keep silence; that you may fear the superior of the monastery as a master and love him as a parent; that you may believe whatever he commands to be for your salvation; and that you may not judge the decision of an elder, since your office is to obey and perform what has been commanded.

And later, after enumerating certain vices from which most solitaries seem to suffer, he added: “When you are in a monastery, you will not be permitted to do these things; and as habit gradually grows, you will begin to will what at first you were compelled to will.”

It is wholly clear why Jerome invites Rusticus to the coenobium: not because the rank of anchorites is not higher, but because it is more dangerous, so that one who has chosen to fight in higher things scarcely succeeds in glorying in the titles of victory. For the enemy attacks more urgently and presses more fiercely the one whom he sees standing higher, hoping to gain greater glory if he casts down the man whom he sees above the rest.

## CHAPTER XCVII
This same reason is why the same Jerome recalls Heliodorus from the clerical rank and invites him to the haven of monks: namely, lest, placed on high, he be forced to endure the enemy’s fiercer assaults and, unable to bear the sharper struggle, finally fall ingloriously. For because he sees clerics pre-eminent in a loftier rank and exercising a dangerous office in that rank, he fears that, if this dignity or office is sought by any weak person, he may finally be compelled to collapse beneath a burden unequal to him. It is indeed the dignity of clerics to preside over all the faithful of the Church; it is their office to teach them the way of truth, to administer spiritual things alike to noble and ignoble, wise and foolish; to visit married women, widows, and virgins; to know the consciences of all, instruct the thoughts of all, shape the actions and conduct of all, and correct the errors of all with every patience and authority. And because, as debtors of this office, they must live bodily among those over whom they preside and whom they instruct, lest through the pastor’s absence the wolf make an attack upon the people’s flock. But because it is difficult and rare to touch pitch and remain wholly undefiled, to live among secular people and not be burdened by their company, some clerics had happened to be weakened by association with secular persons, so that the laity seemed not so much to imitate them for the better as they themselves to imitate the laity for the worse.

Therefore [Col. 0799B] Jerome strives to deter Heliodorus, Paulinus, and Rusticus from this rank, lest under the pretext of clerical office they should wish to mingle with secular people, and lest they think this rank either lower or more relaxed, even though many clerics do not live worthily within it. For they, so far as may be understood from Jerome’s letters, proposed to live in the monastic order, but, still clinging to certain carnal ties, wished to be constrained by the rule of religion while nevertheless refusing to be separated either from their kindred or from the crowds of the people. Heliodorus, among other things, was held by affection for a certain little nephew, Nepotian; Paulinus found it painful to leave his sister; Rusticus still [Col. 0799C] lived together with his mother in one house. And thus, entangled in these and similar attachments, they seemed insufficiently unencumbered for walking the path they had set before themselves.

Jerome, indeed, seeks in various letters thus to confront them: to show in each case that it is by no means expedient for a monk either to delight in living among relatives and popular crowds or, setting aside monastic quiet, to become entangled in tumultuous affairs. And lest those who could not endure this quiet should object by appealing to the order of clerics, whom they see lawfully living in cities and amid the people, he took care to meet this objection more carefully and to bring them—or others in their ignorance—back to its true understanding. Thus he says to Heliodorus: “Though your little nephew hang from your neck, fly to the standard of the Cross with dry eyes; in this matter the only kind of piety is to be cruel.” And below: “Interpret the name *monk*: it is your name. What are you doing in a crowd, you who are alone?” And shortly afterwards: “From this calculation arises the conclusion that a monk cannot be perfect in his own country.” And because he knew that words of this kind did not please many monks, whom he endeavours to remove from dwelling with parents, from the company of crowds, and from attachment to their native country, he immediately adds what he knew Heliodorus, or any such person, would answer: “But, he says, driven from this rank, you will appeal to clerics.”

As though he were saying: If you find it burdensome to attain the monastic perfection to which I exhort you, since for its sake you are warned to leave the crowds and forget your parents and native country, perhaps, seeking holy [Col. 0800A] orders, you will hasten to advance yourself to clerical office, so that under the pretext of this office you may remain more freely in city, among people, at home, and in your native land. For you suppose that a more relaxed life is granted you in this rank, while it is nevertheless considered fully sufficient for perfection. But I shall not exhort you to monastic life in such a way as to presume to cast any reproach upon clerics, nor, by disparaging the holy and exalted rank of clerics, to carry the praises of monks beyond what is just. This is what follows: “Or shall I dare, he says, to say anything about those who certainly live in their own cities? Far be it, he says, from me to speak anything ill of them.”

It would seem to be speaking ill of clerics if he declared their rank either inferior or more relaxed; if he presumed that those must be judged blameworthy who are necessarily detained in cities, not by entanglement but by office. “Far be it,” he says, “from me to speak anything ill of those who, succeeding to the apostolic rank, make Christ’s body with sacred mouth; through whom we too are Christians; who, holding the keys of the kingdom of heaven, in some manner judge before the day of judgment; who preserve the Lord’s Bride in sober chastity.” As though he were saying: Those whose rank possesses so great a dignity in the Church, whose office possesses so great a holiness, I do not dare judge inferior to monks, though I see them dwelling in cities. “But,” he says, “the case of monks is one thing, that of clerics another: clerics feed the sheep; I am fed.” That is to say: no necessity compels me, who am fed, who am a monk, [Col. 0800C] to endure the disturbances of the popular throng—disturbances which pastoral necessity compels the cleric to endure. Yet for that reason he is not reckoned inferior; indeed, a cleric is judged as much more worthy than a monk as a shepherd is than a sheep.

But the more worthy a place the cleric holds, the holier a life he must necessarily have, lest, if greater dignity lacks greater holiness, the cleric incur greater and more grievous harm from dignity itself. And because it is rare to stand unbendingly in this summit of dignity, and deadly to turn aside, I do not advise you to ascend to a higher place, lest you be unable to stand and encounter a graver fall. “It is not,” he says, “easy to stand in Paul’s place or hold Peter’s rank. You look at Peter, but consider Judas too; you behold Stephen, but look also at Nicholas.” Therefore, because it is difficult to obtain the place of Peter, Paul, and Stephen in the Church when one cannot easily have their merits, Jerome exhorts Heliodorus to the monastic order, not because this order is considered either more worthy or holier than the clerical order, but because, the humbler it is, the safer it is judged to be. For if anyone who holds Peter’s or Stephen’s place does not also imitate their merits with diligence, one must fear that he may slip into the company of Judas or Nicholas; and the higher the rank he has attained, the graver the fall he will find when cast down to the depths.

## CHAPTER XCVIII

In the same way, writing to Paulinus, Jerome seems [Col. 0801A] to testify that the clerical order ought to be judged superior to the monastic; and, while seeking to call him back from the crowd and exhort him to monastic quiet, he says that clerics may lawfully live in cities because of the office they perform. “I think there are differences of place: if, leaving cities and the crowds of cities, you live on a little farm, seek Christ in solitude, pray alone on the mountain with Jesus, and enjoy only the neighbourhood of holy places—that is, so that you lack the city and do not lose the monk’s purpose.” “What I say, I do not say of bishops, presbyters, or clerics, whose office is different, but of a monk, who for this reason laid the price of his possessions at the apostles’ feet, teaching that money must be trodden underfoot, so that, living humbly and in secret, he may always despise what he once despised.”

And shortly afterwards: “If you wish to perform the office of presbyter, if the work or perhaps the honour of the episcopate delights you, live in cities and towns, and make the salvation of others the gain of your own soul. But if you desire to be what you are called, a monk—that is, alone—what are you doing in cities, which surely are not habitations of persons alone but of many?” And because this same Paulinus was somewhat held by affection for his sister and seemed to love the popular crowd more than monastic quiet, Jerome adds a little below: “I beseech you, since you are bound by the tie of your sister and do not proceed with a wholly unencumbered step, flee crowds of people, official duties, greetings, and banquets, whether here or there, as certain chains [Col. 0801C] of pleasures.”

## CHAPTER XCIX

So also, when he saw the monk Rusticus clinging rather too tenaciously to his possessions, and wished to remove him both from them and from his mother’s company, he says: “But if you wish to be a monk and not merely appear one, take care not of your household property, by renouncing which you began to be this, but of your soul.” And below: “I wish you, for the reasons set out above, not to live with your mother.” And because some clerics seemed both to give attention to household property and to live everywhere, as though lawfully, with mothers or sisters, he took care to excuse himself more carefully on this point, lest he seem to accuse them through indirect attacks. “It is not,” [Col. 0801D] he says, “within the humility or measure of my station to judge others and say anything ill of the ministers of the Churches.”

Therefore, lest Rusticus should suppose he could fortify himself by their example and oppose their manner of life to unwelcome admonitions, he says again: “But do not let the crowd of passers-by disturb you, so that you think silently: ‘What then? Will all who live in cities perish? Look, they enjoy their possessions, serve the Churches, visit baths, do not reject perfumes, and yet move amid every elegance.’ To this I previously replied, and now briefly reply: in the present little work I am not discussing clerics but training a monk.” Clerics are holy. It is therefore plain that Jerome does not seek to invite those whom we have mentioned to monastic quiet because he presumes to judge the clerical order inferior, but because this rank is of such dignity in the Church that scarcely anyone can be found whose merit of holiness corresponds to it. It is easier, however, and far safer, to earn salvation in a lowly rank and condition than to attain worthy virtue on a high and slippery height; for assaults of the winds are repelled from the valley below by the obstacle of the mountains, while upon those same mountains the fury of the winds rages more freely.

Therefore he commends the order of monks neither from envy of friends nor by disparaging clerics, but advises that the danger of the clerical office be feared and avoided, lest one who scarcely suffices to flee from the face of a pursuer presumptuously seize the place of one who resists. For not everyone who gains salvation by fleeing can also deserve victory by resisting; nor is the one who hastens to flee lest he be defeated accused of base cowardice or shameful dishonour. Thus, the easier it is, the safer it is to flee from the midst of Babylon and be saved; but the more difficult it is, the more glorious it is to be crowned victorious in the midst of Babylon. Thus monastic perfection, though rightly commended for its merit, is judged inferior to the clerical order in proportion as it is easier. Therefore Jerome instructs those whom we have mentioned with friendly counsel, lest they break out into flight by way of, or under cover of, clerical office; because sometimes one who lives well while pressing a regular footstool slips and falls when seated in a teacher’s chair.

## CHAPTER C

This our Augustine expressly stated [Col. 0802C] when he elegantly checked the pride of certain monks. Speaking to Bishop Aurelius, he says: “It is much to be lamented if we raise monks to such ruinous pride, when even a good monk scarcely makes a good cleric.” Augustine saw certain monks growing weary of quiet and silence and, failing to preserve monastic humility, shamelessly aspiring to ecclesiastical honours. They did not consider how much a footstool differs from a chair: on the former one sits more safely, on the latter more dangerously. Therefore, showing both the dangerous eminence of clerics and checking the brazen insolence of monks, he says, “when even a good monk scarcely makes a good cleric,” plainly showing that not only a wicked monk ought to be entirely excluded from clerical rank or office, but that even a good monk is scarcely worthy to be promoted to them.

For some who live quite honourably in monastic humility, when ecclesiastical necessity raises them to perform the office of a cleric, not only fail to retain their former discipline of life, but succumb to failure beneath a burden unequal to them—or rather, to ruin. Too weak, indeed, to hold clerical eminence, shaken by trials greater than usual, they sink into secular life; and at last they learn by experience how a good monk differs from a good cleric, when what suffices for the former is found by no means to suffice for the latter. The Lord also indicated through Isaiah that they differ, when he distinctly commended his benefit toward them: “Blessed is Egypt, my people; but Israel is my inheritance” (Isa. 19).

In Egypt, as was said above, Mark’s preaching is found to have flourished; there, while he preached, the monastic order is found to have had its origin; there, through the inspiration of grace, it advanced so greatly that the abounding coldness of former iniquity was surpassed by the new ardour of charity. Egypt, which was formerly called an iron furnace, in which varied error and manifold idolatry were forged: when fire is sent from heaven, it becomes a saving workshop in which regular conduct is shaped by the hammer of discipline. And such conduct becomes so fruitful that it makes populous what had been deserted, and the solitude which had hitherto claimed uncultivated and arid places for itself is occupied by an innumerable [Col. 0803B] multitude of monks. These persons live locally in Egypt, yet are held there not so much in mind as in body; casting errors aside, they walk by a path of light, so that they have nothing in common with Egypt except its dark clothing.

For because “Egypt” is interpreted as “darkness,” and they themselves had lived in the darkness of sins, they wish the memory of their former state to remain with them, lest, forgetting what they were, they fall into the vice of pride and deserve to lose what they had received freely. Thus they wish to retain in their clothing the black colour which they knew accorded with darkness, though expelling it from their minds, so that at every moment they may remember their former blackness and, lamenting the past, glory in the present with greater safety because with greater humility. Thus outwardly dark in black and rough clothing, but rich in the inward light of the mind, while a pleasing harmony arises from these contrasting elements, they sound forth in harmonious melody that saying from the Song: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1). Black because of the memory of Egyptian antiquity, but beautiful because of the grace of newness discovered; black because of the place in which we still dwell in reality, but beautiful because of him toward whom we hasten in hope and desire.

Therefore, because Egypt first and chiefly abounded in monks when the true East visited its darkness by the outpouring of his light, the Lord beautifully foreshadowed such grace by a prophetic spirit when through Isaiah he proclaimed Egypt his blessed people: “Blessed,” he says, “is Egypt, my people” [Col. 0803D]. But lest the blessing foretold to monks should appear to be conferred in such a way that the ancient benefit was thought to be removed, conversely, from clerics, when the divine utterance had said, “Blessed is Egypt, my people,” it added: “But Israel is my inheritance.”

By Israel the clerical order seems to me to be signified. Originating among the people Israel, it deserved there also to be exalted, since among that people it deserved to receive for its increase apostles—and those whom the apostles chose—presbyters and Levites, true Israelites in flesh and spirit. Among that people Christ trained the clerical order; among it he bestowed ecclesiastical dignity upon it; among it the clerical order heard Christ; among it it obeyed him even to the cross and stones; among it Christ suffered, died, rose again, and in their sight was raised into heaven, to the right hand of the Father. Israel, then, is rightly called the clerical order, to which greater spiritual grace was given by Christ, to which it was said especially: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke 10); and: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Matt. 12). Seeing Christ in flesh and spirit, it deserved to cleave to him more intimately than the rest and to remain faithfully with him in his temptations.

## CHAPTER CI

To this order Christ entrusted, in Peter, both the honour and ministry of governing the Church; to it, in John, he entrusted the Virgin Mother to a virgin; to it, in both, he revealed his glory upon Mount Tabor; to it, in Stephen, opening the heavens, he showed himself standing at the Father’s right hand; this order, in Paul, he raised to the third heaven [Col. 0804B] to hear unspeakable words; this order, in all the apostles, he appointed in his own stead in the Church for preaching, baptizing, and binding. This order, therefore, is called not only heir of God or co-heir of Christ, but more expressly and appropriately an inheritance: Christ embraced it not, like the rest, by a general love or benefit, but claimed it with a certain tender affection and allotted it to himself by a special lot.

Hence he says in the Psalms: “The lines have fallen to me in splendid places” (Ps. 16). And because he saw some who either, recalling the luxuriant Maecenas, despised the poverty of this apostolic order, or presumed to feign greater holiness by raven-black colour, after saying, “The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places,” he immediately adds: “Indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me” (ibid.). As though he said: Although my inheritance is cheap in your eyes—you who either disdain apostolic humility with swelling pride, or rather you who take pride in a dark image of holiness—yet to me my inheritance is both dear and splendid: dear indeed because of the benefit of holiness bestowed upon it, but splendid because of the lofty height of ecclesiastical dignity.

Because of this splendid, pre-eminent, special allotment, this order has from ancient times rightly been called clerical, so that, when such an order was designated by such a name, its prerogative might be marked in its very name. For *cleros* is Greek, “lot” in Latin; and a lot is called an inheritance because an inheritance is divided by lot. Thus through Moses the Lord said: “To each one, as the lot falls, so the inheritance shall be allotted” (Num. 33). Therefore, since no earthly inheritance is granted to this order, but God himself and God’s sanctuary are assigned to it as its part or portion, as again it is said through Moses, “The Lord himself is their inheritance” (Deut. 18), the order itself is rightly, in reverse relation, called God’s inheritance, because he allots it by the special cord of grace to govern the Church in his stead. To this inheritance it is said in the Psalm: “If you sleep between the two lots (*cleri*), [you will be] the silvered wings of the dove” (Ps. 67).

By *cleri* he means the two inheritances promised by the two Testaments, of which the first and lower is temporal, the second and far more excellent eternal. For in the first Testament are promised length of days upon earth; in that length, sound bodily health; invincible strength against enemies; abundance of grain, wine, and oil; and, not to make the matter long, such an extent of temporal goods that the profound breadth of earthly desire would not presume to seek more. But in the second Testament are promised immortal life, eternal peace, unfailing light, spiritual joy, the delightful fellowship of angels, full satisfaction without weariness, the radiant vision of God himself, and the glorious permanence of that vision.

## CHAPTER CII

These are the two inheritances which, as was said, are promised in the two Testaments and bestowed through them upon their worshippers. In one they are lulled to a heavy and deadly sleep; in the other, to a sweet and saving sleep. In the first inheritance, he is said to sleep who embraces temporal goods with all his efforts, who pants after possessing them and takes more delight than is right in what he possesses; who, blinded in heart, clings only to visible things and rests in that blindness, in wretched security, as though asleep. Paul knew that some slept in this way among the Corinthians, saying: “Therefore among you many are weak and infirm, and many sleep” (2 Cor. 11); and to the Thessalonians: “Those who sleep, sleep by night” (1 Thess. 5). And Isaiah: “Watchmen,” he says, “all of you are blind, sleeping and loving dreams” (Isa. 56).

Our Lord likewise rebuked his disciples for this sleep when he himself, awake, was in agony at the very moment of his passion. “He came,” he says, “and found them sleeping” (Matt. 24): that is, still carnally attached to love of this life. “For,” he says, “their eyes were heavy” (ibid.): that is, darkened by fear of death even to the peril of flight or denial. Therefore he rebukes Peter, who had promised that he would in no way sleep but would remain faithful with him unto death: “Simon, are you sleeping? Could you not watch one hour with me?” (Matt. 14). You who had said, “I lay down my life for you; even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you”—you, I say, sleep when the moment of death is imminent, when you ought especially to have watched, so that by the brief span of one hour you might avoid eternal loss.

But in the second inheritance, he is judged, as it were, to sleep who, temporal care removed, rejoices in the security he has found; who glories in the longed-for company of angels; who, with unveiled face, contemplates the Lord’s glory, when no interruption impedes his vision, when peace kisses justice, when justice is transformed into judgment, when charity begun is consummated without obligation. David foresaw this sleep in the Spirit and, in humble confidence, declared that he would attain it: “In peace,” he says, “in the selfsame state I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. 4).
