Blessed is that peace into which, when the righteous person comes, he is said to fall asleep: that is, he is believed to find a security so delightful and so everlasting that no discordant adversity, no opposing diversity, can either confront or prevail against him; rather, free from every injury, he rests delightfully in the selfsame state.

The Lord seems elsewhere also to designate such peace or sleep when in Leviticus he promises the land of promise to the children of Israel: “I shall give peace in your borders; you shall sleep, and there shall be none to terrify you” (Lev. 26). For the borders of that heavenly country are so peaceful, the gates, bolts, and bars of that Jerusalem so strengthened, that there one sleeps in long and delightful sleep, and no one is terrified even by the sound of a flying leaf. In these two *cleri*, as was said, there is sleep: that is, in the first a deadly rest, in the second a saving rest, is found.

But he sleeps between the midst of the *cleri*, that is, between the two inheritances, who neither strives to seek temporal things nor has yet attained the heavenly things he desires. For when someone is separated from the turmoil of public affairs, opposes carnal desires, and despises honours, glory, and riches; when he remains thus in the flesh without embracing the things of the flesh, what does he seem to do except in some manner already to leave the temporal inheritance and, forgetful of what lies behind, fall asleep in the bosom or lap of quiet? Yet because he has not been wholly freed from this body of death and does not yet behold the inner things of the sanctuary with the veil removed, what does he seem to do except, as though asleep outside in the vestibule, dream of those things whose fragrance he deserved to taste beforehand by love?

He therefore sleeps between two inheritances who has already somewhat departed from this one but has not yet wholly entered that one; who grows weary, in praiseworthy torpor, of the desire for this inheritance and longs for the other, which he is not yet able to obtain. Thus God commanded the person mentioned above to sleep between the midst of the *cleri*, and for this reason also willed him to be marked by the clerical name, so that when he considered himself designated by such a name, he might know whence and whither he ought to advance. For, sleeping between the *cleri*, clerics become the wings of the dove, because then the Church is raised by their word and example from earthly things to heavenly, when both their life and teaching repose in quiet and leisure.

Therefore at supper Christ affectionately reclined upon his breast the disciple whom he loved most, whom he intended to set before clerics as their teacher and leader; and, when he was asleep—not for dreaming but for contemplation—breathed into him grace for living and teaching. In this he showed that he wills the order by whose wings the Church must be raised on high to rest delightfully in peace and leisure. But this one, thus put to rest, possesses God’s sanctuary as an inheritance [Col. 0806D], and himself, in reverse relation, becomes God’s inheritance; so that, just as the sanctuary or priesthood is assigned to him by hereditary right, so he himself may be specially reckoned, beyond others, as God’s possession or inheritance.

This, indeed, as was said above, the Lord indicated through Isaiah; this he commended by an apt distinction when he called Egyptian monks his people generally, but reserved the hereditary name especially for clerics: “Blessed is Egypt, my people; but Israel is my inheritance” (Isa. 19). Therefore, when monks see that they have advanced through the gift of blessing, let them not suppose that clerics have fallen from their former dignity, since clerics are specially called the inheritance and Israel, for the reasons mentioned above.

## CHAPTER CIII

I could fittingly have ended the present answer at this point, had not the written disputation of a certain monk compelled me to extend it somewhat, since it strongly opposes our assertions by which we sought to show that clerics are more worthy than monks. I neither wished nor ought to pass over this disputation in silence, lest, should it happen to come into your hands, you be left in doubt about whom you ought chiefly to agree with.

When that monk, whom I know not by face but only by name, was disputing with a cleric of his city, whom I know well both by face and name, he endeavoured, wishing to commend monks beyond what was just, to assert that they were more worthy than clerics. Because the cleric did not readily yield to the opposing monk, the monk produced testimonies from Jerome’s letters; and because he kept them by use and memory, selecting what seemed suitable to his own side, he bent them to his own purpose. But the cleric had either not read Jerome’s letters, it seems, or had not committed them to memory; and, because he did not presume to resist the authorities of so great a man, he finally gave assent when he heard the testimonies.

Yet if he had read them and retained what he had read in memory, he could, I think, have responded fittingly and confidently removed opposing arguments by opposing arguments. If anything concerning the reading of Porphyry or Aristotle had been debated between them, I do not doubt that the cleric would have been judged not at all inferior to the monk, indeed far superior; for he was exceedingly learned in secular literature and unimpeachably ready in proposing or answering arguments. Nor did he lack knowledge of sacred literature; indeed, he exercised himself in it so diligently that, when he once debated seriously about it with the same monk, the consulted authority of the masters of Laon judged his opinion sounder.

Therefore, that he yielded to the monk, who exalted monastic dignity beyond what was just and produced testimonies from Jerome’s letters as a defence of his cause, seems to me to have arisen from the reason already stated: namely, that I do not believe he had knowledge of those letters. Although some clerics of that city assert—and their assertion is considered quite plausible—that this very monk was the notary of the written disputation: that he himself took it down, wrote it, and described the cleric as defeated and himself as victor according to his own pleasure. But let us set aside that judgment for the present and come to what the monk asserts.

## CHAPTER CIV

He says that monks are more worthy than clerics because they are adorned by monastic profession and, while serving in sacred orders as clerics, minister at the altar; whereas the latter are merely clerics, the former are considered at once monks and clerics. “For,” he says, “since clerical status is not tonsure, not dress, not knowledge of letters, but the office of the altar, and monks perform the office of the altar, it is clear that they too are clerics, since they do the things proper to clerics; and to the fullness of their dignity are added monastic dress and profession.”

But it seems fitting to insert the monk’s own words into the present work, so that you may know more certainly what and how one must answer him. “A monk speaking to a cleric: Clerical status,” he says, “is not knowledge of letters, nor your tonsure or dress, but the office of the altar. And it is designated by such a name for this reason: when in the old law the Lord divided the land among the tribes of Israel, perhaps by the measuring-line of distribution, the tribe of Levi, which was to minister in the sanctuary, received as its lot none other than the Lord himself, that is, the Lord’s altar, so that one serving the altar might live from the altar. Therefore all who serve the altar are clerics, and clerical status signifies nothing other than the office of the altar. Hence you must grant that you are called, or are, a cleric for no other reason than because you perform the orders of the altar. But I too perform those same orders; indeed, with the authority of my rule I have performed priestly service; therefore I too am a cleric.”

Thus, by proposing, assuming, and inferring, the monk maintains that he is a cleric and persists inflexibly in the same assertion, adding that for this reason he must be judged more worthy than a cleric: because, along with clerical status, he is also adorned by monastic profession. For he says: “But I, who together with the splendour of the monastic [Col. 0808C] order also exercise the honour of priestly and Levitical order, do not permit you to seem at all equal to me. For, as someone has most truly said: ‘Mary is a virgin, and John is a virgin; but Mary has the greater fullness, because John is only a virgin, whereas Mary is both mother and virgin.’ So indeed I have a greater fullness than you, because you are only a cleric, whereas I am both monk and cleric. You now understand that I, who am a monk, am also a cleric: namely, because I have performed the orders of the sacred altar.”

By these words the monk both maintains that he is a cleric because he has performed sacred orders, and contends that he is more worthy than a cleric because he is also a monk. But which monk he refuses to allow to be called more worthy than a cleric, or to which monk he admits a cleric is equal, is more plainly declared in the same disputation. For he says to the opposing cleric: “These things appear opposed to you—namely monasticism and clerical status. They are indeed distinct, and each can exist without the other: as in you or that man, clerical status without monasticism; and likewise in any converted layman, monasticism without clerical status. I do not deny that you are equal to such a man, on the authority of the canons, which prescribe for a monk holding no rank of the altar, if he falls into a crime, the same manner of penance as for a cleric of Levitical rank.”

You see that he declares a layman—if he becomes only a monk and does not perform the ministry of the altar—to be equal to a cleric of Levitical rank. He relies upon the argument that, if a monk of this sort slips into the pit of sin, the authority of the canons imposes upon him the same manner of penance as upon a Levitical cleric. But, in my judgment, this is not a sufficiently necessary argument, nor a sufficiently adequate support for that argument; and there is no need to labour greatly anew in refuting what he thus strives to affirm. For it has been abundantly demonstrated above that monasticism ought not to be equated with clerical status, nor need this be repeated so often that weariness is produced in hearers by superfluous repetition of the same thing.

Indeed, what sound-minded person would patiently allow a lay monk to be asserted equal to a cleric who is a Levite, when the former is not even permitted to utter a word in the Church, while the word of the Gospel is entrusted to the latter’s mouth? The latter, though he is not yet able to consecrate Christ’s body with sacred mouth, nevertheless ministers so intimately to the one consecrating that he is commanded to lay his hand upon the chalice and is reckoned a necessary fellow-worker in so great a mystery, lest the bishop appear to perform it alone, but a deacon as a participant be admitted to the sacred office.

## CHAPTER CV
What is assigned to a monk, if he has fallen into crime, namely the same measure of penance as to a cleric of the Levitical order, does not signify equality of rank; rather, ecclesiastical censure is administered with just moderation: it acts more mildly toward one who, under the compulsion of his office, associates with secular people, but pronounces a stricter sentence upon one who, though withdrawn from the world, is nevertheless entangled in the world’s crimes. For when a levite performs clerical ministry, when the demands of office bring him into contact with the common throng, when, whether a presbyter is present or absent, he is obliged to console others, visit widows, instruct married women, exhort virgins, when he must be occupied with these and similar duties, what wonder if he is found burdened by attendant troubles?

[Col. 0809C] What wonder, I say, if hay upon the mountains, exposed to the sun’s rays while Cancer blazes, dries up; if, when it dries up, the little flower of chastity withers—a flower which, so long as it lies hidden in a sheltered valley beneath the covering of trees, nourished by fitting moisture, grows green in its proper beauty? Indeed, it is strange and worthy of wonder if, when a levite is mixed with secular crowds because of the office of the clergy, he is not caught, even amid abundant grace, in the birdlime of secular vices; if, while he labours to impart his spiritual obligation both to men and women, he can pass through the assaults of the fire encountered without injury to his step.

[Col. 0809D] Therefore, just as his fall is reckoned graver because of the higher degree of his rank, so, because of his burdensome office, he is judged more worthy of pardon; and the bishop rebukes his minister in a spirit of gentleness, considering how difficult it is to maintain an unbending state of the holiness one has undertaken. But if a monk, who is not bound by ecclesiastical care, who by the law of his order is removed from the crowd of the people, whose duty it is to give himself to tears, to sit in a solitary corner, to flee the encounters of men—and especially of women—to see nothing that flatters in the world, to recoil at the admonition of his habit, to lie hidden in silence, and to have nothing in common with outward things—if such a man, I say, having broken down the barrier of his singular continence, and restrained by no shame,

[Col. 0810A] bursts forth into the obscenity of a brothel, who would not judge him worthy of a heavier punishment, since he has, as it were willingly, abandoned the shadow of a safer hiding-place? For the more easily he could have preserved continence, since it was his duty to hide beneath the shadow of silence, the more severely ecclesiastical censure is exercised against him, and the sharper remedy is applied to his disease.

Thus, in the same measure of penance prescribed by the authority of the canons for monk and levite, equality of rank is not signified; rather, their unequal security is weighed, so that the cleric, whom occasion arising from his ministry presses upon, may be punished somewhat more indulgently, whereas he whom monastic profession renders more advanced [*senriorem*, perhaps *seniorem*] is not spared by strict judgment. To be sure, the cleric would deservedly be punished much more severely, inasmuch as the higher the rank, the graver the fall is held to be; but if judgment were exercised against him without mercy, perhaps scarcely anyone could be found to perform clerical ministry.

Now I wish to reply a little to the monk’s assertion that he is also a cleric—if God grants me both to perceive what is true and to explain what I have perceived. For a poor spirit is found narrow and slow in apprehending subtle matters, and is very often impeded by still greater constraints in explaining what it has apprehended; because, even if by investigation it can at last discover something through understanding, yet through lack of words it cannot successfully set forth what it has discovered. Therefore he is greatly necessary to our poverty who is both the Wisdom of God and the Word of God, God himself: that, by his bounty, he may illuminate our understanding with knowledge of the truth, and that at last

[Col. 0810C] our scant store of words may not constrain that knowledge.

## CHAPTER CVI

The monk says that he is a cleric because he serves the altar. “For,” he says, “the tribe of Levi, which had to minister in the sanctuary, received no other portion than the altar of the Lord”—namely, that by serving the altar it might live from the altar. “Therefore,” he says, “all who serve the altar are clerics.”

I wonder why he did not also infer: “Therefore all who live from the altar are clerics.” For just as it belongs properly to clerics to serve the altar, so it also belongs properly to them to live from the altar. For it was established for the priests and levites, for whom the Law ordained service at the altar, that they should also live from the altar; so that among their brothers

[Col. 0810D] they should receive no portion other than the altar: that is, they should render it spiritual ministry and receive from it temporal sustenance.

Or did he decline also to infer, “Therefore all who live from the altar are clerics,” as he inferred, “Therefore all who serve the altar are clerics,” lest such an inference should appear superfluous, since this was held as certain and unquestioned? For it is established that, just as the tribe of Levi was appointed to serve the altar, so it was appointed to live from the altar; no tribe other than that was assigned to the altar’s office, nor was anyone other than that tribe divinely assigned to live from the altar.

If, then, our argument refers to that period in which the Levitical tribe alone, all others being set aside, was preferred for serving the altar, and no other inheritance among its brothers was given to it, it follows quite appropriately, in my judgment,

[Col. 0811A] that all who live from the altar are of Levitical stock. But can the same apply to our time, in which not one tribe of Levi alone, but persons both from Jews and Gentiles are found serving the altar; when we no longer shed the blood of calves in the Temple or in the ancient tabernacle, but in Christ’s Church offer the calves of confessing lips?

Does it, I ask, suit our time to say, “All who serve the altar,” or “all who live from the altar,” “are clerics,” when this could be said of the sons of Levi, who were the predecessors of clerics in this office and whose successors in the Church clerics are? Yet the condition of the present Church seems to me different from that of the Synagogue; and not everything that could plausibly be asserted there about the tribe of Levi can in every respect be applied to the clerics of our time.

To repeat one of the points made above: who would say that all who live from the altar are clerics, when we see many receiving temporal sustenance from the Church whom no one would presume to call clerics? Many, indeed, even laypeople, are permitted to possess ecclesiastical revenues for purposes of administration; and this concession now seems to have acquired such force that no one either ought, or could easily, abolish it, with almost everyone protesting that such a practice ought to prevail by the privilege of antiquity.

[Col. 0811B] In many monasteries we also see women gathered together for the sake of religion, whom common usage calls *sanctimoniales* (“consecrated women”) or nuns; and since offerings and tithes are certainly allotted for their support, it is sufficiently clear that not all who live from the altar are clerics. Finally, the Apostle (1 Tim. 5) wills that a widow of sixty years be enrolled, so that she may receive temporal sustenance from the treasury of the temple; and he earnestly exhorts every believer to provide for his own widows, lest the Church, burdened thereby, have insufficient means for those who are widows in truth. From this it is clear that, although it properly belongs to clerics to live from the altar, nevertheless not all who live from the altar are now clerics.

But just as not all who live from the altar are clerics, so conversely not all clerics live from the altar. We see many clerics to whom no ecclesiastical revenues are granted, who derive no temporal advantage from the altar, but are worn down by poverty,

[Col. 0811C] whether voluntary or perhaps involuntary, or endeavour to procure for themselves elsewhere the necessities of this life. Finally, Paul (1 Thess. 2), although he served the altar, nevertheless did not wish to live from the altar; and although, in proclaiming the Gospel, he fully discharged the demanding duty of a cleric, he nevertheless did not wish to obtain temporal advantage from the Gospel.

Accordingly, as has been said, just as not all who live from the altar are clerics, so not all who are clerics are obliged to live from the altar, although the Law established that the Levitical tribe should live from the altar and that no one other than it should live from the altar.

## CHAPTER CVII

Likewise, unless I am mistaken, not everyone who is a cleric

[Col. 0812A] serves the altar; nor, conversely, is everyone who serves the altar a cleric. The service by which the altar is served may, it seems to me, fittingly be understood in two ways.

For in one sense we serve the altar when we assemble in church before the altar and sound forth in harmonious voice with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, solemnly chanting the hours called regular or canonical. In this way not only clerics or monks, but also nuns or consecrated women are found to serve the altar. For that reason they also maintain, not without justification, that they ought to receive from the Church the necessities of this life, since they perform, as clerics do, that spiritual office—that is, the musical rendering of the written text.

But let this form of service be set aside here, since our monk does not speak of it.

There is another manner of serving, by which service is rendered to the altar more closely and more sacredly. A minister is marked out by sacred orders in order regularly to carry it out; and only one who is found superior to the rest in life and learning is called to those orders, with discernment and to salutary effect. This office has such a prerogative that it is no small harm to those who intrude upon it unworthily; but to those who approach it with humble presumption, or presumptuous humility, it is indeed productive both of perfect salvation and of saving perfection.

[Col. 0812B] A nun does not perform this office, nor does a consecrated woman—not because they possess no holiness or literary learning, but because ecclesiastical authority, which entrusts the altar’s sacraments to holiness and learning, nevertheless does not admit the female sex to perform them.

Accordingly, the presbyter, whose hand has been anointed with sacred oil, makes the body of Christ at the altar by his sacred mouth: applying the sign of the cross and the power of the words, he renders the truly corruptible substance of bread and wine incorruptible, enrolled [*ascriptam*], ratified, through the Spirit’s effective operation, without any doubt whatever; in such a way that the visible appearance is not seen by the eyes to be transformed, while the substance is held by certain faith to have been invisibly changed into another.

A deacon is assigned as the presbyter’s second minister in this office. He is said to be so necessary for carrying out holy things that through him, in the midst of the sacred solemnities, the word of the Gospel is proclaimed, and through him the chalice to be blessed is presented to the presbyter himself.

[Col. 0812C] These two, namely presbyter and deacon, are said to be marked out by sacred orders; therefore they ought to be more learned than others in knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, so that, laudably bound not by the fetters of ignorance but by those of wisdom, they may be found ready both to teach what they have learned and to do what they teach.

Besides these there are others who are also occupied in the ministry of the altar and are ordained by bishops to carry it out. Although they are not denied a degree of holiness, their orders are nevertheless not called sacred. For no one will deny that a subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, or doorkeeper holds a place of holiness, although it is clear that they are subject to presbyters and deacons. For those things which they must provide by right of their order are holy;

[Col. 0812D] and those which presbyter and deacon are commanded to perform are most holy, if anything more can be said.

## CHAPTER CVIII

Since it belongs properly to clerics to hold such orders, and since some monks also hold them, the monk of whom I speak declares himself also to be a cleric for this reason: he too is elevated by sacred orders, which are the cleric’s prerogative. He says that Jerome likewise agrees with this assertion and demonstrates the same point in his works, especially in the letter which he is found to have addressed to Nepotian. In it he carefully instructs both Nepotian and others who are monks and clerics together. This, says the monk, is indicated both by the title of the letter itself

[Col. 0813A] and shown more clearly in the course of the work.

For he says concerning Jerome [Note: [Col. 0813D] Book II, Letter 12]: “Moreover, he writes to Nepotian concerning the life of monks and of those clerics who are at once monks and clerics.” And below: “Nepotian, to whom or on whose account he writes, is one and the same person, both monk and cleric.” And further: “In this one Nepotian he instructs how those who belong to both orders—that is, clerical and monastic—ought to conduct themselves.” And shortly afterward: “For that reason,” he says, “the letter bears this title: *On the Life of Clerics and Monks*, whose priesthood, as Jerome himself says in it, is adorned by their religious purpose, and whose religious purpose is adorned by priesthood.”

With the monk’s permission, neither is the title of the letter found to have that form,

[Col. 0813B] nor is the letter itself known to exhibit such a treatment. The manuscripts which I have been able to inspect promise nothing about monks in the title, but state only that Jerome writes on the life of clerics. Even if, in our manuscripts or in any others, such a title had been introduced through a scribal error, sensible persons would not trust it, since they could find far truer evidence by which they might arrive more certainly at the truth of the matter.

At the very beginning of this letter it is made sufficiently clear that Nepotian earnestly asks Jerome [Note: [Col. 0813D] Jerome, *Letters*, Book II, Letter 12] to write to him how either a cleric or a monk ought to live, one who, abandoning the vanity of the world, has undertaken to serve God more perfectly. But since Nepotian’s uncle Heliodorus, a bishop and a monk, had written him a little book on the formation of monks, Jerome does not presume to repeat the same thing, lest he seem to offer injury to a holy man by placing a second little book upon his little book and brazenly preferring, as it were, his own knowledge to that man’s learning.

[Col. 0813C] Therefore, passing over monks, whom his uncle had instructed in every detail, he writes only about clerics, about whom Nepotian had also requested him to write—lest by writing about the former he deserve to be accused of presumption, or by keeping silent about the latter he seem to disregard a brother’s request.

[Col. 0814A] For he says: “From across the sea, my dearest Nepotian, you ask me by letter—and ask repeatedly—to set forth for you in a short volume precepts for living, and by what rule one who, having abandoned the service of the world, has begun to be either a monk or a cleric may keep to Christ’s straight path, lest he be swept away into the various byways of vices.” And below [Note: [Col. 0814D] There]: “I know,” he says, “that from your blessed uncle Heliodorus, who is now a bishop of Christ, you have both learned holy things and learn them daily, and that you possess the rule of his life as an example of virtues. Yet receive also ours, whatever they may be, and join this little book to his little book: so that, when he has trained you as a monk, this one may teach you to be a perfect cleric.”

You see that, although Nepotian asks him to write a little book of instruction for both clerical and monastic life,

[Col. 0814B] Jerome nevertheless promises to instruct him only as a cleric; and he plainly pursues this point through the whole body of the letter, while he speaks of monks only incidentally two or three times at most.

Finally, when Jerome wrote a letter to a certain Rustic concerning the formation of monks, he stated that the letter mentioned above had been written on the formation of clerics. For he says to him concerning clerics [Note: [Col. 0814D] St Jerome, Book II, Letter 13]: “Let them have their own order; if you keep it, the published book addressed to Nepotian will be able to teach you how you ought to live in it.” Therefore, while Jerome sends Rustic a little book on monastic formation, why does he refer him, for instruction in clerical perfection, to the little book published for Nepotian, unless

[Col. 0814C] because, as the monk is instructed in the one, so the cleric is instructed in the other, and the perfection not of both together in both letters but of each separately in its own letter is defined?

Jerome’s statement to Nepotian—“whose priesthood is adorned by their religious purpose, and whose religious purpose is adorned by priesthood”—is not, as our monk says, spoken conjunctively of persons who are monks and clerics together. Rather, it must be understood disjunctively of clerics and monks, as the very order of the words makes clearer if one attends a little more carefully. For he says: “How much more [is this true] among monks and among clerics, whose priesthood is adorned by their religious purpose, and whose religious purpose is adorned by priesthood!” And shortly after: “This is forbidden by law to clerics and monks alone.”

By saying “how much more among monks and among clerics,” and below, “to clerics and monks alone,” he makes sufficiently clear that he does not mean the same monks as clerics. Instead he speaks distinctly of both groups: their religious purpose is adorned by the dignity of priestly office, and their priestly office by the holiness of religious purpose.

[Col. 0814D] For both groups—clerics and monks—are adorned by religious purpose and graced by priestly office. “How much more,” he says, “among monks and among clerics.” The conjunction *and*, placed between them, regularly joins the two ablatives in the sentence but distinguishes what they signify, so that monks and clerics must be understood as different persons; the meanings of these names are in no way confused by the insertion of *and* or *among*.

## CHAPTER CIX

As for the monk’s statement that Nepotian, to whom or for whose sake Jerome wrote this letter, was one and the same person, monk and cleric together, I do not see how he can prove this. For it is not read in the letter that he was a monk, nor do I recall ever reading it anywhere else. Although his uncle Heliodorus wrote him a little book explaining how a monk ought to live, this does not show that Nepotian was a monk. Even if he wished to be instructed by reading in monastic perfection, perhaps he did not wish to experience monastic life by living it.

Jerome, however, is found to call him a cleric not only in this letter, in which he wished to instruct both him and, in him, other clerics, but also elsewhere, when he mourns grievously and beyond repair the loss occasioned by Nepotian’s premature death.

[Col. 0815A] Writing to Bishop Heliodorus, whom he knew to be inconsolably grieved at his nephew’s death, and wishing to console him in compassionate speech, he says among other things about Nepotian [Note: [Col. 0815D] Jerome, *Letters*, Book II, Letter 22]: “Why say more? He becomes a cleric and is ordained presbyter through the customary grades.”

Nor should it trouble anyone if Jerome, or any other saint, is sometimes found to call monks “clerics,” adorning them with another’s title on account of some incidental reason. For sometimes a monk either intrudes himself into performing a cleric’s function or perhaps is invited to do so, and because of the office he has undertaken is called a cleric. Jerome indicates this when he earnestly exhorts the monk Rustic to live in monasticism in such a way that he may eventually deserve to become a cleric [Note: [Col. 0815D] Book II, Letter 13]: “Conduct yourself and live in the monastery so that you may deserve to be a cleric when you have reached mature age; provided that life attends you and either the people or the bishop of the city chooses you as a cleric. Perform the duties of clerics, and among them follow the better men.”

[Col. 0815B] So too my Augustine, in the statement cited above: “When a good monk scarcely makes a good cleric.” But your charity should know that this manner of speech is improper; nor is the sequence of the divine Scriptures so clear and serene as to be altogether free from the obscurity of impropriety.

Therefore I wonder that the monk, whom I know to have been exceptionally learned, did not notice that this is more commonly used in the Scriptures: when someone does what is assigned as proper to another, he takes from that other a borrowed name. Thus the Lord in the Gospel called an apostle a devil, because that man had claimed for himself a devilish office. “Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6). He did not say, “One of you does what belongs to the devil,” which could properly have been said; but “One of you is a devil,” which is plainly said improperly, because the name was suitably applied to him only by an improper form of speech—he whose work or office he performed.

[Col. 0815C] There is no doubt, however, that what that apostle pursued was the work of the devil, concerning whose work the Lord elsewhere spoke to the Jews: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the works of your father” (John 8). This impropriety is also found to have a considerable place in ordinary speech; anyone who attends more carefully will readily be able to perceive it.

## CHAPTER CX

You know that applying oneself to knowledge of the Scriptures belongs so properly to clerics that whoever wishes to become a cleric must necessarily be educated in letters, and without at least some knowledge of them scarcely anyone—or no one—is considered a cleric. Hence common usage has prevailed that, whenever we see someone learned, we immediately call him a cleric; and because he does what clerics do, we assign him the name from their office.

If anyone compares a learned soldier with an illiterate presbyter, he will confidently exclaim and affirm on oath that this soldier is a better cleric than the presbyter: for the soldier reads, understands, dictates, composes verse, and, when speaking Latin among clerics, is approved as ignorant of solecism; whereas the presbyter not only does not know how to compose a grammatically irreproachable sentence, but perhaps cannot even chant Compline alone in the prescribed manner.

[Col. 0816A] Yet we know without doubt that the soldier whom we call a better cleric than the presbyter is not a cleric. But the use of improper speech has become so prevalent that one who applies himself to letters, which is a cleric’s task, is called a cleric, although it is not at all doubted that he is not one.

Finally, when, for kindness and charity’s sake, we visit a monk concerning whom we do not yet know whether he knows letters or not, we ask him whether he is a cleric—not seeking to know whether he has been ordained to perform the altar’s office, but only whether he is learned. In answering the question accordingly, he says that he is a cleric if he is literate, but conversely a layman if he is illiterate.

Among consecrated women and monks who serve God in the Church through literary labour, if any person is found more thoroughly educated in letters, she is called a “good cleric” by improper, not proper, speech; and in this nothing other than her learning is praised.

[Col. 0816B] Once, in my presence, a man religious in conduct and dress entered a certain church and found a consecrated woman, mature both in age and learning, standing before the altar with a little book in her hands. Among the other things they seriously discussed, he asked her what she was holding—namely, what the little book held in her hands contained. She replied: “The life of a certain virgin, which I composed and committed to writing when I was a young woman.” And she added: “For I was a good cleric.”

[Col. 0816C] By these words I understood nothing other than that she had been well educated, since in her youth she had written a virgin’s life. Likewise, concerning certain other women whom I know either to be, or to have been, highly learned, I recall frequently hearing that, when discussion arose concerning the learning of any one of them, she herself was said to be a “good cleric.”

And I wonder why, when clerical learning is praised in a woman, she is called not *bona clerica* (“a good female cleric”) but *bonus clericus* (“a good cleric”), although it would seem much more fitting that, as *monacha* is derived from *monachus*, so *clerica* should be derived from *clericus*. Those whom it is known live in a monastery under a religious habit I find called *sanctimoniales*, *nonnae*, or *monachae* in the works of the Fathers; but whether I have ever found them called *clericae* in writing I cannot recall,

[Col. 0816D] nor do I hear anyone who speaks Latin call any women so.

Why this is the case is not sufficiently clear to me, unless perhaps it serves to refute our monk’s opinion: he supposes that monks whom he hears called clerics are clerics, without noticing that even a well-educated woman, though she is not a cleric, is nevertheless judged to be a “good cleric.” The monk himself also plainly admits in this disputation that the reality of clerical status does not consist in knowledge of letters. Thus, undoubtedly, his own testimony proves that not everyone who is called a cleric is truly a cleric.

## CHAPTER CXI

Finally, if one who does what a cleric does is a cleric, is not one who does what a monk does also a monk, and one who does what a soldier does a soldier? If so, the order of things will be no small measure confused; no profession will be distinguished; it will not be easy to know what each person ought to be called. For in every profession there is very rarely a person who does not perform something proper to another profession.

You know that riding a horse has from ancient times been assigned as something almost proper to soldiers, so that the very name *eques* (“horseman, knight”) is derived from the horse, and the equestrian order is named from the *eques*, that is, the soldiers of whom it is said to consist.

[Col. 0817A] Will everyone who is permitted to ride a horse then claim to belong to the equestrian order? And because he does what a soldier does, will he compare himself with a soldier? We now see permission to ride granted so widely and extensively to everyone that we do not find even monks forbidden it; indeed, scarcely any monk can now be found who can or wishes to experience on foot the labour of a long journey.

What village, street, or market-place does not have monks riding horses? Who, on leaving his house, does not immediately find them coming to meet him? What festival, what fair is celebrated without monks? What assembly of men, what clash of soldiers is brought to an end without them? When soldiers gather from every direction and from different regions for the sake of fighting, rejoicing with the collision of shields, the crash of lances, and pitiable fury, if monks were denied the privilege of riding, perhaps so great a multitude of them would not be seen there.

[Col. 0817B] But who could predict the imminent destruction of wretched corpses unless a multitude of ravens flew together for plunder, so that from their unwelcome presence one might easily know in advance that such a customary spectacle will not end without loss of souls? Hence some soldiers are often violently angered when, having spurred on their horses, they strive vigorously to advance against their opponents, but are met by monks on horseback and are either ineffectually turned aside from their purpose or shamefully collapse in the very engagement, disappointed of their hope.

One of them, coming to himself, says: “Now I know that, when a monk mounted on a horse met me—or rather, when the devil mounted upon that monk met me—such a meeting foretold nothing prosperous for me; and by such an omen this kind of defeat could easily have been avoided, if my mind had not been ill-omened.”

Therefore we must not assign everything belonging to a soldier to all who sit upon a horse, lest we be compelled to attach the military name to monks as well.

It is also proper to a soldier to be girded with a sword, so that whoever among us enters upon the military profession is girded with a sword at the very entrance to that profession; nor does he presume to enter its threshold unless protected by such a sign.

[Col. 0817C] For since one who contends in the contest of battle is judged readier with his loins girded, and manly boldness for fighting is considerably strengthened by taking up the sword, secular military custom very fittingly decided that its novice should be girded with a sword-belt. By such a mystery, at the very threshold of service, the novice must be taught how he ought both to free himself from the wrinkled confines of harmful timidity and to fortify himself manfully with a keen and vigorous spirit; lest, with a slack heart, he inflict a disgraceful loss full of cowardice, but rather let manly boldness provide the triumphant defence.

For the sake of this triumph the Redeemer of the human race is likewise exhorted to gird himself with a sword when he is said to come to defeat the ruler of the world: “Gird thyself with thy sword, O most mighty one.” What does “O most mighty one” mean? That he may not ungird himself until victory is completed after the enemies have been subdued.

## CHAPTER CXII

Isaiah also clearly indicated that a soldier ought not to ungird himself before victory when he prophesied that the Roman army would come against Judaea: “Behold,” he says, “it will come swiftly and speedily. There is none faint or weary among them; none slumbers or sleeps,

[Col. 0817D] nor is the belt of his loins loosened” (Isa. 5).

For because the Jews had killed Christ, divine vengeance stirred up the Roman soldier against them with such fury, and the avenging spirit inspired him with such love of battle, that, as he hastened impatient of delay to subdue the Jews’ insolence, eager to conquer, he was not overcome by weakness or weariness; he did not sleep through dullness or cowardice; nor, finally, did he loosen the sword-belt from his loins until he had triumphed over his enemies with a successful outcome and placed the victorious eagles in the security of peace and glory.

For a soldier should neither glory while he is still in battle, until he is ungirded, nor is it fitting that he should ungird himself before he has obtained victory. Thus Ahab, king of Samaria, is read to have answered Ben-hadad, king of Syria, and in doing so to have wisely instructed every soldier.

When Ben-hadad threatened that he would shortly overthrow Samaria and leave not even dust in it, he sent messengers to Ahab king of Israel, through whom he insolently taunted him, already swollen with hope of victory as though the deed were accomplished.

[Col. 0818A] “May the gods do so to me, and add yet more, if the dust of Samaria will suffice for the handfuls of all the people who follow me” (3 Kings 20). But Ahab, considering that the outcome was still uncertain, and that the end of a matter often does not accord with its beginning, bore the king’s threats patiently enough and sent back an apt reply to the man who threatened him: “Tell him: Let not one who is girded boast as one who is ungirded.”

For a soldier is girded with a sword when he prepares for battle, but ungirded when he is rather crowned with victory. Therefore it belongs to one who is girded to strengthen himself manfully in hope and silence; but to one ungirded, having attained peace and leisure, to glory beneath the shelter of security.

It was therefore well said that the sword-belt is assigned as proper to a soldier, since by its aid battle is brought to its due conclusion. But will every person who girds himself with a sword, which is a soldier’s implement, properly be—or be called—a soldier? Has the military profession been able to obtain this: that a sword may be permitted to no one but a soldier, and that whoever is girded with a sword, whether at home or on campaign, should consequently be regarded as a soldier?

[Col. 0818B] No. On the contrary, in our times swords are manufactured in such abundance that much iron is consumed in making them, because scarcely anyone among the people can now be found who, intending to travel any considerable distance, does not hasten to fortify his side with a sword. For even if no need should arise during the journey to draw the sword, its carrying nevertheless seems a commendable custom, lest the traveller be reproached as unprudent and faint-hearted if he walks with womanish security, without the protection of a sword.

## CHAPTER CXIII
Here, however, the use of the sword—which military rank ought to have secured for itself as though its own special possession—is now granted not only to those who everywhere belong to the common people; I also hear that some clerics arrogate something of this kind to themselves, and cloak the stain of this usurpation with the covering of necessity. In the province of Auvergne, in the town of Brioude, the blessed martyr Julian has a church, in which it is known that several canons, noble by birth and exceedingly rich in wealth [Col. 0819D] and honor, serve in clerical office, and receive considerable revenues from that church. But because that province is not held under laws of firm peace, and because the stronger does not hesitate to inflict injuries upon the weaker, neighboring princes have often presumed to seize for themselves by rapacious assault the goods of the aforesaid church, and, without any regard for God, to make restitution for what they had taken.

Since for a long time no more powerful person took care to prevent this violence, nor could ecclesiastical censure restrain them within the bounds of peace, the clerics, unable longer to endure the loss of their possessions, adopted a new plan against the wickedness of the plunderers. For it seemed good to them that those whom they could not deter from robbery by the spiritual sword, they should try more effectively to prevent by the material sword [Col. 0820A], and that they should protect the goods of their church by military vigilance, lest through clerical patience they should at last be reduced to nothing.

They therefore take up arms, gird themselves manfully with swords, summon both relatives and other dependents, and advance into the very forefront of the affair. They not only refuse altogether to suffer what is theirs to be taken away, but also endeavor violently to reclaim what has been taken—indeed, to render the plunderers a fitting return with their own hands. They resist attackers and labor to overcome those who resist them: no longer bringing forth the sword of the word of God, which their insensible enemies despised as ineffective, but striking with the visible sword, whose weight the carnal perceive carnally to hang over them.

Thus even today they are found to perform both offices in turn: namely [Col. 0820B], when necessity requires, to threaten enemies severely; and, when arms have been laid aside and stored at home, to devote themselves to spiritual songs. Outside, they guard the temporal goods of the church by hand and sword; inside, regularly chanting psalms and hymns, they serve that same church. This, certainly, does not escape ecclesiastical shepherds, bishops, and apostolic authorities. But because they see it done not so much voluntarily as necessarily, they are compelled somehow to tolerate it, lest the church be forced to suffer irreparable losses, though they themselves cannot otherwise provide for its peace and tranquility.

But when, as I have heard, certain apostolic authorities once tried to prohibit such an impropriety, maintaining that it was utterly alien to the clerical calling, either the practice itself, or rather [Col. 0820C] necessity, proved so powerful that they could not secure its abolition without greater scandal. Clerics, then, perform military service, whether by usurpation or, as they prefer to say, by permission: thus properly carrying out what belongs to a cleric in church, while, when necessity demands, they incidentally do what belongs to a soldier.

But why have I said these things about men whom I do not know by sight, though I have learned of them from persons who both saw and knew them? Clearly, that you may see that not everyone who does what belongs to another is thereby also what that other is, although he may sometimes be called what that other is. For although those clerics may be called soldiers by someone on account of their usurped function, they do not themselves profess to be soldiers; indeed, they consider it a grave injury [Col. 0820D] if anyone, calling them clerics, insists that soldiers must also be included under that designation. For they are not at once clerics and soldiers: they are clerics only, although they are sometimes found to do, by usurpation—or, as was said shortly before, by permission—what belongs to a soldier. Likewise, not everyone who performs a monk’s office is a monk.

## CHAPTER CXIV

Above you heard that a monk’s work is fasting, vigils, labor, mourning, and silence. Jerome also says that the monk has the office of one who mourns. Is everyone, then, who is found doing these things a monk? So far as I can see, he is not. For even if the name “monk” is applied to someone because he is afflicted by labor, fasting, grief, and tears [Col. 0821A], such speech is not rightly judged proper, nor is he thereby truly affirmed to be a monk.

It often happens that someone placed in a secular rank or dress chooses there to live somewhat more modestly: while others devote themselves to idleness, he occupies himself with some useful work; while others run about through the streets, he perhaps remains in church; while others feast joyously, he wears himself down by fasting and abstinence; while others give themselves to laughter and loud merriment, he weeps silently within the chamber of prayer. Because this harshness of life is especially prescribed to monks, one who has lived in this way is sometimes called a monk. Yet although the dress and profession of one living thus are far from those of a monk, the improper speech of an observer gives him that name: “This man,” he says, “whom I see living in this way deserves to be called not so much what he is as a monk.”

Hence it is that, in the little book in which you hear the feasts of the saints recited and their virtues and merits briefly commended, Queen Radegund—who was compelled to lie in Clothar’s bed by right of marriage—is nevertheless called not a wife but a monk [Col. 0821B]. For it says: “Radegund,” it says, “queen, who, reclining in the bed of Clothar, king of the Franks, was called rather a monk than a wife.” If, with her husband’s permission, the queen, fervent in spirit, shrank from sexual union and in the royal bed devoted herself to continence, vigils, prayers, and tears, would she therefore truly be affirmed to be a monk, even though some call her a monk by an usurped manner of speech? The truth of the matter does not appear to be so [Col. 0821C].

Likewise Jerome commends Nepotianus, of whom we spoke above, because, while he honorably fulfilled the office of clerics outside, upon returning home he embraced the austerity of monks: outside acting as a cleric, exhorting widows and virgins with chaste words; inside imitating a monk, mortifying his flesh with tears, vigils, and fasts. “Honor,” he says, “the widows and virgins of Christ as mothers; exhort them as sisters, with all chastity.” This concerns the office of clerics. And he adds: “But after he had withdrawn home, and left the cleric outside, he gave himself over to the austerity of monks: frequent in prayers, watchful in supplication, he offered tears to God, not to men; he regulated fasts according to fatigue and the strength of his body.” This concerns the austerity of monks.

In these matters Nepotianus imitated his maternal uncle, both bishop and monk, as Jerome himself declares a little earlier: “In one and the same person,” he says, “namely in his uncle, without doubt he both imitated the monk and revered the bishop” [Col. 0821D]. From these words our monk seems to me to have inferred that Nepotianus should rightly be considered a monk, as though only a monk could imitate a monk. Yet Nepotianus unquestionably also imitated that same uncle as bishop, and nevertheless was not considered a bishop. If anyone stubbornly wishes to affirm that he was a monk, I yield, lest, while disputing, I seem to do what is unfitting for a servant of God—provided only that this be held certain: if he properly was a monk, he is improperly called a cleric.

Otherwise, if one who is a monk were also properly called a cleric, so that, because he does what belongs to a cleric, he were truly considered a cleric, then as much honor and distinction as this would confer upon the monastic order, so much disgrace would be brought upon it from another direction by the same reasoning [Col. 0822A].

## CHAPTER CXV

For just as Jerome calls one who is a monk also a cleric when he does what belongs to a cleric, so he calls the same person a bridegroom when he does what belongs to a bridegroom. He saw that many monks wished for this reason to be elevated to sacred orders: that, once ordained, they might deserve to be invited to ecclesiastical responsibilities, and, once invited, might be able not so much to fulfill the clerical office more religiously than others as, under this pretext, to attach themselves to pleasures.

For when those brought out of the cloister were assigned the governance of the people, in order that by religion and learning they might supply the role or office of clerics [Col. 0822B], they so loosened the reins of their rule and regular purpose that they displayed themselves not so much as clerics as bridegrooms, by the character of their secular lives. Abhorring monastic lowliness, they appeared so refined in face and dress, and sought women’s conversations with such unrestrained habits, that in them there shone not so much monastic religion, or even clerical religion, as the extravagance of worldly behavior and the license of married life.

Speaking to the virgin Eustochium of such men, Jerome says:

> “There are others,” he says—“I speak of men of my own order”—“who seek the presbyterate and diaconate in order that they may see women more freely. All their care is for their clothing: that they may smell pleasant; that the foot may not swell in loose skin; their hair is curled with the curling iron; their fingers shine with rings; and, lest a damp road splash their soles, they scarcely set down the tips of their feet. When you see such men,” he says, “consider them bridegrooms rather than clerics.”

[Note: [Col. 0821D] Jerome, *To Eustochium*, “On the Guardianship of Virginity.”]

You see that monks who hurry to be ordained not for the sake of religion, but in order that they may roam more freely in the broad field of secular life and take pleasure in fine clothes and the sight of women, ought to be regarded as bridegrooms rather than clerics. By what arguments, then, can our monk resist the conclusion that monks of this kind must truly be affirmed to be bridegrooms, since they both do what undoubtedly belongs to bridegrooms and are known to be called bridegrooms by Jerome?

Jerome likewise represented Jovinian, of whom we spoke above, as such a person: abhorring monastic dirtiness, he showed him to possess the luxuries of bridegrooms. “That handsome monk,” he says, “fat, sleek, whitened, and always walking about as though he were a bridegroom” [Col. 0822D]. If, then, they are both monks and bridegrooms because they embrace bridal license and are called bridegrooms by Jerome, I grant that they should similarly be considered clerics because they do what belongs to clerics and are adorned with their name. But if they are not bridegrooms, although Jerome calls them so because of their bridal actions, perhaps they will not be clerics either, although they are sometimes called clerics because of clerical office.

Finally, I do not think Jerome ought to be indignant with me if I say that one who is a monk is properly called neither bridegroom nor cleric; rather, he may all the more freely be called either, because he properly can be called neither. For, unless I am mistaken, one who is a monk cannot properly be called either bridegroom, soldier, or cleric; nor, conversely, can any of these properly be called a monk, although one often seems to perform another’s office in such a way that neither is considered content with his own proper identity [Col. 0823A].

## CHAPTER CXVI

It is fitting, then, that we finally see who is properly a cleric, lest, darkened by ignorance, we wander into the path of error by stubbornly affirming that one who is not a cleric is one, or conversely denying that one who is one is a cleric. Just as there is a monastic order, and just as there is a military order [Col. 0823B], so too there is a clerical order or profession.

When someone seeks to enter the threshold of this order or profession, in order to serve God there more familiarly, at the very entrance he takes up the clerical tonsure and dress, knowing that among the wedding guests he is not counted who has not a wedding garment. Therefore, when he promises to live as a cleric, so that his vow and undertaking may be evident to others as well, he shaves his head and changes his clothing, according to the customary practice among clerics; and so by voice, appearance, and dress professes himself a cleric.

Such, indeed, was the institution of the Fathers’ careful wisdom. Thus the Church maintains to this day that one who has not taken up this manner of profession is not properly called a cleric; while one who has maintained what he assumed is undoubtedly considered a cleric. Our present discussion does not concern the holiness which such a profession is commanded to possess. Without it, as was said above, clerics are not sufficiently and truly what they are called, because they are called so to no purpose. For he falsely—that is, in vain—glories in the clerical name who does not endeavor to adorn the name with merits. Therefore, when a person of this sort is denied to be a cleric, the title of the profession is not annulled; the degenerate life of the professed person is condemned.

Accordingly, one who has assumed and maintained this profession is called a cleric in the proper manner of speech, because this name is assigned as proper not to religious devotion but to profession. For the assumption of this profession is a kind of seal of religion [Col. 0823D], not religion itself; and so long as the outward display remains upon the professed person, even though inward religious affection does not cultivate his conduct, the unanimous assertion of all nevertheless commonly declares him a cleric.

Otherwise, if everyone who is not religious thereby ceases also to be a cleric, not only would an innumerable multitude of clerics suffer loss of its number, but perhaps the countless army of monks too would be reduced to its former smallness. Nor do I think religious monks would be offended if I said that their order contains within its bounds a great many who boast that they maintain the monastic profession in speech, appearance, and dress, yet apply either no care or only the slightest care to reforming their lives worthily.

Therefore, lest an intolerable injury be inflicted on both the monastic and clerical orders, let each retain its privilege unimpaired: namely, that one who is enclosed under the title of an assumed profession must not be denied to belong to the order whose character he bears [Col. 0824A].

Finally, Christ wishes the person whom He wishes truly to honor with the dignity of the Christian name to be adorned also with the title of Christian profession, lest anyone perhaps think himself to be counted a Christian who refuses to be enclosed under the sacraments of faith. “Baptizing them,” He says, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” And: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess before my Father.” Baptism, therefore, and oral confession of the Christian faith are a kind of outward manifestation. To lack this is undoubtedly so harmful that one who does not retain the manifestation of faith is not even called a believer.

Hence, when the Apocalypse was read, you heard that Christ promises each believer as a great gift: “I will write upon him the name of my God, and my new name” (Rev. 3) [Col. 0824B]. Christ writes the name of His God upon one whom He enrolls in the number of the faithful, so that he is no longer called a son of Adam, from whom he is carnally begotten unto death, but a son of God, by whom he is adopted unto life through the grace of Christ Himself. Hence it is written elsewhere: “He gave them power to become children of God” (John 1).

But since no one now deserves to be called a son of God unless he has received from Christ the name Christian, Christ promises to write His own new name likewise upon the one whom He admits among His adopted children. “And my new name,” He says. The new name is the Christian name [Col. 0824C], by which every believer, with new grace shining forth, is so adorned that without this splendor of the name he is considered neither a believer nor a son of God.

But because it is not enough for someone to embrace in his heart, as a matter of memory, the name of God or the name of Christ, unless he is also instructed outwardly through the saving sacraments of faith, Christ does not say, “I shall place the name in him,” but, “I shall write upon him,” so that from the inscription written over the threshold all may know to whom that dwelling should be assigned.

For a person is said, as it were, to wear the title of faith on his forehead when he professes the Christian religion by visible signs: when he is washed in the flowing water of baptism under its judgment, and confesses with his mouth. Whoever despises being inscribed with such a seal will deserve not to be enrolled among the children of God.

## CHAPTER CXVII

[Col. 0824D]

Accordingly, later in the same Apocalypse John says that he saw a multitude of the elect, whom he declares to have had such writing upon their foreheads:

> “I looked, and behold, the Lamb stood upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name and the name of his Father written upon their foreheads” (Rev. 14).

This Lamb is Christ, who, leaving in the heavenly wilderness the ninety-nine little sheep that were nourished by life-giving sustenance beneath the Father’s hand, came to seek the hundredth—that is, human beings wandering through the paths of death. Since every animal is more easily turned toward what is like itself, He who was God became a Lamb, in order to recall the lost sheep with a matching bleat, lest it wander longer, straying amid the flocks of goats.

Having become a Lamb [Col. 0825A], He was seen standing upon Mount Zion because He had come to aid His elect: He who was to sit in the Church, granting it the glory of reigning with Him, first stood among it, bestowing the grace of assistance. Isaiah, filled with the divine Spirit, ardently desired this and, raised into hope and impatient of delay, prophesied in prayer: “Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16).

By the name “wilderness” he wished to signify heaven, which man or angel deserted by sinning, and in which each might have remained securely, as upon a rock, had he wished to cling more faithfully to his Creator. Or perhaps heaven is called a wilderness because Christ, as it were, deserted it when, having assumed flesh, He appeared visible to us; when, leaving the ninety-nine sheep there, as though He had no further concern for those He knew to be safe, He came to seek the hundredth, so as to carry it back to the sheepfolds upon His shoulders.

The rock of the wilderness is the solidity of the heavenly dwelling, which Christ is said, as it were, to have deserted in satisfying the will of the Father’s command. He who, according to the prophet, ineffably went forth from the highest heaven (Ps. 18), mercifully undertook our unstable course of life [Col. 0825B]. “I came forth from the Father,” He says, “and came into the world” (John 16).

The prophet therefore prays that God the Father may make the Son—ruler indeed over the multitude of heavenly angels—the ruler of earthly human beings; and that from the rock of the wilderness, that is, from that hidden dwelling, He may send the Lamb, innocent and recalling human flocks to the pastures of life, to Mount Zion—that is, to the Church, then already contemplating heavenly things in its few members through hope and desire. “Send forth,” he says, “O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16).

What Isaiah so earnestly prays may come to pass, John the apostle rejoices to have seen already accomplished: for he saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, that is, above the height of the elect who contemplate, and with Him one hundred and forty-four thousand who were sealed. For none is now found with Christ except one marked by the inscription of the Christian name, who has chosen to have His name and the name of His Father visibly written on the forehead—that is, to display himself as a Christian and a son of God under the title of profession [Col. 0825C].

> “Having,” he says, “his name and the name of his Father written upon their foreheads” (Rev. 22).

Perceiving this, Antichrist, who seeks to be thought Christ and to oppose Christ most vehemently both in action and name, wishes those whom he compels, whether by entreaty or threats, to serve him also to be marked on their foreheads with his own character. For he too has his own character, by which all who are seduced into his retinue are more visibly inscribed. By this title they are separated from the worshipers of the true faith, and it is known, both among themselves and to everyone else, whose they are.

Thus it is also read in the Apocalypse:

> “He will cause all, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, to have a character upon their right hand or upon their foreheads, so that no one may buy or sell unless he has the character of the beast” (Rev. 13).

That lost man, who deserves even more expressly to be called not merely beastlike but a beast—because, wholly given over to bodily hay, he savors nothing but earth—wishes, I say, that no commerce of human society should be permitted among his apostates unless it is secured by a certain seal of apostasy, unless one rejoices to bear on forehead and hand the character, that is, the mark of crime: on the forehead, so that profession may be displayed; on the hand, so that action may be displayed [Col. 0826A].

Hence later, when the victory of saints, martyrs, and confessors is proclaimed, this is laudably assigned to them as their merit: that they received the character of this beast neither on their foreheads nor on their hands—that is, they showed themselves to be his followers neither by profession nor by action.

> “And I saw,” he says, “the souls of those beheaded on account of the testimony of Jesus, and those who did not worship the beast or its image, nor receive its character on their foreheads or on their hands; and they conquered and reigned with Christ” (Rev. 20).

Therefore Christians will be those who bear Christ’s character; and anti-Christians will be those who bear Antichrist’s character [Col. 0826B].

## CHAPTER CXVIII

Those who are enclosed within the wide compass of the Christian name, and thereby, as said above, separated from anti-Christians, are also distinguished among themselves by certain particular marks. By that distinction one knows not what faith they hold, but to what order they belong. For among them one order is clerical, another monastic, another military [Col. 0826C]. Each is designated by its own properties, so that, as they are distinguished by names, so too they are distinguished by characters.

Each person has his own name, by which he is, as it were, properly named, and his own character, which is assigned as proper to that name. Thus no one should be marked with such a character without such a name, nor found among those who bear that name without such a character. A cleric, therefore, will be one who has assumed the clerical profession and maintained what he assumed, so that in him one considers not merit but purpose, when judgment concerns him not according to conduct but according to character.

For whoever has lawfully acquired the manner of making that profession which the Fathers instituted for making a cleric—namely, that he profess himself a cleric by voice, tonsure, and dress—must undoubtedly be accounted a cleric [Col. 0826D]. There are indeed certain grades or orders by which one approaches the altar; through advancement in them, an acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, or priest is said to stand at the altar. Authority willed these orders to be assigned to clerics, so that in the primitive Church none but they might lawfully minister at the altar.

But not all clerics are promoted to these orders, because such promotion does not make a cleric; assumed profession does. For many, having undertaken to profess themselves clerics, either do not wish or are unable to be promoted to these orders. Yet no sane person claims that they must be removed from the number of clerics; indeed ecclesiastical censure says that they ought to be kept within their stated commitment [Col. 0827A].

I remember that, when as a rather young boy I was living in a certain city for the sake of study, there were there two men who in childhood had assumed the clerical profession but, repenting of their commitment, had lapsed back into the lay condition. Persisting in it, they had spent the years of youth; and now, their heads sprinkled with gray, they were preparing to enter the threshold of old age.

The bishop thought it good to admonish them to return to their commitment, lest the clerical order continue any longer to be exposed to mockery because of them. For rumor frequently circulated that they had been clerics, and the mockery of many people repeatedly cast this in the teeth of clerics. When, therefore, people were coming from every direction in the usual manner to hold a synod [Col. 0827B], so that ecclesiastical affairs might be dealt with canonically, what seemed useful might be established by due authority, and whatever had perhaps been weakened might be compelled to return to its former state, the bishop publicly admonished the men just mentioned to return to the clerical profession which they had abandoned, threatening to bring a sentence of condemnation upon them unless they obeyed the admonitions.

But they answered that, while as boys they had studied letters for some time in schools, they had never at all been clerics. In response, the harmonious testimony of certain clerics was heard; especially the dean of the church, a man noble in birth and mature in age, affirmed that they had indeed devoted themselves with him to literary study in the schools and had been marked with clerical tonsure and dress. On hearing this, the synod judged without hesitation that they must return to the clerical state; and the bishop confirmed the judgment by due authority. When the council was dissolved at the approach of evening, each returned home.

The next day, when the clerics had gathered and the synod was again in session, and no public discussion concerning those apostates was taking place, behold: one of them, having shaved his beard, shaved his tonsure, cut his hair round, and put on clerical dress, came to the synod and sat among the other clerics. Many rejoiced and marveled that he had been changed both in spirit and in dress, and that he had not delayed returning to the honor and order of clerical status [Col. 0827C]. The other, though somewhat more slowly, was nevertheless compelled to return, not daring to oppose ineffectually either the synodal judgment or the bishop’s command.

Thus both renounced the lay condition, and from that time remained and continued in clerical manner of life and dress. Neither has yet been stripped of the bodily burden; indeed each is still living this temporal life. Therefore a person is judged to be a cleric not because of the orders through which one ministers at the altar, but because of the profession he has assumed. For those who were removed from lay status by synodal judgment were promoted to no ministry of the altar either before or afterward [Col. 0827D].

## CHAPTER CXIX

Not only among those who, because they hold the reins of life more loosely, are called secular clerics, but also among those who, because of a stricter commitment, are called regulars, many may be found who do not hold altar-orders and yet are truly affirmed to be clerics, with no one dissenting [Col. 0828A].

When, as a boy already somewhat grown, I was presented to the bishop so that he might make me a cleric, I bent before him on my knees as I had been instructed. Over my head he chanted the psalms which he knew to be suitable for this office, and, removing me from the lay condition, transformed me by a change of appearance and dress. For he clothed me in clerical attire and marked the crown of my head with the sign of tonsure, so that henceforth not only my own speech would acknowledge me to be a cleric, but, even if that were silent, my appearance and dress would speak.

The bishop, certainly, commended this by devout prayer and confirmed it by due blessing. Yet at that time he did not ordain me to perform the office of the altar, but merely made me a cleric according to the practice instituted by the Fathers. For some years, then, I remained in the state which I knew I had attained, seeking nothing more than what I knew I had assumed: thus gladly proclaiming myself a cleric by voice, appearance, and dress, yet neither holding nor seeking those grades or orders by which one approaches the altar [Col. 0828B].

Remaining in what I had professed from boyhood, I eventually entered the bounds of adolescence. Powerful nature, eager to make me, as it were, another person by years rather than merits, was clothing my cheeks with a slight down. Driving away the tender and hitherto boyish face, it strove by forceful effort to bring on a youthful one, granting an increase of new age while not knowing, or being unable, to grant at the same time any new holiness [Col. 0828C].

But the grace of God, stronger than nature, struck me with the blow of fear and knocked from my hands the frivolities of former vanity, warning—indeed compelling—me that I, who rejoiced to profess myself a cleric, should no longer delay submitting to the laws of clerical religious life. Drawn, therefore, by a welcome compulsion, I did not shrink from obeying these admonitions. I fled to the harbor of the monastery for the sake of religion, and there I placed my feet in the fetters of the regular life, whose binding seemed to me a saving bond.

There I lived for almost a whole year before I was promoted to orders, before I was in any way assigned to minister at the altar. I lived among clerics in such a manner that no one denied that I too was a cleric, and no one separated me from either their number or their name [Col. 0828D]—not because of any worthy height of virtue or office of the altar, which I did not deserve to obtain, but because of the clerical profession, under whose title or character I was included.

You too, brothers, often see some living among you who, having renounced their former habits and secular life, enter the cloister to live under the discipline of regular obedience. No one doubts that they are already counted among clerics both in fact and in name, and yet they have not been promoted to orders. For not all who become clerics immediately desire or are compelled to minister at the altar. Indeed, very many are delayed from orders, either unwillingly or willingly, yet are not removed from under the clerical title. Finally [Col. 0829A], that title does not declare them ordained, but merely made clerics; it does not indicate by what grade or order they come to stand before the altar, but of what profession they ought to be judged.

## CHAPTER CXX

For it is fitting that each profession be designated by its own character. Otherwise its identity could not easily be known if one erred in the title, as it were, and at the doors: if one who rejoices to be a cleric wishes to appear a monk, or one who wishes to be a monk rejoices to be included under the clerical title.

A certain teacher of clerics is found to have carefully forbidden this practice, wishing each profession to retain its own title as proper to it, so that when the outward sign is seen, the inward identity may not be doubted [Col. 0829B]. For some clerics, not knowing what boundary ought to contain the clerical profession, when in times of affliction they wished to conduct themselves more religiously, would temporarily take up monastic clothing, so that their devotion might be displayed by black and rough dress and the borrowed abasement might seem fitting to the occasion.

He rebukes them for erroneous vanity, because they wrongfully assume for themselves the title of falsehood: the clerical profession ought not to be darkened by monastic dress, just as the monastic profession ought not to be designated by a clerical character. Each person, he says, ought to be dressed in the way which is known by customary right to be assigned to his profession, so that, when the professed person does not continually speak for himself, the continual proclamation of his clothing may reveal what his profession is.

He therefore says that one who is a cleric ought not to appear a monk, unless perhaps, laying aside the cleric, he wishes to profess himself a monk; lest, if the title does not appear to accord with his profession, he be thought falsely to be what he truly does not wish to be [Col. 0829C]. Here he makes no mention of the orders through which one approaches the altar, nor does he say that monastic dress is inconsistent with them. Rather, he says it is inconsistent with that profession by which one is lawfully made a cleric, a profession designated by its own character, just as monastic profession is.

For one is not a cleric because he is promoted to minister at the altar, but because he professes himself a cleric by clerical manner and custom—that is, because he is found to have assumed the clerical profession and, by definite signs, to remain in what he assumed. But one who either has not assumed such a profession or has abandoned it after assuming it is not a cleric, just as one who does not profess himself a monk is not a monk.

Therefore, when we see many monks who have never assumed the clerical profession and have never borne its character, but have passed from lay rank into monastic rank without passing through clerical rank and have remained in it by grace’s favor, who, I ask, would call such men clerics, even though he sees them standing at the altar [Col. 0829D]?
