Who, I ask, presumes to call himself a monk if he does not assume the monastic profession, if he never wishes to be clothed in monastic dress, if he refuses to be marked with monastic character?

So too, no one rightly calls himself a cleric who does not commit himself to the clerical profession in due manner; who does not, as stated above, put on clerical dress; who, having chosen the clerical character, does not put away other characters from himself [Col. 0830A]. But if he abandons the clerical profession which he had assumed, throws off its character, and determines to remain in another state or order, he will no longer be a cleric. For just as one does not become one unless, as stated above, the clerical profession is assumed, so one ceases to be a cleric if what was assumed is abandoned.

## CHAPTER CXXI
By two causes, as I see it, clerical profession is abandoned: one, namely, proud vanity; the other, religious humility. Proud vanity is at work when someone, having cast aside the tonsure and garb of clerics, relapses into the state and order of laymen, so that he may more freely [Col. 0830B] indulge his pride there and, with looser reins, serve the vanities of the world. Religious humility is at work when someone, more carefully considering the pre-eminent dignity of the clerical order, sees that he does not possess holiness commensurate with it; and, since he is unable to win victory upon a high and slippery mountain, wishes at least to deserve escape by hiding in a low and humble place. Therefore, abandoning a profession which he knows to be loftier than the others in the Church, and in which very many live more laxly by occasion of their office, he flees to the monastic hiding-place, that he may lie concealed there more safely and, removed far from ecclesiastical cares, rest beneath the shade of mourning and silence.

Those two men mentioned above had given themselves to proud vanity. Having violated the covenant which they had entered into by their clerical profession, they persisted in that violation with obstinate minds; and thus deserved to be called apostates. For an apostate is interpreted as a transgressor: one who, having cast aside a stricter resolve and the very mark by which that resolve is signified, bends back to what he had formerly left, as to vomit, so that the unrestrained breadth of life may again possess him—the sphere in which the multitude seems to find freer opportunity for sinning. Thus those apostates were no longer clerics, who had abandoned their profession and clerical garb, who with perverse mind had returned to lay latitude. The holy synod judged them inexcusable, and justice recalled them, bound under the bishop’s judgment. For if they were clerics, there would have been no need either to accuse or recall them [Col. 0830D], nor would anyone have borne witness against them, since this coercion was inflicted on them for no other reason than that they had abandoned the clerical profession. They were what it was altogether unlawful for them to be; they were not what it was necessary for them to be. For the lay highway in which they moved was forbidden them, while the narrow clerical path which they had abandoned had been lawfully imposed upon them.

We have indeed seen, and do see, very many such persons, who, abandoning the clerical state imposed upon them, have returned to lay vomit; and are so perverse in that unjust resolve that they neither wish to be called nor to be what they ought to have been—indeed, they wish to be called and to be what, headlong in error, they chose. Those whom we know to have cast off the clerical mark and resorted to lay license, we say are no longer [Col. 0831A] clerics, but were clerics. No one calls such a man a cleric, except perhaps when that name is recalled publicly because of his disgrace.

Many, having spent childhood, adolescence, and perhaps still longer in the clerical state, and having perceived themselves burdened there by certain disadvantages—whether by difficulty in literary learning, lack of family resources, or desire for military activity—renounce that clerical state. Returning among laymen, they either practise some trade in order to become rich or become soldiers in order to behave more insolently. Certainly no one now maintains that these are clerics, because neither the clerical mark nor profession persists in them. Rather, just as they were called and were clerics while bound by the laws of that profession, so now they are called and are [Col. 0831B] what they profess, though unlawfully, by word and dress.

For many years I knew a certain man so devoted to military pursuits that in soldiering—or rather wrongdoing—he would not be judged inferior to others. As a boy he had been brought up as a monk in a monastery of monks, and in time had been ordained deacon among them. At last, breaking the barriers of obedience and casting off the monastic habit, he leapt from the cloister, driven by youthful impulse. Resuming the appearance and dress of a layman, and taking up shield, lance, and sword-belt, he became a soldier, though never before trained in military pursuits, but marked from childhood by the badges of monastic rule. He openly professed the military life, in whose pursuit he engaged, though unlawfully; and no one admitted that he was anything but a soldier, though it was beyond doubt known [Col. 0831C] that he had been a monk.

Thus proud vanity drives monks or clerics away from their religious resolve; thus the apostate spirit shamelessly thrusts them into the pit of apostasy. Once the barrier of fear and shame has been broken, the more extensively and abominably they conform themselves to the world, the more expressly and miserably they will be found conformed to the same devil in the endurance of punishments.

## CHAPTER CXXII

Religious humility, however, seems to work in a cleric when, under the visitation of grace, he begins to loathe the latitude of his own will; when, fervent in spirit, he begins to abhor whatever shines with merely superficial brilliance, and strives to remove as though unlawful whatever is permitted but not expedient [Col. 0831D]; when he desires to cleave to God so inseparably that he endeavours to exclude from his inward retreat whatever opposes itself through the cares that arise.

And because there are many clerics in whom due holiness is not found, whom especially the fleeting beauty of the world delights, whom the unbecoming ugliness of secular life deforms, while a multitude, through corrupted laws, makes them unpunished: when he cannot attain fitting religious devotion among them, he does not dare remain longer in their company. For a weak mind cannot equally endure the troubles of living among others: through association with secular persons it contracts the contagion of sinning, and among them the harmful liberty of one’s own will chokes the conceived desire for holiness.

Considering, therefore, both the lofty summit of dignity to which clerics [Col. 0832A] are raised and the dissolute path of life in which they rejoice as though mad, he judges it more fitting to be cast aside and hide in a corner in the wedding-house than to sit in a prominent place and, when the bridegroom comes, be degraded. Therefore, bidding farewell to the profession and name of clerics, to which he does not doubt that he is unequal through lack of fitting merits, he humbly turns aside to the life and order of monks. He knows, on the testimony of Scripture, that it is better to be humbled with the meek than to be powerfully tortured with the mighty. “For the mighty,” as it is written, “shall suffer mighty torments” (Wisdom 6).

Thus, laying aside the clerical state which he had held by profession and dress, he assumes monasticism likewise by profession and dress; and just as he was a cleric by bearing the clerical title, so he becomes a monk by assuming the monastic mark [Col. 0832B]. In abandoning the former, he accuses not the order but the morals of clerics; in assuming the latter, he commends not the dignity but the holiness of monks. For he knows that the former, if he judges rightly, are worthier of ecclesiastical eminence, while he considers the latter holier in life and conduct.

Therefore he does not dishonour the clerical order which he leaves, nor arrogantly honour before it the monastic order which he assumes, since he declares himself wholly unfit to attain the former and does not despair of being able to suffice for the latter. For, as was said, it is far easier to attain monastic than clerical perfection; and a good cleric is a far more precious, and consequently rarer, thing to find than a good monk.

Once made a monk, he is no longer correctly considered to be what he was before, and therefore is no longer properly called a cleric, although he may be allowed to retain certain things belonging to clerics, or perhaps later be advanced to certain clerical functions. For although the orders which he possessed are not taken away from him, and perhaps greater ones are conferred in the course of time, nevertheless he ought not properly to be called a cleric. For a cleric is not one who is promoted to orders, but one who professes the clerical state in the manner described above [Col. 0832C].

If any soldier, anticipated by grace and fervent in spiritual desire, casts aside the profession and military habit under which he had lived and becomes a monk, submitting himself to regular discipline, then, I think, he is no longer properly called what he formerly both was and was called. For who would say that a man who has left military service and is a monk is still a soldier, although he is permitted to do certain things known to belong properly to a soldier? Not everyone who performs what seems specially assigned to a soldier is a soldier, just as not everyone by whom a monastic duty is performed is a monk. “A monk,” says Jerome, “has the office of one who mourns.”

When, therefore, discussion arises concerning any monk, and someone asks what condition he had held before becoming a monk, the person questioned answers that he had been a cleric, soldier, or something of the sort; but he does not say that he now is any of these. Rather, just as he asserts that he was a soldier if he had been a soldier, so he asserts that he was a cleric if he had been a cleric. But if someone still wishes to call him either cleric or soldier, he will appear to inflict an injury by leading the hearer into error [Col. 0833A], because his speech will assert one thing about him while his profession and habit show another.

For whoever hears that he is called either cleric or soldier and sees him designated by monastic appearance and dress will complain that he has been deceived, and the man who said this will not undeservedly be charged with lying. If he replies that he says it not for the sake of lying or deceiving, an explanation of that statement will consequently be required: namely, how he wishes it to be understood that he presumes to call cleric or soldier one whom he sees beyond doubt shown by profession and dress to be a monk.

When the hearer requires an explanation, perhaps the person questioned will answer nothing else than that the man who is a monk is called a cleric because he is learned or ministers at the altar. But it is both true, and the monk under discussion himself declares, that no one ought to be judged a cleric because he is learned [Col. 0833B].

## CHAPTER CXXIII

As for the altar service for which that monk wished to maintain that he was a cleric, reason itself seems sufficiently to show that he ought not claim the name cleric on that account, since we see many clerics who nevertheless do not stand at the altar in that manner. Although in the beginning none but clerics performed the altar service, because monks either did not yet exist or were very few, nevertheless, in the course of time, when the number of monks increased, many things proper to clerics were granted to them.

For ecclesiastical teachers judged it quite inhuman and unfitting that, when a cleric turned to the monastic order for the sake of religious devotion, ecclesiastical discipline should exclude him from altar service, when he desired that order for no reason other than that thenceforth he might live more holy and humble. And when he strives to give greater care to holiness and humility, he seems all the more suited to altar service—provided, however, that the other gifts of grace are not lacking, namely the prescribed soundness of body and learning [Col. 0833C].

Rightly, therefore, one who professes monasticism for the sake of humility is not barred from altar service; yet he is no longer properly called a cleric when he is not bound by clerical profession and dress. But if, impatient of the self-abasement he proposed, he shamelessly presumes to cast off the monastic order which he adopted with a view to religious humility, and resumes the clerical habit which he formerly wore, he is accused of pride—indeed, of intolerable apostasy—because ecclesiastical discipline does not grant such liberty to a monk.

A person is permitted to pass from lay to clerical order; or, if he has perhaps relapsed into the former, he is still admonished—indeed compelled—to return, because the broad lay highway of liberty cannot attain this narrow purpose of holiness. But when a cleric transfers himself to the life and habit of monks, not condemning but honouring the clerical order, he humbly strives to yield place to a greater dignity so that he may give greater care to holiness [Col. 0834A]. He therefore leaves the clerical state lest, on a loftier summit, exposed as it were to winds, he vanish away; he desires monasticism so that there he may lie concealed more holily the more lowly he is.

Since in this humble transfer the postponed lofty dignity suffers no loss, while humble holiness seeks greater increase, a convert of this kind, after assuming the habit of monastic humility, is not allowed to return to the habit of his former dignity; otherwise, if a higher order humbly laid aside could be more easily resumed, it would seem more contemptible than is right. For since in laying it aside nothing but holy humility, or humble holiness, is professed, in resuming it the same purpose is judged changed. Therefore no slight injury is inflicted upon it if a monk, having laid aside humility, is freely and indiscriminately allowed to return to it.

Clerical authority therefore does not admit this return, nor does it permit a monk such broad liberty of wandering. Rather, it requires that his chosen abasement be found complete, provided that it was lawfully—that is, in due order—begun. But if a cleric unlawfully transferred himself to the monastic order, if, guilty of proud disobedience, he assumed the habit of humility, he ought not persist in that obstinate course. Willing or unwilling, he must be recalled to his former state, lest humility feigned under an obedientless raven’s covering be found to be not innocent simplicity, but doubled iniquity [Col. 0834B].

## CHAPTER CXXIV

Finally, clerical dignity considers itself somewhat burdened if anyone abandons it contumaciously; and monastic humility itself is no little defiled if, like a rebellious handmaid, it behaves insolently toward its mistress. Thus the harmonious reverence and reverent harmony which ought to be preserved between the two orders is sometimes compelled to weaken when the poison of anger or envy has been poured over it. Sarah then tries to instruct rebellious Hagar not by caresses but by blows, while Hagar, though recalled by an angel, scarcely at last endures obedience.

But if what properly belongs to each is preserved with peace between them—so that clerical dignity does not threaten imperiously, nor monastic humility resist contumaciously—no small fruit will be gathered from both alike. One will command piously and humbly, and the other will hasten to anticipate the commander with humble obedience [Col. 0834D].

Thus clerical dignity will tolerate its own clerics passing to the monastic order when fervent desire for concealment and silence, labour and mourning possesses them; and thereafter it will not hesitate to recall some to ecclesiastical service, provided it perceives them fit by life and learning. This is indeed the ancient custom of the Church: when suitable learning, eloquence, and holiness appear in monks, they are compelled, though unwilling, to come forth from the welcome refuge of silence and are set over the peoples, who require them to perform a clerical role or office.

For who can more familiarly or fittingly fill the place of a cleric than a monk eminent in religious devotion and learning, when that order is joined to the clerical order by such close affinity that a cleric, although of greater dignity, is permitted to transfer to it alone for humility’s sake? Who is nearer or worthier to be substituted in a cleric’s place than one judged to possess suitable religious devotion? Moreover, we see so many things proper to clerics granted to monks that, except for the name and garment, almost everything else is now common to them [Col. 0835A].

Therefore, when no suitable person among the clerics is found to govern the people of the faithful, the Church’s authority appropriately has recourse to monks and commands the one whom it sees eminent among them in religion and learning to preside over the people in a cleric’s place. Yet, lest anyone judge him a cleric because he occupies a cleric’s place, ecclesiastical authority does not wish his monastic habit to be changed. It entrusts him with clerical oversight in such a way that he nevertheless retains monasticism in profession and habit.

Thus the monk does what belongs to a cleric, yet is not a cleric. He exercises the care of the people lest he contumaciously recoil from the command laid upon him; he wears the monk’s habit lest he presume to be proud from the cleric’s chair [Col. 0835B]. If, on account of such an office, he is sometimes called a cleric—since that office is clearly assigned especially to clerics—such speech must be judged improper. Since enough has been said above about this, there is no need to repeat it.

For he is called a cleric in many writings of the Fathers not so much because of the orders through which he is presented at the altar as because he is sometimes summoned from the cloister to govern the people; and in that designation strictness of speech is not preserved. Since, therefore, such fellowship exists between the clerical and monastic orders that one passes from the one to the other—though in different ways, as was said—it is especially fitting that peace and concord be maintained between them, without which, as the Apostle testifies, no one beholds God.

It is fitting, I say, that Solomon’s litter, which is chiefly constructed from them, gathered from virtues on every side, be spread in the middle with charity. That charity neither acts perversely nor is puffed up; it is neither ambitious nor seeks its own interests. Without it, even the cedars of Lebanon are corrupted by rot, the silver columns are broken like reeds [Col. 0835D], the golden couch is deprived of its gift of rest, and the purple ascent is turned into a precipice.

As I see it, because of the approaching failure of this charity, ignorance of the truth long held very many clerics and monks alike. The former did not strive to attain the summit of holiness laid upon them, and the latter did not wish to remain within the proposed and most wholesome boundary of humility and lowliness. Both, therefore, walking in darkness while imagining that they saw, refused carefully to consider the dignity of either order. Searching out superfluous things, they did not sufficiently know themselves: “wise,” according to the prophet, “to do evil, but knowing not how to do good” (Jeremiah 4).

## CHAPTER CXXV

[Col. 0836A]

But in our times, when divine mercy chose to show itself more generous than usual, both orders alike seemed to flower again through the grace of virtues. Those who had almost failed through winter frost and had been dried by the long blasts of the North return to their former condition, warmed by a new sun and breathing west winds. Welcome mildness wears away winter’s harshness; impatient of oldness, it clears away the frost and brings back spring’s newness.

Thus monastic religious life, languishing and worn-out, grows strong again as a more ardent emulator of God; sprinkled with fresh dew, it flowers anew. In monasteries, like trees, no small fruit grows; the workshop of all holiness, fire sent from above and driven by mighty blasts, glows intensely. This praiseworthy workshop, in which a new discipline of life is forged [Col. 0836B], is first found to receive a welcome place at Cîteaux. There, in the furnace of poverty, the little fire of religious devotion is first nourished.

There, I say, the monastic order, long dead, is revived; there, its old ashes having been driven away, it is reformed by the grace of renewal; there, by file and diligent effort, it is restored to its proper condition. It abhors the soft delicacy accepted by other monks and insatiably embraces labour, poverty, mourning, and silence. It does not hang its mind upon popular tithes, but extends its hands with vigorous readiness to labour, striving by this means to acquire for itself humble food and clothing and showing that it has in no way forgotten its first origin.

Because modern monks had turned into luxury and ostentation the measure or colour of the former habit, which their predecessors had adopted to show penitential mourning or sorrow, this community judged it right to adopt a coarser garment of another colour: such a garment as a simple sheep produces in its wool, uncoloured by dye or cosmetic falsehood, and made neither delicate by artifice nor softness [Col. 0836C].

Some worldly scoffers mock and disparage this, and even more frequently and bitterly do many monks. Since they do not stretch out their hands to imitate the good they see, they at least sharpen their teeth to blaspheme it impudently. For when at first there were only black monks, they are astonished, as they say, to see monks now in brown or grey, and accuse them of not keeping the former custom of life—as though this new holiness had arrived with pepper and palms.

But just as true love does not know how to envy good or better things, so true humility does not know how to make insolent reproaches. Holy men are ready to endure calmly the tongues of detractors and in no way to hold back their foot from their resolve. They choose rather to make themselves a spectacle to angels or to men than, together with those who do not maintain it, not to maintain monastic truth. They thus adhere to the Rule of that Benedict under which they live, so as to persevere in everything it commands literally or exhorts them to do, judging that they could not observe it in every detail unless they applied the utmost care to small things as well as great [Col. 0836D].

From this monastery called Cîteaux, in which in our times the Rule of Benedict is restored to the truth of its letter, proceeds the distinguished Clairvaux, fruitful in offspring, which surpasses the other monasteries of the same order in the brilliance of its renown and name. It very fittingly deserved to be called Clairvaux—“Bright Valley”—for there monastic humility is known to be reforged into its former state with new anvil and hammer, and from it the sweet savour of that same humility is spread far and wide. Its humility of life makes it a valley, and its glorious humility a bright valley.

For its humility is made manifest by such light and glory that its fame is now spread even to the furthest parts of the world; and, through the generosity of the Spirit, who works where and as much as he wills, a great number is added to this order day by day [Col. 0837A–B].

## CHAPTER CXXVI

After Christ, as said above, visited the monks with gratuitous goodness, he also directed the fountain of the same grace toward clerics. In the place called Prémontré he gathered certain men fervent in spirit, through whom he stirred up others far and wide toward due religious devotion. There such holiness of clerics boiled over, such strength against temporal enticements, that the apostolic life itself seems truly to have been restored in them—a life oppressed almost to extinction by the weariness of prolonged languor.

There, I say, casting aside the purse of monetary resources, execrating the deadly blandishments of their own will, leaving the ecclesiastical offices which they either possessed or sought [Col. 0837C], and counting as nothing dignities destined swiftly to pass away, they devoted such zeal to labour, silence, and poverty, and finally such diligence to holiness, that among them might be found both the laborious affliction of monks and the holy and devout religious life of clerics.

God particularly willed this to be done in a valley, so that the form of the place might accord with the saving work and plainly show that, for clerics whose lofty dignity and freedom of rule provided occasion for ruin, voluntary lowliness and the humility of repentance were fitting. The valley itself is appropriately called Prémontré, “Fore-shown,” indicating that this humility of clerics was not begun rashly or through chance inventions, but that divine mercy set it forth beforehand as an example to others, showing them through it the way of return to himself [Col. 0837D].

Nor is it without purpose that divine providence formed this valley thus, and conformed it to the present work—or the present work to it—so that the very appearance of the place seems to forewarn something grave and severe, while the humble obedience of the clerics responds to that warning. For the valley spreads out in the form of a cross into four arms, and its plain ends in four corners. Its length extends from east to west, and its breadth from north to south. What does this appearance of a place, stamped with so great a likeness of the cross—this valley, as it were crucified not by human contrivance but by nature’s work—teach or forewarn, except that those who gather there should no longer take care to live for the world, but should conform themselves by a fitting crucifixion to it—indeed, to Christ? [Col. 0838A]

Moreover, one enters that valley by its four arms, and in them there is a meeting at the centre, as at a four-way crossroads: so that a welcome multitude of arrivals may flow to it from the four parts of the world, and from it the fame of religious devotion may spread to the four parts of the world.

This is that estate of Gethsemane into which Christ comes with his disciples and prays; in which, as the hour of his Passion approaches, he labours in sorrow and sweat; in which he rouses his disciples, oppressed by the heavy sleep of fear and unbelief, to pray, lest they be led into the irrevocable precipice of temptation. “And they come,” he says, “to an estate called Gethsemane,” which is interpreted “valley of fatness.” It is beautifully called the valley of fatness, because it is overshadowed from above by the Mount of Olives. For Christ, who is truly called the Mount of Olives, overshadows and protects the vale of tears and makes it fertile—not with the oil of the sinner, but with the most devout love of the Creator [Col. 0838B].

In this valley the sleepiness and harmful torpor of clerics are rebuked; in this their earnest care to watch and pray is more urgently aroused. Here Christ endures to be troubled and afraid with them and for them, so that they too may not refuse to endure for his sake the hardships of repentance. Upon this valley Christ pours the gifts of his blessing; through it he pours out with lavish force the oil of his charity. He fills it wholesomely, as we are taught by the sure witness of John; and David specifies with what he fills it: “The valleys,” he says, “shall abound with grain” (Psalm 65).

Perhaps this grain is Christ himself, who, falling into the earth, sprang up more fruitfully; who, ground by the mill of suffering, fed his humble ones with the bread of life; who grants humble clerics the nourishment of saving refreshment and, when they have now grown to maturity, confers upon them the adornment of glorious beauty. For this reason, in the Song of Songs he wished to call himself the lily of the valleys, showing that he hastens to crown with honour and glory those who, for his sake, do not find the hardships of self-abasement burdensome. Those who do not refuse, as the Apostle exhorts (2 Corinthians 7), to grieve unto repentance, he makes rejoice without end when mourning is changed into joy. The whiteness of the lily signifies the festal joy with which he will reward the humble grief of clerics [Col. 0838C–D], when he shows himself to them face to face.

## CHAPTER CXXVII

As a type of this joy, those same clerics gathered in the valley of Prémontré for humility’s sake, who have set aside ecclesiastical dignities and embraced contempt for temporal things, cast off soft linen garments and clothe themselves in woollen white. Thus, in white wool, they proclaim the grace of remission received and prefigure the hoped-for glory of heavenly joy.

That forgiveness of sins is symbolized by white wool is made clear by the Lord, who mercifully promises through Isaiah: “Though your sins be red as the worm, they shall be white as wool” (Isaiah 14 [an apparent citation error]). Since the worm is blood-red in colour, through it—as also through blood—is understood the grave iniquity of the sinner, which is called not only carnal and bloody but sometimes “flesh and blood”; and these two do not possess the kingdom of God, as the Apostle declares (1 Corinthians 15). “If, therefore,” he says, “your sins are bloody, if they are unclean, nevertheless I will wash them; pouring out innocence, I will mercifully make them white like wool, so that greater iniquity may obtain a greater washing, and unless the former abounds, the latter may seem superabundant” [Col. 0839A].

Finally, in the whiteness of his clothing the Lord prefigured the future glory of heavenly joy when he showed himself transfigured on Mount Tabor to the disciples: “And he was transfigured before them; and his face shone as the sun, but his garments became white as snow” (Matthew 17). Peter, judging that this was not a transitory vision but the abiding dwelling of heavenly joy which he desired, wished to remain there with him whose face he saw shining with solar splendour and whose garments gleamed with snowy whiteness. He spoke with burning desire, though not sufficiently instructed: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles: one for thee, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matthew 17) [Col. 0839B].

The angel—or angels—who announced the glory of Christ risen, having cast off the sadness of the present life and already attained the state of enduring joy, chose to appear to the women in shining white clothing, that they might be conformed to the joy of the heavenly life which they came to announce. Mark the Evangelist says: “They saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe; and they were astonished” (Mark 16). John says: “Mary saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been laid” (John 20) [Col. 0839C].

Thus the aforesaid clerics prefigure this solemn joy when they conform themselves to Christ and the angels by the whiteness of their clothing. By the wool in which they are clothed after discarding linen, they manifest the grace of innocence by which they are washed from former sins; by the whiteness they signify that they will attain heavenly joy and remain in it without end with Christ and the angels [Col. 0840A].

Truly blessed is this life of clerics, who, though still placed upon earth, nevertheless live after the manner of angels. They are conformed not only to angels but rather to the King of angels, not merely by the whiteness of their outward dress but more especially by the whiteness of their souls. Of him Solomon says: “My beloved is white” (Song of Songs 5); and another Wise Man says: “It is the brightness of eternal light” (Wisdom 7).

If those who have hitherto delayed to flee to this life—where clerics are made white inwardly as well as outwardly, and by that whiteness are conformed, as said, to the white Christ—now flee to it; and if those who have perhaps already embraced it hold it perfectly, they need not fear mockery from either laymen or monks, since neither can accuse their merit. This life has first a hundredfold perfection and afterward a thousandfold recompense, because in the present it is granted perfection of merits and in the future consummation of rewards [Col. 0840B].

How great a reverence is due to this life or order, in which dignity adorns holiness and holiness supports dignity, I judge it superfluous to commend to you again, especially since this response calls for its conclusion. Having shown, as best I could, what is ascribed to clerics and monks respectively as common or proper, and what honour each owes the other by right of dignity or merit of holiness, it is fitting at last to set a limit to this response, lest either its length or perhaps its uselessness be considered burdensome longer than necessary [Col. 0840C].

## V. ON THE OBEDIENCE OF CLERICS

[Col. 0839]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0839C]

Having completed the third response, I came to the fourth stage of my intended journey. Finding its ascent both obscure and exceedingly steep, I confess that for some time I kept silence; unequal to the task, I waited in silence and hope for one who might raise my soul by a new help of grace, while it clung to the ground beneath the weight of its weakness.

From every side I am assailed by the differing counsels of different persons—and would that they were not opposed to one another—so that, when I yield to one, I may not offend the other, and may seem to satisfy one at the cost of the other’s peace. Fear and hope join me as though from opposite sides in the middle, and speak quite differently to one another. Fear urges me not to undertake what I cannot bear; hope suggests [Col. 0839D] that, trusting in the Lord, I should humbly presume to do so.

Fear says: “Do not search into things stronger than yourself” (Ecclesiasticus 3). Hope says: “Blessed are they who search his testimonies” (Psalm 118). Fear says: “Before you speak, learn” (Ecclesiasticus 18). Hope says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80). Fear says: “There is a time for keeping silence” (Ecclesiastes 3). Hope says: “A time for speaking” (ibid.).

Thus hope often escapes the burdens of fear by its swiftness; but often, overcome by great fear, it falls. Yet because hope, as was said, does not disappoint when charity is poured out in our hearts, I shall at last undertake this task—not for the sake of any earthly advantage, but out of regard for fraternal charity. I shall undertake, I say, with grace preceding, so to fear that I shall no longer delay to answer what has been asked.

Along the narrow and slippery way I shall walk with two feet: leaning upon hope with one, while with the other I do not depart from the moderation of fear [Col. 0840D]. Thus, if hope perhaps tries to leap farther than is due, fear may compel it promptly to draw back a little; and if fear begins to sink into the abyss and pit of despair, hope, recalling and strengthening it, may give it confidence to cross over [Col. 0841A]. God in his grace will deign to grant me this, since in this little work I desire to obey both his will and that of his servants.

## CHAPTER ONE
Obedience, brothers, is asked about: what sort of virtue it ought to be judged, and whether we must obey it in all things, or whether perhaps in some matter it is permitted to resist. Obedience is indeed a consummate virtue, and from the beginning is so variously commended in the Scriptures that no other virtue seems to possess the merit of perfection unless it is fortified by this safeguard. Even charity itself, which is affirmed to be greater than the rest, if it attempts to love anything contrary to obedience, is not only rejected by sound judgment, but is not judged to be true charity; for it is found truly to oppose God [Col. 0841B] if it loves Him otherwise than obedience prescribes.

Therefore every rational creature is bound by the bonds of obedience; and by the Creator of all, all creatures are commanded. Nor is there any creature of such exalted and pre-eminent dignity that it does not accept obedience to a higher power, although it sometimes, through the perversity of its own will, declines into the flat country of perverse and deadly liberty. Yet not even thus is it released from the bonds of obedience; rather, it is wonderfully—or, more truly, miserably—bound by them. For whereas, by following and obeying, it could deservedly be crowned eternally with glory and honour, because it drives obedience away and flees from it, it deserves to be tormented by the punishments that follow.

God therefore wills that all creatures serve Him obediently, and that each of them in turn obey another [Col. 0841C], so that no rank, profession, city, or nation may abuse its own will, but all may be brought under another’s authority. Kings, although they are not compelled to be subject to other kings, nevertheless ought to render obedience to God; and, in God’s stead, they ought to incline their ear to the bishops of the Church, regulate their own conduct by their admonitions, defend mother Church against assailants, and overthrow the enemies of the faith by arms obediently employed. To kings themselves are subjected consuls, centurions, tribunes, and captains of fifty; and some of these rightly and most orderly rule over others, so that whoever, with proud neck, despises the authority set over him falls into the guilt of disobedience not only before men but also before God.

Soldiers therefore owe their commanders, and commanders their kings, the service of military obedience [Col. 0841D], so that, when necessity arises to fight for peace, country, or Church, subordinates may not delay to prepare themselves at the command of their superiors, knowing that they fight God’s battles more than men’s. But if the madness of their superiors attempts to rage against peace, country, or Church, it ought not to find subordinates ready to assist it; and, if they are admonished, they ought to remember that “we must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5). If, however, through a perverse fear or love of their superiors, they yield to their will, though they may seem excusable, they will not be excused from being found truly to oppose God if they consent to attack ecclesiastical peace.

Peoples also, assembled to live according to law, are commanded reverently to obey the just laws of the city [Col. 0842A], so that no one among the rest may strive to obtain the privilege of his own liberty, lest, by living badly according to his own judgment, he disturb the peace of the united community. For a multitude of citizens could not remain at peace within the bosom of peace unless the strength of obedience protected it; because the natural diversity of so many persons, and the vicious instability peculiar to their minds, would more often make the crowd disturbed, and, once disturbed, incite it to quarrels and hatreds.

Thus neither a city, nor a village, nor any popular assembly is permitted to live like a solitary wild ass or “a sparrow alone upon the housetop”; but although the condition and manner of life called secular may remain free, the saving bond of obedience is nevertheless imposed upon it. Yet this obedience benefits [Col. 0842B] the earthly welfare of the city, but does not suffice for the virtue of perfect holiness. It is useful for market-place profits and temporal peace, but does not sufficiently cultivate conduct by spiritual advancement. It restrains the tongue so that it may not run wild in reviling a neighbour; it holds back the hand so that it may not strike or violently commit robbery. It adds the necessary constraints of fear, but does not pour voluntary charity into hearts. It forbids the evil of outward action, but does not prescribe the good of inward religion.

## CHAPTER II

For the sake of that obedience by which it has been granted to merit the salvation of the soul, we ought to consider obedience more closely: the obedience by which it is evident that evil works are not so much servilely restrained as good works are more diligently fulfilled. [Col. 0842C] This, certainly, is that obedience by which we obey God, the true Creator of all; by which we keep His commandments, once learned by reading or hearing them—abstaining, that is, from those things which He commands not to be done, and doing those things which He commands to be done.

We assuredly find in the Scriptures this way of obedience to be twofold; as by a forked road, we arrive at its summit without straying into error when we freely reject with abhorrence those things which He commands not to be done, and devote willing diligence to the things to be done. This twofold way is set before every rational creature and has the promise of the life that now is [p. 487] and of that which is to come; for in the present it makes the traveller perfected in virtues, and in the future, when he reaches the end, crowned with both [Col. 0842D] honour and glory.

All who, from the beginning, have pleased God through the merits granted them by His grace and have happily deserved to attain His fellowship, advanced in this twofold way—provided that they had time to live and progress. Yet, although it is clear that all the righteous hold both ways, since otherwise they could not sufficiently please God, some are found to shine more brightly in the praises of one of them and, as though by one virtue alone, to obtain merit before God. Some are found to be commended not a little because they strive more diligently to perform what they are commanded to do; others, likewise, deserve worthy praise because they refuse to do what is divinely forbidden.

To those who do what must be done, the Lord promises in the [Col. 0843A] Gospel that He will grant them the kingdom of life prepared from the beginning: “Come,” He says, “blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25 [the source reads 29]). And why is this? “For I was hungry,” He says, “and you gave me food,” and the other works of mercy that follow there; because they strove to do these, they attain the unfailing kingdom.

But Scripture elsewhere both proclaims blessed and admires as praiseworthy the person who resolutely rejects what is forbidden. “Blessed,” it says, “is he who has not gone after gold, nor placed his hope in treasures of money. Who is he? We shall praise him” (Ecclus. 31). As those are blessed for doing what has been enjoined upon the faithful, so this man likewise is blessed because he rejects what is prohibited: for they strove to apply greater [Col. 0843B] diligence to doing those things, while he was found to strive more vigorously, and more commendably, to reject the forbidden things. Hence Isaiah says: “Blessed is the man who keeps his hands from doing every evil” (Isa. 36 [citation as printed]).

This, surely, can be seen more certainly by one who wishes to review the Scriptures consecutively from the beginning. But because I have acquired neither knowledge of the Scriptures nor retained them in memory, I cannot at present compile many examples. Therefore I wish at least to bring forward two men, Adam and Abraham, in whom obedience seems to shine forth not a little. Abraham satisfied God when He commanded difficult things (Gen. 22): he willingly did what he was commanded; and therefore he is set before all future generations as an example of obedience, for those who will attain the same glory through the same obedience. Adam, however, did not avoid the light things which he was commanded to avoid (Gen. 3), but turned aside to do what was forbidden; and in him also it is plainly shown to all posterity what follows contempt for obedience.

Just as obedience is commendably proclaimed in Abraham, so in Adam it is likewise commended by contrast: Abraham, by keeping the commandments through doing them, is adorned with such great glory; Adam, by not avoiding what was forbidden and so rejecting obedience, is disfigured with such great shame. And here it should be observed that Adam was forbidden to touch, whereas Abraham was commanded to kill. Light matters are forbidden to the first man; difficult matters are laid before the patriarch. Adam, who had not yet sinned and ought to have been stronger, would not endure a light obedience; Abraham, already entangled in sins and hindered from doing good by those same nets, was able to fulfil a difficult obedience. The one failed when the easier path of obedience was set before him; the other advanced when the narrower was set before him, because it seems easier to abstain from lighter matters than to prevail in more arduous ones. Adam, forbidden, ate the fruit with harmful effect; Abraham, commanded, sacrificed his son with a willing disposition. I confess: the hidden meaning of this matter cannot be penetrated by my understanding; it seems obscured to me by such great perplexities.

## CHAPTER III

At a mystery so profound, the mind is amazed beyond what can be said, because for me, unworthy as I am, that desirable day has not yet dawned on which the fountain of the house of David is opened for the inhabitants of [Col. 0844A] Jerusalem. When a repentant sinner has been watered by its stream, he is made glad; for, once the stains of sins have been driven away, spiritual knowledge grows in him more abundantly.

Through the prophet Zechariah the Lord promises this fountain to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, by which their conscience will be more effectively washed and the ignorance of those washed will be wiped away—if, however, the day dawns on which this is judged worthy to occur. “On that day,” He says, “there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruating woman” (Zech. 13).

By David, Christ is undoubtedly prefigured; by the house of David, the Church of Christ is figuratively signified. The fountain of David’s house is the spiritual knowledge of the Scriptures. It remains with those whom the Church has made more perfect, because more perfect knowledge is found only in the perfect, and is opened to them more and more for the increase of their merit. “Therefore an open fountain of the house of David shall be”: open indeed to the house of David itself, because those who are Christ’s special house and dwelling will receive a more abundant infusion of spiritual understanding of the Scriptures.

But when will this be? “On that day,” he says. On what day? On that day, of course, which I have commended to you so often and so greatly, which I have so often prophesied would come, which I have desired with such longing to arrive: when my Christ, who is the true light, will arise in your hearts [p. 488]; when knowledge and love of Him will be poured into you more abundantly; when He will no longer die in you under the pressure of any danger; when He will not be sought as one living among the dead, but will be truly known as risen, [Col. 0844C] ascending, and seated at the Father’s right hand.

“On that day, therefore, there shall be an open fountain of the house of David”: open, as has been said, to the house of David itself, because in those whose conscience possesses Christ perfectly there will be perfect knowledge of the Scriptures—and this not hidden, not sealed under the covering of fear or oppressive negligence, but an abundant and overflowing fountain of springing water.

But what grace is bestowed upon us by this, if the grace of perfect spiritual knowledge is granted to the perfect, when we are so far from the degree of perfection that we cannot even aspire to it, much less attain it? What then does this mean for us: “On that day there shall be an open fountain of the house of David”? Indeed, it means much for us. For in them the perfect knowledge of the Scriptures so abounds [Col. 0844D] that it is not shut up within them by either poverty or envy, but overflows; it does not steal itself away from the eyes of those standing around, like a sealed well, but is conveyed as it were by a little channel to us who stand outside.

For holy teachers rejoice in their knowledge and in the abundance of their merits in such a way that they are also concerned for the salvation of their neighbours. Therefore, grieving over our errors, they instruct us by their manifold teaching and, once the soot of our sins has been wiped away, reform us into the image in which we were made. Hence, after it has been said, “On that day there shall be an open fountain of the house of David,” there is added: “and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruating woman.”

The fountain will not be open only to those who are Christ’s intimate dwelling; the inward subtlety of the Scriptures will not appear only to Christ’s chamberlains. It will also be poured outward to those who are citizens of Jerusalem, and will flow through the greater to the lesser, as down slopes. [Col. 0845A] Through the teaching of the greater, the imperfection of the lesser is instructed; through the former’s spiritual riches, the latter’s poverty is relieved, so that they may know and be able to remove the present stains of sins and guard against those that come upon them.

This is what is meant by “for the washing of the sinner and the menstruating woman.” The sinner and the menstruating woman stand for lighter and graver sins: the sinner is one sprinkled with the stains of lighter offences; the menstruating woman is one defiled by the uncleanness of grave sins. By the decree of the Law, the menstruating woman is judged unclean, and whatever she touches is reckoned defiled; and by her is fittingly represented more expressly that soul which is disfigured by the disorderly flow of carnal pleasures.

Yet she is washed, if she wishes to remain within the walls of Jerusalem; if she wishes to submit herself to the stream of this fountain; if she wishes to be silent amid the external tumults of sins; if she wishes to lend a willing ear to the sound counsels of her elders. Thus that agriculture is deservedly rejected as accursed in which Esau, with mind gone astray, delighted to labour; nor is the tangled darkness of the forests praised, in which the same man hunted in wretched pleasure. Therefore every wise person should either dwell at home with Rebekah, preserving the grace of chastity, or at least, after hearing Solomon’s decree, remain constantly within the walls of the city, from which that same Solomon commanded Shimei not to depart any farther (3 Kings 2), and because he did depart, he deserved to perish without remedy [Col. 0845C].

Thus the open fountain of the house of David becomes, for the inhabitants, a washing for the sinner and the menstruating woman, when those who dwell within these walls of Jerusalem—not so much in body as in spirit—are cleansed from sins both lighter and graver: those, namely, who love to remain in peace and leisure, quiet and silence, and to be healthfully watered by the streams of the divine Scriptures.

Jerusalem, as you know, is called “vision of peace.” Therefore those are not unfittingly said to dwell in Jerusalem who withdraw some distance from worldly noise and are kept within the enclosures of silence for the sake of peace, so that there they may occupy themselves with spiritual duties; love to read the divine Scriptures constantly and suitably; ponder with grateful remembrance what they have read and not neglected [Col. 0845D]; repel at hand the obstacles of occasions; banish idle conversations by mature counsel; and prudently arrange necessary matters according to place and time.

These are the inhabitants of that holy city: forgetting what lies outside, they live within under the rule of holiness; abhorring not only deeds but also words of superfluous vanity, they apply diligence so as at last to attain knowledge of the truth. To these people that open fountain of David’s house is conveyed; to them its saving water is offered in a fruitful cup, by which both their conscience is purified and their understanding of the Scriptures is made clear. “On that day,” he says, “there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruating woman.”

Would that that day might dawn, even faintly, for me [Col. 0846A], and that the depth of my darkness might be dissolved by its first light. Would that even a small drop from that fountain might trickle down to me, and that, by its dripping, the dryness of my ignorance and conduct might be somewhat driven away; and that, when those same conduct habits had been chastened by a stricter judgment, an understanding of truth might glimmer for me beneath the covering of Scripture.

## CHAPTER IV

Yet although I seem to dwell in the Jerusalem spoken of above, because a regular cloister contains me with holy brothers, [p. 489] my spirit, which a bodily enclosure cannot hold back, seems often to fly away like a little bird. Though it would be far better for it to remain within its proper bounds, patiently to endure quiet, to rejoice in the silence imposed upon it, and to be fed by the wholesome nourishment of the Scriptures’ set-out feast [Col. 0846B], nevertheless, through a levity long since acquired, it more willingly returns to its accustomed ways. It seeks, as it were, through the rough places of the forests, the pleasure of its wretched will, where it endures a loss that is more grievous, though pleasing to it.

A certain pagan seems aptly to have described the natural restlessness of such a little bird, as I recall reading as a boy in school:

> “Though the daughters of Pandion are well shut up in a cage,  
> Yet each strives to return to her own woods.”  
> —Ovid

The pagans tell that certain little birds were born from Pandion. When they are caught by some fowler’s means and presented at home to young girls, the girls delight in keeping them more carefully enclosed in a cage, in setting before them choice foods and freely supplied drink; perhaps they also urge and urge again that they speak, so that, forgetting their woodland chatter, they may praiseworthily make use of our words. Yet although these birds see that all necessities are ready to hand, that heat, rain, and the discomforts of cold are absent, and that the violent attacks of larger birds do them no harm, if they happen to discover that the door of the cage has been left half open, they fly and fly out, eagerly seize upon their former woods, and there, suffering hunger, heat, frost, rain, and weariness of flight, hang in distress.

Because they do not recognize that this misery is voluntary, the prophet Hosea seems to have expressly signified this birdlike restlessness when he says that Ephraim flew away like a bird: “Ephraim,” he says, “flew away like a bird” (Hos. 9) [Col. 0846D]. Ephraim is interpreted “fruitfulness” or “abundance.” Therefore our spirit, which could bear abundant fruits if it wished constantly to dwell within the walls of Jerusalem, is rightly said to fly like a bird when, unable to endure quiet, it is found returning to love the things outside. There, although it works more laboriously, its work earns no glory; for, once it does not remain in its appointed place, it is not owed the reward of glory for its labour.

Hence Hosea adds: “Their glory [shall depart] from birth, from the womb, and from conception” (ibid.). By conception, recent thought seems signified; by the womb, deliberation; by birth, action. We seem to conduct ourselves in worldly matters in these three ways: what we are newly considering is, as it were, in conception; what we carry through deliberation is in the womb; what we now complete in deed is in birth. Their glory, therefore, departs from birth, womb, and conception, because whether they devise, deliberate upon what they have devised, or perform what they have deliberated, they will have no glory before God if they do not keep themselves within the established bounds of Jerusalem’s peace; if they stubbornly withdraw—not in bodily step, perhaps, but in spirit—from spiritual things; if they cling in heart and mind to worldly concerns [Col. 0847A].

And if they wish, as though reasonably, to excuse themselves and, after great works as they suppose, dispute with God, they are broken by judgment, because they went after filth, since they loved worldly things more than spiritual things. Thus Hosea says elsewhere: “Ephraim is broken by judgment, because he began to go after filth” (Hos. 5).

Since, then, my mind or spirit does not remain within the regular cage, but wanders inconstantly through empty things like a bird in flight, Christ certainly does not offer it the spiritual food of the Scriptures, nor nourish it as a fugitive with their understanding. Of this Solomon aptly says in Proverbs: “Like a bird flying away from its nest is the man who leaves his place” (Prov. 27).

If Christ sometimes deigns to recall such a man so that he may sit, be silent, read, or hear something salutary, he returns with wings smeared by the accumulated dust of worldly affairs and is found building not so much a wine-cellar as a muddy nest [Col. 0847B]. For just as a swallow flying outside plunges its wings into waters and, once they are wet, gathers the dust it touches, then returns and builds itself a muddy nest from it, so that frivolous spirit, when with harmful love it runs through every byway, weighs down its wings—now with the violent waters of thoughts into which it rushes, now with the unclean dust of actions which it meets. And if by chance it runs inside in order to provide better for itself, it nevertheless does not free itself from the things it gathered outside, but wraps itself in them as they cling to it, like a muddy nest.

Therefore, when I see that my heart has abandoned me, what can I say except: “May it please you, Lord, to deliver me?” For I cannot, except by His good pleasure, be freed from these muddy bonds by which I seem to be inextricably entangled; nor can I be instructed in the divine writings unless, freed on both sides, I deserve to be heard through His grace. But if I have not deserved—or rather, because I have not deserved—to obtain perfect knowledge, may He at least show me what mystery seems contained in the fact that the first man was found not to keep the lightest commandment, whereas Abraham manfully fulfilled the gravest.

## CHAPTER V

Perhaps in these two men, under the hand of the one who commands, are figuratively represented two kinds of subjects of differing merit. The first is lowly and weak and cannot withstand even a light wind, because, like a newly planted shoot, it does not yet stand firmly upon a foundation and does not enjoy the assistance of practice or training for resistance. The other, however, because it is [p. 490] now frightened by the example of those who went before and were weak, and encouraged by the praise or reward of the strong, once it has been strengthened by use and exercise, does not know how to bend beneath the weight of commandments, but has a heart ready for all things.

When someone newly becomes a weak beginner in [Col. 0848A] obedience and is bound by the prohibition of a superior not to do this or that, he is often more sharply incited toward what is forbidden; he strives after the prohibited thing and desires what is denied. At times, because what is forbidden is judged a trivial thing, he does not think that doing it will cause great harm; and, in doing it, he does not reckon himself bound by a very grave guilt, but thinks it can be more easily erased. For untrained childhood does not know how to provide for itself by prudent counsel; it does not know how to endure present discomforts in hope of the future. If something pleases it, it does not think it impermissible; and if it does happen to know it is unlawful, it nevertheless prefers to cling to the sweetness of present things.

This is figuratively demonstrated in that first man, when he is placed as a novice in the cloister of obedience. After he heard himself commanded not to eat the fruit [Col. 0848B], he desired it all the more eagerly at the serpent’s and his wife’s urging. Or perhaps, because he despised the forbidden fruit as a thing of no or little worth, he did not adequately weigh the obedience which forbade it; and although by true knowledge he perceived that the devil who persuaded him was lying, he did not realize that God would be so severely angered.

Or rather, Adam, like an infant at the threshold of beginning life, had not yet learned to guard himself against the assault of discomfort that would come afterward. Little concerned for the future and greatly concerned for the present, he despised what was to come and yielded to the present enticement. In that first beginning of his, when he was found not a little child in an infant’s body but already grown, and although he was endowed by God the Creator with no small knowledge [Col. 0848C], nevertheless, because he did not fear sufficiently—having experienced no evil—he ate what was forbidden and, by eating, was abandoned from his first grace.

For when, at the beginning of the world, he too had received a beginning and, as I have said, had received from God no mediocre knowledge, he must be believed to have known good and evil alike: good through experience, but evil only through knowledge. Since that seems to be more perfectly known which a person is said to experience by possessing or suffering it, he knew less fully the evil he had not experienced, and therefore sought it more heedlessly. When by wretched fall he cast himself into that unknown evil, he lost the good which he seemed to hold more perfectly; and when he wished, he could not stretch out his hand toward the good he had lost, because an angel set in the way and a flaming sword immediately did not permit him [Col. 0848D].

What this means, since it is explained in the answer concerning the salvation of the first man, need not seem necessary to repeat here, lest, while what was said there is unnecessarily repeated here, the discourse return more slowly to its subject. Therefore, when that first man did not merely fail to raise himself with firm step toward the good which he knew through experience, but also turned himself through unstable curiosity toward unknown evil, he sufficiently indicated how the first age works similarly under the hand of obedience if grace is removed and it is released to its own judgment.

For at that time both the first age of the world and the first age of man were in progress; hence both the one and the other were in a sense held to be weak. Although Adam, as I said before, was not infantile in body, he was not mature in time or old in years. Such maturity of time, although it does not always give to all sufficient growth in holiness, nevertheless, by grace’s cooperation, gives necessary assistance to many.

This world runs through six ages from beginning to end; and so does man, who is called the lesser world. As the former, by the increase of its ages, is found to have holier men, so the latter ought through the passage of time to cultivate his conduct more holily, so that according to the stages of life he may ascend to higher degrees of obedience, and the advance of his days may invite him to worthier advances of mind.

The first age of the world began with Adam. The second began with Noah, in whose time the flood occurred. The third began with Abraham, who was commanded to sacrifice his son. The fourth with David, who, in accordance with his name, is found bravely to defeat his enemies. The fifth with Jeconiah, when the people of Israel were exiled in Babylon. The sixth with Jesus Christ, who, dying and rising again for us, also raised us as having died with Him.

The first age of man is infancy; the second, childhood; the third, adolescence; the fourth, youth; the fifth, mature manhood; the sixth, old age. Thus also by the sixth degree one reaches the summit of obedience, than which nothing more perfect is found in this life. In those six ages of either world or man there is a figure; in these degrees there is the reality—not a reality destined to end in old age along with those ages, but one that will bring the consummate obedient person with Christ to the Father’s right hand.

Those six ages of the world or man could be fitted to these six degrees, and it could be shown in order which belongs to which, were it not that this demonstration appeared to require lengthy labour [Col. 0849C], while Adam’s and Abraham’s obedience is now in hand. But since each of them is contained within those ages, and when the discussion turns to those ages we shall not depart from these men either, it is not unfitting if at this point I attempt to show how each of these seems to correspond with each; provided that I, in attempting it, have the ability—for, as I see, no small difficulty also threatens this work.

[p. 491]

## CHAPTER VI
In the first age of the world God fashioned man from the clay of the earth; and to the man whom he had made he imposed no great or burdensome command, but forbade him to eat the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil, foretelling that, if he ate, he would die on that very day. And fittingly God showed the first man [Col. 0849D] the first degree of obedience: to one newly made he commanded nothing arduous, but tempered the command of obedience with easy possibility, since he did not desire the destruction of the being whom he had made.

For the first degree of obedience is to restrain someone newly entered upon it, as though an infant, from things not necessary, and to train the little athlete on the level ground of light commands, so that, when he has learned not to cling to lighter prohibited things, he may be able to advance his foot to the second degree of obedience. Therefore the same novice is not inappropriately forbidden the fruit “which was, as we read, beautiful to look at and pleasant to eat” (Gen. 3), although abundance of other fruits is granted him for food. For infants are accustomed to yearn more inquisitively after everything beautiful that they see, [Col. 0850A] and, unless perhaps they are forbidden, to stretch out their hands and bring it to their tender mouths.

Thus he, although not deceived by infantile ignorance, was nevertheless led on by his wife’s counsel; he rashly seized what was forbidden, and, eating what he had seized, learned by a true and miserable experience both what obedience bestows when it is maintained by unfailing service, and, conversely, what it brings upon one when it is abandoned in unlawful contempt. He could indeed have sufficiently kept the command he received, if he had wished steadfastly to obey it; unless perhaps, after this had been kept, some other thing might afterward have been granted him, which he too would have been commanded to accomplish under a greater injunction.

For when someone is forbidden one thing and is not commanded to do anything else, abstinence alone is virtue enough; and because of this abstinence it gives the eternal rewards of salvation. Hence those held in the condition of ordinary people, and in the public sphere of this life by secular manners and habits, are not compelled by the divine law so much toward great achievements as repelled from forbidden things, so that those weighed down by infantile weakness, which is common to very many, may at least be saved by easy abstinence from what is forbidden.

This is more clearly declared in the Acts of the Apostles, where the multitude of believers is commanded only to abstain from prohibited things. “It has seemed good,” they say, “to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no burden beyond these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication; if you keep yourselves from these things, you will do well” (Acts 15). You see that the apostles impose nothing else upon the people except that they separate themselves from what is [Col. 0850C] forbidden; and although by these things they are not joined to apostolic perfection, neither are they excluded from the number of believers who are to be saved.

“Like newborn infants,” Peter says, “desire milk” (1 Pet. 2); and Paul says to the Corinthians: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3). And if one asks why he gave them milk and not solid food, lest the teacher seem to begrudge his disciples spiritual progress: “For,” he says, “you were not yet able; indeed, even now you are not able” (ibid.). No one ought easily to be removed from this milk unless he is fit to be advanced to stronger food—that is, one who is growing up and for whom the milky observance of light commands no longer suffices, but who now hastens to the crumbs [Col. 0850D] that fall from the masters’ table.

Thus we read (Gen. 21) that Abraham weaned his son Isaac and celebrated a feast with joy at his weaning, because it is fitting for a father to feast and rejoice when his son aspires to greater advances, when, not content with milk, he desires stronger foods—as Paul rejoiced over the Thessalonians, whose spiritual progress he observed. “You are,” he says, “my crown and joy” (1 Thess. 2). Hannah too, we read, weaned her son Samuel (1 Kings 1) and, once he was weaned, presented him to the Lord at Shiloh, because those who still partake of milk and do not eat solid food are not worthily offered for ministry at the sacred altars. Paul knew the Hebrews to be such people when he said to them: “You have become those who need [Col. 0851A] milk, not solid food” (Heb. 5).

But one who does not spring forward from this milk in order to grow up, but recoils backward in order to become defiled—whose corrupted mind falls into doing what has been forbidden—incurs that prophetic curse: “As one weaned upon his mother, so is recompense in my soul” (Ps. 130). A little child is weaned upon his mother when, under the pressure of illness, he lacks strength even to suck milk; and, oppressed by hunger, he suffers the loss of death, because he has not gained strength for nourishment suited to his age.

Adam, newly created, suffered from this illness when he did not care to obey light commands, when he rejected the nourishment of permitted fruits and inclined his diseased ear to his wife’s poisonous counsel. By this illness he also weakened the succession [Col. 0851B] of his posterity and bound it with the chains of sin so inextricably that all, conceived and born in sins, also die in sins—except for the very few who are freed by grace alone.

Hence that first age, which spread itself into a plentiful multitude of nations, advanced from bad to worse; it so confused its thoughts and deeds that the more numerous it became, the worse it became, and, as though a horse had been given its head, it was borne headlong as a whole into vices. Not to mention many other things in which it did not fear to entangle itself—all of which this place and time do not permit us to recount—it relaxed the reins of modesty to such a degree and violated the lawful rights of chastity so greatly that few within it remained bound by the just law of marriage, while men everywhere and without discrimination mingled with women.

[Col. 0851C] The law, although not yet inscribed on parchment or tablets, was nevertheless already written in their hearts. It taught that each person should lawfully take a wife of his own, and should not presume to desire one whom another had taken; for just as he does not wish to give his own wife to another, so neither should he join another’s wife to himself. Indeed, they knew that God joined only one wife to that first man, thereby clearly showing later generations that each person ought to be confined within his own wife’s embrace, not beastlike and unrestrained among those of others.

Disdaining these laws, which they ought to have obeyed, and failing to refrain from neighing after a neighbor’s wife, the sons of God, as it is written, when they saw the beautiful daughters of men, rushed with lustful violence into their embraces [Col. 0851D] (Gen. 6). The beauty of women presented to their eyes pleased them so greatly that the strength of men yielded to it; conquered, they preferred captivity in a woman’s pleasant bedchamber to being crowned through the laborious victory of manly resistance.

Scripture is understood to call “sons of God” those descended from Seth, who remained in the worship of God; but “daughters of men” those born from Cain’s descendants, who, worshipping foreign gods, were held in wandering error. Thus that people of God committed a double sin, mingling themselves both with women who were not their own and with idolaters; either one of these would have been more than enough to merit wrath and to bring eternal punishment upon themselves from an angry God.

For when we read that, seeing that the daughters of men were [Col. 0852A] beautiful, the sons of God “took wives for themselves from all whom they chose” (ibid.), it is plainly understood that they carried off married women from weaker men as well as virgins whom they knew to be free from the bond of marriage—especially since no restraint of any law checked those unbridled men, and they were pleased not by holier life but by more beautiful form. If, however, they are thought to have chosen not married women but virgins alone, and to have joined the women they chose to themselves in marriage, even so they incurred no slight guilt, because worshippers of God ought never to have been joined to worshippers of demons.

By these and many other things God was at last stirred to unappeasable anger. He did not wish their great wickedness to roam unpunished any longer; but because the whole world was held guilty of disobedience, he willed that the whole world should be submerged by the overhanging [Col. 0852B] flood. “Behold,” he says, “I will bring the waters of a flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh” (ibid.).

Quite rightly God threatens to bring the waters of the flood over flesh that was borne by no desire for heavenly things, and to destroy all flesh that refused to obey the spirit but chose to serve its own pleasures; that refused to detest the passions of the body but wallowed in them with ruined understanding. Thus, that which is pleasantly immersed in the streams of luxury and in moist places is punished by being submerged in the flood of tribulations, as though by a deluge of waters.

But if, though this is difficult, someone is found who, living among the wicked, is intent upon guarding himself, and who does not refuse to draw milk from tender breasts—that is, to give more diligent care to light commands—then he certainly ought not to perish when the waters of tribulation overflow, but should pass from infancy to childhood through progress of mind. For one who does not burn, together with other sinners, to do what is forbidden, but rests from the heat of wickedness in the shade of obedience, is worthy to be called righteous Noah, who alone with his household deserved to be delivered from the flood.

For Noah means “rest.” Upon this man the Lord gladly rested when, angry with those upon the earth, he destroyed all wickedness. He remained in this man’s spirit, finding in it a freely given dwelling for himself, whereas his spirit did not remain in other human beings because they were flesh. “My spirit,” he says, “shall not remain in man, because he is flesh. He repented,” as Scripture says, [Col. 0852D] “that he had made man upon the earth” (Gen. 6), because all man’s thought slipped, through carnal instability, toward evil, and his life opposed in every way the will of him who had made him so that the world might be inscribed by him as though with letters and the Creator praised by him in vocal harmony.

But because the same Creator knew this writing to be already confused and full of blasphemy, he wished to erase every creature from the face of the earth, so that a more legible letter might be written in his book and a better posterity given to righteous Noah. “I will destroy,” he says, “the man whom I created from the face of the earth; for I repent that I made them” (ibid.).

And fittingly, “I will erase.” For a prudent writer wishes to erase an old writing in such a way that he does not abolish parchment or tablet together with it, but, preserving the base as though it were the prior and immovable foundation, places upon it another building, of a firmer structure. Hence a certain pagan, while teaching his pupil and earnestly advising him to correct what came before, said:

> Often turn your stylus: you are about to write again things worthy of being read.  
> —Horace

The wise poet wishes that, if what has been written seems not to suit the purpose, the prudent writer should not hesitate to erase it, so that, when the unsuitable material is corrected more carefully, what remains may be preserved more fittingly. But because I judge the testimonies of prophets rather than poets more pleasing to devout ears, God, speaking through the prophets, also declares that he erases, [Col. 0853B] so that, when the stylus is turned, the tablet is not destroyed but, once it has been smoothed, a more durable inscription is written anew. “I will erase Jerusalem,” he says, “as tablets are usually erased; erasing, I will turn and repeatedly draw the stylus over its surface” (4 Kings 21).

It is as though he said: What has been written does not please me, and therefore I shall not preserve for myself writing of such a kind. Rather, drawing the stylus repeatedly, I shall straighten what is crooked and level what is rough; and there, setting forth a better writing, I shall inscribe it legibly. It is of such a writing that he says to Habakkuk: “Write the vision and set it forth upon tablets, that he who reads may run” (Hab. 2).

Therefore God rightly declares that he will erase man, in whom, because he is flesh, his spirit does not remain; for those who are permanently enrolled upon the fixed foundation of faith are written by his spirit, not with erasable ink. As Paul says to the Corinthians: “You are the letter of Christ, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God” (1 Cor. 3). Noah alone with his household deserved to be delivered, through whom the human race might be restored. In him the course of the preceding age comes to an end, while the restoration of the following one begins.

## CHAPTER VII

In this subsequent age the world now grows somewhat, as it were; and what had thus far been an infant becomes a child by the ordered course of progress. With nearly all that its infant newness had done washed away and erased, a greater grace succeeds, and childlike vigor proceeds. This childhood gives the world a more numerous people, [Col. 0853D] and makes that same people somewhat more instructed; for although not yet wholly perfect lovers of the Creator, they are nonetheless, by a useful fear, in some measure providers of useful things.
