Thus Noah, to whom the divine judgment assigns a testimony of praise, and who lived many years in this childhood of the world, is said, having become a farmer, to have planted a vineyard after the flood—of which there is absolutely no mention before the flood (Gen. 9). Since he knew that that first age had perished through the excess of waters, and that he and his household had scarcely escaped the flood under the shelter of the ark, taught by the divine Spirit he fittingly plants a vine in due order and prefers noble Falernian wine to tasteless water, lest the world fear a similar punishment again and, once the distress of such fear is driven away, rise confidently into joy.

For wine not only gives drink to the thirsty but also gladdens the drinker. When someone suffers and dries up from thirst, and his mind is in addition constricted and made sick by some distress, if he drinks wine soberly, he sometimes recovers from both ailments: his understanding is sharpened, his spirit is kindled, his speech becomes readier, and his face brightens. And fittingly the cup of wine is offered not in the first but in the second age of the world, because the infant who must still be nourished on milky foods does not yet dare to drink wine’s harsh liquid; though perhaps, if it is offered, he rejoices in the strength he has tasted.

But the child, already nourished with stronger foods, is found fitter to drink a cup of wine; and such a drink is judged to profit him considerably, provided moderation and temperance are maintained in taking it. So too that age of obedience which, by analogy, is called infancy is shaped, as was said above, by gentle and infantile commands; whereas childhood is now beneficially burdened with harsher ones, provided it is not weighed down beyond its strength by the burden of this severity.

The former is moved more feebly to avoid what is forbidden; the latter advances more vigorously to do what is commanded, rejoicing to enjoy a freer field, now somewhat released from the bonds by which infancy is still impeded, as though wrapped in swaddling clothes. At this degree or age the obedient person’s mind begins to expand; it is no longer burdened by its former slowness, but dares to undertake the commander’s injunction not only patiently but gladly, and eagerly springs forward with commendable quickness to perform it.

This child, fit for bending and nimble for running, does not know how to disdain even very humble things, provided they are not burdensome; but, eager for the things promised, he hastens to obey the commands of the one who promises. Because of this readiness by which the advancing mind inclines toward obedience, the person making progress is, I think, frequently called a child in the Scriptures. By this designation not a small number of years is indicated, but a ready obedience is signified.

I judge the people of Israel once to have been such a child, whom God declares through the prophet Hosea that he loved: “For Israel was a child,” he says, “and I loved him” (Hos. 11). In Egypt the dullness of infantile ignorance held the children of Israel, when the superstitious religion of the Gentiles deceived them by diverse error, and when they thought the false gods whom they saw honored by sacrifices and offerings were likewise worthy of their own divine worship. Therefore the same prophet says there: “They sacrificed to the Baals and offered sacrifice to idols” (ibid.).

Yet divine patience bore with them for a long time in this error, and at last summoned them from the darkness of that Egypt through Moses and Aaron. They did not sufficiently understand that his forbearance and summons intended nothing other than mercifully striving to heal them, resistant though they were. Hence it is added there: “And I, like a nurse, carried Ephraim in my arms, and they did not know that I was healing them” (ibid.).

But after they were led out of Egypt under Moses’ leadership and were instructed, according to their capacity, by his admonitions to worship God, [Col. 0855A] they came somewhat to know the God whom they had previously not known, and loved him once known; so that they were no longer carried in his arms after the manner of infants, but followed him as children when he called and drew them. Concerning this drawing the Lord continues through the same prophet: “I will draw them with the cords of Adam, with the bonds of love” (ibid.).

Lest Adam, after sin, should wander any longer and be irrevocably estranged from his Creator, the same Creator cast the cord of his mercy after him as he fled, and by the gift of his grace caused him to turn and return to himself. When he had returned, he entangled him in the soft bond of love, so that he might follow the one drawing him by the choice of his own will.

> Each person is drawn by his own pleasure.  
> —Virgil [Col. 0855B]

With the same cord he drew back the children of Israel from the yoke of Egyptian slavery; and, having led them out of Egypt, he drew them after himself with the bond of love, going before those who followed in a pillar of fire and cloud, while they promised him voluntary obedience (Exod. 13). “All that the Lord has commanded,” they say, “we will do, and we will be obedient” (Exod. 24).

Therefore it is rightly said: “Israel was a child, and I loved him,” because “I,” he says, “love those who love me” (Prov. 3); and those who are loved first understand, and rejoice that they are loved by God, when they begin to delight in his commands. Many testimonies may be gathered from Scripture in which those who obey are called children. If anyone thinks they are called children because of their age, closer attention will show him repeatedly contradicted.

When Abraham had received angels, appearing as men, into his hospitality and wished to prepare a meal for those he had received, “he ran,” Scripture says, “to the herd, took from it a very tender and excellent calf, and gave it to a servant-boy” (Gen. 18). Of this servant-boy it adds: “He hastened and cooked it” (ibid.). You see that the child did not delay in doing the light task commanded, but hastened—as is characteristic of a child—so that not only might the commander’s order be fulfilled, but the cheerfulness of the fulfiller might deserve favor.

When the same Abraham was commanded to sacrifice his son Isaac and saw from afar the place which God had wished to point out beforehand, “he said to his servants: Wait here, and when we have worshipped, [Col. 0855D] we shall return to you” (Exod. 24). Here too I judge that “children” indicates not persons small in age but those ready to obey: ready both to go with their master and to await his return when he departed.

Likewise, when Lot met the two angels appearing to him and, devoted to hospitality, humbly invited them into his house, he said: “I beg you, my lords, turn aside into the house of your servant (puer)” (Gen. 19). I do not see why this man should call himself a child, when Scripture attests that he already had a wife and two daughters, unless it was because he was ready to obey the angels’ wishes and had resolved to serve strangers and guests.

When Jacob, by the Lord’s command, was returning to the land of his birth and, fearing his brother Esau, sought to appease him with gifts, “he sent,” Scripture says, “separate herds, each by the hands of his servants, and said to his young servants: Go before me, and let there be a space between herd and herd” (Gen. 32). But to show that Scripture calls these men children because of obedience, it adds: “And he commanded the first, saying: If you meet Esau,” and so forth (ibid.); and below: “Likewise,” it says, “he gave commands to the second and third” (ibid.). You see that they are designated by the name of children because obedience to commands is imposed upon them—not because they take upon themselves again the small age that has already passed, but because they do not presume to oppose the order of the one commanding.

The centurion in the Gospel testified that he had such children, when he earnestly besought the Lord for one of them. “Lord,” he says, “my servant-boy lies at home paralyzed [Col. 0856B] and grievously tormented” (Luke 7). And he added: “I have soldiers under me, and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it” (ibid.). These are the centurion’s children: those who strive to obey him according to their strength, faithfully going or coming in the service of his household, and serving with obedient submission at their commander’s nod—unless a harmful sickness prevails to hinder them. “I say,” he says, “to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

Thus the obedient person, who was previously called a child, is later called a servant, because, with neck bent beneath the Lord who commands, he serves him. Although he does not yet rejoice in perfect readiness to fulfill every command, he nevertheless does not dare to resist him with stubborn insolence.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0856C]

For just as it belongs to servants to have masters, so, if they do not love their masters, it belongs to them at least to fear them; thus those whom the gladness of a complete love does not lead into service may at least be compelled by the necessity of an incipient fear. Therefore, when the Lord invited the children of Israel in the wilderness to serve him and bound them through Moses’ hand by many commands, he carefully affirmed that he was the Lord and repeated this very point often. “Keep my Sabbaths,” he says: “I am the Lord” (Lev. 26). “Do not turn to idols: I am the Lord. Keep all my commandments: I am the Lord” (Lev. 19). And many similar statements.

Because they needed to obey—which is nothing other than to serve—their teacher vigilantly declares himself to be their Lord, so that from this they might understand themselves to be servants. For as son is related to father and father to son, so master is related to servant and servant to master. These are mutually relative names: neither is there a servant without a master, nor a master without a servant. Therefore, when God gives them precepts for living, wishing that they should have ears to hear, he frequently inserts, “I am the Lord,” so that servants may know that nothing is more beneficial for them than to serve their Lord through obedience.

Those who obey serve, or those who serve obey: if they are somewhat perfected, they do so through love of progress; if they are imperfect, through fear of punishment. For, according to Horace:

> The good hate to sin out of love of virtue.

And according to Isaiah: “We conceive the spirit of salvation from [Col. 0857A] fear.” But those whom neither love nor fear brings to obedience are indeed servants, but wicked servants; and therefore, their hands and feet bound—that is, with all capacity for good works taken away—they are cast into outer darkness and punished by the blindness of everlasting death.

But those who strive to obey the Lord’s commands either through love of virtue or from the obligation of necessary servitude, yet cannot attain the result because they are hindered by an obstructing weakness, ought to be helped. Divine mercy should be implored for them, so that those who have at hand some measure of will to act may also receive some ability to carry it out.

Such, it seems to me, was the centurion’s child or servant: because the will lies near to him, he deserves to be loved by the centurion; but because he does not find how to accomplish the good, he is said to be tormented by sickness. What sickness can more greatly afflict anyone than to will and not be able to fulfill what he wills? When this impossibility resists the will like a hateful illness resisting health, I see no remedy that can be given for so grave a burden unless at last either the will yields to impossibility, or perhaps impossibility yields to the will.

Despair leads us to the former; the grace of God alone brings us to the latter. For we commonly withdraw the will from its purpose when we wholly despair that it can be fulfilled; but we attain the effect of that same will when the grace of divine generosity makes possible what is impossible. A certain comic poet wisely recalls presumptuous persons to the former course; Christ mercifully encourages his lovers toward the latter. The former says: “Since what you wish cannot happen, wish for what you can do.” [Note: [Col. 0857D] Terence.]

The pagan gives prudent counsel to the proud: if they have presumed to attempt something impossible, they should hasten to direct their minds toward attempting what can be done. But Christ so exhorts his faithful to hope for impossible things that their hope may be placed in God, not in man; and such hope will remain unconfounded through the true love poured into their hearts (Rom. 5). “What is impossible,” he says, “with men is possible with God” (Luke 18).

Observing this, the centurion does not despair of the recovery of his servant or child, but confidently affirms that the sick man can be healed if it pleases the divine majesty dwelling in Christ, whose invincible power makes nothing impossible. “Only speak the word,” he says, “and my servant-boy will be healed” (Matt. 8). Great faith! He believes that his servant-boy, whom he cannot heal because he is a human being, can be healed by him who is a human being. For he knows that, although he commands his servant-boy as a master, so that he may render obedient service, he does not thereby grant him the grace effectively to carry out what he has been commanded. But he sees Christ not only visibly to be human: he also believes him invisibly to be Lord. Therefore he believes that Christ can not only command whatever he wills, but also grant whatever he commands.

For this reason Christ says: “I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Matt. 8). In Israel according to the flesh, which regards me too carnally; which neither fears me as God nor even reveres me as a righteous man; which does not confess that I have any power, or perfect power; which with unbelieving mind denies either that I am from God or that I am one with God—in this Israel, I say, to which I came sent in a special way, I have not found such perfection of faith as I see excelling in this foreigner, who could foresee with a believing heart the divine majesty hidden by flesh.

Therefore Christ heals the sick servant-boy on account of this man’s merit, so that, once the obstacle of sickness had been removed, he might perform the even light obedience that he wished to perform. Christ knows that this obedience is accomplished not by the man’s own strength but by divine generosity, which works in him both to will and to accomplish, according to its good will.

Such children are also invited in the psalm to praise the Lord, because those who either do not yet speak through infantile inexperience or are weighed down by languid incapacity are unable to voice divine praises, though they do not wish to lie hidden in torpid silence. “Praise the Lord, children,” it says; “praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 112). Those who have driven away sickness and infancy, and eagerly seek to obey with quick movement, can in some measure pour forth praises pleasing to God; when they hear through the Scriptures what God has willed not only to forbid but also to command, they strive, according to their strength, to respond in speaking obedience.

For the age of childhood abounds in talkativeness and is curious to hear; it delights in the garrulous novelty of speaking, all the more inclined to roam through this breadth because the earlier age seemed to have been confined longer within the narrow bounds of silence. Infancy is not granted a fully developed ability to speak; a certain innate difficulty restrains it as it eagerly watches those speaking, and it can scarcely at last attempt a few words that it hears more frequently repeated at home by its parents.

But childhood, seeing a greater power of speech granted to itself, can no longer endure confinement within the paternal household. It wanders abroad, strives to rival greater speakers, hates silence, and loves to chatter with those of its own kind. It is fit not only to retain its mother tongue, which it learned at home, but also to acquire any new one offered to it; indeed, a child can more easily acquire several languages or arts by learning them, and is said thereafter to remember them more tenaciously.

Therefore children are rightly entrusted especially to teachers of letters or of any arts, and are trained in every branch of knowledge during childhood, so that, when they have received in these matters a suitable foundation of learning, they may more easily and more firmly acquire a further completion in subsequent years. Perhaps for this reason too the first age of the world is found to have had one language or speech, while diversity of languages is granted to the second age: so that nothing arduous beyond its powers might be imposed on the former, nor anything suited to its powers withheld from the latter.

Thus, at the second degree obedience is not inappropriately judged more talkative, since, once commands have been heard, it is prepared to act more readily than usual [Col. 0859A]; and it not only performs things suitable and lighter for its own strength, but, like a talkative child, promises that it will accomplish greater things.

## CHAPTER IX
But because one who, still acting as a child, presumes to promise great things is often found to incur anger, obedience must also in some manner be removed from this stage and advanced, in its proper order, to the third and higher degree of progress. At this degree the obedient person no longer chatters lightly in a childish way, but, like an adolescent, is stirred more ardently to obey; and he so rejoices in this new increase of strength within himself that he also aims to be of help to others. For, seeing certain blameworthy persons accused, and seeing the weak corrupted by their example [Col. 0859B], he is ashamed not merely to seem like them, but burns to attain a merit unlike theirs. He desires indeed so to obey the divine commands that he may also impart to his neighbours a pattern of obedience, lest he seem to live for himself alone if another is not brought to life through imitating him.

For he understands that it is a lesser merit to serve in the camp of obedience if, by looking on, no other person is invited to the same service. Someone lukewarm may wish to maintain an obedience so slight that the bushel placed over it can keep it enclosed under its own authority; whereas obedience itself ought rather to burn so brightly that it deserves to appear commendable to all who are in the house. But obedience which thus stands out, luminous as though upon a lampstand [Col. 0859C], undoubtedly becomes abundantly fruitful: for its progress offers others a useful encouragement, and others’ benefit increases its own progress. For whatever another commendably performs by its example is rightly credited to its merits; and, like a mother, it seems to give birth to as many children as it earnestly labours to impart to its neighbours a pattern of life.

Finally, when the childhood of the years yields place, the adolescence that succeeds it now reaches puberty; and within the workshop of the loins a certain new fire grows, which, when it burns, the flesh scarcely bears to be confined by the barrier of continence, but is expanded by desire for offspring to seek generation. For this law is naturally assigned to human flesh: when, established in infancy or childhood, it cannot beget, then, upon entering the bounds of adolescence [Col. 0859D], it begins not to love barrenness, but, in order to bear fruit, seeks to join to itself a partner.

Thus the first and second ages of a human being remain, as it were, unfruitful through natural weakness. Although the passage of time gives each, according to its measure, sufficient development, it nevertheless brings neither to the accomplishment of begetting. The third age, however, is advanced by a natural benefit so that, as though unable to bear solitude, it rejoices in social love; and, now fit for the marriage union, desires to be made fruitful in children. So too an obedient person is then said, as it were, to have reached the third degree when he is found to obey commands with such affection that he is judged useful not only to himself but also equally to others, and deserves profitably to be set before them for imitation.

For when he burns inwardly to obey as though in a furnace [Col. 0860A], and when, according to place and time, his unfeigned humility shines outwardly, his progress is rightly judged commendable, and he encourages all the untrained and tender to make progress. “Strengthen me with flowers,” she says, “surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song of Songs 2). The torch of love is wont so to inflame an adolescent that he is often compelled to reach an unbearable languor; and at last, through impatience, he seems to himself to be perishing unless some consolation hastens to aid him. Since he has been accustomed to feel either no stings of love or only rare ones, and now a somewhat greater fire has arisen within his tender loins, that untrained age does not know how patiently to bear an unfamiliar burden, but immediately desires to cling in embraces to the thing it loves.

When it is prevented from this by the unwelcome obstacle of difficulty [Col. 0860B], it is prompted to desire something that it can meanwhile obtain, so that its impatient mind may be drawn away a little by this presence, lest it be intolerably weighed down by that absence. The adolescent therefore desires to be placed in a flourishing garden and to dwell amid the various delights of flowers and apples. By these, both relief is given to his languor, lest through impatience it grow beyond measure, and aid is given to his love, lest, what seems more disadvantageous, it grow cold. For just as, when what is desired is deferred, the mind sometimes burns more intensely, so it often grows cold, falling through excessive delay into despair; and what it despairs of being able to attain because it is too difficult, it chooses, as though consulting its own welfare, to forget.

But when the adolescent has been ensnared by welcome love, he strives so to bring his desires to fulfilment [Col. 0860C] that, if they are delayed, he nevertheless does not wish to call them back from their purpose—preferring to be worn away by love rather than, under the pressure of sloth, not to love at all. Rightly, therefore, he asks to be strengthened and surrounded by flowers and apples, by whose beauty and fragrance the lover’s mind is usually delighted, so that through this diversion impatient intensity may be moderated, while by the same encouragement a torpid desire may nevertheless be awakened. “Strengthen me with flowers,” she says, “surround me with apples, for I languish with love.”

The fervent obedient person at the stage of adolescence says this rightly when opposing difficulty resists his endeavours; when, because he cannot reach the one he loves as though by a sudden leap, he desires at least to find some consolation among those with whom he lives. For he thinks that his obedience alone does not sufficiently please God if he does not love to have other obedient persons with him; if he does not embrace, as the pleasant blossoms of a flourishing garden, the first beginnings of their good disposition [Col. 0860D]. Those are called flowers who, when the frost of hardened depravity has been loosened and the springlike mildness of holiness poured in, burst from the bark of oppressive oldness and assume for themselves the tender beauty of flowering newness.

Apples, however, may be called those who, instructed by weightier admonitions, have attained the more pleasing fruit of good works, offer their neighbours the fragrance of a good reputation, and now nourish their cultivators with a fitting progress in obedience. This obedient person desires to be surrounded and strengthened by apples and flowers of this kind, so that his adolescence may be found fruitful. He rejoices in his fruit—that is, in the progress of his neighbours [Col. 0861A]—and, strengthened by this nourishment, loves more earnestly and awaits more patiently the one he loves.

## CHAPTER X

That patriarch Jacob says that he had been thus fed from his adolescence, when, considering death to be near, he blesses Ephraim and Manasseh. “May God,” he says, “who has fed me from my adolescence, bless these boys” (Gen. 48). God indeed fed that patriarch from his adolescence, from the time, that is, when He inspired in him an obedience so fervent that by it he bestowed upon his neighbours an incentive to live well, and was fed, as it were, by their progress as by the labours of his own hands.

For an obedient person seems to find this nourishment for himself from the time when he rejoices that his obedience serves others’ benefit; from the time when, just as he himself was borne [Col. 0861B], he begins also to bear others, and, having advanced to the years of puberty, to support others’ infancy. This is the burden, or yoke, which the Apostle urges us to bear, so that the law of Christ, which is charity, may be fulfilled. The infancy or childhood of earthly littleness cannot fulfil it: living only for itself, it does not know the ardour of brotherly charity. Therefore Jeremiah says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his adolescence” (Lam. 3).

When someone has, as it were, completed the years of puberty; when fruitful maturity in holiness has grown together within him; when the love of begetting has grown warm in the secret place of heart and loins—then charity patient in bearing others is also generated, or, once generated, strengthened. For who would not be believed to love the one whom he desires to beget by word or example? And who does not bear patiently with the one whom he loves [Col. 0861C]? It is good for a man—that is, pleasant and useful—when he has borne this yoke, when, in God’s service, he has joined others to himself. This happens once, like an adolescent, he has completed the years of puberty; that is, through the progress of obedience, he has received the grace of this holiness.

It is good, I say, for a man when he has laboured in the Lord’s cultivation in such a way as to seek benefits not only for himself but for others as well; so that he may be neither a wild ass, whose chief concern is solitude, nor a discordant beast that kicks against the yoke. Finally, the word *yoke* (*jugum*) seems to be derived from joining (*jungendo*), because it does not admit a single wild animal [Note: [Col. 0861D] An allusion to Psalm 79:11.], but through the grace of love transfers the number from singular to plural and joins two together, lest anyone wander unrestrained in the reins [Col. 0861D] and perish in solitary wandering when he has no one to lift him up if he falls.

For those held together in the union of the yoke cherish one another, and do not easily turn aside from what they desire together, because for the sake of refreshment they lean one upon the other. Therefore the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you; for my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11). As though He said: If you wish both to be and to seem mine, love to be held beneath my yoke, so that zeal and contention may not divide you, but brotherly love may join you in an indissoluble bond. “For by this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 15).

By the benefit of this union, what is judged harsh and intolerable for one who loves solitude is made no little lighter [Col. 0862A], because my yoke is not weighed down by a bundle of troublesome heaviness, but is lifted upward by the support of winged lightness. The prophet Samuel bore such a yoke for a long time; but he took to himself a companion of stiff neck. Although he loved him and wished, as it were, to draw him with himself together to the threshing, that companion kicked and violently rushed against the yoke.

For when the prophet, in the affection of sincere charity, judged the people Israel and laboured to lead them along the path of obedience for threshing, it, impatient of repose and judging obedience’s burden too hard, rendered evil for good and eventually sought another teacher. Yet the holy man, “peaceful while dwelling with those who hate peace” (Ps. 119) [Col. 0862B], did not cast off the yoke he had devoutly assumed, nor did he reject concern for those by whom he was rejected. Rather, from his adolescence to old age, he bore them patiently, loved them, and, with untiring ardour of spirit, interceded for them, both when they resisted and when they obeyed.

Hence he seems in a manner to glory before them that he was found to live peacefully among the restless; nor did he ever oppress anyone by the eminence of his authority, but presided over them with charity alone in view. “I,” he says, “have grown old and grey. Thus I have conducted myself before you from my adolescence to this day; behold, I am here. Speak before the Lord and before His Christ whether I have taken anyone’s ox or donkey; whether I have falsely accused anyone; whether I have oppressed anyone; whether I have received a gift from anyone’s hand.” And they said: “You have not falsely accused us, nor oppressed us, nor taken anything from anyone’s hand” (1 Sam. 12). And below: “Pray,” they say, “for your servants to the Lord your God, that we may not die” (ibid.) [Col. 0862C]. And he said: “Far be it from me that I should sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you” (ibid.).

You see that the prophet patiently bore the yoke from adolescence and diligently prayed for those whom he bore, because he judges it good for himself to be held by love for multiplying offspring, provided that he may always be found fruitful among those whom he loves. But when an obedient man is inflamed by the desire to beget, and his desire is brought to completion by a prosperous result; when he labours to offer himself to others as worthy of imitation, and sees them applying diligence through his counsels or examples [Col. 0862D]—then that light burden, or sweet yoke, is borne not only patiently but beneficially for both parties, because those who bear it do not bring upon one another the annoyance of kicking back.

This, I think, is what the divine word promises Abraham: namely, that in his seed blessing will be bestowed upon the nations; that his faith and obedience will be set before posterity as an example; and that from it there will arise a harvest of imitators comparable to a multitude of stars. “In your seed,” He says, “all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 15). And again: “Look up to heaven,” He says, “and count the stars, if you can; so shall your seed be” (ibid.). Because Abraham obeyed in going out from his land and from his kindred [Col. 0863A], he deserved to find such grace with God that he was made father of many nations, and his posterity was reckoned abundant not so much according to the flesh as according to the spirit.

“Go out,” He says, “from your land and from your kindred and from your father’s house; and come into the land which I shall show you. I shall make of you a great nation, and bless you, and you shall be blessed; and in you all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 12). And below: “I have made you father of many nations” (ibid.). Abraham is fittingly endowed with the grace of this blessing, and his offspring fittingly compared with the stars by merit of obedience, because the third degree of obedience is made fruitful with spiritual offspring, and the third age of the world was then in progress.

For, as was said above, the third age of the world begins with Abraham and, running through fourteen generations, is completed in David [Col. 0863B]. This number is suitably adapted to the age of generation, because from this number of years the capacity to beget is granted to a human being. But the two preceding ages of the world, which in their generations do not exceed the number ten, do not attain this abundance of blessing. For although the age of ten years advances to the point of seeing, it is still, hindered by the laws of nature, insufficient for begetting.

But if four is added to ten; if the Decalogue of the Law is increased by the grace of the Gospel; if one comes from the first rudiments of childhood to the puberty of adolescence; if one passes from carnal and self-directed love to spiritual love of one’s neighbour [Col. 0863C]—then a human being begins to be able to beget spiritual children, because he has now banished disordered movements and animal affections.

But if anyone assumes the role of one who begets at an immature time; if, still situated in childish years, he presumes to seem an adolescent; if, when he ought still to lie concealed, he wishes to come out in public; if the untaught attempts to teach, or the weak to govern the stronger—let him hear what follows upon the presumption of one who ventures such things, as the true judgment of a certain wise man cries out—or rather thunders—“Woe to you, O land, whose king is a child” (Ecclus. 10).

The adolescence of the world, therefore, is rightly marked with the titles of fervent obedience; rightly, by its merits, is it adorned with the fruitfulness of spiritual offspring. For in Isaac, who was begotten not according to the flesh but through promise, and whose name is interpreted “laughter” or “joy,” the joyful promise is fulfilled for obedient Abraham [Col. 0863D]. “In Isaac,” He says, “shall your seed be called” (Gen. 21). Thus ought our adolescence to be made fruitful; thus should it rejoice in prosperous fruitfulness: it should not grow sluggish under the winter shadow of frozen barrenness, but, beneath the summer sun, grow fruitfully ardent in loving its neighbour.

The Apostle Paul wishes such an adolescence to be present in Timothy, his son—one that may, by the example of its virtues, be fruitful for others—lest he should be found, contrary to the purpose of benefiting rather than ruling those whom he ought to help, to harm them through the burden of a contemptible pre-eminence. “Let no one,” he says, “despise your youth; but be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, in chastity” (1 Tim. 4).

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0864A]

This obedient adolescence—or adolescent obedience—which burns to offer itself as an example to the faithful, which wishes to flourish in merits not only for its own sake but also for brothers and neighbours, is granted, as grace advances, to enter the bounds of youth in order to attain more fully this gift of virtue. In this youth the obedient man is strengthened by an increase of powers, since he does not count it burdensome to endure troubles for the same obedience: he is fit not only to resist invincibly adverse attacks, but also boldly to attack every obstacle in the hope of victory.

For just as the holiness of obedience grows fervent in adolescence, so in youth the strength of that same holiness grows mighty: the former burns to obey for the progress [Col. 0864B] both of itself and of its neighbours; the latter does not refuse to die for the laws of that same obedience. Finally, that obedience does not seem to flourish in adequately worthy praises which, being somewhat delicate, is accustomed to rejoice only in prosperity; which can fulfil commands that are indeed smooth and easy, but which, although the will desires them, weakness compels it to shrink from those that threaten sufferings.

Therefore youth must necessarily be added to fervent adolescence. In it, the obedient man, not content with easy fulfilment of the commandments, becomes readier for greater things, intent upon the honours of victory to such a degree that he does not refuse, for God or neighbour, to undergo the varied outcomes of war. To such young men the Apostle John writes: “I write to you, young men, because you are strong and have conquered the evil one” (1 John 1).

When the Apostle John writes to these young men, he notably ascribes to them nothing else than that they are strong and have conquered the evil one, thereby indicating that strength belongs, as it were, particularly to obedience in its youth; and that one found strong subjects the evil one to servitude. For at this fourth degree of obedience the evil one is overcome, wherein the vigorous young man imitates the suffering Christ. As He, by His Father’s command, was willing to suffer death for His brothers, so this obedient person does not refuse to spend his life for charity [Col. 0864C].

For this is what our adversary fears; this is what most heavily brings about his ruin: that in the camp of obedience our flesh wastes away through the afflictions of death. The more it is worn down, the more our spirit rejoices. That wicked one does not lightly dread such a battle or contest, in which the obedient combatant grows strong with youthful courage. The more that crafty foe swells up to attack it, the more forcefully he is struck back and, his powers finally exhausted, grows weak.

For just as an enemy attacking more feebly makes the defender slow and weak—because strength is not needed except against one who attacks more strongly—so a strong attacker makes a proven fighter stronger, because the victor deservedly finds the palm sought in a mighty contest more pleasing. A certain pagan also judged this worthy of belief and committed it to memory in a brief verse:

> “It is well that you fight: a good fighting enemy makes you so.” —Ovid

[Col. 0865A]

Likewise, our obedient person is found more commendable when greater difficulty is discovered in fulfilling commands and, in those difficulties, his spirit dreads nothing harsh and nothing base, provided only that he deserves to obtain the strength of youth. For in none of the preceding degrees is he strong enough to despise, at obedience’s command, the threats of death. But in this one he is clothed with confidence of triumph; having banished fear through the strength to suffer, he meets every adversity, “terrible as an army arrayed in battle.”

Finally, the fourth age of human life, which follows adolescence and is called youth, is fittingly strengthened first for the tasks of war. A young man can sufficiently bear military arms and respond with suitable strength to attacks by enemies. An adolescent, however [Col. 0865B], does not grow strong enough to carry out acts of war, but his effort proves insufficient. For even if some presumption urges him to persist, age recalls him, since it does not supply his body with sufficient strength.

A young man, however, because he displays stronger arms, will certainly gain surer triumphs. If camps stand against him, he is not troubled by weakness of strength; if battle arises, he rejoices all the more, placing his hope in it. This seems plainly indicated also in the divine Scriptures, when the strength or power of Judas Maccabaeus is commended: “Judas Maccabaeus, strong in powers from his youth, shall be your leader in war, and he himself shall wage the people’s battle” (1 Macc. 2).

Judas is declared strong in powers from his youth, because in earlier ages the gift of nature does not grant a person sufficient bodily strength [Col. 0865C], without which fullness of praise and glory is not gained in battles. Therefore he is rightly declared outstanding in the praise of this strength from the time when he could obtain sufficient strength, so that it may be understood that praise of bodily power is in some manner a gift and benefit of youth.

Thus, in the following book of Maccabees, when Scripture spoke of certain besieged persons bravely resisting their besiegers, and much farther on of others manfully defeating their enemies, it significantly called both groups young men. By this, I think, it clearly indicated that the incomplete tenderness of childhood or adolescence does not naturally possess the perfect bodily strength that accompanies it. “Strong young men,” it says, “standing upon the walls, were resisting bravely” (2 Macc. 12). And later, concerning Judas Maccabaeus, it says, after choosing the bravest young men: “In the camp he killed four thousand men” (2 Macc. 13).

When that learned man was about to go against the enemy to battle, he wisely chose as helpers those whom he knew to be not only lovers of praise and glory, but stronger in power and boldness through the gift of youth [Col. 0865D], so that they might either happily gain the desired palm after overcoming their enemies, or bravely undergo a praiseworthy death while their enemies triumphed. For this is, as it were, the chief concern proper to young men—provided they are not degenerate: they love those things which they know will benefit their honour, so that they may attain the praise of courage in deeds of war and, through its protection, either escape gloriously or die more gloriously.

For they think it neither inglorious nor far removed from virtue if, flourishing in the strong and verdant youth of body, they disdain to be subjected to enemies in disgraceful servitude and choose rather to die bravely avenged among fighters than either to undertake shameful flight, forgetful of praise, or to lead a degenerate life under the servile rule of those who mock them. On this account Scripture declares the sons of Israel commendable when it elegantly praises their courage: “They are prepared,” it says, “either to live or to die bravely” (1 Macc. 4).

Whether, therefore, they live or perhaps die, young men are not deprived of the glory of courage: they either deserve to preserve life through a victorious sword, or obtain in strong battle the victory of a glorious death [Col. 0866A]. Judas Maccabaeus finely showed this in word and deed when, about to die in battle, he wisely strengthened his companions in order to attain such glory: “Far be it from us,” he says, “to do this thing, to flee from them; and if our time has drawn near, let us die bravely for our brothers, and let us not bring reproach upon our glory” (1 Macc. 7).

You see that Judas, flourishing in noble youth, abhors shameful flight and desires to die bravely, lest love of a degenerate life bring upon his glory the reproach of dishonour; rather, honour and glory are bestowed on one who dies nobly. Plautus too, in the *Captives*, seems wisely to have held that one who dies in courage must by no means be thought to perish:

> “He who perishes through courage does not perish.”

The same author in the *Amphitryon*:

> “Courage has all things within itself; every good is present to him who possesses courage.”

[Col. 0866C]

Therefore no loss or disgrace is to be thought incurred by one who, whether living or dying, is found to have obeyed courage. Indeed, praise of courage is deservedly bestowed upon the person who manfully prefers an honourable death to a degenerate life.

Perhaps for this reason, after Judith the widow had killed Holofernes, commander of the Assyrians, and his army, swollen with hope of victory, had fallen from that hope, Scripture relates both that the Assyrians fled shamefully and that the sons of Israel pursued bravely. Thus it shows the former as deserving reproof for womanish weakness and degenerate fear, while, conversely, it commends the latter as young men with the praise of courage. “When,” it says, “the whole army heard that Holofernes had been beheaded, stirred by trembling and fear alone [Col. 0866D], they took refuge in flight, so that no one spoke with his neighbour” (Judith 15).

You see that the Assyrians, shaken with fear, shamefully sought refuge in degenerate flight and deserved neither the glory of a commendable life nor that of an honourable death. For when the courage necessary in military affairs fails, the disgrace of either life or death necessarily follows. But the sons of Israel, who were judged able bravely either to die or to live, were encouraged by hope of victory as their enemies fled. To reduce to nothing the enemies’ enfeebled courage, they sent chosen youth to pursue them. “Every district,” it says, “and every city sent armed chosen youth after them, and they pursued them at the sword’s edge” (ibid.).

They rightly sent armed youth [Col. 0867A] to pursue their enemies—that is, those whom they knew armed with courage—so that the hope of the hostile army might be turned to its opposite: those whom it had hoped to overcome would instead overcome it by their courage. For the Assyrian hoped easily to overcome the courage of the Jews, as Judith recalls when, after victory, she sang a hymn to the Lord: “Assyria,” she says, “came from the mountains of the north in the multitude of its strength; it said that it would burn my borders and kill my young men with the sword” (Judith 16).

## CHAPTER XVIII
The fact that strength is sometimes signified by a young man seems also to be intimated covertly by the angel Raphael himself. When he came to men, intending to show himself strong on their behalf, he chose to appear to them in the form of a young man. “Tobias went out,” it says, “and found a young man standing there; and, not knowing that he was an angel of God, he greeted him and said: ‘Where are you from, good young man?’” (Tobit 5). And below, the elder Tobias says: “Can you take my son to Gabael, in Rages, a city of the Medes?” (ibid.). And he says: “I will take him and bring him back to you” (ibid.). The angel was indeed able to take Tobias and return him to his father: he who powerfully overcame the demon that had killed seven of Sarah’s husbands in succession, and who, lest he should injure Tobias as the eighth husband, bound him fast with strength. As it is written: “Then he bound the demon in the desert of Upper Egypt” (Tobit 8).

The same angel indicated both by name and by appearance the strength through which he was able to bind the aforesaid demon and free Tobias, now married, from the demon’s malice. He presented himself as a young man and called himself Azariah, son of Ananias: “I am Azariah,” he says, “the son of the great Ananias” (Tobit 5). Now Azariah is interpreted “helper.” Fittingly he appears in the form of a young man, since he had come in order to help: weakness is not capable of offering sufficient assistance, but prevailing strength triumphs over a powerful adversary. Therefore, when the angel both calls himself a helper and shows himself stronger in power through the advantage of youth, he seeks to lead the doubting man into hope of victory and, as it were, to place his wavering mind upon the rock of confidence.

501 But lest this promise of help and strength should appear presumptuous—for swelling presumption is not useful but harmful—he elegantly commends it by expressly showing the source from which he derives his origin. “I am,” he says, “Azariah, son of the great Ananias.” Ananias is interpreted “grace of the Lord.” Thus he wished his strength to be attributed to the Lord’s grace: by that strength he was able, after binding the demon, to help Tobias; and that grace itself brought forth the young Azariah, that is, helping strength. The same strength humbly acknowledges Ananias—its generating grace—as its parent. “I am,” he says, “Azariah, son of the great Ananias.”

By these words Azariah not only commended himself as Ananias’s son, but also proclaimed Ananias himself worthy of commendation. For he recalled that he was not simply the son of Ananias, but the son of the great Ananias, so that, as strength might appear commendable because it comes from grace, so the greatness deserving proclamation might commend that same grace. There is, as it were, a small grace of the Lord, and there is also a great grace of the Lord. The Lord’s small grace may be called that by which he grants us bodily vigor, beauty of face, physical appearance, honors, riches, reputation, power, acute intelligence, tireless application, literary learning, and other such things as bring worldly delight. But the Lord’s great grace is rightly called that by which holiness of life is granted us, together with strength so effective and sufficient for that holiness that Satan, our adversary, is crushed beneath our feet; that the hammer of the whole earth is shattered; and that we are able not only to free ourselves from his bonds, but also to bind him strongly by our own strength so that he may not harm others.

This great grace, which is figuratively called the great Ananias, requires helping strength—namely, the young son Azariah—who is said to have bound the demon in the desert of Egypt by mighty power, and who confesses that he possessed this power not from himself but from the great grace of the Lord. Understanding this, as it were, wisely, Tobias replied: “You are of a great family” (ibid.). Truly, that helping strength proceeds from a great family, from great nobility; neither dull ignorance nor swelling arrogance precedes it. Rather, the great grace of the Lord grants such an abundant increase of power and goodwill that it imparts the aid of salvation not only to itself but also to others.

[Col. 0868C] So too obedience, which is strengthened by courage at its fourth degree, and which, once strengthened, glories not in itself but in the Lord, possesses a firmer defense of sure hope and supplies others with a more effective encouragement to obey. For one who, though delicate himself, refuses to endure burdensome commands cannot suitably invite others to obey serious precepts. The beauty of praiseworthy obedience is aired only in his speech; solid strength is not found in the performance of his work.

There are indeed some who know well enough how to commend obedience and discourse admirably upon its virtue or reward; if they have subjects, they imperiously impose every burden upon them, considering not so much what those subjects are able to do as what they themselves wish. Yet they themselves do not deign to obey either the decrees of their elders or the commandments of Scripture; rather, they either utterly despise them or attempt to lighten them according to their own judgment. But since the most commendable authority for speaking is the prior demonstration of doing, those who argue about obedience or issue imperious commands are not sufficiently heard unless they too submit to the laws of obedience; unless, when they command others humbly to fulfill the precepts of holiness, they themselves also labor to appear truly holy and humble.

Whatever must be commanded is communicated more effectively by doing it beforehand than by introducing it with the noise of words alone—especially if what is easy to command is known to be difficult to fulfill. This was not unknown to Ehud, judge of the children of Israel, who, when ordering his men to go into battle, himself went before them. “Ehud,” it says, “sounded the trumpet in the hill-country of Ephraim; and the children of Israel went down with him, with him going before at their head. He said to them: ‘Follow me.’ They went down after him and struck down about ten thousand Moabites” (Judges 3).

The very valiant judge properly exhorts the children of Israel to battle when he himself advances more eagerly at the head of the column. He knows that a serious undertaking is not commendably commanded if the commander reveals himself weakened by soft idleness. Abimelech too seems to have shown this during the siege of the tower of Shechem: what he commanded by word, he chose to demonstrate by example. “Taking up an axe,” it says, “he cut off a branch from a tree; carrying it upon his shoulder, he said to his companions: ‘What you see me doing, do quickly’” (Judges 9). And it adds: “Then, eagerly cutting branches from the trees, they followed their leader. Surrounding the stronghold, they set it on fire; and so it happened that a thousand persons were killed by smoke and fire” (ibid.).

You see the army swiftly obeying commands when it sees its leader going before it not so much in words as in deeds; for the very example of one who goes strongly before makes the obedience of the follower considerably strong. I think Judas Maccabaeus likewise did not fail to understand this. Having commanded all his men to come to battle, he is read to have crossed over to the enemy first. “When Judas approached the watercourse,” it says, “he stationed the scribes of the people beside the watercourse and commanded them, saying: ‘Leave no man behind, but let them all come to battle.’ And he crossed over to them first, and all the people after him; and they were all crushed before them” (1 Maccabees 5). And in the following book: “He himself,” it says, “the first Maccabee, having taken up arms, urged the others to undergo danger together with him” (2 Maccabees 1).

It is plain that he commands confidently who also obeys the law, who judges it dishonorable that one who imposes anything difficult or troublesome upon others should languish in idleness. But one who weakly languishes like a woman when great things must be done is certainly ashamed to impose the same things upon others. And if, setting shame aside, he swells insolently into command, then his wordiness, supported by no authority of life, is not received but despised.

For who would obey if a judge commanded the army to march into battle, to endure calmly the discomforts of heat and cold, to count fasting, vigils, and the hardships of camp as light in hope of victory, and to fight bravely unto death for peace and country—if the judge himself were not equally ready for the same things? If he languished in idleness, entangled in bodily luxuries, delighting in the steam of baths, with his hair arranged in womanish fashion, softened beneath shade in a chamber by the softness of feathers, and indulging the desires of his loins amid elaborate foods and repeated cups of wine?

It is therefore fitting that the commander who imposes war upon soldiers should be, as it were, one of those same soldiers; and, though regarded as commander by rank and dignity, should show himself a soldier by equal exercise of virtue. Hence in a certain writer a military commander is commended who, wishing effectively to exhort his companions to battle, endeavored among them not so much to make a noise with words as to fight with a strong hand: “He fought much himself, frequently struck the enemy, and performed at once the duties of a brave soldier and a good commander.”

Thus strength is necessary for everyone in obedience. Through it, distinction of merits is gained both by the commander and by the obedient person: the one who commands strives to present himself as a worthy example to those whom he commands, while the subject obeys by courageously adhering to the example set before him.

## CHAPTER XIII

Finally, David—by whom the fourth age of the world is said to have begun—is believed to have reached this fourth degree of obedience. Having been made ruler of the people, he did not think it fitting to delight in shade and idleness, but, obedient to their welfare, rejoiced to fight with tireless strength. The interpretation of his name also appears to agree with this, for it is found to signify strength: David is interpreted “strong of hand.” He is rightly called strong of hand, since by the Lord’s command he fights the Lord’s battles; having attained the vigorous youth of obedience, he offers God a service pleasing in battle.

Wicked Saul gave him a salutary admonition concerning this, and the king imposed fitting service upon his faithful soldier: “Only,” he says, “be strong, and fight the battles of the Lord” (1 Kings 18). Abigail too wisely commended this when she sought to bend David himself toward mercy: “The Lord,” she says, “will surely make my lord a faithful house, because, my lord, you fight the battles of the Lord” (1 Kings 25).

He fights the battles of the Lord who lives in the camp of obedience; who opposes with all his strength the enemies of the Church; who does not find it burdensome to endure any hardships for the peace of the faithful; who is troubled by continual afflictions for God’s sake and gladly glories in his own weaknesses; and who, in all that he does vigorously and faithfully, reveres the Lord whom he has resolved to obey and please. David eagerly desired these battles. For carrying them out diligently he wore away his youth in invincible strength and welcome labor; in them he obeyed God faithfully even unto old age.

And because he saw that he possessed within himself this strength for battle, from which he had an unfailing hope of triumphant victory, while truly recognizing that this strength came to him not from himself but from God, he rightly loved God, the giver of so great a gift, in order that he might possess it more strongly and perfectly. Gratefully he called God both his strength and his hope: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength” (Psalm 17); and elsewhere: “O Lord, you are my hope from my youth” (Psalm 70).

He calls the Lord his strength and also his hope, because the commendable strength belongs to God’s gift, and the effective certainty of hope is likewise God’s gift. “O Lord, my hope from my youth.” It is as though he said: From the time when you bestowed upon me the strength of youth, you also bestowed the hope of salvation; for when you act, bold strength in battle consequently gives confidence in triumph. Otherwise, if the strength of divine gift does not go before, the effective certainty of hope does not follow. A man despairing because his powers are weakened does not labor to obtain glory, and sad shame disfigures one who languishes in idleness.

Conversely, David says in another psalm: “I will enter unto the altar of God, unto God who makes my youth glad” (Psalm 42). God makes our youth glad when he supplies our strength with both the power and the certainty of sure hope; just as that strength is contracted and sickened by sorrow when no hope of glory renews it for the performance of brave deeds. But joyous youth, loving to obey bravely, promises that it will enter God’s altar; for then at last can each person offer himself to God as a burnt offering, when he has first loved to prefer brave deeds to soft idleness.

This is that youth to which the enemy, the world, is greatly opposed, and whose strength he admires while yielding to its power. The ineffective tempter constantly devises snares against it and supposes that it can be bent by any deceit. But it is greatly strengthened by the practice of suffering; once strengthened, it rejoices not vainly in hope of praise and glory. For though enemies can wickedly set every obstacle before it, yet by grace’s gift they cannot prevail. Of them he says elsewhere: “They have often attacked me from my youth; yet they could not prevail against me” (Psalm 128).

[Col. 0871C] It is as though he said: For this reason they do not cease to repeat their attacks, because they cannot trample down my youth. If it had ever submitted itself, ruined, to their dominion, their malice, victorious, would certainly have ceased from attacking. “They have often attacked me from my youth”; and: “I have been in labors from my youth” (Psalm 87). For from the time when I received youthful strength, I have been assailed by the greater attacks of enemies, because the faithful God does not give these enemies power or license to attack unless he sees that I have strength to resist.

Therefore I have suffered grievous assaults of enemies from my youth; but resisting them, overcoming through long and unwearied labor, from the time when I could fight I have been pressed by a great multitude of assailants, yet, strong in him who strengthened me, I have not been overwhelmed by the flood of tribulations poured over me.

Saul, David’s persecutor, was able to foresee in spirit this power by which David was found to prevail against his enemies. Knowing that he could not restrain it, the wretched man was not ashamed both to praise out of envy and, while praising, to envy: “Blessed are you, my son David; indeed you will accomplish what you undertake, and you will be mighty” (1 Kings 26). And above: “Saul, angry with Jonathan, said: ‘All the days that the son of Jesse lives upon the earth, neither you nor your kingdom will be established. Therefore send now and bring him to me, for he is a son of death’” (1 Kings 20).

An envious person is accustomed to endure nothing more painfully than seeing another excel by prosperous success. Although compelled to commend him for the merit of his virtues, he is nevertheless tortured by the intolerable torment of envy. Because Joseph is loved by his father more than all his sons, their hatred against him is stirred up; and after he, in his simplicity, related the dream he had seen to his brothers, that speech supplied greater fuel for envy and hatred. Finally, according to a certain pagan writer:

> The Sicilian tyrants found no greater  
> Instrument of torture than envy.

For although the tyrants kill the body, a brave spirit does not know how to bend; but envy, to greater harm, first makes the inner spirit rot, and then the body wastes away in sympathy. Hence that comic poet Plautus says in *The Captives* that it is characteristic of the wretched always to envy those whom they see to be good:

> “It belongs to the wretched to be ill-disposed and to envy the good.”

Thus Saul is tortured by envy when he sees David’s power. Nor is his perversity contained in silence; rather, he is unrestrained in word and deed to display the misery of his envy. For that wicked prince, not held by the bonds of obedience and not afraid, in obstinate thought, to offend his Creator, considers nothing more grievous than seeing others courageously obey the laws of holiness and arrive through victorious obedience at honor and glory.

Then his kingdom is irreparably weakened when the obedience of the righteous is strengthened by courage. Then his vessels or spoils are plundered, and his ruined strength is taken captive, when the fullness of strong obedience is granted to this man. Then that king, with his wretched army, is defeated and disfigured by fitting shame, when this man, strong of hand, is raised to the throne of the kingdom. For to be strong in this obedience is undoubtedly to be a king: one who bravely serves the heavenly commands rules imperially over hostile powers. And the more earnestly he strives to show himself a humble servant to virtues, the more strongly he is found to preside, by royal right, over vices.

Finally, that fourth age of the world, at whose beginning David is said to have been king, is read to have had kings after David until its end; and the world, flourishing in the development of youthful age, is also found to have flourished beneath the scepter of royal power. Worldly youth is fittingly found to excel under the rule of kings, and the succession of kings to preside over worldly youth, so that it may be understood that the fullness of youth possesses royal strength, and royal strength presides over that youth as though familiarly.

For this reason strength is rightly called royal: it is assigned, as though properly, to kings themselves. Without it they cannot retain their kingdom or penetrate the territories of enemies with victorious eagles. Hence, when it was said to hostile princes concerning the King of kings, “Lift up your gates, O princes, and the King of glory shall enter” (Psalm 25), those princes replied: “Who is this King of glory?” (ibid.). It is as though they said: If your king seeks to enter our gates, tell us who he is that dares even to utter a threat against them, when through so many days past none has come here with such confidence, nor has anyone violently broken through these gates.

And since it was known that he was not only eminent in the royal name but also excelled in strength—which is proper to a king—the question, “Who is this King of glory?” received the answer: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (ibid.). This is to say: If among you the question of the King of glory is being discussed, this man is proved to be king more in reality than in name, because he will obtain the triumphal throne against all opposing principalities, crowned with honor and glory (Psalm 8). “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.”

[Col. 0873B] At this voice all those wicked princes fled, and the gates of hell stood open when their bars were broken; and the strong armed man could no longer guard his court (Luke 11), when the King of glory, stronger and mightier, deigned to come there. He was deservedly called king not only when he powerfully triumphed over hell, but also when he endured mockery, blows, spittle, and reproaches before the judge. For it is royal not only to possess the lands of enemies by happy victory, but also to endure their injuries with invincible patience.

Christ himself confirmed this when, questioned by the judge who treated him as though more powerful, he answered very briefly and truthfully: “I am a king.—You say,” he says, “that I am a king” (John 18). It is as though he said: You think that you possess royal power over me; but your power cannot endure much longer, because the exalted splendor which you love so greatly is not lasting beauty but passing beauty. My kingdom, however, though here assaulted by the momentary sadness of suffering, is nevertheless sustained without decline by the invincible strength of obedience; it is advanced by the certainty of unashamed hope; and it is brought to perfection by the unfailing brightness of heavenly glory.

Truly, therefore, I am a king, because whether I suffer or die, I do not depart from the strength of obedience. Rather, with unyielding step I walk the narrow path of obedience, so that, although upon it I appear to endure the grievous assaults of enemies, I am nevertheless found to prevail by royal power.

Although no other obedient person can be equal to this king, each must nevertheless strive to imitate him according to his measure. He will imitate him if he is equipped not only strongly for obedience but also wisely instructed in that undertaking. For it is fitting that the obedient person should not only be strong, so as steadfastly to suffer for the divine law, but also instructed, so as to know what and how he ought to perform. Otherwise the dullness of inadequate understanding may disfigure what strength confidently undertakes or pursues. Rather, while unbending constancy is maintained in acting, sufficient prudence and counsel for action must also be possessed.

Obedience which relies only on strength and remains without counsel is still quite uncultivated; by the very impetuosity of its strength it sometimes suffers harm, unless instruction comes to its aid with prudent counsel. Therefore the Lord says to those to whom he says, “Be strong in battle and fight with the ancient serpent,” elsewhere, “Be prudent as serpents” (Matthew 10), so that it may be understood that prudence, as well as strength, is fitting for one who wishes to obey more perfectly. As he is fortified by strength to undertake what is difficult, so he is necessarily instructed to know how he ought to undertake it.

The prophet, taught by the divine Spirit, also indicated this: recognizing men to be strong, he invited them to learning and understanding. “And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Psalm 2). And the Book of Wisdom says: “To you, O kings, are these my words, that you may learn wisdom and not fall away” (Wisdom 6). He calls them kings in whom the strength proper to kings excelled, perhaps men raised up against their enemies by confidence in that strength. But lest either their own presumption or hostile craftiness deceive them, he wishes intelligent instruction to draw this strength about with the bridle of counsel.

## CHAPTER XIV

This is the fifth degree of obedience, to which one must necessarily arrive. This is the age of manhood, by which the obedient person is appropriately marked: the strong constancy of battle makes him young, while prudent counsel in ordering things also makes him a man. For he will not readily obtain sufficient victory who, in doing brave deeds, does not maintain the necessary order, imagining that he can accomplish everything by violence and caring little if he acts imprudently.

For although the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it, that kingdom is by no means attained through violence unless prudent counsel moderates it. Only the prudent virgins were able to enter the wedding feast, and the Lord wished to instruct the apostles in serpentine prudence. Therefore, just as youthful years are followed in the order of life by manhood, in which one who is strong in bodily powers becomes, with the passage of time, mature in prudence, so discerning prudence is added, in the order of progress, to the strength of obedience; by its counsel, as though by a man’s counsel, the obedient person’s steps are wisely directed.

Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “A prudent man will direct his steps” (Proverbs 15). Strength for walking does not suffice to keep to the path of obedience unless prudent counsel for directing is also at hand. Often one runs strongly outside the path, and by a wandering course incurs only loss.

That counsel is regarded as somehow worthier and higher than strength is shown more clearly in the prophet Isaiah. When he recalls that seven spirits rested upon the flower of Jesse, he names counsel first and strength afterward. Beginning from the higher and proceeding downward in order, he says at last: “And there shall rest upon him the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength” (Isaiah 11). This shows that, although strength has no small value in the catalogue of spirits, the fullness of prudent counsel has something more exalted; for strength, though it may not yield to an enemy’s force, nevertheless yields when caught in seductive snares unless protected by the careful governance of counsel.

For this reason a certain wise man says: “Wisdom is better than strength, and a prudent man than a strong one” (Wisdom 6). Finally, if divine Scripture is considered more attentively, it declares how much prudent counsel avails in wars. When Mattathias, about to die, was giving his sons careful instructions and arranging diligently which of them should excel the others in what respect, he said: “Behold, Simon your brother—I know that he is a man of counsel; always listen to him. And Judas Maccabaeus, strong in power from his youth, shall be your commander in war, and he shall conduct the war of the people” (1 Maccabees 2).

Thus the father wishes that Judas, strong in power, should be placed over the army, yet that Simon, the man of counsel, should first be listened to in all things, lest anyone strong should presume to go to war without hearing him and be compelled to gain ruin rather than victory. Hence it is found later that some fell because, trusting in their own strength, they went to war without counsel: “On that day priests fell in battle, because they wished to act bravely like Judas, going out into battle without counsel” (1 Maccabees 5). And below: “Simon and those who were with him fought against Bacchides; he was crushed by them, and they afflicted him severely, because his counsel and his attack were futile” (1 Maccabees 9).

You see that victory did not come to Judas and those with him, because counsel did not go before them when they fought. But Simon, the man of counsel, afflicted and crushed adversaries whose strength prudent counsel had not fortified. Therefore Jesus son of Sirach, instructing the righteous man, says: “My son, do nothing without counsel, and after the deed you will not repent” (Ecclesiasticus 32).

Hostile and crafty malice, always striving to subdue the righteous, confidently attacks when it sees his strength deviate from the rectitude of counsel. And if it cannot overcome him by force, it knows that it can bind him in the nets of flatteries, since strength often yields to the sweet speech of a deceitful little woman: “For the lips of a harlot drip honey” (Proverbs 5). Of her Solomon says in Proverbs: “The harlot is a deep pit; she lies in wait on the road like a robber, and she will kill those whom she sees to be unwary” (Proverbs 23).

This harlot, lying in wait like a robber, is fittingly said to kill not the prudent but the unwary, because hostile craftiness detests not so much the strength of the righteous as their prudence. Indeed, the stronger it sees them to be, the more it glories if their unwary strength should perhaps be seduced by its flatteries.

By what deceits that same craftiness captures the righteous person’s strength when it discovers it to be unprotected by manly counsel, Solomon has already shown quite elegantly; by that exposition he intends to call us back from such bonds: “I observe,” he says, “a foolish young man passing in the street near the corner” (Proverbs 7). By the foolish young man, I think, the unconsidered strength of the righteous is represented. For as strength seems signified in the young man, so prudence of counsel seems signified in the heart; whoever does not take care to possess it profitably in what he does is rightly convicted of not even having a heart.

Hence it is said below: “A rod is upon the back of one who lacks heart” (Proverbs 10). It is as though he said: He who does not refuse to lack prudence of heart is rightly compelled to endure the scourge of the imprudent. The prophet Hosea also represented prudence by the term “heart,” comparing the imprudent people to a deceived dove: “Ephraim has become like a deceived dove, having no heart” (Hosea 7). Ephraim was like a dove, because he loved his brethren with simple affection; but he was deceived and had no heart, because he did not prudently avoid the hostile traps. For dovelike simplicity is nearly useless unless serpentine prudence instructs it.

“Such a foolish young man,” Solomon says, “I observe passing in the street near the corner; and he walks near the way of her house in darkness, at the coming of evening, amid the night’s shadows and gloom” (Proverbs 7). By darkness, evening, night, and gloom, the young man’s manifold ignorance seems to be signified. Because of it he is found to draw closer to hostile plotting; if he had wisely kept the straight and narrow path while the sun shone, he certainly would not have given easy access to that enemy. “Behold,” he says, “a woman meets him in harlot’s dress, prepared to capture souls” (ibid.).

By this woman, hostile deception is suitably represented. She is prepared in the attire of a harlot to capture souls, so that what she cannot accomplish with spear, sword, or other weapons of war, she may accomplish by the bold deceit of her countenance and the allurements of words. Hence it follows: “Having seized the young man, she kisses him, and, with a bold face, flatters him, saying: ‘Come, let us be intoxicated with breasts until daybreak; let us enjoy the embraces we desire’” (ibid.). It is as though she said: I wish you to be made drunk with carnal and muddy teaching, to delight in the pleasant softness of my embraces, until the day dawns upon us in our mutual rejoicing—that is, until our desire is made glad by its wished-for fulfillment.

Why she does not despair that what she asks can be done, and why she effectively asserts falsehoods as truths to the foolish young man, the woman seems not to conceal an adequate reason. In this Scripture, though it did not intend to make that young man wiser, it did intend to make us wiser. For after saying, “Come, let us enjoy the embraces we desire,” it adds: “For the man is not in his house; he has gone on a very long journey” (ibid.).

Certainly, if he had not gone away on a very long journey, if the man had been in his house as was fitting, the aforesaid woman would not easily have deceived the young man. Rather, he would have resisted her with both prudent strength and strong prudence. “The man,” she says, “is not in his house.” By the man I judge prudent counsel to be meant. Unless it governs strength and dwells familiarly in the heart of the obedient person, hostile power secretly enters in, and the shameless woman overturns the young man who is susceptible to deception.

Of her Scripture adds: “She ensnared him with many words and drew him away with the flatteries of her lips” (ibid.). She attacked him not with bow, sword, or javelins, but ensnared him with the pleasant words of her lips. Knowing him pressed down and overwhelmed by the cloudy darkness of imprudence, she drew and dragged him with the cord of seductive pleasure. Of him it is added: “Immediately he follows her like an ox led to slaughter, unaware that the fool is being drawn to chains” (Proverbs 7).

When strength is darkened by the shadows of imprudence and not trained by manly counsel to avoid an enemy’s snares, it can readily be softened by deceitful allurements and seduced; once seduced, it can be led like an ox to slaughter. Therefore Scripture subsequently exhorts in sweet words the obedient person who glories in youthful strength, lest he be drawn away by the soft bonds of this harlot’s deception, but that he should withdraw with prudent step from her approach and attack: “Therefore now, my son, listen to me: let not your mind be drawn aside into her paths, nor be deceived by her tracks; for she has cast down many wounded, and every one of the strongest has been killed by her” (ibid.).

It does not say, “Every one of the most prudent,” but, “Every one of the strongest has been killed by her,” so that it might more carefully warn the man who considers himself strong not to place hope in his strength alone, but to strive diligently to acquire prudent counsel, without which strength cannot obtain the complete crown of victory. Therefore, after Solomon said, “Who shall find a strong woman?” (Proverbs 31), he added shortly afterward: “She has worked with the counsel of her hands” (ibid.), to show that strength should be praiseworthily proclaimed when it is found to work by the counsel of its hands, and that a praiseworthy life is located not so much in strength as in that counsel. So another wise man appears to declare: “Do everything with counsel, and you shall live.”

Therefore the obedient person ought to celebrate, as it were, certain nuptials in the chamber of his heart, and with an unrelaxed bond join counsel to strength, so that counsel may rule strength by due law and manly discernment may moderate youthful impulses.

## CHAPTER XV
But just as strength of powers suits a young man, so fullness of more mature counsel suits a man; Solomon seems to have indicated this in the same Proverbs, when he expressly wished to assign to each what was his own: “The exultation of young men,” he says, “is their strength” [Col. 0877D] (Prov. 20). And above: “As deep water, so is counsel in the heart of a man” (Prov. 18). And again: “From the fruit of a man’s mouth his belly shall be filled” (ibid.). And this: “Deep water are words from the mouth of a man” (ibid.). He wisely attributes counsel to a man, which youth has plainly not yet deserved to attain; for although love and zeal seem to assist it in acquiring it, the narrowness of time is nevertheless still found to offer some resistance. For no short time is needed by one who wishes to acquire manly prudence and advance by fitting progress to its fullness; rather, when he has girded himself with due ardor in its furnace, he must also be polished by long practice.
