Rightly, therefore, its perfection is first assigned to mature age, in which a brief interval does not prejudice an eager will; [Col. 0878A] but, if grace goes before and dull sluggishness does not hinder, a suitable length of time brings it to perfection.

Observing this, Elihu said: “Therefore, men of understanding, hear me” (Job 34). And below: “Men of intelligence, speak to me, and let a wise man hear me” (ibid.). Elihu judged those fit to hear him whom the sudden learning of youth did not puff up, but whom he knew, through the growth of age, to have reached perfect manhood and acquired fitting prudence of heart through the file of practice. Hence, rebuking Job himself, he marvels that, though he sees him as a man in years, he judges him devoid of prudence; for he knows prudence to suit mature age, to which Job himself ought to have devoted care and study. “Who,” he says, “is a man like Job, who drinks mockery [Col. 0878B] like water, who walks with workers of iniquity?” (Job 34). And he adds: “Therefore, men of understanding, hear me”—as if to say: Because I know that prudence belongs, as it were especially, to men, I ought to summon them to hear me. Job did not deserve to obtain the favor of this thing, because, though able, he was perhaps unwilling to exercise himself in it.

Yet Job had carefully repelled this accusation from himself above, and truly and humbly affirmed that he was prudent: “I too,” he says, “have a heart like you, nor am I inferior to you” (Job 12). Elihu therefore judged him imprudent unjustly, when he stubbornly summoned prudent men to hear him. Yet he did not wholly depart from the rule of truth when he regarded prudence as, in a manner, the particular possession of men. For those cannot easily advance to its height who have long disdained to exercise themselves in it—those who, while they should still be counted among children, boldly promise themselves the prudence of the perfect. Of such perfect persons Paul says: “Solid food belongs to the perfect, who through practice have their senses trained” (Heb. 5). Paul rightly judged those fit for solid food whom the study of long time had formed, whose senses laborious habit of learning had exercised, rather than those whom an affected elegance of an outward title had corrupted.

Such a person a certain satirist declared himself to be, sharply attacking poets suddenly made by presumption:

> “I have not rinsed my lips in the Caballine spring,  
> Nor dreamed upon two-peaked Parnassus.  
> I do not recall that I came forth thus suddenly as a poet.”  
> —Persius, *Prologue*, 1–3.

Sudden learning does not seem sufficiently praiseworthy to the satirist: learning which, despising the workshop, leaps prematurely into public view; which, lacking the file, swells with the presumptuous windiness of self-assurance, and is not led to perfection by finishing polish.

Rightly, therefore, David wished to call him who “did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly,” at the beginning of the book (Ps. 1), a man, and to proclaim that same man blessed. For it belonged to manly prudence not to be seduced by the counsel of the imprudent; and it belongs to the blessed portion of reward to be introduced into the storehouse of the divine law, so that by its continual meditation he may become more learned and, advancing into [Col. 0879A] perfect manhood, be blessed with the praises of prudent obedience.

Finally, Rehoboam son of Solomon, because he did not heed the warnings of prudent men but obeyed the youthful counsel of those who had been brought up with him, made his father’s kingdom—which until then had been united in undivided concord—twofold by an irreparable division. Ten tribes of it passed to Jeroboam son of Nebat, while the other two remained under him, not by his own merit but by David’s. Hence Scripture emphatically calls that same Rehoboam “diminished in prudence,” and not so much foolish as “the folly of the people,” through whose perverse counsel the people departed from their former unity: “He left behind from his seed the folly of the nation, and Rehoboam, diminished in prudence, who turned the nation aside by counsel” (Ecclus. 47).

Because Rehoboam had not been instructed in manly prudence, but had stubbornly been made unwise by youthful counsel, he turned aside his people, so that it did not serve him in the order of succession, but the greater part of the kingdom passed to another tribe. In this it is clear how necessarily prudence must be joined to strength, and how necessarily strong obedience must be fortified by prudent counsel: so that, while it is hindered by no obstacle of difficulty in carrying out what is right, it may also be instructed by the exercise of prudent intelligence.

For Rehoboam’s own strength did not preserve him sufficiently, although he considered it by no means insignificant—so much so that he stubbornly preferred himself to his father on its account, when, in answer to the people’s requests, he preferred the imprudence of youths to the counsel of elders. “My little finger,” he says, “is thicker than my father’s loins” [Col. 0879C] (3 Kings 12), as if to say: Even my least act is made greater and fuller by solid strength, whereas my father is reproved for soft and tender corpulence; for I am prepared courageously to do brave deeds, while my father was effeminately weakened by the softness of his loins.

Rehoboam knew that a ruler ought to be strengthened by fitting courage, but perhaps he did not know that the same courage ought to be governed by prudent counsel. For this reason, he so boasts of his strength that, diminished in prudence, he is also diminished in the glory of his father’s kingdom. Therefore, it is not enough for anyone who is to do brave things to be driven by an impulse of strength, unless he also knows how to moderate the strength he has obtained with deliberative prudence. Thus strength gives him a bold desire for action, while the belt of prudent counsel renders him effectively unencumbered.

For an agile runner does not easily gain the prize set before him if, in running, he is impeded by the loose folds of his clothing. Thus strength for action does not at all glory in hoped-for praise unless it is girded for action with the belt of prudence. Indeed, sometimes the more strongly it thinks itself to be advancing, the more hastily it is compelled to fall into a graver ruin. For this reason the Lord says to Job: “Gird up your loins like a man” (Job 40), as if to say: Your strength is not sufficiently commendable unless it is wisely girded with manly counsel; for, wrapped in the dark folds of imprudence, when it seeks to run, it tumbles headlong into the abyss.

Hence the Prophet also commended the Lord himself: “He rejoiced mightily as a giant to run [Col. 0880A] his course” (Ps. 18). “The Lord,” he says, “has clothed himself with strength and girded himself” (Ps. 92). For the Lord not only clothed himself with strength, but girded himself lest it should, as it were, overflow in excess; knowing that strength works more rightly and perfectly when prudent counsel, encircling and binding it, moderates it.

Thus the angel who appeared to men in human form by divine command, and showed himself to them as a helper not only strong but prudent also, wished to appear as a young man to show that he was strong, and girded to show that he was prudent: “When Tobias went out,” it says, “he found a young man standing, girded, and as if ready to walk” (Tob. 5). He was girded indeed, who wonderfully ordered by prudent counsel the strength through which he bound the demon, so that agile strength might strengthen prudence, while fullness of prudent counsel tempered strength. Therefore he is not sufficiently prepared to do brave things unless he is both fortified by strength and formed by prudence—he who, in the fourth degree of obedience, has clothed himself with strength, and in the fifth order of advancement has attained prudence.

## CHAPTER XVI

Finally, the fifth age of the world takes its beginning from Jeconiah, whose name is interpreted “prepared of the Lord,” because at that time the people of Israel are prepared by the Lord so as to endure the troubles of captivity not only courageously but prudently [Col. 0880C]. For under him the children of Israel, pressed beneath the yoke of the divine command, leave the land of their birth and become inhabitants of Babylon, so that in exile there they may learn by the experience of suffering what they had previously been warned of through the instruction of the prophets.

For that knowledge is judged more perfect which is confirmed through experience: what the teaching of reading resounds in the ears from without, the experience of suffering holds and retains within. Concerning this Paul the Apostle says to the Philippians: “I know how to suffer want” (Phil. 4). Paul means, I think, that knowledge which is acquired not by reading but by suffering the want of which he speaks. And patience, advancing, produces tested character; tested character produces hope, through which the soul is strengthened. Hope, by grace bestowed, does not put to shame, because the love [Col. 0880D] of God is poured out in the hearts of those who thus hope (Rom. 5).

God therefore wished in that age to advance the children of Israel so that they might not only be able to endure every hardship, but might learn endurance by experience. Thus, suitably formed by this instruction, they might be found prepared for obedience both with strong prudence and with prudent strength. Jeconiah, from whom, as has been said, that age began, plainly signified this by the interpretation of his name; and John the Baptist preached it with a terrible voice in the wilderness, he who brought that same age to completion as its boundary and end: “Prepare,” he says, “the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Matt. 3).

Then indeed the way of the Lord is prepared; then one walks in his straight paths, when the work of truth is formed according to the rule of prudence, so that one may remain unswervingly strong both in deed and counsel. And because this is not from us but from God, lest anyone dare to boast, the Prophet humbly wished to entreat God concerning it: “Guide me,” he says, “in your truth, and teach me” (Ps. 34). He saw that a person is not sufficiently directed in the truth of holiness unless he is also formed by the teaching of truth; for though, as he testifies elsewhere, he gains understanding from the commandments, without understanding he does not walk perfectly in the commandments. “Therefore give me understanding,” he says, “and I shall search your law, and keep it with all my heart” (Ps. 118).

The law of God is by no means kept with the whole heart unless that observance is preceded by searching understanding. But when a strong person, obediently instructed by careful examination, is prudently formed, then he is perfect in the divine law, because he obeys it more prudently [Col. 0881B]. David, therefore, understanding that he had advanced to this degree of obedience, and blessing God who gave him understanding, says: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody” (Ps. 107); and again: “I am ready and am not troubled, that I may keep your commandments” (Ps. 118). These commandments cannot be kept by a sufficiently ready heart unless its keeper, as has been said, has endeavored to receive prudent instruction.

When someone has been raised to this degree of obedience—fortified with youthful strength and formed by manly prudence—he must still extend himself further and, not content with what he has attained, stretch out his hand toward something higher.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0881C] There remains that sixth progress in virtue, which is called either the old age of obedience or the obedience of old age. To the extent that this is granted in the present life, it is free from the turmoil of the preceding ages and sits powerful and serene upon the throne of majesty. For youthful strength finds opposing it the excessive weight of our infirmity, while manly prudence finds the blindness of ignorance. To overcome these troubles, no small labor and sweat were necessary, so that their obstacles might be entirely removed.

But this old age of obedience no longer fights, no longer struggles against troubles opposing it; for the hostile enemy neither attacks it as though it were still standing in battle array, nor, when it yields and presents its back in flight, does it overcome it as one master of victory. Rather, as has been said, it sits in the teacher’s seat and humbly rejoices in the honor of triumph. No adversary boldly contradicts it; and if one should murmur against it, the majesty of its hand commands silence. Its enemies and vices reverence that command when issued; the other virtues revere it when spoken, since the former yield to it, as is fitting, in reverence, and the latter honorably prefer it through devotion.

For venerable old age is not that which is long-lasting or calculated by the number of years—an old age often troubled by sickness, disturbed by coughing, weighed down by the bent mass of the body, disfigured by wan pallor and a face furrowed with wrinkles. Rather, it is that which a more mature advance removes from the tumult of conflict, and which peace, won through purity, makes serene in the height of concord [Col. 0882A]. It is, indeed, a certain pure peace—or prepared purity—of old age, which neither manly prudence nor youthful strength could attain. With the grievous trouble of warfare lulled to rest, it is not provoked, but rests upon the lofty throne of judgment. “The spiritual person judges all things, and is himself judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2).

Finally, among the ancient pagans, when manhood had reached its appointed limit and a man entered, by the law of nature, the adjoining threshold of old age, he was released by a general privilege from the obligation of fighting. Like one discharged from service, at sixty he was cherished in rest and leisure. Thereafter sufficient sustenance was supplied to him from public resources; and he was held in such honor and fear among the rest that, by the privilege of his age, he was the censor of younger persons, an exhorter to virtues, and an unrestrained reprover of vices.

For this age seemed especially fitting for the purpose: when the blood had grown cold, a man was already far removed from the commotion of vices, having been polished to the utmost in the school of strength and prudence by the file of practice, and having crushed, through the purity of freedom, the desires of former luxury, vain praise, and glory. They also thought that some mystery was contained in this number of years, by which they wished all to be more diligently warned what degree of perfection ought to be found in a man of sixty, and what reverence ought deservedly to be accorded him for his perfection.

Six multiplied by ten, or ten multiplied by six, makes sixty. Ten is called perfect by arithmeticians because counting proceeds continuously up to it; once it is completed, one must necessarily return to one in order for the number to increase by repeated counting [Col. 0882C]. Perhaps for this reason God wrote the ten commandments of the law for the people of Israel by the hand of Moses. By them he imposed a rule of life in such a way that whoever obediently fulfilled it would be considered perfect, nor would anything further be required of him at that time.

They also assert that six is perfect because it is the first number composed from its own parts. This is by no means to be lightly regarded among them, except by one who does not attend with due consideration to the force of numbers. For it is divided in equal portions into six units, three twos, and two threes. If one, two, and three—the three portions of six—are added together, they are found so to complete the number of which they are parts that they cannot exceed that same perfect number. For one, two, and three, the parts of six, if joined together, yield nothing less and nothing more than that same six.

Therefore, since that number is commended as perfect, when it either multiplies ten or is multiplied by ten, it is plainly evident how great the perfection of the number thereby produced is considered to be, and how much perfection of prudence and reverence is due to the age of sixty. The perfection of this number six is also commended from the beginning, when God—who wisely works all things in measure, number, and weight—completed on the sixth day the things he wished to make materially. On that day he also made man in his own image, whom, by the merit of reason, he set over all earthly things.

Perhaps in this he figuratively intimated [Col. 0883A] that man, whom, as has been said, he formed on the sixth day—and in whose formation God completed his works—ought more perfectly to obey his Creator with a pure and peaceful heart; and that all other earthly things ought likewise perfectly to serve that obedient man. But that man departed from this state of obedience through the working of the serpent’s cunning, bending the excellence of the reason he had received toward the womanly counsel of his wife. Sold under sin, he likewise bound the succession of his posterity, from which bond neither angel nor prophet, but only the grace of God—grace given to whom he wills—set them free.

Since man had fallen from the perfection of six, in the sixth age of the world God became man, that he might conform himself to human beings not in sins but in sufferings, and reform disfigured man into the likeness of his own perfection. In himself as man, whom he showed to be truly capable of suffering, he displayed beforehand to other human beings the perfect path of obedience, by which one obeys God the Creator not only unto the straits of death, but also preserves in that obedience the tranquility of a pure mind. This tranquil purity suits the old age described above, in which the perfect obedient person is not subject to slavery, but obeys from a pure heart and good conscience in such a way that he may worthily be set forth as an example to one whom he precedes in perfected age.

## CHAPTER XVIII

As a type of this, the Apostle Paul proposes a widow to be chosen: not the younger one, who, having lived luxuriously against Christ, now intends to marry. In instructing Timothy, he carefully warns that she must be avoided, lest either the life [Col. 0883C] or the reputation of that priest should deserve to be defiled by her company. Rather, he proposes an aged widow, not less than sixty years old, who has ceased to be troubled by the wanton passions of younger persons and does not move amid the harsh and uncertain conflict of vices; whose blood has grown cold, whose former vigor has faded, whose womanly impulses have failed, whose wanton navel has withered. “Let a widow,” he says, “be chosen not less than sixty years old; if she has brought up children, if she has received strangers, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has assisted those suffering tribulation, if she has pursued every good work” (1 Tim. 5).

For that soul ought to be numbered among the company of the saints, and everyone in the Church ought to venerate her with due honor: the soul which has loved to apply enduring diligence to good works; which, in affection and deed, has compassion upon the needs of the saints; which offers herself as an example for younger people to imitate; which rejoices now to offer God a pure and tranquil obedience; which, through love of heavenly things, restrains from itself every carnal thing. “She who is truly a widow and desolate,” he says, “let her hope in God and continue in supplications and prayers night and day” (ibid.).

The soul which no longer cares for carnal desire and does not fashion itself after the passing world; which does not depend on any temporal consolation and yields not only to unlawful things but not even to lawful things—this soul, I say, is truly a widow and desolate. She is a widow because the world is judged dead to one truly living; she is desolate because she is strengthened by no thing or hope of transitory joy. “But this widow hopes in God and continues in supplications and prayers [Col. 0884A] night and day.” Since she has turned all her hope away from the slippery world, she freely turns herself wholly toward hoping in God, diligently forgetting the things behind, so that she desires to obtain from him nothing but himself.

Since her desire is still deferred from its blessed fulfillment, lest anything harmful from without should befall this delay, she continues in supplications and prayers with anxious attention of mind, so that the devout widow does not cease from them by night or day. “She continues,” he says, “in supplications and prayers night and day.” If the adversity of any difficulty comes upon her, she does not lose confidence in despondency or weariness; if the grace of advancement smiles upon her, she does not rashly trust in herself, lifted up by empty joy. Instead, fervent and humble in either condition, she so regulates her desire that anxiety is not separated from hope, nor hope from anxiety.

This is the prayer which the Apostle commands to be offered without ceasing, and in which the true widow ought to remain amid adversity and prosperity: burning with desire to be heard, yet not refusing to bear delay, and by bearing it deserving more abundantly to obtain with greater favor what she asks. The Apostle himself persevered without ceasing in this prayer, as he declares at the opening of his Epistle to the Romans: “Without ceasing,” he says, “I make mention of you in my prayers” (Rom. 1). He says the same thing to the Philippians, to the Colossians, to the Thessalonians, to Timothy, and also to Philemon: namely, that he makes continual mention of them in his prayers—perhaps praying that they too, through grace going before, may attain the peace of old-age obedience, and may obey the heavenly commandments with the serene agreement of mind and body.

Therefore, to these and to almost all the others to whom he sends his epistles, he places at the beginning of each letter this salutation: first, that grace, and then peace, may be bestowed upon them by God. By this gift obedience, once begun, advances and is brought to its fitting completion: “Grace to you,” he says, “and peace from God” (1 Cor. 1 and elsewhere). Paul wrote such a salutation to the churches and such a salutation to his disciples, except in the Epistle to the Hebrews—if indeed he wrote that epistle. For, as some say, it was written not by him but by another under his name; or rather, if he himself wrote it, he appended the salutation for a reason known to himself.

Paul beautifully places in the salutation not grace alone [Col. 0884D] but peace also; and, joining both together, he significantly puts grace first. By grace he understands the gratuitous remission of sins; by peace, the fitting perfection of merits. For through grace alone sins are first remitted to the heart; once they are remitted, good works follow more effectively. Through their discipline and study, one finally deservedly reaches old-age obedience, when the conflict of flesh and spirit has been lulled to rest and one obeys God more serenely.

That generosity of remission is preceded by no merits of works; and therefore it is rightly called grace, because divine goodness grants it freely. But this tranquility of an advanced mind, although it is not denied to be a divine gift, is given as a reward in some sense due to one who labors and sweats. Of this reward Paul says elsewhere: “Godliness is useful for all things, having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” [Col. 0885A] (1 Tim. 4). In this life which now is, a reward is rendered to godliness when tranquil perfection of mind is granted to holiness already begun; when holiness itself is said to arrive at that hundredfold reward which it sometimes deserves to find before possessing eternal life. “He shall receive a hundredfold,” he says, “and shall possess eternal life” (Matt. 19).

Whoever has fully despised earthly things is said to obtain this hundredfold, and, rewarded with it, afterward to possess eternal life. Thus the perfection of one fruitful state of perfection precedes another, and the latter completes the former far more fruitfully; it does not exclude it. For when this present life ends, this hundredfold perfection does not yield place but goes before; it does not fail but advances; it suffers no loss of itself but receives a sufficient increase. Although it deserves in some measure of life to be called perfection, it nevertheless needs to be completed by the benefit of future perfection.

Hence it is not unfittingly called a perfect imperfection—or, rather, an imperfect perfection: perfect, indeed, because according to the measure of this life it has deserved to attain peaceful obedience or obedient purity; imperfect, because it is not yet granted to possess eternal life. It is therefore perfection of the present life, but imperfect in relation to the life which follows; for what is perfect here is still only in part, and when the future perfect comes, that which is in part will be done away (1 Cor. 13). Yet it is not perfect imperfection that will be done away, but the imperfection of perfection itself, because that imperfection will then be utterly annulled when completed perfection finds its consummating end.

If anyone wishes to taste more perfectly there the end of that consummation, he ought in the course of this life to taste it beforehand by diligent study, striving to attain old-age purity or pure obedience: that is, to obey the heavenly commandments with a pure heart and a body not impure [Col. 0885C]. Such old-age purity, such pure obedience, renouncing its own dominion and subject with unrelenting love to the command of superiors, is plainly near the divine vision—if the evangelical promise is believed, or rather because it is believed: “Blessed,” he says, “are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

Here it should be noted that he does not say, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they see God,” but “for they shall see God.” Thus he makes clear that he speaks of present purity of heart, not future purity, but of the vision of God as not present, rather as future: purity is to be possessed here first, and one comes afterward to the vision of God. For if he had said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they see God,” he would seem to speak of angels or holy persons to whom the vision of God is already granted in present actuality, and not of us or of any others who are to come—persons who do not see God as one not to be seen, but who will see him.

Therefore, blessed are the pure in heart: those, that is, who have deserved to attain purity of heart in this life. Blessed, I say, not because they see God presently or have seen him, but because they shall see God. They shall see him indeed when that which is in part has been done away, when their hope has passed into reality; when, after faith has yielded its primacy, love alone will occupy the whole person, and that same abiding and enduring love will bring to completion the purity which faith has wrought.

For faith works purity, as Peter declares in the Acts of the Apostles: “Purifying their hearts by faith” (Acts 13). And Paul says to Titus: “All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Tit. 1). He calls clean those whose inward conscience unfeigned faith has thoroughly cleansed; conversely, he calls defiled those whom unbelief has defiled. Thus perfection of faith produces the virtue of purity, and purity produces the welcome old age of obedience, when obedient progress burns so with the desire for purity that it grows cold and languid toward doing or loving the works [Col. 0886B] of carnal pleasure.

For good old age not only does not burn for fulfilling unlawful desires, but is even sluggish in performing things that are lawful. And if, from companionship with this flesh, the beguiling attraction of pleasures smiles and becomes cheerful, old age nevertheless rests in its purity in praiseworthy silence.

## CHAPTER XIX

As a type of this, King David, I think, is read to have grown old, and the young woman Abishag the Shunammite to have slept in the bed of the aging man. The king neither removed her altogether from his chamber nor knew her, though the girdle of his loins was loosed. “King David,” it says, “had grown old and was advanced in age; and though he was covered with garments, he was not warmed. And his servants said to him: Let us seek for our lord the king [Col. 0886C] a young virgin; let her stand before the king and cherish him; let her sleep in his bosom and warm our lord the king. Therefore they sought throughout all the borders of Israel for a young woman beautiful in every respect, and they found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king. The girl was exceedingly beautiful and slept with the king; but the king did not know her” (3 Kings 1).

David, as is well known, is interpreted “strong of hand.” He is quite fittingly said to grow old when the strong obedient person advances to the summit of tranquil purity: when conflict between flesh and spirit is no longer found within his bounds, and when neither has power effectively to resist obedience. “He had,” it says, “many days of age.” The many days of this old man are the accumulation of virtues with which the consummated obedient person rejoices to be imbued. Having received the blessing of the heavenly Giver, advancing from progress to progress, he now draws near to the vision of the Creator. Hence it is written: “The lawgiver shall give blessing; they shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83).

He had indeed gone from strength to strength who had already attained the old age of obedience; the age of his advances was now cleansed from its former torches, “for old age is an immaculate life.” In this old age, one is found to have many days—that is, to be distinguished by many and perfect virtues. As we read, some of the Fathers ended their present course in that state and passed from the summit of old age to behold God in Zion. For of Job it is written: “He died old and full of days” (Job 42). But of Abraham: “He died,” it says, “in a good old age, advanced in years and full of days” [Col. 0887A] (Gen. 13).

Happy Job and Abraham, whom fullness of days made elders, and whom, by the merit of that fullness, length of days received: that length, I say, which no boundary or limit can confine, in which God shows his salvation to his faithful ones. “With length of days,” he says, “I will satisfy him and show him my salvation” (Ps. 90). While living here, the Prophet longs for this vision; with fear and trembling he earnestly entreats God not to permit him to be deprived of the hoped-for fullness of days, but mercifully to bring him to it by his power: “Do not call me back,” he says, “in the midst of my days” (Ps. 101).

A person is said to be called back in the midst of his days when he is not permitted to be brought to completion in the progress of spiritual gifts; when, having acquired some of them, while he anxiously presses toward those ahead, he is seized, as it were, by an untimely death in the middle of his advance. The Prophet, therefore, desires with burning longing to be brought to fullness of days, that through it he may deserve more perfectly to be introduced into length of days. He knows that if here he is gifted with the blessed old age of virtues, there he will enjoy the vision of God without end of days. Therefore he says elsewhere: “Even unto old age and gray hair, O God, do not forsake me” (Ps. 70).

The same Prophet at last attained that gray old age for which he had anxiously prayed, as Scripture testifies; and the same scriptural narrative goes on to describe commendably the condition in which he stood in that old age: “Though he was covered with garments, he was not warmed” [Col. 0887C]. A good old man is one who has so forgotten the natural affections of the body that he cannot be turned back toward their bold or disordered appetites. Though, by the corruption of mortality, his soul is burdened, he is not compelled to be slavishly subjected to its rule.

The garments with which this aged king is said to be covered may fittingly be understood as the corruption of mortality, which the first man miserably acquired for himself and his descendants when he stubbornly transgressed God’s command in the paradise of delights. Created naked in the purity of a holiness coeval with him, by sinning he was clothed in the covering of a skin-like perversity; and human nature has been so severely infected by this disease that henceforth it is necessarily mortal and corruptible.

Although our elder, as has been said, is clothed in these burdensome garments, although his humanity is enclosed by the nights and infirmities of this life, he is not inflamed by their demands to desire carnal things. He neither fears their threats nor is softened by their flatteries. They press and bear down upon him in order to affect—indeed infect—his old age, as they are accustomed to weigh down, and perhaps overwhelm, the tender youth of anyone, so that he may be inflamed by the torches of gluttony, anger, or avarice and the maturity of old-age obedience may be relaxed from its due strictness.

But this old age, though driven by many and varied blasts, nevertheless remains unmoved like a tree with firm roots. And though in the furnace of this life [Col. 0888A] its leaf grows heavy under the assault of fire, it by no means grows hot so as to be softened. Therefore it was rightly said: “Though he was covered with garments, he was not warmed.”

## CHAPTER XX
“Then his servants said: ‘Let us seek for our lord the king a young virgin, and let her stand before the king and cherish him; let her sleep in his bosom and warm our lord the king.’” Although an abundance of the aforesaid garments is laid upon this old and enfeebled man, yet his wasting coldness—which is, as it were, proper to old age—is not removed. His servants therefore take counsel and seek a young virgin, that he may be warmed by her companionship, one who may sleep with him and caress him with feminine softness. Under the modest name of sleeping, I judge that carnal intercourse is here indicated, by which these shameless servants think the king’s old age may be stirred: so that one whom the other vices or necessities of this flesh cannot soften may perhaps be more effectively ensnared by the more delicate pleasure of lust. Thus Potiphar’s wife, having seized Joseph’s garment, says to him: “Sleep with me” (Gen. XXXIX).

The servants who seek the young woman are our thoughts. They are not improperly called servants, because they rightly owe service to reason; although they sometimes presume to chatter against it, they nevertheless ought, in just order, to serve it. The young woman whom they seek is the pleasure of lust, which is accustomed to assail certain holy persons by deceits and, if they at last judge it conquered by reason, to attack them more fiercely. It once cast down David himself—perhaps while he was still moving about upon the roof of swelling youth, and had not yet reclined in the chamber of tranquil old age. It made Solomon’s wisdom foolish; it weakened Samson’s strength; it marred many others with a blameworthy stigma, though much uprightness of life had formerly adorned them.

Wandering thoughts sometimes shamelessly bring this pleasure of lust before a righteous man and introduce it into the chamber of his memory, so that, with his strength weakened, the spirit may embrace what is offered, or at least bend its gaze toward it for a while. Nor is it surprising that she is found when sought, since she frequently comes even when she is not sought; before she is called, she rushes in, bold and shameless, according to that saying of the pagan poet:

[Col. 0888D] “[Though] you drive her out with a pitchfork, yet she will always return.”

For this vice is so proper to human nature, so naturally implanted in our generation, that the succession of posterity is not propagated without it, nor is the propagation of generation completed without it. From the time when the first human being presumed to do what had also been forbidden, such a wound was inflicted upon his flesh as a punishment that, willing or unwilling, he suffers the desire of lust and is moved to beget only through the working of that same desire.

By this disease the same man so infected—indeed, unless divine grace comes to their aid, killed—all his descendants, that whoever is generated through the concupiscence of the flesh, infected by the same contagion, deserves to be condemned by original sin. Since the generation of us all is thus infected, all who are so generated now suffer this vice as nature; and concupiscence itself, by which our nature is thus originally corrupted, is called “nature,” because it can no longer be avoided.

Therefore by nature we are children of wrath, deserving to perish on account of natural concupiscence, unless, as I said, divine grace is willing to aid us and freely and mercifully release us from nature’s covering. For this reason God the Father willed that his Son should become human, and that in this becoming-human the concupiscence of the flesh should have no part whatever: rather, that a chosen virgin should become pregnant without intercourse with a man, and that Christ should be brought forth from her through the working of the Holy Spirit.

Because he was conceived in a manner and by an operation not carnal—or, to say it more plainly, not by the itch of the loins, not by marital concupiscence—his flesh was not infected with the natural contagion common to us all. [Col. 0889B] Rather, he drew to himself only pure and simple matter from the virginal womb. In order that this might be possible, or that what had happened might more readily be believed, he willed that no man should be carnally joined to the virgin; so that, once it was believed that the mother had wondrously conceived without intercourse, it might consequently also be believed that in conceiving she had experienced no concupiscence of the flesh.

Therefore this flesh of Christ, which knew not the burning workshop of lust, could provide us with sufficient medicine: through its purity God might mercifully pardon our concupiscence, even though he does not yet wholly abolish it while we live here. For pleasurable concupiscence naturally remains in our flesh, brought upon us by the sinful generation of our parents. It burns within and is shamefully unrestrained without, unless it is checked by the firm and discerning governance of reason.

Since this appetite of the flesh operates so strongly in those who beget that none of us is generated without it, it is not inappropriate to say that it itself, as it were, begets us, since by its prompting the begetter is moved to generate. Hence she whom David’s servants seek and bring to him is called Abishag, a name interpreted “my father is superfluous.”

## CHAPTER XXI

“They sought,” he says, “a beautiful young woman throughout all the borders of Israel; and they found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king.”

Abishag, as has been said, is interpreted “my father is superfluous.” That appetite of the flesh is called father because it so possesses human nature that, as though by a right properly its own, it precedes the generation of us all; and it is said, as it were, chiefly to effect that generation, since without its condemnable yet pleasurable presence generation cannot be completed.

But this same father is rightly called superfluous because the human race could sufficiently have been created without him, had not that first man been held guilty of disobedience and deserved to bring this penal stain both upon himself and upon his descendants. This was added to us as something superfluous by that ancient enemy, a most bitter enemy of the holy purity in which humanity had been created. Seeing—and envying—its pure and simple nature, wholly undefiled by any contagion, he inflicted this stain upon its purity by the counsel of disobedience.

Hence that enemy deserved to be called Leviathan (Job III; Isa. XXVII), a name interpreted “their addition,” because upon the nature of human beings, whom God had created pure from every contagion of vices, that wicked and envious one wished to impose this thing, not from his nature but from his malice, which could not be removed from them or their descendants. Thus he took care to introduce the stain of lust into that purity, without which our supper might sufficiently be conducted, according to the pagan saying. But now, although this is regarded as superfluous or overflowing, it accompanies us inseparably, both those who beget and those who are begotten.

Thus that wicked one now rejoices that he possesses, as it were, a certain proprietary right in a human being, whose flesh he sees clinging to the concupiscence of sin. No human being can naturally free himself from this except Christ, [Col. 0890B] in whom alone the prince of this world could find nothing of his own (John XIV). Apart from him, all others are weighed down by the aforesaid concupiscence and suffer in their flesh the tumultuous malice of a raging lion: either they are hurled headlong by unrestrained heat of lust, or they are worn down by many cares and labours in restraining it.

This agrees with the fact that the aforesaid name Abishag is also interpreted “the roaring of my father.” In a certain manner the devil was the natural father of all, not because he begot us from his own flesh, but because he begot us through carnal concupiscence and impressed upon us the image of his depravity. By this image he cast us down, lest we should be able to rise again to the divine likeness.

For removing this image, divine goodness did not fail us: it instituted circumcision under the Law and baptism under grace, [Col. 0890C] so that those whom concupiscential generation had made children of the devil, spiritual regeneration might make children of God. Yet concupiscence remains so deeply implanted in us that it is not wholly abolished even after baptism; rather, by a kind of roar of nature it still makes a noise against purity—not in order to harm, but rather to exercise those who devote themselves to holiness.

Thus Abishag is rightly interpreted either “my father is superfluous” or “the roaring of my father,” because this appetite, which still clamours against us, was formerly introduced as a superfluity. It would not be necessary if man had not transgressed the commandment; after sin, it either incites human beings to guilt or urges them to vigilance. Abishag is also aptly called a Shunammite: “They found,” he says, “Abishag the Shunammite.”

[Col. 0890D] “Shunammite” is interpreted “scarlet.” Scarlet bears the appearance of blood and signifies sin. Hence the Prophet says: “Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, my God” (Ps. L). And the Lord says through Isaiah: “Your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I); and a little later: “Though your sins are as scarlet, they shall be whitened like snow” (ibid.). Therefore Abishag the Shunammite is sin, because she is a superfluous roaring. For what is superfluous to human necessity, what wickedly clamours against nature’s holiness—what can it rightly be judged to be except sin? By it the transgression of the first human being is avenged, and his hereditary depravity in us is made manifest.

## CHAPTER XXII

“The young woman,” he says, “was exceedingly beautiful.” I wonder why excessive beauty is ascribed to this Shunammite, since so much ugliness is known to reside in carnal concupiscence. Yet because lovers of women are plainly accustomed to admire nothing beyond their beauty, to recoil from their ugliness, and to delight especially in their appearance, I consider that nothing is more suitably signified by her beauty than the pleasure of concupiscence—than which none greater is thought to be allotted to the human body.

For among all the things in which human flesh wickedly delights, the delight of the loins holds chief place by a wretched law. In its fulfilment the flesh is said to be so enervated that even the spirit itself, as though sympathizing, is carnally weakened. For this reason she is also called a girl or young woman, so that the pleasure may seem more welcome through the bloom of age; for whoever gives himself over to this activity, although not young in age, is shown to be young in deed.

Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: “Flee youthful desires” (II Tim. II). And when a son is promised to Abraham and Sarah in their old age, Sarah says: “After I have grown old, and my lord is old, shall I give myself to pleasure?” (Gen. XVIII). Thus Abishag is rightly said to have been an exceedingly beautiful girl; for if she had been described as ugly and old, she would surely have seemed less pleasing, and no one would reasonably have been drawn to intercourse with her.

Herein the perfect continence of our old man is further commended: though he lives in one chamber with such a young woman, he is not at all inflamed toward her embraces, but merely allows her to sleep with him. “She slept,” he says, “with the king, but the king did not know [Col. 0891C] her.”

This, surely, was the intention of the aforesaid little servants: that the young woman brought in should sleep with the king and warm him—that is, that carnal concupiscence, presented to memory, should be accepted in such a manner that the old man, made young again, might be drawn into consenting to it. For thus they say: “Let us seek a young woman for our lord the king, and let her sleep in his bosom and warm our lord the king.” But now it is said: “She slept with the king,” and it is not added that she warmed him; rather, it is subjoined: “But the king did not know her.”

This sleeping, then, is a suppression: carnal pleasure is pressed down and overpowered with a heavy sleep, so that it does not come forth but lies torpidly hidden in its chamber. Of such suppression Jonah is asked: “Why are you weighed down with sleep?” (Jonah I). The servile multitude of thoughts sets before the old man the deeds of youth; but he, remaining and persevering in the purity of mature old age, bears the memory of the image that meets him as though it were the presence of one sleeping in quiet silence.

Though he senses her within himself as in his own chamber, he does not embrace, approve, or consent to her. For, withered and cold in the icy solidity of purity, he neither burns nor melts under the fire of wanton depravity. “But the king,” he says, “did not know her.” For the old man by nature does not know her whose embraces he does not seek to enjoy; he judges every pleasure of this world forbidden to him, lest he be unable to cling to God if he clings to a harlot.

For whoever wishes to become a friend of this world is, as it is written, made an enemy of God; and he is proved, through a ruined mind, to hate God if he chooses to cling to the world in effeminate ways. Hence Solomon sentenced Adonijah, son of Haggith, to death because that man, guilty of folly, loved Abishag the Shunammite.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“Bathsheba said to Solomon: ‘Let Abishag the Shunammite be given as wife to your brother Adonijah’” (III Kings II).

Not only does he refuse to draw his burning mind back from its purpose, but he also wishes to cloak his incontinence under the name of wife. He does not wish anyone to presume to restrain him in anything; whatever he pleases, he wishes also to be permitted to do. So many people, even though they know that something is forbidden to all by public law, nevertheless refuse to have anyone oppose it in their own case. They think that they can rightly be called happy if they freely bring their wretched desire to its unhappy effect.

Against this, that prudent man Tully thought far better. Looking upon a man of this sort, he said: “O wretched man, to whom it was permitted to sin!” Tully regards the licence to sin as great misery when someone whose understanding is ruined does not refuse to carry out an unlawful desire. Neither fear of the law is sufficient to recall a person so disposed, nor, after the crime is committed, does its severity presume to punish him.

Yet not only the completion of an intended depravity deserves punishment, but also the depravity of an unfulfilled will. Before God, to whom the secrets of hearts are naked and open, it makes no difference whether evils have been completed in the heart or in deed. For when a corrupt mind desires something deadly, and only possibility fails it in accomplishing it, the consent itself of captive reason suffices for guilt; and it deserves to be condemned by the true judgment of Solomon.

Therefore, when Solomon heard that Adonijah wished to take Abishag the Shunammite to himself as a wife—that is, to devote himself freely, both in desire and in act, to the pleasure of carnal things—he denied the fulfilment of his desire and condemned the desire alone to deserved death. “Why,” he says, “do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask the kingdom for him also” (ibid.).

As though he said: If one is allowed freely to carry out what he has wickedly desired, this is nothing other than to reign. For he is not so much king who holds the sceptre of royal dignity in his hand as he who exercises in action the dominion of his own will. But this kingdom, which is not subject to the divine command, in which one’s own will is preferred to worthier reason, is not from God. God neither knows its rulers nor accepts them; rather, he has together rejected and repudiated both kingdom and kings.

Of such persons he says through Hosea: “They have reigned, but not through me; they have been princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. VIII). Therefore upon such kingdoms and kings, to whom God does not impart the grace of his recognition, he pours out his wrath in righteous judgment. Those whom he does not promote unbridled to the eminence of his light, he does not allow to lie unpunished in the darkness of their own malice. “Pour out,” says the prophet, “your wrath upon the nations that have not known you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name” (Ps. LXXVIII).

Thus Solomon, angered when he heard Adonijah’s unjust desire, neither permitted it to be fulfilled nor left it unpunished; rather, he ordered the sprouting wickedness to be cut off by swift death, lest a will brought to its goal should have cause to glory wickedly. “King Solomon swore, saying: ‘Adonijah has spoken this word against his own life’” (III Kings II). And below: “As the Lord lives, Adonijah shall be put to death. And the king sent by the hand of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who killed him, and he died” (ibid.).

Thus he ought to have been punished: he wickedly swelled with pride; not content with his own possessions, he stubbornly desired another’s; he wished to plunge weakly into the pleasure of carnal things and to remain there without restraint, as upon a throne of kingship.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Scripture therefore rightly states beforehand: “Adonijah, son of Haggith, was exalting himself, saying: ‘I will reign’” (III Kings I).

Adonijah is interpreted “ruling lord”; Haggith, “festive” or “solemn.” Thus the person who loves to be called lord is said to exalt himself stubbornly toward reigning. Festive solemnity, as though his mother, has brought him forth, having nourished him with maternal caresses to seek lofty things.

Whoever humbly remains hidden within the bounds of lawful desire does not know, as though unborn, the offspring of present pleasure; he does not wish to be brought to the womb of carnal concupiscence or brought forth into the open air of wretched action. But one whom solemnity—that is, the common shamelessness of evildoers—casts into the light of perverse freedom, so that he no longer blushes at the desire or act of harmful insignificance, is appropriately called Adonijah, “ruling lord.” For, regarding whatever is pleasing as permissible, he miserably rules, either in fact or in hope.

“Adonijah,” he says, “was exalting himself, saying: ‘I will reign.’” Great presumption! Foolish pride promises itself a kingdom and does not fear vainly to hope for what it wickedly desires, so that, if it perhaps does not deserve effectively to obtain what it seeks, it may at least meanwhile delight in unstable hope, like a flying wind.

Of him Hosea aptly says: “Ephraim feeds on wind and follows the heat” (Hos. XII). A person is said to feed or nourish the wind when he rejoices to soothe his wretched soul with fickle hope; he hopes to obtain what he foolishly desires and persists in cherishing and vainly embracing that same hope. He also follows the heat of wretched will, which burns and shakes off the tender flowers of inward chastity. Once this is corrupted, he becomes more completely the enemy of truth.

Therefore, after saying, “Ephraim feeds on wind and follows the heat,” Hosea adds: “All day he multiplies falsehood and devastation” (ibid.). He multiplies falsehood by continually loving false things as true; but he multiplies devastation by at last suffering destruction according to his deserts. For the magnitude of the ensuing destruction is measured according to the mode or measure of the preceding heat and falsehood.

Thus this Ephraim bears fruit and perversely multiplies such fruits for himself. He could have gained abundant fruits of life and salvation had he wished to live more fruitfully in accordance with his name. By contrast, our old man neither feeds on wind nor follows heat. Casting out and repelling the falsehood of deceptive hope, he pursues—indeed, embraces—the peaceful purity of obedience.

As has been said, the age of old age seems suited to its sixth degree, in which a person is granted to find a certain purity in himself, to which he is not permitted to attain in the preceding ages, while the flesh, still insolent, delights in obstructing the path of purity.

## CHAPTER XXV

The sixth age of the world also corresponds to this purity. In that age Christ not only brought a remedy for our depravity but bestowed upon his faithful such perfection of holiness that they seemed to grow old by the merit of obedience, not by age. By word and example he wished to instruct them toward this end, warning and forewarning them to obey even at the peril of death, and in that obedience to preserve serene purity and, by the purity of life, to anticipate the vision of God.

For this reason he himself willed to be born untouched from a Virgin, nor did he contract uncleanness from her in his origin. Since, conceived and born, he naturally possessed purity, he credibly remained in it throughout the course of this life. The Pure One wished to exhort his people to purity, not so that by being born they could equal him in this purity, but so that, aided by grace, they might strive to imitate him according to their strength and eventually, by discipline and labour, be conformed to him in their own measure.

Choosing Simon Peter, he separated him from marital embraces; he recalled John, son of Zebedee, from the prospect of marriage; and he freed the other apostles from such bonds, by which they had been held hindered—whether lawful or perhaps unlawful. [Col. 0894C] From this he plainly indicated that by the path of continence one comes more easily to the citadel of purity, in which, as has sufficiently been said, God is obeyed more acceptably and perfectly. For the obedient person is freed from carnal desires and bound by the gracious chains of saving wisdom.

John, I think, had attained this citadel of purity when, writing to the Elect Lady or to Gaius, he spoke beforehand of his old age, so that what he was about to write might be made more authoritative when the reader knew at the outset who and how great was the writer. “The Elder,” he says, “to the Elect Lady and her children.” And likewise: “The Elder to beloved Gaius” (III John I).

Why, when writing, does he so expressly call himself “the elder,” unless because he quietly indicates that he has obtained a fuller mercy? Its abundance bestowed upon him a cleaner conscience; a cleaner conscience, a more pleasing obedience. Of this abundance the prophet says: “My old age is in abundant mercy” (Ps. XCI); and below: “They shall still be multiplied in a fruitful old age” (ibid.).

This richer old age, this abundance of the best old age, is an advancement not of decrepit years but of virtue. John significantly places mention of it before the matters he is about to state, thereby offering himself as an example to those to whom he writes. For he desires that they too may grow old in abundant mercy: that they may grow white, not so much in hair as in manners, through the progress of grace; that amid the tumultuous business of vices they may not become defiled, but rest in the lofty place of aged obedience under pure and peaceful silence.

The rest of his fellow apostles also rested in this high place. They grew old not so much by the number of their years as by the abundance of their virtues. The final age of the world deserved to possess them as shepherds and teachers, so that these elders might show the children of grace the path of perfection.

Isaiah perceived their old age by prophetic scent. Looking far back, he spoke beforehand of those still to come: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people and its princes” (Isa. III). By “elders and princes of the people” he means the apostles, who will not merely come with the rest to judgment but will sit in judgment above the rest. They will no longer render account for their own iniquities; instead, by judicial authority they will condemn the iniquities of others.

He calls them elders or princes because of their mature, elderly obedience, through whose merit they attained such precedence over others that they deserve to sit as judges over the twelve tribes, when Christ the Judge comes and is seen to possess with them the throne of glory. Thus Hannah says: “That he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory” (I Kings II).

The old age of the world—that is, its sixth age—deserved to be distinguished by elders such as these. It is fitting that their contemporaries should be instructed after their likeness, so that those who live one after another in the same age may be adorned with the same whiteness of aged obedience. For in this age Christ wishes the one ministering to him to be made perfect, although under the Law or before the Law he did not reject the imperfect, so that obedience may receive greater progress through the succession of ages and be completed in the same number in which disobedience fell into failure.

For the summit of obedience is found in the sixth degree; likewise, in the sixth degree one descends to the depth of disobedience. In old age both obedience and disobedience are completed: the former is judged ascending and advancing, the latter falling and failing. Although the prophet says that proud people ascend, and Paul that evil people and deceivers advance, the advance of the wicked is toward worse things, and the ascent of the proud tends toward ruin.

Paul says: “Evil people and deceivers will advance into worse things” (II Tim. III); and David: “The pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. LXXIII). Elsewhere he says: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. LXXII). A person arrives at this corrupt advance of disobedience, at this ruinous height of inveterate old age, as his mind falls step by step from evil to worse; for, as a certain pagan says: “No one becomes utterly vile all at once.”

## CHAPTER XXVI

The first degree of falling is, as it were, the earliest age of infancy: when contempt for the justice of obedience is freshly conceived in the heart, and the inclination of a corrupt will, proceeding toward action, is immersed as though in the breasts and milk of carnal pleasure. Of such persons it is said through the Prophet: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. CXXXVI).

But if little ones of this sort are not dashed against the rock—that is, Christ—if the offspring of vipers are not more swiftly cut off by the sharp sickle, they advance into worse things and grow with the passage of time. Having cast off the first body, they become childish in the agility of malice. What the slowness of infancy does more feebly, the agility of childhood accomplishes more readily; it is prepared not only to rejoice in itself and those like itself, but also, with shameless chatter, to mock those whom it sees unlike itself.

I judge such were the boys who are read to have mocked the prophet Elisha. With the brow of shamelessness covered by the mane of vices, they pursued him who had the brow of conscience made bald. “The boys mocked him, saying: ‘Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead’” (IV Kings II).

The wretches do not observe that Elisha bore the type of him who was not only man but also God-man, who, as though bald, had no hair through superfluous vices. Though rightly liable to no punishment, he nevertheless endured sinners’ mockery when he deigned to ascend the cross at the place of Calvary, in order to grant us who are stubborn a pattern of obedience.

But many persons not only neglect to imitate the baldness of the obedient; like people painting a stork from behind, they prefer to laugh. With childish chatter they harshly persecute those who humbly obey their superiors though despising themselves. Unless our Elisha swiftly curses them and, sending bears against them, restrains their malicious chatter, they pass from childhood into adolescence, begin to reach puberty, and burn inwardly with the stronger impulses of ampler malice.

For it is not enough for them childishly to mock those whom they see devoted to obedience. To make them like themselves, they also attempt to harm them and corrupt the obedience of their unbroken chastity, casting into them the poisonous seed of depravity. They rejoice greatly if anyone, deceived by their counsel, yields to them; if they can generate, as it were, children in their own likeness, whom they see decline with them from the rule of obedience.

The Lord does not rejoice over such adolescents, as Isaiah declares in truthful prophecy: “Therefore the Lord shall not rejoice over his young men” (Isa. IX). And Moses says: “The thought of humankind is inclined to evil from its youth” (Gen. VIII). A person is shown to be of greater malice, and judged to incur a greater downfall, insofar as he plots to pour the venom of perverse counsel into others and, made shameless, rejoices to make others his associates and followers.

Since the devil wishes to establish his strength in itching loins, he advances such an adolescent to vigorous youth, so that his stubborn disobedience may be strengthened at that stage and may be recalled from its purpose neither by anyone’s entreaty, nor payment, nor threats. Of such young men David says: “Fire consumed their young men” (Ps. LXXVII).

The consuming fire devoured young men of this kind, whom agreeable perversity inflamed with such ardour that they refuse no hardship, however severe, provided that they can fulfil the malice they desire. Hardened by this shield of strength and darkened by the smoke of obscurity through their wretched progress, they pass into mature manhood and attain a perverse prudence by which they no longer even see the precipice into which they are plunging.

For, calling evil good and good evil, making bitter sweet and sweet bitter, they exalt or excuse whatever they do as though it deserved praise; and in anger they reject or accuse their reprovers. Of such persons Paul says: “Their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. I). “For, claiming to be wise, they became fools.” And Isaiah says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. V).

Such prudence is perverse: it wickedly hardens itself in its own error and, swelling with empty wind, does not yield at all to sounder teaching. The higher it is raised, the more deeply it is destined to fall. It gives no heed to present woe and will afterward find eternal woe. And lest anything seem lacking to its destruction, this man, advancing in evil, is completed by the arrival of old age. The strength joined to prudence made him a man or young man; the pleasing habit of proposed malice makes him old.

For the more sweet his perversity becomes to him, the more pleasantly he grows accustomed to living perversely. By wretched practice premature old age comes upon him, perhaps to have no end except death. Such were the elders whose malice falsely accused the innocent Susanna because she refused their intercourse out of love for chastity. A boy exposed the falsity of their testimony, and judicial judgment condemned the exposed falsehood to deserved death: “You who have grown old in evil days, now your sins have come” (Dan. XIII).

These old men—indeed, men made old in evil—were full of days, but evil days; without doubt, they were full of the manifold number of vices. The righteous penitent invokes a curse upon the light of such days, lest, drawn back and deceived by their enticements, he deserve to be extinguished: “The lamp of the wicked shall be extinguished” (Prov. XIII). Job says: “Let the day perish on which I was born; let those who curse the day curse it” (Job III). And Jeremiah says: “Cursed be the day on which I was born; the day on which my mother conceived me, let it be cursed” (Jer. XX).

In these evil and accursed days those old judges had become inveterate. Banished from the true light, they wickedly assailed chastity and condemned the daughter of Judah on a false criminal charge; but when the judgment was reversed, they fell into the pit which they had dug (Ps. VII). Like them were also the elders of the people who later took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him (Matt. XXVI). Though they did not see, with the revealed eye of faith, that he was God, they nevertheless recognized before Pilate the judge that he was an innocent man.

This is that decrepit old age of profound malice, which long-ingrained perversity ploughs and bends. As though especially to complete it, interrupted breathing, frequent spitting, coughing, and phlegm are added; they so press and oppress this wickedly hardened old age that it does not know how to be renewed according to the youth of the spiritual eagle.

Having set aside this old age, which grows wholly numb toward goodness and which a prudent and noble mind rightly abhors as burdened by so many miseries, let us return to that which grows white through the progress of virtues, toward whose desire every wise person rightly burns. For it is—wonderful to say—continent, yet fruitful; weighty in maturity, yet pleasant: neither does its gravity take away its pleasantness, nor its pleasantness its gravity; neither does its fruitfulness take away its integrity, nor its integrity its fruitfulness.

## CHAPTER XXVII
Abraham, however, is beautifully said to have grown old, and, in his old age, to have begotten a son by a free old woman; in whose old age there is a type and commendation of virtue, while in the son the fruit of old age is displayed. “They were both,” it says, “old and advanced in years” (Gen. 18). But how great was the perfection of holiness in these old persons, how great their continence, how great the grace of purity, is more than sufficiently shown by Sarah’s reply when the divine promise invites them to hope for a son. “I shall return to you at this time,” he says, “and Sarah your wife shall have a son.” And Sarah says: “After I have grown old, and my lord is old, shall I give myself to pleasure?” (ibid.).

By these words she indicates that she no longer gave herself to pleasure, no longer burned with carnal desires; that both had already banished the carnal obligation of reciprocal servitude and remained, as it were, widowed through the benefit of a chaste old age. Therefore, when the promise had been made, they did not come together in order to serve carnal desires, but in order to supply the ministry of begetting to the son who was to be born; [Col. 0898C] not in order to set what they preferred above their Creator, but in order to receive what had been promised and, having received it, render it back to the Promiser.

Whatever, therefore, those old persons do who were able, “against hope, to believe in hope,” who chose by sound counsel not carnally to serve themselves but rather to obey God, does not indict their old age as delirious and reprobate; rather, it represents and commends the service of aged obedience. For they were ready both to beget him whom they heard was divinely promised to them and to sacrifice the son they had begotten and loved so greatly. Hence the Apostle declares that this same son was begotten not according to the flesh but by virtue of the promise (Gal. 3), because it was not a work of flesh but rather a miracle that a son should be born from an old and barren woman. He is also called Isaac—that is, “laughter” or “joy”—because both parents rejoice over such promised and bestowed offspring.

But I wonder that God required this very son to be sacrificed to Him—the son whom He had so carefully promised to the aging Abraham, whom Abraham, now old, had obtained and in whom he rejoiced and rejoiced exceedingly as he himself advanced in age; through whom he hoped, according to the divine promise, that his offspring would be multiplied by God, so that, compared to the sand or the stars, it could not be numbered because of its multitude. I wonder, I say, that God asked him to sacrifice this son, and that the obedient father did not presume even slightly to resist.

Yet to this obedience, by which the patriarch Abraham obeyed God when He required from him as a sacrifice the only son whom he loved, our discourse must at last turn back its looser rein, since we made too long a digression from it. [Col. 0899A] For far above we had in hand the obedience of Adam and Abraham; censuring the former and assigning deserved praise to the latter, we were discussing, after some fashion, the former’s failure and the latter’s progress. Then the subject admonished us to recount in order the six stages, or advances, of obedience and compare with them the six ages of the world or of humankind. Our discourse plunged into the treatment of that matter and, laboring there for some time, scarcely emerged—as I must confess—because, although its subtle height may have seemed insignificant to some, the very length of the unequal endeavor commonly exhausts one who labors.

Now, therefore, let us return, as was said, to Abraham, concerning whom the question under discussion was this: that he showed himself ready to accomplish a difficult thing at the command of One who ordered it, whereas that first Adam neglected a small and easy thing through ruinous contempt. Adam, although large in body, was newly made in time and was still regarded as a little child. Therefore, tender as he was, he was commanded to do nothing grave or harsh, but only something light. He was a type of those who, placed in the first stage of obedience, are driven or pressed by fear into liable servitude. If they are assailed by anyone’s threats, or perhaps softened by gentle flatteries, they easily stagger and turn aside like children with trembling knees; scorning useful things, they incline themselves to the love of present things.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

But Abraham, who is reported to have been old and advanced in years, seems not inappropriately to have borne the figure of those who, raised to the sixth stage of obedience, attribute nothing to their own will but everything to the divine will. [Col. 0899C] They not only utterly put away from themselves what is forbidden, but also voluntarily refer to God what is permitted and lawful, so that they do not refuse to offer the sacrifice of their own will for the perfect consummation of desired holiness.

For whatever is sin is generally forbidden to all; and if anyone delights to commit it, guilt will accuse him. Justice does not will that the reward of praise should be bestowed upon the works of the wicked or that disobedient slaves should share in the inheritance of sons. Perhaps this is why Sarah said: “Cast out the slave-woman and her son; for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. 21). Figuratively, the slave-woman is the will of sin; her son is the affection consenting to that will. Justice, which is free from slavery to sin, plainly does not tolerate their possessing a right of inheritance together with virtue.

But it is the work of justice both not to misuse forbidden things and to use rightly what is granted or lawful. For this reason God deigns to make Himself the promiser of such things, and shows Himself a generous fulfiller of His promises: that His faithful may more easily be kept from unlawful things and, restrained from those, may be held more healthfully by love of the lawful things. “I shall come to you,” He says, “and Sarah your wife shall have a son” (Gen. 17). God declares that He will come to Abraham and mercifully grant what Abraham justly desires, because God is said more manifestly to visit His faithful servant when He deigns to make that person’s justice fruitful: so that not only may there be for him a bridal chamber with justice, but offspring of sonship may also proceed from the same chamber.

In the bridal chamber of each faithful person justice is in a sense already present: justice, which inclines toward lawful things and opposes unlawful ones. This is so when the faithful person embraces justice in the secret of the heart and, cleaving to it, thoughtfully considers how to bring forth fruit. Yet this same justice is judged as still barren when the effect of a work is not granted to the righteous affection—when the just person and justice are joined in the hiddenness of the pleasing chamber, but, because some difficulty intervenes, works do not follow as desired. “To will,” he says, “is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good” (Rom. 7).

But when, through grace’s visitation, the affection of the righteous turns into effect; when the imperfection of one who wills is brought to the perfection of working—then Sarah, previously barren, becomes fruitful, and Isaac, desirable and joyful offspring, is begotten. When he has been begotten, the father rightly rejoices in the fields of his desire; he applauds and rejoices greatly as the son grows, [Col. 0900B] because every faithful person, when seeing that he is no longer intent upon former unlawful things, but has also been granted lawful ones and is content with these gifts through grace, fittingly and blamelessly rejoices: for the reward of salvation is not denied to works of this kind.

For one who knows no adulterous bed but remains in the marriage chamber; who, detesting robbery, supports himself by a just inheritance or his own labor; who wrongs no one unjustly but assists those suffering wrong; who wastes away in hatred of no one but bears, loves, and honors all—such a person, provided that he perseveres in his purpose, does not despair of being able to live eternally. Through this lawful work he confidently embraces the hope of salvation and rejoices in the certainty of that hope, just as hoped-for posterity is enlarged through a son and a father rightly takes joy in that son.

Works, indeed, are designated in Scripture by the name of sons, because, just as sons are begotten so that posterity may not fail, so each faithful person gladly performs what is granted and lawful, through which he truly judges that he may escape death and attain life. “Look upon your servants,” it says, “and direct their sons” (Ps. 89). And, as though explaining this, it adds: “Direct the works of our hands” (ibid.).

Since, moreover, in these works the sweetness of the present life is not wholly removed, while hope for the life to come is nevertheless genuinely held, some who receive them through grace embrace them with a certain tender affection as though they were a son. They rejoice that they have lawful wives and children by them; that they possess houses, fields, estates; [Col. 0900D] that their storehouses overflow with grain, wine, and oil; that they abound in these and the other successes of the year. And, considering that by these things they are not only not drawn toward unlawful acts but are even recalled from adultery, theft, robbery, and other unlawful deeds, they give thanks to Him whose generous kindness comforts them, since He both promises future goods and bestows present ones.

That Pharisee seemed to have a son of this kind, in whose embrace he rejoiced greatly: he gave thanks to God for benefits received and preferred himself, as fruitful, to those who were deprived and barren. “God,” he says, “I thank you that I am not like other people—unjust, robbers, adulterers—or even like this tax collector” (Luke 18). He is not rebuked for truly exulting in the receipt of gifts, [Col. 0901A] but because he rashly insulted the tax collector: the truth of the matter is judged insufficient for justice when its appearance is disfigured by the added cosmetic of pride.

Thus humble truth and truthful humility are necessary: so that insolent presumption may not dishonor truth, nor accompanying falsehood discolor humility. “I fast,” he says, “twice in the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess” (Luke 18). You see a man lawfully possessing earthly things which he knew the divine law permitted both to himself and to others. Since he receives them for himself and his own, he ought to respond with grateful praise to Him by whose gift he deserved to obtain them.

But when someone does not incline toward unlawful things through the gift of grace and reclines in gentle repose among temporal goods; when he recoils from whatever he knows to be unlawful, and possession of lawful things does not depart from the rule of justice—it is not surprising if he applies a holy will to his condition, if he rejoices in this, as it were, voluntary holiness, since the will obeys holiness and holiness is pleasing to the will. He is like the son in whom Father Abraham is said to rejoice and to find pleasure, [Col. 0901B] considering that in him he receives hope of offspring that will never afterward cease, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. “In Isaac,” He says, “your seed shall be called” (Gen. 21); as if He said: Do not merely rejoice because a son is given to you in the present, but because through him your offspring will be multiplied in what follows. For when one expends care upon nothing but lawful works for God’s sake, a lasting repayment of rewards surely follows.

## CHAPTER XXIX

But God at times wills that this son be offered to Him; He who must be preferred to all temporal things consoles His faithful with present benefits so that not gifts or things given, but He Himself, the giver of gifts, may be loved. He therefore asks that the beloved son be sacrificed when He admonishes that even granted and lawful things be set aside; when He teaches His faithful not only not to retain prohibited things but also, for His sake, serenely to abstain from things which they rightfully possess.
