The person who does not refuse to offer the son to the One who asks is he who, when admonished to despise his own possessions, does not excuse himself by an unsuitable objection; he does not reply that not everyone can do such a thing, raising that commonplace saying: “Not all of us can do everything.” He is said to sacrifice his beloved son to God who does not refuse to surrender back to God the benefits he has received from Him; who chooses, at God’s bidding, not to possess temporal goods, or bears their lack without murmuring.

That most holy Job appears to have offered a sacrifice of this kind when he declared that God, their giver, had taken away all that he lawfully possessed; when, poor and bereaved, he brings no accusation against the taker-away but, fortified by patience, gives thanks to the giver. “The Lord,” he says, “gave; the Lord has taken away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1).

Long afterward the apostles offered God a voluntary sacrifice. Invited to contempt for temporal things, they left all that they possessed, [Col. 0902A] hearing that he does not attain the worthy fullness of perfection who, when asked, does not lay his son upon the altar; who does not subordinate wife, children, houses, fields, and estates to obedience; who does not prefer God, the giver, to His received gifts. “Whoever does not renounce,” He says, “all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14).

But a certain young man, capable of lesser obedience and regarded as anxious about the greater, asked the Lord what he might do to deserve eternal life. When he confessed that from his youth he had fulfilled the commandments of the Law, he heard the counsel by which he was admonished to offer, as it were, his beloved son: “If you wish to be perfect,” He says, “go, sell what you have and give to the poor; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19). On hearing this, the young man, as Scripture says, went away sorrowful, “for,” it says, “he had many possessions” (ibid.).

He did not wish to sacrifice the son whom he carnally loved; for the sake of perfection he did not wish to despise what he lovingly possessed. Perhaps he was fit not to touch the forbidden fruit, but still too weak to climb the proposed height of perfection. He was indeed stronger than the first Adam, who weakly bent himself toward what was forbidden; but he was far weaker than Abraham, who raised himself to difficult things in such a way as to show, on hearing the command, that he was a strong despiser of present things—ready to sacrifice his son to God, loving not so much the gift as the giver.

Thus he is commanded to offer this sacrifice upon one of the mountains, that he may know he ought to prefer God to all things; and just as a mountain’s height rises above valleys and plains, so the holiness of God ought to be loved above all things loved either unjustly or justly. “Offer him,” He says, “upon one of the mountains which I shall show you” (Gen. 22). Mountains are virtues; but the one mountain not expressed by name is rightly understood, by antonomasia, as the virtue of love. Through it a person is freed from the many and varied bonds of earthly things and united to the one God by the indissoluble bond of obedience.

God also declares that He Himself will show this mountain to Abraham, so that we may know that no one except God Himself will grant us love of God. Rather, by special grace He makes us understand that He is to be loved, and He makes Him whom we understand to be loved. In this love He commands the beloved son to be sacrificed, because it does not suffice—perhaps it does not even profit—to despise what we possess or love if we do not refuse to remain in the valley or plain of a perverse intention; if we do not strive to be raised up to love God; if charity is not found to rule over our works. Hence the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, but have not charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13).

Therefore, if anyone offers either the purse of earthly resources or indeed the sacrifice of his own will, he must offer it upon the mountain of charity, upon which the true Rising One pours the ray of eternal brightness. Perhaps this is why Abraham called that place “The Lord sees,” whence it is said to this day: “On the mountain the Lord will see” (Gen. 22): because the Lord graciously beholds the lofty flame of love [Col. 0903A] and is not shut out from it by any intervening cloud or mist.

But upon the valley, dark with the filth of vices, ignorant of charity’s heat and hateful to every virtue, the bright countenance of the divine regard does not shine. Its clear purity abhors what is vicious; and therefore, if any offering is made there, it will not be fruitful, however abundant in number or magnitude. For, as it is written, God is not a God of valleys but of mountains (3 Kings 20).

Understanding this wisely, Josiah, the most righteous king, took pains to remove the sacrifices made in the valley of the son of Ennon, knowing that sacrifices of deep valleys do not please God. “He defiled,” it says, “Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Ennon, so that no one might consecrate his son or daughter to Moloch” (4 Kings 23). Topheth is a place in the valley of the son of Ennon, to which the children of Israel flocked, and there, with ruined understanding, offered sons or daughters. Wretchedly, they did not fear to become not only murderers but also slaves of miserable superstition (thus the text).

Topheth is interpreted “protection of the mouth,” or “danger of the mouth.” The place in which sacrifice is made to evil spirits is aptly called “protection of the mouth,” because those wicked spirits, rejoicing that sacrifices are offered to them, profess that they will protect their worshippers. But perverse human beings are deceived by their promises, and, deceived, fall into the danger of Gehenna. Hence Topheth is also interpreted “danger of the mouth,” because those spirits deceitfully promise protection, while these people truly deserve danger; with their pestilential mouth the former pledge themselves as protectors of sinners [Col. 0903C] and later show themselves mockers amid the sinners’ punishments.

Topheth is also interpreted “Gehenna,” because their protection is, as it were, a beginning of Gehenna, and their condemnation amid punishments is nothing but the depth of Gehenna. “Topheth,” it says, “which is in the valley of the son of Ennon.” Ennon is interpreted “behold these things,” or “they are,” as if it said: “Behold, these things are.” For when perverse spirits have seduced perverse people into sin and led them with themselves into the danger of eternal death, they say to them: “Behold, these things are”—as though saying: Behold, these are the places or the rewards you have earned in the camps of our warfare, when you chose, with ruined understanding, to remain under our protection; when you refused to avoid the danger of our mouth by reformed conduct; [Col. 0903D] when you consecrated to us your sons or daughters; when you dedicated to our worship those things which were lawful for you; when, despising your king, to whom you ought to have offered sacrifices, you served our king Moloch by offerings of gifts.

Finally, Moloch is interpreted “king.” He is, I think, the son of Ennon: that is, the son of perdition, the son of that eternal condemnation which is prepared for the devil and his angels, by which he is rewarded when his own wickedness and that of his followers has been consummated. Topheth is not inappropriately said to have been in his valley, because whatever he either thrusts upon people in insult or promises in deceit is not illumined by the bright visitation of the rising sun, but is burdened and darkened by the gloomy depression of the valley.

Josiah, therefore, rightly defiled Topheth. A Josiah plainly defiles Topheth when any righteous ruler subtly teaches us that demons must not be served, that none of their wishes must be obeyed, that nothing belonging to them must be mixed into our works, and that none of the things we love must be offered to them. A Josiah defiles Topheth when a teacher of others prudently examines his own obedience also: when he permits nothing carnal, nothing dark, in it; neither a vicious beginning nor a vicious end in his inward intention; but, abhorring the depths of valleys, hastens to reach the heights, and there, fervent in spirit, loves to obey God for God’s sake.

Finally, Mary, having received the Spirit, is said to have gone into the hill country, that she might herself marvel at the citizens of the hills as their fellow-citizen, rejoice in both her own and their mountain-like obedience, and urge us also, by the example of the citizens of the mountains, toward the mountains. Abraham, then, rightly sacrificed his son not in a valley but upon the mountain which the Lord had shown him beforehand, because no useful sacrifice is found that is not seasoned with the salt of loving wisdom or wise love: “You shall season,” He says, “every sacrifice of yours with salt” (Lev. 2).

## CHAPTER XXX

But what does it mean that Abraham, ready to sacrifice his son, is recalled, and that, after the son has been restored to him, a ram presented to him is sacrificed, except that when an offering of our possessions is presented to the Lord with a view to perfection, a hundredfold reward is given to us in the present? Mark the Evangelist says: “There is no one,” he says, “who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or mother, or father, or [Col. 0904C] children, or fields for my sake, who shall not receive a hundredfold now in this time” (Mark 10).

Therefore, when anyone obeys evangelical commandments or counsels, offering to God whatever he previously possessed temporally, he does not judge that he has incurred any loss through dispersing his possessions, considering that he has discovered a more perfect treasure in voluntary poverty. And because the possession of things, even lawful things, is temporal and seems to a perfect person now to belong to the animal life, the ram, as it were, is rightly said to be found and sacrificed when the carnal affection for such things is placed upon the altar of obedience. Thus those things which were formerly gains are now counted loss for Christ (Phil. 3), and what was formerly possessed—especially because it was lawful—seemed useful for living well, but, once offered, or rather sacrificed, is now judged far more useful.

Isaac is restored alive to his father because such perfection and such joy are granted to the will that, preferring what has been restored after being offered, it understands that what divine mercy intended to promise it is thereby more perfectly fulfilled. “In Isaac,” He says, “your seed shall be called” (Gen. 27), as though He said: “You shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life” (Matt. 19). If possession or love of temporal things is sacrificed like a ram, a hundredfold recompense will be conferred upon the sacrificer like an Isaac restored. In it the seed—that is, the operation of the perfect person—[p. 522] no longer suffers loss, but receives the desired increase of future offspring, that is, of lasting recompense.

Divine generosity restored to the righteous man Job, after he had patiently borne the removal of his possessions, with doubled increase, so that it might be known how great is the merit of patient obedience: obedience which, provoked by losses, remains firm in heart and does not overstep with its lips. But our obedient person, formed by evangelical sayings and conformed no longer to the shadow of things but rather to truth, generously lends his money to God at interest and receives from Him, in a far more generous measure, a return. He receives in the present not, like Job, double—or perhaps tenfold, which is more—but, according to the preaching of the Gospel, a hundredfold.

This number does not know the imperfection of the old life but, being perfect, passes more perfectly into perfection. For as perfection becomes a hundred when ten is multiplied by ten, so consummation becomes a thousand when a hundred is multiplied by ten. This number, I think, God mystically promises to Abraham: namely, that his obedience shall be consummated, when He declares that his seed is both called in Isaac and, once called, compared with the stars of heaven. Understanding the mystery wisely, Abraham loosens the reins of obedience and, forgetting what lies behind, stretches eagerly toward what lies ahead: he does not refuse to offer the requested Isaac, and, though he loves him when received, he welcomes him still more when restored. For perfection restored as the proper possession of those who offer is received far more abundantly and far more rightly; for what a hundredfold differs in deserved magnitude from a single amount, that is voluntary poverty in relation to the perfection received as one’s own.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Although, in the offering and restoration of Isaac, I think something more subtle is signified which can be assigned more perfectly to our obedient persons—something which Abraham perhaps saw in spirit when he received his son and received him back after offering him, and, embracing the shadow, did not envy those who would follow the reality of the thing.

Sarah is said to be joined in marriage to Abraham when divine grace offers to assist our spirit, that by her help and service it may be made fruitful and rejoice in the fruitful offspring of good works. Sarah is interpreted “princess,” because spiritual grace rules over good works, without which no one performs anything good. Grace itself mercifully both precedes and follows one who works well: “Without me,” He says, “you can do nothing” (John 13). Yet although this grace is truly spiritual and is called spiritual, in the person whom it helps it does not initially produce spiritual things; [Col. 0905D] it does not make him spiritual through an inverted order of progress, but first supports, cherishes, and embraces the natural or animal person. “The spiritual,” says the Apostle, “is not first, but the animal; afterward, the spiritual” (1 Cor. 15).

While spiritual grace appears to withhold itself from producing spiritual persons, Sarah’s womb is rightly said to be closed, as it were; and a son is not properly forbidden to be born from her, but her bearing is deferred until a more fitting time. For that person is rightly considered her son who, judging all things spiritually, is judged by no one; who is formed in the merits of perfected virtues down to the last detail, and conforms in an expressed likeness to his spiritual mother (1 Cor. 2).

When grace sees that it does not yet have such a son, it nevertheless does not wish the spirit it embraces to remain barren. Rather, meanwhile it strives to invite it to suitable works and joins its maidservant to it by a useful dispensation: “Go in,” she says, “to my maidservant, that perhaps at least from her I may receive sons” (Gen. 16). This maidservant, to whom Abraham goes at Sarah’s prompting, is fittingly understood as the active life, or laborious action. She is appropriately said to be Sarah’s servant because she herself is not fruitful or useful except through grace’s gift.

She first certainly produces fruit when the untrained obedient person, to the extent of his ability, satisfies the grace that inspires him; when he applies himself to performing just temporal actions and intends, through these, to please God especially. Abraham is said to beget a son by the maidservant when the fruit of good work is found to spring from the active life: when each person wisely forms and orders his own conduct; when he arranges and governs his outward affairs with discernment; when he loves to use temporal goods in such a way as diligently to strive not to misuse their abundance; when he loves to have a lawful wife but nevertheless does not refuse to devote himself to prayer for a time; when perhaps, putting aside his wife and abandoning the purse of financial resources, he transfers himself to the assembly of the righteous for the sake of greater holiness, and there labors diligently at good works and applies himself to them at obedience’s bidding, never ceasing humbly to serve the needs of the brothers.

This is the son begotten from the maidservant; these are the matters in which the active life is greatly wearied, in which Martha is frequently troubled with care, until at last our mind, as its merits advance, attains Mary’s repose. In that repose the first human being had been placed and wisely instructed by the divine command to guard himself: namely, to keep himself within the bounds of rest and justice, since he had been made to possess peaceful territories as though by his own right.

But because he consented to the counsel of his deceived wife, he was driven far from the boundary of that peaceful possession; and, wickedly obeying the will of the deceiving devil, he miserably fell, having lost what was his own, into what was not his own. [p. 523] Stripped of the purity of his innate nakedness, he was grievously wrapped in the rags of another’s misery.

Therefore this temporal affliction, by which each person feels himself greatly opposed, should be called not properly a citizen but rather a stranger: it came from elsewhere and, through vexatious invasion, assailed our peaceful borders, when, through the devil’s envy, “death entered into the world,” as it is written (Wis. 2). Yet this stranger now becomes fruitful for us; from it a health-giving remedy is now prepared for us, provided only that it is not at all turned away from service to Sarah, but is directed by maturer counsel to bear fruit.

For laborious activity harms when it runs through the downward paths of pleasures, but helps when it humbly performs service for merciful grace; when it does not rule in the manner of a citizen rejoicing within native boundaries, but, as a guest and stranger, turns to obey the one who commands. Hence the maidservant to whom Abraham is said to be joined at the free woman’s prompting is not inappropriately named Hagar, and the significance of this matter is expressed in her name. Hagar is interpreted “stranger” or “converted.” And she is fittingly called “stranger” or “converted,” because a human being would have known no laborious activity at all, but would have possessed as his own a dwelling-place of unbroken rest, if he had been willing to remain in the state in which he was made and had kept the rule of obedience imposed upon him.

Yet this activity is not now wholly adverse to our salvation, but has been converted into a healing remedy, insofar as it offers the file or exercise of obedience to each imperfect person, through the saving disposition of Him “who forms labor in commandment” (Ps. 93). From this activity a son proceeds, older by birth but lower in precedence. God hears the mother’s desire for him without delay, but does not yet hear Sarah’s desire to give birth. Therefore this son of the servant is called Ishmael; Ishmael means “God’s hearing,” because, when the untrained obedient person vigorously applies strong hands to the labor commanded, God graciously hears this cry not of words but of works: “You shall call his name Ishmael,” He says, “because the Lord has heard your affliction” (Gen. 16).

So also Leah, Jacob’s wife—whose name is interpreted “laborious,” and who is declared by Scripture’s testimony to have been bleary-eyed—is said to have borne children first, while Rachel, whose name is interpreted “sheep” or “seeing the beginning,” was still oppressed by barren confinement. Long afterward, Hannah, whose name is interpreted “grace,” was still considered barren after Phenenna, Elkanah’s wife; and Elkanah himself grieved not a little over Hannah’s barrenness: “To Hannah,” it says, “he gave one portion in sorrow, because he loved Hannah” (1 Sam. 1).

> [Note: [Col. 0907D] The phrase is incomplete.]

In the wives of Jacob and Elkanah alike a certain diversity of manner of life is signified. This diversity contains no blameworthy perversity; rather, there is a distinct usefulness in distinct kinds, and the authority of Scripture mystically commends both that usefulness and its diversity. By Leah, indeed, labor and activity are signified; by Phenenna, the conversion of that same laborious activity is signified, because the active life is converted into salvation for those who, like Egyptian Hagar, embrace the laborious service of obedience.

By Rachel, called “sheep” or “seeing the beginning,” are understood innocent purity and a certain principal vision; by Hannah, spiritual grace. For after the file or exercise of the active life—through which a progressing person ceases to be animal—one comes by more abundant grace to contemplate God. In the hiddenness of His countenance the perfect obedient person is buried; separated from temporal things, by whose concern he is bound for the moment, he at last devotes free diligence to contemplating truth. [Col. 0907D] Therefore a son is first begotten from Leah, Phenenna, or Egyptian Hagar, because from the laborious life the posterity of works is first propagated. Yet this active toil would not produce such works if spiritual grace did not grant it something from its own proper right.

## CHAPTER XXXII
For the fact that our obedient person bends himself to the handmaid of the free woman, and does not turn away from her vigorous union for the sake of offspring, is a gift of grace. By the privilege of freedom grace commands whatever it wills, and by the lavish generosity of its goodness supplies the power to fulfil it. [Col. 0908A] The handmaid, therefore, must be reproved if she grows insolent against her mistress; that is, if the active life swells up against spiritual grace, if, made fruitful by its abundant gift, she scorns with a rebellious spirit its gentle lordship. “I,” says Sarah, “gave my maid into your bosom; and she, seeing that she has conceived, holds me in contempt” (Gen. 16).

For the conceiving handmaid then appears to despise Sarah when the active life begins to lift itself somewhat proudly on account of the fruit of good work; when it suggests to the mind that it should not take great care to apply itself to spiritual occupations, but should rather devote its attention to external matters; and flatters it with the usefulness of the work proposed, since this is found in itself more ready and more immediately available. This handmaid seems to me to represent those who, when they see themselves prevailing in outward matters [Col. 0908B] and their brethren somewhat in need of their service, suppose themselves to excel them in the merit of virtues—those brethren whom they observe clinging more closely to spiritual leisure. Since the usefulness of their own ministry is, as it were, immediately before their eyes and is not deferred, whereas the spiritual leisure of those who are free for it does not quickly show its fruits, they value their own life as presently fruitful and, with lofty disdain, despise the others’ 524 barren leisure.

When such presumption enters into the mind of one who is obedient and proceeds to seduce him with a stealthy, silent step, if he does not immediately wipe this mist of deception from the threshold, if by giving assent he turns, even a little, in the other direction, spiritual grace intervenes: it condemns the judgment of falsehood, rebukes the departing spirit, and recalls it to the rule of equity. [Col. 0908C] “You act unjustly against me,” it says. “I gave my maid into your bosom; and she, seeing that she has conceived, holds me in contempt. Let God judge between me and you”—as though it said: It is not right that you, whom I wished to train in outward occupations because you were too weak to devote yourself to spiritual studies alone, should allow your active life rashly to grow proud of its fruit and, in presumptuous arrogance, oppose the contemplation of spiritual things; or that you should consent, either in judgment or through forbearance, to its boldness, which plainly departs very far from the rule of justice.

“Let God judge between me and you.” Between me, by whose gift you approached the fruitful handmaid, and you, who allowed the swelling pride of that same handmaid to proceed even a little: let God judge and distinguish [Col. 0908D] our cause, commending as is fitting the benevolence of my bounty, and rebuking and correcting the consent of your will.

When divine correction thus strikes the spirit of a righteous person, in whom no poisonous purpose of evil is predominant—who does not eagerly embrace the counsels of the malignant enemy, but, whether willing or unwilling, endures his temptations—when, I say, such a spirit feels itself restrained by divine admonition and gladly learns more fully through inspiring grace, it seems to make a sufficiently prudent reply and, by that prudent reply, to remove whatever guilt it had incurred: “Behold, your handmaid is in your hand; use her as you please” (ibid.).

I know, it says, that the contemplative life rightly rules the active; spiritual leisure governs laborious occupation; Martha, busily laboring, is wearied in the service of Mary who listens. [Col. 0909A] The fruitful action of the laborer serves spiritual grace, by whose generous gift it is honourably made fruitful with the burden of its desired fruit. It is therefore fitting that she should not be ungrateful for this benefit, but always bow before you in humble service; that you should hold her subject under the hand of your power and use her in due order according to your will.

But if, through feminine fickleness, she should presume to think otherwise, or, contrary to right order, should dare to mutter with chattering insolence, my manly discernment will not give her its assent, but will adhere spiritually to your spiritual fellowship. For I approached her not in the heat of lust, but rather through the grace of begetting; and I do not wish her carnal pleasure so to entice me that I withdraw from the sincere holiness of spiritual things.

“Therefore,” it says, “when Sarai afflicted her—that is, Hagar—she fled” (ibid.). [Col. 0909B] Hagar is afflicted when any obedient person is inwardly instructed that he ought not to glory in his external work; when outward progress entirely vanishes if inward love grows cold under the blast of vanity. Hagar is also fittingly said to flee when that obedient person is, by the impulse of grace, removed from the desire for praise; when, knowing that the person who hopes for a passing reward from the merits of his works is deceived, he now profitably abandons that hope. The external activity of obedient persons becomes, in a sense, fugitive when, being better instructed, it is compelled to withdraw from presumptuous hope; when it understands that no good work comes from itself to itself, and that, if spiritual grace is abandoned, nothing remains but failure and misery.

“And when the Angel of the Lord found her in the wilderness, he said to [Col. 0909C] her: ‘Hagar, Sarai’s handmaid, whence do you come and where are you going?’ She answered: ‘I flee from the face of Sarai, my mistress.’ And the Angel said to her: ‘Return to your mistress, and humble yourself under her hand’” (ibid.). And again: “‘Multiplying,’ he says, ‘I shall multiply your seed, and it shall not be numbered because of its multitude’” (ibid.).

The Angel of the Lord is said to find Hagar as she flees, and, having found her, to address her with consoling speech, when the divine Word permits our active life to be tested beyond its strength, yet graciously comes to console it with manifold teaching. It exhorts and admonishes it to turn away from what it had foolishly presumed, and humbly to return to obedience to spiritual grace. “Return,” it says, “to your mistress, and humble yourself under her hand.”

This, indeed, is what the divine Word is found to admonish in many places; this is what divine Scripture teaches in both the New and the Old pages: namely, that no one should presume to glory in his own works, but should attribute to grace whatever good he is enabled to do. [Col. 0909D] If anyone has been instructed by this teaching as though by the visitation of an angel, and humbly obeyed it with lowered pride, he will consequently hear what that divine visitation promises him, what its benevolence or mercy will grant to one who humbly obeys: “‘Multiplying,’ it says, ‘I shall multiply your seed, and it shall not be numbered because of its multitude’” (ibid.). It is as though it said: If one who is vigorously exercised in outward matters does not find it burdensome humbly to obey the command of spiritual things; if he attributes not arrogantly to himself, but to spiritual grace, whatever progress he happens to make in active labor; if, while occupied and busied with Martha’s service and labor, he nevertheless understands the part of Mary sitting still to be the better one—then he will assuredly feel his seed, that is, his activity, multiplied in so many ways that its increase cannot be numbered because of its multitude. [Col. 0910A]

525

## CHAPTER XXXIII

After these things God said to Abraham: “You shall call your wife Sarah, and I shall bless her; and from her I shall give you a son, whom I shall bless. Abraham fell upon his face and laughed, saying in his heart: ‘Shall a son be born to a man a hundred years old, and shall Sarah at ninety bear a child? Would that Ishmael might live before you!’” (Gen. 17).

After Ishmael is begotten for Abraham from the handmaid, after the progress of good work is propagated from the laborious life; after our obedient person has humbly obeyed the command of spiritual things and has attained worthy merit of praise in external occupation—God, who according to the Apostle is rich in goodness (Rom. 2), visits his obedient servant with a new abundance, so that one who has exerted himself courageously in active occupation may receive greater progress in spiritual leisure. [Col. 0910B] “‘From her,’” he says, “‘I shall give you a son, whom I shall bless’” (Gen. 17). To one who has a son by the handmaid, a son is promised also by the free woman, because one who has shown himself faithful in a small matter, by begetting Ishmael at Sarah’s command, seems worthy to be advanced to something greater, in which he may deserve to obtain a greater blessing.

What, then, does divine condescension promise him when it introduces him, as it were, into a vestibule of contemplation, and when to him as he gazes there begins already, however faintly, to shine forth how pleasant and good it is to cleave to God in the embraces of rest and leisure? When he feels himself suffused with the faint ray of this light, and God’s love already poured into his heart through the Spirit, he cannot but rejoice at the newness of the promised joy—that is, he delights to rejoice at the coming benefit. “Abraham,” it says, “laughed, saying in his heart: ‘Shall a son be born to a man a hundred years old?’” [Col. 0910C]

When the spirit of an obedient person begins to behold invisible things through a glass, understanding that God promises him more than usual, it laughs; and, as though what is promised were incredible, faithfully awaits it, silently marveling within itself at the greatness of the promise. “‘Shall a son,’” it says, “‘be born to a man a hundred years old?’” [Col. 0910D] He says this not in despair but rather in wonder. For one who is unable to offer adequate praise for benefits received wonders how he will deserve to obtain still greater things.

That obedient person is rightly called a centenarian who is perfected by the labor and study of the active life; who is granted to attain such a summit of it that he then perceives the perfect fruit of good work proceeding from it. When he considers himself to possess this perfection and sees in the spirit another, greater one impending for him, he rejoices, marveling at so great a bounty of God; and, presuming nothing of himself, is astonished at so great a benefit.

But lest he appear to direct his attention to the coming benefit in such a way that he negligently despises the gifts already received, he shows that he does not regard it as insignificant or contemptible if what he has already attained is preserved for him by the gift of grace. “‘Would that Ishmael,’” he says, “‘might live before you!’” [Col. 0911A] Would that what I have labored at in the active life under the burden of obedience, whatever merit I have gained from that labor and sweat, might live before you—that is, might be worthy to please your sight—and that I might deserve to remain in it with steadfast step.

For I do not think it a small benefit to obtain if I can also retain what I have acquired; if, in that place in which your benevolence has willed to set me, you may also deign to strengthen or preserve me, lest I fail when tested. “‘Would that it might live before you!’” And he significantly says, “before you.” For often a person seems to work zealously in his own sight or in the sight of other people, yet is judged dead in the sight of God, because he alone, whose eye is darkened by no film and no dust, perfectly sees which work deserves to live, and with what fruit and for what end labor is bestowed upon good works. [Col. 0911B]

“Would that it might live before you”: that which I have acquired by labor and study; that in which I obeyed your command, attending to external matters; that active life which, at your command and in hope of offspring, I embraced; that in which, by your gift, I have gained some small profit. But if, after these benefits of your bounty, you promise to add the greater gifts of a new holiness, so that the inward beauty of spiritual things may receive and soothe the person pressed and afflicted by the daily concern of outward things, who would not, in astonished joy, rejoice beyond comprehension at so great a grace? [Col. 0911C]

Since one truly fervent in desire can scarcely endure delay, and nothing suffices him so long as he understands that he does not have what he desires, when I say, “Shall a son be born to a man a hundred years old?” I say it not in despair, beyond doubt, but rather affirming that my desire is eager and impatient.

But lest his desire should faint under the burden of excessive delay—or rather, so that the longer it is deferred, the more it may desire—God elegantly both repeats the promise and delays the gift: the repeated promise does not permit the expectant person to grow weary beyond his strength, while delay makes what is delayed be awaited more eagerly. “God said to Abraham: ‘Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac; and I shall establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant’” (ibid.). [Col. 0911D]

God wished not only to repeat his promise to him, but to make that repeated promise more commendable by a welcome addition, when he indicates what name the son whom he declares that he will give to his obedient servant shall have. “‘You shall call his name Isaac’” (ibid.). Isaac is interpreted “vision” or “joy.” It is a good promise, one worthy to be called laughter or joy, which cannot be darkened by the gloom of failing 526 sorrow. Through it our obedient person already tastes heavenly things in delightful sweetness, and no difficulty will oppress him in the future. For this godliness has the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come (1 Tim. 4): by it the begun height of contemplation receives the obedient person in the present life, and its consummated breadth perfects him in the life to come. [Col. 0912A]

Hence he adds: “‘And I shall establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant’” (ibid.). Indeed, what is begun here spiritually and completed eternally, God establishes as his covenant into an everlasting covenant: just as he makes temporal things end in time, so after the end of time he makes this more blessed thing reach its consummation.

And lest it appear vain that the obedient person has taken such pains to apply diligence in outward matters, because those things are not said to endure eternally like spiritual things, God shows that they should not be judged useless, though they are in no way comparable with spiritual things. “‘Concerning Ishmael also,’” he says, “‘I have heard you: behold, I shall bless him, and increase him, and multiply him exceedingly.’”

Then Abraham is heard concerning Ishmael; then greater progress is found in the works of the active life, [Col. 0912B] when the obedient person desires those works to live before God—that is, to please God—yet values adherence to spiritual things more highly. That their difference may be known still more certainly, what was said a little earlier is repeated again; and the more this repetition binds the promisor, the more certain it appears to make the one to whom the promise is given. “‘But I shall establish my covenant with Isaac,’” he says (ibid.).

To make the obedient person’s desire glad, he names a definite time for fulfilling the promise, because often a promise is more welcome, or its certainty is held more securely, when it is not burdened by the limitless length of time. Therefore he says: “‘Whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time next year’” (Gen. 18). At this time Isaac is promised to be born [the text perhaps reads *nascitur* for *nasciturum*], when our obedient person hopes and foresees that he will attain the sweetness of divine taste—not only in that life when God is revealed face to face to all the faithful, but also in this life, when our eye has not yet been made wholly clear. [Col. 0912C]

“‘At this time next year’” (ibid.). By “year,” I think, perfection is signified; for just as a year is said to be completed by the accumulated number of days, so the perfection of the active life grows through the gathering of temporal works, and spiritual perfection through progress in spiritual works. The one, or first, year is the perfection which each obedient person seems to acquire when he endeavors to apply himself to temporal concerns and works, prudently carries out the outward duties imposed upon him, and in carrying them out attains progress toward perfection. [Col. 0912D]

The other year is that perfection which is attained after the exercise of the laborious life, when the obedient person’s mind is freed from outward concerns, immerses itself with entire desire in spiritual studies, and wipes its face with the hand of devotion in order to behold God. In this perfection, as in the second year, God promises that Isaac will be born, so that our obedient person may rejoice in hope of his birth, knowing not only how great, but also when at last, the son will arise for him—namely, when this other perfection is granted to him at this time.

And God, observing him both sufficiently soothed for the time by the pleasing hope and made more fervent by the delay of the thing itself, at last fulfils what he had promised, so that the realities which accomplish the promise may refresh more welcome and more perfectly the one whom the words of promise had long held in expectation. [Col. 0913A]

## CHAPTER XXXIV

“‘The Lord,’” it says, “‘visited Sarah; she conceived and bore’” (Gen. 21).

The Lord visits Sarah when he increases for his obedient servant the benefit of spiritual grace, removing far from him the turmoil of temporal business; when he grants his desire more abundant restful leisure and makes the grace of that leisure, or repose, fruitful. It becomes fruitful when the obedient person, resting and ardently striving through contemplation toward perfection, feels himself affected in that very progress with such sweetness that the same sweetness seems now like a worthy reward for which devotion to contemplation is not unreasonably bestowed.

Forgetting what lies behind, he burns to seek and hold the truth, and with tender affection embraces its purity when found; he is ineffably delighted by this embrace, and through this delight, with Paul, “is preserved in the heavenly places” (Phil. 3). [Col. 0913B] For when spiritual reading occupies the perfect obedient person, pure and clarified prayer soothes him after reading; meditation holds him suspended by the benefit of reading or praying; and grateful devotion pierces—or rather anoints—him amid all these things. It is evident that he is in some manner present among the choirs of angels: not in body, but in spirit standing before the divine countenance; and, caught up in ecstasy, he thinks that nothing is now lacking to him, while, longing after what is set before him, he says with Peter: “It is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:4).

This good, this fruit, this as it were son—who that thinks rightly would not desire to obtain it? Who, having obtained it, could sufficiently rejoice? Who would not smile with such joy? “Abraham,” it says, “called the name of his son, whom Sarah bore to him, Isaac” (Gen. 16 [probably 21]); Isaac, however, is called “laughter” or “joy.” [Col. 0913C]

And rightly: “laughter” or “joy.” For the perfect obedient person, though still placed amid the misery of this life, when he has attained this fruit of sweetness by the gift of grace, scarcely comprehends his own joy within the narrow bounds of the human mind; 527 he finds none greater or even like it. Though he had formerly rejoiced in the progress of outward works, while he was still wholly without spiritual things, that joy is nevertheless judged to have been far different, since it was in some sense passing, being found in temporal and transient things.

To labor wisely in those outward things, and to rejoice in merits advancing through their labor and study, has its beginning here and likewise ends here; for nothing of this kind is found at all in the heavenly dwelling. There no one is exercised by cares and labors; no one is said to rejoice in transient things. Rather, for all who dwell there, there is joyful rest, jubilant silence, tranquil joys. [Col. 0913D] Their sweetness is already tasted in this life by those to whom it is given lavishly, by those who, through abundant grace, taste the sweetness of contemplation—when, that is, their mind is emptied of the disturbance of earthly thoughts and is enlarged by serene love to tread the path of purity.

Thus this joy begins here, but does not also end here; begun in this life, it is more perfectly consummated in heavenly glory. In it, as in Isaac, there is said to be called the seed of more serene action, and in that seed the unfailing posterity of contemplation is blessed. [Col. 0914A]

Therefore Sarah, seeing that Ishmael, now somewhat older, was playing with the little Isaac, and prudently understanding what was signified by such a game—or rather mockery—said: “‘Cast out the handmaid and her son, for the son of the handmaid shall not be heir with my son Isaac’” (Gen. 21).

Ishmael, somewhat older, is said to be with the little Isaac and, while playing, tries to mock him when the pleasantness of temporal activity—which grows strong sooner and more easily—behaves somewhat insolently against spiritual activity, still as it were undeveloped and tender; when, flattering obedient persons, it wishes to seem more ready and available, and to draw those obedient persons away from the difficulty of spiritual things. [Col. 0914B] For what is obtained more easily commonly presents itself more familiarly; what is more customary returns even when expelled. This coming and returning is rightly judged a game or deception, since by its enticement the sharpness of contemplation is sometimes blunted.

When the gratuitous mercy of God sees this play developing in the contemplative person’s heart, and does not wish him to fall into the error of harmful consent, it deigns to instruct him by severe admonitions, as it were, and swiftly to assist one who is almost in doubt. “‘Cast out,’” it says, “‘the handmaid and her son, for the son of the handmaid shall not be heir with my son Isaac.’”

I do not want you to think, it says, that the active life is in any respect equal to the contemplative; that by its pleasure it obtains the dignity of spiritual joy; or that its tumultuous labor, though fruitful in its own measure, passes into the heavenly dwelling and there obtains the divine vision through its former activity, care, or exercise. [Col. 0914C] Drive this opinion from the secret place of your conscience. By its presence you greatly dim the nobility of Isaac, if you compare the eternal with the active life or its temporal joy, if you suppose that what passes with time remains forever.

“For the son of the handmaid shall not be heir with my son Isaac.” The perfection of outward works will not obtain the right of inheritance together with the spiritual perfection; rather, when the former has ceased, the latter will possess eternally what is its own, and what it now deserves to feel in sweet delight it will there rejoice to find so much more sweetly as it finds it more manifestly.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I shall see you, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16). [Col. 0914D] God sees his own when he reveals to them the eye of contemplation, when he pours into those who contemplate the grace of foretaste, when he gives them great joy from a taste of his sweetness, promising that no end threatens this joy.

But because in the condition of this life there are no delights to which temptations do not threaten—for “human life upon earth is temptation”—after so many benefits divinely granted to our obedient person, temptations are nevertheless also brought upon him by God himself. “God,” it says, “tested Abraham, saying: ‘Take your son Isaac, whom you love, and offer him as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I shall show you’” (Gen. 22). [Col. 0915A]

A wonderful thing! God had promised Abraham long before that a son would be born to him, even foretelling what name that son would bear; in that son Abraham’s seed would be called, and in that seed blessing would be bestowed upon the nations. Yet now God demands that this same son be sacrificed to him, as though, once sacrificed, he could be more fruitfully multiplied. But the righteous Abraham, whose faith is proclaimed as praiseworthy, considers that God promises nothing superfluous. Fully knowing that God is able to accomplish whatever he has promised, he does not refuse to sacrifice his son to him who, just as he had given life, was also able to raise him from the dead.

## CHAPTER XXXV
Then God wills Abraham’s son to be offered to Himself when, after all His gifts, He requires that He Himself be preferred above them [Col. 0915B]: so that the righteous man, who rejoices to contemplate “through a glass, in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13), may know that this joy ought to be ascribed not to himself but to God. Abraham is commanded to sacrifice the son whom he loves when the person granted, through contemplation, a taste of the sweetness of heavenly things understands that he must love them not on account of himself to whom they are given, nor on account of what is given, but on account of Him from whom they are given; and that the love of the sweetness tasted must be referred back to Him who bestowed it.

For when someone gratefully embraces the benefits God has bestowed upon him, and, rejoicing because of those very benefits, accordingly comes to love God the giver, he indeed possesses a not inconsiderable fruit, spiritual joy; yet something still somewhat animal remains attached to that joy. Very many people not only do not love God, but even pursue Him with hatred, and wretchedly misuse His temporal gifts [Col. 0915C], clinging carnally to visible things, so that no blows can drive them away from them, just as no blows can drive a dog from a greased hide. Of such persons David says: “The pride of those who hate thee ascendeth continually” (Ps. 73). And through Amos: “I sent death among you, and I smote your young men with the sword; and ye returned not unto me, saith the Lord” (Amos 4). And through Jeremiah: “In vain have I smitten your children; they have received no discipline” (Jer. 2).

Others, however, seeing temporal things which they love abound for them, begin to praise God the giver: ready indeed, if they are full, to render thanks, but conversely murmuring if they should begin to be in want. Hence David also says: “He will praise thee when thou hast done well to him” (Ps. 48). And when the people of Israel stayed in the wilderness, they are reported to have murmured because of a lack of water [Col. 0915D].

But some, considering how terribly God threatens those who despise Him, and, on the other hand, what and how great things He professes that He will confer upon those who love Him, beginning from fear progress toward a tender relish for loving, or toward the wisdom of loving. The more richly they are endowed with the prudent sweetness of love, the more confidently they await greater gifts in the future; and the fuller the hope of heavenly gifts they receive, the more they love the Giver Himself. For, observing how great a strength He gives His faithful in their journey, and how great a salvation He gives in their homeland as the reward of strength, stirred worthily by such great goodness, they respond by loving [Col. 0916A] to His goodness: they love Him who loves, choose Him who chooses, and burn to turn toward Him with complete devotion, having already experienced Him as gracious to them through many benefits.

In their person the Prophet says: “I will cry unto God most high, unto God who hath done good to me” (Ps. 56); and elsewhere: “Return, O my soul, unto thy rest, because the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee” (Ps. 114). Yet when these people rejoice in spiritual benefits received, and on their account are laudably inflamed to love God, they seem to embrace Isaac their son in very tender arms, hoping through him to extend the succession of their posterity. But in order that their hope may be held more firmly and perfectly, and be brought to fruition far more effectively, God wills that this same joy be offered to Himself by the perfect: that is [Col. 0916B], that He Himself be preferred to His gifts, so that they rejoice not so much in those gifts as in Him who bestowed them.

Thus he offers his joy to God who now rejoices not in his own gifts (2 Cor. 6), but in Him whom he loves “from a pure heart and a good conscience”; not because He confers temporal or spiritual gifts upon those who love Him, but because He is supremely good in nature—He whose radiant purity no darkened mind attains. Sacred Scripture strives to instruct the faithful toward this love of Him; but only the perfect person is capable of obeying such instruction. For the troubled activity of beginners who are still on the way does not know this obedience; rather, it belongs to the pure contemplation of perfect persons, as though already triumphant.

“Give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. 117). It is not enough, he says, for attaining the full measure of perfection if you consider God to be loved because of benefits bestowed upon us; if you follow Him because you ate of the loaves; if you give thanks because you have received His benefits. I desire you to perceive the perfection of obedience somewhat more subtly: to obey and give thanks to the Lord because He is good; not because He is good *to you*—for such thanksgiving is, as it were, mercenary—but because He is good: good, I say, in His own nature, good in Himself. It is good to cleave to that Good, so that one may love to rejoice in Him only because of Him. Therefore Abraham was told: “Offer him for a holocaust upon one of the mountains which I will show thee.”

Nothing of a holocaust is left for food; it is entirely consumed by divine fire. By this is plainly understood the offering brought to completion: when the mind of the righteous person [Col. 0916C] is so consumed by the fire of charity that, retaining for itself nothing of its own joy or love, as though forgetful of itself, it passes wholly into love of the Creator. But to one offering this love or joy in a benefit received, and laudably immersing his whole self in the hiddenness of the divine countenance, the Lord says: “Lay not thine hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him” (Gen. 22); “now I know that thou fearest God, and hast not spared thine only-begotten son for my sake.”

Know, He says, that by offering Me your joy you have obeyed Me, and yet have lost nothing of that joy. Rather, I have restored it to you far more pleasantly and far more firmly, now that you understand and love that whatever you have received, you have received from Me. For now you love Me for My own sake [Col. 0917A], and have no joy except in Me. Although you gratefully embrace My gifts, you rejoice chiefly not in them but in Me; and you do not love Me because of them, but love them because of Me.

Thus beloved Isaac is offered, yet is undoubtedly not taken away from the offerer; rather, he is preserved safe and pleasing both to God and to his father, in whose place the ram found nearby is sacrificed. For as long as the obedient man rejoiced in God’s spiritual benefits and, rendering a fitting return, loved God because of them, then—even if such joy or love was deemed commendable—there remained within it something rightly called animal. For the animal man knows how to love one whom he either perceives (1 Cor. 2) or hopes will be useful to him; but if no advantage shines forth for him, he is in no way inflamed to love.

This is indeed bestial and earthly; although it is held to be quite near [to true love], it is nevertheless so entangled in the brambles of our ignorance or weakness that its blameworthiness cannot readily be detected by everyone, or, perhaps when detected, reproved by suitable uprooting. But when the mature obedient person has come to the mountain of perfect charity and has deserved to be flooded by the ray of divine brightness, he perceives with keen sight whatever in himself had been animal; and, once that is sacrificed, he retains nothing but what is spiritual. “Abraham,” it says, “lifted up his eyes, and saw behind him a ram caught by its horns among the brambles; and, taking it, he offered it as a holocaust in place of his son” (Gen. 22).

And Scripture rightly records that the animal which Abraham sacrificed in place of Isaac was a ram [Col. 0917C], which, as you know, is the leader and forerunner not of goats, but of the harmless flock—namely, sheep or lambs. In this ram is appropriately signified that animal intention through which a man is shown to love God because of His benefits: when he sees that some things are already bestowed upon him by God and hopes that greater things will be repaid in the future. One such person seems to me to have been he who said that he had obeyed the divine commands with a view to recompense: “I have inclined my heart to perform thy justifications for ever, for the sake of recompense” (Ps. 118).

This regard for recompense, like a ram, goes before the flocks of many persons, leading them as if to pastures and guiding them toward observance of the commandments—commandments which perhaps they would not greatly observe [Col. 0917D] if they did not desire recompense for themselves. Our studies and works follow such leadership with sheep-like simplicity when, in hope of reward, they humbly obey the heavenly commands and consider no small grace to be granted them in this: that, even through love of reward, they are effectively moved to obedience.

And truly God bestows no small grace on His faithful when He sets before them the commendable fruit of obedience and so kindles them on their journey by hope and desire for it that anyone who does not strive to attain it rightly seems unworthy of them. If, perhaps through overflowing grace, they are raised to the summit of contemplation, and there behold, though in an enigma, the glory of the divine majesty [Col. 0918A], they become so intoxicated with longing for the sweetness they have tasted that, in commendable ecstasy, they are wholly carried over into it. There, with the inner eyes lifted toward Him who gives His lovers no better gift than Himself, they love Him with embraces so pure and cleansed that they love His gifts only because of Himself.

But when, in this lofty and commendable ecstasy, they are raised up, and with countenance lifted and cleansed they admire nothing except the face of God, then they who a little before had pursued the prospect of recompense with mercenary desire discover it now behind them, through a progress marked by thanksgiving; and, desiring even to cling to what lies behind, they immediately seize it manfully, and, lest any part of it remain, not only sacrifice it upon the divine altars but burn it. “Abraham,” it says, “lifted up [Col. 0918B] his eyes and saw behind him a ram caught by its horns among the brambles; taking it, he offered it as a holocaust in place of his son.”

Once the ram has been offered and wholly consumed in divine fire, Abraham rejoices that his beloved son has been restored to him. So too the mature obedient person then feels that he rejoices more pleasingly and more perfectly when he rejoices to remove his eye from self-love and loves to cleave inseparably to God alone. He loves, I say, to set aside all things for God’s sake, and to love nothing except for God’s sake; in loving Him, he considers not the benefit accruing to himself as lover, but weighs the worth and merit of the beloved—namely, that He is in Himself such and so great that, even if He did not reward, He nevertheless deserves to be loved because of the goodness that is His own.

But when a man loves God not for the sake of fruit [Col. 0918C], he nevertheless does not love Him without fruit. Rather, in a wonderful way, when he does not lay claim to the fruit of his own love, when in loving he does not ascend the mercenary chair, he consequently obtains a far greater fruit; for God pours greater gifts of His bounty into the one who loves Him freely. These gifts seem to be commended not so much through their Author as to commend themselves through Him, since every perfect person loves and embraces them not for their own sake but for His sake; and while the Author of gifts alone satisfies his longing, His gifts also become precious—gifts which their Author makes precious (*sic*).

## CHAPTER XXXVI

For when He who gives is loved perfectly, whatever He gives is loved for His sake also; and His goodness, gracious by its own merit alone, makes precious what it bestows upon those who love Him. Hence a certain wise man [Note: [Col. 0917D] Cicero] says: “For it is not so much the advantage gained through a friend as love itself that delights; and then that which proceeds from a friend becomes pleasant.”

For the wise men of the age, since they were ignorant of the love by which God is loved and were discussing that by which human beings love one another, said that the love which grows from regard for an external advantage is not sufficiently commendable, since it vanishes if gain or the hope of gain fails. Hence the aforementioned wise man says: “Most people love friends as they do cattle: they especially love those from whom [Col. 0919A] they hope to receive the greatest profit.” Thus they lack that most beautiful and most natural friendship, which ought to be sought for its own sake. And elsewhere: “If utility were the glue of friendships, a change in utility would dissolve them.”

But having examined more subtly the power of true love, these same wise men, fixing—as they supposed—their lynx-like gaze upon the truth, judged commendable that love which laudably begins from a mutual consideration of virtue, and which is strengthened in an indissoluble bond not by the impulse of poverty but by love of uprightness. Hence the same wise man says: “Let us understand that the feeling of love and the affection of goodwill arise from an evident manifestation of uprightness; for nothing is more lovable than virtue, nothing draws us more strongly to love.” And again: “I, through a certain admiration of his virtue [Col. 0919B], loved him; and he, in return, perhaps through some opinion which he held of my character, loved me; and although many and great advantages followed, the causes of our loving did not arise from hope of those advantages.”

You see that Tullius Cicero—or Laelius, whom he introduces as speaking—does not allow the pursuit of advantage to bind together perfect love, but rather the demonstrated excellence of character; and that in loving, ambition for reward is not to be preferred, but virtue is to be embraced from love of virtue. When virtue is loved chiefly in a friend, the advantage which proceeds from him consequently becomes pleasant also; and a fitting order results when a friend rejoices in a friend in such a way that virtue is preferred to utility, not utility to virtue.

But because a sudden conversion does not make anyone perfect in the love of God—for the human condition is not capable of taking in sublime things so quickly—God, rich in goodness, who does not disregard the weak and little ones, mercifully condescends to our weakness. He gives fitting nourishment to His newly planted growth, and, with the passage of time, stronger increase toward progress. Therefore, wishing to advance some people to the excellence of a better life—those whom He knows from eternity belong to His grace—and seeing that they are not yet fit for the spiritual summit, He first caresses them with a temporal benefit, so that, when they receive things by which their carnal mind is soothed, they may turn to Him who thus indulges their desires [Col. 0919C].

When they have turned to Him, God increases the gifts of His bounty, by which the infancy of their tender littleness longs for Him more and more. This littleness is not easily drawn from the bosom of misleading habit unless the guiding maturity of its educator bends down to play before it. Therefore, while they are still little children, He prudently gives them lesser things; and, as they already long for Him, He shows greater things beforehand. By such a prelude He draws them away from worldly conduct and desire, and causes Himself to be loved to some extent because of what He has bestowed and what He promises.

As the days pass, He causes them to despise the world and the world’s deceits, to cast away worldly things and rejoice in attaining spiritual things; to be more greatly inflamed by the sweetness that has affected them through heavenly promises, and to embrace God more eagerly because of these things. Thus God, desiring the salvation of the elect and piously condescending to the limitations of the weak [Col. 0920A], does not disdain to attract them to Himself through earthly benefits and strengthen them to love Him through hope of heavenly rewards.

But those whom He mercifully advances toward fuller progress, whose obedience He desires to become holier, He commands not to be reluctant to offer God whatever they rejoice in or hope for: that is, freely to prefer God to their own advantages. He commands, I say, that they love nothing before Him and nothing except for His sake; that they direct their gaze toward Him in such a way as almost to forget even themselves, and love even themselves only for His sake. Then they are found to love themselves far more holily and fruitfully when, by loving themselves for His sake, they seem to neglect themselves: not lowering their flickering eye toward their own advantage, but fixing an untiring gaze upon His sweetness [Col. 0920B], ready thus to rejoice in gifts bestowed or hoped for, only that they may rejoice to cleave to the Author of gifts.

This is the obedient love, or loving obedience, of angels; this is also that of the faithful already received into their fellowship; and it is likewise that of certain—though few—persons in the arena of this life who, while still set on earth, attain the summit of perfection and obey heavenly commands after the manner or in the love of angels. Though it cannot easily be reached, and though nature’s imperfection cannot experience it, we nevertheless ought not to measure others by our own standard, because God is able to impart to whom He wills, when He wills, and as great a grace as He wills.

Accordingly, by His grace and through the passage of days and growth in virtues, some mature and grow old in such ripeness of progress [Col. 0920C] that whatever was bestial and self-regarding in them is weakened and, like a ram, sacrificed upon the divine altars; while whatever is spiritual and divine is not delayed in being returned to God, so that they rejoice not so much in the gifts as in the Author of gifts.

This obedience, indeed, is not ours, nor that of weak persons like ourselves, whose visual power is dimmed by much dust; it belongs to those whose pupil is made clear by a precious eye-salve, and who contemplate the obscurities of the commandments with a lynx-like understanding. For there is much obscurity, or subtle obscurity, in the commandments through which the excellence of the divine majesty speaks to His faithful; in them are contained the secrets of His will, which cannot be seen through unless the inner eyes are revealed when their cloudiness has been wiped away.

Considering this, the Prophet says: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall behold [Col. 0920D] wondrous things out of thy law” (Ps. 118). Truly, unless the eyes are unveiled through the working of grace, the wonders of the divine law are not seen; for the law possesses a shadow so subtly joined to its own cloud that it deceives an eye dimmed even by a slight film. There is, indeed, great diversity among God’s commands, but no perversity can ever be found in them. For although in many of them there seems to be a kind of opposition, far be it from us to suppose that He who commands is governed either by error or by inconstancy.

Since there is in them such multiplicity that it can scarcely be comprehended, and since the apparent opposition of some must in no way be blamed, it remains to know what is irrevocably enjoined upon all human beings in every age; what is separately imposed upon a different “kind of human being” (*generari hominem*, sic; the wording is corrupt or uncertain) and condition of time; and what is at times imposed so specially or singularly upon certain persons that such a thing is heard of thereafter only once or rarely [Col. 0921A].

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Accordingly, there seem to me to be three kinds of commandments, to which God invites and advances the obedience of the elect. I think that no one has ever attained perfection of merits unless he has been granted progress in one of these kinds.

The first kind may fittingly be called unchangeable, because it is found never to vary at any time for any reason whatsoever. Since it was necessary in itself for all persons, it remains fixed and immovable before the Law, under the Law, and after the Law [Col. 0921B]. Of this kind are charity, humility, patience, gentleness, temperance, fortitude, and other virtues of this sort, which are enjoined generally upon everyone. Without them neither the righteous of the New Testament nor those of the Old attain salvation. It is evident that they are so good in themselves and so stable in that goodness that they can never in any way be otherwise or different. These virtues always have been and always will be good, and have made and will make their possessor good. Even God Himself is not to be thought ever to change them from being good, by teaching or commanding anyone to choose to depart from them.

The second kind of commandments may be called variable, because it is found to be enjoined upon a different class of people [Col. 0921C] or a different condition of time in such a way that either not every person is commanded to observe it, or the same thing is not binding at every time. Under this kind, I think, are included the commands laid upon the children of Israel concerning sacrifices or legal ceremonies, by which other nations are in no way bound by command, although some among them are known to have pleased the Lord.

Even among the people of Israel themselves, certain things were specially enjoined upon the Levites which were forbidden to the other tribes, because the former were commanded to minister at the altar and tabernacle, while the latter were excluded from the dignity of that ministry. Very many things commanded at that time to the children of Israel through Moses were not read as commanded earlier to any peoples or persons [Col. 0921D]; and when Christ came, these were not only not regarded as natural, but are very harmful if literally observed in the ancient manner.

Christ Himself also, when He came, carefully instituted certain new things in which He established the salvation of His faithful, so that no one should hope to be saved who did not faithfully take care to observe this institution. For cleansing the stains of one’s preceding life and more surely obtaining the eternal rewards to follow, He consecrated the washing of baptism and the bread and cup of the altar, and commanded His faithful thereafter to celebrate what He had consecrated. As you know, these were not actually assigned to anyone under the Law or before the Law, but were only prefigured mystically through figures and enigmas.

The third kind of commandments seems to be placed, as it were, between these two [Col. 0922A]. It cannot altogether be called unchangeable like the first, nor is it found to be assigned specially to any class of people or condition of time like the second; rather, from the beginning it has been laid generally upon all, in such a way that only He who imposed it has the right to change it. Because He Himself is read to have changed it very rarely, and because He has commanded something contrary to it according to the counsel known to Himself, this kind may properly be called scarcely changed, or scarcely changeable: its stability seems to be contradicted to some degree by God alone.

In this kind are contained the sayings: “Thou shalt not kill, thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not steal” (Exod. 20), and whatever is of this sort. These are judged to be observed before the Law, under the Law, and after the Law; those who observe them are commended by the testimony of divine Scripture [Col. 0922B], while their despisers are charged with an intolerable transgression and, unless worthy repentance should intervene, are punished with deserved condemnation.

Thus, as you know, Cain is condemned for homicide. Joseph, because he is falsely accused of having wished to commit adultery with his mistress, is consigned to prison for a long time in punishment of the crime he is alleged to have intended. The same Joseph later, when he distributed grain to the starving Egyptians and spoke more harshly to his brothers, not unmindful of their sale of him, accused them of having unlawfully returned evil to him for good, and of daring to steal from him his cup, in which he had been accustomed to practise divination.

Since these things are found unlawful before the Law and prohibited in writing under the Law through Moses, it is clear that God did not wish them to be commonly and freely practised [Col. 0922C], but wished His obedient people to be recalled from their unlawful performance. Yet because observance of such matters is commended not by the holiness or worth of the thing itself but by the authority of Him who commands, the same Author who willed to forbid these acts from being done willed, when He could, also to command that these same acts be done.

At His command, the obedient person is not only excused, but is greatly accused if he does not obey. For just as one who presumes to do what is forbidden is guilty, so one who scorns to do what is commanded deserves rebuke. Therefore God, when He willed, commanded the children of Israel, as they were about to leave Egypt, to borrow abundant silver, gold, and clothing from their neighbours and hosts, and, under cover of night, to despoil the unsuspecting Egyptians by theft; so that their wealth might pass in this way to the Israelites, and they might not pass empty-handed from Egypt into the wilderness.

“When ye go forth,” He says, “ye shall not go empty; but every woman shall ask of her neighbour and of the woman lodging in her house vessels of silver and gold and garments, and ye shall despoil the Egyptians” (Exod. 3). And much later: “The children of Israel did as the Lord had commanded Moses, and asked of the Egyptians silver and gold vessels and abundant clothing; and they despoiled the Egyptians” (Exod. 12) [Col. 0922D].

How could this deed be judged worthy of pardon if it did not rejoice in being covered by the veil of a command? How could the authority of the commander make just the plunder of one who steals secretly? Yet to some, the Egyptian’s being secretly despoiled by the people of God seems not a command but a permission: that is, the people were not ordered to do this, but were left free to act according to their own will. For they think that it does not accord with divine purity ever to command what is contrary to holiness, lest God be proclaimed the author of theft, though elsewhere He prohibits theft with such diligence.

Against this, some hold that God did command this also to the children of Israel, and yet did nothing contrary to holiness. For just as it is holy for that not to be done which He commands not to be done, so it is holy for it to be done if He happens to command that it be done. As His prohibition makes any work unlawful, so His command makes that same work lawful [Col. 0923A], provided only that a subtle eye discerns what is enjoined generally upon all and what specially upon some.

For He commands neither all persons to do everything, nor does He wish them to repeat everything that He commands once. Rather, He commands certain things to certain people in such a way that He wishes those things to be done only by them, and certain things in such a way that He wishes them to be done only once. That God not only permitted but also commanded the children of Israel to despoil the Egyptians seems clearly shown by Scripture. If anyone wishes to examine it a little more carefully, I think he will not venture long to contend against its words, lest he be charged with defending his own opinion against the truth of the matter by obstinate contention:

“The children of Israel did as the Lord had commanded Moses, and asked of the Egyptians silver and gold vessels and abundant clothing, and despoiled the Egyptians.” You see that, in despoiling the Egyptians, the children of Israel are read to have acted just as the Lord is read to have commanded them through Moses [Col. 0923B]. And doubtless, whatever the excellence of that authority commands them, they can and ought to do without violating the rule of holiness.

And what wonder is it if that most just Distributor of rewards willed to be fulfilled both the loss which the Egyptians deserved to suffer and the benefit which, perhaps, the children of Israel deserved to receive, rendering to both different rewards according to their merits? What does it matter whether divine equity willed this to be done openly or secretly, by war or by theft—divine equity in which no injustice can ever be found? Who can examine, or having examined condemn, His will, in which irreproachable equity is certainly always present?

Moreover, lest anyone thereafter flatter his own avarice by the example of this deed and, satisfying not divine obedience but his own covetousness, commit theft [Col. 0923C], God afterwards willed to command nothing of the kind even to these same children of Israel, but recalled them from theft by many words and punishments. For after the words through Moses, “Thou shalt not steal” (Exod. 20), and later through Joshua, “Take heed lest ye touch any thing of those things which are commanded” (Josh. 6), when Achaz, son of Charmi, transgressed the Lord’s command and concealed silver, gold, and a scarlet garment from the spoils of Jericho, God was angry. He not only sentenced the perpetrator of the crime to deserved death, but also struck down many of the people before their enemies in punishment for the same crime:

“An accursed thing is in the midst of thee, O Israel; thou canst not stand before thine enemies until he who is defiled by this crime is removed from thee” (Josh. 7). And Joshua said to Achaz: “Because thou hast troubled us, may the Lord trouble thee this day. And all Israel stoned him” (*ibid.*) [Col. 0924A].

From this it is clear that, although God willed the Egyptians to be despoiled by the children of Israel, He did not will theft to be practised on that example. Rather, He commanded it then at that time according to a counsel known to Himself, in such a way that later He did not command—and indeed prohibited—anything similar. So He commanded the prophet Hosea (ch. 1), first, to take a harlot as his wife, and second, an adulteress. In doing this, the prophet would have incurred a very shameful offence if he had not truly obeyed the divine will rather than his own pleasure.

He knew indeed that Moses had said: “Thou shalt not commit adultery”; and surely he is said to commit adultery who does not fear to join himself to an adulteress. So too the skilled interpreter of the Law, Paul, later says: “He who is joined to a harlot becomes one body” (1 Cor. 6). Therefore, that the prophet is joined to a harlot or adulteress and yet is not stained with the blemish of adultery is rightly attributed to the divine command [Col. 0924B], which is shown to command only what is right. For, by commanding, it changes by ineffable power into what is right that which both before and afterward is judged not right.

But the clouded eye of the heart does not readily behold this, an eye whose dimness divine brightness does not heal. Yet it appeared quite plain and clear to the Prophet, to whom and in whom the Lord spoke. For he says: “The word of the Lord which came to Hosea, and the beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea” (Hos. 1). Therefore, he beheld with cleansed eye the somewhat obscure commandment who heard the Lord speaking not only to him but also in him, understanding that whatever was commanded while He spoke was good. Hence he was deservedly called a seeing one—a prophet.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII
It is therefore likewise good when the same Lord commands killing, who most certainly also commands that no killing be done; so that, just as one who kills inhumanly against the commandment is guilty of wrongdoing, so too one who, commanded to kill, does not kill deserves rebuke. For it was said through Moses: “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX). Before and after Moses this has been holy by decree of divine justice, and has been most diligently observed by obedient persons. In those who presumed to despise it, it was punished more severely, as you know: the Lord gravely rebuked Cain when He discovered his killing—indeed, his fratricide—and vengeance following seized both him and other killers.

But although killing is not to be done, as the goodness of that supreme Author willed both to be written and observed, the authority of that same goodness made certain exceptions, so that a person may be killed without violating the rule of holiness, provided that the killer understands the commands wisely.
