For that divine authority granted that those who fight the battles of the Lord under the standards of justice may kill those who wickedly oppose them, in order to preserve the territories of faithful peoples; nor should we fear to shed the blood of barbarians. Hence in the holy Scriptures many are found greatly commended who are known to have been commendably stirred to kill enemies; while, conversely, some incurred the stain of rebuke because they languished in feeble negligence when it was time to shed blood.

Ehud, judge of the children of Israel, is commended because he boldly drew a double-edged sword against Eglon, king of Moab (Judg. III), and, relying on bold prudence, killed that exceedingly fat king. Once he had been killed, the children of Israel in turn subdued the Moabites who had oppressed them; and, after these had been subdued, they rested in peace and ease for eighty years. Saul is reproved because, although he had overcome the people of Amalek in a successful outcome of war and ought, by the Lord’s command, to have killed all of them—from man to woman, child, and nursing infant—he nevertheless, overcome by degraded cowardice, did not kill Agag their king, and did not foresee with careful prudence the evil that would arise for him from this. Samuel, wishing as it were to correct what Saul had neglected, undertook to do what he had not done. “Bring Agag king of Amalek to me,” he said; and below: “Saul struck Agag before the Lord at Gilgal” (I Sam. XV).

Divine authority also grants that, if persons acting under God’s authorization bear the office of public power and see the enactments of laws and the rights of the state being corrupted, they may, after due consideration, inflict death on criminals, lest, by sparing the wicked, they provide an increase to their wickedness and, as the wickedness of a few spreads, the commonwealth suffer harm. Phinehas the priest judged this worthy to be done when one of the children of Israel turned aside to a Midianite prostitute before all the people. Inflamed with zeal for God, Phinehas seized a dagger and hurried to enter the brothel; and he pierced both the man and the woman through their genitals (Num. XXV). No one can doubt that this vengeance pleased divine justice, since God Himself gave him favourable testimony: “Phinehas, son of Eleazar, has turned away my wrath from the children of Israel, because he was moved by my zeal” (ibid.).

Besides these exceptions—which the general permission you have heard made for those who wage just war or exercise authority in the commonwealth—there is also a particular command to kill. Though those who investigate cannot comprehend why it was given, those who are ignorant ought not to rebuke it. For God commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son to Him (Gen. XXII), so that the son whom he had received in hope of a continuing offspring he might present as an offering upon His altars. Neither He who is read to have commanded such a thing nor he who courageously obeyed the Commander—more in disposition than in outcome—was worthy of rebuke.

This command was not given generally to all fathers, but by some hidden counsel was narrowed entirely to such singularity that God issued such a command to this man alone, unless he alone, when asked, offered his son. For although Jephthah is read to have offered his daughter (Judg. XI), he is not read to have received this command from God; nor does Scripture offer clear testimony establishing that he pleased God by such a sacrifice. He could indeed have displeased God in sacrificing his daughter and nevertheless pleased Him by other righteous works; he could, while still alive, have repented of this committed crime and erased the stain of sin by fitting fruits of repentance. Yet that Jephthah pleased God, no one may lawfully doubt, since the Apostle is found to name him in the catalogue of saints (Heb. XI).

Moreover, Scripture speaks plainly concerning the command to Abraham, and the prudent reader needs no conjecture to prove it; where plain and evident proof shines forth, an argument is contemptible in proportion as it is also shown to be useless when produced. The same God also commanded that mighty Samson should kill himself and crush the Philistine revelers in his death (Judg. XVI); and so, by the collapse of the house, he both completed the obedience of the Nazirite and ended the laughing malice of the mocking people.

But if Scripture is found to make no mention of this command—for Samson is not read to have received such an order—the Apostle’s words nevertheless furnish an argument strong enough to support this judgment. For since the Apostle places him in the catalogue of saints, and since no one is holy except through keeping the commandments, it is clear that, in killing himself, he obeyed a commandment—not one formerly written on tablets, but one newly inspired inwardly. Otherwise, according to the Apostle, he could by no means have been considered holy if, in killing himself, he were held guilty of disobedience; for after death one acquires no merit for oneself by repenting, if one refused, by dying, to keep the commandment to repent.

It remains, therefore, to believe that God, who had deigned to work wonders—indeed, miracles—through him, wished secretly to inspire this new command in him: so that he who had previously subdued his enemies with a strong hand might now, through stronger obedience, give himself to death together with his enemies; and so that he who had lost his hair by sleeping in the lap of a deceitful little woman might, in dying, recover the strength of his mind rather than that of his body.

This command to kill—by which either Abraham is commanded to kill his son or Samson himself—is found to have been assigned by the divine word to them so privately and specially that neither were they permitted to resist this new and unfamiliar order, nor is anyone else found invited to anything similar. It is therefore necessary that whoever wishes to obey the heavenly commands more perfectly should diligently strive to free his feet from the stains of ignorance, so as to discover the subtlety and subtle diversity of those commands, and by fitting progress attain the breadth of mature obedience. For, as I think, one does not easily attain this unless its subtlety is first made clear: unless, when one sees more subtly the diversity of the commandments, one also discerns alike to whom each applies, whether to all or only to some.

But because we know that such things as we have said were commanded to Abraham, Samson, and Hosea are no longer commanded to persons of our own time, setting those matters aside we must take more careful concern for what Scripture’s testimony commands us to observe. This is what is commanded generally to all, from which absolutely none of the faithful is exempt: namely charity, patience, courage, and the inward beauty of other virtues of this kind, without which neither the multitude of common people, ancient or recent, nor the exalted rank of the great obtains salvation.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Each profession also has a law, as it were its own, which it is commanded to observe and under whose dominion it must serve especially. For that law has a certain prescribed definiteness, outside or against which uprightness does not easily stand. Every class of the faithful is divided into laity and clergy; among the laity, once subdivided, one order consists of farmers and another of soldiers; among the clergy, one is the humility of monks and another the dignity of clerics.

Whatever one’s profession, each must know more certainly what truth declares fitting to that profession, so that he may not presume in swollen frivolity to overstep its recognized boundaries, but may strive, with bowed neck, to obey its prescribed laws. Furthermore, one must attend more carefully to who ought duly to be set over whom and who ought to be placed under a superior, so that, when each knows his own instructor, he may show himself a devoted hearer in all things.

Thus Christ gathered the Church from the four quarters of the world; thus, solicitous for our salvation, He ordered her once gathered, placing the apostles, who were worthier to preside, at the head, and bending the remaining multitude to obedience to them. Yet lest He should seem to have given this pre-eminence to the Apostles alone, and lest useful order should deserve to be confused when they were gone, He also appointed seventy-two other disciples, whom He sent into every place where He Himself was about to come, so that in the apostolic office—indeed, in His own office—they might everywhere among the nations preach the word of life and, by saving teaching, form the chosen for the catholic faith.

That their teaching might be esteemed by their hearers, and that He who sent them might truly be believed to speak in them or through them, He said to them: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X). It is evident, therefore, that those whom God wished to ordain as shepherds and teachers to govern the people, and to whom He entrusted the honour of presiding—indeed, the labour of training those subject to them—must not be despised by those same subjects with unbent necks. Rather, they must be heard with fear and reverence as heralds of the Judge, because whatever honour is conferred upon, or disgrace inflicted upon, the envoy unquestionably rebounds upon the sender.

But although reverence is due to those sent, both the Apostles and their successors, and although their despiser deserves no slight rebuke, those are bound by stricter bonds of obedience who are gathered in the furnace of discipline to live according to a rule: those who, renouncing the world, choose to possess nothing of their own and, imitating the apostolic life, possess all things in common. Having by their own choice selected one father for themselves from among many, and having submitted their necks voluntarily to his command, they must indeed not listen to him at all when he commands against God, but must obey him in everything he commands according to God.

His commands are said to be according to God if they do not oppose God’s commands; and, finally, if in them is preserved with stable consistency the rule which both he and his subject profess—whether Augustine’s canonical rule or Benedict’s monastic rule. For when a subject is warned by a superior to observe this or that rule, and promises obedience to him according to it, the superior ought not thereafter, by commanding otherwise, to override this vow; nor is the subject compelled to obey one who commands otherwise, unless the necessity is so great that the matter cannot be omitted without detriment to charity.

For the regular tradition, established by the vigilant care of its author and promulgated to preserve the order of charity among brethren, is not subject to the personal will of any successor for alteration; rather, it serves only that charity for whose sake it was promulgated. If, then, the successor should at some point see that what the former man carefully wished to promulgate for nurturing the order of charity conflicts with ordered charity, he may temper it—not by dissolving it, but by prudent discernment—and faithfully administer it, not under the slippery impulse of his own will but under the impulse of devoted charity. But if no reasonable necessity compels the administrator, he undoubtedly does not infringe a rule once undertaken without guilt; rather, both he and the subject deserve to be charged with transgression if either, by commanding or by acting, does not fear to abandon its tradition.

For as both have vowed to keep the rule, so both must fulfil their vow by keeping it, and so apply themselves to the holiness they have proposed that their will may be subject to the rule, not the rule to their will. Otherwise, someone would promise in vain to live according to the rule if he did not diligently observe its prescriptions; or if a superior, changing the rule without the pressure of reasonable necessity, wished everything to be done according to his own will. In vain, I say, would a rule be set before those professing religious life as a common standard, if the superior’s will were preferred to the rule; for that will itself would then become the rule, since life would be conducted according to it rather than according to the rule.

Therefore one who proposed to profess the regular life under a superior ought to promise obedience not according to the rule but according to that superior’s will, so that thereafter he might be commanded not by rule, not by reason, but by will—according to the satirist’s saying:

> Thus I will, thus I command; let my will stand in place of reason.

But our Augustine, who wrote the Rule for clerics, giving superiors and subjects an appropriate distinction of precepts, granted neither party freedom for personal will, but imposed the yoke of the rule, as it seems, upon superiors as well as subjects. For in that same rule, after he had instructed both superiors and subjects in many ways, offering now counsels common to both and now warnings proper to each, he finally bound all alike by one precept, by which he indiscriminately tied them to the prescribed rule:

> “But so that you may be able to look at yourselves in this little book as in a mirror, lest through forgetfulness you neglect anything, let it be read to you once a week. And wherever any of you find yourselves doing what is written, give thanks to the Lord, the giver of all good things. But wherever any of you sees that something is lacking in himself, let him grieve for the past and beware for the future.”

Since he wishes none of what he wrote to be neglected even through forgetfulness, and therefore commands that the little book itself be read once a week to everyone; and since, wherever either superior or subject sees something lacking in himself, he wishes him to grieve for the past and take more careful precaution for the future, it is clear that he subjected not the rule to will, but will to the rule, and granted neither of them voluntary liberty against the rule.

Therefore all who have undertaken the Rule must keep it and, according to it, render their vows to God, which they have articulated with their own lips. None of them may presume to overstep it, since according to it the superior has vowed to command and the subject to obey. As was said above, none of them relaxes the strictness of this vow or permissibly changes or omits the precepts of the rule—unless perhaps the person entrusted to preside in the position of dispenser sees a reasonable necessity approaching. Then he is found to be not a condemner of the rule through self-will, but the most faithful administrator of its precepts through necessity: keeping them as long as he sees that they serve charity and salvation, and omitting or relaxing them when he knows that they truly conflict with these.

## CHAPTER XL

The things we know to be promulgated directly by God cannot be relaxed by the prudence of an administrator. “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX), and every similar command, are delivered to us by divine tradition in such a way as to admit no human dispensation whatsoever. But the things we know to have been beneficially ordered by a human being according to his own will, so that charity may be fostered among brethren and, once fostered, more strongly preserved—things which before a vow people are not compelled to undertake, though after the vow they become necessary—may, it is said, be omitted or relaxed by that person or his representative, but only when reasonable necessity presses. For although they arise from his will, necessity is not bound by law.

The faithful administrator is therefore one who, though he surpasses those entrusted to him in office and dignity, does not withdraw from the Rule through contempt or injury; nor does he wish his own people to obey him in such a way that they neglect to preserve the truth of the common Rule. Likewise, the subject is said to be faithfully obedient when, in his obedience, he looks to what pleases God, and strives to carry out what a human being commands him in such a way that he does not thereby become a persecutor of heavenly precepts.

For some, not knowing—or rather despising—the truth of the divine will, which is especially necessary to both subjects and superiors by the testimony of the Scriptures, take such pleasure in serving the wills of superiors that they are found to obey not so much God as human beings (Acts V). Perhaps because they see that their masters have itching ears, becoming angry at harsh words, even truthful ones, while rejoicing in flattering words, even deceitful ones, they too are deformed by a heavy rust as they conform their conduct with anxious care to such masters.

Therefore, setting aside serious matters, which they know find no welcome place with such persons, they present flatteries, to which they perceive their masters cling somewhat more tenaciously. By this traffic, superiors become accustomed to command nothing unless it is pleasing and agreeable, and subjects do not fail to respond with a corresponding obedience. And while, through such concord, master and disciple conform themselves mutually to one another, they commend one another considerably by welcome testimony: the disciple declares such a master to be a discerning instructor, and the instructor calls the disciple a most obedient hearer.

On the contrary, a truly obedient person renders obedience to a superior because he judges that the superior’s command pleases the Creator. He does not choose to please a human being by offending God, nor, while he placates a human being, does he carelessly displease God. For he knows that if he strove to please his superior with flattering words—by which God is unquestionably said to be gravely offended—he would thereby be considered a servant not of God but of a human being. This the apostolic pronouncement expressly prohibits to the Corinthians: “You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings” (I Cor. VII).

The Apostle wishes those to be understood as slaves of human beings who, when they see their masters more than properly inclined toward empty flattery, do not oppose the manly constancy of just severity, but place themselves beneath their masters’ lax minds in soft complaisance. While they strive to soothe their itching ears with agreeable words and obey their affections, not spiritual but carnal, it is clear that they serve not God but a human being; not righteousness but sin; and by degraded servitude they come to death. Hence he says also to the Romans: “Do you not know that, to whom you offer yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey—either of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?” (Rom. VI).

Because Christ redeemed us from that death at the price of His own death, and released us from the chains of our slavery into the freedom of His Spirit, obedience and service must be rendered to Him—that is, the obedient person ought to attend to His good pleasure, not to the carnal desire of a human being. “You were bought at a price,” he says; “do not become slaves of human beings” (I Cor. VII). Whose servants, then? The same writer says to the Colossians: “Serve the Lord Christ” (Col. III).

And lest he should seem by this saying to remove us altogether from obedience to human beings, as though he wished us to serve Christ in such a way that we should not also render obedience to human beings, he had shortly before stated: “Children, obey your parents in all things” (Eph. VI). Therefore children ought in all things to obey their parents—which is nothing other than to serve through obedience. And lest the Apostle perhaps be thought inconsistent with himself, he adds what removes such an impression. For after saying, “Children, obey your parents in all things,” he adds, “in the Lord” (ibid.), so that children’s obedience may be in the Lord, not against the Lord; and so that they may serve not human beings—that is, their empty and human affections—but Christ the Lord.

Speaking also to the Ephesians, he says: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord; for this is just” (ibid.). Thus, as has been said, not against the Lord but in the Lord; for this is just. No one, however, doubts that every sin truly opposes the Lord, and that whoever gives it free rein acts against the Lord. Nor does merely the open instrument of cutting persecution displease the Lord; perhaps equally displeasing is the soft caress of deceitful service. For often one whom clamorous persecution did not crush has been weakly softened by creeping flattery; and one who did not bend even slightly beneath thundering cruelty has inclined his itching little ear beneath hissing deception.

The Prophet, rightly perceiving such a pestilence of a smooth, harmful, deceiving tongue, dripping from the harlot’s lips like a poisonous honeycomb, curses it and anxiously prays that it be removed from him: “Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Ps. CXL). The sinner’s oil is the speech of a flatterer, fashioned and uttered according to the pleasure of one whose ears itch. When that person’s head—that is, the inner mind—is made fat by it, the whole body of works is burdened by the harmful outpouring.

The Prophet therefore prays that serpentine softness may not pour itself into his heart by its slippery course, nor pour harmful poison over works of virtue; and that the itch for listening may harm not himself alone, but may also bring to his associates a ready ruin through compliance. For he understands that this plague obtains no small claim among subjects as they strive to please their superiors with gracious speech, and that among superiors very few can be found who do not delight to be obeyed with favourable compliance.

Hence canonical Scripture declares more plainly how great a ruin often follows. It says that Joash king of Judah came to idolatry, but only after his princes had softened him with flattering observances: “The princes of Judah entered,” it says, “and worshiped the king; and, softened by their observances, he consented to them” (II Chron. XXIV). Scripture adds the result for which both they wished to soften the king and the king to agree with those softening him: “And they abandoned the temple of the Lord God of their fathers, and served groves and carved images” (ibid.).

You see what fountain and origin of evil were the smooth tongue of flatterers and the itching of ears; and how, because of the accepted soothing of deceitful service, both king and people incurred the ruin of idolatry. They advanced so far from bad to worse that they neither returned to the God whom they had forsaken nor heard the prophets sent to them by the Lord. Indeed, at the king’s command the people presumed to stone the prophet Zechariah because he had endeavoured with free speech to call them back from idolatry: “He sent prophets to them,” it says, “that they might return to the Lord; but they would not hear those who testified to them. They gathered together against him, cast stones at him at the king’s command, and killed him” (ibid.).

Therefore, because, according to a comic poet, truth produces hatred and compliance friends, few are willing for truth’s sake to endure the hatred of their superiors. Many hasten to please them by flattering compliance, choosing, of course, to become their intimates and friends rather than, by speaking unwelcome truth, their enemies when they cannot endure it. And because scarcely another Peter is found who patiently endures Paul’s rebuke (Gal. II), scarcely anyone like Paul is found who confidently rebukes Peter. Instead, we wish subjects to devote themselves to our holiness in such a way that they do not prefer unwelcome truth to our will.

Yet this is not the obedience that ought to be required by superiors or rendered to them when required; rather, it is that obedience whose integrity does not endure to be disfigured by a patch sewn on, whose truth does not know how to flatter with smooth words. Since every religious person is commanded to obey superiors in order that by the merit of obedience he may obtain divine grace, it is certain that it is in no way expedient for either superiors or subjects to strive, whether by commanding or complying, to attain anything else.

But if a superior, in commanding, loves the truth of the rule and chooses diligently not his own will but God’s, he must not be rejected as a human being like ourselves, but heard as God, whose office he holds. Although we cannot compel those who have vowed nothing other than to observe the proposed rule to advance beyond it by the law of that vow, nevertheless one who wishes to be considered perfectly obedient ought not to be confined within the narrow limits of his vow. Rather, as charity is more fully extended within him, he should be advanced to greater things by free will.

For the author of the Rule, though he did not wish us to dare anything against it, did not prohibit our doing many things beyond it. Thus he wished regular observances to be observed, but did not wish superabundance to be prohibited. While a certain necessity of the vow already compels us to those observances, the sweetness of free charity leads us to this superabundance. Nor is it a greater merit that the ardour of charity freely makes us obey than that the Rule we have undertaken and vowed does not permit us to transgress it.

The Apostle appears to have indicated this obedience when, speaking of Onesimus, he commended his disciple Philemon: “Confident in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say” (Philem. XXI). Therefore, beyond what the author of the rule has commended to us, beyond the precepts for living which he has expressly promulgated for us, a good obedient person does not refuse to act. He is unwilling, as a miserly fulfiller, to be confined by the bounds of a vow; rather, breaking forth into a kind of plain of boundless generosity, he readily undertakes in charity whatever is commanded.

For whatever a human being commands in God’s stead, provided that it is not contrary to Him and that it is clear neither to conflict with the authentic commands of superiors nor to depart from the Rule of right living, the subject ought not dispute against it merely because it is sudden and perhaps unfamiliar, but accept it with the ear of faith as a divine oracle.

## CHAPTER XLI
Thus the sons of Jonadab heard their father’s severe and unusual command, and held fast to what they had heard with unbending constancy: he commanded them henceforth neither to taste wine nor to live in houses, but in tents. Although they knew that God had imposed nothing of the kind upon them, they nevertheless kept their father’s prohibition unshaken, knowing that children ought to obey their parents—unless, perhaps, it is evident that their parents’ command conflicts with God.

And since those who rightly advance from virtue to virtue [Col. 0933A] do not endure to be confined within a narrow and debased slavery, these men, remembered as obedient, are fittingly called sons of Jonadab. *Jonadab* means “willing” or “spontaneous.” The sons of the willing, therefore, are those who refuse to be restricted by the prescribed limits of a vow, but are enlarged in a freer field by spontaneous affection: they strive not only to fulfil the things God commands, but also, no less, the commands of the person who is known to hold the ministry of commanding. For in the one to whom He chose to entrust His own office or ministry, He declared that He Himself is both despised and heard. Thus a person is not to be heard on account of his ministry if he commands against God; nor, because he is a human being, is he to be scorned if he commands in accordance with God.

For it befits a hearer, if he wishes perfectly to practise judgment and justice, not to be overborne by either love or hatred [Col. 0933B]: neither may he presume, because of a harmful attachment to his instructor, to do anything against the Creator’s righteousness; nor may he disregard the command of one whom he sees to be a man because of hatred or contempt for him, when that person is manifestly God’s representative in commanding what is right. This is most clearly shown in the Gospel, where the Lord condemns not the Pharisees’ words but their deeds: “Do what they say,” he says, “but do not do what they do; for they say, and do not do” (Matt. XXV).

“I wish,” he says, “that you should utterly condemn what they do badly, yet embrace with the broad scope of obedience what they say well. For their deeds draw their followers into ruin, while their speech proclaims the discipline of the rule. Therefore, although you may perhaps hate them—or rather, their deeds [Col. 0933C]—do not on that account despise anything they rightly command. Rather, leave to them, as their own, that which is discordant in their conduct; and ascribe to me, because it is mine, that which agrees with me in their words.”

But it must be understood that this is the obedience of the perfect: to attend not to the character of the person commanding, but to the weight of the commands. Among God’s people, however, there is a greater number of the weak, and they do not readily obey their superiors’ admonitions if the life of those offering the admonitions is found unjust or hateful. Therefore the Lord—who does not wish the gravest punishment to be inflicted upon those who trouble his little ones by causing scandal—wishing to provide not only for subjects but also for prelates, is found to have carefully forewarned those same prelates to make themselves worthy and imitable to their inferiors. “Let your light shine,” he says, “before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

He who said in Luke, “Whoever hears you hears me” (Luke X), also said in Matthew, “Let your light shine before people” (Matt. V), so that by the former saying he might instruct subjects to obey their superiors, and by the latter invite prelates to make themselves imitable. For he knew that a subject does not readily obey a superior if the commanding person’s life does not first set an imitable example. Nor can anyone readily imitate another unless the one proposed for imitation makes every effort to be loved: so that he may appear righteous not only before the divine gaze, but may also show himself lovable and welcome to his brothers. For just as the eyes turn with an eager gaze toward what is loved [Col. 0934A], so they turn away from what is not loved; and no one can readily show himself a follower of one whom he does not even wish to see.

Therefore the Apostle, wishing love to be preserved between fathers and children, without which a child cannot imitate his father, after saying, “Children, obey your parents in everything in the Lord” (Eph. VI), immediately added: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger” (ibid.). Since he saw that it was not beneficial for children to be released by a loose bond of life and, relying upon harmful liberty, to wander through the byways of conduct, with fatherly care he fixed necessary boundaries for them and bound them with the fetter of saving obedience. “Children,” he says, “obey your parents in everything in the Lord; for this is pleasing” (ibid.).

But lest fathers should grow proud in this arrangement with a presumptuous spirit, and, taking occasion from the piety granted them, rage freely against their children, he also instructed them with fitting admonitions; and, recalling them from the latitude of their own will, bound them in tight fetters. “Fathers,” he says, “do not provoke your children to anger, lest they become faint-hearted” (ibid.) [Col. 0934B]. “Do not pour into them the poison of anger, when you ought to anoint them with the welcome oil of love. Do not provoke them to any vice, when you ought to call them back from every vice. Do not inflict an unwelcome and destructive injury upon children hastening with tender step toward the vision of God; lest those who ought to obey your commands with filial affection be driven by your violence to recoil from that very obedience.”

For a good father, not lifted up by the eminence of authority bestowed upon him, but turning over and over in his mind the burden of care imposed upon him, does not breathe threats upon the trembling necks of those subject to him; rather, he can scarcely breathe while he frequently sighs under grave concern for his children [Col. 0934C]. A good father prepares for his children no snare and no ruin, but gives them saving instruction, not so much by words as by conduct. He tempers necessary discipline with such weight and measure that he joins the serpent’s shrewdness to the dove’s gentleness. The former prudently corrects the twisting crookedness of vices; the latter gently draws to itself the yielding tenderness of minds. He corrects, I say, lest they flow away—or perhaps overflow—with no barrier to restrain them; but he draws them, lest they fail and recoil from the path under an intolerably harsh uproar.

By the former a father instils reverence and fear in his children; by the latter [Col. 0934D] he suggests patience and love: lest love without fear make them negligent, or fear without love make them hate—which is more grievous. Hence Paul, when instructing the Philippians, said, “Whatever things are holy,” and immediately added, “Whatever things are lovable, think on these” (Phil. IV). Thus he indicates that holiness is to be acquired and retained in such a way that charity must necessarily be joined to it.

And lest he seem to admonish others concerning what he himself perhaps either could not or would not fulfil, he consequently added: “What you have learned and seen and heard in me” (ibid.). Speaking also to the Thessalonians on this point, he briefly instructs prelates, saying: “Reprove the unruly, comfort the faint-hearted” (1 Thess. V). By these words he clearly gives [Col. 0935A] us to understand that correction does not sufficiently produce holiness in subjects unless consolation also builds charity in them. For the faint-hearted spirit grows weary under the burden of correction unless it is revived by the welcome benefit of consolation.

Therefore the Apostle does not wish a father to be merely feared by his children, lest fear lapse into hatred; rather, he wishes him to be so feared that he is loved still more, because ready obedience accompanies love. “Give no offence,” he says, “to the Church of God, just as I please everyone in everything, seeking not what is useful to me, but what is useful to the many, that they may be saved” (1 Cor. X). He sees that one does not effect the salvation of those subject to him with sufficient efficacy if he does not take care and strive to be loved with tender affection; nor can his admonitions rightly please if the admonisher happens to displease his hearers.

Our Augustine, clothed in this understanding, as though placing fear and love together in a balance, wishes fear to have the lesser weight, so that when a subject obeys his prelate with fear and love, the love of that same prelate may outweigh the fear in a just and salutary order. For, speaking of a prelate, he says: “Although both are necessary, yet he should desire to be loved by you more than feared.” Therefore, since a prelate ought both to be feared and loved by his subjects, he is plainly commanded carefully to seek to be loved more; and assuredly he is not deemed sufficiently free from fault if, so far as lies in him, the person who fears him does not love him more [Col. 0935B]. For unless he is loved, he will not go before the subject people with an admired footprint, nor will that people gladly come out to behold him, since hateful justice does not sufficiently offer itself as worthy to be seen, and scarcely anyone rejoices to look upon it for imitation.

## CHAPTER XLII

This, it seems, is why Christ commended John, son of Zechariah, in the Gospel, and declared the crowds of ordinary people commendable: John knew how to make himself pleasing not only to God but also to people, and people streamed to him from every side, going out to learn from him how to live. “John,” he says, “began to say to the crowds concerning John: ‘What did you go out into the wilderness to see?’” (Luke VII).

By the name “crowds” are suitably denoted those who, though held for some time in the harmful quiet of sins, are at last stirred by divine fear—painfully indeed, but healthfully—and are driven out by the mighty hand of divine shaking [Col. 0935D]. Of such people the prophet says: “You have shaken the earth and troubled it; heal its breaches, for it has been shaken” (Ps. LIX). A good disturbance, a good breaking, a good shaking, when a people complacently at rest in evil is moved to repentance; and when God’s abundant goodness graciously has mercy upon them once they have been stirred, so that, rejecting the enticement of their former peace, they may now love Christ who sustains them and may be nourished by Christ through the life-giving benefit of spiritual food: “I have compassion on the crowd,” he says, “because they have now remained with me three days and have nothing to eat” (Mark VIII).

When such a crowd has been awakened by the divine regard and driven, by the onset of unfamiliar fear, from the welcome softness of bodily passions, it goes out in a love of novelty to see, understanding that the gift of grace is to be preferred to its former pursuits [Col. 0936A]. Thus Abraham too was told: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. XII), that we may know we ought not to linger in things that are carnally ours, but to migrate to spiritual things through a religious departure. Of this Isaiah says: “Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from its midst” (Isa. LII).

A good departure is that by which one leaves the midst of unclean wickedness; by which one leaves the tomb of deadly oldness; by which Lazarus does not delay to come out at the voice of the Lord who calls (John XII), and is released from the bands of sins by the deeds of the attendants. A good departure, I say, is one by which a person goes out from the midst of shamefulness, not one by which he comes into the midst of shamefulness; good is the departure by which a weaker person goes out to imitate the stronger, not that by which he goes out, with erring intention, to see those worse than himself [Col. 0936B].

Thus Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, though she would have been better kept in the inner chamber of her father’s house (Gen. XXXIV), went out to see the women of that region. When Shechem, son of Hamor, saw her go out, he desired the virgin; and, having taken away the flower of her virginity, he soothed her grief with caresses. That most wicked Cain, having first contemplated murder within himself (Gen. IV), went out into the field to carry it out in deed. After committing it, he declares that he is driven from the face of the earth and hidden from the divine presence, and by the merit of his sin wanders as a fugitive upon the earth.

Since, therefore, departure is shown to be both good and contrary to the good, Christ rightly asks the crowds, as he speaks to them, about their departure—not that he might learn through their answers what he did not know before, but that he might show us what he knew as he questioned them. Having said, “What did you go out into the wilderness to see?” he himself answered his own inquiry: “A reed shaken by the wind” (Luke VII) [Col. 0936C].

If this is uttered as a simple statement, nothing needs to be supplied in thought; but if interrogatively, one must supply “truly,” or “indeed,” or “it is so,” or something of that sort. “What,” he says, “did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” Truly, it is so. “Truly,” he says, “you went out to see a reed, which you found not in the market or street but in the quiet of solitude. For the bustling street of public life is occupied by the multitude of sinners, while a watery and trackless solitude is congenial to the reed.”

Solitude, or wilderness, is the perfection of a better life, in which the wantonness of young men, choruses of maidens, and citizens’ disputes have no place; rather, they are condemned both in word and conduct. Nor does the wandering, noisy multitude of the many dwell there; neither the odours of flesh and fleshly things nor the sickness of vices contaminates it. It is soothed not by a harsh north wind but by the whisper of a gentler breeze, and is bathed in the welcome murmuring of a purer stream—water, I say, which washes away the stains of conduct without suffering harm itself, and leaps up with gracious force into eternal life [Col. 0936D].

Such perfection is rightly represented by the name “wilderness,” because many abandon it through weakness or negligence; indeed, so few effectively seek it that its narrow path is scarcely worn even lightly by them. David declares that he fled to this wilderness, and we read that there he was safe from the attack of enemies: “Behold,” he says, “I fled far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. LIV). For when Saul pursued him, David dwelt as an exile on the mountain in the wilderness of Ziph, and by the protection of the place escaped the pursuer’s malice. The solitude friendly to fugitives enabled him not to be conquered, though the presumed strength of resistance had not enabled him to conquer. “David,” it says, “remained in the wilderness in very secure places; and he remained in the wilderness of Ziph, on the shady mountain” (1 Sam. XXIII) [Col. 0937A].

*Saul* means “asked for” or “request.” By him the world lying in wickedness appears suitably to be signified: in its desire you see the brutish multitude of the people running unchecked, unwilling to be restrained by the humble teaching of righteous Samuel and loving to roam across the plains under royal power. *Ziph* means “flower.” Thus David is a good fugitive: he hastened to flee the world that persecutes the saints, and, fleeing, hid upon the mountain in the wilderness of Ziph, so that the lofty height of spiritual progress might fortify the fugitive, and the flowering beauty of that height might delight him once fortified.

“On the mountain,” it says, “in the wilderness of Ziph, on the shady mountain.” This solitary, flowering, shady mountain is the loftiness of the holy Scriptures, to which the righteous man hastens to transfer himself when he refuses, with a servile neck, to bear the threats of worldly assaults [Col. 0937B]. Scripture is called a mountain because of the dignity of its lofty excellence; solitary because of the rarity of those who seek it; flowering because of the flourishing beauty of conduct or virtues that it contains; shady because of the dense obscurity of spiritual understanding.

Of it Habakkuk says: “God will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran” (Hab. III), which another translation gives as: “from a shadowy and thickly wooded mountain.” And Haggai says: “Go up to the mountain, bring wood, build the house” (Hag. I). Each wise person indeed goes up to the mountain when, fleeing from the face of the persecuting world, he grasps the height of Scripture; when he stretches himself beneath its shade upon flowering grass for refreshment and defends himself under its protection from the injury of sun or heat. He carries wood and builds a house when he takes from the Scriptures the examples of preceding saints and applies them to his own use with prudent skill, so as both to remove from his conduct the beast-like disgrace of nakedness and to build within himself a spiritual house for God [Col. 0937C].

“David departed from the mountain in the wilderness of Ziph,” it says, “and remained in the wilderness of Maon. And, departing from the wilderness of Maon, he remained in the wilderness of En-gedi” (1 Sam. XXIV). This change of places indicates not a timid despair of remaining, but progress in flight. For although the righteous man rejoices that he has fled to the fortified places of solitude, so long as anything is lacking he does not yet think he has made enough progress.

“Thus David remained in the wilderness of Maon.” *Maon* means “dwelling-place.” The good fugitive rejoices not only to hasten to the height of the wilderness and eagerly to taste in advance its flowering sweetness; but with unremitting spirit he chooses to dwell there, stretched toward what lies before and never returning at all to what lies behind (Phil. III). “Here,” he says, “will I dwell, for I have chosen her” (Ps. CXXXI).

He dwells in wilderness or solitude who loves to meditate upon knowledge of the Scriptures, to live amid their commands with due meditation, to be removed from the contradiction of tongues and the disturbance of people, and to delight in peace and leisure for the sake of progress [Col. 0938A]. The Israelite people did not rejoice to dwell in the wilderness, for in a tumultuous spirit they returned to the dark allurements of Egypt, were burdened by distaste for the solitude they had found, and lived there in body while dwelling in Egypt in spirit.

“David departed from the wilderness of Maon and remained in the wilderness of En-gedi.” *En-gedi* means “spring of the kid,” and by it baptism is rightly understood: by baptism the humble sinner is washed, who, though advancing from virtue to virtue toward the summit of perfection, nevertheless, according to Christ’s counsel, declares himself an unprofitable servant. “When you have done all good things,” he says, “say: ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke XVII).

There is a baptism of washing, a baptism of repentance, a baptism of tears, a baptism which not only washes the unclean sinner but makes the washed person a fervent lover. For the more fully one is whitened by sprinkling with humble hyssop, the more abundantly and fruitfully one is inflamed to love [Col. 0938B]. Since very few are baptized with this baptism, they are said, as it were, to remain in the wilderness, because the purity of a more perfect life is a kind of solitude in which the noisy multitude of the imperfect does not dwell.

## CHAPTER XLIII

In this solitude dwelt John, of whom we have spoken above. By the merits of his virtues he occupied the citadel of purity; with figurative baptism he baptized very many who came to him [Col. 0938C], and invited them, by both word and conduct, to fruits worthy of repentance. Those whose desire was stirred by his reputation and who wished to receive from him a pattern of life rightly streamed together to see him, hastening to leave their own places in such a way as both to see him and, having seen him, gladly to obey.

“What did you go out into the wilderness to see?” he says (Luke VII). He rightly asks what they went out to see, for it matters greatly what one sees. There is a harmful vision, and there is also a useful one. Harmful is the vision when the unwary eye roams abroad and the mind of the person seeing is stirred to sin: the eye ranges through useless things, released in harmful freedom, while the mind seethes, enveloped in carnal desires. Of such seeing the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks upon a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her” (Matt. V).

Job indicates that he had kept this vision far from himself when he says: “I made a covenant with my eyes, not to think upon a virgin” (Job XXXI). Against it the Prophet prays: “Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity” (Ps. CXVIII) [Col. 0938D]. Useful vision, however, occurs when the simple eye looks upon outward things in such a way that the inward mind is stirred to praise the Creator; when, as the former opens with eager attention for sight, the latter is kindled for devotion as though by the blast of bellows.

The Prophet seems to indicate this when he says: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (ibid.). God is said to unveil a person’s eyes when that person more attentively contemplates God’s wonders: when, setting earthly things aside, he cannot admire enough God’s saints as they think upon heavenly things [Col. 0939A]; finally, when he both sees them as wonderful and, seeing them, loves to imitate them. “I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. VIII). By “heavens” he wishes the saints to be understood, stretching toward what lies before by the working of spiritual grace. One is said to see them when he rejoices in their progress and, stirred by their example, is commendably inflamed to imitate them.

For the vision by which we see the righteous confers upon us no little grace and no small progress, when we desire both to imitate their righteousness and to be aided by richer merits. Christ, I think, foresaw this progress when he urged two disciples in the Gospel to see where he lived. When they said, “Rabbi, where do you live?” he replied: “Come and see” (John I). He would by no means have urged them to see if this kind of vision bore no fruit, or if what the prudent eye found useful outwardly did not pass into the progress of the inner mind [Col. 0939B].

Likewise Philip, announcing Christ to Nathanael, said: “We have found Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth, whom Moses wrote of in the Law and the Prophets.” When Nathanael replied, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Philip added: “Come and see” (ibid.). Philip saw that this vision lacked no great fruit when the wisely inquisitive eye delights to have a righteous person before it; when, rejecting the harmful vanity of the world, it loves inwardly the holiness of whatever righteous person it sees outwardly.

The Lord therefore rightly asks what they went out to see, and, showing that he knew what he asked, does not delay to answer his own question: “A reed shaken by the wind?” (Luke VII). “I ask,” he says, “what you went out to see, and I do not wish you to be unaware of what you saw: for he whom your curiosity was commendably stirred to see is like a reed shaken by the wind.”

But if the words “a reed shaken by the wind” are read as a question, “truly,” “indeed,” or something similar must be understood—something which answers the question affirmatively, so that when the explicit question is presented, the hidden answer of the implied affirmation follows: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” “Truly, truly,” he says, “it is so: truly you went out into the wilderness to see a reed, because it is plain that the one who strives to instruct his hearers through the office of preaching performs the function of a reed” [Col. 0939C].

A reed is a pen. The Hebrews customarily wrote with a reed or pen, tracing lasting marks upon thin parchments, so that what lay hidden in the deep learning of the more educated might, through the service of the pen, pass into the knowledge of others. Therefore an eloquent preacher is not unfittingly called a pen or reed: through his preaching the rule by which we ought to live is shown to us; through him God writes his laws in our ears; by his tongue and speech God so sets before us the way of righteousness that no one at all may now doubt, if he is willing humbly to incline his ear to the speaker.

Hence the Prophet says: “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Ps. XLIV). Our scribe is God; our scribe is the Holy Spirit [Col. 0940A], whose pen is the prophetic tongue. Through it he sets forth for us the rectitude of spiritual life, when he moves and directs that tongue to speak as a scribe moves a pen or reed to write. This scribe is said to write swiftly because his swiftness is restrained by no barrier: whenever he chooses to take up a pen or reed for himself, nothing can prevail against his will. Hence elsewhere: “His word runs swiftly” (Ps. CXLVII).

His word runs swiftly—works effectively—when this pen or reed is moved by the impulse of the mighty Spirit; when he pours into it the grace of spiritual knowledge and a sick conscience does not blunt the edge of that knowledge; when that stronger south wind, the dispeller of the harsh north wind, blows through it. Of this south wind, or to it, the true wisdom of Solomon speaks: “Arise, north wind; come, south wind; blow through my garden” (Song IV).

By the mighty breathing of this south wind Solomon’s garden is blown through, and the reed or pen is moved by a favourable wind, when suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a violent rushing wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting (Acts II), so that thereafter they dared to speak the word boldly before rulers and authorities; indeed, fervent in spirit, they could no longer refrain from speaking what they had heard and seen [Col. 0940B].

Thus John too is not unfittingly called a reed, being moved by the mighty breath of the divine Spirit, so that, setting an end to silence, he lovingly exhorted the crowds coming to him to repentance; indeed, he did not fear freely to condemn Herod’s adultery in rebuke. If a wind of this kind had not driven John, placed as he was among a brood of vipers, he would either have kept silence or his speech would not have had commendable power. For all who are not led by God’s Spirit, though children of the world, either do not speak against that same world at all or speak vainly.

“For all who are led by the Spirit of God,” says the Apostle, “are children of God” (Rom. VIII). But God’s children do not know how to conform themselves to this world; rather, with solicitous affection they reform others, deformed as they are, into due beauty. They are bent neither by the threats of opponents nor by the flatteries of sycophants, because good reeds are strengthened by the action of a commendable wind [Col. 0940C].

But a reed which is not moved by the breath of a mighty spirit breaks when someone leans upon it, and pierces the hand of the person leaning on it. So if anyone presumes to be a teacher without the divine Spirit moving him, he is found to harm his hearers rather than benefit them. John is therefore rightly called a reed shaken by the wind: his tongue was so urged by the impulse of the divine Spirit that, though he chose to live in the wilderness far from the tumult of the cities, he could not hide there beneath the shadow of harmful silence. Rather, like a roaring lion and menacingly growling, as the tongue of a swiftly writing scribe, as the voice of one crying out, and as the herald of the Judge, he thundered and roused sluggish peoples far and wide to a saving remedy.

“Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near” (Matt. III). Of him there is fittingly added: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A man clothed in soft garments” (Luke VII); or, if this too is stated interrogatively, “A man clothed in soft garments?” One must supply, as above, “truly, it is so,” or something similar.

## CHAPTER XLIV
For John, who was called a reed shaken by the blast of a mighty spirit, is also declared to have been clothed in soft garments, so that, just as the commendable strength of preaching is signified by the reed moved by the wind, so the incomparable beauty of living is signified by the soft garments. Parents are accustomed to dress in soft clothing the children whom they love to keep close—especially their daughters—so that the delicate tenderness of the girls may not be harmed by the roughness of their clothing, and their inborn beauty may be enhanced by more elegant adornments. So too God the Father clothes in delicate garments those whom He loves above others: that is, He fortifies and beautifies them [Col. 0941B] with carefully cultivated merits and virtues, so that the more delicate soul may, as it were, repose in their soft silk, and its delicacy may not be weighed down by the coarse mass of vices sprinkled over it.

But if that soul, perhaps degenerating from the nobility of bestowed holiness and becoming subject to its own will, falls into forbidden perversity, God often turns away from it the affection by which He delighted to hold it close, and takes away the delicate adornments with which He had clothed it in softness and tenderness. Through Isaiah He threatens this to the sinful soul which formerly lived in delights like a tender virgin, but now, bending itself toward the weak and needy things of its own will, deserves to be stripped both of the reality and the name of its former dignity. “Come down, virgin; sit in the dust; sit upon the ground. You shall no longer be called soft and tender; take the millstone and grind flour” [Col. 0941C] (Isa. 47).

For the faithful soul sat on high when, forgetting the things behind, it clung to more perfect commands; when it dwelt among the choirs of heaven through likeness of life; and when, though in the flesh, it was held by the desire of the Creator alone, beyond the flesh. It was not undeservedly called soft and tender when it was guarded in the hidden place of God’s countenance from the disturbance of men; when, joined to Christ alone, it dwelt within the bridal chamber, so that neither a scorching wind might strike its face nor a corrupter assault its virginal chastity.

But when, like Dinah, it went out to see the women of a foreign land, setting aside the brightness of inward vision, it was sought with impure embraces by that Shechem who is the corrupter of virgins; and, its modesty [Col. 0941D] deflowered, it was enticed by his deadly flatteries. Therefore it is said to it: “Come down; sit in the dust; sit upon the ground.” You who until now sat on high by the merit of virginal holiness, come down, since you have clung to deceitful counsels; and sit in the low and depressed place of earthly perversity, enduring the deserved disgrace of unclean baseness. “For,” He says, “there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans” (ibid.). There is indeed a throne of most exalted dignity for the daughter of the citizens above; but the daughter of the Chaldeans lacks such a throne. Deprived of native tenderness, by which either a noble virgin or the nobility of virginity is commended, she is assigned, like a servant-girl, to harsh and servile labor: “You shall no longer be called soft and tender; take the millstone; grind flour.”

Because you despised the virginal tenderness which was My gift, take upon yourself the millstone of grievous sins, or the circular course of the world. Pressed—or rather crushed—by it, an incomprehensible multitude of thoughts will arise, by the flying cloud of which the sinful soul deserves not so much to be fed as blinded. The miserable woman is compelled to come to this millstone or flour because she refused to delight herself with the soft garments of virtues. For noble leisure it is fitting that soft and royal attire should distinguish it, whereas shameful nakedness seems suited to servile work.

The Lord threatens through Isaiah that He will bring precisely this nakedness upon them: stripped naked, they may transfer themselves in miserable freedom to servile labors, because, having lost their understanding and refusing to bear His soft and tender yoke, they chose to prefer their own will to the divine command. “The Lord,” he says, “will make bald [Col. 0942B] the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion, and will lay bare their hair; and He will take away the ornament of their shoes, and their crescents, necklaces, pendants, bracelets, turbans, headbands, anklets, little chains, perfume-vessels, earrings, rings, gems hanging upon the forehead, changes of dress, cloaks, linen garments, pins, mirrors, fine linen, bands, and veils” (Isa. 3).

These are the ornaments of which the soul is stripped if it departs from God; but if it persists in His love, it is laudably adorned with them. John—of whom we are speaking—shone with these ornaments, as the Lord bore witness concerning him: “A man clothed in soft garments.” Of such soft garments He also says through Ezekiel: “I clothed you in embroidered garments and shod you with hyacinth; [Col. 0942C] I girded you with fine linen and clothed you in delicate fabrics. I adorned you with adornment, and put bracelets upon your hands and a necklace about your neck; I put an earring upon your mouth, rings in your ears, and a crown of beauty upon your head. You were adorned with gold and silver, and were clothed in fine linen, embroidery, and many-colored garments” (Ezek. 16).

With these soft garments, as I have said, John was clothed: that is, he was distinguished, in the manner of nobles, by the varied texture of virtues. He neither knew nor wished to become entangled in sullied and servile pursuits, choosing and commending delight in spiritual leisure. Hence Christ adds: “Behold,” He says, “those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings” (Luke 7).

By kings He means those who disdain to be subject to vices with a certain religious loftiness; who tame the carnal affections and rule over them when tamed; who, prudently trained to execute judgment in their own land, are made vigorously ready to overcome every resistance. Of such persons the prophet says: “And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Ps. 2). And in another psalm: “Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth” (Ps. 148).

The houses of these kings are the virtues, which, joined together with strong and prudent workmanship and brought by a fitting connection into one structure, provide their architect both a strong defense against the storm from without and, within the hidden conscience of the one who presides, a peaceful seat of royal authority. Of such houses Isaiah says: “They shall build [Col. 0943A] houses and inhabit them” (Isa. 65); and Ezekiel: “They shall build houses and dwell securely” (Ezek. 28).

For a man builds a house and lives in its dwelling when he gathers virtues and steadfastly delights in their shelter; when he earnestly piles up for himself merit through virtue and much more earnestly remains and preserves himself in those virtues. But he builds a house without being said to dwell in it if he does not strive to complete what he has rightly begun; if, prudently admonished to do what is just, he applies his heart for a time, but does not give his wholesome purpose its due end. Since this does not seem fitting for the perfect or the elect, the Lord rightly promises through Isaiah: “They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat” (Isa. 65 [Col. 0943B]).

They build, but another inhabits; they plant, but another eats—those who labor vigorously to construct the edifice of good works, yet through negligence allow an intruding destroyer to spoil their labor; those who plant nurseries of virtues, who set the fruitful vine in order, yet do not provide adequate protection against beasts and robbers.

In this regard Scripture seems to commend Jacob, the younger in age, because he, a simple man, chose to dwell at home, whereas Esau, the elder of the brothers, not content with a similar manner of life, preferred outward things and devoted himself to hunting. Finally, because the midwives in Egypt feared God, He built them houses, it says (Exod. 1); or, according to the Septuagint interpreters, they made houses for themselves—like the wise man who, seeking an inviolable foundation against winds and floods, builds his house upon the foundation of solid rock.

In houses of this kind God, as David declares (Ps. 48), will be known, because knowledge of Him is attained in the progress of virtues, when, according to Isaiah (chap. 40), what was rough is turned into level ground: that is, things hard and iron-like are softened by the strong fire of love. “Behold,” He says, “those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings” (Luke 7). For those who have been tenderly softened by divine love and more delicately instructed in the hidden things of mysteries by worthy knowledge are said to be in these houses—that is, in the merits of virtues—which cannot be possessed except by those who have prudently governed themselves.

Since John shone, according to Christ’s testimony, with this precious garment of virtues, he showed himself worthy in the sight of the crowds [Col. 0944A] gathering to him, writing and setting before them in learned discourse the rule of holiness and commending saving teaching by carefully ordered conduct. For he bent the minds of his hearers more effectively toward obedience when the sweetness of his morals commended his teaching; when he did not thunder with words of command alone, as though authority were sufficient, but the love of the one imposing the command made the required obedience light.

It is therefore clear to attentive observers how necessary it is that one who commands others should deserve to be loved by them: his justice must not only furnish them a pattern of holiness, but the grace of his conduct must also arouse in his hearers the affection of charity. Finally, perhaps charity is called the end of the command because without it the command is not perfectly fulfilled, since the command requires both that the teacher render himself more acceptable to those under him, and that those under him love their teacher in reciprocal affection, or with due return.

If this happens through the operation of grace, nothing more pleasant and nothing more fruitful can be found; no fellowship is more fitting to itself than the gracious fellowship of one commanding and one obeying. For when a father shows plainly that he bends himself to command a son only with loving concern, and the son rests himself against the father’s bosom in tender affection, obedience, finding in neither party anything of which to complain, becomes joyful and grows strong for every great undertaking through health-giving gladness. But if anger, dispute, power, arrogance, and stubbornness give commands, while sadness, murmuring, quarrelling, and resentment obey, the serene face of obedience is certainly darkened to no slight degree, and neither the commander nor the obedient person is excused from blameworthy guilt.

Therefore, because the end of the command is charity from a pure heart and a cleansed conscience, and because obedience is not complete without charity, let superior and subject alike rest in its bosom and be inflamed by mutual embrace to love one another. When they see themselves bound indissolubly by the bond of perfect love, and see that the due measure and order are preserved among them both in commanding and in obeying, they will no longer need instruction from our words, rejoicing that they are already conformed to God beyond what can be spoken.

Our answer may therefore fittingly end here. Once the matter has been completed, it would be superfluous to prolong it further, since its principal purpose was to lead obedience, by fitting progress, to perfection.

## VI. ON THE SILENCE OF CLERICS

[Col. 0943]

### PROEM

[Col. 0943D]

The question is asked, brothers, what silence ought to be kept, by whom, when, and why; and, conversely, when it ought commendably to be set aside. For in the Scriptures silence is often found approved, yet often likewise condemned. This question, however—as I seem to see—cannot easily be answered, nor can one advance one’s hearers sufficiently toward understanding, unless one has first chosen to restrain oneself within the enclosure of silence and there acquired an intimate knowledge of it by a fitting manner of life.

For that teacher is especially found suitable who learns by experience, not merely by knowledge, that what he preaches is true; who does not chatter merely from knowledge, like a torrent driven by winter rains, but is shown rather to bring forth truth from inward judgment, as from a living spring. That wise man considered himself to be such a teacher, and, in order to urge others to imitate him, said: “God gave me to speak from understanding” [Col. 0945A] (Wis. 7). You see that he did not speak merely from knowledge, which is sometimes gathered from another’s hearing, but rather from the inward judgment produced by interior taste—just as one knows that wine is good not merely because report has circulated the fact, but more perfectly because taste itself judges it to be good.

Since, then, my own experience has not sufficiently tasted the mystery of the question proposed, its solution certainly troubles me greatly. I see it entangled in such great perplexities that I, being inexperienced, cannot explain it with complete clarity. But the more difficult it is to explain, the more readily pardon is due to the one explaining it, because the discerning judgment of judges does not accuse the person who does not refuse, to the extent of his ability, to bear the burden laid upon him.

Indeed, angels not only rejoice with and minister to people of perfect capacity, but also announce peace to people of good will (Luke 2), so that those who have merited to be perfect in work may persevere by their aid, while those who have good will may not despair. Therefore I undertake, in hope, to answer concerning silence, trusting in Him whom I know to preside over people of good will, [Col. 0945B] who in His own goodness will either grant grace to one who undertakes the task or will not deny pardon to one who proves insufficient.

## CHAPTER I

Silence is by no means lightly commended by religious men; it is more carefully observed in religious cloisters; and in our times no cloister is considered sufficiently worthy of praise in which regular silence is not maintained by diligent observance. For, as Isaiah says (chap. 32), silence is the cultivation of justice: one who takes care to render service to justice cannot find sufficient favor with it if he presumes to pour out whatever comes into his mouth.

And truly, when very many are gathered together in order to live justly and according to rule, and remain in the same chamber with doors shut for fear of the Jews, they will not easily restrain their restless tongues from quarrelling unless they are restrained from the wandering license of speech by an imposed law of silence. “For when there is jealousy and contention among you,” says the Apostle, “are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to man?” [Col. 0945D] (1 Cor. 3).

Those gathered together, therefore, for regular life must necessarily be bound with the rein of silence, so that, when for the sake of religion people do not talk idly with people, they may converse more familiarly with God in the secrecy of their hearts and, through His spiritual converse, may deserve to become not men but gods. Yet, in order to merit the grace of this gift, silence of the mouth alone does not suffice; nor does the inward mind rest whenever the tongue is silent. Indeed, often the more stubbornly the tongue is mute outwardly, the more angrily the mind burns inwardly.

But if it releases the same anger from which it suffers by breaking through the barrier of silence in clamorous words, it subsides, as a sore subsides when its pus breaks forth; and gradually, like a furnace whose vent has been opened, it cools. Therefore, as I see it, silence of the mouth is not always commended; nor is this the only silence named in the pages of Scripture. Another silence may be found in them; and perhaps each person may discover it more carefully in himself.

## CHAPTER II

There are, indeed, types of silence to be found in the Scriptures. If anyone wishes to define each of them more plainly, he may understand it better by its opposite and provide his hearers with a fuller understanding of it. There is silence from speech. There is silence from good things. There is silence from evil things.

Silence from speech is ceasing or resting from speaking. Speech, however, is made in one way by words and in another by signs. Speech made by words is so properly and generally called speech that not even a simple person would seem to doubt that it should be called speech; and many think that speech has been given to the human race for this reason, lest silence be kept among men as among cattle.

And indeed, in the creation of the world, before God made the mute living creatures of diverse kinds, which we know to be distributed on land, in water, and in air—and these were established not for themselves, but for the human being yet to come—at last He made man in His own image. He set man over all the rest, beasts, fish, and birds alike, so that, endowed with reason, man might understand and love that he had been created to serve his Creator; and the other irrational creatures render service to him thus created.

Reason is a certain natural power and capacity for discernment by which a spiritual nature can distinguish good from not-good, and just from unjust. God, who is Spirit, is truly believed to possess it; and He wished naturally to impart it to other spirits, whether human or angelic. For the Creator gave reason to created spirits, the spirits of angels and of human beings, by which they might naturally possess knowledge of good and evil, so that, by its benefit, discerning between the just and the unjust, they might, through the accompanying freedom of choice, incline themselves toward the proposed option.

But some angelic spirits used this reason and freedom badly. They were cast down from the heavenly light of blessedness into the darkness of profound misery; and although implanted reason remained in them, their rational obedience toward their Creator did not remain. Others, however, as they were rational spirits by nature, so they persevered rationally in obedience to their Creator; and, not following their fellow citizens, they obtained by fuller grace the merit of perseverance.

These contemplate the divine will with a pure and spiritual eye, and perceive one another’s consciences with their implanted keenness. They have no need to be taught anything by clamorously spoken words, nor to be commanded anything, whether by God or by one another, through speech as a medium. Since they are not wrapped in coverings of dullness but are wholly free from every weight and grossness, they see with spiritual subtlety what divine grace shows them beforehand; and, with every veil entirely removed, each apprehends the other’s naked conscience.

After their creation, God formed man from the clay of the earth [Col. 0947A] and breathed into the formed man the spirit of life, so that, made in the image of his Maker through the gracious benefit of his first creation, he might be capable of reason. Therefore man, like the angel, was rational by nature; but, because he possessed a human body—unlike the angelic creature—his rational soul was covered by the enveloping flesh. What was visible was not the soul itself but its earthly covering.

It therefore seemed fitting to the most gracious Creator and the most faithful Provider of all that He had created to grant speech to man, who consisted of soul and body, and to assign him a certain natural aptitude for speaking. Thus, when reason conceived something useful or honorable, one human being could make it known to another by speaking. It was fitting that a welcome exchange should be carried on among men in this way, and that they should be joined together through speech as a medium, so that, while their consciences were veiled within them by the garment of flesh, they might easily be conveyed outward into mutual knowledge by means of the voice.

Finally, because man is endowed with natural reason and necessarily uses speech to express reason’s counsel, it is said that he uses language. God Himself and angels also often spoke with sounding words and carried out in fitting ways what was necessary for human beings. Although it is certain that they, being spiritual—indeed, being spirits—have no need of vocal speech, nevertheless for the sake of human beings they chose sometimes to appear visible and audible. Taking on a material voice and form, they showed themselves for a time in such a way that man could both hear [Col. 0947C] and see them bodily.

Thus, when God placed the first man in paradise, which abounded in countless fruitful trees, He told him in material words which trees he should eat from, and likewise forbade him to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. “From every tree,” He says, “that is in paradise, eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat. For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death” (Gen. 2).

Since God had made man capable of reason and, as has been said, had given him the office of speech for expressing hidden things, He wished, in accommodation to him, Himself also to use material words, that He might teach him more plainly not to abuse the benefits he had received. In this way God or an angel of old made Himself audible to the ancient Fathers, and often appeared visibly in whatever form He chose, taking on temporarily whatever material creature might enable Him to be seen and heard, though by nature He was invisible and inaudible.

Adam too seems to indicate this when, after sin, he tries to hide his discovered nakedness, declares that he heard the voice of God walking in paradise, and says that he feared God’s sight because of the shame of his new nakedness. For, when God said, “Adam, where are you?” he answered, “Lord, I heard Your voice, and I was afraid because I was naked” (Gen. 3). He heard God’s voice and feared being seen by Him, though previously he had been seen by Him without being ashamed to be seen. Before sin, because he felt no injury of resistance in his body, he did not fear the bodily sight of God or an angel present in bodily form.

But after, at the woman’s persuasion, he fell away from the saving command, he endured by divine punishment rebellion from that which had been subject to him. Poorly advised to follow intemperance as a guide, he fulfilled what was later said: “He who does evil truly hates the light” (John 3). Therefore he flees and hides in the shade beneath fig leaves. Yet divine goodness does not on that account fall silent; it finds him in hiding, speaks to him, rebukes him, calls him back to salvation, and imposes on him, as a remedying gift, the involuntary servitude of vanity.

In the same way God is said to have spoken to Cain, who, overthrown by envy, did not fear to kill his undeserving brother; when asked where he was, Cain stubbornly denied knowing, lest he humbly expiate his accomplished crime by the confession due. Later, when Jacob was returning from Mesopotamia, an angel in the form of a man not only allowed himself to be seen, but also suffered himself to be bodily held; and by a wondrous mystery he wrestled with Jacob until morning, speaking as they wrestled words well known to you: “Let me go,” he says, “for dawn has now risen” (Gen. 32). And again: “What is your name? You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name” (ibid.).

In the New Testament likewise, it is easy to find such things. An angel is read to have met Zachariah as he stood at the altar, announcing that John would be born to him in his old age and that, because his faith had failed, he would remain silent until that time (Luke 1). Shortly afterward, the angel Gabriel is sent to Mary (ibid.); appearing to the solitary Virgin in the form of a man, he greets her, declares that the Lord is now with her, comforts her in her alarm, and affirms that she will conceive by the Spirit and give birth in a new manner to her Savior and the Savior of all.
