At other times, in both the New and Old Testaments, an angel is found to appear and to hold conversation with human beings in material words, so that he might make known to them his will or God’s will. For the sake of knowledge of hidden things, they were granted the faculty of speech. Happy they would have been had they used the grace of this gift so as to abstain from making unlawful matters known; had they not abused the benefit bestowed; had they not used the aid of speech to teach one another harmful things or provoke the Lord to anger by His own gifts.

Then every kind of speech would be commendable and constrained by a great barrier of silence, because no one would utter either a deadly word for which he deserved condemnation, or even an idle one for which he would be compelled to render an account.

## CHAPTER III

But in the second age of the world, when all nations everywhere spoke one and the same language, and some used the received benefit more perversely than the rest, divine judgment willed to call them back from their purpose. Confusing their language, it caused them to be separated from one another. For they wished to build a tower of astonishing size, whose height might approach the height of the heavens, so that by this deed their name might be spread abroad in celebrated fame and a memorial of their presumptuous wickedness might be transmitted to generations far in the future.

“Come,” they say, “let us make for ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach heaven, and let us make our name famous before we are scattered over all lands” (Gen. 11). Perverse speech! Perverse, I say, and worthy to have silence imposed upon it, so that through the aid of silence its desired perversity might be set aside; lest it seem either harmless or perhaps profitable to itself, if it were permitted to accomplish in deeds what it had uttered in words.

For wickedness which the fellowship it has sought favors and supports, once brought out into the open, does not easily desist from what it has begun. If a strong hand does not resist its evil design and persist in destroying what it undertakes to build, it will not cease. Seeing this, the Lord said: “They have begun to do this, and they will not desist from their thoughts until they fulfill them in deed. Come then, let us go down [Col. 0949B] and confuse their language there, so that no one may hear the voice of his neighbor” (ibid.).

God rightly willed to punish sinners in this way: seeing them agree with one heart with one another in evil and entangle one another by effective words to accomplish what they had wickedly conceived, He struck them in their language and compelled them not to hear one another’s voices. With their hearing obstructed, they would fail to understand and cease to obey one another.

But both the fault and the punishment fitting the fault may be more clearly perceived if we review in order the things said a little above, in which the rise of their wickedness is found and its great advance is contained, so that it could not, or ought not, be endured any longer by the righteous Judge. For the Apostle says: “Evil men advance toward worse things” (2 Tim. 3). And the Lord says through the prophet: “I have labored in enduring” (Jer. 6).

Speaking, therefore, of the sons of Noah’s sons, who were born after the flood and divided into many nations and peoples throughout lands and islands, Scripture shows in mystical speech the order in which their wickedness grew and the degree of pride to which malicious impiety came by its wicked progress. “As they journeyed,” it says, “from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and dwelt in it” (Gen. 11).

The east is named from the rising of the sun, because from that quarter the sun rises again for us. By its rising it rebukes and dispels the darkness of night and, the world’s gloom cleared away, pours forth its shining daylight. Therefore, by the east divine illumination is not unfittingly signified. When our blindness has been driven away through it, the Sun of righteousness is presented to us, so that henceforth we may not be darkened as children of night or of darkness, but, clothed in “the armor of light, may walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. 13).

Of this Zachariah says: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke 1). For light has risen upon those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death (Isa. 9). Everyone taught by the divine Spirit rejoices to turn toward the rising of the true light, so that with eyes and hands he may receive it when it is offered; indeed, so that his face may seek that Face, and, having sought it, may in no way be turned aside by the Seeker. “My face has sought You,” he says; “I will seek Your face, O Lord” (Ps. 26). To what end? To what profit? He adds: “Do not turn Your face away [Col. 0950A] from me” (ibid.).

God does not turn His face away from a face seeking His. Rather, He turns toward that face awaiting Him with a gracious gift; and, having in some sense revealed Himself to the one awaiting Him, He advances that person from strength to strength and afterward brings him by the merit of virtues to salvation. Hence the Prophet says: “O Lord God of hosts, turn us, show us Your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79). It is as though he said: Turn us, and turn Yourself toward us, so that when Your face has shone by faith upon our face, we may deserve to attain the glory of the promised vision.

As a figure of this reality, when we pray for divine grace to be present with us, whether we stand in prayer or bend down with knees bent, we turn our bodies toward the eastern region, as though refusing to look upon the west, so that we may show by the position of the body the disposition of our mind. For we ought to oppose, as losses, the western darkness of sins and await with desire turned toward Him the rising of the Sun of righteousness, so that when He comes—that is, when He rises—He may find us not turned away, but turn toward those who have turned to Him the face of illuminating grace. As it is written: “Turn to Me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. 1). And Jeremiah says: “Look around, Jerusalem, toward the east, and see the joy that will come to you” (Baruch 4).

The people mentioned above are said to depart from this east when they are found, by their own will, to have forgotten the true light that illuminates those turned toward it. They did not fear to incur, in proud spirit, the crime of apostasy: that is, to turn away from God and fall headlong into their own inventions. “For the beginning of pride is apostasy from God” [Col. 0950C] (Ecclus. 10).

Perhaps Balaam the diviner is also remembered as having come from this east when he was invited by Balak, king of the Moabites, to curse the children of Israel. The divine face did not shine sufficiently upon Balaam’s face, since he did not shake off from himself every gift because of regard for Balak. “Balak, king of the Moabites, brought me from Aram,” he says, “from the mountains of the east” (Num. 23). For Balaam would not have consented to Balak’s summons if he had not turned away from the Sun of righteousness; nor would he have sinned with malevolent feeling against the people whom the Lord had blessed had he not abandoned the mountains of the east—that is, righteousness. “Your righteousness,” he says, “is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 35).

Of such persons who leave the east the Lord says through Jeremiah: “They turned their back to Me and not their face” (Jer. 3). And below: “I shall show them my back and not my face on the day of their destruction” (Jer. 18).

## CHAPTER IV

“But when those sons of Noah were journeying from the East, they found,” it says, “a plain in the land of Shinar” (Gen. 11). Having abandoned the East, or the mountains of the East, they rightly find a plain in the land of Shinar, because broad and spacious is the way by which men arrive at the precipice of death. The perverse mind, not caring to be illuminated by the face of the true light, gladly wanders with looser reins across the flatland of pleasures.

Now in Scripture a plain is sometimes commended, and humility or equality of conduct is signified by it, because the roughness of pride is left behind, the level ground of humility is sought, and brotherly love is gained through the ordered equality of conduct. “I,” He says, “am the flower of the field” (Song 2). And the Prophet says: “The word walked and went forth into the plains”: that is, it appeared to the humble and gentle. Of these another prophet says: “We found her in the plains of the wood” (Ps. 131).

The plains of the wood are said to be the nations of the Gentiles. At Christ’s coming they humbly confess that, uncultivated by the roughness of sins, they have become wild; and by the merit of humble confession they are faithfully and savingly made level, so that, like a bitter wild olive, they may deserve to be grafted into the sweetness of the olive tree.

And the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Go out into the plain, and there I shall speak with you.” “And I went out,” he says, “into the plain, and behold, the glory of the Lord stood there, like the glory which I saw by the river Chebar” (Ezek. 3). This plain not unfittingly signifies the breadth of charity. Whoever goes out to it from the hiding place or narrowness of earthly and self-will feels God speaking to him, sees God appearing to him more fully—indeed, feels God abiding in him and himself likewise abiding in God. “For,” as we read, “God is charity; and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him” (1 John 4).

Therefore the Apostle says to the Corinthians as to children: “I say to you: be enlarged, you also” (2 Cor. 6), as though saying: Go out from the narrow hut of earthly affections, and pass over to love and desire for eternal things, so that, when the flowering breadth of this command has received you, the glorious greatness of the divine majesty may appear to you more freely and fully.

But sometimes a plain signifies the unrestricted breadth of vices, when the height of virtues appears rough or narrow to the sinful soul, and the soul, unable or unwilling to strive toward its arduous gravity, falls back upon itself and embraces a broad freedom to sin. Hence perhaps it is that the righteous king Josiah, fighting in the plain of Megiddo, is wounded by archers, disappointed in his hope of victory, and is carried away dead by his triumphant enemies from the very place from which he vainly expected to bring back not only life but victory.

“He went,” it says, “to fight in the plain of Megiddo, and there, wounded by archers, he died” (2 Chron. 35). And in the Book of Kings: “His servants carried him dead from Megiddo” (4 Kings 23). Megiddo is interpreted “temptation.” Temptation is whatever we see smiling upon us in temporal things. When we wish to gain what seems like victory in its pursuit, we set before ourselves the harsh and narrow discipline of inward religion; and the desired success of outward things turns into spiritual ruin for us.

Therefore, in the plain, as it were, the righteous king Josiah is killed when, amid a broad appetite for outward things, whatever righteousness our mind may possess is overthrown. He is carried away in sudden death from Megiddo—that is, from temptation—when the inward mind is rejected from the things it desires and its hope is frustrated.

Finally, a certain poet says:

> Wars, more than civil, across the Emathian plains,
The right to crime is granted—we sing … [lacuna] (Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.1)—plainly indicating that by the Emathian, that is, blood-stained, [Col. 0952A] plains nothing prosperous is signified, where crime and wars “more than civil” are found to hold unjust dominion by right.

King Nebuchadnezzar also sets up a golden statue on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon (Dan. III), and by manifold music invites the people of that region to worship it, doubtless wishing that, when the multitude summoned by his command had assembled, the spaciousness both of the place and of idolatry might receive it into a welcoming bosom. Yet the three youths Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, rejecting the king’s command and worshipping not so much his statue as the true God with the worship due to Him, prefer to endure the furnace of tribulation, bound by the bonds of divine love, rather than freely traverse the proposed breadth of idolatry.

Such also is this plain which the aforesaid men found, [Col. 0952B] who, having turned away from the east, sought the west by a wandering error, and spread themselves into such a breadth of malicious intent that, enclosed in the unheard-of darkness of presumption, they desired to assail heaven.

## CHAPTER V

“And they found a plain in the land of Shinar” (Gen. II). Such a perverse expanse is rightly said to be found in the land of Shinar, because where the strength of spiritual virtues perishes and the native brightness of good repute is held in contempt, there the unbridled and untamed amplitude of wickedness obtains its kingdom. Shinar is interpreted “the shaking out of teeth,” or “their stench.”

Teeth are like millstones, by which bread is ground and crushed so that it may pass more suitably into the stomach and there impart its life-giving juice to the veins that converge there, [Col. 0952C] so that this nourishment, through the service of those veins, may be distributed through the remaining limbs; and, once distributed, it makes the whole body more healthful and vigorous. Now bread is Holy Scripture, which ought to instruct the inner person, so that he may reach the perfect man by fitting stages. For when the bread of the Scriptures is withheld, one who fasts and abstains becomes weak; but when it is received more eagerly, the heart of man is strengthened and gains force.

The teeth by which this same bread of the Scriptures is crushed and the life-giving food is conveyed into the stomach of memory are rightly understood as intelligence and diligence, which, meeting one another, produce in us salutary progress. For when intelligence is bestowed upon our mind, as though from above, and our diligence, as though from below, is laid beneath it, there results a pleasing grinding or eating, fruitful to our spirit for spiritual life. Intelligence, indeed—which may also be called natural ability—is known to be given to us not by our own choice but by divine gift; and for this reason it is not unfittingly reckoned the upper molar tooth, which, as the more worthy, presides over our food—that is, over our progress.

But diligence—or, if preferred, study—is applied, as it were, by our own choice, through the natural powers of understanding; and it may deservedly be called the lower molar, which, meeting the upper one, is found to work together with it. Hence the Prophet says: “Give me understanding, and I shall search your law” (Ps. CXVIII). For when he asks that understanding be given him by God, and subsequently promises [Col. 0952D] that he will search God’s law with diligent study, he indicates both that it is God’s proper work to bestow understanding on a human being and that it is the human being’s work to pursue understanding by study. Yet neither understanding nor study is possessed apart from divine gift; and they advance and increase through the benefit of each other. For when someone understands what he has investigated, he is stirred to investigate more zealously; and through the zeal of investigation, understanding itself is made clear.

Such teeth, which are bestowed upon us only by divine gift yet are not brought to perfection without our effort, are made sound and strong by devout humility, but are shaken out and weakened by pride. For studious natural ability, or intelligent study, is found to make progress and persist in progress when the mind of one desiring to advance is first furnished with due humility—when, that is, it seeks to break the bread of the Scriptures in order that by that breaking it may work for the salvation of souls. “Work,” he says, “not for food which perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life” (John VI).

Indeed, after saying what was quoted above—“Give me understanding, and I shall search your law”—the Prophet adds: “And I shall keep it with all my heart” (Ps. CXVIII), clearly showing that he desires to obtain understanding, and promises to devote study to searching the law, for no other purpose than that he may be found a more effective keeper of that law once it is known; for unless it is known, it cannot be kept.

But when the inward mind swells against God and, through the working of pride, recoils from keeping the divine law, whatever understanding may perhaps have been naturally present in it is darkened; and diligence in searching vanishes, overwhelmed by contempt and disgust. And while that same pride takes no care to recover toward the better, but with obstinate malice strives to advance toward the worse, it rejoices not merely to shake these teeth of which we have spoken, but to shake them out once shaken: so that the wretched mind neither loves to exercise understanding through study nor understands that it is declining into failure.

When the teeth have been shaken out—that is, when intelligence and diligence have been put to flight, by which the solid food of truth ought both to have been understood more diligently and loved more intelligently—the same wretch feeds on the empty fodder of falsehood and establishes therein for himself a seat of destructive firmness. For just as commendable strength is nourished and perfected by the food of truth, [Col. 0953D] so a contrary kind of firmness grows through deceptive vanity, so that the perverse mind cannot be recalled from its purpose but delights to be strengthened in the blind progress of malice.

This is the land of Shinar: namely, the stubborn obstinacy of perversity, in which the mind full of vanity fixes a stable footing, having neglected and cast away understanding and the study of spiritual commandments, and is borne by blind impulse through the desired expanses of vices. Of this the Apostle says: “They became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. I).

But since, as has been said, Shinar is interpreted “their stench,” it must be understood that this interpretation too agrees with the character of the wicked, who, even if they possess understanding and apply diligence to the Scriptures, nevertheless do not love heavenly things [Col. 0954A] but plunge their minds into transient matters. For there are some whose natural intelligence is not blinded but, with labour added day by day, is clarified by study; they heap up much knowledge for themselves by diligent care, yet do not observe in their conduct the precepts of justice that they comprehend by knowledge. They do not desire to know much in order to live more holy lives, but desire their knowledge to serve passing pleasures: namely, so that by it they may attain temporal profits more effectively, or swell with haughty brow among others, perhaps even above others.

And while this intention gnaws at the wretched mind inwardly and becomes outwardly manifest to others through deeds, that very intelligence and diligence which seemed to make progress in knowing are proved harmful, both to themselves and to others, in living. Blindness does not remove these things far away as though shaking them out; rather, the worm of perverse intention corrupts them while they are present. Perhaps it would be healthier for someone not to possess them than to hold them swollen with noxious moisture and corrupted by rottenness.

Many afflicted by diseased teeth, when prompt treatment does not restore them to health, judge it more useful to pull them out entirely than both to endure their pain and to offer their stench to those with whom they converse. So, indeed, when anyone grasps knowledge of the Scriptures through intelligence and study but does not strive to live according to those same Scriptures, he is proved exceedingly harmful both to himself and to his neighbours: he sins knowingly, and his neighbour is polluted by his perversity. He who ought [Col. 0954C] to offer himself as the good fragrance of Christ in every place is found instead to emit a harmful stench. When his teeth are gnawed by the worm of avaricious vanity, his mouth grows large, his words swell, and his hearers are corrupted by the rottenness administered to them.

Hence Scripture says: “Balaam son of Beor has spoken, who knows the doctrine of the Most High and sees the visions of the Almighty, who falls and has open eyes” (Num. XXIII). This man, seeing visions of the Almighty, understood through anxious inquiry what was just; but he did not direct the edge of his wretched will toward doing those things. Rather, with open eyes rushing into the blaze of avarice, he gave King Balak an abominable counsel for Israel’s death.

The reprobate are said to come to such a Shinar [Col. 0954D] and there find a plain—that is, the sought-after breadth for sinning. Having found it, they do not hasten, like guests, to pass through it within the space of one day, but resolve to establish in it a lasting dwelling, a city: “They found,” he says, “a plain in the land of Shinar, and dwelt in it” (Gen. II [probably XI]).

## CHAPTER VI

This dwelling signifies a lingering abode: when, that is, the mind makes, or resolves to make, a divine stand in its purpose; when, cleaving to what it desires, whether badly or well, or to what it has been granted to attain, it is unwilling to turn either foot or affection away from it through entreaty, reward, or any threats.

Thus Scripture, speaking of evil inhabitants, says: “The sons of Benjamin did not destroy the Jebusite; and the Jebusite dwelt with the sons of Benjamin unto this present day” (Judg. I). But of the good it says: “He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever” (Ps. CXXIV).

In Scripture, dwelling is also used for dominion: when someone is said not merely to remain in a condition but to exercise a kind of rule by right of power, so that he may enjoy, as a king, the command of free will, which the rational creature commonly possesses without receiving it from another. “Joseph dwelt in the house of his master” (Gen. XXXIX). A little later this dwelling is explained, as it were: he had been set over all things and governed the house entrusted to him and everything delivered to him.

And David says: “Dwell in the land, and you shall be fed on its riches” (Ps. XXXVI); that is, rule your body and you shall obtain fruit from it. Therefore, in what is said of those men—“They dwelt in it”—whether one chooses to understand “dwelling” as habitation or as abiding, Scripture intended to designate their obstinate will: they strive to bring to completion by effective power what they had wickedly begun.

## CHAPTER VII

And since to each perverse person the wickedness of his own self alone is judged insufficiently effective unless another is joined to him in doing likewise, they eagerly strive to invite accomplices and to stir them more vehemently by exhortatory words to the work they desire. “And one said to his neighbour: Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire” (Gen. II).

When the tumult of malice burns in the furnace of the heart, it dreads nothing more than silence; judging it intolerable to be confined within its native narrowness, it loves, once the barrier of silence is broken, to wander abroad through the expanses of words. Just as new wine is contained in a flask and, if perhaps no outlet for breathing is provided to what is enclosed, it seethes and, unable to endure restraint, swells; and its swelling intensifies until it bursts the flask—so perversity often agitates and bursts the perverse mind if, denied licence to speak, it does not break forth.

Eliphaz the Temanite aptly intimates this when he says: “Who can restrain a conceived word?” (Job IV). Thus one said to his neighbour. And rightly, he who cannot restrain within silence the malice he has conceived is said to exhort no one but a neighbour to carry it out: for if he addressed someone remote or far away, his speech, heard more slowly or perhaps not at all, would fail. But this neighbour is near not so much in place or lineage as in effect: one who does not withdraw wicked hands from a like-minded desire; who, lest he abandon his evil purpose through the conversation or company of the just, flees them and approaches the person whom he sees to be like himself.

I heard someone say that he feared association with religious persons to such an extent that he avoided even conversation with a brother of his who was a monk, lest through the conversation of religious persons he too should come to desire religion—whose desire and effect he did not yet wish to be present in himself. Astonishing perversity! He feared becoming good, whereas he ought to have feared remaining evil; and he ought to have inclined his ear, if not to the Gospel, at least to the pagan warning, “It is permitted to hope for one who fears.” Perhaps it was permitted to him to hope, but it did not please him, because he not only strove not to be considered holy but feared lest divine grace grant him this will.

Thus every perverse person, with the rein of chatter loosened, does not care to associate with one who gladly keeps silence; and if it should happen that he is kept in the same place with such a person, he is nevertheless far from the one whose conduct and justice he does not follow. He loves instead to obtain the company of one whose manners he knows to answer to his own, who not only bears heard verbosity patiently but displays himself twice as garrulous and a son of Gehenna.

Such a person is not undeservedly judged a neighbour also by lineage, because whoever does the works of the devil is proved to be from him as from a father, like a son, as Holy Scripture plainly testifies. Paul says to Elymas the magician: “Son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness” (Acts XIII). And John the Apostle: “He who commits sin is of the devil” (John VIII). And the Lord in the Gospel: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (ibid.).

Therefore all who wickedly carry out the devil’s will are shown to be his children; just as, conversely, those who obey God’s will in faith and works are transferred into the children of God. “As many as received him,” he says, “he gave them power to become children of God” (John I). But who can deny that those who are children of one father are of one race, when *genus*, “race,” or *generatio*, “generation,” is named from that from which one is begotten? And since the devil is proclaimed father or begetter of all evils, while God is proclaimed father or begetter of good things, Scripture surely speaks of a twofold generation: one intends to mark every evil person, while the other embraces all good persons under the same name.

Of the evil: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign” (Matt. XVI); and through Moses: “A depraved and perverse generation” (Deut. XXXIII). But of the good: “The generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Ps. III). Those who belong to one generation or race are surely neighbours; indeed, every just person rightly acknowledges the just person as his neighbour, and the unjust is likewise declared neighbour to the unjust.

Thus one said to his neighbour: that is, the wicked to the wicked, who, begotten from the one devil not in substance but in malice, are related not by flesh or blood but by likeness of conduct. And just as the just person loves his neighbour as himself, wholly desiring that he be saved as himself, so the wicked person hates and entangles his neighbour as himself, always loving evil and drawing that neighbour likewise to himself.

In this he is like his father, who, after falling through the impulse of pride into the abyss of wickedness, did not wish man to ascend to the place from which he himself had fallen. Taking a form and approaching the woman with suitable words, he overcame her simplicity by crafty deception. “You shall by no means die,” he says, “for God knows that on whatever day you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened and you shall be as gods, knowing good and evil. And the woman took of the fruit and ate, and gave to her husband” (Gen. III).

You see how great a ruin perverse speech works: when the simple woman does not fear a snare in the food and poison in the tongue, she is unbridled, with the laws of self-restraint relaxed, to eat what was forbidden; and the uxorious man is enervated by her persuasive words. The devil rightly appeared in the form of a serpent when he counselled the unsuspecting woman to transgress the commandment, because this animal insinuates itself by crawling and slippery motion and, carrying poison in its tongue, pours it upon the unwary and unsuspecting.

For that ancient Satan, the twisting serpent, not moderately hateful to lovers of righteousness, does not walk or make noise lest, heard from afar, he be avoided. Rather, he creeps and glides so that his coming is unknown; and he is said to bite silently the person whom he finds off guard. In his bite there is not so much poison as death, the inseparable companion of poison. His silence is his very hidden intention; his bite is poisonous speech: that is, he plots each person’s destruction secretly within himself and then, employing whatever devices he can, brings it about outwardly.

For he always burns within himself with the torches of malice, and, impatient of delay, scarcely keeps silence even briefly, judging nothing more burdensome than lurking in silence and resting, as though idle, from harmful action. Therefore, breaking silence, he quickly chatters with his viperous tongue and contrives to pour poison into his hearers, so that, once he has infected them, he may rejoice that they have become like himself; and evil is all the more pleasing to him as it spreads more widely among many.

Those who set out from the east, departed from the true light, and said, “one to his neighbour,” made themselves like this poisonous father, lest they offend their father by prolonged silence. The speech exchanged among such children, by which one diligently exhorts his neighbour, like exhorting like, is thus carried from within outward into public view, so that it is recognized as not degenerate or unlike its source.

## CHAPTER VIII

“Come,” they say, “let us make bricks and bake them with fire. And they had bricks for stones, and bitumen for mortar” (Gen. II).

A work worthy of its maker. The ancients made bricks from mud mixed with straw, baked their watery softness by applying fire, and used them once hardened in place of stones; from them they constructed both city walls and the walls of houses. By soft and watery mud, carnal pleasure is not unfittingly signified, in whose filth the devil wallows like a sow, because the sow is a friend of mud, as a certain pagan writer is found to recall; and in Job Behemoth is read to dwell in wet places.

But empty and windblown straw bears the figure of proud vanity. The discriminating winnowing-fan, reproving its fruitless lightness and not allowing it to remain among the grains of solid truth, tosses it, shaken and cast out, into the winds of wretched [Col. 0958A] liberty. There it is carried here and there by the wind of its own frivolity, and no certain dwelling is afforded it in the cloudy air, until at last it falls to the earth, adheres more tenaciously to the mud of the streets, and there, as though received into a welcome bosom, rests in a soft reclining place.

For when the just, by severe judgment, shake empty vanity from their works, considering that nothing but the solid truth of virtues pleases God, it flees and flits away to the muddy works of the wicked, plunges into them, and enjoys, as it were, rich repose. Thus the just person says: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). But David says of the unjust: “Those who hate you have gloried” (Ps. LXXVIII). And Solomon: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. II). And Paul again: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their outpouring” (Phil. III).

There are indeed some who, though they ought to devote care to good works or, if they have done something wicked, at least not transgress the bounds of shame but rather blush when they incur the slipperiness of youth—for there is some hope of salvation in a shamefaced person—nevertheless are not at all ashamed of the wicked works they have committed. Instead, as though attaining what they desired, they are puffed up with empty glory, thinking themselves worthy to be crowned with the title of praise because, in doing evil, they have been able either to surpass others or to equal them.

These are rightly said to mix straw with mud in order to make bricks: they do muddy deeds and are unwilling to restrain them in silence; indeed, they are as rash in performing deeds they know to be unclean as they are verbose and garrulous in boasting of them with ruined judgment. Yet fire, as it were, must be applied to such works, and by its intense heat the material of the bricks is hardened. For it is known by experience that mud, unless it is made firmer by applying heat, is broken by the lightest touch.

The fire by which filthy and fluid works gain strength and harden more vehemently so as not easily to be undone is rightly judged to be the malice of the mind, which in some people produces the precipice of despairing contempt. “When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he will despise” (Prov. XVIII). Malice exists when someone leaves the way of justice not through weakness, ignorance, or any negligence, but sins now by a decree of perverse will and the heat of wickedness, so that he neither hopes nor desires, in the present or the future, to be removed from his purpose, nor can be frightened away from it by any threats, like a dog from an oiled hide.

Such malice hardened Pharaoh’s heart more violently. Despising Moses, he even denied the Lord himself; and although, as the plagues increased, he was afterwards compelled both to know and confess Him, this did not suffice to dissolve his perversity. “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. V). And later: “The Lord is just; I and my people are wicked” (Exod. IX). And later: “Take care not to see my face again, for on whatever day you appear to me, you shall die” (Exod. X).

It is plain with what heat of malice Pharaoh’s wicked heart is obstructed: though scourged by many grievous plagues, it is not softened into fitting repentance but is changed by divine chastisement much for the worse, so that his chastiser might seem to be washing a brick. Finally, Pharaoh himself in Egypt was intent upon making bricks and pressed the children of Israel to make them (Gen. II), desiring nothing more eagerly than to be polluted by muddy and carnal things and, in them, to be reprehensibly hardened, both himself and others.

Of this kind are the bricks of which it is said: “They had them for stones, and bitumen for mortar.” Stones, naturally strong, rightly signify works of holiness. If a prudent builder joins them together with the mortar of charity, they rise and advance the structure of a spiritual building, [Col. 0959B] which neither the violence of winds, nor the inundation of rivers, nor temporal temptation overthrows. With such stones and mortar they ought to have built their edifice, if they truly wished to draw near to the height of heaven, to God’s exalted throne. But through wandering error they had bitumen and bricks in their place, so that everything which they laid one upon another in their building was muddy.

When bitumen and bricks are thus prepared as they please, the perversity of incipient wickedness does not fail but advances; and the insolent, irreverent, unbridled tongue is raised on high, and nothing is more perverse than unpunished loquacity. For when above one invited his neighbour to make bricks, and the tongue, though small, set the whole forest ablaze, according to James, divine patience did not extinguish so grave a fire or restrain their wandering loquacity beneath the yoke of silence.

Thus unrestrained and unbridled presumptuous speech, knowing no fixed limit and containing none of its own incitements, disdains the earth, wanders through the plains of the air, and, not content with them, now plots to reach heaven itself. For it follows: “And they said: Come, let us make for ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach heaven.” Loquacious presumption, unwilling to bear the yoke of silence or to tolerate a fixed measure and due boundaries, wishes to inflict violence upon the very seat of God and refuses to yield to anything that it sees can resist it.

But the kingdom of heaven does not yield to one who seizes contumaciously, nor is it plundered by plunderers of this sort. Rather: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but he has given the earth to the children of men” (Ps. CXIII). And through Obadiah: “Though you are exalted as an eagle, and though you set your nest among the stars, from there I shall bring you down, says the Lord” (ch. IV).

Therefore God, wishing to scatter the boastful tongue lest it rejoice to bring its wicked purpose to completion, in a sense desires silence for himself as well, and interrupts their perverse conversations by an instrument of a new kind.

## CHAPTER IX

“For the Lord came down,” he says, “to see the city and tower which the sons of Adam were building, and said: Behold, they are one people, and all have one language; and they have begun to do this, nor will they desist from their designs until they complete them in deed. Come, therefore, [Col. 0960A] let us go down and confuse their language there, so that no one may hear the voice of his neighbour” (Gen. XI).

In Scripture God’s descent is often found pleasing and desirable, when he is known to bestow his benefits upon those below. Thus, pitying the people of Israel oppressed in Egypt under Pharaoh’s rule, the Lord himself declares that he descended to set them free: “I have come down,” he says, “to deliver them from the hands of the Egyptians” (Exod. III). And you know that elsewhere he is said to descend like rain upon the fleece, and then “righteousness,” he says, “and abundance of peace shall arise” (Ps. LXXI).

But sometimes, when God is mentioned as descending, that descent foretells the punishment that will follow it. Thus when he prepares to strike Sodom and Gomorrah, he states beforehand, as it were, that he will descend: “The outcry of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans is multiplied; I will go down and see” (Gen. XVIII).

Likewise God’s seeing sometimes grants grace and sometimes brings wrath. It grants grace when it is said: “I have seen the affliction of my people, and I have come down to deliver them” (Gen. III). And in the Gospel: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John I). But it brings wrath when it is said: “The face of the Lord is upon those who do evil, to destroy the remembrance of them from the earth” (Ps. XXXIII).

And through Amos: “I will set my eyes upon them for evil, and not for good” (Amos IX). So here too, when it says, “The Lord came down to see [Col. 0960C] the city and tower which the sons of Adam were building,” his wrath and punishment are signified, because he foretells that a stronger vengeance will resist their mighty pride. However great the height that rises against him, the strength of his unconquerable hand strikes and overthrows it.

“They are one people,” he says, “and all have one language” (Gen. XI). This is the perverse unity that bound that people with a mutual bond and joined their lips to speak great things, so that, abhorring the enclosure of silence, they might be freed from the rule of discipline and wander with equal thought and consent through the widespread spaces of speech. But into this unity God sent, as it were, a great stone, and with fitting dissension divided it into many parts, so that they abandoned what they had begun contrary to their intention, although perhaps they persisted in agreement upon the same will.

They were punished all the more severely and painfully because they were more violently hindered from carrying out their will; and nothing is endured more intolerably by anyone than when his desire burns fiercely yet cannot be brought to fulfilment. “Come,” he says, “let us go down and confuse their language there.” They had said: “Come, let us make for ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach heaven.” The Lord says: “Come, let us go down and confuse their language there.”

They thought the multitude of their own people flourished with greater strength and that their multitude contained very great power. But God too was not without a multitude of strong ones, or the strength of many, by whom he was able either to delay or frustrate their wicked purpose. “Let us go down,” he says, “and let us confuse”—perhaps he speaks to the angels, who rejoice continually to obey his commands, and to whom, as they stand before him, he is accustomed to assign such service: either to destroy and scatter the actions and counsels of the perverse or to build up and plant the affections and endeavours of those who are converted.

“Are they not all,” says the Apostle, “ministering spirits sent forth for ministry on behalf of those who shall inherit salvation?” (Heb. I). Whether the elect are supported by angelic ministry or the reprobate are deservedly punished according to their merits, it surely benefits the elect toward the inheritance of salvation, who often wash their hands in the blood of sinners.

Therefore God says to the angels: “Come, and let us go down,” because descent is credibly attributed to no one else; and through them he works vengeance and wrath upon sinners and reprobates. What he does through them Scripture rightly declares them to do; and what they do at his command is likewise rightly attributed to the one commanding. “Let us go down,” he says, “and confuse their language there, so that no one may hear the voice of his neighbour.”

Because they do not speak what is just and salutary but stubbornly speak against the just and against salvation, let their tongue, wickedly harmonious with itself, be confused, lest poisonous speech be harmfully spread according to its purpose. Divine vengeance wishes to confuse it in such a manner “that no one,” he says, “may hear the voice of his neighbour”: so that one who does not voluntarily impose silence upon himself and, for the sake of religion, does not put his finger upon his mouth, may nevertheless, whether willing or unwilling, be compelled either to speak more sparingly or to be silent when he finds no one able to answer him.

Indeed, one who cannot bear silence and delights in verbosity is undoubtedly not moderately distressed if a hearer is withdrawn from his chatter, or if his hearer offers him no response.

## CHAPTER X

But when someone boils over too eagerly with the itch to speak, if he finds a hearer he becomes childishly cheerful, and often clings to that person with garrulous importunity until, as it were, fullness turns to vomiting, according to a certain pagan writer:

> The leech will not release the skin unless full of blood.

Some, if while speaking they find a listener, nevertheless still complain if they do not also have a respondent; and, as they judge it, intolerable injuries are done them if words are not returned for words in reciprocal exchange. Thus when Rabshakeh was sent to Jerusalem at the command of Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, and with threatening and voluble clamour urged the children of Israel to serve the Assyrians, Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah, the rulers of the city, requested that he speak to them in another language, lest the people, understanding, should be stirred up to make a voluble reply. “Speak, they said, to your servants in the Syrian language, for we understand it; do not speak to us in Judaean in the hearing of the people who are upon the wall” (IV Kings XVIII). They wished the people to be unable to understand Rabshakeh as he spoke, lest they should answer his verbosity in a like tongue, knowing that even the faint breath [Col. 0962A] of answering increases the blaze of babbling.

But he, unwilling to be restrained from his flood of speech and desiring that ampler material should be supplied him by those who answered, did not at all comply with the moderate counsel of those making the request, but spoke in the Judaean language in the hearing of the Judaeans. “Rabshakeh, it says, stood and cried with a loud voice in Judaean, and said: Hear the words of the great king, the king of the Assyrians” (*ibid.*), and so forth. Since prudent admonition could not temper his loquacious insolence, King Hezekiah, by an elegant stratagem, wished silence to be imposed upon the people, so that, seeing that no answer at all was made to him, he might be tortured all the more and thus at least be compelled to abandon his purpose. “They were silent, it says, and did not answer him a word; for the king had commanded them, saying: Do not answer him” (Isa. XXXVI).

[Col. 0962B] A prudent counsel: if the importunity of talkers is directed against anyone, let not word be returned for word, but silence; and let the mouth of those speaking wickedly be stopped by the obstacle of silence, and, as it were, the planned tower of bricks be destroyed. But because those building the city and tower possessed both a care for speaking first and a vehement desire to answer one another in equal word and deed, all had to be struck by an equal punishment and restrained from one and the same purpose by the same sentence. Their language therefore was confused, so that no one heard the voice of his neighbour, nor did speech, as intermediary, disclose their wishes to one another; rather, the hearer, stupefied at the voice of the one speaking first, fell silent, and did not willingly grant a hearing even to one whom he could not understand.

And when they were unwilling to hear one another and could not understand each other’s [Col. 0962C] voices, sudden difficulty compelled them to be silent; and what they had refused by nature to maintain out of regard for justice, they incurred as a punishment by God’s just judgment. Yet, deeming it intolerable to remain together in one place and to be restrained by unwelcome silence from completing their wickedness, they chose alike to be separated far from one another and to associate only with those whom they could understand when they spoke. For they had already been dispersed into a multitude of seventy-two nations; and by the same gift of languages they were, deservedly for their perversity, confused—namely, so that all languages were not possessed by all together, but each nation spoke only its own single language.

When the Paraclete poured himself out upon the disciples gathered on the day of Pentecost, he did not confuse their language by the abundance of this gift; rather, all languages were distributed to them all in such a way that not individual languages were given to individual persons, but all were granted to all. Therefore that was not believed to be a punitive confusion, but a spiritual outpouring for their consolation; by its gift one understood another’s new and diverse voices, and did not turn understanding and grace into an injury against the Giver. But those who attempted to build a city of brick, although they were of one speech, were struck by the divine sentence, so that, inasmuch as they had already been variously dispersed into so many nations, they might be confused in punishment by an equal number of languages. For seventy-two nations were already contained in the assembly of one multitude, which until then had been held together both by one place and by one speech; but on the plain of Shinar they are confused by as many languages [Col. 0963A] and are then divided from one another into as many parts.

For this confusion was assigned to them by divine ordering in such a way that a distinct language was attributed to each nation; and since in their excessive perversity they refused to keep silence, one nevertheless could not answer another. Thus each person was separated from the one with whom he was compelled to maintain silence and joined only to the one to whom he could speak; and so, driven by the divine sentence, they divided themselves locally among nations and languages, and, divided from one another, ceased from building the city they had proposed.

## CHAPTER XI

“Thus, it says, the Lord divided them from that place over all lands, and they ceased to build the city; and therefore its name was called [Col. 0963B] Babel, because there the speech of the whole earth was confused” (Gen. II). Rightly is the city which they had begun to build—while babbling, neglecting the bridle of justice, 555 and mutually exhorting one another to complete the work of wickedness—called Babel, or Babylonia, that is, “confusion.” For whoever refuses to restrain a voluble tongue by measured silence undoubtedly devises for himself a structure of confusion, where there is no rest, order perishes, and religion is scattered.

Hence also Nimrod, the leader of those building such a city, is said to have been a mighty hunter before the Lord (Gen. X). His name does not seem to oppose his occupation, nor his occupation confusion; indeed, in accordance with his name, his work was confused. For Nimrod means “transgressor” or “tyrant.” And he is not inappropriately called a transgressor or tyrant who presides over others not with the affection of charity but rules in tyrannical fashion; who, transgressing the bounds of justice, makes others transgressors and by his command or example renders his subjects worse.

He is significantly called a mighty hunter before the Lord, because he considers the destruction of himself alone insufficient unless he also pursues others in a violent hunt, unless his strength wickedly prevails against the Lord, so that a captive multitude of those like himself may serve him. By this Nimrod the eminence of certain persons seems to be figured: when, by God’s hidden judgment, they find themselves set over others, they do not cheer them by the majesty of a gentle hand, nor remove them from the confusion of noisy words; but by restless habits they take away from them the benefit [Col. 0963D] of repose and, by their burdensome instruction, provide them matter for speaking.

For when a perverse person obtains a position of authority and compels his subjects, as it were, to the duty of obedience, those same subjects either become dissolute by imitating their ruler or, abhorring his wickedness, frequently complain about his instruction. Thus silence, the guardian of religion, perishes among them; and not the peace of Jerusalem but the tumult and confusion of Babylon is built. For a ruler who hates discipline and orderly conduct, and whose laxity loosens the bridle of religion so that the people subject to him do not keep silence, builds not a city of peace, rest, or justice, but disturbs and confuses the unity of the gathered multitude.

For because he does not hold fast the unbending rectitude of religion, nor rest from the noise of unlawful deeds, his subjects, banishing the silence of repose, raise a tumult, acclaiming his perverse will with unworthy favour; or, in the words of the prophet Nahum, moaning like doves and murmuring in their hearts. But once peaceful silence has been banished, confusion possesses the disturbed crowd: it knows neither the proper time, order, nor measure for speaking, and yet boils over all the more immoderately into speech. Such confusion must be followed by division: those confused are divided from one another, lest their perverse fellowship carry them through to completion; and this division is compelled to turn away from one another unto failure.

Thus that hunter Nimrod and those who were with him are confused by many languages; being confused, they are divided from one another locally and desist from enlarging Babylon’s walls or towers, in which [Col. 0964B] they used bricks instead of stones and bitumen instead of mortar. From this it is clear how much confusion a ruler brings about, and with what force he erects Babylon’s walls or buildings, if, through prevailing negligence, he does not walk along the narrow path of religion; if he does not go before his subjects in excellence of rank or order of merits; if, presenting himself to them as an ill-advised leader, he breaks the silence of peace and incites them to tumult.

For, holding too eagerly the loosened rein of his own will, he provokes those fettered by the bond of subjection to clamour; and whereas he ought to have preceded them in living quietly, he labours restlessly to find persons like himself. Of him Moses says: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has been multiplied” (Gen. XVIII); and Isaiah: “I expected that he would do justice, and behold, a cry” (Isa. V).

## CHAPTER XII

A cry is excessive and harmful speech, displaying oppressive negligence and a disturbed spirit. When this spirit is disturbed and neglects to stand guard over itself, it delights to let loose its voluble tongue for harmful speech. For when justice’s restraint is more freely loosened, its rectitude is not maintained; as David declares, a man of many words shall in no way be directed—one who either does not put his finger upon his mouth or does not order his speech in judgment. Therefore David himself says: “I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue” (Ps. XXVIII).

For as, according to Isaiah, our strength shall be in hope and silence, so, according to Solomon, sin will not be lacking in much speaking [Col. 0964D] (Prov. X); nor does pure religion make serene the hidden recesses of the heart if it does not restrain the unstable tongue with the bolt of silence placed against it. “If anyone thinks himself religious,” says James (ch. I), “while not restraining his tongue, that man’s religion is vain.” The tongue is indeed known to be a small member, yet it can harm all the rest so greatly that it may, as it were, seize and set ablaze the whole forest, unless manly discernment strives to restrain it.

For this reason it is also sometimes called a sword in the Scriptures: when wickedly unrestrained, it works the destruction of death, either by separating the soul from the body, so that a person is killed temporally, or God from the soul, so that the person dies all the more grievously because inwardly. “Their teeth,” it says, “are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” [Col. 0965A] (Ps. LVI). Their tongue both caused Christ to be killed temporally and killed those same people spiritually; had they wished to restrain it beneath 556 just silence, they could, by repelling the desert of death, have attained life more happily.

Therefore death and life are rightly said to be in the power of the tongue, because by a certain privilege of power it obtains what it desires; and when by free choice it extends itself either toward death or toward life, it effectively lays hold of that which it has chosen and loved. “Death and life,” says Solomon, “are in the hand of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII). Death, certainly, when it swells insolently into speech; life, when it hides beneath welcome silence. Death, when it wanders abroad with laws dissolved; life, when it is restrained by discerning moderation. Death is in the tongue when someone by speaking either unjustly gives offence to a neighbour or stores up for himself the wrath of the supreme Judge as an avenger, with the bridle loosened for wicked folly that flatters him—unless, perhaps, it is tightened by the hand that imposes silence. Of this Solomon says: “He who imposes silence on a fool mitigates wrath” (Prov. XXVI).

For God’s wrath or a neighbour’s is easily provoked when the tongue of the imprudent is not constrained beneath silence. Even if it is found, perhaps, to say something good, yet because it does not know the proper time for uttering it, that very thing is reproved. Hence Jesus son of Sirach: “A parable is reproved from the mouth of a fool, for he will not utter it at its proper time” (Prov. XXV). Rightly, then, is the fool confined within the barriers of silence, lest hostile wickedness freely plunder him when he wanders abroad; for a city not enclosed by the defence of walls easily suffers loss when a multitude of enemies rushes in. Solomon, indicating this, says: “Like an open city, without an encircling wall, is the man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (*ibid.*).

But if he can restrain his spirit in speaking and wishes to apply diligence to maintaining silence, trusting in this protection he will be able both to remove certain inconveniences and to obtain very many things of no small advantage. For just as no one is found who, if he gives way to much speaking, does not sin—for much speaking is nearer to acquiring folly than silence is—so he who loves silence either deserves to become wise, because hearing rather than babbling is closer to acquiring wisdom, or, even if he is not wise, is nevertheless thought to be wise, since his folly is not disclosed to others by words bursting forth. On this Solomon says: “A fool, if he keeps silent, shall be considered wise; and if he presses his lips together, intelligent” (Prov. XVII).

And to a certain man who wished to be considered wise but could not endure being constrained within silence, another is said to have made an elegant reply, as the prudent Boethius is found to have related to us: “I would have understood you to be a philosopher, had you kept silent.” Therefore a person may seem a philosopher or wise man if he chooses to remain within the bounds of silence; and a virtue which in truth is not possessed in the heart is thought to be possessed when the veil of silence is drawn over it.

Finally, a man of less wisdom does not know how to moderate his words, and is found to bring about his own ruin or that of others when he speaks indiscriminately—either things wholly useless or things undoubtedly harmful. Gospel teaching invites us to silence concerning matters that do no good, and terrifies the despiser with fear of the account to be rendered; for an idle word, though human negligence makes light of it, divine severity strictly reproves in judgment. “Every idle word,” it says, “which men shall have spoken, they will render account for it on the day of judgment” (Matt. XII). And Isaiah: “If you cease,” he says, “from pointing the finger and speaking what does no good” (Isa. LVIII).

The wise man Philo likewise says: “Keep yourselves from murmuring that does no good, because obscure speech shall not go away empty” (Wis. I). Obscure speech is speech that does not strike the minds of those who utter it with the manifest noise of harm, but silently insinuates itself into the unwary and less prudent; and, just as it does not claim that it will greatly benefit them, so by lying it suggests that it will do them no harm at all. Obscure speech is that upon which the ray of truth does not shine, or in whose truth charity does not spread itself abroad; that is, whose arising is not preceded by an intention of right usefulness, and in which either simplicity is not joined by prudence or prudence by simplicity.

Such speech, according to Scripture, shall not go away empty, because it does not leave its author innocent, but makes him liable to accusation, if not for malice, at least for idleness—the former damnable, the latter, though lightly, yet inevitably to be punished. Perhaps for this reason the prophet Elisha recalled the sons of the prophets from idle speech and more diligently invited them to silence, when he was himself greatly anxious lest Elijah should be taken up into heaven in his absence. For the sons of the prophets who were at Bethel, and others afterward who were at Jericho, went out and said to him: “Do you know that the Lord will take your master from you today?” He answered: “I also know it; be silent” (IV Kings II).

There is no need, he says, for you to utter uselessly what you ask me as though it were unknown, though it is known to me, lest, while I am compelled to incline my ear to your empty words, I be found to turn aside, even slightly, from that toward which I was tending. Be silent, then, lest through loquacious levity you incur vain speech, and through heedless vain speech incur offence; for idleness immediately condemns useless speech, and it is a service of justice to keep silence concerning it.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0966D]

If idle speech is so greatly reproved—a speech which levity produces and no fruitful effect follows—how ought speech to be rebuked and condemned when it is faulty both at the root and at the surface, poisonous with pride, envy, rage, and imprudence? Of it the Psalmist says: “Your mouth abounded in malice, and your tongue devised deceits; sitting, you spoke against your brother, and placed a stumbling-block against the son of your mother” (Ps. XLIX). And Jeremiah: “They stretched out their tongue like a bow of falsehood” (Jer. IX); and shortly below: “Their tongue is a wounding arrow” (*ibid.*). And he adds: “Shall I not visit for these things, says the Lord, [Col. 0967A] or shall not my soul take vengeance upon such a nation?” (Jer. IX).

A lying, wounding, irreverent, unbridled tongue shall not go unpunished before the judgment of the strict Judge; divine scrutiny will visit it and, taking vengeance, judge it more severely in judgment. Isaiah confirms this: “You shall judge,” he says, “every tongue resisting you in judgment” (Isa. LIV). The Lord judges the tongue that resists him so that it may resist no longer; so that, willing or unwilling, it may now desist from its evil speech; so that, having refused silence in pursuit of the holiness proposed to it, it may at last be silent in life because its faculty of speaking has been removed. Indicating this above through the same Isaiah, he says: “I will take vengeance, and no man shall resist me” (Isa. XLVII). And he adds: “Sit, be silent, and enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans; you shall no longer be called lady of kingdoms” (*ibid.*).

When, he says, the time of strict vengeance comes, in which human disputation of reason will not resist me, you who enjoyed the broad freedom of your own wandering and babbling will, though you seemed to sit like a lady upon the throne of rule, become mute with your throat stopped and your jaws choked; and when your day is interrupted, you will hide in the secret place of darkness. “Sit,” he says, “be silent.” For nothing is more burdensome to one wandering and unstable than sitting, and nothing more intolerable to one loquacious and babbling than silence. Sit and be silent, so that as you formerly rejoiced to do things opposed to me, so now in reciprocal recompense you may suffer what is burdensome to you.

For just as those who love me and obey my commands are brought, through the gift of my love, into the haven of their own will, so those who maintain continual hatred against me and rail against me with unbridled voices are compelled in turn to endure my hatred. This is what the Lord likewise indicates through Jeremiah, saying: “My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; it raised its voice against me; therefore I hate it” (Jer. XII). The Lord likewise hates the inheritance that presumes to raise its voice against him and, according to the prophet Ezekiel, persists in confirming itself by speech; judging severely, he disinherits it and at last imposes a limit, so that it may proceed no longer according to its pleasure, and so that what, through prevailing wickedness, did not lay aside its will to rail may, under the punishment of divine justice, lose its wretched capacity.

For, if they continue in their purpose, both the perversity of unbelievers and heedless talkativeness are reproved, and neither can by hereditary right possess salvation. The former knows not faith, and, not illumined by the light of faith, is wholly darkened; the latter is already adorned by conspicuous faith, like the morning radiance of the sun, but is discoloured by an incontinent tongue, like a cloud rushing in. Therefore, after saying through the prophet Jeremiah, “It raised its voice against me; therefore I hate it,” he added: “Is my inheritance a speckled bird to me? Is it a bird dyed all over?” (*ibid.*).

A bird is variegated with speckled markings when a soul is indeed illumined by the right title of faith but stained by the vice of immoderate speech; when it does not depart from the form of ecclesiastical religion, yet does not walk within the bounds of enjoined silence. And because two masters are not rightly served, its Creator himself refuses to possess the bird found thus speckled, since he wishes to have nothing in common with an alien master. For this bird has clothed itself in varied colours: while it has joined a discordant tongue to the religion it has undertaken; while it has restrained itself by the bonds of an outward rule, but unbridled its mobile tongue irregularly. God himself, who wishes to possess all things alone, wholly rejects it, because he is not permitted to possess one of its two parts.

“Is my inheritance a speckled bird to me?” By no means. “A speckled bird,” he says, “shall not be my inheritance, any more than a bird dyed all over.” For just as no one belongs to my portion who more shamelessly rejects religion and, casting aside native whiteness, is darkened by the adulterous dye of soot, so neither does the one who more suitably professes himself religious, if he does not fear, by the open gate of unchecked speech, to raise his voice against me.

Therefore from speech of this sort, which is proved contrary to God, one must keep silence with the utmost care and utmost zeal, so that by this silence the desert of death may be driven away and this repulse may produce the life-giving justice. This silence must be maintained always, everywhere, and by everyone; it must never, nowhere, and by no one be set aside. For just as divine law gives no one permission to sin, so it imposes upon all a command diligently to perform what is just.

## CHAPTER XIV

Therefore the silence described above is imposed upon the aforesaid speech; and, conversely, forbidden silence must be put away, for Scripture declares that it opposes divine justice, and divine goodness, compassionately caring, forbids it to everyone. Accordingly, it diligently commands the wise man not to be silent, not to confine his learned tongue behind the lock of silence; but, after spending a fitting time in silence according to the command, he may now appropriately open the gate in speech.

Indeed Socrates the philosopher, who bound his disciples by oath to silence, did not take from them forever the liberty of speaking; rather, he imposed upon them a fixed period of silence, so that over the course of five years he might make each one learned, knowing that a silent listener is instructed far more effectively, while a babbler is hindered by the untimely noise of words. Another wise man aptly indicates this, saying: “But if the raven could feed silently, he would have more food and far less quarrelling.” From this it is clear that the wise pagans do not wish anyone being instructed to be oppressed by silence, since, by keeping silence, he deserves to receive more nourishment and wisdom; and when he has been suitably fed and taught under silence, he is permitted—indeed perhaps plainly commanded—to speak.

I judge that these pagans received this from our Scriptures. Although they did not grasp their spiritual understanding, they received at least some moral understanding; commending in them what they knew suited their own purpose, they, being unbelievers, left the rest to believers, and being natural persons, to spiritual persons. One of these spiritual persons says: “Teach me, and I will be silent” (Job VI). Another says: “Before you speak, learn” (Ecclus. XVIII). And Ecclesiastes indicates that one who wishes to learn must keep silent, and that, after being taught through silence, he must speak: “There is,” he says, “a time for silence and a time for speaking” (Ecclus. III). Thus a prudent man knows that the time for silence comes first and that the time for speaking follows in second place, according to its proper order.

Therefore divine law commands a wise man to speak; his orderly speech is not inappropriately compared with a honeycomb, since his persuasion sweetens the hearer’s soul, heals acquired weakness, and strengthens health. Hence Solomon says: “An orderly sweetness of speech is a honeycomb to the soul, and health to the bones” (Prov. XVI). And above: “The tongue of the wise is health” (Prov. XII). Since the tongue of the wise is health, who can doubt that it ought not to be restrained by silence, but applied to the unlearned and infirm, so that, as dogs licking the foulness of sores, they may alleviate pain, drive away disease, and restore health? Of this David says: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies” (Ps. LXVII).

In the figure of this, the dogs in the Gospel are said to lick the decaying Lazarus, because wise persons are employed for the less wise, that by the medicine of the mouth and the manifold care of speech, as with iron, oil, drink, poultice, and bandage, they may cut away what is harmful and diligently apply what is beneficial. Wise men ought not, indeed, keep such words silent, but should stir the less learned by untiring speech—unless perhaps they see those same hearers to be so obstinate that, having heard the word of life, they become worse. To such persons Paul said: “Because you reject the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

Concerning this Ecclesiasticus warns: “Where there is no hearing, do not pour out speech” (Ecclus. XXXII). And Solomon in Proverbs: “Do not speak,” he says, “in the ears of fools, because they will despise the instruction of your eloquence” (Prov. XXIII). Because of men of this sort, who obey none of the teachers’ admonitions but, the more they are warned, pursue their persecution with the greater bitterness, those same teachers often veil their knowledge in silence and do not reveal what is holy to dogs or pearls to swine. This is not because they begrudge those to whom they ought to supply the nourishment of teaching, but because they await a time when they can more suitably fulfil it.

Therefore Ecclesiasticus says: “A wise man will keep silence until the proper time, and rightly until the proper time” (Ecclus. XX). When the wise man sees the time approaching in which not being silent is either honourable or useful for him, he will not hide the lamp of knowledge beneath the covering of a bushel, hearing the wholesome admonition of Scripture’s command: “Do not hide your wisdom in its beauty; for wisdom is known in speech, and understanding, knowledge, and instruction in the word of the sensible man” (Ecclus. IV).

Since understanding, knowledge, and instruction are in the word of the sensible person, silence must not be imposed upon so great an excellence; for knowledge hidden away is likened to an unseen treasure. A certain philosopher declares that it is vain for its thoughts not to be uttered: “Since it teaches that joys should gladly be brought forth, it is vain not to speak fitting thoughts.” Just as those who, oppressed by pride, do not speak fitting thoughts are reproved not only by secular but also by divine writings, and are called by the prophet “mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. LVI), loving to sleep unto both their own destruction and that of others, so those who speak what they rightly think in fitting places and at fitting times are exalted with deserved praises.

For these are the ones whose knowledge is not held contemptible, and whose tongue is said to adorn their knowledge; for they know what should suitably be said, to whom, when, and how, and a ready tongue serves that very knowledge. Of them Solomon says: “The tongue of the wise adorns knowledge” (Prov. XV). The knowledge of the wise is fruitful with its due adornment when the tongue is suitably eloquent in bringing it forth: that is, when what knowledge has deserved to obtain by understanding and study, the tongue confidently undertakes not to conceal, for the sake of usefulness.

In this flight from silence, both the inward meaning of the speaker shines out and the hearer’s mind rests in welcome repose; thus no small benefit grows for them both, since one is fittingly and delightfully strengthened to speak and the other to hear. Solomon aptly indicates this: “Golden apples in silver settings: one who speaks a word at its proper time” (Prov. XXV). By “apple” is signified fruit; by “gold,” the precious brightness of wisdom; by “silver,” eloquence; and by “setting,” the gracious sweetness of that same eloquence. If these are united, nothing more useful and nothing more welcome among human beings is found—as one knows far better who experiences it by possessing rather than merely speaking.

Therefore one is rightly said to place golden apples in silver settings [Col. 0970C] who knows how to dispense fruitful wisdom in sweet eloquence, who inclines to declare fitting thoughts while speaking at the appropriate time, and in whose sweet speech the hearer reclines more gently. “Golden apples in silver settings: one who speaks a word at its proper time.” And rightly, “at its proper time”: for the wise man is found to speak only at his proper time, and by this he is plainly known to be wise. For just as Scripture declares, “A wise man will keep silence until the proper time” (Ecclus. XX), so that same man, when the time for speaking draws near, will not be silent.

## CHAPTER XV

Such watchmen, Isaiah writes, the Lord set upon the walls of Jerusalem; and he expressly commanded them to speak without ceasing, because by the speech of watchmen the hope of enemies lying in ambush is frustrated, while the citizens’ diligence in resistance is not wearied by continual labour. “Upon your walls, Jerusalem,” he says, “I have set watchmen; all day and all night they shall never be silent” (Isa. LXII).

The walls of Jerusalem are the multitude of believers in the Church: invincible strength, compacted by the mortar of charity, makes them firm. Each of them, as Peter declares, is called a living stone, and they make walls out of themselves when they are joined by the covenant of mutual love. “And you yourselves,” he says, “as living stones are built up into spiritual houses” (I Pet. II). Upon walls of this sort God places Peter, Paul, and the other watchmen of this kind, and so imposes upon them the concern of guarding that he wills them not merely to avoid the sluggishness of soft drowsiness, but, vigorous in alertness, never to be silent. “All day,” he says, “and all night they shall never be silent.”

Whether the day shines with temporal prosperity or favour, or the night’s darkness of loss or threats pours itself forth, the wise and faithful watchman does not know how to sleep beneath silence, but, mindful of the Master’s command, loves to preach it with unwearied zeal. Therefore, after the Spirit had said through the prophet, “All day and all night they shall never be silent,” he added, addressing those same watchmen: “You who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give him no silence” (Isa. LXII). You who remember him who set you over the walls, know that you will not please him by sluggish silence; and therefore you will rightly give him none of those things that are not pleasing to him, but will speak tirelessly for the guardianship of the walls.

Peter and his fellow apostles remembered both this command and the one who gave it. Though the Pharisees prohibited them, they stood firm in speaking; and although the night of threats, insults, prisons, and beatings was poured over them—things which they endured altogether—they could not keep silent about what they had heard and seen: “We cannot,” they said, “but speak the things which we have heard and seen” (Acts IV). A wonderful thing! They were so inflamed with ardour for speaking and so strongly detested unwelcome silence that they not only confidently spoke what they knew, but, intoxicated by the new wine of the Spirit, could no longer refrain from speaking.

## CHAPTER XVI

And rightly: in order that they could not refrain from speaking, the Holy Spirit came upon them; upon those to whom the omnipotent Word had earlier come from the royal seats, that he might himself overcome the hardened silence of old and unlock silent mouths with David’s key. For the world was held guilty of long-established silence and was oppressed as it were by the palpable darkness of a most dreadful night, when the Word of God the Father gently poured himself out, like dew upon our fleece, and a virgin womb brought him forth before human eyes.

The wise man Philo, indicating this, said: “For when quiet silence held all things, and night in its course had reached the middle of its journey, your omnipotent Word, O Lord, leaped down from heaven, from the royal seats, as a stern warrior into the midst of the land of destruction” (Wis. XVIII). He calls this silence “quiet” by an epithet—that is, a property of the thing—for it belongs to silence to be quiet; otherwise it is not silence if it is not quiet.

Although, in saying “quiet,” he seems to designate that silence which is known to take place at midnight: when the noises of evening have more fully ceased, and those of morning have not yet begun. For although approaching night seems to bring silence, as though warning people to rest from daytime labour and noise, some nevertheless are accustomed still to work during its first part, and likewise to rise for work during its last. But in its middle part all more generally rest, either occupied with sleep or at least hidden in their chambers. At this untimely hour silence becomes quiet, whereas at the boundary of the departing or returning day it is more often disturbed.

But quiet silence is known especially to occur at midnight. Hence another translation has not “quiet silence” but “silence holding the middle,” by which it seems to signify nothing other than that silence is known to be more quietly observed at midnight: “While all things held the middle silence.” That by “middle” it plainly designates the silence of midnight is subsequently indicated when it adds:

560 **CHAPTER XVII.**
“And night in its course had reached the middle point” (Wisdom 18). In this silence of the dead of night, when people give themselves more deeply to sleep, the harlot in the Book of Kings is said to have risen—the one whose own child had died because she lay upon him through negligence—and to have taken the living child from the side of the other woman while she slept. When the latter perceived this in the morning as she wished to nurse her son, she complained and accused her of having dared to commit theft; and, since their dispute could reach no conclusion between them, both were brought before Solomon’s truthful judgment. One of them said: “Rising in the silence of the dead of night, she took my son from my side while your servant was sleeping, and placed him in her own bosom; but her son, who was dead, she put in my bosom” (3 Kings 3).

This woman complains that, in the silence of the dead of night, her fellow lodger rose to perpetrate the crime of theft, when she ought rather to have been sleeping—or perhaps, if awake, at least resting from work.
