For this is why midnight is called the dead of night: then especially is not the time to do anything. Yet this woman did not consider that she should have feared this hour more, and guarded against it with greater vigilance and concern; for one who delights in bringing some injury upon another by deceit or ambush chooses an untimely time, in order to be less guarded against. Thus, when the Egyptians are overwhelmed by heavy sleep at midnight, their firstborn are slain by the destroying Angel; forewarned of his coming, the children of Israel await it with watchful concern, and, awaiting it, are not afflicted by a similar misfortune.

Remembering this, David did not wish to sleep at midnight, but to forestall the coming Lord with anxious expectation, so that, should He perhaps come again to disturb the quiet, or middle, silence, He might find him on His arrival not only awake but intent upon praises. “At midnight,” he says, “I rose to give thanks to You” (Psalm 118).

For he knew that the kingdom of heaven, which is compared with ten virgins and which is entered only by those who keep watch and possess the oil of praise, is especially declared by a true judgment to be either offered or taken away when it is least expected by the heedless or sleeping. For when the cry was made at midnight, the bridegroom came, excluding those whom he did not find prepared and supplied with oil, but bringing with him to the wedding those whom neither sleep nor a delayed purchase of oil had deceived. Thus the Lord is accustomed often to come when the careless watchman has settled into deeper silence; when only a few, solicitous for Him, have persisted in praise and vigil, while all the rest have kept silence as if in the dead of night—that is, in the middle of the night. This middle or quiet silence held all things, and night, as it were untimely, was pursuing its middle course, when the Word of God the Father chose to become man for the salvation of us all and, by His human presence, powerfully to wage war against harmful silence.

For at that time the fifth age of the world was in progress, said to have begun with Jeconiah. It was so overwhelmed by silence that in it there was scarcely anyone who spoke God’s word openly with confidence. From Abraham to Jeconiah there had unfolded a succession of two ages, in which a multitude of patriarchs and prophets had spoken more abundantly; but this age is found to have had no prophets, except the very few whom we read to have arisen at its beginning. For at its beginning there appeared Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi—whom the Hebrews maintain to be Ezra [Col. 0973B]. Like twilight in the night, they resisted for a little while the approaching silence; while they were present, truth preached shone faintly, like glittering stars, and did not wholly lead the minds of their hearers away into the error of ignorance.

But after they were taken away, night, sinking into the depths, grew darker still; heavy sleep crept on, and it rested from the sound of preaching. That whole age ran its very long course in this fashion: no preaching encountered the darkness, nor did light encounter the silence. Therefore, when the whole world had fallen silent from the zeal of preaching, and the night of ignorance held its middle course—that is, its deepest point—“the almighty Word of God leapt from the royal thrones, and, as a most stern warrior, sprang into the midst of the land of destruction.”

The royal thrones are the diverse multitude of dwelling places which God prepared according to the merits of diverse deeds, so that in them each person might enjoy, according to his merit, kingship or dominion, while He Himself is acknowledged as King of kings and Lord of lords. By the land of destruction is signified the earthly sinfulness of humankind. The Son of God, the Word of the Father, the almighty Speech, is remembered as coming to it so that He might drive away the aforesaid silence in a blessed destruction and, as a stern warrior, dispel by His light the darkness of ignorance. And when that same Word is said to leap from heaven and spring into the midst of the land of destruction, the name “leap” commends the suddenness of His coming. He delights to come to those by whom He is not expected—those whom deep darkness, heavy sleep, and quiet silence held fast, so that they did not see the One who was mercifully preparing to save them.

Yet Zechariah, Simeon, Anna, and Elizabeth forestalled Him as He came. Taught by the prophetic Spirit, they foresaw that He would soon come; perhaps they sang something concerning Him, like cocks at midnight, but they could not awaken those held by heavy sleep with their slender sound. He alone, therefore, could awaken them; He alone could effectively disturb the wrongly quiet silence in which they lay. For He is read to be not merely powerful but almighty Speech, who, coming in His own person, tirelessly speaks the command of the Father.

## Chapter XVIII

Finally, when He chose to be born and to appear as a man before human eyes [Col. 0974A], the actual night was found to have reached its middle course; and angels came upon a few shepherds keeping watch over their flock in that region, in a new and wondrous vision. They turned the nocturnal darkness into light and quiet silence into a cry, while with great rejoicing they announced to the shepherds the Savior’s birth. At His birth the angels of surpassing brightness rejoice in heaven, and on earth peace is bestowed upon people of good will (Luke 2).

On hearing this, the shepherds rejoice beyond measure; when the angels depart, they too break the silence of the night and encourage one another to go as far as Bethlehem, to see the word that has happened, and to render a new service to the new child. Nor was it enough that angels and shepherds broke quiet silence and burst forth in joyful voices into divine praises during that same hour of the night: heaven too brought forth a new star, to perform the office, as it were, of one who speaks, since it spoke not with a tongue but with a mystical light of a new kind. Its visible appearance, revealing a welcome mystery, stirred astrologers in the regions of the East; guided by its shining, three Magi hurried to Jerusalem, hoping to find the newborn child in the royal city. “Where,” they say, “is He who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw His star in the East and have come to worship Him. Then Herod,” it says, “was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him” (Matthew 2).

You see that at the birth of the new King Chaldeans and Jews alike, though in different ways, were disturbed, and that both were strongly incited to search. The former did so in order, when they found Him, to render humble service with gifts offered; the latter, burning with envy, to persecute the same One. When the Chaldeans found Him, they worshipped Him according to their purpose; and, warned in dreams, they refused to obey Herod’s command, returned by another road to their own country with joy, and proclaimed to the peoples of the nations the mighty deeds of the King whom they had found.

But when Herod saw that the Magi, by not reporting back to him, had deceived him and had by prudent counsel shut him out from what he had hoped for, he could not restrain his rage or keep silence. Rather, he burned more openly and obstinately to persecute the King. He therefore orders all boys born in Bethlehem under two years of age to be slaughtered, so that He might not be able to escape among the rest; he preferred that there be no child at all in those regions rather than that the One he sought should survive along with the others. For this reason that same Child both allowed and willed these things to happen: so that the renown of His name might spread more widely, and so that, when silence had been driven far away, the Word made flesh for the salvation of all the elect might become speech in every nation and place.

Nor only when He was born did Christ disturb quiet silence and stir both good and wicked people to speech; when He had suffered and died, He also chose to rise on the third day and to have His resurrection proclaimed far and wide to all. This resurrection took place when the upper regions of the world were darkened by the sun’s absence, and the presence of night covered the face of the earth; when deep sleep removed human concerns; when, in the deep course of night, silence contained all things; when cocks, girded as it were about the loins with wakeful concern, sang together, distinguishing the various hours of the night by their announcing song. At this untimely hour Christ chose to rise from the dead, when mortals, freed from cares, are not accustomed to be awakened.

But in the very early morning the diligence of the women is displayed. As they go forth in sorrow, an angel consoles them, telling them that He has risen whom they did not sufficiently believe could be enclosed in a tomb; that He lives in His resurrection, whom in feminine error they were seeking among the dead. Why, I ask, are all these things done at night, when people are oppressed by sleep, silence, and darkness, except that those who had fallen into torpor might by such a benefit be restored to vigour; that those held in harmful silence might speak divine mighty deeds; and that those whose understanding was darkened might long to gain the light of knowledge?

## Chapter XIX

Moreover, to crown grace: after Christ returned to the place from which He had come and set the body He had assumed from us at the Father’s right hand, He did not delay to send from there to the apostles the Holy Spirit, as He had promised. Once He had sent Him, He inflamed their hearts so that they even despised death, and opened their mouths wide so that they could no longer refrain from speaking. This is fittingly proclaimed as occurring in the full brightness of day, when its third hour is already drawing near to noon. At noon the sun shines more brightly from the summit of heaven’s axis and, its course now completed, burns more fiercely.

By this it is indicated that, through the gift of such great generosity, such force of love was poured out in them that, for the sake of the word of preaching entrusted to and undertaken by them, they advanced in bearing the sufferings of passion. In a manner of speaking, the sun seems to approach noon, where it is said to be both brighter and hotter, when the righteous person, under the Spirit’s urging, not only does not depart from righteousness but presses on more strongly to preach it and advances. The more a strong adversary confronts and resists him, the more clearly and confidently he preaches and persists. And while, for love of preaching and persistence in truth, he endures threats and the hatred of human perversity, through the grace of progress he is far from the morning rising and becomes like the sun at noon, or like glowing gold in a furnace: more precious in bright heat or fervent light of merits the more he burns in enduring the seething malice of the reprobate.

For that person Christ died; for that person He who died rose again: the person whose darkness He did not disdain to remove, whose ignorance He did not disdain to wipe away, whose languid torpor and old silence He banished, and whose conscience He trained for living and whose knowledge He trained for speaking. Upon that person, suddenly coming down as at the third hour, the consoling Spirit is poured forth in tongues of fire. He makes that person’s conscience so secure and bold, and the tongue so eloquent, that he cannot keep silent about the things that must be spoken; for their sake he is ready to endure the blazing furnace of suffering.

Such were those upon whom the Pharisees tried to impose silence, forbidding them to speak any further to the people in Jesus’ name. Yet, though forbidden, they did not keep silent under the Spirit’s urging, but willingly and gladly endured the insults laid upon them. “They went,” it says, “rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). The rage of persecutors inflicted the insult, while spiritual anointing soothed the mind of the sufferer; and the more fiercely the former rages, the more powerfully the latter is accustomed to bring relief. For the persecutor is not as powerful to inflict what is grievous as the consoling Spirit is to endure it; indeed, the Spirit is much more effective in removing silence than the persecutor is in imposing it.

Accordingly, having received the Spirit in fire, the apostles speak while their adversaries persecute them with threats, scourges, and prisons. Although their preaching is assailed in many ways, impatient of silence it casts aside its covering and is laid bare; and though it is burdensome to many who do not possess the same Spirit, it is nevertheless made manifest to all, in season and out of season.

## Chapter XX

Perhaps this is why they were commanded not to use shoes, but, being sent to preach, to walk with bare feet, possessing only sandals, by whose interposition they are separated from the ground and are not harmed by thorns, briars, and serpent bites. Thus the lower part of the foot is covered, while the upper part remains uncovered, so that preaching may neither cling shamefully to earthly filth nor hide with equal shame beneath the shadow of silence.

For when preaching chiefly hunts after earthly gain; when it is entangled in the thorns of avarice and the prickles of empty glory [Col. 0976C]; when, rash or untaught, it does not avoid the poisonous bite of false speech; when it regards this and similar things as no loss to itself—then surely the speaker’s foot seems to have no sandal but to cling wholly and carnally to the earthly pavement. But when that same preacher wastes away because of the tongues of detractors, or trembles at the threats of persecutors, and through anger or fear falls silent when he ought to speak, his foot, as though pressed beneath some covering, is not exposed above, and vile dead flesh grows over the form of the word.

Indeed, when Moses was called to be sent to lead the children of Israel out of Egypt and was mystically taught how he ought to persist in preaching, the Lord said: “Remove the footwear from your feet” (Exodus 3), so that your preaching may be revealed to all and not darkened by a covering superimposed by resentment or fear. Likewise the apostles are commanded to walk barefoot in preaching, so that no terror and no detraction may obscure their preaching; rather, it may be set like a lamp upon the height of a lampstand, and the light shining before people may bring about not its own glory but God’s.

This also seems to be indicated by prophetic speech, when the voice of preachers is commanded to be raised, lest it be shamefully repressed by harmful fear, but, its covering driven away, be boldly expressed. “Cry out,” the Lord says through Isaiah, “do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet, you who proclaim good news to Jerusalem. Lift it up; do not fear. Say to the cities of Judah: Behold your God” (Isaiah 58; 40).

The Lord wishes the preacher not only to cry out but not to cease crying; and He commands him to raise his voice not softly or moderately, but in the manner of a trumpet—perhaps so that he may effectively rouse his hearers to battle. For the trumpet was formerly used in battle: when it sounded in advance, the battle was fought, since an army became more courageous upon hearing its sound, but seemed to act more feebly when it did not hear it. This trumpet fittingly represents the preacher who exhorts the minds of the faithful to overcome invisible enemies. His exhortation is not useless or ineffective if he strives to raise it and commends it with worthy strength. “Lift up,” He says, “your voice in strength; lift it up; do not fear.”

Due strength raises the voice of the person whose holiness so strengthens his conscience that he neither fears to be wounded by adversaries’ threats nor delights to be softened by flatterers’ favors. Once he is fortified with worthy strength against both, he will be manfully ready to speak freely; he will oppose and exclude whatever confronts him, and no importunity will close his open mouth. Indeed, after saying, “Lift it up; do not fear,” He adds: “Say to the cities of Judah: behold your God.” For the person who speaks what is right to the cities rightly is one whom no fear effectively opposes, who, laying aside fear of all hostile pressures, loves in an affection of piety the peace and salvation of the cities.

The cities of Judah are said to be faithful souls, which confess their Creator in word and deed. The preacher is commanded to give them the wheat of the word in due measure, so that he may return to the Lord with increase what was entrusted to him. If he says, “Lord, your mina has gained ten minas” (Luke 19), he will hear from Him: “You will have authority over ten cities” (ibid.). And if he says, “Lord, your mina has made five minas,” he will hear from Him: “And you, be over five cities” (ibid.). For he receives, as it were, the rightful authority of power over as many cities as those to which he imparted the word of saving truth, as many cities as he fortified with the rampart and defenses of preaching—that is, as many souls as he gained for God through the word entrusted to him.

For the souls whose instruction he labored to assist are rightly said to be under his leadership as well, since to him as teacher and guide the rewarder of all good things credits whatever good their instructed and obedient humility accomplishes. This teacher or guide is commanded not merely to speak but to cry out, and by crying to raise his voice like a trumpet, so that the understanding or reason divinely poured into the spiritual mind may be fruitful when speech is joined to it in a marital covenant. For it is like a modest virgin kept in a shut chamber, who remains barren because she does not know a man, when contemplative reason delights in the privacy of silence and is not made fruitful by the marital union of assumed speech. It does not suffice for anyone wise to possess reason unless he joins speech to that reason, so that he may make in himself a kind of nuptial marriage from which a spiritual benefit may proceed as offspring.

## Chapter XXI

In a figure of this matter, a certain philosopher invents a marriage celebration [Note: [Col. 0977D] Martianus Capella, *On the Marriage of Philology and Mercury*. See book I, p. 132; book II, p. 179 ff.; [Col. 0978D] edition of Ulrich Friedrich Kopp, Frankfurt am Main, 1836, quarto.], and assembles the very multitude of heavenly gods to approve it. Though they perhaps have differing views on certain points, they all give one and the same consent to this marriage. All of them judge it entirely fitting that Mercury—whom that philosopher understands as representing speech—should take a wife in marriage at the age of puberty, when he is of mature and suitable age for taking a wife. Thus, when Jupiter declared that the marriage ought to take place, he is said to have spoken of Mercury before the assembled heavenly beings:

> “The ages, enriched by accomplished labours,  
> urge that he be lawfully joined in marriage;  
> and added strength calls for the marriage chamber.”

Because, he says, he has gained the strength appropriate to his age and has already experienced many labours in due season, these appropriate circumstances seem to demand the bridal chamber, so that he may delay no longer to unite a worthy wife to himself. Concerning her Jupiter adds:

> “But a maiden has pleased us, indeed exceedingly learned,  
> and equal in zeal.”

Since this Mercury, who is said to represent speech, ought now at a mature age to take a wife, the prudent young man rightly finds pleasing above all others the woman whom he sees to be devoted both to commendable learning and to an equal purpose. When he is bound to her in a marital covenant, he is found to acquire worthy children by her, and this marriage makes him very fruitful; without it, as though living a celibate life, he becomes idle. Therefore Jupiter concludes his speech:

> “Let them be joined; for it is fitting that, under like auspices,  
> they should enrich the stars with our descendants.”

What, then, is the maiden to whom Mercury ought to be joined and from whose embrace and marital covenant he ought not to be separated? Jupiter himself is found above to indicate this: “Know,” he says, “that Mercury seeks marriage with Philology.” And above: “I perceive,” he says, “that he has long been inflamed with love for Philology.”

By Philology is represented spiritual reason, which the supreme Craftsman works in the soul of every person. By it the soul perceives within itself what is just and unjust, and prudently examines and distinguishes what ought to be retained and what rejected. Speech seeks and adopts marriage, as it were, with this reason; burning with love for it, speech desires to join it to itself, because there is no propriety or usefulness in speech which the bosom and prudence of reason do not nourish and advance. Without its inward offspring and embrace, outward speech is either called babbling and held cheap, or, restrained by fear and distrust, grows cold and blushes to come before the ears of the wise, since it does not shine with bridal ornament and rational learning.

But if reason is present within, dwelling as though in a chamber; if there it delights to preserve and cultivate its native beauty; then there too it wisely instructs and forms the person who is to speak prudently, and fittingly shapes the speech that is to come forth as from a bridal chamber. Hence Juno says: “Yet he ought to submit to the bond of that same virgin, who cannot endure to join him even when he wishes to rest.” The union with this reason does not weaken speech—Mercury as bridegroom—but rather heaps up his honor and merit. Concealed in the chamber of the heart, it does not allow him to languish, as it were, under his blanket, but causes him to spread forth into eloquent branches [564], having living confidence in the root.

As Paul spread such public branches and spoke more copiously at Lystra, the crowds bestowed honor on him—miserably mistaken in this, that they declared him not a man but the god Mercury. “The gods,” they say, “have come down to us in the likeness of men. And they called Barnabas Jupiter, but Paul Mercury, because he was the leader in speech” (Acts 14). Do not such marriages seem to you to be celebrated in Paul, and Mercury to be joined to Philology in a kind of marriage? For love in the inward secrecy of reason makes him learned, and from there speech comes forth polished, like a bridegroom from his chamber.

Thus speech and reason came together in him in a pleasing covenant; thus they found a pleasing dwelling together in him, so that reason proved useful and fruitful through the ministry of speech, while speech was nourished in reason’s lap or bosom. For just as speech is not sufficiently commended if it does not rest upon reason, so reason is judged barren if it does not proceed to union with speech. Separated from one another, neither is accounted sufficiently fruitful or useful; joined together, the two are mutually nourished with fruitfulness. Therefore it is fitting and right that Philology be betrothed to Mercury, that inward reason be married to outward speech, because what inward reason has dictated for expression ought not to be crushed beneath the torpor of silence. Indeed, that alone, and especially that, ought to be said concerning which reason has judged that silence ought not to be imposed.

Accordingly, as the nine Muses sang in succession the praises of this maiden appropriate to the aforesaid marriage, each wished her own *symbolum* [refrain] to end in such a way that they might sing responsively and, in their singing, affirm that she was worthy to be joined to Mercury. When the song of each Muse had ended, all together repeated in harmonious chorus:

> “Ascend the temples of heaven, maiden  
> worthy of so great a covenant.”

The second-to-last of them, Euterpe, says:

> “Rightly ascend  
> the council of the Thunderer,  
> you whom alone it is fitting  
> to join in Mercurial  
> covenant.”

How worthy she is held to be of the honor of so great a covenant, and how fittingly she alone should be joined to this Mercury, the last, Thalia, declares in her song, carefully intertwining praises suited to them both:

> “He is learned among the gods,  
> but the maiden is more learned;  
> now, now are blessed the arts  
> which you both thus consecrate.”

Speech founded upon sound reason is indeed learned; more learned is reason whose doctrinal beauty shines forth in speech. The arts are blessed at the worthy summit of praise when they are consecrated through the common presence of these two. For no art and no discipline of knowledge is fittingly pursued if it is not fashioned in their common workshop—if, in treating it, either the keenness of reason does not assist speech, or fitting speech does not attend reason as its guide.

Therefore, after Thalia had set forth their praises in many ways—for she had extended her song rather more fully [Col. 0980B]—she brought that very extension to a conclusion in the form of a prayer, and, having uttered the closing words, rested in silence:

> “Consecrate all disciplines  
> and us sacred Muses.”

“You,” she says, “without whom no discipline of knowledge is commendably pursued, and of whom neither is sufficient without the other for those who wish to advance—you, I say, consecrate our knowledge of the Muses: that is, adorn it by your sacred presence in sacred marriage. For I know that speech is of little benefit to you—indeed, perhaps not a little harmful—if it wishes to stand among us alone like a wild ass, and that the integrity of reason produces fruits not sufficiently fitting if it refuses to enter into speech’s embrace.”

## Chapter XXII

Finally, in the old Law Moses in some sense gives a command that neither of these two should choose such celibacy, since the same Moses sternly pronounces a curse upon one who is not found to bear fruit. “Cursed,” he says, “is he who does not leave seed upon the earth.” Hence too Jephthah’s daughter, a Gileadite, already grown to maturity, remaining in her father’s house a marriageable but unmarried virgin, laments that she has held on to her virgin modesty longer than was right and has not at a mature age entered into marital union. “Let me go,” she says, “that I may mourn my virginity with my companions” (Judges 11).

Reason, which seems like a virgin to remain barren when it delights excessively in silence, refuses to appear outside, loves to keep itself from speech’s embrace, and excludes every disturbance whatever from its repose, at length mourns sorrowfully, penitently, and groaning, as it considers that its silence is its barren virginity. The prophet Isaiah considers this more carefully, observes it, and severely reproaches himself for having kept silence uselessly; indeed, he declares and shows that his silence is harmful, perceiving with true understanding the punishment that threatens it: “Woe is me,” he says, “because I have kept silence!” (Isaiah 6).

But why he kept silence, he immediately humbly confesses; by this confession he deserves thenceforth to speak more confidently, so that the prudent hearer may understand that he ought not to keep silence, and, if perhaps he has kept silence, at least ought not to conceal the reason for his silence. For after saying, “Woe is me because I have kept silence,” as though someone had asked why he had kept silence, he adds: “Because I am a man of unclean lips” (ibid.). “I kept silence,” he says, “because my lips are unclean and wrapped in the covering of defilement, so that they cannot speak; for one whose conscience is not clean for dictating has, consequently, lips unclean for speaking.”

But if the inward recesses are cleansed with diligent concern; if, according to the Gospel, what is within the cup and dish is clean, inward purity makes the outward mouth, as it were, washed, and, by the benefit of this washing, free to speak. “Clean first,” He says, “what is inside the cup and dish, so that what is outside may also become clean” (Luke 11). Therefore, because the prophet knew that the cause of his silence was uncleanness of lips, and did not deny it but humbly confessed himself guilty, he deserved to be mercifully visited by an angel and cleansed by the coal which the angel had taken from the altar with tongs. “One of the seraphim,” he says, “flew to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken from the altar with tongs; and he touched my mouth and said: Behold, I have touched these lips of yours, and your iniquity shall be taken away, and your sin shall be cleansed” (Isaiah 6).

By the coal, burning and taken by the angel from the altar, I judge that nothing is more aptly signified than charity. Whoever is touched by it does not know how to grow cold, but is set ablaze, because beyond doubt nothing is found more fervent than it. By the touch of this burning coal iniquity is taken away and sin cleansed, because fire burns and consumes the straw of wicked deeds; and “charity,” as you have read, “covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4). Just as, when sin or iniquity is present but burning charity absent, the inner conscience languishes and the outward tongue is mute, so likewise when iniquity is removed by stern rebuke and charity is made present with a gracious countenance, the conscience rejoices more abundantly in the welcome gift of health, and the tongue consequently burns, as it were uncontrollably, to speak.

Therefore, after the coal had touched his lips, when the Lord said: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Isaiah at once answered: “Behold, here am I; send me” (Isaiah 6). The prophet does not wait to be compelled to go, but at the signal of the One who asks he offers himself voluntarily for service, because he to whom the divine coal gives the flame of burning power, impatient of delay, gladly renders the service of his own obedience. Thus putting far away the “Woe!” which he had deserved by withholding truth longer than was right, when his lips had not yet been cleansed by burning charity, now cleansed he raises his voice, as it were, in strength and spontaneously obeys the One sending him, to teach his people with diligent concern.

Paul wished to serve and obey in this way, and to impart to others a fitting concern for speaking; with fatherly affection he instructed him as a son and earnestly testified, restraining him from the plague of silence. “I testify,” he says, “before God and Christ Jesus, who shall judge the living and the dead, and by His coming and His kingdom: preach the word; persist in season and out of season; rebuke, entreat, reprove in all patience and teaching” (2 Timothy 4). And to Titus: “Speak,” he says, “what befits sound doctrine” (Titus 2). And below: “Speak,” he says, “and exhort and rebuke with all authority” (ibid.).

## Chapter XXIII

[The supplied source ends here.]

But since the silence of which we have so far discussed—whether it ought to be maintained or not—is silence from speech made by words, and since we have said that there is also speech made by signs, let our pen at last turn to this kind of speech, so that we may likewise consider what benefit there is in being silent from it or not being silent. For just as speech made by words is found to be either harmful or necessary—harmful, indeed, when in speaking it opposes the divine will, but necessary when through it one obeys the same will’s commands—so certainly speech made by signs is found in Scripture sometimes to be condemned and, unless I am mistaken, often to be commended there as well. Therefore one must both be silent from signs and not be silent from signs: silent, indeed, from those which malignant perversity devises; but not silent from those which discerning charity performs.

There are many signs of many different kinds, by which people mutually disclose the secret of their will. Among these, words seem to hold the first and principal place and to convey knowledge of hidden things more certainly and plainly. For words are signs, and those who speak are undoubtedly affirmed by Scriptural testimonies to signify; thus it is certain that words are nothing but signs by which we make known whatever we wish to be known. Hence, when the Lord said to Peter: “When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish” (John 21), the Evangelist added: “This he said, signifying by what death he was to glorify God” (ibid.). By such words he signified that Peter would not merely die, but would also suffer the perils of death against the desire of human weakness—a death by which he would truly be shown to glorify God, since he appeared to prefer God’s will to his own weakness.

The same John says in the Apocalypse: “Which God gave him to make known openly to his servants, and he signified it by sending through his angel to his servant John” (Rev. 1). And Paul, writing to the Corinthians: “It has been made known to me by those who belong to Chloe that there are disputes among you” (1 Cor. 1). This kind of signification is truly judged to have been made by words, since the truth of the matter itself is communicated not by silence but rather by speech. Thus, as was said, we know that words are signs, holding among all other signs the first and chief place.

The other signs, though they are not equal to words in the same effectiveness, are nevertheless judged very powerful, and are said to be so closely related to speech that those who make signs are in a sense proclaimed to speak. Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “A faithless man, a worthless man, walks with a perverse mouth; he scuffs with his foot, signals with his eyes, speaks with his finger” (Prov. 6). You see that the faithless man, although he does not seem to loosen his tongue to speak, is nevertheless not improperly said to speak when he makes signs with his finger; for the scuffing of the foot and the signaling of the eyes are not audible but visible speech of the perverse. For when perverse people wish their secrets to be detected only by others like themselves, not wishing them either to be frustrated by others or even reproved, they do not speak openly before everyone by vocal speech and ordinary, generally known usage; rather, they misuse silent signs suited to their purpose.

Thus lovers of shameful lust, when they do not wish or cannot restrain their burning thought, and desire to convey to one another the secrets of their desires, make furtive signs because the opportunity for free conversation is often unavailable—provided, at least, that there is a place or time for doing so. One of them says:

> “I shall speak words without voice, speaking with my eyebrows;  
> You will read words, words marked by fingers drenched in wine.”

They also rub hand or foot with a friction that certainly causes no injury, but gives no small pleasure to the corrupted minds of those burning with desire; one rejoices in the other’s rubbing, so that the things they desire are hoped for more eagerly and more confidently as about to occur. They also signal with their eyes and converse with one another by gestures; what is not permitted to the tongue they accomplish by familiar signs. Even with the voice suppressed, they delight in signaling as a substitute for speech, doing little or scarcely less by gestures than by speaking. As the aforesaid pagan poet affirms:

> “In your gestures, a good part of speech was present.”

So traitors, so robbers, so utterly wicked people who devise signs appropriate to themselves—thus by foot, hand, or any bodily gesture—perform deceitful speech, so that among those like themselves or their accomplices they are not mute, though to the ignorant they seem to remain silent.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0983C] Did Judas Iscariot not seem in some manner to you to speak when he presumed to kiss both his Lord and Master, when he perversely abused the sign of peace and changed it—no longer in kind—into a sign of wickedness? “He gave them a sign, saying: ‘Whomever I shall kiss, he is the one; seize him’” (Matt. 26). This wicked man makes the kiss a detestable sign of his betrayal, as he carefully instructs his followers to pass over the others and cautiously lay hands on the one whom he, the disciple, has chosen to kiss.

In former days a kiss was a sign of affection: by it those who had withdrawn into the troubles of anger, discord, and faction were customarily recalled to the favor of goodwill, or were confirmed more openly and firmly in that same favor. Since in a kiss the lips of two people are joined together, and by mutual drawing their spirits are perceived by one another, it was rightly thought fitting that the grace of affection should be signified by a kiss, through which the minds of two persons are known to be joined in a pleasing bond. Hence, when the sacraments of the altar or the sacred mysteries are celebrated, those present kiss one another at their completion, signifying that through love we are one spirit with him in whose sacred mysteries we delight to participate. “For he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6).

This union of the Spirit is signified, certainly, by that kiss which Scripture assigns to holy and faithful persons, when either the patriarch Isaac is read to have kissed Rebecca or the Bride in the Song of Songs rejoices in the Bridegroom’s kiss. Therefore, because from ancient times the kiss has been found to be a sign of peace, a sign not of feigned but of true goodwill, Christ himself seems in some manner to marvel when he sees it corrupted by an inverted and perverse order: “Judas,” he says, “do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22).

A strange thing! By a kiss the discordant are accustomed to be recalled to harmony; those in harmony are confirmed in the firm grace of perseverance; two or more persons are united in one spirit and bound together, as it were, into one sheaf from different directions. But now, by a detestable pretense, you confuse right and wrong, since you overlay a sign of goodwill upon hidden malice. You corrupt the order of things; you violate the ordinances of laws, when an unprecedented appearance veils conceived wickedness. You have invented a wonderful—indeed, evil-working—kind of deception and injury; in discovering it and effectively carrying it out, you were first, you alone, and you last. You hate me; you betray me. Though you have no charge to bring, you do not openly extend your hand, but prepare and display the friendly favor of a kiss.

Finally, Joab son of Zeruiah (2 Sam. 20), although he seized the chin of Amasa, commander of Judah’s army, as though to kiss him, as is recorded, nevertheless did not give him a kiss in any concern for his own safety. Instead, he drew from its sheath the sword so made that it could come out with a slight movement, hanging down to the groin, and struck him in the side and killed him, though he was innocent. But you both greet me as Master and hate the one greeted; you kiss me as a friend and betray the one kissed. Thus you alone appear to have corrupted this sign of love, this bond of peace, and you alone are held first and last guilty of so great a crime.

For even robbers who pursue either travellers’ money or their lives do not use a kiss to deceive them. They endeavor to devise other signs for themselves by which they satisfy their purpose, yet are not charged with so great a crime. They have a whistle of the mouth; they have the sound of a horn or trumpet, or something similar, by which they both warn their accomplices who are present and call back those absent, gather the scattered, summon those gathered; and although their ready tongue is not loosed to speak, such signs nevertheless have considerable power to harm. By these they communicate with their helpers in the manner described, and severely pursue their enemies; and they are found to do little or no less harm by horn or whistle than if they wished to carry out their purpose by explicit words.

## CHAPTER XXV

Finally, when God proposed to stir up the peoples of the nations against the children of Israel and determined that their heavy armies should be punished by the attack of those peoples, he is read as intending to do this not so much by a word as by a sign, choosing a whistle from the great abundance of signs. Isaiah speaks of this: “He will raise a sign among the nations far away, and whistle to him from the ends of the earth” (Isa. 5).

Because none of us can fittingly speak of the movements of the divine will, God endures to have human characteristics attributed to himself, so that by them his will may in some manner become known to us, since our smallness can scarcely comprehend it otherwise. Therefore, in our manner of speaking, he is said to raise a sign and whistle in order to summon a hostile army from remote regions, so that, summoned by this sign, it may fulfill its intention against the children of Israel, while God himself exacts a deserved vengeance for their merits.

This whistle by which God summons his helpers so that they may oppress the children of Israel is the very inspiration, or conspiracy, by which those utterly wicked people assemble; once assembled, they plot to defeat the children of Israel. They can neither do nor accomplish anything of this kind unless they are sent—or permitted—by him who orders all things justly. And since there is no doubt that this occurs by divine anger and just judgment, God himself is not improperly said to do it; he is said to inspire those through whom he, by a wise ordering, fulfills the counsel of his will.

Whatever God ordains to be done, whether through himself or through any ministers whatsoever, clearly does not delay beyond his pleasure. For even a wicked minister hastens to satisfy his own perversity in such a way that he at the same time obeys the divine will, though unknowingly. Isaiah adds concerning this: “Behold, he will come swiftly and speedily; there is no one fainting or weary among them” (ibid.). Having received the sign—that is, the inspiration or whistle of the divine ordinance that intends to strike the children of Israel with the sword of vengeance—the wicked minister hastens quickly to come, intending to obey his own pleasure more than God’s.

For thus God’s goodness works good from evil: although God loves nothing but good, wickedness is nevertheless compelled to serve the divine order. What becomes harm to the reprobate and a necessary purification to the elect is, for God who orders all things well, an instrument in both cases. Hence in what follows the same prophet says that God whistles to the fly and the bee, because even a fly or a bee cannot fly toward anyone to harm them unless it has been prompted by the whistle of divine sending or permission, and is given freer rein to perform what it desires, insofar as it has received leave. “The Lord will whistle,” he says, “for the fly that is at the extremity of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria” (Isa. 7).

By the fly and the bee, one and the same plague seems to me to be signified, though called by different names because of different effects. It is the plague which the more severe judgment of an offended God imposed upon us as punishment when our first parent ate the forbidden fruit. This plague is unlawful enticement, which flies and rushes upon us more importunately in the manner of flies, and, though it is sternly repelled, still returns repeatedly. Indeed, this plague or enticement presses some people with such severity that it greatly diminishes their holiness and turns the grace and fragrance of a good name into stench by introducing the stain of shamefulness. Ecclesiastes indicates this: “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of ointment” (Eccl. 10).

The ointment is a good name: good reputation, good fragrance. Solomon says of it in the Song of Songs: “Your name is ointment poured out” (Song 1). And in Proverbs: “A good name is better than great riches” (Prov. 22). Paul writes to the Philippians: “Whatever is of good report, if there is any virtue, if any praise of discipline, think on these things” (Phil. 4). And to the Corinthians: “We are the good fragrance of Christ” (2 Cor. 2).

Dying flies spoil the sweetness of this ointment when fleshly enticements, exceeding the fitting limits of continence, corrupt the whole freshness of the mass of virtues and defile the purity of religious chastity. “A little leaven,” he says, “corrupts the whole mass” (1 Cor. 5). Finally, where flies settle more stubbornly, they are found to foul cleanliness once attained and stain whiteness once acquired; the former beauty loses no small measure of its grace when so great and indecent a shamefulness clings to it.

But if decaying flies are more importunately immersed in ointment, and die there after being immersed, they inflict much graver, much more intolerable damage, corrupting and turning the pleasant perfume into nausea. So fleshly enticements, when they immerse themselves too immoderately in the catalogue of virtues and stain and bespatter them with deadly filth, destroy the perfume and sweetness of the entire composition, making holiness guilty of all things when it offends in one. For what discolors the brightness of holiness more than the unclean filth of this perversity, which inundates our corruptible nature with its vicious flood and dulls the consenting spirit with dark obscurity?

Therefore the aforesaid fly is said to be at the extremity of the rivers of Egypt, so that its uncleanness may be shown by its very dwelling-place. For as pure virtue delights in cleansed and more austere retreats, so the unclean filth of vices delights in muddy and damp places. Peter speaks of it: “The washed sow [returns] to the wallowing in the mire” (2 Pet. 2). And the Lord says of the unclean spirit to Job: “He sleeps under shade, in the hiding place of reeds, in damp places” (Job 40). The fly is therefore rightly said to be at the extremity of the rivers of Egypt: “the fly which is at the extremity of Egypt’s rivers,” because, although rivers in Scripture often signify spiritual delights, the rivers of Egypt seem to suggest only harmful and carnal ones.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 0986D] For there are rivers of Paradise, rivers of wisdom, rivers of Babylon, and rivers of Egypt. Whether these are beneficial or harmful is plainly indicated by their own qualifying terms. Who would deny that the four rivers of Paradise ought to be commended—the rivers by which Paradise itself is said to be watered, which issue from it and flow into diverse regions, and by their onward course enrich and gladden arid nations?

The Church is, indeed, the paradise of due delight. From it flows and streams forth the fourfold teaching of evangelical purity. It waters not only those whom it could find within its boundaries in the earliest times, but has deigned, in abundant goodwill, to reach those situated outside. In order to gather all, it freely channels itself to all and rejoices to wipe away their ignorance by the benefit of its outpouring. It knows that that which is wholly unknown cannot be loved with greater care. Therefore, so that diverse and scattered peoples of the nations may both know and love God, the rivers of Paradise water the boundaries of various regions; and none, or scarcely anyone, can now excuse himself on grounds of ignorance, since the will of the ignorant rather than impossibility ought to be blamed.

Of the rivers issuing from Paradise: “The name of one,” it says, “is Pishon; the name of the second, Gihon; the name of the third river is Tigris; and the fourth is Euphrates” (Gen. 2).

## CHAPTER XXVII

Pishon is interpreted as “the mouth of the pupil,” or “a change of speech.” The pupil is of such keen and subtle nature that it sees, and it signifies understanding, which with wonderful sharpness sees invisible things—unless, perhaps, grave dullness presses it, as bleary inflammation often affects the pupil of the eye. But “the mouth of the pupil” is the speech of understanding: that is, when, by grace’s gift, someone both understands wisely and is granted eloquently to express what has been understood.

For one who does not see truth with lynx-like understanding, but bleary-eyed or blinded dreams up falsehood—what does he utter except falsehood corresponding to his vision? Of this the prophet Ezekiel says: “They see vanities and divine lies” (Ezek. 13). Although such people have a mouth, since they speak volubly enough, or perhaps more than enough, they do not have the mouth of the pupil, since they attain no understanding or only little understanding. Certainly it does not benefit them sufficiently—indeed, it usually harms them—to have a mouth if they have not deserved to possess the mouth of the pupil as well. The Apostle observes this: “Some, having wandered away, have turned to empty talk, wishing to be teachers of the law while understanding neither what they say nor what they affirm” (1 Tim. 1).

But if the pupil is cleared by infused spiritual eye-salve, so that divine grace grants understanding to the bleary heart, the mouth is consequently changed so as to speak truthfully. What formerly seemed to flow out in falsehood and empty talk now, with understanding made clear, declares true and commendable things. Finally, Pishon is also interpreted as “a change of speech,” because when he who said that light should shine from darkness cleared Paul’s pupil, clouded by grave bleary inflammation, he changed Paul’s mouth as well. Previously Paul, as a blasphemer and persecutor, had denied Christ the Son of God; afterwards he freely preached that same Christ in the synagogues. And when the Jewish people did not sufficiently assent to his preaching, he passed on, in the manner of a river, to water the nations of the Gentiles.

“The name of the second river,” it says, “is Gihon.” Gihon is interpreted as “breast” or “steep height.” The breast is the dwelling-place of the heart, by which wisdom is figured. Thus Hosea says: “A dove without a heart is called deceived” (Hos. 7), because anyone not fortified by prudent wisdom is easily ensnared in the stains of the deceiver. Therefore the breast can not improperly be called spiritual teaching, which neither deceives nor is deceived, but, overflowing from its inexhaustible spring, pours out abundant streams of welcome and necessary truth of the most subtle purity.

Or perhaps John, as is recorded, reclined upon the Lord’s breast (John 21), not because at the supper he had no other space or place in which to recline, but because the spring of spiritual wisdom lay hidden in that breast, and from it a desirable stream flowed to the one reclining there. Since access to that reclining-place upon the breast is not easily gained, and hidden water is not drawn indiscriminately by anyone, Gihon is rightly also interpreted as “steep height.” What is called steep is high, lofty. And what is higher, what loftier, than wisdom? It is never attained by one who expends no diligence, who does not direct a studious mind to the desire for it. Yet even one who seems to strive for it does not grasp it, but sometimes withdraws from it all the farther the more he stretches himself toward it.

Solomon says of this: “Wisdom is too high for a fool” (Prov. 24). And again: “What does it profit a fool to have riches when he cannot buy wisdom?” (Prov. 17). And in Ecclesiastes: “I said, ‘I shall become wise,’ and it withdrew farther from me; and its deepness is high—who will find it?” (Eccl. 7). Truly it is a lofty depth, which not only the foolish and negligent do not reach, but which even the diligent and understanding scarcely attain. Therefore, the more difficult it is for anyone to be granted access to it, the more gratefully and diligently he should devote care to attaining it.

Gihon is thus beautifully interpreted as “breast” or “steep height,” because the spiritual wisdom with which a learned preacher overflows and is enriched is inaccessible to the imprudent, the foolish, and those who do not attend to heavenly things, surpassing by reason of its excellence the infinite number of fools.

“The name of the third river,” it says, “is Tigris.” The tiger is a swift and rapacious beast. The slower are greatly astonished at its speed; the weaker no less dread its rapacity. This river is given the name of that beast because it too is especially said to be swift; and the swifter it is, the more rapaciously it sweeps away and carries off anything that stands in its path, drawing it by violent force into a deep abyss.

By this river the word of wisdom is not improperly figured. Struck by a mighty spirit, it is not delayed by a base obstacle, but is channelled with ready diligence to water willing hearers; and it is more abundantly unleashed with most rapacious speed to refute the reprobate. Of this the Prophet says: “His word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147). And the Apostle writes to the Thessalonians: “Pray that the word of God may run” (2 Thess. 3).

The overflowing word of wisdom runs swiftly because the languishing sloth of harmful fear or love does not stand in its way; or, if it stands in its way, spiritual force crushes it, and the river’s flood hurls it down like light chaff. Paul indicates this to the Ephesians: “I discharge an embassy in chains, so that in it I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak” (Eph. 6). And to Timothy: “In which I labor even unto chains” (2 Tim. 2)—“but the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 4).

And below: “Preach the word; press it in season and out of season” (ibid.). And to Titus: “Speak, exhort, and rebuke with all authority” (Titus 2). What was such a word except something running swiftly and flowing on, ignorant of obstacles, with most rapacious force—so that, like a tiger, it was carried off to prey with fear set aside, or like a cleansing river rushed downhill in a precipitous course?

Finally, in the Syrian language Tigris is called Diglath, which is interpreted “sharp” or “narrow,” because “the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword” (Heb. 4). Its sharpness is found not in the marketplace or street, but on the heights and, as it were, in trackless country; nor is it reached except by a confined and narrow path.

“The fourth river,” it says, “is Euphrates.” Euphrates is interpreted “fruitful” or “increasing.” Whoever is distinguished by the grace of the aforesaid number is certainly shown to increase and bear fruit: advancing in himself from virtue to virtue, and by word and example calling others to salvation. “I have appointed you,” he says, “that you may go and bear fruit” (John 15).

Divine grace so orders these people and sets them before others in rank and merit that they not only deserve not to be reproved for unprofitably hidden money, but merit praise for what has been doubled more diligently and faithfully. “You gave me two—or five—talents; behold, I have gained another two—or five.” And the Lord says: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, I shall set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

These rivers water the delightful pleasure of Paradise. Their health-giving current gladdens the city of God. They descend, drop by drop and thinly, to those who are untrained in understanding and obedient to greater and more learned persons.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Such, I think, are also those called rivers of wisdom, which Wisdom pours from its own inexhaustible and hidden bosom, flooding different hearts with different and fitting measures. When that same Wisdom spoke through someone concerning these rivers, and seemed to compare David the king—or perhaps his son—with them, it declared more clearly that it had poured them forth, thereby commending to us their honorable origin: “I, Wisdom, have poured out rivers” (Sir. 24).

What rivers it has poured out it plainly suggests when it first says: “He has set David his servant to raise up from him a most mighty king, seated forever on a throne of honor, who fills wisdom like Pishon, and like Tigris in the days of new fruits; who fulfills understanding like Euphrates, who sends forth instruction like light, and stands by like Gihon in the day of vintage” (ibid.). Having expressly named the rivers, it adds what was said before: “I, Wisdom, have poured out rivers.”

Therefore those rivers which Wisdom is read to have poured out were certainly not contemptible, for she is the one who makes fruitful the teaching which her presence has made luminous. Of her it adds: “I illuminate instruction like the dawn” (ibid.). And below: “I shall pour out instruction like prophecy, and leave it for those who seek wisdom” (ibid.).

Wisdom rightly testifies that it pours out instruction like prophecy when it grants the gift of spiritual knowledge so abundantly to many that, in fuller grace, after the manner of the seeing prophets, they perceive and expound the secret utterances of Scripture. For one who is given to reveal hidden things concerning the future, the present, or the past is undoubtedly said to prophesy. Hence those who in former times were filled with the spirit of prophecy to reveal mysteries were called “seers” in common speech. “Saul said to Samuel: ‘Tell me, I pray, where is the house of the seer?’ But he said: ‘I am the seer’” (1 Sam. 9).

To these seers Wisdom says that it pours out instruction like prophecy, and promises to leave it for those who seek it, so that both the gratuitous gift of the one who pours out and, consequently, some merit of the seeker may be commended. For if the gift of instruction is freely poured out upon anyone, it must be sought more diligently by that person; otherwise that person already sins through negligence, and the author of grace does not leave with the despiser what he had offered.

Therefore David says: “Blessed are those who search his testimonies; with my whole heart I shall seek him” (Ps. 118). And the Lord: “He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7). And again: “He who drinks the water which I shall give him” (John 4). You see both grace ready at hand from the giver and the merit of the seeker’s faith not lacking from the gratuitous gift, so that a prudent person neither hopes to be able to do anything without grace nor ceases, in seeking, to persevere with faithful diligence in grace.

For the persevering diligence of the searcher draws waters, as it is written, “with joy from the fountains of the Savior” (Isa. 12): waters, I say, which lack tumult and are not held by mud, but are said to flow without mud and with silence. Those who reject them are sternly rebuked through the same Isaiah, and waters of another kind are promised them; when these swell over them in roaring waves, they will certainly not rest in desirable silence. “Because this people has rejected the waters of Shiloah, which go with silence, behold, the Lord will bring upon them the strong and many waters of the river” (Isa. 8).

Shiloah is interpreted “sent,” signifying Christ, who says: “I have been sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). The waters of Shiloah, then, are Christ’s spiritual teaching, whose taste and savor the natural person does not perceive; for the fleshly dullness has neither sufficient depth for this well nor a worthy vessel for drawing from it. In these waters of Shiloah, tranquil with blessed silence, in these rivers channelled from the hidden place of Paradise or Wisdom, the filthy fly mentioned above does not dwell; rather, its foulness is opposed to their purity.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Let us therefore find other waters and rivers, as I suppose, which seem more fitting for this fly, in which it finds a pleasant dwelling, wallowing and, although wickedly, delightfully defiling itself in such mire. These are perhaps those called the rivers of Babylon, which a prudent man, remembering that eternal dwelling, although he cannot wholly drive them away from himself, nevertheless strives from his elevated position to trample underfoot. “By the rivers of Babylon,” he says, “there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion” (Ps. 136).

For one who is not immersed in the rivers of unclean pleasure, but sits above them by the authority of royal power, rejoices indeed that he is not bound by the glue of fleshly enticement, but grieves that he does not yet dwell more fully in the Zion or Jerusalem which he loves. But those who rejoice to be immersed in the mud of such rivers and not to wipe away from themselves the stains of so many filths, having lost firmness, are shaken and unstable; and avenging angels are sent to punish them. “Go,” says the Lord through Isaiah, “swift angels, to a nation torn apart and trampled underfoot, whose land the rivers have plundered” (Isa. 18).

Because the rivers—that is, the currents of fleshly pleasure—have plundered their land, the strength of their due steadfastness, go, angels: go, I say, and swiftly fulfill the service of the vision you have received, lest they laugh if they escape the sentence of just vengeance.

## CHAPTER XXX
Thus also through Ezekiel he threatens Pharaoh king of Egypt, who rejoices to lie amid the rivers, although the rivers of Egypt ought to be kept far from the resting-place of the righteous, or at least restrained by the barrier of strict moderation. “Behold,” he says, “I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, who lie in the midst of your rivers [Col. 0991C] and say: ‘The river is mine’; I will put a bridle in your jaws” (Ezek. 29).

Pharaoh represents that evil spirit who, since he himself did not remain steadfast in the truth granted him at first, infected humankind also, once made, with a like perversity. He persuaded man not to fear in any way the transgression of the commandment, asserting that he would not die as God had said. By his counsel, inexperienced man passed beyond the limits prescribed for him; and divine vengeance immediately punished his negligence—or contempt—by imposing upon his members the law of concupiscence, which should contend against the spirit in harsh conflict. But because that wicked spirit is proclaimed to be the author of sin, while this concupiscence is admittedly both sin and the law of sin, he boasts, to the increase of his own destruction, that he has made for himself such a river [Col. 0991D] as this: he both instils its inclination and rejoices more fully in its effect. “The river is mine,” he says, “and I made it.” I made it so that created man might incline toward sin; I stir up in his loins the movements of carnal pleasures; in these pleasures I exercise my power; I disturb the thoughts of the inner person; I trample holiness underfoot.

Hence below the Lord says to him: “You brandished your horn in your rivers, and disturbed their waters with your feet, and trampled down their rivers” (Ezek. 32). He is said to brandish his horn in his rivers when he appears to exalt his own dominion in the pleasures of the flesh; when he can, as it were with his feet, disturb by evil thoughts the waters—that is, the spiritual affections—of those whom he deceives, and trample down their rivers, that is, the torrent of inward pleasure [Col. 0992A].

But because divine justice leaves nothing unpunished, the sentence of vengeance sometimes strikes the unbridled enemy: either he receives what he deserves for past acts, or he is restrained from present and future acts as though by a bridle imposed upon him. “I will put,” he says, “a bridle in your jaws” (Ezek. 29, 38). And below: “Because you have said, ‘The river is mine, and I made it,’ therefore behold, I am against you and against your rivers” (Ezek. 29). Because you not only do not grieve in worthy repentance over your own malice, but moreover glory in it as though it were righteousness: “Behold, I am against you, against your rivers,” so that I may indeed abandon you, perverse as you always are, to your inclination, and may at some time, whether you wish it or not, prevent the malice you have desired from reaching its effect. “I will put,” he says, “a bridle in your jaws.” And below: “I restrained,” he says, [Col. 0992B] “his rivers and checked his many waters” (Ezek. 31).

Then indeed the many waters are restrained by the obstacle of difficulty: in their flood the perverse are not worthy to draw near to God. Then the rivers, flowing with abundant force, are checked and, driven back upon themselves as their waves subside, are restrained as if in silence—when the house founded upon the solid foundation of rock does not collapse under the troubles rushing upon it, but sets against them an inviolable strength. “The rivers came,” he says, “and the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house; and it did not fall, for it was founded upon the rock” (Matt. 7). And in Luke: “The river dashed against that house,” he says, “and could not move it” (Luke 6). And Solomon in the Song of Songs: “Many [Col. 0992C] waters,” he says, “cannot extinguish love, nor shall rivers overwhelm it” (Song 8).

Winds and rivers do not overthrow the firmness of a building thus founded; nor, as you have heard, can waters or rivers extinguish or overwhelm love. For he who is the Rock gives to the building placed upon him the defence of fitting holiness; and he who is Love preserves the surpassing structure of love. The river or rivers which dash threateningly against the founded house, the many waters which, by flooding, strive to bring on a deluge—he himself, by the majesty of his hand, compresses and restrains them, and by interposing difficulties powerfully turns them aside from their desired effect. Hence Isaiah: “He will raise his hand over the river in the strength of his spirit, and strike it into seven streams” (Isa. 2).

[Col. 0992D] The Lord appears to raise his hand over the river and strike it into seven streams when, in merciful purpose, he comes to the aid of the tossing mind: with the power of his Spirit he thunders at its waves, that they may be still, and divides them in many ways from the channel of their former course, that they may dry up. For as long as the flood of passions runs freely through its accustomed channels, it does not grow gentle but more violent; unchecked, it carries everything away with it. For it has this characteristic: the more freely an open way is granted it, the more insatiably it pours forth to accomplish what it desires. But if its desired liberty of overflowing is shut off, and its little path is divided through many narrow passages, then surely its swelling abundance first diminishes, and the disordered flux is dried up by the prevailing heat of chastity.

Isaiah indicates this much later: “The water shall dry up [Col. 0993A] from the sea, and the river shall be desolate and dry; the rivers shall fail, and the channels of the embankments shall be diminished” (Isa. 19). Such waters or rivers overflow and increase with their flooding outpouring when, restrained by no barrier, they swell more freely in their desired channel. Then they provide a fitting lodging and an agreeable dwelling to the fly of which Isaiah seems to speak: “The fly,” he says, “which is at the end of the rivers of Egypt” (Isa. 7).

Egypt is interpreted as “darkness.” The rivers of Egypt, therefore, are the fluid impulses of carnal pleasures. Whenever they gain mastery in anyone, they overturn and cast down one weakened by soft allurements, banished from righteousness, and darkened by heavier shadows. This aforesaid fly is said to be not at the beginning, not in the middle, [Col. 0993B] but at the end of those rivers, because among the things in which the flesh takes vicious and wicked delight, nothing seems more pleasing, yet nothing more burdensome; nothing more enjoyable, yet nothing more unclean; nothing more familiar, yet nothing more deserving of punishment, to that same flesh than the pleasure of the loins, which—even if the will resists—nevertheless naturally clings to it.

Appropriately, therefore, the fly which is at the end of the rivers of Egypt signifies the pleasure of the loins. By its pestilential touch it infects the purity of the virtues; occupying the furthest place of dark and carnal perversity, it attacks, and very often captures, the stronghold of pure and snowy chastity. “The Lord,” he says, “will whistle for the fly that is at the end of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land [Col. 0993C] of Assyria” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXXI

Through the bee likewise the unlawful appetite of the flesh is not without reason represented. For the bee is shown to bear not only honey and honeycomb, but also a sting; and though it delights the throat with the food of honey and a sweet drink, it is nevertheless bitter in the severe puncture of its sting. Yet the pleasing delight of honey’s taste passes swiftly, whereas the venomous puncture of the sting weighs upon one longer; and the former does not appear to possess nearly as much charm or sweetness as the latter has trouble and severity.

So also the appetite of the flesh caresses the reins or loins with a certain sweet enticement to lust, but it stings the conscience with a certain natural bitterness [Col. 0993D] of repentance. And in proportion as it smiles upon them with its blandishment in the act’s fulfilment, so—indeed, in a greater measure—it torments the wounded conscience with harm.

The prudent Boethius carefully observed this and plainly expressed it in careful writing, wishing the reader not to love the first appearance of an action whose end bears the tail and sting of the scorpion:

> Pleasure has this way:
>
> It drives those who enjoy it with goads,
>
> And, like a swarm of flying bees,
>
> Once it has poured forth welcome honey,
>
> It flies away and with an all-too-tenacious
>
> Bite strikes the hearts it has wounded.
>
> (BOETHIUS, *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, III.7, metre)

[Col. 0994A] You see that pleasure, in the manner of a flying bee, pours out honeys and flies away. For what pleases in it—and from this it is called *libido*, “lust”—comes suddenly, as if on the wing, seeming almost like a little bird, and swiftly passes when its miserable effect is consummated. But once that is consummated, whose enticement the willing flesh experiences and by whose present experience even the carnal mind is delighted, the wretched heart is struck with a grievous bite and wound, and is arraigned under severe judgment for the act completed.

Therefore the taste of this sweetness is by no means greatly to be desired, since it must be closed by so bitter an end; nor should honey rightly indulge the greedy throat in miserable intoxication, when gall impresses upon its sweetness the poison of its own bitterness.

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Col. 0994B] Rightly—when in the Law many things are commanded to be offered, so that, once offered upon the altar, they may be burned either as a holocaust or as a sacrifice, and those who offer and burn them may deserve to propitiate God for themselves (for, taught by Moses, they judge that he is propitiated by such things)—rightly, I say, no honey is mixed with offerings of this kind. Nothing of it at all is commanded to be burned upon the altar; rather, honey is carefully prohibited from the divine fire and, as forbidden, is found to be wholly removed.

For the Lord says to Moses: “No leaven or honey shall be burned in sacrifice to the Lord upon the altar; it shall not be placed as an odour of sweetness” (Lev. 2). In honey I consider the enticing sweetness of carnal pleasure to be represented. The Lord does not wish it to be presented upon his altar [Col. 0994C]; he forbids our flesh to be softened by its enticement, and instead wishes it to be seasoned with the sternness of preserving justice. Hence the same Leviticus adds: “Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt; you shall not take away the salt of the covenant of your God from your sacrifice. In every offering you shall offer salt” (ibid.).

For salt applied to naturally soft and weak flesh makes it firm; undoubtedly keeping worms and stench far away, it preserves—indeed improves—its sound condition and flavour. So sternness, fittingly applied, preserves our corruptible nature when enervating blandishment has been removed. Seasoned with the justice of wisdom, and with soft enticement and the worms of vices driven away, worthy strength and the integrity of chastity flourish in it.

Therefore let every sacrifice be seasoned with savoury salt, but let honey’s enticement not be placed upon the altar. For the presence of Wisdom, the attendant of your throne, O Lord, is to be desired (Wis. 9), while the “dripping honeycomb of the harlot’s lips” is to be removed far away (Prov. 5). A honeycomb, as you know, is the work of a bee, containing honey in wax; and the dripping of the harlot’s honeycomb is not pure. Nor is only distilled honey found forbidden from the altar: wax also is not applied to the divine lights.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

When lights are arranged in the tabernacle of the covenant, if I remember rightly, one does not read that wax or candles are supplied, nor is there any mention of them at all among those lights. Instead, clear and most pure olive oil is used. “Command,” he says, “the children of Israel to bring you most pure and clear olive oil [Col. 0995A] for continually preparing lamps. Outside the veil of the testimony, in the tabernacle of the covenant, Aaron shall set them from evening until morning before the Lord, by a perpetual rite and observance; they shall be placed upon the most clean candlestick, always in the sight of the Lord” (Lev. 24).

What does it mean that Aaron by no means brings candles into the tabernacle, and that the divine ordinance does not admit them among its lights, but that Aaron sets before the Lord olive oil of the greatest purity and places only its lamps upon the most clean candlestick? In wax is signified a certain fragile fluidity, or fluid fragility; this is in no way attributed to those who shine perfectly in the Church. Divine grace wills them to be pure from fragile softness and to have the flux of carnal impulses checked by the frost of purity.

For this reason the Apostle, forbidding those whom he instructs to be leavened, carefully exhorts them to keep festival with the unleavened bread of sincerity, making it understood that sincere unleavened bread is nothing other than a pure [Col. 0995B] manner of life without wax. “Let us keep festival,” he says, “not with old leaven, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity” (1 Cor. 5). The Apostle does not want us to be, in the manner of wax, fragile or easily bent, loose or readily flowing. Perhaps he recalls that the poet reproved the beardless young man as waxen in life, and that the Prophet found sinners to perish like melting wax:

> “The beardless youth,” says the poet, “once his guardian has been removed,
>
> Is wax, to be bent toward vice.”

[Col. 0995C] And David: “As wax melts,” he says, “before the fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God” (Ps. 67). And again: “Like wax which melts, they shall be taken away” (Ps. 57). Therefore the Apostle says: “We ought to observe the things which we have heard, lest perhaps we drift away” (Heb. 2).

God does not admit into his tabernacle the fire of those who, according to the poet, are bent like wax toward vices and, according to the Prophet, are carried away like melting wax. Instead, he either sternly commands or permits them to walk in that fire, so that because they refused to be kindled by the fire which he wished to send upon the earth and to burn, they may burn in the fire which they wickedly kindled for themselves, and, burning, may perish. Of this Isaiah says: “Walk,” he says, “in the light [Col. 0995D] of your fire and in the flames which you have kindled” (Isa. 50).

But, having rejected that fire which the wretched kindled for themselves, by whose heat they became waxen and fragile and melted away into vices, God wished that fire to be given to himself and placed in his tabernacle and on his candlestick, to which olive oil supplies such unfailing nourishment that it suffers no loss of its due brightness. Oil checks swellings, soothes pains, restores the weak, and consoles the afflicted; and therefore mercy is rightly represented by it, since mercy grieves with a tender heart over a neighbour’s fall and brings the medicine of consolation with compassionate affection.

Christ, anointed with this oil, deigned to visit us in our weakness and mercifully to summon us back, refreshed with wholesome consolation, to the hope of salvation. Pouring upon us the grace of his abundance, he wiped away the long-standing [Col. 0996A] languor of our dryness. Was not Saul dry when he did not know Christ, the Son of God? When he thundered threats of slaughter against Christ’s disciples? When, travelling to Damascus, he was recalled from his purpose by a voice falling from above, and, falling to the ground, was blinded with his senses troubled? When the scales fell from his eyes, he cast off the blindness poured into them; when he recovered inward sight and observed the dryness of his former wickedness, he understood that the one speaking to him was Christ, whom God had anointed, and did not neglect to approach the Anointed One while dry.

Finally, a certain poet, who plainly did not know that Christ was anointed, nevertheless gave his hearers prudent counsel, so that clearer truth may become known not only through the teaching of believers but may also shine upon us from the mouth of unbelievers. For he says:

> If you wish to benefit your own people and to treat yourself somewhat more kindly,
>
> you will approach the anointed one dry.

But since Paul did not despise the sayings or counsels of the pagans when he saw that they were not contrary to usefulness, he hastened, in accordance with the counsel just quoted, to approach Christ, so that that anointing might wipe away his dryness. He was received by him so mercifully and obtained the abounding grace of such great consolation that he himself could impart consolation to others and, by the benefit of the anointing he had received, assist those who approached while dry.

Hence to the Corinthians: “Blessed,” he says, “be God, the Father of mercies and the God [Col. 0996C] of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we too may be able to console those who are in every affliction” (2 Cor. 1).

And because oil not only gives consolation to the weak and heals, but is also said to rise above other liquids, it rightly represents not only mercy but also love, which by its excellence holds primacy among the other virtues. Of it Paul says: “The greatest of these is love” (1 Cor. 13). God wishes its fire to burn in his tabernacle: not to be hidden while burning beneath a bushel, but to shine upon a candlestick, so that the inner house may not be oppressed by the troubles of darkness, and one who enters the threshold may rejoice at seeing the light.

Rightly, therefore, oil is chosen and wax rejected, so that unfailing mercy [Col. 0996D] or love may be kindled in the house of God, while the fire of foolish concupiscence may in no way rule there, but may grow cold and turn to ashes, so that it is not even named there. In this passage I find nothing of the works of bees approved: wax is rejected from the candlestick and honey from the altar.
