From this it is clear that the soft appetite of the flesh is not incongruously signified by the bee, which loves to produce reprobate fruits.

The same Isaiah says that this bee, for which, according to the Prophet, the Lord whistles, is in the land of Assyria; so it should not seem strange if the bee is said to signify such a thing, since it dwells in such a fitting abode. “And for the bee,” he says, “which is in the land of Assyria” (Isa. 7). Assyria (*Assur*) is interpreted as “one who presses down” or “one who is exalted.” The one who presses down or is exalted is that ancient [Col. 0997A] enemy, a most harsh exactor of tribute, who hinders and harasses the paths of travellers, and as the accuser of the brethren presses and troubles them with grave calumny. He does not care by what blandishments or troubles he makes anyone a sinner, provided that he sees himself victor over that person, pressed down and oppressed.

But the victor is wickedly raised up into pride and, swollen with it, glories vainly: a wretch who is to receive no remedy for his own destruction but is to enjoy the company of the destroyed. Therefore he is rightly called both one who presses down and one who is exalted: the more he presses down, the more exalted he is found; and the more exalted he is, the more grievous an oppressor every ruined person experiences him to be.

The land of this Assur is his possession, which from ancient times he deserved to obtain as his own and to possess for ever by a certain established right. [Col. 0997B] I judge that nothing more rightly can be called this land or possession than sin, to which the devil himself is so certainly assigned—or which is so assigned to the devil—that it is principally attributed to him as its author and inventor, and he himself rules over it in miserable power as over his own right.

He fell from heaven, as you have read the Lord recalling in the Gospel: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven to earth” (Luke 10). He is undoubtedly said to have fallen, as Isaiah the prophet likewise sang: “How have you fallen, Lucifer, who rose in the morning? You have fallen to earth” (Isa. 14). But what is it to fall from heaven to earth except to fall from the lofty hidden realm of the heavenly virtues into the lowest [Col. 0997C] firmness of sin, whence no return to lost brightness lies open to him?

For the devil bound himself to his own sin so indissolubly and secured his ruin with such strong bars that not only was the power of returning taken from him, but, all hope wholly lost, he has no will to return either. Man, miserably following him in his fall by sinning, was himself cast down into such firmness and such inextricability that he could in no way have returned thence to the former glory of life, but would have perished in his sin through that firmness which served it—unless God had found a fitting remedy and soothed our wounds with the poultice (*malagma*) of flesh assumed.

Christ indeed entered the hell into which man had fallen by sinning; he who was stronger bound the wicked strong man armed, and by the nail of his cross, in which he had mercifully dipped his garment, he powerfully shattered the fortress of that abode. Hence, when he returns in triumph, the angelic spirits marvel; wondering and astonished, they ask who and how great he is, seeing that he had broken into hell with such confidence and, by an unheard-of miracle, burst forth from it bearing the trophies of victory.

They marvel, I say, that Christ overthrew the great strength of hell and returned, surrounded by the company of his own, to the heights of heaven, showing that he had fulfilled the ministry of the eternal command and offering him the garment dyed with the blood of his Passion. “Who is this,” they ask, “who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63).

Edom is Esau himself. Edom is interpreted as “earthly” and signifies the world, which proposes to those who come to it the allurements of this life by a marvellous manner of deception, and brings the losses of eternal death upon those who love them. But Bozrah is a city in Moab and is interpreted as “fortified” or “strong”; it signifies hell, which was so defended by so many and such great guards, walls, bars, and bolts that there was no easy return to the upper regions for anyone entering it.

Those whom that enemy, skilful in doing harm, deceived in the world and led into sin, either by flattery or perhaps by oppression, he brought down to the fortified and strong recesses of hell. From there no grace and no power afterwards led them out to salvation. Therefore, when Christ by dying had triumphed over both the world and hell, and, rising from the dead, returned victor to heaven, the angels, as has been said, are amazed at so great a novelty of miracle—or rather rejoice that their number is being completed by the new arrival of the faithful. “Who is this,” they ask, “who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?”

Who is this who, shattering the age-old fortress of hell and its strength inviolable throughout all preceding ages, returns from there as victor, bearing no instrument of war but the garment of assumed flesh dyed with blood?

Moreover, although God, in the grace of his goodness, had mercy on man and redeemed him, taking him out of the prisons of hell that seemed fortified and strong, he nevertheless did not take from the devil—whom no one’s deception, but his own perversity alone, destroyed—his own land, that is, the solid right of sin. The just goodness of God did not invade that possession of his, nor, pitying him, persuade him to saving repentance. But because he is the first inventor of malice and has sinned, God left his invention as his own.

Therefore the devil wishes to claim every sin as his own; and God, the just Judge, does not cease to claim it as reprobate. The former delights in it as a most welcome food; the latter abominates it as contrary to himself. Therefore he says to him: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. 3). And through Isaiah: “For the serpent, dust shall be his bread” (Isa. 65).

For as God is fed upon heavenly things—that is, righteousness, purity, truth—so the devil upon earthly things, namely sin, impurity, falsehood. And as the one, so the other seeks and desires foods like himself; the food of the one does not delight the other. Therefore Paul says: “Putting away falsehood, speak truth” (Eph. 4). And to the Colossians: “Mortify,” he says, “your members which are upon the earth” (Col. 3)—not, therefore, those which are above heaven.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

For righteousness, prudence, temperance, and fortitude are not commanded to be mortified. Supported by these, man is received by the heights of heaven, because they make him far removed from the earthly contagion of sin and, in affection and merit, a participant in things highest and heavenly. Nor did the prudent Apostle compel us to mortify even those things by which God our Maker joined us together bodily, which are destined to die in their own time, not through our action but through his, and to pass into the heavenly life by the benefit of resurrection [Col. 0999A].

Rather, the crafty serpent deceived us by those things which the Apostle just mentioned commanded us to mortify as members [the construction is uncertain]; by their enticements that perverse worker of evil infected us wretches and by miserable infection made us like himself. So that we may not perhaps plead ignorance, he wishes us to note the consequence of this command, subsequently naming in careful detail those things which he commands to be mortified. For after saying, “Mortify your members which are upon the earth,” he added: “Fornication, impurity, lust, evil concupiscence, and avarice, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3). And a little later: “Put away,” he says, “anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy” (ibid.).

These are the members which, having been made far from heaven or heavenly things, have by their own desert been brought down upon the earth, or into the earth. Left to the devil himself as his own possession, they have also been inflicted upon his servants for their very destruction. These are the members of which the body of the unrighteous is composed (Rom. 6); this is the earth which the head of the lost eats. The eminent teacher wishes either that we should not have it at all, or at least that it should obtain in us neither kingship nor dominion. “Let not sin reign,” he says, “in your mortal body” (ibid.).

The Apostle wishes sin either not to be in us, or not to hold the privilege of dominion. But even if it perhaps shamelessly murmurs against our command, it must nevertheless be subjected, though unwillingly, to our rule. Through Isaiah the Lord both mercifully promises this and does not fail to grant it through his grace to his faithful, saying that he presides over their exalted virtues and that their sin lies beneath them as they trample it down: “Heaven,” he says, “is my seat, and earth the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66).

By the name of heaven I judge virtues to be signified, which by their proper dignity deserve to be separated from low and muddy things. The more sublimely they withdraw from these by refined purity, the more intimately they present themselves to the divine sight. God is said to have his seat in them because it is clear that they please him not a little; seated, reigning, and judging in those very virtues whose purity delights him when offered to his sight, he rests in them.

But earth is sin, which, because it appears to abhor the highest and heavenly things, has deserved to be placed in the lower regions. Removed from the summit of the virtues, it coheres with itself as it were in one lump and mass, so that, like a leaden weight, it always remains in its own place. Yet God not only placed this sin far from his hand, right hand, and arm, but by abundant grace subjected it beneath the feet of his own, so that they may both stoutly resist its assaults and, as victors, trample it down like the mud or dust of the streets.

The hand, right hand, or arm of God is Christ, who waged absolutely no struggle against sin of his own, because iniquity and sin did not approach him at all. But he allowed sin to mingle somewhat with the feet of his own, so that, in its warfare, Israel might be trained, as Scripture says. His feet are his elect, who bear him by word and example to willing hearers, so that these too may become fighters by receiving the word of faith. Of them Isaiah says: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of one announcing and preaching peace” (Isa. 52).

When these feet of the Lord wage war against the assaults of sin, with the Lord himself presiding, they reduce it to a footstool for themselves. He deigns to preside over their virtues as over heaven, and makes earth—that is, sin—lie under them like a footstool beneath their feet.

The bee of which we are speaking is said to dwell in this earth, because the unlawful appetite of the flesh is certainly counted among the vices, over all of which that wicked adversary is permitted to rule as over earth, while he does not cease to oppose heaven and the heavenly virtues of the righteous. Finally, when Paul set forth a catalogue of vices in order, he explicitly placed this same appetite of the flesh among them and judged it not to be excluded from the members which are upon the earth; nor did he consider free from sin one who feels himself deceived by its enticement. “Mortify,” he says, “your members which are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust” (Col. 3), and so forth.

Whoever, therefore, is touched even slightly by such a passion, whether soothed by its enticement or wounded by the bite of its sting, certainly has not wholly confined himself within the bounds assigned to him, but has usurped something from the devil’s right, from his land. When that same wicked spirit recognizes this in him, he clamours and demands back what is his with tumult and deceitful craft. The malicious artificer wishes what has been usurped to be held more greedily, so that it may deserve to be claimed back all the more fiercely in proportion as it is more justly claimed.

Yet he does not thereby recover what he wishes and possess alone those things taken from man. Rather, after first sending out scouts, the tyrannical robber himself then hastens deceitfully to arrive; and, if he has ascertained the matter through those sent ahead, he carefully reclaims it and violently exercises dominion as though by his own right. This violence, just as it occurs only when the devil wickedly introduces it, occurs only when God most justly permits it. This permission, by which the devil is unbridled as though at a signal received, is called a whistle in Isaiah. “The Lord,” he says, “will whistle for the fly and the bee that is in the land of Assyria, and they shall come and rest in the torrents of the valleys” (Isa. 7).

The Lord whistles for the fly and the bee when he does not bring forth the battle-line of strength against them; when, in his just judgment, he withdraws himself from guarding us; when, without grace, he leaves the freedom of our will to itself; when he does not preserve our chastity by the defence [Col. 1000D] of continence. And what else is it not to do these things than a sign of one angered and leaving us far from himself in the hands of enemies? What else, I say, than a sort of whistle that summons and invites malevolent plunderers to their preferred prey?

For he seems in some way to provoke them when, though they press themselves forward, he does not, because of sins demanding it, take care to call them back; when he sets a wretched sheep before a ravening wolf and does not stretch out his hand with a staff to frighten it away. So too, food is sometimes exposed from a most secure store-room; no guards are set over it when exposed, and no barriers are placed against the more avid puppies [Col. 1001A]. What is this except that neglected food is in some way set before them? They run to that neglected food even uninvited, as though called by voice or whistle; and their appetite, as if by its own right, drives them there, from which no present guard repels them.

## CHAPTER XXXV

Therefore it is said of the fly and bee: “They shall come and rest in the torrents of the valleys” (Isa. 7). When God whistles to them—that is, when he loosens the rein of our chastity and continence, and, by the counsel known to himself, relaxes his strict guarding of us; when he does not gird our loins as the Apostle commands, and does not bind our reins and heart with a strong girdle—then the fly and bee, that is, carnal allurements, burst forth as if from ambushes. Rushing into our dwelling in a great swarm and receiving free licence to buzz, they boil over more abundantly and, as though they had obtained what they desired, rest in the torrents of the valleys.

The torrents of the valleys are the impetuous waves of thoughts. Torrents, swollen not from the abundance of a natural spring but by drops of rain, carry away mountain ridges and level plains in precipitous flow. Rushing with great force into the depths of valleys, they pollute those valleys with dirt gathered and swept along, and by such abundance make unclean pools in them. So the impulses of carnal pleasures, generated not from the living spring of purity but strengthened by the small and many rains of temptations, find neither place nor rest in the lofty and level meditations of the righteous. Nor do they restrain the impurity gathered in their precipitous flow, but flow down to the depressed and faint-hearted thoughts of the weak, and, as in a welcome receptacle, build in them a cesspool of vices.

Yet the divine presence, judging sternly, causes thoughts of this kind—however great the swarm in which they are collected, however hardened and frozen by long usage—to be split apart and melted like wax or ice before fire. The prophet Micah indicates this: “The mountains,” he says, “shall be consumed beneath him, and the valleys shall be split like wax melting before fire, like waters running headlong downward” (Mic. 1). For when the stern Judge comes, beneath him the mountains—that is, the accumulated deeds of the perverse—will be consumed; and the deeds which had proceeded proudly into action will be reduced to nothing. The valley also—that is, the secret and deep hiding places of thoughts—will be torn open, and those things which had hoped to lie hidden unpunished will be severely punished. Just as no swelling confidence in deeds will endure his grievous presence, so no one’s deep thought will remain hidden from him; rather, he will bring into light what was thought to lie concealed in darkness, just as that Cumaean prophetess, the Sibyl, declares prophetically:

“[God] will cast down the hills,” he says, “and raise up the valleys from the depths.” He will cast down the hills when, by a manifest vengeance brought upon them, he powerfully tramples down their deeds; he will raise up the valleys when he presents to himself, who sees all things, their hidden thoughts, when he, the searcher of things and hearts, presses heavily upon them, [Col. 1002A] and exercises his judgment over them with grave power. This he threatens terribly through the prophet Joel when he declares that he will come to judge, saying that he will bring those to be judged into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and there swiftly inflict punishment upon them according to their deserts:

> “When I restore the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, I will gather all nations and lead them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and there I will contend with them concerning my people and my inheritance Israel, whom they scattered” (Joel 3).

When God has turned toward the certain liberty secured by the covenant of hope those who in the world do not desire the world’s enticements; whom the seductive pleasures of this life’s imprisoning captivity do not delight; who humbly confess their sins and truthfully confess the living God; who behold true and eternal peace with inward eyes—when, I say, God has turned them [Col. 1002B] toward that liberty—then he will gather the rest to endure severe justice. “I will gather,” he says, “all nations and lead them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat.”

Jehoshaphat means “the judgment of the Lord.” God gathers and leads the nations into the valley of Jehoshaphat when he calls and brings each person back, to be judged, to the depths of his own thoughts: so that there he may strictly rebuke and accuse them, where no verbal excuse can exculpate them. For he questions not any outward matters concerning the quality of their merits, but their inward thoughts. When every perverse person has been recalled to these by strict judgment, he will be compelled to know both what commanded things he neglected and what forbidden things he loved. Hence it is written: “There shall be an examination in the thoughts of the ungodly” (Wisdom 1).

Meanwhile, in the torrents by whose overflowing the depths of such valleys are befouled, the fly and the bee gladly rest; for when carnal allurements inflame the workshop of the loins, they welcome the ravenous flow and cesspool of thoughts. 577 These assuredly would neither come nor prevail unless divine justice whistled to them, unless God, by his permission, opened for them their desired entrance. For when, as a just judge, he seems to forget us because we have not deserved well, he permits those deadly creatures to advance against us at their pleasure.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

Having received this whistle, they broke forth powerfully against King David; having found him upon the roof, they made him captive [Col. 1002D] in mind and wandering in eyes. Enervated by their soft enticements, he obeyed them, and, violating the laws of continence, desired Uriah’s wife in unlawful embrace.

They had also received it—the whistled permission of God—when they assailed learned Solomon, exalted upon his father’s throne. They made his wisdom foolish and his strength feeble, and polluted the beauty of chastity with the filth of intemperance. For he had, as is read, sixty queens and eighty concubines; or, according to some, seventy wives and three hundred concubines. Beyond these, moreover, he wandered and incontinently extended himself toward young women and passive prostitutes, whose number Holy Scripture does not at all record.

In this whistle of God his anger is plainly shown, [Col. 1003A] when a grievous temptation, sent or permitted, rages against us. Unless his justice ceases from that permission or whistle by imposing silence, our weakness cannot withstand so many and such great vexations of temptations. Therefore we need God to remove this whistle from us and deign to bring near to himself a quiet silence: that his anger may not boil up more tumultuously over us, but, taking pity on us though unworthy, may rest beneath welcome silence.

For while it whistles, our valley is polluted by the flood of torrents and the strength of our mind is bent with a bowed knee. Once its uprightness has been bent, the following multitude of enemies passes through it. These are those who, according to Isaiah, say to the soul: “Bend down, that we may pass through” (Isa. 51). But after they have passed through, they no longer speak or talk; rather, according to Zephaniah, they are said to whistle. By speaking, the counsel of the wicked is poured into the wretched; by whistling, the chatter and triumphant dancing of conquerors are poured forth.

> “Everyone,” says Zephaniah, “who passes by her shall whistle and shake his hand” (Zeph. 2).

What, then, are this whistle and the shaking hand but a kind of speech by which the deception of those who, seeing themselves to have passed through a bent soul, rejoice and mock is plainly declared to all? They do not keep silent, according to their purpose, once they have conquered. Great indeed is the exultation of a triumphant people: much laughter, much insulting whistling, a great gathering and great noise of those conversing, and finally the great arrogance of victors dividing spoils according to custom. [Col. 1003C] Hence Isaiah says: “As conquerors rejoice over captured prey when they divide the spoils” (Isa. 9).

This whistle of the enemies, this exultation or mockery of theirs, does not grow mild; this noise of mockers does not hide away in any silence, unless God also wills to fall silent from the aforesaid whistle and, by his own act, wring silence from them. Of this silence Zephaniah, already cited, says: “The Lord your God, mighty in your midst, shall be silent in his love” (Zeph. 3).

For when God purposes to love us more tenderly, he strongly restrains and removes the aforesaid whistle; he changes the hail of his anger into the dew of mercy, and the winds that whistle threateningly into the lament of a gentle breeze. When the dawn-breeze blows, the enemies formerly unrestrained are forcibly checked, [Col. 1003D] and their dances are crushed beneath grave silence. Our sea is levelled into calm plains; the waves are silent; the ship rejoices in their silence.

> “He made his storm a breeze,” says David, “and its waves were silent; and they rejoiced because they were silent” (Ps. 106).

When the storm is driven away, a gentle breeze blows. The mind, shaken by the blasts of winds, breathes again at the advent of silence; and the more abundantly welcome serenity shines upon it, the more serenely it rejoices in the presence of the welcome gift. For in this it understands God to be present to it, not absent from its prayers or desires; and him whom it had felt angry in the storm, winds, and whirlwinds, it feels gently merciful in the breath of the gentle breeze.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Perhaps this is the breeze which Elijah the fugitive is read to have felt, [Col. 1004A] when oppressive fear compelled him to flee swiftly, when, by the protection of flight, he escaped the threats of the raging queen, and, hidden in a cave, attended to God as in some sense present to him.

> “And after the fire,” Scripture says, “a whistling of a gentle breeze” (3 Kings 19).

It is a sign of spiritual grace, by which the prophet, fleeing with a fearful heart, is met and granted the hope of consoling grace or the comfort of a present one. For as God sometimes signifies himself angry by a breath or whistle, so by breath or whistle he often signifies himself appeased; and these signs speak his wrath or favor, as becomes clearer when different effects follow.

> “Your spirit blew,” says Moses, “and the sea covered them; they were submerged in mighty waters” (Exod. 15).

What does this breath declare except the will of an angry and commanding God, purposing to punish the perversity of the pursuing Egyptians? The sea, as though immediately understanding the sign of wrath, hastens to cover the unbelievers in mighty waters.

Likewise, there the whistle plainly signifies wrath where Job portrays the eternal destruction of the rich sinner, when the most severe judge is found, beholding his destruction at hand, either to laugh in anger or, as though laughing, truly to be enraged:

> “He shall clap his hands over him and whistle over him, beholding his place” (Job 27).

For God, seeing the rich man obstinate both in avarice and wickedness and destined by hardened evil for his own destruction, claps his hands over him as though laughing, signifying by the clapping of his hands that he rejoices to see such devotion rewarded with such a price. [Col. 1004C] He also whistles over him, indignant and regarding as nothing the obstinacy of one who presumptuously spends continual time and labor upon his own evil, “beholding his place”: that is, seeing that he will not return from his purpose but will go to his own place—that is, to a place fitting for him—like Judas Iscariot.

Conversely, when after the resurrection Christ showed himself to his disciples and bestowed on them new gifts of his generosity, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20). What grace his breathing upon the disciples signified, he made known by the following words, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit.” Thus it is certain that, just as a word explaining the breath is found to follow it, so the following word reveals the hidden mystery of the sign. Shortly afterward, when again they were shut together in one room, whether held by fear of the Jews or expectation of the promised gift, “there came suddenly,” it says, “from heaven a sound like a violent rushing wind, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2). By such a breath, such a sign, such a whistle, God first spoke; then he fulfilled his speech by the effect of the work. What he signified by mystical breath or whistle, he accomplished by giving them a mighty outpouring of the Spirit.

Perhaps this is why, when those born carnally are reborn through the spiritual washing and cleansed in the water of baptism by the ministry of a priest, we see that minister breathe upon the mystical font: namely, that he may signify the approach of the life-giving Spirit to that font. From this breath or whistle we desire God not [Col. 1005A] to be silent, or rather, to answer our prayers and cries, so that he may pour into us the grace to seek him and may himself, graciously, not delay the benefit of answering.

> “To you, O Lord, I shall cry; my God, do not be silent toward me, lest you be silent toward me” (Ps. 27).

And elsewhere:

> “Do not be silent, for I am a stranger with you and a sojourner, like all my fathers” (Ps. 38).

God is not silent toward us when he purifies the baptismal font by a mystical breath; when he gladdens those anxiously waiting by the forceful breath of the Spirit; when he deigns to refresh the fearful by the whistle of a gentle breeze; and, finally, when he remains with us until the consummation of the age. Of this whistle Zechariah says: “I will whistle for them and gather them, because I have redeemed them” (Zech. 10).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Col. 1005B]

Not only breath or whistling seems to take the place of speech and, in the ways we have mentioned—and perhaps in more besides—to drive away silence; the trumpet, horn, and many instruments of this or another kind have likewise been devised both to dispel silence and to fulfill the office of speech. Thus we read, Scripture testifying, that in wars, where all need to be summoned by the loudest voice and alike urged to press on bravely or resist more bravely, trumpets and horns are employed, since spoken words seemed not sufficiently suitable or effective. Since no voice loud enough could be found to be heard by everyone over so great a distance and extent, human prudence judged it fitting to devise instruments more fully adequate to issue such exhortations more suitably.

Likewise the Lord is found not to be silent when through Moses he instructs the children of Israel, not only concerning what they should do in time of peace, but also how they should proceed into the hazards of war:

> “If you go out to war against enemies who fight against you, you shall sound the trumpets with a piercing blast; and you shall be remembered before the Lord your God, so that you may be delivered from the hands of your enemies” (Num. 10).

God does not wish them to go forth to battle unless they have sounded the trumpets: not to attack hostile enemies stealthily and silently, but to advance more abundantly and eagerly with a loud blast, and to terrify their opponents by breaking their power of resistance. For warriors, stirred by the trumpet’s sound, gather in great numbers and become courageous to undertake war more boldly. Those who feel themselves strong and eager breathe threats and slaughter; the faint-hearted, perhaps ashamed by the example of the stronger, take heart.

Even the animals or beasts of burden used by the warriors, which contribute no small assistance in a cavalry line, are more fiercely excited by the trumpet sound; their cowardice born of fear driven out, they rejoice in the hope of approaching battle. The proud horse could scarcely be kept within proper bounds, resentful to be restrained in silence by its rider’s command: it foams at the mouth, snorts through the nostrils, paws the earth with its hoof, and, scarcely held back though impatient of delay in running or fighting, unable to stand still, repeatedly circles about in a small space. That elephant also, whose strength is said to be so incredible that a great tower is set upon it and, in the tower, a multitude of soldiers is carried—as it is more sharply aroused at the sight of blood, Scripture attests—may perhaps be borne forward more boldly when it hears the blasts of horns.

Therefore God rightly commands trumpets or horns to be used among those whom he wished to show themselves vigorous in war, so that that present carnal people might thereby obtain a temporal benefit and thereafter, through mystical understanding, a future spiritual one. 579 For God wished to order their wars in such a way as chiefly to instruct spiritual warriors, who wrestle not against flesh and blood—that is, material human beings—but resist aerial spirits by spiritual strength.

Anyone who considered more carefully the Lord’s own words, by which he seems to admonish that people, could clearly see this. They so weave a literal history for that people as all the more to demand that a spiritual meaning be received from it. For after the Lord had said, “If you go out to war against enemies who fight against you, you shall sound the trumpets with a piercing blast,” he added: “And you shall be remembered before the Lord your God” (ibid.). As it appears, he commands them not to fight without sounding trumpets so that, at the trumpet-blast, he may remember them—as though he did not easily remember those fighting unless the trumpets awakened him to remember them.

And perhaps this is indeed the truth of the matter. When God’s people wish to go forth to battle and seek victory after their enemies have been overcome, God is found, as it were, to forget the combatants unless compelled by the trumpet blast to remember them. For when the same people are about to undertake the peril of spiritual combat and to contend against spiritual wickedness with an uncertain outcome, if their rulers and teachers do not instruct them with their admonitions and teaching, their adversary will rejoice in their downfall while God does not remember them.

For the discourse and instruction with which the watchful ruler of a people ought to resound, and to ring out tirelessly like a trumpet or horn, driving away the torpor of ignorance, makes the people learned and, by the benefit of instruction, equipped to wage battle bravely. God, merciful in justice and just in mercy, remembers this people, beneficially formed by suitable teaching and usefully encouraged by wholesome formation to resist enemies, [Col. 1006D] so that he may grant it victory over adversaries in battle.

> “You shall be remembered,” he says, “before the Lord your God, so that you may be delivered from the hands of your enemies” (ibid.).

And lest it perhaps remain unknown who ought to be the people’s trumpeters, to whom, that is, the ministry of sounding the blast is particularly assigned, the same Lord who commanded that trumpets and horns be possessed made this clearer in the same chapter: “The sons of Aaron the priest shall sound the trumpets” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXXIX

It is clear that those entrusted with the care of souls are likewise especially commanded to sound trumpets and horns, and those who are particularly rulers of others must also be teachers. Hence later [Col. 1007A] in the same book of Numbers, when Moses sent a thousand from each tribe to fight against the Midianites and commanded Phinehas the priest to lead those forces, he is read to have given him, among the other things which he both commanded and bestowed for conducting war bravely, trumpets also for sounding:

> “Moses sent a thousand from all the tribes with Phinehas son of Eleazar, and added: ‘He also delivered to him the holy vessels and the trumpets for sounding’” (Num. 31).

Moses the lawgiver—for, as it is written, “the law was given through Moses”—bears the type of Christ. When Christ sends his faithful ones to conquer invisible enemies, he does not allow those sent to suffer from the disease of ignorance, but in prudent order gives them such a ruler that, through his merits and teaching, they may find God a ready helper to them.

To the ruler he gives holy vessels and trumpets for sounding; these are useful not only to that ruler, but also by no means unnecessary to the people at war. “Holy vessels and trumpets,” he says. Good gifts, and a good ordering of gifts. The vessels are our bodies. Although their material is said to be clay and fragile, an invisible treasure is nevertheless contained in them, since our souls dwell in their little hut; through the souls’ presence those very bodies are quickened. Of these Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4).

These vessels are adorned by no small grace of holiness if they shine cleanly with the due brightness of chastity; if, in the sight of him to whom we must show ourselves acceptable, abhorring unlawful things, we also love to abstain from lawful ones.

> “We have kept ourselves from women,” says David, “since yesterday and the day before, and the vessels of the young men were holy” (1 Kings 21).

I judge this holiness of continence fitting no one more than rulers of churches. As they ought to surpass those subject to them in the honor of rank, so they should surpass them in the merit of holiness. They offer them no sufficiently suitable model of life unless they have gone before them by the modest and honorable path of continence.

Or perhaps our souls may be called vessels, in which, when grace withdraws, iniquities and vices gather and are deservedly broken by the iron rod; or, when God gives generously, gifts of virtues gather and are preserved by the Giver himself through the merit of his gifts. Those that are for dishonor deserve rejection; those that are for honor deserve preservation by their Maker. Golden and silver vessels are admitted into the treasury; unclean and clay vessels are broken and cast into the dung-heap. Those that are for honor and burn with the gift of holiness are pleasing to God himself through the inward fervor of charity: when, that is, not merely the surface, like a deceitfully whitewashed wall, [Col. 1007D] but the purified recess of conscience presents itself to him.

## CHAPTER XL

Finally, the foolish virgins, because they had no oil in these vessels—that is, because they neglected to possess within the recesses of the soul the burning fervor of true holiness—came to the Bridegroom’s door with an empty conscience and found it shut, not to be opened by any prayers:

> “Lord, Lord,” they say, “open to us.” But he says: “Amen, I tell you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25).

Their foolishness and foolish emptiness are truly proved in this: at Christ’s wedding, it is not the one who has cried out but the one who has brought something who is heard; the door is opened not by voices but by gifts, and that Bridegroom is gracious not to the caller but to the giver.

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7).

And therefore in Exodus: “You shall not appear before me empty-handed” (Deut. 16).

The Gentiles transferred this from our writings into their own pagan literature; later generations favorably praised those who transferred it, and what they had received from our earlier and better forebears, their descendants accepted with approving use and memory:

> “If you bring nothing,” says a certain writer, “you shall go outside, Homer.”

And Plautus in the *Asinaria*:

> “If you bring something, then the doors stand open; if you have nothing to give, the house does not stand open.”

Which scholarly cleric who frequents the reading of secular literature does not very often mention these verses? Who, having pleasantly and memorably retained this saying, does not commend its authors as though it had been their invention?

Yet those writers in some way distorted this sentiment and turned it toward showing the avarice of certain persons who, according to Isaiah (ch. 1), “loving gifts and pursuing recompense,” do not regard anyone with due honor unless they discover that he brings them gifts. Among such persons, whoever appears empty is also thought foolish; conversely, one from whom much money is counted is not thought foolish. For their sake the popular saying is often repeated: “Empty purses make the mistress foolish,” because the wisdom of someone whose needy hand lacks gifts to offer does not appear commendable in their eyes.

But God, who does not know the disease of avarice, does not demand our gifts for his own sake. Rather, providing for us, he wills us not to be found empty and void but to be presented, laden and rich, to his majesty. He wills us to be vessels not empty and deserted, on account of the foulness of heaviness, but clean and filled with an abundant gift of holiness: that his gracious goodness may choose us, and, having chosen us, may love us by reason of our fruitful will.

Such a vessel he willed that man to be, and by the grace of his own will made him so: though not chosen on account of preceding merits, he obtained mercy when he had deserved wrath.

> “This man,” he says, “is a vessel of election to me” (Acts 9).

In this type Moses gives holy vessels to Phinehas son of Eleazar, so that he may prefigure him whom he wishes to set over a people going to war as holy through mystical gifts, and so that his body, soul, or rather both, may be enlarged with such holiness that the people following him ought rightly to imitate him. And because it is not fitting that one appointed by God to preside over a people should be mute, Moses therefore gave trumpets to Phinehas the priest, so that, as he sounded the trumpet, the warriors might gather more quickly and be more strongly encouraged to conduct the war.

For it is not enough for one set over others to show himself a leader unless he also shows himself a teacher: having displayed the way to followers by walking ahead, he must know how to encourage them toward it by preaching fitting words. Therefore, after the Lord said of Paul, “This man is a vessel of election to me,” he added: “That he may bear my name before nations and kings and the children of Israel” (ibid.), making it understood that in him would be not only the truth of holiness but also holy preaching of truth: so that, while he truly loved God in the secret place of his heart, he might also preach him to Jews and Gentiles in fitting speech.

For one who burns inwardly to love God, if, lacking the trumpet’s sound, he hides in sluggish silence, however he may provide for himself alone, gives no necessary help to others by exhortation; and when they flee, as Isaiah warns, does not meet them with water and bread. If such a man is appointed as the leader of others in battle-array, and the care of warriors in a great undertaking is committed to him, then as much as he benefits them by boldly fighting, so much—indeed, more—does he harm them by lacking the sound of exhortation.

## CHAPTER XLI

Ehud, judge of the children of Israel, understood this wisely. When he wished to fight bravely against the Moabites and effectively exhort the children of Israel to the same battle, “he sounded the horn,” it says, “on Mount Ephraim; and the children of Israel went down with him, himself going at their head” (Judg. 3).

You see that, on receiving the judge’s signal, the children of Israel assemble and, at the horn’s sound, are manfully encouraged by their love of battle. Perhaps none, or very few indeed, would have assembled had the judge wished to proceed silently to war. But now, who among the people would not hear the judge? Who, having heard, would not obey more diligently, when he sounded the horn powerfully, and did so on Mount Ephraim, so that its sound might reverberate more clearly?

Just as a standard is sometimes placed upon a mountain so that it may be seen far and wide by many people, even those at a distance, so a trumpet or horn is also sounded upon a mountain by prudent counsel, so that the cry may be heard both better and farther away.

> “He sounded the horn on Mount Ephraim” (ibid.).

Ephraim means “fruitfulness.” Therefore, upon the fruitful mountain—that is, in the fruitful eminence of merits, in the fruit and advancement of exalted works—a good judge endeavors to sound the horn and invite the people subject to him to the grave hazard of battle. Since its signal or sound does not come from a barren valley, while he goes before his hearers in the merits of fruitful works, they assent, obey attentively when they hear, and eagerly follow him who goes before them.

> “They went down with him, himself going at their head” (ibid.).

Such a man, when he speaks, wishes to be loftier than the rest; and when he goes forward, likewise to be before them. Thus he is not accused, while silent, of harmful silence, nor seen, while speaking unworthily, as presumptuous and loquacious; he does not incur, while advancing, the fault of refined sluggishness, but in all things, before all people, sets forth and displays a worthy model of holiness.

This is what Isaiah appears mystically to show when he warns the one who evangelizes to ascend a high mountain, as though no one ought to usurp the ministry of preaching who has chosen to dishonor it by a lowly mode of life:

> “Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isa. 40).

If ascent onto the high mountain has preceded, one need not condemn the presumption to preach which follows, because that preaching is found to have worthy strength when it is fortified by the lofty summit of the mountain. Therefore it follows there: “Lift up your voice with strength” (ibid.). For when one about to preach has climbed the mountain and, by a certain preeminence of life, raised something like the standard of victory, he rightly deserves to be heard far and wide by those below, having first labored to be found lofty and conspicuous through the merit of his life.

Hence the same prophet elsewhere says:

> “Raise the standard and lift up the voice; raise the hand, and let the leaders enter the gates” (Isa. 13).

If the standard is raised, if the voice is more clearly lifted up, and if the hand of teaching—that is, action—has been elevated, our leaders will not return driven back from battle, but will enter the enemies’ gates with victorious eagles. At their watchful urgency, moved by their insistent presence, the opposing bars are loosened, the enemies’ strength is weakened, and finally the walls all around utterly collapse; everything that formerly resisted is overthrown in a great destruction.

## CHAPTER XLII

Joshua son of Nun beautifully prefigured this in that battle by which he overthrew the stronghold of the city of Jericho. Bow and sword [Col. 1010C] were not found able to prevail in conquering it; rather, the priests’ horns won the chief title of victory. For Joshua commanded, by the Lord’s precept, that seven priests with horns should precede the ark of the covenant; that they and the entire army should circle the city of Jericho once each day for six days; and that on the seventh day they should repeat the circuit seven times and, while going round, make sound not with words but with horns.

> “Go around the city,” he says, “once each day; thus you shall do for six days. But on the seventh day the priests shall take seven horns used in the jubilee and go before the ark of the covenant; and you shall circle the city seven times, while the priests sound the horns. And when the trumpet sound grows longer and sharper, all the people shall cry out with a great shout, and the walls of the city shall fall utterly” (Josh. 6).

By this sound of trumpets or horns is signified the speech which is assigned in a particular and special manner to prelates and priests, who are commanded not to silence the new grace of the sevenfold Spirit. The hostile Jericho could not withstand their great proclamation.

For the hammered-metal trumpets with which these priests sound are evangelical preaching, uttered by the apostles and their successors. Chosen by a divine gift, they are leaders and teachers of peoples; with speech drawn out and unfolded from the hidden darkness of mystical meanings, they destroy in those subject to them the raised and fortified masses and contrivances of vices.

As the number ten commonly signifies the law given through Moses, because the Decalogue of commandments is literally set forth in it, so the number seven signifies the fullness of our present age, in which the sevenfold Spirit gives the perfect holiness of new grace. For the number seven contains three and four, one added to the other to make seven: grace to retain faith, hope, and charity is poured out through the four regions of the world; the four Gospels plainly preach faith in the Trinity; in the human being the fourfold body is subjected to the threefold soul; and the soul itself, cleaving to God, rejoices to become one spirit with him.

Therefore there are said to have been seven priests, seven trumpets, seven days, and seven circuits on the seventh day. By the power of this mystery the towers and walls of Jericho are overthrown; in that overthrow the choir of priests prevails by its merits, and the subject people of God rejoice when the marks of victory have been gained.

Finally, the horns used are those whose use is in the jubilee. “Let the priests,” he says, “take seven horns whose use is in the jubilee.” The Hebrews called the fiftieth year *jubilee*, in which, by the Lord’s command, pledged possessions returned to their former owners, debts were freely remitted, and slaves were released into restored freedom. Since such numerous and great benefits abounded in that year, they called it, as stated, *jubilee*, that is, the year of remission; in it they sounded mystical trumpets or horns and matched festive blasts to the desired remission.

Nor did they use mystical trumpets only in the jubilee, but also in other festivals. They seemed to correspond to the solemnity of the days with harmonious blasts, displaying by outward signs the joy of the present feast to those who were carnal, and prefiguring future spiritual things to those who understood spiritually. Hence in Numbers:

> “Whenever you have a feast,” he says, “or festival days or Kalends, you shall sound the trumpets over the burnt offerings and peace offerings, that they may be a remembrance of your God to you” (Num. 10).

And David:

> “Sound the trumpet,” he says, “at the new moon, on the notable day of your solemnity” (Ps. 80).

What Numbers calls the Kalends, the psalm calls the new moon (*neomenia*). The *neomenia* is called the new moon. The Hebrews reckoned the new moon as the Kalends, that is, the beginning of the month. At this time, by the Lord’s command, they broke silence with sounding trumpets; and when, according to the prescribed custom, they celebrated this or any other feast day, they sounded the horn so as to correspond with the feast—or rather, to weave its mystery.

The Church has not wholly rejected the practice which the synagogue received from the divine institution of the ancient law. Rather, it has changed the hammered-metal trumpets with which that synagogue sounded at that time into bronze signs of another form. When it has a feast—that is, when at the altar it consecrates the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood and, through the hands of ministers, gives this spiritual food to the faithful; when it observes a festival day; when it celebrates the *neomenia*, the new increase of the month—that is, when it solemnly commemorates the laying aside of the loss of the old life and the beginning or increase of a more perfect fullness of grace—it customarily rings out a solemn joy with bronze signs, which common usage among us more frequently calls bells.

Such a celebrated ministry of these signs is employed in churches so generally that scarcely any church or monastery is found in which the people of the faithful are summoned without such signs, or the divine office celebrated without their proclamation. When they sound, the sluggish silences of night are dispersed; sleepers are stirred to wakeful eagerness; ministers go to church to celebrate the synaxis or morning praises; and lay workers awake in their different workshops to do the work of their hands. The bells sound and, with a necessary kind of jubilation, speak beforehand; the others carry out their appointed task in song or work. Nor does confused ignorance of the hours trouble them by night or day, since the loud prior speech of the signs makes the distinctions of the hours plain.

The cry of these signs—their speech—is so resonant that it penetrates the farthest spaces of the air. Though held together in one place by a fastening bond, when struck by an iron clapper they are heard far away. These signs therefore act not only among those present but also among those absent, because, serving hearing rather than sight, they dispel silence. For just as silence occurs when the ear is said to hear nothing, so silence is certainly removed, or rather destroyed, when any resonant utterance is found to pass through to people near or far away.

Finally, when the high priest of the law enters the Holy of Holies for the purpose of prayer, he is commanded to wear bells upon a hyacinth-blue garment, so that, though he cannot be seen by those standing outside because of the intervening veil, he may nevertheless be heard more significantly by a mystical sound or sonorous mystery.

## CHAPTER XLIII
Nevertheless, certain other signs are found which serve sight more than hearing. They are so properly said to be signs of words that they are often called, by a figurative manner of speaking, not signs but words. These are letters: as it were, bonds by which any flat surface is inscribed, and, when prudently joined together, a sequence for reading is arranged. Hence, according to grammarians, *littera* (“letter”) is named as though *legittera*, because through it a path is afforded to readers [Col. 1012D]; or because the ancients wrote upon waxed tablets, they named letters from *liturae*, erasures.

Prudent antiquity, which has gone before us not only in time but also in care and foresight, devised this benefit of letters for this reason: since no one could fix fleeting words, he might in some fashion preserve them by a memorial writing, engraving their marks and signs—that is, letters—upon parchment or tablets, and, by looking upon them, recall to memory what had passed. Between words and the signs of words, that is, letters, such close affinity is found, and signification and signifier are bound by so great a kinship, that we often metaphorically call the words which we utter with the mouth “letters”; and conversely, we improperly call the letters which are written “words.”

Thus a written codex is said to contain many words, although in truth it contains not fleeting words but enduring letters [Col. 1013A]. And one who has uttered Latin words in speech is said to have uttered Latin letters, although it is certain that he could have uttered not the letters adhering to the book, but passing words. Finally, when the Lord had set Moses over the children of Israel and on Mount Sinai had taught him, through many discourses, what He wished them to do, Moses himself is said to have written down the sequence of those discourses, so that it might be read not only among those then present, but might also not be erased among future generations by any blot of forgetfulness. Hence in Exodus: “Moses,” it says, “wrote all the words of the Lord” (Exod. XXIV). And much further on:

“When Moses had fasted for forty days [Col. 1013B], so that he might deserve to receive the Law a second time, and when the Lord spoke familiarly with him on the summit of the mountain: ‘Write for yourself these words,’ He says, ‘by which I have made a covenant both with you and with Israel’; and Moses wrote upon the tablets the ten words of the covenant” (Exod. XXXIV).

From this it is evident that discourses or words, which are of course uttered in speaking, are improperly understood as the letters which are written; and that letters, which are signs of words, are commended by the Lord when He commands them to be inscribed upon tablets.

Long before Moses, as the apostle Jude reports, Enoch, seventh from Adam, prophesied; and he carefully committed his prophecy to letters, wishing that what he had written might be conveyed to posterity by the vehicle of letters—though that writing is held neither among us nor anywhere in the canon. For although the authority of so great a man was not to be despised [Col. 1013C], very ancient antiquity made his writing suspect, since men of sound faith doubted whether everything ascribed under the heading of his name had been written by him. For many have committed many things to writing and letters while placing before them not their own names but those of others, either so that they might establish their own writings under titles of better men, or weaken the titles of great men by reprehensible writings.

Many also, when they found writings of their forebears worthy of praise, wasting away with envy inserted something of their own, and by adding dregs disturbed the purity they had found; and, sowing tares over it, obscured the truth of the wheat. But because the writing of Enoch did not reach posterity free from suspicions of this kind, it did not obtain canonical authority among them [Col. 1013D]. For although he existed as nothing but a writer of truth, later generations regarded letters of so great an antiquity as suspect.

Whether for this reason or any other, his writing is not placed in the canon; yet there is no doubt that he wrote, because, as has been said, the apostle Jude attests this in his Epistle, which is confirmed with canonical authority in the catalogue of divine Scriptures. Whether Enoch himself first invented letters, or received them as invented by someone earlier, I do not judge to be certain from canonical Scripture, though it has in some manner been ascertained from other writings. But whoever invented them, no one earlier than he is found in canonical Scripture to have written [Col. 1014A]; no one prior to him is truly found to have committed his discovery to letters. Although his writing cannot be found among us, or anywhere, or in the canon, the office of writing is most certainly first ascribed to him.

And rightly does canonical authority affirm that he first wrote—the man who, by the order of generations, was Adam’s seventh descendant—for this office could fittingly be attributed to none more than to one known to have received the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. For the fact that Enoch is read to have reached the seventh degree of generation indicates that he attained the sevenfold grace of the Spirit: beginning with fear, he deserved to advance to wisdom; and, taught wisely, to become a teacher of those less wise.

Finally, perhaps the Spirit of God is called the finger because through Him wisdom is written upon the tablets of hearts: He is the inward writer, and likewise the writing itself, which no overwriting or erasure removes from the hearts of the elect. When this Spirit had raised the aforesaid Enoch step by step to wisdom, He consecrated him, in a certain new manner, to His own office: what the Spirit breathed familiarly into Enoch’s heart, Enoch might legibly inscribe outwardly for the knowledge of others [Col. 1014B]. Thus the one writes inwardly with the spiritual pen; the other writes outwardly by the ministry of letters. The one presides, as in a temple consecrated to Himself, over the wise heart; the other, as one consecrated, serves the Lord who presides.

This accords with the fact that Enoch is interpreted “dedication.” For when someone is advanced to such wisdom that by writing he is himself conformed to the inward scribe, a certain solemn and festal dedication is celebrated: namely, when the scribe works through the obedient pen, or the pen works under the scribe’s direction. “My tongue,” says the prophet, “is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Ps. XLIV).

Nor, I think, should it pass unworthily in silence that Enoch, having been translated, is nowhere found among human beings. For no human being—one who delights in knowing only what is human and transitory—can attain or find him who deserved to enter the secret sanctuary of the inward scribe and reach the chamber of His wisdom. That height of spiritual wisdom which is granted to every perfected person is altogether inaccessible to one who is wise merely in human things; for while the former is made serene by spiritual pursuits, as by the hiddenness of the divine face [Col. 1014D], the latter is troubled by human and transient affairs. “You shall hide them,” it says, “in the hidden place of Your face from the disturbance of men” (Ps. XXX).

Rightly, therefore, is Enoch mystically reckoned seventh in descent from Adam; rightly, he who, having found the seventh [gift], is struck by the disturbance of men; rightly, I say, is the grace and ministry of this office assigned to him, so that by canonical testimony he may be declared the first of all to have woven a book with letters, even if he is perhaps thought also to have invented those letters. For it seemed fitting to the inventors of letters that through this sign not only might people present speak with those absent, but those who followed long afterward might know the words of their predecessors; so that those who had already lost the power of speaking—indeed, of living—might not, through their enduring writing, be silent to future readers or hearers.

## CHAPTER XLIV

[Col. 1015A]

A certain writer of Jewish antiquity relates that the sons of Seth—namely Enos and his brothers—imitated their father in good conduct, banished idle sloth, devoted themselves to honorable pursuits, and, vigorous alike in application and native talent, discovered certain hidden mysteries of knowledge unknown to others. Since they did not wish these to perish through forgetfulness or neglect, but to come to the knowledge of future generations by an indelible display, they prepared for themselves two pillars, one of brick and the other of stone, and inscribed upon them what they had prudently discovered.

For they had heard their grandfather Adam prophesying to them that the progress of time would so increase human wickedness that the divine power would not endure it with an even mind; and that, as evil grew more grievous, a grievous destruction threatened human affairs, and the human race would be destroyed at one time by fire and at another by flood [Col. 1015B]. Accordingly, using prudent counsel, they wished, as stated, to prepare one brick pillar and another stone pillar, and to entrust their new knowledge to a durable writing. They considered that if the brick one were compelled to dissolve under a flooding deluge, the stone one would remain indissoluble; and if the violence of fire pressed for the dissolution of the stone one, the brick one, able to endure fires, would remain inviolate.

Thus they believed that their discovery could be delivered to posterity, since their writing would not be destroyed by whichever catastrophe came first. They were uncertain whether fire or flood would be inflicted first, but certain that, when one threatened, the other would be postponed for a longer time. It is clear that these men possessed letters, since they are said to have written their knowledge on pillars; and perhaps they themselves first invented letters, having surpassed the people of their age by a new knowledge and a new zeal for knowledge [Col. 1015C].

That first age, therefore—whose people had but one speech and one language—both consulting the present and providing for those who followed, established written signs for itself, so that it might have some inscribable and durable memorial of the word that passes away and perishes in its swift passage, and that this invention might be transmitted to posterity by a most useful conveyance. That speech or language used by the people of that time bore no particular name, because no other, dissimilar language could yet be found among any nations, in distinction from which it ought to be marked with its own designation.

So likewise the letters which that age first inscribed, I think, it called by no name at that time; they were simply called “letters” or “writing,” and were to acquire a distinctive name much later. For in the second age, when Noah’s sons had set out from the east, found a plain in the land of Shinar, and devoted earnest labor there to the building of that famous tower, they were confused by a multiplicity of languages through the intervention of divine justice; their design was frustrated, and they were separated from one another and dispersed far and wide among nations and families [Col. 1015D].

Because the original language remained in the family of Heber—within which the religion of divine worship had also earlier in some measure remained—the Hebrew people was named from that Heber, as his family was called. Within this Hebrew people and language, the letters formerly invented, though separated from those of others, persisted; and those who held this distinctive designation by what was virtually hereditary succession had Hebrew letters just as they had the Hebrew language.

We know, therefore, that letters existed among the Hebrews in the second age; yet we do not know who among them wrote, or what writings they left. Either that whole age was silent and inactive in the making of books, or antiquity, by a design hidden from us, effaced what had been produced [Col. 1016A].

But the third age, which began with Abraham, furnished us with skilled and authoritative writers. In it Moses was found and reared by Pharaoh’s daughter, and in the course of time was trained to the utmost in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. Through his hand God delivered the children of Israel and instructed them, once established in the wilderness, by legal commandments, commanding that the words of that Law be committed to letters, so that they might be retained in unfading memory through the aid of letters.

This ministry of writing was assigned to Moses so that he who was leader of the people might also be considered their teacher. For one who presents himself as leader ought to supply his subjects with the nourishment of doctrine; and I judge that nothing is more fitting for a teacher than to surpass in the merits of virtues those whom he instructs. Thus Moses leads and teaches the carnal people, and, by the Lord’s command, entrusts spiritual doctrine to letters, so that not only those immediately present might be instructed by the present admonition, but also those who would read long afterward might follow the prescribed rule [Col. 1016B].

God further willed that both the precepts necessary for the formation of conduct be inscribed in letters and the creation of the world be recalled to the knowledge of those present; that things past be revealed to Moses himself by the prophetic Spirit; and that he should recount in writing the sequence of events to both those present and those to come. After Moses, Joshua son of Nun, by the Lord’s command, led the same people and brought them into the land of promise, something denied to Moses. There he divided the inheritance among the ten tribes by the measuring-line of distribution, and did not permit his own deeds to be buried in silence.

For he too took up the pen and inscribed written characters; imitating the master as a minister, he ordered the history of events, commending writings which he judged pleasing to those present and useful to posterity [Col. 1016C]. In these he not only explained the events, so that they might be retained in memory, but marked profound mysteries, so that they might be apprehended more pleasingly by subtle understanding.

After that time are described the succession of judges and their deeds, who are known to have existed in this same third age; perhaps knowledge of them would long ago have been removed from our midst by forgetfulness, had it not been committed to memorial writing. During the long span of this age, in which this Scripture of ours proves these things to have happened—the Scripture first established among us by canonical authority—the peoples of the nations invented letters for themselves, and some among them first became distinguished by knowledge of letters.

Before Moses was born in Egypt, when Isaac, in the land of Canaan, had already become the father of the twins Jacob and Esau, Inachus is read to have ruled first over the Argives, that is, the Greeks; and after him his son Phoroneus to have held the sovereignty [Col. 1017A]. His daughter Io, who was also called Isis, illustrious indeed by birth but far more illustrious in intellect, left the bounds of Greece and came to Egypt. There, ruling widely and justly, she first invented letters.

For it seemed to her not only elegant but necessary that one person should sometimes speak to another in silence, and that when separated from each other and unable to hear their mutual words, they might disclose the secrets of their wills through the mediation of letters. Because this gift pleased the Egyptians greatly—especially since no one, or scarcely anyone, knew that it had yet been granted to the nations—they mourned Io, or Isis, as was fitting, even when she had died; and after her death, in wandering error, worshipped her as a goddess.

Not forgetting so great a benefit, they built her a temple in pitiable devotion, in which, in order to represent her memory, they wished also to set up an image, to which they decreed that prayers and sacrifices should be offered. They fashioned this image with such prudent intent that it seemed to place a finger upon its mouth, thereby indicating that Io herself had avoided superfluous speech and, as a teacher, invited her pupils to silence [Col. 1017B]. For this reason she was believed to have invented letters and to have taught those over whom she ruled the art of letters: so that, when anyone wished either to indicate more clearly a secret in another’s presence or recall past matters to memory, he need not always employ the noise of words, but might accomplish it more elegantly by letters while the tongue was silent.

For the prudent queen knew that nothing is considered more unbecoming than for a woman, having broken the barrier of silence, to be talkative; and that she deserves to be censured in the judgment of prudent persons who especially does not deserve often to be heard by prudent men. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Let women keep silence in the churches; for they are not permitted to speak, for it is shameful for a woman to speak in church” (I Cor. I). And to Timothy: “Let a woman learn in silence” (I Tim. II).

Solomon also, in the Proverbs, when he brings forward an immodest woman hostile to an unwary young man through deceits and flatteries, is found to censure her among other things because she is not restrained by silence, but is talkative and impatient of quiet. “Behold,” he says, “a woman meets him in the dress of a harlot, talkative and wandering, impatient of quiet” [Col. 1017C].

Therefore, although the queen lived among many people, she considered it unsuitable to be heard speaking often among them. She accordingly took pains to cultivate silence and to transact every matter that arose not so much with words as with letters, so that she might plainly show herself not disgracefully unbridled by talkative boldness, but modestly and diligently, honorably and actively instructed. So that her prudence may be recalled to memory and all who behold it may be invited to the modesty of silence, her image, though it imposes no such command by word, places a finger upon its mouth in order to signify this.

## CHAPTER XLIV

[Col. 1018A]

Or perhaps that image is said not to place its finger *upon* its mouth, but to place it *at* its mouth, so that thereby not silence but speech may be figured: just as placing the finger upon the mouth is found to restrain speech, so placing it at the mouth is figuratively understood to express it. For, since Io modestly refused either to appear talkative or chattering, or wished more discreetly to announce her intention to persons far away, she is said to have discovered a new kind of speaking, which clearly pleased the Egyptians greatly. The Egyptians marked this on her image, since they wished to place its finger not upon, but at, its mouth.

For speech is fittingly figured by the mouth, since speech is undeniably made properly by the instrument of the mouth; and the very inscription of letters is called a kind of speech, although the office of writing is assigned not to the mouth but to the hand [Col. 1018B]. Therefore, when the statue of Isis puts its finger to its mouth, it perhaps does not impose silence on those who look upon it, as was said before, but wishes by this indication to recall that the prudent queen Io strove to discover a kind of speaking.

Her discovery instructed the unpolished Egyptians and freed them from the stains of their own ignorance. Greatly stirred by its benefit, they more subtly and diligently searched out the depth of certain mysteries. Having acquired an honorable and necessary knowledge of letters, they especially set themselves to investigate the order of the stars; and what earlier men had perceived through subtle inquiry and careful experience, they committed to letters so that the same knowledge might come more widely to others.

Thus, making progress through love of learning and zeal for reading, the Egyptians in the course of time became wise and in some measure stretched themselves heavenward beyond other nations, as they discovered the stars, their courses, their fixed positions, and their abodes [Col. 1018C]. Some are found to have pursued this kind of knowledge with such eagerness that, in the Prophet’s words (Ps. LXXII), they seemed to have set their mouths in heaven; and because of the knowledge of the stars which they are said to have attained in some measure, those skilled in this art came everywhere to be called astrologers.

Foremost among them is remembered that great astrologer Atlas, concerning whom the lying chatter of poets tells the fable that his stature was so great and strong that the height of heaven rested upon his shoulders. Those who testify that mystical meanings lie within many fables judge that nothing else should be understood in this case except that this man certainly possessed such great knowledge that he was believed beyond others to have attained an exalted understanding of the stars [Col. 1018D].

His brother was that remarkable craftsman Prometheus, whom the error of the Gentiles asserts to have formed men from clay, not sufficiently understanding that it is false to ascribe such a thing to any human being, since God alone, not Prometheus, could accomplish it. But because at that time there was an innumerable multitude of fools, whom dull ignorance held fast as mud holds a street, prudent Prometheus gathered some from the midst of that unskilled and foolish nation and impressed upon them wise instruction as though it were the form of human reason.

When he had educated these crude and unformed people and, in his wise school, polished them thoroughly by skillful art, he rendered them distinguished by a worthy standard of knowledge, as though by human form—those whom he had found muddy through a gross and shapeless bleary dullness [Col. 1019A]. While these brothers, Atlas and Prometheus, abounded in knowledge and took no small care to teach others, Moses was born in Egypt, cast into the reeds of the river, and thence compassionately received and nourished by Pharaoh’s daughter; in the course of time he acquired all the wisdom of the Egyptians.

## CHAPTER XLV

[Col. 1019B]

Long after Isis, the Phoenicians, lest they should be considered without letters and appear inferior to the Hebrews or Egyptians, also made new characters and figures useful for their speech and memory, in order to make words or voices, naturally fleeting in their headlong transience, fixed and stable by the bond of letters. Concerning them a certain poet says:

> “The Phoenicians first, if report is to be believed, dared  
> to mark enduring speech with rough figures.”

Cadmus, son of Agenor, brought this discovery into Greece and there made known seventeen Phoenician letters. The Greeks gratefully received his instruction and learned from him both the knowledge and practice of learning and reading. Because the Phoenicians had first invented such letters, the Greeks who learned them under Cadmus chose to adorn the beginnings of their books with Phoenician-red color, and by this sign recall the benefit they had received [Col. 1019C].

This practice first grew up among the Greeks, and neither the antiquity nor forgetfulness of time has erased it even to the present day. Indeed, having come down even to us, it is observed so generally that scarcely a book is written whose beginning is not furnished with Phoenician color. After the letters invented by the Phoenicians, which Cadmus made known to the Greeks as stated above, Palamedes added three others during the Trojan War; and after him Simonides is said to have invented three more. Added to the earlier ones, they completed the number of twenty-three letters.

With the aid of these letters Greece began to possess learned sages. Devoting earnest care to acquiring knowledge, they diligently committed to letters the praises of the gods whom they served in various ways under deception of error, in order to enlarge their remembrance. Since their pursuit was to compose wordy poems about the gods, they deserved generally to be called theologians, gladly receiving such a name as one that might mark out their allegedly divine office.

The earlier and more ancient among them are reported to have been Orpheus, Linus, and Musaeus, who surpassed their contemporaries in reputation and learning. Through their literary labor, praises and poems were offered to false gods, and agreeable teachings were provided to erring people [Col. 1019D]. At the time when poets flourished in Greece and attained, by the testimony of reputation, the literary art of learning, the people of Israel were already dwelling in the promised land and were governed there by judges—and, as some think, by Deborah the judge [Col. 1020A].

After those poets whom we said were called theologians because they chose especially to tell tales about their gods, that Sibyl too made Greece illustrious through her reputation for learning; inspired by a truth-speaking spirit, she prophesied many things concerning Christ. Ten Sibyls are said in the writings of the Gentiles to have existed, three of whom are extolled by later writers with no small praises. By their deserved distinction in literary learning, they are found not only to have equaled the men of their age, but, by the testimony of many, truly to have surpassed many of them.

One of these three was the Erythraean; another, the Cumaean; the third, the Samian. The Erythraean—or, as some more strongly suppose, the Cumaean—is said to have composed the prophecy in which Christ’s coming, passion, resurrection, and final judgment seem to have been made manifest. These Sibyls existed and flourished in literary learning at the time when the fourth age of the world, which began with David, was already unfolding, and the people of Israel were held under the rule of kings [Col. 1020B].

The Erythraean Sibyl made Greece illustrious by her fame when King Ahaz—or, according to some, his successor Hezekiah—ruled the Jews. The Samian Sibyl is said to have lived afterward, when Judaea was already ruled by Manasseh, son of Hezekiah. After the Erythraean Sibyl, Thales of Miletus is said to have arisen. He is said to have been one and the first of the seven sages of Greece, and to have flourished in natural philosophy at the time when Judaea rejoiced under the more just rule of the aforementioned Hezekiah, and Rome, recently founded, was ruled by Romulus.

After Thales of Miletus, six others are remembered; with him added as the first, they were called the seven sages of Greece. These six are said to have flourished when the children of Israel were already held captive in Babylon. Their names are: Pittacus of Mytilene, Solon of Athens, Chilo of Lacedaemon, Periander of Corinth, Cleobulus of Lydia, and Bias of Priene [Col. 1020C].

Because these men excelled others in life and learning, they were called by the general name *sophi*; the usage had not yet prevailed whereby those learned in letters, as distinct from the unskilled multitude, were called philosophers. Anaximenes and Xenophanes, successors of Thales of Miletus, were also called *sophi*, which in Latin means “wise men”; in investigating the causes and natures of things they imitated the same master, yet, each abounding in his own judgment, they held very diverse opinions.

They too flourished in literary learning at the time when the Babylonians held the children of Israel captive, and when Pythagoras is remembered to have flourished in that part of Italy which is now near Greece and was then called Greater Greece.
