Because, out of humility, he did not wish to profess himself a *sophus*, that is, a wise man, observing that very many were called *sophi* rather than truly being such, he first named himself a *philosophus*, that is, a lover of wisdom. In this name he modestly claimed for himself not the thing itself but love for the thing [Col. 1020D].

When this expression was brought to the knowledge of others and seemed to all modest, humble, and fitting for this profession, a pleasing and elegant practice grew up among them, which has not been abolished from that time onward by the antiquity of time: whoever burned with love of letters and excelled in their learning would acquire for himself the name not of *sophus* but of philosopher.

This new philosopher invented the new letter Y. In its shape he figuratively indicated that the first age of life is lived with undifferentiated judgment, but when it has ended, a kind of fork in the road is found, as one comes either to the right hand of wisdom or to the left hand of folly. The left-hand way, at first broad and spacious through the pleasing enticement of pleasure, leads into final narrowness, deservedly because of its sought-after perversity. The right-hand way, initially restricted and narrow, is made smooth toward progress by the grave appearance or beginning of holiness, and passes into the perfection of expansive love [Col. 1021A].

Of these Solomon says: “The Lord knows the ways that are on the right; but those on the left are perverse” (Prov. IV). For this reason the left branch of this letter, beginning from breadth, ends in a narrow outlet; whereas the right branch, narrower at first, widens at the end. For the pleasingness of seductive injustice is shut in by the constrictions of punishments, while the narrow way of righteousness is received into the welcome breadth of rewards.

In this fifth age, which Matthew declares to begin from the Babylonian captivity and, prolonged through many years, to end in the advent of the Lord, such a multitude of philosophers arose among the Greeks, and so great a love and pursuit of writing possessed them, that the region shone in letters beyond other nations, while among its other cities Athens held pre-eminent and celebrated renown. For Athens was regarded as a kind of gymnasium of learning, in which the naked agility of philosophers wrestled in tireless exercise; there were the furnace, or forge, the anvil, the hammer, and the workshop, through whose aid or labor philosophical discipline was forged [Col. 1021B].

There Socrates and Plato, native sons endowed with marvelous genius, were educated; there, burning with remarkable zeal, they were most thoroughly instructed in letters. There Plato’s Academy resounded with the clamor of disputants, whence a learned posterity of Platonists sprang up in fruitful growth. Therefore those who wished to be more fully trained in letters flocked with special eagerness from every direction to that city, believing that learning could not be polished to perfection in letters unless the Athenian file had most carefully refined it [Col. 1021C].

588

## CHAPTER XLVI

After the Greeks, whose learning, as has been said, flourished in the city of Athens, the use of letters passed to the Latins; and the nymph Carmentis bestowed on them a welcome benefit by teaching them, still uncultivated, new letters. This nymph, whose proper name was Nicostrata, was also called Carmentis because she spoke of future things in songs. She first gave, they say, seventeen letters to the Latins, by which they formed their words and various utterances [Col. 1022A]; not content with that number, in the course of time they added others.

For H, K, Q, and X, which the prudent woman is not thought to have invented, are said to have been added by learned posterity, so that, because the woman’s discovery sometimes seemed insufficient, a fitting supplement might be supplied by a later invention. Y and Z, however, are Greek letters, which the Latins adopted through preference rather than necessity: namely, so that when they sometimes used Greek names in Latin speech, those Greek names might be written with the aforesaid Greek letters.

The Hebrews therefore had twenty-two letters, and the Greeks twenty-four. The Latins held a kind of middle position between the two, having twenty-three characters with which to compose their writings; some were invented by the aforesaid woman, others by others. When such elements or letters in the course of time came to the knowledge of many, and studious people far and wide wished to be taught them, this teaching at last especially flourished at Rome, and the workshop of this discipline glowed with a great throng of assembled people [Col. 1022B].

For just as Athens was a kind of fountain and overflowing abundance of Greek letters, from which no small multitude of teachers flowed forth and shone, so at Rome the learning of Latin letters boiled over, as a great multitude of poets gathered and studied there. There they were furnished with much material for writing; there a welcome reward was rendered for their labor; there their fame was spread abroad with celebrated praise, as the copious eloquence of these writers told of what the bravery of combatants accomplished.

The Romans’ highest purpose was to conquer foreign nations by a strong hand and rule the conquered with power, aspiring not so much to greater riches of gold as to the supreme dignity of empire, so as to make their own city the head and mistress of the world. Hence one of them, despising weights of gold and valuing highly the praise of victory and the generous spirit of a conquering ruler, did not submit gold and riches to one who offered them, but gave an elegant answer:

> “The Romans do not seek gold, but seek to rule those who possess gold.”

Those who spoke these and similar things, lovers of glory, wished them diligently committed to writing, so that their memory might be carried even in the present to distant persons and thereafter not be erased by any soot of forgetfulness [Col. 1022C]. For this reason writers zealously devoted themselves to literary labor, striving to extol in praise both the deeds and sayings of noble persons. They received both monetary payments, which they needed temporarily, and the title of vain glory, which they often sought more eagerly and intensely.

With this reward in view, not only the more learned but also the less learned publicly rushed into writing; and, keeping no measure, they chattered like frogs in marshes. They considered nothing more shameful than to possess even a very small amount of literary learning and yet not compose books and be included among the poets. Seeing some run everywhere to writing as though to a market or a summons [Col. 1023A], a certain man flings at them a mocking curse, so that those whom imperfect restraint cannot hold back from their presumptuous boldness may at least be confounded and silenced by satirical derision:

> “Let scabies occupy the last place; it is shameful for me to be left behind.”

So many and such persons arrogated to themselves the office of writing, and, though unable to speak, refused to be kept silent; thus even those endowed with greater perfection of learning were greatly displeased by so much presumption among the unskilled. Yet both the learned and the unlearned, strangers to divine truth and either not knowing God or not following with the affection of love the God whom they knew in some degree, did not make their writings worthy of commendation, because in them they had no desire at all to please the true God.

For, with understanding darkened by the gloom of unbelief [Col. 1023B], they did not know how to distinguish the imperfect from the perfect; they pronounced worthy of praise only those whom they observed to devise more subtly and speak more ornamentally in their writings. Few indeed—or scarcely any—illumined by true light, bore worthy witness to eternal truth; and though many delighted in practicing literary labor, it was granted to few of them to behold God more discerningly.

Among the other things which that prophetess, the Sibyl, wrote with much industry—and, in writing, entangled in many obscurities, as those who have read her affirm—there are certain passages to be found which seem applicable to Christ as God and man. I have indeed declined to insert them into this little work, because I judged their length would be burdensome to hearers; [Col. 1023C] and if perhaps you wish to hear or read them more attentively, they will be readily available to you upon consulting the volumes of certain Catholic writers. That noble poet too, Virgil, who undertook to recount the overthrow of the Trojans, 589 and in sequence the ancient origin of the Romans, perceiving that a slender ray of truth was shining upon him, did not wish to suppress in silence the spark he had received:

> “Son, my strength, my great power, thou alone.”

And elsewhere:

> “Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven.”

Some judge these words, certainly, to have been spoken mystically of Christ, although historically they seem to allude to others; for no one doubts that very many things are so proclaimed concerning Christ [Col. 1023D] that it is certain that the same things may be assigned, according to the letter, to others. Yet because these poets or prophets did not attain sincere faith, but spoke without knowing what they said—as Caiaphas did in the Passion—the divine judgment did not sufficiently approve their eloquent writings; and those alien from faith it deservedly rejected from life. Therefore, whether their eloquence proclaimed anything concerning God more obscurely or perhaps more clearly, that supreme Judge judged them worthy to be silenced, since, although they foretold many things true and fitting to God, they were nevertheless not worthy of the office of prophets because they lacked faith. They say certain things which appear consonant with truth, and yet Truth itself commands them to be silent: as when demons are permitted to utter Christ’s praises, yet are restrained from their purpose by the command of silence. [Col. 1024A] “I know,” says one, “who thou art, the Holy One of God.” And he says: “Be silent, and come out of him” (Luke IV). And below: “Demons,” he says, “came out of many, saying: We know who thou art, the Son of God; and rebuking them, he did not allow them to speak” (ibid.). If those who bear witness to truth are commanded to be silent because, in bearing it, charity of faith is not joined to faith joined with charity, how much more rightly are those driven back from the flood of speech who prate of falsehoods, errors, and things contrary to God.

Thus the philosophers of the nations, both Greek and Latin, who resounded in many and varied writings and, while being led astray by diverse error, accorded with one another in the same literary labor, were vehemently checked when the Gospel trumpet sounded; and, like frogs on hearing thunder, they plunged into their marshy hiding-places. [Col. 1024B] Not without reason are James and John called sons of Boanerges—that is, sons of thunder: when they thunder, chattering frogs are terrified; at their writings philosophical loquacity is struck dumb and, overwhelmed by a mighty cry, falls wholly silent or grows hoarse. For the defenders of Catholic truth spoke things so subtle and so lofty, and pursued saving doctrine with such power of the Spirit and such constancy, that the pagan hearers were wondrously astounded, having nothing they could reasonably answer to what they heard. And because, stubborn and wretched as they were, they could not draw in deep mysteries by any vessel of understanding, they reproached the Catholic teachers, supposing those whom they heard pouring out new and marvelous things like a river to be mad, like persons possessed, through a wandering mind.

[Col. 1024C] When Paul, grievously accused before the governor Festus and King Agrippa, was arguing his case and strengthening his words by the invincible testimony of the Scriptures, Festus, amazed that he thundered so fearfully and fluently, and having no means by which he could effectively meet this thunder, said: “You are mad, Paul; much learning drives you to madness.” And he said: “I am not mad, most excellent Festus, but I speak words of truth and sobriety” (Acts XXVI). And shortly afterwards Agrippa said: “In a little while, Paul, you persuade me to become a Christian” (ibid.). So great was Paul’s learning, and so great his constancy in speaking before kings and governors, that no fear of them could deter him from his undertaking, nor could anyone resist him in argument while he spoke. [Col. 1024D] Therefore God, in wise counsel, willed that the words by which he steadfastly resisted adversaries and vigorously pressed upon them the Catholic faith should be committed to writing, so that through the benefit of writing they might be conveyed not only to the knowledge of those then living but also of those yet to come.

For as Christ, upon coming, willed to obscure the writings of the pagans and, shaking off their ancient bloom, assign them to nocturnal silence, so he stirred the apostles and apostolic men—whom he flooded, as it were, with the morning light of Catholic faith—to speak and write by a certain incitement of vehement spirit. The more they shine in faith and works, the more ardently they burn to write, according as God imparted to each his own grace and instructed him by spiritual gifts not only for living but also [Col. 1025A] for writing. In the course of time, therefore, many composed many Gospels; by divine counsel four of these deserved to take precedence—four which searching truth strengthened with canonical authority and the sacred mystery of the number four commended. Moreover, many undertook to write treatises, letters, sermons, homilies, and other kinds of Scripture, fervent in literary zeal; and, as day by day faith is more widely spread among all nations and, by grace bestowed, the number of believers increases, more persons in various places and times gird themselves for writing, and the mighty acts of divine praise are celebrated in manifold fashion in both Greek and Latin letters.

But while the truthful writings of Catholics prevail solemnly with great strength and a great multitude, [Col. 1025B] the vanities and lying madness of the pagans grow languid and weak; and while the former, as though hastening toward the noonday pole, grow bright in prosperous progress, the latter, by a westward course, are darkened in the deep gloom of night. Eager watchfulness worthily adorns the writings of Catholics; sluggish indolence hastens to put pagan writings to sleep. For every believer wishes to bestow due care upon writing or reading the former; toward the latter he is commanded to fall asleep in heavy slumber and commendable contempt. If, perhaps, a Catholic appears at some time to open his heavy eyes upon them, because he judges that he finds in them something befitting honesty and useful for morals, then, although he reads, he does not choose with a pleasure-seeking affection to cling to their darkness. Rather, he gathers what is good and [Col. 1025C] loves to turn what he has gathered to uses fitting for himself. The writings of the gentiles ought either not to be read by Catholics, or to be read with this intention: that what in them is false and useless may by no means be loved, but what is useful may be chosen, like grain from chaff.

It has certainly become known to almost everyone, and in the course of time we see matters have come to this: among the pagans there are now no writers, or exceedingly few, and their ancient writings are scarcely read by religious Catholics today. So great a multitude of Catholic writers has grown together and prevailed, so great a holiness has appeared and been pleasing in their writings, that we see silence now deservedly imposed upon pagan writers and the new [Col. 1025D] writings of our people preferred to their old writings. Nor is it unfitting that in our times pagan literature has fallen silent and pagan writers, struck by the ecclesiastical trumpet, have kept quiet. For the presumptuous fabric of their edifice ought not to advance but to decline: religious truth did not furnish it with a noble and immovable foundation, but inflated vanity both laid beneath it and piled upon it deceptive and unstable flattery.

The mysteries of heavenly grace have deservedly been unveiled to the understanding of the others, and the door of writing has been opened to many who understand: applying themselves to the pursuit of knowledge and wisdom, they gladly forget the things behind in contemplation of what lies ahead, and, working for their own salvation and that of their fellows, seek God principally. These men are certainly not only permitted to write what they have understood, [Col. 1026A] but are not even allowed to be silenced, lest, if they can and neglect to return their talent doubled to the lender, they be accused and delivered to the exacter for eternal destruction. Although there have never been, nor will there be at any time, lacking detractors who bite and tear such writers with satirical tooth, nevertheless their ill will is not to be feared in such a way that the good will of these writers should be restrained from writing.

If the succession of teachers is traced backward from modern writers up to the apostles—of whom an innumerable multitude is remembered to have existed, one after another and together—scarcely any one of them, I think, could be found to have enjoyed so fortunate a state of affairs that he could truly rejoice that he had endured no detractor and no rival. “Our fathers,” says the rival, [Col. 1026B] “have already written enough; with sufficient diligence they have examined the canonical Scriptures. Their subtlety was sufficient for writing and their sufficiency has supplied us with material for reading. What need is there for new writers to go on writing again and to toss their learning about on the fan of fame, as though the secrets of Scripture had not reached the earlier writers but these younger men at last saw them with lynx-eyed understanding?”

Thus and thus do certain detractors speak against writers of their own time, pursuing them with poisonous abuse so as either to call them back from writing, burdened by such injuries, or at least to make their writings contemptible by disparagement. You know a certain man of our order who, having already begun to expound the Song of Songs and having completed almost four books upon a few of its verses, [Col. 1026C] would have carried a work of no small size to its conclusion in the tenor in which he had begun it. But he wished, somewhat prematurely, to submit what he had written to the reading of outsiders, perhaps hoping that others would take pleasure in a labor pleasing to himself. When certain persons learned this, they took it very ill and, angry with him, mocked both the work and its author—as if, in the words of a certain pagan, they had seen a third Cato fall from heaven; or, in the language of our Scriptures, Saul suddenly rush in among the prophets of the Lord.

Since this new scribe could not bear with sufficient equanimity the grievous vexations they caused, and preferred silence to suffering their bites, he cast down his pen and did not complete the work he had begun; taking silence upon himself, [Col. 1026D] he satisfied his detractors. Yet when divine goodness willed to impart its grace to our forebears and to open for them, with ready hand, the door of knowledge and writing, it did not shut within that inner chamber all who were their contemporaries; neither did it exclude from the same sanctuary the many who would come after. Indeed, it willed to advance certain persons to this office both later and earlier, though not all deserved to obtain equal grace in writing. When gracious God embraces one who surpasses others in knowledge, by the mercy that is his, he does not reject any inferior person; rather, he wills to be praised no less by the spoken and written word of diverse persons—he whose praises none of them can adequately unfold.

But whoever wishes to prevent any diligent person from writing [Col. 1027A] wishes, as it were, to set some limit to divine praises: namely, that no one should presume to write of God except one to whom it has been given to shine with the highest and perfect knowledge. Yet, in my judgment, no cleric is rightly barred from this, provided that he performs the same office with sound faith and doctrine. This, indeed, seems to me to be the clerical office; this is the special task assigned to a cleric above others: that, loving God and separated from the affairs in which secular life is entangled, he should spend his chief diligence in reading and writing. But since, as I think, enough has been said concerning letters as concerning the other signs, and sufficient indication has perhaps been given as to whether a person ought rightly to be silent about them or not, it now seems we must proceed to that silence which, it is said, is kept by one who returns nothing. [Col. 1027B]

## Chapter L

For there is silence not only from speech but also from repayment: namely, when someone is found to bring or confer something upon another, and the recipient returns nothing. This return or recompense is twofold, since one kind is like and the other unlike. Like recompense returns agreeable things for agreeable things, or disagreeable things for disagreeable things. Unlike recompense returns agreeable things for disagreeable things, or disagreeable things for agreeable things. This twofold—or rather fourfold—recompense may appear more clearly if someone wishes to recount testimonies from Scripture, in which certain persons are found responding now in one way, now in another, and abstaining from those very responses in a kind of quiet silence.

Concerning that recompensing [Col. 1027C] response which is called like, and rejoices to return agreeable things for agreeable things, the Lord did not wish to be silent through Moses when, setting it forth, he wished to urge the children of Israel to obedience: “If,” he says, “you keep my commandments, I will give you rains in their seasons, and the earth shall yield its growth, and the trees shall be filled with fruit, and you shall eat your bread in fullness” (Lev. XXVI). And in Deuteronomy: “If you keep,” he says, “the commandments of the Lord your God, the Lord will make you abound in every good thing: in the fruit of your womb, the fruit of your cattle, and the fruit of your land” (Deut. XXVIII).

Because I know that heavenly things do not yet sufficiently please you, weak and carnal as you are, but that with animal affection you cling to earthly and visible things: if you love to keep the things laid upon you, [Col. 1027D] I shall lovingly bestow upon you with generous hand those things which I do not doubt are pleasing to you. Since you are in some measure obedient to me, I shall not keep a miserly silence, but shall answer your desires with ready generosity, so that you may perceive him whom you do not love without reward or payment to be a benevolent recompender of the service you render.

In this, divine equity set before us a form of recompense, which it imposed upon every living creature as a kind of law of nature: namely, that every animal is naturally stirred to return agreeable things for agreeable things, and is, as it were, rightly to be reproved if it is not bound by the bond of this law. Hence dumb animals become gentle not only toward animals of their own kind but even toward those of another kind; they grow accustomed mutually to soothe and to please one another; and scarcely anything is found to possess such fierceness that it does not at least incline its affection toward one like itself. [Col. 1028A] Observing this, the Wise Man says: “Every animal loves its like, and all flesh is joined to what is like itself” (Ecclus. XIII). If this nature has such power among dumb animals as to unite them by the bond of a certain mutual good will, far more rightly ought the human creature to be bound by a like tether, since by merits it is destined to attain the vision of the Creator of virtues. For it is not fitting that, while affectionate fellowship or social affection softens wild beasts, bestial savagery should render a human being inhuman; nor that he should not only fail to aspire to the offered height of spiritual merit but even be found devoid of natural fellow-feeling.

Commending this, a certain pagan says:

[Col. 1028B]

> “The will to preserve a human being is fitting for a human being.”

This prudent pagan judged nothing more fitting, nothing more becoming to a human being, than that he should judge worthy of preservation, by natural judgment, the person whose form he sees to be like his own. To him divine Scripture says: “Visiting your likeness, you shall not sin” (Job V). A human being’s likeness is another human being, who by the right of similarity deserves to be visited by a human being’s bestowed kindness. And lest perhaps, when he shrinks from being urged to return this kindness, a person should say that he cannot imitate the invisible God, he is commanded at least to resemble dumb animals, which by native affection love to associate with their fellows; so that, when a man excuses himself on the ground that the loftiness of the higher God cannot be imitated, he may at least not refuse [Col. 1028C] to imitate the lower things placed before him.

For when Ecclesiasticus had said, “Every animal loves its like,” he added, “So also every human being loves his neighbor”; and, having added, “All flesh is joined to what is like itself,” he again appended, “So every human being is joined with one like himself” (Ecclus. XIII). Thus, when any sluggish person cannot sufficiently prevail in imitating God, he may blush in shame at being unable even to imitate dumb animals; indeed, he who does not fear to be harder than a beast in returning a kindness should rightly be judged to have put off humanity and put on stone. Perhaps for this reason God is said to raise up children for Abraham from stones (Matt. III): because, by the working of his power, human hardness is softened to this end—that it is no longer content to resemble dumb animals, [Col. 1028D] but strives, in returning agreeable things for agreeable things, to imitate righteous Abraham (Gen. XXI).

When Abraham rejoiced in receiving the son for whom he had hoped (Rom. IX), trusting that in Isaac his seed would be called, as had been promised (Gen. XXII), he was neither ungrateful nor unbelieving toward the gracious and truthful promiser; he was ready to return to the giver the gift he had received and requested. Thus every wise person must imitate righteous Abraham, so that he does not begrudge returning to God what he receives from him, lest the brightness of the received light be hidden, as it were, under a bushel, or the entrusted talent be wickedly buried, as it were, in a hole in the ground.

The same Abraham seems to shun this course, choosing rather to speak than to restrain his tongue in silence, 592 knowing that before God he has no glory who does not wish to answer the giver of gifts with a grateful [Col. 1029A] heart. “I will speak,” he says, “to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes.” “Although,” he says, “I am wrapped in the covering of earthly dust, although I am not yet wholly freed from the bonds of sins, yet in response to the Lord who has first spoken with freely bestowed gifts and moved me beforehand to render like things in return, I shall hasten to answer not so much in words as in deeds. I shall return his gifts to him with open scale; and when I, according to my ability, have followed with recompensing liberality him who in his own goodness first spoke to me, though I am little, then my desired son—laughter or joy—will arise for me, in whom unfailing length of days or posterity will be granted me.”

In Abraham there is prescribed a certain form of recompense which is inaccessible to the weak and is specially assigned to the perfect: those whose concern it is not only to avoid the shame deserving blame for stinginess, but more eagerly to aspire to the fuller glory of generosity.

[Col. 1029B] There are, indeed, certain actions which, if performed, confer greater glory, but, if not performed, bring no greater blame; nor is the neglecter of them to be reproved nearly as much as the diligent performer is to be praised.

But there are other actions which do not greatly adorn their author, while they more gravely dishonor one who despises them; nor is as great an honor or merit gained from performing them as disgrace and stain are incurred from neglecting them. Those things, namely, which are more ordinary and lesser, are easily performed, are imposed generally upon all as necessary to salvation, and, when performed, do not confer a distinguished name and glory on the performer, but, when despised, inflict upon the despiser the stain of more serious guilt. [Col. 1029C] For one who keeps what is written—“You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal” (Exod. XX)—and other such commands is undoubtedly not held guilty, but does not thereby deserve glory; he does not incur the punishment owed for crimes, but does not acquire the title of exceptional praise.

A certain pagan is found to have shown this aptly, when he elegantly makes one man answer another who was guilty of no theft. For when one man wished to boast of his supposed justice and claim for it something great and special: “I have not committed theft,” he said. The other immediately replied: “You will not feed ravens on [Col. 1029D] the cross.” That is to say: if you have chosen to keep your innocent hands from theft, you have escaped the punishment and disgrace of the cross; your flesh will not be given as food to birds—a penalty which civil judgment inflicts upon those guilty of crimes. Yet, just as you see that you have escaped a shameful punishment, do not suppose that you have also acquired the special glory of praise; for if someone is found free from disgrace, he is not immediately marked out by glorious praises. But one who does not fear to become entangled in theft, homicide, or any similar crime deserves to be tortured grievously and disgracefully; he obtains no such great reward or glory by abstaining as he incurs punishment and dishonor by doing these things.

This is indicated by a certain satirist, when it is loudly declaimed through streets and squares: [Col. 1030A] “They say, ‘Sejanus is being dragged by the hook.’” This Sejanus, as one guilty and convicted of crimes, was, through the hatred of all, consigned to such punishment and mockery that either he himself or perhaps his statue was dragged in the most disgraceful fashion by a hook through the middle of the city, while many people everywhere cried out in exultant derision: “Sejanus is being dragged by the hook.” Who does not see that this man, wrapped in so many stains of crimes and hatreds, incurred such a punishment and such infamy as no corresponding praise or glory would have been granted him had he been free of such calamities? There are, then, very many things which produce little glory if they are diligently observed, but much punishment and much disgrace if they are carelessly neglected; and whose contempt leads into profound misery, [Col. 1030B] while their observance does not lead to the summit of glory.

No more perfect person wishes to be content with these things, which he knows to be slight and common to many; rather, with generous affection, he tends toward harder things, in which he gains the glorious title of praise. Nor did praise of this kind escape even the pagans, whose valor sought to surpass others, since in returning a benefit it shrank from no hardship, no arduous undertaking, and did not even evade facing the risks of death. Their writings discuss at length and proclaim everywhere, as worthy of readers’ remembrance, that Pylades and Orestes were bound together by so great a tie of mutual love that, lavish of this life, they were ready to die for one another.

In Scythia there is a place which in ancient times was called Mount Taurus, [Col. 1030C] where there was a marble temple in which the virgin Diana was worshipped. No one but a virgin served as priestess of that virgin, and with her virgin hand she sacrificed victims on the sacred altars. There impious antiquity established a remarkable—or rather pitiable—rite, which later posterity preserved for a long time: if any stranger happened to arrive there, he was led away as a victim and perished in honor of the virgin Diana. When Pylades and Orestes had been driven there by adverse winds, seized in accordance with the custom and destined to be sacrificed before the altar, the virgin Iphigenia, who unwillingly performed the office of priestess, had compassion on those about to die and delayed carrying out the sacrifice.

At last she said: “One of you [Col. 1030D] must be sacrificed and, according to the harsh rite, must venerate Diana by the shedding of blood; but the other will be allowed to return home, so that the sacrifice of one may be reported by the return of the other.” 593 On hearing this, Pylades said that he would be the victim and that Orestes, as more worthy of life, should return home; and Orestes in turn ordered Pylades to depart, maintaining that he himself should perish in fulfilling the sacrifice. A loving contest, a new dispute, took place between the young men, because to each it seemed grievous and unjust that he should be forced to survive while the other died—indeed, that another should survive unless he himself first died. The Getae, the Sauromatae, and the other Scythian barbarians marveled at such a deed; marveling, they confessed it worthy of remembrance, and all paganism judged that it should not be buried in silence [Col. 1031A] but transmitted to posterity in writing for the praise of these young men.

Something similar is also reported in pagan writings concerning the two Pythagoreans Damon and Pythias. When one of them, condemned in judgment, was ordered to be led to death, he requested permission to visit his own people briefly, in order to make provision for them, and to return on the appointed day for the decreed execution. The ruler who, according to the sentence of the law, had ordered his death, thinking that he could not find anyone to stand surety for him, said: “Your request and the delay you request are not denied, provided that you furnish someone who will die for you if you do not return.” The man offered his companion, who would undergo the punishment in his place if he failed to keep his promised pledge by not returning. The man offered as security for the one offering him did not refuse to become guarantor; but when the other departed, he fearlessly awaited the day under the judge’s authority. [Col. 1031B]

The day arrived on which the accused man had promised to present himself; and, because his delay made it seem that he had not fulfilled his promise, the man who had served as pledge was led to execution and calmly prepared to die for the absent man. While he was displaying marvelous constancy amid the preparations for death, behold, the other returned, lest he be held guilty of falsehood; and, because he had presented himself, though somewhat late, on the appointed day, he declared that he rather ought to be killed, his guarantor being wholly released. All marveled that such friendship had bound them, such constancy had strengthened them to die for one another; so that the ruler released both from their obligation to death and devoutly requested to be admitted into their friendship. [Col. 1031C]

But lest such contempt for life and desire for death for the sake of love should seem to belong only to pagans—or lest what has been said should perhaps be pronounced fabulous and trivial—something similar is found to have occurred among our own people at Antioch, where a certain man suffered martyrdom for a Christian girl. For she, beautiful in face, fervent in spirit, loving religion, had resolved to preserve the integrity of her body; and, avoiding public gaze, had chosen to live privately. The more, by common report, her suitors despaired of obtaining their desire, the more she began to be desired by many of them. When she consented to none of their entreaties and no one found the access he desired, intemperate love, deeply wounded by rejection, at length turned to inflicting suffering upon the virgin.

Thus the girl, burning with such love of purity that she did not refuse to suffer death to preserve the gift of chastity, was brought forth; she feared more that an shameless lover might deflower her virgin modesty than that a hostile executioner might take away her bodily life. [Col. 1031D] Seeing her steadfast in her profession, strong in religion, exposed to punishments, lavish of life, miserly with modesty, concerned to preserve her integrity, ashamed before masculine looks, and unafraid of approaching death, they considered how they might turn her from faith and religion; how, in order to turn her, they might instill fear of the loss of chastity, so that, once they had shaken the foundation of the religious commitment she had undertaken, they might then inflict damage upon her virginal modesty.

They therefore ordered her either to worship the gods by offering sacrifice, or to be prostituted to a filthy brothel for the corruption of her integrity; so that whichever she chose, her purpose would be nullified and, that purpose broken, the persecutor might rejoice in his victory. The virgin hesitates, her mind is tossed in different directions, and, repeatedly turning over every possibility, she is entangled on every side in astonishing straits. She considers it grievous that virginal modesty should be violated by the shamelessness of pimps, but far more grievous that the mind should be defiled by the filth of idolatry. [Col. 1032A] Addressing herself about this, she says: “What shall I do? Where shall I go from the evil spirit, and where shall I flee from the face of sin? If I descend into the hell of idolatry, eternal ruin is near at the doors. If I abandon my purpose of chastity, I am likewise worthy of punishment: for faith broken incurs eternal destruction, and no small punishment follows if promised chastity is corrupted.”

[Col. 1032B] “But, as I judge, chastity is not truly judged corrupted when the mind, wholly intact, resists a violent ravisher while the flesh is overpowered; when, although weak flesh feels the wound of violence inflicted upon it, the stronger mind does not consent to seductive corruption. I will enter the brothel, relying on the defense of faith; and, though I must suffer a pimp, I shall not give consent to corruptible allurement. Although I think that God, the lover of chastity, is not absent from a brothel, indeed that he is everywhere present to all who call upon him—he who delivered Susanna from the hands of the unchaste elders (Dan. XIII) and preserved unharmed [Col. 1032C] the chastity of the widow Judith in the house of Holofernes (Judith XII)—the same God can preserve my chastity in a brothel and the holiness of faith amid the hands of persecutors, so that faith may be strengthened by chastity and chastity by faith, and my adversary may not plunder my purpose in either respect.” 594

Strengthened by these and similar thoughts, the virgin is shut up in the brothel, and a dissolute crowd hastens to assemble for such a spectacle. The curious man does not wish to be found slower in coming to see; every lustful man fears being anticipated by another. Within, she sighs and trembles violently like a tender lamb, but is not broken by fear, because in mindful possession of God she gains strength. Outside, they rage in turbulent fury like wolves, joyfully supposing her to have been enclosed in their nets.

[Col. 1032D] While they roar, behold, a certain man distinguished by military dress makes his way through the midst of the others into the brothel. He alone knows for what purpose he is entering; all perhaps suppose that he intends to indulge in wantonness with the girl. At his entry the virgin is struck dumb with uncertainty, since the reason for his coming is not yet wholly known. She doubts whether he has come to take away her virgin modesty or rather to kill her with a soldier’s sword. He says to her: “I beg you, virgin, do not be alarmed at my entrance; do not fear me as an enemy and a man of blood. I have come only to provide both for your life and for your modesty, provided that you listen to one who offers you counsel. I wish you to be clothed in my garments and I in yours, so that, our dress having been exchanged, I may appear to be a woman and you, conversely, a man. You shall leave this hut [Col. 1033A] wrapped in male clothing, and, while I remain amid the stains, you shall fly forth more freely, released.”

“And because those who surrender themselves to wandering and shameless lust are, when such an act has been accomplished, confounded as though overcome by repentance, hide your head and face beneath the covering of this cap of mine, so that your flight may be safe amid the snares of those clamoring around you by means of this disguise.” The virgin marvels and refuses to contrive the proposed deception, judging it unfitting to gain anything at another’s loss and to bind so benevolent a man by her own release. Yet, overcome by his urgings, she at length yields; and, after giving and receiving the garments, she leaves and departs in the guise of a man.

When she had gone out, one of those who were clamoring outside the door, scarcely able to endure delay in satisfying his lust—one whom a more vehement heat of lust or perhaps malice consumed—rushed in before the others to satisfy his lust. [Col. 1033B] Seeing a man, though he knew a woman had entered, and ignorant of the contrivance of the deception, he thought a miracle had taken place: that, with the clothing unchanged, a woman had been transformed into a man, a thing which pagan fabulous writings sometimes report to occur. “What,” he says, “does it mean that you entered the brothel as a woman, and behold, have assumed a man’s appearance? There has been no change or damage in the garments, and yet sex, face, and nature have been altogether made other. Must this place not be believed to have a God so powerful, bringing such contrary effects upon different persons who come to it, that either a man is transformed into a woman or a woman into a man, and is forced either not to be what it was or to be what it was not?”

“It is therefore prudent that we flee from here swiftly, while it is clear that we are still what we were before; lest, if we remain here longer, through the god of the place working what belongs to him, we too be changed into something else. Although I seem already to myself changed, and altered beyond what can be said or imagined: I who entered the brothel an unchaste fornicator leave it, my purpose broken, chaste and modest.”

But when it became known that the soldier had contrived the deception on behalf of the virgin, malice gaining strength, he was assigned to death in the virgin’s place; and, as the wicked and pestilential people rushed upon him, he was led out of the brothel to the place of execution. On hearing this, the virgin hurried back as though running eagerly to market, thrust herself into the crowd, and bitterly protested that the soldier had forestalled her:

> “I—yes, I am the one to whom death is due; what has this soldier, this innocent man, deserved?” [Col. 1033D]

But he said: “I am the one whom they found in a place of shame; the one whom, as their merits required, they declared to be liable to death. What has by common judgment been decreed to be inflicted upon a man ought not, by a base design, to be turned back upon a woman. In short, your flight, once undertaken, in some manner already excuses you; and, as before, the wrath of the judges does not accuse you. Having once been released from the debt of death and from the bonds of the noose, you seem, through womanly importunity, to have returned to demand the same things.”

To him the virgin replied: “I did not choose you as the protector of my life or blood, but of my chastity: that chastity might be preserved under the protection of one stronger, because it was not my life but my integrity that was exposed to danger, and my captivity feared not a killer but a corrupter. When, by both your counsel and your kindness, I escaped outside, I certainly escaped not martyrdom but disgrace. I left you behind not so that you might die for me with your blood shed, but so that, secure in your presence, I might preserve my modesty.” [Col. 1034A]

For it was maidenly modesty, not a man’s modesty, that was in danger of being crushed; and against it raged not a sword, but youthful shamelessness. Its loss is irreparable, however anyone may suffer it; its breach can be repaired by no effort. If, then, the issue is death, I am ready; and I who fled for the sake of preserving virginity shall willingly undergo it, choosing rather to suffer more than to prolong life longer in weariness. If I returned quickly, I must certainly not be refused; if I am not late or negligent, I must even be excused. And she whose patience failed her for enduring the loss of modesty has a sufficient defense of courage for bearing death. If you inflict that death upon me, I shall think that I have not been redeemed by your kindness but ensnared by a more cunning design; nor will you seem mercifully to have provided for my necessities, but secretly to have begrudged my present advantage. Take care, then, lest, while you begrudge me martyrdom, you inflict injury also upon my modesty; lest, while I remain alive, I be subjected to a corrupter, and him whom I had hoped would be the kindly defender of chastity I find, on the contrary, when my hope has been overturned, to be its certain destroyer. But if you allow present martyrdom to be granted to me, no result of uncleanness will remain to my corrupter; you will be the most welcome author to me of a double benefit, and you yourself will suffer nothing harmful, no such misfortune.” [Col. 1034B–C]

In this manner the soldier and the virgin contended with one another, each desiring to forestall the other by dying; and while each feared for himself lest he should remain alive when the other died, the death they desired was inflicted equally upon both. There is now no ground upon which either can justly complain of the other, since neither is permitted to survive, since the executioner pursues both with equal peril, so that each receives martyrdom as a most welcome gift. Who would choose to pass these persons over in sluggish silence, when one can rarely find their like—people who were united only in this, that they wished, in rivalry with one another, to die for the other? For they did not pass through their lives in silence, these people who with magnanimous spirit performed something so noble and excellent that even the bravest could scarcely imitate them, and that people everywhere could not keep silent about the renown of so illustrious a deed. [Col. 1034D]

## CHAPTER LI

A certain historian seems not to have kept silent about persons of this kind; indeed, he urges them all the more diligently to strive, not content with lesser deeds, to attain the summit of excellence, and not to be cast down, like degenerates, in obscure silence.

> “All men who endeavor to excel the other animals ought to strive with their utmost power not to pass through life in silence.”

For those are said to pass through life in silence who seem not to perform anything worthy of special praise, whose conduct is not regarded as so upright, their excellence so distinguished, that it is often celebrated among others by spoken proclamation. But by these words this pagan perhaps seems to instruct those whom he wishes to shape after himself in writing and example, whom, with human praise in view, he wishes to devote themselves to excellence, preferring passing respectability to religious holiness. When people like himself strive to obey him and, in accordance with his teaching, devote their effort to distinguished works, they do indeed have glory, but not before God: they obtain among the people a temporary title to admiration, but receive nothing eternal from God, whom they either do not know or despise. Such, certainly, were those mentioned above, who, rejected from the faith, are said to have chosen death for one another; and because they were found zealous to perform great deeds from a love not divine but human, they are glorious not in heaven but on earth, not before God but among men. [Col. 1035A–B]

But those who rise, by their own efforts joined with grace, to love God, and who sincerely embrace their neighbor in accordance with the second and like commandment, do not remain in the school of the pagans, which does not know the purity of faith; rather, they hear Christ’s teaching and the truth of sacred Scripture. For there it is said that every one of the faithful must serve God even unto death, and likewise assist the needs of a neighbor even unto death—yet in the love of God he must acknowledge no measure, weight, or limit, whereas in the love of his neighbor he must extend himself according to the prescribed rule:

> “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. VI). [Col. 1035C]

The person is proved to love his neighbor as himself who does not begrudge mercifully giving that to another which he wishes given to himself: whether money, if the other is heavily burdened by poverty, or indeed his own life, if necessity seems to demand it.

> “Whoever has the substance of this world,” says John, “and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him—how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John III.)

And above:

> “He laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren” (ibid.).

And Paul to the Corinthians:

> “Most gladly,” he says, “will I spend and be spent for your souls” (1 Cor. XII). [Col. 1035D]

And to the Thessalonians:

> “Eagerly,” he says, “we wished to impart to you not only the Gospel of God, but also our own souls” (1 Thess. II).

This is the pattern by which Christ wished to instruct his disciples and conform them to himself in a pleasing likeness. Not only the apostles, but many after the apostles, are found to have attained it more fully: they strove with all their strength not to be wrongly and idly mute. For those disgracefully fall silent through degenerate weakness who grow sluggish in offering their brethren a welcome benefit, who, through either laziness or malice, despise the just and noble height of excellence and give others no subject for speech by any exercise of virtues. But those who strive more diligently to devote themselves to excellence, and who expend not only their possessions but themselves upon divine or brotherly love—these, having put aside degenerate silence, speak glorious things; indeed, their praiseworthy action itself becomes eloquent. [Col. 1036A]

Did not Christ wish to speak to us through the benefit of his passion, and does not that same passion also speak on our behalf, so that no one who does not begrudge lending his ear to Christ’s words has cause to complain rightly of his silence? The apostle Paul says:

> “You have come to the sprinkling of blood that speaks better than Abel” (Heb. XII). [Col. 1036A]

The killing of Abel (Gen. IV), or the sprinkling of his blood, does not incite us to anger and insult; rather, by a kind of instruction in virtue, it invites us to patience, since we read that his brother inflicted an unjust death upon him, and that Abel endured what was inflicted without returning anything wickedly. His patience is for us a kind of speech, a warning not to be despised but surely to be heard by all wise people: namely, that if trouble, persecution, or even death itself is inflicted upon us by anyone whatsoever, hatred must not be returned for hatred, nor persecution for persecution. [Col. 1036B]

But while Abel’s killing thus speaks to us, seems thus to call us back from anger and to summon us to humble patience, Christ’s own passion and the sprinkling of his blood are found to speak much better, because they impart a worthier model and a more perfect example. Abel rendered nothing like his wicked brother’s deed; Christ, however, gave himself for his brethren. Abel was prepared rather to suffer death than to inflict it; Christ was found willing and voluntary to offer himself. Thus Abel spoke well, but Christ better: Abel practiced patience, Christ benevolence. Abel, speaking as it were more gently, made himself imitable by many; Christ, to be imitated by fewer, offered prayers to God with loud cries and tears, pleading acceptably.

Concerning him Paul says:

> “Offering prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears, he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. V). [Col. 1036C]

Christ is frequently read in the Gospel to have offered prayers, and sometimes, while offering them, to have shed tears. The Father seems to have heard them more fully because in them was found a loud cry. A loud cry is the chief and foremost form of love, by which Christ encounters the hardness of our perversity, wishing to impress upon us that we should especially heed him as leader and forerunner, and, following his example, voluntarily expend our lives for our brethren. Therefore the Apostle says:

> “See that you do not refuse him who speaks” (Heb. XII). [Col. 1036D]

Those who stubbornly strive to excuse their own hardness are convicted of wickedly refusing Christ speaking in this way; for to furnish the patronage of a defense to an obstinate heart is nothing other than to remove farther away Christ’s word and his example of generosity. But where the affection of a new will has taken root, though the strength of perfect love has not yet become firm, its tenderness ought not to be abhorred as accursed, but nourished by the watering of wholesome instruction so that it may advance to better things. For not all are able to imitate Christ sufficiently in this respect, so as to be wholly conformed to him in the abundance of love and to be willing, after his pattern, to suffer death for their brethren, although they desire to obtain grace or strength of this kind. [Col. 1037A]

Observing that they could not yet be brought to perfection, the Apostle nevertheless does not abhor their imperfection or judge it condemnable. Rather, he cherishes and advances what has been begun more tenderly, and commends it by affirming that it is truly acceptable to God.

> “Let a widow,” he says, “first learn to govern her own household and to render a return to her parents; for this is acceptable before God” (1 Tim. V).

It is as if he said: Let her whose husband is as though dead through the violent force of oppressive vices, but who does not yet possess a ready desire for spiritual advancement, learn to govern the household of her mind manfully in the role of its ruler, and to respond with thankful benefits to those whom she has experienced as earlier benefactors. And because such a work is not yet wholly perfect, lest anyone suppose it unacceptable to God, he says: “For this is acceptable before God”—to whom, it is certain, things perfect and weighty are pleasing in such a way that things imperfect and light are nevertheless not believed to displease him as reprobate. [Col. 1037B]

For it pleases him when someone repays a benefit with a benefit as due return; but perhaps it pleases him more when someone bestows the same benefit freely, because what is given without preceding merits belongs to a greater grace than what answers, in equal balance, merits and a preceding benefit. Indicating this, the Apostle diligently instructs the widow to render a reciprocal return to her parents, and then declares that the widow who is freely generous ought to be chosen, making it understood both that one who does not repay an accepted benefit is to be rebuked and that one who extends herself to confer free gifts is worthily to be commended. For after saying, “Let a widow first learn to govern her own household and to render a return to her parents,” he adds shortly afterward:

> “Let a widow be chosen who has testimony in good works: if she has received guests, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has assisted those suffering tribulation, if she has pursued every good work” (ibid.). [Col. 1037C]

By these words he instructs both that widow concerning repayment of a benefit as a due return, and this widow, in turn, concerning freely bestowing benefits; showing what ought to be preferred to what in point of time, and what in dignity of merit ought to be preferred to what, since unquestionably regard is due to each according to place and order. First each person ought to lend a teachable ear to the teacher, so that he may learn thankfully to repay a benefit to one who confers it; then, by fitting progress, he should endeavor to advance so far as to love being beneficent even without return.

And although silence is prescribed for a woman by the Apostle (1 Tim. II), and she is rebuked by Solomon as talkative and unable to endure quiet (Prov. VII), a prudent widow is nevertheless not exempted from this kind of speaking. Indeed, by useful commands she is invited both to return thanks and to grant free gifts. Thus divine Scripture (3 Kings XVII) proclaimed the widow of Zarephath praiseworthy and declared her worthy of remembrance by later generations, because when the hungry Prophet demanded something for food from her with a loud cry, she did not choose to be oppressed by grasping avarice and silence, but heard the petitioner’s cry with a generous answer and, though hungry herself, bestowed oil and meal with a liberal hand. [Col. 1037D–1038A]

The Proverbs of Solomon also commend that strong woman (Prov. XXXI), whose manly spirit is not constricted by enervating stinginess, whom fear of poverty or desire of possession does not make base, but who opens her hand to the needy and stretches out her palms to the poor.

That Samaritan too, who, moved by compassion, lifted onto his beast a man almost killed by robbers (Luke X), led him to an inn, entrusted his care to the innkeeper, and, to make him more attentive, produced two denarii for him—that Samaritan, I say, is declared by the lawyer’s assertion to have been neighbor to the man whom the priest and Levite, moved by no mercy, are said to have passed by. [Col. 1038B]

Conversely, that rich man who rejoiced in the abundance of his crops and had no barns sufficient to store them, because in his greed for money he bestowed nothing upon his neighbor from them, is condemned as a fool when his soul is demanded in the night.

> “Fool,” he says, “this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?” (Luke XII.)

That other rich man also, seeing Lazarus hungry before his door and refusing to bestow a welcome benefit upon the hungry man, begs in hell that a drop of water be given him, feeling his tongue tortured by the burning of a fierce flame. And rightly the tongue suffers especially grievous punishment: when Lazarus endured a double injury, of wounds and want (Luke XVI), it spoke to him no good word, no word of consolation; and though it could have acted by a word alone, it performed no work of mercy. Therefore the tongue that had been wrapped in the folds of avaricious silence when it was time to confer a benefit is set free in hell to utter talkative complaints; compelled by divine judgment, it cannot keep silent about its own torments, since it had refused to comfort its needy neighbor with a welcome word. [Col. 1038B–C]

Finally, when the Lord spoke to Jerusalem through Ezekiel and complained that Jerusalem had justified Sodom by acting more wickedly, among the other vices by which he recounted that Sodom and her daughters had grievously sinned, he pointedly recalled their grasping avarice:

> “They did not stretch out their hand to the needy and poor” (Ezek. XVI). [Col. 1038D]

What does it mean that he does not say Sodom and her daughters took something from anyone or committed violence against any needy or poor person, but only that they bestowed no free benefit, and for this endured a sentence of condemnation? Surely it is to show that those people ought not vainly to boast who, when they see their neighbors perhaps in need of something, are shut up in hard stone and give them no assistance, imagining it enough that they inflict no harm, although the divine law commands not merely that people should not harm one another but that they should diligently take care to help one another.

And just as these persons are rebuked for conferring no free benefit, so many others receive benefits yet return no thanks. Though they are clamorous in demanding what they wish to obtain, they become fruitful in no gift of generosity when it comes to freely returning what is welcome. I think the lepers in the Gospel were such people: we read that they pressed Christ with loud cries to obtain healing. Having received their desired result, they were weighed down by the more serious weakness of silence and did not return to give the physician his due thanks.

> “Were not ten cleansed?” he says. “And where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner?” (Luke XVII.) [Col. 1039A]

Those who rejoice in desired health yet are ungrateful for the benefit received are rebuked; they not only bestow no gift upon their healer, but do not even honor him with easy praise. But the tenth man is commended by the judgment of truth because he does not follow the flight or silence of the other nine, but returns quickly and gives thanks to his healer, knowing that what is welcome ought to be repaid to a welcome giver.

Each person, I say, ought not to keep silent in this duty, but either give what is welcome or respond in a like manner to one who gives—provided that honorable holiness adorns and strengthens this exchange, and the enervating baseness of vices does not darken or weaken it. For welcome things ought not either to be freely given or freely repaid if they are known to be contrary to the rule of holiness—if, that is, someone, wishing to please another, bestows something which the uprightness of divine justice rebukes as departing from what is honorable and useful. [Col. 1039B]

This is what the greedy softness of some people demands, and what the blameworthy generosity of many provides when demanded: their ears itch to hear what they wickedly desire, and their overly yielding tongue becomes ready to say the same things. In Isaiah such demanders speak: people weakened in character who refuse to endure stern admonishers, but demand that the latter set aside the weight of sincere truth, bend themselves, and utter soft flatteries of falsehood:

> “Do not show us what is right; speak pleasing things to us; show us errors” (Isa. XXX). [Col. 1039C]

You see that errors, not what is right, please these people; with remarkable imprudence they presume to instruct their admonishers to set aside the serious things by which they had determined to abolish their vices, and to speak pleasing things which certainly depart from truth. Such instruction, it seems, had been given to those who, wishing to satisfy the will of King Joash, worshipped him, pursued him with gratuitous flatteries, and spoke perversely pleasing things to his perverse ears:

> “The princes of Judah entered,” he says, “and worshipped the king. Delighted by their services, he yielded to them; and they abandoned the temple of the Lord God of their fathers and served groves and carved images” (2 Chron. XXIV). [Col. 1039D]

The princes knew that the king’s ears itched and that, abhorring truth, he more eagerly heard the proclamation of vanity. Recognizing what pleased their lord, they complied with sufficiently submissive spirit in order to obtain his favor. Under the pressure of their welcome submission, truth in him turns to ashes; at the voice of his praisers, malice, as though driven by great blasts, blazes up; and miserable error grows so strong in him that, abandoning God’s temple, he served groves and carved images and entangled others by his example in the same idolatry.

Of this malice Jeremiah says:

> “At the sound of loud speech a fire was kindled in it” (Jer. XI). [Col. 1040A]

Loud speech is flattery, which greatly puffs up and exalts a miserable soul; having been raised by this inflation, it weakens and softens it utterly, deprives it of the dew and rain by which it flourishes and grows green through the protection of strength, and—relying on no shelter—more quickly dries it up and sets it ablaze. Thus, “at the sound of loud speech a fire was kindled in it,” because when flattery, breaking open the enclosure of modesty, produces the miserable caress of praise; when, casting aside the linen cloth of truth, it draws over the deceptive covering of vanity; then in the miserable soul that has deserved no aid of divine grace, the fire of malice receives its desired increase. For the evil which in us grows faintly, as in a furnace, through our own fault, burns more fiercely when the breath of loud speech is added—when, namely, we hear the perverse desires of our soul called worthy of praise, and what we do wickedly blessed by the judgment of deceivers. [Col. 1040A–B]

Of such deceivers the Lord says through Isaiah:

> “My people, those who call you blessed are deceiving you” (Isa. III).

Such blessing is deception when we proclaim in a loud voice that those whom we wish to please by yielding service, and from whom we seek to extort a similar benefit, are blessed in whatever they have done; and when, by welcome flattery, we strengthen them in their wickedness. For the lover of vanity hears nothing more willingly than that a flatterer smiles upon and applauds his error; desiring to do whatever pleases him as though it were lawful, he wants others like himself to answer, “a pleasing ‘Well done!,’ an approving ‘Well done!’” [Col. 1040B–C]

But even the pagans themselves sharply rebuke this “well done,” though they understand moral knowledge somewhat more subtly; and they fiercely attack both those who demand it and those who delight in giving it, striving to call them back from so enervating a purpose. Hence a certain satirist says:

> “. . . . . . . . I reject  
> your ‘Well done!’ and ‘Fine!’ For examine that whole ‘fine!’ closely:  
> what is not contained within it?”

—Persius, *Satires*, Book I, Satire 1, line 49. [Col. 1040C]

This wise man knows that the flatterer, alert and girded for praising useless things, has nothing upright or sound within; though the outer surface of his lips is whitened, his inward parts are full of dead men’s bones. For when a certain beauty of words shines outwardly, deceitful ugliness lies hidden in that very beauty: his “well done” is born not of understanding and love of truth, but of yielding flattery and the duplicity of vanity. [Col. 1040D]

If, then, the prudent pagan rejects and refuses a false “well done” and a deceitful “excellent,” and gravely rebukes and accuses those who delight in such things, how much more should a holy man, a lover of sincere truth, reject the flattering voices of falsehood with the prophet:

> “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done! Well done!’ be turned back at once and put to shame” (Ps. LXIX). [Col. 1040D]

David saw that this vice prevailed not only among pagans but also held a very great place among God’s people; he saw that both prelates and subjects could more easily be led onto this slippery downward slope, and could scarcely be brought back from the same precipice. Therefore, not wishing his own people to fall into this pit of flattery, and fearing that he himself might someday agree with their flatteries, he says: “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done! Well done!’ be turned back at once and put to shame”—so that their empty praise may not be admitted even a little, nor the mind gradually relax and flow away from its firmness. [Col. 1041A]

For nothing is more grievous than for one person to offer yielding flatteries, for another to rejoice at being made like him through those flatteries, and thus for them mutually to lick one another, scratch one another’s itch, and return welcome things for welcome things—so that the judgment of divine truth may complain equally of both:

> “The prophets prophesied falsehood, and the priests applauded with their hands, and my people loved such things” (Jer. V).

Through Jeremiah the Lord complains that the prophets deceived the people by lies, the priests in equal madness applauded with their hands, and that miserable people loved the same deceits; thus both prelate and subject neglected the destruction hanging over them. [Col. 1041A–B]

Therefore let no one strive either to confer or return such welcome things as attentive discernment or discerning intention does not commend. For although the Gospel commands us to do to another what we want done to ourselves, we must not believe that, just as we ought mutually to confer lawful things, so also unlawful things. Luke says:

> “As you wish men to do to you, do likewise to them” (Luke VI).

And Matthew:

> “Whatever things you wish men to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. VII). [Col. 1041B]

Will lovers of shamefulness excuse their wickedness by this command and refuse to devote themselves to holiness that is unwelcome to them, judging that, just as they want others readily to grant them whatever perverse things, so they are commanded to grant others whatever those others perversely wish? But the words “whatever things you wish” must undoubtedly be understood of things which the law of justice upholds as to be done, not of things which it rebukes as unlawful and contrary to itself. For the teacher of truth commands nothing other than what is holy and useful in either willing or doing; he knows nothing of the shamefulness of perverse pleasure. Thus, through the prophet:

> “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers”; 

and he adds:

> “I will rebuke you and set you before your face” (Ps. XLIX). [Col. 1041C]

Whom do you think the supreme Judge mentions here, who runs with a thief and places his portion with adulterers, except one who wickedly delights in thefts and adulteries and rejoices to have helpers and companions in them? Therefore he says:

> “You wickedly imagined that I would be like you; I will rebuke you and set you before your face” (ibid.),

so that you may see what you now neglect—that you are filthy in your own dregs—and know that the things pleasing to you are likewise not pleasing to me, and that I am not like you in your perverse love, even if I keep silent for a time and do not oppose your pleasures. [Col. 1041D]

## CHAPTER LII

Having therefore set aside those things which are not done without violating the seal of justice, we must return to those things which are justly and reasonably demanded, which every rightly generous person ought to provide to one who asks, and for which a grateful recipient ought to respond to the giver with more abundant generosity. To such a person Wisdom says:

> “Pay your debt, and answer peaceably with meekness” (Ecclus. IV). [Col. 1042A]

Whoever receives something welcome from another ought to regard it as if lent to him, so that he may not swell with pride as a superior because of the gift received, but may gently dispose himself, with due humility, to make a like response. The Apostle Paul also exhorts us to such response or repayment. By his exhortations every wise person is instructed never to think himself free from debt, since the very love by which he is bound makes him a debtor:

> “Render to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; tax to whom tax; fear to whom fear; honor to whom honor” (Rom. XIII). [Col. 1042A–B]

And lest anyone should say that he owed none of these things to anyone and was therefore subject to no debt, the Apostle added that obligation from which he wished to excuse no one, but to bind all indissolubly:

> “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (ibid.).

It is as if he said: Granted that you owe no one any of the things mentioned, you nevertheless do not rightly consider yourselves free from debt, because love makes you mutual debtors, and you ought to be true and constant payers of that debt. Indeed, God wishes people to be bound by such a debt, and to show himself propitious to his lovers as though from obligation. When he more freely hears their voices from his own treasury, bound by this tie he more willingly answers and grants their request.

As Isaiah affirms:

> “At the sound of your cry, as soon as he hears, he will answer you” (Isa. XXX). [Col. 1042C]

The voice of the cry by which someone is said to approach God is the action by which God shows himself gracious. For that voice is especially pleasing to God which, having set aside degenerate silence, becomes clamorous. The cry of this voice is love; unless the voice itself, or action, is made clear by the aid of love, it does not resound sufficiently in God’s ears but grows hoarse. But if action is strengthened by a cry—that is, by love—the request of the one crying out to God is not disappointed. Rather, God answers more welcome things to a welcome deed that speaks before words, and divine goodness returns greater things to one who offers willingly.

Promising this through Isaiah, he says:

> “To those who keep my Sabbaths and choose the things that I have willed, I will give in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than daughters” (Isa. LVI). [Col. 1042D]

This is the recompense from which God certainly does not keep silent, but answers the voice of the preceding cry with a welcome reward. In this he wishes us also to be conformed to himself and to imitate with benevolent affection his generosity.

He has graciously wished to teach us not only to return welcome things freely given, but also to return unwelcome things to the ungrateful; and he has bestowed upon us in himself a welcome pattern, so that following his example we may not grow sluggish in returning welcome things for welcome things, and may maintain discerning judgment in returning or not returning unwelcome things to the ungrateful. He certainly does not begrudge repaying whatever welcome thing is bestowed upon him, although a person’s merit is not always sufficient to attain salvation. Thus the rich man clothed in purple is read to have come to the punishments of hell, and yet to have received good things in his life according to his merits:

> “Son,” he says, “you received good things in your life” (Luke XVI). [Col. 1043A]

There is no doubt that this rich man must be understood to have offered God something pleasing, and that God, the just judge, returned something pleasing to him. Thus it is certain that, though God does not accept everything we do, he does not refuse to repay whatever he has accepted. But what is offered to God and is unacceptable, he is sometimes found to endure in silence; at other times he does not keep silent in returning like things—so that in his silence his mercy or patience may be proved, while in his returning like things his truthful justice may be shown.

But because mercy precedes judgment, as David declares:

> “I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. C), [Col. 1043B]

I think I should first speak of that concerning which he is merciful or patient in silence, and afterward of that concerning which he, being just and true, more fiercely burns to speak. For God, unwilling hastily to pronounce a harsh sentence of punishment, grants the sinful conduct of men a space for repentance. Through Isaiah he says:

> “I have been silent; I have always kept silent; I have been patient” (Isa. XLII),

lest, if sinners were struck at once by impending vengeance, they should seem to complain rightly about so precipitate a judgment. For often, when a sinner is entangled in the pleasant bonds of vices and yet is not struck in the present according to his deserts, he is confined within his conscience and confronted by a most grievous torturer; and, devoutly repenting, he trusts more confidently in the mercy of him whose judgment he experiences to be so patient in delaying it. [Col. 1043B–C]

But when swift vengeance, God judging more strictly, strikes the man whose wicked heart and hands have become free for sins, that same sinner sometimes murmurs and complains that worthy mercy has not been shown him. He says that, if not today, perhaps tomorrow—if not yesterday, then the day after tomorrow—he would have repented, if divine goodness had granted him tomorrow for repentance. Therefore God often keeps silent and does not immediately restore to us what we deserve, so that with the passage of time we may be prompted to repentance. He knows to whom, when repentant, he may mercifully grant his grace; by the gift of that grace the penitent person returns so as to merit salvation. [Col. 1043C]

For if God’s anger and vengeance struck us immediately when we sin, and justice raged with equal balance against the mass of our crimes, in a short time no one would remain to whom that same mercy could bring aid, to whom it could grant life and salvation—which none but the righteous attains—when it could scarcely find any righteous person among human beings, and almost every person, justly lost, would perish. Good, therefore, is the silence commended by God’s mercy, when time for repentance is not denied to any sinner; when God, by the goodness of his nature preferring to be loved rather than feared, seeks occasions by which he may fittingly have mercy upon sinners. [Col. 1043D]

For he does not spare every offender from a degenerate fear—lest, that is, at some time missiles be lacking to the one who strikes, and, when the weapons by which he might overcome the stubbornness of sinners have failed, the stubborn may more securely presume to resist one who is unarmed and powerless. This is what babbling poets fabulously tell of the gods of the nations: they think that those gods sometimes refrain from striking men’s perverse behavior lest, if their quiver were emptied all at once, as though its arrows had been shot, no further supply might be available to them for striking. [Col. 1044A]

> “If Jupiter,” says a certain poet, “should send his thunderbolts whenever men sin,  
> he would be unarmed in a short time.”

God does not wish, like Jupiter, to hurl thunderbolts whenever people sin; rather, he generally bears with their faults, postponing vengeance, lest, if zeal for revenge drove him to strike at every individual offense, thunderbolts should fail before people deserving to be struck down for their manner of life. But our God does not refrain from vengeance whenever someone, whether unknowingly, through weakness, or perhaps wickedly, lays hold of what has been forbidden [Col. 1044B]. Indeed, he keeps silent for this purpose: that the sinner may at some point be beneficially put to shame and, once ashamed, may be endowed through a more abundant favor with the gift of the Spirit. For where sin has abounded, grace has generally abounded still more (Rom.
