V); and the one forgiven more loves more, and we sometimes see one who recognizes that he was the greater debtor become more generous in repayment.

But if anyone, abusing strong mercy, neglects repentance, and divine judgment postpones rendering to the unrepentant person what is due according to merit, in this the greater patience of God himself is shown: he does not refuse to endure even those whom he is not appeased by in mercy. Of such persons he says through the prophet: “I have labored in bearing with them” (Isa. I). He says that he labors when the inner Searcher investigates the ungrateful conduct of people and considers that [Col. 1044C] penitence, piercing them, does not correct them; rather, the more he is silent, so that he seems, as it were, not to see what ought to be punished, the more their unpunished iniquity hardens them in sinning. Rebuking this through the same Isaiah, he says: “You did not consider in your heart that I was silent and, as though not seeing, and you have forgotten me” (Isa. LVII).

When the soul, in perverse inward thought, does not consider that divine goodness does not repay it its crimes because of merciful silence, and that, turning away his face, God chose for a time, as it were, not to see, so that through patience he might lead it on to repentance, then the very source from which that wretched soul ought to remember divine mercy more gratefully and devoutly is found to make it forget more harshly and perversely. “And you have forgotten me,” he says. But God, whose mighty [Col. 1044D] patience does not grow weary, whose patient strength is not shaken by the prolonged assault of our crimes, often places no obstacle in the way of our grave purpose, but sometimes allows us, according to our own desire, to run on until the end of this life. And when our iron neck is not softened by fear or love of him, his patience, restraining vengeance, falls silent, considering to what result our perversity is being hardened, or by what end or recompense that very hardness will be consumed. Indicating this through the same prophet, he says: “I will rest and consider in my place” (ibid.).

God is said to rest in his own place because, in the sanctuary of his divinity, there is neither wrath nor retribution, from which he seems, as it were, to go out toward us when he delays to strike us according to the purpose known to himself. Yet while delaying, he considers that, [Col. 1045A] while he rests, our perversity does not rest; rather, the more it is unpunished, the more violently it hardens, and, advancing toward worse things, until it is brought by a miserable desire to completion, it is plunged in that completion into irreparable ruin.

[p. 601]

## Chapter LIII

Finally, when the same prophet spoke of the Son of God himself, considering what and how great were the sufferings he endured while no merit of his own required them, he wished not only to foretell his Passion itself but also to make gracious mention of the accompanying silence. “He was offered,” he says, “because he himself willed it; and he did not open his mouth. Like a lamb before one shearing him, he will be silent, and he will not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII).

When Christ allowed himself to be killed by the gracious gift of his own will, though those killing him were corrupted by the vice of voluntary perversity, relying on prudent counsel he chose not to open his mouth—that is, not to strike back at the insults of those striking him with the sword then at hand. Hence to Peter, who had not yet bowed himself to such humble silence, but, rather boldly in speech, draws the sword of hasty retaliation, he says: “Put your sword back into its sheath; for all who take up the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. XXVI). Do not hasten to strike with the sword while you wish too quickly to avenge injuries just received; but, taught by a sounder master, now put it back—that is, hide yourself, pressed down and subdued beneath patient silence.

For all who take up the untimely sword of striking, ignorant of or despising the health-giving silence of endurance, [Col. 1045C] shall perish by the sword: that is, they will incur divine vengeance by an equal judgment, unless perhaps, changing their purpose, they put the drawn sword back into its sheath. And Christ is fittingly said to be like the lamb which is patient and kindly, or which is shorn in his Passion, so that no prudent person may indignantly, in any pride as though superior, reject an invitation to imitate that lamb of Christ by his admonitions. “Behold,” he says, “I send you as lambs” (Matt. X).

For if anyone beats a lamb, remarkable patience is shown in it: it does not resist the striker by biting or by any blow, but is found to restrain every violent movement in such silence that, when struck on one cheek, it seems rather to offer the other. But if anyone shears it, it does not violently reclaim its fleece through avarice; rather, it presents itself so willingly to give it back that, like one who does not refuse to yield also his cloak to one taking his tunic, the commanded—or proposed—perfection of the Gospel does not reproach it. Thus the lamb is good: if it is beaten, it does not know how to return the blow; if it is shorn, it remains silent nonetheless; and amid all that it sees the violent onset of its persecutor do to it, patient as well as kindly in rendering like for like, it refuses to open its mouth.

And in this it fittingly bears the type of Christ, who did not refuse to suffer scourges and wounds for us, nor refuse to be shorn when the covering of humanity was laid aside; who instructed us by the form and example of humble patience and clothed us in the fleece of his incorruptible flesh. But the silence of that lamb, which Isaiah asserts Christ maintained in his Passion, Christ himself is found to have predicted long before through another prophet. Isaiah therefore seems not so much to have prophesied something new as to have repeated what had already been prophesied in order to confirm it.

[Col. 1046A]

For when, through David’s mouth, he set forth the ill will of his persecutors and accused their talkative vanity, deceits, and persistence, he consequently took care to mention his own silence in response, showing that he had not at that time returned retaliation for their malice. “Those who sought evils against me,” he says, “spoke vanities and meditated deceits all day long. But I, as though deaf, did not hear, and like a mute man did not open my mouth” (Ps. XXXVII). And again: “I became,” he says, “like one who does not hear and who has no rebukes in his mouth” (ibid.).

Wonderful silence! Though Christ was not unaware of the vain speech of his ill-wishers, [Col. 1046B] indeed of their deceitful plotting, and though he was able to repay their ungrateful deeds in kind, he nevertheless kept silent as though deaf, as if he had not heard their words or counsels, as though he had had a mute and powerless mouth for rebuking them. But why this, unless to invite us likewise to the same silence, to restrain us by effective admonitions from returning ungratefulness for ungratefulness, knowing that an admonition works more effectively when what is to be done is demonstrated both by word and by deed?

For many days long ago, in the continuous course of the ancient Scriptures and through the testimony of many prophets in succession, he had warned us that, when a persecutor brought us any trouble, our humble disposition should not repay like for like in restless speech. What he would eventually display personally and visibly in himself, [Col. 1046C] he had long before wished to teach in writing through his prophets, so that humble silence might be known in advance from their writings and, once foreknown, might be held more commendably because it had been confirmed by his own display of it.

## Chapter LIV

Speaking therefore through Isaiah, he says: “Be silent, you who dwell in the island” (Isa. XXIII). He fittingly undertakes to invite to silence those who are said to dwell not just anywhere but on an island—not because he judges silence to be of no benefit to others, but because he knows it to be especially necessary for these persons.

For every earthen vessel seems suitably to possess its integrity, though it can often scarcely be kept whole in the hands of those holding it. Yet when a violent fire comes near it, or any other [Col. 1046D] severe pressure openly bears upon it, endurance is especially necessary for it, lest, in the crash of its breaking under the misfortune that has befallen it, its conspicuous distress make reply. So too, when a person is refreshed in the garden of delight beneath most pleasant shade, when, brought into the harbor of his own will, he lies hidden as though in a chamber, it is no wonder if he rejoices in the peace and leisure he desires and keeps silent, since his mind is distressed by no tumult or cautery.

But if the hand of a striker delivers a heavy blow, if a blazing furnace, a persecuting assault, the crash of waves, or the rage of winds afflicts him, then a person especially needs strength to stand firm: so that, as evils grow heavier, he may not abandon the tranquil resolve of his heart; so that, when the grievous injury of any tribulation bears down more fully upon him, he may make no reply by breaking, like a weak and impatient vessel. [Col. 1047A] Silence is therefore rightly commanded with diligence to dwellers on an island, because it is judged especially necessary when a person is wearied by many and varied troubles: namely, that he may strive to endure inflicted wrongs with equanimity, lest, when patient silence is broken, he presume to return the like.

An island is a smaller tract of land, surrounded on every side by waters and separated from the wider extent of the lands by the waters flowing between. Its surface is neither compelled to be covered by the neighboring waves nor, when they have entirely fled, able to be joined to the remaining land. But because the sea spreads more widely than other waters and occupies much space through its broad expanse, an island of this sort is found most often especially within it, [Col. 1047B] rising a little above the level of the waters and surrounded by the sea.

By the name “island,” moreover, is signified the religious life, which is made firm by a steadier purpose, as by a certain weight of its own, and which, rising above the more dangerous and, as it were, more slippery element of secular life, provides those who come to it with a firm place to dwell. Another prophet certainly rejoices greatly that he has found this and, leaving behind the unstable flood of carnal actions, has reached a firmer purpose, in which he is no longer driven, as formerly, by winds and gusts, but advances from progress to progress with a straight and steady step. “He led me,” he says, “out of the pit of misery and the mud of dregs; he set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” (Ps. XXXIX).

The pit of misery [Col. 1047C] is the overflowing flux of perverse actions, which occupies and swallows an infinite multitude of wretches; and its gulf sometimes leads those sunk in it into eternal misery, unless the hand of mercy first draws them back from its deep abyss. The mud of dregs, or conspicuous dregs, is the very impurity of a hidden will, in which the wretched mind clings, delighting in the mire of wicked pleasure; and even when it perhaps does no evil outwardly, it nevertheless wallows in this residue through miserable delight. Divine merciful regard draws us out of both this pit of misery and this mud of dregs; after washing us by the grace of forgiveness, it introduces us, as it were, onto an island; it sets our affections upon the rock of a firmer purpose and directs our actions while disposing us to return to salvation. [Col. 1047D]

But because the sea or lake does not withdraw far from the island, it does not grant its inhabitants the desired peace in full. Those whom it has not been able to keep within its waves it nevertheless never ceases to menace with various threats and terrors. For people of secular life, stirred by the winds of anger, envy, and avarice and raised in a swelling mass by bold malice—who can describe what attacks, and of what kind, they bring upon people of a better purpose, especially if a more powerful hand does not perhaps impose silence upon them?

Because religious persons hold a firmer degree of holiness while secular persons occupy a worse position and endure less patiently, the latter stretch themselves out with untiring fury to attack the former, whom they discover to be unlike themselves in life and character. Nothing, therefore, is more useful to such dissimilar persons [Col. 1048A] than silence and than not answering inflicted injuries with biting insult, lest those unlike their malicious assailants in keeping silent should eventually, defeated by troubles, become like them in answering. “Do not,” says Solomon, “answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him” (Prov. XXVI).

Christ too seems to confirm this not so much by word as by deed. He refused, in answering, to become like his assailants; according to Peter, “when he was reviled, he did not revile; when he was struck, he did not strike back” (1 Pet. II). Rather: “I set,” he says, “a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me” (Ps. XXXVIII). By this example the island-dweller is commanded to guard his mouth and more diligently to fortify it with the strong bar of silence, lest, impatient under tribulations, he presume to utter a word of [Col. 1048B] vengeance and, with a disturbed spirit, repay the injuries of those striking him. “Be silent,” he says, “you who dwell in the island” (Isa. XXIII).

You, he says, who by grace already have no unstable and shifting way of life in the sea, but by sounder counsel possess a more solid religious purpose; who, like fertile land, now reap fruits in joy—for religion possesses the promise of the life that now is and that which is to come—while meanwhile the sea roars around you, while the frequent flood of waves threatens, while it strives by various assaults to drive you down into the depths, while the powerful iniquity of secular people rages harshly, which is accustomed to press island-dwellers more toward decline than advance: take care that your patience does not languish, but, placing the finger of humility upon the mouth, keeps silent; lest, if you wish to repay persecutors [Col. 1048C] in kind through similarity of conduct, you appear no longer to dwell on an island but in the sea.

[p. 603]

And perhaps any religious person may somehow bear the heavy assaults of secular people and, with a sufficiently even mind, not return their injuries for injuries, when he recognizes that he stands upon a firmer height and does not strive to become like those below him. But when the turbulent air swells from above, when snow, hail, thunder, and the lightning of fires press heavily, when the floodgates of heaven seem threateningly opened, when the whole island seems altogether covered by storms from above, what inhabitant of it would not tremble more violently? Indeed, who would not faint under such a weight, deprived of every refuge? [Col. 1048D]

For when the raging sea promises nothing favorable on every side, and heaven rains, thunders, and flashes lightning far more grievously, promising death; when there is no escape to be found from the sides and the storm of the air does not cease to rage upon the island, I wonder whether anyone possesses strength so unconquerable that he is not, like a tree, torn up by the roots with a tremendous crash.

Thus the roaring sea seems to signify the turbulent wickedness of secular people, which never ceases to assail religious persons by evil deeds or at least by conduct. Likewise, by the name of heaven or air is signified the loftier rank of teachers, by whose instruction our lower humility is governed like earth lying beneath. When the face of this heaven grows clear at evening, when it is lightly moistened by morning dew, when it shines more brightly upon the earth by the sun’s ray [Col. 1049A], when it is richly fertilized by timely rain in welcome succession, the person born for labor rejoices not a little because the earth he inhabits is made fruitful by such a benefit.

In the same way, when an ecclesiastical teacher rests, as it were, beneath the low roof of a tranquil will; when he rises and moistens others with the truth of profound knowledge; when, like the rays of the midday sun, he burns and shines by the merits of his works; when he is not weary of watering those subject to him by teaching and speech: then the subject person, the soot of his mind wiped away, is made cheerful because his religious life flourishes more abundantly, perhaps, under such instruction.

But if the one who ought to be the fruitful distributor of these gifts is instead found to be a harmful persecutor; if he loves to exercise grievous power over those subject to him; if, in place of the order of dignity, [Col. 1049B] he acquires tyrannical right; if he thunders and lightens; if he rages in intemperate conduct; if he delights that his own malice is turned into the misery of his subjects—then the little flock has no sheltering shade under which it may be protected, when the one it had hoped would be its protector is found to be a more grievous enemy.

When someone at sea fears or is already enduring an approaching storm, he hastens with all desire to attain the solid stability of land, so that he who seems likely to perish in peril at sea may at last be safe when he has gained the desired shore. But if, having gained land, he is assailed by thunderbolts from above, he neither flees nor is strengthened by remaining hope, because any mortal falsely promises himself life when vengeance does not permit him to live either on land or in the waters.

[Col. 1049C]

And whereas the danger at sea seemed quite serious to him, in which nevertheless hope remained that he might strive toward land, he declares the danger upon land itself much more grievous—a danger in which I, wretched and perhaps more than wretched, have learned by experience, as one now despairing of mercy: no persecution rages more fiercely; none is more accustomed to press down or crush; by no burden is the miserable soul so weighed down; by no oppression is hope more languidly weakened than when the one whom natural or perhaps spiritual order had promised as a defender presents himself, violating the laws of mercy, as an oppressor. Of such persons Isaiah says: “A man shall not spare his brother, and each shall devour the flesh of his own arm” (Isa. IX). And Micah: “A man hunts his brother unto death” (Mic. VII). And Matthew: “Brother,” he says, “will hand over brother to death, and father his son” (Matt. X).

[Col. 1049D]

But when brother delights in troubling brother, father son, and in harassing by plots, hatreds, and persecutions one whom he ought to have cherished in his bosom, silence is not easily maintained by the person so harassed. The more unjustly he judges himself oppressed, the more urgently he is driven to answer. “If my enemy,” he says, “had cursed me, I would certainly have endured it” (Ps. LIV). But because a man at one with me, my guide and my familiar, not only confers no benefit on me but, violating the law of love, troubles me with the poison of rancor and envy—although I am compelled to restrain a timid or perhaps weak hand, how can I at least restrain the tongue of mouth or heart, so as not to cry out, cry back, and demand vengeance, and so as not to do in will what is not granted to my hand? [Col. 1050A]

But since there is “a time to keep silence and a time to speak”: “Be silent,” says the Lord, “you who dwell in the island” (Isa. XXIII). The time, he says, has not yet arrived for taking vengeance but for bearing whatever happens with equanimity, according to Solomon’s saying: “Whatever happens to him will not grieve the righteous” (Prov. XII). Be silent, especially since your dwelling itself seems to admonish you, and because you ought, in regard to me, to endure more patiently whatever I endure. For your island, continually hemmed in on every side by waves of the sea and frequently troubled by the harsher inclemency of the air, admonishes you to hide silently beneath the shield of patience and to allow what befalls you by my judgment to pass without anger or murmuring. David says: “All your heights and your waves have passed over me” (Ps. XLI). [Col. 1050B]

## Chapter LV

Finally, Christ himself, who had received flesh from the Jews and who ought by a certain natural right to have been loved by them, endured many oppressors without any [p. 604] merit of his own; yet he found the scribes and Pharisees much more grievous to him. For although Pilate, the soldiers, and many other Gentiles harmed him, handing him over to the Passion with violent hands, those are nevertheless shown to have been more grievous, far more wicked, who, corrupted by malice, are certainly known to have pressed for this with tireless cries.

For the Jews and Jewish rulers accused the innocent Christ and, wasting away with envy, defamed him by false reports; and though they should not have publicized even genuine [Col. 1050C] faults of his among the Gentiles—for according to the law, “cursed is he who presumes to uncover the shame of brother or son” (Lev. XVIII)—they undertook to proclaim by fabricated lies that he was guilty of death and the cross. By their cries they compelled Pilate to preside and, through persistent malice, drove the Roman soldiers to kill the one whom they did not know to have incurred a capital charge, though he had been accused by the malicious cries of his own nation.

Hence Pilate says: “Your nation and its rulers have delivered you to me” (John XVIII). And he says to them: “What evil, then, has he done?” (Mark XV). Since Pilate therefore knew that he had done no evil, though he says that his own nation and rulers had handed him over, it is plainly implied that Pilate himself was not chiefly armed for this by his own malice, but was incited by the anger and venomous hatred of the Jews. [Col. 1050D]

In what both the obedient Gentile and the instigating Jew inflicted, what an inhabitant of the island Christ was—how, that is, he stood as though deaf and mute before injuries inflicted on him, and, fortified by wonderful patience, did not return ungratefulness for ungratefulness—is well known to one who gives more diligent ear to the Gospel, whose sequence of events, reviewed, makes this clearer. And what Christ himself carried out in reality in the Gospel he had spoken prophetically through Isaiah, so that prophecy might bear witness to the future event and the reality of the event might display what had been foretold.

“To me,” he says, “let the islands keep silent” (Isa. XLI): as if to say, Let those keep silent in my example, after my pattern, in imitation of me, in confirmation of me, who not only dwell on an island but also deserve more expressly to be called islands, while they are pressed on every side by many and grave [Col. 1051A] troubles; while they are not only submerged by the encircling flood of secular people but also silently and courageously endure the graver thunderbolts of teachers. For just as those whose manner of life is in heaven are called “heaven,” according to what he says through the same Isaiah, “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. LXVI), and David says, “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII), so those who dwell on an island may rightly be called islands: dwelling amid scribes and Pharisees, they choose to imitate Christ, are grievously assailed by those by whom they ought to be protected, and in enduring them contemplate Christ’s silence and patience.

Of them he says again: “The islands shall wait for me” (Isa. LI). [Col. 1051B] Those, he says, who endure persecution from their superiors look to me; they wait for me to render them what is due according to their merits, knowing that the awaited one does not defraud those who wait for him of the reward of recompense. Whoever judges rightly praises them worthily for the merit of this silence.

Finally, even Gentiles who do not heed Christ because of their misguided understanding nevertheless value manly patience and proclaim that those who know how to endure adverse events equably surpass others in an admirable way. Hence that distinguished orator says: “That great and admirable praise is commonly thought to be this: to have borne adverse events wisely, not to have been broken by fortune, to have retained dignity amid hardships.” For he retains firm dignity amid hardships who does not cast off, in a faint-hearted mind, his mature [Col. 1051C] gravity; who is not carried away like chaff when a strong wind blows; who is not shaken when the hammer of adversity bears down even to ruin.

That person, I say, retains dignity amid hardships whose inward honor is not degraded by the harshness of circumstances, whose serene mind no cloud of persecution discolors, who does not labor in fury and hatred to avenge himself. He seeks to banish such fury or hatred from us and to make serene the hidden recesses of our minds amid hardship—he who, when we often labor under anger or perhaps ignorance, wishes vengeance forbidden to us to be assigned to himself in this book: “Vengeance is mine,” he says, “I will repay, says the Lord”; or, as our translation has it, “Mine is vengeance, and I will repay them in due time” (Deut. XXXII).

## Chapter LVI

[Col. 1051D]

For he who commonly does not take vengeance because he wishes to have mercy on sinners and to lead them to repentance by granting them time, according to the Apostle’s saying, “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. II), certainly, when he sees that the appropriate time is at hand, shows himself relentless toward sinners whom he strikes. Hence through the Prophet he says: “When I receive the time, I will judge justices” (Ps. LXXIV). I, he says, who for some time openly chose to endure your injustices and to restrain the judgment of vengeance in silence, when I see that a fitting time for vengeance has arrived, will judge even that which you judge yourselves to have done more justly, because, although the will is present, you are darkened by ignorance. [Col. 1052A]

Nor should it be thought that God always remains silent concerning vengeance and that anyone may with impunity presume upon forbidden things; rather, the fixed judgment of truth has determined that before that Judge no guilt whatsoever remains unpunished. Considering this, Job says: “I was afraid of all my works, knowing that you would not spare the offender” (Job IX). Although God is not denied mercifully to spare those who sin—otherwise none of us, having received forgiveness, would be saved—Job nevertheless rightly declares that he does not spare the offender, because no fault whatever is released from the vengeance necessary to it.

For although he spares the sinner so that he is not assigned to the punishments of hell, which sin certainly deserves if forgiveness does not come to aid, he nevertheless does not spare him in such a way that the same sin is not struck by purgative [Col. 1052B] punishment, so that, once it has been purged, the sinner may attain salvation through repentance. Therefore, he who spares the repentant by his mercy undoubtedly does not spare the offender when justice demands it: both because the repentant person is not saved without mercy that spares, and because it is just that sin should be bitten by fitting bitterness.

For this reason Job rightly declares that he fears all his works, considering that the divine judgment wishes to show mercy to no offense, since it strikes whatever is perpetrated against justice, even though it may be contracted not through malice but perhaps through weakness or ignorance. Finally, Lazarus too, who certainly shines by the merits of great works and, as the Gospel proclaims, rests joyfully in Abraham’s bosom, is said to have fittingly received evils for sins which he is thought perhaps at some time to have incurred. For when Abraham had said to the rich man tormented in hell, “Son, you received good things in your life,” he added: “And Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke XVI), making it understood that, just as the just Judge did not permit the rich man to be defrauded but restored to him in this life the good things due for the good he had done, so he must be believed not to have spared the offending Lazarus, but to have repaid evil things for evil things by an even reckoning. [Col. 1052C]

For this is the Creator’s justice: that just as, before it, a good work is not defrauded of its worthy reward, so an evil work is struck by fitting recompense; and it holds as determined by a sure judgment that neither good remains barren nor evil unpunished. But because the patient God generally does not hasten to render like for like to sinners or draw the sword of vengeance [Col. 1052D] against them immediately after they sin, some, thinking that he is sleeping in negligence, do not fear to entangle their hands in the many and long-standing stains of vices. To them he says through Isaiah: “I was silent; I was patient; like a woman in labor I will speak” (Isa. XLII): as if to say, I showed you my patience when I kept silent, when I still made no response to your transgressions by blows; but I shall bring my hidden justice forth into the light in your pain, when I strike you, hardened as you are, with a heavier punishment.

Another translation has: “I was silent; shall I always be silent?” “Although,” he says, “for a time I endured your iniquities in silence, delaying punishment while waiting for your repentance, do you think I shall always keep silent in the same way—that is, return no bitterness for your ingratitude?” To this there is an answer elsewhere through the same Isaiah: “I will not keep silent,” he says, “but I will repay” (Isa. LXV). I seem to you to be silent while you sin, while all things fall out for you according to the desire of your corrupt will; but I shall not be silent when justice thunders against you, when, in order to strike every offense, I more strictly recount your evils. [Col. 1053A]

Finally, Gentiles, though blinded by the darkness of unbelieving ignorance, nevertheless give somewhat more diligent attention to moral decency. They do not judge it right that the chatter of wicked persons should always be heard and that a degenerate person's patience should never strike it with a fitting reply. One of them says:

> “Shall I always be merely a listener? Shall I never reply?”

[Col. 1053B]

This satirist was listening to a rustic multitude of poets who, though possessing extremely little literary knowledge, nevertheless with remarkable impudence appropriated to themselves the position and name of learned persons and composed books and poems in hoarse and useless verbosity. Since this had displeased him for a long time and he had not yet answered them with fitting rebuke, he finally thought it should no longer be endured in silence but that some annoyance ought to be returned for so burdensome a nuisance. “Since I am certain,” he says, “that you are obscure poets, knowing little or nothing, giving little care to literature and none to improvement, shall I always hear you babbling in hoarse impudence, heedlessly pouring out rustic poems, and return nothing for such great insolence, by which you presume to vex me? [Col. 1053C] Shall I not apply the hellebore necessary to cleanse such madness?”

So also, when wicked people do not become softened toward repentance as time passes, but the more they are endured, the more severely they harden themselves in sinning, that highest chastiser is generally prepared to strike, lest, should he decide to spare them longer, they sin more obstinately. For just as young shoots of trees, when left to their own freedom, spread out into an untrimmed breadth of branches or a lofty height, and if they are perhaps permitted to grow into aged maturity, then, their strength hardened and made solid, are no longer bent by human powers; so, surely, when new-born iniquity is allowed to flourish while vengeance is set aside, it hastens to spread through the freedom it has received, and if vengeance, as though forgetful, is silent too long, that iniquity, advancing toward worse things, hardens into invincible and incorrigible malice. [Col. 1053D]

Therefore God often threatens those who cease from good work, so that the thunder of the threat may terrify the sluggish soul and, knowing that punishments are imminent for its negligence, it may fear to turn hand or mind toward more wicked action.

[p. 606]

## Chapter LVII
The first offense by which God is said to be provoked to anger occurs when the wretched, sluggish soul neglects to do what is good; the second, when, no longer content with sluggishness and idleness, it becomes more vehemently intent upon doing what is evil. When it is not recalled from sluggishness and idleness by prayers or threats, it wanders, as though license had been granted it, into a certain broad field of sinning [Col. 1054A]; and because the first shoot of the disease is not cut back by any biting hoe, it proceeds from vice to vice and, through harmful liberty, is strengthened.

But if, while it languidly grows numb in good works as though weighed down by sleep, it is more watchfully terrified at the lightning-flash of threats, it not only does not direct its voluntary mind toward doing worse things, but reproves itself with fitting repentance for that in which it had already become sluggish. Therefore, when in Jeremiah the divine word accused certain persons and showed them deserving of accusation because of negligence—“They have not upheld the cause of the orphan, nor judged the judgment of the poor”—it added: “Shall I not take vengeance upon these things, says the Lord, or shall not my soul be avenged upon such a nation?” (Jer. VI). As though He said: [Col. 1054B] If people devoted to idleness have grown sluggish in good works, and, though able to perform what their brother’s need required, refused to do so, shall I endure such an injury and not rather exact fitting vengeance for these things? For I do not wish them to suppose, because I am silently inactive, that I sleep; so that what they have negligently despised I should leave unpunished with still greater negligence. Rather, I shall strike the root that has been wickedly driven into the earth before the tree becomes wild and spreads into a multitude of branches.

For contempt of justice is a kind of root of injustice: first, through it, one negligent in doing what is just fails to apply diligence; then, advancing in evil, he later gives himself over to doing what is unjust. But when divine benevolence purposes quickly to show mercy, it does not allow contempt of itself, as though a root, [Col. 1054C] to grow into greater things; rather, with the terror of correction, as with a hoe, it cuts off the evil first growth, lest by abusing license it receive a more wicked increase. But if sleeping vengeance is silent in striking such contempt or root, or if perhaps an evil mind is hardened against its threats and lashes, the root once implanted grows strong, sprouting with pestilential force; and, through wretched progress, a multiplicity of branches grows together.

For nothing is more fruitful, nothing is found to prosper so swiftly according to its wish, than perversity of mind, which, diligently seeking not the difficult heights of merits but the downward paths of vices, finds its progress in these and is borne by precipitous fall to completion. When it rejoices ruinously in its pleasures and judges them either unworthy of vengeance [Col. 1054D] or perhaps consigned to forgetfulness, the righteous Judge—who, for reasons known to Himself, chose silently to endure evils while they were germinating—at last undertakes to answer them, once grown, with a more grievous sentence. Hence in Ezekiel: “The iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great, and the land is filled with blood, and the city is filled with apostasy. For they have said: ‘The Lord has forsaken the land, and the Lord does not see’” (Ezek. IX).

Because God in His patience chose not to strike the sins of the children of Israel at their outset, but endured their disposition until it reached greater wickedness, they, blinded in heart, supposed that God had no concern for earthly matters and did not closely see what they perversely did. From this they assumed greater confidence—or rather, hardness [Col. 1055A]—and, more negligently abusing God’s patience, sinned more freely and added graver things to grave things, as though God did not see such deeds.

This is also plainly proclaimed elsewhere by a certain fool who, supposing that God does not see what he himself shamelessly does, prepares himself more confidently for further sin because God, postponing vengeance, patiently bears with the sinner. “Who sees me?” he says. “Darkness surrounds me, walls cover me, and no one looks around me. Whom should I fear? The Most High will not remember my sins” (Ecclus. XXIII). This man, besieged by darkness and enclosed by the hard wall of an obstinate mind, has no experience of that light which is God and softens those whom it penetrates. [Col. 1055B] Those in darkness do not regard with fitting reverence either His stern justice or His gentle mercy; for although the light shines in darkness, the darkness does not comprehend it. This man, I say, because he does not see that light, supposes that he too is not seen; and, with hardened heart, he dares not fear the strict Judge. Though he knows Him to be the Most High, he thinks that He dwells so far above that He does not care to remember what is perversely done below. “The Most High,” he says, “will not remember my sins.”

Yet this Most High so bears with the sinner for a time that later He shows Himself a strict requiter. One must not suppose that He is negligently patient toward him, since Scripture proclaims Him not only patient beforehand, but also a requiter afterwards. [Col. 1055C] For a wise man says: “The Most High is a patient requiter” (Ecclus. V). And David says: “Merciful and compassionate and just” (Ps. CX). Again: “Patient and abundant in mercy and true” (Ps. LXXXV).

Therefore, since Scripture’s testimony declares Him patient and a requiter, compassionate and just, abundant in mercy and true, it must not be believed that He endures anyone’s vices either in ignorance or through negligence; 607 nor that He punishes the Gentiles in such a way as not also to punish those instructed in the divine laws, or strikes Israel in such a way as to leave the Gentiles unpunished. He strikes all indeed, but inflicts heavier penalties upon those whose faults He finds greater: perhaps those who, having attained a fuller knowledge of Him through the benefit of teaching, nevertheless, setting aside fear and love, are entangled in greater vices. Finally, [Col. 1055D] the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall rightly be beaten with many stripes.

Thus the master wishes to punish with a stricter sentence the servant to whom he deigns to impart fuller knowledge of himself, when that servant offends. Nor does He pity with debased compassion one who does not duly fear, in humility, Him whom he knows as his Creator and Lord. Hence, when the children of Israel and Judah said in Ezekiel, “The Lord has forsaken the land, and the Lord does not see” (Ezek. IX), the Lord immediately added there: “Therefore my eye too shall not spare, nor will I have mercy; I will repay their ways upon their head” (ibid.).

Because, He says, they confess me as Lord with their own voice, yet think that I, as though far away, do not see their perverse actions because I delay to hurl the dart of vengeance against them—[Col. 1056A] therefore I too shall at last not spare, nor shall I appear continually merciful to such sinners; rather, I shall answer their grave pride with graver punishments. For, insofar as they presumed proudly and obstinately to sin, neither loving nor fearing Him whom they knew to be Lord, it is fitting that a corresponding recompense be visibly returned upon their head, so that not I so much as their own pride may seem to answer them.

For then each person’s own iniquity plainly answers him, when grave adversity presses upon him by its merit; when, just as he formerly exulted in contempt of justice or loss, so afterwards he is made sorrowful by penalties equal in number or measure. Hence through Isaiah: “According to the greatness of the work, their visitation” (Isa. XV). And again: “In measure against measure He will visit her” [Col. 1056B] (Isa. XXVII). And the prophet Hosea says: “The arrogance of Israel shall answer in his face” (Hos. V).

What it means for the arrogance of Israel to answer in his face, the prophet then wished to explain more plainly: “And Israel,” he says, “shall fall in his iniquity” (ibid.). Because Israel did not fear to entangle itself in more wicked deeds and to despise the divine commandments through swelling pride and arrogance, that same arrogance shall fittingly answer him when the vengeance pressing down upon him forces him grievously to fall.

Indeed, one whom the very judgment of a servant of God so blinds that he greedily embraces what flattering flesh or the deceitful world offers seems, in his lost understanding, to stand firm as long as no adversity confronts such a purpose. [Col. 1056C] But if the wrath of God, meeting this carnal flattery, cuts it away like a physician with some surgical instrument of vengeance, that sick and weak man now, as though punished, falls: he is prevented by new adversities from carrying out his customary acts, and, through the merit of his faults, experiences the exceedingly heavy hand that strikes him. Surely the measure and severity of vengeance are fashioned according to the measure or merit of perverse action, so that when the offender is struck harshly or more harshly, he has no ground rightly to complain of the justice of the one striking.

Hence Hosea adds much later concerning Israel: “According to his ways and according to his inventions, He will repay him” (Hos. XII). What can excuse Israel as undeserving to be struck, or accuse as indiscriminate the justice of Him who strikes, when the former’s iniquity and arrogance are named, [Col. 1056D] while the latter is proclaimed not so much to give as to repay according to ways and inventions? That one, wicked and arrogant, does not fear to offend his God. God, just and true, does not negligently pity the offender; rather, the more He knows him to be His familiar and member of His household, the more expressly He wills every offense he has incurred to be avenged.

Indicating this through the prophet Amos, He says: “You alone have I known among all the families of the earth; therefore I will visit upon you all your iniquities” (Amos III). Because, He says, I know you more intimately than the rest, I therefore do not excuse you when you sin, but will rehearse and turn over before your face all that you commit wickedly, so that, when I have rendered the fitting recompense, I may acquit you.

[Col. 1057A] For a good Judge, even when He does not spare, spares; and even when He does not show mercy, shows mercy: when He both punishes sin and works the healing of the sinner; when, visiting His people, He strikes them in order that they may be cleansed; when that person, as a sick man, is urgently brought back to health by severe cautery. He does not spare and yet spares when, according to David, “He visits their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges; but He does not take away His mercy from them” (Ps. LXXXVIII): that is, when He brings grievous discipline upon those who stray, and that very grievousness is transformed into saving medicine.

## CHAPTER LVIII

Paul also, taught by this discipline, threatens the Corinthians and declares that he will be severe with them when they sin; yet with what affection [Col. 1057B] and with how great mercy he heals their sickness he shows more than sufficiently in his Epistles. “As though I were not coming to you,” he says, “some have become puffed up; but I shall come to you soon. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Cor. IV). And in another Epistle: “I have foretold,” he says, “and I foretell, that if I come again, I will not spare” (2 Cor. XIII).

He who thus roars, thunders, and terribly threatens that he will come—and that, if he comes, he will not, so to speak, spare—has no other concern in this than to provide for them 608 or heal them, and to rage against the sickness in such a way as to be found merciful toward the sick themselves. For he whom zeal and love of justice so urge to severity nevertheless loves those whom he chastises so deeply that, while he rebukes and accuses their vices more harshly, he does not refuse [Col. 1057C] mercifully to spend himself for their souls: “Most willingly,” he says, “I will spend and be spent myself for your souls” (2 Cor. XII).

Hence Joseph seems to rage more severely against his brothers, though he was assisting them toward salvation. He vexes and grinds them harshly as though with iron teeth, and more fiercely seems to close and stop his ear against their groaning entreaties. Because he knew that they were grievously ill and that so great an illness could not be cleansed except by severe cautery, he assumed a severe expression and did not pity them with womanish softness, lest by pitying them weakly he should rather seem to hate them. For it is written: “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Prov. XIII).

Therefore, he does not pour the soothing oil of flattery into their wound, but [Col. 1057D] forcefully applies the instrument of fear and distress. The inward wound, which either long duration or, rather, impunity had caused to rot with harmful infection, the wise physician compels to become raw again by cutting and burning. For the sin which, because it had long remained unpunished, had already been put to sleep among them by a kind of forgetfulness, is recalled to memory by the onset of grievous penalties and renewed in their consciences by a severe reminder.

Hence they themselves say: “We deservedly suffer these things because we sinned against our brother, seeing the anguish of his soul when he begged us, and we did not listen; therefore this tribulation has come upon us” (Gen. XLII). Because our malice did not pity our brother, in whom no iniquity was found, [Col. 1058A] it must be certain that we are now punished by the merit of this deed and experience at present such great troubles for so great a crime. The tribulation which this ruler brings and threatens against us sets that fraternal crime before our face, and makes the truth of just judgment now openly answer the malicious falsehood which we spoke against him.

Of such persons Isaiah says: “The recognition of their face shall answer them” (Isa. III). For the recognition of the face is found to answer sinners when they take care to recall past sins in memory and openly acknowledge that they endure the grave evils which they see threatening them by the merit of those sins. Recognition of the face answers when old sins are struck by the novelty of evils, brought back as it were before the face into memory; when both the causes of evils [Col. 1058B] and the penalties of sins are compared with one another. Thus the discerning judges speak through the aforementioned Isaiah: “Our iniquities have been multiplied before you, and our sins have answered us” (Isa. LIX).

Therefore Joseph inflicted accusations on his brothers and afflicted them more repeatedly by prudent counsel so that the penalty due for the crime committed might be returned before their face, and that this repayment might heal them with a saving effect. “By the life of Pharaoh,” he says, “you are spies” (Gen. XLII). And shortly afterward: “Having returned,” it says, “he spoke to them, taking Simeon and binding him in their presence” (ibid.). And below: “Terrified, they said to one another: ‘We have been brought in because of the money which we formerly returned in our sacks, so that he may bring a charge against us and violently [Col. 1058C] reduce both us and our asses to slavery’” (Gen. XLIII). And below: “Rise,” he says, “pursue the men; and when you have seized them, say: ‘Why have you returned evil for good? The cup which you stole is the very one in which my lord drinks and in which he is accustomed to divine. You have done a very evil thing’” (Gen. XLIV).

Again: “All,” he says, “fell down together before him upon the ground. And he said to them: ‘Why did you wish to act thus? Do you not know that none is like me in the knowledge of divination?’ To him Judah said: ‘God has found out the iniquity of your servants. Behold, we are all my lord’s servants, both we and he with whom the cup was found.’ Joseph answered: ‘Far be it from me that I should do so. He who stole the cup shall be my servant!’ To him Judah said: ‘Let me myself [Col. 1058D] be your servant, for I received him into my own pledge and promised, saying: “Unless I bring him back, I shall be guilty of sin against my father all my life.” For I cannot return to my father while the boy is absent, lest I stand by as witness to the calamity that will crush my father’” (ibid.).

You see how harshly Joseph assails his brothers, how heavy a penalty of vengeance he devises against them, how he labors to burn or cut away their inward corruption and to avenge with a just sentence what had gone unpunished in them. Why does he do this, except that by cutting and burning he may make them healthier, and, when they are healed, have them more grateful and show himself benevolent and serene toward the more grateful? [Col. 1059A] From that manifestation, indeed, he commands every stranger to be removed: “He commanded,” it says, “that all should go out, and that no stranger should be present at their mutual recognition” (Gen. XLV).

Resentment, envy, and poisonous hatred are strangers to brothers; they exclude and keep far away gracious affection. Casting over the covering of malice, they veil the eye of the mind and conceal Joseph’s face, lest he be recognized. For as long as the hateful malice of the envious injures the wretched mind and fitting repentance does not come to cleanse it, it certainly does not recognize Christ, though He is near and present; rather, with blinded understanding, it thinks Him dead or absent. “We are twelve brothers,” they say, “born of one father; one is no more” (Gen. XLII). Him whom the brothers neither recognize nor understand to be present, they do not even suppose to be alive, because Christ, whom the envy of those who hate Him buried shut within a hard 609 stone, [Col. 1059B] lives and reigns with unveiled face only in the hearts of those who love Him.

For this reason, then, Christ cleanses the eyes of the envious with a kind of cleansing cloth; and, pouring in the biting eye-salve of repentance, wipes away the stain or rheum from their eyes, so that when the pupil of the heart has been uncovered by purgative medicine, the unveiled face of Christ Himself may be revealed. Christ pursues His brothers, who are enemies through their deserts, so that pressing spurs may convert them into friends. In anger against their vices He inflicts heavy vengeance upon them, so that, through this recompense, He may grant them a clearer knowledge of His own vision. “I am,” He says, “Joseph your brother” (Gen. XLV). I am He, He says, who, gravely angered against your vices, yet embraced you all the more eagerly with brotherly love; I wished to strike what I knew ought to be rebuked in you, [Col. 1059C] in order to give myself to you to be known with unveiled face.

Surely with this purpose Christ rages severely against the vices of the elect, and with this end, when severe, He is accustomed to strike them: that wrath may work medicine, the blow salvation, and that He may glory in them or because of them when they have been healed to the uttermost. Concerning them He says through Moses: “I will strike, and I will heal” (Deut. XXXII). And Eliphaz the Temanite says to Job: “He wounds and heals; He strikes, and His hands shall heal” (Job V).

## CHAPTER LIX

For this reason perhaps the prophet Habakkuk complained, grieving at God’s silence because the wicked were presently spared according to their desire; grieving because divine correction did not answer them [Col. 1059D] sternly and profitably, because it did not abolish their iniquity by the imposition of some bitterness. “Why do you not look upon those who act wickedly,” he says, “and remain silent while the wicked devours one more righteous than himself?” (Hab. I).

Why, he says, when the unjust oppresses the just, do you not intervene? Why do you not help not only the oppressed but rather the oppressor, so that by a useful blow he may be turned more quickly from injustice and converted to pursue the justice which he attacks? Why do you not take up arms and shield mercifully rather than cruelly, defend him who suffers injury, and swiftly inflict a heavier penalty upon him who causes it, so that by looking upon him you may shake him usefully into trembling? For you are He who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble (Ps. CIII).

Why, then, do you not [Col. 1060A] look upon him who acts wickedly? Why are you silent while one more righteous is devoured by the wicked and ungodly? While you do not call that same ungodly person back, you are already allowing him to tumble into the abyss; and you do not release the just person from a double anguish and sorrow. For the righteous man grieves not only for the hardship he suffers, but rather for the malice of the one inflicting it; perhaps he wishes in some manner to become accursed, so that a more biting and salutary poultice may be applied to the sick person.

Seeing, therefore, both grave evils brought upon himself by the ungodly and that the latter is not recalled from his purpose while unpunished, the righteous man, knowing no other remedy for his pain, ventures to address the God in whom he trusts through Isaiah: “Will you restrain yourself in these things, O Lord? Will you remain silent and afflict us exceedingly?” (Isa. LXIV). When you see us harassed by many grave injuries, [Col. 1060B] and the ungodly freely unleashed to harass us, can you contain yourself in silence concerning these things and not rather hasten to answer those who do wrong? Will you be silent and greatly afflict us by your silence, while patiently allowing both them to inflict suffering and us to suffer it, rather than striking with a hard word those who labor in malice, that they may be healed and, their neck’s hardness broken by your ordinances, may resist no longer?

Thus the righteous groan not only because they are afflicted by the injuries of the wicked, but because those same wicked persons are not yet corrected by stripes. They know without doubt that those whom the Lord desires to call back to justice and salvation are scourged by Him. Conversely, those whose advancement God does not care for and whose blameworthy life [Col. 1060C] He despises—those whom, for reasons known to Himself, He does not determine to save—He commonly permits to fulfill their wicked desires and leaves them presently unpunished in a kind of harmful silence. Because a reprobate will harshly binds them against repentance and more freely loosens and incites them to heavier sin, He does not chastise those hardened in malice with present blows; and, because a stricter wrath drives them far from salvation, He does not scourge with angering gentleness those whom He does not receive as sons. “He scourges,” Solomon says, “every son whom He receives” (Prov. III; Heb. XII). And David: “The reprobate are not in the labor of men, nor shall they be scourged with men” (Ps. LXXII).

## CHAPTER LX

[Col. 1060D] This gentleness, by which He is found to spare such persons—and in which every malicious person miserably rejoices or flatters himself—though it works wrath in the present and death afterwards, nevertheless does not appear grievous and troublesome to the carnal eye. For they suppose God burdensome and angry, intolerably indignant at their life and habits, when they see that those whom He regards do not possess the good things He loves and do endure the present evils that He hates.

Hence, when that Judge determined not to strike in the present the city of blood, which He perhaps foresaw would perish irreparably in the future, He says: “My zeal shall be taken away from you, and I shall rest and no longer be angry” (Ezek. XVI). Because, He says, you no longer heed the scourges by which I wished to correct you; indeed, your wicked and reprobate heart hardens itself against them. Therefore my justice shall henceforth rest from its purpose of scourging [Col. 1061A] 610 and shall not grow angry at your transgressions by inflicting present troubles. I shall not be zealous for you, wickedly hardened and given over to shamefulness; nor shall I be indignant against your crimes through useful vengeance. Rather, with the rein loosened, abandoned to your free will, without any obstacle you shall plunge at will into sins.

From this it is plain that it is no small benefit when God is immediately angry with sinners; when He mercifully corrects by present vengeance what is sinned; when He rebukes the offender in judgment rather than in fury, so that, chastised by a medicinal stroke, he may repentantly serve God in fear. “O Lord,” David says, “rebuke me not in your fury” (Ps. IV). And Jeremiah: “Correct me, O Lord,” he says, “yet in judgment and not in fury” (Jer. X).

[Col. 1061B] The wise prophet wishes rather to be chastised by present judgment than to have the due vengeance reserved for the last day, when the implacable wrath of God shall be poured out upon every reprobate person, every evil deed shall be punished according to measure and number, and the desirable salvation shall not follow those painful penalties. Hence through Isaiah: “I shall measure back their work into their bosom” (Isa. LXV). Therefore the prophet wishes God to answer those crimes healthfully by present judgment rather than to restrain His hand from vengeance through negligent silence; for at the final examination He promises Himself a more severe Judge outwardly to those for whom purgative punishment does not presently answer.

For He who chooses in the present, as though patient, to remain silent toward reprobate sinners and to prevent them by no obstacle from their evil purpose [Col. 1061C] is afterwards found gnashing and thundering in fierce anger, and rehearsing before their faces in punishment all that they have done wickedly. His avenging answer is not delayed, nor is patient silence preferred to answering for long, except so that those who are in filth may, through wretched progress, desire to become more filthy; and, having become more filthy, may deserve to endure not only many but also the most grievous things. For they receive not only what they wished to do wickedly, but also punishment because, though long awaited after their wicked deeds, they refused to blush with shame. And the longer divine equity bore with them, the more harshly their own iniquity brings them to judgment in return.

[Col. 1061D] Concerning them Ezekiel says: “According to their way I shall deal with them, and according to their judgments I shall judge them” (Ezek. VII). And to Tyre and Sidon: “I shall repay your recompense upon your head” (Joel III). And through Obadiah to Edom: “As you have done, so shall it be done to you; your recompense shall return upon your head” (Obad. 15). The most just Judge repays and requites them according to their way when He brings the due end upon their evil works; when He lays aside the patience He had shown toward them; when He no longer purposes to maintain silence instead of retribution; when He sets before their conscience all that they have done wickedly; when, finally, He lays the due curse upon their deserts: “Go,” He says, “you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV).

## CHAPTER LXI

[Col. 1062A] These words by which He rages so terribly against those described above, by which He either assigns the accursed to fire or fire to the accursed, do not pass away as mere words; rather, they blaze like abiding fire. Wasting away in their grievous burning, the ungodly become ashes; and those who, hardened, refused to prefer admonitory words to their pleasures cannot endure avenging words that have the effect of fire. Concerning them Jeremiah says: “Are not my words like fire, and like a hammer breaking a rock?” (Jer. XXIII). And Isaiah: “His tongue is like devouring fire” (Isa. XXX).

The words of God and the tongue that inflict a curse upon those who perish, never again to return to repentance through any regard of grace, are rightly proclaimed to be like fire; by their burning the ungodly are reduced to nothing. For as fire, while burning gold or silver, [Col. 1062B] makes it brighter, but does not brighten wood, hay, and stubble but consumes them, so the word of wrath which the Lord speaks on the day of vengeance does not consume the elect but compels the reprobate to come to nothing.

For those who, through the demands of their deserts, reach the point where it would be much better for them never to have existed are in Scripture sometimes said not to be, because, being wretchedly lost, they do not possess true being. Of them Esther says: “Do not hand over your kingdom to those who are not” (Esth. XIV). And Isaiah: “Your spirit is like an overflowing torrent, to destroy nations into nothing” (Isa. XXX). And Ezekiel says to the prince of Tyre: “You have become nothing, and you shall not be forever” (Ezek. XXVII).

Those, therefore, who deserve to perish irreparably plainly [Col. 1062C] come to nothing, as has been said: for just as hay and stubble do not withstand fire, so the children of perdition do not stand before the word of the Judge. Job, fearing this, says: “Why do you not take away my sin, and why do you not remove my iniquity? Behold, now I sleep in the dust; and if you seek me in the morning, I shall not remain” (Job VII). If sin is not taken away from the sinner and iniquity from the wicked, when at last sleep—that is, bodily death—is brought upon him, he does not stand before the Judge because paternal justice does not assist him and his merit fails.

“If you seek me in the morning,” he says, “I shall not remain” (ibid.). In the morning—that is, when, the darkness of this life left behind, day is now breaking, when the more perfect light of His justice shines upon one according to one’s deserts—if you seek me, that is, examine me, investigate me, search me out—for you are God who searches hearts and reins—I shall not merely fail [Col. 1062D] to answer worthily when you search the inner things of my merits; I shall not even be able to stand before the face of your fire. 611

“Forgive me, therefore,” David says, “that I may be refreshed before I depart and am no more” (Ps. XXXVIII). If, before I depart from here, you do not forgive me; if you do not send healing refreshment into my consuming wound, I shall indeed depart and be no more, because I shall not be led into the light of glory which truly is, but brought into the shadows of true death, which are nothing. And those who are in the shadows that are nothing are themselves in some sense nothing. Therefore Jeremiah says: “Do not reduce me to nothing” (Jer. X).

[Col. 1063A] He clearly understands that those who are not with Him with whom it is good to be—as Peter says, “It is good for us to be here” (Luke IX)—are quite reasonably said not to be, because they possess only a miserable existence. For one who exists badly, compared with that which is truly good, is nothing. Therefore, just as that Jerusalem is which has merited to attain the vision of its Creator, and in which its Creator deigns to make a welcome dwelling, so that wretched Babylon, upon which the stricter Judge inflicts harsh vengeance, must be believed not to be.

That Babylon not only fails reverently to desire good things, but has negligently despised them in its lost understanding; and because divine justice patiently bore with it in these things, it burst shamelessly forth, with the rein loosened, into doing evil. When the [Col. 1063B] Judge had endured its shamelessness for some time and it observed neither measure nor reverence in sinning, He summoned avenging ministers to end this silence and commanded them to punish Babylon according to its deserts: “Do not,” He says, “be silent concerning her iniquities, for it is the time of the Lord’s vengeance; He Himself will repay her recompense” (Jer. LI).

Because in my silence Babylon, stiff-necked, made no progress; and while I awaited its repentance, it did not cast off its malice—I do not wish you whom I have prepared as my avengers to be silent any longer, but, laying delay aside, to render to it what it deserves. Hence above, through the same Jeremiah: “Declare in Babylon; stand against her round about, and let none escape. Repay her according to her work; according to all that [Col. 1063C] she has done, do to her, for she has risen up against the Lord” (Jer. L).

Because God saw that He was excluded in every inhabitant of Babylon, He wills that all alike be enclosed in a general destruction, so that, because none had been moved by the love of repentance, no one may be granted the means of escape when vengeance comes upon them. Thus Babylon is repaid according to its work when all its citizens are subjected to divine vengeance; when, just as it refused to refrain from ungratefulness toward God, so it is finally compelled by just judgment to endure ungrateful vengeance.

But since it is now enough to have discussed this recompense, lest the reader grow weary of a discourse too long drawn out upon it, the pen is urged to pass to that recompense which is said to return favorable things to the ungrateful.

[Col. 1063D] The twofold recompense discussed thus far is called similar because it repays like things: that is, favorable things to the grateful and unfavorable things to the ungrateful. But the twofold recompense that remains is called dissimilar because it is proclaimed to render unlike things: either favorable things to the ungrateful or unfavorable things to the grateful.

To repay kindness to the ungrateful with kindness, that supreme Master of all instructs us, since he wills mercifully to teach what he does powerfully, and to display in deeds what he has taught. When he endured from the Jews spitting and blows, mockery and reproaches, and finally the cross, though he was able by a strong hand to repay them in kind, he instead pitied their error, humbly entreated the Father, and by the intervention of his prayers obtained pardon for them. “Father,” he said, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” [Col. 1064A] (Luke 23). Some among those who had assembled at such a spectacle with malicious intent received this benefit with such grace that they did not afterward refuse to die for him whom they knew had prayed to the Creator on behalf of their undeserving selves. And so that teaching might accord with such an example, and both might reach posterity in worthy remembrance: “Do good,” he says, “to those who hate you, that you may be sons of your Father, who makes his sun rise upon good and evil, and rains upon just and unjust” (Matt. 5). If you wish, he says, truly to show yourselves to be God’s sons, you must apply your greatest zeal to doing good, conversely, to those who hate you, and repaying their ungrateful hatred with a welcome benefit. For thus your Father in heaven [Col. 1064B] makes his sun rise upon the undeserving; thus he wills to bestow necessary rain even upon all manner of evil persons, and does not refuse generously to make fruitful the land of evil persons no less than that of good persons, so that they may abound in temporal goods.

You too must maintain the pattern of this benevolence, so as to make yourselves like that same Father God in this respect. Those whom he admits within the number or order of his children, he does not wish to be content with the righteousness or merits of the heathen. “For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? And if you greet only your brethren, what more do you do? Do not even the heathen do this?” (ibid.). You see that, although spiritual religion does not make tax collectors perfect, yet a certain natural law draws them to this: as they return hatred to those whom they recognize as their enemies, so they are found to have a kindly disposition toward friends. Likewise, the heathen do not refuse at last to embrace even this law: those who know themselves to have been greeted return the greeting, judging it fitting for anyone wishing to live humanly to render reciprocal kindness to one who loves him. 612 Finally, you have heard that it was said: “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy” (ibid.). Therefore, the same law which inward nature gives to the heathen, outward Scripture gives from heaven to the Jews; or perhaps Scripture does not truly impose upon them a law of hatred, but, for the sake of forbearance, indulgently tolerates and permits it.

But Christ does not wish us to resemble either these heathen or the Jews, nor does he wish evangelical men to adhere literally to their law [Col. 1064D]—that is, to choose as the sole measure or manner of love that we should love only those who love us. Therefore, when he had said, “You have heard that it was said: You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy” (ibid.), he immediately added: “But I say to you: Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (ibid.); as though he said: You have heard that the law which God sent you, who were harder of heart, through Moses permitted you to repay your enemies in kind. But I, who invite you to evangelical perfection, certainly do not admit among the perfect those who embrace only their own lovers tenderly, while pursuing their enemies with equal balance and hatred. [Col. 1065A] Therefore I will that you be bound in no way by the law of heathen or Jew, but be advanced farther by abundant zeal, so that not only those who love you may find you repayers of this obligation, but those who hate you may also find you their lovers.

The apostle Paul, setting out to obey this teaching, chose not to strike back at one who struck him according to the Mosaic law; and, as he himself affectionately taught the Corinthians in Christ’s place, he wished them not to be unaware of this same benevolence of his. “We are cursed,” he says, “and we bless; we endure persecution; we are slandered, and we entreat” (1 Cor. 4). What he clearly affirms of himself to the Corinthians, he confidently commands the Romans as well, observing that a preacher rightly speaks good with authority when neither his will nor his conduct contradicts what he says. “Bless,” he says, “those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse” [Col. 1065B] (Rom. 12). And lest anyone think it sufficient to show himself benevolent by word alone and not confer a necessary benefit upon an enemy, Paul expressly stated this more clearly in what follows and left no room for our ignorance. “If your enemy is hungry,” he says, “feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink” (ibid.).

This, he says, is a repayment gracious by reason of its perfection, fruitful even for enemies themselves: namely, when we repay them not with the fleeting emptiness of words, like leaves, but with the welcome reality of a deed springing from a more sincere affection. A welcome deed truly bestowed upon enemies [Col. 1065C] is not only useful to the friends who confer it, but is often changed into a spiritual benefit for those whose minds, previously disturbed by hatred, are brightened by the ray of love. The Apostle indicates this when he adds: “For in doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head” (ibid.). If, he says, you feed an enemy when hungry and give drink to him when thirsty, you will heap coals of fire upon his head; that is, you will strike his mind with grave compunction, and, breaking his hardness, provoke him to repentance, and, conquered by kindness, gladly call him back from hatred. For sometimes one who, assailed by evils, did not desist from malice, yielded when more effectively conquered by contrary good deeds; and one whose hardness the hatred inflicted by persecutors did not break has been compelled by benefits received to become a friend. This is also sometimes found to have occurred among those to whom it had not been granted to attain the summit of religious faith: though ignorant of both the command and fruit of Catholic or evangelical truth, they nevertheless repaid benefits to those who hated them, solely through the grace of human gentleness.

## Chapter LXII

When Lucius Cinna assailed the Emperor Augustus with bitter hatred and plotted by deceit to kill one whom he could not openly kill, it happened that this utterly wicked affair did not escape Augustus’s notice; for one of the conspirators chose to become an informer. The emperor therefore, wishing to take vengeance upon his most wicked enemy, ordered those whom he knew to be his friends to be summoned, so that [Col. 1066A] he might report to them the criminal’s wicked purpose and, by their counsel, pronounce upon him a fitting sentence. Meanwhile he was troubled and anxious with fear; a sleepless and restless night passed for the anxious man, while he considered what safeguard he should prepare against plots and ambushes, and what injury he should inflict upon those who ambushed him. Turning these matters over and over, he was grievously distressed; drawing frequent sighs, he spoke variously with himself, still uncertain what might at last be the more fitting decision in this affair: whether he should let his enemy live or instead compel him to die.

“Am I,” he said, “to allow my assassin to live? Am I, while anxious, to allow him to be safer? Am I, who so often won the prize of battle as victor on land and sea, now to die by a shameful death and the plots [Col. 1066B] of wicked men? Am I to allow him to exult, joyfully having attained the object of his wish; to allow him, victorious over me when I am conquered, to insult me? Rather, should I not set upon him, entangle him in his own snares, and by swift vengeance forestall the accomplishment of his intended deceit?”

Having said this, Augustus was silent for a while; what he had said did not sufficiently please him, and it seemed to him that such cruelty did not become royal majesty—that whoever fell under suspicion should immediately be exposed to the danger of death. “What am I to do?” he said. “If so many seek to rage against my head, if their settled purpose is that I should perish, 613 who could so often withstand the plots of so many and find a sufficient remedy for this serpent-like disease? But if I arrange that their work be repaid into their own bosom, and inflict upon each of them the death they contrive for me, what limit or end to killing could be found? Who would be so inhuman as not to fear undergoing this? What life would be worth so much that, for its sake, so many should be removed from the midst, and that, for it alone to survive, countless others should die—a life which desires to be so pleasing to itself alone that it does not care to become hateful to everyone else? Yet what wise man would not protect himself rather than others? Who would be found such a lover of another’s life and so prodigal of his own that he would allow such wicked enemies to live unpunished, while he himself, cowardly and base, dies like a lamb for sacrifice?”

For Cinna had planned to attack him at a time when he would be engaged in devotion at the sacred altars of the gods, when, out of religious reverence, he would be sacrificing victims to his gods and, intent upon divine things, would fear human dangers less [Col. 1066D].

While the anxious emperor spoke these or similar things, still uncertain what choice he should finally make, his wife Livia approached him. “Do you wish,” she said, “O king, to hear a woman’s counsel and, laying aside for a little while your manly authority, to obey my advice? Those who know how prudently to apply medicine for the healing of bodies, so that they can either expel a present pain or prevent one that is coming, when they see that customary remedies do no good, try contrary ones. For as harsh remedies benefit and heal harsh conditions, and gentle remedies gentle conditions, so likewise gentle remedies are often usefully applied to harsh conditions and harsh remedies to gentle conditions. Since, therefore, you have thus far gained nothing by severity—for plotters spring up again, though you have previously put many to death one after another—try whether clemency might perhaps serve you better, whether by sparing rather than killing you might be safer. Behold, Lucius Cinna has now been apprehended, and you can repay him according to his desert; when he suffers his due punishment beneath the avenging sword, he will no longer harm you in your present anxiety. But if you spare him, if you pardon him mercifully, if you grant life to the undeserving man, perhaps he will not harm your life, and without doubt he will benefit your reputation; and he who now, by reason of his treachery, is deservedly an object of hatred or fear to you will, by the gift of your clemency, contribute to your glory and honor.”

Augustus was pleased that the prudent woman had dissuaded him from cruelty and murder and, by pleasing speech, persuaded him toward worthy clemency. Dismissing the friends whom he had ordered summoned to him, [Col. 1067B] he commanded that Lucius Cinna alone be brought into his chamber. When Cinna had been brought in, he ordered a chair to be placed beside himself; and when Cinna, still unaware of the plan, had sat down at his command, Augustus dismissed everyone else.

“Cinna,” he said, “I wish you to be silent for a while and to endure in silence whatever I say, so that, while I am speaking, you do not burst out in haste or impatience to speak, nor interrupt the course of my words with the noise of an objection. Nor do I say this to take from you hope of speaking; rather, after I have spoken, I will give you ample time to reply. Thus what belongs to each of us will be freely granted, since the speech of us both will be offered not confusedly but one after the other.

“Cinna,” he said, “I made you fortunate, rich, and honored; I heaped upon you countless benefits; I raised you above others to this summit of dignity and, by the abundance of good things bestowed on you, stirred up against you the envy of many great men. And although I have deserved so much from you, you do not render due return, but, restoring evil for good, plan to kill me, without duly considering that my benevolence toward you does not deserve this, nor is such recompense owed to my generosity.”

At this speech Cinna, no longer able to keep silent, cried out and most vehemently denied what the emperor had said: “Far be such madness from me, that I should lay a hand upon my king and lord, or admit this crime even in secret intention.”
