Augustus replied: “Cinna, this was not our agreement: that you should not allow me to speak, that while I am still speaking you should interrupt me [Col. 1067D]; but rather that, while I spoke, you should be silent, and after my words, should it seem fitting to you, reply. You, Cinna, who ought to offer me loyalty, obedience, and protection, in a reverse and perverse exchange prepare to kill me. And lest you think that I do not so much truly know as idly suspect what I say, do you wish the day, place, and accomplices of this crime to be named for you?”

When he set all these things out for him by name and related in order how the crime had been decided upon and was to be carried out, Cinna fell silent not so much because of what they had agreed between themselves as because of his guilty conscience, since he could not at all refute the crime laid to his charge. The emperor added: “I should like to know, Cinna, with what purpose you desired this crime; what honor or glory you thought you would gain if you accomplished it; on what account my safety was hateful to you [Col. 1068A], or through hope of what reward my death was, conversely, welcome. Was it that you might alone possess my empire, and exercise your own dominion or tyranny over all who are subject to it? Do you suppose that, apart from me, no obstacle to this can be found? Do you not reckon that another may hinder you in this, and have you found the time so favorable to your desires that, in fulfilling them, you have no one troublesome but me? But let it be so: in that way, or perhaps in any other, I at last yield to your wish, and now grant that you shall reign and rule as you please. Will Paulus and Fabius Maximus, the Cossi and Servilii, and many other great men whose names are displayed, who are magnified as great and noble by their ancestral images—will they, I say, endure this with such patience? And will those whom you now have as rivals rejoice in your advancement? Ill does fortune now flatter the Roman people, ill the fortune of the commonwealth, and imperial dignity finds itself burdened and ill-served, if so easy an entrance to sovereignty lies open to you, if this ambition of yours is hindered only by me.

“Yet though, guilty of treason, you are judged unworthy of life, and though you deserve rather to suffer the death you wished to inflict upon me, nevertheless, with more welcome clemency, I utterly lay aside my just anger. And, Cinna, traitor though you are, I now give you life a second time, so that, conquered by an overflowing benefit, you may be changed into a friend—you whom, without any fault of mine, I had hitherto had as an enemy. Henceforth let friendship between us begin more graciously, and from day to day be strengthened by fitting growth; and observe, when injustice and treason have deserved punishment and disgrace, what reward or honor faithfulness and love obtain.”

Having said this, the emperor voluntarily bestowed the consulship upon Cinna, so that he might enrich him not merely with words but with gifts, complaining that Cinna had not dared to seek it when he ought not at all to have doubted that he would receive it. In this way Augustus tempered his anger with merciful patience; as a good emperor he ruled his own mind with strength; and, employing prudent counsel, he did not refuse to repay evils with good. He changed Cinna’s malice into benevolence, and they were found to cling to one another by so indissoluble a bond of strong friendship that thereafter they are not reported to have differed even slightly.

## Chapter LXIII

[Col. 1068D] If, among the heathen, repaying kindness to the ungrateful with kindness is proclaimed commendable because by such repayment hatred is sometimes changed into friendship, much more fittingly and much more sacredly should the same repayment be practiced among the faithful, who ought to imitate their God in life and morals. For this purpose God grants the benefit of his generosity to all who are ungrateful; for this purpose, when they provoke him, he displays toward them, in return, an affection of mercy: that, as though coals had been heaped upon their heads, they may turn away from their wicked purpose, and, pierced by the benefit received, be converted to loving him who loves them.

Thus, when Judas Iscariot wandered far from the path of uprightness and, guilty of treachery, wickedly thirsted for Christ’s death, Christ nevertheless did not expose him [Col. 1069A], though aware of the secret; the kindly Master did not dishonor him with reproaches; he did not avenge violated faith or the horrible crime by sudden violence. Instead, he admitted the hand of the man eating with him into the dish; he called friend the man whose conscience he saw through and abhorred; meek and patient, he kissed the accursed traitor. Why did he do this, if not that the fire of malice might be extinguished by the infusion of welcome dew; that the wicked traitor, piously admonished, might come to his senses; that his iniquity might be checked not harshly by an avenging blow or a deadly punishment, but that a mind wickedly armed might be salutarially confounded by being softened with such sweet oil? Since he had said in the Gospel, “Do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5), he wills his deed to accord with his teaching and attempts to soften his enemy by benefits, thereby showing it commendable if one employs benevolence toward a malicious person, though that person, stubbornly wicked, abuses the grace expended upon him.

He found Judas guilty of avarice and condemned by crime, yet stretched out to embrace him with the broad bosom of clemency. But that wretched shipwrecked man seized neither the offered ship nor plank; rather, rushing headlong into the deep, he finally, in evil repentance, hanged himself. If it is commendable, then, to offer a benefit to one who despises it, much more does it accord with reason to confer it more abundantly upon one who seeks it; and not to inflict something like his preceding ungrateful deserts, but freely to render him a welcome recompense. This, the father of the household is said in the Gospel both to have done and commended. When a debtor of ten thousand talents was brought before him and asked that he might mercifully deem fit to defer their payment, he is recorded not merely to have deferred it in accordance with the humble request, but to have forgiven, beyond the debtor’s hope, the whole debt [Col. 1069C].

The ten thousand talents are the countless sins by which a wandering human being provokes his Creator and makes himself in many ways indebted to him. He is always so needy and poor that he cannot pay such a debt to the last farthing; indeed, as guilty, he is sold, unless the creditor releases him from every debt. Yet such goodness is found in this creditor, and frail man experiences such mercy in him, that, if he humbly bends himself in supplication with a bowed heart, he is released from the most tenacious bond of that ungrateful debt. But God either does not grant this release to a human being, or does not continue it once granted, if that same person does not also conform himself to the benevolent God: namely, just as God freely releases his servant from debt, so that servant must not refuse to release his fellow servant.

For this purpose God not only does not repay in kind the ungrateful deserts of human beings, but shows himself generous and benevolent by the goodness that is his own: that human beings may learn and love to show one another what they know they have obtained from him; and, conformed to him by this likeness, may cling in likeness to the Like One, whom it is certain that no one can please more perfectly except by merit of likeness. If a human being does not diligently apply himself to this pattern and reform his deformity; if, in the mirror set before him, he does not make himself conformable according to his measure; if he does not freely pour out upon his neighbor what he receives freely from the Lord [Col. 1070A]; if, like a wicked man, he does not multiply but hides the talent of divine benevolence—then God, who is good by nature, will seem to turn cruel and rage harshly against one whom he finds unfaithful in what was entrusted to him.

This the Gospel reading showed figuratively, in which the aforesaid master released his servant from the debt of ten thousand talents, teaching not so much by word as by deed what ought to be repaid for the ungrateful deserts of one’s neighbors, and how mercy ought to be granted to them when they plead. When this servant had departed free from debt, a fellow servant who owed him money met him as he was leaving. Forgetful of the remission he had received, he began to rage violently against him and harshly press him by words to pay the debt. “Pay,” he said, “what you owe.” [Col. 1070B] And the other said: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything” (Matt. 18). I willingly wish, he says, to pay the debt to the man demanding it, but I presently lack the means to pay; therefore I ask you patiently to defer your demand a little longer, and I will carefully restore to you all that I owe.

But he would in no way yield to the petitioner. Instead, blazing more fiercely with anger and rage, he seized and choked his fellow servant, pressed him cruelly, and, throwing him into prison, exacted the debt with grave injury. When the fellow servants saw this, displeased by such cruelty, they reported to their lord how mercilessly servant was pressing fellow servant. The lord at once ordered that same servant brought before him; when he had been brought in, he began to be strongly indignant. “Wicked servant,” he said, “I forgave you all the debt because you asked me; ought you not therefore also to have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” (ibid.).

You, he says, were bound to me by a great and unpayable debt. Driven by want, despairing, and having no escape, you appealed solely to your prayers; I forgave all this debt and set you free by a free remission. In this I had prescribed for you a pattern of mercy and of responding with welcome gentleness to your debtors: that you should not hold them bound by debt, but should yield to their need and show yourself merciful. But because you despised my teaching with a stiff neck and poured out upon your fellow servant no benevolence from what you had drawn from me, whatever was mercifully forgiven you [Col. 1070D] will be demanded again by exacting justice, and the whole debt will be exacted from the first farthing to the last. “And the Gospel says, in anger his lord delivered him to the torturers, until he should pay the whole debt” (ibid.).

As he had done, so it was done to him. Since he had not acted mercifully toward his pleading fellow servant, but had harshly and violently exacted the debt from him, the wretched man is caught in his own judgment and his own snares; and, at the Lord’s command, his own iniquity is brought back upon his head. This lord is almighty God, who, when we have fallen repeatedly into sins, freely grants pardon to us who deserve punishment, dismisses us free when the debt has been forgiven, adds grace, and promises glory.

Seeing and admiring this, David says: “What shall I repay to the Lord for all that he has repaid to me?” [Col. 1071A] (Ps. 115). Though punishment is due by a just reckoning for my offenses, divine goodness, forgetting my deserts, has mercy on me; for my evils it mercifully returns its own goods; to me, ill-deserving, it bestows gifts of its grace. What, then, shall I repay him who repays such great things for such things? By what labor, by what desire, shall I stretch myself out to answer him, when I realize that I am in no way sufficient to accomplish this, even if I spend myself for him in death? Yet because I have nothing greater or better than myself, I voluntarily give myself to drink the cup of his Passion; and because I cannot do even this except by his gift, I shall perform it through him by invoking his name. “I will take,” he says, “the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord” [Col. 1071B] (ibid.).

When we are unwilling not only to make such a return to this Lord, but even to show welcome benevolence, at his grace, to a fellow servant who pleads, that same Lord in anger orders whatever he had forgiven us to be paid; he does not order us, delivered to the torturers, to be released until we have paid everything. But who could pay the debts of ten thousand talents? Indeed, who could make satisfaction for the guilt of innumerable offenses? Who could endure it if every sin he had committed were charged to him, if, mercy removed, penalties corresponding to the measure or number of his faults were calculated?

I think that no one can be found who sets foot within the joy of his Lord unless that same Lord first forgives his debt, since that inward joy is promised only to the good servant, and no one becomes good unless he is released from the bond of guilt. Therefore, when Christ invited his disciples to pray, he also taught them how they ought to pray, so that absolutely no person may hope to obtain salvation who judges himself not to need this prayer. “Thus,” he says, “you shall pray: Our Father who art in heaven, forgive us our debts” [Col. 1071C] (Matt. 6). For none of us is able either to be born so righteous or, once born, to live so righteously in this life that his mortality is not entangled in the stains of debts. No one, I say, born of a woman can say, “I am clean from sins,” since the Scripture of truth does not even declare an infant of one day clean. Rightly, therefore, everyone asks that his own debts now be forgiven him, lest on their account the Lord later command him to be cast into prison.

This petition is heard by the same Lord, and the petitioner is released from the guilt of debt in accordance with his desire, when he himself is not held by the sickness of avarice toward his neighbor and has generous benevolence toward his own debtor. Therefore, after Christ had said, “Forgive us our debts,” he added: “As we forgive our debtors” (ibid.), plainly teaching that God will repay us, who are debtors, according to the measure in which we grant remission to our debtors. Therefore Christ wished his disciples not to be silent in making this repayment, by which each person shows himself kinder toward the ungrateful, repaying the offenses of neighbors with more generous benevolence [Col. 1072A]; for he so carefully wished to teach them this kind of prayer. And just as he judges commendable those whom manly courage encourages to repay kindness to the ungrateful—a goal to which the malicious multitude of the perverse does not aspire—so by his just judgment those deserve rebuke who, conversely, do not deserve to repay unkindness for kindness.

This repayment, as it is said to be last in the order of the others, must likewise be called far worse than all the rest. For I think that nothing more unjust or more detestable can be said than that perverse people are found to be enemies even to those who love them. Of such people the Prophet says: “They have set evils against me for goods, and hatred in return for my love” [Col. 1072B] (Ps. 108). David bestowed good things upon his people, good things upon those subject to him, and loved their advancement with sincere affection, knowing and teaching that “he who has no care for his own, and especially for those of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5). Yet they did not render due return to this benevolent man; they did not show him deference for his sovereignty or for his beneficence; they did not return good things, greater or equal, for good things; but with astonishing perversity wickedly inflicted evils upon one who had deserved well of them.

You know how many curses Shimei the son of Gera, a Benjaminite, hurled against him when David fled the city, his home, and seat of kingship, abandoned through fear—showing himself greatly delighted by David’s flight, and not fearing to hurl stones and insults at him. “Shimei son of Gera came out,” it says, “and cursed, and cast stones at David. Thus he spoke: ‘Go out, go out, man of blood and man of Belial; behold, your evils press upon you, because you are a man of blood’” [Col. 1072C] (2 Kings 16). When Abishai, son of Zeruiah, moved by anger, wished to rush upon him and exact fitting vengeance from the cursing dog, patient David recalled his sword to its sheath and moderated his inflamed rage in view of the greater injury. “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah?” he said. “Behold, my son, who came forth from my womb, seeks my life; how much more now this son of Benjamin?” (ibid.).

Why do you wonder, he says, that the son of Gera dares to assail me with insults, when my own son takes up arms against his father, when he rages against me freely with fury and hatred—he whom a certain natural affection is accustomed to make gentle even among wild beasts? For what beast, although lacking human and rational understanding, inflicts bites or the wound of a sting upon its parents? Does it not rather become tame through a certain natural affection and, laying aside its wildness, recognize the source of its own flesh? But the man whom David begot, whom his father had advanced to full manhood by paternal care, forgetful of his birth and oblivious of his begetting, oppresses within himself the force of nature by a kind of stony hardness. What could be found harder, or more contrary to nature, than that a son seems softened by no affection toward his parent, but, blinded by malice, should so seek that kingdom’s throne as joyfully to open his jaws for his father’s blood and destruction?

Great cruelty! The son hates, persecutes, and attacks his father, and with astonishing shamelessness makes his hatred manifest to all when, at Ahithophel’s counsel, he orders curtains spread upon the roof and does not shrink before all Israel from entering his father’s concubines. Perhaps recalling and abhorring this or something like it, the prophet Micah says: “The son dishonors the father, and a man’s enemies are those of his own household” [Col. 1073A] (Mic. 7). For when God said through Moses: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father or the nakedness of your mother; she is your mother, you shall not uncover her nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife, for it is your father’s nakedness” (Lev. 18)—when, I say, he is declared to have said these things in order that reverence might be rendered to parents—the son is said to inflict no slight dishonor upon his father when, insolent and shameless, he presumes to touch his father’s bed and by unlawful touching violates not only the written law but also the natural law. For parental reverence wishes to possess a kind of sanctuary, from which both nature and Scripture seem to restrain children, lest anyone wantonly descend either to defile his father’s bed or return to know his mother, the source of his own origin.

## Chapter LXIV

Even barbarian nations knew this decree of the law. Though they wandered freely and through countless shameful passions, they nevertheless bound themselves more tightly with this bond and judged its transgressors detestable and abominable. Thus the histories of nations detest that criminal man, and their readers attest his accursed crime: having long before been carnally born from the same mother, he was later, unknowingly, joined to her in an abominable marriage. When, in misery, he had successively begotten miserable children by her and at last learned of the long-unknown pitiable crime, he so grieved and so abhorred having confounded the order of nature that, in his mother’s—or wife’s—very lap, he is said to have dug out his own eyes with his hand [Col. 1073C].

As he turned all these things over, full of anger and frenzy, and though repentant, yet not taking hold of the path of a better life, just as Judas Iscariot, repentant of his deed, turned aside to the noose, so he turned to Ctesiphon, chief of the Furies, begging and imploring her not to end such great malice in himself, but, transferring it to his children, to bind them under their father’s condemnations:

> Grant, Ctesiphon, and favor my perverse prayers,  
> if I have deserved this well; if, falling from my mother,  
> you cherished me in your lap; if, rejoicing, I entered upon  
> my mother’s lamentable marriage, and often endured  
> that abominable night, and prepared children for you  
> —you yourself know it. Come hither, and devise for punishment  
> all my descendants. Go among the brothers; let the bonds  
> of kindred be sundered by the sword . . . .  
> nor will the minds of the young men be slow to follow.  
> Only come worthily: you shall recognize my pledges.

A strange—indeed dreadful—prayer of a madman! The father wishes that the evils he has perpetrated should not be erased by any washing of expiation, but that his sons should be bound as though by some original bond; that the vices of the corrupted root should spread into branches and leaves; and that his wretched sons should be confounded by the crime of their father’s desert [Col. 1074A].

A similar malice seems also to have held the Jews, who are read to have pressed for Christ’s death not so much with hand as with tongue. Not only were they not turned from their undertaking by any repentance, but, beginning a web for themselves, they wove it for their own children. “His blood,” they say, “be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). Just as good parents, with inclined affection, assign paternal inheritance to their children, earnestly desiring it to remain with them as though forever, so all who are wicked and malicious do not wish their malice to end quickly, but wish it to pass by hereditary possession to their children and their children’s children.

Therefore Oedipus, whom the heavy burden of his crime oppresses and grieves, heaping evil upon evil, prays to Ctesiphon that she may come to his aid, that what is undoubtedly hers to do even unasked, she may do when asked—indeed, may accomplish thoroughly. That infernal Fury did not reject his impious prayers; instead, in accordance with his wish, she infected the young men with anger and hatred such that they disturbed not only Thebes but all Greece with war and at last breathed out the spirit of life by each other’s sword [Col. 1074B]. When their father, still alive, learned that they had fallen by mutual wounds, and that what in madness and turmoil he had wickedly requested had come to pass, he was lifeless with grief: worn out with old age, bereft of sight, scarcely supporting his trembling limbs on a staff, he had himself led, with his daughter going before, to their funerals; and, weeping over and kissing the bodies he found, he threw himself upon them.

“Alas,” he says, “what divine power, what fortune has from the beginning proved so grievously hostile to me, [Col. 1074C] that the entire course of my life is held accursed, beginning in evil and ending in a worse conclusion? Thus, brought forth in misery from the darkness of my mother’s womb, and then returned to that same mother in a carnal marriage, pursuing an ill-starred succession of almost every crime, I have surely incurred the implacable wrath of the heavenly gods. And because in their sight I have been guilty beyond measure and number, at my disastrous marriage no Juno stood as bridal attendant, no joyful Hymenaeus was present; divine law fled and recoiled from our marriage-bed; and when you were born, Erynis stood by, not Lucina.

“But when at last the order of events became known to miserable me, the light of day became hateful to me; and, to exact punishment from myself, I voluntarily turned my own hands against myself [Col. 1074D] and blinded myself; shut within a cage, I banished the joys of this whole life. To complete my evil, because you despised your father’s grey hairs left bereft, and did not guide his feeble old age with kindly affection, I—confused by madness—cursed you, whom I had begotten from whatever kind of bed, and by invoking upon you your father’s crimes consigned you to a wretched inheritance. What god—or rather what infernal Fury—heard me, accursed as I was, in this way, and too favorably heard my wicked prayers, so that, in accordance with my evil wish, my offspring should at last lie thus, slain by one another and held fast in one another’s mutual embrace?

“Whose breast, though made of stone, would not be softened by the hammer-blow of such a fate? Whose wrath or hatred would not grow cold when Boreas breathes thus? Whose cruel spirit would not at last be shaken by the impulse of pity, when Lachesis allots you such a life and [Col. 1075A] Atropos such a death? Whom shall I first, whom later, embrace with trembling arms? Which of you, most miserable as I am, shall I kiss more tenderly? Though I hold you, I am not allowed to see you; and, though I cannot see you, is it granted me—what is more grievous—to hold you thus? Who will grant me,” he says, “that for your sake I might again tear out my eyes—or rather, that I might quickly die, piercing my aged breast with a sword? The gods above rightly abhor my present life sufficiently; perhaps the gods below will abhor even my shade. Whither then shall I go? Whither flee? Where will the burden of my evils not weigh me down, where will the shame of my wicked deeds not cover the face of my heart, where will the harassing memory of my sons not torment me—the ill-starred birth of those who arose, the grievous destruction of those now dead? Alas! How hostile to heaven, earth, and perhaps also [Col. 1075B] hell was that birth: a birth which none preceded and none like it will follow, which has transgressed every law and right through the horror of its crimes—618—whose wicked beginning, you may take it, is destined to end in ruin.”

When the complaining old man had uttered these or similar words, and wished to inflict death upon himself in order to complete the punishment of his evils, his daughter, who had been his guide on the way, restrained his headlong hand; taking away his sword, she prevented him from accomplishing his purpose. If the school of the Gentiles abhors such a man—indeed, if he himself judges death more worthy of him than life—who, though unwittingly, desired what his father had done to him unlawfully, what more hidden nature wills to be inaccessible to sons, how must a man be held accursed among the people of God, though instructed in the Law and [Col. 1075C] Scripture, whom neither Law nor nature restrains? How can Absalom be proclaimed worthy of pardon, who does not fear to uncover his father’s shame; who not only does not fear to molest his father as a son ought not, but even aims to dishonor him by crafty counsel?

But if anyone should say that he of whom I have spoken beforehand for the sake of this matter deserved far more grievous wrath and judgment—he who is said not only to have dishonored his father’s bed but also to have taken that father’s life—then Absalom does not seem less blameworthy in this respect, since parricide may also be detected in him. Oedipus, indeed, while seeking his father, is said to have killed his father without recognizing him; once conscious of the deed, however, he afterward [Col. 1075D] grieved not moderately. And because he knew that both his father’s death and his father’s dishonor were forbidden to him by the laws of nature, impatient of grief he prepared both hands and eyes for punishment. His avenging hands inflicted blindness on his eyes; his eyes endured the violence of that blindness. Thus, because he had sinned against his father through an eye deceived—by deed, not intention—he first voluntarily exacted a sufficiently just punishment from his sight. At last, when such vengeance seemed insufficient to him and his grievous conscience was oppressed by overpowering grief, dread Ctesiphon would have driven him to inflict death upon himself, had not the maiden Antigone, present as has been said, taken away the sword.

Absalom, by contrast, knowingly presumed both to violate his father’s bed and to kill that same father with the sword [Col. 1076A] of his perverse will. And although his conscience did not rejoice in the result he desired, his parricidal malice nevertheless remained in his purpose without repentance. Which of the two, then, seems to you to have sinned more grievously? Which sought parricide more shamelessly? He who, lacking written law, is said unknowingly to have fallen upon his father, and who, once conscious of the deed, repented and grieved deeply? Or rather he who, taught in the Scriptures, maliciously attacked his father, and of whom no repentance is recorded as having escaped from the entanglement of this plague?

Great is the difference; great the perversity! The son hates—and obstinately hates—a father who loves him; he drives away one who is well-disposed and pursues one fleeing him; he arms everyone, prepares war, exhorts the assembled army to it, and already rejoices in the utterly vain hope of his father’s downfall. If earlier he suddenly drew the sword against the neck of his brother Amnon [Col. 1076B], if by treachery he killed one caught off guard while sparing his other brothers at the feast, perhaps this could in some degree be excused: namely, because the unlawful violation of his sister deserved vengeance. Thus, when Absalom was believed to have killed all the king’s sons, and the king, hearing this report, was distressed with inconsolable grief, Jonadab, son of Shimeah—of degenerate and long-remembered lewdness—undertook to soothe the king’s grief by reporting the truth:

“Let not my lord the king suppose,” he says, “that all the king’s sons have been killed. Amnon alone is dead, because Absalom had set himself against him from the day when he violated Tamar his sister” (2 Kings [II Reg.] 13).

Let the king not suppose that Absalom laid hands upon all [Col. 1076C] his sons, or committed such a dreadful crime against innocent brothers; rather, let him hold it certain that, while the rest survive, he alone especially fell—the man who unlawfully lay with Absalom’s sister.

This same man now, with greater madness, prepares war against his father; he gathers supporters from every side and, by warnings as well as gifts, makes them readier for the crime he intends. His purpose is that the man whom he sees prudently escaping his deceits and snares by the protection of flight may, when enclosed by the net of war, be violently crushed. But the father lovingly embraces the son who hates him, fears for him, and is tortured by astonishing concern for him. Lest perhaps he see that son’s ruin, he does not enter the battle, but gives commands and intercedes earnestly on his behalf: “Preserve the boy Absalom” [Col. 1076D] (2 Kings [II Reg.] 18).

“Preserve,” he says, “the one who, deprived of manly reason and counsel, has wickedly clothed himself in childish and foolish understanding; the one who stirs up the anger of an ignorant multitude against a loving father. You who understand better, keep him safe. Although he repays my good with evil, I nevertheless do not wish your sword to render to him what is his due; for my prudent strength loves, in quietness and peace of spirit, the one whom childish and foolish dullness drives to hatred.”

Perhaps this is what is figuratively signified in the interpretations of their names: David is proclaimed “strong in hand,” and Absalom “the father’s peace,” so that the very interpretation of the names may in some manner serve that mercy by which a good father has compassion upon a wicked son. For *abba* means “father,” while *salem* means “peace”; hence he is called Abbessalon, “the father’s peace.” With one syllable removed from the middle, this is contracted, and he is called no longer Abessalon but Absalon by syncope. Absalom, therefore, means “the father’s peace”—not because he had peace toward his father, but [Col. 1077A] because the father had peace toward his son. Though sustained by a strong hand, this childlike folly did not bend him to hatred; rather, pitying and embracing the madman, he did not love only his madness. “Preserve the boy Absalom”; and below: “Who will grant me that I might die for you, Absalom, my son, my son, Absalom?” (ibid.).

And what wonder if David is found patient and kindly toward his son [Col. 1077B], when Saul himself also experienced David’s strong goodwill? David bestowed nothing on Saul except many and great benefits, while Saul returned nothing to his benefactor except many and grievous evils. Of him Jonathan says: “Let not the king sin against your servant David, because he has not sinned against you, and his works are very good toward you” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 19). And Ahimelech says: “Who among all your servants is so faithful as David, the king’s son-in-law, obedient to your command, and glorious in your house?” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 22).

Although David remained faithful and good in the king’s house, and both Jonathan and Ahimelech bore worthy witness concerning him before the king, Saul did not embrace him worthily for this faithfulness. On the contrary, he hated one who loved him and pursued his friend as though he were an enemy. “Saul sought him all his days, and God did not deliver him into [Col. 1077C] his hands” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 23). And below: “Saul, taking three thousand chosen men from all Israel, went to seek David.” When David was hiding with his companions in a cave, and Saul went aside into that same cave without a companion to relieve himself, David, at his companions’ prompting, could have repaid his persecutor in kind. But he merely cut off the hem of his cloak, preferring to spare one who did not deserve it. “May the Lord be merciful to me,” he says, “that I should do this thing to my lord, the Lord’s anointed, that I should put forth my hand against him” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 24).

In this deed a certain honorable pride is displayed in David: it disdains to conquer an enemy except honorably, and clearly shows that a victory is to be shunned when it dishonors the victor with a mark of baseness.

[Col. 1077D] There is indeed also a humility which divine Scripture fittingly rebukes: namely, when the soul does not consider where or how it falls, when it burns with so great a heat of seductive pleasure that it has scarcely any regard or concern for honor. Hence Isaiah says to such a soul: “You received an adulterer, enlarged your bed, and humbled yourself even to hell” (Isa. 57). The soul which the Word of the Lord had joined to himself by the grace of bestowed holiness—if it should turn away from the marriage of fruitful chastity, enlarge its bed in order to embrace more freely the adulterer introduced within, and be defiled by the uncleanness of the corrupting demon through the unrestrained expansiveness of the mind—then indeed, having fallen from among the heavenly beings through the fault of its own negligence, it humbles itself to hell by its own will.

For as long as it clung to God, it moved among the angels and enjoyed the lofty throne of incomparable glory. But when it enlarged the chamber of its inward conscience to receive an adulterer, it surely bent the summit of its dignity down to things excessively low. Great indeed was the height of its former integrity; by contrast, lowly and abject is the shame of the abyss of lust. In that former state its bright beauty merited heaven; now the bright appearance of earthly things holds it cast down and lowly. Of this the Lord says through Amos: “The virgin Israel has been cast down to the earth” (Amos 5). And through Ezekiel, to Jerusalem: “You were cast upon the face of the earth in the abjection of your soul” (Ezek. 16).

[Col. 1078A] When a person to whom God gave an uplifted face nevertheless does not look toward the heights of heaven, but with gaze bent downward casts himself [Col. 1078B] upon the face of the earth, his soul, already infected by the contagion of earthly things, becomes vile and abject in the sight of the supreme Judge. And, because it does not retain its former dignity, being abject gives unclean spirits the opportunity to pass through it. They seem vigilant and intent upon nothing else than to bend that wretched soul so that they may pass through it. Of them Isaiah says: “They say to our soul: ‘Bend down, that we may pass through’” (Isa. 51). For when the soul bends toward the love of carnal pleasures, the malice of unclean spirits gains strength to pass through it. When this passage is frequently repeated to its hurt, that soul, lying low and abject, is trampled in its own blood; concerning it Ezekiel says: “I saw you trampled in your blood” (Ezek. 16). And Micah says: “Now she shall be trodden down like the mud of the streets” (Mic. 7). And David says: “If I have repaid evil to those who repaid me, let the enemy pursue my soul, overtake it, and trample my life to the ground” (Ps. 7).

The more a soul is trampled, the more surely it grows sick; and as the sickness gains strength, it grows soft in womanish fashion. Not only does it become foul through its enervating softness, but through prolonged use it also rots in its own filth. Micah says of it: “Because of its uncleanness, it shall be corrupted with the worst rottenness” (Mic. 2). And Joel: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1). And a certain penitent says: “My scars have rotted and become corrupt” (Ps. [Col. 1078D] 73).

Yet sometimes divine mercy visits the sickness of one lying thus, and with a healing hand wipes away the scab of one who is rotting. It gives strength, through infused grace, to one exhausted in weakness; and, pitying her, raises to salvation that bent woman of the Gospel: “Raising the needy from the earth, and lifting up the poor from the dung” (Ps. 112). And in the Gospel: “Woman, you are released from your infirmity”; and immediately she stood upright and glorified God (Luke 13). When he has raised her, he bestows upon her the gifts of new holiness; multiplying gifts upon gifts, he sets her, as it were, on a lofty throne of dignity, so that she may recoil from low things and disdain to bend shamefully toward them; longing for higher things, she may love to remain in them; she may no longer endure to be burdened with what is abject and vile, but may ardently seek to be honored by what is more eminent and splendid.

## Chapter LXV

[Col. 1079A]

When a soul is found not merely to pass by the seductive allurements of vices as contemptible out of regard for religion, but also to disdain every shameful thing for honor’s sake, what does it seem to do but take pride in a certain noble and free excellence of mind, inasmuch as it refuses to soothe its mind with things unworthy? Such great care for religion, first and chief, possesses it that whatever it knows will certainly harm either life or reputation, it abhors and flees as though it were the burden of harshest and heaviest poverty. It desires to be enriched only by the proud riches of most honorable holiness. This is beautifully promised it through Isaiah: “I will make you the pride of ages, unto generation and generation” (Isa. 60).

[Col. 1079B] The soul which God ordains to transfer into the fellowship of angels is rightly said to be established in the pride of ages, since he both grants it, in the present, great and outstanding riches of merits, and in the future far greater and more excellent rewards. And lest, conscious of its own weakness, it should be too greatly afraid and grow faint in hoping for and loving the promised height, God wills it to be strengthened by the example and teaching of those who have gone before, so that with their aid it may be fortified for every arduous undertaking. “You shall suck the milk of the nations,” he says, “and shall be nursed at the breast of kings” (ibid.).

That is: those who have been converted from the darkness of the nations to the Israelite light, who have left the wide way of the world and entered upon the path of a narrower life, who have first been instructed and trained in the gymnasium of discipline, will diligently pour into you the milk of teaching. “You shall be nursed at the breast of kings” [Col. 1079C]. Why is the breast of kings promised to this soul rather than that of servants, unless because those oppressed by the degrading slavery of vices are not yet fit or useful to teach, and silence must deservedly be imposed on them because of their weakness? Therefore, servants being silent, those are admitted to the office of teaching who are guided on the straight path to obtain righteousness; who are manfully equipped to govern their own conduct and are laudably trained to teach others. The Psalm admonishes them: “Understand, O kings; be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Ps. 2). And another Wise Man says: “Love righteousness, you who judge the earth” (Wis. 1).

[Col. 1079D] Those, therefore, who strive to be distinguished by fitting learning and devote earnest care to acquiring wisdom are rightly admitted, as has been said, to the office of teaching; and teachers for the soul’s instruction are promised by the Lord. Blessed is the soul that is not nursed at the unworthy breast of servants; that is not harassed by the wicked conduct of teachers; that is not led astray into wandering error by the perverse preaching of its elders, nor brought to anger and scandal by their corrupt way of life. Blessed is the soul to which such grace is proclaimed, that it is nourished only by the care and attentiveness of kings; grown to maturity and strengthened by the royal riches of such noble persons, and by more fully imitating them itself established in the pride of ages.

Does not that soul seem to you to have been placed in this pride, which, considering how high it is raised by the summit of virtues, is not held within the hiding places of silence by miserly ingratitude, but bursts forth into joy, so that through Solomon it may gloriously boast: “With me are riches and glory, proud wealth and righteousness” [Col. 1080A] (Prov. 3). In calling these riches and glory, or the pride of wealth, it is certainly not indicated that anything blameworthy exists in it. For even though it joins glory to riches and pride to wealth, righteousness, its companion, does not at the same time admit vice. Rightly, therefore, such glory and pride are judged praiseworthy when righteousness—which knows no vice—accompanies them. That righteousness makes their fruits better than gold, precious stone, or silver, as is clearly intimated by the following teaching of the same Wisdom: “My fruit is better than gold and precious stone, and my offspring than choice silver” (Prov. 8).

[Col. 1080B] Why these fruits and offspring are commended, and why nothing visibly commendable is rightly compared with them, is shown more clearly in the following verse, so that no doubt on this point may remain for the reader: “I walk in the ways of righteousness, in the midst of the paths of judgment” (ibid.). Wisdom is seen to walk when it acts; it is found to judge more strictly when subtle rectitude guides its narrow paths and strength leads it to the rectitude desired. And lest it seem to labor in all these things for itself alone, gathering the aforementioned riches to itself in greedy zeal without concern for others, it next wished to show us what it intends when it commends itself with such riches and such praise: “That I may enrich those who love me and fill their treasuries” (ibid.).

“For this purpose,” it says, “I wished to commend my proud riches, and for this purpose to proclaim to you my righteousness and my judgment: that you who hear these things may rightly love me; that by loving me you may be enriched with the same magnificence of wealth; and that your treasuries may be filled by my generosity—treasuries which, once filled, need not fear thieves and are not damaged by rust or moth.” Wisdom therefore wills that those who are to attain its lofty pride should be mature in discernment, judgment, and righteousness. For one reaches righteousness only after judgment has gone before; and entrance to its height is opened only by righteousness. Indicating this through another wise man, it says: “Do nothing weighty without judgment” [Col. 1080D] (Ecclus. 33). By “weighty” it means not something unbearable or harsh, but something just and mature, in which each person must exercise himself manfully if he wishes to be numbered among those who offer worthy praises to God. Hence David also says: “I will praise you among a weighty people” (Ps. 34).

A weighty person is one not carried away like a leaf by the wind of instability, not separated from a just purpose by fickleness of conduct; rather, seeking just things justly, he remains fixed and immovable in them. No amount of strength or effort can attain to this weightiness—understood not as hateful heaviness but as maturity, which allows no power to vices or place to instability—unless judgment first precedes everything that must be done. Paul indicates this when he says to Timothy: “Doing nothing without previous judgment” (1 Tim. 5). [Col. 1081A] Whatever a discerning person determines must be done, he first prudently tests by subtle judgment, so that, after the height of a discerning examiner’s judgment has gone before, the breadth of the work that follows may be mature and secure.

Thus Wisdom rightly called them both ways of righteousness and paths of judgment, distinctly assigning to each what belongs to it: in judgment there must be a certain narrow and rare subtlety, while in the ensuing work there is broad security. Therefore, after saying, “I walk in the ways of righteousness,” it significantly adds, “in the midst of the paths of judgment” (Prov. 8), so that one who hopes to attain the secure breadth of deeds may know that he must pass through the middle paths of examining judgment. For this reason the Psalm says: “He will guide the meek in judgment; he will teach the gentle his ways” (Ps. 34), [Col. 1081B] clearly showing that God does not lead persons into the perfect breadth of his works unless he first brings them into the narrow rectitude of judgment. In bringing and teaching them in this way, he certainly makes them meek; and he wills to make only the meek discerning for this purpose. Wisdom therefore rightly proclaimed its proud riches and glory, and rightly commended the paths of judgment and ways of righteousness, so that it might invite those who love it and enrich them with the grace of merits, and, as said above, establish those who have merited well in the pride of ages.

## Chapter LXVI

David, while a fugitive, seemed rich in these possessions and established upon the eminent throne of such pride when an opportunity of place and time was offered him for easy vengeance upon his enemy, yet he honorably disdained to stoop to touch him [Col. 1081C].

For, I think, he saw that he bore the type of a more righteous soul, which by the merit of righteousness obtains the seat of a worthier throne. Although many urge it to turn aside toward the contemptible things of a baser life, it considers it unworthy to bend the neck of its stronger purpose. Indeed, David means “strong in hand.” Those who urge him to lay hands upon Saul, not to allow his persecutor to depart freely as it were, prefigure all wicked or malicious spirits. Accompanying the righteous soul, they repeatedly whisper that it should now, as though at an opportune time, turn from the path of holiness; that it should loose the bridle of righteousness and bend itself toward the unclean works of the world.

Saul means “asked for,” and [Col. 1081D] bears the figure of the world, which is chosen for themselves by those who despise the duty of religion—those who, with utmost zeal, love pleasures more than God. With Saul rejected, they said: “Give us a king to judge us” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 8). And in the Gospel, rejecting Christ: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19); and again: “Not this man, but Barabbas” (ibid.). This world, therefore—violently desired by very many, for according to Solomon the number of fools is infinite—this world, I say, is like a sepulchre full of the bones of the dead, which does not cover up this carrion but brings it forth to the notice of others through an open throat: “Their throat is an open sepulchre” (Pss. 5, 13).

[Col. 1082A] Whoever is defiled by wicked works as by the bones of the dead, and rejoices to infect those who approach with their wretched stench, is not properly called *mundus* (“clean”) but is so called by antiphrasis—that is, either from the uncleanness in which it is foul, or rather from the cleanliness of which it is deprived. Whoever touches that which is “clean” in name alone but in truth unclean becomes not clean but unclean through the attraction of its uncleanness. Moses says concerning this: “Whoever touches anything unclean, whose touch is defiling, shall be unclean” (Lev. 22). And much earlier: “Whoever touches the uncleanness of a person or of anything which can defile shall perish from among his people” (Lev. 7). Therefore the Lord says later through the same Moses: “You shall teach the children of Israel to beware of uncleanness, lest they die in their filth” (Lev. 25).

[Col. 1082B] When Saul, turning from the way and wandering from the straighter path, brings forth into the light of action the filth of his thoughts and its miserable stench, David rightly disdains to lay hands upon him, lest he too be defiled by the base touch of turning aside. Although freedom to sin is granted for the present, and a seemingly opportune time or opening is offered, the righteous person ought not consent to the prompting of those who urge him, nor should the wickedness suggested reach the effect of action.

David’s servants said to him: “Behold the day of which the Lord spoke: ‘I will deliver your enemy into your hands, that you may do to him as pleases your eyes.’” David said to his men: “Unless the Lord strike him, or his day come that he die, or he go down into battle and perish, [Col. 1082C] may God be merciful to me, that I should put forth my hand against the Lord’s anointed” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 24).

“Although,” he says, “no bar prevents me from sinning, and divine equity patiently awaits me while I do whatever I choose, nevertheless I shall not desire what seems lawful to you, and my cleaner hand shall not cling to the filth of this world.” This world is not undeservedly called figuratively “the Lord’s anointed,” because it is ordered by God either for the destruction of the wicked or for the exercise of the good. For God, who makes peace and creates evil, forms light and creates darkness, is proclaimed in Isaiah’s prophecy, since he is not denied either to make or to dispose good and prosperous things, evil and harsh things.

## Chapter LXVII

A little later, when the same Saul pitched camp upon the hill of Hachilah [Col. 1082D], and was weighed down there in his own tent with his commanders by deepest sleep, David came upon him and could have fulfilled his will against him. But with the same spirit and similar noble pride he rejected the opportunity offered. For Abishai said: “God has shut up your enemy today into your hands; now therefore I will pierce him with the spear into the ground once, and there shall be no need for a second blow.” David answered: “Do not kill him; for who shall stretch forth his hand against the Lord’s anointed and be innocent?” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 26).

Saul sleeps when this world and any lover of the world grows weak under the weight of vices. He rests in filthy sickness with wretched security when he closes the eyes of his mind to the true light of righteousness and, in the manner of a deaf asp, does not hear the voice of those who wisely charm him. [Col. 1083A] Isaiah speaks of such people: “Sleeping and loving dreams” (Isa. 56); and Hosea: “He slept all night” (Hos. 7). If anyone wishes, as it were, to repay this persecutor in kind, if anyone lays hands upon him so as to give favor or consent to the sinner, what does he seem to do except kill him and block the way of truth? He drives headlong one already falling, and by pursuing and joining in wickedness makes that person’s fall precipitate. Hence Isaiah says: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps” (Isa. 3). And Solomon: “If sinners entice you, do not consent to them; for their feet run to evil and hasten to shed blood” (Prov. 10).

[Col. 1083B] David therefore does not wish, in the manner of a sinner, to shed the blood of one asleep; he does not cast his own sin upon another or another’s sin upon himself. Rather, leaving to divine judgment the life or death of one whom God himself wills to live even while he sins, he says: “Unless the Lord strike him, or his day come that he die, may the Lord be merciful to me, that I should not stretch forth my hand against the Lord’s anointed” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 26). Though the apparently favorable face of an opportune place and time flatters him, and the troublesome prompting of companions urgently presses him to sin, he, being stronger, does not turn from the straight path nor bow his rigid neck to their urgings.

[Col. 1083C] They say, in Isaiah’s words, “Bend down, that we may pass through” (Isa. 51): that is, once your uprightness is bent, let us who pass through trample your noble holiness; and let that excellence of proud virtues, which is seen raised high with face turned upward, not recoil from rolling in our filth after it has been cast down in abasement. But David—or rather any righteous person whose honorable strength is at hand, to whom shameful humility is loathsome and abject baseness contemptible—chooses to answer with the great and necessary saying of Joel, and desires in affection and deed to obtain what he answers: “Jerusalem shall be holy, and strangers shall no longer pass through her” (Joel 3).

Jerusalem means “vision of peace” and bears the figure of the soul. As long as the soul loves to serve God through contemplation of true peace, keeps its heart lifted to the Lord, and obeys his commandments and wills, such strength of holiness is found to surround it that strangers—that is, wicked spirits—cannot pass through it.

## Chapter LXVIII

[Col. 1083D] To this soul the prophet Nahum also says: “Belial shall no longer pass through you” (Nah. 1). The same Saul, repaying evil for good, does not cease to persecute the one who refuses to grant passage through himself to strangers or Belial and resolves to keep his hands clean and innocent from touching Saul. Sometimes he ceases, however, not from goodwill but rather from cunning. At times the crafty persecutor seems to repent of his purpose, and seeks to restrain his hand rather than his intention, so that, when the person he hates has been deceived by the appearance of peace and supposes himself no longer disliked, Saul may suddenly come upon him and overwhelm him more effectively while unprepared.

[Col. 1084A] “Saul lifted up his voice,” it says, “and said to David: ‘You are more righteous than I; for you have rendered me good, whereas I have rendered you evil. You have shown today how the Lord delivered me into your hand and you did not kill me’” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 24). And below: “I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I will no longer do you harm” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 26). Saul promises that he will henceforth do David no harm, so that, setting aside fear, David may remain secure in the future. But David is unwilling to place any confidence in Saul’s promises; he does not believe himself loved, though Saul seems to smile with a gentle face. For he knows—knows by experience—the ill will of his persecutor, his faithless character, and the instability of his promises. [Col. 1084B] In the world, the rays of the sun are repeatedly veiled by a cloud spread over them; and just as light follows darkness, so, in alternating order, darkness follows light.

David therefore suspects Saul even when Saul suspends his wicked purpose and, with an outwardly serene face, already promises good and prosperous things. Lest he fall by entering Saul’s deceits and snares, David prudently seeks the protection of flight: “One day I shall fall into Saul’s hands. Is it not better that I flee and be saved? I will therefore flee from his hands” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 27). The prudent man, instructed by the Spirit, rightly foresaw the Gospel counsel when he determined for his own welfare to flee his persecutor, knowing grave danger threatens the person who either touches evil or does not fear to endure its touch: “When they persecute you in one city, flee to another” [Col. 1084C] (Matt. 10). Likewise the prophet Jeremiah says: “Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each save his own soul” (Jer. 51).

David wisely recognizes that any soul is scarcely saved if it disdains to flee the deceits and assaults of the world. Since in it there is much frenzy but no order, and all things are confused, what hope has a soul if it is enclosed in its nets or snares? David therefore flees one who gives no trustworthiness to promises, who returns evil in exchange for deserved good—as Saul himself, stung as though by acknowledged guilt, is compelled by the pressure of truth openly to confess: “You have rendered me good; I have rendered you evil” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 24).

[Col. 1084D] Saul is infected by such poison and such burning criminality, and his understanding is pressed down and overwhelmed by such malice, that even though he knows David has been good and courageous toward him, and has remained innocent although provoked by injuries, he nevertheless does not love or embrace him. Instead, readily turning from a promised kindness to hatred, he acts under the pressure of malice. This malice not only prevents him from softening toward David, his servant, despite David’s deserved benefit; it also makes him rage violently against his son Jonathan because Jonathan proclaimed David’s commendable righteousness and exposed his father’s blameworthy malice. “Saul, angry with Jonathan, said to him: ‘Son of a woman who takes men by force, do I not know that you love the son of Jesse?’” (1 Kings [I Reg.] 20). And shortly afterward: “Saul seized a spear to strike him” (ibid.).

## Chapter LXIX

[Col. 1085A]

Some within the Church may be found like this: when they see themselves distinguished by the eminence of office, they rage with such envy against their inferiors and subjects that they seem not fathers and rulers, but rather enemies. Forgetting how they ought to provide for their necessities, how much care they ought to devote to their peace and quiet, with what affection they ought to show themselves gentle and lovable toward them, and with what zeal they ought to offer themselves to all, and in all things, as a model of life, they become, on the contrary, burdensome in life, troublesome in conduct, lovers of their own interests, wholly unconcerned for the common good. Since they observe both that others are subject and that they themselves rule over those others, they wish everything that pleases them to be lawful to themselves by the privilege of office. Thus, serving their own will with pleasing flattery, and bending what belongs to law and to order to their own pleasure, because they are endured by their subjects on account of their assumed mastery, they seem, as it were, to break down the barriers and rush headlong into unrestrained excesses. [Col. 1085B]

If any of their subjects perceive that such conduct is displeasing, refuse readily to assent to the wicked deeds of their superiors, do not approve vices for a man's sake nor hold a man dear for the sake of vices, but, from zeal for uprightness, abhor whatever departs from it, they at once judge such a subject insolent and senseless, because they see that he does not agree with their corrupt ways. In their eyes, he deserves stern rebuke for stubborn hardness—indeed, like an enemy, he deserves to be pursued with bitter hatred—if he does not soften into welcome compliance with a favorable hand toward his superiors, if he does not exalt their deeds, whatever they may be, [Col. 1085C] with flattering praises. He must be rebuked, they say, who has presumed even to murmur against his superior's actions and to pour out any reproach against whatever he does; since, as they say, it does not become a subject either to do anything but agree with his superior in all things with submissive goodwill, or to put his finger to his lips and fall cautiously and humbly silent.

Thus he does not complain of his superior's life with impunity who gladly obeys God's will rather than a human being's; nor does he come off creditably among men, nor prosperously in the superior's eyes, who does not, by favor or silence, join in consenting to corrupt conduct. For the higher any perverse persons stand in rank of office, the more heavily they threaten such a subject, commanding, like Rehoboam, a harsh rule in the present [Col. 1085D] and promising, with hardened heart, that it will be harsher still hereafter. Of such people the prophet Micah speaks well: “If anyone does not put something into their mouths, they consecrate war against him” (Mic. 3). Because their conscience is not made sound and rich by the nourishment of inward truth, their greedy mouth opens outwardly to seek vain things, ever gaping and panting for subjects to bring them whatever they please, and for the pleasing sweetness of flattery—not the hateful harshness of truth—to be offered them in abundance.

If anyone does not give their mouths the coveted gift, they judge such a desire alien to religion, if he chooses to obey the law rather than the king when he sees that law and king do not think alike: “they consecrate war against him.” That is, by the authority through which they know and recall [Col. 1086A] that they stand above others, they threaten and declare that severe troubles hang over him. They do not embrace in tender arms one burning 624 with zeal for justice; rather, they persecute with threats and insults the man whom they ought to have cherished. And if they see any who are not held by the same hatred against him, they do not delay to be fiercely angered against them.

“Will the son of Jesse,” he says, “give fields and vineyards to all of you, and make all of you tribunes and centurions, because all of you have conspired against me, and there is no one to report it to me, none of you to grieve for my plight?” (1 Sam. 22). “Is he,” he says, “to be favored, who has not received a rank or station equal to mine, who, so far inferior, does not bestow worthy gifts on you? Ought you not rather to exercise the same hatred against him with me, [Col. 1086B] so that you may deserve my greater gifts and obtain my favor?”

Accordingly, when the Ziphites reported to Saul that David was hiding among them on the hill of Hachilah, and declared that they would hand him over into Saul's hands, Saul gratefully received their perverse service and favor. As he had shown himself harsh to those mentioned above, so he was gentler to these flatterers: “Blessed are you by the Lord,” he says, “because you have grieved for my plight” (1 Sam. 23). Conversely, when he learned from Doeg the Edomite's report that Ahimelech the priest had consulted the Lord for David and had supplied him with the loaves of the Presence and the sword of Goliath the Philistine, he summoned Ahimelech himself and his entire father's house, and said to the attendants standing around him: “Turn and kill the priests of the Lord, for their hand is with David” (1 Sam. [Col. 1086C] 22).

You see the evil ruler raging against the servants of the Lord, in whom he can find no other ground deserving death except that they had not obeyed his perverse wishes or joined him in pursuing innocent David with bitter hatred. He was tortured by such venom of envy and such wickedness that, if any subject seemed to prefer truth to vanity, or refused to serve him with flattering approval, that person deserved in his eyes to become hateful as an enemy.

Therefore, he desires to harm not only innocent David, but also the others whom he sees unwilling to harm David. By a marvelous perversity, he becomes David's enemy, although David himself is Saul's friend. And because the evil ruler does not repay his friend [Col. 1086D] as he deserves, but even dares to oppress him and return evils for benefits, it is clear that he does not fear the severe judgment which God declares through the prophet to be imminent for such persons: “Woe,” says Jeremiah, “to him who oppresses his friend without cause and does not pay him his wages” (Jer. 22).

When everyone is commanded to love his enemy and to return favor for his hatred, that he may deserve to become like his Father who is in heaven, how great a woe does he deserve to incur who not only does not love an enemy, but, through prevailing wickedness, attacks a friend with grievous hatreds? Surely he ought not to devise anything wrongful against that friend, nor assail him, even secretly, with the darts of ill will; for even if someone happens to refrain from outward action, the divine judgment nonetheless condemns inward thoughts alone. Zachariah indicates this: “Let none of you think evil in his heart against his friend” (Zech. 5). [Col. 1087A] If an evil thought does not seem fitting toward a friend, how much more strictly is the completion of the deed forbidden, when someone endeavors by deliberation and effort to bring to completion that which was conceived within the conscience as the seedbed of wickedness? On this Solomon says: “Do not devise evil against your friend” (Prov. 3).

The aforesaid rulers oppose these and similar warnings of Scripture. They possess the appearance of piety and dwell among the sheepfolds of sheep, yet pursue with a lion's roar or a wolf's fury those who, steadfast in what is right, do not comply with the corrupt conduct of their superiors. They bite and tear those whom they see to be inferior to themselves in rank of dignity, but perhaps superior to themselves [Col. 1087B] in merit of holiness. Since they see a greater testimony of virtue borne to them by grace, they fear that they may be advanced to an equal rank or station of honor.

“Saul,” they say, “has struck down thousands, and David tens of thousands. Saul was exceedingly angry, and this saying displeased him. ‘What remains for him,’ he says, ‘but the kingdom alone?’ And from that day onward Saul did not look upon David with a favorable eye” (1 Sam. 18). Behold the tinder and seedbed of envy and hatred: that more honor is paid to the soldier than to the prince, to the servant than to the master; that, by the testimony of women playing tambourines, one serving under the king is preferred to the king; and that he who ought to have become favored because of his bravery is, through a reversal and perversion of the order of things, made hateful.

## CHAPTER LXX

[Col. 1087C] We read not only that this was fulfilled figuratively in David, son of Jesse, but know that the same was more fully displayed in Christ, made from David's seed. Because he stretched out his hands manfully to perform mighty deeds, he greatly displeased the scribes and Pharisees and the other rulers of the Jews. “The chief priests and Pharisees assembled a council,” it says, “and said, ‘What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him.’ From that day, therefore, they planned to kill him” (John 11).

The chief priests and Pharisees, whose special duty it was to serve God and to instruct others both by example and teaching in his commandments, ought with benevolent affection to have rejoiced in Christ's signs and merits; but, having lost their miserable judgment, they chose rather to envy. Since their perversity would neither venerate his signs nor listen to his admonitions, and since he would not soothe the ears of the teachers according to their pleasure 625 with soft compliance, their envy increased; they preferred to plunge themselves into the pit of murder rather than let him, who taught wonderful things and worked miracles, go free. [Col. 1087D] “If we let him go on thus,” they say, “all will believe in him” (John 11). And below: “You see,” they say, “that we are accomplishing nothing. Look: the whole world is going after him” (John 12).

Some of the people, wickedly instructed by their teaching and eagerly prepared in criminal inclination to imitate their teachers, observe that what differs from the chief priests in teaching is displeasing to them. They wish to crush him with stones and win human rather than divine favor. “The Jews took up stones,” it says, [Col. 1088A] “to stone him. And he said: ‘I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of these works do you stone me?’” (John 10.)

“Because I told you that the seductive enticements of vanity must be avoided and that, by sounder counsel, the narrower path of truth must be held; because I strengthened useful teaching by life and conduct, and healed your sick and raised the dead in order to bring you to faith: I ask you, for which of these works do I receive this benefit of your generosity, that you should overwhelm with stones one who has deserved so well, with such unanimous agreement? Do you judge me worthy of this reward of favor among you—that I, who wished to be so gracious to you above the other peoples of the nations, should receive such an answer for doing good to you, that, as a recompense, you should at last hasten to the stones?”

But they know that evils ought not to be repaid for good; yet, unwilling to restrain either heart or hand from their purpose, they endeavor to remove not the wickedness but the reproach of that purpose, and to twist Christ's uprightness in another direction. [Col. 1088B] “We do not stone you for a good work,” they say, “but for blasphemy, because you, though a man, make yourself God” (ibid.). All malicious people, while pursuing an innocent person with envy and hatred, labor and strive all the more either to impute to him the stain of an invented falsehood or to corrupt and condemn the uprightness of truth which they have heard.

Thus the worst of the Jews, seeing nothing blameworthy in Christ and envying his reputation and name with the infected venom of malicious corruption, do not stone him “for a good work,” as they say, lest they be proved to return ingratitude for kindness; rather, they stone him for blasphemy, so that they may appear to do it for justice's sake. They consider it blasphemous and in no way fitting that he, being a man, calls himself God and the Son of God, because his humanity can plainly be known and seen by everyone, whereas no one can behold his divinity except by faith.

Because the wicked returned evil for his good deeds, and finally inflicted nails, a cross, and an impious death upon him, Christ also foretold that his followers would receive the same and there endure similar things through the malice of the envious: “If they persecuted me,” he says, “they will persecute you also” (John 15). [Col. 1088C] For this reason that wise teacher and guide wished to forewarn them: that they might endure evils more stoutly when foreknown, and, when they felt the hatreds of the envious threatening them more tumultuously, might learn to answer not with hatred and like wickedness, but with silence and patience.

For he is the good David: strong of hand, full of the Spirit, humble of heart, mighty in speech, an instructor in present things, watchful concerning those to come. He saw that Saul, Doeg, the malicious accusations of the Ziphites, the scribes, chief priests, Pharisees, and finally the hateful Jews who stoned him would not be absent—those who would apply mind, tongue, and hand most eagerly to this final recompense of all others, hastening to return evils for benefits and ingratitude for good deeds. Although they do not think that an end ought to be placed upon this tumultuous recompense by the imposition of silence, yet our rather lengthy discourse about it must at last be concluded, [Col. 1089A] so that our purpose may turn its silence to discussing something else, lest the third subject be delayed from coming forward by the prolonged obstacle of the two.

## On prudent silence concerning good things. CHAPTER LXXI

There is also silence concerning good things. Things are called good that are either useful or pleasant. Concerning them, some people are at times silent by prudent counsel; others hold their peace culpably; and still others become mute as punishment. Although some good things ought to be held in great esteem because of their own merit, they should not nevertheless be spoken to everyone at every time—namely, to those who not only do not embrace good and salutary things with any reverence, but, becoming more wicked, pursue them with more grievous hatreds.

Of such persons the Gospel says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7). The holy thing is the word of God, by which, as it were, the children of like character are nourished: those who are divinely chosen to obtain the Father's inheritance, who discern what pleases God and what does not, and, rejecting harmful things, gladly submit to what is better. [Col. 1089B] Dogs, however—that is, those indecent in life and conduct, ungrateful to teachers, enemies of those who love them—do not receive in a humble heart the word of salvation that they hear, but bark and quarrel against it with rabid mouths.

Whether you wash them or prick them, according to the common proverb, they do not change; rather, with wandering judgment they delight to remain what they were. As they are ready to repay the one who strikes them, so, with undiscerning judgment, they prepare a bite for the one who caresses them. It is therefore not wise to take the children's bread 626 and throw it to such dogs: frenzied animals that do not distinguish household members from strangers, that do not carefully distinguish holy from profane, that are not turned from their wickedness by any benefit of teaching, or perhaps, after a proposed conversion, return still more wickedly to their vomit. “Nor pearls,” he says, “to swine.”

The pig is an unclean animal that delights in mud. It signifies those who, lax in affection and conduct, do not discipline their uncultivated manners in the sight of heavenly things, but, with hearts bent down, greedily search only for earthly things. If someone offers them the commendable pearl of God's word, for its grace or love they do not moderate their former desire; instead, they venture to value the same word as cheaper than mud and to trample it underfoot in earthly pursuits. [Col. 1089C]

For this reason the legion of demons said: “If you cast us out from here, send us into the herd of swine” (Matt. 8). For when an evil spirit is not permitted to remain in any of the elect, when divine grace desires to free them from its rule, it chooses to dwell in those wholly immersed in muddy pleasures, those finally overwhelmed by the carnal flood through persistent wickedness. When a prudent man sees such persons obstinate in their wickedness and hardened with stopped ears at the voice of those who wisely charm them, he prudently imposes silence upon himself concerning good things and does not set the pearls of teaching before despisers.

Thus the prophet Amos says: “Therefore the prudent man shall keep silent at that time, because it is an evil time” (Amos 5). [Col. 1090A] The time is evil when scoffers do not give credence to their teachers, when they hold the life-giving word which they have heard in contempt, when, as speech gains greater strength for teaching, the wicked hearer's mind grows correspondingly harder. Therefore, at the time when a hearer is found so irreverent, obstinate, and undisciplined, everyone wisely instructed by the divine Spirit keeps silence. He is silent, I say, either out of deference to God's word, lest it be cheapened, or perhaps out of sparing his neighbor, lest one who is in filth become filthier still.

For he hears that the inward Spirit enjoins this silence upon him and forbids him to speak good things to the wicked. At that Spirit's command or prohibition the ready tongue clings to the hearer's palate, and he becomes mute regarding good things which the wicked no longer deserve to hear. Thus it says to Ezekiel: “I will make your tongue cling to your palate, and you shall be mute and not like a man who rebukes, because they are a provoking house” (Ezek. 3). [Col. 1090B] You see that the Spirit of God considers the hardness and fault of the hearers: with hardened heart, they embitter the one whom they ought to appease; and deservedly the same Spirit makes the prophet mute because they embitter him, lest he presume to pour out the word of life to those hardened and advancing toward worse things.

By the same Spirit Jeremiah is forbidden to pray, to labor in vows and prayers for a wicked people, lest both the prophet's devout prayer be poured out in vain and the intercessor be put to shame when he meets with refusal. “Do not pray for this people,” he says, “nor raise for them praise and prayer; do not stand against me, for I will not hear you” (Jer. 7). Because, he says, the perverse neck of this people has been hardened, and such great wickedness has not deserved to obtain pardon, see that you do not presume anything superfluous for them; do not take up praise and prayer for the restoring of the lost.

The intercessor takes up praise when, desiring to obtain divine mercy, he lovingly brings forward God's ancient benefits, recalling how God did not wish them, or their forefathers, to perish when they sinned, but mercifully granted pardon to their errors. [Col. 1090C] When praise of this kind is repeated to God, as it were, to his face, and so great a kindness is recalled to his memory, present wrath is softened by humble entreaty, and former mercy is urged to grant a benefit once again. But when anyone persists more devoutly in praises of God in this way and does not withdraw from his purpose until he is heard, he indeed meets and withstands God in his anger with the force of prayers, while God does not persist in what he had threatened.

God indicates this when speaking to Moses: “I see,” he says, “that this people is stiff-necked; let me alone, that my anger may rage against them and that I may destroy them” (Exod. 32). Why does he ask to be let alone so that his wrath may rage more freely, except because he was held back by Moses' powerful prayer, lest his anger and sentence rage against the sinful people and, in that raging, the sinner perish according to his desert? “For Moses,” it says, “prayed to the Lord his God, saying: ‘Why, Lord, does your anger rage against your people?’” (ibid.). Scripture indicates to what end that devout man prayed to God, and how strongly he restrained God's wrath by praying, [Col. 1091A] when it adds: “And the Lord was appeased, so that he did not do the evil which he had spoken against his people” (Exod. 32).

From such prayer, by which every devout person is said never to cease opposing God, God warns him whom he does not wish the justice of the angry Judge to hear not to presume to pour out superfluous prayers. For although both the intercessor and his prayer appear good, while he begs some good thing either for himself or another, a good person ought obediently to be silent even about that good when he truly knows that silence itself pleases God, the supreme Good. Repeating this much further below, he says: “Do not pray for this people for good” (Jer. 14).
