Peter understood that prayer should not be offered for good on behalf of the one to whom the Spirit has made known that salvation is not to be granted. Therefore he did not pray for Ananias and Sapphira, because through the Spirit he knew both the sin and its penalty. Similar is what John says: “There is a sin unto death; 627 I do not say that anyone should pray for that one” (1 John 5). [Col. 1091B]

## CHAPTER LXXII

Taught by this Spirit, Paul is found to pray for certain sinners; but, a little above, when another sinned, he is found to refrain from prayers, knowing that the faults of the former could more easily be forgiven by the gift of grace, whereas the latter's wickedness could not be erased by the remedy of pardon. Speaking to Timothy, he says: “All deserted me; may it not be charged against them” (2 Tim. 4). And above: “Alexander the coppersmith,” he says, “showed me many evils; the Lord will repay him according to his works” (ibid.).

What does it mean that he prays that such guilt may not be charged against those who deserted him, but does not pray for Alexander and instead declares that he will receive what he deserves, except that, taught by the Spirit, he knows that his prayers are accepted for the former but that Alexander's obstinate wickedness is not remitted through his prayers? [Col. 1091C]

Again, when he saw the Jews hardened against saving teaching and, prodigal of salvation, detesting both the medicine and the physician, he prudently set an end to his undertaking and resolved, with a renewed plan, to turn to teaching others. “The Jews,” it says, “were filled with jealousy and contradicted what was being said by Paul, blaspheming. And Paul said to them: ‘It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles’” (Acts 13).

Because Paul saw that the Jews, on hearing the word of life, did not believe but exceeded into contempt and blasphemy through obstinacy of mind, he bade farewell to those blasphemers not in hatred but by prudent judgment; nor did he continue to speak to those dying from the good fragrance. “We are,” he says, “the good fragrance of Christ to God among those being saved and among those perishing: to some, indeed, a fragrance of death unto death; but to others, a fragrance of life unto life” (2 Cor. 2). [Col. 1091D]

Just as many, fed by the good fragrance of the word, make progress and through that nourishment and progress arrive at spiritual life, so some, whose inward parts are corrupted by the gall of bitterness, die, as it were, through the same good fragrance by a certain incongruity. Finally, a human being is advanced toward perfection and life by solid bread; but a rapacious hawk is kept away from the eating of that same bread. Although a similar nourishment—or indeed precisely the same—is set before both, it nevertheless works very differently in things so dissimilar.

And rightly: to the human being, to whom divine generosity has given reason, by which, understanding God, he ardently desires God's vision alone—to him, I say, the nourishment of solid bread is fitting, and by the good fragrance of the word he receives the support of indissoluble life. But for the one who, in rapacious wickedness, burns toward the destruction of others; who tears the flesh of the weak with greedy claws; who in headlong pride despises the health of fruitful faith; who in proud flight passes by the humble truth of teaching—for him, I say, life-giving nourishment is changed into its opposite, while he stubbornly opposes with blasphemous spirit that which he ought to have loved. [Col. 1092A]

Those human beings who either live through the good fragrance or, conversely, die through it cannot easily be perfectly distinguished by the steward of the word: that is, the teacher cannot perfectly know to whom the word of life ought rightly to be entrusted, or who, reprobate in mind, ought wholly not to be admitted to its aid. Paul indicates this when he adds: “And who is sufficient for these things?” (2 Cor. 2). Who, he says, can be a steward endowed with so great a grace? Who can be found so prudent and discerning that, with penetrating understanding, he may perceive for whom the same antidote is harmful and for whom salutary—when the door should be opened for speaking good things, or when silence should more rightly be imposed?

This summit of virtue, this perfection, seems inaccessible unless perhaps discernment of spirits has been granted to someone. For as one is found to have, through the Spirit, the word of wisdom, and another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, so that same Spirit grants prophecy to one and discernment of spirits to another. [Col. 1092B]

The Apostle himself wished Titus to possess this discernment of spirits, and earnestly instructed him in acquiring it, lest a needless teacher speak the word of salvation to those whose reprobate mind gives no hope of salvation. “Avoid,” he says, “a heretical person after a first and second correction, knowing that one of this kind has been subverted” (Titus 3). If, he says, heretical depravity has already subverted anyone, and the grace visiting him does not convert him when you give a first or second correction, let your discernment be more surely instructed by this sign: take silence concerning good things upon yourself, and avoid him altogether.

For since, condemned by his own judgment, he sins in such a way that, as a blasphemer against the divine Spirit, he leaves himself no place for repentance, it is right that a prudent teacher should not strive to apply medicine to a wound whose hardness is so great that, when corrected, it does not accept discipline. The Apostle also saw that he possessed this same discernment of spirits when, abandoning the Jews, he turned to preaching among the Gentiles; when, leaving those whom he loved more affectionately by the claim of kinship, he went to outsiders whom, taught by the Spirit, he foresaw to be worthier in life. [Col. 1092C]

After saying to the Jews what was quoted above—“It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13)—after saying this, he immediately added: “For thus the Lord commanded us: ‘I have set you as a light to the Gentiles, that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth’” (ibid.). You see that 628 Paul is not blinded by the wickedness of envy or the fault of ignorance when he leaves the Jews and seeks the salvation of the Gentiles. Rather, he professes that he acts so at the Spirit's command and instruction—though, insofar as one may understand, he would have preferred above all to be sent to his own people.

Finally, when this same preacher visits the cities of the Gentiles in diligent journeying, he first enters the Jewish synagogues found in them, trying whether perhaps God may deign to grant them his grace, so that they may be willing to obey his saving admonitions. [Col. 1093A] But everywhere he finds them so stiff-necked, so perverse, and with hearts so obstinately opposed to the faith preached, that he plainly understands that he is not sent as an Apostle to teach them and that the word of life ought not at all to be entrusted to them.

“For when he came to Thessalonica, he entered the synagogue of the Jews according to his custom, and for three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures. But the Jews, in their jealousy, taking certain evil men from the rabble, stirred up the city, crying out and saying: ‘These all act against Caesar's decrees, saying that there is another king, some Jesus’” (Acts 17). And below: “When he had departed from Athens and come to Corinth, and was disputing in the synagogue, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ—when they contradicted and blasphemed, he shook out his garments and said to them: ‘Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from now on I will go to the Gentiles’” (Acts 18). [Col. 1093B]

[Col. 1093C] While he was at Rome, he expounded to the Jews, testifying to the kingdom of God and persuading them concerning Jesus from the law of Moses and the prophets. And when they did not agree among themselves, he said: “Let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will hear it” (Acts 28).

In different places Paul wishes to teach the unbelieving Jews and earnestly to advance them toward the catholic faith; but, with the Spirit opposing, he is compelled to turn his mind from his purpose, understanding that whatever labor he spends upon them has no effect. As, taught by the Spirit, he understands that they are rejected and declares the rejected unworthy of saving teaching, so, instructed by that Spirit, he promises to turn to teaching the peoples of the Gentiles. Yet the Spirit who is teacher does not permit him to speak to or go to certain of them: “Passing through Phrygia and the region of Galatia,” it says, “they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they came to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16). [Col. 1093D]

Paul rightly restrained himself in silence in Asia and, his plan broken off, did not go to Bithynia, since the Spirit of Jesus is found graciously to have taught him concerning this, indicating what, when, and to whom is fitting.

So too Jesus himself—whom no dullness of ignorance obscures, but in whom all fullness of wisdom dwells—is found at times to have been silent concerning good things when he is confronted by his Jewish or Gentile persecutors. “The chief priests and scribes brought him into their council, saying: ‘If you are the Christ, tell us’” (Luke 22). “Just as we wish you not to presume falsely to take the name of Christ for yourself,” they say, “so we wish you not to maintain an unwelcome silence concerning it; rather, make the truth known to us who are ignorant, lest our opinion hold falsehood in its place.” But he says: “If I tell you, you will not believe me” (ibid.). [Col. 1094A]

“It is not fitting,” he says, “that I disclose to you what you ask or dishonor divine mysteries by superfluous explanation, since, if I tell you, you will not believe and will not receive the holy pearl with fitting reverence.” Thus Mark says that, when the high priest questioned Jesus, saying, “Do you answer nothing to the things these men bring against you?”, “he was silent and answered nothing” (Mark 14). And Matthew: “When he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing” (Matt. 27).

Jesus does not wish to answer his accusers, whom he knows beyond doubt lack ears to hear; whatever he might say to them, he foresees would be turned rather into contempt and slander, and that their wickedness would not convert them, hardened as they are, to love truth. Yet when, according to John, he answered the high priest who questioned him about his disciples and teaching, and his answer contained nothing blameworthy, “one of the attendants standing by struck him, saying: ‘Do you answer the high priest thus?’ Jesus answered him: ‘If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness concerning the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?’” (John 18). [Col. 1094B]

“If I had spoken improperly to you or the high priest, and you had pursued it with fitting testimony or even with a blow, it would not seem remarkable, or perhaps blameworthy at all, because one who judges justly is not liable for injustice. But when you find no falsehood in my speech, and have spoken no unjust truth either to you or to anyone else, why do you not merely refuse to approach in love what I say, but strike me thus while I speak useful things?” Therefore, because Jesus sees that his answers, though good, do not benefit the Jews who hear, but rather make them readier to return insults, he judges it fitting sometimes to remain silent concerning those same good things, so that by his example the goodness of such silence may become known. [Col. 1094C]

## CHAPTER LXXIII

As he gave this silence to the Jews, so also to the Gentiles, when he did not perceive them kindly disposed to obey him; when, considering that he was mocked by their stiff-necked pride, he saw the narrow path of faith closed against those mockers. “Herod questioned him 629 at length,” it says, “but he answered him nothing. Herod despised him and mocked him, clothing him in a white garment” (Luke 23). It is clear that Jesus gave Herod no answer because he knew it was unnecessary, recognizing that Herod was not a kindly hearer of his teaching but greedy for signs and a proud mocker of both those signs and of Jesus himself. “For he hoped,” it says, “to see some sign performed by him” (Luke 23). [Col. 1095A]

In Herod's presence Jesus not only worked no miracle, but did not add any answer at all to his questioning, lest, by answering, he appear to fear authority, or, by working miracles, to flatter Herod by fawning upon him. Thus, when some people elsewhere said to him, “Go away and depart from here, because Herod wishes to kill you,” he said to them: “Go and tell that fox: ‘Behold, I cast out demons,’ etc.” (Luke 13). “My spirit, though absent,” he says, “does not fail to know the deceitful wickedness in which Herod labors; but my power does not abandon its purpose through fear of him, nor does the sly and feeble little fox stand against stronger wisdom.”

Jesus does not care to answer one such as this, who wishes with curiosity to hear the Jesus brought before him and yet does not at all intend to obey what he hears, lest good things owed to a humble and earnest person be indiscreetly offered to a proudly curious one. Likewise, according to John, when Pilate said to him, “Where are you from?”, “Jesus gave him no answer. Therefore Pilate said to him: ‘Do you not speak to me?’” (John 19). [Col. 1095B] Because Pilate did not present himself as a teachable disciple and sought the unknown not through the merit of humility but through the terror of authority, Jesus disdains to instruct him concerning it; and the judge, as though more powerful, is angered at his silence. “Do you not speak to me?” he says. “Do you not know that I have power to crucify you and power to release you?” (ibid.).

And according to Mark: “Pilate questioned Jesus, saying: ‘Do you answer nothing? See how many things they accuse you of.’ But Jesus answered nothing further, so that Pilate marveled” (Mark 15). Pilate marveled that Jesus did not answer him more readily, that the one being judged did not fear the judge's power, and that, although he dared to expose the Jews' malicious falsehood, he did not at least fear the judicial authority of the governor. But Jesus, whose Spirit imposed silence concerning good things upon Paul when it prohibited him either to go to Bithynia or to speak the word in Asia, himself knows when he too should keep silence, when he should speak, to whom, and with what purpose. [Col. 1095C] Whoever despises such distinctions, or fails to discern them through ignorance or negligence, deserves rebuke not only for speaking evil, but is also not excusable when he speaks good things indiscreetly.

## CHAPTER LXXIV
[Col. 1095D] Therefore, when Peter speaks good things but does not consider when he ought to utter them, and, through over-hasty judgment, lays hold of the summit of perfection, Christ, who knows secrets, rebukes him and, wisely, forewarns the ignorant man of his imminent fall. “All of you,” Christ says, “will suffer scandal because of me this night.” To this Peter replied: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I shall never be scandalized.” And he added: “Even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you” (Matt. 26). What better answer could a disciple give his master than to pledge himself so devoted and subject to his service that, though the others are scandalized, he himself will suffer no scandal and no threat of death will tear him away from him?

Paul too is found to have said something similar in his letters [Col. 1096A], and yet no one charged him with blame for it; indeed, both the speaker is judged praiseworthy and what he said is proclaimed worthy of remembrance. “Neither death,” he says, “nor life will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8). But Christ’s death and resurrection brought with them so great a benefit: they bestowed this grace of courage upon the apostles and their followers, so that, seeing him who first rose from the dead for their sake, they would not fear in return to suffer death for him. For Christ’s death removed the old burden of sins, while his resurrection advanced them toward the righteousness of merits, so that, once the old weight of burdens had been removed and the newness of virtue received, they might now both wish and be able to suffer with Christ—indeed, to die with him—and, living and reigning with him, sit together in the heavenly places.

Peter recalls this when he says: “Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you may follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 1). And Christ himself, in the Gospel, foreshadows this mystery of his passion: “I have given you an example,” he says, “that, as I have done to you, so you also should do” (John 13). Thus, through the reality of his passion—not foretold but now accomplished—the apostles obtained such ready firmness of spirit that they followed this example with resolute purpose and, in fitting sequence, died for Christ who had first died for them. For it was not fitting that the disciples should suffer death for their master before the master suffered death for his disciples, lest the disciple’s death seem necessary to the master. Rather, in the right order, he was first to die who was to furnish the others with both example and grace.

Accordingly, no apostle had attained such grace; none of them could be found so perfect that he could, with courageous spirit, die for Christ before Christ had died, 630 and, not yet redeemed, render the service of death to his Redeemer. Hence, when Christ was being sought by the crowd of persecutors in order that, once found, he might be delivered to death according to Judas’s plan, he said to them: “Whom do you seek?” And they: “Jesus of Nazareth.” But he: “If you seek me, let these go” (John 18). “I do not wish,” he says, “that, while you seize me, you should seize these also and compel them, unprepared, to suffer death with me—those whom I know still to be lame in faith, weak in works, and not yet advanced by life-giving grace to contempt of death.” Since I see that they lack, although they do not know it, those things which are evidently necessary for true salvation, I wish them to depart from here while you seek me, lest they be compelled by an untimely death to perish eternally.

The Evangelist, indicating this, adds: “That the word which he had spoken might be fulfilled: ‘Of those whom you gave me, I lost none’” (ibid.). By these words he indicates that, if the apostles had not been permitted to depart and had died at that time, being weaker in faith they would undoubtedly have perished; and the saying in which he had previously spoken of their salvation would not appear to have attained its proper effect. For a little earlier he had said: “Those whom you gave me I have kept, and none of them perished except the son of perdition” (John 17).

[Col. 1097A] “Those whom you gave me,” he says, “with that goodness which is yours for saving, I did not wholly abandon for condemnation, though they were weaker in merits; nor did I depart from your will in guarding them, but I kept all who were given to me with fitting care.” Therefore, although much tribulation presses or comes upon them, none incurs perdition except the son of perdition—whom, certainly, you had not given to me, though perhaps he seemed to have been given, while he still associated, before the judgment had been made manifest, with those who had been given.

But in order that the saying Christ had uttered concerning them might be fulfilled, he did not wish any of them to die together with him in his death—not because, through that prediction, a violent necessity of salvation was imposed upon any of them. Certainly, no one is saved unless grace goes before and merits follow. For they are not necessarily to be saved because Christ spoke such a saying; rather, because they were going to be saved, he who foreknew it foretold this. He is said to foretell their salvation in such a way that neither the grace of the One saving nor the free will of those to be saved is taken away.

Therefore, in order that the apostles whom the Father had given to the Son might be saved, and thus that what had been foretold concerning their salvation might be fulfilled, when Christ heard himself sought for death, he did not wish them to be driven to die with him. For what they thought of themselves with the bleary eyes of their inward sight, what they rashly boasted in unconsidered speech, he, the searcher of hearts, knew better not to be so; and the tribulation that came upon them made this very thing known to them.

Peter indeed said that, though the others were scandalized, he too would not be driven into scandal, and that even if he had to die with him, he would nevertheless not be torn from him in confessing him. This all the others likewise answered with one voice, promising that they too would remain steadfast. For when Peter had said, “Even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you,” the Evangelist adds: “Likewise all the disciples said” (Matt. 26). But just as Peter did not keep the faith owed to this promise and, disturbed by fear, turned aside blameworthily with a slipping foot, so all the others sinned through the same inconstancy of mind and, guilty of falsehood, abandoned their master by taking flight. Thus Matthew says: “Then all his disciples left him and fled” (ibid.).

[Col. 1097D] Those who suffered under so grave a failure and so deadly a weakness, and who, with the dullness of heart darkened over, were unable to recognize him, would have done far more honourably and profitably to restrain themselves in modest silence than, in reckless outpouring, to utter pompous, airy, and empty boasts. For when darkened judgment makes them presumptuous, fear immediately makes them cowardly fugitives; when their words, promising remarkable courage and constancy, are thus nullified and made foolish by fearful denial, it is clear that a person greatly offends by speaking if he does not carefully discern what he ought to say and when.

## CHAPTER LXXV

This is especially seen in Peter, who, confidently declaring that he would not be troubled by scandal, deserved to hear that he would not merely suffer the scandal he had denied, [Col. 1098A] but, contrary to what he had promised, would deny both his master and his Lord. “Amen, I say to you: this very night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times” (Matt. 26).

Peter does not know the magnitude of the sickness from which he suffers, but the wise physician does not fail to know it. Peter, accountable for his vow, had strayed far from his presumed constancy; and the event proved this physician truthful. For fear, coming upon Peter a third time, bent him to denial. Yet his truthful and merciful master did not despise him when he denied him; rather, with a gracious look he caused him both to remember what Christ himself had foretold and to grieve over what Peter had subsequently done. “Peter,” it says, “remembered the word of the Lord, and, going out, he wept bitterly” (ibid.).

Recognizing that he had been reckless and headlong in speaking and promising good things, and that afterward he had fallen in denying once and again—indeed, a third time—Peter, repentant of his deed, does not take up speech and no longer presumes to trust in deceptive words. For the place which he had found slippery and harmful to himself, 631 where he had fallen both in loving and in fearing, as though with right and left foot, cannot, after being grievously wounded, fail at present to be suspect to him; both the prior injury and the ensuing suspicion lead him to despise it. Repentant of his deed, then, he hesitates and doubts where to turn, by what remedy to obtain saving pardon, and by what silence he ought to hold himself in order to obtain it, since speaking anything now seems neither useful nor fitting to him.

Considering his fall silently within himself, and deliberating what he can do about it at present, he says: “What shall I do, or what shall I say? If I deny my master again, if, careless of salvation, I add fault to fault, who will patiently bear one who repeats the offence so often, rather than restrain the erring man with swift punishment? But if I immediately wish to confess my sin with my own mouth, if I promise henceforth abstinence from evil and constancy in good, who will incline a favourable ear to one confessing? Who can believe one who has proved false in promising? Shall I not seem insolent and shameless? Shall I not deserve to be charged with wordiness if I return to speaking so quickly, so easily, so confidently, when in so brief a span I have fallen there so often?”

[Col. 1098D] Turning these matters over and over within himself, Peter did not know what he could rightly say; indeed, wounded by speech, he no longer dared say anything, lest by speaking he should be thought, as before, too hasty, and should again deserve blame for unconsidered talk. Finally Solomon says: “Have you seen a man hasty in speaking? More hope is to be placed in folly than in his correction” (Prov. 26).

For sometimes one who promises many or great things quickly abandons those same things just as quickly; and one found rather too unconsidering in proposing lofty things soon experiences a grave fall through weakness or negligence. Therefore Ecclesiastes says: “Do not speak anything rashly, and let not your heart be swift to utter a word” (Eccles. 5).

[Col. 1099A] It is no small rashness when someone is too swift to speak and, with precipitate purpose, promises things unequal to his powers; when, by grace’s inspiration, he is not taught what and when he should say, and does not fear to utter both good and evil without discriminating judgment. And who is more rash than the man deceived by his own words—when speech and truth are far apart, when the tongue says freely and indiscriminately whatever comes into the mouth, and the course of events contradicts its saying? Thus words that, through unconsidered judgment, affirm falsehood, or that, through cowardly fear, deny truth, are often exceedingly harmful both to the speaker himself and to the hearer, since they bring ruin by deception upon one or perhaps upon both.

[Col. 1099B] The pagans rightly observed the force of such words and in their little works used “words” for deceptions. This figure of speech seemed quite appropriate to them: the efficient cause is sometimes put for the effect. One of them says: “Every lover gives words.” For everyone who is inwardly inflamed by erotic love in a wounded conscience, and is not concerned to heal it, has, upon neglecting the wholesome remedy, this as an ensuing characteristic: fraudulently to weave and cast networks and snares of words. For, burning and hastening to fulfil an unchaste desire, he finds nothing more familiar to himself than verbose falsehood. By its flattering entanglements he tries to bind and seduce the unwary woman—or, while seducing her, to bind her—through whose miserable passion he is compelled, miserable himself, to perish.

[Col. 1099C] Therefore every lover gives words, that is, deceptions, because whoever sees himself held under the unjust law of desire and does not wish to be free of its yoke or dominion takes care to cover what he says more carefully in a wrapping of fraud, so that, like a deceitful fowler, he may ensnare the bird he desires. Thus the serpent too is found in paradise to have seduced the woman by speech, and by deceitful promises to have induced her not to fear touching the forbidden fruit, guilty of the commandment; and she in turn urged the same transgression upon her husband with feminine importunity. Hence she herself says to the Lord who rebukes her: “The serpent deceived me” (Gen. 3).

Since, therefore, much deception and falsehood are found in speech—as Peter is discovered to have learned not so much by speaking as by falling—having recently fallen through speech, he does not immediately entrust himself again to the same thing: he does not confess, he does not pray, nor finally does he promise again that he will be steadfast.

## CHAPTER LXXVI

Having set aside the clamour of words, which he perceived was not then suitable for him, he turns by prudent counsel to modest silence. In it, repentance for sin poured bitterness into his heart, and that inward bitterness of heart suffused his outward eyes with tears. Recalling and grieving that he had not shown to his Lord and master what he had earlier promised, but had answered the word of the doorkeeper with a word of denial, he wishes to try another way of obtaining remedy. Leaving the praetorium [Col. 1100A] and entering the enclosure of silence, he weeps bitterly.

There, in the recesses of conscience, considering both his fault and himself, he sits, as before a tribunal, and judges himself. Examining what he had done by word and by an unguarded tongue, he attacks the offence as he attacks the tongue—indeed, with a heavier judgment. He restrains and chastises his loose and unstable tongue with silence, 632 while he pursues and investigates his offence with bitter repentance. He presses the one down and closes it, drawing bolts and bars across his lips; the other he washes and wipes away by pouring over it many great floods of tears.

Thus he does not despair, with respect to mouth and tongue by which he had fallen grievously, of the fruit of tears and silence, perhaps remembering that in tearful silence a certain voice is sometimes found that worthily awakens God, although it is not heard by human beings. Hence the Prophet says: “Receive my tears with your ears” (Ps. 38). Though tears are normally said to be visible rather than audible—for the ear cannot hear them, while the eye may behold them—the Prophet nevertheless wishes God in his mercy to deign to hear his tears, he who is able both to see and to hear audible things.

With him contrition and devotion of spirit do not grow hoarse, nor does tearful silence become mute. Though, because sins demand it, a too-talkative tongue clings to the palate, the inward mind is nevertheless often gladdened by its heard weeping. The Prophet indicates this when he says: “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping” (Ps. 6). Weeping therefore has its own voice—indeed, its own cry—but in God’s ears; for just as the mouth of one speaking is opened to strike human ears, so the efficacious outpouring of tears is found to strike the ears of God.

[Col. 1100C] Accordingly the wise man says: “Do not the tears of the widow run down upon her cheek, and does not her cry rise against the one who causes them to fall? For from her cheek they descend even to heaven, and the Lord who hears will not take delight in them” (Ecclus. 35). You see that when the widow is watered with tears from a devoted heart, no house, nor even the vastness of this air, confines their cry; penetrating heaven, it is heard and answered by the merciful goodness of God presented with it.

For he who often does not heed the loud voices of those who speak, but rebukes those who say to him with hardened heart, “Lord, Lord,” has pity on the afflicted soul, for whom the now more defiled world no longer lives; the good guardian has mercy on her, whom priest and Levite passed by rather carelessly as though half-dead, lifts her upon his beast, and, soothing her pain, supplies the aid of salutary medicine. The wise perfumer turns that person’s voice of groanings or speech into a remedy for her; and he who does not look upon the ungrateful and their voices or offerings, which are ungrateful, does not despise the eloquent groaning of the devoted widow. Of her the aforementioned wise man first says: “He will not despise the widow if she pours out the speech of groaning” (ibid.).

Warned by these and similar things, Peter, though he does not dare after falling through speech to be verbose again lest his offence be deservedly increased by shamelessness, chooses, with afflicted heart, to weep in silence, in the hope that perhaps God may accept even this small offering. [Col. 1101A] Inner devotion indeed releases him for weeping, while shame restrains his tongue from speaking; and the infusion of the visiting Spirit, which grants him tears, makes him at the same time hold back through fear of the strict Judge.

Hence certain penitents in Jeremiah say: “Come, let us enter the fortified city and be silent there, because the Lord our God has made us silent; for we have sinned against the Lord” (Jer. 8). Some, when after sin they turn to repentance and inwardly are ashamed of their past deeds, so reverence the inward Judge in fear that they do not unrestrainedly pour forth prayers in hasty speech. It seems to them that vocal prayer does not effectively reach the divine ears unless it is preceded by the modesty of silence; nor is a louder voice adequately received with worth unless it is commended by prior fear and discriminating judgment.

“We shall be silent,” they say, “because the Lord our God has made us silent” (ibid.). The Lord then makes us silent when, by a gracious regard, he makes us repent our transgressions; and he instils in us, being penitent, such fear of judgment that a hasty and talkative confidence in prayer seems unfitting. For our weakness often experiences error and falling in hasty speech, whereas greater security is found in devout silence. Therefore what is harmful or suspect seems for the present to be laid aside, while what is at present safer ought to be preferred.

[Col. 1101C] Remembering that they have sinned, then, they blush deeply and, having a conscience confused and fearful, fall silent, lest, if they do not attend with balanced judgment to the fitting time for speaking, they offend more by hasty speech the One whom they desire to be appeased. The Lord is said to effect or confer this silence because his severity is feared by a conscience wounded by sin; that is, those who, inspired by him, groan deeply over their sins, tremble as though brought before his judgment, supported by no merit.

“The Lord our God,” they say, “has made us silent, for we have sinned against the Lord” (ibid.). Because by sinning we have shown ourselves wicked servants toward our Lord, fear of him takes from us our present confidence in prayer; holiness no longer seems to stand for us in sounding words, but the strength of penitents will lie in the devotion of hope and silence. For although God’s abundant mercy pours hope into penitents, the true and severe fear of that same justice so checks them that they dare approach him rather in a devout and compunctive disposition than insolently open an unworthy mouth for verbose prayers or praises.

This too he teaches the penitent soul through Ezekiel: “That you may remember and be ashamed, and no longer have your mouth opened because of your shame, when I have been appeased toward you” (Ezek. 16). “When,” he says, “in the goodness that is mine I have restored myself as appeased toward you, when your former will no longer gives you over, as formerly, to headlong sin, I wish you not to be forgetful at all of your past deeds. Rather, humbly recalling them, be wholesomely ashamed; and, though the recent sickness has been driven away, do not, still insufficiently prepared, presume to take my covenant into your mouth, 633 nor presume confidently to speak, as belongs to those who have made progress.”

For it belongs to those who have made progress to dare open their mouth and, strengthened by merits, approach God confidently: those, namely, whose intention and conduct are no longer foul, whom a guilty conscience of present vices does not gnaw. To one of these the Lord says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80). And another says: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118). In the Acts of the Apostles: “Philip, opening his mouth, preached Jesus to him” (Acts 8). And Paul says: “My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians” (2 Cor. 6).

But to the sinner God says: “Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant into [Col. 1102B] your mouth?” (Ps. 49). And elsewhere: “You have sinned: be still” (Gen. 4)—as though he said: “If you have polluted your inner conscience with the contagion of sin, and have not yet washed away its uncleanness by fitting repentance and enduring satisfaction, do not at once, as one insolent and shameless, take my covenant into your mouth. But, strengthened by humble hope, first resort to the protection of silence, so that, constrained there by the saving bond of discipline (Ecclus. 15), you may learn more diligently when, how, and what you should say.”

For just as praise is not becoming in the mouth of a sinner, so waters are drawn in joy from the springs of the Saviour (Isa. 12), when, according to Jeremiah, each person chooses to await the Lord in silence (Lam. 3), until, after the manner of Isaiah, he sends to him the angel with a coal from the altar (Isa. 6). The angel, once sent, finds him not dissolved in presumptuous effusion of speech, but wrapped in the folds of silence, fear, and reverence. He touches and cleanses his mouth or lips with the burning coal, so that thereafter neither his speaking of good things may confound him with dissimilar vices nor the reproachful objection of hearers strike him down.

For those who presume to preach righteousness in speech, while their conduct does not yet appear sufficiently reformed to agree with the righteousness they preach, are either severely reproached by their own conscience or readily denied assent by the indignation of their hearers. Of such people Jeremiah says: “Do not believe them when they speak good things to you” (Jer. 12). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “How can you speak good things when you are evil?” (Matt. 7).

[Col. 1102D] But those who are burned by the fiery coal—that is, by the cautery of fear-filled repentance—and who are refined by the altar’s little fire and by the inward ardour of the compunctive Spirit, have their sin and iniquity removed. Once these have been worthily removed by gracious use, they are granted freedom of speech (Isa. 6), indeed, a more abundant grace is bestowed upon them. “Behold,” the angel says to Isaiah, “I have touched your lips; your iniquity shall be taken away, and your sin shall be cleansed” (ibid.). And the Prophet adds: “And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Go, and say to this people: ‘Hear, you who hear,’” and so forth (ibid.).

He says that he kept silent while he was still a man polluted in lips, before he was cleansed by the burning coal of fitting repentance. After fitting cleansing, he receives the command to speak, and with a good conscience is sent to speak good things to the people. Just as he rightly kept silent before receiving the command to speak—or, if perhaps forbidden to speak, ought not insolently to have broken restraint—so, having heard the voice commanding him, he does not refuse to proclaim what he is ordered, since sin or iniquity no longer accuses his now cleansed lips.

[Col. 1103A] Therefore, when a little earlier he complained that he had been silent, saying, “Woe is me, because I kept silent!” (Isa. 6), I think he reproves not so much the silence as the preceding state of merit: namely, because he had not devoted sufficiently worthy diligence to correcting his conduct, and because, owing to the very depravity and uncleanness of his lips, he realized that freedom to speak and teach had been denied him. But after he understands himself to have been cleansed by the coal taken by the angel from the altar, and that the office of teaching has been assigned to one cleansed, he lays aside the burden of silence by which he was previously weighed down and speaks with confidence—something judged both worthy and useful.

It is therefore wise counsel sometimes to keep silent about good things; nor is he found prudent who does not know how to restrain his tongue with discriminating silence. Good is the word which judgment precedes, truth accompanies, and the just authority of the sender commends.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On Culpable Silence

But one who is sent and commanded not to be silent, but to teach others by necessary speech, is undoubtedly blameworthy if, despising the command, he remains silent through sloth or envy. “Wicked and slothful servant,” he says, “you knew that I reap where I do not sow [Col. 1103C] and gather where I have not scattered; therefore you ought to have entrusted my money to bankers, and on coming I would indeed have received what was mine with interest” (Matt. 25).

By the talent or money which the Lord deigned to give to the slothful servant, that he might strive to gain profit from it rather than negligently bury it in a dug hole, the word of teaching is fittingly signified. He who receives a command to speak ought to dispense it. If perhaps he wastes away through an inward sickness of mind and, at the time for speaking, is held silent by sloth, he deserves rebuke from the One who calls in what was entrusted, just as the person who has prudently fulfilled the task is, conversely, pronounced praiseworthy.

“Who do you think,” he says, “is the faithful and prudent servant whom his lord has appointed over his household to give them food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant” (Matt. 24). This servant, appointed by the Lord over his household, because he faithfully and prudently supplied them at the proper time with the food they needed, is counted worthy of no reward other than eternal blessedness, rejoicing that, after his ministry is fulfilled, he is admitted to the joy of his Lord. “Well done,” he says, “good servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

But what does this mean: “That he may give them food at the proper time” (Matt. 24)? Why, in praising the servant who strove to carry out his Lord’s command, does Scripture make such pointed mention of time, so that he is not praised because he gave food, but commended because he gave food at the proper time?

[Col. 1104A] Certainly, the gifts which the prudent servant distributes to the household do not sufficiently please the Lord if they are not timely: that is, if before receiving the command he rashly gives himself over to lavish giving, or if he presumes to speak while the Lord has not yet imposed this office upon him. Of such a time the Lord himself says through the Prophet: “When I receive the time, I shall judge justices” (Ps. 74). “I,” he says, “who, when I became human, underwent by the Father’s decree the judgment—or the injustices—of the unjust, because the Father wished me first to endure, rather than inflict, the punishments of sinners: once obedience has been fulfilled, I myself—or I by the power which is his or mine—shall rise again. Having likewise received the command or the time, I shall judge justices.”

For as one made mortal I endure, because I have a command to endure; so, rising again and made immortal, I receive the time to inflict judgment, so that neither my passion nor my action may depart from the Father’s command, since neither is marred by an untimeliness of season.

Hence through Isaiah: “I have been silent,” he says, “I have endured; shall I always keep silent? Like a woman in labour I shall speak” (Isa. 42). “I know,” he says, “that a time for silence was first appointed for me and thereafter, likewise, a time for speaking. At first I was silent and patiently bore every obstacle; afterward I shall speak and forcefully repay those who inflict evil.” And elsewhere, through the same Prophet: “I shall not be silent,” he says, “but shall repay” (Isa. 65).

[Col. 1104C] “And though I now seem silent toward the perverse and negligent, because according to the command I must endure their harassment, yet when, likewise according to the command, the fitting time to speak comes, my judgment—which is good because it is just—will answer their wickedness.” Christ, as you have heard, does not negligently pass over such a time. For just as Scripture declares wise the one who keeps silence until the time, so conversely it declares negligent the one who keeps silent when he has received the time for speaking: “Wicked and slothful servant” (Matt. 25).

This wicked, slothful man, worthy of darkness, fetters, or torture, is rebuked by the just exactor not for a loss, but because, when he received profitable things at the fitting time, he pressed them down in silence as though in a pit and did not return them with interest.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

[Col. 1104D] The Prophet fears being charged with this sloth when, wearied by the disposition of evil people, he keeps silent about good things beyond what is right; when, observing more closely that through sluggish softness the rigor of justice is growing feeble within him, he comes to his senses from his incipient failure through visiting grace. “When the sinner stood against me,” he says, “I became mute and kept silent from good things” (Ps. 38).

“When,” he says, “the sinner would not hear the word of justice, when, hardened in wickedness, he would not agree with our preaching; when he did not devoutly stand by, inclining a willing ear to one willing and teaching just things, but, becoming more shameless, openly stood against me, pressed down and oppressed by weariness I resolved to become wholly mute and, with the rudder of hope broken, to withdraw from uttering good things. For I thought it would be better for me if I were silent, if by speaking I did not move my helpers toward what was worse, if, looking to my own safety, I were silent, safe beneath the covering of silence, since my teaching was no help to the perverse and alienated.”

But when I had made this resolution, I understood and saw clearly that the rule of justice was not so ordered that one commanded to speak should, in despair, fear, or weariness, fall silent. For the word of salvation, just as it is offered suitably to those who are willing, must sometimes also be pressed upon those unwilling, inopportunely. Observing and seeing this, he wastes away in sorrow of spirit; and, with pain renewed, his heart grows warm within. As in a furnace an almost-dead coal blazes up more fiercely, so eagerness to speak burns like a flame-bearing fire. Therefore: “I spoke,” he says, “with my tongue” [Col. 1105B] (Ps. 33).

To me indeed silence seemed timely, though wrongly, when I saw that my discourse was not so much useful as harmful to the hearer. But, seeing the will of him who commands more clearly and being suffused, as it were, with the morning light, I found that my purpose of silence was being cast down by a kind of evening fall or decline. Therefore, using sounder counsel, I did not carry out my purpose, but spoke the good things that I had wrongly kept silent; and in proportion as I had been pressed by more languid negligence to be silent because of the opposition of those standing against me, so I set about speaking with more fervent diligence because of the command of the One who commands.

Jeremiah likewise, when he sometimes saw that the word from his mouth did not prosper as he wished, but that his hearers, instead of improving, grew hardened for the worse, and when he was greatly burdened by their hardness and shameless wickedness, resolved to rest from good things, setting a guard upon his mouth. “The word of the Lord,” he says, “has become to me a reproach and a derision all day long; and I said: ‘I shall not remember him, nor speak any longer in his name’” (Jer. 20).

[Col. 1105C] “Whereas my hearers ought to have made themselves attentive and well-disposed, offering a humbly believing ear to our hearing, they dare instead, hardened in wickedness, to mock and turn the benefit offered them to its opposite. Since this is so, and I truly perceive it to be so, I proposed and resolved to embrace silence, that, when I waste away wounded by intolerable injury as I speak, I might hide somewhat more easily beneath the shade of silence.”

Indeed, among some people the word of the Lord is not precious if it is abundant from a kindly teacher; and what by its own merit ought to become gracious to all becomes hateful to them through more lavish abundance. Seeing, therefore, both that the word was becoming cheap and that mockers did not improve but were perverted, I fled according to my purpose to silence. But he who wished me both to teach and to endure an oppressive hearer did not wish me, a fugitive, to hide in harmful repose. “And it became in my heart,” he says, “as a burning fire, shut up in my bones; and I failed, unable to endure it” (ibid.).

The inward Judge did not delay to recall publicly one who wished to hide more quietly and safely in a corner: for in my heart I felt his word burn like fire and, shut up in my bones, scarcely endure delay and restraint. “I failed, unable to endure it” (ibid.), because the inward mind becomes so concerned for progress that it seems to fail if the tongue is idle; and what, languid through torpor, it had negligently proposed, now lively through fervour it cannot patiently endure.

[Col. 1106A] Therefore, setting aside both fear and torpor, under whose pressure he had resolved to keep silence, he no longer kept silent about the good things he knew, lest he too deserve to be charged with harmful silence and the foolish people suffer loss through his silence.

## CHAPTER LXXIX
Moreover, justice—or rather, the just mercy of God—judged it fitting in the case of the Ninevites that, though they were sinners, the good and necessary word should be preached to them, even against their will; and he commanded Jonah to hasten to them for the purpose of preaching [Col. 1106B], and to announce to them both their deserts and the rewards of their deserts. “Arise,” he says, “and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it, because the cry of its wickedness has ascended before me” (Jonah 1).

“I wish,” he says, “that you should go to that great city Nineveh and, by a fitting warning, forestall its overthrow; so that, when perhaps it pays the penalties it deserves, it may not blame the justice of him who inflicts them, on account of the desert already foretold.” For what makes it great or large is not so much the manifold extent of its walls or towers, nor the height of its houses or the multitude of its inhabitants, as its very wickedness, which has grown stronger for the worse with the passage of time and now grows foul in my sight with an intolerable cry. That “great” or “large” is often said both in praise and in blame cannot rightly be disputed, either as to the fact or the manner, provided that the attentive hearer considers both our writings and those of the pagans, in which greatness often signifies greatness of vices.

[Col. 1106C] In Zechariah: “What art thou, O great mountain, before Zerubbabel?” (Zech. 4). And in the Gospel: “If you have faith,” he says, “and say to this mountain, ‘Remove yourself and cast yourself into the sea,’ it shall be done” (Matt. 21). What does it mean that this is called both a mountain and possessed of greatness, unless its swelling is indicated rather than any solid fullness? That is, it swells greatly with a great heap of vices and does not diminish from its harmful swelling through correction or repentance. [Col. 1106D] Thus we find a great thief and a great harlot; and the more anyone especially and pre-eminently strives to be entangled in vices, the more he may be called greater, first, or foremost. Hence the Apostle, when he said that “Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners,” added: “Of whom I am the first” (1 Tim. 1). By this he intended it to be understood that he was the greatest and foremost sinner, since, as it seemed to him, he had offended the Savior more than others, breathing threats and slaughter and grievously persecuting his Church—although he was enveloped not so much in darkness of malice as still in that of ignorance.

[Col. 1107A] Conversely, when he showed himself visited by divine grace and reduced from that swelling savagery to the humility of faith and patience, he wished to call himself Paul—that is, “little”—although he was found to labor more than all others in the Church. “Paul,” he says, “a servant of Christ Jesus” (Rom. 1). And to the Ephesians: “To me, the least of all the saints, grace has been given” (Eph. 3). In Ezekiel also the sinful soul is reproachfully called great, since she is accused of having fallen into the impurity of fornication not equally with, but more than, the rest: “Filthy, noble, great in destruction” (Ezek. 22). This greatness or nobility is not reckoned sufficiently evident unless defilement, as though ruling over it, is first attributed to it. Indeed, just as that woman must be rebuked whom only blameworthy things follow, so those things that obey the commands of this preceding ruler must also be rebuked.

[Col. 1107B] But she is great because she is greatly, or magnificently, defiled: she commits fornication with the Egyptians, who are likewise swollen with greatness; and, committing fornication, she is joined with fornicators in equal wickedness. Clearly, greatness is accumulated not by bulk, but by some blameworthy heap. Of these it was said above in the same prophet: “You committed fornication with the sons of Egypt, your neighbors, great of flesh” (Ezek. 16). What is this so emphatically expressed greatness of flesh, unless it is the great, overflowing—indeed, utterly overflowing—shamefulness of carnal pleasures, into which the Egyptians, having cast continence far away, dissolve, [636] and like beasts roll down into the deep and broad abyss of lust? Of them, much later on, it is said: “Their flesh is like the flesh of asses, and their emission like the emission of horses” (Ezek. 23).

[Col. 1107C] This is the greatness of the Egyptians: forgetting that they ought to be human beings endowed with reason, and to seek with a contrite and humble mind the vision of their Creator, they have been so subjected to the heat and itch of fornication that they have been reduced to dumb animals, bent down and wholly devoted to the body. For whoever makes no eager effort of mind to awaken to the things of the spirit, but desires to attain only bodily things with enfeebled softness and a certain stupid sluggishness, is no longer judged a human being by the privilege of reason, but, according to a certain philosopher, is proved to live like a swine or an ass.

For Boethius was not unacquainted with our writings, nor had he devoted his efforts merely to knowing the fables of poets; but, reading more attentively both the writings of the New Law and the ancient prophets, by grace bestowed he had understood the truth of the Scriptures [Col. 1107D]. He knew, therefore, that a human being subject to the body, given over to luxury, neglectful of virtues, and delighting in the filth of vices, is often called in those same Scriptures by various names of beasts, because, having darkened the image of the Creator, he rejoices to live in a beastly manner. This same philosopher, an attentive student of such teachings from our writings, at length received by wholesome counsel the mysteries of our faith; and advancing in merits, he raised his eagle-like eye to the Trinity itself and did not neglect to write for us what he beheld there, imitating our Augustine.

Considering how ruinously anyone is changed into, or grows into, a beast who, according to the Prophet, rots away in his own dung, he preferred humbly to perform works of holiness under the wings of faith than, through philosophy and vain deceit, to boast of himself as somewhat great. [Col. 1108A] For the city of Nineveh swelled with the faulty greatness described above; the cry of its wickedness grew intolerably foul before God. Therefore God, as was said, warned Jonah to frighten that wrongly great city by fitting preaching.

## CHAPTER LXXX

“But he arose,” he says, “to flee to Tarshish from the face of the Lord” (Jonah 1). The dove-like prophet feared to preach harsh things, lest, at his grave word, the city should perish according to its deserts. He did not yet know by what counsel or to what end divine goodness wished to frighten it—this goodness which wished and knew that it would be instructed toward faith and repentance.

[Col. 1108B] Or perhaps the simple prophet did not wish to go there and impart the good word, the word of warning, to the peoples of the nations, lest, if on hearing the word they hastened to be raised from stones into children of Abraham, he should see the Jews, his own nation, rejected for the desert of unbelief. For he knew, as Isaiah said, that the Lord would blind the heart of this people (Isa. 6), would dry up the fatness of the olive tree by the heat of unbelief sent upon it, and that then its former holiness would fail when the converted multitude of the Gentiles entered into faith. He did not wish outsiders to enter thus at the end, so as to see—and sorrow over—his own people wickedly falling away from the same faith; and, lest the foretold blinding should overtake the Israelites in his presence, he wished either to prevent or to delay the Ninevites’ entrance into faith.

[Col. 1108C] Therefore the prophet, not very wisely seeking an escape from his fear, thought that nowhere could he flee better than into silence, so that there, hidden from the disturbance of people, he might lie concealed and explore the joy of quiet and contemplative leisure. For *Tharsis* is interpreted “the exploration of joy.” The prophet had perceived how great a joy is found in silence, when a mind desiring rest is freed from the tumult of public affairs; when divine goodness is encountered in devout meditation; when, in the fitting wine-cellar, the Spirit sometimes bestows the sublime sanctuary of prophecy; when, forgetful of present things, the mind feels itself borne wholly into heavenly things, and, as though it had already left the body behind, does not consent to the body’s desires, and, joined to the choirs of angels, does not dissent from their pure desire.

Yet this is not granted continuously or constantly to one who is bodily, even if he has at times deserved to be made drunk by it. Rather, he feels himself promoted to that benefit swiftly and, as it were, for a moment; then, whether willing or unwilling, he is quickly compelled to be turned back to his own affairs [Col. 1108D]. The prophet, judging this gift of grace not to have been lost, eagerly seeks again what had been interrupted. But since the sweetness of contemplation is not tasted contrary to God’s will, and no one burdened by the stains of disobedience reaches it, the prophet, while refusing to obey the good command, justly does not deserve fully to find the joy he explored. For as long as one obeys not God’s will but one’s own, the sweet joy of desired contemplation is not felt, and the eye is wholly blinded or darkened for searching out spiritual things, unless it seeks them in pure and simple obedience.

[Col. 1109A] Thus another Prophet says: “From thy commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. 118 [119]). “When,” he says, “I kept your commands more diligently, when I obeyed perfectly not my own will but rather yours, then I felt [637] that greater understanding was given to me, and that the inner eye was cleared of dust for seeing inward things.” Conversely, because Jonah was found disobedient, he was hindered from reaching Tarshish in accordance with his purpose; and while he thinks to find the joy of contemplation through the protection of flight, by just judgment he is compelled to come to grievous sorrow. For when a storm arose at sea because of the disobedience of the fugitive, the sailors cast him into the depths of the raging ocean; and a great sea-creature, at the Lord’s command, swallowed him when he had been cast out, while the monstrous beast [Col. 1109B] kept the man unharmed in its belly. A wondrous thing! A human being endowed with reason does not fear to oppose heavenly commands, while a sea-creature loves to obey; and when the Prophet is mistaken in thinking flight a safe remedy, the fish voluntarily offers itself and receives ears for hearing.

Accordingly, the obedient fish detained the disobedient prophet and, when he had repented, vomited him forth again at the Lord’s command. For the justice of the one who commanded wished to punish him in such a way that his mercy nevertheless did not wish him to perish. But the Lord did not allow him, punished and chastened by the cautery of repentance, to go to Tarshish; rather, he sent him back to preach to the Ninevites, knowing it would be most beneficial both for the prophet to place the command above his own will and for the saving message to strike terror into the city.

## CHAPTER LXXXI

[Col. 1109C]

And, he says, the word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying: “Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach the preaching which I shall speak to thee” (Jonah 3). Since you are commanded to utter not your own words but mine, there is no reason why you should fear to undertake such preaching. For even if, whether sparing the Jews or envying the Gentiles, you choose again to remain silent, it is certain that my purpose will not remain ineffectual. Since Nineveh swells with the magnitude of its crimes and, as though fed by wind, does not know how to waste away from its diseased emptiness, I wish the thunderbolt of preaching to make its sickness more fully known to it, and that it may be reduced from its swelling not by your sting, but by the piercing and compunctive sting of my word.

[Col. 1109D] But who are you, that you should be able to weaken my will and, when it is weakened, establish your own purpose? Soft and feeble clay does not resist its maker; and if perhaps it strives to do so, the powerful and benevolent potter does not cease from his work. “Go therefore,” he says, “and preach the preaching which I speak to thee” (ibid.). At this word the prophet did not resist again. Chastened by the scourge, he no longer seized upon flight as a refuge, but chose rather, under the guidance of good obedience, to preach than, with obedience wounded, to explore joy in harmful silence. “Therefore he arose,” he says, “and went to Nineveh according to the word of the Lord, and he cried and said: ‘Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown’” (ibid.).

[Col. 1110A] Greatly terrified by such thunder, the Ninevites, laying aside their swelling pride, were reduced to such humility that, led by repentance, they covered themselves in cheap sackcloth; and when a fast had been proclaimed, both animals and people went hungry in sackcloth and ashes. For they had heard that the supreme Judge is moved to wrath by sins, but shows himself kind and merciful to those afflicted in repentance. Therefore they hope that if their great iniquity is powerfully overthrown by the battering-ram of sorrow, he too may perhaps mercifully turn from what he had threatened. “Who knows,” says the king, “whether God may turn and forgive, and turn from the fury of his wrath, so that we shall not perish?” (Jonah 3).

You see the king, who a little before had been wickedly unbridled, now healthfully instructed by inspiring grace; and he not only leaves his royal throne in the condition of his body, but, with his mind humbled, does not entertain any presumptuous thought. [Col. 1110B] “The king,” he says, “arose from his throne, cast off his garment, clothed himself in sackcloth, sat in ashes, and cried out and said: ‘Let neither people nor animals taste anything; let them be covered with sackcloth and cry to the Lord mightily, and let each man turn from his evil way’” (ibid.). And he added what was stated before: “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive?” etc. (ibid.).

Although the king knows that God is turned from wrath by the repentance of some, he does not know whether his own humility deserves acceptance. For though every penitent feels himself afflicted by mourning and sorrow, still, clothed in flesh, he does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or of love. [Col. 1110C] Thus, considering on the one hand God’s merciful clemency, he takes up hope; on the other, the blind ignorance of human beings, he does not presume with insolent confidence, lest perhaps something profitable, growing through the irrigation of compunction, should be quickly emptied at its very beginning by the breath of presumption.

When divine goodness perceived both his outwardly abased repentance and his inwardly discerning hope, it did not despise the king and people who felt alike. Rather, God, who together granted them the grace to repent and pray, also graciously heard their groans and prayers. A good king, who did not inflict reciprocal threats or blows upon the threatening prophet, nor contradict the divine word with royal arrogance; but, casting off purple, he put on thin sackcloth; forgetful of his throne, he threw himself humbly upon the ground; laying aside the diadem, he defiled his head with ashes; and he bowed down devoutly and humbly everything in him that had swelled high.

[Col. 1110D] A good king, who, having heard the preaching, first of all afflicted himself; fasting and abstaining, he forbade food to animals and people alike. Having shortly before surpassed them in arrogance and pleasure, he now went before them in mourning and repentance, and did not permit his followers [638] to place their hope in a human being. “Let animals and people,” he says, “cry mightily to God” (ibid.). The king commands that the public cry be directed not to himself but to God, and that this cry be strengthened by inner contrition, so that, since the greatness of him who is asked is great, unwearying strength may be able to reach it. For he knows that God is stirred to great wrath by the magnitude of crimes, and that his great anger is not appeased except by strong contrition. And because a worthy recognition of past deeds now gnaws at the conscience, he wishes satisfaction not to be out of harmony with that recognition.

[Col. 1111A] Therefore, just as he had been chief and foremost in contracting guilt, so he wished to be first and conspicuous in abolishing it, lest his eminence should contribute more to the detriment of justice than to its more honorable and useful increase. The common people, following both his example and command, abhorred and cursed the dissolute works of their former life; freed from their bonds by contrition of spirit, fasting, and tears, they won, when the Judge was appeased, the merit of justice as well. “God,” he says, “saw that they had turned from their evil way, and he had mercy; and concerning the evil which he had spoken of doing to them, he did not do it” (Jonah 3).

When God sees king and people not at variance with one another, but sitting as most attentive hearers before their instructor; [Col. 1111B] truly repenting inwardly of their past deeds and outwardly presenting themselves as afflicted and utterly abased, his immeasurable mercy cannot fail to be moved by the vows and prayers of such people, nor fail to pity them in their repentance with his innate compassion. Because mercy now prevailed, he did not carry out the evil which he had previously declared under the demands of justice. Rather, covering the sight of their monstrous sins with the veil of forgiveness, he turned away, and changed the flashing thunderbolts of threats into the dew of clemency.

He heard their voices—or rather, their devout desire—and did not punish their iniquities as he had said. [Col. 1111C] This does not mean that God, who must be believed true, uttered a lie, although it is certain that on the fortieth day he did not bring upon them the foretold overthrow. For the statement, “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (ibid.), must be understood thus: on that day it deserved to be overthrown, and because of the desert of its wickedness the overthrow would not be delayed beyond that day; but through the intervention of repentance, it is removed as night is removed when the sun’s ray rises. Therefore, when the truthful word assigned the city what appeared to be a fixed term of overthrow, it did not truly designate destruction, but subtly designated desert: namely, that it was bound by such guilt of crimes that, by its merits, no further delay would be granted to it.

But what is sometimes brought upon it, or upon any sinner, [Col. 1111D] by desert is freely remitted when justice gives way for a time; the inner mind is visited with the bitterness of repentance; and thus, by free forgiveness, vengeance long deserved is forestalled.

## CHAPTER LXXXII

Or perhaps merciful God, whose care for sinners is great, seeing immediately what for us is past or future, at last looked mercifully upon a chosen but neglected people and wished the prophet to utter what even he who uttered it did not understand. For the overthrow which merciful God arranged to bring about for the better, the dim-sighted prophet thought would occur for the worse; and, hearing the word, he did not perceive clearly enough that, just as the just God overthrows unto evil, so the merciful God overthrows unto good. Hence the wise man says: “Overthrow the wicked, and they shall not be” (Prov. 12). For when God, forgetting wrath, turns himself to mercy, he removes and overturns our wickedness from its foundation, and [Col. 1112A] renders wholly null by beneficial overthrow the structure that had wickedly been raised against justice.

God intended that such an overthrow should occur among the Ninevites, but Jonah, who was still announcing it, did not see this; uncertain what end or benefit the preaching imposed upon him would have, he preferred to remain in the joy of quiet, leisure, and silence. But because God, who wills that necessary good things not be kept silent, intended to have mercy both upon those to whom the message is addressed and upon those who deliver it, he did not allow the prophet to persist in his purpose. Instead, after fitting correction, he sent him back to teach the Ninevites. In this he wished not only to remove the prophet’s fault—for, neglecting the command, he had chosen to be held in harmful silence—but also to frighten the aforesaid Nineveh by his good word and, shaken by strong terror, to advance it more swiftly toward good.

[Col. 1112B] “You grieve,” he says, “over the ivy for which you did not labor; and shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which are more than one hundred and twenty thousand people, and animals?” (Jonah 4). It seemed fitting to that goodness which is incomprehensible that he should spare all the more a city enveloped in extensive crimes, and, although its deserts deserved nothing but the losses of overthrow, should nevertheless save within it people and animals by the gift of grace.

Good animals are those who, when gifts of salvation are divinely bestowed, are perhaps joined in this grace to the elect among human beings: rejecting the freedom through whose precipitous course they would have perished, they take up Christ’s yoke and do not kick against the bond. Of such David says: “Thou shalt save people and animals, O Lord” (Ps. 35 [36]). [Col. 1112C] For he saves not only those who excel in reason and knowledge and now pursue heavenly things alone, but also those who obey those leaders, presenting themselves to their teacher, like animals to a rider, [639] bowing down in order to receive the teachings of salvation. Of these it is said: “I became like an animal before thee” (Ps. 72 [73]). For the devout and humble man showed himself an animal before the one whose command he openly—or perhaps diligently—bore; whose yoke or burden he preferred to harmful freedom; and whom, as his rider and protector, he honored in grateful obedience.

Thus the Lord, going to Jerusalem, is said to have sat upon an animal—not because, weak in his feet, he needed its assistance, but so that the healing rider, by his riding, might restore to health the animal [Col. 1112D] that had been made sick by unbridled injury. He has mercy on animals of this kind at Nineveh when Jonah is prevented from going to Tarshish as he had intended, and when Nineveh does not undergo overthrow on the fortieth day. For this purpose he wished it to be frightened by the prophetic word: that, repenting, it might hasten to restrain itself from its presumed license to sin; and, when it had been changed for the better by saving terror, the harshness of threats might also be changed into the sweetness of pardon.

[Col. 1113A] By the stern judgment of a strict judge he likewise wished to frighten King Hezekiah when he sent Isaiah to him in his sickness, so that the king, shaken by the prophetic word, might be restored to devotion, and death foretold might more graciously be deferred by the merit of devotion. “Hezekiah,” he says, “was sick unto death; and Isaiah entered to him and said: ‘Thus says the Lord: Set thy house in order, for thou shalt die and not live’” (Isa. 38).

A good message: it does not soothe a sick king with hope of life, but rather shakes him with terror of death and shows what royal height can accomplish—or indeed, how it is nothing—when the severe and austere power of death comes upon him. Death does not fear royal insignia or throne or purple; it is not held back by gate, bar, or iron bolt, nor prevented by the circuit of walls or the height of towers. Rather, according to a certain pagan writer (Horace, *Odes* I.4), it is said to strike the towers of kings and the huts of the poor with equal foot.

At its stroke every wise person trembles; mindful of the past and provident for the future, he groans, and like a good householder he now sets his house in order, adding no further things that must be cut away as harmful [Col. 1113B]. The foot or hand by which death strikes the towers of kings and the huts of the poor—a force whose violence their strength cannot repel—is that suffering, that sickness of our body, by whose harsher onset vigor, health, and beauty wither. Death, which seems to envy all mortals, is rightly understood not to see those whom it envies: raging in obstinate harshness, it despises all, and does not distinguish whom it despises less or whom more. Of it a certain pagan also says:

> “That dark hand lays hold upon all.”

[Col. 1113C] You see that death does not fear to lay hands on everyone; but these hands are said to be dark because it has no merciful regard either for those whom it should have spared longer, or for those whom it should quickly have crushed. Delaying the latter negligently, it seems not to see. Thus many crowned with the spring flowers of adolescence, many fortified by the reliable strength of pleasing youth, many exaltedly distinguished by wealth and honors, many sweetly instructed through growing learning—whose life was burdensome neither to themselves nor to others and would have been fruitful not only now but much later—death, caring nothing for them or such as they, unexpectedly seizes in its blind onset before their time.

[Col. 1113D] Conversely, those oppressed by the heavy burden of poverty, rendered inglorious by the shameful disgrace of low condition, dishonored as dull and foolish by the languid torpor of ignorance, disfigured as perverse and harsh by depravity of character, bent over and made troublesome both to themselves and to others by the infirmity of complaining old age—those in whom there is no virtue and no appearance of virtue—death sometimes does not know how to find. Yet they live, if it is life not to experience the advantages of living. Therefore many are found to complain greatly about death’s judgment: unhappy and impious, it does not measure the claims or weights of things; it blindly fails to find those who ought rightly to die, while it comes with unexpected harm upon those whose life is more welcome.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

[Col. 1114A]

But, according to a certain philosopher (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy* I, metrum 1), the death of human beings would be considered happy if, with its dim sight cleared, it possessed somewhat greater discernment: namely, if it did not bring itself upon sweet years and, when summoned, did not too often delay its coming to sad ones. Hence, just as it does not comply with the wishes of the happy, so neither does it heed the plaintive vows of the unhappy; rather, it proves more grievously troublesome to both, since by undiscriminating judgment it denies itself troublesome to all. For just as it is blind, so it is deaf. It frequents too often the dwellings of the happy, where it is unwelcome, but in a kind of arrogance or neglect turns away from the presence of the wretched; and their cry scarcely reaches its ears, which become still more stubbornly and severely deaf to hear it. The aforesaid philosopher also complains of it:

[Col. 1114B]

> “Alas! With what a deaf ear she turns away from the wretched,  
> And cruelly refuses to close their weeping eyes!”  
> (*Ibid.*)

A remarkable turning away! As was said, death does not sport with the laughter of the happy, but unexpectedly cuts short their breath of life too soon; yet it offers no smaller cup of distress to the wretched when, by its unwelcome withdrawal, it does not hasten to close their weeping eyes. Thus it rages more importunately in both cases. It is accustomed truly to pity no one and properly to defer to no one; [640] and it is found more remarkable and much more severe in this, that anyone afflicted does not experience it as quickly as he wishes. While he wastes away through its delay or absence, death remains absent and unheeding toward that wretch. [Col. 1114C]

Since death’s office is not to accord with the conditions of life, but, on the contrary, to grant the end of living beings in differing manners and circumstances, if anyone is compelled to die in its course contrary to his own will, and if a more welcome life is forced to yield to a stronger power, the dying person has no reason to complain fittingly of death’s justice, since death truly performs what belongs to it as death. But when some are shaken by many and varied troubles, and amid many grievous things suffer nothing more grievous than life, it is remarkable why death itself does not come at their desire, since in doing so it would agree with them and would not depart from what is proper to it.

[Col. 1114D] But perhaps death, which in a sorrowful course snatches away the happier life, does not quickly visit the more sorrowful life with welcome arrival because it has decreed for itself this penal monstrosity and, if you consider more carefully, is accustomed to keep this decree: not to attach itself with a compassionate disposition to anyone’s wishes, but more gladly and frequently to oppose them by blind and deaf withdrawal. In this death recognizes that it is doing its own work: it does not intend to fulfill anyone’s will, nor does it stand favorably beside their desires and prayers, but, rejoicing in victorious cruelty, confronts and resists them.

For just as to wish to live and be unable is death, so too to wish to die and be unable is likewise a kind of death.
