In this latter death the body is no longer separated from the soul, but the will is tortured while both, or one of the two, suffers. I think Paul spoke of such death when his body was tormented by various toil or his spirit by excessive weakness, and neither was released from the other by the loosening of invisible bonds; rather, both—or one—were miserably tossed in a kind of lake of sorrow. [Col. 1115A] “Every day,” he says, “I die, brethren” (1 Cor. 15). And David: “For thy sake we are put to death all the day” (Ps. 43 [44]).

Were the Prophet and Apostle, all day or daily, released from bodily bonds? Or were they not rather enveloped in the stains of grievous sufferings, so that their death should be called not a release hostile to the union of soul and body, but tribulation perversely inflicted on the will? Because they saw themselves burdened by many pressing troubles, they earnestly wished to be freed from them by the benefit of release, suffering heavily not so much what the world, set in evil, [Col. 1115B] inflicted, as the fact that release delayed the remedy they desired. Hence the same Apostle says: “I desire to be dissolved” (Phil. 1). And David: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. 119 [120]).

For the disease by which the Prophet and Apostle were afflicted—namely, their endurance of the unwelcome burden of the present life—they judged no remedy more fitting than bodily death, whose absence they rightly considered a kind of death. Although death did not yet come to free them, and the body still enfolded the soul in tenacious union, the very delay of release seemed a kind of death, since often nothing is held more grievous than to live against one’s will. [Col. 1115C] Hence a certain pagan says:

> “I live, if it is life to possess a kind of death.”  
> (Ovid)

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

Because this man endured the hatreds of his elders, the absence of his own people, loss of his country, and unwelcome exile, he was untried in future things and impatient with present ones. He thought that perhaps he would be considered happier, or at least less miserable, if the welcome hand of death closed for him the gate of living. There is indeed in one who suffers a kind of natural changeableness: he more grievously dreads what he harshly endures in the present, and judges somewhat sweeter what has not yet happened for him to experience through suffering. Even if he knows by report or perhaps by experience that the other condition is more grievous, he nevertheless more gladly flees what he feels to be harmful at hand; and, desiring to pass over to what he undoubtedly knows [Col. 1115D] will harm him when attained, he thinks there is at least some remedy in the transition itself.

Because this pagan could not yet obtain such a remedy according to his wish, but the present life seemed to hold him against his will, he declares that he possesses not life but a kind of death, because it is death when death refuses to present itself to one who longs for it. It is death, I say, when what the mind ardently desires is not granted, and what it hates remains obstinately or is imposed upon it. Nothing is more grievous, even if it ought perhaps to be judged pious or beneficial, than that to which the will is found to be more ardently opposed. Indicating this, Boethius says:

> “Impious life prolongs unwelcome delays.”

[Col. 1116A] Troubled with sorrow, Boethius calls life impious because it harshly opposes his will: though hateful, it still wishes to remain longer, while he himself wishes it to end sooner. The more burdensome life makes its own presence through importunity, the more welcome death, if it came, would make its presence; and Boethius would judge it happy and prosperous for himself if, as was said above, desired and summoned, it did not delay in coming.

Yet for some, to whom the present life seems not merely useless but harmful, as oppressive heaviness contracts and crushes their wills, death passes them by the more fleetingly the more miserable they are, and rejects both their words and their feelings by deaf refusal. Of such John says in the Apocalypse: “People shall seek death and shall not find it; [Col. 1116B] they shall desire to die, and death shall flee from them” (Rev. 9). The fifth angel, sounding the trumpet, declares that those upon whose foreheads the sign of God cannot be found will experience such tribulation that the presence of life will be exceedingly burdensome to them and the absence of death no less hateful.

For it was not given to the locusts or scorpions to compel them quickly to die, but to afflict the living more harshly with a longer punishment, lest that same punishment should appear slight and negligible and be more quickly ended according to the sufferer’s wish. Therefore they seek death, but cannot at all overtake it as it flees; they desire to die, but are compelled against their will to live; and they seem to themselves to die all the more grievously and miserably because they are not allowed to die according to their desire.

[Col. 1116C] The prophet of prophets himself likewise foretold in his Gospel this kind of death, in which those living die more grievously: those who endure the intolerable troubles of this life and complain bitterly both of life’s present burden and, inconsolably, of death’s absence. Set in the agony of his Passion for the salvation of us all, he said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. For behold, days are coming in which they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us’” (Luke 23).

You see how great is the misery which the daughters of Jerusalem must suffer, and how insatiable is the desire for death in those who suffer. Abhorring what they are presently compelled to undergo, they long to be covered by mountains or hills in the desire for an unknown death. So greatly is the fury of their persecutors inflamed against them, and so craftily does malice rage against them, that their persecutors prefer them to waste away under prolonged torture rather than find the remedy they desire in a swift death.

The persecutors of Christ also wickedly gave heed to this: certain persons demanded, not that a spear or sword be driven into him so that he might die quickly, but rather that he be crucified, so that he might suffer longer and, as they thought, more fittingly. Christ alludes to this when he adds, addressing the daughters of Jerusalem: “For if they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” (ibid.).

Green wood is that whose root lives and whose trunk flourishes, so that in its proper season it can bud forth and spread out branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit. Even if it lies concealed in the cold of winter as though dead, it becomes green again in springtime through an inborn vigor. But dry wood is that which, deprived of the power of budding, withers languidly: in neither spring nor winter does it swell with budding shoots, smile with flowers, or bend beneath the abundance of fruit. Though it may appear to be wood in a form not deceptive, it nevertheless lacks within itself an effective power at will.

[Col. 1116D] Therefore Christ is not inappropriately called green wood: his inward power is held back by no obstacle; violence of death cannot be imposed upon him when he wills to live, nor, when he wills to accept it, can death be delayed by anyone’s cunning plan. For this purpose, as has been said, they wished to prepare for him the gibbet of the cross: that while alive they might torture him more severely and for longer, and, sated with the immense and extended weight of his punishments, might satisfy their perversity by such a welcome spectacle.

But he, in whose power it lay both to die and not to die, who did neither according to the desire of his persecutors but rather according to his own will, showed himself more plainly to be powerful and to be green wood when, though they did not yet wish it, he himself willingly entrusted his spirit into the Father’s hands. For just as the violence of the wicked did not force him into a swifter death, so their craftiness did not compel him to a longer life. Free from the necessity which binds the weakness of all our corrupted nature, he is known to possess, by the singular privilege of voluntary power, both life and death.

If, then, those who persecute the justice of the good in their wicked will seek to exercise their malice upon the green wood in such a way that they wish it both to be tortured with severe punishments [Col. 1117A] and to be kept from death for longer—though it is certain that it is bound neither by their laws nor by their wishes—how fiercely will their malice rage against us, and to what misery of life will it bring you, who are dry wood because your sins demand it and who cannot resist their malice by an inborn power? For it is not within man’s own power, by his own strength, either not to die or, conversely, to die at will. Rather, he is often compelled to die unwillingly, and often compelled to live, fettered by unwelcome stains.

## Chapter LXXXV

The aforesaid Jonah, utterly weary of living, prays to be taken away; but his request is not granted. His prayer being frustrated, he is compelled to live longer, though he judges death itself to be better for him than life.

“Lord,” he says, “I beseech thee, take my soul from me, for death is better to me than life” (Jonah 4). And Elijah: “It is enough for me, Lord; take my soul, for I am no better than my fathers” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19).

You see Jonah and Elijah rejecting the weariness of this life, wishing to exchange present things, known by experience, for future things, unknown by experience. For when the mind is more grievously offended by present evils, through hatred of what it feels it counts light whatever experience has not yet felt. Yet death does not then close life’s door to those who desire it, because death, blind and deaf, neither sees anyone’s groans nor hears them. Rather, being judged dull and senseless because it lacks these senses, it works effectively upon those whom it finds by touch alone.

For it is said to wander about, touching whatever lies in its path with hand or foot; and in touching it is not restrained by merciful goodwill. [Col. 1117B] It disturbs the health of small and great alike by even the slightest touch; and if it presses more harshly, it brings on the burden of dying. For when it lies heavily upon anyone it has found and persists, neither that person’s craft nor strength can withstand its grievous touch. But, according to the philosopher Boethius: “The lowly head and the lofty alike are wrapped up, and from life’s high station are rolled down to the final end.”

Since death did not know that Christ the man possessed so surpassingly excellent a power that to die or not to die lay within the choice of his own will, it attacked him too with its customary confidence, more harshly; and it entangled in its bonds not only one living, but Life itself.

Yet death did not win a triumphal victory over him, because Christ received it not under compulsion but voluntarily. Though, as man, he could by his inborn power have escaped experiencing it, nevertheless by that goodness which is his own he chose to submit to our laws. But what he chose not to delay in himself at the fitting time, he chose not to inflict upon the terrified king Hezekiah. When death strongly struck Hezekiah with hand or foot, Christ—who alone was able—more powerfully repelled it from him.

“Set thy house in order,” he says, “for thou shalt die and shalt not live” (Isaiah 38). Hezekiah, whom the height of imperial rank had made illustrious, was oppressed as though by a present hand of death in the bodily sickness that pressed upon him; and the dreadful force of the divine threat which followed shook and terrified him, so that no certainty of continued life remained for him.

[Col. 1117C] For he knew that death showed deference to no human being. Just as it did not prefer the least person to the greatest, so neither did it prefer the greatest to the least; but upon whomever it more stubbornly laid hand or foot, it utterly crushed not only that person’s health but also life itself. Pressed down by illness, therefore, he fears imminent death; and, as the goad of fear presses him, his grief grows greatly heavier—not because he was paying nature’s debt, which he knew his fathers had paid and from which no human being thereafter had wholly freed himself, but because in his present death he saw the hope frustrated which he had believed would rather be fulfilled with a prosperous outcome.

He recalled that God had long ago promised his fathers Abraham and David, and had sent them away, strengthened by that promise, into the refreshment of peace: that in the course of time one would be born from their stock in whom and through whom blessing would be granted to the nations. Since this same king traced the line of his descent from Abraham and David in a direct succession extending from them down to himself, he had hoped that Christ would issue from that same line and believed that he himself would be the author of this offspring.

But because he was still without children, and both sickness and the prophetic word threatened him with death, the approaching pressure of unwelcome death shattered his consoling hope; and, with that hope shattered, he was tortured by inconsolable grief. “In the midst of my days,” he says, “I shall go to the gates of hell” (ibid.). “The span of life which I had hoped for has not yet been fulfilled; the course of my days is checked as if halfway through; and already I am compelled to reach too soon the gates of hell, to which I had thought I would come only after leaving behind offspring.”

[Col. 1117D] “My life has been cut off like a weaver’s web; while I was still beginning, he cut me down” (Isaiah 38). “Still immature in age,” he says, “and unfruitful in works, I was beginning my task; mindful of what lay behind, I was anxiously stretching toward what lay before. Like an eager merchant entering the marketplace, I awaited the best end; set in the racecourse, I thought I would reach the goal. And behold, the hasty weaver now cuts down the web begun and, with an untimely sickle, cuts short its fruitful completion.

“Therefore, suffering violence, where shall I go? With the anchor of hope broken, whither shall I pass? Into whose court shall I enter, that I may offer prayers? What fruit will there be for anyone when I perish as a dry stock? ‘Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me’” (ibid.).

Rightly, one suffering violence does not plan to resist by his own power, but, being weak, places his cause in a strong hand. Clearly knowing that neither royal power nor riches can prevail against death, he asks the mighty God to answer for him who is powerless. He is the one who can by his own power lift the heavy hand or foot of death, who can restore the sick and despairing person by his healing hand; at whose command infirmity flees, death trembles, the dying recover strength, and the dead return to life.

[Col. 1118A] When he saw the devotion, tears, and prayer of this sick man, being supremely good and free from envy, he did not begrudge his progress. Rather, pleased that the king had wholly abandoned his swelling self-confidence, he powerfully and mercifully sent death, which was near, far away. “I have heard thy prayer,” he says, “and I have seen thy tear; behold, I will add fifteen years to thy days” (ibid.).

Death was pressing the king with a strong hand, and the prophetic word increased fear in the oppressed man. For this reason divine goodness chose to hear him while he wept and, having heard him, to grant him the foretold span of life, so that within those added days Manasseh might be born to the same king, and through him the line of descent might be woven anew through restored succession.

The king obtained both this span of time and this son by prayer and tears: when, afflicted by illness, he groaned at the prophet’s word; when the prophet, at the Lord’s command, had threatened him with imminent death; and when the king was stirred not to anger or threats, but to prayers and tears.

Therefore, when the prophet was commanded to speak to the sick king and to urge him by threatening words to set his house in order, he ought not, through insolence and stubbornness, to oppose the One commanding him; nor ought he, by imposing silence, to conceal the good things which had to be spoken. [Col. 1118B] By this utterance the prophet gained for himself the merit of obedience; the terrified king anxiously sought God; God graciously heard him as he sought anxiously; and, having heard him, granted a span of life and, within that span, the son he desired.

And even if perhaps the king had not listened to the threatening prophet with a haughty brow, and even if God had not heard the king in his hardness of heart as described above, it would nevertheless not have been the prophet’s counsel to keep silent. Commanded to speak, if he did not speak, he would render himself guilty and blameworthy. For whether or not the person commanded to be admonished listens, the one commanded to admonish must not be kept silent; rather, as he owes necessary instruction to a ready hearer, so, when the hearer is hardened, he nevertheless owes obedience to the commander.

## Chapter LXXXVI

Thus the Lord says to Ezekiel: “If, when I say to the wicked, ‘Thou shalt surely die,’ thou hast not spoken” (Ezekiel 3), so that the wicked person may guard himself from his way, that wicked person shall die in his iniquity, but “his blood I will require at thy hand.” If the prophet, commanded to speak, does not speak because negligence weighs upon him, and the sinner is overwhelmed by the onset of death because the prophet did not speak, the sinner indeed perishes by the merit of his own offense, but the danger arising from him is required from the hand of the one who did not speak.

But if the prophet has spoken what he was commanded, and the hearer rejects what he has heard and is not restrained by due fear, the person who did not heed the prophet’s warnings dies, while the monitor is delivered because he obeyed the divine commands by speaking. This is added concerning Ezekiel: “But if, when thou hast announced to the wicked that he should turn from his ways, he has not turned from his way, he shall die in his iniquity; but thou hast delivered thy soul” (Ezekiel 3).

Therefore one commanded to proclaim good things to the wicked has no reason to refuse the command. Even if benefit is not granted to the evil hearer, fitting usefulness is nevertheless not denied to the good admonisher.

Thus Moses is sent to warn Pharaoh; nevertheless Pharaoh, though warned, is hardened against his warnings. And although the admonisher tries to excuse himself so as not to speak, he is not permitted to refuse the authority of the One commanding. “Come,” he says, “I will send thee to Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring my people out of Egypt” (Exodus 3). And below: “I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go” (Exodus 4).

[Col. 1118C] Hearing that he was to go among the Egyptians and speak to King Pharaoh words that, though good, would not be welcome, Moses, untrained for the assigned ministry, trembles as he obeys and, fearful in heart, longs rather to hide in silence. Since the command of a greater person is not fittingly refused unless an appropriate—indeed, sufficient—reason is advanced, he does not hesitate to accuse himself of being unequal to this command, so that he may more excusably refuse what is commanded.

“I beseech thee, Lord,” he says, “I am not eloquent from yesterday and the day before yesterday, nor since thou hast spoken to thy servant; I am of a more impeded and slower tongue” (ibid.). “I beseech thee,” he says, “do not impose upon me the office of speaking, and do not add the burden of thy command to one whom weakness already oppresses; for no small harm, either to himself or to another, is incurred when one undertakes to speak whom eloquence does not assist.”

“I am not eloquent from yesterday and the day before yesterday.” Before thy majesty spoke to me, he says, and before the incomparable sublimity of thy word was heard by me, so insignificant a person, I thought myself somewhat learned and ready to speak, and perhaps some regarded me as sufficiently eloquent. But after the trumpet of thy word sounded in my ears and thy wisdom became known to me through the more abundant gift of fresh grace, I seem impeded by so many tongues and obstacles that I cannot possibly be found competent to relate worthily the things which thou hast set forth more worthily.

[Col. 1118D] For just as the full disk of the moon seems to hide the lesser stars, and the brilliance of the noonday sun dims a faint lamp, so surely, when thine incomparable majesty speaks and the greatness of the speaker is considered, my childish and ineffective dullness is as though veiled and counted as nothing.

And he said: “Who made man’s mouth, or who fashioned the dumb and deaf, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I?” (ibid.). It is certain that God, the creator of all things, made the human mouth and naturally endowed it with the capacity both to speak and not to speak, so that in alternating circumstances it may be modestly covered for silence, as though by a seal, and may be willing and able to be opened for speaking good things.

What has been made ought without doubt to reverence its maker; and, when he commands, it must not be restrained by any obstacle, but, renouncing its own will, should devote itself to the decision of the greater. In nothing should the work contradict the workman, nor the thing formed the potter. Therefore, one whom the supreme craftsman has commanded not to speak may justifiably—indeed commendably—remain silent; he is then made dumb not by his own resistance, but by the One whose command he fulfills through the silence imposed upon him.

For who else rightly makes a human being dumb but the wise maker who holds clay in his strong hand, lest by its natural softness it spread out into something worse, but instead, by the maker’s grace, become a praiseworthy vessel? Moses, however, thought that he would be judged praiseworthy, or at least excusable, if, because he was slow to speak, he could remain in the silence he desired. He did not adequately perceive what sort of evil he would wrongly suffer if, by keeping silent, he indulged his own will in matters of good.

[Col. 1119A] But none except God, the creator of good things, makes a commendably dumb person. He declares, as stated above, that he made the human mouth, so that a person may then alone be commendably silent or speak when he serves not the pleasure of man but that of God.

“Who,” he says, “has fashioned the dumb?” You are preparing to make yourself dumb, and you apply no due care to seeking what is just. While you do not set the Creator’s will before your own, you lay upon your weak self the heavy burden of guilt. But who are you, that you so arrogate to yourself the privilege of your own will and rashly—indeed, presumptuously—assume what belongs to me alone: namely, that you will not use your mouth at the command of one greater, but will live by your own rule and abuse the gifts received?

It belongs to me, your Creator, to command you whom I have made, according to my will; but it belongs to you, who have been made, to prepare a ready ear for the command. Thus you should not try to make either a human being or yourself dumb, nor seek to make the thing formed equal to the potter in the privilege of power.

“For I am he who makes the dumb and deaf, the seeing and the blind.” The Lord once made the prophet Ezekiel dumb when, because the people’s sins required it, he forbade him to speak, lest a word of correction be delivered to those ungrateful and undeserving people, since no benefit would result for them from it. “I will make thy tongue cleave to thy palate,” he says, “and thou shalt be dumb, and shalt not be as a man rebuking them, for they are a provoking house” (Ezekiel 3).

[Col. 1119B] Just as Ezekiel, when commanded to speak, did not reject the authority of the One commanding, so conversely he did not stubbornly make himself dumb; rather, he himself was made dumb by the One whose command he obeyed through silence.

Likewise, the Lord commanded Jeremiah, placed among evil and incorrigible people, to become as though dumb, ordering him not to undertake concern and prayer for these reprobates and not to presume to intercede with him for the unworthy. “Do not pray,” he says, “for this people for good” (Jeremiah 14). Since the Lord sees that the benefits of prayers do not profit the people, he commands the prophet living among them to be dumb, judging it unfitting that he should rashly be wordy for people for whom, grace standing in the way, he cannot become fruitful.

## Chapter LXXXVII

God also makes a person deaf when, by his grace, he closes someone’s ear; and, with the ear closed, that person either does not hear the most wicked voice of the exacting devil, or, as though not hearing, does not bite back at malicious tongues with a retaliatory tooth, so that he may not differ from his Redeemer, whom he remembers as patient.

Thus a certain wise man, when his enemies spoke vain and harmful things against him and labored to devise and advance deceits all day long, declared that his ears, sated with many and various insults, had notably been stopped by the grace of a divine gift. “But I,” he says, “as one deaf, did not hear” (Psalm 37 [38]); and again: “I became like a man who does not hear and who has no rebukes in his mouth” (ibid.).

[Col. 1119C] Happy is the person who does not hear the loud malice of the envious and does not delight to strike back at slanderous tongues with an equal tooth; to whom divine grace grants the discipline of maintaining such conduct, that I may offer a dove-like ear to the clamor of wicked words.

On the other hand, the person who shuts his ear to a good word, an admonitory word; who does not hear the voice of those wisely uttering incantations; who, clinging to earthly and lower things, becomes deaf like an asp, and does not grow warm with any stretching of spirit toward the things that lie ahead—such a person suffers miserably and is grievously sick, and is all the more wretched because he hardens more wickedly in his purpose.

Since divine goodness does not know how to make such a deaf person, his maker deserves blame. The obstinacy of this deafness has not glory but disgrace, and its author is not God’s grace but the malice of one’s own will.

## Chapter LXXXVIII

God also makes one seeing when, by the abundant medicine of merciful grace, he lessens the swelling caused by phlegm that heavily weighs down the eye; and, wiping gently away the diseased blearedness of a cataract, cleanses the eye by the benefit of a luminous infusion. Once cleansed, it perceives things formerly unknown by experience; with the veil of ignorance driven away, it rejoices that they are laid open to it. And what lies hidden in God’s sanctuary, useful or honorable, it recognizes as made manifest to it when entrance has been opened.

On account of this vision, by which he contemplates secrets and hidden things, such a person is also called a *seer* (*videns*), receiving his name from the reality. He is marked with this designation as with a title increasing his glory, since divine goodness bestows upon him the grace of seeing.

[Col. 1119D] Thus Samuel, to whom it was granted to contemplate divine things, deserved, as Scripture shows, to be called a seer; and those now called prophets, because they perceive hidden things, were also formerly called seers in common usage. “Where,” they ask, “is the house of the seer?” And Samuel says: “I am the seer” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 9).

Jacob likewise, because he struggled mightily with an angel and, as he says, contemplated God face to face, laid aside the name which signifies the labor of struggle and received another which denotes the grace of divine vision: “Thou shalt no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be thy name” (Genesis 32). Jacob means “wrestler”; Israel, however, “a man seeing God.” And rightly: he who was willing and able to wrestle—indeed, to prevail—is called Israel. For the eye of one who is soft and womanish is not so purified that it is willing and able to aspire to see invisible things and that God may breathe into its inward face the grace of this spiritual breath.

Accordingly, Ezekiel displays certain blameworthy persons who presume for themselves the office of prophesying and, although they are unable to contemplate anything but false and empty things, falsely desire nevertheless to glory in the name of seers. “Woe,” he says, “to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and see nothing; they see vain things and divine a lie, saying, ‘The Lord says,’ when the Lord has not sent them” (Ezekiel 13).

[Col. 1120A] Lest those deceived, and themselves deceivers of others, continue for long to maintain that what they have seen is true and persist in confirming their proposed utterance in the ears of the simple, the divine word not only rebukes them threateningly but also charges them with the falsehood which it has truly discovered in them. “Have you not,” he says, “seen an empty vision and spoken a lying divination?” (ibid.).

Lest they suppose that such lying will go unpunished, and boast both of the deceitfulness of their alleged visions and of the avenger’s negligence, the judge of prophets then more openly threatens them. The truth of his threats is confirmed by an unalterable outcome, unless perhaps the sinner turns and he himself turns mercifully. “Because,” he says, “you have spoken vain things and seen a lie, my hand shall be upon the prophets, because they have deceived my people, saying, ‘Peace,’ when there is no peace” (ibid.).

These are the prophets who, deceived by their own spirit or by an evil spirit, and led by the deceiving angel of light into the deepest errors, hasten to entangle their wretched hearers in the same stains and to soothe itching ears with words that are false indeed, but welcome.

For from those whose life is corrupted by vices, yet to whom a certain authority for teaching others is entrusted; whose inward eye is held by a corrupting cataract, yet whom presumptuous opinion asserts to be seers—from these, I say, great evil and contagion are spread among the people, who rightly honor as seers those who deceive and are deceived on the basis of their proclaimed vision.

[Col. 1120B] Concerning them the Lord says through Jeremiah: “From the prophets of Jerusalem pollution has gone forth over all the earth” (Jeremiah 23). Though they ought to cleanse the defiled with holier words, to make those sterile through ignorance fruitful with the watering of saving teaching, to lead the blind and dull by the way of truth, and by both word and example to provide an incentive to holiness for those living perversely, they instead make those who are in filth still more filthy. They cause those darkened by ignorance, covered over with the cloud of falsehood, not to see at all; having lost inward sight, they wander headlong through the byways of errors and, entangled in evils, are involved in worse evils.

Though they call themselves prophets of Jerusalem because of their excellence of vision and preach peace without reliance on the support of a divine commission, they are in fact found to be rather false prophets of Babylon, stirred by an evil spirit through the allure of a deceptive command. As the poisons of its command are more gently poured into their hearts, their minds and tongues, having lost true peace, are thrown into confusion; and what has wickedly been infused into them as into a full vessel is poured out again into everything near at hand and spilled more ruinously upon all who savor only earthly things.

God mercifully seeks carefully to call his own people back from hearing them, and prudently instructs them not to be rashly deceived, showing that such prophets ought not to be heard at all, since it is clear that they are shamelessly trained to speak by their own spirit rather than God’s. “Do not,” he says, “listen to the words of the prophets who deceive you. They speak a vision of their own heart, and not from the mouth of the Lord. I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied” (ibid.).

[Col. 1120C] You see these people running to preach but not being sent; understanding, as they say, but not being admitted into God’s sanctuary; putting forth the vision of their own heart without consulting the mouth of the Lord; following their own spirit rather than the due command of the One who sends. In contrast Paul says: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10).

Therefore those who preach while not being sent, who utter false and deceptive things from their own heart, have not been made prophets by truthful inspiration, nor seers, but merely presumptuous persons by false opinion and deceptive pride. But those whose life is no longer defiled by voluntary conduct, whose inward conscience does not reproach their tongue and speech, and from whose affection and action the coming Spirit freely removes every offense—such persons he sometimes illumines with more abundant grace for prophesying.

The same Spirit is also found at times to make them blind, when in prudent counsel he does not yet grant them knowledge of hidden things, so that, when the grace of sight has been withheld, it may be sought with the concern of more fervent earnestness and, once perhaps found, may be held in the most eager embrace of humbler diligence.

Elisha indicates this when he says to Gehazi: “Let her alone, for her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has concealed it and has not revealed it to me” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 4). Elisha, although he had already long perceived many things with inward eyes instructed by the Holy Spirit, nevertheless did not know at that moment what the Shunammite woman sought from him. Perhaps he was obscured in respect of knowing it not through his own fault or desert, but divine grace was displaying in this matter its own glory alone.

[Col. 1120D] Finally, in the Gospel: “Neither this man sinned,” he says, “nor his parents, that he should be born blind, but that the glory of God might be manifested in him” (John 6). Neither his own iniquity nor that of his parents made this man blind; and no human being ought rightly to be blamed for this blindness, which divine goodness chose to appear solely in order that its glory might shine forth more excellently in it.

But the one who, fleeing the inward light, does not fear to plunge, through the fault of a corrupted will, into the abyss of harmful blindness, is not only excused by no testimony of the supreme Judge, but, as the author of his own loss, is justly and truly accused. Of such persons the Gospel says: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit” (Luke 6).

Therefore, since the person who makes himself dumb, deaf, seeing, or blind deserves blame, whereas the person whom God makes such is called praiseworthy, or at least excusable, Moses is rightly warned not to follow the error of his own will but wisely to obey the command of the greater, whether in speaking or keeping silent. “Who has fashioned the dumb and deaf, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I?” (Exodus 4).

[Col. 1121A] “I,” he says, “and I alone ought, and rightly can, be the maker of such persons, because I am the most just worker of all things that are just. If anyone else presumes to undertake this contrary to me, then, while wishing to be independent, he is found to be a blameworthy usurper over others.

“Go, therefore, and I will be in thy mouth and will teach thee what thou shalt say.” Go, he says, renouncing the decision of your own will and confidently obeying the command of the most high Majesty; and I, mighty—indeed almighty—will put into your mouth what you are to say, so that, taught by my power and benevolence, you may be considered learned and eloquent.

But Moses, not yet sufficiently strengthened by these admonitions, clinging to his purpose and remembering his own weakness more than was fitting, said: “I beseech thee, Lord, send whom thou wilt send” (ibid.). “I do not see how I can be sufficient for this command: how, by approaching Pharaoh, I can bring the children of Israel out of Egypt. But send quickly the person whom I foresee that thou wilt someday send, whom I know will powerfully accomplish whatever thou commandest.”

“And the Lord was angry with Moses” (ibid.). Because Moses does not incline a ready ear or mind to his commander, but still stubbornly recoils and withdraws from what he is commanded, Scripture declares that the same commander grew angry and assigned to Moses his brother, because of the latter’s greater grace of eloquence. “Aaron,” he says, “thy brother, I know that he is eloquent; he shall speak for thee to the people, and he shall be thy mouth” (ibid.).

[Col. 1121B] Hearing this, Moses at last yields and, giving ear to the command, no longer withdraws from it, clearly knowing and recognizing that one commanded to speak good things is not judged blameless if he strives to remain silent.

For this reason Jeremiah too could not be excused when, called to such a task, he chose rather to remain inactive, considering his youth and the lack in youth of experience in speaking, and judging that the time was not yet fitting for this inexperience to teach. “Behold,” he says, “I do not know how to speak, for I am a child. And the Lord said: Do not say, ‘I am a child,’ for thou shalt go to all to whom I send thee, and thou shalt speak whatever I command thee” (Jeremiah 1).

“Even if you seem to yourself still burdened by immature age, so that you are not yet capable of fulfilling the duty of service imposed upon you, you will nevertheless not be sufficiently excused in his sight if, having heard the command, you stubbornly resist.” Therefore Jeremiah went; forgetting his younger age, he did not delay to obey the worthy hearing of his commander, lest, if he continued stubbornly to recoil from him through blameworthy silence, he should, under the requirement of righteous judgment, arrive at punitive silence.

## Chapter LXXXIX: On Punitive Silence

For we find many persons held in punitive silence whom we know, by the merit of their sins, to have incurred wrath. When they have fallen negligently into offenses either by silence or by speech, silence is subsequently imposed upon them as a punishment.

Luke relates that when the scribes and chief priests came together against Christ in order to find something blameworthy in his speech, they carefully asked whether tribute or tax ought to be given to Caesar, or whether this seemed rather contrary to the rule of justice.

[Col. 1121C] When this question had been carefully proposed, Christ, seeing the deceit and fraud in their words, commanded that a coin, or denarius, be brought to him, and asked whose inscription, likeness, or image was upon it. They said, “Caesar’s.” And he said: “Therefore, if you wish deservedly to be commended for justice—which commands that each person be given what is his—render undiminished to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and likewise do not deny to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22).

He has indeed marked the light of his countenance upon us, and by that seal designated us as belonging to himself, so that, just as we render to Caesar what we acknowledge to be due to royal authority, we may, by an equal law, render to God what is his, justly and faithfully.

“And,” the Evangelist says, “they could not rebuke his word before the people; and, marveling at his answer, they were silent” (Luke 20). When Christ replied, his deceitful hearers did not criticize his word, lest the remaining crowd judge them lovers of falsehood; and they stood amazed at his praiseworthy answers. Being astonished and stunned, they fell silent under the pressure of justice.

For since they saw nothing blameworthy in his answers, and begrudged those answers the praise they received, they were struck by the worthy judgment of avenging justice: those who do not rejoice in truth are compelled to lie low. They would rather have had him answer in a blameworthy manner and plainly afford them an opportunity to accuse him; or at least they would have preferred that the people then present not be there, so that in their absence they might accuse him more freely, even falsely.

[Col. 1121D] Since no such occasion whatsoever was granted to them, and every opportunity for accusation was removed, they were struck with a most grievous punishment, lest they perhaps rejoice that they were unpunished: they were restrained in silence not by their own choice but by coercive vengeance. For malicious people judge that nothing more grievous can befall them than being forbidden to exercise the malice they desire—if, finally, powerful vengeance restrains them with so great an obstacle that against truth they are unable, or do not dare, to answer.

## Chapter XC
Matthew indicates this when he brings forward the Sadducees, and, once they have been refuted, then the Pharisees also. The former, lame in faith, deny that there is a resurrection; the latter, truly dull-witted, cannot solve the question put to them by Christ. The Sadducees inquire rather carefully about the wife of seven husbands, whom they declare to have had seven brothers successively as husbands, according to Moses’ command to the children of Israel that the surviving brother of a deceased brother should take his wife in marriage. “In the resurrection,” they say, “whose wife of the seven will she be? For they all had her” (Luke [Col. 1127B] 20). And the Lord says: “You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God; for in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22).

He says: A very great error has taken hold of you; your wickedness has cruelly blinded you. You do not know what kind of truth is proclaimed in the Scriptures, or how effectually God’s power works in the dead. “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; he is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (ibid.). Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob undoubtedly entered upon the way of all flesh and, being of the earth, returned to earth by the common law of all. Yet eternal Truth declares himself to be their God, so that they may be known now not to be dead but to live forever. For he would not truly be their God if it were not certain that they live, since he who is undoubtedly the true God cannot truly be God of those who are not. Therefore they live in spirit; and though they are known to be dead in the flesh, whoever does not overstep the true bounds of sound faith believes him to be their God—the living, true, limitless One—rather than God of the dead.

The Sadducees could make no effective reply to this saying; and the enemies of truth, confounded by their confusion, fell silent, bearing with great difficulty that they could neither weaken his judgment nor support their error with true answers. “When the Pharisees heard,” says the evangelist, “that he had imposed silence upon the Sadducees, they came together; and one of them, a doctor, questioned [Col. 1127D] him, testing him: ‘Master, which is the great commandment in the Law?’” (ibid.). Seeing that the Sadducees answered absolutely nothing and could in no way withstand Christ in disputation, the Pharisees supposed that they would inquire more successfully and answer much more cleverly against one seeking to solve what had been asked.

The Pharisees and Sadducees were accustomed to disagree with one another and, with discordant opinion, to oppose the truth greatly. Whenever one party could get ahead of the other in some matter, they seemed to themselves to have found no small claim to praise. For this reason the Pharisees gird themselves to inquire more subtly and endeavor to spread verbal nets for the one questioned, so that, when it becomes evident that they can both inquire better and oppose the respondent more cleverly, they may seem to overcome those whom they envy. But Christ, answering their questions more wisely still, checks their wicked design with a ready solution; and he so strives to undo their snares or traps that thereafter they can neither repair them nor dare to do so.

For when the Pharisee asks, “Which is the great commandment in the Law?” he says, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” and so forth (ibid.). And lest they be only slightly struck down by so explicit a solution, but be further confounded by an added question, he questioned the same assembled Pharisees, saying: “What do you think concerning Christ? Whose son is he?” They say to him: “David’s.” He says to them: “How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying, ‘The Lord said to my Lord,’” and so forth. “If then David,” he says, “calls him Lord, how is he [Col. 1128B] his son?” (ibid.).

The Pharisees, who presume to envy Christ just as they envy the Sadducees, being blinded by malice cannot perceive the question set before them. Since they know no fitting answer to it, they are compelled by their embarrassed ignorance to fall silent as a punishment. For, having nothing by which they might more suitably criticize his answers, and lacking understanding by which to grasp more subtly what was asked, they now set aside their presumptuous hope of empty victory and do not venture in his presence to raise similar questions further. Of them Matthew adds: “And no one was able to answer him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day onward to question him any more” (ibid.).

Likewise in Matthew and Luke demons are restrained by fear, lest, having assumed liberty, they speak according to their own pleasure. They are struck with imposed silence not on account of the blasphemy that belongs to demons, but are even stopped from praises of Christ already begun. “A demon,” he says, “cried out, saying: ‘What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God.’ And Jesus rebuked it, saying: ‘Be silent’” (Luke [Col. 1128C] 4). Since “praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15), because the inward examiner attends not to the outward lip but to the inner conscience of the one giving praise, Christ does not accept his praises when he hears them uttered by demons’ mouths; rather, he commands the reprobate praisers to be tormented by silence.

When the powerful indignation of a punishing judge afflicts someone who has not deserved well, the misery of the sufferer has at least this sort of remedy: to pour out inward pains in lamenting cries, if he is permitted to approach the judge with prayers or praises. But if a wretch is compelled under the judge’s hand both to suffer and, while suffering, not to utter a word of remedy because silence has been imposed, inward pain, with its outlet closed, increases more severely; and, like a burning furnace, the wretch is miserably tormented. Therefore, when Jesus wishes to punish demons more severely, he commands them by stern judgment to be mute, so that those unwilling to put their guilt to sleep by worthy repentance may not even find a remedy for punishment through speech.

## Chapter XCI

In the same manner Paul, when he heard his own praises proclaimed by a Pythian spirit and his righteousness made known to the ignorant by that spirit’s proclamation, considered its wicked character rather than its praise. He did not value the proclamation, but imposed penal silence upon that spirit. “The spirit,” he says, “cried out: ‘These men are servants of the most high God, who announce to you the way of salvation.’ And it did this for many days. But Paul, being grieved, turned and said to the spirit: ‘I command you in the name of Jesus Christ, come out of her’” (Acts [Col. 1129A] 16).

Knowing that it does not accord with God’s good pleasure for praise to be uttered by one whose tongue is rebuked by a ruined mind, Paul preferred that the Pythian spirit should be silent rather than that his own righteousness should become known to the people through its praises. And what wonder if, guilt requiring it, an unclean spirit is found to be made mute, when even the righteous man Zechariah deserves to receive the same punishment? That is, because he was found unbelieving toward God’s word through the angel, he is swiftly punished with silence in vengeance for his fault.

“The angel said to him: ‘Do not fear, Zechariah, for your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son.’ And Zechariah said: ‘How shall I know this? For I am old, and my wife is advanced in her days.’ To him the angel said: ‘Behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things come to pass, because you did not believe my words’” (Luke [Col. 1129B] 1).

When the angel announces that his aged wife will bear by a new gift, and that offspring of good disposition will be born from elderly parents, human dullness does not sufficiently accord with the heavenly message, and limping faith binds Zechariah’s tongue. Rightly, therefore, he who will not give a fitting answer to the speaking angel, who will not lend a believing ear to the heavenly proclamation, is found judicially liable to this punishment: when he wishes to speak, he is compelled instead to be silent.

For this reason, finally, that Virgin of virgins is commended, and when Elizabeth announces it (ibid.), is deservedly proclaimed blessed for her faith. For when the angel proposed to make known to her things hidden and untried throughout all preceding ages, when he announced to her the imminent accomplishment of a birth which would surpass nature’s power in a wondrous and ineffable manner, she, though as a young woman she seems to have been womanishly alarmed by the speaking angel, is nevertheless found to have maintained the constancy of wondrous faith and to have answered fittingly enough to one speaking great things.

For the tender virgin, though amazed at the outcome, does not doubt the fulfillment of the gratuitous promise. Having certain faith concerning a matter not moderately full of grace, she becomes commendably curious only concerning the manner of the event. “How shall this be?” She says: I do not doubt that what you have said will truly happen; but because you have not said how it is to happen, as I confess myself certain of what has already been said, so I am naturally concerned about what has not been said. Tell me, therefore, how this shall be. For since I have not yet consented to a man’s embraces and, what is more, have not resolved to consent to them in the future, I carefully ask how that may be fulfilled which, unless a man be known, is declared not to have been fulfilled in any previous age.

“And he said: ‘The Holy Spirit shall come upon you’” (ibid.), and so forth. Because the Virgin does not resist the angelic announcement, she does not remain long in suspense concerning the manner she has asked about. When she has heard all the great and wonderful things announced by the angel, she commends her faith in a concluding word of humility: “Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.).

This answer, this faith, this humility experiences neither wrath nor judgment. Neither angel nor higher Judge is found to be angry with her; shameful correction does not afflict her, nor does harsher punishment; the avenging hand does not impose penal silence upon her. For the angel accepted the humble word of the Virgin, who, though questioning this novelty in doubt, did not dispute in resistance. And the Spirit who came upon her not only made her pregnant without burden by new offspring, but, with womanly silence set aside, also made her abundant in praiseworthy speech.

Thus, once John had already been conceived by his aged parents, the Virgin wished to greet and visit his mother [Col. 1130B] in the hill country, so that those about to give birth beyond the bounds of hope or nature might receive mutual comfort in reciprocal speech concerning the children conceived. Elizabeth, knowing and sensing that the arriving Virgin already bore in her womb one who was from the Spirit, wished fittingly to rejoice at so great a novelty. She proclaimed the Virgin’s faith, since she had firmly believed the angel—indeed, the Lord—and prophesied that the things foretold would be fulfilled.

“Elizabeth,” he says, “was filled with the Holy Spirit and cried out with a loud voice: ‘Blessed are you among women,’” and so forth (ibid.). And below: “Blessed is she who believed, because those things which were spoken to you by the Lord shall be fulfilled” (ibid.). At this utterance of the prophetess, Mary is not held in silence but, full of the Holy Spirit, is moved to utter a song, choosing so to rejoice in the newness of the gift she has received that she is found also to comfort future generations by grateful speech. “My soul magnifies the Lord,” she says, and so forth (ibid.).

You see women sitting together in one room, conversing not with feminine frivolity but with the prophetic Spirit, singing praises and weaving prophecies; from these things unbelieving Zechariah is grievously excluded for a time. For the Virgin and the woman remain in the same chamber for three months, where they comfort one another not only in affection but also in mutual speech, delighting in being together—not that they might apply industrious hands more urgently to textile work, but that they might unfold divine praises more pleasingly in joyful conversation. But while these women are occupied in religious zeal and diligent praises, while they speak tirelessly of him with whose Spirit they are filled, that priest of the Law, because he did not answer the speaking angel with worthy faith, hides himself, confounded under penal silence.

Thus the Lord is found through Isaiah to threaten terribly certain people whose ears do not hear in faith, so that it may be more plainly understood alike from the Gospel and from the oracle of the prophets that penal confusion follows hardened hearing. “Because I called,” he says, “and you did not answer; I spoke, and you did not hear: behold, my servants shall rejoice, and you shall be confounded” (Isa. [Col. 1130D] 65). When the servants rejoice who heard the Lord speaking, who faithfully answered with a receptive ear to him who mercifully called, those are certainly deservedly confounded who are more clearly known either not to have heard him or not to have answered when they heard.

What Isaiah foretells of hardened hearers, Jeremiah, speaking in the same Spirit, also declares. Although the prophets are separated from each other by place and time, they are nevertheless joined by the operation of the Spirit of him who is always the same. “Do they provoke me to anger?” says the Lord (Jer. 7). Do they not rather provoke themselves to the confusion of their own faces? When the wicked presume to provoke the Lord to anger, they cannot inflict anything harmful on him; for though we know that our works, when evil, displease him greatly, it is nevertheless certain that whatever we do cannot harm him. Therefore, when what we do is condemned by the true judgment of justice, punishment and confusion are owed to us. Justice does not repay either guilt or punishment upon our Creator; rather, wounded conscience or the experience of punishment confounds us, the authors of evil.

Moreover, the Lord makes clear through the same prophet a little earlier how they had first offended him and then been confounded: they had not heard with due humility the words of their admonisher, and for that reason had incurred his wrath and the judgment of his anger. “Because I spoke to you,” he says, “and you did not hear; I called you, and you did not answer: I will do to this house in which you place your confidence as I did to Shiloh, and I will cast you away from my face” (ibid.).

This house to which the Lord threatens so terribly, which he declares that he will destroy because the people’s sin demands it, is Jerusalem, in which he had commanded a temple to be built for himself and his name to be invoked there by devout and humble persons. Long ago the tabernacle and ark of the covenant were kept at Shiloh, while the aged Eli, and after Eli Samuel, performed the priestly office. All Israel assembled there at the Lord’s command and offered before the ark praises, prayers, and sacrifices to him. But when that same people implacably provoked God to anger and heaped old sins up with new ones, God rejected that place by stern judgment and, when the ark was removed, annulled its former religious service.

Hence David later says: “He rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle, where he dwelt among men” (Ps. [Col. 1131D] 47). Once the tabernacle in which God had first dwelt was rejected, the people no longer hastened there for prayer; they no longer offered their gifts there devoutly and eagerly; neither the vows of suppliants nor praises nor songs sounded there. Thus that place, formerly dedicated to religion and thronged by the presence of priests and by crowds of worshipers, was at last, when wrath prevailed, counted as nothing; its celebrated honor having ceased, it was assigned to penal silence.

God wished its honor to pass to Mount Zion and, by the breath of his Spirit there, to rekindle the extinguished ashes of worship; indeed, he wished that place to be consecrated with the privilege of greater holiness and honored with far greater glory and riches. Of it David says: “He chose Mount Zion, which he loved” (ibid.). By David’s design, but through the ministry of his successor Solomon, God wished a temple to be made for himself on the mount of vision, where Abraham had formerly not refused to sacrifice his son Isaac, yet, when the angel recalled him, as an obedient father inflicted no harm upon the boy.

In that temple God wished his name—his, as it were, presence—to be so present, and his goodwill to be so ready for those who asked worthy things of him, that all who wished to go there might be certain that God was truly in that temple and place. Of it the Lord says to Solomon: “I have sanctified this house which you have built, that I may put my name there forever; and my eyes and my heart shall be there all days” (2 Chron. [Col. 1132A] 7).

This house or temple was proclaimed by fame from the rising of the sun to its setting. Everyone who heard of its wonderfully splendid form marveled, and whoever experienced its holiness in person became bound to it with much more devout affection. Thus even the queen of Sheba came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon (1 Kings 10), earnestly desiring to gain sight of the work she had heard about. When she saw it, the greatness of the report seemed of no account, because the present certainty of those marvelous realities surpassed it. For although report commonly exceeds the reality of a thing and, according to a certain pagan writer, “gathers strength as it goes,” yet, in proclaiming what and how Solomon accomplished, its wandering talk is overcome by the magnitude of the facts.

This house of the Lord, which Solomon had built at great expense and with much labor, remained in worthy honor in Solomon’s own time and under many succeeding kings, until Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, held the kingdom; his father was the most righteous king Josiah. At that time the wickedness of king and people so increased, and iniquity, surpassing nearly every justice, so destroyed it, that God, no longer enduring it, decreed to overthrow that great and marvelous work of Solomon—indeed, all Jerusalem—by Babylonian fire or army.

Cruel Nebuchadnezzar seized Zedekiah and blinded him; he stripped both the house of the Lord and the royal house of their coveted wealth; and, after setting the city on fire, he carried the citizens, pressed hard by the impending divine vengeance, into Babylon, over which he ruled with royal power. There they were oppressed under harsh dominion for seventy years and compelled to pay for ancient errors by their present exile, because neither long-standing guilt except by bitterer discipline nor a hardened disease except by stricter medicine can be effectively cured.

During the time when the tribes of Judah and Benjamin inhabited harsh Babylon, the worship of the temple which devout Solomon had instituted at the Lord’s command did not flourish at all in its due manner or customary honor. Rather, the temple, the city, and the entire land of Judah were condemned to such silence that no festive solemnity, no customary rejoicing, no voice of worshipers was heard there. Before this happened, God wished it to be proclaimed in prophetic speech and announced long beforehand through Jeremiah, so that it might either be avoided by hearers who repented, or that those who did not repent might be condemned more inexcusable. [Col. 1133A] This is what was said: “I will do to this house as I did to Shiloh” (Jer. 7). Just as that place is no longer commended by its former holiness, no longer has priests or crowds of people frequenting it, but is held in deserved disgraceful solitude, penal silence, and the ugliness of decay and neglect, so I shall make this house, likewise dedicated to my name, desolate in silence when just judgment comes upon it.

Nor shall I inflict grievous injury merely upon the house which Solomon especially dedicated to divine worship and adorned, rich in gold, with mystical beauty; I shall also destroy the whole region of Judaea through grievous injury to the entire city. “I will make Jerusalem heaps of sand, and the cities of Judah a desolation, because there will be no inhabitant,” he says (Jer. 9). And through the prophet Micah he threatens similar things: “Zion shall be ploughed like a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the house shall become the high places of forests” (Mic. [Col. 1133B] 3).

By saying that Zion will be ploughed like a field and Jerusalem changed into heaps of stones, he plainly indicates the overthrow of the ruined city. Having incurred the loss of its former holiness through perverse conduct, it deserves by the enormity of its crimes and the criminal magnitude of its depravity to be overthrown, leveled like an empty field, and to have its precipitous buildings reduced to worthless heaps of stones. Those who overthrew captured cities in mighty hatred, wishing them neither easily restored nor returned to their former condition, commonly leveled them to the ground with a plough like a field and reduced the necessary houses to an empty pile of stones.

When this had been done, neither citizen nor inhabitant remained there, since, with everything lost, there was nowhere and no way for anyone to remain. The former possessor did not inhabit the ruined place, which hostile savagery held after reducing it to desolation. When the possessor had been driven out and removed far from his own boundaries, the buildings overthrown and the place wholly laid waste, nothing good or joyful was heard there according to custom; and when this is not heard, what is found but silence?

This is what the Lord threatens the Jews through the aforesaid Jeremiah: “I will cause to cease from the cities of Judah and from the streets of Jerusalem the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of bridegroom and the voice of bride, for the land shall become a desolation” (Jer. [Col. 1133D] 7). For, as was said above, “I spoke to you, and you did not hear; I called you, and you did not answer” (ibid.). Your prosperity will not increase; rather, your land will suffer the loss of desolation. Once it is desolated, the speech of your solemnity will fall silent, and from your cities the voice of joy and gladness will cease.

No one will announce the joy you desire; no one will stir you to spiritual gladness; no one will sound Paul’s exhortation to you; no one will offer David’s song in welcome ministry. “Rejoice in the Lord,” says Paul, “again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4). And David: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous” (Ps. 31). Nor will the Bridegroom, that is Christ, admonish you whom he hates; nor will the Bride, that is ecclesiastical faith, answer him; nor, finally, will the watchful teacher win glory from the progress of his hearers, nor will the obedient man proclaim distinguished victories.

The voice of this joy, this gladness, this bridegroom, and this bride shall cease from Judah and Jerusalem when, the inhabitants having been removed, the land becomes wholly mute; when the curse foretold to those sinners in prophetic speech comes upon them because repentance has not averted it. Of this it is said much later through the same Jeremiah: “If you do not hear me, I will make this house as [Col. 1134A] Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse” (Jer. 26). You see that those who have offended the Creator and have scorned to hear their admonisher with hardened heart, when no prohibition can recall them from their wickedness, are at last subjected to the grave curse of desolation.

No curse seems heavier or more intolerable than if Jerusalem should perhaps be made equal to Shiloh—if, just as no inhabitant or singer of divine praises can now be found there, Jerusalem too is compelled to undergo a similar punishment.

## Chapter XCII

To the fullness of the penal punishment inflicted is added this: the coming of that same curse is not delayed, and it is not the children’s teeth that are set on edge while their parents eat a sour thing; rather, those who eat it themselves deservedly waste away in the stupor inflicted upon them.

Long before, when Hezekiah had behaved somewhat arrogantly toward the envoys of the king of Babylon, Isaiah was sent by the Lord’s command to rebuke him. The desolation which Jeremiah later foretold as imminent, Isaiah prophesied by the divine Spirit as far in the future. “Behold,” he says, “days are coming when all things which are in your house, and which your fathers have stored up to this day, shall be carried away into Babylon; and of your sons who shall come forth from you, whom you shall beget, they shall take some away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon. And Hezekiah said: ‘Good is the word of the Lord which he has spoken; only let peace and truth be in my days’” (2 Kings [Col. 1134C] 20).

When the prophet declares certain future misfortunes to the king, he greatly consoles that same king by saying that the things truly foretold as harmful will be fulfilled not in his own time but in that of his children. “They shall take of your sons,” says the prophet, “and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.” And he says: “Only let peace be in my days.” “Although,” he says, “it is grievous that evils shall be inflicted upon my descendants and that some of them shall suffer mutilation among the Babylonians, I nevertheless perceive in this that God comes to my aid favorably: I am not compelled to experience these evils in person; peace is enjoyed in my own time according to my wish; and a future generation will suffer the fulfillment of the prophecy.”

Jeremiah did not grant his hearers in his prophecy the kind of consolation which Hezekiah received from delay. For he assigned the grievous imminence of calamity which he foretold neither to sons nor to grandsons in such a way as to suggest that the parents then present would not see it; rather, he asserts that those who deserved it would endure it in person. Because they had become hardened so as not to hear divine admonitions or, believing the prophetic message in no way, to obey it, the stricter avenger displayed in reality before their own eyes the desolation which the Lord had announced to their ears through him. “Behold,” he says, “I will take away from this place, in your sight and in your days, the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of bridegroom and the voice of bride” (Jer. [Col. 1135A] 7).

It is fitting that those who act wickedly with unrestrained license should have evils inflicted upon them according to their deserts, and that those unwilling to abstain from vices while happy circumstances are available should be compelled, when those happy things fail, to endure sorrowful ones.

It should be noted that the angry judge threatens to impose silence upon those whom, because their sins require it, he wishes to make suffer sorrowful things, because just as sorrow is the punishment of wickedness, so silence is the work of sorrow. For just as a certain talkativeness accompanies joy and gladness—since one who is cheerful can scarcely restrain himself from speaking what he feels, because the mind itself is more soothed in its joy when inward delight is poured out in outward words—so, when the night of sorrow envelops any wretch, it consequently brings upon him grievous silence, so that the wretch is found to be tormented more miserably to the degree that he either may not speak sweet things or has no desire to speak of harmful feelings.

That each person more willingly speaks of pleasant things, and that, when happy circumstances are present, grievous silence is banished, the Lord indicates through the same prophet when, after the evils and sorrows he has set forth, he mercifully promises better and happier things to the city. “Behold,” he says, “I will restore the restoration of the tents of Jacob, and I will have mercy on his dwellings; the city shall be built on its height, and the temple shall be founded according to its order; and from them shall go forth praise and the voice of those playing or praising” (Jer. [Col. 1135C] 30).

You see that when desired prosperity is restored to the sorrowful, when the frost of grief has been wiped away and spring gladness spreads over the hills, this very outpouring is not held back by the heavy barrier of silence; rather, praise and the voice of those praising or playing are said to go forth from them. Finally, when, after a long winter, its hardships are now driven away; when snow and ice melt in spring’s mildness; when waters, their course restored, now flow in their customary freedom; when the earth’s surface has been loosened and produces new grass; when plants put forth shoots, smiling meadows grow green, the bark of trees comes back to life, buds swell, and twigs now leaf out; when the sun is brighter and the air purer; when this whole lower world is distinguished by welcome newness—then the birds, unable to contain their discovered joy and giving outward expression, in such speech as they can, to their inward secret, delight to resound with wondrous song or chirping and to fly talkatively through woods, gardens, and trees.

Because they sense the earth to be more open in the new mild weather, the woods more pleasant, and the air gentler—where they find food more plentiful than usual—they judge it unfitting to suppress these things in prolonged silence rather than render chattering praise to their giver. The Lord also exhorts to such praises those whom, after the misery described, he consoles by a gratuitous promise. He wishes their prosperity not to hide as beneath a bushel, but, silence removed, to become known in clamorous praises: “Exult in the gladness of Jacob, neigh against the head of the nations, make a sound, sing, and say: ‘Save, O Lord, your people and the remnant of Israel’” (Jer. [Col. 1136A] 31).

When the Lord deigns to visit afflicted Jacob and, after long sorrow, restore him to joy and gladness, Jacob will sing, neigh, and make a sound against the head of the nations by which he had been oppressed; at last, having been restored to freedom after defeating it, he will exult over it and devoutly and publicly call upon his deliverer: “Save, O Lord, your people and the remnant of Israel.” When this man, after long sorrow, is refreshed with desired joy, he is urged by a twofold cause to break silence: he both exults in worthy praises for his helper and greatly rejoices to exult over his oppressor.

For one who, after receiving a benefit, refuses to give thanks seems in a certain way to begrudge his helper; so too does one who declines to confess him with praise, though by that one’s gift he knows himself not to be held in the heavy chain of calamity. Those freed from Babylon do not incur this fault. They offer talkative praises to divine generosity and, returned to the place which mournful desolation had made deserted, proclaim their deliverer in joyful voice. This is foretold below through the same Jeremiah: “There shall yet be heard in this place the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of bridegroom and the voice of bride, the voice of those saying: ‘Give thanks to the Lord of hosts, for he is good’” (Jer. [Col. 1136B] 33).

When they have been brought out of Babylon and recover their former homes, they will not cherish inward joy in sluggish silence, since whatever prosperity the inward mind experiences has less grace if an outspoken tongue is not found to accord outwardly with it. Therefore, breaking the bars of silence, they will resound with vocal joy and proclaim the power—indeed, the powerful benevolence—of their deliverer, lest they be ungrateful for his generosity if they offer no praises, or diminish their own joy by submitting to idle silence.

To complete their joy, they also delight to exult over their former oppressor, whose power had been able, by God’s just judgment, to hold them captive. Since, when at last rescued, they cannot repay him in kind by oppressing him similarly, they love at least to repay him in speech. The Lord speaks to them also through Isaiah: “You shall take up this parable against the king of Babylon and say: ‘How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning? You have fallen to earth’” (Isa. [Col. 1136D] 14).

When the Babylonian king held the children of Israel captive as he pleased and subjected their weakness to his powerful hand, he rejoiced as though ruling heaven, bathed in morning light and not fearing that his rising would be brought low by evening decline. But when a stronger hand weakened his power and strengthened against him, with welcome courage, those who had been oppressed, he was cast down from the presumptuous height of his throne and fell in abject weakness to the deep and dark earth. Seeing this, they rejoice not only in the benefit by which they are delivered from the most wicked hand, but equally in the fall of the most wicked man. Reckoning his ruin as their own glory, they cannot avoid chattering, singing the work-song of treading men. Of this Jeremiah says: “A work-song like that of treading men shall be sung against all the inhabitants of the earth” (Jer. [Col. 1137A] 25).

If a vine bears an abundant crop of grapes through the favor of autumn, the farmer rejoices while it still offers only hope and has not yet reached the vintage. He receives the noble delight of hope, but he does not yet sing as though he no longer feared loss. He is still anxious lest some weather prove harmful to it, lest it perish through untimely rain, hail, or frost, lest it be damaged either by excessive heat or icy breath. Content with the promise of hope, he refrains from a triumphal song.

But when, maturity completed, the heavy grape-cluster is cut with the knife and gathered into the narrow vat for treading, hope now having become reality, the treader rejoices confidently and, at the success he has long desired and awaited, glories as though master of victory. Since he has at last deserved to obtain what he wished, he can no longer contain his joy in silence, but hastens to pour out his inner affections in the pleasing sound of a work-song (*celeuma*) and to soothe his undertaken labor of treading with vocal song.

In the same way, those who were once captives, beaten down in affliction and misery beneath the strong hand of enemies, if they see themselves freed after the snare has been broken and see their enemies diminished in strength, even if not in malice, rejoice. They do not wish their joy to remain hidden beneath a bushel; rather, with the work-song of treading men—that is, the triumphal song of those rejoicing—they delight to exult over their enemies.

For joy is talkative and chattering; it does not know how to be contained beneath the tongue. It flees solitude and wishes to be widely known in streets and marketplaces. It abhors silence and wishes to be expressed in wandering abundance of speech; impatient of quiet, it wishes to be carried to the knowledge of many. This is significantly indicated in the Gospel by the man who, though healed and commanded not to presume to reveal it to anyone, declared throughout the whole region, saying that silence was a heavy yoke, and, receiving the benefit, commended the giver of the benefit with worthy praises.

From such praises or exultations, in which joy grows more talkative, grievous sorrow, conversely, as has been said above, falls silent; and where, joy being absent, afflicting grief is found, no voice of praise, triumphal song, or work-song of treading men is heard.

## Chapter XCIII
Even this the Lord makes known through Isaiah: when, after guilt, he grievously oppresses and afflicts the guilty, when, withdrawing the benefit by which he had been wont mercifully to sustain them, he threatens sinners with sorrow and imposes silence upon the sorrowful. “Joy and gladness,” he says, “shall be taken away from Carmel; and in the vineyards there shall be neither exulting nor shouting; he who was accustomed to tread shall not tread out wine in the press: I have taken away the voice of the treaders” (Isa. 16). When the overflowing wine is not trodden in the press, when wine fails and he who was accustomed to rejoice is made sorrowful, the grievous punishment of sorrowful silence is added as punishment for failing to render due reverence to the Creator. For the vine-dressers no longer sweetly shout in the vineyards, nor do the treaders sing the treaders’ chant beside the vat [Col. 1138A]; rather, when the wine is lost—which was wont to make its cultivators cheerful and talkative—the owners abandon the very place, confirming its silence.

Far below, Isaiah declares that the same thing had happened, saying that joy, harp, and song had failed—things which, to be sure, had resounded with frequent noise when cheerful inhabitants thronged the place more fully. “The joy of tambourines has ceased,” he says; “the sound of those rejoicing has fallen quiet; the sweetness of the harp with song has been silent; they shall not drink wine” (Isa. 24). And he adds: “Every house is shut, with no one entering; desolation has been left in the city, and calamity oppresses its gates” (ibid.). When desired prosperity flourished in the city, when the welcome sweetness of success caressed it, when the fullness of festive joy occupied its streets and squares, a great multitude of inhabitants flowed together like bees [Col. 1138B]; and the yoke of silence did not weigh upon the happy crowd, but it rang with tambourines, harps, and diverse songs. But when grievous calamity fell upon that same city, when heavy adversity pressed and crushed it, the tambourines ceased, the harp’s sweetness was silenced, the songs fell mute, and the sound of those rejoicing was hushed.
