And, that silence might be more firmly established, the inhabitants’ crowd abandoned the city itself: no one entered its closed houses and opened them; immense solitude possessed its streets and crossings; deprived of citizens, the broad expanse within its walls lay empty.

What misery produces such solitude or silence is not left unspoken in the same chapter of Isaiah. “All joy,” he says, “has been deserted; the joy of the earth has been carried away.” Sorrow follows upon abandoned gladness [Col. 1138C] and joy carried away; and no strength remains to the citizens for bearing it with equanimity. Their intolerable distress, abhorring the place itself as though it were a witness to their grief, leaves it willingly or unwillingly; and when they depart, solitude occupies the city. If anyone, however, either of his own accord or compelled by a robber’s violence, remains in that same city, if he inhabits a place made monstrous by the scarcity of its residents, he will nevertheless not sing talkative praises, not chant a triumphal proclamation, not sound the treaders’ refrain or sweet melodies. Rather, sympathizing with the misery that the desolated city suffers, the citizen will follow it with mourning and silence.

For the mouth which, when joy loosens it, opens more freely for such things, is closed by constricting sorrow beneath the weight, as it were, of a stone; its voice is shut up and buried as in a dark tomb, and in that tomb is lulled to sleep beneath a kind of sleep-like heaviness of silence. For as joy makes men wakeful for speaking, so sorrow, surely, weighs them down with sleep for silence; and this sleep does not restore the sick unto improvement, but afflicts them and, having afflicted them, casts them down into ruin. The apostles were somewhat burdened by such sleep when, in Christ’s Passion, fear and sorrow unmanned them; since they could find no escape from the impending evil, they were compelled by weary exhaustion to fall asleep in heavy silence. Thus Matthew has it: “He came to the disciples and found them sleeping. And he said to Peter: Thus could you not watch with me one hour? Watch and pray” (Matt. 26). And below: “He came again,” he says, “and found them sleeping, for their eyes were weighed down” [Col. 1139A] (Matt. 16). You see that the disciples are depressed by oppressive heaviness: those who ought eagerly to have watched dissolve into slothful sleep; those who ought stoutly to have maintained the loud defense of prayer are found, as punishment, subject to destructive silence.

Luke makes still clearer by what cause such silence or sleep arose, and in a brief verse shows both the definite origin of the ensuing punishment and the harmful offspring of the preceding fault. “He found them,” he says, “sleeping because of sorrow” (Luke 22). Such sorrow held them, while the loss of this present life threatened and the promise of eternal life had not yet sustained them more perfectly, that their inward eyes being weighed down, they lapsed into the harmful torpor of sleep; with faith wounded and hope shaken, they labored under heavy silence [Col. 1139B]. Their wise and benevolent Master seeks to remove them from this sleep or silence, to sustain them by a good and consoling word, so that they may be restored by medicinal remedy to a condition of salvation, lest through irremediable obstinacy they be brought into the imminent temptation. “Watch,” he says, “and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (ibid.). Let not incipient sleep, he says, let not heavy silence deceive you; let it not bring you into the irrecoverable abyss of temptation. Watch more earnestly, you for whom snoring is not necessary; pray more vigilantly, you who are silent as punishment; drive sleepiness far away, and rise up, you who lie down. “Rise,” he says, “and pray.”

For he who in Matthew and Mark says, “Watch and pray” [Col. 1139C] (Matt. 22; Mark 14), in Luke says, “Rise and pray” (Luke 22), clearly indicating that one who so sleeps is held down, lying in a heavy bed; but one who rises from degrading sleep is not oppressed by penal silence: “Rise,” he says, “and pray, lest you enter into temptation.”

## Chapter XCIV

He who does not carefully avoid entering into temptation is miserably compelled, with foot slipped, to come to that confusion in which every ruined person is found to sleep perpetually—sleeping, to perish in silence, of which we are speaking. Of this Isaiah says: “Behold, my servants shall rejoice, and you shall be put to shame” (Isa. 65). “And the wicked themselves,” through Jeremiah, say: “We shall sleep in our confusion, because we have sinned against the Lord our God” [Col. 1139D] (Jer. 3). Because all who are perverse spread themselves abroad in wakeful malice while sinning, they are confounded beneath strict judgment while suffering punishments, and in that very confusion sleep perpetually in heavy sleep, since they are neither struck by punishments nor brought to repentance from their malice.

For they are steeped in so great a poison of wickedness, so imbued with the sweet and welcome allurement of sinning, that, their sense as it were lost, they are plunged into the gulf of a kind of drunkenness; plunged and overthrown, they are put to sleep in the obstinacy of that same overthrow. When the ungodly, having fallen into the depth of sins, do not rise again; when, pressed down by the weight of punishments, they do not rise to hope for anything better; when, having fallen into the pit of misery, they do not desire to remember divine mercy [Col. 1140A]—what are they but those who will not, or cannot, awaken while sleeping? Concerning such people the Lord says through the same Jeremiah: “I will make them drunk, that they may fall asleep and sleep an everlasting sleep and not rise” (Jer. 61). And a little later: “I will make her princes drunk, and they shall sleep an everlasting sleep and shall not awaken” (ibid.). You see what the more severe Judge, angered against Babylon, threatens, and to what end their hardened wickedness is brought: namely, that, made drunk, they may sleep an everlasting sleep—that is, be buried forever in hell beneath penal silence.

Finally, in the divine Scriptures the city Babylon, whose princes the Judge declares to be threatened with such punishment, is said to bear the type of hell; and the interpretation of its very name is found fitting to this type, since Babylon means “confusion,” which is found in its chief form in hell [Col. 1140B]. For although among all things that owe obedience to their Creator, angel and human being ought always and everywhere to render foremost praises to the Creator, within the enclosure of hell, right being violated and order lost, all things are so confused that the voice of all alike is shut off from divine praises. That multitude of so many thousands is oppressed by silence so heavy that a vast solitude seems to hold the courts of that region. For since among them no one has any concern whatever for virtue, and none of the living has any hope of salvation, they do not lift in grateful proclamation the Savior whom they do not recognize as the giver of virtue and justice. Of such people the prophet Amos says: “Many shall die; in every place silence shall be cast forth” (Amos 8).

In contrast David says of the righteous: “The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous” [Col. 1140C] (Ps. 117). The righteous, knowing and feeling how great is the abundance of divine sweetness, how manifold and sweet the greatness of his good will, exult in him who advances them from virtue to virtue, who grants salvation to those advanced and raised to the heights of virtues. Received into the mysteries of that saving dwelling, in which they rejoice in the attained vision of divine glory, they do not wish or are unable to obscure by degrading silence what they see and hear; rather, with triumphant song and loving praises they delight to make it bright. Of such people Isaiah says: “They shall come into Zion with praise, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads” (Isa. 35).

Zion is the lofty height of that city [Col. 1140D] in which the righteous behold the magnificence of the eternal Godhead; there, in David’s words, they are granted to see the God of gods. The rewards of seeing are preceded by merits suited to them; but upon the heads of those who see—that is, upon their minds, poured forth without restraint—everlasting joy is poured, and eternal praise is gratefully poured out from their tireless voices, while they see the walls of that same Zion fully occupied by the defense of salvation and the entrances of its gates gloriously strengthened with bolts and bars. Isaiah, foreseeing this concerning Zion, says: “Salvation shall occupy your walls, and praise your gates” (Isa. 60). Seeing that Zion’s walls are weakened by no troubles but that their broad spaces are established by the invincible protection of salvation, its citizens rejoice to mark its lofty gates with titles of praise. As no one once admitted through them is thereafter compelled to go out, so no enemy is permitted to enter them [Col. 1141A].

And the author and ruler himself of the fortified city, seated in its midst upon the throne of royal majesty—he who, loving his citizens, blesses them with a share in his Godhead, while himself shining as the sun, far above the sun in the glory of holiness—him, I say, they all praise, glorify, reverence, and love; to him they cry; to him with tireless voices they make confession. Thus Isaiah, that most noble of prophets, in the year when King Uzziah died, saw the Lord seated upon a lofty throne, and the throng of heavenly spirits confessing to him as he sat: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isa. 6).

Therefore we also, standing at the altar, sing praises according to our measure, ask that our voices may be admitted with theirs, and delight to repeat the same “Holy, holy, holy,” conforming ourselves in this respect, however lowly, to those higher beings [Col. 1141B]. For they, standing around their Creator and Lord as though he were in their midst, and exulting ineffably in his vision, are secure in their own salvation and glory, to suffer no more fall, fear, or troubles. They praise him whose great benefit they have deserved to receive: enjoying his present glory, they do not fear coming wrath or judgment. Him they so see in their midst, so desire to see, that they do not wish to turn either eye or desire away from him to other things.

To those standing round him, he who is in the midst is thus present, and the surpassing vision of him is bestowed on all from every side in full measure, so that eternity is granted equally, although one differs from another in glory as stars do. Addressing those who have attained the joyful and glorious vision of him who deigns to make in them a dwelling pleasing to himself, Isaiah says: “Exult and praise, O dwelling of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One” (Isa. 12) [Col. 1141C].

By Zion the prophet intended to name that heavenly court in which its King and Author rejoices to dwell in presence. It always sees him and always desires to see him; neither does desire grow weary through satiety, nor satiety through desire. He says that the Lord is in the midst of this Zion, not in one part or corner, because the prophet understands him to be so present to all who stand there that he does not incline to one as though abandoning another, nor, approaching one, withdraw from another. To all who stand there he reveals himself equally as God and Lord; he stretches himself forth to protect all by merciful power, or powerful mercy. Far from none, near to all, he gives life to all—not a life of one day, but one bestowed with full hand, equal balance, and unending duration [Col. 1141D]. If he should incline in his bestowal of benefit toward anyone, even a father, or by however little, he would surely incline the other part toward ruin; and as, by approaching some, he would preserve them as more intimate members of his household, so, by withdrawing from others, he would condemn them more strictly.

## Chapter XCV

[Col. 1142A]

This, indeed, seems to have happened at the beginning of things in a wonderful and awe-inspiring judgment, when God is found to have distinguished some angels from others, and, inclining toward these, to have admitted them more firmly within his grace, while, being far from those, he left them to their own will alone. Those who were left, since they neither could nor would cleave to him who left them, were found to suffer irreparable ruin; and when the inward pillar, upon which they ought more firmly to have leaned, was removed, they fell apart like stones into the depths of an alien night. But those who remained by grace within the inner sanctuary of their original condition received their Creator in their midst then and thereafter in such a way that he became to them the wholly unbending strength of a pillar, and they cleaved to him as the beauty of an indissoluble crown [Col. 1142B].

Whenever righteous persons are taken from the prison-house of this life and raised to heaven, they are inserted into that same crown like living stones; joined to the angels, they contemplate God in their midst with unveiled face, and, all trouble driven away and desire fulfilled, they glory in security. Zephaniah, seeing them and filled with the prophetic Spirit, exhorts them to rejoice and praise, like Isaiah: namely, since they hold God in their midst and rejoice continually to see him, they should take care to render due praises to so great a joy. “Praise,” he says, “daughter of Zion; rejoice and exult, daughter of Jerusalem: the Lord is in your midst; you shall fear evil no more” (Zeph. 3); and below: “The Lord your God,” he says, “is in your midst; he himself is mighty; he will save” (ibid.).

And although long ago many angels fell from the heavenly throne, so that the remainder could have feared a like fall, nevertheless, now that those who remain are strengthened by more abundant grace, no evil, fear, or oppressive distress remains for them [Col. 1142C]. I know also that human beings, who, through love of the faith they professed while living here, suffered many and heavy things both in flesh and spirit, when released from their bonds and carried into the courts of that heavenly assembly, enjoy, as in a freer field, the spaciousness of freedom. Surely they are no longer shaken by any evil or by fear of any evil, through the blessed vision of him whom they embrace in their midst with loving bonds.

Therefore those angels and humans alike, joyful in the fellowship of one dwelling, blessed, as has been said, by the benefit attained of the divine vision—that harmonious multitude of heavenly citizens, that fortified height of the royal city—are rightly invited by the prophets’ exhortations to praises and songs. For they rejoice to see the King of ages in his beauty; and he who is in their midst so loves to unite and fortify his city that no adversity disturbs the unity of all its assembled inhabitants, and that by the Creator’s help it may forever be secure, always free both from the contagion or injury of sin and from every disturbance [Col. 1142D].

## Chapter XCVI

Not only to angels and humans already gathered in the heavenly court, but also to the present Church, he so manifests the loving kindness of his Godhead that, among those to whom he intends more tenderly to show mercy, he declares himself to be in their midst in order to protect and console them. Through the prophet Zechariah: “I have returned to Zion,” he says, “and I will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem; and Jerusalem shall be called the city of truth” (Zech. 8) [Col. 1143A]. Just as the multitude of the blessed who rejoice to see God in heaven is called Zion or Jerusalem because of the very glory of that vision, so too the assembly of righteous persons now living, though still wearied on earth by the troubles of affliction, is called by a like name in Holy Scripture. For there is one city, some of whose citizens are known already to reign in heaven, while others still labor on earth under pressures and beatings.

Divine goodness brings these out from the iron furnace of Egypt, from the darkness of vices and grievous servitude, from the midst of ruined Babylon, where there is much confusion of life; and it leads them into the sanctuary of its truth [Col. 1143B], so that, abandoning wandering error, they may be held fast by love of saving holiness. Thus that which previously, while serving vices, was rightly called Egypt or Babylon, becomes Zion or Jerusalem, since it now beholds God in hope and desire. God also graciously delights to show himself in their midst, making them cling to him with undeviating affection and advancing them from virtue to virtue, so that neither their work nor their intention deviates in any way from salvation.

“For whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” (Jas. 2). The person occupied with diverse and mutually opposing works, who in one matter seems to please God but in another does not fear to offend that same God, is certainly not regarded as having God in his midst; God draws nearer to one who abhors evil and practices good. Of such persons Jeremiah says: “He is near to their mouth, and far from their reins” (Jer. 12). God is said mercifully to draw near to their mouth, whom he loves to instruct in speaking what is just, so that they may be found more diligently serving divine praises and teaching their neighbors by the word of truth with sound faith [Col. 1143C]. But he is removed far from their reins when, their girdle of chastity loosened, they honor a mouth equipped and well ordered by the allurements of lust—a mouth unfitting to the loins, which the disorder of their reins defiles.

Therefore God’s presence is not in the midst of those whom he does not guard on every side with equal custody: he places in their mouth the word of faith or doctrine, but their loins do not sufficiently breathe forth discipline. Thus God’s condescension promises a great benefit to those whom he so admits into the sanctuary of his love that, by the goodness which is his own, he says that he dwells in their midst, lest they be found culpably to turn aside in this direction or that. “I will dwell,” he says, “in the midst of Jerusalem, and Jerusalem shall be a city of truth.” As that city in which God disdains to dwell under strict judgment is rightly called a city of confused falsehood, so it deservedly is called a city of truth in which—indeed, in whose midst—he who is truth itself is attested to dwell (John 14) [Col. 1143D].

For God is truth by the testimony of truth itself; and he diligently invites the converted multitude of the city which he inhabits to make melody in exultation with praises, as is read much earlier in the same Zechariah: “Praise and rejoice, daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and will dwell in your midst” (Zech. 2) [Col. 1144A]. You see that the testimonies of Scripture invite both those who see on earth through a mirror and those who contemplate in heaven with unveiled face to rejoice and praise, because he who is in their midst wishes to be praised by all the citizens of Zion or Jerusalem, and by his presence likewise wishes them all to be saved.

The citizens of Babylon, however, are excluded from such praises and, as though their vital breath were cut off, are restrained beneath silence; since, having ceased to be good through the vice of a perverse will, by the laws of divine justice they are also made silent regarding good things. Thus in the psalm God sternly rebukes the sinner and withdraws the despiser of justice from the presumed office of the righteous, lest he utter praises or doctrine with impudent tongue while neglecting the saving discipline in his life and conduct. “Why,” he says, “do you recite my righteousnesses and take my covenant in your mouth, when you hate discipline?” (Ps. 49) [Col. 1144B]. God does not wish his righteousnesses to be honorably recounted by one whom he perceives not to love them commendably; nor does he wish the wordy remedy of that person’s tongue to be offered when, because of his life, he wills the due punishments to be inflicted upon him.

Conversely, a little earlier in the same psalm, God deigns to console his people Israel, recalls it from silence, and more diligently exhorts it to the proclamation of praise, so that the one whom grace allows to contemplate him with the eye of the mind made clear may hear: “Hear, my people, and I will speak, Israel: I will not accept calves from your house; but sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and render your vows to the Most High” (ibid.) [Col. 1144C]. Whomever God mercifully deigns to enrich with his vision, so that he is worthy through contemplation to be called Israel, he does not wish disgracefully to be idle in empty silence; rather, mindful of benefits received, he wishes him to be occupied in grateful praises.

But the Babylonian citizens, whose eyes are darkened both now by the smoke of the pit and afterward blinded in that same pit by unavoidable darkness—who, while living here, neither love heavenly things nor worthily hope for invisible things, and who there persist in their wickedness unto final despair—these, I say, divine justice does not exhort to offer it a sacrifice of praise. It does not open their mouth or rejoice to fill it when opened; rather, it alike abhors the works and proclamations of those whose evil life and obstinate purpose corrupt them, and it shuts their mouth in silence lest it utter good things [Col. 1144D].

Such silence, by which, as we have said, those who are sternly excluded from uttering good things because they are evil are compelled to be silent, often begins here and is without doubt completed there; and, with the gates buried in hell, it is secured with bars and bolts. For although, while people live here, many evil persons are permitted to say good things, and demons in the Gospel speak good words while their conduct is evil, nevertheless both these and those, when they fall into the pit of infernal misery, are wrapped in such straits, pains, and darkness that, as if pressed beneath a millstone, they are ground down beyond remedy; and, severely crushed, they are held in eternal silence.

God himself is also said to be silent toward such persons, lest he console them with even his speech while they suffer deservedly; for those whom he wills to be tormented without remedy by penal silence, he does not will to sustain by any speech. Seeing this, the Prophet says: “Do not be silent toward me, lest at any time you be silent from me and I become like those who go down into the pit” (Ps. 27) [Col. 1145A]. When God, in the counsel known to himself, permits us to sin; when he leaves us longer hardened in our wickedness; when he does not draw us back, recall us, exhort us to repentance, or finally console us with the benefit of visiting grace—then, sins demanding it, he is found to be silent or mute toward us, since our misery experiences none of his benefits.

When he is silent, we miserable people are made like those descending into the pit, and are compared in condemned likeness to those laboring there. If, God being hardened against us, we do not thereafter perceive his visiting grace, we finally come to their fellowship in that same place of misery. In that pit a miserable multitude is tortured by miserable pain; and it is not lightened by the remedy either of a voice heard or of one uttered, since surely a sufferer receives some alleviation, whatever its kind, if even in torment he is permitted to have a voice. Hence a certain pagan says: “Alas, how miserable is pain that has no voice in torment!” And through Ezekiel the Lord says: “You shall not mourn, nor weep, and your tears shall not flow; groan in silence” (Ezek. 24); and below: “You shall not mourn nor weep, but shall waste away in your iniquities” (ibid.) [Col. 1145C].

You see that these endure miserable inward pains and yet are silent amid pains; inwardly they groan, waste away wickedly, and are tormented, yet are forbidden mourning and tears, lest, if they were permitted to utter a voice in torment or a lament in pain, they might, though worthy of continual misery, obtain even such consolation. For when any weak person is harshly oppressed by one who is powerful, without any merit of his own or power of resistance, he surely reckons that some remedy, of whatever kind, is granted him if he is allowed to offer his punisher either pleasing praises or plaintive prayers. But if the powerful one does not cease to torture the person who has deserved ill, and nevertheless wholly refuses to permit him to speak, severe pain grows fiercer and more intolerable—just as an ignited furnace burns more fiercely when all ventilation is denied [Col. 1145D]. Hence the Prophet says: “You shall make them like a furnace of fire at the time of your countenance” (Ps. 20).

The Prophet rightly says that they burn like a furnace who are shut up in hell, never to find any remedy, whose suffering is enclosed in such constrictions that they are excluded not only from remedy but even from the hope of remedy. Since they feel themselves relieved by no remedy and by no hope of remedy, they no longer desire to remember him who could have delivered them; and, not held by his welcome remembrance, as though not knowing him, they make no confession to him at all. The aforesaid David indicates this when he says: “There is none in death who remembers you” (Ps. 6). And he adds: “But in hell who shall confess to you?” (ibid.). It is as though he said: Since one dead in death is not found mindful of you, who in the region of death, being dead, confesses to you? For none but one who lives can confess to you, and you do not deign to show mercy except to those who confess.

“The dead,” he says, “shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all who descend into hell” (Ps. 113). And again: “Will dust confess to you, or declare your truth?” (Ps. 29) [Col. 1146A]. Those whom a raging wind scatters like dust from the face of firmer ground, and whom the violent Judge hurls, dying in death, into the depths of hell—those the same stricter Judge does not allow even to mutter, but oppresses with such silence that they are said to sleep amid their torments. For, as was said above through Jeremiah, those whom divine wrath casts down into the lower hell sleep an everlasting sleep, never to awake; and in that same sleep they are constrained by so many pressures and pains that they hope for, love, or speak of no good thing further.

Of them Hannah says: “The wicked shall be silent in darkness” (1 Sam. 2). But since silence from good things is found to be fully consummated there among them—as anyone who experiences it in person knows more expressly—when, by speaking, we have arrived there, it is at last fitting that we should be silent concerning that same silence, and by being silent leave to those who are present what belongs to them.

## Chapter XCVII. On silence from harmful evils

Concerning the fourth silence, which at the beginning of this response I asserted to be silence from evils, and which, as I wove their catalogue, I placed last in order: having now finished with the three concerning which I have spoken as best I could, place and time at last require that I discuss it as I proposed [Col. 1146C]. For as there is silence from good things, so there is silence from evil things. Evils are either harmful or sorrowful. Harmful evils bring war against our holiness; sorrowful ones are those which oppose the will. Let us first see from what harmful things, and in what manner, we ought to be silent, so that, instructed by this teaching, we may be able to keep silence with the help of the divine gift.

The divine law, wishing humanity to be exercised in the struggle of obedience and, by the merit of that exercise, advanced from good to better, commanded him to strive to fulfill what was enjoined just as it commanded him wholly to reject what was forbidden. It willed that the things commanded to be done should be called good, because it saw them to accord with the pleasure of the one commanding; but it called the things commanded not to be done evil, because, on the contrary, they were judged not sufficiently pleasing to that same commander. Therefore God willed the human being whom he had made to devote himself to the former and wholly abstain from the latter: to be watchful, outspoken, and active in fulfilling the former; but quiet, silent, and inactive in regard to the latter [Col. 1146D].

Thus, when faithless Cain envied innocent Abel and his countenance fell because Abel’s offering was accepted and his own was not, the Lord said to him, according to another translation: “You have sinned; be still” (Gen. 4). It is as though he said: If, while your mind meditates a crime which you have not yet brought into word and deed, you have already brought an intolerable tumult to my serene ears, at least now blush as one guilty of the crime you have contemplated; confounded by shame, now be still in modest silence. Finally, much later, through Jeremiah, certain persons deserved to be rebuked because, not being ashamed with shame, they did not know how to blush [Col. 1147A]. For as an impudent brow or irreverent heart rushes headlong into vice, so modest shame produces silence, when the penitent now casts off the turbulent wickedness of the heart and, ashamed, takes care not to do anything at all similar.

The Lord rightly therefore invites the sinner to be still, that after contemplating the crime he may repent and blush, lest repeated fault be gathered as into a bundle and an intolerable cry be brought to the divine ears. The son of perdition, hardened in wickedness, did not care to hear this counsel of recall or humbly obey it; but, despairing in despair and as though renouncing his monitor, offering bound hands, he exposed his whole self to the deceiver. Indicating this in words, he says: “My iniquity is greater than I deserve to receive pardon for” (ibid.) [Col. 1147B]. This man declares his own iniquity greater than God’s goodness; clothed in a wayward mind, he now despairs of salvation and forgiveness. Therefore he does not resolve to assume fitting quiet and useful silence, but rather gives himself up as restless, wandering, and fugitive. “I shall be,” he says, “a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth” (ibid.).

The wretched man is most miserably a wanderer and fugitive when, abandoned on every side by grace, he is not held fast by one vice alone but, his reins loosened, is carried about through many and varied things, unable to resist any, driven before all that pursue him. Hardened in wickedness, obstinate against every counsel of the one who recalls him, remembering no forgiveness and destined for ruined death, he is borne, by the vice of his own levity, like stubble at every breath or impulse of whatever perversity; he is swept away like chaff. Confirming this, as it were, he adds: “Everyone who finds me will kill me” (ibid.) [Col. 1147C].

Everyone who finds such a sinner is said to kill him, because the miserable man is compelled to fall by the violence of whatever finds him; because whatever oppressive passion attacks him, he—his mind lost in deceptive ignorance and knowing no escape—offers his neck to the sword and his fleeing back to the wound. In this victory, in which not only the victor but the conquered man judges himself to have obtained his desire, and, seized by inward frenzy, rejoices in his own destruction, there is no rest from evils and no commendable silence; rather, a conscience wounded by incurable sickness rages wildly. And when the wickedness of the tempter brings forth its nefarious voice, and the listener’s answer sounds in harmony with that voice, such agreement—or rather collision—brings the harsh cry of a more grievous noise to the serene ears of the Creator [Col. 1147D].

That exacter is the one who whispers a deadly suggestion to us. Unless our vigilance—or rather divine grace—swiftly meets this whisper, the poisonous persuader endeavors to water it with certain allurements and carefully makes the little shoot, as it were, sprout. Growing from evil into worse, it gradually takes root; taking root, it grows strong like a perverse tree; and, growing strong, it hastens to spread its broad branches so widely that the birds of heaven—that is, evil spirits—are found to dwell in them. The one who plants a suggestion in us demands that it be so fruitful that whoever has heard its first voice should hear the second also, and thereafter that his speech should be heard to its conclusion, until one comes to the irrevocable ruin of complete damnation.

For if he perceives that the mind is seduced by the first motion, he immediately demands that the suggestion be brought into action; then that habit be added to the action like a heap upon it, so that the structure thus strengthened may not be overthrown by a slight impulse—or indeed by any impulse afterward [Col. 1148A]. When he sees that a mind gives itself feebly to the first suggestion, he seems to obtain a kind of proprietary right over it; and from the one who has begun to be his, he exacts step by step as tribute the aforesaid order established by his own laws. Both are miserable: the exacter and the obedient hearer alike are accused. The latter rejects nothing poisonous, nothing harmful; once he has heedlessly lent an attentive ear to the first voice, the now-prevailing enemy violently demands the consequences from him [Col. 1148B].

## Chapter XCVIII
Such, we find, was that first woman whom the serpent is said to have deceived with a crafty voice; and she in turn brought her husband into partnership in guilt, so that both carried their perverse design through to its wicked end. Since at the first word of the exacter they fell away from righteousness, they made us, who were to come long afterward, equally miserable; and the curse poured upon them as voluntarily deserving it has also, by a marvellous—or rather, more miserable—law, been poured punitively upon us even though unwilling. It so hampers our wretched nature that we are now scarcely able, or not able at all, not to heed that exacter; and whereas the first human beings could readily have sprung back from his snares, we now cannot disentangle our faltering steps from them except with grievous struggle. [Col. 1148C]

But when grace is absent, we cannot—or will not—make progress by struggling; and the exacter, gaining strength, compels us in our weakness to fail. Speaking according to his own will, he strives to recommend evils all the more openly as he does so more confidently; and we, taken captive, not only do not refuse but even delight to answer with a damnable consent. This response sometimes resounds so loudly, rages so wildly, and is so wretchedly increased in accordance with the pleasure of a corrupted will, that it infects those near at hand with a grave contagion of example, and an intolerable cry is carried even to the ears of God.

A cry of this kind was grievously heard at the time when the people of Sodom, burning with an illicit lust, [Col. 1148D] and wickedly prepared to fulfil it, hurried in one body, as though an army assembled, to the doors of righteous Lot, having crossed the bounds of modesty and wishing abusively to couple with the new guests.

When wickedness within sought to call them back, and, to the rioting crowd, he offered the two daughters whom he had, that ruined people by no means yielded to the sounder counsel. Instead, increasing their violence and multiplying their outcry, they persisted urgently in their more wicked purpose. Astonishing perversity! Those perverse men would not hear the righteous man’s more honourable counsel, nor would they spare guests of a single night. With such fury did they seek things altogether unlawful that they rejected what, though not permitted by divine law, was nevertheless made permissible by the order of nature. But the angels, whose concern was purity, unable to endure such shamelessness, struck with severe blindness the brutish men who were violently assailing the doors of the righteous man, so that an entrance could not be found; and, departing thence, they shook off the dust from their feet, as it were. [Col. 1149A]

Nor did this seem sufficient to divine equity. Though it mercifully bears with and spares human perversity for a long time, it is at last constrained, even unwillingly, to render like for like when perversity has reached its end and has been softened neither by threats nor by prayers. “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah,” He says, “has been multiplied. I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the cry which has come to Me, or not” (Gen. XVIII). The righteous Judge wishes to punish the vices of criminals in such a way that no one can utter even a just complaint against Him: before their destruction is determined, He is able, as it were, to experience their wickedness in immediate presence. Therefore, descending in the two angels, He enters the accursed city; invited to the house of righteous Lot, He lodges there as a guest. To that house, as has been said, the citizens of Sodom flocked from youth to old age, and deserved to be struck with the blindness you have heard described. [Col. 1149B]

But because the whole city was corrupted by an abominable vice, the blindness inflicted was not enough to punish so great an abomination. The stern avenger applied a sickle that cut away all harmful things so completely that it removed not merely the disease but the sick person from the midst. “Therefore the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of heaven, and overthrew these cities and all the inhabitants of the cities” (Gen. XIX). Rightly are those accused of such a fault, such an unlawful crime, struck with such an irremediable punishment; the angry Judge saw that He could find nothing more fitting for abolishing deeds so vile. For fire burns and sulphur stinks; both are joined together, and vengeance hurls an unheard-of rain upon the wretched cities which shameless lust inflamed when modesty had been driven far away, and which the stench of luxury polluted once nature’s laws had been crossed. [Col. 1149C]

Because shameless lust is a companion of stench and burning, the shameless are worthily punished by their own, as it were, kindred things; and those whose enticements they formerly obeyed with pleasure finally compel them to perish by their stings. Thus stricter judgment sometimes punishes contraries with contraries, and sometimes like things with like things. When it no longer wishes to bear the unruly cries of sinners, it knows how, by the majesty of its weighty hand, to restrain the clamorous beneath an unwelcome silence. Yet divine goodness is seen to be more intent upon this: by bearing with them and warning them, it restrains itself from vengeance, wishing that, with punishment deferred, the repentant sinner may be ashamed and may cease from the wicked clamour of vices, not so much compelled as willing. Therefore, admonishing through Isaiah, He says: “Cease to do perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. I). For nothing is found to sound more grievously in God’s ears, nothing to provoke Him more to anger, than the manners of the perverse, corrupted by the gall of wickedness—a shameless life devoted to clamorous depravity. [Col. 1149D]

For as long as perversity delights to possess the mind as its ruler, to occupy its gates, and to sit with power upon its throne, such fury and such joy are celebrated there that nothing health-giving is admitted. “Those rejoice,” says Solomon, “when they have done evil, and exult in the worst deeds” (Prov. II). Joy or exultation of this kind blinds the mind and utterly kills the vital spirit; and since one who is dead takes delight only in what is dead, he does not pursue what is living or healthful. Thus, when the Lord is about to say through Isaiah, “Learn to do good,” He first says, “Cease to do perversely,” indicating that unless the fire of wickedness first cools in the mind, unless garrulous joy and clamorous exultation grow somewhat still, the hard ear, overgrown with thorns, is not opened to hear what is good, and the understanding grows more heedlessly dull toward learning what is right. [Col. 1150A]

Indeed, a mind inflamed by evil desires and occupied in its own destruction by perverse deeds does not learn to do good so long as no repentance brings it to its senses from its purpose and it gives no attention to more useful teachers. Finally, when someone undertakes to instruct another, he first diligently invites him to silence; for the speech of the teacher is superfluous where the listener’s diligent attention does not provide silence. “Be silent for a little,” says Job, “that I may speak” (Job XIII). And a little earlier: “You are fabricators of falsehood; would that you were silent!” (ibid.). Job, burning with zeal for righteousness, seeks to teach truth to those who fashion falsehood both in heart and speech; and the good teacher calls his listener to silence so that, by being silent, he may hear his teacher more fruitfully. [Col. 1150B]

For since nothing clamours more against truth than falsehood, and noisy iniquity resists or murmurs against equity, one who teaches good things wishes his hearers to be silent from harmful evils, knowing that these things and those cannot share a place or concord. And lest he be accused of saying this while contradicting the saying by his conduct, and lest consequently his teaching be found the more deserving of rejection, he loves to show himself, for learning like things, to be such as he wishes them to be for hearing useful things. Hence he says: “You will not find in my tongue iniquity, nor shall foolishness resound in my throat” (Job VI). And much further on: “My lips shall not speak iniquity, nor shall my tongue meditate falsehood” (Job XXVII). [Col. 1150C]

The righteous man knew that when iniquity, foolishness, and falsehood are not pressed down by silence—when they sound, clamour, and are let loose in harmful freedom—the ear stopped by such things does not admit the word that brings salvation and does not let useful teaching enter the innermost seat of the heart. Therefore, trusting in sound counsel, he strives to restrain these harmful things by silence and to remove them far from mind, throat, and lips, so that they may neither assail nor prevail against the desired quiet, and may offer no obstacle to health-giving teaching. For the Spirit of God, by whom this holy man is inwardly taught, and by whose gift and grace he is freed from the tumult of worldly snares, does not teach those who wickedly, foolishly, and falsely love to be wordy, who do not wish “to be delivered from the snare of the hunters and from the harsh word” (Ps. XC). [Col. 1150D]

For the teaching Spirit is not heard by those whom sins demanding this keep at a greater distance, who are divided from Him by intervening iniquity and do not enjoy the countenance of grace as though His very face. To such persons Isaiah says: “Your iniquities have divided between you and your God, and your sins have hidden His face from you” (Isa. LIX). The prophet then indicates what a mass of iniquities and sins brings about this harmful schism between them and God, so that there is no meeting and no mutual agreement: “Your lips have spoken falsehood, and your tongue speaks iniquity” (ibid.). When tongue and lips are found to detest silence, and, having rejected silence, to serve iniquity and falsehood, surely equity and truth do not care to come to such clamourers; and, if they should come, they hasten to spring back from the tumult they find. [Col. 1151A]

As, according to the Gospel, “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI), so these different and opposed things cannot coexist. So long as falsehood and iniquity hold the rule of the heart, equity does not enter that same heart, occupied by such contraries. Further on through the same Isaiah, some are found to confess that, after their faults, when they are compelled to incur the punishments of those faults, they recognize both by what deserving they have fallen into their subsequent evils and what evils they had incurred by preceding deserving: “We have spoken from the heart words of falsehood; and justice stood far off, truth fell, and equity could not enter” (Isa. LIX). Because these persons, as they say, spoke falsehood from their heart and, abhorring silence, were enveloped in malicious tumults, justice did not care to approach them in their restlessness; truth did not enter the liars, nor equity the unjust. [Col. 1151B]

For hostile to virtue are the multitude of carnal passions, a mind devoted to tumult, and the foulness of a wounded conscience. Like a public street, it lays itself open to whatever vices happen to meet it, and, hardened in evil, does not resolve to rest from worldly clamour. While it labours with welcome unrest to serve such things, while it follows the tracks of the flocks and, grazing the kids, miserably fails to know itself, it no longer speaks to itself, lost as it is, anything health-giving or useful; it imposes neither rest nor silence upon its labour. Rebuking it, Isaiah says: “In the multitude of your way you have laboured; you did not say, ‘I will rest’” (Isa. LVII). [Col. 1151C]

The way of one who walks perversely is sin, by which every lost person walks and does not refuse to labour as he walks. The more sin is accumulated by adding sin to sin, the more he delights in the labour of his manifold way. This pleasing, though very burdensome, multitude of ways that the lost man heaps up for himself so enervates him as he heaps it up, by a certain heavy softness—or soft heaviness—that, like a heifer given over to welcome toil and to threshing, he no longer either wishes or is able to restore his captive mind to the rest that would benefit it. [Col. 1151D]

A little further on, the same prophet says of such people: “The impious are like a boiling sea, which cannot rest.” The sea, which by its own nature has a shifting and unstable movement and is unable at any time or in any manner to maintain a motionless state, is nevertheless said, when its surface is spread out in level beauty, not to boil but somehow to be at rest. At times its expanse itself, with rippling back, is gently made even; and from such evenness it is properly called *aequor*, “the level sea,” when its surface is made calm like a plain, and the sailor rejoices in grateful sailing upon the tranquil sea. But when an unwelcome onset of winds comes upon that same sea, when the thrust of the following wave harshly drives the wave before it, when its disturbed level rises into heavy heaps and is now sunk as if into an abyss, now lifted and stretched aloft, then the sea itself is said, as it were, to be stirred to anger and to roar so that it cannot be restrained by silence. [Col. 1152A]

From this roaring it is called not now *aequor* but rather *fretum*, “a turbulent strait,” because, having lost its evenness, it rages in swollen boiling; its anger grows heavier under the pressure of the winds, and its troubled face swells with roaring waves. So too, when the impious have been inflamed by the heat of vices and, falling step by step from bad to worse, have reached the depth of sins, pressed and oppressed by clamorous enticements, they neither can nor wish to rest, but are both compelled and delighted to persist in their heat and roaring. For those who, by the choice of a will abandoning grace, are depraved and rejoice not merely to sin but to add sin to sin, grow more wickedly hardened against God in their multiplied fault and therefore do not readily cease from their purpose. Hence the Lord says to Job: “Does one who contends with God so easily grow quiet?” (Job XXXIX). [Col. 1152B]

The person who dares to contend with God, as with swollen neck he presumptuously offends Him again, hardened by the clamour of offences, does not know how to find an entrance to rest. Delighting in forum and street, he cannot enter the sanctuary of peace. The aforementioned Job affirms this: “Who has resisted Him and had peace?” (Job IX). If the creature delights in resisting the Creator by sinning, and in its hardness does not fear to persist until evil is piled high, it cannot forget the wickedness in which it has hardened, nor attain the peace or silence that it does not love. For as long as anyone does not fear to sin wickedly and, through love of sinning, neither fears God nor respects a human being, he certainly does not deserve to find rest or attain peace, being without that grace apart from which harmless peace is not possessed. [Col. 1152C]

## CHAPTER XCIX

Therefore, when Eliphaz the Temanite spoke to Job himself, struck and afflicted by troubles, thinking that Job suffered the evils pressing upon him because his own faults demanded it, and that in his suffering he was regarded as insolent and impatient, he seemed to offer him honourable and salutary counsel. By hearing it, Job, he thought, could find peace and silence. For observing him tormented with hard blows, and judging still more that he was weighed down by inward sins, he rashly dared to reproach him with those same faults; and, not sufficiently examining himself, he grievously accused an innocent man. “You have stripped the naked of their clothing,” he says; “you have not given water to the weary; you have withheld bread from the hungry; you have sent widows away empty; and you have broken the arms of orphans” (Job XXII). [Col. 1153A]

Eliphaz then indicates what evils Job had deserved, as he supposed, and into what unrest he had fallen while descending from evil to evil: “Therefore,” he says, “you are surrounded by snares, and sudden terror troubles you” (ibid.). Because, he says, you have offended God in many ways, bringing no good gift but instead inflicting evil on the needy, you are therefore bound by blameworthy obstinacy as though by snares or fetters, so that you may not turn to repentance or to recognition of your own iniquities. And you who formerly rejoiced foolishly and securely in transitory prosperity are now troubled by its sudden loss, and fear the adversity that you feel has befallen you more harshly—though you ought more prudently to have feared it while future than when present. [Col. 1153B]

Thus Eliphaz the Temanite thought Job to be troubled; thus he, who himself was to be judged, judged Job’s hidden conscience. He supposed Job had heedlessly incurred grave faults and, with the peace of his heart utterly shattered, had more turbulently resisted God.

Having clearly identified the disease as grievously pressing upon him, he offered a remedy reasonably suited to that disease, giving counsel by which Job’s harsh perversity might be overthrown and, once the tumult had been lulled, he might return to the peace he had lost. “Therefore,” he says, “submit to Him and have peace” (ibid.). Eliphaz rightly understood what inward silence ought to be maintained and by what manner or order one comes to the peace of that silence; and he would have offered a quite fitting command or counsel on the matter, had he more carefully considered to whom it ought to be offered. [Col. 1153C]

But righteous Job had no need of this advice, because he did not commit the evils for which he was unjustly accused, and it is certain that he possessed, both by grace and by corresponding merits, the inward silence and peace that he was thought not to possess. Since Eliphaz did not look more subtly into his conscience and, blinded by pride, did not understand his innocence, he wished to counsel one who was wiser, to teach one more learned; and though not sufficiently sound himself, he nevertheless put forward sounder teaching. “Submit to Him,” he says, “and have peace.” Surely he does not rest in the wholesome and happy bosom of peace who does not diligently submit to God the Author; nor is he worthily struck by the harmful tumult of evils who does not humbly incline himself to hear His words. [Col. 1153D]

Therefore he adds: “Receive the law from His mouth, and lay up His words in your heart” (ibid.). Since he had advised Job to submit to God, he adds how one ought to submit to Him. For a teacher is judged prudent, and teaching more effective, when it shows not only what must be done but also how it must be done. The person is proved to receive the law from God’s mouth and to lay His words up in his heart who both hears the divine commands and tenderly embraces what he has heard; who eagerly warms himself by attentive hearing in order to know them, and does not grow cold in inward diligence in doing them. But because peace is not one thing only, but is found to be varied and manifold, and its variety is experienced in the diversity of those who seek it, the following statement clearly and usefully defines what kind of peace that is to which the course just described leads. [Col. 1154A]

“If you return,” he says, “to the Almighty, you will put iniquity far from your tent, and the Almighty will be against your enemies” (ibid.). When anyone returns to God with devout affection, receives His law, and embraces His words in the heart, he earns peace from vices and silence from harmful evils; iniquity is removed far from his tent. Our tent is said to be the dwelling-place either of body or of mind, because the soul is contained in heart or body and intention in the mind. He therefore removes iniquity far from these who does not defile either the mind with perverse intention or the body with carnal deed. Then the Almighty is found to oppose that person’s enemies, when He takes care to repulse malignant spirits from him, makes the recesses of the mind clean and serene by grace poured in, and by a mighty hand removes from them whatever clamours wickedly. [Col. 1154B]

In this peace or silence, the person rests hidden who, according to Eliphaz’s statement, submits to God the Creator: the person whose mind is not deceived by serpentine suggestion, whose strong spirit is not led by feminine softness to carry out a wicked deed.

For when a wicked suggestion fraudulently steals into the heart; when consent of the will, much more wicked, is joined to the suggestion; when the corrupted will, making evil progress, is given over to effect; when, for the advancement of wickedness, the sinner holds his salvation in contempt—then inward peace and the silence of the mind are disturbed, and, like a boiling sea that cannot rest, the conscience rages with faults as with swelling waves. And if such a sinner sometimes comes somewhat to his senses, is shaken by fear, and desires to rest from the harmful heat, he nevertheless cannot immediately gain tranquil silence or remove the bond from his neck and the fetter from his foot. [Col. 1154C]

He who has wholly subjected himself to enervating softness, and has not rejected its harmful poison at the first, second, third, or fourth stage, does not easily withdraw his neck from its heavy yoke; for even if he expels it, the cord of habit draws it back. Job speaks grievingly in the person of this sinner and complains bitterly of so great a misery; in complaining, he indicates by what fall or order wickedness reaches consummation, and, once consummated, how silence is not readily retained from evils. “Why,” he says, “did I not die in the womb? Why did I not perish at once when I came forth from the womb? Why was I received upon the knees? Why was I nursed at the breasts?” (Job III.) The first movement of sin is suggestion: when the devil, seeking to disturb the purity of our mind, secretly presumes to pour his poison into it, so that, once it has been poured in, the affection of the mind may be led astray and the impulse may be brought by harmful advance into effect. [Col. 1154D]

Then, as it were, seed is conceived in the womb when an evil suggestion is collected in the heart; and the sinner dies in the womb of conception when the suggestion is not at all permitted to advance by any consent.

“Why did I not die in the womb?” Why, he says, did I not come forward to meet the first suggestion? Why did I not crush the seed cast in with a strong foot? Why did I not drive off the approaching flies with a watchful hand? And why, before I lived to sin, did I not choose rather to die to it? The sinner would be dead in the secret of the womb if, attending to the beginning of evil living, he resisted it with prudent counsel; if he restrained himself against the first motions with such justice that, like one dead, he offered no collusion at all to sin at play. [Col. 1155A]

But if he does not stretch out a ready hand to wipe away the poison cast in, if he does not crush the first seed of wickedness as though it were the serpent’s head, the suggestion is plainly allowed to pass into delight, and, like Eve, our carnal sense is deceived. In this deception the sinner is said, as it were, to come forth from the womb, when what had been conceived in evil is advanced into worse: when the wicked seed not only does not wither under the injury it deserves, but, irrigated with added delight, grows stronger in greater wickedness. Recalling that he had fallen into this advancement toward worse, the aforementioned man complains sorrowfully that he had not perished even then; for although he had not chosen to die while hidden in the womb, he ought at least to have perished once he had come forth from the womb. [Col. 1155B]

“Why did I not perish at once when I came forth from the womb?” Since, he says, I was not overcome in the womb by a fortunate death, why did I not at least perish as soon as I came from the womb, so that, seeing the danger and understanding that I had perished, I might destroy what I was—though it would have been better for me not to have been? Hence the Gospel says: “It would have been better for that man had he not been born” (Mark XIV). Indeed, it was better that the wicked seed should fail in the womb than advance by being born from it; better that both the born thing and the conceived thing should be turned back and cease to be, than that it should be evil to others and most evil to itself. “Overturn the wicked,” says Solomon, “and they shall not be” (Prov. XII). Happy is the person whose impiety divine grace so overturns, whose back it so turns aside from the impending burden, that it perishes either in the womb, while the disease is fresh, or at least immediately perishes after coming forth from the womb. [Col. 1155C]

“Why was I received upon the knees?” When this offspring has newly emerged from the womb and advances from the first to the second stage of progression, if it then finds its own maker hostile, it is immediately destroyed at its very birth, as it were by the hand of midwives. But if the author of evil does not yet dread its birth, but stubbornly burns for its advancement, unhappy midwives receive it upon their knees, stroking and handling it tenderly. After that wicked whisper which serpentine craft hisses, after the wicked hearing by which feminine softness is deceived, that husbandly Adam not only pursues the woman’s fault with no correction, but, weakly conquered, obeys her enticing words. What the wicked serpent proposed by poisonous fraud, what pleased the deceived woman to whom it was proposed, Adam, himself induced, gave a very yielding consent; and, to carry it out, he placed his working faculties beneath it, cherishing it as though upon knees. [Col. 1155D]

So too, when primal suggestion steals into our mind, and deceptive sensuality delights in it with a certain native softness, reason itself and the spirit are sometimes weakened by its flatteries; and, through the connivance of the weakened powers, the begun prelude is confirmed in action. Once the spirit is defeated, the whole array of senses is applied to carrying out the wicked deed, so that it may be cherished through them and in them as upon knees. For he does not apply effective diligence to its fulfilment who does not, by consenting to it, place beneath it the harmony of his senses as though knees. But would that even then he restrained the loose reins of sinning and held back the wicked desire stretched out toward further things; so that, if by the knees placed beneath the harmful offspring he supplied the caress of consent, he might at least not add the nourishment of milk being poured in. “Why,” he says, “was I nursed at the breasts?” [Col. 1156A]

The sinner himself is said to provide himself with the nourishment of milk when he not only loves to consent to delight in order to carry out the wickedness in his heart, but adds to that consent a false hope or the boldness of self-defence. Strengthened most wickedly in these things, he does not abandon his purpose of sinning. Thus Adam too, bound by social affection to Eve, who thought carnally, gave his consent and, at her word, put the forbidden fruit to his mouth. Once the deed was committed, he did not immediately repent in compunction; rather, believing that God would not easily be angry with a human being—indeed, that for the sake of a new wife He would indulge an offender more leniently—he made light of what he had done, hardened his heart more heedlessly, and, soothed by false hope, persisted too long in the fault he had committed. [Col. 1156B]

In a similar manner, much later, when Shechem son of Hamor had violated Dinah as she wandered abroad and had perhaps taken the blossoms of her virgin modesty while she did not sufficiently resist, he took care, skilled in such matters, to soothe the distressed girl with caresses, lest, corrupted and repentant, she should hasten to recoil from the experience. Softened by flatteries of this sort, Adam not only did not immediately rebuke himself with any repentance, but, when questioned by the Lord, swelled with boldness in self-defence. He attempted to hurl the dart of guilt at the woman given to him, or rather, indirectly, to turn it back upon Him who had given her. “The woman,” he says, “whom You gave me, gave to me, and I ate” (Gen. III). [Col. 1156C]

Adam seems to think that, if a woman—or such a woman—had not been given him, he could by no means have been held guilty of this transgression. Therefore he thinks it just that guilt should not be heavily imputed to him, since in some fashion its cause derives from the Giver Himself. Thus he nursed himself at the breasts both of such false hope and of swollen self-defence; sucking harmful milk, he strengthened himself in his purpose. And to the thing which the susceptible woman did not reject when the serpent suggested it, he himself, consenting, added the strength of habit. By these four modes or stages we turn aside inwardly in the heart from righteousness and wickedly incline the wretched mind to sin, so that, even if the guilty hand is not seen outwardly in the deed, wickedness is nevertheless gradually consummated in thought. [Col. 1156D]

Considering this, the Lord says: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from before My eyes.” Divine goodness does not wish to behold the worst thoughts—wicked thoughts which, restrained by no rein from their advance, do not cease to advance from progress to progress toward worse, until they reach completion. [Col. 1157A]

## CHAPTER C

By the same modes through which the wickedness of thoughts is consummated in the mind, sin also grows outwardly in deed; and, when grace to repent has at last been infused into him, the sinner complains and laments each stage of his transgression.

“Why,” he says, “did I not die in the womb?” (Job III). The sinner is said to live in the womb when he does not fear to commit an unlawful deed in secret, when he despises the knowledge of Him who alone knows all things, while he has not yet offended the eyes of men. Because he fears to undergo punishment for sin, or, though he may wish to be a sinner, is ashamed nevertheless to be seen as one, he therefore takes care either to commit theft deceitfully, or to seek the embrace of another person’s wife secretly, or to burn wickedly for carrying out any other deed, while still delighting to hide in darkness as though within walls. Of such a person the Gospel says: “He who does evil hates the light” (John III). [Col. 1157B]

Sometimes a person who wishes to be restrained by no obstacle from fulfilling wickedness carefully arranges not to be seen by people, and, in order to sin more securely and more confidently, diligently avoids their testimony. “Who sees me?” says one. “Darkness surrounds me, walls cover me, and no one looks around me; whom should I fear?” (Ecclus. XXIII). Within these walls, within the womb, within this hiding-place, the sinner would die if he confessed himself dead through humble repentance; if divine grace, visiting the confessing sinner mercifully, awakened him as though from the dead and made him more righteous.

“Why did I not die in the womb, or at least perish immediately after coming forth from the womb?” If the sinner or hidden sin does not die within the womb, then, advancing in evil, it comes forth alive as though from the womb: what was formerly done with some restraint in hiding is now done shamelessly in public. For one who does not hasten to crush fault while it lies hidden, who does not put forth his hand or draw his sword to cut it down while it crawls upon the ground, gains strength in time to the point that, once the barrier of shame has been broken, he does not fear to leap forth and come with shameless face to the knowledge of many. [Col. 1157C]

Of such people Jeremiah says: “They were not ashamed with shame, and they did not know how to blush” (Jer. VI).

And again: “You have acquired the brow of a harlot; you refused to be ashamed” (Jer. III).

Sometimes a woman who formerly delighted in a hiding-place for sinning and admitted her lover into a closed chamber advances to the point of delighting in wandering abroad once shame has been wiped away; abandoning the room, she delights in the open brothel. For after someone presumes to leap beyond the bounds of modesty and the limits of shame, he does not care to what vices he may direct his harmful hands, and he pays little attention to who says what about him, judging slight the fault whose good name or ill repute he despises. [Col. 1157D]

It does not suffice for such a person to pollute his own life alone with blameworthy actions; he is also found, so far as lies within him, to disturb others greatly. For he not only does not incite them to live, but, by living perversely before them, urges them to do like things. Just as when a corpse has been buried within the blind confines of a tomb, if after some days the structure of its covering is opened, the eyes and nostrils of those around are offended by horror and stench, and scarcely anyone is protected from the offence unless perhaps at a greater distance; so too, when anyone burns more shamelessly for sinning, neither fears God nor is ashamed before people, he grievously burdens those to whom his perversity becomes known. And when he eats a sour grape, another’s teeth too are set on edge. [Col. 1158A]

Such were those rebuked by the prophet, who are said to have proclaimed their sin like Sodom; they not only refused to hide the works of darkness, but, sinning publicly, wished to draw others into their company. In this condition the sinner would perish happily if he came to a worthy recognition of his danger; if, after coming to human notice as though he had emerged from the womb, he forestalled the third stage of evil living by swift repentance.

## CHAPTER CI
“Why was I received upon the knees?” (Job 3). If the sinner, after coming forth from the womb, does not at once perish; if the sling that meets him does not quickly crush his shameless brow; then habit gladly receives him into its soft lap and, placing knees beneath him, receives him so that he may rest upon them with pleasure. [Col. 1158C] Having received him, it carefully softens him by so many enticements, binds him by so many bonds, ensnares him in such gentle embraces, so that, once ensnared, he not only refuses to abandon his wicked purpose, but can scarcely—or cannot—do so even if the will sometimes seems present.

For the sinner whom habit attracts to itself, whom, having welcomed evil, it strives to make worse, it wraps in so subtle and inextricable a knot of blandishment that, deceived, he thinks himself held by the force of nature. Hence that much-discussed proverb, which declares the bond of this habit to be stronger: because it readily grows and does not readily cease from its growth, it has no slight kinship and no slight partnership with nature: “Habit,” it says, “is a second nature.” It rightly chose to call habit [Col. 1158D] nature, because just as a person cannot prevail in uprooting nature, so indeed what he has allowed to take root through the vice of habit he will not at once be able to abolish, even should he wish to do so.

Sometimes, when he begins to contemplate this difficulty and weighs attentively how hard it is to eradicate, if perhaps someone advises him, for his own better welfare, to reject what will harm him, the wretched man complains, in excusing himself, of nature. For when habit contradicts sounder counsel, he, attracted and deceived, calls it a defect of nature; and, either overlooking or failing to understand habit’s subtle and scarcely disentanglable bond, he ascribes to nature what truly brings him this loss. “You advise me,” he says, “to pursue these and similar harmful things no further [Col. 1159A]; not to offend by wicked deeds the kindly lover of my salvation; to forget them and, with deliberate purpose, stretch toward the things of greater worth and take hold of the narrower paths of a better life. I admit indeed that this would truly benefit me: my conscience would thereby be healed, and honourable advantage would result. But I see that my nature is so constrained by its own softness that by no means can I advance to these difficult matters. I cannot abstain from soft and pleasant things; I cannot, like very many others, endure hard and rough things. Such an inborn softness is found to press upon me that I cannot apply myself to grave and unfamiliar matters.”

Thus this foolish man, by excusing ruined habits and blaming nature’s feeble softness, does not set a vigorous hand even to better things; but, clinging to accustomed evils, [Col. 1159B] he heaps the greatest sins upon great ones. A certain pagan, Sallust, is found not to agree with this judgment. He recognizes, as I think, how far it departs from truth, and in refuting it invites us to think more rightly, lest anyone through sloth or ignorance omit to undertake anything more honourable. “Falsely,” he says, “does the human race complain of its nature as though it were weak: you will find that human industry fails more often than nature’s power.”

The pagan does not think that our nature ought to be accused of weakness, or that our perversity ought to be excused through it. Rather, he believes that people should be blamed because they do not propose what is honourable and useful, nor set the industry of the mind to accomplish what nature is doing. For he does not judge that it belongs to nature [Col. 1159C] to lack strength; rather, he wishes the mind’s cooperating industry to be present. If that industry slackens and becomes feebly numb, nature delays, since by itself it has no power at all to compel anyone.

But when that industry delays, crafty habit puts itself forward; gradually slipping in, it shamelessly sets itself before nature. The longer it lasts, the stronger it proves; and, once it has acquired strength, it finally pretends to be nature. For that deceitful thing wishes to be regarded under nature’s name; assuming nature’s appearance, it wishes to be seen as nature, so that anyone deceived may more freely incline himself toward it and gladly rest his languid head upon its knees. Yet would that even this were enough for the sinner, and that he did not proceed to inflict a greater insult upon the Creator: received upon the knees, he should rest there so gently as to seek [Col. 1159D] decline rather than a greater and stronger encouragement.

“Why was I nursed at the breasts?” For the one received in a soft resting-place and placed upon knees is then sweetly offered breasts, so that, drinking milk, he may grow fittingly, and suitable nurture may make the one who grows great. When the sinner is bound with the soft cord of harsh habit and, grace being absent, is not freed from it—whether because he is unwilling or unable—what previously seemed sufficiently blameworthy and condemnable is now made light of by his blinded conscience. Reprehensibly, he induces himself to a certain hope—a miserable hope whose sweetness deceives him, miserable as he is—while he hopes that God will more readily forgive him, although he himself is unwilling to repent in order to obtain forgiveness.

For he hears that God has pardoned many faults equally great, indeed greater [Col. 1160A], and bestowed his benefit upon many who deserved evil. Setting before himself those to whom he knows God’s abundant generosity has been shown, he judges that God is not restrained by stinginess even toward himself. Thus seductive hope caresses this ruined person; thus it strives, as it were, to milk out for him twin breasts: from the left breast, making his sins appear to him lighter than is just; from the right breast, making him judge God’s mercy to be greater than is due.

For when he does not direct his eye to look upon his sins, or treats those which confront him as extremely slight—thinking that they are either not liable to a charge of injustice or are unworthy of severe punishment because they carry little weight—then indeed he is wickedly nourished from the left breast of hope and softened by the ruinous allurement of this nourishment. But if he judges God’s mercy so great that God is regarded as nothing but merciful toward one who sins obstinately [Col. 1160B]; if, while he himself hardens wickedly through sinning, God is supposed to soften feebly through showing mercy; while he himself, choosing injustice, rejects holiness, God is supposed not to love justice or behold equity in his face; while he himself does not recall his unbridled heart from its evil purpose, God is supposed, through base negligence, to leave him unpunished—if, I say, he feels, imagines, and supposes that God will be such toward him, and will be present to one sinning for however long and render only the rewards of justice, then, nursed from the right breast of hope, he grows badly; and, growing badly, clings quite childishly to the nurse.

## CHAPTER 102

Divine Scripture wisely addresses the man, although in his hardness he does not follow its speech, finding it sweeter to be nursed in his sin by deceptive hope than [Col. 1160C] to be weaned by Scripture’s harsher words. “Do not add sin to sin,” it says, “and do not say: ‘God’s compassion is great; he will have mercy upon the multitude of my sins’” (Ecclesiasticus 5).

Holy Scripture, which very often commends and extols God’s mercy, and raises us up to hope in it by praiseworthy exhortations, nevertheless does not wish us to proclaim its greatness with reckless confidence so long as we voluntarily remain subject to condemnable vices. [Col. 1160D] For just as no work is found saving in us unless it is preceded by fitting and necessary hope, so neither does the hope of one whose perverse and obstinate will is darkened by vice shine forth sufficiently fittingly or commendably.

Therefore David says: “Hope in the Lord and do good” (Psalm 36). I wish, he says, and admonish you to hope in the Lord God and affirm that his mercy is of great magnitude or great abundance; but know that in hoping you will not be disappointed only if, with a disciplined will, you love to do what is good. Otherwise hope is proved to be not so much beneficial as deceptive; and each person deceived by its blandishments delights in it to his ruin—drawing from the right breast so as not to regard God as wholly just in punishing the obstinate, and from the left so as not to weigh his own sins in a just balance and with equal weight.

Since this man’s wickedness increases through the aforesaid stages, Job, carefully considering them, laments and, adopting the person or, as it were, the appearance of a penitent man, bewails the miserable birth and progress [Col. 1161A] of the offender. “Why,” he says, “was I nursed at the breasts?” But as such nursing is rightly lamented, so, conversely, the weaning of the person being nursed is commended: when, that fleshly deceiver’s flow of milk having been driven away and dried up, he hungers for bread from heaven and thirsts for waters from the fountains of the Saviour.

Thus Abraham is rightly read to have weaned his son Isaac and joyfully celebrated a feast on the day of his weaning, because both angels and human beings who are concerned for our salvation diligently draw us back from the yoke of deceptive slavery; and when they see us repent after carnal desires have been driven away, they gladly rejoice in our sorrow and our progress. “There is joy,” he says, “among the angels over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 15). And Paul says to the Corinthians: “Who,” he asks, [Col. 1161B] “is it that makes me glad except the one who is made sorrowful by me?” (2 Corinthians 47 [as cited]). And much farther on: “I rejoice,” he says, “because you were made sorrowful unto repentance” (ibid.).

When, instead of deceptive laughter, we are watered with devout tears; when, instead of the oil of gladness, we are cast down by weeping and ashes; when, instead of tender milk, we do not find it burdensome to feed on rough bread; when we are sorrowful with fitting repentance for past evils—then indeed our Paul, who had formerly grieved that we were being nursed by the enticement of sin, now rejoices and exults, as Abraham at the weaning of his beloved son.

Likewise another diligently weaned the son whom he trained by watchful care and saving admonitions, wishing him not to be nursed by deceivers’ blandishments nor, with his natural tooth broken, to delight in deadly milk. “My son,” he says, “if sinners have nursed you, [Col. 1161C] do not consent” (Proverbs 1). If the hissing of a deceiving tongue is heard, he says, when each wretched person is praised in the desires of his sinful soul, see, my son, that your strength does not soften childishly, and that, your tooth broken or knocked out, you do not consent to milky pleasures.

Whoever chooses either not to perceive at all the sweetness of this milk, or at least, having perceived it, to recoil from it manfully, will surely deserve to fall asleep in blessed sleep and, with the noise of harmful evils driven away, will find silence while sleeping. Of this Job also adds: “For now, sleeping, I would be silent and would rest in my sleep” (Job 3). Rightly, he says, do I lament that I have incurred the stains of sin and have come by ruinous stages to deserve death, because, if I had more strictly kept my feet from them, I would rest in my sleep and, sleeping, [Col. 1161D] would now be silent.

Just as sleep or sleeping sometimes deserves rebuke in the Scriptures, so it is at other times described in the same Scriptures as commendable. For the sinner lies numb, as though asleep, in the harmful security of a bed of vices; while the righteous person likewise rests, as though asleep, in the soft repose of virtues. Of sinners Isaiah says: “Sleeping,” he says, “and loving dreams” (Isaiah 56).
