In the Gospel, Lazarus, who dies as a figure of sinners and is said to have been held in the tomb for four days, is testified by the Lord not only to die but also to sleep, so that by the name of sleep the harmful repose of sin may be signified. “Lazarus,” he says, “our friend sleeps” (John 11).

The Lord complains that the sinner grows numb in his sins as though asleep, that he hardens in evil obstinacy in his torpor, having incurred ruin through the four stages of perdition and, like one dead four days, filled the tomb with a grave stench. “Lord,” Martha says, [Col. 1162A] “for he has been dead four days” (ibid.). The four days during which Lazarus is held in the tomb, I judge to be the four stages by which every wretched person is said to come to the height of wickedness. When he reaches it, pressed by a hard stone, he falls into a heavier sleep, since, made evil and obstinate, he scarcely comes to his senses from his purpose.

Yet God’s abundant benevolence does not always wholly abandon one who, falling from evil into worse, sins in this manner; rather, thundering with a loud voice, it deigns to awaken him from grave sleep and mercifully raise him from four-day death. “I am going,” he says, “to awaken him from sleep” (ibid.). I wish, he says, that this sick man, dead four days, should not sleep so long; I wish to free him from the hard bonds of his obstinacy; I wish him not to be held in wicked death, but to be refreshed by the welcome benefit of another kind of sleep.

[Col. 1162B] The disciples’ reply agrees with this: “Lord,” they say, “if he sleeps, he will be safe” (ibid.). In the literal sense, the Lord had spoken of bodily death, but they thought that he spoke of the sleep of slumber. In the mystical sense, however, that sleep signifies the deadly repose of sin, whereas this other works the repose of more serene grace unto lasting salvation. “If he sleeps,” they say, “he will be safe.” Truly, the one to whom divine grace grants such sleep as to silence the restless clamor of his vices; to obey the heavenly commandments with a conscience at peace [Col. 1162C]; to be free from sin and serve justice alone; to flee present things and direct desire toward things to come; to spurn transient things and sigh after those which [are without] end and abiding—such a person will undoubtedly, according to the Gospel word, enjoy salvation and obtain peace upon peace and grace for grace.

For this sleep is a kind of foretaste or figure of that which, by the gift of grace, is to come to the merits of the righteous: after they reach that peace in which they strive to be released from the noise of vices, they will attain the peace which no disturbance can upset. Therefore this sleep is rightly commended, and every wise person is worthily invited to it—blessed indeed if he deserves to find this grace, so that amid the laborious course of this life he may be able to sleep a little.

[Col. 1162D] To this end that good teacher also more diligently exhorted the disciples; near his Passion, seemingly neglectful of himself, he appeared to be caring for them, warning them to hide during the troubled time in a kind of bed of hope and, their fear softened, rest beneath the wings of steadfast faith. “Sleep now,” he says, “and rest” (Matthew 26). A little earlier, coming to them and finding them asleep, he had rebuked them, saying: “Could you not watch with me one hour? Watch and pray” (ibid.). Because they had heard their master and Lord preached as immortal, but now saw him in no way resisting imminent death, their love having grown cold and their faith greatly weakened, they were wholly unprepared to die with him or for him. They are therefore said rightly to be held by the sleep of a certain weakness and sloth, from which they are restrained by their master’s kindly rebuke. [Col. 1163A] Hence in Luke: “Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray” (Luke 22).

Why, he says, have you fallen away from the faith which I diligently preached to you and, through fear of death, fallen into the base drowsiness of sorrow, when the death and Passion which shall come upon me according to the law of human flesh will benefit the salvation of you all, if only you believe? “Therefore rise and pray” (ibid.). For if you raise yourselves, at my word, to steadfastness in faith, and direct the urgency of prayer to the true God, then he himself, being merciful, will certainly not lead you into deadly temptation, but his good Spirit will lead you in the straight way.

But because the disciples could not rise suitably to watch and pray, nor emerge from the depth and profundity of drowsy weakness, unless he who warned them also mercifully deigned to help them and either give or obtain that this might be effectively fulfilled, he first went away and prayed. Matthew relates how often he found them asleep; he first went away, he says, and prayed, signifying that in dying he would not leave them like orphans in their weakness, but, when the work of his Passion was completed, would bestow the greater gifts of grace. [Col. 1163B]

First he prays, and coming to them finds them sleeping; a second time he prays, and coming to them finds them sleeping; he prays a third time, and coming to them says: “Sleep now and rest.” Because in his death their violently shaken faith grew weak, and with faith weakened their very activity consequently hid away as though pressed under a bushel, [Col. 1163C] Christ, moved by mercy for their limping condition, prays; and, lest they fail entirely, he himself keeps watch and labours for those who sleep. This is what he says elsewhere to Peter: “But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (ibid.).

He prays first that the shame of wounded faith may be washed away; second, that the numbed negligence of slumbering action may be removed; third, that, once vices are cleansed, the welcome rest of conscience may be bestowed.

## CHAPTER 103

That he is said to pray three times for the removal of these evils, but once for the acquisition of goods, indicates that it is difficult for anyone to be freed from their bonds, while, once freed, these goods can be acquired more easily. For if someone labours to cut thorns, briars, brambles, and brushwood away by the root; to plough up suckers, tamarisks, and ferns; to uproot utterly wild trees and their deep roots; [Col. 1163D] to level heavy masses of rubble and the rocky swellings of hills; to make a field new by clearing it of these and similar things—he must surely labour with great sweat and no small delay of time in order to prepare the cleared place for the necessary seed.

But once it is prepared, the labor that follows is judged lighter and more bearable: good seed is easily sown there; once sown, it grows together through the welcome balance of moisture and warmth; once established, it becomes green; once it has put off its greenness, it ripens; and when it has ripened, the cultivator’s welcome security becomes joyful. Therefore, when the Lord spoke figuratively to Jeremiah of such cultivation and earnestly exhorted him to undertake the cultivator’s office, he sufficiently indicated both that evils are uprooted only with much labour and that good things are afterward introduced with more pleasant care. [Col. 1164A] “Behold,” he says, “I have appointed you to pluck up, to destroy, to ruin, to scatter, to build, and to plant” (Jeremiah 11 [as cited]).

He set forth four acts by which the tenacious evil of vices is cast out; he added two by which fruitful virtue is planted. For, according to a certain pagan also, “this fern is scarcely tamed by any plough”; and once it has at last been expelled, a good field is then more easily enriched with good seed.

For this reason Christ is remembered to have prayed twice for those whom he found sleeping twice, but only once when he either wished, commanded, or urged them now to sleep. No one among them can either be free of vices or abound in virtues unless the Son takes care to offer sacrifices of prayer to the Father. His prayers are indeed offered in humble devotion before the Passion, but after [Col. 1164B] the Resurrection they are more manifestly known to be fulfilled, when their old weakness was removed by the gift of new grace and a larger gift of serenity of mind and security was bestowed.

For Christ, rising from the dead and appearing with many proofs for forty days, restored their faltering faith—indeed, trained them far more strongly in a fuller faith. Having made them firm in faith, he likewise stirred them to action, so that the virtue of faith might not only be held in their hearts but also be commended in word and deed. “For faith without works is idle” (James 2).

Accordingly, when the Jews, in the harsh rage of envy, persecute them and strive to extinguish in them either faith itself or at least the work of faith, they nevertheless are not bent by prayer, money, threats, or beatings. Rather, they gladly suffer insults for Christ’s name. As it is written: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). You see that they not only endure many grievous things for Christ, but that in enduring them they do not grieve from weakness or distress of spirit; indeed, they are enlarged by a more abundant benefit, a certain inward joy, and take delight in security of mind as though at a banquet. [Col. 1164C] “For a secure mind,” as it is written, “is a continual feast” (Proverbs 15).

[Col. 1164D] This security is not inappropriately judged to be a kind of sleep, when the inward mind is lulled in quiet silence, so that some seclusion is claimed amid the public square of this life, and, with domestic tumults removed, one rests in the inner chamber of strength. Even if the unruly flesh opposes it with deceitful allurement, or any adversity of envious people struggles against it with loud murmuring, striving and straining in every way to seduce the righteous person’s mind and draw it, as it were, from its chamber to the noise of the market-place, that mind nevertheless keeps the door closed and does not admit the presence of those making noise. Rather, as though in a cloistered dormitory, it entrusts itself to the sleep of silence.

For when it yields in no softness to carnal blandishments; when it is not terrified by persecutors’ threats or beatings; when, barring the door with the bolt of constancy against everything hostile to salvation, it does not hear the taskmaster’s voice through the intervening strong wall—what else can it be said to do but sleep securely in a certain retreat of rest, [Col. 1165A] to whose inner chamber neither violent nor crafty robber can find entrance?

Therefore it is fitting that, after the Resurrection, the disciples are reported gathered in one chamber and the doors carefully shut for fear of the Jews. With the enemies excluded, Jesus wished to show himself present and refresh the besieged men’s anxiety by the gift of the grace of peace. [Col. 1165B] “When,” it says, “the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered for fear of the Jews, Jesus stood in their midst and said to them: ‘Peace to you.’ The disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. He said to them again: ‘Peace to you’” (John 20). A little later: “After eight days,” it says, “his disciples were again inside, and Jesus came when the doors were shut and said: ‘Peace to you’” (ibid.).

The Lord wishes carnal affections, like Jews, to be shut out from our minds and spiritual affections alone enclosed in the chamber. Once they are enclosed, he loves to bestow upon them the peace of quiet strength, so that, vices excluded, they may sleep more securely in silence. “With the persecutors excluded,” he says, “I wish you to have saving peace; and, setting aside fear of them, to possess the tower of strength, so that by the majesty of the hand from on high you may drive away their assaults, gather your thoughts in safety as though upon a bed, and sleep under the desired silence in composed peace.”

Christ designated this peace, this silence, this repose of sleepers at the time of his Passion, when he later invited to sleep those whom he had earlier rebuked for sleeping. He did not give them such a benefit at that moment, but wished them to possess it and strengthened them with a gratuitous promise. [Col. 1165C] “Sleep now,” he says, “and rest” (Matthew 26). But after the Resurrection he wished to fulfill what he had promised before; proclaiming peace to them, he wished to render them calm, giving them the Spirit so that they could effectively resist opponents and delight, within their consciences, in a kind of sleep or silence.

For the person who by the Spirit’s gift does not entangle his feet in the rope of evils, who does not multiply for himself a bundle of cords by sinning—once the disease has been driven away and the conscience cleansed, he is made serene and is judged to sleep in silence, the tumult of vices having been lulled. Of this Jeremiah says: “It is good,” he says, “to await in silence the salvation of the Lord” (Lamentations 3). At some time the Lord will visit each one of us, when he separates the soul bound to us from the flesh; he will put an end to our work and our time for working, [Col. 1165D] and will not delay in rendering to the work its fitting reward according to its merit.

Some people are found not at all to await this coming: hardened, they do not wish to think of it; blinded, they do not know how to think of it. With perverted affection they cling so closely to present and passing things that, like beasts, they take no care for the future. Others do not deny that the Judge will come and await his coming with utmost certainty of knowledge, yet in awaiting they appear neither calm nor removed from the tumult and clamor of perverse works. But, supposing that he will come either more gently than is just or after a long delay, they entangle themselves in harmful evils all the more confidently, in proportion as they judge that judgment will be milder or further delayed. [Col. 1166A]

The Lord indicates this in Luke: “If that servant says in his heart, ‘My lord delays in coming,’ and begins to beat the boys and girls, and to eat and drink and get drunk” (Luke 12). You see that this servant does not deny at all that the Lord will come, but declares that he delays in coming; and, foolishly flattering himself by promising himself a desired interval, he prefers tumult to quiet and is not held within the enclosure of silence. For, harshly beating boys and girls—or, according to another Evangelist, fellow servants—he loves to give himself over to eating and drinking, to the vice of drunkenness. Addicted to these evils, he certainly does not accept Jeremiah’s counsel and does not await the coming Lord in fitting silence. [Col. 1166B]

This conduct is found to displease the Lord himself greatly. He does not indulge the ruined desire of his tumultuous servant, but comes upon him quickly when he is not expected and repays the one who strikes harshly with a most harsh blow. The Gospel adds accordingly: “The lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him, and at an hour which he does not know, and will cut him in two and assign him a portion with the unbelievers” (ibid.).

Whether the servant wishes it or not, the Lord will not delay in coming, and he will restrain the dissolute servant under strict judgment. Separated from those who awaited the Lord in silence—like a goat from the sheep—he will place him with those who wholly failed to recognize his coming. “He will assign his portion,” he says, “with the unbelievers.”

The good servant says with Jeremiah: “The Lord is my portion, says my soul; therefore I shall await him” (Lamentations 3), and with David: “My portion in the land of the living” (Psalm 141). He earnestly does what he judges pleasing to the one whom he chooses and loves above all others as his portion; and his portion is assigned with those who, devoting themselves to holiness, faithfully awaited the coming Lord in fitting silence. [Col. 1166C]

But the evil servant, who possesses the form of faith but not the reality of the thing; who knows the will of the coming Lord but did not do it, is separated from those who make their faith fruitful by hope and love. Separated from them, he receives his portion with unbelievers. Because he chose, while awaiting the Lord, not to preserve silence, to persecute his fellow servants, and to indulge his own will rather than God’s, he deserves to receive his portion and reward with those to whom neither the work of faith nor even faith itself is granted. For as nothing but condemnation is owed to the unbeliever, so the wicked believer merits no other reward; both are remembered as receiving their portion together, since, being far from salvation, they are alike assigned to fitting punishment.

Therefore, according to Jeremiah’s word, it is good to await the salvation of the Lord in silence; it is good, while awaiting, to rest from the harmful tumult of vices; it is good from youth to bear his gentle yoke and most light burden; it is good, in bearing it, to refrain from harmful evils. Of this he adds: “He shall sit alone and be silent” (Lamentations 3). Whoever is not burdened to obey diligently the Lord’s gentle yoke and burden will sit alone with God [Col. 1167A] and rest; he will not yield to crowds of business or to tumults of desires. “No one,” says the Apostle, “serving God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Timothy 2).

He will sit alone with God, I say, and be silent, because with most steadfast hope he will cling to God alone, seeking nothing eagerly in this life except him, hoping and desiring him alone, and his peace alone, in one and the same purpose. Of this the Psalm says: “You, Lord, have established me singularly in hope” (Psalm 4). And again: “I have become,” he says, “like a solitary sparrow” (Psalm 101).

[Col. 1167B] The solitary person, fleeing marketplaces, crossroads, and streets, hides as though in a corner; rejecting business, desires, and every harmful thing, he clings exclusively to God. He is silent, indeed, because he does not play along with the noisy blandishments of vices, does not attach himself to them, and does not deceive himself by enervating dalliance. Nor, finally, does he excuse himself as Adam did, because he has no need to be excused: he takes care not to do that for which he ought rightly to be accused.

That sinner did not take such careful precaution. Later, in the Psalm, he recalled his unwary negligence, showing both what stains of guilt had wrapped him about and what punishment he had deserved through guilt. “My bones,” he says, “grew old while I cried out all day” (ibid.). Because I did not hear the saving counsel of him who said, “You have sinned; be still”; because I did not humbly obey his command with a willing ear; because I did not give heed enough to the one reproving and urging me to repentance; because I did not sit alone with him and rest, according to Jeremiah—but, entangled in many and diverse sins, [Col. 1167C] I moreover cried out, while stubbornly excusing those very sins with brazen self-defense. Since, I say, both by sinning and by excusing myself I raised a harmful cry, my bones—that is, the necessary strength of virtues—grew old, and the inner beauty of the soul was disfigured by the decay of age.

## CHAPTER 104

This old age seized that first parent of our race when, after taking the forbidden fruit, he stubbornly excused his sin. Shaken with fear at the voice of God walking, he fled indeed into hiding, but when sought out there did not refuse wickedly to cry out. For when he was caught by him whose command he had received not to sin, not to touch the tree of knowledge and eat the fruit of disobedience, he ought, as a guilty man, to have washed away his fault with tears. Instead, he presumed to provoke the Creator to anger with a harmful cry.

Setting aside the saving medicine of serene devotion, his spirit troubled, he did not fear to excuse himself. He not only failed to wipe away the filth of sin in the bath of renewing repentance, but, heaping it up by his defense, he plunged himself into a certain abyss of old age. “The woman,” he says, “whom you gave me, gave to me, and I ate” (Genesis 3). By this word he accused the woman who had been given him—indeed, perhaps the one who gave him the woman—and excused himself as innocent or undeserving of severe punishment. By excusing himself, he drew over his bones, that is, his virtues, the wrinkled ugliness of old age, by which he darkened [Col. 1168A] and, as it were, furrowed the beauty of holiness laid upon him.

And because his inner beauty was obscured by the wrinkle of sin and old ugliness prevailed as though the flower of youth had been shaken off, he is called the old Adam, the author of our race; all his posterity is darkened by such old age. For, having infected us with a like sin because we are born in the flesh of sin, he himself, being old, made us old through hereditary transmission. Stripped of the first robe, flourishing with the comely beauty of newness, he clothed both himself and his descendants in the tunic of oppressive old age.

Divine mercy did not wholly abandon those thus oppressed, but established a fitting remedy to raise them up. It admonished them that, to wipe away the disease of hereditary perversity by which they are held, they should be burned by the biting cautery of healing repentance. [Col. 1168B] To them it says through blessed Job: “Hear, I pray, my words, and do penance” (Job 21). Hearing this, every penitent says: “I have laboured in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed; I shall water my couch with my tears” (Psalm 6). And in another Psalm: “I am afflicted,” he says, “and exceedingly humbled” (Psalm 37).

Paul had heard this; urging others also to hear, he says: “Put off the old man and put on the new” (Ephesians 4). By “the old man” he wishes to understand the sinful person, whose purpose bends more readily down toward earthly things through a kind of failure of strength, whose inner face is darkened by senile ugliness, and who, an imitator of the first man, does not refuse to add sin to sin, since, hardened in wickedness, he excuses himself with swollen self-defense. [Col. 1168C]

We put off this person, or the oldness of this person, according to Paul’s command, when, led by repentance, we lay aside the desire to sin; when, tearing not our garments but our hearts, we obey the prophet’s admonitions; when we anticipate the coming Judge with purifying confession; when we restrain with a strong girdle the fleshly enticements introduced by the first Adam; when we prevent ancestral vices from retaining in us a hereditary right.

But we put on the new person when we receive the newness of justice which Christ brought and bestowed; when, according to Paul’s admonitions, laying aside falsehood, we speak truth; when, after the former weakness has been driven away, we make fitting progress in virtue; when, our old age broken as against a rock, we return, like the eagle, to honourable youth. [Col. 1168D] Finally, when the cry of vices, which is found grievously to make noise in God’s ears, has been lulled, our minds, having found the silence of new purity, cause our bones that had grown old to become young, and the inner parts of the soul, the frost having been wiped away, grow green again in springtime’s tempering air. Indeed, our whole person blooms again in a certain new manner, while the spirit more diligently clings both to chastity and truth.

Therefore Job rightly laments that, having fallen by ruinous stages into deserving death, and grace having departed, he did not attain such silence, in which a sound conscience might rest as in soft sleep or repose and, the cries of vices being lulled, might find the desired solitude. “Now,” he says, “sleeping, I would be silent, and in my sleep I would rest with [Col. 1169A] kings and consuls of the earth, who build solitudes for themselves” (Job 3).

## CHAPTER 105
Those to whom the abundant goodness of God deigns to impart this gift, so that they deserve to find the aforesaid sleep or silence, He has called by no other names than those of kings and consuls; nor has He judged that they should be reckoned under other titles. By kings, I think, are meant not those who rule over many towns, villages, and cities; not those who hold dominion far and wide over diverse peoples and nations; who rejoice not so much in benefiting many as in presiding over them; who glory in the obedience of their subjects and in the reverence paid them; who, though feared by many, both subjects and neighbours, 671 nevertheless serve with base humility one vice, and perhaps many. [Col. 1169B] For these may more properly be called slaves than kings: ruling men, they deign to be subjected to vices; and while they labour and delight to extort from lower peoples the servitude due to royal power, they do not refuse, with womanish weakness, to render it to unworthy passions.

But he who does not let loose his hands, tongue, and other members to sin; who keeps unlawful desires far from their fulfilment; who does not exalt rebellious flesh against the spirit, nor soften that same spirit through the enticement of the flesh; whose spirit is one with God, who loves to cleave to God, and to exercise royal rule and dominion over the senses of the body—he, I say, is rightly distinguished by the title of king, in whom are found uprightness of judgment, strength of life, and seriousness of character. For [Col. 1169C] since he delights to seat and set reason over the height of his heart, and grants it, as ruler, free choice—so that it may by rightful authority subject animal passions to its own dominion, and, the order of things being well arranged, they may obey its command—he is indeed a king and is rightly proclaimed to be one, since he is proved to rule himself and rightly order what is his own.

Job not inappropriately also calls such kings consuls, because he knows them to be useful not only to themselves but also to others: as they rule themselves in the manner and order I have described, so they exhort others to rule by honourable counsel. For, hating sin through the contemplation or love of virtue, [Col. 1169D] they give their hearers counsel for salvation in brotherly charity; and thus they are rightly called consuls—from giving counsel—because they show themselves useful to their hearers by word and teaching. Scripture fittingly named kings first and consuls afterward, thereby commending the time and order of ruling and counselling, since those whose conduct has not first been restrained by strict rule are not considered sufficiently fit to counsel others.

He is found worthy of praise in giving counsel whose tongue and teaching are preceded by disciplined conduct; who is found first to possess and love in himself the word of counsel which he more diligently imparts to his neighbour. For one who rebukes an unlearned person with learned speech, yet shows himself equally blameworthy in his own actions; who desires to instruct any fool with prudent counsel, yet by his conduct proves himself no less ill-advised—for such a man's word and counsel are not heard with due reverence, because they are not seasoned, for the sake of life, with the prior salt of good morals. [Col. 1170A] A hearer scarcely, or never, greatly values as his counsellor one whom he sees does not rightly govern his own conduct and acts; and, finding him to live foolishly after losing his own kingdom, he gives neither ear nor mind to his counsel. But when he sees a man's conduct and works restrained under worthy rule and advanced by fitting progress from good to better; when he observes his mind or spirit so reigning over its affections that good work agrees with word and word stands in harmony with work—then he does not hesitate to receive such a one as counsellor and teacher; the humility of the hearer rightly reveres his counsel. [Col. 1170B]

Of such kings and consuls it is rightly said: “Who build solitudes for themselves.” He who loves to embrace the world and what belongs to it; to be raised high by the summit of passing honour; to be enriched with money; to be enlarged in his own desires; to outstrip his equals and make himself equal to his betters—such a man seems to frequent a kind of marketplace and to labour beneath the dense throng of pressing crowds. For when the perverse mind, intent only upon visible things, is headlong swept in various directions by the evil desires that meet it; when now anger, now avarice, now lust, now ambitious hope scatters it; when fear torments it on one side, envy twists it on another, pride lifts it up here, grievous sorrow distresses it there, and empty joy dissolves it elsewhere—when, I say, it is oppressed by these and other assaults [Col. 1170C] of vices, what else does it do but move about as though in the midst of tumultuous peoples, so that, seeing countless foes standing about it—or rather opposing it—on every side, it can scarcely discern by which of them it is touched more particularly?

“The crowds press upon you,” they say, “and you ask, ‘Who touched me?’” (Mark 5). They marvel that their master declares himself touched by someone when he is being pressed not so much by one person as by crowds on every side, and when, as they think, he ought more fittingly to complain of the oppression of all than anxiously to inquire about one touch. But they, cleaving to visible things, answer concerning bodily pressure; he, understanding quite otherwise, speaks of a spiritual touch, which no outsider could perceive, but only he himself felt, since he was unwilling to restrain the devout person from touching him. [Col. 1170D] “Someone touched me,” he says, “for I perceived power going out from me” (ibid.). He had perceived that a certain person had touched him with a discerning touch, whom he knew had received, by his grace, the power to touch; but the disciples say that the other crowds pressed him, whose urgency it is not at all clear pleased the Lord.

But the wretched man assailed by the vices mentioned above, whose uprightness of mind is subjected to their rule—so long as their powerful multitude besieges him—does not know what useful or honourable solitude is. But if, visited by grace, he begins to recoil from the grievous crowd; if he shrinks from enduring so great a multitude; if he refuses to allow its heavy assaults to prevail; if he loves to restrain fleshly desires under the rule of reason; 672 if [Col. 1171A] he strives more zealously, with provident hand, to keep them from desire, then assuredly he no longer dwells in the forum, the street, or the clamour of popular wickedness, but like a wild ass in the wilderness or a solitary sparrow on a building. For when he moderates anger, subdues avarice, bends down pride, extinguishes envy, chastens lust, restrains ambition, and denies these and their like their former place within himself—when by a kind of royal authority he drives and banishes them from his borders—he builds for himself a certain secret retreat in the withdrawal of his own mind, and, having expelled outward disturbances, now nests there in peace.

There he rejoices to dwell alone; there to cleave uniquely to God; there to cherish pure thoughts with the fervent spirit of charity; there, with the popular tumult driven far away, to be silent in the repose of peace. Of this Jeremiah says, as stated above: “He shall sit alone and be silent” (Lam. 3). And elsewhere: “I sat alone because of your hand, for you filled me with threats” (Jer. 15). By the hand of God His blow is to be understood, because He, the Just One, wills at last to strike with severe judgment those who do not fear to serve the multitude of vices; and before striking, He threatens terribly, so that the sinner, more quickly coming to his senses, may deserve saving pardon. [Col. 1171B] Thus Jeremiah, shaken by the terror of threats, flees from being found within the aforesaid multitude, knowing that whoever does not flee from belonging to such company is compelled to experience the hard hand of the living God and to endure His avenging blow.

Finally, in the Gospel the demons complain that they are tormented and suffer the most severe hand of Christ with irremediable pain, because their Judge detests that wicked multitude which, fleeing solitude, rejoices in the ruinous society of many. “They cried out, saying: ‘What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?’” (Luke 8). And in Mark: “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.” And he asked him: “What is your name?” And he said: “My name is Legion, because we are many” (Mark 5). [Col. 1171C]

Jeremiah, therefore, knowing that a vicious multitude is not commended and that the heavy hand of the Judge hangs over it, prudently withdraws from the face of the one striking and sits alone, far removed from the fellowship of the sinful crowd. David too, clothed in this spirit, says that he withdrew far away and, fleeing the crowds, dwelt in a place of solitude, awaiting Him who in kindly and customary generosity delivers from the faint-hearted spirit and the destructive tempest. “I withdrew far away,” he says, “fleeing, and I remained in solitude.”

## CHAPTER CVI

That woman also, who in the Apocalypse is said to have borne a male child, and beside whom the envious dragon is read to have stood while she was giving birth, fled into the wilderness, so that there she might lie safely hidden and rest far from the serpent under the shade of silence. “The woman fled,” it says, “into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, that there He may feed her” (Rev. 12).

By the name woman any soul is rightly signified which, subject to its Creator, is made pregnant by His Spirit and, as grace advances, brings forth offspring that are wholly male—that is, it produces strong and unconquered works, free from feminine softness born of ignorance. [Col. 1172A] While this soul gives birth, that deceitful serpent secretly stands by; after the birth he labours to press upon it more openly, in order either to steal from the proposed work the ability to advance, or, once it has been accomplished, to inflict upon it the manifest burden of violence. But she, fearing his deceits and violence, yet not growing lukewarm either in affection for good works or in their performance, hastens by no ignoble flight to gain solitude: that is, in the secrecy of her mind, to cleave uniquely to God.

In this solitude God prepares a place for the fugitive: by supporting hand He gives the resting one a soft couch, and with pleasing bounty supplies health-giving pastures, pouring more abundantly spiritual grace into her desire. Hence David says: “In a place of pasture He set me” (Ps. 22). And elsewhere, as was said a little earlier: “I withdrew far away, fleeing, and remained in solitude” (Ps. 54). David and the woman are rightly said to flee to this place of pasture or solitude, in order that, with base sluggishness put away, the agility of a devout mind may be commended—a mind which does not grow weak in seeking heavenly things with slow step or drowsy eyelids, but, impatient of delay, burns with eager desire.

Thus both David and the woman are said to have feathers or wings, by whose swift oarage they are borne to the desired solitude; [Col. 1172B] and such solitude is attained neither by dull slowness nor by sluggish dullness, nor does it admit sluggish dullness. “Who will give me wings,” says David, “and I shall fly?” (ibid.). And lest he seem to have asked without obtaining, he adds: “I withdrew far away, fleeing, and remained in solitude” (ibid.). And in the Apocalypse: “Two wings were given to the woman, that she might fly into the wilderness from the face of the serpent” (Rev. 12).

These wings are understood as the twofold love by which God and neighbour are loved according to the prescribed rule: namely, when the soul burns to cleave especially to God alone and desires that its neighbour obtain the same grace. By this twofold ardour it is raised from the desire for earthly things and carried in swift flight to the place of solitude, so that, having passed beyond the hissing malice of the envious serpent and entered the quiet chamber of the solitary mind, it may rejoice to shut out evil noises as though by a closed door, and, praying inwardly to the Father, hear Him answer through Isaiah: [Col. 1172C] “Iniquity shall no longer be heard in your land” (Isa. 32).

Happy is the land in which iniquity is not heard, 673 within whose bounds nothing but equity is found; it is not reached for habitation with a limping foot or languid desire, but attained by rapid flight and fervent spirit. Happy is the land to inhabit which no popular multitude streams together; rather, with that multitude far removed, solitude holds its bounds—a solitude not marked by rocky dryness, uncultivated harshness, or horrid ugliness, but by sweetness of fragrance, pleasant greenness, and flowering beauty. Burning with desire for it, Jeremiah says: “Who will give me a place in the wilderness, that I may leave my people and depart from them? For they are all adulterers, an assembly of transgressors” (Jer. 9).

Jeremiah, observing his people grievously sinning, polluted by adulteries and guilty of transgression, desires to make his dwelling far from them, lest perhaps he run with the thief and place his portion with adulterers. [Col. 1173A] Provided someone might be willing and able to grant him the choice, he chooses to come to the place of solitude, so that there he may deserve to find the grace of desired security. For there the spirit climbs more freely to the height of reason; there it rejoices more securely in the benefit of an unveiled vision; there, with dust cleared away and the cloud of falsehood more carefully removed, it discerns more keenly the judgment of truth that has been sought out. Isaiah indicates this when he says: “Judgment shall dwell in solitude” (Isa. 32).

In a forum or street, indeed, where the people strive to satisfy their own will and each person more freely clamours against truth according to his own desire, the uprightness of subtle judgment either scarcely or not at all dwells, because an undiscerning multitude prevails over the few who are better. Judgment is therefore rightly said to dwell in solitude, where there is no concourse of people or disturbance of strangers; where the dust of streets does not obscure the eye of the judge, and the gift of avarice does not close the ear of understanding. [Col. 1173B] There the mind sees what is right more freely and clearly; there it directs spiritual sight more effectively straight ahead, when, by the gift of grace, it is freed from harmful evils—that is, from the stains of vices—even though it is not yet found free from sorrowful evils.

## CHAPTER CVII. On silence from sorrowful evils

For although one is granted to banish harmful evils far from one's borders, one cannot immediately and completely calm sorrowful evils as well. Rather, while the desired silence is already maintained with respect to the former, the mind is nevertheless often still harshly exercised by the latter. That sorrowful evils, no less than harmful ones, are sometimes called evils is attested by many passages of Scripture, in which we find both classed together under this single term, although in reality they are discovered to differ widely from one another.

We have called harmful those things which oppose justice and are contrary to virtue; which by their own nature benefit no one, place some obstacle in the way of salvation, and by which angel and human being are miserably bound under a grievous law, whereas neither the Creator nor any other creature is bound by a similar law. But sorrowful evils are those which anyone suffers unwillingly and severely; which are felt by the sufferer as bitter and harsh in some respect; and which, although perhaps useful, are not altogether pleasant and for that reason are not inappropriately called evils. [Col. 1173C] Thus fever, paralysis, famine, poverty, and many things of this kind are called evils, not because they are sins, but because they oppose the will of those who suffer them. Whatever is found to afflict, burden, or injure us is, according to the testimony of Scripture, classed under the name of evil.

“Lord,” he says, “my servant lies at home paralysed and is grievously tormented” (Matt. 8). And later, speaking of Peter’s mother-in-law: “He saw her lying sick with fever; and he touched her hand, and the fever left her; and he healed all who were ill” (ibid.). You see that those afflicted with fever, paralysis, or such sufferings are said by evangelical testimony to be ill and grievously tormented; and as the discipline of repentance is needed to wipe away the evil of sin, so a fitting medicine is required to cure the evil of sickness.

Of this same matter Matthew says elsewhere: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do” (Matt. 9). [Col. 1173D] By “those who are ill” he means those pressed by the discomfort of sickness, detained by any burdensome affliction, for whose infirmity a physician must necessarily be applied, so that, the unhealthy disorder having been driven away, desired health may be restored.

When a severe famine afflicted the land of Canaan and all the surrounding provinces, while Egypt alone abounded in grain and bread: “All the provinces,” it says, “came into Egypt to buy food and alleviate the evil of want” (Gen. 41). Here Genesis calls the lack caused by famine an evil, not because the authority of justice or of a just law forbids it, but because its grievous presence subjects us to sorrow and its oppression contradicts the will of those who suffer it.

So too Jacob, considering the many hardships threatening him—himself in need of bread, lacking the full number of his children, and unable with an adequately even mind to endure so many and such grievous things—cannot, in his sorrow, keep himself from mourning and complaint. “Joseph,” he says, “is no more; Simeon is held in chains; you will take Benjamin away; all these evils have fallen upon me” (Gen. 42). The loss of Joseph, Simeon’s detention, and Benjamin’s removal harshly shake the father’s heart and inflict exceedingly grievous pain upon his inward affection. 674 [Col. 1174A] Yet these evils do not make the sufferer’s soul evil; they affect his loving tenderness almost to the extremity of death. Hence he says: “You will bring down my grey hairs with sorrow to the grave” (ibid.).

So great is the father’s love for his sons, and so intensely is he distressed for those who have been sent away or lost, that in their absence no consolation seems capable of being given him; his afflicted old age will be brought down with sorrow to the grave. If Joseph is lost, or if Benjamin suffers any misfortune, the father does not wish to live, lest by living he be more grievously tormented; for from the moment that he is told Joseph has been devoured by a most savage beast, the father seems to himself not to live but rather to die. Although the bite of the fiercer beast did not injure his flesh, the death of sorrow harshly touched his loving spirit; and the cruel beast rages far more mildly against the son in a brief fury than the anguish of sorrow against the father, whom it has now long been accustomed to torment.

Even if nothing evil or dangerous had happened to that son, the father alone would still have fallen into grievous anguish; because, believing lies, he considered Joseph lost in death and laboured, as it were dying from the greatness of grief, over a long course of days. [Col. 1174B] On the other hand, when Joseph’s brothers reported to their grieving father that Joseph lived, and set before him in order Joseph’s words, commands, and gifts, and he was finally compelled to believe those who told him, unable to contain within the bounds of silence the greatness of his joy, “his spirit revived,” Scripture says, and he said: “It is enough for me if Joseph my son is still alive” (Gen. 45).

When Scripture says that his spirit revived, it surely implies that he had in some way been dead: as the bitterness of sorrow brought him the pains of death, so the arrival of joy brought him back a more welcome life. Likewise, a tree is sometimes called evil, and its fruit evil, because it is found bitter or useless; although such things, created well by a good Creator, are known to remain in their proper state, they may nevertheless be called evil when only their bitterness is blamed. “Every good tree,” he says, “produces good fruit, but an evil tree produces evil fruit” (Matt. 7:17; printed “XLVII”). Just as Matthew proclaimed a good tree and its good fruits, so he likewise affirmed an evil tree and its evil fruits, so that we may know that this evil is not what is found contrary to the laws of justice, but the sorrowful bitterness which anyone’s discernment experiences as unsuitable. [Col. 1175A]

## CHAPTER CVIII

Jeremiah’s prudence distinguished such evil when the Spirit of prophecy showed him two baskets, one of which was understood mystically to contain joyful and prosperous things, while the other was found to pertain to sorrowful and disadvantageous things. “The Lord showed me,” he says, “and behold, two baskets full of figs. And the Lord said to me: ‘What do you see, Jeremiah?’ And I said: ‘Good figs, very good; and bad figs, very bad, which cannot be eaten because they are bad’” (Jer. 24).

We can find no greater badness in these figs than that they do not seem suitable for eating: that is, anyone may shrink from their bitterness from afar, or perhaps the teeth of those who taste them more closely may be painfully numbed. [Col. 1175B] But what the Lord intended to signify by this badness of the figs He chose to show in the words that follow; and although He Himself, the good One of good things, testifies that He is the giver of all good things, He nevertheless shows Himself to be the author of this evil. “As the very bad figs,” He says, “which cannot be eaten because they are bad, so will I give Zedekiah king of Judah and his princes; and I will give them over to vexation and affliction in all the kingdoms of the earth, to reproach, proverb, and curse; and I will send upon them sword, famine, and pestilence, until they are consumed” (ibid.).

This is the evil or curse; these are the evils which God works by His power, though the testimonies of Scripture prove Him to be supremely good. Nor is it asserted or allowed that this is alien to His goodness, if His justice compels us to suffer the evils and sorrows we have deserved. Isaiah indicates this when he says: “I am the Lord, and there is no other: forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil; I, the Lord, do all these things” (Isa. 45). Since the eye is alert in light, the mind is made cheerful, each person becomes more vigorous for conducting whatever business is at hand, and the world itself is pleasantly formed with a kind of new appearance as each thing in its variety resumes its own aspect, it was right to signify by light the joyful and prosperous things which God in His innate goodness loves to accomplish. [Col. 1175C]

But because, when darkness is present, the eye grows dim, the hand stiffens and becomes numb, the foot is bound, and the mind languishes; because introduced darkness in some sense confounds the world itself, and superimposed confusion takes away from varied colours what is their own—darkness rightly signifies sorrowful adversity, which is sometimes inflicted upon us by the just Judge according to our deserts. Hence Job says again: “After darkness I hope for light” (Job 17). The just man, considering himself troubled by the judgment of Him who desires not the destruction but the purification of His faithful ones, does not despair of mercy while feeling His anger. Though God strikes, he perseveres in his own innocence; and, after the sorrowful and harsh things he is compelled to endure as darkness, he believes that he will more fully obtain joyful and prosperous things as light.

For he hopes that the Judge will not rage against him always, but that after anger and blows 675 He will mercifully grant grace; because He who is proclaimed in Isaiah’s prophecy to create darkness is also declared to form light: “Forming light and creating darkness.” [Col. 1176A] Repeating this in other words, He adds: “Making peace and creating evil.” By evil He means sword, famine, pestilence, and other such things which afflict us harshly, distressing lovers of peace and quiet with burdensome suffering; by these God wills either justly to punish the unjust or to exercise the patience of the just for greater merit.

Thus in Jeremiah: “Behold, I will bring evils upon them” (Jer. 11). Explaining a little later what these evils are, he says: “The young men shall die by the sword; their sons and daughters shall die by famine; and no remnant shall remain to them, for I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth” (ibid.). And much farther on: “Behold, I will watch over them for evil and not for good; and they shall all be consumed by sword and famine” (Jer. 44). You see that God calls sword, famine, and whatever seems to afflict us in this way evil, which in anger He undertakes to inflict upon us. We suffer nothing of this kind unless He more justly brings it upon us; indeed, no evil of this sort occurs unless He beyond doubt brings it about.

Although no evil is believed to cling to the good God, this assertion must nevertheless not be thought to depart from the truth: namely, that the good God makes such evil; indeed, unless He makes it, no such evil at all comes to pass. [Col. 1176B] Amos of Tekoa likewise does not dissent from the statement just made; for the prophetic Spirit thinks the same thing in different people, and though prophets are separated from one another by place or time, they are joined in the same meaning and the same Spirit. “Can there be evil,” Amos says, “in a city which the Lord has not done?” (Amos 3). The prophet does not suppose that a city can suffer any adversity—be shaken by pestilence, sword, or battering-ram—unless it is done by Him who cannot bear it to go unpunished when it is rebellious against holiness, devoid of virtues, and guilty of obstinacy.

Often, when He is about to bring evil, He deigns to foretell the evil and, before striking, to instil threats and terrors, so that the sinner, shaken with fear, may hasten to abandon his purpose, and the avenger, now appeased, may turn the blade back into its sheath. For when the angry Judge declares that He will do evils and grievous things, and bring upon the sinner punishments deserved according to his merits, if that person, terrified by the threats, hastens to repent, the Judge rejoices not to carry out the evil He had spoken of. Jonah affirms this: “God saw,” he says, “that they had turned from their evil way, and He had mercy concerning the evil which He had said He would do to them, and He did not do it” (Jonah 3). [Col. 1176C]

By “evil” he means the overthrow which God had announced beforehand as a threat, but which He did not carry out as though He had changed His mind; for, when the evil of overthrow had been foretold, Nineveh turned itself to repentance, and He, moved by mercy, did not overthrow the repentant city. Observing the devotion of the mourners and the discipline of those repenting, He turned back His hand and returned the sword to its sheath, so that, once the fire of anger was quenched within it, it might grow cool, and the same sword, content with its place, might lie hidden in silence.

For when sent forth, this sword makes a great clamour: when, forgetful of patience, it is borne headlong into fury; when, as though its bridle were loosened, it rages more harshly against whatever wretches [it encounters], and their misery is grievously stirred to mourning and cries.

## CHAPTER CIX

When Jeremiah mentioned the Philistines and said that Pharaoh was coming to make war on them, he expressly displayed the fury, onset, and evil of the attacker, and conversely the wailing, outcry, and misery of those who endured it. “Behold,” he says, “waters come down from the north, and they shall be like an overflowing torrent; they shall cover the land and its fullness” (Jer. 47). [Col. 1176D] By the waters he means Pharaoh and his men, who advance mightily to make war on the Philistines, spread over the face of the earth like waters, and rush into battle with grievous force like an overflowing torrent: they spare no one and plunder everything.

Lovers of battle are rightly compared with waters or a torrent, because, with silence stilled, they rage with a grievous uproar; and just as the force of roaring water sounds harshly, rages, and thunders, so does the headlong soldiery—or rather wickedness—of a raging people. Hence, above, the same prophet says of a warlike people: “It is cruel and will not have pity; its voice sounds like the sea” (Jer. 6). When a people is driven to war by the breath of an evil spirit and, swollen with grievous fury, spares none of its enemies, its voice is rightly said to sound like the sea, because it contains much confusion, no order, and no measure of wickedness.

But when the sword of the assailant rages with so great a cry, and the tumultuous chatter of the besieger sounds like the sea, certainly the besieged too are not oppressed in silence; pressed by evils, they are compelled to cry out far and wide in another manner. [Col. 1177A] For the attackers are elated with fury and exultation, while the attacked lament miserably in mourning and sorrow; their discordant voices are heard far and wide, and silence is found to be kept by neither party.

Therefore, when Jeremiah said that the aforesaid Pharaoh was coming to make war on the Philistines, he added concerning those same Philistines: “Men shall cry out, and all the inhabitants of the land shall howl, at the sound of the pomp of his arms and warriors, at the shaking of his chariots, 676 and the multitude of his wheels” (Jer. 47). You see the pomp of weapons, the din of warriors, the shaking of chariots, and the multitude of wheels, when Pharaoh suddenly pours in like a torrent for war; at his coming the Philistine cries, groans, grinds his teeth, and howls.

But lest this affliction, harshly inflicted upon the Philistines, should be attributed to the military strength of Pharaoh and his men, the prophet shows to whom it should more truly and fittingly be ascribed, so that the author of this evil or malice may be known more certainly: “The Lord,” he says, “has laid waste the Philistines” (ibid.). Although Pharaoh’s wickedness put its hand to the work of war, the supreme justice of God nevertheless ordained that the war should take place thus; and, as He justly disposed that the Philistines should reap their deserts, He willed them to be punished in this manner through Pharaoh sent against them. [Col. 1177B]

Of such persons David says: “Sendings through evil angels” (Ps. 77). Evil angels are sometimes sent to punish particular persons and, by the just judgment of God, are permitted to carry out their will upon them. Although wickedness or hatred is ascribed to those who are sent or permitted, the supreme ordering of the work is undoubtedly ascribed to God Himself. The prophet therefore rightly did not say, “Pharaoh has laid waste the Philistines,” but: “The Lord has laid waste the Philistines”; for although Pharaoh rejoices that he has been an instrument in crushing them, the prophet knows that the Lord has been the commander.

Accordingly, considering how great a tumult occurs in this crushing, while the sword of the indignant Lord rages against His people, the prophet, as though pitying and grieving that same people’s destruction, begins to address the tumultuous sword: “How long,” he says, “shall you cut down, O sword of the Lord? How long will you not rest? Enter into your sheath; be cool, and be silent” (Jer. 47). [Col. 1177C] The prophet sees that the wretched people do not cease from mourning and howling, so long as the divine indignation does not cool the fury of its anger, and so long as the sword which the Avenger draws from its sheath with outstretched hand to strike does not hasten, its purpose changed, to return to the sheath. (Thus.)

For as long as the sword of the striker does not cease from anger and fury, the misery of the sufferer does not cease from mourning and crying; and therefore the sword is rightly invited to silence in the coolness of its sheath, so that, once it is put away, the wretched sufferer too may be allowed silence. [Col. 1177D] But that same sword cannot be restrained from its purpose, return to its own place, and remain in desired silence unless the divine hand which lets it loose or draws it forth at its own will brings it back to its proper place by the command of grace. The prophet adds this: “How shall it rest, when the Lord has commanded it and appointed it?” (ibid.). “Although,” he says, “I ask that the sword return to its place, and that anger turn to coolness and its tumult to silence, I nevertheless know that in raging it obeys a greater power, and will not rest unless it first pleases the divine will.”

For just as divine power grants silence from harmful evils when His patience no longer wills to endure them, so without His gift there is no silence from sorrowful evils, when His benevolence has mercy upon the sufferer. [Col. 1179A] When divine providence wills to impose silence upon harmful evils—so that they are either not desired in the heart or, when desired, are not more openly displayed—it either infuses into us its grace, so that we do not wish for those harmful things, or removes the harmful opportunity, so that we cannot accomplish them at will.

After the sin involving Uriah, David devoutly desired that this grace should be poured into him; and, that he might put an end to harmful evils, he asked for the secret place of his heart to be cleansed, so that, just as he had been wounded not only in desire but also in the deed of abominable wickedness, so he might be made clean not only from the act but also from the vice of a harmful will. “Wash me yet more from my iniquity,” he says, “and cleanse me from my sin” (Ps. 50).

He is washed “yet more” when the hand that performs sin no longer touches it, and the shattered softness of the inward will no longer desires it; when he is now able not only to free his steps from its stains, but to reject in free horror even the memory of it when it occurs. He is washed “yet more” when he both withdraws the bodily senses from the performance of sin and, by fuller grace, purifies the inward conscience from its desire; when he drives harmful suggestions far away by a kind of repelling power of virtue, or gives no assent, even for a little while, to their presumptuous assaults. [Col. 1179B] Hence he adds below: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (ibid.). When the Prophet earnestly desires a clean heart to be created in him, he plainly desires to be cleansed from harmful evils, so that not only may the depravity of impurity be washed from his conduct, but no willing stain may defile the hidden place of his heart.

Divine goodness imparts such a benefit to some, and the happiness of those people experiences this bounty, when, with chilling evil driven away, they burn with the breath of the Holy Spirit, and, their icy hardness dissolved, are softened more tenderly to love God.

Of these the Lord speaks through Ezekiel: “I will give a new spirit within them, and I will take away the heart of stone from their flesh, and I will give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in my commandments, and may be my people, and I may be their God” (Ezek. XI). He calls a heart of stone that which is frozen in such obstinacy and hardness that it is not struck by the hammer either of divine love or of fear; so that, even if Moses or Aaron promises that the dangers of plagues are impending, that hardened heart nevertheless does not admit wholesome counsel. God sometimes looks compassionately upon the obstinate hardness of such a heart [Col. 1179D], has mercy through his own grace upon the perishing soul, and, when he no longer wishes to defer its conversion, takes care by his mighty hand to remove from it its heart of stone. Once the stone has been removed, by which that wretched soul was weighed down and held, as it were, in a hard tomb so that it could not rise to life, God’s abundant mercy gives it a heart of flesh; and his new love makes it soft and tender.

For divine grace is said to give a heart of flesh to one into whom it deigns to breathe a soft and tender disposition of love, so that one who had been rigid in hatred or contempt may be bent toward the purpose of loving, and may embrace with a certain gentle tenderness whatever he has resolved to love. For if the torch of love kindles the heart somewhat more strongly, then, once its hardness has been set aside, it is softened more tenderly [Col. 1180A]; and what, in love’s absence, is found excessively hard and harsh is discovered, in its presence, to exchange harshness for tender softness. Hence a certain pagan, who was held in a particularly affectionate love toward his own people and, laying aside manly authority, was dissolved as though into womanly softness, says:

> Whether you call this dutiful or womanly,  
> I confess that I, unhappy man, have a tender heart.  
> —OVID

The poet who burns with the torches of a vain glory to be attained, who swells with the pride of knowledge like a bladder exposed to the wind, nevertheless, because he feels himself held toward his own by tender love, does not disdain to confess quite plainly that he has a tender heart.

## CHAPTER CX

[Col. 1180B] Jacob too loved his son Benjamin tenderly. Sending his other sons into Egypt, he would not allow Benjamin to depart far from him; and when at last he was compelled to send him, he was oppressed by grave distress and fear lest, if some misfortune should befall the younger son, the elder should be brought down to the underworld in sorrow. Of him Judah says: “Our father loves him tenderly.” And the father says: “If you take this one also, and anything should happen to him on the journey, you will bring my gray hairs down to the underworld with sorrow” (Gen. XLIV).

You see the father possessing a soft and tender heart toward his son; and, as Judah says, his soul depending upon that son’s soul. The power of love, having taken away manly severity and the stone of a harder disposition, had made him wholly, as it were, fleshly [Col. 1180C]. God is said to bestow such a heart of flesh upon us when he deigns to soften us with the fire of his love—when he so disposes us that, whatever we find contrary to his holy will, we, united with his good pleasure in one judgment, do not wish. Thus his goodness alienates harmful evils from us: not only does it now restrain the hand from wicked action, but grace infused into us also heals our will, so that it assents to no depravity even in the secret place of the heart.

But when our will is not healed by divine benefit and contrives some depravity in the inner workshop’s hidden chamber, the supreme Judge often does not grant efficacy to the evil inclination, and the conceived wickedness does not proceed outward into a criminal deed. [Col. 1180D] Although, by the counsel known to himself, he does not take away the will to sin, yet by an equitable judgment he removes the power to carry it out. Thus wicked desire burns within the conscience as fire in a furnace, but, with its vent stopped, no outlet for bursting forth lies open. Hence through Isaiah: “I will cause the pride of the unbelievers to cease, and I will humble the arrogance of the strong” (Isa. XIII). And through Ezekiel: “I will cause the pride of the mighty to cease” (Ezek. VII).

The pride of unbelievers, or the arrogance of the strong, in a sense becomes quiet when it lies hidden, pressed down and oppressed as if beneath a bushel; when its poisonous root indeed reaches down into the depths, but the earth above, as though bound by frost, does not extend itself into branches of deeds. This too is indicated through Hosea: “Behold, I will hedge your way with thorns, and I will fence it with a wall, and she shall not find her paths” [Col. 1181A] (Hos. II). Certainly our way is then hedged with thorns or a wall, and no clearer path for proceeding is found, when the heart burns with unlawful passion as though inside a chamber, but the inward cry of wickedness is not heard outside, as though the door were shut.

For God sometimes shuts the door upon an inward inclination; he does not permit that which rages and longs to burst forth within to do so. Though it wishes to go out like overflowing waves from the chamber of a spring, he refuses to open the channel, placing obstacles of difficulty before it. Therefore, although carnal affections are regarded as fluid and unstable like waters, and always strive toward their consummating effects as toward the depths of valleys, nevertheless the stricter censure which meets and resists them makes those which a more downward-driving nature impels to flow [Col. 1181B] remain, as it were, steady in their place. Of them the Psalm says: “And he made the waters stand as in a skin-bottle” (Ps. LXXVII).

Because a skin-bottle is made of hide, our flesh is rightly signified by it. Within its enclosure, fluid desire is held fast as by a firm strap, when it gathers turbulent impulses in the recess of the heart but, because of opposing difficulty, does not channel them through the bodily senses into effects. For the supreme justice of God does not will that, when the torrent of carnal affections is poured from the heart’s bilge, it should spread freely through the streams of deeds as it desires. Rather, with a strict hand it keeps stopped up within the bottle the accumulated bitterness of perverse wills. Hence in another psalm: [Col. 1181C] “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a skin-bottle” (Ps. XXXII).

The sea is at times disturbed by a certain natural agitation, and at times stirred by the onset of winds. Its overflowing waves would often occupy spaces spread far abroad, if the height of the shore did not set itself against its tumult. Thus the raging sea is confined within these narrow bounds; beating back its waves upon itself, it does not wander at will. It is stirred by a weighty and implacable anger, yet, as though shut within a skin-bottle, it is restrained within set limits. So, indeed, the malice of some people often burns in the secret places of their hearts, but the desired door for proceeding into action does not open. Within, the sinner, boiling over, gnashes as though with his teeth and wastes away; evil in the hidden place falls silent outwardly from harmful wicked acts.

## CHAPTER CXI

[Col. 1181D]

Just as God’s grace or power makes us silent from evils of this kind—when, that is, it deigns to remove either the will to sin or the ability to carry it out—so the same divine benevolence makes us rest from grievous evils when it finally wishes our labors to be lightened by the benefit of desired repose. For those whom the grace of future rest appoints to be refreshed, it first permits to be exercised by certain sorrows; and it makes the gifts of subsequent grace more welcome to them in proportion as they have felt and tasted more deeply the draughts of preceding bitterness.

Why he should wish those whom he graciously predestines to attain the desired refreshment of rest [Col. 1182A] to experience hardships and sorrows is made clear by evident causes found in Scripture, so that the diligent reader may be freed from the stains of ignorance. At times, indeed, the elect suffer hardships and sorrows for this purpose; in this wretched life they are shaken by miseries and troubles, so that the depravity of their vices, as though melted down in a furnace, may turn to ashes, while the purity of virtues acquired may shine forth like silver or gold. Hence in the Psalm: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; but I will not take away my mercy from him” (Ps. LXXXVIII). And through the prophet Amos: “You alone have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will visit upon you all your iniquities” (Amos III). And in the book of Maccabees: “Not allowing sinners for a long time to act according to their purpose, but applying punishments at once, is a sign of great kindness” (II Macc. VI). And a little later: “Though correcting his people in adversities, he does not abandon them” (ibid.).

You see that God does not permit the vices of his elect to accumulate to the utmost, but wishes them to be cut off sooner by punitive affliction, so that the more wretched they are found at present through suffering for Christ, the worthier they may become of his mercy; and the more they are restrained with their necks bowed beneath the afflicting yoke of punishment, the more, when the time of glory comes, they may be exalted. Addressing them, the apostle James says: “Be wretched and mourn; humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (Jas. IV).

[Col. 1182C] At times, however, God wills hardships and sorrows to be inflicted upon his elect, and wills them, though undeserving, nevertheless to endure troubles and affliction, so that, where there is in them no fault to be burned more severely by a biting cautery, the merit of virtue and patience may be increased. Thus they may obtain not so much a happy pardon through a punishment discharged for sin, as deserve the rewards of victorious glory through patience. This is apparent in Job, of whom it is written: “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips” (Job I, II). And later: “You moved me against him, that I should afflict him without cause” (Job II). Any righteous person is said to be afflicted “without cause” when the punishment of sinners is imposed upon one who has not sinned; when no lead, no tin, nor anything else needing purification is found in him, yet he experiences purifying fire as gold in a furnace [Col. 1182D] (Prov. XXVII).

So too Scripture relates that Tobit, blinded by a swallow’s nest dripping into his eyes, was not suddenly disturbed by the event of his blindness, but bore so great an adversity with so wholly serene a spirit that it did not hesitate to compare him with blessed Job. “The Lord allowed this trial to befall him,” it says, “that he might give to posterity an example of his patience, as did holy Job” (Tob. II). You see that this trial, this punishment of blindness, did not so much expiate a past sin as bring the man’s hidden patience to light. It increased the merit of his virtue, since, after the pattern of Job, he furnished an example both to those of the future and to those of the present.

At other times someone is restrained by grievous evils [Col. 1183A], and, though he has deserved nothing, is oppressed by an undeserved punishment, so that God’s virtue and power may be displayed in him and, once displayed, honored by the fitting praises of those who behold it. The author of Gospel truth indicates that this was fulfilled in the man who suffered from the congenital affliction of blindness from the womb. The disciples perhaps thought that children are born sightless only because sin demands it, and inquisitively asked whether he had sinned or his parents: “Rabbi,” they say, “who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” (John IX).

The disciples rightly perceive that the sins of parents often turn to the ruin of their children, and that when the former offend, the latter pay the penalties of their offences—by the severe indeed, but true, judgment of supreme and incomprehensible equity, which exacts penalties for sins from those who have sinned as well as from those who have not sinned. For when parents do not fear to offend God and, having incurred offense, deserve to pay its penalties, God permits those whom they begot from their own flesh and tenderly desire to prosper to be bodily afflicted by his judgment. Thus the evils by which children are tortured in body without personal desert are transferred to the souls of their ill-deserving parents, so that parents may feel punishments coming upon themselves in, or from, those in whom or from whom they hoped to find the welcome benefit of consolation.

But in this the disciples are mistaken: they do not think that anyone is bodily afflicted unless he has been burdened through his own sin or that of his relatives; and, wishing to discover whether Christ is 679 hidden [Note: [Col. 1183D] The phrase is defective.]. But he says: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but that the works of God may be made manifest in him” [Col. 1183C] (ibid.). The man whom the Creator, forming him in the womb, left as it were naturally incomplete—neither his parents nor the son himself sinned; rather, the supreme Author, who is God and Lord of nature, withheld or bestowed upon his birth whatever he willed. He withheld light, not in order to repay parents or son with punishment for sins, but in order to show all people the magnificence of his power. Seeing a man deformed from the womb for many years, and suddenly restored by Christ’s mighty hand through light infused, the Jews might not in any way doubt that this same Christ was God and the Son of God; firm in faith and ready in speech, they might praise his divine works.

[Col. 1183D] Of those upon whom God wills sorrows to be inflicted for the causes we have mentioned, and to whom he wills subsequent goods to be granted after evils inflicted, he wills some to be consoled in this present life by the refreshment of some measure of rest; others he wills to be freed from certain sorrows only after this life. In the Gospel: “Because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart” (John XVI). And below: “Therefore you now have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice” (ibid.). Christ does not wish his disciples, once they have heard the word, to be tormented for long or swallowed up in small waves of sorrow. Rather, as a woman in labor is said to have sorrow, but once she has given birth, forgets her distress and is refreshed with joy, so they are weighed down by storms of trouble when they hear or behold the mystery of his passion [Col. 1184A]; and when the glory of the resurrection is revealed, they are consoled, through increase of faith, certainty of hope, the grace of love, and the visitation of the Spirit.

Thus also, when the Job of whom we spoke above had been harshly afflicted by innumerable losses and the blows of the adversary, and when, to complete his misery, his friends had agreed to visit him in his stricken state, divine mercy did not endure to leave him troubled by so many and such great adversities. It restored him to health and rest, with wealth doubled and offspring restored. Likewise, when a wicked guest, a nesting swallow, had injured the quite innocent Tobit, and for many days he had not seen the light of heaven or the face of the earth, when at last his son returned with the daughter of Raguel as his wife, he recovered his lost sight through Raphael’s welcome remedy. Thus divine mercy wiped away the clouds of his sorrow [Col. 1184B], and, strengthened, he rested as it were in silence, rejoicing both in his son’s return and in the recovery of light, once the evils by which he had been grievously distressed had been driven far away.

Nor are only those who suffer sorrows said to become silent or rest from them when, after the evils have gone far away, they are refreshed by consolation. Those who inflict them are likewise said to rest and be silent when, having changed their purpose, they cease to inflict evils upon sufferers. Those who suffer do not readily rest or enjoy silence unless those who inflict suffering rest either unwillingly or willingly; and in a proper order some rest or silence begins in the latter, and, passing to the former, is consummated in their welcome experience.

Therefore, so that those who endeavor to inflict sorrows on others may be silent, and those upon whom such things are inflicted unwillingly may be consoled, divine speech is sometimes found admonishing the former; for, so far as lies in itself, it wills to remove all evils from human beings. “Cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is accounted exalted” [Col. 1184C] (Isa. II). And to Ezekiel: “You shall speak my words to them, perhaps they will hear and cease, for they are a provoking house” (Ezek. II).

Isaiah sees, Ezekiel sees—indeed, the prophetic Spirit sees—that a popular fury would assemble against Christ the Lord, and that the tumult of the raging people would come to such a point that the afflicted misery of the sufferer would be compelled to cry: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI). Since this one is weak and yet strong, humble and yet exalted, man and yet God, the Jews are rightly admonished by prophetic speech to cease from him: namely, lest they provoke the one whom they behold as a true man, because he who makes the weak, the humble, the man sorrowful will be judged in power by him when he appears as the more exalted one.

Likewise, when the power of the commander Holofernes became known far and wide among diverse peoples and their weakness trembled at the report of him, certain persons came forward and earnestly prayed that he might cease, and that his indignation toward those subject to him might grow gentle, lest he proceed to rage more harshly against those ready faithfully to serve both his command and that of the king. “Let your indignation cease against us,” they say, “for it is better that we, living, should serve King Nebuchadnezzar and be subject to you” (Judith III). And later: “Come to us as a peaceful lord [Col. 1185A], and use our service as may please you” (ibid.).

But he is softened neither by prayer nor price nor their devoted obedience. Rather, he foams against them like a boar and rages like an untamed lion; and the more their misery wastes away beneath his fury, the more his raging mind delights. The source from which the sad and parched mind of the afflicted sickens makes fat the insolent mind of the afflicter. Ruined in mind, he thinks that he becomes glorious if by mighty malice he makes himself hateful to all. But when divine mercy wished to visit those suffering sorrow, it removed their oppressor from their midst in the manner it willed. It sent the widow Judith—beautiful in countenance, endowed with chastity, eloquent in speech, commendable in holiness—to seduce the commander with Bacchus and Venus, and to slay him with his own dagger by a woman’s hand [Col. 1185B].

Because grievous evils flourished while he lived and inflicted them, they likewise ceased when he ceased; and, though his wicked will was not changed for the better, the possibility of acting was taken away from him by just judgment. God himself, who is said to inflict sorrows only justly, is sometimes also urged to be silent or rest from them; for if his anger or judgment does not cease from inflicting them, the misery of us unworthy people does not rest from suffering them.
