When the people had induced Aaron the priest to make new gods, and he, wickedly fearful, had committed gold to the fire and produced a molten calf, the Lord—who on the mountain was instructing Moses by pleasant discourse and directing commandments of life down to the people on the plain—said: “Let me be, that my fury may be enraged against them and that I may destroy them” (Exod. XXXII).

God wished to answer the provoking people with a corresponding punishment and suddenly restrain the idolatry of their rejoicing with grievous penalty, so that those who despise salvation and reject the discipline of life might feel the sorrowful hand of their angry Creator bringing ruin. To him Moses says: “Let your anger cease, and be appeased concerning the wickedness of your people.” Although the provoking house is held guilty of idolatry, I pray that it may not be utterly destroyed according to its desert; that your anger may not be found raging in sorrows even unto extermination; that you may not seem to furnish the Egyptians material for mockery.

For the Egyptians hated the children of Israel and were grievously distressed at their prosperity. If, because God was angry, the Israelites should come to destruction according to their merits, the Egyptians would leap out as though from ambush to insult and disparage them, babbling that they had been led out of Egypt without a prosperous outcome and, through the failure of their promiser, had not at all been brought into the desired land. “Let not the Egyptians say,” he says, “He cleverly brought them out in order to kill them in the mountains and destroy them from the earth” [Col. 1185D] (ibid.).

Moses wishes the angry Judge not to inflict sorrows upon the people according to his purpose; he wishes the sinning people not to suffer what they deserve according to their merits, lest the envious enemy be found rejoicing at their ruin and wickedly insulting their Author as though he were their deceiver, with mocking applause. He wishes, I say, that those who had sinned should not be wholly destroyed, although he desires their faults to be removed by fitting correction. For he knows that God’s justice admits no faults within its sanctuary [Col. 1186A], yet his mercy often does not permit the guilty to perish.

For he knows that divine grace, when it wishes sinners more seriously to be saved, does not allow them, uncorrected, to be brought to grief by sudden death. Rather, it first takes care that they be chastened through sorrowful repentance and, once chastened, consoled by the sure hope of pardon.

## CHAPTER CXII

But those whom God does not purpose to save in his just judgment, he does not apply to them the healing poultice of repentance. Instead, he either strikes them with swift death, lest they become arrogant for longer, or permits them to live so that the filthy may become filthier still. While they live, moreover, he often does not make them sorrowful by sending blows, lest any adversity resist their perversity. Thus he allows them to use the broad latitude of their own will [Col. 1186B], so that, advancing from evil to worse, they may freely fall into sins.

Thus the more severe Judge is silent and at rest among such persons; for the present his punishing anger does not burn against them, while they are carried and run about by harmful evils with loosened reins, and no sorrows meet their course. Indicating this through Ezekiel, he says to the sinful soul: “My jealousy shall be taken away from you, and I will rest and will be angry no more” (Ezek. XVI). “Because,” he says, “I no longer care to save you, as your sins demand, I too now harden my heart against you, hardened as you are. I apply neither a present iron, nor poultice, nor oil, nor bandage to your wound; but at last I leave you to yourself, to perish by your own decision.

“For if I had resolved to save you through both my grace and your merit, I would surely have cut your wound with the iron of sorrow, and would not have allowed you to prosper at will in your own purpose. Rather, I would have wished harmful evils quickly to be cleansed away by grievous evils. Therefore I shall rest and not be angry; for the present I shall not inflict what you deserve. Though committing every kind of harm, you will suffer no sorrows; rather, you will possess the latitude of your own will so widely extended that, as under its shelter, you will delight in quiet and silence” [Col. 1186C].

Conversely, those upon whom divine benevolence purposes to have mercy it commonly wills to be exercised by present punishments. Like one enraged, it roars, thunders, strikes, and heals; not sparing the wound, it mercifully has compassion on the wounded person. Hence in the Psalm: “You were angry, and you had mercy on us” (Ps. LIX). And Habakkuk says: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. III).

For the anger of a physician, by which he is believed to rage against the wound when cutting putrid flesh in order to reach the furthest extent of its corruption, can be called mercy, because he wills not that the sick person should wholly perish, but that, healed by the grievous iron, he may return to the benefit of health. It is fitting that one who did not more carefully guard against contracting sickness, when, like Adam, knowingly and intelligently departed from righteousness—or perhaps did not care to understand how to do good—should eat medicinal bread only in sweat, and should find what he foolishly contracted healed with sorrow. Therefore the just Judge takes care to apply a biting remedy, even against their will, to those abandoning healing discipline, willing that whoever, sick through the seduction of flesh or spirit, strays from virtue [Col. 1187A], may rejoice in health again only through the bitterness of sorrow.

For this reason, when the children of Israel are reported to sin in the book of Judges, they are consequently said to be delivered into the hands of plunderers; their harmful acts are punished with grievous sorrow, and, when vengeance has been completed, they at last return to rest and silence. “The children of Israel,” it says, “did evil in the sight of the Lord, and forgot their God, serving the Baals and Astaroths. And the Lord was angry against Israel, and delivered them into the hands of Chushan-rishathaim; and they served him eight years” (Judg. III).

You see that the sinning people do not long enjoy their purpose, but, by swift vengeance, become subject to a hostile lord. Those who, by the decree of a corrupted will, had undeservedly served foreign gods afterward bowed their necks against their own will beneath oppressive masters [Col. 1187B]. The provident dispenser beautifully ordered the punishments of the wicked and assigned them rewards corresponding to their merits: those who had refused to obey the true God with due worship, he made, by an equitable balance, serve such oppressors.

“He delivered them into the hands of Chushan-rishathaim” (ibid.). This lord, to whom divine judgment subjected the children of Israel, treated those enslaved to his jurisdiction with harsh dominion in such a way that for eight years he grievously distressed those subject to him and granted no opening of relief to the distressed. Indeed, the very name, or names, by which Scripture chose to designate the oppressor seems, as I see it, suited to his function; and, as though on the forehead or threshold, it readily shows the beholder what dwelling and what benefit of the dwelling lie within. For *Chushan* is interpreted “their Ethiopia,” while *Rishathaim* means “their impiety.”

Since Ethiopia, which is interpreted “darkness” or “gloom,” has black and ugly peoples, it rightly signifies a certain inward darkening. When impiety is joined to it as an inseparable companion, they so darken the wretched mind forgetful of its God, press down what they have darkened, and harden what they have pressed down with gloom, that, ignorant of the true light, it is neither warmed by the fire of the Holy Spirit nor wholesomely made joyful by the oil of spiritual gladness. Instead, oppressed by nocturnal frost, it is darkened with the cloud of impiety; producing foul and ugly thoughts, it wastes away in bitter sorrow.

Thus the children of Israel are placed beneath Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, when they are grievously weighed down with darkness [Col. 1187D]; when, pressed down and exhausted, they groan beneath the burden, as it were, of royal power and, deprived of free choice, cannot breathe the air of freedom. They have indeed fallen so heavily and impiously into the depths, have been enclosed in prison and wrapped in such great darkness, that they cannot free their necks from bonds or their feet from fetters; groping in darkness, they do not know how to find the joyful day in the heights above.

Hence the same king, said to oppress them with a sorrowful yoke, is in another translation called *Chusarsathon*, because, holding in the depths, whether they wish it or not, those who had long despised the true and supreme light, he brings them more grievous darkness. For *Chusarsathon* is interpreted “their humiliation.” Upon those, namely, who did not duly render reverence to the true God [Col. 1188A], who stubbornly raised themselves against him with stiff neck and uncircumcised heart, who chose to serve the creature rather than the Creator when, despising him, they worshiped Baals and Astaroths—upon these King Chusarsathon rules with grievous dominion. He delights to afflict, distress, and oppress them; and the more effectively he exercises his power over them, the more harshly he shakes, presses, bends, and humiliates their will.

For when they wished to prosper in their idolatry, to celebrate feast days, rejoice in corrupt worship, and glory in rest, leisure, and festive silence, he delights to assail them with such power and such mighty malice that they are permitted to rejoice neither in their erroneous will nor in voluntary error. Thus the king roars and rages as he inflicts sorrows upon the children of Israel; they gnash their teeth and waste away as they suffer them. So on both sides peace fails, rest perishes, silence is banished, war resounds, discord flourishes, and strife rules—if, however, strife or quarrel may properly be named where, according to a certain pagan poet (HORACE), one party is shown only to strike, the other only to be struck.

But while the grievous malice of the inflicter strikes and the sad misery of the sufferer is only struck, they learn that it would have been far better to cleave faithfully to God and be subject to him than, by sinning, to expose themselves to the souls of those who trouble them. In God’s worship joyful and peaceful silence may be found; when they chose otherwise, they were compelled to experience the sorrowful hand of punishment. Therefore they sigh from the depths and cry to the Lord from the belly of hell [Col. 1188C]. Although they now know that he always justly punishes the insults of sins, they nevertheless know that he is commonly not lacking to the prayers and groans of the afflicted.

He bends his ear to hear their groaning and cry; having mercy on those who cry out, he raises up for them a savior, by whose prudence and courage he wills King Chusarsathon to be overcome, and, when he has been overcome, the rest and silence of his people to be restored. His name was Othniel, which is interpreted “the answer of God,” or “God’s time for me.”

He is rightly called “the answer of God” who answers God, or to whom God answers. He answers God who voluntarily raises his ear to God’s command; who presents himself ready to the one calling or commanding; who hears what the grace of the instructor pours into him as one subject to him, and passes on nothing else to his own hearers. “I heard,” Isaiah says, “the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? And I said: Here I am; send me” [Col. 1188D] (Isa. VI). Such a person not only does not refuse to go where he is sent, nor merely fail to complain of the heavy command of the one who commands; he even voluntarily and readily offers himself to the divine will, answers with obedience, and renders reverence to majesty. David says: “I am ready and am not troubled, that I may keep your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII). Such a man is the answer of God.

Sending Ezekiel, the Lord says to him: “You shall speak my words to them” (Ezek. III). And below: “You shall hear words from my mouth and announce them to them from me” (ibid.). And to Jeremiah: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth” (Jer. I). Each of the two sent by the Lord says: “Thus says the Lord.” He too is very fittingly called “the answer of God” who, sent to the people, does not devise words from himself or utter falsehoods in many words, but first humbly applies a listening ear to his instructor and then passes on to his hearer what he has drawn from him [Col. 1189A].

He can also be called “the answer of God” because God answers him as well. God answers him when he seems to obey not the person’s command but his desire; when he is found to grant his grace to one devoutly longing for it; when, in response to one who asks worthily, he shows humble regard by giving generously and opens his ear in abundance. To one who says, “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII), he answers: “I will give you understanding and instruct you” (Ps. XXXI). To one who says, “Teach me to do your will” (Ps. CXLII), he answers: “He will show you, O man, what is good” (Mic. VI).

He also answered Solomon, when Solomon anxiously asked that wisdom might be given him, so that as ruler he might rightly govern the people committed to him; so that under his rule ignorance might wither away, the injustice following upon it might languish, discernment might flourish, just judgment bloom again, strife cease, war be restrained by a strong barrier, and righteousness, going before, might grant a kiss to peace coming to meet it. “You will give your servant,” he says, “a teachable heart, so that he may judge your people and discern between good and evil” (III Kings III). And God says to him: “Because you have asked for wisdom to discern judgment, behold, I have given you a wise and understanding heart” (ibid.). And in Chronicles: “Give me wisdom and understanding” [Col. 1189C] (II Chron. I). And God says to him: “Because you have asked for wisdom and knowledge, so that you may judge my people, wisdom and knowledge are given to you” (ibid.).

To whom God deigns to show himself so benevolent, to whose vows and prayers he responds with so abundant a benefit, to whom he grants prosperous days and a season bringing salvation, whose desire he graciously hears from his sanctuary—to such a one “the response of God” rightly belongs as a name. By this name, the first judge in the Book of Judges is said to be designated. Or he was called, “God’s time is mine.” This does not differ from the same sense. For one who understands, as has been said, that God responds to him in a familiar manner, consequently confesses that a prosperous time smiles upon him [Col. 1189D]; and lest he seem ungrateful to so kindly a respondent, he attributes the welcome time to none other than his own benefactor. “God’s time,” he says, “is mine.” A favorable time is at hand for me, a day of salvation (2 Cor. 6): a time in which I do not put my neck, bent down, beneath my enemies; in which I do not lay heavier burdens upon the peoples entrusted to me, already burdened as they are; but in which I place myself as a strong mediator between oppressors and oppressed, and, thus interposed, put an end to evils and impose silence upon sorrows.

“This time,” he says, “is at hand for me—not a time brought by the revolutions of the firmament or the course of wandering stars, but one bestowed by God’s grace and God’s wisdom in a wondrous order of providence: so that the people who sat amid darkness and the tumult of martial sorrow may breathe again, strengthened by the radiant coming of peace and silence.” [Col. 1190A] Therefore the judge rightly calls this God’s time: it grants him grace, denies power to his enemies, puts an end to battles, commands silence to sorrows, favours him, and successfully resists hostile malice. Although Othniel rejoices that this is granted to him, he nevertheless knows that whatever is his must be rendered back to its author; and therefore he claims it as present to himself in such a way that he says it belongs not to chance or merit, but rather to God. “God’s time,” he says, “is mine.”

Of such a time it is said also in the Book of Maccabees: “Jonathan saw that the time was helping him, and he sent to Rome to establish and renew friendship with them” (1 Macc. 12). And the Apostle says: “While we have time, let us do good” (Gal. 6). Rightly, because the time was helping him, that man hastened to renew the friendship of the Romans toward himself [Col. 1190B], hoping that his purpose would prosper through the favor of the time. And this worker likewise exhorts us to work, lest, when time has failed, anyone should strive in vain to go out to his work. Thus, when one asks for five loaves at an importunate hour, he is said to have closed his door; but at another, fitting hour he is said to give food to those who hope for it. By this the giver’s grace is commended through the suitability of the time, without which there is no successful way to the remedy of peace and tranquil silence.

For this reason the Lord also says: “My time has not yet come” (John 7). The reason, he says, why your hearers’ unbelief does not heed my words; why present prosperity does not attend upon my will; why my sorrow is not permitted to find silence; why I do not wish to distinguish myself at this feast day [Col. 1190C] with passing praises; why my humility cannot suit your intention—is that I know that my time, favorable and fitting to me, has not yet come. But when the welcome fullness of my time arrives; when spring’s mildness and summer’s beauty breathe forth; when autumnal ripeness has been brought into the wine-cellar—then indeed the mournful rage of winds, winter’s harshness, the swelling onset of threats, and the destructive instability of waves will fall far away; and triumphant joy will set its throne in the harbor of silence.

The aforesaid judge Othniel is named as a type of this time. Through the favor of merciful grace he rules the children of Israel, 683 so as to draw over their grievous sorrow, as it were [Col. 1190D], a sheltering veil of consolation; indeed, having driven far away the constriction of grief, to introduce them into the joyful sanctuary of silence. Having therefore assumed the leadership, the judge sets himself against the enemies and does not abandon his resolve to fight for victory until, having conquered the king of Mesopotamia, beneath whom the sorrowful people had been heavily oppressed, he restores peace and renews the silence which, long lost, had been sought with long sighing. Once this was found, the land is said to have rested for forty years; the sorrow of wars was lulled to sleep, peace and silence flourished; and those whom an importunate king had removed from rest and leisure for eight years, the excellent judge advanced to tranquil silence for a more ample span of time. “He subdued,” it says, “the king of Mesopotamia, and the land rested forty years; and Othniel died” [Col. 1191A] (Judg. 3).

And whereas in the same Scripture the succession of judges is described one after another—whence the book itself is properly called Judges—all are found to devote their diligence to this end: that they may refresh in tranquil silence the people disturbed by grievous war.

## Chapter 113

For the disturbance of war is no small thing, and sorrow is unbearable when, under its pressure, each person’s prosperity seems doomed to be crushed; or when, crushed beneath the hostile hand, it groans and is burdened, and is relieved from that very burden neither by its own help nor by another’s. Wars, indeed, are rightly called sorrowful because they are wholly opposed to the silence that is desired: no combatant hides beneath the shadow of that same silence so long as war and the peril of war [Col. 1191B] grow more severe. Of this Jonathan says: “My father has troubled the land” (1 Sam. 14). And Elijah says to Ahab: “I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father’s house” (1 Kgs. 18).

Since it belongs to a good ruler to make the land entrusted to him serene, and, having restrained the din of wars, to preserve it beneath peaceful silence, Saul and Ahab are rightly rebuked by the clear and free speech of a wiser understanding, since they were discovered to be guilty of malice and authors of sorrow. For when the trumpet blares, the horn sounds, and war’s discordant cry is heard; when men with savage hearts converge from both sides upon an uncertain contest; when discord reigns, rivalry thrives, and praise is sought; when confidence is forestalled by fear and victory by toil—then the land is disturbed, the inner parts of hearts are crushed, and, as sorrow prevails, peace and silence [Col. 1191C] are unknown. Showing this, the Lord says through Jeremiah: “The sound of war in the land, and great destruction” (Jer. 50); and below: “The sound of a cry from Babylon, and great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans, because the Lord has laid Babylon waste; and their waves shall roar like many waters; their voice gives forth its sound, because a destroyer is upon her” (ibid.).

You see that the sound of war, rather than silence, is proclaimed, and Babylon, oppressed by war, is said to cry out. For while each person experiences sorrowful misery in his own crushing, he is truly not soothed by peace, rest, or serene silence. For their voice gives the sound of sorrow: theirs, upon whom the destroyer has come; whom the trumpet shakes with terror; whom the sword pierces; whom destruction [Col. 1191D] presses. And while the clash and confusion of warriors make heavy sounds, a sorrowful cry and the lament of misery resound from the houses of those who have been crushed. The same prophet, indicating this much earlier concerning the children of Israel, says: “Let their young men be pierced with the sword in battle; let a cry be heard from their houses” (Jer. 18).

When the hostile sword rages and becomes drunk with blood in battle; when, overthrowing wretches on every side, it exercises a grievous rule of sorrow; when the prudence of men and the strength of youths fall; when hope is reduced to nothing and certainty is turned into its opposite; when laughter becomes tears and joy is changed into grief; when the trumpet gives a mournful sound and the horn a wretched blast—then surely no small grief is found in their houses, and neither in them nor from them is heard anything but [Col. 1192A] the cry of sorrow, the lament of misery, and the voice of rage and anger. Thus the wrath of the supreme Judge is found raging against wretches when he wills to punish their wickedness with grievous sorrow: either to bring them back to saving repentance after severe chastisement, or perhaps to make the hardened perish utterly without mercy.

For those who wickedly exalt themselves against God, who babble arrogantly and are not restrained by due fear, who do not impose healing silence upon harmful clamour, who do not apply the remedy of healing repentance to corrupting joy—these he, with whom nothing at all goes unavenged, at some time shakes with roaring and scatters into tumult. Affirming this through the same prophet, he says: “I will make heard over Rabbah of the children of Ammon the roar of battle, and it shall be scattered into tumult” [Col. 1192B] (Jer. 49). Because Rabbah, the city of the Ammonites, offends me by the clamorous din of vices and does not spread the covering of repentance over its grievous offences, my wrath will at last not be silent from rendering like for like, while that same city endures the roar of war and the tumult of sorrow.

But when divine grace intends to have mercy on its people, willing to remove from them sorrowful things and the mournful roar of war, it deigns, as stated above, to raise up for them a judge able and willing to transform tumult into silence and sorrow into joy. This is Othniel, in whom, as it is written, was the Spirit of the Lord; by whose power he overcame the aforesaid king of Mesopotamia. When that king was conquered, the people, long oppressed under the burden of grievous sorrow, breathed again.

And Scripture rightly declares that the Spirit of the Lord [Col. 1192C] 684 dwelt in him, who both wills and is able to free the people from the yoke of slavery. For effectiveness is given to the will only by the divine Spirit, and only the Spirit restores the sorrowful and wretched to freedom. “For where the Spirit of the Lord is,” says the Apostle, “there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3). In this freedom, the people who had formerly been accustomed to groan under King Chusarsathon afterward rested for forty years; and under the aforesaid judge peaceful tranquillity and welcome silence took root, since he abolished with a strong hand the oppressive tumults of sorrow.

After his death, the people, deprived of the happy presence of their defender, again added to their wrongdoing and fell back into the hands of an oppressor. Under Eglon, king of Moab, they were consigned to grievous sorrow and were intolerably afflicted for eighteen years [Col. 1192D]. Crying from the depths to the Lord, they deserved to be visited; and, when the Lord visited them, to be freed from sorrowful toil and misery. This accords with Isaiah’s promise, made in the fullness of the divine Spirit as he contemplates on the one hand the people’s misery and on the other God’s mercy: “He will have mercy on Jacob and will yet choose Israel, and will make them rest upon their own ground” (Isa. 14).

He who, while God is angry, is pressed by the long burden and toil of war; who bears the heavy yoke of slavery in mourning; who is compelled to lament and waste away under his enemies’ hand; whose inner self is darkened by an afflicted spirit—when God, having mercy upon him, shines upon him as from above, when grace smiles upon him, when justice grows gentle, then, with the cloud of grief wiped away, he rejoices in the new light of the gift [Col. 1193A] and rests upon his own ground, the din of sorrow having been stilled. This heavenly mercy graciously showed to the aforesaid children of Israel, when God powerfully delivered them from their enslavement under Eglon’s hand and again raised up for them a saviour named Aoth, who used either hand as his right hand and killed the very fat Eglon with a sword. This good judge, by the strong sharpness both of his prudence and of his courage, broke the yoke and snapped the fetter of harsh and long-lasting slavery; and once it was broken, the sorrow that had cruelly oppressed the children of Israel for eighteen years, bringing them lamentation, groaning, and grievous tumult, yielded and departed.

## Chapter 114

Finally, Eglon is interpreted as “calf of sorrow,” or [Col. 1193B] “their festivity.” A calf is a frolicsome, inconstant, wandering animal, impatient of the stall and delighting in freedom. If it is perhaps permitted to follow its own free will, this is regarded by those who allow it as a sort of festivity, since by its running and agility it delights observers who heed the present indiscriminately and attend less carefully to what is to come. But when, in the course of time, it grows strong in age and vigor, and its horn and hoof have developed, its swiftness becomes dangerous. The more freely it has hitherto held the reins of license, the more grievous threats and assaults it now inflicts upon all it meets: sparing no one, yielding to no one, and offering no one any kindly encounter. Thus both outwardly and inwardly it is a calf not of joy but of sorrow.

[Col. 1193C] Concerning such a calf Moses says: “If an ox was accustomed to gore yesterday and the day before, and they warned its owner, but he did not confine it, and it kills a man or woman, the ox shall be stoned and they shall kill its owner” (Exod. 21). By such a calf is rightly signified the wandering instability of the mind: a fugitive from the law, ignorant of discipline, rejoicing in wide-open latitude; driven, as if by a fan, by its inborn lightness; unable to stand still, delighting in motion, possessing nothing of mature steadiness; carried through everything attractive and harmful by the impetuousness of wanton desire; and, dissatisfied with one thing, rushing from many things to still more through love of novelty.

While it is thus allowed to be tossed about according to its own will, a game and festive amusement indeed seem to be enacted, because every steadfast person [Col. 1193D] finds nothing more pleasant or festive to behold than his own many and varied desires held by no restraint. While he wallows in this likeness to himself with freer license and rejects from it nothing foul or voluntary, he is fattened by such enticements as by taverns and brothels, so that he is reckoned to be not merely fleshly but wholly flesh, more through vice than material substance. “For Eglon,” it says, “was exceedingly fat” (Judg. 3).

The people of Israel are delivered to this oppressor when our senses, which ought to obey their Creator, are, after offending him, carried captive into another law; deprived now of free will and compelled to serve disease rather than God, flesh rather than spirit. Thus the Israelite people are subjected to King Eglon when frivolous inconstancy rules upon the throne of our mind [Col. 1194A] and drives both our inward and outward senses through the downward and wandering paths of manifold perversity, with no one resisting its rule of power. When they consent to it, when wretches delight in serving it, when they obey eagerly, when they wholly love to obey, that very inconstant frivolity, that frequent movement from great evils to greater, that experience of diverse pleasures adding heavier burdens to heavy ones, becomes for them a certain exultation and agreeable festivity, in which the lost sense wanders and the mind is scattered abroad.

But if at some time fear of impending punishments comes upon one, or if the wretch perhaps incurs the deserved penalties of error; if harmful deception is at last exposed through fear and anguish; if a spark of truth, struck out by the hammer of punishments, falls and shines forth—then the rule of King Eglon begins to seem more sorrowful than usual, and gradually the wantonness of our calf [Col. 1194B] becomes displeasing. The yoke which the sport of poisonous pleasure had previously made welcome is rendered unwelcome by fear or by the experience of its heaviness. For when a burdened person considers the danger in obeying Eglon’s commands, and the end and eventual recompense that await present pleasure, he now grieves and is sad that he has fallen into Eglon’s snares and voluntarily put his neck beneath a yoke which is not sweet but now heavy.

Pressed by sorrow, therefore, he now wishes and desires to depart from there; abandoning the king’s rule, he wishes to return to his former freedom. He is no longer held by his customary affection for the latitude of vices; he wishes to leave free at once, but he is held fast by such a hoof. [Col. 1194C] For with the ease with which he turned himself from the heights to the depths, he does not turn himself back again to recover the summit he left behind: the broad and spacious way lay open as he declined, but a closed and barred door is found by one seeking to breathe again. Although the breadth of vices is great and almost limitless, and its expansiveness receives any wretch as it were in an open bosom, it nevertheless knows how to bind one whom it has received with tight knots and cunningly impede him in his broad and spacious wandering, so that, even if he wishes, he cannot immediately free himself or retrace with an unobstructed return the path from which he came.

He therefore grieves, groans, sighs, and is tormented, while he longs to be dismissed free but is held; while, just as he fell into vices through the choice of free will, he cannot rise again with an equal privilege of freedom [Col. 1194D]. And what can anyone know that is harsher or more burdensome, sadder or more bitter, than to will something with eager desire and not be able to do it—especially since, if I am not mistaken, sorrow consists precisely in this: that a will loving freedom sees obstacles set against it? He grieves, I say, and is distressed when he feels himself deprived of his own choice and enslaved unwillingly to the troublesome service of a ruler; when he wishes to leave the wide and spreading expanse of vices but cannot discover a way out.

For one who thinks and resolves to cast off the filth of perversity, change his habits, put off the garment of oldness, renounce harmful things, henceforth undertake better things, put the former things far away, and seek what is nearer to salvation—for one who thinks these things, I say, so great a difficulty presents itself that there is utterly no power to accomplish what he desires. That very fat Eglon [Col. 1195A], into whose dominion he had declined through the fault of his will, to whose injustices his deceived heart had voluntarily bent, whom he had already served for some time, and whose commands and laws he had obeyed with a sufficiently eager heart—that Eglon, unwilling that what is his should pass into another’s right, strives to enclose it with rampart, wall, locks, and bars. Seeing any wretch wish to leave the bounds of his power, he obstructs his departure with the enticement of former pleasure; frequently troubling him, he sometimes makes him more prone to vices than before; he declares the path of departure narrower, and, piling up vices on every side, takes care to make him so burdened that by his own judgment he cannot pass through the narrow way.

Thus the person whom devout thought, a compunct heart, and hatred of sin lead outside for an hour [Col. 1195B], that craftsman of deceit more quickly leads back with the leash of habit. Lest he be idle, he occupies him with mud and brick like Pharaoh; and lest he return to Jerusalem, he keeps him bound within the enclosures of Babylon. But when this good will is thus repeatedly opposed, when possibility does not come to the aid of one badly occupied and miserably captive, when the unruly flesh desires against the spirit, and—what is far more grievous—when at times the spirit itself seems to grow weary into flesh, the wretch does not know by what exertion or art he can free himself from so hard a prison, seeing himself held captive by so miserable a law. By a momentarily sound resolve of mind he wishes to escape, but in the time of temptation he finds himself slipping back into it; thus, wishing to be freed from the same bonds, he grieves that the first impulses of his will are entangled by the blemish of habit.

He grieves, I say, turning matters over and over and not knowing where to turn or whose help he should implore in faith and trust. For he feels that he is held in his present misery by his own desert, and that, held fast as he is, he does not deserve the mercy of anyone who might help him. Pressed and oppressed, therefore, he at last strives to cry out, intending by his cry to rouse a gracious hearer, so that, when the hearer’s mind has been struck by his plaintive cry, he may consequently obtain however small a grace of mercy. “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” [Col. 1195C] (Rom. 7). He is truly wretched, and may rightly be called most wretched, who, subjected to King Eglon, feels himself consigned to such misery that, when he wishes to leave that kingdom and undertake [Col. 1195D] better things, he falls back—even unwillingly—into worse things by the law of habit.

“And who,” he says, “will visit me in this prison of difficulty and furnish the power to depart? Who will free me from this body of death, release one who is sorrowful into joy and one who is wretched into grace?” Rightly he asks, “Who?” For there is no one who frees, or very rarely anyone—indeed, so rarely that there is only one: “There is none who does such good; there is not even one” (Ps. 13). That one is God, who alone withdraws whom he wills from the power of enemies and by his grace alone restores them to saving freedom. Understanding this, he says: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 7). Therefore the person hindered by the stains of vices, who wishes no longer [Col. 1196A] to be deceived by the enticement of harsh habit and to be led out by effective power from the grievous rule of King Eglon, rightly cries to God himself, whose grace alone is known to be supremely powerful.

## Chapter 115

“The children of Israel,” it says, “cried to the Lord, who raised up for them a saviour, Aoth” (Judg. 3). Happy is that people which, after long losses of salvation, is permitted to cry out; which, after long sorrow, can rouse God by cries; which at last can breathe a little after being long and grievously oppressed; which can aspire by the efforts of hope toward the life long ago lost. Much more good is God, who does not turn away his kindly ear from the people’s cry, who turns toward the vows of the humble and the prayers of the sorrowful, who deigns in the gift of his grace to have mercy on those whom he sees sorrowful and unwillingly pressed by hostile rule.

Having mercy upon them, God raises up a saviour who, [Col. 1196B] breaking the prison, opens a wider gate to the captives and stretches out his hand against him who appeared to be the author of evil and prince of sorrow; he draws the sword and fights with a strong arm. His name was Aoth. Aoth is interpreted “praise” or “glorious.”

A judge of this kind is rightly raised by the Lord to free the people: one proclaimed praiseworthy in the merit of his life and conduct; indeed, to say more, one who deserves himself to be called “praise,” so that his excellence may be commended more fully by this name. For he may not unfittingly be called praise who wishes God, the Father of lights, to be praised not so much in himself as through himself; who wishes his mighty deeds to shine before men for this purpose: that those who see them may be pleased not by the excellence of the doer, but by that of the giver [Col. 1196C]. For when he does not ascribe to himself whatever difficult thing he accomplishes, but returns to the giver whatever is commended in him through the giver’s gift, he himself is praise—not his own praise, but rather the Creator’s—to whom alone he gives, and desires to be given, the title of praise and honor.

The more earnestly he devotes himself to the praise of God alone, honorably zealous to spread God’s name, ascribing nothing to himself and being fruitful only for God, the more he is found worthily and deservedly glorious. Since he does not retain within himself a love of personal praise, he presents himself without scruple to the inward Searcher. The more he renders his conscience pure from the desire of glory, the more ample glory he finds in that same hidden place of conscience. Of this Paul says to the Corinthians: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1). As a wounded conscience, containing [Col. 1196D] evil and perverse thoughts, inflicts penal torments upon the reprobate, so inward purity and the conscience of clean holiness bring glory and the joyful testimony of truth to the righteous.

This glory is not false and empty but true and solid when, knowing no pride, it remains within its appointed bounds: that is, when conscience glories only in and concerning him whom it joyfully recognizes, by familiar grace, as both dwelling within it and ruling over it. If conscience did not truly have God as its president in its inmost recess, and carelessly rejoiced in some other, whether introduced or seductive, it would rightly be said, having gone beyond its proper bounds, to wander abroad and to glory vainly not within itself but outside itself. Recalling the Galatians from this error, the Apostle says: “Let each one prove his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone and not in another” [Col. 1197A] (Gal. 6).

Each person proves his own work—that is, makes it approved—when in the secret place of the mind he wishes to have God alone, to have him, and no other, presiding as his Lord; when he keeps himself with God as though in an inner chamber, and strongly excludes whatever alien thing may appear. When he has done this and rightly realizes that it has been done, he will no longer have glory outside himself in another, but within himself concerning, or in, him to whom he adheres alone. One thus declared glorious, as has been said, deserves worthily to be appointed judge of the people, so that through him the sorrows by which the people are distressed may be mitigated, disturbed silence restored, and lost rest repaired.

Trusting prudent counsel to restore that rest, Aoth fashioned a two-edged sword, hid it fastened upon his right thigh beneath the garment with which he was clothed, and approached King Eglon in the summer upper chamber as if to speak privately with him. He drove it into Eglon’s belly so forcefully that the hilt followed the blade into the wound. “He did not draw out the sword,” it says, “but left it in the body as he had struck; and immediately the excrement of the belly burst out through the natural passages. When he had died, the land rested for eighty years” [Col. 1197B] (Judg. 3).

God rightly wills him to become a minister for the restoration of peace in whose work nothing sinister is found, on whose right thigh a two-edged sword is carried, and by whose drawn sword hostile malice is manfully slain. [Col. 1197C] By “sword” I understand that the sharp rigor of discipline is signified. Whoever desires to be glorious rather than merely called so is rightly believed to carry it prudently beneath his garment when he studies to chastise himself more strictly within his conscience. The same sword is placed on the right thigh when the censure of discipline cuts off his perverse pleasure, so that nothing fleshly, sinister, or deadly remains in the flesh, but everything is regarded as, so to speak, right-handed and suited to salvation.

Afterward the sword is suitably drawn from its sheath to crush the enemy when discipline is vigorously exercised upon one’s neighbors, when their instability, dissolution, and wantonness are cut away by the sharpness of correction, and when, under the pursuing zeal of justice, they are slain in the very hidden place of the heart. They are slain, I say, [Col. 1197D] when the judge has made the discipline of a biting cautery penetrate into the very den or cesspool of the mind and has expelled, by the efficacy of penetrating medicine, everything that flows there, as into a belly of dung 687 or fat.

As the belly gathers the greater amount of fat to itself and contains within its walls the decay of foods, so the more the wretched mind swells against God with a fat neck, the more inwardly foul becomes the gathered uncleanness of its vices. Therefore, just as the prudent Aoth inflicts greater injury upon fat Eglon where more refuse flows together in him, so sharper-than-any-sword discipline is rightly applied where the entrails of the mind hold, as it were, dung and fat. When once the salutary cautery [Col. 1198A] has been applied and received, a prudent person must not recall from its purpose the work he has begun, but must confirm by perseverance the medicinal rigor both in himself and in his neighbor; he must not be like the Gospel man who began and could not finish (Luke 14).

This is perhaps what is meant by the account that Aoth drove the sword into the fat belly and, not drawing out what he had driven in, left it as he had struck: namely, that he understood and saw that the sword had succeeded according to his purpose, that the enemy had been struck firmly, and that the malice of the one struck had failed. The divine text indicates how he perceived this: “Immediately the excrement of the belly burst forth” (Judg. 3). Thus, when a prudent person administers saving discipline to himself or his neighbor, persuading hatred of sin and a spiritual affection for justice, he perceives that his adopted purpose [Col. 1198B] is working effectively and that the author of malice is being slain in the inner chamber of the mind, if no beauty of that evil presents itself as pleasing, but its foul ugliness is set before his nostrils and eyes.

This surely happens when, through the strong inspiration of grace, we abhor the uncleanness of vices; when continual rigor does not relax for any of their enticements; when the bed of the deceiver sprinkled with myrrh and aloes, and the honey-dripping lips of the deceitful harlot, no longer become sweet to us as formerly when they recur to memory. Rather, a generous and free mind abhors the encounter with such things; and, considering that according to Paul their end is truly nothing but death, it judges whatever of this sort occurs to be like foul dung. [Col. 1198C] By this sign—that the conscience of a righteous person is thus struck when the memory of sin occurs—a prudent teacher learns that his sword has advanced, and does not withdraw it from its progress, lest, if he grows faint even a little and the rigor of justice is removed, guilt revive, if only slightly.

## Chapter 116

Once she is dead—or rather, dead in this manner—the land rests for eighty years. This land is our mind. While it is occupied by earthly desires, agitated by the various impulses of vices, subjected voluntarily to that to which it has once submitted itself and afterward subjugated even unwillingly; while it is not master of itself but is taken captive by its lost freedom of choice—it is truly shaken and tossed about with the great tumult of anguish, fear, sorrow, and misery; and, its base having been shaken, it does not rest, but hangs suspended as in a kind of motion.

[Col. 1198D] But when it pleases him who willed to set us apart from our mother’s womb and who, having triumphed over enemies, deigns to free us from their rule; when our mind truly feels itself fortified by effective grace and no longer impeded either by the occurrence of sin or by harsh habit—then grief yields, distressing sorrow is banished, and, as though Eglon had died, our land rejoices in rest. For when it senses that it is no longer moved as before, shaken by frivolity, held by the forced services of slavery, required to pay tribute, or subject to its exacter; when it senses that this exacter has failed, that its hope is not frustrated, and that its desire has attained fulfillment—when our land senses this, it is silent in the face of sorrows and rests; and, its author of sorrow defeated, it rejoices in the grace of the gift it has obtained.

As a type of the same matter, much later the people of Israel, driven by sin into Babylon, were, after the debt of punishment had been paid, brought back from there after many years. When divine grace had removed the heavy clouds of their sorrow, the land, as we read, rejoiced and rested in silence. Before this happened, Isaiah foresaw it and wished to foretell it; and after him Jeremiah likewise, with the same Spirit, was found to instruct the people by prophetic speech, threatening them indeed with sorrowful things but comforting them with promised silence. Isaiah says: “When God gives you rest from your toil, from your shaking, and from the hard slavery in which you formerly served, you shall take up a parable against the king of Babylon and say: ‘How has the exacter ceased! Tribute has rested; the whole earth has grown still and silent; it has rejoiced and exulted!’” [Col. 1199A] (Isa. 14).

Isaiah sees that, once the king of Babylon has been conquered, those who had been captive will rejoice; and, with him defeated, they will in turn triumph and mock him [Col. 1199B]. The frost of sorrow having been wiped away, the land will bloom again with new joy; the tumult lulled, it will rest in desired silence. Concerning this Jeremiah also says: “Jacob shall return and rest, and there shall be none whom he fears” (Jer. 30). Jacob will, because of sins demanding it, be led into the souls of those who afflict him; under the hand of enemies the wretch will suffer sorrowful things. But when God has mercy, he will return from there to his own place and, with fear of sorrows removed, enjoy rest and silence.

Happy is one whom words of promise comfort; happier still one whom their fulfillment renders possessed of what he desired. Thus, when Aoth rules, the people rejoice not in hope but in reality, and, when Eglon has died, our land rests in gladness. I have said that in the aforesaid Book of Judges judges are appointed to obtain this end: namely [Col. 1199C], that the rest of a troubled people may be restored both by their ministry and by their teaching. I cannot in this present little work include all of them by name, 688 nor can I either understand or set forth in sequence what mystery their names and deeds contain.

Yet although in that same book, if I am not mistaken, thirteen judges are found to have presided, the land is said to have rested under only four of them; and although perhaps all laboured for its advancement, Scripture records that no more than four attained the advancement of peace and silence. That Scripture is found to contain thirteen judges seems to me to foreshadow the figure of the Apostles. For although in the Gospel catalogue they are commended as twelve [Col. 1199D], it is not denied that they were in truth thirteen. When another succeeded Judas Iscariot in his episcopal office—as David prophesied and Luke narrated—namely Matthias, and when Paul, last of all, joined the apostolic lot by his own testimony, then, while preserving the mystery commendably proclaimed in the number twelve, we have a thirteenth, lest he who laboured more abundantly than the rest should be excluded as superfluous.

This number, which Scripture chose to assign both to the Apostles when Paul is added and to the judges, is found, upon closer consideration, not to be devoid of mystery; and the significant sacrament of the same number offers a useful reminder to those who count them. For thirteen is completed from six and seven. Six, because it consists of its own parts, is called a perfect number; and the dignity of such perfection is first assigned to it because no number before it was worthy to have its parts able to make up its total. For it is divided equally into six units, into three twos, and into two threes; and one, two, and three—the equal parts of six—when joined together, make up that same six and do not exceed it. Because this number first attained that property, it deserved, as has been said, to be called perfect. Thus God, in fashioning the world by his works, chose that they should be completed in it, wishing the perfection of those works to be commended by the perfect number of days.

Finally, he is reported to have made the first human being on the sixth day. To that being, above the other works of the world, he showed himself more generous and gracious: he declares that this one alone was made in his own image [Col. 1200A–B], and it is shown that he made not the human being for the sake of other things, but other things for the sake of the human being. He chose to form him on the sixth day in order to teach more plainly that he ought to be perfect in life and conduct, and that, considering on which day he had the beginning of his creation, he should cleave to his Creator who created him with a perfect bond of love.

God likewise assigned six ages both to humanity and to the world, through which he ordained their life or course to be completed. Him whom he made on the sixth day, and brought to perfection through the stages of six ages, he willed to come to its setting; and by the mystical six he made their end correspond to their beginning, their setting to their rising. In the sixth age of this world God chose to become human, to accomplish human salvation by assuming humanity, and, while accomplishing this work, to undergo death also on the sixth day of the week, and by the power of his shed blood [Col. 1200C] to wipe away the long-standing stains of sin. For it seemed fitting that he whom he had made on the sixth day, when disfigured by the shame of disobedience, should be re-formed by him dying for him on that same day; and that, as creation, so re-creation should be consecrated by the dignity of six, and that the creature, consecrated by the mystery, should be held worthy of commendation.

But seven, which follows six, ought to be proclaimed worthy of commendation because we read that the Spirit of God is and is called sevenfold. Although he is believed to be one in the undivided essence of the Godhead, he is nevertheless called manifold because of the sevenfold grace of his bounty. Thus in a certain wise man he is found to be called both one and manifold, whereby the singularity of essence [Col. 1200D] and the plurality of gifts appear to be commended, so that unity does not detract from multiplicity, nor multiplicity from unity, since this accords with such great majesty without injury to either: “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “is one, manifold, subtle,” etc. (Wisdom 7).

Having first said “one,” he added “manifold,” understanding the nature or substance of the Spirit to be uniform, but his grace, in abundant fullness, to be multiform. His unity, by instructing us in faith, cleanses us; his multiplicity, through the sevenfold gift of graces, makes us fruitful. Of him Isaiah says: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11).

Isaiah, as it appears, named many spirits, yet did not deny the unity of the undivided Spirit [Col. 1201A]. For just as the threefold distinction of persons does not make many gods, so the sevenfold division of graces does not naturally make many spirits. The Apostle intimates this when he says: “There are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12); and below: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills” (ibid.). Although apostolic truth confesses that the Spirit who works by distributing many varied things to each according to his will is one and the same, the aforesaid wise man confidently calls him manifold, and Isaiah the prophet shows him to be sevenfold in gift.

For there are seven gifts, as it were principal gifts, which the Spirit is found to impart to spiritual persons; yet he does not distribute all to everyone, but gives to each as he wills. These gifts are sometimes called by the name of the giver [Col. 1201B], and in Holy Scripture are called the seven spirits. Hence in the Apocalypse: “These things says he who has the seven spirits of God” (Rev. 3); and below: “Seven burning lamps before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God” (Rev. 4). Again: “I saw the Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth” (Rev. 5).

John calls the seven eyes, or seven spirits, the seven principal gifts by which God the Father endowed with sight the innocent Lamb—that is, Christ as man—who was sent to take away the sins of the world and shone with the light of every grace, since, according to Paul, “the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” in him [Col. 1201C] (Col. 2). Zechariah likewise says of him: “Upon one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. 3); and below: “These seven are the eyes which range through all the earth” (Zech. 4).

This stone is Christ, who, according to the Psalm, was “made the head of the corner” (Ps. 117), joining the two walls together; whom Daniel proclaimed to be cut from the mountain without hands (Dan. 2). He shone, as it were, with the sevenfold light of eyes, because he abounded more fully and perfectly than all others in the sevenfold Spirit of graces. Scripture declares that his seven eyes are sent or range through all the earth because the sevenfold Spirit is sent everywhere in the world to work. Breathing where and as much as he wills, he is believed to effect those churches of the Apocalypse which, by a like mystery, are commended in the number seven [Col. 1201D].

For although, by Scripture’s testimony, the Church is truly proclaimed to be one, consecrated to one Lord, one faith, and one baptism—in whose type Solomon commended one dove, one beautiful woman in the Song of Songs (Cant. 2), and the Apostle Paul betrothed a chaste virgin to one husband (2 Cor. 11)—yet because it is spread through every place and adorned with the sevenfold gift of the Spirit, it too is correspondingly commended in the number seven. Thus John testifies that he writes to the seven churches which are in Asia, by which the universality of churches is signified. Though distributed from east to west and from north to south in place and merit, they are united by the tenacious bond of one and the same faith.

Finally, after completing the works of the six days, God is said to have rested on the seventh day [Col. 1202A]. This does not mean that he should be believed to have suffered any labour or weariness in making them; rather, it shows that, although he makes things naturally subject to vanity, he himself is ever devoted within himself to tranquil truth. For he is that Day of which the Psalmist says: “Day utters speech to day” (Ps. 18); and the Evangelist: “If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble” (John 11). This Day is not inappropriately called seventh, because it is revealed by the sevenfold ray of light; or because, as the seventh is the last of days in the order of creation, so he is rightly believed to be not only the first but also the last of all things.

Therefore, when Scripture says that God rests on the seventh day (Gen. 2), it plainly makes known that he is tranquil and peaceful in himself: the eternal rising who is never darkened into evening, but, knowing no setting, shines upon all things with the light of good. A diligent reader can indeed find many other things that seem to accord with the sacrament of this number. I do not perceive that all of them have reached my knowledge, and those which perhaps do occur are not fitting to set forth here or now.

When this seven is joined to six, it is proved to complete the number mentioned above, which divine wisdom assigned to those ancient judges appointed after Joshua’s death to govern the children of Israel. By this number God wished to teach both them and their successors how great a title of perfection ought to shine forth in one who is set above others in excellence of dignity [Col. 1202B–C] and commanded to offer those subject to him a pattern of character and an example of life. For the perfection of holiness generally imposed upon those of lower rank, though perhaps advancing them, is nevertheless insufficient for prelates. What may fittingly appear saving to the former in a certain single measure is judged necessary for the latter in double, or even greater, measure.

## CHAPTER 117

That the land is said to have rested under only four judges seems, upon closer consideration, to intimate that only that judge proves fit to confer the benefit of this rest who, relying on four-square justice, embraces steadfast morals. Since he ought to bring living stones to the building, he himself diligently sets the squareness of his own life before them in the structure [Col. 1202D].

For the world too is proclaimed to be composed of four elements; the lower world, the earth, is watered by the four rivers of Paradise; and in Job’s house his offspring feast, supported by its four corners. They cannot be crushed unless that same fourfold structure is first shaken. The ark of the covenant and the table of presentation are mentioned as having four distinct corners, carried by poles inserted into four rings. The faith of the Church is strengthened by four Gospels, and there are four virtues by which the perfection of life is completed.

When a clean conscience secretly rejoices in this perfection, it rests, like a land or city free from tumult, as was shown figuratively when Joash reigned: with the people rejoicing, the city is said to rest. “All the people of the land rejoiced,” he says, “and the city rested” (2 Chr. 23) [Col. 1203A]. When a righteous king reigns, the subject multitude rejoices; and when the people rejoice, the city is shown not to be disturbed but to rest. For as sorrow produces mourning, lamentation, roaring, and crying, so peace brings silence and rest, rendering the people more joyful.

The cry which invading sorrow compels to arise is softened by the sweeter arrival of joy; and the consoling grace that introduces silence calms and drives far away the plaintive voices formed and uttered by anger and grievous misery. Jeremiah speaks of this crying: “Wail, Heshbon; cry aloud, daughters of Rabbah; gird yourselves with sackcloth, lament, and go about among the hedges” (Jer. 49).

And a little below: “At the sound,” he says, “of their ruin the earth was shaken; the cry of its voice was heard” (ibid.) [Col. 1203B]. The prophet Amos says: “In all the streets there shall be lamentation, and in all places outside it shall be said, ‘Alas! alas!’ They shall call the farmer to mourning, and to lamentation those who know how to wail” (Amos 5). And Jeremiah again: “A voice was heard on high, of lamentation and weeping and mourning: Rachel weeping for her children” (Jer. 31).

These are the voices, this is the cry by which sorrowful misery roars and wails when powerful affliction presses upon it and rages more fiercely; when the mind grieves that it is oppressed by so great a burden that its excess cannot be restrained in silence. For when divine wrath burns against wretched people, when protection withdraws, when oppression grows more grievous, they judge that they have found some remedy if what they feel within may be poured out in groaning cries.

Thus the miserable cry when crushed by adverse events; cities howl when struck by the hard peril of war; streets, strewn with the corpses of the slain, resound with lamentation; farmers harmed by the loss of ruined crops cry, “Alas! alas!” [Col. 1203C]. Rachel, spreading out her bosom and raising her voice into the air, laments; in the death of her children she judges no present consolation other than this to be necessary, hoping to receive something greater and better at the fitting time, if only she bears this loss patiently in the present.

Yet for those known to be thus pressed by inward sorrow, and by the cries of whose ruin the earth is shaken, as was said, relief is effectively supplied by counsel when the supreme Consoler ordains mercy for those who ask. He sometimes permits his faithful, whom from the beginning he has willed to ordain unto salvation, to labour harshly amid adverse events, so that they may strike heaven with their cry, move earth with their tearful lamentation, implore help, and obtain silence by a fruitful cry.

God’s grace does not immediately grant silence of this kind, but neither does he turn his face away from those in sorrow. He delays, he appears to disregard them, and for a while closes his ear to their voices; yet he has mercy on them unto salvation and hears the miserable. He delays either in order that, by punishing longer, he may cleanse sinners more perfectly, or so that the delay may make them keener in asking and persisting, and so that, when it is finally granted, the gift may be held more gratefully and what has long been awaited and scarcely at last obtained may be held more sweetly.

But to those to whom he gives the benefit of this silence, he grants it in this life only imperfectly [Col. 1203D–1204A]; no one is allowed to attain it utterly while compelled to remain in this body of death. For, to say nothing of other matters, the very fact that one lives in the body—where, in familiar discord, flesh opposes spirit and spirit flesh; from which one desires to be released and to be with Christ, “which is best,” and because one does not yet prevail, the same spirit groans under its burden—this itself disturbs rest. It does not allow one to be altogether free from sorrows and does not perfectly admit the desired silence into the recesses of the heart.

John aptly shows this in the Apocalypse: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8). Heaven may not inappropriately be called the present Church or any righteous soul, which dwells in heavenly things by desire and resolve, and in which God’s grace works a certain joyful silence, since it both hates evil, loves justice, and embraces heavenly glory with firm hope [Col. 1204B].

But because it still walks by faith and not by sight, and what is partial is imperfect, it is said to be silent not wholly but beneficially, as it were for half an hour, being prevented from having complete joy in the place of sorrow. When that which is partial has been abolished and that which is perfect has come, then sorrow will more fully wither away—indeed, it will have no place whatsoever in heaven or among heavenly beings. Since there will be nothing from which anyone can or ought to grieve, each will rejoice and be silent, gladly rejoicing in silence.

If divine grace does not seem to grant this to anyone at present, it nevertheless promises it to its faithful by benevolent condescension [Col. 1204C]. Whoever is sustained by the true hope of such great blessedness, even if not yet completed, is already not without a beginning of that silence.

For the sorrow of every righteous person is greatly alleviated when he reads and loves what truthful Scripture declares, what prophecy and the Gospels promise in concordant spirit: namely, that the tears and groans of the elect will be changed into joy and silence. Isaiah says: “The Lord will take away the tear from every face” (Isa. 25).

And John says in the Apocalypse: “The Lord will wipe every tear from the eyes of the saints” (Rev. 7 and 21). Because the saints unwillingly suffer the troubles of the present life and are delayed from the kingdom of glory which they desire, they grieve [Col. 1204D], their faces are bathed with tears, and they are compelled by mournful crying to disturb silence.

But when, according to Isaiah, they are gathered away from the face of evil, the tears are wiped from their eyes by the gracious hand that gathers them, and the peace that comes upon them makes them rejoice more fully, as the Spirit says that henceforth they rest from their labours. For when Isaiah had said, “The righteous person has been gathered away from the face of evil,” he added: “Let peace come; let him rest in his chamber” (Isa. 57). And John says: “Henceforth,” says the Spirit, “let them rest from their labours” (Rev. 14).

When the righteous person is gathered, incoming peace is said to rest in his chamber, because it produces the grace of rest in the heart of the righteous person, causing bow, sword, and everything that makes harsh noise to recoil far away [Col. 1205A]; and, with the din driven off, it enables the gathered person to sleep securely. The Lord intimates this through Hosea: “I will break bow and sword and war from the earth, and I will make them sleep securely” (Hos. 2).

Blessed is the land which the righteous person will at last be allowed to possess through more abundant grace. Every adverse and sorrowful assault will be broken, and its inhabitant will enjoy glory so great beyond the former manner that it will be called, in a new sense, the land of the living [Col. 1206A]. The Gospel also speaks of it: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. 5). The soul was called the land of death or of the dying because death rightly rules in it or from it as by hereditary title; but when it receives the glory of resurrection and incorruption, the human being, granted immortality, will securely possess it incorruptible and promised to him by the Father of lights.

> [Note: This manuscript codex was damaged here; consequently some material is still lacking, which we would gladly have added had we been able to recover it from elsewhere.]

[Col. 1205]

# LIFE OF THE BLESSED AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1205B]

Inspired and aided by the grace of the Holy Spirit, who, breathing where he wills and as much as he wills, can do impossible things, I have ventured to write about the life and deeds of the blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo. Yet I ask you who will read this to attribute it not to my presumption but to brotherly love. For the brothers among whom I lived, inflamed with devotion, wished to preserve the memory of his deeds and character. They found somewhat burdensome to read, because of its length, the book written concerning his life; yet that book seems to omit some things worthy of narration. They asked me to attempt a briefer account of that blessed confessor, so that truth might be more fully known to diligent readers and length might not cause weariness to those reading [Col. 1205C].

Considering myself unequal to the task, I confess that I proposed to hide in the harbour of silence, lest, if I undertook it and could not prevail, that saying of the Gospel should strike me with a blow: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke 14). But recalling that brotherly love could obtain grace and divine generosity could supply it, I finally consented to obey their request, lest by keeping altogether silent I should be thought a philosopher.

Therefore I want you who will read—if indeed any will read—to know that in this little work you will find nothing falsely invented and nothing coloured by flattery. That holy man, a perfect friend of truth, does not desire to be honoured by the praises of falsehood. Accordingly, I have inserted in this work those things which he himself humbly said about himself, or which another truthfully wrote concerning him, insofar as, with his help and grace obtained, I have been able to gather them in reading [Col. 1205D]. What is said here about him has been written elsewhere, if not in the same words, nevertheless in the same sense, and perhaps better there. But it is briefer here, so that one who has no leisure to gather these matters by reading there may, if he wishes, read them here already gathered.

Let the Prologue end here; thereafter let the Catalogue of Deeds follow.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1206B]

Augustine was born in the town of Thagaste, of honourable descent, among the municipal curial class. His father was named Patricius and his mother Monica. The former was a pagan; the latter a Catholic. Led by divine counsel without knowing it, they gave him instruction in literary studies. Divine mercy, foreknowing the future, granted him such ability in understanding and exposition that, by the quickness of his learning, he surpassed not merely the efforts of those of his own age but even of older persons.

Thus, in a short time he learned grammar in his native town and in the neighbouring city of Madaura, to which his parents sent him. On returning, when he was in his sixteenth year, he planned to go farther away to teach rhetoric [Col. 1206C]. His parents rejoiced greatly at such progress and diligently supplied what he needed. Many neighbours marvelled at the care they lavished upon their son, not considering what they were spending while he was advancing according to their desire.

Yet at that time, certain circumstances intervening, he remained for a while with his parents and had a break from school. In the years of fervent youth, he wandered down the slopes of sensual dissipation. His father, recently a catechumen, took little care; his mother, so far as she could, called him back. By entreating and reproving her son, she gave him this counsel: that he should not, through the impulse of slippery youth, rush into the precipice of fornication or adultery. But he—as commonly happens at that age—regarded such warnings as old women’s talk and counted them as nothing, preferring to listen to companions of his own age and disposition rather than obey his mother. Hence divine Scripture says: “The thought of the human heart is inclined to evil from its youth” (Gen. 8). And the secular poet says:

> “The beardless youth, once his guardian is removed,  
> is wax to be bent toward vice.”

## CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 1207A]

At last Augustine bade farewell to his parents and, by God’s ordering though without knowing it himself, went to Carthage to pursue learning. There he was taught everywhere in the school of a certain rhetor with incredible speed. Applying himself to Tully’s flowers and Quintilian’s colours of style, he soon appeared superior to all his fellow pupils, so that all marvelled and praised him.

There, when in his twentieth year he was studying books of eloquence among fellow pupils of similar age, eager to flourish in that art and delighted by popular applause like a creature living on wind and air, he came in the course of study to a book of Cicero called *Hortensius*. This book exhorts one to philosophy—*philosophia* being interpreted “love of wisdom”—a name said to have arisen from Pythagoras of Samos. Previously those were called wise who seemed to surpass others in life and knowledge. But when Pythagoras was asked what profession he followed, he replied that he was a philosopher, that is, a lover of wisdom, lest, if he called himself wise, he might appear arrogant [Col. 1207B]. Since all approved this answer, the custom grew among pagans of calling a wise person among them a philosopher.

Since that book exhorts to philosophy without commending any particular sect, it powerfully inflamed Augustine to love, seek, and hold fast to wisdom. It displeased him only somewhat because it did not contain Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God. From his tender years he had heard this name preached and commended by his mother. Therefore he did not wholly approve anything lacking it, however elegantly and truthfully expressed.

He therefore resolved to devote himself to reading the divine Scriptures, to see what they contained. But he found their face veiled and marked by the cloud of mysteries; he who was accustomed to run through pagan letters could not even enter their doorway. “O Lion of the tribe of Judah, it is yours alone to open the book and loosen its seals.” Thus taking leave of the divine Scriptures, he fell into the sect of the Manichaeans, cloaked in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For although everything among them was full of manifold falsehood, they discoursed at length, at least in sound, about simple truth [Col. 1207C–D].

Augustine therefore hung upon their words all the more ardently because he sighed day by day more intensely for God, of whom they spoke. He was perniciously held in this error for nine years; but through his mother’s unceasing prayer and God’s merciful deliverance, he was eventually rescued.

## CHAPTER THREE

The great consolation divinely given to his mother, who was almost overcome by grief for his ruin, must not be passed over in silence. She mourned inconsolably for her son’s spiritual death, continually weeping for one who recklessly laughed. She had even begun to refuse him fellowship at her table—not because she hated her son, but because she detested the vice as a disease rather than the sick person [Col. 1208A]. Yet God had mercy on her tears, and she saw a dream in which she began to receive moderate consolation.

She seemed to be standing on a certain wooden rule or measuring-staff. Then a young man came, splendidly dressed and cheerful in countenance, and smiled upon her as she wept. “What,” he asked, “is the cause of your continual mourning and sorrow?” She answered: “The ruin of my son.” The young man said to her: “Be secure, and see: where you are, there he is also.” Immediately the woman turned her eyes away from him and saw Augustine standing beside her on the same rule.

When she awoke, she recalled this clearly. As a prudent woman of great faith, she interpreted it truly, plainly recognizing and affirming to herself that someday she would see Augustine on the same rule of truth and Catholic faith on which she saw herself. She regarded it not as a dream but as a divine reply: “Woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.”

Accordingly, when she recounted the vision in order to her son, and he tried perversely to interpret it by saying, “Where I am, mother, there you also will be,” she, a little woman not open to deception but a woman of manly spirit, at once said: “No. For it was not said to me, ‘Where he is, there you also are,’ but, ‘Where you are, there he also is.’” Thus defeated by reason, he yielded; yet he nevertheless remained in that sect for another nine years [Col. 1208B].

## CHAPTER FOUR

She also received another divine answer for her consolation through a certain bishop, a Catholic man learned in the sacred writings. When she came before him in supplication, weeping and devoutly asking him to meet Augustine and to summon him back from his error to the Catholic faith, he answered: “Your son is certainly still unteachable, puffed up proudly by the novelty of that heresy, more ready to weave little questions than to submit to one teaching him. Therefore endure for a while and pray without ceasing. By reading, he will discover how detestable is the sect he loves. For I myself, when I was a young man, was foolish in the same error, and by reading and understanding I learned how much it should be fled, and I fled.”

This answer did not suffice for her. With a woman’s importunity and an excessive outpouring of tears, she persisted, asking him to deign to speak with her son and exhort him to better things. He, as if overcome by weariness, said: “Go, woman; live as you do. The son of such tears cannot perish” [Col. 1208C–D]. The answer pleased the woman as much as if a prophecy from heaven had sounded to her.

## CHAPTER FIVE

Then, when Augustine was in his twentieth year, the teacher at Carthage was reading Aristotle’s ten *Categories* to his pupils. While they were astonished—for they scarcely understood them—he rebuked them sharply. Augustine, supposing it to be some great matter, obtained the little book and, reading it alone at home, understood by himself whatever lay hidden in it. What the best students judged difficult to understand even under expert teachers who not only spoke but also drew diagrams in the dust, Augustine, comparing notes with them and reporting nothing except what he had understood by himself, affirmed to be very easy [Col. 1209A].

Whatever he heard them disputing argumentatively concerning the properties of substances and their accidents, he grasped by hearing alone and regarded as a light matter under discussion. He read all the books of the arts called liberal that he could find; whatever he could read, he understood by himself. In short, lest I lead you on too long: without any human teacher, with God alone supplying him, he came without great effort to a clear knowledge of all the intricacies of dialectic, the dimensions of geometry, the harmonies of music, and the difficulties of arithmetic. He did not realize that all these things were grasped with difficulty by other studious and gifted people until he wished to explain them to them and saw that they could scarcely understand.

A marvellous thing!
