Such was his quickness of understanding, capacity for retention, fluency in exposition, and keenness in disputation that it would seem wholly unbelievable, unless he himself humbly confessed it [Col. 1209B]. Let us judge nothing unworthy of God if he pours so great an abundance of his generosity even upon the unjust. Of him it is written that “he makes his sun rise upon the good and evil, and rains upon the just and unjust” (Matt. 5).

Thus divine generosity flooded this soldier of his—though not yet his—with an abundance of secular learning; afterward it flooded him with the willing rain of saving wisdom. But he, not yet having received the Spirit of God, gave God no thanks for any of these things, but gloried in them as though they were his own, not yet having read: “Let him who glories, glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1). For although he had known God, he did not glorify him as God, but became futile in his thoughts, thinking himself wise when he was foolish (Rom. 1) [Col. 1209C]. Thus, by not glorifying through confession the humble Son of God, he repelled the Spirit of God from himself, as it is written: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7).

## CHAPTER SIX

Then, in his twenty-eighth year, Augustine left Carthage, where he had been head of a school and taught rhetoric; earlier, in his own town of Thagaste, he had taught grammar. Persuaded by certain friends, he came to Rome. Many pupils flocked to his lecture room, and through them he quickly became known to the whole city.

Since he was held in high esteem by everyone in Rome for the rhetoric he taught [Col. 1209D], a message was sent from Milan to Symmachus, the prefect at Rome, requesting that he provide and send to Milan a teacher of rhetoric. By divine ordering Augustine was chosen before all others and was sent by the prefect to Milan to teach rhetoric.

At that time blessed Ambrose was guiding the chariot of the Church of Milan. Divine merciful counsel led Augustine to him, saying to him, though he was still deaf: “He will tell you what you must do” (Acts 11). The man of God kindly received the newcomer; and Augustine at first loved not his holiness but his kindness toward himself. Augustine was often present when Ambrose spoke God’s word to the people, not in order to hear the truth, but to discover whether the eloquence for which he was famous matched its reputation [Col. 1210A]. He had heard Ambrose’s eloquence praised and eagerly listened, delighted more by the sweetness of the discourse than by the truth of the matter.

Then, as he attended the preaching frequently, he gradually began to direct his mind more to the things said than to the words: to attend not to how it was said but to what was said. At last, as truth began a little to dawn, he resolved that the Manichaean sect which he had long held must be abandoned, and determined to remain a catechumen in the Catholic Church until the truth that he should hold shone more fully.

## CHAPTER SEVEN
Meanwhile, with Alypius and Nebridius, who were bound to him by the right of friendship, he was an anxious seeker after truth and wisdom, sighing together with them and tossed by the same waves, when he saw what was to be abandoned but did not yet clearly perceive what was to be retained. [Col. 1210B] He now marvelled within himself at the long fluctuations of his mind, recalling his nineteenth year, when, after reading the *Hortensius*, he had resolved to abandon the vanities and deceitful madnesses of his desires and thenceforth to devote himself to wisdom alone, which the *Hortensius* seemed to commend. And behold, he was now thirty years old and yet not truly wise, although during that time he had frequently seemed to ascend to that height, and yet, compelled by the weight of habit, had fallen back into the depths.

Nevertheless, the words of the divine Scriptures, to which he had hitherto passed by with a deaf ear, no longer seemed absurd to him; nor did he oppose those who maintained that one thing is read in the Law and the Prophets and another understood, especially [Col. 1210C] as he frequently heard Ambrose preaching to the people: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3). Yet when he strove to raise the sharpness of his mind so that he too might understand spiritually what he had read or heard literally, he could not accomplish what he wished; and although zeal was present, grace was not at hand. Struck back by his own weakness, he was unable to fix his eye upon the ray of the eternal Sun; and when he strained to do so, he recoiled in terror.

Thus, sighing after God, he found himself to be far from Him—not by an interval of lands, but by unlikeness—as though he heard His voice saying: “I am food for the mature; but you are little: grow, and you shall eat me.” And lest one who did not yet know how to savour the spirit should take this carnally: “Nor,” He says, “will you change me into yourself, as you do the food of your flesh; rather, you shall be changed into me: for I am He who am” (Exod. 3). Having received this, not through an outward hearing but through inward inspiration, he felt and experienced that it is no wonder that bread, sweet to a healthy palate, is punishment to an unhealthy one, and that light, lovable to sound eyes, is hateful to bleary eyes. When he was raised above himself, he knew this food to be for the mature; when he fell back upon himself, he carried away almost nothing except a loving memory, desiring, as it were, what it had smelled but was not yet able to eat.

## CHAPTER VIII

Then indeed he beheld more fully the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made; and although he could not fix [Col. 1211A] his gaze upon them, yet from creation he understood the Creator. He anxiously sought how he might be made fit to enjoy God, but did not find it until he embraced by faith the Mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ. Hearing Him proclaimed as a just and holy man of outstanding wisdom, and—what was more wonderful—as born of a virgin, he thought Him such a one as no human being could equal; but what mystery there was in the words, “The Word was made flesh” (John 1), he could not even suspect. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (ibid.), he perceived in some fashion; but “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.) he did not understand.

For he had understood that the former was proclaimed in certain Platonic books, not in the same words but [Col. 1211B] in the same sense; but he had not found the latter there. Therefore he could attain no perfection until he came to Christ, as it is written: “There is none that does good, no, not even one” (Ps. 13). Nor is this surprising. For one cannot attain Israelite security who has not first held Jewish truth, as the prophet plainly intimates to those who understand devoutly: “In those days,” he says, “Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely” (Jer. 3). For the person whom the merit of true confession saves is precisely the one received by the secure dwelling of divine visitation.

Accordingly, he began most eagerly to read the books of divine Scripture, and especially Paul; and at last he understood that the tenor of Paul’s discourse was not opposed to him but agreed [Col. 1211C] with the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets. Now that the covering of the mysteries had been removed, the one countenance of the pure sayings appeared to him; and, rejoicing with trembling, he learned what God has hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to little ones (Matt. 10). Thus, the knot of blindness being torn apart, he burned with desire for holiness; and although he now saw where he ought to go, he still hesitated about the way by which he should go. For he saw the Church full of believers, one proceeding in this way and another in that; and though all the good were going well, one nevertheless went before another.

## CHAPTER IX

When he was now in some measure free from the bond of error, whatever he did in the world displeased him; and, delighted by spiritual sweetness, he was greatly burdened by worldly life. Therefore he thought it good to consult Simplicianus, a just and holy man, 695 [Col. 1211D] whom he had heard had lived most devoutly for God from his youth. Now old and full of days, Simplicianus himself had spent his life in the pursuit of holiness, having learned much, experienced much, as it seemed—and truly it was so.

Revealing to him the heat of his heart and the wanderings of his error, Augustine devoutly asked that the holy man should set before him what manner of life was suitable for one thus disposed, as he was, to walk in the way of God. For many travelled upon that way and, as we have said, various people went in various ways. Simplicianus, greatly commending the humility of Christ, especially invited Augustine to it; and in inviting him, recalled the conversion of Victorinus, [Col. 1212A] formerly a Roman rhetorician.

For many years at Rome that Victorinus had been a teacher; and because of the distinction of his eminent instruction, he had deserved to have a statue in the Roman forum. But when God, who made light shine out of darkness, shone in his heart (2 Cor. 4), reckoning as losses what had formerly seemed gains, he devoutly turned to God; abandoning his talkative school, he became a humble disciple in the school of Christ. He rejected all the pride of his former rank and, retaining nothing of himself for himself, gave his whole self to God. The blessed Jerome had this same man as his teacher of rhetoric, having previously had Donatus as his teacher of grammar.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 1212B] Stirred by this example, Augustine grew inflamed with the desire to imitate it; and, setting aside all that belongs to the world, he resolved to devote himself to God alone. But though willing lay close at hand, he did not find the power to act. For as he burned and sighed for what was unfamiliar, what had become ingrained reproached him; and when he wished to rest in the former, he felt the latter raising an outcry against him.

He experienced in himself that saying of the Apostle: “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. 5), because the new man, driving out the old, was now as it were at the door, while the old resisted the new as far as it could. He heard it said to him: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and you shall be enlightened” (Eph. 5); yet still drowsy, he delayed to rise. Though he knew that wakefulness was better than sleep, he was nevertheless more willingly overtaken by heavy slumber.

He wondered at the discord in the one self—yet no longer one—of two affections, [Col. 1212C] one of which brought on sleep while the other urged him to wakefulness. The one, now thirsting for the things of God, tugged at the sides of the sleeper; the other, savouring the things of the world, pressed down the temples of the one rising. The former, by instilling fear of judgment, broke the barrier of torpor; the latter, by coaxing and deceiving, delayed him a little longer. Augustine himself was indeed astonished at such a spectacle, when he saw that he both wished, and did not wish, to despise the world.

## CHAPTER XI

While he was thus torn inwardly by such a conflict and troubled both in expression and in mind, he entered a garden belonging to the lodging where he stayed; Alypius, his intimate friend, followed slowly after him. Having found [Col. 1212D] a place suited to grief—for solitude is a friend to sorrow—he began more violently to be angry with himself and, in his anger, to abhor his own hesitation. The customary vanities of his thoughts pressed upon him, no longer confronting him face to face or turning him aside from the path so that he could not proceed rightly, but whispering behind his back and, as it were, tugging at him so that he might at least look back.

At last, when the depths of his heart had been overturned and the whole mass of his miseries had been heaped before the eyes of his mind, a tumultuous storm of tears arose. To pour it out more freely, he left Alypius at the place where they had sat and withdrew a little farther away. Now unable to contain his grief, he threw himself beneath a certain fig tree, perhaps that the Lord might say to him: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1). [Col. 1213A] Rolling himself upon a grassy bed, he removed the restraint upon his tears and gave them full rein; and as the stream of his eyes flowed down, he abundantly watered his couch over its yielding slopes.

Nor were groans and cries full of pain lacking, as he tearfully addressed God, who looked upon his tears with delight—not out of cruelty, but compassion. “And you, Lord,” he said, “how long?” (Ps. 6). How long, forgetting your mercies, will you remember my iniquities? How long will my conversion be postponed until tomorrow and tomorrow? Why does my shame not end today—why not at this very hour? As he spoke these and similar words through tears, and was pierced by bitter contrition of heart, behold, from a neighbouring house he heard what seemed the chanting voice of a boy or girl, repeatedly [Col. 1213B] singing: “Take up and read; take up and read.”

Hearing this, he was astonished and silently began to consider whether children in some game were accustomed to sing anything of that kind. Nothing came to mind. Therefore he understood that he was divinely admonished to take up a book, read it, and do whatever it instructed him. For he had heard that Anthony, the Egyptian monk, had done something similar. When Anthony was preparing to convert, he happened to arrive as the Gospel was being read and saying: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19). And, as though what he heard had been said to him, he obeyed the command.

Recalling this, Augustine restrained his tears, returned to the place where Alypius sat, and seized the apostolic book that he had left [Col. 1213C] beside him when he rose from there. Opening it, he quickly cast his eyes upon it and silently 696 read the first passage that met him: “Not in feasting and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, not in strife and pride; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13). Having read this, he ceased reading, judging this sufficient for himself. As soon as this admonition had entered his heart, every covering of languid doubt was driven away and a certain light of assurance was poured in.

Closing the book and marking the place, he joyfully told Alypius what he had read. Alypius asked to see it and, receiving the book, looked. Seeing what followed beyond what Augustine had read—Augustine himself not knowing [Col. 1213D] what came next—he found and read: “Receive the one weak in faith” (Rom. 14). Applying this to himself, he joyfully proclaimed it to Augustine. At once strengthened by this admonition, he too joined Augustine, putting aside every hesitation, in the same purpose of living well.

## CHAPTER XII

Then Augustine went in to his mother and disclosed to her in order the visitation from on high which was dawning, so that she who had grieved for him might now receive consolation. For she had left her homeland, crossed the sea, and travelled over a great expanse of lands to come to him, after the death of her husband, whom at the end of his temporal life she had won for God.

Hearing that Augustine had been strengthened for the service of God, for whom she had wept for so long, [Col. 1214A] she rejoiced and gave thanks to God, who had granted her more than she had asked. For she saw him kindled not only with the love of faith but also wholly with contempt for the world. Thus her mourning was turned into joy, her lamentation into dancing, as her son stood firm in that rule of faith which had been revealed to her so many years before.

The anxieties of cares and the sweetnesses of trifles, by which Augustine had until then been hindered from the path of salvation, were cast out; and what he had formerly dreaded to lose, he now rejoiced to abandon. Therefore, telling his pupils to provide themselves with another seller of words, he cast aside the profession of rhetoric, burning with desire to be free for prayer and to embrace the Catholic religion. And in order that his location might suit his purpose, he left the tumult of the city and went into the country. There, with friends burning with the same desire, he devoted himself to divine reading. As he read, he was affected by its sweetness; and while reading, drawing deep sighs, he drenched his face with a rush of tears. He cursed his obstinacy against God and marvelled at God’s patience toward him, as he read the Psalms of David and understood them under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XIII

Taking up, indeed, the fourth psalm and attentively reading each of its verses, and reading them again still more attentively, he roared from the groaning of his heart; and, since weeping did not suffice, uttered cries suitable to his grief. For he heard in it the errors of men rebuked—men who pursue vanities and deceitful madnesses—by that striking verse: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4). [Col. 1214C] He knew without doubt that he himself had been such as those whom the verse rebuked.

He read: “Know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful; the Lord will hear me when I cry to him” (ibid.), knowing certainly that whoever has not known the Lord’s holy one to have been made wonderful—Christ suffering, dying, and raised again—will not be heard when he cries. He heard the Prophet, enlightened by the seal of God’s countenance, made rich by the increase of grain, wine, and saving oil, glorying in the hope of eternal refreshment and crying out with humble confidence: “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the selfsame thing” (ibid.).

[Col. 1214D] He read and reread, and for joy exclaimed: “O ‘in peace’! O ‘in the selfsame thing’! O city whose participation is in the selfsame thing! O blessed person who, having banished the flux of mutability, sleeps and rests in the selfsame thing!”

Amid these and many other benefits of divine consolation, bitter draughts of temptation were not lacking to Augustine—perhaps that he might be chastened and taught, according to what is written: “Whom the Lord loves, he chastens” (Heb. 12), and elsewhere: “He who has not been tempted, what does he know?” (Ecclus. 34). For while he was staying in a country house with friends and was continually occupied either in reading, writing, or disputation, it happened that he was afflicted by a serious disease of the teeth, so that through excessive pain his faculty of speech was blocked.

Faithfully recalling [Col. 1215A] the verse, “The Lord will hear me when I cry to him” (Ps. 1, as printed), he thought to admonish those who were present with him to pray for him. Since he could not speak, he wrote on wax and gave it to them to read. When he knelt with them in supplication to pray, the pain fled so swiftly that he himself marvelled and trembled while praising God, to whom, as it is written, “the power to act is at hand when He wills” (Wis. 12).

## CHAPTER XIV

Then, through a letter, he made known to St Ambrose his former errors and his present purpose, asking that the holy man advise which of the sacred books he ought especially to read in order to become more fit to receive Christian grace. Ambrose directed him to read the prophet Isaiah, perhaps because Isaiah more openly than the others foretold the calling [Col. 1215B] 697 of the Gentiles. For it is written: “The wise man shall seek out the wisdom of the ancients, and shall devote himself to the prophets” (Ecclus. 39).

But because he did not understand this reading at first and supposed the whole book to be of the same kind, he put it aside for a time, intending to return to it when he had become more practised in the Lord’s discourse. Yet he was not secure from his former evils, because he had not yet been regenerated by the saving bath. He had not yet entirely put off the garment of oldness, because he had not yet put on Christ through baptism. “All of you,” says the Apostle, “who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3).

Leaving the country, therefore, and returning to Milan, he was baptized by the blessed Ambrose. With him, too, the boy Adeodatus, born carnally of Augustine but [Col. 1215C] reborn spiritually, was baptized. This boy was fifteen years old when he became the blessed Augustine’s contemporary in the grace of baptism; his own intellect was so swift that, by agility of understanding, he surpassed many men of advanced age and great learning. Augustine indeed marvelled and was awestruck at such an intellect when he heard him, at sixteen years old, questioning subtly and arguing by his questions, so that he attended more to the boy’s questioning than to his own reply.

For the boy was a most ardent lover of truth and a diligent investigator of hidden things, according to what is written: “Blessed is the man who devises the ways of the Lord and understands in His hidden things” (Ecclus. 14). There is a book entitled *On the Teacher*; another, *On the Greatness of the Soul* [Col. 1215D]; and certain others written from their conversations with one another. Whoever reads them will discover how much was there investigated subtly and discussed carefully.

But that youth, burning with both desire and zeal to live well, was soon taken from their midst; and, reaching the end that cannot be passed over, he was gathered to his fathers (Job 14). By the benefit of divine grace and by the merit of his own holiness and innocence, I believe that he attained what he so greatly desired: living eternally, reigning in Christ, and with Christ for ever.

## CHAPTER XV

The blessed Augustine, having received the gift of saving baptism, when anxiety over his former life had fled from him, could not be satisfied with contemplating the wonderful sweetness of the height of the divine counsel concerning the salvation of the human race. [Col. 1216A] Frequenting the thresholds of the church and attentively listening to the modulation of hymns and the melody of psalms, he was delightfully moved, joyfully refreshing not his belly but his mind with such food, according to what is written: “My tears were my bread day and night” (Ps. 41); and again: “You will feed us with the bread of tears” (Ps. 49).

For the Church of Milan had only recently begun to devise this kind of consolation, under the compulsion of a certain distress of the times—or rather, through the gentle ordering of divine wisdom. In the year just past, the Empress Justina, mother of King Valentinian, seduced by the error of the Arians, violently persecuted the blessed Ambrose. [Col. 1216B] The faithful dwelling at Milan, ready to die with their bishop, kept vigil in the church. For that royal beast was fiercely hostile to the Christian faith. Hence Ecclesiasticus says: “There is no head more wicked than the head of a serpent, and there is no wrath beyond the wrath of a woman” (Ecclus. 25). And a certain satirist says:

> “Nothing is more intolerable than a rich woman.”

And Plautus, in the *Asinaria*, speaking of two evil women, says: “The sea is not the sea, but you are a most fierce sea.”

Then that same bishop, pitying the affliction of others more than his own, instituted the singing of hymns and psalms in church according to the custom of the eastern regions, so that the faithful, attentive to spiritual songs, [Col. 1216C] might forget their present sorrow and weariness.

## CHAPTER XVI

At that time the bodies of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, which had long lain hidden in the secret places of the earth, were revealed in a vision to that bishop. When they had been dug up, they were transferred with great honour to the Ambrosian basilica. As many miracles occurred at their translation, one in particular: a man well known to the city, a citizen who had been blind for many years, touched the bier with faith preceding and received sight.

When the report spread and the city resounded with divine praises, the mind of that queen was softened—not so that she became a Christian, but so that she ceased to persecute Christians. [Col. 1216D] When the persecution had ceased, the custom of psalm-singing nevertheless remained in the Church and has spread throughout the whole world down to the present day.

Greatly moved by these chants of hymns and psalms, the blessed Augustine burned with eager longing to take part in those angelic choirs that sing hymns; and since he could not yet obtain his wish, he wept for the consolation of his present misery. Then, taking with him Evodius, who came from the same town as himself, together with his other friends, he set out to return to Africa. While they were at the mouth of the Tiber, his holy widowed mother rendered her devout soul to God.

For she had no reason now to love this temporal life or to wish that death should be delayed, when she saw the blessed Augustine, despising earthly prosperity, eagerly serving God and devoutly obeying the perfect commandments of the Gospel. Seized by a fever and near the danger of death, as 698 Augustine and his companions stood around [Col. 1217A] while she lay upon her bed, she earnestly begged only this of them: that they should make remembrance of her at Christ’s altar. Thus, falling asleep in peace, she entered into the joy of her Lord.

## CHAPTER XVII

After her funeral rites had been celebrated according to custom, Augustine returned to Africa; and, arriving at Carthage, he was received as a guest by a certain religious man named Innocentius. This man was suffering from a severe illness in his posterior parts. Physicians had cut open and healed the fistulas—which were innumerable and intricate—that he had; but through carelessness they had left a certain cavity to be cut. [Col. 1217B] They promised to treat what remained with a milder medicine, without the harm of any cutting.

But when medicines achieved nothing and merely consumed time and expense in vain, he consulted other, more capable physicians and learned that he could not be completely healed unless he permitted what remained to be cut to be cut. He was terrified, grew pale, and nearly lost consciousness from fear, because in the first operation he had almost died from prolonged and bitter pain. Yet because one is said to wish to perish who refuses to obey, he at last unwillingly submitted to the physicians’ advice and allowed that operation to be performed on the following day.

The appointed day arrived. His friends assembled; on the preceding day, despairing of his recovery, he had asked them to be present in the morning rather at his funeral than at his suffering. His household, unable to bear the pain, [Col. 1217C] bewailed him aloud as though dead, believing he would die in the physicians’ hands. The physicians entered and instruments were brought forth. All stood astonished and tense; but those of greater authority sought to console the sick man and to raise him, perishing under inconsolable fear, to hope.

Augustine pitied his host’s wretched lot; seeing both him and many of his people despairing of the physicians’ help, he fled to the remedy of prayer, kneeling and praying to Him “who alone does great wonders” (Ps. 135), that He might mercifully assist a man so generous, hospitable, and religious in such danger, and—if it is lawful to say so; indeed, since He is God—that God might obey human prayers. For Scripture tells that God obeyed Joshua while he was fighting and praying: at Joshua’s [Col. 1217D] command, the sun stood motionless over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Aijalon, forgetting their course, until he overcame the tyranny of the five kings.

Armed with the same faith, Augustine, a devout novice (*tyro*), prayed and obtained the result from that same God, under whose standards he himself served as a distinguished soldier. Meanwhile Innocentius lay face down upon his bed; the bandages were loosened and the place exposed. The physician, armed with iron, approached; he sought with his eyes and fingers for the cavity to be cut, and—wonderful to relate—found it healed, not by human but by divine medicine.

There was joy, there was a cry of joy, there was such exultation among the people as, though it may somehow be imagined, cannot be expressed in words. Their mourning being turned into music, God was praised, glorified, [Col. 1218A] and blessed by every mouth: “He heals the broken in heart and binds up their wounds” (Ps. 146).

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 1218A] After these events, Augustine left Carthage and went to his own estates. There, devoting himself with his companions to fasts and prayers, he lived for three years in the lay order. During that same time, intent upon reading and writing, he wrote books and taught the unlearned; he read and was not negligent, for this is the piety which is useful above all things for all things. For, according to the Apostle, labour “even if useful, is useful for a little; but piety is useful for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4).

This piety, as the holy teachers explain, is understood in no more fitting way than as exercise in the divine Scriptures, when they are devoutly read, fulfilled, and taught, according to the Prophet who says: “How sweet are your sayings to my throat! I lifted up my hands to your commandments” (Ps. 118)—“I will recount all your wonders” (Ps. 9). [Col. 1218B] Devoting himself diligently to these studies, he fulfilled the office of Martha and Mary: with Martha, teaching his neighbours and feeding the Lord; with Mary, reading, meditating, and hearing the Lord.

At that time, since the light of so great a holiness could no longer remain hidden and ought to be visible to all who were in the house, a certain citizen of Hippo heard of his reputation. He pondered and reconsidered within himself that, if he might deserve to see Augustine and speak [Col. 1218C] with him, he would, following his advice, leave the world and turn to the Lord. When this became known to the blessed Augustine through a messenger, the holy man, wishing to win a soul for God, went to Hippo. He exhorted the aforesaid man as far as he could to despise the world and love God. The man rejoiced at Augustine’s presence and received his exhortation very gratefully; nevertheless, through God’s hidden counsel, he delayed for the present to fulfil what he had promised.

But divine wisdom, which “orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 13), made the arrival of the holy man—who now seemed useless to himself—benefit many. While he taught that he was making no progress with the one person whom he wished to help, he was compelled to benefit many; and this caused him still greater distress.

For it happened that the blessed Valerius, who at that time governed the episcopate of Hippo, [Col. 1218D] 699 while speaking the word of God to the people, sought, in the course of his address, the counsel and assent of that same people concerning the election of a presbyter in the Church. The blessed Augustine was present in the crowd, hearing the word of God with the crowd. Since Valerius knew Augustine’s reputation and had heard that he was learned, eloquent, and religious, he chose him for ordination at the prompting of the divine Spirit; clergy and people alike unanimously agreed and requested that it be done without delay.

When he learned this, the holy man groaned deeply, having read and understood how many dangers threaten those who are appointed judges of the people. Therefore he wept greatly and wavered in uncertainty: the prophetic saying terrified him, “Woe to those who feed themselves and not [Col. 1219A] my sheep” (Ezek. 34); but the Gospel saying compelled him, “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21). At last Valerius separated him from the crowd while he wept and resisted in vain and ordained him presbyter, although unwilling.

Knowing his desire and purpose—namely, that he wished, owning nothing, to live with clerics who possessed nothing—Valerius gave him a garden. There Augustine promptly built a monastery and began to gather brothers of the same purpose, living with them according to the manner and rule of the holy apostles: namely, that all things should be held in common by them, that no one should call anything his own, and that each should receive what was necessary (Acts 4). Augustine himself had already done this when he had returned to his own country from overseas.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Col. 1219B]

The holy Valerius, who had ordained him, rejoiced and gave God more abundant thanks because He had granted him, in accordance with his desire, such a man as could build up the Church by sound word and doctrine. Valerius foresaw that he himself was not sufficiently fit for this task, being Greek by birth and less well instructed in the Latin language and literature. Therefore he granted Augustine authority to speak the word of God to the people even in his own presence, although this had hitherto been considered unusual in the African churches.

Some bishops, murmuring, criticized this and maintained that it ought not to be done contrary to custom. But the holy Valerius, knowing that this was practised in the eastern churches, paid no heed to the tongues of his detractors; seeking not his own glory but [Col. 1219C] God’s, he preferred that the people of God should be instructed by another rather than remain uninstructed through himself.

Afterward, as the report of this practice spread and the good example advanced, certain presbyters endowed with fitting and learned eloquence, having received authority, began to speak the word of God to the people even in the presence of their bishops. And rightly so, since the Apostle teaches that this is not unsuitable: “If something is revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first be silent” (1 Cor. 4, as cited).

## CHAPTER XX

At the same time, in the city of Hippo, the pestilence of the Manichaeans had infected many citizens and strangers alike. They were chiefly deceived by a presbyter of that heresy [Col. 1219D] named Fortunatus, through his verbose cunning. Living in that city and going around houses to seduce little women, he was highly regarded by many. He spoke much about the holy Scriptures, which he wrongly interpreted to his own destruction and theirs.

Meanwhile, many people of Hippo, both Catholic Christians and Donatist heretics, approached the blessed Augustine and urgently requested that he meet the aforesaid Fortunatus, whom they considered learned, and dispute with him concerning the law of God and the holy Scriptures. Augustine, ready to give an answer to everyone who asked him concerning the faith and hope that were in him, and able both to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradicted it, did not refuse what was asked; but he inquired whether Fortunatus too wished this to take place.

They immediately [Col. 1220A] went to Fortunatus and earnestly asked him not to refuse. Because he had known the holy Augustine at Carthage while Augustine was still held in the same error with him, he appeared inclined to avoid the encounter. But, compelled by shame and their insistence, he at last promised that he would come to the conference and undertake the contest of disputation.

On the day and at the place appointed they assembled. Many came together to hear them out of eagerness to know the truth; many also from the impulse of curiosity. The tablets of the notaries were opened to record each speaker’s words. Their disputation began on the first day and ended on the second. In it the Manichaean teacher could neither weaken the Catholic assertion of the blessed Augustine nor establish the sect of the Manichaeans by the support of truth [Col. 1220B]. Failing in his answer and suffering deserved disgrace, he yielded, willingly or unwillingly, to the truth; and shortly afterward left the city, never to return.

Thus, through the man of God Augustine, the deception of the aforesaid error was uprooted from the hearts both of those present and of those absent to whom that disputation reached; and the religion of Catholic truth was made known and confirmed.

## CHAPTER XXI

He preached everywhere and publicly, speaking the word of God with all boldness, overthrowing every heretic and instructing Catholics. The Holy Spirit poured into him an ineffable grace, and all marvelled at his discriminating 700 eloquence. The Church, not only in Africa but also overseas, now knew the fame of his name [Col. 1220C], rejoicing beyond expression that God had granted it such a man—“Incernam” in the printed text, materially uncertain—whose word and example it had deserved to be enlightened by.

[Col. 1220C] While the aged Valerius rejoiced more than all others, he began, as human weakness does, to fear that another might seek out his presbyter, take him away, and choose him as bishop. This would certainly have happened at some time, unless Valerius, foreseeing it, had caused him to be hidden so that, if sought, he could not be found. Greatly shaken by still greater fear, especially since he was weak in body and worn out by age, Valerius sent confidential letters to the primate, the bishop of Carthage, praying and beseeching him that Augustine should be ordained bishop for the Church of Hippo—not so much [Col. 1220D] to succeed to his chair as to join him as fellow bishop.

The primate, taking account of Valerius’s weakness both of body and age, graciously yielded to his pious prayers and, by a written reply, granted that what he requested should be done. Then Megalius, at that time primate of Numidia, came to the Church of Hippo. Valerius was present, as were all the clergy and people; all agreed and acclaimed the election. Augustine was chosen bishop, though he made strenuous efforts to refuse it when his bishop arrived.

But when all compelled him, and it was shown by examples from both the African and overseas churches that this was customarily done, he at last yielded under compulsion and held both the episcopal place and office with the blessed Valerius. Later he both said and [Col. 1221A] wrote that this ought not to have been done, when he had learned the decrees of a universal council, which at that time had been unknown to him.

## CHAPTER XXII
Having become a bishop, the greater the dignity in which he shone, the greater the zeal and authority with which he preached the word of God—not only in his own city, but wherever an ecclesiastical need summoned him, whether to instruct Catholics or to overthrow heretics. For he defeated in public disputation the heretics Felix, Maximinus, Pascentius, Felicianus, and many others, whom it would be both tedious and superfluous to enumerate, striking them with fitting confusion. Throughout all Africa they had been deceiving weak hearts by their crafty wit and perverse authority, and, blind themselves, were leading the blind to destruction. Many of those who, while their error prevailed, had long been corrupted and turned away, were, through divine inspiration and Augustine’s disputation, converted and restored to the Catholic faith. [Col. 1221B]

Seeing, moreover, that a bishop had necessarily to show continual humane hospitality to all who came or passed through—for otherwise, if he did not do so, he would be charged with inhumanity, while the abandonment of this practice in monasteries would be irreligious—he wished to maintain in his episcopal household a monastery of clerics. Thus he who, as a priest, had lived according to rule in a garden might likewise, as bishop, serve God under a rule, poor among the poor. As his sound and holy teaching advanced, many clerics, inspired by the divine Spirit and bidding farewell to the world, flocked to [Col. 1221C] his monastery. There, having abandoned secular property and their own wills, they served God devoutly under and with so great a teacher.

Their holy continence, voluntary poverty, and humble obedience spread the fragrance of good repute far and wide; and throughout Africa they diffused, with renewed vitality, the marks of apostolic religion, which had until then been almost dead. Accordingly, some bishops, becoming emulators of so great holiness, asked that many brothers from the same monastery be granted to them; under their care and custody they entrusted many churches to God’s service. These men, mindful of their purpose and bearing the savour of the wholesome teaching which they had received from the holy vow, established monasteries also, after gathering clerics together. From these they subsequently sent forth many, as their religious life and the devotion of the faithful advanced, to instruct other monasteries. Thus this religious purpose and canonical rule of profession gathered many servants of God and ordered many churches, not only in Africa but also in lands beyond the sea. [Col. 1221D]

## CHAPTER XXIII

When the heretics saw this holiness advancing and themselves declining more and more, they were angry, gnashing their teeth and wasting away; for although they lacked the power to resist, they retained liberty to envy. Yet their desires perished. For they were unable to harm blessed Augustine—whom they regarded as the glory and pillar of this religious life, but as, so to speak, the head and leader of their own destruction—either by force or by deceit, though they attempted this many times.

Thus, on one occasion, [Col. 1222A] when armed men lay concealed in ambush and planned to kill him as he went, according to custom, to visit and instruct the Catholic people, it happened by divine ordering that, having missed and abandoned the particular route, the holy man arrived by another road at the place to which he was making his way, and escaped their hands through the protection of that mistaken turn. Learning this afterward, he gave thanks to Him who delivers, in whatever way He wills, those whom He purposes to save.

Nevertheless, shaken by fear, he did not cease from preaching God’s word. Rather, always and everywhere, whenever time and place required it, he pressed and suppressed their error; and he frequently interceded with secular rulers on behalf of those heretics when they had sometimes been condemned and sentenced to death. For he knew the Scripture that instructs us thus: “Do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6). Invited by them, he attended councils of bishops, synods of priests, and conferences of rulers; [Col. 1222B] and in them he sought and loved not what was his own, but what belonged to Jesus Christ, so that what was just might be duly confirmed, and what was unjust discreetly corrected.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Finally, in countenance and bearing, speech and conduct, he presented himself to all in such a manner that he became all things to all for the benefit of all. To religious persons he was honourably grave; to secular persons, agreeably cheerful. Thus by his example he confirmed the former in the holiness they had begun, and by fitting cheerfulness invited the latter to holiness. For the holy man knew for whom an appropriate gravity was beneficial, and for whom a discerning cheerfulness was most useful. [Col. 1222C]

His clothing and footwear maintained the measure suitable to religious life: they were neither defiled by empty ostentation nor rendered shabby by affected abasement. For just as excessive elegance in clothing is censured, so too is its excessive ugliness as a mark of pride. He wished to offer himself to others as a model for living, not as material for disparagement.

His speech was gracious, seasoned with salt, full of honourableness and truth, full of counsel and strength; it possessed a frank humility and a humble abundance, dispensing the debt of spiritual nourishment alike to the wise and the foolish, able to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradicted it. Finally, he was guarded with such vigilance and enclosed by such protection that he avoided not only falsehood and perjury, but every oath; and he warned that every oath should be avoided. This was not because the truthfulness of one who swears is sinful if the distrust of an unbeliever requires it, but because one who swears frequently will at some time commit perjury. [Col. 1222D]

He strongly maintained that the evangelical saying must be observed: “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; No, no” (James 5), lest someone, through the habit of swearing, fall into the snare of perjury. For one must abstain not only from unlawful things but also from lawful things, lest, while a person wanders everywhere among lawful things, he incur unlawful ones. Therefore he shunned, with the utmost care and diligence, as though it were a plague, every oath—even such expressions as some religious people use frequently and which certain simpler persons do not regard as oaths: “God is witness,” “God knows,” and the like—because he wished to be perfectly united with Him [Col. 1223A] of whom the Apostle says: “There was not in him Yes and No, but in him was Yes” (ibid.).

His habits, according to the same Apostle, were free from avarice, and he was content with what was at hand. He loved poverty as a treasure found; he embraced it and clung to it, knowing that the virtue of voluntary poverty is the guardian of holiness.

## CHAPTER XXV

The vessels in his house were of marble, wood, or earthenware—not from the compulsion of need, but by the choice of his purpose. He did indeed use wine, though sparingly; and among vegetables and pulses, he ate meat also for the sake of guests or any who were ill. Poor for himself, he was considered rich and generous toward others; fasting for himself, he feasted others. His door stood open to the traveller; [Col. 1223B] his table served guests. At it, refreshment was supplied not so much to the belly as to the mind, because trifles and idle stories were banished, and disputation and reading were the chief course.

But because amid meals intended for necessary refreshment the superfluous—indeed, the deadly poisons—of speaking ill of one’s brethren often intrude, he had two verses written on his table to suppress this plague, so that, when he himself was silent, they might speak:

> Whoever loves, with words concerning the absent, to gnaw at another’s life,  
> Let him know that this table is forbidden to him.

If any member of his household or any bishop, who frequently shared his table, forgetful of this inscription, presumed either to speak idly or to disparage persons who were absent, he was sometimes so sharply stirred that he said either he himself would leave the table and go away, or that man must obey the verses. [Col. 1223C] This indeed sometimes happened: he rose and went into his chamber when someone spoke more than was proper at table. Thus he restrained his guests not only from disparaging speech but also from superfluous words, compelling them to attend either to reading or disputation.

He himself applied himself to these pursuits with such earnestness that he banished from himself not only what was harmful, but rejected even things that appeared necessary as though they were harmful. Therefore he never wished to buy houses, fields, or estates; although he did not altogether forbid the Church from accepting such things when offered. At times, indeed, he voluntarily returned inheritances that had been offered, judging it just that they should rather be possessed by the children or heirs to whom their fathers had not wished to leave them at death. [Col. 1223D]

Because he always wished to keep his mind free from temporal concerns, he never took an interest in constructing new buildings. Yet he did not forbid others to build them, unless perhaps he saw someone applying himself to such matters more than was proper. Nor did he ever wish to accept property entrusted to his keeping, lest one who was more intent on asking concerning his own affairs than retaining them should become occupied with preserving the goods of others. Even in matters possessed by the Church, he was neither held by love nor moved by fear; but, intent upon higher and spiritual things, he descended at times to arrange temporal concerns, not led by his own will but compelled by [Col. 1224A] the necessity of the brethren. When these matters had been settled for the time being, he called his mind back from thorns and briars and returned the gaze of his understanding to those higher and inward realities, so that he might either reflect upon discovering divine things, dictate something from what he had discovered, or correct something already dictated and copied out.

Since the day was insufficient for this work, the holy man kept vigil and worked by night, that the words might be fulfilled: “But his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he shall meditate day and night” (Psalm 1).

## CHAPTER XXVI

In order that every evil suspicion might be removed both from himself and from his own household, and that no opportunity might be given to those seeking an opportunity, he never permitted any woman to reside within his house—not even his own sister, although it was certain that, as a widow and truly a widow, she devotedly served God. [Col. 1224B] For although councils of bishops had exempted such persons as a mother, a sister, and the like from those who were to be kept away, nevertheless, because such women cannot be without other women, and holy men are not without other clerics or laymen living with them, the holy man said that such cohabitation could cause offence among the weak, or disturb some of them by human temptations, or expose them to the evil suspicions of people and to defamation.

For this reason he maintained that it was improper for any woman, however chaste, to live under one roof with servants of God, lest, as I have said, temptation or evil suspicion arise from such cohabitation. [Col. 1224C] Accordingly, if any such woman asked that he would deign to speak with her, he never allowed her to approach him without clerics as witnesses; he never spoke alone with a woman alone, not even if what she said to him was confidential.

He visited only orphans and widows in distress, and the sick, when requested. Laying hands upon them in response to their entreaties and offering prayer, he drove away their infirmities. For he had received the gift of healing from Him who said: “They shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall be well” (Mark 16). He did not visit women’s monasteries unless grave necessity required it. For he maintained that it did not befit a religious man to seek a wife for any secular person, lest, while the married pair quarrelled with one another, one of them should curse the man through whom they had been joined. And surely it seems sufficiently incongruous for a holy man who has professed continence to invite others to bodily union. [Col. 1224D]

He maintained that these and many other things, which it would be tedious to recount, must be strictly observed by religious men; and he judged that both their life and their reputation ought to be kept whole, both among those within and among those without. For there are many who, although they seem religious, nevertheless do not refuse to become entangled in secular affairs: either they thrust themselves forward voluntarily, or, when invited by anyone, they fear to resist by refusing. But the holy man did not wish anyone who had professed religious life, whether led by personal frivolity or induced by another’s importunity, to comply with anyone’s request if the thing requested would bring either a stain upon his life or discredit upon religion. Indeed, Plautus also seems to declare this in the *Amphitryon*: “It is not fitting,” he says, “that unjust requests should be obtained from just people.” [Col. 1225A]

## CHAPTER XXVII

Finally, he trained the servants of God whom he had gathered to live according to rule in such moral habits that their continence, poverty, and obedience kindled many, far and wide, to abandon private possessions and hasten together into one community, where all things might be common to all. So that this religious life might endure without diminution not only among those then present but also among those far in the future, he took pains to write for them a rule of holy institution. In it he elegantly set forth what a subordinate ought to do, what a superior ought to do, what is fitting for all generally, and what for individuals [Col. 1225B] particularly.

And lest anything be neglected through forgetfulness, he commanded that this same rule be read once each week, so that both superiors and subordinates might have a faithful reminder and none might put forward any excuse. He also offered himself to those whom he taught as the model of the whole religious life. As it is written, he was among them as one of them, like them in worship and outward habit, differing only in episcopal dignity, not in fraternal and inward humility.

Accordingly, he himself says in one place: “I do not want Your Holiness to offer such things as I might use in a manner seemingly more becoming. For example, he may offer me a costly cloak: perhaps it befits a bishop, but it does not befit Augustine, a poor man born of the poor. If he wishes me to have a garment, let him give one of such a kind that I need not be ashamed of it. For I confess to you that I am ashamed of costly clothing, because it does not befit this profession, it does not befit this admonition.” [Col. 1225C]

Augustine wished, therefore, to be clothed in such garments as suited the other brethren, while maintaining the tenor of his purpose. For he had heard, and truly heard, the saying of a certain wise man: “Never glory in your clothing, nor exalt yourself on the day of your honour” (Ecclesiasticus 11).

For the benefit of both those present and those to come, he wrote so great an abundance of books that scarcely could anyone suffice to read them, though he himself had sufficed to write them. After the Apostles, by whose teaching the Church shines, he shone foremost in the grace of dispensing the word of God: a true apostolic imitator, a learned scribe, a Catholic teacher. He dictated many books while still a layman, many after becoming a priest, and very many as bishop. Before the day of his death he diligently revised those that were uncorrected; and whatever he recognized that he had set down in them contrary to ecclesiastical rule when he was still inexperienced and had not yet acquired familiarity with the divine Scriptures, he corrected exactly. Accordingly, he wrote two volumes to which he gave the title *On the Retraction of Books*. He also began certain writings which, prevented by death, he did not complete. [Col. 1225D]

For throughout his lifetime he exercised himself tirelessly in this pursuit; in this arena he toiled and endured the cold; in this gymnasium he contended; in this—and, with due respect to the saints who then were and thereafter would be, I say it—he laboured more than all.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 1226A]

Finally, when after a long course of years he saw himself already an old man, and perceived that the end which no one can escape in the natural order was not far away, he feared that after his departure someone who sought what was his own rather than what belonged to Jesus Christ (Philippians 2) might ambitiously seize the episcopal chair by force, money, or secular favour, and that, with some desiring and others unwilling, a schism might arise in the Church. Therefore he humbly took counsel with all and, by taking counsel, admonished them that while he was alive they should unanimously elect a religious bishop who, after his death and with all contention removed, would assume the episcopate.

They all alike agreed to this counsel and imposed upon Augustine himself the responsibility for this election, so that he, who knew religious men better, might select one of them to succeed him upon his death without delay or dissension. [Col. 1226B] Accordingly, he chose as his successor a religious man of good reputation, named Eraclius, whom Augustine himself had trained in Christ’s school and had excellently formed in both holiness and learning. He publicly named the man chosen; and both clergy and people acclaimed his election with unanimous consent.

Then he said to the people: “You know that some years ago, when at the two councils—namely those of Numidia and Carthage—my holy brethren and fellow-bishops, the Fathers, imposed on me the care of the Scriptures, I asked you to allow me five days a week for uninterrupted leisure—or rather, for the literary labour which I served—and to defer the turmoil of external affairs to the remaining days. For I could not continually bear your affairs and at the same time provide the holy bishops with what they asked. You granted this at that time; but compelled by frequent necessity, you forcibly broke in upon it. [Col. 1226C]

“Since, therefore, I could not then obtain what I wished, I now ask again that the burden of my occupations be transferred to this Eraclius whom I have chosen, and that what was brought to me be brought to him. Go to him; listen to him; let him answer you; let him, according as God shall direct, arrange your affairs. But whenever my counsel is opportune, I shall not refuse assistance. He will consult me; he will listen to me; what he has drawn from me, he will pour back out to you. And thus my labour, devoted to literary duty—or rather, literary work—will serve both your benefit and mine. Therefore I await your answer on this matter; I seek your assent; I ask for your acclamation.”

Upon hearing this, all unanimously replied; recognizing that what had previously been impossible could now be done, they gave their assent to this honourable request. [Col. 1226D]

## CHAPTER XXIX

Some time afterward, by the ordering of divine justice, the fierce and impious people of the Vandals came forth from lands beyond the sea. Joined by an innumerable multitude of Alans and Goths, they entered the African region as enemies under arms and utterly destroyed many cities, towns, and estates there. That people raged with such cruelty that it spared neither age, sex, condition, churches, ecclesiastical ornaments, priests, nor ministers: it burned buildings, slaughtered people, or—what seemed more grievous to all than anything else—reduced them to wretched slavery.

While such savagery brought disaster upon the whole province, scarcely three churches remained surviving out of all: namely, those of Carthage, Hippo, and Cirta. Their cities, supported by the protection of God and men, had not yet fallen under hostile destruction. Nevertheless, after almost the whole region had been laid waste, that hostile onslaught came to the city of Hippo, as though it counted for nothing that it had made progress while it saw any city remaining alive. [Col. 1227A] Having assembled an innumerable army, it besieged that city and remained encamped immovably all around it for almost fourteen months. It oppressed those trapped within by a prolonged and unceasing siege and finally overwhelmed it by God’s just, though hidden, judgment.

At that time Augustine saw his country and city afflicted by so many and such great evils; he saw all the faithful endangered, churches entirely overthrown, and the ecclesiastical order turned away from the worship of God under the compulsion of persecution. He wept with those who wept, sympathized with those who suffered, and consoled those who were with him, maintaining that this was the will of God, who works good out of human evils. [Col. 1227B]

Many priests and bishops from neighbouring cities had fled to Hippo, both that they might be fortified by the city’s protection and refreshed by Augustine’s conversations. Addressing them, the holy man recounted the divine Scriptures and said that many in former times had suffered, so that those in error might be corrected and those who were less good might be made better. He perceived that such had been, and was, the divine purpose; and he earnestly admonished others to perceive it, lest, by womanish faint-heartedness, they lose manly endurance, in accordance with that memorable saying of a certain wise man: “He is not great who regards it as a great thing that trees and stones fall, and mortals die.” [Col. 1227C]

## CHAPTER XXX

Meanwhile, one day, when the aforesaid bishops were together at his table discussing the present calamity and humbly praying that God the Comforter would be with them, blessed Augustine said to them: “I shall pray God at this present time either to repel from this city the disgrace of the enemy, or to grant his servants the patience pleasing to himself, or rather to deign to lead them out of this wretched world and transfer them to eternal peace and glory.” This promise pleased the bishops, and both they and those with them asked this very thing from God; they also devoutly urged the whole population of the city to ask the same.

And behold: in the third month of the siege, Augustine was laid low by fever, and he did not lack the fruitful effect of the prayers which he had poured out to God with tears. For it is written in the Book of Psalms: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears unto their prayers” (Psalm 33). [Col. 1227D]

While he was suffering from his final illness and expected his approaching end from day to day, a householder who had a sick man afflicted by a severe illness heard in a dream: “Go to Augustine, and by laying on his hand he will restore him to health.” Augustine had indeed previously healed many sick persons and, after prayer, had freed many demoniacs from demons. For, hearing that a certain virgin of Hippo was troubled by a demon, he prayed devoutly for her and, while praying, dropped his tears into oil which he had at hand. When this was sent to her, the aforesaid virgin was anointed with it and healed.

He also prayed for a certain young man whom he had not seen, and by prayer freed him from a demon. He himself is found to have recounted these two miracles. Therefore the householder took his sick man and came to Augustine, begging him to lay his hand upon him and restore his health. Augustine, being readier to answer elegantly than to presume, said: “If I had power in these matters, I would first have bestowed it upon myself.” [Col. 1228A] But when the householder begged more insistently and declared that he had been warned in a dream, Augustine, observing the petitioner’s faith, laid his hand upon the sick man and, after praying, the sick man restored health to the sick.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Because he had frequently preached that a priest ought not depart from the misery of this life without mourning and repentance, he had the seven penitential psalms, which he had caused to be written during his illness, placed upon the wall opposite his bed. He read and reread them, and wept copiously as he read. Indeed, ten days before he died, he had humbly asked those who were with him that no one should enter to him except to bring food or some other necessity. [Col. 1228B] During that time he applied himself continually to prayer, devotion, and weeping.

He lived sixty-six years: nearly thirty-three before baptism, three as a layman after baptism, and forty as a professed cleric. Until his final illness he preached the word of God in church unfailingly and vigorously, with sound mind and sound judgment, his sight and hearing unimpaired and all the limbs of his body whole. But on the final day of his illness, that is, the fifth day before the Kalends of September [28 August], with the community of brethren standing by and commending his departure in prayers, he, old and full of days, fell asleep in peace. At last that for which he had groaned in part was done away, and he more fully found what he had long desired.

He made no will, for Christ’s poor man had nothing from which to make one. [Col. 1228C] He left monasteries of men and women full of those who practised continence, trained in conduct and adorned with books which he himself had dictated. In these he still lives for us, although he has died in the flesh. For he lives to God, and he lives also to us, because he clings perfectly to God and speaks to us through his writings.

A certain secular poet also aptly expressed this, commanding that the following verses be inscribed upon his tomb by those whom he left behind at his death:

> Traveller, do you wish to know whether the poet lives after death?  
> What you read—behold, I speak: your voice, surely, is mine.

Therefore let all Catholics—and especially clerics—venerate such and so great a man, so Catholic a teacher, since his teaching is instruction for all [Col. 1228D] Catholics and his life is a model for clerics. For if the grammarian Priscian, gratefully remembering his teacher Theostus, does not disdain to call him the glory of all eloquence, and reverently attributes to him after God whatever learning is in himself, then, in my judgment, anyone who professes himself a cleric is to be blamed no little if he does not love to hold Augustine as his teacher, remember him devoutly, and venerate him diligently. For Augustine is the glory and model of this our profession; he is the mirror and rule of our religious life. [Col. 1229A]

## CHAPTER XXXII

Let others choose whatever ambition suggests to each; but if Philip were given the choice, he would prefer the holy poverty with which God enriched the bishop Augustine to the kingdom and riches by which he exalted King Alexander. [Col. 1229B] He would prefer Augustine’s wise learning and keenness of intellect to the miracle-working by which the Egyptian magicians swelled with pride. He would prefer to be distinguished by the virtues that flourished in Augustine rather than to raise the dead, as Saul and the Pythoness were able to do.

I am unequal to recounting the virtues and merits of so great a man, and the rewards of his merits—poor as I am in life, words, and intellect. Yet I have undertaken to say some things because I received this boldness from the brethren; I did not presume it of myself. Therefore, if I have said anything truly, anything worthily, about him, pray, you who read, that it may please God, who approves and recognizes what is worthy and true, but often forgives what is otherwise. For at his command the heralds of that heavenly city say: “Peace,” they say, “to people of good will” (Luke 2). [Col. 1229C]

May blessed Augustine himself also come as an intercessor, that the God of customary mercy may grant us all alike his favour. Before him no adversary can stand against us, if so great a helper stands with us. For I believe, and truly believe, that he, received into the fellowship of angels, sees in Zion the God of gods (Psalm 83); he sees the Beginning amid the splendour of the saints. Yet he is not forgetful of his brethren; rather, as far as I hope and presume concerning him, he reconciles us who are subject to him with God. This fruitful presumption is aptly supported by that venerable vision, worthy of remembrance, which is found in the text of a certain history.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Col. 1229D] A certain householder, inflamed with religious devotion, celebrated daily with reverence the commemorations of certain saints. Among them he loved Augustine with a rather more tender affection, and although he invoked him with the others, he nevertheless invoked him more devoutly than the rest every day. For this religious man hoped to be delivered from every necessity if, in the day of necessity, he should deserve to be aided by such a patron.

When, by the law of human destiny, he came to his end and prayed that the saints whom he had loved might be present with him, it happened that, undergoing an ecstasy of mind, he was caught up to behold invisible things, as often happens to those who are dying, who, placed in their final struggle, gain a kind of certain knowledge of the future. Thus, with his bodily senses temporarily lulled, being in the Spirit, he saw the saints whom he had intimately loved and faithfully invoked standing present beside him, to console him as he lay in the peril of death and to guard his departure. [Col. 1230A]

As he looked upon them gratefully and recognized without doubt who each one was, he perceived only that Augustine was absent. Since he had loved him above the rest, he would have preferred his presence above that of the rest. On discovering this, he groaned deeply; and he was as troubled by Augustine’s absence as he rejoiced in the presence of the others.

Then an angel—perhaps the one who stood by him as he was dying to guard him, for Christ, the Angel of the Lord, sends an angel or angels around those who fear him, to deliver them—said to him: “Why are you sad? Do not fear; you shall be safe.”

But he replied: “Rightly I grieve, because I do not see him whom I loved above the rest present with the others. I loved Augustine especially, and, while the others are present to me, I perceive him alone to be absent.” [Col. 1230B]

The angel said to him: “Do not grieve at his absence, for it is by no means due to contempt or neglect of you. While Augustine lived in this world, he applied himself to the word of God with the utmost care and diligence, perfectly setting aside not only what was unlawful but even what was lawful for its sake. Embracing it with unrelenting ardour, meditating upon it day and night, he fixed upon its rays an eagle-like gaze; and although he lived bodily on earth, he nevertheless lived in spirit in the heavens.

“Therefore even now he applies himself more fully to the same word of God. Drawing thirstily from the streams of the eternal fountain, he reclines, as it were, familiarly upon Christ’s breast. He clings to him without ceasing, whom he loved perfectly, and from whose love he never turned the sight of his mind toward temporal things. Thus he cannot be separated from him in order to visit you, nor can his attention be relaxed even for a little while from him whom he ardently desires. [Col. 1230C]

“Yet although, having entered into the joy of his Lord, he is made drunk with divine abundance, he nevertheless remembers you with fatherly concern. He beholds and worships for your sake Him whom he ardently embraces; and for you, whom he knows to be subject to him, he prays without ceasing. Therefore do not suppose that he is absent from you: by continual prayer, rather than by merely making an appearance, he takes greater care to benefit you.”

When the angel had spoken these very words, or words of equal force, the man’s spirit, which had been weakened by grief, was strengthened and revived. As though awakening from sleep, [Col. 1230D] he related to those standing by his bed all that he had heard; and shortly afterward, paying nature’s due, supported by such consolation, he fell asleep in peace.

Now it seems fitting—if your charity is not wearied—that, since it has been said to the best of my ability concerning blessed Augustine’s birth, course of life, and due end, something should also be said, however inadequately, concerning his translation.

Accordingly, when the blessed Augustine had died in his own city of Hippo, in the third month of its siege, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September [28 August], he was buried there with lamentation and grief by the holy fellow-bishops who were present and by his brethren. Later, however, by God’s ordering counsel, he was translated thence to Sardinia. When, how, or by whom he was carried there [Col. 1231A], I have neither wished nor ought to commit to writing, because I have been unable to find it recorded. There he lay honourably for almost two hundred and eighty years after his death, until, by God’s hidden but not unjust judgement, that city too succumbed to destruction. For the Saracens rushed in, smote it with the sword, and, knowing not God, overthrew all things belonging to God; and, what was more detestable, casting off all reverence, they shamefully defiled even the sacred places themselves.

Nevertheless, when that city fell beneath hostile devastation, divine providence did not permit the fame of the holy man to be effaced by silence. At that time the devout King Liutprand, by God’s ordering, ruled Italy; loving the things of God, he held the holy Church in the highest reverence. [Col. 1231B] For it is written: “Happy is the land whose king is noble” (Eccles. 10). Noble, I suppose, not so much by dignity of birth as by innate uprightness. For, as a certain pagan says: “It is not a great thing to be born of great people, but to be great.” Solomon too seems to commend this nobility: “Her husband,” he says, “is noble in the gates” (Prov. 31), when speaking of the strong woman.

This Liutprand, stirred by no slight devotion, built, in honour of the blessed apostle Peter, a basilica beyond the walls of Pavia. Distinguished by royal adornment, he called it the Golden Cell. While he was diligently applying himself to this undertaking, he heard that the hostile impiety of the Saracens was laying Sardinia waste and that the venerable place in which [Col. 1231C] blessed Augustine had long rested in honour was being held in contempt. Therefore, choosing envoys whom he judged energetic and trustworthy, he sent them thither with a great weight of gold and silver, praying—and obtaining through prayer—that by entreaty, payment, or whatever means they could, they should endeavour to remove that holy body from Sardinia and bring it to him. For the devout prince said that his church would shine with worthy splendour if it deserved to be enriched by so great a treasure.

Faithfully carrying out their assigned office, they travelled to Sardinia; having taken up the body and paid a great price, they returned with joy. Protected by so great a guardian and secure under so great a safeguard, they entrusted themselves to the sea; and, as the west wind filled the sails, the favonian breeze whistled, and the surface of the sea rippled, they ploughed [Col. 1231D] the deep with swift oars and entered, on a favourable voyage, the harbour of a city called Memiensis. There, having cast anchor, they rested for a while.

When King Liutprand learned that the messengers were returning with the fulfilment of his desire, he joyfully went to meet them there, attended by many soldiers. Falling upon his face with bent knee, he humbly adored that holy body. In its presence God performed many miracles there through blessed Augustine, so that he whose life had been wondrous might after death likewise appear praiseworthy. For it is he of whom it is written: “Who is this? And we shall praise him; for he performed wonders in his life” (Ecclus. 31).

Then, leaving their naval station, the king and his company departed from there with the body. Coming into the bishopric of Terdona, they entered a certain royal village, commonly called Mount [Col. 1232A] Samarius. Since their day’s labour was complete, the sun was now preparing to set, and the approaching evening was bringing the day to its end, they set down the body there and rested. With candles and lamps, hymns and praises, they made the whole night festive.

But in the morning, when the rising morning star was driving away the departing stars, and the red dawn, as darkness thinned, was flooding the neighbouring horizon with new light, the king, impatient of delay, ordered the body to be lifted at first light, hoping to proceed as usual without any difficulty. Hearing the king’s command, the bearers seized the bier and discovered something full of wonder.

For the body was found to be of such heaviness, of such weight, that it could not only not be lifted by [Col. 1232B] those former bearers, but could not even be moved by everyone together. They were terrified and amazed, wondering what offence they had incurred during the night just passed, if, by psalm-singing and praise, they had provoked so great a displeasure. At last the king, admonished by divine inspiration and recalling what is written, “Give alms, and all things are clean for you” (Luke 2), offered a gift to placate the holy man, saying:

“If you, Father Augustine, permit yourself to be carried to the place which I have chosen, I shall give you in perpetuity this estate in which we stand, and all that belongs to it, for the use of those who minister to you.”

A wonderful thing! That blessed saint who, according to Scripture, “has shaken his hands free from every gift” (Isa. 33) is placated by a gift of this kind; and his body, which shortly before was altogether immovable, once it had heard the offering [Col. 1232C] became portable. Yet, so far as I perceive and dare affirm, it was not desire for a temporal gift that drew him, but the spiritual benefit of the devout king; for he knew that this is true and fruitful devotion, the kind confirmed by action. The affection of devotion may indeed then be sufficient, when the means are lacking for its effect to follow. But if the means for action are granted, the will is not fruitful if it remains idle.

Therefore, prudent reader, if you wish to review the Holy Scriptures, both New and Old, you will find many things requested there and many carefully offered, in which there appears not so much the greed or need of the one requesting as the benefit of the one offering. Thus God asked Abraham to sacrifice to him his only son, not seeking a parricidal victim, but awaiting the father’s obedience. Thus the servant of that same Abraham, having found Rebecca at the well, asked water of her—the water which she drew with much labour. In this, the benefit was prepared not so much for the servant as for the girl, as the result that followed in the narrative makes clear to anyone reading the text.

Thus Elijah, who had abundance of bread and meat through the ministry of a raven, was sent to the hungry widow of Zarephath of the Sidonians, that he might be fed by her—though, her little flask of oil and jar of flour exhausted, she said that she was immediately about to die of hunger with her son. “Go,” he says, “and from that very little flour first make me a small hearth-baked cake and bring it to me; then you shall make something for yourself and your son” (3 Kings 17). Here perhaps an unlearned hearer will judge the prophet blameworthy for [Col. 1233A] lack of self-restraint and importunity, as though ignorant of brotherly charity, because in such want he asked—indeed, loudly demanded—that bread be made first for himself, who was not yet hungry, before it was made for the widow, already almost dying of want. But if you consider the purpose for which this was done, you will understand that provision was being made for the widow rather than the prophet. Thus was woven that embroidered garment, varied with diverse virtues, which the strong woman wrought upon the loom of righteousness. Of her Solomon says: “She put her hand to the distaff; her fingers grasped the spindle” (Prov. 31). What thread that same woman spun, or with what comb she wove the incorruptible garment, he indicates when he adds: “She opened her hands to the needy and stretched out her palms to the poor” (ibid.). This prophecy was indeed fulfilled when the prophet was fed by [Col. 1233B] the widow.

Likewise, Christ himself asked the Samaritan woman for a drink (John 4), not, as it seems to me, thirsting for water from the well, but for the streams of faith.
