Likewise, when the apostle Paul praised the honourable generosity of the Philippians, after shortly before having indirectly reproved their former stinginess, he said: “Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit” (Phil. 4). You will find many such things in the Holy Scriptures which do not occur to me at present. Yet not everything that occurs ought to be set down here, lest, by too long a digression, weariness be produced in readers while the return to the subject is delayed.

Once the gift devoutly promised by King Liutprand had been given and confirmed, the bearers lifted that holy body, every difficulty removed. Setting out upon their desired journey, they arrived together at Pavia with joy. When messengers had run ahead, the whole city was stirred by unutterable gladness, and an innumerable multitude of both sexes came forth to meet them with hymns and praises. Praising the Lord, by whose incomprehensible grace they had deserved to receive such relics, they returned to the royal basilica and honourably deposited them there on the fifth day before the Ides of October [11 October]. I would call that church blessed which is enriched with such a treasure, rightly judged more precious than all gold and more splendid than jewels. Blessed, I say, is the church which has deserved to contain in the present time such relics as the whole world does not deserve to retain for ever.

If things that perhaps seem unbelievable ought to be believed, believe, you who read; believe, you who hear. I would rather that our church were enriched and adorned with the bones of Augustine preserved in the church of Pavia than with silken garments, many of which, as I have heard, are offered for sale in the marketplace of Pavia. I would rather that the precious relics of Augustine were kept in our church than the sumptuous riches of Croesus. Rightly, therefore, the apostolic church of Peter rejoices in these relics, for Peter himself rejoices in Augustine’s fellowship in the heavenly court. There, although both he and the other apostles rejoice in the blessedness of all the righteous, they rejoice especially in Augustine, who was their perfect imitator and who lives—and will live for ages of ages—with them in God and from God.

[Col. 1233]

# LIFE OF SAINT AMAND, BISHOP OF MAASTRICHT

(From the edition of Godfrey Henschenius, *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, February, vol. I, 6 February, p. 815.) (G)*

## PREFACE

Philip of Harveng, commonly called “of Almsgiving,” second abbot of the Premonstratensian monastery of Bonne-Espérance near Binche in Hainaut, a contemporary and intimate associate of Saint Bernard, wrote the Life of Saint Amand in an elegant style. In the eulogies of the abbots of Elnone the following is transmitted concerning him:

> I must not pass over the praise of eloquent Philip,  
> Whose fragrance of speech spreads everywhere;  
> He flourished in Hugh’s age; under that ruler,  
> O Bishop Amand, he set his pen to your deeds.

Philip wrote the first letter of the Life of Saint Amand, placed before it as a prologue, to this Hugh. When Hugh died in A.D. 1169, Philip wrote a second letter to Abbot John, his successor; under him he published the Life of Saint Amand about the year 1170. Finally, he died in 1183, having relinquished the burden of governing the monastery some months earlier. The following epitaph is read for him:

> Philip, the flower of flowers, the way of morals, withers;  
> Beneath me, O Christ, may Philip share the company of your saints.  
> Christ Jesus, do not allow Philip to be harmed  
> By the second death, but grant him to live for ever.

Vossius discusses Philip in three places in his books *On Latin Historians*. In book II, chapter 49, he calls him Philip of Almsgiving, abbot of Bonne-Espérance; then, in book III, part II, under the letter P, he lists Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, as though he were different from the preceding man; and shortly afterward he names Philip, abbot of the monastery of Elnone, as author of the Life of Saint Amand, cited by Meyer under the year 661 in the *Annals of Flanders*. Possevino likewise treats the abbot of Elnone as distinct from the abbot of Bonne-Espérance. Josias Simler has only one Philip and makes him abbot of Elnone, relying also on Meyer’s authority. These are his words: “Philip, abbot, on the location of that monastery [Elnone]: ‘It is,’ he says, ‘a place within the territory of the Menapii, adjoining the Propontii and Nervii.’” Philip has these words below, section 64.

We have transcribed this Life from manuscripts of the monastery of Blandin and of Nicholas Belfort, and have collated it with the Douai edition of the works of Abbot Philip and with another ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Elnone. There is also a manuscript [Col. 1235] in the library of Saint-Vaast. Miraeus, in the *Fasti Belgici* and *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and Valerius Andreas, in the *Bibliotheca Belgica*, mention this Life as written by Philip. But in the first edition Andreas calls Saint Amand bishop of Utrecht, and in the second bishop of Liège—thus sufficiently indicating that the Life itself was unknown to him. We correct Philip’s chronology, which is not sufficiently accurate.

# DEDICATORY LETTER TO ABBOT HUGH

[Col. 1235A]

1. To the reverend father in Christ, Hugh, by God’s grace venerable abbot of the monastery of Elnone, and to the brethren there assembled in the Lord: Brother Philip of Almsgiving, counted among the seed which the Lord has blessed.

[Note: [Col. 1235D] This Hugh, as appears from the records of Elnone, was Burgundian by birth, distinguished for eloquence, judgement, and gentleness of character. Formerly prior of the monastery of Saint John at Laon, then abbot of Humolaria, he afterwards became the forty-second Amandinian abbot, and second of his name, in 1150, after Walter II had been removed for inactivity. He raised to a great height a tower which had collapsed by fire from its upper windows; dug two fishponds; repaired the cloister; built a dining hall; enlarged the possessions; and died in 1169. Philip celebrates his praises in the following letter.]

To adorn the merits of the saints with the flowers of discourse, and through the office of writing to embellish the praises of the chosen race, is proved difficult and arduous—especially where neither one’s life is suitable nor one’s learning provides support. For one who undertakes to proclaim the conduct of the blessed, expound their life, and recount their deeds ought to live as he speaks and adorn by deeds what he commends in speech, lest, reproved by the testimony of his own voice, he fail to approve by imitation [Col. 1235B] what he pursues by assertion.

From your desirable and holy fellowship I have received for correction the Life of most blessed Amand: so that, by diligent labour, obscure passages may receive light, superfluities measure, gaps connection, and deficiencies supplementation. But who am I, or what am I, to whom neither merit of life, seasoning of wisdom, cultivation of learning, nor practice in writing promises the excellence of so renowned a work? I indeed praise the diligence of the first writer and reverence its antiquity; I approve his industry; if his style lies low, I do not reject his arrangement. But envy readily attends those who mint new things, and seething jealousy is not without the stings of detraction—especially when novelty seems seriously introduced to censure the ancients. Thus [Col. 1235C] injury to the ancients is lamented, as though whatever is added by the new must perish for them.

But the judgement of truth is awaited more securely than the murmur of envy is feared, for envy has no place in the court of charity. This charity supplies support for my incompetence, furnishes strength, provides boldness, and drives the little vessel of timid diligence onto the stormy sea. Yet if humility be given as its sailor, obedience as its rudder, truth as its mast, discretion as its yardarm, diligence as its oarsman, and authority as its sail—which the favourable breeze of heavenly grace may lift—it will easily be able, on a favourable course, to swim through the wave-crests of the turbulent salt sea and the grim bays of envious agitation.

Therefore, since I am bound to your sincerity by the affection of charity, I cannot refuse whatever you command, especially since execution ought always to attend honourable commands as their companion, and to bring the fruit of gladness to those who give holy orders. For what uprightness [Col. 1235D] commands ought not to be troublesome; what love dictates, difficult; what usefulness persuades, burdensome.

2. What, moreover, can be judged more useful than to fashion examples for spiritual exercises, sow discipline among conduct, celebrate the virtues of the saints, and hand down to posterity the things that they may follow in holiness and righteousness before God? Indeed, what is the life of a bishop worthy of God but an outstanding light for living well, a mirror of holiness, a title of righteousness, a school of piety, a pattern of doctrine, an ordinance of discipline [Note: [Col. 1236D] The manuscripts read *satio*, “a sowing.”], and an example of religion? Every sex, age, condition, rank, order, and state has in him something to choose; and the holy brightness of this light pours forth abundantly upon all.

In him childhood finds what to admire; youth, what to imitate; mature strength, what [Col. 1236B] to seek; and watchful old age, what to pursue. Nobility is instructed by him to seek delights of the soul more than those of the flesh, and to adorn the dignity of birth with the beauty of virtues. The condition of every order is taught humility and obedience, lest the mind, vainly swept upward above itself by the wind of a perverse whirlwind, swell with ambitious pride and seem to belong to him who is king over all the children of pride. Authority is taught not to think lofty thoughts but to fear; and the eminence of earthly exaltation to submit humbly to heavenly commands and not reject the divine will.

Episcopal authority is taught to rise against offenders with zeal for righteousness in such a way that it does not abandon the gentleness of meekness, and to pursue the equity of judgements in such a way that indulgence does not smell of laxity nor vengeance of cruelty. The life of preachers is called upon not to place the Gospel in learned words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of spirit and power, lest, seeking glory from human beings, it fail to obtain the glory which comes from God alone, and, poured out abroad, be left empty of the gift of inward reward. The condition of peoples is ordered not to depart from the foundation of faith, to persevere in the law of the covenant, to be subject to princely decrees, and not oppose public acts of enforcement. Thus all are made fruitful by one man’s example, and in all his work the worship of piety and the path of truth shine forth.

3. Let us praise the Lord who made him, who, just as he is always and everywhere wondrous in his saints, is likewise wonderfully praiseworthy in the virtue of most blessed Amand. [Col. 1236D] In him he gives glory to his name: he who magnified him in praise, made him exalted in a word of glory, and subdued monsters by his words. Therefore, with the supporting aid of your prayers, timid indeed because of my incompetence but confident because of charity, with obedience as my guide, I undertake what you command, satisfying to the best of my ability the command of charity.

Yet I do not undertake to correct what has first been set down, lest I seem insufficiently reverent toward antiquity, and lest variety of style produce an ill-proportioned work which fails to bring the weight of the thoughts and the glory of the subject into the unity of a coherent composition. Therefore, retaining the thread of the theme and arranging the chapters under fixed headings [Note: [Col. 1237D] We place in the margin this division into chapters made by the author.], I begin the commissioned work with the help of divine mercy and of your devotion, and with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

# LETTER OF THE SAME AUTHOR TO ABBOT JOHN

[Col. 1237B]

To his beloved father and friend in Christ, JOHN, by God’s grace abbot of the monastery of Elnone, and to the holy community of that place: Brother PHILIP of Almsgiving, [wishes them] to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

[Note: [Col. 1237D] John II, forty-third abbot, formerly superior of the same monastery, was compelled, after fourteen years, to resign at Arras in the presence of William, archbishop of Rheims. His successor was Eustace, treasurer of the church of Blandin, an excellent man.]

By a perpetual rite fire is commanded to burn continually on the altar, while each day the priest supplies wood to it, furnishing fuel for the consuming of the sacrifices. The authority of the letter of the Law keeps watch before the doors of the tabernacle, the Holy Spirit signifying inwardly by this that the altar of the heart ought always to blaze with the fire of charity, to which the faithful and diligent worker must continually furnish, as daily fuel, works of piety. For the form of a burnt offering is not praiseworthy unless the incense of mutual love rises in the sight of the Lord as an odour of sweetness.

This reflection does not permit me, in love for you, to cultivate an avoidable failing [Note: [Col. 1238D] Thus the manuscript codex; another reads *fructicare*, “to bear fruit.” The printed edition reads *fructicarum*.], but, in the affections of devout devotion toward your service, my studious mind watches with the movement of sincere charity, so that our service may be reasonable before God and the saving sacrifice of this offering may profit us both. But when I had lately intended to come to meet your holiness, “a lion was in the road, a horned viper in the path”: a grievous onset of suddenness. “I heard, and my belly was troubled; at the sound my lips trembled” (Hab. 1). My senses were confounded and the state of my mind withered, because so suddenly there was removed from our midst a lofty pillar, powerfully impressed by the hand of the supreme craftsman with the mark of holiness, [Col. 1237D] glory, and honour.

The good shepherd has departed: the glory of the order, an example of piety, a sower of discipline, an ornament of religion, a dwelling-place of virtues, a counsellor of peace, a way of uprightness, a surveyor of the common good; a comforter [Note: [Col. 1238D] The manuscript reads *solator*, “comforter”; the printed edition, *solutor*, “one who releases/pays.”] of the poor and an arbiter of equity. The flourishing state of the monastery in the worship of righteousness before God, and its splendid buildings in the sight of human beings, give ample testimony to his abundant wisdom and renowned industry.

Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may mourn—not the sons of my people slain by the sword, but the passing of our common father, the sad sundering from a most sweet friend, the lamentable misery of public desolation? This occasion of necessity confronts us, that we may pay tears in funeral observances. Yet nothing is lamentable for him who, stripped of the chaff of flesh, happily passes into the heavenly granary. Though we lack his delightful presence, we nevertheless ought to store up in the treasury of memory what we may admire in him [Note: [Col. 1238D] Thus the manuscript; the printed edition has *meremur*, “deserve.”], what is sweet to imitate, and what is gracious to set before others.

5. Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place: in the setting of so great a light it defended your place against darkness, restrained the storms of divisions amid so great a disturbance, and brought back the grace of holy consolation after [Col. 1238B] grief. Rejoice, shepherd, in the praiseworthy unity, faithful constancy, and singular grace of the chosen flock. Rejoice in the advancement of the order and the exercise of discipline; rejoice in the worship of righteousness and works of holiness. Rejoice, sacred community, in the appointment of a new shepherd, who entered not through Simon’s gates or the tunnels of falsehood like a hireling, but, with your harmony serving him, was called by the Lord like Aaron and made Peter’s minister and Amand’s successor.

May he be found steadfast with Peter and lovable with Amand, as I desire. If anyone judges his age less than sincerely, or unequal to the burden or honour, let him hear the Apostle saying to Timothy: “Let no one despise your youth” (1 Tim. 4). Let him read and understand that Jeremiah was called as a boy to preach [Col. 1238C] (Jer. 1); that Daniel, a boy, rose against shameless elders in a spirit of judgement and a spirit of ardour, sternly and humbly (Dan. 13); that at about that age David was chosen by the Lord and anointed king (1 Kings 16); and that John the Evangelist was raised to the apostolic order. Youth possessing the habits of old age is more useful and far more commendable than aged old age entangled in the sports of youth and subject to frivolity: “For the grey hairs of a person are understanding, and useful old age is an unstained life” (Wis. 4). We rejoice in the Lord, brothers, that you are thus united by a spiritual covenant: that the zeal of your charity may burn toward one another, displaying the light of honour and the example of piety.

6. And behold, what you sought is at hand; what [Col. 1238D] you ordered has been completed; what you commanded has been supplied. It has not indeed been written as it ought, or as reverence for so great a patron or the dignity of the subject demanded, but as the slenderness of poor talent and manifold occupations have allowed. And now my mouth is open to you and my heart is enlarged toward you; but the fruitful progeny of my necessities begrudges you my presence and so drags and distracts me that I do not do what I wish, but am often compelled to discharge what I hate. [Col. 1239A] Our common son, Brother Albert, will deliver on our behalf what we send to your charity. Fare well always in the Lord, and pray for us.

[Note: [Col. 1239C] This table of chapters was appended in the manuscripts and printed editions. We mark those items in brackets. We have, however, divided the Life in our customary manner into longer chapters. We nevertheless note here summaries of the author’s own chapters.

# LIFE OF SAINT AMAND

## CHAPTER ONE. Saint Amand’s birth, childhood, and monastic life

7. Therefore the glorious confessor of Christ, Amand, born of parents illustrious in faith and lineage, made the dignity of his birth illustrious by the merits of his life. His father was named Serenus and his mother Amantia; by names so distinguished they foretold, with a happy omen, both the name and glory of their holy offspring. Herbatilicus is the name of the place, distinguished by his birth; and, just as it lies not far from the Ocean, so it borders upon Aquitaine.

As the father’s prudent care was exercised concerning the child entrusted to him, he was committed to the diligence of a teacher for instruction in sacred letters, so that the distinguished cultivation of the first liberal studies might raise the earliest rudiments of his tender age, and so that, grace making doctrine sweet, he might draw from the breasts of wisdom an understanding of the divine law. Already at that time the signs of future holiness shone brightly in the boy, and the appearance of a radiant flower displayed the abundance of the fruit that would follow. For the hand of the Lord was with him; through its effective power, like a young calf destined to be brought to the plough, he put forth horns and hooves, with which he would trample the uncleanness of the ancient enemy and scatter his wickedness.

The practice of heavenly discipline flourished in him; and his devout mind, about to contend in royal camps, bore fire and sword for the sacrifice. 711 His speech was faithful, his faith affectionate, his affection [Col. 1239C] sincere, his sincerity firm, his firmness constant, his constancy [Col. 1240A] persevering, his perseverance unerring. He practised, indeed, a celibacy marked by disciplined conduct and by a certain adornment of old age; in his fragile body there met a manly spirit and mature counsels. And because esteem for truth always restrains vanity, and “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3), his devout spirit yearned to be transformed into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. Already the offspring of salvation, which his holy mind had conceived from fear of the Lord, longed to break forth into the light, and faithful desire was already sighing in advance for flight from the world.

8. [CHAP. II.] Therefore, prompted by holy desire, he left his parents and his father’s house and sailed on a favourable voyage to the island of Ogia, which is about forty miles from the shore of the Ocean. There he was received with the pleasant devotion of brothers serving God; he brought the hidden purpose he had conceived to a celebrated fulfilment, and by the reasoning of heavenly philosophy crushed worldly glory. He renounced the distinction of lineage in order to live as one cast down in the house of God; he fled fleshly enticements and rejected the shows of vanity; he renounced the insignia of dignities, set limits to desires, imposed bounds upon curiosity, declared war upon vices, gave precedence to service of virtue, and took up the way of truth with an unfeigned heart.

Having become poor, he followed the poor Christ; and, a novice monk, he embraced with all diligence the observance of regular discipline. He was nourished by fasts, refreshed by vigils, gladdened by labours, restored by prayer, and filled with the dishes of reading. He overcame weariness through occupations, wiped away disgust by variety, adorned silence with meditation, composed his impulses by stability, delighted in the zeal of the brethren, advanced by imitation, was set aflame by examples, and formed by exhortations. He made the way of righteousness bright by the services of charity and adorned the grace of his labour with the fitting ornament of wholesome obedience. The faithful community of the brethren marvelled at so great an adornment of perfection in an age so frail; they marvelled at the rising, as it were, of a new star. In the presence of the Lord, they resounded with thanksgiving and a voice of praise for the fellowship of so great a fellow-soldier.

9. [CHAP. III.] Gnawing envy is accustomed to waste away at another’s advancement, and it belongs to wickedness not to behold the progress of innocence with a serene countenance. “The sinner sees and is angered; he gnashes his teeth and wastes away” (Ps. 111). In turbulent indignation he is confounded at the glory of holiness. The enemy of humankind renews the snares of his ancient deceit, and through an instrument familiar to himself strives either to extinguish or to disturb the radiant flame of this new light.

Once the holy boy was travelling alone across the island, summoned by the order of his superiors. He did not decline the service by which he might earn favour. He went, wholly intent upon himself and contemplating heavenly things in his mind; before the golden altar which is in the sight of God, he burned the incense of devout devotion. He appointed a solemn day amid dense thickets, even to the horn of the altar; he feasted joyfully from the table of the Presence and delighted in gladness. Pleasant rest often becomes the origin of danger, and from the harvest of joys there arose a plant of sorrow.

Stirred by the stings of envy, the enemy of humankind came upon him, assuming the same form and the same nature by which he dealt the wound of death to the first-created human beings and, having broken them by the seductive fraud of a promise, consigned them to the yoke of wretched captivity. Suddenly, a monstrous serpent in body, dreadful in form, horrifying in appearance, presented itself to his sacred gaze and changed the sabbath of his mind into stupefaction. Unexpected events easily shake inexperienced minds, and a sudden assault readily overthrows their settled state. At the monster’s approach, the boy of the Lord was seized with fear, troubled by distress, confused by trembling; anxiously he considered flight, yet he dreaded the dragon’s attack, and he could not decide whether it was safer to flee or remain.

10. The Lord’s regard is always upon the elect, and he does not abandon his saints in the day of evils, nor leave them without help in the time of the proud. Divine mercy suddenly restores one who is wavering and revives one who is trembling; it raises the agitations of an anxious mind toward the strengthening of confidence. Therefore, returning to his heart, he warmed again into his former fervour. He gathered anew the weapons of happier hope, and awaited from the treasury of divine mercy the badge of a blessed victory. Thus, prostrate upon the ground, he was indeed pierced with compunction for his earlier disturbance, yet gave thanks for the visitation; and a brief, effective prayer for assistance was carried to the throne of grace. His cry was heard on high, and from the heavenly mercy-seat the gift of an answered prayer was brought as help.

Immediately he rose fearless; and, making the sign of the cross against the enemy, he commanded by the powerful force of his words that the dragon’s malice should depart from the bounds of the island, and henceforth bring no harm upon its inhabitants. Struck as though by a sling-shot [Note: Col. 1241D: Thus the manuscripts; the printed edition has “by a heavier engine.”], the serpent’s power was crushed by the force of that mighty command. With lowered head, confounded, it departed, and did not resist the decree of its commander. In the serpent the devil was conquered, and clothed, as it were, in a double garment of his own confusion. In return for the fear he had inflicted, he received sheaves of pain and anguish; and the weaker the victor’s age appeared, the more grievously was he tormented by madness. He was more violently troubled and more deeply put to shame.

11. [CHAPTER IV.] An unbridled mind does not take warning from past events, but insolent irreverence continually frequents the tents of slander [Col. 1242B]. The adversary, whom he had been unable to break by terror, tried to weaken by blandishments; and, with the abundant retinue of cautious piety [Note: Col. 1241D: Manuscripts, “cautious.”], he strove to recall him from his holy resolve. Concern for visiting him beat upon the father’s heart; affections that had grown cool revived within him. By new suggestions he awakened old desires, and kindled in the parent’s mind a new ardour [Note: Col. 1242D: Printed editions, “sometimes.”].

Sprinkled with these shadows, the mind of Serenus the father ceased to be serene. He could not endure to be without so sweet a pledge; though his son lived, he believed himself bereaved, as though after the ashes of the grave. Accordingly, casting aside regard for divine fear, he resolved to tear from the monastery one whom no willing offering of paternal authority had assigned there, and determined to call back to the right of the despised inheritance the heir who had fled.

Having crossed the sea, therefore, he came down to the island [Col. 1242C]. On arriving at the monastery he was gladly received; and, after greeting the brethren, he asked for and obtained from the prior of the place an interview with his son. Calling him aside to a more private place, after affectionate kisses and miscellaneous conversation, mature arguments were advanced and earnest persuasion introduced: he was to cast off the garb of sacred religion, return to his homeland, and reclaim his inheritance. The father’s state of bereavement was set before him; the mother’s unceasing and anxious grief over her son’s tender age; the injury done to their nobility; the repeated complaints of their fellow-countrymen; and the general wish of all who lived with them for his return.

12. All this was reckoned by the boy of the Lord as the whisper of a light breeze. His father’s prayers were rejected, his blandishments spurned, his counsels condemned beforehand. Serenus put on a cloud of indignation that was anything but serene [Col. 1242D]. He swelled in spirit and rose wholly into anger; he heaped up threats to terrify him and could not bear his own contempt with equanimity. Stricken inwardly, therefore, by grief of heart, he disowned his son, annulled his rights of succession, and pronounced a declaration of disinheritance [Note: Col. 1242D: In another manuscript, “speech” (*eloquium*)].

But he, stationed upon the lofty watchtower of his mind and raised above the world, regarded all these things as nothing and emptiness. Unmoved in face and mind, he looked down alike upon his father’s coaxing and threats—yet without violating the claims of reverence or breaking the duty of filial affection. Retaining, indeed, the balance of inward self-control, he “orders his words with judgment” [Col. 1243A] (Psalm 111). “Keep your inheritance, father,” he said; “the Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; he himself will restore my inheritance to me” (Psalm 15). Heavenly lineage is worthier than earthly. It is fitting to prefer the immortal Father to a mortal father.

The father, frustrated in his hope and disturbed by these words, departed. His labour defeated, he withdrew empty-handed and returned home. Thus for the second time “the Lord made marvellous his holy one” (Psalm 4), glorifying the man who feared him; and before him the malignant perversity of the ancient deceiver was reduced to nothing.

13. [CHAPTER V.] It is not shameful to change one’s plans when circumstances change, nor unreasonable to adopt a course of action when pressing reasons require it. Moved, as is believed, by this impulse, the servant of the Lord resolved to travel as a pilgrim, so that the discipline of the flesh, undertaken through the urgency of toil, might increase more excellently, and that he might avoid similar attacks in the future. For just as vices must be fled along with their causes, so too must the occasion of an imposed temptation be avoided. The influences of fleshly kinship incline a person to evil more readily than the terror of swords or the cruelty of power can do; and human nature is always readier to follow than to be dragged.

Therefore the first steps of his vowed pilgrimage were directed toward the city of Tours, so that the purpose thus undertaken might be guided by the patronage of blessed Martin and the work begun advanced by the intercessions of the saints. Approaching the tomb of the glorious confessor in a spirit of humility, amid the devout approaches to that sacred shrine, he particularly asked that, through the merits of the holy Father, this might be obtained for him from God: that every possibility and occasion of returning to his homeland should thereafter be closed off. For just as it is unsafe to sleep beside a serpent, so there is no secure companionship for those professing piety among acquaintances and relatives devoted to worldly life.

After remaining for a while in that place, he offered to God the first-fruits of his head: he received the sign of the royal priesthood and was initiated into the clergy by ecclesiastical tonsure [Col. 1243C].

14. Afterwards, having sought the blessing of the brethren of that place, he went forward and resumed his interrupted journey. Thence, guided by the Lord, he came to Bourges and turned aside to its bishop for lodging. At that time the church was governed by the blessed father Austrigisilus, a man venerable in life [Col. 1243D]; his company was adorned by Sulpitius, archdeacon and distinguished confessor, who by merit of life and grace of character was soon to become bishop after that holy man. These received the arriving servant of God with the due office of hospitality and, in the benevolence of charity, supplied assistance suited to his need.

15. [CHAPTER VI.] Blessed Amandus was in the years of puberty, in the first bloom of youth. He did not separate the fervour of his spirit from the ardour of his age, so that the strength of his soul might grow together with his body, and so that in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth he might consecrate his devoted youth to the Lord. This man, full of God, understood that something more secluded must be undertaken by him, so that by a stricter guard, a more ready zeal, and purer vigilance, he might weaken the unformed impulses of slippery youth and the native stirrings of the flesh [Col. 1244A]. For those tending toward eternity must apply the discipline of severe chastisement to domestic impulses, lest the soul miserably serve when it ought nobly to rule.

The chosen man earnestly desired to eat this Passover with the perfect, and by a solitary conflict to seek victory over the enemy, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “Blessed is the man who has borne the Lord’s yoke from his youth; he shall sit alone and keep silence, and shall raise himself above himself” (Lamentations 3). A holy intention readily obtains fitting success, and possibility scarcely fails the desire that the pursuits of piety have raised.

At his request, men of mercy—the holy bishop and the faithful archdeacon—swiftly built a cell above the city wall. There, in the happy manner of pilgrimage, a stranger to the world [Col. 1244B], a stranger to the flesh, a stranger to the senses and to the companionship of vanities, he might more freely cling to God alone, devote himself more ardently, serve more faithfully, and fight more fruitfully. Into this prison of voluntary necessity the man of God entered, bound by the fetter of charity, intending to fight with humble and modest vigilance against the vices of flesh and spirit, against worldly glory, and against spiritual wickedness.

16. In battle, sackcloth became his clothing; barley bread his food; ordinary water his drink; and the ground, covered with cheap scraps, his couch. His life became one of unbroken abstinence, frequent vigils, untiring prayer, faithful silence, continual meditation on the sacred law, and effective devotion to divine reading. Thus his manifold occupation was balanced, so that hostile idleness could find no opening, the crafty enemy lacked access, and, with the outer door shut, divine protection might preserve the righteous man concealed within the ark of wisdom against outward storms [Col. 1244C].

For almost fifteen years the man of God lived in this way; and in such things the life of his spirit drew shoots of virtues from the eternal vine, and, budding from the drops of grace, brought forth holiness. After the outstanding labours of his chosen prison, the faithful watches of extraordinary conflict, and the continual sufferings of his mortified body—after the movements of age had been powerfully subdued and the period of time already mentioned had elapsed—the desire for his vowed pilgrimage revived, and memory of his earlier purpose vigorously raised him toward the journey first planned.

## CHAPTER II. Saint Amandus’ First Journey to Rome. The Word of God Preached.

[Col. 1244D]

17. [CHAPTER VII.] He left his solitary dwelling; the busy leisure of his sweet retreat was released into public life; the hiding-place of his concealed way of life was brought out beneath the sun’s gaze. Yet we must not suppose that the servant of God acted here from frivolity, or set out without a familiar command imprinted upon the page of his heart by the pen of a swiftly writing scribe. The spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one. Although the virtue of the saints must always be imitated, their acts are not always capable of imitation; many of their deeds declare not a rule for living but a privilege of divine gift, in which they have been handed down for admiration, not as examples.

It is permitted to marvel at the servant of God in this matter; it is not permitted to imitate him, because a private concession does not become a general decree [Col. 1245A], nor is a special grace spread abroad to all. For the Holy Spirit does not breathe everywhere, but where he wills; and he gives precedence to the voice of power over his own voice, so that one taught inwardly may hear what he says, and may understand from the commandments, choosing the paths of truth.

Thus, as is fitting to believe, the holy man departed content with one companion only, and undertook the journey which, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, he had conceived, to be endowed with the profit of spiritual grace. Having completed the journey—after the dreadful and steep Alpine route, the winding and slippery summits of the Apennines, and the dangerous, difficult crossings of rivers—he joyfully entered Rome, city of the apostolic summit, delighted by his happy arrival.

There, at the confession-shrine of blessed Peter, he reverently prostrated himself with tears and prayer [Col. 1245B]. Devoted in mind, he gave himself to holy petitions; he sought what would profit the remaining time and order of his life; he rested wholly upon divine mercy; and in the joy of his heart he renewed thanksgivings for freely granted aid. Thence he eagerly went about the memorial shrines of the holy martyrs [Note: Col. 1245D: Printed edition, “tombs”], seeking from the Father of lights, through their intercessions, that fruit might be granted to his work.

18. [CHAPTER VIII.] Just as righteousness strives to perform what belongs to it, so wicked envy does not withdraw from its deadly purpose. The persistent malice of Satan besets the paths of the righteous and circles them by ambush, seeking to turn the works of piety into a stumbling-block. One day blessed Amandus returned, as was his custom, from the vowed circuit of sacred visitation, so that the day might be completed and prayer continued in the basilica of blessed Peter [Col. 1245C].

After the evening synaxis, when the others had gone away, he wished to remain there alone for this purpose. One of the sacristans came, searching the holy places in the course of his watch, lest anything should occur that might disturb the service entrusted to him. When this man found the servant of God, unknown to him, in a hidden place, he was disturbed by a sudden impulse; laying hands on him rather uncivilly and not without insulting words, he violently and irreverently drove him from the enclosure of the church.

But Amandus, confining himself within the bounds of patience, bore the injury in a spirit of gentleness, despised the slanders, and endured the vexation. Roused by reproach, he did not withdraw from his work of holiness; rather, in hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs, the service of heart and voice sounding together, he paid to the Lord the due measure of his service with all humility [Col. 1245D]. Here too the ancient deceiver was beaten back and mocked by the judgment of truth, because humility, when struck down, carried away consolation, while fraudulent impiety found no rest in the desire of its own heart.

19. [CHAPTER IX.] Thus excluded, he sat upon the steps of ascent before the church doors. After the course of prayer, the tears of piety, and the holy sighs of inward love [Col. 1246A], he was suddenly caught up and, in an ecstasy of mind, saw blessed Peter standing beside him, radiant in shining apparel, with cheerful countenance and serene face. After granting the gift of this pious visitation, after the communion of sweet speech and the gentle consolation of holy familiarity, Peter announced that he must turn his journey back toward Gaul, in order to labour more diligently in the Lord’s field and watch as a ready minister over the harvest which had grown so abundant.

Strengthened by the heavenly oracle and fortified by the apostolic voice’s exhortation, he turned his road toward Gaul and showed by deed that he understood what came from the commandments.

20. [CHAPTER X.] At that time Lothair reigned in Gaul [Note: Col. 1245D: This is Chlothar II, on whose death in 628 his son Dagobert succeeded; under him the events that follow were more properly carried out], a man energetic in military affairs, no less great in virtue than in glory, and an outstanding defender of the Christian faith. Fourth from Clovis—whom it is established was baptized through the ministry of blessed Remigius [Col. 1246B; Note: Col. 1245D: Fourth from Chlodovech I not in the order of reign but of descent: he had him as great-grandfather, Chlothar I as grandfather, and Chilperic as father]—he joined clemency in authority with moral distinction at the height of dignity, and in abundant worldly prosperity maintained the grace of gentleness.

He honoured the pastors of the Church with reverence, adorned churches with frequent gifts and estates, and enlarged the glory of his kingdom by continual gains. When the renowned reputation of the blessed man reached him, the distinguished men Audoenus [Note: Col. 1246D: Commemorated 1 October. On his age and the baptism of Chlodovech, we have treated at this date in the Life of Saint Vedast; likewise on the king’s baptism, 5 February, in the Life of Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne] and Eligius actively urged the matter. Though still wearing secular dress, they held no insignificant position among the leaders of the court. Amandus was summoned to the king; and, after pontifical authority had been brought forward, by the prince’s will and with the approving agreement of the great men, he was ordained bishop for the office of preaching, as the custom of that time required [Col. 1246C]. With everyone’s favour and goodwill he was sent to spread the Gospel ordinances among the nations, proclaim Christ’s name to unbelievers, and lay the foundations of faith.

21. Reverently accepting the office imposed upon him, the holy man strove diligently to fulfil the work of an evangelist. He strove to profit all alike by word and example; faithfully to invest in spiritual gain the talent entrusted to him; to distribute with grace the bread of faith to those who did not know faith; and to recall the erring from idol-worship to the way of truth. Because he preached the grace of eternal redemption, he compassionately devoted himself to redeeming captives, so that he might free in them alike the yoke of worldly and diabolical slavery, and so that the esteem of his mercy might lend weight and grace to his holy preaching [Col. 1246D].

If misfortune assigned any children to redemption, he purified them in the water of baptism and applied them to the study of letters, lest lack of discipline disgrace those reborn, or ignorance overwhelm those to be advanced. With the blessed Father’s help, some of these later became outstanding defenders of truth, chosen priests, teachers of churches, and superiors of monasteries who professed holy monastic life.

[Col. 1247A] 22. [CHAPTER XI.] While the blessed man crowned the beginnings of his episcopal ministry by such transactions, he was invited by the distinguished man Audoenus, whom we mentioned above, to consecrate a monastery which he had established by command of the aforesaid king [Note: Col. 1247D: Rather, after Chlothar’s death, Saint Audoenus asked and obtained the site from King Dagobert and built the monastery, as is clear from the Life of Saint Agilus, first abbot of Rebais, 30 August, chapters 11 and 12].

Blessed Faro, bishop of Meaux [Note: Col. 1247D: Saint Faro is commemorated 28 October], was summoned; and together with blessed Agilus [Note: Col. 1247D: In another manuscript, *Agasilo*, less correctly], he worked diligently to complete the appointed task. When all had been duly performed and the holy bishops approached to consecrate the altar, the marble slab placed upon it was found to lie unevenly. They deferred the sacred mysteries for a time, prepared to correct the discovered unevenness, and diligently sought to restore the sloping surface of the altar-table.

While the holy men held the slab in their hands after moving it from its place, and handled it incautiously, the marble suddenly slipped and fell to the ground; striking it violently, it split at once into two pieces. Troubled and alarmed, the venerable men were greatly distressed and marked the misfortune of this pressing accident with words of lamentation. Then blessed Amandus, with blessed Faro and Agilus, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, fell prostrate in prayer with tears; and, as their affection penetrated heaven, they awaited from the clemency of the eternal Father relief from the grievous mishap.

Rising from prayer, they made the sign of the life-giving cross over the stone and saw the marble restored and made whole in its former condition [Note: Col. 1247D: The same miracle is narrated in the Acts of Saint Agilus, chapter 15, and of Saint Faro; in both, Saint Amandus is said to have been present]. Yet, as a sign and memorial of the miracle, a fine line appeared in the middle where it had split, like a ruled division [Col. 1247C].

There was solemn rejoicing at the divine gift; the work of consecration was completed in joy; and abundant thanks were offered to the giver of so renowned a mercy. Therefore Audoenus, the distinguished man, lest age consume so worthy a work or forgetfulness hide it, ordered the aforesaid marble to be marked with prominent letters containing the definite statement that this altar had been consecrated through the ministry of blessed Amandus.

Moreover, the holy Fathers directed that the inhabitants call the place Jerusalem [Note: Col. 1248D: Aimoin, *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 41, writes: “Blessed Audoenus built a monastery within the forest of Brie, which indeed is called Jerusalem, but, from the river upon which it stands, the monastery is called Rebais”], because of the frequent visions of spiritual revelations and the continual benefits of miracles which divine mercy deigned there to perform abundantly through its servants.

23. [CHAPTER XII.] Then, lest anything be lacking from the title of glory or the abundance of reward, blessed Amandus, beloved by God and humankind, went out to more remote regions [Col. 1247D] and to peoples entangled in the worship of idols, in order to give the Lord’s people knowledge of salvation in the remission of their sins: that Christ’s light might shine in darkness, the Lord’s saving help be made known, worship of righteousness be revealed to unbelievers, and the grace of truth disclosed. This was the labour and zeal of the man of God: he applied himself to this work by day and night and increased in spiritual gains, with the Lord working together with him and confirming the word by the signs that followed.

## CHAPTER III. Saint Amandus’ Second Journey to Rome. The People of Ghent and Others Instructed.

24. [CHAPTER XIII.] True humility never presumes upon itself; and the higher it is lifted to the citadel of virtue, the more closely it gathers its own refuse into itself, considering itself less than those whose estimation calls it more exalted. Heavenly authority and the faithful command of the apostle Peter, at whose bidding he had undertaken the burden and work of preaching, might have sufficed for the man of God. Yet, lest the spirit of envy brand him with the mark of presumption if he preached Christ among the nations without the Vicar of Christ [Col. 1248B], he set out for Rome a second time.

Before the supreme pontiff he humbly disclosed the whole extent of his labour and purpose in submission; in shining speech he expressed his heart’s desire and brought the flame of his holy longing before the holiness of the supreme Father. He showed that the abundance of the Lord’s harvest needed labourers, and asked that his own need be relieved by paternal help.

The bishop worthy of God marvelled at the man of God’s zeal, approved his diligence, commended his teaching, revered his purpose, praised his persistence, extolled his labours, shared his concern amid dangers, and delighted in his progress. Therefore, to increase his companionship and labour, he assigned to Gaul with blessed Amandus, by apostolic authority, capable and industrious men: Landoald, archpriest [Note: Col. 1248D: We have shown in §12 that Saint Landoald and his companions were given by Pope Saint Martin to Saint Amandus as assistants on his third journey to Rome], and Amantius, deacon, set apart for the work of holy ministry, with others whose names we do not retain [Col. 1248C].

Having obtained his desire, he left the City with the Father’s blessing and was carried by ship to Centumcellae. He conceived great hope and rejoiced in the fullness of his faithful company.

25. [CHAPTER XIV.] The ancient transgressor always hangs over the joyful, seeking to stain the blessed persons’ joys with his foul sprinkling. Toward evening, as was his habit, the man of God was engaged privately in prayer when the malignant spirit seized one of the boys, shook him violently, and dragged him out toward the sea to drown him. Surrounded by the terror of night and the horror of the enemy, the boy cried out with a dreadful shriek as often as he could, repeatedly invoking Christ’s name, tearfully imploring Christ’s help [Col. 1248D], and faithfully commending himself to Christ.

The wicked assailing invader [Note: Col. 1248D: In another manuscript, “perverter”] mockingly answered the crying boy: “Who was this Christ to whom he so diligently commended himself?” When the boy was silent, the blessed man was angered at these words and called out strongly to him: “Answer, son: Christ is he who was born of the Virgin, [Col. 1249A] suffered for us, and rose from the dead.” At this confession the demon vanished in confusion, and by the merit of holiness the boy was delivered from imminent drowning.

26. [CHAPTER XV.] Then they boarded ship and traversed the regions of the Tyrrhenian sea, passing swiftly by the winding bends of the shores. As Amandus, according to his custom, poured out to those sitting with him in the ship the nectar of the divine word, like a heavenly cupbearer, a great fish suddenly appeared before the sailors and began to press against the ship in repeated attacks. The crew, skilled in fishing, watched it closely, surrounded it with their equipment for sea-hunting, and hauled it up.

Joyfully, therefore, they gave thanks for the divine gift, and from so remarkable a catch provisions for a common meal were prepared [Col. 1249B]. They feasted and rejoiced, spending the day in festivity and celebrating the welcome reward of their happy success. Mortal frailty is always uncertain of itself and scarcely understands either causes or outcomes. Amid their meal and words of joy, the face of the sea suddenly grew dreadful; the sky, with the sun withdrawn, passed into gloomy darkness; and the spirit of storms, pressing more violently upon them, overwhelmed the minds of those rejoicing and their state of security by the force of the whirlwind and the repeated assaults of waves.

Everything stored for food was thrown into the sea; baggage was cast out; vessels together with utensils were thrown overboard; the ship was emptied of everything, so that it might float over the wave-crests with lighter motion and, though their possessions were lost, life alone might at least be saved. Everywhere was fear; everywhere the many images of death; and despair, the companion of miseries, thought of nothing but the end [Col. 1249C].

They therefore begged the man of God to intervene on their behalf with the Judge’s mercy and offer the sacrifices of prayer to the Redeemer for their common danger. The blessed man comforted those struck with terror and urged them to turn to the Lord with all their heart and hope for a saving outcome from the Almighty’s mercy. Then he turned to prayer, the familiar refuge in every affliction, and offered earnest entreaties to the supreme Majesty for his own safety and that of his companions. His affections struck heaven; his devotion rose beyond the heights; and with the strong advance of his mind he summoned the Father of mercies and God of all consolation to the remedies of his customary compassion.

27. [CHAPTER XVI.] While praying, the man of God was suddenly carried away into sleep [Col. 1249D], and, amid the intense travail of his spirit, the weakness of his flesh gave way. The heavenly key-bearer came to him as he rested and led him, through the door of gentle consolation, into the private chamber of mercy, saying: “Rise, Amandus; do not fear. You shall not perish, and those whom the fellowship of this necessity has joined to you shall escape the danger.”

With these words, sleep and storm alike dispersed, and the joyful serenity of desired calm shone forth. When morning came, they left the ship and all returned to dry land. Giving thanks for their deliverance, they went to their respective homes. Glorious is God in his saints: he heard his servant crying to him so mercifully, helped him powerfully, and delivered him effectively [Col. 1250A]. And Amandus himself is worthy of praise: through his eminent merit, praiseworthy life, and outstanding work, he obtained so much from his Lord’s grace that he profited not only himself but others also for salvation, and drove away by the benefit of holy prayer the grievous danger which had arisen for the common destruction.

28. [CHAPTER XVII.] Meanwhile King Lothair entered the way of all flesh [Note: Col. 1249D: Philip states that Saint Amandus died in 661; therefore he anticipates events here, treating as under Chlothar II occurrences that took place under his son Dagobert and grandsons Chlodovech II and Saint Sigebert]. Dagobert was appointed his successor, a vigorous imitator of his father’s virtues and piety as well as of his rule.

During Dagobert’s reign, blessed Amandus returned from the city and began, as he was accustomed, to exercise the ministry of the word more diligently and to produce spiritual gains for souls through the advance of the divine gift. For this purpose he went to Ghent and strove to fill the barrenness of an unbelieving people with the fruitfulness of the divine seed [Col. 1250B]. In order that he might rise more freely and securely to the work of Gospel sowing, through the intervention of Aicharius, bishop of Noyon, of holy memory, he received letters from the aforesaid king directing that no one should reject the word of life, the yoke of faith, or the sacraments of grace. Thus, with the earthly king serving the heavenly King, the holy word might run swiftly; and, for the destruction of death and the devil’s throat, the two swords might join, since happy and pleasant is the union when the retinue of earthly rank is raised at the trumpet-call of spiritual warfare.

29. [CHAPTER XVIII.] That people, barren and hungry for the abundance of grace just as it was rich in soil, devoted itself to the cults of frenzied error and sacrifices to idols. Thus, at the instigation of the enemy of salvation, it rejected with hard brow and unyielding heart the counsel of eternal peace, and resisted saving admonitions with stiff-necked effort [Col. 1250C].

Nevertheless, the man of God laboured by persistent zeal and continual effort to lead those drawn into the lodging-places of death into the kingdom of life through the grace of sanctification. Impiety opposed the services of piety and repeatedly attempted by ambush to drag the minister of life to death. Disregarding the death of his own body, he was often beaten, treated with insults, struck with injuries, provoked by reproaches, and frequently thrown into the river; he endured the violence of persecution even from little women. The more fragile their sex, the more wicked their judgment, and the more depraved and brazen their inclination to malice is accustomed to be.

The brethren who had followed him, bound to him by excessive affection, and who supplied familiar companionship in God’s work, were compelled by fear of death and the squalor of hunger. Broken in spirit, they departed and returned home, leaving him behind [Col. 1250D]. He, so as not to burden anyone or make the Gospel cost-free, worked with his own hands for his living and, insofar as he was able, to provide for those suffering need.

30. [CHAPTER XIX.] Nothing is so arduous or difficult that persistent labour cannot conquer and frequent filing smooth; especially when grace, the companion of diligence, gives assistance. At last a great door was opened to his holy labours. As magnates came with the people in a stream to the faith, the holy man, through God’s power, shattered idols [Col. 1251A], destroyed temples, demolished altars, excluded the worship of wretched superstition, and cast off the errors of deceived paganism.

Therefore, to the praise and glory of God’s name, the triumphant standard of the life-giving cross was raised. With the rite changed, saving sacrifices were offered for the faithful; and, once the blood of slaughtered offerings had been removed, the worship of Catholic religion was established through the Eucharist. At the expense of the faithful a notable structure was built in the same place, elevated into a dwelling of faith by solemn sacraments and consecrated through the ministry of blessed Amandus in honour and in the name of the Prince of the Apostles.

Another church for divine worship was also built in the place which ancient paganism, devoted to pleasures, had customarily called Blandinium, because it seemed gentle in its delights and especially pleasant. There [Col. 1251B], having established the approved offices of clerics serving God, he entrusted the office of pastoral care to his disciple, the venerable man Florebert. Under Florebert’s blessed instruction, Saint Bavo entered the secrecy of vowed enclosure after being converted from worldly vanity by the preaching of blessed Amandus and receiving tonsure by the grace of blessing according to ecclesiastical rite. There, diligently devoted to vigils, fasts, and prayers, he faithfully strove to offer himself to God the Father as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable, according to the instruction of the man of God.

31. [CHAPTER XX.] Divine favour, ever glorious and effective toward its own, sets better things beneath good things [Note: Col. 1251D: Thus the manuscripts; printed editions have “sets better things above”], and crowns the best with the attainment of perfection. Great and wonderful was Amandus’ glory in holy salvation [Col. 1251C]: the Lord had placed great glory and beauty upon him. But how great the perfection of his power and holiness was is shown by the testimony of the following miracle.

The blessed man had gone up to the city of the Menapii [Note: Col. 1252D: We have established this seat of the Menapii in §3], commonly called Tournai, making his homeland illustrious by the glory of holiness and pouring the grace of sweetness upon a people now believing. Count Dotto, a judge appointed by the king for the province, was sitting there, in order to give order to public affairs, an end to disputes, form to judicial proceedings, punishment to offenses, and justice to those suffering wrong.

As he sat upon the tribunal, a man was brought by the lictors: stained by public disgrace, seized in guilt, pitiable in punishment. The people were dreadfully shouting for a sentence of death against him. The judge, being somewhat too harsh and more indulgent toward anger than was right, hurled upon the wretch, in response to the people’s cry [Col. 1251D], the deadly decree of hanging.

But the blessed man, who always overflowed entirely with the bowels of mercy in the Lord, took pity on the condemned man. He humbly intervened with the judge, offered prayers for the acquittal of one about to perish, and asked that the life enveloped by the sentence of final condemnation might be given to him. Arrogance commonly produces obstinacy, and merciless contempt is born from obstinacy. The judge’s determination remained unmoved; he did not heed the merit of holiness. Rejecting the supplication of the prayers, he decreed that the condemnation once imposed must remain irrevocable.

Accordingly, the wretched man was dragged to the gallows, more wretched in his suffering than in the cruel sentence itself; and he was by then almost wholly consumed by blows, so that he appeared not a man but a corpse torn apart by a beast [Col. 1252A].

32. A humble mind is not confounded by rejection, but takes breath in the mercy of Him who does not abandon utterly nor turn away the prayer of the poor. At once the holy man departed from the judge’s presence and hurried to the place of punishment; but the steps of mercy had preceded the violent hands of the officers, and the life wrenched out by the noose had brought about the sad separation of flesh and spirit. He therefore took the lifeless body down from the gallows and ordered it carried by the hands of those attending to the cell in which he was accustomed to pray. Then, after all had been dismissed, he gave himself wholly to prayer. Holy sighs issued from his inmost breast; he drenched his face with a copious outpouring of devout tears [Col. 1252B], and, with all the strength of his soul, rose to meet the divine mercy, that the man thus extinguished might return to life and be restored anew to the remedies of salvation. The stream is not cut off from its fountain, nor is the vein deprived of the benefit of its own source. A devout affection is received into the embrace of mercy by goodness meeting it halfway, and the Father’s condescension does not turn aside the petition of the son. The fugitive spirit returns to the right of the possession from which it had been torn away; and the dead flesh, granted renewed senses, is raised up. Darkness having been expelled, the eyes return to the light; and, the stiffness imposed upon the body being relaxed, the function of speech is renewed in the language formerly spoken.

When morning came, the holy man summoned the brethren and ordered water to be brought, so that the devoted attendant might wash away the filth of the wounds and the spattering of flowing blood [Col. 1252C], lest anything be lacking to the office of mercy. They supposed that they were being summoned to render the service of washing for a funeral, and thought that the body was to be granted the benefit of burial. But when they entered the cell, they saw—to their astonishment and amazement—the man whom they had left dead conversing with and sitting beside the man of God. They magnified the Redeemer’s mercy in so solemn a work. The holy man humbly begged and adjured them in the Lord not to make this secret public, but to suppress it in more careful silence: it had been granted not by the merit of human frailty, but by the indulgence of divinity. For the holy mind, never departing from the tenor of humility, sought nothing in its works except the splendour of the divine Name and the glory of the heavenly kingdom; the enticements of human favour [Col. 1252D] and the praises of men it abhorred as a dreadful poison. When the body had been washed, he closed the rents of the flesh and the gaping wounds so completely that no trace of its former corruption remained. Thus endowed, he sent the man back to his own home and restored him sound and unharmed to his parents.

33. [CHAPTER XXI.] A hiding-place is sought in vain when fame speaks openly; nor is one deprived of the adornment of glory whom eternal Majesty has determined to glorify. Day by day the beloved name and glory of Amandus increase and spread widely; and, as from a storehouse of light, the pure brightness of a more splendid magnificence flashes forth from the wonder of so great a miracle [Col. 1253A]. From the eminence of so great a power he receives a more abundant grace. The harshness of the Gentiles having been laid aside, necks formerly stiff grow soft; the stings of hatred having been buried, the envy of persecution melts into love; and the briars of malice yield the sweetness of charity. They voluntarily submit their necks to the sacraments of faith; and, after the seats of idols have been overthrown, they bring both an end to error and extermination to brutality. They raise the splendid standards of the Lord’s Passion; they establish churches and holy altars in honour of the Saviour; and with faithful obedience they follow the admonitions of the holy Father.

## CHAPTER IV. The conversion of various persons to monastic life. The exile and return of St Amandus. The baptism of St Sigebert.

[Col. 1253B]

34. 719 [CHAPTER XXII.] For a long time the blessed Gislenus had desired to see him [Note: [Col. 1253D] St Gislenus is commemorated on 9 October.]. Like an outstanding star, whose gleaming splendour appears from east to west, he had migrated from the borders of Greece into Gaul, led by a heavenly oracle [Note: [Col. 1253D] That is, into Belgium, where, on the river Haine, from which the county of Hainaut takes its name, he founded a monastery. From him the town called Gislenopolis grew up around it.]. When he had been instructed by both the sight and conversation of the man of God [Note: [Col. 1253D] He visited him after leaving the bishopric of Maastricht, in the year 650.] and was advancing in the holy work through continual fruitfulness, he took the occasion of the dedication of his monastery, which he had newly built, to invite the servant of God with special diligence, that, together with the blessed Autbert, bishop of Cambrai, he might consecrate the structure of the new work as a dwelling-place of heavenly grace [Note: [Col. 1253D] Fulbert, in the Life of St Autbert, 13 December, likewise reports that this consecration was performed by Saints Autbert and Amandus. It occurred about the year 653.].

While both were jointly labouring at the sacred mysteries and striving fittingly to impress upon the minds of the faithful the pattern of the visible form, Count Madelgarius [Col. 1253C], also called Vincent [Note: [Col. 1253D] He is commemorated on 14 July; the same matters are related in his Life and in that of St Autbert.], was converted by the devout hearing of the assembly from the vanities of the world to the services of divine mercy. Though he was regarded as illustrious and noble among the magnates of the palace, and most pleasing to the king, he renounced the world at the prompting of life-giving preaching. In accordance with the saving teaching of the blessed bishop, he learned to turn his heart away from his own desires, to resist the affections of the flesh [Note: [Col. 1253D] Another manuscript: “pleasures.”], and to possess nothing as his own. He became a citizen of voluntary poverty and crowned the praiseworthy purpose of holiness with the glorious outcome of completion.

35. [CHAPTER XXIII.] A tree is praised by its fruits, and balsams are proved by their fragrance. Quality and use assign value to wares; the beauty of the work commends the craftsman. The noble fruitfulness of the offspring whom, in Christ, he begot through the Gospel composes a celebrated adornment for the servant of God [Col. 1254A]. The illustrious virgin Aldegundis [Note: [Col. 1253D] We have given three Lives of St Aldegundis under 30 January.], whom the gifts of beauty and nobility of birth, together with the grace of character and faithful instruction, had rendered still more worthy, fled suitors and the enticement of the marriage bond. With greater ardour she longed to attain the eternal bridal chamber of incorruption while bearing the title of virginity.

Escaping the hands of those seeking her by the aid of a secret flight and a woodland hiding-place, she learned that the aforesaid bishops had come to the monastery of Altimont [Note: [Col. 1253D] We have dealt with the monastery of Altimont under 16 January, in connection with the Life of Pope St Marcellus, whose relics were translated there.]. Without allowing bodily delay to hold back her desire, she hastened to them as to a city of refuge. Falling therefore at the saints’ feet, she explained what she feared, disclosed what she desired, and asked to be instructed concerning what was expedient. The blessed Amandus refreshed her wavering mind with eloquent speech, raised her to the height of a loftier purpose, and, imposing the use of the sacred veil, consecrated a virgin bride to the virgin Bridegroom [Note: [Col. 1254D] We have related this above; it occurred about the year 661.]. Having happily obtained her vow and been strengthened [Note: [Col. 1254D] We have dealt with Malbodium, a town of Hainaut from which the monastery of Altimont is one league distant, in connection with its Life.], she returned to Malbodium, where she had first hidden herself. There, with the holy bishop’s support and the assistance of King Dagobert’s [Note: [Col. 1254D] Rather, of St Sigebert, whom we have said, under 1 February, to have then been king of Austrasia and to have founded very many monasteries.] generosity, she built a monastery for women serving God.

36. [CHAPTER XXIV.] In like manner the blessed Rictrudis [Note: [Col. 1254D] We have dealt with these matters in the Life of St Adalbald, husband of St Rictrudis, 2 February.], with her daughter St Eusebia, encouraged by the admonitions of the glorious bishop, fortified by his counsels, aided by his prayers, and raised by his support, vowed and paid to the Lord the celibacy of saving continence at the monastery of Marchiennes, or Martianus [Note: [Col. 1254D] We have dealt with the monastery of Marchiennes, or Martianus, there and above, §4. Buzelinus elegantly describes it in book I of *Gallo-Flandria*, chapter 41.], which the holy Father had founded earlier [Note: [Col. 1254D] In the year 645.], under Abbot Jonathas, his disciple [Note: [Col. 1254D] St Jonatus is commemorated on 1 August.].

[Col. 1254C]

37. Her son Maurontus [Note: [Col. 1254D] Huchaldus relates the same story in the Life of St Rictrudis. We have said above, §14, that it happened in the old age of St Amandus.], while the holy Father was celebrating the divine mysteries and he stood reverently at the sacred altars, was seen by that holy bishop with his head encircled by the flight of a bee. The perceptive mind of the man of God conceived a deeper meaning; and because the little bee is a minister of sweetness and mother of chastity, he inferred by a faithful augury that, through the merit of chastity, the grace of perpetual sweetness would be propagated in him. Then, calling the young man aside more privately, he told him what he had seen, explained what the vision portended, and invited him to adopt the pattern of a holier [Note: [Col. 1254D] Another codex: “stricter.”] purpose.

Although, at the urging of friends, the connivance of his mother’s counsel, and the threatened loss of an inheritance left without an heir, he was being drawn rather strongly toward marriage, he broke the bonds of these necessities, bowed both mind and head to the saving admonitions [Col. 1255A], solemnly made a vow of continence, and was tonsured through the ministry of the blessed bishop according to ecclesiastical custom. Thus he was effectively given wholly to divine service.

38. [CHAPTER XXV.] Holy diligence leaves nothing untried; nor does the obstacle of difficulty crush the affection of true mercy, nor does a matter of fear produce distrust in holy love. The man therefore, lest any merit or favour with the Lord should slip away from him, resolved to spare himself in no way in order to provide for the salvation of others; and, that he might gather together those who were perishing, he did not refuse to offer the sacrifice of his own blood. Accordingly he directed his journey to the Slavs [Note: [Col. 1255D] About the year 633, as was said in §10.], to whom Christ had not yet been proclaimed, so that he might gather strangers into the camp of faith and teach them to serve beneath the heavenly standards for the glory of the eternal King [Col. 1255B], resisting Satan’s tyrannical laws.

But faith is not possessed by all, nor do all obey the Gospel, because darkness does not comprehend the mystery of light; nor is soil suitable for seed when it is not made fruitful by the outlay of its own moisture. Yet after a few had been converted to the faith, he entrusted to them the care of the divine word and arranged sacred ministries, so that nothing necessary for those to be saved might be lacking. He himself returned to his own sheep, since the rest of the multitude lay stubbornly and indiscriminately entangled in the wrappings of their errors. It did not seem fitting to him to cast the Lord’s pearls before swine or to dispense what is holy to dogs. Therefore, having shaken off against them the dust of his feet in accordance with the Lord’s command, he was happily called into Gaul and resumed the interrupted work of preaching.

[Col. 1255C]

39. [CHAPTER XXVI.] Meanwhile Dagobert, rendered prouder by great victories and successes beyond belief, turned his heart from the path of justice to crime and defiled royal dignity with disgraceful acts. He violated the sacrament of marriage and, rejecting his lawful wife [Note: [Col. 1255D] Gomadrude, because she was barren.], went over to the embraces of a concubine whom he had taken. When this came to the holy bishop’s hearing, he was overwhelmed with grief. With anxious mind he considered the injury done to innocence, the ruin of virtue, the affront to royal majesty, and the stigma of a deadly example. Because the righteous are as bold as a lion, and tested virtue reproves the foolish, he entered boldly before the king. Thus he rebuked the man while showing deference to his rank; and he presented the word of reproof without seeking an occasion either for offence or for favour.

The fierceness of a lion [Col. 1255D] is governed not by the lash but by flattery; royal dignity is not corrected by rebuke but leaps into fury. At the admonitions of the man of God, the king’s spirit swelled into anger. Trampling upon the honour of divinity and banishing all regard for mercy, he ordered the minister of truth to depart from the borders of his kingdom, imagining that cruel vengeance would bring relief to his shame if it removed the presence of the man of God. But he, mindful of the divine saying, “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10), gave place to wrath. In response to the king’s threat, he departed and penetrated more remote places [Note: [Col. 1255D] In exile he went, in the year 634, to the kingdom of Charibert, Dagobert’s brother [Col. 1256D].], seeking in exile and labour a resting-place of peace [Col. 1256A].

40. Yet the mind never goes into exile from divine things. The Lord grants a word with great power to one preaching the Gospel, and consoles His innocent servant on the day of cloud and darkness. He inflicts punishment upon the guilty and deprives the adulteress of the fruit of her womb, for, according to the saying of Wisdom: “The bastard shoots shall not put down deep roots, and seed from an unlawful bed shall be exterminated” (Wisdom 4). The king therefore, despairing of succession, sent away the adulteress and transferred all his affection elsewhere. This above all he desired and earnestly sought in continual prayers: that the sceptres might not lack rulers and royal dignity might not be deprived of descendants.

A third marriage-chamber was prepared, and, according to the king’s will, a noble and fruitful virgin was brought in [Col. 1256B], so that she might endow her husband with offspring, the subjects with a ruler, and the kingdom with a successor. Meanwhile Dagobert, not forgetful of the transgression he had committed, turned from the misery of sin to the Lord when the terrible thorn of judgment was fixed in his heart. He redeemed sins through alms, frequented heaven through supplications and altars through gifts. The Lord looked upon the humility of His servant, and by a divine gift a son was given him: his parents’ glory, the restoration of the line, a pledge of good hope, and the joy of his subjects. Therefore the father, happy yet anxious, considered to whom above all he should entrust the little child for receiving the saving sacraments of holy rebirth; whom he wished to make guardian of so great a gift, protector of his hope, minister and nurturer of the royal succession.

[Col. 1256C]

41. [CHAPTER XXVII.] As he pondered many things, the memory of the Saint came to his mind. By an unhesitating judgment of estimation, he alone was found especially worthy to receive so sweet a burden of such great reverence. At once messengers were dispatched in every direction by the king’s command to seek the servant of God. After much labour he was found and brought back with joy and exultation. Dagobert came to meet him as he returned, cheerful and glad; mindful of the wrong he had done and forgetting his royal rank, he humbly embraced the footsteps of the man entering, asked pardon for his sin, and with humble confession denounced his own error.

The precious confessor of the Lord, always gentle and humble in heart, and readier to grant [Note: [Col. 1256D] In another manuscript, “to exercise.”] forgiveness than vengeance, anticipated the obeisance of humility. He raised up the man thus prostrate and lying down [Col. 1256D], and repaid injury with grace. Made more confident by the kindness of the man of God, the king disclosed his request and earnestly begged, with many entreaties, that the little child granted him from heaven might be renewed by heavenly sacraments. The man of the Lord, who sought nothing in the world except the Lord’s will and nothing except heavenly command, initially refused, lest he seem to have wished to exploit the familiarity of an earthly king for such an exchange. But at the urgent entreaty of the king, and through the further persuasion of the illustrious men Audoenus [Col. 1257A] and Eligius—whom royal familiarity still distinguished among the magnates of the palace as a special example of affection and faith—he reverently consented to the request and promised his devout service to the royal will.

42. [CHAPTER XXVIII.] Accordingly, when the magnates and leading men of the kingdom had assembled at Orléans [Note: [Col. 1257D] In the year 635.], in accordance with the king’s edict the little child was brought to the baptistery to be renewed by sacred mysteries through the ministry of the holy bishop. While he was making him a catechumen by the solemn signing, according to ecclesiastical custom, divine mercy revealed by a wonderful judgment before men how great was his power and grace with God. For the child, being about forty days old, when the prayer had ended, and no unlearned person in so great an assembly was available to make the response, answered in a clear [Col. 1257B] voice, “Amen,” and turned toward himself the eyes and hearts of all who heard. They marvelled and were astonished at so unusual and solemn a miracle. They declared the king blessed for the happy omen attending the birth of his child, foretold signs of the boy’s future excellence, and in this new event commended the goodness of God, the merit of the holy man, and the grace of the sacrament.

Thus the little child was renewed by the saving sacraments and, by a divine gift, transferred into a new creation. All shared in rejoicing; all gave thanks to the Giver of so great a gift; and each returned home bearing sheaves of joy. Thus the favour and grace of the servant of God were gloriously increased, and the more widely they were spread abroad, the more sweetly they shone.

## CHAPTER V. The bishopric of St Amandus at Maastricht. Letter of Pope St Martin.

[Col. 1257C]

43.
