[CHAPTER XXIX.] Certainly, after the death of the blessed John [Note: [Col. 1257D] In the year 646, 25 July.], bishop of Maastricht, through the fervent affection of King Dagobert [Note: [Col. 1257D] Rather, of St Sigebert, three years after Dagobert’s death.] toward the man of God, the election of the clergy, the petition of the people, the assent of the eminent men, and the wish of the neighbouring provinces, the servant of the Lord was reverently and urgently sought. Resisting and unwilling, he was drawn to the episcopal chair; worthy of pastoral care, he was acclaimed by the voice and desire of all. He steadfastly declared himself unworthy of the honour, confessed himself unequal to the burden, insufficiently useful for the care, and less suited to the dignity.

But the efforts of many, supported by zeal for piety, prevailed, and by the universal and favourable assent of all he was placed in the episcopal chair [Col. 1257D]. For all judged it unworthy that so illustrious a see should not be adorned by the comfort of so great a Father; that so great a Father should serve for so long without a title; and that the royal household should be deprived of so faithful and sweet a counsellor. The blessed man yielded, though complaining, sorrowful, and anxious, to the urgency of such sincere devotion. The more he called himself unworthy, the more worthy all considered him; and the display of holy humility was commended by the worthy acclaim of all.

When, therefore, the things customarily and necessarily performed with solemnity in the ordination of a bishop had been completed, the holy man strove with every sagacity and effort to honour his ministry: correcting what was wrong, sustaining the weak, strengthening the broken, preserving the sound, and gathering again the scattered [Col. 1258A]. He did not exercise the model of one ruling over the clergy; but, having become an example to the flock, he offered himself to all as an example of humility, a path of justice, a mirror of innocence, an ornament of chastity, and a title of holiness. He showed himself even-handed toward the humble; against the proud he rose in zeal for uprightness. He corrected sinners with gentleness and restrained rebels through the correction of devout severity. He cultivated his subjects with diligence; he treated equals with service and superiors with reverence; he was a restorer of the poor, consoler of the grieving, delight of the people, glory of the great, and a propagator of salvation and grace to all.

44. [CHAPTER XXX.] But, as it is written: “Behold, those who serve Him are not steadfast, and in His angels He finds perversity” (Job 4) [Col. 1258B], an unhappy calamity was found among the ministers of the altar, and their wretched conduct was found wanting in the weight required by the sanctuary. For priests and Levites, who ought to have been bound more strictly and sincerely to heavenly rites, had cast aside the fear of God. They gave themselves to feasting and drunkenness, beds and shameless acts; making provision for the flesh in its desires, they fulfilled the desires of their father the devil through the obscenities of pleasure.

The blessed man was distressed in spirit and, raising himself in the zeal of strength with just severity, resolutely opposed those in error. He argued, rebuked, and exhorted in season and out of season; he preached the way of innocence, and with the hoe of correction tried to uproot the dense thickets from the Lord’s vineyard [Col. 1258C]. A desperate disease does not readily yield to treatment, nor does hardened malice willingly receive the word of truth. The salamander lives amid devouring flames, and poisons that bring death to a human being give life to the serpent. So unhealthy impiety rests in its own dregs, and an ill-starred fruitfulness sends forth the shrubs of transgression from an evil root. When caught, the hedgehog rolls itself into a ball and bloodies the hand that touches it with the pricks of its spines. Thus the rebellious and deceitful crowd of evildoers not only refuses to obey saving admonitions, but also seeks to harm the innocent through destructive schemes; and in return for the benefit of holy aid, it stirs up persecutions and offences.

[Col. 1258D]

45. [CHAPTER XXXI.] Meanwhile King Dagobert closed his final day [Note: [Col. 1258D] In the year 644, 19 January.], leaving his sons to reign in his place: Clovis in Francia [Note: [Col. 1258D] In Neustria, or Western Francia, as the ancients called it.], and Sigebert in Austrasia, whom the blessed Amandus had received from the sacred font. The same man of God, seeing that his own industry accomplished nothing, his solicitude contributed nothing, and his goodwill earned nothing but the stings of opposition and the tunnels of hatreds, resolved to withdraw and depart from the midst of that crooked and perverse nation. Thus neither might the burden of sin increase for them through their rebellion, nor, through the demands of their sins, might his labour appear more fruitless [Col. 1259A].

But because it is the part of a wise man to examine counsels and not precipitately to rush into new courses with facile fickleness, as Solomon says: “Do everything with counsel, and after the deed you will not repent” (Ecclus. 32), he sent envoys to Rome and set forth, in a sealed letter to the blessed Martin [Note: [Col. 1259D] St Martin was created pope in 647, deported into exile in 653, and is commemorated on 12 November.], then Roman pontiff, the troubles of the work he had undertaken and his heart’s desire. He wished to employ the counsel of him under whose authority he stood. The Apostolic man read this letter with eyes full of reverence and pious understanding, and wrote in reply a letter full of consolation and reverence, exhorting him to the virtue of perseverance, by which the merits of all the faithful are crowned.

For already, as the proclamation of fame spread abroad, the holiness of his life, his zeal in preaching, and the grace of his powers had become known to the blessed pope; and he whom God had suffused with grace was loved by him more sincerely [Col. 1259B] and ardently. Moreover, he sent him the relics of saints which he had requested, an excellent volume of synodal decrees, which he himself had copied out in five divided books [Note: [Col. 1259D] The Acts of the Roman Synod held under Pope St Martin, in the eighth indiction, on 3 October of the eighth year of Constans, A.D. 649, are divided into five secretariates, proceedings, or sessions.], and commands to be conveyed to King Sigebert [Note: [Col. 1259D] In the Acts of St Martin it is said: “making copies,” which “he had caused to be copied out”; for below he says: “We have foreseen your attachment to the volumes.”].

From this it may be understood that the blessed Amandus was a man of great merit and renown: so great a confessor, a pillar of the faith and Father of the universal Church, honoured him with marks of such condescension; he embraced the presence of the absent man with a familiar gaze, and remembered him more worthily and sweetly in this part of himself, because the bond of friendship is possessed more faithfully and pleasantly. In order, therefore, that the assertion of our preceding account may be confirmed after the cloud of uncertainty has been wiped away, we have thought fit to append to this discourse the aforesaid letter sent by the same pope to the blessed Amandus [Col. 1259C]. Its form is as follows:

46. [CHAPTER XXXII.] To the most beloved brother Amandus, Martin [Note: [Col. 1260D] This letter appears at the end of the said Synod and in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul* edited by Sirmondus. We collated it with the manuscripts of Elnone, Blandinium, and four others.].

Our mind is known to be relieved upon receiving the letter of your brotherhood, filled with zeal for piety [Note: [Col. 1260D] Others read: “receiving,” and “those receiving.”]. For it is certain that, despising the unstable and passing pleasures of this world, you seek those eternal and sublime gifts bestowed for the service of our Lord God. From the report of the bearer of this letter, in accordance with the tenor of your brotherhood’s letter, we have learned of the struggle of your labours. From these, the gifts of future joys are to be bestowed upon you for your ascent to the heavenly homeland through humble minds and bodies made contrite [Col. 1259D].

For what is recompensed by our Creator for good service cannot be made equal by any comparison, since the labours which we endure for His love come to an end in a brief and small span of time. In consideration of refreshment, ought we not willingly to bear the straits of this present life? Yet as greatly as the accomplishment of your labours brings us abundant joy [Col. 1260A], so greatly are we grieved by the hardness of the priests of that people, who, laying aside the aids to their salvation and despising the service of our Redeemer, are weighed down by the bonds of vices. We must press upon them with urgent preaching for the preparation of their salvation, just as the double return of the talents entrusted to us is required in the business of perfect stewardship, and the declaration of the Lord’s word urges us to receive His rest.

For it has been reported to us that presbyters, deacons, and others in priestly office are defiled by falling after their ordinations; and that your brotherhood is thereby oppressed with excessive grief, desiring to lay down pastoral service because of their disobedience, to choose release from the labours of the episcopate [Col. 1260B], and to live in silence and leisure rather than remain in those matters entrusted to you. Yet the Lord says: “Blessed is he who perseveres unto the end” (Matt. 10). Whence comes blessed perseverance except from the virtue of patience? For, according to apostolic preaching, “All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecutions” (2 Tim. 3). Therefore, dearest brother, let not the bitterness of afflictions compel you to depart from the devout purpose of your mind. Consider how much our Creator and Lord endured for our absolution and liberation, and to what insults He gave Himself up, in order to free us from the bonds of diabolical power.

47. Therefore, in no way show compassion toward those who commit such a sin, to the overthrow of the canons [Col. 1260C] [Note: [Col. 1260D] Gratian cited these words of the pontiff in the *Decretum*, distinction 50, chapter 2, “Qui semel post.”]. For anyone who, after his ordination, has once fallen into sin shall thereafter be deposed and may attain no rank of priesthood. It must suffice him, by continual lamentations and tears for as long as he lives, to persevere in that same penitence, so that by divine grace he may be able to blot out the sin he has committed.

For if we seek for promotion to holy orders such persons as are hindered by no wrinkle and no contagion of life, how much more, if anyone after ordination has fallen and is found liable for the sin of transgression, must he be altogether forbidden to handle, with muddy and defiled hands, the mystery of our salvation? [Note: [Col. 1260D] Gratian also cites this in distinction 50, chapter 12.] Thus one of this kind, always deposed in this life in accordance with the ordinances of the sacred canons [Col. 1260D], may be reconciled at the terrible judgment by Him who searches the inward parts of the mind and takes no delight in any sheep going astray, when He sees that person’s sincere repentance.

Therefore we again exhort your charity, after the example of Him who willed to suffer and die for us, to remain ready in all His services [Col. 1261A]. Let us not be reluctant to endure temporal sufferings for Christ’s name, but let the profits of future recompense persuade us to endure the vexations of this world. For it is written: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that He has rendered to me? I shall receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115). For only as much is required of us as we are able to furnish in the services of our ministry. And since, through the generosity of the clemency of heavenly Majesty, all things that could minister to the strengthening of the minds of your brotherhood are doubtless known to you, it remains for us to communicate to your brotherhood concerning the other matters about which it has consulted us through its letters.

48. We believe that word has reached you how, amid the disturbance of the true faith and the trampling-down of the Catholic Church, about fifteen years ago [Note: [Col. 1261C] Therefore about A.D. 634, in the twenty-fourth year of Emperor Heraclius, in which Sophronius the orthodox was made patriarch of Jerusalem. Under him the heresy of the Monothelites, which had begun in the twentieth year of Heraclius, A.D. 630, was condemned [Col. 1261D].], an execrable and abominable heresy, renewing the error of the Apollinarians [Note: [Col. 1261D] Thus in the said Synod, in the Secretariat, Pope St Martin states that “Sergius established one will and operation in Christ according to the impious Apollinaris.” This heresy began under the emperors Valens and Valentinian and was condemned by Pope St Damasus at Rome in a synod of A.D. 373; Sozomen treats of it in book VI, chapter 25.], Severians [Note: [Col. 1261D] Severus lived under Emperor Zeno. In the cited passage Pope St Martin says: “Cyrus of Alexandria preached one operation in Christ after the likeness of the Acephalian heretics.”], Eutychians [Note: [Col. 1261D] Eutyches abolished every distinction of natures in Christ; he was condemned at the ecumenical Synod of Chalcedon [Col. 1262D].], and Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 1262C] The Manichaeans had invented many fables concerning Christ, which Timothy the presbyter reports in Combefis, *History of the Monothelites*, p. 451 [Col. 1262D].], sprang up through Sergius, false bishop of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 1261D] Sergius was made bishop in the seventh year of Emperor Phocas and one year before Heraclius’ accession, therefore in A.D. 609; he died in indiction VIII, according to Nicephorus’ *Breviary*, in A.D. 636.], aided by the emperor Heraclius then reigning [Note: [Col. 1261D] He then died in the thirty-first year of his reign, A.D. 641, eight years before this letter was written.].

His successor Pyrrhus [Note: [Col. 1262D] Sergius’ successor was expelled under Constans in A.D. 642.], likewise a bishop who seized the see of Constantinople in the arrogance of ambition, increased it for the worse. On this account the Apostolic See repeatedly [Note: [Col. 1262D] Especially St Martin’s predecessors John IV and Theodore.] admonished them through many persuasions, appeals, and rebukes, that they might withdraw from such error and return to the light of piety from which they had fallen [Col. 1261C]. Not only did they utterly refuse to do so, but now his successor Paul [Note: [Col. 1262D] Paul sat from the first to the eleventh year of Emperor Constans, from A.D. 641 to 652.], a violator of the faith and bishop of Constantinople, devised another more wicked undertaking to the prejudice of the Catholic faith. As though overturning what his predecessors had heretically set forth, by sacrilegious audacity he persuaded our most clement prince [Note: [Col. 1262D] In the sixth indiction, A.D. 648.] to issue an imperial *Typos*, wholly filled with perfidy, which all Christian peoples were commanded to believe [Note: [Col. 1262D] The author of the Life of St Martin calls the “Typos” “the disease of the invented heresy, by which Catholic doctrine is destroyed and all utterances of the holy Fathers are enervated; and neither one nor two wills or operations may be confessed in Christ the Lord.”].

Therefore, lest we be bound by the guilt of blame because of some negligence and the loss of souls entrusted to us, we found it necessary [Col. 1262A] to gather a general assembly of our brethren and fellow bishops in this city of Rome. In their presence the wicked writings of the aforesaid heretics were examined and laid bare; and with one voice and one spirit we condemned them by the apostolic sword and the determinations of the Fathers, so that all might recognize the error contained in them and in no way be defiled by their pollution. Accordingly, we have arranged to send you at present the volumes of the synodal proceedings [Note: [Col. 1262D] As is read in his Acts, “St Martin sent copies through all the churches of East and West, and sent them by the hands of orthodox faithful persons.”], together with our Encyclical, from whose sequence you may learn all things carefully and, as children of light, extinguish their darkness together with us.

[Col. 1262B] 49. Therefore let your brotherhood strive to make all these things known to everyone, so that they may execrate with us so abominable a heresy; and so that they may be able to learn the sacraments of their salvation, and, after a synodal assembly of all our brethren and fellow-bishops in those regions has been held, may celebrate in writing, according to the tenor of the Encyclical sent by us, and send the documents to us together with your subscriptions: thereby confirming and assenting to those measures which we have recently decreed for the orthodox faith and for the destruction of the newly arisen madness of heretics. And most wisely admonish and entreat our most excellent son Sigebert, king of the Franks, for the welfare of his Christianity, to send us from the body of our brethren [Col. 1262C] most beloved bishops, who, by God’s propitious grant, may discharge an embassy of the Apostolic See; and we shall without doubt cause what was done in our council, together with these our synodal letters [Note: [Col. 1262D] Sirmond, in the *Councils of Gaul*, reads: “your.”], to be conveyed to our most merciful prince, so that, having become a participant in our labours, he may obtain an abundance of reward and find as protector of his kingdom Him whose cause he is known to be petitioned for. For we know that this is also urged upon him in his letter.

[Col. 1263A] 50. As for the relics of the saints, concerning which the bearer of this letter has reminded us, we have ordered them to be given. For the books in our library have already been exhausted, and we had absolutely no means of giving him any; nor could he have them copied, because he hastened to depart quickly from this city. Since these matters have thus been set forth beforehand, we exhort your brotherhood to see that what has been written to you by us in this letter is carried into effect. May God keep you safe, most beloved brother.

## CHAPTER VI. The establishment of various institutions. Miracles performed by St Amandus. Monasteries constructed.

51. Having received the admonitions of so great a Father, the blessed man continued in the ministry of the rule entrusted to him, enduring grievous stings of sorrow over the transgression of those subject to him [Col. 1263B] and, with wise insistence, calling back to remedies of salvation those who refused them. But, as it is said through the Prophet: “We have healed Babylon, and she has not been healed” (Rom. X); hardened perversity rejected the antidote of holy medicine, so that the blessed man could deservedly say: “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people who do not believe, but contradict me” (Jer. LI), “who walk in paths that are not good, but after their sins.” [CAP. XXXIII.] Thus, after three years [Note: [Col. 1263D] The author confines both the reign of Dagobert and the pontificate of St Martin within the three years of Amandus’s episcopate at Maastricht; these points have been refuted above.] had passed from the time of his entry, when he saw that all his labour among them was being utterly wasted, he withdrew from them, choosing to dwell privately in the house of God rather than to excel among transgressors under the title of high office. For the innocence of poverty and the lowliness of private retirement are safer than the luxury of sinful wealth and [Col. 1263C] the proud exaltation of swelling power. He therefore went away bitter in spirit, in the indignation of his soul, grieving over the malice of the wicked, fearing their destruction, and displaying amid a sad danger the affection of holy compassion. Nevertheless, the hand of the Lord was with him, strengthening him, so that he who had been left because of barrenness might yield an abundance of precious fruit.

52. [CAP. XXXIV.] In that same region there was a noble matron named Itta [Note: [Col. 1263D] We shall treat of Blessed Itta, or Iduberga, on 8 May.], surpassing the glory of her birth with the distinction of her manner and conduct of life. Recently widowed by the death of the glorious Duke Pippin [Note: [Col. 1263D] In the year 646, 21 February.], she bore in sorrowful mind the sad separation from a happy union. Temporal affliction often becomes the joyful beginning of a holier purpose, and hard necessity is sometimes transformed to the service of virtue. The dove flies back to the bosom of the ark when, amid the reigning flood, it finds no place on which to stretch out its feet in rest. This holy woman too, left without the consolation of a husband amid her distresses, considered how she might please Christ alone and bring the vowed beauty of chastity into the treasury of the heavenly sanctuary; for after shipwreck it is a second plank of salvation that the loss of virginity should worthily be repaired by widowly continence. The blessed man turned aside to her in order to console her, prompted by the holy intercourse [Col. 1264A] of a friendship begun long before. Courteous cheerfulness was shown to him as he entered, services fitting for his holiness were rendered, and a welcome exchange of modest conversation was woven between them. When the man of God had been admitted to the secret of her inmost will and could discern the object of the holy widow’s devout longing, he encouraged her faithful purpose of holy desire with congratulations, raised her up by admonitions, and confirmed it by examples. Made stronger by the exhortation of the holy bishop, she bound herself by a vow of chastity and obligated herself to stricter rules of good living. And because love cannot be idle, but declares its measure by deeds, blessed Itta consecrated to the heavenly Bridegroom whom she had chosen her wealth and estates; and, having purified her house by the heavenly sacrament, she asked that it be consecrated as a church. There, amid the sacred solemnities of the Masses, she received from [Col. 1264B] the hand of the holy bishop the sacred veil, the sign of humility and chastity. Afterwards, gathering there a community of women serving God, she enlarged the place itself with possessions [Note: [Col. 1264D] The monastery of Nivelles.] and adorned it with manifold ornaments of different kinds, striving to become in every respect an example of obedience and humility.

53. 725 [CAP. XXXV.] She had an only daughter named Gertrude, distinguished by the gifts of birth and beauty, who aroused many suitors. Her devout mother, wishing to free her from the filthy whirlpool of corruption, cut off her hair, changed her clothing, attached her to the sacred altars, and presented her to the holy bishop for consecration. For she greatly desired that the integrity of the shoot might display what had withered in the root, and that she might possess in her daughter the title of virginity which she herself could not possess. Thus initiated into the sacred mysteries and crowned with the mystical veil, Gertrude began to surpass the other virgins greatly in conduct, grace, faith, character, and discipline. Not long afterwards, by the working of divine mercy, she was placed over the monastery of Nivelles and, by the harmony that brought about a canonical election, was appointed Mother of the Virgins by the arrangement of the holy bishop. There afterwards, full of good works and most renowned for the merit of her virtues, she rested in Christ in a blessed end [Note: [Col. 1264D] In the year 664, 17 March.].

54. [CAP. XXXVI.] Departing from there, the man of God joyfully made his way to the monastery of Blessed Gislenus, of which we have spoken, and, gratefully received by the brethren, generously shared the sustenance they sought. Narrow poverty often suffers grievous want; and what is insufficient for itself cannot provide sufficiency for the altar. Since they had nothing which they considered worthy of the table of so great a guest, the holy bishop went out without having dined, not without the repeated complaint of the brethren, whose generous feeling endured want and whose hands could not find what their hearts desired. He was therefore led to a boat, to cross the river Haine [Note: [Col. 1264D] The monastery of St Gislenus lies beside the Haine; from it Hainaut and Henegau are so named.], as the need of his journey required. And now, as the holy men [Col. 1265A] Amandus and Gislenus [Note: [Col. 1265D] The same account is related in the *Life of St Gislenus*, 9 October.] were bidding one another farewell, a great fish, called a pike, suddenly leapt of its own accord from the river onto the land; by its size it could refresh many diners. At the sight of this new event all gathered with rejoicing, and followed God, the author of the gift, with thanksgiving and a proclamation of praise. By this benefit the distress of their former embarrassment was relieved, the holy bishop’s devout compassion was gladdened, the harsh necessity of fasting was removed, a meal was prepared, and the man of God was joyfully brought back to the monastery. There arose among the holy Fathers a humble and devout contention: the holy bishop attributed this gift to the merits of Gislenus, while Blessed Gislenus, with simple and devout judgement, ascribed it to the holy bishop. It was an argument [Col. 1265B] without rancour, disagreement without vexation, a contest without transgression; on both sides their judgement varied without prejudice to truth, because discord is always alien from peace of soul, and unity of will is not violated among those who think alike. After the divine gift had been received, they returned joyfully to the river; greeting each other with a holy kiss, they were separated from one another’s sight as the boat served them in its course down the stream. He then proceeded [Note: [Col. 1265D] Philip, in the *Life of St Gislenus*, says that he went from there to Elnone, as we proved above, §12.] to an island commonly called Canelaus [Note: [Col. 1266D] Calloa is meant.], near the Scheldt and not far from Ghent, and decided to make it a brief resting-place from his labours, with the God-fearing men living there.

55. [CAP. XXXVII.] After some delay, once his name had become public, [Col. 1265C] he began to proclaim the way of truth to the neighbouring people and, through the benefit of saving doctrine, earnestly endeavoured to turn sinners from the error of their ways. But the physician’s service is lost when the sick person refuses healing, and words of wisdom do not reach those whose minds are deranged for correction. The inhabitants reject an appetite for life-giving food and, as though afflicted with a foul abscess, reject the draught of salvation with a languishing stomach. God’s servant is despised by the impious—or rather, Christ is rejected in his servant, He who had come in him to seek and save what was lost. In return for their rejection, the Lord gives them a writ of divorce; in the mire of the deep he abandons those deserters who have despised mercy. And because, just as humility earns pardon, obstinacy earns punishment, heavenly vengeance proceeded against them as against traitors to majesty; [Col. 1265D] and for nearly two continuous years a ravaging plague violently afflicted them, until all who had proudly resisted the beneficial teachings of the man of God were consumed.

56. 726 [CAP. XXXVIII.] Not long afterward, as the man of God diligently and carefully visited his brethren whom he had left in various places for the salvation of souls, he entered the territory of the Basques, whom he had heard to be occupied with idol-worship, divination, and various errors. Therefore, while in a public assembly he preached the word of truth and the way of salvation to the faithless multitude, a certain man from the crowd, [Col. 1266A] shallow and unstable, raising his voice out of the abundance of a perverse heart, began to pour forth shameful blasphemies and, not without laughter, to hurl at the servant of God and the teaching of the faith utterly absurd words full of insults. Immediately seized by a demon, he began to attack himself with his own bites and, made the butcher of his own body, began more horribly to open to his own destruction the mouth which he had irreverently raised against the holy bishop. Yet amid those very torments he confessed that he suffered such things because of his insult to God’s servant; and thus, driven to the end, under the pressure of punishment he breathed out his insolent spirit.

57. [CAP. XXXIX.] Then, when he had entered one of the towns to preach, he was reverently received as a guest by the bishop of that place. When the aforesaid bishop, in the service [Col. 1266B] of devout hospitality, had provided water for his hands, he ordered that what had been used be stored in the sacristy. A man, blind for a long time and begging, sat at the door of the church. The faithful bishop approached him and said: “Son, if you can believe, trust in the Lord and wash your eyes with the water in which the man of God Amandus washed his hands; you will receive sight, freed from the affliction of blindness.” Encouraged by the bishop’s word in faith, the man conceived a fuller hope; bathing his eyes, oppressed by a cloud of darkness, in the water of washing, he was recalled from darkness to light and received the service of the sun, which he had formerly not known. Thus the Lord saves the humble in spirit and restrains the malice of the wicked with the rod of wrath. And by God’s just judgement, confession [Col. 1266C] of truth does not free the blasphemer from punishment, while the faithful man is released from the bond of blindness. Thus the Lord glorifies the life of his servant, glorifies his work, commends his merit, and shows by certain signs that He lives in Amandus.

58. [CAP. XL.] Meanwhile the man of God, leaving the territory of the Basques, returned to Francia; and coming to Hilderic, king of the Franks, he requested a place where he might suitably build a monastery. In accordance with royal magnificence, the king granted him an estate named Nanto [Note: [Col. 1266D] Among the Rutheni in Aquitaine I.]. There the holy man, with ready eagerness, persevering zeal, and diligent work, began to lay the foundations of a new planting and, gathering there sons of grace, to prepare suitable buildings. But a certain Mummulus, bishop of Osindum [Note: [Col. 1266D] Rather, of Uzès.], resentfully [Col. 1266D] bearing the king’s generosity and the holy man’s undertaking, infected with the poison of deadly envy, sent forth sons of Belial, set apart for an evil work, to destroy the works of holiness and cruelly drive God’s servant out of that place. Coming to him, therefore, they spoke peaceful words deceitfully and promised that soon they would show him a place more suitable for building. Holy simplicity followed the agents of wickedness; and although, through the Spirit’s revelation, he was not ignorant of the mechanism of their impious plot, he nevertheless aspired with heart and soul, devotedly, to martyrdom, and wished by the shedding of his blood to crown the end of labour long sustained. Yet he would not disclose this to his disciples, lest they either hinder one hastening to his end or be more grievously disturbed by the imminent danger.

59. When, therefore, they had come to the summit of the mountain, where the executioners had decided to murder God’s servant, justice, turned to judgement, looked down from heaven, scourging the wicked and protecting the righteous with the aid of loving defence. A sudden storm arose; the face of heaven was thickened into darkness, the air was filled with the terror of gloom, and a tempestuous whirlwind enveloped the splendour of the sun. The appearance of things was hidden and folded into uniform confusion; light was taken from the attendants, and, struck with sudden blindness, they shuddered at the danger of imminent death. Cruelty turned to fear, [Col. 1267B] ferocity passed into supplication, stubbornness bowed into abasement; and him whom they had come to kill they humbly and urgently begged to permit them to depart free. The compassion of the man of God was moved to pardon; bathed in a great flow of tears, he steadfastly gave himself to prayer and asked forgiveness of sin for the wretches. The door of mercy was opened to him who knocked; calmness, which had been taken away, returned; when the storms were lifted, the condition of the air was restored; and when their eyes were released to light, the wretches, with blindness removed, were restored to the use of daylight. 727 Thus, led by repentance, they gave thanks for their deliverance, venerated God’s servant with due admiration, and, returning peacefully to their homes, more fully related the mighty works of God which they had seen. Thus the Lord [Col. 1267C] protected him from deceivers: their malice, like flowing water, was reduced to nothing before him; yet it neither escaped the scourge of deserved severity nor remained excluded from the benefits of mercy.

60. [CAP. XLI.] In about the fifth year [Note: [Col. 1267D] In the royal charter cited above, the second year of Christ 666 is stated.] of the aforesaid king Hilderic, while he was staying at Laon [Note: [Col. 1267D] Laon, or Lugdunum Clavatum, a city of Gaul on the borders of Picardy and Champagne.], the most blessed Father Amandus came to him and, through God’s action, found favour in his sight. Therefore, to enlarge the service of divine worship and extend the order of regular discipline, the king, by royal liberality and with due freedom, conveyed to the blessed man a noble estate named Barisy, together with all its appurtenances. Receiving it graciously with thanksgiving, Amandus, as place and time allowed, suitably established a monastery there; [Col. 1267D] and, gathering in it God-fearing men who had professed the warfare of Christ, he prudently appointed over them his venerable and God-worthy disciple Andrew [Note: [Col. 1267D] We shall treat of Blessed Andrew below on this day.], who would soon become his successor in the monastery of Elnone.

61. [CAP. XLII.] As was his custom, while he travelled through neighbouring places for the sake of evangelising, he came to Ressumthum, which is known to be situated in the district of Beauvais on the river Aronne. There was there an unbelieving woman who endured the penalty of unbelief, the affliction of blindness; [Col. 1268A] and, because of works of darkness, being given over to darkness, she led a useless life fully bearing the image of death. Entering her house, the man of God inquired into the causes of her misfortune. The distressed woman confessed that it had justly befallen her because of the worship of demons and the observance of omens. Then she showed him the tree beneath which, initiated into profane rites, she had customarily sacrificed to the demon. The holy man said to her: “If you wish to recover your former health, first, in contempt of superstition, take an axe to cut down the tree, and you will be healed from the horror of blindness.” Trusting the man of God, the woman, led by the assistance of her maidservant, eagerly raised the iron against the tree; and what she could not accomplish by her own strength, she encouraged and rejoiced to see completed by the hands of those standing by. Therefore the man of God, standing over her, invoked God’s name and, by the sign of the cross, touched [Col. 1268B] the organs of light and restored them by divine grace to the service of sight. Then, having instructed her how she ought henceforth to live, he taught her in the fear of God to guard her heart with all vigilance and to keep the actions of her life more carefully, so that just as outward light shone in her head, so the inward splendour of truth might radiate in her mind. Thus the woman, faithfully instructed by the admonitions of the holy bishop and made more upright in everything, lived before God in holiness and righteousness all the days of her life.

## CHAPTER VII. St Amandus’s third journey to Rome. Praise of the monastery of Elnone.

62. [CAP. XLIII.] About the same time [Note: [Col. 1268D] Rather, he left Maastricht in the year 650, as stated in §12; thus it was twenty-six years before the foundation of the monastery of Barisy.], the holy man resolved [Col. 1268C] to set out for Rome for the third time, so that, by the toil of pilgrimage and the fruit of prayers, he might advance the final years of his life just as he had dedicated its beginning. Undertaking the journey, he turned aside to the house of Blessed Humbert [Note: [Col. 1268D] The monastery of Maroilles.] for hospitality. Humbert received him with every reverence of charity, and every kindness was carefully shown in providing for him. During the meal, the holy man asked his host whether he wished to expend with him the burden of this undertaken labour, share in the reward of the labour, and present himself at the apostolic thresholds. Blessed Humbert assented and most cheerfully joined the holy bishop’s company.

63. One day, as is the custom of travellers, while they had sat down near a forest beside the road to take a meal, a bear came out and tore apart the animal with which they were accustomed to carry their baggage. Binding the bear by the power of the divine name, they led it to the baggage and used it in place of a beast of burden, making the robber carry their household goods. As the men of God approached the City, the Roman bishop, secretly informed by an angel acting as a messenger, announced to them in familiar conversation that they should release the beast from this service, lest they seem to enter the city more ostentatiously than religiously—a city which ought to be the head of religion and honour [Col. 1269A] among the nations—and lest, through the novelty of the spectacle, they stir up crowds of people and draw to themselves the eyes and voices of all. The holy Fathers obeyed the apostolic command and allowed the beast, released from its imposed obedience, to return to the hiding-places of the woods, 728 repeatedly looking back and showing its service by such signs as it could. They then entered the city and were received worthily and reverently by the supreme pontiff; having accomplished all for which they had come and sought the intercessions of the saints, they returned joyfully to their own country.

64. Blessed Humbert turning aside to Maroilles, the man of God Amandus withdrew to Elnone, a place which the generous hand of King Dagobert [Note: [Col. 1269D] In Dagobert’s second year, A.D. 638.] had long before granted him and solemnly assigned with liberality in order to enlarge the worship [Col. 1269B] of God. The place itself lies within the territory of the Menapii, adjoining the Propontii and Nervii; just as it is the boundary of the German and Roman empires, so it is known to be a portion of Belgica Rheims and a frontier of the Franks. Here, where the two rivers Elnone and Scarpe meet in one, a spacious angle stretches out between them; around it there extend meadows watered by the streams, abundance of pasture, and fruitful fishing, while beyond it a forest, suitable for hunting, offers a more extensive retreat. The soil is neither exceptionally fertile nor barren; it provides for the inhabitants an abundance of milk and honey. Coming here, God’s servant, with the foresight of his mind, decided to make it the resting-place of his labour, the dwelling of peace, the habitation of repose, and the title of his completion. But because he had not yet established there buildings suitable to religious life, he began carefully to consider where he should lay the foundations of a new construction. Entering, therefore, the angle of the aforesaid interval, he began to cut down thickets, tear up shrubs, root out sedge-beds; felling the trunks of riverside trees and demolishing reed-beds, stripping the ground of its native covering, he levelled the dreadful density of its former growth into a clearing and prepared a most suitable place for the regular buildings. Having thus laid foundations, he founded a church in honour of Peter, prince of the apostles, whom he had often had as the chief author of his preaching, the guide of his labour, and the comforter of his hardship. With ardent zeal he built there the buildings suitable for a monastery, such that [Col. 1269D] they neither savoured of superfluous luxury nor of the constriction of threadbare poverty. Then the diligent fisherman cast his nets [Col. 1270A] for a catch and gathered from every side vigorous helpers in the work he had undertaken and most faithful guardians of regular observances. Men fervent in spirit came to him, zealous for God’s law, eagerly embracing the commandments of life and pursuing with distinguished diligence the school of divine service which had been established. The faithful shepherd rejoiced at the growth of the good flock, while the devoted flock in turn was made cheerful, under the governance of so great a Father, by the progress of its common goods. Then he ordered a new church, from its foundations, to be built in honour of Blessed Andrew the apostle, and adorned it with the worthy services of those who served God. Like an excellent steward, he now undertook the storms of outward affairs, now entered the inner sanctuary, not without the incense of prayer and the fire of holy fervour, [Col. 1270B] that he might hear what the Lord God spoke within him and ask peace and advancement for His servants.

65. [CAP. XLV.] Not long after these events, Blessed Humbert, returning from the City for the second time, came down to Elnone to visit the man of God. When he was already near the place, an angel of the Lord came to Blessed Amandus and warned him to go out to meet God’s servant and to recognise, by the sign displayed upon his head, how great was his merit before God. The blessed man went out, rejoiced at the arrival of so great a guest, and, after giving the kiss of peace, uncovered Humbert’s head and saw the sign of the cross shining on its crown. This was not granted for all to behold, but only to those whose eyes divine power illumined. A shared and immense [Col. 1270C] joy arose between them, breathing not the pretence of flattery but the character of holy sincerity; nor did it bring forth anything unusual that was not fitting to the purpose of each, to holiness, and to religious order, or that could resist the laws of holy hospitality. Having remained with him as long as he pleased, for two days, after sacred exchanges of mutual exhortation and sweet conversations of holy devotion, and having given each other a blessing, Blessed Humbert joyfully returned home.

66. [CAP. XLVI.] There was in the monastery of Elnone 729 a certain provost named Chrodobald, assigned to the brethren’s [Note: [Col. 1269D] Rather, to the monastery of Marchiennes. Concerning him Gualbert, a monk of Marchiennes, relates in Buzelin, book I of *Gallia Flandria*, ch. 41: “In the fifth place, near and adjoining blessed Abbot Jonatus, is commemorated in famous and worthy memory the holy Chrodobald, glorious in merits, monk and provost of the most holy confessor and bishop Amandus. Yet, because of obstinacy, boasting, and wilfulness, he was struck by God; but, when he had been humbled by that same bishop, the joined structure of his limbs, broken by the sickness of paralysis because of the fault of disobedience committed against the blessed man—when the master commanded and the disciple did not obey the duty of charity—was healed and corrected by the Lord’s power. To show his merit to posterity, such a miracle concerning him became known in the monastery of Marchiennes. For when in former times the church of that same monastery was burned, the carpet placed beneath his sarcophagus, although covered on every side with burning coals and while flame raged throughout the whole monastery, as related by the ancient Fathers, remained entirely unharmed. To renew daily before the eyes of future as well as present persons the distinction of this miracle, the carpet is still kept stored away—or rather, laid up in the vestry, where albs, copes, and the other ornaments are placed. Raissius also mentions this miracle in the *Hierogazophylacium* and calls him Blessed.”] services and, by the command of the holy Father, appointed to external care. Receiving an order from him to serve drink to the brethren at the proper time according to the usual allowance, [Col. 1270D] he despised the just command of his superior. But he did not escape the vengeance of the just Judge. Preparing to go up to the man of God, in order to make excuses for his sins and cloak the obstinacy of his guilt with the veil of a pretext, he was suddenly seized by the terror of paralysis. His senses were ruined, his memory dulled, his sight grew dim, his hearing was blunted; and with all his limbs as though dead, the vital spirit still beat only in his breast. Yet with such voice and effort as he could, he continually confessed that the guilt of disobedience had brought upon him such evils. Therefore, placed in a boat by the brethren’s assistance, he was carried by the river’s current to Elnone [Note: [Col. 1271D] The Scarpe, beside which lie the monasteries of Marchiennes and Elnone.]. These things were reported to the man of God, who is said to have smiled and said: “He will yet suffer greater things, because he follows boasting and pays no heed to the grace of obedience.” Then, through a faithful priest, he sent a piece of bread and a little wine, after bestowing a blessing; ordering that he be refreshed with these, [Col. 1271B] he commanded him to come without delay to meet him on the following day, when he would visit him. Having tasted the Father’s blessing, the provost was restored to his former health, and obedience restored the strength which the guilt of disobedience had taken away. On the following day he presented himself joyfully to God’s servant when he came to him, asking pardon for his fault and giving thanks for the benefit. The whole community of brethren marvelled when they saw sound and vigorous in body the man whom they had seen brought in wretchedly, nearly lifeless and lying helpless in others’ hands. Praise to God was offered in common, and the power and merit of the holy Father were proclaimed more gloriously. But Amandus gently and mildly sent the corrected brother back to Marchiennes, exhorting him to take heed for the future and strive to reform his conduct more profitably.

[Col. 1271C] 67. Meanwhile Blessed Florebert, whom Amandus himself had long ago placed over the monastery of Blandinium, was gathered to his fathers [Note: [Col. 1271D] In the year 664, 2 November, when we shall give his Life. His death was discussed above, §13.], entered into the joy of his Lord, and obtained the kingdom and glory of immortality. But the brethren of that place, with one vow and unanimous will, sent an embassy. With such petition as they could make and with unfeigned entreaty, they appealed to the affection of their Father’s compassion, asking the holy man to come down to them, provide for the monastery which he had founded, nourish the sons whom he had received through spiritual generation, water more abundantly the plants he had set, and not suffer the devoted flock to go away into the loss of dispersion. Blessed Amandus, moved by his sons’ petition and suddenly pierced alike by fear and love, wished neither to leave Elnone [Col. 1271D] nor to send away his suppliant sons without counsel. Thus divided by the concern of piety, after many movements of holy deliberation and careful counsels, he answered the petitioners with gentle humility: “Do not, sons, do not disturb your Father’s rest; do not call me back from the harbour into the sea. My poverty is enough for me, to be reckoned as riches. ‘This is my rest for ever and ever; here will I dwell, because I have chosen it.’ By God’s favour you will not lack the strength of heavenly aid or the help of our concern.” [Col. 1272A] At this response, the brethren, prevented from pursuing the intention they had proposed, begged lest they return empty-handed; and with all devotion they sought the wisdom of the holy Father, asking what he thought and judged should be done concerning the ordering of the monastery of Blandinium. Holy Father Amandus, unable either to abandon his Elnone brethren or to be wanting to the desolate flock, gave them his disciple John [Note: [Col. 1271D] We have said in the same place that John presided until the year 683, [Col. 1272D].], a man of proved conduct, distinguished in character and outstanding in moderation. With a blessing, he committed the care of the brethren to John and sent him joyfully back to Blandinium.

68. [CAP. XLVIII.] Blessed Father Amandus now felt the failure of his body, worn out by labours and old age, and by secret inspiration foresaw that the day of his departure was not far distant. Therefore, calling to himself [Col. 1272B] the venerable Andrew, whom he had formerly appointed abbot at Barisy, he placed him [Note: [Col. 1272D] In the year 683, as stated in §15.] over the household which, with the Lord’s help, he had gathered, so that under Andrew’s hand the strength of order and the strictness of discipline might flourish in prudent moderation, while for Amandus himself a more secluded and freer entrance into devotion to God might lie open. Yet he decreed that whatever he had previously possessed at Barisy through the generosity of King Hilderic should be restored to the perpetual right of the monastery of Elnone; this, according to the man of God’s disposition, has been inviolably maintained down to the present day.

## CHAPTER VIII. The testament, death, and burial of St Amandus.

69. 730 [CAP. XLIX.] A father’s affection is usually more inclined toward offspring born later, and [Col. 1272C] reserves the ardour of natural love for its final affections. Thus the Master of piety, when he loved them, gave the still weak and unformed disciples the life-giving remedy of his death. Imitating Him, blessed Father Amandus, knowing that the moment of his departure was near, summoned the brethren to himself. After words of exhortation, gentle discourses of devout consolation, and repeated injunctions concerning eternal salvation, he declared that the time of his calling was approaching; and he made clear by manifest signs how deeply he had loved them while living, since even in death he could not endure separation from their sweet fellowship. Therefore, having made a testament for them, as it is preserved in the archives of this monastery, he confirmed a binding decree concerning his body. He earnestly adjured, entreated, admonished, exhorted, and commanded that it be inviolably observed. Drawn to him by the fame of his holiness, the report of his virtues, the fruits of his merits, and the signs of his works, there assembled Fathers of revered authority and distinguished eminence: Reolus, metropolitan of Rheims; Mummolenus, bishop of Noyon; Vindicianus, father of the people of Cambrai; the abbots Bertinus and Aldebertus; and John, the excellent shepherd of the monastery of Blandinium [Note: [Col. 1272D] Reolus is honoured on 25 November; Mummolenus on 16 October; Vindicianus on 11 March; Bertinus on 5 September. Note: [Col. 1272D] Molanus, under 1 November in his notice of St Florebert [Col. 1273D], calls this man “adorned with every excellence of character”; Sanderus likewise lists him in the *Hagiology of Flanders*.], together with other God-fearing men. By their authority and counsel he strengthened the effect of his disposition. He decreed, under the dread sentence of a terrible threat, that no ecclesiastical or secular person should be permitted to remove his body from the monastery of Elnone or transfer it under any pretext whatsoever; rather, that with the brethren who through his guidance had conquered the world, the place of his burial should immovably possess the presence of his body, and that he should faithfully await with them the day of the final resurrection—those whom he could not endure to abandon while living, nor allow to be separated from him in any way when dying. Therefore, to remove every uncertainty in this matter for those who wish to know it, we think it fitting to insert into this work the testament of the devout Father.

70. [CHAPTER L.] [Note: [Col. 1273D] We have compared this testament with the Elnone and Blandin manuscripts and three others. Miraeus published it in his *Belgian Fasti* [Col. 1274D].] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I, Amandus, most wretched and a sinner. We believe [Col. 1273B] that the divine mercy rules us everywhere and wills mercifully to save us, since before the ages he himself foreknows both our entry into the world and our departure from the world. Therefore it is known to all how we have journeyed far and wide through all provinces and nations for the love of Christ, to proclaim the word of God and administer baptism; and the mercy of God has delivered us from many dangers and has deigned to bring us down to this time.

But now, with our body worn out and exhausted by many labours, in extreme old age and with the body almost already dead, we hope that our departure from this world is near. And since God has deigned to bring us to this little place [Note: [Col. 1274D] Elnone manuscript: “in this little place.”], called Elnone, which, through royal generosity and by our own labour, we seem to have built [Col. 1273C], if God decrees that we shall depart this world there, I ask and presume to adjure before Christ Jesus, the Son of God, that no bishop, abbot, secular person, or any authority whatsoever shall oppose this: that my little body may rest in that monastery, Elnone, mentioned above, among those brothers to whom we have already commended ourselves both in body and soul.

71. And if our end should come while travelling [Note: [Col. 1274D] The same manuscript: “from that very place.”], or wherever it may occur, let the brothers or abbot of the monastery of Elnone have permission to bring our little body back thence to the place mentioned above. But if anyone should wish to oppose this, violently to remove my body from that monastery [Col. 1273D], or rashly to resist, let him first incur the wrath of the Holy Trinity; let him stand excommunicated from all Catholic churches and become alien to the fellowship of the saints. Let him suffer the condemnation endured by Dathan and Abiram, whom hell swallowed alive; and let him be *anathema maranatha*—that is, perdition—at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Nor may he thereby prevail in changing our will; rather, this our determination shall remain firm and inviolate for ever.

And, that you may believe more certainly [Col. 1274A], I have subscribed with my own hand; and we entreat and ask all God-fearing persons to subscribe. We asked our brother Baudemund, priest, to draw up this letter. The letter was made in the monastery of Elnone, in the second year of the reign of our lord Theuderic, the glorious king, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May [17 April].

I, Amandus, a sinner, have consented to and subscribed this letter made by me.  
I, Reolus, though a sinner, have subscribed in Christ’s name.  
I, Mummolenus, bishop, have subscribed in Christ’s name.  
I, Vindicianus, bishop, though a sinner, at the request of lord Amandus have consented to and subscribed this letter in Christ’s name.  
I, Bertinus, abbot, have subscribed.  
I, Aldebertus, abbot, have subscribed.  
I, John, asked by lord Amandus, consenting, have subscribed this letter [Col. 1274B].  
I, Baudemund, a sinner, at the command of my lord Amandus, have written and subscribed this letter containing his determination.

72. [CHAPTER LI.] Praiseworthy zeal, unconquered love, delightful grace, pleasant sweetness, marvellous unity of charity, which had bound the holy man’s soul with an indissoluble bond of devotion, so that at the moment of his own dissolution he judged separation from his brothers to be a breach of the holy covenant.

Therefore, when the day of the glorious bishop’s revered passing was at hand, he was in the oratory of blessed Andrew. After the offering of prayers and after receiving the sacraments of the heavenly mystery, he departed to the Lord in the hands of his disciples, having completed the course of life; and he was gathered to his fathers in glory. Happy in the merit of his works, happy in the grace of holiness, happy in his praiseworthy consummation [Col. 1274C], he was divinely granted to render up his last breath before the altar of the Blessed Virgin, whose merits he most devoutly sought as aid, and whose sacred footsteps he had striven with all the effort of his mind to imitate.

For no one’s intercession with God can be more intimate, no one’s grace more effectual, than hers who merited to be mother of him whose Father is God. In her, by the wonderful operation of the Holy Spirit, the properties of the divine and virginal natures remaining intact in their union, she shares in the begetting of the eternal Word.

73. The holy solemnity of the funeral was deferred until the fourth day, so that devout men might gather from every direction, the due rites might be rendered to the saint’s burial, and the laying down of the precious treasure might be celebrated more favourably. Neighbours, aroused by the report [Col. 1274D], came together in a great throng from towns and villages, that they might venerate the funeral of so great a Father and attend, in the office of devotion, him whom they had loved living and now followed lifeless. The holy multitude of his disciples, summoned from different regions, was present. The clergy and neighbouring people, children of devotion, were present; and the faithful throng accompanied with psalms, hymns, and heavenly songs the bier bearing the most holy body from the place of his death to the place of burial.

Although they dared to believe in the great Father’s blessed victory, devotion nevertheless drew tears of grief from them [Col. 1275A]. From one and the same spring, flowing with equal course but stirred by different causes, there issued a stream of mourning and joy: devotion required them to rejoice for the triumphant man, while funeral observance properly required them to grieve.

He was therefore buried in the oratory of blessed Peter, which he himself had founded, so that he who had been the author of preaching, a helper in times of need, and a comforter in tribulations, might stand ready in the last things, open the gates of righteousness to one entering, and cherish in earth’s bosom the one who rested there. Splendid benefits are granted at his tomb to those who ask, more fully attesting the merit of the holy Father. The divine visitation commends its confessor with shining miracles, and Christ shows by glorious signs that he lives in his servant. He, God, lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

74. [CHAPTER LII.] Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints. Though it may appear an annihilation to those of limited understanding, heavenly authority magnifies them and proclaims in the dead the glory of eternal resurrection.

When blessed Amandus, having laid down the burden of flesh, departed to the Lord on the Lord’s night, Aldegundis, the illustrious virgin, in the monastery of Maubeuge, was praying and keeping vigils with special fervour before the venerable altar of the holy and perpetual Virgin. [Note: [Col. 1275C] It was said in §15 that St Amandus died on the Saturday before Septuagesima Sunday.] Suddenly, caught up in an ecstasy of mind [Note: [Col. 1275C] Indeed, we said above that this vision occurred rather while St Amandus was alive.], she saw a man of venerable grey hair, splendid in priestly vestments and supported by a pastoral staff, ascending to the heights amid the immense glory of shining light. An innumerable host of white-clad persons went before and followed him. She longed to follow immediately in their footsteps, to be joined to their sweet company, and to share in their blessed joys; and with all the strength she could, she followed their tracks.

The angel guiding her journey asked whether she knew who was that old man of such reverence and glory, attended by so solemn a company of white-robed people. [Col. 1276A] When the virgin of the Lord confessed that she did not know, he said: “This is the servant of the Lord, Amandus. Having laudably and innocently completed the course of this present life, he hastens to enter into the joy of his Lord with sheaves of gladness, so that after his labours he may have a delightful dwelling-place of rest and, translated from hope to sight, be satisfied with the glory of manifest contemplation.”

That splendid throng of white-clad people, which follows or precedes him, consists of those instructed by his sacred teachings and foreordained by divine judgment to life: they are the sign of his apostleship in the Lord, companions of his holy glory and reward through imitation.

75. The virgin of the Lord kept the vision silent and would reveal it to none of her own household. But she sent a messenger to her sister, blessed Waldetrudis, asking her to come and speak with her [Col. 1276B], and likewise summoned the man of God, Saint Gislenus. Meeting them at the place called Mervius [Note: [Col. 1275C] Rainer calls it Menrisuum.], she explained in intimate conversation the mystery of the holy vision.

The holy man, understanding it wisely, said: “Give thanks to God, faithful virgin, whose gracious will has chosen to make known to you both the merit of his servant and the near day of your own departure. Therefore carry out fittingly and diligently what you have begun, so that, having embraced the counsel of his exhortation, you may be united with him in the fellowship of eternal glory.” Having said this, they departed from one another; and her faithful death fulfilled the faith of his words.

76. Blessed Amandus died on the Lord’s night, on the eighth day before the Ides of February [6 February], in the six hundred and sixty-first year from the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1275C] The year 684.], in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Vitalian [Note: [Col. 1275C] St Vitalian, whom we treated on 27 January, began his pontificate in 636; therefore his third year was A.D. 659 and his fifth, 661.], in the twenty-third year of the reign of Constantine [Note: [Col. 1276C] Rather, Constans, grandson of Heraclius and son of Constantine, began to reign in 641; his twentieth year corresponds to A.D. 661. Constans was father of Constantine Pogonatus, under whom St Amandus died. The cause of the errors was discussed in §16.], [Col. 1276C] the third ruler of the commonwealth after Heraclius; while Theuderic reigned in Francia [Note: [Col. 1276C] Theuderic began to reign in 680; only he is mentioned in St Amandus’s testament.]. It was the ninetieth year of the blessed bishop’s life. By the favour of the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honour and glory through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[MIRACLES OF ST AMANDUS.]

[Col. 1277]

PROLOGUE TO THE MIRACLES OF ST AMANDUS. [Note: [Col. 1277C] From the Douai edition.]

[Col. 1277A] Although the human mind is sometimes deceived by imaginary visions, it cannot be deceived by miraculous signs, which the Lord who works virtues deigns to perform in his faithful people. For the king of Memphis, together with all Egypt, was taken in more by phantasmal delusion from the Egyptians, holding false and imaginary things as true. But after the divine wonders of power had been displayed, even the magicians themselves, though at first unbelieving, afterwards confessed with the rest that this was the finger of God.

The heavens—that is, all the faithful—declare the glory of God, and the sound of his mighty works goes forth into all the earth. Therefore, according to the measure of our ability, in speech admittedly unpolished but in no ignoble subject-matter, I shall endeavour to convey certain notable acts to the knowledge of posterity: how, in our own age upon earth [Col. 1278A], the immortal King revealed his soldier, namely blessed Amandus, to have been endowed by himself with the glorious gift of immortality in heaven.

But if anyone, in obstinate mind, should try to rebuke our undertaking in this style, thinking that we wish to follow nothing but common rumours, we set against him the weapon once used by the shepherd and first captain of the Church against those rejecting the truth: “We cannot but speak of what we have heard and seen.” For this pen sets forth in its running lines nothing except what the eyes of the writer have manifestly proved, with testimony supplied by monks, clerics, and laypersons of the same period, men of venerable memory and distinguished reputation.

THE CHAPTERS BEGIN.

[Col. 1277]

[Col. 1277B]

I. Concerning bells which rang while burning, though no one struck them.  
II. Concerning a madman at Cambrai restored to reason.  
III. Concerning a sick woman restored to health.  
IV. A mute man’s mouth and tongue are opened.  
V. Concerning a disabled boy healed.  
VI. Concerning a madman at Laon restored to reason.  
VII. Concerning a crippled woman set upright beneath the bier of Saint Amandus.  
VIII. Concerning a blind woman restored to sight.  
[Col. 1278B] IX. Concerning a woman mute from birth, who spoke there.  
X. Concerning a boy with open eyes who did not see, enlightened through Saint Amandus.  
XI. Concerning a blind woman at Noyon enlightened.  
XII. Concerning a cripple healed.  
XIII. Concerning a woman at Douai suddenly crippled and set upright before the bier of Saint Amandus.  
XIV. Concerning a prisoner at Coceium freed through the invocation of Saint Amandus.

THE MIRACLES OF ST AMANDUS, WHICH TOOK PLACE THROUGHOUT GAUL, BEGIN.

[Col. 1277]

CHAPTER I.

[Col. 1277C]

Accordingly, in the year 1066 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and the forty-sixth from Amandus’s death, on the third day before the Ides of February [11 February], houses in the marketplace at Elnone caught fire about the third hour. From there, through the roof-tiles beneath the lead sheets, the flame broke into the church of the aforesaid bishop itself, which was roofed with lead plates—through, as we believe, the envy of the ancient enemy. That church, together with all its cloisters, was immediately devastated by fire, as also was the other church of the prince of the apostles. The bells melted and were reduced to powder; all the church’s ornaments were ruined—its columns of Parian marble, I mean, together with the handsome structure of the lectern. What was heard there also cast many into no small amazement: to readers, I think [Col. 1278C], it will seem like a prodigy.

For as soon as the bells themselves were seized by the flame, they began all together to ring, moved by no one except God alone, as though divinely instructed to lament their own ruin and that of the church, until, as has been stated, they were reduced to powder. In order to restore that dwelling, the brothers, with the abbot of the place, took through Gaul the bier in which the little body of the venerable Father lay, acting on the advice of the marquis of the land and at the urgent request also of the Frankish bishops. Everywhere the Gauls received them with much treasure, honourably and with the utmost devotion.

We departed from the monastery on the seventh day before the Ides of June [7 June], and returned to it on the fourth day before the Nones of July [4 July]. What, during this interval of four weeks, was often accomplished through the merits of the oft-mentioned bishop before an immense multitude in that region, Mother Church does not judge should be kept silent. She rejoices that her orthodox children, preserving her filial bond everywhere in good perseverance, have been invested with the honour of heaven [Col. 1279A]. But, passing over these things, let us now turn our admittedly feeble pen to those matters which we have resolved to record and commit to memory.

CHAPTER II.

As we travelled through various places, we at last came to Cambrai, resplendent with its episcopal see.

There, beside the gates, sat a madman with his feet tightly confined in irons. As the inhabitants openly told us, in the extreme madness of his mind he had wounded one of his female relatives [Col. 1279B]. When we had been honourably received by Bishop Herberthus and all the clergy of that place and had stayed there as guests, we requested that he be given to Saint Amandus, so that, released from bodily chains, the saint to whom he was entrusted might obtain from divine mercy his release from demonic bonds. And so it came about. The bishop assented to our petitions, and our bishop, whose body was being carried, obtained from Christ the supreme bishop a free mind for the man hitherto held captive. Thus the man proceeded with us thereafter, showing no further sign of an unsound mind.

CHAPTER III.

Turning our steps from that city with an immense company of citizens, we were making our way toward the town [Col. 1279C] called Coceium, where many injuries were inflicted by the townsman, or judge, of that place upon the household of Saint Amandus that lived around the town. But when we drew near to the place whither we had intended to go, behold, we met a priest named Milo, of a church built in honour of Saint Remigius, with a considerable mixed-sex crowd. He humbly begged us to allow the shrine of so great a bishop to be carried into the church of Saint Remigius and to rest there for a little while.

Not far from that place is a village called Vernulium. A woman lay there upon a bed because of an overwhelming weakness of her limbs; for twice five years she had been unable to leave her bed [Col. 1279D]. When she heard the sounds and songs of the people turning aside there, she asked the cause. On learning that the body of Saint Amandus was being borne there by throngs of the faithful, she immediately burst out in these words: “O, if only I were allowed at least to crawl on my hands, like a four-footed creature, to meet him, I would entreat the saint to aid my weakness by his sacred intercession!”

But as she burned with eager longing that what she desired might be fulfilled, the merciful divinity, through the intercession of so great a Father, forestalled her vows—he for whom it is easy to grant things which mortals do not even dare to desire. At once the blood coursing through her sinews strengthened her weak limbs, drove out the infirmity, and established them in vigour. So she lightly sprang from the bed on which long illness had confined her [Col. 1280A] and began gradually to walk to the threshold of the house. Not content, as women commonly are, merely to walk, she ran swiftly, seized the bier, and related, with competent witnesses, what and how great things that eminent worker of miracles had done for her through his protection. Then she placed a strap around her neck like a slave’s yoke and, though free, made herself subject to the saint’s lordship. Nor without reason: he had enabled her, who through natural infirmity had been reduced to go about like a four-footed creature, to come joyfully to meet him upright on two feet according to nature’s use.

CHAPTER IV.

A young cousin of this woman, likewise free, is also mentioned. He was more than thirty years old, mute from birth, though fully possessed of hearing and understanding [Col. 1280B]. He had visited many churches of saints, seeking the divinely granted use of his tongue; but, with no disrespect to them, this gift had been reserved for the merits of so great a Father. Ancient miracles are renewed in him, and we recognize, as it were, another age of Zechariah arisen.

Zechariah’s relatives indicated by signs what name he wished to give his son; this man’s relatives likewise indicated by signs upon what terms he wished to subject himself to the saint’s service. Zechariah asked by gesture that a writing tablet be given him, so that his fingers might record what his tongue could not; this man likewise indicated by gesture that he would pay the saint four silver coins each year as the poll-tax for his head. What Zechariah wished to put upon the page, he soon declared in open speech when the use of his tongue was restored. Let us see how this man too imitated him in a pleasant miracle, when, standing before the bier [Col. 1280C], he put a strap around his neck.

Then the priest Milo, mentioned above, in whose diocese this man was said to have been born and raised, came forward and addressed him briefly: “What, brother, are you promising? If you cannot speak, at least indicate with your fingers, before these witnesses, what you have in mind.”

All fell silent and held their faces attentive. VIRGIL.

Then, while he was trying with two pairs of fingers to signify the same number of silver coins, he declared in a clear voice, for the first time, what he had been endeavouring to express by signs. O what applause, and how great, you would have seen, had you been present, from the crowds streaming together in companies from every side [Col. 1280D], praising God with us in hymn-singing voices and, in immense joy, wetting their cheeks with floods of tears.

What shall I say of the very age at which he was instructed in speech? Christ, by his Passion, restored in this same age to life a person dead in sins and mute in the praises of God, opening his mouth to divine praise. And blessed Amandus, by sacred intercession, as it were gave speech-life to this servant of his, who in some manner was comparable to a dead person; he made him extol God’s praises and obtained from divine mercy that he might form words for rendering thanks to God.

CHAPTER V.

I consider no less worthy of proclamation what we saw wonderfully accomplished [Col. 1281A] at the very threshold of the gates of the aforesaid fortress. As the litter carrying the saint’s corpse was held crosswise, so that the people might in deepest devotion place their necks beneath it, a woman hurried up, carrying in her arms a disabled son who, for almost a full year, had been unable to set foot upon the ground. When his mother placed him beneath the bier, he began to cry out, in the hearing of all: “Mother, set me down at once from the vehicle in which I am carried, for I think I can now follow you on foot. I beg you, do not oppose my welfare and your own joy.”

But she, believing that he said this in childish—or even irrational—words, replied: “Do not, my son, do not, lest you be crushed by the crowd pressing upon us, while you are unable to accomplish what you say” [Col. 1281B].

And the child said: “I can, mother, I can.” After this, without waiting for his mother’s answer, he immediately wrenched himself from her arms; testing the way little by little, he joyfully broke into a run. By performing these and similar miraculous signs around that fortress, the merciful bishop preferred, I believe, to restrain the townspeople gently from harassing his household rather than to terrify them with threats. But since we have dealt with these according to the capacity of our little talent, let us turn the pen to the things remaining, which shine brighter than light; invoking the protection, for their completion, of him to whose merits we believe such remarkable deeds are to be ascribed.

CHAPTER VI.

At the end of the following dawn we came to the hill of Laon [Col. 1281C] and immediately climbed it. There we were received with great veneration by Bishop Elenandus and all the clergy of the place, and rested that day. Meanwhile the sun was turning toward sunset, and behold, they brought a man of deranged mind, bound hand and foot in chains. Night fell from Ocean; meanwhile boys and unmarried girls, young men together with old, surrounded the shrine of that most precious treasure and began devoutly to keep watch with burning torches and lamps.

Then, when night held the middle of the world and the setting stars invited sleep, the man suddenly, lying beneath the bier, burst out with these words: “I ask you who stand around to tell me why these bonds bind my arms, or where I lie cast down” [Col. 1281D].

Astonished by wonder, they thought he was uttering wandering words as before; nevertheless they told him what he asked: “Because of the excessive madness of your mind, you have been brought, bound by knotted fetters, to the protection of Saint Amandus, whose body, you should know, lies at present in the church of Saint Mary.”

“Give thanks to God with me,” he said, “for the monstrous force of madness has departed; let the mouths of the chains now be opened.” As soon as he had been freed from every bond, he signed himself with the sign of the holy cross. Beating his breast, he confessed himself guilty if, prompted by the devil, he had uttered in that error any word against the purity of the faith. Thereupon he gave himself as a servant to Saint Amandus, whose prayers he continually regarded as the support of his mind. And rightly he submitted himself to the saint’s service, through whose aid he knew himself, once powerless in mind, to have been freed from the prison of a savage torturer [Col. 1282A].

CHAPTER VII.

Nor should those things be passed over in silence which, as we returned from there on the Lord’s Day, were performed before all eyes upon that same hill [735]. As we passed the gates of the city set upon the brow of the hill with a great mixed company of both sexes, in the heat of midday, behold, a woman came forward with twisted legs, creeping on her hands and with her face fixed upon the ground. As everyone made way, she approached the bier. A wonderful and exceedingly astonishing thing! Once she joined herself to the bearers, her sinews loosened; she rose upright and—marvellous to tell!—firmly grasped the bier itself.

O what a roar rang out from the people’s mouths, and what a great cry of monks, clerics, and laypeople echoed in the praises of God! Then one could see crowds streaming from every side to this wonder, so pressing upon the bearers in their eagerness to see the woman that scarcely any of them could move his feet [Col. 1282B]. Therefore, using prudent counsel, we caused the holy body to rest for about three hours upon a certain rock in that same place, so that, having thus recovered our breath somewhat, we might afterwards descend from the hilltop.

CHAPTER VIII.

Foolishly I relate a marvellous thing, seeking a believing hearer; yet I narrate only matters accomplished, as the sight of the writer attests, within scarcely the space of one hour. Immediately a woman came up who had spent the course of seven years in the sorrow of blindness. As soon as she touched the shrine with her eyes, the darkness having been wiped away, she recovered the loss of her vanished light [Col. 1282C]. Restored to her former sight, she proceeded with us and began to proclaim the mighty works of Christ performed upon her.

CHAPTER IX.
