A girl was also brought by both parents. They said that, from the time she had issued from her mother’s womb until that very day, she had lacked the use of speech. When she likewise kissed the receptacle of the venerable body, the instrument of her tongue was loosened, and the organs of speech were raised in praise of God.

The people of Laon rejoiced in heart at these and many other miracles [Col. 1282D]. They gave thanks to the majesty that thunders from heaven for things which an innumerable gathering of people of every sex and age had kept from our eyes, and which were afterwards reported to us by truthful believers. Not only the inhabitants of that city but also of other cities flocked to these spectacles, lifting up their voices in hymnic song to God and praising the divine power because the occasion had arisen to bring the saint there. They believed that such things would never have been made manifest to their eyes by so great a patron unless fire had devastated his church; for otherwise they would not have rejoiced that he had been brought to their borders.

CHAPTER X.

Then, turning our steps amid an immense and joyful press of people, we proceeded toward [Col. 1283A] the walls of Noyon. The golden sun was preparing to plunge its course into Ocean when we arrived at the little fortress called Calneium. We were received there hospitably and rested through the night. In the morning, after the night vigils, we saw a woman holding in her lap a boy who carried a lamp without light—his little eyes, I mean, having in their sockets no lamp at all. She came forward and began to speak, but broke off in mid-sentence, shaken by sobbing as she expressed the grief caused by her son’s congenital blindness:

“With this boy I have kept watch throughout this night beneath the bier of Saint Amandus. I bore him into the world without natural sight, and I brought him here so that he might be enlightened by the rays of this saint’s merits.

[Col. 1283B] But since I have not yet obtained my request, I beg you: touch the places of his eyes with some relic of this saint, if in some way divine mercy may condescend to me in my supplication and enlighten him by its grace.”

Then we took a tooth of the oft-mentioned Father, honourably set in gold by a craftsman, and also the staff by which the bishop had guided his episcopate of preaching, and laid them upon the places of his eyes as the mother had requested. After a brief interval, the boy’s little eyes immediately performed their function, shining by divine power with no darkness at all impeding them.

Then all those standing by—first the father and mother—wished to put this beyond doubt by experiment. They offered him necklaces, little candles, and other things which delight a child’s mind; and he, clearly distinguishing them [Col. 1283C], swiftly seized everything, then promptly threw it back in play to those who offered it in turn. They also made signs with their fingers, and he similarly responded. Without delay, the canons rushed to the bells, while we with the people burst forth in divine praises.

CHAPTER XI.

Next we arrived at Noyon, where we were proceeding. There we encountered two shrines of Saint Eligius—formerly a most intimate friend of Saint Amandus while both were alive—one borne by the monks and the other by the clerics. Suburban residents and townspeople of every order, clerics together with monks, were present. Receiving the shrine of our patron [Col. 1283D] with immense reverence and the highest devotion, they carried it into the church of the episcopal see.

After our tent had been pitched in the city square, they, together with Baldwin, bishop of that place, reverently received it and carried it there, rejoicing in so great a guest [736]. When the customary night vigils had been completed and our morning offices likewise performed, behold, a woman appeared oppressed by the immense pain of vertigo, so that she could not turn her head upward, to the right, or to the left and was deprived of the joy of sight. Standing beside the bier, by the middle of daylight she was restored so completely to health that she rejoiced openly in the remedies of which pain in her head had deprived her. For, at once crowned again with her former sight, she looked up to heaven [Col. 1284A] in thanksgiving to God; turning her eyes about, she looked here and there at those standing around and recounted the Lord’s powers marvellously displayed upon her.

CHAPTER XII.

When this had occurred and the report immediately spread through the mouths of the people, a man walking with a distorted foot was brought forward. Not trusting his own steps upon the ground, he was supported by another’s aid. Thus, seeking the help of the most holy confessor, he put the grace of the saint’s merits to the test. Remaining for a long while, trembling, before his presence, he invoked the prayers of so great a bishop, to avail him before divine mercy. At last he found what he sought, and he who had come by another’s feet returned on his own; he felt that the saint’s protection would not fail him [Col. 1284B].

These and very many similar manifestations of power were shown not only in these but in other cities of Gaul through this our patron, as we have said. They could not reach the knowledge of our own sight because of the pressure of the immense crowds. But because we did not wish to exceed our undertaking, we record for the present only those wonders which did not escape our eyes.

CHAPTER XIII.

Nor do we think it fitting to be silent about what we witnessed gloriously accomplished at Douai.

Among the other people a woman came out to meet us in health; but, being liable to I know not what guilt, she was not found worthy to meet the saint—perhaps guilty of some blasphemy against him, for which she had not yet offered worthy penance [Col. 1284C]. For the judgments of the Lord are a great abyss.

Accordingly, as soon as she returned home, her feet clung to her buttocks and her hands to her breast, as if fixed by nails, and so she lay half-dead. We ourselves saw her brought in a vehicle to the refuge of our patron, like one dead and showing no breath of life at all. But not long afterwards we saw her, her feet released and her hands reversed in position, standing erect before the bier itself.

These are the things by which the Lord has deigned to declare, in the Gallic province and in this time, the merits of most blessed Amandus, together with other things related to us by the sick persons themselves after their health had been restored, under the testimony of faithful people [Col. 1284D]. Whatever these may be, however great both these and those other things are: in all his works may the name of the Lord be blessed for ever. Amen.

**Concerning a young man hanged in the district of Noyon and restored to life through blessed Amandus**
A certain remarkable miracle performed by blessed Amandus in the district of Noyon, as we have learned from the report of certain persons, we shall take care to make known in some sort of writing to those who wish to read it.

While blessed Amandus was staying with twelve brethren in the district of Laon, in a place called Baresetum, it happened that King Dagobert of the Franks came one day to Compiègne. When he learned of the king’s arrival, blessed Amandus resolved to go there. When he reached an estate called Melincotum, he turned aside for lodging in the house of a certain widow [Col. 1285A], who had an only son.

Meanwhile, certain robbers coming from the region of Beauvais were leading before them some booty which they had stolen and carried away from there. When they saw the inhabitants of that same region pursuing them swiftly and close behind, they plunged deep into a darker forest with their booty. Yet, not feeling secure concerning their lives, they fled at a rapid pace from their pursuing adversaries.

By chance, the widow’s son, in whose lodging blessed Amandus had turned aside, was walking alone through that same wood. Since he was completely unaware of the matter, the robbers left their booty with him as though it were to be guarded; wishing only to save themselves, they then began to flee more swiftly. But the men who were hastening to seize the booty from the robbers [Col. 1285B] found the youth alone in the wood with the booty abandoned by the robbers. Believing him to have been one of the robbers, they seized him and immediately [Col. 1286A] hanged him.

Without delay, the report spread and a cry was raised: the widow’s son had been hanged and was already dead. Almost all the inhabitants dwelling round about ran to see. The mother of the hanged youth also came running with blessed Amandus, whom she had received as a guest, wailing with pitiable cries. Why say more? The holy man was so moved by compassion for the woman that, prostrate upon the ground and full of tears, he remained long absorbed in prayer, until, by God’s favour, he restored the youth alive and unharmed to his rejoicing and exultant mother.

Therefore, in memory of this extraordinary and venerable event, a small chapel was built at slight expense in that same place, 737 in honour of blessed Bishop Amandus, to the praise of God our Saviour Jesus Christ, [Col. 1286B] who wonderfully glorifies his saint in heaven and on earth. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Prologue to the Miracles of Saint Amandus

[Col. 1285]

[Col. 1285B] In many and frequent ways, if we take care to notice, divine grace deigns to visit us and to rouse us when we are weighed down by the torpor of sloth. At one time it threatens with terrors; at another it consoles human weakness with fatherly encouragements. With terrors it rebukes sinners, so that they may repent [Col. 1285C]; with encouragements it exhorts those doing good to advance toward better things. Sometimes it acts within us by inward inspiration; sometimes, by presenting unusual things to the outward senses, it shakes off our indolence.

For, seeing the complaints of certain people who murmur that it displays no miracles in our times, as it did in antiquity, God sometimes renews miracles through the bodies or even ashes of departed Fathers—signs which he granted them to perform while living, outward manifestations of inward virtues. For what else do the divine works which the wisdom that created all things performs through its saints set before our senses, except that we should understand that the maker of all things dwells within them, as in his own temple, speaking and acting?

Although, moreover, to demonstrate his omnipotence, he also performs many miracles through wicked persons, for the benefit of his own people and to confute the perversity of unbelievers—miracles which Scripture customarily calls figuratively “powers,” as Truth itself testifies in the Gospel: [Col. 1286B] “Many will say to me: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name perform many powers?’” (Matthew 7).

But when miracles are divinely performed at the bodies of saints, what else is thereby indicated to us from heaven except that we should at least be stirred to imitate them [Col. 1286C] and apply ourselves to good works, whose merits, we do not doubt, bring about such deeds? Let the minds of men sleeping in death-bringing torpor therefore awaken, and let them understand the works of divinity brought before their senses, so that healings of bodies may become causes of the salvation of souls. For this reason health is often restored to dying bodies, so that, through such an occasion, the souls of those who see it—souls that will never die—may be raised from inward sickness.

The Creator’s kindness provides for all: according to each person’s capacity, it bestows on each fitting benefits with moderation. Thus it raises the prudent and those strong in faith to contemplate heavenly things, yet does not abandon the simple and weak. By bringing certain visible and bodily things before those devoted to the senses of the flesh, it nourishes and raises them toward greater [Col. 1286D] things, the invisible and spiritual. Let us now come to the matter for which we have said these things beforehand, lest our longer preface seem burdensome to readers.

## The Chapters Begin

[Col. 1285]

[Col. 1285D]

I. The beginning of the account of the event, and concerning a woman healed.  
II. Likewise, concerning another woman healed of contraction of the hand.  
III. Likewise, concerning a third woman healed of weakness of the whole body [Col. 1286D].  
IV. Concerning a circle seen in the air above the saint’s body.  
V. Concerning a girl blind from birth, enlightened by the saint’s merits.  
VI. Concerning a contracted boy who was made erect.  
[Col. 1287A] VII. Concerning another girl, blind from birth and deaf, healed by the saint’s merits.  
VIII. Concerning a deaf man recovering his hearing at the saint’s arrival.  
IX. Concerning a woman healed at Tournai.  
X. Concerning a woman’s contracted arm and its healing; and that not all the miracles performed during the saint’s conveyance are set forth in this little work; and that the remedies for souls divinely effected through them are to be embraced more than those for bodies [Col. 1288A].

## The Miracles of Saint Amandus Performed through Brabant Begin

[Col. 1287]

## Chapter I

[Col. 1287B]

Just as many faithful people, stirred by divine inspiration, are accustomed to build churches or monasteries from their goods and estates for the remission of their sins, so utterly wicked men, persuaded by the devil, daily strive to invade, plunder, and carry away the goods handed over by the faithful to churches and monasteries.

Because a necessity of this kind pressed upon us—namely, because evil men desired to take away, and were already 738 violently retaining, things that had long ago been bestowed upon God and Saint Amandus in the district of Brabant by kings and devout princes for the salvation of their souls—in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1107, when Lord Abbot Hugh presided over the monastery of Elnone, in the twenty-second year of his ordination, the body of the saint was carried into Brabant on the Monday of Pentecost.

They came to the saint’s estate called Anduennium, and to another called Saint Saviour’s. A great crowd ran together there. A certain woman, sick for eighteen years and lying in bed, was weakened in the lower part of her body—that is, in her legs and shins. Hearing that the saint was passing by, she had herself carried there and was placed beneath the saint’s bier. There, after writhing for several hours in extreme pain while the people watched, she suddenly rose up. She stood healed; a cry arose from the people, and praises were offered together to the Creator.

## Chapter II

When the saint’s body had been carried from Anduennium to Gerald’s Mount [Col. 1287D], and was being brought from Gerald’s Mount to Herlengona, an estate belonging to it, as we crossed a stream called the Lota, a certain woman joined the whole crowd. Her right hand was so weakened by contraction of the sinews that she could perform no task with it at all. She came, I say, to the saint’s bier, faithfully applied her disabled hand to it, and went away; as she returned, she received complete healing of her hand.

## Chapter III

They arrived at the aforesaid estate. At dawn on the following day, because of the crowd of people gathering together, the saint’s body was carried out of the church, which was too small to contain them, and placed in the open air beneath a wooden structure suitably arranged with curtains hanging around it.

There another woman, weak throughout her whole body and wretchedly contracted in the legs, was brought and laid beneath the saint’s bier. At first she was in torment [Col. 1288B], and twice almost expired as her strength failed because of the agony of pain; but at last she was stretched out, and returned home healed by her own steps, though she had been brought there by another’s.

## Chapter IV

At about the third hour, as they began to celebrate Mass before the most sacred body, marvellous to relate, so that it might plainly appear to all by whose merits these signs were performed: in a clear and pure sky, without thick clouds, a circle of white colour was seen shining in heaven above the saint’s body. It remained until the priest had completed the Mass.

A considerable crowd of people was present. The unfamiliar sight struck the eyes of all who marvelled at it; appearing to everyone in the upper regions of the air, it could not possibly be concealed. [Col. 1288C] Let the prudent reader consider inwardly what divine goodness was effecting through that sign in the hearts of those who looked upon it. Certainly sighs and tears mingled with joy bore witness to the devotion of the people who beheld it in astonishment.

The same precious body was then carried over the land where certain wicked men had been violently injuring the saint—through woods and lands which they had unjustly invaded. The saint, most justly subjecting them without resistance, also made these men his subjects. In the presence of the saint’s body, to whom the holy apostle Peter, while he lived, had given the power of binding and loosing, all who thereafter presumed to inflict any injury upon the saint concerning those lands and woods were excommunicated, with the agreement, will, oral declaration, and proclamation [Col. 1288D] of the brethren accompanying the saint and of the people standing around.

## Chapter V

As evening fell on that same day, after the saint’s body had already been brought back into the church, while some of the brethren who had accompanied the saint were resting and others were still awake, a five-year-old girl blind from birth was led there by her mother and placed beside the bier. Through the merits of Father Amandus, the darkness of her eyes was driven away, and she was suddenly enlightened by divine power.

When she cried out to her mother that she could see, and rejoiced exceedingly with the unfeigned delight of simple childhood—for such an age neither knows how to pretend what is not, nor can conceal what is—and was greatly astonished at the forms of the surrounding things which she had never previously seen, her mother, the first to perceive what had happened to her daughter, cried out. The people, hearing at once what had occurred, raised an uproar at the novelty of the event [Col. 1289A]. They ran to the church; the bells rang; the brethren hastened up; and they marvelled at the girl’s joy, beyond all words.

To test the matter, they held bread and other things before her eyes. She stretched out her hands and followed with her face and arms whichever way the objects presented to her were moved. What more fitting response could there be than to praise you, God, the giver of all good things?

## Chapter VI

On the following day, as the parents were going to Ghent, a boy of about fifteen years, from the village called Nineveh, the son of a certain rich man, was brought there. Both his shins were contracted so that his calves adhered to the backs of his legs, to such an extent that the two limbs had become a single skin. He was brought [Col. 1289B] and placed beneath the saint’s shrine. Suddenly, when the calves and legs were separated, he cried out terribly; 739 blood flowed copiously and for a long time from the place of rupture, as though the limbs had been cut with iron. Rising with his legs straightened, he stood sound upon his feet and began to walk.

## Chapter VII

On the following feria, the Monday after the octave of Pentecost, while the saint’s body had been carried over certain land concerning which a knight, Razo of Mont, was wronging the saint, a girl from Ghent, about twelve years old, blind and deaf from birth, was brought by her parents and placed before the saint’s bier. By divine compassion, through the merits of so great a Father, she was granted hearing and sight.

Seeing this, the knight was seized by divine fear. He confessed his fault concerning the injury, made amends [Col. 1289C] to the saint for his offence, sought pardon, and obtained forgiveness.

## Chapter VIII

As we were now returning and bringing home, with immense joy, a treasure of such great value, we had to pass through Tournai. Among the innumerable crowd that came from the surrounding villages to meet the saint, a certain man from the countryside of Rungiacum, deprived of hearing in both ears, arrived at Tournai with his neighbours and began with them to await the saint’s arrival.

[Col. 1290A] When some delay occurred, he turned aside with his companions and began to dine. Suddenly the church bells sounded for the saint’s arrival. While the others heard them, he was the first to cry out that he himself could hear; confessing that he had recovered his hearing through the assistance and truly worthy merits of Father Amandus, he later devoutly fulfilled his vow at the monastery in our sight, carrying a band of wax around his head.

## Chapter IX

As we passed through the city and had already gone out through its gates, suddenly the cry of the people following us rose behind our backs. A disabled woman, who was being carried after the saint’s bier, was announced to have stood upright. The saint’s body, carried back by the force of the crowd to the place where the healed woman stood, was compelled to halt [Col. 1290B]; all voices were turned to the praise of the Creator.

## Chapter X

During this carrying of the holy Father along roads and through the countryside, some other events occurred while we were absent, though we later learned of them from the report of the faithful. We pass over some of them, but record one: a certain woman who lived at Anduennium had an arm which, through infirmity, was twisted back and adhered to her shoulders so tightly that she could neither move it at all nor bring it to her mouth.

Water was brought to her which they applied to the saint’s shrine as a remedy for the sick. She washed her arm with it and stretched it out. She effectively grasped a distaff and spindle, a woman’s work implements, so that she could work with them, something she had previously been unable to do.

Let others marvel at such marked manifestations of powers brought before the bodily senses [Col. 1290C], namely bodily healings; let us rather embrace the healings of souls thereby accomplished. For what wise person would not rejoice more at minds divided by strife reconciled to peace, at deadly hatreds calmed—that is, at souls raised from death—than at bodily health restored only to last for a short time? In all things let us praise, glorify, and bless the Creator and Restorer of body and soul. Amen.

## A Miracle Performed through His Intercessions in the Church of Saint Amandus within the City of Rouen, Concerning a Woman Who Killed Herself by a Noose and, through Christ’s Assisting Grace, Received Life Again

[Col. 1289]

[Col. 1289D] To the most beloved and greatly venerable Bovo, a member of Christ and abbot of the monastery of Elnone, and to the whole blessed community entrusted to him by God: Marsilia, least of the abbesses of the handmaids of Christ, and the whole congregation of sisters serving God and the holy bishop Amandus in the city of Rouen, wishes that you may advance from virtue to virtue, so that you may worthily behold the God of gods in Zion.

Among the virtues and miraculous signs which God performs for you through our holy and common Father, a certain distinguished miracle, divinely accomplished in our church and in our presence through the merits of that most holy Father of ours, should be included. We have judged it worthy to set down briefly in writing and report it to your holiness. For it is fitting that, just as in the camp of the eternal King, though different in sex yet equal in purpose, we serve under one and the same patron, so we may unanimously rejoice at the triumphant proclamation of his powers, to the honour of God.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1107, a certain noblewoman in the district of Lisieux, not so much because her own sins demanded it as so that the glory of God might shine more widely 740 [Col. 1291A] in his holy bishop, suffered such cruelty from the ancient enemy that she was first deceived and tormented by malignant and various phantasms of thought. Finally, after losing her natural reason, she determined upon this alone: how, when everyone was absent, she might lay hands upon herself and somehow end her life, whether by hanging from a noose or by drowning in a river.

And she would have done so, had not her husband’s sudden appearances repeatedly prevented it. For she had been deceived by a certain little woman, restless and garrulous, who came to her in houses, fields, and streets with deceitful talk, asserting that her husband hated her and, loving another woman more, preferred that woman to her in carnal union. Immediately, credulous toward the liar as Eve of old had been toward the serpent, she fell into the sorrow that works death. Forgetful of God and of the Christian faith, she continually contrived and laboured by every means to end her wretched life through some diabolical artifice.

But divine mercy, which wills no one to perish, prevented this from happening, in order to multiply the praise and glory of its holy confessor Amandus. When her husband understood such madness, he often tried to soothe her with gentle words and consolations, so that she might recover from this devilish understanding and make both him and his household joyful rather than sorrowful by such a calamity. But in answer to his exhortations she gave this response of wretched despair: [Col. 1291B] “This can by no means happen; let me go to hell with the devil, to whom I have been predestined and given.”

No persuasion, promise, or threat could tear this wicked utterance from her mouth. Then, having adopted a salutary plan, they brought the deranged woman to the church of blessed Amandus, to whom this particular kind of power is believed to have been granted by the Saviour: that no demonic force can resist him. Hence we do not doubt at all that his merit is numbered among the heavenly powers, to whose authority hostile powers are subjected.

When the woman was earnestly asked by certain persons of sound faith, of both sexes, who were gathering to her for the purpose of visitation and exhortation, to fortify herself with the saving sign of the cross, she utterly refused. Repeating the aforementioned pronouncement of her unhappiness, she complained insistently that she was being delayed so long from going to the ruin of destruction.

[Col. 1291D] When certain religious men of more discerning intelligence among them approached her more closely and spoke with her privately, she replied in composed speech that she had been wholly delivered over to infernal flames and sulphurous punishments; that while detained in this world she had even felt a share of them; and that she expected the remainder, which would come upon her before long.

Then those who were sounder in faith and keener in understanding decided that water should be poured into a cask and blessed, and that on the following day it should be set there by the hands of priests, with the invocation of Christ’s name and of his power and authority. Hearing and understanding this shrewdly, she was greatly astonished, began to be more sharply agitated, and drew frequent deep sighs.

Then, after looking around at everything, she feigned outward modesty through diabolical cunning, though inwardly the enemy’s madness raged. [Col. 1292A] When evening came, she was led outside the choir and placed before the altar at which Saint Amandus had been accustomed to celebrate Mass. Then, as night’s darkness came on and guards had been appointed to watch over her, those who had brought her withdrew.

O cunning of the devil! O deceitfulness of the ancient serpent, bent upon the destruction of the human race! As soon as the unhappy woman found a suitable time for death, she craftily urged the watchmen, after the vigils and labours they had expended upon her, now to rest and, exhausted by so great a trouble, give themselves to sleep. She also pretended that, being extremely weary with them, she wished to rest. For seven days and as many nights had already passed since she had been brought there.

When a bed had been prepared and suitably arranged, she lay down upon it a little, as though to sleep. Looking around and perceiving that no one was present, clothed only in a shift, she secretly climbed a wall which seemed higher than the others. She fastened part of the veil with which she covered her head to the summit of a column in that wall; from the remaining part she marvellously fashioned a running noose, put her neck into it, and leapt down violently. She bent her neck with such force that a jet of blood issuing from her throat stained part of the wall opposite.

Midnight had already passed when one of the guards awoke and rose. Not finding her in the bed, he searched the whole church and finally found the place where she was hanging. Struck with great horror, he perceived the body to be stiff [Col. 1292C] and wholly lifeless.

Immediately he raised a great cry and announced by shouting what had happened. On hearing it, nuns rushed together from every side; cries arose all around; the wretched dead woman was pitifully lamented; Saint Amandus was invoked with many groans and tears, that he might not allow the dignity of his place to be lost, but might mercifully come to the help of those running to him.

Then a light was kindled, the neck of the hanging woman was pulled from the noose, and her lifeless corpse was cast down upon the pavement of the church. Three of the sisters, who appeared bolder or more prudent, because it was night, sought out the archdeacon and tearfully asked what should be done. He gave them this answer and 741 counsel: before daylight, the corpse should be dragged from the church and thrown into any ditch whatsoever.

When they returned, the archdeacon himself followed them and stood there with those crying and gathered around, marvelling at the great cunning of the devil’s fraud. Meanwhile, as certain nuns came nearer, one of them felt a living spirit stirring again in the woman’s breast. She perceived that at times her face gradually reddened, at times she gradually opened her eyes, and at times drew faint breaths.

Those around her, examining this more carefully, called with a great cry upon the aid of their holy patron Amandus, beat their breasts, and multiplied their vows of prayer. While these things were taking place, they suddenly knew, through the power of almighty God and through the intervention of his glorious and wonderful bishop Amandus, that the soul had returned to the body [Col. 1293A].

Nevertheless, on that day and the following night, after she had been restored to life, she remained unable to speak. Such strength of force was in her that she could scarcely be held by four people. But on the following day, as dawn broke, her first words were: “Holy Lady, merciful Mother of God Mary, help me.” Then she opened her mouth to praise our Saviour and his beloved confessor, and, with manifold rejoicing, offered vows of thanks to almighty God.

After these events, a priest was summoned. She made a full confession of her former sins and humbly received absolution.

Then she added: “I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus, who through your grace and through the merits of Saint Amandus, my lord, have raised me up and delivered me from the hands of the most destructive enemy and from the gulf of hell. I faithfully believe in you with the Father and the Holy Spirit; I worship you; and I renounce all the pomps and snares of Satan.”

When this wonderful miracle resounded far and wide, the glorious and wonderful God was magnified in his holy bishop, through whom he works so many signs marvellously. For just as, when he was once in the world, he raised by prayer a thief fastened to a gallows and dead, so now, living in heaven with Christ, he recalled to life by his precious merits the unhappy woman who had died by hanging—to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone and everywhere lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages.

## Sermon on the Elevation of the Body of Saint Amandus

[Col. 1293]

## Chapter I

[Col. 1293B]

Since we are taught by Raphael the archangel, bearer of heavenly medicine, that it is honourable to recount the works of almighty God, we judge it fitting—indeed necessary—not to pass over in silence the memorable elevation of the body of the most sacred bishop Amandus. For in it there is no small portion of divine miracle, and inexhaustible material for praise of the same blessed man and of his holiness.

Therefore, in the year 809 of the incarnate Word—that is, of the Son of God, for the salvation and redemption of the human race—which was the hundred and fiftieth year from the passing of the man of God Amandus, an extraordinary flooding of waters surpassed its boundaries in many places. It stripped the fields around the rivers [Col. 1293C] bare through the destructive loss of their crops. This dangerous evil grew so great that even inhabitants dwelling near the rivers were forced to abandon their ancestral homes and, changing their dwellings, live upon elevated hills until the waters subsided.

## Chapter II

This abundance of swelling waters, rising day by day with increased rainfall, had also filled the banks of the river called the Scarpe to overflowing. The river lay almost adjacent to the tomb of our most blessed patron Amandus, no more than twenty paces away. Overflowing through its daily increase, it rose so high that it reached the most sacred burial place of the most sacred body and filled with overlying water all the space of its little shrine lying near the feet, denying dry passage to those who wished to walk there [Col. 1293D].

The distressing consequence of this misfortune brought no small sorrow to the minds of the monks, and especially struck the venerable Lothair, keeper of the sacred church [Col. 1294B] at that time, with considerable alarm. Although human speech should fall silent, the structure of the buildings proclaims the resourcefulness of his discerning mind and the effectiveness of his works, as do the volumes of books entered into our archive and the improvement and enlargement of the whole monastery.

Disturbed by the novelty of the unprecedented flood, he began to consider with discerning thought how he might meet the threatening danger, or by what aid he might withstand so grave and so great a destruction. For he was anxious lest that same abundance of waters might penetrate as far as the deposit of the most precious treasure—the holy Father’s little body, buried deeper in the earth, as we said in another sermon, by Bishop Eligius of blessed memory—and, flowing around it, dampen and violate it by its insolent touch.

At last, putting aside his wavering uncertainty, he rose to this salutary counsel, inspired, as is fitting to believe, by God 742: that he should raise the urn containing the holy little body from the lower place to a higher, and thereafter, through his foresight, make it entirely safe from all this flooding and wholly removed from the muddy marsh [Col. 1294C].

## Chapter III

When the appointed day came, he assembled a company of clerics for so great a task, engaged the necessary diggers, and took great care in raising the sarcophagus. Once it had been raised with the utmost caution, as was fitting, he had it set down on the left side. Then, with festive solemnity, in the broad spaces of the church and with lamps shining, he began and devoutly completed the solemn rites of Mass over that same tomb in honour of so great a bishop [Col. 1294D].

Although watery moisture lay outside all around the sepulchre, no entrance was opened within to muddy filth or drops of water. Nor is it unfitting to believe that God—who transforms the natures of all creatures, according to his will, into whatever forms of things he chooses, and by his own command restrains swelling seas with sands as with strongest reins—could also bestow upon the corpse of his beloved servant this benefit of so great an honour: that no defilement might enter the vessel of that urn in which the precious deposit was contained, so that the merit of that venerable bishop might be made manifest to all [Col. 1295A].

When the solemn rites of Mass had been completed, he retained with him only such monks as he wished and dismissed the rest. Not so much in rash daring as in the ardour of faithful devotion, he judged it fitting to investigate with loving curiosity what the vessel set before his eyes held within its enclosure. At the same time, he considered it necessary to take some small portion of relics from the dust of the flesh or from the bones, for the devout veneration of those who might seek them [Col. 1295B].

## Chapter IV

Meanwhile, all hesitation having been removed, the same chief guardian humbly approached the tomb, now placed upon the surface of the pavement, and, having carefully removed the stone cover by which it was closed, looked within.

And behold: there presented itself to his sight a venerable man, white-haired, pale from the emaciation of abstinence and fasts by which he had lived, outstanding in holiness of conduct and merits; fragrant as with spices through the incorruption of his limbs, and uncorrupted throughout his whole body. Lying in the tomb, he closely resembled one asleep, adorned with the dignified beauty of episcopal vestments [Col. 1295C].

The thing was exceedingly marvellous in its rarity, and scarcely expressible in human speech because of its magnitude. He who had thought he would find the remains of putrefied flesh, as usually happens with the dead, found beyond expectation the memorable prodigy of an unviolated body. No eloquence of human intelligence can express what miracle was worthy of this sight or how near it was to immeasurable astonishment; still less can the barrenness of our speech set these things forth as is fitting in its meagre words.

Astonished as was proper at the sight of so unexpected a prodigy, he blessed God with praises due to him and gave thanks to the giver of such great gifts. Rejoicing also at the discovery of so great a treasure, he again began to be tormented by no small anguish of anxiety [Col. 1295D], considering many things in his mind: what he ought to take from it as a gift for the remembrance of later generations.

## Chapter V

When the anchor of counsel had steadied his wavering mind, he took from the most sacred neck the chasuble with which the saint was clothed. Turning him to either side, he removed the river reeds which had formerly been placed beneath him because of the moisture of the water. Yet he judged this too little for his desires unless he also took some portion from the unviolated limbs of the body. He therefore turned, as I may say, bold hands toward the venerable corpse and cut the nails which projected like the horns and hooves of a spiritual calf [Col. 1296A]. After the saint’s death these had grown, contrary to nature, so much that their growth even pierced the sleeves over his hands. He also cut the beard of our bishop—our Aaron—which had grown again after his burial.

Having stored all these things away for himself with the highest devotion, yet judging them insufficient for himself and his desires, he dared to put his hand to the most sacred mouth, through which frequent prayers had been poured out to divine mercy and abundant preaching directed to diverse peoples. He attempted to see whether he could remove one of the saint’s teeth.

But, since he could not accomplish this because of their firmness, he used a craftsman’s instrument, namely a strong pair of forceps, and drew two teeth from the gums of that most beautiful mouth [Col. 1296B], teeth more precious, as one must believe, than ruddy ivory and ancient sapphire. Marvellous to tell—let him find a faithful hearer—drops of blood flowed, contrary to nature, from the teeth drawn from the dead man’s body. To this day, an ivory container bears witness to this event, still stained with the same blood with which it had been filled when the teeth were placed there for safekeeping—marvellous to tell—743.

## Chapter VI

In this deed we venerate a renewed—indeed, repeated—work of the divine majesty, recalling what we read was done at the first beginning of the world’s creation: when, in paradise, a rib was drawn from the side of the first parent while he slept, and we hear that it was fashioned into a woman’s form [Col. 1296C] (Genesis 2).

We also recall the mystery figured by that same act: namely, that from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross came forth blood with water, when the fountain of life was opened by the soldier’s spear; the price of our redemption flowed out, and, when the pouch of treasure was torn open, the fullness of the bridal pearl came forth. The stipulation of the marriage covenant written above the cross also appeared upon a most beautiful white tablet, expressed in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters.

From these things the Church, re-formed in the likeness of her Creator and Redeemer, was made the life-giving Eve, mother of all believers, the former calamity having been removed.

The miracle of which we spoke before does not seem altogether incomparable in every respect: when the mouth of our Father—who begets us in Christ through the Gospel—was opened, drops of most precious blood flowed. Through this, the whole beloved congregation of the Church deserved truly to receive an increase of faith and to become worthy and faithful in the chaste bond of marriage [Col. 1296D].

## Chapter VII
Then that ancient Adam slept in Paradise, and received Eve—fashioned from his own bone—into the fellowship of marriage. Later the new Adam, the creator of that ancient first-created man, rested in the punishment of the cross, and from the blood of his side fitted to himself the Church, pledged to him in marriage, having neither spot nor wrinkle, but immaculate in body and spirit. Our own father and parent of this people represented both of these to us by a certain likeness: he, not long ago, [Col. 1297A] slept in the tomb one hundred and fifty years after his death, representing the likeness of the first Adam in the bone removed, and presenting the image of the second Adam—that is, Christ—in the blood poured out. By these two wondrous acts he seems to have acquired for himself the Church gathered before him for his solemn rites, as a true bride in the purity of love and faith, the mother of us all. She bears children for him from her own womb—that is, from the sacred font—and, wondrous to say, remains both mother and virgin. Of her fellowship I too belong, I who now supply these things, though through his indescribable mercy I am a degenerate member of her.

Indeed, the history which relates the true judgment upon the ancient Israelite nation will seem not altogether unlike the matter of which we speak. They tell how Samson, strongest [Col. 1297B] of all the leaders, when seeking marriage encountered a roaring young lion in his path, and, upon returning, took a honeycomb from the jaw of that same lion which he had violently slain; and how he proposed a dark riddle to his wedding guests. These things correspond in some small part to the present matter; moreover, they instruct the wavering minds of those who hesitate to believe, in whom faith still either lives while charity grows cold, or rather, if it may be so said, believes itself to live though dead.

Therefore we do not, in the manner of frenzied poets, invent empty fables devoid of truth; nor, following the fiction of the Mantuan bard and the example of Aeneas, do we draw blood-stained spears from the tomb of Polydorus, slain through the accursed hunger for gold. Rather, we desire to set forth in fitting adornment the merit for the praise of the Lord and the beloved name of the holy bishop Amandus. But if those tales, adorned with meretricious language and ornament, could persuade pagans as though true, what fitting rebuke can be found for Christians if they doubt certainties with less faith than those men gave to falsehoods and uncertainties? It remains, then, for them either to deny God’s omnipotence or to doubt the holiness of so great a man; and in this madness to prove worse even than pagans. But enough has now been said on these matters.

## CHAPTER VIII

Accordingly, he laid the aforesaid relics removed from the body of the man of God in a suitable place with due honor. He also employed stonecutters and masons, and procured many other things which seemed suitable for this [Col. 1297D] work. He allowed the venerable body to remain above ground for thirty-two days, from the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, when it was raised, until the tenth day before the Kalends of November, when it was restored. On that same day, with a great assembly of clergy and people gathered, he replaced it in the prepared place. He placed the tomb-chest not, as it had been before, in the deeper part, but in the upper part, so that its foundation could be seen and a light could be kindled beneath it; and upon it he inscribed that verse of the Psalm: “This is my rest for ever and ever.” He made both occasions—the elevation of the body and its restoration—celebrated festivals, and decreed that they should remain perpetually honorable to his successors. To this day [Col. 1298A] we observe this most devoutly in the present celebration, and urge our descendants to ensure that such care may endure.

744 Since we heard these things from fathers who were present at them and who still survive in considerable numbers, recounting them repeatedly, we were not permitted to consign them to unprofitable silence; but we have transmitted them to posterity in humble composition, to the praise of Christ and of that bishop himself. By such and so great miracles his celebrated tomb is honored even to the present day. We refrain here from recounting some of the healings performed in the basilica in which he rests through the intercession of his merits, since we know that they have been sufficiently set forth in the little book of his Life. For at his memorial blindness receives sight, deafness hearing, weakness the power of walking, and dumbness the use of speech. [Col. 1298B] We omit to relate these, as it were the common gifts of saints, because my feeble pen hastens toward the fire divinely kindled at his memorial; toward it my dull mind runs in lowly devotion.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the heavenly fire wondrously kindled by divine power at the memorial of Blessed Amandus

Finally, in the eight hundred and fifty-fifth year from the Incarnation of the Lord, the one hundred and ninety-fifth from the passing of most blessed Amandus, and the forty-seventh from the elevation of his body, on the twentieth day of September, the annual celebration of that aforesaid elevation was approaching. It was observed with a devotion less worthy than it ought to have been. For [Col. 1298C] it was neglected on ordinary days and was honored by no regular liturgical observance. How this negligence was corrected by a divine miracle will become clearer in the following account. For, to say something even in passing, we do not believe that the miracles of almighty God, whether performed through his servants, are wrought merely to arouse the noise, applause, and favor of the crowd. Rather, we hold it altogether certain that heavenly works are shown to those on earth in order to strengthen believers’ faith and correct wandering souls: so that, since we are not reformed by the daily admonitions of the sacred commandments, we may be corrected by certain portents, like the goads of spurs. And because, hardened after the manner of Lot’s sons-in-law, we refuse to obey when bidden to flee, turning our backs upon doomed Sodom, [Col. 1298D] and to ascend the mountain of virtues, it comes about that we see the divine word, figured by Lot, as though speaking in jest to us; and, as the prophet says, we turn fearful commandments threatening death and destruction into a song upon our lips.

## CHAPTER X

What, then, ought we think ourselves admonished by this sign of which we have begun to speak—namely, the kindling of the divine fire—except that we should kindle in our hearts the flame of the twofold love, of God and neighbor, by which we may shine in the sight of the supreme Majesty? By the heat of that fire which our Lord sent into the earth—that is, into earthly hearts—let us thoroughly purge from our deeds the rust of vices; so that, casting off the weight of lead, that is, of iniquity and sin, we may prepare ourselves like purest gold for the heavenly diadem of our king. But enough of these matters. Although they ought to have been said in a later order, we have stated them beforehand; now let us approach the magnitude of the sign itself with the plectrum of speech and the pen of the scribe.

## CHAPTER XI

On the day, therefore, which in the sequence of time preceded the aforementioned elevation, the service of the evening celebration having ended, night was approaching, with neither such abundance of light as was fitting nor such a festive gathering of the common people as was proper. When Compline had been performed, the darkness now required lamps; and because the hour of rest had come, the monks [Col. 1299B] each went to his prepared bed, leaving guards in the court of the basilica. These men, according to their usual practice, lit the lamps which were accustomed to burn during the night hours, and extinguished all the candles throughout the spaces of the church. When one of them, after a very short interval, returned while keeping watch over the church, he found the candle customarily burning at the saint’s feet—extinguished a little before—shining with a brightness of fire poured forth from heaven. Thinking that someone else had lit it, he believed it should again be extinguished. Thus, when the guards relieved one another in turn, it was extinguished a third time; yet a third time it appeared glittering with heavenly fire. Thereupon, gathering together, each recalling that he had himself extinguished it and seeking who had relit it, they resolved once more to extinguish it, [Col. 1299C] even removing with pinched fingers the glowing coal which remained in the wick, wishing to test whether it would again appear radiant with renewed brightness of light. For they had not yet fully recognized the significance of so great a miracle, though by every means they were already beginning to feel a certain anxiety about this occurrence. But when they saw the same candle kindled for the 745 fourth time, they were astonished—indeed terrified—that they had tried, by what might be called a rash presumption, to oppose this prodigy by extinguishing it. They yielded it, so often vindicated by the light, to itself. Why say more? They allowed it to belong to him whose power’s majesty had appeared unconquerable on so many occasions. Long stunned with highest joy at the novelty of this sudden miracle, they at last went to sleep and gave their bewildered eyes to sleep-bringing rest.

## CHAPTER XII

That night, now almost spent, had been illuminated by so great a light, and as the dawn reddened the solemnity of Matins approached. Meanwhile the guards rose from the pallets on which they had rested and found, of the seven largest candles placed beneath the very mausoleum, within the railings, at the head of the man of God, two blazing with double brightness. They did not doubt that these candles set at the head had been lit from the one placed at his feet which they had seen lighted a little earlier. [Col. 1300B] When the solemnities of Matins were completed and daylight had already come, news of the event having spread, the whole body of monks came into the basilica and blessed the supreme, holy, and undivided Trinity with exalted praises and joyful voices. Then, in honor of that same father, they celebrated the solemn rites of Mass with devotion beyond their custom. I myself, who write these humble things, was present and heard with my ears the song of its unutterable melody, drawn out at length; I saw the fire with my eyes, and amid those chants I spoke these verses to the bishop:

> You showed your monks, Bishop Amandus,  
> The light in which you shine in ethereal Olympus.
>
> Grant your servants to strive for fellowship in your life,  
> That they may share in your gifts.

[Col. 1300C] Therefore those present celebrated with the highest rejoicing of devotion this twofold gift of divine benefits—namely, the wondrous elevation of the sacred body and the memorable giving of fire sent from heaven. They decreed that it should be honored by their descendants, believing that those who keep his memorial with the due rendering of thanks will obtain eternal relief.

[Col. 1299]

# PASSION OF SAINTS CYRICUS AND JULITTA (G)*

## LETTER OF LORD PHILIP, ABBOT OF ELEEMOSYNA, TO ABBOT JOHN OF THE CHURCH OF ST. AMANDUS, CONCERNING THE PASSION OF SAINTS CYRICUS AND JULITTA

[Col. 1299D] Brother Philip, a little thing of what he is, to the reverend father in Christ John, by God’s grace abbot of the monastery of Elnon, and to the venerable and holy community: greetings.

Just as the failing vein of a barren intellect and an impoverished command of unpolished speech diminish the dignity of deeds, so the decay of antiquity and the faulty corruption of manuscripts disfigure the ornament of an honorable composition. For what grows old and ages is near to destruction; and a stream, unless it lives by the bounty of its source, dries up. We believe this has happened in the history of the passion of blessed Cyricus and Julitta, which both the mist of antiquity obscures and the low quality of its uncomposed form overshadows. Though it is reckoned among apocryphal writings, [Col. 1300D] it does not therefore cast a cloud of falsehood over the victory of the martyrs. The universal Church solemnly venerates them as having suffered for the truth, and in the kingdom of glory the embraces of eternal blessedness refresh them before the face of Christ Jesus. By signs and miracles divine mercy testifies that they are his own and declares that their lot is among the elect, as is said through Isaiah: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples.” The testimony of Jesus bound them to the discipleship of faith, and the law of truth was sealed in their hearts through the Holy Spirit. Faithfully tested by its affirmation, they deserve to possess the crown of life and the kingdom.

“Apocryphal” indeed denotes a closed secret, not the fault of falsehood, [Col. 1301A] when the author of a manifest event is unknown and the narrator of a clear deed hidden; just as the book of blessed Job, although called apocryphal because its author is uncertain, is nevertheless numbered among the hagiographa on account of the excellence of its merit. Thus, although the triumph of the blessed martyrs is celebrated with glory, who wrote the account of their deeds remains unknown. Your authority compels me to correct them, and the affection of charity urges me on; in that charity I owe you whatever I can do, not in word or tongue but in deed and truth. Therefore, setting aside what verbosity exaggerated, ignorance debased, age corrupted, carelessness ruined, the careless copying of manuscripts confused, and the accompanying suspicion of falsehood cast down, I have expressed in the style of truth what was drawn from more corrected writings, preserving not the order of words but the majesty of the deeds.

But because it is envy’s characteristic always to gnaw at another’s work, distort what is sound, and envelop what is bright in the cloud of detraction, I do not doubt that the poisons of insolent murmuring will confront my undertaking without the judgment of charity. Therefore I beseech the sincerity of your love that the wound inflicted by the pricks of raging hostility may be soothed by the poultice of holy intercession; and that their sword may enter their own hearts, who zealously sharpen their tongues so that they may defile a brother’s work with wicked whisperings.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1301]

[Col. 1301B] The wondrous sublimity of divine wisdom, as it is of surpassing glory, so grants to its faithful abundant material for praise. According to the riches of his goodness, he has deigned to make known to them his excellent power and the glory of the magnificence of his kingdom. By his praise he restrained them from perishing and stirred them to confess his name, so that what they cannot penetrate by strength of mind they may pursue with the urgency of love. Let them praise his power in his works, his wisdom in his ordinances, his mercy in his benefits, and admire the unity of his majesty in contemplating greatness. The manifold course of these his works comprehends all things by its definition, yet our weakness separates us from comprehending them, and the greatness of that power overwhelms the efforts of our understanding.

Yet mercy opens a way to misery tossed by the waves; it crowns its utterances with the surrounding reality of truth and does not expect that what it has deigned faithfully to utter for the building up of our strength will prove vain. We are indeed perplexed, but do not fail, because “we know in part and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. XIII); and, following the Apostle, we stretch ourselves toward the prize of perfection which we are altogether unable to grasp in the present life. For whose perception can be so penetrating, whose understanding so subtle, reasoning so acute, memory so lively, or intellect so effective, as to dare profess itself conscious of this totality? For, as the Apostle says, “The works of the wisdom of God are incomprehensible, and his ways unsearchable” (Rom. XI). Yet in their effects a certain path of knowledge shines forth, so that at least we may see his back parts, though we cannot behold his face; and we are transformed from brightness to brightness, as by the Spirit of the Lord, striving in the steps of faith toward the embrace of eternal attainment.

For just as we behold a ray of the sun in a cloud, which we cannot bear to gaze upon directly as it flashes in the light of its power, so, in the struggle of martyrs, when we consider the weakness of the flesh and the dreadful torments of penal injury, we proclaim the wondrous triumph of divine power. It broke the ferocity of persecutors, reduced the cruel engines of torture to nothing, and, contrary to the law of the flesh, invests endurance with glory and the torturer with confusion. These most credible testimonies of his will, made in every age and sex, commend themselves to every human conscience—not to those who hold down God’s truth in unrighteousness, but to those whose senses have been trained and who confess the wondrous God in wondrous deeds. What nature does not possess, custom does not accept, reason does not admit, understanding does not conceive, and the manifold compass of human perception does not attain, must be reached by the steps of faith; and in the magnificence of his works it is fitting to venerate the power of Majesty.

For when the deeds of blessed Cyricus are read, when the renowned history of his passion is recited, who would not recoil in mind from a three-year-old child prudent in answers, brave in tortures, eloquent in confession, faithful in thanksgiving, and wondrous in the contest of martyrdom, and judge this foreign to the laws of nature? If weakness is fashioned into strength, if frailty is girded with might, if infancy rises to manly courage, if a stammering tongue speaks eloquently, if feebleness does not yield under suffering, who would believe another to be at work here than the coming of divine power? If the female sex is girded with fortitude; if at the torments of her little child a mother’s heart does not fail; if the nature of affections and their effects is transformed; if the natural order is changed from its course: who is the author? Surely he whose omnipotence works wondrously in all things and above all things, who is blessed [Col. 1302D] for ever.

In all these things the radiant beam of his operation shines forth, and he illumines the works of the faithful with the light of his visitation, as it is written: “You have wrought all our works in us, O Lord” (Ps. LXVII). This incomprehensible power raised up the unique trophy, to be proclaimed through all ages, of the martyr Cyricus and his mother Julitta, granting merit to faith, glory to the contest, constancy to frailty, power to confession, rest in return for labors, and a crown in return for torments.

# PASSION OF THE HOLY MARTYRS CYRICUS AND JULITTA, HIS MOTHER, WITH THEIR COMPANIONS

[Col. 1303]

[Col. 1303A] 747 Blessed Julitta, a woman of no obscure origin from the province of Isauria and of the foremost families of the city of Iconium, derived her physical lineage from them; but by the adornment of her character, the grace of faith, and the pursuit of virtue she stood above the rank of her birth. Deprived of a husband’s support, she was still raising a little child three years old, Cyricus by name. Along with the milk of the flesh, she had raised him in the first elements of faith and taught him to believe in him by whose word the heavens were established, and by whose Spirit all their power and adornment endure and subsist. Inflamed by spiritual desires, she adorned faith with works, righteousness with meditation on the divine law, holiness with the power of chastity; and, after the pattern of the heavenly image, she formed herself by diligent watchfulness.

While Aurelius Alexander held the fasces—who was the twentieth to rule the Roman Empire after Augustus Caesar—a harsh storm arose against the Church. Decretal edicts were sent throughout the world, and the imperial command thundered cruelly that those who professed the sacred faith must either sacrifice to idols or be subjected to severe punishments. The storm’s spirit swelled beyond measure, its waves rose to overwhelm the faithful, and the rage of the thankless whirlwind bore down more violently upon the children of grace. Priests of the Lord were dragged to shrines; the people, together with their leaders, were compelled to make abominable libations; those whom inviolable strength united in confession of faith were subjected to punishments. Because they refused the sacrifices of impiety, they offered themselves to God as a saving sacrifice of sweet odor. Heavy smoke rose in wrath, and fire blazed forth from his presence, mounting into the neighboring regions of the East; it shook Isauria, Pamphylia, and the bordering places with its terror.

Alexander, heir alike to impiety and to its name, was the wicked governor who held sway over those regions. Like a roaring lion prepared for prey (Ps. XVI), he bore himself insolently in the spirit of savagery against the servants of the Lord, eager to win the emperor’s favor, the Senate’s approval, and glory for his own name through the blood of the saints, the slaughter of the faithful, and the ministry of cruelty. He swallowed up many, terrified some, and dictated flight or compelled hiding upon others, through the madness of this storm and of this wicked disturber, whom headlong impiety armed and singular arrogance emboldened to scatter and destroy Christ’s sheep.

The faithful matron, taking thought for herself and her child—fearing not so much for herself as for the child—fled from her own city to another, in accordance with the saving prudence of evangelical counsel, and reached Tarsus of Cilicia in hidden flight.

[Col. 1304A] If the holy woman avoided the onset of fury, this was not a sign of a troubled mind or broken courage, but the surest mark of prudent discretion and a humble soul. For the mind that cultivates humility never presumes upon itself, nor walks in great matters nor in wonders above itself; rather, it wisely searches out the counsels of the divine will and entrusts everything to the judgment from above. An accepted end crowns beginnings, and intention gives an act both its name and merit. The history on the following page declares the intention with which our heroine withdrew. She fled the familiar affections of her neighbors and the blandishments of flesh and blood, lest, when the evil of persecution broke out, they should instill something into her holy ears that would soften her resolve, overthrow the constancy of her courage, or recall her holy mind from the way and testimony of truth.

Meanwhile Alexander, the agent of wickedness, having traversed the regions of the adjacent province, came, led by a spirit of insolence, to the place where blessed Julitta intended to lie concealed. There, in accordance with his customary malice, he ordered the worshippers of the holy faith to be diligently sought out by officers and brought before his tribunals. He issued a cruel command that they must either offer libations to the gods or pay for the offense against the injured divinity by the infliction of punishments. The investigation having been made, the venerable matron was found by the ministers of wickedness and brought before the governor. Asked her name, family, homeland, and religious profession, she gave a steadfast declaration and publicly proclaimed herself a Christian in ready speech.

Her ready devotion, confident mind, cheerful countenance, wise eloquence, renowned confession, and faithful constancy, as they proclaimed God’s glory, so brought a cloud of confusion upon the tyrant. Yet, restraining inwardly the vexation of his embittered heart, he courteously urged her, as if with wholesome advice, not to depart from the rites of the ancient religion, from the general reverence for the gods, or from the command of imperial majesty. Rather, in order to earn the favor of both powers, she should redeem her safety with victims and incense. For just as favor is prepared for those who submit, so an inglorious end and the terror of torments threaten those who despise them.

But the matron’s heart, established upon firm ground, admitted neither the deadly poison of this counsel nor, through fear of punishment, was loosened into sin. The governor repeated his admonitions and redoubled his threats in order to drive the holy mind to ruin. But the sacrilegious design was blunted like a wave dashed against rocks, and the faithful mind, like an immovable pillar in the building of truth, bent to neither side.

[Col. 1305A] Meanwhile, the tender memory of the little child whom she had left behind entered the holy mother’s mind, and she was deeply distressed that she had entered the conflict without him. It is credible that the holy woman feared lest, without the restraining comfort of a mother, the child’s weakness might be overcome if seized; or that she was unwilling to receive the sweet fruits of her own contest without so dear a pledge. For when she saw that the moment of her own consummation was at hand, she did not consider it sufficiently safe that the weak child should remain alive after her, exposed to the mockery of another’s cruelty and ignorant of so great a contest. Nor did the devout mother judge it pious, if she abandoned her son, to advance to the eternal crown—a son whom she had devoutly raised for this very end, that he might become a citizen of the saints and heir of Paradise. For she preferred to be translated by death to the kingdom rather than to begin the campaigns of everlasting death through the commerce of an unhappy life.

Accordingly, following her indication, the child of the Lord was sought out and brought into public. At first the governor, in keeping with humanity and the child’s age, tried him with blandishments and the enticement of honeyed speech; then he assailed him with terrors and the stings of threats.

But the faithful God, who does not abandon his own in temptation; who taught John, enclosed in his mother’s womb, to leap for prophetic joy; who without the ministry of human speech disclosed the mysteries of Scripture to the simple and unlearned; who taught men of one language to speak in the tongues of all peoples through tongues of fire—supplied even to his child, still three years old, the adornment of trained perception and an instructed tongue.

[Col. 1305C] Therefore, at the first encounter of interrogation, he openly professed himself a Christian and declared that he would by no means depart from this profession.

The governor marvels and urgently asks how he had acquired so solemn a memory of this name, how he had received the doctrines of this religion. “I marvel,” says blessed Cyricus, “at the foolishness of wishing to inquire this from a child who has neither time for study, nor understanding for comprehension, nor age for instruction.”

The savage cruelty of the harsh judge flared into anger, and the wicked possessor stirred himself wholly to rage. And just as the foolish prophet was rebuked and confounded by the mouth of his beast of burden, so the confession of the holy child clothed the judge of iniquity in confusion.

[Col. 1305D] Flashing eyes, a flushed face, threatening gestures, disordered speech, harshness of voice, and the unstable posture of his whole body plainly reveal the madness of his mind. Wickedness belches forth the flame of its heart, and, speaking wrath upon the earth, orders the child to be beaten who had uttered beforehand the Savior’s proclamations. The confession of truth is accused by torments, and impiety feeds its wrath upon the punishment of innocence. It spares neither nature nor age; transformed into a savage beast, it thunders threats against the child of the Lord, rages with blows, and rises to the summit of fury. But he who chooses the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and in the contemptible condemns the contemptuous, grants his champion constancy amid the lashes and inspires him from the abundant sweetness of fatherly consolation with holy delight.

[Col. 1306A] Therefore, reverently stretching innocent hands and simple eyes toward heaven, he gives thanks to the Giver of graces and, taunting the officials, repeatedly cries: “I am a Christian, I am a Christian.” As often as he utters the voice of sacred confession, so often are his powers renewed in him; and new strength grows together with endurance. The governor is overcome with astonishment, and the confused ferocity of the lictors is more broken in spirit while inflicting punishments than could be the one who seemed subjected to afflictions.

Thus wickedness, beaten back upon itself, subsided for a while and, after an interval, lowered its madness and restrained its stubborn passions.

But when the appointed interval had elapsed, the governor ordered venerable Julitta and her son to be brought before his tribunals. He repeated his admonitions, suggested counsel, accumulated inducements, and pressed her with persuasion to yield from her obstinacy and obey the worship of the gods and the emperor’s edicts. The faithful matron remained immovable, and with a deaf ear passed over everything uttered by the governor. When he saw that neither entreaties, admonitions, nor counsels accomplished anything, he ordered different kinds of torments to be prepared and renewed the instruments of cruelty for an assault upon courage. Blessed Julitta was tortured, and Cyricus too was tortured; yet the engine of impiety did not consume the strength of faith and constancy of truth. The venerable heroine stood firm: an example of fortitude, an emblem of patience, an oracle of piety, a seedbed of faith, a foundation of constancy, a witness to holiness, a crown of righteousness. She yielded neither to the horror [Col. 1306C] of punishment nor, wearied by tortures, was diminished in spirit.

The governor blushed and was more deeply distressed because the unconquerable courage of the martyrs, inviolable faith, joyful constancy, and fearless confession did not yield beneath interrogations; because amid torments they remained great-souled, amid insults cheerful, amid pressures upright and firmly persevering; and because they stood out stronger through suffering than the mad torturer did through punishing. What breast, even of iron, or what entrails harder than metals, would not be struck with amazement and wonder when the bitterness of punishment does not break a woman’s spirit or extinguish a little child? When a fragile vessel, a woman, a little boy tender in age, unequal in strength and immature in understanding, resist tortures with brave spirit? The unworthiness of the conqueror defeated is a grave kind of confusion, when the inferior exults over the fall of the strong and one who seemed superior withdraws ingloriously. The injustice of this reversal strikes the governor, and he grows bitter in his whole disposition because weakness exults victorious amid so many afflictions.

He therefore ordered the illustrious fighters, withdrawn from the torments, to be shut in the most confined prison, raging with a harsher stratagem than if he consumed them by a sentence of final condemnation. For he believed that, afflicted by the filth of prison, worn down by tedium, and emaciated by hunger, they would endure renewed punishments less bravely and turn more readily from their profession of faith. But this capacity is not a power of human virtue; it is a divine gift. Nor is the triumph of martyrdom due to merit, but is dispensed through grace.

[Col. 1307A] By grace strength is perfected in weakness, and in tribulation righteousness shines more beautifully. Heavenly authority flashes in the confessors of faith, and victory is granted from heaven to the humble. The Judge of righteousness turns the governor’s devices to their opposite purpose: what was prepared for destruction the Lord ordains for grace, increasing for his saints both glory and merit.

There were in the same prison about four hundred and forty-four men, whom one sentence had thrust into prison confinement for various causes. The adversity of the present life pressed upon them, wrapped in the darkness of ignorance and the bonds of sins, and the hard onset of eternal death awaited them. Blessed Julitta, pitying their peril, sharing their sufferings, and grieving over their error, came suitably to meet their condemnation. She disclosed the mysteries of faith, unfolded the order of redemption, proclaimed the grace of baptism, and promised again the eternal joys promised to the saints, if they obeyed the ordinances of the Christian religion. With prudent speech she explained that those publicly worshipped are not gods. She firmly declared that an idol has nothing in common with the divine nature, but is a work of humankind, empty of perception, lacking reason and power: a mockery of the demon, contrary to salvation.

[Col. 1307B] She proclaimed that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one saving Godhead, and that no other name has been given under heaven to human beings in which they must be saved. No narrowness of beginning or end confines his majesty; no spaces of time or place measure it. Rather, abiding eternally in himself, he renews all things; and just as he mercifully raises up those who trust, so by the judgment of truth he overwhelms the hardened.

By the holy woman’s so diligent exhortation and the singular example of the little confessor, that entire multitude assigned to punishments was converted. They rejected the error of paganism, reverently received the teachings of faith, asked to be marked with Christ’s name, and were restored through faithful ministry to the liberty of the glory of the children of God.

In name alone liberty is sweet; in experience it is more pleasant, and in use most joyful. At first they were distressed by fear of death, guilt of conscience, expectation of punishment, the squalor of prison, the injury of hunger, the assault of despair, and the cruelty of officials. Now, encouraged by faith, reborn to a living hope, and raised by the power of divine [Col. 1307D] charity, with free minds and public voice they proclaim Christ’s praises. They despise present things, sigh for eternal things, and glory in the gift of the heavenly benefit. They judge it happier to lay down life for Christ than to live clothed in purple amid the world’s pleasures.

Alexander was informed that the children of the prison had rebelled and, to the injury of the divinity and against the decrees of rulers, had become associates in the Christian name; that with blasphemous mouth they detested the worship of the deities and proclaimed the glory of the Crucified One. Seized with madness, the governor ordered them brought before him so that he might test by present evidence what had been reported. Led out from custody, the confessors of faith, unchanged in spirit and not wavering in terror, declare with one voice that they are Christians.

[Col. 1308A] The governor, conceiving indignation, hurls forth the fire of his rage like a furnace and, pronouncing sentence, orders that the saints be put to death by the sword. He decrees that their bodies, cut into pieces and scattered partly through the fields, should remain unburied. The hands of the lictors carried out the deadly command of their savage master and scattered the entrails of the beheaded in cruel dispersal, so that they might become examples of terror to others and so that the faithful might not believe that they could offer benefit after death. You accomplish nothing, wicked Alexander; you gain nothing. Those whom you slaughter are joined to angels and carried into the heavenly kingdoms. What you cast out so irreverently cannot perish. The glory of the resurrection will restore whole those whom you destroy, and blessed incorruption will possess the loss caused by present decay. He does injury to himself who overturns the laws of nature, [Col. 1308B] and he does not differ from a madman who examines by torments things without perception or exercises vengeance upon a corpse under interrogation.

They live with Christ and reign in blessedness; they belong to the blessed orders, though you persecute them with such cruelty. Dead flesh does not feel what you threaten, nor can bodily injury disturb the blessed spirit. The Lord, the God of vengeance, will act freely: he will recompense them with glory for endurance and you with everlasting punishment for malice.

With the holy martyrs thus brought to their end, when the time was already at hand for blessed Julitta to complete the praiseworthy course of her glorious contest with her son, and to bring into the harbour of a tranquil shore the precious rewards rescued from the shipwreck of this sea, the fierce wickedness of Alexander began to revive [Col. 1308C] 750; and he began to devise new kinds of tortures against the saints of God, by which he might either break their constancy or prepare for his fury a feast of reparative vengeance. For the disposition of the wicked is unchangeable, and “the pride of those who hate thee, O Lord, continually rises” [Ps. 74:23]. The stirring of anger tormented him more grievously, and he burned more fiercely, because the patience of the lowly had greater power than the terror of princes and the eminence of authority. It tortured him that they judged it more glorious to die than to obey the exalted, or to retain peaceful fellowship among the great ones of the earth.
