Therefore he ordered all the weapons of his cruelty to be deployed with greater care, and that particular instruments of his fury should be applied one by one to each of the saints’ limbs. [Col. 1308D] But the praiseworthy matron and the boy of outstanding courage, with stout heart, serene countenance, and cheerful steadfastness, patiently received whatever was inflicted upon them and persevered in blessed endurance, to the praise of Christ.

When Alexander saw that his cruelty availed nothing against them, he ordered them punished by capital sentence; and, himself overcome by the injuries of the sufferings which he ordered to be inflicted upon the victorious, he left to the saints the victory which they desired with all their prayers. For the more grievous the punishments by which the saints’ bodies were scarred, the more glorious was the triumph over the tyrant which raised them up; and, in return for their double confusion and shame, they bore away sheaves of joy together with the palm of victory, destined to possess double portions in their land. The upright shall praise their portion, [Col. 1309A] and he who made them shall be praised in them: he who raised their labours into rest, their punishments into refreshment, and their contest into the palm of victory. Truly praiseworthy and wondrous is that victory, when through the sufferings of this present time eternal light is revealed in the saints; and this momentary and light tribulation works in them an eternal weight of glory, that they may behold the goodness of the elect of God, so that he himself may be praised with his inheritance, and the throne of incorruption may be as the sun before him, and as the moon perfect for ever, and Christ Jesus, the faithful witness in heaven, may display in them the dignity of perfect likeness.

Here the blessed mother and unconquered martyr Julitta, conqueror of her sex and of the world, glories and exults, fearing neither for herself nor for her child; but with him she glories in the fullness of the heavenly benefit, and, beholding the Redeemer with unveiled face, [Col. 1309B] she renders repeated thanksgiving to the divine majesty for the unfading glory of herself and her son, to whom is honour through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## Here begins the Translation of Saint Cyricus

“Let us praise glorious men and our fathers in their generation, to whom the Lord gave much glory by his magnificence.”

Long ago, in the place of the monastery of Elnone, where Saint Amand rests in the body, the riches of salvation—that is, wisdom and knowledge—abundantly overflowed and spread their fragrance in every direction, so that many drew from there the draught which they offered to their own. But because “knowledge puffs up, whereas charity builds up” [1 Cor. 8], through the puffing up of knowledge wise charity, and beloved wisdom, seemed to become scarce in that place, as will be seen in what follows. [Col. 1309C]

Accordingly, there flourished there, in learned study, a certain wise man named Milo, who fostered beneath the wings of the schools his nephew Hucbald, with the benefit of the liberal arts. This follower, indeed, wishing to test his own talent, composed an antiphonal setting concerning Saint Andrew, and also the beginning of certain praises containing a truly pious commendation. When at last the teacher barely recognized this, he took it badly and denied him access to the schools, complaining that he wished to usurp above him the name of philosopher. Since the place then lacked an abbot, he approached the prior and accused the pupil of excessive arrogance, declaring that he and the latter could by no means live in the same dwelling. The prior summoned Hucbald [Col. 1309D] and asked him to yield to his elder, until his anger, then freshly inflamed, had been softened, and then to return peacefully to his own place.

Accepting this counsel, he sought the city of Nevers, which a certain Nivo had founded. While he stayed there with the bishop, he attached himself so closely to his household that he became his companion in every affair. For that bishop admitted him into such familiarity that he entrusted his household goods to him. And because the prelate had received his upbringing to maturity at Rheims, he ordered him to become a composer for the history of blessed Cilinia, mother of Saint Remigius. The aforesaid bishop also had with him, among his sacred ministries, the body of Saint Cyricus, a little child and a great martyr.

It happened that the bishop was worn down by a sharp bodily pain and felt the peril of death [Col. 1310A] to be at hand. Then he summoned Hucbald and addressed his friend in these words:

“I am afflicted with the weariness of a most grievous illness to such an extent that I understand that I can be helped by the assistance of no medicine, nor relieved by any remedy. Therefore, most beloved brother, because until now I have known you devotedly to have served my needs, I do not wish now to leave you unrewarded. Since all that I possess is known to you, disclose what I have by which a worthy recompense may be made for you.”

On hearing this, Hucbald, now more cheerful, replied to the bishop:

“There is one thing, lord father, in your possession which, if it should fall to me to have, I would esteem highly the devotion of my service. I seek no quantity of gold or silver, or anything else of that sort, but only the body of Saint Cyricus.”

On hearing this, the bishop, with a somewhat sorrowful face, answered Hucbald: [Col. 1310B] “Your request indeed exceeds measure; nevertheless, lest I seem to wish to defraud you of what I promised, depart as quickly as possible, taking the holy body.”

Then he secretly carried off the martyr’s bones and placed them among his baskets, joining shrewd ingenuity to faithful theft: namely, so that so clean a treasure would not be sought among unclean vessels. Meanwhile, the clerics and servants, occupied with various business, after learning that Hucbald had departed, began to discuss among themselves whether he had left any loss behind him, since the bishop had entrusted the care of the household to him. At last, when he had already gone farther from the city, they came in their discussion to the place where they thought the martyr’s body was kept. Not finding it there, they realized that they had been craftily forestalled in a loss to the household. [Col. 1310C]

Why say more? As he hastened his flight, they hurried to pursue the fugitive. But Hucbald, looking back, when he saw that he was surrounded by enemies, entered a wood before him, dismounted from his horse, bent his knees, poured forth prayer, and made this vow: that, if the holy martyr, with Christ’s help, allowed him to be conveyed to the monastery of Elnone, he would be placed in the middle of the church’s court and singularly venerated by the people. Then, mounting his horse, he quickly crossed that thicket as he wished. But since they could not find even his tracks, they wandered through the wood and returned, supposing that he had taken another route. Rejoicing that he had escaped with that heavenly treasure, he continued in haste to the monastery of Elnone. [Col. 1310D]

On the night preceding the day upon which he was to enter the oratory of Saint Amand, Saint Amand himself appeared to a sick monk in the infirmary, whose limbs had been disjointed by paralysis. Touching the man’s breast, the seat of life, with his finger, he said: “Rise whole, and by this sign warn the brethren to prepare themselves to meet Hucbald with crosses and candles, as he brings the body of Saint Cyricus the martyr.” Obeying the command of the one who ordered him, the monk took part in the procession, not without the very great astonishment of those who saw it.

Then Hucbald, mindful of his vow, hastened the woodworkers and caused a fitting resting-place, as far as possible, to be constructed in the middle vault of the church, in which the holy bones might be placed. This was done with all [Col. 1311A] speed, and the sacred relics were placed there.

For this reason an altar was built there, before which Hucbald frequently lay prostrate and addressed the martyr in devout prayers. From this there befell him a certain forewarning which we have by no means judged should be suppressed in silence. At midnight on a certain night, while he rested with the brethren, Saint Cyricus appeared to him in a vision and terrified him with this address:

“Know that the course of your life will soon be ended: namely, this year, on the fifth day after the triumph of my passion. Therefore seek some one of the chief men of the heavenly court who may be your advocate before the strict Judge.”

Hucbald immediately awoke from sleep, but did not give credence to the vision until, prostrate before the holy martyr, he sought the matter from God. For, coming to the church [Col. 1311B] and lying on the ground before the altar as usual, he prayed with devout feeling that, through the martyr’s intercession, he might be made certain whether it was a true vision or an illusion of a phantom. While he prayed intently, sleep stole upon him; and behold, he perceived the saint standing before him with the eyes of the mind and repeating in friendly words what he had said:

“Do not doubt what I have told you; but because until now you have laboured in the commemoration of many saints, now, before you depart this life, take pains that through you there may be made in the church a commemoration of the heavenly key-bearer greater than usual.”

Awakening at these words, he waited until the brethren assembled; then, with due acknowledgment, he made known to all what he had seen and heard. Although [Col. 1311C] he was troubled by a certain weariness of spirit, since he believed that his last day was imminent according to the common lot, he began, sick with illness, to set to music the history of Saint Peter, beginning with the words: “The sick were laid in the streets.” As the day drew near on which he had learned that he would depart from here, his limbs grew weak and his bodily strength failed. Having come, so to speak, even to the gates of death, he received the viaticum of the Lord’s body and sacred unction, [Col. 1312A] and, about ninety years old, in the year of the Lord 930, on Sunday, the twelfth day before the Kalends of July [20 June], he died, just as he had heard in his sleep.

When the brethren saw that the aforesaid vision was in no way void but came true in sequence exactly as they had heard it, all who had previously wavered in mind concerning the saint’s presence, moved by repentance—both they themselves and all the others—gave themselves to the praises of God. But because they lacked the means to adorn the mausoleum of so great a martyr, they languished in spirit. In the course of time, however, the mercy of the Saviour aided their successors in this matter.

A noble and very powerful matron, namely Queen Susanna, came to the place to pray. Seeing that the bones of so great a martyr had a shrine less worthy than was fitting, she began to ponder in the secret places of her heart [Col. 1312B] how she might correct what had until then been neglected concerning him. At last, strengthened in purpose, she did not delay to set craftsmen and masons to work. She also gave the monks much gold and silver, ordering that a shrine in relief-work, a panel before the altar, and above it the deeds of his passion should be made; and that the attractive structure should be suitably distinguished around about with Parian stone and black stone. 752 The craftsmen, applying themselves skilfully to the work, executed it wonderfully according to her discerning intention. This work, worthy of every admiration, endured until the burning of the church.

Therefore, brethren, do not be reluctant to frequent his commemoration, to whom so great a treasure was brought of its own accord; for, as has been said before us, praise spoken of the members is not doubted to be referred to the head. Thus, by his present aid, his venerators shall at last be delivered from every evil, through the bounty of the heavenly King, who supplied strength to that tender child to endure the bitterness of torments and bestowed eloquence upon the infant; through whose intercession, we pray, may he deliver us from every enemy—he who, with the Holy Spirit, reigns as God in the majesty of the Father. Amen.

[Col. 1311]

# The Passion of Saint Salvius, Martyr

## Prologue

[Col. 1311C] To Lord Hugh, venerable prior of the Church of Saint Salvius: Brother Philip, humble prior of the Church of Bonne-Espérance, greetings and prayers.

Your charity asks of me what I neither felt nor now feel myself able to do. For I do not know how to commit to enduring writing the lives and merits of the saints, since I can neither claim nor ought to claim either practice or skill in writing. Yet one who confidently undertakes such a task, if he does not carry it out sufficiently, or at least suitably, seems both to detract from the merits of the saints of whom he speaks and to impose upon himself the stain of presumption.

I wonder, therefore, why you lay such a work upon me—or rather, cause it to be laid upon me by [Col. 1312C] my abbot—when you are wholly unaware whether I can carry it out. As I have heard, it was indeed told you that I wrote some account of the life of my Augustine, bishop of Hippo and outstanding doctor, in which I related what I knew of him, not as desire but as ability was granted to me. Frequent urging by certain of my brethren compelled me to undertake this, as did the tender love with which I embraced that confessor. Yet, to confess the truth, I did nothing of the kind either before or afterwards, since I have made no sufficient progress, whether in talent or in study, for adequately undertaking such a work.

Therefore, asked by you—or rather by my abbot at your request [Col. 1313A]—to write the life of blessed Salvius, your patron, I am not a little distressed, since both to refuse what I am commanded is the stubbornness of rashness, and to fulfil what I am commanded appears beyond my ability. Nevertheless, because your charity requests it [Col. 1314A] and reverence for my abbot commands it, I shall say what I can concerning your martyr—indeed, mine also, if through your intercession I can find him to be mine, that is, favourable to me—so that he may mercifully assist me as I speak of him.

## Here Begins the Passion

[Col. 1313]

## Chapter One

[Col. 1313A]

Blessed Salvius, then, as I have learned from the testimony of a truthful account, was born in Auvergne, which lies in the regions [Col. 1313B] of Aquitaine. By the ordering of divine wisdom, which “orders all things sweetly” [Wis. 8:1], he was educated in literary studies, and in the course of time was distinguished by the rank of priesthood and, what is more, by episcopal dignity. For he was adorned with such holy manners that he was worthy of the height of the episcopate. Yet the more highly God exalted him, the more he humbled himself, remembering well what is written: “It is better to be humbled with the meek than to divide spoils with the proud” [Prov. 16:19]. For he is unworthy to be raised to the summit of the priesthood who does not know how to humble himself with the meek, since that is a savoury ornament of the priesthood to which true humility supplies seasoning.

Mindful of this, the holy man rejoiced not so much in the dignity of priesthood as in [Col. 1313C] humility of heart, singing the Davidic saying more with his heart than with his mouth: “It is good for me, Lord, that thou hast humbled me” [Ps. 118:71]. Moreover, this same saint shone with so many virtues as a necklace with precious stones, a garden of delight with words and flowers, or the ethereal heaven with diverse stars. To crown all, such grace of preaching was given him that no sane wise person could doubt that the Spirit was speaking in him, of whom the Lord said to the disciples: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” [Matt. 10:20].

Since he possessed both such power of living well and, as I have said, did not lack the grace of preaching, he rendered no small praises to God, while he caused God to be praised far and wide by many. [Col. 1313D] For the Lord did not wish this lamp, so burning and so light-bearing, to lie hidden beneath a bushel, but, providing for the souls whom he purposed to save through it, took care to set it higher upon a lampstand. Accordingly, by his ordering the holy man departed from his own land and from his kindred [Gen. 12:1], because of the saying: “No prophet is accepted in his own country” [Luke 4:24]. So great an ardour of divine charity had kindled him that the grace of his own holiness seemed almost fruitless to him unless he also won others for God, through whom he might deserve to please that same God more abundantly. For as long as he was compelled to remain in this life and unwillingly kept from seeing God, for whom he sighed, it seemed to him no slight consolation that he rejoiced not so much in his salvation alone as in that of his brethren.

Having therefore departed, as I said, from his own land [Col. 1314A], accompanied by a certain disciple who followed the same master not so much in footstep as in conduct, he travelled through the regions of Gaul, in which, by God’s infusing grace, he abundantly preached the word [Col. 1314B] of God. But because Christian religion already flourished there, and his highest zeal burned for gaining souls, he turned his journey toward the perverse peoples of Hainaut, whom, perhaps by report spread abroad, he understood still to be rebellious against God. The Catholic faith had indeed already been preached there and an assembly of believers had already been gathered; but such traces of ancient perversity remained that not only unbelievers but even believers possessed the bestial perversity of savagery. Nor is that people known to have been hard-necked and uncircumcised in heart only at that time; it is found stubborn even to the present day.

Nevertheless, because the holy man was lavish of this life and did not make his soul more precious than himself, he fearlessly went there with his disciple and first entered a town of Hainaut called Valenciennes. [Col. 1314C] There he publicly preached the word of God to the people and, by his honeyed preaching, encouraged them to worship and love God. Having spoken to the people, he departed from Valenciennes and, not far away, saw a church consecrated in honour of blessed Martin. Learning that it was a church of this confessor, he said: “Let us go there and seek the aid of so great a man; and through his intercession let us ask that our journey be directed. For blessed Martin was of such great merit before God that he restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, walking to the lame, health to those suffering from every illness, and, what is more, raised the dead.”

The holy man therefore went to the aforesaid church and celebrated Mass there. Going out to refresh himself a little, he returned to it. When evening came, and the day’s labour compelled rest and the fitting time invited sleep, the holy man nevertheless did not depart from the church, but spent the night there with his disciple, occupied in psalms and praises.

## Chapter Two

When morning came, as the people hastened according to custom to gather at church and to hear the solemnities of Mass and the divine rites celebrated there, report spread everywhere that blessed Salvius was staying there, a man whose life was regarded as exemplary and whose preaching persuasive. Therefore a larger multitude than usual assembled, eager to see and hear a man of such holiness, especially because they had leisure owing to the feast-day of the Lord’s resurrection. When the innumerable crowd had gathered, the holy man offered to all the word of life and first commended to them the Catholic faith through fitting exhortation. [Col. 1315A]

Afterwards he carefully admonished them that, laying aside the ragged tunic of their inborn oldness, they should strive to be clothed with the gentle linen garment of newness. He knew indeed that their necks were hard and inflexible and that they were not so much inclined toward better things as fixed in what was worse. Having completed his sermon, he put on the sacred vestments in order to celebrate Mass. Woven with gold and silver and likewise shining with gems, they showed him to be a bishop not only by adorning him but also by their symbolism. For a bishop ought to be so arrayed when he comes before the altar to offer sacrifices that the very clothing may figuratively show both the dignity that is his and the holiness he ought to possess.

Blessed Salvius thus possessed very rich ornaments in which he ministered at the sacred altars, and a golden chalice in which he reverently handled the sacrament of the Lord’s body. He always carried all these things with him, not prompted by desire for temporal value but venerating the divine mystery with such service. After he had joyfully celebrated the solemnities of Mass before the people, a man named Genard, steward of that village, earnestly entreated him, in the name of the holy charity which he seemed so greatly to preach and commend, to deign to enter his house for refreshment. [Col. 1315B] Blessed Salvius, in order to satisfy not so much his own need as that man’s devout wish, entered his house, reclined at table, and, having tasted bread and given thanks [Luke 18], prepared to depart.

Then there came a certain man called Winegard, son of the aforesaid Genard, who was frivolous and unstable, proud and envious, fearing neither God nor respecting man. Observing all that the holy man carried with him—namely the golden chalice and the precious vestment which he wore while standing at the sacred altars—he began to burn with the torches of greed and to consider carefully how he might acquire these things. That wicked man therefore inquired where and by what route the holy man intended to go, so that by either going ahead of him or following him he might certainly seize him. [Col. 1315C]

## Chapter Three

[Col. 1315D]

Blessed Salvius, having given the people his blessing, left Genard’s house with his disciple and set out on the road leading to Condé, in which town there was a church consecrated in honour of the blessed Mother of God. While travelling, he came to a certain stream called Bontion by the inhabitants. After he had crossed it, the aforesaid Winegard met him with several accomplices. When Winegard asked where he was going, the holy man replied: “I am making for the church of blessed Mary, situated not far away, if indeed God grants fulfilment to what I intend.”

Winegard said to him: “I have on my estate a church which ought shortly to be dedicated; most earnestly, holy man, I should like it to be consecrated by your hands. [Col. 1316A] Come with me, therefore, so that so holy a work may be completed by so holy a bishop; for it is not fitting that some unworthy person be brought in to perform this work.”

Understanding the snares in his words, and not unaware through divine revelation of what threatened him, the holy man said: “It is not fitting that this should be done, so that I should obey your will before I visit the holy places as I have proposed. Therefore, if permitted, I shall first go to venerate the remembrance of the saints, through whose intercession I desire to commend myself to God.”

Having said this, he began to hasten somewhat more quickly, as though wishing irrevocably to complete the journey he had begun. But Winegard, not restraining the fury once conceived, secretly ordered his servants to take from the holy man everything he carried and to lead him and his disciple into custody, placing them in chains. To complete his own destruction, that accursed man further ordered that his own saddle and bridle should be gilded from the holy man’s golden chalice, so that not only he but even his horse might delight in being adorned with royal equipment.

After they had been led into custody, Winegard came to his father as though to report some great achievement and carefully explained in order everything that he had cruelly done to the holy men. His father said to him: “You have acted badly in presuming to cast into prison a man of such renown and such holiness. Perhaps this wickedness will work destruction not for you alone but for us all, and through you the iniquity of our forebears is brought down upon us again by hereditary succession.” [Col. 1316B]

The son said to him: “What then should I do, father? Should I correct what has been done and desist, or should I complete what I intended?”

His father answered: “It is not expedient, son, that what has been wickedly begun should be completed, lest the blood of the righteous be required of all our race.”

But Winegard, whose heart greedy avarice had seized and in whom unquenchable rage had been kindled, did not incline his ear to his father’s truthful advice, listening rather to those whom he knew to be his equals in wickedness or age. Returning therefore to his house, he ordered his doors to be carefully barred, lest the desired crime might in any way be delayed by the arrival either of his father or of anyone else. Then he summoned a certain servant named Winegarius, whom he had appointed prison guard, and ordered him quickly to enter the servants of God and hasten to kill them. [Col. 1316C]

Winegarius, having received the order, went down into the prison and found blessed Salvius praying, steadfast in face and mind and in no way afraid of the death that threatened. At the sight of him such fear seized the servant that he could neither carry out nor wished to carry out what he had been ordered; instead he began humbly to warn the holy man.

“I have been ordered, holy man, to kill you. But as it seems to me, my master ought not to have commanded this, nor is it fitting that I, his servant, should perform it. For I judge it a crime that you, who deserve no such thing, should be killed—especially since, as I look upon you more carefully, you seem almost an angel. Hear therefore and do what I tell you, so that you may escape bodily death and I may escape spiritual death. Leave this prison with your disciple, since I allow you an exit, and flee my master’s hands, while I myself flee with you. For I do not think that my master’s rage will cease in any way unless you are killed before dawn. Therefore, trusting in the shelter of night, let us leave together while we may, lest you by dying and I by killing should incur his grievous sentence.” [Col. 1316D]

## Chapter Four

To this blessed Salvius replied: “Brother, divine Scripture speaks thus: ‘Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks’ [Matt. 12:34; Luke 6:45]. It is the custom of certain servants to lie rather easily; and when ingrained wickedness urges them to do some evil thing, they say that they are ordered and compelled to do it, in order that they may somehow excuse themselves. Yet your master thinks nothing of the sort, takes no pleasure in having anything of the sort done, and, as I judge, does not command that either we or any other person be unjustly killed.”

Winegarius said: “I call as witness the God whom you desire to please: I have said nothing falsely and promised nothing deceitfully. Rather, as I said, my master has commanded it, and, as I promised, my mind is ready. Therefore go out, I beseech you, and take me with you; and I shall be your servant, the servant of you both, ready with all my heart to remove and clean the shoes from your feet. For such fear and trembling have seized me at the prospect of accomplishing what I have been ordered that this very house seems to be shaken by a divine impulse, so that no timber may be left upon timber and no stone upon stone [Matt. 24:2]. But my master is so savage and cruel that, if I do not obey commands of whatever kind, he will inflict upon me punishments of unbearable severity. Yet if I kill you, in whom I find no cause of death, I shall undoubtedly incur the wrath of divine mercy. You will therefore make provision for yourselves and for me alike if, as I have said, you are willing to escape, lest I, a servant wickedly obeying, be forced to bring to completion the purpose of a master who wickedly commands.” [Col. 1317A]

Blessed Salvius answered: “Son, if God’s will is such that we must suffer, we can neither escape nor ought to escape, but must endure with constant heart whatever happens to us. But do not be troubled at all if you are commanded to commit such a deed, because it is fitting for a servant to obey his master. For, according to the Apostle, masters must be obeyed not only when good and gentle, but also when harsh [1 Pet. 2:18].”

While they spoke these things to one another and contended in a pious debate, behold, a messenger of Winegard arrived, ordering the servant to return to his master and quickly report whether what he had commanded had been done. When he came, Winegard said: “Why have you delayed so long? Have you fulfilled the order or not?”

The servant answered: “I beseech you, my lord, hear me for a little while; and, with your anger calmed, give me, your servant, leave and opportunity to speak.”

Winegard said: “Speak.”

The servant replied: “You, lord, sent me, your servant, to do what you commanded. But, to confess the truth to your majesty, when I entered the prison door, such sudden fear seized me that I failed both in body and mind and could by no means endure the man’s face because fear prevailed. [Col. 1317B] Prostrate before his feet, I thought that the earth would at last open its mouth and, as my merits required, swallow me irrevocably. It seemed to me that the man’s face shone like an angel’s and that the ray of his brightness condemned the darkness of my conscience. Would that divine grace, my lord, might also open your eyes, so that you might perceive how great a brightness God has bestowed on that man and how great is the love that man possesses toward God!”

At this Winegard was violently moved to anger and, scarcely restraining himself from rushing upon the servant, sharply rebuked him for such cowardice and threatened him with the most grievous punishments unless he obeyed the orders without delay. Calling one of those standing by, he said: [Col. 1318A] “Go with him to the prison to which I first sent him, so that strengthened by your support he may more confidently fulfil what I commanded. Perhaps because he was alone, he was afraid to undertake such a thing and, through his fear, showed himself not so much a servant as a worthless servant.”

At these words the two men left the presence of their commander and entered the aforesaid prison, where they found blessed Salvius occupied in prayer and fearlessly awaiting the crown of martyrdom. At the sight of him both were afraid; pressed both by the command they had received and by their own accusing consciences, they kept silence for some time. At last the man sent to encourage the servant by his presence said: “Why do you stand? Why do you hesitate? Why do you delay? Why do you not quickly fulfil what you have been commanded?”

Then Winegarius took an axe to strike the holy man [Col. 1318B] and began to tremble all the more; with the blow suspended in the air, he stood for a long time in fear over the man’s neck. Blessed Salvius addressed him as he hesitated, saying: “Son, courageously do what your master commands, so that I too may suffer what my Lord commands. You must obey your master who commands, and I must depart when my Lord calls.”

Thus, as blessed Salvius humbly exhorted him and Winegard’s messenger threateningly pressed him, Winegarius at last completed the deed; and, by killing the man of God, he conveyed him to the heavenly kingdoms. For while he was cut down in prison, he was freed from every prison, and granted the enjoyment of a freer region as he entered into the joy of his Lord.

His disciple, who had been kept a little apart from him [Col. 1318C] in the same prison, so as to show reverence to his master—not in order either to escape or delay martyrdom by flight—when he saw that his master had died, or rather had departed and gone away, cried out in a tearful voice:

“Look, holy father; look, I say, lest you offend or violate the laws of inviolable charity, if you leave me, your disciple, in the misery of this mortal life. While you lived mortal life, you wished me to share your journey and labour; now that you live the life of life, do not refuse or defer having me as a participant in your reward and glory.”

After blessed Salvius had been killed, the executioners likewise killed his disciple. Thus they both rested in peace on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June]. In peace, I say; for, brought forth from the bodily and penal prison and conveyed into the fellowship of angels, [Col. 1318D] they live and reign in God and with him for ages of ages.

## Chapter Five
Winegard, having learned that the holy men had been killed, had them secretly removed from prison and secretly buried in a pit dug in the earth, in the stable where his cattle assembled. Nor is it surprising that Salvius, when he died, was placed in a stable, since Christ deigned to be placed in one when he was born. They were buried in such a way that blessed Salvius was first laid in the tomb, and then his disciple was placed crosswise upon his breast, so that the bodies of the dead might form the figure of the cross, whose burden they had borne with composure while alive. That lost man thought this deed entirely hidden from human knowledge, but divine providence [Col. 1319B] arranged matters better. For, to reveal the secret of this hiding-place, an event worthy of a miracle occurred.

There was in Winegard’s herd an exceedingly large bull, which seemed the leader and guardian of the herd and, because of its fierceness, was feared by everyone. 756 When the herd returned from pasture and gathered at its accustomed stalls, this bull began to gaze most intently upon the place of burial and to reverence it with due honour. A marvellous thing! The saints whom that wicked man had held in contempt and, with bestial savagery, handed over to an undeserved passion, the untamed bull did not disdain; rather, laying aside its natural fierceness, it stood in awe, loved, and reverenced them. Circling their burial-place, it allowed none of the animals to approach or do anything indecent upon them; and in a stable where there was nothing clean, nothing decent [Col. 1319C], it kept the place altogether spotless, out of reverence for the holiness concealed there.

If any of the things brought there for the animals’ use—hay, straw, or anything of that sort—fell within the circle, whether through the negligence of the herdsmen or the force of the winds, the bull, perceiving it, hastened to drive it away and, sweeping the surface of the grave, to cleanse it perfectly. But if one of the animals, whether a leaping heifer or a frolicking young bullock, came nearer than was fitting, or perhaps rashly ventured to enter the very circle, the bull, enraged, gave a terrible bellow and immediately exacted punishment with horn or hoof; it did not leave such an offence unpunished. Thus all the animals came to understand that the bull wished that place to be kept for himself and disturbed by no molestation; [Col. 1319D] and, from fear of that reverent fierceness, they too rendered to the place the reverence due to its dignity.

## CHAPTER VI

When the course of three years had passed, that which had already become known to dumb animals God wished to become known to human beings as well, lest man should for too long be surpassed by cattle, or an incomparable jewel lie concealed any longer in dung. There was in the same village of Breviticum a certain old woman named Rasuera. At night she often left her house while the others slept, either to guard her own property with vigilant care or, more probably, to devote herself to prayer.

One night, having gone out through her little door as usual, while she anxiously surveyed her house from outside [Col. 1320A] and at the same time meditated upon her little prayers, she happened to look toward Winegard’s stable, which was near, or perhaps adjoining, her garden. She saw that it shone within with an immense radiance. Thinking it was a fire, and fearing that it would harm both herself and all her neighbours, she hurried to see more closely what it might be, so that she might not disturb the silence of night with an outcry before she had become certain. Approaching and looking in through certain openings in the wall, she saw the little burial-vault gleaming with such radiant brilliance as if a summer sun were glowing there with noonday splendour. Two lamps were fastened to the horns of the aforesaid bull, and they shone with incredible light throughout the whole extent of the stable.

At this sight [Col. 1320B] the woman was beyond measure astonished. Lest she do wrong to the vision by failing to have it seen by others too, she hastened to awaken and summon some of her neighbours and household, whether prompted by feminine curiosity or, rather, by divine inspiration. For God wished it to be made known not merely to the woman, but through the woman to others also, how great a treasure lay hidden in the stable and what a sweet fragrance that rich dung-heap exhaled. Thus Christ first announced the glory of his resurrection in a garden to a woman, and then through the woman to others, so that she who had first been the agent in bringing in the taste of death might not be later in announcing the joys of life.

The neighbours, having been summoned, came to the aforesaid stable, [Col. 1320C] and, astonished, saw for themselves the light which the woman had seen. And lest the vision of a single night seem insufficient, they gathered on the following night, and the same thing was again revealed, so that the welcome repetition of this manifestation might confirm the vision. Therefore all said, each and every one:

“Truly marvellous and wonderful is this vision of the stable. Although we are wholly ignorant what it portends, we do not in the least doubt that it is divine and angelic.”

Therefore, by common counsel, they summoned clerics far and wide and humbly begged them to consult God about this matter.

“You,” they said, “to whom it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God (Matt. III; Mark I; Luke VIII), pray more intently that this mystery may be revealed to us, so that, once revealed, it may be honoured with due reverence.”

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 1320D]

At that time divine grace revealed another vision to Charles, king of the Franks, by which it stirred him to make a more diligent inquiry into this secret. One night, when the king himself had withdrawn somewhat from his daytime occupations and cares and given himself to rest and sleep, someone seemed to stand beside him and say:

“Send, O king, send to Valenciennes, and have diligent inquiry made into what divine providence wishes you to discover concerning Saint Salvius, martyr and bishop of Christ.”

The king awoke and retained a sufficiently clear memory of what he had dreamed; but because the vision of dreams is often empty, he judged this one empty as well. On the following night, when he had again yielded himself to sleep, he seemed once more to be warned in these words. [Col. 1321A] Yet negligence prevailed—or perhaps God so ordained it—and he had not yet obeyed the command, reasoning within himself that a person is judged rashly credulous who does not hesitate to believe every spirit before he has tested it. 757

On the third night, when the second watch had already passed and profound silence held all things, an angel stood before him, gleaming with marvellous brightness, reproaching and rebuking him for having still delayed obedience. Striking the king’s side, he said:

“Behold, once and again I have already commanded you diligently to investigate where Salvius, martyr of Christ and bishop, rests, so that through you his merit may become known to peoples far and wide. I commanded you, I say, and you neglected it; as though the command were trivial, you scorned to carry it out. Is there no one greater, to whom you ought to obey, because you see a people serving you as one greater than they? [Col. 1321B] Is there not a King of kings who contains the whole world, beneath whom, as Scripture testifies, those who bear the world bow down? (Job XIII.) Go then, go; and, taking with you your bishops and princes, do not delay to investigate where God has hitherto willed the blessed martyrs Salvius and his disciple to remain hidden.”

He spoke, and both angel and dream departed from the king. Recognizing that this was not the phantom of a superfluous vision but the course of a divine dispensation, the king summoned those whom he judged wisest and set before them in order what had been revealed to him—what, when, and how. Having received their counsel, he sent messengers into Hainaut, to precede him, for he himself would follow shortly, and to endeavour to discover what had happened to blessed Salvius.

[Col. 1321C]

On arriving at Valenciennes, they summoned the princes and judges of that province and earnestly inquired whether they knew anything about these matters. When the provincials heard the king’s command and feared incurring his judgment, some swore that they knew absolutely nothing; others reported what they had heard through common rumour. Among them Genard was brought forward, perhaps accused by certain persons. Being questioned more subtly and rigorously, he was forced to confess that the men had indeed entered his house and eaten with him at the hour of refreshment. Then, when asked what they had done after the meal or where they had gone, he answered that he knew nothing at all, fraudulently concealing the truth of the matter by lying.

Angered, those who had been sent said:

“By the king’s safety, you shall suffer innumerable punishments unless you tell the truth which you falsely deny knowing.”

[Col. 1321D]

Then they seized Genard himself, his son Winegard, and Winegard’s servant Winegarius, and presented them to the king, saying:

“These are the two, my king, who, as very many have told us, dared to kill the holy men for whom you sent us here.”

Looking upon them, the king said:

“What madness, what such presumption overthrew you, that within the kingdom in which you knew I possessed authority, you dared to exercise so monstrous a tyranny? Who granted you this power, that you should rage not only against those men, but against my own majesty as well? For you inflicted no slight [Col. 1322A] injury not only upon them but upon me also, when, without my command or utterance, you killed innocent men. Do you not know that whatever in a kingdom arrogantly abounds beyond measure and contrary to justice rebounds upon my head, as ruler by imperial authority? For just as it is my praise and glory if peace and justice are firmly maintained, so, conversely, it is disgrace and shame if they are feebly corrupted at each person’s whim?

“Since, therefore, what has been done cannot be undone, at least it must not be left unavenged, lest my negligence appear to consent, to the heightening of disgrace, in your crime, which is judged so execrable. Therefore you yourselves—yes, you—tell what you cruelly perpetrated against the holy men, or where you took care to hide them, so that the shameless tongue [Col. 1322B] may not delay to confess what the impious hand did not fear to do.”

At this they were struck with such terror that they seemed almost lifeless. Long hesitating, they neither denied the truth of the matter nor confessed it. For they kept their eyes fixed upon the ground, almost motionless, and did not dare, in anger, to look upon the king’s face. Their conscience accused them: they could neither deny so great a crime nor presume to hope for pardon by confessing it. At length, with all hope of life abandoned, fearing not so much death as a wretched manner of dying, they began to recount in order all that they had done, expecting nothing other than to undergo death or something worse than death.

Having heard this, the king considered that he would not delay to punish them according to their deserts, but that he would nevertheless not take away their opportunity for repentance. He would permit them to live in such a fashion that life itself would be a burden rather than an honour to them. [Col. 1322C] For he judged it inappropriate for their punishment to end in a swift death, lest both their disgrace and the royal justice exercised against them be more quickly consigned to oblivion. He therefore commanded his executioners to cut off the genitals of Genard and Winegard his son and tear out their eyes, so that by living thus they might instil fear into others and provide for themselves by repentance.

Indeed, it contributed not a little to the glory of the saints who had been killed that a swift death did not terminate the punishments of their executioners: for the more this misery of theirs was displayed day by day to many people, the more greatly was the saints’ memory celebrated with veneration. Then the king ordered Winegarius, Winegard’s servant, merely [Col. 1322D] to be blinded, not also, as with the others, to have his genitals cut off; for although he was known to have sinned in killing innocent men, yet in this he had satisfied not his own will but the command of the one ordering him.

“For,” he said, “it belongs to servants humbly to obey their masters, lest, if they scorn obedience, they be accused of insolent contumacy. 758 He ought therefore to undergo a lighter punishment, because he was compelled to obey in the death of the saints.”

## CHAPTER VIII

When these things had been done, the king commanded bishops, priests, and clerics to be assembled, so that they might raise those saints from the place where they lay dishonourably and place them elsewhere with dignity and veneration. Clergy and people alike gathered and solemnly celebrated the same feast. [Col. 1323A] Raising the holy bodies with hymns and praises, they clothed them in precious garments and, placing them upon a new cart, wished to transfer them in honour to the church of Saint Vedastus.

But divine power weighed down the cart itself so heavily that, although human effort applied yokes of oxen to draw it, it remained fixed and immovable. All were astonished, and, adding an innumerable multitude of people, they wished to draw the cart to the basilica of blessed Pharaildis; but divine counsel opposed them, and they could not do so. They all stood amazed and could not sufficiently wonder what such immovability might mean; they grieved that the divine counsel was hidden from them so incomprehensibly. Therefore they endeavoured humbly to entreat the martyrs themselves in prayer, that they might deign to reveal, [Col. 1323B] even to an unworthy people, whether they wished to remain in the stable or to be moved elsewhere.

At length, by the inspiration of divine mercy, the bishops and priests said to the people:

“It does not seem to us that these saints have chosen to remain in the places which we have chosen; but we do not know to what other place they may perhaps wish to be conveyed. Therefore yoke only two oxen to the cart and leave them to their own freedom, so that, human guidance removed, they may choose the place pleasing to the divine will.”

All assented to this counsel. They yoked two oxen and left them to their own choice. With no one to lead them, they made for the church of Saint Martin, in which Saint Salvius had most recently celebrated Masses, by so direct a road [Col. 1323C] as though they were being led by a drover preceding them, and with such speed as though they bore no weight. On arriving there, they stopped without any human being moving them and showed clearly enough to all the place which the martyrs had chosen for themselves.

Thus, once God’s will had become known, all extolled him with praises. With hymns and songs, with candles and lamps, with incense and spices, they placed the holy martyrs in a new tomb. So that King Charles might obtain their favour, he gave them the third part of the fisc which he had been accustomed to possess there. Genard himself also, in order to make them propitious toward him, gave them everything that he possessed.

## CHAPTER IX

That this burial of the martyrs might inspire fear and honour [Col. 1323D] in all, God wished to commend it also by another miracle, so that those who for a long time, by his arrangement, had lain hidden in the stable might now deservedly shine forth far and wide. While King Charles was still staying in the same place, and an innumerable multitude both of clergy and people gathered around him, there appeared among the rest a certain nobleman who was disinheriting his two sisters. Leaving them no share of their inheritance, he was unjustly claiming all of it for himself.

The sisters came before the king and made complaint against him, praying and tearfully begging that the king command—or rather entreat—their brother to deign to restore to them the share of the patrimony that belonged to them. Moved by their prayers, the king began to address that nobleman quite humbly, partly because he was regarded as a person of some consequence in worldly affairs, but chiefly because the king seemed to love him.

[Col. 1324A]

“It is not right, brother,” he said, “for such injury to be inflicted by you upon your sisters, lest your nobility be charged with inhuman violence. Since it is just that you should embrace them with fraternal love and, if they need you, be regarded as their merciful protector, you will disgrace your upright character not a little if, as the stronger, you oppress their weakness. Restore, therefore, to them an abundance of their paternal estate.”

But he would not at all accept the king’s counsel and refused to restore anything whatever to his sisters, asserting that their complaint was unjust. The king replied:

“Although you seem to me to act unjustly, I do not wish you to complain of my power. [Col. 1324B] I shall therefore commit the matter to divine judgment, so that no violence may be inflicted upon you by me, yet the matter may not be left undiscussed. We have here blessed Salvius, whose favour has lately been revealed to us and whom this whole people venerates for the merit of his holiness. Go and swear upon his tomb, so that, if your cause is not guilty of injustice, his merits may reveal this to us all.”

On hearing this, the miserable man immediately agreed. Coming to the tomb, restrained by no fear, he swore, saying:

“I swear by this place and by blessed Salvius who rests in it that my sisters complain unjustly against me, since I take nothing from them by violence and steal nothing from them by fraud.”

Hardly had the wretch completed his oath when divine vengeance struck him. [Col. 1324C] His entrails burst, he split open in the middle, and blood flowed from his ears, eyes, and mouth. He spread so great a stench all around that those who came to see this miracle could not endure the heaviness of the odour. 759 Some of his household and friends removed him from the crowd surrounding him and withdrew apart; there he struggled for a little while in their hands, and shortly afterward, as his sickness grew worse, he expired.

At the sight or report of this, all feared blessed Salvius and thereafter did not dare to swear falsely upon him. God adorned him with these and many other miracles and showed, to future generations as well as the present, how great was his merit.

Let us therefore pray to him, brothers, that what our weakness does not deserve before God, he may deign to obtain for us [Col. 1324D] by his own merit; and that those whom he sees serving him in whatever fashion upon earth, he may cause to glory with himself in heaven. For it is certain that, if so great a martyr should wish to commend us to God and enrich whatever diligence we have with his own merits, we shall indeed be able to cross the deep perils of this life in a happy vessel and bring our little boat into the harbour of salvation.

For what human mind could conceive, or what eloquent tongue adequately tell, how glorious a dwelling this man obtained in heaven, who endured so vile a passion for Christ? Should he not be believed to have received a seat near John the Baptist, since he is known to have endured a similar passion in prison? As I judge, he enjoys with John the unfettered liberty of rejoicing, [Col. 1325A] because with him he endured such great straits in dying. Surely he whose body passed from prison to a stable had his spirit ascend from the body with Christ to heaven’s upper chamber; and whereas a passing ray of brightness honoured that body, the vision of the eternal Deity glorifies this spirit.

Without doubt, therefore, holy brothers, commend yourselves to his merits, you who devoutly celebrate his memory; and hope that he will be present with you, since you labour continually in his service. [Col. 1326A] For this reason I too, poor little man that I am, have laboured as best I could in writing his passion, so that, if I may share in your service, I may also become a sharer in salvation; and that together we may receive dwellings with him in harmonious brightness, although in a brightness unlike his and unequal to it. May that God of gods deign to grant, and not to defer, this gift—he whose vision Salvius enjoys in Zion through infinite ages of ages.

[Col. 1325]

# LIFE OF SAINT FOILLAN, MARTYR

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1325B]

You have asked, indeed urgently asked, that I should recount in another manner of writing the life of the holy martyr and bishop Foillan, which you possess described in verse, and free it from metre, bringing it onto the plain ground of prose freedom, as likely to please devout ears somewhat more through the grace of mature novelty. But since for a long time now I have been unable either to dictate or to write what has been dictated, I long refused this kind of undertaking, repeatedly excusing my leisure while delaying to take up again the pen I had laid aside.

Since I perceive that this excuse is not sufficiently pleasing to your affection, I have judged it right to force myself, contrary to my intention, to undertake this task and devote care to it, rather than offend you by failing to serve the aforesaid martyr. [Col. 1325C] First, therefore, I commend myself to your prayers; trusting in them, I put my hand once more to the work, hoping that, if some difficulty delays me in bringing it to completion, your devotion and the martyr’s intercession will nevertheless assist me in sustaining it.

## CHAPTER I

That the life of the martyr of whom you wish me to speak may become more agreeably known to you, I have judged it fitting that the narrative, drawn back as if from a double egg, should become clear; for things which follow sometimes derive praise—or perhaps blame—from their origin or primitive form.

In the regions of the West, at the ends of the earth, the encircling sea makes the province of Hibernia into an island. [Col. 1325D] On one side it approaches the Scots, on another the Britons; on another it is confined by the meeting Ocean; and, as far as the circuit of the sea permits, it stretches from south to north. There a ruler named Funologa held power. He carefully brought up a son born to him, until he distinguished him with the sword and the military honours customary among nobles.

When the youth Philtanus had become a soldier, no longer content with his paternal home, he went over to the king of the Scots, so that there he might both be made more diligent in honourable conversion and gain a more illustrious reputation through devotion to upright conduct. 760 As the new recruit conducted himself bravely in the royal household and pleased both King Agiulphus and all the Scots by his courage, Gergehes, the king’s daughter, embraced him with a special love and wished to be joined to him in the bond of marriage, if [Col. 1326B] God so willed.

He did not disdain the maiden—fair of face, modest in speech, chaste in conduct, and without presumptuous pride—but understood that both their present love and their future marriage were pleasing to God. Fearing the king, however, they did not make this plan public. Through certain intimates they arranged the whole course of the affair and, with equal consent and due marriage rite, entered into matrimony, God so ordering it, whom they found a gracious father.

The matter remained hidden from the king until, in the course of time, the new bride’s belly swelled. When he learned this, the father’s savage anger blazed beyond measure, and he determined to burn his daughter as though she were guilty of fornication. A pile of wood was prepared; fire kindled beneath it burned; and the rumour, herald of evil, raged as the city [Col. 1326C] hurried to gather. Whoever was present wept abundantly and recoiled from the father’s crime; the father alone, clinging to anger, was not softened by the tears of others.

The pregnant bride was brought out and ordered to be quickly burned, led like an innocent sheep to sacrifice. No longer looking to human beings, she chose to imitate Susanna: with a contrite heart she groaned and prayed more devoutly to God. And behold, a voice from heaven declared plainly to all present that the king raged unjustly, grievously wronged his daughter, killed a pregnant woman who was not guilty, and incurred the guilt of murder. The voice refuted, but did not change, the wrath or intention of the father-killer. Thinking that the voice he heard had arisen through the deception of an apparition, and judging royal majesty unworthy of being deceived by trickery, ignorant of pity, he exercised harsh authority over his daughter. [Col. 1326D]

But she did not cease from prayers and tears:

“O God, who didst temper the flames of fire for the three children, who didst deliver Susanna from the hands of her false accusers, defend me, wretched as I am, who trust in thy mercy alone; temper my father’s wrath, which rages more fiercely than fire. But if perhaps I am not worthy to be delivered from the flames now present, at least protect with thy mighty hand the burden of my womb; seal it for thyself. And what I vowed to thee from its very birth, save for thyself, so that it may not perish with me in untimely death.”

Divine goodness heard her tearful prayers. From the earth, watered by tears, a most abundant spring immediately issued forth; by its flow it powerfully quenched the threatening flames and, in a wondrous miracle, changed burning heat into coolness. Seeing this, all the king’s [Col. 1327A] relatives boldly reproved him and almost forcibly snatched his daughter from his hands, crying out and praising the mercy and power of God, who consoles those who mourn and gives salvation to those who hope in him.

The father, moved, now abandoned his desired frenzy of parricide, yet still did not come to love his daughter. Rather, he ordered her to be removed quickly from his house and from all Scotland, and, having once hated her, could no longer bear even to look upon her. Philtanus, rejoicing at the restoration of his wife, left Scotland. Yet he did not return to Hibernia, whence he had come, thinking that his father Funologa would take it grievously, even for a short time, that he had entered a marriage which had not been disclosed to him and seemed almost clandestine.

Therefore, accompanied by a few companions, he entered the land of the Hebrides and confidently approached his uncle Brendan, who then presided over that land from an episcopal see and was pleasing both to God and people through the merit of his life. When that bishop had kindly received his nephew and the nephew had spent a short time with him, Gergehes his wife reached the time of giving birth, and became mother not of one child only but of three at once.

He wished the first to be called Furseus, the second Foillan, and the third Ultan. In them, it seems, nature chose to enact a mystery: for in three persons the supreme Deity is made known to us, and, according to Solomon, a threefold cord is not quickly broken. There is moreover something quite fitting in Foillan’s being found born in the middle, since he was fortified on either side by manly strength; no softness, no womanliness was produced in him by a debasing manner of life [Col. 1327C], and his life is proclaimed holier, his death more glorious.

Holding his brothers on both sides, he bound them to holiness; joined together by the middle nail, they did not differ from one another. One Lord, one faith, one baptism bound and united them; one profession likewise united them, and death alone separated them. Bishop Brendan instructed them after their birth and growth in letters; and in the course of time divine grace distinguished them by holy conduct. According to their age—indeed, beyond their age—they proved to be of good disposition, and with diligent zeal always applied themselves to increasing the merits of their virtues. For they did not seek earthly kingdoms or royal wealth; but, out of love for poverty, they despised the abundance promised them, and when their paternal inheritance seemed to smile upon them, they chose rather to have no hereditary right in it. [Col. 1327D]

## CHAPTER II

For King Agiulphus of the Scots, hearing that his daughter was fruitful and that the sons were of so illustrious a character, was led to repentance and swayed by the counsel of many. Taking with him friends and relatives, 761 he visited his daughter by ship; and, calling both her and her husband back to Scotland, he assigned them his realm.

A little later, the death of Philtanus’s father Funologa was announced to him; and when he died, Philtanus was raised to the royal sceptre of both Hibernia and Scotland.

The sons’ humility did not turn its attention to these joyful and prosperous events, but extended itself rather toward the narrow and arduous merits of religious life. They knew and remembered that whatever transient thing the world promises its lover does not correspond in a fitting balance to the lover of heavenly things. As their religious devotion increased day by day with worthy progress, and as their fame and reputation were celebrated and commended far and wide, Foillan, whom the bishop had exalted by reason of his greater prudence and learning, was ordained bishop amid the acclamation of clergy and people alike. [Col. 1328A]

Once ordained, he did not become proud; rather, he feared both burden and honour, lest the preeminence he had taken up should disturb his desire and love. He loved—or rather desired—to live in this life humble and private, rather than depart from his purpose through the office of the episcopacy which he had assumed. Therefore he began to beseech God more devoutly and frequently, that God might deign to reveal his will to him, direct and guide his steps into the path of the poverty he had purposed [Col. 1328B], and keep and increase in him the desire for holiness alone.

The most merciful hearer did not fail his righteous prayers. He taught the holy man and warned him through an angel to leave house, country, and parents, go forth, cross over to unknown regions, and bear fruit among other nations both by example and doctrine. Foillan quickly reported this to his brothers Furseus and Ultan; taking them and others who had attached themselves to him for the sake of religion, he sailed, under God’s guidance, to England.

King Sigebert devoutly received them there and, on hearing from them the word of life, advanced to such contempt for the world that, taking the religious habit and tonsure, he did not delay to profess himself a monk. [Col. 1328C] In his own land he built a monastery, which he carefully endowed with a suitable site, appropriate buildings, sufficient possessions, and religious inhabitants. Casting aside royal power, he subjected himself there to the rule.

The care and guardianship of this monastery were principally entrusted to Foillan, because among great men he seemed to possess greater prudence and learning. Living there in holiness and piety, he presented himself to all as an example to imitate, and his reputation exhaled a sweeter and more fruitful fragrance in inviting others. Both Sigebert’s conversion and Foillan’s leadership rendered that place renowned, as many flocked there to offer God the devoted service of religious life.

Not long afterward, a divine revelation made known to Furseus that a hostile invasion would devastate that place—indeed, the whole province—and that he himself should leave England and move to Gaul for the sake of religious life. When he had announced this to Foillan and the other brothers, he took a few companions, bade England farewell, came into the regions of Gaul, and found no small favour with King Clovis and his nobles. [Col. 1328D]

## CHAPTER III

Foillan, however, wishing to comfort the religious men whom he had assembled in each of the monasteries, chose to await the coming evils with them, lest, once the shepherd had been struck, the sheep should be found disturbed too hastily, and wander more freely through the absence of one who consoled them than through the presence of one who attacked them.

England was therefore troubled when a king named Penda, accustomed to rule its fourth part, sought to exercise wicked power and powerful wickedness over the remaining three. As he raged, King Sigebert was forced to return from the cloister; and with those who recalled him he fought not with hand and sword, but with a word of consolation. [Col. 1329A]

Although he conducted himself in battle religiously and bravely, and unconquered in spirit suffered death for his country, so many and such great princes fell in that same destruction that I consider it long and superfluous to set forth in sequence either the manner and order of the event or the men themselves by name. Once the defenders had fallen, a band of pirates freely raged through the province. Attacking the monastery over which Foillan was said to preside, they carried off the brothers as captives and plundered their possessions. [Col. 1329B] Nor did they spare the holy man, though by divine counsel he was preserved.

Observing that the province had been laid waste, its princes had fallen, the monastery had been despoiled, and religious men had come into the hands of enemies, he addressed his brother Ultan and showed himself given over to such grief that, for the life of the others, if it pleased divine counsel, he wished to die. Thus they both prayed together, persisted diligently in prayers, confidently desired that divine help be present with them, and more surely hoped that God’s good pleasure would be revealed to them—that the righteous prayers of righteous men would not be defrauded of their just desire.

God did not delay to visit Foillan by sending an angel, and to change his sorrowful tears into a new consolation: “Do not,” he said, “while evils press upon you, be worn down beyond measure or grieve excessively; rather be prepared to endure whatever the world may bring upon you. For a reason known to himself, God has for the present set aside this place, and has ordained that you should go elsewhere and make progress among many people. He does not now grant you your appointed end; rather, time for labor remains to you, and no slight labor.”

Admonished by such speech, the man of God restored courage to those with him; and he ransomed, by prayer or by payment, such captive brethren as he could. Leaving the place which the intolerable fury of war had disturbed, and taking the equipment needed for divine services, he entrusted both himself and his companions to favorable winds and to a ship; and, having made a happy voyage, he was received by lands beyond the sea. Having left the sea, he resolved to go to Rome, that he might be worthy to find the favor of Peter and Paul. Pope Martin, who then presided there, honored him with especial devotion and, recognizing his religious distinction, enriched him with the gift of his blessing. And because he knew that Foillan had received episcopal rank, and had left that very place both for the sake of humility and at a divine command, he enjoined him that, although he no longer held his former see, he should nevertheless exercise the office of a bishop: namely, by ordaining, confirming, and preaching, he should be a source of salvation to his hearers, and, as formerly in his own country, so now in exile, should discharge the episcopal ministry.

Afterward a heavenly vision strengthened him in a dream. It earnestly commanded him to return to Gaul, foretelling both the course of his life and the outcome of his future death, and even naming for him the place of his martyrdom and the place of his burial. Instructed by this oracle and retaining the vision in his memory, he revered the prophecy and already longed for the passion of which he had foreknowledge. Having bid farewell to the holy apostles, whose protection he had begged might be present with him, he returned to Gaul, accompanied by his brother Ultan and certain others.

When he came to the monastery which his brother Furseus had built at Péronne, and learned that he was now dead and had been buried there, he was moved by natural affection. He could not but grieve, and, compelled by flowing tears, rendered the service due to his devotion. After mourning and rendering these rites, he remained there for several days and ministered the spiritual nourishment of the word to the crowds that came together. But because his spirit could not yet find rest there, he left the province of the Germans and wished to pass into the region of Hainaut. When he had departed from Hainaut, the virgin Gertrude gladly received him; and, finding in him both teaching and a pattern of life, she seemed to embrace him with such longing that she loved him with a singular affection as though he were her own father.

## Chapter IV

That virgin was noble by birth, distinguished in character, and reputed rich in patrimony. Her religious devotion was renowned and her reputation praiseworthy. From childhood her pursuit had been a virginal life, not the desire, affection, or intention of married union. Since she had already laid aside the kingdom of the world and all its adornment, and had placed a veil upon her head to show this, desiring Christ alone, she clung to him with all her strength. At the monastery of Nivelles, together with many women of the same purpose, she served him. Burning with holy ardor, she rejected whatever the world loves; she abstained not only from all unlawful things, but also from many lawful ones. She wore down her body with fasts, vigils, and rough clothing, and, beyond what was customary for her age or rank, appeared despised and contemptible.

When Foillan understood and loved her as so devout, attached to spiritual things and so far removed from carnal ones, he judged it fitting to remain with her for some time, that through her he might advance to better things and perhaps advance her also. He admired in the virgin so devout a youthfulness of years; he admired in the young man a venerable old age full of grace; he admired in the fragile sex such robust strength; in one despised and neglected, such lovely beauty of mind. The virgin’s face was indeed bright through nature’s gift, but muddy with the dust poured over it by labor and tears. The dignity of her lineage and the law of nature strove to adorn her; but opposition to perishable beauty prevailed.

Over the virgins, widows, and continent women whom she governed, she presented herself neither as greater nor as their equal, but as though subject to them. What she commanded others to observe strictly, she herself first observed, and more rigorously—mindful of her charge and forgetful of her birth. This woman, who was regarded as supported by such great and numerous merits, greatly admired the holy man, the great bishop: his angelic countenance, his honeyed mouth in teaching, his worthily ordered conduct, endowed with wonderful discipline. The virgin admired that he was not puffed up by episcopal mitres, that he made no claim from a supreme patron or royal lineage, that he had left home, country, and parents, lived in exile, stood firm in his purpose, and counted every land as his homeland.

She heard and approved him as he discoursed excellently from the Scriptures, speaking most profoundly, as though returning from the third heaven; concerning God—who was not new—he brought forth things new and unknown to the unlearned, and thereby won great favor in the ears of his hearers. The virgin therefore wished the holy man to remain longer with her, and that he might not perhaps wander farther in exile, to be bound to her by whatever means. Having formed a plan for calling him back more firmly from his journey, she sought a place in which he might serve God more devotedly and in greater seclusion.

For she knew that the bishop did not love gatherings and tumultuous crowds of people, and did not gladly or frequently have recourse to quiet and silence; and therefore she sought to find a suitable and solitary place. She sought it, I say, and rejoiced that the place she found suited so well such a desire.

## Chapter V

At that time the place was a valley, wooded and enclosed by hills, rich in springs, not abundant in grain but productive enough to provide sustenance; it was fruitful in cattle, pleasant with adjoining meadows and a stream flowing through it. In this valley, the surrounding forest concealed a certain small village, inhabited from ancient days by only a few very poor people. For a multitude of people does not greatly love a barren or uncultivated place, nor does a grim place and vast solitude gather many fellow citizens.

Those who first lived in that place or village named it from its character: they properly called it Fosses, “Ditches,” because the natural site of the place, low and sunken, is enclosed as though by a surrounding rampart formed by the overhanging hills. And because, just as tumult belongs naturally to a populous city, so solitude is friendly to a small number of religious persons, the holy virgin wished to present this place to the righteous man. There, withdrawing himself, he could be absent from the bustle of public affairs; and when weary with tedium and afflicted by the labor of preaching, he could there breathe freely and refresh his spirit in the welcome repose of contemplation.

Foillan, with those who were with him, went to inspect the place thus presented and offered. Having found it, walked about it, and examined it carefully, he accepted it and declared that it suited both his own purpose and that of his companions. Moreover, reflecting that the inhabitants, as stated, called the place Fosses, he recalled to mind that vision which, while he was in Rome, had named for him both the place of martyrdom and likewise that of burial. Thus, now knowing the place of his burial, he did not delay to give thanks. There he celebrated Masses, prayed that God might preside over both himself and that place, and urged his brethren finally to settle there permanently. As they remained and devoted themselves to God, he loved to remain with them.

Accordingly, many persons assembled and hastened with great zeal to cut down the forest. With axes they cut away the brushwood; with hoe and digging-tool they uprooted the willows; they stripped the rough and uneven ground of rubble and trees, and in a short time made it arable and fit to yield crops. The reputation of that place, and of the bishop himself who inhabited it in a particularly religious manner, spread far and wide and attracted very many persons. Some bestowed generous gifts for his needs; others transferred themselves there to live with him. Thus, in the course of time, the number both of possessions and of possessors increased. Foillan, ever more devout, embraced the devout newcomers with most tender arms. He rejoiced to be among them as one of them, not to preside over them but simply to be with them—indeed, to be regarded among them as far beneath them, abject and humble.

All whom he perceived to please God, he loved to rejoice with; he suffered with the suffering and grieved with the sad and failing. Becoming all things to all men (1 Cor. 9), he desired to be devoted to God alone. Forgetting the things that were behind, he spent himself wholly in the courts of the Lord; urgent in devout prayers, he hid himself in the hidden place of the divine countenance. Having passed beyond faith and hope, he seemed to cleave to the vision itself.

## Chapter VI

When the holy virgin Gertrude saw that Fosses had made no small progress and had raised its head, as it were, from a lowly place to the height of virtues, she rejoiced. She earnestly endeavored to urge the holy man Foillan to return to her without delay and comfort her by his presence. For she could not calmly bear that he should continually be present among the gathered brethren, so caring for them that he did not also benefit others in need. Rather, she wished that, while he attended to Fosses and to the needs of its people, he should also not be absent, at a fitting time, from the virgin herself and her virgins.

Foillan neither could nor would oppose the desire of the saint, since he knew that God himself sometimes obeyed the prayers of a virgin. Without delay he consulted more carefully with his brother Ultan about the matter, placed the care upon him, and arranged all things as he knew to be expedient for the monastery. Ultan had chosen to remove his dwelling farther from the community, and there, devoting himself to God, to remain solitary and silent. Released from earthly matters, he wished to live with Paul in heavenly things, to attend continually to praises, and to delight in angelic ministry. Yet, reminded by his brother, he did not pursue the inclination more pleasing to himself. Setting aside quiet and leisure, he undertook care and labor, fearing that he might be found to have strayed greatly from the path of rectitude if he presumed to oppose Foillan’s command even a little.

Therefore, with affairs arranged and Ultan presiding over the brethren, the bishop returned to the virgin, God sweetly ordering all things. With her he devoted himself to God and applied himself to the pursuit of holiness; those attending him he taught the rule of religious truth. Those who attended and listened, who worthily observed the bishop and the virgin, and who gladly obeyed their commands and examples, rejoiced in their fellowship, in their shared life, in their mutual affection, and in their spiritual love.

Thus the bishop and virgin together ran in the way of God’s commandments; thus together they strove in the contest; thus, disregarding bodily suffering, they watched over the healing of souls, so that they seemed to rival one another and hasten competitively toward the prize for which they had long hoped, leaving spectators uncertain which of the two ought to be preferred. Such abundant fruit, and indeed such a discipline of good living, issued from their manner of life, their shared dwelling, their conduct, and their teaching, that not only those who served under them imitated them more zealously, but even those far away reverenced their celebrated fame and illustrious testimony.

## Chapter VII
