While they lived and progressed in this manner, and were thus useful to very many, Foillan resolved to visit the brethren who lived under Ultan’s direction; but first he intended to visit Maldegarius, who was also called Vincent, a man known and intimate to him and most dear in religion.

When she heard this, the virgin Gertrude, although she could scarcely bear even his brief absence, nevertheless could not fittingly oppose this purpose. She only earnestly required and begged of him that, once his business had been accomplished, he would set delay aside and return more quickly. The holy man therefore took leave of the holy community, humbly commended himself to its prayers, and repeated this very request with such weeping, again and again, that he seemed thereby somehow to foresee that he would not return, although he believed that he would return.

Taking only a few companions, he set out, intending to go to Sonegias. He entered the forest of Charbonnière, and while passing through it found an extensive plain enclosed by trees and beautiful with its grassy surface. There was in it a somewhat elevated and lofty mound, and a clear spring which sent forth a brook with pleasing murmur. To this place neighboring shepherds often gathered, refreshing both their flocks with pasture and themselves with play and conversation. From a lookout which they had fixed upon the said eminence of the mound, they surveyed the surrounding places and watched their flocks, scattered farther away to graze.

When the holy man came there, attracted by the pleasant appearance of the place, he stopped to rest. After remaining there for a little while, he saw some persons passing along the public road and addressed them in peaceful speech: “You who pass along the road, tell me where you are going; what is that village to which you hasten to go, or perhaps to return? And since the appearance of this place in which we stand seems to have some significance, tell me whether it is known among you by any name.”

They replied: “The neighborhood calls the place in which you stand Ampolines; the village toward which we are going is called Seneffe. Since the sun is considering its setting and evening hastens to draw near, it is good that you should turn aside with us for lodging.”

That place is rightly called Ampolines, that is, “rich in circuit” or “powerful in enclosure,” because, naturally surrounded by the forest about it, it excelled in its broad plain and pleasant surface, and its fruitful abundance smiled upon both men and cattle. Its overflowing fruitfulness of pasture and the murmuring vein of its spring made it fertile and delightful. But the village to which the most wicked men were proceeding was rightly called Seneffe, because, without faith, covenant, or peace between them, they led the holy man out of his way and drew him aside. Under the appearance of hospitality they promised him a kindness and deceived him.

For while they promised to lead him, as it were, by certain shortcuts, they brought him into some mean shepherds’ folds. With treacherous malice, violating the law by which a host should carefully receive a guest, they plotted and murmured deceitfully about killing the man. The holy man, considering the name of the place, which he had long before committed carefully to memory because the divine vision had named it both as the place of burial and the place of martyrdom, understood that death was truly and imminently near to him. Though his spirit was ready, his weak flesh could not but fear. He spared his companions the disclosure of this fear lest they should be troubled; but he commanded and admonished them to be strengthened in the Lord, to remember and hold fast that they would obtain unfading life if they endured the impending death with courageous steadfastness.

“Brethren,” he said, “these wicked men, who promised and ought to have given us lodging, seem instead to be devising a ruinous plan. So far as I understand, they are driven by anger—indeed, by fury—and, faith having been violated, they meditate not kindness but murder. Therefore stand firm and be diligent while time is granted you; while the wicked murmur wickedly, let your devotion work more earnestly, so that, when their malice has been confirmed in an accursed resolve, your steadfastness may be found prepared to endure.”

Foillan spoke and stood thus, and he himself likewise watched and persevered in prayer. Both prelate and subjects did not cease from vigilant attentiveness until the malicious executioner came threateningly and stood before them. Finding the holy men watchful and wakeful in prayer, he condemned men guilty of no fault to the sentence of the sword; and, having slain the innocent, the wretch rejoiced in his triumph of malice.

But the holy man Foillan, as he had been wholly engaged in devotion and prayer, so, when slain by the sword, remained steadfast in the same purpose. In a miracle worthy of the event, his head having been cut off, he seemed not to know death: while the others were silent, he himself did not cease from the prayers he had begun. Hearing this, the executioner was astounded beyond expression and marvelously horrified at a thing unheard of before. Fearing that the dead man’s speech might reveal the murder he had committed, he rushed upon him again and did not fear to add wounds to wounds.

Having killed him anew and more cruelly torn him limb from limb, he hid him in a trackless place, shaded by branches and foliage. Yet the natural savagery of beasts and birds reverenced and guarded the man whom bestial inhumanity had not spared. Nor do I doubt that the holy man, afflicted in death by a second, repeated martyrdom and a double passion, now rejoices in a doubled gift of reward or crown; and that he whom the cruel executioner made, though dead by death, die again, the supreme Craftsman glorifies with a more splendid gift. For if one star is truly said to differ from another in glory (1 Cor. 15), it follows that one martyr likewise differs from another; and for him over whom a double death rules so mightily in time, the crown is undoubtedly doubled in reward.

## Chapter VIII

No one was present at their murder to report it; no one performed a funeral lament; no one rendered the customary funeral rites. No human care buried their bodies; no one recited prayers or psalms at their tomb; no one sang funeral chants; finally, no one offered the saving sacrifice for the slain. Thus the murder long remained concealed, until the day set for his return had passed. When it had passed and the bishop did not return to the virgin Gertrude, the piously anxious virgin sent a messenger to ask Ultan what he thought of the bishop’s prolonged delay.

He replied: “When recently I was standing at the altar celebrating Mass and offering the sacrifice, and was remembering that bishop as usual, it seemed to me that a dove flew before my face, showing a snow-white body but blood-red wings. Hence, groaning, I infer and am distressed by this inference: that he is overwhelmed by an untimely death, his blood having been shed; and, though I rightly grieve over the loss of my brother taken away, to complete my grief I fear that perhaps he lacks burial.”

Hearing this, the holy virgin was inconsolably sorrowful. With tears she urged all who were with her, clergy and people alike, that they should not delay to entreat God privately and publicly not to permit this report to remain hidden longer. At the virgin’s command, clergy and people hastened to implore God, to persist in vigils, and to fast with devout spirit. They did not cease from the prayer and fast imposed upon them until the truth of the matter became known to the virgin herself.

For one morning, when the morning office had been completed, an angel, suddenly shining with light, stood beside the virgin as she prayed. He spoke familiarly to her in his accustomed manner and gently refreshed her sorrowful ignorance with these words: “Virgin, that father of yours most dear to you, concerning whom you ask, grieve, fear, and are so anxious—he and those who went with him have been killed by the sword of wicked men; having attained what he desired, he has been received into heaven.”

The holy virgin was greatly comforted by such speech, rejoicing that the truth she longed for had at last been more certainly disclosed. Taking many persons of both sexes with her, she set out and hastened to find the man she loved, although dead. When they had arrived together where they were heading, and had found the bodies of the dead by a guiding light, piety took precedence over religious observance, and human feeling over faith: psalms were postponed, chant set aside, and overwhelming cries intervened. When the crying had subsided, fitting psalms and funeral hymns followed. The devout clergy performed the duty required by religion; they commended the souls and prayed that angels might come to their aid—though it is beyond doubt that praises rather than prayers are fitting for holy martyrs.

The virgin gathered the bodies of the saints, dried their wounds, wiped away their blood, washed them carefully, and clothed them in clean linen. While the others performed the solemn office for the souls, she drenched the bishop’s body with an abundance of tears. It is remarkable that these bodies had lain for a long succession of days beneath branches or in the open air and had already suffered from their situation, rain, and corrupting air; nevertheless, contrary to the usual condition of bodies long without burial, they gave off no foul smell whatever, but sent forth far and wide a fragrance like balsam or incense.

The bodies, therefore, having been washed, as stated, and wrapped in linen cloths, were placed upon biers and carried to Nivelles amid a great throng both of singers and mourners. It was uncertain whether they grieved more for those unjustly and wickedly killed, or, grief wiped away, at last rejoiced more over their discovery. The virgin herself also placed herself beneath the bishop’s bier to carry it; having taken it up, she did not set it down except when her body was exhausted. Strong love gave strength to her weak body, and even when her powers were wearied, love knew neither weariness nor failure.

## Chapter IX

When they came to Nivelles, they placed the bodies of the dead in the church and celebrated Masses with the utmost devotion of the people. While they deliberated whether the bodies should be buried there or elsewhere, Abbot Ultan came and addressed them thus: “By divine counsel it was the bishop’s will, his fixed purpose and earnest concern, that after his death he should receive burial at Fosses. If anyone should intend or strive to bury him elsewhere, he would seem to oppose both the will of God and that of the bishop.”

The virgin agreed; the multitude of the people agreed; and Dido, bishop of Poitiers, agreed. At that time he had come there for prayer, and, warned by a divine vision, he had joyfully gone to meet the dead Foillan. “Rise,” the angel said, “and quickly go to meet Elijah as he comes.” He repeated this three times to the listener. This warning suddenly broke his sleep, and upon awakening he at once burst out in words of this sort: “What can such a warning about Elijah mean? Is it an empty dream, as often happens in sleep, or perhaps a prophecy? How could Elijah, the most ancient prophet, come here, so that I could go out to meet him as he comes?”

While he considered and reconsidered this, and Bishop Dido could not sufficiently marvel, behold, people arrived announcing that Foillan was being brought dead. Hearing the people’s lamentation and the clergy’s mournful melodies, he went to meet them and said: “This, I judge, is Elijah. So far as I perceive, as his fame and reputation attest, as the age which he has spent wholly without stain proclaims, as the purity of his heart, the sequence of his conduct, and the order of his life show—he who, from boyhood, renouncing the flesh, passed readily through the world—just as John, son of Zacharias, deserved to be called Elijah because of a certain likeness, so this man truly possesses not Elijah’s person but his resemblance.”

Considering this, Bishop Dido reverently honored Foillan. Conferencing with Gertrude, he gladly accepted what was proclaimed so solemnly concerning him; and, seeing how great was Ultan’s devotion and care concerning Foillan’s burial, he approved whatever pleased Ultan in this matter. Therefore the holy virgin and an innumerable company of clergy and people, hindered neither by domestic concerns nor by business, did not delay to bring the body, placed on a cart, back to Fosses. Many of them ran ahead to announce the coming of the funeral procession.

When they had hastened to the River Sambre and found that, swollen by winter rains, it had overflowed far beyond its channel, they had to stop their intended course, willing or unwilling. They and the others remained there until the cart arrived. But when the draught animals of the cart came, they were moved neither by driver nor by goad, as was customary. Rather, fortified by a certain confidence, they did not fear to enter the swelling waters; and no obstacle whatever prevented their entrance or progress, because they trusted more manifestly in the burden they carried.

For as soon as the hooves of the young oxen touched the water, by a wonderful event the swollen waves subsided. That former swelling seemed so suddenly annulled that the ford could now be crossed easily not only on horseback but even on foot. Hence that ford was from then onward called Gertrude’s Ford; it was said to be better and safer than other fords because the prayers of the virgin and the merit of the martyr seemed to obtain an easier crossing there, since they themselves had crossed it with easy step.

Having crossed it, they quickly came to Fosses, their destination. There they found many religious persons and laypeople coming to meet them. As all ran together, unbearable grief was renewed, and the whole crowd lamented the bishop as though he had newly died. Devoutly celebrating his funeral rites with mourning and chant, they buried him with the greatest honor in a fitting place. When the solemnities of Masses and psalms had been completed, they took leave of Ultan and, imploring rest, blessed him all with one voice.

He is held to be present not only among those standing near him and ministering there, but he also deigns to be present to all who worthily seek him. Indeed, whoever gladly celebrates his memory in any place finds him favorable and experiences the saving help of his protection. Therefore I also, who have labored as best I could in writing what has been said above, and who, when I began it, asked that he might be present with me, now commend myself to his prayers and merits, that through his intercession I may one day be able to attain what I seek. For he so rejoices in heaven, among the angels, in the desired rest and in the divine countenance, that he is remembered as a merciful helper of those of his own who labor on earth. Thus he, free of all misery, mercifully has compassion on his own with his own benevolence, and eternally glories with and in him who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1337]

# Life of the Blessed Confessor Gislenus

## Prologue

[Col. 1337C]

The saints who, by the law of mortals, have been led out of the prison-house of this flesh and brought by ampler grace into that long-desired joy of their Lord, are said to bear such tender affection toward us who live and remain behind that, although they certainly have no need of human praises, they nevertheless wish and desire to be proclaimed praiseworthy among us, so that both preachers and hearers may love to imitate their praiseworthy deeds.

Hence a sufficiently honorable and useful custom has grown up: that the holiness of those believed to be outstanding should sometimes be commended in writing, recounting how great their courage was in this life, and by whose worthy merits they are granted an unfailing length of days. Therefore, brothers, not refusing to obey your prayers, yet acknowledging myself to be far unequal to this task, I undertake, as best I can, to write the praises of your confessor: by what labor and by what grace he is believed to have obtained the crown of glory and honor.

I ask, however, that you commend me in your prayers, as I minister to you in this work, to that same saint to whom you show yourselves devotedly committed in service, so that in his goodness he may deign to accept the present little work and obtain for me the favor of God, before whom he stands.

## Chapter I

God, the author of all things, who is said to do nothing on earth without cause, whose will is only just although it is sometimes unknown to us, willed—and, willing, ordained—that the blessed confessor Gislenus should be born in Greece but should dwell far from Greece in the district of Hainaut.

When his Christian parents lovingly cared for him from birth into adulthood, and with paternal concern perceived that he possessed a good natural disposition, they committed him, with a devout regard for religion, to be educated in letters and trained in the schoolroom under a master’s rod. For they had heard that, through the benefit of learning, the error of ignorance is driven away; the darkness of the mind is cleared and the path of life made plain; elegance of conduct and ordered speech are formed; and, far more importantly, the hidden or obscure wisdom of heavenly things shines forth. Knowledge of eternal things, and love of the things known, are kindled in devout minds; and whatever is judged rightly necessary for either future or present life is tasted beforehand, grace assisting through the instruction of letters.

Having heard and understood this, his parents wished their son to be educated in letters, desiring that, once educated, he should be distinguished not by empty praises but by the abundance of his merits. They loved him as born of flesh with spiritual affection, and therefore wished him to advance by literary study and knowledge toward the knowledge of God.

Now in Greece, at that time, the noble city of Athens still flourished in its reputation and learning. For the sake of greater advancement, they sent him there and entrusted him to teachers for instruction, having paid a great price. But he, by the talent which the generous hand of the Creator’s benevolence had poured into him, diligently added watchfulness in study and labor. Rejecting games and amusements by which the age of boys is often ensnared, he hastened to be found wiser not only than his equals but than very many older persons.

As he read and advanced in both learning and age, he did not care to hunt after the praises of passing vanity. Rather, from the very things from which some gather material for glory or self-importance, he acquired a greater merit of grace. Having read the books written by pagan poets or philosophers—men who, not knowing God, described worldly and transient things—he set aside the error in which their blindness had darkened them and carefully retained the truth which they proclaimed through them.

Therefore, despising the things which their writings taught were to be despised, and which the doctors of the Church judged to be destructive, the boy Gislenus, while still of tender years, so directed his mind toward desiring those things which he divinely understood to be abiding and saving, that, though he labored energetically and earnestly with the others in literary study, he surpassed the others in spiritual advancement and wisdom.

But when he observed that those who, childhood receding, had entered the bounds of adolescence and were growing to maturity, and others whose youthful privilege clothed their cheeks with a slight down, fell more grievously into failure of virtue and salvation in proportion as they advanced further in age and learning, he resolved, with a stricter purpose, to hasten more ardently toward perfection, lest malice coming upon him should change his understanding while it was still unformed and weak.

Therefore, at the persuasion of his mother, who was deservedly called Philosophy and who urged her son toward the love of wisdom with every admonition she could offer, he bade farewell to the teachers and pupils of the schools and entered a regulated cloister. There, made a monk, he began to serve God according to the rule.

## Chapter II
There the Rule of Saint Basil was observed; according to its decree the saints who had assembled lived. Their elders strove to impart both example and teaching to the younger; the younger obeyed the teachings and commands of their elders; all forestalled one another with due honor, and thus, as if in competition, found favor with the supreme Judge.

The more diligently blessed Gislenus observed their manner of life, and the more fully he understood from day to day that it pleased God, the more completely he despised all that he had left outside, and the more devotedly he applied himself, with watchful zeal, to imitating them. While he strove to imitate them through devout conduct, and, thinking humbly of himself, regarded himself as inferior to the rest [Col. 1339D], they especially exalted him with praises and, by their own worthy judgment, preferred his merits to their own. For among them he was as a humble and abject servant of all: sparing in speech, loving silence, remarkable for vigilant circumspection, devoted to reading, given to prayer, and so moved by continual devotion that, through the merit of his virtues, he was acceptable both to God and to his neighbor.

As time went on, when his holiness was no longer held in any doubt, he was advanced step by step to ecclesiastical orders. After the ministry of acolyte and the dignity of subdeacon, he was adorned with the Levitical rank; and finally, to complete his dignity, he was raised to the honor of the priesthood. Having been promoted to orders, he burned also to advance to greater heights of virtue, to remove entirely from himself whatever he believed hindered him, and [Col. 1340A], that he might be accounted conformed to that holy Abraham, he embraced with devout longing Abraham’s faith and obedience.

Neither his country, his kindred, nor his father’s house could hold Abraham back, but appeared to reject what was known for what was unknown, and what he possessed for what was yet to be acquired. At the command of Him who ordered him, counting all that lay before him as loss, he hastened to obtain the increase of the promised gifts. So too this our novice Gislenus—not with the sudden impulse of an unstable mind, not by a breath of fickleness, not led by his own spirit but by the divine Spirit—setting aside the cloister in which he rejoiced in silence, as though drowsing for a time in womanly fashion [reading uncertain]—desired to keep watch and be worn down by the labor of pilgrimage. For He pressed him by a hidden command, who intended to accomplish great things concerning him and through him; He who now willed that the lamp of religion, once kindled [Col. 1340B], should not be hidden beneath a bushel, but placed upon a lampstand and proclaimed far and wide to many.

Having therefore sought a blessing from the father who presided over the monastery and from the holy community which there served God according to rule, they indeed grieved tenderly at the future absence of so great a brother, but they would not resist divine appointment with human obstinacy. At length, having exchanged the holy kiss with the abbot and brothers, Gislenus undertook his purpose. Burning with desire for holiness, he first proceeded humbly and devoutly to Rome, wishing to serve the holy apostles not so much with gifts as with the services of prayer.

He entered their churches with a suppliant countenance and a joyful heart, now mindful neither of journey nor labor, not wearied by hardship. Visiting the holy places, he did not distinguish which he preferred to another; but everywhere he poured forth prayers, prostrated himself more devoutly upon the ground, and joyfully, as though soothed by the sweetness of consolation found, repeatedly bent his knees and pressed kisses upon the pavement [Col. 1340C]. While he venerated the holy apostles with all the devotion he could, and humbly begged them to direct his way and life, he was instructed, in the secret place of understanding, by the admonitions of divine revelation that he should travel far from Rome, across the Alps, into Gaul; and that in the district of Hainaut, which was a part or province of that region, amid a crooked, perverse, and pestilential people, he should dwell in a place which the inhabitants call Ursidongus. There he was to prepare a house of prayer for the aforesaid apostles and, by the word of preaching, gather servants of God there to live according to rule [Col. 1340D].

When he received this instruction, the holy man gave devout thanks to the Creator, the ever-faithful provider for His faithful servants, who had care for him and had wished to reveal to him the place where, according to His pleasure, he ought to finish his present life. Commending himself to the patronage of the apostles, in whom he placed great confidence, and taking with him two companions whom he especially loved, Lambert and Belliricus, he left Rome and undertook a long and difficult journey. After much labor and time had been spent, he crossed the ridges of the Apennines and the Alps; having forded the Rhône and the Danube, he entered the flatter lands of Gaul, and, not content with this, traveled onward as far as Hainaut.

## CHAPTER III

At that time the holiness of the confessor Amandus was held in high esteem in those parts [Col. 1341A], and his fame was everywhere spread abroad with celebrated praise. On hearing his name, Gislenus earnestly desired to behold his face, converse with him, and be refreshed by his good and consoling word. Divine goodness did not disappoint him of his desire, but granted him the desired opportunity of seeing and speaking with him. When he saw him, Gislenus declared his desire and the duty laid upon him; and Amandus, with a gracious answer, strengthened him in his purpose.

Having accomplished this, Gislenus, now joyful because he had spoken with the holy man as he had wished, pursued his journey with a more devout spirit and came to a certain place commonly called Mount Castrilocus, which seemed suited to religion and the solitary life.

Two rivers, flowing on either side, protected it [Col. 1341B]; between them lay the green of meadows and the pleasantness of woods. The very beauty of the place’s natural setting, the absence of inhabitants, and a solitude friendly to religious life invited one to remain there. Thinking, therefore, that perhaps this was the place revealed to him by the divine promise—the place which, while he was still at Rome, had been foretold to be in Hainaut—he began with diligent care to prepare a little dwelling for himself there, intending to live in it with those who had come with him.

At that time King Dagobert, under whose scepter the Gallic realm was governed, was hunting in the district of Brabant. His dogs, pursuing a she-bear which they had found in those regions, came with her in swift flight to Mount Castrilocus. The she-bear, swifter in flight, saw the righteous man intent upon manual labor [Col. 1341C]; trusting in his protection, she now dared to withstand the dogs and rested securely beneath his garment, which he was accustomed to hang upon a tree branch while working, as though she had found a defense.

But the dogs, immediately struck by a strange terror and driven back from their purpose as if by some opposing barrier, stood fast: their hope frustrated, their rage laid aside, made gentler, and stunned with astonishment, they awaited the hunters, whom they knew to be following close behind. When the hunters arrived, they became more savage than their dogs; and, because the good man was good, they became worse through the clouded eye of their minds. What they saw occur, they did not venerate as a miracle but cursed as though it were the sorcery of an enchanter. Showing their malice with canine teeth and charging the righteous man with a fault of which he knew nothing, they said [Col. 1341D]:

“Who are you, who have driven back the dogs of our king from their purpose by Circean spells, and changed a fierce beast into sheep-like gentleness, so that the appetite of these dogs, their scent lost, now lies numb, while the madness of that beast lurks peacefully beneath the shadow of your cloak? Who could endure with impunity that you have inflicted so great an injury upon us and shown no reverence for the royal majesty? You ought to have known that nothing displeases so great a king more than that you should not fear to prevent his dogs from succeeding in the hunt.”

With these or similar words, the king himself also followed the dogs and attendants and addressed the righteous man at first somewhat harshly: “Who are you,” he said, “or whence do you come, that you have taken here, I know not, the confidence to root me out? By what sign or spell have you deceived the dogs and the beast, so that, forgetting both custom and nature, they are near one another and yet inflict upon one another no threat or harm?” [Col. 1342A]

But he replied: “O king, I have known no maleficent arts of spells; neither as a boy nor when older did I devote myself to such folly. I am Greek by nation, a priest by rank, though humble and abject; I have been cast into these barbarian peoples as an exile. As for what you see, do not suppose that it has come about through some wicked human contrivance, but by the command and power of the heavenly Majesty. For that supreme King, the author of all creation, exercises sovereign command over every nature.”

Observing that the holy man answered wisely and humbly, and that in his simple face the modest appearance of religion shone brightly, the king calmed his spirit and rested from the anger he had displayed [Col. 1342B]. For the generous temper of kings is accustomed easily to yield. Commending himself to the man’s prayers, he called his servants back from their assault and gave both them and himself again to the pursuit of the hunt, seeking what might follow from the labor of hunting, for game caught seemed more pleasing to a royal mind than food cooked.

## CHAPTER IV

Meanwhile the confessor Gislenus persisted in the work he had undertaken, because he intended to remain longer in that place. But divine appointment ordered matters far otherwise: it reserved Mount Castrilocus for another inhabitant. By its will, that she-bear which had found the man as her defender seized in her mouth the little basket which Gislenus held dearer than all his possessions [Col. 1342C], in which he carried with him the venerable garment in which he was clothed when he celebrated the divine sacrament at the altar. The she-bear, I say, snatched up the basket and began swiftly to depart, in this matter being far more ready to obey God than the man.

Gislenus took this grievously and wondered that, in a short time, her mind had so changed that she turned away from him with robbery and injury. Hoping for nothing better, he turned to the refuge of prayer, trusting in Him who alone does not unjustly apportion evils:

“Lord God,” he said, “if I have rendered You pleasing service in this garment, do not allow it to perish or be ruined by an unworthy loss, lest in anger You charge me with having neglected and omitted Your commands. Strengthen one who is undeserving; according to Your will, preserve what I have lost” [Col. 1342D].

While he remained for a considerable time in prayer, as was his custom, and earnestly entreated God concerning the intolerable loss, the she-bear carrying off the spoil did not delay in proceeding far away, heedless, it seemed, of the defender she had left or of his distress. But when he rose from prayer and no longer saw the beast, having no certainty whatever where or by what route to pursue her, behold, an eagle came, descending from the high air, and by such signs as it could offered itself as guide of this way.

To the hesitating man it came face to face in gentle flight; then immediately, turning its head, it flew ahead at a measured pace. It spoke to him not with words but with bodily gesture, making it plainly understood that it was following the beast by the direct road. Perceiving this, he was restored to firm hope [Col. 1343A]. Leaning on his staff, he followed the guide that went before him. Farther down, finding shepherds, he most diligently asked whether such a beast had perhaps passed by in their sight.

They replied both that it had passed shortly before and, to establish their testimony, produced sure evidence of its burden. They added that close by was the place or den called Ursidongus, where the she-bear was accustomed to rear her cubs. On hearing this, he followed the eagle with greater confidence; not long afterward he reached the place whose name he had learned, and found preserved among the bear’s cubs what he had lost—torn by no damage, violated by no defilement.

At this sight he became joyful and was greatly strengthened in faith. He knew that this place had truly been prepared for him, where his foot, its dust at last wiped clean, might rest, and where, in a place of horror and vast solitude, he might remain hidden in hope and silence [Col. 1343B]. At once, therefore, he commanded the she-bear with her cubs to depart from there and, leaving the hiding-place of her young, to find another suitable place for herself; henceforth never to harm anyone in the neighborhood of this place, indeed never in any manner or at any time to return.

O new thing! A wild beast, endowed with no gift of reason, heard and obeyed the words of a sudden command, striking us human beings with a blow of shame and embarrassment, who are unwilling to obey the saving command of the Creator. It heard, I say, and in hearing yielded to the new guest. It so relinquished its long-hereditary right that from then onward it did not resume what it had once laid down, and according to the man’s word did not dare to inflict any injury upon the whole neighborhood.

[Col. 1343C] Then the holy man cleansed and cultivated with much care and labor the place, now empty of its former possessor. He leveled its until-then uncultivated and solitary natural terrors, and by skill and manual labor made it suitable. There, in honor of the apostles whom he venerated with spiritual affection, he built a cell, and ordained that it should be called “the Cell” by that special name.

In it he bound himself strictly to the monastic rule and denied himself desires and pleasures of bodily goods. He disciplined his body by fasting, vigils, cold, and nakedness; but he nourished his spirit by devoted and unceasing purity in reading, meditation, and prayer. He rejoiced in the solitude of the place and the absence of tumultuous crowds, knowing and sensing the presence with him of a multitude of ministering angels [Col. 1343D].

## CHAPTER V

Yet a jewel in dung, gold in dust, and light in an earthen vessel do not remain hidden long. When their enclosures are broken, their native brightness shines forth. Thus the humble and modest purpose which wished to be concealed was made manifest by the height of the divine counsel.

For the fame of the man and the strictness of his regular life reached the ears and knowledge of the common crowd. Very many, moved by religious desire, came to him, wishing both to be instructed by his discourse and more effectually formed by his example. He sternly rebuked those who came for their negligence in sin and taught them to live well by better promises, pouring wine and oil into the wounds of the sick, wisely discerning what was suited to the salvation of this one, of that one, and finally of very many [Col. 1344A].

His name and good fragrance did not merely fill the neighboring district, but spread with beneficial effect to those far away; nor could it escape the notice of blessed Autbert, who at that time appeared to adorn the Church of Cambrai with his episcopate. He sent a messenger and humbly invited Gislenus to come to him, that he might carefully confer with him in person and, after seeing and hearing him, might be more certainly informed who he was, whence he came, by what spirit he was guided, and what way or rule he followed.

Having received the bishop’s command, Gislenus rejoiced that so great a man had deigned to remember him and hastened with due humility to Cambrai. He lamented only that he had been found so slow and negligent that the holy bishop had anticipated him in seeking their conversation [Col. 1344B]. On his way he came to a certain village which the inhabitants call Roisin. Since weariness pressed upon him and evening was drawing on, a rustic invited him to lodging and received him with a generous hand, but cared for him with a still more generous will.

The man also asked him and strove with many entreaties to obtain that, after completing the business which he had decided to perform at Cambrai, he would, God willing, return by the same village and again turn aside to lodge with him. When morning came, the holy man continued the journey he had begun, finally presented himself to the bishop, and, being asked many questions by him, explained everything in order.

“I am,” he said, “a Greek by nation [Col. 1344C], a monk by profession, a priest by order, and a sinner in merits. In the place which the people from ancient times call Ursidongus, but which I have ordained should be called ‘the Cell’ in honor of the apostles, I have resolved to build a house of prayer, as divine revelation instructed me from afar, and as counsel known to itself led me here from foreign regions. Concerning this, holy bishop, I ought to have sought both your counsel and your favor; but I confess that through delay or negligence I have sinned not a little. Though it befitted me to forestall your majesty with worthy services, detained by a base delay, I seem to have come late.

“But perhaps He who has distinguished you with the excellence of greater dignity has also endowed you with the ampler gift of holiness; and those over whom you have deserved to preside from the episcopal seat or by rank, you have worthily surpassed by the grace both of wisdom and humility” [Col. 1344D].

The holy man’s prudent answer, holy purpose, more devout will, assumed profession, countenance, modesty, evenness of character, and worthy religious life pleased the bishop. Rejoicing in the work which he perceived had been begun by divine prompting, he sent Gislenus back to his own place, strengthened by the grace of his blessing.

## CHAPTER VI

On returning, he did not forget his devout host, from whom he had received both generous kindness and many pressing requests. Coming to Roisin, he again turned aside to him, and the host ministered to him as before with a cheerful countenance. That night it happened that, when her days were fulfilled, the hostess went into labor and, because of the difficulty of childbirth, came almost to the point of death [Col. 1345A].

When he learned this, her husband threw himself at the feet of the guest whom he had brought in, and, anxious for her, implored him with many tears. “My wife,” he said, “is tortured in childbirth, lying in the room about to give birth; in the very act of childbirth, and because of childbirth, she will, as I see it, immediately die. Come to the aid and rescue of both mother and newborn child—indeed also of their father, who will die with them and for them.”

And he, as one in whom and through whom the Spirit of God spoke, said: “Rise. Your wife, now delivered of childbirth, rejoices; the child lives and cries, not deprived of the full number of limbs; through the attendance of midwives, it is fed at the breast and wrapped in swaddling clothes.”

At these words the father, scarcely still able to restrain his weeping, ran inside and found all that had been said already fulfilled. His spirit, which had almost failed from grief, restored, he ran again to his guest and rendered thanks with honor [Col. 1345B].

“The mother,” he said, “was not, as I feared, afflicted by pain even to death; the child thrives unharmed; my spirit has come to life again. Since I have begun, I shall still speak, if only I find that your gentleness is not burdened. I desire grace to be heaped upon grace, and joy upon joy. For I ask—and would that my longing as petitioner may be fulfilled!—that the child who has been born may be born again through your ministry, and that he who is my son by the law of flesh, by mortal birth, may become your little son by a work holier than nature.”

He gladly assented to the petitioner’s prayers and desire; and when daylight came, he performed the office of baptism. Taking the little child from the sacred font, he devoutly commended him to the Lord [Col. 1345C]; and when all had been duly completed, he returned to the cell from which he had come.

Prompted both by his example and kindness, this new co-father in baptism went with him. On seeing the place suitable for religion, he was so moved by humble devotion that, like those who lived there under a strict purpose or discipline, he too resolved, with eternity in view, to set aside transient things. Therefore, inspired by the Spirit, he transferred to the brothers who would serve God there forever whatever he possessed by right at Roisin; and, lest he should seem to offer his possessions rather than himself to the Lord, he labored earnestly to become holier and more pleasing to God.

## CHAPTER VII

At that time blessed Amandus, returning from Maastricht, where he had been compelled to remain as bishop for three years [Col. 1345D], heard Gislenus and his place commended for the renown of religious life. Moved by charity, he turned aside to visit him. He was received with honor and ministered the word of life to the brothers assembled there. They were fed and refreshed by the word and spiritual consolation; yet, since they had nothing at hand with which to refresh the man with bodily food, they were greatly saddened and troubled, and allowed him to depart unfed. They accompanied him as far as the flowing river Haine.

While the holy man remained for a while on its bank and the boat in which he was to embark was being made ready at the sailors’ urging, Gislenus again began to lament—not his own poverty, which he seemed to bear with a sufficiently even mind, but the hunger of this new and great guest, which distressed him greatly. He did not dare constrain him to the straitened table of a poor man, and he had nothing with which to refresh him more fully and honorably [Col. 1346A].

And behold, the Lord heard the devout desire of the poor man: from the aforesaid river a fish called a pike suddenly leapt onto the land. Its size appeared so great in the eyes of those present that a multitude of diners could be refreshed by it. At this sight Gislenus rejoiced, both in the generous gift and in the grace of the Giver.

“Let us return home,” he said, “strengthened by the consolation of a better hope, for God does not permit our guest to leave here fasting, he whose merit has made Him willing to distinguish our table with so great a feast.”

But Amandus said: “This kindness ought not to be attributed to my merit, but to yours. God knew that you were somewhat saddened, because neither fasting nor temporary hunger troubled me, while affection and the humane duty of hospitality pressed upon you more heavily” [Col. 1346B].

Thus among holy men arose an honorable and modest dispute in words, as each worthily ascribed the merit of this gift to the other. Both, stubbornly, yielded to one another in no way, yet in their unconquered contention did not depart from mutual peace. Therefore they left the boat and returned together to the cloister. A meal was prepared and set upon the table, and they ate together. Refreshed with food and cheerful with fuller joy, they sang praises and gave thanks to the Creator.

After again exchanging the kiss, Amandus returned to the river which he had left. Blessing his hosts, he entered the boat which had been offered him, and by its conveyance was carried to his monastery at Elnone, rejoicing that, tranquility having been recovered, he had been freed from the burden of the episcopate [Col. 1346C].

Blessed Gislenus, however, persevered in his purpose: he built an oratory and manfully prepared himself and his followers for service to God. The fragrance of his name spread more and more through the whole province, and his fame, with ever more welcome influence, entered the ears of all. Moved by it, the aforesaid King Dagobert, as he passed along a road adjoining that place, encountered the holy man coming toward him with a Gospel-book, candles, and a censer. The king returned his greeting and addressed him quite humbly; he followed their mutual greeting with an offered gift.

For he did not merely commend himself to the holy man’s prayers in words, as most people do. Adding deeds to words, he adorned the place with royal generosity. He gave both Hornutum and Ursidongus [Col. 1346D], and whatever there belonged to him by right, to the man and to the brothers who would serve God there forever. This done, the king hastened to turn his feet and mind back to his own affairs. Gislenus, strengthened by the gift received, rendered worthy service to God, completed the temple he had begun through expenditures and labors, and solemnly had it consecrated by the hands of bishops when it was completed.

The aforesaid Amandus and Autbert, bishop of Cambrai, attended its consecration. They refreshed the people with the word of God and heavenly food, teaching that not so much stones as every righteous person becomes a temple of God—those who furnish others with examples of righteousness both in word and deed.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 1347A] Count Malgerus, a nobleman, did not turn his ear or mind away from their teaching. Aided by grace, he turned himself with all desire toward loving God; renouncing all that he had hitherto loved to possess in the world, he chose, as a lover of poverty, to own nothing of his own.

Accordingly, receiving the tonsure at the hands of the bishop of Cambrai, he resolved to profess himself a monk and to be restrained under a rule of stricter life in the place called Hautmont. There he gathered with himself many despisers of temporal things, lovers of the same purpose and strict order. His wife Waldetrudis did not immediately place herself under a religious profession, but remained in her own home and took care of household and family. In this she satisfied her husband: she lived in continence as though he were dead [Col. 1347B], and remained in a widow’s purpose according to Paul’s counsel.

For she was a matron noble in birth, mature in conduct, powerful in riches, richer in offspring, removing herself and her children from contact with unworthy and unlawful wickedness and advancing them toward the love of what is right and the excellence of virtue. By divine command blessed Gislenus was ordered to visit her and invite her more fully to despise temporal things, so that, as her husband had received instruction in religion through bishops, so the matron might receive through Gislenus’s teaching an increase of a better purpose.

Joyfully obeying the divine command, he hastened to approach the noble matron and preached to her the word of life with much gentleness. He taught both that it was great merit to forget earthly things for love of heavenly ones, and that it was a far greater reward to gain those same heavenly things eternally [Col. 1347C]. The matron gave open ear to his word and teaching, exchanging love of present things for desire of things to come. She was now earnestly concerned to find a solitary place suited to voluntary poverty and her purpose of holiness.

As she considered and reconsidered this, she seemed to herself to enter a small church. As she entered, Bishop Gaugericus—whom she knew to be dead—seemed to come to meet her. With generous hand and gentle face he gave the anxious matron a piece of bread and a cup of wine, encouraging her both by the gifts offered and by his speech:

“Prudent handmaid of Christ, do not abandon what you have begun; rather, do quickly what you are doing and persist. For such a work pleases me; indeed, it obtains God’s favor for itself, and a better end will follow this beginning of yours” [Col. 1347D].

The widow did not delay to recount this vision to her Gislenus, desiring to know what the most holy man might deign to answer concerning it. Nor did she doubt that whatever Gislenus might affirm and the bishop in the vision might forewarn would please in the sight of the eternal Judge. When he heard it, the holy man, worthily discerning its meaning beforehand, could not but rejoice. He understood that nothing but prosperity was signified in the vision: the hungry widow would be filled with the living bread, and her sobriety would be made drunk with the exceedingly splendid cup in which she rejoiced.

Therefore he strove to encourage her with gentle words, condemning earthly things and commending heavenly things alone to her. Thus, having placed far away whatever might smile upon her in temporal life [Col. 1348A], she might cling with an undivided affection of mind to eternal things invisible. When she heard his warnings and promised herself more willingly to obey, she still remained concerned that she did not have a suitable little place. The holy man showed her a place known to him by divine revelation, which the people had from ancient times called Mount Castrilocus.

In the Spirit he had foreseen many souls passing thence to heaven. In the course of time, divine appointment brought them together there, and Waldetrudis strove to instruct them by both word and example. God’s abundant goodness willed to bestow upon her much grace for this purpose.

## CHAPTER IX

It did not suffice the holy man that he had brought about the conversion of Waldetrudis unless she should also call her sister Aldegundis to the same end, and indeed the two daughters whom Waldetrudis herself had borne, one of whom was Maldeberte and the other called Aldetrudis [Col. 1348B]. To them he spoke concerning contempt for temporal glory, conflict, victory, and the reward of virginal continence. The widow diligently urged herself upon the virgins at opportune and inopportune times, and did not cease her persistence until she brought to effect what she desired.

Thus Gislenus, with grace accompanying him, arranged a noble four-horse team and joined the widow and virgins to the yoke of religion and continence. Though not one place or the same dwelling united them, one Spirit and the same religion bound them into a single bundle. For the virgin Aldegundis made herself a cell at Maubeuge; there, through hope of heavenly things, she put far from herself love of temporal things [Col. 1348C], and, according to Gislenus’s teaching, preserved for God not only bodily integrity but labored through fasts and prayers to cleanse her mind as a linen cloth.

But while Aldegundis at Maubeuge and Waldetrudis on Mount Castrilocus diligently served the Lord, and humbly obeyed Gislenus as daughters obey a father and disciples a teacher, it pleased the divine counsel at last to end his strenuous struggle and carry him, now a veteran, to the eternal glory of the palm. When, by revelation of the Holy Spirit, he foresaw this and willingly assented in spirit to the Lord’s call, he summoned the holy monks who were with him in devout humility and revealed with great joy that he would soon depart from here.

They could not bear the words they had heard with equal patience, but showed the inward grief of their hearts by lamentation and tears. “Lord God,” they said, “who will defend us from the assaults of the wicked? Who will show the narrow path of religion to those darkened by ignorance, if You command the man who has hitherto cared for his own with such great concern to be carried away by untimely death, as though You had forgotten us?” [Col. 1348D]

He strove to comfort them with gentle discourse and carefully admonish them to trust with firm faith in the Lord, declaring that hope is not to be placed in man but in Him from whom salvation comes and in whom alone eternal rest is to be had. When he had instructed the brothers as was fitting, he requested the saving viaticum. Fortified by it, he expired amid the hands of those standing by, as the distress of fever pressed upon him. By his death he made the minds of those left behind inconsolable in sorrow, but he no less gladdened [Col. 1349A] the attending choirs and multitude of angels, who bore his holy soul with great rejoicing and offered it before the divine presence, cleansed of vices and endowed with virtues. It was placed in Abraham’s bosom, in the land of the living, where, knowing nothing of evils, it happily enjoys the vision of the present God.

The holy monks who remained took care to bury his body and to pay it the diligence worthy of his funeral rites. They laid him in the church of the apostles Peter and Paul which he had built, and venerated his tomb with the fitting devotion of the faithful. There, from that time onward, God’s great favor toward him has been displayed, attesting that he lives rather than dies, both through virtues and miracles [Col. 1350A]. Those who pray to God and implore the aid of His devotee rejoice when, freed from afflictions, they obtain the benefit they sought.

For many sick persons recover bodily health; many who are wearied by vices are healed in their will—a healing far greater still. They find Gislenus favorable and helpful to them, present to their prayers, and most gracious to devout minds. Therefore we also, holy brethren and monks, ask so great a man together with you, that we may likewise experience the benefit of him whom you diligently serve, and that through his intervention we may deserve to become companions of the angels, among whom he lives now and forever, unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1349]

# LIFE OF BLESSED LANDELINUS, CONFESSOR

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1349B] Just as one who beholds men of good conduct in person is often moved with compunction of heart to live rightly, so, when their past conduct is recounted in a truthful account, the devout hearer is soothed as though by sweet music.

Therefore a custom, by no means unprofitable, has long prevailed in the Church, and posterity, extending even to our own time, has not yet abolished it: namely, that the character and deeds of the saints should be committed to lasting writing, so that they may be recited in the ears of the devout as examples. Accordingly, pressed by your prayers, which I do not dare sufficiently to resist, since I have resolved to serve the righteous wills of God and of those who belong to God, I undertake, however inadequately, to set down the life of this confessor and recount his virtues to the praise and glory of the Creator [Col. 1349C], so that a devout reader or hearer may love to venerate so great a man and strive to imitate him, worthy of veneration, through worthy deeds.

In this I judge that some profit is not lacking even for me: as you see, though unequal to the task, I nevertheless stand ready for your requests. Sincere charity will excuse my presumptuous boldness, and your devout prayer—indeed, the prayer of your confessor—will reward the labor I have undertaken.

**774 CHAPTER ONE.**
When the breadth of the sky is no longer brightened by the setting sun, but, with night already present, the whole face of things grows dark, the evening rising of Hesperus has no small charm; Saturn lies hidden in the middle of the night, and Lucifer rises in the morning. Thus divine providence [Col. 1349D] willed to order things, thus to supply many and varied lights of the stars at the different hours of night, so that, since nocturnal birds are given no opportunity to gaze upon the visible sun, their infirmity might be more greatly comforted by the faint shining of the stars.

Accordingly, at the time when the northern region was governed under the power of King Dagobert, and the flourishing Church of Cambrai rejoiced under Bishop Autbert, God willed that, in the province of that same Cambrai, a new star should appear, as it were—a star which deserved to occupy no insignificant place [Col. 1350B] in the night of this life. For the village called Vallis, which seemed to possess neither name nor merit, brought forth a morning star under a most favorable rising, when, through the regard of heavenly grace, it gave birth to Landelinus. Since the brilliance of noble birth adorned his parents and the eminence of secular power distinguished them, they wished that Bishop Autbert, receiving the child from the sacred font, should grant him the first fruits of blessing, so that the distinction of his rebirth might correspond to that of his birth.

When the boy had grown older, they sent him back to the same bishop and entrusted their welcome offspring to his holiness, that the holy bishop might instruct the child, still small in age, in letters and, with diligent care, distinguish him by good morals. Receiving him with paternal affection, the bishop raised him as a son, taught him letters, and formed him in morals [Col. 1350C], rejoicing exceedingly because in him shone a specimen of no small integrity: he showed himself teachable to his masters and lovable to all.

For the boy inclined a ready ear to the counsels of his elders; as he grew and became an adolescent, he did not yet depart from the path pointed out to him. Rather, in a measure—indeed beyond the measure—of his age, possessing a quick understanding, he hastened by labor and diligent study more fully toward perfection. When the bishop more joyfully observed that he had made honorable progress and had surpassed the years of puberty in morals and learning, he entertained no slight hope for the salvation of one whom he had now brought to the threshold of youth. He wished to distinguish this recruit of good disposition with the grace of a higher rank, judging that a stricter commitment was suited to his age and progress.

He therefore decreed [Col. 1350D] that Landelinus should be removed from the lay rank and order and be adorned with tonsure and clerical dress, so that, having professed himself a cleric, he might live in a monastery; renouncing secular affairs, he might be devoted to psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. For it seemed to the holy bishop that if Landelinus remained in what he had begun, if, continuing in the monastery, he applied unbending diligence to the cultivation of his morals, he would be fruitful for himself, pleasing to God, necessary to the Church; and from him and through him much benefit would be conferred upon many [Col. 1351A].

But that ancient enemy, who does not know how to rejoice in the progress of the good, seeing and envying this, could not but grieve. The crafty artificer did not thunder terrors or threats against the spirited recruit, but with cunning malice spewed forth upon him the poison of deadly persuasion. He found certain relatives and kinsmen of Landelinus especially suited to this purpose. Through them he ensnared his tender age; having deceived and gathered them, he sent them to him under the appearance of giving counsel, though the whole intention alike of sender and sent was to seduce him.

“Brother,” they said, “we too wish to provide for you, and you ought to lend your ear to our counsels. The greatest concern for you rests upon us; your advantage as well as your loss is counted as our own. See therefore, beloved, that no one deceives you, lest, deceived, you perhaps be led into such madness that you should wish to remain longer [Col. 1351B] in a monastery, to waste away in idleness, loitering with muttering clerics.

“These men undertake nothing vigorous, nothing hard. Given over to sleep and feasting, they prattle false or useless things; they keep their hands folded and do not exercise them in any strong work. They are comparable to brute animals, passing their lives in silence. But you possess the blooming beauty of youth, a manly spirit, and strength suited to the time; you can be pleasing and most useful to your parents, foremost in supporting their plans and taking part in their affairs. Your nobility calls for courage and military vigor, not clerical leisure and sloth. Let shield, lance, sword, and weapons of war occupy your hands, not tablets, stylus, or little books. Your worthy [Col. 1351C] youth, devoted to more vigorous exertion, will surely be glory and honor to us all. You will be your parents’ glory and the ornament of your whole family; you will leave to posterity a worthy monument of your inborn excellence.”

With these or similar words they shook the untutored mind of Landelinus and, by deceitful flattery, struck him a heavy blow. They prevailed upon him to withdraw from the monastery and the fellowship of the clerics and to expose himself wholly to the life and habits of the depraved. God yielded to their wishes for a reason known to himself; yet his care did not entirely withdraw from his chosen one. Rather, for a time he kept silence and, as it were, patiently endured whatever they chose to advise and he chose to do negligently.

Perhaps divine grace withdrew itself for some time and did not at once draw him back from his deviation at the beginning [Col. 1351D], so that after grave sins he might repent more devoutly and humbly, and, having experienced [775] the contagion of evil, might abhor it more cautiously and perfectly. Thus David, after the sin concerning Uriah, asks to be washed with a fuller cleansing; and Peter, after the threefold denial, is read to have wept more bitterly. Each, after his fall, is restored more devout and stronger: execrating the evil he has experienced, he holds discipline more eagerly and much more firmly.

So too our athlete, abandoned for a little while by grace, now sins, now his heart is led astray, now his former strength leaves him. Having forsaken the bishop, he listens to and follows the members of his household and family as friends, not yet sufficiently understanding that they are truly enemies. Seeing this, the holy bishop is inconsolably saddened; oppressed with heavy grief [Col. 1352A], he laments over the lost youth. He offers no other relief, nor asserts that any ought to be offered, for his sorrow than unwearied prayers, tears, and sacrifices to the Creator on his behalf. Since this bishop does not despair of God’s goodness, he prays, mourns, and perseveres without failing, determining and resolving not to cease from such a purpose until divine goodness restores his foster-son to him.

## Chapter II

Meanwhile his seducers drove Landelinus headlong through the byways of vice and urgently solicited him to sin both by words and examples. Him whom, according to their promise, they ought to have distinguished with riches and honors, they hastened to entangle with themselves in plunder and robbery. They rejoiced that they had found so vigorous and eminent [Col. 1352B] a companion: although they had preceded him in this militia by time, they nevertheless hoped that he would not prove inferior to his predecessors, but would surpass the rest in wicked agility and advancement.

To confirm their hope, he wished his name to be changed; Landelinus being put to sleep, he determined to call himself Maurosus, so that, as a new robber, he might be known by a new name, and no one might know whence he had come or who he had formerly been. Thus he might devote himself more freely to new deeds, since the recollection of his old name would not recall him. Headlong Maurosus therefore freely employed his hands in every crime, and in carrying them out considered neither measure nor danger. He no longer followed his companions as a novice, but was regarded as their teacher, leader, and standard-bearer, as though they were his disciples.

Once, when by night [Col. 1352C] he planned to break into the house of a rich man and violently seize his abundant wealth, divine dispensation recalled him from this design; leaving the rich man what belonged to him, it changed the wicked robber’s plan. For that very night one of his companions, overtaken by swift death and released from the body, was entangled in the nets of his sins. The malignant spirits whom he had hitherto served received him bound, with rejoicing; rendering to him what he deserved, they cast him into the depths of hell.

When Maurosus learned of his death, he wasted away in grief, groaned, and wailed. So greatly did sudden sorrow weigh upon him that, since neither forgetfulness nor consolation could soften it, he was compelled, his eyes heavy with sadness, to fall asleep. As he slept, a man seemed to stand beside him, bearing a gracious countenance, venerable [Col. 1352D] hair, and splendid clothing. He opened the inner eyes of his mind and showed him what place received his companion and what fruit there was for wickedness.

“See,” he said, “to what place this companion of yours has come; what torturers, what place, what reward he has now found; and because, while it was permitted for a little while, he carried out your wickedness, into what misery he has been cast for eternity. Know without doubt that you too will come to this place and receive a like punishment for a like life, unless you quickly leave the life and fellowship of the wicked and return to the holy order of clerics.

“There Bishop Autbert, not content with concern only for his own salvation or merit, mourns your peril and is held in inconsolable anxiety. While drowsy [Col. 1353A] death holds you, he weeps; he labors for you in vigils, prayers, and sighs. You must therefore return to him as soon as possible; leaving the works of darkness, obey his saving admonitions. If you do this, you will not be drawn into the abyss of your companion, but in heaven you will enjoy the fellowship of us angels.”

Having said this, the monitor fell silent, as though his task were completed. Maurosus awoke greatly terrified and judged that this was neither an empty nor deceptive dream, but revered it as a divine oracle inspired by God’s grace.

At once, therefore, laying aside his love of sin and the fury of his mind, he did not delay to renounce his wicked purpose. Abandoning the companions through whom he had been drawn toward the perils of death, he presented himself to the bishop, that henceforth he might obey him. He cried out [Col. 1353B], wept, and lamented miserably, praying that pardon might be granted to one unworthy of it, if this could be done. By words and tears he displayed the ruin of his soul so that he moved even his hearers to lamentation.

Observing with how much feeling the young man wept, the bishop too was moved to tears and rejoiced. With great joy he stretched forth kindly hands to the returning man, recalled him to hope, and promised forgiveness to the penitent. For some time he made him remain in the monastery in lay dress, devote himself to prayers, and persevere in devotion and fasting, until the file and washing of saving penitence had washed away whatever he had contracted through the allurement of secular life.

When the bishop saw him cleansed by fitting satisfaction and now ready to receive gifts of greater grace [Col. 1353C], he dedicated him to a new order after he had renounced his former state. Distinguished by crown and habit [776], he made him a cleric with the appropriate blessing.

Having become a cleric and obtained the grace of so great a dignity, Landelinus considered worthily the burden of the matter. He burned with a greater desire for holiness and, so that he might deserve to attain the highest glory of clerics, resolved to go to Rome for the sake of pilgrimage. There, as he had heard, rest the holy apostles, known to all the faithful through their blessed martyrdom; as leaders and princes of clerics they do not cease to be present to their representatives who humbly sit or stand before them in devotion.

Having received permission from the blessed bishop, he went to Rome. Worn out by much labor, he entered the churches of the apostles, counting as nothing whatever hardship [Col. 1353D] he seemed to have endured on the road, since he had at last been granted to reach that which he desired. In devotion he prostrated himself upon the pavement with lamentation and tears, and petitioned the blessed apostles more by vows than by words: that they might protect their cleric from demonic assault and grant the humble representative the benefit of their intercession. What he did not hope to accomplish by his own strength, he believed could be granted in every detail through their prayers—in whom the dignity of the clerical order shines solemnly and its spiritual holiness flourishes more perfectly.

When he had completed his prayer and the service of due devotion, in which he had venerated the relics of the saints with sufficient humility, and had accomplished everything his fervent desire required, he bade the apostles farewell and returned whence he had come. On returning [Col. 1354A], he devoted himself to the instruction of the blessed bishop. At the bishop’s word he forbade himself the delights of this life, desiring nothing more eagerly or insatiably than labors, persistence in prayer, fasts, vigils, and cold. Seeing him make worthy progress in holiness so that he might serve God more intimately and devoutly, the holy bishop ordained him deacon, so that rank and office might correspond to his devotion.

## Chapter III

Having become a deacon, he resolved to set out for Rome, that he might more perfectly merit the apostles’ favor, and that, while he exercised the diaconate in preaching the word of the Gospel, he might be aided by their protection to accomplish what he had begun. Having seen Rome a second time, he returned, as before, to Cambrai and presented his lowliness [Col. 1354B] to the holy bishop with due humility. Rejoicing in him, the bishop after some days invited him to a higher dignity and, anointing him with sacred liquid, ordained him priest.

When he exercised the priesthood in so lofty a station, lest he be regarded as overconfident and ungrateful for so great a benefit, he again resolved to visit the holy apostles at Rome and, by a third visit, obtain their intercessions more perfectly. For the faith and learning of clerics proclaim God as Trinity, and God delights in an odd number, according to the saying of the pagans. Though pagans and Catholics differ and contend with one another in many matters, they nevertheless agree in this: that they especially exalt and commend the number three.

Therefore, going to Rome for the third time [Col. 1354C], he commended himself to the apostles’ protection. This done, he hastened back again to Bishop Autbert. The greater the distinction of his dignity beyond what was customary, the more fervent did he become in the love and desire of holiness. Therefore, mindful of the past, anxiously striving toward what lay ahead, and reckoning present suffering of no account in view of future things, it seemed to him that the cloistered life, although rightly judged by very many to be perfect, was not sufficiently adequate for one who had sinned more grievously.

For as a moderate sinner can be content with a lighter washing, so one more heavily burdened needs a greater purification. Thus he who remembered having committed so many and such unforgivable acts sought harsher things, inaccessible to those whose penitence was merely moderate. Accordingly, after consulting the bishop [Col. 1354D]—who kindly rejoiced in his desire and truly declared that his disciple’s progress was his own—he left the city and bade farewell to the multitude, taking with him two companions, Andelinus and Domitianus, whom he did not reject because they desired the same things.

Divine providence willed that he should come into the district of Hainaut, beside the River Sambre, where a stream called Laubicus enters that same river. Receiving this place, Landelinus prepared monastic cells for himself there, and called both the cells and the place Laubias after the aforesaid stream.

## Chapter IV

There, bringing with him Adelino and Domitianus, he subjected himself to stricter discipline, making his body a servant and wearing it down with fasting and abstinence. At last, in accordance with the threats of the prophets, he offered scant bread [Col. 1355A] and little water to the one who asked; he did not satisfy the murmurer with wine or delicacies.

Although he perhaps wished to remain hidden, he could not do so long, and a bushel could not conceal the access of such great light. Once it was removed, the burning star cast its flashing rays far and wide, and his good reputation spread throughout the whole neighborhood. When it had spread, very many gathered there, rejoicing that they had found an incomparable treasure in one who was humble. Many placed themselves under the same superior; others offered temporal possessions with a generous hand.

Thus within a short time that place prospered both spiritually and materially. Religion grew; sustenance did not fail the religious. Many came together and brought many gifts, which by law were to remain as possessions for the use of those dwelling there. But Landelinus [Col. 1355B], seeing that the place had prospered beyond his expectation, that many from different regions had come together to live more religiously, and that others had bestowed lands, villages, households, and other such things, blessed the brothers gathered in that monastery and crossed the River Sambre out of love and desire for poverty.

Coming to a place called Alna, he prepared a dwelling for himself there too, rejoicing that in solitude, with a few companions, he served God with sufficiently devout devotion. Though now worn in body, he did not relax the rigor of his way of life, but day by day laid heavier burdens upon burdens. Some also contributed many things to that place, and, while he presided, built a monastery there, lest the man’s labor seem vain and useless—if, that is, it proved fruitful only for himself and not also for others.

When by labor and diligence he had completed [Col. 1355C] the monastery of Alna and enlarged it with households and possessions, he departed and similarly began another in the district of Templurum. The undertaking thus begun he enlarged in no short time through the generosity of the faithful. Since he had visited blessed Peter at Rome three times and had commended himself to him as the first and chief of clerics and a poor representative, he wished to dedicate these three monasteries to him and assign his threefold labor both of pilgrimage and of building to the apostles.

Nevertheless, the priest of Christ was not to rest in any of these places or receive there the desired end of this life. Divine dispensation designated for him another place [Col. 1355D], to which it directed him after he had completed the things mentioned above.

## Chapter V

Taking the aforementioned companions Adelino and Domitianus, he came above the River Hon and wished to settle where the forest called Ambligis appears adjacent to that river. The place was commendable to him not because of the fertile levelness of its fields or the blooming beauty of vineyards, but because of the deep shade of its woods and its solitude given over to terror.

Seeing that the whole surrounding area was occupied by the vast forest and that little or no open ground remained where they could set up their new huts, they together took up tools to level the place and, in order to work more freely, laid aside their clothing. While they labored, the master of the household [Col. 1356A] happened to arrive and harshly confronted them as invaders, because they had presumed, without consulting him, to clear a forest which he was accustomed to claim by hereditary right.

Lest he seem to endure without compensation the damage to his own inheritance, he seized their clothing in vengeance for the act, so that shaken by this loss they might repent of the past and not dare to proceed further in such an undertaking. As he departed with the clothes, divine punishment pursued him and addressed him more harshly by a blow than by a word. It inflicted on him such bodily injury that, suddenly lying stunned upon the ground, he believed that only the suffering of death remained.

Pressed by so great an affliction, he understood that he had been struck by God. Thus admonished, he no longer despised the holy man, but humbly began to beseech him as best he could that he might deign to entreat God for these offenses. If the holy man, pitying one unworthy, obtained forgiveness for them, then through his hands this man would surrender to God the middle [Col. 1356B] part of the forest; henceforth the holy man might do there as he pleased and, with no one opposing, serve God in due peace.

Seeing him almost dead and bereft of strength, the kindly priest, desiring not so much the offered gift as the man’s salvation, devoutly poured forth prayers for him to heavenly mercy. By the prayer he had poured out, he restored the sick man to his former health. Strengthened by the welcome comfort of divine mercy and made strong in spirit to bear the labor he had begun, he prepared there a small oratory in honor of blessed Martin. With the aforementioned disciples, he there offered humble sacrifices of penitence to God.

## Chapter VI

[Col. 1356C]

Although he rejoiced that water from the river was not lacking for the brothers’ use, he nevertheless knew and regretted that no living spring was present in that place. He knew that, even though river-water is not denied as a provision for necessity, waters are more pleasing when drunk from the spring itself, as the pagans proclaim.

Running therefore to his customary aid of prayer and fortified by humble trust, perceiving that his more devout desire had been heard by God, he broke the surface of the earth with a single stroke of his staff. By a miracle worthy of the event, a living spring at once burst forth. The holy man observed its clear waters bubbling up more abundantly from the depths, the rippling surface gushing in trembling waves, and the very course of the little stream [Col. 1356D] murmuring with a pleasing whisper, inviting anyone to remain there by such grace of its own. Delighted by the appearance that he noticed to be crisp and trembling, he immediately named the place in which he had settled Crispinum.

After he experienced this and perhaps many other proofs of God’s favor toward him, and the place to which he had come was distinguished by the grace of a new name, the ointment of good reputation having been poured out, its fragrance—or report—was carried far and wide. The remedy being made known, healing was not delayed for those who came together. Indeed, though the desire to remain hidden burned within him, its effect was wholly annulled: whether he wished it or not, his light was raised above a mountain or a lampstand. Many ran and sought the living and clear spring of truth, that they might be healed by drinking or washing in the irrigation of such purity—not so much seeking for dying bodies the remedy of passing [Col. 1357A] health as for souls that would live the enduring grace of holiness.

The man, fervent in spirit, did not reject them from his company or drive them far from the bright spring of goodness by a harsh rebuff.
