Rather, gathering them together, he undertook to teach them a rule of life, presenting himself by stricter living as a model to his hearers. But seeing them now properly restrained under the prescribed rule and ready and agile to advance from good to better, he wished for a little while to withdraw from their companionship, so that, being free for God alone, he might practice his resolve more freely.

There also, in honor of the Apostle Peter, he had a small oratory built for himself. He chose to live there in solitude, so that he might not spend what remained of his time amid somewhat turbulent cares, but, once the affairs of the brothers had been rightly arranged, might freely stretch himself toward things more inward and serene. And lest he seem to be providing only for himself and begrudging the same progress to Adelino and Domitianus, his first companions, he caused them also to be separated from the community and from one another, and each to remain in a separate dwelling [Col. 1357B]. Those whom mutual communal life had advanced as examples to one another were thus brought to completion by solitude, perpetual silence, and spiritual contemplation.

He so devoted himself by study within his own dwelling, setting aside outward matters and occupying himself only with interior things, that, forgetful of the body, he took part for the sake of contemplation in the choirs of angels and stood ready with suspended desire for the divine countenance. This continual trial so burned him in the furnace, and so shook away whatever chaff seemed to be in him, that, purified to the utmost, he became more precious than refined gold, and, as a purified offering [Col. 1357C], was judged more worthy of heaven than of earth.

## Chapter VII

[Col. 1357C]

At length heavenly grace, wishing to bring to its close his old age, worn down severely in rendering devoted and long service, weighed down his frail body with the heat of fever. Its coming announced to him, who desired it greatly, that death was near. Feeling himself burdened by the onset of fever and hoping soon to be freed from the prison of this flesh, he summoned his brothers before him and joyfully announced his death to those who mourned.

On hearing this, they came together, spoke to him while he assented, and bitterly lamented his future absence. They had rejoiced in his life beyond what could be expressed; once he was dead, they said, they no longer wished to survive.

“Why, Father, good Father, best teacher [Col. 1357D], do you leave us? Though you may provide for yourself, why do you abandon us miserable people? Why do you presume to depart while we remain here? Or at least, why, in departing, do you not take us also with you? Do you not know that death breaks into a sheepfold deserted by its shepherd, that the rushing wolf scatters the gathered multitude of the weak, that when unity is weakened order perishes, religion is scattered, the defeated side groans, and the triumphant adversary rejoices? Why did you wish to gather us from different regions [Col. 1358A], only to decide to leave us at so untimely a time, when we are still uncertain of salvation and reward and are about to lose your presence and protection?”

But he said: “Dearest ones, your brotherhood does not lose me, but sends me ahead; and my devotion, such as it is, commends you to him toward whom I am tending, that he may preserve you and advance you [Col. 1358B] while you still struggle for some time, until, when it seems good to him, you follow to that place to which you send me before you. Therefore let not my absence disturb or grieve you, for heavenly grace will not cease to be present with you and to preside over you. I wish and ask that you commend me by your prayers, and by supplicating vows amend that in which I am deficient.”

After they had addressed one another with these and other similar words and had pursued in reciprocal speech what seemed fitting, the holy man’s soul was released from the bonds of the body among the hands of those standing by. Carried by angels, it was admitted into the joy of its Lord, where, with those same angels, it joyfully enjoys God with unveiled face, receiving the first robe and doubting nothing concerning the second.

His devoted disciples embraced his body, left in ashes and sackcloth, and rendered him the fitting service customary among the faithful. In his monastery, where to the end [Col. 1358C] he had endeavored to serve God, they honorably undertook to bury him with mourning and tears, psalms and prayers. Thereafter and henceforth, he does not withhold his protection from those who stand by him and serve him, but presents himself to their vows and merits with abundant favor. Standing so before the divine countenance upon which he desires to gaze, he nevertheless does not cease to be present to the devout petitions of his own people.

May this follower of God come graciously to my aid also and lend a kindly ear to my petition. To please him, I have labored as best I could in writing this present little work, and have offered him, according to my ability, the labor and service of my devotion. Nor do I doubt that, although he now possesses what he sought more fully, he is nevertheless present to his Philip, who commends himself to his patronage [Col. 1358D]; and he himself commends the one entrusted to him to him before whom he stands—the King of kings and Lord of lords, to whom belong power, honor, and glory through endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1359]

# Life of the Blessed Virgin Oda

## Prologue

[Col. 1359A] [779] If the blind error of the pagans has diligently commended with great praises poets who contrive foolish old wives’ tales—poets who, covering truth with a cloud of falsehood, have resolved to cultivate vice as virtue and to enlarge their names with more splendid titles—then much more ought our philosophers, defenders of truth and lovers of justice and virtue, to be extolled with exceptional praises. For whatever anywhere shone forth as praiseworthy in the sayings of teachers or illustrious in the deeds of famous men, they have more diligently recorded in the bond of writing and handed down to the knowledge of posterity, to be read and not neglected, through enduring remembrance.

The prudent purpose of these men, carried down to us through the succession of passing ages, was that a worthy catalogue of remembrance should be woven not only for men but also for women who shone wondrously in virtue beyond their sex [Col. 1359B], so that anyone touched by the wholesome breeze of such great renown might be stirred by zeal to live likewise. If in the night of this world, amid its declining times, a lamp of this kind should shine anywhere, it must not be hidden under a bushel, but raised upon a lampstand to give light to all who are in the house of God.

Just as one incurs no small mark of blame who, whether puffed up by knowledge or corrupted by envy or weighed down by sloth, chooses to know alone what he has learned rather than extend it to the ears [Col. 1360A] of many, so too one makes himself praiseworthy and adds grace to his own head who exalts worthy men in the churches and proclaims them at the head of every crossroads. The first of the apostles took care to do this when the scribes and Pharisees forbade him to speak in the name of Jesus, and he aptly answered them: “We cannot but speak of what we have heard and seen” (Acts 4).

For, as someone has said, “In a certain manner, he seeks a share in praise who is the first to proclaim another’s words or deeds, well spoken or well done.” No possession of any good is pleasant without a companion. Therefore, although the file of literary learning has insufficiently polished the roughness of my talent; although I have by no means attained the sophistical conclusion of Socrates, the enthymeme of Demosthenes, or the richness of Ciceronian eloquence; nevertheless, trusting in devotion [Col. 1360B] more than learning, I shall undertake, however haltingly, to recount in plain speech the life of a certain virgin who in our days and before our eyes shone conspicuous in virtue. I commend myself to her merits, that she may deign to open my mouth in her praise, so that a better fortune may follow my weak beginning. Nor shall I fear the venom of a jealous reader or dread a babbling judge, while secure beneath the covering of her prayers I hide myself from such storm and rain.

## The Life Begins

[Col. 1359]

[Col. 1359C] Just as, in the middle of the night, the sky is beautifully painted with grateful variety by the stars shining through, and the dreadful fleece of shadows is gradually wiped from the world by the benefit of light, so, in the profound blindness of this pilgrimage, the assembly of saints is wondrously clothed in the diverse brilliance of merits. While it casts forth through the world manifold rays of virtues, it is found brighter than all the beauty of the stars.

The variety of this diversity delights the eye that beholds it, because it knows nothing confused and admits nothing discordant into itself, but always returns to unity. So it is in that dwelling of the heavenly city, “whose participation is in unity”: there are many mansions, distinct orders, and diverse brightnesses; yet the one God is all things to all—light that cannot be extinguished, life that does not die [Col. 1359D], peace that does not fail, beauty that does not wither.

In this order of eternal seats, some surpass the rest by more illustrious titles, endowed with a higher gift of blessedness: namely, those who in the pressure of this world’s winepress [Col. 1360C] have worn down their bodies for God’s covenant, or who, denying themselves, have ground flesh and spirit in the frying-pan of temptations, laboring through many fasts, vigils, and works. Above all these, virginal chastity rightly holds precedence by a higher rank and a certain prerogative of dignity: the more like the King of glory, the spotless Lamb, it is, the more closely it follows him.

The venerable virgin Oda desired to undertake this height of life. The author and consecrator of that same virginity, favoring her vows, kept her undefiled until the glorious end of her life.

[780] At the time when Pope Innocent guided the chariot [Col. 1360D] of the universal Church, Lothair administered the Roman Empire in the western regions, Louis, son of Philip, held royal authority among the Franks, the venerable Remald governed the metropolitan see of Rheims, Liethard the diocese of Cambrai, and Baldwin of Hainaut held the principality of Hainaut, this virgin was born of illustrious parentage in the aforementioned district, in a village popularly called Allodium [Col. 1361A]. Her father was Wibert and her mother Thescelina; both shone by their sincere piety in divine worship as well as by nobility.

Thus the wise virgin, deriving noble descent in the flesh from both parents, did not wish to obscure the splendor of her birth by a degenerate life. Instead, cutting off at its very germ the lust of the flesh, which powerfully weakens feminine softness, she wholly banished from herself the deceptive blandishments of the world and unlawful desires. Giving herself altogether to the school of virtue, she fittingly adorned her earliest age with the flower of chastity and the title of modesty.

For she felt, according to a certain pagan, that one relies on the titles of one’s parents in vain unless aided by one’s own merits. Hence Boethius says [Col. 1361B]: “If you have no splendor of your own, another’s brilliance does not make you splendid.” She therefore resolved in her heart and vowed, while still a young girl, to dedicate the privilege of her virginity to that heavenly Bridegroom. Daily, like a dove, she pondered how, abandoning the marshy places of earthly pleasure, she might more suitably and freely swim up to the mountain of holier life and place her little nest in the hollow of the humble rock.

Already all her desires aspired toward that saying of the Song of Songs: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hills of Lebanon” (Song 4). For she saw many upon the plain of secular life, through harmful liberty, running unbridled down the slopes of conduct into licentiousness. Knowing that what is crooked is not corrected except according to a rule, she desired to be raised [Col. 1361C] to the mountain of myrrh—that is, to the steep discipline of the monastic rule. And because the lily of chastity is often compelled to be swallowed up among the thorns of passing vanity and by the muddy flood of the valley, she wished to be transferred to the hills of Lebanon—that is, to gatherings of religious women, which blossomed anew with the most pleasing radiance of every holiness.

Indeed, after making her vow, she remained hidden under her parents’ guardianship until the years of puberty; and, with her mind withdrawn from worldly concerns—which is the first sign of a well-ordered mind—she trained herself to withdraw into herself and dwell with herself. And lest envy in any way cast a stepmotherly shadow over the reputation of her innocence, she avoided as vipers the gatherings and conversations of girls whose hearts were set on luxury and idleness; admitting to herself only Sabine women [*sabinas*], [Col. 1361D] whose conversation concerned honor and friendship, and whose private conduct did not belie their public testimony. Although the natural bloom of her complexion wonderfully adorned her outward face, and with virginal restraint she shared the honeyed cups of her speech with those who spoke with her, all her beauty and glory were nevertheless within; for her Beloved dwelt delightfully between her two breasts, and with him she spoke continually in the secret chamber of her conscience, as in a bridal chamber.

Accordingly, she shrank from—or rather despised—the wanton addresses and looks of young men, whose eye announces indecency and whose mouth speaks vanity; who walk with breasts thrown back, exalting themselves vainly above themselves and rushing headlong into every pleasure of lust. Therefore, while nothing earthly had settled in her mind, while she resolved daily to fulfill her vows, while she burned irresistibly, though happily, with the love she had conceived, she summoned a kinsman who was more intimate with her than the rest. Although fearful, she unfolded to him fully her holy ardors, begging and adjuring him with many tears that the secret she had entrusted to him should be concealed from her parents with the greatest care, and that through his assistance she might be worthy to attain her desired end. But because, to a mind that longs, nothing comes quickly enough, she repeated her entreaties: let her present vow not be delayed until tomorrow, but be carried as swiftly as possible to Lord Odo, then abbot of Bonne-Espérance, so that from him and under him she might without delay receive the habit of holy religion.

But since faith is safe nowhere, and a friend cannot easily be guarded against if he wishes to betray, while [Col. 1362B] the virgin, in dove-like simplicity, believed her vow was being managed in deepest secrecy, he turned back. Not fearing to wound the heart of a friend, he went on to her father and mother and disclosed the secret; and, reversing and perverting the proper order, he strove to obstruct the course which he ought to have prepared. When her parents heard this matter concerning their daughter, they were troubled and greatly distressed by the news; and, after taking counsel with their household, they resolved to weaken her purpose of chastity by the fetter of marriage.

A bridegroom was therefore sought for the virgin: one found suitable for her marriage in family, character, wealth, and rank. A multitude of friends and relatives having been summoned from every side, they deliberated concerning the union in marriage of the children. The young man, named Simon, received with eager approval and with the unanimous assent of his people the bride offered by her father and parents; and he almost gloried, though in good hope, that he would be made happy by so great a marriage. He urged that the promises be fulfilled as swiftly as possible, and this was confirmed without delay by an oath. A pledge having therefore been given by both sides, a day was finally fixed for the celebration of this union.

Meanwhile, while the consecrated virgin wavered, suspended between hope and fear, and diverse and doubtful thoughts possessed her mind, she was terrified by the sad and unexpected portent of this report: namely, that the secret which she had deposited in the ear of one person to be kept concealed, she heard being publicly bandied about by everyone; and she who had resolved not to know the marriage-bed of a man in sin learned that [Col. 1362D] her own wedding must shortly be celebrated. She who had already prepared to leave her father’s house and, with her way made clear, to go to the place of the holiness she had purposed, was impeded by a grave obstacle and shaken by a new fear: that she might lose the seal of virginal chastity.

But who knows what he has not experienced? Moreover, that is not virtue—or does not seem to be virtue—which a diligent athlete is not compelled to sweat over through frequent exercise in the gymnasium of temptations; which no headstrong south wind presses with all its strength, nor the Thracian north wind repeatedly drives with its free blast; which, weighed down by harmful torpor, does not vigorously repel the poisoned arrows of enemies. For virtue is so called because, relying on its own strength, it is not overcome by adversities. Virtue, however, which has nothing contrary within itself does not become conspicuous, nor does it become splendid without testing. What has not been tried and examined is not virtue; nor can one bring great courage to contest who has never been bruised.

Therefore the Lord of hosts, who permits his champions to be tempted in such a way that the temptation can nevertheless be endured with a favorable outcome, wished his handmaid—whom he intended to engage in a triumphal contest with the enemy—to be more diligently trained in this wrestling-ground, so that she might gain practice in fighting. For practice makes the endurance of hardships easier. He permitted, I say, and willed her to be tempted, not so that, failing under the burden through womanly weakness, she might be driven about by the enemy, but so that a spectacle wonderful to all might be displayed: an unarmed and humble girl sent into single combat against that armored and lofty Goliath [Col. 1363B], and, bravely defeating the enemy in a manly encounter, might deservedly obtain the palm of victory according to her merit.

Thus the virgin, perceiving the various storms of temptations stirred up against her and the enemy preparing war against her with all his powers, returned into herself and awakened her Beloved, delightfully resting in the humble lodging of her heart. She laid before him her plaintive words and announced that the enemy lay in ambush at the gates. She asked that aid be sent her from the sanctuary and that her loins be girded with strength, knowing that strength is needed against one who fights fiercely. She also more earnestly commended to Christ the privilege of her chastity, which she had entrusted to him while still of tender age; and she prayed that the bonds which Satan had prepared for her ruin and stumbling might be broken, so that she might run the way of truth which she had chosen with uninjured foot and unstained path.

While she thus persisted at the door of her friend with welcome importunity, repeating her prayers, he awoke and inclined the ear of mercy to the voice of his bride, opened to her, and graciously comforted the tender spirit of the woman who loved him, imprinting upon her the kiss of inward [*intrariae*, sic] charity. And so that she might not fear the terror of the night or be alarmed at any onset of temptation, he refreshed her with the bread of strength, containing every delight and every savor of sweetness; and he promised that he himself would be her protection in the day of tribulation.

Having received this divinely given fragrance, and as though receiving a most powerful seed into fertile ground, the virgin dismissed her empty fears. She who a little before could have been bent by the faintest breath of any breeze now remained steadfast and laughed at the wrath of heaven, the roar of the sea, and the storms of the winds. While the enemy employed manifold snares around her, so that the flower of virginity might suffer inevitable injury, she resolved with a more burning vow to fulfill the purpose of good living which she had once conceived, and in free flight swam out to the protection of the solid rock. Therefore, with her tent fixed in the strongest places, she no longer feared the thousands of people surrounding her. Knowing how to fight, if camps should stand against her, she gloried in this hope; she challenged the enemy more than she herself was challenged, now secure to say with Paul: “Neither tribulation, nor sword, nor death, nor any creature shall be able to draw her away from the love of Christ” (Rom. 8).

At last the wedding day pressed near, and its fame was widely spread to the ears of very many. The house was adorned with varied decoration and painted hangings; the household moved about more splendidly and joyfully than usual; elaborate ornaments for the virgin’s attire were provided with the utmost care and effort. Yet she did not walk in great things, nor in wonders beyond herself, nor did the gravity of her countenance change in different directions. For she had put on a manly spirit, apart from which, as someone says, “Nothing is wonderful to one for whom nothing great is great.” Her father, seeing that his daughter was in no way inclined toward the object of his desire, was pressed by excessive fear: lest, while he exerted every effort to marry her against her will, overwhelming grief might seize her mind and compel her into an incurable sickness, or perhaps she might attempt a flight from which she could not easily be recalled.

While he turned such anxious considerations mournfully in his heart, he at last resolved to meet them with a false argument. As evening fell—the evening before the wedding day—he addressed the virgin with flattering words, veiled in deceit: “It is not fitting, daughter, that the flower of your youth should fall and wither at its very rising, lest your natural color be stained by the black ink of some sorrow. Rather, rejoice in your youth; enjoy abundant possessions and many riches; and, the cloud of sadness wiped away, put on the adornment of joy. I beg you, drive all heaviness from your mind, and do not wound a parent’s affection with a sad countenance. Nor fear what need not be feared: I have postponed the day of the marriage union—which you think is to be celebrated tomorrow—because I am occupied with certain affairs, for its more convenient performance at another time.” [Col. 1364C]

Hearing the word which her father spoke to her heart from his own heart, she took it as an omen; not knowing falsehood from truth, she embraced it, and, ignorant of what the coming day would bring forth, gloried as though the first assault of battle had been broken.

Indeed, when the night had passed and the sun, its course revolving, shone with the morning light of day, the bridegroom arrived at the appointed time with a great company of his own people. Girls, parents, many noble virgins, and matrons also came, splendidly adorned with much care and costly attention to dress. Since the church was not nearby, the crowd of guests assembled in the courtyard of the girl’s father. She too was ordered to come; and because she knew that parents must be obeyed, she did not hesitate to comply and came forth—not as one about to marry in a hall, but as one about to fight in a theatre, intending to demonstrate more clearly by deeds as well as words how great a love of chastity remained in her breast.

And when the priest, as was customary, addressed the bridegroom Simon with a threefold question, asking whether he voluntarily consented to be lawfully joined to the virgin Oda, he replied that he had come for this purpose and promised that he would fulfill with all zeal what marital law commanded. But when they came to the virgin and asked whether she wished to accept the aforesaid bridegroom according to custom, she, her face suffused with blushes and her delicate forehead bowed, regarding as vain and proud [perhaps “superfluous”] whatever assailed her eyes or ears, [Col. 1365A] gave no answer whatsoever to the priest.

Some of those standing by attributed this silence to arrogance, others to modesty, and they tore apart her pure conscience with differing judgments. Then one of the matrons, who stood more intimately at her side, having regard for the virgin’s modesty, gently and mildly addressed her thus:

“Do not hesitate, noble virgin, to utter in a lawful reply your assent of will to those matters about which you are questioned. For as it was honorable and modest for you, when prompted once and twice, to remain silent, so you will be charged with ignorance and contempt if, where and when it is proper, you either do not know or do not wish to open your mouth. For there is a time to speak and a time to be silent (Eccles. 3). And although wisdom counsels a young person scarcely to speak even in her own cause, lest she incur blame deserved by excess, it nevertheless teaches that, when she has been questioned a second time, she should begin her reply. Therefore, lest you shame too greatly the faces of so many and such important persons; lest you offer girls of your own age an example of silence—indeed, of contempt for answering—at the priest’s question, now uttered three times, I beg you, open your noble mouth and give a welcome reply.”

To this the virgin said: “Since you inquire so insistently whether it is fixed in my mind to have this bridegroom whom you name to me, know with complete certainty that I wish to accept neither him nor another. For I am joined in love to him, to him alone I keep faith, to whom, while I was still a little girl, I wished the title of my virginity to be entrusted as a virgin. From his embraces neither another’s love or gifts, nor my parents’ threats or beatings, can ever separate me.” [Col. 1365C]

At the novelty of this reply, all the multitude present stood amazed in wonder. Simon, however, blushed deeply at being rejected; and, seeking to cover the shame of his rejection with some pretext of haughtiness, he falsely declared that he did not want a woman deprived of the benefit of speech. Then, with his brow lowered, he turned away and went off in indignation; and, as though an enemy pursued from behind, he returned rapidly on horseback to his house with his companions.

The virgin’s parents and those who remained with her, considering themselves no less humiliated, were fiercely enraged against her. They sought to infect with the leaven of malicious suspicion the word which had been uttered from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. Thus indeed, thus the human eye, when it willingly grows dim with the bleared sight of envy, investigates the judgment of truth less carefully in doubtful matters; and it often chooses to twist into a reproachful sense what is done with good intention, rather than, keeping a sound eye, to judge nothing rashly about hidden things.

Thus, when Hannah prayed to the Lord in the temple with tears poured out and no voice at all could be heard from her lips, which merely moved silently, Eli the priest—whose sight was now dimmed by blameworthy old age—watched closely, as Scripture says, the mouth and face of the woman praying. The deluded old man judged that she was not so much pouring forth the groans of speech as belching forth excessive drinking: “Digest for a little while the wine with which you are drenched,” he said (1 Sam. 1). [Col. 1366A]

But a mind firmly adhering to sound reason is not easily removed from the uprightness of its state, and a pure conscience cannot be frightened by the barking tongues of envious persons. Therefore the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day” (1 Cor. 4). The prudent virgin therefore stood, with tranquil mind and serene expression, in the midst, so to speak, of Babylon. Nor could the fierce blast of the north wind shake the fortress of her virginity; for, a daughter of Jerusalem enclosed by the valley of complete holiness and chastity, she scorned the suitors of luxury and the eye of impudence, and had nothing in common with the daughters of Ashkelon.

But her father, fearing that he might be charged with falsehood or perjury and that a mark of reproach might be laid upon his name, took with him certain necessary companions and went to recall the humiliated young man as quickly as possible, [Col. 1366B] so that, whether she wished it or not, he might join his daughter to him in the promised marriage. “But in vain is the net cast before the eyes of winged creatures” (Prov. 1).

When she learned what her father was plotting against her, while the crowd that remained was troubled and murmured over what had occurred, she seized an opportunity and slipped away secretly. Coming home, she withdrew into her mother’s chamber. Having fastened the door, she prayed that God would attend to help her. Seizing a sword which she saw hanging at the head of the bed, she hastened to cut off her nose. But her hand trembled, untrained in striking with a sword; and because with a woman’s blow it could not overcome the tougher upper resistance of the sinews, she said to herself in indignation: “O sword, how blunt is your edge, that with biting sharpness you cannot destroy the beauty of my face!”

Saying this, she raised herself against herself, pressed the iron more harshly, and with an oblique wound cut off her nostrils. She let a precious stream of rosy blood drip into a basin, and thus grievously disfigured the natural splendor of her face. O wondrous heart of the virgin! In order not to be fit for conformity to this wicked age, she chose to live with a mutilated nose and to disfigure the appearance of her attractive form, rather than to be painted with false beauty by adulterous cosmetic and have wanton eyes brazenly fixed upon her. I say, she preferred, as Christ’s handmaid, to remain abject in his house with unclean skin and humble clothing and to be reckoned, even among David’s maidservants, the least of his handmaids, rather than, in superfluous finery, wipe dust in the manner of foxes’ tails and soothe her body with prostitutes’ ointments, by which the nauseated appetite of adulterers is customarily provoked. [Col. 1366D]

We read of certain holy women, married as well as virgins, whose chastity was assailed by impure men: some thrust a sword into their breasts with courageous force; others immersed themselves in deep waters; some perished by fire or by a precipice, forestalling by voluntary death the rash attempts of their assailants, and thus purchasing the venerable name of martyr by the glorious price of death. Yet I seem to see that the virgin Oda endured no less martyrdom than they. Although she did not put off the garment of her flesh by a momentary blow dealt either by herself or by a persecutor, and although the harshness of penal tortures did not crush her, she nevertheless washed herself in the blood of the Lamb and kept her garments white until she should be taken from the midst.

For how, if necessity arose, could she evade dying for Christ, when, disfiguring herself thus for his love, she lived in this body beyond the flesh? For I think this kind of martyrdom greater, surpassing every form of torture: if one lives in the flesh beyond the flesh, provided that one has made oneself a eunuch for the kingdom of heaven. Finally, a universal command is laid upon everyone: when the cause of faith requires it, they must lay down their lives in death and must not put houses, wives, children, or themselves before this foundation. But this is prescribed by no law and handed down as no command; it is proposed as the highest and best course, and no one is accused of transgression except one who has bound himself by a vow or rashly violated what he voluntarily undertook. “He who is able to receive this, let him receive it,” says the Lord (Matt. 19). And the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7). Blessed Fulgentius also, commending virginity in a certain sermon, says: “Virginity cannot be commanded, but it may be desired.”

Moreover, we find many distinguished men who have bravely overcome many powers of vices and assaulted with mighty attack many fortifications arrayed against them, yet whom their natural heat afterward dried up from the full greenness of holiness; whom the itching of the loins almost exhausted; whom womanly softness shamefully subjugated as weak and unwarlike men. But whoever, aided by grace, prevailed against this flood, against this enemy, and gave no place to corruption either in flesh or in mind, is worthy of praise, because he performed wonders in his life. Therefore Oda is both martyr and virgin, for virginity cannot exist without martyrdom. She restrained the inciting rebellion of the navel with the girdle of strong chastity; and, abhorring as harmful the beauty that displeased her in herself, she marked her face with the sword’s cautery, saying not in voice but in deed that saying of Agnes: “I have set a mark on my face, that I may admit no lover except Christ.” But let us return to our subject. [Col. 1367C]

When those then present in the house became suspicious about what secret thing the girl was doing in the chamber, and inquisitively sought information now with their ears, now with their eyes, they heard the sound of her murmuring to herself. Knocking at the door, they asked with much entreaty and insistence that it be opened to them. But when she gave no reply and would not open it, they suspected that she was perishing either by the sword or from excessive pain. They rushed together against the door and brought it down with axe and adze.

When they saw that she had so cruelly raged against herself, that the great loss of blood had rendered her almost bloodless, and that a chilly pallor had already thoroughly colored her face, they burst into loud cries and were seized with astonishment beyond expression. Her mother, seeing her daughter’s disfigured face, fell upon her own face, beat her breast—bent by age, her skin slack—and, drawing long sighs from her depths, poured forth heavy waves of tears. Weaving a tearful tragedy, she proclaimed herself the most unfortunate of all women. [Col. 1368A]

The report sped to the ears of her father, who was then absent from that place. Stricken with inward grief of heart, he returned home swiftly on horseback. Seeing the wave of blood flowing from his daughter’s face; seeing the old woman, her companion, tearing out the gray hairs of her head amid bitter weeping; seeing the whole household, as though she were dead, performing the offices of mourning with lamenting voice—unable to bear it, he burst into tears and was overwhelmed by inconsolable sorrow. He neither softened his grief nor moderated his tears with the self-command of a manly spirit.

The harp was turned to mourning and the voice of joy to grief. That festive applause clapped sorrowing hands, and, interrupted by a heavy sigh, redoubled its fresh pain. The chorus of virgins that had prepared to lead festive dances abandoned the song of sweet melody and was compelled to begin mournful strains. All that splendid array for the wedding was darkened with grimy soot and covered with mourning dress. And what is more astonishing: while all wept, she herself remained without tears. As one who had attained her vow, she passed the sad lamentations about her with a deaf ear, nor was she shaken by any fear.

When the aforesaid Odo, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, learned this through a reliable report, and was moved by the woman’s so celebrated virtue, he summoned two religious men from among his own brethren and sent them there under the pretext of lodging. He earnestly instructed them to comfort her with the hand of godly consolation and to ask what she intended to do. The virgin’s father received them on their arrival with the greatest generosity and showed them every cheerful countenance. She herself reverenced those sent as messengers from the heavenly court and served them with devoted ministry.

When, in secret questioning, she had explained in full her vow and purpose, and had received in trusting faith the assurance that their assistance was available to her in this matter, she asked her father not further to impede, by any marital union, the path of chastity which she had chosen. Rather, because she was now useless to him and as if already repudiated, she asked that he grant her, with kindly favor, permission to leave the world. He would by no means yield to this request, but opposed to it the barrier of a contradictory refusal. He considered it foolish that she should seek voluntarily to enter the narrow hiding-place of voluntary poverty and strict religious life when, with the illustrious title of many inherited possessions, she ought rather to be distinguished and, in her flourishing and verdant youth, be joined by the law of marriage to a man of her own marriageable age. [Col. 1368D]

Then she said: “If you do not receive the voice of my plea and do not permit me to set out with free foot for the place of my heavenly calling; if, because you obstruct me, I cannot attain the prize for which I am sent to run in this stadium, I shall so destroy and cut down the flower which you call that of my youth that it shall be desired not only by no nobleman, but not even by a common man. And I shall add to your head a grief which, even if you wish it, you will not be able to forget. Why do you strive with such great and such vain concern to marry me against my will? Why do you not more carefully consider that one dead to the world cannot live for the world again? Truly, father, know this: if no other hope at all smiled upon my vows; if, I say, no favorable success on my journey were available to me except on this sole condition—that you, laid beneath my feet in any mud whatever, should supply me a bridge with your body—if you bent yourself for me to cross over, I freely confess that I would not delay to pass over you; and, despising you—indeed, trampling you underfoot—I would hasten joyfully to the place I have chosen.”

While she contended with her pious father in these or similar words, and he utterly despaired of making her give way, his heart was deeply troubled. At last, though sorrowful, he assented to her wishes.

[Col. 1369B] Having received permission, she met the aforesaid guests and begged that, under their guidance or protection, she might be worthy to depart swiftly from Egypt. Inclining a benevolent ear to her request, they returned as quickly as possible to the monastery and began to relate the matter in order to the abbot. Delighted by their report, the abbot rejoiced; taking certain brothers with him, he hurried to meet the virgin. Seeing him, she humbly ran to his feet and explained her purpose to him in sufficiently eloquent speech.

After they had exchanged godly conversation and arranged the matter for which they had met, she bade farewell to her parents and to the world, left her house and kindred, and received from that abbot the habit of holy religion. She entered under him into the cloister of obedience and courageously undertook, with the devout women there, the discipline of monastic profession. I lack understanding, life, words, and talent to tell with what fervor of holiness and zeal she advanced in a short time, or how great was the perfection in her of humility, obedience, and the other virtues.

For, so that the best end might follow a good beginning, she first sat down and counted the costs needed before she set foot to build the tower, lest perhaps cost or material should fail her in the work she had begun, arousing the laughter of passersby and suffering the ridicule of an unfinished wall, begun but not completed. Otherwise, the foundation rashly laid would correspond not so much to the building of a tower as seem to provide a cave for robbers or a tomb fit for storing corpses. Therefore, avoiding the lofty summit of the mountain and the shifting sands that drink in water, she first set her feet in the trench of profound humility. And so that the structure of her building might rise straight up and grow into a holy temple in the Lord, she strove to direct her steps according to the line of evangelical instruction.

Since, therefore, bowing her neck, she placed upon herself the light and sweet yoke of Christ’s burden; since, chanting the Song of Ascents, she arranged ascents in her heart in the valley of tears, the Lord placed in her mouth a new song, which no one can sing in a strange land save that company in the Apocalypse, “led in number, hundreds of thousands of virgins” (Rev. 14). This song belongs to virgins alone: only to those [Col. 1370A] who follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 22 [sic]).

Moreover, she subdued her flesh by such great abstinence from food and drink that the impulses of natural rebellion found no room for resistance in her, so to speak, arid belly; and neither delicate softness nor engorged heaviness softened her chaste and sober mind into sexual excess. Hence a certain pagan says: “Without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold.” But whenever the martial tumult of vices grew fierce against her, whenever an adverse wind rose, she did not yield to impatience. Instead, with the strong battering-ram of patience she dashed her little ones against the rock, and forcefully crushed to earth beneath her heel the head of the serpent lying in ambush for her (Gen. 3). How greatly she strove and labored in this workshop of virtue, the following evidence will be able plainly to show.

[Col. 1370B] For when, rejecting the seductions of worldly glory, she had only recently bent her pliant neck beneath the yoke of obedience, and had put aside soft clothing and sweet nourishment, binding her willing foot as though with fetters of poverty and frugality, harsh clothing and scanty food wasted her tender and delicate body and weakened it from its former strength. That fresh and robust compactness of her limbs was loosened by the undigested rawness of food; and, her humors being corrupted, the surface of her bright skin was infected with blotched swellings.

When the sisters saw the virginal appearance of her face so quickly changed to a deathly pallor and the skin that had been clearer than glass now wrinkled in certain places by diseased swelling, they suspected that she was burdened with the contagion of leprosy. They began to murmur among themselves that she should be separated from the fellowship of the others, as from the midst of the camp. When this was openly discussed by all, and some who seemed wiser in this matter had examined the place more carefully and pronounced her leprous, she was ordered to have a little hut built apart. Thus, by the bleary judgment of human beings, though pure in mind and body, she lived outside the others as though unclean. [Col. 1370C]

But Christ’s humble handmaid did not take the disgrace of this contempt badly. Indeed, knowing that virtue is perfected in weakness, she gladly endured the unjust rejection attached to her name; and, setting aside any attempt to oppose the false suspicion which lied about her, she did not delay to withdraw to the place designated. When one of the sisters of mature age was chosen as her companion, to console the young woman with maternal affection and diligently provide necessities, the unhappy woman—though her brow was wrinkled, yet irreverent in mind and untamed—refused to obey the order. She said that she was so faint-hearted—or, to speak more truly, so foolish—that she could not possibly endure contact with such uncleanness, and that she preferred to incur the offense of disobedience rather than bear the burden of attending to her illness.

The rebellious obstinacy of that woman was deservedly punished by the sentence of regular discipline; and the youthful age of virgin girls afterward gave ready service to the one for whom her gray-haired childishness had refused its aid. But Oda herself was unmoved amid all these crashes of adversity. Rather, her spirit grew from the difficulty of circumstances, and through endurance of suffering she was advanced to the summit of highest holiness. Made the refuse of all and, as it were, the useless sweepings of a house, she always kept before her eyes the image of him who for us was struck, had neither form nor beauty, and did not refuse to undergo the torment of the cross.

She spoke this to herself, reflected on it diligently, and had turned her thoughts back upon it, frequently looking upon and kissing the hand which the rejected swelling had seized. For the prudent virgin knew that whoever has professed this warfare needs patience, because, as a certain pagan says:

> Whatever it is forbidden to set right becomes lighter through patience.

[Col. 1371B] HORACE, *Odes* 24.

And the Apostle says: “Tribulation produces patience; patience, testing; testing, however, hope; and hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5). For, as Symmachus says, hope, which always counsels endurance of adverse events, is secure. Therefore she prayed to the Lord all the more devoutly because she prayed more secretly, that in the favorable time he might grant her to emerge in a sound ship from so many dangers. She did not think it a great thing, for love of him, if she were now to endure anything hard or harsh, certain that she would receive eternal life as the fruit of labor and patience.

But after she had been much winnowed upon the threshing-floor of this trial, after her hoof had been duly hardened on rough ground, he who does not allow his own to be tempted beyond what they are able to bear moderated the scourge of his chastening. With the foulness of diseased humor removed, he called her back, sound and unharmed, into the camp with the others.

Yet she attended the school of obedience with such careful skill and skilled diligence that she allowed no one to surpass her in this discipline. She embraced the observance of its rules so completely that she regarded nothing commanded her as harsh or unbearable, but as welcome and light. [Col. 1371C]

786 Therefore, not long after her conversion, the father of the aforesaid monastery chose her as mistress over her fellow disciples; and, because she surpassed her companions by the merit of her virtues, she was set before the rest as a kind of mirror or rule. Yet when she was made prioress, she did not swell with the empty breath of pride because of the eminence of her office; [Col. 1371D] rather, the care imposed upon her and the obligation of a more extensive service made her humbler and more devoted. Recognizing herself as a mother rather than a mistress, she cherished her daughters with such affection and advanced them toward so lofty a summit of religious life that they unanimously embraced her with filial fear and love, and rejoiced that, with her as leader and guide, they were being compelled by their own willing progress toward better things.

Her life was in some sense a sermon. With mature discernment she was so available alike to the wise and the foolish that, while remaining everywhere consistent and the same, she nevertheless accommodated herself to each individual—not so that harmful lukewarmness or lax indulgence might weaken in any degree the firmness of her strict purpose, but so that she might draw them by love and bind them by affection, thereby more fully imprinting Christ upon their hearts through a welcome influence. [Col. 1372A] And because, as someone says, “it is shameful to speak one thing and think another,” her deeds answered to her words, and, as though struck into one mould, corresponded with one another. Thus, with a teacher’s authority, she rebuked the faults of those subject to her and exercised regular discipline, so that, once the corrupt diseased matter had been cut out at the root, she might apply a kindly poultice and place a healing remedy upon the wound inflicted.

Toward the sick and the poor—being herself poor and afflicted for Christ—she overflowed with such bowels of mercy that she not only provided necessities for those over whom she presided with motherly care, but, if she knew anyone near her to be suffering from the disadvantage either of poverty or some illness, she strove, through a certain most faithful agent of this her secret, somehow to relieve their need from her own scant means. [Col. 1372B] For she told him that it was a pious theft by which he mercifully assisted the sick and clothed Christ in the naked poor.

In short, such holiness shone in her countenance, such uprightness in her conduct, maturity in her counsel, usefulness in her speech, integrity in flesh and spirit, and lavish charity in loving all, that the greatness of her virtue surpassed the measure of frail nature and displayed, in a mortal body, the pattern of that heavenly manner of life. Nor is it surprising that she savoured of the draught which she had drawn from a full vessel, she who could say with the Apostle that her citizenship was in heaven (Phil. III). The radiance of her grace could not be confined within the hiding-place of walls, but flashed far and wide in vast outpouring beams. [Col. 1372C] The excellent ointment of her name, broken in the house of obedience, spread such fragrance everywhere that it invited many of both sexes to run in the good way in the fragrance of her ointments. Nor did popular favour or the approving voices of the crowd, which perish with their very sound, make her famous; rather, the proven virtues of the soul, which bring their possessor—though placed in a corner, though hidden in a rock—to the everlasting knowledge of ages through the judges of virtue.

Accordingly, when she had completed the number of her days and the crown of righteousness had already been laid up for her in reward for her labours, it pleased Him who called and justified her to bring the way of her pilgrimage to an end after her appointed course, and by this glorious removal to convey her from the shipwreck-prone dwelling of this world [Col. 1372D] to a place of peaceful abode. For she was seized by a final fever and worn down by prolonged illness; a deadly pain raged within the dwelling-place of her breast with repeated stings. It gnawed, as it were, with a hard tooth upon the remnants of a body exhausted by long penitence, and pressed ever more heavily upon her vital breath. A diseased humour repeatedly obstructed the passage of the upper instrument [the throat], cutting off her breathing; and, exercising the tumult of cruel tyranny within the cavity of her stomach, it brought forth an importunate cough. Thus the disease gradually put down and spread its roots, increasing day by day.

Indeed, thus it was fitting, thus it was proper, that in this furnace her dross should be refined to purity, so that, thus tested, [Col. 1373A] thus smelted, she might deserve to be fittingly engraved in the diadem of the supreme King. Therefore, although she had little strength, she bore this oppression with great courage, giving thanks to God that He had struck her with so great a blow and had willed her to undergo this threshing. She therefore devoted herself more earnestly to prayer by day and night, and anticipated the face of the Lord in confession. Setting herself before herself, she examined her cause with careful scrutiny beneath the eyes of that strict Judge; and, correcting with stern rebuke whatever displeased her in herself, she watered His feet with tears like Mary.

When the crushing sickness had already worn her down for half a year and, gathering all her strength, had bent her utterly over the bed of illness, renewed pain, beating more sharply upon the inmost heart, indicated that she must soon be dissolved and that her vessel—which she had hitherto possessed in sanctification and honour—must be involved in the common lot of mortals. [Col. 1373B] For her natural, appetitive, and retentive powers had so completely failed her that she no longer desired any food; rather, her stomach resisting, she immediately rejected what she had taken. Anointed, therefore, with the liquid of holy oil, and with the offices of nature now lulled—or rather buried—her holy soul, in a half-living body, was wholly intent upon heavenly things; forgetting the things behind, it stretched itself forth to those before. Commending herself to Christ in constant prayers and tears, whom in her life she had earnestly endeavoured perfectly to serve as a handmaid, she awaited the consummation of her struggle in a joyful end.

And when her sorrowing daughters stood around their holy virgin-mother and, with tearful prayers, begged that when she had passed to heaven she might deign to care for them, she, shunning the sickness of self-exaltation, was troubled by this speech. Breaking into tears, she answered them thus: “Why, daughters, do you address me, a sinner, with words such as these? Why do you ask from me—who am of no account, who am scarcely conscious of any good in myself—those things which belong to the apostles and the other saints? Spare yourselves, I beg you, such words; instead implore that pardon be granted for my sins, and commend my end more earnestly in your prayers, that when I depart from here the bosom of Abraham may receive me—to Him for whom all live and through whom all things are.” [Col. 1373C]

[Col. 1373D] At length the solemn day of Easter came. When, having completed her course, she had now drawn near to the final stretch of her race for the palm; when prolonged sickness had thoroughly purged the old leaven of her body; after the most holy mysteries of our redemption had been celebrated, she received that saving viaticum. As day declined toward evening, in the presence of the abbot, brothers, and sisters, who according to custom commended her departure with prayers and psalms, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May [20 April], in the year 1158 from the Incarnation of the Word, she rested in peace.

When the holy virgins learned that she had fallen asleep, they were moved by such affection and weighed down by such sorrow of heart that their faces were darkened by an exceeding pallor of grief, and they gave expression without restraint to their desolation in tears and sighs. [Col. 1374A] Keeping devout watch over her holy funeral with prayers and tears, they escorted her holy soul with psalms and hymns to the mountain of the Lord and into His holy tabernacles. When daylight broke on the following day, her holy body was carried by the brothers to the abbey. There, after holy offerings had been presented to God in her commemoration, it was committed to burial with the great honour that was fitting by the venerable Gregory, abbot of Aulne; Philip, abbot of that place; the aforesaid Odo; priests; and a great company of brothers. Though it was sown in weakness, I believe that it shall rise in power; sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption; sown in mortality, it shall rise in immortality; sown in dishonour, it shall rise in [Col. 1374B] glory.

Happy, therefore, and blessed was her soul, which deserved to leave Egypt on that day on which the true Paschal Lamb restored freedom to the true Israelites, on which Christ rose from the dead, no longer to taste the bitter fruit of this vine. Happy, I say, and blessed was she who deserved on that day to pass into Galilee, on which the new glory of the Resurrection was first made known to the world; who then deserved to see King Solomon in his splendour, when His mother crowned Him on the day of His solemnity and joy, on the day of His espousals. Happy, I say, is the virgin Oda, and worthy of praise according to her name—indeed, *Oda* means, emphatically, “praise.” As the Psalmist, mindful of God’s benefits, calls Him not merely merciful, [Col. 1374C] but Mercy itself in an eminent sense: “My God,” he says, “my mercy” (Ps. LVIII [59]). Now indeed the pious virgin sees and tastes how sweet the Lord is (Ps. XXXIII [34]), no longer so much through a mirror and in an enigma (I Cor. XIII), for the former things have passed away; but she walks in the light of God’s countenance and exults all day in His name, together with those choirs of the blessed who remained steadfast in the struggle of the contest. She sleeps a happy sleep in the embraces of her heavenly Bridegroom, made drunk with the abundance of God’s house; nor does she permit anyone to awaken her or make her rise, for as long as she wishes to yield herself to the sleep of such blessed rest.

Although secure in the lot of her blessedness, her loving care nevertheless ever keeps watch for her brothers and sisters. For their peace and salvation she appeals to divine mercy, praying that He may drive far away from their minds and dwellings all the assaults of their adversaries. [Col. 1374D] Therefore I hope that she will also grant pardon to me, who have undertaken, at the request of the sisters and with the zeal of love and devotion, to write her life as best I can—if anywhere I have stumbled in expression, if I have exceeded the permitted manner of writing—and obtain for me fuller grace. May she, by the oarage of her prayers, lead me, still struggling amid the waves of the great and spacious sea, to the desired end by a very easy course, though I am carried in a frail vessel.

Therefore, that, when death has at last been swallowed up in victory, we too may deserve to please God with her in the land of the living, let us confess His holy name and glory in His praise—He who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1375]

788 **THE LIFE OF ST WALDETRUDIS (G)\***

## Prologue

[Col. 1375A]

The custom of the ancients, who have left us so many volumes concerning them that they can scarcely be counted, declares that the venerable deeds of the saints ought to be committed [to be committed] to writing for the stirring up of those who live. Moved, therefore, by their examples and compelled by the charity of certain religious brothers and sisters, I have presumed to undertake this work. I humbly beseech every prudent reader to spare the rusticity of the writer and to be a kindly corrector rather than a malicious critic, knowing that my concern has been more to set forth clearly, for the brothers who requested it, the truth of the matter proposed than to observe the rules of grammarians.

## Chapter I. Preface concerning the examples of the saints

[Col. 1375B]

To illuminate the way of eternal life, the Redeemer of the world deigned, after His Ascension, to send to all faithful Christians the apostles and chosen followers of the apostles. By living rightly, enduring adversity with equanimity, despising visible and temporal things, desiring invisible and eternal things, preaching and awaiting, they proclaimed to those who wandered the lost joys of eternity; and, shining with the great grace of the Spirit, they showed, like stars amid the darkness of errors, the way to those who wished, so to speak, to return to these joys.

## Chapter II. Why miracles were given to the saints: that faith might be spread throughout the world

[Col. 1375C]

But because in the earlier age the people were carnal, believing that visible things alone existed and not desiring invisible things because they did not even suppose them to exist, the examples or preaching of the saints alone could by no means suffice to establish faith in invisible things. Miracles were therefore added, so that the power displayed might give credence to words. Those visible miracles then shone forth for this purpose: that they might draw the hearts of hearers to faith in invisible things, and that through what was wondrously done outwardly, that which was far more wondrous within might be perceived.

Now, however, because through God’s working the number of believers has increased in the world, those bodily miracles have for the most part ceased—not because there are now lacking in the Church people who possess a life of virtues while not performing signs in the body, [Col. 1375D] but because they are no longer necessary in our times. Hence the Apostle says: “Tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (I Cor. XIV). For a miracle is performed outwardly in vain if that which works inwardly is lacking. For it is life, not signs, that must now be sought. The proof of true life lies in the virtue of deeds, not in the display of signs. Yet when such things do occur, they bear witness to a good life [Col. 1376A] and stir the hearts of neighbours to imitation.

## Chapter III. That the examples of saints are greatly able to benefit believers

We therefore believe without hesitation and hold with steadfast faith that it will be no small benefit to those who desire utterly to abandon worldly affairs and who wish to forsake the broad and spacious paths of this world that lead to destruction, and to enter the narrow and strait way of our Redeemer which leads to life, if examples are brought forward from the lives of holy men and women who have gone before on this very way, under grace’s guidance, and have left it trodden by their footsteps. Thus everything which they might have thought impossible for themselves becomes so much easier for them to hope for, because they see that others have already passed through it. [Col. 1376B] For often the examples of saints move and awaken sluggish hearts toward the love of God and the desire for eternal life more than sermons do, because when people consider their sublime deeds or miracles, they are ashamed to lie disgracefully in low places themselves. Hence the Lord also says: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

## Chapter IV. The fleshly lineage of blessed Waldetrudis

Accordingly, with the help of Christ’s grace, we shall endeavour to reveal in writing, for the praise of God and the edification and advancement of neighbours, some things—though few out of many—concerning the life, manner of life, and miracles of the holy and most blessed handmaid of Christ, Waldetrudis. These events occurred not far from our own times, [Col. 1376C] according to the trustworthy report of truthful witnesses who deserved either to see or hear these very things.

Therefore, while Dagobert, son of Lothair the Great, was king, God’s mercy set many stars in the firmament of His Church, which drove away the darkness of vices from the people by their radiance. The see of Cambrai shone with the light of the holy bishop Autbert; Elnon rejoiced in the merits of Saint Amand; the city of Metz was cherished by the patronage of Saint Arnulf; the see of Maastricht venerated its bishop Remaclus; the chair of Noyon embraced its chosen Eligius; [Col. 1376D] the metropolitan city of Cologne reverently honoured the pious Cunibert. Moreover, the district anciently called Martensis from the shrine of Mars, but by modern people called Hainaut from its river, wore a flourishing crown through the merits of certain saints.

There Landelinus, ordained by Saint Martin, archbishop of the Roman See, cultivated Crespin with the divine plough; Gislenus, exiled from his homeland through love of God, inhabited a vast wilderness. Nor was the lamp of such great men hidden under a bushel (Matt. V). It had also kindled with divine ardour the princes who then governed worldly affairs. For the sons of the aforesaid king—Sigibert and Clovis—listened to their counsels and gladly served their undertakings. Sigibert, grieved that he lacked private offspring, built twelve monasteries for an unfailing line of descendants, where holy men might live by a holy rule. [Col. 1377A] The wife of Clovis, named Balthild, after she had brought the noble church of the martyr Saint Quentin to complete perfection, enlarged the monastery called Chelles with many benefactions. Pippin also, son of Carloman and then mayor of the royal household, endowed with many estates his daughter Gertrude, betrothed by the bishop with the ring of faith, and rejoiced that she presided over no few nuns. He likewise rejoiced that Begga, widowed by her husband Ausigis, had preserved the chaste holiness of widowhood.

A rival in these things was the most noble and kindly prince Walbert, pre-eminent among the princes of Gaul in nobility of blood and extent of possessions. By divine providence, from which nothing can be hidden, he married a most noble virgin, renowned both for the nobility of royal blood and the beauty of her fair lineage, named Bertilia by her parents. Her brothers were Landeric and Cundeland, whom our annals report to have been standard-bearers of an army. [Col. 1377B] Though our pen and tongue may be silent about their wealth and nobility, their estates and the buildings upon those estates—known by everyone to have been theirs and to have come to God’s churches through their beneficence—affirm them.

While, therefore, the aforesaid Walbert and Bertilia were joined in the bond of holy marriage and nevertheless, according to the Apostle (I Cor. VII), devoted themselves to prayer for seasons; while, I say, they cultivated well the plants of their own life, they bore precious fruit through God’s gracious generosity. For there was born to them a most flourishing rose and, as will later be clear, a most brilliant star: namely, the girl whom they had long sought from God with sighs. Washed in the laver of divine baptism, she was named Waldetrudis by her elders. We have resolved to describe briefly the examples of her life, because we believe them beneficial to present and future people alike. [Col. 1377C] No order in God’s Church is excluded for which the life of so great a mother cannot suffice as an example.

From her, hermits may gain an increase in their former way of life, hearing how this handmaid of God fled from people and withdrew herself, remained in solitude, and maintained herself upon the height of divine contemplation. From her, married people may conceive a love of continence, when they hear how she urged her husband toward the monastic order. From her, virgins may more readily choose the hundredfold crown, when with the hand of their minds they understand how she offered sacred virgins a model for imitation. From her, bishops who are shepherds of the flock, provided they lend a patient ear to instruction, may learn with what diligence they ought to govern those entrusted to them. She, I say, as she still offers herself ready to hear those who pray to her, so while living she offered herself to all for imitation. But now the time presses for the thread of the narrative to be taken up.

She was thus born, in the time of Dagobert, illustrious king of the Franks, [Col. 1378A] from exceedingly distinguished and noble parents and of royal descent. She also had a sister, a most holy virgin named Aldegundis, who led a life full of many virtues, guarded herself on the height of continence, and presided for many years over the monastery of Maubeuge. There exists a little book published concerning her life and manner of life; whoever wishes to know how pleasing she was to God and the angels, how beloved to human beings, and how many and what great acts of power the Lord deigned to show through her, will readily be able to discover it. But let us return the pen to our purpose.

## Chapter V. That she was given by her parents to a husband in marriage

[Col. 1378B]

While the blessed Waldetrudis was still a young girl, being brought up in her father’s house and greatly loved by her family, it seemed good to her parents that, according to God’s ancient ordinance and the example of the patriarchs, they ought to give her to a husband in marriage. She was beautiful in face and fair in appearance, but fairer in faith, modesty, and chastity. Yet not even the union of the flesh could alter the hidden dispensation of the Lord God, who had betrothed her with the ring of His faith and predestined her to become the companion and co-heir, in the glory of the eternal kingdom, of her aforesaid virgin sister Aldegundis.

For almighty God swiftly drew her back from worldly involvement by the gratuitous gift of His compassion, and, kindling her heart with the fire of His love, easily restrained her from all carnal allurements and from an excessive desire for earthly things. [Col. 1378C] When her mind was transformed, those things which had pleased her suddenly began to seem worthless, and what had formerly delighted her heart afterwards became exceedingly burdensome. Meanwhile, she strove gradually to set aside worldly cares and to long only for eternal desires: to distribute all her substance joyfully to the poor, orphans, and widows; to ransom captives; to receive guests and pilgrims; and utterly to root out vices not only from bodily action but also from the thought of her heart.

## Chapter VI. That she persuaded her husband to preserve chastity

[Col. 1378D]

Meanwhile, not content merely with her own salvation, she also took care every day, by gentle and saving words, to stir her husband, the nobleman Madelgarius, toward love of God, desire for the heavenly homeland, and the preservation of chastity. With the fire of charity in which she herself sweetly burned, she laboured to kindle his mind. Since the pleasure of carnal affection commonly lashes the mind’s attention severely and clouds its sharpness, she began greatly to dread the union of the flesh—not because she despised God’s gift, granted to human beings for the propagation of offspring, but because she knew that the Apostle taught in Scripture: “The unmarried woman and the virgin think upon the things [Col. 1379A] of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and spirit” (I Cor. VII). But she who is married thinks upon the things of the world, how she may please her husband. Therefore, desiring to devote herself to God alone, she feared carnal marriage as a kind of impediment and daily prayed with groaning and tears that, by God’s will, it might be dissolved and the will of the Lord fulfilled in her.

## Chapter VII. That her husband Madelgarius sought the monastic life

But almighty God, who mercifully suggested these things in the heart of His handmaid by a hidden dispensation, also powerfully helped bring them about. For her aforesaid husband Madelgarius, pierced by divine inspiration and kindled with the torches of inward love, dissolved the bonds of marriage while charity remained, hastened to the monastery called Hautmont, received the monastic habit there, and passed the temporal course of this life in holy deeds. [Col. 1379B]

## Chapter VIII. How, while still clothed in secular dress, she was strengthened by a heavenly vision

The most religious handmaid of the bishop, Waldetrudis, although still wearing secular dress, relaxed none of the vigour of her soul, but administered the care of her own household. She devoted herself to works of mercy, gave attention to good works, cultivated hospitality, and served in fasts and prayers night and day. Almighty God, who knows how to cultivate every branch that bears fruit so that it may bear more fruit, deigned to call His handmaid—who faithfully ministered the gifts she had received—to greater gains in holiness by a heavenly vision.

For one night, after labour, when she had laid her weary limbs upon a bed for a brief refreshment of the body, she soon fell asleep and saw in a dream that she entered the basilica situated in the estate which the common people call [Col. 1379C] Buxutum. And behold, the most holy bishop Gaugericus appeared to her, shining with great splendour. He received her with the highest honour and reverence, and in the vision gave her a cup full of wine. When she had drunk it, he said to her with a serene and joyful countenance: “Continue what you are doing, for the things you do are exceedingly pleasing to me.” Strengthened by this vision and, so to speak, made drunk with the wine of divine grace, she began to despise earthly things and burn more vehemently with love of her heavenly homeland, and to seek more eagerly the sweetness of eternal life which she had, as it were, tasted a little.

## Chapter IX. Concerning the slanders brought against Christ’s handmaid by diabolical instigation

But where the ancient enemy grieves that good people are advancing, there he tries, by the arts of his wickedness, to drag the wicked toward worse things. When the handmaid of almighty God humbly recounted this vision to certain women who served with her, and it was—as often happens—carried by them to the ears of the ignoble crowd, the enemy of humankind, wishing to resist this holy purpose at its very beginning, immediately kindled the hearts of certain reprobate people with the fires of envy. [Col. 1379D] He incited them to bring against her detractions, mockeries, and false reproaches, and, so to speak, armed himself with their venomous tongues in order to wage war against Christ’s handmaid. Hence it is written: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI [57]). But almighty God swiftly helped His handmaid when she was wavering amid diabolical snares.

## Chapter X. How she was comforted by an angel sent from heaven

For when her spirit, still inexperienced, was greatly disturbed by such mockeries and disparagements, and she, crushed by heavy sorrow, had taken to her bed, an angel sent from heaven suddenly appeared in the form of a man, shining with great beauty. Standing near and speaking with her familiarly, he asked the causes of so great a grief: “Why,” he said, “are you weighed down by so heavy a burden of sorrow? Why do you improperly cloud the cheerfulness of your soul with a cloud of sadness?” When she answered how many disparagements, mockeries, and slanders she endured from her fellow citizens at the instigation of the ancient adversary, the angel added: [Col. 1380A] “Take courage and be strong against those who speak against you and slander you, for it is written: ‘He shall not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully’ (II Tim. II). You should not, therefore, be greatly troubled by the empty sparks of words, which, once kindled, are quickly and easily extinguished. For the prophets, apostles, and martyrs who were before you suffered these things. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: ‘The disciple is not above the master’ (Matt. X); and a little later: ‘If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household!’ [Matt. X:25.] Elsewhere Scripture also admonishes us, saying: ‘My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation’ (Ecclus. II). You must therefore bear bravely this sort of temptation, which is made for testing, so that, when you have been tested, you may receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love Him” (Prov. I).

Strengthened by these and similar words and testimonies of Scripture, [Col. 1380B] she immediately repressed the useless sadness of heart which diabolical fraud had suggested, as spiritual joy came upon her. Oh, how beloved the Lord regarded her, whom He did not permit even for a little while to be saddened!

## Chapter XI. That the servant of God Gislenus designated for her a place to build a monastery

Meanwhile, there was a certain priest named Gislenus, dwelling in deserted places near the river called the Haine. He showed in his conduct the monastic habit which he wore outwardly, and because of the merit of his holiness he was greatly venerated by all who could know him. Warned by a divine command, he had often been accustomed to visit the aforesaid handmaid of Christ, Waldetrudis, for the purpose of exhortation, and took care to refresh her mind with the nourishment of God’s word.

When this man of God learned that she had grown cold toward the allurements of this world, was inflamed with heavenly desire, and eagerly sought the habit of holy living, [Col. 1380C] he designated for her a certain mountain, now called Castrilocus. With earnest exhortation he urged her, once she had received the sacred veil, to build there a little cell for herself in which to serve almighty God. This mountain lay about four miles above the cell of the aforesaid man of God Gislenus, in the upper part of the wilderness. It was far removed from secular dwellings, wooded and uncultivated because of the thick growth of thorns and brambles, but appeared most suitable for a holy and religious manner of life.

## Chapter XII. That Hildulfus first built her a house there

[Col. 1381B]

The blessed Waldetrudis gladly and gratefully received the admonition of the man of God, and did not delay to fulfil in deed what almighty God had deigned to show her through His servant. She immediately sent to a distinguished man named Hildulfus, who at that time was very illustrious and noble and, in the temporal dignity of this world, most powerful; through his wife he was related to that handmaid of Christ. She earnestly asked him to buy from its owners, at a price, the aforesaid place which divine clemency had designated for her through His servant, and not refuse to prepare there a dwelling in which she could serve the Lord.

He readily assented to her prayers. He arranged to purchase the place which Christ’s handmaid had requested and, having cut down the shrubs and brambles at the roots, carefully prepared for her a house to live in upon the summit of the mountain. [Col. 1381C]

## Chapter XIII. How the house displeased her, was overthrown by God, and another was built in its place

We must not pass over in silence the miracle which almighty God displayed at the very beginning of her holy undertaking, in order to show how great a care He had for His handmaid. When this most devout novice in Christ came to the house prepared for her and saw that it was broad, spacious, and lofty, she recoiled; its very size greatly displeased her eyes. For, with a humble mind, she sought on earth a humble dwelling hidden from human sight, in order that she might deserve to possess in heaven a high and lofty dwelling amid the multitudes of angels.

A marvellous and utterly astounding event followed at once. After Christ’s handmaid had departed, in that same night the entire structure of the house was suddenly torn from its foundations by a whirlwind and cast far away by divine power. [Col. 1381D] Then the aforesaid Hildulfus rebuilt for her, on the side of that mountain and at the place she herself had indicated, a small dwelling suited to holy religious life, together with an oratory dedicated in honour of Saint Peter the Apostle.

## Chapter XIV. That, having received the sacred veil, she devoted herself to the Lord’s service

[Col. 1382A]

Meanwhile, the dearly beloved handmaid of Christ, Waldetrudis, fervent in spirit and breathing ever more eagerly after heavenly desire, followed the admonition of the man of God Gislenus, whom we mentioned above. She approached the most blessed bishop Autbert and asked that she might be worthy to receive the sacred veil; and she obtained this without delay.
