Having received from him the garments of a nun, she immediately gave herself and all that she possessed to almighty God, enclosed herself in the cell which she had caused to be built, and there provided notable examples of holy conduct in every direction.

For she was incomparably endowed with gravity of conduct, sobriety of mind, gentleness of meekness, and moderation of speech; perfect in charity toward God and neighbour; attentive to the needs of poor people and pilgrims; and devoted to vigils, prayers, and fasts. [Col. 1382B] Meanwhile, with all the effort of her mind she strove to mortify the flesh, break her own wills, avoid the tumults of people, and daily offer herself to the Lord upon the altar of her heart in tears.

## Chapter XV. What temptations she suffered from the enemy and overcame
Accordingly, the ancient enemy, the foe of the human race, who from the beginning strives to oppose good deeds, inflamed by the torches of envy, rose against her with all his strength in temptation. At length, grieving that by grace he had previously lost the open war, he again renewed himself for hidden contests. For by a subtle temptation concerning the faith and hope which are in Christ Jesus, he conceived the design of wickedly assailing her mind: importunately suggesting to her heart various unlawful thoughts—first, by bringing to mind her possessions, the nobility of her lineage, the protection of her household, love of material things, the fleeting glory of the world, the varied pleasure of food, and the other enticements of a more indulgent life; then the arduous goal of virtue, the immense effort needed to attain it, the frailty of the body, and the long extent of life. By these and such temptations he raised in her a great darkness of thoughts, trying whether in some way he might draw her away from her holy purpose.

But the mighty hand of almighty God easily frustrated these deadly schemes of the devil. Through the visitation of divine grace she swiftly returned to herself; and, finding herself standing in battle-line amid Satan’s bands, she at once ran to her weapons. She immediately gave herself to lamentation, beseeching the Lord with groans and tears that in such a contest he might deign to grant her aid, lest she should succumb. And while day and night she sought a remedy from the Lord in frequent and prolonged prayers, it happened once that for this reason she spent the night in prayer.

And behold, suddenly that same ancient enemy appeared in the form of a man, as though mocking her, and stretched out his hand and placed it upon her breast. But when she swiftly invoked Christ’s name, the enemy immediately sought flight. She, undaunted—strengthened, that is, by angelic aid—boldly pursued him as he fled here and there, with reproaches and fitting insults:

“Well has it befallen you, wretch; well has it befallen you—you who said in your heart: ‘I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I shall be like the Most High’ [Isa. 14]. Behold: because of your pride you were driven from the seat of heaven and condemned, as you deserved, to Tartarean death; and now you are put to flight by a woman. The place which you in your pride abandoned, Christ in humility restored to the human race redeemed by his blood.”

On hearing this, the enemy, ashamed of his humiliation, at once vanished like smoke. Nor did he presume thereafter to harass the mind of Christ’s handmaid with this temptation; and he whom he had willingly brought into contests was compelled, by the power of almighty God, unwillingly to furnish her with occasions for victory.

## CHAPTER XVI. That, freed from temptation, she became a mistress of virtues.

When temptation had therefore withdrawn, blessed Waldetrudis, her thorns plucked out, like cultivated ground bore more abundant fruit. For when the fame of her outstanding manner of life spread far and wide, certain women of nobler birth began to flock to her instruction and to serve the Lord in consecrated chastity. Rightly, freed from temptation, she became a mistress of virtues.

## CHAPTER XVII. That, though urged by her sister, she refused to leave her cell.

[Col. 1383C]

Her sister too, namely the most holy virgin Aldegundis, whom we mentioned above, was accustomed on appointed days to come from her monastery to visit her, so that they might exchange sweet words of life with one another and, since they could not yet enjoy perfectly the sweet food of the heavenly homeland, might at least taste it in longing.

When Aldegundis saw the smallness of the place and observed that as yet only a few consecrated women were attending her sister, moved by human affection and, as it were, pitying her poverty, she began with earnest entreaties to persuade her to leave that small place and hasten to her own monastery. But the handmaid of almighty God, desiring more to be wearied by labours for God than to enjoy the passing honours of this life, did not consent at all. She feared to lose the security of her poverty just as covetous rich people customarily guard riches destined to perish.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning a miracle divinely displayed before them.

Nor should the miracle which almighty God deigned to show to his handmaids be passed over. For one day, when according to custom they had met together to enjoy discourse concerning eternal life, a reason suddenly arose why, for the benefit of the monastery, they were compelled to go a little way beyond the enclosure. Having gone out and duly arranged everything for which they had gone, they suddenly returned to the monastery and wished, as usual, to enter the church. But, in the absence of the portress, they found all the doors shut and secured with bolts.

Yet a wonderful thing immediately happened. As the handmaids of Christ came to the entrance of the basilica, the doors, shaken by divine power, opened with such exceeding speed as though they greatly feared to hinder their prayers.

## CHAPTER XIX. She asks an angelic power concerning herself and her sister.

Thereafter the venerable handmaid of Christ, Waldetrudis, because she had not refused humbly to submit herself to the service of the heavenly King after abandoning the world’s enticements, deserved again to be lifted on high to contemplation of the citizens of heaven. For she again saw in spirit a man descending to her from heaven. Recognizing through the Spirit that he was an angelic power, she was at once filled with trembling and sought to inquire what had been ordained in the divine judgment concerning herself and her sister, and humbly took care to ask him whether they deserved in any measure the grace of the divine regard.

The angel gently strengthened her and taught her that the Lord always looked upon them with the serene gaze of his mercy, just as he himself says through the prophet: “To whom shall I look, if not to the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” [Isa. 66.] Hence the Psalmist also says: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears upon their prayers” [Ps. 33].

## CHAPTER XX. That by a heavenly revelation she learned that she and her sister would possess the same blessedness.

[Col. 1384C]

After this it was divinely revealed to her that she and her sister, namely blessed Aldegundis, would possess one dwelling-place and the same blessedness in the kingdom of God, in recompense for their labour; that blessedness to which, as it is written, they come: “Some in this way, but others in that” [1 Cor. 7].

Instructed by these divine revelations, the handmaid of almighty God did not lift her mind up into pride through empty boasting; rather, guarding herself in the citadel of humility, she became all the more devoted thereafter to rendering thanks to her Creator, as she recognized his benefits toward her to be greater. She became more diligent in good work insofar as she was more certain of the promise.

Meanwhile, almighty God was unwilling for his handmaid to remain more richly hidden within herself, but deigned to declare by signs and miracles how great was her merit in his sight, so that the lamp placed upon a lampstand might shine and give much light to all who are in God’s house [Matt. 5]. We shall recount a few of the good works of power that come to memory, so that from these few the many others which occurred may be estimated.

## CHAPTER XXI. She resolved to redeem captives.

Therefore, as she meditated day and night on the law of God and ardently sought how she might increase for herself the gains of mercy, it occurred to her mind that she ought to redeem certain captives. Calling one boy from among her attendants, she took money with which she intended to redeem those captives and placed it in a balance, so that she might know whether it would suffice for what her purpose required.

But, as it is written, “To everyone who has, more shall be given, and he shall abound” [Matt. 13], the money itself placed in the balance began in a wondrous manner to increase and outweigh the scale. When the trembling boy saw this, he was greatly amazed. She immediately gave him a stern command, saying that while he lived in the body he should reveal this miracle to no one. She feared, of course, lest, stirred by human favour because of the power of the deed, she should wither inwardly through that by which she appeared great outwardly to men. She also followed the example of the Master, who, in order to instruct us in the way of humility, commanded his disciples concerning himself, saying that they should tell no one what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead [Matt. 17].

## CHAPTER XXII. How a cup spilled upon the ground by a girl was divinely refilled.

At another time, when the aforesaid handmaid of Christ, Waldetrudis, had reclined for a meal, one of the girls entered the storeroom according to custom and filled a little vessel with drink to carry to Christ’s handmaid as she dined. But as she was returning carelessly, her foot suddenly slipped. Falling down with the vessel itself, she spilled on the ground all the drink that she was carrying. Trembling as she rose, she intended to return to the storeroom to fill the vessel again. But when she suddenly turned her eyes back to the vessel, she found it so full in her hand as though not even a drop had spilled from it.

## CHAPTER XXIII. She cured a sick man.

[Col. 1385C]

After this, a certain man was severely afflicted with an illness and lay long in distress. It happened that one day he fell into a trance of mind. And behold, he saw himself, as it were, being dragged away by demons. With loud cries he called upon blessed Aldegundis and her sister, holy Waldetrudis, that he might be aided through their merits and prayers. Suddenly rescued from the demons’ hands and power, he became silent and uttered no mad cries.

Then he urgently begged those present that he might be carried before the presence of Christ’s handmaid Waldetrudis. When this was granted, and he had been brought before her seated in a chair, Christ’s handmaid, seeing him afflicted by extreme emaciation and weakness, was moved by pity. Stretching out her hands in prayer, she placed them upon his head; and, making the sign of the cross, she immediately drove away all the sickness by which he was held. Restored to his former health, he at once rose and walked from the chair in which he had been carried there, and took food as usual—though for thirty days, as those who had brought him asserted, he had touched no food at all with his mouth.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Where she restored a half-dead little boy to health.

On the fourth day thereafter, a certain woman came to her with her small son, oppressed by a grave illness, begging her with earnest prayers to deign to touch her sick son with her hand. Christ’s handmaid, being most compassionate and sharing the mother’s grief, assented and humbly placed her hands upon the half-dead child. He immediately recovered strength, received food and drink from her table, and sucked his mother’s breast as usual, although for four days already he had touched no food at all with his mouth.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning a yet-unbaptized boy healed by her.

Thereafter another small boy was brought to her, likewise half-dead and not yet washed in the water of baptism. His mother begged with urgent prayers that, through Waldetrudis’s merits and intercessions, he might at least deserve to live to receive the grace of baptism. Christ’s handmaid, immediately trusting in divine help, laid her hands upon him; and when she had impressed the sign of the cross upon his head, the whole little body of the boy at once trembled in a wondrous way. He gave voice, opened the eyes which before had been shut, and from that hour was made well. Afterwards ordained a priest, he continued in life into old age.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That signs continue to occur at her tomb.

There are also many other works of power wonderfully performed by her which we have been unable to recount partly because memory has perished and forgetfulness increased, and partly because we have not wished to set them down in the brevity of a compendium, lest prolonged reading produce weariness. For these few things which we have said, together with those which we see occurring daily at her most sacred relics, can sufficiently serve readers as testimony to her life.

For what need is there to recount much concerning her life, when even now such proofs of powers appear at her body? For she continues without ceasing, even at her dead bones, to do what she was accustomed to do while living: to restore light to the blind, give walking again to the lame, and heal the sick whenever this is sought in faith. It is therefore no wonder if she was able wonderfully to do many things in her life, since her dead bones still live in so many miracles.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning her happy passing.

[Col. 1386D]

Blessed Waldetrudis died on the fifth day before the Ides of April [9 April], received by angels and led into the heavenly dwellings. She lives with Christ; she rejoices with patriarchs and prophets; she exults with apostles; she triumphs with martyrs; she is equal to virgins and companion to confessors.

Therefore let us pursue her with such prayers and praises as we can, praying that she may deign to remember us, so that he may grant us forgiveness of sins who has lavishly rendered to her the reward of all her labours: to whom belong honour and glory, praise and power, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1387]

# PASSION OF ST AGNES, MARTYR (G)*

[Col. 1387A]

May holy Agnes gild the pen of her writer,  
and sprinkle my tongue with nectar-bearing rain.

I attempt to depict her martyrdom in metrical flowers,  
that the Passion, once written, may teach faith.

The city of Rome flourished at the birth of the virgin named before,  
and all the earth shone brightly as in this mirror.

The girl’s rising sprinkled Rome with new light:  
noble in lineage, lovely in face, beautiful in faith.

As the moon’s starry radiance buries the stars,  
so the virgin outshone her companions with rosy beauty.

Nature’s grace poured such gifts upon her  
that after her own gifts it was, as it were, a beggar.

She imitated, reproduced, and equalled stars, privet, and roses—  
fiery in brightness, ruddy in radiance, forehead, and cheeks.

Her eyes shone like stars, her head like the rainbow;  
her brow was like snow, her face like a rose, her tooth like ivory.

Beyond all these resplendent mirrors of gifts,  
the nobler jewel of faith blessed her above all.

A virgin in sex, a man in deed, fair-haired,  
grey in judgment, small in body, great in faith.

When her Passion made Rome purple for faith’s title,  
the thirteenth year after the tenth had come.

As she prepared to return from her studies,  
the prefect’s son fastened his eyes upon her; she pleased him.

The flower of her face, the light of her eyes,  
the fleece of her brow, her cheeks’ purple, her teeth’s ivory, enticed the youth.

This beauty strikes back the young man’s gaze,  
wounds him within, and from it love takes its food.

The murmur of cares creeps beneath his breast;  
the light of reason, darkened by love’s wound, grows dull.

Armed with tricks, words, and gifts of the flesh,  
the lover attempts to pluck the lilies of virgin chastity.

Love touches her with entreaty, approaches with gifts, exhausts her with art;  
neither prayer, nor gifts, nor love’s art avails anything.

He promises estates, boasts of beauty, exalts his lineage;  
estate, beauty, and lineage found no place.

He loves; she hates. He begs; she resists.  
He gives; she scorns. He desires; she refuses.

All madness conspires to ruin chastity,  
but that flourishing chastity remains without stain.

Chastity stands unmoved; the lover’s love is mocked;  
and she addresses the youth in words like these:

“O whirlwind of peace! O leader of death! O disgrace of the world!  
Suppress your words, break off delay, depart far away.

What do you give? What do you hope? What, fool, do you sow? Without profit  
are gifts; without substance, hopes; without honey, labour.

Another lover binds me, whom nobility of lineage,  
beauty’s grace, and eminence of wealth place above you.

From his fingers I claim jewels for myself,  
from his eyes light, from his mouth honeycomb.

In his chambers, at his tables, in his halls,  
plectra sound, honey flows, and stars glitter.

In his gardens flower, incense, and bird smile, smell sweet, and sing;  
the flower smiles, the incense gives fragrance, the bird plays the lyre.

He is the one at whose beauty the moon’s disc, the sun’s circle,  
and the flame of the stars are accustomed to marvel.

This radiant one surpasses the moon’s rays, the sun’s brightness,  
and all heaven’s lamps.

All the splendid necklaces of the stars  
take from his mirror whatever honour they possess.

He has enriched my arms with bracelets, my breast  
with crystal, my neck with a torque, my cheeks with beauty;

my limbs with a robe, my hand with gems, my head with garlands, my ears  
with sapphires, my table with nectar, my bed with flowers.

He is the one who enriched heaven with stars, earth with grass,  
air with birds, and the sea with fish.

His fragrance, his touch, his beauty heal the sick,  
raise the dead, and surpass the stars.

To him I vow myself; to him I owe my betrothal; to him  
I submit my mind, render service, and keep faith.

He stains snowy chastity with no blemish,  
but preserves pure beauty by pure love.

O renowned condescension of a chaste Bridegroom—  
whose kisses are chaste, whose touch sacred, whose love honourable!

Him I follow, him I confess, him I seek by night and day.  
I follow with my mind, confess with my mouth, seek with prayer.”

Her words ended; madness twists the youth,  
care oppresses, grief torments, deceit drives, love burns.

He yields and departs, feigns illness,  
and veils every allurement of his madness under the name of fever.

His breast feigns fever; his cheek feigns brightness; his breast becomes short of breath,  
his cheek pale, his brightness dull.

The father, consulting a doctor, learns everything;  
he caresses his son, probes his heart, promises aid.

He rises and goes, pouring the virgin’s prayers into her ear  
and supporting his prayers with golden gifts.

By giving and begging the prefect’s arts seek nothing successfully:  
the gifts lack weight, the breeze carries off the prayers.

The virginal purity which is due as the emblem of a first lover  
refuses to violate itself.

The prefect asks a servant who the lover is  
to whose love Agnes devotes herself; the servant tells him.

He indicates that the girl is so deceived by great fraud  
that she thinks she has made a covenant with Christ.

At these words the judge is wholly delighted and tells Agnes’s parents  
that she is guilty of a capital crime.

For because the virgin’s parents shone with a renowned name,  
he feared to inflict violence without legal pretext.

It was law that the Roman sword should punish Christ’s servants;  
by this device the judge veils his crime.

Thus madness ordered her to be brought before him;  
his wish smiles upon the command; the virgin is summoned and appears.

He soothes and rebukes her, now flatters, now terrifies;  
now he showers prayers, now he thunders threats.

But neither the dew of prayers pollutes her pure ears,  
nor does his thunder shake her mind.

The judge, discovering that he was ploughing the shore  
and seeing that the seed failed its master, breaks out thus:

“If your chastity wishes to preserve this course,  
you must perform the sacred rites of renowned Vesta.

Vesta seeks those whom flourishing purity adorns;  
the virgin’s altar requires a virgin’s hands.”

To this the virgin replies: “I do not pray to stone,  
I do not worship wood; I do not know Vesta; I despise gods.

Your Vesta is indeed a stone, whose golden form falsely  
pretends to you that she is a goddess.

No distinguishing mark consecrates her as divinity,  
nor does life provide her with any sense.

She lacks the touch of hands, the sound of a tongue, hearing of ears,  
sight of brow, and scent of nostril.

She does not feel by flesh, see by brow, smell  
by nostril, hear by ear, or speak by mouth.”

The judge says: “Your still-childish age pleads for you  
and postpones your punishment.

But why do we deceive the time with barren speech? Behold,  
there are two things that I command: do whichever you choose.

Either you shall undertake the commanded rites, or, made a prostitute,  
you shall incur the stain of dishonour, wholly dedicated to criminals.”

She wounds the man’s mind with this reply:

“You are mistaken and plough the shore with a barren ploughshare.  
The coal of an altar shall not pollute faith’s purity,

nor shall any lover stain the flower of the flesh.  
Christ has consecrated both body and faith to himself,

preserving the body from stain and faith from the enemy.  
This one is indeed my husband, my guardian, and my author—

husband of my mind, guardian of my body, author of my wealth.  
For Christ is hope, light, and medicine for his own:

hope for the wretched, light for the blind, medicine for the guilty.  
With him as guide, punishment does not break me, the sword

does not terrify me, deceit does not conquer, nor does a whirlwind shake me.  
He is the one who enriches light with Phoebus’ lamp,

and adorns the path of night with the moon’s mirror;  
who makes smiling gardens purple with saffron flower,

ruffles groves with foliage, and adorns fields with harvest.  
To depict him for you in brief words: he knows

all things, orders each thing, and has power over all.  
How broad the field of his titles is, neither tongue can unfold,

mind comprehend, nor pen write.  
Since this my Jesus shines with the gold of so many gifts,

no grace ennobles your gods.  
Your gods neither live in mind nor move in body;

they do not breathe with life nor shine with divinity.  
They lack walking—not feet; feeling—not body; touch—

not hands; words—not mouth.”  

The torch of this speech kindles the prefect’s anger into flame;  
anger compels the man to crime.

Anger orders Agnes to be mocked, given to procurers,  
scourged with lashes, and stripped of garments.

The order is carried out: an impious hand strips the girl of clothing,  
yet the naked girl frustrates the gaze.

Such grace flowed into her virginal hair  
that her hair shaded the honour of her entire body.

So celebrated a marvel could not soften the raging man’s mind,  
nor could a chaste cause move him.

Adding new spurs to his commands,  
he drives on his servants, piling threats upon orders already given.

The threats therefore are followed by execution: the chaste virgin begins  
to be dragged to the cell of an unclean house.

At her entrance the evil cell wholly expels  
darkness and the odour of filth.

Christ makes the cell shine with angelic brightness;  
the light proves that the author of light is present.

Here is an angel; there is light; there is fragrance:  
the angel consecrates the cave, light irradiates it, fragrance fills it.

The virgin pours forth prayers; her petitions do not fail the suppliant:  
there a shining cloak appears to cover her sacred limbs.

It suits her body’s measure so perfectly  
that one might think an angelic hand had made it.

O happy condescension of Christ, under whose guidance such chastity  
swims across the great shoals of lust!

No lover violated her; but each, worshipping  
the trembling rays of light, returned rejoicing.

Now the love of the young men had grown numb when the youth who authored the crime  
flew here swiftly to accomplish his desires.

Entering the place, he separates himself from his companions;  
alone he enters the cave, girded with artifice, frenzy, and deceit.

He had scarcely begun to use the light at his entrance  
when the splendour of holy light struck his gaze.

The lover despises so great a glory and gives no titles  
of honour to such singular brightness.

Unaware of delay, he rushes into the abyss  
of the intervening splendour and orders his own hand forward.

And when lust wished to touch with his hands the sacred flesh,  
death seized him, avenging the crime.

The companions’ hope of the youth’s return is disappointed:  
he does not return; fate holds him in its own chain.

Why does the young man delay so long in returning? One  
of his companions investigates the cell and enters the cave.

Surveying the cell with wandering gaze, he encounters  
the corpse, calls his companions, and asks help.

There gather all the young men’s lust, a cry arises,  
murmurs resound, hearts are tumultuous.

Report of the new disaster wounds the father’s ear;  
terrified, he flies there, with the city following the man.

His eyes indulge in tears, grief troubles his heart,  
his cheek is stained with clouds of sorrow, his hair torn by his nails.

Tear, tongue, and heavy uttered grief question, shake, and burn  
face, place, and mind.

The father’s tearful voice attributes the extinguished flower  
of the youthful body to Agnes’s deceits.

He charges her with the crime, as though the virgin  
had used her arts to bring about the young man’s death.

Agnes answered thus: “You err if you believe  
that our hand, using arts, brought your harm.

Why the avenging Angel harvested this one alone  
from so great a crop of youths—the fitting reason is plain.

This light struck the minds of the young men, but this man  
was not touched in mind by honour for this light.

While he violently attempted to touch me with an impure hand,  
a fitting vengeance struck down his crime.”

The prefect replies: “If you restore my son to me with life,  
this event will give weight to your word.”

The virgin replies: “I do not owe this work to your merits;  
such grace differs from your faith.

But because the time has come for Christ’s shining power  
to come into light, have what you ask.

Let that company of youths withdraw from this cell,  
so that I may be more intent upon my prayers.”

She spoke. At these words, every flower of the youths immediately flies outside;  
the blessed virgin pours forth prayers.

The grace of her petitions smiles on her vows;  
the dead youth rises and judges the gods worthy of fire.

Jesus sounds on his tongue, Christ is honeycomb in his mouth,  
light in his heart, melody in his ear.

The new event stirs and presses worshippers of the temples;  
care urges their minds, fear shakes them, anger burns.

All conspire against one woman; they cry that she deserves death  
and is guilty of magical arts.

Joy at his son’s recovery tests the father’s heart;  
the savage winter of grief is calmed.

Now his rage grows numb, now the swell of threats subsides,  
now he wishes to grant pardon, now prepares to be merciful.

He wishes to spare the snowy flower, unless law, the populace,  
and the throng of priests oppose him.

His mercy is conquered and broken by the storm of such great pressures;  
his pious mind does not carry its work to completion.

Yet he then withdraws, placing the burden and honour upon  
Aspasius, by legal right and in his own place.

Turning the reins of law at the people’s nod,  
he unjustly performs the prefect’s office.

As popular fury presses him concerning the virgin’s death,  
he commands that she be given to flames.

The priest girds himself to fulfil the crime,  
kindles the fire, and piles dry wood onto the pyre.

The hungry fire feeds on the aid of sulphur;  
the bloody flame boils and overflows exceedingly.

O crime! That flesh which had known no fire  
of seduction is given as food amid the flames.

Yet the present burning accomplished nothing against her;  
the flame, ignorant of itself, forgot its powers.

It did not dare to use its strength against the virgin,  
but seemed to sympathize with and pity her.

But a fiery globe enveloped in its own power  
certain men who fed the flames with sulphur.

There are two things at which I marvel: a wicked leader and a merciful fire—  
the judge was unjust, and the flame just.

The priest burns with desire for the virgin’s punishment; the fire  
is cold and inactive, possessing no heat.

In the midst of the flame, sprinkled with a cloud of heavenly  
nectar, Agnes spoke in these words:

“To you I render proclamations of praise, fulfil vows,  
offer thanks, and pour forth prayers—

you whose sweetness, love, and grace  
fortify, cherish, and guard your own from the enemy.

With you as guide I despised the executioner’s scourges,  
the Charybdis of lust, the force of flame, and the young men’s threats.

Amid so many shoals you became my anchor;  
under your guidance this chastity endured no shipwreck.

For you, Christ, I have endured so many bitter things; but add  
rewards justly answering to my labour.

Now I possess what I hoped for; I see what I loved;  
joyful, I touch what I desired and possess what I purchased.”

The voice of the virgin’s mouth flies to Christ,  
filling his nostrils with the fragrance of its incense.

After her death, all the violence of the flame so ceased  
that the fire’s smell never again lived.

Thus the fire, not daring to breathe rage,  
lays aside fury, loses force, and restrains threats.

The novel grace of the sign throws the crowd into confusion:  
the populace sees the sign, envies it, and gives a roar.

The populace urges Aspasius into crime; therefore he commands  
the sword to drink innocent blood.

The executioner’s hand hastens the crime;  
the sharp point, hungry for punishment, arms the hand.

The virgin makes the lictor’s sword drunk with her blood;  
the purple of shed blood paints the ground.

A triple distinction of merit beautifies Agnes:  
a pure body, a rosy Passion, and steadfast faith.

By these titles of virtues Agnes claims for herself  
the Lamb who took away the sin of the world.

[Col. 1391]

# VARIOUS POEMS. (G)*

## I. Verses on the destruction of Rome.

[Col. 1391D]

(They are by Hildebert of Le Mans. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXI.)

## II. Response of the city of Rome.

(See above.)

## III. Verses of the bridegroom against his bride.

(See likewise in Hildebert.)

## IV. Response of the bride.

(It appears above.)

## V. Response of the judge.

(See there.)

## VI. On the praises of Samson.

[Col. 1392D]

Touch your hand to the pen; paint Samson’s triumph,  
by whose honours the Gallic land blooms.

Make for yourself some little bundles of these flowers;  
from them a great garland may be woven.

Wax-light of the Church, royal seat of virtues,  
line of law, clasp of the discordant: hail, Samson!

By your deeds you declare that Samson, mighty in name, shines;  
our age marvels that the strong Samson lives.

May his honour, praise, and fame pour serene  
light over the lands: live, I pray.

## VII. Epitaph of Pope Urban.

Here while living he was the light of the City; slain by death, he was night.  
The City stood while Urban stood; falling, it falls.

Ruling you by law and fostering you by peace, O Rome, he blessed you,  
preserving you from vices within and enemies without.

Wealth did not bend him, renown did not exalt him, nor did any powerful man ever terrify him  
by gifts, praise, or threats.

Eloquence adorned his tongue, wisdom his breast, honour his character,  
and beauty his outward form.

Behold, through him the holy City lies open, our law triumphs,  
the nations are conquered, faith increases throughout the world.

But the rose that blooms more richly in the garden is snatched sooner;  
so fate bore away the flourishing man.

Death releases the man, rest cherishes the spirit,  
and the deep cistern covers the corpse.

## VIII. Epitaph of Ivo, bishop of Chartres.

[Col. 1393B]

Affection made him a father, learning a teacher,  
the rule a canon, and rank a bishop.

Integrity made him beautiful, nature humble,  
his calm life venerable, long age and chastity holy.

In former times, when a bishop died, it was customary for the prince  
to claim his possessions; Ivo purchased this custom from the prince.

The injured found his help, the people his teaching, the tyrant his restraint,  
the needy his wealth, God his prayers for the flock.

## IX. Epitaph of the bishop of Sens.

(It is by Hildebert. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXI.)

## X. Epitaph of Anselm, bishop of Canterbury.

(See there.)

## XI. Epitaph of Seneca.

[Col. 1393C]

Care, labour, merit, honours received as reward—  
go and trouble other souls after this.

God calls me far from you; once earthly business is done,  
farewell, earth, a land in which I was a guest.

Yet receive my body, greedy earth, beneath solemn stones,  
for we render the soul to heaven and the bones to you.

## XII. Epitaph of Master William.

Gaul sighs, deprived of its serene ray;  
the star that shone more brightly than the stars grows dim.

Night passes into mourning, and day follows without sun;  
there is a day without William; there is a day without sun.

His Greece wept for Apollonius, Rome for Maro;  
Gaul mourns William, father of both.

Normandy was made illustrious by his birth,  
Gaul by his life, Paris by his body, heaven by his mind.

## XIII. Epitaph of Master Peter.

The morning star has set, you lesser radiant stars,  
whose light he dimmed as inferior to his own.

At his setting you at last came to your rising,  
and the anchor of your ship found harbour through his shipwreck.

Mature, teachable, and devout, he completed his course in due time, upheld law by law, and gained  
heaven by faith.

## XIV. Epitaph of Master Lanfranc.

You lived wisely and justly, venerable Father;  
you lived while living, and death too was life to you.

Amid riches, Lanfranc, you were poor;  
abounding in wealth, you were a lover of the poor.

Through you the flourishing Latin arts had strength;  
behold, grace triumphs rejoicing because of you.

Italian by birth, you raised the Gauls by teaching;  
Britain’s pivot holds you as its primate.

Living on earth, you sought heavenly things in mind;  
freed from earth, you go freely to the stars.

The sun had occupied Gemini with fire for ten days;  
the moon brings forth the day; released in the night, you depart.

## XV. Epitaph of the kings of Jerusalem.

(See Hildebert, as cited above.)

## XVI. Epitaph of King Henry.

[Col. 1394B]

England, once humble, once the glory of lands,  
now tosses and lies submerged with its helmsman drowned.

She who shone over the whole world with titles of praise  
suffers eclipse, abandoned by her sun.

With his death she dies; while he lived, she enjoyed peace;  
while he stood, she stood; falling, she falls.

By laws he restrained treachery, by arms enemies;  
gentle to those made peaceful, subduing the unsubdued.

Happy in his rule, he used it well;  
a lover of peace, renowned for generosity, mighty in war.

At his death glory perishes, and with it perish  
peace, leisure, the sanction of laws, rights, and faith.

Now seas lack ships, markets goods, fields cultivators,  
the people protection, and the clergy honour.

Now the judge restores perjuries, the tyrant wars,  
the thief his dagger, the robber weapons, and the pirate his ship.

Therefore England mourns the fall of so great a man,  
and, cast down by his sudden fall, herself falls headlong.

## XVII. Epitaph of the dean of Orléans.

The Church’s bridegroom has fallen, defender of honour—  
Cato in mind, Tully in speech, Numa in skill.

Peace dies with the man’s death; discord lives;  
wickedness reigns, and every best thing collapses.

Death rages, weapons ring out, the order of things is overturned,  
and what had been first is now made last.

Liberty serves, generosity ceases, honour grows foul,  
virtues languish, strength perishes, order lies low.

Fraud prevails, ambition flourishes, Fury rules;  
uproar arises, scandals increase, wars roar.

Cease, Rome, to boast of magnanimous peers and your ancestors’ deeds,  
and to count your tribes.

He alone surpassed the Fabii in courage, Camillus in gravity,  
Aulus in counsel.

While he cultivates law and protects liberty,  
a bloody hand pierces his innocent side.

O evil mind, criminal hand, wicked conspiracy,  
savage blow, daring attack, horrible purpose!

That death was the death of the homeland which took him away;  
in his fall the whole homeland falls.

## XVIII. Epitaph of the abbot of Clairvaux.

(See Hildebert, as cited above.)

## XIX. Comparison concerning the Incarnation of the Lord.

[Col. 1395A]

The sun, crystal, and water offer some image  
and teach faith in the virginal birth.

If the stone is soaked with water and placed beneath the sun,  
it remains whole yet sends forth sparks.

Thus, washed by the Holy Spirit and placed beneath the Sun  
of righteousness, the virgin, remaining whole, bore God.

## XX. Verses on the gifts of the Magi.

The Magus gives gold, incense, and myrrh. The King receives gold,  
God incense, and myrrh he who was to die.

By prayer we give incense, by wisdom the gold of heavenly things,  
and myrrh when the work of the flesh is mortified.

## XXI. Of the same subject.

[Col. 1395B]

(See Hildebert, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXI.)

## XXII. On the threefold house of the righteous.

(See there.)

## XXIII. On the threefold house of human beings.

Three houses are prepared for us: home, tomb, and heaven.  
Wood provides the home, the spade the sarcophagus, devotion heaven.

A companion in the household prepares disasters [*occasus*]; the worm is in the urn,

The angel in heaven, the household spirit for punishment, the tomb for sleep.

Heaven for joy: by a different allotment these are named;

Fault gives the first two, grace alone the heavenly one.

[Col. 1395C]

(By Hildebert. See the same place.)

XXVI. 804 Verses on a bad woman.

XXVII. On the rich man who desires and the avaricious poor man.

Who is rich? He who desires nothing. And who is poor? The avaricious man.

What is the work of the wise? Not to wish, and to be able, to do harm.

What is characteristic of the fool? Not to be able, yet to wish, to do harm.

What is the most beautiful dowry of a married woman? A chaste life.

XXVIII. On the mouth, sight, and mind.

[Col. 1395D]

The present table seeks for itself three guests;

It prepares three dishes, three things given in name alone.

It feeds the mouth with foods, delights the sight with painted images, and instructs the mind with examples; each teaches its respective one.

The mouth wants food for itself; sight is delighted by the image of things;

In examples, recognize the dishes of the mind.

The first table pleases the sick, the second the idle, but the third the learned,

Providing strength, leisure, and doctrine.

XXIX. Logogriphs and riddles.

A three-syllabled word commends me excessively by changing me;

Take away my first syllable: in Latin I fight for a wife.

[Col. 1396A] If I lack the middle, I do not need medicine;

If you remove the end, there is no ruin in the belly.

What the cruel axe is accustomed to cut from a tree—

A two-syllabled word remains, marked by five shapes.

It will become *vir* (“man”) if you drive the end from the name;

If A is changed into O, it is scarcely found among a thousand girls.

High mountains: let L be taken away from *montibus*. If they

Live, they make honey; let those who can explain it, explain.

I afflict girls’ hearts with wanton diseases;

Turn my name backward, and the whole world will serve me.

I owe torments to sinners inclined toward evils;

If B is removed, I shall be called a thing suitable for farmers.

Nature gives a certain bird a dark color;

Take its heart away, and it will surpass the swan in whiteness.

The art joins for me a foundation, wall, and roof alike;

[Col. 1396B] If *do* is changed into *ha*, my point pierces a fish;

Life smiles upon me; I rejoice in youthful bloom;

Let E fall into nothing, and I burn with excessive heat.

A crack gives me a path; I run through a different cavern;

Let the first letter fall, and I drive away darkness with a lamp.

While I wish, I become a letter; flying, I am nearest to Phoebus;

If you cut off my head, I shall please the rustic crowd.

Yet I serve the writers’ pens not without a *gramma* [Greek “letter”];

In a Roman word, my name is almost a double axe.

I am a spark of evil, which incites hearts to wars;

Let L be joined to me, and now I make sweet music for hearts.

With B put in place of R, if the letter D is removed,

I shall be a fish through which a living man is often devoured.

It adorns kings, being dyed with the blood of a fish;

[Col. 1396C] If L is changed into R, it swims on the foot and chirps in the mouth.

I displease peace and seek deadly ruin;

If S is changed into E, I sink sailors’ hulls.

805 I arise in the woods; by a breath I am driven out upon the waters.

Take N away from me: the air will be furrowed by my flight.

The mother hen labors to bring me forth;

If *um* is changed into *is*, white wool adorns me.

I am the husk of grain which the wind carries everywhere;

Without P, wanton youth will make sport of me.

The highest Creator commands me to go on two pairs of feet;

Let two syllables fall away: without me no one becomes a traveler.

In appearance I feed the sight, in fragrance the nostrils;

If you remove A from me, you will make a liquid from a flower.

I always love dung and cannot look apart from it;

I remain what I was before, although turned backward.

[Col. 1396D] I am surrounded by six ribs and three times seven little eyes;

With M put in place of T, I am driven and struck by storms.

I am wine, arising from the vine, to serve the drinker;

If V is formed into E, I am full by a sinister name.

I am a river; the Trojan region drinks from me;

If X is driven out from S, Christ endows me in heaven.

Pythagoras divided me into a certain cleft;

This rite of the altar prepares a double passage for me.

I embrace the body; I bind flowing garments tight;

If *zo* is changed into M, I set minds aflame with desire.

By the witness of sound I am double, by the witness of form simple;

I join my first part with the future part.

I am woven from wood; a thief labors to open me;

Join M to me, and the rich miser adores me.

[Col. 1397A] Three threes sound in the same part of the letter:

The third of the sixth, the fifth of the second, and the first of the fourth.

Sitting in a laurel tree and seeing twice six doves fly about,

A dove happened to give this sound.

If your number increased twice by a double order,

You would be a hundred while I was flying together with you.

So that the total of the flying troop may not escape you,

That troop consisted of thirty-three.

Divide twice six loaves among twice six guests,

Among clergy, farmers, and soldiers alike.

[Col. 1398A] Give two loaves to the clergy, a fourth part of a loaf to the farmer,

And let half a loaf feed the soldier’s mouths.

That there may be as many men as loaves, let there be for you five

Clergy, farmers three times two [*ruricolae ter duo*, reading uncertain], and one horseman.

A collection of one hundred steps builds a staircase;

One dove alone sits on the first step.

Then two birds, afterward three, then four:

This sequence orders the hundred steps.

I asked for the total with fifty doves;

The sum contains five thousand doves.

ORDER OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME.

[Col. 1405] PHILIP OF HARVENG, ABBOT OF BONNE-ESPÉRANCE.

LETTERS.

LETTER I. Philip to Weberic.—He asks concerning the works of the six days: whether God performed them all at once or successively; and concerning the time of the creation of the angels and of the fall of the first parents. 1

LETTER II. Philip to Hervard.—He teaches that three things are necessary for one reading the Holy Scriptures; asks and resolves how Christ contracted original sin from Adam and yet was contained in him according to the flesh. 16

LETTER III. Philip to Heroald.—He rebukes the name “Fortune.” He teaches that Christians ought not to linger over the books of the pagans, but hasten to the Holy Scriptures. Praise of the Parisian academy. 26

LETTER IV. Philip to Engelbert.—The study of letters must be directed to the spiritual perfection of the inner person. 32

LETTER V. Philip to John.—He defends the books of Blessed Hilary *On the Trinity* and explains two difficult propositions of his: (1) that Mary did not give origin to Christ’s body; (2) that Christ’s body was incapable of suffering. He shows the Catholic meaning of these statements. 34

LETTER VI. Philip to John.—On the same subject. 46

LETTER VII. Philip to John.—On the same subject. 57

LETTER VIII. Philip to Gregory.—A religious ought not to disparage other religious orders. 74

LETTER IX. Philip to Bartholomew.—Concerning the unjust persecution inflicted upon him. 78

LETTER X. Philip to Bernard.—He complains concerning a member of Prémontré received by the Cistercians against the will of the Premonstratensians. 85

LETTER XI. Philip to Bernard.—He wonders that, as new reforms of religious increase, their mutual charity does not increase. 93

LETTER XII. Philip to Pope Eugene III.—He asks the pontiff for help against his persecutors. 96

LETTER XIII. Philip to ***.—He gives a fine discussion of the virtues of prelates. 105

[Col. 1406]

LETTER XIV. Philip to Ralph.—He offers an excellent philosophical discussion of manifold death and martyrdom. 127

LETTER XV. Philip to Adam.—A letter of remonstrance. 142

LETTER XVI. Philip to Philip.—He commends virtues worthy of noble men. 147

LETTER XVII. Philip to Henry.—On the same subject. 151

LETTER XVIII. Philip to Richer.—Literary studies are necessary for ecclesiastical men. 157

LETTER XIX. Philip to Raynald.—He congratulates a noble, learned, and pious man upon his elevation to ecclesiastical prelacy. 160

LETTER XX. Philip to Richer.—He commends the study of letters. 173

LETTER XXI. Philip to William.—A letter of recommendation. 176

LETTER XXII. John to Philip.—On statements of Blessed Hilary in the book *On the Trinity*. 178

LETTER XXIII. John to Philip.—On the same subject. 178

LETTER XXIV. John to Philip.—On the same subject. 180

LETTER XXV. Hunald to the provost.—On the same subject. 182

LETTER XXVI. Philip to Pope Alexander III.—He congratulates Alexander upon his elevation to the highest dignity, and states that he met with the kings of England and France in order to draw them to Alexander’s side. 188
